The threshold of heatwave is higher in low-latitude regions (e.g., southern Asia) than high-latitude and high-altitude regions (e.g., the Qinghai Tibet Plateau), while the extreme runoff threshold is higher in low-latitude regions (e.g., southeastern Asia and northwestern South America) than other regions (Fig. S1 ). Based on the identified extreme runoff and heatwave events, the SRHE events can be identified by the incidence analysis method (He and Sheffield, 2020 ).(1) SRHE = ∑ j = 1  N R   θ ∑ i = 1  N H   I 0 , 7      t i H  - t j R                where t i H     and t j R     represent time series values of heatwave events (i  = 1, 2, 3, …, NH  ) and extreme runoff events (j  = 1, 2, 3, …, NR  ), respectively. θ    and I  can be expressed as:(2a) θ x    = 0 , x ≤ 0    1 , x > 0             (2b) I x    = 0 , x ∉ 0 , 7        1 , x ∈ 0 , 7                 where x  in equation (2a)  represents ∑ i = 1  N R   I 0 , 7      t i H  - t j R         ; x  in equation (2b)  represents the heatwave time series minus the extreme runoff time series (t i H  - t j R    ). Notice that when multiple extreme runoff or heatwave events occur successively, only the first extreme runoff or heatwave event is considered in order to avoid the redundancy. The interval between extreme runoff and heatwave (IRH, in days) during one SRHE event is the time from the end date of extreme runoff to the start date of heatwave. The duration of these various events is the number of days from the starting to the ending date of an event. The land exposure of SRHE is defined as the percentage of grids with at least one SRHE occurrence within a year, which can be expressed as:(3) P = N SRHE   / N     where NSRHE   represents the number of grids with at least one SRHE occurrence per year, and N  (=13927) is the total grid number of global land (excluding Greenland and Sahara regions).  2.3 Mann-Kendall trend test The Mann-Kendall (M−K) trend test is a nonparametric method for analyzing the trends of meteorological and hydrological sequences recommended by the World Meteorological Organization (Kendall, 1948 ; Mann, 1945 ). The advantages of M−K trend test are mainly that it does not need follow any specific distribution and it is resilient to the non-stationary data and missing values (Ali and Abubaker, 2019; Daneshvar Vousoughi et al., 2015 ). The Sen’s slope estimation is a nonparametric method for estimating the magnitudes of trend in the time series (Sen, 1968 ). The M−K trend test and the Sen’s slope estimator have been widely used in numerous hydro-meteorological studies (Almazroui and Şen, 2020; Dabanlı et al., 2016; Khalid et al., 2023 ). In this study, the M−K trend test and Sen’s slope estimation methods are applied to detect the trend significance and magnitude of SRHE characteristics (frequency, IRH, and duration). The significance level of the M−K trend test is set to 0.05.  2.4 The fraction of attribution risk The difference in SRHE characteristics between ALL and NAT simulations can be attributed to the impact of ACC. The contribution of ACC to the SRHE probability can be quantified based on FAR. FAR is an indicator measuring the change in the probability of climate incidents due to ACC (Allen, 2003; Stott et al., 2016 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ) defined as:(4) FAR = 1 - P NAT   P ALL        where PNAT   and PALL   represent the probability of SRHE occurrence in ALL and NAT simulations, respectively. Here the SRHE probability at each grid is defined as the SRHE duration (in days) divided by the total number of days in the study period (Bian et al., 2022 ). A positive (negative) FAR indicates that ACC increases (decreases) the probability of SRHE events.  2.5 Partial correlation Partial correlation analysis is a method used to describe the relations between two variables while eliminating the effects of another variable or several other variables on the relationships (Waliczek, 1996 ), which has received wide applications in multivariate analysis in meteorology and hydrology (Han et al., 2018; Ross et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2021 ). The partial correlation coefficient (PCC) is calculated as (Brown and Hendrix, 2005 ):(5) r 12 , 3   = r 12  - r 13  r 23   1 - r 12  2    1 - r 13  2          where r 12,3  refers to the PCC between the first and second variables, while the third variable remains unchanged; r 12 , r 13 , r 23  refer to the correlation coefficients between variables 1 and 2, 1 and 3, and 2 and 3, respectively. The range of PCC is from −1 to 1. A greater absolute PCC value represents a stronger correlation between two variables. In this study, PCC is used to evaluate the relations between the ACC impacts on SRHE, extreme runoff, and heatwave occurrence at the grid scale for six global continents. The significance level of PCC is set to 5 %.   3 Results This section first evaluates the ALL simulations of CMIP6 (section 3.1 ), analyzes the long-term mean changes (section 3.2 ), temporal changes (section 3.3 ), and trends (section 3.4 ) of the SRHE characteristics (frequency, IRH, duration) under the ALL and NAT simulations, and then explores the FAR (Fraction Attributable Risk) of SRHE occurrence with different characteristics (sections 3.5 and 3.6 ). 3.1 Evaluation of ALL simulations from CMIP6 The ERA5 daily temperature data and GLDAS daily runoff data are used for validating the ALL simulations of CMIP6. Fig. 1   plots the Taylor diagrams of the multi-model simulated mean daily Tmax  , Tmin   and runoff at the global scale. The indicators of the Taylor diagram measure the degree of difference between ALL simulations and ERA5 (GLDAS), with the correlation coefficient and relative standard deviation close to 1 and the Centered Root Mean Square Error (CRMSE) close to 0 indicating better performance of simulations. The ALL simulations perform well in capturing the daily variability in Tmax   and Tmin   with a relative standard deviation around 1, a correlation coefficient of 0.99, and a CRMSE of 0.13. For the daily runoff, a high correlation coefficient (0.85) is found between ALL simulations and GLDAS, but its relative standard deviation (1.15) and CRMSE (0.61) are slightly larger than those of daily Tmax   and Tmin  , indicating that the daily temperature simulation is better than daily runoff at the global scale.  3.2 Global analysis of 1950–2014 long-term mean changes in SRHE characteristics The global and latitudinal distributions of the long-term (1950–2014) mean SRHE characteristics (frequency, IRH, duration) extracted from CMIP6 simulations forced by ALL and NAT forcings are compared in Fig. 2  . Similar comparisons, but for the long-term mean extreme runoff and heatwave characteristics (frequency and duration) are provided in Figs. S2 and S3 , respectively. The percentage change (%) in CMIP6-simulated SRHE characteristics forced by ALL forcing relative to that forced by NAT forcings are also compared. In ALL simulation, the SRHE occurs more frequently in southeastern Asia and central South America (> 80 events, Fig. 2 a) than other regions, while the low SRHE frequency is found in the central North America, northern South America, central Africa, and northern Asia (< 30 events). No SRHE event is identified in some parts of northern North America, southern/northern South America, most of Europe, western/northern Asia, and the Indian Peninsula. The IRH of ALL simulations is mostly between 2–4 days/event (Fig. 2 b). The ALL simulation identifies a short IRH in the low-latitude areas (∼1 days/event around the equator) and a long IRH in the 30°N and 80°N regions of the Northern Hemisphere and around 30°S in the Southern Hemisphere (2–4 days/event). The SRHE duration in ALL is 5–20 days/event in most global regions, and a longer duration is found in the northern North America, Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, and southeastern Asia (> 25 days/event, Fig. 2 c). Fig. 2 g shows that the SRHE frequency in ALL simulation is higher than that in NAT for most global regions, especially in central South America, central Africa, and southeastern Asia (> 18 folds). This suggests that ACC enhances the SRHE frequency during 1950–2014, mainly attributed to more frequent extreme runoff and heatwave occurrence (Figs. S2 e and S3 e). On the contrary, the decrease in SRHE frequency due to ACC is found only in some regions of northern North America, Europe, and Asia (mostly < 1 fold). The IRH changes caused by ACC are distributed more scattered across global regions (Fig. 2 h). A decrease in IRH (< 1-fold) is commonly found globally (e.g., the northern North America, southwestern Asia, and western Australia), indicating that ACC results in more intermittent SRHE occurrence. On the other hand, ACC increases the SRHE duration in most global regions, especially in northern South America, central Africa and southeastern Asia (1–4.5 folds), mainly due to the longer heatwave duration (> 2 folds) caused by ACC (Fig. S3 f). In contrast, ACC shortens the SRHE duration in some parts of central North America and northern/eastern/southwestern Asia (< 1 fold) mainly due to the decrease in extreme runoff duration (Fig. S2 f). In order to investigate the temporal changes and trends of global SRHE characteristics, the 1950–2014 study period is further divided into 1950–1979 and 1980–2014 sub-periods. The probability density distributions (PDFs) of global SRHE characteristics (frequency, duration, IRH) from ALL and NAT during 1950–2014, 1950–1979 and 1980–2014 are displayed in Fig. 3  . Similar PDF comparisons, but stratified into each of the global six continents, are given in Fig. S4  for more demonstrations of global patterns. As seen, the PDF peak of the SRHE frequency was shifted from the first (1950–1979) to the second 1980–2014 for ALL at both global scale (Fig. 3 a) and six continents (Figs. S4 a, d, g, j, m, p). In contrast, the difference in SRHE frequency PDFs between two sub-period is small in NAT, suggesting the relatively limited influences exerted by nature forcing on the temporal changes of SRHE occurrence. The SRHE frequency in ALL is larger than that in NAT during both 1950–1979 and 1980–2014 period (in particular during 1980–2014), which can be explained by the higher extreme runoff and heatwave frequencies simulated by ALL than that simulated by NAT (Figs. S5 a and S6 a), suggesting that the promoting impact of ACC on SRHE occurrence has increased over time during the study period. Similarly, the NAT forcing impact on SRHE duration is still limited from the first (1950–1979) to the second (1980–2014) sub-period at both global (Fig. 3 b) and continental (Figs. S4 b, e, h, k, n, q) scales. However, the ACC significantly increases the likelihood of long SRHE duration especially during 1980–2014, which is mainly due to the longer heatwave duration during 1950–2014 simulated by ALL (5–25 days/event) than that by NAT (3–15 days/event) (Fig. S6 b). From the first to second sub-periods, the probability of IRH within 1.9–3.8 days is increased in ALL, but little change can be found for NAT between two periods (Figs. S4 c, f, i, l, o, and r). Comparisons of ALL and NAT indicate that ACC increased the probability of IRH within 2–3.7 days during both sub-periods (in particular 1980–2014).  3.3 Temporal analysis of changes in global mean SRHE characteristics Fig. 4   compares the 1950–2014 interannual changes in global-mean frequencies of SRHE, extreme runoff, and heatwave (relative to the 1950–1979 mean) obtained from ALL and NAT. As seen, ALL shows a significant increasing trend in SRHE frequency (+0.002 event/year, p  < 0.05), but NAT shows a slightly decreasing trend in SRHE frequency (−0.0001 event/year) (Fig. 4 a). A large discrepancy can be found between ALL and NAT over recent decades (especially after 1980s). The SRHE frequency due to ACC (i.e., trend magnitude in ALL minus that in NAT) is increased by 0.0021 event/year during 1950–2014, which can be attributed to the significant increasing trends in the heatwave (+0.027 event/year) and extreme runoff (+0.009 event/year) frequency forced by ACC (Figs. 4 b and c). However, the spread in the simulated SRHE frequency under ALL increases with time over recent decades (Fig. 4 a) is similar to the spread in simulated extreme runoff frequency under ALL (Fig. 4 b), suggesting that the uncertainty in simulated SRHE frequency is mainly caused by the uncertainty in extreme runoff frequency. Fig. 5   compares the 1950–2014 interannual changes in global-mean duration and IRH of SRHE between ALL and NAT simulations. As shown in Fig. 5 a, a significantly increasing trend (+0.0442 days/event/year, p  < 0.05) in SRHE duration is detected in ALL simulation especially after 1980s, while an insignificantly decreasing trend is found in NAT simulation (−0.0005 days/event/year). Overall, ACC results in an increase of 0.0447 days/event/year in SRHE duration during 1950–2014 (Fig. 5 a). The IRH of SRHE shows a significantly decreasing trend in ALL simulation (−0.0008 days/event/year, p  < 0.05) during 1950–2014 (Fig. 5 b). Comparisons of ALL and NAT suggest that the IRH of SRHE is decreased by 0.0009 days/event/year, implying the more intermittent SRHE occurrence over time caused by ACC. Fig. 6   compares the 1950–2014 interannual changes in global land exposure of SRHE, extreme runoff, and heatwave (relative to the 1950–1979 mean) from ALL and NAT simulations. The changes in global land exposure are quantified by the changes in the proportion of grids globally with at least one extreme event occurrence within one year. A significantly increasing trend is found in the land exposure of SRHE (+0.109 %/year), extreme runoff (+0.016 %/year) and heatwave (+0.148 %/year) for ALL (Fig. 6 ). The trends in the land exposures of SRHE and extreme runoff estimated by NAT are weak and insignificant (−0.003 and −0.003 %/year, respectively), while that in the heatwave land exposure in NAT is significantly decreasing (−0.009 %/year, p  < 0.05). Comparisons of ALL and NAT suggest that ACC increases the land exposures of heatwave and extreme runoff, resulting in an increase in SRHE land exposure (+0.112 %/year, see Fig. 6 a). Furthermore, the increase in heatwave land exposure (+0.157 %/year, Fig. 6 c) contributes to the increase in SRHE land exposure more than that of extreme runoff exposure (+0.019 %/year, Fig. 6 b).  3.4 Global analysis of 1950–2014 trends in SRHE characteristics The M−K trend test is applied at each grid globally to estimate the (1950–2014) trends in the SRHE characteristics (frequency, IRH, duration) simulated by ALL and NAT. The global distributions of trends in SRHE characteristics are plotted in Fig. 7  , while that of trends in extreme runoff and heatwave characteristics (frequency and duration) are plotted in Figs. S7 and S8  respectively. Notice that the trend of SRHE frequency is estimated based on the total number of SRHE events per year, while the trends of IRH and duration estimated based on the SRHE event sequences. As seen, the trend pattern of SRHE frequency estimated by ALL is both weak and insignificant in most global regions. For ALL simulations, a significant increasing trend (p  < 0.05) is detected only in some regions of southeastern Asia and northwestern South America (+0.05 events/year), consistent with the increase of heatwave and extreme runoff frequency (Figs. S7 a and S8 a). For NAT simulations, the SRHE frequency shows no significant trend over the entire global land (Fig. 7 d) due to the weak trends in extreme runoff and heatwave frequencies nearly globally (Figs. S7 c and S8 c). Comparison between ALL and NAT reveals that ACC intensifies SRHE frequency with a trend of < +0.1 event/year in southeastern Asia and some parts of central South America by enhancing the frequency of both extreme runoff and heatwave, while it reduces SRHE frequency (> -0.05 event/year) in some regions of western South America by decreasing the frequency of heatwave occurrence. The trend magnitude of IRH exhibits a large global variability especially in ALL and NAT simulations (Figs. 7 b and e). The increasing (decreasing) IRH trends estimated by ALL are < +0.5 (> -0.2) days/event, while the increasing (decreasing) IRH trends estimated by NAT are < +0.5 (> -0.4) days/event. In general, ACC exerts the increasing (decreasing) IRH trends by the magnitude of +0.5 (−0.4) days/event or less. For SRHE duration, the ALL simulation generally shows increasing trends globally (< +1 days/event), with a significant upward trend (p  < 0.05) found particularly in northern/southern North America, western South America, southern Africa, central/eastern/southeastern Asia, and central Australia (Fig. 7 c). On the contrary, the NAT simulations shows generally decreasing trends of SRHE duration globally, such as in the northern/southern North America, southern South America, southern Africa, Arabian Peninsula, eastern Asia, and central Australia (> -0.5 days/event). Comparison between ALL and NAT reveals that ACC results in an increase (decrease) of SRHE duration in most of northern/southern North America, central/eastern Asia (in some regions of South America, southern Africa and Australia, and scattered regions of North America and Asia). Moreover, this increase in SRHE duration is mainly due to the increase in heatwave duration (< +0.1 days/event, Fig. S8 f), while the decrease in SRHE duration is attributed to the decreased IRH (Fig. 7 h) and little change in extreme runoff and heatwave durations (Figs. S7 f and S8 f).  3.5 Fraction attributable risk of SRHE occurrence To further investigate the impacts of ACC on SRHE occurrence, the attribution analysis of SRHE, extreme runoff, and heatwave occurrence is conducted by using FAR based on ALL and NAT simulations during 1950–2014. Note that as PALL   is in the denominator of equation (4) , the regions where ALL simulation identifies no SRHE occurrence need to be excluded. As shown in Fig. 8  a, the FAR of 1950–1979 SRHE is larger than zero in many global regions especially South America, Africa, southeastern Asia, and Australia (0.6–1), indicating that ACC has enhanced 60–100 % of SRHE probability there. In contrast, a negative FAR of SRHE is found in North America and Asia during 1950–1979 (Fig. 8 a), mainly related to the decrease in heatwave probability caused by ACC (FAR mostly < 0) in the Northern Hemisphere (Fig. 8 g). From 1950–1979 to 1980–2014, the regions where the SRHE probability increases due to ACC (FAR > 0) are further expanded to almost all global regions, including southern North America and southeastern Asia (Figs. 8 a and b), which can be attributed to the enhanced influence of ACC on heatwaves (FAR up to 1) over the Northern Hemisphere from 1950–1979 to 1980–2014 (Figs. 8 g and h). Overall, the ACC exacerbates SRHE probability during 1950–2014 in most global regions especially the Southern Hemisphere (> 60 % increase in probability, Fig. 8 c), consistent with Fig. 2 g where it shows that SRHE frequency is larger in ALL than that in NAT. The FAR of extreme runoff events shows large spatial variability, suggesting the relatively large uncertainty in extreme runoff attribution. ACC leads to the increased extreme runoff probability during 1950–1979 in many global regions such as eastern North America, central South America, central Europe, eastern Africa, central/southeastern Asia and eastern/central Australia (up to 80 % increase, Fig. 8 d). From 1950–1979 to 1980–2014 (Figs. 8 d and e), the extreme runoff probability due to ACC has increased significantly (FAR from < 0 to up to 0.8) in central Africa, northeastern Asia, and most of Australia. This is supported by Fig. S2  showing that during 1950–2014 the extreme runoff frequency in ALL is 0.25–3 folds higher than that in NAT there. In high-latitude and −altitude regions such as northern North America, northeastern Asia, Qinghai Tibet Plateau, and the Andes Mountains, the FAR of heatwave is mostly larger than that of extreme runoff events during 1950–2014 (especially for 1980–2014, Figs. 8 e and h), suggesting that ACC contribute more to the increase in heatwave probability than that of extreme runoff probability there. Such increase in heatwave probability is conducive to snow melting and exacerbate the risk of extreme runoff events and SRHE events. The global-mean FAR of SRHE is mostly > 0 with a larger increasing trend after 1970 (+0.01/year, p  < 0.05), and a mean FAR value of 0.4 in 2014 (Fig. 9  a) indicating that the ACC has led to a 40 % increase in SRHE probability by 2014. This result resembles the heatwave interannual variability which shows an increasing trend especially during 1971–2014 (+0.0103/year, p  < 0.05) with a 40 % increase in heatwave probability in 2014 due to the ACC (Fig. 9 c). In contrast, the global-mean FAR of extreme runoff shows a relatively small increasing trend after 1970 (+0.0012/year, p  < 0.05) with a mean increase < 10 % in extreme runoff probability by 2014. This indicates that ACC has a greater promoting effect on heatwave probability than extreme runoff, and the increase in heatwave probability is more dominant in dictating the changes in SRHE probability. We further quantify the relations of FAR between SRHE, extreme runoff, and heatwave during 1950–2014 at continental scale using the partial correlation analysis. As shown in Fig. 10  , all PCCs between the FARs of SRHE, extreme runoff and heatwave are positive, indicating that the intensification of extreme runoff and heatwave contributes to the increased SRHE probability. Furthermore, the PCC between the FAR of SRHE and heatwave (0.04–0.53) is larger than that between SRHE and extreme runoff (0.01–0.23) in nearly all continents (especially Africa, Australia and South America), indicating that the heatwave intensification contributes to SRHE probability more than extreme runoff. In contrast, a similar PCC is found between the FAR of SRHE and heatwave (0.039) and that between SRHE and extreme runoff (0.036) in Europe, suggesting the comparable contributions of extreme runoff and heatwave to the SRHE probability under ACC. We also evaluate PCC between the FARs of heatwaves, extreme runoff events, and SRHE in the polar climate regions (according to Köppen-Geiger climate classification, Beck et al., 2005 ) located in high-latitude and −altitude areas covered by snow. Results show that the PCC between the FAR of heatwave and SRHE (0.203, p  < 0.05) is larger than that between extreme runoff and SRHE (0.187, p  < 0.05), indicating that the heatwave intensification contributes to SRHE probability more than extreme runoff over these regions. Therefore, the heatwave caused by ACC in high-latitude and −altitude areas can lead to snowmelt, potentially causing extreme runoff and increasing the SRHE risk.  3.6 Fraction attributable risk of SRHE with different characteristics We computed the FAR of SRHE from both ALL and NAT simulations with different IRHs (from 1 to 6 days) and with different durations (0–5, 5–10, 10–15, 15–20, > 20 days). Fig. 11   displays the violin diagrams of FAR for the global SRHE occurrence with different IRHs (durations) during the 1950–1979, 1980–2014, and 1950–2014 sub-periods. The nuclear density curve of the violin region is plotted based on the FAR values of all global grids. As shown, the mean FAR of SRHE with IRHs from 1 to 6 days is 0.03, 0.03, 0, 0, −0.01, and 0.02 respectively, suggesting that ACC leads to a larger increase in SRHE probability with a shorter IRH. During 1980–2014, the FAR of SRHE is generally > 0 for different IRHs (Fig. 11 b). Furthermore, there are more grid points with the FAR close to 1 (especially for IRH=1 day) during 1980–2014 than 1950–1979, suggesting a significantly increasing impact of ACC during 1980–2014 relative to 1950–1979. Overall, ACC increases SRHE probability during 1950–2014, and this increase is greater for the short than the longer IRH (Fig. 11 c). For the SRHE with different durations, the FAR with the duration > 20 days is larger than that < 20 days during 1950–1979, and there are more grids with FAR close to 1 for the duration > 20 days (Fig. 11 d). During 1980–2014, the FAR of SRHE with different durations ranges between 0.04–0.78 (Fig. 11 e), obviously larger than that during 1950–1979. This indicates that ACC increases SRHE probability with all durations during 1980–2014, and a greater increase is found in the longer SRHE duration. In general, the ACC increases SRHE probability during 1950–2014 with a mean FAR of 0.08–0.69 for five different durations (Fig. 11 f), suggesting that ACC has resulted in an 8-69 % increase in the global SRHE probability with the different durations.   4 Discussions 4.1 Reasons for changes in SRHE risk under anthropogenic forcing This study conducts an attribution analysis of changes in SRHE occurrence during 1950–2014. Results show that FAR exhibits an increasing trend particularly after 1970 (Fig. 9 ), indicating that ACC has intensified the SRHE occurrence risk over time. This can mainly be attributed to the increased heatwave risk caused by ACC almost globally in 1950–2014 (Figs. 8 g and h), also consistent with the findings in previous findings (Bo-Tao and Jin, 2021; Christidis et al., 2014 ; King et al., 2015; Kishore et al., 2022 ). On the other hand, ACC also leads to more frequent and intense heavy rainfall in most global regions and results in an increased extreme runoff probability (Fischer and Knutti, 2015 ), which also exacerbates the SRHE risks globally (Figs. 8 d and e). Our study highlights that under ACC the intensification of heatwave contributes to the SRHE occurrence more than extreme runoff, especially in the Southern Hemisphere (Fig. 10 ). ACC exacerbate warming by emitting the greenhouse gases and enhance atmospheric vapor transport and heavy rainfall, thereby accelerating the water cycle and increasing extreme runoff risks (Fung et al., 2021; Mikhaylov et al., 2020; Trenberth, 2011; Yeh and Wu, 2018 ). The large amount of aerosol particles produced by humans increases the cloud condensation nuclei in the atmosphere and release the potential heat, triggering strong convection and resulting in more extreme precipitation (Feichter et al., 2004; Rémy et al., 2015; Rosenfeld et al., 2014 ). In addition, anthropogenic activities have changed land surface characteristics during urbanization and industrialization, such as albedo, surface roughness, leaf area index, and fractional vegetation coverage, together altering the regional climate and water cycle to be more prone to local heavy precipitation and extreme runoff occurrence (Fu, 2003; Huong and Pathirana, 2013; Li et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2017 ). The role of ACC in affecting heatwave risk has greatly changed globally from 1950–1979 to 1980–2014 (Figs. 8 g and h and Fig. 9 c). The ACC during 1950–1979 tends to reduce the heatwave risk in the mid-latitude (around 40-50°N) in the Northern Hemisphere while exacerbate this risk in the Southern Hemisphere, generally consistent with the findings of previous studies (Ma et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2022 ). From 1980 to 2014, the ACC impact on heatwave intensification spreads nearly globally (Fig. 8 h), mainly due to the significant increase in atmospheric greenhouse gases during the late 1970s and 1980s caused by burning of fossil fuels and deforestation, which led to global warming intensification by changing surface energy balance (Hansen and Sato, 2004; Seong et al., 2021; Trenberth, 2018; Wallington et al., 2009 ). In addition, the global coverage of cropland and vegetation was decreased and the impervious surface increased due to expanded urbanization after the 1980s (Huang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2016; Luo and Lau, 2017 ), leading to warmer urban climate and the increased frequency and intensity of heatwave (Wang et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2020 ), as supported by the findings in this study showing that the Pearl River Delta has experienced higher frequency and longer duration of heatwaves than other regions in southern China (Figs. S3 a and b).  4.2 Spatial variability of FAR for the occurrences of SRHE, extreme runoff and heatwave Fig. 12   plots 1950–2014 annual variations of the spatial standard deviations (SSTDs) of FAR for the occurrence of SRHE, extreme runoff, and heatwave in the global scale and the six continents. SSTD is calculated as the standard deviation of FAR and represents the spatial variability of FAR at the global and continental scales. The SSTD of FAR for SRHE occurrence decreases over time in all six continents (especially Europe and Africa) with a decline rate ranging from 0.0026 to 0.0079 year−1 . Moreover, the SSTD of FAR for heatwaves shows a larger decreasing trend than that for extreme runoff in all continents except Africa, suggesting that the decrease in SSTD of FAR for heatwaves contributes to the decrease in SSTD of FAR for SRHE more than extreme runoff. At the global scale, the SSTD of FAR for SRHE decreases significantly from 1950 to 2014 (−0.007 year−1 , p  < 0.05), indicating that ACC on the global variability of SRHE risk is decreased over time. This is mainly due to the decreases in the spatial variability of ACC on heatwave (SSTD decreases by 0.029 year−1 , p  < 0.05) and extreme runoff (SSTD decreases by 0.0043 year−1 , p  < 0.05) (Fig. 12 g). It is also found that the global SSTD of FAR for extreme runoff (2.0674) is significantly larger than that for heatwaves (1.0561) during 1950–2014, and the difference in the global SSTD of FAR between extreme runoff and heatwave tends to increase over time (Fig. 12 g). This indicates that ACC on extreme runoff exhibits greater spatial variations than that on heatwaves especially during recent years, as supported by previous studies (Davenport et al., 2021; Zou et al., 2021 ), indicating that ACC on extreme runoff exhibits significant regional differences around the world since the greenhouse gases and aerosols affect atmospheric circulation and vapor transport and lead to large spatial variability of precipitation (Davenport et al., 2021; Zou et al., 2021 ). The spatial variability of extreme runoff is also closely related to varying surface conditions such as restoring farmland to forest (Sajikumar and Remya, 2015; Wang et al., 2017; Wang and Stephenson, 2018 ), urbanization (Chithra et al., 2015; Li et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2018 ), and construction of water conservancy projects (Biswas, 1990; Wang et al., 2021 ). These human activities have significantly changed runoff generation processes of the underlying surface and hence the enhanced spatial variability in extreme runoff occurrence.  4.3 Limitations of this study This study uses the peak-over-threshold method to identify the extreme runoff at the grid scale, which is considered a potential indicator for monitoring floods (Zhou et al., 2023 ). However, not all the extreme runoff events will eventually evolve into the flood events. Therefore, this method used in the present study may potentially overestimate the frequency of flood events, particularly in some high-mountain areas (e.g., Andes) where the floods rarely occur. This is evidenced by Fig. 8  showing the higher FAR of floods in Andes if the peak-over-threshold method is used to identify flood events. On the other hand, the use of extreme runoff as the flood indicator is unable to distinguish various flood types such as the fluvial versus pluvial floods (Wang et al., 2019 ). Both flood triggering and evolution mechanisms are complicated (Tarasova et al., 2020 ) and are related to precipitation variability (Breugem et al., 2020; Tabari, 2020 ), topography (Kuksina et al., 2017; Torre Zaffaroni et al., 2023 ), and land use (Brath et al., 2006; Saghafian et al., 2007 ). In future work, it is necessary to use the global-scale hydrodynamic model (e.g., Uddin et al., 2023 ) to simulate the daily streamflow process and identify the flood events at the catchment scale to improve the result robustness of successive flood-heat extreme event identification. In this study, we use FAR to explore the ACC impact on SRHE occurrence. Notice that the FAR calculation depends on the simulations under ALL and NAT forcings. Thus, the credibility of this attribution analysis depends highly on the selected GCMs, and the multi-model ensemble can be a sufficient choice for the attribution analysis (Qian et al., 2022; van Oldenborgh et al., 2021 ). Meanwhile, the CMIP6 GCM simulations may also have limitations in simulating local precipitation and runoff due to complex terrain or urbanization (Abdelmoaty et al., 2021; Rahman et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ). For example, the performance of CMIP6 models is still unsatisfactory in high latitude and −altitude areas (Hou et al., 2022; Lalande et al., 2021 ). The FAR method can only quantify the risk of disaster occurrence, but not the impact on the magnitudes of disaster characteristics. This study only quantified the ACC impact on SRHE occurrence without differentiating individual impacts due to greenhouse gases, aerosols, and land use. More advanced attribution methods (e.g., optimal fingerprint method) can be used to explore the influences of individual anthropogenic factors on SRHE and its characteristics in the future study.   5 Conclusions Based on the daily simulation data of five selected CMIP6 GCMs under the ALL and NAT forcings, this study investigates the global changes in the SRHE characteristics (frequency, land exposure, duration, IRH) during 1950–2014. The ERA5 temperature data and GLDAS runoff data are used for validating the ALL simulations of CMIP6. The impacts of ACC on the SRHE predictability with different durations and IRHs are analyzed quantitatively by using the FAR (Fraction Attributable Risk) method. The individual contribution of heatwave and extreme runoff to the increasing SRHE occurrence due to ACC is explored by using the partial correlation analysis. The main findings of this study are summarized as follows:(1) From 1950 to 2014, the ALL forcing leads to a significant increase in SRHE frequency (+0.002 event/year), duration (+0.0442 days/event/year), and land exposure (+0.109 %/year), but a significant decrease in IRH (−0.0008 days/event/year). Spatially, the ALL forcing simulates more SRHE events in southeastern Asia and central South America (> 80 events), the longer IRH (2–4 days/event) in the 30°N and 80°N regions of the Northern Hemisphere and around 30°S in the Southern Hemisphere, and the longer SRHE duration (> 25 days/event) mainly in northern North America, Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, and southeastern Asia.  (2) The SRHE frequency under ALL simulation is higher than that under NAT simulation during 1950–2014 in most global regions, especially the central South America, central Africa, and southeastern Asia (> 18 folds). ACC (i.e., ALL minus NAT) lengthens SRHE duration in most global regions, especially northern South America, central Africa, and southeastern Asia (1–4.5 folds) due to the larger increase in heatwave duration (> 2 folds), and shortens SRHE duration in some parts of central North America and northern/eastern/southwestern Asia due to the decrease in extreme runoff duration there.  (3) Attribution analysis indicates that ACC exacerbates the probability of SRHE occurrence in most global regions especially the Southern Hemisphere (> 60 % increase), with a global mean increase of 40 % in SRHE occurrence probability by 2014. Furthermore, the SRHE events with a short IRH and long duration tends to occur more frequent than other types of SRHE events. Overall, the impact of ACC on the spatial variability of SRHE occurrence decreases over time. The intensification of heatwave due to ACC contributes to the SRHE occurrence more than that of extreme runoff in nearly all global regions, especially the Southern Hemisphere.
1 Introduction Terrestrial evapotranspiration involves the transpiration of vegetation, evaporation from the soil, and the interception occurring within the vegetation canopy (Wang and Dickinson, 2012 ). It constitutes a fundamental process within the water cycle and heat exchange, playing a pivotal role in the global water balance (Huntington, 2006; Jensen et al., 2016 ). Roughly two-thirds of precipitation on a global scale is returned to the atmosphere through ET (Oki and Kanae, 2006 ). Despite being second only to precipitation in significance within the land water cycle, estimating ET remains the most challenging aspect. In recent times, the escalation of global temperatures due to climate change has led to a notable increase in the occurrence of record-breaking high temperatures and widespread droughts worldwide. This surge in climate extremes poses a substantial threat, causing severe harm to both natural ecosystems and socioeconomic systems (Song et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2020; Pérez et al., 2021 ). A recent study has shown that due to climate change, precipitation has dominated the recent decline in global water resource availability (Zhang et al., 2021 ), and the average global surface temperature in the 2020s is approximately 1.09℃ higher than at the end of the 18th century (IPCC, 2021 ). High temperature, high VPD and drought are three common extreme climatic conditions that can have multiple negative impacts on plants (Qian et al., 2023 ). When plants encounter extreme climate, they reduce transpiration to conserve water, which can lead to a significant reduction in carbon dioxide absorption and photosynthetic efficiency (Chen et al., 2021 ). Additionally, protein structure and enzyme activity, as well as inhibition of root development, growth, and normal metabolism, can all be negatively affected to varying degrees (Buttlar et al., 2018; Li et al., 2021 ). These impacts are not limited to individual plants, but may also trigger chain reactions throughout the ecosystem, with long-term effects on ecological balance. The process of evapotranspiration (ET) is intricately linked to alterations in vegetation and the broader phenomenon of climate change. (Zhang et al., 2019 ), so the frequent occurrence of extreme climates worldwide will further increase the uncertainty of ET, which is already difficult to estimate. Conventionally, the measurement of evapotranspiration (ET) involves techniques such as laser meters, eddy covariance, and other methods, but these are constrained to point and local scales (Qian et al., 2022 ). Although the FLUXNET project furnishes local-scale ET observations through flux towers (Baldocchi et al., 2001 ), achieving global coverage with such measurement sites is evidently impractical. The representativeness of field measurements at a point scale for broader areas is currently a subject of ongoing research. To address this constraint, researchers have devised various regional and global ET products featuring diverse spatial and temporal resolutions. Despite these advancements, there remains a substantial degree of uncertainty when it comes to precisely determining the magnitude and spatiotemporal characteristics of ET at regional or global scales (Tian et al., 2010; Mueller et al., 2011; Miralles et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2022 ). Currently, some studies indicated that the accuracy of ET products under extreme climatic conditions, may be compromised due to deficiencies in model structure, input reliability, and insufficient ground data (Jia et al., 2012; Xia et al., 2015 ). For instance, Qian et al. (2023)  discovered a notable decline in the accuracy of nine global ET products under three extreme climate conditions (high temperatures (over 95 %), high VPD (over 95 %), and drought (SPEI<-1.5)) during their evaluation. When evaluating whether current ET datasets can detect variation in ET in the Heihe River Basin, Wu et al. (2023)  discovered that the majority of mainstream ET products, such as MOD16A2, PMLv2, and FLDAS, produce considerable ET inaccuracies in comparison to observed values during periods of high temperatures and droughts. Wang et al. (2023a)  found that the consistency of ET estimates in both space and time is significantly influenced by droughts and vegetation greenness. Yao et al. (2023)  discovered that the complementary-relationship-dependent (CR) and Noah Land Surface Model (NOAH) datasets exhibited elevated uncertainties in warmer temperatures (summer) when comparing the uncertainties of three high-resolution ET products in China. Majozi et al. (2017)  assessed the precision of four ET products in two arid ecological regions in South Africa, revealing suboptimal performance in both regions for all ET products. Jung et al. (2019a)  identified that certain satellite-derived ET datasets are unsuitable for application in arid regions, displaying increased uncertainties. In Australia, Bai and Liu (2018)  noted a substantial deterioration in the effectiveness of four ET products during arid summers, with correlations to observed values dropping below 0.36. Mueller et al. (2011)  scrutinized a global ET dataset spanning multiple years based on 30 observations from 1989 to 1995. Their findings revealed that the majority of ET products significantly overestimated evapotranspiration in arid and semi-arid regions, such as Western Australia, Western China, and the Western United States. Moshir Panahi et al. (2021)  identified deficiencies in estimating ET in arid and semi-arid regions for three ET products, emphasizing the importance of considering water input fluxes in these areas. Ochege et al. (2021)  documented below-par performance of four ET products, including GLEAM, across four arid biomes in Central Asia. In their examination of evapotranspiration trends in the upper and middle reaches of the Yellow River basin, Wang et al. (2022a)  underscored the adverse influence of VPD on both precipitation and evaporation. Similarly, Bai and Liu (2018)  carried out a comparative assessment of three ET products in the Chinese region and observed that elevated VPD imposed specific constraints on the ET products. Xiong et al. (2015)  also detected that the uncertainty of ET products is more conspicuous in arid regions. In summary, various studies have indicated that extreme climatic conditions, encompassing high temperatures, drought, and dry air, may exert varying degrees of adverse effects on prevailing ET products. This complex phenomenon involves multiple factors and interrelated processes, which can be attributed to various factors. Firstly, high temperature and high VPD can impose stress on vegetation, leading to increased rates of water evaporation. However, the rate of water uptake by vegetation roots may fail to meet the demand, resulting in a reduction or instability in transpiration. This poses a significant challenge for estimating ET products (Lu et al., 2017; Massmann et al., 2019 ). Simultaneously, vegetation may adopt physiological mechanisms to reduce transpiration, mitigating water loss. This can involve the closure of stomata or a decrease in transpiration. The rapid depletion of soil moisture also restricts water supply, further limiting the transpiration capacity of vegetation (Zhang et al., 2014a ). Secondly, an increase in temperature intensifies the movement of water molecules in the air, thereby accelerating the rate at which water molecules escape from water bodies or soil. However, elevated temperatures also increase the saturation vapor pressure of water in the air. This means that, after a certain point, water molecules encountering the saturation vapor pressure cease to evaporate. This non-linear relationship between the amount of water evaporated and temperature is referred to as the saturation vapor pressure effect (Zhang et al., 2014c; Qian et al., 2023 ). Therefore, when the temperature increases to a certain extent, even though the evaporation rate of water molecules increases, the enhanced saturation vapor pressure effect gradually slows down the rate at which water molecules evaporate. This may contribute to a decrease in the accuracy of ET estimation and, in many cases, result in overestimation (Allen et al., 1998; Green and Hay, 2002; Hatfield and Prueger, 2015; Yuan et al., 2019 ). Finally, the majority of current ET products may struggle to accurately capture the complex non-linear dynamics of vegetation and soil moisture under extreme conditions. This increases the uncertainty of the models, as the occurrence of extreme events can trigger dynamic changes in ecosystems, such as slowed vegetation growth and shifts in vegetation types. In addition, incomplete observational data, model parameter constraints, and insufficient simulation of physical processes contribute to the uncertainty of these products under extreme climatic conditions (Umar Waqas Liaqat and Choi, 2017; Abatzoglou et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019 ). Nevertheless, there is presently limited systematic evaluation in this regard, with many studies concentrating on the performance of ET products on annual and quarterly scales. Therefore, it is necessary to improve the uncertainty of existing ET products under extreme climatic conditions (Wartenburger et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016 ). In recent years, the application of machine learning techniques in hydrology and ecology has been on the rise (Abrahart et al., 2012; Kousari et al., 2017; Crisci et al., 2012 ). Compared to other methods, machine learning models can autonomously uncover hidden relationships among data and provide higher-precision simulations of complex systems (Reichslein et al., 2019 ). Particularly in predicting reference ET and evaporation, machine learning methods have been shown to offer more accurate results than traditional meteorology-driven approaches (Tramontana et al., 2016; Yaseen et al., 2016; Mehdizadeh et al., 2017; Granata 2019; Jung et al., 2019b; Hu et al., 2021 ). These techniques not only accurately estimate ET but are also utilized to address other ET-related issues such as data gaps, sensitivity analysis, and climate variable estimation based on flux tower data (Abudu et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2012 ). Presently, a growing cohort of researchers is employing machine learning methodologies, including RF and XGB, for the estimation of ET (Knipper et al., 2023; Han et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2022 ). Recently, Wang et al. (2023b)  successfully employed a RF to obtain hourly ET data for the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, and their estimates surpassed those of SEBS, Maximum Entropy Production (MEP), and ERA5. However, due to the weak ability of machine learning in processing complex data and mining high-order features, as well as its high dependence on data volume and feature engineering, its performance on certain complex tasks is limited. To date, research on deep learning models for ET estimation remains limited (Bennett and Nijssen 2021 ), and most of it has been conducted at local scales or under normal climatic conditions. The use of deep learning to improve ET estimation under extreme climatic conditions on a global scale is indeed quite scarce (Qian et al., 2023 ). Deep learning (DL) represents a facet of machine learning (ML) characterized by a sequence of sophisticated investigations into artificial neural networks (ANN). Since 2012, it has garnered substantial traction, demonstrating superior efficacy compared to alternative ML approaches (LeCun et al., 2015; Shen, 2018 ). Studies indicate that the accurate estimation of ET at a singular scale exhibits remarkable performance (Li, 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022b ). The CNN model, a widely employed DL architecture, possesses the capability to capture enduring correlations between input and output within the network. Its application extends to simulating runoff, soil moisture, and various facets of the hydrological cycle (Kratzert et al., 2018; Kratzert et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2020a; Fang et al., 2020b ). However, its utilization in large-scale ET estimation studies remains infrequent (Wang et al., 2022b ). In contrast to traditional machine learning approaches, CNNs autonomously extract relevant features, finding extensive utility in image recognition and classification, including applications in ET estimation (Gebrehiwot et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Panahi et al., 2020 ). Wang et al. (2022a)  observed that, in regions with limited observation data like the Tibetan Plateau, DL models exhibit greater flexibility in simulating ET compared to traditional machine learning methods. Dong et al. (2022)  conducted an assessment of three machine learning models for computing reference evapotranspiration across various spatio-temporal scales in China, encompassing CNN, extreme learning machine (ELM), and multiple adaptive regression splines (MARS). Their findings indicated that CNN surpassed ELM and MARS in both daily and monthly modeling accuracy and robustness. Meanwhile, Chen et al. (2023)  demonstrated that integrating flux footprints and physical mechanisms into the CNN model effectively enhances the precision of urban ET simulation while significantly minimizing estimation errors. Ferreira and da Cunha (2020)  investigated the viability of CNN and three alternative machine learning approaches for estimating ET in both regional and local contexts. Their findings revealed that, particularly when utilizing hourly data as input, CNN demonstrated the highest accuracy in ET estimation. While DL exhibits significant potential for ET estimation, its applicability across diverse global regions and land cover types remains inadequately explored. Furthermore, the assessment of estimation accuracy under extreme climatic conditions has been overlooked in prior studies. Existing research has predominantly concentrated on specific regions or particular ET products (Khan et al., 2018a; Bai and Liu, 2018; Guo et al., 2022 ). Lastly, there is a scarcity of studies investigating the synergies of ET product data and deep learning algorithms for assessing ET outcomes. In summary, against the backdrop of frequent occurrences of extreme climate events globally, the ET products are no longer able to accurately and stably reflect ground observational data under climatic conditions (Qian et al., 2023 ). Therefore, the purpose of this study is to assess the estimation accuracy of ET products under high temperature and high VPD conditions. We attempt to enhance the estimation accuracy of ET products under extreme climatic conditions by integrating ET products into a deep learning CNN using ERA5 meteorological data as a foundation. Additionally, three machine learning models (RF, XGBoost, and GPR) are selected as references to investigate novel approaches for improving the accuracy of ET product estimation, simultaneously calculate the contribution rate of ET products and meteorological data to model estimation to understand whether ET products play a major role in improving accuracy. The study also explores the capabilities of these models to enhance accuracy in different regions, land cover types, and climate types. Finally, we comprehensively considered data from 35 neighboring flux towers as independent validation sites to assess the model's applicability. This investigation contributes to optimizing water resource management, enhancing agricultural productivity, preserving ecosystem health, assessing natural disaster risks, and deepening the understanding of the impact of climate change on the water cycle. Accurate estimation of evapotranspiration through the utilization of deep learning and ET products proves effective in addressing issues related to water scarcity, drought disasters, and ecological balance, providing valuable support for sustainable development.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Eddy covariance ET and study area The eddy covariance (EC) technique stands out as a prevalent approach for measuring energy flux, enabling the continuous assessment of water and energy exchange (Mu et al., 2011 ). The FLUXNET2015 dataset, as outlined by Ma et al. (2021) , supplies uninterrupted measurements of carbon and energy fluxes on an hourly basis through the utilization of the eddy covariance method. This study amalgamated latent heat flux (LE) data extracted from 150 flux towers situated globally, consolidating the information into daily values (Fig. 1  ) (the basic information about flux towers can be found in attachment Table S1 ). These daily values were employed to assess the performance of different ET products and models. Additionally, considering factors such as distance, land cover type, and climate type, 35 nearby flux towers were selected as independent validation sites to evaluate the model's applicability, please refer to the specific distribution in Fig. S1  (the basic information about 35 validation sites and corresponding site relationships can be found in attachment Table S2 and S3 ). The data from the aforementioned sites can be accessed online at https://fluxnet.fluxdata.org/ . These sites are categorized geographically into three regions: the Americas (AM), Europe-Africa (EA), and Asia-Russia-Australia (ARA). Simultaneously, based on the global 1-kilometer climate type distribution provided by Beck et al. (2018), this study classifies the flux towers into the following climate types: 8 Aw (1Af + 2Am + 5Aw), 2 Bwh, 7 BS (3 BSh + 4 BSk), 13 Csa, 2 Cwa, 22 Cf (14 Cfa + 8 Cfb), 5 Dsb, 7 Dw (1 Dwa + 2 Dwb + 3 Dwc), 84 Df (9 Dfa + 47 Dfb + 28 Dfc) (Specific explanations for different climate types can be found in Table S4  in the attachment). Furthermore, according to the International Geosphere-Biosphere Programme (IGBP) classification system, different flux towers are distributed across various land cover types (Friedl et al., 2010 ). The specific types and corresponding quantities are depicted in the histogram in Fig. 1 . (For detailed information about flux towers and corresponding references, please refer to Table S2  in the attachment). The FLUXNET2015 dataset has undergone quality control and preprocessing to enhance consistency and comparability among different sites. The specific methods employed are detailed in Pastorello et al. (2020) . Blank gaps in the dataset were filled using two independent methods: marginal distribution sampling (denoted by the suffix_F_MDS) and ERA-Interim (denoted by the suffix_F_ERA). Therefore, the final gap-filled product (variables with the suffix_F) includes both directly measured records and gap-filled records. In this study, the flux tower data filled by MDS method (LE_F_MDS) is used and removing lower quality data. The eddy covariance (EC) method, after nearly 50 years of development, undoubtedly remains the most advanced and preferred flux observation method in current land–atmosphere exchange research (Stocker et al., 2018 ). However, the analysis of energy balance closure issues associated with fluxes has raised significant concerns about the reliability of the EC method. Virtually all land–atmosphere exchange models are built on the fundamental principles of energy and mass balance. In ecosystem observations, when energy enters the system from above, the net radiation (Rn ) takes a positive value; conversely, Rn is negative when energy leaves the system. The surface energy balance equation is expressed as:(1) R n  - G - S - Q = H + L E     Where R n    represents the net radiation, G   is the soil heat flux, S   is the heat storage in the vegetation canopy, Q   is the sum of additional energy terms, H   is the sensible heat flux, and H   is the latent heat flux. Since S   and Q   are often negligible and ignored, in this context, R n   - G       is referred to as the available energy, and H + L E      is termed turbulent energy. Therefore, when the available energy equals the turbulent energy, it is referred to as energy balance closure; otherwise, it is considered energy balance non-closure. However, the turbulent energy observed by the eddy covariance (EC) method is often 10 %-30 % lower than the available energy (Chen et al., 2018 ). To rectify this energy imbalance, we presupposes the precise measurement of the half-hourly Bowen ratio, which represents the ratio of sensible heat flux to latent heat flux, in turbulent flux observations. That is, the Bowen ratio remains constant before and after correction. The energy deficit is then compensated by utilizing the difference between available energy and turbulent energy. In our study, the Bowen ratio (Jung et al., 2010 ) for each site was estimated using the sensible heat (H_F_MDS) and latent heat (LE_F_MDS) fluxes filled with the MDS method. In the effort to eradicate white noise from the initial data set, in addition to directly eliminating gaps or duplicate values (e.g., '0000′ or '9999′) at the commencement or conclusion of the time series, this research utilized effective techniques such as Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) or k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) for gap filling. (Lin et al., 2022 ). These methods effectively address data gaps (with at least 1 year of valid data) while maintaining the original distribution pattern, thus enhancing data quality and reliability. Moreover, FLUXNET ET can be derived by calculating the ratio of latent heat flux (LE) to the conversion factor λ (λ = 2.45  MJ/ kg) (Qian et al., 2023 ).  2.2 Data 2.2.1 Definition of extreme climatic conditions and uncertainty The definition of extreme climate varies by region and country, typically relying on statistical analyses of meteorological and climatic data (McPhillips et al., 2018 ). To facilitate comparisons across different sites in various regions, this study opts for a more suitable percentile method (relative threshold method). Specifically, it compares the maximum temperature and maximum VPD for a given day with the corresponding daily maximum values within the entire time range. If these temperature and VPD values exceed a specific percentile (in this study, the 95th percentile), they are considered extreme high temperature and high VPD (Stefanon et al., 2012 ). Additionally, the study uses the flux environmental factors TA_F and VPD_F as proxies for temperature and VPD, respectively. This study defines that when the accuracy of ET products declines by more than 20 %, it can be considered as uncertainty. For instance, if the original R2  is 0.6 and it decreases to below 0.48, or if the RMSE increases from 0.8 mm/d to over 0.96 mm/d, it indicates the presence of uncertainty.  2.2.2 ERA5 reanalysis data and NDVI data Building on previous research efforts (Tramontana et al., 2016; Jung et al., 2019a; Liu et al., 2021 ), this study selects NDVI data and meteorological data from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset that is most closely associated with ET as input factors (Table 1  ). This approach overcomes limitations related to geographical and temporal constraints. These predictor variables include maximum temperature (Tmax ), minimum temperature (Tmin ), relative humidity (RH), surface solar radiation (Rs ), 10-meter wind speed (WS), precipitation (Pre), and soil moisture content (SMC), with 0.25° × 0.25° spatial resolution. Additionally, daily Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) data were obtained from the NOAA Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR) product (Version 5) of NOAA Climate Data Record (CDR) (Vermote et al., 2014 ; Pedelty et al., 2007 ). It provides measurements of surface vegetation cover activity globally, spanning from 1981 to 2019, with a spatial resolution of 0.05°. The aforementioned ERA5 data and NDVI data can be accessed online at https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/  and https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/climate-data-records , respectively. Finally, since the ERA5 reanalysis meteorological data and NDVI data are part of a gridded dataset, there is a need to address the issue of matching these data with flux tower measurements. Consequently, this study addresses the issue by applying the Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) technique, which interpolates meteorological data from four adjacent grid points to the flux tower locations. IDW is a deterministic interpolation method that assigns weights according to distance. The core idea is to use a weighted moving average, with weights determined by the spatial distance between the interpolation point and the data points. This method ensures that the meteorological data aligns with the specific flux tower sites, improving the precision and relevance of environmental data integration. The calculation formula is available in the attachment. The calculation formula can be found in the attachment. Our study also used the IDW method to interpolate the ET values of grid ET products into flux towers.   2.3 Input data 2.3.1 GLEAM GLEAM (https://www.gleam.eu/ ) is a dataset of actual evapotranspiration (ET) and soil moisture generated by the GLEAM algorithm, which decomposes evaporation into four components: plant transpiration, interception loss, and other parts (Bai and Liu, 2018 ). It extracts evaporation information from remote sensing data, relying on meteorological and environmental variables (Martens et al., 2017 ). GLEAM uses the correlation between potential evaporation (PET) and soil moisture stress when computing ET and is unique for its low input data requirements (Zhang et al., 2015 ). It employs a simplified Penman-Monteith (PM) equation and Priestley-Taylor (PT) equation (Priestley and Taylor 1972 ), considering factors like microwave vegetation optical depth (VOD), soil root moisture, and aerodynamics (Zhou and Wang, 2015 ). The GLEAM version v3.6b was used in this study. The reasons for the decrease in GLEAM accuracy under extreme climatic conditions may include: GLEAMv3.6b estimates ET using the Priestley and Taylor equation based on surface net radiation and near-surface air temperature (Martens et al., 2017 ). However, this equation doesn't account for vegetation water stress or physiological responses like stomatal closure, particularly under extreme conditions. While GLEAM incorporates vegetation type and soil moisture to convert potential evaporation to actual evaporation via an evaporation stress factor, this factor may be inaccurate under extreme climates. Additionally, GLEAM's assimilation of surface soil moisture for correcting errors is limited due to rapid soil moisture variations under extreme conditions (Yang et al., 2017; Khan et al., 2018a ).  2.3.2 GLDAS_CLSM GLDAS_CLSM (https://ldas.gsfc.nasa.gov/gldas/ ) (Li et al., 2018 ) is a global-scale land surface modeling system. Its fundamental feature lies in the integration of multisource data on land surface and atmosphere with advanced land surface models and data assimilation techniques to provide an accurate simulation of land surface states and flux scenarios (Rodell et al., 2004 ). In this study, we opted for the CLSM model-simulated surface parameter dataset due to its spatial resolution (0.25° × 0.25°) and temporal coverage (1948–2014). Unlike traditional land surface models, CLSM employs watersheds as the basic computational units instead of rectangular grid cells (Koster et al., 2000 ). The reasons for the decrease in CLSM accuracy under extreme climatic conditions may be that CLSM is a land hydrology model, and its performance depends on the model's parameters and configuration. Under extreme climatic conditions, different parameter settings and configurations may be required to more accurately simulate processes such as soil moisture and evapotranspiration. This adds complexity to the accurate estimation of CLSM (Yang et al., 2017; Khan et al., 2018b ).  2.3.3 REA REA (https://data.tpdc.ac.cn/home ) (Lu et al., 2021a ) adopts three widely used model-based ET products, including ERA5, MERRA2, and GLDAS2-Noah reanalysis data. It selects regions with high consistency using the coefficient of variation and fuses them based on the reliability ensemble average method to obtain a long-term global daily evapotranspiration product (REA ET) with a spatial resolution of 0.25° from 1980 to 2017 (Lu et al., 2021a; Lu et al., 2021b ). The dataset has a longitude range of −179.875E∼179.875E and a latitude range of −59.875 N∼89.875 N. The reasons for the decrease in REA accuracy under extreme climatic conditions may include: it merges ERA5, MERRA2, and GLDAS using a reliability ensemble averaging method, which has certain limitations. This study found that GLDAS and ERA5 have notable stability declines under extreme climate conditions. Furthermore, REA relies on GLEAM and flux tower observations for reference and validation (Lu et al., 2017 ). However, under extreme conditions, insufficient or low-quality observational data can make it difficult to accurately assess ET products, creating uncertainty in evaluating their performance.  2.3.4 ERA5 ERA5 (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu ) (Tarek et al., 2020 ) stands as an upgraded global dataset representing the land surface component of the European Reanalysis 5 (ERA5), released by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) in 2021 (Wang et al., 2023c ). At its core is the ECMWF surface model, which flattens the exchange of carbohydrate water in the land surface. ERA5 employs the ECMWF integrated forecasting system (IFS) 4D data assimilation technology, featuring 137 isobaric surfaces at intervals of 0.01 hPa vertically. ERA5 demonstrates superior performance in comparison to the latent heat data from 65 EC instruments worldwide, this improvement can be attributed to enhancements made to the ECMWF surface model (Albergel et al., 2018 ). ERA5 covers the time span from 1979 to 2021, featuring a spatial resolution of 0.01°. The reasons for the decrease in ERA5 accuracy under extreme climatic conditions may be that reanalysis data typically begin with initial conditions and are then subjected to spatiotemporal interpolation using models. If the initial conditions are inaccurate, especially prior to extreme meteorological events, this may result in subsequent inaccuracies. The model may fail to capture the correct ET values. Finally, the annual average ET distribution of four ET products from 2003 to 2014 is shown in Appendix Fig. S2 .   2.4 Models The estimation accuracy of ET products under extreme climatic conditions may experiences a significant decline compared to non-extreme conditions, demonstrating high uncertainty and potentially falling short of the increasing demands of practical applications. To address this issue, the study attempts to use ERA5 meteorological data, which is not constrained by geographical and temporal limitations, as input for the CNN model (with three machine learning models as references). Additionally, ET products are incorporated into this input. So we selected CNN as the deep learning model for estimating ET and used models such as RF, XGB, and GPR as references. Through testing, these models proved to be among the top-performing ones, with their advantage being lower computational costs. 2.4.1 Convolutional neural network CNN belongs to the domain of deep learning and stands out as a neural network type that distinguishes itself from traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) by incorporating convolutional layers or convolutional filters (Goodfellow and Bengio, 2016 ). These layers execute an automatic feature extraction process, crucial for deriving pertinent features from input data, facilitating the mapping of input variables to the desired output. For an in-depth understanding of CNN, LeCun et al. (2015)  and Goodfellow and Bengio (2016)  serve as comprehensive references. In the convolutional layers of this study, there are 100 convolutional filters with a size of 3x3. The stride is 1, padding is set to “same”, and the ReLU activation function is used. The pooling layers are in average pooling mode with a stride of 5. The number of neurons in the fully connected layer is 200. Early stopping is used to define the number of training epochs, with a maximum of 150 epochs and patience set to 10 epochs. The learning rate is 0.001, and the batch size is 512.  2.4.2 Machine learning models RF (Random forest) is an algorithm rooted in decision trees, as introduced by Breiman (2001) . This model operates by combining multiple decision trees, each fitted on different subsets of the training data. While individual trees may have relatively weak learning capabilities, the ensemble of trees collaboratively forms a single model with high predictive power (Huang et al., 2019 ). For an in-depth exploration of RF, Tyralis et al. (2019)  serves as a valuable reference. The number of decision trees is 200. The number of randomly selected features used for each tree construction (mtry) is 12. XGBoost (Extreme Gradient Boosting), recently introduced by Chen and Guestrin (2016) , is another algorithm based on decision trees, similar to RF. The key difference between XGBoost and RF lies in the way they construct the ensemble of decision trees. XGBoost adopts the gradient boosting approach, where each tree created is informed by the information from the trees built previously. For a more comprehensive understanding of XGBoost, refer to Chen and Guestrin (2016) . The number of iterations is 200. The learning rate is 0.01. The subsample ratio is 0.65. The maximum depth of each tree is 15. The L2 regularization parameter is 1. The minimum sum of instance weight needed in a child node is 6. The number of threads is 2. GPR (Gaussian process regression), introduced by Rasmussen and Williams (2005) , is a regression method that employs Bayesian inference to obtain a distribution describing all possible functions of the target variable based on the prior distribution and likelihood of the training data. The prior distribution represents prior knowledge about the target variable and is formulated as a multivariate Gaussian distribution with a mean vector and covariance matrix. For further insights into GPR, consult Rasmussen and Williams (2005)  and Karbasi (2018) . Radial basis function kernel is used for Gaussian process regression. The noise variance is set to 1, and the model convergence tolerance is 0.0005.   2.5 Experimental set up and Pearson correlation coefficient analysis Before commencing the experiments, we conducted Pearson correlation coefficient analysis. In this section, we examined the strength of the correlation between input parameters (ET products and meteorological factors) and FLUXNET ET as shown in Fig. 2  . The correlations of meteorological factors may vary with changing climatic conditions, but Tmax  and Tmin  exhibited strong correlations with observed data across all climatic zones. Therefore, we chose Tmax  and Tmin  as the primary inputs. Among the ET products, we selected the two with the highest correlations as the main inputs (REA and GLEAMv3.6b). The specific experimental settings are provided in Table 2  . In this study, we divided the input combinations into six groups based on the number of meteorological factors, increasing them in order of their correlation strength, from Group (1)  to Group 6. Within each group, we added different ET products to test if the inclusion of ET products as inputs could improve the model's estimation accuracy. As an example, for Group I, the most correlated meteorological factors were Tmax  and Tmin , which served as the basic inputs (Combination 1). We then added REA and GLEAMv3.6b separately as Combination 2 and Combination 3 to examine if these highly correlated products could be interchangeable. Finally, Combination 4 and Combination 5 were set up to investigate if increasing the number of input parameters could enhance model accuracy.  2.6 Statistical indicators In this study, the fitting degree of estimated values to observed values is evaluated using the Pearson correlation coefficient (R2 ). The errors between estimated and observed values are quantified using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE), while the magnitude of overestimation (positive) or underestimation (negative) of the estimated values is measured using Percent Bias (PBias). The optimal values for these metrics are R2  = 1, RMSE=0 mm, MAE=0 mm, and PBias = 0. The specific calculations are detailed in Qian et al. (2023) .   3 Result 3.1 Assessment under extreme climatic conditions Fig. 3   presents Taylor diagrams for four ET products (The specific R2  and RMSE of ET products under extreme and non extreme climate conditions can be found in attachment Table S5 ), illustrating their estimation of FLUXNET ET results under extreme climate and non-extreme conditions. Different colors represent distinct ET products, while various symbols denote different climatic conditions. Pentagrams represent FLUXNET ET, with symbols closer to the pentagrams indicating higher estimation accuracy. For a more detailed description of Taylor diagrams, refer to Taylor (2001) . The Taylor diagram results indicate that under non-extreme conditions, the performance of ET products is commendable, with most products having correlation coefficients (R) concentrated above 0.8. The ratio of standard deviation to FLUXNET ET is in the range of 0.7 to 0.9 mm/d, and RMSE is primarily concentrated within 1.000 mm/d. However, under extreme climatic conditions, the estimation accuracy of all ET products for FLUXNET ET significantly deteriorates. The R for most products are concentrated in the range of 0.6 to 0.7, with the ratio of standard deviation to FLUXNET ET being less than 0.5 mm/d, and RMSE mainly falling between 1.000 and 2.000 mm/d. However, there are notable differences in the performance of different products. Firstly, except for CLSM and ERA5, the performance of the other products is better under non-high VPD conditions than under non-high temperature conditions. For all ET products, the performance under high VPD is better than under high temperature conditions. Specifically, under high VPD, the average decrease in R2  for ET products is approximately 35.4 %, and RMSE increases by 37.8 %. Under high temperature conditions, the average decrease in R2  is around 39.6 %, and RMSE increases by 42.3 %. Additionally, when considering overall performance, REA and GLEAM exhibit relatively good estimation performance, while CLSM shows poorer correlations with FLUXNET ET, and ERA5 maintains good correlation but with larger errors.  3.2 Assessment of different regions and land cover types under extreme climatic conditions To further assess the performance of ET products, this study calculated the R2  and RMSE for these products under high temperature and high VPD conditions in different regions (Fig. 4  a−d). It can be observed that the estimation accuracy of ET products is negatively impacted by high temperature and high VPD in all regions, leading to an increase in errors. Under extreme climatic conditions, GLEAMv3.6b and REA exhibit good correlation and error performance across all three regions, while ERA5 shows more significant errors (with RMSE above 2.0 mm/d). Performance varies across different regions, with the estimation accuracy being highest in the ARA region and poorest in the AM region. Both regions exhibit relatively high errors, with GLEAMv3.6b under extreme climatic conditions having an average RMSE below 1.0 mm/d. The study also computed the performance of ET products under high temperature and high VPD conditions across different land cover types. The results reveal significant limitations on estimation accuracy under extreme climatic conditions. In terms of R2  (Fig. 4 e−f), the performance patterns under high temperature and high VPD are quite similar. CLSM and MOD16A2 exhibit the lowest R2  under both extreme climatic conditions, with CLSM showing the largest decline under high temperature (R2  decreases by 0.368), and REA experiencing the most severe decline in correlation under high VPD (R2  decreases by 0.315). On the other hand, under high temperature and high VPD, ET products perform relatively well under SAV and WSA land cover types, while their performance is generally poor under other land cover types. Moreover, there is a significant decline in performance under MF and WET land cover types (R2  decreases are concentrated around 0.4). Regarding RMSE (Fig. 4 g−h), ERA5 exhibits the highest RMSE under both extreme climatic conditions, and the magnitude of error increase is the largest (RMSE increase is concentrated around 0.6 mm/d). Except for ERA5, CLSM shows the largest increase in accuracy under high temperature conditions (RMSE increases by 0.417 mm/d), and REA has the largest increase in error under high VPD conditions (RMSE increases by 0.334 mm/d). On the other hand, under high temperature and high VPD, ET products also demonstrate relatively good error performance under SAV and WSA, while experiencing a significant decline in accuracy under CRO and GRA land cover types (RMSE increases ranging from 0.407 to 0.768 mm/d). Finally, the study calculated the performance of ET products under different climate types under high temperature and high VPD conditions (Fig. 4 i−l). Overall, under extreme conditions, ET products perform relatively poorly in Cwa and Df, while showing relatively good performance in AW and Csa. Under non-extreme conditions, ET products exhibit poor performance in Bwh and Df, and good performance in Csa and Dsb. Additionally, the largest decline in accuracy for ET products occurs in Cf, Dw, and Df.  3.3 Performance of deep learning under overall climatic conditions The performance of four ET products and four models under various input combinations is detailed in Table 3   and Table 4  , respectively. From the table, it can be observed that when ET products are used as inputs for the machine learning model, there is a significant improvement in estimation accuracy compared to using only meteorological data as input. Moreover, CNN outperforms the other three machine learning models in most input combinations, and the performance gap between CNN and the three machine learning models widens with the increase in input meteorological parameters. Additionally, Random Forest (RF) is the best-performing model among the three machine learning models. The result found that as the number of input parameters increases, the estimation accuracy of all models improves. On one hand, when the meteorological parameters transition from 1 (GⅠ) to 2 (GⅡ) (i.e., adding parameter Rs ), the improvement in accuracy is most significant (average increase in R2  by 13.2 %, average decrease in RMSE by 14.88 mm/d). This improvement diminishes with the addition of more meteorological inputs, and when the model includes SMC and WS, the improvement in model accuracy becomes quite limited. On the other hand, when REA and GLEAMv3.6b are added on top of meteorological data, the latter's performance is slightly better in most cases. When all eight meteorological factors and four products are used as inputs, CNN achieves its highest estimation accuracy (R2  = 0.924, RMSE=0.323 mm/d). Compared to the case where only meteorological data is used as input (R2  = 0.888, RMSE=0.369 mm/d, MAE=0.224 mm/d), the addition of ET products leads to a significant improvement. Furthermore, compared to the well-performing products REA and GLEAMv3.6b, R2  increases by 39.3 %, and RMSE decreases by 62.1 %. Furthermore, the distribution of PBias for the four models across different sites can be found in attachment Fig. S3 . The results indicate that the CNN model exhibits a relatively balanced distribution of overestimation and underestimation at most sites, with PBias ranging within −9% to 9 %. In contrast, the three machine learning (ML) models predominantly display underestimation at most sites, and this tendency is more pronounced in higher latitude regions, where PBias may exceed −15 %. This study also discusses the contribution of each input parameter under the optimal input combination C30 in the CNN to the final estimation results (See details in attachment Fig. S4 ).
