Our study highlights the importance of ongoing monitoring and evaluation to ensure the long-term effects of restoration efforts and the sustained success of peatland rewetting projects. Furthermore, a crucial aspect to follow up in rewetting projects is vegetation dynamics. Shuttleworth et al. (2019)  demonstrated in their study that vegetation, due to its surface roughness, can significantly influence peatland runoff response. Degradation, such as drainage, has a direct impact on vegetation dynamics; therefore, vegetation recovery and changes are important variables to consider in assessing long-term consequences and planning future studies. The findings of this study can be utilized to support and guide decision-makers by valuable insights into the anticipated initial ecosystem responses in the context of restoring wetlands in boreal climates following rewetting activities. This is particularly important in Sweden, where such information is generally lacking.   5 Conclusions In our study of a Swedish boreal peatland, we investigated the impact of rewetting on the GWL and runoff dynamics during ice- and snow-free periods. Using two nearby natural peatlands as controls, we observed significant positive effects on the hydrological functioning of the rewetted site. Rewetting significantly shifted the GWL position toward the ground surface, resulting in a more stable GWL condition that more closely resembled that of the control sites. The study also highlighted a substantial increase in baseflow at the rewetted site, particularly during low-flow periods. Moreover, rewetting appeared to enhance water storage and hydrological buffer capacity, as indicated by a higher GWL threshold for runoff initiation. Additionally, there was a reduction in the runoff coefficient, generally considered a good indicator of peatland water storage and hydrological buffer capacity, especially during wet periods.
1 Introduction Flooding is one of the most frequent and disastrous natural hazards that can cause catastrophic impacts on infrastructure and human societies. In recent years, in the context of global warming, severe weather events such as tsunamis, storm surges, and extreme rainfall have occurred frequently (Ekwueme, 2022; Faye, 2022; Gayaz et al., 2019 ). The resulting extreme flood disasters are characterized by strong suddenness, large peak heights, and wide damage areas. (Francesco et al., 2016; Russo et al., 2021 ). In 2020, China suffered a severe flood disaster. According to statistics, floods across the country in July 2020 caused 38.17 million people to be affected, 27,000 houses collapsed, 38.68 million hectares of crops were affected, and direct economic losses were 109.74 billion yuan. These severe water conditions have significantly endangered lives and properties, inflicting substantial economic losses (Pan and Liu, 2019; Demirdjian et al., 2018 ). In the domain of water disaster management, the significance of numerical model cannot be overstated, serving as a key tool for swiftly acquiring accurate disaster information. It plays a crucial role in providing theoretical support for flood control decision-making, early warnings, and forecasting (Hu et al., 2017; Jean et al., 2017 ). Despite the accuracy achieved by current hydrodynamic numerical models, computational efficiency remains a notable challenge. The traditional approach of employing a global time-stepping scheme (GTS) becomes inefficient when refining only small areas within the computational domain, leading to increased computational effort (Ni et al., 2020 ). In previous attempts, Sanders (2008)  applied the local time-stepping method (LTS) to solve 2D equations, which is based on the idea of using its own time stepping to advance each cell to bring it closer to its maximum allowable value, and the simulated speed of was improved to a certain extent; Hu et al. (2019)  applied the local time-stepping method (LTS) to unstructured grids. These studies have shown promise in improving simulation speed. However, these models were limited to CPU calculations, leaving room for further enhancement in efficiency. Combining the local time stepping approach with the GPU parallel computing method maybe is a good attempt. In addition, the application to flood simulations over complex areas with non-uniform grids remains limited and few studies have focused on implementing local time-stepping algorithms on non-uniform grids. The existing hydrodynamic numerical model in this study shows a certain accuracy, but the computational efficiency has the potential to be further improved. In order to overcome the limitations of current numerical hydrodynamic models, this study aims to address the existing gap in computational efficiency by proposing a novel approach. The focus is to establish a two-dimensional hydrodynamic numerical model based on GPU acceleration, local time stepping method and non-uniform grid method, and maximize computational efficiency by integrating these advanced methods. This comprehensive integration is novel, offering a holistic approach to address the complexities of flood prediction. In addition, bridging these aspects is essential to achieving computational efficiency in hydrodynamic models, particularly for large-scale flood simulations in complex terrains. The proposed model is applied to the simulation of basin flood and urban inundation with complex terrain, compared with the traditional prediction models in previous studies, the model proposed in this study greatly improves the computational efficiency while ensuring accuracy, and is more suitable for practical applications. Especially in simulating urban inundation of complex land use types, it represents a unique contribution to the field. The subsequent sections of the paper are organized as follows. Section 2  introduces the method of generating the non-uniform grid, and describes the efficient GPU implementation of the local time stepping scheme based on the non-uniform grid and the second-order FVM format. In Section 3 , the proposed local time stepping (LTS) model based on non-uniform grid is applied to basin flood cases. This paper evaluates the accuracy and efficiency of the model in predicting flood scenarios through comparison with measured data. Comparative analyses of computational efficiency and accuracy against different models are presented. Section 4  applies the model to actual large-scale urban areas with complex terrain to predict urban floods. By predicting the distribution of water accumulation points and the extent of flooding at different times, researchers can identify effective measures to reduce flood risks and improve the area's resilience. Finally, brief conclusions are drawn in Section 5 .  2 Methodology 2.1 Non-uniform grid optimization method The division of grids significantly impacts the calculational accuracy of the hydrodynamic model. In updating flow variables, the commonly employed methods for computational time stepping include global time step and local time step approaches. For grid cells of equal size, the global time step algorithm represents the conventional method for temporal integration and stands as the most prevalent stepping technique currently utilized. The fundamental principle behind this approach involves advancing the solutions of all cells to the same time point, ensuring stability across all computational grid cells, thereby effecting a series of temporal updates to resolve relevant phenomena. The implementation of the global time step method involves selecting the minimum time step size among all grid cells as the time step for the entire computational domain to maintain numerical stability in explicit schemes. This primarily relies on controlling the time step size through the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) condition.(26) Δ t n  = CFLmin Δ x i   |  u i  | +  g h i      , Δ y i   |  v i  | +  g h i             where: h i    is the water depth, Δ x i     and Δ y i     are the size of grid cell i  in the x and y directions, respectively. u i    and v i    are the velocity components along the x and y directions, respectively. Compared to the global time step method, the concept of the local time step method entails individual grid cells within the computational domain utilizing their own permissible time steps. Consequently, integration of different cells occurs at distinct time points. This strategy involves employing the maximum stable time step for each cell, rather than a global value, theoretically resulting in improved efficiency and reduced computational time. First, we consider a set of homogeneous conservation laws to briefly illustrate the concept of local time stepping. For any given cell i , the update from time level n  to n  + 1 can be written as:(27) U i n + 1   = U i n + 1   - Δ t  Δ x i    F i + 1 / 2  n  - F i - 1 / 2  n          When using the global time stepping approach, Δt is calculated based on the stability criterion and the same value is used throughout the grid. The GPU is mainly responsible for graphics-related rendering tasks. As people's requirements for the fidelity of graphics display continue to increase, GPUs begin to support more and more complex calculations. Due to the high degree of parallelism in graphics, GPUs increase processing power and memory bandwidth by adding parallel processing units and memory control units. In terms of single-precision floating-point processing, mainstream capabilities can reach about 10 times that of the same period (Xia and Liang, 2016 ). In order to improve the computational efficiency of the model, on the basis of non-uniform meshing technology and GTS method, this study uses GPU parallel computing technology to run the solved 2D shallow water equations on the GPU, and runs variable initialization on the CPU. Fig. 6   is a flowchart of GPU calculation.(1) Allocate memory space on the host side using the function malloc (), and allocate graphics memory space on the GPU using the function cudaMalloc (). The input data is read and stored in the CPU memory, and variable initialization is performed on the CPU.  (2) Copy the initialization data from the CPU to the GPU through the function cudaMemcpy ().  (3) Combining with CUDA language, different Kernel functions are executed on GPU to perform corresponding numerical calculations, including flux calculation, spatial second-order accuracy reconstruction of variables, processing calculation of wet and dry interfaces, boundary calculation. The synchronization function cudaDeviceSynchronize () is used to ensure that the previous kernel function is executed before the next kernel function is executed in sequence. Therefore, when some grids participate in the calculation, other grids need to wait.  (4) A Kernel function can call many independent thread blocks, each composed of many threads. Therefore, when each Kernel function is started, a large number of threads can be started to run GPU codes, achieving large-scale parallelization of computation through thread management. In this article, 64 thread blocks are allocated for each Kernel function, and 64 threads are allocated for each thread block. A total of 4096 threads participate in the calculation of each Kernel function.  (5) After all Kernel functions complete the calculation in sequence, the results are copied to the host side to update the calculation results. If the iteration is not completed, the updated data of the host side is transmitted to the device side for calculation until the end of the iteration.  (6) After the calculation is completed, the calculated value is transferred to the CPU for output, and the memory of the host side and the device side is released respectively.       3 Simulation of flood evolution process 3.1 Dam-break flood evolution of three humps The flood evolution process of three humps proposed by Kawahara and Umetsu (1986)  was used to test the ability of the proposed model to simulate the complex alternating dry and wet processes. At the same time, the case can also reflect the ability of the model to deal with complex terrain and the stability of the model. The hydrodynamic model is used to simulate the process of flood rising and retreating between three humps after the dam break at t = 0 s. During the propagation of dam break waves, the phenomenon of inundation and flow around hump will appear when encountering a hump, with obvious processes of rising and retreating water. The computational domain is a rectangular area with 75 m × 30 m, which is discretized into 150 × 60 regular square grids with a grid size of 0.5 m. There are two humps of 1 m at X =30 m and one hump of 3 m at X =47.5 m. The dam is located at x  = 16 m, and the dam width is ignored, and the dam willl collapse instantaneously when t = 0 s. The definition of the bottom elevation is determined by the following formula and is shown in Fig. 7  .(36) z b  x , y    = m a x 0   1 - 0.125 x - 30    2  + x - 6    2       1 - 0.125 x - 30    2  + x - 24    2       3 - 0.3 x - 47.5    2  + x - 15    2                Considering that the non-uniform grid used in the proposed model is generated based on the initial uniform grid, grid sensitivity analysis is first conducted on the initial uniform grid. Because of the small number of grids in the calculation domain, two conditions are set, that is high density grid (0.5 m resolution, a total of 9000 cells) and low density grid (2.5 m resolution, a total of 360 cells). Since there is no measured data for this case, this study determines the mesh scale by observing the simulation results of different mesh densities. From the comparison of modeled results at different grid scales (Fig. 8  ), it can be seen that compared to high-density grid, the results of low-density grid are relatively poor, with low accuracy, and the contour shape of the water flow is relatively fuzzy, which cannot better reflect the actual situation. In addition, and the simulated time of the two grids is similar is close. Therefore, in order to improve the calculation accuracy of the uniform grid model and the subsequent local time stepping model based on the non-uniform grid, the uniform grid scale adopts high-density grid (0.5 m grid accuracy). Then, the non-uniform grid is divided based on the uniform grid, and two levels of thresholds are defined. If the grid elevation gradient change in the area is greater than grcr 1, the grid will be refined for the first time; if it is greater than grcr 2, the second level of grid refinement will be performed. The obtained non-uniform grid situation is as shown in Fig. 9  , with the total grid cells being 3216. At first, the calculation domain is enclosed by wall boundaries, and the local time step (LTS) model based on non-uniform grid is used to simulate the process of flood evolution for 300 s after the dam broke (Fig. 10  ). From Fig. 10 , it can be seen that when t = 1 s, the flood flows downstream after the dam broke; when t = 2 s, the flood first inundates two small humps; when t = 5 s, the two small humps are completely submerged by the flood, the flood mainly rushes to the large humps from the middle gap and the front of the flood reaches the large hump. When t = 12 s, the flood does not inundate the large hump, but flows from both sides and spread to the downstream, with obvious circumfluence phenomenon. When t = 20 s and 24 s, the flood inundates the whole pool, and the water is blocked by the bottom and reflected back to the large hump. Finally, due to the interaction between the dam break flood and the river bed, and the resistance of the bottom, the water tends to be static. Since the research area is strictly symmetrical about y = 15 m and the water depths of 1 s to 20 s (Fig. 10 ) have a certain symmetrical relationship. Since the research area is strictly symmetrical about y = 15 m, it can be inferred that the results at any time should remain symmetric with respect to y = 15 m. As can be seen from the water depth (t = 2–20 s) in Fig. 10 , the water depth is distributed symmetrically. Therefore, the simulation results are consistent with the physical law. This case proves that the proposed local time stepping (LTS) model can effectively capture the alternating phenomenon of dry and wet interfaces under different hump effects. In addition, the initial water volume is 900 m3 , and at the end of the calculation, the water volume is 899.9975 m3 , the relative error of mass is (900–899.9975)/900 = 0.0003 %, the proposed model can well satisfy the mass conservation law of water volume. Therefore, within the discretization error, it means that the multi-time scale non-uniform grid based on local time stepping (LTS) is conserved and has certain stability. In addition, the model based on the uniform grid, the non-uniform grid model based on the global time stepping scheme (GTS) are also used to simulate the same flood process. Fig. 11   shows the water depth simulation of different models at different times. From the water depths at different times simulated by different models, it can be seen that the trend of flood evolution simulated by three models is similar. In order to further verify the simulation accuracy of the multi-time model, different models were compared by analyzing the water level changes at three points that are more sensitive to hydraulic elements. The following figures and tables show the simulated water levels of different models at the P1, P2 and P3 (Fig. 4 ). Fig. 12   and Table 1   show that the proposed model is in good agreement with the simulated water level of the traditional uniform grid model and the global time stepping (GTS) model. The RMSE of the LTS model and the uniform grid model at points: P1, P2, P3 are 6.2 %, 7.3 %, 0.9 %, respectively, and the average value of RMSE is 4.8 %; The RMSE of the LTS model and the GTS model at points: P1, P2, P3 are 3.8 %, 5.3 %, 1.6 %, respectively, and the average value of RMSE is 3.6 %. Therefore, the proposed local time stepping (LTS) model can ensure certain simulation accuracy, it can effectively simulate the complex flow process and is suitable for simulating the evolution and inundation of dam break flood. In terms of computing efficiency, the uniform grid model consumes 27 s, while the global time stepping (GTS) model consumes 10 s and the local time stepping (LTS) model needs 6 s. Therefore, the proposed model has higher computational efficiency, its efficiency is about 4.5 times that of the uniform grid model and 1.7 times that of the global time stepping (GTS) model.  3.2 Flood evolution of Toce In order to further verify the ability and stability of the proposed local time stepping model (LTS) based on non-uniform grid to handle unsteady flow under two-dimensional complex terrain, this paper selects Toce as the study area to simulate the process of the flood evolution, given its certain representativeness. The physical model of this dam-break test was built in ENEL (Italy) to represent a 5 km reach of the Toce River in the Northern Alps in Italy. The dam-break flow was triggered by sudden release of flood water from an upstream inflow tank. This study area is about 50 m × 10 m (Fig. 13  (b)), and the resolution of the initial uniform grid is 0.05 m, with a total of about 210,000 square cells. After being divided into non-uniform grids, the total number of non-uniform grids is 110,745 (Fig. 13 (c)). The input conditions of the proposed model include terrain data (Fig. 13 (c)), inflow data (Fig. 14  (a)), and Manning data. The Manning n  is 0.0162 s/m1/3 . The upstream is set as the inflow boundary, the downstream is the outflow open boundary, and others are the closed boundary. The proposed GPU-accelerated and local time stepping model (LTS) based on non-uniform grid are used to simulate the process of flood evolution (Fig. 14 (b)). It can be seen from the dam break flood process that the dam began to break after t = 10 s. After the dam broke, the floodwater rushed downstream through the low-lying valley. The water flow were very fast and almost filled the river channel at t = 120 s. In addition, in order to verify the simulated accuracy of the proposed model, this paper also employs both the uniform grid model and the non-uniform grid model based on global time stepping algorithm to simulate the process of flood evolution in this area (Fig. 15  ), and compares the simulated results of different models with the measured values. Fig. 15  shows that the water depth simulated by the different models are similar. However, compared with the other models, the flood process simulated by the proposed model is slower. To further analyze the simulated accuracy, three points with measured data are selected. Fig. 16   and Table 2   show the simulated water levels and measured data at different points. It can be observed that the trend of water level simulated by the proposed model is similar to the measured value and other models. The RMSE of the proposed model and the measured value at different points (P4, P9, P21) are 0.8 %, 0.9 %, 1.5 %, respectively; The RMSE of the proposed model and the uniform grid model at different points (P4, P9, P21) are 0.5 %, 0.9 %, 1.7 %, respectively; The RMSE of the proposed model and the non-uniform grid model based on global time stepping algorithm at different points (P4, P9, P21) are 0.4 %, 1.0 %, 1.2 %, respectively. Therefore, the simulated results of the local time stepping and non-uniform grid model align well with the measured values and the simulated water levels of other models. The proposed model demonstrates excellent solution accuracy and is suitable for simulating the process of flood evolution. Additionally, the proposed local time stepping algorithm model based on non-uniform grid demonstrates enhanced computational efficiency. The simulation of the flood evolution takes 145 s using the uniform grid model and 95 s using the global time stepping (GTS) model. In contrast, it only 32 s when calculated with the proposed model, achieving an efficiency approximately 3 times that of the global time stepping (GTS) model and 5 times that of the uniform grid model. Therefore, the GPU-accelerated lobal time stepping (LTS) model based on non-uniform grid significantly enhances computational efficiency while ensuring simulated accuracy. Compared with other models, it is more suitable for simulating actual flood evolution processes.  3.3 Dam-break flood evolution of Malpasset In order to test the performance of the proposed model in simulating water flow in actual terrains, this paper selects an actual complex terrain as the study area to simulate the process of dam-break flood evolution. The dam is located on the Rhine River in France and is located 14 km away from the sea entrance. Due to multiple heavy rainfall events, water levels rose rapidly, leading to the dam's collapse in 1959. The process of dam-break was rapid, and in this study, dam-break is considered instantaneous, with a primary focus on analyzing the process of flood evolution after dam-break. The computational domain covers an area of approximately 18 km × 9 km, with the initial uniform grid resolution of 10 m, totaling approximately 1.58 million square grid cells (Fig. 17  (a)). Three key points (P1, P2, P3) are strategically positioned within the computational domain, guided by considerations such as river channel bends and significant hydraulic influences, to analyze the trend of water level changes. Utilizing the non-uniform grid method to divide the initial grid, refining regions with pronounced changes in terrain and coarsening areas relatively insensitive to water level variations. Finally, approximately 0.8 million non-uniform grid cells are obtained for the entire study area (Fig. 17 (b)). Different models are used to simulate the process of flood evolution for 3000 s, respectively. The upstream is set as the water level boundary condition, the downstream is the outflow open boundary, and other boundaries are closed. The upstream water level is 100 m, and the downstream water level is 0. The Manning n  is 0.033 s/m1/3  (Cao et al., 2019 ). The accuracy of the proposed GPU-accelerated local time stepping model based on non-uniform grid is analyzed by comparing simulation results with other models (Fig. 18  ). From Fig. 18  and Table 3  , we can see that the trend of water level change simulated by the proposed model is similar to other models. The R2  of the proposed local time stepping model (LTS) model and the uniform grid model at points (P1, P2, P3) are 0.91, 0.95, 0.95, respectively; the R2  of the proposed local time stepping model (LTS) model and the global time stepping (GTS) model at points (P1, P2, P3) are 0.92, 0.97, 0.95, respectively. Therefore, the model shows good capabilities in actual flood with complex terrain. The process of flood evolution simulated by the proposed model is as follows: It can be seen from Fig. 19   that the water flow rapidly evolves downstream. When t = 100 s, the flood begins to flow through the long and narrow river channel, when t = 1500 s, the flood reaches the downstream plain., when t = 2500 s, the flood has submerged basically most of the downstream area. In addition, the uniform grid model and the non-uniform grid model based on global time stepping algorithm need 775 s and 330 s respectively to simulate the flood evolution process for 3000 s. In contrast, the proposed model only needs 120 s. The computational efficiency of the proposed model is 6.5 times that of the uniform grid model and 2.8 times that of the non-uniform grid model based on global time stepping algorithm. Therefore, the proposed model greatly improves the calculational efficiency under the combined action of the non-uniform grid method, the local time stepping algorithm and the GPU accelerated parallel method, while ensuring the simulated accuracy. It is more suitable for simulation of actual large-scale flood evolution processes.   4 Simulation of urban inundation process 4.1 Overview of the study area In this study, the paper selects the core of Guyuan city in China as the study area to simulate the urban inundation. The study area is situated in the semiarid region of the Loess Plateau, characterized by various land-use types. Rainfall is unevenly distributed throughout the year, with a concentration in July and September, resulting in frequent urban flood disasters. Therefore, selecting this area for urban flood research is representative. The digital elevation map data is obtained by scanning with a drone. After processing the point cloud data, the high-precision terrain with a resolution of 1 m and a total of 3.65 million initial square grid cells can be obtained (Fig. 20  ).  4.2 Calculational conditions of the model In order to explore the inundation situation of the study area under the extreme rainstorm condition, this paper selected the return period of 50-year design rainfall as the rainfall file, calculated it using the rainstorm intensity formula, and obtained the rainfall process through the Chicago Rainfall Pattern Generator (Fig. 21  ). Considering that the study area is very broad and the number of the initial square grid cells is large, we use the non-uniform grid to simulate the process of inundation. For different land use types, two thresholds are established: grcr 1, grcr 2. For grassland, bare land and road, all situated at relatively low elevations, the thresholds are set as follows: grcr 1_grassland = grcr 1_bare land = grcr 1_road, and grcr 2_grassland = grcr 2_bare land = grcr 2_road. For woodland and residential land, the thresholds are defined as follows: grcr 1_woodland = grcr 1_residential land, and grcr 2_woodland = grcr 2_residential land. If the gradient change of the grid is greater than grcr 1, the gird will be coarsened for the first time; if it is greater than grcr 2, the grid will be coarsened for the second time. Compared to the traditional hydrodynamic numerical model, although the proposed model can improve the efficiency, non-uniform grids divided based on certain situations may not be optimal. In order to balance the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed model, different non-uniform grid divisions are obtained by constantly changing the thresholds. Table 4   shows the different non-uniform grid divisions of the study area under the conditions of changing the thresholds (Table 5  ).  4.3 Analysis of simulation results To achieve optimization of threshold division, the proposed local time stepping algorithm model is employed to simulate urban inundation under various non-uniform grid divisions. In addition, the simulation results are compared with the simulation results based on the uniform grid model. The simulated results of main inundation points under different non-uniform grid divisions are shown in the tables below. Fig. 22   shows the relationship curve between the average error of the inundation area and the simulation time. It can be seen that with the increase of the number of non-uniform grid cells, the simulation time of the proposed local time stepping (LTS) model is continuously increasing and the calculation efficiency is continuously decreasing. Compared with the results of the uniform grid model, the average error of the inundation area at major inundation points (4 inundation points) is decreasing, that is, the calculation accuracy of the model is gradually improving at the same time. Furthermore, prior to reaching the Eth threshold condition, the trends of the two curves exhibit faster changes, leading to continued increase in simulation time, albeit with a decrease in the average error of the inundation area. Following the Eth threshold condition, the changes in the two curves become slower, and they intersect near the Eth threshold condition. Therefore, the Eth threshold condition is approximately the optimal value, considering that the average topographic gradient changes of the first group of land use types (relatively low elevation) and the second group of land use types (relatively high elevation) are 0.73 and 1.10, respectively, so when the threshold value is 32 %–48 % of the average topographic gradient change in the area, the computational accuracy and efficiency of the multi-time scale model are optimized near this threshold. In this case, the inundation situation is as shown in Fig. 23  . From the comparison of inundation scenarios, it is evident that the locations of inundation simulated by the local time stepping model are relatively consistent with the actual situation, matching at four locations. In this case, compared with the uniform grid model, the average error of inundation area is about 12.74 %, and the efficiency is about 4.67 times that of the former. The complete urban inundation process in the study area is as shown in Fig.24  . The model was used to simulate the waterlogging process for a total of 14400 s. It can be seen from the predicted urban flooding process that as rainfall intensity increases, water accumulation begins to increase. When t = 5400 s, the water accumulation situation is the most serious, mainly concentrated on roads and residential areas. Then, as the intensity of rainfall decreases and the effect of soil infiltration occurs, the accumulated water gradually decreases. The flood prediction model proposed in this study can rapidly and accurately forecast the urban inundation process, aligning closely with actual conditions. It can anticipate the distribution of inundation points in urban areas at different times, the area and depth of waterlogging at various points, as well as the timing of flood arrival and recession. The introduction of the new urban flood prediction model plays a pivotal role in flood prevention and disaster mitigation efforts. By accurately forecasting flood events, this model equips city authorities and emergency management agencies with essential information to implement timely and effective flood preparedness measures. This proactive approach not only helps minimize property damage and economic losses but also safeguards human lives by enabling early evacuation planning and emergency response coordination.   5 Conclusions With the increasing occurrence of extreme rainstorms triggered by global climate change, floods have inflicted significant losses on human society. Efficient and accurate prediction of flood processes can provide emergency management agencies with timely information to implement necessary response measures, thereby minimizing losses to the greatest extent possible. This paper proposes the local time stepping scheme (LTS) and GPU-accelerated model based on non-uniform grid to efficiently predict flood process. The main findings are as follows.1) The proposed local time stepping scheme (LTS) and GPU-accelerated model can increase the computational efficiency through the non-uniform grid method, local time stepping scheme and GPU parallel computing technology. A constant water flow is considered to test the calculation accuracy of the model and the effectiveness of the dynamic change between wet and dry boundary treatments. The results show that it can capture the alternating change process at the dry-wet interface, and no obvious numerical diffusion is found, which verifies the stability of the model.  2) The proposed model is applied to the prediction of flood evolution processes. The results show that the trend of the flood evolution simulated by the proposed model is similar to those simulated by other models and observed values. The computational efficiency is 5–7 times that of the uniform grid model and 2–3 times that of the traditional non-uniform model based on global time stepping method. Therefore, the proposed local time stepping (LTS) method and GPU-accelerated model can greatly improve the calculation efficiency of the model while ensuring the accuracy of the simulation. It holds greater promise for simulating flood processes and offers significant value in enhancing large-scale shallow water flow simulations.  3) In recent years, floods caused by climate change such as extreme weather have had a huge impact on society. In addition, in order to further validate the ability of the proposed model in simulating water flow in two-dimensional complex terrains, this study applies the model to the simulation of urban inundation in a real large-scale area with complex land use types. The results show that it can predict the urban inundation situation and waterlogging point distribution more efficiently, which provides technical support for strengthening joint prevention and control of flood disasters. Through threshold sensitivity analysis, the optimal value of threshold division is found, which provides reference for the future threshold value in urban area. When the threshold value is 32 %–48 % of the average topographic gradient change in the area, the computational accuracy and efficiency of the proposed model are optimized. At this time, the average error of the inundation area is about 12.74 %, and the proposed model can be 4.67 times faster than the conventional GPU-accelerated hydrodynamic model. It has greater application prospects in actual large-scale urban inundation prediction.    In flood prediction, computational accuracy and efficiency are crucial. This paper establishes the local time stepping (LTS) and GPU-accelerated model, which enhances computational efficiency through the utilization of non-uniform grid method, the local time stepping scheme and GPU parallel computing technology. By integrating these approaches, the model significantly improves calculation efficiency while maintaining simulation accuracy. Consequently, the proposed model demonstrates promising potential for simulating flood processes and holds value in enhancing large-scale flood simulations. It can quickly predict extreme flood process, providing the basis for formulating disaster reduction and relief plans for exceeding standard floods. Additionally, the implementation of the model underscores a commitment to proactive risk management strategies, fostering resilience against the increasing threat of urban flooding exacerbated by climate change.
1 Introduction As a common geological event in humid karst regions around the world, floods generally submerge farmland, villages, and industrial and mining establishments, causing large reductions in crop yield, traffic congestion, and environmental pollution (Blackstock et al., 1993; Prohic et al., 1998; PEI, 2001; López-Chicano, 2002; Bonacci et al., 2006; Skeefington and Scott, 2008; Bailly-Comte et al., 2010; De Luca et al., 2013 ). Due to the unique underground hydrological setting (sinkholes, cracks, and subterranean streams) and its connection to surface rivers, drainage in karst depressions is often weakened by the backwater effect of subsurface rivers when large-scale rainstorms occur. In addition, the sediment from soil erosion and litter from hillslopes can clog the sinkholes and cracks in karst depressions, increasing the threat of flooding (Li et al., 2019c ). Southwest China contains one of the largest contiguous karst areas in the world (Fig. 1  a). The most typical landscape found in southwest China is the peak-cluster depressions of similar dimensions with overlapping steep hills and ridges surrounding a flat center (Feng et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019c ). According to the disaster statistics of the Guangxi Civil Affairs Bureau, over the past four years (2015–2018), a total of 37 floods occurred in this region with one large-scale flood disaster each year. These floods caused about a total of $1.51 billion of direct economic losses, 34.3 % of which was agriculture-related losses [https://www.gxmzt.gov.cn ]. However, the increasing impact of global warming may increase the risk of extreme rainfall events in Southwest China (Easterling et al., 2000; Liu et al., 2014; Westra et al., 2014; Pendergrass and Knutti, 2018 ). As a result, the increasing floods will further affect the agricultural systems in this region. Meanwhile, other countries suffer from the same problems such as Northern Italy, South Spain and Croatia (López-Chicano, 2002; Bonacci et al., 2006; De Luca et al., 2013 ). Therefore, it is of utmost importance to understand how karst agriculture systems respond to extreme rainfall events. Humid regions of Southwest China have 55 underdeveloped and overpopulated ethnic minorities (Xia, 2008; Zhang et al., 2015 ). In past years, economic development and population growth have led to unfavorable land use practices such as deforestation, over-grazing, and farming in this region, especially on hillslopes with shallow soil layers (Li et al., 2019c ). These detrimental land use practices coupled with steep slopes and abundant rainfall have led to severe soil erosion (Li et al., 2019c ). After 1999, the “Grain for Green” project was implemented to help achieve sustainable development of the socio-economic-environment with a majority of the arable areas on hillslopes abandoned (Yang et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019a ). For example, Maize (Zea mays ), a crop that is more disruptive to the soil (Rodenburg et al., 2020 ), is prohibited from being planted in peak-cluster, while Napier grass (Pennisetum purpureum ), an environmentally friendly crop, can still be planted on slower slopes. This led to depressions becoming the main arable areas as they were a source of fertile soils in Southwest China. However, the low location and flat terrain in the karst depression made farming systems highly susceptible to flooding. With respect to plant responses to flooding, numerous studies have been conducted around the world, particularly in prone-flood areas such as riparian zones, river marginal wetland environments, and flood plains. Previous studies have found that species richness and composition were impacted by flooding (Violle et al., 2011; Fischer et al., 2016 ). Specifically, species richness displayed a bell-shaped response to disturbance (i.e., water depthmax ), and longer durations of flooding lowered species richness and the biomass of terrestrial species (Violle et al., 2011 ). Other studies have demonstrated how plants respond and adapt to floods through their physiological and ecological functions. It was discovered that plants could maintain oxygen exchange (for example, shoot elongation, aerenchyma production, and plant height) to increase their tolerance to flooding, therefore mitigating this process (Dı́az and Cabido, 2001; Wright et al., 2017 ). They can also remain dormant until the water has receded and then recover (Striker et al., 2012 ). However, the plant responses to flooding were still unclear in karst depressions where are susceptible to extreme rainfall (Tockner, 2008; Li et al., 2019c ). The main crops of agriculture system in karst peak-cluster depressions are Napier grass and Maize. Most previous studies had focus on analyzing the responses of individual species under controlled static flooding conditions and plant communities under field conditions (Beumer et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2009; Vashisht et al., 2011; Violle et al., 2011; Garssen et al., 2015 ). Few studies were conducted to quantify individual species' response to natural flooding in field conditions. Therefore, the restructuring of farming systems by the residents to adapt to the future flooding is lack of scientific support. The 2016-floods in Guangxi Autonomous Region affected 55 counties (districts) in 10 cities and caused 54,250 ha of crops destroyed and 273.3 million yuan of agricultural losses. Along the line from Mulian Demonstration Base to Bagong town within 85 km (Fig. 1 b), 90.5 % of depressions were flooded except for 2 depressions with higher elevations. Understanding the characteristics of flood resistance within an agricultural ecosystem is essential for the planning of agricultural structures in karst depressions for mitigation against floods. By investigating and assessing the influence of the 2016-flooding on agricultural ecosystems, this study therefore aimed to explore: (1) How do current farming systems respond to flooding status? (2) What are the implications for agriculture plans in subtropical humid karst peak-cluster depressions?  2 Materials and methods The study area (24°54–24°55′N, 107°56–107°57′E) is a typical karst peak-cluster depression in Southwest China (Fig. 1 c-f) (Zhang et al., 2019 ). The main crops within the study area are Napier grass and Maize. Napier grass is suitable for cattle, rabbits, pigs, fish, and other animals. It has been planted on more than 500 km2  in Southern China in recent years (Liu, 2006 ). The total Maize planting area in Southwest China was 26,400 km2  by 2009 (PRC Ministry of Agriculture, 2010). This catchment covers 1.686 km2  with elevation ranging from 375 to 816 m above sea level and contains 0.176 km2  of farmland mainly located in the depression. Soils are developed from limestone, with some outcropping rocks distributed sporadically (Chen et al., 2011a ). The climate of the catchment is a subtropical, mountainous monsoon climate, with rain and heat occurring simultaneously. The mean annual temperature and precipitation are 15.1 ℃ and 1638 mm, respectively (Li et al., 2019b ). However, rainfall is not evenly distributed, with May to September occupying 70–80 % of the total annual rainfall (Li et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019 ). Flood events predominantly occur during the main growing season. 2.1 Rainfall frequency analysis Long-term rainfall of 1989–2018 was obtained from the automatic weather station near the catchment (Fig. 1 b). The meteorological station is 26 km away from the study area but with similar topographic features. Therefore, it is considered that this meteorological station is representative of the rainfall data in the study area. The cumulative rainfall for 10 consecutive days (Rx10day) of each year was extracted from 1989 to 2018. The rainfall frequency analysis was conducted by hydrological frequency distribution curve fitting software (developed by the State key laboratory of water resources and hydropower engineering, Wuhan University), and Rx10day of different return periods (T=2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 a) was obtained. The Pearson type-III (P-III) distribution is used for fitting the hydrological frequency distribution of Rx10day.  2.2 June 2016 flood The rainfall in June 2016 lasted for 11 days from June 8 to June 19. After the flood receded, a typical water-level-fluctuating zone appeared within this catchment from highland to lowland. Flood height was measured from 0.00 m (soil saturated conditions) to 7.64 m (water level above soil level) and soil flooding duration from 0 to 17 days. In addition, 0.00 m is the relative elevation of A(sinkhole) in Fig. 1 d. The mortality of Napier grass and Maize in the flooded area of this catchment was investigated by two field investigations, comparing depression photos before and after the flood. Mortality is the dead area of crop planting area as a proportion of the total planting area. Napier grass was defined as dead when the aboveground stems and leaves were withered and no further leaf development occurred in the remaining growing season. Maize was defined as dead when the cobs were rotten, meaning Maize cobs had failed. To further explore the effect of flooding on agricultural ecosystems, the Napier grass and Maize sampling strips with six and five gradients were respectively selected. The direction of the sampling belt, and the relative position, height, and horizontal distance of plots are shown in Fig. 2  . Six gradients (N1-N6) of Napier grass were separated into three groups (A, B, and C) according to their managements: group A (N1-N2), group B (N3-N5) and group C (N6). Group A and B were located in the depression and had been mown on Jun 2013 and Dec 2013 separately, while Group C was located on a slope and mown on Dec 2015. Five gradients of Maize (M1-M5) located in the depression had the same management and genotypes as surrounding local farms. Maize was planted at a density of 8 plants/m2 , in soil containing 10–20 % bare rock. In this flooding event, Maize was in the ‘milk stage’-87 days post-sowing. To compare floods across gradients, flood indexes such as SFD (soil flooding duration), PSD (plant submerged duration), CSD (cob submerged duration), and D (the difference between plant height and the maximum flooding height; positive and negative D means plants above water and below water, respectively) were quantified (Fig. 3  a). Site level:(1) y sl   = H sl        Cob level:(2) y cl   = k 1  x + H cl        Canopy level:(3) y ca   = k 2  x + H ca        Therefore, the coordinates of the two intersection points of the site level and the water level on the dynamic curves of one flooding event are (xs1 , ys1  ) and (xs2 , ys2  ), respectively. In addition, the coordinates of the two intersection points of the cob level and the water level are (xc1 , yc1  ) and  (xc2 , yc2  ),  respectively, and the coordinates of the two intersection points of the canopy level and the water level are (xca1 , yca1  ) and (xca2 , yca2 ) , respectively. As the height of the cob and plant does not change during the flood, k1   and k2   is 0.(4) SFD = x s 2   - x s 1       (5) CSD = x c 1   - x c 1       (6) PSD = x c a 2   - x c a 1       (7) D = k 2  x + H ca   - y pk        Hsl  , Hcl   and Hca   is the relative elevation of planting site, cob and plant canopy to sinkhole, respectively. ypk   is the height of the highest water level point. Due to the strong collinearity of these indicators, stepwise regression was selected to identify the highest correlation between the index and the remaining crop green ratio or biomass. The remaining green ratio can indicate the condition of the crop after a flood event (Rajcan and Tollenaar, 1999 ). The flood index data was calculated through subtraction of the intersection values between the water level curve, and the soil surface, plant, and cob level of each gradient (Fig. 3 a). The water level curve can be divided into an increasing phase and a receding phase. The increasing phase was inferred by the water level recorded on 8, 9, and 12 June and meteorological data (estimated from the automatic weather station near the catchment). The receding phase was quantified by the height of the recorded water level and UAV (DJI Phantom 3 Standard unmanned aerial vehicle) images taken from 17 to 24 June. In addition, the relative elevation of each gradient to the sinkhole was measured by Electronic Total Station (NTS-332R4; precision at 0.001 m).  2.3 Crop physiological ecological responses to flood The calculation of the remaining green ratio differed with crop type. Napier grass is a tussock-type crop, while Maize has a more erect growth pattern. Therefore, the remaining green ratio of Napier grass is the ratio of the green aboveground biomass to the total aboveground biomass. The Maize remaining green ratio is the ratio of the green leaves to the total leaves. Dry matter distribution (leaf, stem, cob, bract, and inflorescence) was calculated by determining the proportion of each biomass component as a percentage of the total aboveground biomass. Sampling was conducted on 7 and 8 July 2016 (two weeks after flood water had receded), to allow for the withering of leaves due to post-anoxic injury to become visible (Nabben et al., 1999 ). Three 1 × 1 m2  sample areas were selected for Napier grass in each gradient. Aboveground biomass was harvested near the soil surface and separated into green and withered components. The green components of Napier grass branches were separated into leaves and stems, and then weighed after drying at 70 °C for 48 h. Ten branches were selected randomly in each sample area and measured for shoot height. For Maize, ten plants were randomly selected in each gradient, measured for shoot height, and then separated into green and withered components of leaves, stem, cob, bract, and inflorescences. Components were then weighed after drying at 70 °C for 48 h. In addition, weeds and foreign materials were carefully removed from both crops before drying. When analyzing dry matter distribution, the Maize components included dead material only, as live and dead parts of stems and cobs were difficult to identify accurately. To represent the major axis of plant functional variations, 11 functional traits were measured, such as plant height (PH), percentage of leaves biomass (PLB), fine root biomass (FRB), leaf area (LA), specific leaf area (SLA), phosphorus concentration per leaf unit mass (Pm ), nitrogen concentration per leaf unit mass (Nm ), maximum CO2  assimilation rate per unit area (Aa ), stomatal conductance per unit area (ga ), leaf chlorophyll content (SPAD) and transpiration rate per unit area (E). PH, PLB, and FRB are biomass-related indicators. Fine roots (<2 mm in diameter) play a crucial role as the primary pathway for water and nutrient uptake of plants (Jackson et al., 1997 ). Soil cores were collected (10 cm diameter, 10 cm depth) within three soil layers (0–10, 10–20, and 20–30 cm) from each sample area of Napier grass to measure FRB. Three replicates for each sample area were collected with total of 162 soil cores. These were immersed in water for eight hours to loosen attached soil particles, and fine live roots were separated by washing and sieving. Fine roots were dried at 70 °C for 48 h and then weighed. For Maize, the belowground roots of each plant were collected at the same time as the aboveground sampling. The collection of live fine roots was the same as Napier grass. Leaf area, SLA, Pm,  and Nm  are considered part of the leaf economic spectrum (Reich et al., 1997; Wright et al., 2004 ). The measurement of these indexes is consistent with previous research (Sauvadet et al., 2021 ). Aa , ga , SPAD and E are indexes of light-capturing strategies. Aa , ga,  and E were measured between 9:00 and 11:00 am on sunny days with a Li-6400 portable photosynthesis system (Li-6400, Li-Cor). Based on preliminary trials, the photosynthetic photon flux density was set at 1600 μmol m−2  s−1  to ensure that light-saturated photosynthetic rates were reached for Napier grass and Maize. Ambient CO2  and air temperature was maintained at 390 mol−1  and 28 °C, respectively. For each crop, five to ten fully-expanded, sun-exposed leaves were measured. SPAD (SPAD 502 Plus Chlorophyll Meter) was conducted on these leaves to measure chlorophyll content.   3 Results 3.1 Flood characteristics Rx10day (cumulative rainfall of ten consecutive days) of (1989–2018 Historical) eight different return periods at the Guzhou catchment (T=2, 5,10, 20, 50, 100 a) ranged from 197 mm to 386 mm, respectively (Fig. 3 b). In 2016, the Rx10day was 280 mm, which was close to the once-in-a-decade flood (Table 1  ). On 8th June 2016 a total of 61.3 mm of rain fell, causing a temporary waterlogging in the depression. The deepest depth is at 7.64 m. Depth at this temporary waterlogging reached its peak on 17th June after several days of rain, with water receding on 24th June (Fig. 3 a). The water level was dynamic, along with the plant height above the water level. The longest soil flooding duration (SFD) was 14.6 days for N1, followed by 12.8, 11.7, 10.4, 9.5, and 1.5 days for N2-N6, respectively. The longest plant submerged duration (PSD) was 11.7 days for N1, followed by 10.1, 7.4, 5.5, 4.0, and 0 days for N2-N6, respectively (Fig. 3 c). SFD is positively related to PSD, but negatively related to the plant height minus water level (D) (Table 2  ). Maize had the longest SFD of 10.3 days for M1, followed by 9.5, 8.4, 5.7 and 4.1 days for M2-M5, respectively. Maize had the longest submerged duration of Maize cob (CSD) of 6.7 days for M1, followed by 5.2, 4.1, 1.3, and 0 days for M2-M5, respectively (Fig. 3 d). SFD of Maize is positively related to CSD, but negatively related to D and no relation with PSD (Table 3  ).  3.2 Response of crops According to Fig. 1 d, 78.6 % of the Maize planted area was destroyed, while Napier grass died in 20.4 % of its planted area. Aboveground biomass of Napier grass differed significantly (p < 0.05; Fig. 4  a1) among sampling gradients. For example, aboveground biomass was significantly higher in N4-N6 than in N2-N3, and it was significantly higher in N2-N3 than in N1 (0 t·ha−1 ). This suggests that there is a mortality threshold between N1 and N2 and a threshold of yield reduction between N3 and N4 when Napier grass is flooded. Note that there were no significant differences in plant height between N1 and N2, N3 and N4 (Fig. 4 a1), which means the original aboveground biomass (represented by plant height) before flooding would not affect the above comparison analysis on aboveground biomass among different sampling gradients. Cob biomass was significantly lower in M1-M3 than in M5 on the sampling strips (Fig. 4 a2). Cob biomass of M1, M2, M3, and M4 were 23 %, 25 %, 35 %, and 76 % of M5, respectively (Fig. 4 a2). Meanwhile, Cob biomass of M1-M3 were lower than that of their stem, whereas that of M4-M5 was higher (Fig. 4 b2 and 4c2). This suggested that M1-M3′s cobs growth stopped, but M4-M5′s cobs continued to grow post-flood, and there should be a flooding threshold for corn extinction between M3 and M4. Plant functional traits showed how plants adapt to flood events. Napier grass and Maize fine root biomass (FRB) had a significant negative correlation with soil flooding duration (SFD) (p < 0.05). Napier grass FRB (362–1500 kg/hm2 ) was two orders of magnitude higher than that of Maize (6.8–42.2 kg/hm2 ) (Fig. 5  a), and therefore had great potential to control soil erosion (Li et al., 2015b). Leaf area (LA), specific leaf area (SLA), phosphorus concentration per leaf unit mass (Pm ), nitrogen concentration per leaf unit mass (Nm ) were the leaf economic spectrum functional traits (Fig. 5 b–e). LA of Napier grass and Maize decreased with SFD (p > 0.05, Fig. 5 b), and no significant correlation between SLA and SFD existed (p > 0.05, Fig. 5 c). Meanwhile, Napier grass’s Pm  was positively correlated with SFD, while Maize’s Nm  and Pm  decreased with SFD (Fig. 5 d–e). As for functional traits related to leaf light-capturing strategies, such as maximum CO2  assimilation rate per unit area (Aa ), stomatal conductance per unit area (ga ), leaf chlorophyll content (SPAD) and transpiration rate (E), Napier grass and Maize showed contrasting responses to flooding (Fig. 5 f-j). Positive significant correlations were observed between these functional traits (Aa , ga  and E) of Napier grass and SFD (p < 0.05, Fig. 5 f-j), whereas those (Aa , ga , SPAD and E) of Maize were negatively correlated with SFD (p < 0.05, Fig. 5 f-j). The results of principal component analysis (PCA) are shown in Fig. 6  . The first two principal components accounted for 79.2 % of the variance, with 48.4 % in the first axis. PCA axis 1 was closely related to vegetation resource (FRB and percentage of leaves biomass), leaf nutrient concentrations (Nm  and Pm ), and basic traits (plant height and leaf area). PCA axis 2 accounted for 30.8 % of the total variation, and primarily comprised of photosynthetic-related traits (Aa , ga,  and SPAD) and the transpiration trait (E). The loadings of Napier grass gathered in the center of PC2, whereas Maize separated along PC2. This indicates that Maize is more sensitive to flooding than Napier grass. Napier grass and Maize are well separated from each other along the first two axis, indicating that there are different survival strategies between the two crops.  3.3 Flood tolerance thresholds for crops The relationship between flood indexes and plant state shows that the remaining green ratio and biomass of Napier grass and Maize has a decreasing linear trend with increased SFD and PSD/CSD, and increases linearly as D increases (Fig. 7  ). Furthermore, there is a piecewise regression between flood indexes and plant state of Napier grass (The numbers in the figure indicate the split point of the piecewise function). Therefore, taking the minimum value of the flood indexes to determine the tolerant values, we can get the tolerant durations of Napier grass to soil flooding and plant submersion at 12.6 and 10.2 days, respectively, and the tolerant submerged depth of Napier grass canopy at 2.71 m under the water (Fig. 7 f). In contrast, it indicates that most Maize can survive when the plant height above the water level is > 150 cm and may potentially die if < 50 cm. Where the relative height of the Maize is above the water level by 50–150 cm, the remaining green ratio of Maize varies (between 0 and 90 %). PSD is the most vital factor that affects the remaining green ratio of Napier grass and the remaining biomass of Maize, while CSD and D are the most vital factors that affect the remaining green ratio and cob biomass of Maize, respectively (Table 4  ). According to Equations (1)–(7) , the survival space for Napier grass and Maize under submerged water is 4.55 m and 1.43 m, respectively (in Fig. 8   green space). In response to the extreme rainfall event in 2016, the safe planting heights for Napier grass and Maize are 3.09 m and 6.21 m, respectively, relative to the lowest point of the depression elevation (set at 0.00 m).   4 Discussion Karst depressions are sensitive to extreme precipitation since they are easily influenced by both surface runoff and shallow subsurface flows (Gutierrez et al., 2014; Garssen et al., 2015; Parise et al., 2018 ). Crop security (crop survival and biomass) in depressions will face an increasing number of challenges because of extreme rainfall events are becoming more frequent. Napier grass is more resistant to flooding than Mazie. The PSD threshold for Napier grass survival and biomass was found to be 10.2 days, while the CSD threshold for Maize cob survival was 1.3 days. Syvertsen et al. (1983)  found that anoxic conditions within the soil are attained within a week of flooding and kernels become rotten and stopped in growing when submerged in water for several days. Maize protruding 1.5 m above the water level has a greater chance of survival, as they have decreased SFD and can grow more green leaves out of water level, thus allowing for increased aerial gas exchange (Voesenek et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2011b ). Functional traits of roots and leaves for the two main crops (Napier grass and Maize) changed with increasing flood severity. For Napier grass, root and leaf damage increased with flooding. Fine root biomass decreased; large, older leaves senesced, but small, young leaves replaced older leaves and became the main source of metabolism during post-flood. These young leaves conducted a stronger physiological activity for recovery and growth. The result was concordant with that of Mollard et al. (2008) , in which flooded plants of Paspalum dilatatum  in lowland positions had 35 % higher photosynthesis compared to controls (watered daily) because the rapid growth of new foliage, which promotes plant recovery. Similarly for Maize, root and leaf damage increased with flood severity. Fine root biomass decreased and leaves yellowed and withered. The net photosynthesis rate of the leaves decreased sharply; subsequently, the whole plant began to senesce and could not recover. This result was consistent with those obtained by Bragina et al. (2002) , and Yordanova and Popova (2007) . No matter what growing stage Maize was at, the rate of photosynthesis decreased sharply after soil flooding or the plant completely flooded. This is due to root oxygen deficiency caused photo-oxidative damage in leaves, when Maize subjected to flood (Yordanova and Popova, 2007 ). Results of PC1 indicate that plant functional traits divide Napier grass and Maize into two groups (Fig. 7 ). Napier grass has a higher remaining green ratio with higher nutrient resource input (higher fine root biomass, higher percentage of leaf biomass, and lower SLA) and an economical nutrient use strategy (smaller leaf area, lower plant height, lower Nm  and Pm ) compared with Maize. Results of PC2 indicate that Napier grass has stable and quiescence carbon fixation rates (Aa , ga,  and SPAD) and transpiration (E), concentrated in the center of PC2 (Fig. 7 ). Traits associated with plenty of resources can resist anoxic environments for longer periods of time (Klimešová, 1994; Mommer et al., 2006; Fischer et al., 2016; Purcell, 2016 ). In addition, Napier grass can survive after flooding, and this could be due to it being more efficient in resource uptake post-flood (Klimešová, 1994; Mommer et al., 2006 ). This is consistent with flood-resistant plants such as Poa pratensis  which has high fine root density (Fischer et al., 2016 ) and Lotus corniculatus  which maintains stable carbon fixation rates (Striker et al., 2005; Striker et al., 2012 ).  Ultimately, this is a typical quiescence strategy. Maize has opposing trait patterns, as it has a low remaining green ratio and carbon fixation rate. Different gradients of Maize were separated along PC2. It was found that Maize maintains a stable carbon fixation after 2–3 days of flooding, and the chlorophyll content starts to deteriorate after 6 days of flooding (Yan et al., 1996 ). Maize is typical of an escape strategy plant, using death to escape harmful environments. Plants are more sensitive to climatic extremes during the growing season (Klimešová, 1994; Van Eck et al., 2004 ). It was found that species survived winter floods for longer periods compared to summer floods (Van Eck et al., 2004 ). Within our study area, flood disturbance usually occurred during May to September, and particularly in June. During this time, Napier grass has not yet begun to develop flowers and fruit (June 2016). This indicates that Napier grass is less affected by submersion, and only some aboveground biomass is lost (Garssen et al., 2015 ). However, Maize is at the grain-filling stage during this flood period. A waterlogging depth of 30 cm for more than 5 days or 50 cm for more than 3 days can both cause significant reductions in Maize yield (Zhou et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013 ). Various landform types are subject to different flood water level curves, subsequently affecting crop survival. When comparing a depression flood to a plain flood under similar rainfall and seasons (Wright et al., 2015; Wright et al., 2017 ), the karst depression flood had a shorter waterlogging duration, but a deeper water level than the plain flood, and crops in karst depressions were impacted more severely than flood plains. This indicates that closed landforms with surrounding steep hills are more susceptible to damage to plants under similar conditions. Plants that are partially or fully submerged in flood waters are affected more negatively than plants in saturated soil without submersion (Wright et al., 2015; Wright et al., 2017 ). This is due to a deficiency in oxygen in the soil, limiting root function and submerged leaves experiencing oxygen deficiency thus limiting gas exchange and photosynthesis (Garssen et al., 2015 ). These anaerobic fermentations cause a rapid depletion of carbohydrate reserves (Bailey-Serres and Voesenek, 2008 ), causing plant death (Fox et al., 1995; Gibbs and Greenway, 2003 ).  5 Implications This study may have several implications for sustainable agriculture in karst landscapes. Modifying the planting layout from traditional rows to concentric rings parallel to the contours is not only beneficial in reducing economic loss during flooding but also maintains sustainable development of agricultural ecosystems in depressions. Additionally, flood-resistant crops are recommended to be planted in relatively low-lying areas (Sarangi et al., 2016; Rumanti et al., 2018 ), particularly to close to sinkholes. Crops with a low tolerance to waterlogging should be planted at relatively high elevations. Grass strips not only reduce edge-of-field runoff by 90 % (Melville and Morgan, 2001 ) but are also an effective way to reduce nutrient pollution and sediment loss, thus improving water quality and mitigating the risk of congestion within the underground drainage system (O’Connell et al., 2007; Wilson et al., 2014; Rapidel et al., 2015 ). These provide efficient guidelines for the local government to mitigate against flooding by adjusting the planting layout by analyzing depression areas to find a safe planting locations for crops. This is particularly important in large and dense agricultural activity depression areas with large populations. Additionally, it is noteworthy that tree species are beneficial for prolonging flood duration. In the future, it is necessary to develop ecohydrology models to assess the impacts of continuous total precipitation on karst depression agroforestry ecosystems in different recurrence periods in the history and the future and to select the optimal layout of the agroforestry ecosystems through quantitative simulations. In this way, it is possible to cope with the effects of future climate change and realize the sustainable development of agroforestry ecosystems in karst depression. We need to emphasize that this study aimed to propose a framework which can be used to determine a safe planting height of plants by exploring the relationships between plant survival rate and flooding (waterlogging) processes. The basic ideas of this study can be flexibly applied to other regions or for other crops. However, it should be noted that the flooding processes in different regions/Landscapes is not necessarily consistent, and the flooding tolerance of different plants is not necessarily consistent, so the extension to other regions or landscapes needs some experimental calibrations and validations according to the local hydrological environment and plant species.  6 Conclusions In June-2016 flood, a once in ten years flood,78.6 % of Maize and 20.4 % of Napier grass failed to persist. The critical tolerance time of flooding to Maize cobs and Napier grass was 1.3 and 10.2 days, respectively, and the survival space for Napier grass and Maize under submerged water was 4.55 m and 1.43 m, respectively. Napier grass performed better than Maize when submerged, due to higher fine root biomass and the stable photosynthetic capacity of the leaves. In response to the extreme event in 2016, the safe planting heights for Napier grass and Maize are above 3.09 m and 6.21 m, respectively, relative to the lowest point of the depression elevation (set at 0.00 m). In the follow-up research, it is necessary to obtain the future inundation status of depressions based on model predictions of future climate change and depression hydrological processes. Then combined with the crop inundation threshold, set the safe planting height of crops, rationally layout agroforest ecosystems to be adapted to the future climate change.  7 Consent to participate.
