1 Introduction Urbanization, which is increasing globally, has deleterious environmental impacts. Urban land has been expanding at a rate of 5 % per decade over the past several decades (Güneralp et al., 2020 ). Urban expansion often involves the clearing of natural lands, thereby leading to habitat fragmentation and loss (Kowarik, 2011 ). Impervious surfaces can be a large proportion of the new land cover (Elvidge et al., 2007 ), and these surfaces intensify air temperatures (Memon et al., 2008) and stormwater runoff (Miller et al., 2014 ). Urbanization also introduces and increases emissions of substances that degrade air quality (Zhang et al., 2022 ) and water quality (Malmqvist and Rundle, 2002 ). It could be argued that urbanization has one of its largest impacts on streamwater quality, due in part to the many processes involved. In the United States, for example, five water-quality variables that are continuously monitored at thousands of sites by the United States Geological Survey (USGS) include temperature and specific conductance, which are true physical properties, dissolved oxygen and pH, which are concentrations, and turbidity, which is an expression of the optical properties of water (Wagner et al., 2006 ). Increased solar heating from a lack of riparian shading (Hewlett and Fortson, 1982 ), storm runoff flowing across heated impervious surfaces (Herb et al., 2008 ), and relatively warm wastewater discharge in winter (Kinouchi et al., 2007 ) increases temperatures. Increased temperatures as noted above along with excessive algal growth from nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilizers, atmospheric deposition, and sewage (Hochmuth et al., 2012 ) and the oxidation of ammonia by microorganisms (Beaulieu et al., 2011 ) decreases dissolved oxygen levels. The use of salts for deicing roads (Corski et al., 2010 ) and the leakage of sewage from sanitary-sewer system (Rose, 2007 ) increases conductivity, while the weathering of concrete infrastructure (Tippler et al., 2014 ) increases conductivity and pH. Accelerated streambank erosion (Nelson and Booth, 2007; McCarney-Castle et al., 2017 ), the erosion of exposed soil at construction sites (Lenat and Crawford, 1994; Russell et al., 2017 ), the production of street residue (Devereus et al., 2010 ), and the outflow of solids from wastewater treatment plants (Carter et al., 2004 ) increase turbidity. Streams in urban watersheds generally have higher conductivity, higher temperatures, lower dissolved oxygen, and higher pH than streams in nearby forested watersheds. Urban land cover (e.g., building density, percent imperviousness, percent urban land, percent developed land, etc.) is positively correlated with conductivity (Bolstad and Swank, 1997; Busse et al., 2006; Ding et al., 2015; Haidary et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2019; Pratt and Chang, 2012; Tu, 2011 ), temperature (Bolstad and Swank, 1997; Chang, 2008; Ding et al., 2015; Nelson and Palmer, 2007; Pratt and Chang, 2012; Somers et al., 2013 ), and pH (Bolstad and Swank, 1997; Chang, 2008; Hasenmueller et al., 2017; Kaushal et al., 2017; Pratt and Chang, 2012 ), and negatively correlated with dissolved oxygen (Bolstad and Swank, 1997; Chang, 2008; Ding et al., 2015; Haidary et al., 2013; Pratt and Chang, 2012; Tu, 2011 ). Comparisons of most urbanized sites with least urbanized sites also show urbanization associated with increased conductivity (Lenat and Crawford, 1994; Klose et al., 2012 ), temperature (Lenat and Crawford, 1994 ), and pH (Hasenmueller et al., 2017 ) and decreased dissolved oxygen (Lenat and Crawford, 1994 ). The strong relationships between urbanization and conductivity, temperature, dissolved oxygen, and pH are not always observed: some studies (Beganskas and Toran, 2021; Booth et al., 2014 ) show that percent urbanized and impervious cover of a watershed are not strongly correlated with temperature, while other studies find no difference in pH (Lenat and Crawford, 1994; Haidary et al., 2013 ), conductivity (Haidary et al., 2013 ), and dissolved oxygen (Haidary et al., 2013 ) between urban and forested streams/wetlands. Compared to conductivity, temperature, dissolved oxygen, and pH, there is more uncertainty about urbanization impacts on turbidity. Comparisons of urban and forested streams also have mixed results: there have been both increased turbidity for urban streams (Brett et al., 2005; Lenat and Crawford, 1994 ) and no difference in turbidity between urban and forested streams/wetlands (Haidary et al., 2013; Hasenmueller et al., 2017; Mallin et al., 2009 ). But only positive correlations (Brett et al., 2005; Chang, 2008; Pratt and Chang, 2012; Tu, 2011 ) between urban land cover and turbidity have been observed. While the existing research on urban impacts on water quality does provide useful results at the annual scale, studies in general provide insufficient information about intra-annual variations in urban impacts on water quality. There may be as few as two studies that provide information showing how correlations between urban land cover and water quality or differences in water quality between urban streams and other streams differ among seasons. In the southeastern United States, Bolstad and Swank (1997)  show – for spring and summer compared to autumn and winter – larger correlations between building density and temperature, and – for autumn and winter – larger correlations between building density and turbidity. In the northwestern United States, Pratt and Chang (2012)  shows the presence of urban variables as predictor variables in temperature and pH models for the wet season and not the dry season. The existing studies on urban impacts on water quality also tend to have a small number of sites, short time periods, and have limited statistical analyses. Only five studies (Chang, 2008; Ding et al., 2015; Pratt and Chang, 2012; Somers et al., 2013 ; Tu et al., 2011) have ≥ 30 sites. Only four studies (Brett et al., 2005; Chang, 2008; Pratt and Chang, 2012 ; Tu et al., 2011) use more than four years of data. Finally, only one study (Haidary et al., 2013 ) uses both correlation – or regression – and testing for differences among groups. Therefore, this study attempts to fill in the research gaps noted above by using a robust number of sites and years along with multiple statistical approaches to determine intra-annual variations in urbanization impacts on water quality. The objectives are as follows: (1) to assess month-specific differences in water quality between stream groups with different levels of urbanization and (2) to determine month-specific relationships between the urban intensities of watersheds and streamwater quality.  2 Study region The chosen study region, the Atlanta–Sandy Springs–Gainesville combined statistical area in the southeastern United States, was an ideal locale for examining urbanization impacts on water quality (Fig. 1  ). Of the 90 watersheds examined in Diem et al. (2021)  for the 2013–2020 period, 38 watersheds had sufficient water-quality data during 2014–2021. Those 38 watersheds were used in this study. All watersheds had a humid-subtropical climate (Beck et al., 2018 ) and – due to existing entirely within the Piedmont physiographic province – had similar geology (i.e., igneous and metamorphic rocks) (Miller, 1990 ).  3 Data and methods 3.1 Data Daily water-quality data for 2014–2021 were obtained for the 38 gauges from the National Water Information System of the United States Geological Survey (U.S. Geological Survey, 2023 ). Boundaries of the watersheds associated with the gauges were obtained from Diem (2021) . The daily water-quality variables, which were summaries of continuous-sensor data, available for download were mean specific conductance, mean temperature, mean dissolved oxygen, median pH, and median turbidity. If a gauge was missing more than 25 % of daily values for a water-quality variable, then that gauge-variable combination was eliminated. The screening resulted in 37, 37, 24, 24, and 38 gauges with specific-conductance, temperature, dissolved-oxygen, pH, and turbidity data, and for the five variables the stations were missing on average 12.9 %, 11.6 %, 12.9 %, 13.1 %, and 25.7 %, respectively, of daily values (Table S1 ). Missing daily values at each gauge for each variable were replaced using the following procedure: (1) the gauge with the largest correlation with the gauge in question was identified; (2) regressing the daily values at that gauge on the daily values at the strongest-correlated gauge yielded predicted daily values; (3) if there were still missing values after replacing the missing values with the predicted values, then the gauge with the second-largest correlation was used in the regression; and (4) the steps were repeated with other gauges until there were no missing daily values. For all the linear-regression models developed, assumptions of linear regression were ignored because the regression models were used only for prediction and not inference. Correlations between each pair of gauges for the five water-quality variables are in Figs. S1–S5 . Gridded land-cover and developed-imperviousness data for 2014–2021 were obtained from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) of the Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium (Dewitz and U.S. Geological Survey, 2021 ). All data had a spatial resolution of 30 m. Land-cover data were obtained for 2013, 2016, 2019, and 2021. The land-cover composition of each of the 38 watersheds was determined for each of the four years, and values for the intervening years (i.e., 2014, 2015, 2017, 2018, and 2020) were estimated using inverse-distance weighting. Developed-imperviousness data were obtained for 2016. The land-cover product had 15 classes for the Atlanta region (Fig. 1 ) and the imperviousness product had for each grid cell the percentage of developed surface that was impervious surfaces. An additional variable, the change in developed land cover from 2014 to 2021, was calculated for each watershed. Land-cover composition data for NLCD classes were obtained from Diem (2023) . These data are the mean percentages of forest, grass, water, and impervious surfaces for the 15 NLCD classes in the Atlanta region. The data are used in Diem et al. (2023) . Population and housing data at the block-group level were obtained from the U.S. Census Bureau’s American Community Survey 5-year estimates for 2010–2014 and 2015–2019 (U.S. Census Bureau, 2014, 2019 ). Population and housing totals were converted to density values, and weighted means – which were based on the areas of block groups within a watershed – were used to estimate population and housing densities within the watersheds. The final density estimates for the 2014–2021 period were one-eighth the 2010–2014 estimates plus seven-eighths the 2015–2019 estimates. Land-use data were obtained from the Atlanta Regional Commission for 2012, which was the most recent year with data. The dataset had 29 land-use classes. The proportional coverage of all land-use classes was determined for each watershed. The urban land-use coverage was the sum of the proportions of the following: commercial and services; industrial; transportation, communication, and utilities; industrial and commercial complexes; other urban; high-density residential; multifamily residential; intensive institutional; and limited-access highways.  3.2 Testing for differences between watershed groups Differences in monthly values of mean daily water-quality – along with watershed-level variables – between watershed groups with differing levels of urbanization were assessed using Mann-Whitney U  tests (α = 0.05; two-tailed). Principal components analysis (PCA) was used to divide the 38 watersheds into groups. A Q-mode input matrix (i.e., watersheds as the rows and variables as the columns) was used with the following five highly collinear land-cover variables: population density (PD), housing density (HD), proportion of watershed that is high-intensity developed land (HID), imperviousness (Imp), and proportion of watershed that is urban land use (ULU). A similar procedure is performed in Diem et al. (2022)  for 90 watersheds.  3.3 Correlations between water quality and urban and development variables Correlations between monthly values of the five water-quality variables and the watershed-level variables were assessed using Pearson product–moment correlation tests (α = 0.05; two tailed). The urban/development variables included PD, HD, HID, Imp, and ULU along with an urban-intensity index (UII) and the change in developed land from 2013 to 2021. The UII is described in Section 4.1.1 . Watershed development was included because construction activities can be major sources of sediments (Nelson and Booth, 2002; Russell et al., 2017 ).   4 Results 4.1 Watershed groups 4.1.1 Differences in watershed characteristics There were three groups of watersheds (i.e., exurban, suburban, and urban) with roughly equal numbers of members, and those groups had distinctly different watershed scores on the first component from the PCA (Table 1  ). The first component was the only component with an eigenvalue equal to or greater than one, and that component contained 77 % of the variance of the dataset (Table 2  ). Loadings of PD, HD, HID, Imp, and ULU on the first component were similar (i.e., ranged from 0.836 to 0.910) (Table 2 ); therefore, scores for the watersheds on the first component were essentially urban-intensity scores (i.e., the UII). The urban, suburban, and exurban watershed groups had substantially different land-cover characteristics, population densities, and housing densities (Figs. 2 and 3   ). In general, urban areas are much more built up than suburban and exurban areas, with suburban areas typically congruent to urban areas and exurban areas being the least built up and proximate to rural landscapes (Davis et al. 1994; Newburn and Berck, 2011 ). Urban watersheds were located primarily in and near the City of Atlanta, while suburban watersheds were mostly located in nearby DeKalb County and exurban watersheds were mostly located at least 25 km northeast of the city in Gwinnett County (Fig. 2 a). Compared to exurban watersheds, urban and suburban watersheds had significantly larger PD, HD, HID, Imp, and ULU (Fig. 3 a-e). The largest differences involved HID and ULU: the values for those two variables for urban watersheds were 7.4 and 5.3 times larger, respectively, than the values for exurban watersheds. Compared to suburban watersheds, urban watersheds had significantly higher HD, HID, Imp, and ULU (Fig. 3 b-e). Urban and suburban watersheds had significantly less proportional coverage of forest and grass compared to exurban watersheds (Fig. 3 f,g), while urban watersheds had significantly less forest and grass compared to suburban watersheds (Fig. 3 f,g). Nevertheless, urban watersheds usually had substantial (>30 %) forest cover. The largest differences between urban and suburban watersheds involved HID and ULU: the values for those two variables for urban watersheds were 2.1 and 1.8 times larger, respectively, than the values for suburban watersheds. Finally, exurban watersheds had a significantly larger increase in developed land from 2014 to 2021 compared to suburban and urban watersheds (Fig. 3 i).  4.1.2 Differences in water quality For all months, urban and suburban watersheds had significantly higher specific conductance than exurban watersheds and urban watersheds had significantly higher specific conductance than suburban watersheds, with the differences largest in winter and spring (Fig. 4  a). Across all months, mean specific conductance for exurban, suburban, and urban streams were 77 µS cm−1 , 109 µS cm−1 , and 155 µS cm−1 , respectively. During December-May, urban streams had 84 µS cm−1  (114 %) higher specific conductance than exurban streams, suburban streams had 34 µS cm−1  (47 %) higher specific conductance than exurban streams, and urban streams had 50 µS cm−1  (46 %) higher specific conductance than suburban streams. Those three differences decreased to 73 µS cm−1  (90 %), 29 µS cm−1  (36 %), and 44 µS cm−1  (40 %), respectively, during June-November. Urban and suburban stream temperatures were significantly higher than exurban stream temperatures only during non-winter months, and there were no significant differences between urban and suburban stream temperatures (Fig. 4 b). Stream temperatures exhibited the expected seasonality of lowest values in January and highest values in July. During March-October, urban temperatures were 1.0 °C higher than exurban temperatures. The difference decreased to 0.2 °C during November-February. Differences were maximized at 1.3 °C during June and July. During May-October, suburban temperatures were 0.7 °C higher than exurban temperatures. The difference decreased to 0.3 °C during November-April. Differences were maximized at 0.9 °C during June and July. There were no significant differences in dissolved oxygen, which had the highest values in January and the lowest values in July (i.e., the inverse seasonality of temperature) for all watershed groups, between urban and exurban watersheds; however, suburban watersheds did have significantly higher dissolved oxygen than the other two watershed groups (Fig. 4 c). Dissolved oxygen was significantly higher in suburban streams than in urban streams during April-November, with a mean difference of 0.4 mg L-1  (5 %). The difference was maximized at 0.5 mg L-1  (7 %) in July. Significant differences in dissolved oxygen between suburban streams and exurban streams were restricted to October and November, with dissolved oxygen 0.4 mg L-1  (4 %) higher in suburban streams. While there were no significant differences in pH between the stream groups, urban streams did consistently have the highest pH, especially from late autumn to early spring (Fig. 4 d). Across all months, mean pH values for exurban streams, suburban streams, and urban streams were 6.95, 7.03, and 7.07, respectively. Only urban streams had increased pH values during November-March: the mean values for the three groups were 6.93, 7.03, and 7.09, respectively. There also were no significant differences in turbidity between the stream groups, but – unlike what occurred for pH – exurban streams – rather than urban streams – consistently had the highest turbidities (Fig. 4 e). Across all months, median turbidity values for exurban streams, suburban streams, and urban streams were 12.9 FNU, 11.3 FNU, and 11.0 FNU, respectively. From May-October, exurban turbidity was 2.3 FNU (22 %) larger than urban and suburban turbidity, while during November-April, the difference decreased to 1.2 FNU (10 %).   4.2 Correlations 4.2.1 Urban intensity There were strong, significant positive correlations between specific conductance and urban intensity for most months, with the largest correlations typically during winter and spring (Fig. 5  ). The mean correlations across all months for PD, HD, HID, Imp, ULU, and UII were 0.34, 0.48, 0.60, 0.61, 0.66, and 0.61, respectively. All variables except PD had significant correlations during all months. The largest and smallest correlations for all variables typically existed for January-April and July-October, respectively. There were positive correlations between temperature and urban intensity for all months, but the largest – and significant – correlations were restricted mostly to the non-winter months (Fig. 5 ). The mean correlations across all months for PD, HD, HID, Imp, ULU, and UII were 0.38, 0.40, 0.26, 0.29, 0.33, and 0.38, respectively. The strongest correlations existed for March-October. There were no significant correlations for December and January. There was a mix of weak positive and weak negative correlations between dissolved oxygen and urban intensity during the non-summer months, but during summer there were strong, significant negative correlations for most of the variables. During November-March, PD and HD were positively correlated with dissolved oxygen, with mean correlations of 0.27 and 0.21, respectively, while HID, Imp, and ULU were negatively correlated, with mean correlations of −0.25, −0.15, and −0.15, respectively. UII, which as noted previously was developed from the other five urban variables, had both positive and negative correlations during Noember-March. Significant negative correlations existed during May-September for HID and ULU and during June-August for those two variables along with Imp and UII. The mean correlations for HID, Imp, ULU, and UII during June-August were −0.52, −0.47, −0.55, and −0.44, respectively. Similar to the results for specific conductance and temperature, positive correlations between pH and urban intensity prevailed; however, significant correlations were confined mostly to winter and nearby months. Only HD, ULU, and UII had significant correlations, with those correlations occurring during January and February for HD, during October-April for ULU, and during November-February for UII. Somewhat similar to specific conductance, the largest correlations for all variables typically occurred during November-April. The mean correlations for PD, HD, HID, Imp, ULU, and UII for the period were 0.27, 0.35, 0.31, 0.29, 0.43, and 0.40, respectively. Nearly all correlations between turbidity and urban intensity were weak and negative (Fig. 5 ). The mean correlations for PD, HD, HID, Imp, ULU, and UII were −0.22, −0.21, −0.17, −0.22, −0.17, and −0.23, respectively. Only PD, HD, Imp, and UII had significant correlations, and those correlations were restricted mostly to May.  4.2.2 Urban development Significant correlations between the water-quality variables and development from 2014 to 2021 were generally weak except for significant positive correlations with turbidity (Fig. 5 ). There were negative correlations with specific conductance and temperature, and the significant correlations were generally restricted to February and March. There were mostly positive correlations with dissolved oxygen and pH, but none of the correlations were significant. All correlations with turbidity were strong and positive (e.g., the mean correlation was 0.44), with significant correlations occurring for all months except August.    5 Discussion 5.1 Urbanization has the largest and most consistent impact on specific conductance Among the five water-quality variables, specific conductance is most impacted by urbanization, and the impact is largest during winter and spring. Urban streams have significantly larger specific conductance than exurban and suburban streams during all months. On average, urban streams have 78 % and 47 % larger specific conductance than suburban streams and exurban streams, respectively. These results are not surprising, since either positive correlations between urbanization and annual conductivity or urban streams having higher annual conductivity than forest streams have been found in other studies (Busse et al., 2006; Ding et al., 2015; Haidary et al., 2013; Klose et al., 2012; Lenat and Crawford, 1994; Moore et al., 2019; Pratt and Chang, 2012 ; and Tu, 2011 ). The seasonal findings in this study are roughly similar to those in Bolstad and Swank (1997) , where higher correlations between urbanization and specific conductance exist during autumn and winter compared to spring and summer. In this study, for each of the five urban-intensity variables, specific conductance has the largest correlations among the five water-quality variables. Urban watersheds have on average 42 % coverage by impervious surfaces, compared to 18 % coverage for exurban watersheds. Therefore, throughout the year, there is increased weathering of concrete in urban watersheds leading to increased transport of major ions into streams (Kaushal et al., 2017 ). Urban watersheds in this study also have on average 58 % coverage by urban land use compared to 12 % coverage for exurban watersheds, and urban land use is correlated with sewer density. Exfiltration from sewers has been shown to be a significant source of salts in Atlanta streams (Rose, 2007 ). Differences in specific conductance between urban and exurban streams are maximized during January-April and a likely cause of this specific conductance enhancement in urban streams is the occurrence of road salts for deicing (Peters, 2009; Baker et al., 2019 ). The winter/spring increase in specific conductance is, however, much smaller than the increase in urban streams in Baltimore, MD (Baker et al., 2019 ), where area-normalized road-salt use might be 50 times higher than in the Atlanta region (Panno et al., 2005 ).  5.2 Impacts of urbanization on temperature and dissolved oxygen are generally restricted to non-winter months Urbanization increases stream temperature and decreases dissolved oxygen but only during late spring to early autumn. Other studies have only looked at annual temperature and annual dissolved oxygen, and either positive (negative) correlations between urbanization and temperature (dissolved oxygen) or urban streams having higher (lower) temperatures (dissolved oxygen) than forest streams have been found (Chang, 2008; Ding et al., 2015; Lenat and Crawford, 1994; Haidary et al., 2013; Nelson and Palmer, 2007; Pratt and Chang, 2012; Somers et al., 2013; Tu, 2011 ). Bolstad and Swank (1997)  show higher correlations between urbanization and temperature during spring and summer compared to autumn and winter, but they show the most negative correlations with dissolved oxygen occurring during spring and autumn. In this study from May-September, urban streams are 1.2 °C warmer and 0.4 °C warmer than exurban streams and suburban streams, respectively. For those same months, urban streams have 0.45 mg L-1  (6 %) less dissolved oxygen than suburban streams. A comparison with exurban streams is not made here, since only three exurban streams have dissolved oxygen data. There are significant positive correlations between temperature and PD, HD, and ULU and significant negative correlations between dissolved oxygen and HID and ULU. The likely causes of the warm-season maximum in urbanization impacts on stream temperature are a relative lack of riparian forest canopy in urban watersheds and the seasonally varying surface urban heat island. Increased riparian canopy – and associated decreased solar heating – decreases extreme and mean stream temperatures only during warmer months (Beganskas and Toran, 2020). For humid climates in the middle latitudes, surface urban heat islands are most intense during late spring and summer (Zhou 2016; Manoli et al., 2020 ). And since the solubility of oxygen in freshwater decreases with increasing temperature (United States Geological Survey, 2020), a temperature-induced decrease in dissolved oxygen will occur in summer.  5.3 Urbanization impacts on pH may be restricted to cooler months Urban streams appear to have higher pH than exurban and suburban streams, but a dearth of statistically significant results only allows a claim of urbanization being positively correlated with pH during mid-autumn to mid-spring to be made. More significant results were expected, since runoff from concrete infrastructure is a major cause of increased stream pH (Kaushal et al., 2017 ). There were no significant differences between any pairs of stream groups for any month, and this might be due to the fact that pH data were only available for three of the 13 exurban streams. In general, the urban streams were slightly alkaline and exurban streams were slightly acidic. There were positive correlations between urbanization and pH during all months, which is similar to what studies have found at the annual scale or for all seasons (Bolstad and Swank, 1997; Chang, 2008; Hasenmueller et al., 2017; Kaushal et al., 2017; Pratt and Chang, 2012 ). The significant positive correlations are centered on the winter months and only involve HD and ULU. In the Atlanta region, December-April is the soil–water surplus period, and baseflow during these months decreases with increasing urbanization of watersheds (Diem et al., 2021 ). Inflow and infiltration of groundwater into sewers might be the major cause of the decreased baseflow of urban streams (Diem et al., 2021; Pangle et al., 2022; Diem et al., 2023 ). Since groundwater in the Piedmont physiographic province, in which the Atlanta region resides, is slightly acidic (Sonon et al., 2006; Donahue and Kibler, 2007 ), the lower pH of exurban and suburban streams compared to urban streams during winter and spring might be caused by increased groundwater flow into those less urbanized streams.  5.4 Development activities within a watershed, rather than the degree of urbanization, are the causes of increased turbidity Urban streams do not have higher turbidity than exurban and suburban streams; in fact, exurban streams, which tend to be in watersheds that have undergone the most development in recent years, have the highest turbidity. Unlike what is shown in other studies (Brett et al., 2005; Chang, 2008; Lenat and Crawford, 1994; Pratt and Chang, 2012; Tu, 2011 ) and despite much higher maximum streamflow for urban streams (Aulenbach et al., 2022; Diem et al., 2021 ) – and thus more potential for streambank erosion (MacKenzie et al., 2022 ) – compared to other streams in the Atlanta region, urbanization does not yield increased turbidity in this study. There are no significant differences in turbidity between stream groups; thus, the results are similar to those in Haidary et al. (2013), Hasenmueller et al. (2017) , and Mallin et al. (2009) . Strong, positive correlations between turbidity and watershed development indicate that land-disturbing activities are the likely major cause of turbidity differences among streams. In the Atlanta region, the proportion of a watershed undergoing development is at least three times and five times larger in exurban watersheds than in suburban and urban watersheds, respectively. Therefore, this situation matches the conceptual model first shown in Wolman (1967)  and later revised in Gellis et al. (2017)  and Russell et al. (2017) , where sediment yield is increased during urban construction phases. This temporal phenomenon is observed in the Atlanta region by Aulenbach et al. (2023) .   6 Conclusions This study has shown that – by analyzing a large number of streams over a robust number of years – urbanization impacts on water quality vary throughout the year, with urbanization not having impacts on water-quality variables during certain periods. During all months, urban streams had significantly higher specific conductance than suburban and exurban streams and the urban intensity of a watershed was strongly positively correlated with specific conductance. Differences and correlations were intensified during winter and spring, and a likely cause was the use of deicing road salts, which was assumed to be most prevalent in urban watersheds. Only during non-winter months did urban streams have significantly higher temperatures and significantly lower dissolved oxygen as well as significant positive correlations between urban intensity and temperature and significant negative correlations between urban intensity and dissolved oxygen. Urbanization impacts on temperature – and by extension dissolved oxygen – peak during the warmest months because, during those months, cooling via shading by the riparian forest is maximized in non-urban watersheds and the urban surface heat island is most intense. Urban streams, which were slightly basic, had the highest pH during all months, but none of the differences were significant. Among the urban-intensity variables, only housing density and urban land use had significant positive correlations with pH, and those significant correlations were restricted generally to winter and spring months when there is presumably more groundwater – which is slightly acidic – flowing into exurban and suburban streams than into urban streams. Runoff from concrete infrastructure is the most plausible cause of the increased pH of urban streams. Turbidity was the only water-quality variable that both did not have significant differences between stream groups and did not increase with increased urban intensity. However, exurban streams did have the highest turbidity among stream groups during all months and this is probably due to increased development-related land disturbance in exurban watersheds. All findings in this study are likely applicable to other urban areas in the Piedmont physiographic province of the southeastern United States and most findings could be applicable to urban areas in humid subtropical climates.
1 Introduction Groundwater extraction accounts for 35 % of total water withdrawals and 42 % of irrigation water, exceeding one trillion tons annually in 2007 (Döll et al., 2012 ). One of the negative consequences of continued groundwater extraction is depletion in many major aquifer systems (Döll et al., 2012; Wada et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2020 ). The decline in groundwater levels caused by groundwater extraction also reduces groundwater recharge to surface water bodies (Kollet and Zlotnik 2003 ; Li et al., 2020a ), exacerbating the intensity and frequency of global droughts (Wada et al., 2013 ). Additionally, groundwater extraction for irrigation can affect climate by altering land–atmosphere interactions (Kåresdotter et al., 2022; McDermid et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2017a ). Therefore, a quantitative description of groundwater extraction activities under climate change and assessing their impact on the terrestrial water cycle is essential for sustainable water management and climate adaptation. Limited groundwater monitoring is difficult to use for the broad range of spatial and temporal scales hydrological studies, and it is difficult to distinguish between the effects of climate change and human activities in observations (Condon et al., 2021 ). Land surface and global climate models that consider human water use are effective for studying the impact of climate change and groundwater extraction on the terrestrial water cycle (Xie et al., 2018, 2020 ). Several studies have demonstrated that groundwater extraction alters the spatial and temporal distribution of soil water and groundwater, causing changes in evaporation, runoff, and infiltration processes (de Graaf et al., 2019; Dominguez et al., 2009; Douglas et al., 2006; Ozdogan et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2020 ). In particular, groundwater extraction for irrigation significantly alters water and heat fluxes, increasing local atmospheric humidity and the probability of convective precipitation (Dominguez et al., 2009; Douglas et al., 2006; Zeng et al., 2017b ). These studies have advanced the understanding of anthropogenic effects on the terrestrial water cycle, but the focus has been on historical variations, and there is a lack of future projections. Future projections from global climate models have been used to quantify the impact of climate change on the terrestrial water cycle under various climate scenarios (Arnell et al., 2019; Graham et al., 2020; McColl et al., 2022; Pokhrel et al., 2021 ). As population growth and socioeconomic development increase energy and food demand, water demand will also rise. With population growth, the consequent increase in agricultural water demand is one of the largest sources of groundwater depletion, especially in arid and semi-arid areas (Aeschbach-Hertig and Gleeson, 2012; Siebert et al., 2010; Wada et al., 2012 ). Socio-economic development, including increased industrial activities and living standards and the potential dependence of industry on groundwater for cooling and cleaning, will lead to increased groundwater extraction, thereby altering the natural water cycle (Sharma et al., 2021; Wakode et al., 2018 ). However, few studies have integrated the combined pressures of climate change and socioeconomic development or examined their impact on the terrestrial water cycle. Future climate warming and socioeconomic development will exacerbate global water scarcity, particularly affecting arid and semi-arid regions (Huang et al., 2021 ). By the end of the twenty-first century, crop water consumption could increase by 70 % in regions with significant irrigated area expansions, such as Central Asia, China, and the Middle East (Huang et al., 2019 ). These studies provide scientific guidance on the impact of climate change and socioeconomic development on water resources, but the changes in the terrestrial water cycle remain unclear. A recent study identified human effects on key water balance variables using a global hydrological model (Kåresdotter et al., 2022 ). However, potential hydrological responses under various future scenarios still need to be more understood. Currently, the literature lacks a systematic analysis of groundwater extraction projection that combines pressures of climate change and socioeconomic development and their effects on the terrestrial water cycle at the global scale. To address these research needs and contribute to bridging current gaps, this study aimed to assess the effects of climate change and groundwater extraction on the terrestrial water cycle under various future scenarios. To achieve this aim, we developed a groundwater extraction projection scheme based on the Shared Socio-economic pathway (SSP) and the Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) scenarios. We incorporated it into a global climate model, the Flexible Global Ocean–Atmosphere–Land System model grid-point version 3 (CAS-FGOALS-g3) (Li et al., 2020b ). Subsequently, numerical simulations assessed the effects of climate change and groundwater extraction on the terrestrial water cycle under five scenarios. We also explored the repercussions of groundwater extraction on groundwater storage within four key aquifers. The following sections discuss the potential effects of groundwater extraction on climate. We present a summary and further discussion in Section 4 .  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Climate model and experimental design The climate system model CAS-FGOALS-g3, developed by researchers at the Institute of Atmospheric Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, includes atmosphere, land, ocean, and sea ice components (Li et al., 2020b ). The land component is the Chinese Academy of Sciences land surface model (CAS-LSM), containing the human water regulation (HWR) scheme (Wang et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2018, 2020; Zeng et al., 2017b ). CAS-LSM utilizes a sub-grid hierarchy with land units, soil columns, and plant functional types in each grid cell. Weighted averages of sub-grid quantities represent the average value of a grid cell. Groundwater is considered as an unconfined aquifer lying below the soil column. The HWR scheme includes irrigation, industrial, and domestic water withdrawal from surface water or groundwater (Wang et al., 2020 ), focusing on groundwater extraction in this study. The groundwater extraction scheme updated the unconfined aquifer storage by subtracting the groundwater extraction quantities from the original unconfined aquifer storage (without considering groundwater extraction). Water used for irrigation is considered as precipitation into the surface soil. A portion of the water used for industrial and domestic is served as wastewater added to surface runoff, and the remainder is considered as evapotranspiration. The proportion of wastewater comes from Zeng et al (2017b) . This study estimates future terrestrial water cycle changes under five scenarios (Table S1 ): combinations of SSPs and RCPs in the Scenario Model Intercomparison Project (ScenarioMIP) (O’Neill et al., 2016 ). SSPs describe the society evolutions, consisting of sustainable development pathway SSP1, middle-of-the-road pathway SSP2, regional rivalry pathway SSP3, inequality pathway SSP4, and fossil-fueled development pathway SSP5 (O’Neill et al., 2016 ). RCPs describe the concentrations of greenhouse gases, aerosol emissions, reactive gases, and atmospheric constituents, influenced by changes in demographics, socioeconomics, energy consumption, and land use (Moss et al., 2010 ), including a high-emission pathway RCP8.5, two medium-emission pathways (RCP4.5 and RCP6.0), and a low-emission pathway RCP2.6. The SSPs and RCPs are combined to explore a wide range of possible future scenarios incorporating socioeconomic developments and climate policies. These combinations provide a more reasonable description of future scenarios and help determine the necessary mitigation and adaptation strategies (Nature Climate Change, 2019 ). Here, we focus on five scenarios (Table S1 ): a low vulnerability, low mitigation stress, and low radiative forcing scenario SSP126 (SSP1-RCP2.6, abbreviated as SSP26, similarly hereafter); a medium social vulnerability, medium radiative forcing scenario SSP245, high social vulnerability; a relatively high radiative forcing scenario SSP370; a medium forcing scenario SSP460; and a high radiative forcing scenario SSP585. Two simulation groups were conducted from 2015 to 2100 (Figure S1 ). The first group of simulations considered groundwater extraction, denoted as GW. The second group of simulations did not consider groundwater extraction, denoted as CTL. Each group comprised five future scenarios: SSP126, SSP245, SSP370, SSP460, and SSP585. The spatial resolution was set to 2° × 2° (decimal coordinate system), and the temporal resolution was to 1 h. Initial conditions were based on the outputs from the historical branch run of CAS-FGOALS-g3 in the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6). The physical scheme settings align with historical simulations, except for external forcings (including greenhouse gas concentrations, ozone concentrations, optical properties of anthropogenic aerosols, land use changes, etc.). Model results are sensitive to initial conditions due to internal variability. Performing ensemble simulations using different initial conditions and averaging the ensemble simulation results is one way to reduce the sensitivity (Koster et al., 2002, 2006 ). Ensemble simulations were performed for each scenario in CTL and GW simulations. Each scenario involved four simulations with different initial conditions labeled 1–4. Ensemble members with the same number (e.g., CTL-SSP126-2, GW-SSP126-2) shared the same initial conditions. To streamline the computational effort of the coupled simulations, the CTL experiments used outputs from the ScenarioMIP run with the CAS-FGOALS-g3 (Pu et al., 2020 ). Maintaining consistency with the CTL, the GW-SSP460 scenario contained one simulation. Consequently, there were two groups of CTL and GW, each containing four simulations per scenario (except for SSP460), totaling 34 simulated results. For each scenario, the difference in the ensemble mean between GW and CTL was used for analysis. Before starting the simulation, water used for irrigation, industry, and domestic needs to be estimated for each scenario.  2.2 Estimating future groundwater extraction For each scenario, we estimated the spatial and temporal distribution of irrigated, industrial, and domestic water demand at a global scale (Figure S1 ). The ratio of water supplied by groundwater followed historical statistics (Zeng et al., 2017b ). GDP and population data are common and readily available explanatory variables for industrial and domestic water demand estimation (Hanasaki et al., 2013 ). Two datasets were used for non-irrigation water demand (industrial and domestic). The first set from the Inter-Sectoral Impact Model Intercomparison Project (ISIMIP) provided the spatial distribution of population and GDP under the SSP126 scenario at 0.5° spatial resolution (Murakami & Yamagata, 2016 ) and was interpolated to 2° resolution. This data explicitly takes into account the spatial and socio-economic interactions between cities, and it captures the differences between urban and non-urban areas in a more rational way (Murakami & Yamagata, 2016 ). The second dataset comprised country-level population and GDP data at five-year intervals from the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) and the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) for various scenarios from 2010 to 2100 (Dellink et al., 2017 ; KC & Lutz, 2017 ; Riahi et al., 2017 ). The dataset takes a more comprehensive view of the drivers of economic growth, is calibrated for 184 countries, and provides forecasts for the entire 21st century (Dellink et al., 2017 ). We downscaled the country-level data to gridded data for 2015–2100 based on the ISO 3166–1 code. Subsequently, non-irrigation water demand in 2003 (Zeng et al., 2017b ) served as a reference. Selecting 2003 as the baseline for non-irrigation water demand estimation was underpinned by the availability of comprehensive and well-documented data in the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations global water information system for the year. This dataset encompasses global irrigation statistics and the water utilization ratio for agricultural, industrial, and domestic purposes. Notably, non-irrigation water use exhibits a stronger correlation with population and economic expansion (Wang et al., 2020; Zenget al., 2017b ). Hence, it is logical and pragmatic to extrapolate future industrial and domestic water demand patterns under varying climate scenarios by anchoring the analysis on the 2003 non-irrigation water use statistics while considering population and economic data. We used three datasets to estimate irrigation water demand in this study. The first dataset was the monthly output data of five climate scenarios for 2015–2100 from the climate system model CAS-FGOALS-g3 (Li et al., 2020b ). The dataset contained precipitation, net radiation, soil heat flux, wind speed at 2 m height, and air temperature at a spatial resolution of 2° × 2°. The second dataset was the land cover change under five scenarios provided by the Land-Use Harmonization 2 (LUHv2) project (Hurtt et al., 2020 ). It was developed by various integrated assessment models (Popp et al., 2017 ) to obtain changes in the irrigated and rain-fed crop areas globally from 2015 to 2100, and the resolution is 0.5° × 0.5°. Since the LUHv2 data was produced based on the SSP storylines, no additional assumptions were made for this study. The LUHv2 provides only changes in irrigated area for C3 and C4 crops.
