This data, derived through a top-down approach and combined with statistical data (including water use, irrigated area, etc., provided by FAO global water information system), has been fully validated for its reliability in reproducing hydrological variables (soil moisture, groundwater table depth, etc.) and successfully employed in global and regional modeling (Xie et al., 2018, 2020 ). Fig. 1   shows the temporal changes in global human water demand from 1965 to 2100. Global human water demand is projected in the SSP370 scenario to grow from 4,500 km3  in 2010 to almost 8,000 km3  in 2100. For irrigation, the changes in water demand for varied scenarios are consistent with the irrigated area (Figure S2 ). For instance, in the SSP370 scenario, LUHv2 predicts that the irrigated area could reach 3.8 × 106  km2  in 2100 (Figure S2 ), a reasonable estimate compared to the globally available irrigated area of 4.03 × 106  km2  (Bruinsma, 2003 ). Consequently, the water demand for irrigation in this scenario is projected to be nearly 5000 km3  year−1 . Domestic water demand varies according to population growth, with the SSP3 scenario showing a significant increase in population (Figure S3 ) and, consequently, a higher predicted domestic water demand. Industrial water demand also varies significantly between scenarios, with the SSP5 scenario evincing a notable increase in industrial water demand, primarily attributed to increased production. Despite the close GDP values of the SSP1 and SSP2 scenarios, the industrial water demand in the SSP1 scenario is slightly lower than in SSP2, owing to the lower water intensity in the former (Section 2.2 ). The verification of water demand accuracy in this study is challenging due to variations in methodologies and assumptions across various socioeconomic scenarios. Comparisons with previous studies (Alcamo et al., 2007; Hanasaki et al., 2013; Hayashi et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2008 ) reveal that this study's projected water demand falls within reasonable ranges (Fig. 2  ). Hayashi et al. (2013)  assumed that the model parameters were consistent with the historical period and obtained results that closely align with the projected water demand (both domestic and industrial) in the SSP2 scenario present in our study. Alcamo et al. (2007)  estimated domestic water demand using an intensity change rate of 400 L person-1  day−1 , close to the SSP3 scenario assumption in our study. Consequently, Alcamo et al. (2007)  estimated domestic water demand comparable to the projected results in the SSP3 scenario. Overall, the water demand projection in this study is consistent with the scenario description and previous studies and includes the main scenarios of future socio-economic and climate change. The spatial distribution of groundwater extraction under different scenarios throughout the 21st century within 2015–2100 (Figure S4 ) indicates no significant difference in groundwater extraction patterns. The hotpots of groundwater extraction remain concentrated in the central United States, India, and the North China Plain. However, there are notable variations in groundwater extraction trends among scenarios. Specifically, in the central United States, there is a clear increasing trend in groundwater extraction under SSP585 (Fig. 3  ). In India and Pakistan, groundwater extraction increases substantially under SSP370 and SSP585, associated with the expanded irrigated area. The apparent reduction in groundwater extraction in the North China Plain under sustainable and unequal development scenarios (SSP126 and SSP460) is mainly related to the reduced irrigated area under these scenarios.  3.2 Spatiotemporal changes in terrestrial water cycle We used the coupled modeling results to investigate the impact of climate change and groundwater extraction on the terrestrial water cycle under various future scenarios. First, we examined the spatial and temporal variations in terrestrial hydrological variables. The temporal trends of precipitation, surface runoff, evapotranspiration, and surface soil moisture (0–10 cm) simulated by the GW experiment for 2015–2100 are presented in Figure S5 . Globally, the annual precipitation increases under all scenarios, most significantly under the medium-to-high and high-emission scenarios (SSP370 and SSP585). The annual temperature rises before 2060 under all scenarios but gradually reduces under the medium emissions scenarios (SSP245 and SSP460). The temperature increase in the medium-to-high emission scenario, SSP370, falls between the medium and high forcing scenarios. As a result of the rising temperature, evapotranspiration tends to increase in all scenarios, the surface runoff decreases, and surface soil moisture decreases significantly (−4.2 × 10-5  mm3  mm−3  year−1 ). Fig. 4   illustrates the spatial distribution trends in annual average (2015–2100) surface soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and runoff under different scenarios obtained from the GW ensemble simulation. Surface soil moisture exhibited a drying trend in all scenarios, with rates of 9 × 10-4 , 3.6 × 10-4 , 7 × 10-4 , 7.1 × 10-4 , and 4.7 × 10-4  mm3  mm−3  year−1 . Under the low emission scenario SSP126, 22 % of the areas show a notable surface soil drying trend. For the medium emission scenarios (SSP245 and SSP460), 25–33 % of the areas undergo significant drying. Meanwhile, under the medium-to-high and high emissions scenarios (SSP370 and SSP585), 25–29 % of the areas exhibited a considerable drying trend. Overall, there was an approximately equal distribution between areas experiencing soil drying (51–56 %) and those undergoing soil wetting (44–49 %) under all scenarios. Notably, a higher proportion of soils displayed drying tendencies under the medium emission scenario, while the low emission scenarios (especially in the tropical rainforest region of South America and central Africa) demonstrated more substantial changes in soil conditions. Evapotranspiration increases under all scenarios, with a substantial increase in 11–13 % of the area under the medium-to-high and high emissions scenarios (SSP370 and SSP585) and 9 % under the low emission scenario SSP126. For the medium emission scenarios (SSP245 and SSP460), 10 %-12 % of the areas show an increase in evapotranspiration, representing an intermediate trend between the low and high emission scenarios. From Fig. 4  (c, f, i, l, and o), the surface runoff increases under the SSP245 and SSP585 at 0.007 and 0.012 mm year−1 , respectively. In contrast, SSP126, SSP370, and SSP460 evinced decreased runoff rates at −0.035, −0.017, and −0.04 mm year−1 , respectively. Similar to evapotranspiration, changes in surface runoff under the medium emission scenarios (SSP245 and SSP460) fell between the low and high emission scenarios. As depicted in Fig. 4  and S6, the spatial patterns of the hydrological variables trends under various scenarios are relatively consistent with changes in precipitation in most regions of the world, except for the United States, the Middle East, and Australia. The Midwest region of the United States shows a significant drying trend in the SSP460 scenario, while the other scenarios show either a drying or no pronounced trend. In contrast, the Middle East exhibits a significant wetting trend in the SSP245 scenario, while other scenarios indicate a drying trend. Additionally, evapotranspiration significantly increases in Australia under the SSP460 scenario, while other scenarios demonstrate either localized increases or no prominent trend. Tropical rainforests in South America, southern Africa, India, and southeastern Australia exhibit notable soil drying accompanied by reduced evapotranspiration and surface runoff due to declining precipitation and rising temperatures. In contrast, southern South America, northeastern Asia, and central Africa experience increased precipitation, resulting in increased soil moisture and surface runoff.  3.3 Potential effects of groundwater extraction on terrestrial water cycle The effects of groundwater extraction on the terrestrial water cycle under various scenarios are depicted in Figs. 5-7    . These figures present differences and relative differences in surface soil moisture, surface runoff, and evapotranspiration averaged over the 2015–2100 period, as simulated by GW and CTL. Fig. 5  illustrates the persistent influence of groundwater extraction on surface soil moisture across all future scenarios, with notable effects in the central United States, the North China Plain, and northern India. Irrigation is considered as precipitation into the surface soil in the model. Even with a declining trend in groundwater extraction in the North China Plain under the SSP460 scenario, it substantially affects soil moisture. Notably, the North China Plain and northern India reveal a significant increase in soil moisture, with approximately 0.03 mm3  mm−3  and a remarkable 40 % rise. Conversely, the increase in soil moisture is less but still notable, ranging from 5 % to 10 % in the central United States compared to the North China Plain and northern India. This is because the magnitude of groundwater extraction in the central United States is smaller than in northern India and North China Plain (Figure S4 ). The irrigated area reduced in most of the North China Plain in SSP126 and SSP460 scenarios and the irrigation-induced increase in surface soil moisture is smaller than in the other scenarios. Changes in surface runoff due to groundwater extraction from wastewater generated by industrial and domestic water use. Fig. 6  depicts the influence of groundwater extraction on surface runoff. In regions characterized by intensive groundwater extraction, such as the central United States, northern India, Pakistan, and the North China Plain, surface runoff experiences a notable increase of approximately 10–20 mm year−1 . The increase is statistically significant at a 95 % confidence level in a Student's t -test under the SSP370 and SSP585 scenarios. The surge in surface runoff in these scenarios can be attributed to population growth and the expansion of manufacturing industries, leading to increased water utilization for industrial and domestic purposes and enhanced surface runoff resulting from industrial and domestic wastewater discharge. Industrial water demand in the central United States shows a decreasing trend of 0.15 mm year−1  under the SSP370 scenario, and the change in surface runoff in this region is small compared to the other scenarios. In northern India, industrial water demand shows a significant increase trend (0.84 mm year−1 ) under the SSP585 scenario but no significant increase in surface runoff due to the gradual decrease in domestic water demand as a result of the decline in the population (Figure S3 ). Fig. 7  presents the implications of groundwater extraction on evapotranspiration. Regions with extensive groundwater extraction show a prominent increase in evapotranspiration (0.1 to 0.3 mm day−1 ), statistically significant at a 95 % confidence level. The heightened evapotranspiration is primarily attributed to the augmented soil moisture in irrigated areas. Under the SSP585 scenario, the influence of groundwater extraction on evapotranspiration is more pronounced, driven by increased irrigation water use. This effect is mainly ascribed to the Middle East, where evapotranspiration increases by approximately 30 %. A portion of the increase in evapotranspiration also comes from industrial and domestic water use. Under the SSP370 scenario, industrial water demand in the central U.S. shows a slight downward trend (0.15 mm year−1 ), and groundwater extraction is less than in northern India and the North China Plain, so the increase in evapotranspiration in this region is weaker than in the other scenarios and other areas.  3.4 Potential effects of groundwater extraction on groundwater storage The above analysis emphasizes the significant impact of groundwater extraction on the terrestrial water cycle in over-exploited regions. Prolonged groundwater extraction has continuously declined the groundwater table, directly affecting groundwater storage. Consequently, we further explored the repercussions of groundwater exploitation on groundwater storage. Figure S7  illustrates the groundwater storage trends under various future scenarios, revealing a significant reduction in groundwater storage within regions of extensive groundwater exploitation, such as the North China Plain, central United States, and northern India. Changes in groundwater storage are less pronounced in other areas, prompting a more detailed investigation into the impact of groundwater extraction on water storage changes within four key aquifers (Fig. 8  ). Considering the general spatial consistency in groundwater storage changes across the five scenarios, we focused on the average value of groundwater storage changes for the scenarios. Fig. 8  provides the time series of groundwater storage changes in major aquifers modeled by the GW experiment under future scenarios. Notably, in major agricultural regions, such as the Southern Plains of the USA, the Middle East, northwest India, and the North China Plain, a significant decline in future groundwater storage is projected when accounting for groundwater extraction. In the bar chart, the red and blue colors represent the trends in groundwater storage modeled by the GW and CTL experiments, respectively. This result underscores that excessive groundwater pumping alters the groundwater storage trend compared to scenarios without groundwater extraction, especially in the Southern Plains of the USA, where the increasing trend in groundwater storage becomes negative. Subsequently, the attribution of groundwater storage changes using regression methods (Wu et al., 2020 ), as Figure S8  depicts. Due to the similarity of the attribution results between various scenarios, only the results under the SSP245 scenario are shown here. The findings indicate that when the model only considers the influence of climatic factors (in humid regions, such as Southeast Asia and South America), changes in groundwater storage are mainly associated with precipitation. In high-latitude regions, groundwater storage changes are predominantly correlated with snowfall variations. However, in irrigated agriculture regions, changes in groundwater extraction emerge as the crucial factor affecting groundwater storage. Combined with the results presented in Fig. 8 , it is evident that future human groundwater extraction will perpetuate groundwater depletion in crucial irrigated regions without water conservation policies. This deduction presents a severe challenge to conserving terrestrial water resources.   4 Discussion 4.1 Potential effects of groundwater extraction on climate This study assessed the effects of climate change and groundwater extraction on the terrestrial water cycle under various future scenarios. Groundwater extraction and utilization alters land hydrological processes, providing a climate feedback through land–atmosphere interactions. In the subsequent analysis, we utilize the results from two ensemble simulations presented in the above sections, GW and CTL, to assess the influence of groundwater extraction on near-surface temperature, precipitation, wind, and vapor advection. Our previous studies have explored the historical climatic impact of groundwater extraction, with a particular emphasis on the cooling effect in the Indian and Pakistani regions (Wang et al., 2020 ). As such, our current focus is evaluating the effects of groundwater extraction on near-surface temperatures in the Indian region under various scenarios. Fig. 9   illustrates the difference in 850 hPa temperatures between the GW and CTL ensemble simulations for varying periods under varied future scenarios in the Indian region. Notably, in the short-term future (2015–2040), the cooling effect attributed to groundwater extraction will remain prominent (Fig. 9 ). During this period, there is no significant distinction in the cooling impact between the medium emission scenarios (SSP245 and SSP460) and the high emission scenarios (SSP370 and SSP585). This absence of differentiation can be attributed to the relatively consistent levels of groundwater extraction across these scenarios in the Indian region (Figure S4 ). Nonetheless, it is essential to underscore that the cooling effect attributed to groundwater extraction diminishes in the mid-term (2041–2066) and end-term (2067–2100) under the medium emission scenarios (SSP245 and SSP460). This decline in the cooling effect could be attributed to the stabilization of irrigation water during the mid-to-late 21st century, as indicated by the reduced irrigated area under the medium emission scenarios (Figure S2 ). Consequently, it results in a reduced cooling impact associated with irrigation. Further, we investigated the climatic implications of groundwater extraction by comparing the difference between the summer precipitation, the summer 200 and 850 hPa wind fields, and the vertically integrated water vapor advection field simulated by the GW and CTL. Similarly, the climatic effects of groundwater extraction are studied only for the focal areas. Fig. 10   shows the spatial distribution of ensemble-averaged GW-CTL differences in climatic variables averaged over 2015–2100 for the Indian region. The summer precipitation reduced in the Indian region at a rate of 0.3 to 1 mm day−1 . This reduction is particularly pronounced under the medium emission scenarios (SSP245 and SSP460). Notably, the impact of groundwater extraction on precipitation remains insignificant under the low-emission scenario SSP126. The changes in summer precipitation correspond to alterations in the circulation and the water vapor advection fields. Within regions experiencing reduced summer precipitation, the circulation anomalies in the 850 hPa pressure surface opposite the Indian monsoon during the summer counteract the monsoon precipitation. Concurrently, water vapor advection anomalies, moving from the continent to the ocean, diminish water vapor transport from the ocean to the land by the monsoon, resulting in decreased summer precipitation. Figures S9 and S10  present the discrepancies in climatic variables for eastern China and central United States, with values representing multi-year averages from 2015 to 2100. Notably, the impact of groundwater extraction on summer precipitation aligns with historical findings. In eastern China and the central United States, summer precipitation slightly increases at approximately 0.3 to 1 mm day−1 . In eastern China, groundwater extraction for irrigation increases localized soil moisture, which in turn causes land–atmosphere interactions (Zeng et al., 2017b ), enhancing convective precipitation and increasing summer precipitation. This increase in eastern China is statistically significant, with a 95 % confidence level in a Student's t -test. For the central United States, groundwater extraction is less than in eastern China and northern India, and there is less variability in the wind and water vapor advection fields, resulting in less variability in summer precipitation (Figure S10 ). Acknowledging the considerable uncertainties in assessing the climatic effects of groundwater extraction is crucial. These uncertainties arose from the imperfect representation of physical processes, the complexity of atmospheric dynamics, and the limited number of ensemble members used in the simulations. The results provided in this study, particularly concerning the cooling and precipitation effects in the Indian region, explain potential mechanisms based on simulation results.  4.2 Implications for water management and adaptation measures This study highlights regions where groundwater storage will change with changes in climate and groundwater extraction, which can be applied to water resources management to reduce the impacts of climate change and human activities, reducing water scarcity. Specifically, suppose a region does not experience a significant increase in the irrigated area in a future scenario, but the irrigation water demand increases. In that case, we can understand the region's climatic and socio-economic drivers, leading to more efficient and rational water resource management. For example, for northwestern India, groundwater extraction shows a significant increasing trend under SSP126, SSP370, and SSP585 scenarios (Fig. 3 ). Comparing the changes in the irrigated area, precipitation, and temperature, the increase in irrigated area is the main factor behind the increase in groundwater extraction in the SSP1 scenario (Fig. 3 ). In contrast, in the SSP370 and SSP585 scenarios, it is related to agricultural water deficit due to a warming climate (Figure S6 ). For the vast water demands arising from expanding irrigated areas in the SSP126 scenario in northwestern India, efficient agricultural management techniques can improve yields; for example, diversified and intense cropping systems and additional tile drains and increased fertilizers (Niroula et al., 2023 ). In the SSP370 and SSP585 scenarios, distributed policy scheme (Du et al., 2022 ) and the development of water transfer systems may help reduce the local water scarcity in northwestern India. In the SSP370 scenario, technological processes develop slowly, accompanied by high GDP; more water will be consumed for industrial production, especially for densely populated and industrially developed regions such as northern China. Keeping a balance between continued water demand and water sustainability remains a challenge. Industrial water recycling and reuse and distributed stormwater management systems may be helpful in urban water management. In the Southern Plains of the United States, results indicated a reduction in groundwater storage due to groundwater extraction even though there is no significant expansion in irrigated areas. Mitigating groundwater scarcity by creating new agricultural infrastructure, reusing wastewater, and recharging aquifers. Equally important is that encourage lower water demand and increase water efficiency. In addition, our results indicated that excessive groundwater extraction in northern India may alter circulation and the water vapor advection fields and then reduce summer precipitation. Projected precipitation shows a slight decrease almost for all future scenarios in northern India, accompanied by excessive groundwater pumping and reduced summer precipitation; future water supply is a challenge. Thus, potential adaptation measures that could help mitigate the adverse effects of groundwater extraction on climate are urgently needed. For example, optimizing cropping systems, improvements in water use efficiency to reduce irrigation water consumption, and mitigating impacts on climate without compromising food security and economic benefit (Yin et al., 2022 ).  4.3 Limitations and uncertainties This study underscores the complex interplay between groundwater extraction and hydroclimate within an evolving environment, emphasizing the critical need for effective water resource management to mitigate future water stress. However, it should be acknowledged that there are still some limitations in the present study. First, estimates of groundwater extraction can be further refined. Limited by data availability, we only considered the main drivers and made simple assumptions for different scenarios, and although the overall projections are consistent with the scenario descriptions and previous studies (see section 3.1 ), more detailed descriptions and assumptions (such as industrial transformation and human lifestyle) are needed for the future. Estimates of future irrigation water demand also need to take into account the impact of agricultural policies, such as constraining irrigation water demand with targets for enhancing crop yields and reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Climate change and extreme events (like heat waves) also influence it, increasing urban domestic and industrial cooling water demand. The current industrial and domestic water demand estimation primarily relies on demographic and economic data. Future work should focus on refining the groundwater extraction estimation process, explicitly accounting for the impact of extreme climate events on water demand. In addition, quantifying the impacts of climate change projections on water demand and their possible climate feedbacks using multiple global climate models and assessing the uncertainties associated with climate projections also require further consideration. On the other hand, the description of the HWR in the model could be further refined. The construction and operation of reservoirs and large-scale water projects, such as the Three Gorges Dam and the South-to-North Water Diversion Project, profoundly impact ecosystems and alter the water and material cycle processes (Long et al., 2020 ). These projects significantly modified land surface and subsurface characteristics, subsequently affecting land surface processes and atmospheric interactions. While this study primarily considers HWR as groundwater extraction, future work should incorporate the dynamics of reservoirs into land surface models to represent human activities more comprehensively. In addition, groundwater extraction can affect surface–groundwater interactions by changing groundwater levels. The model used in this study included a groundwater lateral flow module. Still, this module was not activated due to the large computational resource requirements of the global ensemble simulations and the specific question to be addressed in this study. Future studies are needed to more closely examine the effects of groundwater extraction on hydrological processes in climate system models. Moreover, note that the model used in this study has a relatively coarse spatial resolution (2° × 2°), thus missing some detailed processes, such as the influence of topography and heterogeneity in hydraulic properties. However, this study focuses on the global scale and some overexploited plains areas. The model's sub-grid structure can characterize the average state of each 2° grid, making it suitable for large-scale studies. High-resolution simulations are necessary for future in-depth studies at regional scales.   5 Conclusions This study developed groundwater extraction projection schemes incorporating climate scenarios, global population density, GDP, and irrigation data. We conducted two group-coupled simulations from 2015 through 2100 using the climate system model CAS-FGOALS-g3 to illustrate the consequences of groundwater extraction on the terrestrial water cycle under various scenarios. The results indicate that expanding irrigated areas will significantly influence the variation in irrigation water demand. The irrigation water demand under SSP370 scenario is projected to be nearly 5000 km3  year−1 . Meanwhile, industrial water demand is closely associated with manufacturing production and water use intensity. Under future scenarios, variations in soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and runoff align with changes in precipitation. The proportion of surface soil drying due to warming is 3 %-11 % more in the medium- and high-emission scenarios than in the low-emission scenario. Excessive groundwater pumping alters the trend of groundwater storage, with more pronounced effects in the Southern Plains of the United States. In major irrigated areas, such as the central United States, the Middle East, northwestern India, and northern China, groundwater extraction is the primary driver of declining groundwater storage. In the northern India regions, the cooling effect of groundwater extraction weakens under the medium emission scenarios (SSP245 and SSP460) during the mid-to-late 21st century, coinciding with stabilized irrigation water usage and reduced irrigated area under these scenarios. Over-exploitation in northern India may cause a reduction in summer precipitation, suggesting that future adaptation measures are imminent to mitigate the negative climate impacts of localized over-exploitation. This study quantitatively analyzed future groundwater extraction and evaluated its implications on the terrestrial water cycle and climate. This study will provide scientific guidance for policymakers to manage and plan for water resources supply under future climate scenarios. Future research can perform detailed case studies in regions with significant groundwater extraction issues, such as the North China Plain, the Southern Plains of the United States, and northern India, to develop region-specific insights and solutions. Moreover, exploring innovative water resources management practices, such as managed aquifer recharge to enhance groundwater sustainability, ultimately contributes to more sustainable water resource management practices.
1 Introduction Floods are among the most catastrophic natural disasters, impacting enormous sections of the Earth's surface and having long-term consequences (Amiri et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024 ). Coastal flooding, on the other hand, is a severe environmental and socioeconomic concern threatening the livelihoods of people in coastal regions across the globe (Edmonds et al., 2020; Nicholls and Cazenave, 2010 ). These effects are not only destructive to infrastructure, including roads, buildings, aquaculture, and agricultural land but also to coral reefs and coastal wetlands (Asiri et al., 2024; Ebtehaj and Bonakdari, 2022 ). The convergence of coastal and inland flooding has emerged as a pressing issue due to the intricate interplay between oceanic phenomena (such as storm surges, astronomical tides, and wave runups) and hydrological processes (including rainfall and land use changes) (Ganguli and Merz, 2019; Najibi et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023 ). Extreme river flows caused by severe rainfall can have devastating downstream consequences; compound flooding can dramatically exacerbate flood risks and have an even greater impact on the coastal areas (Fang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2023 ). With the increasing global mean sea level rise (IPCC, 2021 ), it is critical to understand the complex interplay of coastal and inland flooding in order to develop appropriate and effective coastal flood adaptation strategies. Investigation into the causes of compound flooding has been brought to attention recently (Du et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024 ). Researchers have used estimates of increasing sea levels and changing weather patterns to predict the escalation of compound floods (Wahl et al., 2015 ). Several factors were also taken into account, including the effects of tide, river flow, rainfall, and wind (Du et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024 ), sea level rise, land subsidence, and tropical cyclones (Wu et al., 2024 ). This phenomenon was further investigated by taking into consideration the extreme sea level rise, as mentioned by (Harrison et al., 2022; Liang and Zhou, 2022 ). Despite various study attempts, there is a limited comprehension of the oversight of coastal regions that are entirely encircled by the ocean rather than being impacted by individual areas. Specifically, when high tides occur, the outlets may get immersed in ocean water, leading to water flowing back into the drainage system and significantly reducing its capacity (Wang et al., 2019 ). While tides might have spatially nonuniform variations between locations, addressing ocean water fluctuations simultaneously in a particular event could be complicated for regional models, particularly for an island. This is because the discontinuity of the loose coupling at the ocean boundary may result in specific gaps and mismatches between the inland and coastal models (Yang et al., 2023 ). Moreover, the reflection of hydro infrastructure (e.g. bridge and culverts), which is an important factor for flood models, might also be complex because of the enormous number of structures or missing dimension information that cannot be easily integrated within flood models. Traditional approaches often focus on individual watersheds depending on available data (Kang et al., 2009; Mourad et al., 2022; Mukherjee et al., 2024 ) or using machine learning for the inspection of the structures based on historical data. However, implementing these techniques in the context of pluvial floods might be difficult owing to limited data availability and the need for extensive manual configurations in regional models. Therefore, this study aims to fill the gap by (i) carrying out a comprehensive flood model on coastal communities under current and future climate and (ii) proposing an automated approach for determining hydro infrastructure within the basins. The novelty of this research is that it employs a regional flood model to address the current gaps in combined coastal–inland flooding for an island, which somewhat differs from traditional studies when dealing with loose coupling at the ocean boundary. Prior to the simulations, a sensitivity analysis was undertaken, which included evaluating alternative warm-up durations and model parameters. In addition, the automated detection of the hydro infrastructure technique may be helpful for large-scale flood studies. In particular, each model configuration process has been optimized rigorously through the use of several automated procedures. The adoption of both municipal and island-wide models reveals important constraints in model simulations regarding mesh refinement and hydro-connection aspects. These limits present an important opportunity for future studies to identify the most effective ways for model designs. Surrounded by the Atlantic Ocean, Prince Edward Island (PEI), the smallest province in Canada, is susceptible to climate change, consisting of intense and frequent storm surges, coastal erosion, and floods (Chown and Froneman, 2008; Pang et al., 2023 ). In spite of the endeavours undertaken by the Government of PEI, including the recently introduced Coastal Hazards Information Platform (CHIP) (EECA, 2023 ), which furnishes maps of coastal flooding based on various storm surge and sea level rise scenarios, the region continues to lack information depicting pluvial flooding, typically caused by heavy rainfall associated with sea level rise. Therefore, PEI was selected as a particular case of this study. The findings of this research will be used by the Government of PEI to plan and manage flood hazards for adapting to future climate change in PEI (Government-of-PEI, 2024 ).  2 Study area The province of PEI is situated within the Gulf of St. Lawrence along the eastern coast of Canada between latitudes 45°57′ and 47°04′ N and longitudes 61°55′ and 64°25′ W, stands as the smallest and most densely populated province in Canada (see Fig. 1  ). The province has an area of 5,681 km2  and has a population of more than 154,000 as of 2021 (Statistics-Canada, 2023 ). According to the Census of Statistics Canada, PEI has a total of 98 Census Subdivisions (CSDs) in 2021. The City of Charlottetown, City of Summerside, Town of Stratford, Town of Three Rivers, and Town of Cornwall, together with the Town of Tignish, are PEI's most populated community centres, serving vital urban functions for the residents. Lennox Island and Abegweit-Scotchfort are the island's largest two Mi'kmaq First Nation reserves. Geographically, PEI has altitudes ranging from sea level to 140 m, with characteristic red soil, red sand beaches, coastal sand dunes, and vast agricultural areas. The Land Use Land Cover (LULC) types across PEI are dominated by cropland and mixed forest, covering 45 % and 39 % of the total land area, respectively (Government-of-PEI, 2003 ). The remaining land consists of wetlands (6 %), transportation (2 %), residential (2 %), urban (1 %), industrial (1 %), and others (4 %) (Dau et al., 2023 ). PEI typically experiences a cool and humid climate, marked by prolonged and mild winters (November – April) with temperatures ranging from −3 to −11 °C, while the summers (June – August) tend to be moderately warm, with temperatures ranging from 20 to 34 °C (Dau et al., 2023 ). The annual average precipitation measures around 1,100 mm, with 80 % attributed to rainfall and the remaining 20 % to snowfall (Bhatti et al., 2022 ). PEI streams are small, shallow, and short, with lengths of less than 16 km; therefore, the flows cannot accelerate rapidly but rather meander and spread out. The province is vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change, notably the increased frequency of storm surges and extreme rainfall, causing flooding in both inland and coastal zones.  3 Materials and methods 3.1 Data sources The High-Resolution Digital Elevation Model (HRDEM) with a 1 m × 1 m resolution is obtained from Natural Resources Canada (NRCan). The HRDEM is derived from airborne LiDAR data and refers to the Canadian Geodetic Vertical Datum of 2013 (CGVD2013), which is the reference standard for heights across Canada. The LULC data in 2020 with a 10 m × 10 m resolution was obtained from the Environmental Systems Research Institute (ESRI). The LULC data is developed using Sentinel-2 satellite imagery from the European Space Agency (ESA) in collaboration with Microsoft and Impact Observatory partners. It was later reclassed based on the United States Geological Survey (USGS) National Land Cover Database (NLCD). The LULC requires soil data to estimate the infiltration and rainfall losses in rainfall-runoff models. The soil data was obtained from the Government of PEI based on survey data between 1970 and 1978. It is further reclassified into four Hydrologic Soil Groups (HSG) based on the soil’s runoff potential according to the Natural Resource Conservation Services (NRCS) guidelines. Although the roadway and watercourse network are not direct inputs in modeling, they are essential to guide model setups, such as mesh refinement, culvert setup, field visits, DEM breaching, etc. Therefore, it is imperative to include this network in the model to reflect the physical conditions in the basins. These data are freely available from the Government of PEI’s Open Data Portal (https://data.princeedwardisland.ca ). Other hydraulic structures, such as culverts and bridges, were also derived from the PEI Department of Transportation and Infrastructure (DTI). Due to data limitations that only cover culverts with a span width greater than 1.2 m, information on certain key dimensions is still unavailable. As a result, field visits have been conducted to the major communities, like Charlottetown, Summerside, Stratford, Cornwall, and Three Rivers (mainly Montague and Georgetown), in the summer of 2023. The CHIP prepared by the Department of Environment, Energy and Climate Action (EECA, 2023 ) for PEI was referred to as ocean boundary conditions in hydraulic models.  3.2 Rainfall IDF curves and climate change Rainfall data is crucial for pluvial flood modeling as it aims to simulate floods caused by extreme rainfall events. This study used the existing rainfall Intensity-Duration-Frequency (IDF) curves (Kourtis et al., 2023; Padulano et al., 2021; Skougaard Kaspersen et al., 2017 ) under current and future climate conditions developed by the Environmental on Climate Change Canada (ECCC). In particular, two sets of IDF curves (current climate and future climate) were developed to generate pluvial flood maps for PEI. The current climate condition is based on the historical rainfall IDF curves, which are solely based on historical rainfall data from existing weather stations. In contrast, future climate conditions are based on the climate change-scaled IDF curves under the SSP5-8.5 for 2071–2100, obtained from the ECCC. In detail, future rainfall rates are estimated by scaling the historical IDF values according to the Clausius-Clapeyron relationship. This implies that for every 1 °C of temperature increase, the water-holding capacity of the atmosphere would increase by about 7 %. The difference between projected future temperature and historical temperature is then combined with historical rainfall rates underlying the Clausius Clapeyron relationship to scale the rainfall rates and the 95 % confidence limits for future climate conditions. The Annual Maximum Series method was later used to estimate precipitation amounts corresponding to return periods based on the Gumbel distribution. Four commonly used return periods were considered in this study, consisting of 10-year, 25-year, 50-year, and 100-year. In order to provide time series rainfall inputs for hydraulic models, the Chicago method (Keifer and Chu, 1957; Lopes da Silveira, 2016 ) was used to generate the 24-hour hyetographs from the selected IDF curves, as described in Eq. (1) .(1) i t  = a t + b    n       where, i t    is the rainfall intensity (mm/hour); t   is the duration of rainfall (minutes or hours); and a , b , and n  are IDF constants that represent local conditions and the return period. In association with the IDF curves, an additional parameter required for computation is r,  which is the ratio of time to peak over the total storm duration. Based on the internal investigation, it was found that the average concentration–time for all watersheds in PEI is around 8.4 h. Therefore, a symmetric hyetograph (i.e., r = 0.5) is used here to allow sufficient time for surface runoff to concentrate.  3.3 Flood simulations with HEC-RAS 2D model The two-dimensional Hydrologic Engineering Center – River Analysis System (HEC-RAS 2D, version 6.4.1), developed by the US Army Corps of Engineers (Brunner, 2016 ), was used in this pluvial flood modeling. HEC-RAS is a widely used tool for flood modeling, sediment transport, and water quality analysis (Costabile et al., 2021; Dau et al., 2017; David and Schmalz, 2020; Desalegn and Mulu, 2021; Zeiger and Hubbart, 2021 ). The unsteady flow analysis, governed by the principle of conservation of mass and momentum, was used for model simulation. By assuming a constant water density, the mass conservation (or continuity equation) for shallow water flow is formulated by Eq. (2) , and the momentum conservation for a non-conservative form (Newton’s Second Law) is expressed by Eq. (3) . The system of mass and momentum equations is called the Shallow Water Equations (SWE), sometimes referred to as the Full Momentum or Navier-Stokes equations (Brunner, 2016 ).(2) ∂ h  ∂ t   + ∇ ∙ h V    = q     (3) ∂ V   ∂ t   + V  ∙ ∇   V  + f c  k  × V  = - g ∇ z s  + 1 h  ∇ ∙ v  t  h ∇ V    - τ  b  ρ R   + τ  s  ρ h       where, ∂ h  ∂ t     is the rate of change of water depth h   with respect to time t  ; ∇ ∙ h V       is the divergence of the product of water depth h   and the velocity vector V   ; q   is water source/sink; ∂ V   ∂ t     is the rate of change of velocity vector V   ; V  ∙ ∇   V     is the convective acceleration, which represents the change in velocity; f c  k  × V     is the Coriolis acceleration (a result of the earths’ rotation), where f c    is the Coriolis parameter and k    is the unit vector in the vertical direction; - g ∇ z s     is the gravitational force, where g   is the acceleration due to gravity and z s    is the bed elevation; 1 h  ∇ ∙ v  t  h ∇ V       is the diffusion, representing the effects of viscosity where v  t    is the turbulent viscosity; τ  b  ρ R     is the bottom friction where τ  b    is the bottom shear stress, ρ   is the water density, and R   is the hydraulic radius; and τ  s  ρ h     is the surface stress, accounting for wind stress or other surface forces. The HEC-RAS 2D model has several advantages, such as (i) its ability to represent hydro-infrastructure such as bridges, culverts, etc. accurately, (ii) supporting mesh refinements that allow for increased model resolution at specific areas, and (iii) allowing additional detail to be considered within a grid cell so that the numerical method can account for the fine input elevation data through mass conservation. However, the model is unable to reflect urban stormwater systems directly. A practical solution is subtracting the 2-year return period rainfall intensity from the design flood rainfall intensity for the entire domain. This assumption of a 2-year return period was based on a conservative estimate of the service levels provided by the stormwater management infrastructure. Further work would be required to confirm this. Given the above limitation of the HEC-RAS, a subtraction of the 2-year return period rainfall intensity was applied to these urban settings.  3.4 Boundary conditions PEI is bounded by the ocean; hence, considering ocean boundary conditions is of the utmost importance in this flood modeling. Moreover, literature reviews have observed the increasing risks of compound floods in PEI (coastal and pluvial floods) in recent years, especially during some extreme storm events, e.g., the post-tropical storm Fiona in 2022 (Bonnington et al., 2023; Mulligan et al., 2023 ). This may suggest that the return periods of ocean boundary conditions should be appropriately adjusted to match the return periods of rainfall IDF curves. However, due to the lack of research on compound flood risks in PEI, it is challenging to determine the appropriate return periods for coastal boundary conditions. Based on the CHIP data, the 1.6-year return period Designated Flood Elevations (DFEs) under the 2020 High Flood Hazard and 2100 Moderate-Low Flood Hazard scenarios were used to drive the pluvial flood modeling under the current and future climate conditions, respectively. At the City of Charlottetown, the 1.6-year return period DFE is equivalent to 0.4 m above the HHWLT (Higher High Water Large Tide). It is, however, worth noting that using the 1.6-year return period ocean boundary conditions might not be able to fully reflect the increasing compound flooding risks in the context of climate change. On occasions when there is an open-end reach from the downstream that is not connected to the ocean, another boundary condition, such as Normal Depth, was used. This approach solely employs Manning's equation to determine the stage for each downstream reach. This requires a friction slope, which is called the energy grade line. The Normal Depth is typically useful when detailed stream downstream stage information is unavailable, and it was used in this study.  3.5 Model parameters HEC-RAS has incorporated rain-on-grid capabilities in its 2D modeling framework, which allows for simulating directly rainfall on each computational grids. Infiltration rates measured in depth per unit of time are used in the HEC-RAS model to quantify the amount of water infiltrating the soil surface. The Soil Conservation Services (CSC) Curve Number (CN) method is an empirical surface runoff method developed by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) NRCS in 1985, which was selected to estimate direct runoff resulting from rainfall. To better understand how the model performance would react to different parameter settings and to select a better combination of model parameter values, a set of sensitivity analyses was initially performed in HEC-RAS model under seven configurations: (1) AMC II, n min , I min , (2) AMC II, n mean , I mean , (3) AMC II, n max , I max , (4) AMC III, n min , I min , (5) AMC III, n mean , I mean , (6) AMC III, n max , I max , and (7) AMC III, n mean , I min , where AMC II  and III  are Antecedent Moisture Condition under normal and wet conditions; n  is Manning coefficient; I  is infiltration rate; min , mean , and max  are minimum, mean, and maximum values. Based on the internal sensitive analysis, the parameter settings in configuration 7 indicated a better performance in reproducing the observed peak flow for the July 3–4, 2024, heavy rainfall event in Prince County, and it was used in this study.  3.6 Model resolutions Since this research focused on two perspectives: (i) a detailed flood model for major municipalities and (ii) a regional flood model for island-wide, it’s imperative to mention model resolutions for each configuration. An overall resolution of 10 m with a refined 2 m resolution was applied to enhance spatial flood maps for municipalities, along with the key infrastructure. The processes of defining mesh resolutions consist of three main steps: (i) establish a model domain by delineating all sub-watersheds within the administrative boundary, (ii) generate the domain with 10 m × 10 m resolution, and (iii) refine the existing stream and road networks with 2 m × 2 m resolution. For an island-wide pluvial flood map, the study divided the entire island of PEI into three regions by merging the related watersheds with reference to the administrative boundaries of three counties (i.e., Prince, Queens, and Kings). As for the mesh generation and refinement in HEC-RAS for each county, the study first generates 100 m × 100 m grid cells for the model domain and then applies 20 m × 20 m refinements along with the hydro and road networks.  3.7 Representation of hydraulic structures Two approaches were carried out to represent hydraulic structures (culverts and bridges) for the municipal and island-wide models: (i) individual structures with detailed dimensional information are explicitly reflected in the HEC-RAS 2D model for municipal models, and (ii) all structures are breached (hydro-connection) for island-wide models. Fig. 2   presents detailed hydraulic structure reflection steps for these two models. For the municipal model, since the hydraulic structures data provided by the PEI DTI only have a width dimension equal to or greater than 1.2 m, any structures less than this threshold are unavailable. To address this issue, the study took a unique approach, examining the intersection of hydro and road networks within the municipal domains. First, any intersection points that coincide with PEI DTI data will be omitted. At the same time, the remaining spots that lie outside of this coverage (less than 1.2 m) will then be manually reviewed by conducting field trips to collect data (see Fig. 2 a). It is worth mentioning that several major bridges are already hydro-connected in the current HRDEM data; hence, they were excluded from HEC-RAS, as the water flow at these points is assumed to have limited affected in the model. It is unrealistic for the island-wide model to include all hydraulic structures (1,440, according to PEI DTI data). Therefore, an automated approach was employed to breach HRDEM for structures connecting rivers at road crossings. To do this, the study will first overlook any large bridges that are already hydro-connected in the existing HRDEM. Then, a 75 m buffer circle was formed at each crossing point (note that this 75 m threshold was selected through many testing experiments by considering road width, pavement, and so on). These buffer circles are then used to cut the hydro network in order to get a line segment with a length of 75 m. To determine the dimensions of each line segment in relation to the structural dimension, deck length data from PEI DTI was utilized as width and the lowest elevation from HRDEM, where each segment was placed, as height. Similar to the municipal areas stated above, dimensions for these structures only apply to deck lengths equal to or more than 1.2 m; meanwhile, structures smaller than 1.2 m are unavailable. As a result, any remaining segments smaller than 1.2 m in width will be assigned a deck length of 1.2 m. Representing this threshold (=1.2 m) for smaller structures still makes sense because HRDEM's resolution is 1 m; therefore, any DEM breaching less than 1 m cannot be properly reflected. Finally, 2,895 points (1,183 culverts, 98 bridges, and 1,614 intersections of hydro and road networks) were identified in the DEM breaching process for the island-wide model. This new DEM dataset is then used for island-wide pluvial flood modeling.  3.8 Model calibration and validation The flood occurrence in Charlottetown on September 2, 2021, was chosen for urban flood modeling due to the availability of flood data. Video footage from social media was utilized to validate the model. In particular, a focus was placed on two locations in downtown Charlottetown: the parking lot of Holland College and the junction of West Street and Richmond Street. In order to estimate the flood depths available from the footage, various field trips were carried out at these two locations in the summer of 2023. This is to help determine the flood depths at the points of interest by cross-referencing existing inundated landmarks for the September 2, 2021 flood event. Note that because hydrometric stations are unavailable in urban domains, the study did not conduct a quantitative comparison in these areas. For island-wide pluvial flood modeling, the measured flow rate for a heavy rainfall event on July 3–4, 2023, was collected from the hydrometric stations maintained by ECCC. Three stations were chosen based on their data availability and spatial representation throughout three PEI counties: #01CA003 in Prince, #01CC010 in Queens, and #01CD005 in Kings.   4 Results and discussions 4.1 Model warm-up In order to properly estimate the initial conditions for soil moisture and water filling up for rivers, streams, and ponds, a warm-up period needs to be added before the simulation for the design rainfall storm. This is due to the absence of initial conditions for natural water bodies in the watersheds. Improperly representing this criterion would have an influence on surface runoff as it would alter the travel time (lag time) in the simulation. Accordingly, a 2-year return period rainfall event was used for the warm-up period. Using a trial-and-error approach, four potential options were tested: (i) placing the peak of 2-year rainfall event at 6 h before the design rainfall storm; (ii) 12 h before; (iii) 24 h before; and (iii) 36 h before (see Fig. 3  a). The observed flow rates from three ECCC hydrometric stations (i.e., #01CA003 in Prince County, #01CC010 in Queens County, and #01CD005 in Kings County) during this rainfall event are collected for evaluation purposes. Fig. 3 b shows the comparison results of four warm-up options and no warm-up in terms of their performance in capturing the observed flow rate at the station in Prince County. The testing results suggest that a warm-up period is important to initiate the model simulation as the flow rates from the no warm-up run are significantly lower than the observed ones. As for the four warm-up options, the results suggest that the peak of a 2-year rainfall event 12 h before the storm event can produce the best simulation. Considering that the other two hydrometric stations in Queens County and Kings County represent much smaller watersheds than the one in Prince County, the testing results for Prince County here are deemed representative of other major watersheds in PEI. Therefore, the warm-up option of “12-hour before” was considered in this study.  4.2 HEC-RAS 2D model performance Fig. 4   shows the comparison of observed and simulated flood depths at two locations (the parking lot of Holland College and the junction of West Street and Richmond Street) in downtown Charlottetown. There is a good agreement between model simulation and observation in both flood depth and extent in the parking lot of Holland College. However, the model simulation seems to overestimate the observed flood depth near the junction of West Street and Richmond Street. After some investigation of the potential causes, the study found that the main reason is that the HRDEM data used in this study was collected in 2020, and there were some major developments (e.g., new residential properties and road repairs) in this location after the HRDEM data collection and before the September 2, 2021 rainfall event. Overall, the validation results in the City of Charlottetown demonstrate the good performance of the municipal model setup for HEC-RAS 2D. Note that this study did not undertake a quantitative comparison in urban domains, as previously stated, because of the lack of hydrometric stations. Fig. 5  a–c present the validation results of flow rates for the July 3–4, 2023 rainfall event at three hydrometric stations for the island-wide model. The results show that the observed flow rates for the station in Prince County are significantly larger than those of the two stations in Queens and Kings counties. This is because these two stations only represent a small watershed, and their flow rates are susceptible to the representation of local topography and landscapes. Since the island-wide model runs at a resolution of 20 m along with the hydro network, it is unsurprising that the observed flow rates for small rivers or streams are not accurately captured. However, it is worth noting that the model well-simulates the observed flow rate pattern for these two stations. As the station in Prince County receives water from a much larger watershed and is thus more representative of PEI’s topography and landscape, the good agreement in simulated and observed flow rates at this station (Nash Sutcliffe Efficiency = 0.643 and R2  = 0.765) confirms the acceptable performance of our island-wide model setup.  4.3 Quality assurance and control To ensure the quality of the pluvial flood maps, the study has taken some quality assurance and control measures throughout the model runs and the post-processing of output maps. Initially, an inspection was made for the output flood maps from the design storm events. The regions where modelled flood depths exceed 1.5 m on each flood map will be manually evaluated to ensure accuracy and rationality. In most cases, these areas typically fall into two categories: (i) rivers or ponds filled with more water after heavy rainfall events, and (ii) low-lying coastal areas which are usually inundated by ocean water. The experience and knowledge from the local residents and field visits were also used to help inspect those commonly flooded areas. Following the foregoing validity and reasonableness inspection, compare the flood maps from municipal models to the maps from the island-wide model to verify the consistency for urbanized areas. This is because two sets of flood maps are available for the eight selected municipalities: one is from their own high-resolution municipal models, and one is from the island-wide model. Since both models used different resolutions and approaches to reflect hydraulic structures, it is not surprising to see some differences in the output flood maps between the municipal and island-wide models. The significant difference resulting from the difference in model resolution is that the high-resolution municipal model can produce more detailed maps, which are helpful for flood risk assessment for individual properties and key civil infrastructures (say roads and highways), while this level of detail is out of the reach for the island-wide map. As shown in Fig. 6  , the major difference resulting from the different approaches for the reflection of hydraulic structures is that the island-wide model tends to generate lower flood depths and thus smaller flood extent on the upstream side at the crossing of hydro and road networks where a culvert typically exists. This is mainly due to the limitation of DEM breaching, which ultimately cuts the land and leads to no limits on the height of the channel. In other words, more water will flow from upstream to downstream in the hydro-connected DEM (used by the island-wide model) compared to the explicit representation of culverts in the municipal model. While the abovementioned differences in the pluvial flood maps for urbanized areas are understandable from the scientific perspective given the limitations in the island-wide model, it realizes that this may cause some potential confusion for the map users who do not necessarily understand the reasons. Since detailed maps from municipal models can generate more reasonable results in urbanized areas, the island-wide flood maps can be updated by replacing the maps for the selected municipalities and Indigenous communities with the maps from their high-resolution municipal models. Note that the detailed flood maps from municipal models are not clipped into the municipal boundary before the replacement. This is to avoid any potential mismatches between the island-wide map, municipal model, and municipal boundary.  4.4 Pluvial flood mapping The pluvial flood maps generated for six municipalities, two Indigenous communities, and the entire island of PEI, are presented in Figs. 7 and 8   , respectively. More details of these flood maps are available online in the PEI Climate Hazard and Risk Information System (CHRIS, https://chris.peiclimate.ca ). The CHRIS is a GIS- and web-based platform that provides free and easy access to all the pluvial flood maps generated by this research (see Fig. 9  ). The platform offers maps of not only inland flooding alone but also coastal erosion and flooding. It is important to note that a 10 cm threshold of flood depth was used in this study to extract the flood extent maps. In other words, flood depths less than 10 cm will be ignored because they can quickly penetrate the ground surface or stormwater system. Moreover, Table 1   summarises the flooded areas corresponding to different return periods for current and future climates in this study. Quantitative analysis of the social risks due to flooding for coastal societies is further discussed by Pang et al. (2024) .   5 Conclusions In this research, municipal and island-wide (regional) models were developed for PEI. Four return periods (10-year, 25-year, 50-year, and 100-year) under current and future climate conditions were considered. The study's results suggest that the model warm-up period would influence the flow variations in flood modeling. However, in most cases with heterogeneous topographical conditions and many water bodies, the warm-up period is highly recommended in flood models to capture the natural characteristics of surface water bodies before the simulation. In the context of climate change, the study underlines the possibility of a 20 % increase in food extent in the future, notably for PEI; hence, adaptation measures should be put in place to minimize future consequences. Compound flooding is a complicated process in flood modeling. This is because the combined impacts of high tide levels, storm surge, and intense rainfall events within the inland watershed lead to more flooding than these phenomena occur individually (Yang et al., 2023 ). As global warming continues, the compound flooding risk is likely to increase. Therefore, there is an urgent need to consider this complex interplay in coastal studies. By considering tides, surges, relative sea level change, and wave setup, the study used a 1.6-year return period DFEs as reported by (Richards and Daigle, 2011) for Nova Scotia and PEI areas. For future studies, other joint probability approaches can be preferred to improve compound flooding, such as using Copula functions analysis (Chen and Huang, 2007; Zhang and Jiang, 2019). Due to the enormous number of structures, reflecting hydro infrastructures in a regional flood model would be a barrier. In this regard, an automated DEM breaching technique may be feasible to address this gap. The approach is practical as it represents culverts/bridges for connecting waterways blocked by roads and other structures. Breaching is particularly useful for confronting the absence of hydrostructural information. For instance, it found that out of 1,440 structures with a dimension exceeding 1.2 m provided by the Government of PEI, potentially another 1,455 structures had a dimension < 1.2 m in PEI, thanks to the automated DEM breaching approach. However, a few drawbacks should be brought to attention, such as the hydro-connected dimension of DEM not being comparable to actual structural sizes, leading to less flood accumulation from the structure's entryway. Despite these shortcomings, the method may still be recommended, particularly for large-scale flood studies or limited information on the hydro infrastructures. Notwithstanding the efforts made, the study still has a few limitations. The HEC-RAS 2D model is limited in reflecting the urban stormwater systems in urban areas. The 2-year return period rainfall intensity under current climate conditions is subtracted from the large return period rainfall intensity for the entire model domain to approximately represent the capacity of urban stormwater systems. However, the capacity of urban stormwater systems can be affected by many factors (e.g., tidal changes from ocean water) and can also vary significantly by time and location. The current approach in this study is certainly unable to reflect the spatiotemporal complexity of urban storm systems. Other flood models that explicitly represent the capacity of urban stormwater systems say PCSWMM (Bibi et al., 2023; Smith et al., 2005 ), should be used for further projects to generate more reliable pluvial flood maps in urban areas. Due to the limited hydrometric stations in urban areas, calibration and validation are also restricted in quantitative comparison. The results of this study serve as an essential tool for PEI local governments in flood mitigation and planning. High-resolution flood maps generated from this research are now officially implemented by the EEAC, Government of PEI (Government-of-PEI, 2024 ), as well as Natural Resources Canada.
1 Introduction Understanding the long-term and short-term effects of chemical weathering is essential for a comprehensive evaluation of the global carbon cycle. Chemical weathering rates are complex functions and are influenced by several factors, including mineral dissolution, mechanical erosion, lithology, tectonics, biota, climate, hydrology, and various human activities (Donnini et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2015; Mortatti and Probst, 2003 ). This natural phenomenon of chemical weathering serves as a pivotal mechanism for sequestering atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2 ) by transforming it into dissolved solutes within continental aquatic systems (Das et al., 2016; Deka et al., 2015; Moon et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2021 ). Moreover, the chemical weathering and CO2  consumption in the riverine ecosystem reflect the influence of atmospheric factors like precipitation as well as the origins of solutes through physical and chemical erosions. Hence, quantifying the effects of chemical weathering and determining the CO2  absorption through rock weathering are major determining processes of the long-term carbon cycle and its relation to climate change (Zhang et al., 2021a ). The chemical weathering of carbonate and silicate minerals is the paramount process that could control the long-term climate change effect by providing atmospheric CO2  drawdown during the weathering process (Liu et al., 2011; Quade et al., 2003 ). Notable, silicate weathering is an important process to deposit atmospheric CO2  due to the weathering of silicate minerals (Donnini et al., 2016; Hren et al., 2007 ). Previous studies have suggested that the water chemistry of the world’s major rivers is mostly dominated by the weathering of minerals, particularly carbonates and silicates (Chen et al., 2002; Gaillardet et al., 1997; Qu et al., 2019; Bishwakarma et al., 2022 ). Rock weathering processes dominate the long-term global CO2  balance and play a significant role in the global water cycle, and rivers are the primary conduits for balancing global CO2 , connecting terrestrial ecosystems with the ocean (Zhang et al., 2021b ). The following chemical reaction formulas (Eqs. The ongoing upliftment of the Himalayas-Tibetan Plateau, coupled with heavy rainfall due to the Asian and Indian monsoons, accelerates chemical weathering in the region (Kajita et al., 2020 ). Since the 1990's, several studies have been done in this region focused on large river basins such as the Ganges, Brahmaputra, Mekong, Ayeyarwady, Indus, etc. These studies highlighted that the chemical weathering in the Himalayas is significantly higher than the world average of about 200 × 106  tons/yr, consuming more than 10 % of total global CO2  (Gaillardet et al., 1999; Galy and France-Lanord, 1999; Hren et al., 2007; Kajita et al., 2020; Sarin et al., 1989 ). Some studies done in the middle-scale rivers in the Himalayas region, such as Yamuna, Lasha, Teesta, Narayani, etc., have underlined the spatiotemporal variations of chemical weathering and CO2  consumption, strongly influenced by river discharge (Dalai et al., 2002; Das et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019 ). Additionally, researchers have explored weathering and/or CO2  consumption rates in small-scale Himalayas river basins such as Trisuli, Bheri, Marshyangdi, etc., explaining the effects of erosion in the high-elevation regions (Galy and France-Lanord, 1999; Wolff-Boenisch et al., 2009 ). More recently, studies focused on mechanisms of chemical weathering and CO2  drawdown in the glacierized area, signifying the importance of meltwater in the Himalayas (Biswal et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2020 ). These studies collectively deepen our understanding of the complex interactions between geology, climate, and hydrology in driving chemical weathering and CO2  consumption processes in the Himalayas. Overall, natural factors like bedrock composition, lithology, hydrological regimes, relief, climatic features, and vegetation are dominantly controlling riverine hydrochemistry in the Himalayas region (Das et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2019 ). Climate factors such as air temperature and precipitation also play a pivotal role in controlling chemical weathering (Godsey et al., 2019 ). Other physical factors, including denudation of vegetation cover, the thickness of soil layers, terrain steepness, river gradients, and permafrost, also influence the chemical weathering processes (Pant et al., 2018, 2021; Zhang et al., 2021a; Zhang et al., 2019 ). Thus, exploring riverine hydrochemistry in rock weathering-dominated river catchment is important in quantifying the contributions of potential sources of dissolved solutes and estimating the chemical weathering and CO2  consumption rates. The rivers originating from the Third Pole Region in the Himalayas serve as lifelines for downstream countries, supporting more than 240 million people across China, Nepal, Pakistan, India, Bhutan, Afghanistan, etc. (Wester et al., 2019 ). As the rivers are substantial networks for material exchange between land and sea, the rivers from the Himalayas region play a fundamental role in the global land-sea energy exchange process (Liu et al., 2019 ). Snow cover in the Himalayas highly influences the water availability downstream of the major river basins (Immerzeel et al., 2010 ). About 20% of snowmelt contributes to the annual discharge in the central Himalayas region (Bookhagen and Burbank, 2010; Lutz et al., 2014 ). However, the supply of meltwater from the snow mass to many rivers has changed over the past decades due to climate change. Particularly, in the central Himalayas, the snow cover area is decreasing trend due to the increasing temperature and precipitation owing to global climate change (Khadka et al., 2014; Kraaijenbrink et al., 2021; Thapa et al., 2020 ). Additionally, the Himalayas snow-pack has been losing mass at a rate of 4.55 Gt per year between 2000 and 2018 (Nie et al., 2021 ), and it is estimated the melt runoff will continue to increase up to mid-century (Immerzeel et al., 2010; Lutz et al., 2014; Nepal, 2016 ). In addition, the snowmelt runoff in the Himalayas is also projected to increase trend, and it is projected that the contribution of snowmelt runoff will increase by 3 % to 13 % by the mid of century (Bhattarai and Regmi, 2016; Khadka et al., 2014 ). Therefore, it is imperative to study hydrochemistry, integrating it with chemical weathering, CO2  consumption, and hydrology in the Himalayas region. Such studies are crucial for understanding spatiotemporal changes in freshwater resources and their valuable contributions. The Koshi River, the largest tributary of the Ganges River System, annually transports approximately 6.2 billion tonnes of water and 19.5 million tonnes of sediment (Li et al., 2020; Sinha et al., 2019 ). With more than 8 % snow cover, the snow melt contribution to the Koshi River’s total runoff is substantial, contributing approximately 15 % on average (Budhathoki et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2019; Gyanwali et al., 2023; Khadka et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023 ). However, the snow cover area of the Koshi River catchment has declined at the rate of 0.47 % per year since 2000, have a significant role in the alteration of the runoff budget (Gurung et al., 2017; Xiang et al., 2018 ). Owing to the headwater region in the high glacier area and major freshwater source for Nepal and India, the Koshi River has received significant attention from chemists, hydrologists, and geologists since the 2000s (Bharati et al., 2014; Mishra et al., 2019; Quade et al., 2003; Tripathee et al., 2016 ). Nonetheless, there are still gaps in our understanding, particularly regarding the process of basin scales chemical weathering, CO2  consumption, and hydrological influence on aquatic geochemistry. Therefore, this study focuses on the Koshi River, a transboundary river basin in the Himalayan region, encompassing both the upstream alpine mountainous regions (leeward side of the Himalayas) and downstream rainfall influenced temperate plain areas (windward side of the Himalayas). The study aims to achieve three main objectives: (1) specify the characteristics of the river water chemistry and controlling factors; (2) quantify chemical weathering and CO2  consumption rates, comparing the differences in the upstream alpine mountains and the downstream temperate plain regions; (3) describe the effects of glacier melt runoff, snowmelt runoff, rainfall runoff, and base flow on river hydrochemistry, chemical weathering, and CO2  consumption rates.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The Koshi River Basin (KRB), one of the major Himalaya River systems, originates in China and flows through the Himalayas to the Ganges plain area covering 54,000 km2  (Fig. 1  b ). The KRB is often recognized as ‘Saptakoshi ’ due to its major seven tributaries namely Tamor, Arun, Dudhkoshi, Likhu, Tamakoshi, Bhotekoshi, and Indrawati (Fig. 1 a ). The climatic pattern of KRB varies significantly, ranging from dry and cold climates in the upstream region to humid and sub-tropical climates in the downstream plain area (Nepal, 2016 ). The upstream region of the KRB lying on the leeward side of the Himalayas, experiencing a low average annual precipitation of about 400 mm, whereas the downstream region of KRB is on the windward side of the Himalayas with a tropical climate and receives high monsoonal precipitation about 1800 mm annually (Xue et al., 2017 ). Geologically, the KRB includes three major east–west striking geological sections from north to south, namely Tethys Himalaya, Higher Himalaya, and Lesser Himalaya (Fig. 1 c ). These geological sections constitute 43 %, 41 %, and 15 % of the total basin area, respectively, and are separated by the major Himalayan thrust namely, the South Tibetan Detachment System, the Main Central Thrust, and the Main Boundary Thrust (Dhital, 2015; Zhang et al., 2016 ). The Tethys Himalaya, situated on the northern slope of the Himalayas, primarily consists of fossiliferous sedimentary rocks such as shale, limestone, sandstone, etc. (Montgomery and Stolar, 2006 ). On the other hand, the Higher Himalaya covers the high mountain region, which is characterized by high-grade metamorphic rocks and igneous rocks like aquamarine, ruby, quartz, schist, gneiss, marble, etc. The Lesser Himalaya is in the lower reaches of tributaries and primarily comprises sedimentary and metasedimentary rocks such as quartzite, limestone, phyllite, schist, slate, dolomite, gneiss, etc. are common in this section (Li et al., 2020 ).  2.2 Sampling and laboratory analysis For this study, a total of 46 surface river water samples were collected from the upstream, downstream, and mainstream of the KRB during post-monsoon (November 2017) and monsoon (July 2019) (23 samples for each season). In total, five sampling points are located in upstream, 17 sampling points are located in downstream, particularly from the tributaries, and one sample is collected from the mainstream of the KRB (Fig. 1 a ). All the upstream sampling points are located in China, and all the downstream and mainstream sampling points located in Nepal. The pH, electrical conductivity (EC), and total dissolved solids (TDS) were measured onsite during fieldwork using a multiparameter device (HI–98129, HANNA, Romania). The samples were collected at ∼10–15 cm water depth, and before collection, the bottles were pre-rinsed with the same river water to avoid contamination. After collection, samples were filtered through a millipore nitrocellulose filter (0.45 µm) to remove suspended sediments and stored in pre-washed ultra-clean high-density polyethylene bottles. The samples were stored at 4°C until the laboratory analyses were done at the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences (ITP–CAS), Beijing. Major cations (Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Na+ , K+ ) and dissolved silica (Si) were determined using an Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometer (ICP–OES) with a detection limit of 0.05 ppm for major cations and 0.1 ppm for Si. In addition, anions (SO4 2 – , Cl– , and NO3 – ) were measured using Ion Chromatography of Dionex ICS 900, the USA, with a detection limit of 0.1 ppm for each anion. Due to the physical constraints and the transportation complexity in the KRB, onsite titration for HCO3 –  concentration measurement was difficult during the sampling time. Therefore, we applied the charge balance relation to determine the concentration of HCO3 –  which is also proved reliable with the titration process (difference within 10%) in Himalayan rivers (Tipper et al., 2006 ). To ensure data quality, the correlation between the measured TDS vs. calculated TDS was examined following the reference of Liu et al. (2020) . The slope equation and correlation between the measured and calculated TDS (TDS Calculated  = 1.01 × TDS Measured  + 7.19, R2  = 0.85) suggested that the hydrochemical data are of good quality for the analysis.  2.3 Chemical analysis The Forward model (Fig. S2 ) is principally designed for quantifying the contributions of precipitation inputs, minerals weathering, and sulphide oxidations to the major ions (Galy and France-Lanord, 1999 ). The forward model is based on the mass budget equation (Li et al., 2019 ) for the concentration of major ions (X) in riverine water as in Eq. (9) .(9) X riv   = X precp   + X sil   + X carb   + X sulf        Where, riv: river, precp: precipitation, sil: silicate weathering, carb: carbonate weathering, and sulf: sulfide oxidation. The details of the forward model are mentioned in the supplementary file . The chemical weathering rate of the river catchment is used to determine the total chemical denudation during the weathering processes of silicate and carbonate minerals. By combining the cation concentration produced by the weathering of silicate and carbonate minerals, river discharge, and basin area, the silicate rock weathering rate (SWR) and carbonate weathering rate (CWR) can be quantified using the Eqs. (10) and (11) , respectively (Jiang et al., 2015 ).
