The SPHY model relies on several input datasets, including a digital elevation model (DEM) obtained from HydroSHED (90 m), land use and land cover information from GLOBCOVER (300 m), hydrological soil properties derived from HiHydroSoil (800 m), and glacier distribution data from the Randolph Glacier Inventory version 4.0. Additionally, daily air temperature (minimum, maximum, and average) and precipitation data necessary for runoff simulation were sourced from ERA5 (0.1°). The model was calibrated for the period from 2011 to 2015 and validated for the subsequent four years, from 2016 to 2019, using observed daily discharge data from the Chatara hydrological station (Fig. 1 a ). The total discharge for the Chatara Station has been collected from the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, Nepal. The calibrated parameters used in this study are listed in Table 1  . The sensitivity of simulated results was analyzed at a daily time scale using Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) and percentage bias (PBIAS). During the calibration period, NSE and PBIAS values were 0.82 and 12.57, respectively, while during the validation period, NSE was 0.85 and PBIAS was 2.09. These sensitivity results and hydrograph (Fig. 2  ) display the simulated results closely, representing the real hydrological scenarios. Based on the simulation data, we obtained information on total runoff, precipitation, and runoff components such as rainfall runoff, snowmelt runoff, glacier melt runoff, and base flow of every sampling point during sampling periods.   3 Results 3.1 Characteristics of the river water chemistry The statistics of the ionic composition in the KRB are summarised in Table 2  . The Koshi River water is slightly alkaline in nature, with pH values ranging from 7.20 to 9.00 with a mean value of 8.10 ± 0.34. The EC and TDS range from 36 µS/cm to 476 µS/cm and 18 mg/L to 238 mg/L with a mean value of 147 ± 106.43 µS/cm and 75 ± 58.80 mg/L, respectively. Notably, the KRB exhibits relatively lower TDS and EC concentrations compared to the global average. The average concentrations of major cations, including Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Na+  and K+  ranges from 6.03 mg/L to 65.02 mg/L, 0.28 mg/L to 14.60 mg/L, 0.29 mg/L to 15.86 mg/L, and 0.37 mg/L to 3.07 mg/L with an average value 18.01 ± 16.11 mg/L, 4.34 ± 2.86 mg/L, 4.77 ± 3.73 mg/L, and 1.66 ± 0.55 mg/L, respectively. Likewise, the Si content in the KRB ranges from 0.41 mg/L to 5.65 mg/L with an average of 3.42 ± 1.12 mg/L. On the other hand, the average concentrations of anions, including HCO3 – , SO4 2 – , Cl– , and NO3 –  ranges from 17.68 mg/L to 170.66 mg/L, 2.03 mg/L to 117.07 mg/L, 0.27 mg/L to 8.72 mg/L, and 0.00 mg/L to 3.78 mg/L with an average value 68.95 ± 42.56 mg/L, 14.42 ± 20.90 mg/L, 1.55 ± 1.82 mg/L, and 0.64 ± 0.77 mg/L, respectively. The pattern of cationic dominance based on mean values (mg/L) is in the order of Ca2+ > Na+ > Mg2+ > K+ , showing the dominance of alkaline earth metals on alkalis. Similarly, the average anionic concentrations follow a pattern of dominancy order as HCO3 −  > SO4 2− > Cl−  > NO3 −  exhibiting the dominancy of weak acids over strong acids. The total cationic budget exhibits that the Ca2+ , Na+ , Mg2+ , and K+  account for 62 %, 17 %, 15 %, and 6 %, respectively. Similarly, the total anionic budget shows that the HCO3 – , SO4 2 – , Cl– , and NO3 –  account for 80 %, 17 %, 2 %, and 1 %, respectively. The ionic dominancy order of KRB is also comparable with the other studies, especially from the Himalayas region and within the WHO drinking water limit, as presented in Table 2 . Fig. 3  a  illustrates the spatial variations of major ions. The upstream region is characterized by the significantly higher (p < 0.05 ) average concentration of most of the hydrochemical variables, including pH, TDS, EC, Ca2+ , Na+ , Mg2+ , HCO3 – , SO4 2– , Cl– , and NO3 –  as compared with the downstream. Specifically, the average concentrations of Na+  and Mg2+ , Cl–  and HCO3 – , TDS and Ca2+ , NO3 – , and SO4 2-  are observed 2, 3, 4, 7, and 8 times, respectively, higher in the upstream region. However, the ionic dominancy order for both upstream and downstream follow the same order as Ca2+ > Na+ > Mg2+ > K+  and HCO3 – > SO4 2- > Cl– > NO3 –  for cation and anion, respectively, exhibiting the dominancy of Ca2+  and HCO3 –  in the total ionic budget. The higher concentrations of major ions in the upstream region are primarily attributed to the intense physical erosion and chemical weathering in the northern slope of the Himalayas. In contrast, a relatively higher concentration of dissolved Si was measured in the downstream region than in the upstream region, suggesting relatively more silicate weathering in the downstream region. Fig. 3 b  illustrates the seasonal variations of major ions. During the post-monsoon season, there is a notable increase in the average concentrations of most ionic variables, including pH, TDS, and EC, when compared to the monsoon season. On average, all the parameters are observed slightly higher during the post-monsoon season except NO3 –  and Si (2 times higher in post-monsoon). However, only the dissolved Si and NO3 –  are significantly higher (p < 0.05 ) during the post-monsoon season. The ionic dominancy order for both the monsoon and post-monsoon seasons follows the same order as spatial variations, i.e., Ca2+ > Na+ > Mg2+ > K+  and HCO3 – > SO4 2– > Cl– > NO3 –  for cation and anion, respectively exhibiting the dominancy of Ca2+  and HCO3 –  in the total ionic budget. The lower concentrations of major ions during the monsoon season are associated with high chemical dilution in the river channel due to increased total discharge by the monsoon-driven climatic system (Baronas et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2005 ). The milli-equivalent percentage (meq%) of the ionic composition provides insight into the major dissolved ions in rivers through the Piper Diagram (Piper, 1944 ) (Fig. 4  ). In the anion plot, most of the samples are plotted in the left corner of the right ternary plot near the HCO3 –  apex indicating the dominancy of HCO3 –  in total anionic budget. In the cation plot, most of the samples are plotted in the lower-left corner near the Ca2+  apex, indicating the dominance of Ca2+  in the total cationic budget. The results plotted in the central diamond section show the Ca2+ –HCO3 –  of river hydrochemistry, indicating the alkaline earth metals (Ca2+ +Mg2+ ) exceed alkali metals (Na+ +K+ ) and weak acid (HCO3 – ) exceed strong acids (SO4 2- +Cl- ).  3.2 Controlling factors and source apportionment of major ions 3.2.1 Rock weathering inputs and chemical weathering The Gibbs plot explains the controlling factors of river hydrochemistry in the KRB (Fig. 5  ). Most of the water samples are characterized by medium TDS values and low ratios of Na+  versus (Na+  + Ca2+ ) and Cl-  versus (Cl-  + HCO3 – ), and thus located on the left side of the central zone, indicating the rock weathering as a predominant source of major ions. When comparing temporal distribution, the post-monsoon samples have relatively higher concentrations of TDS. Additionally, comparing upstream and downstream indicates the relatively higher TDS in the upstream. Mainly in the downstream region, some of the samples also exhibit low TDS (<70 mg/L), indicating the sources of major ions are also influenced by rainfall-runoff interactions. The hydrochemistry of the KRB is also illustrated by the mixing diagrams of Na-normalized molar ratios (meq) of Ca2+  versus HCO3 –  and Ca2+  versus Mg2+  (Fig. 6  ). In this study, all the sampling points are plotted in between the silicates and carbonates domain suggesting the deposition of both carbonates and silicates minerals in the KRB. Some samples collected from the Tamor River section tend to move towards silicate end members, likely due to the higher deposition of silicate minerals in the Tamor River catchments (Dhital, 2015 ). Chemical weathering and evaporite dissolution produce several dissolved ions that play a vital role in the controlling mechanisms of river hydrochemistry (Pant et al., 2018 ). The results of ionic ratios for the upstream and downstream regions of the KRB during the monsoon and post-monsoon seasons are summerized in Table 3  . The notably high mean molar ratio of Ca2+ /Na+  (7.01) indicates the dominancy of Ca2+  in the total cationic budget, suggesting intensive weathering of carbonate minerals. In general, the ratio of HCO3 – /Ca2+ , ∼2, indicates the dominance of carbonate weathering in river hydrochemistry (Thomas et al., 2014 ). In the KRB, the grand mean molar ratio of HCO3 – /Ca2+  is 1.27, indicating that hydrochemistry is influenced by carbonate and silicate minerals. Furthermore, the elevated ratios of (HCO3 – /Na+ ) (7.78) and HCO3 – /(Na+ +K+ ) (5.78) provide additional support for a river basin controlled by both carbonate and silicate minerals. Similarly, the high ratios of (Ca2+ + Mg2+ )/(Na+ + K+ ) (6.78) and (Ca2+ +Mg2+ )/TZ+  (0.84) underscore that the chemical composition of the KRB is largely controlled by carbonate weathering with a notable contribution of silicates weathering (Das et al., 2016; Pant et al., 2018; Tsering et al., 2019 ). In summary, the hydrochemistry of KRB is largely dominated by weathering of carbonate minerals. The molar ratio of HCO3 – /(SO4 2-  + HCO3 – ), known as C–ratio, provides insights into the weathering processes, whether they involve carbonate, sulfide, or both. Principally, the C-ratio ∼ 1 typically indicates carbonation reactions (Thomas et al., 2014 ). In the KRB, the molar C-ratio ranges from 0.50 to 0.98 with a mean value of 0.80, specifying the carbonate weathering due to the carbonic acid is more significant. However, the weathering of sulphuric acid also has a major role in the weathering of carbonate rocks. Moreover, the ratios of Ca2+ /SO4 2− , HCO3 –  /(Ca2+  + Mg2+ ), SO4 2- /(Ca2+  + Mg2+ ) also support the carbonate and silicate weathering. The concentration of riverine HCO3 –  increases when weathering involves more H2 CO3  and the concentration of riverine SO4 2-  increases if more H2 SO4  is involved (Zhang et al., 2021a ).  3.2.2 Quantitative analysis of the river hydrochemistry-source contributions The forward model is used to quantify the input sources of the riverine dissolved solutes, and it also has an important implication in exploring the association between the chemical weathering rate and its controlling factors (Galy and France-Lanord, 1999 ). As described in previous sections, the hydrochemistry of the KRB signifies that the carbonate weathering is mainly due to the carbonic or sulfide acid. The contribution of the precipitation, sulfide oxidation, silicate weathering, and carbonate weathering has been estimated using the Forward model and summarized in Table 4  . In the basin scale, the annual average contribution of precipitation, sulfide oxidation, silicate weathering, and carbonate weathering was 5 %, 8 %, 38 %, and 50 %, respectively. As consistent with the ionic dominancy order and ionic ratios, the contribution of rock weathering (carbonate and silicate) is dominant for the hydrochemical budget for both the upstream and downstream of the KRB. More than 85 % of the contribution of rock weathering (both the silicate and carbonate) is estimated to be in the total chemical budget. Additionally, the deposits of clasolite, limestone, mudstone, sandstone, etc., regulate the sulfide oxidation in the KRB (Zhang et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2021 ). In the upstream region of the study area, a predominantly dry and cold climate prevails. During the post-monsoon season, the average contribution of precipitation, sulfide oxidation, silicate weathering, and carbonate weathering of the upstream is 1%, 19%, 27%, and 53%, respectively. In comparison, the average contribution of precipitation, sulfide oxidation, silicate weathering, and carbonate weathering during the monsoon season is 1%, 19%, 17%, and 62%, respectively. The relatively higher contribution of carbonate weathering during the monsoon season is closely linked to the dominant monsoonal climate in the study area. This climatic system leads to increased river discharge, which, in turn, plays a significant role in physical erosion during the monsoon season. As previously discussed, the downstream region of the KRB experiences significantly different climatic conditions than the upstream region. During the post-monsoon season, the average contribution of precipitation, sulfide oxidation, silicate weathering, and carbonate weathering is 5%, 6%, 43%, and 46%, respectively. Likewise, during the monsoon season, the average contribution of precipitation, sulfide oxidation, silicate weathering, and carbonate weathering is 8%, 7%, 43%, and 43%, respectively. The relatively higher contribution of the precipitation inputs in the downstream region is particularly linked with the strong Indian monsoon influencing the windward side of the Himalayas region (Fig. 1 e, f ).   3.3 Chemical weathering and CO2  consumption rates Assessing the relative contributions of silicate and carbonate to chemical weathering is important in quantifying atmospheric CO2  consumption during the weathering processes (Manaka et al., 2015 ). The weathering cycles of the river basin play an important role in increasing CO2  consumption and mitigating climate warming as well. The chemical weathering rates in the KRB, in terms of silicates and carbonates during the post-monsoon and monsoon seasons, are calculated and presented in Table 5  . To determine these rates, the total discharge at each sampling point was simulated using the SPHY model, and the basin area was calculated using ArcMap, a GIS software. In the basin scale, the average annual CWR and SWR are calculated 26.35 tons/km2 /yr and 7.37 tons/km2 /yr, respectively. At the same time, the average CO2  consumption rates due to the carbonate weathering and silicate weathering are calculated 3.82 × 105  mol/km2 /yr and 3.40 × 105  mol/km2 /yr, respectively. Based on our estimation, the CO2  consumption by silicate and carbonate rock weathering accounting for ∼0.15% and ∼0.26% of the global CO2  consumption fluxes by carbonate (12300 × 109  mol/yr) and silicate (8700 × 109  mol/yr) weathering, respectively (Gaillardet et al., 1999 ). However, the total catchment area of the KRB is about 53,000 km2 , accounting for only 0.035% of the global continental (150 × 106  km2 ) (Li et al., 2009 ). The chemical denudation and CO2  consumption in the KRB are also comparable to those neighboring river basins, particularly originating from the Third Pole region, including the Ganges River, Brahmaputra River, Indus River, Yamuna, and Lhasa Rivers basins (Table 5 ). Generally, the rapid rock uplift, higher glacier depositions, and intense physical weathering due to the steep slope of catchments are major components for the higher chemical weathering in the Himalayas river basins (Das et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2021a ). As mentioned in the above section, the upstream part of the KRB is regulated by the dry and cold climate with intense physical weathering; however, the downstream region is mostly dominated by wet and humid climates. During the post-monsoon season, the average carbonate and silicate weathering rates in upstream of the KRB are estimated 2.33 tons/km2 /month and 0.55 tons/km2 /month, respectively ( Fig. 7  ) . Whereas, during the monsoon season, the average carbonate and silicate weathering rates are estimated 5.07 tons/km2 /month and 0.86 tons/km2 /month, respectively. Similarly, during the post-monsoon season, the average carbonate and silicate weathering rates in downstream of the KRB are estimated 0.69 tons/km2 /month and 0.26 tons/km2 /month, respectively ( Fig. 7 ) . Whereas, during the monsoon season, the average carbonate and silicate weathering rates are estimated 6.62 tons/km2 /month and 2.58 tons/km2 /month, respectively. In the upstream of the KRB, the average CO2  consumptions due to carbonate and silicate weathering are estimated 0.30 × 105  mol/km2 /month and 0.28 × 105  mol/km2 /month, respectively, during the post-monsoon season. Whereas, during the monsoon season, the average consumption rates are 0.67 × 105  mol/km2 /month and 0.44 × 105  mol/km2 /month, respectively ( Fig. 7 ) . Likewise, in the downstream region, the average CO2  consumptions due to carbonate and silicate weathering during the post-monsoon are estimated 0.10 × 105  mol/km2 /month and 0.13 × 105  mol/km2 /month, respectively. Whereas, during the monsoon season, the average consumption rates are 0.91 tons/km2 /month and 1.24 tons/km2 /month, respectively ( Fig. 7 ) . Differences in chemical weathering and CO2  consumption rates are evident between the upstream and downstream regions of the KRB during distinct seasons. In the post-monsoon season, weathering and CO2  consumption rates are notably higher in the upstream region than in the downstream region. This phenomenon may be attributed to increased physical erosion in the arid environment of the leeward side of the Himalayan region, driving higher rates of chemical denudation and CO2  consumption. Conversely, during the monsoon season, all these rates are higher in the downstream region of the KRB. This increase is primarily linked to the greater volume of water in the river channel. Higher river discharge plays a significant role in accelerating the processes of chemical weathering and CO2  consumption within the river catchment.   4 Discussion 4.1 Runoff components of the Koshi river basin The summary of simulated results of the hydrological regime of the KRB at Chatara gauge station for post-monsoon (November 2017) and monsoon (July 2019) are presented in Table 6  , and details of each sampling point are provided in the supplementary file  (Table S1  ). The total contribution of glacier melt, snowmelt, rainfall, and base flow in every sampling point has been quantified for both sampling periods. The KRB is characterized by distinct spatial and seasonal variations in climatic, hydrological, geological, and topographical perspectives. Total contributions of glacier melt, snowmelt, base flow and rainfall at the Chatara station are estimated 14%, 13%, 15% and 58%, respectively. The simulated results also align with the previous studies (Devkota and Gyawali, 2015; Sinha et al., 2019 ). The upstream and downstream regions of the KRB exhibit distinct hydrological characteristics, with marked variations in the contributions of glacier melt, base flow, snowmelt, and rainfall during different seasons (Fig. 8  ). Notably, during the post-monsoon season, base flow dominates the hydrological regime, while rainfall becomes the dominant contributor during the monsoon season.  4.2 Influence of hydrological regime on the river water chemistry Examining the characteristics of the river runoff and their contributors has important repercussions for the inclusive application of the basin's physical, chemical, and biological properties (Ma et al., 2019 ). River runoff and atmospheric inputs are crucial parameters to determine the characteristics of the hydrochemical features of a river basin. Considering the seasonal changes, the variability of runoff and precipitation during post-monsoon is lesser than average and higher during the monsoon season (Table 6 ). Additionally, the pattern of the hydrochemistry also differs during the post-monsoon and monsoon seasons. The concentration of most of the chemical attributes is measured higher during the post-monsoon season and lower during the monsoon season. The contradictory phenomenon suggested that the runoff/precipitation significantly influences the chemical loadings in the river waters. Through correlation analysis between major ions and hydrology of the KRB, it is exhibited that most of the ions are negatively correlated with river discharge and precipitation (Fig. 9  ). The dissolved Si and NO3 –  have a significant negative correlation with runoff and precipitation, whereas TDS, Ca2+ , Mg2+ , and HCO3 –  display a significant negative correlation with precipitation. To deepen understanding, correlation analysis has been applied to the concentration of major ions and major runoff contributors such as glacier melt, snowmelt, base flow, and rainfall. Most of the major ions, including TDS, negatively correlate with the glacier melt, snowmelt, and rainfall contribution. Still, a positive correlation exists with the base flow contribution (Fig. 9 ). Only Na+  has a significantly negative correlation with glacier melt. In contrast, major ions have no significant correlation with snowmelt contribution. Likewise, TDS, Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Si, SO4 2– , NO3 – , and HCO3 –  are significantly negatively correlated with the rainfall contribution (Fig. 9 ). Whereas, TDS, Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Na+ , Si, NO3 – , SO4 2– , and HCO3 –  that have a significant positive correlation with base flow contribution (Fig. 9 ). Correlation analysis of major ions with river discharge, precipitation, and runoff contributors indicates the major role of the hydrological characteristics in the chemical signatures of aquatic systems. The higher contributions of surface water, mainly rainfall, have the ability to decrease the concentrations of major ions due to the chemical dilution. Meanwhile, the higher contribution of ground flow, mainly base flow, can increase the concentration of chemical attributes due to the higher chemical weathering of bedrock minerals. The long-time contact of river water with the minerals and bedrock significantly increases the chemical loads in the river water.  4.3 Influence of hydrological regime on chemical weathering and CO2  consumption Using hydrological analysis, we examined the influence of precipitation, discharge, and major discharge contributors on weathering and CO2  consumption using Spearman’s correlation analysis. The correlation matrix, presented in Fig. 10  , clearly illustrates the significant impact of discharge and its components on weathering rates and CO2  consumption. Notably, except for glacier melt contribution, precipitation, total discharge, and other discharge contributors exhibit positive correlations with chemical weathering and CO2  consumption rates. These findings emphasize the crucial role of surface flow in influencing chemical denudation and atmospheric CO2  consumption, with both increasing and decreasing trends being linked to these factors. Interestingly, we observed that the snowmelt contribution only has a significantly positive correlation with the CWR and [CO2 ]car . This result is closely related to the Himalayas having a higher snow coverage area and subsequent deposition of the carbonate minerals. This result also suggested that silicate weathering in the KRB occurs in low-altitude areas rather than in highly glacierized Himalayas region. The increasing trend of the snowmelt runoff in the Himalaya Rivers due to climate change (Bookhagen and Burbank, 2010; Khadka et al., 2014 ) may significantly weathered the carbonate minerals and ultimately decline the water quality of the downstream by the increasing concentrations of the inorganic dissolved solutes. Hence, these dynamics in the Himalayan snow/glaciers will significantly influence the weathering pattern of the meltwater-dominated river basin. Therefore, the implications of climate change should be carefully considered in our efforts to combat global climate change.   5 Conclusion This study reveals that the hydrochemistry of the Himalayas River Basin is mostly influenced by the weathering of carbonate and silicate mineralswith significant spatiotemporal variations in the KRB. The major findings of this study are as follows: (1) River water of the KRB is mildly alkaline with a moderate TDS content and major ions concentrations. Hydrochemistry of the KRB is primarily influenced by the weathering of bedrock minerals, i.e., the silicate and carbonate. (2) The forward model clearly depicts that the contribution of the carbonate/silicate weathering accounts for > 85 % of the total cationic budget in both the upstream and downstream regions, with the remaining 15 % attributed to precipitation and sulfide oxidation. (3) The average SWR and CWR of the KRB are 7.37 tons/km2 /yr and 26.35 tons/km2 /yr, resulting in corresponding average CO2  consumption rates of 3.82 × 105  mol/km2 /yr and 3.40 × 105  mol/km2 /yr, respectively. (4) The average SWR and CWR are relatively higher in upstream during the post-monsoon season, while in the monsoon season, the reverse applies, mainly due to the greater volume of water. (5) The significant positive correlation of chemical weathering and CO2  consumption rates to the runoff components underscores the strong positive influence of surface flow like rainfall-runoff and snowmelt-runoff on chemical denudation of the Himalaya region. The study reveals that hydrology has a very significant role in regulating atmospheric CO2  consumption during chemical weathering. However, this study is based on twice sampling during the higher and lower discharge periods, which may not fully represent the whole-year seasonal variation dynamic. Future research should involve long-term monitoring at several available stations to better understand hydrochemical mechanisms. It will also be worth estimating chemical weathering by considering single geology to know the possible influence of geology in the Himalayas. Furthermore, isotopes (13 C, 42 Ca, 44 Ca, etc.) and inverse models can be applied in the future to more accurately estimate chemical weathering rates in a large basin scale.
1 Introduction Dam construction has significantly impacted fluvial systems worldwide, reducing water flow and increasing residence time by deepening the water depth, thereby altering their ecological dynamics (Dudgeon, 2000; Wang et al., 2019 ). Over two-thirds of the world's long rivers are no longer free-flowing (Zhang and Gu, 2023 ), leading to alterations in water column physicochemical properties and interconnected ecological disturbances (Visser et al., 2022; Winton et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2022 ). Phytoplankton communities, pivotal in aquatic ecosystems, have been greatly affected by anthropogenic activities such as dam construction and reservoir impoundment. These impacts manifest as alterations in phytoplankton growth, composition, and increased micro algal bloom risks (Baxter, 1977; Chen et al., 2020; Reynolds, 2011 ). While many studies have delved into the primary environmental determinants of phytoplankton dynamics in freshwater ecosystems, the majority have focused on lakes (Chellappa et al., 2009; Schulhof et al., 2019; Sommer et al., 1986; Summers and Ryder, 2023; Zhang et al., 2021a ), lake-type reservoirs (Liu et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015 ) or natural rivers(Ibáñez et al., 2012; Qu et al., 2019 ), and a significant knowledge gap persists, particularly concerning the unique ecological nuances of large deep channel-type reservoirs like the Xiangjiaba Reservoir (XJB). With their difference in water flow, nutrient availability, and physicochemical properties from lakes and natural rivers, it is imperative to scrutinize their ecological consequences (Qu et al., 2018; Wang, 2020 ). Notably, large channel-type reservoirs marked by their considerable depth and extensive runoff, circulation patterns are driven by a combination of inflow-induced barotropic and baroclinic forces, differing from the meteorologically driven circulations in lakes and lake-type reservoirs, contributing to the complexity of algal dynamics (Shi et al., 2023b ). Additionally, phytoplankton dynamics can vary regionally (Arcifa et al., 2023; Becker et al., 2010; Bulti, 2021; Xiao et al., 2011 ), and understanding their interplay with hydrological forces at specific regional scales remains an area of exploration. Moreover, the recent surge in hydropower development along the Yangtze River, particularly the construction of upstream cascade reservoirs-Wudongde, Baihetan, Xiluodu, and Xiangjiaba (shown in Fig. 1  a) with a total regulating capacity exceeding 20 billion m3  and an installed capacity of 44800 MW (Shi et al., 2023a ), has transformed the river-reservoir ecosystem, bringing forth new regionally ecological challenges that demand in-depth investigation. The Xiangjiaba Reservoir, collectively providing an installed capacity of 6,400 MW, stands as the final installation in the sequence of four cascade hydropower stations. This prestigious station is recognized as the fifth-largest hydropower facility in China and the eleventh-largest globally. It serves a pivotal role in China's ambitious West-to-East power transmission program, acting as a cornerstone in the country's energy infrastructure. Its strategic role in energy provision underscores the reservoir's societal importance, while it also offers unparalleled opportunities for academic exploration into the ecological and hydrodynamic nuances of large channel-type reservoirs, characterized by its deep, narrow channel-type morphology (Shi et al., 2023b ). During its ten-year operation, certain sections of the XJB have transitioned from a riverine to a lentic lake phase (Qu et al., 2020 ), presenting an unparalleled opportunity to study the ecological transformations induced by such large-scale hydrological modifications. While the ecological impacts of the adjacent Three Gorges Reservoir (TGR) in the Yangtze River mainstream have been extensively studied (Xu et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2022b ), with a more focus on algal issues in typical tributaries such as the Xiangxi Bay(Huang et al., 2020; Jin et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2022a ), these areas often exhibit lake-like characteristics with relatively weak inflow conditions(Li et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2013 ), making them fundamentally different from channel-type reservoirs in the mainstream like the XJB. The hydrodynamic mechanisms in channel-type reservoirs, driven by both temperature differences and significant runoff, introduce a layer of complexity not present in the more static environments of tributary bays which are primarily driven by tributary-mainstream temperature differences (Shi et al., 2023a ). Consequently, less attention has been given to upstream cascade reservoirs like the XJB, where the hydrodynamic mechanisms and their ecological implications, particularly in the main channel, remain less understood. This oversight highlights a critical gap in our understanding of potential algal bloom threats and the broader ecological impacts of reservoir construction on riverine ecosystems, underscoring the need for comprehensive studies in these areas. The construction of these vast, deep reservoirs has introduced a new set of ecological challenges, necessitating a thorough exploration of their aquatic environments, phytoplankton communities, and the driving environmental factors. This is a crucial issue in the conservation of the Yangtze River. Preliminary investigations have examined the reservoirs’ ecological conditions of the downstream Jinsha River (JR), providing initial glimpses into the XJB’s phytoplankton community (Gao et al., 2019; Gong et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020 ). However, most of these studies have spanned on the entire JR basin, lacking the granularity in sampling within the XJB to obtain detailed spatio-temporal phytoplankton patterns to decipher the complex dynamics. Moreover, given the relatively nascent operation phase and ongoing impacts from the upper cascade reservoirs, the river-reservoir ecosystem is yet to achieve equilibrium, and requires continuous follow-up studies. This dynamic context underscores the necessity for ongoing, detailed research to monitor and understand the evolving ecological conditions. This study aims to fill these gaps by conducting a detailed examination of the XJB, utilizing high-density and contemporary sampling methods to capture the most recent data, elucidate the spatio-temporal phytoplankton patterns within the XJB, their responses to the changing environmental conditions, and the overarching hydrodynamic influences shaping these patterns. Furthermore, by drawing comparisons with the pre-dam natural river conditions and the well-studied TGR, this research endeavors to shed light on the broader ecological implications of dam construction and reservoir impoundment. Such comparative analyses are crucial for understanding the transformative effects of such hydrological interventions on riverine ecosystems and for informing effective management and conservation strategies. Through this comprehensive approach, our study seeks to contribute significantly to the ongoing efforts to preserve the ecological integrity of the Yangtze River, amid the expanding network of large channel-type reservoirs and the escalating environmental pressures they entail.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Study area The Xiangjiaba Reservoir is a typical channel-type reservoir with a dam height of 162 m, which controls a watershed area of 45.88 × 104  km2  downstream of JR (Fig. 1 ). The XJB’s normal storage water level is 380 m since its impoundment in 2012, with a total storage capacity being 5.163 km3  (Wang et al., 2022 ) and the reservoir surface area being ∼ 95.6 km2 . It has a considerable backwater length of approximately 160 km, and the water depth of the reservoir increases from ∼ 10 m upstream to ∼ 120 m downstream. The main tributaries include the Xining River, Zhongdu River, and Dawen River, all of which are located within the backwater area throughout the year, with the average discharge being 44 m3 /s, 6 m3 /s, and 11 m3 /s, respectively (Yin et al., 2021 ). With the operation of the hydropower dam, the ecological environments in the forming riverine-reservoir system has been changed dramatically and need more deeply investigation.  2.2 Sample collection and analysis Field investigation and sampling in the XJB were conducted from September 2020 to October 2021, covering spring (April and May 2021), summer (June 2021), and autumn (September 2020 and October 2021). Sampling sites (J01 to J12) were distributed along the deep water stretch of XJB, as depicted in Fig. 1 . The downstream section of the JR experiences its flood season from June to August. During this period, the river has a high flow rate, which reduces the likelihood of algal blooms. Additionally, due to logistical constraints encountered during that period, June was the sole representative month for the summer season. In September 2020, sample collection was limited to sites J03-J09 due to unfavorable meteorological conditions. Besides the mainstream, sampling was also conducted in three major tributaries of the XJB. Selected data from these tributaries, including chl-a concentrations, are referenced in our comparative analysis to provide context, without detailed elaboration. We employed a portable YSI multiparameter electrodes with pre-correction (EXO, Xylem Co. New York, USA) to measure physical indicators, including water depth (±0.04 %), water pressure (±1.5 mmHg), water temperature (Tem, ±0.01℃), pH (±0.1), conductivity (±0.5 %), turbidity (±2%). The EXO electrodes were carefully lowered to each site’s bottom and then slowly pulled back to the surface using a controlled winch. We used data only during the descent process from 0.2 m to the maximum depth and data collected during the ascent were discarded due to the disturbed water layers by the instrument. Additionally, the Secchi disk depth (SD) was employed to determine water column transparency. For chemical analyses, surface and bottom water samples were procured from all sites using pre-acid-washed plastic containers and subsequently transported to the laboratory. These samples were analyzed for a range of chemical constituents, including ammonium nitrogen (NH4 -N), nitrate nitrogen (NO3 -N), nitrite nitrogen (NO2 -N), organic nitrogen (ON), total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), orthophosphate (PHOS), dissolved oxygen (DO), potassium permanganate index (COD), and silica (SiO2 ), in accordance with the standard protocols delineated by the standard guidelines (State Environment Protection Bureau, 2002 ). However, due to constraints during the sampling periods in April and September, SiO2 measurements were not conducted, resulting in the absence of SiO2 data for them. For Chlorophyll-a (chl-a), 500–750 ml of water was pressurized and filtered through a 0.45 μm glass fiber filter using the Nalgene filtration system. Subsequently, the chl-a filters were extracted with a buffered acetone solution (comprising 90 % acetone and 10 % saturated magnesium carbonate) and stored under refrigeration for 24 h before colorimetric determination (Jespersen and Christoffersen, 1987; Tq et al., 2020 ). Qualitative samples of phytoplankton were collected with a 25# phytoplankton net, which were dragged in an “∞” shape for 3 min at 20–30 cm/s at a depth of 0.5 m below the water surface, and the concentrated liquid was transferred into a 30 mL brown reagent bottle and fixed with 1.2–1.5 mL of formalin solution using a plastic dropper (Xu et al., 2021b ). In the laboratory, samples were classified, transformed into temporary specimens for microscope slides, and identified using literatures (Hu and Wei, 2006; MoWRot, 2016; Shi, 2004 ). Quantitative samples were collected from the surface layer of each sampling site, fixed with Lugol's solution, and analyzed using an Olympus BX51 microscope at × 400 magnification, with classification and counting performed according to established standards and books (Hu and Wei, 2006; Needham and Needham, 1962; Utermohl, 1958 ). Phytoplankton species were classified taxonomically and grouped according to Reynolds functional groups (FGs), a classification system based on energy utilization, nutrient uptake, algal morphology, and growth characteristics (Reynolds et al., 2002 ) and then expanded by Padisák et al. (2009). FGs based on individual physiological, morphological, and ecological attributes (Huang et al., 2017 ) are essential tools for summarizing community environmental characteristics and analyzing changes in phytoplankton biomass (Affe et al., 2019 ). That can better assess and predict potential structural and functional impacts on aquatic ecosystems (Wang et al., 2020b ).  2.3 Data analysis The analysis of chl-a was referred to the water quality standards for the Yungui Lake region and the central and eastern lake region in China, which includes XJB (The Ministry of Ecology and Environment, 2020 ). A chl-a baseline of 3.4 μg/L was adopted to evaluate the ecological effect of algae growth, and if the concentration exceeds the baseline, algae growth may endanger the ecosystem function. The dominant species index of phytoplankton proposed by McNaughton (Austin, 1968 ) was used to determine the dominant species (Y>0.02), Y = n / N × f i    , where n / N    represents the proportion of the number of individuals of the i-th species in the community to the total number of individuals, and f i    is the occurrence of the species in the sample. Species with Y exceeding 0.1 were considered absolutely dominant. The same formula, replacing n / N    with the ratio of the number of individuals of the i-th phylum or genus to the total number of individuals in the community, was used to determine dominant phyla and genera. To quantify the stability of the water column, we introduced the RWCS/H index R W C S / H = ( ρ b  - ρ s  )  / ( ρ 4  - ρ 5  )  × H  - 1     , where ρ s    and ρ b    represent the surface and bottom water densities, respectively; ρ 4     and ρ 5    are water densities at 4 °C and 5 °C, respectively; and H is the water depth. This parameter reflects water column stability in response to thermal stratification (Wang et al., 2020a; Zeng et al., 2016 ). This method is based on a single relative water column stability (RWCS) coefficient (Becker et al., 2009; Padisák et al., 2003 ), and it is then divided by the water depth for calibration, which is a more effective thermal stratification stability measurement by considering the effect of water depth while emphasizing the difference in density between the surface and bottom water column. RWCS/H between 0.17 m−1  and 1.56 m−1  indicates the stratification formation or extinction period; values between 1.56 m−1  and 6.99 m−1  is the stable stratification period, and RWCS/H<0.17 m−1  is the homo-thermal mixing period (Zeng et al., 2016 ).   3 Results 3.1 Spatial and temporal analysis of environmental and ecological indexes Monitored environmental factors in the XJB reservoir were illustrated in Fig. 2  . The average surface chl-a concentration in the reservoir was low, measuring 2 μg/L during the survey period, but it exhibited wide variability, ranging from 0.02 to 26 μg/L (Fig. 2 a). Compared to the chl-a baseline (3.4 μg/L) for lakes in central and eastern China, 85 % of the monitoring sites in the reservoir’s mainstream had lower concentrations, indicating a low overall risk of algae bloom. Nevertheless, there were significant spatio-temporal variations, with higher chl-a values observed in spring and summer, and notable differences between upstream and downstream sites, except in autumn. Spatially, two clusters of sites with higher chl-a concentrations were identified: one near the dam and the other at the junction of the mainstream and tributaries. Some sites near the dam had slightly elevated concentrations than average but did not exceed 5 μg/L (e.g., J12 in April: 4.71 μg/L; J11 in May: 3.68 μg/L; J12 in June: 3.54 μg/L). Conversely, sites at the junctions exhibited much higher concentrations, such as J08 at the confluence of Dawen River and mainstream in May (6.86 μg/L). During that month, the chl-a concentration range in Dawen River was 3.17–32.35 μg/L, with a mean value of 14.31 μg/L, suggesting the tributary significantly influenced the chl-a in the mainstream. Another site with a high chl-a concentration was J10 station at the confluence of Zhongdu River and mainstream in September (26 μg/L). The chl-a concentration range of Zhongdu River during that month was 57.85–78.89 μg/L, with a mean of 69.77 μg/L. In both May and September, some sites in the tributary had chl-a concentrations above 30 μg/L, and algal blooms were visible. Overall, surface chl-a concentration in XJB demonstrated spatial and seasonal variations, with higher values in spring and summer. Some sites near the dam and at the junctions of the mainstream and tributary had chl-a concentrations above 5 μg/L, which were strongly influenced by the algal blooms in the tributary. Water quality in the XJB reservoir is generally moderate, with environmental indicators like COD, DO, NH4 -N, and TP meeting Grade III of National Surface Water Quality Standards (Fig. 2 b, c, f, i). However, the TN concentration (Fig. 2 e) was relatively high in April (average: 1.2 mg/L; range: 1.0–1.4 mg/L), and it also exceeded 1.0 mg/L (the threshold of Grade III) at some sites in May (J08 and J11), June (J01) and September (J04). NO3 -N and ON were the primary forms of nitrogen in spring, while NH4 -N dominated in autumn. In April, when the TN concentration was highest, NO3 -N (average: 0.83 mg/L, Fig. 2 g) and ON (average: 0.3 mg/L, Fig. 2 h) accounted for 70 % and 25 % of it, respectively. Compared with previous observation data, the TN concentration in the XJB reservoir has increased since the reservoir was impounded (Zhang, 2022 ), likely due to longer nutrient retention time. The reservoir's pH was weakly alkaline, except in September (Fig. 2 d). Concentrations of certain indicators differed between the bottom and surface layers, with higher values observed in the bottom layer for TP, phosphorus (PHOS), silicon dioxide (SiO2 ), and ON, potentially due to nutrient deposition (Li et al., 2022 ). Conversely, the surface layer exhibited higher COD, DO, NH4 -N, TN, and NO3 -N concentrations. Although the DO concentration in the bottom layer was slightly lower than the surface layer, it remained above the Grade I water quality threshold of 7.5 mg/L, indicating the absence of hypoxia commonly observed in other large reservoirs post-operation (Yu et al., 2020 ). Water transparency (SD, Fig. 2 m), often used to estimate algal biomass and nutrient status (Carlson, 1977 ), varied from 0.6 to 5.5 m in the reservoir area. SD was highest in April and fluctuated in other months without significant difference. The surface water temperature ranged from 16.09 to 23.11℃, with the lowest value in April and increasing values in May and June due to higher air temperatures. The water temperature decreased in September and October after the summer heat. From April to June, the water temperature along the mainstream differed more due to upstream water inflow and internal temperature gradient, with higher values near the dam.  3.2 Relative water column stability The RWCS/H in the XJB reservoir (Fig. 2 o) reflected the hydrodynamic impact of the reservoir construction and operation on the water components, especially nutrients (Wang, 2020 ). It also affected the habitats of tributaries near the dam, which might change the algal density and dominance in the downstream section (Wang, 2010 ). The RWCS/H index ranged from 0.006 to 2.0 /m, with higher mean and variance in spring and summer than in autumn. In spring and early summer, the RWCS/H was more elevated in May and June, with values above 1.56 /m at some sites (J11 in May; J08, J10, J11, and J12 in June), indicating water stratification (Wang et al., 2020a ). In autumn, the water stability was low, the variance was slight, and the stratification disappeared by October. The simultaneous observational data in the XJB showed a seasonal stratification phenomenon in the XJB with a vertical temperature gradient from April to August and uniform water temperature in other months, which agreed with the results calculated in this study (Shi et al., 2023a ). Spatially, the upstream sites had smaller temperature differences and lower RWCS/H than the downstream sites near the dam. Moreover, the XJB reservoir had a cooling effect on the mainstream water temperature from April to June due to its regulation and storage function in the Xiluodu-Xiangjiaba section (Li et al., 2021 ). The water temperature in the XJB Reservoir in April and June of 2021 was about 5℃ lower than that in April and June 2011 (Gong et al., 2014 ), due to the cascade reservoirs operation upstream of the Jinsha River. The phenomenon matched the theoretical prediction that the warming period after the cascade reservoirs' construction and operation was delayed by one month and shifted from April to July (Wang et al., 2022 ).  3.3 Structure of phytoplankton community A total of 8 phyla, 47 genera, and 78 species of phytoplankton were identified in the XJB reservoir, as shown in Table 1  . Bacillariophyta and Chlorophyta were the most abundant phyla, with 32 and 21 species, respectively (Fig. 3  ). The spatial and temporal distribution of phytoplankton abundance showed a range of algal cell densities from 0.07 to 3.06 × 106  cells/L, with an average of 1.43 × 106  cells/L (shown as dots in Fig. 3 ). The highest algal cell densities were observed primarily at the main confluence of the mainstream and its tributaries, like J04 in September, J08 and J03 in May, and J03 in April. The correlation between algal cell density and the number of algal species varied among different phyla (Table 1 ). Bacillariophyta accounted for the most species but had a lower density (23.29 %) compared to Chlorophyta (38.15 %). Cryptophyta, despite having only four species, significantly contributed to algal cell density (21.14 %). The dominant genera included Cyclotella , Nitzschia , Melosira  (Bacillariophyta), Chroomonas , Cryptomonas  (Cryptophyta), Scenedesmus, Oocystis, Ankistrodesmus, Chlamydomonas, Coelastrum, Pandorina, Eudorina (Chlorophyta), Tribonema  (Xanthophyta), Pseudanabaena  (Cyanophyta), and Gymnodinium  (Pyrrophyta). The abundance analysis showed different prevalent phyla and genera (Y>0.02) each month. Cryptophyta, Chlorophyta, and Bacillariophyta were absolutely prevalent (Y>0.1) in April and May, with Cryptophyta being the most abundant. In May, the diversity of phytoplankton increased, with seven phyla present. Cryptophyta decreased in abundance over time, while Bacillariophyta, Chlorophyta, Pyrrophyta, and Euglenophyta remained prevalent in different months. In September, Chlorophyta and Bacillariophyta were absolutely abundant, and Pseudanabaena  (Cyanophyta) became an active predominant genus with the Y of 0.074. In October, diatoms (also called Bacillariophyta) had a definite advantage of 0.693, while the prevalence of other phyla decreased. The most abundant phytoplankton indicated an increase in water nutrient levels and the potential for algal blooms. Cryptophyta, Chlorophyta, and Bacillariophyta were representative algae in spring and autumn. Chroomonas acuta , a Cryptophyta species, showed absolute prevalence in spring, with flagella adjusting its position in the water to obtain the best lighting conditions (Wang et al., 2021 ). It was often an indicator species of moderately polluted water, favoring growing in the environment with rich organic matter and nitrogen, and was sensitive to water mixing, and Tribonema  (Xanthophyta) appeared in large numbers in autumn and became a unique prevalent group in the region, but no dominant phenomenon of Tribonema  was found previously (Gong et al., 2014; Wei et al., 2020 ). Tribonema was a common type of filamentous algae that was highly adaptable and liked to live in continuously mixed water layers (Chen et al., 2014 ). That likely related to the convergence of tributaries because a large amount of Tribonema was also present in the Xining River in September of the same year. Euglenophyta was the most abundant phylum only in June and preferred freshwater rich in organic matter(Hu and Wei, 2006 ). Overall, the construction of cascade reservoirs in the JR resulted in changes to the phytoplankton community structure, as evidenced by the monthly variations of predominant phyla detailed in Table 1 . Bacillariophyta and Chlorophyta remained prevalent throughout the year, while other phyla showed temporal fluctuations. The ecosystem shifted towards a more stable lake-type water body, impacting the distribution and prevalence of phytoplankton species. This transformation signifies a broader shift from a riverine to a more stable reservoir ecosystem. While the hydrodynamic conditions have rapidly evolved due to reservoir construction (Ting et al., 2020; Xuan et al., 2018 ), the ecological adaptation appears to be more gradual, suggesting an ongoing period of adjustment.  3.4 Classification of phytoplankton functional groups and spatial and temporal distribution characteristics The phytoplankton in the XJB are categorized into 21 FGs, namely A, C, D, E, F, G, J, Lo, MP, N, P, S1, T, TB, TD, W1, W2, X1, X2, XPh and Y during the study period. The species comprising each of the groups are detailed in Table 2  . This paper selects the dominant FGs with relative biomass greater than 5 % for each month for comparative analysis, which are X2, J, G, Lo, F, C, MP, A, Y, W1, S1, T, and P. The dominant FGs changed monthly, as shown in Table 3   and Fig. S1 . Among them, X2 had the highest frequency of occurrence and the most significant proportion among the functional groups, representative genera including Chroomonas  (Cyanophyta) and Chlamydomonas  (Chlorophyta). The representative algae for J is Coelastrum  (Chlorophyta), for G are Pandorina  and Eudorina  (Chlorophyta), for S1 is Pseudanabaena  (Cyanophyta), for A is Cyclotella  (Bacillariophyta) and for T is Tribonema  (Xanthophyta).   4 Discussion 4.1 Comparative analysis of phytoplankton changes in the XJB reservoir To gain a deeper insight of the phytoplankton community structure after the construction and operation of the XJB, we sought to collate all available historical data pertaining to the XJB sites. This effort was challenged by the limited number of studies exclusively focusing on the XJB. Consequently, we incorporated data of the XJB area dating back to 2007, prior to the dam's construction. These findings are detailed in Fig. 4  , with a particular emphasis on the representation of diatoms within the community. We observed a significant increase in both the cell density and diversity of phytoplankton after the reservoir's establishment. The algal cell density in the downstream region of the Jinsha River, where the XJB is situated, has surged almost tenfold over a decade. During the construction phase, the algal cell density ranged from 0.35 to 2.73 × 105  cells/L(Gong et al., 2014; Yu, 2008 ). In 2014, the average cell density was 2 × 105  cells/L (Gao et al., 2019 ). From 2017 to 2018, the phytoplankton density remained at 0.193 × 105  ∼ 3.41 × 105  cells/L (Wei et al., 2020 ). In 2019, the average algal cell density in spring and autumn was 2.3 × 106  cells/L (Zhang et al., 2020 ), while the algal cell density in the Jinsha River basin in summer was 5 × 105  cells/L (Yang, 2021 ). This increase in abundance of algae after the reservoirs’ construction and operation is observed in other cascade reservoirs, i.e., on the Lancang River (Jinpeng Li et al., 2013 ) and Paraná River (Nogueira et al., 2010 ). However, if the cell density of a specific species increases too much, there is a risk of algal blooms. The composition and structure of phytoplankton in the XJB have also undergone significant changes. Before the reservoir operation, diatoms (also called Bacillariophyta) were the dominant group, accounting for a high proportion of the total biomass (up to 70 % or more) (Gong et al., 2014; Yu, 2008 ). However, after the operation, while diatoms remained dominant, their proportion gradually decreased, and other algal groups emerged and showed dynamic changes (Gao et al., 2019; Wei et al., 2020; Yang, 2021; Zhang et al., 2020 ). The composition of phytoplankton in the XJB is now characterized by multiple algal groups commonly dominating, including Chlorophyta, Cryptophyta, Bacillariophyta, and Xanthophyta (Fig. 3 ). This shift from a single-phylum-dominance to multi-phylum-dominance mode indicates a change in the ecological structure of phytoplankton in the reservoir. Building on prior research, our findings indicate an upward trend in phytoplankton diversity, with the community structure becoming increasingly diverse (Fig. 4 ). While the swift alterations in hydrodynamic conditions due to reservoir construction align with earlier findings (CTGC, 2019; Shi et al., 2023b; Ting et al., 2020 ), the ecological responses appear to unfold over a more extended period, suggesting an ongoing ecological recalibration (Table 4  ). This transition pushes the ecosystem towards a more stable lacustrine configuration, influencing the distribution and dominance of phytoplankton species. Nevertheless, as the impacts of reservoir impoundment continue to emerge, sustained monitoring becomes vital to identify the core drivers and anticipate long-term consequences, ensuring the reservoir's ecological integrity. However, this study, constrained by the limited data available, emphasizes the importance of long-term, multi-annual research, beyond mere seasonal changes, to fully understand the impacts of anthropogenic stressors like damming on phytoplankton community structures. Afterall the four-decade-long monitoring of the Jiulong River mainstream, marked by numerous algal blooms (Ruan et al., 2024 ), contrasts with the limited research on the XJB Reservoir. While multi-year scale studies on the impact of reservoir construction on phytoplankton community structure are more well-studied in lakes(Fu et al., 2020; Lv et al., 2014; Reinl et al., 2021; Rugema et al., 2019 ), reservoir studies often focus on algal blooms in specific tributary sections post-operation or within annual seasonal cycles, leaving a gap in our understanding of long-term ecological impacts in such environments.(Nwankwegu et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2021a; Zhu et al., 2013 ). Our preliminary findings, indicating a significant rise in algal cell density and a shift in phytoplankton species dominance, underscore the imperative for more detailed research to unravel these complex, long-term ecological transformations, thereby addressing a notable gap in reservoir ecological studies. We also compared the phytoplankton structure with the neighboring Three Gorges Reservoir (TGR), both large deep-water reservoirs located in the mainstream of the Yangtze River, revealing distinct differences in phytoplankton structure. We used the results from Wei et al. (2022) as a reference for the phytoplankton status of the TGR during the same period as our study. The mean abundance of phytoplankton in the TGR was 1.97 × 105  cells/L, while it was tenfold higher in the XJB with a mean abundance of 1.43 × 106  cells/L. The XJB exhibited alternating dominance of Chlorophyta, Cryptophyta, and Chrysophyta, while diatoms were dominant in the TGR throughout the year. Cyanobacteria also played a significant role in the TGR, but favorable growth conditions for Cyanobacteria were not observed in the XJB. We hypothesized that the difference in hydrodynamic conditions between the mainstream of the TGR and the XJB might be one of the critical reasons for their different phytoplankton habitats, as the TGR has a larger runoff and flow velocity and has not shown water stratification compared with the XJB (Ren et al., 2018 ), the strong vertical mixing in TGR can extensively explain the differences of the two reservoirs.  4.2 The response of phytoplankton functional groups and chl-a to environmental factors Specific habitat conditions and environmental factors in water bodies play a crucial role in shaping the composition of FGs (Reynolds, 2011; Tian et al., 2014 ). In our analysis, we concentrated on chl-a as a proxy for phytoplankton abundance, given its established role as an indicator of algae density (Guo et al., 2011). Correlation analysis revealed significant associations between chl-a and several environmental factors, including relative water column stability coefficient (RWCS/H), total nitrogen (TN), nitrogen-phosphorus ratio (TN/TP), Secchi depth (SD), and phosphorus (PHOS) (Fig. 5  ). RWCS/H exhibited the highest positive correlation with chl-a (r-correlation coefficient = 0.703), followed by TN, TN/TP, and SD. In contrast, it showed a negative correlation with PHOS (r = -0.449). These findings highlight the importance of water hydrodynamics and nutrient levels in shaping phytoplankton diversity in the XJB. Further exploration of the response of FGs to RWCS/H and nitrogen-phosphorus nutrients revealed distinct patterns (Fig. 5 ). FGs X2 and L0, predominantly composed of flagellated algae, showed significant positive correlations with RWCS/H (R values of 0.585 and 0.613, respectively). These algae, including Chlamydomonas , Chroomonas , Peridinium , and Gymnodinium , thrived in stable water layers due to their motility advantages (see Fig.S1  for specific distribution). Other FGs demonstrated correlations with RWCS/H, albeit not as pronounced as X2 and L0. FG J, consisting of Chlorophyta such as Coelastrum , Actinastrum , and Scenedesmus , preferred high-nutrient and mixed shallow water body with weak mobility (Zhang et al., 2021b ). FG A and TB, primarily comprising non-flagellated diatoms with a siliceous shell, faced limitations in surface water due to their density and immobility (Huang, 2007 ). Therefore, when the water column was stratified and the vertical mixing was weakened, the increase of RWCS/H was one of the main factors limiting the diatoms’ growth. Although the overall correlation between nutrients and biomass was not as strong as RWCS/H, different FGs exhibited varied responses. FG X2, consisting of Chlamydomonas  and Chroomonas , showed a significant positive correlation with TN (r = 0.624), indicating their preference for eutrophic conditions. FG T, mainly composed of Tribonema , demonstrated a negative correlation with TN (r = -0.589), as high nitrogen levels inhibited its growth. Low phosphorus stress also inhibited the growth of Tribonema  (Guo et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2020b). These results emphasize the differential responses of FGs to specific environmental factors, underscoring the need for a comprehensive analysis beyond chl-a. TN/TP ratios also played a crucial role in nutrient dynamics (Fig. 6  ). In freshwater systems, TN/TP ratios above 16:1 typically indicate phosphorus limitation (Downing and Q, 1992 ), and similar patterns were observed in the XJB. The TN/TP in most sites exceeded 16:1, particularly in areas with high chl-a concentrations. Notably, FG X2 exhibited relatively abundant nitrogen and thrived within a TN/TP range of 30–85. However, although the TN/TP ratio of the site in October was closer to 16:1 (ranging from 15.5 to 27), the corresponding chl-a concentration remained markedly low. This anomaly could be attributed to the extensive water mixing observed during this period, which compromised water column stability and favored diatom predominance. Diatoms, thriving under such hydrodynamic conditions, outcompeted other algal groups, thereby diminishing the influence of nutrient ratios on phytoplankton community structure. This underscores the complex interplay between hydrodynamics and nutrient availability, suggesting that in the XJB, hydrodynamic conditions may eclipse the TN/TP ratio's role in dictating phytoplankton functional group dynamics. Changes in silicon content might also be associated with the shift in non-diatom proportions of phytoplankton communities in September. Silicon plays a vital role in diatom growth, and alterations in nutrient structure, with decreased silicon and increased nitrogen and phosphorus, have been observed in the Yangtze River mouth after the operation of TGR, resulting in decreased diatom biomass and increased dominance of non-diatom phytoplankton (Liu et al., 2021 ). The 6–8 mg/L concentration of silicon dioxide in the XJB was lower than the optimal growth conditions (15 mg/L) for diatoms (Liu et al., 2021 ), which necessitates further investigation into the effects of changes in silicon content resulting from cascade reservoir operation on diatom growth. Furthermore, due to thermal stratification and the consumption of dissolved oxygen in the water column, some large deep-water reservoirs often experience seasonal dissolved oxygen deficiency (Bellanger et al., 2004; Han et al., 2018 ). However, for the XJB, there was currently no evidence of vertical deficiency. Our analysis did not reveal significant correlations between dissolved oxygen and FGs, potentially due to the duration of reservoir operation and the biomass levels of phytoplankton. Further studies involving monitoring and simulations are required to examine dissolved oxygen distribution and its impact on phytoplankton biomass in the XJB.   5 Conclusions In this study, we undertook a series of field surveys and laboratory analyses to examine the phytoplankton community and associated environmental factors in the XJB, one of the Yangtze River’s prominent reservoirs. We delved into the driving factors behind algae distribution and their temporal variations. The main findings are as follows:(1) The phytoplankton density and composition in the XJB has shifted significantly since its construction in 2006. The overall algae density has gradually increased over the past decade, from ∼ 2 × 105  cells/L initially to 1.43 × 106  cells/L in our recent observations. More than a quantitative change, there's been a notable shift in the phytoplankton structure from a single-phylum-dominance mode, primarily represented by Bacillariophyta, to a more diverse multi-phylum-dominance mode. Notably, Cryptophyta dominates in spring, Xanthophyta peaks in autumn, and both Bacillariophyta and Chlorophyta co-dominate in the annual cycle.  (2) While the average chl-a concentration remains relatively low, it exhibits high spatial and seasonal fluctuations. A discernible upward trend is observed along the channel, starting from 0.02 μg/L upstream and culminating at 4 μg/L near the dam, averaging at 2 μg/L. It's worth noting that concentrations can spike to 26 μg/L at the confluence of the mainstream and the Zhongdu tributary. Overall, the reservoir's water quality is generally moderate, with TN values ranging from 0.5 to 1.5 mg/L and TP below 0.05 mg/L.  (3) The stratification in water column restricts diatom growth and favors specific algae with flagellum, i.e., Chlorophyta and Cryptophyta, whereas other environmental factors do not impose significant constraints on algae distribution. This stratification effect also elucidates the differences between the XJB and its neighboring mega-reservoir, the TGR, even with comparable nutrient profiles. The TGR retains a diatom-dominant ecosystem due to its pronounced vertical mixing.  (4) Overall, the shift from a riverine to a reservoir ecosystem, significantly alters the hydrodynamic processes within the reservoir, profoundly impacting the biological ecosystem's response. This change underscores the critical importance of proactive and sustained monitoring to ensure the reservoir's ecological stability and vitality.
1 Introduction Microplastics (MPs) refer to plastic particles with a diameter less than 5 mm (Thompson et al., 2004 ). The pollution of microplastics is significantly attributed to industrial activities (Grbić et al., 2020; Brožová et al., 2023 ), agricultural production (Li et al., 2022; Jia et al., 2024 ), urban runoff and sewage (Liu et al., 2024; Rasmussen et al., 2024 ). Microplastics are ubiquitous in freshwater systems (Cook et al., 2021; Stride et al., 2023 ), including natural rivers (Nash et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Nihei et al., 2024 ) and lakes (Free et al., 2014; Dusaucy et al., 2021 ), urban settings and water transportation infrastructures (Stride et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024 ), and even urban water supply systems (Adediran et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2024 ). The extensive dispersion of microplastics amplifies the potential for biological and human exposure to these particles. A variety of organisms are more likely to ingest microplastics and gradually transfer them through the food web (Castro-Castellon et al., 2022 ), which could eventually pose a potential threat to human health (Liu and You, 2023; Wang et al., 2024 ). It is evident that microplastic pollution has emerged as a significant environmental issue. Rivers play a crucial role as pathways for the transportation of microplastics to the ocean (Besseling et al., 2017 ), making them pivotal in comprehending the dynamics and fate of microplastics. Confluences are widespread and serve as important control nodes for habitat (Li et al., 2023b; Nazari-Giglou et al., 2016 ) in drainage networks. The layout of spur dikes in confluences will enhance flow regimes and alter fish habitats (Koken and Constantinescu, 2008a; Ma et al., 2020 ). The unique flow structure of spur dikes facilitates the provision of nutrients to fish, thereby offering them a suitable habitat for shelter (Kang et al., 2012 ). However, the layout of spur dikes may affect the transport properties of microplastics and disrupts their spatial distribution patterns in confluences. Harmful substances such as microorganisms (McCormick et al., 2014 ) and viruses (Lu et al., 2022 ), which are adsorbed onto microplastics, can adversely affect organisms and populations (Mughini-Gras et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2023a ) in confluences containing spur dikes. Therefore, the investigation of microplastic behavior at the confluence with the spur dike is crucial for both ecosystems and human health. Best et al. (1987)  defined six zones in the confluence: flow deflection, flow separation, flow stagnation, maximum velocity, flow recovery, and distinct shear layers. Some researchers have demonstrated, through various research methods, that the hydrodynamic characteristics of confluences are intricate and possess significant three-dimensional features (Bradbrook et al., 1998; Herrero et al., 2016; Li et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2023a ). The layout of spur dikes in confluences will inevitably impact the hydrodynamic characteristics. The complex turbulent structure and low velocity zone (spur dike field) are generated downstream of the spur dike (Han and Lin., 2018 ). The hydrodynamic characteristics mentioned above are important drivers in the transportation of dissolved pollutants and nutrients. For example, the concentration distribution of dissolved contaminants is governed (Tang et al., 2018 ) by the coherent structures (Sukhodolov and Rhoads, 2001 ) that exist in the shear layer. In addition, the spiral flow accelerates the mixing of pollutants in the water column (Yuan et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2023b ). The dissolved contaminants have the potential to diffuse into the spur dike field (Montazeri et al., 2022 ). The transport and diffusion mechanisms for dissolved pollutants in confluences containing spur dikes have been relatively rich. However, as a particle pollutant, microplastics may exhibit distinct behavior in confluences compared to other pollutants. The current study has demonstrated the distinctive transportation patterns and spatial distribution of microplastics in confluences. For example, the occurrence of intricate confluences will lead to an augmentation in the fluxes of microplastics (Zhao et al., 2020 ), while higher microplastic abundances have been observed in natural river confluence (Klein et al., 2015; Haque et al., 2024 ). However, the hydrodynamic influence of spur dikes on the transport and fate of microplastics in confluences remains poorly understood. Furthermore, the density of microplastics plays a pivotal role in governing their vertical transport dynamics within the water column (Yuan et al., 2022 ). For instance, high-density particles will be deposited within the riverbed (Stride et al., 2024 ), whereas low-density particles will be transported upwards in the upper water column (Shen et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2024 ). The density of microplastics can also impact the terminal velocity (Bagaev et al., 2017 ) and residence time of microplastics in the water column. However, the influence of density on the behavior of microplastics in confluences with spur dikes remains inadequately addressed in existing literature. Therefore, it is necessary to investigate the hydrodynamic transport mechanism of microplastics considering the influence of layout spur dikes and density effects. Current research methods for microplastics rely on prototype observations (Reisser et al., 2015; Saarni et al., 2023 ), laboratory experiments (Van Melkebeke et al., 2020; Waldschläger et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020 ), and numerical models (Bondelind et al., 2020; Holmes et al., 2020; Yazir et al., 2022 ). The prototype observations are influenced by the weather and hydrological conditions in the study area. There are still some major challenges and limitations in monitoring microplastics in rivers (Ali et al., 2023 ). It is difficult to understand how microplastics are transported and cycled (Range et al., 2023 ). Numerical simulation offers a cost-effective approach to acquiring the motion of microplastics. The CFD is considered to be an effective method for capturing turbulence characteristics around buildings (Zhu et al., 2022 ). The DEM is a computational approach utilized for simulating particle motion, enabling direct acquisition of comprehensive insights into particle dynamics. The CFD-DEM coupled method integrates continuous phase and dispersed phase simulation calculations, thereby overcoming the limitations of Eulerian methods in modeling discrete phase motion. The method has been widely used in the simulation of sediment transport (Alihosseini and Thamsen, 2019; Sun et al., 2016; Yazdanfar et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2018 ), erosion (Liu et al., 2022; Mu et al., 2023; Zhang and Liu, 2023 ), and fluvial sediment transport (Lei et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2022 ) with good accuracy. However, sediment transport modeling is not applicable to microplastics (Kowalski et al., 2016; Goral et al., 2023 ). Thus, the study presents an innovative three-dimensional hydrodynamic-microplastic transport model, which is simulated using a one-way CFD-DEM method. The behavior of microplastics was accurately tracked in the confluence with the spur dike under intense turbulent conditions. In summary, previous studies of confluences have been limited to flow structures, dissolved pollutants, and habitat studies. The studies have primarily focused on the terminal velocity of microplastics in static water and their transport distribution in dynamic water (Jiang et al., 2024; Dittmar et al., 2024 ). There is a lack of insight into the hydrodynamic motion mechanism of microplastics in confluences, considering both the layout of spur dikes and the properties of microplastics. The objective of this work is to clarify the microplastic motion patterns and hydrodynamic retention mechanisms in the confluence with a spur dike, rather than solely focusing on investigating microplastic concentrations and sedimentation under static water. The laboratory-scale numerical simulations investigated the influence of different angles (60°, 90°, 120°) of the spur dike, various materials (polyethylene, polystyrene, polyamide), and microplastic diameters (0.5 mm, 1 mm, 1.5 mm, 2 mm) on the dynamics and accumulation of microplastics. The findings of this study will provide novel insights into the motion of microplastics in a laboratory-scale confluence, particularly under the disturbance of the spur dike. The novelties of the present work are (i) the detailed analysis of the impact of spur dike angles, microplastic properties (material, diameter) on the motion of the microplastics, (ii) the retention process of microplastics from the mainstream to the spur dike field and flow separation.  2 Materials and methods In this work, we employed the coupled CFD-DEM method, which was implemented using ANSYS FLUENT and Altair EDEM software via a coupling interface. During the CFD calculation stage, ANSYS FLUENT acquired fluid motion by solving the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations within the fluid domain. The identification of appropriate turbulence closure models was imperative. The standard k - ε    model exhibits certain inaccuracies in the computation of intense rotations and streamline curvature (Hanjalic, 2004 ). The RNG  k - ε   model, however, mitigates the aforementioned issues and enhances the suitability of this model for simulating hydrodynamic properties in confluences. Currently, the RNG  k - ε   model has gained widespread application in simulating the bed erosion (Jing et al., 2013; Bahmanpouri et al., 2021 ), the hydrodynamic characteristics of dam break (Khoshkonesh et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024 ) and confluences (Bradbrook et al., 2000; Shi et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2024 ). Furthermore, Shen et al. (2022)  demonstrated that the RNG  k - ε   model exhibits superior capability in capturing the hydrodynamic characteristics of confluence when compared to standard k - ε    and RSM models. The RNG  k - ε   model, in conjunction with the Volume of Fluid (VOF) multiphase flow model, also demonstrates remarkable accuracy in capturing water surface elevation (Shen et al., 2023 ). Therefore, the RNG  k - ε   closure model was selected for this work based on previous works. The VOF multiphase flow model was selected to accurately capture the water surface elevation at the confluence. The control equations were discretized in space using the finite volume method. For near-wall treatment, the standard wall functions were employed. The solver employed a Pressure-Based approach with the transient time scheme. To solve the algebraic equations on each control volume, the SIMPLE algorithm was adopted. The pressure interpolation format used the PRESTO! format. For enhanced precision, the second order upwind scheme was used as the momentum interpolation method. The discretization of turbulent kinetic energy and turbulent kinetic energy dissipation rate was implemented using a first order upwind scheme. For better accuracy, in the FLUENT, a separate precursor calculation of the fluid was required. After achieving a steady state in the flow field, the one-way coupling between CFD and DEM was subsequently conducted. During the coupled computation, the stream within a computational time step was initially computed using the FLUENT solver. When the residual convergence condition (less than 10-4 ) was satisfied, the stream data was passed to the coupling interface. The drag and buoyant forces of each microplastic were calculated. Subsequently, the forces were transferred to the EDEM via the coupling interface, resulting in an update of microplastic positions and velocities, thereby completing a time step for coupling calculation. 2.1 Numerical model of fluid 2.1.1 Governing equations The governing equations include the mass conservation equation and the momentum conservation equation.(2.1) ∂ ρ  ∂ t   + ∂ ρ u i      ∂ x i    = 0     (2.2) ∂ ∂ t   ( ρ u i  )  + ∂ ∂ x j    ( ρ u i  u j  )  = - ∂ p  ∂ x j    + ∂ ∂ x j    ( μ + μ t  )  ∂ u i   ∂ x j    + ∂ u j   ∂ x i          + S i       Where, ρ  (kg/m3 ) is the density of water; The dimensions of the flume and the location of the spur dike are indicated in Fig. 1  . The width (B ) of the flume is 0.5 m. The material of the flume is organic glass. To ensure a smooth transition of the stream downstream, a semicircular type spur dike head is selected. The effective length (d ) of the impermeable non-submerged spur dike is 0.1 m, while its height stands at 0.3 m. The origin of the model coordinates is defined as the right bottom point at the inlet of the tributary. (Fig. 2  ). The computational domain was discretized into structured hexahedral meshes using ICEM CFD software. The meshes with numbers 1604188, 875220, 604,831 and 401,166 were divided. The average resultant velocity (vxy  ) in the X  and Y  directions was employed to test mesh dependency, as it better captures the hydrodynamic characteristics of flow direction. In Fig. 3  , When the number of cells is less than 604,831, there is a large variation in vxy   for different mesh densities. The variation in vxy   is merely 0.23 % when the number of grids increases from 875,220 to 1604188. Therefore, the mesh with a number of 875,220 was selected, considering both accuracy and computational efficiency. The minimum volume of the fluid domain grid is 6.83 × 10-8 m3  and the maximum volume of the particles is 4.19 × 10-9 m3 . It is obvious that the maximum particle volume is less than 10 % of the minimum fluid domain grid volume, which satisfies the requirements of the Euler-Lagrange method. Fig. 1  and Table1   illustrates the boundary conditions for the simulation. The gravity acceleration (Z -direction) was set to −9.81 m/s2 . The pressure in the pressure inlet was set to standard atmospheric pressure. The pressure outlet maintained a water level of 0.2 m. In the particle simulation, the microplastic materials were set as polyethylene (PE), polystyrene (PS), and polyamide (PA) to consider the influence of material properties on the transport of microplastics (Table 3 ). Microplastic shapes are varied, but due to limited computational resources, the complex microplastic shapes were uniformly simplified to spherical in this study.
