We have conducted an extensive investigation into the findings of previous studies on microplastics and determined that microplastics within the particle size range of 1 mm to 0.5 mm exhibit dominance. (Eriksen et al., 2013; Ghanbari et al., 2022; Kılıç et al., 2023 ). Therefore, microplastics with particle diameters of 0.5 mm, 1.0 mm, 1.5 mm, and 2.0 mm were selected in this work. The microplastic injection position was uniformly distributed on the plane where the water inlet 1 and water inlet 2 were located. The five cases are listed in Table 2  , and the migration test duration of microplastics is 140 s in each cases. To guarantee the accuracy of the calculation results, we set the time step ratio for DEM and CFD calculations to 1:100.   3 Results and discussion The computational domain was discretized into Grid Bins, with dimensions of 0.1 m*0.1 m*0.2 m and 0.05 m*0.05 m*0.2 m, to accurately quantify the spatial distribution of microplastics. The collection of distinct Grid Bins was defined as a Grid Bin Group. In Fig. 4  , a total of three longitudinal Grid Bin Groups (L1, L2, L3) were defined along the flow direction, while five crosswise Grid Bin Groups (C1, C2, C3, C4, C5) were defined perpendicular to the flow direction. 3.1 Validation of the DEM-CFD model Accurate fluid simulations are the fundamental basis for coupling CFD with DEM. We used the RNG  k - ε    turbulence model, which had been shown to better capture turbulence characteristics in our previous study. Therefore, we validated the applicability of the CFD-DEM method for investigating microplastics in streams only through settlement experiments of microplastics in static water. The experimental data were obtained from the previously published literature by Waldschläger et al (2019). In their experiments, microplastics were ordered online, while the density of expandable polystyrene (EPS) was 22 Kg/m3 . Referring to the experimental method, glass sinks of the same dimensions (Fig. 5  ) were modeled. The results were quantified using the same indicator (terminal velocity). During the simulation, the EPS spherical particles with diameters (d) of 0.84823 mm and 1.06099 mm were released from the center of the bottom of the glass sink, and each particle was subjected to three repeated simulations. The terminal velocities were determined once the particles reached a state of zero acceleration. The measured value (V M ) and simulated value (V S ) of the terminal velocity were presented in Table 4   . Additionally, Table 4  includes the values of the relative error (E ) between VM   and V S  . The simulated values of terminal velocity in Table 4  exhibit excellent agreement with the experimental values, demonstrating a maximum relative error of only 10.541 %. It is shown that the 3D coupled model used in this study provides relatively accurate results for the motion of microplastics in the stream, and this coupled model can be used to further describe the transport and retention behavior of microplastics in the confluence containing the spur dike.  3.2 Influence of microplastic composition and particle diameter on their transport and fate characteristics In Fig. 6  , low-density PE particles float to the upper water column, while high-density PS and PA gradually sink after entering the flow field. These microplastics disperse and migrate along the bed of the flume. Furthermore, the spatial distribution of microplastics varies significantly along the flow direction, even within the same material. To gain a deeper understanding of the fate of microplastics with varying densities in the water column, Fig. 7   illustrates the fluid velocity (V F ) and microplastic residence time (PRT ) in both the upper water column (Z/B =0.2 ∼ 0.42) and lower water column (Z/B =0 ∼ 0.2). The PRT  is defined as the cumulative duration experienced by particles from their initial entry into the computational domain until their final exit from it. In Fig. 7  (a, b), Microplastics with extended PRT  are observed in both the upper and lower water columns during periods of flow stagnation and separation. However, the number of microplastics is higher in the lower water column. Meanwhile, a distinct region characterized by lower concentrations of microplastics can be observed in the lower water column (e.g., the purple transparent area depicted in Fig. 7 (b)). In contrast, the distribution of microplastics in the upper water column is more uniform. This phenomenon primarily arises due to the higher average flow velocity in the upper water column compared to that in the lower water column, facilitating the preferential transport of low-density microplastics towards the core of the mainstream. In Fig. 7  (c, e), significant stratification is observed among the particles due to their different materials. The low-velocity zones pose a greater threat from high-density microplastics compared to low-density microplastics. In Fig. 7  (d, f, g), the particle size distributions of the three materials in the flow stagnation exhibit similarities, with a slightly higher abundance of particles measuring 2 mm. The small-size microplastics (0.5 mm, 1.0 mm) exhibit a clear numerical advantage in the flow separation and spur dike field. Consequently, these small-size microplastics possess a higher potential for environmental impact within confluences containing spur dikes. Thus, a single particle diameter of 0.5 mm was used to explore the pattern in subsequent work. Taken together, our findings indicate that the vertical movement of microplastics is governed by their density and diameter. Previous studies have shown that microplastic density influences the distribution between the water surface and sediment surface (Lenaker et al., 2019; Stride et al., 2023 ), which is consistent with our findings. Significant variations exist in the vertical distribution of the particles composed of the same material within the water column have been observed, potentially influenced by microplastic diameter (Reisser et al., 2015 ). Moreover, the retention of microplastics in key areas (flow stagnation, flow separation) was observed during their transportation with the stream. The key areas exhibit lower velocities in comparison to the main stream (Best et al., 1987; Yuan et al., 2018 ), resulting in reduced transport capacity for microplastics. Consequently, these key areas gradually transformed into hotspots for the accumulation of microplastics. The behavior of microplastics exhibits certain similarities to that of sediment (Nizzetto et al., 2016; Horton and Dixon., 2018 ). The transport patterns of microplastics and sediment at the laboratory scale were further discussed in our study. The comparison reveals some similarity in the spatial distribution of sediment and microplastics, i.e. both sediment (Yuan et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2020 ) and microplastics are retained in areas of flow separation and stagnation. The area with a reduced distribution of microplastics (Fig. 7  (b)) in lower water column is in close proximity to the scour hole (Best, 1988 ). The low concentration of microplastics in this area may be attributed to the convective acceleration of flow and intense turbulent conditions (Leite et al., 2012 ), which are also responsible for the formation of the scour hole. Additionally, the distribution characteristics of microplastics differ from those of sediments in some respects. For instance, in Fig. 5 (b), a peripheral region of microplastic aggregation is observed at the flow separation, extending downstream. The primary factor contributing to this phenomenon is the compression of the tributary by the mainstream, which subsequently drives the aggregation of microplastics. Relevant studies have also reported increased microplastic concentrations in natural confluences (Klein et al., 2015; Li et al., 2023; Zong et al., 2024 ). Distinct quantities of microplastics, varying in terms of materials and diameters, are observed across key regions. The number of PS microplastics exhibits a higher magnitude in the flow separation. The number of microplastics with small particle sizes (0.5 mm, 1 mm) is found to be higher in the flow separation and spur dike field. This implies that PS microplastics with smaller particle sizes (0.5 mm, 1 mm) may present a heightened risk. Notably, the shape of the microplastic is another factor that affects the vertical motion (Jalón-Rojas., 2022 ). Therefore, refining the composition of microplastic shapes is our next stage of the work.  3.3 Impact of spur dike layout on microplastic fate and motion patterns at confluence 3.3.1 Hydrodynamic characterization In Fig. 8   (a, b), the spur dike induces a reduction in the size of the flow separation, resulting in the generation of a large-scale counterclockwise reverse current within the spur dike field. From Fig. 8  (d), the water surface elevation (WSE ) of Case 3 is observed to be higher than that of Case 2 in the upstream section of the confluence. This suggests that the presence of the spur dike reduces the area of the flow cross-section and allows back-water to occur upstream. After spur dike (X/B =0.6), WSE  of Case 3 was significantly lower than Case 2. Suggesting the water surface has a more pronounced 3D character in the vicinity of the spur dike. The fluid velocity in the maximum velocity zone is larger in Case 3 compared to Case 2, as shown in Fig. 8  (c). The velocity in Case 3 exhibits a significant increase beyond the spur dike location and attains its peak value at X/B =1.5.  3.3.2 Distribution and retention characteristics of microplastics The distribution of microplastic concentration in the crosswise direction of the computational domain is illustrated in Fig. 9   (a, b). In Case 2, all crosswise Grid Bin Groups exhibit a comparatively lower concentration of microplastics (Fig. 9 a) at Y/B =0.7. The concentration of Grid Bin Group C3 is observed to be lower at Y/B =0.7 in Case 3 (Fig. 9 b). It becomes evident that the perturbation caused by the confluence and spur dike induces a high-velocity flow (Fig. 8  (a, b)), thereby altering the crosswise distribution of microplastic concentration within the water column. The findings of Liu et al. (2022) also demonstrate the impact of flow velocity on microplastic accumulation, which is consistent with our results. The longitudinal microplastic concentrations in the left bank of the flume exhibits a substantial disparity between the two cases (Fig. 9 c).The existence of angular eddies upstream of the spur dike (Han et al., 2022 ) may result in an increased concentration of microplastics at X/B =1.2 in Case3. The longitudinal concentration of microplastics in the middle of the flume (Fig. 9 d) exhibits minimal influence from the spur dike. On the right bank (Fig. 9 e), in downstream of the confluence, there is a fluctuating upward trend in concentration for both cases, but Case3 microplastic concentration is higher. It is suggested that, affected by the compression of the tributary, part of the microplastics is transferred along the right bank and accumulated over time. This retention trend has also been observed in sediment injection experiments. The sediment injected from the tributary is influenced by the mainstream and primarily distributed along the side of flow separation (Yu et al., 2020 ). The microplastic components retained in flow stagnation and flow separation are predominantly composed of PA and PS, as illustrated in Fig. 10   (a, b). The flow stagnation exhibits a higher proportion of PE particles in comparison to the flow separation. Despite the greater number of microplastics in the flow stagnation (Fig. 10 (a, b)), PRT  is larger in the flow separation and spur dike filed (Fig. 10 (c, d)). Therefore, the distribution of microplastics in the flow separation and spur dike field should be focused on. The microplastics in the flow separation exhibit a distinct retention center, where they reside for an extended duration, as depicted in Fig. 10  (c, d). The PRT  of microplastics in the periphery of the retention centers is relatively short. In contrast to Case2, the Case3 spur dike field exhibits a circular distribution of long-standing microplastics. The particle retention center is consistent with the reverse current center, and the PRT  in the center is the largest. Our initial estimate is that microplastics gradually enter the center of the reverse current through the periphery and accumulate in the center of the reverse current. In summary, the confluence is a critical zone for the accumulation of microplastics. The layout of the spur dike in the confluence leads to significant microplastic retention in key areas, including flow stagnation, flow separation, the spur dike field, and downstream of the flow separation. Enrichment of these key areas may give rise to additional ecological consequences. The flow separation is possible refuge for fish (Shen et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2019 ). The microplastics trapped in the flow separation will increase the risk of ingestion of fish. The presence of microplastics in the spur dike field poses a potential threat to the habitat (Pinn et al., 2005 ) of juvenile fish. Hence, the identification of microplastic retention areas will serve as an initial reference for ecological conservation at confluences. The localized presence of microplastic pollution in the spur dike field cannot be disregarded while achieving the purpose of river regulation. Further in-depth investigation into the mechanisms governing the movement of microplastics under hydrodynamic conditions could offer valuable insights to effectively address this potential risk.  3.3.3 Motion patterns of microplastics in the confluence containing the spur dike To elucidate the underlying mechanism governing microplastic retention in key areas, we conducted an analysis of microplastic motion. Fig. 11   (b, d) illustrates a comparison of the movement trajectories of microplastics at different initial positions for Case2 and Case3. In these cases, the trajectories of the microplastics (Others) remain unaffected by the low-velocity zone during their transportation. The microplastics (flow stagnation) are transported along the flume walls and accumulate in the flow stagnation. The trajectories of microplastics (Flow separation) entering the flow separation exhibit distinct disparities between the two cases. In Case 2, the microplastics enter the reverse current through the upstream of the flow separation. In contrast, microplastics in Case 3 enter the reverse current from downstream of the flow separation. In Fig. 11 (e, f), at the origin of the confluence, Case 2 and Case 3 have a negative directional maximum in vorticity, which deflects the direction of microplastic motion near the origin. The vorticity magnitude in Case 2 is significantly higher, leading to a more pronounced deviation of microplastic motion. The deflection of Case 2 results in a broader distribution of negative vorticity bands in the stream, compared to Case 3. Thus, in Case 2, microplastics (Flow separation) are more likely to enter the reverse current from the upstream. Furthermore, the microplastics (Spur dike field) entered the reverse current downstream from the spur dike field. To investigate the mechanisms by which microplastics enter the reverse current downstream of the spur dike field. The thickness of the mixed layer is introduced. The calculation equation: (Mignot et al., 2016 ):(3.1) δ = U m  ( x )  - U g  ( x )   ∂ u  ¯    ∂ y     max        Where, U m  ( x )    (m/s) and U g  ( x )    (m/s) are the overall mean streamwise velocities at the streamwise coordinates of the mainstream and spur dike fields, respectively. The absolute value of the velocity gradient at the corresponding position of U m  ( x )    (m/s) and U g  ( x )     is negligibly small. In this study, 0.5 s - 1     was chosen as the velocity gradient threshold. ∂ u  ¯   / ∂ y    max    is the maximum lateral gradient of velocity corresponding to each streamwise position at the interface. In Table 5  , the mixed layer thickness tends to increase linearly along the stream direction. The larger mixed layer thickness promotes mass exchange (Mignot et al., 2017 ). Thus, with an increase in the mixed layer thickness (Fig. 11 d), there is a higher likelihood of microplastics being transported into the downstream reverse current from the spur dike. The analysis further validates the conjecture derived from the microplastic distribution in section 3.3.2 . From the above analysis, there are two microplastic motion patterns: (i) The microplastics initially located on the right bank of the mainstream and on the left bank of the tributary are retained in the flow stagnation. The microplastics originating from the right bank of the tributary enter the flow separation from its frontal region. The microplastics on the left bank of the mainstream gradually move downstream. (ii) The microplastics (located on the right bank of the tributary) will enter the flow separation after the layout of the spur dike. The entry point is located downstream of the flow separation. The microplastics captured by the flow separation exhibit a clockwise movement and gradually accumulate in the reflux center. The microplastics (located on the left bank of the mainstream) will bypass the spur dike and enter the spur dike field. The entry point is located downstream of the spur dike field. The microplastics in the spur dike field move counterclockwise and are gradually retained in the reflux center. In the existing study, the sediment originating from the tributary can also be captured by the flow separation (Best and Reid., 1984; Yuan et al., 2023b ), which is consistent with our results. The flow separation can also entrain large woods (Yuan et al., 2024 ), and the movement patterns significantly differ from the microplastics. This phenomenon can be attributed to the lower mass and reduced generation of centrifugal force exhibited by microplastics during curved motion. This enhances the likelihood of microplastics being captured by flow separation in comparison to large woods. Furthermore, in our work, the shapes affecting the motion of microplastics (Nguyen et al., 2022 ) are simplified to spheres. The maximum diameter of microplastics is limited to 2 mm. Thus, there is a difference between the motion patterns of microplastics and large woods. Furthermore, we elucidated the hydrodynamic mechanism underlying the retention of microplastics in flow separation, i.e. The microplastics are influenced by the larger vorticity magnitude at the confluence origin, leading to alterations in their movement direction. And the entry of microplastics into the flow separation is influenced by the vorticity. After the deployment of the spur dike, there was a significant increase in the absolute value of vorticity at the confluence origin, leading to a notable alteration in the trajectory of microplastics into the flow separation. This further substantiates the rationality of the mechanism. The hydrodynamic influence mechanism of microplastic retention in the spur dike field was also elucidated, i.e. the greater thickness of the mixed layer facilitates the entry of microplastics into the spur dike field after they have bypassed the diked dam. The sediment entrained by the scouring of the spur dike is also deposited in the spur dike field, which is consistent with the behavior of microplastics. The sediment is also transported to and deposited in the spur dike field (Koken and Constantinescu., 2008b ), which is consistent with the behavior of microplastics. The longitudinal distribution patterns of the average per-particle rotational kinetic energy and kinetic energy within the longitudinal Gird Bin Groups of Case2 and Case3 are characterized in Fig. 12  . The trends of rotational kinetic energy and kinetic energy in microplastics exhibit similarities. The kinetic energies of both components exhibit significant growth in the confluence region and near spur dikes. On the left bank, the confluence in Case 3 intercepts microplastics through the layout of the spur dike, resulting in an immediate reduction in both kinetic energies. In contrast, in the absence of the spur dike obstruction, Case2 microplastics can undergo accelerated transport with the stream. On the right bank, the Case2 flow separation has a greater range of influence, which makes the two energies for Case2 smaller than for Case3. With the layout of the spur dike, the microplastic mobility decreases significantly on one side of the spur dike, while it increases significantly at other part of the flume. The implication is that the layout of the spur dike not only locally influenced the confluence but also enhanced the downstream transportability of a fraction of microplastics. Analogously, the experimental results on sediment transport demonstrated that the presence of a spur dike significantly enhanced the mobility of suspended sediment in the mainstream (Gu et al., 2011 ). Furthermore, the layout of spur dikes may give rise to potential ecological consequences. With the increase in microplastic transportation capacity, the downstream of the confluence may be at risk from a significant amount of ecotoxic microplastics (Stapleton et al., 2023 ), unlike sediment. In natural rivers, wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) serve as important point sources of microplastic contamination (Browne et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2020 ), exhibiting notably elevated concentrations downstream (McCormick et al., 2016 ). Microplastics close to shore tend to be susceptible to retention in the confluence due to hydrodynamic features. If a WWTP is near the confluence, the microplastics may accumulate in the key areas of retention. This situation poses a potential threat to localized ecology. The findings of this study can make a contribution to the mitigation of microplastic pollution. In specific cases where the confluence exhibits a similar pattern to that observed in this study (asymmetric confluence), it is recommended to implement targeted cleanup efforts focusing on the key areas of microplastic retention. Alternatively, microplastic pollution can be controlled using ecological spur dikes (Chen et al., 2022; Rao et al., 2018 ). Submerged plants can be planted along the microplastic flow paths within the areas of flow separation and spur dike fields, harnessing their inherent water purification capabilities (Wang et al., 2023 ) to mitigate the transportation of microplastics.   3.4 Impact of varying spur dike angles on the transport and fate of microplastics In Table 6  , we focused on the hotspot areas of microplastic retention, and counted the number of particles. According to the findings presented in Table 6 , an increase in the angle of the spur dike leads to a corresponding increase in the accumulation of microplastics both upstream of the spur dike and the flow stagnation. In Fig. 13  (a, b) and Fig. 8 (b), it can be observed that the extent of the low-velocity region before the spur dike is maximized in Case 5. Thus, this region exhibits a higher propensity for the retention of microplastics in Case 5. In the spur dike filed, Case3 exhibits higher particle counts, while Case4 and 5 particle counts have a smaller gap. The increase in the angle of the spur dike resulted in an expansion of the spur dike field (Giglou et al., 2018 ), however, no significant trend was observed regarding the accumulation of microplastics within this field. This is mainly due to: Firstly, Cases 4 and 5 have a larger deflection angle of the mainstream left bank streamline compared to Case 3 (Fig. 13 (a, b) and Fig. 8 (b)). This effect causes more microplastics on the left bank of the mainstream to enter the center of the flume. Secondly, Case 5 has the highest particle-averaged kinetic energy at the location of the spur dike (Fig. 14  (d)). In summary, a larger spur dike angle allows more microplastics to move transversely to the high-velocity zone in the middle of the flume. This gives the particles greater kinetic energy to be transported downstream without being trapped by the low-velocity zone of the spur dike field. The distribution of microplastics in the spur dike field exhibits significant variations among the three cases, as illustrated in Fig. 14 (a ∼ c). This is mainly due to the different fluid velocities in the dike field (Fig. 13  (d)). Relevant research has previously demonstrated that reduced flow velocities in rivers facilitate the deposition of microplastics (Tibbetts et al., 2018 ). The findings of this study suggest that the localized enrichment of microplastics is significantly influenced by the flow velocity in regions where they accumulate, too. To assess the local retention of microplastics within the spur dike field, we computed the standard deviation (σ P   ) of microplastic concentrations across various Grid Bins as presented in Table 6 . The presence of a larger σ P    indicates limited mobility of microplastics, which in turn leads to their potential accumulation in a localized area. The reduced σ P    indicates enhanced mobility of microplastics, thereby reducing the likelihood of their aggregation in a localized area. It can be found that microplastics in Case 5 are less likely to aggregate locally. In order to quantify the impact of angles of the spur dike on the standard deviation of microplastic concentration at the spur dike field, we established a linear correlation between the dimensionless angle α N   (α / 90   ） of the spur dike and the dimensionless standard deviation σ N   (σ / 8.5362   ). The relation equation is:(3.2) σ N  = - 0.7269 α N  + 1.7891 ( R 2  = 0.9528 )       Where, σ N    and α N    are the non-dimensional standard deviation and non-dimensional spur dike angle, respectively. The increase in spur dike angle is associated with a decrease in the risk of local high concentration in the spur dike field. The layout of a 90° spur dike angle resulted in a reduced risk of localized microplastics retention within the spur dike field and minimized the overall accumulation of microplastics at the confluence. Therefore, we conclude that a spur dike angle of 90° is the most favorable for microplastic transport downstream and exhibits a lower risk in the low fluid velocity zone. The angle of the spur dike also influences other pollutants. The optimal efficiency for ammonia nitrogen purification in the flume is achieved when the spur dike angle is set at 60° (Wang et al., 2024 ). The angle of the spur dike chosen for microplastic pollution control in this study differs from that chosen for ammonia nitrogen. And the main reason for this difference is the difference in prevention and control objectives. Furthermore, the layout of the spur dike gives rise to a riverbed scouring predicament (Pandey et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2022 ). Therefore, the next stage of research aims to consider microplastics and riverbed scour.   4 Conclusion A coupled hydrodynamic-microplastic model was established. The microplastic retention hotspots were characterized at the 90° flume confluence with the spur dike. The retention mechanisms of microplastic were analyzed under the combined influence of hydrodynamic characteristics and microplastic properties. The role of the spur dike in regulating the distribution of microplastics at confluences was highlighted. This study will enhance the theory of microplastic motion at confluences with spur dikes, and reinforce the engineering design of ecological spur dikes with theoretical support. The major findings are summarized as follows:1. The hydraulic zones formed by the confluence and the layout of the spur dike, namely flow stagnation, flow separation, downstream of flow separation, and spur dike field, significantly contribute to microplastic accumulation. In these particular zones, low-density microplastic pollution has less impact on the upper water column. The retention of high-density microplastics with small particle diameter (<1mm) strongly impacts bottom water quality.  2. The layout of the spur dike will increase microplastic concentrations in front of the dike and downstream of the flow separation.  3. The retention patterns of microplastics: (i) The microplastics initially located on the right bank of the tributary enter the separation zone through the flow separation upstream. (ii) After the layout of the spur dike, microplastics initially located on the right bank of the tributary enter the separation zone through downstream of the flow separation. The microplastics initially located on the left bank of the mainstream enter the spur dike field from downstream of the spur dike field.  4. The dimensionless angle of the spur dike (αN  ) exhibits a linear and inverse relationship with the dimensionless standard deviation (σN  ) within the spur dike field. The total number of microplastics retained at the confluence did not exhibit an increase with an increasing angle of the spur dike. The decrease in the risk of local high concentration in the spur dike field is associated with the increase in spur dike angle.    This study provides insights into the hydrodynamic motion of microplastics at the confluence, specifically focusing on their behavior in relation to a spur dike. Compared with the motion theory of microplastics in turbulent environment (Goral et al., 2023; Stride et al., 2024 ), this study investigated the retention patterns of microplastics at the confluence, enriching the theory of microplastic motion in turbulent environments. The significance of this study will be further amplified as the influx of microplastics into freshwater is projected to escalate in the future (Wu et al., 2024 ). When addressing the actual problem, practical measures can be implemented based on the proposed microplastic motion patterns in this study. These measures include the planting of submerged plants and the layout of ecological spur dikes, among others. However, this study is conducted at the laboratory scale, without accounting for the interaction (Sun et al., 2022; Glaser et al., 2023 ) between microplastics and other substances in numerical modeling. Microplastic motion in the case of a dynamic bed has not yet been considered. The future research should focus on further enhancing the hydrodynamic-microplastic transport model by incorporating these intricate factors.
1 Introduction Oscillating water levels are not rarely observed in groundwater monitoring wells. In addition to atmospheric pressure fluctuations, periodical aquifer disturbances are considered to be a major cause of water level oscillation, stemming from various disturbance sources, such as seismic waves, tides, and aquifer testing. The monitored water levels have been widely used for aquifer characterization (Allègre et al. 2016, Cardiff et al. 2020, Fischer et al. 2018, Wang et al. 2021 ) and interpretation of seismic hydrological phenomena (Brodsky et al. 2003, Candela et al. 2015, Manga et al. 2012, Roeloffs 1998 ), which have received increasing attention in recent years. In applications of contaminated site remediation or nuclear waste storage safety, periodic oscillations of water levels triggered by earth tide or oscillatory pumping tests are widely utilized for investigating aquifer characteristics, due to their high signal-to-noise ratio and logistical convenience of requiring no water injected into or extracted from the aquifer (Cardiff et al. 2013, Lan and Gu 2021, Shalev et al. 2016, Trglavcnik et al. 2018, Zhang et al. 2019 ). In earthquake hydrology, co-seismic and post-seismic water level responses are intensively analyzed to reveal the mechanism of seismic waves interacting with aquifers (Liao et al. 2021, Shi et al. 2015, Sun et al. 2015 ). Periodical aquifer disturbance sources can mechanistically be divided into two categories, the pressure diffusion (PD) source and the volumetric strain (VS) source (Xing et al. 2022 ). PD sources cause water level oscillations through the process of pore pressure diffusion in the aquifer, e.g., ocean tides and oscillatory pumping tests. In contrast, VS sources first induce the elastic volumetric strain of the soil skeleton to cause pore pressure changes, and then lead to water level oscillation, which is a complex coupling process. Fig. 1   illustrates some of the typical PD and VS disturbance sources in aquifers. In order to model these two different mechanisms, generalized well-aquifer coupling models have been developed. Bredehoeft et al. (1966)  modeled the response of a well-aquifer system to pressure disturbances using an electric analog, exploiting the behavior similarity between the well-aquifer system and a mechanical spring-mass system with viscous damping. This model has successfully been used to investigate water level responses triggered by seismic waves, slug tests, and pumping tests. Another coupled well-aquifer model was developed by Cooper et al. (1965)  and has been refined to investigate water level responses induced by earth tides (Bredehoeft 1967, Hsieh et al. 1987, Liu et al. 1989 ) and oscillatory hydraulic tests (Black and Kipp 1981, Kipp 1985, Van der Kamp 1976 ), although it was originally developed for seismic waves. Xing et al. (2022)  developed a general well-aquifer numerical model considering all aforementioned disturbance sources, where the various disturbance sources were represented by different boundary conditions. In these coupled well-aquifer models, water level responses are considered to be influenced by multiple factors related to aquifer properties, wellbore structure, and source characteristics. To comprehensively understand the complicated well-aquifer system and the mechanisms governing water level responses, a global parameter sensitivity analysis can be beneficial. However, existing studies have shown that the model’s influential parameters are different for different types of disturbance sources. Water level response to PD sources is thought to be primarily influenced by aquifer parameters (i.e. hydraulic conductivity, specific storage, and aquifer thickness), while the process of water column movement in the wellbore is usually ignored (Cardiff et al. 2013, Jiao and Tang 1999, Li and Jiao 2001, Renner and Messar 2006 ). Carr and Van Der Kamp (1969)  also highlighted that the aquifer diffusivity and the distance from shoreline are the main factors causing time lag and amplitude attenuation in ocean tide-induced water level response. Li and Jiao (2002)  incorporated the aquifer thickness in their analytical solution to describe tidal groundwater level fluctuations in coastal subsurface systems. Similar to ocean tides, oscillatory pumping tests are another way of triggering aquifer disturbances, offering the benefit that the amplitude and period of the source signal can be artificially controlled. Black and Kipp (1981)  formulated an analytical solution for groundwater level responses during sinusoidal pumping tests, relating the response to aquifer parameters and the distance between the pumping and observation wells. For the VS source, the water level responses are influenced not only by aquifer parameters, but also by wellbore effects and source characteristics (Bredehoeft 1967, Cooper et al. 1965, Gao et al. 2020, Lan and Gu 2021, Sun et al. 2019, Wang et al. 2018 ). Cooper et al. (1965)  derived an analytical solution for water level response to seismic waves, which took into account the impacts of source period and wellbore construction including water column height, well radius, and screen length, in addition to aquifer parameters. Considering water column inertia, they analyzed a spectrum of amplitude amplification factors (defined as the amplitude ratio of in-well water levels to the pressure head in aquifers) based on the period of disturbance sources. Hsieh et al. (1987)  stated that earth tide-induced water level response is mainly sensitive to aquifer transmissivity, well radius, and the period of disturbance sources. In recent years, studies on parameter sensitivity have primarily focused on analyzing earthquake-induced water level responses based on field measurements. Sun et al. (2019)  compared water level responses between two closely located wells caused by barometric, tidal responses and slug test results. Permeability and confinement of aquifer systems are identified to be the important parameters. Zhang et al. (2021)  analyzed the different sensitivities of two wells to earthquake-induced water level responses by comparing the seismic energy, aquifer properties, and well configuration. However, these analyses are often limited to the specific site conditions and a scarcity of field measurements, making it is challenging to fully understand the sensitivity of water level response to all pertinent parameters. Specifically, field measurements primarily provide information from those monitoring wells that are sensitive to aquifer disturbance. Consequently, utilizing field measurements alone makes it difficult to ascertain the parameter sensitivities that dictate whether and how water levels respond to various disturbance sources in aquifers. Addressing these gaps is critical for the effective design of seismic monitoring wells, the evaluation of underground waste repositories, and the accurate estimation of aquifer parameters. In this study, a coupled well-aquifer numerical model is employed to conduct a global parameter sensitivity analysis, which provides a strategy to efficiently and comprehensively examining how water levels respond to changes in relevant parameters. Initially, we analyze uncertainties pertaining to aquifer properties, source characteristics, and wellbore construction parameters based on the application scenarios for PD and VS sources. To address the complex issues of whether a monitoring well will respond to aquifer disturbances and how it will respond under the influence of wellbore effects, seven sensitivity indices were identified. To improve computational efficiency and thoroughly encompass parameter uncertainty, Monte-Carlo based surrogate models that relate parameters to sensitivity indices were then built. This approach provides a detailed analysis of global parameter sensitivity of the well-aquifer model, as well as insightful recommendations for the design of monitoring wells and the interpretation of measured water levels.  2 Methodology 2.1 Coupled well-aquifer model for water level response to harmonic aquifer disturbance Water level responses to aquifer disturbances are governed by three fundamental processes: pore pressure diffusion in the aquifer, pore pressure rebalance adjacent to monitoring wells due to wellbore storage, and water level oscillations affecting by water-column inertia and friction losses on the well wall. In accordance with the coupled well-aquifer model developed by Xing et al. (2022) , pore pressure diffusion in aquifers is abided by the Darcy’s law, and water level oscillation in the wellbore is governed by the Navier-Stokes (NS) equation. These two sets of equations are coupled through continuity conditions of pressure and groundwater velocity at the well screen. Pore pressure rebalance adjacent to monitoring wells is the combination effect of the Darcy flow and Navier-Stokes flow influenced by gravity effects. To track the oscillating water level, a free-moving boundary is specified on the water level surface using an arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) method. The Xing et al. (2022)  model was developed for partially penetrating wells situated in confined homogeneous aquifers, with both the upper and bottom boundaries assigned as no-flow zones. In case of PD disturbance sources, line mass-flux and surface head boundary conditions were designed for oscillatory pumping wells and ocean tide, respectively. Conversely, VS source-induced pressure disturbance can be simulated by imposing a harmonic pore pressure at the well screen, a common simplification of the complicated pore pressure-stress coupling process in aquifers (Bredehoeft 1967, Cooper et al. 1965, Gao et al. 2020, Lan and Gu 2021, Sun et al. 2019, Wang et al. 2018 ). Fig. 2   depicts the well-aquifer conceptual model and traces the evolution of the pressure head from the source to water level oscillations. The detailed model description and numerical implementation can be found in Xing et al. (2022) .  2.2 Parameter uncertainties for the PD and VS sources Based on the Xing et al. (2022)  model, water level responses to aquifer disturbance can be influenced by an array of parameters related to source characteristics, aquifer properties, and well construction. Harmonic disturbance sources are defined by three main characteristics: the amplitude (A 0    ), period (T 0    ) of the source, and the distance (D   ) to monitoring wells, with D    being applicable only for PD sources. The aquifer properties, including hydraulic conductivity (K   ), specific storage (S s    ), and aquifer thickness (B   ), can predominantly influence the pore pressure diffusion in the aquifer. The well construction parameters, such as the well radius (r w    ), water column height (H w    ) from the top of the well screen to the water level, and screen length (L s    ), may play a significant role in affecting the movement of the in-well water column. In practice, each of these parameters can exhibit substantial variability, reflecting the diversity in site geologic conditions, types of disturbance sources, and configurations of monitoring wells. Typically, groundwater monitoring wells designed for VS sources are deeper than those for PD sources. For instance, wells set up to monitor pore pressure changes induced by earthquakes should reach depths of several hundreds of meters. In contrast, monitoring wells for PD sources are primarily designed for local hydrogeological surveys and usually do not exceed a few hundred meters in depth. Since hydraulic conductivity generally decreases with depth (Kuang and Jiao 2014 ), lower average K    values should be considered targeting VS sources. Adding to the complexity are the distinct periods associated with various disturbance sources. The period of far-field seismic waves can be relatively short, approximately a few seconds, and the earth/ocean tides exhibit a much longer period of around twelve hours. In contrast, oscillatory pumping tests stand out with their adjustable periods, which can be artificially controlled from a few seconds to several minutes. Previous studies observed a diminishing impact on water lever responses when source period exceeds hundreds seconds (Cooper et al. 1965, Xing et al. 2022 ). Therefore, in this study, the main focus is on short-period (less than hundreds of seconds) sources to analyze their influence on water level responses. The uncertainty of all impact parameters for the PD and VS sources are listed in Table 1  . The selection of the parameter ranges associated with the source features is based on Manga and Brodsky (2006)  and Rabinovich et al. (2015) , while parameters related to aquifer properties and well construction are set based on the assumption of a shallow confined aquifer. In this study, a well radius varying from 0.02 m to 0.1 m is applied for all sources. Given the possibility for greater lengths in monitoring wells for VS sources in actual field settings, the assumed water column heights span from 50 m to 500 m for VS sources and with a shorter range from 5 m to 100 m for PD sources. To consider the constraint of well screen length by aquifer thickness, a screen length ratio (sl   ) is introduced, defined as the ratio of screen length to aquifer thickness. To prevent boundary effects at the top and bottom of the aquifer during numerical simulations, the sl    is controlled within a range of 0.1 and 0.9. Considering different application scenarios, aquifer thickness is assumed to vary from 1 m to 50 m for the PD source and from 10 m to 100 m for the VS source. Due to the depth dependence, the selected range of K    values for the VS source varies from 10-9  m/s to 10-4  m/s, which is lower than the range of K    values for the PD source (10-7  m/s to 10-2  m/s). The same range of S s     values is selected for all sources, changing from 10-6  to 10-3  1/m. According to previous studies, water level response is only sensitive to changes in source periods that occur within a few hundred seconds. Additionally, a period of 5 to 100 s is selected for the VS source, and a relatively wide period ranging from 10 to 200 s is selected for the PD source to allow greater adaptability during oscillatory pumping tests. For the PD source, the disturbance distance between the source and the monitoring well is also taken into account, with a range from 10 m to 100 m. To analyze the influence of these parameter uncertainties, a global parameter sensitivity analysis using Monte Carlo simulations, based on the integrated well-aquifer model, can be performed.  2.3 Global parameter sensitivity of the coupled well-aquifer model Amplitude (A   ) and phase (P   ) are two primary attributes utilized for describing harmonic pressure signals. A disturbance source, represented by A 0     and T 0    , exhibits amplitude attenuation and phase delay during the pressure diffusion process in aquifers, attributed to the damping effect of the porous medium (Black and Kipp 1981, Cardiff et al. 2013 ). When considering wellbore effects, such as the water column inertia and wellbore storage, water level amplitude (A wl     ) can be either attenuated, remain equivalent, or amplified, and the phase (P wl     ) might be delayed, stay in-phase, or even advanced (Cooper et al. 1965, Liu et al. 1989, Sun et al. 2019, Xing et al. 2022 ). Despite these insights gathered from previous studies, it is necessary to clarify the following practical issues: (1) determining the conditions under which the monitoring well reacts to aquifer disturbances, (2) understanding the potential response mechanisms of water level amplitude and phase, and (3) identifying the impact of wellbore effects on water level responses. To effectively address these questions, a global parameter sensitivity analysis is needed. 2.3.1 Response indices To determine whether a monitoring well responds to aquifer disturbances, the amplitude of water level (A wl     ) simulated by the coupled well-aquifer model is utilized. In practice, water level oscillation can be properly measured only if its amplitude surpasses the resolution of sensors (R s    ). Therefore, an index A YN    ¯      of the yes/no water level response in monitoring wells can be expressed as,(1) A YN    ¯   = response , A wl   ≥ R s     n o r e s p o n s e , A wl   < R s               where R s     is assumed to be 1 mm in this study as a critical value. Furthermore, when there is a measurable response in monitoring wells, it is critical to understand how the amplitude and phase of water level respond to aquifer disturbances. In cases where the influence of wellbore effects is minimal, the amplitude and phase of water level should be closely equivalent to those of pore pressure at the investigated aquifer location. Otherwise, as mentioned above, the water level amplitude can be attenuated or amplified relative to the pore pressure of aquifers, and the phase can be delayed or advanced, due to wellbore effects. This suggests that the water level cannot accurately represent the pore pressure in aquifers, and directly utilizing of water levels may introduce errors in the estimation of aquifer parameters. To determine when the water level can truly represent pore pressure changes in aquifers, a theoretical pore pressure signal (A nw      and P nw     ) situated at the monitoring well but unaffected by wellbore effects is selected. The A nw      and P nw      can be simulated by a traditional groundwater flow model that only considers the pressure diffusion process in aquifers. For comparison, the amplitude ratio (A wl   / A nw     ) and phase shift (P wl   - P nw     ) between water level and pore pressure of the aquifer are employed. To characterize the difference in amplitude and phase between water level and theoretical pore pressure, an amplitude index (A WE    ¯     ) and a phase shift index (P WE    ¯     ) are introduced,(2) A WE    ¯   = amplified ,    e q u i v a l e n t ,    a t t e n u a t e d ,         A wl   / A nw   > 1.1    A wl   / A nw   ∈ [ 0.9 , 1.1  ]     A wl   / A nw   < 0.9          (3) P WE    ¯   = advanced ,    i n - p h a s e ,    d e l a y e d ,         P wl   - P nw   > 0.1    P wl   - P nw   ∈ [ - 0.1 , 0.1  ]     P wl   - P nw   < - 0.1           When categorizing response types, a certain degree of inclusiveness (about 0.2) is taken into account for the cases of equivalent A WE    ¯      and in-phase P WE    ¯     . Additionally, in order to further clarify the mechanism of wellbore effects on water level responses, the in-well water column inertia and wellbore storage are investigated. For comparison, the pressure head signal (A ws      and P ws     ) at the mid-depth of the well screen is selected, which can be simulated using the coupled well-aquifer model. When compared to water levels, the results can reflect the impact of water column inertia, whereas comparison with pore pressure at the monitoring well unaffected by wellbore effects reflects the role of wellbore storage. Therefore, two different types of response indices related to amplitude ratios and phase shifts are defined as,(4) A IN    ¯   = A wl   A ws        (5) P IN    ¯   = P wl   - P ws       (6) A ST    ¯   = A ws   A nw        (7) P ST    ¯   = P ws   - P nw        where indices with subscript IN    and ST    denotes the effects on the variable mainly caused by water column inertia and wellbore storage, respectively. In order to quantitatively characterize the relationship between the wellbore effect and its main influencing parameters, different from the previous three indices, the response indices defined in Eqs. (4)-(7) are all numerical types.  2.3.2 Global sensitivity of coupled aquifer-well model using a surrogate model Since the coupled well-aquifer model becomes considerably nonlinear and computationally time-consuming following the integration of the NS equation, exploring the sensitivity of the aforementioned indices in the full parameter space presents a significant challenge. To this end, a random forest (RF) surrogate model is employed, capable of being constructed through training with relatively small input–output samples, to approximate a complicated nonlinear model (Dasari et al. 2019 ). The RF is a supervised machine learning algorithm that leverages an ensemble of decision trees for prediction, offering computational efficiency while minimizing overfitting and bias. In the RF, each decision tree is created by randomly selected subsets of the training samples and yields a prediction. Aggregating these predictions through either a majority vote or an average can yield the most accurate prediction. First, to generate the training samples for the RF surrogate model, a total of 1600 Monte-Carlo simulations were performed for PD and VS sources using the coupled well-aquifer model. In this process, the parameters were sampled using Sobol sequence to uniformly cover the full parameter space. Second, two types of RF surrogate models were established for different sensitivity indices. How the water level responds to aquifer disturbance, e.g. the type of response in both amplitude and phase, as described in Eqs. (1)-(3), belongs to classification issues. In building the RF surrogate for classification, a total of 100 decision trees is set, and the number of nodes in each tree is unlimited until a pure-feature node is reached, which means that all instances in each leaf node can be classified into the same class and the optimal split for branch nodes of each decision tree is selected by minimizing the Gini impurity (Rodriguez-Galiano et al. 2014 ). The sensitivity of the indices defined as Eqs. (4)-(7) to varying parameters is more modeled as a regression problem because it involves quantifying a continuous relationship between the indices and their influencing factors. This approach allows us to explore how changes in parameters such as water column inertia and wellbore storage quantitatively affect the water level responses, reflecting a spectrum of possible outcomes rather than distinct categories. This continuous spectrum is more aligned with the nature of the physical processes involved, which exhibit gradual variations rather than discrete, categorizable states. For regression, the criterion to minimize as for finding optimal split locations in RF is the mean squared error (MSE). The optimal split is achieved by selecting the split that minimizes the total MSE of the two child nodes, after evaluating all possible splits for all features. The total MSE of the child nodes is derived by calculating the average of the squared differences between each predicted value and the actual target value. The total number of decision trees is set to 500 in order to get a higher regression accuracy, and the number of nodes in each tree is also unlimited. Regardless of classification and regression, all training samples are divided into a 75 % in-bag portion for training the surrogate model and a 25 % out-of-bag portion for testing. Global parameter sensitivity of the identified indices can be realized by analyzing the parameter importance in the established RF surrogate models. In RF classification, parameter importance can be determined using the mean decrease in accuracy (MAD   ), defined as the decrease in model score (s   ) when the value of a single parameter is randomly shuffled,(8) MAD  j  = s - 1 C  ∑ i = 1  C  s i , j        where i    is the number of random shuffles of the j   -th parameter, ranging from 1 to C   . The model score s    can be obtained by the ratio of the number of correct predictions to the total number of predictions. A higher mean absolute deviation (MAD) for a parameter means that the parameter has a greater impact. Sobol’s method, a variance-based sensitivity analysis algorithm, assesses the contribution of each input parameter and their interactions to the overall variance in model output (Sobol 1993, Zhang et al. 2015 ). Within the array of Sobol indices, which includes the first-order index and second-order index, the total Sobol index of a given parameter reflects the sensitivity of both first-order effects and all the higher-order effects involving that parameter (Chiogna et al. 2024 ). The total Sobol index (S T    ) is defined as the complement of the conditional expectation variance of the response indices across all parameter values except the specified parameter (X j    ),(9) S T  = 1 - V a r E Y |  X  j          V a r Y           where Y    here represents the four response indices defined in Eqs. (4)-(7), and X  j      denotes the set of all parameters excluding X j    . Var    means the model variance and E    denotes the conditional expectation. Cooper et al. (1965)  reported an interaction effect (i.e., second-order effect) of K    and T 0     on the sensitivity index A IN    ¯     . Considering the potential higher-order effects, the total Sobol index is selected as a metric to measure the parameter sensitivity for the regression task. Fig. 3   illustrates the implementation steps of the global parameter sensitivity analysis method used in this study. It should be noted that in order to assess the stability of the parameter importance estimates, the mean and standard deviation of the MAD or S T     indices were calculated using Monte Carlo methods with random samples of the testing set.    3 Global sensitivity analyses Based on the proposed framework, this chapter conducts a global parameter sensitivity analysis of water level response to aquifer disturbance based on the coupled well-aquifer model. First, the global parameter sensitivity of the yes/no water level response is investigated for PD and VS sources, respectively, in Section 3.1 . For those with a water level response, the question is whether the water level can truly reflect the pore pressure changes in the aquifer. To this end, global parameter sensitivities of the response type of water level amplitude and phase are carried out in Section 3.2 . Wellbore effects can lead to amplitude and phase differences between water levels and aquifer pore pressure changes. To quantify the impact of wellbore effects, global parameter sensitivities of water column inertia and wellbore storage are conducted in Section 3.3 . 3.1 Global parameter sensitivity of the yes/no water level responses A total of 1600 Monte-Carlo simulations (MCS) were performed for PD sources and VS sources. The sample size was examined based on the variance of total Sobol index for the parameters as the sample size increased in the MCS, see Figures s1 and s2  for more details. Of the 800 simulations performed for the PD source, 355 simulated responses that could be recognized as “response” in A YN    ¯     , i.e., water level amplitudes exceeding the assumed sensor resolution of 1 mm. This implies that with the parameter uncertainties listed in Table 1 , the probability of being able to observe a PD source-induced water level response is approximately 44 %. Therefore, it is necessary to analyze the parameter sensitivity associated with the binary (yes/no) water level response, which is beneficial to optimize the experimental design to minimize instances of non-response. The parameter sensitivity of the yes/no water level response is performed by measuring the MAD    values of each parameter based on the RF surrogate model. Initially, the RF surrogate model is trained using 600 groups of randomly sampled parameters and corresponding A YN    ¯     , and then is tested using the remaining data. The performance of the trained RF surrogate model during the validation phase is shown in Figure s2 . For the PD source, the MAD including mean (bar graph) and standard deviation (top black line) of each parameter are shown in Fig. 4  a . It indicates that hydraulic conductivity K    is the most influential parameter, followed by the specific storage S s    , the disturbance distance D   , and the source amplitude A 0    . This implies that water level response to PD sources is predominantly governed by aquifer parameters and source characteristics, having minimal relation to the wellbore construction parameters. This also highlights that the PD source-induced water level is primarily affected by the dampening effect of the aquifer on the pore pressure diffusion process. Fig. 4 b  depicts the relationship between the A YN    ¯      with respect to the four most influential parameters. Diagonal plots represent the probability density of each parameter in each column using kernel density estimation, providing insights into the central tendency, distribution, and distribution shape of each parameter for yes/no water level responses. Results indicate that water level response is more likely to be observed when conducting tests in aquifers with larger K    and/or smaller S s    . For instance, when K    exceeds 5 × 10-5  m/s or S s     is less than 2 × 10-5  1/m, the probability of observing a response is greater than the probability of non-response, as shown by the intersection points in Fig. 4 b . In contrary, a larger D    and a smaller A 0     tend to increase the probability of no water level responses. Similarly, for the VS source, after the validation of the surrogate model (see Figure s2 ), the sensitivities of the binary yes/no water level response on eight model parameters are analyzed by measuring the MAD and standard deviation (SD). The results are illustrated in Fig. 5  ,  including the permutation importance and the scatterplots of the A YN    ¯      regarding the four most influential parameters. Approximately 82 % of the A YN    ¯      simulations are quantified as “response”. A 0     and K    are identified as the two most influential parameters, followed by S s    , and B   . The larger A 0     and K    are, the higher is the likelihood of observing the water level response. This suggests that aquifer properties and source characteristics are the primary factors influencing the observability of a water level response in a monitoring well. It further confirms that the water level response to aquifer disturbance depends primarily on pore pressure diffusion processes within the aquifer, rather than on water column movement within the wellbore.  3.2 Global parameter sensitivity of response type of water level amplitude and phase When a water level response is observed, it is important to clarify whether the observed water level can truly represent the pore pressure in the aquifer. It is primarily because in practice, the measured water levels are generally considered as a proxy of the total pore pressure in aquifers, aiding to interpret aquifer properties or the mechanisms of various hydrological phenomena. According to Eqs. (2)-(3), the amplitude index A WE    ¯      and phase shift index P WE    ¯      represent the difference between water levels and theoretical pore pressure unaffected by wellbore effects, calculated based on the Monte-Carlo simulations. The parameter sensitivities of these two indices were again assessed through calculating the MAD    values utilizing the RF surrogate model. For the PD source, the RF surrogate model is trained and tested utilizing the 355 responsive samples. The performance of the trained RF surrogate model during the validation phase is shown in Figure s3 . The index A WE    ¯      contains three categories, i.e., amplitude attenuation, equivalence, and amplification, which account for approximately 34 %, 58 %, and 8 % of all samples, respectively. Correspondingly, three categories on index P WE    ¯      are phase delay, in-phase, and phase advance, which account for about 58 %, 40 %, and 2 % of the total samples, respectively. This suggests that the water level induced by the PD source is more likely to be amplitude-equivalent and phase-delayed. The parameter sensitivities of each category are analyzed and shown in Fig. 6  . The K    and T 0     are the two most influential parameters influencing whether the water level amplitude can maintain the pore pressure amplitude in the aquifer. Fig. 6 b  indicates that when K    is greater than 10-4  m/s and T 0     is larger than 46 s, the amplitude of the water level has the highest probability of accurately representing the amplitude of the pore pressure in the aquifer. When the K    is less than 10-4  m/s, the water level amplitude is highly likely to be attenuated due to wellbore effects. And the amplitude of water level can be amplified only if the T 0     is below 72 s. In Fig. 6 c and 6d , the two most influential parameters for in-phase cases are K    and T 0    , which also influence the phase delay significantly. When K    is lower than 6.3 × 10-4  m/s, there is a probability for the water level phase to incur a delay. Just five cases of phase advance are recorded, congregating predominantly around a T 0     equal to 13 s and K    value exceeding 6 × 10-4  m/s. For the VS source, out of 654 “response” samples, the majority exhibits amplitude attenuation and phase delays. The proportions of amplitude attenuation, equivalence and amplification are about 92 %, 4 % and 4 %, respectively. And the proportions of phase delay, in-phase, and phase advance are about 91.9 %, 7.8 % and 0.3 %, respectively. After validation of the surrogate model (see Figure s4 ), Fig. 7   presents the parameter sensitivities of all the categories in A WE    ¯      and P WE    ¯     . The K    and T 0     are the two most influential parameters determining whether the water level amplitude can truly represent the pore pressure in aquifers. The amplitude of the water level is likely to be equal to the amplitude of the pore pressure only if K    exceeds 2.5 × 10-6  m/s and T 0     is larger than 20 s. In contrary, K    and S s     are the two most influential parameters for the phase delay and in-phase categories, as shown in Fig. 7 c . Given that only two simulations exhibited phase advance, its parameter sensitivity is not investigated. Fig. 7 d  illustrates that the in-phase cases are clustered in two regions, where K    is either lower than 10-8  m/s or greater than 10-5  m/s, underlying two different mechanisms. In case of aquifers characterized by low K    values, a considerably larger S s     (>10-4  1/m) is required to synchronize the water level in phase with the pore pressure. This is because the high-S s     aquifer can rapidly release water to balance the pressure disturbance. On the other hand, when K    is large (>10-5  m/s), the pore pressure disturbance can be balanced majorly by driving groundwater flow to the monitoring wells. Notably, the phase advance cases are only observed in region with high K    values, specifically larger than 10-5  m/s.  3.3 Global parameter sensitivity of water column inertia and wellbore storage Wellbore effects are the main reason of the differences in water levels and pore pressure changes in aquifers, i.e., the changes in A WE    ¯      and P WE    ¯     . According to Eqs. (4)-(5), the impacts of water column inertia on water level responses can be evaluated by the amplitude ratio A IN    ¯      and phase shift P IN    ¯     , which represent the differences in amplitude and phase between water levels and the pressure head at the midpoint of the well screen. To quantify how the A IN    ¯      and P IN    ¯      are affected by the model parameters, global parameter sensitivities are performed by measuring the total Sobol index (S T    ) using the RF regression. For the PD source, the RF regression model is built using the 355 responsive samples and the validation results are shown in Figure s5 . Fig. 8   shows the importance of all parameters based on the S T     and the relation between the most influential parameters and the response indices A IN    ¯      and P IN    ¯     . The source period T 0     is the most sensitive and almost the unique influential parameter for both A IN    ¯      and P IN    ¯     . In Fig. 8 b , scatter plots of simulated A IN    ¯      and P IN    ¯      exhibit a forced harmonic behavior. Specifically, A IN    ¯      first increases and then gradually stabilizes to 1 as T 0     increases, as illustrated in the upper plot in Fig. 8 b . A significant amplification of the amplitude (A IN    ¯   > 1   ) can be observed when T 0     is about 20 s. According to the P IN    ¯      curve delineated in the bottom plot of Fig. 8 b, a  significant hysteresis can be observed when T 0     is smaller than 20 s, and this hysteresis gradually vanishes as T 0     increases. To quantify the impacts of T 0    , the scatter points are curve-fitted using general solutions of forced harmonic motion, i.e. the amplitude A T    = c T  2   ( T  2  - a  2  )  2  + ( b T )  2       . The 95 % prediction interval and 95 % confidence interval are also included in Fig. 8 b . The 95 % confidence interval is approximated by adding and subtracting two standard deviations from the mean of the parameter estimate. In a similar fashion, the 95 % prediction interval is calculated by adding and subtracting two standard errors of the regression estimate to and from the predicted values. A resonance period of 17.5 s in the well-aquifer system disturbed by PD sources can be identified by T 0     corresponding to maximum A IN    ¯      and P IN    ¯      at - π / 2   . This indicates that when the T 0     of the PD source is about 17.5 s, the amplitude of water level could be considerably amplified due to the water column inertia and the phase can experience a delay of greater than π / 2   . The maximum of the simulated amplitude ratio A IN    ¯      is 7.1, and the minimum of P IN    ¯      is close to - π   . For the VS source, the source period T 0     is the most influential parameter for A IN    ¯      and P IN    ¯     . All 654 responsive A IN    ¯      and P IN    ¯      observations varying with T 0     are depicted in Fig. 8 d . According to the fitted curves, the resonance period of the well-aquifer system disturbed by VS sources can be identified to be around 35 s. The maximum value of the fitted A IN    ¯      is about 2.5, which is much lower than 3.8 observed for the PD source. Furthermore, the amplitude amplification zone (A IN    ¯   > 1   ) and phase transition zone (P IN    ¯   < 0   ) induced by the VS source are considerably wider than those induced by the PD source. These comparisons suggest that water level induced by the VS source experience more significant damping effects from the water column inertia than the PD source. This phenomenon can be attributed to the extended average wellbore length considered for the VS source (Table 1 ), which can be akin to an inertia mass damper. Wellbore storage is another important factor that can attenuate the amplitude of water level responses and affect their phase shifts. The impact of wellbore storage is quantified using the A ST    ¯      and P ST    ¯      defined in Eqs. (6)-(7), which represent the disparity between the pressure head at the well screen and the theoretical pore pressure at the same location unaffected by wellbore effects. Global parameter sensitivities of A ST    ¯      and P ST    ¯      are also investigated based on the total Sobol index (S T    ). Fig. 9   illustrates the sensitivity analysis results and the relation between the A ST    ¯      and P ST    ¯      indices and their most influential parameters. For PD sources, K    is identified as the most influential parameter for both A ST    ¯      and P ST    ¯     . The simulated A ST    ¯      and P ST    ¯      show a stepwise increment as K    increases, and the relation between the two indices and K    can be curve-fitted employing a step function. The fitted curve reveals a transition zone where A ST    ¯      changes from 0 to 1, when K    varies from 10-6  m/s to 10-3  m/s. Concurrently, P ST    ¯      increases from - π / 2    to 0 with the increase of K    values. These results indicate that wellbore storage can lead to an evident amplitude attenuation and phase delay in an aquifer with a K    less than 10-6  m/s. The phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that when the permeability of the aquifer is low, the ability of the wellbore storage to rapidly equilibrate aquifer disturbances is suppressed. In contrast, for the VS source, the most influential parameter of A ST    ¯      and P ST    ¯      are K    and T 0    , respectively. The fitted curves in Fig. 9 d  indicate that the relation between the A ST    ¯      and K    is relatively similar to the of the PD source. A significant attenuation in amplitude becomes apparent when K    is smaller than 10-6  m/s, which is attributed to the wellbore storage. However, the fitted P ST    ¯      exhibits a stepwise decrease from π / 2    to - π / 4   . The positive P ST    ¯      here means the phase is advanced after considering the effect of wellbore storage. The cutoff point for positive and negative P ST    ¯      is located at around 35 s, i.e., the averaged resonance period of the well-aquifer system disturbed by the VS source. This is because when the disturbance period T 0     is smaller than the resonance period, wellbore storage has to respond at a rate that exceeds the resonance frequency of the system in order to balance the aquifer disturbance. This, however, triggers the inertial effect of the water column, which in turn leads to a phase advancement of the pressure head at the bottom of the wellbore. Moreover, when T 0     exceeds 60 s, the P ST    ¯      stabilizes at - π / 4   , which can be attributed to the overall lower K    values considered for VS sources. This is due to the fact that lower K    values dampen the water exchange between the well and the aquifer.   4 Discussion 4.1 Key factors affecting water level response to PD source disturbances in aquifers Based on the global sensitivity results, aquifer properties and source characteristics emerge as the paramount factors influencing water level response, with K    and T 0     being especially significant. For the PD source, K    is the most important parameter that determines the extent to which a monitoring well responds to aquifer disturbances and whether the measured water level can truly represent the pore pressure in aquifers. In a high-K    aquifer (>10-4  m/s), sensors with a resolution of 1 mm can essentially detect the water level response, independent of the other parameters (Figs. 4 and 6 ). Moreover, the measured water level can basically reflect the actual pore pressure in the aquifer, except when T 0     is lower than 46 s. In a low-K    aquifer (<10-4  m/s), water level response might experience substantial attenuation in amplitude and delay in phase, or even be unobservable by sensors (Figs. 4 and 6 ). The another influential parameter T 0     predominantly affects the water level response through inertial effects of the water column. T 0     can considerably affect the magnitude of water level response, but it is insensitive to whether the wellbore responds to aquifer disturbances. When T 0     is approximately 17.5 s, the amplitude of the PD source-induced water level can be significantly amplified in a high-K    aquifer, resulting in a pronounced phase delay. The discovered global sensitivity reveals the fact that when utilizing measured water levels to investigate aquifer properties, the influence of wellbore effects can be disregarded if the aquifer has a high permeability and is subject to long-period disturbances, such as the ocean tide or an oscillatory pumping with a period longer than 50 s.  4.2 Key factors affecting water level response to VS source disturbances in aquifers For the VS source, K    is one of the most important parameters. Given that the elastic dynamic stress is exerted on the entire aquifer, a VS source-induced water level response can be often observed even in a very low-K    aquifer. The value of K    determines the response types of the water level in terms of amplitude and phase. In Figs. 7 and 9 , a notable amplitude attenuation occurs when K    is lower than 10-6  m/s, and significant phase delay emerges when K    varies between 10-8  m/s and 10-5  m/s. The impact of K    on water level response is mainly through wellbore storage as a lower K    aquifer can inhibit the water exchange between wells and aquifers. Consequently, the water level induced by the VS source usually suffers from amplitude attenuation and phase delay, both accounting for approximately 92 % of all the simulated samples (Fig. 7 ). Similar to the PD source, short-T    disturbances typically cause amplitude changes and phase shifts in water levels. The water column inertia can evidently amplify the water level amplitude in a high-K    aquifer, and introduce a phase delay when T 0     is around the resonance period of 35 s. Furthermore, the phase can advance when T 0     is shorter than the resonance period, progressively delaying thereafter to a value around π / 4   . From a practical perspective, a VS source-induced water level can be commonly (98 %, according to the Monte-Carlo simulation results) observable in aquifers with K    exceeding 10-7  m/s, particularly when the amplitude of the source A 0     is larger than 10-3  MPa. Moreover, given that T 0     of a seismic wave typically ranges from a few seconds to tens of seconds, the amplitude and phase of water level can be significantly influenced by wellbore effects. The relation between A WE    ¯      and T 0     shown in Fig. 8 d  is similar to the findings of Cooper et al. (1965) , except the discrepancy in the scale of amplitude amplification, which might exceed 100. This divergence might stem from the analytical solution basis of Cooper et al. (1965)  allowing the A WE    ¯      at the theoretical resonance period to be explicitly delineated. In some filed measurements, however, seismic wave-induced A WE    ¯      was also reported to be typically less than 10. Considering the long period-earth tide, the impact of T    on water column inertia can be essentially disregarded. However, the consideration of amplitude attenuation and an approximate π / 4    phase delay due to wellbore storage remain crucial when interpreting the earth tide-induced water levels.  4.3 Other important influential factors in practical scenarios Besides K    and T 0    , some additional factors should be further investigated when explaining the measured water level in practical scenarios. For instance, the degree of aquifer confinement has been considered as an important factor in various field studies (Zhang et al. 2021 ). While this study assumes a homogenous aquifer, it is essential to acknowledge that the subsurface environment can exhibit substantial heterogeneity. Unique geological structures, such as faults and highly conductive fractures, can considerably affect water level response. Furthermore, it is important to note that the sensitivity results were derived based on the parameter uncertainty listed in Table 1 . Extrapolating these results beyond the defined parameter ranges might result in inaccurate estimates.   5 Conclusions Based on different disturbance mechanisms, aquifer disturbance sources are categorized as pressure diffusion (PD) sources and volumetric strain (VS) sources. In order to understand whether a monitoring well responds to various aquifer disturbances and to study the nature of its response under the influence of wellbore effects, a comprehensive analysis of the global parameter sensitivities was performed based on a coupled well-water layer model. Sensitivity results show that the two parameters affecting the observability of a water level response are hydraulic conductivity and specific storage for the PD source, and source amplitude and hydraulic conductivity for the VS source. The most influential parameter affecting whether monitored water levels can truly represent pore pressure changes in aquifers is hydraulic conductivity for both sources, with a critical threshold observed at approximately 10-4  m/s. Monte-Carlo simulations show that within the context of the analyzed parameter uncertainties, PD source-induced water level responses have approximately a 50 % probability of being representative of aquifer pore pressure. In contrast, VS source-induced water level responses have a 92 % probability of occurring phase delay and amplitude attenuation. Additionally, sensitivity analysis of the wellbore effect reveals that the impact of the in-well water column inertia on water levels becomes most significant when an aquifer is influenced by disturbances from short-period sources. Significant amplitude variations and phase shifts can be observed when the disturbance is induced by PD sources with a period less than 50 s or by VS sources with durations less than 100 s. The impact of wellbore storage on water levels is mainly reflected as amplitude attenuation, especially in cases when the hydraulic conductivity is less than 10-6  m/s. Furthermore, water level responses show no sensitivity to the parameters of well construction. Sensitivity results obtained from this study offer valuable insights for the experimental design and interpretation of observed water levels. In order to reduce the impact of wellbore effects, oscillatory pumping tests should have a period of greater than 50 s and should be avoided in formations with hydraulic conductivity less than 10-6  m/s.
