Despite the long period of ocean/earth tides, wellbore storage can still result in amplitude attenuation and phase shifts when water levels are measured in formations with hydraulic conductivity less than 10-4  m/s. In addition, it is recommended to consider the impacts of both water column inertia and wellbore storage when interpreting water levels induced by far-field seismic waves. It should be noted that this study assumes a homogeneous confined aquifer. In addition, the sample size in Monte-Carlo simulations is limited and the method of optimal splitting branch nodes in tree selection process is classical, which may bring uncertainty to the results. Consequently, it is also necessary to fully assess the uncertainty caused by the above factors on the results considering the future practical applications.
1 Introduction Since the Industrial Revolution, the concentration of CO2  in the atmosphere has risen sharply due to the extensive use of fossil fuels, which has caused severe greenhouse effect and thus endangered human survival and development. Moreover, fossil fuels still dominate the global energy system at present. Therefore, how to reduce net CO2  emissions while ensuring energy supply security is a global challenge. For this purpose, many researchers have focused their attention on geological carbon storage (GCS) in recent years. Injecting CO2  into saline aquifers is regarded as one of the most promising GCS methods, which can effectively mitigate environmental degradation and energy constraints (Bachu, 2003 ; Bui et al., 2018 ; Metz et al., 2005 ; Michael et al., 2010 ). The CO2  migration in saline aquifers is often described as the immiscible two-phase flow in porous media (Bakhshian & Hosseini, 2019 ; Guo et al., 2022 ; Hu et al., 2017 ; Kohanpur et al., 2020 ; Ott et al., 2015 ; Reynolds & Krevor, 2015 ). The macroscopic responses of a multiphase seepage system depend heavily on the multiphase flow behaviors at pore scale (Liu et al., 2022 ; Raeini et al., 2015 ; Shams et al., 2021 ; Singh et al., 2017 ; Xu et al., 2017 ; Yang et al., 2021 ; Zhu et al., 2016 ). Therefore, deepening the research on pore-scale multiphase flow can provide an in-depth understanding of the interplay between pore structure, interface behavior and transport process, contributing to improving the quantification, prediction and optimization of CO2  storage performance (Bakhshian et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., 2022 ). Multiphase seepage is a complex physical process which is influenced by many factors, such as capillary number (Ca  = u c μ in /σ , where u c  denotes the characteristic flow velocity, μ in  denotes the kinetic viscosity of the invading phase, and σ  denotes the interfacial tension (IFT)), viscosity ratio (M  = μ in /μ d , where μ d  denotes the kinetic viscosity of the defending phase), wettability (denoted by the contact angle θ ) and pore-throat characteristics (e.g., heterogeneity and geometry). Many studies have been conducted to clarify the influence of one single factor on multiphase seepage, in which there are always uncertainties due to the interplay between the factors considered and those ignored (Bakhshian et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2022 ; Najafi et al., 2023 ; Rabbani et al., 2018 ; Ramstad et al., 2012 ; Yang et al., 2022 ). Therefore, to gain a deeper understanding of multiphase seepage physics, the comprehensive effects of multiple factors are attracting more attention (Ambekar et al., 2021 ; Bakhshian et al., 2019 ; Fan et al., 2019 ; Holtzman & Segre, 2015 ; Hu et al., 2018 ; Suwandi et al., 2022 ; Trojer et al., 2015 ; Tsuji et al., 2016 ; Zhao et al., 2016 ). In particular, in GCS scenarios, M  tends to be fixed at ∼0.1 due to the inherent thermodynamic properties of the reservoirs and fluids (Kestin et al., 1981 ; Linstorm, 1998 ; Nordbotten et al., 2005 ). By contrast, there are wider variations of Ca  and θ . Therefore, the pore-scale comprehensive effects of Ca  and θ  on GCS is a more valuable research topic. The environmental and economic benefits of GCS depend mainly on two properties, namely, the CO2  storability and injectivity, which denote the maximum amount of CO2  stored in a reservoir and the ease of injecting CO2  into a reservoir, respectively. Generally, these two properties can be expressed in terms of saturation and relative permeability, respectively (Burnside & Naylor, 2014 ; Suwandi et al., 2022 ; Tsuji et al., 2016 ). However, previous studies have shown that multi-factor interplay results in the uncertainties of the variations of these two indicators with Ca  and θ . For instance, Bakhshian et al. (2020)  showed that the variations of invading phase saturation with θ  in a homogeneous media differ from those in a heterogeneous media. Liu et al. (2022)  found that a higher Ca  leads to a higher invading phase saturation in imbibition, different from the finding of Bagheri et al. (2023) . The variations of relative permeabilities with θ  reported by Landry et al. (2014)  are the opposite of those reported by Nemer et al. (2020) , even though the identical mechanism was adopted to interpret the findings. Therefore, a comprehensive parametric study addressing saturation and relative permeability is necessary. On the other hand, it has been demonstrated how Ca  and θ  influence pore-scale multiphase flow behaviors. For example, Holtzman and Segre (2015)  demonstrated that increasing θ  promotes cooperative pore filling stabilizing the invasion, but viscous instabilities resulting from increasing Ca  suppress this effect. Hu et al. (2018)  demonstrated that the crossover from fingering to stable flow is a function of Ca  and θ  at a favorable M . Zhao et al. (2016)  demonstrated that the fluid-fluid displacement at a high Ca  is dominated by wetting films and that increasing θ  promotes an evolution from cooperative filling to corner flow. Accordingly, the variations of relative permeability and saturation with Ca  and θ , the macroscopic response indicators of a multiphase seepage system, are supposed to be closely related to the evolutions of pore-scale multiphase flow behaviors. Therefore, a high-precision dissection of pore-scale multiphase flow behaviors is the crux in clarifying the aforementioned uncertainties. Advances in imaging technology have enabled pore-scale multiphase seepage visualization tests. For example, Rücker et al. (2015)  and Singh et al. (2017)  investigated the ganglion dynamics in imbibition and the dynamics of snap-off and pore-filling events, respectively, using X-CT. Nonetheless, there are pore-scale non-equilibrium and inertial effects during a multiphase seepage, which can cause an abrupt increase in interface velocity, as exemplified by the burst, i.e., the Haines jump (Zacharoudiou & Boek, 2016 ). It's difficult to capture these events accurately through visualization tests due to temporal resolution limits. In addition, it's a challenge to reveal and dissect pore-scale multiphase seepage behaviors entirely through laboratory tests solely. To this end, numerical simulation provides a promising avenue for the exploration of multiphase seepage physics. The most interesting feature of a physics problem is accessible in a 3D realistic model (Bakhshian et al., 2020 ; Zhao et al., 2016 ; Zhou et al., 2010 ). In other words, a 3D natural porous media model has the potential to elucidate multiphase seepage mechanisms under real reservoir conditions. In recent years, digital rock physics (DRP), combining micro-imaging techniques with numerical simulation, has become progressively popular thanks to improved computer performance. DRP allows one to characterize and analyze the pore-scale multiphase flow behaviors in a 3D complex model under extensive reservoir conditions. The most widely-used methods of DRP include the pore network model (PNM) method (Bensinger & Beckingham, 2020 ; Blunt et al., 2013 ; Xiong et al., 2016 ), the Lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) (Chen & Doolen, 1998 ; Dye et al., 2016 ; Suwandi et al., 2022 ; Tsuji et al., 2016 ) and the computational fluid dynamics (CFD) method (Gunde et al., 2010 ; Najafi et al., 2023 ; Raeini et al., 2014 ; Zhao et al., 2018 ). PNM greatly simplifies pore structures and is thus highly computationally efficient. However, it's a challenge to reveal pore-scale flow mechanisms entirely through PNM. Parallel computation is accessible through LBM. Nonetheless, LBM makes it difficult to cope with the flow problems with large densities or high viscosity ratios. As an alternative, CFD couples the solution of the Navier-Stokes and interface equations in a mesh model with both accuracy and efficiency (Kohanpur et al., 2020 ), hence is recognized as a practical approach to investigating fluid flow physics and interfacial dynamics at pore scale. The phase field method (PFM) is a CFD method derived from physics, which is highly credible due to its strict adherence to thermodynamic consistency and conservativity (Cahn, 1959 ; Cahn & Hilliard, 1958 , 1959 ; Jacqmin, 1999 ; Yue et al., 2004 ). Moreover, many studies have demonstrated that PFM is capable of depicting the complex topological variations of interfaces to capture pore-scale two-phase behaviors accurately (Amiri & Hamouda, 2013 , 2014 ; Rokhforouz & Amiri, 2018 ). In this study, the comprehensive effects of Ca  and θ  on CO2  saturation and relative permeability in GCS scenarios were systematically investigated based on DRP. We first performed a 3D reconstruction of the pore structure of Berea sandstone based on CT scanning. Next, we simulated dynamic CO2 -water displacements in the obtained pore structure using PFM under extensive Ca -θ  conditions, and calculated the corresponding CO2  saturations and two-phase relative permeabilities. Then, we analyzed the corresponding pore-scale mechanisms based on the high-resolution visualization results. Finally, we organized our results into comprehensive Ca -θ  diagrams, based on which the general patterns of CO2  storability and injectivity and the overall benefits of GCS were discussed.  2 Methodology The overall workflow of this study, including sample preparation, CT scanning, image processing, 3D reconstruction, quantitative description and two-phase flow numerical simulation, is shown in Fig. 1  . Berea sandstone sample was used in this study. CT scanning was performed through the "spiral extension" method. The binarized slice images of the sample were obtained through image processing, and were spatially stacked to achieve 3D reconstruction deriving the 3D voxel model of the sample. The pore-throat characteristics of the sample were obtained through quantitative description. Two-phase flow numerical simulations were carried out based on the above work. 2.1 Sample preparation Berea sandstone sample was collected from the deposit in Northern Ohio, USA, with helium porosity and gas permeability of 22.07 % and 494.10 mD, respectively. XRD analysis shows that the mineral components of the sample include quartz (89.8 %), muscovite (4.1 %), feldspar (3.6 %), calcite (0.8 %) and clay (1.7 %). A plug (5.2 mm i.d., 5.5 mm height) was extracted from the sample utilizing the wire-cutting method for the subsequent work.  2.2 3D reconstruction of pore structure based on CT scanning 2.2.1 CT scanning CT scanning was performed utilizing the Sanying nanoVoxel-3000 Computed Tomography System. The high-resolution grayscale slice images of the plug were obtained with the accuracy of 2 μm/pixel. 1000 slices in each of three directions were selected for the subsequent work to minimize the burdens of data processing.  2.2.2 Image processing and 3D reconstruction To reconstruct an accurate pore structure, image processing, including image filtering and image threshold segmentation, must be performed on the original images, as shown in Fig. 2  (a). Image filtering aims to eliminate the effects of noise from the CT device (Buades et al., 2005 ). The median filtering method was used due to its excellent performance in removing noise and preserving pore integrity (Fan et al., 2020 ; Fang et al., 2020 ). Image threshold segmentation aims to binarize the images (Wang et al., 2023 ). The grayscale images in Fig. 2 (a) show the presence of clay (light gray), consistent with the XRD results. The intraparticle pores contained in the clay with dimensions smaller than the resolution of CT scanning, whose effects on immiscible multiphase flow are minimal, were not considered. The cylindrical 3D voxel model of the pore structure (Fig. 2 (b)) was obtained through 3D reconstruction, with the porosity of 16.53 %, lower than the helium porosity due to the inability of CT scanning to capture the intraparticle pores. To improve computational efficiency, extracting a smaller model as Representative Elementary Volume (REV) is necessary. As shown in Fig. 2 (b), a cube of 150 × 150 × 180 voxels, with the permeability of 769.57 mD, close to the gas permeability, was extracted as REV from the better-developed area of the cylindrical model, where contains key pores dominant in overall seepage performance (Nishiyama & Yokoyama, 2017 ; Wang et al., 2023 ).  2.2.3 Quantitative description of pore structure Quantitative description of pore structure can facilitate accurate pore-scale multiphase seepage simulations. Pore decomposition and labeling were performed through the watershed method, which is easy to implement while maintaining satisfactory accuracy (Zhao et al., 2020 ). Two pore radius probability density functions were plotted based on the pore decomposition and labeling of the cylindrical model, and the mercury intrusion porosimetry (MIP) measurement of the plug, respectively, as shown in Fig. 3  (a, b). It can be seen that these two curves are in good agreement within the range of CT scanning resolution (>2 μm), with peaks occurring near 10 μm, which is sufficient to demonstrate the accuracy and feasibility of the watershed method. Therefore, the watershed method was applied to REV, as shown in Fig. 3 (c). The average pore diameter of REV, D a , was obtained at 30.7 μm.   2.3 Two-phase flow numerical simulation 2.3.1 Phase field method for two-phase flow modeling The immiscible two-phase flow modeling was developed through the phase field method (PFM). The numerical solution was performed in the FEM solver of COMSOL Multiphysics. In phase field modeling, ϕ , known as a phase field variable, is used to identify different phases to depict the evolutions of the interfaces. All physical properties of the phases, such as density (ρ ) and dynamic viscosity (μ ), can be expressed as the functions of ϕ . The governing equations with only four independent variables, i.e., flow velocity (u ), pressure (p ), phase field variable (ϕ ) and phase field auxiliary variable (ψ ), are obtained by coupling the Navier-Stokes and Cahn-Hilliard equations (Jacqmin, 1999 ):(1) ∇ · u = 0     (2) ρ ∂ u  ∂ t   + ρ ( u · ∇ )  u =  −  ∇ p + μ ∇  2  u + G ∇ ϕ     (3) ∂ ϕ  ∂ t   + u · ∇ ϕ = ∇ · ( γ λ  ε   2   ∇ ψ )      (4) ψ = − ∇ · ( ε   2  ∇ ϕ )  + ϕ ( ϕ  2  − 1 )      where G  is the chemical potential, γ  is the mobility. The chemical potential, obtained from the interfacial mixing energy through the calculus of variations, is expressed as:(5) G = ϕ ( ϕ  2  − 1 )  λ ε   2   − λ ∇  2  ϕ     where λ  is the mixing energy density, ε  is the capillary width. The mobility is expressed as:(6) γ = χ ε   2      where χ  is the mobility tuning parameter. Considering that the interfacial mixing energy is physically equivalent to IFT (σ ), σ  = (22   /3)λ /ε  is introduced into the modeling. Wetting condition can be characterized through geometric characteristic (Ding & Spelt, 2007 ; Yue et al., 2010 ):(7) n · ∇ ϕ = − | ∇ ϕ  |  cos θ     where n  is the outward normal vector defined at the solid wall. According to the phase field theory, pore-scale two-phase flow physics is closely related to the structures of the interfaces and the convection-diffusion interactions. The capillary width ε , a measure of the interfacial thickness (Yue et al., 2004 ), is essential for determining the interfacial mixing energy and IFT. The interfaces are expected to be thin enough to allow the modeling to converge to the sharp-interface limit, which is a physics convergence, and to be resolved by sufficient meshes, which ensures that ϕ  is described smoothly. The mobility γ , a parameter determining the relaxation time of the interfaces, controls the competition between the convection and the diffusion in the domains of the interfaces. The higher the γ , the stronger the diffusion, and conversely the stronger the convection. The convection induces chemical potential perturbations, which are counteracted by the diffusion to ensure numerical stability. However, excessive diffusion can, in turn, damp the flow, deviating the modeling from a real physical state (Jacqmin, 1999 ). Nonetheless, the diffusion will affect weakly if the modeling converges to the sharp-interface limit (Zhou et al., 2010 ). To depict the phase field system accurately and efficiently, the physics convergence of the modeling was quantified by Cahn number (Cn  = ε /l c , where l c  is the characteristic length of the porous media); ε  was defined as h c /2, where h c  is the maximum cell size of the mesh model; l c  was defined as D a . Consequently, decreasing Cn  by decreasing h c  improves the physics convergence while ensuring that the interfaces are resolved by sufficient meshes. The physics convergence is achieved as Cn  approaches a small critical value (Yue et al., 2010 ). The numerical stability was guaranteed by adjusting γ .  2.3.2 Computational domain and conditions The unstructured tetrahedral mesh models of REV, suitable for FEM, were obtained after processing which consists of smoothing and meshing processes. The optimal meshing scheme maintaining efficiency and accuracy contains 1.53 × 106  tetrahedral meshes (Fig. 4  (a)). Generally, in GCS, CO2  is injected into the saline aquifers 1000-3000 m underground, where the temperature and pressure are within the ranges of 35°C - 110°C and 10.5 MPa - 31.5 MPa, respectively (Nordbotten et al., 2005 ). Therefore, 92°C and 16.8 MPa were used as the temperature and pressure conditions, respectively. The reservoir-fluid salinity was considered to be zero. Table 1   lists the corresponding properties of the fluids, which are collected from the related literatures (Adams & Bachu, 2002 ; Batzle & Wang, 1992 ; Kestin et al., 1981 ; Li et al., 2012 ; Linstorm, 1998 ). Notice that the viscosity ratio, M , is fixed at 0.105, a value of typical GCS scenarios, representing an unfavorable displacement condition. During the simulations, a 40 μm domain near the inlet (the bottom of the model) was filled with CO2 , serving as the invading phase, for buffering; the remaining domain was filled with water, serving as the defending phase (Fig. 4 (b)). The inlet and outlet (the top of the model) were set as the velocity and pressure boundaries, respectively. The lateral and internal boundaries were set as the slip and no-slip boundaries, respectively. The simulation schemes are shown in Table 2  . The simulations were performed under extensive injection velocity (v in , ranging from 0.001 m/s to 0.05 m/s) and contact angle (θ , ranging from 30° to 90°) conditions to investigate the comprehensive effects of capillary number and wettability systematically. The logarithm of Ca , lgCa , ranges from -3.38 to -1.68, representing the flow conditions in the near-well region of GCS. The Reynolds number (Re  = ρ in u c l c /μ in , where ρ in  denotes the density of the invading phase) ranges from 0.16 to 8.15, representing the conditions of the laminar flow (Alpak et al., 2018 ; Fan et al., 2020 ; Hassanizadeh & Gray, 1987 ). Five values of θ  from 30° to 90° were considered since CO2 -water-sandstone systems are usually water-wetting (Iglauer et al., 2012 ; Lv et al., 2017 ; Saraji et al., 2014 ). Homogeneous distribution of θ  was adopted.    3 Results and analysis Firstly, modeling convergence analysis was performed to find the sharp-interface limit and optimize the meshing schemes, ensuring the accuracy and efficiency of the simulations. Then, several transient two-phase flow simulations were performed to investigate the comprehensive effects of Ca  and θ  on CO2  saturation and two-phase relative permeabilities. The data in the domains of 40 μm near the inlet and 20 μm near the outlet were not analyzed to avoid the boundary effects. 3.1 Modeling convergence analysis As listed in Table 3  , two-phase flow simulations were performed on the models with three different meshing schemes, based on which the pressure difference curves, related to the pore-scale events, were calculated. The obtained pressure difference curves tend to converge as Cn  decreases (Fig. 5  ). Nevertheless, the case of Cn  = 0.24, i.e., Scheme 2, achieves satisfactory accuracy with moderate computational costs and thus was considered to be the optimal scheme, which would be used in the subsequent simulations.  3.2 Comprehensive effects of Ca  and θ  on S CO2  The CO2  saturation (volume fraction) at the breakthrough moment, S CO2 , was calculated based on the simulation results. Fig. 6   shows that the comprehensive effects of Ca  and θ  on S CO2  are nonnegligible. On the one hand, overall, S CO2  decreases linearly as Ca  increases (Fig. 6  (a)). On the other hand, the S CO2 -θ  curves show different trends under different Ca  conditions (Fig. 6  (b)). At the high Ca  (lgCa  = -1.68), S CO2  monotonically increases as θ  increases, whereas at the moderate (lgCa  = -1.99) and lower Ca  (lgCa  = -3.38, -2.68, -2.38), the S CO2 -θ  curves show ascending and then descending trend. In particular, at the slightly high Ca  (lgCa  = -1.81), as θ  increases, the curve ascends, descends, and ascends again; furthermore, at this Ca , the S CO2  are higher than those of lgCa  = -1.99 at θ =  45° and 90° meanwhile is lower than that of lgCa  = -1.68 at θ =  60°, which is not in line with the overall monotonic trend shown in Fig. 6 (a). To interpret the above phenomena comprehensively, in-depth pore-scale analyses will be launched in this section. 3.2.1 Analysis based on microscopic forces To visually illustrate the dynamic competition between microscopic forces, the snapshots of the pore pressure fields in different Ca -θ  scenarios are compared in Fig. 7  . Fig. 7 (a) illustrates that under a higher Ca  and lower θ  condition, a higher magnitude of pressure appears due to the higher viscous and capillary pressure drops. By contrast, of more interest is the correlation between pressure field and the positions of the interfaces. According to Fig. 7 (a-c), there are always pressure jumps at the interfaces, whose magnitudes, representing the strengths of the capillary force, are related to Ca -θ  conditions. As shown in Fig. 7 (a), increasing Ca  always blurs the pressure jumps at the interfaces, indicating that the effects of capillary force fade while those of viscous force are strengthened. Under a lower Ca  condition, due to the dominant effects of capillary force, the main pathway for dissipating energy is interfacial motion, which causes the interfaces to sweep through more pore space, and hence the displacement efficiency is higher. However, the effects of viscous force gradually dominate as Ca  increases. Consequently, the two-phase flow system tends to dissipate energy through viscous force, which reduces interfacial motion, and hence the displacement efficiency is lower. Therefore, the decreasing trends of the S CO2 -lgCa  curves (Fig. 6 (a)) are directly related to the dynamic competition between the two microscopic forces, i.e., capillary and viscous forces. The reason for the tiny fluctuations in the slopes of the S CO2 -lgCa  curves with θ  is that the effects of the pore-scale behaviors on the macroscopic responses are amplified in the small-scale system. Similarly, the variations of the S CO2 -θ  curves are also related to the evolutionary characteristics of the pressure fields. On the one hand, at the high Ca  (lgCa  = -1.68), there are no significant pressure jumps at the interfaces no matter how θ  varies (Fig. 7 (a)), indicating that the effects of viscous force are dominant and those of capillary force are weak. For the rest cases (lgCa  = -3.38, -2.68, -2.38, -1.99, -1.81), the pressure jumps at the interfaces become significant with decreasing θ  (Fig. 7 (a)), suggesting that the control of the capillary force on the flow is enhanced and that of viscous force fades. On the other hand, the S CO2 -θ  curves show different trends under the aforementioned high and other Ca  conditions (Fig. 6 (b)). It can be concluded that the intricate variations of the S CO2 -θ  curves are inextricably linked with the dynamic competition between capillary force and viscous force. Nonetheless, it is difficult to clarify the mechanisms adequately by the analysis based on microscopic forces alone, and hence a further pore-scale analysis is necessary.  3.2.2 Analysis based on phase diagram The high-resolution visualization results show that there are regular and observable variations of the macroscopic displacement patterns with Ca  and θ , which are speculated to be related to the variations of the S CO2 -θ  curves in Fig. 6 (b). Therefore, the snapshots of the displacement patterns with similar morphology were marked with the same color to obtain a phase diagram marked with four colors, i.e., green, blue, orange and gray (Fig. 8  (a)). Based on this phase diagram, the evolutions of the displacement patterns with Ca  and θ  can be demonstrated qualitatively. Similar pore-scale interface behaviors, i.e., the same type of pore-scale displacement mechanism, were observed in the snapshots marked by the same color (Fig. 8 (b-e)). At the high Ca  (lgCa  = -1.68), the dominance of the effects of viscous force results in the dominance of the finger-like invasion (Fig. 8 (b)). Under this condition, CO2  breakthroughs rapidly along a shorter path, leading to limited pore space swept by the interfaces and significant trailing films (Zhao et al., 2016 ). As θ  increases, the affinity of rock surface for CO2  increases, decreasing the capillary resistance on the interfaces. Consequently, as shown in the green-marked snapshots in Fig. 8 (a), CO2  invades the corners of pores easily, which thins trailing films and thickens the finger, and hence induces a higher S CO2  (black line in Fig. 6 (b)). At the moderate (lgCa  = -1.99) and the lower Ca  (lgCa  = -3.38, -2.68, -2.38), the enhanced effects of capillary force lead to more active interface behaviors, inducing diverse displacement mechanisms. When θ  is low, there is a large distinction between the affinity of rock surface for CO2  and that for water, which causes CO2  to flow toward the middle of larger pores. Furthermore, the interfaces at different positions advance intermittently and pore-by-pore due to the significant effects of capillary resistance. Consequently, the burst (Fig. 8 (c)) dominates at this time, corresponding to the blue-marked snapshots in Fig. 8 (a). As θ  increases, the affinity distinction decreases, resulting in decreasing capillary resistance, and most of the interfaces advance simultaneously. Accordingly, the cooperative filling (Fig. 8 (d)) gradually replaces the dominance of the burst, corresponding to the orange-marked snapshots in Fig. 8 (a). The burst induces an incomplete displacement, resulting in a lower S CO2.  By contrast, the cooperative filling induces a more compact displacement pattern, resulting in a higher S CO2 . Considering the above, as shown in Fig. 6 (b), the S CO2 -θ  curves ascend with θ  until the weak water-wetting condition is reached. The tiny fluctuations in this trend arise from the sparser θ  schemes and the amplified effects of pore-scale behaviors on the macroscopic responses in the small-scale system. Intuitively, when θ  reaches 90°, the affinities of rock surface for the two fluids are equal, resulting in a thorough cooperative filling, and hence, the displacement efficiency is expected to be the maximum. However, as shown in Fig. 6 (b), the values of S CO2  are counter-intuitively low at θ  = 90°. As can be seen in Fig. 8 (a), the displacement patterns under neutral wettability condition (gray-marked) highly differ from those under other wettability conditions. The coexistence of concave and convex interfaces was found under neutral wettability condition (see the I and II of Fig. 8 (e)), implying drainage and imbibition occur simultaneously. Additionally, as shown in the III of Fig. 8 (e), the saddle-shaped interfaces were observed, which are the transitional interfaces between concave and convex interfaces with negligible capillary force (Lin et al., 2019 ). Actually, the two-phase flow physics in a heterogeneous media is extremely complex. The effects of pore geometry on interfacial dynamics are amplified as the wettability approaches neutrality, resulting in the dominance of the coexistence of concave and convex interfaces (Bakhshian et al., 2020 ; Rabbani et al., 2018 ). From this, the differences among the pressure gradients of the interfaces drive concave and saddle-shaped interfaces to advance preferentially while pinning convex interfaces, leading to an incompact displacement pattern. In the scenarios of this study, as the displacements proceed, the displacement fronts evolve the branching paths flowing reversely due to the combined effects of capillary force and pore heterogeneity. The interfaces advancing reversely trap and capture the bulk water with the interfaces advancing forward (see the IV in Fig. 8 (e)), causing the counter-intuitively low S CO2 . In addition, the coexistence of concave and convex interfaces dominates at θ  = 75° of the moderate Ca  (lgCa  = -1.99), differing with the lower Ca  (lgCa  = -3.38, -2.68, -2.38), suggesting that the higher viscous pressure drop caused by a higher Ca  can exacerbate the instabilities of concave and saddle-shaped interfaces, resulting in the early emergence of this mechanism. At the slightly high Ca  (lgCa  = -1.81), due to the same mechanisms discussed above, the burst, causing the lower S CO2 , dominates at θ  = 30°, while the finger-like invasion, causing the increasing S CO2  as θ , dominates from θ  = 60° to θ  = 75°. In particular, from θ  = 30° to θ  = 60°, the fading effects of capillary force lead to the slightly stronger, but not sufficiently strong, effects of viscous force. Consequently, the two-phase flow system is unable to dissipate energy through the effects of viscous force via the preferential path solely, and hence more interfacial motion is necessary, contributing to the transition from the burst to the finger-like invasion, as confirmed by the snapshot at (45°, -1.81) in Fig. 8 (a). However, the dramatic transition from a typical capillary-dominated mechanism to a typical viscous-dominated mechanism leads to the phenomena (see Fig. 6 (b), the S CO2  of lgCa  = -1.81 is higher than that of lgCa  = -1.99 at θ =  45° whereas is lower than that of lgCa  = -1.68 at θ =  60°) contradicting the overall trend demonstrated in Fig. 6 (a). Similarly, the transition from the finger-like invasion to the coexistence of concave and convex interfaces appears at (90°, -1.81), due to more interfacial motion caused by the fading effects of viscous force from lgCa  = -1.68 to lgCa  = -1.99, contributing to a higher S CO2  (see Fig. 6 (b), the S CO2  of lgCa  = -1.81 is higher than that of lgCa  = -1.99 at θ =  90°). Therefore, the R2  fluctuations in Fig. 6 (a) can be attributed to these cross-mechanism transitions.   3.3 Comprehensive effects of Ca  and θ  on k CO2  and k w  Two-phase relative permeabilities, k CO2  and k w , were calculated based on the simulation results. The relative permeabilities were calculated by (Raeini et al., 2014 ):(8) k i  = Q i  Δ  P i    · Δ  P i , s    Q i , s        where Qi   and ΔPi   are the total flow rate and Darcy-scale pressure drop of phase i  in a two-phase flow system, respectively. The variables with subscript s  denote those in a single-phase flow system. The data fluctuations in the small-scale system were avoided through nonlinear fitting using orthogonal distance regression. Three representative θ  conditions were selected to demonstrate the effects of Ca  on relative permeabilities (Fig. 9  ). For CO2 , k CO2  increases with Ca  (upward shift of the curves), on which θ  has no significant effects (Fig. 9 (a-c)). The reason is that increasing Ca  enhances the transient instabilities on the interfaces, which, together with the local potentials linked to interfacial motion, will add extra driving forces to the flow, enhancing CO2  flux and thus increasing its relative permeability. This is in agreement with Ramstad et al. (2012) . For water, as shown in Fig. 9 (d-f), there are intricate patterns. In the low S w  range, k w  increases with Ca , a trend insignificantly correlated with θ ; however, in the high S w  range, k w  at a moderately lower Ca  tends to be the maximum. Actually, the flow capacity of defending phase stems from the direct driving effects exerted by invading phase and the viscous coupling effects. To elaborate on the effects of Ca  and θ  on k w , the following definitions are made. On the one hand, increasing Ca  undoubtedly enhances CO2  flux and the effects of viscous force so that enhances the direct driving and viscous coupling effects, which is defined as A. On the other hand, according to Fig. 11 , at a lower Ca , increasing θ  curtails trailing films and drives the interfaces to advance via contact-line motion, which is piston-like, decreasing the area of the interfaces parallel to the flow direction so that weakening the viscous coupling effects (Li et al., 2005 ; Yiotis et al., 2007 ) but enhancing the direct driving effects, which is defined as B. During the initial stage of a displacement, i.e., in a high S w  range, the viscous coupling effects are weak due to the smaller area of the interfaces. Consequently, at a moderately, but not absolutely (if so, A is faint), lower Ca , as θ  increases, the synergies of A and B favor k w . As a displacement proceed, i.e., in a low S w  range, the viscous coupling effects are significant due to the increasing area of the interfaces. Thus, A is too significant to be dominated by B, causing k w  to increase with Ca . Three representative Ca  conditions were selected to demonstrate the effects of θ  on relative permeabilities (Fig. 10  ) For CO2 , k CO2  increases with θ , on which Ca  has no significant effects (Fig. 10 (a-c)). Increasing θ , implying the increasing affinity of rock surface for CO2  and the decreasing that for water, weakens the impediment to the flow from capillary force (Fig. 7 ) and thins trailing films (Fig. 11  ). Consequently, at a higher θ , CO2  passes through channels with less resistance and higher flow rates, leading to greater k CO2 . For water, k w  increases with θ  (Fig. 10 (d-f)). Similarly, increasing θ  allows water to escape from films and flow toward the middle of pores, inducing the piston-like interfacial motion (Fig. 11 ), which promotes the direct driving effects but weakens the viscous coupling effects. The net effect of these two effects ultimately increases k w  with θ . Furthermore, at a lower θ , trailing films are more significant (Fig. 11 ), and decreasing Ca  can diminish the role of these films in the viscous coupling effects to a greater extent compared to a higher θ . Consequently, as shown in Fig. 10 (d-f), decreasing Ca  enhances the correlation between k w  and θ .  3.4 Comprehensive Ca -θ  diagrams After the comprehensive effects of Ca  and θ  on S CO2 , k CO2  and k w  were confirmed, three comprehensive Ca -θ  diagrams were created (Fig. 12  ), which provide a clear overview of the main results of this study and help to demonstrate the evolutions of CO2  storability and injectivity with capillary number and wettability. As shown in Fig. 12 (a), the color bands of Ca -θ -S CO2  contour map are intricate, reflecting the complex comprehensive effects of Ca  and θ  on S CO2 . A higher S CO2  is accessible under a lower Ca  and weak water-wetting condition. As shown in Fig. 12 (b) and Fig. 12 (c), the color bands of Ca -θ -k CO2  and Ca -θ -k w  contour maps are distributed along the diagonal overall, similar to the distribution of the dominant pore-scale displacement mechanisms, which suggests that the variations of relative permeability are related to the interplay between capillary and viscous forces. This is in line with the analyses in Section 3.3 . However, k CO2  is less sensitive to Ca -θ  compared to k w  for the pore structure and parameters used in this study.   4 Discussion In this study, we utilized PFM, a reliable method derived from physics, to simulate CO2 -water dynamic displacements in a 3D natural porous media. Our study confirms that the high-resolution results from PFM, which can depict pore-scale two-phase behaviors clearly, provide a powerful tool to elucidate pore-scale two-phase flow mechanisms. In addition, our unsteady-state simulations were performed with the lgCa  ranging from -3.38 to -1.68, contributing to the understanding of the two-phase flow mechanisms in the near-well region during the injection stage of GCS. Saturation is a measure of the displacement efficiency in a multiphase seepage system. In this study, we found that the correlations between S CO2  and Ca -θ  are intricate. Most previous studies have shown that a higher Ca  decreases the displacement efficiency (Bagheri et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2016 ) while a wettability closer to neutral increases the displacement efficiency (Bakhshian et al., 2021 ; Hu et al., 2017 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2016 ). As expected, we also observed the above patterns (see Fig. 6 (a) and the black curve in Fig. 6 (b)). We confirmed that the dynamic competition between viscous force and capillary force directly leads to the negative correlation between displacement efficiency and Ca , and also induces the finger-like invasion contributing to the positive correlation between displacement efficiency and drainage θ  at a high Ca . Additionally, we found that at a lower Ca , the displacement efficiency shows a non-monotonic relationship with drainage θ , with a peak occurring under weak water-wetting condition and a minimum occurring under neutral condition (see the orange, red, blue and pink curves in Fig. 6 (b)). We suggested that the ascending trend (before the peak occurs) in the above relationship originates from a more compact displacement pattern induced by increasing drainage θ , consistent with previous studies (Ambekar et al., 2021 ; Holtzman & Segre, 2015 ; Hu et al., 2017 ; Trojer et al., 2015 ; Zhao et al., 2016 ). We attributed the descending trend (after the peak occurs), alternatively, the minimal displacement efficiency under neutral condition, to the effects of the coexistence of concave and convex interfaces, which is similar, but not identical, to a handful of studies. For example, Zhao et al. (2016)  attributed the decrease in displacement efficiency with increasing drainage θ  to the corner flow, which was not observed in our visualization results. As another example, Bakhshian et al. (2020)  demonstrated that the coexistence of concave and convex interfaces leads to a more compact displacement pattern, i.e., a higher displacement efficiency, in a 3D heterogeneous model, contrary to our argument. We assess that the discrepancies between our two results stem from the distinctions between the pore structures or the displacement conditions (Ca  = 1 × 10−6  in their study). In addition, Rabbani et al. (2017)  demonstrated that the coexistence of concave and convex interfaces induces a counter-intuitively low displacement efficiency under neutral condition in a 2D heterogeneous model, similar to our view. Our study, by contrast, was conducted in a 3D heterogeneous model. To sum up, our study provides new insights into how the pore-scale interplay between capillary number and wettability influences displacement efficiency. Relative permeability is a measure of the flow capacity of a fluid in a multiphase seepage system. In this study, we found that the correlations between two-phase relative permeabilities and Ca -θ  are obvious. We interpreted these correlations through the effects of pore-scale two-phase behaviors on the flow capacities, a method similar to previous studies. We used high-resolution pore-scale 3D visualization results as the evidence for the corresponding interpretations, which have not been addressed in previous studies (Fan et al., 2019 ; Huang & Lu, 2009 ; Landry et al., 2014 ; Nemer et al., 2020 ; Ramstad et al., 2012 ; Suwandi et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2019 ). However, it is still a challenge to make definitive assertions about the variations of relative permeabilities with Ca  and θ  in GCS. On the one hand, multiphase seepage is a complex physics process that is significantly influenced by many factors, such as pore geometry and heterogeneity (Bakhshian et al., 2020 ; Rabbani et al., 2018 ), which are highly uncertain. The distinctions among the pore-scale multiphase behaviors in different pore structures lead to the uncertainties in flow capacities, i.e., the uncertainties in relative permeabilities. On the other hand, according to the results of this study and some previous studies (Huang & Lu, 2009 ; Landry et al., 2014 ; Li et al., 2005 ; Nemer et al., 2020 ), the evolutions of relative permeabilities with Ca  and θ  involve the competition among multiple effects, whose net effect is often uncertain in different conditions. Nonetheless, it is certain that the pore-scale analysis based on high-resolution visualization results is an effective means of investigating the evolutionary mechanisms of relative permeability. In GCS, CO2  storability and injectivity must be considered (Suwandi et al., 2022 ; Tsuji et al., 2016 ). For this purpose, we created the comprehensive Ca -θ  diagrams (Fig. 12 ). Generally, the better the CO2  storability and injectivity, i.e., the higher the CO2  saturation and two-phase relative permeabilities, the greater the overall benefits of GCS. However, we found that due to the comprehensive effects of Ca  and θ, S CO2 , k CO2  and k w  may not necessarily evolve toward the direction of favoring GCS simultaneously. For instance, k CO2  and k w  tend to be higher at a higher Ca  and higher θ  condition, overall. By contrast, this condition is not conducive for a higher S CO2 , but a lower Ca  and weak water-wetting condition is. The comprehensive effects of viscosity ratio M  and Ca  are similar to the above. For example, Tsuji et al. (2016)  and Suwandi et al. (2022)  performed CO2 -brine simulations and found that k CO2  is higher at a higher M  and higher Ca  condition, while S CO2  is higher at a higher M  and lower Ca  condition. Therefore, to improve the overall benefits of GCS, it is necessary to consider the site-selection and injection schemes carefully. Our method can provide a reference for the selection of an optimal scheme. In addition, the above discussion demonstrates once again that studying the coupled effects of multiple factors is necessary. One future research direction is to create Ca -θ -M -α  multidimensional diagrams, where α  represents an important multiphase seepage response indicator, to evaluate the overall benefits of GCS more comprehensively. During our analyses, we created a Ca -θ  phase diagram (Fig. 8 (a)). Different from the classical two-phase flow Ca -M  phase diagrams based on macroscopic invasion patterns (Chen et al., 2018 ; Lenormand et al., 1988 ; Tsuji et al., 2016 ; Zhang et al., 2011 ), we found the identical pore-scale displacement mechanism in the similar displacement patterns, based on which the domains of our Ca -θ  phase diagram were classified. The process we creating this phase diagram once again demonstrates that macroscopic multiphase seepage responses depend heavily on pore-scale behaviors. Ambekar et al. (2021)  presented a phase diagram similar to ours, which did not report the coexistence of concave and convex interfaces found in our study. The reason may be the distinctions between the pore structures or the displacement conditions (M  = 1 in their study). Admittedly, we did not explicitly identify the transitional domain in the phase diagram, which is not the focus of our study. Nevertheless, we confirmed that the alternation of the dominant mechanism is not abrupt but transitional, in line with previous studies (Ambekar et al., 2021 ; Cottin et al., 2010 ; Ferer et al., 2004 ; Tsuji et al., 2016 ), and that these transitions, inducing considerable variations of the macroscopic response indicators in a two-phase seepage system (see Fig. 6 (a) and the purple curve in Fig. 6 (b)), are crucial. In the future, more efforts are necessary to improve the phase diagram by extending the parameter schemes and deducing a theoretical model quantifying multiple mechanisms.  5 Conclusions To deepen the pore-scale understanding of GCS, we systematically investigated the macroscopic influences and pore-scale effects of capillary number (Ca ) and drainage contact angle (θ ) on CO2  saturation (S CO2 ) and two-phase relative permeabilities (k CO2  and k w ) in GCS scenarios using PFM-based DRP technique. The main conclusions are as follows.(1) Pore-scale two-phase flow behavior, on which Ca  and θ  have comprehensive effects, is the fundamental factor leading to the macroscopic physics evolutions of a two-phase seepage system.  (2) The dynamic competition between microscopic forces directly leads to decreasing S CO2  with increasing Ca . The dynamic evolutions of pore-scale displacement mechanisms lead to the intricate correlations between S CO2  and θ . At a high Ca , the finger-like invasion increases S CO2  with θ ; at a lower Ca , the dominant pore-scale displacement mechanism evolves from burst to cooperative filling to coexistence of concave and convex interfaces with increasing θ , causing S CO2  to ascend and then descend; the cross-mechanism transitions play a role in S CO2 .  (3) The transient instabilities on the interfaces increase k CO2  with Ca . Increasing θ  weakens capillary resistance and thins trailing films, resulting in increasing k CO2  with θ. k w  is determined by the net effect of the direct driving and viscous coupling effects. The net effect increases k w  with Ca  in a low S w  range, and causes k w  at a moderately lower Ca  to be the maximum in a high S w  range. In addition, the net effect increases k w  with θ ; however, a lower Ca  diminishes the role of films in the viscous coupling effects to a greater extent at a lower θ , reducing the correlation between k w  and θ .  (4) S CO2 , k CO2  and k w  may not necessarily evolve toward the direction of favoring GCS simultaneously due to the comprehensive effects of multiple factors. The comprehensive Ca -θ  diagrams created in this study can provide valuable insights into the selection of an optimal GCS scheme.
1 Introduction Fractures are ubiquitous in rocks, and commonly play a large role in fluid flow applications including carbon storage and sequestration, fate and transport of solutes, geothermal energy, petroleum extraction, and water resources (Fatemi and Kharrat, 2011 ; Guihéneuf et al., 2014 ; Reeves et al., 2017 , 2023 ; Fu et al., 2017 ; Li et al., 2020 ; Feng et al., 2020 ). Geometric and hydraulic attributes of networks of interconnected fractures generated by tectonic stresses are controlled by current and past stress field orientations and magnitudes (Jaeger et al. 2009 ; Matthäi et al., 2004 ; Schultz et al., 2008 ; Wu and Wong, 2013 ). The connectivity of tectonically generated fracture networks can span a continuum ranging from well-connected to poorly connected systems (Smith and Schwartz, 1984 ; Reeves et al. 2013 , 2023 ; Trullenque et al., 2016 ), although sparse networks where only a subset of fractures conduct the majority of fluid flow are more commonly reported (Matthäi et al., 2004 ; Zhang et al., 2013 ; Reeves et al., 2013 , 2014 ; Wu and Wong, 2013 ; Akara et al., 2022 ). In contrast, networks formed by volumetric contraction can be extremely well-connected, particularly for mature systems with columnar patterns where fracture spacing is controlled by the rate of cooling and size of the exposed surface. Unlike studies of tectonic fracture networks which are well represented in the literature, fluid flow and solute transport characteristics of volumetric contraction networks have received very little attention and remain largely unknown (Schultz, 1995 ; McGrail et al., 2006 ; Douglas et al., 2007 ; Burt et al., 2009 ; Fernandes et al., 2016 ). Volumetric contraction refers to a Mode I fracturing process (i.e., fracture displacement is normal to fracture walls) that can produce a series of irregular polygons within a solid medium due to loss of volume over time. This pattern is present in desiccation mudcracks (Goehring et al., 2010 ; Goehring, 2013 ; Miedema, 2015 ; Seghir et al., 2015 ; Shepidchenko, 2020 ), rocks that are initially deposited hot, such as basalt and rhyolite (Spry, 1962 ; Budkewitsch and Robin, 1994 ; Goehring, 2013 ; Charlier and Grove, 2012 ), patterned ground and polygonal terrain in permafrost subjected to freeze-thaw cycles (Goehring, 2013 ; Jan et al., 2017 , 2019 ; Painter et al., 2023 ), or any other solid that loses considerable volume over time. Patterned ground, polygonal terrain and volumetric contraction patterns have also been observed within craters on Mars (Milazzo et al., 2009 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ). Mechanisms of polygonal fracture formation are specific to both the medium and the set of conditions responsible for the volume loss (Goehring, 2013 ). The expression of these polygons describes a natural phenomenon that will occur anywhere a solid is losing volume. Columnar jointing in basalts is one of the more common volumetric contraction processes. For columnar jointing to occur, a singular and relatively instantaneous pulse of initially hot lava deposited over relatively flat terrain is required. Upon solidification, fracturing begins to occur as the basaltic unit cools and thermal contraction commences. The edges and top of the domain will cool first due to a large temperature gradient between the cooling rock unit, surrounding rock, and ambient air. The first fractures to form, denoted as master joints by Spry (1962) , originate along the outer edges of the rock unit and then propagate into the interior. These initial fractures are relatively long and straight. As the rock unit cools and fractures continue to propagate, triple junctions begin to form. This fracture configuration characterized by the intersection of three fractures at a specific point optimally releases the greatest amount of stress during the volumetric contraction process (Goehring, 2013 ). Over time, networks of fractures connected by triple junctions emerge (Spry, 1962 ; Degraff and Aydin, 1987 ; Budkewitsch and Robin, 1994 ). Ambient air temperatures create a much sharper thermal gradient at the most inwards part of the fractures compared to any other location on the outcrop. Stress is released through fracture propagation into the interior of the rock mass as the well-connected fracture pattern grows into the rock mass in intervals that can be expressed by a unit width. (Spry, 1962 ; Budkewitsch and Robin, 1994 ; Goehring and Morris, 2008 ; Lamur et al. 2018 ; Akiba et al., 2021 ). The order that individual fractures form during downward propagation varies for every triple junction in the network (Degraff and Aydin, 1987 ; Budkewitsch and Robin, 1994 ; Lamur et al., 2018 ; Akiba et al., 2021 ). This leads to the emergence of new fracture patterns during each successive downward fracture growth interval that deviates from the original fracture pattern (Kattenhorn, 2008 ). In situ field studies have been conducted in flood basalts, which commonly form columnar fracture systems, investigating the hydraulic properties of these systems (Newcomb et al., 1972 ; Barker and MacNish, 1976 ; Versey and Singh, 1982 ; Carahan, 1982 ; McGrail et al., 2006 ; Douglas et al., 2007 ; Burt et al., 2009 ; Fernandes et al., 2016 ). Most of this work investigated the connectivity of differing rock units with respect to aquifer recharge, map aquifer responses to differing pumping rates, assessing the potential for CO2  sequestration, and contaminant remediation. These studies are important for understanding hydraulic properties of the fractured basalt unit but largely ignore how volumetric contraction fracture patterns contribute to the measurements recorded. Secondary features, like a series of tectonically formed faults, often get more attention than the volumetric contraction networks themselves (Spane et al., 1985 ; Lavenue et al., 1986 ; Seitz et al., 1987 ; Schultz, 1995 ; Burt et al., 2009 ; McGrail et al., 2014 ). Fernandes et al. (2016)  concluded that columnar networks have little impact on fluid flow properties at a site located near Sao Paulo, Brazil due to the presence of mineral precipitates within the fractures. However, the minerals present within the fractures (silica, calcite, and zeolites) precipitate from groundwater indicating paleo circulation of groundwater within the volumetric contraction network (Bernhard and Barth-Wirsching, 2002 ; Lee et al., 2003 ; Drake et al., 2012 ). Characteristics of fluid flow in volumetric contraction networks have largely been ignored. To our knowledge, only four studies related to fluid flow in basaltic columnar networks are present in the literature with no studies investigating solute transport. Khaleel (1989)  numerically investigated length scales required to establish an equivalent hydraulic conductivity tensor using spatially consistent network patterns. Based on the network pattern and hydraulic properties used in their model, variations in the hydraulic conductivity tensor stabilized at a domain size of 30 m  × 30 m. Vasseur and Wadsworth (2019)  modeled a quasi-2D columnar basalt using regular hexagons in a grid comprised of four polygons in the x -direction and three polygons in the y- direction. Each polygon was bounded by fractures with symmetric triple junction intersections of 120° Enhanced fluid flow was found to occur in fractures aligned in the direction of flow with substantially less flow occurring in fractures perpendicular to the flow direction. Chao et al. (2020)  and Niu et al. (2023)  studied changes in bulk permeability as a function of dip angle for an artificially jointed columnar basalt with application to dam failure. The impact of irregular polygons and fracture aperture variability on regional solute transport has been neglected in all volumetric contraction hydrology studies. Several studies have demonstrated relationships between fracture properties, such as length, orientation, density and aperture, and resultant fluid flow and solute transport in poorly- to moderately-connected networks formed by tectonic stress (Smith and Schwartz, 1984 ; Reeves et al., 2008a , 2008b , 2013 ; Frampton and Cvetkovic 2011 ; Makedonska et al., 2016 ; Maillot et al., 2016 ). We hypothesize that such relationships with fluid flow and solute transport behavior must also exist for volumetric contraction networks for fracture properties denoted by aperture, column radii, triple junction geometry, and the presence or absence of more transmissive mega column fractures and their radii. The primary objective of this study is to systematically investigate the influences of mega columns and distributions of fracture aperture on the transport of conservative solutes. Large-scale, fully mature columnar basalt networks consistent with observations of natural volumetric contraction networks are numerically generated. A discrete fracture network (DFN) simulator is used to solve for fluid flow and track conservative particle trajectories through the networks. A total of 9 network parameterizations, encompassing variability in fracture aperture and mega column diameter, are used to identify how fracture properties influence ensemble fluid flow and solute transport. The organization of this paper details a conceptual model describing the formation of volumetric contraction networks, and the numerical framework used to generate columnar networks and simulate fluid flow and solute transport in Section 2; results from the evaluation of particle transport for all network types and their parameterization, contrasting results between volumetric contraction and tectonic networks, and study limitations in Section 3; and highlights major findings in Section 4 .  2 Methodology Fully mature volumetric contraction networks consistent with physical observations of columnar basalts are generated numerically and imported into a 2D DFN flow and particle tracking simulator. A total of 9 network parameterizations investigating aperture variability, the presence or absence of mega column fractures, and mega column radii, when present, are used to systematically characterize flow and transport properties. A Monte Carlo approach incorporated uncertainty in network geometry by generating 250 master network realizations. Transmissivity of fractures in the generated networks are then modified per the nine network parameterizations belonging to one of three network types (Table 1  ). Transport properties of the networks are assessed by analyzing ensemble particle breakthroughs and plume snapshots. 2.1 Model justification Two dominant conceptual models have been proposed to describe the formation of volumetric contraction networks and their evolution during cooling. One of them is the Budkewitsch-Robin (1994)  model of quasihexagonal joint formation which proposes that fractures migrate throughout the domain with time and network maturity. Immature networks exhibit irregular fracture junctions that divides the rock mass into irregular polygons. As the fractures migrate, it is assumed that all fractures in the domain maintain equal or near-equal apertures removing any memory of the early forming fractures in the network. This model describing network evolution and maturity appears to reasonably explain well-studied columnar basalt networks, like Giants Causeway in Ireland and Devils Postpile in California (Budkewitsch and Robin, 1994 ) (Fig. 1  a). However, observations from other columnar basalts indicate that this conceptual model is not universal (Spry, 1962 ; Müller, 1998 ; Moore, 2019 ; Akiba et al., 2021 ) (Fig. 1 b,c). The second conceptual model describes a hierarchal volumetric contraction pattern where early fracture patterns are preserved and later influence secondary fracturing at the column-scale. Master joints initially propagate within a rock unit, and once fully connected, form mega columns which are defined as polygons of substantially larger size than the average basalt column diameter (Spry, 1962 ). The boundaries of these mega columns are typically represented by large aperture fractures (Fig. 1 b,c). Mega column fracture orientation is often influenced by the geometry of the outer surfaces of the domain where the rock mass has the greatest strain, which in turn, controls the geometric orientation of all subsequent fractures (Spry, 1962 ). Stress created by cooling concentrates around the tip of previously formed fractures, and continued fracture growth releases this stress as opposed to the domain losing surface area (Akiba et al., 2021 ). As the domain continues to cool from the outside towards the inside, smaller polygons within the mega columns form later as a secondary volumetric contraction process (Fig. 1 b,c). Similar to the Budkewitsch-Robin model of quasihexagonal joint formation, a relatively well-connected fracture pattern dividing the rock unit into a series of irregular polygons eventually emerges (Spry, 1962 ; Peck and Minikami, 1968 ; Budkewitsch and Robin, 1994 ). Comparing these two conceptual models of volumetric contraction, Spry's model accounts for the hierarchy between larger polygons bounded by mega column fractures formed during the initial cooling stages, and smaller polygons bounded by shorter fractures formed at later cooling stages within the mega columns. The Budkewitsch-Robin model assumes all fractures will impact future fracture patterns equally and does not consider that initial fracture patterns may influence subsequent fracture growth; however, in some networks, early forming fractures are clearly preserved and serve as boundary conditions to the internal propagation of smaller polygons within the mega columns (Bohn et al., 2005 , 2005 ; Mal et al., 2005 ) (Fig. 1 ). The degree to which these features are expressed in volumetric contraction networks appears to be controlled by rates of cooling and subsequent fracture growth. Instead of parallel fracture propagation in outcrops retaining the original fracture orientation described by Spry (1962) , each period of downwards growth will contain altered fracture orientations as described by the Budkewitsch-Robin model. This process continuously alters the expression of triple junctions present within the outcrop with the geometry of the junctions taking the shape of a “T” or a “Y” creating jagged fracture surfaces. “T” junctions are commonly formed during the early stages of fracture propagation when a third fracture attempts to orthogonally intersect one of the preexisting fractures at a thermodynamically favorable 90° angle. “T” junctions are comprised of roughly 90°−90°−180° angles on the surface of the outcrop (Budkewitsch and Robin, 1994 ; Goehring, 2013 ). Over time and with successive downward fracture growth, fractures tend to from “Y” junctions with symmetric triple junctions where fractures are separated by three 120° angles. If the mega column structures are preserved, they will have greater apertures than smaller columns forming within the mega columns and serve as less tortuous, higher transmissivity pathways for fluid flow and solute migration. These mega column fractures are more likely to retain their original orientation during future periods of fracture growth. Downwards propagation of fractures within volumetric contraction networks have been found to extend 3–25 cm into the rock mass during cooling (Ryan and Sammis, 1978 ; Gray, 1986 ; Goehring and Morris, 2008 ; Tanner, 2013 ). The pattern of fractures in each interval of downwards growth will remain consistent as fracturing continues into the outcrop (Gray 1986 ). Angles between fractures at different depths can be measured and record the cooling history of the outcrop. Full network maturity is often reached after 15 growth intervals, typically extending through the upper 45–375 cm of the basalt unit (Gray, 1986 ; Goehring et al. 2010 ; Miedema, 2015 ). This network maturation process occupies a small percentage of a columnar basalt unit because a typical columnar basalt is tens of meters thick. Currently no code exists that can accurately model the immature region of any volumetric contraction network so the transport properties of these regions will remain unexplored. Once network maturity is achieved, fractures may deviate around a hypothetical central plane during each period of downwards growth (Fig. 2  a). Fig. 2 b,c illustrates a mature 3D network comprised of multiple horizontal slices of the same network with the same seed, i.e., initial Voronoi center locations. Each layer contains a unique fracture pattern represented by one growth interval downwards with similar fracture orientations at a network scale and roughly the same number of 120° angles (Fig. 2 b). Fracture orientations are slightly different for each period of downwards growth but retain similar orientations overall (Fig. 2 c). A representative network highlighting network scale fracture orientations for all intervals of downwards growth is highlighted in red. Within-fracture aperture variability will naturally occur in volumetric contraction networks similar to that found in tectonic networks, but has been shown to minimally impact flow and solute transport within fracture systems, (Makedonska et al., 2016 ).  2.2 Network generation and parameterization Two-dimensional volumetric contraction fracture networks are generated using a MATLAB code originally from the Qhull library using the methodology proposed by Brassel and Reif (1979) . The code does not explicitly model evolving stress fields and fracture propagation associated with volumetric contraction. Rather, volumetric contraction is emulated as a quasi-2D geometrical process where fracture height is undefined, and iterative changes in fracture patterns capture stages of the evolution of the network associated with each downward fracture growth interval. The final fully mature network utilized represents a 2D slice of a volumetric contraction network where the final fracture position is influenced by all the previously generated networks. Fig. 2 b shows a representative 3D network maturation process with multiple periods of downwards growth present. The fractures highlighted in red display the orientation of one iteration of fracture growth. The X-Y locations of the fractures highlighted in red are very similar to the fracture orientation of every interval of network growth indicating one slice of a 2D network can effectively model a 3D network. To generate each network, a series of Voronoi centers is initially placed on a 250 m  × 250 m grid. When placing the Voronoi centers, a circular region is generated with a radius of 1/100 the domain size where no new Voronoi center can be placed. Once all Voronoi centers are placed, a Voronoi diagram is generated and Voronoi centers are updated for each successive iteration. Delaunay triangulation ensures that each network iteration contains mature 120° fracture junctions creating symmetrical polygons (e.g., “Y” junctions) with the interior angle of each vertex being approximately equal. The distribution of Voronoi centers becomes more evenly dispersed at each successive iteration creating more mature networks. Once the code reaches its final iteration, the mature fracture network is output as a 2D map of the fracture pattern containing locations of each fracture segment. This process is repeated to generate a total of 250 statistically equivalent networks. Differences in spatial patterns of the fracture networks are created by randomizing initial locations of the Voronoi centers. A master set of 250 networks with an average radius of 2.5 m is generated by placing 8000 Voronoi centers within the model domain and performing 6 iterations to ensure full network maturity. Each of the final networks contain roughly 10,000 fractures that are either connected to other fractures or domain boundary, with individual fracture segments preserved as a series of points. All 9 parameter sets utilize this master set of networks and modify transmissivity assigned to individual fracture segments. This approach facilitates direct comparisons of each parameter set by holding network geometry constant (Reeves et al., 2023 ). Mega column fractures are mapped directly onto the networks after generation of a consistent mega column node pattern and identifying fractures that form the most direct path between these nodes. Base-case cubic law apertures of 250 μm, corresponding to a 2D transmissivity of 1.3 × 10−5  m2 /s, are initially assigned to all fractures within the 250 network realizations. Cubic law apertures of 1000 μm (transmissivity equal to 8.1 × 10−4 m2 /s) are assigned for the mega column fractures (when present) to provide a large (64 times) contrast with the non-mega column fracture apertures. The transmissivity values are determined assuming laminar flow between parallel plates (uniform aperture) over unit thickness or height of the columns according to the cubic law: T  = (ρg /12μ )b 3 , where b  is aperture and fluid properties density (ρ ) and viscosity (μ ) are expressed at standard temperature and pressure (Snow, 1965 ). A total of 3 network types are generated through the inclusion/exclusion of mega columns, varying mega column radii when present, and either holding transmissivity constant for all fractures or using a lognormal distribution over the fracture population (Table 1 ). Natural fractures commonly exhibit a lognormal distribution of transmissivity with a log10 σT   range of 0.5–1.0 (Paillet, 1998 ; Stigsson et al., 2001 ; Anderson et al., 2002a , 2002b ; Kozubowski et al., 2008 ; D.M. Reeves et al. 2013 ). This range of log10 σT   is used to vary transmissivity 5–8 orders of magnitude for both columnar and mega column fractures. Network type I is divided into 3 parameter sets each by modifying the logarithm of standard deviation in the distribution of transmissivity (log10 σT  ). Network type II maps mega column fractures with varying radii onto parameter set 1 (log10 σT   fixed at 0.0) while network type III maps mega column fractures with varying radii onto parameter set 3 (log10 σT   fixed at 1.0). Network type II and III required a mega column fracture pattern to be mapped onto preexisting master networks without modifying the orientation of the original fractures. Keeping the original fracture pattern ensures that any differences in breakthrough and plume behavior is caused by the modification of fracture transmissivity, not the modification of the fracture orientations. Mega column radius was determined by multiplying the original average radius of the network (2.5 m) by scalar value (4,6,8) ensuring that multiple small-column polygons would be present within the mega column. The scalar value describes the average number of small-column polygons that constitutes the radius of the mega column with smaller scalar values creating networks with a higher density of mega column fractures.  2.3 Fluid flow and conservative particle transport The DFN model described in Parashar and Reeves (2012)  is used to solve for fluid flow in the volumetric contraction networks. The head value at all interior nodes is calculated by combining Darcy's Law, Q  = −T •∇h , with the conservation of mass principle where Q  is the volumetric flow rate per unit fracture width normal to the flow direction (m2 /s), T  is the transmissivity of the fracture (m2 /s), and ∇h  is the hydraulic gradient. The minimal residual method (MINRES), similar to the conjugate method, iteratively solves these equations until an internal convergence criterion of 1 × 10−7  is met. Parashar and Reeves (2012)  numerically vetted and verified the DFN against using a diverse set of iterative matrix solvers in Minitab. A linear hydraulic gradient boundary condition of 0.01 is applied to the networks to induce a north-south flow direction (D.M. Reeves et al., 2013 ; Akara et al., 2021 ; Akara et al., 2022 ). The east and west boundaries have open flow conditions where the gradient is linearly propagated along each boundary. The 2D solution to flow assumes 1D line segments of unit width connected to nodes where hydraulic head is solved. Flow is linearly proportional to the product of transmissivity assigned to each fracture and head across the fracture. Thus, hydraulic attributes of the networks, including global flow and velocity, are solely captured by the distribution of transmissivity. The velocities in this model intended for comparative purposes rather than exact times of transport to a distant receptor. A total of 10,000 conservative particles are placed into all fracture intersections (nodes) located within a 100 m  × 8 m input box centered on the domain, and located 2 m downgradient from the upgradient domain boundary to eliminate the potential for boundary interference. On average, 89 fracture nodes are present within the source box region for all 250 network realizations. The particle tracking algorithm utilizes a Lagrangian approach to individually move each particle from node-to-node according to advection. At each node, the particle tracking algorithm flux weights each outflowing fracture segment to determine the exiting trajectory for each particle independently where P (Si  )=qi  /(∑qi  ) where P (Si  )=probability of particle entering a segment Si ,qi   is determined by the flux of the segment (Akara et al., 2021 ). Consistent with other DFN simulators, matrix diffusion is not simulated in the model (Schwartz and Smith, 1988 ; Benke and Painter, 2003 ; Hyman et al., 2015 ). The execution of all 250 DFN simulations for each parameter set required 8–16 h using a personal computer with an Intel(R) Core(TM) i7–10750H CPU @ 2.60 GHz 2.59 GHz processor. Ensemble breakthrough curves for particles exiting the bottom domain boundary are comprised of all 250 realizations. A quantile analysis similar to that used by Akara et al. (2021)  using quantiles of 5 %, 16 %, 84 %, and 95 % of particle breakthrough at the bottom of the model domain is used to examine the behavior of particle migration within the networks, where quantile pairs Q0.16 , Q0.84  describe the bulk behavior of the plume and Q0.05 , Q0.95  describe the leading and trailing plume edges. The distribution of these quantiles within individual realizations of the 250 network realization ensemble are illustrated as boxplots of median, interquartile range (IQR), 95 % confidence internals, and outlier values for each parameter set. Percentages of particles initially placed in mega columns (as opposed to columnar fractures) and exiting the domain through mega columns, and mean ensemble particle velocity also serve as quantitative metrics. Ensemble plume snapshots are generated by determining the normalized density of particles at every X-Y point on a fine grid.  2.4 Network validation A comprehensive set of validation checks were performed involving checking a subset of generated networks against hand drawn fractures to ensure consistency in nodal locations, column radius, and overall geometry. Consistency in nodal locations between the original MATLAB networks and the DFN flow and transport solver were used to verify that errors were not introduced in the workflow between the two codes verifying that the networks were mapped in the correct locations. Comparisons of nodal locations verified that mega column fractures are mapped at the correct locations. The postprocessor utilized to read in individual particle plume locations and boundary breakthroughs performed an additional check to ensure the assigned head convergence criterion of 1 × 107  in the DFN flow solution was satisfied for each realization. Fig. 3  a shows a representative fracture network realization comprised of small column fractures. The same network with mega column fractures mapped directly to the network is illustrated in Fig. 3 d. Figs. 3 b and 3 e display fluid flow through individual fractures for both networks with line thickness proportional to flow. Consistent with the findings of Vasseur and Wadsworth (2019) , the flow solutions indicate that fractures parallel to the direction of flow transmit more water than fractures perpendicular to the direction of flow. Thicker blue lines in Fig. 3 e confirms, as expected, greater flow in the designated mega column fractures regardless of orientation. Figs. 3 c and 3 f highlight changes in the spatial distribution of exit locations for the networks shown in Figs. 3 a and 3 d (without and with mega columns) using colored dots on the edges of the domain. The red and blue dots denote exit locations where greater than 75 particles or 75 particles or less leave the domain, respectively. Ensemble-averaged particle velocity within the domain is computed from exit times for all 10,000 particles over 250 realizations (Table 2  ).   3 Results and discussion Fluid flow and particle tracking results from a total of 9 parameter sets are organized into three network types that explore: (i) transmissivity variability in the small column fractures (type I), (ii) presence of mega columns and mega column radii (type II), and (iii) aperture variability for both small column and mega column fractures (type III). Ensemble particle breakthroughs at the downgradient model boundary for network types I-III (Fig. 4  ) and plume snapshots for selected parameter sets (Figs. 5-7    ) are used to systematically illustrate how these properties influence conservative particle transport. 3.1 Type I networks: network geometry and aperture variability Plume snapshots in type I networks (parameter sets 1–3) illustrate how the combination of network geometry and aperture variability influence transport properties of the networks in the absence of mega columns for 500, 1000, 1500 and 2500 days after particle release (Fig. 5 ). These very-well connected networks, comprised of short fractures intersecting mostly as triple junctions with an average length of 2.6 m (slightly longer than the 2.5 m average column radius), generate ensemble particle plumes with leading edges resembling Gaussian-densities and a pronounced trailing plume edge. All fractures in parameter set 1 networks are assigned the same transmissivity, and thus, longitudinal and transverse dispersion is an emergent phenomena as particles sample the velocity and orientation of each fracture segment. Particle breakthroughs from these networks exhibit the least amount of dispersion (Fig. 4 a). Given the constant transmissivity assigned to all fractures, the internal distribution of velocities within parameter set 1 networks arise as the linear gradient boundary condition propagates through the complex network structure. Fractures more strongly aligned with the hydraulic gradient conduct more flow, and hence, have greater velocities than weakly aligned fractures and is consistent with observations made by Vasseur and Wadsworth (2019)  (Fig. 3 b). The trailing plume edge reflects the initial source condition where particles are evenly applied to all fracture nodes within the input domain regardless of velocity. Placing particles into nodes connected to fractures of lower velocity results in significantly slower transport as these fracture segments serve as a ‘bottleneck’ that modulate transport. Influences of aperture variability on transport are explored by systematically increasing log10 σT   for parameter sets 2 and 3 to 0.5 and 1.0, respectively, from the parameter set 1 constant transmissivity case where log10 σT   = 0 (Table 1 ). As log10 σT   increases, growth of the leading plume edge and transverse dispersion noticeably increase, while the center of plume mass (bulk of the plume) migrates more slowly (Figs. 3 and 4 ). Peak particle breakthroughs at the downgradient boundary of the domain systematically decrease in both time and magnitude (indicating increased dispersion) with increases in log10 σT   (Fig. 4 a). The effect of increasing log10 σT   on ensemble-averaged particle velocity is also reflected in Table 2  for parameter set 1 (log10 σT   = 0, v  = 5.4 × 10−2  m/d), set 2 (log10 σT   = 0.5, v  = 5.2 × 10−2  m/d), and set 3 (log10 σT   = 1.0, v  = 4.8 × 10− 2 m/d). Ensemble-averaged network flow ranges from 5.5 - 6.0 m2 /d in a trend similar to that observed for particle velocity. Histograms and probability plots illustrating the distribution of global network flow for all network types are shown in Figures S1 and S2. These findings can be explained by the presence of preferential pathways of connected higher transmissivity fractures in some portions of the network, along with areas of lower transmissivity where particles must undergo more tortuous routes that generate larger transport times.
