The prevalence of both earlier and later breakthroughs at greater values of log10 σT   is shown in Figs. 3 a,b. Similar trends to these results were also observed in lattice bond network simulations with heterogeneous distributions of transmissivity (Fan and Reeves, 2023 ). The quantile analysis in Fig. 4 b further distinguishes the influence of aperture variability on particle transport for the bulk of the plume (Q0.16 ,Q0.84 ) and leading and trailing plume edges (Q0.05 ,Q0.95 ). If the plumes were fully Gaussian, pairs Q0.16 ,Q0.84  would describe 1σ  shift from the mean, where σ 2  represents the variance of particle displacement (Reeves et al., 2008a , 2008b ). Increasing values of log10 σT   from 0.5 to 1.0 delays the arrival of ensemble-averaged Q0.05  by 19 days, Q0.16  by 34 days, Q0.84  by 86 days, and Q0.95  by 90 days, and produces greater variation in interquartile range (IQR) (Table 3  ). This indicates that the random assignment of transmissivity values within the networks tend to reduce transport rates overall, despite the small subset of particles that migrate within higher transmissivity pathways and produce faster breakthroughs as log10 σT   increases. Parameter set 3 networks also have the greatest inter-realization variability in particle breakthroughs along the leading and trailing plume edges (as denoted by IQR for Q0.05 , Q0.95  in Table 3 ) with parameter set 1 networks having the least inter-realization variability (Fig. 4 b).  3.2 Type II networks: mega columns Type II networks are defined by the inclusion of mega column fractures. Both small column fractures and mega column fractures are assigned constant transmissivity given cubic law aperture values of 250 μm and 1000 μm, respectively (Table 1 ). Three parameter sets for type II networks explore both the presence of mega columns and the influence of mega column radii on particle transport, where parameter sets 4, 5, and 6 have mega column radii of 10, 15, and 20 m, respectively (Table 1 ). Each mega column pattern is generated externally from the networks and mapped onto existing fractures within the master set of 250 network realizations by assigning the higher transmissivity value (Fig. 3 d). Mean global flow values for type II networks range from 44 - 86 m2 /d (Table 2 ) with a distribution that is approximately normal (Figures S1 and S2). Instead of the symmetric, well-defined peaks in type I networks, breakthrough curves generated by type II networks exhibit three peaks (Fig. 4 c). The first peak consists of very-early time particle breakthroughs corresponding to those particles which are initially placed into mega column fractures and exclusively migrate within these preferential pathways until exiting the model domain. The percentage of particles initially placed in mega column fractures increases with decreasing values of mega column radii due to a higher density of mega column fractures (Table 2 ). Breakthrough times of the first peak within all type II networks are similar indicating that particles are transported downgradient at approximately the same rate of enhanced velocity. The second breakthrough peak in Fig. 4 c occurs for particles that were originally placed in smaller-column fractures, migrate to the mega column fractures, and are then transported exclusively in the mega column fractures until exiting the model domain. The third peak is comprised of particles that travel through a combination of smaller-column and mega column fractures and tend not to remain within the mega column fractures, unlike particles contributing to the first and second peaks. Decreases in mega column radii led to delays in the second and third breakthrough peaks (Fig. 4 c). These delays are attributed to a higher density of highly transmissive mega column fractures that increase both overall flow through the networks and velocities in nearby smaller-column fractures. Mega column radius also adds more variation between networks, especially for particles contributing to the late time tailing (Figs. 3 c,d). Type II quantile breakthrough times are an order of magnitude faster than the quantile breakthrough times of type I networks (Table 3 ). Q0.05  and Q0.16  breakthroughs, dominated by mega column fractures, vary by roughly 10 days with differing mega column radii with an IQR of approximately two days. Q0.84  and Q0.95  have more variation than network type I due to the interaction between mega column and non-mega column fractures. The observed trends will be different if dual-domain mass transfer of solutes between fractures and matrix was simulated. Differences in breakthrough times between the three peaks reflect the timescales particles travel through smaller-column fractures until reaching mega column fractures. Using mega column radii of 10 m (scalar multiplier of 4), 15 m (scalar multiplier of 6), and 20 m (scalar multiplier of 8), 11–31 % of the input nodes are occupied by mega column fractures (Table 2 ). Particles not placed directly in a mega column node are located between 2.8 and 8.0 m away from a mega column fracture, with positive correlations in breakthroughs observed between mega column radius and average distance to mega column nodes. Magnitudes of the three peaks are significantly influenced by mega column radii which control mega column density and the probability of particle placement either in or near a mega column fracture (Table 2 , Figure c). Approximately 12–25 % of the exit nodes are mega column fractures in type II networks, yet 83–89 % of the particles exited through these nodes depending on mega column radii. The high percentage of particles exiting the mega column nodes indicates that particles became concentrated in the mega column fractures when moving downgradient due to higher values of velocity in those fractures. The particle breakthrough behavior discussed above is also supported by observations of ensemble particle plumes. The density of mega column fractures increases at smaller mega column radii and acts as a barrier for the transverse growth of the plume at the input locations. The location of the leading edge of the plume is consistent within all parameter sets within type II networks, regardless of the assigned radius (Fig. 6 ). For the same transport times, a significantly higher percentage of particles move downgradient in parameter set 4 compared to parameter set 6 because the smaller mega column radius results in more high transmissivity pathways within the network. The center of plume mass has less distance to travel to intersect with a mega column allowing shorter residence time in lower velocity, small column fractures before entering a mega column (Table 2 ). Particle velocities decrease overall with increases in mega column radii due to longer travel distances to mega column fractures. This leads to more pronounced late time tailing of the larger mega column radius networks leading to slower particle velocities within the parameter set. The vast majority of particles within the type II networks exit the domain before any particles in the parameter set 1, type I networks (Fig. 4 c). This reflects the high transmissivity and transport velocity of the mega column fractures where ensembled average velocity for parameter sets 1–3 have a range of 4.8 × 10−2  m/d - 5.4 × 10−2  m/d and sets 4–6 have a range of 3.1 × 10−1  m/d-5.8 × 10−1  m/d (Table 2 ). The presence of mega columns in type II networks substantially increases longitudinal and transverse dispersion compared to type I networks as particles along the leading plume edge follow the mega column pattern. Late-time plume snapshots indicate higher particle mass in both small column and mega column fractures perpendicular to the flow direction. In the plume snapshots, each band of particles moves downgradient at 1 m/d which is consistent with the calculated mega column velocity of 0.9 m/d (Table 2 , Fig. 6 ).  3.3 Type III networks: mega columns and aperture variability Type III networks explore the influence of aperture variability on small column and mega column fractures. For each fracture type, a lognormal distribution based on cubic-law apertures of 250 μm and 1000 μm as a mean, and log10 σT   equal to 1.0 is used to randomly assign transmissivity values. Consistent with the progression of type II networks, mega column radii in parameter sets 7–9 incrementally increase from 10 m to 20 m. Thus, parameter sets 7–9 reflect the same mega column structure in sets 4–6 while simultaneously incorporating aperture variability. The distribution of global network flow suggests that a normal distribution fits all 250 networks with the mean DFN flow reducing from 66m2 /d to 32 m2 /d as parameter sets change from set 7 to set 9. Times of peak breakthrough for all type III networks approximately correspond to the third peak for type II networks, highlighting the decreased influence of the mega columns (Fig. 4 e). The first two peaks of type II networks disappear because the fast pathways associated with the leading edge of the plume are disrupted by lower transmissivity fractures. This would also occur if matrix porosity was simulated by allowing mass transfer of particles into and out of the rock polygons. On average, particle velocities associated with network type III are 24 % slower than type II networks due to the increased aperture variability. For type III networks, the average velocity of particles exiting from mega column fractures decreases by an average of 39 % from type II networks. Slightly less particles (3–5 %) exit the domain through mega column nodes (Table 2 ). Clearly, the broad continuum of transmissivity assigned to both smaller column and mega column fractures in the type III networks diminishes the role of mega column fractures in influencing large-scale transport behavior (Fig. 4 f). Breakthrough observations are also supported by comparing differences between ensemble plumes for type II and type III networks. The leading edge of plume for parameter set 9 migrates more slowly than parameter set 6 over the same amount of time (Fig. 7 ). This occurs because particles must exit the mega column fractures when low transmissivity fractures restrict flow. The edges and center of the plume for type III networks all have breakthrough times slower than type II networks with identical mega column radii, and the assigned log10 σT   to type III networks generated larger IQRs (Table 3 ). Consistent with type II networks, breakthrough times for type III networks are still an order of magnitude faster than type I. Within type III networks, increased mega column radii delayed the breakthrough time for all particles within the plume consistent with the observations of type II networks.  3.4 Flow and transport comparisons in volumetric contraction and tectonic networks Comparisons can be made noting similarities and differences in fluid flow and solute transport properties of columnar volumetric contraction and tectonic networks. Generally, tectonic fracture networks are more challenging to characterize due to greater spatial heterogeneity in fracture location, orientation, length, and connectivity than columnar volumetric contraction networks which tend to form very well-connected networks of vertical fractures that are restricted in length to column diameter and in height to the thickness of the rock unit. Unlike tectonic fractures that may exhibit a wider range of fracture interaction and intersection types (Dershowitz and Einstein, 1988 ; Peacock et al., 2018 ) resulting in erratic spatial connectivity that can vary both horizontally and vertically, volumetric contraction fractures terminate as triple junctions that maintain a high-level of horizontal connectivity. These differences can lead to challenges in intersecting dominant water bearing fractures by wells or horizontal hillslope drains in tectonic networks (D.M. Reeves et al., 2013 ). Hydraulic conductivity and transmissivity of tectonic fractures have been shown to range 5–8 orders of magnitude over a single site (Paillet, 1998 ; Stigsson et al., 2001 ; Anderson et al., 2002a , 2002b ; Kozubowski et al., 2008 ; D.M. Reeves et al. 2013 ). This caused by a wide range of apertures, particularly with respect for joints, which proportionally scale with fracture length (Schultz et al., 2008 ; R.A. 2013 ). Contrary to tectonic fractures, lengths of fractures in columnar volumetric contraction networks are restricted by column diameter. The combination of well-connectedness of volumetric networks and regular fracture length in columnar networks may imply that fracture aperture is less variable in these networks. However, the hierarchy between smaller column fractures and mega column fractures (Fig. 1 c) and the variance in hydraulic conductivity observed in the Hanford basalts show that similar ranges in hydraulic conductivity and transmissivity may also be present in volumetric contraction networks. Detailed tracer experiments are typically conducted in tectonic fracture systems that have been well characterized with care taken to isolate the system for greater tracer mass recovery (Hadermann and Heer, 1996 ; Winberg et al., 2000 ; Dershowitz et al., 2001 ; Andersson et al., 2002a , 2002b ; Kosakowski, 2004 ). These studies all show the critical role of molecular diffusion in promoting dual-domain mass transfer between fractures and unfractured matrix blocks. Currently, there have been no tracer tests conducted in columnar volumetric contraction networks for direct comparison. However, inferences may be made with respect to the role of molecular diffusion and network connectivity. For example, fracture spatial patterns are highly complex in tectonic networks resulting in broad distributions of sizes of the unfractured matrix blocks, whereas the high fracture connectivity, regular column diameter, and spatially similar pattern exhibited by volumetric contraction networks may simplify the modeling of diffusive processes to a characteristic matrix block size. The results of numerical simulations describing flow and transport properties of volumetric contraction networks do not vary greatly compared to similar studies based on characteristics of tectonically formed networks (Painter and Cvetkovic, 2005 ; Matthäi et al., 2009 ; Reeves et al., 2014a,b ; Wang et al., 2020 ; Akara et al., 2021 ). Fracture orientation, length, transmissivity, network density, and connectivity all directly play a role in the transport properties of these networks (Schwartz and Smith, 1988 ; Painter and Cvetkovic, 2005 ; Reeves et al., 2008a , 2008b ; Frampton and Cvetkovic, 2011 ; Maillot et al., 2016 ; Akara et al., 2021 ; Reeves et al., 2023 ). Unlike tectonic networks, volumetric contraction networks are well connected, fracture density is controlled by the small column radius and consistent through the entire domain, and fractures have similar lengths. Fracture orientation, density, and transmissivity are the dominant fracture attributes impacting flow and transport within volumetric contraction networks. Variation in fracture transmissivity, provided by the presence of mega columns or fracture aperture variation within smaller column fractures, creates preferential flow paths unlike tectonic networks where preferential flow paths reflect fracture connectivity.  3.5 Study implications Groundwater systems comprised of volumetric contraction networks are poorly studied, yet understanding flow patterns within these systems is extremely important for the remediation of contaminated sites, understanding the movement of nutrients essential to biological activity, and future extraterrestrial exploration where columnar basalts are more prevalent. Previous volumetric contraction studies on fluid movement through fractures utilized simple and idealized polygons due to ease of generation and solution of flow. However, irregular polygons more accurately reflect observations from natural volumetric contraction networks, and combined with larger network scales for network flow and contaminant migration, provide needed realism. Our simulations indicate that irregular polygonal geometry alters flow and transport properties of a network by disrupting the continuity of straight-line flow paths that are perfectly parallel to the direction of flow leading to perturbations in flow velocities and solute retention. Other factors, such as dual-domain mass transfer of solutes between fractures and matrix, paleo-orientation of the stress field, weathering history, mineral dissolution, and precipitation also play a role in the transport properties of these networks but are not captured in the model. These effects become even more pronounced when variability in fracture transmissivity is incorporated. Plutonium processing at the Hanford site in Washington, USA has resulted in radionuclide contamination within a series of horizontal, flood basalt units (Harvey, 2000 ). Fracture studies at this site have focused on basaltic units largely comprised of tectonic fractures (Spane et al., 1985 ; Lavenue et al., 1986 ; Seitz et al., 1987 ; Schultz, 1995 ; Burt et al., 2009 ; McGrail et al., 2014 ). The presence of columnar jointing has been briefly mentioned in several reports, but little work was dedicated towards characterizing their hydrogeologic properties, with the exception of pumping tests conducted within the columnar jointed zones within the Grand Rhonde basalt yielding hydraulic conductivity values ranging from 10−1  to 10−3  m/d (Newcomb et al., 1972 ; Carahan, 1982 ; Burt et al., 2009 ). This three order-of-magnitude range is consistent with the variability in hydraulic conductivity computed from global network flow (10 to 102  m/d) in our simulations (Table S1). Both sets of hydraulic conductivity values fall within the range of fractured basalt systems (Heath 1983 ; Domenico and Schwartz 1990 ), although the values at Hanford are more reflective of aquitard systems than the groundwater systems simulated in this study. Columnar basalt flow and transport properties have applications to aquifers on extraterrestrial planets. On planets like Mars, sedimentary rocks formed by natural hydraulic processes are unlikely to form because wind governs the movement of modern weathered grains (Favaro, 2020 ). Uncertainty exists about surface water being present and the location of these surface water bodies on Mars in the past potentially impacting the formation of volumetric contraction networks (Baker, 2001 ; Nazari-Sharabian et al., 2020 ; Jakosky, 2021 ). Regardless of the presence of surface water, volumetric contraction patterns seem to be abundant and common through the subsurface (Milazzo et al., 2009 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ). They have been observed on several crater edges and multiple columnar basalts appear to be stacked on top of each other. It is very likely that most Martian aquifers will have a volumetric contraction fracture pattern causing a strong influence on the flow and transport properties of these networks. There is potential to find life within these fracture networks on extraterrestrial planets due to how these fractures influence the movement of nutrients and how microbes respond to this influx of nutrients on Earth (Ross et al., 2001 ; Castegnier et al. 2006 ; Bochet et al., 2020 ; Cheng et al., 2021 , Kolbe et al., 2019 ). It is important to understand the flow and transport properties of these networks if sustainable water is to be achieved on another planet.   4 Conclusions This study explores the effects of mega columns and aperture variations (as transmissivity) on particle transport properties in large-scale volumetric contraction networks. Particle transport in a constant transmissivity network provided a basis for defining baseline dispersion attributed solely to network structure and connectivity, with the other 8 networks allowing for more detailed investigation into the role of mega column fractures and transmissivity variability on fluid flow and solute transport. Major findings of this study include:• Unlike tectonic networks, fracture orientation, density, and transmissivity are the dominant fracture attributes impacting flow and transport within volumetric contraction networks.  • Preferential flow paths in volumetric contraction networks emerge due to variance in fracture apertures, unlike tectonic networks where fracture connectivity controls the formation of preferential flow paths.  • Fracture connectivity and network structure contributes a baseline amount of dispersion that is then further enhanced by variations in fracture transmissivity and the presence of high-transmissivity mega column fractures.  • Mega column fractures when present serve as preferential pathways leading to faster breakthroughs and enhanced concentration of particles where roughly 80–90 % of particles exit the domain through mega column fractures.  • A binary distribution of transmissivity utilizing constant values for small column and mega column fractures illustrated three distinct particle pathways (fast, intermediate, slow) within the network; the majority of fast particle pathways were disrupted when a broad distribution of transmissivity is assigned to the networks.  • Smaller values of mega column radii lead to greater network-scale fluid flow and overall faster breakthroughs due to a higher density of these features.    Aside from this study, the authors are not aware of any research conducted on flow and transport properties of a volumetric contraction fracture network utilizing irregular polygons, leaving many aspects of this system uninvestigated. The full range of transport behavior in our simulations is likely not captured by our simulations given that fracture connectivity is expected to change at different stages of network maturity. Immature volumetric contraction models do not currently exist due to the increased complexity of modeling these networks compared to more mature networks. Mega column fractures are mapped ad-hoc onto an existing mature network which likely does not capture a more realistic pattern and connectivity between mega column and small column fractures. Finally, future work should also consider systems with permeable polygons. The authors intend to address these outstanding aspects of volumetric contraction networks in future studies. 1 Introduction Human activity influences largely the subsurface, and particularly the unsaturated vadose zone. This part of Earth located below the land surface and just above the water tables is most of the time only partially saturated with water. It plays a key role in hydrogeology, as the refilling of aquifers usually takes place in this part of the subsurface. The vadose zone can be impacted by pollution, coming from agriculture or industrial activities, which impairs the water resources. Furthermore, the water saturation level may vary, notably during periods of droughts or heavy rainfall. Therefore, it is crucial to be able to predict contaminant transport for various saturation conditions in the vadose zone. In contrast to unsaturated media, transport in heterogeneous, saturated porous media has been the subject of numerous studies, e.g reviewed in Dentz et al. (2011, 2023) . However, dispersion in unsaturated porous media still remains a significant research topic, notably because of the complex multiphase flow interactions with the porous structure, which are not yet fully understood. The difficulty lies in the fact that the volume of pores accessible to pollutants depends on the interaction of the non-miscible air/water flow with the porous medium. Indeed, the presence of air clusters induces a greater flow heterogeneity. As a result, the velocity field presents stagnant zones with very low velocities as well as preferential paths with high velocities (Jiménez-Martínez et al., 2015; Jiménez-Martínez et al., 2020; Leontidis et al., 2020 ). Flow, and consequently transport, will thus depend on both the saturation and the medium heterogeneity. In stagnant zones, transport is controlled by diffusion and is, therefore, very slow. Transport in the preferential paths, however, is mainly advective and much faster, leading to extreme solute displacements (Hasan et al., 2019 ). As a result, dispersion in unsaturated porous media is far more complex than in saturated ones. Further comprehension on the joint influence of the pore topology and the two-phase non-miscible air/water distribution on the macroscopic transport is crucial to fully understand dispersion phenomena in the unsaturated subsurface. A large number of experiments have been performed to determine the dispersion coefficient or the dispersivity in porous structures at various saturations. However, authors have different points of view on the influence of saturation on dispersion. Many authors note an increase of dispersion/dispersivity in unsaturated porous media, compared to saturated conditions (e.g. Bromly and Hinz, 2004; Maraqa et al., 1997; Nützmann et al., 2002; Haga et al., 1999 ), related to an increase in heterogeneity. In contrast, other works highlight non monotonic relations between the saturation and the dispersivity, or the dispersion coefficient (Padilla et al., 1999; Karadimitriou et al., 2016; Raoof et al., 2013 ). Few other articles show different tendencies from those mentioned above (e.g. Vanderborght and Vereecken, 2007; Birkholzer and Tsang, 1997 ). These discrepancies could be explained by the limited number of experiments, which leads to statistical incoherence; and by the different experimental approaches and different ways of interpreting the data. The determination of a constant dispersion coefficient also assumes that transport is Fickian, i.e. governed by a advection–diffusion equation (ADE). It is worth mentioning that Fickian regime is very frequently observed. Indeed, the central limit theorem states that transport becomes Fickian in an asymptotic regime if the variance of the displacement is finite. However, it has been shown that a Fickian transport model often fails to predict dispersion in unsaturated porous media (Bromly and Hinz, 2004; Triadis et al., 2018; Velásquez-Parra et al., 2022; Cortis and Berkowitz, 2004; Hasan et al., 2019; Dou et al., 2022 ). A key feature of Fickian transport is the linear growth of the second moment of the concentration field over time. Thus, the most convenient way to determine the Fickian nature of the transport is to analyse the time evolution of the second moment. Often non-Fickian behaviour is characterized by a power law time evolution of this moment, referred to as ‘anomalous’ dispersion (Berkowitz et al., 2000; Triadis et al., 2018; Velásquez-Parra et al., 2022; Talon et al., 2023c ). The main objective of this paper is therefore to assess and quantify the nature of transport in unsaturated porous media by analysing the temporal evolution of the second spatial moment. The effect of saturation on dispersion has been the subject of numerous studies. In particular, three-dimensional column experiments are often used to study dispersion in unsaturated sand, rock or soil samples (e.g. Maraqa et al., 1997; Haga et al., 1999; Padilla et al., 1999; Nützmann et al., 2002; Bromly and Hinz, 2004 ). In such configurations, due to the opacity of the samples, transport is often analysed using breakthrough curves (average concentration at the outlet). Dispersion in unsaturated porous media can also be studied by means of transparent micromodels. Indeed, micromodels allow direct visualization of the solid structure, two-phase distribution and concentration pattern. Dispersion is then determined from the spatial moments of the concentration profiles as well as the breakthrough curves (Bromly and Hinz, 2004; Hasan et al., 2019; Leontidis et al., 2020; Jiménez-Martínez et al., 2020 ). The first step in assessing the influence of saturation on the dispersion is to understand the spatial distribution of the immiscible phases. A simple way to generate realistic unsaturated porous media is to co-inject the two immiscible phases. Immiscible multiphase flow processes have been extensively studied using micromodel experiments (e.g. Zhang et al., 2000; Tallakstad et al., 2009; Chevalier et al., 2015; Kazemifar et al., 2015; Haque et al., 2021; Talon et al., 2023a ). Multiphase configurations mainly depend on the capillary number, on the saturation of each phase and on the flow history (Chevalier et al., 2015 ). Many tracer experiments have been performed in micromodels in either saturated (e.g. Wan et al., 1996; Corapcioglu et al., 1997; Watson et al., 2019 ) or unsaturated (e.g. Wan and Wilson, 1994; Karadimitriou and Hassanizadeh, 2012; Karadimitriou et al., 2016; Hasan et al., 2019; Leontidis et al., 2020; Jiménez-Martínez et al., 2020; Karadimitriou et al., 2017 ) conditions. However, transport experiments in micromodels are limited by several aspects. As dispersion tends to increase in unsaturated conditions, the micromodel size may not always be appropriate. Furthermore, as saturation decreases with flow rate, it is difficult to investigate a wide range of Peclet numbers (ratio of advection time to diffusion time) for a given saturation. In addition, as discussed in Leontidis et al. (2020), Jiménez-Martínez et al. (2017) , it is difficult to experimentally obtain neat tracer injection conditions due to the dispersion in the inlet tubing. Consequently, the experimental uncertainties compromise the analysis of the nature of dispersion. To overcome these difficulties, several authors have used numerical simulations. The critical factor for these simulations is to ensure an accurate representation of the immiscible phase distribution. Images can be obtained either experimentally or numerically (from two-phase flow simulations or machine learning methods) (Aziz et al., 2018; Jiménez-Martínez et al., 2020; Dou et al., 2022; Velásquez-Parra et al., 2022 ). The main disadvantage of numerical simulations is the high computational cost of solving the two-phase flow equations. However, numerical simulations allow a more accurate resolution of the transport equation with a neat inlet condition, a wider range of Peclet number and are less limited in size than experiments. Highly parallelizable Lattice Boltzmann simulations are commonly used to simulate flow and transport in complex porous media (Talon et al., 2012; Zaafouri et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024 ). Further understanding of the coupling between pore structure, immiscible phase distribution and transport requires a statistically relevant amount of data. Indeed, as the saturation decreases, heterogeneity becomes more important, as the air cluster size distribution widens. To address this augmented heterogeneity, one can either increase the sample size or the number of configurations with identical statistical properties. Jiménez-Martínez et al. (2020)  considered a machine learning approach based on multiple-point statistical simulations (MPS) (Straubhaar et al., 2020 ) to generate two-phase distributions in a given two-dimensional porous structure consisting of irregularly arranged spheres. The MPS approach, initially developed for geological modelling, makes it possible to generate images with complex features that are derived from a reference image, referred to as the Training Image (TI) and representing the expected structure. In this work, we extend the machine learning approach considered by Jiménez-Martinez et al. However, unlike Jiménez-Martinez et al. who only generate the air–water distribution for a given solid configuration, we use an MPS algorithm to generate both different solid and water/air configurations. The training images represent two fluid-phase distributions (air/water) in porous media obtained experimentally, when a steady state is reached and air clusters are immobile. By this approach, the coupling between saturation and pore topology can be easily studied for different structures. Moreover, this method allows a significant statistical analysis.  The article is structured as follows: we begin by presenting experiments on two-phase flow in a micromodel that represents a 2D natural rock formation. These experiments enable the acquisition of a training image database for different phase configurations. In the following section, we introduce the MPS algorithm used to generate the image database with various configurations and different saturations. Then, we will introduce the Lattice Boltzmann simulations performed to solve flow and transport in these images. Finally, we analyse the distribution of air and water in the porous medium as well as the dispersion, Fickian or non-Fickian, depending on the saturation and Peclet number.  2 Experimental and numerical methods In the following, we briefly present the experimental and numerical methods developed and their validation. Further details can be found in the Supplementary Information. 2.1 Multiphase flow in a micromodel This section provides an overview of the experiment conducted in an irregular porous glass micromodel to obtain air/water distributions at different saturations. To this end, we apply co-injection of air and water. We performed experiments at various fractional flow rates in order to obtain images at different saturations. We hereby present the micromodel structure and the experimental setup. 2.1.1 Experimental setup Micromodel. We use a glass micromodel with an inner etched irregular network. The dimensions of the micromodel are L  y   = 10  mm    wide by L  x   = 17  mm    long. The model is wet-etched with depth of L  z   = 40  μ m   . The interior model network is based on an image of a 2D slice of Bentheimer sandstone rock, obtained from X-ray tomography. It was modified to ensure percolation in 2D leading to a final porosity higher than the one of the original rock. The micromodel is presented in Fig. 1 a. The porous medium is characterized by a total number of 2600    grains. The average porosity of the micromodel is ϕ = 66  %    and the permeability including inlet and outlet tubings is 4.7 Darcy (taken from Yeates et al., 2020 ). The micromodel can be considered as strongly water wetting as it is made of glass.  Microfluidic set-up. The micromodel is connected to a Vinduum pump (delivering a continuous flow rate) at lateral inlets for water injection and to a Harvard syringe pump at the centre inlet for gas injection. The outlet is connected to the pressure and flow rate sensors. The gas used is ambient air and the liquid is MilliQ water. We used Parker Quink ink as tracer. The value of the diffusion coefficient at our experimental conditions is around 2 . 71 0  − 8    mm  2    s  − 1      following the measurement of Lee et al. (2004) . The micromodel is inserted in a holder and placed horizontally on the optical bench (avoiding gravity effects), above a flat dome red light with adjustable intensity. A high speed camera with a lens is placed above the system to visualize the air–water distributions. The camera JAI (SP-12000M-CXP4 model) provides a 12-megapixel monochrome resolution (4096 × 3072 pixel), the full-field framerate is 189 frames per second (fps). The acquisition is performed by the Hiris software. The experimental setup is presented in Fig. 1 b. The pressure drop of the water phase is measured to determine the permeability of the system. The room temperature was regulated at 21°C.  Co-injection experiments. The objective of the experimental part is to obtain a homogeneous distribution of trapped air clusters in the micromodel at different water saturations. To this goal, we chose to inject air and water simultaneously in the micromodel at different fractional flow rates, resulting in uniform distributions of the air and the water phase in the micromodel. Modifying the fractional flow rate between air and water results in different water saturations at steady state. The flow rates were in the range of 0 . 1  μ L  min  − 1      and 1  mL  min  − 1     . Co-injection is not maintained over a long period of time but is stopped once the air distribution reaches a steady state after several seconds. Then we preform the transport experiment. Please note that similar experimental protocols were used for example in Tallakstad et al. (2009), Chevalier et al. (2015), Talon et al. (2023b), Anastasiou et al. (2024)  providing a deeper analysis of the two-phase distribution resulting from a co-injection procedure.  Image processing. The solid, air and water phases are distinguished through segmentation of the images using a thresholding technique. Each phase is then associated to a specific grey level. Fig. 2  shows the original two-phase distribution in the micromodel (a) and the segmented image (b). Further details on the image segmentation can be found in the Supplemental Information (SI). The segmented image is analysed using the ImageJ Analyse Particles tool to obtain structure properties: grain and air cluster size as well as shape characteristics. Pore size distribution is computed using ImageJ plugin for Watershed separation on the binarized porous structure.     2.1.2 Characterization of non-fickian dispersion with spatial moments Fractional dispersion has been introduced to describe anomalous dispersion where the spatial and/or temporal moments vary according to a power law (e.g. Benson et al., 2000; Cushman and Ginn, 2000 ). For example, it can be associated with random walk models such as the Levy walk and Levy flights, which are characterized by broad distributions of temporal or spatial random steps (Meerschaert et al., 1999, 2002; Metzler and Klafter, 2000 ). To characterize non-Fickian dispersion, we determine the temporal evolution of the second spatial moment (see Supplemental Information). We then fit the second moment with a power law with exponent α   and a fractional dispersion coefficient D  α  f r a c    : (1) σ  f i t  2   = D  α  f r a c   t  α   .     The coefficient α   characterizes the nature of dispersion. If α   is close to 1  , dispersion is Fickian, it is non-Fickian otherwise. D  α  f r a c     quantifies the magnitude of the dispersion (Fickian or not). However, it is worth noting that comparing different values of D  α  f r a c     is meaningless as soon as α   is different. For this reason, when comparing the evolution of D  α  f r a c     for different parameters (Peclet number P e   , S  ), we are led to impose α  .   2.2 Flow and transport equations We treat the non-wetting phase as immobile because we assume that the flow rate for the tracer experiment is small enough not to displace the gas. Considering higher flow rates would require the use of a two-phase flow solver, which has a much higher computational cost. Consequently, we treat the gas as solid and consider flow and transport only in the water phase. In the following, we first detail the flow and transport equations solved in order to obtain the velocity and concentration field for each configuration. We then briefly present the numerical method used for the resolution of the equations. Finally, we present a comparison between experimental and numerical data. Flow equation. The local velocity field u   in the fluid phase is computed by solving the Darcy–Brinkman equation (Brinkman, 1947 ): (2) − ρ ν  k   u − ∇ P + ρ ν ∇  2   u = 0 ,     where ρ   is the density of the fluid, ν   represents the kinematic viscosity and P   is the pressure. The Darcy–Brinkman equation is used to compute the depth-average velocity. This allows to describe a 3D velocity field with a 2D equation as demonstrated by Zeng et al. (2003) . The permeability k   can be computed from the depth as k = L  z    2   / 12   . Physically, the Laplacian term models the transverse diffusion of momentum. It can be used, for example, to describe the boundary layer introduced by the no-slip condition at the wall. In principle, the viscosity in front of the Laplacian should be slightly different from that in the Darcy term (Zeng et al., 2003 ). However, in our case the permeability is so low that the boundary layer is very small and therefore has almost no effect on the dispersion (Jarrige et al., 2010; Soulaine et al., 2021 ). For simplicity, we have chosen to assume that the two viscosities are equal. And for the same reason, we assume a no-slip condition at the air–water interface.  Advection–diffusion-equation. Transport is simulated by solving the local advection–diffusion equation given by (3) ∂ c  ∂ t   + u ⋅ ∇ c − D  m   Δ c = 0 ,     where c   is the solute concentration in the fluid, u   the local velocity vector obtained from the resolution of the Darcy–Brinkman equation and D  m     the molecular diffusion coefficient. Similar to previous work, Jiménez-Martínez et al. (2020) , we use a constant diffusion coefficient here. We note however that because the flow profile is not homogeneous in the depth, one should expect that the local flow velocity increases the local dispersion coefficient (Taylor dispersion). By neglecting this effect, we thus assume that the molecular diffusion is dominant over advection at the scale of the gap depth (see also Soulaine et al., 2021 ). Indeed, the Peclet number defined with the depth is lower than the one defined using the pore diameter.  Lattice Boltzmann simulations. Two-Relaxation-Time Lattice (TRT) Boltzmann simulations were used to solve Eqs. (2) and (3)  to obtain the flow and concentration field in the porous structures. Details on Lattice Boltzmann schemes for the resolution of Eqs. (2) and (3)  and the applied boundary conditions are provided in the Supplemental Information file or can be found in Ginzburg et al. (2015), Ginzburg (2012) . Parameters chosen for the simulation can also be found in the Supplemental Information file. LB computations were performed by adapting the open framework software Walberla (Bauer et al., 2021; Godenschwager et al., 2013 ).   2.3 Comparison of experiments and simulations We consider continuous tracer injection starting at a specific time t = 0   , where molecules are injected at the inlet. Fig. 3  shows an image of the micromodel with the three phases (water, air, solid), the porous structure on which simulations are performed (supposing that the gas behaves as the solid), the velocity field in the fluid phase and the concentration field.  We evaluate the influence of these simulation assumptions on transport and the suitability of the method for studying transport in unsaturated micromodels. This is achieved by performing a comparative analysis between the experimental work and Lattice Boltzmann simulations for three different saturations as shown in Fig. 4 . Since the numerical and experimental injection conditions are not the same, the comparison requires to shift the origin of time and position. Notably, as the front is more dispersed in the experiments, a position relative to the real position in the experimental case is defined with an offset subtracted to compensate for the spreading at the inlet. Qualitative agreement is then observed, in particular the preferential paths and stagnant, dead end zones are fairly well reproduced. To be more quantitative, we plot the experimental and numerical concentration profiles (see Fig. 5 a–c) at different time. As can be seen, there is an agreement between the two profiles that persists over time. This agreement is then confirmed by comparing the time evolution of the second moment of the profiles in Fig. 5 d. However, there is a difference at long times for low saturations. This is due to the high degree of heterogeneity within the system, that is reflected in the concentration profile. It is important to acknowledge that this heterogeneity represents the main challenge in understanding transport in unsaturated porous media. Consequently, the system might not be inherently representative, as the size of the micromodel may be insufficient to achieve a smooth enough signal. As mentioned in the introduction, one way to overcome this difficulty consists in generating a large number of different synthetic but realistic porous media with the adequate characteristics to capture the transport behaviour. We propose here to investigate the use of the MPS algorithm to generate such images. Another way consists in increasing the size of the system, which is unfortunately more time consuming.     2.4 Generation of unsaturated, artificial porous media: multiple-point statistics modelling (MPS) In order to generate unsaturated, artificial porous media having the same structural and statistical properties as the experimental ones, we apply here the multi-scale MPS algorithm described in Gardet et al. (2016), Gardet (2014), Doligez et al. (2015), Gardet and LeRavalec (2014)  to the experimental images. MPS algorithms allow to generate images with complex shapes and structures. Their leading idea consists in retrieving information about the desired shape, spatial distribution and connection of the objects from a training image (TI), that represents a model of the expected structure. This information is then used to fill iteratively the simulation grid, resulting in a synthetic medium with a spatial distribution based on the previous characteristics. Further details on the multi-scale MPS algorithm used in this work can be found in the Supplemental Information. The MPS algorithm is applied here with training images derived from experiments and consisting of two-fluid-phase distributions (air/ water) in porous media. The training images considered here are not the experimental images, but cleaned versions of these images obtained by removing non-physical artefacts resulting from the image processing, such as some air clusters completely enveloping grains or water contained in grains. Elements of small size whose effect on the flow is negligible are also suppressed. As detailed in the Supplementary Information, the MPS algorithm parameters are chosen as a trade-off between the simulation time and the quality of the results. The generated images present small defects that are not physical: discontinuities of the different phases, absence of water meniscus between grains and air clusters, inclusions in grains or air clusters. These defects may be lessen with other configuration parameters for the MPS algorithm, but at the cost of longer simulation times. Instead, we apply here a post-processing algorithm to the generated images to suppress these defects (see Supplemental Information). 2.4.1 Validation of the MPS algorithm method for flow and transport in MPS generated images The quality of the resulting generated images was assessed on three different saturation values (S  w   = 1 ,   S  w   = 0 . 87    and S  w   = 0 . 70   ). We conducted a comparison of various structural characteristics between the experimental and the MPS generated images. These characteristics include the distribution of pores and throats, as well as the size distribution of air clusters. The MPS algorithm proved to be effective in accurately replicating the structural properties of unsaturated porous media as discussed in the Supplemental Information. In addition, we compared flow and transport properties of the generated structures and the experimental ones. To this goal, we simulated the velocity and concentration fields using the Lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) described above. As presented in the Supplemental Information, the velocity fields show a very good agreement. Furthermore, Fig. 6  shows the concentration fields in the experimental and generated images for three saturations. The patterns of dispersion, such as the preferential flow paths and the stagnant dead end zones, are correctly reproduced for the three saturations. Also, the transport properties, characterized by the concentration profiles and the second moment of the dispersion, showed a very good agreement as well (see Supplemental Information file). In summary, the dispersion behaviour showed consistency between the generated and experimental porous media over all investigated saturation levels. The methodology presented in this study provides a valuable means of investigating dispersion in unsaturated porous media over a wide range of saturations, including different phase configurations and porous media sizes.      3 Numerical results 3.1 Image datasets By conducting multiphase flow experiments, we obtained phase distributions from co-injection, covering a saturation range from 0.55 to 1  . Our dataset resulting from experiments consists of 25    images. From this dataset, we extracted sub-images, called “training images” (TI) to generate new realizations. Using a sufficiently large number of training images, we can create a training image dataset that covers the various phase configurations present in the micromodel and takes into account their inherent variability. As explained above, two different approaches are employed to deal with the heterogeneity of the unsaturated porous media. We can either analyse a large number of small generated images, or we can analyse one single, larger image. This results in two different sets of data: • The “small size” dataset: This dataset comprises images that are approximately equivalent in size to the micromodel (L  y    ∗   = 1980    pixels, L  x    ∗   = 3780    pixels or L  y   = 0 . 90    cm, L  x   = 1 . 73    cm). To capture the system’s variability, we generate multiple realizations from each training image. This dataset enables us to study short-term dispersion phenomena within a computationally feasible time-frame.  • The “large size” dataset: the images within this dataset are approximately four times longer (L  y    ∗   = 1980    pixels, L  x    ∗   = 18000    pixels, or L  y   = 0 . 90    cm and L  x   = 8 . 3    cm). However, due to their larger dimensions, simulating flow and transport in these images involves significantly higher computational costs (9000    processors were used in this case, compared to 180    for the shorter images). Therefore, only a limited number of these longer images was used.     3.2 Influence of water saturation on flow properties (small size dataset) In this section, we investigate the influence of saturation on the flow properties, such as permeability, tortuosity and velocity distribution which are computed from the velocity fields (see Fig. 7 ).   3.2.1 Permeability Considering the fact that many permeability models incorporate the water content as a parameter, we define θ = ϕ S  w      to allow comparisons, where ϕ = 0 . 66    is constant. Fig. 8 a illustrates the evolution of the effective permeability k k  r   ( S  w   )    , where k  r     is the relative permeability corresponding to the water content θ  . k k  r      increases as the water content, or saturation, increases. In the fully saturated medium (S  w   = 1   , θ = ϕ = 0 . 66   ), the permeability equals 20    Darcy. As the saturation decreases to its minimal value (S  w   = 0 . 55    and θ = 0 . 40   ), the relative permeability tends to zero. Please note, that in this case, the effective permeability of the fully saturated micromodel is much higher than values provided in the Experimental setup. This is due to the fact, that inlet and outlet tubings included in the experimental acquisition of the permeability reduce the latter. Numerous experimental and numerical studies have extensively explored the relationship between porosity, water content and permeability in saturated and unsaturated media (see for instance Bear, 1988; Dullien, 1991 ). Many of them propose a power law relationship with the porosity or the saturation (e.g. Brooks, 1965; Bernabé and Maineult, 2015 ). Because the effective permeability tends to zero for a non zero value of water content, we fit our data using the following relation: k k  r   = R ( θ − θ  0   )   c     , with R = 153   , c = 2 . 2   , and θ  0   = 0 . 3   . And thus (4) k k  r   ( S  w   )  = R ϕ  c   ( S  w   − S  0   )   c   ,     with S  0   = θ  0   / ϕ   . In summary, the evolution of the effective permeability of the medium is consistent with certain classical models that establish the relationship between permeability and porosity in experimental systems. Consequently, the effective permeability k k  r      of the generated images can be modelled by empirical laws with physical parameters.    3.2.2 Tortuosity Tortuosity quantifies the complexity of the flow paths within the porous material. A simple approach to calculate tortuosity is as follows: τ = 〈 | u |  〉   〈 | u  x   |  〉      , where | u |    is the velocity norm and 〈 | u  x   |  〉    is the average streamwise velocity component. In Fig. 8 b we show that tortuosity decreases with increasing saturation, suggesting that flow paths become more tortuous at low saturations, which can be observed from the velocity fields shown in Fig. 7 . At lower saturations (or water content) the tortuosity reaches a value of 1.4, indicating that the transverse and longitudinal velocities are of the same order of magnitude. Here again, there is a lack of consistency in models that incorporate the connection between tortuosity and saturation. However, numerous models exist to explain the relationship between tortuosity and porosity (see Ghanbarian et al., 2013  for more information), among them logarithmic models as for example proposed by Koponen et al. (1996) . We applied this logarithmic model to fit our data: (5) τ = 1 − p ln θ ,     with p = 0 . 43   . In summary, the evolution of flow tortuosity aligns with classical models that describe the relationship between tortuosity and porosity in experimental model systems. We remind that we include the gas in the definition of porosity (water content).  3.2.3 Flow velocity distribution In Fig. 9 a, the distribution of normalized velocity, | u |  / 〈 | u |  〉    , is plotted for various saturation values. It is observed that as the saturation decreases, the velocity distribution becomes wider, and the tail of the distribution extends towards lower velocities. This widening suggests the formation and expansion of dead-end regions within the medium. Notably, at lower saturation levels, a second peak emerges at very low velocities (| u |  / 〈 | u |  〉  ∼ 1 0  − 5     ), indicating the presence of nearly stagnant zones in the flow. Additionally, there is a spreading towards high velocities with increasing saturation, especially below S  w   = 0 . 70   . These high velocities arise from the formation of preferential paths with high velocity. This flow heterogeneity can be quantified using the velocity standard deviation σ  u    . Fig. 9 b reveals that the standard deviation decreases as the saturation increases. For the lowest saturation values, the standard deviation is approximately three times higher than that in saturated conditions. The velocity standard deviation can be reasonably fitted with a power law: (6) σ  u   ≃ a S  w  c   + b     with ( a , b , c )  = ( 0 . 62 , 0 . 02 , − 1 . 8 )    .      3.3 Effect of water saturation and peclet number on transport (small size dataset) We perform LBM simulations on MPS generated images, covering the experimental range of saturation [ 0 . 55 , 1 ]    and explore the following range of Peclet numbers: P e ∈ [ 0 . 001 , 1000 ]    , where the Peclet number is defined as (7) P e = 〈 | u |  〉  d  pore    D  m     .     〈 | u |  〉    is the mean local velocity, d  pore     the mean pore diameter of the porous medium and D  m     the molecular diffusion coefficient.   3.3.1 Effect of saturation on dispersion Fig. 10  shows the time evolution of the concentration fields for different saturations and P e = 100   . At full saturation the concentration front is relatively flat. As the saturation decreases, the front becomes more heterogeneous and spreads faster with time. In particular, preferential flow paths and dead end zones become more pronounced. We characterize dispersion by the second moment as a function of time, as shown in Fig. 11 a. For this Peclet number, we observe that the second moment is not proportional to time, in saturated and unsaturated conditions. The dispersion is therefore non-Fickian for any saturation. To quantify the dispersion magnitude, we compute the mean of the power law coefficient α   for all the realizations and saturations, which is equal to 〈 α 〉  = 1 . 5   . We then compute the fractional dispersion coefficient with this exponent using Eq. (1) . Results are presented in Fig. 11 b. The fractional dispersion coefficient increases by more than a decade as the saturation decreases from S  w   = 1    to S  w   = 0 . 55   . Roughly speaking, the decay follows an exponential trend for the unsaturated cases, with a small inflection around S  w   = 1   . This trend is consistent with the observation in 3D porous media by Padilla et al. (1999), Sato et al. (2003) , although these authors fit their data with a function different from ours (power law decay).  3.3.2 Effect of the peclet number on dispersion In this section, we explore the influence of the Peclet number on dispersion, starting with saturated conditions followed by unsaturated conditions. Saturated medium. Fig. 12  illustrates how the power law index α   evolves with the Peclet number. At high Peclet numbers, α   exceeds one (∼ 1 . 4   ) and decreases as the value of the Peclet number decreases. The exponent reaches 1   for Peclet numbers less than one. In other words, for high Peclet numbers, the dispersion is dominated by advection, leading to non-Fickian behaviour. The non-Fickian character slowly diminishes with decreasing Peclet number as diffusion becomes more effective. When diffusion and advection are of the same order (P e ∈ [ 1 , 10 ]    ), α   reaches 1   (Fickian transport). We also compute the pure diffusion case (P e = 0   ) and observe, as expected, that the transport is Fickian (α = 1   ) and the value of the dispersion is below the molecular diffusion coefficient, allowing to define a diffusive tortuosity τ  d   = 1  D  ∗   ( P e = 0 )    = 2 . 15   . The effect of Peclet number on dispersion has been thoroughly studied in the literature for saturated porous media (Perkins and Johnston, 1963; Fried and Combarnous, 1971; Mostaghimi et al., 2010 ). Most of these studies report the evolution of the dispersion coefficient, i.e  assuming Fickian transport α = 1   , as a function of the Peclet number. For comparison, we thus compute in Fig. 12  a normalized effective dispersion coefficient, imposing α  i m p o s e d   = 1   : D  ∗   = D  α = 1  f r a c   / D  m     . For high Peclet number values, D  ∗     is approximately proportional to the Peclet number. As the Peclet number decreases, D  ∗     slowly converges to a constant value smaller than 1  . This evolution with the Peclet number is thus in good agreement with the literature. In conclusion, we have shown that while the evolution of the dispersion coefficient with the Peclet number is qualitatively consistent with the literature, the transport deviates from the Fickian one for P e ≳ 10   . In this range, the value of α   rises above 1  .  Unsaturated medium.  We now examine the influence of the Peclet number on α   and D  ∗   = D  α = 1  f r a c   / D  m      for different saturations. Fig. 13 a displays how the exponent α   changes as the Peclet number varies. For all saturations we observe a similar dependence on the Peclet number as in the saturated case. Namely, there is a transition from Fickian behaviour (α = 1   ) at low P e    to non-Fickian behaviour (α ∼ 1 . 4   ) at higher Peclet number. However, we note that the Peclet number of the transition depends on the saturation, with the transition occurring at lower P e    (almost two decades) for the lowest saturation. Also, for lower saturations, the transition is stiffer. Fig. 13 b shows the evolution of the normalized effective dispersion coefficient D  ∗     (α = 1   ) with the Peclet number. Similarly to the saturated case, the dispersion coefficient increases with the Peclet number. As for the saturated case the dispersion coefficient is constant for low Peclet number. At a given Peclet number, D  ∗     starts to increases with the onset of the transition depending on the saturation. For lower saturation, the onset occurs at a significantly lower value of the Peclet number. For a given Peclet number, D  ∗     is therefore higher at lower saturation. Interestingly, the onset of the transition for α   and D  ∗     is of the same order of magnitude of Peclet number. Note that the value of D  ∗     in purely diffusive conditions (P e = 0   , straight line in Fig. 13 ) decreases with reducing saturation: the diffusive tortuosity of the medium thus rises with saturation.   Fig. 14  shows the evolution of α   with saturation for different, specific Peclet numbers. For high Peclet numbers, α   is relatively independent of saturation, but as the Peclet number decreases, the dependency becomes more pronounced. In 2D regular structures, Velásquez-Parra et al. (2022)  observed a transition from Fickian to non-Fickian behaviour with decreasing water saturation. 3D transport experiments using NMR imaging in homogeneous rock with various degrees of saturation (Guillon et al., 2013 ) show non-Fickian dispersion even in saturated conditions, with a non-Fickian character enhanced by lower saturations. Our results are therefore representative of a general tendency and most likely not constraint by the geometry of the porous media. As discussed in the introduction, similar micromodel transport experiments have been performed by Jiménez-Martínez et al. (2015), Jiménez-Martínez et al. (2017, 2020), Ben-Noah et al. (2023)  using cylindrical pillars of different diameters. Although they observed non-Fickian transport for the unsaturated case, the exponent α   is difficult to compare quantitatively. For example, ballistic behaviour (α = 2   ) was observed in Jiménez-Martínez et al. (2017) , whereas in our case α   is below 1.5 even at high Peclet number. This difference could be attributed to the porous structure of the micromodel, which strongly influences the immiscible distribution. To conclude, dispersion is non-Fickian for a larger range of Peclet numbers in unsaturated conditions. At high Peclet number, transport is dominated by advection even in saturated conditions and transport is non-Fickian. For intermediate Peclet number, dispersion is Fickian only for high saturations but not for smaller saturations. For sufficiently low Peclet numbers, dispersion is dominated by diffusion and becomes Fickian even for the lowest saturations.    3.4 Large size dataset simulations In the previous section, we observed a non-Fickian behaviour for a large range of parameters. However, it is worth recalling that asymptotic non-Fickian behaviour is only expected for non-finite variance of the velocity distribution. As shown in Fig. 9 , the variance of the velocity field increases with decreasing saturation while remaining finite. This means that one should expect the dispersion to be Fickian in an asymptotic regime, suggesting that the observed non-Fickian regime would only be transient. For this reason, we performed several simulations with a very large domain as described above. Fig. 15 a shows the variance as function of time for five different saturations with an intermediate Peclet number, P e = 5   . The evolution of the variance confirms the non-Fickian tendency over longer times, but no change in the temporal behaviour (e.g. transition to the asymptotic regime) was observed for any saturation. We conclude that our domain is still too short to reach an asymptotic regime. However, since the exponents α   in the large size domain (Fig. 15 b) and the smaller one are similar (α   increases with decreasing saturation), it indicates that the small size samples are large enough and more efficient for quantifying the transport properties in partially saturated porous media.     4 Conclusions and discussion In this article we investigated passive transport phenomena in two-dimensional unsaturated porous media coupling experiments and numerical simulations. Two-phase distributions (air/water) for different saturations were obtained by means of co-injection experiments in a micromodel reproducing the topology of a Bentheimer sandstone. From these experimental images, we generated new images using a multi-scale MPS algorithm. Using Lattice Boltzmann method, we computed velocity and concentration fields in both experimental and generated images, for saturated and unsaturated conditions. We showed that the velocity distributions were very similar. The concentration profiles were in very good agreement and the variance indicates that the dispersion characteristics of the experimental images are well reproduced by the MPS images. Consequently, MPS allowed the generation of a large number of unsaturated porous media images having a new topology but similar properties. For a large number of samples covering the saturation range between 0.55 and 1  , we computed transport for different Peclet numbers. The main result of this study is the observation of non-Fickian behaviour for a wide range of these parameters. This behaviour is characterized by a variance that increases with time according to a power law with an exponent α  . We have determined the evolution of this exponent as a function of saturation and Peclet number. Overall, α   increases with decreasing saturation due to the increase in flow heterogeneity, and increases with the Peclet number. This behaviour has been confirmed by large size simulations. However, these large size domain simulations did not exhibit the expected transition to a Fickian regime. As discussed in the introduction, the physical origin of anomalous transport lies in the strong heterogeneity of velocity field and residence time (see also Ben-Noah et al., 2023 ). It is therefore not surprising to find that decreasing the water saturation enhances anomalous behaviour, as it increases both the extent of the velocity distribution, but also the number of stagnant zones. What is more interesting, however, is the fact, that while saturation greatly increases the prefactor of the power law D  ∗    , it changes only slightly the exponent α   (around 1.5 at high Peclet number). The exponent seems to depend mainly on the Peclet number: 1   for low values and 1.5 for high values. In fact, diffusion increases the exchange rate between different velocity zones. Reducing the Peclet number therefore decreases the effects of extreme velocity values and thus favours normal transport. However, we observe that decreasing saturation shifts the Peclet number value of the transition by increasing the extent of the high and low velocity zones. We also note, that, while the α   exponent in our case becomes relatively constant for high Peclet number, other studies in different geometries show higher exponents (Jiménez-Martínez et al., 2017; Triadis et al., 2018; Velásquez-Parra et al., 2022 ). This suggests that the exponent value may depend on the geometry of the porous structure. There are several ways to extend this study. First of all, it would be worthwhile to repeat this method for 3D geometry. If 3D X-ray tomography allows the determination of air and water distribution in natural media, the main drawback is the small sample size. A 3D MPS algorithm could therefore be used to generate many other configurations to perform statistical analysis on more realistic rock. This would also allow lower saturation values to be investigated. Another possible direction could be to analyse more carefully the origin of the non-Fickian regime. For example, one could use the CTRW framework to determine the resident time distribution. One possible outcome of such approach would be the estimation of the duration of this transient non-Fickian regime.
1 Introduction Transport phenomena within porous media play a pivotal role in multiple environmental and industrial processes. These applications encompass a wide range of processes, ranging from underground carbon or hydrogen storage to the migration of pollutants and contaminants in groundwater flow (Blunt, 2017 ). The majority of these processes occur at multiphase conditions, where two or more fluids coexist, often referred to as “unsaturated”. In many cases, the fluids (e.g. gas and liquid) are immiscible, and the fluid–fluid interface serves as a boundary for solute transport, confining the tracer to a single phase only, referred to as the carrier phase. Mapping fluid–fluid interfaces and the transport of solute particles in the carrier phase are the key physical processes that need to be integrated to predict the fate of solute particles at unsaturated conditions. Depending on the application and flow condition, the stationary percolating pathways for solute migration can be formed by either the simultaneous flow of wetting and non-wetting phase (Jimenez-Martinez et al., 2017 ) or the displacement of one phase by the other phase (Karadimitriou et al., 2017 ). In drainage (displacement of wetting fluid by non-wetting one), the focus of the current study, the spatial fluid distribution is controlled by the interplay of various forces, including viscous, capillary, gravitational, and wetting forces, in addition to the pore morphology of the media (Holtzman, 2016 ). The carrier phase can be categorized according to its topology into (i) interconnected regions that are reachable by the solute, featuring mobile∖  flowing and immobile∖  stagnant zones, and (ii) isolated regions that are unreachable for solute (De Gennes, 1983; Khayrat and Jenny, 2016 ). Mobile∖  flowing zones constitute the fully connected segments of the flow network, where all the fluid flow takes place, while immobile∖  stagnant zones do not contribute to fluid flow and primarily act as a diffusion-controlled sink for the tracer. In unsaturated media, solute transport is governed by the competition between advection and diffusion, which occur predominantly in the mobile (advection-dominated) and immobile (diffusion-dominated) regions, respectively (Karadimitriou et al., 2016 ). This competition is quantified by the ratio between the relative strength of advection and diffusion via the Peclet number, P  e   = U L  D  m       , where U   is the fluid velocity, D  m     denotes the molecular diffusion coefficient, and L   is a characteristic length. Both fluid flow and solute transport are directly impacted by the microstructural heterogeneity of the porous domain (Schlüter et al., 2012; Timms et al., 2018 ). Structural heterogeneity is an inherent feature of natural porous media, and it has been shown that macroscopic responses at large scales are governed by the distribution of solid obstacles at smaller scales (Scheibe et al., 2015; Tahmasebi and Kamrava, 2018; Armstrong et al., 2021 ). Unlike Darcy-scale models, pore-scale models allow for the inclusion of such small, localized properties and mechanisms by considering the domain as discrete void and solid phases (Mehmani and Balhoff, 2015 ). Different pore-scale modeling approaches have been developed to study pore-level mechanisms, including Pore Network Modeling (PNM), Lattice Boltzmann Modeling (LBM), and Volume of Fluid (VOF). PNM simulates fluid motion on idealized pore bodies, typically represented as cylindrical shapes, connected by constraining throats. PNM incorporates simplifications to reduce computational costs and enable simulations at larger scales but at the expense of precise medium geometry and pore-scale mechanisms. In contrast, VOF and LBM techniques offer more accurate modeling with sub-pore resolution (i.e. control volume smaller than pores/throats) but they demand more computational resources and parallel simulation on high-performing clusters. These methods are capable of capturing pore-scale processes on exact porous structures and are often referred to as direct modeling approaches (Saeibehrouzi et al., 2024 ). In many natural porous materials such as soils and rocks, the medium is characterized by spatially correlated disorder in pore sizes. Overall, few studies investigated solute transport in partially saturated media, mostly considering random disorder without any spatial correlation with transport happening within the wetting (Raoof and Hassanizadeh, 2013; Jimenez-Martinez et al., 2015, 2017; Ben-Noah et al., 2023 ) or non-wetting phase (Karadimitriou et al., 2016, 2017; Aziz et al., 2018, 2020; Hasan et al., 2019; Gong and Piri, 2020 ). Enhancing oil recovery by low-salinity water flooding in oil-wet media or surfactant flooding in petroleum-contaminated soil as a clean-up strategy (Li et al., 2016; Qin et al., 2019 ) can be mentioned as examples of unsaturated transport within the non-wetting phase. Much less attention has been given to the effects of correlations on unsaturated transport. Babaei and Joekar-Niasar (2016)  investigated single-phase transport considering the impacts of different correlation lengths and Peclet numbers. Using PNM, Dashtian et al. (2018)  evaluated the relation between throat size correlation and the rate of brine evaporation within drying porous media. Borgman et al. (2019)  conducted a numerical and experimental investigation to quantify the effects of correlation length on the displacement pattern and sweep efficiency across a range of injection rates and wettability states. An et al. (2020b)  employed quasi-static PNM to study solute transport and multiphase flow interactions within correlated structures. Although the above-mentioned studies tried to account for the relation between correlation length and flow or transport mechanisms at the pore level, there is still no accurate, yet efficient numerical study for evaluating unsaturated transport within correlated media. For instance, the common Mixed-Cell Method (MCM) in PNM considers perfect mixing inside pore bodies and ignores the effect of parabolic velocity profile on solute shearing (Mehmani et al., 2014; Mehmani and Tchelepi, 2017 ). It is also well-established that the fate of solute species in unsaturated porous media fundamentally differs from saturated conditions with unsaturated transport exhibits non-Fickian behavior and long tailing in Breakthrough Curve (BTC) (Guillon et al., 2013; Jimenez-Martinez et al., 2020; Aquino and Velásquez-Parra, 2022; Velásquez-Parra et al., 2022 ). Therefore, results from the single-phase transport cannot elucidate unsaturated transport. Even in unsaturated media, while it is known that dispersivity (Hammel and Roth, 1998; Sato et al., 2003; Nützmann et al., 2002; Vanderborght and Vereecken, 2007; Raoof and Hassanizadeh, 2013; Karadimitriou et al., 2017 ) and mixing (Ursino et al., 2001; Kapetas et al., 2014; Jimenez-Martinez et al., 2015, 2017 ) behaviors are influenced by multiphase conditions, the way it affects these features is unclear and one finds contradictory findings in the literature. These ambiguities underscore the necessity of establishing a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying physical mechanisms governing transport in unsaturated porous media. Another open question is how transport characteristics depend on fluid–fluid interface locations in correlated structures. This can be of utmost importance, as the most common approach in evaluating transport under unsaturated conditions involves a one-way analysis of transport. This means that solute solution is injected into the domain only after the establishment of either fully steady-state (i.e. fully stable fluid–fluid interfaces) (Karadimitriou et al., 2016; Aziz et al., 2018; Hasan et al., 2019 ) or dynamic steady-state conditions (i.e. statistically constant saturation, pressure drop, and fluids distribution) (Jimenez-Martinez et al., 2015, 2017; Ben-Noah et al., 2023; Velásquez-Parra et al., 2024 ). Recent studies highlighted the complex dynamics of interfaces within the pore-space, showcasing frequent shuffling of flowing pathways during steady-state conditions (Reynolds et al., 2017; Spurin et al., 2020, 2021; Mathiesen et al., 2023 ). For instance, in the drainage scenario, it is demonstrated that displacement under unfavorable viscosity ratios can lead to multiple “breakups” of invading phase networks even after the breakthrough, attributed to mechanisms such as snap-off (Andrew et al., 2015; Chang et al., 2019; Wei et al., 2022 ). Currently, it remains uncertain how correlated disorder affects the establishment of steady-state conditions in drainage scenarios. Furthermore, the impact of alteration in fluid connectivity on the one-way analysis of unsaturated transport under dynamic steady-state conditions is still poorly understood. Here, we use high-resolution direct simulation to investigate correlated microstructural heterogeneity under unsaturated conditions in 2D coordinates. This is achieved by coupling multiphase displacement and advecting-diffusing solute solution within the stationary, non-wetting phase. We employ a methodology to reduce the computational costs of modeling by fabricating a mask of drainage fingering pattern at steady-state conditions for transport modeling, allowing analysis of wider numerical cases. We find that the coupled effect of high local disorder and drainage non-local performance can destabilize the fluid–fluid menisci. This instability results in the frequent alteration in fluid connectivity and the establishment of dynamic rather than fully steady-state conditions. Our numerical modeling results indicate that the size of numerical domains needs to be tuned based on correlated heterogeneity. Simulations also show that the magnitude of dispersivity is influenced not only by the invading phase saturation but also by spatial heterogeneity with higher dispersion at higher correlation length. Analyzing the transport in terms of mobile/immobile regions shows that diffusive mass flux from mobile paths to immobile zones is primarily influenced by the saturation of the invading phase and the distribution of mobile and immobile zones.  2 Methodology 2.1 Direct numerical simulation OpenFAOM (Open Field Operation and Manipulation) framework (w w w . O p e n f o a m . o r g   ) is employed for simulation of flow and transport in porous media. Incompressible Navier–Stokes (NS) equations for conservation of mass and momentum are solved for each phase i   to model multiphase flow as: (1) ∇ ⋅ u  i   = 0     (2) ρ  i   ∂ u  i    ∂ t   + ρ  i   ∇ ⋅ ( u  i   u  i   )  = − ∇ P  i   + ∇ ⋅ μ  i   ∇ u  i   + ∇ u  i  T       + F  s       where, ρ   denotes density, μ   is viscosity, u   is the velocity vector, P   is the fluid pressure, and F  s     represents interfacial forces. The evolution of fluid–fluid interfaces in both time and space is accomplished through the VOF technique, using interFoam  solver. This method utilizes an indicator (also called color) function (γ  ) to distinguish between phases as: (3) γ =   0  for Ω  1     (Phase 1)    ( 0 , 1 )   for Γ   (Interface)    1  for Ω  2     (Phase 2)          (4) ∂ γ  ∂ t   + ∇ ⋅ ( γ u )  + ∇ ⋅ γ ( 1 − γ )  u  r     = 0     where u  r     is the relative velocity between two fluids.
