The contact angle (θ  ) is defined for the interface-solid moving line to satisfy the following equation: (8) n = n  s   cos ( θ )  + τ  s   sin ( θ )      with n  s     and τ  s     showing vector normal and tangent to the solid wall, respectively. Pressure and velocity values are determined by using the Pressure-Implicit with Splitting of Operators (PISO) algorithm (Issa, 1986; Moukalled et al., 2016 ). A relative tolerance of 10−8  for both velocity and pressure is considered. To improve the stability of all simulations, the time step (Δ t   ) is determined such that the Courant number (Co=U  m   Δ t  Δ x    , where U  m     shows the magnitude of velocity, and Δ x    is typical mesh size) remains below 0.5. While the VOF method has been extensively used for modeling multiphase flow in porous media (Rabbani et al., 2018; Suo et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021; Shende et al., 2021 ), this study conducts verification of the employed model against micromodel experiments by Roman et al. (2020)  to confirm the accuracy of the utilized numerical schemes. Further details and the conditions of the numerical model validation can be found in the Supplementary Material (SM) section in Fig. S1 and S2. The transport of solute in porous media is modeled by solving the Advection–Diffusion Equation (ADE): (9) ∂ C  ∂ t   + ∇ ⋅ ( u  C )  − ∇ ⋅ ( D  m   ∇ C )  = 0 ,     where C   is the species concentration and D  m     is molecular diffusion. In Eq. (9) , the first term refers to the temporal evolution of the solute, while the second and third terms correspond to transport through advection and diffusion, respectively. A typical molecular diffusion coefficient of 1 0  − 9    m  2   / s    (Cussler, 2009 ) is adopted for all simulation scenarios investigated in this study. The time derivative is discretized using a 1st order Euler implicit scheme. The diffusive and advective terms are discretized using Gauss linear corrected (2nd order) and Gauss Van Leer (2nd order) schemes, respectively. The transport matrix is solved with the stabilized preconditioned bi-conjugate gradient solver with a relative tolerance of 10−10 .  2.2 Porous media geometry In this study, the domains under investigation are square structures containing cylindrical pillars in square lattices. The size of the numerical domain is L = 70 a   , where a=60 μ m    is the lattice length, corresponding to the distance between the center of two adjacent pores. The cylindrical pillars have a constant height of 20 μ m   , and an average radius of 20 μ m    with a standard deviation of 4 μ m   . The mean value of the throat radius is 40 μ m   . The spatial correlation length is generated by making a random rough surface (surface with non-symmetric height distribution), where pillar radii (z-axis) are plotted as a function of their location in the x–y plane, whose Fourier transform is characterized by a Gaussian distribution of intensities centered around zero. This is accomplished by incorporating 1 0  4      sinusoidal waves, with wave numbers extracted from a uniform distribution, and their amplitude, orientation, and phase chosen from random uniform distributions. The correlation length (λ  ) of the surface has an inverse relationship with the width of this distribution in the Fourier domain, measured in units of the lattice length. A higher λ   increases the likelihood of similar-sized pillars residing adjacent to each other. More information on the creation of this type of rough surface can be found in Persson et al. (2004), Borgman et al. (2017) . In this study, porous media with λ   of 1 (60 μ m   ), 3 (180 μ m   ), and 5 (300 μ m   ) at three different realizations (domains with different random seeds but with same statistical attributes) are generated to obtain statistically representative numerical results. Porosity of generated media is approximately 64%.  2.3 Domain discretization and boundary conditions The numerical domains are created in a two-dimensional Cartesian coordinate system utilizing the OpenFOAM S n a p p y H e x M e s h    utility (Daniels et al., 2019; Boccardo et al., 2020 ), and by employing the porous structures in S T L    format. Mesh sensitivity analysis follows the method outlined in Ferrari and Lunati (2013) . Ferrari’s study showed that differences in results between simulations using a mesh length of Δ x = d / 12   , where Δ x    denotes the typical cell size and d   is mean pillar diameter, and finer mesh sizes (d / Δ x = 15 , 24 , 48   ) are below 10%. To enhance simulation precision, all numerical domains are discretized with a typical cell size of 1.68 μ m   , resulting in nearly 4 million cells for each realization (d / Δ x ≃ 24   ). Constant injection rate at the inlet face is imposed, while the no-slip boundary condition is applied to the side walls of the domain and the fluid–fluid–solid contact line. To generate simulation results with various degrees of saturation, distinct injection rates are applied, quantified through dimensionless capillary number C a = μ  i n v   u  inv   / σ   , where μ  i n v     and u  i n v     denote the invading phase viscosity and injection velocity, respectively. Multiphase simulations are performed at three injection velocities, C a = 1 0  − 4     , 10−5 , and 10−6 , for all realizations, resulting in a total of 27 cases (three realizations x   three correlation lengths x   three injection velocities). In this study, the viscosity of invading and defending fluids is set to 10−3  Pa.s and 10−1  Pa.s, respectively. The density of both invading and defending fluids is also set to 1000 kg/m  3    . The interfacial tension between the fluids is set to 70 m N  m    . Initially, the domain is fully saturated with the defending fluid, and the invading fluid, acting as the non-wetting phase, is introduced into the domain with a constant contact angle of 120°, mimicking the drainage scenario at an unfavorable viscosity ratio. After reaching steady-state conditions (i.e. fully stable fluid–fluid interfaces), a mask, with identical mesh density to the initial multiphase model, is generated based on the fingering pattern of the invaded fluid for each realization. The fabricated masks contain only the connected network of the invading phase and it excludes the residing phase and any disconnected (i.e. isolated) parts of the invading phase. However, we note that for some scenarios, the fully steady-state condition is not achievable, and a dynamic steady-state condition is established (see Section 3.1 ). Solute migration is then modeled within the invaded fingers using the fabricated masks, which serve as new numerical domains. This involves establishing laminar, steady-state velocity fields within the invaded fingers by solving single-phase Stokes equations. This technique reduces the computational cost by solving the transport equation in the single-phase scenario and ensures a fixed fluid map without diffusive mass flux between the phases. See Fig. S3 and S4 in SM for details on the boundary conditions and the mask extraction process. For all cases, the no-slip boundary condition is applied at fluid–fluid interfaces. While simplifying the calculation, this boundary condition has a negligible effect on transport characteristics (Guédon et al., 2019; Triadis et al., 2019; Jimenez-Martinez et al., 2020 ). Our analysis also shows that imposing free-slip boundary conditions on interfaces makes no appreciable impact on results. See Fig. S5 in SM for more details. In our simulation, the solute concentration is dimensionless and ranges from 0 (no solute) to 1 (fully saturated with solute). Initially, the invading fingers are solute-free, and the solute is introduced into the domain from the inlet with a concentration of 1. Solute solution is injected into the domains at macroscopic P e  ¯  = U  i n l e t   ∗ L  D  m     = 280   , and 28 with L   being the length of the domain and U  i n l e t     showing the solute solution injection velocity. All simulations are compiled on High-Performance Computing (HPC) clusters with 32 to 64 CPUs (depending on mesh density).  2.4 Averaging concentration fields Whilst simulations are done at the pore level with data of concentration fields in cells smaller than a pore throat, macroscopic properties, such as dispersion coefficients, are defined for the Representative Elementary Volume (REV) of the system. On this account, it is required to upscale simulation results to examine properties at the Darcy scale. This involves upscaling the concentration values obtained at each time step to the macroscopic scale, allowing us to determine the BTC and overall concentration–time curves within the domain. The BTCs are determined by calculating the average concentration values over the outlet cells, weighted by the flux of each cell (q  i    ): (10) C  ¯   e   = ∑  i  N   C  i   q  i    ∑  i  N   q  i          The concentration–time evolution within the domain is estimated by averaging the concentration value in each cell, with weighting based on the volume of each cell (V  i    ): (11) C  ¯  = ∑  i  N   C  i   V  i    ∑  i  N   V  i          2.4.1 Estimating dispersion coefficient Dispersion mainly accounts for deviation of velocities in pore-scale compared to the macroscopic velocity (Neuman and Tartakovsky, 2009; Sahimi, 2012 ). For a purely advective transport, the frequent fluctuation in velocity fields, happens, for instance, by the recurrent divergence and convergence of flow pathways within a porous medium, leads to hydrodynamic dispersion. In addition to the advective spreading, dispersion is also impacted by diffusion and the way that the spectrum of velocity fields is sampled by solute particles (Puyguiraud et al., 2021 ). Curve fitting of data to analytical solutions is one common methodology to determine the dispersion coefficient (Karadimitriou et al., 2016; Aziz et al., 2018; Hasan et al., 2019; Erfani et al., 2021 ). This study adopts the analytical solution proposed by Ogata and Banks (1961)  to estimate the longitudinal dispersion coefficient in the domains. For the Dirichlet boundary condition applied in the simulation (with continuous injection of solute), the 1D analytical solution of the advection–dispersion equation for the inlet solute concentration of C  0   C ( 0 , t )  = C  0   , t ≥ 0      in a solute free domain [ C ( x , 0 )  = 0 , x > 0 ]    with a zero concentration gradient condition at the outlet can be written as (Ogata and Banks, 1961 ): (12) C ( x , t )  = 1  2   C  0   erfc x − v t  2 D t       + e  x v / D   erfc x + v t  2 D t             where, D   is longitudinal dispersion coefficient, and v   is average pore-level velocity. Curve fitting is done by using the nonlinear least-squares solver in MATLAB (l s q n o n l i n    function), where it is tried to minimize an objective function Φ ( x )  = ∑ ‖ F ( x  i   )  − y  i   ‖  2     , where F ( x  i   )     is the solution to a nonlinear function (Eq. (12) ) for given input values and y  i     shows the input concentration–time data. The Ogata and Banks (1961)  analytical solution was proposed for single-phase scenarios with Fickian behavior. However, it is well-known that immobile zones alter transport characteristics to non-Fickian (Ben-Noah et al., 2023 ). The computational data generated by Aziz et al. (2018)  has indicated that transport in flowing regions can still be approximated as Fickian during the early stages of the process. Hence, we use the solution proposed by Ogata and Banks (1961)  for mobile regions exhibiting Fickian behavior. To mitigate the effects of tailing observed in the BTCs during the fitting procedure, we employ the procedure proposed by Karadimitriou et al. (2016), Hasan et al. (2019) . Longitudinal dispersion coefficients in flowing pathways are found by fitting data up to a time where the concentration fields in flowing fingers are nearly fully developed (i.e. averaged concentration of 0.99). On this account, the value of C  0     is set to the maximum value of concentration in the curve fitting procedure (i.e. 0.99). The distinction between mobile and immobile regions is accomplished by using pore-level P e = u ∗ R  ̄   D  m        with R  ̄    being average pillar radius, and u   showing velocity in each cell (Aziz et al., 2018 ). Here, we consider the pore-scale value of P e   =0.01 as a threshold to distinguish between diffusion- and advection-controlled zones, as suggested by Babaei and Joekar-Niasar (2016) .  2.4.2 Mass exchange rate between mobile and immobile zones Mixing is a key parameter for determining transport characteristics in porous media, especially in the presence of chemical reactions. It plays a crucial role in facilitating encounters between solute particles already present in the domain and those introduced into the domain, aiming to homogenize concentration values in space (Borgman et al., 2023 ). In unsaturated media, the diffusive mass exchange between mobile and immobile regions is a significant factor in characterizing the mixing, directing solute particles from flowing networks to stagnant zones (Karadimitriou et al., 2016; Jimenez-Martinez et al., 2017 ). In this study, the non-Fickian Mobile-Immobile Model (MIM) is employed to analyze the simulation results. The MIM estimates the mass flux between flowing and stagnant zones by employing a non-equilibrium mass transfer model (Van Genuchten and Wierenga, 1976 ): (13) S  s   φ ∂ C  s    ∂ t   = α C  f   − C  s         where, S  s     is stagnant saturation, φ   denotes porosity, C  s     and C  f     refer to macroscopic concentration in stagnant and flowing regions, respectively, and α   is the mass transfer rate. Stagnant saturation is defined as S  s   = V  s   / V  P     , with V  s     denoting the total volume of stagnant zones (i.e. zones of invading fingers with pore-scale P e ≺   0.01) and V  P     is the total pore volume of the medium. The temporal evolution of C  s     and C  f     can be found by using Eq. (11) . The derivative term in Eq. (13)  is also determined numerically through the forward difference method. While MIM assumes a constant α   over time for each saturation (Zhuang et al., 2021 ), Karadimitriou et al. (2016), Aziz et al. (2018), Zhou et al. (2019), Hasan et al. (2019)  employed MIM and found that the mass transfer rate between mobile and immobile zones is time-dependent. An et al. (2020b)  later derived and validated a semi-analytical solution to determine the temporal variation of mass transfer rate between mobile and immobile zones. The model was based on the assumption of zero concentration at t  =0 and diffusive-governed transport in immobile zones. The derived model was highly similar to the non-equilibrium model in Eq. (13) . Given that, we also pick the MIM for our analysis to facilitate comparing our results with those of previous studies.    3 Results and discussion 3.1 Effect of drainage non-local dynamics on the establishment of multiphase steady-state conditions In a pore-scale modeling approach such as quasi-static PNM, which excludes viscous forces, every drainage event occurs independently, and each pore body is considered as a single simulation node. The percolation theory mainly considers capillarity as a local mechanism, quantified based on the idealized geometrical shape of throats (Dashtian et al., 2018; An et al., 2020b; Wang et al., 2021 ). Under such circumstances, achieving a fully stabilized fluid distribution is feasible since the model needs to predict whether a pore is drained, and once a flow path is established, it remains unchanged. However, experimental and numerical evidence has shown that the assumption of percolation theory does not always hold, and the location of menisci can play a crucial role in drainage dynamics (Moebius and Or, 2012; Armstrong and Berg, 2013; Raeini et al., 2014; Andrew et al., 2015 ). Armstrong and Berg (2013)  highlighted the non-local behavior of the drainage, with the existence of a capillary pressure difference across multiple pores. It was observed that several pores could contribute to a single pore event by providing the non-wetting phase from neighboring throats, leading to imbibition in nearby throats (i.e. receding of interface) and possible redistribution of the invading phase. Similar results were obtained by Andrew et al. (2015)  using X-ray microtomography imaging in a cm-long core. The authors observed frequent snap-offs and re-connections of the non-wetting phase fingers, which can occur near the advancing front or further away from it, challenging the traditional assumptions of percolation theory. Contrary to the PNM approach, direct simulations with control volumes smaller than a single pore enable us to investigate and evaluate drainage non-local behavior and its impact on multiphase steady-state conditions. In porous media, fluid–fluid interfaces advance through pore-scale mechanisms, such as Haines jumps and cooperative pore-filling. The prevalence of these mechanisms depends on the wettability and the rate (C a   ) (Holtzman and Segre, 2015 ). During drainage, the pressure of the invading phase increases until it reaches the threshold required to overcome the local capillary pressure of a constriction (throat). The interface then “jumps” to the next equilibrium state within the pore body. The sequence of such events leads to fluctuations in the pressure drop along the domain, as depicted in Fig. 1 , for different λ   at two injection rates. Similar pressure fluctuations were observed in the drying of correlated media (Biswas et al., 2018 ), and forced drainage in uncorrelated media (Ambekar et al., 2021a,b ). In all cases, the inlet pressure increases with some oscillations until the first breakthrough, which is followed by a reduction in pressure.  Fig. 1  highlights varying post-breakthrough pressure behavior across different λ   values tested in this study at identical periods. In the most correlated medium, λ  =5, the pressure nearly stabilizes with a small reduction after all fingers breakthrough, indicating unchanged fluid–fluid interfaces. However, pressure fluctuations persist for lower correlation lengths, particularly for λ  =1. The oscillation in the pressure gradient during the post-breakthrough phase is indicative of variation in the invading phase topology. The intensity of fluctuations after the first breakthrough depends on the applied C a   . For instance, while significant post-breakthrough oscillation fades away after a period of time for λ = 3    at C a   =10−6 , the opposite can be seen at C a   =10−5  with pressure experiencing a continuous upward and downward trend after breakthrough. To better understand this, Fig. 2  displays the occurrence of a snap-off event within an already established finger in a domain with λ  =1. As depicted in the figure, the propagation in one finger (shown in yellow) leads to interface receding in the other finger (shown with black). Recruiting some parts of the non-wetting phase for pore-level drainage events in one finger from another finger can reduce the capillary pressure far from the invasion front, and potentially destabilize the interface in the “source” finger. The destabilization of the interface continues until the pressure reaches the snap-off threshold, and the swelled wetting phase rapidly fills the throat, disconnecting parts of the invading phase network (green arrows in Fig. 2 ). These non-local (“distal”, as termed by Andrew et al. (2015) ) snap-offs can result in immobile or mobile ganglia. As the broken-up finger attempts to attain equilibrium, it starts propagating again within the domain, either to coalesce with the disconnected region or bypass it. For both injection rates (C a   =10−5 , 10−6 ), while interface receding still occurs for λ  =5, distal snap-off does not take place. The absence of such pore-level events may be related to the underlying porous microstructure, as follows: the higher correlation length increases the likelihood of larger throats residing next to each other. The snap-off threshold depends on the throats’ size, with invading phase snap-off occurring in the smallest throats at the highest capillary pressure (Andrew et al., 2014 ). The pore space morphology at higher correlations λ   generates very low capillary snap-off pressure (due to greater throat size) within the preferred pathways of the invading phase that may hardly be reached. Forcing the non-wetting phase to smaller throats at higher injection rates increases the maximum value of the snap-off capillary threshold and raises the chance of non-wetting phase break-up as shown in Fig. 1  for λ  =3. These findings show the influence of correlations on the distal snap-off occurrence. We hypothesize that increasing correlation length reduces the local instabilities of menisci, and enhances the stability of the fluid–fluid interface. This aligns with the observation of Wu et al. (2021)  on the greater local instability of interface evolving in domains with more local disorder (corresponding to the lower correlation length in the present study).  From the analysis of numerical simulations, we find that for low correlation length (more random disorder), fully stable interfaces may not be achievable due to drainage dynamics associated with the disorder, and the dynamic steady-state condition is established. Our analysis indicates that even a minute perturbation caused by a local p o r e − s c a l e    event during the d y n a m i c    steady-state regime, can cause an evident change in interface morphology with a direct impact on unsaturated transport. To exemplify this, Fig. 3  illustrates the evolution of pressure and saturation for a domain with λ  =1 and corresponding fluid configuration at two different times with similar displacement patterns but varying by a single pore invasion. While the saturation of the invading phase reaches a plateau, marginal fluctuation in the pressure gradient can affect the topology of the invading phase causing a snap-off (highlighted with red circles in Fig. 3 c,d). Such variations in displacement pattern (e.g. snap-off event) can occur repeatedly with further finger thinning and advancement in other locations, according to the pore space characteristics and snap-off pressure. Based on the considered criteria for the dynamic steady-state condition (i.e. statistically constant saturation or fluids distribution), each of the fluid configurations (Fig. 3 c and d) can serve as the stationary, steady-state displacement pattern for one-way examining of unsaturated transport. However, the probability distribution of pore-level P e    in Fig. 3 b reveals that the transport behavior, at an identical injection rate, varies among the two patterns. The breakup (by snap-off) of a finger that reaches the outlet can alter the streamlines and thus the distribution of flowing-stagnant clusters. This alteration in velocity pathways evidently affects the spreading and mixing properties of solute particles. To further elaborate, Fig. 4  displays the variation of solute Residence Time Distribution (RTD) for the displayed invading phase displacement patterns in Fig. 3 c and d. For a domain with a continuous flow of solute solution, the RTD can be viewed as the probability distribution with respect to the time for which the solute particles will remain at one location. RTD variation over time is calculated using the time derivative of BTC. For the Fickian regime, RTD corresponds to a Gaussian distribution (i.e. bell-shaped curve). However, Gaussian distribution is hindered in the non-Fickian regime and RTD shows an early breakthrough with long tailing (Zhang et al., 2021 ). As can be seen from Fig. 4 , the a c t i v a t i o n    and d e a c t i v a t i o n    of flowing pathways affect the temporal variation of RTD and its tailing. For instance, in Fig. 4 , a single peak is observed for the pattern extracted at time 0.47 s. However, at 0.49 s, the a c t i v a t i o n    of an additional flowing pathway causes a second solute breakthrough with a distinct breakthrough time, leading to the emergence of a second b u m p   . In this study, to minimize the effects of alterations in fluid pathways in domains with high local disorder, the quantities (e.g. in Section 3.6 ) are determined by averaging them from all realizations and cases with the least alteration in fluid connectivity are mainly considered for analysis. Interfacial redistribution at steady-state is also a common observation in intermittent flows (i.e. during co-injection of the two phases) (Spurin et al., 2019, 2020 ). The continuous alteration in fluid connectivity causes the phases to move within porous media through periodic events of disconnection and coalescence. A common approach to study solute transport at dynamic steady-state conditions is to select a fluid arrangement when the saturation of the wetting phase in the domain is nearly constant with minimum variation in fluid pathways (Jimenez-Martinez et al., 2015, 2017 ). We note, however, that at a constant saturation, interfaces can evolve affecting relative permeability (Armstrong et al., 2016 ). Given the high sensitivity of transport to the connectivity of pathways under dynamic steady-state conditions (e.g. shown in Fig. 3  for a single snap-off), a more complex transport behavior is expected for intermittent flows compared to the drainage case.     3.2 Correlated disorder increases the representative elementary volume size Fluid invasion patterns, and hence the required size of REV and the domain, are sensitive to pore-scale heterogeneity, including both random and spatially correlated disorder (Holtzman, 2016; Borgman et al., 2017, 2019; An et al., 2020b ). Macroscopic models, from the fundamental conservation laws such as the advection–dispersion equation to the empirical constitutive relations such as Brooks–Corey relative permeability correlations, are computed assuming that domain size is much larger than the REV. This assumption requires the input variables to be spatially and temporally independent (Neuman and Tartakovsky, 2009; Mehmani et al., 2020 ). A common approach for finding the REV of a medium is determining Darcy-scale properties, e.g. porosity, at various fields of view (Erfani et al., 2021 ). However, in this study, the extensive number of cases, including different realizations for each λ  , inhibits the implementation of such a technique (i.e. determining REV by finding properties at different fields of view). To ensure that results are independent of the specific realization, we use numerical–statistical evaluation to find the REV-λ   relation. The employed technique is similar to previous studies, where the variation of an objective  parameter   is evaluated across multiple realizations (Ukrainczyk and Koenders, 2014; An et al., 2020b; Shi et al., 2024 ). On this account, if the domain size is insufficient to be representative, the variability of the calculated macroscopic properties across different realizations will be increased. Fig. 5  shows the BTCs and the corresponding dispersion coefficients, obtained using Eq. (12) , for all realizations under saturated conditions at P e  ¯  = 280   . The accuracy of fitted dispersion coefficients can be evaluated by calculating the Normalized Mean Square Error (NMSE) between the fitted and numerical results as NMSE =‖ X  i   − X  ˆ    i   ‖  2     / ‖ ( X  i   − X  ̄    i   )  ‖  2    , where ‖  2     shows the 2-norm of a vector, and X  ˆ    i    , X  i    , and X  ̄    i     are curve fitting output values, curve fitting input values from simulation, and mean values, respectively. In all fitting cases, the NMSE value was below 0.01. As can be seen from the figure, similar dispersion coefficients are estimated for λ = 1    and λ = 3    with superimposed BTCs. However, for the most correlated structures, the dispersion coefficient’s value varies markedly from one case to another and is realization-dependent. Another evidence is provided by comparing the saturation values at the steady-state condition for all realizations across the range of applied C a    (see Fig. S6 in SM). Contrary to λ  =5 with scatter values, the invading phase saturation remains nearly the same for all realizations of λ  =1 and λ  =3 at each injection rate. This shows that the structural heterogeneity of media with λ  =5 results in a REV larger than the dimensions of the domains, making the results realization-dependent. For the model investigated in this study, the domain size should be at least 23 times the correlation length (considering the domain size as 4.2 mm and correlation length of λ  =3 or 180 μ m   ) to obtain quantitatively representative porous media. This is aligned with the findings of An et al. (2020b) . This is particularly relevant as a common approach to measure flow and transport characteristics is using images captured from X-ray microtomography, with specimens often on the order of mm, depending on the device specifications (Moreno-Atanasio et al., 2010; Scanziani et al., 2017 ). In carbonate rocks, for instance, characterized by multiscale heterogeneity and correlation length in the range of ≫   1 mm (Vik et al., 2013a,b ), utilizing samples smaller than the REV can lead to misinterpretations. In such cases, a marginal shift in sample volume can result in substantial changes in determined bulk properties (Nordahl and Ringrose, 2008 ). Given these considerations and due to the runtime costs of rerunning simulation cases with larger domain sizes, the transport analysis is focused on domains with λ   of 1 and 3.    3.3 Fluid-fluid displacement topology and diffusion-controlled zones The final fingering patterns across the range of applied C a    are illustrated in Fig. 6  for one set of realizations. For the lowest injection rates (C a    of 10−6  and 10−5 ), the flow is predominantly governed by capillary forces. Pore morphology controls the displacement pattern and the invading phase enters throats and follows pore bodies with the path of least resistance, as shown in the seminal work of Lenormand et al. (1988) . Similarly, the developed transversal branches conform to the structural disorder of the domain and grow within pores created by the smallest solid obstacles. This is also highlighted for some branches in Fig. 6  with ellipses. In λ = 1   , high local randomness leads to the formation of fingers that grow more randomly without any particular shape. However, we note that even at λ = 1   , the f o o t p r i n t    of correlated heterogeneity on fingering topology can still be seen and similar fingers can grow for the two lowest injection rates, shown with red ellipses in Fig. 6 . An increase in the injection rate intensifies viscous forces, resulting in the emergence of additional pathways (fingers) for the invading phase. At a higher injection rate (C a = 1 0  − 4     ), the developed branches from a sole finger stretch out less in the perpendicular direction. For instance, compare the highlighted branches in Fig. 6  with red ellipses at C a = 1 0  − 5      and 10−6  with the highest C a    for λ =   3 and 5. However, the lack of high correlation in pillar distribution at λ = 1    limits the considerable transversal movement of the invading phase. For C a = 1 0  − 4     , the coupled effect of the capillary with pore morphology causes some fingers to advance obliquely and not straight, reaching the outlet diagonally (e.g. observe the formed diagonal fingers in λ  =3 and 5 in Fig. 6 ). Non-wetting phase still stays away from some parts of the domain with low conductivity and bypasses them, highlighted with red squares in Fig. 6 . Hence, the displacement pattern at this injection rate (C a = 1 0  − 4     ) can be ascribed to a transitional zone between capillary and viscous fingering. This is also in agreement with previous experimental and numerical findings (Zhang et al., 2011; Wei et al., 2022 ).  At an identical C a   , the variation in λ   significantly influences the injection phase saturation and the number of formed fingers. As shown in the bottom panel of Fig. 6 , higher values of λ   introduce spatial heterogeneity that results in the formation of clusters of regions with similar pillar radii, ranging from 16 to 24  μ m   . Zones with smaller pillar radii (a few are highlighted with ellipses in the bottom panel of Fig. 6 ) exhibit larger throat sizes. The capillary pressure (Δ P  c     ) along an interface can be determined based on the Young–Laplace equation, Δ P  c   = 2 σ C o s θ / r    with r   being the throat radius (Young, 1805 ). Accordingly, the non-wetting phase requires a lower pressure to invade a throat with greater size. Similar to the concept of PNM developed by Fatt (1956) , which is based on current in electrical resistors, the non-wetting phase tends to flow preferentially through pathways of least resistance, or possesses higher fluid conductivity. The developed contrasts in medium local permeability, characterized by pathways with high fluid conductivity coexisting with pathways of low conductivity, not only reduce the number of formed fingers but also lead to the development of larger branches in the lateral direction (e.g. compare patterns for λ  =1 and λ  =3 at C a = 1 0  − 5      in Fig. 6 ). According to the pore-scale P e   , the interconnected fingers of the invading phase can be decomposed into two parts: (i) zones mostly in the direction of flow with very high velocity and dominated by advection, and (ii) stagnant zones, mainly developed in the transverse orientation with small pore-scale P e    and governed primarily by diffusivity. The influence of λ   on the volume of diffusion-dominated zones of the invading phase network can become evident by comparing the value of stagnant saturation at different degrees of invading phase saturation, S  i     (displayed in Fig. 7 ). To provide a comprehensive analysis and expand the dataset range, two additional drainage simulations are conducted for realizations with λ   equal to 1 and 3 at C a    of 10−3 , resulting in higher S  i    . In Fig. 7 , each S  i     value corresponds to one C a    ranging from 10−3  to 10−6 . A monotonic increase in stagnant saturation is observed for λ  =1 and 3 versus S  i     increase (Fig. 7 ). Increasing injection rates boost not only the number of longitudinal fingers but also the transversal branches. The majority of formed transversal fingers belong to diffusion-dominated zones (P e ≺   0.01), and consequently, the volume of stagnant saturation increases at higher injection rates. Later in Section 3.4 , we will analyze the contribution of each zone (mobile and immobile) to transport. Fig. 7  also highlights that increasing λ   corresponds to a reduction in the volume of diffusion-governed zones across all S  i    . This is attributed to the lack of favorable pathways at lower λ   values, characterized by higher randomness in the local conductivity. At the same C a    (injection rate in our case), the lack of favorable pathways for domains with lower correlation length results in the formation of more fingers that remain dead-end, i.e. do not reach the outlet, and hence are reachable for the solute mainly by diffusivity due to small values of pore-scale P e   . The nonlinear relationship observed in Fig. 7  between injection rates and S  i    , i.e. an order of magnitude reduction in C a    leading to a distinct reduction in S  i    , can be explained by the dynamics of the drainage process. In drainage, the preferential pathways of the non-wetting phase and its saturation are primarily determined by the interplay between the applied pressure drop, capillary pressure (Δ P  c     ), and the pore space morphology, i.e. pore connectivity and distribution. The pressure drop is primarily a function of the injection rate and viscosity of the fluid and, for instance, can be found using Poiseuille’s equation for a tube (Loudon and McCulloh, 1999 ). In accordance with the Young–Laplace equation, when a non-wetting phase enters a saturated domain, the local potential energy of the non-wetting phase accumulates until it surpasses the capillary entry pressure of the widest throat, and then draining the connected pore body (Moura et al., 2020 ). Based on the applied pressure, only a subset of pores are available for the penetrated phase at each C a   , as the invading phase preferential pathways can alter in accordance with the spatial connectivity of pores. Consequently, the variation in accessible pore bodies versus injection rate can exhibit a nonlinear relationship, leading to distinct S  i     value (An et al., 2020a ).    3.4 Contribution of mobile and immobile zones to transport The fluid–fluid interfaces segment the penetrated phase network into mobile and immobile regions with distinct transport characteristics in each zone (i.e. mostly advection or diffusion in mobile or immobile zones, respectively). To evaluate the contribution of each zone to the transport process, the probability of pore-level P e    at different invading phase saturation for λ = 1    are compared in Fig. 8 . In the saturated case, a single peak is evident, predicting the dominance of advection in regions predominantly characterized by P e > 0 . 01   . For the unsaturated cases, two zones with a bimodal variation can be observed across all saturation ranges, demonstrating the migration of solute with significant contributions from both advective and diffusive forces. Zone 1 corresponds to regions with high-velocity values, where advection is the primary transport mechanism, i.e. mobile zone. The formation of dead-end fingers and transversal branches leads to a second peak (Zone 2), characterized by low-velocity values and governed by diffusive forces. As the influence of diffusive forces intensifies, the transition from Zone 1 to Zone 2 results in the emergence of regions with an interplay of both forces (intermediate P e   ), followed by regions where advection plays a minimal role (i.e. considerably small P e   ).  A notable difference among unsaturated cases is the magnitude of each peak. Comparing the overall distribution of pore-scale P e    probabilities shows that an inverse relationship exists between the S  i     and the prevalence of completely diffusion-dominate zones (the peak in Zone 2) within the medium. For instance, for invading phase saturation S  i   = 26 %   , the probability of both peaks in the pore-scale Peclet number distribution is similar, indicating a nearly balanced contribution from both advection and diffusion to the transport process. At higher saturation levels (e.g. S  i    =58%) the peak in Zone 2 is smaller than the corresponding peak in Zone 1. The contribution of stagnant zones to transport shows consistent behavior across examined realizations, and a similar trend can be observed for them, displayed in Fig. S7 for two more realizations. While according to Fig. 7 , reducing S  i     decreases the overall volume of immobile zones (Zone 2), Fig. 8  shows that at lower S  i     Zone 2 is constituted mostly by totally diffusion-dominated regions with very small P e   . Multiphase pore-scale mechanisms control this behavior. At a high C a    like 10−3  (resulting in S  i     =58% for λ = 1   ), the displacement pattern exhibits viscous fingering, facilitating the flow of the non-wetting phase predominantly in the direction parallel to the applied pressure drop. As a result, fewer dead-end fingers and l o n g    transversal branches, corresponding to the peak in Zone 2, are formed. However, at lower injection rates multiple fully dead-end fingers can develop in the direction of flow and branches move more deeply in the transversal direction, resulting in an increase in the probability of considerably small pore-scale P e    (e.g. compare mobile and immobile zones in Fig. 9  for saturation of 58% and 22%). It is worth mentioning that the indicated contribution by each zone to unsaturated transport is prevalent for cases with P e  ¯  ≫ 1   , where solute migration happens by the combination of advection and diffusion. For scenarios with small P e  ¯   , such contribution may not be applicable.    3.5 Solute concentrations Next, we show the impact of fluid velocities in solute transport under partially-saturated conditions. As predicted above from the P e    distributions, solute concentration in immobile zones increases more rapidly (with injected volumes) for higher S  i    , see Fig. 10 . The cumulative volume of injected solute required to raise concentration in the immobile zones also increases with the macroscopic (sample-averaged) Peclet value, e.g. compare P e  ¯    of 280 with 28 in Fig. 10 . This is due to the relatively low diffusivity in the domain: the weak advective forces in the immobile zones make diffusion the primary transport mechanism. Provided that solute is present in the mobile zones (i.e. P e  ¯   ≫   1), diffusivity requires a similar amount of time to direct solute from mobile pathways to the immobile zones at both P e  ¯    levels for each saturation degree. This indicates that at higher P e  ¯   , a large number of introduced solutes exit the domain without being diverted toward the stagnant zones. Increasing the P e  ¯    by injecting at higher rates primarily boosts advective forces in the mobile zones without any appreciable effect on transport in immobile zones. The longer time required to increase concentration fields in immobile zones than in mobile zones contributes to the dual characteristic time scales of non-Fickian transport, including an early breakthrough of the solute with the rapid development of solute concentration fields in mobile zones (marked with red circles in Fig. 10  for the concentration of 90%), followed by a prolonged period of slow mass transfer between mobile and immobile regions. In Section 3.7  we analyze the mass flux between these zones.    3.6 Dispersion–saturation relation It is widely acknowledged that transitioning from single-phase to multiphase transport scenarios can amplify tracer dispersivity by order of magnitudes, due to the constriction of available pathways for solute migration. However, there is no clear agreement regarding the behavior of dispersivity in unsaturated media. For instance, some studies have reported an increase in solute spreading with decreasing saturation (Nützmann et al., 2002; Sato et al., 2003 ), whereas others demonstrated a reduction in dispersion coefficients (Hammel and Roth, 1998; Vanderborght and Vereecken, 2007 ). Some studies also presented a non-monotonic trend between dispersion coefficients and carrier phase saturation (Raoof and Hassanizadeh, 2013; Karadimitriou et al., 2017; Zhuang et al., 2021 ). To improve understanding of the equivocal nature of the dispersion–saturation relation, we compute the dispersion coefficient at various invading phase saturation for different media (spatial correlations, λ  , of 1 and 3) and macroscopic Peclet values (Fig. 11 ). We find that increasing λ   enhances the solute spreading by up to 50%, regardless of the value of P e  ¯    (injection rate). This can be explained by the reduced number of developed fingers at higher λ  . At the same applied injection rate, a lower number of formed fingers results in a faster spreading of the entered solute and a shorter period of time for it to leave the domain. The non-monotonic dependence of dispersion on S  i     (Fig. 11 ) can be attributed to the tortuosity of velocity streamlines, with the maximum dispersivity at a fluid configuration with the most heterogeneous pathways (Gong and Piri, 2020 ). The simulation results show that the dispersion coefficient peaks at invading phase saturation of S  i   ∼   37%, which belongs to the transient regime between capillary fingering and viscous fingering. The formed diagonal fingers at the transient regime increase the path length, tortuosity, for the solute and finally lead to an enhancement of the dispersion coefficient. At identical saturation, increasing the macroscopic P e  ¯    from 28 to 280 enhances the advective force and helps the solute to travel faster in flowing areas, manifesting itself by a higher dispersion coefficient. The comparison of the variation in dispersion coefficients versus P e  ¯    in Fig. 11  reveals that increasing the injection velocity by ten times leads to an approximately equivalent increase in the dispersion coefficients. Generally, dispersion coefficient is linked to dispersivity (A  ) as D ≈ A v  β     , where β   is an empirical parameter and is set commonly to one (Raoof and Hassanizadeh, 2013 ). For the considered modeling scenario in our study, P e  ¯  ≫ 1   , the observed variation in Fig. 11  for P e  ¯   -D is in line with the notion of dispersivity’s independence from applied dynamic conditions.    3.7 Mobile-immobile mass flux The common perspective on mixing under unsaturated conditions suggests that concentrating the transport process into a limited number of pathways restricts mixing by reducing the residence time for tracer particles (i.e. shorter period of time for mixing) (Kapetas et al., 2014 ). However, Jimenez-Martinez et al. (2015)  demonstrated experimentally that fingering in the longitudinal direction can also lead to a concentration gradient in the transverse direction, enhancing mixing by promoting diffusive flux to immobile zones. Findings from multiple physical and computational studies have outlined the time-dependency of mass exchange rates between mobile and immobile parts of domain (Karadimitriou et al., 2016; Aziz et al., 2018; Hasan et al., 2019; Li and Berkowitz, 2019; An et al., 2020b ). However, the variation of the mass exchange rate over time was inconsistent in the literature. For instance, Aziz et al. (2018)  demonstrated a non-monotonic trend for the mass exchange rate coefficient in an uncorrelated medium, concluding two stages for mixing, including an initial increase in the mass exchange rate followed by a subsequent decrease. However, An et al. (2020b)  showed a monotonic reduction in the mass transfer rate over time for both correlated and uncorrelated structures.  Fig. 12  depicts the temporal variation of mass transfer rate (α   in Eq. (13) ) for λ  =1 and λ  =3 at two P e  ¯   . A non-monotonic trend can be observed for P e  ¯   =280 at both λ   values. Prior to the complete development of concentration fields in the mobile zones at the early stages of the process, the mixing zone (i.e. the contact boundary between mobile and immobile zones that is formed by concentration gradient) increases, leading to the enhancement of diffusive mass flux. Due to the rapid development of concentration fields in mobile zones, the duration of this stage is relatively short. This stage is followed by a gradual decrease in diffusive mass flux as the concentration gradient among mobile and immobile zones fades away, and the tracer is directed to significantly low-velocity zones far from the mobile pathways. However, for the highest saturation at both correlation lengths, the mass exchange rate displays a monotonic decrease. For the same injection rate, the concentration fields in flowing pathways require a longer period of time to fully develop, which is related to the larger clusters of flowing regions at the highest saturation. This delay postpones the rapid formation of the mixing zone between mobile and immobile zones, and subsequently, masks the initial increase of α   at the beginning of the process. Similarly, for P e  ¯   =28, the mass exchange rate shows a continuous decrease for both correlation lengths at all degrees of saturation. Here, the delay in the development of concentration fields in mobile zones, caused by a reduction in advective forces within the domain, is responsible for masking the initial increase of α  . These results clearly underline the significance of fingering topology, affecting the mixing zone between mobile and immobile zones, and the ratio of advective to diffusive forces in determining the mass exchange rate. For instance, compare the difference in the magnitude of diffusive mass flux for λ  =3 at the saturation of 55% with lower degrees of saturation in Fig. 12 . The temporal evolution of the mass exchange rate can vary depending on the spatial distribution of mobile and immobile clusters, and the injection rates for each fluid configuration.   4 Conclusion The transport of solute species under unsaturated conditions is a complex process exhibiting non-Fickian characteristics. We employed pore-scale modeling to study unsaturated transport in porous media with correlated disorder. By upscaling the results from high-fidelity direct simulation, we investigated the macroscopic properties, including dispersion coefficient, mass transfer rate between mobile/flowing and immobile/stagnant pathways, and correlation length-stagnant saturation. It was demonstrated that correlation length in pore sizes can significantly impact the REV of the system (requiring a larger domain), and, consequently, derivation of upscaled quantities. Due to the dependence of the results on the realizations for λ = 5   , we limited our analysis on unsaturated transport to two correlation lengths. Correlated heterogeneity was indicated as an influential parameter on the fingering topology of the invaded, non-wetting phase. We found that an increase in the number of developed fingers in media with greater local randomness reduces the dispersion coefficient of the solute species by up to 50%, exhibiting a non-monotonic trend against saturation. Additionally, our results showed that media with higher correlation lengths reduce the volume of stagnant zones. Through the analysis of pressure drop along the domains, we speculated that increasing the correlation length can potentially enhance fluid–fluid interface stability, leading to a time-independent distribution of fluids. We demonstrated that full or dynamic steady-state conditions can be established depending on the C a    and correlation length. Our direct comparison revealed that even minor perturbations in the connectivity of the invaded phase, such as a snap-off in a single pore during dynamic steady-state conditions, can significantly impact the one-way analysis of solute transport by altering mobile zones to immobile zones or vice versa. While further caution is warranted in the one-way analysis of unsaturated transport during dynamic steady-state conditions, we attempted to minimize the impact of dynamic steady-state conditions on unsaturated transport by examining quantities across multiple realizations. The MIM was used to determine the mass transfer rate between mobile and immobile pathways. We selected the MIM due to its extensive application in the literature and its straightforward implementation. While the MIM assumes a constant mass transfer rate, our results indicated its sensitivity to time. We found that the mass transfer rate can exhibit either a monotonic or non-monotonic temporal variation, depending on the level of saturation and dynamic conditions. For low P e  ¯   , we observed a monotonic reduction in the mass transfer rate, regardless of invading phase saturation. The non-monotonic trend was observed for cases with high P e  ¯    and saturation below 40%. The simulation results across multiple realizations clearly highlighted that the contribution of diffusive forces to transport is enhanced at lower degrees of saturation. We observed an inverse relationship between the saturation of the invading phase and the volume of fully diffusion-dominated zones. This phenomenon is linked to the increased formation of fully dead-end fingers and long transversal branches at lower C a   , which exhibit significantly lower P e   . Our direct simulations in correlated media have yielded new insights into the complex dynamics of unsaturated transport. Although we did not account for the effects of medium wettability or the viscosity ratio between the invading and defending phases, our findings suggest that future studies may not need to analyze multiple realizations for each correlation length. This advancement facilitates the investigation of the combined impact of various factors on unsaturated transport while significantly reducing computational costs by minimizing the number of required realizations.
1 Introduction Hydrogen (H2) plays a crucial role in the shift towards sustainable and renewable energy. Its versatile applications, including fuel cells for transportation, synthetic methane production, and integration into existing natural gas networks, contribute to a wide array of solutions. The utilization of hydrogen in power-to-gas concepts facilitates the storage of surplus electricity, addressing the intermittent nature of renewable energy sources. Large-scale underground storage in geological formations like salt and hard rock caverns, deep aquifers, and depleted gas fields stands out as a promising technology. This method ensures substantial storage capacity while prioritizing safety (Tarkowski, 2019; Sainz-Garcia et al., 2017 ). Furthermore, large-scale hydrogen storage mitigates the challenges associated with the intermittency, seasonality, and geographical constraints of renewable energy generation (Navaid et al., 2023 ). In regions where deep geological formations are unavailable or lack the necessary criteria for quality reservoirs and impermeable seals-often due to geological factors such as the predominance of igneous or metamorphic rocks—lined caverns present a viable alternative. These caverns are especially advantageous because they do not involve additional fluids or rocks, simplifying both safety and management analyses (Masoudi et al., 2024 ). Hydrogen injection into saline aquifers provides a geographically independent and flexible solution for energy storage (Sambo et al., 2022 ). Aquifers are particularly attractive storage options due to their abundance, stability, and capability to efficiently store hydrogen at high pressures (Gholami, 2023 ). The requirements for utilizing aquifers include having a storage zone with higher capacity, a nearly impermeable caprock with high capillary entry pressure to seal the storage, a dome-shaped trap structure to prevent lateral gas spreading, and sufficient permeability for ease injection and extraction processes at reasonable pressures. The fluid properties of hydrogen-water mixtures, including density, viscosity, thermal conductivity, diffusivity, and surface tension, play crucial roles in controlling the hydrogen’s underground behavior and its performance during cyclic injection/production operations. Injecting hydrogen into porous formations like aquifers involves complex interactions, including hydrogen flow-induced brine displacement, as well as associated diffusion, mixing, capillarity, and dissolution processes (Sainz-Garcia et al., 2017 ). Numerical simulations are crucial for modeling subsurface energy storage in porous media, particularly in Underground Hydrogen Storage (UHS). These simulations are done with different numerical formulations, where standard reservoir simulation can be categorized into two broader mathematical models for flow: the general multi-component description, often referred to as compositional simulation, relies on the equation-of-state for resolving the mixing process by phase equilibrium calculations during the simulation. This formulation is general in that it accommodates any number of components, but can be computationally expensive due to the number of degrees of freedom required to describe the components, and the flash equations that must be solved in every cell of the reservoir. The second option is the black-oil model and its variants that typically accounts for up to three fluid components with limited miscibility: oil, gas and water. The black-oil model relies on explicitly tabulated properties for prediction of PVT which are accurate in the region where data is available, and efficient to evaluate. The main limitation is that tables become memory intensive and difficult to create as more components and dependencies are added. Compositional simulations excel at handling complex fluid systems, but the computational cost can be prohibitive for large-scale or numerous simulations needed for optimization or uncertainty quantification. Conversely, black-oil models provide equilibrium property predictions with reasonable accuracy at a significantly lower computational cost. Even for a single simulation run with limited budget, a trade-off between higher accuracy in terms of fluid physics and geological resolution must be made. For these reasons, it is crucial to rigorously evaluate the capabilities and limitations of each formulation to ensure a realistic representation of the fundamental processes specific to each storage type (depleted gas, aquifer, salt dome, etc.). Performing accurate reservoir-scale simulations is essential in assessing the viability of UHS at a prospective site. A fundamental aspect of this process, vital for both formulations, involves validating thermodynamic models that precisely consider the solubility of H  2     in brine systems and the water evaporation in the H  2    -rich phase under varying thermodynamic conditions. This step ensures the reliability and accuracy of simulations, especially given the limited availability of experimental data relevant to the underground storage of hydrogen in porous formations. Exploring the solubility of hydrogen in water, particularly in saline water, under laboratory conditions with elevated pressures and temperatures presents significant challenges. This is primarily due to the extreme flammability of hydrogen and the presence of salt, which escalates the risks of leakage and corrosion. Safety concerns have limited direct experiments, so researchers rely on modeling to accurately predict how much hydrogen can dissolve in brine (Li et al., 2022 ). Recent advancements involve the creation of predictive models fine-tuned with a constrained dataset, incorporating available experimental data (Li et al., 2018 ) or generating pseudo-data through molecular simulations (Lopez-Lazaro et al., 2019 ). Chabab et al. ’s work addresses this data gap by employing an experimental setup based on the static-analytic  method to predict hydrogen solubility under geological storage conditions. The pseudo-measurements obtained were then employed to parameterize and assess the effectiveness of three predictive EoS models. In his research, (Jafari Raad et al., 2023 ) introduced a modified Redlich–Kwong (RK) equation that incorporates the Pitzer expression to account for salting-out effects. The model was accurately fine-tuned using equilibrium data from the hydrogen-water system and subsequently validated with reported experimental data. For a more in-depth analysis of experimental equilibrium data and predictive models, we refer the reader to Torín-Ollarves and Trusler (2021), Chabab et al. (2019), Zhu et al. (2022), Gholami (2023) . Our objective is to develop a thermodynamic model suitable for black oil and compositional simulations, balancing accuracy with computational efficiency. To achieve this, we fine-tune three equation-of-state models, spanning from a complex formulation to a rather simple algebraically explicit model, and finally, a correlation-based approach for modeling H2 -water/H2 -brine mixtures. We assess the accuracy of the perturbed-chain statistical associating fluid theory (PC-SAFT) and an explicit version of Redlich–Kwong cubic EoS (RK) in predicting phase equilibria (solubility of hydrogen in brine and water content in the hydrogen-rich phase). We additionally present a thermodynamic model employing a modified Henry–Setschenow (HS) equation. This model enhances the traditional Henry’s law, providing predictions of hydrogen solubility under specific temperature and pressure conditions while considering the impact of salinity. Therefrom, we employ black-oil simulations for feasibility assessments and numerical simulations of underground storage in saline aquifers. In these simulations, we aim to comprehensively explore critical processes including H2 dissolution, salinity effects, molecular diffusion, lateral spreading, potential leakage, periodicity, and various injection/production scenarios. This work is structured as follows: In Section 2 , we introduce the models and address associated regression problems aimed at enhancing their predictive accuracy using experimental data. We then assess their ability to predict mutual solubilities and compare density computations using ePC-SAFT against correlation-based models and the NIST database across various temperatures and pressures. Section 3  presents the application of these thermodynamic models in black-oil flow simulations through tabulated PVT data. Section 4  presents numerical simulations, exploring H  2     loss from the mobile gas due to dissolution, salinity, leakage to the caprock, and other pertinent parameters to assess the feasibility of underground hydrogen storage by numerical simulation.  2 Thermodynamic models We employ both implicit and explicit thermodynamic methods to model the liquid–vapor equilibria of the H  2    -H  2   O    and H  2    -H  2   O   -NaCl systems. These models can be used to tabulate the PVT model for integration into the black-oil simulator. In terms of usage in a numerical reservoir simulation model, two things are required: (i) Performing a flash that converts a overall molar composition at a given grid block pressure and temperature into a vapor mole fraction and liquid and vapor mole fractions for individual components, and predicting density and saturations after a flash is converged. (ii) Models should also be able to compute the derivatives with respect to these variables for inclusion in a Newton solver. In addition, viscosity and saturation functions are needed, but these are not intrinsically tied to the thermodynamic model and can be obtained from correlations or empirical data. 2.1 ePC-SAFT EoS SAFT EoS represents a contemporary class of equations of state rooted in statistical mechanical theories developed by Gross and Sadowski (2001), Chapman et al. (1990) . These models use a coarse-grained representation of inter- and intra-molecular interactions, assuming an underlying molecular framework. By relying on statistical mechanics, SAFT EoS offers advantages compared to empirical models or cubic equations of state. Unlike those models, which are fitted to limited experimental data and typically exhibit poor extrapolation capabilities, SAFT models benefit from a physically based derivation, namely an estimate of the molar excess Gibbs energy, thus encompassing a wider range of conditions beyond the confines of the experimental data used to tune the model coefficients. Theory and model The electrolyte PC-SAFT equation of state (ePC-SAFT) which can account for ionic effects, see Cameretti et al. (2005)  is expressed in terms of the dimensionless residual Helmholtz energy A  ̃    res     defined as (1) A  res    R T   = A  ̃    res   = A  ̃    hs   + A  ̃    ch    ︸   A  ̃    hc     + A  ̃    disp   + A  ̃    assoc   + A  ̃    ionic   ,     where R   is the universal gas constant, and T   is the temperature. The superscripts r e s   , h s   , h c   , c h   , d i s p   , a s s o c   , and i o n i c    denote the residual, hard-sphere, hard-chain, chain, dispersion, association, and ionic contributions, respectively. These contributions are illustrated in Fig. 1 .  All thermodynamic properties can be estimated through derivatives of the residual Helmholtz free energy. In contrast to traditional cubic EoS models, where critical temperature, critical pressure, and acentric factor serve as the pure-components parameters, the PC-SAFT model requires three parameters for each pure component to account for the non-associating components: The number of molecular chain segments (m  ), the dispersion energy between segments (ɛ  ), and the diameter of the chain segment (σ  ). For pure components with association interactions, two additional parameters are included: The association volume (κ  A B    ) between sites A   and B   and the association energy between sites (ɛ  A B    ). In phase equilibria and flash calculations (Vidal et al., 2020 ), we work under a specified reservoir pressure. Consequently, the density solver mentioned above, operating at a constant temperature, pressure, and composition, is employed (see Fig. 2 ). This computation emerges as the most resource-intensive task in ePC-SAFT, given its repetitive nature within phase equilibria calculations, Diamantonis et al. (2013), Parvin et al. (2020) . The phase behavior of the binary hydrogen/brine mixture is highly influenced by the binary parameter k  i j     in Eq. (7a) , which dictates the cross-dispersive interactions between molecular segments of different components. The presence of salt plays also a significant role in influencing the solubility of dissolved gas. With constant values, the EoS cannot accurately represent the hydrogen-bonding network responsible for water’s typical density anomaly. This anomaly involves unusual changes in density with temperature, particularly around 4°C, which differ from the behavior of most liquids. Consequently, there is a need to adjust the parameter k  i j     based on experimental liquid–vapor equilibrium data (Eller et al., 2022; Alanazi et al., 2022 ).    Adjusting binary parameters The molar fraction of H2  in the liquid phase exhibits a parabolic trend with a minimum at 330 K and decreases with increasing salinity, requiring both temperature and salinity-dependent parameters for an accurate model, (9) k  i j   ( T  r   , m  NaCl   )  ≔ A  0   ( m  NaCl   )  T  r   + A  1   ( m  NaCl   )   T  r     + A  2   ( m  NaCl   )  log ( T  r   )  ,     where A  k   ( m  NaCl   )  = a  k   ( 1 + α  k   m  NaCl  β  k     )     for k ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 }    , T  r   ≔ T / T  c      represents the reduced temperature, m  NaCl     is the salt molality in water (mol/kg), and a  k    , α  k    , and β  k     are adjustable coefficients. This formulation closely resembles the empirical form suggested by Søreide and Whitson (1992)  for binary parameters. However, we observe a better prediction where a logarithmic term is employed instead of an exponential one.    The optimization process uses a regression algorithm to calibrate the ePC-SAFT model against Vapor–Liquid Equilibrium (VLE) experimental data. The regression problem is formulated to represent percentage deviations, defined as Error  r   × 100 / N   , where Error  r     is the relative error between the experimental and computed mole fractions of the mixture components. Here, N   denotes the total number of data points considered in the calibration process. The optimized coefficients are presented in Table 2 , while the corresponding binary parameters for varying salinity are illustrated in Fig. 3 . The average deviation between calculated and experimental data is approximately 1.5% for salt-free mixtures, and this deviation rises to 2.8% with increasing salinity. Fig. 4  compares ePC-SAFT to measurements at 298.15 K (top left) and 323.2 K (top right), showing good agreement with experimental data. Note that more data were used in the fine-tuning phase. Fig. 4  (bottom figures) illustrates the mutual solubilities as functions of pressure and temperature. The findings support the observed parabolic trend in the H2  mass fraction within the liquid phase, indicating an increase with pressure. Additionally, the mass fraction of H2 O in the hydrogen-rich phase demonstrates an increase with temperature and a decrease with pressure. Note that, our empirical correlation requires only three parameters for pure water, in contrast to Fernández-Prini et al. (2003) ’s correlation, which necessitates over 10 parameters. Our correlation employs the reduced temperature, resulting in a computationally efficient optimization process and a well-scaled correlation, as evident from the model coefficients (Eller et al., 2022 ).   2.2 A non-iterative RK-EoS model While equations of state like the ePC-Saft model are powerful tools for predicting thermophysical properties, their implicit nature often demands extensive calculations, making them significantly more expensive than tabulated properties or cubic EoS. This is especially important when the flash is used inside a simulation workflow, where potentially thousands or millions of flash computations need to be performed. In the context of a thermodynamic model that is to be coupled to a flow simulator, the need for practical solutions that alleviate the computational burden is clear: We present here a non-iterative version of the RK-EoS Model described in Jafari Raad et al. (2023)  to convert hydrogen-brine phase equilibrium compositional data into black-oil PVT data. The model closely adheres to the CO2 model established by Spycher and Pruess (2010) , employing an efficient back-substitution method. Additionally, we introduce an activity coefficient based on the Pitzer formulation. General considerations This approach, which extends previous work presented by Hassanzadeh et al. (2008)  for CO2-brine mixture, relies on equating chemical potentials and utilizes the Redlich–Kwong equation of state to account for deviations from ideal behavior.
