1 Introduction The study of multiphase reactive flow in porous media is motivated by multitudinous energy and environment applications, such as CO2  geological sequestration (Boot-Handford et al., 2014 ), proton exchange membrane fuel cell (Zhang et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ), oil and gas stimulation (Jew et al., 2022 ), groundwater pollution remediation (Pak et al., 2020 ). Naturally, the multiphase flow dynamics and reactive transport are two decisive physicochemical processes significantly controlling the potential physical alterations and systematic performance (Wang et al., 2023 ; Meakin and Tartakovsky, 2009 ; Chen et al., 2022 ). A comprehensive understanding of the interaction and feedback mechanisms between multiphase flow and reactive transport contributes to the accurate prediction and optimize strategy implementation in practice. Much efforts have been devoted to study the multiphase flow in static porous media with theoretical, experimental or computational tools. An essential foundation of fluid-fluid displacement is the competition between viscous and capillary forces as characterized by viscosity ratio M  between invading and defending fluid and capillary number Ca  (Lenormand et al., 1988 ).  With the two dimensionless parameters, different flow patterns including stable displacement (M  > 1, high Ca ), viscous fingering (M  < 1, high Ca ) and capillary fingering (low Ca ) are characterized (Lenormand et al., 1988 ; Zacharoudiou et al., 2020 ). However, the wettability measured by the contact angle θ  within the fluid-fluid-solid system is not accounted for in the original phase diagram (Zhao et al., 2016 ). A number of studies have been conducted to probe the two-phase dynamic behavior during imbibition process (θ <90°) and drainage process (θ >90°) (Zhao et al., 2016 ; Primkulov et al., 2019 ). As a result, with cumulative effort in this flourishing field, the original two-dimensional (2D) M -Ca  phase diagram was extended to a novel three-dimensional (3D) M -Ca-θ  phase diagram (Primkulov et al., 2021 ). The extended 3D phase diagram benefits from an unprecedented parameter sweep in the M -Ca-θ  space with 7560 simulations in total using a dynamic pore-network model (Primkulov et al., 2021 ). In the study of multiphase flow in porous media, the effective combination of modern experimental techniques and advanced numerical models can reveal the pore-scale physical mechanisms and macroscopic displacement patterns. Zhao et al. (Zhao et al., 2019 ) performed a comprehensive comparison of experimental benchmark dataset with pore-scale models from fourteen leading teams, in which the dataset provided high-resolution microfluidic results across a wide range of wettability and Ca  numbers, and the numerical models included lattice Boltzmann method (LBM), stochastic rotation dynamics, volume of fluid (VOF), level-set, phase field, and pore network model. The comparison results showed that although single method with excellent predictive performances under all conditions was currently impossible, especially for thin films and corner flow, most methods were able to reproduce the multiphase dynamics from strong drainage to weak imbibition (Bakhshian et al., 2020 ). In the context of actual 3D heterogeneous porous media with mixed-wet conditions, the more accurate pore-scale models are promising tools to explore multiphase flow processes (Irannezhad et al., 2023 ). Multiphase flow in various static heterogeneous porous structures is of great interest (Bakhshian et al., 2020 ; Hu et al., 2019 ; Lei et al., 2022 ; Lei et al., 2023 ). Hu et al. (2019)  studied the effect of disorder on the immiscible displacement in a wide range of wettability, and found that the invasion morphologies were destabilized as pore structure disorder increases at weak imbibition condition. Lei et al. (2022 , 2023 ) systematically studied the non-monotonic wettability effects on displacement process in heterogeneous porous structure under preferential flow conditions, and proved that different pore-scale mechanisms resulted in the formation of the non-monotonic wettability effect for uniform and disordered pore structures. However, the study of multiphase flow in an evolving porous medium is still lacking, in which the interaction between multiphase flow dynamics and structural evolution remains unclear. The solid structural evolution, caused by dissolution and/or precipitation reaction, further complicates the reactive transport in porous media (Deng et al., 2018 ; Wang et al., 2022 ). The single-phase reactive transport in porous media with solid structural evolution has been extensively studied in the literature (Deng et al., 2018 ; Soulaine et al., 2017 ; Maheshwari et al., 2013 ; Deng et al., 2022 ). It was shown that the reactive transport process with mineral dissolution is controlled by many factors including injection rate, reactant properties, reaction kinetics, initial physical heterogeneity, chemical heterogeneity, and so on (Seigneur et al., 2019 ). Fortunately, using two dimensionless parameters, the Péclet (Pe ) number and Damköhler (Da ) number (Bekri et al., 1995 ), typical mineral dissolution regimes, such as compact (face) dissolution, uniform dissolution, conical wormhole dissolution, ramified wormhole dissolution, and dominant wormhole dissolution, were characterized either in experimental studies or numerical studies (Maheshwari et al., 2013 ; Hoefner and Fogler, 1988 ). Actually, the relative magnitude of Pe  and Da  reflects the competition between convection, diffusion and reaction, in which Pe  measures the relative strength of convection and diffusion, and Da  denotes the relative strength of reaction and diffusion (Bekri et al., 1995 ; Chen et al., 2014 ). Molins et al. (2020)  proposed a benchmark problem set for single-phase reactive transport with structural evolution, and remarkable agreement was obtained among five codes widely used in pore-scale studies, including Chombo-Crunch, OpenFoam-DBS, LBM, Vortex, and dissoFoam. Further, Dutka et al. (2020)  conducted an integrated set of microfluidic experiments and numerical simulations on a dissolving mineral cylindrical disk, and compared the time-dependent shapes both in experiments and simulations. They confirmed that the microfluidic experimental results can be predicted by the pore-scale reactive transport models under well-controlled conditions. Due to the disposable pore structure during the mineral dissolution process, the verified pore-scale reactive transport models may play a crucial role in deciphering the impacts of physical and chemical heterogeneities on reactive transport process, which are open interesting issues in this field. Al-Khulaifi et al. (2017 , 2019 ) conducted a reactive transport experiment using CO2 -saturated brine in a chemically heterogeneous rock composed of dolomite and calcite. The results showed that the heterogeneous flow characteristic in the upstream dolomite can change the dissolution pattern from uniform to preferential channeling in the downstream homogeneous calcite (Al-Khulaifi et al., 2017 ). Yang et al. (2020)  experimentally studied the dissolution processes of limestone with homogeneous, fractured, and vuggy pore structures by CO2 -saturated brine injection, and found that the dissolution became more nonuniform as the physical heterogeneity increases. Recently, Zhang et al. (2022)  evaluated the physical heterogeneity using the Euler number, and studied the mineral dissolution patterns with different Pe, Da  and Euler numbers. As a result, the diagram with six dissolution regimes for single-phase reactive flow was established. Further, Wang et al. (2022)  generated porous media with increasing physical heterogeneity quantified by standard deviation of local porosity, and provided the diagrams of dissolution patterns within different heterogeneous porous structures. To sum up, deep understanding of the single-phase reactive transport processes with solid structural evolution has been obtained in the literature, while the mystery of multiphase reactive flow in porous media with structural evolution remains elusive. What is the impact of nonaqueous phase on the interaction between diffusion, convection and reaction? How to construct a diagram for multiphase reactive flow with solid dissolution in porous media? To this end, much efforts need to be paid to improve our understanding of fundamental physics during the multiphase reactive transport processes with structural evolution. In fact, the simultaneous occurrence of multiphase flow and reactive transport processes in porous media is prevalent, and the related study is getting more and more attention. For example, during oil and gas stimulation process, the tight formation is saturated with oil or gas prior to acid invasion (Kumar et al., 2017 ). Likewise, in CO2  geological sequestration, the mineral dissolution arises in a CO2 -brine-rock environment (Jiménez-Martínez et al., 2020 ), or even a CO2 -brine-oil-rock system (Sha et al., 2022 ). Consequently, multiple interfaces including fluid-fluid interface and fluid-solid interface are evolved during the multiphase reactive transport process, which in turn greatly complicates the interplay and feedback mechanisms among multiphase flow, species transport, chemical reaction, and structural evolution (Song et al., 2014 ). Previous core-scale studies have found that the presence of an immiscible phase before acid injection would promote wormhole formation and reduce the breakthrough volume of injected acid (Babaei and Sedighi, 2018 ; Mahmoodi et al., 2018 ; Shukla et al., 2006 ). Recent experimental and numerical studies of reactive/nonreactive fluids co-injection into porous media have shown that the mineral dissolution became more homogeneous and the wormhole dissolution pattern was suppressed with the existence of nonreactive fluid (CO2  bubble) (Jiménez-Martínez et al., 2020 ; Ott and Oedai, 2015 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ). Such dissolution pattern was ascribed to the negative feedback between multiphase flow and structure evolution, while such feedback is positive in single-phase reactive transport processes leading to the formation of wormhole dissolution (Chen et al., 2014 ; Kang et al., 2003 ). In addition, as gaseous CO2  phase may be produced by acid-rock reaction, the mineral could be locally enveloped by gaseous CO2 , and the emergence of wormholes will be prevented (Song et al., 2018 ; Soulaine et al., 2018 ; Wei et al., 2024 ). Such interaction between nonreactive CO2  and mineral dissolution not only generates novel dissolution regimes, such as “nongaseous”, “gaseous breathing”, and “gaseous nonbreathing” (Xu and Balhoff, 2022 ), but also impacts accurate estimation of overall dissolution rate depending on surface-volume correlations in continuum-scale reactive transport modeling (Ling et al., 2022 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ). These studies imply that multiphase reactive flow in porous media is extremely intricate, and unfortunately the underlying interactions are not well understood. To probe the dynamic behaviors and interaction mechanisms during multiphase reactive flow, the experimental setups need to provide both real rock mineralogy and pore-scale real-time visualization (Song et al., 2014 ). To this end, geomaterial-functionalized microfluidic device is an attractive solution for multiphase reactive flow with interfacial phenomena (Zhang et al., 2020 ). The popular micromodel functionalization approaches used in multiphase reactive flow studies include geomaterial based chip-off-the-old-rock method (Jiménez-Martínez et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2014 ), surface coating/modification, microbially induced calcium carbonate precipitation (Song et al., 2018 ), and dissolution-after-precipitation method (Xu and Balhoff, 2022 ; Lee et al., 2016 ). Particularly, well-controlled initial samples with identical physicochemical properties are needed to conduct a parameter sensitivity analysis for revealing underlying mechanisms. Such a requirement for sample fabrication could be challenging, expensive and time consuming, due to the one-time use of the pore structure during mineral dissolution (Xu and Balhoff, 2022 ). From the literature review in multiphase flow in static porous media and single-phase reactive flow, the idea of computational microfluidics has emerged as a potential solution for multiphase reactive transport modeling (Zhao et al., 2019 ; Molins et al., 2020 ; Soulaine et al., 2021 ). Computational microfluidics is the digital counterpart of experimental microfluidics which solves the fundamental equations of continuum mechanics in complex geometries and intends to complement and augment laboratory experiments (Soulaine et al., 2021 ). The advantages of the computational microfluidics include (Ⅰ) the real heterogeneous porous media with exact microstructure can be directly employed to quantify the flow and transport processes, (Ⅱ) the multiphase reactive flow under extreme conditions, such as temperature and pressure that are difficult to operate in the laboratory without dedicated device, can be explored, and (Ⅲ) the validated numerical models can be easily combined with the digital rock physics technique for complex 3D modeling. With the tremendous progress in high-performance computing technology and high-resolution robust numerical algorisms (Deng et al., 2022 ; Ling et al., 2022 ; Datta et al., 2023 ), the computational microfluidics is expected to play an increasingly critical role in complementing laboratory experiments, understanding complex reactive transport process, and fostering practical engineering applications to a low-carbon future (Zhao et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ). In this work, a 3D computational microfluidic framework based on the LBM is proposed, and then reactive transport processes with solid dissolution and self-induced multiphase flow are comprehensively investigated in a microfluidic channel, a microfluidic porous chip and further a 3D digital core. The computational microfluidic framework can be extended to simulate the complex reactive transport processes coupled multiphase flow, interfacial mass transport, chemical reaction, solid dissolution/precipitation and structural evolution. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first 3D numerical study to investigate multiphase reactive flow with mineral dissolution, and the 3D effects will be discussed in the present study. By conducting a series of computational microfluidic simulations, the interactions between multiphase flow, species transport, chemical reaction and structural evolution are elucidated, and the variations of important structural and reactive parameters are quantified. Particularly, the interfacial area between the reactive fluid and solid will be quantitatively evaluated, which is believed to be one of the important factors explaining several orders of magnitude of significant difference between laboratory experiments and predictions of continuum-scale models (Zhou et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2008 ; Qin and Beckingham, 2021 ).The remaining of the study is arranged as follows. In Section 2 , the physicochemical process is introduced, and the computational microfluidic framework for the multiphase reactive flow based on the LBM is established. In Section 3 , the computational microfluidic studies of multiphase reactive flow in a channel, microfluidic porous chip, and digital core are conducted sequentially. Finally, in Section 4 , main conclusions in this study are summarized.  2 Methodology 2.1 Physicochemical problem The present study focuses on the multiphase reactive flow with mineral dissolution and bubble generation. To perform a computational microfluidic study, a dissoluble mineral is embedded in the chip with an inlet and an outlet. As shown in Fig. 1(a)   and (b ), the acidic brine is injected with constant flow rate, and then the chemical reaction occurs as the hydrogen ion in the solution contacts with the calcite (Soulaine et al., 2018 ). As a result, the solid is dissolved and the bubble may be generated (Song et al., 2018 ). Such chemical reaction can be expressed as follows(1) CaC O 3 ( s )    + 2 H  +   ( aq )   → C a  2 +    ( aq )   + C O 2 ( g )    + H 2  O ( l )        The secondary phase CO2  generated leads to the occurrence of the multiphase reactive transport process (Soulaine et al., 2018 ). In turn, the structural evolution and bubble movement will affect the reactive fluid transport, and thus various solid dissolution patterns will be formed. In a word, as shown in Fig. 1(a) , the multiphase flow, species transport, chemical reaction, and structural evolution are fully coupled and interacted with each other. For the heterogeneous chemical reaction given in Eq. (1) , the reaction kinetics r α  [mol/m2 ⋅s−1 ] is expressed as (Chen et al., 2014 )(22) r α  = k s  ( C R ( aq )    − C P ( aq )    / K eq   )      where C R  and C P  are the concentrations of reactant and product in the solution, herein hydrogen ion and calcium ion, respectively. k s  is the surface reaction rate constant and K eq  is the reaction equilibrium constant (Chen et al., 2014 ; Soulaine et al., 2018 ). At the fluid-solid interface, the reactant is consumed and the product is released during the mineral dissolution process. Such chemical reaction is implemented by the boundary conditions (Chen et al., 2014 )(23) D R ( aq )    ∂ C R ( aq )     ∂ n   = k s  ( C R ( aq )    − C P ( aq )    / K eq   )     D P ( aq )    ∂ C P ( aq )     ∂ n   = − k s  ( C R ( aq )    − C P ( aq )    / K eq   )         where the balance between diffusion flux and reaction flux is considered, and n  is the direction normal to the reactive surface and points to fluid. In addition, the CO2  and H2 O are both products of the reaction, and the corresponding source terms are expressed as (Chen et al., 2021 ; Guo et al., 2022 )(24) S C O 2    = 1 V  ∑ i = 1  6  ξ P  M P  J P  A =  1 V  ∑ i = 1  6  1 2  M C O 2    r α  A     S H 2  O   = 1 V  ∑ i = 1  6  ξ P  M P  J P  A  = 1 V  ∑ i = 1  6  1 2  M H 2  O   r α  A          where i  is indicator for the 6 surfaces of a cubic computational node in 3D, and V  is the total volume of node and A  is the reaction area of one face. ξ P  is stoichiometric coefficients, J P  is reaction flux determined by the surface reaction (Eq. (22) ), and M  is the molar mass. The mass increase caused by the solid reaction is responsible for the self-induced multiphase flow, which induces the phase separation for forming secondary phase.  2.2.4 Solid structure update The VOP method is used to update the volume change of solid dissolution, and expressed as follows (Kang et al., 2006 )(25) ∂ V M ( s )     ∂ t   = − A V  ‾  M ( s )    k s  ( C R ( aq )    − C P ( aq )    / K eq   )       With Eq. (25) , the solid volume at each solid node is updated at each time step using the time forward difference(26) V M ( s )    ( t + Δ  t )  = V M ( s )    ( t )  − A V  ‾  M ( s )    k s  ( C R ( aq )    − C P ( aq )    / K eq   )  Δ  t      In fact, The VOP method has been widely applied in the pore-scale reactive transport studies (Chen et al., 2015 ; Xu et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2019 ; Liu et al., 2020 ), which is also consistent with the porosity evolution equation in continuum-scale studies (Maheshwari et al., 2013 ; Jia et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2019 ; Panga et al., 2005 ). Once the volume of the solid node reduces to zero, the solid node is converted into a fluid node, and then the node information and distribution functions of the new fluid node are initialized (Chen et al., 2015 ; Chen et al., 2013 ). In this way, the moving fluid-solid interface during mineral dissolution process is tracked.   2.3 Computational microfluidics setup In order to perform a computational microfluidic study of multiphase reactive flow with mineral dissolution and bubble generation, three computational domains are employed to explore the dynamic behaviors and subsequent physical alterations during the reactive transport processes, including a microfluidic channel, a microfluidic porous chip, and a 3D digital core as shown in Fig. 1 (b-d). For the microfluidic channel (Fig. 1(b) ), the size is N x ×N y ×N z =320×160×16 lattices with the channel width of 50 lattices, representing a physical size of 3.2 × 1.6 × 0.16 mm3 . 20 additional lattices are fixed at the inlet and 100 additional lattices are added at the outlet. The size of the embedded cuboid dissolution mineral is 200×55×14 lattices. Similarly, for the microfluidic porous chip (Fig. 1(c) ), the size is N x ×N y ×N z =600×400×16 lattices, representing a physical size of 6.0 × 4.0 × 0.16 mm3 . 50 additional lattices are fixed at the inlet and 30 additional lattices are added at the outlet. The size of the porous chip domain is 520×400×14 lattices with an initial porosity of 0.56. At last, for the digital core structure reconstructed by packing spheres (Fig. 1(d) ), the size is N x ×N y ×N z =320×100×100 lattices, representing a physical size of 3.2 × 1.0 × 1.0 mm3 . The size of the porous packing region is 260×100×100 lattices with an initial porosity of 0.52. 40 additional lattices are fixed at the inlet and 20 additional lattices are added at the outlet. Additionally, all parameters used in the simulation are presented in lattice units, and the conversion between physical units and lattice units is listed in Table 1  . Consist with the experimental microfluidic setup, the boundary conditions are carefully implemented. At the inlet, the constant flow rate with constant concentration is fixed. The nonequilibrium extrapolation scheme is adopted for constant velocity boundary condition (Guo et al., 2002 ). The unknown concentration distribution function is obtained by minus the known distribution functions from the constant concentration. At the outlet, the outflow boundary is applied for the fluid flow and the fully developed boundary is set for the species transport. The convective boundary condition with second-order is employed for the co-outflow of multiphase fluids and the Neumann boundary condition is adopted for the fully developed boundary (Lou et al., 2013 ). The other sides of the computational domain are set as walls. Therefore, the no-slip boundary for fluid flow and no-flux boundary for mass transfer are implemented respectively. For the fluid-solid interface in the computation domain, the no-slip boundary is set for fluid flow. In particular, the reactive fluid-solid interface is the reactive boundary expressed by Eq. (23) , where Kang's scheme is applied (Kang et al., 2004 ). While, the nonreactive fluid-solid interface is no-flux boundary. The bounce back scheme is adopted for the no-slip boundary and no-flux boundary. The accuracy of the multiphase flow LB model and CST-LB model have been validated in our previous work (Zhang et al., 2024 ), and several additional validations are presented in the Supplementary material.   3 Results and discussion In an effort to unveil the complex interactions between multiphase flow, species transport, chemical reaction, bubble generation and structural evolution, the computational microfluidic studies of multiphase reactive flow coupled mineral dissolution and bubble generation in a simple channel, a microfluidic porous chip, and a digital core are conducted sequentially, as shown in Fig. 1.  Overall, the mineral dissolution patterns are the combined results of convection, diffusion and reaction, and two dimensionless numbers, Pe  and Da , are used to characterize the mineral dissolution patterns (Bekri et al., 1995 ; Hoefner and Fogler, 1988 ; Daccord et al., 1993 )(27) P e = u 0  l c   D     D a = k s  l c   D         where u 0  is the inflow velocity, l c  is the characteristic length, set as the channel width of 50 lattices. To account for the impact of reactant concentration on reactive transport, the dimensionless acid capacity number N ac  is introduced (Panga et al., 2005 ; Daccord et al., 1993 )(28) N ac  = C 0  V m   ‾       where C 0  is reactant concentration at the inlet. In addition, the Ca  number (Ca =u 0 ρν /σ ) and Reynolds number (Re =u 0 l c /ν ) are all provided, where ν  is the kinematic viscosity of inflow fluid and σ  is the interfacial tension (Lenormand et al., 1988 ). Both Ca  and Re  numbers are determined by inflow velocity in this study. It should be noted that the dimensionless numbers are used to characterize the initial setup of the simulation cases, and the magnitude of dimensionless numbers will change as the pore structure evolves during the multiphase reactive flow. 3.1 Multiphase reactive flow in a microfluidic channel First, to understand the complex interactions between convection, diffusion, reaction, bubble generation and mineral dissolution, multiphase reactive flow in a simple straight channel is studied with Pe  and Da  varied in the range of {0.01, 0.1, 1, 5, 10, 50}×{0.01, 0.1, 1, 5, 10, 50} by tuning values of u 0  and k s , leading to the corresponding Re  numbers as {0.003, 0.03, 0.3, 1.5, 3, 15} and Ca  numbers as {1.85×10−5 , 1.85×10−4 , 1.85×10−3 , 9.25×10−3 , 1.85×10−2 , 9.25×10−2 }, respectively. A total of 72 simulation cases are all listed in Table S1 in the Supplementary material. The above range of Pe  and Da  studied is relatively wide compared with existing studies (Zhang et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ). For example, in the experimental study of multiphase reactive flow of Xu and Balhoff (2022) , Pe  is set in the range of 0.0065∼11.2, and Da  is set in the range of 1.2∼76.36. Note that the reaction capacity computed by Eq. (28)  is N ac =0.038 and N ac =0.076, which has the same magnitude in continuum-scale study with N ac =0.05 and N ac =0.1 (Panga et al., 2005 ). The wider range in the present study is helpful for obtaining more comprehensive understanding of multiphase reactive flow and solid dissolution which are shown in Fig. 2  . 3.1.1 Coupling mechanism between multiphase reactive flow and solid dissolution From the viewpoint of solid structure evolution, the dissolution pattern can be roughly divided into two kinds, namely the uniform dissolution and wedge dissolution. Uniform dissolution indicates that compared with reaction, the mass transport (either by diffusion or convection) is much stronger (Zhou et al., 2022 ), leading to uniformly expanded channel as shown by the results under relatively low Da  in Fig. 2.  As the reaction gradually becomes stronger or as Da  increases, the supply of reactant to the channel downstream is suppressed as more reactant is consumed at the upstream, leading to reduced channel dissolution along the flow direction and generating the wedge dissolution pattern as shown in Fig. 2 . While the solid dissolution is roughly classified as uniform and wedge dissolution, the details of the solid dissolution still show difference caused by the secondary phase (green phase) generated. It can be found that both single-phase and two-phase reactive flow patterns can be obtained. The former one is generated under relatively low Da  (Da =0.01), because under such circumstance the secondary phase generated is too little to induce phase separation for forming bubbles. As reaction gradually becomes stronger, the secondary phase emerges in the domain (Da ≥0.1). Depending on the bubble generation rate and the flow rate in the domain, several interesting two-phase patterns can be observed, such as slug flow, film flow, bubble flow as well as transition flow pattern between the above different two-phase patterns. Under relatively high Da  and relatively low Pe  (Da ≥0.1 and Pe≤ 0.1), slug flow of the secondary phase is generated, as the convection is too weak to prevent the coalescence of bubbles from the side walls of the microchannel. The convection becomes gradually stronger as Pe  increases, where the bubbles generated on the side wall has no chance to contact with bubbles from the other side, leading to the formation of film flow (Pe =1). For extremely high Da  and Pe , bubble flow pattern can be observed, as the Pe  is extremely high which decreases the detachment size of the bubble, leading to the presence of discrete bubbles. In a word, the multiphase reactive flow affects both the mass transfer as well as the reactive surface area, and is more complex compared with the single-phase reactive transport processes. In addition, the reaction capacity of the reactive fluid will also affect the reactive transport process, while the current Pe  and Da  numbers cannot quantify the magnitude of reaction capacity. In other words, the reactant concentration determines the instantaneous reaction volume, and thus affects the structural evolution processes. It is reported that as acid was injected into a carbonate core with the same Pe  and Da  numbers, the complete dissociation hydrochloric acid (HCl, strong acid) produced the compact (face) dissolution, while the wormhole dissolution pattern was generated by CO2  saturated brine, namely partial dissociation H2 CO3  (weak acid) (Vafaie et al., 2023 ). Therefore, with the same Pe  and Da  settings in Fig. 2 , the simulations of multiphase reactive flow in the microfluidic channel with N ac  doubled as 0.076 are also implemented, as shown in Fig. S4 (see Supplementary material). It can be observed that the gas saturation (the fraction of pore volume occupied by the bubbles) increases due to the enhanced dissolution volume caused by the high concentration reactive fluid injected. Such two-phase dynamics will induce more serious blocking effect on species transport, and decrease the accessible reaction area. For example, at Pe =1 and N ac =0.038 with relatively high Da  numbers, the elongated bubbles extend along the solid surface (Fig. 2(a) ), acting as a barrier to preventing solid dissolution. Such similar temporary shielding effect of the bubble film on continuous dissolution was reported in the recent experimental microfluidic study of multiphase reactive flow in a fracture carbonate matrix (Zhou et al., 2023 ). Further, at N ac =0.076 under the same Da , much thicker film is generated which almost blocks the channel (see Supplementary material Fig. S4). In addition, it is noted that compared with the results with Da =0.01 in Fig. 2(a) , in Fig. S4 (see Supplementary material), the case with Pe =1 and Da =0.01 leads to the presence of two bubbles, while for other cases under Da =0.01 the secondary phase is absent. This clearly demonstrate the complicated interaction between convection, diffusion and reaction. A too low Pe  less than 0.1 cannot provide enough reactant for generating enough secondary phase to generate multiphase flow, while a too high Pe  will dilute the CO2  generated in the bulk fluid to prevent the formation of secondary phase.  3.1.2 Solid dissolution pattern The solid dissolution diagram under different Pe  and Da  was widely studied in the single-phase reactive transport studies (Bekri et al., 1995 ; Hoefner and Fogler, 1988 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ), and also recently studied in the experimental studies of multiphase reactive transport (Song et al., 2018 ; Xu and Balhoff, 2022 ). The characterized dissolution diagram can provide optimal injection rate to effectively stimulate the formation with minimum cost during oil and gas stimulation (Maheshwari et al., 2013 ). For CO2  geological sequestration, the different dissolution patterns will play important roles on storage capacity and security assessments. Recently, several dissolution patterns were summarized in the experimental microfluidic studies. For example, three distinct patterns, including single-phase dissolution at small acid fluxes, separate CO2  bubble generation at moderate acid fluxes, and stepwise dissolution with solid engulfed by separate CO2  phase at large acid fluxes, summarized by Song et al. (Song et al., 2018 ), as well as nongaseous, gaseous breathing, and gaseous nonbreathing regimes proposed by Xu and Balhoff (2022) . Therefore, in the present study, we try to propose such solid dissolution patterns considering the effects of multiphase reactive flow with wide range of Pe  and Da  studied, as shown in Fig. 3  . According to the results in Fig. 2 , six typical solid dissolution patterns for multiphase reactive transport are identified, including single-phase uniform dissolution, bubble-flow wedge dissolution, bubble-flow uniform dissolution, slug-flow wedge dissolution, slug-flow uniform dissolution, and film-flow wedge dissolution. In Fig. 3 , the single-phase region and multiphase region separated by the grey dotted line, as well as the wedge dissolution region and uniform dissolution region separated by the blue dotted line are clearly observed. In the multiphase region, slug-flow region (labeled by circle), film-flow region (labeled by square) and bubble-flow region (labeled by triangle) are further distinguished. Comparing the two diagrams in Fig. 3 , it can be found that similar dissolution patterns are obtained, while the transition regimes between different patterns may change. For example, for the case of Pe =1 and Da =1, a bubble-flow uniform dissolution is formed at N ac =0.038, while a bubble-flow wedge dissolution appears at N ac =0.076 under the same Pe  and Da , due to the increased bubble volume at higher reaction capacity which impedes reactant transfer to the downstream, and thus local upstream dissolution is enhanced. To the best of our knowledge, the pattern diagram proposed in Fig. 3  is the most comprehensive dissolution patterns for the multiphase reactive transport processes, with several new regimes identified.   3.2 Multiphase reactive flow in a microfluidic porous chip In this section, multiphase reactive flow in a microfluidic porous chip with relatively complex structures compared with the simple channel in Section 3.1  is further studied under different reactive transport conditions, namely (a) Pe =5, Da =10, (b) Pe =1, Da =10 and (c) Pe =1, Da =0.1. The initial porosity ϕ 0  is 0.56, and the simulation is terminated when the normalized porosity ϕ/ϕ 0  exceeds a critical value of 1.60. The normalized porosity ϕ/ϕ 0  is defined as the current porosity ϕ  during the reactive transport processes divided by the initial porosity ϕ 0 . The multiphase distributions and the corresponding reactant concentration distributions during multiphase reactive flow are displayed in Figs. 4   and S5 in the Supplementary material, respectively, where the normalized porosity ϕ/ϕ 0  and the corresponding total injection pore volume (PV) of reactive fluid are provided. It can be observed in Fig. 4(a)  that for the case of Pe =5 and Da =10, the gas saturation is relatively low during the continuous mineral dissolution process, because of the strong convection. Most of the domain is distributed with tiny bubbles, and only near the outlet large bubbles can be observed. The higher concentration of the reactant in preferential pathway with lower flow resistance clearly demonstrates the relatively stronger convection (see Supplementary material Fig. S5(a)). While bubbles of the secondary phase can be observed in the preferential pathway, bubbles also exist in the surrounding high-resistance porous regions with low fluid velocity, some of which are trapped inside the porous region, and the remaining are trapped by the top and bottom walls of the microfluidics. By reducing the relative strength of convection while maintaining the strength of reaction (Pe =1 and Da =10), generally the solid dissolution becomes more compact and the accumulation of the bubbles inside the domain occurs as shown in Fig. 4(b) , and the bubble size increases significantly compared with that in Fig. 4 (a). It can be found that the solid parts are seriously enveloped by the bubbles, thus completely separating the solid parts from the reactant species, which can be proved by the lower concentration of the reactant in the porous region in Fig. S5(b) (see Supplementary material). Compared with Fig. 4(b) , in Fig. 4(c)  the relative strength of the reaction is remarkably reduced with Da  as 0.1. Under such circumstance, the mass transfer is dominant compared with reaction, leading to more uniform distribution of the reactant concentration (see Supplementary material Fig. S5(c)). Large bubbles also can be observed in the domain and these large bubbles tend to distribute discretely in Fig. 4(c)  rather than connected to each other in Fig. 4 (b). This is exactly due to the more uniform distribution of the reactant and thus the corresponding secondary phase generated. Combining two-phase distribution and reactant concentration distribution, the three multiphase reactive flow cases can be regarded as bubble-flow wedge dissolution, film-flow wedge dissolution, and bubble-flow uniform dissolution patterns according to the diagram in Fig. 3(b) . In the few existing microfluidic studies of coupled two-phase reactive flow and solid dissolution processes (Song et al., 2018 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ; Xu and Balhoff, 2022 ), only the in-plane phenomena can be visualized while the observation of the out-of-plane (the thickness direction of the microfluidic) is difficult. Thanks to the 3D numerical simulation, such out-of-plane transport phenomena also can be explored. The porosity ϕ  and gas saturation S B  of each layer along Z -direction are displayed in Fig. 5  . The interesting phenomenon are that on the one hand, as shown in Fig. 5(a) , the gas saturation near the top and bottom of the microfluidic is higher than that in the middle, and the maximum discrepancy is 0.0147 presented in Pe =5 and Da =10. On the other hand, as shown in Fig. 5(a) , the porosity in the middle is higher than that near the top and bottom positions, and the maximum discrepancy is 0.0053 presented in Pe =5 and Da =10. To explain the above results, the bubble distributions along Z -direction at ϕ /ϕ 0  = 1.10 for Pe =1 and Da =10 case are displayed in Fig. 5(c)  as an example. It can be clearly observed that many tiny bubbles appear near the corners of the mineral and top/bottom plate, such as Z  = 2 or Z  = 15, while the tiny bubbles disappear gradually in the middle layers. It can be inferred that the reaction-induced bubbles firstly emerge at these corners where the convection is weak and the tiny bubble are concentrated. Then, the growing bubbles near the top and bottom positions coalesce to form large bubbles, moving in the pore space. Subsequently, the reactant transport is enhanced in the middle region, and thus facilitating the mineral dissolution as the zoom in insets of solid shown in Fig. 5 (c). As a result, the enhanced dissolution in the middle region and bubble enrichment near the top/bottom region are formed as shown in Fig. 5 . Such heterogeneous distributions of porosity and gas saturation overall become uniform at the later stage of solid dissolution as shown in Fig. 5  at ϕ /ϕ 0  = 1.50, but locally there may still exist remarkable disparity such as the porosity curve of Pe =5 and Da =10. However, such 3D heterogeneous distributions are difficult to characterize in the experimental microfluidic study, in which the solid grain is abstracted into a cylinder or a hemisphere depends on the basal area obtained from 2D images (Xu and Balhoff, 2022 ). The computational results of the heterogeneous distributions may initiate new insight to improve the porosity and saturation calculation method in experimental microfluidics. Compared with experiments, one of the advantages of the pore-scale simulation is its capacity to provide detailed distributions and evolutions of key variables such as velocity, pressure, concentration, saturation, solid volume as well as interfacial areas between different phases. Note that in the continuum-scale models for reactive transport processes in porous media, as the pore-scale transport processes are not directly resolved, several macroscopic transport properties are required to close the governing equations, such as permeability, effective mass diffusivity, effective thermal conductivity, etc. (Chen et al., 2022 ). Further for the chemical reaction, while at the pore-scale the actual reaction rate is expressed as k s C s , where C s  is the concentration at the fluid-solid interface which can be predicted in the pore-scale simulation (Xu et al., 2018 ). However, in the continuum-scale models, the averaged concentration C R   ‾    in a mesh is employed for calculating the reaction rate. Obviously, in a mesh C s  differs from C R   ‾   , thus the mass transfer coefficient k c  is usually adopted to take in account such difference (Panga et al., 2005 )(29) r a  ( C s  )  = k s  C s  = k c  ( C R   ‾  − C s   )       Thanks to the pore-scale simulation, k c  can be calculated using Eq. (29)  based on the pore-scale results (Panga et al., 2005 )(30) k c  = k s  C s   ( C R   ‾  − C s   )   = k s  ( C R   ‾   /  C s   − 1  )        Comparing k c  and k s , the reactive transport processes can be divided into the reaction limited process when k s  << k c , or transport limited process if k s  >> k c . In addition, the overall effective reaction rate r eff  can be calculated by (Menke et al., 2015 )(31) r eff  = 1 V m   ‾  A As    Δ  ϕ  Δ  t        where A As  is the specific interface area between the reactive fluid and solid, and Δϕ  is increase of the porosity due to solid dissolution in the time interval Δt . Thanks to the pore-scale simulation, the above two variables can be recorded during each simulation step. Fig. 6(a)   displays the comparison of mass transfer coefficient k c  and reaction rate constant k s , while Fig. 6(b)  shows the evolution of effective reaction rate r eff . It can be clearly observed that k s  is greater than k c  for the cases of Pe =5, Da =10 and Pe =1, Da =10, indicating transport limited process, while k s  is less than k c  for the case of Pe =1, Da =0.1, implying reaction limited process, consistent with Eq. (30) . It suggests that the consistent controlling mechanisms are identified by the relative magnitude of k s  and k c , or the dimensionless numbers of Pe  and Da . By comparing the first two cases with the same Da  (Da =10) but different Pe , it can be found that the magnitude of k c  is related to the Pe  number, that is, the larger Pe  is, the larger k c  is. This is because a higher Pe  can enhance mass transfer and thus reduce the difference between C s  and C R   ‾   . For the two cases with the same Pe  but different Da , at the early stage (ϕ/ϕ 0  < 1.14), due to the rapid dissolution induced lower C R   ‾   , k c  of case Da =10 is higher than that of Da =0.1, which decreases rapidly owing to the continuous bubble generation raising mass transfer resistance. In the middle stage of the multiphase reactive flow (1.14<ϕ/ϕ 0  < 1.4), the discrepancy of k c  between the two cases can be roughly neglected. At the later stage (ϕ/ϕ 0  > 1.4), k c  of case Da =10 is higher than that of case Da =0.1 again, due to the formation of the dissolution channel reducing the mass transfer resistance. It is worth mentioning that in continuum-scale modeling reactant concentration at solid surface C s  is required, which however is not directly resolved, to calculate the chemical reaction rate. Therefore, empirical expression of k c  is needed to determine C s  based on Eq. (29) . In fact, similar to the heat transfer coefficient h  in convective heat transfer problem which is expressed as the relationship between Nu  (Nusselt number, Nu =hl /λ  with l  as the character length and λ  as the thermal conductivity of fluid) and Re  number, k c  is determined by the relationship between Sherwood number (Sh ) and Pe  number or Re  number and Schmitt number (Sc ), in which Sh =k c l c /D , and Pe =ReSc  (Panga et al., 2005 ). The pore-scale results in Fig. 6(a)  can help to build such empirical relationship. Nevertheless, considering the complicated variations of k c  during the dynamic reactive transport processes, it looks like very challenging to propose a general formula for such empirical relationship under different Pe  and Da . Now attention is turned to the effective reaction rate r eff  displayed in Fig. 6 (b). Considering the mass transfer and reaction, measured by Pe  and Da  numbers respectively, the r eff  of case Pe =5 and Da =10 is largest, followed by case Pe =1 and Da =10, and finally the case Pe =1 and Da =0.1. Note that r eff  is a function of the specific reaction interface area between the reactive fluid and the solid, namely A As  as defined in Eq. (31) . Therefore, fluctuations of the variation of r eff  during the multiphase reactive flow process can be observed, as A As  also dynamically changes due to the multiphase flow as well as the solid dissolution. For the two cases with the same Pe  but different Da , since the Da  varies by one hundred times, one may expect that the effective reaction rate also varies by one hundred times. However, this is not the case as shown in Fig. 6(b)  where the difference between the two effective reaction rates is relatively lower of about three times (r eff ≈3.4 × 10−5  at Pe =1 and Da =10, r eff ≈1.0 × 10−4  at Pe =1 and Da =0.1), and the two values even quite close at early stage of solid dissolution (ellipse region in Fig. 6 (b)). This is due to the mass transport limitation as well as the multiphase coverage. Al-Khulaifi et al. (2019)  conducted an experimental study of single-phase reactive transport in a multimineral carbonate mainly consisting of dolomite and calcite, in which the initial Da  number of calcite was two orders of magnitude higher than that of dolomite, however, the r eff  of them is in the same order of magnitude due to the mass transport limitations in the higher heterogeneous pore space. Herein, the reduced discrepancy of reff  shown in Fig. 6(b)  is ascribed to the mass transfer limitations caused by solid as well as nonreactive secondary phase under multiphase circumstance. As discussed above, the A As  plays an important role on the effective reaction rate which is of engineering interest. Therefore, the variation of A As  is further provided. In fact, in the continuum-scale models, the empirical relationship of A As  is also required for closing the continuum-scale governing equations (Emmanuel and Berkowitz, 2005 ). The ratio between A As  and A fs , which is called contact efficiency f , can be related to the saturation of the reactive fluid S A  (Wei et al., 2017 ).(32) f = A As  A fs   = a ( S A  − b  )   c       where a, b , and c  are fitting parameters. Note that A As  is the interfacial area between the reactive fluid and the solid, while A fs  describes the total interfacial area between the fluid and the solid. Since the secondary phase is not reactive, A fs  is higher than A As  as part of the solid surface is covered by the secondary phase. A fs  can be obtained by the following correlation (Steefel et al., 2005 )(33) A fs  A fs 0    = ϕ ϕ 0   ( ϕ 0  ( 1 − ϕ )   ϕ ( 1 − ϕ 0   )    )   β      where the script 0 refers to the initial values before reaction, and β  is pore cementing parameter. Hence, combining Eqs. (32) and (33) , A As  can be predicted after two steps of fitting(34) A As  = a A fs 0   ϕ ϕ 0   ( ϕ 0  ( 1 − ϕ )   ϕ ( 1 − ϕ 0   )    )   β  ( S A  − b  )   c             Fig. 7   displays the relationship between specific interface area, porosity and saturation in the microfluidic porous chip studied in the present study. First, for the contact efficiency-saturation relationship shown in Fig. 7(b) , it can be observed that the original correlation with a  = 1.02, b  = 0, and c  = 0.244 overestimates the current results (Wei et al., 2017 ), and such correlation was proposed in the study of porous-packing trickle-bed reactors (El-Hisnawi et al., 1982 ). What's more, different dissolution patterns have important impact on the contact efficiency, and thus three sets of fitting parameters are recommended to correlate the relationship between contact efficiency and saturation. For the case of Pe =5, and Da =10, the fitting parameters are a  = 1.981, b  = 0.913 and c  = 0.287. For the case of Pe =1, and Da =10, the fitting parameters are a  = 1.527, b  = 0.763 and c  = 0.291. For the case of Pe =1, and Da =0.1, the fitting parameters are a  = 1.567, b  = 0.590 and c  = 0.505. It can be found that a higher Pe  and/or a higher Da  leads to smaller contact efficiency f  which indicates that the solid surface is more seriously covered by the secondary phase. Again, from the results in Fig. 7(b) , it can be observed that it is really challenging, if possible, to propose a general formula for the contact efficiency f  under different reactive transport conditions or different Pe  and Da . In fact, in the literature, even for single-phase reactive transport process, there have been attempts to propose a general relationship for the effective transport properties or statistical structural parameters during the solid dissolution (Soulaine et al., 2017 ; Chen et al., 2014 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ). However, due to the complicated mechanisms of solid dissolution under different reactive transport conditions, to date there has been no such general relationship proposed. Thus, alternatively, researchers even turn to machine learning to predict the values of the effective transport properties or statistical structural parameters during the complicated dissolution processes (Wang et al., 2022 ). Then, for the specific interface area-porosity relationship shown in Fig. 7(a) , as multiphase reactive flow processes, the porosity increases and the specific interface area between fluid and solid decreases. The fitting parameter β =0.895 is suggested for all the cases. Finally, A As  can be predicted using Eq. (34)  with the acquired two-steps fitting parameters. As shown in Fig. 7(a) , the predicted A As  is roughly consistent with the simulation results, indicating the present correlations can be used in the continuum-scale multiphase reactive transport modeling.  3.3 Multiphase reactive flow in a digital core While the numerical studies in Sections 3.1 ∼3.2  are of great help for understanding the underlying coupling mechanisms between multiphase reactive flow and solid dissolution as well as the variations of important parameters, in this section the pore-scale study is further extended to a 3D digital core shown in Fig. 1(d)  with the same Pe -Da  numbers in Section 3.2 . The evolutions of the bubble dynamics and reactant concentration distributions during multiphase reactive flow with solid dissolution in the digital core are shown in Fig. 8   and Fig. 9  , respectively. It can be observed that for the case of Pe =5 and Da =10, the discrete bubbles induced by continuous dissolution are migrated in the porous structure. With relatively high Pe  and Da  numbers, a preferential dissolution channel is gradually formed, in which the reactant is enriched and transported rapidly at later stage of mineral dissolution. For the case of Pe =1 and Da =10, due to the decreased inflow velocity, which leads to relatively weak convection and reduced reactant supply, the gas saturation increases and the reactant concentration distribution becomes more compact. At last, for the case of Pe =1 and Da =0.1, the reduced reaction rate renders residual reactant to be transported deeper, forming a more uniform concentration distribution. As a result, more uniform mineral dissolution pattern is generated although the gas saturation is relatively high. During the multiphase reactive transport process, both the solid dissolution and bubble generation are evolving continuously. As shown in Fig. 10  , the pore size distribution (PSD) and bubble characteristics corresponding to Fig. 8  are further analyzed. The PSD of initial structure (ϕ/ϕ 0  = 1.00 in Fig. 10(a–c) ) is unimodal and approximately follows a normal distribution. It can be clearly observed that the PSD presents remarkable difference during solid dissolution with different Pe  and Da  numbers. In detail, for the case of Pe =5 and Da =10 shown in Fig. 10(a) , an initial unimodal PSD is gradually transformed into a bimodal distribution at 1.20≤ϕ/ϕ 0  ≤ 1.40 because of the occurrence of dissolved pore, and finally a trimodal distribution is formed at ϕ/ϕ 0  = 1.60 because of the formation of preferential dissolution channel. For the case of Pe =1 and Da =10 shown in Fig. 10(b) , a bimodal PSD is obtained in the compact dissolution, in which the left peak mainly ascribed to the original pore at the downstream goes down, while the right peak induced by the upstream dissolved pore goes up, indicating the dissolved pore is enlarging during the solid dissolution process. At last, for the case of Pe =1 and Da =0.1 shown in Fig. 10(c) , the unimodal PSD is maintained in the uniform dissolution pattern, but the range of PSD extends, meaning the mean and the standard deviation increase. In addition, the bubble characteristics during the multiphase reactive flow process are quantified, as shown in Fig. 10 (d –f ), including number, volume, surface area, and shape factor of discrete bubble clusters. The shape factor describes the regularity degree of bubble cluster shapes, defined as (Lv et al., 2023 )(35) S F = A  3  36 × π × V  2        where A  is the surface area, and V  is the volume of discrete bubble clusters. SF  is equal to 1 for a perfect sphere and not equal to 1 for other irregular shapes. The shape factor is normalized as log(SF )+1.0 shown in Fig. 10(d–f) . As shown in Fig. 10(d)  for the case of Pe =5 and Da =10, taken ϕ/ϕ 0  = 1.05 as an example, it can be counted that 73 green round bubble symbols are presented, meaning there are 73 discrete bubble clusters existed in Fig. 8(a)  at ϕ/ϕ 0  = 1.05, and the volume of each bubble as well as the shape factor denoted by the size of the green round bubble symbols are calculated. For example, the volumes of the maximum and minimum bubbles are 11,200 and 21, the corresponding normalized shape factors are 2.10 and 0.27 respectively, and the total bubble volume at ϕ/ϕ 0  = 1.05 is 83,048. Furthermore, for the case of Pe =5 and Da =10, it can be observed that many discrete bubbles grow and link together, forming huge bubble clusters with increased total bubble volume during the multiphase reactive transport process. While for the other two cases shown in Fig. 10 (e , f ), due to the relatively weak convection at Pe =1.0, a huge bubble cluster is formed quickly and accounts a dominant share of the total bubble volume. Such huge bubble cluster occupies numerous pores and envelopes a large amount of residual solid, with a normalized shape factor exceeding 3.0. Comparing the three images in Fig. 10 (e -f ), generally a high Pe  will lead to relatively dispersed distribution of bubbles while bubbles tend to coalesce into large bubbles as Pe  decreases. In this study, the digital core is sliced into 5 equal-sized layers along mainstream direction, as shown in Fig. 8 (a). Then, the multiphase reactive flow on each layer is tracked as follows (Parmigiani et al., 2011 )(36) ϕ i *  = ϕ i  − ϕ i , min    ϕ i , max   − ϕ i , min         where ϕi   is the porosity of the i th layer during the multiphase reactive flow, ϕi  ,min  and ϕi  ,max  are the minimum and maximum porosity of the i th layer, namely the porosity of the initial porous structure and the porosity at last moment with all dissoluble mineral dissolved of each layer, respectively. Fig. 11   displays the evolutions of ϕ i *    during multiphase reactive flow in the digital core corresponding to Fig. 8 , in which the horizontal axis PV/PVf  is the normalized pore volume of injected reactive fluid with PVf  as the PV at ϕ/ϕ 0  = 1.60. The interesting discrepancy among different cases is the onset of dissolution and porosity increase pattern of each layer under different reactive transport conditions. For example, in the case of Pe =1 and Da =10 shown in Fig. 11(b) , as the first layer is almost dissolved with ϕ l *    over 0.8, the onset of dissolution of the second layer starts. Such pattern is repeated on the remaining layers. When the overall porosity is ϕ/ϕ 0  = 1.60, the last layer is still intact. Such dissolution characteristics of each layer suggests a compact dissolution pattern for the case of Pe =1 and Da =10. While in the case of Pe =1 and Da =0.1 shown in Fig. 11(c) , the onset of dissolution on each layer emerges early as PV/PVf  is over 0.3. Although mineral dissolution volume at the upstream is higher than that of the downstream, the residual dissoluble mineral is remained near the inlet when the overall porosity is ϕ/ϕ 0  = 1.60. Thus, a uniform dissolution pattern is generated in this case. In contrast, as shown in Fig. 11(a) , for the case of Pe =5 and Da =10, the onset of dissolution time is between the above two cases shown in Fig. 11(b)  and (c ), and the formation of preferential dissolution channel reduces the dissolution rate at the downstream (layers 3–5) because of concentrated reactant transport in the preferential dissolution channel. Compared with the heat transfer dominated melting process with injection of superheated invading fluid in Ref. Parmigiani et al. (2011) , in which the melting process started almost at the same time on each subregion due to heat transfer takes place both in solid and fluid, and finished with all meltable solid vanished in the upstream, there are complicated interactions between multiphase flow, mass transfer, and solid dissolution existing in present multiphase reactive flow, inducing various evolutions of normalized subregion porosity as show in Fig. 11 . In the end, as shown in Fig. 12  , the mass transfer and reaction metrics during multiphase reactive flow in the 3D digital core are discussed. Fig. 12(a)  shows the evolutions of overall normalized porosity ϕ/ϕ 0  and specific reactive interface area A As . It can be observed that during the mineral dissolution process, the increase of ϕ/ϕ 0  is fastest for the case of Pe =1 and Da =10, followed by case Pe =5 and Da =10, and finally the case Pe =1 and Da =0.1. This is because the relative comparable effects of convection and diffusion at Pe =1, and the higher Da , resulting in rapid mineral dissolution. Besides, strong convection at Pe =5 induces discrete bubble distributions with a lower gas saturation (Figs. 8(a)  and 10(d) ), and thus a higher reactive fluid-solid interface area A As  is observed at early stage of multiphase reactive flow. Then, the A As  decreases rapidly, even lowest among the three cases shown in Fig. 12(a) , due to the increasing bubble clusters link together and envelope residual solid at the later stage with the formation of preferential dissolution channel. In contrast, for the other two cases, the same Pe  has similar reactant delivery and bubble transport capacity (Fig. 10(e)  and (f )), thus the evolution of A As  shows a small discrepancy, whereas the case of Pe =1 and Da =10 has a slightly lower A As  because of the higher bubble generation rate. Similar to the discussion in Section 3.2 , then the mass transfer coefficient is shown in Fig. 12 (b). Either comparing the relative strength of diffusion, convection and reaction quantified by Pe  and Da  numbers, or comparing the metrics of mass transfer coefficient k c  and reaction rate constant k s , the consistent results of dominant mechanisms in the multiphase reactive flow can be obtained, as shown in Fig. 12 (b). In detail, the cases of Pe =5, Da =10 and Pe =1, Da =10 are transport limited processes, while the case of Pe =1, Da =0.1 is a reaction limited process. Due to the breakthrough of the preferential dissolution channel with reduced mass transfer resistance in case of Pe =5, Da =10 (Fig. 9(a) ), the k c  increases at the later stage of multiphase reactive flow. For the cases of Pe =1, Da =10, and Pe =1, Da =0.1, the same Pe  number induces the roughly equal mass transfer coefficient as ϕ/ϕ 0  > 1.20. It is observed that a sudden fluctuation of k c  occurs in cases of Pe =1, Da =10, since nonreactive bubbles detach rapidly from mineral into dissolved pore space. Finally, the effective reaction rate during the multiphase reactive flow in a digital core is analyzed shown in Fig. 12 (c). It can be found that for the two cases with the same Pe  number and different Da  numbers, the evolutions of effective reaction rate r eff  have similar trends with the evolution of k c , indicating presence of nonreactive bubbles significantly influences the reactive transport processes. However, for the case of Pe =5 and Da =10, the evolution of r eff  is obviously different from the other two cases. The r eff  increases quickly as ϕ/ϕ 0  is over 1.40, due to the reduced reactive surface area caused by bubble coalescence of increasing discrete bubbles (Fig. 10(d)  at ϕ/ϕ 0  = 1.40). Then, the increasing nonreactive clusters engulf partial mineral, preventing the mineral from being dissolved. Consequently, with the strong convection and reaction, such two-phase distribution renders the reactant delivery deeper, contributing to the formation of preferential dissolution channel (Fig. 9(a)  at ϕ/ϕ 0  = 1.50). It can be confirmed by the evolution of r eff ⋅A AS , derived from Eq. (31)  asr eff  · A As  = Δ  ϕ  / V m   ‾  Δ  t      , denoting the rate of overall porosity change during solid dissolution, where r eff ⋅A AS  decreases dramatically due to limited reaction as the preferential dissolution channel formed. Notably the similar formula of Δ  ϕ  / Δ  t     was employed to calculate the mineral dissolution rate in a recent multiphase reactive flow microfluidic study, in which the effects of reaction area are lumped into a correction factor (Zhou et al., 2023 ). The completely opposite trends of r eff  and r eff ⋅A AS  at later stage of multiphase reactive flow implies that the reaction area estimation plays a pivotal role in explaining the significant discrepancy of reaction rate with several orders of magnitude between laboratory and field (Li et al., 2008 ; Qin and Beckingham, 2021 ).   4 Conclusions In this study, a computational microfluidic framework is established to study the pore-scale multiphase reactive flow with mineral dissolution and secondary phase generation, which has potential to complement the experimental microfluidics widely used in relevant research areas. The complicated multiple physicochemical processes including multicomponent multiphase flow, interfacial mass transport, heterogeneous chemical reaction, and solid dissolution induced structural evolution are taken into account. Using the computational microfluidic model, the multiphase reactive flow processes in a simple channel, a microfluidic porous chip, and finally a 3D digital core are systematically explored to reveal the interaction and feedback mechanisms between reactive transport and solid dissolution in the framework of multiphase flow. The main conclusions are as follows.(1) A diagram of multiphase reactive transport considering solid structure evolution and flow characteristics in a simple channel is established, in which several dissolution patterns are identified, including single-phase uniform dissolution, bubble-flow wedge dissolution, bubble-flow uniform dissolution, film-flow wedge dissolution, slug-flow wedge dissolution, and slug-flow uniform dissolution.  (2) For multiphase reactive flow in a microfluidic porous chip, the interesting 3D heterogeneous distributions, including the enhanced dissolution in the middle region and bubble enrichment near the top/bottom region are discovered. The transport limited cases of Pe =5, Da =10, and Pe =1, Da =10, as well as reaction limited case of Pe =1, Da =0.1 are obtained using the relative magnitude of reaction rate constant and mass transfer coefficient. The mass transfer limitation caused by solid and secondary phase reduces the effective reaction rate discrepancy between the cases with Da  of one hundred times. Further, the correlation for reaction area prediction using porosity and saturation is proposed, in which the relationships between contact efficiency and saturation depending on different dissolution patterns are quantified.  (3) For the multiphase reactive flow in a digital core, pore structure evolution and bubble characteristics are quantified under different reactive transport conditions. The different dissolution patterns are recognized with the evolution of normalized subregion porosity. The same Pe  number provides similar reactant delivery and bubble transport capacity, and thus the similar mass transfer coefficient and effective reaction rate. While in turn, the increased secondary phase volume can reduce the reaction area and impede the solid dissolution.
1 Introduction Waves, tides and storm surges cause highly dynamic conditions in the coastal zone that result in mixing of terrestrial groundwater and seawater. The subsurface mixing zone has been termed ‘Subterranean Estuary’ (STE) (Moore, 1999 ). STEs were intensively studied over the past two decades because they have the potential for biogeochemical transformation of solute species prior to discharge (Slomp and van Capellen, 2004 ; Kroeger and Charette, 2008 ). Hence, it is believed that they play a major role for chemical fluxes from land to sea, which ultimately discharge via ‘submarine groundwater discharge’(SGD) to the coastal oceans (Burnett et al., 2003 ; Windom et al., 2006 ; Hays and Ullman, 2007 ; Anschutz et al., 2009 ). The physical behavior of STEs and the response to oceanic forcings has been addressed by several studies. They generally show that sandy STEs are characterized by an upper saline plume in the intertidal zone (USP; also referred to as ‘intertidal recirculation cell’), which overlays a fresh/brackish discharge tube that pinches out at the low water line (Michael et al., 2005 ; Robinson et al., 2006 , 2007 ; Greskowiak, 2014 ; Beck et al., 2017 ; Kuan et al., 2019 ). The flow regime in the STE is governed by hydrogeological factors, such as surface slope, hydraulic conductivity, geological heterogeneity, terrestrial freshwater inflow and oceanic forcings (Robinson et al., 2018 ). Depending on the latter, the conventional picture of flow and transport in the STE may change, and more than one USPs might develop (Grünenbaum et al., 2020 ). Yet, the flow regime in the STE is likely more dynamic as suggested by the conventional picture of STEs if spatio-temporal variations, e.g., a variable beach topography and seasonal floodings, play a role (Greskowiak and Massmann, 2021 ). The biogeochemical functioning of STEs is linked to the physical flow characteristics. High loads of labile (marine) organic matter (OM) via infiltrating seawater promote the reactivity of STEs (Charbonnier et al., 2013 ; Kim et al., 2020 ; Rakhimbekova et al., 2022 ), the sediments of which are usually poor in organic carbon (e.g., Boudreau et al., 2001 ; Seibert et al., 2019a ). USPs are hotspots for biogeochemical reactions due to large volumetric fluxes, forced by waves and tides, and associated supply of OM, nutrients, oxygen and other electron acceptors. Aerobic respiration (Charbonnier et al., 2013 ), denitrification (Kim et al., 2017 ) and iron oxide reduction (Reckhardt et al., 2015 ) are dominant redox processes along flow paths in the STE. In addition, the seasonality of the seawater endmember composition may cause fluctuating redox conditions and process rates over the year (Charbonnier et al., 2013 ; O'Connor et al., 2018 ; Ahrens et al., 2020 ). Mixing of different water endmembers in the STE triggers a series of geochemical reactions. If fresh groundwater equilibrated with calcite and high PCO2  mixes with calcite-supersaturated seawater, calcite dissolution can occur, a process also known as ‘mixing corrosion’ (Bögli, 1978 ; Appelo and Postma, 2005 ). Mixing-induced carbonate reactions may ultimately change the carbonate chemistry of SGD and even alter aquifer properties (Sanford and Konikow, 1989 ). Moreover, reduced species in anoxic groundwater, such as dissolved manganese (Mn2+ ) and dissolved iron (Fe2+ ), will further react with oxygenated seawater to form metal oxides (Spiteri et al., 2006 ; McAllister et al., 2015 ). The process of mixing-induced precipitation of iron oxides in the STE has been termed ‘iron curtain’ formation, since it may act as a barrier for dissolved species, including phosphorous (P) (Charette and Sholkovitz, 2002 ; Spiteri et al., 2008b ), trace metals and organic compounds (Linkhorst et al., 2017 ; Sirois et al., 2018 ) due to co-precipitation, adsorption or surface complexation. Phosphorous can further be removed from solution by formation of hydroxyapatite and vivianite (Slomp and Van Capellen, 2004 ; Seibert et al., 2021 ) or be sequestered as surface complexes on iron oxides (Dzombak and Morel, 1990 ; Spiteri et al., 2008b ). The formation of iron sulfides caused by the reaction of dissolved sulfide (HS- ) with Fe2+  or iron oxides presents another important process in the STE (Roy et al., 2013 ; McAllister et al., 2015 ; Reckhardt et al., 2015 ; Seibert et al., 2019a ,b). Vice versa, (reductive) dissolution of the latter minerals may act as source for dissolved solutes, such as trace metals (Reckhardt et al., 2021 ). In contrast to the many field-based research efforts, the number of studies applying reactive transport modeling (RTM) to constrain chemical reactions and quantify solute fluxes in the STE is limited. Spiteri et al. (2008a)  were among the first to apply a RTM approach to a STE, simulating species transport in Waquoit Bay, USA. Their reaction network accounted for aerobic respiration, denitrification (also via Fe2+  and pyrite), iron oxide reduction, nitrification, Fe2+  oxidation, P adsorption to iron oxides, pyrite oxidation as well as hydroxyapatite formation. They demonstrated that nutrient dynamics in their investigated STE were governed by denitrification and P sorption. They also found that biogeochemical reactions were strongly dependent on model set-up and aquifer parameters, such as hydrodynamic dispersion and groundwater flow rates. It is worth noting that the effect of pH was not explicitly regarded in the kinetic RTM approach by Spiteri et al. (2008a) , which served as basis for several subsequent RTM studies. An overview of key studies that advanced the understanding of the STE biogeochemistry by integrating RTM approaches are presented in the following. Anwar et al. (2014)  investigated the impact of dynamic oceanic forcings (i.e., tides and waves) on species transport, redox reactions and dissolved OM (DOM) degradation in a STE. Their kinetic reaction network was based on Spiteri et al. (2008a ,b), focusing on aerobic respiration, denitrification/nitrification as well as iron oxidation and P sorption. Subsequently, Heiss et al. (2017)  assessed the physical control of oceanic forcings as well as hydrogeologic factors on mixing-dependent (denitrification) and mixing-independent (microbial sulfate, SO4 2- , reduction) reactions. Kim et al. (2017)  conducted a field study on the biogeochemistry of a STE in Cape Henlopen, Delaware, and supported aerobic and denitrification zones observed in the field with a RTM approach, accounting for aerobic respiration and denitrification. Moreover, Kim et al. (2020)  explored the contribution of particulate organic carbon (POC) to the biogeochemical STE reactivity, employing a kinetic RTM approach including aerobic respiration and denitrification. The effect of groundwater and seawater temperature on nitrate (NO3 - ) removal in a STE was explored in a study by Cogswell and Heiss (2021) . Rakhimbekova et al. (2022)  expanded the work by Anwar et al. (2014) , focusing on the role of time-varying wave conditions for species transport (aerobic respiration and denitrification) in a STE. More recently, Greskowiak et al. (2023)  showed that the redox zonation of a sandy STE, represented by RTMs accounting for dynamic model boundaries, was primarily a function of varying beach topography as well as seasonal storm floods. While the aforementioned RTM studies considerably advanced the understanding of the biogeochemical functioning of STEs, they employed kinetic reaction networks, where the effects of pH, pe, ion activity or mineral saturation on species concentrations, e.g., via precipitation/dissolution of minerals or complexation of dissolved species to charged surfaces, were usually disregarded or only considered in a more simplified manner (e.g., Spiteri et al., 2008a ,b; Anwar et al., 2014 ; Heiss et al., 2017 ; Kim et al., 2020 ). A lower degree of complexity, faster simulation run times as well as increased numerical stability are in favor of purely kinetic modeling approaches. However, a more realistic representation of the complex and non-linear hydrogeochemical processes in the STE may be obtained when employing comprehensive RTM, integrating the aforementioned species and processes. We hypothesize that mineral reactions as well as surface complexation exert important influences on the STE biogeochemistry. Hence, neglecting these processes upfront in modeling studies could potentially lead to wrong outcomes. The aim of this study was to test if and how OM degradation, mineral reactions (calcite, goethite, siderite, iron sulfide (FeS(ppt)), vivianite and hydroxyapatite) as well as surface complexation play a role for the fluxes of dissolved oxygen (DO), NO3 - , ammonium (NH4 + ), dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), Fe2+ , HS-  and PO4 3- . For this purpose, a comprehensive RTM approach, i.e., accounting for the effects of pH, pe, ion activity, mineral equilibria and surface complexation, was applied to a STE setting. Separate model variants for a generic, idealized sandy STE were developed to determine the relative importance of the different reactions on the transport and fate of selected species as well as to derive flux and budget estimates, which is important to assess the source/sink characteristics of STEs. Parametrization of the generic RTMs was partly based on an unconfined sandy nearshore coastal aquifer on Spiekeroog Island, Germany (Beck et al., 2017 ; Seibert et al., 2018 , 2019 b; Grünenbaum et al., 2020 ; Greskowiak et al., 2023 ). The conclusions of this study contribute to a better understanding of the biogeochemical functioning of STEs in sandy beaches and raise awareness for the important role of RTM for an improved process understanding. Note, however, that our generic models are not directly comparable to field observations from a specific STE field site. Moreover, the assessment of physical controls on biogeochemistry, such as time-varying waves, tides, storm floods or topography changes, was beyond the scope of this study.  2 Material and methods 2-D numerical models were developed, representing a cross sectional transect perpendicular to the shore of a sandy high-energy beach. Parametrization of the models was partly based on previous studies conducted at an unconfined sandy nearshore coastal aquifer on Spiekeroog Island, Germany (Beck et al., 2017 ; Holt et al., 2019 ; Grünenbaum et al., 2020 ; Greskowiak and Massmann et al., 2021 ; Greskowiak et al., 2023 ). In a first step, variable-density groundwater flow and salt transport were simulated using the software package SEAWAT v.4.0 (Langevin et al., 2008 ), which couples the software packages MODFLOW (Harbaugh et al., 2000 ) and MT3DMS (Zheng and Wang, 1999 ). Subsequently, the reactive transport was simulated based on the SEAWAT-generated flow fields, applying the software package PHT3D v2.17 (Prommer and Post, 2010 ). PHT3D couples MT3DMS to the hydrogeochemical software PHREEQC (Parkhurst and Appelo, 1999 ). Model construction was carried out using the Python packages FloPy (Bakker et al., 2016 ) and PHT3D-FSP (Seibert and Greskowiak, 2024 ). All simulations were run on the high-performance computing cluster ROSA at the University of Oldenburg. 2.1 Groundwater flow and transport model Models consisted of 60 layers and 200 columns (Fig. 1  ). Horizontal and vertical extents were 500 m and ∼44 m (left boundary) to ∼36 m (right boundary), respectively. The dune base with an elevation of 4.08 masl served as x origin, following Grünenbaum et al. (2020) . The beach surface was linearly sloping from 4.08 masl to -4.12 masl (beach slope ∼1:60), and the aquifer base was assumed at -40 masl (Holt et al., 2019 ; Grünenbaum et al., 2020 ). Models had a horizontal discretization of 2.5 m. The vertical cell size was increasing geometrically from 0.1 to max. 2.45 m over depth. Ocean high, mean and low water lines were located at 1.36, 0 and -1.36 masl, characterizing the site as mesotidal with an average tidal range of 2.72 m (annual means from 1995 to 2015, Federal Waterways and Shipping Administration [WSV], 2017 ). Fresh groundwater inflow into the models was realized using the MODFLOW WEL package, i.e., a Neumann-type constant-flux boundary (second-type boundary), which was assigned to all model models cells in the first column located below 1.00 masl (Fig. 1 ). Rates of each WEL boundary cell were related to the cell thickness, so that the total inflow via all WEL boundary cells corresponded to 0.5 m3  d-1  m-1  shoreline, i.e., the average terrestrial freshwater discharge at Spiekeroog (Beck et al., 2017 ). Interaction with the sea was realized applying the MODFLOW CHD package, i.e., a Dirichlet-type boundary (first-type boundary), which was assigned to the top cell of each column at all locations below 1.36 masl (mean high water, Fig. 1 ). The tide phase-averaged head approach was used for the prescribed CHD heads, following Grünenbaum et al. (2020) , Greskowiak and Massmann (2021)  and Greskowiak et al. (2023) . Thereby, the effect of tides on the flow regime in the STE was approximated by averaging groundwater heads over a tidal cycle. The advantage of this approach is that the overall effect of tides on groundwater heads can be replicated without the need to temporally resolve tidal dynamics, which would be computationally heavier. For salt transport, non-dispersive flux boundaries were assigned at all WEL and CHD boundary locations, using salinities of 0.3 and 32 g TDS L-1  for inflowing fresh groundwater and seawater, respectively. Groundwater flow and salt transport models were parametrized as shown in Table 1  . The simulation time for each model was 60 years, after which a quasi-steady-state situation (“dynamic equilibrium”) for the salt transport was reached. Seawater salinities (32 g TDS L-1 ) were used as initial concentrations.  2.2 Chemical reaction model The developed reaction network consisted of two sub-types of hydrogeochemical reactions: (i) primary redox reactions, i.e., consumption of electron acceptors coupled to the degradation of organic matter, and (ii) secondary reactions, i.e., nitrification of NH4 +  to NO3 - , mineral equilibria as well as surface complexation. Separate model variants were constructed to explore the individual effects of the different reactions on the modeled hydrogeochemistry (see Section 2.3 ). Degradation of OM was implemented using the ‘Partial Equilibrium Model’ approach (Postma and Jakobsen, 1996 ), where degradation is divided into a rate-controlled fermentative step and a fast electron accepting step that approaches equilibrium. Hence, it was assumed that OM (i.e., CH2 O(NH3)0.151 (H3 PO4 )0.00944 ) was added to the model solutions as a function of electron acceptor concentrations, while the terminal electron accepting step was controlled by thermodynamics (Table 2  ). For simplification, it was assumed that OM contents and characteristics were not rate-limiting. The effect of OM transport via the endmembers was, thus, not regarded in our study.
