The employed network of primary redox reactions was adopted from previous studies (e.g., Seibert et al., 2019b ; Greskowiak et al., 2023 ). Rate constants, half-saturation concentrations and inhibition concentrations for the primary redox reactions as well as NH4 +  reoxidation are provided in Table 3  . Mineral equilibrium reactions were included for calcite (CaCO3 ), siderite (FeCO3 ), goethite (FeOOH), iron sulfide (FeS(ppt)), vivianite (Fe3 (PO4 )2 :8H2 O) and hydroxyapatite (Ca5 (PO4 )3 OH) (Table 2 ). Calcite (Cinitial =28.4 mM) and goethite (Cinitial =15 mM) were initially present in the models, reflecting in-situ mineral contents at Spiekeroog (Seibert et al., 2019a ). Note that the observed calcite (∼0.2% d.w.) and Fereactive  (∼10 mmol kg-1 ) contents were converted to molar concentrations of porewater for better comparability with the dissolved species concentrations, employing a bulk density of 1.42 kg L-1  and a porosity of 0.3 (Seibert et al., 2019a ). All other minerals were allowed to precipitate during simulation only but could potentially dissolve again once formed. Surface complexation reactions were coupled to goethite, using the surface complexation model by Dzombak and Morel (1990) . Thermodynamics constants for all redox processes, mineral equilibria as well as surface complexation reactions are provided in the standard PHREEQC database ‘phreeqc.dat ’. Equilibrium solubility products of all minerals are presented in Table 3 . The surface complexation model integrated into ‘phreeqc.dat ’ regards multiple cations (H+ , Fe2+ , calcium, strontium, barium, cadmium, zinc, copper, lead, magnesium and manganese) and anions (OH- , PO4 3- , SO4 2-  and borate). However, we focused on the effect of surface complexation on PO4 3-  in this study, which is regarded as a major process controlling phosphorous concentrations in STEs (e.g., Spiteri et al., 2008b ). The compositions of inflowing fresh groundwater via the WEL boundary and seawater via the CHD boundary (compare Fig. 1 ) were based on Spiekeroog freshwater and seawater endmembers (Table 4  ; Seibert et al., 2018 ). Note that Fe2+  and HS-  concentrations in groundwater inflowing via the WEL boundary above an elevation of -20 masl were set to zero ('WEL (top)' endmember), while groundwater inflowing via the WEL boundary below an elevation of -20 masl contained Fe2+  and HS-  ('WEL (bottom)' endmember), reflecting more reducing conditions in deeper fresh groundwater (compare Table 4 , Fig. 1 ). To enhance numerical stability, all inflowing solutions were charge-balanced using chloride and equilibrated with calcite and goethite. Initial STE groundwater had the same composition as seawater (Table 4 ), yet, without any DO and NO3 -  but instead containing low concentrations of Fe2+  (<1 µM), PO4 3-  (4 µM) and NH4 +  (22 µM), as reported for the freshwater lens groundwater endmember.  2.3 Set-up of model variants The impact of the different primary and secondary reactions (Table 2 ) on the simulated STE hydrogeochemistry was investigated employing separate model variants (Table 5  ). For simplification and to study the general chemical processes, we focused on a few major minerals and a subset of possible mineral combinations. Certainly, many more realizations for the applied reaction networks, e.g., other mineral combinations, would be possible. The set-up of the groundwater flow and salt transport model as well as the hydrochemical composition of the initial and boundary conditions remained the same for all model variants.   3 Results 3.1 Species distribution and mineral formation A USP developed in the central part of the models, i.e., from ∼180 to 320 m, with a brackish interface reaching down to the aquifer base (Fig. 1 -b). A brackish discharge tube, resulting from the mixing of terrestrial freshwater and recirculated seawater, pinches out close to the low water line. The observed salinity features are in line with previous investigations on flow and salt transport of STEs impacted by tides (e.g., Robinson et al., 2007 ; Beck et al., 2017 ; Grünenbaum et al., 2020 ). Model VAR-conservative, i.e., the conservative model variant, shows that evolving species concentrations in the STE result from endmember mixing, if other reactions were turned off (e.g., Fig. 2  -1, -3, -4). Accordingly, DO and NO3 -  (only present in the seawater endmember) track seawater flow paths, respectively (Fig. 2 -3, -4). HS- , which is the transformation product of microbial SO4 2-  reduction, was absent due to the lack of SO4 2-  reduction (Fig. 2 -6), and DIC was nearly constant in the STE due to similar endmember concentrations (Fig. 2 -2, compare Table 4 ). The absence of DO and NO3 -  in the lower right part of the model demonstrates that a quasi-steady state situation was only reached for the salinity distribution after 60 years simulation time (Fig. 1 ), but not the remaining endmember species. Consequently, residence times in the lower right part must be >60 years, which explains the highest accumulation of reduced species in this zone in model variants including OM degradation (see following paragraphs). Note that the incomplete equilibration with the seawater endmember in the lower right part of the model, indicated by the DO an NO3 -  patterns in VAR-conservative (Fig. 2 -3, -4), has no further impact on the species distributions in the remaining model variants because (i) the initial and seawater compositions are almost identical, except for the absence of DO and NO3 -  as well as the presence of Fe2+ , NH4 +  and PO4 3- , respectively, in the initial solution compared to the seawater endmember (Table 4 ), and (ii) because initial Fe2+ , NH4 +  and PO4 3-  concentrations are very low compared to the addition of these species resulting from OM degradation (e.g., Fig. 2 -14 to -16). Model VAR-OM, i.e., the model variant including OM degradation, demonstrates the impact of primary redox reactions on evolving pH and species concentrations (Fig. 2 -9 to -16). DO was almost completely exhausted due to aerobic respiration (Fig. 2 -11), and denitrification reduced NO3 -  concentrations in most parts of the USP (Fig. 2 -12). However, nitrification of OM-derived ammonia increased NO3 -  concentrations at the left boundary of the USP above freshwater endmember concentrations (Fig. 2 -12). Since iron oxide was not included in VAR-OM, SO4 2-  was the dominant anoxic electron donor, causing an accumulation of HS-  in the lower right part of the model (Fig. 2 -14). Here, groundwater flow was slow and, thus, residence times high compared to the fast flow conditions in the USP. Furthermore, pH values decreased and DIC, NH4 +  as well as PO4 3- , all of which are released during OM degradation, accumulated in the zones characterized by long residence times (Fig. 2 -9, -10, -15, -16). Adding calcite as well as goethite to the reaction network in VAR-C/I lead to the accumulation of Fe2+  in the stagnant model parts, caused by OM degradation coupled to iron oxide reduction (Fig. 2 -21). Because iron oxide reduction consumes protons and the system was buffered by calcite, an overall increase of pH was observed compared to VAR-OM (Fig. 2 -9 vs 2–17). Along the sub-oxic interface of the USP (Fig. 2 -20), zones of goethite formation as well as dissolution evolved in close spatial vicinity (Fig. 3  -2). The pH buffering effect of calcite is demonstrated by its formation/dissolution behavior, opposing the formation/dissolution trends of goethite (Fig. 3 -1, -2). The addition of siderite to the reaction network in VAR-C/I/S decreased Fe2+  (Fig. 2 -29) as well as DIC concentrations (Fig. 2 -26) due to siderite precipitation (Fig. 3 -10). Siderite formation in the USP further triggered goethite dissolution as well as calcite precipitation (Fig. 3 -8, -9). The latter was an effect of goethite dissolution induced pH elevation, outcompeting the effect of decreasing DIC due to siderite formation which would have triggered calcite dissolution. Overall, OM degradation coupled to the complex mineral dynamics had an increasing effect on the developing pH in VAR-C/I/S (Fig. 2 -25). Adding FeS(ppt) to the reaction network in VAR-C/I/P resulted in iron sulfide formation, which precipitated large quantities of Fe2+  (Fig. 2 -37) as well as all HS- (Fig. 2 -38). pH and DIC concentrations were less affected by FeS(ppt) formation, compared to the effect of siderite formation in VAR-C/I/S (Fig. 2 -25 vs. 2–33). The fate of dissolved PO4 3-  was explored in VAR-C/I/P/H (incl. hydroxyapatite), VAR-C/I/P/V (incl. vivianite) and VAR-C/I/P-Co (incl. surface complexation). Both hydroxyapatite and vivianite precipitated PO4 3-  from solution (Fig. 2 -48, -56 and 3–26, -34). The effect of hydroxyapatite and vivianite formation on pH and other dissolved species was low, which becomes evident when comparing to results of VAR-C/I/P (e.g., Fig. 2 -33 vs. 2–41 vs. 2–49). Dissolved PO4 3-  was also scavenged from solution via complexation to goethite surfaces in VAR-C/I/P-Co (Fig. 2 -64, 3–42). Moreover, the implementation of surface complexation increased the pH (Fig. 2 -57) and decreased DIC concentrations (Fig. 2 -58). Because surface complexation is pH dependent and ultimately coupled to the content of goethite, the pattern of adsorbed PO4 3-  (Fig. 3 -42) illustrates the dynamic behavior of calcite and goethite as well (Fig. 3 -36, -37). All minerals (i.e., calcite, goethite, siderite, FeS(ppt), hydroxyapatite and vivianite) as well as surface complexation were regarded in VAR-all. Compared to VAR-C/I/P-Co, formation of siderite (Fig. 3 -45) increased the pH and decreased DIC concentrations (Fig. 2 -65, -66). Furthermore, calcite, goethite and siderite dynamics were linked (Fig. 3 -43, -44, -45), as previously described for VAR-C/I/S (Fig. 3 -8, -9, -10). In addition, hydrochemical conditions became favorable for hydroxyapatite formation within the USP at locations where siderite was forming and goethite dissolving (Fig. 3 -47). Adsorbed PO4 3-  concentrations decreased where hydroxyapatite was forming (Fig. 3 -49). Vivianite formation was not observed in VAR-all (Fig. 3 -48). Removing calcite in VAR-all (no C) demonstrates the important role of calcite for pH, which increased in most parts of the STE but the USP, where pH was decreasing (Fig. 2 -73). Moreover, removal of calcite resulted in higher DIC concentrations in the saltwater wedge (Fig. 2 -74) and caused locally more intense FeS(ppt) as well as hydroxyapatite formation (Fig. 3 -53, -54) compared to VAR-all. On the other hand, less PO4 3-  was adsorbed to goethite surfaces in VAR-all (no C) (Fig. 3 -56), possibly resulting from higher pH.  3.2 Solute fluxes in discharging groundwater A brackish discharge tube emerged in vicinity to the low water line at ∼320 m (Fig. 4  -a). pH as well as DIC of discharging groundwater varied between the different model variants (Fig. 4 -b, -c), depending on the applied reaction network. VAR-C/I, VAR-C/I/P, VAR-C/I/P/H and VAR-C/I/P/V showed similar results for both pH and DIC (Fig. 4 -b, -c). Elevated DIC fluxes, which were up to ∼50 % higher than in VAR-conservative (Fig. 4 -c), demonstrate the contribution of OM degradation to the DIC pool. The inclusion of siderite into the reaction network in VAR-C/I/S resulted in a drop of DIC fluxes as well as an increase of pH (Fig. 4 -b, -c), caused by the precipitation of siderite and its complex interaction with calcite and goethite, compare Section 3.1 . Accounting for surface complexation in VAR-C/I/P-Co lead to a pH increase (Fig. 4 -b) as well as a drop in DIC fluxes (Fig. 4 -c) compared to VAR-C/I/P. Combining OM degradation with calcite, goethite, siderite, FeS(ppt), hydroxyapatite and vivianite mineral reactions as well as surface complexation in VAR-all yielded intermediate pH and DIC concentrations compared to the aforementioned model variants (Fig. 4 -b, -c). DO became fully depleted due to aerobic respiration and, hence, was only present in discharging groundwater of VAR-conservative (not shown). Similar results were found for NO3 -  fluxes, which were only observed in the USP at ∼220 to ∼250 m, except for high concentrations in VAR-conservative (Fig. 4 -d). Fe2+  fluxes were highly dynamic between model variants, underlining the important role of the applied reaction network for Fe species (Fig. 4 -e). Integration of goethite in VAR-C/I resulted in maximum Fe2+  fluxes. On the other hand, the formation of siderite and FeS(ppt), which was regarded in VAR-C/I/S, VAR-C/I/P and VAR-C/I/P/V, VAR-C/I/P-Co and VAR-all, respectively, precipitated large quantities of dissolved Fe2+ . HS-  fluxes were highest for VAR-OM and VAR-C/I (Fig. 4 -f), i.e., model variants including OM degradation but without additional S-mineral sinks. Compared to VAR-C/I, HS-  fluxes were reduced in VAR-C/I/S (Fig. 4 -f) due to the complex interaction of calcite, goethite and siderite, leading to preferential consumption of Fe3+  as electron acceptor (Fig. 3 -2 vs. 3–9) and, thereby, less SO4 2-  reduction (Fig. 2 -22 vs. 2–30) and slightly lower HS-  fluxes (Fig. 4 -f). HS-  was effectively precipitated from solution via FeS(ppt) formation in VAR-C/I/P, VAR-C/I/P/H, VAR-C/I/P/V, VAR-C/I/P-Co, VAR-all and VAR-all (no C), setting HS-  fluxes to zero (Fig. 4 -f). NH4 +  accumulated in similar concentrations in groundwater of all model variants (row 7, Fig. 2 ), resulting in comparable NH4 +  discharge fluxes (Fig. 4 -g). Low NH4 +  fluxes in VAR-conservative illustrate the important role of OM degradation for N export to the sea. Highest PO4 3-  fluxes were observed for model variants without P-minerals or surface complexation, i.e., VAR-OM, VAR-C/I, VAR-C/I/S and VAR-C/I/P (Fig. 4 -h). Hydroxyapatite and vivianite formation in VAR-C/I/P/H and VAR-C/I/P/V, respectively, precipitated large quantities of dissolved PO4 3-  (Fig. 2 -48, -56), subsequently reducing PO4 3-  fluxes (Fig. 4 -h). Furthermore, surface complexation included in VAR-C/I/P-Co removed PO4 3-  from solution (Fig. 4 -h). Similar P-removal was observed for VAR-all and VAR-all (no C), integrating P-minerals as well as surface complexation (Fig. 4 -h).  3.3 Element budgets of the subterranean estuary OM degradation produced DIC, NH4 +  as well as PO4 3-  (compare Section 3.1 and 3.2 ). Accordingly, the STE became a source for the latter species in most model variants (Fig. 5  -a, -f, -g), while it was a sink for the electron acceptors DO, NO3 -  (Fig. 5 -b, -c) and SO4 2- , indicated by the HS- surplus (Fig. 5 -e). Adding goethite to the reaction network resulted in the STE being a Fe2+  source (Fig. 5 -d). Formation of siderite in VAR-C/I/S precipitated DIC as well as Fe2+  and triggered goethite as well as calcite reactions (compare Section 3.2 ). These processes turned the STE into a sink for DIC and reduced the released amounts of Fe2+  in VAR-C/I/S (Fig. 5 -a, -d). The integration of FeS(ppt) in VAR-C/I/P precipitated all HS-  and large quantities of Fe2+  compared to VAR-C/I (Fig. 5 -d, -e). Hydroxyapatite as well as vivianite formation reduced the source functioning of the STE for PO4 3-  in VAR-C/I/P/H and VAR-C/I/P/V compared to VAR-C/I/P (Fig. 5 -g). Surface complexation and its impact on dissolved species, pH as well as mineral dynamics in VAR-C/I/P-Co (compare Section 3.1 and 3.2 ) further decreased the source functioning of the STE for DIC, Fe2+  and PO4 3-  (Fig. 5 -g) compared to VAR-C/I/P (Fig. 5 -a, -d, -g). Integrating all minerals as well as surface complexation in VAR-all resulted in sink functioning of the STE for DIC, DO, NO3 -  and HS-  (Fig. 5 -a, -b, -c, -e) as well as lower Fe2+  and PO4 3-  discharge fluxes compared to VAR-C/I (Fig. 5 -d, -g). Neglecting calcite in VAR-all (no C) turned the STE into a DIC source and decreased the discharge fluxes of Fe2+  and PO4 3-  compared to VAR-all (Fig. 5 -d, -g).   4 Discussion 4.1 Relevance of OM degradation, mineral dynamics and surface complexation While previous RTM studies in STE settings have focused on the interaction of groundwater flow and OM degradation coupled to electron acceptors (e.g., Anwar et al., 2014 ; Heiss et al., 2017 ; Kim et al., 2017 ), the roles of secondary mineral reactions and surface complexation were less frequently regarded (e.g., Spiteri et al., 2008a ). The relevance of the considered processes in this study and their implications for fate and transport of dissolved species in the STE is discussed in the following. Goethite played a key role for primary and secondary biogeochemical processes. Firstly, anaerobic OM degradation was largely driven by consumption of solid Fe3+ , producing dissolved Fe2+ . Dissolved Fe2+  then served as an important driver for subsequent mineral formation processes, including siderite, vivianite and iron sulfide formation. We observed that siderite had a strong impact on pH and DIC but also Fe2+  concentrations. Its formation/dissolution dynamics were further linked to the formation/dissolution behavior of calcite and goethite and vice versa. Accordingly, Postma (1981)  reported that the presence of calcite may control the saturation state of siderite. The formation of siderite under iron-reducing conditions has been described in laboratory studies (Frederickson et al., 1998 ; Roh et al., 2003 ) and observed in the field (Postma, 1981 ), including coastal dune aquifers (e.g., Coos Bay, Oregon, USA, Magaritz and Luzier, 1985 ). More recently, Van Beek et al. (2021)  reported that Fe2+  concentrations in Dutch fresh groundwater are largely controlled by siderite and that iron oxide reduction and siderite precipitation occur simultaneously once saturation with respect to siderite has been achieved. Further indications for siderite formation in coastal aquifers were provided in our previous RTM study (Seibert et al., 2019b ), in which including siderite formation was required to accurately simulate observed pH and bicarbonate concentrations of an evolving barrier island freshwater lens. Vivianite formation took place under iron reducing conditions in our models, where it served as an important P sink. This observation is in line with Slomp and Van Capellen (2004) , who stated that P removal under anaerobic conditions mainly occurs via precipitation of vivianite and hydroxyapatite. Vivianite formation under iron reducing conditions has been reported in laboratory studies (Frederickson et al., 1998 ), observed in the field (Ahmed et al., 2004 ), and it was previously speculated that vivianite formation also occurs in anaerobic coastal sediments based on the calculation of mineral saturation states (Seibert et al., 2018 ; Seibert et al., 2021 ). However, vivianite formation is complex, often associated with organic remains and favored within microzones (Rothe et al., 2016 ). Hence, saturation calculation based on bulk chemistry may fail to predict vivianite occurrence when ignoring small-scale heterogeneity. The absence of vivianite formation in VAR-all and VAR-all (no C), i.e., the model variants where also siderite and hydroxyapatite formation as well as surface complexation were regarded, underlines that vivianite is very sensitive to the bulk chemistry. Small-scale heterogeneity may, therefore, result in favorable in-situ hydrochemical conditions for vivianite formation, despite the overall trend of the simulated bulk chemistry. The fate of P was further controlled by the formation of hydroxyapatite and surface complexation. Both mechanisms effectively immobilized dissolved PO4 3-  in our models. The role of hydroxyapatite for P removal was previously noted by Slomp and Van Capellen (2004) . Moreover, indications for hydroxyapatite formation were found in coastal groundwater based on saturation calculations in a previous study (Seibert et al., 2021 ). Similarly, Anschutz et al. (2007)  and Dang et al. (2014)  reported hydroxyapatite formation as possible P sink in coastal sediments. Besides P removal, hydroxyapatite traps heavy metals (Fuller et al., 2002 ; Simon et al., 2008 ). Hence, hydroxyapatite formation may also be relevant for heavy metal dynamics in STEs. Surface complexation at iron oxide surfaces (Dzombak and Morel, 1990 ) was another important process in our models scavenging large quantities of PO4 3- . The role of surface complexation for the fate of P was previously described by Spiteri et al. (2008b)  and is a well-recognized process for pH-dependent P removal in aquatic systems (e.g., Elzinga and Sparks, 2007 ). Iron sulfide precipitation was the key process removing virtually all HS-  and large quantities of Fe2+  from solution in our models. Iron sulfide formation has been well described in laboratory studies (Luther, 1991 ; Wilkin and Barnes, 1996 ; Rickard and Luther, 1997 ) and observed in organic-rich marine environments (Berner, 1970 ; Middelburg, 1991 ; Lyons and Berner, 1992 ) but also permeable (organic-poor) sediments (Reckhardt et al., 2015 ; Seibert et al., 2019a ). The role of iron sulfide formation as HS-  sink has also been recognized for STEs (e.g., Roy et al., 2013 ; McAllister et al., 2015 ; Reckhardt et al., 2017 ). Iron sulfide formation has further implications for the fate of trace metals and toxins (e.g., Pb, Hg, Tl, and Tc) via co-precipitation/sorption of the latter (Jeong et al. 2010 ; Fan et al. 2013 ). We demonstrated that the dynamics of the previously described minerals potentially affect the STE biogeochemistry. Since other studies reported authigenesis for at least some of the discussed minerals, we think that more complex reaction networks accounting for mineral formation/dissolution as well as surface complexation need to be regarded in future work for or an advanced understanding of the STE biogeochemistry. The application of comprehensive RTM approaches, i.e., accounting for pH, redox states, species activities and ion strength, is inevitable for this purpose. While it is well known that calcite in form of calcareous shells as well as iron oxides and iron sulfides prevail in coastal sediments (e.g., Seibert et al., 2019a ), further in-situ investigations are needed to clarify if the other discussed minerals, i.e., siderite, vivianite or hydroxyapatite, are relevant to the STE biogeochemistry. On the other hand, some species, such as DO, NO3 -  and NH4 + , were virtually not impacted by both mineral dynamics and surface complexation. Hence, investigations focusing on the fate of the latter species using kinetic reaction networks seem justified.  4.2 STE source/sink functioning and species fluxes We found that the discharge of pH, DIC, Fe2+ , HS-  and PO4 3-  as well as the source/sink functioning of the STE are strongly dependent on the chosen reaction network. For example, the STE was a source for DIC to the coastal ocean due to OM degradation in model variants excluding siderite. The addition of siderite to the reaction network, in turn, resulted in a sink functioning of the STE concerning DIC. Similarly, the source/sink functioning of HS-  depended on the integration of FeS(ppt). Some processes, such as microbial SO4 2-  reduction or P release during OM degradation and subsequent hydroxyapatite and vivianite formation, might be completely masked when only evaluating in-situ species concentrations of discharging groundwater. This finding underlines the important role of the STE as biogeochemical reactor and the great value of process quantification via RTM. Model-based species fluxes derived in this study are in good agreement with field-based observations. This underlines that the applied reaction networks seem to generally capture the relevant biogeochemical processes and that the model parametrization is reasonable. For example, Beck et al. (2017)  reported NH4 +  as well as PO4 3-  fluxes of 117 and 55 mmol d-1  m-1  shoreline, respectively, for the Spiekeroog beach aquifer, which is very similar to the here derived fluxes of 150 to 166 (NH4 + ) and 3 to 14 (PO4 3- ) mmol d-1  m-1  shoreline. Anschutz et al. (2009)  found a similar PO4 3-  flux of 15.2 mmol d-1  m-1  shoreline for a beach aquifer at the French Aquitanian coast. Furthermore, simulated Fe2+  fluxes of <1 to 421 mmol d-1  m-1  shoreline are on the same order of magnitude as the calculated Fe flux of 185 mmol d-1  m-1  shoreline at the Spiekeroog beach (Reckhardt et al., 2017 ). However, as also noted by Reckhardt et al. (2017) , fluxes of redox-sensitive species might be overestimated, taking into account re-oxidation and/or precipitation close to the sediment-surface water interface. Finally, the maximum simulated DIC fluxes of ∼50 to 130 mmol m-2  d-1  agree with previous studies. Cai et al. (2003)  reported a DIC flux of 171 mmol m-2  d-1  for the North Inlet basin, South Carolina, Faber et al. (2014)  found a DIC flux of 130 to 450 mmol m-2  d-1  for a macrotidal embayment at Western Port, Australia, and Stewart et al. (2015)  calculated a DIC flux of 156 mmol m-2  d-1  for the embayment Moreton Bay, Australia. Somewhat higher DIC fluxes were, for instance, reported by Chen et al. (2018)  for the mangrove-dominated tropical bay Maowei Sea, China, (250 to 700 mmol m-2  d-1 ). Note that the intention of the previous comparison of our model-based species fluxes with other field-based studies was to generally assess if the chosen reaction networks are meaningful, rather than to identify which model variant is most representative of real-world STEs. The fact that hydrogeological conditions vary strongly between field sites, e.g., considering the prevailing geology, coastal forcings, climatic conditions or endmember compositions, prohibits a direct comparison of our simulations for a generic, idealized sandy STE with other field sites. Therefore, the proposed reaction networks, which highlight the important role of mineral dynamics and surface complexation reactions, should be integrated into RTM studies attempting to model real-world STEs for further process validation. Note that this study was carried out within the DFG funded project 'DynaDeep', which aims at gaining a deeper understanding of the physical and biogeochemical processes in the subsurface of high-energy beaches (Massmann et al., 2023 ). Subsequently, the here proposed reaction network will be adopted and further validated by a field-scale model of the DynaDeep study site on Spiekeroog, Germany.  4.3 Limitations The applied model boundary conditions were steady, leading to a dynamic equilibrium situation of flow and salt transport after several years simulation time. Accordingly, the evolving salinity distribution was at quasi steady-state, and an equilibrium situation for the other dissolved species was reached in most parts of the aquifer, except for the lower right part, where groundwater flow was slow and the initial seawater endmember was still present. Yet, it is likely that groundwater flow is much more complex and transient in coastal STEs, particularly at high-energy sites (Greskowiak and Massmann, 2021 ), owing to the tidal dynamics, wave forcing, storm floods as well as a transient beach morphology. Recently, Greskowiak et al. (2023)  demonstrated that the latter factors potentially also have an impact on the developing redox zones in STEs. The effect of transient oceanic forcings and variable beach morphology on biogeochemistry and mineral dynamics in the STE was beyond the scope of this study but should be explored in future work. The degradation of OM was implemented as kinetic process following the Partial Equilibrium Model by Postma and Jakobsen (1996) , with the overall rate being coupled to electron acceptor concentrations. The subsequent electron accepting step was purely thermodynamically driven. Similarly, precipitation/dissolution of the considered minerals were integrated as equilibrium processes, occurring instantly and depending on the solution saturation state. The latter assumption seems valid, considering that groundwater flow velocities are usually slow and that kinetics of many minerals are fast, e.g., of carbonates (Svensson and Dreybrodt, 1992 ). However, mineral reactions may not necessarily proceed at equilibrium but rather as kinetic reactions, particularly if flow velocities become fast in the USP, or if inhibiting mechanisms play a role (e.g., Mucci, 1986 ; Zhang and Dawe, 2000 ). Therefore, future work should explore the kinetics of in-situ mineral formation in STEs. In addition, we note that the effect of mineral dynamics, e.g., calcite dissolution, on aquifer properties, e.g., sediment porosity, was neglected in our modeling approach. However, the effect is small, considering that the annual absolute porosity change related to calcite dynamics would be only ∼0.004 % if a maximum calcite rate of ∼1200 µM a-1  (compare Fig. 3 ), a molar mass of 100.09 g mol-1  and a bulk density of 2.71 g cm- ³ for CaCO3  were assumed. The reaction network used in this study was rather complex, involving electron acceptor consumption coupled to OM degradation, dynamics of relevant mineral phases as well as surface complexation. However, though complex, it remains a simplification of reality. Firstly, many more mineral phases might be present in-situ and, hence, influence the evolving STE chemistry. Rhodochrosite (MnCO3 ), as an example, has not been regarded in this study due to relatively low observed Mn2+  concentrations (Reckhardt et al., 2017 ; Seibert et al., 2018 ), but may still play a role for the fate of Mn2+ . In addition, surface complexation to other minerals apart from iron oxides, e.g., pyrite, calcite, siderite but also manganese oxides, possibly influence the fate of PO4 3-  or other dissolved species. Secondly, the complex characteristics and provenances of (dissolved) OM (Seidel et al., 2014 , 2015 ; Kim et al., 2019 ; Waska et al., 2021 ) and its interaction with other dissolved species and minerals, such as iron (Linkhorst et al., 2017 ; Sirois et al., 2018 ), was not regarded. Yet, it is clear that OM in its different forms is a key parameter controlling the STE biogeochemistry. Thirdly, the described hydrochemistry was constrained to major dissolved water constituents, while other trace compounds, e.g., trace metals, were not included. The fate of the latter adds even more complexity, considering their redox-sensitivity and interaction with mineral phases as well as OM (Reckhardt et al., 2021 ). Finally, the applied reaction rate constants for OM degradation were adopted from our previous study Seibert et al. (2019b) , where rate constants were adjusted to match observed electron acceptor concentrations in the barrier island freshwater lens of Spiekeroog. Although the applied rate constants agree with other groundwater studies (e.g., Diem et al., 2013 ; Henzler et al., 2016 ; Greskowiak et al., 2023 ), further investigations, e.g., incubation experiments with in-situ sediments and porewater, are needed to constrain the reaction network and its rate constants. In addition, a rigorous sensitivity analysis for relevant parameters of the proposed reaction network, e.g., rate constants, equilibrium constants, surface areas, endmember concentrations and OM contents, could be useful to further assess the sensitivity of the STE biogeochemistry.   5 Conclusion This study investigated the fate of dissolved species in a sandy STE, considering the complex interactions of OM degradation, mineral formation/dissolution as well as surface complexation. A comprehensive RTM approach was developed for this purpose, accounting for the effects of pH, pe, ionic strength and ion activities. This was essential to quantify equilibrium reactions, e.g., mineral formation/dissolution, as well as to accurately simulate pH-pe dependent processes, e.g., surface complexation. Findings show that biogeochemical processes in STEs are highly complex and cannot be disentangled by field data alone. Further conclusions are:• pH and DIC chemistry are controlled by both OM degradation, mineral formation and surface complexation.  • Surface complexation at iron oxide surfaces as well as formation of hydroxyapatite and vivianite control the fate of PO4 3- . HS-  concentrations are controlled by precipitation of iron sulfides.  • The biogeochemical functioning of STEs is very sensitive to the chosen reaction network. Wrong conclusions regarding element fluxes to coastal oceans might be drawn if relevant processes are not accounted for.  • DO, NO3 -  and NH4 +  were virtually not impacted by both mineral dynamics and surface complexation. Hence, investigations focusing on the fate of the latter species using kinetic reaction networks seem justified.  • Field and laboratory studies, e.g., incubation experiments, are needed to shed light on relevant processes shaping the STE biogeochemistry, such as mineral formation and surface complexation, and to derive site-specific rate constants for OM degradation.  • The role of transient groundwater flow for the biogeochemical processes in STEs requires additional model and field-based investigations. This is particularly relevant at sites which are exposed to dynamic oceanic forcings.  • Combining field, lab and RTM techniques is key to further advance our process understanding.
1 Introduction Understanding how fluids and solutes navigate through porous structures is of great interest in many industrial, environmental, and biological applications including, but not limited to, subsurface (Carbonell and Whitaker, 1983; Dejam et al., 2014; Picchi and Battiato, 2018; Ling et al., 2022; Jew et al., 2022 ) and surface flows (Papke and Battiato, 2013; Ling et al., 2021 ), lithium-ion batteries (Hossain et al., 2019; Korneev et al., 2020; Weber et al., 2022a ), membrane filtration (Ling and Battiato, 2019; Sitaraman and Battiato, 2022 ), carbon capture and sequestration (Hidalgo and Carrera, 2009 ), and geological hydrogen storage (Boon and Hajibeygi, 2022; Okoroafor et al., 2022; Alms et al., 2023 ). While such applications span a large variety of systems and scales, ranging from engineered designs at the cm-m scale to environmental systems at the m-km scale, they share intrinsic multiscale features and dynamics, i.e. topology at the nm-μ m    scale has a dramatic impact on the system’s macroscopic behavior. Pore-scale models fully resolve flow and transport at the fine-scale and can guarantee the highest fidelity, since they are based on the numerical solution of conservation laws based on first principles (e.g., Icardi et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2016a; Molins et al., 2017, 2021; Gouze et al., 2021a; Li et al., 2022 ). However, despite significant advancements in computational tools which have dramatically expanded our capability to model at high spatial and temporal resolution domains of increasing dimensions, the separation of physical scales typical for environmental applications involving geological porous media can easily span 9 orders of magnitude, from the sub-μ m    to the km scale. The computational cost associated with such a dramatic scale disparity is prohibitive. A cornerstone of subsurface hydrology, upscaling theories provide a formal mathematical framework to build effective-medium (continuum, macroscopic) representations of averaged pore-scale phenomena. A review of different upscaling methods is provided by Battiato et al. (2019) . Such approaches allow one to resolve macroscopically averaged variables, while still accounting for vital pore-scale information, such as particle morphology, through the definition of effective parameters. Two critical effective parameters associated with flow and solute transport at the macroscale are the permeability and effective dispersion tensors. Permeability depends only on the specific morphology of the porous structure considered, whereas the dispersion coefficient additionally depends on the flow conditions – described by the Péclet number which relates advective and diffusive time scales. Many empirical correlations have been proposed to estimate permeability and dispersion (Delgado, 2007; Koch and Brady, 1985; Rose, 1973 ). Yet, their validity and accuracy across a broad range of porous media configurations and dynamic regimes have been amply questioned (e.g., Valdes-Parada et al., 2009; Schulz et al., 2019; Wagner et al., 2021 ).  Recent advancements in visualization techniques, combined with ever increasing computational power, have allowed direct calculations of effective parameters based on realistic microstructural information obtained from, e.g. X-ray microtomography images (Bodla et al., 2014; Egan et al., 2015; Prodanović et al., 2007; Hasan et al., 2020 ), and to overcome the limitations of the aforementioned empirical correlations. Direct numerical simulations are used to solve pore-scale equations over microstructures of macroscopic size containing hundreds or thousands of pores. Effective parameters, such as permeability, are then determined by postulating a relationship between numerically measured fluxes (i.e. Darcy flux) and driving forces across the sample (e.g. pressure gradient) (e.g., Yang et al., 2016b; Ferguson et al., 2018, 2021; Gouze et al., 2021b ). Such simulations are however computationally intensive since fine-scale solutions need to be determined for domains of macroscopic size, i.e. larger than a typical Representative Elementary Volume. More recently, machine learning approaches have been successfully deployed to limit the computational burden associated with direct numerical simulations of flow and transport in complex macroscopic microstructures, once the network has been trained (e.g. Wang et al., 2020; Marcato et al., 2021; Santos et al., 2021; Marcato et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2022; Marcato et al., 2023 ). However, the computational cost of building sufficiently representative training sets is significant and can lead to the development networks trained over a narrow set of physical parameters (e.g. small ranges of porosity values, or idealized grain shapes). A number of approaches have been proposed to overcome these limitations, including computationally efficient multiscale neural networks approaches (Santos et al., 2021 ) or homogenization-informed convolutional neural networks (Weber et al., 2022b ), where the computational gain is associated with training the network on the numerical solution of closure problems solved over a unit cell of the macroscopic domain. In this work, we focus on upscaling approaches, since such methods offer a rigorous and self-consistent framework for the calculation of effective permeability and dispersion tensors, as well as a priori error bounds on upscaling approximations and well-defined applicability (permissibility) conditions under different dynamic regimes (Battiato et al., 2019; Pietrzyk et al., 2021; Pietrzyk and Battiato, 2023a ). In particular, we employ homogenization theory (Hornung, 1997  Chapter 1, pp. 1–25), which conceptualizes the macroscopic porous medium as a collection of repeating unit cells. Upscaling through homogenization results in the decoupling of micro- and macro-scales where effective properties, i.e. permeability and dispersion tensors, can be determined through the calculation of a closure variable which satisfies a local boundary value problem (also known as closure problem) over the unit cell. In this formulation, the closure problems for permeability and dispersion are inherently linked as the latter solution is dependent on the former (see, e.g., Battiato and Tartakovsky, 2011; Boso and Battiato, 2013 ). The closure problem dramatically reduces the computational cost of characterizing the effective properties of the porous medium because only a representative subset of the domain is needed, namely the unit cell. One technical challenge associated with the solution of the closure problems for permeability and dispersion tensors is that the closure variables must satisfy global constraints for the theory to rigorously hold. These global constraints, which require that the average of the closure variables be equal to zero over the unit cell, guarantee the uniqueness of the solution and can be difficult to satisfy for complex and arbitrary pore-scale geometries, particularly under high flow conditions. Guaranteeing the uniqueness of the solution is critical to ensure that a priori  error estimates hold true and that pore-scale fields can be accurately reconstructed from the closure variable. We emphasize that, while each upscaling method has unique features, such global constraints are present in other upscaling formulations, including, but not limited to, the method of volume averaging (Whitaker, 1999 ). Although multiple works have employed the solution of local closure problems to determine effective properties including permeability (Wagner et al., 2021 ) and dispersion (Guo et al., 2015; Shende and Mani, 2022; Valdés-Parada et al., 2016; Wood et al., 2003 ), to the best of our knowledge, current methods cannot provide estimates that rigorously satisfy such global constraints. While this may have no effect on the accurate estimation of effective parameters, the reconstruction of pore-scale quantities from the closure solution cannot be uniquely performed when such global constraints are not satisfied. In this case, full pore-scale simulations become necessary. Ling and Battiato (2020)  introduced an algorithm that allows one to satisfies the global constraint associated with the permeability closure problem, and hence allows for a unique pore-scale reconstruction of the velocity field from the closure solution. In this work, we extend the algorithm proposed by Ling and Battiato (2020)  to the closure problem associated to dispersion, and refer to it as τ  2    -SIMPLE algorithm. We achieve this by introducing two artificial time scales τ  1     and τ  2     into the OpenFOAM SIMPLE loop (Ferziger and Perić, 2002 ) to satisfy global conditions for both the permeability and dispersion closure variables, respectively. The algorithm is designed to work for arbitrary particle morphologies and Péclet numbers, within the model applicability conditions. The paper is structured as follows. Section 2  summarizes the homogenization model used and the closure problems for both permeability and effective dispersion. In Section 3 , the τ  2    -SIMPLE algorithm is described in detail. Section 4  presents the numerical convergence analysis of the algorithm and verification by direct comparison of the upscaled solution with fully resolved pore-scale simulations for various unit cell structures in both two and three-dimensions and varying topological properties.  2 Homogenization and closure problem Let us consider the incompressible flow of a Newtonian fluid and solute transport through a porous medium Ω  ˆ     with boundary ∂ Ω  ˆ      and characteristic length L  , as depicted in Fig. 1 (a). Homogenization theory assumes that the medium is composed by a collection of spatially periodic unit cells Y  ˆ     with a characteristic length ℓ  , as shown in Fig. 1 (b), with (1) ɛ = ℓ  L   ≪ 1     and ɛ   the ratio of scales between the microscopic and macroscopic domains referred to as scale separation parameter. The unit cell Y  ˆ   = B  ˆ   ∪ G  ˆ      consists of the pore space B  ˆ     and the impermeable solid matrix G  ˆ    , separated by the smooth surface Γ  ˆ    . The pore-space B  ˆ     in each unit cell forms a multi-connected pore-scale domain B  ˆ    ɛ    , bounded by Γ  ˆ    ɛ   = ⋃  i   Γ  ˆ    i     , with i   indexing across all unit cells contained in Ω  ˆ    . The geometry in Ω  ˆ     is defined in a Cartesian coordinate system x  ˆ   = x  ˆ    1   , x  ˆ    2   , x  ˆ    3       . The coordinates spanning the unit cell domain are y  ˆ   = y  ˆ    1   , y  ˆ    2   , y  ˆ    3       . Homogenization theory provides a rigorous framework for deriving macroscopic equations by using effective medium properties that are calculated on a representative unit cell of the porous media microstructure, as briefly outlined in the following. For detailed derivations, we refer the interested reader to Battiato and Tartakovsky (2011, Appendix)  and Battiato et al. (2019, Section 7) . 2.1 Governing equations and dimensionless formulation At low Reynolds numbers, the single phase incompressible flow of a fluid in the pore-space B  ˆ    ɛ     is governed by the Stokes and continuity equations subject to the no-slip boundary condition at the fluid–solid interface Γ  ˆ    ɛ    , i.e. (2) μ ∇  ˆ    2   u  ˆ    ɛ   − ∇  ˆ   p  ˆ    ɛ   = 0 ,  x  ˆ   ∈ B  ˆ    ɛ   ,    (3) ∇  ˆ   ⋅ u  ˆ    ɛ   = 0 ,  x  ˆ   ∈ B  ˆ    ɛ   ,    (4) u  ˆ    ɛ   = 0 ,  x  ˆ   ∈ Γ  ˆ    ɛ   ,       where u  ˆ    ɛ   ( x )     is the velocity field, μ   is the fluid dynamic viscosity and p  ˆ    ɛ     is the pore-scale pressure. The fluid contains a dissolved species M   whose pore-scale concentration c  ˆ    ɛ   x  ˆ   , t  ˆ        satisfies the advection-diffusion equation in the pore domain B  ˆ    ɛ    (5) ∂ c  ˆ    ɛ    ∂ t  ˆ     + u  ˆ    ɛ   ⋅ ∇  ˆ   c  ˆ    ɛ   = ∇  ˆ   ⋅ D  ˆ   ⋅ ∇  ˆ   c  ˆ    ɛ     ,  x  ˆ   ∈ B  ˆ    ɛ   ,  t  ˆ   > 0 ,     where D  ˆ     is the molecular diffusion coefficient which, for generality, is here represented as a second-order tensor. The first step in homogenization is to formulate the governing equations in dimensionless form. Dimensionless quantities for all variables and parameters are defined as (6) x = x  ˆ    L   ,  y = y  ˆ    L   ,  u  ɛ   = u  ˆ    ɛ    U   ,  D = D  ˆ    D   ,  c  ɛ   = c  ˆ    ɛ    c  ̄     ,  p  ɛ   = p  ˆ    ɛ   ℓ  2    μ U L   ,     where U  , D  , and c  ̄     are characteristic values for velocity, diffusion, and concentration respectively. Additionally, we define diffusion and advection time scales, t  ˆ    D     and t  ˆ    A    , as (7) t  ˆ    D   = L  2    D   ,  and  t  ˆ    A   = L  U   ,     respectively. The Péclet number is defined as the ratio between the diffusion and the advection time scale, (8) Pe = U L  D   ,     such that higher Péclet number corresponds with faster advection compared to diffusion. Using the above formulation, the dimensionless version of Eq. (2)  is (9a) ɛ  2   ∇  x  2   u  ɛ   − ∇  x   p  ɛ   = 0 ,  x ∈ B  ɛ   ,    (9b) ∇  x   ⋅ u  ɛ   = 0 ,  x ∈ B  ɛ   ,    (9c) u  ɛ   = 0 ,  x ∈ Γ  ɛ   ,       and Eq. (5)  is recast as (10) ∂ c  ɛ    ∂ t   + u  ɛ   ⋅ Pe ∇  x   c  ɛ   = ∇  x   ⋅ D ⋅ ∇  x   c  ɛ     ,  x ∈ B  ɛ   ,  t > 0 ,     with non-dimensional time t   scaled with the diffusive time scale t = t  ˆ   / t  ˆ    D      .  2.2 Macroscopic equations and closure problems After formulating the pore-scale equations in dimensionless form, macroscopic equations can be derived together with their effective/macroscopic properties, calculated on the pore-scale unit cell via the solution of a closure problem. Many works have focused on upscaling Eqs. (9) –(10)  from the pore-scale to the continuum-scale, including approaches based on homogenization via multiple-scale expansions (Marušić-Paloka and Piatnitski, 2005; Mikelic et al., 2006; Wall, 2007; Battiato and Tartakovsky, 2011 ), the focus of this work. For completeness, we provide a brief outline of the method and present the corresponding continuum-scale equations, while we refer the interested reader to classical works on homogenization by, e.g., Auriault and Adler (1995)  and Hornung (1997, Chapter 1, pp. 1–25) , or reviews on upscaling methods by Battiato et al. (2019)  for more information. Homogenization is based on the identification of a slow variable, x  , which spans the macroscopic domain, and a fast variable, y  , which spans the repeating unit cell. These variables relate through (11) x = ɛ y ,     so that all spatial derivatives are written as (12) ∇ = ∇  x   + 1  ɛ   ∇  y   .     First, the pore-scale variables – velocity, pressure, and concentration – are expanded in integer powers of the scale separation parameter ɛ  , i.e. (13a) u  ɛ   ( x , t )  ≔ u ( x , y , t )  = u  0   + ɛ u  1   + ɛ  2   u  2   + O ( ɛ  3   )  ,    (13b) p  ɛ   ( x , t )  ≔ p ( x , y , t )  = p  0   + ɛ p  1   + ɛ  2   p  2   + O ( ɛ  3   )  ,    (13c) c  ɛ   ( x , t )  ≔ c ( x , y , t )  = c  0   + ɛ c  1   + ɛ  2   c  2   + O ( ɛ  3   )  ,       and substituted into the governing Eqs. (9) –(10) , while accounting for (12)  (see, e.g., Battiato and Tartakovsky, 2011; Battiato et al., 2019 ). After collecting terms of like-power of ɛ  , a cascade of equations is obtained and solved iteratively through the introduction of a closure problem, which relates the leading order to higher order terms. Additionally, the operators for the superficial and intrinsic averages ⋅     and ⋅    B     are defined as (14) ⋅   = 1  | Y |    ∫  B   ⋅ d y ,  ⋅    B   = 1  | B |    ∫  B   ⋅ d y .     After performing these steps (Battiato and Tartakovsky, 2011 ), it can be shown that the macroscopic flow field is governed by Darcy’s law, (15) 〈 u 〉  = − K ⋅ ∇  x   p  0   ,  ∇ ⋅ 〈 u 〉  = 0 ,  x ∈ Ω ,     where p  0     is a function of x   only (see Auriault and Adler, 1995 ) and K   is the dimensionless permeability tensor calculated as (16) K = 〈 k y   〉  .     The closure variable k   is the solution to the boundary value problem in the unit cell (17a) ∇  y  2   k + I − ∇  y   a = 0 ,  y ∈ B ,    (17b) ∇  y   ⋅ k = 0 ,  y ∈ B ,       subject to (18a) k = 0 ,  y ∈ Γ ,    (18b) a   = 0 ,    (18c) k ,  a  periodic in y ,       where a   and k   are closure variables introduced in the homogenization process and I   is the identity tensor. Similarly, the upscaling of the advective–diffusion equation (10)  for a nonreactive scalar leads to a macroscopic formulation (see, e.g., Battiato and Tartakovsky, 2011; Pietrzyk et al., 2021 ), (19) ϕ ∂ 〈 c 〉   B    ∂ t   = ∇ ⋅ D  ∗   ⋅ ∇ 〈 c 〉   B   − Pe 〈 c 〉   B   〈 u 〉    ,     where ϕ   is the porosity of the domain and D  ∗     is the effective dispersion tensor, which can be calculated as (20) D  ∗   = 〈 D ⋅ I + ∇  y   χ   〉  + ɛ Pe 〈 χ k 〉  ⋅ ∇  x   p  0   .     The closure variable χ ( y )     is periodic in y   and is defined as the solution to the local problem (21a) − ∇  y   ⋅ [ D ⋅ I + ∇  y   χ   ]  + ɛ Pe u  0   ⋅ ∇  y   χ = ɛ Pe 〈 u  0   〉   B   − u  0     ,  y ∈ B ,    (21b) − n ⋅ [ D ⋅ I + ∇  y   χ   ]  = 0 ,  y ∈ Γ ,       where u  0   = − k ⋅ ∇  x   p  0      and p  0     is the solution of Eq. (15) . Therefore, the determination of the dispersion tensor through Eqs. (20) –(21)  requires a prior calculation of the permeability closure problem, Eq. (17) –(18) , within the unit cell. For the model described by Eqs. (19) –(21)  to be valid, the following conditions must be satisfied (Battiato and Tartakovsky, 2011 ): (22a) ɛ ≪ 1 ,    (22b) Pe < ɛ  − 2   ,    (22c) 〈 χ 〉  = 0 .        While the conditions (22a) and (22b)  control the accuracy of the approximations employed in homogenization by multiple scale expansions, condition (22c)  ensures that a unique solution to the closure variable χ   exists. Similar to condition (18b) , Eq. (22c)  is a global condition imposed on the closure variable χ   and it ensures both uniqueness as well as the possibility to reconstruct pore-scale fields for concentration, if needed. It is worth emphasizing that the closure problem (21)  holds, not only for passive tracer transport, but also for reactive transport of a solute undergoing a mild heterogeneous reaction (i.e. when Damköhler number is smaller than 1 (Battiato and Tartakovsky, 2011 )), if the additional condition (23) 〈 χ 〉   Γ   ≈ 〈 χ 〉   B       is satisfied, where 〈 χ 〉   Γ   ≔ 1  | Γ |    ∫  Γ   χ d y   . For full derivation of this additional constraint see Battiato and Tartakovsky (2011, Eqs. (A.27) and (A.28)) . In other words, if 〈 χ 〉   B   = 0    per (22c), and also 〈 χ 〉   Γ   ≈ 〈 χ 〉   B     , then the closure variable χ   satisfying (21) can also be employed to derive the dispersion coefficient for mildly reactive solutes, as showed in Battiato and Tartakovsky (2011) . Also, it is important to point out that even as ɛ → 0   , the advective terms in Eq. (21)  (i.e., the terms premultiplied by ɛ Pe   ) are not negligible when ɛ  0   < Pe < ɛ  − 2     . Instead, for Pe ≤ ɛ   , the closure problem simplifies to a purely diffusive one (Figure 1, Battiato and Tartakovsky, 2011  for further discussion).  The next section presents an algorithm to solve the permeability and dispersion closure problems for arbitrary geometries and flow conditions within the appropriate bounds on Pe  , while enforcing global conditions on both closure variables. We emphasize that, while the algorithm is numerically verified for passive tracer transport, it can be readily applied also for mildly reactive systems (i.e., whose Damköhler number is less than one) since, as shown in Section 4 , also condition (23)  is satisfied.   3 τ  2    -SIMPLE algorithm In this section, we outline the algorithm to solve the dispersion closure problem (21) , after the permeability closure problem (17) –(18)  has been solved. The overall objective of the algorithm is the following: to find a solution for χ   by numerically solving (21)  while enforcing (22c) , for a given Pe, ɛ  , ∇  x   p  0      (assumed constant) and k   (the latter obtained as solution of the permeability closure problem). The “τ  -SIMPLE” algorithm (Ling and Battiato, 2020 ) introduces an artificial temporal scale τ  1     into the SIMPLE algorithm (Ferziger and Perić, 2002 ) to solve the permeability closure problem, Eq. (17) , while enforcing the global condition, Eq. (18b) . This algorithm is summarized on the left side of Fig. 2 . Here, the algorithm is extended by introducing a second artificial time scale τ  2     that solves the dispersion closure problem, Eq. (21) , while enforcing the global condition, Eq. (22c) . The introduction of an artificial temporal scale allows us to achieve numerical stability and convergence to the unique solution for the closure variable χ  . In particular, we search for the stationary solution  to the equation 〈 χ 〉  = ∂ χ / ∂ τ  2      with τ  2     an artificial temporal scale, such that the global constraint 〈 χ 〉  = 0    is recovered when τ  2   → T   , T ≤ ∞   . In other words, as τ  2     increases to a sufficiently large value, we ensure that the global constraint, 〈 χ 〉  = 0   , is satisfied, effectively driving the solution towards the true stationary state of the closure problems. This algorithm is thus referred to as τ  2    -SIMPLE, which is detailed below and summarized on the right side of Fig. 2 . The algorithm is structured as two sets of double nested loops — the first set to solve for permeability (gray portion of Fig. 2 ) and the second set to solve for effective dispersion (yellow portion of Fig. 2 ). Here we focus exclusively on the solution steps of the dispersion closure problem, i.e. the yellow portion of the algorithm in Fig. 2 , and their integration with the outputs of the permeability closure problem. The steps to calculate permeability are detailed in the work by Ling and Battiato (2020) . Before detailing the steps of the algorithm, we present how the solution of the permeability closure problem (17) –(18)  algorithmically integrates with the dispersion closure problem (21) –(22)  in a non trivial fashion. Once the unit cell geometry is defined and the permeability closure problem has been solved through the procedure outlined in Ling and Battiato (2020)  and summarized for completeness on the left (gray) side of the chart in Fig. 2 , the following quantities become known: k  , K  , ϕ  . First, we note that, differently from the permeability closure problem, the dispersion closure problem requires the specification of the prescribed macroscopic pressure gradient driving the flow, ∇  x   p  0     , as well as the Pe   number. It is critical to emphasize that these two quantities cannot be independently defined and are related to each other through the definition of the Péclet number (8) , and Darcy’s law (15) , which provides a scale for the characteristic velocity U  . As such, Pe   and ∇  x   p  0      have to be prescribed and calculated consistently. Here, we start by prescribing Pe and representing, without loss of generality, ∇  x   p  0      as (24) ∇  x   p  0   ≔ G g ,     where g = g  1   , g  2   , g  3        is the known direction of the pressure gradient with | g |  = 1    and G   its unknown magnitude, to be calculated consistently with the prescribed Pe. Given Pe and g  , we present how to determine the magnitude of ∇  x   p  0      so that the dispersion closure problem can be solved. For a given Pe number, the characteristic velocity scale in (8)  is chosen such that U ≔ | 〈 u  ˆ   〉   B   |    , which implies | 〈 u 〉   B   |  =  1   . This condition combined with Darcy’s law (15)  requires that (25) | K ⋅ ∇  x   p  0   |  = ϕ     with ϕ   porosity and ϕ 〈 u  ˆ   〉   B   = 〈 u  ˆ   〉    . Combining (24) and (25)  provides a condition to uniquely determine G   as (26) G = ϕ  | K ⋅ g |    ,     where | K ⋅ g |  = ( K  i j   g  j   )   2        and Einstein notation convention is implied over the repeated indices. Eq. (26)  ensures that the characteristic velocity U ≔ | 〈 u  ˆ   〉   B   |    , or alternatively, | 〈 u 〉   B   |  = 1   , and that the magnitude of macroscopic pressure drop is calculated such that the resulting flow field is characterized by the prescribed Pe number. Once G   is calculated consistently for a given Pe, the algorithm for the solution of the dispersion closure problem can be initiated. The algorithm is based on a double nested loop which ensures its convergence. The outer loop (n  -loop) ensures the closure problem given by Eq. (21)  is satisfied, while the inner loop (τ  2    -loop) ensures the convergence to steady state for the artificial time scale τ  2    , i.e. 〈 χ 〉  → 0    as τ  2   → ∞   . As such, each numerical iteration is divided into two main steps: (i) solving Eqn (21)  with χ   from the previous iteration as the initial condition, and (ii) applying a correction to χ   based on the global constraint and a relaxation technique to ensure numerical stability and convergence. Specifically, the solution at each iteration, denoted as χ  n    , is constructed by first calculating an intermediate solution χ  n  ∗     and then adjusting it with a correction term χ  n  ′    .   The algorithm is composed of the following steps: Step 1.  Retrieve permeability solution K   and k  , calculated from solving the closure problem (17) –(18)  (Ling and Battiato, 2020 ), and calculate ∇  x   p  0   ≔ G g    and u  0   = − k ⋅ ∇  x   p  0     .  Step 2.  Set n = 1   . Initialize χ  0    .  Step 3.  Solve numerically the following equation for χ  n  ∗    (27) − ∇  y   ⋅ [ D ⋅ I + ∇  y   χ  n  ∗     ]  + ɛ Pe u  0   ⋅ ∇  y   χ  n  ∗   = ɛ Pe 〈 u  0   〉   B   − u  0     ,  y ∈ B     subject to (28) − n ⋅ [ D ⋅ I + ∇  y   χ  n  ∗     ]  = 0 ,  y ∈ Γ       Step 4.  Relax closure variable by using (29) χ  n  ′   = α χ  n  ∗   − χ  n − 1        (30) χ  n   = χ  n − 1   + χ  n  ′         where α   is a relaxation variable. The parameter α   prevents numerical instabilities that arise from rapid changes in the solution between successive iterations. By applying relaxation, the solution updates are tempered, ensuring smooth convergence while maintaining numerical stability even under high flow rates and complex geometries. In this work, α = 0 . 1    was selected to achieve an optimal balance between convergence and stability. The update to χ  n     in each iteration effectively refines the estimate of the true solution to better satisfy both the closure problem and boundary condition.  Step 5.  Set τ  2   = 0   . Determine 〈 χ  n , τ  2   = 0   〉   .  Step 6.  March in time (31) ∂  τ  2     χ  n   = − 〈 χ  n , τ  2     〉      until steady state is reached. Once τ  2    -convergence is reached, then the global condition 〈 χ  n   〉  = 0    is satisfied.  Step 7.  Check n  -convergence. If n  -convergence is reached, χ  n     is the final closure problem solution. If not, set n = n + 1    and return to Step 3.    The following section shows how using the algorithm above enforces the global condition on the closure variable for the dispersion closure problem in unit cells with different pore structures.  4 Algorithm convergence and validation    The implementation of the algorithm described in this work is conducted in OpenFOAM, an open-source CFD software. The τ  2    -SIMPLE algorithm is built into the openly available SIMPLE loop. The algorithm is tested on six periodic unit cells – five 2D (UC-01, UC-02, UC-03, UC-04 and UC-05) and one 3D (UC-06) – with various topological properties, shown in Fig. 3 . Each unit cell is simulated for Péclet number up to Pe = 100   , which allows one to span dynamic regimes ranging from diffusion-controlled to advection-controlled. We emphasize that Pe = 100    corresponds to the theoretical upper bound for the validity of the upscaled Eq. (19)  and its corresponding closure problem, Eq. (21) , when ɛ = 0 . 1   . The geometries considered here include both isotropic and anisotropic structures, as well as solid domains with random shapes and varying channel sizes meant to represent a large variety of realistic porous media of different complexity levels. In all simulations ɛ   is set to 0.1. In the following, we first test the ability of the algorithm to enforce the global condition for all geometries and three Pe numbers, Pe= { 1 , 10 , 100 }     (Section 4.1 ). Subsequently, we perform numerical verification tests, in which we compare the solution of the upscaled equations with the corresponding spatially-averaged pore-scale solution (Section 4.2 ). 4.1 Convergence The global conditions for the dispersion closure problem require that the average of the closure variable over the unit cell is 0, i.e. 〈 χ 〉  = 0   , Eq. (22c) . For completeness, we also show that the average of the closure variable in the pore-space and on the solid boundaries within the unit cell are of the same order, i.e. 〈 χ 〉   B   ≈ 〈 χ 〉   Γ     (23) . In Fig. 4 , the magnitudes of 〈 χ 〉   B     (top) and 〈 χ 〉   Γ     (bottom) are plotted for the six unit cells considered and all Pe numbers. The relaxation parameter α   is set to α = 0 . 1    for all simulations, and convergence is reached when | 〈 χ  n   〉  |  < 1 0  − 12      – though all simulations are ran for 30,000 iterations for comparison, even if convergence has already been reached. Fig. 4  shows that the τ  2    -SIMPLE algorithm ensures that both global conditions are satisfied for all unit cells, as averages for the closure variable in the pore-space and surface converge to 0 for each unit cell and Péclet number. It is worth emphasizing that while only Eq. (22c)  is explicitly enforced when solving the closure problem, Eq. (23)  is satisfied as well. Fig. 4  also illustrates that convergence becomes slower as Péclet number increases, which is expected as higher flow rates introduce more complex dynamics. We note that the homogenization procedure requires Pe < ɛ  − 2      (Battiato and Tartakovsky, 2011 ). Since ɛ = 0 . 1    in this study, the upper limit of Péclet number simulated is Pe=100, strictly beyond the applicability regime. In Fig. 5  the solution for UC-02 and UC-05 is plotted for different Péclet numbers. Fig. 6  plots the magnitude of χ   for the three-dimensional unit cell UC-06 and three Péclet numbers. Both Figs. 5–6  show the impact of increasing Pe number on the closure variable, where higher Pe numbers lead to a distortion of the closure variable field from its diffusive solution at Pe = 1   . Particularly apparent is the shift from a diffusive solution at Pe = 1    to a more advective solution for Pe = 100   , with a preferential flow path in the center of the unit cell, for UC-06. Once the closure variable is determined, the dispersion coefficient can be calculated from (20) . Plots of | χ |    for all unit cells and all simulated Pe are available in the Supplementary Materials, together with the components of the dispersion tensor. For completeness, the Supplementary Materials contain also the components of the permeability tensor and the spatial distribution of | k |    for all unit cells. In Fig. 7 , the four components of the dispersion tensor for all unit cells and Pe = [ 0 , 1 , 2 , 5 , 10 , 20 , 50 , 100 ]     are plotted, so the entire applicability range for ɛ = 0 . 1    is shown. Fig. 7  shows that the growth rate of the diagonal components of D  ∗     with Pe is strongly dependent on the pore-scale structure, with, e.g., D  11  ∗     experiencing more than a 4-fold increase for UC-01 between Pe = 1    and Pe = 100   , while remaining nearly constant for UC-05, across the same range of Pe. This analysis highlights both the challenges in the development of empirical correlations between dispersion coefficient, porosity and Pe number for porous structures of arbitrary geometries, as well as the opportunity of using theoretically established formalisms, e.g. homogenization theory, to determine effective properties from the solution of closure problems for complex pore-structures and different dynamic conditions.   Fig. 7  also shows negative off-diagonal components of the dispersion tensor for unit cells UC-03 and UC-04. From a physical standpoint, a negative off-diagonal component of the dispersion tensor indicates, for example, that a pressure drop driving the flow in the positive y  1    -direction (i.e. flow from left to right) leads to a net mass flux in the negative y  2    -direction (downward mass flux). The impact of flow directionality and channelization (augmented by local geometric anisotropy) becomes more pronounced with increasing Péclet number. Unlike unit cells UC-03 and UC-04 (Fig. 7 ) which have pore-scale structures which lead to negative off-diagonal tensor components as mass flux tends to be driven in the negative y  2    -direction (down) as flow moves in the positive y  1    -direction (left to right), UC-05 demonstrates how strong unit cell anisotropy can cause significantly positive off-diagonal components under high Péclet numbers, where flow in the positive y  1    -direction (to the right) simultaneously enhances transport in the positive y  2    -direction (upward). An insightful analysis on the magnitude and sign of the components of the dispersion coefficient is offered by Dejam and Hassanzadeh (2022) .    4.2 Verification Once the effective Darcy-scale parameters K   and D  ∗     have been determined from the closure variables, the continuum-scale Eqs. (15) and (19)  can be numerically solved on a macroscopic effective domain provided appropriate boundary conditions and initial conditions are defined. Numerical verification of the upscaled equations and effective parameters is performed by comparing the numerical solution of Eqs. (15) and (19)  against the spatially averaged fully-resolved pore-scale solution governed by Eqs. (9) and (10) , while ensuring that the absolute error between the two solutions is bounded by ɛ  , as prescribed by homogenization theory. A direct comparison against the fully resolved pore-scale model demonstrates that the algorithm can accurately reproduce the true benchmark it is designed to emulate. Simulations of the macroscopic and pore-scale domain with the same boundary conditions (see Fig. 8 ) are ran. The domain consists of ten repeating unit cells aligned in the x  1    -direction (horizontal). Thus, the total macroscopic domain length is L = 1   , and the unit-cell size is ɛ = 0 . 1   , as illustrated in Fig. 8 . This horizontal direction is where the pressure gradient is applied. In the x  2    -direction (vertical), the model includes only three layers of unit cells. Despite this, periodic boundary conditions applied at the top and bottom boundaries render the domain effectively infinite in the vertical direction. Following Pietrzyk and Battiato (2023a, b)  and for the current validation, we find that the choice of ɛ = 0 . 1    is a good balance between (i) testing the model under the most challenging theoretical conditions, i.e. for ɛ   as large as possible, but still smaller than 1, as required by homogenization theory, and (ii) computational cost, since reducing ɛ   would dramatically increase the computational burden of the pore-scale simulations due to larger domains and finer grid requirements. The boundary conditions for concentration are designed to simulate a pulse of solute entering the domain from the central region of the left inlet boundary. Initially, a Heaviside Dirichlet boundary condition is imposed on the left boundary, by setting c  ɛ   = 1    for 0 . 1 < x  2   < 0 . 2    and c  ɛ   = 0    elsewhere, creating a sharp concentration front. This condition is maintained for 0 ≤ t  ˆ   ≤ t  ˆ    A     , which corresponds to the time it would take for the concentration pulse to travel across the domain in the absence of diffusion. At t  ˆ   = t  ˆ    A     , the inlet concentration is switched off (c  ɛ   = 0    across the entire left boundary). The top and bottom boundaries are treated with periodic boundary conditions, while a zero-flux condition n ⋅ ∇ c = 0    is enforced at the outlet (right boundary). See Fig. 8 . The diffusion coefficient D   is set to 1 for all simulations, and the characteristic velocity U = 〈 u 〉     is adjusted via ∇  x  1     p  0      to achieve the desired Péclet numbers of Pe = 1 , 10 , 100     , as discussed in Section 3 . The detailed setup and boundary conditions for both the pore-scale and macroscopic simulations are summarized in Table 1 . The verification is based on assessing whether the absolute error between the continuum scale solution and the averaged pore-scale solution is bounded by ɛ  , the a priori  upscaling error guaranteed by homogenization theory. Specifically, the error is defined as | 〈 c 〉   B   − 〈 c  ɛ   〉   B   |    for all points in the macroscopic domain. The maximum and mean error can then be computed for each time step and are plotted in Fig. 9 . The equations for calculating maximum and mean error, δ  max     and δ  ̄     respectively, are (32) δ  max   = max  i   | 〈 c  i   〉   B   − 〈 c  i , ɛ   〉   B   |       (33) δ  ̄   = ∑  i   | 〈 c  i   〉   B   − 〈 c  i , ɛ   〉   B   |        where i   represents each cell modeled in the continuum domain. The pore-scale concentration, c  ɛ     is averaged over the pore-space to allow for comparison with the macroscopic model. Fig. 9  shows that, for all cases with Pe < ɛ  − 2     , i.e, Pe < 100   , the maximum error is on the order of ɛ   or below, as guaranteed by homogenization theory (Pietrzyk et al., 2021 ), when the applicability conditions are satisfied. We emphasize that when Pe = 100   , the maximum error slightly exceeds ɛ   for UC-05, while it remains below the error-threshold for all other unit cells although the applicability condition is strictly violated. However, for all Pe numbers, including Pe = 100   , the mean error is always of order less than ɛ  . This demonstrates the robustness of the closure problem approach and accuracy of the algorithm. Fig. 10  shows the pore-scale (inset (a)), averaged pore-scale (inset (b)) and upscaled (inset (c)) concentration distribution for UC-04 at t = 0 . 01    and Pe = 100   . Despite the averaged pore-scale and upscaled concentration fields are very similar (see absolute error in inset (d)), the majority of the error is concentrated at the inlet at early times, when the solute entering the domain has not had the ability to diffuse yet across a full unit cell. Videos comparing the macroscale and pore-scale simulations for all unit cells are available in the Supplementary Material.   5 Conclusions Homogenization of the Stokes and the advection-diffusion equations describing passive solute transport in porous media results in two boundary value problems (or closure problems) to calculate the permeability and dispersion tensor over a repeating unit cell describing the local periodic structure of the medium. This process defines applicability regimes for the macroscale formulation as well as global conditions which require that the average of the closure variables are equal to zero in the unit cell. Ensuring that such global conditions are satisfied is important to guarantee the accuracy of both the upscaled solution and the reconstructed pore-scale field, when that is necessary. In this work, a novel algorithm was developed to efficiently and accurately solve the permeability and dispersion closure problems while satisfying such global criteria. The algorithm developed is tested against a number of 2D pore-scale geometries with different levels of anisotropy and for one 3D unit cell. Once the closure solutions are determined, the corresponding dispersion tensor is determined for different pore-scale geometries and Pe numbers. The accuracy of the effective coefficients calculated from the closure variables is finally numerically verified by comparing the spatially averaged pore-scale and the upscaled concentration field in a transient injection scenario. Although the algorithm has been tested and verified on flow and transport of a passive tracer, this formulation is valid for mildly reactive systems where the solute is subjected to both homogeneous and heterogeneous reaction at Damköhler numbers less than one. Future work involves the development of algorithms that can enforce similar types of global conditions on closure variables for precipitation–dissolution problems for moderately reactive cases in which flow dynamics, transport and moving boundaries may be coupled in the closure problem formulation (?).
1 Introduction Biofilms are sessile communities of microbial cells that are attached to mineral surfaces and other substrates (Hall-Stoodley et al., 2004 ). In the subsurface systems, e.g., geological repositories, the microorganisms can form biofilms on mineral surfaces (Carrel et al., 2017 ; Coombs et al., 2010 ; Escudero et al., 2018 ) and cause mineral precipitation (Cosmidis and Benzerara, 2022 ; Zhu and Dittrich, 2016 ). Such microbial activities can cause alterations of rock properties, e.g., porosity, diffusivity/dispersivity, permeability (Kone et al., 2014 ; Vogt et al., 2013 ) and pore water chemistry, e.g., pH, redox conditions (Mitchell et al., 2019 ) and affect the adsorption of radionuclides on the host rock's mineral surfaces (Behrends et al., 2012 ; Lopez-Fernandez et al., 2021 ). Consequently, consideration of microbial activities is of importance in the accurate estimation of contaminant transport in the subsurface, which is a key in the risk assessments of radioactive waste disposal. Recently, laboratory experiments have been performed to study the effect of microbial growth on the changes in rock properties. In these studies, different imaging techniques and tracers were applied to provide the spatial distribution of the biofilm materials in the porous media. For example, Kildsgaard and Engesgaard (2002)  visualized biological clogging during a two-dimensional flow experiment. By analyzing the image data, they found the dispersion increased due to the clogging by microbial growth. Charbonneau et al. (2006)  performed diffusion experiments in a total of 11 diffusion cell pairs where biofilm growth was stimulated. The experimental results demonstrated that the effective porosity and diffusivity were reduced due to the development of a biofilm in the pores of the rock matrix. Carrel et al. (2017)  proposed an iron sulfate method to provide images of the morphology of biofilms during biofilm growth. In this method, contrast agents such as barium sulfate were used in the X-ray tomography technique to image the biofilm for a better understanding of the biofilm development and bioclogging mechanisms in the porous media. These studies revealed the changes in rock properties due to the microbial growth, which impacts not only fluid flow but also the solute transport. As another important microbial activity in the subsurface, microorganisms can induce mineral precipitation (e.g., calcite precipitation), which can be built as a by-product of different microbial metabolic activities, including photosynthesis, ureolysis, denitrification, ammonification, sulfate reduction, methane oxidation (Görgen et al., 2020 ; Zhu and Dittrich, 2016 ). Among these metabolic activities, ureolysis is the most common and best studied. Ureolytic bacteria were found in different soils and aquatic environments (Arias et al., 2018 ; Bibi et al., 2018 ; Nasser et al., 2022 ) and can be also used for biotechnological applications (Fang and Achal, 2019 ; Jeong et al., 2017 ; Nasser et al., 2022 ). Among different ureolytic bacteria, Sporosarcina pasteurii  (formerly known as Bacillus pasteurii ) has been extensively used as the model urease-producing organism in ureolysis-driven calcite precipitation studies, due to its high ureolytic activity (Yoon et al., 2001 ). Several factors seem to be beneficial for the superior performance of this bacterium such as the strong negative cell surface charge of S. pasteurii , which is favorable for binding calcium ions, and a high correlation between biomass growth and urease production (Ma et al., 2020 ). The biomineralization of calcium carbonate by this bacterium was also studied in the presence of trivalent europium, an analog for trivalent actinides, using time-resolved laser-induced fluorescence spectroscopy (TRLFS) and a variety of physicochemical techniques (Johnstone et al., 2016 ). During the calcite phase transformation, the Eu(III) speciation changed and resulted in the incorporation of several species in the calcite phase, either substituting at the Ca2+  site or at a previously unidentified, low-symmetry site. Most of the studies with S. pasteurii  for calcite precipitation were performed under aerobic conditions and S. pasteurii  seems to be unable to grow anaerobically (Martin et al., 2012 ). The ureolytic activity previously shown under anoxic conditions can be a consequence of the urease enzyme already present in the cells of the aerobically grown inoculum (Martin et al., 2012 ). It was also observed that variations in the ureolytic capabilities and associated rates of calcite precipitation between species and even strains must be considered in subsurface engineering strategies that utilize microbial amendments (Mitchell et al., 2019 ). Reactive transport models (RTMs) are widely applied to simulate the contaminant migration in the subsurface in the presence of microbes. The RTMs enable simulation of the coupling processes of fluid flow, solutes transport, chemical reactions, and biogeochemical reactions from the pore scale to the larger scale (Ebigbo et al., 2013 , 2010 ; Steefel et al., 2015 ; Zhang and Klapper, 2010 ; Zivar et al., 2021 ). In the RTMs, the microbial growth rate can be estimated using the Monod model (Monod, 1949 ), which describes the growth rate as a function of the mass concentration of substrate. At the field scale, Ebigbo et al. (2010)  developed a numerical model to simulate the biofilm growth in a CO2  storage reservoir. The model described the biofilm growth, flow, and transport in the geological formation and the interaction between the biofilm and the flow processes. At the core scale, an RTM was presented to simulate microbial-induced calcite precipitation through ureolysis (Zhang and Klapper, 2010 ). Their model can predict the temporal and spatial evolution of rock porosity due to microbial-induced calcite precipitation. At the pore scale, a coupled RTM was presented to study the impact of microbial activity on the efficiency of underground hydrogen storage (Ebigbo et al., 2013 ). In their model, three microbial species (i.e., methanogens, acetogens, and acetotrophs) were considered to be active in the presence of high concentrations of hydrogen.
