The simulation results demonstrated that hydrogen was consumed by these three microbial species. These studies proposed different numerical models at different length scales to simulate the microbial activities (e.g., growth and induced mineral precipitation) and corresponding physical and chemical processes. However, the study of the effects of microbial activity on mineral surface topography evolution was not included in these investigations. As a surrogate parameter to quantify the evolution of surface topography, surface roughness has a significant impact on various processes, such as mineral dissolution (Deng et al., 2018 ) and the adsorption of contaminants (Yuan et al., 2021 ). Therefore, at the pore scale, the increase of microbial activity on minerals causes changes in the substrate surface topography, affecting contaminant transport at the core scale and beyond. Consequently, a comprehensive understanding of the evolution of surface topography due to the microbial activity at the pore scale is beneficial to improve the estimation of contaminant migration in the subsurface. In this study, we focus on the influence of microbially induced calcite precipitation on the evolution of a material surface at the pore scale. Among the six common microbial metabolic activities, i.e., photosynthesis, ureolysis, denitrification, ammonification, sulfate reduction, and methane oxidation, ureolysis is the most common metabolism to induce calcite precipitation in soils and rocks (Zhu and Dittrich, 2016 ). Therefore, we present a pore-scale reactive transport model to simulate the physicochemical processes owing to microbially induced calcite precipitation through ureolysis occurring on the solid surface in porous media. The model of ureolysis contains three parts: (1) urea hydrolysis catalyzed by ureolytic bacteria; (2) dissociation of carbonatic acid, bicarbonate ion, and ammonia; and (3) calcite precipitation in the presence of dissolved calcium ions. The numerical investigations focus on modeling the reactive transport in a flow-through cell and quantification of the evolution of surface topography by a statistical parameter, surface nanoroughness, and applying the power spectral density (PSD) analysis. The sensitivity analysis focuses on the effects of advection, diffusion, and reaction on the evolution of surface topography. We quantify the resulting surface nanoroughness and PSD based on two dimensionless numbers, Péclet (Pe ) and Damköhler (Da ) numbers, which determine the dominancy among the advection, diffusion, and reaction. This pore-scale study presents insights into the microscopic physicochemical processes of biomass-solid substrate material-fluid interaction and its impact on surface topography and solute transport. Overall, the generalizable approach presented in this study contributes to improve the predictability of contaminant transport at the pore scale.  2 Methodology 2.1 Investigated cementitious material Low-pH model cementitious material, created by mixing Ordinary Portland Cement (OPC) with colloidal silica, was cast into a 4 × 4 × 16 cm3  mold by colleagues from the Institute for Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety (IRSN) in France (Neji et al., 2023 ). After one year of hydration in a sealed bag, the paste was cut into 1 cm slices. A layer of resin (Resoltech 3030) was applied to each slice. The sample material was examined for integrity using micro-computed tomography, and the topography was then analyzed using vertical scanning interferometry (VSI). A Sensofar microscope was used in VSI mode with a 50 × objective. For general details about the data acquisition and analysis see Fischer and Luttge (2007) . Resulting field of view (FOV) size = 350 µm × 260 µm, and spatial resolution is 258 nm × 258 nm.  2.2 The pore-scale reactive transport model In this study, we employ the micro-continuum approach (Soulaine, 2024 ; Soulaine et al., 2017 ; Soulaine and Tchelepi, 2016 ) for modeling the coupled processes of fluid flow, solute transport, and microbial-induced calcite precipitation at the pore scale. In this approach, each control volume contains a pore region, or solid region, or both, which are differentiated by the volume fraction of void space, ϕf  . In the pore region, ϕf   = 1. In the solid-fluid interface, 0 < ϕf   < 1. In the solid region, the solid phase is described by a fictitious low-porosity material (i.e., ϕf   = 0   0.001), which results in near-zero velocities in the solid regions and a no-slip boundary condition at the solid-fluid interfaces (Soulaine et al., 2017 ). In the mathematical model, the Stokes-Brinkman equation (Brinkman, 1947 ) is utilized for modeling fluid flow in both solid-free and porous regions in a single framework (Soulaine and Tchelepi, 2016 ; Yuan et al., 2016 ). We then couple the Stokes-Brinkman equation, the reactive transport equations, and the petrophysical model for simulating the coupled processes. Stokes-Brinkman model . The Stokes-Brinkman equation has been widely applied to model fluid flow in fractured porous media (Popov et al., 2009 ; Yuan et al., 2016 ), as it provides a single set of equations for simulating fluid flow in the entire domain. The general formulations of the Stokes-Brinkman equation for incompressible single-phase fluid are given as follows (Brinkman, 1947 ; Popov et al., 2009 ; Yuan et al., 2016 ):(1) μ K perm  − 1   v + ∇ p − μ  *  Δ  v = 0 ,     (2) ∇ · v = 0 ,     where v  denotes the physical velocity of the fluid in the solid-free regions and the Darcy velocity in porous regions, p  represents pressure, K perm  is a permeability tensor, μ is the physical viscosity of the fluid, and μ* is the effective viscosity, which is a key parameter for matching the shear stress boundary condition at the solid-fluid interface (Martys et al., 1994 ). The effective viscosity μ* is set equal to the fluid viscosity μ in most applications (Popov et al., 2009 ; Yuan et al., 2016 , 2019 ). In this study, the fluid viscosity μ is the water viscosity, which is 1 × 10–3  Pa·s. The Stokes-Brinkman equation tends toward Stokes momentum in solid-free regions and Darcy's law in porous regions, a feature that enables the efficient modeling of the evolution of the interface between porous and solid-free regions without involving complex re-meshing or interface-tracking strategies. The readers are referred to Yuan et al. (2016)  for more details on discussions of the Stokes-Brinkman equation. Reactive-transport model . The reactive transport equations describe the coupled processes of solute transport and geochemical reactions. In the model, the aqueous species are classified into primary species and secondary species (Steefel and Lasaga, 1994 ). The general mass balance equations for the primary species α are written as:(3) ∂ C T α    ∂ t   + ∇ · ( v C T α   − D ∇ C T α    )  = R α m i n   ,  ( α = 1 ,  ⋯ ,  N p   )  ,     where C T α  are the total concentrations of primary species, Np   is the number of primary species, and R α m i n     are the kinetic reaction rates of primary species. In this study, the chemical reactions (i.e., Eqs. 6 - 10) are calculated using PHREEQC v3.7 (Parkhurst and Appelo, 2013 ). To solve the reactive-transport equations (i.e., Eq. (3) ), we couple the PHREEQC/IPhreeqc with a previously developed numerical simulator (Yuan et al., 2019 ) using a non-iterative operator-split approach (Steefel et al., 2015 ). Following the execution of PHREEQC/IPhreeqc, the change of volume fraction of the solid phase, ϕs   in a control volume during the precipitation processes is calculated by (Lu et al., 2022 ):(4) Δ  ϕ s  = Δ  b s  ρ f  ϕ f  V m  ,     where Δbs   is the amount of precipitated calcite per kg of water (in a unit of mol/kg), which is calculated by PHREEQC/IPhreeqc. ρf   is the fluid density (in a unit of kg/m3 ), and Vm   is the molar volume (in a unit of m3 /mol). Petrophysical model.  In this study, the Kozeny-Carman equation is utilized to estimate the local absolute permeability from the porosity. The Kozeny-Carman equation is written as (Soulaine et al., 2017 ):(5) K p e r m  − 1   = K p e r m 0  − 1   ( 1 − ϕ f   )   2  ϕ f 3   ,     where K perm 0  is the initial permeability. The initial permeability K perm 0  of 10−15  m2  is chosen to ensure no-slip boundary conditions at the solid/fluid interfaces (Soulaine et al., 2017 ). The proposed mathematical model (i.e., Eqs. 1 - 5) is solved numerically using a decoupled approach (Yuan et al., 2019 ), which contains four sub-steps within each time step: (1) solution of the Stokes-Brinkman and continuity equations resulting in velocities and pressure; (2) solution of the reactive-transport equations using the calculated velocities, resulting in solute concentrations and updated volume fractions of solids; (3) the fluid-rock interface will be updated based on the updated volume fractions of the solid phase; (4) The local permeability is then calculated based on the volume fractions of porous regions using the Kozeny-Carman equation. The updated permeability will be used for the calculations in the next time step.  2.3 Biogeochemical reactions In this study, we employ the kinetics of calcite precipitation induced by hydrolysis of urea (CO(NH2 )2 ) by bacteria (Zhu and Dittrich, 2016 ), which are based on the reactions by equations 6 – 10 (Mitchell et al., 2019 ; Zhang and Klapper, 2010 ). Firstly, the ureolytic bacteria produce the urease, which catalyzes the hydrolysis of urea, resulting in the product of ammonia (NH3 ) and carbonic acid (H2 CO3 ) (Eq. (6) ). The ammonia and carbonic acid equilibrate in circumneutral aqueous conditions to form bicarbonate (HCO3 - ), ammonium ion (NH4 + ), and carbonate ion (CO3 2- ) (Eqs. 7 - 9). In the presence of the dissolved calcium (Ca2+ ), the saturation state of the system shifts and as a consequence solid calcium carbonate (CaCO3 ) is formed (Eq. (10) ).(6) CO ( N H 2   )  2  + 2 H 2  O   → 2 N H 3  + H 2  C O 3  ,     (7) H 2  C O 3  ⇌ HCO 3 −  + H  +  ,     (8) HCO 3 −  ⇌ CO 3 2 −   + H  +  ,     (9) NH 4 +  ⇌ N H 3  + H  +  ,     (10) C a  2 +   + CO 3 2 −   ⇌ CaC O 3  .       2.4 Pore-scale simulation setup In this study, we first present a numerical investigation to validate our numerical model. In the numerical experiment, we assume a constant concentration of biomass (Mitchell et al., 2019 ), which is attached to a flat material surface (Fig. 1  ). The computational domain has 100 × 50 pixels and the size of each pixel is 40 × 40 µm2 . The pore water contains 25 mM CaCl2  and 333 mM urea at pH 6 (Mitchell et al., 2019 ) as the initial condition. We consider the diffusive transport of aqueous species due to the concentration gradient to mimic the batch reactions. All the boundaries are non-flux conditions. The ureolysis rate coefficient (kurea  ) and calcite precipitation rate (kp  ) are 0.55 day-1  and 0.2 mmol l-1 day-1 , respectively (Mitchell et al., 2019 ; Zhang and Klapper, 2010 ). These kinetic data for microbially induced calcite precipitation are from studies with planktonic bacterial cells in solution, not from studies with biofilms developed on solid surfaces. We compare the temporal evolution of the pH value in the solution with the experimental data under a batch reaction condition from Mitchell et al. (2019) . Next, we perform the simulations of fluid flow through a two-dimensional (2D) channel with a rough surface. In the 2D simulations, the fluid-mineral interface is defined using the rough surface topography of a cementitious material measured by vertical scanning interferometry (Fig. 2  ). The computational domain has 1360 × 200 pixels and the size of each pixel is 258 × 129 nm2 . Constant velocity and constant pressure are applied at the inlet (left side) and outlet (right side) boundaries, respectively. “Open boundary” is applied to the upper boundary and the “no-slip” condition is applied to the bottom boundary. The biomass is assumed to attach to the rough surface. Since biomass can lead to a permeability reduction by a factor of 2000 if the biomass completely fills the pores (Dupin et al., 2001 ), we assume for simplicity the biomass is the solid phase with a significantly low permeability. Therefore, no explicit differentiation is made between the biomass and solid phase in the model. Since the concentration of biomass is assumed to be constant, the thickness of the biomass does not change during calcite precipitation. Therefore, the thickness of the biomass does not affect the temporal evolution of the material surface due to calcite precipitation. In this study, for simplicity, we assume that we can ignore the thickness of the biomass. Moreover, we assume the calcite precipitation only occurs at the interface between water and solid phases with the following steps: (1) locate the interface cells that have a volume fraction of void space of one (i.e., ϕf   = 1) and at least have one neighboring cell of solid phase (i.e., ϕf   = 0   0.001); (2) update volume fractions of the solid phase of the interface cells (0 < ϕf   < 1) based on the calculated precipitated calcite (cf. step 3 in numerical solution procedure); (3) repeat the growing process of (2) until the volume fraction of the solid phase of the interface cells reaches one (i.e., ϕf   = 0   0.001); (4) repeat the steps (1) and (2) for the next interface cells. In this study, we consider that one cell has four neighbors in four principal directions (i.e., ±x  and ±y  directions) with identical growth probability in the 2D Cartesian coordinates. In this section, to quantify the importance of advection, diffusion, and reaction rates, two dimensionless parameters, Péclet (Pe ) and Damköhler (Da ) numbers are used under different flow and transport conditions. The Péclet (Pe ) is defined by: P e =  u i n   L  D    , where uin   is the injected velocity, L  is the length of the domain, and D  is the diffusion coefficient. The Damköhler (Da ) number is defined by (Deng et al., 2018 ): D a =  k p  L  u i n   C a e q       , where kp   is the calcite precipitation rate (set to 0.7 mol/L/day after model validation), Caeq   is the calcium concentration in the pore water. In this study, three case studies have been performed for various diffusion coefficients (D  = 1.15  × 10−15  − 1  × 10−10  m2 /s) and injected velocities (uin   = 1.15  × 10−10  − 1  × 10−4  m/s), resulting in various Pe  and Da  numbers listed in Table 1  . We first present case 1 (cf. Table 1 ) to study the temporal evolution of surface topography caused by microbial-induced calcite precipitation. In this case, the Pe  and Da  numbers are 3500 and 9.8, respectively, which indicate that the flow is dominated by advective transport. In order to quantify the evolution of surface topography, we calculate the overall surface nanoroughness, which is the root-mean-square deviation of the surface height (i.e., Sq  parameter). Note that the RMS roughness of a profile is sometimes referred to as Rq , as opposed to the RMS roughness Sq , which is calculated from multiple profiles that form a surface. For simplicity, we will use Sq  to describe RMS roughness in general. The calculation of Sq  can be written as (Thomas, 1999 ): S q =  1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  ( h i  − h ¯   )   2       (in a unit of micron), where N  is the number of points in the surface height profile (i.e., N  = 1360). hi   is the surface height of point i  in the surface height profile (in a unit of micron), and h ¯    is the mean surface height (in a unit of micron). The temporal evolution of the Sq  parameter demonstrates the effect of calcite precipitation on the surface topography. Moreover, we apply the power spectral density (PSD) analysis on the surface topography data at different reaction times (e.g., Duparre et al., 2002 ). The fractal dimension and the Hurst exponent parameters are quantified by fitting the fractal models to different PSD curves. The temporal evolution of the Hurst exponent parameter will provide both the lateral and vertical distribution of surface nanoroughness and the scale dependency of roughness. Next, we study the effect of advection, diffusion, and reaction rates on the temporal evolution of surface topography. We varied the reaction and transport conditions at the surface by changing flow velocities and diffusion coefficients (cf. cases 1 – 3 in Table 1 ). The flow velocities are used to control surface precipitation rate limitations, with low flow velocities leading to transport-limited conditions and high flow velocities leading to reaction-limited conditions. Here, we consider cases 2 and 3 with different Pe  and Da  numbers. In cases 2 and 3, the Pe  and Da  numbers are 350 and 1.13 × 10–3 , and 35 and 980, respectively. The different temporal evolutions of the Sq  parameter, PSD profiles, and Hurst exponent parameters are compared, respectively, among cases 1, 2, and 3.  2.5 Power spectral density analysis The power spectral density (PSD) of a surface is a mathematical tool that deconvolves the surface height distributions into contributions from different spatial frequencies (Jacobs et al., 2017 ). Mathematically, the PSD is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation function of the height signal, which contains the power across a range of wavevectors. The application of PSD is capable of understanding the effects of surface morphology on the properties of material systems (Pfeifer et al., 1989 ). Specific PSD profile behaviors can be described by the fractal model, in which the surface fractal dimension (D ) and Hurst exponent (H ) describe the spatial distribution of surface nanoroughness on various complex surface geometries and the scale dependency of roughness (Gong et al., 2016 , 2018 ). The general formulation of the fractal model can be expressed as (Gong et al., 2016 ):(11) PS D f r a c t a l   = K f  s   ,     where K  is the spectral strength and s  is the slope of logarithmic plots (PSD vs. spatial frequency). The fractal dimension, D , can be determined as(12) D = { 2 ,  0 ≤ | s |  ≤ 1    0.5 ( 8 − s  )  ,  1 < | s |  ≤ 3    1 ,  3 < | s |       .      The Hurst exponent, H , is the roughness scaling factor, which has a value between zero and one and is related to the fractal dimension by H  = 3 − D . In this study, we first quantify the fractal dimension and the Hurst exponent parameters with the following three steps: (1) the PSD profiles are generated based on the surface topography data. (2) The K  and s  are determined by fitting a function to the PSD plot through the fractal model. (3) The fractal dimension and the Hurst exponent are quantified based on the fitted value of s . Next, we quantify and compare the different fractal dimensions and the Hurst exponent parameters based on the temporal evolution of PSD profiles. The different fractal dimensions and the Hurst exponent parameters demonstrate the effect of calcite precipitation on the surface topography due to microbial activity.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Model validation We simulate the microbially induced calcite precipitation at a flat surface under diffusive transport conditions to mimic a batch reaction and compare the numerical results with the laboratory experimental data from Mitchell et al. (2019) . The temporal evolution of the pH and concentration of calcium ions (Ca2+ ) in the solution of our model results are compared with experimental data, as shown in Fig. 3  . Fig. 3 a illustrates that the pH value increases from 6.0 to 9.1 after 30 h of reaction and then reaches a plateau, corresponding to steady-state conditions of the reaction. Fig. 3 b shows that the Ca2+  has decreased by an order of magnitude after 30 h of reaction, as the Ca2+  in solution is consumed to form calcite on the material surface. More generally, Fig. 3  demonstrates that microbial-induced calcite precipitation can cause changes in water chemistry (e.g., pH, Ca2+  concentration), affecting the solute transport. The good agreement between the model results and the experimental data indicates that our proposed reactive transport model is capable of simulating microbially induced calcite precipitation at the pore scale. Note that, since experimental micromorphological data are not currently available in the literature, model validation is focused on quantitative analysis of microbially driven reactions using data from Mitchell et al. (2019) . Our colleagues are conducting ongoing experimental work on biofilm formation and surface evolution due to microbially induced calcite precipitation. Future work will aim to improve model validation as these data become available.  3.2 The temporal evolution of the surface topography due to calcite precipitation We utilize the rough surface (cf. surface profile in Fig. 2 b) in the 2D pore-scale model, as shown in Fig. 4  a. Fig. 4 b illustrates the relative velocity distribution (u/u0 ) of case 1 (cf. Table 1 ) based on the rough surface. The constant injection velocity (u0 ) is applied at the inlet boundary (left side). Thus, a certain length parallel to the flow direction is required for developing the Stokes flow situation, resulting in the calculated velocity distribution based on the momentum balance. The temporal evolution of the Sq parameter of case 1 is shown in Fig. 5   (cf. Equation in Section 2.5 for Sq calculation). In Fig. 5 , the temporal evolution of Sq shows a periodic fluctuation pattern. Specifically, Sq first decreases to the first local minimum value at point B and then increases to the first local maximum value at point C after about 19 h of precipitation. After 43 h of precipitation, Sq rises again to reach the second local minimum value at point D and then increases to the second maximum value at point E. The increased surface heights due to calcite precipitation at B (black line), C (red line), D (blue line), and E (green line) are shown in Fig. 6  . The dynamic changes in Sq value and surface heights are caused by the temporal alterations of Δϕs   within the interface, which are influenced by the amount of precipitated calcite, Δbs   and volume fraction of void space, ϕf   (cf. Eq.4). In case 1, the flow is dominated by advective transport (Pe  = 3500). The calcium ion (Ca2+ ) rich zone is initially located near the pore wall at the inlet and is predominantly displaced downstream along the pore wall (see Fig. S1a for Ca2+  concentration after a 19 h period), resulting in a larger precipitated calcite Δbs   near the inlet (cf. Fig. S3a). Consequently, the increased surface height is greater near the inlet (e.g., ROI I in Fig. 4 ) than near the outlet (e.g., ROI II in Fig. 4 ) (cf. black line in Fig. 6 ). Therefore, the larger values of increased surface height near the inlet causes a smoothing of the substrate surface, resulting in an initially reduced value of Sq (points A – B in Fig. 5 ). After 19 h, the concentration of calcium ion (Ca2+ ) near the outlet is increased due to the advective transport of Ca2+  to the outlet (cf. Fig. S1a). Such increased Ca2+  concentration leads to a rapid increase in Δbs   near the outlet, resulting in similar values of Δbs   between the inlet and the outlet (cf. Fig. S3b). However, the values of ϕf   in the interface cells near the inlet are significantly lower than near the outlet due to the larger precipitation near the inlet (cf. Fig. S4a and b). Consequently, the values of Δϕs   in the interface cells near the inlet are smaller than near the outlet. This larger Δϕs   results in a rapid increase in surface height near the outlet. As shown in Fig. 6 , the increased surface heights in ROI I and II between 19 h and 43 h of precipitation are about 18 nm and 95 nm, respectively (cf. red and black lines). As a result, the material surface becomes rougher, resulting in an increased value of Sq (cf. points B – C in Fig. 5 ). After 43 h, the period from C to D involves updating the interface cells near the inlet (see thicker layers of deposited calcite in ROI I in Fig. S3c), resulting in larger values of ϕf   in the interface cells near the inlet (cf. Fig. S4c). Consequently, according to Eq. (4) , the Δϕs   in ROI I is larger than in ROI II, despite having a similar value of Δbs   (cf. Fig. S3c). This larger Δϕs   leads to a rapidly increased surface height near the inlet (cf. blue and red lines in Fig. 6 ), which causes a less rough material surface again, resulting in a reduced Sq value (cf. points C – D in Fig. 5 ). Moreover, the values of Δbs   and ϕf   in the interface cells near the outlet exhibit relatively homogeneous distributions (cf. Figs. S3c and S4c), which causes an almost uniform Δϕs   resulting in a plateau near the outlet (cf. blue line in Fig. 6 ). From points D to E, the larger Δϕs   near the outlet causes the rapid increase in surface height, consequently resulting in an increased Sq value (cf. green and blue lines in Fig. 6 ). This behavior is similar as observed during the period from B to C, as explained above. Therefore, the consistent dynamic trends between the sub-periods A – C and C – E can be found in Fig. 5  due to the differently increased surface height from the inlet to the outlet (cf. Fig. 6 ). Eventually, the microbial-induced calcite precipitation causes a wave-shaped curve of the temporal evolution of the Sq parameter. Moreover, the local maximum values and local minimum values of Sq decrease versus time, indicating that the calcite precipitation causes a generalized decrease in Sq value. This can be indicated by the linear correlation of the Sq value and time with a negative slope (cf. red dashed line in Fig. 5 ). Therefore, microbial-induced calcite precipitation can eventually cause a less rough material surface for case 1. For Da  = 9.8 > 1 in case 1, the advection time scale is higher than the reaction time scale, resulting in a transport-limited precipitation regime. At the same time, the advective transport dominates the fluid flow (Pe  = 3500). Fluid mixing strength exerts control over the chemical gradient inside pore space. Consequently, a larger increased surface height can be observed near the inlet (e.g., ROI I in Fig. 4 ), as shown in Fig. 6 . Moreover, the various values of the increased surface height along the surface at a specific reaction time (cf. four colored lines in Fig. 6 ) demonstrate the heterogeneous calcite precipitation due to the microbial activity. Such heterogeneous calcite precipitation causes dynamic changes in the material surface topography (cf. Sq values in Fig. 5 ). Therefore, under the advection-dominated transport and transport-limited conditions, the microbial can induce heterogenous calcite precipitation on the material surface at the pore scale. The heterogeneous reaction pattern under the same conditions can be found in the previously reported pore-scale studies (Agrawal et al., 2020 ; Soulaine et al., 2017 ), where the authors observed the heterogeneous calcite dissolution on the material surface based on the pore-scale simulation results. Figs. 5 and 6  demonstrate that the microbial can induce the heterogeneous calcite precipitation on the material surface under the advection-dominated transport and transport-limited conditions, resulting in eventually a less rough material surface at the pore scale. Fig. 7  a and b illustrates the PSD versus spatial frequency calculated from the 2-D surface topography data (cf. Fig. 2 a) and the 1-D surface profile data (cf. Fig. 2 b), respectively, before the microbial-induced calcite precipitation. The curve for 1-D surface data shows large variances of PSD in the high spatial frequency region (> 106  m-1 ) compared to the curve for 2-D surface data. Such large variances of PSD indicate that the graph is exceedingly noisy in the high spatial frequency for the 1-D surface profile data. Due to the given spatial resolution of the topography profiles, the statistics of the PSD analysis are too weak for spatial frequencies above 1 µm wavelength. Since the 2-D surface data contain 1024 1-D surface profiles with the same pixel size and number as the data in Fig. 2 b, the PSD calculated from the 2-D surface data can be considered as an ensemble average of PSD calculated from such 1024 1-D surface profiles. Therefore, such an ensemble-averaged method can reduce the variance sufficiently in the high spatial frequency region (Elson and Bennett, 1995 ), resulting in a smooth PSD curve as shown in Fig. 7 a. Certainly, spatial resolution affects the high-frequency components and the regression line bends upwards for the highest spatial frequencies in Fig. 7 a. Fig. 8   visualizes the evolution of PSD due to calcite precipitation. The black solid line represents the PSD calculated from the surface data before calcite precipitation, and the red solid line represents the PSD calculated from the surface data after calcite precipitation of 97 h (cf. points A and E in Fig. 5 ). In Fig. 8 , the PSD curves between point A and point E have almost identical values in both the low-frequency region (< 105  m-1 ) and the low-medium frequency range (105  m-1  – 5 × 105  m-1 ). However, compared to the PSD curve for point A, the PSD curve for point E appears to have less variance in the high-frequency region of 106  m-1  – 107  m-1 . The spatial resolution leads to a statistical limit to the possibility of comparison. However, it can be stated that the critical range of changes is close to the 1 µm value. In the model, calcite precipitation is realized by adding surface building blocks of the size of the original resolution (∼ 250 nm). This then causes the observed accumulated surface changes expressed by the lower variance of the PSD around 1 µm. Moreover, the fitted coefficients of the fractal dimension and the Hurst exponent of PSD curves calculated from the surface height data at points A – E are listed in Table S1 (cf. points A – E in Fig. 5 ). All Hurst exponent coefficients in Table S1 are below 0.5, indicating a negative autocorrelation of surface roughness with a continuous alternating feature of high and low values (Gong et al., 2016 ). As shown in Table S1, the fractal dimension coefficient decreases from 2.8775 to 2.8590 and the Hurst exponent coefficient increases from 0.1225 to 0.1410 after calcite precipitation of 97 h. The slight changes in the fractal dimension and the Hurst exponent coefficient over the entire frequency demonstrate the consequences of calcite precipitation on the surface topography. Overall, Fig. 8  and Table S1 demonstrate that the microbial-induced calcite precipitation affects the surface topography via two aspects: (1) general changes in the distribution of surface roughness over the entire spatial frequency (i.e., fractal dimension and Hurst exponent), and (2) local changes in the variance of PSD in the high spatial frequency range.  3.3 The influence of advection, diffusion, and reaction rates on the temporal evolution of surface topography As a next step, we investigated the effect of advection, diffusion, and reaction rates on the temporal evolution of surface topography due to microbial-induced calcite precipitation. Fig. 9   shows the temporal evolution of the Sq parameter (a) and increased surface height (b) of cases 2 (black line) and 3 (red line). The reaction times of cases 2 and 3 are 43 h and 50 days (i.e., 1200 h), respectively. In cases 2 and 3, the Pe  and Da  numbers are 350 and 1.13 × 10–3 , and 35 and 980, respectively (cf. Table 1 ). Fig. 9 a illustrates a constant surface roughness for case 2, which indicates a uniformly changed surface height due to calcite precipitation, as shown in Fig. 9 b (black line). In case 2, calcium ions are uniformly transported along the pore wall (see Fig. S1b) under elevated flow velocity conditions (i.e., v  = 0.1 mm/s), which leads to homogeneous calcite precipitation along the surface (see Fig. S2b) under reaction-limited conditions (Da  < 1). In the reaction-limited regime, the residence time for precipitation reactions seems to be the dominating factor rather than the residence time for fluid mixing, resulting in a uniformly changing surface topography (Agrawal et al., 2020 ), which is shown in Fig. 9 b (black line). In Fig. 9 a, Sq for case 3 decreases from 3.17 µm to 2.72 µm after 50 days of calcite precipitation (red line). For case 3, the solutes transport is dominated by diffusive transport (Pe  = 35), which causes a higher concentration of calcium ions at the inlet (see Fig. S1c). Consequently, a higher amount of calcite precipitates at the inlet (see Fig. S2c), resulting in a larger value of increased surface height at the inlet as shown in Fig. 9 b (red line). Therefore, this leads to heterogeneous calcite precipitation under the transport-limited condition (Da  > 1). Moreover, a decreased Sq for case 3 indicates that microbial-induced calcite precipitation leads to a smoother surface. Fig.10 shows a comparison of PSD versus time calculated from two different surface data for case 3. Black and red solid lines represent the surface data before the calcite precipitation and after 50 days of precipitation, respectively. In Fig. 10  , the smaller variance of the PSD curve can be observed in the high-frequency region (106  m-1  – 107  m-1 ), in which the consistent trend of variance can be found in case 1 (cf. Fig. 8 ). However, compared to the case 1, a larger difference of PSD curve can also be observed in both low- and intermediate-frequency regions. Such large differences in PSD indicate that calcite precipitation can affect the surface topography in all frequency regions under diffusion-dominated transport and transport-limited conditions. Overall, the coupling of transport and reaction rates has a significant impact on the evolution of surface topography due to microbial-induced calcite precipitation. In reaction-limited regimes (Da  < 1), homogeneous precipitation leads to a uniformly developed surface, while in transport-limited regimes (Da  > 1), heterogeneous precipitation causes non-uniform changes in surface topography and a smoother surface. Similar uniform and non-uniform reaction patterns can be found in the previously reported pore-scale studies with respect to calcite dissolution (Agrawal et al., 2020 ; Soulaine et al., 2017 ). Note that, a recent study estimated that the biofilm (i.e., Lactobacillus casei ) has a permeability of 500 mD (Hassannayebi et al., 2021 ). This high permeability indicates that solutes can be transported within the biofilms. Therefore, consideration of solute transport within the biofilms will be a focus of future work to improve the model.   4 Summary and conclusions In this study, we developed a pore-scale reactive transport model for describing the coupled processes of flow, multi-component transport, microbially induced calcite precipitation, and evolution of the solid surface. The developed model is validated using published experimental data. The numerical experiments focus on fluid flow through a 2D channel with a rough surface. Our results show that heterogeneous calcite precipitation causes a generally decreased surface roughness under advection-dominated and transport-limited conditions. Moreover, the results of power spectral density analysis demonstrate that microbially induced calcite precipitation affects surface topography both through general changes in surface roughness over the entire spatial frequency range (trend of fractal dimension change) and via local modifications in surface topography in the micron wavelength spatial frequency range. Sensitivity studies clearly show that uniform and non-uniform types of precipitation can be caused by different flow rates, which result in different Pe  and Da  numbers. Such different types of precipitation lead to different surface shapes. Quantitative insights into the evolution of surface height under different flow and reaction conditions provide a comprehensive understanding of surface evolution by microbially induced calcite precipitation at the pore scale. This has implications for enhanced predictability of contaminant transport in the subsurface with microbial activities at the core scale and beyond.
1 Introduction The phenomenon of wetting and drying (WD), where initially dry land becomes inundated or vice versa due to changing flow, is a common occurrence in various water-related domains globally, including storm surges (Garzon and Ferreira, 2016 ), urban flooding (Liang, 2010 ), coastal tidal flows (Sobey, 2009 ), river-lake systems (Chen et al., 2012 ), among others. The cyclic transition between wetting and drying poses inherent challenges to hydrodynamic simulations in these water bodies (Yuan et al., 2008a ), manifesting as: 1) susceptibility to numerical oscillations near flow boundaries; 2) dry cell conditions with realistic velocities and water depths reaching 0, necessitating appropriate numerical processing methods to prevent divergence; 3) potential impacts on mass and momentum conservation arising from hypothetical flow between dry and wet cells. Therefore, it is imperative to employ suitable algorithms that effectively address these challenges for stable and accurate hydrodynamic simulation. In balancing calculational cost and accuracy, WD simulations are commonly simplified to two-dimensional in most cases (Schuttelaars et al., 2022 ). The existing 2D techniques for dealing with WD can be broadly categorized into two categories: moving mesh methods and fixed mesh methods (Yuan et al., 2008a ). Moving mesh methods, also referred to as mesh adaption algorithms, dynamically adjust the boundaries of the calculation mesh over time based on the calculation results to trace the water front. While this approach can effectively simulate the fluid domain changes caused by WD and has demonstrated efficacy and accuracy in certain applications (Baines et al., 2011 ), it comes with high computational costs, especially in cases involving complex terrain and large changes in water depth. Additionally, integrating moving mesh methods with implicit time scheme proves challenging (Lee and Lee, 2016 ). Meanwhile, as highlighted by Bunya et al. (2009) , mesh adaption algorithms may not necessarily produce more accurate computational results compared to fixed mesh methods. Therefore, current research on WD algorithms mainly focuses on the improvement and innovation of fixed mesh methods. The fixed mesh method is further categorized into four distinct approaches (Medeiros and Hagen, 2013 ): (1) thin film method (TFM), (2) depth extrapolation method (DEM), (3) element removal method (ERM), and (4) negative-depth method (NDM, also known as the artificial porosity method). TFM is prone to numerical oscillations and incurs high computational costs during calculation (Karna et al., 2011 ; Medeiros and Hagen, 2013 ), and DEM requires the introduction of additional techniques to ensure mass conservation (Bradford and Sanders, 2002 ; Begnudelli and Sanders, 2006 ). These defects limit the widespread application of these two methods. Instead, ERM and NDM are currently the most commonly used WD methods. ERM involves a thorough examination of mesh elements, where dry elements are identified and subsequently excluded from the computational domain. These excluded elements undergo separate processing, often entailing the adjustment of variables such as velocity to 0, with no momentum or mass transfer occurring (D Greenberg et al., 2005 ). Renowned for its robustness and effectiveness, this method has demonstrated favorable results in various scenarios, including one-dimensional dam break tests and two-dimensional water flow simulations (Matsumoto et al., 2002 ). Noteworthy for its simplicity of implementation, the method has gained widespread adoption, such as finite element models like TELEMAC (Moulinec et al., 2011 ) and ADCIRC (Dietrich et al., 2012 ), as well as finite difference models such as Delft3D-FLOW (Zhang et al., 2015 ) and MIKE 21 (Ma et al., 2022 ). However, despite its merits, this method exhibits certain limitations. The discontinuous nature of the switches involved renders it generally unsuitable for implicit or semi-implicit methods and makes it notably sensitive to round-off errors (Hof and Vollebregt, 2005 ; Medeiros and Hagen, 2013 ). Additionally, the structured mesh used in the finite difference models is not as adaptable to complex boundaries as the unstructured mesh. NDM allows the water level to drop below the ground, regulating the flow in the dry cells through porosity terms. This method eliminates the need for the separation of wet and dry cells, requiring only slight modifications to the governing equations and avoiding issues related to artificial pressure gradients. One early instance of the negative-depth is the slot method  proposed by Tao et al. in 1984, which envisions a narrow slot beneath the ground within a unit width (Tao, 2020 ). Numerous improvements and applications of the slot method followed (Yuan et al., 2008b ). Yuan et al. (2008a)  developed a linked groundwater and surface water flow model capable of implicitly handling moving boundary problems, though introducing an extra groundwater equation adds computational complexity. Hof and Vollebregt (2005)  introduced the concept of a virtual water level , allowing the shallow water equation to naturally resemble a groundwater equation, thereby eliminating the need for additional solutions (Chen et al., 2012 ). Martins et al. (2018)  conducted experiments comparing various WD methods, indicating higher accuracy for the negative-depth method compared to simple element removal methods. Previous studies have demonstrated the negative-depth method's advantages, including high simulation accuracy and compatibility with various discrete methods, particularly implicit time integration schemes (Barros et al., 2015 ). Despite these strengths, scholars have noted that in simulations of severe water level changes, such as dam break problems, the negative-depth method may exhibit divergence in calculations (Medeiros and Hagen, 2013 ). In summary, both the element removal method and negative-depth method are widely used in dealing with WD, each with its own strengths and limitations. Proposing a novel WD method that can effectively mitigates the drawbacks of ERM and NDM is of great significance for promoting numerical simulation of shallow water systems. The Navier-Stokes/Brinkman (NSB) model, incorporating Brinkman's description of Darcy resistance as a volumetric penalty term directly into the momentum equations, was first proposed by Arquis and Caltagirone (1987)  to compute natural convection flow inside a fluid-porous cavity. Angot and Caltagirone (1990)  applied the NSB model to complex fluid-porous-solid systems, distinguishing different media within the computational domain by characteristic permeability, i.e., a finite value for porous, infinite for pure fluid, and zero for pure solid. The presence of the Brinkman penalty term effectively enforces zero velocity within solid regions (Olesen et al., 2006 ). Rigorous mathematical analysis and numerical validation of this model, confirming its convergence, have been documented in the literature (Angot, 1999 ; Khadra et al., 2000 ; Romain et al., 2014 ). One advantage of this model is its ability to avoid explicit expressions for flow conditions between different media, allowing the same governing equations to be solved throughout the entire computational domain. This feature is particularly valuable when the geometric shape of solid regions changes, eliminating the need for mesh redivision, thus finding wide application in fields like topology optimization (Bastide et al., 2018 ; Manuel et al., 2018 ) and fluid-structure interaction (Gerosa and Marsden, 2024 ). Notably, the computational domain in WD problems can also be regarded as a multi-medium system coexisting with solid and liquid phases, where solid regions correspond to dry cells, and fluid regions to wet cells. Based on this similarity, some scholars have attempted to use the NSB model to solve the WD problem and achieved satisfactory results (Dissez et al., 2005 ; Nicolsky et al., 2011 ). However, these methods present obvious limitations and have not received widespread attention, such as introducing an additional phase equation to determine the dry cells, which increases the computational burden. Therefore, inspired by the NSB model, this study incorporated a flow resistance term into the shallow water equations based on the negative depth method and proposed a new method for solving the WD problem, named the flow resistance method (FRM). This method identifies dry cells based on pseudo-water depth, without the need to solve additional equations, and is suitable for implicit schemes and unstructured mesh, enhancing adaptability in various scenarios. Additionally, in FRM, when the cell is identified as dry, the flow resistance term rapidly reduces the flow velocity to close to zero, avoiding numerical instability caused by supercritical flow at the water front due to tiny water depth. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2  provides a concise introduction to the governing equations and delves into a detailed derivation of FRM. Section 3  describes the discretization of the governing equations and outlines the numerical solution steps. Following that, Section 4  conducts a comprehensive series of numerical experiments and evaluates the proposed model using a real-life case. The concluding insights and findings are summarized in the last section.  2 Modified shallow water equations This section introduces the derivation of FRM, encompassing the modification of the shallow water equation and the determination of model parameters. The primary objective is to devise a method where the velocity within dry cells undergoes a rapid reduction to near-zero, addressing key challenges associated with the simulation of WD scenarios. 2.1 Modification to shallow water equations For numerous flow scenarios, such as coastal tidal flow and floodplains, the vertical velocity component is often significantly smaller than the horizontal velocity component. At this point, the SWEs derived by integrating the Navier-Stokes equations along the water depth can effectively capture the flow dynamics:(1) ∂ ζ  ∂ t   + ∇  · ( h u  )  = 0     (2) ∂ ( h u  )   ∂ t   + ∇  · ( h uu  )  − ∇  · ( h ν eff  ∇  u  )  = − 2 h Ω  × u − C f  | u |  u − g h ∇  ζ     where, ζ = water stage; h  =ζ  − zb  = water depth; zb  = bed elevation; u  = depth-averaged horizontal velocity; ν eff = ν  + ν t   = efficient viscosity; Ω = rotation rate of the Earth; Cf   = gn 2 h −1/3  = friction coefficient; n  = Manning's roughness. When the bed is exposed, the conventional application of SWEs becomes impractical, necessitating special treatment for Eqs.(1) and (2). To address this, Hof and Vollebregt (2005)  introduced the concept of a "pseudo–water stage" ψ , which is allowed to freely drop below the bed elevation in SWEs instead of the usual water stage ζ  for calculation purposes. Correspondingly, a "pseudo–water depth" H , calculated as H  = ψ  − zb  , might be negative. To ensure that the water depth h  used in calculations remains positive and physically meaningful, a mapping relationship is applied between h  and H  (Chen et al., 2012 ):(3) h = h ( H )  = {     H ,           H > δ    δ  2  2 δ − H   ,        H ≤ δ              where, δ = user-defined positive small threshold, allowing for adjustment according to the specific needs of the calculation. In wet states (H  > δ ), h  is equal to H , while in dry states (H  ≤ δ ), h  smoothly transitions from 0 to δ . This ensures a seamless and continuous transition between the dry and wet states of the equation. In porous media theory, the Darcy force, proportional to velocity, is often used as f  = αu   to characterize the fluid flow resistance in an ideal porous medium (D Gersborg et al., 2005 ; Olesen et al., 2006 ). The Navier-Stokes-Brinkman (NSB) model, which takes into account Darcy resistance, can be used to simulate viscous flow including complex shaped solid obstacles in a fluid domain, with an in-depth mathematical analysis found in existing literature (Arquis and Caltagirone, 1984 ; Angot et al., 1999 ; Carbou and Fabrie, 2003 ). In shallow water systems, the exposed bed can be regarded as a porous medium with permeability approaching zero, and the flow resistance tends to infinity. Inspired by the NSB model, a flow resistance term αhu   is introduced in Eqn.(2) to describe the flow resistance in the wetting and drying transition region in this proposed method. For a smooth and continuous transition between the fluid and the exposed bed, a blending factor α  = α max χ (γ ) is incorporated. The dimensionless interpolation function χ (γ ) varies from 0 to 1, and its specific form will be further discussed in Section 2.2 . The Brinkman penalization term plays a crucial role in effectively simulating the spatial variation of flow resistance and the fluid domain during the WD process. When the penalization term incorporates χ (γ ) = 1 and is sufficiently large, it approximates the no-slip boundary condition (Dilgen et al., 2018 ).  2.2 Parameters determination The transition between dry and wet cells is realized through the function χ (γ ), which must adhere to the specified requirements outlined as follows:(7) {  0  ≤  χ ( γ )   < 1 ,    0  <  γ  ≤  1    χ ( 1 )   =  0 ;   χ ( 0 )   =  1            where γ  = the characteristic porosity distribution across the simulation domain, with the porosity being inversely proportional to flow resistance. When γ  = 1, it refers to wet cells, indicating that the fluid can flow freely (Fig. 1  ), while the γ  of dry cells approach zero, meaning the flow resistance infinite. The impact of flow resistance induces a rapid decay in flow velocity to 0, indicating the presence of an exposed bed. The distribution of γ  is mapped from the pseudo-water depth H :(8) { γ = 1 ,                      H > δ    γ ( H )  = δ 2 δ − H   ,      H ≤ δ          In this study, the function χ (γ ) is defined as(9) χ ( γ )  = c 1 − γ  c + γ       where the parameter c  controls the curvature of the interpolation function. Fig. 2   shows three curves of χ (γ ) for different values of c , highlighting that an increase in c  amplifies the curvature of the interpolation function, causing a sharper transition between the fluid and the exposed bed. The impact of c  on computational stability will be discussed in Section 4.3 and 4.4  with the default value being c  = 10 unless specified otherwise. In research on the NSB model, numerical experiments have shown that α  should be sufficiently large to generate sufficient Darcy resistance in the solid region. On the other hand, being too large can also lead to computational instability (Lundgaard et al., 2018 ; Abdelhamid and Czekanski, 2024 ). Similarly, the value of α max  in Eqn.(5) should be typically selected just high enough to enforce near zero velocity in non-fluid elements, yet small enough not to introduce numerical instabilities. Considering the importance of α max , we employed the trial-and-error method for selecting a proper α max  in the study. The effects of α max  on simulation performances will be discussed in Sections 4.4 and 4.5 .   3 Numerical approaches A set of techniques are embedded in the standard 2D hydrodynamics model T-WUMM2 developed by Chen et al. (2012)  and Yu et al. (2019)  to solve the SWEs. T-WUMM2 was developed on the OpenFOAM (Weller et al. 1998 ; Liu et al., 2017 ) platform with the finite volume method. The governing equations used in this study just made several necessary modifications to the SWEs, with the addition of the flow resistance term and the introduction of the function ψ  instead of ζ . Therefore, the discretization method and solution algorithm applied in T-WUMM2 are practical for FRM, also indicating that FRM is easily accommodated in any existing SWEs solver. For details regarding loop and relaxation iteration processes for solving the modified shallow water equations, please refer to Yu et al. (2019) 's research. Here, we focus on demonstrating the wetting and drying treatment procedure within each time-step (Fig. 3  ):Step 1: Pseudo–water depth calculation. Input the existing pseudo–water stage field ψ 0  from the previous moment or iteration, and calculate the pseudo–water depth field by H  = ψ 0  − zb  ;  Step 2: Water depth and resistance coefficient calculation. Compare H  with the user-defined positive small threshold δ , and calculate the water depth h  and coefficient fields κ, γ  and χ (γ ) according to Eqs.(3), (6), (8) and(9);  Step 3: Governing equations solution. Based on h, κ, γ  and χ (γ ), solve Eqn.(4) and Eqn.(5) to obtain the unit discharge q   = hu   and iterative stage field ψ ;  Step 4: Return to step 1 to update the pseudo–water depth field according to the newly obtained ψ .    In conclusion, the proposed wetting and drying method in this study involves straightforward modifications to SWEs, obviating the requirement for extensive alterations to the program dedicated to solving SWEs. This simplicity underscores its high universality and portability. Notably, the proposed method can be used for both explicit and implicit solutions, showing significantly better applicability compared to ERM. This study does not involve a comparative analysis of the computational accuracy between ERM and FRM. Therefore, subsequent numerical experiments will focus solely on a quantitative comparison between FRM and NDM.  4 Results and discussion A set of numerical experiments has been selected to validate the efficacy of FRM, including assessments such as the still water test for stability (Liang and Marche, 2009 ), the Balzano 3 test case (Balzano, 1998 ), the Thacker test case (Thacker, 1981 ), the laboratory dam-break over a triangle obstacle (Soares-Frazão, 2007 ) and the Nansi lake real-life case (Wang et al., 2019 ). The former four representative numerical experiments is aimed to evaluate the accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency of the proposed WD method, and the real-life case is applied to assess the capability of simulating actual wetting fronts. For comparative analysis, a kind of negative-depth method proposed by Hof and Vollebregt (2005) , referred to as HVM, is also applied in the same cases, providing a basis for demonstrating the enhancements achieved by FRM.  4.1 Still water test The well-balanced property of a model is often assessed using the still water test constructed by Duran et al. (2013) . This test scenario involves a frictionless channel with dimensions of 2 m in length and 1 m in width. The channel is enclosed by solid wall boundaries. The elevation of the terrain in this context is defined as follows:(10) z b  ( x , y )  = {  0.5 exp ( − ( 25 ( x − 1.2 )   2  + 50 ( y − 0.7 )   2  )  )  ,     if   x  >  0.68  m     − 0.5 exp ( − ( 50 ( x − 0.45 )   2  + 100 ( y − 0.4 )   2  )  )  ,    elsewhere               At the beginning of the simulation, the water in the channel is stationary, with the water stage of 0.2 m and the bump at the center of the channel partially exposed (Fig. 4  ). The total simulation took 500 s, with the time step determined by the CFL criteria and δ  = 0.0001 m, α max  =1000 s-1 . Using an unstructured quad mesh, Δx  = Δy  = 0.008 m with a total of 31,250 cells. After 500 s, the velocity calculated by FRM basically remains at 0, with the water surface staying still at the initial time, which verifies the well-balanced property of FRM (Fig. 5  b). However, Wu et al. (2014)  tested the model proposed by Bryson et al. (2011)  using the still water test and found unphysical discharges at wetting front, violating the actual situation, which could not guarantee the model's well-balanced property. Compared with HVM, the maximum flow velocity error calculated by FRM is significantly reduced by nine orders of magnitude (Fig. 5 ). To further demonstrate computational error, the following error formula is defined for the water depth h  and the discharge per-unit-width q  =h u  :(11) L ( h )  = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  ( h i  − h i a    )   2    ,   L ( q )  = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  ( q i  − q i a    )   2        where N  = the total number of grids, and hia   and q  ia   = the theoretical solutions for h  and q  . The errors of HVM for h  and q   are 4.81 × 10–8  m and 3.12 × 10–10  m2 /s, respectively, while the errors of FRM for h  and q   are 1.60 × 10–9  m and 2.59 × 10–16  m2 /s, respectively. The computational results indicate that compared to HVM, FRM can reduce the error of h  by an order of magnitude and the error of q   by six orders of magnitude. This improvement is attributed to the flow resistance term in FRM, which effectively suppresses unrealistic flow patterns in dry areas and at water front (Fig. 5 b), thereby minimizing flow rate errors. This case have indicated the ability of FRM to ensure the hydrostatic state when the computational area contains dry areas (e.g., islands and coasts). 4.2 The Balzano 3 test case Balzano (1998)  investigated three idealized 1D test cases commonly utilized for evaluating various WD methods. The Balzano 3 test case imposes particularly stringent conditions, featuring a sloping basin with a triangular reservoir, making it valuable for assessing the accuracy and conservation properties of WD methods. Initially, the simulation domains for the Balzano test cases were 1D basins with a length of 13,800 m, and the elevation of the basin is defined as follows (Fig. 6  a):(12) z b  ( x , y )  = {  − x / 2760 ,     x ≤ 3600  m   and   x ≥ 6000  m     x / 2760 − 60 / 23 ,      3600  m  ≤ x ≤ 4800  m     − x / 920 + 100 / 23 ,     4800  m  ≤ x ≤ 6000  m               However, considering that FRM is designed to address 2D WD problems, a width of 7200 m has been incorporated to modify the origin domain, as illustrated in the grid division in Fig. 6 b, Δx  = 144 m,   Δy  = 138 m with a total of 5000 cells. In the simulation, the left boundary was designated as a no-slip wall, while the right boundary served as an outlet boundary with a decreasing water stage. Coriolis force, surface stress, and horizontal viscosity were neglected, the time step was set to 400 s, and the model parameters of FRM were specified as δ  = 2 × 10−12  m, α max  =200 s-1 . Over a 12-hour simulation period, the water stage of the outlet boundary decreased from 3 m to −3 m, remaining constant thereafter to assess the potential for water leakage from the small reservoir through the dry area (see Eqn.(13)). In HVM, the calculation tends to diverge when δ  = 2 × 10−5  m, and it can converge when δ  = 2 × 10−4  m. The simulation concluded after 48 h, and the temporal evolution of the pseudo-water stage is shown in Fig. 7  .(13) ζ = {  3 cos ( 2 π t  86400  )  ,      0  s   <  t  <  43200  s     − 3 ,                43200  s   <  t  <  172800  s               After 48 h of simulation period, the water stage in the reservoir should theoretically be close to the top of the triangular bulge, while the downstream water stage equals to 3 m, with the flow velocity of 0. As Balzano (1998)  noticed, several methods yielded unrealistic water stages higher or lower than the proper level in conducting this test. In addition, Le et al. (2020)  pointed out that the impermissible water transfer from wet cells to dry cells is often observed in the negative-depth methods, leading to a lack of mass conservation (Gourgue et al., 2009 ). This issue arises mainly because it is usually necessary to increase the control height δ  for the calculation to convergence. From Fig. 7 , it can be observed that the pseudo-water stage calculated by HVM would significantly drop below the bottom, resulting in negative water depth, while the pseudo-water stage of FRM slightly droped below the bottom and was highly consistent with the theoretical results, with less unreasonable water leakage. Referring to Eqn. (11) , the errors for h  of HVM and FRM are 1.18 × 10–2  m and 7.36 × 10–5  m, respectively, indicating that FRM can significantly reduce the required control height during calculation and effectively avoids the common problem of mass conservation deficiency in HVM. In this case, the accuracy of water depth calculation has been improved by three orders of magnitude, and the conservation properties have been successfully verified.  4.3 The thacker test case In order to further quantitatively test the accuracy of FRM in solving WD problems, consider a simple but rigorous test case with analytical solutions - the Thacker test case (Thacker, 1981 ). This test is conducted in a closed parabolic basin (Fig. 8  ), and the initial water depth satisfies the following equation:(14) h = h 0  ( 1 − x  2  + y  2   R  2    )      where, h 0  = the depth at the center of the basin, and R  = the radius at the reference plane (z  = 0). Without frictional resistance and Coriolis acceleration, the analytical solutions of free oscillation on water surface are as follows:(15) ζ = h 0  { 1 − A  2    1 − A cos ( ω ′  t  )    − 1 − x  2  + y  2   R  2   [ 1 − A  2   ( 1 − A cos ( ω ′  t  )   )   2   − 1  ]   }      (16) u = 1 2  ω ′  x A sin ( ω ′  t  )   1 − A cos ( ω ′  t  )        (17) v = 1 2  ω ′  y A sin ( ω ′  t  )   1 − A cos ( ω ′  t  )        where,(18) ω ′  = 2 π  T  = 8 g h 0    R      (19) A = ( h 0  + ζ 0   )   2  − h 0 2   ( h 0  + ζ 0   )   2  + h 0 2         ζ 0 = the initial water stage at the center of the basin (t  = 0), and T  = the oscillation period. In this study, R  = 430.62 km, h 0  = 50 m, ζ 0 = 2 m, and the calculated parameters T  = 43200 s = 12 h, ω′= 2π/43200, A  = 51/1301 with the time step of 10 s and δ = 0 . 001   m   , α max  =1000 s-1 . The radius of the simulation area is 600 km with a total of 30,685 cells and the simulation time is 129,600 s, corresponding to 3T . Fig. 9  a shows the magnified plots of the water stage near the water front during an oscillation period, which indicates that the results are in good agreement with the analytical solutions. The time evolution of the water stage changes at the domain center throughout the entire calculation are also highly consistent with the analytical solutions (Fig. 9 b), while the maximum amplitude decreases slightly over time due to the numerical dissipation caused by the discretization (Le et al., 2020 ). Further comparing the velocity distribution near the water front, it can be seen that the numerical velocities are generally very close to the analytical solutions (Fig. 10  ). Quantitatively, according to Eqn. (11) , the errors of FRM for h  and q   are respectively 6.67 × 10–4  m and 1.19 × 10–3  m2 /s, which could verify the mass conservation and computational accuracy of FRM. Notably, certain numerical oscillations can be observed near the wetting front. Considering the difficulty of simulating frictionless situations, this small undulations is acceptable (Balzano, 1998 ). And compared with some existing studies, the numerical results near the water front in this study are generally more stable and present smaller fluctuations (Casulli and Zanolli, 2007 ; Yuan et al., 2008a ). Additionally, under the same settings, the simulation of HVM proceeded to divergence at 2140 s. This may be because, under frictionless situations, the supercritical flow may form near the water front with extremely low water depth due to insufficient reduction in flow velocity, resulting in violent velocity gradients and vortex structures, which can lead to the inability of the convergence. In FRM, with the presence of the flow resistance term, the flow velocity at the wetting and drying boundary rapidly decreases to 0 (Fig. 10 ), avoiding the occurrence of the supercritical flow near the water front. At the same time, the flow resistance term also enhances the diagonal dominance of the coefficient matrix, which could improve the stability and convergence in numerical solutions. In conclusion, the mass conservation and accuracy of FRM have been once again verified through the Thacker test case, and FRM has shown better numerical stability compared to existing research and HVM.  4.4 Laboratory dam-break over a triangle obstacle Following the recommendations of the EU CADAM project, the proposed WD method is applied to simulate the laboratory dam-break flow over a triangle obstacle using detailed laboratory measurement data. The simulation domain spans 38 m, with the dam situated 15.5 m away from the upstream end, and a symmetrical triangular obstacle with a height of 0.4 m and a projection length of 6 m positioned 13 m from the dam (Fig. 11  ). The setup assumes a static reservoir with the water depth of 0.75 m upstream of the dam, an initial dry floodplain, and a constant Manning coefficient of 0.0125. Six gauges recorded time series of water depth at distances of 4 m (G4), 8 m (G8), 10 m (G10), 11 m (G11), 13 m (G13), and 20 m (G20) from the dam. Assuming solid wall boundaries at the upstream and downstream ends of the domain, the simulation lasted for 90 s after dam break, with a time step adjustable by the courant number Co, and α max  =100 s-1 , Comax  =0.4. Using an unstructured quad mesh, Δx  = 0.05 m, Δy  = 0.19 m with a total of 152,000 cells. Fig. 12   shows the comparison between calculated water depth and experimental measurements at different gauges, revealing ongoing complex wave interactions and wetting and drying processes until the flow momentum is suppressed by friction effects and mass loss downstream of the obstacle (Liang and Marche, 2009 ). Both FRM and HVM exhibit good agreement with measured values, accurately predicting the wave arrival times and water depths G4, G8, G10, G11, and G13. However, the water depth predicted at G20 exceeds the measured value, consistently observed even with smaller time steps (not shown), aligning with findings from prior studies (Liang and Marche, 2009 ; Wu et al., 2018 ). This discrepancy may be attributed to the highly complex and unstable nature of water flow behind the obstacle, rendering shallow water equations based on a hydrostatic assumption less suitable. Notably, the arrival time was accurately predicted, a crucial aspect in dam break simulation. Overall, the simulation accuracy is satisfactory at most measurement points, effectively capturing the dynamics of the wetting and drying process. Six groups of conditions were conducted to explore the improvement of FRM and how the parameters Comax , δ, c  and α max  will affect the calculation time and convergence (Table 1  ). It can be obtained that properly increasing Comax  is beneficial for reducing the time required to complete the calculation with larger time steps. However, an excessively large Comax  can easily lead to large time steps, gradually accumulating errors and causing computational divergence. Compared to HVM, FRM can obtain a smaller δ  and larger Comax , and the total time for calculation is shorter under the same setting, with a maximum reduction of 11.32 %. This is because FRM can rapidly decrease the velocity near the water front, avoiding computational instability caused by supercritical flow due to δ  being too small. It could be inferred that the numerical stability and computational efficiency of FRM are improved to a certain extent, and FRM tends to make up for the deficiency of convergence in HVM when the water level changes dramatically. By changing the curvature coefficient c , it was found that sharper transitions are beneficial for robust convergence, which is consistent with the findings in topology optimization (Borrvall and Petersson, 2003 ). Because sharper transitions can generate sufficient flow resistance near the water front to cause timely attenuation of flow velocity (Lundgaard et al., 2018 ). In addition, the experiments also prove that excessively large α max  is not conducive to computational convergence and a suitable α max  can be selected through the trial-and-error approach (Lundgaard et al., 2018 ).  4.5 Nansi lake real-life case The accuracy, mass conservation, and robustness of FRM in solving WD problems were initially demonstrated through the four numerical experiments above. This section will further highlight the applicability of the method proposed under complex conditions through a real-life case. The study applies FRM to investigate the water level changes of Nansi Lake, one of the four major storage lakes in the world's largest water transfer system - the Eastern Route of the South to North Water Diversion Project (Fig. 13  ). Nansi Lake features complex underwater topography, with waterways, lake grass, reeds, and other elements intricately distributed throughout the lake (Zhao, 2020 ). Large aquaculture production areas are situated on the west side of the lake, and the elevation of the pond embankment is 0.5 m higher than the normal storage level (34.6 m in this study). Most of the time, this area does not belong to the water diversion area, and is generalized as a large area of exposed bed. The purpose of this case is to assess whether FRM can effectively simulate the moving boundary under complex real-life conditions. The mesh of the calculation domain is shown in Fig. 14  a, comprising a total of 3795 cells and an approximate cell size of 400 m. The riverbed roughness varies across different areas. Through a literature review and multiple calibrations, the roughness values of the waterway, reed, lake grass, and lake surface (areas without aquatic plants) were set to 0.02, 0.58, 0.196 and 0.064, respectively (Fig. 14 b). Time steps were adjustable according to Comax  =0.8. Other parameters applied in the calculation using FRM and HVM refer to Group(a) in Table 2  . Water level time series spanning 293 days from January 31, 2023, to November 19, 2023, were set as boundary conditions for the Erji dam and Liangji Canal. The calculation was validated by the changes in water levels at Makou station. Selecting two monitoring points in the lake and its adjacent pond, respectively, to test the accuracy of simulating wetting and drying(Fig. 13 ). The results of the water level are basically consistent with the measured values, and the water level changes in the pond are similar to the lake when the water level is higher than the pond embankment (Fig. 15  ). It appears to suggest that when wetting and drying occur, FRM can simulate the actual water level well and capture the water front. The times taken to finish the case simulation using FRM and HVM were 688.33 s and 717.34 s, respectively, with a 4.04 % decrease in time consumption, while FRM can save 68.55 % of calculation time under the condition of group (b) in Table 2 . It tends to indicate that, when δ  decreases, FRM can effectively prevent the supercritical flow near the water front, and then increase the calculation stability with less iterations, consequently consuming shorter time. Eight groups of experiments similar to 4.4 were conducted, and the same pattern was obtained (Table 2 ). In summary, in the simulation of real-life shallow water systems, FRM has significant augmentations compared to HVM, achieving smaller control height and larger time step, which both improve mass conservation and computational efficiency. In order to gain a balance between calculation accuracy and efficiency, it is not advisable to make δ  too small. Besides, the larger the curvature of interpolation function χ (γ ) the more conducive it is to computational convergence. Generally, c  = 10 can meet the computational demands in most cases. Under special conditions, increasing the c  value can be considered to obtain more robust calculations.   5 Conclusions Based on the negative-depth method and the Navier-Stokes/Brinkman (NSB) model, a robust and well-balanced method for dealing with wetting and drying problems, known as the flow resistance method (FRM), was proposed. A flow resistance term was introduced into the momentum equation of shallow water equations, making the flow resistance of the dry cells large enough and rapidly reducing the flow velocity of dry cells to 0 during simulation. In comparison with the most widely used WD methods, including ERM and NDM, the improvement of FRM can be summarized as follows:(1) By increasing the flow resistance, the flow velocity of the dry cells approximately equals to 0, implicitly limiting the mass transfer between the dry and wet cells, which compensates for the inadequacy of ERM in implicit solving.  (2) The insufficient velocity gradient near the water front is often the main reason why NDM is prone to divergence in simulating severe water level changes. In order to calculate convergence, it is usually necessary to increase the control height, which may affect mass conservation. FRM can accelerate the velocity attenuation at the dry cells and reduce the control height, thereby effectively increasing the numerical stability and ensuring mass conservation.  (3) The accuracy and robustness of FRM have been tested through three numerical experiments, a dam break experiment, and a real-life case. In addition, this method can effectively increase the time step in the calculation, thereby shortening the time consumption and improving the computational efficiency.    The flow resistance method can accurately simulate the water front with high universality and portability. It can be directly implemented into existing two-dimensional shallow water models to solve the WD problem, and promise a wide application in hydrodynamic simulation for river-lake systems, natural flood prediction and management.
