1 Introduction Gas invasion in porous media is an essential process for many emerging subsurface applications like aquifer energy storage (i.e., solar thermal (Mouli-Castillo et al., 2019 ) and hydrogen (Tarkowski, 2019; Bacon et al., 2014 )), geological carbon sequestration (GCS) (Singh et al., 2020; Bakhshian and Sahimi, 2017; Soltanian et al., 2017 ), and geothermal utilization (Axelsson, 2010 ). All of them are of great significance and have been practically applied to mitigate the greenhouse effects and global climate change (Halland, 2022 ). In many geological gas sequestration processes, the invading fluid such as CO 2     or H 2     is injected into aquifers bearing multi-fluids, e.g. depleted oil reservoirs that the exploitation has been almost finished after water/brine flooding. Often, to achieve higher efficiency of the storage or the later-on extraction process, the operation modes can also be enriched by alternating injection of multiple fluids such as tertiary gas injection (Qin et al., 2019 ) and water-alternating-gas (Wang et al., 2023, 2022 ). Therefore, it is crucial to have a thorough understanding of mechanism of gas invading into a multi-fluid system in porous media. The state-of-the-art on-chip system provides an instrumental platform for investigating the microscopic fluid displacement in porous media (Osei-Bonsu et al., 2018, 2020; Yang et al., 2021 ). Together with other conventional microscopic experimental and numerical approaches such as X-ray micro-CT scanning (Alhosani et al., 2023, 2021b, 2020 ) and Lattice Boltzmann methods (LBM) (Liu et al., 2016; Li et al., 2021a,b ), effects of saturation history (Oak, 1989; Oak et al., 1990 ), wettability (DiCarlo et al., 2000; Lei et al., 2022; Blunt et al., 2021 ), pressure (Primkulov et al., 2019 ), spreading (Fenwick and Blunt, 1998 ), and layer drainage (Sahni et al., 1998; Alizadeh and Piri, 2014 ) on the flow characteristics have been explored on three-phase relative permeability in porous media. With microfluidic imaging, Osei-Bonsu et al. (2020)  characterized the effects of fluid properties on phase topologies for three-phase displacements. Suo and Gan (2021)  offer a comprehensive understanding of managing fluid–fluid displacement within hierarchical porous medium, spanning various flow scenarios from capillary-dominated to viscous-dominated regimes. Their findings provide the reference for the development of microfluidic devices and customization of porous materials (Suo et al., 2020 ). Qin et al. (2019)  performed a series of core-scale flooding experiments at high pressure and temperature, and showed the influence of surface wettability on pore-scale displacement events associated with tertiary gas injection. Li (2022)  also reported that the interfacial force is significant in governing the transient flow behavior and trapped-phase mobilization at pore-scale by using LBM modeling and microfluidic flow imaging. In Zhu et al. (2022) ’s study, a range of typical microscopic complex behaviors, such as coalescence and split-up, pinch-off, double and multiple displacement, and parallel flow have been observed on the three-phase displacement process at the pore scale. In three-phase displacement, the hydrodynamics of gas invasion into multi-fluids G→  (L→  L) is more complicated than that of liquid invasion L→  (L→  L). The gas has extremely low viscosity as the invading phase, and flow instability usually occurs due to the huge viscosity ratio during G→  (L→  L). Meanwhile, in comparison with G-L two phase flow, the extra third phase also induces significant flow complexities because of the coupling interfacial interactions at G-L and L-L interfaces. To date, experimental research on the effect of liquid properties, injection sequences, and phase interactions on G→  (L→  L) is rarely reported. Alhosani et al. (2021a)  and Singh et al. (2019)  have identified the key pore-scale processes and double/multiple displacement events for capillary-dominated flow conditions, and highlighted the need for further research in this area. However, the pore-scale physics for viscous-dominated three-phase displacement has not been fully revealed. In particular, the dynamics of gas invading into the multi-fluid system with low-viscosity and high-viscosity fluids is still not fully understood (Alhosani et al., 2021a ). In this study, a microfluidic platform with high-speed imaging system is built to study viscosity-dominated displacement in a porous media chip. By varying the defending phase from a single liquid to a two-liquid system, we comparatively investigate the fingering dynamics for the two-phase and three-phase displacement. In the two-phase displacement, gas invading high-viscosity (G→  HL) and low-viscosity (G→  LL) liquids are characterized by using the highly viscous Glycerol solution (HL) and the lowly viscous Hexane (LL) as the defending fluid, respectively, to have the viscosity contrast. In the multi-fluid system, by alternating the occupation sequences of the low-viscosity and high-viscosity fluids in the chip before gas injection, we further investigate the different three-phase displacement scenarios G→  (HL→  LL) and G→  (LL→  HL). Here the self-developed image processing approach is used to extract the fingering pattern, followed by quantitative analysis on saturation, invading time, and displacement efficiency. The transient fingering patterns are analyzed to reveal the viscous-dependent displacing dynamics in multi-fluid system. The local invading dynamics are also examined to reveal different invasion mechanisms between G→  (HL→  LL) and G→  (LL→  HL). Connection types of ganglia mobilization are analyzed by tracking the movement of all gas ganglia. Finally, the topological connectivity of gas finger is estimated by Euler numbers.  2 Experimental method and flow image processing 2.1 Experimental setup and flow imaging procedures  To perform fingering displacement experiment, a microfluidic platform with porous media chip was built as illustrated in Fig. 1 . First, a vacuum pump was used to remove the air from the microchip until the vacuum degree reached approximately 10−2  bar. The buffer bottle was in place to prevent liquid from entering the vacuum pump and causing any damage. Next, Liquid 1 was injected into the porous media using a syringe pump (New Era NE-4000). Due to the high vacuum, a low liquid flow rate of 20 mL/h was carefully maintained to ensure that the microfluidic chip was fully saturated without any bubbles. This saturation process before the experiment is challenging during the experiment procedure, which requires a high sealing performance of the chip. Typically, it takes several hours to complete saturation process. The cameras can be used to monitor the filling process. After saturating, the displacement experiments were ready to begin. For G→  L displacement experiment, gas phase (N 2    ) was introduced into the chip at a controlled flow rate using a mass flow meter to displace liquid phase 1. To conduct G→  (L→  L) experiment, the L→  L multi-fluid system was first created in the chip by injecting the liquid phase 2 to displace liquid phase 1 using syringe pumps (see Fig. 1 ). Steady state is defined as the state when the invasion area no longer expanding (Yang et al., 2022 ). After L→  L displacement reaches the steady state, the gas phase (N 2    ) was then injected to have G→  (L→  L) displacement. Throughout the displacement processes, a high-speed camera (Phantom V611) with a micro-NIKKOR 105 mm lens was used to record the behavior of fingering invasion. A 1280 × 256 recording window at 24∼  2000 frames per second was performed on the entire porous domain to capture the process. A light source (Motic MLC-150C) provided brightness. Digital image processing was used to extract the each phase from the images captured by the camera based on an in-house code in MATLAB. Detail information can be found in our previous research (Yang et al., 2022 ). Subsequently, quantitative analysis, including invading velocity, saturation and Euler number, can be performed.  The porous media chip used in the experiment was fabricated by Dolomite company. Fig. 2  displays the schematic diagram of the microchip. To fabricate the chip, the HF (hydrofluoric acid) etching method was first used to generate lattices on a lower plate. The thermal bonding method (Barth, 1990 ) was used to bond the flat upper plate and lower plate together. The microchip has a 60 × 10 mm rectangular porous domain with a porosity ω   of 0.633. The pore-throat networks of the porous domain are designed to model a complex porous sandstone rock structure. As shown in Fig. 2 (b), the porous domain is constructed by replicating a 2 × 2 mm grid 150 times. The micrograph in Fig. 2 (c) shows differently shaped lattices are randomly arranged in the grid to form straight channels and two types of constricted throats (labeled as Throat#  1 and Throat#  2). Their widths are 110 μ m   , 85 μ m   , and 63 μ m   , respectively, but with the same depth, 100 μ m   . The grid has 50 Channels, 40 Throat#  1, and 38 Throat#  2. The probability distribution of throats and channels in the grid is illustrated in Fig. 2 (d). The cross-section of the straight channel is approximately circular, as illustrated in Fig. 2 (e). To ensure uniform inflow and outflow of the porous media, the inlet and outlet are equipped with tree-shaped layouts. The material of microchip is quartz glass with an inherent hydrophilicity (measured contact angle is 38.3°for 60 w t . %    Glycerol solution, 0°for Hexane) due to its 5 nm surface roughness (Ra). The etching process increases surface hydrophilicity.  2.2 Fluid properties and experimental conditions In order to investigate the influence of fluid viscosity on the mutual three phase displacement dynamics in porous media, we have to carefully chose the gas phase (G) with extremely low viscosity, low-viscosity liquid phase (LL), and high-viscosity liquid phase (HL). In this work, we use 60 w t . %    Glycerol solution as HL, Hexane as LL, and N 2     as G to have high viscosity differences. Because they have different brightness, it is easy to distinguish each phase from the other. It is not necessary to add dye into the liquid phase to enhance contrast. Table 1  shows the physical properties of these three fluids.     3 Results and discussion 3.1 Displacement pattern morphology of different multiphase scenarios  In order to investigate the invading behavior under different multiphase scenarios, that is G→  LL, G→  (HL→  LL), G→  HL, and G→  (LL→  HL), we compared the fingering morphologies of different fluid pairs at a 20 mL/h flow rate of invading phase, as shown in Fig. 3 . Colors golden, red and blue represent G, LL and HL, respectively, for ease of distinction. Unless otherwise specified, this color scheme will be used in the following figures. The breakthrough moment (BT) is defined as the time when the gas cap reaches the outlet, and the steady state (SS) is defined as the state when the invasion area no longer expands. As shown in Fig. 3 , the thin and elongated finger can be observed both in G→  LL and G→  HL displacement at breakthrough moment. Because of the lower viscosity of the defending phase LL, the finger in G→  LL displacement appears wider in general. Checking the local behavior of both cases, early compact invasion both appeared near the outlet in G→  LL and G→  HL displacement (dash box in Fig. 3  BT1 and BT3). As the interface gradually became unstable, the compact displacement was broken by the formation of preferential flow paths. In the case where the defending phase is LL, the area of compact invasion is wider than that in the case where the defending phase is HL. In both cases, the gas continued to invade new area after the breakthrough until the invaded area remained constant, termed as steady state. After reaching the steady state, a larger uninvaded area was left in the G→  HL displacement compared with the G→  LL displacement (see SS1 and SS3 in Fig. 3 ). In the three phase flow, the gas finger during G→  (HL→  LL) displacement exhibits a similar pattern with G→  L flow. However, a unique and previously unobserved yarn-liked pattern is found in G→  (LL→  HL) displacement experiment (see BT4 in Fig. 3 ). The video in Supplementary materials of Appendix shows the entire formation process of yarn-liked pattern vividly. Note that the defending phase was essentially the same co-existing LL and HL mixture, but completely different gas invading patterns are observed in the G→  (HL→  LL) and G→  (LL→  HL) process. The apparent reason is the different occupation sequences of LL and HL in the pore spaces, which potentially induces different liquid distribution and saturation. Previous research has also reported that the fingering pattern of the invading phase is highly sensitive to the initial liquid distribution in porous domain (Zhu et al., 2022 ). The underlying reasons are explored through the invading dynamics analysis and a detailed discussion is presented in the later sections.  The saturations S   of each phase after gas invading into single- and multi-fluid system are calculated: (3.1) S = A  L  t o t a l   W  t o t a l   φ   ,     Here, A   is the occupied area of each phase. L  t o t a l     and W  t o t a l     are the length and width of the porous domain, which are 60 mm and 10 mm, respectively. φ   is the porosity of the porous domain. Fig. 4  demonstrates the displacement scenarios categorized into two distinct parts based on the different initial liquid phases, represented by the various colors of the curves. For all the displacement scenarios, the saturation of initial phase at steady state is lower than that of the breakthrough moment. Here, we define the displacement efficiency as 1 minus the saturation of the initial phase. The low saturation of the initial phase means the high displacement efficiency. From Fig. 4 , we can also find that alternating to gas phase injection after the L→  L displacement reached steady state, that is G→  (L→  L), can further improve the displacement efficiency. In another word, after saturation reaches the limit in the L→  L displacement, a third phase can be injected to break the limit and further increase the displacement efficiency. In summary, the displacement efficiency follows the order of G→  (L→  L) >   L→  L >   G→  L. The lowest saturation of the initial phase is observed in the three-phase displacement. Specifically, in the G→  (HL→  LL) displacement, most of the initial phase is displaced, and its residue saturation is close to 20%. In many subsurface energy applications, the residue saturation of the initial phase is an important parameter in evaluating the extraction efficiency. By showing that the G→  (L→  L) tops the highest displacement efficiency, the three-phase flow offers great potential for the enhancement of subsurface extraction.  3.2 Influence of injection flow rate This section mainly focuses on the influence of injection flow rate and phase viscosity, which is divided into two parts: G→  (HL→  LL) and G→  (LL→  HL). In order to investigate the viscous-dependent fingering dynamics, the injection rate is required to be high enough to locate displacement at the viscous flow regime. Meanwhile, a large range of C a    number needs to be covered to reflect the impact of C a    number. Based on the flow regime diagram (Yang et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2020 ), three different injection rates 20, 200, and 2000 mL/h were chosen in the experiments after considering the limitation of the flow meter and syringe pump. To locate the flow regimes of each invading conditions in the phase diagram (Hu et al., 2019; Primkulov et al., 2021 ), the capillary number C a    and the viscosity ratio M   are respectively calculated by: (3.2) C a = μ  i   u  i    σ  d     ,     (3.3) M = μ  i    μ  d     ,     where u  i     is the Darcy velocity of the invading phase; σ  d     is the surface tension between invading and defending phases; μ  i     and μ  d     are dynamic viscosity of the invading and defending phases, respectively. In case of G→  (L→  L), the viscosity of the defending phase is calculated as the saturation-averaged values μ  a v e     based on the liquid saturation after L-L displacement reaches equilibrium and before the gas invasion: (3.4) μ  a v e   = S  H L   μ  H L   + S  L L   μ  L L   ,     Here, S  H L     and S  L L     are the saturation of the low-viscosity liquid phase (LL), and high-viscosity liquid phase (HL) after L-L displacement reaches equilibrium. μ  H L     and μ  L L     are their viscosity. In Fig. 5 , it is noted that all gas invasions in our experiments are located in the area of viscous fingering regime and crossover regime of the flow phase diagram defined by Zhang et al. (2011) . In these flow regimes, the fingering dynamics is mainly governed by viscous effect, which is aligned with our research focus on viscous-dominated gas invasion.   According to Eq. (3.2) , the higher the flow rate, the higher the capillary number C a   . When gas invades into the high-viscosity liquid (G→  LL), the displacement pattern seems to become more compact with the increased C a    number, as shown in Fig. 6 (a). By looking into the finger details in the three images of the first column, an obvious increase in finger numbers is observed as the increase of C a    number. Under the high C a    number, these paralleled fingers are generated near the inlet and move forward together, resulting in a such compact pattern (see videos in supplementary materials). Correspondingly, the gas invaded area is also increased. In the case of G→  (HL→  LL) in Fig. 6 (a), the fingers are more fractal than those in G→  LL. With the increase of C a    number, the number of fingers does not have an obvious increase either. Instead, the finger width increases a lot. Different fingering dynamics leads to the variation in phase saturation and displacement efficiency. Fig. 6 (b) presents the residue saturations of the initial phase after gas invasion. Under the same injection rates, the maximum displacement efficiency of initial phase still appears in G→  (HL→  LL) displacement, which aligns with our previous observation. Fig. 6 (b) also illustrates that the displacement efficiency has a positive relationship with the injection rate in the same injection scenario. When the invading and defending fluids are fixed, the higher the injection flow rate, the higher the C a    number. The stronger viscous force allows the invading phase to displace more initial phase. However, when it comes to actual underground storage/extraction strategies across different geological contexts, it is important to evaluate not only the displacement efficiency but also the overall economic benefits. The faster injection flow rates mean higher energy consumption and the need for pumping systems that can deliver high pressures. As shown in Fig. 6 (b), When the injection flow rate increases by 2 orders of magnitude, the initial phase saturation decreases from 21.4% to 7.7% at steady state of G→  (HL→  LL) displacement. The substitution efficiency is roughly 3 times higher. Our conclusions can be used as a reference when considering whether the additional cost of adopting faster flow rates can be compensated by higher economic revenues from higher displacement efficiencies. Another important finding is that when using the lowest flow rate (20 mL/h) in the G→  (HL→  LL) displacement, the residue saturation of LL remains much lower than that of using the highest flow rate (2000 mL/h) in the G→  LL and HL→  LL displacement. In other words, the G→  (HL→  LL) three-phase displacement efficiency is the highest even using a low injection rate in spite of the fact that the increase of injection rate is able to reduce the LL residue. A low injection rate means low energy consumption of pumping equipment, which is of great economic benefits for the practical geo-applications.  Different finger patterns of three-phase displacement have been observed in the experiments when switching the initial phase to the high-viscosity liquid (HL). Fig. 7 (a) shows the fingering patterns of G→  HL and G→  (LL→  HL) under various gas invading speeds. The fingers in G→  HL displacement tend to expand in width with the increase of C a    number, which is similar to patterns in the G→  (HL→  LL) displacement. In G→  (LL→  HL) displacement, the yarn-liked structure appeared (see the images of the last three rows in Fig. 7 (a)). When the C a    number is low, the yarn-liked branches are less in number but more twisted. In the last row of invading speed at 2000 mL/h, the threads of yarn-liked finger densely appear and move in parallel. As a result, the invaded area at steady state exhibits a positive relationship with C a    number, which aligns with the result in the viscous fingering regime of Chen et al. (2017) . Fig. 7 (b) shows a similar trend of displacement efficiency as the cases in Fig. 6 (b) with the low-viscosity liquid as the initial phase. Displacement efficiency of initial HL phase is maximum in G→  (LL→  HL) displacement. However, because the thin yarn-liked fingers, yet of great number, have limited invading area, the increment is not as obvious as G→  (HL→  LL) displacement.  3.3 Underlying invading dynamics  As previously mentioned, the gas invasion dynamics is dominated by viscous effect based on the phase diagram. To find out the underlying reasons of different gas invading behavior of G→  (HL→  LL) and G→  (LL→  HL), we first checked the viscosity of the defending phase. For the HL and LL co-existing multi-fluids, the saturation of each liquid phase before the gas invasion is shown in Fig. 8 (a), and the saturation-averaged defending viscosity μ  a v e     is then calculated and shown in Fig. 8 (b). Due to distinct invading phases during L→  L displacement, Fig. 8 (b) exhibits a contrasting trend in μ  a v e     for G→  (HL→  LL) and G→  (LL→  HL) as the increase of flow rate. Obviously, the μ  a v e     in G→  (HL→  LL) is higher than that in G→  (LL→  HL). From the gas invasion experiments, we also measured the breakthrough time T  B     and steady-state time T  S     in Fig. 8 (c–d). T  B     is the time from the start of the invasion to the arrival of the finger cap at the outlet, and T  S     is the time from the start of the invasion until when the invasion area no longer expands. Often, high viscosity means high resistance from the defending phase for the gas invasion. However, when comparing the results in Fig. 8 (c–d), the gas invading time does not completely follow the same order of averaged viscosities of defending phase. In G→  HL, the defending fluid has the highest viscosity, and the gas invading time T  B     and T  S     are the longest as expected. But, the T  B     and T  S     of G→  LL are not the fastest even though its viscosity of defending phase is the lowest. Surprisingly, the G→  (LL→  HL) has the shortest invading time. In another word, after having the high-viscosity phase HL before gas injection, the invading time is counterintuitively shortened. Furthermore, the position of the finger cap was captured, which is defined as the frontmost pixel of the finger. Fig. 8 (e) plots the finger cap position X  c a p     as a function of time t  . The finger cap gradually moves forward over time until it arrives outlet. A linear fit was made to the curve to obtain the slope, which is the cap speed. It was found that the finger cap speed has a positive relationship with injection flow rate in the same injection scenario. The speed of finger cap during G→  (LL→  HL) displacement is much faster than that during G→  (HL→  LL) displacement. To reveal the mysteries of ultra-fast invading speed of G→  (LL→  HL), the special yarn-liked finger might be the key.    Fig. 9 (a, c) shows the time evolution of the gas invasion process in three-phase displacement. The animations of three-phase displacement process are also included in the supplementary materials. The images of finger patterns are color-coded based on specific time periods ranging from 0 to T  B    , which enables the identification of the invasion location during each of these periods. The invasion process started as soon as the gas entered the porous domain, with the fingers gradually forming at the interface between the gas and liquid. As the gas invasion proceeds, the previously unobserved yarn-liked pattern was observed in G→  (LL→  HL), which is completely different from the common fingering pattern in G→  (HL→  LL). Its pathways were restricted within a single channel. To reveal the cause, the mechanism behind different patterns was studied by local dynamics analysis as shown in Fig. 10 . The different local gas invasion behavior in G→  (HL→  LL) and G→  (LL→  HL) was observed. In G→  (LL→  HL), interconnected LL pattern and scattered HL form after LL→  HL displacement became steady state. In multi-fluid system, gas preferentially displaces the pore space where low-viscosity liquid occupies due to smaller resistance. Therefore, gas mainly invades the LL channel. This is also confirmed by the saturation evolution of the HL and LL phase in Fig. 9 (d), where the LL saturation drops much faster than the one of HL. Note that the LL (Hexane here) is also the wetting phase, which is completely hydrophilic on quartz glass (see Table 1 ). According to the Alhosani et al. (2021a) ’s report, the liquid with the highest wettability tends to occupy the smallest pores and throats within the pore space, as well as wetting layers. Conversely, the phase with the lowest wettability tends to trap in the centers of larger pores. Therefore, in the LL→  HL process, the LL tended to form a thin wetting layer in the constrained spaces. Meanwhile, the scattered HL further limits the growth of the route width. Eventually, the yarn-liked fingering pattern rapidly forms during the G→  (LL→  HL) displacement. Contrary to G→  (LL→  HL), in G→  (HL→  LL), HL is invading phase during HL→  LL displacement. After steady state, LL becomes scattered and HL interconnects as shown in Fig. 10 (a). When gas invasion, there is no interconnected LL channel for gas to break through, resulting in the gas having to displace the HL. high-viscosity liquid suppresses the quick breakthrough of gas and promotes the bypass invasion, leading to the increment of finger width. Therefore, the yarn-liked fingering pattern disappears during G→  (HL→  LL) displacement. Under the same volume flow rate, the flow speed increases within narrow flow paths. Therefore, such a thin yarn-liked finger pattern is the reason for ultra-fast invading speed in G→  (LL→  HL). As shown in Fig. 9 (c), the yarn-liked structure becomes denser but less twisted at higher C a    numbers. Near breakthrough, the disconnected gas ganglia is observed, as shown in the pattern painted in white. Especially at the highest C a    number, lots of scattered gas appeared near outlet. Furthermore, compared with G→  (HL→  LL), frequent gas ganglia movement is found during G→  (LL→  HL). They can move independently, either slower or faster than the main finger fronts. The movement of the ganglia has a significant impact on the dynamic connectivity and reorganization of the flow path, thereby influencing the phase distribution (Reynolds et al., 2017 ). It is necessary to explore ganglia mobilization and connectivity.  3.4 Ganglia mobilization and topological connectivity By tracking the movement of all gas ganglia before breakthrough, we notice that ganglia movement and connection are mainly divided into 2 categories, i.e. “catch up to connect” and “expand to connect”, as illustrated in Figs. 11 (a, b). As for the first type, gas ganglion (highlighted in red color) moves with a higher speed than the finger front. It moved in its own, finally caught up, and actively re-connected to the main invading finger (highlighted by white color). Its movement is mainly driven by the pushing of liquid behind it. As for the second type, the gas ganglion did not completely break away from the gas behind, so it expanded forward with the continuous supply of invading gas, although sometimes it was still disconnected. Upon contact with the anterior main invading finger, reconnection of the ganglia is completed. From the observation of the invading process from breakthrough moment to steady state, we also find that most ganglia got reconnected to the flow path after breakthrough due to the continuous expansion of fingers. As shown in Fig. 7 (a), almost all the gas is interconnected together at steady state. To understand how they are connected, the evolution of topological connectivity is investigated. Here, Euler number (or Euler characteristic) χ   was measured, which is a topological invariant that characterizes the fluid connectivity of fingering patterns in porous media. χ   can be calculated from the family of Betti numbers: (3.5) χ  G   = β  0   + β  1   + β  2   ,      Here, χ  G     is the Euler number of the gas phase. β  0    , β  1    , and β  2     represent the number of disconnected fluid elements, “handles” or loops within each fluid element, and isolated voids or cavities in the fluid elements, respectively. β  2     is 0 for our two-dimensional chip. According to the equation, the lower χ  G    , the higher connectivity. Fig. 11 (c) illustrates the temporal evolution of χ  G     throughout the gas invasion process, spanning from the initiation to steady state. At the flow rates of 200 and 2000 mL/h, χ  G     demonstrates an ascending trend as the gas invasion progresses, implying the generation of disconnected ganglia and lower connectivity. The higher C a    number, the steeper the upward trend. It is noteworthy that χ  G     fluctuates around 0 at the flow rate of 20 mL/h, indicating ganglion disconnection equivalent to the connection. After breakthrough, χ  G     continues its ascent, followed by a rapid descent. The decline is attributed to the persistent expansion of fingers and the subsequent reconnection of ganglia after breakthrough, as previously mentioned. Eventually, the downward trend slows down and stabilizes, signaling the arrival of a steady state. At steady state, χ  G     is below 0 at higher flow rate of 200 and 2000 mL/h, suggesting that the number of loops surpasses that of disconnected ganglia. As depicted in Fig. 11 (c), χ  G     at steady state decreases with the increase of flow rates, meaning that connectivity has a positive relationship with C a    number.   4 Conclusions This work has investigated the gas invasion into the single- and multi-liquid systems in porous media by using a microfluidic chip with a porous domain. From the digital image processing and quantitative analysis on the images captured by a high-speed imaging system, we have reported the following new insights on the viscous-dependent displacing dynamics, which is promising for subsurface extraction/storage enhancement through enriching multi-fluids injection scenarios. (i) Gas invading into multi-liquids achieves the highest efficiency, followed by liquid-invading-liquid and gas-invading-liquid, in terms of the displacement of the initial phase in porous spaces. This is evidenced by the quantitative analysis of the residue saturation of the initial phase after displacement. Even at a low injection rate of 20 mL/h, the displacement efficiency of three-phase displacement remained higher than that in two-phase displacement at a high rate of 2000 mL/h, shedding light on the innovative extraction enhancement strategies for energy savings without the cost of expensive pumping power.  (ii) When gas displaces multi-fluids, the gas fingering pattern highly depends on the historical occupation sequences of the liquids. A unique and previously unobserved yarn-liked gas (G) fingering pattern is discovered in the G→  (LL→  HL) displacement when the initial phase is high-viscosity liquid (HL) and the second occupation phase is low-viscosity liquid (LL) before gas invasion. Breakthrough and steady state time show that the yarn-liked gas fingering has a much faster invasion speed even though the co-existed LL and HL defending fluid has higher saturation-averaged viscosity than that of G→  LL.  (iii) To reveal the mechanism behind the formation of yarn-liked fingers, local dynamics analysis was conducted. In G→  (LL→  HL), gas prefers to invade interconnected LL channel and the scattered HL further prevents the growth of the finger width. On the contrary, in G→  (HL→  LL), LL channel is dispersed, so the gas needs to invade HL. high-viscosity liquid provides high drug and promotes bypass invasion, resulting in the disappearance of yarn-liked fingering pattern.  (iv) By tracking the movement of each individual ganglia, two types of ganglia movement and connection were identified in G→  (LL→  HL), i.e. “catch up to connect” and “expand to connect”. To access the connectivity of gas fingering in G→  (LL→  HL), Euler number χ  G     was measured. The time evolution of χ  G     shows an initial ascending trend, attributed to the generation of disconnected ganglia. Following the breakthrough, a rapid descent of χ  G     ensues, indicating the expansion and reconnection of ganglia after breakthrough. When a steady state arrives, the descent trend slows down and stabilizes.

1 Introduction Flooding, as a severe natural disaster, significantly impacts human life and economic development. Globally, frequent flood disasters can lead to casualties, property loss, infrastructural damage, and ecosystem destruction (Apurv et al., 2015 ). According to the 2022 statistics released from the Ministry of Emergency Management of the People's Republic of China, five out of the top ten natural disasters in the country were attributed to heavy rainfall and flooding. Additionally, between 1975 and 2001, a total of 1,816 inland flooding events worldwide affected over 2.2 billion people (Serinaldi et al., 2018 ). These underscore the crucial importance of accurate flood forecasting for the human society. Rain forecasting, as a prerequisite for accurate flood modeling, is a significantly challenging task for data-sparse regions like in Northeast China due to the lack of observation stations and the spatially and temporally strong variability of rain distributions. Currently, the rain forecasts, either driven by the physics-based weather models such as Global Forecast System (GFS) or provided by machine learning techniques, mainly sourced from measurements by rain gauges, weather radar, and remote sensing (Chiang et al., 2022 ) with various advantages and limitations. Ground-based rain gauges offer relatively precise rainfall data at the point scale, but their uneven network due to the accessibility and economic constraints, poses difficulty for accurately interpolating the rain distributions over watersheds or mountainous regions with insufficient gauges (Canli et al., 2018 ). Ground-based radar transmits and receives electromagnetic waves to obtain the information of spatial targets. Radar-based rainfall observations deliver a wide-ranging coverage and high spatiotemporal precision, but they may not fully capture the actual rainfall distribution. The presence of complex terrain and issues like ground clutter interference and attenuation effects could compromise the accuracy of radar measurements (Martens et al., 2013 ). Satellite rain products, utilizing the technologies like infrared or microwave sensors, provide even broader coverage including the inaccessible areas and enhance the potential for analyzing rainfall intensity and distribution (Bitew and Gebremichael, 2011; Stampoulis and Anagnostou, 2012 ), These products, however, are affected by the sensor performance, cloud conditions, and the local terrain disturbances, leading to discrepancies between the measured and actual rainfall. To reduce the errors generated from a single source, the fusion of multi-source rainfall datasets became a research focus in recent years. Combining satellite or radar rain estimates with gauge observations leveraged the strengths of both sources, enhancing the accuracy and spatial coverage of the fused products (Nan et al., 2023 ). The methods of data fusion can be classified into the global fusion and the local fusion. The global fusion method employed a smoothing function but overlooked the spatial differences among rainfall data sources (Lekula et al., 2018; Woldemeskel et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2017 ), thus potentially ignoring the geographic heterogeneity and adding the subjectivity in data correction weights. Narkhedkar et al. (2008)  fused the satellite data with daily rainfall data observed from stations in India's monsoon region by the global fusion method, resulting in the higher spatiotemporal resolutions in the fused product. Tian et al (Tian et al., 2010 ) corrected the TRMM 3B42RT product using ground observations in the U.S., which were found to reduce the errors of the satellite forecast by 47 % to 63 % in regions with a less extensive network of ground-based rain gauges. The local fusion approach, on the other hand, considered the spatial variations in the merged rainfall dataset by statistical methods such as interpolation (Mahfouf et al., 2007 ). By optimally fusing multi-source data from weather model forecasts, rain gauges, and radar, the data quality could be significantly improved. Hu et al (Hu et al., 2015 ) introduced a geographically weighted regression method to merge satellite and station data. This model has been proven to be superior in addressing the spatial heterogeneity and temporal variability of precipitation (Wang et al., 2022a; Xie et al., 2017 ). Recently, the evolution of machine learning has created new possibilities for rainfall fusion techniques. Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have been extensively utilized in rainfall-runoff modeling, demonstrating their reliability in flood prediction (Guo et al., 2013; Hung et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023, 2022; Young and Liu, 2015 ). Specifically, ANNs can effectively improve the rainfall forecasts by associating the historical rainfall data with reanalysis data or the related meteorological variables. Hong et al (2021)  employed ANNs to merge measured data with ERA5 reanalysis data, producing a multi-source precipitation dataset that more accurately represented the precipitation distribution in data-rich regions. Additionally, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) models considered the spatial and temporal patterns of the rain data with the complex geographic features and, thereby, enhanced the accuracy of precipitation predictions. Pan et al. (2019)  investigated the method of CNNs trained for precipitation estimation across various regions in the U.S., which suggested that the precipitation estimates forecast by the CNN could surpass those of the reanalysis products in terms of accuracy when adequate training data were available. The Transformer, as a new-generation network architecture proposed by Google in 2017 following the CNN model, has increasingly attracted research interests, especially due to its self-attention mechanism in handling complex tasks requiring an understanding of the context and interrelationships within the data (Vaswani et al., 2017 ). Established on the Natural Language Processing (NLP) analytics often used for applications such as machine translation (Xiong et al., 2020 ), the Transformer's innovative architecture has inspired the development of new algorithms in other domains including computer vision and time series analysis (Fan et al., 2021; Nascimento et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2021 ). In this study, considering its potential for processing time series data, the Transformer model was explored to be adopted for improving the rain forecast and flood simulations. Especially, the self-attention mechanism enabled the Transformer model to handle the spatial and temporal dependencies in meteorological data, while the latter was often a challenging task for the conventional CNN models. While machine learning and deep learning techniques exhibited considerable potential in predicting meteorological variables, they may still face difficulties when applied to a specific meteorological forecasting dataset if the rain gauges were required (Yu et al., 2023 ). Meanwhile, in spite of the superiority of time series analysis, the Transformer remained constrained in handling complex meteorological data especially with uneven rainfall distributions due to its sensitivity to sparse data (Nan et al., 2023; Sayeed et al., 2023 ). Additionally, certain regions like Northeast China lacked supportive observations such as meteorological stations or radar data, which further reduced the amount and quality of the training sets. Rain intensity is the main factor affecting the results of flood simulations (Chen et al., 2023 ). Due to the completely missing or underestimated rain amounts provided by the numerical weather predictions, the performance of the driven hydrologic models could be extremely constrained in terms of flood forecasting. For instance, although the Global Forecast System (GFS) provided the long-term weather forecasts, its performance across all seasons had not met expectations yet (Sun et al., 2023 ). Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), a class of machine learning frameworks, have proven promising across a wide range of applications, including image and speech generation and data augmentation. GANs operate through a dual-structural mechanism, consisting of a generator that creates a dataset mimicking the observations and a discriminator that evaluates the fidelity of the generated dataset (Goodfellow et al., 2014 ). This setup enables GANs to learn and replicate complex data distributions, making them particularly suited for enhancing the quality of meteorological data predictions (Hess et al., 2022 ). One of the standout advantages of GANs in handling meteorological data is their ability to generate realistic, complex data distributions that can account for spatial and temporal variability in rainfall patterns. By learning from existing data, GANs can interpolate or extrapolate to fill in gaps in sparse datasets, offering a robust tool for correcting uneven rainfall distribution in GFS data. To address the above-mentioned key challenges in rainfall forecasting and flood simulations, this study introduced the Attention-Enhanced Meteorological Prediction Generative Adversarial Network (AEMP-GAN) for improving the GFS rainfall prediction during the flood season in Northeast China. The AEMP-GAN model shared the benefits of self-attention mechanisms and GANs, enhancing the processing of time series data and effectively managing the nonuniform rain distributions, which was critical for predicting the extreme flood events. Through this novel approach, AEMP-GAN was shown to be able to improve the accuracy of rain forecasting and consequently the flood forecasting.  2 Methodology 2.1 AEMP-GAN model The Attention-Enhanced Meteorological Prediction Generative Adversarial Network (AEMP-GAN) was proposed as the forecasting model (Fig. 1  ), which was inspired by the work of Sayeed et al (Sayeed et al., 2020 ) and merged with the self-attention mechanism from the Transformer model. Given the interdependent nature of meteorological variables, convolutional networks could serve as an effective tool for establishing connections among such variables (Wang et al., 2020 ). As Complex nonlinear interactions among the features of meteorological variables played a crucial role in the precise forecasting of rainfall events, the developed model employed an attention mechanism that dynamically identified and accentuated the pivotal, interactive spatial features within the GFS dataset, which enhanced the accuracy and robustness of the prediction of the evolving rain distributions. The AEMP-GAN model encompassed an encoder, a decoder, and a discriminator. The encoder was responsible for extracting the key features from the rain grids and encoding them into a multi-channel feature matrix of a 2D image. On the 2D domain, the spatial information was continuously compressed and refined, while the pixel size gradually increased and the feature values conveyed higher-level semantic characteristics. Additionally, the increase in the channel number or the dimensionality of the matrix created more variations for the extracted information. The encoder's convolutional layer with a 4 × 4 kernel size performed the feature extraction to achieve spatial downsampling by setting a stride of 2 and padding of 1. Within each pooling, the spatial dimension of the feature map was halved, while nonlinear feature selection was achieved by the ReLU activation function that accelerated convergence and improved accuracy. During the encoding process, the convolutional layer utilized a 3 × 3 kernel size for feature extraction, and a 2 × 2 pooling size for spatial downsampling. Each pooling step reduced the spatial dimension of the feature map by half, further aided by the ReLU activation function to introduce nonlinearity, thereby accelerating convergence and improving prediction accuracy. During decoding, the decoder reconstructed the data structure from the highly-abstract encoded features through a series of transposed convolution layers, which doubled the size of the input feature maps through each layer. Subsequently, the features were gradually upsampled to generate the revised rainfall forecasts. The discriminator from the GAN framework, which was responsible for evaluating data, was used to distinguish the actual rain distributions from those generated by the predictive model and fed the errors to the generative model to improve the latter. Architecturally, the discriminator comprised of multiple convolutional layers to extract features, an adaptive average pooling layer to resize the feature maps, and a fully connected layer to convert the feature values by the Sigmoid function into the probabilities of the input features belonging to the real rain distributions. The AEMP-GAN model utilized 8 meteorological forecast variables as inputs, the same used by WRF-Hydro. Each of the 8 variables for the 0–24 h prediction range was arranged as a channel, respectively. The Climate Prediction Center (CPC) precipitation data were used as the ground truth and processed into a single channel with the dimensions of 96 pixels in both width and height. Due to the need for grid data to effectively address the inherent spatial variability of rain patterns in the study area, the CPC precipitation data analysis product is more suitable as ground truth than station data. As the primary focus of this study was the flood seasons of Northeast China (June to October). The flood seasons from 2015 to 2020 were designated as the training period, while the flood season of 2021 was reserved for testing. During the training process, the Mean Squared Error (MSE) reconstruction loss function and the Adversarial loss were employed for training the model. The MSE evaluated the pixel-level reconstruction accuracy and was calculated as follows:(1) L rec   = 1 n  ∑ i , j   I pred  i , j   - I GT  ( i , j )    2  ,       where n   is the number of samples in one data batch, I p r e d   ( i )     and I G T   i      are the i  th     sample of predicted image and ground truth image, respectively. The adversarial loss function is provided below:(2) L adv    = E I GT   ∼ p GT      l o g D I GT       + E I pred   ∼ p pred     log 1 - D I pred         ,         where D ·    represents the probability output by the discriminator to determine whether the input image I P r e d     is a real image. p GT     is the distribution of real images, and p Pred     is the distribution of generated images. Therefore, the total training loss (L total   ) for the model is given by:(3) L total  = L r e c   + 0.001 × L adv  .        Pytorch was used for the construction and training of the neural network. The learning rate and the batch size were optimized as 0.001 and 32, respectively, and the Adam optimizer was selected.  2.2 Evaluating indicators The percent bias (PBIAS), Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) were used as the major indicators to evaluate the runoff simulations:(4) PBIAS = ∑ i = 1  n  P i  - ∑ i = 1  n  O i   ∑ i = 1  n  O i    × 100 % ,       (5) NSE = 1 - ∑ i = 1  n  O i  - P i    2   ∑ i = 1  n  O i  - O ¯    2    ,       (6) RMSE = ∑ i = 1  n  O i  - P i    2   n   ,       where O i    and P i    represent the observed and predicted values, respectively, and O  ¯     is the mean of observed values. To comprehensively evaluate the overall quality of the model's predictions, the Index of Agreement (IOA) was further applied as an additional metric:(7) IOA = 1 - ∑ O i  - P i     2   ∑ abs ( O  i  - O  ¯   ) + abs ( P  i  - O  ¯   )     2    .          IOA varied between 0 and 1, which reflected the degree of model prediction error. A value of 1 indicates a perfect match and 0 stands for no agreement at all (Willmott et al., 1985 ). The IOA serves as an effective metric for reflecting the model's prediction accuracy across various conditions, including different rainfall intensities. It offers a relative measure of the congruence between predicted and observed values, thereby encapsulating the overall consistency of the model’s predictions. This metric does not solely focus on the magnitude of prediction errors but also considers the directional agreement between the model outputs and observed data, ensuring a comprehensive evaluation of model performance in simulating rainfall events.   3 Experiments 3.1 Data 3.1.1 Numerical weather prediction (NWP) dataset The GFS dataset provided by the National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) was used as a source of rain forecasts for this study. The GFS data had a temporal resolution of 6 h with runs at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00, and 18:00 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) and a spatial resolution of 0.25° × 0.25°. The daily 00:00 UTC GFS data were selected with a 3-hour interval between forecasts covering a 0–24 h prediction period, providing eight data per day. The GFS range was cut to 30°N-54°N, 111°E-135°E with 96 grid points in both the zonal and meridional directions to cover the study area (Northeast China).  3.1.2 Observation datasets The observed precipitation dataset was collected from the CPC of the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) (Xie et al., 2010 ), which provided the global-scale precipitation observations. The data spanned from 1980 to the present, aggregating observations from satellites, ground-based stations, and meteorological radars. The CPC precipitation dataset offered the daily precipitation grids with a horizontal resolution of 0.5° × 0.5°, which has been widely applied in research fields such as climate change, hydrology, and agriculture. The GFS forecast data were aggregated to match the daily resolution of the acquired CPC dataset, ensuring that consistency in temporal resolution between the two datasets was achieved. The daily time series of the observed runoff were collected for the flood season from 2015 to 2021. Due to data limitations, the Chaersen and Suolun stream gauges at the outlet and the middle of the studied watershed were selected for the calibration and validation for the hydrologic model (Fig. 2  ).   3.2 WRF-Hydro setting WRF-Hydro 5.2.0 was a parallelized, physically based, and distributed hydrologic model developed by the U.S. National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) (Gochis et al., 2020 ), which supported the simulations of hydrologic processes and the land–atmosphere interactions. The WRF-Hydro modeling system simulated the runoff generation process based on the Noah-MP land surface model and separately simulated subsurface flow, overland flow, and channel routing (Fig. 3  ). The subsurface flow was simulated based on the Dupuit-Forchheimer assumptions. The simulation of the overland flow employed an unsteady, spatially explicit diffusive wave equation. Regarding channel routing, WRF-Hydro had multiple options including the Muskingum, Muskingum-Cunge, and diffusion wave methods. The Noah-MP LSM grids were generated with a spatial resolution of 1.5 km by the WRF Model Preprocessing System (WPS) (Skamarock et al., 2021 ). The routing grid for the studied watershed was generated from a 90 m digital elevation model (DEM). The domain included 76 east–west cells and 34 north–south cells. The time steps for Noah-MP, channel routing, and terrain routing were 180 min, 10 s, and 10 s, respectively. The corrected rainfall forecasts were processed to be compatible with WRF-Hydro using the Earth System Model Framework (ESMF). The model was spun up for 3 months before the formal calculations. 3.2.1 Forcing The uncoupled WRF-Hydro model required meteorological forcing data to drive the hydrological simulation. Eight variables from the GFS forcing were extracted, which included rainfall rate (RAINRATE), long-wave radiation (LWDOWN), short-wave radiation (SWDOWN), air temperature (T2D), specific humidity (Q2D), surface pressure (PSFC), and near-surface wind in the u-component (U2D) and v-component (V2D) (Table 1  ). It is important to note that for operational flood forecasting, the rainfall data must be corrected before being employed by the hydrologic model.  3.2.2 Model calibration As a distributed hydrologic model, the WRF-Hydro model involved numerous parameters that significantly affected the results of flood simulations. These parameters could be broadly categorized into two groups: one group had direct influence on runoff generation including surface infiltration rate (REFKDT), surface retention depth (RETDEPRT), and the coefficient for deep drainage (SLOPE); the second group indirectly affected runoff processes such as Manning's coefficient (MannN) and surface roughness (OVROUGHRT). In the calibration process, Based on the previous sensitivity analyses (Ryu et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020 ), the five most sensitive parameters were calibrated in this study: REFKDT, saturated soil lateral hydraulic conductivity (LKSATFAC), SLOPE, RETDEPRT, and MannN. The calibration process was characterized by an iterative optimization approach, whereby various combinations of parameter values were adjusted to identify the set that best matched the observed streamflow. In this approach, key parameters that influence the model's total water output, specifically REFKDT and RETDEPRT, were initially calibrated to ensure the model's output was aligned with the observed data. Subsequently, parameters affecting the shape of the hydrograph curve and the temporal distribution of water flow, such as MannN, were then subjected to calibration. Throughout this iterative process, the optimized value for a parameter was fixed in the subsequent calibration for the remaining less sensitive parameters, and the calibrated values were also restrained within the normal ranges of the parameters (Table 2  ). A total of six historical events from 2015 to 2020 were picked for model simulation and calibration (Fig. 4  ). The Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) of the calibrated model exceeded 0.5 for all events and the root mean squared error (RMSE) percentages dropped significantly, except for the event on July 21, 2018 (Table 3  ). The relatively lower NSE value observed for the event on July 21, 2018, might be attributed to a few interrelated factors. Firstly, the capability of WRF-Hydro itself in terms of simulating events with multiple peaks was not ideal (Gu et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022b ). This challenge was further exacerbated by the underestimation of rainfall intensity in the Global Forecast System (GFS) forecasts for this event. Such underestimation led to inaccuracies in predicting soil saturation levels, critically affecting the generation of excess runoff. These discrepancies significantly hindered the model’s capability to simulate the secondary, smaller peak in runoff.    4 Results and discussion 4.1 Performance of AEMP-GAN in rain forecast The average RMSE of the GFS rainfall of the training dataset from 2015 to 2020 was initially 13.50 mm/day, which dropped to 5.90 mm/day when using the AEMP-GAN model, equivalent to a 56.30 % decrease. For the test set, the RMSE of GFS rain predictions was originally 8.64 mm/day but dropped to 6.16 mm/day after implementing AEMP-GAN, which represented a 28.7 % reduction. The monthly performance of the raw GFS rainfall and the AEMP-GAN rainfall were compared by a Taylor diagram on a grid-by-grid basis for the test set (Fig. 5  ). The diagram clearly demonstrated that AEMP-GAN rain forecasts outperformed the raw GFS rain forecasts in every month of the flood season across three metrics: RMSE, Pearson correlation, and standard deviation. Notably, except for October with relatively lower rainfall, the AEMP-GAN rain forecasts showed significant improvements in the three metrics for all other four months, indicating that AEMP-GAN was particularly effective in predicting medium to heavy rain events compared to medium to light events. The monthly IOA values were calculated for both the raw GFS rain forecasts and AEMP-GAN forecasts during the flood season (Table 4  ). An average 11.3 % increase in the IOA values was found across all grid cells, while the average IOA values rose from 0.626 to 0.696. Notably, the IOA in September exhibited the most significant (nearly 20 %) increase. The rain forecasts corrected by the AEMP-GAN model showed a significant increase in the medians of the monthly IOA values compared to the raw GFS rain forecasts (Fig. 6  ); the former was more consistent with the observations indicating the stable performance of the AEMP-GAN model. The spatial distributions of the RMSE of the rain grids forecast by GFS and AEMP-GAN for the test set were compared across Northeast China (Fig. 7  ). The RMSE of each grid was calculated based on the comparison with the CPC data. In Northeast China, the highest RMSEs for the raw GFS (exceeding 5 mm/day) were found in Inner Mongolia and Liaoning provinces with values of 5.81 mm/day and 8.11 mm/day, respectively, which, however, decreased to 4.53 mm/day and 6.57 mm/day, respectively, when using the AEMP-GAN model. Overall, the RMSE distributions of the AEMP-GAN rains in Jilin, Heilongjiang, Liaoning, and the upper part of Inner Mongolia provinces were significantly better than that of the raw GFS rains, which indicates that the AEMP-GAN model can significantly reduce the RMSE in Northeast China spatially.  4.2 Sensitivity experiments To evaluate the impact of the attention mechanism on the accuracy of the rainfall forecasts, this study compared the original AEMP-GAN model with the CMP-GAN (Conditional Meteorological Prediction Generative Adversarial Network) model with the attention module commented out. The comparison was conducted based on the identical datasets and training conditions to make a fair comparison. As shown in Table 5 ,  the RMSE for rainfall predictions by GFS, CMP-GAN, and AEMP-GAN reveals that the AEMP-GAN model, with the attention module activated, achieves a lower RMSE compared to CMP-GAN. The percentage decrease in RMSE on the test set for AEMP-GAN and CMP-GAN compared to GFS is 28.7 % and 20.2 %, respectively, demonstrating that AEMP-GAN outperformed CMP-GAN.  4.3 Flood forecasting Leveraging the time series of rain grids forecast by AEMP-GAN, WRF-Hydro could be employed to simulate runoff, which was then evaluated in comparison with streamflow observations. Throughout this process, the same parameter settings were consistently maintained as those used in the calibration phase. The model's spin-up period extended from May to the end of July, which was aligned with the spin-up duration of the calibration process. To minimize the influence of other meteorological variables within the forcing data on the simulation, only the rain datasets corrected by the AEMP-GAN model were imported into the WRF-Hydro, while other variables from the GFS forcing were directly used without corrections. The simulated flood flows for the three rainfall events from August to September 2021 were generated using 3-hourly intervals by WRF-Hydro, with rain forecasts by the GFS and AEMP-GAN models serving as inputs (Fig. 8  a). It's important to note that while WRF-Hydro was operated at a 3-hour resolution to capture the detailed dynamics of these events, the validation of model performance was conducted against observed daily runoff data (Fig. 8 b). This approach was necessitated by the unavailability of observed runoff data at a finer temporal resolution as a common challenge in the data-sparse region. It appears that the flood flows driven by the AEMP-GAN rain forecasts were generally higher than the actual flows except at the flood peaks. In contrast, when the raw GFS rain forecasts were used as the input, the simulated hydrographs were typically lower than the observations, which suggests that the modelled runoff driven by the GFS rains may lead to an underestimation, whereas AEMP-GAN compensated for the deficiency in the forecasted rain amounts that led to the overestimation of the floods. The PBIAS, NSE, and RMSE of the simulated flows driven by the GFS and AEMP-GAN models were calculated based on the measured flows for the three events (Table 6  ). The simulations utilizing rainfall data predicted by AEMP-GAN demonstrated an improvement in NSE over GFS rains by 8.42 %, 4.98 %, and 1.01 % for the three events, respectively, while the RMSE was reduced by 4.53 %, 3.54 %, and 0.55 %, respectively. The analysis of PBIAS values reveals that the runoff simulation, enhanced by rainfall data corrected using the AEMP-GAN model, effectively compensated for the underestimation observed in the GFS simulation. Notably, this adjustment not only addressed the underestimation but, in some instances, led to slight overestimation. Another stream gauge at the middle of the watershed, Suolun Station, was selected for further validation during the same period (Fig. 9  , Table 7  ). The results indicate significant improvements in NSE for two events following the implementation of AEMP-GAN, accompanied with the reductions in RMSE; specifically, the increases in NSE were 23.96 % and 3.90 %, respectively, while decreases in RMSE were 20.1 % and 7.86 %, respectively. As the fluctuation of the measured data at the Suolun station was significantly lower than that at Chaersen, the NSE values of the Suolun station was generally higher than that of Chaersen. The PBIAS values for the Suolun site exhibited a resemblance to prior observations, as the AEMP-GAN model still outperformed the GFS with slight overestimation. However, the correction for the event on September 5, 2021, was less effective, possibly because the uncertainty in rain forecasts inherited from the inability of GFS in capturing the local weather patterns and the influence from terrain and land use. These factors could add uncertainty to the spatial distributions of rain forecasts, resulting in the inaccurate prediction in certain parts of the watershed that exhibited sensitive hydrologic responses. Further, as the GFS yielded robust rain predictions by itself, the improvement by AEMP-GAN became modest. But overall, owing to the corrected rain forecasts, the accuracy of the flood simulations was enhanced for five out of the six events, with an average 6.9 % increase in NSE and an average 6.1 % reduction in RMSE. The results above highlighted the potential of AEMP-GAN in flood forecasting and also identified limitations. It has been observed that AEMP-GAN tended to overestimate flow in certain cases. This overestimation might stem from inadequate representation of extreme precipitation events in the model training phase or due to intrinsic limitations of the model in handling such extreme scenarios. Additionally, AEMP-GAN did not effectively correct the peak flows. On one hand, since CPC was an interpolation product, it might not precisely capture the extreme rainfall events in certain spots. Such minute differences in localized rainfall, while potentially detected in actual runoff station data, could be smoothed over in interpolated data. On the other hand, predicting peak flows required considering the complex meteorological and surface hydrological dynamics, which were not fully taken account by pure data prediction. In refining the analysis for the peak flow corrections, the importance of a comprehensive correction was recognized that ought to include not only rainfall but also other critical meteorological variables like radiation and temperature. These elements may also play a significant role in the hydrometeorological processes that affect the forecasting of peak flows. Future studies should investigate integrating advanced methods that encompass a wider range of meteorological anomalies to enhance the prediction accuracy for extreme events. Nevertheless, the observed improvements in NSE and RMSE indicate that AEMP-GAN could significantly strengthen the reliability of rainfall predictions, which was an important enhancement for flood forecasting and the risk management.   5 Conclusions Hydrologic models such as WRF-Hydro required meteorological forcing such as GFS as a prerequisite to drive the runoff simulations and flood forecasting. Global rain forecasts as a major input for rainfall-runoff modeling, however, had plenty of room for improvement in terms of the forecasting accuracy. Inspired by the successful use of deep learning in image processing, this study introduced the AEMP-GAN, a deep learning-based approach, to enhance the overall accuracy of GFS rain grids, in terms of the temporal and spatial dimensions, for Northeast China during the flood seasons. With the rain forecasts corrected by the AEMP-GAN model for six events, the NSE and RMSE of the predicted floods had a 6.9 % increase and a 6.1 % decrease on average, respectively. The AEMP-GAN models with and without the attention module were further compared. The results indicate that the AEMP-GAN model, with the attention module activated, showed a greater improvement in rainfall prediction than the CMP-GAN model without such mechanism. This underscores the crucial role of the attention mechanism in improving the GFS rain predictions in Northeast China. However, the current model still faced limitations in accurately predicting flood peaks. Future efforts would be needed to integrate a module of outlier detection to further improve the performance for extreme events.
