1 Introduction Flooding is the most common and costly natural disaster globally (Doocy et al., 2013; Razavi et al., 2020 ). It is therefore of critical importance to understand how climate change may impact flood risk as greater flood severity leads to increased economic losses (IPCC, 2023; Wasko et al., 2021b ), while decreases in flooding can have adverse impacts on water supply (Dykman et al., 2023; Sharma et al., 2018 ). Extreme rainfalls are widely accepted to be increasing with increasing temperatures due to climate change (Barbero et al., 2017; Fowler et al., 2021; Jayaweera et al., 2023 ), with the rarer the rainfall, the greater the increase (Gründemann et al., 2022; Jayaweera et al., 2023 ). Long duration (daily) extreme rainfall intensities are generally accepted to be increasing at a rate around 7 %/°C (Barbero et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2021; Westra et al., 2014 ), consistent with the Clausius-Clapeyron relationship, which is a key thermodynamic driver that governs the relationship between temperature and atmospheric moisture. However, changes in atmospheric dynamics (i.e. atmospheric circulation patterns) leads to regional patterns of change, shifting the frequency and mixture of storm types (Pfahl et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2021 ). Consequently, decreasing trends are often observed for more frequent long duration rainfall magnitudes such as annual maxima, (Jayaweera et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2021 ). For short duration (hourly) extreme rainfalls, intensification at rates above the Clausius-Clapeyron relationship are expected due to changes in latent heat fluxes (Fowler et al., 2021; Lenderink et al., 2017 ). For example, a recent meta -analysis of Australian extreme rainfalls found that short duration extreme rainfall intensities (≤1 h) are expected to increase by a median of 15 %/°C. Conversely, long duration rainfall intensities (≥24 h) are expected to increase by a median of 8 %/°C (Wasko et al., 2024 ). Importantly, increases in rainfall do not necessarily relate to increases in flood severity, as catchment conditions, in particular antecedent wetness, also modulate flooding (Sharma et al., 2018 ). Ivanavic and Shaw (2015) demonstrated that flood peaks are more severe on wetter catchments, with extreme 99th percentile precipitation leading to 99th percentile extreme streamflow 62 % of the time during wet periods, and only 13 % of the time during dry periods. Trend studies in frequent floods such as annual maxima often show decreasing trends in large parts of the world (Do et al., 2017; Sharma et al., 2018; Wasko et al., 2021a; Wasko and Sharma, 2017 ). But for flood events of increasingly rarer AEPs, an increasing positive trend in flood peaks emerges (Brunner et al., 2021; Wasko et al., 2021a; Wasko and Nathan, 2019 ). One potential cause of this dichotomous response of floods – where small floods are decreasing, and large flood are increasing – is that antecedent soil moisture is decreasing, leading to an increase in rainfall losses (i.e. rainfall that does not become streamflow, herein referred to as losses). For small flood peaks, this increase in losses offsets rainfall increases, leading to decreasing flood peaks. However, for larger floods the increase in rainfall outweighs the increase in losses, leading to an increase in flood peak (Sharma et al., 2018; Wasko and Nathan, 2019 ). This competing behaviour between changes in rainfall and catchment response creates a large degree of uncertainty for flood risk managers about the direction and magnitude of changes in flood risk in the future. Attempts to understand this change through ‘top-down’ assessments, where a future scenario is chosen and then propagated down a hydrologic modelling chain to produce estimates of future risk (Wasko et al., 2021c ) are confounded by large uncertainties in projections of hydroclimatic variables in General Circulation Models (GCMs). This makes top-down projections sensitive to the choice of climate scenario and GCM. Particularly relevant to flood projections, GCMs are not detailed enough to represent the important rainfall processes such as convection, and therefore rainfall products from these models are often biased and at a resolution too coarse for understanding catchment dynamics (François et al., 2019 ). Downscaling and bias correction techniques are available to improve the resolution of outputs and correct biases, but the choice of method introduces additional uncertainty (Chiew et al., 2022 ). Improvements can be made by using Regional Climate Models (RCMs), but again the choice of model and scenario introduces its own uncertainty, with RCM outputs often requiring further bias correction also (Vogel et al., 2023 ). ‘Bottom-up’ or ‘scenario-neutral’ assessments have been developed as an alternative for considering the deep uncertainty associated with hydroclimatic change (Brown et al., 2012; Brown and Wilby, 2012; Prudhomme et al., 2010 ). These approaches aim to understand future flood risk by stress-testing a system under different combinations of perturbed hydroclimatic variables that may occur as a result of climate change. This process is used to produce response surfaces showing the sensitivity of flood risk to changes in these variables (sometimes referred to as the vulnerability of the system). The projected ranges in the hydroclimatic variables that drive the stress test can then be collected from climate models and used to make an assessment of the likelihood of various future risks (Prudhomme et al., 2010 ). Recently, bottom-up climate change assessments have gained popularity for the estimation of flood risk. Examples include flood studies in the United Kingdom (Kay et al., 2021, 2014; Prudhomme et al., 2010 ) and Ireland (Bastola et al., 2011; Broderick et al., 2019; Wilby et al., 2014 ) with a focus on changes in flood peaks from ranging from an AEP of 1 in 5 to 1 in 100. Collectively these studies find that flood peaks are expected to increase but with considerably uncertainty. For example, in a national assessment to derive uplift factors for flood peaks across the whole United Kingdom Kay et al. (2021)  demonstrated that the regional change in 1 in 20 AEP flood peaks could range from −10 % to 80 % by 2080 under a high emissions scenario. In the United States, Steinschneider et al. (2015)  performed a bottom-up assessment to estimate the sensitivity of economic damages associated with flooding downstream of Coralville Dam to changes in precipitation and mean annual temperature. However, these bottom-up assessments use continuous simulation models, which require long rainfall and PET records to reproduce the streamflow regime, and do not specifically focus on flood drivers like extreme rainfall intensity or losses. The hydroclimatic variables that are used to perform a stress test on the system include changes to the mean temperature, mean annual rainfall, seasonal amplitude or ratios of rainfall to PET, but as noted above, these are not the direct drivers in flood risk. In these studies, the changes in the drivers of flood risk, such as the extreme rainfall or soil moisture, were implicitly, and not explicitly, considered. This means that although such approaches provide information on future flood risks, they do not inform our understanding as to why these flood risks have changed. Despite flood risk managers relying heavily on event-based rainfall-runoff models to estimate flood risk (Ball et al., 2019; Kjeldsen et al., 2005; NRCS, 2004; Pilgrim and Cordery, 1993 ) these models have received limited attention in bottom-up climate change impact assessment literature. However, these models can overcome the limitations above as the key flood drivers such as losses and extreme rainfall intensity can be more easily and explicitly perturbed and the sensitivity of flood peaks to these drivers can be more easily identified and understood. To the best knowledge of the author’s only a small number of bottom-up climate change assessments of flood risk using an event-based model can be found in the literature. For example, Padulano et al. (2021)  present a bottom-up approach to analyse urban flooding, where modelling inputs do not need to be adjusted to represent future climates. Instead, new probabilities are assigned to modelled flood events by considering projected changes to annual maxima rainfall depths. However, such an approach is unable to consider the joint impact of changes in multiple flood drivers. Looking at changes in rainfalls but not losses, Stephens et al. (2018)  found that an event-based model’s inability to account for changes in antecedent catchment conditions led to the overestimation of flood peaks in drying catchments. However, this limitation has now been overcome with the first available projections of losses for use in event-based model modelling published by Ho et al. (2023) . Knighton et al. (2017)  also performed a bottom up assessment using an event-based model. However, this work did not directly investigate the impact of changes in flood drivers on flood peaks, instead they used a framework that considered the risk of a stakeholder defined flood threshold being exceeded in a fixed time period. Here, we present the first known example of a direct assessment of the key drivers on flood magnitude utilising a bottom-up impact assessment. We focus our attention on the sensitivity of flood risk to changes in three key flood controlling factors: rainfall intensity, rainfall arrival frequency and rainfall losses. We separate changes in rainfall into intensity and arrival frequency using a two-step Kappa approach (O’Shea et al., 2023 ) to account for changes in the thermodynamic drivers, which impact rainfall intensity, and dynamic drivers that change regional weather systems, which impact the arrival frequency of storms (O’Shea et al., 2024; Schlef et al., 2018 ). We use an event-based model to derive flood quantiles from probabilistic rainfalls within a joint probability framework that considers the natural variability in rainfall factors and losses (Kuczera et al., 2017, 2006; Nathan and Ball, 2019; Nathan and Weinmann, 2019 ). By doing so we are able to explore the interactions between changes in rainfall intensity, rainfall frequency, and rainfall losses to understand the drivers of altered flood risk for both frequent (1 in 5 AEP) and rare (1 in 50 AEP) events under climate change. We demonstrate our approach for two case study catchments, one in tropical northern Australia and one in temperate south eastern Australia to enable comparison between the two differing climates.  2 Catchment representation 2.1 Data 2.1.1 Catchment selection The details of the two regional Australian catchments selected for this study are summarised in Table 1   with locations shown in Fig. 1  . One catchment, located in temperate south-eastern Australia (temperate catchment), was selected as projected soil moisture decreases in the catchment have been found to modulate rainfall increases leading to a decreased flood risk for more frequent AEPs and increasing flood risk for rarer AEPs (Wasko et al., 2023 ). The second catchment is located in tropical northern Australia (tropical catchment), where soil moisture is projected to increase under some future scenarios (Ho et al., 2023 ). These two catchments were deemed suitable for our analysis as they are:• Part of the Australian Bureau of Meteorology’s Hydrologic Reference Stations (HRS) network. The HRS is a collection of Australian streamflow gauges, selected for their history of minimal stream flow regulation, water extraction and land use change, making them suitable for assessing long-term climate-induced changes in the streamflow regime (Bureau of Meteorology, 2020 ).  • Part of the subset of 167 catchments from the HRS for which Ho et al. (2023)  projected rainfall losses for four different emission scenario pathways and time horizons. In order for Ho et al. (2023)  to project rainfall losses for these catchments, they were required to have suitable quality hourly rainfall and streamflow data to allow construction of an event-based model and demonstrate a statistically significant relationship between rainfall losses and catchment antecedent soil moisture.  • Close to 100 km2  in area, so that the critical duration (the storm duration that leads to the largest flood peak) is close to 24 h.     2.1.2 Rainfall and streamflow data A daily rainfall timeseries of catchment average rainfall was obtained for each catchment from the Australian Gridded Climate Data (formerly Australia Water Availability Project, (Jones et al., 2009 )), which covers Australia on a 0.05° × 0.05° resolution. This daily catchment rainfall data was used for two purposes:1. As the basis for selecting large rainfall events, which were used to calibrate the routing parameters of the event-based model.  2. For deriving the rainfall frequency curves used in the joint probability modelling framework (Section 2.3.1)    For each catchment, instantaneous and daily gauged volumetric streamflow was obtained as part of the HRS dataset (Bureau of Meteorology, 2020 ). To calibrate the routing parameters of each catchment model we make use of an existing dataset of rainfall-runoff events. Ho et al. (2023)  collected paired hourly rainfall and streamflow data for significant rainfall runoff events for all 467 catchments in the HRS network. Events were selected on the basis of three-day precipitation. Precipitation rather than streamflow was used to select events to avoid biasing the sample of events to those with high antecedent moisture and low losses, as these conditions often cause the largest streamflow. This event dataset was derived using the same rainfall and streamflow data described above. Daily rainfall was disaggregated to an hourly timestep using available pluviograph data and matched with the corresponding streamflow data.   2.2 Model description A semi-distributed storage routing model was developed for each case study catchment in which the flood hydrograph is computed by routing storm runoff through a model representing the storage in the catchment. This required construction of a node-link representation of each catchment, as shown in Fig. 1 . Such a modelling approach is the de facto industry standard in Australia and is described in detail in Laurenson and Mein (1995)  and Laurenson et al. (2010) . As shown in Fig. 2  , the important components of the model are as follows, with greater detail provided in Appendix A :• A storm is characterised by a single rainfall depth (or quantile) that is disaggregated by a temporal pattern. Given the small size of catchments considered rainfall is considered spatially uniform.  • Rainfall is partitioned into storm runoff and losses using the initial loss continuing loss model (ILCL), which has two parameters: initial loss (IL   ) and continuing loss (CL   ).  • Storm runoff is routed through a series conceptual storage based on a non-linear power law, with r c    , an empirical coefficient representative of the catchment the only parameter requiring calibration.    The value r c     for each catchment was calibrated to individual flood events using paired hourly rainfall and streamflow data collected by Ho et al. (2023) . r c     and loss parameters IL    and CL    were adjusted to obtain a good match between the observed and simulated streamflow hydrographs, where emphasis was given to ensuring that the modelled hydrograph matched both the timing and magnitude of the peak. The median value of r c     obtained by calibration of the 10 largest events available was adopted for subsequent analysis. Estimating this routing parameter using the largest events was preferred, given the focus on estimating large floods (O’Shea et al., 2021 ). Generally good calibrations were obtained across all flood events with Nash Sutcliffe Efficiencies (Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ) values ranging between 0.6 and 1.  2.3 Flood frequency curve calibration We apply a joint probability approach to simulate catchment flood frequency curves using probabilistic rainfalls. A flood is produced by a combination of many flood producing factors. For example, a large flood peak of the same magnitude could result from either a moderate rainfall on a wet catchment or a large rainfall on a dry catchment (Ivancic and Shaw, 2015 ). Therefore, assuming that a flood peak has the same AEP as the causative rainfall runs the risk of introducing bias into flood probability quantile estimations (Kuczera et al., 2006; Nathan and Weinmann, 2019 ). Here, to estimate the flood frequency curve a joint probability approach was used that mimics the variability of different flood producing factors by sampling each from its own probability distribution (Kuczera et al., 2006; Nathan and Weinmann, 2019 ) to ensure unbiased estimates of flood quantiles. To explore the joint probability of important flood drivers a Monte Carlo sampling framework, summarised in Fig. 3  , was employed whereby flood drivers were stochastically sampled and used to estimate flood peaks thousands of times. For each modelled flood event the following flood drivers were sampled:1. The rainfall quantile (i.e. catchment rainfall depth), which was sampled from the catchment rainfall frequency curve modelled using a two-step Kappa approach fitted to the historic 24 h rainfall maxima. (The two-step Kappa approach involves fitting a coupled Generalised Pareto (GPA) distribution to rainfall intensity and a Binomial distribution for rainfall arrival frequency. See O’Shea et al. (2023)  for more details.);  2. The rainfall temporal pattern, which was randomly sampled from an ensemble of 10 storm patterns; and  3. The initial loss, which was sampled from a non-parametric distribution.    The derivation of each of the three sampling distributions are detailed in Appendix B . Catchment rainfall quantiles were sampled using a stratified approach to allow for computationally efficient exploration of the right-hand tail of the rainfall frequency curve. The three flood drivers were considered to be independent when sampling. The simulated flood frequency curve was calculated from the thousands of simulated flood peaks using the total probability theorem (Haan, 1974 ). Losses (IL    and CL   ) were adjusted (calibrated) to obtain a match between the simulated flood frequency curve and the historic flood frequency curve. This process closely follows existing design guidelines, details of which can be found in Nathan and Weinmann (2019) . The analysis was limited to floods produced from 24 h rainfalls, noting that for rural Australian catchments around 100 km2  such as those considered here, 24 h is typically close to the critical duration (i.e. the storm duration that produces the largest flood peak). A sensitivity test performed in the tropical catchment found that use of rainfalls between 18 and 48 h durations did not lead to material change in the simulated flood frequency curve. A historic flood frequency curve was derived from gauged streamflow for both catchments. This involved extracting a series of annual maxima-based on water years, defined as starting in the month with the lowest mean annual flow in the observed record. A Generalised Extreme Value (GEV) distribution was then fitted to the annual maxima using L-moments (Hosking and Wallis, 1997 ). A parametric bootstrap was performed in order to generate confidence limits for the quantile estimates (Efron and Tibshirani, 1993 ).   3 Bottom-up impact assessment Fig. 4   outlines the procedure undertaken to perform the bottom-up impact assessment. As outlined in Section 1  we chose to focus on the sensitivity of flood peaks to changes in three key flood drivers: rainfall intensity, rainfall arrival frequency, and losses. Section 3.1  describes the process of producing a response surface, which highlights the sensitivity of flood peaks to changes in these flood drivers. Section 3.2  describes the derivation of climate model projections of flood drivers, which are then overlaid on the response surface to indicate possible futures. 3.1 Response surfaces To produce response surfaces, the calibrated flood model described above was run multiple times with different perturbations of three different flood controlling factors (i.e. stress tested):1. Rainfall intensity: changes that notionally represent the thermodynamics drivers of extreme rainfall changes (i.e., related to temperature change);  2. Rainfall arrival frequency: changes that notionally represent changes in atmospheric dynamics (i.e., related to changes in atmospheric circulation responsible for regional weather systems); and  3. Losses: here conceptualised as initial loss (the rainfall absorbed by the catchment prior to a catchment runoff response) and continuing loss (the rainfall absorbed by the catchment after the runoff response).    These factors were perturbed to create a wide range of model simulations, each relating to different combinations of perturbed inputs. We then compared estimates in modelled flood peaks from the multiple runs with the model calibrated to the historic flood frequency curve (i.e. no perturbation). Response surfaces showing change in flood peaks as a function of changes in the rainfall intensity, rainfall arrival frequency, and losses were produced. Each of the three flood controlling factors was perturbed as follows:1. Rainfall intensity was perturbed by multiplying the quantile function of the GPA intensity model within the two-step Kappa model by a factor denoted by percentage change A %    , an approach that achieves the same outcome as multiplying the location and scale parameters of the GPA by this same factor.  2. Rainfall arrival frequency was perturbed within the two-step Kappa model previously fitted to historic data by multiplying the Binomial parameter n    within the two-step Kappa model by a factor denoted by percentage change B %    , whilst leaving the Binomial parameter p    constant. We note that while Binomial parameter n    should theoretically be an integer, the two-step Kappa approach used here allows for non-integer values of n    (O’Shea et al., 2023 ) (see Appendix B  for further details).  3. Initial loss and continuing loss are both perturbed by the same factor C %        For each perturbation factor we independently consider changes between - 40  %    and 40  %    at a spacing of 5  %   , i.e. A %  ,  B %  ,  C %  ∈ { - 40  % , - 35  % , ⋯ ,  35  % ,  40  % }    . To calculate the percentage change in flood peak of Δ Q X , i %      as a result of perturbing model inputs we use the following formula:(1) Δ Q X , i %   = Q X , i   - Q X , 0    Q X , 0    × 100 1      where Q X , i      represents peak flow with an annual exceedance probability of 1 in X using the perturbed climate inputs, with i    denoting a unique combination of change factors A %  ,  B %     and C %    . Q X , 0      represents peak flow with the same AEP using historic inputs (i.e. no perturbation). The same principle is used to calculate percentage change in rainfall quantiles.  3.2 Climate model projections Projections were obtained from the Bureau of Meteorology’s National Hydrological Projections service (part of the Australian Water Outlook, AWO), which includes projections of precipitation as well as soil moisture (Wilson et al., 2022 ) modelled using the Australian Water Resource Assessment Landscape model (AWRA-L). The AWO considered an ensemble of 16 downscaled and bias corrected General Circulation Models (GCMs) from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5). Two emissions pathways were considered: a very high emissions pathway RCP8.5 and an intermediate emissions pathway RCP4.5, which respectively correspond to radiative forcing of greater than 8.5 W/m2  and approximately 4.5 W/m2  for the year 2100 (Meinshausen et al., 2011; van Vuuren et al., 2011 ). Here we consider projections for two nominal future time horizons: 2036–2065 (centered on 2050) and 2070–2099 (centered on 2085). These periods are assumed to be quasi-stationary (Schlef et al., 2023 ) and the change occurring under these periods is assessed relative to a baseline period from 1976 to 2005 (herein referred to historic baseline). These emission scenarios and time horizons were selected to be consistent with projections of IL    and CL    by Ho et al. (2023) . We adopted a 16-member set of climate projections (herein referred to as the “GCM ensemble”) from the National Hydrologic Projections dataset derived using four GCMs and four downscaling procedures (Peter et al., 2023; Srikanthan et al., 2022 ). The four GCMs used were ACCESS 1-0, CNRM-CM5, GFDL-ESM2M and MIRCO5, with a single run (r1i1p1f1) used for each. These models were selected based on three factors: 1) representation of processes important for Australian climate, 2) representation of uncertainty present in the entire suite of CMIP5 GCMs, and 3) availability of daily outputs need to run the AWRA-L model. Climate outputs from each of the four GCMs were bias corrected and downscaled using four different approaches giving an ensemble of 16 members. Three statistical bias correction methods were used: ISMIP2b (Hempel et al., 2013 ), MRNBC (Mehrotra et al., 2018; Mehrotra and Sharma, 2015 ) and QME (Dowdy, 2019 ). A fourth dynamic downscaling method using the CCAM-ISMMIP2b utilised the regional climate model CCAM (Mcgregor and Dix, 2001 ) and the ISMIP2b bias correction method. Hydrological projections for Australia from the more recent CMIP6 experiment are still being prepared (Grose et al., 2023 ) however, initial evaluation suggests that rainfall projections are similar to CMIP5 (Grose et al., 2020 ) and therefore the choice of CMIP should not materially affect the results presented here. To estimate the projected change in rainfall intensity for the GCM ensemble members we adopt a fixed temperature scaling rate based on global average temperature. We adopted this approach rather than using catchment specific precipitation intensity data directly from the GCM ensemble as GCMs are known to poorly reproduce rainfall extremes (François et al., 2019; Kendon et al., 2017 ) and because catchment-specific estimates of intensity change can potentially be influenced by dynamic factors, which we wish to capture in the arrival frequency only. The percentage change in precipitation for a given emissions scenario and time horizon P T , %      is expressed as:(2) P T , %   = P 0  1 + α    Δ T    P 0   - 1    × 100 1  = 100 × ( 1 + α     Δ T   - 1 )      where P 0     represents rainfall intensity in the historic baseline period (which drops out of the equation); α    is the scaling rate, which is assumed to be 8 %/°C, which reflects the median increase in 24 h extreme rainfalls for Australia (Wasko et al., 2024 ); Δ T = T T  - T 0     is the difference in global average temperature between the climate scenario of interest and the historic baseline period. Using this approach the changes in rainfall intensity are assumed to be constant across AEPs. The change in rainfall arrival frequency is estimated by considering the change in the number of exceedances of rain days above 10 mm (i.e. the commonly used R 10     mm index). The percentage change in precipitation for a given emissions scenario and time horizon AF  T , %      is then expressed as:(3) AF  T , %   = R 10 , T   R 10 , 0    - 1    × 100 1      where R 10 , T      and R 10 , 0      are respectively the number of rain days above 10 mm in the 30-year periods for the climate scenario of interest and the historic baseline. Ho et al. (2023)  projected IL    and CL    using soil moisture projections from the Australian Bureau of Meteorology’s National Hydrological Projections dataset (Srikanthan et al., 2022; Wilson et al., 2022 ). These soil moisture projections were derived from relationship between the IL    and CL    and the soil moisture from AWRA-L, which is a semi-distributed hydrologic model of the Australian continent used to estimate surface, shallow, and deep soil moisture stores (Frost et al., 2018 ). Projections for IL    and CL    were then obtained from projections of soil moisture in the AWO whereby projections of precipitation and PET are used to drive AWRA-L to produce projections of soil moisture across the continent.   4 Results 4.1 Model calibration We begin by presenting the results of the calibration to the flood frequency curves for each of the catchments in Fig. 5  . For each catchment loss parameters I L m     (which refers to the median value of initial loss in the non-parametric sampling distribution) and CL    were calibrated in order to match the flood frequency curves derived using the Monte Carlo joint probability modelling framework and the flood frequency curve derived using gauged streamflow data. A reasonable match was obtained between the simulated and historic flood frequency curves, with the simulated curve sitting comfortably within the range of the 5th and 95th% confidence limits of the historic curve for AEPs relevant to the bottom-up simulation (1 in 5 AEP to 1 in 50 AEP). The parameters used to produce these curves are summarised in Table 2  . The lower value of r c     suggests the temperate catchment has a flashier runoff response than the tropical catchment. Higher I L m     in the tropical catchment suggests that less rain is required for runoff to commence than in the temperate catchment, which may be the result of higher typical antecedent moisture conditions.  4.2 Projections of flood drivers from GCMs 4.2.1 Projections in rainfall intensity Table 3   shows projected changes in rainfall intensity for the four GCMs considered for both RCP 4.5 and 8.5 for the two 30-year periods centred on 2050 and 2085 (i.e. 2036–2065 and 2070–2099 respectively). We see that for a given future period (i.e. 2050) the projected intensity increases as we move from RCP4.5 to the more emissions-intensive RCP8.5. We also see that for a given emissions pathway the projected intensity increases as we move further into the future, in line with global temperature projections. The differences between the estimates of intensity change obtained from the four GCMs increase with time, with the greatest spread seen under RCP8.5 in 2085.  4.2.2 Projections in rainfall arrival frequency Fig. 6   shows projected changes in the number of independent exceedances of 10 mm of rainfall in the daily rainfall time series (i.e. the R10 mm metric) for both catchments across the 16-member ensemble for RCP 4.5 and 8.5 for the two 30-year periods centred on 2050 and 2085. Generally, decreasing trends in R10 mm can be seen for both catchments. The magnitude of this negative trend tends to increase when moving to more intensive emissions scenarios from RCP4.5 to RCP8.5 and projections that are further into the future. The median change in R10 mm for the tropical catchment is −2.1 % for RCP 4.5 2050 and −7.0 % for RCP8.5 2085 and for the temperate catchment −4.5 % for RCP 4.5 2050 and −13.6 % for RCP8.5 2085. However, there is some disagreement in the sign of change with a small number of ensemble members projecting a slight positive trend in R10 mm. Typically, the variability in R10 mm projections (i.e. spread of the boxplots) increases as we project further into the future.  4.2.3 Projected losses The projected change in losses are shown in Fig. 7   for the initial loss (top) and continuing loss (bottom) parameters for the tropical (left) and temperate (right) catchments. There is a general trend of increasing losses, with the magnitude of this trend becoming greater with more intensive emission scenarios and time horizons further into the future. For the temperate catchment, the median change from the ensemble is 5.6 % for IL    and 6.2 % for CL    under RCP 4.5 2050, and 12.6 % for IL    14.1 % for CL    under RCP8.5 2085. The only example of median decreasing losses is for the tropical catchment under RCP 4.5 2050. Here, median losses are projected to decrease slightly (−0.23 % for IL    and −0.85 % for CL   ), with more than 50 % of ensemble members projecting a decrease. This behaviour agrees with soil moisture trends for this area showing a shift to wetter conditions for this scenario (Ho et al., 2023 ). Losses are expected to increase for the tropical catchment by 3.10 % for IL    and 12.17 % for CL    under RCP 8.5 2085. For scenarios with a median increasing trend, there is some disagreement in the direction of change within the ensemble, though the number of ensemble members that project a decrease in losses decreases as we move to more emissions intensive scenarios and project further into the future. For the tropical catchment, the variability increases significantly between the 16 ensemble members when moving from 2050 to 2085 (i.e. the spread is greater), most notably for CL   . However, for the temperate catchment, the variability between 2050 and 2085 is similar.   4.3 Bottom-up impact assessment 4.3.1 Changes in rainfall intensity and arrival frequency Before presenting the response surfaces for the flood quantile, we first present the response surfaces for the 24 h burst rainfall quantile (Fig. 8  ). The percentage change in burst quantile (relative to the historic observed baseline) is plotted as a function of change in rainfall intensity and arrival frequency. Response surfaces are shown for both the tropical catchment (top) and temperate catchment (bottom) for the 1 in 5 AEP (left) and 1 in 50 AEP (right) events. For both catchments, the response surfaces show that 24 h rainfall bursts are more sensitive to an incremental change in rainfall intensity than arrival frequency. For example, a 10 % increase in rainfall intensity leads to a greater increase in rainfall burst compared with a 10 % increase in rainfall arrival frequency on all four surfaces. The tropical catchment demonstrates a greater sensitivity to an incremental change in rainfall arrival frequency than the temperate catchment. This can be attributed to the sign of the Kappa shape parameter, k   , in each catchment (k = 0.29    for tropical and k = - 0.12    for temperate), with the positive value of k    meaning that changes in mean arrival frequency result in larger changes in the Kappa location and scale parameter (see Equation (B.4) . Response surfaces for the 1 in 5 AEP and 1 in 50 AEP events for each catchment are more or less identical, with the more frequent 1 in 5 AEP event demonstrating a slight increased sensitive to rainfall arrival frequency than the 1 in 50 AEP event. Symbols overlaid on the response surfaces demonstrate the variability in projected change in rainfall intensity and arrival frequency from the GCM ensemble. Almost all projected futures across the four response surfaces project an increase in 24 h burst quantiles (except for one ensemble member in the tropical catchment for RCP8.5 2050 for the 1 in 5 AEP event). This suggests that increases in rainfall intensity are likely to outweigh decreases in arrival frequency for rainfall extremes in these two catchments. This median increase of the ensemble is slightly greater for the 1 in 50 AEP event in both catchments, owning to the greater sensitivity of the 1 in 5 AEP event to decreasing arrival frequency. Intuitively, quantile increases are larger for more intense emissions pathways and projections further into the future, with RCP 8.5 2085 displaying the largest projected increases. To isolate the impact of the changes in rainfall presented in Fig. 8  on flood peak, Fig. 9   shows response surfaces for change in flood peaks (% − relative to the historic observed baseline) as a function of change in rainfall intensity and arrival frequency, while losses are held constant. As for Fig. 8 , response surfaces are shown for both the tropical catchment (top) and temperate catchment (bottom) for the 1 in 5 AEP (left) and 1 in 50 AEP (right) events. Sensitivities noted for the changes in rainfall (Fig. 8 ) translate to flood peaks (Fig. 9 ), with changes in rainfall intensity leading to greater magnitude changes in flood peaks than the same percentage change in arrival frequency, and the tropical catchment showing greater sensitivity to arrival frequency then the temperate catchment. In contrast, flood peaks in the temperate catchment demonstrates greater sensitivity to changes in rainfall intensity than the tropical catchment. This can be seen as a 50 % or greater increase in flood peak for a wider range of combinations grid cells on the response surface for the temperate catchment. Flood peaks for the 1 in 5 AEP for each catchment appear more sensitive to changes in rainfall than the 1 in 50 AEP event as the number of grid cells with 50 % or greater increase in flood peaks (dark blue shading) is greatest for the 1 in 5 AEP event for each catchment. Symbols overlaid on the response surfaces demonstrate the variability in projected change in rainfall intensity and arrival frequency from the GCM ensemble. As per rainfall burst depths in Fig. 8 , here we see that increases in rainfall intensity are likely to outweigh decreases in arrival frequency when considering flood peaks in these two catchments if changes in losses are not considered. A trend of increasing flood peaks emerges as we projected further forward in time and move to more emissions-intensive scenarios with the RCP8.5 2085 showing the greatest increases in flood peaks.  4.3.2 Changes in rainfall intensity and losses Fig. 10   shows response surfaces for change in flood peaks as per Fig. 9 , except here changes in flood peak are shown as a function of changes in rainfall intensity (y-axis) and losses (x-axis), while arrival frequency is held constant. In order to display change in losses from each GCM ensemble member on a single axis the average of projected changes in initial and continuing losses is used. Comparing the response surfaces of the two catchments, flood peaks in the temperate catchment display significantly more sensitivity to changes in losses than the tropical catchment, with a fixed percentage change in losses resulting in significantly more change in flood peaks for the temperate catchment. The more frequent 1 in 5 AEP event displays greater sensitivity to losses than the rarer 1 in 50 AEP event for both catchments. Similar to Fig. 9 , the temperate catchment again displays greater sensitivity to changes in intensity than the tropical catchment. This, combined with the greater sensitivity to losses, indicates that the temperate catchment is more sensitive to changes in the flood drivers than the tropical catchment, with the greatest sensitivity seen in the 1 in 5 AEP event. The range of projections from the bias corrected GCM ensemble demonstrates the degree of uncertainty in projected flood response for the two catchments. For the tropical catchment, increases in flood peak are projected for all ensemble members, varying from nearly 0 % to >50 % for both in the 1 in 5 and 1 in 50 AEP events. For the temperate catchment there is a small number of ensemble members that project decreases in the 1 in 5 AEP flood peaks (1 member for RCP4.5 2050 and 2085 and 2 members for RCP8.5 2050); all members suggest that the flood peak will increase for the 1 in 50 AEP event. For both catchments, flood peaks are expected to increase with increasing emissions intensity and when projecting further into the future, with RCP8.5 in 2085 demonstrating the largest projected increases in flood peak for all four surfaces. However, there is a large amount of uncertainty in the magnitude of this change. For example, for RCP8.5 2085 changes in the flood peak are projected anywhere from 10 % to more than 50 % for the temperate catchment.  4.3.3 Changes in rainfall arrival frequency and losses Fig. 11   shows response surfaces for change in flood peaks as per Figs. 9 and 10 , except here changes in flood peak are a function of changes in rainfall arrival frequency (y-axis) and losses (x-axis), with rainfall intensity held constant. The same sensitivities for rainfall arrival frequency and losses noted in Figs. 9 and 10  are again apparent, where changes flood peaks in the temperate catchment are more sensitive to changes in losses, and changes in flood peaks in the tropical catchment are more sensitive to arrival frequency. There is strong negative correlation between GCM ensemble projections of changes in arrival frequency and changes in losses, particularly for the temperate catchment. This suggests that decreases in the frequency of large heavy rain days in GCM rainfalls are a major driver for projected decreases in soil moisture and the resultant increases in losses. The majority of projections from the GCM ensemble suggest that we would expect to see a decrease in flood peaks if only changes in arrival frequency and losses are considered. The projected decreases in flood peak are largest for the 1 in 5 AEP event for each catchment. Decreases are larger for the temperate catchment than the tropical catchment, owing to the temperate catchment being more sensitivity to losses.  4.3.4 Combined changes in rainfall factors and losses Fig. 12   shows response surfaces for change in flood peaks in a similar form to the previous sections, but here changes in flood peak are a function of changes in the 24 h rainfall quantile (y-axis), which accounts for the combined impacts of changes in both rainfall intensity and frequency, and losses (x-axis). The projections overlain from the GCM ensemble represent the expected percentage change in 24 h rainfall quantiles when combining projected changes in both intensity and arrival frequency into the two-step Kappa model (with the 1 in X AEP rainfall plotted on the 1 in X AEP flood peaks response surface). As noted in Fig. 8 , the median projected increase in 24 h rainfall quantiles across the GCM ensemble is slightly greater for in the 1 in 50 AEP event the 1 in 5 AEP event for both catchments. Similar to Fig. 10 , Fig. 12  shows rainfall intensity is the dominant driver of change in terms of rainfall processes considered here, though there is reduction in flood peaks projected for GCM ensemble member’s where the change in arrival frequency is negative. For the tropical catchment all ensemble members project increased flood peaks except for RCP4.5 2050 where three GCMs for the 1 in 5 AEP event and one GCM for the 1 in 50 AEP event project a decrease. One ensemble member also suggests no change for both AEP events under RCP8.5 2050. Meanwhile for the temperate catchment nine members (14 %) of the GCM ensemble project a decrease in flood peak for the 1 in 5 AEP event, with at least one ensemble from each scenario projecting a decrease. The most projected decreases are for the RCP4.5 2050 scenario where four GCM ensemble members (25 %) project decreases. The same four RCP4.5 2050 ensemble members project a decrease in flood risk for the 1 in 50 AEP event, while ensemble members for all other scenarios project an increase in risk. The largest projected increase in flood risk is seen under RCP8.5 in 2085, but with a large degree of variability. For the tropical catchment, the projected change in flood peak is between 0 and 45 % for the 1 in 5 AEP event and 5–40 % for 1 in 50 AEP event. Similarly, projections in the change in flood peak in temperate catchment ranges from −10 % to more than 50 % for 1 in 5 AEP, and from 10 % to more than 50 % for the 1 in 50 event.    5 Discussion 5.1 Key inferences about changes to flood risk From our case study catchments, there are a number of general inferences about catchment responses to flooding under climate change that can be inferred. Across the two catchments, projected increases in rainfall quantiles are expected to drive increases in flood risk for both frequent and rare flood events. This increase is partially offset by median decreases in losses under most climate scenarios, with a small number of the GCM ensemble indicating that flood peaks would decrease, with this decrease most apparent for the 1 in 5 AEP (frequent) flood event in the temperate catchment. This is consistent with the findings of studies spanning many regions across the world that more frequent flood peaks show decreasing trends driven by decreasing antecedent soil moisture and therefore higher losses, while larger flood peaks tend to increase, driven by increases in rainfall factors that outweigh the changes in catchment response (Brunner et al., 2021; Wasko et al., 2023, 2021a ). Strong increases in rainfall intensity (related to thermodynamic drivers) are primarily responsible for the increases in rainfall quantiles that are driving increases in flood risk. Rainfall quantiles were shown to increase for nearly all GCM ensemble members despite decreases in storm arrival frequency (related to dynamic drivers) in the majority of the ensemble (Fig. 8 ). The median projected increase in rainfall quantiles from the GCM ensemble is greater for the 1 in 50 AEP event than the 1 in 5 AEP event, due to the greater sensitivity of the more frequent event to changes in arrival frequency. This aligns with studies showing that increases in rainfall quantiles become greater with increasing rarity (Gründemann et al., 2022; Jayaweera et al., 2023 ). Overall, frequent flood peaks, typically driven by moderate rainfalls, are more sensitive to changes in losses. This is seen when comparing the 1 in 5 AEP to the 1 in 50 AEP response surface in each catchment and when comparing the wetter tropical catchment to the drier temperate catchment (the 1 in 50 AEP rainfall is 443 mm for the tropical catchment and 125 mm for the temperate catchment). This aligns with the findings of Grillakis et al. (2016)  who demonstrated that small flood peaks are more sensitive to changes in initial moisture than large flood peaks, and Bertola et al. (2021)  who found that in southern Europe, antecedent moisture was the most important driver for small floods, while both rainfall and soil moisture were important for larger floods. The consequence of this is that changes in losses with climate change are more important when understanding changes in frequent floods and drier catchments. Curiously, the largest expected increases in flood peak percentiles are for the temperate catchment and not the tropical catchment, despite the greater modulating effect of increasing losses in the temperate catchment. We attribute this to the fact that the losses represent a greater proportion of rainfall in the temperate catchment compared to the tropical one, and this means the temperate catchment is more sensitive to the increases in rainfall intensity, which are driving increases in flood risk. This suggests that catchments where losses represent a large proportion of rainfall are more sensitive to future increases in rainfall if the increases in rainfalls outweigh any decreases in losses.  5.2 Future considerations Future bottom-up assessments may benefit from incorporating other dimensions of non-stationarity in flood drivers. For example, changes in the temporal (Visser et al., 2023; Wasko and Sharma, 2015 ) and spatial distribution (Wasko et al., 2016 ) of extreme rainfalls have been studied in the literature and are likely to impact flood peaks. Additionally we only focused on changes in median losses, though changes in the variability of losses have also been observed (Ho et al., 2023 ) and could be considered. Other flood metrics, besides changes in flood peaks used in this study, could be considered. An example of a salient metric is flood volume as this is a key consideration in the design of water supply storages. Alternatively, consultation with flood risk managers and other stakeholders could be used to identify indicators of flood risk that are fit for purpose and enable effective decision making (Knighton et al., 2018 ). For example, the probability of a specified flood threshold being exceeded in a fixed time window (Knighton et al., 2017 ), or using flood depths as an indicator of economic damage (Steinschneider et al., 2015 ). A large amount of uncertainty in projections in flood controlling factors remains. Here we applied a scaling approach based on global temperature to estimate changes in rainfall intensity to separate out the changes in rainfall intensity and rainfall frequency. An alternative could be to use finer resolution Regional Climate Models as these may lead to more reliable projections of rainfall extremes, particularly sub daily extremes (Kendon et al., 2017 ), due to their ability to resolve convective processes, but these are currently unavailable across Australia (Grose et al., 2023 ). Alternatively, the temperature scaling approach used here could be adapted to consider uncertainty in scaling rates (e.g. Wasko et al., 2024 ), but this would need to consider changes in dynamic drivers as well, or else other atmospheric covariates could be considered, for example atmospheric moisture (Kim et al., 2022; Roderick et al., 2020, 2019 ). There is also large variation in projected losses, owing to uncertainty in the direction and magnitude of soil moisture projections, which results from uncertainty in future rainfall patterns (we note the strong correlation between change in losses and heavy rain days observed in Fig. 12 ) as well as evapotranspiration and catchment response (Stephens et al., 2021 ). Ultimately the presence of these uncertainties highlights the value in undertaking bottom-up climate assessments for flood risk. Bottom-up assessments provide a conceptually direct (and computationally efficient) means of investigating the impact of changes in flood drivers and the consequent implications for flood risks in a manner that can be compared directly to estimates used for design and planning purposes.   6 Conclusion In this manuscript we present for the first time a bottom-up climate change assessment for flood magnitude that uses an event-based modelling framework with non-stationary rainfalls and losses. While examples of bottom-up assessments of flood risk are present in the literature these have mostly relied on continuous simulation models, which implicitly, rather than explicitly, model the drivers of flood risk (e.g., soil moisture) through changes in variables such as the seasonality of rainfall and evapotranspiration. This study is the first to attempt to directly understand how changes in flood drivers will influence changes in the flood peak. This approach also allows the investigation and communication of the deep uncertainties associated with catchment response to help flood risk managers make informed decisions about future design and mitigation works. In particular, we believe this event-based modelling approach to bottom-up assessments offers the following advantages:1. Event-based models are widely used in practice for estimation of flood risk in many countries. Therefore, approaches to climate change assessments using these techniques face fewer barriers to adoption.  2. Event-based approaches are more easily tailored to focus on changes in the flood controlling factors that drive large floods. For example, here we found that the case study catchments were most vulnerable to changes in extreme rainfall intensity. In contrast, bottom-up assessments based on continuous simulation must perturb the whole rainfall regime and in doing so may divert attention away from key flood controlling factors, obscuring their impacts.  3. Exogenously specifying catchment initial conditions in an event-based model through the representation of losses means that we can explicitly analyse the vulnerability of the catchment to changes in losses, as well as the joint interaction of changes in losses and changes in rainfalls drivers. Due to implicit soil-moisture accounting of losses in continuously simulation models, the impact on losses is not as clearly represented, and hence such sensitivity is difficult to test directly as they are here.    We demonstrated the utility of our methodology by stress testing how flood peaks will change in two small regional Australian catchments (one temperate and one tropical) in response to both changes in dynamic and thermodynamic drivers of extreme rainfalls as well as changes in rainfall losses. We show that increases in rainfall quantiles are projected to drive an increase in flood magnitudes under most future scenarios despite the dampening impact of decreasing storm arrival frequency and decreasing losses. Rainfall quantiles are projected to increase due to increases in rainfall intensity, despite being partially offset by a decrease in the arrival frequency in some ensemble members. Flood peaks are shown to be most sensitive to changes in losses for more frequent events and in drier catchments (or more precisely catchments in which losses are an appreciable proportion of the incident rainfalls). A small number of the GCM ensemble members imply flood peaks will decrease in future scenarios: this was most pronounced for the 1 in 5 AEP temperate catchment where 14 % of ensemble members indicated a decrease in future flood peaks. Despite large agreement on the direction of change, we found large variability in the expected magnitude of change with flood peaks projected to increase between 0 to 45 % for the tropical catchment and between −10 to >50 % for the temperate catchment under RCP8.5 in 2085 (noting that this varied with AEP). The large variability in projected flood peaks highlights the deep uncertainty associated with projecting flood risk under climate change. We believe this variability demonstrates the utility of using bottom-up approaches to flood risk managers seeking to better understand and communicate the deep uncertainty associated with climate change. Future efforts to undertake bottom-up approaches could consider changes in other drivers of flooding such as changes in rainfall temporal and spatial patterns. Ultimately, our intention in demonstrating this methodology for applying event-based models in a bottom-up framework is to encourage the adoption of bottom-up climate change assessments in practical flood estimation applications. We hope these modelling techniques can be applied in future scientific studies aimed at understanding the key drivers of, and impacts on, changes in flood risk.
1 Introduction Flooding levies a substantial economic burden on communities, leading to the degradation of infrastructure and agriculture, and in extreme cases, fatalities (Allaire, 2018 ). Globally, in 2019 alone, floods were responsible for nearly $45.9 billion in economic losses and almost 4,500 deaths (World Resources Institute, 2020 ). Understanding the behavior of extreme flood events is distinct challenges of applied hydrology, with hydrological models serving as one of the pivotal tools for addressing this challenge. The Xin'anjiang model is currently the most popular model for operational flood forecasting in China (Zhao,1992; Zhao et al., 2023 ). It has been employed in the China National Flood Forecasting System (World Meteorological Organization, 2011 ) and adopted by hydrological departments at various administrative levels. Since its publication, the Xin'anjiang model has garnered widespread attention from hydrologists. Related studies include improving the model structure (Yao et al, 2014; Zang et al, 2021 ), analyzing parameter sensitivity (Hu et al, 2019 ), optimizing model parameters (Lü et al, 2013; Zhou et al, 2016 ), regionalizing model parameters (Gong et al, 2021; Qi et al, 2021 ), and performing real-time error correction (Liang et al, 2021; Wang et al, 2022 ). In hydrological model simulation, a viable strategy for diminishing uncertainties is the correction of the model states or parameters. This is particularly pivotal for operational flood forecasting as it mitigates the accumulation of preceding errors in the initial conditions at the commencement of the forecast, a factor demonstrated to be a predominant source of uncertainty at the start of the forecast period (Shukla & Lettenmaier, 2011; Yossef et al, 2013; Thiboult et al, 2016 ). Enhancing the reliability and reducing the uncertainty of hydrological forecasts can be achieved by recursively improving the initial conditions. A widely adopted strategy for refining initial conditions is the employment of data assimilation, a feedback mechanism or update protocol that amalgamates model estimations with available real-world observations (Reichle, 2008; Liu et al., 2012; Piazzi et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2023 ). This assimilation process, also referred to in some studies as hydrological data assimilation (Walker & Houser, 2005; Clark et al., 2008 ). Within the scope of hydrologic data assimilation, researchers employ observational data derived either from satellite remote sensing (typically soil moisture, evapotranspiration, etc.) (e.g. Zhang et al., 2009; Pezij et al., 2019; Gavahi et al., 2020 ) or from discharge observations (e.g. Clark et al., 2008; Rakovec et al., 2012; Mazzoleni et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2020 ). Practically, discharge observations tend to be a more utilitarian choice due to its direct relevance to flood forecasting. It provides a holistic hydrological overview of the catchment area, with on-site discharge data measurements being notably reliable. Depending on the temporal extent of the assimilated observations, data assimilation techniques can be delineated into either synchronous or asynchronous methods, alternatively termed as three-dimensional (3-D) or four-dimensional (4-D) methods (Rakovec et al., 2015 ). Synchronous methods assimilate observations which correspond to the time of update. The ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) (Evensen, 2003; Evensen, 2004 ) is a widely recognized synchronous sequential assimilation method, which stands distinct for its ability to approximate and propagate probability distribution functions utilizing a Monte Carlo sampling strategy. Unlike the Extended Kalman filter (EKF) which necessitates a linearized model operator (Jazwinski, 1970 ), or variational methods that require an adjoint model (Reichle et al., 2001 ), the EnKF operates without such prerequisites, rendering it a more flexible and straightforward approach for hydrological data assimilation. On the other hand, asynchronous methods encompass an updating methodology wherein the observations assimilated into the model stem from times distinct from the time of update (Sakov & Bocquet, 2018 ). In the realm of sequential assimilation, asynchronous methods find primary application in smoothers, such as the Ensemble Kalman Smoother (EnKS) (Evensen & Van Leeuwen, 2000 ). The Ensemble Kalman Smoother (EnKS) advances the capabilities of the EnKF by incorporating additional information, achieved by propagating the contribution of future measurements backward in time. This retroactive propagation of data significantly reduces the error variance for the past time. However, when it comes to forecasting, including nowcasting, the EnKS and EnKF are identical (Evensen, 2009 ). The crux of differentiation between smoothers and filters is that smoothers assimilate “future observations” whereas filters incorporate “past observation” (Rakovec et al., 2015 ). Therefore, in data assimilation with a forecasting objective, a filter, as opposed to a smoother, is often necessitated. Is it possible to use asynchronous methods in filters? The initial inquiry into this matter was spearheaded by Hunt et al. (2004) , who devised a method called 4D-EnKF. Advancing this line of investigation, Hunt et al. (2007)  later introduced and refined a simpler approach, termed 4D-LETKF. Subsequently, Sakov et al. (2010)  proposed the Asynchronous Ensemble Kalman Filter (AEnKF), demonstrating that the AEnKF is essentially equivalent to the 4D-LETKF, while exhibiting superiority over the 4D-EnKF. The AEnKF executes a forward integration of the model to procure simulated outcomes for use in the analysis step, utilizing past observations within a predefined time window to update the model. Krymskaya (2013)  initially employed the AEnKF technique in history matching problem in the reservoir engineering domain, finding it performs better in parameter estimation than EnKF and utilize the data with comparable effectiveness. Notably, the AEnKF holds considerable appeal in hydrological data assimilation due to its ability to harness a broader spectrum of observational data with little necessitating additional computational time. Moreover, this technique more accurately mirrors the temporal lag between the internal model states and catchment responses. Yet, the current utilization of AEnKF for state updating in hydrological models is relatively scant. Distinguished studies include the work of Mazzoleni et al. (2018)  who evaluated the efficacy of AEnKF within a simplistic routing model, showcasing the AEnKF’s superior performance in both lumped and distributed modeling scenarios. Additionally, Rakovec et al. (2015)  used the AEnKF for assimilation within the distributed HBV 96 model with kinematic wave river routing, illustrating an enhancement in assimilation efficacy as compared to the EnKF. Tao et al. (2016)  employed the AEnKF to assimilate observed discharge data into the Duke Coupled Surface-Groundwater Hydrology Model (DCHM) to enhance the operational hydrological forecasting across twelve catchments in the Southern Appalachians. Although these results are encouraging, current research on AEnKF is based on expert experience setting observation errors for gain matrix calculations and model forcing errors and state errors for generating ensemble perturbations, introducing considerable subjectivity. To our knowledge, there are no studies that have specifically improved and tested the error estimation component of AEnKF. Within the AEnKF framework, the uncertainty surrounding background prediction is discerned via the Monte Carlo method, whereby an ensemble of model states is generated by adding noise to the state variables, forcing variables, and/or model parameters. The uncertainty prevalent in hydrological simulation/forecasting is represented by the spread of these stochastically generated ensemble states. Consequently, the efficacy of the AEnKF substantially relies on the precise characterization of uncertainties inherent in both the model and observations. It's documented that the ill-suited estimations of these uncertainties undermine the performance of ensemble-based Kalman filters (e.g., AEnKF) (Crow & Van Loon, 2006; Reichle et al., 2008; Pathiraja et al., 2018 ). To address the subjectivity and uncertainty associated with the reliance on expert judgment for configuring error models in much of the existing research (e.g., Weerts & El Serafy, 2006; Clark et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2020 ), Li et al. (2014)  propounded a Bayesian inference procedure tailored for ensemble-based Kalman filters, namely the Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) method. Employing historical observations, the MAP method enables global optimization of the hyperparameters, thereby generating an appropriate generalization of uncertainty. Following this, Gong et al. (2023)  refined the prior estimation format of the MAP method and extended its application to the depiction of observational and structural errors in a distributed hydrological model. The advantage of the MAP method is that it doesn't necessitate the independence of observation sequences and facilitates the concurrent estimation of errors emanating from diverse sources. Also, it is relatively simple to implement and easy to couple with the AEnKF method compared to other Bayesian error analysis algorithm. In the AEnKF framework, state variables are assumed to be unbiased, thus, Gaussian perturbation with a mean of zero are typically chosen to generate an ensemble of model states. This ensemble perturbation strategy aims to mirror model uncertainty through a Monte Carlo methodology, all while ensuring the mean performance remains unaltered. This strategy operates under an implicit assumption: during the assimilation, the addition of mean-zero Gaussian noise should not elicit a systematic bias in the model output when comparing the ensemble mean of the perturbed state variables with the unperturbed counterparts (Ryu et al., 2009 ). Nonetheless, the inherent nonlinear processes within hydrological models render the bias in model outcomes inevitable when employing Gaussian noise for ensemble perturbation (De Lannoy et al., 2006; Alvarez-Garreton et al., 2015 ). To address this challenge, Ryu et al. (2009)  proposed a bias-corrected Gaussian error model (BGEM), which is executed by incorporating an undisturbed model prediction in parallel in time within the ensemble predictions of the model. Specifically, while conducting the state analysis, the unperturbed model simulations are utilized to correct the perturbation bias. Ryu et al. (2009)  have demonstrated that the proposed bias correction model effectively removes biases in soil moisture and reduces soil water mass balance errors. However, the effectiveness of this approach in updating hydrological model states using asynchronous data requires further testing. This study aims to reduce the accumulation of hydrological model errors in the initial conditions at the start of forecasting by assimilating observational discharge into model states. To achieve this objective, the study employs the AEnKF assimilation method and introduces, for the first time, enhanced error models designed to refine error estimation within the AEnKF framework. This improvement involves estimating the hyperparameters of the error model via the Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) method and mitigating systematic biases arising from Gaussian perturbations through the Bias-Gaussian Error Model (BGEM) method. Within this research framework, the study initially explores the impact of error models on ensemble simulation and the effect of updating various model state variables on AEnKF’s assimilation outcomes through synthetic cases. Subsequently, we examine the performance variations of AEnKF under different time windows. Finally, we contrast the performance differences between AEnKF and EnKF under the synthetic and real-world cases.  2 Methodology and method 2.1 Asynchronous Ensemble Kalman filter 2.1.1 Ensemble Kalman filter The core idea of sequential assimilation is to incorporate new observational information into the dynamic operation of a numerical model, resulting in a posterior probability density function (PDF) for the model states. Obtaining an analytical solution for the PDF is not feasible in most cases, but it can be sampled and predicted using sampling techniques. Evensen (2003)  integrated ensemble forecasting with Kalman filter theory. This led to the development of a sequential assimilation method to estimate model states and their error covariances through Monte Carlo techniques, termed the Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF). The dimensionality of the state space, observation space, ensemble space, and time space are respectively denoted as N x   , N y   , N e   , N t   . The subscript t  (t = 1 , ⋯ , N t    ) is time index and the subscript n  (n = 1 , ⋯ , N e    ) is ensemble index. The superscript f   indicates the forecasted value from the dynamic model, while the superscript a   indicates the analysis value (updated value) from EnKF. At time t  , the model state vector is denoted as x  t   , and the observation vector is denoted as y  t   .(1) x  t  = ( x 1 , t   , ⋯ , x N x  , t   )  T   ∈ R  N x       (2) y  t  = ( y 1 , t   , ⋯ , y N y  , t   )  T   ∈ R  N y        It is necessary to generate a set of mutually independent model state vectors in the EnKF, and the matrix composed of ensemble members is referred to as:(3) X  t  = ( x  1 , t   , ⋯ , x  N e  , t   )  ∈ R  N x  × N e        The initial X  t = 0     is obtained by the Monte Carlo method. The EnKF approximates the authentic error distribution by assessing the first and second moments of this distribution using statistical evaluation of ensemble members. Consequently, the ensemble mean of the model state variables is the best estimate, while the covariance between ensemble members signifies the analysis error covariance.(13) x   ¯   t  a  = 1 N e   ∑ n = 1  N e   x  n , t  a      (14) P  t  a  = 1 N e  - 1   ∑ n = 1  N e   x  n , t  a  - x   ¯   t  a    ( x  n , t  a  - x   ¯   t  a  )  T      where x   ¯   t  a    is the best estimate of the model state variables, and P  t  a    is the analysis error covariance matrix. In this study, the scheme proposed by Clark et al. Synchronous approaches utilize observational data only at the specific update time step. Conversely, asynchronous methods incorporate observations spanning a period, including both the designated update time step and a preceding interval. Prevailing sequential assimilation filters, such as Ensemble Kalman Filters and Particle Filters, fall under synchronous techniques. This raises the question: Can we transform synchronous filters into asynchronous ones to bolster hydrological assimilation efficacy? Pursuing this objective, this study introduces an asynchronous Ensemble Kalman filter (AEnKF). The AEnKF method, when updating model states, considers observations from both the current time step and the previous tw    time steps. Consequently, the observation vector is modified as follows:(15) y  ∼  t  = ( y  t   T  , y  t - 1    T  , ⋯ , y  t - t w    T  )  T  ∈ R  ( t w + 1 )  ∗ N y        where y  ∼  t    is the joint observation vector, and tw    is the time window of AEnKF; R  ∼  t    is the covariance matrix of the corresponding observation noise, which is also a diagonal matrix, expressed as follows:(16) R  ∼  t  = R  t   ⋯  0   ⋮   R  t - 1     ⋱      ⋮   0   ⋯  R  t - t w              Similarly, the model prediction vector in the observation space from the previous tw    time steps are used to augment the state vector:(17) x ∼  n , t   = x n , t   T  , H x t - 1     T  , H x t - 2     T  , ⋯ , H x t - t w     T    T  ∈ R N x  + t w ∗ N  y        The improvements scheme (Clark et al., 2008 ) can also be applied in AEnKF. As a result, the joint state vector x  ∼  n , t     is modified as follows:(18) x ∼  n , t   = x n , t  '  T  , H x t - 1     T  , H x t - 2     T  , ⋯ , H x t - t w     T    T  ∈ R N x  + t w + 1   ∗ N  y        Additionally, the new state definition introduces a new augmented observation operator H ∼  t    :(19) H ∼  t   = H t   ⋯  0   ⋮   I t - 1     ⋱      ⋮   0   ⋯  I t - t w             where I , with the corresponding subscript, stands for identity elements on the diagonal, matching the dimensions in Eq. (18) . With these augmented equations for x  ∼  n , t    , y  ∼  t   , R  ∼  t   , and H ∼   , assimilation can be carried out directly in the same manner as in EnKF. If only the current observations are assimilated (tw = 0   ), the AEnKF degenerates into the EnKF. In the joint state vector x  ∼  n , t    , all the model prediction vectors in the observation space are treated as diagnostic variables rather than state variables and are not updated in the analysis step. In other words, in Eq. (8) , only the first N x    dimensions of x  ∼  n , t     are computed, and the rest is ignored. Past observation expands the dimension of K  ∼  t    (Eq. (9) ) and P  ∼  t  f    (Eq. (10) ) in both row and column directions. The first N y    columns of K  ∼  t    correspond to observations at each gauge station, while the extra columns correspond to the past observations. The first N x    rows of K  ∼  t    correspond to x  n , t    , while the additional rows correspond to the simulated observations. Hence, it is possible to simply solve the equations for the first rows, which correspond only to x  n , t    . It's worth noting that the first N x    rows of K  ∼  t    already include the influence of past observations on the current state variables, and these influences come from the off-diagonal terms of the joint covariance matrix P  ∼  t  f   .   2.2 Error estimation The EnKF and its variant, AEnKF, adjust the model state using a weighted average of observations and model predictions. This underscores the significance of model error and observation error as pivotal elements influencing the assimilation system's efficacy. In rainfall-runoff simulations, given the unknown nature of both model and observation uncertainties, a judicious generalization of these uncertainties is beneficial for procuring enhanced suboptimal model state estimates. These estimates, in turn, influence the final simulated discharge. It's a common practice to stochastically produce ensembles by incorporating unbiased noise into model forcing and states. Parameters governing this unbiased noise are termed “hyperparameters” (Thiboult & Anctil, 2015 ). By introducing the unbiased perturbations into the model forcing and states, and running the Xin'anjiang model in ensemble mode without assimilation, the operation is referred to as Open Loop (OL). In contrast, deterministic run of the Xin'anjiang model is hereafter noted as DR. 2.2.1 Uncertainty in discharge measurements Observation error was characterized as a function of the discharge observation, as detailed by Clark et al. (2008)  and Weerts & El Serafy (2006) . We introduced perturbations to the measured discharge according to the following scheme:(20) y  n , t  ′  = ( I  + δ  t  y   )  ∙ y  t      where I  ∈ R  N y  × N y       is identity matrix; δ  t  y     is Gaussian perturbation matrix. Assuming that the observation errors are spatially independent, δ  t  y   ∈ R  N y  × N y       is a diagonal matrix:(21) δ  t  y   = δ 1 , t  y   0  0   0   ⋱  0   0   0  δ N y  , t  y          where δ i , t  y  ,  i = 1 , ⋯ , N y     is the perturbation at flow gauging station i  , and δ y   ∼ N 0 , σ y     . Furthermore, a first-order autoregressive model is employed to capture the temporal correlation of discharge observation errors. The perturbation at time step t   is modified as:(22) δ i , t  y  = μ y  + α y  δ i , t - 1  y  - μ y    + φ σ y  ( 1 - α y   2  )  0.5       where μ y  = 0   ; φ   is a standard Gaussian noise; α y    is autocorrelation coefficient for discharge observation errors; σ y    is the standard deviation.  2.2.2 Uncertainty in model forcing Rainfall is the most important model forcing in rainfall-runoff simulation. We utilized the widely recognized lognormal multiplicative error function to address the uncertainty associated with model forcing (McMillan et al., 2011; DeChant & Moradkhani, 2012 ):(23) P  n , t  ′  = δ  t  p   ∙ P  t      where P  n  ′    is the disturbed rainfall for the ensemble n  ; P  = ( P 1  , ⋯ , P N p   )  T   ∈ R  N p      is the rainfall observation vector; N p    is the dimensionality of the rainfall observations; δ  p     is lognormal perturbation matrix. Since the rainfall gauge at each observation station operate independently, its observation errors are not influenced by the errors of rain gauges at other locations. Therefore, it can be assumed that the observation errors are spatially independent (Gong et al., 2023 ). The errors in the precipitation measurement are assumed to be spatially independent, so that, δ  p     is also a diagonal matrix:(24) δ  t  p   = δ 1 , t  p   0  0   0   ⋱  0   0   0  δ N p  , t  p          where δ i  p  ,  i = 1 , ⋯ , N p     is the perturbation at rainfall gauging station i  , and ln δ p   ∼ N μ lnp  , σ lnp      follows a lognormal distribution with the mean of 1.0 and standard deviation of σ p    (Gong et al., 2023 ).
