(2012  and 2015 ), the perturbed model state variables include soil moisture and cumulative channel flow. In this study, soil moisture is represented by a variable called free water storage in the Xin'anjaing Model, denoted as S .    The cumulative channel flow is represented through the variable QC   , which means the outflow from each sub-basin on the routing calculation unit (sub-reaches in this study). According to Li et al. (2014) , Gaussian error functions are used to perturb the model state variables.(26) X  n , t  ′  = X  n , t   + δ  t  x   ∙ X  n , t       where X  n , t   = ( S n , t , 1   , S n , t , 2   , . . , S n , t , N S    , QC  n , t , 1   , QC  n , t , 2   , . . , QC  n , t , N q    )  T   ∈ R  N x      is the state vector; N S    and N q    are the dimensions of the S   and QC   ; δ  t  x     is diagonal Gaussian perturbation matrix and the diagonal elements are ( δ 1 , t  s  , ⋯ , δ N S  , t  s  , δ 1 , t  q  , ⋯ , δ N q  , t  q  )   , in which δ S   ∼ N 0 , σ S      and δ q   ∼ N 0 , σ q     . 2.2.3.1 Bias-corrected Gaussian Error Model The free water storage S   in the Xin'anjiang model reflects the soil moisture of topsoil layer, i.e., the humus layer of the soil (Yao et al., 2012 ). Consequently, the free water storage S   can be considered to lie between the saturated moisture content and field capacity, with its upper limit controlled by the parameter SM    (free water storage capacity, mm) and a lower limit of zero (Yao et al., 2012 ). When S   approaches the upper or lower limit, the perturbations to S   through Eq. (26)  may cause it to violate the physical constraints. In the Xin'anjiang model, to ensure computational stability, it is necessary to truncate the Gaussian distribution to keep the free water storage within physical limits. In the Xin'anjiang model, to ensure computational stability, it is necessary to truncate the Gaussian distribution to keep the free water storage within physical limits. This will lead to truncation errors in the background field and violate the full Gaussian assumption of AEnKF. This study presents the Bias-corrected Gaussian Error Model (BGEM) (Ryu et al., 2009 ) to mitigate biases arising from adherence to physical constraints. It should be noted that the BGEM method can significantly reduce the probability of the free water storage exceeding its physical limits due to perturbations, but it cannot completely eliminate this issue. Therefore, after correction using BGEM, only a very few cases will still have truncation errors, making these errors tolerable. It is achieved by incorporating an undisturbed model prediction in parallel in time within the ensemble predictions of the model. This correction mitigates the truncation error introduced by perturbing the free water storage. At each time step, the average bias δ  b     of the perturbed state variables is calculated as follows:(27) δ  b   = 1 N e   ∑ n = 1  N e   S  n   ′  - S  d         where S  d   = ( S 1  d  , S 2  d  , . . , S N S   d  )  ∈ R  N S      is the free water storage calculated from the undisturbed model; S  n   ′    is the disturbed free water storage. Subsequently, the set of bias-corrected state variables is obtained by subtracting the average bias δ  b     from the perturbed free water storage S  n   ′   :(28) S  ∼  n   ′  = S  n   ′  - δ  b        A bias correction operation is added before the analysis step, and the schematic is shown in Fig. 1  .   2.2.4 Maximum a posteriori estimation method The hyperparameters needed to be estimated in the above error model are σ y   , σ lnp    , σ S   , σ q   , α y   , and α lnp    . The Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) method is employed to obtain the global optimal values for these hyperparameters. The goal of MAP method is to maximize the probability density of the hyperparameters with given the observing historical flood events. In accordance with Bayesian theory, the posterior probability density can be expressed as follows:(29) p ψ    y    ∝ χ ψ    = p ( ψ  )  × p ( y    ψ  )      where ψ  = ( σ y  , σ s  , σ q  , σ lnp   , α y  , α lnp   )    is hyperparameter array; p ( y    ψ  )    is the conditional probability density of the observing historical discharge y    given ψ   ; p ( ψ  )    is a prior probability density, which can be computed as follows:(30) p ψ    = p σ y    p σ s    p σ q    p σ lnp     p α y    p α lnp         where p σ      is a prior probability density of the corresponding hyperparameter. The conditional probability density p ( y    ψ  )    can be obtained by the following equation:(31) p ( y    ψ  )  = ∏ i = 1  N y   ∏ t = 1  N t   p ( y i , t     ψ  )      where p ( y i , t     ψ  )    is the conditional probability density of the observed discharge with given ψ   . In summary, the flowchart of the AEnKF with enhanced error models proposed in this study is shown in Fig. 2  .   2.3 Evaluation metrics We select seven metrics to evaluate the performance of the hydrological assimilation in terms of both the optimal single-value performance and the ensemble performance (Yilmaz et al., 2008; Li et al., 2018; McInerney et al., 2020; Burgan,2022; Wang et al., 2023 ). The optimal single-value performance refers to the best simulation accuracy, i.e., the ensemble mean values of the simulated discharge. Ensemble performance evaluation, on the other hand, assesses the performance of the simulated discharge ensemble from the perspective of ensemble forecasting. It includes the overall performance of the ensemble and ensemble reliability. Quantitative evaluation of the optimal single-value performance employs root mean squared error (RMSE), Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency coefficient (NSE), R-squared (R_sqr), Percent Bias (PBIAS), and percent bias in flow duration curve (FDC) high-segment volume (BiasFHV). The Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) (Hersbach, 2000 ) gauges the ensemble overall performance, while the reliability component of CRPS (denoted as Reli) evaluates ensemble reliability. For the RMSE, CRPS, and Reli metrics, the ratios of AEnKF to open loop are denoted as RRMSE , RCRPS , and RReli , respectively. For the NSE and R_sqr, the differences between AEnKF and open loop are denoted as DNSE  and DR_sqr . Similarly, for the PBIAS and BiasFHV, the differences between open loop and AEnKF are denoted as DPBIAS  and DFHV . These two different subtractions ensure that larger values of DNSE , DR_sqr , DPBIAS , and DFHV  indicate greater improvements compared to the open-loop. Furthermore, the event-averaged values of these ratios and differences are represented as MRRMSE , MRCRPS , MRReli , MDNSE , MDR_sqr , MDPBIAS , and MDFHV , respectively. In synthetic cases, all evaluation metrics utilized the “synthetic true values” as a benchmark. For real-world cases, observed values served as the benchmark. The details regarding the metrics utilized in this study are available in Appendix A .  2.4 Hydrological model Zhao et al. (1980)  proposed the well-known Xin'anjiang model. Due to its logical model structure, clearly defined parameters, ease of calibration, and high accuracy in simulating humid catchments, it remains one of the most widely used hydrological models for flood forecasting in China. Considering the spatial heterogeneity of rainfall distribution and underlying surface, the Xin'anjiang model typically divides a catchment into several sub-basins using methods such as Thiessen polygons. These sub-basins serve as calculation units for runoff generation and routing. The inputs to Xin'anjiang model are the measured areal mean rainfall depth on the sub-basin (P ) and the measured pan evaporation (EM ). Soil evaporation is calculated from measured pan evaporation by the “three-layer soil moisture module”. The method of calculating the runoff generation is derived from saturation-excess mechanism, where net rainfall is first entirely used to replenish soil water, and once the soil moisture content in the unsaturated zone reaches field capacity, all subsequent net rainfall is used to generate runoff. The “lag and route” method is used to produce the sub-basin outflow within each sub-basin. The channel from sub-basin outlet to total basin outlet is divided into a varying number of sub-reaches based on the distance from each sub-basin outlet to the total basin outlet. Flow routing from the sub-basin outlets to the total basin outlet is achieved by applying the Muskingum method to successive sub-reaches. The discharge at the total basin outlet is the sum of discharge from all sub-basins that route to it. The flow chart for the Xin'anjiang model is as illustrated in Fig. 3  . For more information about Xin'anjiang model can be found in Zhao (1992) and Zhao & Liu (1995) . Zhao (1992)  classified the parameters of the Xin'anjiang model into sensitive and non-sensitive categories. Non-sensitive parameters received direct values based on expert knowledge. In real-world cases, the optimal values of sensitive parameters for the two study catchments were determined from historical observational data utilizing the SCE-UA method. In the other hand, in the synthetic data cases designed on the basis of the Tunxi catchment, the sensitive parameters were derived using regionalization techniques, integrating 33 donor catchments. Table 1   provides a summary of the parameters and their estimates. Delving into the estimation of these parameters exceeds this study's focus. For a comprehensive understanding of the methodology, please refer to our previous research (Gong et al., 2021 ).  2.5 Experimental setup The objective of this study is to enhance the AEnKF using enhanced error models and to utilize these assimilation methods to improve the accuracy of the simulated discharge at the catchment outlet. To achieve this objective, we first validated the benefits of using an improved error model (e.g., BGEM) with synthetic data in Tunxi catchment. Secondly, we evaluated the impact of varying time windows on AEnKF performance in synthetic cases. Then, using AEnKF under the optimal time window as an example, we examined which model states should be included and updated during the analysis step. Four partitioned state updating schemes are set up as follows. (1) Scheme 1, denoted as AEnSS, updating of free water storage in sub-basins, which has the most non-linear relation with the discharge at catchment outlet; (2) Scheme 2, denoted as AEnQL, updating the outflow of last sub-reaches at the sub-basin scale; (3) Scheme 3, denoted as AEnQA, updating the outflow of all sub-reaches at the sub-basin scale; (4) Scheme 4, denoted as AEnQS, updating both the free water storage and the outflow of all sub-reaches. Finally, the effect of AEnKF on rainfall-runoff simulations was tested and compared using synthetic and real-world data, including the results under one-step prediction and different lead time. The implementation of a one-step prediction is as follows. Obtain the updated model state x  n , t  a    at time step t   from AEnKF assimilation. Use x  n , t  a    as the initial state for the hydrological model at time step t + 1   , and the simulated states x  n , t + 1  f    and simulated discharge H ( x  n , t + 1  f  )    at time step t + 1    is obtained by the forward hydrological model. The time span of the synthetic data aligns with that of the available observed flood data. The synthetic data is generated in the following manner. Firstly, we use historical flood data to drive the MAP method to generate the optimal set of hyperparameters, ψ  ^  = ( σ ^  y  , σ ^  s  , σ ^  q  , σ ^  lnp   , α ^  y  , α ^  lnp   )    . The σ ^  lnp     and α ^  lnp     are applied to the forcing error model (Eqs. (23)–(25)) to introduce random perturbations to observed rainfall data at each time step, resulting in a set of random rainfall data. This random rainfall process is assumed to represent the true rainfall, named “synthetic true rainfall”. Next, the Xin'anjiang model is driven by this “synthetic true rainfall” and parameters derived from the regionalization methods to simulate the state variables at every time step and to determine the discharge at the catchment outlet. These are assumed to be the true state variables and true discharge, denoted as “synthetic true state variables” and “synthetic true discharge”. Finally, the optimal hyperparameters σ ^  y    and α ^  y    are applied to the discharge measurement error model (Eqs. (20)–(22)) to introduce random perturbations to the “synthetic true discharge”, resulting in a set of random discharge processes referred to as the “synthetic observed discharge”. We tested the assimilation effect for ensemble sizes of 10–100 and chose the optimal ensemble size, i.e., 50. Note that in both the synthetic and real-world cases in this study, we use historical rainfall data as a perfect proxy for rainfall prediction with the aim of assessing temporal persistence of the assimilation effect without introducing uncertainty from numerical weather prediction. Temporal persistence refers to the duration over which the updating applied to state variables by EnKF or AEnKF at the start of forecasting continue to hold in the future. When the ratio metric (such as RRMSE ) falls below 1.0, it is deemed that the assimilation has temporal persistence within that lead time.   3 Study areas and data The Tunxi catchment (located between 117°38′ to 118°29′ E and 29°27′ to 30°5′ N) is located in the mountainous region of southern Anhui Province, China. The drainage area is 2,693 km2 , with elevations ranging from 96 to 1,622 m (Fig. 4  a). The catchment lies within the subtropical monsoon climate zone. The area features well-defined seasons with a temperate climate, characterized by an average annual temperature of approximately 17.0 °C. The region receives ample precipitation, averaging around 1,800 mm annually, but it is unevenly distributed throughout the year, with over 60 % of the annual rainfall concentrated in the period from May to August. Vegetation covers the Tunxi catchment extensively, accounting for more than 70 % of its total area. Dominant vegetation types comprise evergreen coniferous forest, deciduous broadleaf forest, mixed forest, forest land, woodland grassland, pasture, and cropland. Predominantly, the soil types of Tunxi catchment are clay and loam. The Pinghe catchment (117°5′ to 117°25′ E and 117°10′ to 24°26′ N) is located in the mountainous region of Fujian Province, China. The drainage area is 493 km2 , with elevations ranging from 96 to 1,622 m (Fig. 4 c). The region experiences a subtropical maritime climate, characterized by mild temperatures and abundant rainfall. The average annual temperature is around 21.0 °C, and the annual precipitation ranges from 1,400 mm to 1,800 mm. Precipitation is unevenly distributed both within and between years, with approximately 75 % of the annual rainfall occurring between April and September. The main types of precipitation in the catchment are frontal rains from April to June and typhoon rains from June to October, with typhoon rains being the primary cause of significant flooding in the catchment. The hydrometeorological data used in this study, including evapotranspiration, precipitation, and discharge, are provided by the Hydrology Bureau of Anhui Province and Fujian Province. The Tunxi catchment is equipped with nine rainfall gauging stations, while the Pinghe catchment has four. Tyson polygons are employed, centered on these stations, to partition the catchment into nine sub-basins for Tunxi (Fig. 4 b) and four sub-basins for Pinghe (Fig. 4 d). Evaporation data are obtained from daily pan evaporation measurements using the E-601 pan. Hourly values are calculated as 1/24th of the daily measurements. It is noted that there is a single evaporation observatory within each of the study catchment, which leads to the assumption of spatial homogeneity in pan evaporation. Daily discharge data spanning from 2008 to 2020 for Tunxi catchment and spanning from 2004 to 2010 for Pinghe catchment are accessible. Hourly observations are intermittent and exclusively accessible during flood events. Flood events are identified through the peaks over threshold method (Huang et al., 2016 ). There are a total of 26 flood events in Tunxi catchment, listed in Table B1 . Fourteen of these events, spanning from 2008 to 2014, are employed for model calibration, while the remaining 12 events are reserved for validation purposes. In addition, there are a total of 22 flood events in the Pinghe catchment, listed in Table B2 . The first 10 of these events are used for model calibration, and the remaining 12 events are used for validation. An overview of the statistical characteristics of the observations and hydrological model simulations during the flood events can be found in Table B3 .  4 Results and discussion 4.1 Hyperparameter estimation for error models Utilizing the data from observed flood events as detailed in Tables B1 and B2 , a global optimization of hyperparameters was conducted using the MAP method, with the resultant optimal parameters delineated in Table 2  . This set of optimized hyperparameters is subsequently employed in the construction of error models for both synthetic and real-world cases.  4.2 Synthetic cases 4.2.1 The time window of Asynchronous Ensemble Kalman filter The AEnKF assimilates both current and historical observational data over a specified time period, with the length of this period defined by the time window, tw   . Determining the appropriate duration of past observations is crucial for AEnKF. If tw    is set too short, the AEnKF cannot adequately leverage historical information to enhance performances. Conversely, if tw    is set too long, nonlinear systems might incorporate excessive data unrelated to the current period, potentially leading to a degradation in assimilation performance. Four specific time windows, tw =    0, 3, 9, and 18 h, were chosen for AEnKF analysis. The respective runs were designated as EnKF (equivalent to AEnKF0 ), AEnKF3 , AEnKF9 , and AEnKF18 . The RRMSE   of the forecasted discharge at catchment outlet were plotted in Fig. 5  . The most notable observation is that the 3-hours window consistently displayed the best forecasting accuracy across all lead time. For the one-step prediction, the forecast accuracy is ranked as follows: AEnKF3  performs the best, followed by AEnKF9 , EnKF, and then AEnKF18 . As the lead time increases, the accuracy of AEnKF9  declines most rapidly. Around an 8-hour lead time, the accuracy ranking becomes AEnKF3  surpassing EnKF which is roughly equivalent to AEnKF18 , and then followed by AEnKF9 . The reason for the results may be that a longer time window includes too much historical information, which may have a weak correlation with the current state variables. Including too much historical observational information in the assimilation system may lead to a degradation in assimilation performance.  4.2.2 Bias correction based on BGEM In light of the preceding discussion, when the free water storage S   approaches either its upper limit (free water storage capacity, SM   ) or lower limit (0 mm), perturbing S   through Eq. (26)  may lead it to exceed the physical constraints of the variables. Once the hydrological model corrects it, truncation errors are generated, subsequently resulting in a degradation of the performance under the OL mode. In this section, we aim to validate the benefits of utilizing the BGEM method to rectify this bias. This will be achieved by comparing the results between the DR mode and the OL mode employing different error models in synthetic cases. The OL mode using the original Gaussian error model is referred to as OLGEM , while the OL mode incorporating bias correction for perturbations in free water storage using the BGEM is denoted as OLBGEM . Fig. 6   presents scatter plots illustrating the hourly simulated free water storage across 26 flood events. Notably, consistent standard deviations in perturbations result in similar ensemble deviations between the two error models, as observed from the similar distribution of gray dots in Fig. 6 (a) and (b). In Fig. 6 (a), the ensemble mean values (represented by black dots) deviates below the 1:1 line between the [0,35] axis range. This suggests that, in comparison to DR, the OLGEM  model consistently underestimates free water storage. This trend is observed because during flood periods, the free water storage is generally substantial. So, utilizing a Gaussian error function to perturb the free water storage may lead to many instances in the ensemble where S   exceeds SM   . After the Xin'anjiang model adjusts S   to equal SM   , the corresponding ensemble mean consequently decreases, introducing a systematic bias to the originally Gaussian Error Model (GEM). In contrast, Fig. 6 (b) shows that black dots concentrate around the 1:1 line within the [0,30] axis range and display a slight downward deviation beyond S > 30 m m   . This indicates that when the free water storage is less than 30 mm, BGEM effectively corrects the systematic underestimation evident in GEM. Furthermore, as S   nears SM    (S > 30 m m   ), BGEM can alleviate the systematic biases resulting from ensuring the physical plausibility of model variables. Fig. 7   depicts the hourly simulated discharge at the catchment outlet for 26 flood events, as shown through scatter plots. In Fig. 7 (a), there is a noticeable downward deviation of the black dots from the 1:1 reference line, especially in the high flow regions. This trend is attributable to the OLGEM  model's consistent underestimation of free water storage, resulting in a consequent systematic underestimation in its simulated discharge. In contrast, Fig. 7 (b) shows the black dots largely clustered around the 1:1 line in both low and high flow regions, suggesting that the OLBGEM  model's performance in simulating discharge aligns closely with the capabilities of DR.  4.2.3 Partitioned state updating schemes Evaluating the influence of updating various state variables is necessary in nonlinear frameworks, such as hydrological models. In this subsection, we draw upon the partitioned state updating schemes introduced by Rakovec et al. (2015)  to study the implications of updating various state variables on assimilation outcomes. 4.2.3.1 State variables In the context of a one-step prediction, Fig. 8   represents the RMSE values associated with the free water storage under the four partitioned state updating schemes, and compares these results with the OL. A salient observation from the data reveals that the scatter points, spanning all four delineated scenarios, predominantly cluster around the 1:1 line. This clustering underscores their comparable efficacy to the OL in accurately representing free water storage dynamics. Specifically, the mean RMSE values for both AEnSS and AEnSQ schemes are only 0.01and 0.02 mm less than the mean of the OL. Conversely, the AEnQL and AEnQA schemes, having refrained from updating the free water storage, naturally align with the OL's mean RMSE. Moreover, the distribution frequency of the RMSE, as depicted by the histograms within the matrix's diagonal elements, adheres closely to the anticipated normal distribution anchored on its respective mean. This suggests that the simulated free water storage from the four partitioned state updating schemes exhibit no anomalies when benchmarked against the established “synthetic true values”. Fig. 9   depicts the RMSE associated with the simulated hourly outflow from the last sub-reaches of the nine sub-basins. The AEnSS scheme did not update the outflow (QC ), resulting in performance comparable to the OL scheme. As shown in the second plots of the first column, the black dots predominantly cluster near the 1:1 line. In contrast, the AEnQL, AEnQA, and AEnSQ schemes demonstrate performance disparities when compared with the OL. Specifically, within the lower three plots of the first column, the black dots display a discernible downward deviation, indicating that the RMSE for QC  in these schemes is systematically reduced compared to the OL. Additionally, their mean RMSE consistently undercuts that observed in the OL. Hence, the AEnQL, AEnQA, and AEnSQ schemes outperform the OL in simulating QC . On the other hand, there are no particularly significant differences among the three schemes. Specifically, in the scatter plots found in the lower sections of the matrix's third and fourth columns, black dots predominantly align with the 1:1 line. However, from the perspective of mean RMSE, the AEnSQ scheme emerges as the relatively optimal choice among the three four schemes. As can be seen from the diagonal elements of Fig. 9 , the frequency distribution histograms reveal a positive skewness, suggesting the existence of outliers. It's worth noting that such outliers aren't attributable to the state updating process, given that a comparable positive skewness is observed within the OL.  4.2.3.2 Flood forecasting In this subsection, we investigate the variances in flood forecasting, assuming perfect rainfall prediction, across four partitioned state updating schemes. Fig. 10   shows the evolution of the optimal single-value metrics (as defined in Appendix A ) of the forecasted discharge at the catchment outlet over the lead time (LT) spanning 1–24 h. For the one-step prediction, the accuracy hierarchy is denoted as: AEnSQ performs the best, followed by AEnQA, AEnQL, and then AEnSS. This ranking is consistent for PBIAS and BiasFHV up to a lead time of 24 h. For RMSE and R_sqr, after the lead times extend to 11 h and 5 h respectively, the ranking changes to AEnSQ outperforming AEnSS, followed by AEnQL, and then AEnQA. For NSE, after a lead time of 8 h, the ranking becomes AEnSQ better than AEnSS, followed by AEnQA, and then AEnQL. The following analysis examines the progression of MRRMSE  as the lead time extends for each of the four schemes. As the lead time increases, the MRRMSE  for AEnSS gradually decreases, stabilizing around 0.95 when the lead time exceeds 13 h. This suggests that updating the free water storage in each sub-basin can slightly enhance the forecasting accuracy over extended lead times. The MRRMSE  of the AEnQL initially increases rapidly and then slightly decreases, but it is significantly better than the OL scheme only during the first two hours of the lead time. When comparing AEnQL and AEnQA, the RMSE of AEnQL is considerably higher than that of AEnQA within the first eight hours of the lead time. This suggests that by only updating the outflow of last sub-reaches in each sub-basin, the assimilation effect is constrained to a short temporal persistence, and these enhancements are not competitive. When comparing AEnSS to AEnQA scheme, it is evident that updating state variables during the channel routing process might more effectively enhance flood forecasting accuracy. This is attributed to the stronger correlation between the state variables in the flow routing process and the forecasted discharge. Within a 6-hour lead time, AEnQA scheme outperforms AEnSS. Conversely, beyond this 6-hour lead time, AEnSS scheme slightly surpasses AEnQA. This suggests that updating state variables of the runoff generation process benefits the accuracy of flood forecasting for longer lead time. The R_sqr metric exhibits a pattern similar to that of RMSE. However, compared to OL, only AEnSQ shows a sustained advantage in this metric for up to 24-hour lead time. For NSE, aside from the one-step prediction, the AEnQL scheme performs the worst at all other lead times, even falling behind OL after the 2-hour lead time. Conversely, AEnQA outperforms AEnSS for lead times up to 7 h, after which the ranking reverses. Lastly, for the PBIAS and BiasFHV metrics, the performance ranking of the four schemes remains consistent across different lead times: AEnSQ is superior to AEnQA, which is better than AEnQL, which in turn outperforms AEnSS. Last but not least, considering all five optimal single-value evaluation metrics, AEnSQ consistently outperforms the other three schemes and exceeds OL performance at all lead times. This superior performance of AEnSQ scheme is attributed to the simultaneous updating of state variables in both the runoff generation process and the flow routing process. The benefits at longer lead times mainly come from updating the runoff generation variables, while at shorter lead times, they come from updating the flow routing variables. Based on these findings, subsequent research in this study employs the AEnSQ scheme for model state variable updates.    4.3 Real-world cases Considering the optimal performance in the synthetic cases, the time window of AEnKF is set to tw = 3 h    in the real-world cases. In this section, we uses observational data from the Tunxi and Pinghe basins to analyze the outflow simulation accuracy when updating the hydrological model states using the AEnKF with an improved error model. We further examine the temporal persistence of its assimilation effects. All these findings are compared with the results from the EnKF, which corresponds the AEnKF with a time window of zero. 4.3.1 One-step prediction 4.3.1.1 Optimal single-value performance (ensemble mean) The optimal single-value performance of AEnKF in one-step prediction is evaluated. Fig. 11   presents the optimal single-value metrics of both the EnKF and AEnKF assimilation. Under the DR mode, the event-averaged NSE is 0.91 for Tunxi (Table B1 ) and 0.80 for Pinghe catchment (Table B2 ), indicating that the Xin'anjiang model with calibrated parameters offers high simulation accuracy in study catchments. Note that the NSE of the OL mode is essentially the same as that of the DR mode. In the Tunxi catchment, based on the RMSE metric, the RRMSE  of EnKF ranges from 0.41 to 0.68, with an MRRMSE  of 0.55, while the RRMSE  of AEnKF ranges from 0.37 to 0.67, with an MRRMSE  of 0.52. Both EnKF and AEnKF effectively reduce the RMSE of forecasted discharge, with AEnKF performing slightly better. However, AEnKF offers higher improvement caps in some flood events. Taking RMSE as an example, EnKF achieves a maximum reduction of 59 %, while AEnKF reaches up to 63 %. Regarding the NSE metric, the event- averaged NSE of AEnKF and EnKF improved by 0.072 and 0.068, respectively, both reaching above 0.97. For the flood events with the best updating, the NSE improvement reached 0.18 for AEnKF and 0.17 for EnKF. For the PBIAS metric, the MDPBIAS  of AEnKF is 6.35 %, and that of EnKF is 5.67 %, indicating that both reduce the volumetric bias of the forecast results. For the flood events with the best correction, the absolute reduction in PBIAS reached 18.52 % for AEnKF and 15.38 % for EnKF. Based on the R_sqr metric, the MDR_sqr  of AEnKF is 3.81 %, and that of EnKF is 3.77 %, indicating that both improve the fit between forecasted and observed discharge. For the flood events with the best updating, the absolute increase in R_sqr reached 12.90 % for AEnKF and 12.72 % for EnKF. The BiasFHV metric, which reflects the volumetric bias of forecasted streamflow near the peak flow, shows that the MDFHV  of AEnKF is 6.54 %, and that of EnKF is 5.74 %, indicating that both reduce the forecast error of peak flow. For the flood events with the best correction, the absolute reduction in BiasFHV reached 18.27 % for AEnKF and 16.41 % for EnKF. In the Pinghe catchment, based on the RMSE metric, the RRMSE  of EnKF ranges from 0.72 to 1.00, with an MRRMSE  of 0.89, while the RRMSE  of AEnKF ranges from 0.72 to 0.96, with an MRRMSE  of 0.86, indicating that AEnKF outperforms EnKF. The event-averaged NSE for AEnKF and EnKF improved by 0.06 and 0.04, respectively, reaching 0.85 and 0.83. For the flood events with the best updating, the NSE improvement reached 0.11 and 0.19, respectively. Additionally, the DNSE  of AEnKF is positive for all flood events, while DNSE  of EnKF is nearly zero for two events, indicating that AEnKF provided effective updating for all flood events, whereas EnKF failed in two events. Regarding the PBIAS metric, the MDPBIAS  of AEnKF is 3.00 %, and that of EnKF is 2.04 %, both reducing the volumetric bias of the forecast results. The maximum reduction in the absolute value of PBIAS reached 7.83 % for AEnKF and 8.03 % for EnKF. For the R_sqr metric, the MDR_sqr  of AEnKF is 1.16 %, and that of EnKF is 0.85 %, slightly improving the fit of the forecasted streamflow. For the BiasFHV metric, the MDFHV  of AEnKF is 3.91 %, and that of EnKF is 2.28 %, both reducing the forecast error of peak flow. The maximum reduction in the absolute value of BiasFHV reached 14.85 % for AEnKF and 8.24 % for EnKF. Comparing the two catchments reveals that the optimal single-value performance of AEnKF varies between catchments. All metrics indicate that the assimilation effect in the Tunxi catchment is superior to that in the Pinghe catchment. This may be related to the different levels of uncertainty in the Xin'anjiang model across different regions. In Tunxi catchment, the discharge simulation accuracy of the Xin'anjiang model is significantly better than in Pinghe catchment. For example, the NSE values for the two basins are 0.91 and 0.80, respectively. This suggests lower levels of uncertainty in model inputs, structure, and parameters, indicating that the model may more accurately reflect the actual flood processes in the Tunxi catchment. Accurate representation of the regional hydrological processes by the model also benefits the hydrological data assimilation process. Furthermore, in both catchments, the AEnKF with the enhanced error models significantly outperforms the EnKF with the same enhanced error models across all five metrics, with this difference being more pronounced in the Pinghe catchment. These results indicate that the optimal single-value performance of AEnKF with the enhanced error models is superior, and in catchments with lower flood forecasting accuracy, the advantage of AEnKF over EnKF is even greater.  4.3.1.2 Ensemble performance  Fig. 12   delineates the evaluation of the ensemble overall performance and ensemble reliability, employing metrics of RCRPS , and RReli  respectively. In the Tunxi catchment, the RCRPS  values for EnKF span a range of 0.45 to 0.66, with an MRCRPS  of 0.55, whereas for AEnKF, the range extends from 0.39 to 0.68, with an MRCRPS  of 0.51. The RReli  values for EnKF range from 0.14 to 0.89, with an MRReli  of 0.36, in contrast to AEnKF which ranges from 0.07 to 0.74, with a mean MRReli  of 0.30. These results manifest that both EnKF and AEnKF assimilations enhance ensemble overall performance and reliability across all flood events, with AEnKF marginally surpassing EnKF in all these dimensions. Pertaining to ensemble overall performance, the mean CRPS of EnKF observed a reduction of 45 % compared to the OL mode, while AEnKF showcased a reduction of 49 %; in terms of reliability, the mean Reli for EnKF marked a reduction of 64 %, whereas AEnKF exhibited a reduction of 70 %. In the Pinghe catchment, the RCRPS  values for EnKF span a range of 0.71 to 1.05, with the MRCRPS  of 0.91. In contrast, AEnKF values range from 0.73 to 0.97, with the MRCRPS  of 0.87. The RReli  values for EnKF range from 0.56 to 1.58, with the MRReli  of 0.91, whereas AEnKF ranges from 0.45 to 1.00, with an MRReli  of 0.79. Regarding overall ensemble performance, the mean CRPS for EnKF shows a reduction of 9 % compared to the OL, while AEnKF shows a reduction of 13 %. In terms of reliability, the mean Reli for EnKF indicates a reduction of 9 %, whereas AEnKF shows a reduction of 21 %. These results demonstrate that both EnKF and AEnKF assimilations improve overall ensemble performance and reliability, with AEnKF outperforming EnKF in all aspects. Furthermore, the AEnKF assimilation method improves the overall performance and reliability of the ensemble in nearly all flood events. In contrast, while EnKF improves the overall performance and reliability of the ensemble in terms of event averaging, its reliability is lower than that of the OL model in some flood events. Comparing the results of two catchments, it is evident that the advantage of AEnKF over EnKF in ensemble performance is more pronounced in the Pinghe catchment. This further highlights the superiority of AEnKF in regions with higher uncertainty.  4.3.1.3 Discussion of specific flood events In this section, we first discuss four typical flood events selected in the Tunxi catchment, each with varying magnitudes of peak discharges and distinct hydrographs. Specifically, No.2010041008 signifies a multi-peak small flood, No.2011060908 signifies a single-peak large flood, No.2015080908 represents a single-peak small flood, and No.2017062308 denotes a multi-peak large flood. Fig. 13   illustrates the simulated hydrographs for these four flood events. The observed discharge is represented by the black line, the ensemble mean discharge of the OL mode is delineated by the gray line, the gray band delineates the ensemble range of the OL mode, the green line denotes the ensemble mean discharge by EnKF or AEnKF, and the green band delineates the ensemble range of EnKF or AEnKF. It is evident that in the four typical floods examined, the ensemble distributions of either EnKF or AEnKF (depicted by green bands) align more closely with the observed values compared to the ensemble distributions of OL (depicted by gray bands), and exhibit narrower band widths. This suggests that the ensemble performance associated with either EnKF or AEnKF is superior to that of the OL mode, and the ensemble spread is lesser. Moreover, the ensemble distribution during the peak period is observed to be wider than during the rise and recession phases of the flood, a phenomenon attributed to the error models employed. These models afford larger error perturbations to the assimilation system during the peak period, generating adequately wide ensemble distributions, which in turn, ensures a more potent assimilation effect during the peak period. Subsequently, while examining the ensemble mean within the OL model, an anomalous peak emerges around the 268th time step of the No.2010041008 event, which is absent in the observational discharge. A plausible explanation could be that the rainfall occurring in the preceding moments triggered an anomalous response within the hydrological model. Both EnKF and AEnKF have mitigated this anomaly, underscoring their ability to amend the structural uncertainties of the Xin'anjiang model to a certain extent by assimilating the observed discharge. Upon analyzing the flood peaks across the four flood events, it is evident that AEnKF, apart from showcasing a performance comparable to EnKF in the No.2010041008 event, demonstrates superior assimilation efficacy during the peak periods in the other three flood events, most notably in the No.2017062308 event. Throughout the rise and recession phases of the floods, AEnKF and EnKF exhibit comparable performance. In the Pinghe catchment, we select three representative flood events for analysis: No. 2006051704, No. 2006052107, and No. 2007092315, which correspond to a single-peak large flood, a multi-peak small flood, and a single-peak small flood, respectively. It is noteworthy that no multi-peak large flood events are found in the collected data, and thus they are not discussed. Fig. 14   presents the simulated hydrographs for these three flood events. Consistent with the results from the Tunxi catchment, the ensemble distribution of AEnKF is closer to the observed values at most times compared to the ensemble distribution of OL and exhibits narrower band widths. In contrast, the ensemble distribution of EnKF during the peak period in all three events is similar to or slightly wider than that of OL, underscoring the superior performance of AEnKF over EnKF in terms of ensemble performance. Regarding the ensemble mean, AEnKF outperforms EnKF in correcting the peaks of No. 2006051704 and No. 2007092315, as well as the first peak of No. 2006052107. Additionally, AEnKF demonstrates a more pronounced advantage in the recession phase of No. 2007092315.   4.3.2 Temporal persistence of the assimilation effect Fig. 15   presents heat maps illustrating the temporal persistence of the assimilation effect (represented by RRMSE ) of AEnKF with the enhanced error models, compared to EnKF. In the Tunxi catchment, the temporal persistence of AEnKF is significantly better than EnKF in most flood events, such as events 9, 12, 19, and 24. The Pinghe catchment shows similar results, with AEnKF outperforming EnKF in most flood events, such as events 1, 2, 3, 4, and 11. Additionally, in some flood events in both catchments, the temporal persistence of AEnKF can last up to 24-hours lead time. This may be attributed to the effective updating of soil moisture state variables by AEnKF during these events, as summarized from the synthetic data case results: more accurate initial soil moisture states at the start of the forecast contribute to improved assimilation effects over longer lead times. Moreover, Fig. 16   illustrates the trends of five metrics over lead time ranging from 1 to 24 h. The most significant finding is that AEnKF with the enhanced error models surpasses EnKF in all five metrics across all lead times in both catchments. In the Tunxi catchment, the mean values of all metrics for AEnKF are better than those for OL. Except for R_sqr, the mean values of the other four metrics remain better than OL within the 95 % confidence interval. For EnKF, the RMSE and NSE become comparable to OL after a lead time of 13 h, R_sqr slightly underperforms compared to OL after a lead time of 10 h, while PBIAS and BiasFHV show benefits over a 24-hour lead time. In the Pinghe catchment, over a 24-hour lead time, the event mean values of RMSE, NSE, PBIAS, and BiasFHV for AEnKF are superior to those for OL within the 95 % confidence interval. However, the improvement in R_sqr is sustained only up to a 5-hour lead time. For EnKF, improvements in RMSE, PBIAS, and BIASFHV are sustained for 24 h, NSE slightly underperforms compared to OL after a lead time of 3 h, and R_sqr only benefits within a 1-hour lead time.    5 Conclusions This study employs the Asynchronous Ensemble Kalman Filter (AEnKF) to assimilate discharge observations into the Xin'anjiang model, aiming to reduce the accumulation of hydrological model errors in the initial conditions at the start of forecasting. Concurrently, the BGEM model is utilized to diminish the systematic bias brought by perturbating soil moisture, while the MAP method is employed for an objective estimation of the hyperparameters of the error models constructed in this study. Through extensive testing within both synthetic and real-world cases, this study evaluates the performance of this AEnKF assimilation scheme with enhanced error models in updating the hydrological model states. Overall, the AEnKF with enhanced error models can be regarded as an effective model state updating method: (1) it can accommodate more observational data with minimal increase in computational burden; (2) the enhanced error models contribute to the stability and accuracy of the assimilation method. These features make it highly suitable for operational hydrological forecasting. Compared to the EnKF, the AEnKF allows for the selection of a certain assimilation window length, introducing a degree of flexibility to the data assimilation scheme. The assimilation performance of AEnKF is also related to the length of the assimilation time window, and this study discovered that three hours is an appropriate assimilation time window in the study catchments. In the synthetic case, we verified that the BGEM could effectively reduce the systematic bias caused by perturbing the free water storage, rendering the performance of the ensemble run mode without assimilation (OL) essentially consistent with that of the deterministic run (DR) of Xin'anjiang model. Subsequently, we found that updating different model state variables has a significant impact on discharge forecasting. Comparing four different model state update schemes revealed that updating the free water storage enhances the temporal persistence of the assimilation effect. For lead time greater than 7 h, the RMSE, NSE, and R_sqr metrics are all better than those of the scheme updating only the flow routing state variables. updating the outflow of last sub-reaches at the sub-basin scale improves flood forecast accuracy for short forecast times (LT ≤ 2h) but is inferior to the scheme updating the outflow of all sub-reaches at the sub-basin scale in terms of RMSE, NSE, PBIAS, and BiasFHV. All five indicators demonstrate that within a 24-hour lead time, the EnSQ scheme that updates both runoff and routing state variables simultaneously demonstrates higher accuracy compared to the schemes that update either of the two independently. Therefore, we recommend updating both the free water storage and the outflow of all sub-reaches at the sub-basin scale concurrently. In the case study with real-world data, both catchments show similar results, indicating that AEnKF with the enhanced error models outperformed EnKF with the enhanced error models. For optimal single-value performance, higher NSE and R_sqr and lower RMSE indicate that AEnKF can make the flood hydrographs more closely match the observations. Lower PBIAS indicates that AEnKF can make the flood volume more closely match the observations, while lower BiasFHV reflects that AEnKF is more effective in correcting flood peaks. In terms of ensemble performance, lower CRPS demonstrates that AEnKF has superior overall ensemble performance, and lower Reli indicates that AEnKF has higher reliability. The above conclusions demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in humid regions, but it has not yet been tested in semi-arid and arid regions. This is because the Xin'anjiang model used in this study is based on the saturation-excess runoff generation theory, which is a hydrological model suitable only for humid and semi-humid regions. It is important to note that the AEnKF method with the improved error model proposed in this study can be coupled with any hydrological model and is therefore not limited to humid regions. The applicability of this method in arid and semi-arid regions will be tested in future study. Finally, it should be noted that the AEnKF method with the improved error model involves the assimilation of observation data and cannot be used in ungauged catchments.
1 Introduction The sustainable utilization of water resources and ensuring food security are pivotal to the progressive development of human society (UNESCO, 2012 ). Water security serves as the foundation for food security, with water shortages directly impacting food production, a connection highlighted by Kang et al. (2017) . Agriculture, as the primary consumer of water, accounts for approximately 70 % of global water usage (Siebert et al., 2010 ). In this context, irrigation water use (IWU) dominates agricultural water consumption and plays a vital role in food production, especially in arid regions where precipitation is inadequate to sustain agriculture (Puy et al., 2021 ). Accurate estimation of IWU is integral for effective agricultural water management, optimizing cropping systems, irrigation scheduling, and allocating water resources to prevent a systemic decline in crop production. IWU exhibits significant spatial heterogeneity, influenced chiefly by the distribution of water sources, irrigation infrastructure technology, and diverse water requirements across various crops. The complexity of these irrigation environments renders precise IWU estimation challenging. This is further compounded by the lack of comprehensive maintenance of IWU field measurements or regular irrigation water withdrawal surveys over time and space (Zhang and Long, 2021 ). In situ metering data or irrigation district-level survey reports are often inaccessible in China, with irrigation water withdrawals typically reported only at the provincial level (e.g., Water Resources Bulletin of China). Imperfections in agricultural water management and monitoring, particularly in water metering, exacerbate these challenges (Foster et al., 2020 ). Recent advancements in large-scale land surface models, which now include irrigation modules, primarily focus on the natural water cycle or land–atmosphere interactions. However, these models require significant computational resources and incur high operational costs (Lawston et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2020 ). Rapid developments in remote sensing satellite technology and the enrichment of remote sensing data enable the capture of spatiotemporal variations in IWU (Zaussinger et al., 2019; Zohaib and Choi, 2020 ). Numerous studies have sought to estimate IWU via remote sensing inversion, such as deriving IWU from actual evapotranspiration data, surface soil moisture data, or a combination thereof (Foster et al., 2020; Zhang and Long, 2021 ). Despite these advancements, existing remote sensing approaches to IWU estimation face significant uncertainties and are constrained by coarse spatial resolutions. Consequently, these estimations are often imprecise, failing to capture many irrigation effects (Zhang and Long, 2021 ). More importantly, IWU is intricately linked to crop water demand and effective precipitation during the crop growth period. Conventional methods for estimating effective precipitation typically rely on an empirical relationship between mean monthly precipitation and crop water demand, neglecting key factors such as infiltration and precipitation intensity (Doorenbos and Pruitt, 1977 ). Notably, significant water loss can occur through surface streamflow when infiltration is low, and precipitation intensity is high. Furthermore, conventional methods often overlook water losses due to subsurface lateral flow and seepage to groundwater from the root zone. Although these components are included in land surface models, their utilization for calculating effective precipitation to accurately predict spatiotemporal IWU distributions remains rare. Under most climate change scenarios, global surface temperatures are expected to rise by more than 1.5 °C before the end of the 21st century, with regional variations in precipitation patterns due to global warming (IPCC, 2014 ). These changes will directly impact crop evapotranspiration, altering IWU and potentially increasing drought risk during critical crop growth stages. Recent studies have explored IWU responses to climate change, finding significant variability based on geographic location, crop type, and climate scenario (Busschaert et al., 2022; Vahmani et al., 2022 ). Additionally, there is growing research interest in the influence of crop planting area, patterns, and irrigation water use efficiency on IWU (Li et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2017 ). However, there is a notable gap in understanding the most effective water resource management strategies for irrigated agriculture in arid regions impacted by climate change. The establishment of water-suitable agricultural thresholds, crucial for the sustainable development of irrigated agriculture under constrained water resources in a changing climate, has been insufficiently addressed. Water scarcity in the Heihe River basin, an arid inland area in Northwest China, poses serious ecological, environmental, social, and economic challenges. Recent efforts in this region to enhance irrigation efficiency and reduce IWU have included the combined use of surface and groundwater, adjustments in crop planting patterns, and the promotion of water-saving irrigation techniques. However, these improvements have inadvertently led to increased crop planting intensity and an expansion of irrigated areas, resulting in a net increase rather than a decrease in IWU (Liu et al., 2017; Song et al., 2015 ). Furthermore, climate change is undermining the stability of irrigation water systems, exacerbating the mismatch between supply and demand for agricultural water. Addressing these issues, this paper compiled extensive multisource and multiscale data and constructed a distributed hydrological model (i.e., the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT), Arnold et al., 1998 ) that reflected the heterogeneous meteorology–soil–crop–water conditions in the Heihe agricultural area. The primary objectives of this study were: (1) to utilize the five general circulation models (GCMs) of the World Climate Research Programme Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) for predicting future temperature and precipitation trends in the Heihe agricultural area under three representative concentration pathways (RCPs); (2) to develop a spatially explicit, calibrated SWAT model, modifying the conventional method of estimating effective precipitation by incorporating SWAT's distributed hydrological components, thereby improving regional IWU estimation and characterizing the gap between agricultural water supply and demand in both historical and future periods; and (3) to assess the efficacy of changes in crop planting areas, patterns, and irrigation water use efficiency for future agricultural water resource adaptive management, identifying local water resource conditions suitable for agricultural thresholds (i.e., water-suitable agricultural thresholds). The results of this study aim to provide vital theoretical and practical guidance for the sustainable development of irrigated agriculture and water resource utilization in water-stressed regions, particularly in the Heihe River basin, and globally.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The Heihe River basin is the second-largest inland river basin in Northwest China and a pivotal area within the Silk Road Economic Belt, a key component of the One Belt One Road initiative (37°55′–40°00′N, 97°30′–101°43′E). The basin extends from the source of the Heihe River in the Qilian mountains to Zhengyixia, encompassing the upper and middle reaches (Fig. 1  ). The upper reaches, at elevations ranging from 1,680 to 5,280 m, cover an area of 10,009 km2 . The middle reaches, situated between Yingluoxia and Zhengyixia at elevations of 1,300 to 1,680 m, span 25,600 km2 . The region experiences a continental arid climate, with the upper Qilian mountains receiving an annual precipitation of 300–500 mm and an average annual potential evaporation of approximately 700 mm, supported by glacial meltwater and robust vegetation. The middle reaches receive 100–250 mm of annual precipitation and experience a higher potential evaporation rate of 1,200–2,200 mm. This landscape, which harbors over 90 % of the basin's population, is characterized by farmlands and artificial agricultural oases that constitute over 90 % of the region's cultivated land (Li et al., 2016 ). This area is crucial for the majority of grain, vegetable, and seed production in Northwest China, with agricultural production heavily reliant on irrigation primarily sourced from the Heihe River and groundwater extraction (Zou et al., 2017, 2020 ). The cultivated land predominantly lies within Minle County, Shandan County, Ganzhou District, Linze County, and Gaotai County, growing crops such as spring maize, spring wheat, vegetables, oil-bearing crops, cotton, and alfalfa.  2.2 Datasets 2.2.1 Hydro-meteorological and geographical data The datasets employed in this study are detailed in Table 1  . Historical meteorological data encompass daily records of precipitation, maximum and minimum temperatures, wind speed, relative humidity, and solar radiation from eight national meteorological stations (Fig. 1 ), spanning 1964–2014, sourced from the China Meteorological Data Sharing Service System (https://data.cma.cn ). Monthly streamflow data from the Zhamashike and Qilianshan stations (1995–2000) and the Yingluoxia station (1966–1995) were utilized to calibrate and validate the SWAT model. These hydrological observations were provided by the Hydrological Bureau of Gansu Province. The geographic data comprise digital elevation model (DEM) data sourced from the ASTER Global DEM, alongside soil and land use data. The DEM resolution utilized was 30 m, while both the soil map and land use map were scaled at a 1:1,000,000 ratio. All geographical data were acquired from the National Tibetan Plateau Data Center (https://data.tpdc.ac.cn/zh-hans/ ).  2.2.2 Future meteorological data The methodology for generating future meteorological data is illustrated in Fig. 2  . The study considers three emission scenarios, ranging from low to high: RCP2.6, RCP4.5, and RCP8.5. RCP2.6 represents a scenario where radiative forcing peaks at 3 W/m2  before 2100 and then declines to 2.6 W/m2  (approximately 490 ppm CO2  equivalent) by 2100. The RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 scenarios are characterized, respectively, as a stabilization without an overshoot pathway to 4.5 W/m2  (about 650 ppm CO2  equivalent) after 2100, and a rising radiative forcing pathway leading to 8.5 W/m2  (around 1370 ppm CO2  equivalent) by 2100 (van Vuuren et al., 2011 ). Initially, a rank scoring method was employed to evaluate the performance of 23 GCMs in the CMIP5 based on observation data from meteorological stations and ERA-40 reanalysis data. A sensitivity analysis was then conducted to identify the top five GCMs that most accurately project precipitation. These models, namely CNRM-CM5, MPI-ESM-LR, MPI-ESM-MR, MRI-CGCM3, and CanESM2, were selected for future climate element projections in the Heihe River basin. Detailed information about the GCMs, rank scoring methodology, and results of the sensitivity analysis are available in the works of Guo (2017), Liu et al. (2019) , and Wang et al. (2019) . Subsequent to the GCM selection, the statistical downscaling model (SDSM) was utilized to generate future daily maximum and minimum temperatures, as well as precipitation data. The model first identified relevant predictors (atmospheric circulation factors) using daily observed meteorological data and ERA-40 reanalysis data. SDSM then established a statistical relationship between the predictands (climatic elements) and the chosen predictors. This process involved determining the parameters of the multiple regression equation through the effective dual simplex method, essentially calibrating the model. The calibration period spanned 1961–1990, with a validation period from 1991 to 2000. Optimal statistical relationships for each station were ascertained by adjusting parameters, leading to correlation coefficient (R2  ) and Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE ) values for maximum and minimum temperatures during calibration and validation periods, predominantly exceeding 0.9. The root mean squared error (RMSE ) for maximum temperature at most stations was below 2 °C and for minimum temperature within 3 °C. For precipitation, R2   exceeded 0.5 at all stations, with NSE  values ranging from 0.555 to 0.824 during the calibration period and 0.521 to 0.825 during the validation period. The RMSE  for precipitation at each station was within 20 % of the measured values (Guo, 2017; Liu et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019 ). Overall, the temperature and precipitation predictions by SDSM were deemed acceptable. Once the model was parameterized, future maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation data for the RCP2.6, RCP4.5, and RCP8.5 scenarios were downscaled using the GCM scenario generator. To ensure the effective use of statistically downscaled data in driving the SWAT model for future IWU prediction and comparison with historical periods, it is crucial to align future meteorological elements with the trend of historical observations. This alignment involved applying historical observed data to correct the trend of future climate elements (Hempel et al., 2013 ):(1) X = X obs   + ( X rcp   - X base    X base    )  X obs       where X   is the corrected temperature and precipitation data for the future period (2021–2050), X obs     is the observed temperature and precipitation data for the reference period (1976–2005), X rcp     is the future temperature and precipitation data simulated by the five GCMs (2021–2050), and X base     is the temperature and precipitation data generated by the five GCMs for the reference period (1976–2005).  2.2.3 Agricultural management data The growth periods and crop coefficients for each crop type were sourced from Zou et al. (2018) . Irrigation water use efficiency for the entire study area was determined based on the average value from a typical irrigation region, as reported in the Zhangye Water Conservancy Yearbook. Data regarding the planting area and planting patterns were acquired from the China Economic and Social Development Statistics Database (https://tongji.cnki.net/kns55/index.aspx ), the Gansu Development Yearbook, and the Gansu Rural Yearbook (Appendix A , Table S1 ).   2.3 Methods 2.3.1 SWAT model description and evaluation SWAT is a robust, physically based distributed hydrological model. Its technical specifics are elaborated in Arnold et al. (1998), Gassman et al. (2007) , and Neitsch et al. (2011) . Fig. 2  outlines the primary SWAT activities, including data processing, model setup, parameter determination, and model application. For this study, the Heihe agricultural area was divided into 35 sub-basins, which were further partitioned into 828 hydrological response units (HRUs) based on 43 soil types and 13 land use types. The soil water balance equation, a core component of hydrological modeling, simulates processes like surface streamflow, infiltration, evapotranspiration, plant water uptake, lateral flow, and percolation to shallow and deep aquifers. To account for elevation-related variations in precipitation and temperature within the basin, the SWAT model was modified, adjusting for these changes in each sub-basin to enhance simulation accuracy. Details of this model correction process are provided in Zou et al. (2018) . Sensitivity analysis was conducted using the Latin hypercube one-factor-at-a-time (LH-OFAT) method. Following literature on SWAT model parameter sensitivity (van Griensven et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2010 ) and the specific conditions of the Heihe River basin, 15 parameters were selected for this analysis (Table S2 ). The ten most sensitive parameters were then used for model calibration employing the sequential uncertainty fitting algorithm (SUFI-2) (Abbaspour et al., 2007 ). Calibration involved adjusting the relationship between annual evaporation and streamflow until the total evaporation, precipitation, and streamflow values from the watershed simulation appeared reasonable. A detailed account of the calibrated parameters and their optimal values can be found in Table S3 . A warm-up period of two years was set for the model to minimize the impact of initial condition uncertainties. Detailed calibration and validation results for the Zhamashike and Qilianshan stations are available in Zou et al. (2018) . Fig. 3   presents a comparison between the observed and simulated monthly streamflow at the Yingluoxia gauging station. The observed and simulated values were generally consistent in both quantity and trend. For the calibration period (1966–1984), NSE  was 0.79, R2   was 0.85, relative bias (RB ) was −0.92, and RMSE  was 7.02 m3 /s. During the validation period (1985–1995), NSE  was 0.77, R2   was 0.83, RB  was − 1.19, and RMSE  was 7.34 m3 /s. These results, with NSE  greater than 0.75 and R2   greater than 0.80, indicate acceptable model performance. The reliability of these findings is further supported by other streamflow simulations at the Yingluoxia gauging station using different hydrological models (Table S4 ), enhancing confidence in subsequent agricultural water scarcity assessments.  2.3.2 Calculation of IWU The Penman–Monteith (P-M) model is incorporated into the SWAT model to estimate potential evapotranspiration (Monteith, 1965 ), which is:(2) λ E = Δ · H net   - G    + ρ air   · c p  · e z o  - e z     / r a   Δ + γ · 1 + r c  / r a           where λ E    is the latent heat flux density, MJ/m2 /d; E   is the depth rate evaporation, mm; Δ   is the gradient of the saturation vapor pressure curve at air temperature, kPa/°C; H net     is the net radiation, MJ/m2 /d; G   is the heat flux density to the ground, MJ/m2 /d; ρ air     is the air density, kg/m3 ; c p    is the specific heat at constant pressure, MJ/kg/°C; e z o    is the saturation vapor pressure of air at height z  , kPa; e z    is the water vapor pressure of air at height z  , kPa; γ   is the psychrometric constant, kPa/°C; r c    is the plant canopy resistance, s/m; and r a    is the diffusion resistance of the air layer (aerodynamic resistance), s/m. In the Heihe River basin, groundwater contribution to crop water use is not considered due to the groundwater level being generally below 10 m (https://data.tpdc.ac.cn/zh-hans/ ). Additionally, soil salinity and alkalinity are not factors in this model, as recent data indicate low groundwater salinity in the basin (Gao et al., 2011 ). The SWAT model simulated various hydrological components including surface streamflow, lateral flow, and seepage.
