Often, water availability is represented by the mean annual river discharge (Hanasaki et al., 2013 ). In this context, the Yingluoxia hydrological station, situated at the basin's controlled outflow, is less influenced by human activities compared to other stations and accurately reflects surface water changes in the Heihe oasis. Consequently, data from this station are utilized to represent the entire basin's surface water availability. Furthermore, since IWU in this area constitutes over 90 % of the total water withdrawal, the ratio of IWU to streamflow is used to determine the agricultural water stress under different RCP scenarios. The calculation method is as follows:(8) WSI = ∑ i = 1  H  ∑ j = 1  J  IW U ij      Q      where Q   is the average annual streamflow, 108  m3 , and IW U ij      is calculated using Equation (7) . Specifically, when WSI < 0.1   , it indicates no water shortage; when 0.1 < W S I < 0.2   , it indicates mild water shortage; when 0.2 < W S I < 0.4   , it indicates moderate water shortage; when 0.4 < W S I < 1.0   , it indicates severe water shortage; when WSI > 1.0   , it indicates extreme water shortage (Guo and Shen, 2016 ).  2.3.4 Adaptive management scenarios To mitigate the impact of future climate change on IWU in the Heihe agricultural area, adaptive strategies focusing on the control of cultivated land extent, enhancement of irrigation water use efficiency, and adjustment of crop patterns were proposed. Predictions of IWU were made for various combinations of three sets of measures to identify the most effective adaptation strategies. These measures included maintaining crop planting area at levels recorded in 1985, 2000, 2014, or 2020; setting irrigation water use efficiency at 0.54, 0.56, 0.58, 0.60, 0.65, 0.70, 0.75, or 0.80; and altering crop planting patterns by reducing water-intensive crops and increasing low-water-consumption crops (i.e., spring maize 20 %, spring wheat 20 %, cotton 5 %, oil-bearing crops 15 %, vegetables 5 %, and other crops 35 %).    3 Results 3.1 Climate changes under three RCP scenarios To comprehend the impacts of climate change on IWU and surface water availability, changes in maximum and minimum temperatures, and precipitation for the period 2021–2050, relative to the baseline period 1976–2005, were analyzed using three RCP scenarios across five GCMs. Table 2   reveals temperature increases predicted by the five GCMs ranged between 0.76–2.37 °C (maximum) and 0.69–2.17 °C (minimum), with all three RCP scenarios indicating an upward trend. The average maximum temperature rise predicted by the five GCMs was 1.17 °C (RCP2.6), 1.46 °C (RCP4.5), and 1.63 °C (RCP8.5). Similarly, the average minimum temperature increase was predicted to be 1.07 °C (RCP2.6), 1.21 °C (RCP4.5), and 1.46 °C (RCP8.5), with the order of increases being RCP8.5 > RCP4.5 > RCP2.6. Precipitation predictions from the five GCMs varied between a decrease of 11.68 % and an increase of 7.44 %. Notably, the CANESM2 and CNRM-CM5 models predicted a precipitation decrease across different scenarios, while other models showed varied predictions under different RCP scenarios without consistent trends. The average changes in precipitation predicted by the five GCMs were −2.72 % (RCP2.6), −2.81 % (RCP4.5), and −0.37 % (RCP8.5), in descending order of magnitude: RCP4.5 > RCP2.6 > RCP8.5. Fig. 4   illustrates the forecasted variations in monthly maximum and minimum temperatures, as well as precipitation, for the period 2021–2050 in comparison to 1976–2005, as predicted by five GCMs. Despite some discrepancies among the GCMs, a general upward trend in both maximum and minimum monthly temperatures was observed across all three RCP scenarios, with most months and seasons experiencing an increase of 1.0–2.0 °C. Specifically, the monthly maximum temperatures were predicted to rise by 0.42–2.32 °C (RCP2.6), 0.82–2.75 °C (RCP4.5), and 0.49–2.91 °C (RCP8.5). Similarly, increases in monthly minimum temperatures were anticipated to be 0.41–2.23 °C (RCP2.6), 0.62–2.31 °C (RCP4.5), and 0.62–2.59 °C (RCP8.5). The highest average temperature rises predicted by the GCMs were expected in winter (November–January), with the smallest increases occurring in summer (June–August). Additionally, Fig. 4  shows that the monthly precipitation differences for the three scenarios were −14.36–17.55 % (RCP2.6), −16.11–14.35 % (RCP4.5), and −16.32–13.25 % (RCP8.5). The most significant reduction in precipitation was predicted for the summer months under all scenarios, with decreases of 7.89 % (RCP2.6), 8.54 % (RCP4.5), and 5.49 % (RCP8.5).  3.2 Spatial and temporal variations in IWU Assuming consistent planting area, patterns, and irrigation water use efficiency from 2014 for the period 2021–2050, IWU under future climate scenarios was predicted using Equations (2)–(7) , integrating land use, crop distribution, and crop coefficient data. The simulations indicated variability in future IWU among the five GCMs, with the CANESM2 model predicting the most substantial changes. However, a consistent trend was observed across all models, following the pattern RCP8.5 > RCP4.5 > RCP2.6. The average predicted IWU values, aggregated from the five GCMs, were 26.785 × 108  m3  (RCP2.6), 26.827 × 108  m3  (RCP4.5), and 26.865 × 108  m3  (RCP8.5), representing increases of 0.815 × 108  m3 , 0.857 × 108  m3  and 0.895 × 108  m3 , respectively, compared to the baseline of 25.970 × 108  m3  (Table 3  ). These findings suggest a more pronounced increase in future IWU under higher concentration emission scenarios. Table 4   presents the average IWU for different crops as predicted by the five GCMs under the three RCP scenarios. The predicted IWU for spring maize, spring wheat, cotton, oil-bearing crops, vegetables, and other crops constituted 39.58 %, 18.04 %, 0.74 %, 2.89 %, 14.15 %, and 24.60 % of the total IWU, respectively. IWU for each crop was expected to rise under future climate conditions, with the general trend being RCP8.5 > RCP4.5 > RCP2.6. Notably, the IWU for spring maize showed the most significant increase: 0.306 × 108  m3  (RCP2.6), 0.323 × 108  m3  (RCP4.5), and 0.334 × 108  m3  (RCP8.5). Conversely, cotton exhibited the smallest IWU increase: 0.007 × 108  m3  (RCP2.6), 0.007 × 108  m3  (RCP4.5), and 0.008 × 108  m3  (RCP8.5). These trends are largely attributed to spring maize being the most extensively cultivated crop in recent years (Table S1 , Li et al., 2016 ), and its per-unit-area evapotranspiration under future climate scenarios surpassing that of other crops. However, given the relatively minor proportion of cotton in the crop mix (Table S1 ), climate change is anticipated to have a minimal impact on its per-unit-area evapotranspiration. Spatial analysis of IWU within the Heihe agricultural area revealed an increasing trend across all three RCP scenarios, with variability intensifying from southwest to northeast. The central plain areas exhibited the most substantial changes, with IWU increases of 1161.96 × 104  m3  (RCP2.6), 1221.85 × 104  m3  (RCP4.5) and 1276.02 × 104  m3  (RCP8.5). In contrast, the least change was observed in the upstream mountain areas, with minimal IWU increases of only 0.31 × 104  m3  (RCP2.6), 0.32 × 104  m3  (RCP4.5) and 0.34 × 104  m3  (RCP8.5), as depicted in Fig. 5  . This pattern is primarily attributed to the concentration of cultivated land in the middle reaches of the Heihe River, where water-intensive crops such as spring maize and vegetables, significantly impacted in the three RCP scenarios, are predominantly grown (Table 4 , Li et al., 2016 ). The upper reaches, dominated by alpine forests and grasslands with minimal arable land, are expected to experience only slight changes in IWU due to climate change.  3.3 Streamflow availability and agricultural water stress Fig. S1  illustrates the interannual variation in streamflow at the Yingluoxia hydrological station as predicted by the SWAT model under both historical and future climate scenarios. The trend of future streamflow predicted by the five GCMs is consistent. Fig. 6   further depicts the changes for the period 2021–2050 relative to the 30-year average of the baseline period (1985–2014). The annual streamflow variations are notable, with amplitude fluctuations ranging from −5.03 to 4.85 × 108  m3  (RCP2.6), −4.61 to 5.08 × 108  m3  (RCP4.5), and −3.62 to 4.17 × 108  m3  (RCP8.5). Predicted annual streamflow showed a decline in many years, with the average decreases for the five GCMs being 0.28 × 108  m3  (RCP2.6), 0.46 × 108  m3  (RCP4.5), and 0.23 × 108  m3  (RCP8.5), following the order RCP4.5 > RCP2.6 > RCP8.5. Chronologically, the annual average streamflow across the three RCP scenarios is predicted to decrease by 0.22 × 108  m3  in the 2020 s and 1.42 × 108  m3  in the 2040 s compared to 1985–2014, but increase by 0.67 × 108  m3  in the 2030 s. The WSI was calculated to provide a detailed analysis of the agricultural water stress situation. The average WSI values predicted by the five GCMs for the three RCP scenarios were 1.764 (RCP2.6), 1.789 (RCP4.5), and 1.763 (RCP8.5) in the entire agricultural region. These values indicate that the available surface water resources will be insufficient to meet the future agricultural water demand, leading to extreme water shortages. Despite differences in the WSI values predicted by the individual GCMs, future water scarcity is expected to be more severe than in the historical period. This trend suggests that climate change will exacerbate the agricultural water stress situation (Table 5  ).  3.4 Effectiveness of adaptation strategies To assess the potential impact of various adaptation strategies on the increasing discrepancy between irrigation water supply and demand in the Heihe River basin under future climate change, IWU was calculated for different scenarios. These scenarios were predicated on the assumption that irrigation water use efficiency remained at 0.54 and crop types continued as in 2020. Reducing the planting area to the 1985 level of 18.213 × 104  ha would decrease IWU by 11.924–11.955 × 108  m3  for 2021–2050 and reduce the WSI from 1.938 to 1.965 to 1.154–1.170, compared to the 2020 planting area of 26.92 × 104  ha. This reduction also represents a decrease of 8.369–8.425 × 108  m3  from the 1985–2014 level and a decrease in WSI from 1.763 to 1.789 to 1.154–1.170. Reducing the planting area to the 2000 level of 19.855 × 104  ha would result in a decrease of 10.092–10.117 × 108  m3  from the 2020 level and 6.531–6.593 × 108  m3  from the 1985–2014 level, with a corresponding WSI reduction to 1.274–1.292. If the planting area is reduced to the 2014 level of 25.124 × 104  ha, IWU would decrease by 2.684–2.691 × 108  m3  from the 2020 planting area prediction, with a WSI reduction to 1.761–1.786 (Table 6  ). Adjustments in crop planting patterns show that for larger planting areas (e.g., 2020 level), IWU could decrease by about 2.9 × 108  m3  and WSI by about 0.19; for the 2014 level, IWU could decrease by about 2.0 × 108  m3  and WSI by about 0.13. It is evident that there will be a reduction in water usage from 2021 to 2050. However, for smaller planting scales (e.g., 2000 level), IWU might increase by about 0.21 × 108  m3  and WSI by 0.01; for the 1985 level, IWU might increase by about 0.42 × 108  m3  and WSI by 0.03, indicating no water savings (Table 6 ). Predictions for increased irrigation water use efficiency values (0.56, 0.58, and 0.60) for crop types and areas as in 2020, 2014, 2000, and 1985 revealed that for the 2020 planting scale, IWU decreased by 2.849–2.857 × 108  m3  and WSI by 0.188–0.190 when efficiency increased from 0.54 to 0.60. However, IWU was still 0.650–0.729 × 108  m3  greater than in 1985–2014, and WSI did not decrease from its 1985–2014 level. For the 2014 crop area, IWU decreased by 2.590–2.597 × 108  m3  and WSI by 0.170–0.173; for the 2000 crop area, IWU decreased by 1.873–1.879 × 108  m3  and WSI by 0.123–0.125; and for the 1985 crop area, IWU decreased by 1.696–1.701 × 108  m3  and WSI by 0.111–0.113. These results indicate that both IWU and WSI show a decreasing trend compared with 1985–2014, demonstrating a clear water-saving effect. Increasing irrigation water use efficiency to 0.60 and adjusting the crop planting pattern as described above would save about 2.640 × 108  m3  (2020 crop area) and 1.812 × 108  m3  (2014 crop area) more water than if the planting pattern were not changed, with a WSI decrease of 0.174 (2020 crop area) and 0.119 (2014 crop area). However, setting the crop area to the 2000 or 1985 levels would increase water consumption by 0.185 × 108  m3  or 0.378 × 108  m3  compared to not changing the planting pattern; WSI would also increase by 0.012 (2000 crop area) and 0.025 (1985 crop area) (Table 6 ). To identify the most effective adaptation strategies, IWU predictions for various combined scenarios were analyzed. According to Fig. 7  a, maintaining the crop area at the 2020 level requires increasing irrigation water use efficiency to over 0.62 to align IWU with the values from 1985 to 2014. For a crop area consistent with 2014 levels, irrigation water use efficiency needs to exceed 0.56 to match the 1985–2014 IWU values. Conversely, maintaining crop areas at the levels of 1985 or 2000 would lead to a reduction in IWU by more than 8.396 × 108  m3  (1985) and 6.561 × 108  m3  (2000) compared to the 1985–2014 values. These model results indicate that regulating the planting area is the most effective approach for future agricultural water resource management. Further consideration of the WSI values under various adaptation scenarios (Fig. 7 b), along with regional activities such as water-saving irrigation projects, forest and orchard plantings in the Heihe oasis, and increasing water demands from sectors like industry and residential use, suggests that the optimal threshold for planting area should be approximately 25 × 104  ha. This threshold, in conjunction with other measures like adjusting planting patterns and implementing water-saving transformations, is anticipated to lay the groundwork for adaptive water resource management in the future.   4 Discussion 4.1 Future climate change trends The downscaled GCMs indicate a continuing rise in temperatures in the Heihe agricultural area during 2021–2050, aligning with findings from other studies (e.g., Sun et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016a ). Research by Yu et al. (2015)  utilizing high-resolution climate modeling in Western China's arid regions suggested a general trend of decreasing precipitation, particularly pronounced in the summer months, corroborating this study's results. Prior research has often overlooked the specific adaptation of GCMs to individual regions. However, it has been noted that predictions from different GCMs can vary significantly, with accuracy closely linked to the specific study area and selected climate variables (Chen et al., 2011 ). In this study, five GCMs, chosen based on rank score and climate factor sensitivity analysis from Guo (2017), Liu et al. (2019) , and Wang et al. (2019) , were utilized to generate future climate forcing. This selection process was aimed at addressing the challenges of adapting any single model to the region, providing a spectrum of predictions from multiple models and scenarios for different climatic factors. Consequently, this approach mitigates the inherent uncertainty associated with developing future RCP scenarios based on a singular GCM. The methodology employed in this study not only reduces the uncertainty surrounding future predictions of IWU and streamflow, but also enhances the reliability of agricultural water scarcity projections. The outcomes offer a scientifically sound basis for informed water resource management in arid inland areas amidst changing climatic conditions.  4.2 IWU and streamflow estimations The precision in calculating effective precipitation is often hindered by complex factors like precipitation characteristics, soil texture, and crop type, which are not always comprehensively included in models. Prior studies have predominantly relied on empirical formulas for estimating effective precipitation. However, these empirical methods frequently encounter difficulties in accurately capturing the influence of the aforementioned factors, resulting in significant discrepancies in model results under identical conditions (Mohan et al., 1996 ). In this study, the conventional method for predicting effective precipitation was enhanced by integrating the hydrological component simulations of the spatially explicit, calibrated SWAT model. This integration notably reduced errors by considering factors such as precipitation intensity, infiltration rate, lateral flow, and soil water infiltration loss in the root zone, thereby improving the accuracy of regional IWU estimation. The streamflow of the Heihe River primarily originates from snowmelt, glacial meltwater, and summer precipitation in the upper mountains. Previous research indicates that glacial meltwater contributes only 3.4 % to the watershed outlet streamflow in the Heihe River basin's mountain areas (Yang et al., 2007 ). This suggests that variations in summer precipitation will have a more significant impact on streamflow than changes in glacial melting. The precipitation trends predicted by the five GCMs predominantly show a decrease in summer, coupled with the predicted rise in temperature that is likely to augment evapotranspiration, potentially leading to reduced future streamflow. This analysis aligns with findings from other studies, such as those by Zhang et al. (2015)  and Zhang et al. (2016b) .  4.3 Agricultural water stress evaluation The future climate scenarios' temperature and precipitation changes will jointly impact IWU. The statistical downscaling results indicate a continued warming trend in the study area, which is expected to significantly increase crop evapotranspiration. Concurrently, the anticipated reduction in upstream water supply due to decreased precipitation will further constrain agricultural water use, exacerbating the gap between water supply and demand. Moreover, economic incentives have driven an expansion in the area of cultivated land in this region, along with an increased proportion of water-intensive crops like spring maize and vegetables. If current planting scales and patterns persist, irrigation water demand is predicted to rise continually. While not explicitly considered in this study, there may also be growing demands for industrial and domestic water use, intensifying potential water shortages. It is important to note that irrigation often relies on groundwater pumping when surface streamflow is insufficient (Guo and Shen, 2016 ), which can lead to a decline in groundwater levels and possibly the formation of underground funnels, further aggravating ecological degradation. Model projections indicate that in the Heihe agricultural area, future agricultural water needs are likely to surpass available supplies. Various strategies to counteract this imbalance have been explored, such as reducing the extent of crop cultivation, modifying crop planting strategies and patterns, and enhancing the efficiency of irrigation water use. Despite anticipated ongoing deficits in water supply due to climatic shifts, the research identifies a decrease in agricultural scale as the most potent adaptive response. This approach is expected to significantly lower irrigation water consumption, thereby mitigating impending water shortages in agriculture. Consequently, there is an imperative to devise agricultural planting scales compatible with the local water resource capacity, and to implement these plans promptly to foster sustainable agricultural growth in the future. Critically, the prevalent approach of aggressively applying water-saving techniques while simultaneously expanding cultivation into previously unused lands must be reconsidered. Additional necessary strategies include adapting crop planting patterns to align with the available water supply and integrating more efficient water-saving irrigation technologies. These steps are essential for addressing the shortfall in agricultural water resources and reducing reliance on groundwater extraction.  4.4 Limitations of this study While this study provides significant insights, it is important to acknowledge its limitations. One key aspect not considered is the adaptation of crops themselves under future climate scenarios. Research indicates that climate change can significantly impact crop phenology, planting patterns, and crop variety selection (Piao et al., 2010; Song et al., 2019 ), which in turn may alter IWU. Additionally, the increasing frequency of extreme weather events such as droughts, high temperatures, rainstorms, frosts, and fog, known to adversely affect crop production (Xu et al., 2019 ), were not incorporated into our analysis. Another limitation is the exclusive focus on temperature and precipitation in assessing agricultural water demand. The anticipated rise in atmospheric CO2  concentrations is likely to influence the physiological and phenological characteristics of crops, thereby affecting hydrological parameters like evapotranspiration, streamflow, and soil moisture (Niu et al., 2013 ). Elevated CO2  levels can reduce stomatal conductance and transpiration, while simultaneously increasing photosynthetic rate, water use efficiency, leaf area, and plant height, which together can both promote and inhibit evapotranspiration (Li et al., 2019; Liao et al., 2021 ). Future work will entail a more comprehensive analysis that includes the effects of CO2  on IWU. Moreover, due to data limitations, all crops except spring maize, spring wheat, cotton, oil-bearing crops, and vegetables were classified under “other crops”, using average growing stage and crop coefficient data. This approach potentially overestimates IWU, as the “other crops” category includes plants with relatively low water consumption. Additional factors such as groundwater exploitation, reservoir construction, and various agricultural practices, which were not accounted for in the SWAT modeling process, also warrant further meticulous investigation.   5 Conclusions In this study, a refined SWAT model was developed, utilizing multisource and multiscale data, and integrating simulated hydrological components to enhance the precision of IWU estimation in the Heihe agricultural area. This refined SWAT model was then paired with downscaled climate data for three RCP scenarios, derived from five GCMs within CMIP5, to predict IWU and streamflow for the period 2021–2050. Subsequently, we assessed the impending scarcity of water resources for agriculture and evaluated the efficacy of various proposed adaptation strategies in bridging the gap between agricultural water supply and demand. The findings reveal that future agricultural water shortages are predicted to intensify compared to the baseline period of 1985–2014, primarily driven by rising temperatures and diminishing precipitation. Among the adaptation strategies examined, it was determined that controlling the scale of agricultural planting emerged as the most effective measure to address the anticipated water shortages and to secure water-suitable agricultural development for the future. The study recommends that land reclamation in the Heihe agricultural area should be confined to a threshold of approximately 25 × 104  ha. Furthermore, it is crucial to adopt strategies such as modifying crop planting patterns to better align with the available water supply and enhancing irrigation water use efficiency. These measures are essential to minimize agricultural water stress and to sustainably manage water resources in the face of changing climatic conditions. This comprehensive approach not only underscores the importance of strategic planning in agricultural water resource management but also provides valuable insights for policymakers and stakeholders in the Heihe River basin and similar arid regions globally.

1 Introduction Soil water is a crucial component of terrestrial water resources and plays a significant role in the survival, adaptation, and development of plants. Assessing the dynamics of soil water content (SWC) at multiple temporal scales can provide essential guidance for proper reforestation practices. As the global climate continues to warm, along with changes in precipitation patterns, the issue of water resources scarcity has become severe in many regions, leading to increased water stress in plants (Peng et al., 2011; Schwalm et al., 2017 ). Thus, exploring the responses and adaptation strategies of trees and forest ecosystems to soil drought is especially important in areas potentially associated with the risk of water resource deficiency. Forest trees maintain the integrity of their hydraulic systems and ensure water balance by accessing, transporting, and transpiring soil water. Tree species have adapted to escape or resist drought by adjusting their physiology and structure during drought, which involves regulating transpiration through stomatal control and enhancing root water absorption (Du et al., 2011 ). As most absorbed water (approximately 95 %) is lost as transpiration through leaf stomata, soil water budgets are often calculated to estimate the dynamics and environmental responses of transpiration water-use in trees and forest ecosystems (Kozlowski and Pallardy, 1997; Wilson et al., 2001 ). Decrease in soil water availability, either during a seasonal dry period or in rainfall reduction experiment, usually causes transpiration reduction (Kume et al., 2007; Limousin et al., 2009; He et al., 2020 ). When soil water in the shallow layer is low and drought occurs, trees tend to absorb water from deeper soil to meet their transpiration needs (Song et al., 2016; Broedel et al., 2017 ). Studies have shown significant seasonal and inter-annual variations in how trees absorb soil water in certain habitats; for instance, they may primarily rely on water in shallow soil layer during humid seasons but tap into deeper soil layers or groundwater during the dry season (Nadezhdina et al., 2008; Xi et al., 2013 ). However, different response was also reported that Robinia pseudoacacia  (black locust) shifted its water uptake upward to shallow layers after depleting deeper resources (Nan et al., 2019 ). The shift in water uptake depth should play a meaningful role in the adaptation of trees to limited soil water availability. In addition, the dependence of water absorption on the depth of the soil layer varies with differences in climate, soil type, root distribution, groundwater level, and other factors (Dawson and Pate, 1996; Snyder and Williams, 2000 ). Such knowledge is crucial for understanding the relationship between characteristics of plant water uptake and soil water availability, yet further research is needed to determine the underlying strategies, and these are probably species- or climate-specific, in response to changing soil water conditions throughout the vertical profile. The distribution of root systems also reflects the adaptation of trees to soil resources, such as water and nutrients (Jackson et al., 1997; Kuehnhammer et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2022 ). Tree species in drylands generally develop deep roots that enable them to facilitate water harvesting from a large volume of soil (Schenk and Jackson, 2002; Fan et al., 2017 ). Root systems extract water from deep soil layers during periods of soil water stress and high evaporative demands (Jackson et al., 1997; Oliveira et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2024a ). However, contradictory phenomena have also been observed, with fine root distribution and water uptake depth moving to shallow soil layers when deep soil becomes severely dry (Nie et al., 2011; Nan et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020 ). There is evidence that the origin of soil water uptake by vegetation shifts at different spatiotemporal scales and responds with varying sensitivities to climate and anthropogenic forces (Miguez-Macho and Fan, 2021; Chen et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024b ). Therefore, it is not yet clear how the root system and water absorption zone are rearranged in response to a persistent decrease in rainfall input, and whether a specific species in the Loess Plateau exhibits similar or different responses than those found in other studies. In most areas of the Loess Plateau, northern China, precipitation is the only water source that supplements soil water. Plantation forests in the semiarid areas of the Loess Plateau are subject to soil water deficiency owing to insufficient precipitation and high transpiration demand (Wang et al., 2011; Shao et al., 2018 ). While plantations of black locust have been widely implemented for swift revegetation of degraded lands and soil erosion control in this region, they are also frequently linked to the formations of a dried soil layer (DSL) and degradation of mature stands due to their substantial water consumption (Wang et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2015 ). When DSL forms, it signifies alterations in SWC and its spatial distribution. This inevitably constrains effective water availability for evapotranspiration and the sustainability of soil reservoirs (Chen et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011 ). Studies have been conducted on the physiological and ecological mechanisms of black locust adaptation to short- and long-term drought stress from different perspectives. Black locust trees in sub-humid areas generally exhibit quick stomatal regulation in response to increasing climatic driving forces and short-term soil water stress, whereas those in semiarid areas and those subjected to multi-year rainfall reduction treatment in a sub-humid area tend to maintain stomatal opening across a wide climatic amplitude (He et al., 2020; Lyu et al., 2022 ). In addition, declines in fine-root area density and biomass density in black locust forests were observed along an aridity gradient from wetter to drier sites across the Loess Plateau (Zhang et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2021 ). The available information suggests uncertainties in the physiological mechanisms underpinning responses to drought, which could be closely related to the intensity or duration of drought stress. Therefore, it is necessary to conduct quantitative investigations on the water-use characteristics and related mechanisms of black locust under varying SWC, particularly with controlled experiments and seasonal changes. Rainfall exclusion treatment is an effective on-site platform for soil water-controlled experiment which potentially generating soil water deficit in a humid or sub-humid region. In this study, we established an in situ  throughfall exclusion experiment in a black locust plantation at a sub-humid site on the Loess Plateau to investigate interactions between SWC variations and water use by the trees. The specific objectives were to (1) compare the dynamic changes and vertical patterns of SWC between plots of the same vegetation type with and without reduction of precipitation; (2) quantify the seasonal dynamics of the contribution to soil water consumption from different depths with respect to the impact of the rainfall exclusion treatment; and (3) explore the water-use strategies of black locust plantations in response to long-term rainfall reduction. Considering long-term throughfall reduction would decrease soil water availability, our original hypothesis was that soil water consumption and root distribution in the treatment plots would expand to deeper soil layers. The results of this study will contribute to a better understanding of the diverse patterns of water-use of tree species and will benefit future afforestation practices in dryland areas.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Experimental site The study was conducted at a forest station in Yongshou County, Shaanxi Province (34°48′25′′N, 107°58′50′′E, 1430 m a.s.l.), located on the Chinese Loess Plateau (Fig. 1  a). This region has a warm, sub-humid, continental monsoon climate, with an average annual mean air temperature of 10.8 °C, and an average annual precipitation of 617.3 mm (1966–2005). Most rainfall (ca. 70 %) occurs from July to September. The soil is classified as leached cinnamon soil (He et al., 2020 ). The plantation is situated on the upper position of a gentle slope, approximately 150 m higher in elevation than the nearest valley. The groundwater under such a terrain is inaccessible for utilization of plant transpiration and soil evaporation (Chen et al., 2008; Shao et al., 2018 ). The plantation was a monoculture of even-aged black locust (Robinia pseudoacacia ) at approximately 16 years of age when the plots were established in 2018. The understory vegetation is mainly composed of grasses (Artemisia argyi , Humulus scandens , Arctium lappa , and Lisea pungens ).  2.2 Throughfall exclusion In 2018, we established a large plot (20 m × 50 m) for long-term investigation and divided it into two plots (10 m × 50 m) for the rainfall exclusion treatment and a control reference. In the treatment plot, transparent waterproof panels (1.5–2 m in height) were installed between the tree rows to drain the intercepted throughfall away from the plot. Approximately 30 % of the throughfall was excluded, based on the proportion of the plot area covered by these panels (Fig. 1 b, d). To prevent the possible influence of surface runoff and soil water exchange from outside of the experimental plot, we vertically inserted an aluminum plastic sheet into the soil (80 cm below and 20 cm above the ground) around the periphery of the plot. The plots were further divided into sub-plots (10 m × 10 m) for various measurements; the data in this study covered, two throughfall-exclusion sub-plots and two controls all similar in local environments, tree distribution, and growth status. Leaf litter that fell on the panels was regularly transferred back to the soil surface to minimize the influence of factors other than rainfall exclusion.  2.3 Atmospheric measurements Meteorological variables, including solar radiation (Rs , W m−2 ), air temperature (T, °C), relative humidity (RH, %), and precipitation (P, mm), were measured in an open space at the study site. Rs , T, RH, and P were monitored using a pyranometer (Li-200; Li-Cor Inc., Lincoln, NE, USA), a thermohygrograph (HPM 110; Vaisala, Helsinki, Finland), and a tipping bucket rain gauge (Davis 7852; Davis Instruments, Hayward, CA, USA), respectively. All variables were averaged or summed every 30 min from 30 s readings before being stored on a data logger (CR1000, Campbell Scientific Instrument., Logan, UT, USA). Vapor pressure deficit (VPD, kPa) was calculated from T and RH using the formula proposed by Campbell and Norman (1998)  as follows:(1) VPD = 0.611 e  17.502 T  T + 240.97    1 - R H    ,    Daily reference evapotranspiration (ET0 , mm day−1 ) was calculated using the ET0  Calculator (version 3.2) developed by the Land and Water Division of the United Nations Food and Agricultural Organization using input parameters of air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and solar radiation (Allen et al., 2005 ).  2.4 Soil water measurement and data processing Soil volumetric water content (SWC, m3  m−3 ) was measured using 5TM or EC5 sensors connected to EM60 data loggers (Decagon Device, Pullman, WA, USA). In each sub-plot, a soil profile was cut at a representative location (≥1 m apart from a stem and avoiding directly below a canopy gap). At the commencement of the long-term throughfall exclusion experiment in 2018, we only monitored SWC within 0–1 m. Starting in April 2022, we extended the profile to a depth of 2 m. Sensors were installed in each profile at depths of 10, 30, 50, 70, 90, 120, 150, and 190 cm to represent the corresponding horizons along the entire depth range of 0–2 m (Fig. 1 c). In addition, a soil water potential (Ψs ) sensor (METER TEROS 21, Decagon) was installed at 30 cm for collecting paired data of Ψs versus  SWC. All data were recorded at 30 min intervals. The weighted average was calculated for the SWC over the entire 2 m profile (SWC0-2m , m3  m−3 ) according to the relative thickness represented by the sensors (Young et al., 1997; Wilson et al., 2001 ) as follows:(2) SWC  0 - 2   = 0.075 SWC  0.1   + 0.1 SWC  0.3   + 0.1 SWC  0.5   + 0.1 SWC  0.7   + 0.125 SWC  0.9   + 0.175 SWC  1.2   + 0.175 SWC  1.5   + 0.15 SWC  1.9   ,     where SWC0.1 , SWC0.3 , SWC0.5 , SWC0.7 , SWC0.9 , SWC1.2 , SWC1.5 , and SWC1.9  are the corresponding data for sensors at 10, 30, 50, 70, 90, 120, 150, and 190 cm, respectively. The soil water storage (SWS, mm) in a specific soil layer was calculated from the SWC and corresponding thickness as (Cheng et al., 2020 ):(3) S W S = 1000 × S W C × Δ h ,     where SWS (mm) is SWS at a specific layer (e.g. SWC0–2m ), SWC (m3  m−3 ) is mean value of SWC in the layer (e.g. SWC0–2m ), Δh (m) is layer thickness, and 1000 (mm m−1 ) is unit conversion factor. The soil water budget was used to estimate the soil water supplement (from rainfall) and loss (via transpiration and evaporation) in different soil horizons and to evaluate the relative contribution of different horizons to the total transpiration sources (Wilson et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2022 ). This method is effective for estimation of total evapotranspiration without considering its specific components. In this study, we assumed that the proportion of transpiration by understory vegetation (only grasses) and evaporation from soil surface is much smaller than that of transpiration by canopy trees, thus we could analyze the water consumption strategy of black locust in response to soil water variations. We calculated the daily change of soil water storage (ΔSWS, mm) for each soil layer and then summed cumulative values of decreasing and increasing trends separately for a specific period and a specific horizon. For example, daily ΔSWS>0 indicates that SWS has increased during that day and is denoted as ΔSWSi , whereas ΔSWS<0 represents the water consumption on that day and is denoted as ΔSWSd . Therefore, cumulative increment (ΔSWSi ) and decrement (ΔSWSd ) of SWS were calculated for all plus and minus values of daily ΔSWS throughout a specific period, respectively. ΔSWSd  values were used to estimate water consumption via absorption by roots in different soil layers.  2.5 Quantitative evaluation of DSL formation The widely accepted criterion for determining the formation of DSL at a certain soil depth is on the basis of SWC decreasing to less than the stable field capacity (SFC), usually 60 % of field capacity (FC) (Wang et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2010 ). We established a soil moisture characteristic curve for our study plot according to the paired data set of Ψs  and SWC that were measured at 30 cm depth at two profiles (y = 0.591x-0.1386 ). The FC was calculated as 0.369 m3  m−3  which corresponds to 30 kPa, and the SFC was 0.221 m3  m−3  which served as the threshold for the SWC of DSL. Consequently, below the depth of rainfall infiltration, soil layers with a SWC less than 0.221 m3  m−3  were considered as DSL.  2.6 Sampling of fine root distribution To explore the fine root development in response to rainfall exclusion treatment and the consequent changes in SWC along vertical profiles, we comparatively investigated fine root (<2 mm diameter) distribution in both control and treatment plots. Considering the similarity in growth condition among these even-aged trees, we did not survey the root distribution before the implementation of the experiment. At the end of July 2023, three trees with approximately the average stem diameter and canopy area were selected from each subplot. Two soil cores were extracted using a soil auger (6.5 cm internal diameter) 50 cm from each stem on opposite sides. Soil samples were collected for 0–10, 10–30, 30–50, 50–70, 70–100, 100–150, and 150–200 cm, respectively. Fine roots were collected from the soil using forceps, and the remaining root segments in the soil were gently washed in a 0.1 mm sieve. All fine roots were washed to remove fixed soil residue. Finally, fine roots were oven-dried at 70 °C to a constant mass and weighed to the nearest 0.001 g (Sun et al., 2022 ). Root dry weight density (RDWD, kg m−3 ) was calculated by dividing the dry weight of fine roots by the corresponding soil volume.  2.7 Data processing and analyses To investigate the dynamics of soil water consumption in different layers and its dependency on environmental factors, we selected all consecutive rainless days of ≥ 5-day duration during the 2022 growing season (May–September) as dry events for analysis. The longer dry events were separated into multiple events (each lasting 4–6 d) to avoid changes in response relationships. For each dry event, ΔSWS at depths of 0–55, 55–100, 100–160, and 160–200 cm was calculated, i.e. the summation of ΔSWSd  within the horizon and the period as described in section 2.4 . We analyzed the relationships between ΔSWSd  and multiple factors (SWC at different soil depths and ET0 ) using Pearson correlations aiming to tease out the critical factors influencing soil water consumption at different depths. To compare the rooting depths of black locust in the control and treatment plots, the vertical distribution of cumulative RDWD throughout the soil profile was modeled using the following equation (Gale and Grigal, 1987 ):(4) Y = 1 - β  d  ,     where Y is the proportion of RDWD accumulated from the soil surface to depth d  (cm) and β  is a root extinction coefficient showing the fraction of root biomass above depth d , with a value between 0 and 1. A high β  value indicates a greater proportion of roots extending to the deep soil. The programs R 4.2.2 (R Core Team, Vienna, Austria) and SPSS 22.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) were used for statistical analyses. Graphics were generated using the Origin 2021 software (OriginLab Corp. Northampton, MA, USA).   3 Results 3.1 Trends in climatic factors and SWC during the study period Monthly values of precipitation, effective precipitation (>5 mm event−1 ), and ET0  throughout the study period (2021–2023) are shown in Fig. 2  . Although climatic factors showed clear seasonal trends, there were also differences among years for the same months. During the 2021 growing season, precipitation gradually increased and peaked in September. In 2022, monthly precipitation peaked in July, and was much smaller in other months compared to 2021; total rainfall in the 2022 growing season was less than that in 2021. In 2023, although data collection in July, rainfall in May and June were markedly greater than those in previous years. The ET0  values recorded from May to September in 2021 and 2022 were 781 and 754 mm, respectively. ET0  in this area was always higher than precipitation in the corresponding periods, suggesting that the ecosystem is susceptible to water deficits. Around 80 % of total precipitation contributes to effective rainfall, while the remaining 20 % typically occurring in low-intensity events < 5 mm, which hardly supplements soil water. Dynamic variations in daily precipitation and SWC along the soil profiles during the investigative period (2021–2023) are shown in Fig. 3  . The total precipitation was 720, 662, and 412 mm for 2021, 2022, and the early months of 2023 (until July 21), respectively. Precipitation occurred mainly from May to October, coinciding with the general distribution pattern in the region based on long-term records. The SWC of each plot was markedly influenced by precipitation during the growing season (May–September), especially in the top layers (i.e., 0–35 cm), reflecting recharge from rainfall events. Surface SWC (particularly in the 0–15 cm layer) was noticeably sensitive to fluctuations in ET0 . Regarding the vertical trend, the layers of 0–15 cm and 55–100 cm were drier than the other layers, which is attributable to surface evaporation and consumption by the majority of the roots (see section 3.4  in details). The distinct layering of SWC in the treatment plot suggests marked water consumption in 55–100 cm, and formation of a temporary DSL (SWC<0.221 m3  m−3 , see section 2.5  for analyses in details). Despite this soil drying in the treatment plot, sufficient recharge by concentrated rainfalls could induce DSL recovery to SWC of ≥ 0.221 m3  m−3 , as observed in the late months of 2021 and in May–July of 2023.  3.2 Cumulative changes in SWS and vertical contributions to water consumption over the study period Based on the overall trends of SWC as described in the above section, we investigated changes in SWS (ΔSWSi  and ΔSWSd  as described in section 2.4 ) for four major horizons during the growing season of 2022 and 2023 (Fig. 4  ). For both plots, ΔSWSi  corresponded with replenishment by rainfall events across all layers, and the dynamic changes were the same. There were net increases in SWS in both plots during both investigation periods (ΔSWSi  > ΔSWSd ), and replenishment and reduction of SWS mainly occurred in the top 0–55 cm, with the proportions ranging from 41.1 % to 69.0 % during the two periods. Over the 100 cm profile, i.e., including the layer of 55–100 cm, cumulative ΔSWSi  accounted for 70.3 % and 74.5 % of the total increment during the 2022 period in the control plot and in the treatment plot, respectively (Fig. 4 b and c). Corresponding proportions in 2023 were 61.0 % and 70.8 % (Fig. 4 g and h). Thus, replenishment in the treatment plot was less than in the control plot and tended to be limited to the shallow layer, whereas the infiltration in the control plot was deeper. There were differences in the amounts and in the proportional contributions of cumulative ΔSWSd  in different layers between the two plots (Fig. 4 d, e, i, and j). During the 2022 investigative period, cumulative ΔSWSd  was much lower (291.2 mm in total) and the proportion in the 0–55 cm soil layer was much higher (69.0 %) in the treatment plot than in the control plot (366.5 mm and 56.9 %, respectively). Overall, most of the replenishment and consumption appeared within the 0–100 cm soil layer. Particularly, the cumulative ΔSWSd  in the 100–200 cm horizon was only 7.2 % in the treatment plot. Following several large rainfall events in June to early July and the consequent replenishment of soil moisture, water consumption in both plots substantially increased. Nevertheless, in contrast to the condition in control plot, the 100–200 cm soil layer in the treatment plot contributed very little to the total water consumption (Fig. 4 d and e). This low value indicates that trees in the treatment plot minimally utilized soil water deeper than 1 m in depth. This result supports the suggestion of DSL formation in the 55–100 cm layer, as described in the previous section. Similarly, total cumulative ΔSWSd  in the treatment plot (176.4 mm) was less than that of the control plot (197.3 mm) in the 2023 investigative period. However, the proportion of cumulative ΔSWSd  in the shallow layer (0–100 cm) of the treatment plot did not exceed that of the control plot in this period, whereas there was an increased contribution from the next layer (100–160 cm) in the treatment plot around late May. The proportion of cumulative ΔSWSd  in the 100–160 cm layer should include substantial redistribution upward to the DSL which would also contribute to overall consumption. This increasing trend of cumulative ΔSWSd  in the 100–160 cm layer ceased with the substantial recharge by rainfall across the 0–160 cm horizon in June.  3.3 Soil layer contributions to water consumption as related to evapotranspiration controlling factors The possible dependence of soil water consumption and vertical contributions on SWC and the driving force of evapotranspiration was examined by evaluation of correlations between ΔSWSd  across the soil profile and SWC at each soil depth and ET0  for dry events in the 2022 growing season (Fig. 5  ). Rainy days were frequent in the June/ July growing period of 2023, hence there were insufficient dry events for analysis. While of ΔSWSd  of each layer positively corelated with ΔSWSd(sum) , only ΔSWSd(100–160cm)  in the control plot reached statistical significance (p  ≤ 0.01) in this column of the correlation matrices, suggesting a major contribution of this layer to total water consumption in the control plot. A significant correlation was not detected in the treatment plot, although the shallow layers (0–55 and 55–100 cm) tended to have larger contributions. In addition, both ΔSWSd(sum)  and ΔSWSd(100–160cm)  were significantly positively correlated with ET0  (p  ≤ 0.05 or p  ≤ 0.01) in the control plot, suggesting a dominant driving force of evapotranspiration demand (meteorological factors) on water consumption in the control plot. However, in the treatment plot, no significant correlation was detected between ET0  and soil water consumption in any layer, suggesting that water consumption was likely affected most by SWC, and ET0  was non-dominant in the treatment plot. The other columns in the correlation matrices illustrate the potential effects of SWC on water consumption in different soil layers. In the shallow layers (0–55 and 55–100 cm), ΔSWSd  was positively correlated with SWC in both plots, with the correlations of ΔSWSd(0–55cm)  with SWC(0–55 cm)  or SWC(55–100 cm)  being statistically significant. However, ΔSWSd  in the deeper layers (100–160 and 160–200 cm) was negatively correlated with SWC in the shallow layers (0–50 and 55–100 cm) (p  ≤ 0.05 except for SWC(55–100cm)  in the treatment plot). This indicates that the relatively abundant soil water in the shallow layers generally alleviates the consumption in deeper layers, increasing the contribution of the surface layer. The lack of a significant relationship for the treatment plot is consistent with the findings as detailed in the previous section, i.e., that the contribution of ΔSWSd  by the deep layers (100–160 and 160–200 cm) was much less and could not be affected by the limited change of SWC(55–100 cm) . Similarly, ΔSWSd  at 55–100 cm was negatively correlated with SWC in the 100–160 and 160–200 cm layers, suggesting that an increase in soil water in deeper layers could reduce the relative contribution of water consumption in the 55–100 cm layer (ΔSWSd(55–100cm) ). These relationships were highly significant (p  ≤ 0.01) in the treatment plot, supporting the previous inference that a DSL was formed at 55–100 cm and that there was upward infiltration to this layer.  3.4 Distribution of fine roots in response to change in SWC The vertical distribution of roots in the soil profile showed similarities and differences between plots (Fig. 6  ). RDWD decreased exponentially with increasing soil depth in both plots, with roots mainly present in the 0–100 cm horizon. RDWD was generally higher in the treatment plot than the control plot, particularly in the soil surface layer (0–10 cm, 0.83 ± 0.1 vs. 0.38 ± 0.06 kg m−3 , respectively). Changes in the cumulative fine root fractions (y) with depth (d ) were well fitted by the non-linear function (Equation (4)  for both plots (Fig. 6 b); parameters derived from regression analyses are shown in Table 1  . The root extinction coefficients (β ) indicated that root system in the treatment plot were more concentrated in the soil layer near the surface. Both D50  and D90  were smaller in the treatment plot than the control plot. As the plots were based on an even-aged plantation with similarity in growth condition before implementation of the experiment, these results suggest that changes in soil water caused by rainfall exclusion treatment altered fine root distribution pattern, which in turn affected the relevant contribution of water consumption from different soil layers.   4 Discussion 4.1 SWC profile varies with water repenlishment and consumption and affects relative contributions to water consumption from different layers In forest plantations in this region, soil water in the surface layer is subject to frequent fluctuations due to the transpiration of trees and understory grasses, surface evaporation, and inputs from rainfall events. Precipitation affects soil moisture through the infiltration of rainwater (Wang et al., 2012; Cheng et al., 2020 ). Soil water replenishment including the depth to which it is replenished, mainly depends on the characteristics of rainfall events, with very small amounts (e.g., < 5 mm) hardly affecting even the soil surface (intercepted by vegetation canopy). In the present study, the deeper layers were not recharged until concentrated and heavy rains occurred, which was only occasionally (Figs. 3 and 4 ). The result was consistent with the report by Yang et al. (2014) , which indicated no significant differences in deep soil moisture were found between different vegetation types, meaning that soil moisture in deep layers was relatively stable. However, significant effects of precipitation on deep soil moisture were also found in a multi-year observation of a plantation and a natural forest (Cheng et al., 2020 ). The discrepancy may be attributed to the long experimental period, which covered various amounts and patterns of precipitation events. Replenishment in each soil layer and the overall depth of replenishment from each rainfall event were much less in the treatment plot than in the control. In addition, during each rain-free period within the growing season, SWC showed a decreasing trend in both plots, notably in the surface layer (0–15 cm). This is consistent with the general understanding that surface soil water is easily influenced by plant transpiration and soil evaporation (Tromp-van Meerveld and McDonnell, 2006; Seneviratne et al., 2010 ). Another rainfall exclusion experiment conducted in the same region reported that soil water deficits occurred mainly in the 0–100 cm layer but not in deeper layers (Zhang et al., 2022 ). This is supported by our results in that the proportions of cumulative ΔSWSd  and ΔSWSd  were highest in the 0–55 cm layer and then the 55–100 cm layer. The absorption and utilization of soil water by the same tree species may exhibit spatiotemporal variability (Yang et al., 2017; Antunes et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018 ). In our study, the treatment plot showed more consumption of soil water in the upper layers (0–55 and 55–100 cm), with only 7.2 % of the contribution from 100–200 cm, which was much less than that in the control plot. The temporal patterns of soil water absorption also vary with deep-root systems. When roots shift to areas with higher soil moisture due to water stress, the water absorption pattern may become more closely aligned with the distribution of soil water (Gao et al., 2018; Kuehnhammer et al., 2020 ). This difference in deep soil water consumption correlated with the difference in root distribution patterns between the control and treatment plots, in that the treatment plots contained a larger proportion of fine roots in shallow layers (Fig. 6 ). Such variations in water consumption from different layers could be attributed to lowered SWC due to the rainfall exclusion, particularly in the sub-shallow layer (55–100 cm). A study on poplar plantations also suggested that soil water deficit and DSL formation limited the zone of soil water consumption to the shallow layer (Liang et al., 2022 ). Soil water use can also vary interannually following fluctuations in precipitation, because SWC and SWS in different soil layers change with the water consumption and replenishment throughout the seasons. Although the plantation growth may not change greatly within a few years, a wide interannual variation in the precipitation pattern is frequently observed. The uneven distribution of precipitation leads to substantially seasonal variations in soil moisture, with both shallow and deep soil layers potentially experiencing temporary desiccation (Liang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024b ). Concentrated rainfall events, even occasional, may cause substantial infiltration into the relatively deep soil layer, resulting in partial recovery of a temporary DSL (Chen et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2011; He et al., 2022 ).  4.2 Formation of DSL blocked water consumption in deeper layers under continuous reduction in rainfall input Correlation analysis revealed a major contribution of ΔSWSd(100–160cm)  to total water consumption and a dominant driving force of evapotranspiration demand (meteorological factors) in the control plot during consecutive rainless, dry events (Fig. 5 ). This supports the general assumption that trees can increase their utilization of deep soil water under conditions of increasing evapotranspiration demand (Breda et al., 1995; Grossiord et al., 2017 ). We expected to observe a similar response for trees subjected to precipitation reduction (i.e., more uptake of deeper soil water in the treatment plot relative to the control plot). However, our results showed soil water consumption was limited to the upper 0–100 cm in the treatment plot. This deviation from our original hypothesis might have resulted from the formation of a temporary DSL in the 55–100 cm soil layer, which blocked the utilization of soil water in deeper layers (100–200 cm). Water deficits in the deep soil are frequently observed following afforestation of black locust in semi-arid and sub-humid climates (Deng et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020 ). Water demand rapidly increases with forest growth and water consumption temporarily shifts from the upper to deeper soil layers; but the uptake would shift upward again when the water consumption from deeper soil reaches a certain level (Nan et al., 2019 ). Wu et al. (2021)  suggested that deep soil water is not a sustainable water source for tree plantations in semiarid and sub-humid areas, as is observed in humid areas. Therefore, changes in water utilization at different depths is a response mechanism for plants to adapt to changing soil water conditions. The formation of a DSL under continuous reduction in rainfall input, in the treatment plot, blocked the consumption of deep soil water. Water consumption by vegetation is mainly regulated by two factors: atmospheric evapotranspiration demand and soil water supply, and either can be a dominant factor (Novick et al., 2016; Jiao et al., 2019 ). Under soil water deficit, the hydraulic resistance from the soil to the plant canopy increases, and the sensitivity of stomatal conductance to the atmospheric environment tends to decrease (Baert et al., 2015; Jiao et al., 2019; Lyu et al., 2022 ). Based on analysis of evapotranspiration patterns under various SWC, Chen et al. (2022)  quantified the thresholds of SWS that determine different evapotranspiration patterns in two semiarid forest ecosystems. Water consumption in the treatment plot in our study was mostly controlled by soil water conditions, and water availability along the soil profile played an important role in overall water uptake. The ability to modify water use at different depths to cope with effective soil moisture depends on the depth and distribution of functional roots (Ehleringer and Dawson, 1992 ). When surface soil water cannot be obtained in areas with limited water resources, plants are usually deep rooted and utilize deep soil water (Nippert and Knapp, 2007; Yang et al., 2015; Fan et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2021; Zou et al., 2022 ). The root systems of many trees can shift between extracting water from shallow- and deep-sources, based on water availability across the soil profile (Williams and Ehleringer, 2000; Nie et al., 2011; Prieto et al., 2012 ). The distribution pattern of root systems in the treatment plot of the present study did not support the expectation that more soil water would be absorbed from deeper layers, but was consistent with our finding that most water was absorbed from the surface layers. A possible reason for this is that under a continuous reduction in rainfall input, a DSL formed in the major absorption layer (55–100 cm) and blocked water consumption from the deeper layers (Fig. 7  ). There was still uncertainty about the development of root systems in response to changing SWC as the temporal change of root distribution was not investigated in this study. Sampling of fine roots monthly across the growth season is expected in future investigations. Nevertheless, the data of root distribution in this study should represent an integrated result of multiple effects in the previous seasons, as a soil water deficit can affect subsequent water uptake and physiological activity of plants over a longer time period (Yang et al., 2015 ). Thus, the differences in root distribution patterns between the two plots in our study may also reflect the time lag effect of changes in soil water consumption and inputs. In addition, the groundwater level in the Loess Plateau of China ranges from tens to hundreds of meters, and the water absorption depth of the roots is not influenced by groundwater. Trees only use the available soil water for necessary carbon assimilation activity within the reach of their root systems. Variations in the vertical distribution of roots may imply a trade-off between the activity of or allocation to surface and deep root systems (Williams and Ehleringer, 2000 ), reflecting the relationship between soil water status and tree water use strategies.   5 Conclusions During consecutive rainless, dry periods, water consumption in the control plot was significantly correlated with ET0  and SWC in the 100–160 cm soil layer. The treatment plot was subjected to soil water limitation, and the contribution of water consumption was limited to the 0–100 cm layer. The sustained reduction in rainfall input in the treatment plot intensified soil water consumption from shallow layers, resulting in the formation of a DSL at 55–100 cm. Additionally, root distribution in the treatment plot was concentrated in relatively shallower layers than the control plot. Thus, DSL formation hindered root development and water consumption from deep soil layers in the treatment plot. These results contribute to our understanding of the water-use characteristics of black locust plantations under various condition of SWC and provide useful information for water resource management under changing climates in dryland regions.
1 Introduction The International Union for Conservation of Nature’s commission of inquiry on peatlands (Bain et al., 2011 ) identifies peatlands as the largest terrestrial carbon store globally, which, while covering about 3 % of land area, stores more carbon than all other terrestrial vegetation in the world combined. Peatlands can also be important sources of drinking water, such as in the UK, where over 43 % of the population is supplied with water which originates from catchments with peatland areas (Ferretto et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2018 ). However, the degradation and destruction of peatlands continues worldwide despite their known importance. Indeed, drained and damaged peatlands contribute about 3 % of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions (Evans et al., 2021; Leifeld and Menichetti, 2018 ). Anthropogenic activities that can damage peatlands include drainage, urbanisation, agricultural conversion, burning, mining, and climate change. Peatland drainage causes subsidence and compression of the peat, reducing macro porosity and resulting in reduced water storage capacity (Liu et al., 2020 ). The aerobic zone created following drainage can turn peatlands into major sources of carbon dioxide (Bain et al., 2011 ). Channelisation of peatlands, potentially from urbanisation or mining, is associated with increased water discharges and runoff (Cowley et al., 2016 ). Such channelisation has been shown to reduce water storage (Cowley et al., 2018a ) and result in increased fluvial carbon exports and emissions (Cowley et al., 2018b ). Agricultural conversion of peatlands generally involves enhanced drainage or the lowering of the water table (Bain et al., 2011 ). “Managed burning” of peatlands has also been shown to increase carbon exports and decrease primary productivity (Worrall et al., 2010 ), with likely secondary consequences to hydrology. This may include an increased depth to the water-table and increased water table variability, leading to increased dissolved organic carbon concentrations in peatland rivers (Brown et al., 2015 ). Dewatering associated with open cut mining has been shown to increase deep seepage rates (Leclair et al., 2015 ), resulting in deeper water tables, larger downward gradients, and landscape scale subsidence of up to 15 cm (Balliston and Price, 2023 ). Further, longwall mining has been shown to potentially influence the water retention capacity of peatland soils (Mason et al., 2021 ). Climate change impacts on peatlands include hydrologic impacts and the reduction in the carbon sink capacity (Chaudhary et al. (2020 )). Wattendorf et al. (2010)  found that peatlands in Baden-Württemberg, Germany would have longer lasting periods of low water levels despite increases in annual precipitation. Water table drawdown associated with increased evaporative water losses under climate change could lead to greater water table fluctuations and denser, more degraded peat, which would intensify peat degradation (Whittington and Price (2006 )). These potential threats necessitate the need for a detailed understanding of existing and potentially impacted peatland systems, including baseline water budget estimates and hydrology. Research on northern hemisphere peatlands has significantly enhanced the understanding of their hydrology. Reeve et al. (2000)  highlighted the importance of the underlying mineral substrate to broader peatland hydrology, showing that lateral flow in the upper peat layers dominated when the mineral soils were of low permeability. Similarly, Fraser et al. (2001)  showed that there was a large range in hydraulic conductivity between the upper and lower layers of peat (the acrotelm and catotelm, following the Ingram (1978)  diplotelmic model of peat structure) in a Canadian bog, with limited variation below the acrotelm. Further emphasising the importance of peat structure and hydrophysical controls, Rezanezhad et al. (2016)  demonstrated how the relationship between depth and hydraulic conductivity is linked to peat’s dual-porosity properties, with both open/connected, and dead-ended or isolated pores. Lastly, Balliston et al. (2018)  identified how microtopography can drive preferential flow paths in subarctic bogs through solute release experiments. These findings are particularly relevant to our study of upland swamps in the Sydney basin (Australia), as they highlight hydrological processes and dynamics that are critical for understanding of local peatlands. Upland swamps have physical analogues to the acrotelm and catotelm of northern hemisphere peatlands, but the hydrological definition of the catotelm cannot be applied due to wide fluctuations in water table depth (Fryirs et al., 2014 ). Similar to fens, upland swamps are hydrologically dependent on shallow groundwater perched on the underlying sandstone bedrock (Young, 2017 ). These swamps are known for their water storage and water supply functions, as well as their capacity to maintain baseflows to lower catchments during dry periods (Cowley et al., 2020 ). This service ensures their importance within Sydney’s drinking water supply. In addition to hydrologic services, the upland swamps are recognised Endangered Ecological Communities (EEC)(Australian Government, 2005 ) and they provide habitat for groundwater dependent species. This includes the endangered giant dragonfly (Petalura gigantea ) (Baird and Burgin, 2016 ) and the vulnerable Deane’s boronia (Fletcher and Erskine, 2012 ). Many upland swamps in the Sydney basin have been impacted by longwall mining for coal (Krogh, 2007 ). Within the Metropolitan and Woronora ‘Special Areas’ (WaterNSW, 2023 ) the combined area of upland swamps is 29.9 km2 . Of this area, about 16.1 km2  (about 54 %) overlie mining activities (WaterNSW, unpublished data, 2024 ). Coal mining in the Sydney basin has occurred since the early 1900 s (Reynolds, 1977 ), with longwall mining commencing in the Sydney catchment area during the 1960 s (Advisian, 2016 ). Longwall mining involves the removal of a coal seam via rectangular subsurface ‘panels’, typically causing the overlying strata to collapse into the mine void as it progresses (versus board and pillar mining where the mining ceiling is supported) (Commonwealth of Australia, 2014a ). The resultant subsurface fracturing can lead to vertical subsidence at the land surface, typically ranging from one to two metres, or exceeding half the thickness of the extracted coal seam (Commonwealth of Australia, 2014a ). The formation of a collapsed zone above the longwall results in groundwater drainage to a height that has been empirically linked to the width and thickness of the panel, and the depth of the panel below the surface (Tammetta, 2013 ). Considering the international adoption of longwall mining for coal (Lechner et al., 2016 ), there is a need to understand its impacts on surface environments in the context of studies of other mining impacts on peatlands such as Leclair et al. (2015)  and Balliston and Price (2023) , and further the understanding of longwall mining impacts on uplands swamps detailed by Mason et al. (2021) . This need is particularly important when the threatened surface features are already endangered, as is the case for the swamp EECs in the Sydney basin. The longwall mining in the Sydney basin uses panel dimensions that are likely to result in the complete groundwater drainage above many extracted panels, based on the Tammetta (2013)  equation. To date, the impacts of longwall mining on surface water hydrology and swamp soil moisture are documented (IEPMC, 2019; Krogh, 2007; Mason et al., 2021 ), but the changes to swamp storage levels are unknown. Furthermore, the contribution to surface flow from intact swamp sediments is not well understood beyond assumptions regarding the primary water holding textural units of the swamps. Therefore, the major questions remain: how does swamp storage function and contribute to surface water flows, and what are the impacts of longwall mining on swamp storage and discharges? Here, we address this question using the most detailed study (to our knowledge) of peat swamp hydrology before/after a site is undermined by longwall mining. Using a before-after, control impact (BACI) based experimental design (Green, 1979 ), we examine the hydrology of intact swamps, and the impacts of longwall mining on surface water flows and groundwater storage. We consider the implications of our findings in the context of water management in Australia, and the implications for Ecologically Sustainable Development (ESD) and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which are being implemented by Australian governments.  2 Methods 2.1 Regional setting In the state of New South Wales (NSW), Australia, there are two main classifications of peat-forming swamps: Temperate Highland Peat Swamps on Sandstone (THPSS), and Coastal Upland Swamps in the Sydney Basin (CUSSB). Both are listed as endangered ecological communities under state and federal legislation. While the classifications differ based on altitude, Fryirs et al. (2019)  found limited variability in geomorphological structure and function between THPSS and CUSSB swamps, and used the term ‘swamp’ to describe the systems as a whole. This practice has been adopted herein.  2.2 Study swamps We monitored groundwater levels and surface water discharge from two swamps in the Sydney drinking water catchment (Fig. 1  ). The sites were chosen as they reflect typical characteristics of upland swamps, being headwater swamps in broad U-shaped valleys, with a general sequence of vegetation communities of Ti-tree thicket, Cyperoid heath and Banksia thicket, and Restoid heath or Sedgeland (Keith and Myerscough, 1993 ). Accessibility, and their status in the context of mine planning (Swamp 14 was undermined within the study period, Swamp 7 is a reference site) were also factors considered when selecting the monitored swamps. Swamp 7 is at an elevation of around 350 m Australian Height Datum (AHD, equivalent to metres above sea level), has an area of 25,086 m2 , and a catchment area of 671,600 m2 . Swamp 14 is at an elevation of around 385 m AHD, has an area of 24,966 m2 , and catchment area of 392, 020 m2  (to the v-notch). Data collected included topography, sediment depths, soil profiles, rainfall, streamflow, and water table depths. We surveyed the surface topography of the swamps using a Real-time kinematic GPS, and at each survey point a 10 mm diameter steel rod was pushed into the swamp sediments until bedrock or refusal was reached. These data were used to create grids of the surface topography and sediment depth of the swamps, and to guide the locations for installation of monitoring wells. In Swamp 7, 10 monitoring wells were installed, and a v-notch weir was installed in the watercourse about 50 m downstream of the swamp. In Swamp 14, 11 monitoring wells were installed upstream of an existing v-notch weir. The streamflow data from the weir was used in this study. Surface flows from both swamps occur exclusively through the instrumented watercourses. The monitoring well arrays were sufficient to provide lateral and longitudinal coverage of the swamps for the purpose of spatially interpreting water table levels. It is noted that the monitoring well locations shown in Fig. 1  are not all within the swamp boundaries according to the Fryirs et al. (2019)  mapping, but all monitoring wells were installed within swamp sediments, reflecting minor differences in swamp boundary delineation based on field observations as opposed to prior studies which used aerial imagery. Monitoring wells were installed using a hand auger, to the maximum achievable depth at each location. These depths ranged between 1.25 and 3.35 m below ground level (bgl) at Swamp 7, and between 0.6 and 1.85 m bgl at Swamp 14. Each monitoring well was constructed with 50 mm diameter PVC slotted pipe, with a geofabric sock and basal cap. All monitoring wells were screened along their entire length. Each monitoring well was fitted with a Solinst Levelogger 5 pressure transducer, and a Solinst Barologger 5 was installed at each swamp to allow for atmospheric pressure corrections. These instruments were programmed to measure at one-hour intervals. Soil profiles were recorded for each site and each of the major swamp sediment layers as described in Cowley et al. (2020)  were identified. Samples were collected from each of the major horizons encountered, which were later analysed for organic carbon content and to allow for bulk density and porosity estimations. A Solinst Levelogger 5 pressure transducer was installed at the v-notch weir at Swamp 7 to monitor water levels in the weir pool. We were provided with data from the Van Essen TD-Diver pressure transducer installed on the existing weir at Swamp 14. Both pressure transducers recorded data every half hour. As flow can only be reliably measured when water levels are within the ‘V’ of the weir, the geometry of the weirs limited the flow gauging to a maximum of about 500 m3 /day at Swamp 14, and about 2,000 m3 /day at Swamp 7. A meteorological station was installed at each swamp to measure data hourly. Rainfall was measured using 0.2 mm tipping bucket rain gauges that measure precipitation in mm. Air temperature and relative humidity were measured with a digital sensor, which returned data in degrees Celsius and percent humidity. Wind speed and direction were measured using wind monitors that provide data in m/s and degrees. Dew point was measured in degrees Celsius using a psychrometer. Net radiation was measured in W/m2  with a net radiometer. The study period for Swamp 14 was August 2012 to August 2022, and the study period for Swamp 7 was January 2019 to August 2022.  2.3 Data collection and analysis Data were downloaded in the field from the monitoring well and v-notch pressure transducers and corrected using the barometer data. These data were summarised into time series using the mean daily water table depth for the monitoring wells and the daily total discharge over the weirs. Discharge over the v-notch weirs was calculated using the v-notch weir formula (Bos, 1989 ) with a discharge coefficient (Cd ) of 1.365, which is the coefficient given by Bos (1989)  for a v-notch weir without depth and width effects as per Equation (1) , where H is the water depth above the base of the v-notch (m), and discharge (Q) is measured in L/s. Flows above the v-notch limits were calculated the same way and are likely underestimates, but these data have been retained for their use in indicating flow magnitude.(1) Q = 1.365 × H  2.5        Kriging was used to create daily water table grids within the spatial limits of the swamp boundary shapefiles (Fryirs et al., 2019 ). The kriging was implemented in Surfer® (Golden Software, LLC) with the default linear variogram. Volumes between the resulting grids and the bottom of each of the major sediment layers were calculated using the trapezoidal rule. Daily groundwater volumes within the swamp sediments were then calculated based on the average saturated soil capacity (the best available proxy for porosity) of each of the major sediment layers. Saturated soil capacity was estimated as the loss in weight of dried soil (oven dried at 40 °C), divided by the saturated soil weight. Water table lowering during the pre- and post-undermining periods was assessed by identifying periods of three days where the storage volume in the swamp decreased on both the second and third day of the period. Daily potential reference crop evapotranspiration (ET0 ) data for Cordeaux Dam (Station 68018, about 7.6 km north east of Swamp 14) was sourced from Queensland Government’s SILO (Scientific Information for Land Owners) (Jeffrey et al., 2001 ), which is calculated using the Penman Monteith equation from Allen (1998)  (Equation (2) . SILO data were used because of gaps in the data for the on-site meteorological station. A crop coefficient of 0.75 for eucalypt forest (Alves et al., 2013 ) was adopted to convert the reference crop ET to represent the potential ET in the catchment surrounding the swamps in the modelling. For ET from the swamp storage, a crop coefficient of 1 was used, which is typical for wetlands with moist soil or standing water (Allen, 1998 ). As this crop coefficient results in ET values equal to the ET0  − which assumes a reference grass height of 12 cm − it may not be ideal for upland swamps with their variable vegetation communities. However, it is the best available crop coefficient supported by the literature.(2) ET  0  = 0.408 Δ R n  - G    + γ 900 T + 273   u 2  ( e s  - e a  )   Δ + γ ( 1 + 0.034 u 2  )        Where: ET0  = reference evapotranspiration (mm day−1 ]. Rn  = net radiation at the crop surface [MJ m−2  day−1 ]. G=soil heat flux density [MJ m−2  day−1 ]. T=mean daily air temperature at 2 m height [°C]. u2  = wind speed at 2 m height [m s−1 ]. es  = saturation vapor pressure [kPa]. ea  = actual vapor pressure [kPa]. es  − ea  = saturation vapor pressure deficit [kPa].
