Nutrient loading models for rivers in England suggest that concentrations of N and P decrease with increasing flow due to dilution of a relatively constant input, whilst concentrations of N and P from diffuse sources usually increase with increasing flow (Bowes et al. 2008; Bowes et al. 2014 ). These incidences suggest that further work is needed to investigate the frequency and duration of these events to build an improved picture of their impacts within riverine and estuarine systems. Whilst the results from this survey are based on samples taken at the tidal limits of the rivers, these are often above many cities (e.g. London) and inputs from wastewater treatment works may occur below this point. These lower points of discharge, in addition to the input of river nutrients, will help determine the presence of estuarine algal blooms, and will also reflect the residence time of waters within the estuary.  4.5 Wider implications In future, catchment concentrations and export of DSi may be accelerated by climate change, driven by higher temperatures and more extreme precipitation events (Met Office, 2019 ), in similar ways to those that may potentially influence the riverine DIC cycle (Tye et al. 2022 ). This study has demonstrated the role of SAAR in DSi concentrations and fluxes, particularly in the wetter western side of GB. In addition, warming may increase the temperature of groundwater (Hemmerle & Bayer, 2020 ) and this may lead to increased silicate mineral weathering of catchment bedrock, increasing DSi loss via base flow. However, the impacts of climate change on groundwater temperature is presently largely unclear (Egidio et al. 2024 ). However, greater impacts on DSi fluxes may arise from efforts to mitigate rising atmospheric CO2  through the application of crushed basalt rock to agricultural land (a process referred to as ‘Enhanced Rock Weathering’), used to mimic the natural drawdown of CO2  via silicate weathering processes (Beerling et al. 2020 ). Signals representing the application of liming materials have previously been found in DIC behaviour in river waters (Oh et al. 2006), so it is likely that applications of basalt will impact river DSi concentrations. However, much may depend on the distribution of application (likely to be focused on arable land) and application rate (up to 100 t/ha; Harrington et al. 2023; Buckingham et al. 2022 ) which suggests that not all catchments will be equally affected (Kantzas et al. 2022 ). This study provides a valuable baseline against which to monitor and verify changes in the terrestrial to ocean pathway of DSi and will support the assessment of biogeochemical or ecological impacts of this practice.   5 Conclusions Results from this study have demonstrated how riverine DSi across GB is strongly influenced by the interactions of a range of geological, geomorphological, precipitation and landcover variables. Examination of data from the 2017 survey suggests that riverine DSi concentrations are within the range of the long-term HMS dataset, and there was no indication of recent decreases in DSi concentration through the so-called ‘silica loop’. This may be a result of major land-use change in GB having taken place over many centuries. Whilst these factors will largely determine concentrations and yields of DSi from catchments, its ecological importance is in maintaining the stoichiometric safe operating ranges of aquatic systems in which biological processes can effectively self-regulate, and beyond which detrimental impacts, such as algal blooms may occur. For GB, results have shown that the impacts of eutrophication in many rivers and estuaries are partly offset by catchments with lithologies that supply high concentrations of DSi. However, the management of riverine macro-nutrients to improve stoichiometry is complex and currently focuses heavily on source control of N and P. Stutter et al. (2018)  suggest that this emphasis on source controls, including the management of legacy P (Jarvie et al. 2013 ) and N (Wang et al. 2013 ; Ascott et al. 2021) has dominated ‘eutrophication management’ to the possible detriment of considering how the biological regulation of nutrients, such as reconnecting rivers with sources of allochthonous DOC via linking to wetlands and riparian forests, could help decrease N and P concentrations. However, results from the current study have demonstrated the importance of monitoring DSi, along with N and P, when considering ‘biological regulation’ as many wetland-based schemes may involve potential DSi ‘sink’ habitats.
1 Introduction Vegetation plays a crucial role in the exchange of water, carbon, and energy between land and atmosphere. Its growth is co-limited by the availability of water and energy, which in turn significantly affect the ecosystem functions (represented as evapotranspiration, ET) (Jiao et al., 2021; Nemani et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022 ). Changes in vegetation coverage alters terrestrial surface characteristics, including land surface albedo and near surface temperature together with vegetation species and ages, and consequently impacts water-energy exchanges between land and atmosphere and thus water and energy availability (Anderegg et al., 2020; Donohue et al., 2007; Gan et al., 2021; Hoek Van Dijke et al., 2022 ). These changes have the potential to alter the long-term natural equilibrium among vegetation, atmosphere and soil (Eagleson, 2002; Zhang et al., 2018 ), which affects coupling relationship between ecosystem function and water or energy availability. For example, precipitation (P) partition is controlled by vegetation, which increased vegetation coverage (VC) is expected to allocate more portion of P into ET (Yang et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022 ), suggesting that ecosystem function tends to rely more on P. These stress that vegetation has an essential role in regulating the coupling strength between ET and water or energy availability, which strongly regulates the vegetation dynamic and their responses to climate change. Yet, the temporal changes and spatial patterns of the ecosystem constraints to ecosystem function are still less known in the context of large-scale revegetation and climate changes. Large-scale revegetation has long been recognized as a critical and effective strategy to mitigate global warming and extreme drought, and was launched globally (Elizabeth, 2022; Springgay et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2023 ). Since 1999, the Chinese government has implemented the ‘Grain-for-Green Project’ (GFGP) to mitigate severe soil erosion and to improve local fragile eco-environment quality (Feng et al., 2016 ). Numerous evidences have demonstrated that since the GFGP, a trend of increasing VC was observed, resulting in a fundamental augment in VC to nearly double its initial state (Piao et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2022 ). Therefore, the regional water availability decreases dramatically as revegetation accelerates terrestrial water loss through enhanced evaporation from canopy interception and vegetation transpiration (Chen et al., 2023; Deng et al., 2016; Zhang and Wei, 2021 ). Previous research emphasised that declining water availability tended to enlarge water constraint to ecosystem function (Denissen et al., 2022; Jiao et al., 2021 ), however, this seems to contradict with the lush increasing VC and increased ET on the Loess Plateau. These indicated that the impact of the large-scale revegetation on the ecosystem constraints is co-influenced by multiple biogeochemical mechanisms. These mechanisms can be categorised as follows: (i ) The increased VC enhances ET, leading to increased water constraint to ET, owing to drying soil and reduced water availability (Deng et al., 2016, 2020; Mei et al., 2018 ). (ii ) The increased VC enhance P which associates with locally enhanced evaporation cycles and non-locally upwind water vapour flow, and could compensate for water loss driven by increased ET, leading to the increased water availability and the decreased water stress (Cui et al., 2022; Hoek Van Dijke et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023 ). (iii ) Elevated water use efficiency reduces water constraint in the context of higher atmospheric CO2  and increased fraction of vegetation transpiration (f Ev ) (Berg and McColl, 2021; Cheng et al., 2017 ). (iv ) More portion of P into ET because of increasing VC reduces the water constraint from soil moisture (Yang et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022 ). (v ) The equilibrium relationship between VC and local hydro-climatic conditions. When VC remains equilibrium with these conditions, water supply of soil moisture satisfies water demand of ecosystem function (Eagleson, 2002 ). However, the increasing VC augments water demand and water constraint, owing to imbalance between supply and demand. (vi ) Whether this region is water or energy limited (Cui et al., 2022; Forzieri et al., 2020; Pitman et al., 2011 ). For example, the alteration in water availability caused by vegetation changes shows a valid pattern with P and air temperature (Ta ), and the water availability globally decreases in the regions where limited by Ta  while increases in the regions where constrained by P (Cui et al., 2022 ). The joint influences of these mechanisms and the differences in importance make alterations in the ecosystem constraints after the GFGP on the Loess Plateau complex. Additionally, the mechanism of (v ) has not yet been observed or quantified. Therefore, understanding the changes in the ecosystem constraints due to large-scale revegetation and the involved mechanisms are crucial for policy makers and future predictions. Therefore, we quantified the geographical distribution and temporal change of water and energy constraints to ET from 1982 to 2015 to illustrate: (i ) the difference in the ecosystem constraints between before and after the GFGP; (ii ) the relative importance of vegetation and climate changes in regulating the ecosystem constraint; (iii ) the contribution of the equilibrium relationship in controlling the ecosystem constraints from Eagleson’s optimality perspective. This study was conducted on the Loess Plateau, China, where large-scale revegetation has been initiated since 1999.  2 Materials and Methods 2.1 Study area The Loess Plateau, mainly covered arid and semi-arid regions with an area of 640, 000 km2 , is a typical vegetation revegetation area. Precipitation is the main water supply for vegetation, ranging from 200 to 800 mm yr−1  spatially, and the vegetation types from northwest to southeast include grassland deserts, desert grasslands, grasslands, forest grasslands and forests, and the demands on groundwater are relatively minor (Feng et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018 ). The GFGP was implemented to control soil erosion, to recover the ecological environment, and to improve human life quality since 1999, which has been invested $8.7 billion, and converted 16, 000 km2  cropland into planted vegetation (Feng et al., 2016 ). While VC has increased significantly, a host of ecohydrological issues have drawn extensive attention, including decreased runoff, severe depletion of soil moisture, more severe drought, and stunted or “small old” trees (Deng et al., 2016; McVicar et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2019 ). This shift of hydrological states triggered uncertainties on the ecosystem constraints.  2.2 Data sources 2.2.1 Climate data Monthly P data and incoming shortwave radiation (SW) data from 1982 to 2015 were provided by the Chinese Meteorological Forcing Dataset (CMFD) (He et al., 2020 ). Monthly ET data were provided by multiple datasets, including the Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model v3.6a (GLEAM, 0.25°) (Martens et al., 2017; Miralles et al., 2011 ), Global Land Data Assimilation System-NOAH (GLDAS-NOAH, 0.25°) (Rodell et al., 2004 ), and Global LAnd Surface Satellite (GLASS, 0.05°) (Yao et al., 2015, 2014 ), which was represented by the mean value of multiple datasets to decrease the uncertainty caused by a single dataset and algorithm. Daily meteorological records (namely Ta , relative humidity, sunshine hours, and wind speed) from the period 1982–2015 at 69 meteorological stations across the Loess Plateau (Fig. S1 ) were provided by the China Meteorology Administration. These records were integrated into monthly after linear interpolation of missing values and then interpolated into 1-km grids (native digital elevation model spatial resolution) using corresponding optimal ANUSPLIN model (Hutchinson, 1995 ). The monthly gridded datasets were used to calculate potential evaporation (PET) using the open-water Penman equation (Penman, 1948; Shuttleworth, 1976 ). Monthly cloud fraction data over the period of 1982–2015 was taken from the 0.25° gridded averaged ERA5 reanalysis product.  2.2.2 Vegetation data The biweekly Global Inventory Modelling and Mapping Studies (GIMMS) normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), generated from NOAA’s Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR) data, was used to represent vegetation dynamics (Pinzon and Tucker, 2014 ). Furthermore, we calculated the annual VC based on NDVI (Gutman and Ignatov, 1998 ):(1) V C = N D V I - N D V I  s o i l    N D V I  v e g   - N D V I  s o i l         where VC represents the actual monthly vegetation coverage, dimensionless; NDVIsoil  and NDVIveg  represent the monthly NDVI values from bare soil and dense vegetation, respectively. Herein, NDVIsoil  = 0.05 and NDVIveg  = 0.80 (Zhang et al., 2018 ). The mean annual VC was estimated using the average value. Furthermore, we also obtained leaf area index (LAI) as a proxy of vegetation dynamics, and LAI data was obtained from the Global LAnd Surface Satellite (GLASS) LAI product.  2.2.3 Root zone soil moisture data The monthly root-zone soil moisture (SMroot ) datasets were taken from the 0.25° gridded averaged ERA5 reanalysis product, covering the period 1982–2015. The top three soil layers of ERA5 represent 0–7, 7–28, and 28–100 cm, respectively, and they were then aggregated to 0–100 cm based on the soil layer depth weight to represent SMroot . Furthermore, we also obtained SMroot  from GLEAM v3.6a datasets to quantify the robustness of main results.  2.2.4 Land use data To limit the impact of anthropogenic activities on our results, we applied multi-phase land use data (1 km spatial resolution, annually from 1980 to 2015, source: Resource and Environment Science and Data Center) to identify any cells that were at any point during the period 1980–2015 subject to human land use, including cropland and urban construction. Any cells that had one or more human land use cells in at least one year between 1980 and 2015 were removed.   2.3 Data processing After obtaining the data, a series of steps were taken to compute the ecosystem constraints. All growing season (April to October) data were bilinear resampled to a spatial resolution of 1 km (Nicolai-Shaw et al., 2017 ). Detrending was done by removing monthly linear regression fits to minimize biases in the anomaly estimation, and the detrended datasets were then standardized using z -score method. In addition, the monthly cycle was calculated, and the anomalies was resulted from subtracting the monthly cycle from the standardized time series. From the resulting time series, we grouped datasets based on five-year moving average to ensure the size of sample.  2.4 Methods 2.4.1 Estimations of ecosystem constraints to ecosystem function Ecosystem function (represented as ET) was simultaneously controlled by water and radiation (Denissen et al., 2022; Jiao et al., 2021; Nemani et al., 2003 ), and the ecosystem constraints (EC ) of each variable was quantified by the correlation with ET (Denissen et al., 2022 ):(2) EC  W / R   = c o r ( W / R , V )      where ECW/R   represents the ecosystem constraint of water or radiation, respectively; cor (W/R , V ) indicates the spearman correlation between water or radiation and ET, respectively. The correlations were calculated based on five-year moving group detrended and standardized anomaly of variables. We used separately SMroot  and SW as the proxy of water and radiation (Denissen et al., 2022 ). Positive (negative) EC  value denoted that the variable promoted (hindered) ET, and greater magnitude of EC  indicated that ecosystem function was more constrained by this variable.  2.4.2 Contribution of the variation in ecosystem constraints We considered a range of potential factors (including vegetation and climate changes) to express the time series of ecosystem constraints by using multivariate linear regression (Forzieri et al., 2020 ). The specific model was described as follow:(3) Δ EC  Z  = β 0  + ∑ ∂ EC  Z   ∂ X i    Δ X i      where Xi   represents each potential factor. Z  is the ECW   or the ECR  . The derived signal ∂ EC  Z  / ∂ X i     represents the sensitivity between ECZ   and the variable Xi  . Eq. (3)  was based on the difference between two consecutive years (the Δ operator) to disentangle the resulting signal from possible long-term dependencies on covariates (Forzieri et al., 2020 ). Only the cells where the adjusted R2  over 0.3 were included. We assumed that after the revegetation, due to changes in vegetation and climate, the sensitivity can be altered. Therefore, the variation in each ecosystem constraint associated with each relevant variable (δ EC  Z  X    ) could be calculated by the following equation:(4) δ EC  Z  X  = ( ∂ EC  Z   ∂ X i    )  after   δ X i , a f t e r   - ∂ EC  Z   ∂ X i      before   δ X i , b e f o r e       where ( ∂ EC  Z   ∂ X i    )  after     and ∂ EC  Z   ∂ X i      before     are the sensitivity of variable i  after and before the GFGP. δ X i , a f t e r      and δ X i , b e f o r e      are the changes in variable i  after and before the GFGP based on long-term trend.  2.4.3 Inferring water and energy dominant regions We inferred the dominant type of EC , water-dominated or energy-dominated, by comparing the correlations between absolute ECW   and ECR   (Denissen et al., 2022 ). Specifically, the ECW   and ECR   were computed over the whole time series spanning the 1982–2015 period, and we defined water dominant regions (WDR) for absolute ECW   greater than absolute ECR  , and energy dominant regions (EDR) for absolute ECW   smaller than absolute ECR  . Overall, the portion of WDR was significantly greater than that of EDR (78 % versus 22 %), and largely located at arid and semi-arid regions with relatively slight changes in VC (δ VC) (Fig. S2 ).  2.4.4 Trend analysis The trends were based on Theil-Sen slopes (Sen, 1968; Theil, 1992 ). This approach was insensitive to statistical outliers, as the median slope from a rage of possible slopes is selected as the best fit. The significances of these slopes were determined on the basis of Kendall’s tau statistic from Mann-Kendall tests.   2.5 Effects of equilibrium relationship on the ECW   from Eagleson’s optimality perspectives Eagleson ecohydrological optimality theory illustrates the evolution for fraction of soil evaporation (f Es ) and f Ev  with increasing VC, and demonstrates that for a water-limited natural vegetal system, an equilibrium vegetation coverage (VC0  ) will produce minimum water stress, that is minimum ET or maximum SMroot  (Eagleson, 2002 ). Derived from this theory, a conceptually assumed framework was proposed to illustrate the impact of equilibrium relationship (including the state of disturbed, equilibrium, and excessive recovery, and detailed definition can be found below) on the ECW   from Eagleson’s optimality perspectives (Zhou et al., 2024 ). For given environmental conditions (including P, Ta , CO2  concentration, and soil infiltration capacity), there were three main evolution phases of the ECW   following vegetation change.(i) See Fig. 1   (cycle I, from A to B). When VC is far lower than the VC0  , that is the disturbed state, ET is dominated by soil evaporation (Es) that significantly consumes surface soil moisture (SMsurf ), leading to limited P appearing as SMroot . In such case, the constraint of SMroot  to ET is strong (great ECW  ). The reasons are: lower SMroot  cannot be raised to SMsurf  fast enough to satisfy great atmospheric evaporative demand, making insufficient SMroot  to satisfy ET demand which greatly limits ET (Eagleson, 2002 ).  (ii) See Fig. 1  (cycle II, from B to C). With increasing VC (but still below the VC0  ), the reduced f Es  while the enlarged f Ev  jointly decline the constraint of SMroot  to ET (decreasing ECW  ) (Yang et al., 2023 ). Firstly, based on the optimality theory, ET gradually decreases with increasing VC during this phase (Eagleson, 2002 ). Secondly, the decreased Es reduces consumption of SMsurf  (Yang et al., 2023 ). Therefore, a greater fraction of P enters root-zone layer, resulting in increased SMroot . Subsequently, ET gradually receives adequate water supply, resulting in the reducing ECW   (Denissen et al., 2022 ). When VC equal to the VC0  , that is the equilibrium state, both the ET and ECW   are minimum, and SMroot  is maximum (Eagleson, 2002 ).  (iii) See Fig. 1  (cycle III, from C to D). With increasing VC, that is the excessive recovery state (VC greater than the VC0  ), ET gradually increases while SMroot  decreases during this phase (Zhang et al., 2018 ), and the constraint of SMroot  to ET increases (augmented ECW  ). However, considering the threshold relationship between VC and the f Ev  on the Loess Plateau (Fig. S3 ), the evolution of ECW   is driven by different drivers. ①If the VC0   is greater than the threshold point (TP), the f Ev  remains constant. Increased ET enlarges the consumption of SMroot , and augmented canopy interception causes gradually decreased SMroot , leading to insufficient water availability for ET and the increased ECW  . ②If the VC0   is lower than TP, compared with ①, the increased f Ev  and ET significantly enlarges the consumption of SMroot , which markedly decrease water availability for ET, and the ECW   becomes more pronounced until the VC0   over the TP.    To illustrate the impact of equilibrium relationship on the ECW   based on Eagleson ecohydrological optimality theory, the VC0   was estimated during 1982 to 2015 on the Loess Plateau (Eagleson, 2002; Zhou et al., 2024 ), and then was compared with the linear regression values of VC to represent long-term trend, which used to identify valid cells with transitions from disturbed, to equilibrium and subsequently to excessive recovery state. For all valid cells, only cells with a trend of increasing VC were considered to guarantee the transition direction. Then, based on the transition timing for each cell, the period from six years before to six years after the transition was concentrated in order to avoid the influence of significant climate changes (Zhou et al., 2024 ) and to explore the temporal change of ECW   around the equilibrium state. Finally, the matrix with numerous rows (numbers of valid cells) and 13 columns (12 years before and after transitions plus transition timing) were averaged to 1 row and 13 columns. Furthermore, the lag-1 autocorrelation (AR1) was used to identify the critical point of equilibrium shift (Liu et al., 2019; Scheffer et al., 2001; Smith et al., 2022; Smith and Boers, 2023a, 2023b ). This AR1 was calculated using the detrended time series of the difference between VC and VC0  , and the first AR1 identically equalled to 1 was excluded (Liu et al., 2019 ). The abrupt point of equilibrium shift was then identified as the occurrence of the abrupt change in the AR1, including both significant increase and decrease in AR1.   3 Results 3.1 Changes in the ecosystem constraint due to the GFGP under climate changes The findings revealed distinct gradient patterns between ECW   (ECR  ) and two characteristics: aridity index (AI, represented as P/PET), and VC (Fig. S4 ). These patterns indicated that lower AI and VC corresponded to higher ECW   and lower ECR  . The variations in ECW   and ECR   were then analysed based on the AI and δ VC gradient. In general, it was found that the observation-based changes in the ecosystem constraints shown distinct gradient patterns along the AI instead of δ VC, suggesting a dominant role of climate background and an inherent role of vegetation change in driving changes in the ECW   and the ECR   (Fig. 2  A and B). Amid the GFGP and climate changes, the downward trends in ECW   and ECR   were observed in the WDR, resulting in decreased ECW   and ECR   by 0.019 per km2  and 0.064 per km2 , respectively; by contract, the decreased ECW   (−0.154 per km2 ) and the augmented ECR   (0.120 per km2 ) were found in the EDR (Fig. 2 C, D, and Table S1 ). The widespread alleviated ECW   led to reductions in the dominant proportion of ECW   in both the WDR (from 99 % to 91 %) and the EDR (from 40 % to 1 %) (Fig. 2 E). To exclude the confounding effects of climate changes (P and Ta ) on the ECW   and ECR  , the partial correlations shown that without climate changes, the magnitudes of changes in ECW   and ECR   were shrunk, and that the ECW   in the WDR enhanced (0.003 per km2 , 0.8 %) in the context of the GFGP (Fig. S5 ). For example, the variations of the ECW   in the EDR was shrunk from −0.154 per km2  to −0.122 per km2 . These results highlighted the co-regulation of vegetation and climate changes in the ECW   and ECR  , especially the significant effectiveness of climate changes in alleviating the ECW  , which were in line with the gradient patterns of AI and δ VC.  3.2 Drivers for the ecosystem constraints After the GFGP, the enhanced ET and Ta  enlarged the consumption of SMroot , causing a widely significant decrease in SMroot  (Fig. 3  A, B and D). For a mechanistic understanding of why the ECW   was alleviated in the context of soil drying, the geographical patterns of potential factors are explored. In the WDR, with increasing VC, an increase in f Ev  enlarged the coupling strength between SMroot  and ET, resulting in the increased ECW   (Figs. 3 E, S5 C and S6 E). Considering the impact of climate changes, the recharged P was able to replenish SMroot , which significantly alleviated the ECW  . This was confirmed by the fact that regions where P decreased and the f Ev  increased were mostly characterized as increased ECW  , and that the decreased ECW   mainly exhibited a decreased or slightly increased f Ev  and an increase in P (Fig. 3 E and F). In the EDR, due to the threshold relationship between f Ev  and NDVI (Fig. S3 ), the enlarged consumption of ample SMroot  was effective to satisfy augmented ET demand after the GFGP, leading to the reduction of ECW  . Additionally, the increase in ET demand through increased Ta  and the replenishment to SMroot  due to increased P were further alleviated the ECW  . Unexpectedly, it was also found that some certain cells where decreased P and increased f Ev  within AI ranging from 0.15 to 0.65 and δ VC from −6% to 10 % (for example, AI = 0.65, δ VC = 4%), observed decreased ECW  . Regarding variations in the ECR  , the enlarged ET after the GFGP increased the demand of SW on both the WDR and EDR. Insufficient energy supply in the EDR significantly enhanced the ECR   (Fig. 3 D), while it was not the case in the WDR because the enlarged ET can consume ample energy supply, and the relationship between ET and SW was insensitive in the WDR. This was supported by the fact that regions with the significantly increased ECR   were accompanied with significant decreases in SW (AI = 0.5) (Figs. 2 B and 3 C). Besides that, the warming climate increased ET, resulting in greater increase in ECR   in the EDR. Based on the above mechanism explanations, LAI, f Ev , P and Ta  were included into the multivariate linear regression analysis, devoting to explore the contributions of vegetation and climate changes (Fig. S7 ). The VIF test demonstrated that the multicollinearity among variables was weak (Fig. S12 ). Generally, changes in LAI dominated the δECW   before the GFGP in the WDR, supporting this explanation that vegetation changes enhanced the ECW   in the WDR (Fig. 4  A), and similar pattern was also observed after the GFGP (Fig. 4 C). Different with the WDR, in the EDR, climate changes (including P and Ta ) dominated the variations in the ECW   and ECR   before the GFGP (Fig. 4 A and B), while vegetation changes (including LAI and f Ev ) controlled these variations after the GFGP (Fig. 4 C and D), which associated with enlarged sensitivity between LAI or f Ev  and the ECW   and ECR  , and the markedly changes in LAI and f Ev  (Figs. S6 E, G and S7 B).  3.3 Revisiting the changes in ECW   from Eagleson’s optimality perspective To illustrate the importance of equilibrium relationship on the ECW   (mechanism (v ) in the Introduction), it was examined that the variations in ECW   along divergent equilibrium relationship (see Methods). In general, in arid and semi-arid regions, the ECW   diminished from the disturbed to the equilibrium states, and then increased in the excessive recovery state (Fig. 5  ). For instance, on the semi-arid regions, the ECW   decreased from 0.423 per km2  (the disturbed state) to 0.397 per km2  (the equilibrium state), and then increased to 0.407 per km2  (the excessive recovery state) (Table S2 ). While in humid and semi-humid regions, this phenomenon was less pronounced. These results indicated the general importance of equilibrium relationship in regulating changes in ECW  , and also verified the proposed framework in Fig. 1 .   4 Discussion It has been widely reported that the increased ET after the GFGP would significantly amplified the ECW   (Feng et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2023 ). However, when only consider the influence of vegetation changes, there were only slightly augmented ECW   in the WDR and a reduction in the EDR (Fig. S5 C). The significant reduction in the EDR mainly related with the increased ET, which was beneficial to consume excessive soil water (Kreuzwieser and Rennenberg, 2014; Ohta et al., 2014 ), because variations of ET primarily limited by energy availability instead of water availability in such regions. Furthermore, the almost neglectable augmented ECW   in the WDR indicated that there must be another mechanism regulating the ECW   in this region. The equilibrium relationship between VC and local hydro-climatic conditions altered ET demand (Fig. 5 ), exerting critical effects to the ECW   (Eagleson, 2002 ). The results presented in Fig. 5  stressed the significant role of equilibrium relationship, owing to its contributions to water demand (Eagleson, 2002; Zhang et al., 2018 ). More importantly, compared to arid and semi-arid regions, the variations in ECW   in humid and sub-humid regions were less pronounced (Fig. 5 ), which greatly aligns with Eagleson's ecohydrological optimal theory (Eagleson, 1982 ). This mechanism mainly exert its influence on water-limited regions, including arid and semi-arid regions. In contrast, in sub-humid and humid regions, ET is primarily constrained by energy availability (consistent with Fig. S4 C), where the influence of equilibrium relationship is relatively weaker. Additionally, due to the variations in soil infiltration capacity, the ECW   might be lower than the expected level in Fig. 1 . This potential reasons were: increasing VC tended to increase soil infiltration capacity (Poozan et al., 2022; Qiu et al., 2023 ), causing a greater portion of P to enter soil and to replenish SMroot  to a greater extent, which provided more water availability to ET and thus decreased the ECW   to a greater extent. Our results suggested that, after the GFGP, in the context of drying soil and augmented ET (Fig. 3 A and B), reductions in the ECW   were widely observed with regardless of the WDR and EDR (Figs. 2 C and S8 ), which seemingly did not follow previous results that declining soil moisture weakened water supply from soil, intensifying the coupling strength between soil moisture and ET (Denissen et al., 2022; Jiao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022 ). On one hand, the explicit patterns of the variations in ECW   alongside with the gradients of AI and δ VC suggested that vegetation and climate changes co-regulated the evolution of ECW  , which in agreement with previous results (Gong et al., 2023; Nemani et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2023 ). On the other hand, by excluding the confounding effects of climate changes (P and Ta ), an increase in the ECW   was observed in the WDR and lower decreased ECW   was detected in the EDR, which conformed to previous results that the increasing ECW   in soil water-controlled regions (Li et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022 ). These results also demonstrated the benefit of increased P on alleviating the ECW  , while warming climate exacerbated the ECW   (Figs. S5, S6 and S9 ). The reasons mainly came from the following: (i ) greater P supply was effective to replenish SMroot , providing more water availability for ET and a greater proportion of P assigned to ET, which alleviated the ECW  , especially under increasing VC (Koster et al., 2004; Purdy et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022 ); (ii ) increasing Ta  enlarged ET demand through amplifying atmospheric water demand and thus vegetation transpiration (Song et al., 2022; Zhong et al., 2023 ), resulting in the enlarged ECW  ; (iii ) greater influence of P than Ta  on ET over the Loess Plateau (Ma et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019 ), leading to greater impact of P on the ECW   (Figs. S5 and S9 ). The larger ECR   increases occurred in the regions coinciding with larger declines in SW, indicating that the primary factor regulating the ECR   was the imbalance between supply and demand of energy (Figs. 2 B and 3 C). This imbalance could be attributed to: (i ) the influence of background climate; (ii ) variations in the vegetation characteristics. On one hand, due to the fact that energy availability was the primarily constraint factor for ET in the EDR while it was not the case on the WDR (Budyko, 1974; Pitman et al., 2011 ), increased ET after the GFGP and warming climate required greater energy supply to satisfy greater ET demand in the EDR, which enlarged the ECR  . By contrast, ample or excessive energy in the WDR could be consumed due to increased ET, resulting in the decreasing ECR  . On the other hand, in comparison to the significant increase of SW in the WDR (2.79 W m−2 ), the increase in the EDR was smaller (0.96 W m−2 ), leading to a significant increase in the ECR  . The smaller rise in SW in the EDR was linked to higher proportion of forest and lower proportion of grassland (Fig. S10 D), because the number of SW on grassland was significant higher than other types of vegetation (Duveiller et al., 2018 ). The GFGP serves as a crucial ecological barrier that regulates regional water resources and ecosystem function. However, contradiction between water supply and demand, caused by factors such as population growth and extreme weather (Ta et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2023 ), continues to restrict the sustainable development and construction of the GFGP. (i ) The National Development and Reform Commission and the Ministry of Natural Resources of the People’s Republic of China jointly unveiled the “Master Plan for National Key Ecosystem Protection and Revegetation Major Projects (2021–2035)” in 2020. This plan aims to promote the protection and revegetation of the Chinese ecological environment. As part of this plan, the Loess Plateau has been identified as one of the main ecological security barriers. Furthermore, the Yellow River Protection Law of the People’s Republic of China was officially implemented in April 2023. This law provides legal protection for the Yellow River and aims to promote coordinated governance and joint efforts to protect the river. These policies above demonstrate that the ecological revegetation and protection on the Loess Plateau is a long-term process. (ii ) Additionally, the principle of ecohydrological optimality must be considered, as the dynamic equilibrium between vegetation and water resources ultimately affect the process of vegetation restoration under different hydro-climatic patterns, and therefore regulates regional water balance. When restoring vegetation, it is important to consider the equilibrium relationship between vegetation and hydro-climatic conditions, and how this relationship impacts water resource allocation. (iii ) Excessive recovery or disturbance can disrupt the ecosystem equilibrium, and potentially leading to ecosystem instability and affecting regional water security. Our results provided clear evidences of how climate changes and human-induced increasing VC affected the ecosystem constraints and its potential mechanisms. However, the accuracy may be affected by four sources of uncertainty and limitation: (i ) the satellite-based products used in the analysis; (ii ) other potential mechanisms; (iii ) the interactions and nonlinear effects among factors; and (iv ) nutrient constraints, including carbon and nitrogen, should be considered. The robustness of our main findings was assessed by repeatedly conducting the same analysis using SM from GLEAM and SW from ERA5 datasets. The consistency between our main results and this analysis indicated great robustness in the overall variations and trends which may influence the magnitude but not the sign of variations in the ecosystem constraints (Fig. S11 ). Additionally, it should be noted that the current research did not consider the entire potential mechanism. Lage-scale revegetation can contribute to an increase in the water use efficiency through improving LAI and f Ev  (Cao et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2019 ), which has the potential to alleviate the ECW  . However, we found that the widespread increase in f Ev  in the WDR was associated with increased ECW   (Figs. 2 A and 3 E), which may be related to equilibrium relationship transfer from the equilibrium to the excessive recovery state (Zhang et al., 2018 ). Furthermore, vegetation tended to develop deeper roots in response to increased water demand and stress (Fan et al., 2017; Smith-Martin et al., 2020 ), resulting in a greater reliance on deeper soil for growth. Therefore, it should be noted that the study has a limitation in that the root depth is statically set at 100 cm, disregarding the effect of root depth (Stocker et al., 2023 ). Thirdly, the multivariate linear regression was applied to the attribution analysis, based on the linear relationships between the ecosystem constraints and variables. However, this approach was unable to consider nonlinear and interaction effects (Forzieri et al., 2020; Hsu and Dirmeyer, 2023 ). Despite this limitation, our results still supported that the contributions of vegetation and climate changes were significant in regulating the ecosystem constraints, answering our question. Further work is required to explore the nonlinear interactions. The coupling mechanism of soil carbon, nitrogen and nutrient can pose constraints on ET by limiting photosynthesis (Denissen et al., 2022; Gao and Yu, 2020 ), especially when increasing VC required more nutrient supply. However, this research did not quantify these constraints, which is a limitation of the study. Although these were uncertainties and limitations, this study was a significant advancement beyond previous research. It described the evolution of ecosystem constraints and highlighted the significant role of increased P and equilibrium relationship in alleviating the revegetation-enhanced ECW  .  5 Conclusions We explored the influence of vegetation changes and climate changes on the ecosystem constraints (including the ECW   and ECR  ), and then investigated the corresponding potential mechanisms and contributors. The results indicated that, after the GFGP, the ECW   decreased with regardless of the WDR and EDR, and the ECR   decreased in the WDR while increased in the EDR. The variations in the ECW   and the ECR   shown explicit gradient patterns of AI and δ VC, suggesting the co-regulations of changes in vegetation and climate. The contribution analyses showed that, first, in terms of vegetation changes, the increased f Ev  was the most important factors solely in the WDR. Second, in terms of climate changes, P and Ta  were the two most important drivers affecting the ecosystem constraint. The alleviated effect from increased P in the WDR even could reversed the amplified ECW   because of revegetation and warming climate. The theoretical framework based on the Eagleson’s optimality theory succeed in explaining the evolution of the ECW   in arid and semi-arid regions, which illustrated the influences of the equilibrium relationship on the ECW  . The study highlighted the significance of increased P and the equilibrium relationship in alleviating the ECW   in the WDR. This can provide more comprehensive policy for the sustainable development and construction of ecological projects.
1 Introduction Nitrogen is one of the prevalent elements in various layers of the Earth, including the atmosphere and water bodies. However, human activities, especially those related to agriculture, industry, and urban emissions, result in a substantial influx of additional nitrogen into water systems (Morée et al., 2013; Yue et al., 2017 ). When an excess of nitrogen compounds enters rivers, it leads to nitrogen pollution, posing a threat to the health of aquatic ecosystems and potentially causing issues such as eutrophication and cyanobacterial blooms (Chen et al., 2021; Paerl et al., 2020; Schindler et al., 2016 ). This, in turn, poses a threat to both human health and the ecological environment. Moreover, during the decomposition and transformation of nitrogen in water bodies, greenhouse gases like nitrous oxide may be released (Andalib et al., 2018; Webb et al., 2019 ), potentially contributing to the escalation of global warming. Reservoirs serve as vital barriers, capturing nutrient substances (Ding et al., 2019 ) like nitrogen and phosphorus from river flows and causing their buildup within the reservoir. This accumulation subsequently triggers extensive growth of algae and aquatic plants in the water, impacting water transparency and degrading water quality (Lv et al., 2019 ). Following eutrophication, the reduction in dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration poses a threat to other aquatic organisms, potentially resulting in events like fish mortality (Huang et al., 2019 ). The nitrogen within reservoirs is subject to dynamic migration and transformation. Ammonia nitrogen, a prevalent form of nitrogen in water, is typically introduced through processes such as the decomposition of organic matter on land, agricultural fertilization, and wastewater discharge (Xiang et al., 2020 ). Within the reservoir, diverse nitrogen cycling and transformation processes may occur. For instance, conventional nitrifying bacteria further oxidize ammonia nitrogen into nitrate nitrogen, while denitrifying bacteria reduce nitrate nitrogen back to ammonia nitrogen or nitrogen gas (Yilihamu et al., 2020 ). These processes commonly unfold under varying environmental conditions. At present, isotope tracing has found successful applications in various fields, including ecology, agriculture, and environmental science. Nitrogen isotopes (δ15 N-NO3 - ) exhibit distinct characteristics and ratios compared to natural nitrogen, making them useful for identifying different sources of nitrate. However, accurately discerning nitrate sources solely through δ15 N-NO3 -  can be challenging due to the complexity of nitrate origins. The analysis of oxygen isotopes (δ18 O-NO3 - ) is often combined with δ15 N-NO3 -  to enhance the precision of nitrogen source identification. Different δ18 O-NO3 -  proportions are typically observed in soil, atmosphere, and ammonium fertilizers, and the changes in isotope values resulting from nitrogen biochemical processes can provide insights into the nitrogen biochemical status (Yu et al., 2020 ). Therefore, the linear proportional values between δ18 O-NO3 -  and δ15 N-NO3 - , coupled with the numerical changes in isotopes (Batkhuyag et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2021; Panno et al., 2006; Yang and Toor, 2016 ), can serve as a foundation for identifying biochemical processes such as nitrification and denitrification. This paper focuses on the Nuozhadu (NZD) Reservoir, a representative deep and large reservoir in the Lancang River, as the study area. Through the detection and analysis of hydrochemical indices (including T, pH, DO, etc.), nutrients (ammonia nitrogen, nitrate), and the N/O isotopes in stratified water at different typical cross-sections, the study aims to identify the thermal stratification characteristics of typical profiles in the reservoir. It endeavors to explore the characteristics of nitrogen migration and transformation under stratified conditions, providing a scientific foundation for understanding the environmental evolution and ecological impacts of deep and large reservoirs.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The Lancang River is among the 12 key hydropower development bases in China, characterized by abundant water resources in its watershed. The NZD Reservoir represents the fifth tier in the “Two Dams, Eight Cascades” hydropower development plan for the mid and lower reaches of the Lancang River. With a total storage capacity of approximately 23.7 billion m3  and a regulated total capacity of 12.4 billion m3 , it stands as a large-scale, pivotal reservoir equipped with multi-year regulation capabilities. Stretching over about 215 km, the NZD Reservoir submerges a total area of 322.67 km2 , with a pre-dam water depth exceeding 200 m. The reservoir’s jurisdiction encompasses parts of Yunnan Province, specifically the cities of Simao and Lincang, along with nine counties (districts) and 50 townships. Economic activities primarily revolve around agriculture, marking it as a typical agricultural cultivation area in the mountainous region (Yi, 2017). The geographical features of the NZD Reservoir area fall within the Yongping-Simao Zhongshan Canyon subregion, a segment of the longitudinal valley mountainous zone in western Yunnan. The reservoir area exhibits a distribution of three major rock types—igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks—with granite prominently exposed along the reservoir banks. The covering layer, along with the extensively weathered layers, is characterized by significant depth.  2.2 Sample collection The NZD Reservoir area experiences a subtropical monsoonal climate. The temperature in December was about 13 °C, while the average temperature rose to around 28 °C in April, reflecting vast climatic differences. Therefore, the fieldwork was conducted in both April and December 2019, during which the YSI (Yellow Springs Instruments, United States) EXO2 multi-parameter water quality analyzer was utilized. Systematic on-site monitoring was performed across the entire reservoir area, with intervals of every 20 km2 , focusing on various physicochemical indicators such as water temperature (T), pH, electrical conductivity (EC), total dissolved solids (TDS), and dissolved oxygen (DO). Concurrently, to analyze the nitrogen migration and transformation in the reservoir water, three typical profiles were established from top to bottom within the reservoir area: NZD-A (approximately 2 km from the dam site), NZD-B (approximately 15 km from the dam site), and NZD-C (about 150 km from the dam site). Stratified water samples were collected based on variations in water temperature from the surface to the reservoir bottom along these typical profiles (Fig. 1  ).  2.3 Sample analysis Water samples were collected and filtered using a 0.45 μm glass fiber filter membrane (pre-burned for 3 h at 450 °C in a muffle furnace to eliminate residual chlorine). The filtered water was then transferred to bottles with polyethylene samples for the determination of N/O isotopes. Nitrate nitrogen (NO3 – -N) was measured using UV–visible spectrophotometry (UV-8000). The determination of N/O isotopes (δ15 N-NO3 –  and δ18 O-NO3 – ) in the water samples employed the bacterial denitrification method. Under conditions lacking N2 O reductase, denitrifying bacteria converted the NO3 –  in the tested samples into N2 O, thereby terminating the reaction. This ensured that the nitrogen and oxygen compositions in N2 O were entirely derived from the NO3 –  in the samples. The Gas-Bench continuous flow gas introduction system was utilized to introduce gas into the instrument, and a stable isotope ratio mass spectrometer (MAT253, USA) was used to determine δ15 N-NO3 –  and δ18 O-NO3 –  in N2 O-NO3 – . Sample analysis was conducted at the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, with each sample undergoing three analyses, and the average value was used for further assessment.  2.4 Calculation indicators and definitions The thermocline strength index (TSI) is a common index for stratification, calculated by the maximum degree of change with depth(Horne and Goldman, 1994 ). Therefore, it is widely used in the study of stratification in deep water bodies. It is calculated as follows:(1) T S I = Δ T  Δ h        where Δ T   (℃) and Δ h   （m） represents the temperature and depth difference between the upper and lower boundaries of the water column, respectively. The Relative Water Column Stability (RWCS) is a dimensionless parameter used to characterize the thermal stratification status of water bodies (Padisák, J et al., 2003 ). The calculation equation is as follows:(2) R W C S = ( ρ b  - ρ s  )  / ( ρ 4  - ρ 5  )       where ρ b     represents the density at the bottom of the water layer (g / c m  3    ), ρ s     represents the density at the surface of the water layer (g / c m  3    ), ρ 4     and ρ 5     are the densities of water at 4℃ and 5℃, respectively (g / c m  3    ). Studies have shown that when RWCS>50, it indicates stable thermal stratification in reservoirs, thus serving as an indicator for thermal stratification (Chimney et al., 2006; Pu et al., 2020 ). The density of water is a function of water temperature (T), and it can be calculated using the following empirical formula (Lawson and Anderson, 2007 ):(3) ρ T  = 1000 1 - T + 288.9414    / 508929.2 × ( T + 68.12963 )    × ( T - 3.9863 )  2            3 Results 3.1 Characteristics of physicochemical factors in water Monitoring of water quality parameters reveals distinct variations in DO, T, and pH along the depth of profiles in the NZD Reservoir (Fig. 2  ). In April, sections A and B in front of the dam exhibit slow water flow, resembling lake-like characteristics. There are significant differences in various indicators along the vertical direction of the profiles. For section A and section B, the ranges of T, DO, and pH are: 17.11–24.67 °C (18.91 °C), 3.84–10.52 mg/L (6.58 mg/L), 7.38–8.71 (7.60), and 17.12–24.44 °C (18.95 °C), 3.92–10.77 mg/L (7.15 mg/L), 7.34–8.78 (7.70), respectively. In December, Section A and B have distribution ranges for T, DO, and pH as follows: 16.71–21.13 °C (17.18 °C), 2.67––6.55 mg/L (4.21 mg/L), 7.40–8.65 (7.81), and 17.53–20.90 °C (17.63 °C), 2.87–6.51 mg/L (4.18 mg/L), 7.43–8.39 (7.73), respectively. It is evident that the physicochemical characteristics of the water in sections A and B are similar. Section C is positioned at the end of the backflow, and the degree of water mixing is relatively uniform. The hydrodynamic conditions closely resemble river-like characteristics, and the water depth (58 m in April and 44 m in December) is significantly smaller than in sections A and B. The mean values for T, DO, and pH are 18.10 °C, 9.08 mg/L, and 8.22 in April and 17.13 °C, 8.00 mg/L, and 8.29 in December. The mean values of DO and pH in section C are significantly higher than those in sections A and B, while the mean temperature in section C is litter lower than in sections A and B. According to the criterion that a temperature change of > 0.2 °C/m and RWCS>50 indicates a thermocline (WANG Y Z and PU P M, 1982 ), the upper and lower boundaries of the thermocline (TL) can be set as the mixed layer (ML) and the isothermal layer (IL), respectively (Zhang et al., 2015). Therefore, based on the temperature change along the profiles, the 0–5 m depth in sections A and B of the NZD Reservoir is defined as the ML, 5–40 m as the TL, and below 40 m as the constant IL in April. The TSI reflects little temperature stratification in the two months.  3.2 Nitrogen and isotope characteristics analysis As depicted in Fig. 3  , in April, the concentration of ammonia nitrogen in Section A is relatively uniform within a water depth of 100 m but gradually increases beyond 100 m. In Section B, the concentration of ammonia nitrogen oscillates within the first 40 m and then stabilizes beyond 40 m. Section C exhibits significant changes in concentration within the first 5 m of water depth, followed by a stable pattern as the water depth increases. The concentration of nitrate nitrogen in Sections A and C generally follows an increasing-then-constant pattern with water depth. In Section B, there is a sudden decrease in concentration to 0.37 mg/L at a water depth of 20 m-50 m, followed by a gradual increase to 0.50 mg/L. The δ15 N-NO3 -  shows noticeable fluctuations overall, with the most significant fluctuations occurring in the water column above 20–25 m (stable stratification interface). Below 40 m in water depth (IL), the isotope values in Section A remain relatively stable, while Section B exhibits a trend of initially increasing and then decreasing. In December, the changes in the concentrations of various components in the profiles are smaller compared to those in April, indicating the good hydraulic mixing effect.   4 Discussion 4.1 Analysis of nitrogen migration and transformation in the reservoir The δ15 N-NO3 – , δ18 O-NO3 – , and NO3 – -N exhibit distinct concentration variations across the three sections of the NZD Reservoir. Isotopes are commonly used to trace the origin of nitrogen, and their values change during nitrogen cycling processes such as nitrification, denitrification, assimilation, and mineralization. During assimilation, nitrate nitrogen is absorbed by algae, and the nitrogen–oxygen isotopic ratio should be 1:1, accompanied by a decreasing trend in nitrate nitrogen (Tuerena et al., 2021 ). The calculated ε15 N/ε18 O (slope value) suggests that assimilation is not the primary biochemical process in the NZD Reservoir. According to the equation, δ18 O-NO3 –  = 1/3δ18 O2  + 2/3δ18 O-H2 O, it is known that 2/3 of the oxygen in nitrate in water comes from water (Qin et al., 2019 ). Therefore, theoretically, oxygen isotopes in water nitrate can be deduced from the data of N/O isotopes (Fig. 4  a). By comparing the linear fit of water hydrogen and oxygen isotopes with the local meteoric water line (LMWL) and the global meteoric water line (GMWL) (Fig. 4 b), it is evident that the water in the NZD Reservoir primarily originates from atmospheric precipitation. This conclusion aligns with the findings of (Yang et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2023 ). The stable isotope ranges in reservoir water samples are as follows: δ2 D-H2 O ranges from −119.62 ‰ to −77.83 ‰, and δ18 O-H2 O ranges from −16.28 ‰ to −10.70 ‰. In April, the values of δ2 D-H2 O and δ18 O-H2 O are slightly higher than those in December (April δ2 D-H2 O: −87.18 ± 11.09 ‰, δ18 O-H2 O: −12.31 ± 1.74 ‰; December δ2 D-H2 O: −104.17 ± 8.40 ‰, δ18 O-H2 O: −14.47 ± 1.08 ‰), indicating a seasonal significance difference (p < 0.05). The data points for both seasons are located below and to the right of the LMWL but are close to it, suggesting that precipitation and evaporation dominate in the NZD reservoir (Wang et al., 2015 ). The lower slope of the δ2 D-H2 O line in April compared to the LMWL and the GMWL indicates a stronger evaporation effect in April, likely due to the higher temperatures and significant evaporation during this month. Examining the significant differences in δ2 D-H2 O and δ18 O-H2 O between the two seasons reveals that the seasonal differences are due to variations in water temperature. The analysis indicates that the evaporation process is stronger in April due to higher temperatures, causing lighter isotopes such as H1  and O16  to enter the atmosphere more easily, while heavier isotopes like H2  and O18  remain in the liquid phase (Li et al., 2019 ). Consequently, the relative concentration of heavy isotopes increases in December. Based on the vertical distribution of nitrate nitrogen (Fig. 3 ), All data points fall within the range of human wastewater, chemical fertilizer, and soil nitrogen sources. Previous studies show that atmospheric nitrogen contributions via rainfall are negligible. During the wet season, nitrogen-rich soil particles likely enter rivers through erosion due to the region’s steep mountains and long valleys. Local research indicates ammonia volatilization can increase δ15 N-NO3 –  by up to + 4.2 ‰, leading to nitrate accumulation. Dali, located upstream, is a significant city with dense population and industrial activity, contributing to higher regional nitrogen inputs (Liu et al., 2015 ). The slope values for the fitted data points in April and December are 0.76 and −2.15, respectively. It is observed that the slope in April falls within the denitrification range, indicating the presence of denitrification at this section. Analyzing the data in April furtherly, it is evident that the concentration of nitrate nitrogen in the IL of the reservoir (below 20 m) is greater than in the ML, indicating the possible occurrence of significant nitrification in the lower part of the reservoir. According to the analysis of N/O isotopes in the water column (Fig. 4 b), it is found that the nitrogen source in the NZD reservoir mainly comes from soil organic nitrogen, human sewage, and chemical fertilizers. Typically, when the ratio of δ15 N-NO3 –  to δ18 O-NO3 –  is between 1.3 and 2.1, denitrification occurs. After linear analysis of the data from the three sampled sections, the overall linear fit in the study area is 1:6.49, which does not fall within the denitrification zone. Considering the different characteristics of the three sections, individual linear fits for each section reveal that the slope value for section B is 1:1.55, indicating denitrification. Therefore, denitrification may occur in section B of the NZD Reservoir. Additionally, in section B, a trend is observed in the thermocline layer (TL) (30–40 m): δ15 N-NO3 –  increases, NO3 – -N concentration decreases, and DO concentration relatively decreases. This phenomenon also supports the possibility of denitrification in this region. Furthermore, in sections A and C, with increasing water depth, there is an increase in NO3 – -N, while δ15 N-NO3 –  exhibits fluctuating decreases, suggesting the possible coupling of denitrification and nitrification in these sections as water depth increases. According to the analysis of the vertical stratification structure, the top of each section is considered as the initial value for nitrogen biochemical processes. Previous studies have shown that surface water exhibits dual nitrate concentrations similar to those in inflowing rivers (Chen, 2021). By calculating the differences between the monitoring points at different depths in each section and the top of the stable layer, the values of △δ15 N-NO3 –  and △NO3 – -N can be derived (Fig. 5  ). A significant negative correlation between these two Δ values indicates different nitrogen migration and transformation processes in the water. For instance, an increase in △δ15 N-NO3 –  alongside a decrease in △NO3 – -N is typically associated with denitrification and algal assimilation in the water. Conversely, when the concentration trends of △δ15 N-NO3 –  and △NO3 – -N in the water are completely opposite, nitrification is occurring. If there is no negative correlation in the data, it is considered that the water is influenced by anthropogenic disturbances caused by hydrodynamic disturbances or external inputs (Fenech et al., 2012 ). As depicted in Fig. 5 ，a significantly negative correlation is observed in both the TL and IL in April, with all data points falling within the nitrification zone. Given that the DO levels in the majority of the three typical sections are relatively high, ranging from 5 to 10 mg/L(Niu et al., 2019 ), it can be concluded that nitrification is the primary nitrogen conversion process in the NZD Reservoir. However, in December, there is a significant change in ΔNO3 - -N, while the isotopic value of N15  shows little variation. Previous studies have indicated that during winter when there is no thermal stratification and uniformity in reservoirs, mixing processes occur. This promotes the mineralization and decomposition of organic matter, but has little effect on the variation of δ15 N-NO3 –  (Bardhan et al., 2017 ). During assimilation processes, δ15 N and δ18 O are enriched in residual nitrate, and the ratio of δ15 N to δ18 O should be 1:1 (Mayer and Wassenaar, 2012 ). Calculations for different seasons and profiles in NZD reveal that only in April, the ratio for profiles A and B at depths greater than 5 m is approximately 0.76 and 0.87 respectively.  4.2 Analysis of factors influencing nitrogen migration and transformation in water As a typical deep and large reservoir in the Lancang River, NZD Reservoir features a significant elevation drop and favorable hydrodynamic conditions. This leads to an increased depth of oxygen mixing, thereby promoting nitrification and, to some extent, suppressing denitrification. Besides the impact of DO, the nitrogen cycle in the reservoir may also be influenced by environmental factors such as T, pH, and nitrogen forms (Barnard, 2005). Hence, this study employs principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) to identify and analyze environmental factors. As depicted in Fig. 6  a, the first two principal axes collectively explain 94.79 % of the variables, highlighting discernible differences among the layers (ML, TL, and IL). This emphasizes the diverse physicochemical characteristics observed in various water layers within the NZD reservoir in April, thereby necessitating a separate analysis for each layer. Pearson correlation analysis of environmental factors is conducted for the three layers in April. However, due to the good mixing effect of water bodies in December, correlation analysis is only carried out on the upper data (ML). As depicted in Fig. 6 b, no indicators significantly correlated with N/O isotopes were identified in the ML. Typically, in the upper water column, the increased water transparency leads to a higher density of phytoplankton. In this layer, assimilation reactions of ammonium nitrogen may occur concurrently with nitrification, as nitrifying bacteria and phytoplankton compete for assimilation (Yang et al., 2021 ). Referring to the concentration of nitrate nitrogen in the ML (0–5 m) of the NZD Reservoir sampling section, it remains low, increasing with the depth of the water. This can be attributed to assimilation reactions by surface (euphotic layer) phytoplankton, which consume nitrate nitrogen, resulting in a reduction of nitrate nitrogen concentration in the surface layer. As water depth increases and the transparency decreases, adequate DO supply promotes nitrification reactions, gradually increasing nitrate nitrogen concentration. Statistical analysis of the ML in this study revealed no significant correlation between N/O isotopes and environmental factors. The analysis suggests that this may be due to the limited depth of the ML and the relatively small sample size collected, resulting in a weaker statistical relationship between the identified nitrogen migration and transformation and environmental indicators compared to the TL and IL. In most water quality models, the nitrification process exhibits a high correlation with DO and water temperature (Chapra, S.C. et al., 2012; Cole, T and Well, S, 2011 ). Therefore, the thermocline in deep reservoirs can be considered an active zone for nitrogen conversion. As observed in Fig. 6 c, both sections A and B reveal an increase in nitrate nitrogen concentration, a decrease in ammonium nitrogen concentration, and a decline in isotope concentration within the thermocline (5–40 m). This suggests the occurrence of nitrification processes in this region. Temperature plays a crucial role in influencing the activity of microorganisms involved in nitrogen nitrification. Throughout the sampling period, the water temperature in the thermocline consistently remained above 15 °C, promoting the growth of ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) and facilitating nitrification reactions (Yan et al., 2019 ). The PCA results also indicate a correlation between water temperature and the first principal axis. Statistical analysis reveals a significant correlation between N/O stable isotopes and T, underscoring the pivotal role of temperature in influencing nitrogen migration and transformation. Additionally, in the TL, δ15 N-NO3 -  exhibits a significant and positive correlation with DO and pH, indicating favorable environmental conditions for AOB and nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (NOB) involved in nitrification reactions (Ding et al., 2023; Le et al., 2019 ). Furthermore, despite the anticipated decrease in ammonium nitrogen concentration at the bottom of the thermocline after nitrification, an increase in ammonium nitrogen concentration is observed. This could be attributed to the pronounced stratification in the thermocline, with particles residing in the water column for an extended period, releasing particulate organic nitrogen (PON) after microbial decomposition (Yang et al., 2021 ). Moreover, in the TL of section B, at a depth of 30–40 m, nitrate nitrogen concentration reaches a minimum. This may be due to the breakdown of organic matter in the thermocline, resulting in relatively low DO concentrations (normal DO concentrations are generally above 6 mg/L) (Abdel-Tawwab et al., 2015 ), creating favorable conditions for denitrification. Particularly in the 30–40 m depth range, section B exhibits a decrease in nitrate nitrogen concentration and an increase in nitrogen isotope concentration, consistent with the nitrogen transformation characteristics of denitrification. Therefore, in sections with localized DO minima in the water column, there may be a synchronous coupling of nitrification and denitrification processes. In the IL (Fig. 6 d), δ18 O-NO3 -  is significantly correlated with the environmental factor DO. The concentration of DO directly affects the nitrogen migration and transformation processes in the IL. Additionally, in section A, an exceptionally high concentration of ammonium nitrogen is observed at the bottom of the IL. This phenomenon suggests that the release of nutrients from bottom sediment to upper-layer water may contribute to localized increases in nutrient concentrations in the deep water (Noori et al., 2018 ). In the mixed layer data for December, there is no significant correlation between the N/O double isotopes and various physicochemical indicators. This further indicates a weaker nitrogen transformation process in the reservoir in December. This aligns with the earlier mention that the variation of isotopic δ15 N during assimilation processes has little impact, indicating predominantly physical mixing processes. However, in December, there is no significant relationship between nitrogen and oxygen double isotopes and all indicators.  4.3 Analysis of the impact of water stratification characteristics on nitrogen migration and transformation According to the definition of TSI (Eq. (1)  and RWCS Eq. (2) ), when RWCS and TSI exceeds 50 and 0.02℃/m, respectively. The water exhibits distinct features of temperature stratification. As evident from the contour map (Fig. 2 ), sections A and B display stable temperature stratification within the range of 0–35 m. Pearson correlation analysis (Fig. 6 b) found a significant negative correlation (p < 0.01) between RWCS and ammonia nitrogen in the ML. Stable stratification in the mixed layer of the water column (RWCS>50), elevated concentrations of DO prevent the ammonium nitrogen generated through phytoplankton decomposition and synthesis from persisting in the water as ammonium ions. Instead, it promptly undergoes nitrification(Beutel, 2006 ). Higher RWCS values indicate a more stable stratification of the water body with weaker vertical mixing. In this scenario, the nutrient-rich bottom water is less likely to mix with the surface water, resulting in lower ammonia nitrogen concentrations in the surface layer. Conversely, when RWCS is lower, vertical mixing is enhanced, making it easier for bottom ammonia nitrogen to be transported into the upper water layer, leading to increased ammonia nitrogen concentrations in the surface layer (Ji et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2022; Wang et al. 2024a, b ). A significant and positive correlation (p < 0.05) between RWCS in the thermocline and physicochemical parameters such as DO, pH, and δ15 N-NO3 -  (Fig. 6 c). The analysis suggests that the shear force associated with temperature stratification in the water may induce considerable gradients in DO concentration in the upper and lower regions of the thermocline (YoosefDoost et al., 2020 ). This inhibits the rapid transfer of DO to the lower part of the thermocline, resulting in a correlation between temperature and DO stratification. The most immediate consequence of stratification is the occurrence of dissolved oxygen and temperature stratification in the water. Temperature influences the growth of planktonic algae, and higher temperatures in the upper water layers may enhance the growth activity of planktonic algae, potentially leading to nitrogen assimilation by planktonic algae (Reynolds, C.S., 2006 ). In the TL, due to the significant temperature gradient and increased buoyancy, the residence time of particulate matter or dissolved matters in the water increases. This may result in higher nutrient concentrations and microbial decomposition. In the IL, statistical analysis indicates that RWCS is not significantly correlated with various indicators. And the water is relatively uniformly mixed, and nitrogen elements are uniformly blended internally. The DO content satisfies the conditions for nitrification. Therefore, nitrification is primarily dominant (Li et al., 2022 ). Additionally, water stratification may also influence the exchange of substances between sediments and water (Hou et al., 2021 ). Environmental factors at the sediment–water interface (DO, T) directly affect the conditions for nutrient release from sediments (Zhang et al., 2014 ). In recent years, the internal re-release of sediment may continuously impact water quality. Hence, it is essential to monitor changes in environmental factors at the sediment–water interface and understand the characteristics of nitrogen migration and transformation. The positive correlation between the thermocline intensity in the isothermal layer and RWCS reflects the ability of the thermocline to enhance the stability of stratification and prevent the mixing of sub-lithium ions during the stratification process of reservoirs (Jung et al., 2022 ). Correlation analysis of the mixed layer in December indicates that RWCS is significantly positively correlated with temperature (T), and TSI is significantly positively correlated with chlorophyll-a (Chla) (p < 0.05). According to the RWCS calculation formula, as surface water temperature increases, the RWCS value also increases. In winter, the RWCS of the upper layer of reservoir water is positively correlated with temperature, indicating the stabilization of the temperature gradient in the water column. The significant correlation between Chla and TSI suggests that temperatures during the winter mixing period are associated with relatively higher chlorophyll-a content. Typically, the depth of the mixing layer is found to be the primary determinant of Chla in open waters, with surface Chla concentrations varying with temperature (Jiang et al., 2019; Wang et al. 2024a, b ). The significant positive correlation between TSI and Chla reflects the relationship between nutrient levels and algal biomass, thereby determining the trophic status of the reservoir. A significant positive correlation between TSI and Chla indicates that higher TSI values, which denote higher productivity or eutrophic conditions, are associated with higher concentrations of Chla. This relationship is well-documented in studies of lake eutrophication, where increased nutrient levels (e.g., phosphorus) lead to higher algal growth, reflected in higher Chla concentrations and TSI values (Lin et al., 2022; Saturday et al., 2023 ). Based on the above analysis, Fig. 7   provides a conceptual diagram illustrating the nitrogen migration and transformation process under stratified conditions in NZD Reservoir. This facilitates a visual understanding of the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of nitrogen migration and transformation in the vertical dimension of the deep reservoir.   5 Conclusion Through monitoring water quality and N/O isotopes in typical profiles of the NZD Reservoir, it was observed that the reservoir exhibited clear vertical stratification during the sampling period in April. The overall nitrogen transformation in the water body was mainly dominated by nitrification, with localized variations in biochemical processes. In the ML (0–5 m), both assimilation of ammonium nitrogen by phytoplankton and nitrification coexisted. In the TL (5–40 m), evident stratification was observed, with prolonged hydraulic retention times leading to the oxidation and decomposition of particulate organic nitrogen. In regions with minimum DO (30–40 m), simultaneous coupling of denitrification and nitrification was observed. In December, the main process is nitrogen assimilation in reservoir surface with little stratification. Statistical analysis indicated that DO, T, and pH were key factors influencing nitrogen transformation in the water body. DO showed significant correlations with N/O isotopes in both the TL and IL in April. Significant correlations between RWCS and physicochemical parameters were evident. In the ML, RWCS showed a significant correlation with ammonium nitrogen, highlighting the substantial impact of temperature stratification on nitrogen nitrification. In the TL, RWCS exhibited significant correlations with DO and pH, reflecting the characteristics of stratification distribution that directly affect environmental factors such as DO and pH under temperature stratification conditions, thus influencing nitrogen transformation processes. This study highlights the intricate vertical stratification and nitrogen transformation processes within the NZD Reservoir, emphasizing the critical role of factors such as DO, temperature, and pH in shaping these dynamics. The results underscore the necessity for fine-scale monitoring to understand and manage the ecological impacts of deep reservoirs. However, potential limitations exist. The temporal scope was limited to specific months, potentially overlooking seasonal variations. Moreover, localized biochemical processes may differ significantly in other reservoirs with varying depths, climatic conditions, and anthropogenic influences. Future research should incorporate multi-seasonal data and consider broader geographical contexts to enhance the applicability of findings to other deep and large reservoirs.
1 Introduction In the context of global climate change, there is an increasing frequency of extreme rainfall events, posing significant challenges to urban flood control (Deng et al., 2023; Guan et al., 2023; Liao et al., 2023; Qi et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022c; Zhou et al., 2023 ). In inland cities, rainwater is typically managed through drainage networks and discharged into nearby rivers (Chen et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022 ). Urban flooding occurs when the city’s drainage capacity is unable to cope with the volume of rainwater (Wang et al., 2015 ). Furthermore, extreme rainfall often leads to a rise in river levels within the watershed, diminishing the effectiveness of rainwater discharge into rivers and heightening the risk of urban flooding (Moon et al., 2023; Tha et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022b ). For instance, during the period of July 19 to 21, 2021, Zhengzhou, China experienced an unprecedented maximum rainfall of 624.1 mm in a single day (Lv et al., 2022 ). The extreme precipitation, combined with reservoir releases, significantly impacted the Jialu river, the primary drainage outlet of Zhengzhou City, leading to a rapid rise in downstream river levels (Wu et al., 2022 ). The topping effect of the river level hindered the discharge of rainwater, resulting in severe flooding and catastrophic consequences, including 380 fatalities and economic losses amounting to US$6.3 billion (Wu et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2022 ). Hence, it is evident that extraordinary rainfall and elevated river levels are both flood drivers for inland cities, and their compound impact exacerbates flood-related damages. It is imperative for urban flood management to evaluate the augmented flood risk resulting from the compound impact of rainfall and river levels, defining it as amplification flood risk. In addition, the categorization of amplification flood risk and the determination of distinct risk thresholds (i.e., the combined rainfall and river level value) can serve as crucial prerequisites for initiating flood warnings, and establish a scientific foundation for urban flood control and disaster reduction. Urban compound floods, resulting from multiple hazard factors, have been observed to yield more substantial repercussions compared to floods driven by a single factor (Deng et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2021; Muñoz et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021 ). Over the past few decades, an increasing number of scholars focused on compound floods. For instance, in inland cities, compound floods driven by rainfall and river factors (including river levels and flow rates) caught the attention of researchers (Apel et al., 2016; Bermúdez et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2020; Muthusamy et al., 2019; Tanaka et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2023b ). Extensive research on compound flooding resulting from rainfall and river flow indicated a strong positive correlation between the two (Dougherty et al., 2021 ). Neglecting the interaction between rainfall and river flow might have led to an underestimation of urban flooding (Kumbier et al., 2018; Xie et al., 2023 ). Moreover, when extreme rainfall coincided with high river levels, the resulting compound floods often posed greater risks to cities due to increased flood depths and extents (Apel et al., 2016; Muthusamy et al., 2019 ). Similarly, in coastal cities, compound floods triggered by rainfall, river factors, and tides were noted (Bates et al., 2021; Gori et al., 2020; Nasr et al., 2021; Nicholls et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2022; Zeng et al., 2024 ). The interdependencies among these three driving factors was focused on by scholars. For instance, in the United States, higher interdependence was observed between the different drivers during the tropical season in the Gulf of Mexico and parts of the East Coast affected by tropical cyclones, while the West Coast exhibited stronger interdependence during the extratropical season (Nasr et al., 2021 ). Additionally, an assessment of compound flooding in northwestern Europe from 1970 to 2014 highlighted that the simultaneous occurrence of extreme rainfall and high tide levels increased flood risks (Ganguli and Merz 2019 ).
