The combination of heavy rainfall and elevated sea levels presents challenges for the effective discharge of rainwater into the sea (Qiang et al., 2021 ), leading to more severe casualties and economic losses (Fang et al., 2021 ). The assessment of compound floods involves the consideration of various combinations of hazard factors, which can result in different types of compound floods. To evaluate the probabilistic risk of these compound floods and to identify the main hazard factors involved, researchers have employed various research methods (Xie et al., 2023 ). Currently, probabilistic risk assessment of the simultaneous occurrence of multiple hazard factors and hydrological-hydrodynamic model are commonly utilized in the study of compound floods (Saharia et al., 2021 ). As for probabilistic risk assessment, copula functions are commonly used methods to assess the joint risk of multiple hazard factors. The copula function is utilized to discern the multivariate attributes of hydrological extremes (Liu et al., 2020 ), assess various uncertainty parameters within their dependency structure (Gao et al., 2021 ), and derive the concurrent risk probability associated with different hazard factors. The hydrological-hydrodynamic model is another prevalent tool for investigating compound floods (Xu et al., 2023b ). It enables the quantification of flood characteristics, such as inundation depth and area, through simulation calculations (Tanim and Goharian 2021 ). Consequently, the model is frequently employed to evaluate the risk of compound floods and analyze the influence of various hazard factors on compound flood events (Xu et al., 2021 ). For example, Lian et al., (2013)  used a hydrodynamic model to assess the flood risk under different rainfall and tide levels in Fuzhou City, and the results showed that ignoring the additional flood risk due to the tide level would result in an underestimation of the design flood. Lian et al., (2017)  proposed an integrated approach to quantify the hazard of hazard factors based on the calculation results of the hydrological-hydrodynamic model, which showed that the main hazard factor in inland areas is rainfall, while the main hazard factor in island areas is tide level. While existing research has contributed to a better understanding of urban compound flooding, several challenges persist. Firstly, the influence of extreme rainfall and river levels on urban flood management requires further investigation (Gori et al., 2020 ). Under extreme rainfall scenarios, high river levels can significantly impede urban drainage and exacerbate urban flooding disasters. As it was evident, different combinations of rainfall and river levels could present unique amplification flood risk (Liang and Zhou 2022 ). However, to date, the specific research area focusing on the amplification flood risk under the combined influence of rainfall and river levels remained relatively limited. Moreover, for compound floods driven by both rainfall and river levels, there was a lack of unified thresholds that distinguished the classes of amplification flood risk, which could have posed challenges to urban flood risk management. Therefore, a quantitative assessment of the amplification risk associated with various rainfall-river level combinations, along with the determination of rainfall and river level thresholds for different risk classes, could have effectively assisted city decision-makers in enhancing flood management strategies and advancing flood early warning and disaster mitigation efforts in inland cities. The aim of this study is to present a framework for amplification flood risk assessment and threshold determination of extreme rainfall and river levels, with the purpose of providing support for urban flood prevention and management. The potential academic contributions of this study are as follows: (i) the combined rainfall and river level scenarios was stochastically simulated utilizing copula functions and Monte Carlo sampling. (ii) A comprehensive index was proposed for the amplification flood risk assessment by integrating a hydrodynamic-based urban inundation model and entropy weighting method. (iii) The combined thresholds for different amplification flood risk classes were determined through binary return periods of rainfall and river levels. The sections of the study are organized as follows. Section 2  organizes the research framework and introduces the main methods. Section 3  presents an overview of the study area and basic data. Section 4  presents the result of amplification flood risk assessment and threshold determination of extreme rainfall and river levels. At the same time, the discussion on the spatial distribution of urban flooding under different amplification flood risk classes is also in Section 4 . The main conclusions are presented in Section 5 .  2 Methods 2.1 Framework This study proposes a framework for amplification flood risk assessment and threshold determination of rainfall and river levels. Initially, the correlation between rainfall and river level was determined by Kendall rank and Spearman rank correlation coefficient. Subsequently, the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of rainfall and river level were calculated by Generalized Extreme Value (GEV), Log-normal, Normal, Gamma, and Weibull distributions. Following this, the copula function was employed to create a joint distribution model of rainfall and river level. Based on this joint distribution model, the binary return period distribution of rainfall and river level was calculated, and combined scenarios of rainfall and river level were randomly simulated using Monte Carlo sampling. These combined scenarios were input into the urban inundation model to calculate three characterization indicators comparing with the scenarios without considering river levels: the difference in maximum inundation volume (DMIV), the difference in maximum inundation area (DMIA), and the difference in maximum inundation depth (DMID). Finally, the amplification flood risk index (ARI) was proposed by integrating three characterization indicators based on the entropy weighting method. The amplification flood risk caused by combined rainfall and river level was determined by ARI, and the combined thresholds of compound flooding were generated by the binary return period of rainfall and river levels. The research framework is illustrated in Fig. 1  .  2.2 Stochastic simulation of combined rainfall and river level scenarios based on copula functions and Monte Carlo sampling 2.2.1 Copula function Copula function is a multidimensional cumulative distribution function (CDF) defined on the domain [0, 1], capable of capturing the correlation structure among multiple variables (Liu et al., 2020 ). It is not constrained by the type of CDF of individual variables and has found extensive application across various domains (Gao et al., 2018; Xie et al., 2023 ). Methods for Monte Carlo sampling of a specific probability distribution are primarily categorized as direct sampling, rejection sampling, and importance sampling, with direct sampling being the most commonly utilized approach (Groen et al., 2014 ). Let the probability density functions of rainfall R  and river level L  be p ( r )    and p ( l )   , respectively. Step2. The cumulative distribution functions c ( r )    and c ( l )    are obtained by integrating p ( r )    and p ( l )   , respectively, for rainfall R   and river level L . Step3. The joint probability distribution of rainfall R  and river level L  is fitted by copula function and the optimal joint cumulative distribution function c ( r , l )    is preferred. Step4. Based on c ( r , l )   , n  random number pairs ( r i  , l i  )    are generated by Monte Carlo sampling, where i  = 1,2,⋯,n . Step5. Based on the cumulative distribution functions c ( r )    and c ( l )    for rainfall R  and river level L , the corresponding rainfall design value r i ′  i    and river level design value l i ′    for the random number pairs are found, respectively.(7) r i ′  = c ( r i  )  - 1   i = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n     (8) l i ′  = c ( l i  )  - 1   i = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n      In summary, the combined rainfall and river level scenario group is ( r i ′  , l i ′  )   , where i = 1,2,⋯,n .  2.2.4 Binary return period of combined rainfall and river levels A hydrological event can be characterized by two or more variables (Dhital and Kayastha 2013 ). In the context of urban flooding events, both rainfall and river level have a significant impact. The marginal distributions of annual maximum 24-hour rainfall and river level were denoted as F ( r )    and F ( l )    respectively. The marginal distribution of the combined rainfall and river level events was denoted as F ( r , l )   . The probability of both rainfall R   and river level L  exceeding a certain magnitude is referred to as P ∩ ( r , l )   , and its corresponding return period is denoted as T AND   ∩ ( r , l )    (i.e., AND return period) (Lian et al., 2013 ). In this study, the AND return period was adopted to determine the compound flooding thresholds caused by rainfall and river levels. The specific calculation steps were as follows. Initially, based on historical rainfall and river level data spanning from 1980 to 2019, the marginal distributions of annual maximum 24-hour rainfall and river level were separately calculated as F ( r )    and F ( l )    respectively. Subsequently, the correlation between the annual maximum 24-hour rainfall and its corresponding river level was assessed using the Kendall rank and Spearman rank correlation coefficients. The joint distribution of the combined rainfall and river level F ( r , l )    was calculated based on the copula function. Finally, the binary return period was computed according to the formula (9).(9) T AND  ∩ ( r , l )  = 1 P ∩ ( r , l )   = 1 P ( ( R > r ) ∪ ( L > l ) )   = 1 1 - F ( r ) - F ( l ) + F ( r , l )         2.3 Urban inundation model The urban inundation model was established for simulating inundation depth, volume and areas under different rainfall and river level scenarios. The personal computer storm water management model (PCSWMM) is a modeling tool for urban and watershed drainage systems that has been developed by the Canadian Institute for Hydraulic Computing, building upon the foundations of SWMM (Wang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023a ). PCSWMM leverages SWMM’s one-dimensional conduit and river model, complemented by a two-dimensional surface inundation model, which enables the characterization of urban surface inundation processes and has seen widespread adoption (Wu et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2023a; Zhu et al., 2016 ). Moreover, PCSWMM has the capability to input both rainfall and river level data, allowing for the assessment of urban flooding under combined rainfall and river level scenarios (Lian et al., 2017 ). In PCSWMM, the one-dimensional (1D) model is mainly composed of rivers and drainage pipes, and its calculation mode is exactly the same as that of classical SWMM (James et al., 2010 ). In the one-dimensional (1D) model simulation of SWMM, flow calculations in the pipe network were based on the gradual non-uniform flow in the system and the conservation control of momentum and mass through the Saint-Venant equations. Therefore, solving the Saint-Venant equation set is the core of flow computation (Wang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023a ). Common methods for solving the Saint-Venant equation set include the constant flow method, the kinematic wave method, the diffusion wave method, and the dynamic wave method (James et al., 2010 ). Among these methods, the dynamic wave method provides a complete solution to the Saint-Venant equation set by fully considering various flow conditions in the pipes, such as storage changes, backwater effects, pressurized flow, backflow, inlet and outlet losses, making it suitable for all types of pipe networks and currently the most accurate solving method (James et al., 2010 ). In this study, the dynamic wave method was utilized to solve the Saint-Venant equation set. The two-dimensional surface inundation model within PCSWMM is governed by the continuity and momentum equation (Ahiablame and Shakya 2016 ). The one-dimensional conduit and river model is interconnected with the two-dimensional surface inundation model via orifices (Wu et al., 2022 ), with equation (12)  utilized for the calculation of orifice flow.(10) ∂ A  ∂ t   + ∂ Q  ∂ x   = 0     (11) ∂ Q  ∂ t   + ∂ Q 2  / A     ∂ x   + g A ∂ H  ∂ x   + g A S f  + g A h L  = 0      Where, A  is the cross-sectional area, m2 ；t  is the time, s; Q  is the flow, m3 /s； x  is the distance along the conduit, m；H  is the pressure head, m; hL   is the local energy loss, m/m; Sf   is the friction slope, m/m; g  is the gravity acceleration, m/ s2  .(12) Q = C a 2 g h        Where, Q  is the flow, m3 /s ; C  is the flow coefficient ;  a  is the orifice area, m2 ; g  is the gravity acceleration, m/ s2  ; h  is the pressure head at the orifice, m .  2.4 Amplification flood risk assessment of rainfall and river level based on entropy weight method 2.4.1 Entropy weight method The fundamental concept of the entropy weight method is to ascertain objective weights based on the variability of the indicators (Chen and Sun 2022; Xu et al., 2018 ). In essence, a smaller information entropy of an indicator signifies a greater degree of variability in its value, indicating its capacity to provide more information, thus resulting in a higher weight. Conversely, a larger information entropy of an indicator corresponds to a smaller weight. The typical steps of the entropy weighting method are as follows (Chen et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2018 ). Step1. For m  assessed objects and n  assessment criteria, construct the original data matrix X = ( x ij   )  m × n      and standardize the matrix to create a dimensionless matrix Y = ( y ij   )  m × n     . Step2. Calculation of the characteristic weight p ij    for the i  object under the j  indicator.(13) p ij   = y ij   ∑ i = 1  m  y ij   i = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , m ; j = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n       Step3. Calculate the entropy value e j   , the coefficient of variation D j    and the entropy weight w j    for the indicator j .(14) e j  = - ∑ i = 1  m  p ij   ln p ij    ln m       (15) D j  = 1 - e j      (16) w j  = D j  / ∑ j = 1  n  D j        2.4.2 Steps of amplification flood risk assessment and threshold determination caused by rainfall and river levels The amplification flood risk index (ARI) was introduced to quantify the amplification flood risk caused by rainfall and river levels. The ARI was by integrating three flooding indicators based on the entropy weighting method. The steps for amplification flood risk assessment are as follows. Step1. m  sets of rainfall and river level combinations simulated by Section 2.2.3  were input as the boundaries of urban inundation model. The risk of urban flooding is defined by n  flooding indicators (i.e., inundation depth, volume, etc.). For m  sets of combinations, the matrix of flood characteristic indicators are defined as A = ( a ij   )  m × n     , where i = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , m ; j = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n   . Additionally, there are m  sets of identical rainfall scenarios without the influence of river level, resulting in the flood characteristic indicator matrix B = ( b ij   )  m × n     , where i = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , m ; j = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n   . Step2. Based on the A  and B  matrices, the increase in the flood characteristic index C = ( c ij   )  m × n      due to the compound effect of rainfall and river level is calculated as follows:(17) C=A-B     Step3. The matrix C  is standardized to obtain C′ . Step4. The entropy weight of each indicator in C  is calculated from equations (13–16) as w j  j = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n      . Step5. Based on the ARI, the natural-breaks method was used to classify the amplification flood risk for combined rainfall and river level scenarios. Step7. Thresholds for amplification flood risk were determined based on the contour line.    3 Study area and data 3.1 Study area Zhengzhou City is one of the nine central cities of China and serves as the economic and political hub of Henan Province. Among its districts, Jinshui district stands out as the most densely populated and economically developed area. However, the district has been facing increasingly severe flooding, attributed to the combined effects of climate change and rapid urbanization. The latitude and longitude range of Jinshui district is 113°40′ ∼ 113°47′E, 30°50′ ∼ 34°57′N, covering an area of 136.66 km2 . The district has a monsoonal continental climate, with an annual average temperature of 14.8 °C and an average rainfall of 586 mm per year. The district has a dense river network, including the Jialu River, Jinshui River, Dongfeng Canal, Qili River, Xionger River, and others. The levels of these rivers significantly impact flooding in Jinshui district, particularly during extreme rainfall scenarios. For instance, during the intense rainfall event on July 21, 2021, Jinshui district emerged as the most severely flooded area in Zhengzhou City. This was attributed to the extensive river channels in the district, compounded by elevated water levels in all rivers, which hindered the discharge of rainwater through the underground conduits. Consequently, Jinshui district is a very fitting case study to validate the proposed framework. An overview of Jinshui district is presented in Fig. 2  .  3.2 Data The underlying data utilized in this study was separated into two main parts. The first part encompasses essential data required for developing the urban inundation model, such as slope data, building information, Digital Elevation Model (DEM), and river and conduit data of Jinshui district. The second part comprises flooding information specific to Jinshui district, including historical inundation data, records of rainfall and river levels, and the identification of flood-prone areas. Table 1   presents the sources of the data.   4 Results and discussion 4.1 Urban inundation model of Jinshui district 4.1.1 Construction of the urban inundation model Based on the conduit data and river data, a one-dimensional (1D) rivers and drainage pipes model (Fig. 3  a) was constructed for the Jinshui district, which consists of 704 junctions, 739 conduits (main rivers and drainage pipes), and three outfalls. The main rivers were generalized as open channels based on specific parameters such as bed elevation, bottom width, and cross-sectional shape. The outfalls are rainwater outlets for the study area and also allow for inputs into the river level process. The Jinshui district is subdivided into 730 subcatchments based on the distribution of roads, buildings, and rivers, as illustrated in Fig. 3 a. Subcatchments within the vicinity are interconnected with each other or with adjacent junctions. The impediment of rainwater flow by buildings must be considered when developing the surface inundation model. As such, the obstruction layer is created based on the distribution of buildings. Fig. 3 b presents the two-dimensional (2D) surface inundation model of Jinshui district, comprising 395,468 2D junctions, 1190,337 2D canals, and 396,779 2D cells (with a precision of 25 m × 25 m). The one-dimensional rivers and drainage pipes model and the two-dimensional surface inundation model of Jinshui district were connected through 704 orifices (Fig. 3 b). In summary, an urban inundation model of Jinshui district was constructed, which simulates flooding in Jinshui district under a combination of rainfall and river level scenarios.  4.1.2 Calibration of the urban inundation model Flood events, designated as Event A and Event B, occurred on July 26, 2011, and July 20, 2021, respectively, in Jinshui district. Due to limited data availability, the historical inundation depth and flood-prone points from these events were utilized to assess the reliability of the urban inundation model. Fig. 4   depicts the maximum inundation depth distributions simulated by the urban inundation model for Event A and Event B. During Event A, 12 out of 15 flood-prone areas in Jinshui district experienced flooding, accounting for 80.00 % of the areas (Fig. 4 a). For Event B, all 15 flood-prone areas in Jinshui district experienced flooding (Fig. 4 b). Consequently, the distribution of maximum inundation depth obtained by the model aligns with the distribution of flood-prone areas in Jinshui district. Table 2   presents the historical and simulated inundation depth for the observed areas during Event A and Event B. The average relative error between the historical and simulated inundation depth for Event A is 19.91 %, with a Nash efficiency coefficient (NSE) of 0.85. For Event B, the average relative error between the historical and simulated inundation depth is 13.33 %, with a NSE of 0.72. The comparison indicates that the simulated inundation depth calculated by the urban inundation model are in closer agreement with the historical inundation depth. In conclusion, the simulation results of the model are considered reliable.   4.2 Combined scenarios of rainfall and river level based on copula function and Monte Carlo sampling 4.2.1 Joint distribution of rainfall and river level based on copula function Based on historical rainfall and river level data from 1980 to 2019 in Jinshui district, the annual maximum 24-hour rainfall and its corresponding river level were selected for each year. The GEV, Log-normal, Normal, Gamma, and Weibull distributions were employed to model the CDF of the annual maximum 24-hour rainfall and the corresponding river level in Jinshui district. The goodness-of-fit of the rainfall and river level CDFs was evaluated using the RMSE and the AIC. The GEV distribution was selected as the optimal model for rainfall and river level based on the minimization of RMSE and AIC values, as presented in Table 3  . The P-P plot was presented in Fig. 5  a, indicating a satisfactory fit between the theoretical probability and empirical frequency. The assessment of the statistical dependence between rainfall and river level is imperative to verify the suitability of the copula function for analysis. The Kendall rank correlation coefficient and Spearman rank correlation coefficient for rainfall and river level were determined to be 0.41 and 0.54, respectively, with a significance level of 0.01. These values indicate a significant correlation between the two variables. As a result, the copula function can be utilized to ascertain the relationships between rainfall and river level. The Clayton copula, Gumbel copula, and Frank copula were employed to model the joint cumulative distribution function of rainfall and river level. The RMSE values and AIC values for the different copula functions are presented in Table 4  . Based on the minimum RMSE and AIC values, the Gumbel copula was selected to fit the joint CDF of rainfall and river level. Fig. 5 b illustrates the binary P-P plot of rainfall and river level based on the Gumbel copula, with a correlation coefficient of 0.9938. Additionally, Fig. 5 c displays the joint CDF of rainfall and river level based on the Gumbel copula. Lastly, the binary return period of rainfall and river level (Fig. 5 d) was calculated using Equation (9) .  4.2.2 Stochastic combined scenarios of rainfall and river level based on Monte Carlo sampling Monte Carlo sampling is employed to generate 250 random two-dimensional sets (ri ,wi  ) based on the joint cumulative distribution function (CDF) of rainfall and river level. The sets are derived from the CDFs of rainfall and river level to obtain random pairs corresponding to the design values ri   and wi  . The resulting of combined rainfall and river level scenarios is denoted as (ri ,wi  ). Fig. 6   illustrates the 250 sets of combined rainfall and river level scenarios, along with their AND return period distributions. The time series of rainfall and river levels were determined based on design values and historical typical rainfall and river level processes. Building upon previous research (Hu et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022a ), the rainfall time series recorded on August 12, 2017 was identified as the prototypical rainfall time series, and the corresponding river level time series was identified as the prototypical river level time series. Subsequently, based on the prototypical rainfall and river level time series, the time series of combined rainfall and river level scenarios were formulated. In terms of the spatial distribution of rainfall, it was assumed that precipitation was homogenous across all locations within the study area during the specific time period.   4.3 Amplification flood risk assessment and threshold determination for combined rainfall and river level scenarios 4.3.1 Influence on urban flooding by the compound effect of rainfall and river level Maximum inundation volume, area and depth are commonly used indicators to describe urban flooding. Compound floods were simulated for 250 sets of combined scenarios of rainfall and river levels by the urban inundation model. After simulation, 83 sets of combined scenarios were selected due to producing floods in Jinshui district. Correspondingly, 83 sets of scenarios with the same rainfall but no river level were also simulated by the urban inundation model. The thin plate spline method is employed to compute the surfaces of maximum inundation volume, area and depth, as depicted in Fig. 7  a, c, and e, respectively. To characterize the amplification degree of urban flooding by combined rainfall and river level scenarios, the difference in maximum inundation volume (DMIV), difference in maximum inundation area (DMIA), and difference in maximum inundation depth (DMID) between the combined rainfall and river level scenarios and the single rainfall scenarios are chosen as amplification flood risk indicators. DMIV, DMID and DMIA are shown in Fig. 7 b, d, and e, respectively. As shown in Fig. 7 , the inundation volume, area and depth significantly increase when urban flooding is driven by both rainfall and river level. Furthermore, the growth rate of DMIV, DMIA, and DMID slows down with increasing rainfall at the same river level, while under the same rainfall, the growth rate of DMIV, DMIA, and DMID is enhanced with increasing river level. By observing the change of DMIV, DMIA, and DMID with river level (Fig. 8  a, c, and e), it was found that these three indicators followed a similar pattern. With the increase in river level, a turning point (referred to as point D in Fig. 8 a) was identified, leading to a sudden increase in the increments of DMIV, DMIA, and DMID. Furthermore, the river level value at this turning point decreased with increasing rainfall amounts (as shown by points A, B, C, and D in Fig. 8 a). By observing the change of DMIV and DMIA with rainfall (Fig. 8 b and d), they exhibited similar trends. With the increase in rainfall, a turning point (referred to as point H in Fig. 8 b) was identified, leading to a sudden increase in the increments of DMIV and DMIA. Furthermore, the rainfall value at this turning point decreased with increasing river level amounts (as shown by points E, F, G, and H in Fig. 8 b). The distinction between DMIA and DMIV was that a second turning point appeared when both rainfall and river levels were sufficiently high (point I in Fig. 8 d), causing a reduction in the growth rate of DMIA. The DMID differed substantially from DMIV and DMIA. As rainfall increased, a turning point was identified, leading to a sudden decreased in the increments of DMID. Furthermore, the rainfall value at this turning point increased with increasing river level amounts (as shown by points J, K, L, and M in Fig. 8 f). Table 5   presents the percentage increase in DMIV, DMIA, and DMID for the compound flood driven by both rainfall and river level in relation to the rainfall-driven flood. Table 5  presents the percentage increase in DMIV, DMIA, and DMID for the compound flood driven by both rainfall and river level in relation to the rainfall-driven flood. As shown in Table 5 , the maximum inundation volume, area, and depth of the compound flood increased on average by 6.01 %, 10.03 %, and 6.12 %, respectively, compared to the rainfall-driven flood. The maximum percentage increase was 51.15 %, 53.21 %, and 19.88 %, respectively. From this, it could be deduced that the maximum inundation area was most sensitive to the combined effects of rainfall and river level.  4.3.2 Calculation of ARI and assessment of amplification flood risk The ARI was utilized to assess the amplification flood risk under the combined rainfall and river level scenarios, which was computed using the three indicators DMID, DMIA, and DMIV. The weights for DMID, DMIA, and DMIV were calculated using Equations (13–16), and the results are presented in Table 6  . The information entropy of DMID, DMIA, and DMIV was 0.76, 0.83, and 0.85, respectively, while the coefficients of variation were 0.24, 0.17, and 0.15, respectively. Among them, DMIV had the highest weight at 42.62 %, and DMID had the lowest weight at 31.08 %. Subsequently, after determining the weights, the ARI was computed based on Equation (18) . The heat map in Fig. 9   illustrates that the ARI is positively correlated with both rainfall and river level, indicating that higher levels of these factors lead to an increased ARI. Additionally, based on the heat map of ARI, we could roughly infer that the distribution of ARI was similar to the distribution of the binary return period. For instance, when ARI ranged between 0.02 and 0.03 (blue segment in Fig. 9 ), its distribution resembled that of the binary return period of less than or equal to 10 years. Therefore, the binary return period was considered in determining the amplification flood risk threshold. The amplification flood risk was classified as high, medium, and low risk by the natural-breaks method based on ARI (Ke et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2022 ). There are 23 sets of high risk scenarios, 21 sets of medium risk scenarios, and 39 sets of low risk scenarios (Fig. 10  ).  4.3.3 Flooding thresholds of rainfall and river levels for different risk classes Fig. 10  illustrates the distribution of amplification flood risk classes for rainfall and river level scenarios and contour lines of binary return periods. As depicted in Fig. 10 , when the T AND   ∩ ( r , l )     is less than 3 years, the compound flooding of rainfall and river levels will not occur. When the T AND   ∩ ( r , l )     is greater than or equal to 3 years and less than 20 years, the amplification flood risk is classified as low. When the T AND   ∩ ( r , l )     is greater than or equal to 20 years and less than 90 years, the amplification flood risk is classified as medium. When the T AND   ∩ ( r , l )     is greater than or equal to 280 years, the amplification flood risk is classified as high. However, when the T AND   ∩ ( r , l )     is greater than or equal to 90 years and less than 280 years, the amplification flood risk for scenarios of rainfall and river level may be high and medium. In this case, the amplification flood risk is classified as high only when the rainfall exceeds 130 mm and the river level is above 76.88 m (Points C and D in Fig. 10 ); otherwise, it is classified as medium risk. The binary return period thresholds for the amplification flood risk classes are detailed in Table 7  . The threshold for amplification flood risk at different classes is an important prerequisite for initiating flood warnings, providing a scientific basis for urban flood control and disaster reduction.   4.4 Urban flooding distribution under different risk scenarios of combined rainfall and river level Three typical compound flood events were selected from the low, medium, and high risk classes, respectively, and detailed values of rainfall and river level were provided in Table 8  . The maximum inundation depth distributions for these three flood scenarios were depicted in Fig. 11  a, c, and e, respectively. The maximum inundation depth distributions for the corresponding rainfall-driven floods without river level influence were presented in Fig. 11 b, d, and f, respectively. It is evident that only considering rainfall as a single causal factor leads to an underestimation of urban flooding compared to the combined scenarios incorporating both rainfall and river level, especially in areas 1, 2, 3, and 4 of Fig. 11 . Furthermore, this underestimation becomes more pronounced as the amplification flood risk level increases. The comparison of Fig. 11 a, c, and e reveals that the area of flood exacerbation, in contrast to flooding driven solely by rainfall, progressively expands from the southeastern corner of the study area towards the center as the amplification flood risk level increases. The examination of spatial variations in flood exacerbation areas under varying rainfall and river level scenarios serves as a crucial foundation for the precise prediction of urban flooding and offers valuable insights for the development of urban flood mitigation infrastructure.  4.5 Limitation of the proposed framework and future work The FARTD proposed in this study can assess the risk of the amplification flooding driven by the combination of rainfall and river level and determine the binary return period thresholds for different risk classes, which has a potential application in urban flood management. Nevertheless, this study has limitations that necessitate further investigation. In this study, considering the simulation efficiency and timeliness of urban inundation model, 250 sets of combined rainfall and river level scenarios were randomly simulated using the Monte Carlo method to define input boundaries for the urban inundation model. For future studies, expanding the number of combined scenarios could enhance the accuracy of amplification risk assessment. In addition, stochastic rainfall generators are a versatile category of models that stochastically simulate rainfall processes based on the specific rainfall characteristics of the study area (Cowpertwait et al., 2007; Kim and Onof 2020; Onof et al., 2000 ). Due to their capacity to produce long-term, high-resolution rainfall processes, these generators find extensive utility in research and practical applications, particularly in fields like water resources management and flood prediction (De Luca and Petroselli 2021 ). Currently, they are widely employed across the globe, including regions such as China, Germany, and certain parts of South Korea (Vorobevskii et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024 ). In forthcoming research endeavors, utilizing stochastic rainfall generators to produce more precise rainfall processes with spatiotemporal characteristics, combined with other flood-driving factors, could further advance the understanding of compound flood characteristics. Furthermore, this study exclusively assessed amplification flood risk and determined thresholds for different risk classes. Subsequent research could involve regulating river levels based on existing engineering facilities (e.g., reservoirs, pumping stations, etc.) to mitigate flood risk in the inland city.   5 Conclusion This paper presents a framework for amplification flood risk assessment and threshold determination of extreme rainfall and river levels. Taking the region of Zhengzhou City as an example, scenarios combining rainfall and river level in the study area were stochastically simulated using copula function and Monte Carlo sampling. There were 250 sets of combined rainfall and river level scenarios created as input boundaries for the urban inundation model. Subsequently, based on the simulation results of the urban inundation model, it was determined that the maximum inundation, area, and depth of the combined rainfall and river level flood increased by an average of 6.01 %, 10.03 %, and 6.12 %, respectively, compared to the rainfall-driven flood. Therefore, relying solely on rainfall as a singular causal factor may result in an underestimation of urban flooding when compared to combined scenario of rainfall and river levels. Furthermore, based on the entropy weighting method, the ARI of rainfall and river level was proposed, and the amplification flood risk was assessed. Following this, the thresholds for the different risk classes were determined. In particular, Jinshui district will be exposed to more than medium amplification flood risk when the binary return period is ≥20 years. In addition, as the amplification flood risk class increases, the flooding exacerbation areas resulting from the rainfall and river levels gradually expands from the southeast corner of the study area towards the center. Overall, the FARTD proposed in this study can be utilized for urban flood warning and risk management.
1 Introduction Unprecedented changes in global runoff generation have occurred due to intense disturbances from natural landscapes and human activities (Mankin et al., 2019, Yang et al., 2022, Yin et al., 2018, Zhou et al., 2023 ). Particularly, in recent decades, global greening has accelerated at a rate of 2.3 % increase in leaf area per decade, driven by efforts to protect ecosystems (Chen et al., 2019 ). Significant reductions in runoff have been observed in large-scale vegetation restoration areas such as northern China, southeastern United States, and Eastern Europe, with vegetation changes contributing 36.5 % to runoff reduction (Chen et al., 2021 ). The significant changes in vegetation have led to notable fluctuations in global surface and subsurface runoff generation (Liu et al., 2023, Luo et al., 2020 ). It is thus crucial to understand the changes in runoff generation characteristics under vegetation restoration to inform the sustainable usage and development of water resources. Various factors across all compartments of the environment affect runoff generation, such as climate factors in the atmosphere, vegetation cover on the land surface, and soil properties in the unsaturated zone. Precipitation dominates the process of runoff generation, while evapotranspiration and soil moisture can modify the redistribution of precipitation (Kool et al., 2014, McColl et al., 2017, Sun et al., 2018 ). Vegetation has a complex influence on runoff generation. Different vegetation types intercept precipitation within the range of 9 % to 43 % under various climate conditions (Arnell, 2014 ). The growth and decomposition of vegetation root systems reduce soil bulk density, increase soil porosity, and facilitate precipitation infiltration into the soil (Qiu et al., 2022 ). However, it has been estimated that most (approximately 70 %) of the water for vegetation transpiration is sourced from the current-month precipitation stored in the surface soil, and is responsible for returning about 39 % ± 10 % of the precipitation back to the atmosphere, while 18 % comes from past precipitation stored in the deep soil (Ellison et al., 2017, Miguez-Macho and Fan, 2021, Tang et al., 2023 ). Therefore, vegetation restoration profoundly influences the hydrological cycle through its complex interactions with soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and precipitation. Additionally, environmental factors collectively affect runoff generation, but the contribution of each factor to the overall effects remains unclear. To study the effects of the various environmental factors on runoff generation, appropriate quantitative indicators of runoff generation must be used. Runoff generation encompasses surface and subsurface runoff generation. Subsurface runoff generation can be reflected through baseflow and the baseflow index (BFI, the ratio of baseflow to streamflow) (Wu et al., 2021, Yan et al., 2023 ). Surface runoff coefficient, which characterizes the proportion of surface runoff to precipitation, reflects surface runoff generation (Birkinshaw et al., 2021, Jin et al., 2020 ). Peak flow is crucial for determining the scale and frequency of floods generated by rainfall events (Yan et al., 2020 ). The duration of floods and the shape of the hydrograph are the complex results of many interacting factors in the runoff generation process and are important runoff generation characteristics (Linsley et al., 1975 ). Therefore, the surface runoff timescale (Ts   , the ratio of flood volume to peak discharge) has been introduced to measure the duration and propagation of the hydrograph (Gaál et al., 2012 ). The above indicators collectively, rather than individually, help provide a comprehensive understanding of regional runoff generation characteristics (Zheng et al., 2023 ). However, these commonly used indicators alone do not provide sufficient insight into the underlying physical mechanisms, which are important for understanding mechanisms of the hydrological cycle (Li et al., 2017 ). The Soil Conservation Service-Curve Number (SCS-CN) is an important tool in studying runoff responses based on storm events due to its simplicity, ease of application, and robustness (Mishra and Singh, 2013 ). Its parameters may be used to link observed hydrological runoff behavior with the physical characteristics of the regional climates and watersheds (Mahmood et al., 2020, Merz and Blöschl, 2009 ). The key parameters, including Curve Number (CN   ), initial loss (I a   ), and potential maximum retention of the basin (S  ), can account for most of the relevant factors that determine hydrological conditions and runoff generation in the region, such as soil type, land use, hydrological conditions, and antecedent moisture conditions (Li et al., 2023, Shi et al., 2009, Verma et al., 2020 ). Natural factors and human activities induce changes in regional hydrological conditions and thereby result in changes to these parameters (Gao et al., 2012, Lin et al., 2014 ). Hence, identifying the key controlling environmental factors affecting these parameters enables direct evaluation of the causative processes that link anthropogenic and non-anthropogenic activities to changes in runoff generation. The Chinese Loess Plateau (CLP) is the region with significant hydrological and environmental changes in the past several decades. The Grain for Green Project, initiated since the 20th century, has led to a rapid increase in forestland area, with vegetation coverage on the CLP rising from 31.6 % in 1999 to 65 % in 2017 (Chen, 2019 ). Before and after vegetation restoration, the runoff coefficient in 87 % of basins in the CLP decreased, with an average reduction of 0.033 (Miao et al., 2020 ). The runoff coefficient in grassland catchments is approximately ten times higher than that in forested catchments, indicating a strong inhibitory effect of afforestation on storm runoff (Jin et al., 2020 ). Baseflow from groundwater discharge constitutes approximately 64 % of the streamflow, jointly dominating the regional hydrological cycle along with surface runoff (Yan et al., 2023 ). However, groundwater recharge decreased by 38 % ± 15 % at 68 % of the stations, with vegetation directly and indirectly contributing 58 % (Yan et al., 2024 ). With ongoing vegetation restoration, groundwater storage has significantly decreased, leading to an increase in groundwater drought area and intensity (Gao et al., 2015, Han et al., 2020 ). The vegetation restoration in the CLP has pushed water resources to the brink of sustainability (Feng et al., 2016, Huang, 2019, Shi et al., 2021 ). The response of the various hydrological elements to the drastic environmental changes occurring here has been extensively studied (Wu et al., 2020, Yang et al., 2021 ). However, a comprehensive understanding of the physical mechanisms driving the changes in surface and subsurface runoff generation has not yet been obtained. The overall objective of this study is to comprehensively interpret the underlying reasons for surface and subsurface runoff generation changes based on SCS-CN model parameters estimated with data of rainfall-runoff events. Specifically, we will (i) analyze the spatiotemporal variations in runoff generation characteristic values across 13 basins and 56 hydrological stations, (ii) inversely estimate the key parameters Ia   , S  , and CN    of the SCS-CN model from data of rainfall-runoff events and analyze their spatiotemporal variations, and (iii) quantify the contributions of various environmental factors (e.g. demographic changes, revegetation, infrastructure) to changes in these key parameters. Considering the physical significance of the parameters of the SCS-CN model will help to understand the surface and subsurface runoff generation mechanism in a changing environment.  2 Data and methods 2.1 Study area The Chinese Loess Plateau (CLP) is located in the middle and upper reaches of the Yellow River, covering an area of approximately 640,000 km2 . The region transitions from subhumid to arid climate, with annual average temperature ranging from 3.7 to 14.0 °C and annual average precipitation of 144.5 to 812.0 mm. About 72 % of the precipitation occurs from June to September (Li et al., 2012, Zhang et al., 2020 ). The primary land use types are grassland (42 %), farmland (32 %), and forest (15 %) (Li et al., 2016 ). The Grain-for-Green program, initiated in 1999, has led to the conversion of farmland to grassland and forest, resulting in a tenfold increase in NDVI    change speed (Li et al., 2017 ). The region is covered by Quaternary loess, which is layered with varying thicknesses of various loess deposits, and the surface layer varies due to the degree of soil erosion. The thickness of the loess ranges from 0 to 350 m, decreasing from the central region towards the southeast and northwest (Xiong et al., 2014, Zhu et al., 2018 ). The thickness and spatial heterogeneity of the loess profoundly impact the topography and hydrogeological conditions of the region. This study selected 13 basins that stretch across different climatic zones and across the entire CLP, accounting for 57 % of the loess-covered region (Table 1  ). This selection provides a comprehensive reflection of the hydrological conditions on the CLP.  2.2 Data collection We collected daily streamflow data of 1961 to 2019 from 56 hydrological stations located at the outlets of major tributaries and whole basins, which adequately capture the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of the regional hydrology (Fig. 1  ). The data were sourced from the Yellow River Conservancy Commission. Due to data availability, there is a gap in data for the period 1991–2000 or 1991–2005 at the outlets of two basins and tributary hydrological stations. Typically, each 10–12 year time span encompasses a full hydrological wet-dry cycle (Dai et al., 2016, Geng et al., 2021, Yoo, 2006 ). For basins with a data record exceeding 10 years, any errors introduced by interannual variability can be considered negligible (Shao et al., 2021 ). The two data periods we acquired are both at least 14 years in length and adequately represent the hydrological conditions before and after the initiation of the Grain for Green Project. Therefore, these data are suitable for runoff generation studies in a changing environment, and we designate the periods before and after vegetation restoration as t1  and t2 , respectively. To attribute changes in runoff generation, we collected data of influencing factors spanning from the atmosphere to the subsurface aquifer, including atmospheric climate data, surface vegetation, and soil moisture in the unsaturated zone. Daily precipitation and volumetric soil water (VSW ) from 1961 to 2019 with a spatial resolution of 0.1° were obtained from Han et al. (2023)  and the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts atmospheric reanalysis (ERA5-land) (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021 ), respectively. Daily Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI   ) from 1982 to 2019 and monthly potential evapotranspiration (ET  0   ) data from 1961 to 2019 with a spatial resolution of 0.05° were sourced from NOAA-AVHRR and the TerraClimate dataset, respectively (Abatzoglou et al., 2018 ). Soil thickness data were obtained from Zhu et al. (2018) . The topographic index (TI   ) was calculated using the Digital Elevation Model (DEM) from the ASTER dataset with a spatial resolution of 30 m (Beven and Kirkby, 1979, Peña-Arancibia et al., 2010, Post and Jakeman, 1996 ). Clay content data with a spatial resolution of 250 m was sourced from OpenLandMap. Apart from vegetation restoration, human activities influence runoff generation processes through various hydrological engineering measures such as check dams and terracing. Obtaining detailed data on these measures can be challenging, but their intensity is highly correlated with population density. Therefore, in this study, we use population data at the county level to analyze the impact of human activities on runoff generation. The county-level population data from 1981 to 2019 were sourced from the Loess Plateau SubCenter, National Earth System Science Data Center, National Science & Technology Infrastructure of China. The data analysis flowchart was shown in Fig. 2  .  2.3 Determination of characteristic value of runoff generation The characteristics of surface runoff generation are determined for rainfall-runoff events. The Detrending Moving-average Cross-correlation Analysis-Event Separation Routine (DMCA-ESR) was used to automatically identify rainfall-runoff events (Giani et al., 2022 ). DMCA-ESR determines the average lag time between the centroids of rainfall events and runoff events, and detects both rainfall and runoff time series to objectively identify events. This method needs to determine the significant minimum rainfall intensity (R min    ) of the study area to calculate the rainfall fluctuation tolerance, so as to avoid small and isolated rainfall events that prevent the time series from being discretized into different events. The surface runoff coefficient (SRC   ), timescale (T s   ), and normalized event peak discharge (N p   ) were calculated for each event based on the identified events (Zheng et al., 2023 ). SRC    is the ratio of the event surface runoff to the event rainfall. T s    is the ratio of the event surface runoff to the event peak runoff, which represents the shape of the surface runoff hydrograph. N p    is the ratio of the peak surface runoff of the event to the long-term average surface runoff, reflecting the magnitude of the event. The characteristics of underground runoff generation are determined according to the baseflow (Wu et al., 2021 ). Baseflow separation was performed using the Eckhardt method, a two-parameter filtering method suitable for CLP (Yan et al., 2023 ). This method filters surface runoff as a high-frequency signal from the baseflow as a low-frequency signal (Eckhardt, 2005 ). Based on the separated baseflow, the annual baseflow (BF) time series and annual BFI are determined. A higher baseflow means more deep groundwater available for discharge, and a greater underground runoff; vice versa. BFI characterizes the contribution of groundwater discharge from the baseflow to streamflow.  2.4 Inverse estimation of SCS-CN parameters The parameters of SCS-CN were not fixed as traditional methods, but were inversely deduced for each rainfall-runoff event. The varying parameters serve as a foundation for interpreting runoff behavior in response to changes in environmental factors. SCS-CN combines two assumptions (Equations (1) and (2)  and a water balance equation (Equation (3) .(1) Q P - I a    = F S      (2) I a  = λ S     (3) P = I a  + F + Q      where Q  , P  , and F   are surface runoff (mm), rainfall (mm), and cumulative infiltration (mm), respectively. S   is potential maximum retention (mm), which characterizes soil water storage capacity. I a    is initial abstraction (mm), which is the rainfall loss caused by vegetation interception, filling and infiltration before surface runoff occurs. λ   is the initial abstraction coefficient, which is the proportionality coefficient between I a    and S  . Z-value with an absolute magnitude greater than 1.96 indicates a significant trend. The Pearson correlation method was used to identify the controlling factors of runoff parameters. The annual average surface runoff and baseflow were 17 ± 7 mm and 26 ± 14 mm, respectively. The BFI averaged 0.59 ± 0.11, with Tuwei River having the highest value (0.73) and Gushanchuan River the lowest (0.36). The streamflow in these basins has experienced varying degrees of reduction, with an average decrease of 39 % ± 12 % from t1  to t2 . The most significant reductions were observed in the Gushanchuan (−63 %) and Kuye (−61 %) Rivers. Surface runoff and baseflow resulted in a 20 % ± 10 % and 19 % ± 7 % reduction in streamflow, respectively.  3.2 Identified events and runoff characteristic values We determined the R min     of DMCA-ESR in the study area through sensitivity analysis (Fig. 3  a). On a daily scale, we tested a range of R min     from 0.02 to 0.2 mm/h. With the increase of R min    , the average number of events in the sub-basin slightly increased from 759 ± 165 to 760 ± 170, then decreased to 506 ± 150, while the average runoff and rainfall volume in the sub-basin respectively decreased from 1.71 ± 2.83 mm and 27.28 ± 7.69 mm to 1.48 ± 2.40 mm and 26.07 ± 5.77 mm, and then increased to 1.50 ± 2.41 mm and 28.51 ± 5.04 mm. If R min     is too small, small and isolated events hinder the discretization of the time series into different events. As R min     increases, the introduction of more small rainfall as breakpoints between events increases the number of events. If R min     is too large, smaller rainfall events will be ignored. When R min     is 0.06 mm/h, the average number of events in the sub-basin is 739 ± 170, and the average runoff and rainfall volume in the sub-basin is 1.50 ± 2.46 mm and 26.07 ± 5.77 mm. Choosing this value for R min     allows for the separation of continuous rainfall-runoff events without ignoring a large number of small rainfall-runoff events. Therefore, this study selected R min     as 0.06 mm/h for event identification. The mean values of sub-basins SRC    and BF    were respectively 0.028 ± 0.035 and 43 ± 52 mm, showing a spatial distribution with lower values in the central part and higher values in the north and south (Fig. 3  b&e). The mean values of N p    and T s    were 3.1 ± 1.9 and 2.3 ± 0.5, respectively (Fig. 3  c&d). N p    decreased as the basin area increased, whereas T s    exhibited the opposite trend. 91 % of the sub-basins had BFI values greater than 0.5, ranging from 0.35 to 0.77 (Fig. 3  f), suggesting the main component of streamflow was contributed by groundwater discharge. BFI did not exhibit a distinct spatial distribution pattern. Sub-basins SRC    and BF    decreased by approximately 34 % ± 24 % and 26 % ± 23 %, respectively. The extent of reduction varied with basins, but SRC    and BF    showed the largest decrease in the Guanshanchuan (−69 % and −63 %) and Kuye River (−72 % and −53 %). The sub-basin N p    exhibited changes ranging from −65 % to 39 %, with 75 % of the sites showing a decreasing trend and greater reductions in the northern sub-basins. About 82 % and 86 % of the sites showed increases in Ts  and BFI   , with average changes of 14 % ± 15 % and 9 % ± 10 %, respectively. The rate of change in T s    decreased with increasing basin area. Overall, both surface runoff and baseflow decreased, resulting in a more gradual surface runoff hydrograph.  3.3 Spatiotemporal variations in SCS-CN parameters The mean values of sub-basin I a   , S  , and CN    were 16 ± 4 mm, 300 ± 287 mm, and 74 ± 12, respectively. Spatially, I a    decreased with increasing latitudes (Fig. 4  ). S   was highest in the Fen River (755 mm) and lowest in the Tuwei River (79 mm). CN    was highest in the Kuye River (84) and lowest in the Fen River (60). Temporally, from t 1  to t 2 , sub-basin I a    and S   increased by 15 % ± 17 % and 186 % ± 204 %, respectively. The increase in I a    was more significant in the north and south, while it was smaller in the central part, and even showed a downward trend (e.g., Yan River with −15 %). 84 % of the stations had S   increasing by more than 100 %, with the magnitude increasing with latitude. CN    exhibited a decreasing trend (−11 % ± 19 %), with the most significant reduction in the Yan River (−37 %).  3.4 Spatiotemporal changes in environmental factors Spatially, P  , NDVI   , VSW   , and population decreased from southeast to northwest (Fig. 5  a, c, d & e). Meanwhile, clay fraction was higher in the southeast and lower in the northwest (Fig. 5 g). ET  0    was higher in the southeast and northwest regions, and lower in the northeast and southwest (Fig. 5 b). TI    showed a north-high and south-low distribution pattern (Fig. 5 f). The thickness of loess decreased from the central part towards the southeast and northwest (Fig. 5 h). Temporally, there was no significant change in precipitation, but ET  0   , NDVI   , and population all showed a significant upward trend. 75 % of the sub-basins exhibited a significant reduction in VSW   .  3.5 Link between environmental factors and SCS-CN parameters By using factor detector to compare the similarity of spatial distribution between environmental factors and SCS-CN parameters, we found that the spatial distribution of S   was controlled by TI    (0.70) and P   (0.31), while that of CN    was collectively influenced by TI    (0.66), P   (0.40), NDVI    (0.35), and loess thickness (0.35). However, the spatial variability of I a    was not significantly correlated with that of any environmental factors. P   exhibited the strongest temporal correlations with the SCS-CN parameters, showing significant associations with changes in S  and I a  ,  a n d  C N    in 89 %, 50 %, and 84 % of the sub-basins, respectively. Following this, the next most influential factors were NDVI  and population (Fig. 6  a). NDVI   , P  , and population were positively correlated with S   and I a   , while they had a negative correlation with CN   . Averaging the elasticity coefficients for the 13 basins, it was found that for every 1 % increase in NDVI   , ET  0   , P  , and population, the average increase in S   was 3.1 %, 3.3 %, 2.4 %, and 3.1 %, respectively. Similarly, I a    increased by 0.3 %, 0.1 %, 0.6 %, and 0.4 %, while CN    decreased by 0.6 %, 0.5 %, 0.4 %, and 0.5 % (Fig. 6 b). On the other hand, for every 1 % increase in VSW   , S   decreased by 1.3 %, while I a    and CN    increased by 0.1 % and 0.2 %, respectively. We further quantified the contributions of environmental factors from the 13 basins to the changes in the SCS-CN parameters using the elasticity coefficient method (Fig. 6 c). The results indicated that NDVI    and population were the primary factors contributing to the variations in regional S   (32 % and 34 %), I a    (21 % and 18 %), and CN    (−32 % and −33 %).   4 Discussion 4.1 Why is surface and subsurface runoff decreasing in the Chinese Loess Plateau? Our results indicate a decrease in surface and subsurface runoff generation across most of the study area, corroborating previous studies in the CLP (Gao et al., 2015, Liang et al., 2015, Yan et al., 2023 ). Based on rainfall-runoff event estimation, the SCS-CN parameters indicated that the S  increased by over 100 % in 84 % of sub-basins (Fig. 4 b). Underlying driving force was an increase of potential maximum retention for the decrease of surface runoff. The increase in S  was mostly related with increasing vegetation cover (NDVI ) and human activity. S  represents soil water retention (SCS, 1972 ). Therefore, the S  derived from our data can represent water retention across the study basins, and it thus includes the water retention in the soil and some engineering structures such as check dams and reservoirs. An increase in soil water retention could potentially be linked with the wide increase in vegetation cover and soil conservation measures. Vegetation increases surface roughness through litterfall and improves soil structure and properties, and subsequently enhances rainfall infiltration (Zhu et al., 2020, Zhu et al., 2021 ). The soil wetting depths in the revegetated plots increased by 14.7 % during rainfall events, and the soil moisture wetting front velocity rose by 67.2 % (Ge et al., 2022 ). The potential role of increased water retention in artificial structures would be corroborated by the construction in the last decades of check dams and flood-control reservoirs (Guyassa et al., 2017, Luo et al., 2023, Zhang et al., 2008 ). In our results, this could explain the relation between S  and population, assuming that a larger population would indicate a larger density of structures. This has been accompanied by field-scale soil conservation measures such as terracing, further enhancing soil water retention (Wei et al., 2019 ). The implementation of revegetation and soil conservation measures significantly enhances rainfall infiltration into the soil, reducing surface runoff generation. The increased rainfall infiltration is conducive to subsurface runoff; however, our findings and those of others indicate a pronounced decline in CLP soil water and subsurface runoff (Fig. 5 d) (Gao et al., 2015, Huang, 2019 ). This suggests a tendency for soil water redistribution toward evapotranspiration rather than groundwater recharge. Vegetation transpiration accounts for 60–80 % of total evapotranspiration, returning 39 % ± 10 % of precipitation to the atmosphere (Schlesinger and Jasechko, 2014 ). Each tree can transpire hundreds of liters of water daily (Ellison et al., 2017 ). Around 70 % of plant transpiration relies on soil water recently replenished by precipitation (Miguez-Macho and Fan, 2021 ). Due to revegetation, evapotranspiration fluxes in the CLP have increased by approximately 31 × 108  m3 /yr (or 4.90 mm/yr), with a relative increase in evapotranspiration of 93 % (Bai et al., 2019, Shao et al., 2019 ). Therefore, vegetation, taking up soil water for transpiration, may be a primary factor contributing to the reduction in CLP subsurface runoff generation. In addition, the regional water demand increased by 4 % annually with population growth (Feng et al., 2016 ). Approximately 44 % of the water extraction came from groundwater (Han et al., 2020 ). Meanwhile, large-scale coal mining disrupted the geological structure, leading to a substantial loss of groundwater (Chen et al., 2020, Xie et al., 2018 ). The regional groundwater was rapidly decreasing at a rate of 5.50 mm/year, with the continuously declining water table increasing the difficulty of groundwater recharge and, to some extent, resulting in a reduction in subsurface runoff generation (Yin et al., 2021 ). In short, the lower surface runoff generation can be attributed mostly to a higher infiltration, associated with higher vegetation density resulting from the Grain for Green program and other engineering measures. The substantial increase in soil water consumption due to revegetation led to soil drying, which appears to have dominated the reduction in subsurface runoff generation. Therefore, the primary underlying reasons for the decrease in runoff generation were vegetation restoration and soil and water conservation measures that promote infiltration. This then allowed the soil to sustain larger transpiration fluxes, which supports the positive feedback loop of further vegetation growth (Zhou et al., 2022 ).  4.2 Linking changes in runoff generation with the SCS-CN In this study, the SCS-CN model parameters were inversely deduced through rainfall-runoff events to determine the model parameters of each event. In previous research, although it is recognized that model parameters should ideally vary with changing conditions, it is technically infeasible to measure the parameters before each rainfall event (Klemeš, 1986, Lin et al., 2015, Merz and Blöschl, 2004, Rasouli et al., 2019 ). Therefore, CN  is typically determined through the table from the National Engineering Handbook, Section-4 (NEH-4), and S  is calculated based on CN , while I a    is determined as 0.2 times (λ) of S (Mishra and Singh, 2013 ). Assuming that the parameters are known and static ignores their significant impact on hydrological response (Pensoneault et al., 2023 ). The key parameters of the SCS-CN method capture the impact of land cover changes and intervention measures on hydrological behavior (Metselaar, 2023 ). To analyze the variability of model parameters across events, many researchers determine the values of the model parameters being studied in different events by fixing other parameters (Gabriels et al., 2021, Soulis and Valiantzas, 2012, Yan et al., 2020 ). The results show that CN  decreases with increasing precipitation and eventually stabilizes, and it is more appropriate to estimate CN  from measured rainfall-runoff data (Soulis and Valiantzas, 2012 ). The assumption of λ = 0.2 may be a major source of uncertainty in the SCS-CN method (Bo et al., 2011, Durán‐Barroso et al., 2017, Shi et al., 2009, Yuan et al., 2014 ). Many studies suggested that for most regions around the world, this value should be lower than 0.2 (Baltas et al., 2007, Lal et al., 2015, Shi et al., 2009 ), while some research indicated that for different events, this value can be any non-negative number, not limited to between 0 and 1 (Mishra and Singh, 1999, SCS, 1972 ). Recently, in small catchment areas in Poland, it was found that this value is closely related to precipitation, with λ showing greater variability for smaller precipitation events and stabilizing after exceeding a threshold precipitation. The threshold precipitation depends on the landscape features of the study basin, thus, λ is a regional and climatic parameter (Krajewski et al., 2020 ). Our research further confirmed this conclusion (Fig. 7  ). In 13 basins on the Loess Plateau, the median range of λ varies from 0.01 (Wuding river) to 1.04 (Gushanchuan river), with the threshold precipitation range about 20 mm to 100 mm. Therefore, fixing model parameters significantly affects the accuracy of results, limiting the understanding of hydrological behavior. This study used information contained in measured data to determine all key model parameters at the event scale, minimizing conceptual assumptions. The method is objective and repeatable, providing a new scheme for optimizing the SCS-CN method. Our study has identified the event-scale SCS-CN model parameters, enabling the linkage of varying environmental factors with runoff generation behavior based on the physical significance of the parameters. This allows for an in-depth exploration of the underlying mechanisms of runoff generation variations. This research is expected to provide new insights into the analysis of the intrinsic mechanisms underlying the variations in observed rainfall-runoff data.   5 Conclusions Detecting and attributing changes in runoff generation is crucial for informing environmental conservation efforts and the sustainable use of water resources. In this study, we selected 56 hydrological stations from 13 basins in the Chinese Loess Plateau, for which we used a rainfall-runoff event-based approach to estimate the key parameters of the SCS-CN, in order to infer the underlying physical mechanisms that drive changes in runoff generation. Both surface and underground runoff in the region significantly decreased, and the surface runoff hydrograph became flatter. We found that increased rainfall interception and soil infiltration, driven by revegetation and other human activities, has likely led to reduced surface runoff. Revegetation was likely also the key factor contributing to the decrease in subsurface runoff, as an increased water demand for evapotranspiration increases the rate of soil water consumption. Therefore, revegetation is possibly a significant direct cause of the recently observed decrease in surface and subsurface runoff in the Chinese Loess Plateau. Our study offered new insights into the response of surface and subsurface runoff generation under changing environmental conditions. However, the research lacked an accurate description of the physical processes by which vegetation changes affect runoff. In the future, it is necessary to consider integrating vegetation dynamic models with hydrological models to comprehensively simulate the runoff response under vegetation dynamic changes, providing crucial information for sustainable water resource development.
1 Introduction The Earth's ecosystem is undergoing significant transformations due to changes in climate and human-induced disruptions such as land-use changes. Forest restoration (e.g., afforestation, reforestation) emerges as a sustainable and strategic practice to mitigate the loss of biodiversity and enhance the provision of ecosystem services such as carbon sequestration (Filoso et al., 2017; Jones et al., 2022; Verdone and Seidl, 2017 ). However, little is known about the effects of forest restoration on hydrological processes such as streamflow dynamics and water quality (Jones et al., 2022 ). The effects of forest restoration on hydrological processes depend on factors such as tree species, antecedent land-use/cover, and scale (Ellison et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2022; Staal et al., 2024 ). Globally, there is an estimated 0.9 billion hectares of land that could be used for tree restoration (Bastin et al., 2019 ). In the southeast United States (SE-US), efforts are underway to increase the planted area of longleaf pine (Pinus palustris ) ecosystems from 1.7 to 3.2 million hectares by 2025 (McIntyre et al., 2018 ). Longleaf pine trees were once the dominant forest species in the SE-US (Frost, 2006 ). However, extensive timber harvesting, fire suppression, and conversion to commercially valuable species like loblolly pine (Pinus taeda  L.) led to longleaf pine ecosystems having today only 4 % of their original coverage (Noss et al., 2015; Younger et al., 2023 ). Loblolly pine trees are the dominant forest species in the SE-US and the most planted tree species in the country, covering approximately 13 million hectares of land (Bracho et al., 2018; Gonzalez-Benecke et al., 2011; Jokela et al., 2004 ). Highly valued for their rapid growth and timber production, loblolly pine is considered the most important commercial tree species in the world (Will et al., 2015 ) and managed loblolly pine plantations are expected to expand across the SE-US. Afforestation in the SE-US, either because of restoration efforts such as longleaf pine restoration, or driven by economic incentives to increase the planted area of loblolly pine, will likely induce hydrological changes in the region. Additionally, the impacts of afforestation with loblolly pine compared to longleaf pine will probably differ. For instance, longleaf pine forests have a more open canopy with low tree density. This may lead to longleaf pine areas having lower evapotranspiration (ET) rates and more streamflow compared to loblolly pine dominated regions (Brantley et al., 2018; Younger et al., 2023 ). Thus, afforestation efforts must be carefully considered and investigating the impacts of species-specific afforestation on water quantity and quality may provide key insights into water resources management. Few studies have examined the hydrological implications of native forest restoration and compared the hydrology of native tree species with managed forest plantations (Jones et al., 2022 ). Traditionally, afforestation has been shown to decrease streamflow at local scales due to increased water uptake by trees and higher ET (Buechel et al., 2022; Herron et al., 2002; LV et al., 2019; Valente et al., 2021; Webb and Kathuria, 2012; Zhang et al., 2017 ). In contrast to small-scale watershed studies, large-scale modeling research suggests that afforestation might lead to an increase in river flow in certain areas such as downwind of reforestation areas because of atmospheric moisture recycling (Coe et al., 2009; Cui et al., 2022; Hoek van Dijke et al., 2022; Li et al., 2018; Stickler et al., 2013 ). Although extensive evidence can be found in the published literature that afforestation may increase rainfall and water yield at the global and regional scales through atmospheric moisture recycling (Coe et al., 2009; Hoek van Dijke et al., 2022; Li et al., 2018; Stickler et al., 2013 ), there is a notable lack of studies about the potential local (e.g., watershed-scale) implications of moisture recycling (Jones et al., 2022; Keys et al., 2012; te Wierik et al., 2021 ). Hydrologic models can be valuable tools to study the potential effects of large-scale afforestation on hydrological responses. Semi-distributed watershed-scale hydrologic models (e.g., SWAT, VIC) can simulate water fluxes (e.g., surface runoff, groundwater, evapotranspiration, percolation), sediment yield, nutrient loadings, and plant growth at the terrestrial-aquatic interface. Watershed models have been applied from the field to the continental scales (Abbaspour et al., 2015; Arnold et al., 1999; Karki et al., 2020; Schuol et al., 2008 ) and can be particularly useful in predicting the impacts of land-use changes (e.g., afforestation) and management operations (e.g., replanting, irrigation, fertilization) on water quantity and quality at multiple levels. However, current watershed models treat precipitation as an exogenous variable, independent from and unaffected by land-use modifications such as forest restoration during the simulation period (Posada-Marín and Salazar, 2022; Wang-Erlandsson et al., 2018 ). Globally, over 50 % of the terrestrial evaporated water returns to the land as precipitation (Tuinenburg et al., 2020; Van der Ent and Savenije, 2010 ). Moreover, 40 % of terrestrial precipitation originates from terrestrial evaporation (Van der Ent, 2014 ) − 20 % of which originates from vegetation-fed moisture recycling (Keys et al., 2016 ). Thus, neglecting the effects of moisture recycling might limit the reliability of hydrologic models in investigating the effects of large-scale land-use changes such as forest restoration and afforestation. Recent studies such as Link et al. (2020), Tuinenburg et al. (2020) , and Theeuwen et al. (2023)  have developed global databases of moisture recycling ratios using outputs from atmospheric moisture tracking models. Harnessing the power of watershed models and the availability of datasets in Earth system sciences may present a great opportunity to advance watershed modeling and create a more authentic representation of physical processes and real-world scenarios. In the context of forest-water interplays, leveraging readily available moisture recycling data to better inform hydrologic models in capturing land–atmosphere connections may enhance model reliability as a science-based tool to predict the impacts of afforestation on the hydrological cycle and in-stream water quality conditions. In this study, we combine a watershed-scale hydrologic model and a global moisture recycling ratio database to study how large-scale afforestation with loblolly pine and longleaf pine might affect water quantity, quality, and precipitation at multiple scales. Our analysis is in the context of the Mobile Bay watershed-AL, a large and forested watershed draining to the Mobile Bay estuary in the northern Gulf of Mexico. More specifically, we explore three questions: (i ) How does afforestation through increased longleaf and loblolly pine coverage affect water quantity and quality across the study domain? (ii ) What is the importance of considering terrestrial moisture recycling in watershed-scale forest restoration studies? (iii ) Can local moisture recycling offset the effects of afforestation on water quantity and quality? By utilizing the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) model (Arnold et al., 1998 ) and the local moisture recycling ratio (LMR) dataset (Theeuwen et al., 2023 ), we establish a quantitative relationship between model-simulated evapotranspiration (ET) and LMR data for current watershed conditions. This relationship is subsequently utilized to assess the potential effects of large-scale afforestation on precipitation, streamflow dynamics, and water quality loadings across the watershed domain. Our study is novel in realistically investigating the watershed responses of streamflow and water quality to restoring longleaf pine (Pinus palustris ) ecosystems to their native range and in accounting for the potential effects of moisture recycling on rainfall and hydrological predictions. Such a level of detail about the local water cycle and depiction of real-world conditions could never be achieved by solely applying watershed models or simpler water balance models (e.g., Budyko frameworks).  2 Study area The Mobile Bay watershed (MBW) (Fig. 1  ) is formed by the confluence of two large rivers: the Alabama and the Tombigbee rivers, which contribute 52 and 48 %, respectively, to the 1,758 m3 /s of discharge of the Mobile River (Johnson et al., 2002 ). The Mobile River flows approximately 30 miles downstream of its formation, where it splits into several distributaries that contribute approximately 95 % of the freshwater discharged to the Mobile Bay estuary in the northern Gulf of Mexico (GOM) (Johnson et al., 2002; Kemp et al., 2019 ). The MBW is mainly covered by forests (54 %), with loblolly pine being the dominant species. The average elevation above sea level ranges from sea level to 1,280 m, according to the 30-meter resolution National Elevation Dataset (NED). Annual average precipitation and temperature are 1,450 mm and 17 °C, respectively. The climate in the basin is mainly influenced by land-surface altitude and the distance from the GOM. Rainfall is the main form of precipitation, with evenly distributed amounts over the year, and snowfall is rare, averaging less than 25 mm per year. The basin exerts great influence on the Mobile Bay estuary, which is the fourth largest estuary in the U.S. in terms of flow volume and has one of the most biodiverse aquatic fauna and flora in the country. The estuary is a nursery habitat for more than 300 species of fishes and birds, 68 species of reptiles, 57 species of mammals, and 40 species of amphibians (Barnes et al., 2008; MBNEP, 1997 ). During the summer months, when discharge from the upstream rivers is the lowest and water loss through evapotranspiration is the highest, the estuary experiences strong vertical stratification that prevents physical mixing and leads to hypoxic conditions (i.e., low dissolved oxygen concentration) in the bay. This, consequently, underlies a famous natural phenomenon in Mobile Bay: Jubilee , which essentially means large-scale fish kills. It is believed that the Jubilee is becoming more frequent in the Mobile Bay and that this may be due to declining trends in freshwater discharge from the upstream rivers and water quality deterioration (Atkins et al., 2004; Harned et al., 2004; Johnson et al., 2002; McPherson et al., 2003; Montiel et al., 2019 ).  3 Data and methods 3.1 The SWAT model The Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) (Arnold et al., 1999 ) hydrological model was used in the current study to calibrate and validate historical water quantity and quality and investigate the effects of forest restoration on basin-wide hydrology and water quality. SWAT is one of the most widely used hydrological models worldwide and a well-established tool capable of simulating various water fluxes (e.g., surface runoff, lateral flow, groundwater contribution) and plant growth. Additional model components include weather, transport of sediment, and nutrients.
