However, some differences were observed in the peak values at a later time step between the simulation and measurement; the simulation results showed lower peak values than the experiment results. For quantitative evaluation, the temporal change in the spatially-averaged concentration in the storage zone was compared with five experimental and simulation cases. Comparison results between measured and simulated concentration data are shown in Fig. 15 . The measured and simulated cases showed similar decay tendencies. Table 4   shows the calculated RMSE of the concentration–time curve. The RMSE values ranged from 0.019 to 0.075, and the largest errors occurred in Cases E2-2 and NH2-5. The mass exchange coefficient ke   was calculated from the simulated concentration field, demonstrating consistency with the ke   values obtained from the experimental data.  5.3 Application of the numerical solution Numerical simulation was performed for expanded cases to overcome the limitations of the laboratory experiment; the geometric condition of the model weir and the hydraulic condition of the experimental cases were limited due to experiment cost and time. Following the series of experimental cases, the simulation cases were expanded to five or six cases in each series. For the NS series, the spacing between notches ranged from Bn /Sn   = 0.09 to 0.23. For the NH series, the notch height hn /h1   ranged from 0.08 to 0.52. The simulation was performed under two-notch weir (NH2) and three-notch weir (NH1) flow conditions. The NQ series was simulated with different discharges ranging from 0.030 m3 /s  to 0.080 m3 /s , where the upstream water depth h1   varied from 0.20 m  to 0.29 m . Using the simulation results from the expanded cases, the mass exchange coefficient ke   was calculated for different geometric and hydraulic conditions, as listed in Table 5  . For all the series, Fr  and Re  ranged 0.018 ∼ 0.053 and 7,100 ∼ 25,600, respectively. The influence of the geometries of the notched weir and the hydraulic parameters on the mass exchange coefficient ke   was analyzed in detail. The spacing between the notches (Bn /Sn  ) was varied for the NS series, while the other parameters were kept constant. Fig. 18   shows the influence of the spacing between the notches on the storage zone area and mass exchange coefficient. The size of the storage zone area As   increased linearly with the notch spacing. This is expected because increasing the distance between the notches increases the impediment of the main flow by the weir body. Therefore, as previously mentioned, the half-elliptical storage zone increases. As a result, the retention time of the tracer in the storage zone increased. This resulted in a smaller mass exchange coefficient as the distance between the notches increased, as shown in Fig. 18 b. Fig. 19   illustrates the impact of the notch height on the mass exchange coefficient. The storage zone area As   was almost constant and had no apparent relationship with the change in notch height for all three series. This indicated that the notch height had no significant effect on the size of the horizontal storage zone area. For the NH1 and NH2 series, the upstream water depth h1   was kept constant with varying notch height (hn  ). For the NQ series, hn   was kept constant, and h1   conditions were varied. Similarly, Fig. 19 a and b illustrate the influences of the main flow Froude number Fr  and Reynolds number Re , respectively, as hn  /h1  , Re , and Fr  changed simultaneously. The analysis results revealed that for all three series, ke   decreased as hn  /h1   increased. However, the NQ series showed a larger change in the ratio of the mass exchange coefficient than the NH1 and NH2 series. A comparison of the NH1 and NQ series revealed that even under similar Fr  and Re  conditions of the main flow and hn  /h1  , the difference in h1   values affected the mass exchange. These results could demonstrate the effect of the vertical flow on the mass exchange. The weir in this study also generated a forward-facing step recirculation zone, in which a larger h1   increased the volume for fluid entrainment and the mean residence time of the solute mass (Jackson et al., 2013a ). The hydraulic characteristics of the main flow can be determined from the NH and NQ series using the dimensionless numbers Fr  and Re . The Fr  and Re  ranges were 0.018 ∼ 0.053 and 7,100 ∼ 25,600. Notably, Fr  was consistently less than 0.1, indicating a typical low-flow condition. Fig. 20   shows the change in the mass exchange coefficient with Fr  and Re . Fr  and Re  were positively correlated with the mass exchange coefficient. This is consistent with the definition of each dimensionless number: Fr  describes the influence of the main flow on the mass exchange through the shear layer, and Re  describes the influence of turbulent mixing induced by channel irregularities, such as a notched weir structure, on the mass exchange.  5.4 Regression analysis of the storage model parameters The relationships between the mass exchange coefficient ke   and non-dimensional notch geometry parameters (notch spacing (Bn /Sn  ) and weir notch height (hn  /h1  )) and hydraulic parameters Fr  and Re  were determined based on the mass exchange coefficient calculation results. A regression analysis was performed to formulate an empirically derived mass exchange coefficient with the aforementioned non-dimensional variables, and an empirically derived mass exchange coefficient is given by(20) k e  U m   = B n  S n     0.699   h n  h 1     - 0.123   Fr    0.232   Re    0.034        The regression analysis yielded an R2   of 0.87. The empirical relationships proposed in this study can be applied as a useful tool for estimating the mass exchange coefficient for notched weir, as the relations implicate the geometric and hydraulic data into simple relations. Using the proposed empirical equation, the exchange parameters can be easily obtained from measurable parameters at field sites. However, the following terms should be carefully considered when applying the proposed relationships between the mass exchange coefficient and geo-hydraulic factors: First, the mass exchange coefficient relationship was derived for low-flow conditions with a small Fr . This relationship should not be acceptable beyond the proposed flow conditions, such as flow over the weir crest with a high Fr . Second, the roughness of the channel could also contribute to the exchange coefficient. More detailed analyses are necessary to fully derive the relationships between various bed conditions, particularly for channels with high bed roughness, such as complex bed substrates and heavily vegetated systems. Third, only conservative mass solutes were considered in this study. Although most previous studies assumed that contaminants spilled into rivers are non-reactive, several chemical contaminants are reactive in water and should be considered in the solute transport model (Kim et al., 2021 ). Therefore, additional decay terms need to be concerned for exchange coefficient estimations, such as sorption, volatilization, and biodegradation.   6 Conclusions This study conducted a comprehensive experimental investigation involving flow and concentration measurements with planar techniques for a notched weir, including RANS numerical simulation. Laboratory experiments and simulation results for velocity and concentration data were used to calculate the storage zone area and mass exchange coefficient of the transient storage zone model. The results of the hydraulic model test demonstrated that the notched weir structure influenced the velocity distribution. The flow separation and low-flow zone occurred in different transverse directions because of the conversion of the main flow toward the notch opening and the flow obstruction by the weir body. The spacing between the notches and notch height affected the generation of the flow separation and low-flow zone area. The concentration measurement in the storage zone demonstrated that the tracers initially mixed slowly but stretched rapidly in the transverse direction after the tracer cloud reached the storage zone boundary. The tracer cloud showed a longer retention time as the storage zone area increased. The normalized mass exchange coefficient by mean flow velocity, ke  /Um  , ranged from 0.11 to 0.25. This range was approximately one order larger than the values obtained in previous studies on lateral transient storage zones, such as lateral groin fields, and cavities of which dimensionless exchange coefficient ranged from 0.01 to 0.07. Thus it can be concluded that the storage zone generated by the notched weir in this study produced a fast exchange process with a relatively weak storage effect compared with the lateral storage zones along with distinct geometric differences and flow recirculation inside the storage zone. RANS numerical simulations were performed and validated with the measured data from the laboratory experiments. The validation results demonstrated that the numerical solution appropriately reproduced the flow field and tracer transport at the notched weir. The results of the experimental and numerical studies demonstrated that the size of the storage zone area linearly increased with the notch spacing. Moreover, the retention time of the tracer in the storage zone also increased, resulting in a smaller mass exchange coefficient. The storage zone area did not show any significant relationship with the change in the notch height for all three series, whereas the mass exchange coefficient decreased as hn  /h1   increased. The analysis showed that the mass exchange coefficient had a positive correlation with Fr  and Re , where Fr  represented the influence of the main flow on the mass exchange through the shear layer, and Re  represented the influence of turbulent mixing induced by channel irregularities on the mass exchange. An empirical relationship was derived via a regression analysis of the mass exchange coefficient and non-dimensional geo-hydraulic factors, notch spacing, weir notch height, and non-dimensional hydraulic parameters Fr  and Re . The results of the regression analysis yielded an R2   of 0.88. The proposed empirical relationship can be used as an effective method for estimating the mass exchange coefficient of notched weirs using easily measurable field data. However, additional evaluation under a wider range of Fr  over low-flow conditions and field conditions with more complex geometry and topography is necessary for future studies to extend the applicability of the mass exchange coefficient derived in this study for more general applications.
1 Introduction Precipitation exerts a fundamental influence on natural ecosystems and human societies, serving as the principal determinant of freshwater availability and distribution, shaping climate patterns, and supporting agricultural activities (Huffman et al., 2009 ). Reliable and precise precipitation measurement with high spatiotemporal resolution is essential for timely monitoring of extreme weather events, accurately forecasting of natural disasters, and effective governance of water resources (Wanders et al., 2015 ). Measurements acquired from ground-based gauges are universally acknowledged as the most dependable approach for estimating precipitation, but they are confined to capturing precipitation pattern within a finite range surrounding the measuring instruments (Chao et al., 2021 ). Traditionally, precipitation data derived from gauge-based measurements are employed for the purpose of interpolation to derive the precipitation spatial pattern across the entire area. However, the interpolated precipitation derived from limited and uneven distribution of monitoring networks is fraught with uncertainty, particularly in regions characterized by elevated altitudes and complex topographical features (Hong et al., 2006 ). Satellite precipitation products (SPPs) provide unparalleled prospects for estimating quasi-global precipitation patterns with high spatiotemporal resolution. A range of SPPs have been released, such as the Precipitation Estimation from Remotely Sensed Information using Artificial Neural Networks (PERSIANN) (Sorooshian et al., 2000 ), the Climate Prediction Center morphing method (CMORPH) (Joyce et al., 2004 ), the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) (Huffman et al., 2007 ), the Global Satellite Mapping of Precipitation (GSMaP) (Ushio et al., 2009 ) and the Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (IMERG) (Huffman et al., 2015 ). SPPs are conventionally categorized into two groups based on the data processing methods and the time delay in data release (Tang et al., 2020 ). The near-real-time products are typically derived from multiple satellite sensors with a latency ranging from a few hours to several days and possess the potential for utilization in flash flood warnings and other short-term forecasting applications (Wei et al., 2022 ). However, due to the inherent limitations of passive microwave (PMW) and infrared (IR) sensors in accurately detecting precipitation across various conditions (e.g., light rain, snowfall, or complex terrain), and the potential for inaccuracies introduced by the use of forward morphing techniques in extrapolating precipitation estimates, IMERG-E has exhibited poor accuracy in some previous studies. In contrast, post-processed products, which undergo refinement through ground-based precipitation corrections, exhibit greater precision compared to their near-real-time counterparts but are generally accompanied by delays ranging from several days to several months, rendering them inadequate for real-time forecasting applications (Meng et al., 2021 ). Given these challenges, the integration of gauge-based measurements with near-real-time SPPs becomes paramount. This integration aims to combine the dependable, high-resolution spatial coverage provided by SPPs with the accuracy of gauge measurements, addressing the shortcomings inherent in using each method separately. This strategy is crucial not just for improving the accuracy of precipitation estimates but also for guaranteeing their timely availability. Therefore, more consideration should be given to the effective integration of gauge-based measurements and near-real-time products to meet the data utilization requirements in the fields of hydrology and meteorology. Numerous studies have utilized the notable correlations between local environmental variables, namely, topographical, vegetative, and climatic parameters, and observed precipitation to develop correction models for satellite-based precipitation at monthly or annual scales. These approaches are reasonable at monthly or annual scales, based on the assumption that the relationship between precipitation and environmental variables remains relatively stable at these temporal scales. However, this assumption may not remain valid at finer temporal resolutions, including daily and hourly scales, where variability becomes more pronounced. On the other hand, daily precipitation estimation is essential for hydrological simulations, as gridded daily precipitation frequently serves as a necessary input for distributed hydrological models (Bitew and Gebremichael 2011; Shi et al., 2020 ). Given these, conducting research to integrate satellite data with gauge observations to enhance the accuracy of daily precipitation estimates becomes particularly crucial and challenging. Many research efforts have been undertaken from various perspectives to enhance the precision and dependability of openly accessible SPPs datasets through the amalgamation of information derived from different sources. The common merging methods mainly include bias correction (Crow et al., 2011; Wei et al., 2022 ), non-parametric kernel smoothing methods (Nerini et al., 2015 ), Bayesian model averaging (Jiang et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2018 ), geographical difference analysis (GDA) (Duan and Bastiaanssen 2013 ), and geographically weighted regression (GWR) (Chao et al., 2021 ). The aforementioned methods have demonstrated positive outcomes in specific regions; however, their independent application may be hampered by inherent limitations. For instance, the GDA method fails to incorporate the spatial non-stationarity inherent in satellite precipitation error variances, rendering its applicability and accuracy heavily reliant on the interpolation method employed and the spatial density of rain gauge stations in the study area (Duan and Bastiaanssen 2013 ). Furthermore, the GDA method primarily corrects satellite precipitation errors based on the spatial locations of in-situ stations, whilst neglecting the potential impact of environmental variables. Such an oversight of environmental factors may constrain the applicability and precision of such method across various geographical and climatic conditions. The GWR method effectively incorporates environmental factors and adeptly manages the heterogeneity of precipitation errors during model construction. However, the direct application of GWR for merging gauge observations with SPPs may lead to diminished accuracy due to the impact of collinearity issue, as noted by Chao et al. (2018) . Moreover, the direct adoption of satellite precipitation products as the background field may induce instability in the fusion outcomes due to errors in the detection of precipitation events by the original satellite products. In addition to modifying and advancing precipitation data correction and fusion techniques, the incorporation of various methodologies to formulate a multi-step merging framework represents an effective and practical way to enhance precipitation estimation. Many studies have combined multiple methods to integrate multi-source information from a new perspective, yielding a substantial enhancement in the precision of precipitation estimation contrasted with conventional methodologies (Yan et al., 2021; Yumnam et al., 2022 ). Wei et al. (2022)  combined linear scaling with cumulative distribution function to correct daily-scale IMERG-E product for the period spanning from 2015 to 2017 across mainland China. The assessment results indicated that the integrated approach improves the precision of IMERG-E precipitation estimates at daily scale and is superior to the direct application of these two distinct methods. Nevertheless, the ultimate accuracy of the precipitation correction hinges on the precision of the Climate Prediction Center (CPC) data, serving as the benchmark measurement, which carries substantial uncertainties in regions characterized by complex terrain and limited observational density. In addition, rapidly developing machine learning techniques have been extensively employed in precipitation fusion research (Lin et al., 2022 ). However, the application of machine learning for precipitation fusion grapples with challenges such as data scarcity, model interpretability, overfitting, high computational demands, imbalanced datasets, and limited regional generalization (Gavahi et al., 2023 ). Tian et al. (2009)  devised an error decomposition scheme to dissect total errors in satellite precipitation estimates into three distinct components: hit error, missed error, and false error. This error decomposition scheme has been widely employed in satellite precipitation assessment studies in different regions worldwide (Gebregiorgis et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2015 ). Decomposing the errors in satellite precipitation data facilitates a comprehensive delineation of their individual components and sources, a crucial step given missed and false precipitation events have opposing signs and can offset each other. This cancellation effect may lead to the overall bias being actually smaller than the sum of the individual error components, potentially resulting in distortion of statistical metrics traditionally used in precipitation evaluation (Shi et al., 2020 ). Numerous subsequent studies have expanded on the error decomposition scheme, providing new insights into partitioning error sources and quantifying satellite precipitation errors (Chaudhary and Dhanya 2021; Zhang et al., 2020 ). Additionally, Maggioni et al. (2014)  employed the error decomposition method to quantify the uncertainty of SPPs and suggested that this uncertainty quantification method could be employed to estimate potential errors in precipitation estimation by considering topographic and climatic variables in future research. However, to the best of our knowledge, there is currently limited research that employs error decomposition method as the foundational framework for fusing satellite and gauge-based precipitation. Given the discrete nature of precipitation events occurring at daily and sub-daily scales, incorporating error decomposition framework for independent estimation and correction of individual error components followed by aggregation enhances the accuracy of total error estimation in precipitation products. The validation process is imperative for ensuring the reliability and accuracy of precipitation fusion studies. Validation data usually originate from two main sources. Firstly, the spatially gridded precipitation data derived from ground observations represents an effective option, albeit accompanied by significant associated uncertainties. Additionally, ground observations are generally regarded as the most precise data within a certain spatial range and have frequently been utilized as references in previous studies of precipitation data fusion (Khan and Bhuiyan 2021; Lyu et al., 2021 ). To ensure a comprehensive evaluation of these merging methods, comparisons should extend beyond raw precipitation data to include both interpolated and post-processed datasets, as recommended by recent research (Shi et al., 2022; Chua et al., 2022 ). Zhang et al. (2020)  conducted a comparative comparison between interpolation algorithms and SPPs for estimating spatially distributed precipitation. They found that interpolation algorithms provide superior accuracy in daily precipitation estimation compared to TRMM and IMERG, whereas the satellite products offer comparable or improved accuracy for monthly measurements. It is evident that the accuracy of interpolation algorithms is competitive at daily scale, and may even surpass the accuracy of the merged products (Chua et al., 2022 ). Consequently, conducting comparisons of merged products with interpolation algorithms at the site scale proves instrumental in affirming the merged data's superiority. To address the aforementioned concerns, this study constructs a multi-stage merging framework from the perspective of error decomposition to improve the precision of daily precipitation estimates by incorporating the complementary advantages of rain gauge observations and near-real-time SPPs. Based on the classification results from the error decomposition scheme, GDA method was employed to correct the background field for missed and false errors, and GWR method was applied to estimate the spatial gridded errors associated with hit errors. The validity of the proposed framework was assessed at daily scale in the sparsely-gauged YRSR from 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2018, with ground observations serving as the benchmark dataset. The final merged results were assessed through a comparison with the raw IMERG-E, post-processed IMERG-F, global multi-source merged precipitation data, interpolated precipitation data, and the results directly derived from GWR approach. Besides, considering the potential influence of stations contained in Global Precipitation Climatology Centre (GPCC) dataset on the merging procedure, we reevaluated the accuracy of the updated precipitation merging results by excluding stations not present in the GPCC dataset, aiming for impartial evaluation of the merging algorithm's validity. This fusion framework offers new insights into enhancing the precision of the near-real-time product and holds potential for further development in future research.  2 Study area and datasets 2.1 Study area The Yellow River source region (YRSR) is located on the northeast Qinghai-Tibet Plateau over the upstream catchment of Tangnaihai hydrological station between latitudes 32°10′–36°05′N and longitudes 95°50′–103°30′E (Fig. 1  ). It spans an area of 1.22 × 105 km2  and generates an average annual runoff of 168 mm, contributing to 35 % of the total runoff in the Yellow River basin, while representing only 15 % of its total area (Yuan et al., 2018 ). The topography of YRSR exhibits complexity, comprising towering mountains, expansive plains and undulating plateaus, where the elevation gradually declines from southwest to northeast (Meng et al., 2014 ). Climatically, this area exhibits the typical features of plateau continental climate system, characterized by limited annual temperature variation, extended diurnal duration, significant diurnal temperature differentials and intense radiation levels (Shi et al., 2021 ). Due to the combined influence of topography and climate, the annual precipitation in YRSR manifests significant spatial heterogeneity. The annual mean precipitation within the basin is approximately 480 mm, exhibiting a gradient of decrease from the southeast (780 mm/year), to the northwest (210 mm/ year) (Fang et al., 2022 ). Temporally, in terms of intra-annual distribution, precipitation from June to September accounts for 70 % of the annual total precipitation, while winter and spring contribute less than 20 % (Shi et al., 2022 ). The rain gauge stations in the study area are unevenly distributed, with a majority concentrated in the central and southeastern regions. Given the inherent challenges of limited and uneven distribution of rain gauges in this region, refining spatial precipitation estimates at a daily scale becomes crucial for advancing the precision of hydrological extremes prediction, encompassing both flood and drought forecasting.  2.2 Gauge precipitation observation Daily precipitation records (8:00 AM–8:00 AM, UTC +    8) of 12 weather stations (Fig. 1 ) in YRSR were acquired from China Meteorological Data Service Center (http://data.cma.cn/ ). All ground precipitation data have undergone a comprehensive quality inspection process by the China Meteorological Administration to ensure both internal consistency and spatial coherence of the data (Ren et al., 2002 ). The basic information of all 12 meteorological stations is briefly described below (Table 1  ). Among these 12 meteorological stations, 6 stations are included in the GPCC gridded daily precipitation data sets.  2.3 Satellite precipitation products 2.3.1 IMERG precipitation data IMERG is an advanced precipitation estimation algorithm of Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) that employs intercalibration, interpolation, and integration techniques to combine data from multiple microwave satellites, gauge-based analysis, infrared satellites, and other precipitation estimations to provide accurate and reliable global precipitation estimates (Tan et al., 2019 ). The latest IMERG V06B products, released in 2019, provide a series of half-hourly precipitation estimates with a spatial resolution of 0.1°×0.1° spanning both the TRMM (2000–2015) and GPM (2014–present) periods. IMERG-E and IMERG-L are near-real-time products characterized by latencies of 4 h and 14 h, respectively, whereas IMERG-F is a post-processed product with a latency of 3.5 months. IMERG-F undergoes monthly deviation calibration based on the GPCC monthly gauge-based reanalysis data. In-depth details regarding the IMERG precipitation products and the underlying precipitation retrieval algorithm are available in prior articles (Tan et al., 2019; Rajagopal et al., 2021 ). The IMERG data from January 1, 2014 to December 31, 2018 were acquired from the GPM website (https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/ ). To ensure consistency with local precipitation records in the UTC+8 time zone, all three IMERG data underwent local time zone conversion to meet practical requirements.  2.3.2 MSWEP precipitation data Multi Source Weighted Ensemble Precipitation (MSWEP) provides a fully global precipitation dataset with high spatial (0.1°) and temporal (3 h) resolution (Beck et al., 2017 ). MSWEP stands out from other precipitation products by leveraging the integration of ground observations, satellite estimates, and multi-source reanalysis estimates, resulting in enhanced performance specifically in densely gauged regions, convection-dominated weather regimes, and frontal-dominated weather regimes (Beck et al., 2019 ). Further comprehensive details regarding this product are available on the website (https://www.gloh2o.org/ ). In this study, the MSWEP V2.2 dataset was converted to the local time zone (8:00 AM–8:00 AM, UTC +    08:00) for the purpose of data comparisons, aiming to evaluate the accuracy of the generated precipitation data.   2.4 Auxiliary variables The topographic data utilized in this research were extracted from the 90 m Digital Elevation Model (DEM) dataset supplied by the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency and NASA (Slater et al., 2006 ). The DEM data were resampled using the bilinear interpolation method to ensure spatial scale compatibility. Notably, five geographical factors (longitude, latitude, elevation, slope and aspect) were chosen as auxiliary variables in this study because they are well defined and largely independent of each other to reduce the effects of collinearity.   3 Methodology 3.1 Comprehensive merging framework The framework (Fig. 2  ) proposed in this study includes four major modules: data collection, background field correction, error estimation, and additive error model integration. The primary interconnections among these four modules are explained as follows: (1) the Data Collection module provides diverse datasets, including satellite precipitation data, gauge observation data and auxiliary variable data for both constructing and validating the proposed merging model; (2) the Background Field Correction module and the Error Estimation module correct the background field and generate gridded error estimates for various error components, respectively, based on error decomposition processing; (3) the Additive Error Model Integration module aggregates corrected background field with gridded error estimates to yield the final merged precipitation results. The overall merging conceptualization in this study is derived from the well-established additive error model framework (Tian et al., 2013 ). This framework assumes satellite precipitation datasets as the background field given their continuous spatial coverage and estimates spatial gridded errors based on the differences between satellite precipitation data and gauge-based observations (Alemohammad et al., 2015 ). The merged precipitation (P m    ) can be mathematically represented as the summation of the background field precipitation (P b    ) and a function that quantifies the disparity between the observed precipitation (P 0    ) and the background field precipitation:(1) P m  = P b  + f ( P 0  - P b  )       Conventionally, P b     is directly represented by satellite precipitation data, whereas the function f P 0  - P b        employs statistical techniques, such as linear regression, to estimate precipitation background error. In this study, a novel perspective based on the concept of error decomposition was adopted, specifically, the estimated errors of precipitation products were decomposed into three distinct components: hit error, missed error, and false error. Hit error represents instances in which the satellite correctly precisely identifying observed precipitation, missed error indicates that the satellite was unsuccessful in detect observed precipitation, and false error refers to situations where the satellite detects precipitation that was not observed in reality. Further comprehensive explanations of error decomposition scheme can be referenced in the preceding publications by Tian et al. (2009)  and Zhang et al. (2020) . In accordance with the error decomposition scheme's classification outcomes, the missed and false error components were subjected to the GDA method to correct the background field, while the hit error was addressed by employing the GWR method to estimate spatial gridded errors. Ultimately, the corrected background field and the estimated error were arithmetically combined through an addition operation, and the regression residuals generated from GWR were spatially interpolated onto grid cells following the approach employed by Chen et al. (2018) . The final merged product is denoted as IMERG-EDGWR. IMERG-E served as the input dataset for the merging precipitation process, while IMERG-L and IMERG-F were utilized as comparative datasets to reflect the effectiveness of the merging process. The IMERG and MSWEP data have undergone rigorous quality control procedures, whereby data exhibiting substandard quality or containing missing samples were excluded. Additionally, to eliminate the influence of drizzles, precipitation values below 0.1 mm/d derived from IMERG SPPs and MSWEP were set to zero (Tian et al., 2009 ).  3.2 Geographical difference analysis Geographical difference analysis (GDA), developed by Cheema and Bastiaanssen (2012) , has been extensively employed in the merging researches of SPP-gauge datasets due to its streamlined implementation process, reduced dependence on supplementary information, and minimized incorporation of external factors and uncertainties. Most previous studies directly employed GDA method to diminish the differences between gauge-based observations and satellite-derived precipitation data (Duan and Bastiaanssen 2013 ). The GDA method was employed in this study to correct the background field affected by missed and false alarms of precipitation events caused by the misjudgements of satellite sensors. The specific process is outlined as follows: (1) calculating the missed and false errors between the observed and satellite precipitation on the grid where the station is located; (2) interpolating the missed and false errors derived from the previous step into grid cells; (3) adding the interpolation results to satellite precipitation data (initial background field) to obtain the corrected background field. Negative values can potentially arise in certain grid cells of the corrected background field, which were simply set to 0 in this study.  3.3 Geographically weighted regression Geographically weighted regression (GWR) was employed twice in this study, first as a component of the data fusion process and second as a direct application for comparative evaluation against the merging outcome. GWR describes non-smooth relationships between spatial variables and incorporates geographical attributes into the regression parameters (Brunsdon et al., 1998 ). In GWR, the regression coefficients are estimated using local regression estimates with sub-sampled data within a finite radius surrounding the observations to characterize the spatial heterogeneity of precipitation, deviating from the reliance on global information (McMillen 2004 ). The mathematical representation of GWR is as follows:(2) y i  = β i 0   u i  , v i     + ∑ i = 1  n  β ik   ( u i  , v i  )  x ik   + ε i                   i = 1 , 2  , ⋯ n     where y i     is the actual observations at the i    th point; u i  , v i       is the coordinate of the i    th regression point (latitude and longitude); β i 0   u i  , v i        and β ik   ( u i  , v i  )     is the intercept and slope of the k    th variable at the spatial coordinates u i  , v i      , respectively; x ik      is the i    th observation of the k    th independent variable; and ε i     is the regression residual at the spatial coordinates u i  , v i      , which is assumed to follow an independent normal distribution, i.e., ε i   N 0 , σ  2       . Observations close to the estimation point have a greater impact on the coefficient estimates than the observations located further away in line with Tobler's first law in geography (McMillen 2004 ). The GWR model assumes that the regression coefficients are continuous surfaces with similar values in adjacent locations. By establishing a spatial weighting function W    that decays with spatial distance from observations, GWR accounts for the varying impact of adjacent observations on the estimation of regression coefficients at each target point (Fotheringham et al., 2017 ). Regression coefficients in Eq. (2)  were obtained by solving the following matrix:(3) β ^  u i  , v i     = X  T  W u i  , v i     X    - 1   X  T  W u i  , v i     Y     where β ^  u i  , v i        is the vector of regression coefficients subject to estimation at the spatial coordinates u i  , v i      ; X    and Y    is the vectors representing the auxiliary and dependent variables; and W u i  , v i        is the spatial weighting function, which decays as the spatial distance between observations increases. Several methods of determining the spatial weighting matrix have been proposed in past studies, such as Gauss function, inverse distance, threshold and Bi-square method (Wheeler and Calder 2007 ). These four weighting functions were chosen and analysed to determine the optimal choice for the final merged algorithms. The specific descriptions of these weighting functions are shown in Table 2  . Previous studies have demonstrated that the selection of bandwidth for a specific weighting function significantly impacts the outcomes of the GWR model (Waller et al., 2007 ). The main methods for determining the optimal bandwidth are the Akaike information criterion and cross-validation. The optimal bandwidth is determined through the cross-validation method in this study, as used by Chen et al. (2018) . In this study, various combinations of five auxiliary variables and four weighting functions were systematically compared to identify the optimal model based on their respective accuracies. Through computation and analysis, the Gaussian function method was selected for calculating the weighting functions, while longitude, latitude, and slope were determined for the optimal auxiliary variables.  3.4 Interpolation methods Various interpolation methods are frequently employed in hydrological and environmental research to convert point-scale data surface-scale representations. In response to the density and distribution of gauge-based observations within the study domain, different spatial interpolation methods can play their own advantages in specific application scenarios (Haberlandt 2007 ). Li and Heap (2011)  conducted a statistical analysis, concluding that inverse distance weighting (IDW) and Ordinary Kriging (OK) stand out as the most commonly utilized methods in spatial estimates, demonstrating both accuracy and applicability. Consequently, these two methods were applied to estimate spatial precipitation amount and regression residuals. IDW assumes that nearby sampled points are more likely to exhibit similar characteristics to unsampled points compared to those located farther away (Wu et al., 2018 ). IDW estimates the values of unsampled points based on the weights of the existing observed values. The weights are determined through the application of the inverse distance function (Bartier and Keller 1996 ). The general equation of IDW is:(4) Z ^  ( s 0  )  = ∑ i = 1  n  Z s i      d i  p   / ∑ i = 1  n  1 d i  p       where Z ^  ( s 0  )     represents the precipitation estimates at the unknown location s 0    ; n    represents the count of the observed points around the unknown point; Z s i        is the measured value at the known location s i    ; d i     is the Euclidean distance from the estimated point to the i    th observation point; the IDW interpolation method was employed with a power value (p   ) of 2 for background field correction, residual estimation, and direct application in this study, a commonly accepted setting for interpolating precipitation data (Tabios III and Salas 1985). The Kriging method constructs a variogram model that characterizes the main structural features of variables by analysing the interrelationships between known sampled points and to make the best linear unbiased estimate for unknown points (Kleijnen 2009 ). In contrast to IDW, Kriging method derives its weights from a semivariogram constructed from the spatial structure of the observations. Ordinary Kriging (OK) assumes that the regionalized variable exhibits second-order stationarity, and the representation of OK for a spatial process Z ^  s 0        can be expressed as:(5) Z ^  s 0     = ∑ i = 1  n  λ i  Z s i         where λ i     is determined by the Kriging equations:(6) ∑ i = 1  n  λ i  γ x i  , x j     - μ = γ x 0  , x i        ∑ i = 1  n  λ i  - 1 = 0            where γ x i  , x j        is the semivariogram function of x i     and x j    . To determine a more suitable semivariogram function for OK, three different mathematical models, namely, spherical, gaussian and exponential model, were applied in this study. After conducting leave-one-out cross validation experiments, this study ultimately selected the exponential function as the most appropriate semivariogram function with fixed parameters throughout the entire study period.  3.5 Performance evaluation and comparison The leave-one-out cross-validation approach was chosen as the validation method, given the limited number of observations in YRSR. More precisely, validation data were derived from samples at one of all twelve sites in YRSR, while the model was trained using samples from the remaining eleven sites. This step was repeated for all available gauge stations. It is worth noting that throughout the merging and interpolation process, information from the points under estimation was deliberately excluded to maintain fairness in evaluating the accuracy through a comparison between the raw SPPs and MSWEP. Additionally, the evaluation was not based on calculating average values across the entire study area; instead, it involved a site-specific comparison of observed data and model predictions over time series at each monitoring location. Various statistical metrics, such as correlation coefficient (CC), relative bias (RB), mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE) were adopted to evaluate the performance of various precipitation estimates. Besides, probability of detection (POD), false alarm ratio (FAR), and critical success index (CSI) were utilized to assess the effectiveness of precipitation estimates in detecting precipitation events. The formulas of these metrics are as follows:(7) C C = ∑ i = 1  n  ( G i  - G  ¯   )  ( S i  - S  ¯   )   ∑ i = 1  n  ( G i  - G  ¯   )  2    ∑ i = 1  n  ( S i  - S  ¯   )  2          (8) R B = ∑ i = 1  n  ( S i  - G i  )   ∑ i = 1  n  G i    × 100 %     (9) M A E = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  S i  - G i         (10) R M S E = ∑ i = 1  n  ( S i  - G i  )  2   n        (11) P O D = H H + M       (12) F A R = F H + F       (13) C S I = H H + M + F       where n    represents the sample size; G i     and S i     are the observed precipitation and satellite estimates, respectively; G  ¯      and S  ¯      are the average values of observed precipitation and satellite estimates, respectively; H    represents the count of precipitation events documented in gauge-based observations and successfully identified by SPPs; M    is the count of precipitation events documented in gauge-based observations yet undetected by SPPs; and F    denotes the count of events detected by SPPs but not documented in gauge-based observations.   4 Results 4.1 Overall assessment of the merged product Fig. 3   presents the scatterplots depicting the correlation between various precipitation products and observed daily precipitation values at all gauge observations from 2014 to 2018. In this figure, the scatters of IMERG-EDGWR exhibit a closer alignment to the 1:1 line compared to those of IMERG-F (Fig. 3 c, h), and the presence of outliers is effectively mitigated by the proposed merging algorithm. Overall, IMERG-EDGWR attains the top position concerning CC, RMSE, and MAE. Furthermore, the original IMERG-E data substantially underestimates precipitation with a considerable RB of –32.89 %. In contrast, IMERG-EDGWR effectively alleviates these negative biases, reducing RB to 4.63 %. It also enhances CC from 0.61 to 0.77, reduces MAE from 1.30 mm/d to 1.10 mm/d, and diminishes RMSE from 3.52 mm/d to 2.69 mm/d. Remarkably, although IMERG-E and IMERG-L generally exhibit a bias toward underestimating precipitation, noteworthy overestimation outliers are observed for gauge precipitation values below 40 mm. To provide a more comprehensive representation of the quantitative performance of precipitation products from different sources in high-intensity precipitation events, we present their accuracy statistical metrics in Table 3  . IMERG-F demonstrates only marginal improvement in accuracy relative to IMERG-E and IMERG-L for precipitation exceeding 40 mm. This observation aligns with the findings depicted in the scatterplots of Fig. 3 b, suggesting that the monthly bias correction procedure applied to IMERG-F has yielded limited effectiveness in improving high-intensity precipitation estimation. The IDW and OK interpolation methods exhibit significant underestimation in the estimation of high-intensity precipitation values, with RBs of −54.80 % and −73.54 %, respectively. This underestimation is primarily attributed to the smoothing effect of interpolation methods, consequently leading to an underestimation of high-intensity precipitation. IMERG-GWR demonstrates a notable improvement in high-intensity precipitation estimates in contrast to all three IMERG products. IMERG-EDGWR shows superior performance compared to IMERG-GWR, with the best statistical metrics for precipitation exceeding 40 mm. In comparison to IMERG-F, the deviation statistics corrections of IMERG-EDGWR are as follows: RB drops from 97.70 % to 32.04 %, RMSE reduces from 38.24 mm to 30.23 mm, and MAE decreases from 32.83 mm to 27.04 mm (Table 3 ). The Taylor diagram for daily precipitation observations and various precipitation estimates, throughout the entire period and across various seasons, is illustrated in Fig. 4  . The Taylor diagram offers a thorough quantification of the correspondence level between estimates and observations based on three metrics: standard deviation (SD), CC, and RMSE (Taylor 2001 ). The closer the estimated points align with the observed points, the higher the overall accuracy of the estimates (Bosilovich et al., 2008 ). IMERG-EDGWR demonstrates superior overall performance during the whole period, with the closest SD (4.01 mm) to that of the observation, the highest CC (0.77), and the lowest RMSE (2.69 mm). IMERG-F has apparently improved CC across the entire period in comparison to both IMERG-E and IMERG-L, yet the increment in CC during the winter season is relatively negligible. Notably, the CCs of all three IMERG products are below 0.2 in winter, much lower than the CCs observed in other precipitation estimates. The CCs for the interpolation methods (IDW and OK) remain relatively stable, ranging between 0.4 and 0.7 throughout the entire time period and across the four seasons. Nevertheless, it is worth noting that the interpolation results exhibit considerably smaller SD in comparison to the gauge observations. This phenomenon is primarily attributed to the smoothing effect induced by the interpolation methods, resulting in a reduction in the variability of precipitation. Furthermore, the CC values of the interpolated precipitation estimates drop sharply during the summer season, characterized by frequent occurrences of intense rainfall events, consistent with the earlier analysis of scatterplots (Fig. 3 ). This can be attributed to the inherent limitation of interpolation methods in accurately estimating high precipitation values. In contrast, IMERG-GWR and IMERG-EDGWR demonstrate superior performance in this regard. As a global merged precipitation product, MSWEP demonstrates overall superiority in comparison to IMERG-E and IMERG-L. However, its unexpectedly high RMSE compared to other products suggests a degree of uncertainty in the estimation of winter precipitation.  4.2 Spatial evaluation of the merged product Fig. 5   demonstrates the spatial patterns of daily average precipitation estimated from various products from 2014 to 2018. Additionally, statistical indicators of precipitation, including the mean, maximum, minimum, and SD, were calculated to gain insights into its statistical characteristics. As shown in Fig. 5 , the various products provide consistent estimates of the spatial precipitation distribution pattern, depicting lower precipitation in the northwest and higher values in the southeast of the basin. IMERG-GWR and IMERG-EDGWR exhibit superior capabilities in capturing the precipitation spatial variability, as evidenced by higher SD values of 0.4. In comparison to IMERG-E, IMERG-EDGWR exhibits an increase in the estimated precipitation mean from 0.99 mm to 1.58 mm, as well as a shift in the estimated precipitation range from 0.47 mm–2.09 mm to 0.81 mm–2.7 mm. The precipitation estimates for the northwest region of YRSR by MSWEP surpass those of all other products, reaching a maximum mean value of 1.89 mm. Both interpolation methods exhibit a tendency to smooth out precipitation estimates, as reflected in their relatively low SD values of 0.28 mm and 0.16 mm, respectively, implying a constrained ability to capture spatial precipitation variability (Fig. 5 e, f). In contrast, IMERG-EDGWR presents a smoother precipitation pattern, indicating the superiority of the generated precipitation merging data in capturing the spatial variations of precipitation distribution to some extent. Fig. 6   depicts the spatial patterns of CC, RB and CSI at the positions of the 12 meteorological stations from 2014 to 2018. Overall, the CC values of IMERG-EDGWR show a significant improvement compared to IMERG-E, increasing from approximately 0.6 to 0.8 after the merging procedure (Fig. 6 a, h). In comparison to IMERG-EDGWR, IMERG-GWR demonstrates marginally reduced correlation with gauge-based measurements, yet it outperforms IMERG-F. Besides the improved CC values, IMERG-EDGWR effectively restricts the majority of RBs to below 20 %, substantially reducing the extent of precipitation underestimation observed in IMERG-E. Despite both the OK and IDW methods effectively constrain RB values at most weather stations, there is a notable trend of overestimation exceeding 80 % at the Maduo station. One possible reason for the notable estimation bias in precipitation at the Maduo station is its remote location and high elevation compared to other rain gauge stations. The interpolation methods generate precipitation estimates that exhibit a relatively high degree of accuracy for the majority of gauge stations within the basin, although their accuracy diminishes to some extent at the basin boundaries and in valley areas. Although IMERG-F presents superior performance contrasted with IMERG-E and IMERG-L in estimating precipitation amounts, its enhancement in precipitation detection capability is not notably pronounced (Fig. 6 q–s). The main reason could be attributed to the bias-correction procedure of IMERG-F using GPCC precipitation dataset at the monthly scale, leading to limited improvement in the ability to detect daily-scale precipitation events. In contrast to IMERG SPPs, the proposed merged product IMERG-EDGWR demonstrates notable improvements in the capability of precipitation detection with higher CSIs.  4.3 Temporal evaluation of the merged product The boxplots in Figs. 7 and 8    display statistical metrics of all different products at daily scale over the whole period and in each season from 2014 to 2018. In this context, spring spans from March to May, summer ranges from June to August, autumn covers September to November, and winter extends from December to February. Overall, IMERG-EDGWR demonstrates a notably superior performance in terms of correlation coefficients with ground precipitation observations, surpassing three IMERG SPPS, MSWEP, and IMERG-GWR throughout the entire period as well as in all four seasons (Fig. 7 a). In winter, the CCs of IMERG-EDGWR exhibit a minor decrease, with slightly lower values compared to those of the IDW and OK. Meanwhile, the CC values of the three IMERG SPPs during winter exhibit strikingly low values, with medians ranging from only 0.11 to 0.13. This can be attributed that satellite sensors encounter difficulties in accurately detecting and differentiating between light precipitation and solid precipitation in winter. From the perspective of error metrics, IMERG-EDGWR exhibits consistently lower RMSE and MAE values in comparison to other products, signifying its reliability. Both IMERG-E and IMERG-L showed substantial precipitation underestimation, especially in winter (Fig. 7 c). IMERG-F effectively corrects precipitation amounts in the spring, summer, and autumn seasons, leading to consistently low relative error values close to zero. However, during the winter season, IMERG-F struggles to accurately correct errors in precipitation estimates, resulting in a substantial underestimation of 46.8 %. It is noteworthy that MSWEP exhibits a significant overestimation of precipitation during the winter season, indicating instability in its precipitation estimates. Fig. 8  illustrates the computed results of three categorical metrics (POD, FAR, CSI), which collectively assess the effectiveness of precipitation detection. MSWEP, IDW, and OK exhibit the highest POD values, followed by IMERG-EDGWR, IMERG-GWR, and three IMERG SPPs in descending order (Fig. 8 a). The high POD values observed for MSWEP, IDW, and OK are accompanied by elevated FAR values, suggesting a tendency to overestimate the frequency of precipitation events to some extent, particularly during the summer season. Three IMERG SPPs demonstrate significantly low POD values and high FAR values in winter, which aligns with the observed challenges in the precipitation quantity metrics discussed in the preceding paragraph (Fig. 7 a, b). Overall, IMERG-EDGWR demonstrates superior detection capability compared to IMERG-GWR, with significantly improved CSI values relative to IMERG-E, indicating that the proposed merging framework effectively enhances precipitation detection capability. Fig. 9   illustrates the daily variations in mean precipitation, CC, and RB for the IMERG-E, IMERG-F, and IMERG-EDGWR, compared to the gauge-based measurements from 2014 to 2018. To better reveal underlying trends, a 30-day moving average was applied to each time series. Both IMERG-F and IMERG-EDGWR maintain a temporal trend consistent with that of the observed precipitation time series (Fig. 9 a). It is noteworthy that the IMERG-EDGWR demonstrates a more pronounced advantage over IMERG-F in the dry season (October to April). During the rainy season (May to September), the CC values of the three precipitation products are notably higher, whereas in the dry season, these CC values are comparatively lower, as evidenced in Fig. 9 b. The CC curve of IMERG-EDGWR consistently surpasses that of IMERG-E, and it outperforms IMERG-F for the majority of the time, especially during the dry season. In terms of RB, IMERG-E and IMERG-F primarily display significant negative biases, especially noticeable in the dry season, with the majority of RB values exceeding −50 %. The EDGWR method mitigates this systematic underestimation, bringing the RB values closer to neutrality. The performance of the EDGWR approach is markedly enhanced in the dry season, demonstrating its robustness in accurately estimating precipitation during times of scarcity.  4.4 Assessment of precipitation intensities To further assess the impact of precipitation intensity on the precision of precipitation estimates, Fig. 10   illustrates the performance of four indicators under various precipitation thresholds for different products. Overall, IMERG-EDGWR presents optimal performance across diverse precipitation intensities, followed by IMERG-GWR. This indicates that the application of merging techniques improves the precision of precipitation estimates across various thresholds, encompassing not only light and moderate precipitation occurrences. As shown in Fig. 10 a, IMERG-EDGWR exhibits the highest CCs at different precipitation intensities, particularly evident for precipitation exceeding 10 mm. The noticeable decrease in CC values for both IDW and OK interpolation methods for precipitation exceeding 25 mm indicates the inherent limitations of these techniques in precisely estimating high-intensity precipitation. In terms of error magnitude metrics, RBs demonstrate a declining trend as precipitation intensity increases, whereas RMSEs and MAEs display an upward trend. For precipitation exceeding 5 mm, IMERG-EDGWR achieves error control within the range of −16.6 % to −21.7 %, exhibiting a notable enhancement compared to IMERG-E. The two interpolation methods exhibit an amplified underestimation at high precipitation intensities (greater than 25 mm), leading to an underestimation exceeding 60 %. The MAE and RMSE exhibit a consistent trend and a strong dependence on precipitation intensities. IMERG-EDGWR demonstrates the lowest RMSE and MAE values for precipitation exceeding 10 mm, validating the efficacy of the proposed algorithm in mitigating errors associated with high-intensity precipitation (Fig. 10 c, d). The confusion matrix was formulated to quantitatively assess the daily precipitation detection capabilities of different products (Fig. 11  ). The confusion matrix serves as a specific table widely utilized in machine learning for quantifying the performance of matching estimated values with true values, facilitating a comprehensive evaluation of classification accuracy and error rates (Foody 2002 ). In an ideal scenario, the anti-diagonal elements of the confusion matrix would have a value of 1, representing an accurate reproduction of the distribution at the corresponding precipitation intensity level, while the remaining elements would be 0. Compared to the original IMERG-E, IMERG-EDGWR exhibits a notable concentration of high values along the anti-diagonal of the confusion matrix. IMERG-EDGWR exhibits a significant improvement in the anti-diagonal values compared to IMERG-GWR for precipitation exceeding 10 mm, with an increase from 0.38 to 0.47 for precipitation ranging from 10 mm to 25 mm, and an increase from 0.35 to 0.40 for precipitation exceeding 25 mm. MSWEP outperforms both IMERG-E and IMERG-L in detecting precipitation within the range of 0.1 mm to 25 mm, but falls significantly behind them for precipitation exceeding 25 mm. By examining the column corresponding to precipitation exceeding 25 mm at the gauge observations, it can be observed that the interpolation methods have reduced the magnitude of high-intensity precipitation exceeding 25 mm, bringing it within the range of 5–25 mm. This phenomenon, along with the supporting evidence from Fig. 10 , collectively indicates the inaccurate estimation of both the magnitude and frequency of high-intensity precipitation by the interpolation methods, highlighting their inferiority compared to satellite-based precipitation and merged products.   5 Discussions 5.1 Potential advantages of IMERG-EDGWR merging method The EDGWR algorithm proposed in this study offers an innovative and effective solution to the integration challenge between point-based observations and spatial satellite precipitation estimates. The merging procedure has comprehensively and significantly improved the overall spatiotemporal accuracy, precision of winter precipitation, and ability to capture high-intensity precipitation, as demonstrated by the findings in Section 4 . In this study, precision comparisons were conducted on precipitation data derived from our proposed method. These comparisons were made not only against the monthly-adjusted IMERG-F, traditional interpolation techniques, and multi-source fusion precipitation product but also against precipitation data obtained directly through the application of the additive framework and GWR method. The results demonstrate that, compared to traditional GWR method, the EDGWR approach exhibits significant improvements in overall accuracy (Fig. 3 ), precision of high-intensity precipitation (Table 3 ), and enhanced capability in detecting winter precipitation events (Fig. 8 ). The distinctive improvement observed can be primarily attributed to the departure of the EDGWR algorithm from previous studies (Chao et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2015 ) in not employing a straightforward statistical downscaling method to correct the precipitation background field. Instead, it modifies the background field based on the information related to the precipitation event detection inherent in the missed and false error components. The utilization of the GDA method allows for a rapid and effective correction of the background field, thereby enhancing the capability to detect precipitation events. Many prior precipitation fusion studies (Baez-Villanueva et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2023 ) have emphasized the significance and challenges of enhancing the precision of high-intensity precipitation in precipitation merging research. The research performed by Hasan et al. (2016)  and Ma et al. (2018)  emphasized that the direct application of statistical methods is frequently hindered by sample size constraints and method limitations, resulting in significant inaccuracies in estimating high-intensity precipitation. This issue holds particular significance in hydrological investigations, especially in studies related to runoff simulation. In contrast, the merging algorithm proposed in this research offers a meaningful advantage in improving the accuracy of high-intensity precipitation. Compared to IDW, EDGWR exhibited significant enhancements in various performance metrics (Fig. 10 ): CC increased by 208 % from 0.12 to 0.37, RB reduced by 185 % from −61.9 % to −21.7 %, MAE decreased by 41 % from 22.8 mm to 16.1 mm, and RMSE decreased by 62 % from 20.2 mm to 13.1 mm. Interpolation algorithms manifest a proclivity for underestimating both the magnitude and frequency of precipitation events surpassing 25 mm, which is a critical consideration for researchers engaged in flood simulations related to high-intensity precipitation events. Additionally, as shown in Fig. 5 , the spatial estimation of precipitation based on IDW and OK exhibits the phenomenon of the “bull's eye effect”, which is commonly observed in spatial interpolation when weather stations are sparse or unevenly distributed. Schroeer et al. (2018)  proposed that the bull's eye phenomenon around precipitation peaks likely results from radial estimation near rain gauges, which inherently emphasizes local maxima, creating characteristic patterns. Compared to IDW, the OK method displays a more pronounced directional trend, due to its higher sensitivity to the density of rain gauge stations, as indicated by Shen and Wu (2023) . Additionally, the selection of an appropriate variogram function in the OK method can mitigate the appearance of directional trends. In contrast, both the raw and the merged precipitation products show a smoother precipitation pattern in their spatial distribution, containing more spatial information. By effectively integrating existing meteorological data with near-real-time satellite precipitation estimates, the method proposed in this study can provide more accurate and comprehensive spatial estimations of extreme precipitation across extensive areas, including those with limited ground-based observational coverage. This is especially valuable for understanding and anticipating the impacts of extreme weather in remote or under-monitored regions. The winter precipitation estimated by the IMERG SPPs is still deficient due to the interference from snow cover, which disrupts the microwave satellite's ability to discern between frozen snow surfaces and cloud layers, consequently diminishing its capability to identify precipitation particles effectively (Meng et al., 2021 ). Xiao et al. (2022)  conducted bias correction on IMERG SPPs using meteorological stations in the Hanjiang River Basin and found that the correlation coefficients improved most significantly during the winter season, consistent with the findings of this study (Fig. 7 ). Furthermore, this study demonstrates a notable enhancement in precipitation detection capabilities across three categorical metrics (Fig. 8 ). This underscores the effectiveness of bias correction or multi-source information fusion for satellite precipitation products, demonstrating that incorporating ground observations can effectively mitigate the inherent limitations of satellite remote sensing in capturing winter precipitation.  5.2 Impact of input data sources The quality of input data plays a decisive role in precipitation fusion research, manifested by notable disparities in results when the same algorithm is applied to different input datasets (Meng et al., 2023 ). Hence, researchers should not only continually refine methodologies at the algorithmic level but also place increased emphasis on the quality and quantity of input precipitation data. The near-real-time version product IMERG-E employed in this study has garnered extensive application in precipitation assessment and fusion studies, with the additional advantage of demonstrating commendable accuracy in hydrological runoff simulations (Hong et al., 2021 ). From a practical perspective, IMERG-E demonstrates remarkable timeliness, provides data at daily or even sub-daily scales, and demonstrates a distinct advantage in delivering long-term time series data. During the merging process, this study incorporated data from all stations in YRSR, noting that only six of these stations were included in the GPCC data set, as indicated in Table 1 . IMERG-F is the correction of IMERG-E based on information from these 6 stations. For a fair comparison, this study computed new merging results, denoted as IMERG-EDGWR-GPCC, using data from only the 6 stations included in GPCC. The precision of IMERG-E, IMERG-F, IMERG-EDGWR, and IMERG-EDGWR-GPCC was assessed using the 6 stations excluded from GPCC as validation data, and the outcomes are presented in Fig. 12  . Generally, after reducing the number of stations used during merging procedure, IMERG-EDGWR-GPCC demonstrates a slightly diminished level of accuracy compared to IMERG-EDGWR. However, IMERG-EDGWR-GPCC exhibits a substantial improvement compared to IMERG-E and, furthermore, a considerable enhancement in accuracy compared to IMERG-F, especially during the winter season. This indicates the merging algorithm proposed in this study exhibits commendable robustness. Additionally, given the restricted number of stations in YRSR, this study refrained from investigating the influence of varying station densities on the accuracy of precipitation estimates. Contemplating the influence of GPCC stations can be regarded as an exploration of the influence of station density on the performance of precipitation merging algorithm. The findings are consistent with conclusions drawn from previous research (Baez-Villanueva et al., 2020; Chao et al., 2021; Hong et al., 2021 ), indicating that higher station density leads to an improvement in fusion accuracy. Many previous studies employed gauge observation data to perform bias correction or data fusion on post-processed satellite data that has already undergone gauge-based adjustments. This led to the excessive overestimation of the fusion algorithm's accuracy due to the repeated use of the same gauge station data. To the best of our knowledge, this issue has received limited attention in previous research. However, it is of crucial concern in the validation of precipitation merging algorithms, as the accuracy validation of these algorithms constitutes a critical step in demonstrating their rationality and reliability. Especially in studies involving the integration of multi-source precipitation datasets, it is noteworthy that certain datasets may already include information from validation stations, potentially compromising the fairness of the accuracy validation process. In future research, it is imperative to pay attention to this issue and concentrate on the actual benefits of the merging algorithm.  5.3 Limitations and uncertainties Although the aforementioned results confirm the efficacy and validity of the proposed EDGWR algorithm in this study, there are still some limitations to acknowledge. Firstly, the EDGWR algorithm requires the availability of ground observations data, making it inapplicable in ungauged basins. This limitation restricts the applicability of this method on a global scale, despite its excellent accuracy in sparsely gauged basins. Next, the selection of auxiliary variables and weighting functions can impact the precision of the GWR method. Selecting appropriate auxiliary variables plays a crucial role in determining model performance. This importance stems from the underlying assumption of the model that the correlation between the predictive variable (precipitation) and auxiliary variables varies spatially. Our selection of auxiliary variables was strategically limited to those associated with topography, explicitly excluding variables related to climatic patterns. This deliberate choice not only mitigates the impact of collinearity among variables but also enhances the generalizability and applicability of the method proposed in this study across a global context. Only five geographical variables were selected as the auxiliary variables in this study. In future research, the inclusion of supplementary auxiliary variables and an exploration of their collinearity can be considered. Meanwhile, more efforts can be directed towards developing and exploring new weighting methods. The extensive snow cover across numerous areas of YRSR significantly increases the misjudgement rate of IMERG SPPs for winter precipitation events, as reported by Lu and Yong (2018) . The pronounced scattering effect, induced by snow-covered mountainous regions during the winter season, leads to substantial interference in the detection of both light precipitation and solid precipitation by satellite sensors (Gebregiorgis et al., 2018 ). However, this study did not explore the alterations in snowfall detection accuracy before and after merging procedure due to the limited availability of snowfall data. Extensive evaluation studies have consistently highlighted that satellite-based precipitation data exhibit significant limitations in accurately detecting snowfall (Tang et al., 2020; Meng et al., 2021 ). Therefore, it is recommended to develop improved cold-season precipitation correction models based on gauge snowfall data to accurately estimate snowfall in future research. This study posits that the precipitation measured by gauge observations accurately reflects the regional precipitation patterns within their respective grid cells and uses the measured data as references in the model training and evaluation process. However, the issue of spatiotemporal mismatch persists between gauge observations and satellite estimates, influenced by climate, complex terrain, and measurement instruments, can introduce significant uncertainty (Lei et al., 2022 ). Due to the spatial scarcity of observation stations, the evaluations conducted in this study are based on a point-to-point assessment approach rather than a spatially comprehensive evaluation. The point-to-point evaluation, while effective in certain contexts, may not fully capture the spatial variability and complexities that a spatially extensive assessment could provide. Consequently, this limitation must be acknowledged as it could impact the accuracy of our findings. Chen et al. (2018)  highlighted that this uncertainty can be mitigated by downscaling precipitation products with coarse spatial resolutions to finer resolutions. Nevertheless, conducting daily-scale spatial downscaling of precipitation presents challenges owing to the intricate relationship between precipitation and environmental factors, and the utilization of ill-conceived downscaling techniques has the potential to introduce additional uncertainties. Hence, future research efforts can focus on developing rational and effective downscaling methods and rigorously evaluate these methods to demonstrate their capacity in mitigating sources of uncertainty. In future studies, the rationality of this merging framework from the perspective of different error components can be verified by substituting the methods of its submodules with alternative approaches. Furthermore, based on the proposed merging framework, incorporating machine learning and data mining techniques for improved accuracy and uncertainty reduction is a potential avenue for future research.   6 Conclusions This study proposed a framework from the perspective of error decomposition for combining the near-real-time product IMERG-E and gauge observations to obtain improved daily precipitation estimates. GDA is firstly applied to correct missed and false errors in the precipitation background field using the IDW interpolation method, while GWR estimates the spatial distribution of errors in the study area using hit errors. The proposed EDGWR merging framework was applied in YRSR from 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2018, and then evaluated for accuracy by comparing it with data from various sources, including IMERG-E, IMERG-L, IMERG-F, MSWEP, IDW, OK, and IMERG-GWR. Overall, IMERG-EDGWR demonstrates significant improvements over the original IMERG-E and consistently outperforms IMERG-F as well. Furthermore, when compared to commonly used multi-source products like MSWEP, interpolation methods such as IDW and OK, and even the direct implementation of GWR in IMERG-GWR, IMERG-EDGWR consistently exhibits superior performance. In spatiotemporal comparisons, IMERG-EDGWR presents superior performance in capturing the spatial variability of precipitation and shows a smoother precipitation pattern compared to IMERG-E, IDW, and OK. Both interpolation methods display a tendency to smooth out precipitation estimates, indicating their constrained ability to capture the spatial variations of precipitation patterns. During the winter season, IMERG-E and IMERG-F demonstrate notably high RB, low POD, and elevated FAR. In contrast, IMERG-EDGWR produces the most accurate precipitation estimates across the entire period, with a particularly notable improvement during the winter season, by integrating information from IMERG-E, ground observations, and geographical attributes. In contrast to interpolation methods, IMERG-EDGWR effectively improves the accuracy of both the magnitude and frequency of heavy precipitation events, especially when precipitation intensity exceeds 25 mm. Furthermore, experiments involving the removal of gauge observations from the GPCC dataset reveals that reducing the input data led to a decrease in the accuracy of the EDGWR algorithm. Nevertheless, the algorithm still demonstrates varying degrees of enhancement in comparison to IMERG-E and IMERG-F, highlighting its robustness. In summary, these findings affirm the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed EDGWR merging framework, indicating its potential application for improving daily precipitation accuracy in sparsely gauged basins. Therefore, this merging framework has great referential significance for future research and is expected to yield outstanding results when implemented in different regions.
1 Introduction Confluences are essential junctions in river systems and areas of interest in the ecology of river environments (Best, 1987 ; Mosley, 1976; Roy and Bergeron, 1990; Best and Ashworth, 1997; Rice et al., 2008; Lewis and Rhoads, 2015; Gualtieri et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2016; 2022 ). The confluence of two different flow directions produces more complex changes than a single flow structure (Ashmore et al., 1992; De Serres et al., 1999; Rhoads and Kenworthy, 1995; Rhoads and Sukhodolov, 2001 ; Constantinescu et al., 2014 ; Sukhodolov et al., 2017 ). Studies have illustrated the complexity of confluent flows, which are further complicated by the three-dimensional characterization of confluence hydrodynamics. Previous studies on the hydrodynamics of river confluences have focused on flow structures and other possible factors affecting flow characteristics, such as flow ratios, confluence angles, and riverbed incongruencies. The merging of tributary flows with the mainstream induces significant alterations in the flow structure within and downstream of the confluence reach. The interactions of pressure gradients related to flow curvature and topographic streambed features often lead to the emergence of secondary flows. Confluences are characterized by flow shear between two streams, generating vertical eddies at the mixing interfaces and streamwise-oriented vortical cells (SOVs) near the interfaces (Constantinescu et al., 2011; 2012 ). This convergence of flow intensifies riverbed shear stresses and velocities, potentially causing substantial bed scouring (Leite Ribeiro et al., 2012 ). The intense shear near the bed caused by the helical motions of downwelling and upwelling flows is responsible for the formation of midstream scouring holes (Yuan et al., 2018 ). Best (1987)  revealed the importance of this element in his text: “A feature of great significance in this region is that a shear layer is created between the two convergent flows along which powerful, vertical vortices are generated. These are responsible for increased bed shear stresses within the junction which, together with the increase in velocity as both flows enter the confluence, are responsible for considerable bed scour.” Secondary flows, akin to spirals in curved flows, may be induced by imbalances between outward-directed centrifugal forces and inward-directed pressure gradient forces (Ashmore et al., 1992 ). Sukhodolov and Sukhodolova (2019)  linked secondary flow development to lateral diffusion, arising from the mixing of fluids with differing mean crossflow velocities at a confluence. Large-scale secondary motions of confluent flows rearrange within the downstream channel. Pouchoulin et al. (2020)  challenged the notion of secondary flow as a spiral motion, suggesting a lock-exchange-like mechanism proposed by Horna-Munoz et al. (2020) , which is associated with density effects rather than inertial effects and disappears once vertical stratification is reached. Yuan et al. (2021)  observed dual counterrotating cells under high-flow conditions and a single secondary cell under low-flow conditions. Rhoads (2020)  and Yuan et al. (2022)  likened the formation of helical cells at confluences to secondary motions in curved currents, attributing them to an imbalance between centrifugal forces and pressure gradients. Sukhodolov et al. (2023)  theorized that the mixing process of shallow water flows at confluences was controlled by switching between the Kelvin–Helmholtz structural mode and the wake mode.
