Although, the surface temperatures of the entire canopy and the soil are not perfectly equal, this does not matter because the GPP used is the GPP at the ecosystem scale and therefore incorporates the vertical distribution of light and turbulence between the canopy and the soil surface (Li et al., 2019 ). The study excluded data at the time of precipitation and the day after precipitation, so canopy intercepted precipitation was excluded. This is because the observed instability of the flux data during these periods makes it difficult to extract and can easily affect the analysis.   5 Conclusions This study investigated the ecosystem WUE response to SWC and VPD using meteorological and flux data from 76 eddy-covariance sites in the FLUXNET2015 Tier 1 dataset. Our findings revealed a negative correlation between WUE and both SWC and VPD, with WUE showing a greater sensitivity to VPD dynamics.Under low VPD conditions, GPP and ET increased concurrently with SWC, resulting in a weak WUE response. Conversely, high VPD conditions increased ET ahead of GPP, leading to a decrease in WUE. WUE’s sensitivity to SWC primarily stemmed from T/ET, especially under high VPD conditions. Increased VPD levels increased WUE’s sensitivity to the SWC response. For the response of WUE to VPD, a consistent negative correlation between WUE and VPD was maintained, which was more pronounced under adequate soil moisture. Transpiration and evapotranspiration increased with increasing soil moisture, with the increase in transpiration compensated by stomatal closure at high VPD. A significant decrease in GPP/T at high VPD, especially with adequate soil moisture, contributed to the sensitivity of WUE to VPD. Reduced stomatal conductance strongly inhibited carbon assimilation in photosynthesis, decreasing WUE and GPP/T as VPD increased. Overall, VPD emerged as a key determinant of WUE. SWC and VPD affect ecosystem WUE through distinct pathways. These identified ecohydrological patterns offer valuable insights into the global climate change response, with implications for improving ecosystem WUE in water-limited areas and promoting sustainable water use.
1 Introduction With the intensification of climate change and the increase of extreme precipitation events (Slater et al., 2021 ), flash flood, as one of the deadly hazards owing to its rapid occurrence, unexpectedness, and destructiveness, has become more frequent and brought more serious disaster around the world (Borga et al., 2019 ). Flash flood warning is taken as one of the most important means of preventing flash flood disasters through triggering evacuation behaviors before the flash floods coming (Yin et al., 2023 ). The effectiveness of flash flood warnings depends on people’s response processes to the warnings, including receiving the warning, understanding the warning, trusting the warning, personalizing the flood risk, and finally taking risk avoidance action (Mileti, 1995; Parker et al., 2009 ). If people’s response level to the flash flood warnings is low, the warnings are difficult to stimulate their corresponding effective evacuations, and the effectiveness of the warnings is hindered, even if the warnings are reliable and are issued with sufficient lead time. Although both the reliability and lead time of flash flood warning have been significantly improved with the advancements of hydrological research (Han and Coulibaly, 2017; Lei et al., 2018 ), the understanding of the people’s responses to the flash flood warnings has achieved little progress (Bodoque et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022 ). Due to the uncertainty of flash flood forecasting, flash flood warnings are usually issued gradually in stages (i.e., from risk warning to disaster warning, or from suggestive warning to mandatory warning). For instance, three sequential stages for the issuing of warnings are typically found in China. The first stage (i.e., rainstorm red warning) is just a suggestive meteorological warning with a longer lead time but lower accuracy, while the last two warning stages (i.e., the ready-to-evacuate and immediate-evacuation warnings) are taken as mandatory flash flood disaster warnings with higher accuracy but shorter lead time. The rainstorm red warning is usually issued many times for the following reasons. Due to the issuance of the warnings based on administrative region, when some areas within the administrative region may experience disasters, people located in other areas will also receive warnings. Whenever there may be a disaster occurring in a new area, people in the whole administrative region will receive another warning. The similar phenomenon is also reported in other places, such as Europe and South Korea (Pappenberger et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, rolling forecasting leads to real-time changes in the forecast of disaster situations. With the continuous changes of disaster situations, warning administrators repeatedly issue warnings to remind people to pay attention to flood risks. And then the warnings have always been repeatedly issued through multiple channels: television, radio, mobile phones, and social media (Du et al., 2017a ). The impacts of the number of warnings on the people’s response to the warnings have been explored worldwide. For example, Luo et al. (2015)  randomly selected 782 residents as samples and explored the impact of the number of typhoon warning channels on the warning response levels of residents through telephone interviews. Its results indicate that increasing the number of warnings is conducive to improve the warning response levels when it is difficult to receive warnings. Yang et al. (2018)  found that by increasing warning frequency and issuing more warnings, the likelihood of the people receiving warnings and implementing emergency actions can be increased. Krocak et al. (2021)  evaluated the likelihood of US residents receiving and responding to hurricane warnings based on survey data and found that increasing the number of warnings is beneficial for improving residents' confidence in receiving warnings and implementing emergency actions during the late night (i.e., from 0:00 to 4:00). In general, increasing the number of warnings is beneficial for improving the likelihood of the people receiving warnings, thereby improving the warning response levels. However, when the similar warnings are issued multiple times, the additional information amount contained in the subsequent warnings is actually very small, even if all the warnings are reliable and true. And the excessive number of warnings can cause people’s distrust and fatigue towards the warnings, and hinder the warning response levels. For example, in the “720″ event in Zhengzhou, China in 2021, more than seven red rainstorm warnings were issued, but the municipal government and citizens did not pay attention to them (Guo et al., 2021 ). In Liulin Town of Suixian County in the same year, a serious flash flood occurred. Even though seven rainstorm red warnings were issued in advance, the local residents felt tired of the warnings and blocked the information (Wei, 2021 ). In August 2022, during the Longcao Gully flash flood disaster in Pengzhou, China, the upstream administrators monitored the flash flood and issued multiple warnings to downstream tourists, but did not stimulate their responses (Yuwei, 2022 ). Recently, a growing number of studies have reported this negative impact of excessive number of warnings on people's warning response levels. Ancker et al. (2017)  revealed the effects of repeated warnings on warning fatigue through statistical analysis and found that repeated receipt of warnings can cause recipients’ fatigue towards warning, thereby reducing their likelihood of taking action. Lee et al. (2022)  found that due to the relaxed geo-targeting of Korean Public Alert Service (KPAS), the people will receive too many warnings not relevant to themselves. Even if these warnings are all true, the public will gradually lose trust in KPAS after receiving redundant and unnecessary warnings many times, thereby ignoring and blocking the warning information. This phenomenon is referred to as the ”Spam Effect“ (Wang et al., 2010 ). Roberts et al. (2022)  evaluated the effectiveness of the UK's extreme weather warning system through discussions with stakeholders. More and more stakeholders are concerning on the impacts of the excessive number of warnings on the people’s fatigue towards the warnings. Although current studies have explored the impacts of the number of warnings (NOW ) on the warning response levels through the statistical methods, there are very few methods to determine the NOW  for improving the warning response levels. To determine the NOW  that can improve the warning response levels, it is necessary to simulate the effects of warning information on people’s response levels. The simulation of these effects (i.e., simulating the reception, dissemination, and processing of warning information and corresponding response behaviors) should be carried out at the individual scale. Thus, it is important to develop a model that simulates these effects at the individual scale. Agent-based model (ABM) is a computational model that simulates the dynamic decision-making, behaviors, and interactions of agents according to the defined behavioral rules (Janssen and Ostrom, 2006 ). If each agent is treated as a warning response individual, ABM can be taken as an effective tool to determine the NOW  for improving the warning response levels. Furthermore, ABM has also been widely favored by researchers worldwide in simulating the people’s response processes to the warnings (Zhu et al., 2019; Dai et al., 2020; Zhuo and Han, 2020; Du et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024 ). When the ABM describes specific responses of different groups to warnings, these specific responses are influenced by various unknown factors, or there is not enough time and resources to investigate these specific responses in detail. Therefore, the ABM parameters (e.g., risk threshold) are difficult to estimate, and there is even no consensus on parameters’ prior probability distributions (Du et al., 2017b; Zhuo and Han, 2020; Anshuka et al., 2022 ). Owing to the deep uncertainties1  1 Deep uncertainties are defined as the conditions under which parties to the decision do not know or cannot agree on the system model that relates actions to consequences or the prior probability distribution that parameters of the system follow (Lempert and Collins, 2007 ).   of these parameters, it is challenging to apply the ABM to determine the NOW  for improving the warning response levels. As robust decision making (RDM) has been proven to help adaptive decision making of water systems under the deeply uncertain future climate conditions (Herman et al., 2014; Singh et al., 2014; Herman et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2021 ), it can also help determine the NOW  even if there are deeply uncertain ABM parameters. The determined NOW  tries to make the flash flood warning system2  2 The flash flood warning system refers to a system composed of closely coupled modules such as the release, reception, and response of multi-stage flash flood warnings.   perform acceptably under a wider range of possible parameter values. In brief, the determined NOW  is robust. However, even the robust NOW  cannot ensure that the warning system performs acceptably within all possible parameter ranges. RDM can identify the parameter ranges for deteriorating the performances of the robust NOW  to an unacceptable level. Based on these parameter ranges, decision makers can know the applicable scopes of the robust NOW . The aim of our study is to propose an agent-based modeling method to determine the number of flash flood warnings for improving the warning response levels. After the relationship between the warning response levels and the NOW  is quantified by an ABM, RDM is used to determine the robust NOW  and its applicable scopes. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2  introduces the proposed agent-based modeling method. Section 3  illustrates the implementation of the proposed method in our case study. Section 4 and 5  present the determination of the results and discussions. Section 6  summarizes the main contributions.  2 Methodology To determine the number of flash flood warnings for improving warning response levels, the relationship between the warning response levels and the NOW  is firstly quantified. Specifically, the people’s responses to the warnings are simulated through an ABM (section 2.1.1 ), and then the NOW  is taken as an input of the ABM (section 2.1.2 ). The robust NOW  is determined through RDM taking the deep uncertainties from the ABM parameters into account. Specifically, a possible set of parameter values can be regarded as a state of world (SOW), and an ensemble of the warning response levels is generated with the ensemble of possible sets of parameter values and alternative NOW . The robustness measures are then figured out according to the ensemble of the warning response levels to determine the robust NOW  (section 2.2.2 ). And the parameter ranges corresponding to the vulnerable SOW are identified (section 2.2.3 ). If the parameters fall within these ranges, the performance of the warning system is unacceptable or extremely unacceptable for the robust NOW , and the robust NOW  is not applicable within the parameter ranges. Therefore, the flowchart of the proposed method for quantitively determining the number of flash flood warnings is sketched as Fig. 1  . 2.1 The relationship between the warning response levels and the TIW  2.1.1 Simulating people’s responses to the flash flood warnings through the ABM To simulate people’s responses to the flash flood warnings, Zhang et al. (2024)  has proposed an ABM where each agent is referred to a person threatened by flash floods. The agents live in a distributed environment defined by residences, road networks, and shelters. The agents are initially randomly located in the residences owing to the lack of location information. The agents are assumed to move along the road networks rather than freely within the ABM area. Special shelters are taken as the destinations for evacuation. The ABM consists of an early warning sub-module and a social sub-model. The early warning sub-module simulates the issuing of warnings while the social sub-model simulates the processes of the people’s response after receiving the issued warnings. As there are multiple stages in warnings (i.e., the rainstorm red, ready-to-evacuate, and immediate-evacuation warning stages), the early warning sub-module characterizes these three stages and sequentially triggers the social sub-module to simulate the corresponding the people’s psychological and behavioral responses, including whether, when, and how to evacuate (e.g., the choice of evacuation route). The warning sub-module is correspondingly characterized by three lead-time parameters: lead times of the rainstorm red (lead - t i m e - w 1   ), ready-to-evacuate (lead - t i m e - w 2   ), and immediate-evacuation warnings (lead - t i m e - w 3   ). These three parameters determine the times of issuing the three-stage warning. The social sub-module is the core of the ABM. An opinion dynamics model simulates the decision-making process of the evacuation of the j -th agent. The opinion of the j -th agent refers to his/her overall evacuation intention (denoted by a variable S j    , S j  ∈ 0 , 3       ). The decision-making process of the evacuation of the j -th agent can be described as:(1) X j , t   = 0  if  S j , t   < τ    1 ,    if  S j , t   > τ  or  X j , t - 1   = 1              where τ    is an evacuation threshold; X j , t      represents an action of the j   -th agent at time t ; X j , t   = 0    if the agent is taking no evacuation action at time t , or X j , t   = 1    if the agent is taking an evacuation action at time t . Thus, an agent will decide to evacuate if his/her overall evacuation intention exceeds the evacuation threshold at time t  or if he/she has evacuated at time t -1. There are two elements in the S j    : evacuation intention arising from receiving warnings (S j W    , S j W  ∈ 1 , 2 , 3       ), and evacuation intention arising from observing neighbors (S j N    , S j N  ∈ 0 , 1       ). If the j   -th agent has received a warning, S j W     depends on his/her socio-demographic and socio-psychological attributes (SS C j    ) and the stages of the receiving warning from the early warning sub-module (WT ):(2) S j W  = f RF   ( S S C j  , W T )       where f RF   ( . )     can be described by a random forest algorithm as an ensemble of classification and regression trees. The S j W     is divided into three levels (i.e., low, moderate, and high intention). The agents with different SS C j     (e.g., age, gender, income, education level, home ownership, exposure, threat appraisal, coping appraisal, perceived responsibility, and so on) have different evacuation intention after receiving a warning. S j N     is measured by the average of the actions of the neighbors of the j -th agent:(3) S j , t  N  = ∑ i n  X i , t - 1    n       where X i , t - 1      is the action of the i   -th agent around the j   -th agent’s neighbors at time t - 1   ; n    is the number of neighbors of the j   -th agent. The weights of the influence of S j W     and S j N     on the j   -th agent’s opinion are represented by parameters α j     and β j    , respectively, and α j  + β j  = 1   . S j , t      is a linear combination of overall evacuation intention at time t - 1    (i.e., S j , t - 1     ) and the current information:(4) S j , t   = ( 1 - θ j  )  × S j , t - 1   + θ j  × ( α j  × S j , t  W  + S F × β j  × S j , t  N  )       where θ j     measures the weight given by the j   -th agent to the information obtained at the current time. If θ j  = 0   , the j   -th agent will completely ignore current information and insist on past opinion. If θ j  = 1   , the opinion of the j   -th agent will be only influenced by current information. Hence, θ j     determines the speed of change in one’s opinion. If the j   -th agent decides to evacuate, the agent is assumed to evacuate along the shortest road to the shelter. There is often short-distance and the terrible condition of evacuation route during the flash flood disaster, people have to evacuate on foot rather than via vehicles. Thus, the spatial-grid evacuation model (SGEM)) (Lo et al., 2004 ) developed by the City University of Hong Kong and Wuhan University can simulate the process of his/her walking speed, and the interaction with other agents in road networks as follows:(5) v j  = 1.4 ,  if   ρ j  ⩽ 0.75    0.0412 × ρ j 2  - 0.59 × ρ j  + 1.867 ,  if   0.75 < ρ j  ⩽ 4.2    0.1 ,  if   ρ j  > 4.2              where v j     is the speed of the j   -th agent (m/s), and ρ j     is the number of agents within 1 m around the j   -th agent. Further more details of the ABM can be found in Zhang et al. (2024) .  2.1.2 Integrating multiple rainstorm red warnings into the ABM The rainstorm red warnings (i.e., the warnings in the first stage), as suggestive risk warnings, are usually issued multiple times. On the contrary, ready-to-evacuate and the immediate-evacuation warnings (i.e., the warnings in the last two stages) are issued point-to-point by the local government to the affected area. Due to the short lead time, this type of warning is only issued once or even missing. Therefore, the number of flash flood warnings is mainly referring to the number of the rainstorm red warnings. The proportions of people who receive the warnings after issuing a warning are denoted by W I\_ R    and W II\_III\_ R    for rainstorm red warning and the last two warning stages, respectively. As described in the introduction section, the excessive NOW  causes people’s distrust and fatigue in the warnings. If people become distrustful and tired of the warnings, they will not care about and give low weights to the warnings. Thus, the people’s distrust and fatigue level in the warnings can be quantified by a weight parameter, α   , in the ABM. According to the results of global sensitivity analysis on the ABM (Zhang et al., 2024 ), α    is the dominant parameter. Therefore, the impacts of the NOW  can be quantified by the exhaustive estimation of α   . When people receive the warnings only a few times (e.g., one or two times), their weight parameters (α   ) in the warnings remain almost unchanged. However, when the accumulated number of warnings received (NWR ) is excessive, these warnings will bring people’s distrust and fatigue. In other words, when the NWR  exceeds a threshold, their parameter α    decline (Woody and Ellison, 2014; Lee et al., 2022; Roberts et al., 2022 ). As the lower limit of the α    value is zero, if the NWR  further increases, the speed of α    decreasing will slow down and the value of α    will finally approach zero. The process of the α    changing with the NWR  is illustrated in Fig. 2  . And it can be quantified as a S-curve that depicts the loss of α    (L _ α   ) with the NWR  increasing as Equation (6) :(6) L _ α = 1 1 + e - S _ α × ( N W R - β )          where S _ α    describes the speed of the decrease of α   ; β    equals NWR  when L _ α = 0.5   . The range of L _ α    is between 0 and 1. The value of L _ α    can only approach to rather than equal to 0 in practice. Thus, L _ α    is assumed to be 0.001 when NWR  is 0, and β    is ln 999 / S _ α   . As the accuracies of the last two warning stages are different from that of the first warning stages, L _ α    for the rainstorm red warning and the sequent two warning stages are denoted by L _ α _ W I    and L _ α _ W II _ III   , respectively. The equation (6)  can determine the value of L _ α _ W I   . As the reliability of the last two warning stages is higher than that of the first warning stage, a reduction coefficient, K   , is adopted to estimate the value of L _ α _ W II _ III    assuming that L _ α _ W II _ III = K × L _ α _ W I   , K ∈ [ 0 , 1 ]   . Most of the parameters mentioned in ABM are difficult to be measured and there is no general way to calibrate them. Thus, there are deep uncertainties in the relationship between the warning response levels and the NOW  from ABM. As the concept of robustness can help decision making under deep uncertainties, the robust decision making (RDM) is used to determine the robust NOW .   2.2 Determining the robust TIW  through RDM 2.2.1 The components of RDM There are four components in the stakeholders’ RDM: the most important uncertainties (“X”), decision levers (“L”), relationships (“R”), and measures (“M”) (i.e., XLRM). The most important uncertainties (“X”) are the deeply uncertain parameters of the ABM. Decision levers (“L”) quantify an action or policy that can be manipulated by decision makers to change the performance of a system. As our study aims to determine the NOW , the NOW  is selected as decision levers (“L”). The performance of the flash flood warning system is measured by evacuation rate (ER   ). And the performance of the flash flood warning system is considered as unacceptable and extremely unacceptable if the ER    are below 90 % and 50 %, respectively.3  3 Defining the thresholds for dividing acceptable and unacceptable performance of the warning system is a consultative progress completed jointly by project investors, stakeholders, and analysts, which is beyond the scope of this study. However, our research objective is to propose an agent-based modeling method to determine the times of issuing flash flood warnings and provide decision makers with robust information in face of deep uncertainties through a simplified case. Thus, 50% and 90% are just an example threshold to illustrate the processes of the method. Stakeholders can adjust the thresholds in application   Measures (“M”) quantify the robustness of the flash flood system, and a satisficing here is selected to measure the robustness of the warning system. Relationship (“R”) maps the “L” to “M” through ABM. Specifically, it refers to the relationship between the NOW  and the satisficing.  2.2.2 Determining the robust NOW  The robust NOW  can make the flash flood warning system perform acceptably within the maximum parameter space of “X”. To determine the robust NOW , the performance of the warning system is assessed with the uncertainty ensemble. The first step is to sample the deeply uncertain parameter “X” to generate the uncertainty ensemble (i.e., the ensemble of possible sets of values of parameter “X”). Each member in the uncertainty ensemble is regarded as one of the states of world (SOW), representing a plausible set of the values of the parameter “X”. Sampling the deeply uncertain parameters aims to explore the full range of ABM’s behaviors regardless of the probabilities of these samples. Thus, this way of sampling under the deep uncertainties focuses on the impacts of the decision rather than the results of prediction (Bryant and Lempert, 2010 ). A Latin hypercube sample (LHS) can sample over the parameter space of “X” to generate 10,000 SOW to explore the deeply uncertain parameters (Bryant and Lempert, 2010 ). The LHS weights each SOW equally and it samples the ABM’s behavior efficiently over the parameter space. Once the uncertainty ensemble has been generated, the second step is to assess the warning system performance under the uncertain ensemble for alternative NOW . The proposed ABM can simulate the translation from one SOW, x  i   NOW     , to system performance (i.e., the evacuation rate), E R i NOW      with a given certain NOW . The process is repeated over uncertainty ensemble (X   NOW   = x  1   NOW   , x  2   NOW   , . . . , x  n   NOW         ) to generate a set of the evacuation rates (ER   NOW   = E R 1 NOW   , E R 2 NOW   , . . . , E R n NOW         ). The final step is to classify the all SOW into the acceptable SOW (i.e., the SOW under which the performance of the warning system is acceptable) and the vulnerable SOW (i.e., the SOW under which the performance of the warning system is unacceptable or extremely unacceptable). The process of classification can be described as a binary performance function, Λ ( . )   .(7) Λ ( x  i   NOW   )  = 1  if   E R i NOW   > E R T     = 0  if   E R i NOW   ⩽ E R T           Where E R T     is a pre-defined threshold (e.g., 90 % in this study). Λ ( x  i   NOW   ) = 1    means the x  i   NOW      belongs to acceptable SOW while x  i   NOW      is vulnerable SOW if Λ ( x  i   NOW   ) = 0   . Actually, inputted with a given NOW , the satisficing S a NOW      can be quantified by the following equation:(8) S a NOW   = ∑ i = 1  N  Λ ( x  i   NOW   )   N       where N    is the total number of SOW. If the flash flood system performs acceptably under a SOW, the SOW is considered acceptable. S a NOW      is the percentage of acceptable SOW for the warning system with the NOW . Thus, the greater the value of S a NOW     , the performance of the system will meet the acceptable standard under a larger proportion of SOW given the NOW , and the more robust the NOW  will be. The best optimal value of the robustness measure is one, resulting in the NOW  that can make the system perform acceptably under all SOW (i.e., under the whole parameter space).  2.2.3 Identifying parameter ranges corresponding to vulnerable SOW The previous sections can help decision makers obtain the robust NOW . However, the robust NOW  cannot guarantee that the warning system performs acceptably within all possible parameter ranges. The applicable scopes of the robust NOW  should be informed to decision makers. Thus, we use RDM to identify the ranges of the parameter “X” corresponding to vulnerable SOW for the robust NOW  through scenario discovery (SD). If the parameter “X” falls within these ranges, the robust NOW  will make the performance of the warning system unacceptable or extremely unacceptable. Patient rule induction method (PRIM) and classification and regression tree (CART) are two common SD algorithms. PRIM uses a set of multi-dimensional “boxes” to characterize the vulnerable SOW. Each “box” represents parameter ranges that contain predominantly the vulnerable SOW. PRIM can provide interactive visualizations to help decision makers choose alternative “boxes” that balance the measures of box quality: coverage, density, and interpretability. CART is a binary recursive partitioning algorithm that parses the parameter space of “X” into multiple high-purity subregions. And these high-purity subregions contain predominantly one class of SOW. CART can work if there are more than two classes of SOW. As there are three classes of SOW (i.e., SOW where the performance of the warning system is acceptable, unacceptable, and extremely unacceptable), CART is adopted to divide the parameter space of “X” into subspaces. And each subspace is related to a particular class of SOW. CART is run through a statistical R package called “rpart”. The pruned classification trees are automatically developed after a tenfold cross validation. The estimation of misclassification and cross-validation error rates is provided for the trees. The developed classification trees consist of a series of nodes, where each node is a logical expression of the value of an uncertain parameter in “X”. If the logical expression is true, the left branch is followed; otherwise, the right branch is followed. Following a particular combination of logical expressions, we can reach a leaf node where a certain class of SOW has the highest probability.    3 Case study 3.1 Study area When receiving a rainstorm red warning, whether people should evacuate or stay at home is related to the level of flood risk in their location. To ensure that the people receiving the rainstorm red warning need evacuate, Daqiao Street Community, located in Liulin Town, Suixian County, Suizhou City, China, was selected as the modeling area of ABM to test the proposed method to determine the NOW  (Fig. 3  b ). According to the Suixian Mountain Flood Disaster Prevention and Control Project, the Daqiao Street community is listed as a severely high-risk area for flash flood disasters. The community is surrounded by mountains on three sides, with houses distributed along river. Lang River flows through the town from southwest to northeast. Numerous tributaries converge into Langhe River in the town (Fig. 3 a ). The Langhe River in the upstream of the town is wider than that in the downstream, so flow from the upstream is easily congested in the town if there is an upstream rainstorm. Thus, the area is seriously threatened by flood when rainstorm occurs and people should be prepared for evacuation if they receive a rainstorm red warning. A 503 mm extreme rainstorm from 2:00 a.m. to 9:00 a.m. on August 12, 2021 has brought a severe flash flood disaster to the town. The flash flood overflowed the riverbank and severely inundated the houses. Before this disaster, ten rainstorm warnings (including three rainstorm orange warnings and seven rainstorm red warnings) were issued through WeChat, SMS, Weibo, and so on. Furthermore, flash flood disaster warning had been issued through broadcasting and loudspeaker as the disaster was approaching. Unfortunately, 21 people were still dead and four people were still missing in the disaster (Wei, 2021 ). More efforts should be done to improve the warning response levels.  3.2 Parameter setting in the ABM The environment of the agents in ABM was developed on the ArcGIS platform with a digital archive, World Imagery Wayback. As there was no official designated shelter in Liulin Town (Fig. 3 b ), two shelters were assumed to be set up in places that were not easily submerged by floods according to the DEM. The two shelters were located on both sides of the river to prevent the agents from evacuating across the river. The parameter setting in the ABM was shown in Table 1   according to Zhang et al. (2024) . The lead time of the three-stage warning was set by the experience in the study area. We set up four scenarios with different rainstorm red warning lead times to explore the impacts of the lead time on the number of rainstorm red warnings. The hyperparameters in the random forest algorithm (ntree   , mtry   , and nodesize   ) were trained by the survey data (the details of the survey can be found in Zhang et al. (2024) ). Classification accuracy, F1 score, and the area under the curve (AUC) were all greater than 0.70 for training and test dataset. Thus, the performance of the algorithm was acceptable (Jr et al., 2013 ). The socio-demographic and socio-psychological characteristics of the agent were listed in Table S1  . The initial SSC    values of the agents were randomly assigned according to the survey data without its heterogeneity in Liulin Town due to the small area of the town. As the values of parameters in the opinion dynamics model (e.g., weight of warnings, learning rate, and evacuation threshold) were hardly estimated by the empirical data. There was not even enough knowledge to draw their probability distributions of the parameters. According to the definition of deep uncertainties, these seven parameters in the opinion dynamics model can be taken as deep uncertainties (i.e., “X”) and only the uncertainty ranges of these parameters were defined, as shown in Table 1 . The uncertainty ranges of α   , W I _ R   , W II\_III\_ R   , and θ    were set as the maximum possible ranges from a conservative aspect. The larger the uncertainty ranges, the higher probabilities it is to capture the extreme SOW samples. The smaller the uncertainty ranges, the higher probabilities it is to miss vulnerable SOW samples, and the higher risks of the results. According to our survey data, S j  = 2    indicates that the j   -th agent has not yet decided on evacuation, and the agent decides to evacuate when S j  > 2   . Hence, the initial value of τ    was set to 2. The range of τ    was set to 2 ±    0.5 to reflect the uncertainty. The range of S _ α    was set from 1.5 to 3, indicating that the range of NWR  value was [4.6, 9.2] when α    decreased from 1 to 0. The LHS sampled the seven parameters over the uncertainty ranges as shown in Table 1  and generated 10,000 SOW. The ABM was run under these 10,000 SOW to help decision makers determine the robust NOW . The robust NOW  can make the ER    less sensitive to the changes in these parameter values and maintained the ER    at an acceptable level. The simulations covered the period from issuing the first rainstorm red warning to the end of the warning period at a spatial resolution of 9.6 m ×    9.6 m and at a time step of 1 min. A total of 500 agents were assumed to be involved in the simulations. Owing to the inherent randomness of the ABM, the simulation was repeated 1,000 times to reach a stable output. The final outputs were the average values of the 1,000 simulation results. In our case study, the outputs of interest in the system level were the proportions of agents that successfully arrived at shelters at the end of the simulation (e.g., ER ). More details of the ABM settings can be found in Zhang et al. (2024) .  3.3 Developing a surrogate model for the ABM Due to the complexity and randomness of the ABM, it is too time consumption to run the ABM as the requirements in section 3.2  (Confalonieri et al., 2010 ). To improve the computational efficiency, a Bayesian method proposed by Oakley and O'Hagan (2004)  was employed to develop a surrogate model for this ABM. The Bayesian method applies an efficient space-filling design of the input factors. Thus, there are 2–3 orders of magnitudes that are lesser than those in MC-based method. The Bayesian method fits a Gaussian process (GP) emulation to the original code as an accurate and fast surrogate model (O'Hagan, 2006 ). Because most of the inputs in the code have very little impacts on the output, it is possible to train the GP emulation with 200 samples that are generated by Maximin Latin Hypercube designs (O'Hagan, 2006 ). The ABM with 200 different inputs was run to train the GP emulation. A leave-one-out cross validation method checked the accuracy of the emulator fitness. The root mean squared error was 0.11, indicating that the accuracy from the emulator prediction was acceptable. The GP emulation surrogated the original ABM to translate all SOW into a set of ER    for each NOW .   4 Results 4.1 The robust number of warnings To determine the robust NOW , a set of ER    were calculated under all the SOW for each NOW  through the GP emulation. The set of ER    were then classified into acceptable (Fig. 4  a ), unacceptable (Fig. 4 b ), or extremely unacceptable ER    (Fig. 4 c ). Thus, the corresponding SOW to the three types of ER    can be distinguished for each NOW . The percentages of SOW in Fig. 4 a  are equal to S a NOW     , indicating that the higher the percentage of the SOW, the more robust the NOW  is. In contrast, the NOW  is more robust with the lower percentage of SOW in the other two sub-graphs (Fig. 4 b and c ). There are differences among the decision-making for determining the robust NOW  by these three sub-graphs. The performance of the warning system is acceptable within the maximum parameter space of “X” when the NOW  is the most robust in Fig. 4 a , while the warning system avoids to be vulnerable within the maximum parameter space of “X” when the NOW  is the most robust in the other two sub-graphs (Fig. 4 b and c ). For example, if the lead time is 120 min, issuing warnings four times cannot make the warning system perform acceptably while it can avoid the performance of the warning system being extremely unacceptable. Therefore, issuing warnings four times is a conservative decision. If the lead time is 120 min, the robust NOW  is found to be six (in Fig. 4 a ), eight (in Fig. 4 b ), and four (in Fig. 4 c ) times, respectively. If the lead time increases to 180, 240, and 300 min, the robust NOW  is seven, eight, and eight times, respectively, as shown in Fig. 4 a . There are obvious changes in the robustness of warnings when the lead time increases from 120 to 180 min, while these changes are quite small when the lead time increases from 180 min to 240 and 300 min.  Thus, the robust NOW  tends to stabilize at eight times with the increasing lead time. It can also be found that the robustness of warnings with a lead time of 120 min is greater than that with the lead times of 180, 240, and 300 min if the NOW  is less than five in Fig. 4 a . Fig. 4 b  has also shown that the robustness of warnings decreases with the increasing lead time if the NOW  is less than six. These findings show that the longer warning lead time combined with smaller NOW  decreases the robustness of the warning system. The warnings are evenly issued during the lead time period by default. In other words, the warning frequency is a constant during the lead time period. We also want to find the change trends of the robust NOW  if the warning frequency is changed from low to high or is changed from high to low (see Fig. 5  ). If the warning frequency is changed from high to low, the half of the warnings are issued evenly during the first one-third of the lead time period, while the remaining warnings will be issued evenly during the last two-thirds of the lead time period. The warning frequency is changed from low to high means that the half of the warnings are issued evenly during the first two-thirds of the lead time period while the other half will be issued evenly during the last one-third of the lead time period. Fig. 5 a  shows the ranks of the robust NOW  with the three warning frequencies as following: from low to high warning frequency > constant warning frequency > from high to low warning frequency. No matter how the warning frequency changes, there is no big difference among the robustness in Fig. 5 b . The robust NOW  is found to be seven for the from low to high warnings frequency and eight for the other two warning frequencies. The robust NOW  is found to be one, and the larger NOW , the less robust the warning system becomes if the warning frequency is changed from high to low in Fig. 5 c . The orders of the robustness of the warning system for the three types of warning frequencies are: from low to high warning frequency > constant warning frequency > from high to low warning frequency. The robustness of the warnings system with the robust NOW  can reach 19.11 %, 20.52 %, and 20.64 % as the warning frequency is changed from high to low, constant, and changed from low to high, respectively. To improve the robustness of flash flood warning system, the warning frequency is recommended to be gradually increased.  4.2 Parameter ranges corresponding to vulnerable SOW To inform the applicable scopes of the robust NOW , SD was adopted here to figure out the ranges of parameter “X” corresponding to the vulnerable SOW. And if parameter “X” falls within the ranges, the robust NOW  is no longer applicable and the performance of flash flood warning system becomes acceptable and extremely acceptable. If the lead time was 120 min, and its warnings were evenly issued during the lead time period, the ranges of parameter “X” corresponding to the three types of SOW were identified through CART for each NOW  as shown in Fig. 6  . The ER  values of SOW 2 and SOW 3 (i.e., vulnerable SOW) are unacceptable and extremely unacceptable, respectively. The classification trees for the other warnings with different lead times and warning frequencies are shown in Figure S1 - Figure S5  . If the robust NOW  value is one, the performance of warning system becomes acceptable or extremely acceptable unless the weight of warnings (α   ) is greater than 0.57, the probability of receiving ready-to-evacuate and immediate-evacuation warnings (W II _ III _ R   ) is greater than 0.52, the learning rate (θ   ) is greater than 0.2, and the probability of receiving rainstorm red warning (W I _ R   ) is greater than 0.26. If the robust NOW  value is greater than one, the decision makers can also identify the ranges of parameter “X” that deteriorate the performance of the robust NOW  to an acceptable or extremely acceptable level. The class probabilities of the SOW 1–3 are shown at each leaf node. These probabilities indicate the purity of the leaf nodes. If a subregion in the parameter space of “X” contains a single class of SOW, the probability of the class will approach one, and the node will be pure. If CART cannot relate the subregion to a particular class of SOW, the probability distribution across SOW 1–3 will be uniform, and the node will be impure. The probability distribution usually falls in between the two extremes. Thus, there are uncertainties for identifying the ranges of parameter “X” corresponding to the vulnerable SOW. We also summarized the thresholds of the ranges of parameter “X” corresponding to the vulnerable SOW with each NOW . The weight of warnings is always the primary control parameter regardless of the NOW . If the weight of warnings is below 0.57–0.61, the right branch will be followed. Following the right branch, if the weight of warnings is even below 0.38–0.43, the performance of the warning system will be extremely unacceptable. Otherwise, if the evacuation threshold is greater than 1.8, the performance of the flash flood warning system will change from unacceptable to extremely unacceptable. Therefore, the performance of the robust NOW  will be deteriorated if the weight of warnings is less than 0.57–0.61. In the left branch, the control parameters are varied with the NOW . However, the performance of the robust NOW  will be deteriorated if the weight of warnings (α   ) is below 0.65–0.80, the probability of receiving rainstorm red warning (W I _ R   ) is below 0.20–0.34, the probability of receiving ready-to-evacuate and immediate-evacuation warnings (W II\_III\_ R   ) is below 0.51–0.63, the learning rate (θ   ) is below 0.14–0.36, and the evacuation threshold (τ   ) is greater than 1.8–2.3. Through combining the threshold values with available data and expertise, the plausibility of the performance deterioration of the robust NOW  can be estimated. The relative importance of the parameter “X” can be assigned by their locations in the classification trees. For example, the parameter in the first split can be taken as the most importance because it can most effectively divide the parameter space among all parameters. The relative importance of parameter “X” on the class of SOW was summarized for each NOW  as shown in Fig. 7  . The relative importance was represented by color and shown in the legend below the figure. Six warning scenarios had been set: the warnings were evenly issued within lead times of 120 min, 180 min, 240 min, and 300 min, and the warning frequencies were changed from high to low and changed from low to high if the lead time was 120 min. The weight of warnings is the primary control factor regardless of the NOW  for the six scenarios. If the lead time is 120 min, the relative importance of W I _ R    and W II _ III _ R    will exhibit opposite trends with the NOW  increases: the probability of receiving rainstorm red warning becomes more important, while the probability of receiving ready-to-evacuate and immediate-evacuation warnings becomes less important. The people's positive responses to the rainstorm red warning are low owing to a small NOW . It is important to ensure the probability of receiving ready-to-evacuate and immediate-evacuation warnings for acceptable ER   . With the NOW  increases, issuing rainstorm red warning without the other two warning stages has already caused a high ER   . The probability of receiving ready-to-evacuate and immediate-evacuation warnings will become less important if there are many rainstorm red warnings. If the lead time increases to 180 min or more, the importance of W I _ R    shows an increasing first and then decreasing trend, while parameter W II _ III _ R    is unrelated to the vulnerability of the warning system. Therefore, if decision maker does not have enough information about the probability of receiving ready-to-evacuate and immediate-evacuation warnings, the number or lead time of rainstorm red warnings should be increased. Both the learning rate and the evacuation threshold are also two important parameters that are related to the vulnerability of the warning system. The learning rate is the second to fourth split point in the classification trees, and the evacuation threshold is usually third split point in the classification trees. It is interesting that the speed of the loss of α    and the reduction coefficient are not taken as split points regardless of the NOW , and thus they are unrelated to the vulnerability of the warning system.  4.3 The NOW  according to ranges of parameter values As the seven parameters in the opinion dynamics model are deeply uncertain, it is impossible to obtain their priori estimation values or even their probability distributions for determining the NOW . Thus, our study has found a way to determine the NOW  that makes the warning system less sensitive to the variation of the deeply uncertain parameter values. As the determination is based on the insensitivity (i.e., robustness) of the system, each SOW is assumed to be equally possible. However, the likelihood of SOW is different. To determine the NOW  with the different likelihood of SOW, CART was employed to partition the parameter space of “X” into multiple subspaces. And there is a particular optimal NOW  in a particular subspace. The optimal NOW  can achieve a better performance than other NOW  in the subspace (i.e., the ranges of parameter “X”). Thus, the optimal NOW  can be determined according to the ranges of parameter “X”. The results of the partition are shown in Fig. 8  . The results show that issuing warnings one or two times can result in an optimal performance of the warning system if the weight of warnings (α   ) is below 0.35 and the probability of receiving rainstorm red warning (W I _ R   ) is greater than 0.22. The likelihood of this parameter range can be estimated by decision makers according to the existing data, expert knowledge, and experience. If the likelihood of this parameter range is estimated to be the highest, the decision makers can issue warnings one or two times. If the likelihood of other parameter ranges is estimated to be the highest, the decision makers can issue the corresponding NOW  according to Fig. 8 . The results in Fig. 8  are figured out for the warnings that are evenly issued within a 120 min lead time. The results for the other lead times and warning frequencies can be found in Figure S6 - FigureS10  . If both the weight of warnings and the learning rate are below their threshold while the evacuation threshold is greater than its threshold, the left branch is usually followed. As the ranges of parameter “X” reflect the people’s negative responses to warnings, it is recommended to decrease the NOW . If the probability of receiving the three stages of warning is greater than its threshold, the left branch is followed, and the NOW  tends to be decreased.   5 Discussions Even the most reliable flash flood warning cannot be effective without people’s positive responses. To explore the impacts of warnings on people’s phycological and behavioral responses, each person should be taken as an automatic decision-making entity. Therefore, ABM, a model that simulates human behaviors, should receive special attention in addition to meteorological, hydrological, and hydrodynamic models in flash flood forecasting and warning. Recently, with the assistance of the ABM framework, an increasing number of studies have successfully simulated people’s responses to the warnings, including receiving, understanding, and trust the warnings, perceiving flood risk, and evacuation. These studies indicate that warning reception as the initial stage of warning responses has a significant impact on the warning effectiveness (Dawson et al., 2011; Liu and Lim, 2018; Yang et al., 2018 ). And increasing the NOW  is an important means to improve the receiving rate of warnings. However, several empirical studies, especially in the field of social sciences, have emphasized that excessive NOW  may exert a negative impact on warning responses. Due to the flexibility and extensibility of ABM, it provides a convenient channel for incorporating the latest empirical findings into simulation frameworks, thereby supporting quantitative analysis and refined decision-making. Unlike previous ABM simulations that suggested increasing the NOW , this study provides a simulation method to determine an appropriate NOW  by combining ABM and the latest empirical research. There are deep uncertainties in the ABM parameters, especially the parameters in the opinion dynamics model. In order to deal with the uncertainties, traditional risk-based method often assumes the probability distribution of parameters, and simplifies the uncertainties with a small set of characteristics (e.g., a mean or a few moments) of interest properties. However, the deep uncertainties limit the ability of this method to estimate the expected values of the parameters (Milly et al., 2008; Brown, 2010; Brown et al., 2011; Polasky et al., 2011 ). To address the deep uncertainties of parameters, the proposed method samples the ABM behaviors within the parameter space of “X” instead of estimating the expected parameter values. Its simulation results can help the decision makers determine the NOW  that makes the ER    least sensitive to the parameter changes. For example, the results show that the warning system with 4–8 warnings is the most robust if the lead time is 120 min. Briefly, the performance of the warning system is least affected by the uncertainties of parameters and maintains at an acceptable level if there are 4–8 warnings. The method shifts from “How many warnings will make the warning system perform best for the expected parameter values?” to “How many warnings will make the warning system perform acceptably within the maximum parameter space?” Although the robust NOW  can successfully handle a wide range of possible parameter values, the robust NOW  cannot make the warning system perform acceptably under all possible parameter ranges. The information provided by SD can help decision makers understand the applicable scopes of the robust NOW . The decision makers will be informed of the potential risk associated with issuing these warnings, and supporting risk management measures can be implemented. If the applicable scopes of the robust NOW  are not large enough, then small changes in parameters will result in unacceptable performance of the warnings, even if the NOW  is relatively robust. Decision makers need to closely monitor the performance of the warnings, and adjust the NOW  if the parameter values are not within the applicable scopes, especially in complex and constantly changing environments. Moreover, the detection of the important parameters influencing the vulnerability of the warning system can help decision makers reduce the uncertainties of parameters. For example, the weight of warnings is found to be the primary control parameter regardless of the NOW  under the six warning scenarios, thus it is important to reduce the uncertainties associated with the weight of warnings; in contrast, the speed of the loss of α    and its uncertainties are found to slightly influence the vulnerability of the warning system. Our study determines the optimal NOW  according to the ranges of parameter “X”. As the determination method focuses on the choice among alternative NOW , it only requires the rough estimation of the likelihood of the ranges of parameter “X” rather than the accurate estimation of the specific values of the parameters. Moreover, it can help build consensus among parties with different expectations in parameter values to a policy debate. The ranges of parameter “X” that support each NOW  are shown in Fig. 8 . And every party has its own opinions and expectations but there are still various outcomes to satisfy the all parties. The information does not psychologically threaten to those holding different views (Schoemaker, 1993 ). The results as shown in Fig. 8  can also help decision makers understand the outcomes that they might have opposed. Therefore, our method is conducive to policy discussions among groups with the deeply uncertain parameters. Although there are many advantages of our proposed method, some limitations should be improved in our further studies. To describe the distrust and the fatigue towards the warnings caused by excessive NOW , the S-curve quantified the relationship between the weights of warnings and NWR . However, the S-curve is not a conclusive mathematical description of this relationship. A refined quantification equation requires the support of relevant social-psychology theories or empirical data. An interdisciplinary collaboration among the fields of hydrology, psychology, community disaster management, and complexity science should work together to improve the effectiveness of warning system. Any contribution for improving the understanding the system will provide valuable insights into the determination of the NOW . In addition, all the warning messages are assumed to be true in our study while the false warnings are inevitable due to the uncertainties of flash flood forecasting. And the recent false warning ratio undermines people’s trust levels in the warnings and their preparedness actions (LeClerc and Joslyn, 2015; Ripberger et al., 2015; Lim et al., 2019 ). Both the number and the authenticity of warnings affect people's responses to flash flood warnings, and then affect the effectiveness of the warnings. Thus, the impacts of the authenticity of warnings on the relationship between the NOW  and the warning response levels are also worth to be explored in the future.  6 Conclusions This study proposed an agent-based modeling method to determine the number of flash flood warnings for improving the warning response levels. The relationship between the warning response levels and the NOW  was quantified by an ABM. And RDM was used to determine the robust NOW  owing to the deep uncertainties of the ABM parameters. Liulin Town, which experienced a serious flash flood disaster, was selected as a case study area to demonstrate the application of the proposed method. The main conclusions are as follows. The robust NOW  was determined for the warnings with different lead times and warning frequencies. If the lead time of the flash flood warnings increases from 120 min to 300 min, the robust NOW  gradually increases from six to eight times and stabilizes at eight times. The ranks of the robust NOW  with the three types of warning frequencies are: from low to high warning frequency > constant warning frequency > from high to low warning frequency. The method for determining the robust NOW  does not attempt to estimate deeply uncertain parameters, and to answer the “how many warnings can be issued to make the performance of the flash flood warning system optimal under the expected parameter values?” but attempts to determine the NOW  that is least sensitive to changes in uncertain parameters, and to answer “how many warnings can be issued to make the performance of flash flood warning system acceptable in the largest parameter space?” To inform the applicable scopes of the robust NOW , the ranges of parameter values corresponding to the vulnerable SOW were identified. If the parameters fall within the ranges, the robust NOW  is no longer applicable. The weight of warnings is found to be the primary parameter deteriorating the performance of the robust NOW . More efforts should be made to reduce the uncertainty associated with the weight of warnings. The optimal NOW  was determined according to the ranges of uncertain parameter values. Decision makers only need to estimate the relative likelihood of the ranges of uncertain parameter values, and then can choose the optimal NOW . The determination relaxes the accuracy requirements for parameter estimation and builds consensus among parties with very different opinions to a policy debate.
1 Introduction Boreal forests are a significant component of the terrestrial ecosystem, covering approximately one-third of the global forest area (Sexton et al., 2016 ), and contributing 20 % to the global carbon sink (Pan et al., 2011 ). However, it has been demonstrated that climate change and anthropogenic activities have more considerable impacts on the boreal forest ecosystem than on other biomes (Gonzalez et al., 2010; Scheffer et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2021 ), which considerably affect the structures and ecological processes of boreal forests (Wei et al., 2022 ), such as vegetation productivity, tree mortality, vegetation greenness, aboveground biomass, and species composition. In turn, these changes may alter global climate and hydrological processes (IPCC, 2021; Isabelle et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2021; Berner and Goetz, 2022 ). Since climate change impacts (e.g., warming, wildfires) and human activities are projected to persist and be more intensive in the future in boreal regions (Blanken, et al., 1997; Nijssen and Lettenmaier, 2002; Mkhabela et al., 2009; Gauthier et al., 2015; D'Orangeville et al., 2016; Kozii et al., 2020; Hadiwijaya et al., 2021a ), there is a growing research interest in understanding changes in boreal forests and their ecological and hydrological impacts. Ecosystem evapotranspiration (ET ) is the most important component of the hydrological cycle, as it represents a substantial water flux to the atmosphere (Kozii et al., 2020 ). It is not only a strong control on regional water budget and global hydrological cycle (Wang and Dickinson, 2012; Ma et al., 2021 ), but also a critical coupling between carbon and water cycles (Zhang et al., 2019 ). Numerous studies have extensively discussed the ecological and hydrological importance of ET  in water flux in various ecosystems globally (Hadiwijaya et al., 2021a; Kozii et al., 2020; Peel et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2018 ). For example, the relative importance of ET  to precipitation varies considerably (55 to 80 %) due to the differences in climates, forest types, vegetation structures, forest management strategies, and spatiotemporal scales (Peel et al., 2010; Staudt et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2018; Bodo et al., 2023 ). Currently, various approaches such as water budget (Peel et al., 2010 ) and remote sensing (Wei et al., 2017 ) used to estimate ET  in forest ecosystems are modeling-based, providing aggregate estimations across ecosystems at watershed to global scales. In contrast, observation-based methods such as the eddy covariance (EC ) system (Iida et al., 2020; Paul-Limoges et al., 2020 ) and geochemistry (i.e., isotopes) (Wang and Yakir, 2000 ) estimate ET  at the finer scale (e.g., forest stand level). Among all approaches, the (EC ) system is the most widely used method for quantifying ET  and studying ET  partitioning at the fine scale. ET  composes ecosystem transpiration (T ) from plants and evaporation (E ) from soil surfaces (Cui et al., 2020; Kozii et al., 2020; Ma, et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022 ). In a natural forest ecosystem with multi-layer vegetation structures, the entire ecosystem can be conceptually partitioned into the overstory and understory with T  being partitioned into overstory tree transpiration (Tos  ) and understory vegetation transpiration (Tu  ), and E being partitioned into evaporation from overstory canopy (Eos  ) and understory vegetation interception and soil evaporation (Eu  ). Previous studies have often ignored understory processes (Raz-Yaseef et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2021 ). For example, Tos   has normally been viewed as T  due to the difficulty and complexity of measuring transpiration from understory vegetation (Raz-Yaseef et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2021 ), while some studies have solely treated soil evaporation as understory evaporation (Lin et al., 2012 ). Such ignorance might lead to underestimations of T  and E , and consequently, ET . Despite a general perception that Tu   accounts for a small fraction of T , the contribution of Tu   to T  is site-specific, depending on the forest structure and composition (Domec et al., 2012; Bodo et al., 2023 ). Boreal forests have dense understory vegetation and relatively sparse overstory trees (Iida et al., 2009 ), the contribution of understory might differ from other biomes. Thus, there is a critical need to investigate the role of the understory ecosystem in forest ET  and its partitioning in boreal forests. Measuring Eu  , Tu  , and understory evapotranspiration (ETu  ) directly is challenging, and consequently, there are limited studies that investigated the contribution of Eu   to E  (Eu  /E ), Tu   to T  (Tu  /T ), and ETu   to ET  (ETu  /ET ), particularly in China’s boreal forest ecosystems. In addition, there are large variations in ETu  /ET  around the globe, which may be due to varied locations, forest types, and study periods (Black et al., 1996; Ohta et al., 2001; Iida et al., 2020; Paul-Limoges et al., 2020; Jiménez-Rodríguez et al., 2020; Balandier et al., 2022 ). In boreal forests, Iida et al. (2009)  estimated that the contribution of ETu   to ET  can reach 50 %, while a lower contribution of ETu   (18 %) was reported by Hadiwijaya et al. (2021b). These disparities are contingent upon the chosen research methodology and the temporal scale (Balandier et al., 2022 ). In assessing possible factors contributing to variations in ETu  /ET , Iida et al. (2009)  observed that vapor pressure deficit (VPD ) above the forest floor is the dominant driving factor of ETu  /ET  in an eastern Siberian boreal larch forest, while overstory leaf area index (LAI ) dominated ETu  /ET  in a tropical dry deciduous forest (Iida et al., 2020 ). However, there is a lack of assessments regarding potential factors contributing to variations in Eu  /E  and Tu  /T . Clearly, more studies are needed to quantify the Eu  /E , Tu  /T , and ETu  /ET , and their controlling factors in boreal forests. In the past few decades, numerous methods (e.g., eddy covariance, isotopes, and sap flow measurements) have been developed to partition ET  into T  and E  in forest ecosystems (Iida et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2016; Kozii et al., 2020; Cui et al., 2020; Hadiwijaya et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021 ). Although the EC  method directly measures the spatially averaged ET  at a high temporal resolution (Iida et al., 2009 ), most studies have focused on measuring ET  for the entire ecosystem using a single EC  system (Raz-Yaseef et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2018 ). Recently, a few studies have successfully employed concurrent EC  systems to directly measure ETu   and total ET  (Black et al., 1996; Iida et al., 2009; Paul-Limoges, et al., 2020; Iida et al., 2020; Hadiwijaya et al., 2021; Wolf et al., 2024 ), which greatly advance and improve our understanding of water fluxes in forest ecosystems. However, so far, no research has been conducted on the utilization of concurrent EC  systems for assessing ETu   in China’s boreal forests. Additionally, Tu   and Eu   measurements generally include isotope analysis (Jiménez-Rodríguez et al., 2020 ), lysimeter techniques (Young et al., 1997 ), thermometric methods, and water balance equations (Jiang et al., 2019 ). Nonetheless, each approach exhibits pros and cons. For instance, the thermometric method is widely and primarily used to determine Tos   from overstory trees, while upscaling limitations constrain its applicability to measure Tu  . Similarly, using the water balance equation for estimating Eu   does not yield continuous datasets. Without directly measuring T  and E , Zhou et al. (2016)  proposed the underlying water use efficiency (uWUE ) method to quantify T  and E  based on the function between ET , gross primary productivity (GPP ), and VPD  at the ecosystem scale. However, such an application in understory vegetation has not been reported yet. The combination of concurrent EC  systems with the uWUE  method may offer a practical and logical solution to partition ET  and ETu   into various components in boreal forests. The Da Hinggan Mountains, situated on the southern margin of the Siberian zone (Xu et al., 2022 ), are predominantly covered by native, boreal larch forests (Larix gmelinii ) with dense understory vegetation. This study conducted in this region aimed to address the following scientific questions: (1) Can the concurrent EC  systems combined with the uWUE  method be used to quantify ET  and its components? (2) If so, what are the contributions of Tu   and Eu   to T  and E  in the natural boreal larch forest, respectively? (3) How does ETu   contribute to ET ? And (4) what are the dominant driving factors of the variations in the individual components (Tu  , Eu  , and ETu  ) and their respective ratios (Tu  /T , Eu  /E , and ETu  /ET )?  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The study site is located in the Mohe Forest Ecosystem Research Station of northeastern China (53°27′59″N, 122°20′06″E), which is situated on the southern margin of the Siberian zone (Fig. 1  a) with an elevation of 325 m above sea level and a slope of 4 degrees. The natural larch forest (Larix gmelinii ) is the primary vegetation type in the study area (Fig. 1 e). The overstory canopy height is about 20 m. The canopy of Larix gmelinii  is relatively sparse, with a mean overstory leaf area index of 2.0 m2 /m−2  during the growing season (Xu et al., 2022 ). The canopy biomass (i.e., branches, and leaves) is concentrated within the upper half of the tree height (Fig. 1 b and 1c). The understory vegetation is predominantly composed of shrubs, herbaceous plants, and mosses, including Dahurian rhododendron (Rhododendron dauricum ), lingonberry (Vaccinium vitis-Idaea ), ledum (Ledum palustre ), blueberry (V. uliginosum ), and sphagnum (Sphagnum palustre ) (Fig. 1 e). The understory canopy height is about 1.8 m. Larix gmelinii  and the understory vegetation have considerable changes in canopy phenology during the growing season (May to September) (Fig. S1  in the Supplementary Materials ). The mean annual precipitation during the growing season from 1984 to 2017 was 370.5 mm. According to the FAO soil classification, the main soil type is classified as brown coniferous forest soil.  2.2 Meteorological data Meteorological variables were measured by the gradient meteorological observation system. Air temperature (Ta  , ℃) and relative humidity (RH , %) were measured by the Model HMP155 probes (Vaisala, Vantaa, Finland). Wind speed (Ws  , m/s) was measured by the 010C wind speed sensors (MetOne, Grants Pass, USA). Net radiation (Rn , W/m−2 ) was measured by two NR01 sensors (Hukseflux, Delft, Netherlands). One was installed on the flux tower at 23 m (above the forest canopy), while the other one was installed on the flux tower below the forest canopy at 1.5 m height. Solar radiation (SR , W/m−2 ) (Model CNR 4, Kipp & Zonen B.V., Delft, the Netherlands) was measured at the 1.5 m height above the ground by an automatic weather station located in an open area neighboring the study plot. Soil heat flux (G , W/m−2 ) was measured at two locations, positioned at a depth of 5 cm below the ground in eastern and western directions in proximity to the flux tower using two flux plates (HFP01SC, Hukseflux, Netherlands). Precipitation (P , mm) was measured by a TE525 Tipping Bucket Rain Gage (Campbell Scientific, Logan, UT, USA). Soil water content was measured using four CS650 probes (Campbell Scientific, Logan, USA) at depths of 5, 10, 20, and 40 cm below the ground in the study plot, respectively. All meteorological measurements were recorded at 10-minute intervals using a CR3000 datalogger (Campbell Scientific, Logan, UT, USA). The dynamics of meteorological factors can be found in Fig. S2 . In addition, vapor pressure deficit (VPD , KPa) was calculated as a function of RH  and Ta   (Howell and Dusek, 1995 ). The mean soil water content of a profile (SWC , cm3  cm−3 ) was expressed as Eq (1)  (Gao et al., 2019 ).(1) SWC = SW C 1  × L 1  + ∑ i = 2  4    SW C i - 1   + S W C i   2  × L i   L      where, SWC  is the mean soil water content of a profile (cm3  cm−3 ); SWC i  at Li  (i = 1, 2, 3, and 4) represents the soil water contents at depths of 5, 10, 20, and 40 cm, respectively; and L refers the depth of the entire soil profile (40 cm).  2.3 Leaf area index Leaf area index (LAI ) of the overstory in the study site was measured every 5–7 days at 25 to 30 fixed plots during the growing seasons of 2021 and 2022 using the LAI -2200 Plant Canopy Analyzer (Li-Cor, Lincoln, NE, USA). However, to match the study period and obtain overstory LAI  in the 2020 growing season, we also derived LAI  from 2020 to 2022 growing seasons from the MODIS  product (MCD15A3H) with a 500 m resolution at the 4-day time intervals (note: MODIS LAI  reflect the LAI  of the entire ecosystem). Undoubtedly, the existence of clouds can have a considerable impact on LAI  values. As a result, LAI  data with clouds were removed. Subsequently, functional relationships between LAI (both the measured overstory LAI  and MODIS LAI ) and the observation date (day of the year, DOY ) were established (Section 3.2 ). Thus, the daily LAI  values for the entire growing season were derived based on these functional relationships (Wang et al., 2021 ). Finally, the daily overstory LAI  in the 2020 growing season was derived from the relationship between overstory LAI  and MODIS LAI  during the growing seasons of 2021 and 2022. Therefore, the overstory LAI  data from 2020 to 2022 growing seasons were estimated for further analysis.  2.4 A framework for ET  partitioning In the present study, a framework combining concurrent EC  systems and the uWUE  method, was used to conduct ET  partitioning (Fig. 2  ). There are five key steps in this framework. Concurrent EC  systems were adopted to directly quantify ET  and ETu   (Step 1). The uWUE  method was applied to distinguish T  and E  from ET , as well as Tu   and Eu   from ETu   (Step 2). Tos   and Eos   from overstory trees were calculated by T  and Tu  , and E  and Eu  , respectively (Step 3). Cross-validations were performed between Tos   from sap flow measurements or Eos   from the canopy water balance (CWB ) method and differences in T  and Tu   or E  and Eu   from the uWUE  method (Step 4). Finally, the relative contribution of each component to ET  was quantified (Step 5). The details of each procedure can be found in the following sections. 2.4.1 Eddy covariance measurements and data processing In this study, ET  and ETu   were measured by concurrent EC  systems (Step 1 in Fig. 2 ), which were installed at heights of 35 m and 3 m above the ground, respectively, in the study plot (Fig. 1 b and 1c). Both EC  systems in this study consist of an integrated three-dimensional sonic anemometer and open-path infrared gas analyzer (IRGASON, Campbell Scientific, Logan, UT, USA) to continuously measure CO2   and water fluxes below and above forest canopy from 2020 to 2022 at a frequency of 10 Hz and then averaged into 30-minute intervals (Note: the data for EC  system below canopy start on May 23, 2020). The high-frequency data were recorded in a CR3000 datalogger (Campbell Scientific, Logan, USA). ETos   was calculated as the difference between ET  and ETu  . The study area has Larix gmelinii  uniformly distributed within a radius of approximately 1 km around the flux tower. The footprint instance of the EC  system (90 %) in this study estimated by the Kljun footprint model (Kljun et al., 2015 ) can be found in Fig. S3 . The half-hourly CO2   and water flux data were processed using the EddyPro  software (version 7.0.9, LI-COR, Lincoln, USA), which has been widely used to process flux data with 10 Hz. The processing steps involve spike detection, two-dimensional coordinate rotation, corrections for time delay, frequency response correction, and turbulent fluctuations (Paul-Limoges et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021 ). To ensure data quality, the half-hourly CO2   and water fluxes data during the 1-hour before rainfall and 1-hour after the rainfall events were excluded (Ji et al., 2020 ) and then underwent a quality control process (Chi et al. 2019; Chi et al., 2021 ). The energy budgets closing for the whole ecosystem (EC  system above forest canopy) and the understory ecosystem (EC  system below forest canopy) were calculated (Fig. S4 ). The regression slopes were 0.86 for the whole ecosystem (Fig. S4 a) and 0.70 for the understory ecosystem (Fig. S4 e), which is reasonable compared to existing research (i.e., Iida et al., 2020 ). However, the decoupling between below (understory) and above (overstory) EC  systems has been demonstrated in different forest ecosystems (Wilson and Meyers, 2001; Launiainen et al., 2005; Thomas et al., 2013; Jocher et al., 2017; Paul-Limoges et al., 2020 ) due to the topography, canopy phenology, and forest structures (e.g., density and tree height). Thus, there might be a possible decoupling within concurrent EC  systems in the study site. Previous studies have widely used the standard deviation of the vertical wind velocity (σw  ) to evaluate the decoupling thresholds (or unstable conditions) between below and above canopy EC  systems (Launiainen et al., 2005; Acevedo et al., 2009; Thomas et al., 2013; Jocher et al., 2017; Paul-Limoges et al., 2017; Chi et al., 2021 ). Thus, following these studies, the decoupling threshold for the understory EC  system in this study was σw   = 0.06 m/s (Fig. S5 ), which is consistent with the research of Jocher et al. (2017)  who studied boreal forests in northern Sweden. The σw   was used to filter the EC  flux data during the decoupling range, as indicated by the non-linear relationship between the below and above canopy σw   (Fig. S5 ) (Chi et al., 2021 ). Furthermore, previous studies have indicated that although the majority of eddies move upwards, counter-gradient transport (Denmead and Bradley, 1985 ) can cause some eddies to move downwards beneath the canopy, originating from either above or below the canopy crowns. These downward eddies can create biases in the understory contributions when using concurrent EC  systems, as they may be interpreted as negative water fluxes (i.e., condensation) (Paul-Limoges et al., 2020; Chi et al., 2021 ). Thus, the negative water fluxes which were caused by the downward eddies were removed. The detailed calculation processes can be found in Paul-Limoges et al. (2020) . Finally, possible gaps in the half-hourly flux time-series data were gap-filled using the R package REddyProc  (Wutzler et al., 2018 ).  2.4.2 Underlying water use efficiency method The underlying water use efficiency (uWUE ) method (Eqs . (2)–(4) , Step 2 in Fig. 2 ), proposed by Zhou et al. (2016) , was applied to estimate T  and E  from ET  and Tu   and Eu   from ETu  . The uWUE  is an effective method for estimating T  based on the relationship between ET  and GPP  in various forest types worldwide (Zhou et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2021 ). While T  was estimated, E  can be calculated as the difference between ET  and T  (Eq. (5) . More details of the uWUE  method can be found in Zhou et al. (2016) . Similarly, the same principle was applied to estimate Tu   and Eu   using ETu   and GPPu  . GPP  was determined from net ecosystem exchange and ecosystem respiration using a nighttime-based partitioning method based on the flux data (Jin et al., 2023 ). GPPu   was also calculated from the understory ecosystem using the same method. The uWUE  method can be defined as follows:(2) uWU E a  = GPP × VPD    ET       (3) uWU E p  = GPP × VPD    T      (4) uWU E a   uWU E p    = T ET    o r  T = uWU E a   uWU E p      × E T     (5) E = E T - T     where, uWUEa   and uWUEp   are apparent and potential uWUE , respectively, with uWUEp   was determined by the 95th quantile regression method using half-hourly GPP  (or GPPu  ), ET  (ETu  ), and VPD  data, and uWUEa   estimated by the linear regression method at the daily scale using half-hourly GPP  (or GPPu  ), ET  (or ETu  ), and VPD  data (Zhou et al., 2016 ). An example of the uWUE  method to calculate the T /ET  can be found in Fig. S6 . Once E  and T  were partitioned from ET , and Eu   and Tu   were partitioned from ETu   from the uWUE  method, Tos   and Eos   can be estimated as the differences between T  and Tu  , and E  and Eu  , respectively (Step 3 in Fig. 2 ).  2.4.3 Cross-validations 2.4.3.1 Cross-validation between Tos  from sap flow measurements and the uWUE method Tos   from sap flow measurements was used to cross-validate Tos   from the uWUE  method (Step 4 in Fig. 2 ). Several parameters of forest structures, including stand density (1250 trees/ha), mean diameter at breast height (DBH , 13.1 ± 6.7 cm), tree height (17.4 ± 2.6 m), tree age (75 to 90 years), and total sapwood area (SA ) were measured, which can help select sample trees for sap flow measurements. Nine sample trees were selected for sap flow measurements using thermal dissipation probes from May to September (growing season) in 2021 and 2022 based on the frequency distribution of DBH  (Xu et al., 2022 ). The DBH  of sample trees in the study plot ranges from 8.1 to 23.7 cm with a mean value of 14.7 cm.
