These values covered most trees’ DBH  to ensure the optimal representation of the average level of the sample plot and to minimize uncertainties associated with the radial variation. More details of sample trees can be found in Table S1 . All thermal dissipation probes with a length of 20 mm were installed on the north-facing side at the breast height of sample trees. Meanwhile, the probes were mounted with waterproof silicone and covered with reflective, insulating sheeting to mitigate the impact of solar radiation (Song et al., 2020 ). The upper probe contained a heater that was continuously heated with a constant power of 0.2 W , while the lower probe served as a temperature reference. Sap flow data were recorded in a CR1000 datalogger (Campbell Scientific, Logan, UT, USA) at 30-minute intervals. Sap flux density (Js  , g/cm2 /s) was expressed as:(6) J  s   = 0.0119 × Δ T  m a x   - Δ T  Δ T     1.231      where, ΔT  is the temperature difference between the two thermal dissipation probes; ΔTmax   is the maximum temperature difference between sensors at nighttime when Js   is close to 0 (Song et al., 2020 ). The sap flux density was used to determine Tos  . Daily Tos   per unit ground area (mm/day) can be expressed (Clausnitzer et al., 2011 ) as Eq. (7) :(7) T os   = J sa   × S A cum    A S       where, the Jsa   is the average sap flux density of all sample trees (g/cm2 /s); SAcum   is the cumulative sapwood area of the sample plot (0.3 m2 ); and AS   is the sample plot area (400 m2 ). In this study, 25 trees around the sample plot were used to establish the exponential functional relationships between SA  and DBH  (SA =0.6 × DBH 1.7 , R2  = 0.96) (Xu et al., 2022 ). However, previous studies indicated that if the sapwood width was less than the probe length, sap flow density might be underestimated since some parts of the probe were inserted into the nonconductive xylem (Clearwater et al., 1999 ). As shown in Table S1 , there are some trees with sapwood width less than the probe length. Thus, corrections of daily Tos   were conducted according to the method proposed by Clearwater et al. (1999)  (Fig. S7 ). Since the sap flows were only measured in the growing seasons of 2021 and 2022, the cross-validations of daily Tos   were only conducted in these two seasons.  2.4.3.2 Cross-validation between Eos  from CWB and the uWUE method To cross-validate Eos   from the uWUE  method, Eos   was estimated as the difference between P , throughfall (Tf  , mm), and stemflow (Sf  , mm) at the rainfall event level (Eq. (8) ) using the CWB  method. Tf   was collected from three tilted gutters (100 × 20 cm, angles of 5°to horizontal to ensure efficient drainage), which were randomly installed in the study plot. Each collector was connected with a tipping bucket rain gauge (0.2 mm per tip, HOBO RG3-M, Onset, USA) using a plastic tube. Sf   was measured from three standard trees with different DBH  classes based on the frequency distribution of DBH  in the study plot using a waterproof rubber (Fig. 1 d). The Sf   was collected using a halved rubber collar, which spirally wrapped around each selected tree stem and connected to a plastic tube with a tipping bucket rain gauge (0.2 mm per tip, HOBO RG3-M, Onset, USA). More details on the measurement of precipitation interception processes can be found in Sheng and Cai (2019) . However, studies have shown that Tf   and Sf   were underestimated when using measurements from a tipping bucket rain gauge, which may lead to the overestimation of Eos   (Iida et al., 2012 ). Therefore, we corrected Eos   values by assuming static one tip volume reported by Iida et al. (2012) . The dynamics of P , Eos  , Tf  , and Sf   can be found in Table S2  in the Supplementary Materials . In this study, the Sf   can be expressed as Eq. (9) :(8) E  o s   = P - T  f   - S  f      (9) S f  = ∑ i = 1  n  S i  × M i   A s  × 10 3        where, Eos   is canopy evaporation (mm); P , Tf  , and Sf   are precipitation, throughfall, and stemflow, respectively; n  is the number of DBH  classes (n  = 3); Si   is the total stemflow of the i th DBH  class (mL ), Mi   is the number of trees for the selected i th DBH  class; and As   is the sample plot area (m2 ). Since the observations of Eos   by the CWB  method are event-based, this study cross-validated the total Eos   for the growing seasons of 2021 and 2022.    2.5 Statistical analyses In this study, the univariate regression analysis was used to evaluate the bivariate relationships between environmental factors and ET  components. Then, multiple linear regression (MLR ) was employed to determine and assess the integrated effects of key environmental factors on ET  components. Before constructing the MLR  model, the collinearity diagnostics were used to assess the collinearities among significant variables in IBM SPSS 24.0 statistics software (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). The significant level was set as 0.05.   3 Results 3.1 Validations of the uWUE  method for partitioning ET  and ETu   As shown in Fig. 3  a, the daily Tos   obtained from sap flow measurements and the uWUE  method showed a good agreement with the coefficient of determination (R2 ) of 0.91 (slope = 0.95, p  < 0.001). In addition, the differences in Eos   obtained from the uWUE  and CWB  methods were only 7.3 % in 2021 and 4.9 % in 2022, respectively (Fig. 3 b). These results indicate that the estimations of T , Tos  , Tu  , E , Eos  , and Eu   from the uWUE  method are robust and can be used for further analysis in this study. Thus, the relative contributions of each component to ET  can be estimated in the growing seasons of 2020 to 2022 in the study site (Step 5 in Fig. 2 ).  3.2 The dynamics of ET  and its components from the proposed framework Fig. 4   shows that the dynamics of daily ET  and its components were closely related to variations in LAI  during the growing season. Daily T  increased since the beginning of the growing season, with the peak values in the middle of the growing season, and then decreased to relatively low levels at the end of the growing season. Conversely, the variations in daily Tu   remained relatively stable. The daily values of T  and Tu   ranged from 0.2 to 2.1 mm and 0.1 to 0.6 mm (based on a 7-day moving average), with average daily values of 1.0 ± 0.6 and 0.2 ± 0.1 mm (mean ± standard deviation), respectively. Similarly, the temporal patterns observed in daily E  and Eu   were consistent with those of T  and Tu  . The daily values of E  and Eu   ranged from 0.3 to 2.3 mm and 0.1 to 1.0 mm (based on a 7-day moving average), with average daily values of 1.2 ± 0.6 and 0.5 ± 0.2 mm, respectively. Furthermore, the daily values of ET  and ETu   exhibited increasing trends from May to July, followed by consistent decreases from August to September. The daily values of ET  and ETu   ranged from 0.6 to 3.7 mm and 0.3 to 1.2 mm (based on a 7-day moving average), with the average daily values of 2.2 ± 0.9 and 0.7 ± 0.3 mm, respectively.  3.3 T , E , and ET  partitioning 3.3.1 T  partitioning As shown in Fig. 5  a, monthly Tos   and Tu   varied during the growing season from May to September, with ranges of 8.2 to 34.1 mm and 3.8 to 8.2 mm, respectively. The highest monthly Tos   and Tu   were observed in July and June, respectively. Furthermore, the contributions of monthly Tos   and Tu   to T  ranged from 61.8 to 80.5 % and 18.5 to 38.2 %, respectively (Fig. 5 a). The highest contribution of monthly Tos   to T  occurred in July, while the largest contribution of Tu   to T  was observed in September. At the annual scale, total Tos   and Tu   during the growing seasons of 2020 to 2022 were 96.6, 108.0, and 124.4 mm, and 31.2, 33.0, and 26.3 mm, with average values of 109.7 ± 14.0 and 30.2 ± 3.5 mm, respectively (Fig. 5 b). The average contributions of Tos   and Tu   to T  for the whole study period were 78.2 ± 3.8 and 21.8 ± 3.8 %, respectively (Fig. 5 b). These findings indicate that Tu   plays an important role in T  and should not be ignored.  3.3.2 E  partitioning At the monthly scale, monthly Eos   and Eu   varied from 13.9 to 32.3 mm and 8.6 to 20.5 mm during the study period, respectively (Fig. 5 c). The highest amounts of Eos   and Eu   were both observed in July, while the lowest amounts occurred in May. The contributions of monthly Eos   and Eu   to E  ranged from 51.0 to 61.3 % and 38.7 to 49.0 %, respectively (Fig. 5 c). At the annual scale, the contributions of Eu   and Eos   to E  were relatively stable compared to those at the monthly scale (Fig. 5 d). Specifically, the contributions of Eu   and Eos   to E  were 34.6, 44.4, and 44.4 %, and 65.4, 55.6, and 55.6 % during the growing seasons of 2020, 2021, and 2022, respectively (Fig. 5 d). The average contributions of Eos   and Eu   to E  during the whole study period were 58.8 ± 5.7 and 41.2 ± 5.7 %, respectively (Fig. 5 d). These findings indicate that Eu   is a key contributor to E .  3.3.3 ET  partitioning At the monthly scale (Fig. 5 e), the amounts of ET , ETu  , and ETos   were relatively lower in May, and then maintained higher amounts from June to August. Eventually, the amounts decreased in September. In terms of the relative contributions, ETos  /ET  varied from 59.8 to 70.2 %, while ETu  /ET  varied from 29.8 to 40.2 %. The highest contribution of monthly ETu   to ET  occurred in September, while the lowest contribution of ETu   to ET  was observed in July. At the annual scale (Fig. 5 f), the contributions of ETu   and ETos   to ET  were 29.9, 35.5, and 32.3 %, and 70.1, 64.5, and 67.7 % during the growing seasons of 2020, 2021, and 2022, respectively (Fig. 5 f). The average contributions of ETu   and ETos   to ET  during the whole study period were 32.6 ± 2.8 and 67.4 ± 2.8 %, respectively (Fig. 5 f).  3.3.4 Relative contributions of each component to ET  Table 1   displays how ET  was partitioned into Tos  , Tu  , Eos  , and Eu   at the monthly and annual scales. At the monthly scale, the contributions of each component to ET  were considerably different. In May, June, and July, Tos   contributed the most to ET , accounting for 37.9, 44.8, and 35.9 %, respectively. In August and September, Eos   had the largest contributions to ET  compared to other components, with values of 37.2 and 37.7 %, respectively. Although Tu   had the lowest contribution to ET  during the growing season, its average contribution was 9.8 ± 1.6 %. The average contribution of Eu   to ET  was 23.4 ± 3.0 % from May to September. At the annual scale, the contributions of Tos  , Tu  , Eos  , and Eu   to ET  varied from year to year (Table 1 ). The contributions of Tos   to ET  for the growing seasons of 2020 to 2022 were 34.7, 32.5, and 37.0 %, respectively, with an average contribution of 34.7 ± 2.3 %. Similarly, the contributions of Eos   to ET  were 35.4 % in 2020, 32.0 % in 2021, and 30.7 % in 2022, with an average contribution of 32.7 ± 2.4 %. Furthermore, the contributions of Eu   and Tu   to ET  varied from 18.7 to 25.6 % and 7.8 to 11.2 %, respectively, during three growing seasons.   3.4 Controlling factors of ETu   and its components Based on our estimations (Fig. 5 ), the understory ecosystem played a non-negligible role in ET  in the study boreal forest. From the univariate relationships (Fig. 6  ), daily Eu   exhibited significant (p  < 0.05) and positive correlations with Ta  , SWC , LAI , and SR . Conversely, it showed a significant (p  < 0.05) and negative relationship with Ws   (Fig. 6 b). Daily ETu   increased significantly (p  < 0.05) with increasing Ta  , VPD , SWC , LAI , and SR , while it significantly decreased (p  < 0.05) with P  (Fig. 6 e). Daily Tu   displayed significant relationships (p  < 0.05) with all selected environmental factors (Fig. 6 ). For the ratios of individual components (Fig. 7  ), the bivariate relationships revealed that Ta   and P  were the significant (p  < 0.05) influential factors of daily Eu  /E  with positive contributions. Conversely, VPD , SWC , and SR  exerted significant and negative influences on daily Eu  /E . Ta  , VPD , SWC , LAI , and SR  exhibited significant (p  < 0.05) and negative effects on daily Tu  /T , but it was significantly and positively corrected with P . Additionally, Ta  , Ws  , LAI , and SR  were contributing factors that significantly (p  < 0.05) and negatively correlated with daily ETu  /ET . In addition, the MLR  model was used to identify and evaluate the key environmental factors affecting individual components and their respective ratios. Collinearity diagnostics suggested no significant collinearities among key environmental variables (Tables S3 to S8 ), confirming the reliability and robustness of the MLR  model. As shown in Table 2  , the MLR  results showed that 47 % of the variations in daily Tu   were explained by SR , Ta  , and LAI . Similarly, SR , SWC , LAI , and VPD  collectively explained 34 % of the variations in daily Eu  . Moreover, 62 % of the variations in daily ETu   were explained by SR , Ta  , SWC , LAI , and Ws  . Furthermore, the explained variance of key environmental factors on individual components exceeded that of their respective ratios (Table 2 ). Specifically, P , Ta  , SR , and LAI  jointly explained 17 % of the variations in daily Tu  /T . SWC , LAI , P, Ws  , VPD , and Ta   explained 15 % of the variations in daily Eu  /E . Additionally, 25 % of the variations in daily ETu  /ET  were explained by SWC , VPD , Ta  , Ws  , and LAI . These findings indicated that LAI  and SR  are key factors influencing ETu   and its components, while LAI  serves as a key factor affecting their respective ratios.   4 Discussion 4.1 Methodological improvements for ET  partitioning The EC  system is the most effective technique to directly and continuously measure ET  at the ecosystem level (Paul-Limoges et al., 2020 ). Applying concurrent EC  systems provides a unique advantage in effectively capturing the dynamics of carbon and water fluxes in the understory ecosystem and the entire ecosystem, which can greatly improve our understanding of ET  in both overstory and understory ecosystems. However, the concurrent EC  systems cannot be used to measure the ETu   components or ET  partitioning. In this study, we employed a framework combining the concurrent EC  systems and the uWUE  method to partition ET  and ETu   into T  and E , and Tu   and Eu   in a boreal larch forest in China. The cross-validations indicate that the results are robust. However, the limitations of the proposed ET  partitioning framework should be noted. Firstly, although this study successfully partitioned E  into Eos   and Eu  , and T  into Tos   and Tu  , it is limited to further distinguish soil evaporation. However, previous studies have indicated the minimal (Wilson et al., 2001 ) or negligible proportion (Grelle et al., 1999 ) of soil evaporation in natural boreal forests due to the presence of dense surface vegetation. Secondly, the water flux of the understory ecosystem affected by the decoupling effects may be more complex than previously thought. Additional factors should be taken into account in future studies to better assess the applicability of the uWUE  method in the understory ecosystem. To validate the ET  partitioning, we further applied measured sap flow data for Tos   and the CWB  method for Eos   to validate Tos   and Eos   from the uWUE  method (Fig. 3 ). The validation indicates that the partitioning of ET  using the uWUE  method is reliable and robust (R2  = 0.91, slope = 0.95, and differences are less than 7.5 %) (Fig. 3 ). Thus, we conclude that the proposed framework provides an effective and reliable tool to quantify ET  and its components in the study forest ecosystems where concurrent EC  systems can be installed in both understory and overstory layers of forest ecosystems. However, there may be some uncertainties in the cross-validation results. For example, the canopy surface from wetting to drying has a significant time lag following rainfall events. However, the canopy evaporation measurements using the CWB  method in this study did not account for the time lag. As a result, the duration of canopy wetness was ignored, leading to a possible level of uncertainty in the cross-validation between the CWB  and uWUE  methods. Meanwhile, in this study, we observed that the corrected Tos   was higher (27.2 %) than those derived from uncorrected sap flow measurements (Fig. S7 ). However, it is noted that the changes in sapwood water content (Vergeynst et al., 2014 ), long-term wounding or signal dampening (Marañón-Jiménez et al., 2018; Peters et al., 2018; Wiedemann et al., 2013 ), and differences in zero-flow determination or baselining (Peters et al., 2018 ) may also disrupt sap flow measurements. Future studies should consider further calibrations of Tos   and Eos   in research design processes (Fuchs et al., 2017 ).  4.2 The variations in ETu   and its components In this study, our results showed that the temporal patterns of daily and monthly Tu  , Eu  , and ETu   displayed similar trends, characterized by an initial increasing trend followed by a subsequent decrease (Figs. 4 to 5 ). These results are consistent with the previous studies conducted in boreal forests (Iida et al., 2009; Brown et al., 2014; Hadiwijaya et al., 2021 ). For instance, Iida et al. (2009)  found that the dynamics of ETu   exhibited an initial increase and then a decrease from May to September. Additionally, ETu   ranged from 0.3 to 1.2 mm, with a mean value of 0.7 ± 0.3 mm/day over the study period (Fig. 4 ). The estimation is consistent with the previous study by Black et al. (1996) . However, relatively higher daily mean ETu   values of 0.9 and 1.6 mm in boreal forests were observed by Iida et al., (2009)  and Brown et al. (2014) , respectively. The differences in ETu   may be attributed to variations in stand density and precipitation regimes. In our study, the stand density and mean precipitation amount were 1250 trees ha −1  and 452.5 mm, respectively, which were higher than those reported by Iida et al., (2009)  and Brown et al. (2014) . Lower stand density and precipitation levels can lead to more energy and light reaching the understory ecosystem, thereby enhancing ETu   (Bodo et al., 2023 ). Conversely, Paul-Limoges et al. (2020)  reported a daily value of ETu   below 0.7 mm/day, which was lower compared to the present study. One possible reason could be the denser understory vegetation and greater species diversity at our study site. Furthermore, in the present study, the mean Tu   and Eu   were 0.2 mm/day and 0.5 mm/day over the study period, respectively (Fig. 4 ), with Eu   being higher than Tu  . The differences in site-specific conditions mentioned above may lead to different variations in the partitioning of ETu   into Tu   and Eu  . For instance, Yepez et al. (2003)  found that Tu   plays a similar role as Eu  . These findings revealed the complexity of variations in ETu   and its components across the different sites. Thus, more research is needed to deepen our understanding of ETu   partitioning.  4.3 ET partitioning 4.3.1 The contributions of ETu   and its components in water fluxes Our result shows that Tu   contributes 21.8 % to T , while Eu   contributes 41.2 % to E  (Fig. 5 a to 5d), suggesting that ignoring Tu   would underestimate T  in boreal forest ecosystems and Eu   is a key contributor to E . However, there are limited studies that have evaluated the Tu  /T  and Eu  /E  in forest ecosystems. For instance, Wullschleger et al. (2001)  revealed that the Tu   accounted for 17 % of total transpiration in a mixed forest, which was lower than for our study. The possible reasons for this could be the canopy structure (e.g., the closure of the canopy) (Bodo et al., 2023 ) and tree species composition of the overstory (Balandier et al., 2022 ), as well as the understory vegetation density and types (Iida et al., 2009 ). In this study, there are diverse understory vegetation types, including shrubs, herbaceous plants, and mosses, which cover the entire plot (Fig. 1 ). Understory ecosystem with diverse species has a pronounced contribution of Tu   and Eu  through more competitive of these species for water resources (Balandier et al., 2006a; Balandier et al., 2022 ) and more rainfall interception owing to their mass and water holding capacity (Aussenac, 2000; Wilson et al., 2000; Balandier et al., 2006b; Landuyt et al., 2019 ). For example, Zagyvai-Kiss et al. (2019)  reported that the water-holding capacity of litter can exceed 200 % of its weight for spruce, beech, and sessile oak. Moreover, Price et al. (1997)  highlighted a considerable contribution of the moss layer to water balance, as it intercepted approximately 21 % of rainfall in boreal forests. A high water-holding capacity of litter suggests that it has a greater ability to retain and store substantial amounts of water, which is the source of Eu  . Thus, it is reasonable that boreal forests have relatively greater Tu  /T  and Eu  /E  as compared with other biomes. Unfortunately, many previous studies have ignored the role of understory vegetation in hydrological processes, and they often assumed Tos   (or Eos  ) as T  (or E ) (Raz-Yaseef et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2021 ). While such an assumption may be reasonable in some vegetation types, our results from this study clearly suggested that understory vegetation must be taken into consideration when constructing ecosystem water flux models in boreal forests. In addition to the contributions of Tu   and Eu  , our study found that the average contribution of ETu   to ET  was 32.6 % (Fig. 5 f), highlighting that more attention should be paid than before to manage the understory ecosystem in our study area. We also found large variations in ETu   ranging from 10 to 85 % globally (Kelliher, et al., 1997; Iida et al., 2020; Balandier et al., 2022 ). For example, Kelliher et al. (1998)  found the short-term contribution of ETu   to ET  was 54 % during the 18-day study period in mid-summer in a central Siberian pine forest. Conversely, Constantin et al. (1999)  reported that the contribution of ETu   to ET  was only 10 % from 4 June to 23 June in a boreal spruce/pine forest. Furthermore, Iida et al. (2020)  reported that the contribution of ETu   to ET  was relatively stable and ranged between 15 and 20 % when the overstory LAI  was greater than 4 m2 /m2  in boreal forests. Such large variations in ETu   to ET  may be caused by the differences in spatiotemporal scales, understory vegetation compositions, canopy structures of overstory, and research methods (Kozii et al., 2020; Balandier et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2023 ).  4.3.2 The contributions of Tos   and Eos   to ET  Interestingly, we found that the contributions of Tos   and Eos   to ET  during the study period were similar, accounting for 34.7 and 32.7 %, respectively (Table 1 ). This finding suggests an equivalent role of Tos   and Eos   in regulating forest water balance in the study site, which is different from the general perception that the contribution of Tos   to ET  is higher than that of Eos   to ET  (Iida et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2015; Hadiwijaya et al., 2021a; Kozii et al., 2020; Paul-Limoges et al., 2020 ). However, our finding is consistent with some studies (Hadiwijaya et al., 2021b; Sabater et al., 2020 ). For example, Lin et al. (2012)  found that Eos   (75 % of ET ) was significantly higher than Tos   (19 % of ET ) in a coniferous subalpine forest. They inferred that such a high contribution of Eos   to ET  was caused by rainfall characteristics (low rainfall amount, low rainfall intensity, and long rainfall duration), night rainfall ratios, and abundant epiphytes on trees, which considerably influence the interception and evaporation processes in less disturbed or natural forests. The similar contributions of Tos   and Eos   to ET  in this study might be related to forest structure characteristics. The stand age of Larix gmelinii  ranged from 75 to 90 years in our study site, representing a mature stand (Xu et al., 2022 ). Many studies have indicated that the transpiration capacity of mature stands was lower compared to young stands (Dunn and Connor, 1993; Vertessy et al., 2001; Roberts et al., 2001; Forrester et al., 2010 ). For instance, Delzon and Loustau (2005)  demonstrated a significant decrease in Tos   with increasing stand ages in pine forests. Possible reasons for this include decreased stomatal conductance (i.e., leaf-specific hydraulic limitation), sap velocity, sapwood area growth rates, and the ratio of leaf area to sapwood area with stand development (Delzon et al., 2004; Forrester et al., 2010 ). Additionally, due to the energy limitation in high-latitude regions, relatively short growing seasons, and significant canopy phenology patterns (Fig. 4 ), Tos   is constrained, and thus, lower contribution to ET  in boreal forests. In addition, the wet climate during the study period tends to be another factor that contributes to the similar contributions of To  s  and Eos   to ET . The growing seasons had abundant rainfall, especially in 2021 and 2022 with the rainfall amounts of 557.9 and 443.9 mm, respectively (Table S2 ). They were greatly higher than the long-term average (370.5 mm from 1984 to 2017, data from Mohe meteorological station, ID 50136) in the study site. Excessive rainfall might limit Tos   (Xu et al., 2023 ), but increases Eos   due to more canopy interception, and consequently suppresses the contribution of Tos   to ET  while increasing the role of Eos   to ET .   4.4 Controlling mechanisms of ETu   components and their respective ratios The MLR  results demonstrate strong interactions between key environmental factors and ETu   components (Table 2 ). For individual components, Eu   was significantly influenced by LAI , SR , SWC , and VPD . Tu   was affected by LAI , SR , and Ta  , while ETu   was influenced by LAI , SR , Ws  , SWC , and Ta  . Overstory LAI  and SR  affect Tu  , Eu  , and ETu   (Table 2 ). These findings not only underscore significant disparities in the control mechanisms among individual components but also reveal similarities in these control mechanisms. Previous studies have demonstrated that SR  and overstory LAI  play significant roles in promoting transpiration and evaporation by increasing atmospheric evaporative demand and photosynthetic capacity (Oogathoo et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2022 ). Despite the use of overstory LAI , the canopy phenology of the understory is synchronized in the study site (Fig. S1 ). Furthermore, as SR  increase, more energy reaches the forest floor (Wang et al., 2018 ), thereby enhancing Tu   and Eu  , and consequently affecting ETu   (Fig. 6  and Table 2 ). Additionally, the differences in the control mechanisms are likely because transpiration and evaporation processes are controlled by different mechanisms: transpiration is influenced by physiological regulation, while evaporation is affected by physical regulation (Paul-Limoges et al., 2020 ). However, changes in ETu   depend on the differences in sensitivities between Tu   and Eu   to environmental factors. For Eu  /E , Tu  /T , and ETu  /ET , we found that overstory LAI  consistently dominates changes in Eu  /E , Tu  /T , and ETu  /ET  in this study (Table 2 ). Although previous studies have shown that overstory LAI  plays a critical role in ETu  /ET  across different forest ecosystems (Schmidt-Walter et al., 2014; Iida et al., 2020; Balandier et al., 2022 ), limited studies investigated the Eu  /E  and Tu  /T . Overstory LAI  significantly and indirectly influences understory microclimates such as Ta  , Ws  , SWC , and VPD  (Hardwick et al., 2015; De Frenne et al., 2021 ). For example, overstory LAI  directly affects the absorption of radiation by leaves, alters the availability of energy and light, and influences heat retention in the understory ecosystem (Iida et al., 2009, Balandier et al., 2022 ), thus affecting the changes in Eu  /E , Tu  /T , and ETu  /ET . Furthermore, a denser forest canopy amplifies the differences in Ta   and VPD  between below and above the forest canopy (Hardwick et al., 2015; Gaudio et al., 2017; Prévosto et al., 2020; De Frenne et al., 2021 ), particularly in the daily maximum and minimum values of these microclimate variables in the understory (Balandier et al., 2022 ), consequently influencing Eu  /E , Tu  /T , and ETu  /ET . In addition, the explained variance of key environmental factors on individual components exceeded that of their respective ratios (Table 2 ). One possible reason is the complex interactions between overstory and understory water fluxes. As shown in Fig. 5 , the results indicate that the quantities of Tu  , Eu  , ETu  , and Tos  , Eos  , ETos   follow a consistent pattern. However, there are opposing ratio relationships during the growing season. During the early growth stage (in May), the overstory vegetation is in the leaf-expanding stage with relatively low transpiration capacity (Xu et al., 2022 ) (Fig. 4 ), while the soil thawing process at the study site significantly increased soil liquid water with rising temperatures, effectively increasing the contribution of Eu   to E , thus ETu   to ET . During the mid-growth stage (June to August) when canopy leaves are fully expanded, although Tu   and Eu   are constrained by the buffering effect of the overstory canopy, they also increase with increasing Ta   and LAI  (Fig. 8  ) due to the limited buffering effect, albeit to a lesser extent compared to the Tos   and Eos  . These changes result in lower contributions from Tu  , Eu  , and ETu  . However, during the late growth stage (September), leaves defoliate, turn yellow, and lose their physiological functions, and thus Tos   significantly decreases. In contrast, due to the increased light, energy, and water (i.e., SR ), the proportion of ETu   and its components during the late growing season greatly increases. Thus, these traits significantly influence Tu  /T , Eu  /E , and ETu  /ET  in the study site. Although this study identified significant factors driving the individual components and their respective ratios, the current factors may not adequately explain changes in the dependent variables (e.g., Tu  /T , Eu  /E , and ETu  /ET ). The environmental factors selected in the present study are primarily based on meteorological data related to physical processes, and have not fully considered the changes in biological factors, such as canopy conductance. This limitation constrains the interpretation of environmental influences on ET  and its components. Furthermore, the relative impacts of these factors may vary depending on specific forest types, climatic conditions, and geographical locations, all of which influence understory, overstory, and their interaction. Future research should focus on the co-driving mechanisms of environmental and biological controls on ET  components and their respective ratios.   5 Conclusions A framework incorporating concurrent EC  systems and the uWUE  method was employed to partition ET  for overstory, understory, and entire ecosystems in a natural boreal forest in this study. Tu   contributed to 21.8 % of T , Eu   accounted for 41.2 % of E , and ET u  was 32.6 % of ET , suggesting that the contribution of understory vegetation is non-negligible in forest hydrological processes in the study region. SR  and overstory LAI  influence ET u  components and their respective ratios. This highlight similarities in control mechanisms. We conclude that both overstory and understory vegetation must be considered when designing management and protection strategies for hydrological functions in boreal forested watersheds. We also conclude that concurrent EC  systems are not only an effective way to accurately quantify water flux in multi-layered forests but also are critical for assessing water use efficiency and carbon–water coupling in the context of climate change if long-term observations are available.
1 Introduction Hydrologic exchanges fluxes (HEF) at the riverbeds, which mix the groundwater and river water, supply nutrients and substrates that drive biogeochemical reactions (Boano, Harvey et al. 2014, Cardenas 2015, Gomez-Velez, Harvey et al. 2015, Harvey and Gooseff 2015 ). The HEFs significantly impact the time interval between the river water flowing into the subsurface domain and then flowing back into river, which is defined as residence time (RT). The RT and corresponding RT distributions (RTD) of the HEFs have been widely used as a master variable to evaluate the biochemical potential of groundwater-river water mixing (Boano, Demaria et al. 2010, Zarnetske, Haggerty et al. 2011, Harvey, Bohlke et al. 2013, Briggs, Lautz et al. 2014, Gomez-Velez, Harvey et al. 2015 ). Directly measuring these HEFs and RTDs in large-scale natural rivers is extremely challenging (Harvey, Wagner et al. 1996, Gooseff and McGlynn 2005, Payn, Gooseff et al. 2008 ). A practical approach to quantify the HEFs and RTDs in large-scale natural rivers is using the on-site measurements of surface water and in-land well groundwater elevations to calibrate and validate a surface–subsurface water transport model, and utilize the validated model to estimate the HEFs, RT, and corresponding RTDs (Hwang, Park et al. 2014, Zhang, Tejada-Martinez et al. 2014, Tian, Zheng et al. 2015, Shuai, Chen et al. 2019 ). Many pioneering works have demonstrated and reported the modeling approaches for quantifying HEFs and RTDs focusing on one-dimensional (1D) and two-dimensional (2D) numerical scheme (Saint-Venant 1871, Perkins and Richmond 2004, Banda and Seaid 2012, Chen, Murakami et al. 2012, Chen, Glenn et al. 2013 ). Recently, Tripathi et al. (2021)  provided a systematic review on the popular models and the applications in three-dimensional (3D) modeling scheme, such as MODFLOW (Ghysels, Mutua et al. 2019, Zhang, Schmidt et al. 2021 ), HydroGeoSphere (Batlle-Aguilar, Xie et al. 2015, Xiang, Jin et al. 2017 ), HYDRUS-2D/3D (Phogat, Potter et al. 2017 ), PARAFLOW (Frei, Fleckenstein et al. 2009 ), etc. For computational efficiency, most of surface–subsurface water models only considered the surface water depth induced pressure on the riverbed as the driving force. However, laboratory-scale experiments and modeling have demonstrated that the near riverbed flow profile induced hydrodynamic pressure could lead to enhanced subsurface flow transport and may influence the RTDs (Endreny, Lautz et al. 2011, Endreny, Lautz et al. 2011, Sawyer, Cardenas et al. 2011, Zhou and Endreny 2013, Song, Chen et al. 2019 ). In our previous work (Bao, Zhou et al. 2018 , Bao, Chen et al. 2022 ), we developed a modeling framework that couples a 3D transient surface river modeling approach (Chen, Bao et al. 2022 ) with the PFLOTRAN (Hammond, Lichtner et al. 2014, Bisht, Huang et al. 2017, Lichtner, Hammond et al. 2017 ) subsurface transport model and particle-tracking model (Pollock 1994 ). This modeling framework considered both hydrostatic and hydrodynamic pressure on the riverbed as the driving force to influence the surface–subsurface water exchange. The simulation results have been validated with on-site water surface elevation, Doppler current profiler (ADCP) measurements for velocity (Niehus, Perkins et al. 2014 , Chen, Bao et al. 2022 ), and in-land groundwater table for a 10-km river section over 3-year period in our previous work (Bao, Chen et al. 2022 ). Our previous study shows that considering the hydrodynamic pressure slightly lower groundwater level (10 cm on average), which is more consistent with the in-land well observation data. The model validations for the investigated domains in this study are discussed in Section 3.1 . Although transient models can provide a better representation of subsurface flow transport and the associated RTDs of HEFs, it is computationally demanding, so developing a more computationally efficient approach to estimate RTDs is in demand. Hou et al. (2021)  introduced an unsupervised classification approach to divide the investigated river section into seven hydromorphic units (HUs), which is considered as the clustering of bathymetry and surface water hydrodynamic attributes. Additionally, it was demonstrated, through a preliminary modeling test in a small testing area (6 x 6 km), that the river water entering the subsurface domain through the riverbed patches belonging to different HUs provides different RTDs. This indicates that a distinctive relationship possibly links RTDs to HUs. This HU-RTD inferring approach can be considered as an extension of the underlying concept of the NEXSS model that incorporates a greater degree of mechanistic representation (Gomez-Velez and Harvey 2014 ), and could significantly reduce computation time and accelerate the study of biogeochemical reactions in large-scale river reaches. However, this possible HU-RTD model contradicts to some of the pioneering studies. For example, Pujades et al. (2012)  studied the impact of underground semi-permeable barriers on natural hydraulic head gradient in the aquifer. Gomez-Velez et al. (2013)  studied the effect of low-permeability layers on HEFs. Font-Capo et al. (2015)  applied numerical model to show the impact caused by underground impermeable constructions in aquifers. Jing et al. (2023)  demonstrated that the underground barrier plays dominant role in RTDs through both benchmark testing problems and two practical sites. This indicates that without considering the underground structure and properties, it is hard to estimate the subsurface water transport and the associated RTD accurately. In addition, large-scale channel geomorphology also plays a critical role in HEFs. Extensive researches have been reported to show the influence of river meander and sinuosity on HEFs (Wroblicky, Campana et al. 1998, Cardenas 2008, Revelli, Boano et al. 2008, Cardenas 2009a, Cardenas 2009b, Gomez-Velez, Wilson et al. 2012, Gomez-Velez, Harvey et al. 2015, Balbarini, Boon et al. 2017, Gomez-Velez, Wilson et al. 2017, Dwivedi, Steefel et al. 2018, Gonzalez-Duque, Gomez-Velez et al. 2024 ). This indicates that short-distance bathymetry topography attributes, such as slope, aspect (direction of maximum slope), and concavity, which are considered in HUs, are not sufficient to infer HEFs and RTDs accurately. Therefore, the contradiction is whether the HUs map, which only considers bathymetry and surface water dynamics, is sufficient to construct a general relationship to estimate RTDs for any river section, or if the underground structure and large-scale channel geomorphology also need to be considered. This is equivalent to the persistent challenge with most regression models i.e., whether the relationship between the RTDs and HUs identified for one river section remains valid for another. To address this contradiction, this work compared HU-RTD relationships for two 10-km long river sections leveraging the framework we previously developed. The first river section is the one described in Chen et al. (2022)  located at Hanford 100-H Area. The second section is located at Hanford 300 Area, 30-km downstream of the 100-H Area. By applying such a framework at the two selected river sections with similar HUs, we compared RTDs to gain insights into the transferability question of the regression models. Using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (K-S test) (Daniel 1990, Dimitrova, Kaishev et al. 2020 ) and supervised random forest classifications (Ho 1995, Ho 1998 ), we quantitatively proved that the likelihood of transferability of the HU-RTD regression model is extreme low. This means that the existence of general algorithm that can estimate the subsurface water RTDs only according to the easily-accessible surface water hydrodynamics and the short-distance river channel topography data may be nearly impossible. This also confirms the widely accepted understanding that the underground structure and large-scale channel geomorphology are still the dominant factors that control the subsurface water transport and the associated RTDs. The detailed results are discussed in Section 3 .  2 Study domain and methodology 2.1 Study domain The two investigated domains are both located along the Columbia River, which is the largest river in the Pacific Northwest region of the United States and the total drainage area is around 668,000 km2  extending into seven U.S. states and one Canadian province. The Columbia River section in Washington State is shown in Fig. 1  (a). One zoomed in area of the Columbia River section is shown in Fig. 1 (b), which flows through the U. S. Department of Energy Hanford Site and known as Hanford Reach. The two study domains with the bathymetry and ground elevation are shown in Fig. 1 (c) and (d). The two domains are known as Hanford 100-H Area (Fig. 1 (c)) and 300 Area (Fig. 1 (d)). The red block is the domain for OpenFOAM (OpenCFD 2017 ) river water modeling, and the yellow block is the domain for PFLOTRAN (Hammond, Lichtner et al. 2014, Bisht, Huang et al. 2017, Lichtner, Hammond et al. 2017 ) subsurface water and transport modeling. For the Hanford 100-H Area (Fig. 1 (c)), the river section in the red block is about 30 km long, and the subsurface and particle tracking modeling focuses on the 6 km × 7.5 km domain (yellow block). There are six onsite measuring locations (named as 100-B, 100-N, 100-D, Locke Island (LI), 100-H, and 100-F) in Hanford 100-H Area study domain to record the river water surface elevation (WSE), which were used for the river water modeling calibrations and validations as demonstrated in our previous work (Bao, Chen et al. 2022 , Chen, Bao et al. 2022 ). We also have velocity measurements with ADCPs at 12 cross-sections for velocity validations in Hanford 100-H Area. For the Hanford 300 Area (Fig. 1 (d)), the river section in the red block is also about 30 km, and the subsurface modeling and particle tracking focuses on the 7 km × 5 km domain (yellow block). There are many in-land wells in both areas to record the water table variations, which were used for validating the proposed surface–subsurface water transport model framework. The validation is discussed in Section 3.1 . The bathymetry and ground elevation used for the proposed modeling framework (shown in Fig. 1 (c) and (d)) are from the LiDAR (Cracknell and Hayes 2007 ) measured digital elevation model (DEM) combined with Columbia River bathymetry data (Coleman, Ward et al. 2010). The horizontal resolution is 1 m, and the vertical accuracy can reach 3–4 cm. More details about the equipment, methods of measurement and validation for the bathymetry and ground elevation data are available in Coleman (2009)  and Coleman et al. (2010) . The elevation is based on the North American Vertical Datum of 1988 (NAD88).  2.2 Subsurface water residence time simulation framework The RT is defined as the period that elapsed between the time water entered the riverbed and then exited back into the river channel. Numerical particles are used to track the movement of the subsurface water flow, and thus RT is defined as the period that elapsed between the time a particle entered the riverbed and then exited back into the river channel. In this study, the modeling approach for the subsurface water residence time needs three main steps, as illustrated by flowchart in Fig. 2  (a). The first step is the 3-dimsional multi-phase fluid dynamics model, which is used to simulate both the water and air phase for the investigated river section and solved by the open-source CFD package OpenFOAM. Based on our previous demonstration (Bao, Chen et al. 2022 ), hydrodynamic pressure in the proposed 3-dimsional multi-phase fluid dynamics model slightly lower groundwater level (10 cm on average), which is more consistent with the in-land well observation data in Hanford 100-H Area. Therefore, in this study, all the river surface water simulation is based on this model to get more accurate estimation of the exchange fluxes and the RT. The surface modeling domain is in the region defined by dotted lines, as shown in Fig. 2 (b). Pressure outlet boundary condition is applied on the side and top boundaries of the surface modeling domain as marked in Fig. 2 (b). The river surface-water cross section is shown in light blue, and the air above is depicted in light gray. The bottom boundary (riverbed) for the surface-water simulation domain is fluid non-slip boundary condition with calibrated surface roughness. More details about the calibration of surface roughness on the riverbed for the surface-water model is reported in our previous work (Bao, Chen et al. 2022 , Chen, Bao et al. 2022 ). The second step is the subsurface flow simulation by an open-source, state-of-the-art massively parallel subsurface flow and reactive transport code PFLOTRAN (Hammond, Lichtner et al. 2014, Bisht, Huang et al. 2017, Lichtner, Hammond et al. 2017 ). The subsurface domain is bounded by the solid black line in Fig. 2 (b). The dark blue area represents the saturated zone, and the dark gray area represents the unsaturated subsurface region. The land surface of the investigated area is barren land, with limited buildings. The atmospheric pressure boundary is applied on the dry soil surface, and precipitation is neglected. The four side walls boundary conditions (ambient groundwater) are derived from the reach-scale subsurface simulation (Shuai, Chen et al. 2019 ). The bottom boundary for the two investigated domain is 30 m deep, and it is in the low permeability zone, so no flux boundary is assumed as marked in Fig. 2 (b). For the top boundary (riverbed) of subsurface domain, we used the hourly total pressure (p t    ) and volume fraction of water distribution (α   ) on the riverbed, extracted from surface water simulation, to assign the total pressure as boundary conditions for PFLOTRAN riverbed cells that have surface water on top (assuming α > 0.8). More detailed explanation about the proposed subsurface flow simulation configuration and solver is introduced in our previous work (Bao, Chen et al. 2022 ). The third step is the classical semi-analytical particle-tracking scheme (Pollock 1994 ) to simulate the hydrological exchange pathways. This forward particle-tracking scheme imports the subsurface flow field from the PFLOTRAN simulation results from the second step as the driving force, and tracks particles from one cell to the next until the particle satisfies a termination criterion (e.g., a particle reaches a model boundary or the vadose zone) as the sketch shows in Fig. 2 (b). To reduce the sensitivity of results to the spatial and temporal sampling, totally 100 million numerical particles were released from 100 thousand locations on the riverbed over 1000 times from October 2013 to October 2014. We conducted convergence tests to ensure that the number of released particles were large enough to provide consistent results. The modeling framework considered the overall hydrological exchanges between the river water and the surrounding area in the modeling domain. There is part of the water exchanges in the hyporheic zone, but most of the river water can carry the particles leave river, travel a few hundred meters to a few kilometers away from the riverbed where it enters the subsurface domain. The water and the particles can stay in the groundwater over a few hundred days until the low river stage period, that pull the groundwater back to river. The particle traveling paths are discussed in Section 3.2 . The modeling strategy therefore is a one-way coupling approach because fluxes on the riverbed do not feed back into the surface flow region. The strategy is based on the assumption that the magnitude of the HEF volumetric flux is negligible compared to the river discharge. For example, in Hanford 100-H Area river section, the averaged HEF volumetric flux is around 0.075 m3 /s while the river discharge is between 1000 and 7000 m3 /s (Chen, Bao et al. 2022 ). For the 300 Area river section, the velocity of the flow penetrate the riverbed is around 1 × 10  - 5      m/s or even slower, which is equivalent to 0.1 m3 /s HEF volumetric flux at the investigated domain (Bao, Zhou et al. 2018 ). Additionally, the two-way couple for the surface and subsurface flow simulation can be very computationally expensive, it is usually only applicable for small scale (less than 10 m) and fully saturated domain, which simplifies the simulation to single-phase flow simulation (Li, Liu et al. 2020 ).  2.3 OpenFOAM CFD for river Surface-Water simulations In this study, OpenFOAM (OpenCFD 2017 ), an open-source CFD software, was used to simulate multi-phase 3D transient river water flow. The numerical model solves the mass and momentum conservation equations for fluid dynamics and uses the volume-of-fluid method to track the water–air interface of the river flow. The transportation of the water–air interface is governed by a scalar field α which represents the fraction of liquid in each simulation grid cell (Hirt and Nichols 1981, Yazdi, Sarkardeh et al. 2010, Deshpande, Anumolu et al. 2012 ). The velocity of the fluid was solved using the time-averaged Navier-Stokes equation with the k-ω shear stress transport model (Reynolds 1895, Versteeg and Malaasekera 1995, Menter, Kuntz et al. 2003, Wilcox 2006, Liu, Ferng et al. 2012 ). The shear velocity near the solid surface (riverbed) was estimated according to turbulence boundary layer theory (Schlichting 1979 ). The inlet and outlet boundary conditions were derived from a previously calibrated cross-section averaged river model (1D Modular Aquatic Simulation System: MASS1) simulation (Richmond and Perkins 2009 ). The inlet and outlet velocity and water stage are shown in Fig. 3  (a) and (b) for Hanford 100-H Area and 300 Area respectively. The surface-water simulation domain is spatially discretized into 20 ×    20 ×    1 m meshes, where 20 m is in horizontal direction and 1 m is in vertical direction. Therefore, there are totally around 1 million grids for both 100-H and 300 Area surface water simulations. The transient river water model was calibrated using observation data from January 20 to February 16, 2011 (the short time interval between the two blue dash line in Fig. 3 ), and simulations for years 2013 to 2015 were used to generate the transient pressure and wetting information on the riverbed for subsurface flow transport simulations. More details about this 3D transient river water model have been introduced in our previous work (Bao, Chen et al. 2022 , Chen, Bao et al. 2022 ).  2.4 PFLOTRAN for subsurface flow and transport simulations PFLOTRAN is an open-source, parallel subsurface flow and reactive transport code used to model subsurface variably saturated flow (Hammond, Lichtner et al. 2014, Bisht, Huang et al. 2017, Lichtner, Hammond et al. 2017 ). The governing equations used in the code are based on Richard's equation (Richards 1931 ) and the relative permeability is estimated using van Genuchten capillary properties (Genuchten 1980 ). The finite volume discretization method is used to solve the governing equations. The riverbed boundary of the subsurface simulation domain is based on the total pressure and volume fraction of water at the riverbed imported from the surface river water model as introduced in Section 2.3 . More details about the PFLOTRAN subsurface simulation and coupling with the surface river water model have discussed in our previous work (Bao et al., 2022 ). The modeled subsurface domain includes four main soil types as shown in Fig. 4  . Four main soil types comprise the subsurface: Hanford, Taylor Flats, Ringold E, and Ringold LM. The permeability and porosity for these four soil types are listed in Table 1   (Newcomb and Brown 1961, Newcomb, Strand et al. 1972, Thorne, Williams et al. 2006, USDOE 2010, Zachara, Freshley et al. 2012 ). The subsurface-water simulation domain used the mesh resolution of 10 ×    10 ×    1 m, and there are totally about 15 million cells for the study domains. Some previous study has performed sensitivity analysis on the subsurface flow transport model at the similar investigated river sections, so this study directly adopted all the parameters, properties and model setups from Zachara et al. (2020)  work.  2.5 Particle-Tracking model for subsurface water transport To quantify the RTD, a classical semi-analytical particle-tracking scheme (Pollock 1994 ) was adopted to simulate the hydrological exchange pathways. To reduce the sensitivity of results to the spatial and temporal sampling, a large number of numerical particles (100 million) were released from 100 thousand locations on the riverbed and tracked over 1000 times from October 2013 to October 2014. The RTD was estimated by calculating the period between the time a particle entered the riverbed and the time it exited back into the river channel. The particle RTs were weighted by the fluxes corresponding to the location and time of release to estimate the cumulative RTD (CRTD), and the RTD was derived from the CRTD by taking the derivative. More details about the particle-tracking model and the RTD calculation have been introduced in our previous work (Bao et al., 2022 ).  2.6 Hydromorphic classifications Hydromorphic classification can serve as extrapolating results of detailed mechanistic models to large scales for system-scale prediction (Hou, Ren et al. 2021). The classification and the associated hydromorphic unites (HUs) considered various factors and mechanisms of the studied domain. The first category is bathymetric attributes, which include digital elevation from geographic information system (GIS) analysis (Mitchell and Minami 2020 ), slope, aspect (direction of maximum slope), and concavity. The second category is dynamic flow attributes, which include temporal statistical moments (e.g. mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis (NIST 2012 )) of velocity, river depth, and shear stress from 1917 to 2016 from the simulation results of Modular Aquatic Simulation System 2D simulator (MASS2) (Perkins and Richmond 2004 ). All these attributes were mapped on each grid of the investigated river sections. K-means clustering method was used to unsupervised classify the subset of the riverbed. Bayesian information criteria (BIC) were used to determine the optimal number of classes (Joliffe and Morgan 1992, Bradley, Fayyad et al. 1998 ). For the investigated domain, we selected the number of classes to be seven, and they are “Run”, “Fast glide”, “Pool”, “Slow glide”, “Riffle transition”, “Slack water”, and “Riffle”, which were interpreted from descriptors used in standard hydromorphic taxonomies (Wheaton, Fryirs et al. 2015 ). The HUs maps for the two investigated river sections 100-H and 300 areas are shown in Fig. 5  (a) and (b) respectively.  2.7 Random Forest classification model To further study the complex and non-linear relationship between surface water transport and RTs, Random Forest (RF) are developed using the same input parameters as the HUs classification work (Hou et al., 2021 ) as listed in Section 2.6 , and the simulated residence time as the output variable. RF is a tree-based ensemble supervised machine learning method which can be used for classification and regression problem (Breiman, Friedman et al. 2017 ). It works by constructing multiple decision trees during training process and outputs the majority vote (for classification) or average prediction (for regression) of the individual trees. Each tree is constructed using a different bootstrap sample of the training data, which is generated using the bootstrap aggregating (bagging) technique. In addition, a subset of predictor variables is randomly chosen to grow the tree at each node. Both the bagging and the random feature selection make RF robust to the inherent noise or outliers existing in the training data. In this work, due to the heavily skewed distribution of the output variable − residence time, we first take the log10 transformation of residence time and find the multi-modal distribution for residence time in both 100-H Area and 300 Area. To simplify the ML model setup, we then divide the residence time into three classes, which are short (<3 day), medium (>3 day and < 30 days), and long (>30 days). The histogram of the data distribution in the three classes are shown in Supplemental Information Fig. S1 . RF classification models are developed to construct the relationship between all the input parameters and the three residence time classes. Since the developed understanding or relationships for one study domain may have low transferability to other domains, we start with building the RF classification model separately for 100-H Area and 300 Area study domain. For each study domain, 80 % of the dataset are used for training, and the remaining 20 % of the dataset for model testing. Unlike other studies that use random splitting, the 80 % training data and 20 % testing dataset are spatially non-overlapped. For example, in 100 Area, the western portion, which is 80 % of the area, is the training data (NAD88 coordinate < 579500 m), while the eastern portion is testing data (NAD88 coordinate > 579500 m) as marked in Fig. 5 (a). Similarly, the northern portion of 300 Area is the testing data, and the southern portion is the training data as marked in Fig. 5 (b). The purpose of this splitting is to check within-domain transferability of the built ML models. The model trained by using random sampling with 80 % data for training and 20 % for testing provide better accuracy than the model trained with data split by spatial characteristics. However, even though the model with data random split performs better, it cannot adequately test the model’s ability to generalize to the entire spatial regions, or other new regions. The comparison of the two data splitting method has been added into Supplemental Information Fig. S2 . Prior to the training process, random searching is done in the hyperparameter tuning process to identify the optimal settings for RF classification model. The performance of the trained RF model was evaluated by using the precision, recall, F1 score, and balanced accuracy of each class calculated based on the confusion matrix (Grandini, Bagli et al. 2020 ): True positive (TP), True negative (TN), False positive (FP) and False negative (FN). TP and TN are the elements correctly classified by the model, while FP and FN are the elements that have been incorrectly labelled by the model. Precision uses the portion between TP and (TP+FP) to assess how reliable the RF model is at assigning positive events (i.e., short, medium, or long RTs) to the positive classes by comparing true positives with false positives across classes. Recall, the fraction between TP and (TP+FN), measures the RF model's predictive accuracy for the positive class. The F1 score, the weighted average between precision and recall, measures the relative contribution of precision and recall to a model’s accuracy. The balanced accuracy represents the overall correctness for each class by providing an average measure of recall and specificity, which is defined as the fraction between TN and (FP+TN).   3 Results 3.1 Model validation with in-land well observations The subsurface water transport model for the study domains has been validated with observations of the in-land well water level variations from 2013 to 2016. The locations of the in-land wells that used for validating the model are marked in Fig. 4 . The correlation coefficients and root mean square error (RMSE) between the model predictions and the observations were used to evaluate the accuracy of the model, which are shown in Fig. 4 (a) and (b). The correlation coefficients are marked in green color in Fig. 4 (a) and (b), and the RMSE with unit of meter are marked in orange color. The correlation coefficients at the most of in-land wells are higher than 0.9, which means that model can capture the realistic HEFs accurately. In Hanford 100-H Area, the correlation coefficient at one in-land well is 0.75. This may be caused by the heterogeneity of underground properties near this well, which was not well captured in the soil type distribution as discussed in Section 2.4 . In Hanford 300 Area, the correlation coefficient at one in-land well is 0.87, which potentially due to its location near the boundary of the simulation domain, though it is still can be considered as matching the observation data fairly good. The RMSEs between modeling results and observations for the water elevation at in-land wells in Hanford 300 Area are around 0.2 m, while RMSEs in Hanford 100-H Area are around 0.5 m. Therefore, the model accuracy is slightly better in Hanford 300 Area. The direct comparisons of the results data are shown in the scatter one–one plot in Fig. 4 (c) and (d) for Hanford 100-H and 300 Area respectively.  3.2 Particle tracking and RTD Using the transient subsurface water transport simulation results, we extracted all hourly subsurface flow velocity data and then imported it into the particle-tracking model as described in Section 2.5 . For both Hanford 100-H Area and 300 Area, numerical particles (100 million) were released from 100 thousand locations on the riverbed and tracked over 1000 times from October 2013 to October 2014 as shown in Fig. 6  (a). There are approximately 16.7 % and 7.5 % particles did not flow back to river in the simulation domain within the simulated time period (Jan 2013- Jan 2016) in 100-H and 300 Area respectively, either because the particles were trapped in the low permeability zone, or traveled too far away from the river channel and cannot flow back before Jan 2016. There are approximately additional 0.9 % and 6.2 % particles flow out of the domain with groundwater in 100-H and 300 Area. Four particle releasing time snapshots (T1 to T4 in Fig. 6 (a)) were selected to show the particle releasing locations and their corresponding residence time in the subsurface domains. The residence time of particles that were released at time T1 to T4 in Hanford 100-H Area are shown in in Fig. 6 (b)-(e). The red color represents longer residence time of particle releasing locations, while blue color represents shorter residence time. Similarly, the residence time of particles that released at time T1 to T4 in Hanford 300 Area is shown in in Fig. 6 (f)-(i). Several qualitatively similar patterns and relationships can be observed from the comparisons of Hanford 100-H and 300 Area in Fig. 6 (b)-(i). For the particle releasing time T1 and T2, the river water elevation is in a seasonal rising period. This causes the river surface water to flow into the subsurface domain after these releasing time snapshots, resulting in longer particle residence times. For the particle releasing time T3 and T4, the river water elevation is in a seasonal falling period. This causes the subsurface water to flow out of the subsurface domain after these two releasing time snapshots, resulting in shorter particle residence times. These general relationship between the residence time and the river water stage variation can be observed in both Hanford 100-H and 300 Area. More zones in red color, representing longer residence time, are shown in Fig. 6 (b) (c) (f) (g) than in (d) (e) (h) (i). Besides that, there are areas in the upstream zones of the island in the river that always show longer residence time, as the red circle marked in Fig. 6 (b) and (f) in both Hanford 100-H and 300 Area. As introduced in Section 2.6 , the investigated river section can be divided into several sub-domains according seven hydromorphic units (HU) classes that include “run,” “fast glide,” “pool,” “slow glide,” “riffle transition,” “slack water,” and “riffle.” The distribution map of these HUs in the investigated domain Hanford 100-H and 300 Area are shown in Fig. 5 (a) and (b) respectively. The similarity and the transferability of the residence time distribution are studied in each HU for all 100 million numerically tracked particles that were released during October 2013 to October 2014. The comparisons of the RTD at each HU and the whole study domain for Hanford 100-H and 300 Area are shown in in Fig. 7  . The probability density in blue is the RTD for Hanford 100-H Area, and the probability density in red is the RTD for Hanford 300 Area. It is clear that RTDs in Hanford 300 Area show more particles’ residence time distributed in shorter time span. The peaks of RTs in HU ‘Run’ are 100 days and 0.5 day in 100-H and 300 Area respectively. Similarly, In HU ‘Riffle’, the peaks of RTs are 30 days and 0.4 day in 100-H and 300 Area respectively. For the whole reach, the peaks of RTs are 30 days and 0.5 day in the two areas respectively. From this general statistic information and analysis discussed above, the similarity or the transferability RTDs in either HUs or in the whole domain is weak qualitatively. One of the reasons that cause such differences of RTs in the two investigated domains is the large-scale channel geomorphology. The flow paths of particles at the releasing time T4 are shown in Fig. 6  (j) and (k) for Hanford 100-H and 300 Area respectively. Because of the high sinuosity of stream channel in 100-H Area, most of the particle paths are across the bending section, and travel a few kilometers in the groundwater system. In contrast to 100-H Area, the channel in 300 Area is almost straight, and particle paths in 300 Area are mainly near and/or under the river channel.  3.3 Kolmogorov-Smirnov test results To quantitatively evaluate the transferability RTDs in the Hanford 100-H Area and Hanford 300 Area, we applied two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (K-S test) (Daniel 1990, Dimitrova, Kaishev et al. 2020 ). Both K-S test statistics and p-value were used to measure the differences between the distributions. The K-S test statistics measure the maximum distance between the Cumulative Distribution Functions (CDFs) of two probability distributions. The K-S test statistics is a value between 0 and 1, with a value of 0 indicating that the two distributions are identical and a value of 1 indicating the two distributions are completely different. Commonly, the K-S test statistics needs to be lower than 0.05 for the two distributions that can be considered as similar or comparable. The K-S test statistics for all the released particles are 0.27, 0.07, 0.17, 0.15, 0.12, 1, and 0.14 for HUs “run,” “fast glide,” “pool,” “slow glide,” “riffle transition,” “slack water,” and “riffle” respectively. As mentioned in Section 2.5 , particles were released at 1000 different times during October 2013 to October 2014. We investigated the K-S test statistics for the particle RTDs at these releasing times separately as well, as shown in Fig. 8  (a). Each vertical line represents the K-S test statistics for the RTD comparison at one particle releasing time. The K-S test statistics for each HU is shown separately as well in Fig. 8 (a). Because there is no HU “Slack water” in 300 Area, its K-S test statistics is always 1 for all the 1000 particle releasing times obviously. For all the other HUs, the K-S test statistics is above 0.05, which means all the RTDs of the particles, no matter when they are released, are not similar in the two study domains 100-H and 300 Area in any HU. The p-value in the K-S test measures the probability of observing a K-S statistics as extreme as the one calculated from the data, assuming that the null hypothesis is true. The null hypothesis in the K-S test is that the two distributions being compared are the same. If the p-value is less than the significance level, like 0.05, the null hypothesis is rejected, and conclude that the two distributions are significantly different. The K-S test p-value for all the released particles are 6.2 ×    10-322 , 2.1 ×    10-26 , 2.4 ×    10-133 , 5.6 ×    10-98 , 1.7 ×    10-66 , 0, and 4.6 ×    10-86  for HUs “run,” “fast glide,” “pool,” “slow glide,” “riffle transition,” “slack water,” and “riffle” respectively. The releasing time separated K-S test p-value is shown in Fig. 8 (b). Each vertical line represents the K-S test p-value for the RTD comparison at one particle releasing time. It is obvious that all the p-values of the RTDs of the particles, no matter when they are released, are at the order of magnitude of 10  - 10      or lower. The white lines and gaps in Fig. 8 (b) represent the values below the cutoff 10  - 10     . This means the probability of two RTDs are the same is extremely low in any HU.  3.4 RF classification results As mentioned in Section 2.7 , the RF classification models were trained for the three RT classes in 100-H Area and 300 Area, with the optimal model configuration from random searching. And the performance of the built RF models was evaluated on the 20 % testing data area, as marked in Fig. 5 , using the four metrics precision, recall, F1 score and balanced accuracy. The class statistics for 100-H Area and 300 Area using these four metrics are shown in Fig. 9  (a) and (b) respectively. For both 100-H Area and 300 Area, the precision is around 40 %-60 %, the recall is around 10 %-80 %, the F1 score is around 20 %-60 %, and the balanced accuracy score is close to 50 %-60 % for the three classes of RT as shown in Fig. 9 . This indicates the built RF models are not reliable enough to predict the classes of RT for both areas. The particles predominantly enter the groundwater system, as depicted in Fig. 6  (j) and (k), and their flow paths are significantly influenced by the underground structure and large-scale channel geomorphology. However, the RT model input parameters do not include information on both underground structure and large-scale channel geomorphology, making it nearly impossible for the RF model to predict the RT classes.   4 Conclusions and discussion In this study, we utilized the previously established one-way coupled river and subsurface water transport models to simulate the surface and subsurface water transport in two sections of Columbia River and the nearby in-land regions of Hanford 100-H and 300 Area from January 2013 to December 2015. The particle-tracking model was employed to numerically release 100 million particles from October 2013 to October 2014, tracking each particle’s transport in the subsurface domain. All the particle tracking information was then statistically summarized into RTDs for quantitative evaluation of their similarity and transferability in the same HUs in the two regions. Although the RTD spatial distribution (Fig. 6 (b)-(i)) shows some qualitatively similar pattern between the 100-H and 300 Area, the probability density (Fig. 7 ) indicates that the residence time in the 300 Area is generally shorter than it in the 100-H Area. The K-S test statistics and p-value quantitatively demonstrate that the differences between the RTDs in the 100-H Area and 300 Area are significant, and the likelihood of the RTDs in the two regions being the same is below 10  - 10      for all the HUs. This conclusion suggests that the HUs, classified according to the surface water transport information and local riverbed topography, cannot provide reliable information to the RTDs. As discussed in Section 3.2 , for the investigated river sections in this study, the river bend morphology is noticeably different. The river section in Hanford 100-H Area is bent with considerable sinuosity, while the river section in Hanford 300 Area is almost straight. The flow paths in 100-H Area (Fig. 6  (j)) are a few kilometers long and across the river bending section, but the flow paths in 300 Area (Fig. 6  (k)) is much shorter and near or under the river channel. The HU classifications only considered the short-distance river channel topography, such as the slop and concavity. The large-scale and long-distance river channel morphology are not involved by the HU classifications. Additionally, the subsurface hydraulic properties in the study domains, as shown in Fig. 4  and Table 1 , are composed of the complex structures with a 4 orders of magnitude difference in permeability. The more permeable soil type, Hanford, is the main subsurface flow channel and layer. All the other three soil types (Taylor Flats, Ringold E, and Ringold LM) act as barriers. Therefore, the connectivity and the fraction of the Hanford soil play significant role in the residence time and the associated RTDs. This is one of the explanations why the surface water transport behavior and the associated HU classifications show no relationship to the RTDs across the two study domains of Hanford 100-H and 300 Area. In addition to the K-S test, we also used the same input parameters, listed in Section 2.6 , as the HUs classification work (Hou, Ren et al. 2021), and utilized the simulated residence time as the output to implement the supervised learning to construct a regression model for the relationship between surface water transport and residence time. To simplify the model training, the residence time was divided into three classes: short (<3 day), medium (>3 day and < 30 days), and long (>30 days). The training data set covers 80 % of the river section area, and the testing data set covers 20 % of the river section area for both Hanford 100-H and 300 Area domains. The Random Forest approach was applied to construct the relationship between all the input parameters and the three RT classes. The precision is around 40 %-60 %, the recall is around 10 %-80 %, the F1 score is around 20 %-60 %, and the balanced accuracy score is close to 50 %-60 % for the three classes of RT as shown in Fig. 9 . This indicates the trained classification model cannot construct reliable relationship between the input parameters and the of RTs. In summary, all the results from modeling and analysis in this study confirm the widely accepted understanding that, for the large-scale river reaches, the underground structure and large-scale channel geomorphology control the subsurface water transport and the associated RTDs in a more dominant role, even though the surface water transport is one of the main driving forces. For the small-scale stream, where the river water does not exchange with the groundwater system, the surface water hydrodynamics and short distance river channel topography may potentially play a more critical role in controlling the HEFs and RTDs. One possible approach to make the RTDs transferable between different river sections is to include large-scale channel geomorphology information into the input parameters, such as the sinuosity and detailed relative positions of each small patch of the riverbed in the bent channel. Another possible approach is to involve river-bed grain size distribution information and/or shallow depth hydraulic conductivity into the input parameters. Our future work will investigate these possible approaches.  5 Funding information This research was supported by the United States Department of Energy  (DOE) Office of Science , Biological and Environmental Research  (BER) program, through the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory  River Corridor Hydrobiogeochemistry Science Focus  Area (SFA) project (https://www.pnnl.gov/projects/river-corridor ).
1 Introduction Terrestrial water storage (TWS) is a crucial component of the global water cycle, encompassing soil water, canopy water, snow water, glaciers, lakes, rivers, artificial reservoirs, and groundwater (Tapley et al., 2019 ). The southeastern Tibetan Plateau (SETP) is located in Southwestern China, spanning Sichuan and Yunnan, serves as a vital transitional zone between the Tibetan Plateau and its surrounding regions. It formed during the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates, and exhibits complex neotectonic features (Molnar and Tapponnier, 1975 ). Due to the typical subtropical monsoon climate typical of the SETP, terrestrial water storage changes (TWSC) are strongly influenced by seasonal factors. During summer, the southwest and east Asian monsoons bring abundant water vapor from the Indian and Pacific Oceans, increasing precipitation and total water storage. In winter, influenced by the dry inland monsoon, is relatively dry (Wang et al., 2015 ). Therefore, monitoring TWSC in the SETP is critical and assist local water authorities make informed resource management decisions. To estimate TWSC, various hydrological models have utilized to infer the spatiotemporal variations of TWS, such as the Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) (Rodell et al., 2004 ) and the Land Surface Discharge Model (LSDM) (Dill, 2008 ). However, hydrological models often simplify details, which may limit their ability to fully capture dynamic changes in water components (Soltani et al., 2021 ). Since 2002, the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and GRACE Follow-On (GFO) satellite gravity data have been widely used in hydrological research on a global and regional scale. They have been facilitated the study of glacier melting, groundwater depletion, and extreme climate events such as droughts and floods (Rodell et al., 2009; Feng et al., 2013; Long et al., 2014; Thomas et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2017; Velicogna et al., 2020; Jiao et al., 2023; Agarwal et al., 2023 ). However, GRACE/GFO satellites have limited spatial resolution due to orbit height and configuration errors, which restrict the accurate estimation of TWSC for small watersheds and shorter time scales (Schmidt et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2021 ). Previous studies have proposed using high-precision Global Positioning System (GPS) vertical displacements as an indirect method to infer TWSC. This method has been successfully applied in many areas (van Dam et al., 2001; White et al., 2022 ). Many studies have shown that the TWSC results obtained from GPS-only inversion align well with results from GRACE/GFO (Amos et al., 2014; Borsa et al., 2014 ). However, GPS can provide higher temporal and spatial resolutions of TWSC compared to GRACE/GFO, especially when dense GPS networks are available. This demonstrates that GRACE/GFO can detect overall changes in TWSC, while GPS can capture finer details, complementing the broader findings of GRACE/GFO (Chen et al., 2024 ). Therefore, researchers have proposed the joint inversion of GPS and GRACE/GFO in both in the spatial and spherical harmonic domains. In the spherical harmonic domain, Kusche et al. (2007)  implemented a scheme for the joint inversion of GPS and GRACE into low-degree surface mass redistribution fields. In the spatial domain, there are two main methods. One method involves using “virtual” GPS vertical displacements generated by forward modeling from GRACE/GFO as constraints, combined with GPS for inversion (Fok and Liu, 2019; Adusumilli et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023a ). The other method incorporates equal-area 3-degree spherical cap mascon blocks from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) as constraints, combined with GPS for inversion (Carlson et al., 2022 ). Yang et al. (2023)  compared the two joint inversion methods in southwestern China and concluded that the former method is more effective. However, considering the subjectivity of the locations of “virtual” GPS stations and the reliability of the “virtual” GPS vertical displacements generated by GRACE/GFO forward modeling in the first method, we will adopt the second method to perform joint inversion. Researchers have utilized GPS measurements to study TWS in southwestern China, capitalizing on the dense distribution of GPS stations and significant seasonal variations in hydrological loading. Jiang et al.
