(2017)  compared precipitable water vapor and vertical crustal displacement data obtained from 26 GPS stations in Yunnan Province with the equivalent water height (EWH) from GRACE and precipitation data, revealing monsoonal and drought characteristics. Fok and Liu (2019)  proposed considering irregular distribution of GPS stations and terrain effects by utilizing “virtual” GPS vertical displacements from GRACE/GFO. This method effectively monitored TWSC in southwestern China. Jiang et al. (2021a) and (2021b)  integrated variational Bayesian principal component analysis and independent component analysis into the Green's function inversion framework using GPS measurements to analyze extreme hydro-meteorological events in Sichuan and Yunnan. Li et al. (2023b)  compared inversion results in southwestern China using Slepian basis function and Green's function methods, and found stronger signal amplitudes with the former. Li et al. (2023c)  proposed using a priori covariance matrix from a hydrological model as a regularization constraint to estimate TWSC and extreme hydrometeorological events in Yunnan. Zhu et al. (2023)  used variational Bayesian independent component analysis to reconstruct three-dimensional hydrological loading deformations at 43 GPS stations in Yunnan. They combined this with “virtual” GPS vertical displacements from GRACE/GFO to estimate TWSC in three sub-basins of Yunnan. As can be seen, previous studies primarily focused on the spatiotemporal variations of TWS in areas such as Sichuan, Yunnan, and Chongqing. In this study, we investigate the spatiotemporal variations of TWS in the SETP, a region characterized by complex topography and diverse climate types. The SETP serves as a conduit for the gradual southeastward movement of deep-seated materials within the crust beneath the Tibetan Plateau. Our goal is to explore TWS variations in the SETP from 2010 to 2019 using GPS and GRACE/GFO data. Additionally, we will compare the results with GLDAS and hydrometeorological data to analyze the climatic response processes. This study is significant in bridging the knowledge gap regarding TWS, and will contribute to the formulation of water resource management and climate adaptation strategies in the SETP.  2 Data and methods 2.1 Dataset 2.1.1 GPS dataset In this study, we utilized the daily measurement data from 82 GPS stations to infer the TWSC in the SETP from July 2010 to December 2019, as depicted in Fig. 1  . Fig. 1  illustrates the topography of the SETP and its surrounding areas, with red dots representing the spatial distribution of GPS stations used in this research. The solid black line indicates the boundary of study area, while the solid red line represents the expanded boundary with a 2° buffer zone mitigate artificial effects near the edges (Fu et al., 2015 ). The GPS coordinate time series are obtained from the China Earthquake Administration (CEA) and processed using the GAMIT 10.5 software (Herring et al., 2010 ). Specifically, the GPS stations were first consolidated to form an integrated network that is referenced to the International Terrestrial Reference Frame (ITRF). Subsequently, the daily relaxation solutions obtained from this network were processed by GAMIT version 10.5 software, including geophysical correction based on forward models (e.g., the troposphere delay (Vienna Mapping Function), ionosphere delay (Ionosphere-free linear combination), ocean tide effect (FES2004 model) and solid Earth tide effect (IERS2010 model)). In addition to these corrections, a seven-parameter transformation using the GLOBK software was performed to convert the solution to align with the ITRF2014 reference frame. Detailed data processing strategies can be found in the site manual of the Crustal Movement Observation Network of China (CMONOC), available at ftp://ftp.cgps.ac.cn/doc/processing_manual.pdf . Moreover, a range of factors, including seismic events, replacement of receiver antennas, environmental noise, data processing defects, outliers, offsets and post-seismic distortions, are tackled through the utilization of the TSAnalyzer tool, which operates on the basis of the L1 regularization criterion (Wu et al., 2018 ), as shown in Fig. S1  of the supplementary material . As we focus on the TWSC, we correct the non-hydrological loading displacements in GPS vertical time series using the non-tidal atmospheric load (NTAL) and non-tidal oceanic load (NTOL) products provided by the Earth System Modelling group at Deutsches GeoForschungsZentrum (ESMGFZ) (Dill and Dobslaw, 2013 ) with a 3-hour sampling interval and spatial resolution of 0.5° × 0.5° (Fig. 2  (a)). Furthermore, we employ the GNSS Missing Data Interpolation Software (GMIS) developed by Liu et al. (2017) . GMIS combines the Kriging spatial interpolation algorithm with the Kalman time optimal estimation algorithm to interpolate missing data in GPS vertical displacement time series. Fig. 2 (b) demonstrates an example at the GSMA station before and after post-processing, highlighting the successful removal of high-frequency noise and data interpolation. Since the long-term trend of GPS residual vertical displacement time series (GPS with AO-correction) includes contributions from GIA, tectonic, and surface hydrological mass changes, it is challenging to separate individual components. However, considering that the deformation signals caused by GIA and tectonic mainly exhibit a linear trend in the SETP (similar to previous studies by Fu et al. (2015), Jiang et al. (2021a, 2021b), Li et al. (2023a, 2023b, 2023c)  and Yang et al. (2023) ), we remove the linear trend from GPS residual vertical displacement time series. Our focus then shifts to the seasonal and interannual variations of surface hydrological mass changes. Moreover, while long-period nonlinear signals arising from the interior motion of the Earth have been identified (Ding et al., 2020 ), their amplitudes are significantly smaller in comparison to transient nonlinear variations induced by extreme climate events. Thus, upon removal of the linear trend, the influence of non-hydrological factors can be effectively mitigated, allowing for the attribution of interannual hydrological signals to extreme climate events. As with GPS, we also remove the linear trend from GRACE/GFO and GLDAS data when comparing. Furthermore, to match the temporal sampling interval of GRACE/GFO, we resample the daily GPS vertical displacement time series into monthly averages.  2.1.2 GRACE/GFO mascon dataset In this study, we utilize monthly GRACE/GFO mascon solutions of TWSC in the SETP from the University of Texas Center for Space Research (CSR) [0.25° × 0.25°], Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) [0.5° × 0.5°], and Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) [0.5° × 0.5°] (Watkins et al., 2015; Save et al., 2016; Loomis et al., 2019 ). These three mascon solutions do not require post-processing and offer a higher signal-to-noise ratio for immediate use. The degree-1 coefficients of these solutions have been added by using the method of Swenson et al. (2008)  and Sun et al. (2016) . The C 2,0  and C 3,0  coefficients have been replaced with independent solutions from satellite laser ranging (SLR) (Loomis et al., 2019 ). The Glacial Isostatic Adjustment (GIA) effect is corrected with the ICE6G_D model (Peltier et al., 2018 ). To calculate hydrological loading deformation based on GRACE/GFO mascon solutions, we utilize gridded GRACE/GFO mascon solutions with a patched Green's function approach (Chanard et al., 2014 ) and load Love number derived from Wang et al. (2012)  based on the Preliminary Reference Earth Model (PREM) (Dziewonski and Anderson, 1981 ). Moreover, in order to obtain reliable hydrological loading deformation at GPS station locations using GRACE/GFO mascon solutions, we average results from three different GRACE/GFO mascon solutions (Pan et al., 2023 ).  2.1.3 Hydrological model This study uses the GLDAS Noah 2.1 land surface model product with a resolution of 0.25° × 0.25° to verify the inversion results, which has been widely used in many studies, including water resource investigations in China (Rodell et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2020a,b ), and is available on the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) website at https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/ . To determine the TWSC using GLDAS, we aggregate the 0–2 m soil moisture, snow water equivalent and canopy water. It is important to note that the GLDAS TWSC does not consider groundwater changes below the soil layer. Additionally, we compute the hydrological loading deformation at GPS stations using GLDAS and compare it to both direct GPS measurements and hydrological loading deformation calculated from GRACE/GFO.  2.1.4 Hydrometeorological data and climate index Precipitation, evapotranspiration and runoff data obtained from different types of hydrometeorological data are used to verify the inversion results. These data include monthly 0.1° × 0.1° grid precipitation, evapotranspiration, runoff and temperature data from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/cdapp#!/home ), monthly 1° × 1° grid precipitation data from the Global Precipitation Climatology Centre (GPCC) (https://www.dwd.de/DE/Home/home_node.html ), monthly 0.5° × 0.5° grid temperature data from the Global Historical Climate Network and Climate Anomaly Monitoring System Global Historical Climatology Network and the Climate Anomaly Monitoring System (GHCN_CAMS) (https://psl.noaa.gov/data/gridded/data.ghcncams.html ), monthly 0.25° × 0.25° grid evapotranspiration data from the Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM) (https://www.gleam.eu/ ), monthly precipitation, evapotranspiration and runoff data from three GLDAS land surface models NOAH 2.1, Catchment 2.1 and VIC 2.1 (https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/ ), where the NOAH data is 0.25° × 0.25° grid, Catchment and VIC data is 1° × 1° grid, and monthly Southern Oscillation Index (SOI) data from the Climate Prediction Center (CPC) (https://psl.noaa.gov/data/correlation/soi.data ). Furthermore, we use the generalized three-cornered hat (GTCH) method (Galindo et al., 2001 ) to assess the uncertainty of various independent hydrometeorological datasets. Based on the estimated variances, we perform optimal fusion to obtain more reliable data as follows:(1) X = ∑ i = 1  N  P i  X i       where X    is the fused data; X i     is the i -th dataset of the same type; N    is the total number of datasets of the same type; P i     is the weight corresponding to the i -th dataset, and the specific formula is P i  = 1 / w i   ∑ j = 1  N  1 / w j       ; w i     is the variance of the i -th dataset estimated by the GTCH method, and for the specific calculation flow, see Zhao et al. (2019) .   2.2 Methods 2.2.1 GPS-only inversion The theory of elastic loading deformation in the solid Earth describes that the crustal displacements resulting from loading fields can be estimated by convolving the Green's function with the loading field (Farrell, 1972 ). Based on the disk method (Argus et al., 2014, 2017; Fu et al., 2015 ), we perform inversion of the TWSC in the SETP at a 0.5° × 0.5° grid using GPS vertical displacement time series, denoted as EWH. Considering latitude-dependent variations in disk radius, we apply an area-weighted scheme to determine the radius of each grid (Jiang et al., 2021a ). The inversion objective function is constructed by minimizing the combination of data misfit and model roughness as follows:(2) F x GPS      = G GPS   x GPS   - d GPS       2  + β 2  L x GPS       2  → min     where x GPS      is the estimated parameter, i.e. the unknown EWH values; G GPS      is the Green function, where the load Love numbers (LLNs) are derived from Wang et al. (2012)  based on the PREM model (Dziewonski and Anderson, 1981 ), and we calculate the load Green function under the center of figure (CF) frame by using the maximum degree of 20,000 of LLNs; d GPS      is the GPS vertical displacement time series; L    is the Laplacian second-order smoothing constraint matrix used in previous studies (Jiang et al., 2021a, 2021b; Yang et al., 2023 ), which consists of kernels 0  1  0   1   - 4   1   0   1  0          and 1  - 2   1         ; ‖ · ‖  2     is the two-norm of ·   ; β    is the regularization parameter. Based on Eq. (2)  and the least squares principle, we can obtain the parameter estimation of GPS-only as follows:(3) x ̂  GPS   = G GPS  T  E - 1   G GPS   + β ̂  L T  L     - 1   G GPS  T  E - 1   d GPS       where E - 1      is the identity matrix associated with the length of x ̂  GPS     .  2.2.2 GPS and GRACE/GFO joint inversion In this study, the principle for joint inversion is to use the observation equation of JPL mascon as constraint, and the specific constraint equation is as follows:(4) d JPL   = G JPL   x ̂  Joint      where d JPL      comprises q  JPL mascon observations as d JPL   = d 1  , d 2  , ⋯ , d q      T    ; and G JPL      is a sparse matrix as follows (Carlson et al., 2022 ):(5) G JPL   = 1 k 1    1 k 1    ⋯  1 k 1    0   0   0  1 k 2    ⋯  1 k 2     ⋮   ⋮  ⋮  ⋮  ⋮   0   1 k q    ⋯  1 k q    0            where the row of G JPL      corresponds to the number of equal-area 3-degree spherical cap mascon blocks of JPL in the SETP, and the column of G JPL      corresponds to the unknown EWH values where the values inside the equal-area 3-degree spherical cap mascon blocks of JPL in the SETP are 1, and zero elsewhere; k i  ( i = 1 : q )     is the number of grid cells within the i -th equal-area 3-degree spherical cap mascon block of JPL in the SETP. Then, we can obtain the observation vector and design matrix for joint inversion, denoted as d Joint  = d GPS    d JPL          T     and G Joint  = G GPS    G JPL          T    . Further, similar to Eq. (3)  for GPS-only inversion, we can derive the parameter estimation for joint inversion as follows:(6) x ̂  Joint  = G Joint  T  E 1  α ̂  2         - 1   G Joint  + β ̂  1  L T  L     - 1   G Joint  T  E 1  α ̂  2         - 1   d Joint      where E 1  α 2     = α ̂  2  σ GPS  2    0   0   σ JPL  2            is the variance matrix in which σ GPS      and σ JPL      are unit matrices because the standard deviations of observations of the same type are close (Yang et al., 2023 ); α ̂     is the weighting factor between GPS and JPL mascon observations; β ̂  1     is the regularization parameter; L    is the Laplacian second-order smoothing constraint matrix whose kernel is the same as that of GPS-only inversion. Eq. (6)  highlights the importance of determining the optimal weighting factor and regularization parameter for the joint inversion results. Specifically, a high weighting factor can lead to an excessive fit between the TWS estimates and JPL mascon observations, but may deviate from GPS observations, resulting in lower spatial resolution of TWS estimates. Conversely, a low weighting factor can cause an excessive fit with GPS observations. Furthermore, a high regularization parameter yields overly smooth TWS estimates, while a low regularization parameter produce rough results inconsistent with the actual spatial distribution of TWS. The joint inversion model is mainly determined based on the model proposed by Carlson et al. (2022) , and our difference lies in determining the weighting factor and regularization parameter. Carlson et al. (2022)  used the trade-off curve method (Hansen and O’ Leary, 1993 ) to determine the weighting factor and regularization parameter, which may be subjective and computationally expensive. Currently, researchers have conducted extensive studies on methods for determining the parameters of ill-posed problem. However, considering that the generalized cross validation (GCV) method cannot determine the optimal parameter when the curve is too flat; the ridge estimation method has certain subjective randomness although simple calculation; the variance component estimation method takes the parameter as the weight of virtual observation, which may produce negative variance and make the result unreliable; the solution of L curve method is too dependent on the curve fitting accuracy, and the solution result may not converge (Wang and Chen, 2021 ), we will determine the optimal regularization parameter for GPS-only inversion and the optimal weighting factor and regularization parameter for joint inversion based on the Akaike’s Bayesian Information Criterion (ABIC) method. Extensive research and applications have been carried out on the ABIC method, and for the specific calculation flow can be found in Funning et al. (2014), Yang et al. (2023)  and Li et al. (2023a) . The ABIC distribution plots for the GPS-only inversion and joint inversion are shown in Fig. 3  . As can be seen, the ABIC value for GPS inversion is minimized when β ̂  2  = 0.135    is optimal, corresponding to the optimal regularization parameter. Similarly, the ABIC value for the joint inversion is minimized when log α ̂  2     = - 8    and log β ̂  1 2     = 3.5    are reach their optimal, corresponding to the optimal weighting factor and regularization parameter.    3 Results 3.1 Seasonal vertical land motions from various datasets The Earth's crust responds to externally applied forces by causing displacement changes on its surface. This phenomenon arises from the redistribution of land water storage, atmospheric pressure, and non-tidal ocean mass. Surface vertical displacements induced by hydrological mass variations in the SETP are investigated through the analysis of three types of measurements: direct measurements obtained from GPS, model forecasts derived from GRACE/GFO and GLDAS. Fig. 4  (a) shows the area-average outcomes of hydrological loading displacements from GPS, GRACE/GFO and GLDAS. Fig. 4  (b-e) shows the Pearson correlation coefficients (PCCs) and weighted root mean square (WRMS) reduction rates comparing monthly average vertical displacements obtained from GPS with hydrological loading displacements derived from GRACE/GFO and GLDAS. The high values of PCCs and the substantial reduction rates in WRMS suggest a robust correlation between GPS measurements and variations in hydrological mass. In light of the significant seasonal precipitation observed in the SETP (Zhang et al., 2020a ), fluctuations in surface water storage are magnified, resulting in heightened surface elastic loadings related to hydrological signals. These modifications can be more efficiently supervised through the utilization of GPS and GRACE/GFO, demonstrating enhanced coherence. Furthermore, it is evident that the loading displacements forecasted by GLDAS are comparatively smaller than those estimated by GPS, as well as the loading displacements predicted by GRACE/GFO. This phenomenon could be attributed to the fact that TWSC derived from the GLDAS solely accounts for near-surface components of TWS. Fig. 5   displays the semi-annual and annual spatial amplitudes and phases that have been estimated from GPS, GRACE/GFO, and GLDAS hydrological loading displacements. The findings reveal that the semi-annual and annual amplitudes reveal the three datasets demonstrate spatial consistency, gradually decreasing from the southwest to the northeast. Significant variations in amplitude exist among different datasets, primarily attributed to differences in spatial resolution and processing methods across various datasets (Fu et al., 2015 ). Benefiting from the advantage of daily sampling resolution, GPS demonstrates increased sensitivity to the semi-annual signal and provides a more detailed representation of high-frequency information. Nevertheless, accurate separation of high-frequency information, including the actual hydrological mass loading and other sources of noise, is essential for subsequent analysis. The results indicate a relatively high consistency between the semi-annual/annual phases of GPS and GRACE/GFO, whereas the phase of GLDAS shows significant variability. This limitation may arise from the inability of the GLDAS model to accurately replicate the dynamic variations of all water component. To demonstrate the differences between the magnitudes of the same type of data, we perform linear regression comparisons between pairs of GPS, GRACE/GFO and GLDAS. Fig. 6   shows the linear regression analysis comparing the semi-annual and annual amplitudes of vertical displacements obtained from GPS with those from GRACE/GFO and GLDAS. The regression lines fitted for the semi-annual and annual amplitudes exhibit slopes of 0.68 and 0.73 for GLDAS compared to GRACE/GFO (Fig. 6 c and f), which outperform the slopes of 0.44 and 0.66 for GRACE/GFO compared to GPS (Fig. 6 b and e), as well as 0.32 and 0.51 for GLDAS compared to GPS (Fig. 6 a and d). The results indicate that both GRACE/GFO and GLDAS algorithms underestimate displacements resulting caused by hydrological massing loads. This underestimation is particularly pronounced in the case of GLDAS, primarily attributed to variations in observation and modeling methods (Fu et al., 2015 ). For example, GPS technology is sensitive to local and regional hydrological signals (Knappe et al., 2019 ), while GRACE/GFO provides large-scale TWSC estimates (Argus et al., 2014 ). In contrast, GLDAS typically underestimates water compositions due to its limited representation of water and energy cycles (Jiang et al., 2021a, 2021b ).  3.2 Comparison of spatial features from various water estimates As evidenced by prior analyses, seasonality plays a significant role in TWS in the regions of Sichuan and Yunnan. Therefore, our study focuses on examining the annual oscillations in water storage. Fig. 7   shows the spatial distribution of annual amplitudes of TWS as deduced from various sources including CSR, JPL, GSFC, GLDAS, GPS-only inversion and joint inversion. The annual amplitudes of TWS from six water estimates demonstrate consistent spatial distributions throughout the entire study area, with the most significant annual amplitudes observed in the southwestern region. In contrast, the smallest annual amplitudes are observed in the northeast of the study area, exhibiting a decreasing distribution from southwest to northeast, which aligns with the patterns observed in Yunnan and Sichuan (Jiang et al., 2021a, 2021b; Yang et al., 2023 ). This phenomenon is primarily attributed to seasonal precipitation (Zhang et al., 2020b ). The annual amplitudes inverted in this study are both higher than those obtained from CSR, JPL, GSFC, and GLDAS. This disparity can be attributed to the spatial resolution constraints of GRACE/GFO and the limited consideration of surface water components in the GLDAS model. By correlating the elevation of the study area depicted in Fig. 1  with the annual amplitude findings presented in Fig. 7 , it is evident that the annual amplitudes of CSR, JPL, GSFC, and GLDAS are significantly lower compared to the outcomes of this study in the northwestern region of the study area, particularly in the high-altitude zones. This is primarily attributed to the spatial resolution of GRACE/GFO, which is approximately 350 km (Knappe et al., 2019 ), and the significant underestimation of water content in regions characterized by highly intricate terrain in the GLDAS model (Scanlon et al., 2018 ). Moreover, upon comparing the outcomes of the annual amplitude in this investigation, it is evident that the outcomes derived from the joint inversion method demonstrate relatively larger annual amplitudes in the northern region of Yunnan and the southern area of Sichuan, in contrast to those obtained from the GPS-only inversion technique. This disparity can be primarily attributed to the sparse coverage of GPS stations in these areas. The joint inversion method utilizes the JPL mascon as constraints, thereby improving the spatial resolution of TWS. By comparing the outcomes of CSR, JPL, GSFC, and GLDAS, it is evident that the GRACE/GFO results do not exhibit relatively significant amplitudes over northern Yunnan and southern Sichuan, while GLDAS result does due to its high resolution of [0.25° × 0.25°]. Nevertheless, the annual amplitudes of GLDAS are reduced due to the underestimation of water components resulting from the limited representation of water/energy cycles. This conclusion is also supported by Jiang et al. (2017), Jiang et al. (2021a, 2021b) , and Yang et al. (2023) . The inversion results are quite smooth, even compared to GRACE/GFO, this may be because we use a Laplace second-order smoothing matrix with the template which ensures the smoothness of the EWH estimates on the adjacent grids to fit better with the actual spatial distribution of TWS. Furthermore, the high regularization parameter may also result in overly smooth TWS estimates. Recently, numerous studies have examined the effects of Earth models on the inversion results (Wang et al., 2013; Chanard et al., 2014; Swarr et al., 2024 ). In order to illustrate the effects of Earth models on the TWS inversion results in the SETP, we take GPS-only inversion as an example. We use the LLNs of PREMhard model given by Wang et al. (2012) , and the crust structures of this model are constituted by Crust 2.0 in which hard sediment is considered as the outmost layer. In the Fig. S2  of the supplementary material , we show the annual amplitudes of TWS from GPS-only inversion by using PREM and PREMhard models. It can be seen that the results obtained from these two Earth models are almost the same (Fig. S2 (c)), indicating that different Earth models have little influence on the inversion results in the SETP. Meanwhile, Chanard et al. (2014)  and Carson et al. (2012) also pointed out that location-specific elastic structures of the Earth have small improvement in the vertical direction between GPS and GRACE/GFO and so often the simpler PREM model is considered sufficient. Therefore, we will use the inversion results of PREM model for interpretation and application in the later sections.  3.3 Comparison of temporal patterns of various water estimates To examine the time-varying evolution of TWS, we calculate area-average TWS anomaly, and then the missing data are imputed using the Singular Spectrum Analysis (SSA) technique (Yi and Sneeuw, 2021 ). Fig. 8   shows the monthly sampling time series, annual cycles, and spectrums derived from the CSR, JPL, GSFC, GLDAS models, and the two inversion results obtained in this study. The annual variations of TWS exhibit comparable seasonal trends, with the lowest and highest values typically occurring around April and September annually, as shown in Fig. 8 (b). In this study, we use a least-squares fit, including an annual term and a semiannual term, to calculate the annual term and semiannual term of TWS variation and use the fitting residuals to estimate their uncertainties based on the error propagation law (Jiao et al., 2020 ). The magnitude of annual amplitude of inversion is GPS-only > Joint Inversion > GRACE/GFO>GLDAS (refer to Table 1  ). Among them, the annual amplitude of GPS-only inversion is the largest, and that of GLDAS is the smallest. This is reasonable, possibly due to the simplification of the hydrological cycle, particularly the exclusion of deep groundwater, in the GLDAS model. This simplification could result in an underestimation of TWS. The semi-annual amplitudes in this study are notably larger due to the higher sensitivity of GPS to local hydrological loading at daily sampling resolution compared to the monthly sampling resolution of GRACE/GFO and GLDAS. This observation aligns with the findings depicted in the spectrums (Fig. 8 (c)) and the linear regression analysis of semi-annual amplitudes (Fig. 6 (d,e,f)). Moreover, Fig. 8 (c) illustrates that the predominant periods are the seasonal signals, specifically the semi-annual and annual signals, with additional interannual variability signals present (further elaborated in Section 4.2 ). Furthermore, we calculate the PCCs and root mean square error (RMSEs) for various area-averaged TWS time series derived from distinct datasets (refer to Table 2  ). The time patterns of the three GRACE/GFO solutions exhibit a high degree of similarity, as evidenced by PCCs approaching 1 and relatively low RMSEs. By comparing our two methods with the results derived from GRACE/GFO and GLDAS datasets, it is evident that the PCCs exceed 0.9, while the RMSEs exceed 50 mm. This suggests that the methods exhibit strong temporal consistency, albeit substantial discrepancies in magnitude. This phenomenon could be attributed to the simplification of the GLDAS model, the limited spatial resolution of GRACE/GFO, the uneven distribution of GPS stations, and the influence of non-hydrological load signals (Argus et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2023 ).   4 Discussion 4.1 Consistency of TWSC with hydrological and climate variables For a specific region, the water cycle is primarily controlled by precipitation, evapotranspiration, and runoff (Chen et al., 2020a,b ). Therefore, we use the principle of water balance equation to validate various area-average TWS time series, and for detailed information on the water balance equation, please refer to Li et al. (2023a)  and Yang et al. (2023) , which will not elaborated in this paper. Additionally, due to the varying accuracy and reliability of different hydrometeorological data and in order to mitigate the impact of differences from different datasets, this study adopts the GTCH method to integrate various types of datasets, obtaining more reliable precipitation, evapotranspiration, and runoff data for better validation. Figs. 9  (a,b,c) shows the fused precipitation (GTCH P), fused evapotranspiration (GTCH E), and fused runoff (GTCH R) time series obtained from various precipitation, evapotranspiration, and runoff sequences and the GTCH method. Fig. 9 (d) shows the dTWSC /dt  time series calculated based on the water balance equation using the fused sequences, as well as the dTWSC /dt  time series calculated from various area-average TWS time series. Since the area-average TWS time series from three GRACE/GFO mascon solutions are similar, we average and compare them with the average time series, and the GTCH P, E and R in the water balance equation are filtered in advance to maintain synchronous time. As can be seen, the seasonal variations of the dTWSC /dt  time series calculated by GTCH P-E-R are in good agreement with those calculated by other TWS time series, but the amplitudes corresponding to GPS-only inversion is larger than those of GRACE/GFO, GLDAS, and GTCH P-E-R, and the joint inversion is slightly smaller than that of GPS-only inversion. Additionally, we calculate the PCCs and RMSEs between various dTWSC /dt  time series (Table 3  ), where all PCCs are above 0.9, indicating good temporal consistency among them, but there are significant differences in magnitude, especially for our two methods. This may be excessive simplification of the hydrodynamic process in the dTWSC /dt  time series calculated based on the water balance equation, which neglects the soil water and deep groundwater, leading to an underestimation of TWS (Yang et al. 2023 ). The SETP region is influenced by typical subtropical monsoon climate, with significant differences between dry and rainy seasons. Both TWS and precipitation show high consistent and obvious seasonal variations. Therefore, by analyzing the time series of TWS and precipitation in the SETP, we can better reveal land water storage changes in region. Fig. 10   shows various TWS and precipitation time series along with their annual cycles. As can be seen, precipitation reaches its maximum in July with a monthly average of 235.75 mm, while the TWS results obtained from GRACE/GFO, GLDAS, GPS-only inversion and joint inversion all reach their maximum in September. The maximum annual cycle of TWS lag behind precipitation by two months, which may be attributed to the complex transport mechanisms of land water (Long et al., 2014; Hsu et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2021a; Yang et al., 2023 ). Additionally, we provide the PCCs with/without time-lag between the precipitation and TWS time series (Table 4  ). It can be seen that both of our results have higher PCCs with and without time-lag compared to GRACE/GFO, with the highest PCC without time-lag being achieved by GLDAS. This may be because GLDAS only considers shallow surface water, while GPS and GRACE/GFO represent regional hydrological changes, and when rainfall falls to the ground, it quickly converts to shallow surface water, leading to a better time consistency between the GLDAS and precipitation. In order to show the lag relationship between TWS and precipitation time series more intuitively, we manually shift the TWS time series to make them lead the precipitation by two months. As can be seen from Fig. 11  (b), after shifting, the correlations between TWS time series and precipitation are obviously enhanced, and their phases are almost the same, indicating that the PCCs with time-lag are much higher than the PCCs without time-lag.  4.2 The interannual variations of SETP and their response to climate change The interannual variations of TWS on the Tibetan Plateau are significantly influenced by precipitation and temperature resulting from climate change, particularly evident during extreme climatic periods (He et al., 2021 ). To verify the interannual oscillations of the hydrological signal in the SETP, we first deseasonalize the TWS time series. Subsequently, we filter the TWS time series at frequencies lower than 0.5 cycles per year. This process is also carried out for the precipitation, temperature and SOI data for comparison. As depicted in Fig. 12  , the transient mass variations in the interannual fluctuations of TWS data obtained from GPS-only inversion and joint inversion are generally consistent with the changes in precipitation and temperature. However, there is a lack of synchronization between the data from GRACE/GFO and GLDAS. For instance, a reduction in precipitation resulted in a decrease in hydrological mass variations between April 2011 and March 2012, whereas an augmentation in precipitation resulted in an increase in hydrological mass changes from September 2017 to December 2018. Nevertheless, a time delay exists between precipitation and TWS data, suggesting that precipitation plays a crucial role in driving TWS mass variations in the SETP. Moreover, there is a significant correlation between hydrological mass variations in the SETP and SOI data. The SOI is indicative of a climatic phenomenon observed in the equatorial Pacific known as the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), encompassing occurrences of El Niño and La Niña events. The findings indicate that the ENSO serves as a robust indicator of climate anomalies, significantly influencing global climate patterns. Extreme climate events, including atypical precipitation and temperature fluctuations resulting from ENSO occurrences, play a pivotal role in shaping the variations and dynamic evolution of TWS in the SETP.   5 Conclusion In this study, we focus on the TWSC in the SETP. First, a comparison was made among the seasonal surface motions derived from various datasets, including GPS, GRACE/GFO, and GLDAS data (Section 3.1 ). Subsequently, the spatiotemporal variations of TWS obtained by different schemes are compared in Sections 3.2 and 3.3 . Furthermore, we conducted a comparative analysis of the inversion outcomes obtained with the water balance equation, which relies on factors such as precipitation, evapotranspiration, and runoff, in order to validate the reliability of the method (Section 4.1 ). Moreover, the interannual variation mechanisms of the TWS were analyzed by integrating precipitation, temperature, and ENSO time series (Section 4.2 ). The primary findings of this study encompass the following four main aspects: (1) The water resources in the SETP are influenced by the climatic effects of monsoons, leading to notable seasonal variations in precipitation. This phenomenon has been extensively documented in data from GPS, GRACE/GFO, and GLDAS data, demonstrating a high level of consistency in the results. Consequently, it could be inferred that the TWSC in the SETP is evidently influenced by the seasonal precipitation. This influence leads to notable fluctuations in surface water storage, as evidenced by the increased coherence of the hydrological signal of surface elasticity loadings. (2) The results for the TWSC in the SETP obtained from our methods conform with the spatial distribution characteristics and seasonal fluctuations observed in the GRACE/GFO and GLDAS models. However, our inversion findings exhibit larger amplitudes. The sensitivity of GPS data to local hydrological variations contrasts with the higher spatial resolution of GRACE/GFO data, which provide more accurate estimations of large-scale mass changes but may suffer from signal leakage. Additionally, the GLDAS hydrological model generally underestimated the TWSC due to its oversimplified representation of the hydrological cycle. Furthermore, joint inversion could achieve a more refined distribution of the TWSC compared to that obtained by GPS-only inversion in localized areas with sparse sites within the GPS network. (3) Based on the GTCH method and the water balance equation, the reliability of the inversion results was confirmed. Influenced by the subtropical monsoon climate, the peak of precipitation, evapotranspiration, and runoff in the SETP occurred in summer, and among them, precipitation most notably contributed to the TWSC. We have also observed a 2-month time lag between precipitation and the TWSC, which could be attributed to the complex transport mechanisms of terrestrial water. (4) The hydrological changes in the SETP represent a complex and dynamic processes that are responsive to climate variations. We analyzed the interannual fluctuations in different TWS datasets in relation to precipitation, temperature, and ENSO time series. The findings indicated that the interannual fluctuations and sudden shifts in hydrological patterns in the SETP since 2010 closely agree precipitation and temperature deviations. These variations are coupled with extreme climate events associated with the ENSO, illustrating the dynamics of hydrological changes in response to worldwide climate shifts.

1 Introduction Rivers and streams are significant linkages of terrain, river, ocean, and atmosphere (Dean & Battin, 2024 ). Dissolved carbon in them plays an integral role in the biogeochemistry cycle (Drake et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015 ). It influences biodiversity, metal export, and catchment carbon budget. The DOC provides energy for the riverine biogeochemical process, meanwhile, it is the carbon source for either DOC or DIC in riverine (Leenheer & Croué, 2003 ). The DIC is a mixture with signature of rock weathering and organic carbon mineralization (Lehmann et al., 2023 ), so, it is an indicator of rock weathering rate and organic carbon mineralization intensity. DIC dynamics have been demonstrated to vary across heterogeneous landscapes (Campeau et al., 2018; Tank et al., 2011 ) and climates (Clair et al., 2008 ). The Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau (QTP) has a large carbon stock. The estimated data showed that 48 PgC and 73.6 PgC are stored in the upper 1 m and 3 m soil layers, respectively (Zhang et al., 2022 ). With the QTP warming, there is a great potential for the soil carbon to be activated and transported to the riverine and lake (Chen et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, the impact mode of the ongoing climate change on the riverine carbon dynamics remains to be accomplished (Deng, 2024; Huntington et al., 2016 ), and it has attracted great concern. Previous studies had concluded that DIC was the main dissolved carbon in permafrost-affected arctic rivers (Striegl et al., 2007 ; Tank et al., 2012.). In the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau (QTP), DIC concentration is 26 times higher than DOC concentration (Qu et al., 2018 ). However, the characteristics of riverine dissolved carbon transport and their effects on DIC sources across QTP rivers are still poorly understood. The sources of the DIC can be mainly summarized as geogenic via carbonate weathering and biogenic via soil respiration (Campeau et al., 2018 ). To be more specific, the biogenic DIC can originate from organic carbon mineralization (Pipko et al., 2023 ) and the silicate weathered by carbonic acid (Lehmann et al., 2023 ). These transformation processes make interpretation of riverine carbon cycling more difficult. The stable carbon isotope provides a useful tool for identifying the chemical weathering and organic carbon mineralization processes (Palmer et al., 2001 ). The δ13 C value for carbonate rocks and minerals is around 0 ‰ (Das et al., 2005 ). The soil CO2  mainly derives from the residue decomposition and root respiration of plants, and this process is named soil respiration (Wen et al., 2022 ). Hence, the δ13 C value for soil CO2  is equal to that in the origin plant, which is −27 ‰ for C3 plants and −12 ‰ for C4 plants (Campeau et al., 2017 ). For geogenic DIC, the carbonate weathered by carbonic acid generates bicarbonate with half from soil CO2  and the other half from rock, the δ13 C values are the mean δ13 C value for carbonate rock and soil CO2  (Zhao et al., 2023 ). The carbonate weathered by sulfuric acid generates bicarbonate totally from rock, the δ13 C values are same as that in carbonate rock. For biogenic DIC, the organic carbon mineralization generates bicarbonate from plants, the silicate weathering generates bicarbonate totally from soil CO2 , and their δ13 C values are equal to that in plants (Palmer et al., 2001 ). Besides, CO2  evasion in the carbon transfer process increases δ13 C values in order of 1 ∼ 4 ‰ in high latitudes region (Campeau et al., 2018 ). Therefore, to better quantify the seasonal and spatial changes in DIC and the related control mechanisms, it is important to conduct an additional isotope analysis of DIC. In alpine regions, extreme climate conditions accompanied by seasonally changed active layer and high altitudes greatly complicate riverine carbon dynamics (Striegl et al., 2005; Zhong et al., 2021 ). Many researchers made an effort to understand the regulation mechanisms of DIC sources and dissolved carbon dynamics. It has been found that CO2  evasion caused the δ13 C-DIC to be enriched with distance downstream (Song et al., 2020; Telmer & Veizer, 1999 ). Campeau et al. (2018)  pointed out that the mixing of sources influenced δ13 C-DIC on a landscape scale. On a temporal scale, the roles of dissolved carbon transport were explored (Creed et al., 2015; Stewart et al., 2022 ). For example, the DOC in headwater catchments is mainly transported by SSF from terrestrial sources (Battin et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022 ) during the high flow period. However, the impact of the SSF draining process from the slope to the stream on DIC sources was not fully considered in the previous research. Currently, there are still important knowledge gaps on river DOC and DIC transport, and DIC sources: (1) how do FT process affects dissolved carbon transport and biogeochemical process; (2) whether the effects change when considering spatial differences in rock distribution. As the world's third pole, the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (QTP) has unique landform features and climatic conditions that make it particularly sensitive to climate warming (Sun et al., 2021 ).  The significant degradation of permafrost strongly affected the riverine carbon transport and sources (Chen et al., 2022 ). In 2017, the Qinghai Hydroped Catchment in Qianhuli (QHC) was built in the Qinghai Lake Basin, northeastern QTP (Li et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2020 ). The observed changes in the runoff process (Hu et al., 2022 ) and possibly coexisting effects on the mobilization of dissolved carbon prompted us to explore dissolved carbon dynamics in the riverine catchment. To address above mentioned knowledge gaps, it is assumed that the FT-affected SSF process would both change the DOC and DIC transport process and change their transformation process, while spatially rock characteristics determined DIC sources during the FT process. In this study, we collected stream water from the upper headwater to the middle and downward reaches, SSF water in soil, saprolite, and weathered bedrock layers, in an alpine headwater catchment. The DOC, DIC, and δ13 C-DIC characteristics were analyzed. Our objectives of this work are as follows: (1) analyze the influences of FT-affected SSF process on dissolved carbon transport; (2) explore the influences of the transformation process (organic carbon mineralization and chemical weathering) on DIC sources during FT; (3) evaluate the influences of rock distribution on dissolved carbon dynamics and DIC sources. This study would generate valuable information about the impact of the FT-affected SSF process and rock distribution on the DOC and DIC dynamics and DIC sources in an alpine headwater region.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The Qinghai Lake Basin (QLB) is located in the northeastern edge of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (QTP) (Zuo et al., 2023 ). The area is 29661 km2 , with elevation ranging from 3142 to 5286 m. The study area (37°25′ N and 100°15′ E) is located in the middle and lower reaches of the Shaliu River, which is the second-largest river in the Qinghai Lake Basin (Fig. 1  ). The area of the Shaliu River Basin is 1442 km2  (Hu et al., 2022 ). Based on the data collected from the automatic meteorological observing station in the Qinghai Hydroped Catchment in Qianhuli (Hu et al., 2022 ), the mean annual temperature is −0.6 °C and the mean annual precipitation is 389.3 mm, 70 % ∼ 80 % of which occurs in the summer (June-September) by small precipitation events. The soil type is subalpine meadow, and the rock types are primarily granodiorite and monzonitic granite of early Proterozoic age. Kobresia pygmaea , Salix oritrepha,  and Carex atrofusca subsp  are covered in this region.  2.2 Water sampling and experimental design The water sampling in the study sites was carried out from the upper headwater to the downstream, and 6 stream water sites and 1 lake water site were chosen (Fig. 1 ). The water samples were collected weekly or biweekly by hand from June 2022 to December 2022. From headwater to the downstream, the S-1 to S-6 were used to name stream sample sites in order. The Lakew was used to name the lake water sample site of Qinghai Lake. Detailed location information of sample sites was shown and summarized in Fig. 1  and Table 1  . Totally, from the upper headwater (S-1) to Qinghai Lake (Lakw), the elevation ranges from 3195 to 3622 m. From S-1 to S-6, the basin area is 103.72 km2 . All the water samples were filtered with 0.45 μm millipore filters, stored in 100 mL polyethylene plastic bottles, and sealed within parafilm. Before the collection of water samples, the sampling bottles were rinsed with ultrapure water and then dried to prevent cross-contamination. Water samples were refrigerated at 4 °C before analyses. The monitoring data in this study were collected from the Qinghai Hydroped Catchment (Fig. 1 d). The meteorological data from March 24, 2022, to December 31, 2022, were collected from the Bowen ratio energy balance observation system. In this study, the precipitation (P) and air temperature (Ta ) data were collected by a Bowen ratio tower, which is located adjacent to the outlet. ECH2O (Decagon/Campbell, USA) was installed near the Bowen ratio tower, and soil water content and soil temperature data from February 27, 2022, to December 31, 2022, were used in this study. Overland flow and SSF data from May 8, 2022, to December 31, 2022, were monitored by tipping buckets (Decagon/Campbell, USA) and rain gauges (Decagon/Campbell, USA) (Fig. 1 f). A gauging station with an automated flow velocity sensor RG-30 (Sommer Messtechnik, Austria) was installed in the adjacent S-2 (Fig. 1 e). By measuring the cross-sectional area of the river channel and the velocity of the response at different water levels many times, the flow discharge of the river channel was estimated. Li et al. (2018)  and Hu et al. (2020)  published detailed introductions. The data from March 20, 2022, to December 31, 2022 was used in this study.  2.3 Lab analyses The water samples were sent for testing in the State Key Laboratory of Earth Surface Processes and Resource Ecology of Beijing Normal University. The DOC and DIC were analyzed through a TOC-VCSH analyzer (Shimadzu, Japan). The cation of K+ , Ca2+  Na+  Mg2+ , and silica (Si) for water samples was determined with an inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP‐MS, PerkinElmer, USA) after 5 times dilution. The δ13 C‐DIC for water samples were determined with a MAT 253 Stable Isotope analyzer (Thermo Scientific, USA). The δ13 C‐DIC values were reported as per mil (‰) deviations from the standard VPDB.  2.4 Data processing and analyses 2.4.1 Division of FT period Based on the subsurface (SSF) divided method defined in (Hu et al., 2022 ), the FT period was identified in this work. When the daily maximum air temperature (Tamax ) is larger than 0 °C, frozen soil in the deep soil layer is not completely thawed, this period is defined as the thawing period. When the daily minimum air temperature (Tamin ) is larger than 0  °C and frozen soil is not completely thawed, this period is defined as the thawed period. The third period is the freezing period. During this period, the daily minimum air temperature (Tamin ) is smaller than 0  °C and the soil water begins to freeze. The mentioned method involved three kinds of data, namely, air temperature (Ta ), soil water temperature (Ts ), and precipitation data. The constraint and finally calculated period are shown in Table 2  . A more detailed introduction was published in a previous study (Hu et al., 2022 ).  2.4.2 Calculation of runoff depth and dilution effect (b ) The runoff depth was calculated based on the data from the automated flow velocity sensor RG-30 (Fig. 1 d). The runoff discharge in an area of 16.98 km2  from the upstream was measured by the sensor RG-30. The RG-30 automatically recorded data at 5-minute intervals. Considering the water was sampled on a daily scale, the flow data was uniformly calculated into a 1-day interval. Runoff depth and C-Q relation were calculated for S-2 by the following formula:(1) R = Q A      where Q is the runoff flow (m3 ), and A is the watershed area (m2 ). The concentration-discharge relationship (C-Q) well reflects solute concentration with flow conditions. To identify how DOC and DIC concentrations vary with flow conditions and catchment orders, the C-Q relationship was calculated as follows:(2) C = a ( Q ( r u n o f f )  )  b      where C  is the concentration of DOC (DIC) (mg/L), a  is a coefficient (mg/L), Q  (runoff) is the runoff depth (mm), and b  is the deviation from the dilution effect, reflecting the sensitivity of solute concentration to hydrological changes. Generally, if b  < -0.2, the solute concentration is negatively related to the discharge, and the solute displays a dilution behavior, which can also be defined as source limitation behavior. If b  > 0.2, the discharge has a positive effect on solute concentration, and the solute displays enrichment behavior, which means transport limitation behavior, if −0.2 < b <  0.2, the discharge influence on the solute concentration can be ignored, and the solute displays chemostatic behavior (Godsey et al., 2009 ). In addition, the coefficient of determination (r2 ) was used to determine the goodness of fit of the C-Q relationship, and the probability value (p ) at α  = 0.05 was used as the threshold for statistical significance (Gómez-Gener et al., 2021 ).  2.4.3 Identification of DIC source The sources of riverine DIC were mainly generated according to the following reaction processes:(3) C O 2  + H 2  O → H 2  C O 3      (4) ( C H 2  O )  n  + n H 2  O → n C O 2  + n H 2  O      Equations (3) and (4)  represent the dissolution of CO2  in the soil and the decomposition of organic matter in rivers, respectively. The soil CO2  mainly originates from root respiration and plant residue decomposition. Hence, the δ13 C value from equations (3) and (4)  are approximate to native plants.(5) C a x  M g 1 - x   C O 3  + H 2  C O 3  → x C a 2 +   + ( 1 - x )  M g 2 +   + 2 H C O 3 -      (6) 2 C a x  M g 1 - x   C O 3  + H 2  S O 4  → 2 x C a 2 +   + 2 ( 1 - x )  M g 2 +   + 2 H C O 3 -  + S O 4 2 -        Equations (5) and (6)  represent the carbonate weathering by carbonic acid and sulfate acid, respectively. For bicarbonate, half of the carbon originates from soil CO2  with the other half originates from carbonate dissolution during the carbonate weathering by carbonic acid, while total carbon originates from carbonate dissolution during the carbonate weathering by sulfate acid.(7) NaAlS i 3  O 8  + C O 2  + 2 H 2  O → N a +  + H C O 3 -  + 3 S i O 2  + A l ( O H )  3       Equation (7)  represents the silicate weathering by carbonic acid. For bicarbonate, total carbon originates from soil CO2  during this process. According to the analysis of equation (3)  ～ (7), the sources of riverine DIC can be divided into soil CO2  and carbonate rock dissolution. Miller-Tans plot was used to illustrating the DIC source information, which can be expressed as:(8) δ 13  C obs   × C obs   = δ 13  C S  × C S  + δ 13  C B  × C B      where the δ13 Cobs  and Cobs  are the observed carbon isotopic composition and concentration, respectively, they are δ13 C‐DIC and DIC concentration observations in this work. The δ13 CS  and CS  are the δ13 C values of the DIC source and the DIC source concentration, respectively. The δ13 CB  and CB  are carbon isotope values and concentration of the background, respectively. Equation (8)  can be written in the form of y = a × x + b:(9) δ 13  C obs   × C obs   = δ 13  C S  × C obs   - δ 13  C B  ( δ 13  C B  - δ 13  C S  )      the slope of the linear regression in equation (9)  represents the δ13 C-source value (δ13 CS ). The equation (9)  was named as Miller‐Tans plot regression (Miller & Tans, 2003 ). Campeau et al. (2018)  noted that CO2  evasion could change the δ13 C-DIC value by 1 ∼ 4 ‰ for stream water in high-latitude regions.  2.4.4 Statistical analysis Both the mark of the sample sites and the watershed area extraction corresponding to RG-30 were carried out by ArcGIS 10.7. The coefficient of Variance (Cv) was used to reflect the dispersion of DOC, DIC, and 13 C-DIC. The nonparametric pairwise multiple comparisons were performed by the one-way analysis of variance analysis (ANOVA) to calculate statistical differences in water chemistry, DOC, DIC, and δ13 C‐DIC at different periods and sites. Least square linear regressions were used for the Miller‐Tans plots analyses. Relationships were considered significant at p values < 0.05. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) was performed to identify if there were significant differences in slopes for the Miller-Tans plots among different sample sites. All statistical analyses were carried out by the statistical software Origin 2018).    3 Results 3.1 Spatiotemporal variability in DOC, DIC, and δ 13 -DIC The DOC, DIC, and δ13 C-DIC for sample sites exhibited significant seasonality (Fig. 2  ), with mean Cv of 0.5, 0.34, and 0.29, in order. The DOC concentrations had peaks in the 6 sample sites during the thawed period (June to August) when the runoff flow was high, the Peak values for DOC concentration ranged from 9.5 to 35.1 mg/L. From the thawing period to the thawed period (August), the DOC concentrations increased, from the thawed period (August) to the freezing period, the DOC concentrations decreased. The DIC concentrations were higher during the freezing period (September), while the pronounced peak value did not arise. The alternating occurrences of high and/or low values of DIC concentration indicated frequent flush and/or dilution behaviors. The phenomena were particularly evident in upstream (S-1 and S-2). The δ13 C-DIC values kept in high value from thawing to the thawed period. Since the later thawed period (Augu./st), the δ13 C-DIC values decreased. The overall characteristics of the DOC, DIC, and δ 13 -DIC values for sample sites were plotted in Fig. 3  . The mean DOC concentrations were decreased from S-1 (9.53 mg/L) to the S-6 (7.80 mg/L), while the mean DIC concentrations were increased from S-1 (25.08 mg/L) to the S-6 (38.90 mg/L). In terms of the water of Qinghai Lake, its mean DOC and DIC concentrations were 6.42 mg/L, and 44.57 mg/L, respectively. The mean δ 13 -DIC was enriched from S-1(−15.06 ‰) to the S-6(−13.26 ‰), for the δ 13 -DIC of the Qinghai Lake, it was −13.50 ‰ (Fig. 3 b). One-way ANOVA analysis results showed there were no significant differences for DOC and δ 13 -DIC among sample sites, in terms of DIC, only significant differences were found for DIC concentrations between S-1 and S-2 (p  = 0.0002). DOC, DIC, and δ 13 -DIC were divided into three periods based on the FT process (Fig. 4  ). DOC concentration was the largest during the thawed period, with a mean value of around 6.7 ∼ 11.6 mg/L. The DOC concentrations increased from thawing to the thawed period and decreased from thawed to the freezing period. In contrast, the DIC concentrations were small either during the thawing period or the thawed period. Five of seven sample sites reached the largest DIC concentrations during the freezing period, with mean values ranging from 27.6 to 50.4 mg/L. The δ 13 -DIC values were decreased from the thawed period to the thawing period. The one-way ANOVA analysis results indicated that the difference in δ 13 -DIC values is more significant than the DOC and DIC under different FT processes.  3.2 Characteristics of DIC source The Miller-Tans plot analysis showed a highly significant linear relationship for the stream water, lake water, SSF water, and groundwater in sample sites (Fig. 5  ). For the riverine stream water, the slope of Miller-Trans plot regressions ranged from −21.52 ‰ to −11.84 ‰, for the Qinghai Lake water, the slope was −25.2 ‰. During the thawed period, the sampling volume of the δ13 C-DIC was the largest and the more pronounced changing trend was found. Therefore, as shown in Table 3  , the slope of Miller-Trans plot regressions during this period was calculated. For the riverine stream water, the slope of Miller-Trans plot regressions was −16.85 ‰ ∼ −9.84 ‰, with a median of −13.48 ‰. For the Qinghai Lake water, the slope was −13.47 ‰.  3.3 Seasonal and spatial influences on DOC, DIC, and δ13 C-DIC The runoff changed pronouncedly across FT periods (Supplementary Figure 1 ). The relationships between solute concentrations and runoff flow were analyzed for S-2 (Fig. 6  ). In Fig. 6 a, the DOC concentrations were increased with rising runoff. The positive power-law relationship was fitted for S-2 with positive DOC concentration versus runoff slopes (b  > 0). Besides, the enriched DOC concentration arose (b  = 0.21 > 0.2), and the DIC concentrations decreased with the increases in runoff (Fig. 6 b). The negative power-law relationship between DIC concentration and runoff was fitted (b < 0), and the depletion behavior was identified for DIC concentration with −0.27 for b . In terms of the δ13 C-DIC, there was a positive relationship between the δ13 C-DIC values and runoff flow (Fig. 6 c). In summary, an increased runoff would promote the increase of DOC concentration and the decrease of DIC concentration, as well as bring heavy δ13 C-DIC. During the thawed period, δ13 C-DIC values were heavy, and significantly positive relationships between DOC concentrations and δ13 C-DIC values were only clarified for S-1 and Lakw (Fig. 7  ). For the other sample sites, no significant correlations were found. During the freezing period, there was a significantly positive relationship between DOC concentrations and δ13 C-DIC values from S-1 to S-5 (0.19 ∼ 0.66 for R2 ). Only four samples were collected for S-6 and Lakw during the freezing period, so relationships between DOC concentrations and the δ13 C-DIC values were excluded. For each sample site, the δ13 C-DIC values showed no significant correlation with DIC concentrations (Supplementary Figure 2 ). The mean values of DIC concentration and δ13 C-DIC during the sample period were calculated for every site, respectively. 1/DIC versus the δ13 C-DIC values for sample sites were plotted in Fig. 8  (a). With DIC concentration increased from S-1 to S-6, the δ13 C-DIC value tended to be heavier. Additionally, the Si/Ca ratios decreased from S-1 to S-5 (Fig. 8 b). It was noted that to ensure the results are representative, we use three sets of data from the thawing, thawed, and freezing periods to calculate the mean Si/Ca ratio. Additionally, we calculated the standard deviation to reflect the dispersion of the data across these three periods. We analyzed the relationship between the Si/Ca ratio and the δ13 C-DIC value (Supplementary Figure 3 ). There was a negative correlation between the two factors, indicating increased Si/Ca ratio would cause a light δ13 C-DIC value.   4 Discussion 4.1 FT process regulates dissolved carbon dynamics and DIC sources 4.1.1 Dissolved carbon transport changed by SSF process Our high-frequency field measurement results found that b  of C-Q was 0.21 for the DOC, which meant the DOC concentration was increased with runoff (Fig. 6 ). The explanatory mechanisms mainly include the spatial distribution of the DOC sources (Striegl et al., 2005 ) and hydrological connectivity (Laudon et al., 2011 ). Firstly, the frozen soil generally thawed from the shallow to deep layer in this study area (Hu et al., 2022 ), and the DOC concentration for SSF was increased from the soil layer to the saprolite layer and weathered bedrock layer, with mean values of 19.8 mg/L, 21.2 mg/L, and 26.3 mg/L, in order (Supplementary Table 1 ). The nonparametric pairwise multiple comparisons performed by one-way ANOVA analysis showed there were no significant DOC concentration differences in different SSF (p  > 0.1). Pan et al. (2020)  found soil organic carbon would decrease with depth in this study area. Thus, we speculated the DOC-enriched soil water in the upper layer could infiltrate into the deep layer quickly, and a small difference in DOC concentration emerged across the profile. The laboratory analysis results showed there was a high soil water storage capacity for the shallow soil layer (Hu et al., 2020 ), which ensured sufficient extraction of DOC. Besides, the high infiltration capacity was also found for the shallow soil layer, field investigation results showed many animal caves were distributed in the area, which ensured the soil water could quickly infiltrate into the deep layer. All the research findings have verified our previous speculation. It was suggested SSF process in hillslope plays a dominant role in DOC transport. Secondly, the high flow provided good hydrological connectivity (Boyer et al., 2000 ), and the organic carbon stagnated in the soil layers was connected and transported to the stream. In the study area, the high runoff flow occurred during the thawed period, and the low runoff flow occurred during the thawing and freezing period (Supplementary Figure 1 ). Simultaneously, the DOC concentration of SSF was found to be higher during the thawed period than in the other two periods (Fig. 4 ). So, more DOC was transported to the stream, resulting in enriched behavior of DOC (b  > 0.2) during the thawed period. Ultimately, the DOC concentrations showed increased and enriched behavior to increase runoff flow. For the C-Q relationship of DIC, b  was −0.27 (Fig. 6 ). The decreased DIC concentration with increased runoff flow revealed the depletion of DIC supply due to the limited source and good hydrological connectivity (Lupon et al., 2019 ). The DIC concentration in the soil layer (27.3 mg/L) was lower than that in the deeper saprolite layer (33.4 mg/L). Besides, the DIC concentration decreased again from the saprolite layer to the weathered bedrock layer (18.4 mg/L) (Supplementary Table 1 ). The One-Way ANOVA analysis results represented that the significant differences of DIC concentration existed in three kinds of SSF (p  < 0.001). In our study, the Ca2+  concentration in SSF1 and SSF2 was 2.0 ∼ 2.3 times higher than that in SSF3, while for the Si concentration, it was 0.8 ∼ 0.9 times lower than in SSF3. Paired t -test  showed there were significant differences for Ca2+  concentrations in different SSF (Supplementary Table 4 ), and Si concentrations were significantly different between SSF1 and SSF2. These observations indicated that the soil layer and the saprolite layer were controlled by the carbonate weathering process. While, for the weathered bedrock layer widely distributed with silicate rock, the primary chemical weathering process was silicate weathering. According to equations (5) and (7) , 1 mol of CO2  was consumed and 2 mol of HCO3 – were produced in the carbonate weathering process. But 1 mol of CO2  was consumed and 1 mol of HCO3 – was produced in the silicate weathering process. So, compared to the carbonate weathering, silicate weathering would produce less HCO3 – and resulted in a lower DIC concentration in silicates-dominated SSF3. Meanwhile, unlike the DOC, the high soil water storage capacity of the shallow soil layer provides good conditions for carbonate weathering. Additionally, the high infiltration capacity further decreases the DIC concentration in the deep layers, leading to a depletion effect on DIC. With the active layer deepening during the thawed high flow period, the DIC transport would be depleted due to the insufficient DIC in the deep layer. Besides, the hydrothermal condition changed with the FT process (Rehn et al., 2023; Striegl et al., 2005; Walvoord & Kurylyk, 2016 ), and these would eventually affect the carbon transformation process. The change trends of Si, Ca2+,  and Si/Ca in the three kinds of SSF were not consistent during the sampling period (Supplementary Figure 5 ). For example, the Si concentration was 1.38 ∼ 1.58 mg/L for the SSF3 before July 22, however, it increased quickly from 1.38 to 6.44 mg/L in the later period. The mean Si/Ca ratio was 0.13 with a standard deviation of 0.07 (Supplementary Table 5 ). Both for the SSF1 and for the SSF2, the mean Si/Ca ratios were 0.05, about 38 % of that for SSF1. These represented the weathering rates of carbonates and silicates in each soil profile were also inconsistent. Likewise, the Cv of Si/Ca for SSF1, SSF2, and SSF3 were 0.46, 0.20, and 0.54 in order, indicating the relative weathering rates of silicates and carbonates in each layer were changed pronouncedly different during the FT process, which contributed to the changes of DIC concentration.  4.1.2 DIC sources modulated by chemical weathering and organic carbon mineralization processes The DOC concentration, DIC concentration, and the δ13 C-DIC showed high variabilities across the FT process (Fig. 4 ), indicating the FT process affected the chemical weathering and organic carbon mineralization in the study area. The DOC mineralization and rock weathering determined the DIC concentration, and their different transports and mix processes made the δ13 C-DIC different (Campeau et al., 2018 ). The interceptions for carbon dynamics could be expressed based on the δ13 C-DIC variations across the FT processes. The δ13 C-DIC was positively correlated with the runoff flow (Fig. 6 c), reflecting the δ13 C-enriched values accompanied by rising runoff flow. The high flow could increase the reactive surface area of chemical weathering (Torres et al., 2015 ). In the study area, the high runoff flow was synced with high temperature (thawed period), and water was produced by the shallow soil and saprolite SSF. The low runoff flow mainly occurred during the freezing period, during which SSF from the deep weathered bedrock layer contributed more to the stream water. Generally, carbonate weathering consumed half carbon from carbonate rock (0 ‰) and the other half from soil CO2  (−25.9 ‰), so the DIC from carbonate weathering owned the δ13 C of −12.9 ‰. Carbon consumed by silicate weathering was fully from soil CO2 . Thus, the δ13 C-DIC from silicate weathering had the same δ13 C with soil CO2  (−25.9 ‰). In section 4.1.1 , we found the shallow soil and saprolite layer were determined by carbonate weathering while the deep weathering bedrock layer was controlled by silicate weathering. So, the high flow period tended to bring DIC from the carbonate weathering process. It well explained the positive relationship between runoff flow and δ13 C-DIC. Additionally, from the thawed to the freezing period, the δ13 C-DIC also significantly decreased with the decreased runoff flow (Fig. 4 c). This was a further correct verification of the above explanation. In Fig. 6 , we found b  for DIC was −0.27, which meant the change rates of DIC concentration were decreased with runoff flow lowing, indicating additional sources of DIC supply. In Supplementary Figure 4 , the DIC concentration was positively related to DOC concentration during the freezing period. Likewise, five of the six sample sites showed positive linear relationships between the δ13 C-DIC and DOC concentration (Fig. 7 ). The DOC concentration decreased from the thawed to freezing period with δ13 C-DIC tended to be depleted (Fig. 4 ). These reflected that the great magnitude of DIC originated from the organic carbon mineralization during the freezing period. The organic carbon in the deep layer was older than that in the shallow layer (Cory et al., 2013; Mu et al., 2017 ), and it was approved to be easier to mineralize (Drake et al., 2015 ). Hence, the highly biodegradable DOC in the deep SSF made its contribution to the DIC increase from the thawed to freezing period. Moreover, the deep pathways of water and carbon in the deep SSF increased water transit time (Frampton & Destouni, 2015 ), and the buffered temperature decreased (Sjöberg et al., 2021 ). It provided a sufficient reaction time and appropriate reaction temperature for the organic carbon mineralization, and offset the negative effects of temperature reduction on organic carbon mineralization (M. Song et al., 2010 ). In summary, the results highlight the crucial role of both vertical (infiltration) and lateral flows in regulating the transport and transformation of dissolved carbon from soil to streams. During the freeze–thaw process, vertical flow affects the distribution of DOC and DIC within the soil profile, for example, it facilitates the movement of DOC from shallow to deep layers. Meanwhile, lateral flow impacts the transformation of DOC and DIC being transported to the stream, with prolonged transport time of deep subsurface flow potentially promoting organic carbon mineralization.   4.2 Spatial rock distribution Constraints DIC sources From the Miller-Tans plot in Fig. 5 , we found δ13 Cs values in the study area ranged from −21.52 ‰ to −11.84 ‰. It indicated the dominant biogenic and minor geogenic DIC sources based on the summarized DIC sources framework, which suggested the δ13 C values of the biogenic DIC ranging from −25.9 ‰ to −12.9 ‰ (Campeau et al., 2017 ). The biogenic DIC sources included silicate weathering by carbonic acid and organic carbon mineralization. The geogenic DIC sources included the weathering of carbonates by carbonic acid and/or sulfuric acid. On one hand, the negative δ13 C values of the silicate weathering were around −25.9 ‰. The dissolution of silicate carbonates can produce 13 C‐depleted DIC. On the other hand, the carbonic acid carbonate weathering can produce δ13 C‐DIC values around −12.9 ‰. In this study, the δ13 Cs were lower than the carbonic acid weathered DIC from the carbonates, but higher than the carbonic weathered DIC from the silicates, and it was closer to the silicates. Therefore, a 13 C‐depleted source for DIC likely exists. The different δ13 C‐DIC source values among the sample sites may reflect the variabilities in stream sites. Si/Ca ratios were negatively correlated with δ13 C‐DIC (R2  = 0.54, Supplementary Figure 3 ), implying the DIC sources were significantly affected by the spatial rock distribution and organic carbon mineralization process. Water solute was transported from the upper headwater to the middle and/or downstream, mixed with that from adjacent catchments, and finally, input to the lake was the most spatially extensive process (Chiriboga & Borges, 2023 ). In this process, we found the decreased DOC concentration and increased DIC concentration in the study area (Fig. 3 ). For the decreased result of DOC concentration, the stronger organic carbon mineralization or intense dilution effect on DOC from the headwater to downstream were the main two possible reasons. Organic carbon mineralization brings light isotopes (Palmer et al., 2001 ), while the δ13 C-DIC values of stream water in the middle and downstream were heavier (Fig. 3 b) than that in the upper headwater. Additionally, δ13 C-DIC was not significantly correlated with DOC concentration in Fig. 7 . Join the two phenomena, it was supported that the gradual decrease in the DOC concentration from headwater to downstream was due to the enhancement of the dilution effect, and its mineralization had little effect on the DIC concentration. Compared to the effect of organic carbon mineralization on DIC concentration in the SSF generation process, the organic carbon mineralization effect on DIC concentration was weakened in water movement and carbon transfer process among the riverine. It might be related to the faster water transfer velocity in riverine stream water compared to the SSF (Hrachowitz et al., 2009 ), which introduced insufficient time for DOC mineralization. The DIC concentration was increased from the upper headwater to the middle and downward regions, thus, the chemical weathering process was changed (Hélie et al., 2002 ), and organic carbon mineralization intensity was adjusted (Das et al., 2005 ), and CO2  evasion (Liu et al., 2023 ) were the three possible reasons. The CO2  evasion generally increased the δ13 C-DIC but decreased the DIC concentration due to the light carbon isotope escaping first (Van Geldern et al., 2015 ). In this study, the enriched δ13 C-DIC but increased DIC concentration indicated that DIC transport was not strictly regulated by CO2  evasion. It seemed that chemical weathering was the main control on governing the DIC concentrations from the headwater to downstream. In the same sample site, no significant correlation was found between δ13 C-DIC and DIC during the sample period (Supplementary Figure 2 ). However, from the headwater to downstream, the DIC concentration was increased accompanied by enriched δ13 C--DIC (Fig. 8 a). It indicated that the chemical weathered was enhanced in the downstream, and the more DIC was produced. The Si/Ca ratios were decreased from the headwater S-1 (0.14) to the downstream S-5 (0.12) (Fig. 8 b), indicating that the carbonate weathering in the downstream was more intense than the headwater. The previous study found that granodiorite and monzonitic granite were widely distributed in the headwater region (Hu et al., 2022 ), which approved more silicate weathering generated in the upper headwater region. Besides, the δ13 C-DIC values were negatively related with the Si/Ca ratios (R2  = 054 in Supplementary Figure 3 ). The above results showed that the rock distribution in the basin was the main factor governing the DIC concentration and sources.  4.3 Implications and uncertainty of this study Our work provides insight into the impact of subsurface flow on riverine DOC and DIC dynamics in alpine regions and the determinants of riverine DIC sources. We found that the deepening active layer promotes subsurface flow move into deep layers, facilitating the percolation of DOC and activating DIC in these deep layers. Consequently, more dissolved carbon is exported from the deep layer. Under climate warming conditions, the deepening active layer potentially leads to increased DOC infiltration and organic carbon mineralization, reflected in increased DIC concentration and decreased DOC concentration in deep subsurface flow, this should be explored in future work. Additionally, carbonate weathering and organic carbon mineralization jointly regulate the sources of DIC in small hillslope scale. In contrast, the sources of DIC in rivers are primarily influenced by the rock distribution at larger scales. This suggests we may integrate small-scale field monitoring data with models to advance the understanding of carbon transformation processes at the hillslope scale (Stewart et al., 2024 ), which will aid in quantifying and predicting carbon storage and emissions in global cold regions. Our field measurements revealed the characteristics of dissolved carbon dynamics and changes in DIC sources during freeze–thaw processes, enhancing our understanding of the effect of subsurface flow on dissolved carbon transport and transformation in cold regions. However, further exploration is necessary to predict the inter-annual variation of freeze–thaw effects. Additionally, our study periods were thawing, thawed, and freezing periods, lacking data from the frozen period. Therefore, future research should further explore the changes in dissolved carbon during this stage.   5 Conclusion In this study, the dissolved carbon accompanied by the isotope tracing analysis methods was used to explore the characteristics of dissolved carbon and DIC source. Our findings reveal that the FT process significantly impacts dissolved carbon dynamics and DIC sources through its effect on the SSF process. The deepening of the active layer during the FT process enhances the movement of SSF into deeper layers, which activates DIC in these deep layers. Concurrently, DOC from the shallow layer infiltrates rapidly into deeper layers, resulting in minimal differences in DOC concentrations across layers. This leads to the enriched behavior of DOC (b  = 0.21) and depleted behavior of DIC (b  = −0.27) during the FT process. The DIC sources in the deep, silicate-rich layers are produced by increased silicate weathering, and organic carbon mineralization in the deep layer also contributes to DIC. On a spatial scale, the distribution of rocks, particularly the Si/Ca ratio, predominantly controls the chemical weathering process and determines the DIC sources. In contrast, the influence of organic carbon mineralization on DIC sources is reduced. This study elucidates the influencing mode of subsurface flow on dissolved carbon transport and transformation and emphasizes the significant influence of spatial rock distribution on riverine DIC sources.
1 Introduction Nitrogen, an indispensable nutrient, plays a pivotal role in fostering plant growth and development (Alam et al., 2023 ). The mangrove wetland, a critical component of coastal environments, is characterized by an abundant and efficient nitrogen cycling process within its sediments (Wang et al., 2019;Li et al., 2022 ). The nitrogen cycle stands as one of the earth's most essential biogeochemical processes (Xiong et al., 2023 ). Coastal wetlands, being hotspots of biogeochemical activity, significantly contribute to the global nitrogen cycle through their nitrogen cycling processes (Li et al., 2023a;Tian et al., 2024 ).
