It is important to note that, here again, this ranking remains valid in the case of using the average KGE as the performance metric instead of MCCPS. In an attempt to explain the consistency in the ranking of each model’s responses corresponding to the three precipitation products, we employed seven continuous statistical indices:− Six metrics, commonly used in rainfall products evaluation studies (Benkirane et al., 2023 ; Stefania Camici et al., 2020 ; Ouatiki et al., 2017 ; Rachidi et al., 2023 ; Saouabe et al., 2020 ), relating precipitation products to observed rainfall at the catchment scale: Kling-Gupta efficiency score (KGE_P-Pobs), Pearson correlation coefficient (CC_P-Pobs), a bias-related metric (Bias*, see  Table 6 ), root mean square error (RMSE_P-Pobs), mean absolute error (MAE_P-Pobs), and Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ) (NSE_P-Pobs).  − One metric relating precipitation products to observed runoff: Pearson correlation coefficient (CC_P-Qobs).    It is important to note that the evaluation of the precipitation products is beyond the scope of this paper. For information purposes, the boxplots of these seven indices, for ERA5, CHIRPS, and PERSIANN-CDR, across the 30 studied catchments can be found in Appendix D. For all the models, we investigated for each catchment the compatibility between (i) the ranking of the precipitation products with regard to each metric, and (ii) the ranking of models’ responses to these products when used as forcing data. Specifically for each model, a catchment receives a compatibility score of 1 for a given metric if the ranking of the precipitation products according to that metric matches the ranking of the hydrological performances associated with these products. Otherwise, the compatibility score is 0. For each metric and model, we subsequently calculate the cumulative compatibility score by summing the number of catchments that demonstrate compatibility with respect to that specific metric. Therefore, for each model, the cumulative compatibility score of a given metric ranges potentially from 0 to 30, and the metric with the highest cumulative score is considered the most explanatory metric for the hydrological performance of the precipitation products.  Fig. 14  shows that Pearson correlation between precipitation products and observed runoff (CC_P-Qobs) is by far the most explanatory index for the uniformity in the models’ behavior when forced by the various precipitation products since it has the highest cumulative compatibility score for 7 out of 8 models, meaning that the superior hydrological performance of ERA5 (and of CHIRPS compared to PERSIANN-CDR) for all the models is due to its relatively high linear correlation with the observed streamflow of the studied catchments. This finding is supported by the evidence we found in the previous analysis in which we found that this feature is the most important predictor for model performance, which reinforces the similar results found by (Bisselink et al., 2016 ). However, this result does not align with the findings of (Stefania Camici et al., 2020 ) in which they concluded, using a single daily model that was forced by inputs from three precipitation products across more than 1300 catchments in Europe, that RMSE_P-Pobs and Bias are the most reliable indices to select the best-performing precipitation product for hydrological modeling. We hypothesize that this was the case either (i) because, for each used product, RMSE_P-Pobs and Bias were monotonically correlated to CC_P-Qobs in the context of their study area, or (ii) because the structure of MISDc (Brocca et al., 2011 ) – the daily hydrological model used in their study – differs greatly from that of the eight monthly models we employed.   5 Conclusions The aim of this large-sample hydrology study was to assess the performance of eight monthly lumped hydrological models (GR2M, XM, WM, VUB, abcd, DWBM, GR5M, and Wapaba) in 30 Moroccan catchments. As part of this assessment, we examined how model performance, expressed as KGE, relates to model complexity, model structure, and catchment features (more than 200 features were used), and we investigated how the employed models react to three rainfall products (ERA5, CHIRPS, and PERSIANN-CDR) when used as forcing input data. The main findings can be summarized as follows, with each accompanied by its practical implication:− Across all catchments, no hydrological model exhibited consistently superior or inferior performance. Additionally, using a new comparative measure (MCCPS) that offers a more encompassing comparison between the models, Wapaba was found to be the best-ranked model in terms of overall performance, followed by abcd and GR5M that yielded comparable results, then by DWBM, GR2M, XM, VUB, and WM that scored a null MCCPS. Implication : Therefore, when possible, it is important to consider more than one hydrological model in runoff prediction.  − Model performance is affected more by model structure and how runoff generation is described than by model complexity. In particular, the number of storages as well as the number of parameters included in direct runoff calculation seemed to affect positively the model performance. Additionally, the relatively good performance of the 2-parameter model GR2M and bad performance of the 3-parameter model WM were attributed respectively to (i) the detailed description of the hydrological processes and (ii) the simplistic linear representation of the runoff generation process with regard to precipitation. Implication : Therefore, in model development, it is crucial to place greater emphasis on the mathematical equations used to describe runoff generation – with the avoidance of linear relationships between runoff and precipitation – rather than solely relying on using more free parameters.  − Contrary to non-hydro-climatic factors such as the physiographic characteristics, hydro-climatic features especially the calibration-related and the calibration/validation-related features are the only type of characteristics that had a statistically significant link to model performance. Implication : Therefore, in large-sample hydrology studies, it is worthwhile to test various calibration/validation scenarios for each of the studied catchments, and then apply the most suitable scenario for each catchment. This proposed approach is in opposition to the conventional one employed in this study which uses a single scenario for all the catchments.  − Model performance is significantly and positively related to the richness of rainfall and runoff calibration data regarding its content of wet and dry years, both in absolute terms and in calibration relative to validation, with the particularity of the dry conditions being more impactful than the wet ones. Implication : It is then important to find the most relevant index, to model performance, to characterize this richness.  − In response to varied rainfall forcing data, all the models exhibited a consistent pattern: superior performance with ERA5 compared to CHIRPS, and lower performance with PERSIANN-CDR. Implication : Within the study area and in situations where observed rainfall data is unavailable and there is limited capacity to analyze hydrological model responses to different rainfall products, the use of ERA5 precipitation product is recommended.  − The primary factor that significantly impacts model performance is the linear relationship between rainfall and runoff; a stronger linear correlation between these two variables results in enhanced model performance. Implication : Thus, in hydrological applications, it is advantageous for the performance of hydrological models to base the choice of (i) a method for filling missing rainfall values, (ii) a technique for spatially interpolating rainfall data, or (iii) a precipitation product for forcing hydrological models, on the highest linear correlation with the observed runoff.
1 Introduction Drought is one of the most destructive natural disasters and is highly susceptible to serious ecological, economic, and social impacts (Lee et al., 2022 ). Drought forecasting can provide a scientific basis for the monitoring, early warning, and risk assessment of drought in a basin or region (Javed et al., 2021 ). Drought prediction involves studying the mechanism of dry-early occurrence and constructing corresponding dry-early prediction models to predict the occurrence, development, and termination of drought (Dash et al., 2023 ). Drought forecasting helps in the optimization of the operation of the water resource system and the implementation of appropriate drought preventive and mitigation measures, as well as decision-making analysis (Altunkaynak et al., 2021 ). Common drought prediction methods include data-driven, kinetic dry-early prediction, and ensemble drought predictions (Mouatadid et al., 2018 ). Kinetic dry-early prediction models based on forecast product outputs from current climate models have strong physical mechanisms, but coarse resolution, model complexity, and uncertainty in model inputs, structure, and parameters (Wilby et al., 2000 ). Ensemble drought prediction models based on ensemble forecast products use multiple climate models, and multiple model runs are computationally expensive (Ganguli and Reddy, 2014 ). Compared with the kinetic dry-early prediction model and ensemble drought prediction model, the data-driven drought prediction model, which establishes the relationship between the prediction object and the prediction factors based on historical observation data, has the advantages of simple modeling and easy-to-implement methodology and has been widely used (Chakraborty et al., 2021 ). Data-driven drought prediction models can be classified into two categories: statistical and machine learning methods (Rehman et al., 2019 ). Drought is characterized by strong nonlinearity, and statistical methods have limited ability to handle nonlinear problems. Machine learning methods are widely used for drought prediction owing to their inherent nonlinear properties and modeling flexibility (Chaabene et al., 2020, Prodhan et al., 2022 ). Machine learning methods commonly used in hydrology include support vector regression (SVR) and artificial neural network (ANN) methods (Gupta, 2010 ). The main advantages of SVR over ANN are as follows: the number of samples required is relatively small for the same problem complexity, SVR handles the case of linear indistinguishability of the sample data using slack variables (also called penalty variables) and kernel function techniques, and the SVR structure is less risky (Vafakhah and Khosrobeigi Bozchaloei, 2020 ). The ANN method has defects, such as the number of nodes in the hidden layer, that are difficult to determine and can easily converge to local minima, which affects its prediction effect to some extent (Baboo and Shereef, 2010, Ding et al., 2013 ). The results of Mokhtarzad et al. (2017)  and Borji et al. (2016)  showed that SVR-based models predict meteorological and hydrological droughts better than ANN models. Drought predictions are typically based on drought indices (Quiring, 2009 ), and research scholars have done a lot of prediction studies, such as, Sigaroodi et al. (2014)  used the saline Maharloo Lake in Iran as a study area to determine the best variables among 40 indices and identify the proper time-lag between dependent and independent variables for each month by using cross-correlation and stepwise regression techniques. ANN and multivariate stepwise regression methods were used to predict monthly precipitation. Rafiei-Sardooi et al. (2018)  employed the standardized precipitation index (SPI), as a meteorological drought assessment tool, over 3- and 12-month time scales during the years 1970 to 2014 and compared the accuracy of the neuro-fuzzy model with time-series models for modeling of drought. Xu et al. (2020)  calculated SPI using daily precipitation data from 1951 to 2017 at 19 meteorological stations in Henan Province, China, and proposed an ARIMA-SVR model for predicting its drought. From previous studies, the timescales of these studies mainly focus on seasonal and annual scales (Zhao et al., 2021 ), with relatively few studies on drought at the monthly scale and a lack of large samples to verify the reliability of the prediction models. The prediction of monthly-scale droughts is important for the study of short-duration droughts. The monthly-scale drought index series comprised a mixture of high- and low-frequency signals. The SVR single model has a better prediction effect on low-frequency signals, whereas the high-frequency signals are poorly predicted by the SVR model because of the highly nonlinear and drastically varying characteristics, which increases the difficulties in parameter estimation and data learning of the SVR single model and thus leads to the unsatisfactory direct prediction of monthly-scale droughts using the SVR single model (Bian et al., 2016 ). To attenuate the influence of high-frequency signals on the accuracy of the SVR model in predicting the monthly-scale drought index, the monthly-scale drought index series is generally decomposed into several subsequences of high-frequency and low-frequency signals by wavelet transform (WT), empirical mode decomposition (EMD), and extreme-point symmetric mode decomposition (ESMD), which are then predicted using a single SVR model (Wang et al., 2020 ). ESMD is not only able to solve the subjectivity of artificially determining the basic functions of the WT and the modal aliasing problem of EMD but also has a higher decomposition efficiency, which can achieve better smoothing and simplification of the signal (Liu et al., 2018, Ling et al., 2023 ). Except for some subsequences (including the highest-frequency signal), the subsequences obtained by ESMD were relatively stable and had a good prediction effect. However, the subsequence containing the highest-frequency signal obtained by ESMD is still characterized by strong fluctuations and a large absolute value, which makes the prediction results unable to meet the accuracy requirements; therefore, it is generally necessary to perform a secondary decomposition of the subsequence containing the highest-frequency signal (Zhang et al, 2023 ). Most of the secondary decomposition methods utilize the wavelet noise cancellation method for the noise-containing highest-frequency component. However, it is prone to the problem of missing main signals, and the selection of the wavelet function mainly relies on personal experience, which is slightly artificial and fails to solve the problem of low prediction accuracy of the highest-frequency component (Spinosa and Iafrati, 2022 ). The variational mode decomposition (VMD) method can further transform the more complex sequence of the highest-frequency component into several relatively smooth subsequences to adapt to the performance of the SVR model in terms of parameter estimation, data learning, etc., to improve prediction accuracy. In addition, under the premise of ensuring the decomposition effect, it can decompose fewer components to minimize the number of predictions, thus improving prediction efficiency (Yu et al., 2023 ). Therefore, the goal of this study is to address the problem of low accuracy in existing monthly-scale drought prediction models. Based on the primary decomposition of the monthly-scale drought index using the ESMD method, the highest-frequency component after the primary decomposition was decomposed twice using the VMD method. The ESMD, VMD, SVR, and other models were organically integrated to establish a new monthly-scale drought secondary decomposition (ESMD-VMD) combined prediction model. The effectiveness and prediction accuracy of the combined ESMD-VMD prediction model developed in this study were evaluated using 100 meteorological stations in the Pearl River Basin of China as the application object, and the prediction results were compared with those of comparable models.  2 Methods 2.1 Standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index (SPEI) The SPEI is a standard meteorological drought index based on the standardized precipitation index (SPI) proposed by Vicente-Serrano et al. (2010) . The SPEI can measure drought severity based on its intensity and duration and can determine the onset and end of drought episodes. It considers the effect of evaporation on the drought severity and is simple to calculate. The SPEI not only incorporates the effects of temperature and precipitation on drought but also comprehensively considers evapotranspiration by introducing potential evapotranspiration, pooling the sensitivity of palmer drought severity index to evapotranspiration and the multiscale characteristics of the SPI, which is a better drought evaluation index (Kamruzzaman et al., 2022 ). The SPEI calculation method is described by Zuo et al. (2019) . In this study, SPEI-1 was used to denote the monthly standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index.  2.2 Extreme-point symmetric mode decomposition (ESMD) The ESMD method is based on the Fourier transform, which improves the Hilbert-Yellow transform method and can be used in all disciplines involving data processing, such as information science, ecology, meteorology, and hydrology. The ESMD method inherits the advantages of the EMD and uses the least squares method to obtain the final residual modes, calculate the “adaptive global mean” of the entire sequence, and determine the optimal number of screenings. As a data-driven adaptive nonlinear time-varying signal decomposition method, ESMD has strong adaptive and localized properties and is suitable for nonlinear and nonsmooth time series analysis (Li et al., 2020 ). The ESMD method is one of the most recent methods for obtaining the trend and period of changes in an entire time series, which enables the decomposition of the original time series into a series of M−components (high- and low-frequency components) and a trend item, R. The ESMD method can be used to obtain trends and periods of change for an entire time series. The specific process of this decomposition method has been described by Yang et al. (2020) .  2.3 Sample entropy (SampEn) The highest-frequency component after primary decomposition (ESMD) can be determined using sample entropy or a Fourier transform to plot the amplitude–frequency curve. The entropy value is a dimensionless metric used to characterize the complexity of a signal sequence. Sample entropy is a method proposed by Richman, which is similar to approximate entropy but with better accuracy. Sample entropy does not include a comparison of its data segments, which not only improves the calculation accuracy and reduces the calculation time, but also calculates the sample entropy independent of the data length (Yentes et al., 2013 ). The greater the sample entropy, the greater the time series complexity (containing the highest-frequency signal). The sample entropy calculation method has been described by Alcaraz and Rieta (2010) . In this study, we calculated the sample entropy of the M−components obtained by primary decomposition (ESMD) and selected the component with the largest entropy value, that is, the highest-frequency component after primary decomposition.  2.4 Variational mode decomposition (VMD) VMD is a nonrecursive adaptive signal decomposition algorithm proposed on the EMD algorithm by Dragomiretskiy et al. (2013) . The VMD decomposition process consists of two parts: constructing the variational model and solving the variational model. Based on the set iteration threshold, the final decomposed signal was obtained by continuously updating the center frequency and bandwidth. In general, the variational problem involves determining the minimum sum of the bandwidths of each modal function on the premise that the sum of all modal functions is equal to the signal to be decomposed (Dibaj et al, 2021 ). The VMD method decomposes several modes, denoted as VM1 , VM2 , and VMk . The specific process of this decomposition method has been described by Ren et al. (2019) . In this study, the VMD method was used for the secondary decomposition of the highest-frequency component after the primary ESMD decomposition.  2.5 Support vector regression (SVR) The basic idea of SVR is to establish a functional relationship between the input and output data under a limited training dataset. The core involves mapping nonlinear sample points in the input space to linear data in a high-dimensional space via nonlinear mapping φ(.  ), thus constructing the following fitting function: f(x) = w*(x) + b. Here, w and b denote the weight vector and bias term, respectively. This ensures that the prediction error is minimized while keeping the regression function deflated. SVR achieves linear regression of SVR in high-dimensional space by introducing an insensitive loss function ɛ (ɛ > 0, which ensures that the organic sample data under study will be fitted nonlinearly within the accuracy of ɛ) and a slack variable ξ (ξ ≥ 0, which denotes the sample's bias error), thereby realizing SVR in high-dimensional space. The addition of the ɛ and ξ variables changes the problem into a minimization problem for solving the objective function:min 1 2  P ω P  2  + C ∑ i = 1  n  ξ i  + ξ i ∗          S . T . ω ∗ φ x i     + b    - y i  ⩽ ε + ξ i     y i  - ω ∗ φ x i     + b     ⩽ ε + ξ i ∗   ( i = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n )      ξ i  ⩾ 0 , ξ i ∗  ⩾ 0              where ξ i  , ξ i ∗     is a slack variable that represents the input error of the training dataset and reflects the deviation error of the sample; C(C>0) is the penalty factor, which indicates the strength of the penalty when the sample is erroneous and is used to balance the algorithm complexity and fitting accuracy; and ɛ is the insensitive loss function during the training process (Dhiman et al., 2019 ). A small numerical value affects the fitting accuracy, and overfitting may occur if the numerical value is extremely large. Therefore, choosing the appropriate penalty factor C for the predictive performance of SVR is important. In practical applications, the objective function optimization problem is transformed into a Lagrangian function by introducing Lagrange multipliers, replacing the inner product operation in the linear problem with a kernel function, mapping the nonlinear data samples into other high-dimensional spaces, and using a linear function in this high-dimensional space to fit the nonlinear sample size to determine the decision function of the SVR.f ( x )  = ∑ i = 1  n  α i  - α ̂  i      K x , x i      + b     where α i  , α ̂  i     denotes the Lagrange multipliers, n denotes the number of support vector regression machines, and c is the kernel function. Typical kernel functions include linear kernel functions, polynomial kernel functions, and Gaussian radial-basis kernel functions (RBF). Compared to other kernels, the RBF is a highly localized kernel with only one parameter (denoting the width of the RBF, which is used to control the tangent width of the function), which considerably reduces the time complexity and is therefore widely used. The kernel function of the RBF was K x , x i      = exp - P x - x i  P  2   2 σ 2         (Hong et al., 2011 ).  2.6 Sparrow search algorithm (SSA) The kernel function parameter K and penalty factor C have significant impacts on the prediction performance of the SVR model. They are generally determined by optimization using genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization algorithms, and gray wolf optimization algorithms. The SSA is a new heuristic optimization algorithm proposed by Xue et al. (2020) , which has the advantages of simplicity and ease of implementation, high search accuracy, fast convergence, good stability, and robustness. The algorithm performs an iterative optimization search by simulating sparrow foraging and anti-predation behavior. Individual sparrows in the population are categorized into discoverers, joiners, and vigilantes, and the location of each sparrow is iteratively updated to find a globally optimal solution (Rocco S et al., 2013 ). In this study, SSA was used to optimize the kernel function parameter K and penalty factor C. The SSA-SVR prediction model is as follows (Fig. 1  ): Step 1: Determine the parameters of the SVR model to be optimized and assign the parameters to individuals in the SSA. Step 2: Determine the parameters of the SSA: number of populations N, search range [ X min  , X max  ]   , maximum number of iterations, proportion of discoverers, and proportion of vigilantes, using the mean square error obtained from the SVR training as the fitness value. Step 3: Randomly generate the initial solution, calculate the initial fitness of the population, and record the current global optimal and worst individuals. Step 4: Start an iterative optimization search to update the finder, joiner, and vigilante positions. Step 5: Calculate the population fitness after updating the position, and perform greedy selection to select the current global optimal fitness with the corresponding individual. Step 6: Repeat Steps 4 and 5 until the end of the iteration to output a globally optimal individual. Step 7: Reassign the parameters contained in the globally optimal individual to the SVR model, train the model and perform simulation prediction, and output the simulation results (Wang et al., 2020 ).  2.7 Phase space reconstruction (PSR) The prediction of monthly drought-time indices using SVR requires the use of a delayed coordinate state-space reconstruction method to determine its inputs and outputs, which can be solved by PSR. Packard et al. (1980)  proposed the PSR theory and constructed a new system using the dynamic laws of the original system by choosing the appropriate dimension and delay time of the reconstruction space. The new system was a one-dimensional space; thus, the original one-dimensional time series was reconstructed into a multidimensional space. Takens (1981)  proved that a reconstructed space can be found to recover the laws of a system. For a given time series,X = x i  i = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , N              The phase space of its reconstruction can be expressed as follows:x 1   x 1 + τ    ⋯  x 1 + ( m - 1 ) τ     x 2    x 2 + τ    ⋯  x 2 + ( m - 1 ) τ     ⋮   ⋮  ⋮  ⋮   x M    x M + τ    ⋯  x M + ( m - 1 ) τ             where m denotes the embedding dimension, τ denotes the time delay, and M denotes the number of phase points,M = N - ( m - 1 ) T .    By Takens' theorem, the values of m and τ need to be chosen reasonably to obtain the proper phase space and improve the accuracy of time series prediction. The time delay τ is computed by the C–C method and the mutual correlation method, and the embedding dimension m is computed by the G-P algorithm, pseudo-nearest neighbor method, correlation integral method, and Cao method. In this study, the PSR technique was applied to process the predicted time series to form the input of SVR, and the mutual correlation and Cao methods were used to determine the time delay τ and the embedding dimension m (Fan et al., 2018 ).   3 Model construction 3.1 Combined monthly-scale drought secondary decomposition (ESMD-VMD) prediction model The monthly-scale drought secondary decomposition (ESMD-VMD) combined prediction model integrates the ESMD, SampEn, VMD, PSR, SSA, and SVR models. The steps for developing this model are as follows: Step 1. Decompose SPEI-1 using the ESMD method to obtain several subsequences: M1 , M2 , M3 ,…, Mn  components, and a trend item R. Step 2. Evaluate the complexity of the M−components using the SampEn method to determine the highest-frequency component (Mp ). Step 3. Secondary decomposition of the highest-frequency component (Mp ) using the VMD method to obtain the subsequences VM1 , VM2 …VMk . Step 4. Both Steps 1 and 3 decompositions yield subsequences that are input into the SVR model formed using the PSR method. Step 5. Substitute the input from Step 4 into the “SSA-SVR” model to predict the subsequence obtained from Steps 1 and 3. Step 6. Superimpose the Step5 subsequence results to obtain the prediction of SPEI-1, where the prediction of the highest-frequency component, Mp , is the sum of the predicted values of the subsequences (VM1 , VM2 …VMk ). A flowchart of the construction of the combined monthly-scale drought secondary decomposition (ESMD-VMD) prediction model is shown in Fig. 1 .  3.2 Contrasting models To ensure comparability between different models, a comparison model was constructed based on the SVR model, and the following scenarios were considered (Fig. 2  ). (1) Without the decomposition of SPEI-1, the SVR model was directly utilized for prediction, that is, a single PSR-SSA-SVR model was constructed (denoted as Model 1). (2) ESMD was used to perform primary decomposition of SPEI-1 (M1 , M2 , M3 ,…, Mn  components, and a trend item R), rather than secondary decomposition. The SSA-SVR model was used to predict the M1 , M2 , M3 …Mn  components and the trend term R. The predicted series were summed, that is, the ESMD-PSR-SSA-SVR primary decomposition combination prediction model was developed (denoted as Model 2). (3) Based on the primary decomposition of the SPEI-1 using ESMD (M1 , M2 , M3 …Mn  components, and a trend term R), the highest frequency component (Mp ) after the primary decomposition was decomposed quadratically using wavelet noise cancellation to obtain Mw , and then Mw  as well as the other components were predicted using the SVR model. The predicted series were summed. According to the heuristic threshold selection rule, the db3 and db5 wavelets from the Daubechies wavelet family, which are commonly used in the hydrological analysis, were used to remove the noisy high-frequency components. Thus, the ESMD-SampEn-WD(d3)-PSR-SSA-SVR model (denoted as Model 3) and the ESMD-SampEn-WD(d5)-PSR-SSA-SVR combined prediction model (denoted as Model 4) were developed. For ease of expression, the monthly-scale drought secondary decomposition (ESMD-VMD) combined prediction model established in this study is referred to as Model 5.  3.3 Model performance evaluation metrics To verify the prediction ability of the model, four evaluation indexes, the Wilmot consistency index (WIA), Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and root mean square error (RMSE), were used with the following formulas:WIA = 1 - ∑ i = 1  n  y ̂  i  - y i      2   ∑ i = 1  n  y ̂  i  - y  ¯      + y i  - y  ¯           2        NSE = 1 - ∑ i = 1  N  y i  - y ̂  l      2   ∑ i = 1  N  y i  - y  ¯       2        MAE = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  y i  - y ̂  i           RMSE   = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  y i  - y ̂  i      2        where N is the number of samples, y i     is the measured value, y  ¯      is the mean of the measured sequence, y ̂   ¯      is the predicted value, and d is the mean of the predicted sequence. MIA>0.6 indicates that the prediction results are valid, and the closer its value is to one, the higher the prediction accuracy. NSE reflects the degree of fit between the predicted and measured series; the closer the NSE is to one, the better the fit, whereas the smaller the NSE value, the worse the fit. MAE is the average of the absolute error, which better reflects the actual situation of the prediction value error. Compared with the average error, the average absolute error will not be offset by positive and negative errors because the deviation is absolutized; thus, the average absolute error can better reflect the actual situation of the prediction value error. RMSE is highly sensitive to the reflection of exceedingly large or extremely small errors in a set of measurements; therefore, it is a good reflection of the deviation of the predicted value from the true value (Gueymard, 2014 ).   4 Empirical study 4.1 Data sources The Pearl River Basin, located in southeastern China, has an area of 442,000 km2  and a subtropical monsoon climate. The average temperature for many years is 14–22 °C, and the average precipitation is 1200–2200 mm (Jing et al., 2021 ). In this study, monthly meteorological observational data (precipitation, temperature, relative humidity, sunshine hours, and atmospheric pressure, etc.) from 100 stations in the Pearl River Basin (Fig. 3  ) from 1960 to 2020 were selected from the China Meteorological Data Network (https://data.cma.cn/ ).  4.2 Model application For ease of presentation, the four performance evaluation metrics of Model i (i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) are denoted as WIA i, NSE i, MAE i, and RMSE i (i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5). 4.2.1 Performance comparison of models 1 and 2 The performance evaluation metrics of Models 1 and 2 is shown in Fig. 4  . From the figure, we can observe that the WIA1 values of all stations are less than 0.4, indicating that the Model 1 prediction results are invalid. This also indicates that it is not feasible to predict monthly-scale droughts directly using a single SVR model. The WIA 2 values for all stations were better than the WIA 1 values, and WIA 2 was less than 0.6 at only one station, indicating that the predictions of Model 2 were valid; the NSE, MAE, and RMSE of Model 2 were better than those of Model 1 for most stations, indicating that the prediction accuracy of Model 2 was higher than that of Model 1. However, the NSE 2 values of most stations were in the interval [0.2, 0.6]; their values were still small, and the NSE values of the five sites were less than zero. In summary, the predictions of Model 2 were relatively poor for most stations.  4.2.2 Analysis of performance evaluation metrics for models 2, 3 and 4 The performance evaluation metrics of Models 2, 3, and 4 are shown in Fig. 5  . The WIA and NSE values of Models 3 and 4 at most stations increased compared to those of Model 2, whereas the MAE and RMSE values decreased compared to those of Model 2. However, some stations had poorer performance evaluation metrics for Models 3 and 4 compared to Model 2, and some stations had significantly decreased prediction accuracy compared to Model 2. After using the d3 and d5 wavelets for wavelet noise cancellation of the highest-frequency components after primary decomposition (ESMD), the prediction accuracy of most stations is significantly improved. However, the prediction accuracy of some stations still decreases, which may be because the d3 and d5 wavelets are prone to the absence of the main signals after noise cancellation of the high-frequency components that contain more noise.  4.2.3 Performance metrics of comparison of model 5 and models 1, 2, 3, and 4 Model 1–5 model performance evaluation metrics are shown in Fig. 6  . Compared with the performance metrics of Model 1, except for WIA, Models 2–4 failed to result in improved fitting and reduced prediction errors at all stations, indicating that Models 2, 3, and 4 failed to fully address the poor prediction of high-frequency signals (monthly-scale droughts) by a single SVR model (Model 1). The four model performance assessment metrics of Model 5 were significantly better than those of Models 1–4 at all stations (significant increases in WIA and NSE values and significant decreases in MAE and RMSE values), suggesting that Model 5 predicts the monthly-scale drought index better than Models 1, 2, 3, and 4. The majority of stations (more than 90) had WIA 5 and NSE 5 values greater than 0.9 and 0.8, respectively, and the minimum values of WIA 5 and NSE 5 were greater than 0.8, and 0.7, respectively, which shows that Model 5 has high prediction accuracy and a good fitting effect. To further analyze the prediction performance of Model 5, the percentage improvement or decrease in each of the four model performance metrics for Model 5 over Models 2, 3, and 4 is plotted (Fig. 7  ). Model 1 was not compared because the Model 1 predictions were invalid. From the figure, we can observe that for most of the stations (more than 80), Wi, Ni, Ei, and Ri (i = 2, 3, 4) values remain in the range of 10 %–40 %, 50 %–300 %, 50 %–80 % and 70 %–100 %, respectively, which indicates that for most of the stations, WIA 5 and NSE 5 values were enhanced by more than 10 % and 50 %, respectively, compared to the values of WIA i and NSE i (i = 2, 3, 4), whereas the values of MAE 5 and RMSE 5 were reduced by more than 50 % and 70 %, respectively, compared to the values of MAE i and RMSE i (i = 2, 3, 4). Most stations (over 90) had WIA 5 values greater than 0.9, and the minimum WIA 5 value exceeded 0.8. However, owing to the large WIA indicator values of Models 2, 3, and 4, although the improvement of WIA 5 indicator values is smaller than the other three indicator values, Model 5 has high prediction accuracy: approximately half (50) of the stations had Ni values greater than 100 %, with the maximum Ni value exceeding 1000 %, indicating that the fit of the stations can be significantly improved in Model 5 over Models 2–4; The MAE (RMSE) metric values for Model 5 at most stations were reduced by more than 50 % (70 %) compared to the MAE (RMSE) metric values for Models 2, 3, and 4, indicating that Model 5 significantly reduces the prediction error values compared to Models 2, 3, and 4. The four model performance metrics of Model 5 were significantly improved compared to those of Models 2, 3, and 4, with the most significant improvement in the value of the NSE indicator, followed by the improvement in the values of the RMSE and MAE indicators and the smallest improvement in the value of the WIA indicator. (Wi = (WIA 5 − WIA i)/WIA i*100 % indicates the percentage increase of WIA 5 over WIA i; Ni = (NSE 5 − NSE i)/NSE i*100 % indicates the percentage increase of NSE 5 over NSE i; Ei = (MAE i − NSE 5)/NSE i*100 % indicates the percentage decrease in MAE 5 over MAE i; and Ri = (RMSE i − RMSE 5)/RMSE i*100 % indicates the percentage decrease in RMSE 5 over RMSE i, where i = 2, 3, 4).    5 Conclusion In this study, a new combined monthly-scale drought secondary decomposition (ESMD-VMD) prediction model was proposed for application to 100 meteorological stations in the Pearl River Basin of China and compared with the prediction results of four contrasting models. The main conclusions of this study are as follows: (1) The direct prediction of the monthly SPEI using a single PSR-SSA-SVR model was not valid. (2) The accuracy of predicting the monthly SPEI using the combined ESMD-PSR-SSA-SVR primary decomposition prediction model was significantly improved compared to the accuracy of predicting the monthly SPEI using the single PSR-SSA-SVR model; however, the prediction effect is still unsatisfactory. (3) Predicting the monthly SPEI using the ESMD-SampEn-WD(d3)-PSR-SSA-SVR and ESMD-SampEn-WD(d5)-PSR-SSA-SVR secondary decomposition combination prediction models improved the prediction accuracy at most stations compared to predicting the monthly SPEI using the ESMD-PSR-SSA-SVR primary decomposition combination prediction model; however, it failed to solve the problem of the low prediction accuracy of the ESMD-PSR-SSA-SVR. (4) The proposed model in this study, that is, the ESMD-SampEn-VMD-PSR-SSA-SVR secondary decomposition combination prediction model, has better performance index values, and the prediction accuracies of all stations improved compared with the four comparative models, in which the NSE index value improved the most significantly, followed by the RMSE and MAE index values, and the WIA index value improved the least. In this study, when predicting monthly-scale drought at a station, a primary decomposition was first performed. Then, the entropy values of the components obtained after the primary decomposition were calculated, and the most complex subsequence was selected for the secondary decomposition. In the future, a specific criterion could be selected to determine whether further decomposition of other components is required to balance the relationship between predictive accuracy and efficiency.
1 Introduction Soil moisture (SM) serves as a pivot factor that exerts a profound influence on terrestrial carbon, hydrological, and heat systems (Green et al., 2019; Rigden et al., 2020 ). Monitoring the dynamics and trends within a long-period SM time series is essential for exploring how vegetation growth and water cycle respond to climate change (Vereecken et al., 2022 ). Therefore, reliable SM datasets are necessary to support studies of hydrological processes (Zheng et al., 2016, 2018a; WaKigari and Leconte, 2023 ) and land–atmosphere exchanges (Koster et al., 2004; Zheng et al., 2015b; Humphrey et al., 2021 ). While ground observations can offer the most accurate SM data, they are often constrained by restricted spatial representation and limited temporal extent (Vereecken et al., 2008; Crow et al., 2023 ). Hence, numerous SM products developed using remote sensing and reanalysis techniques provide consistent coverage in both space and time, making them viable alternative datasets for various applications. Current SM products are broadly categorized into model- and satellite-based products. Satellite-based products are generated using relevant data observed by microwave sensors, including passive-microwave products retrieved from brightness temperature (TB) data, such as the Soil Moisture and Ocean Salinity (SMOS) (Kerr et al., 2012 ), the Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) (O’Neill et al., 2015 ), and the Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer Version 2 (AMSR2) (Parinussa et al., 2015 ); active-microwave products retrieved from backscatter data, like the Advanced SCATterometer (ASCAT) (Wagner et al., 2013 ); and merged products harmonized from multiple satellite-based SM datasets, such as the European Space Agency’s Climate Change Initiative (ESA CCI) (Gruber et al., 2019 ). Model-based products are often generated by the stand-alone land surface model (LSM), such as the Catchment LSM, Noah LSM, and variable infiltration capacity model (VIC) operated in the Global Land Data Assimilation System version 2 (i.e., GLDAS-2.1 CLSM, Noah, and VIC) (Rodell et al., 2004 ). Additionally, certain model-based products are produced utilizing LSMs integrated within assimilation systems, such as the 5th generation of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) atmospheric reanalysis (ERA5) (Hersbach et al., 2020 ), the Modern-Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Applications version 2 (MERRA-2) (Gelaro et al., 2017 ), and the Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM) (Martens et al., 2017 ). Moreover, a few model-based products are generated by merging multi-source SM data, like the SoMo developed by Sungmin and Orth (2021) . Due to the utilization of different remote sensing retrieval algorithms or LSMs, and different satellite observations or meteorological forcing data, performance of various SM products differs from each other under distinct environmental conditions (Colliander et al. 2017; Liu et al., 2021 ). Therefore, SM products are required to be validated using ground observations before their applications (Chen et al., 2013; Su et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2023 ). Since SM observations measured from the single location are insufficient to represent grid values of SM products, a number of regional-scale SM monitoring networks consisting of multiple sites have been established worldwide, such as the Illinois Climate Network (ICN) (Hollinger and Isard, 1994 ) in the United States, the SMOSMANIA network in southern France (Calvet et al., 2007 ), the REMEDHUS network in Spain (Martinez-Fernández and Ceballos, 2005 ), and many of which contribute to the International Soil Moisture Network (ISMN) (Dorigo et al., 2011; 2021 ). A multitude of endeavors have been undertaken to assess SM products and quantify their uncertainties in various regions around the world, relied on ground observations collected from the above-mentioned monitoring networks. For instance, SM observations collected from over 200 sites across Africa, Australia, Europe, and the United States were utilized by Albergel et al. (2012)  to appraise three SM products, namely ASCAT, SMOS, and SM-DAS-2 from the ECMWF; Zhang et al. (2019)  presented an assessment of the SMAP product using extensive SM observations from 191 sites covering different climatic regions; Recently, Beck et al. (2020)  made a comprehensive assessment of numerous SM products utilizing SM observations collected from more than 800 sites across the United States and Europe. Similar efforts have been made to establish several regional-scale SM monitoring networks (Su et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013 ) over the Tibetan Plateau (TP), known as the third pole (Immerzeel et al., 2010; Yao et al., 2012 ). Correspondingly, the SM data provided by these monitoring networks have been utilized to validate and calibrate currently developed SM products across the TP. For example, Chen et al. (2013, 2017)  assessed the performance of AMSRE/2, SMAP, and SMOS remote sensing datasets, as well as the GLDAS products, utilizing SM observations from the Naqu and Pali networks; Liu et al. (2019)  made an evaluation of five remote sensing products employing SM observations collected from five networks across the TP; More recently, Zeng et al. (2022)  utilized SM observations collected from the Pali, Naqu, and Maqu networks to analyze sources of error in several remote sensing products. The key findings of preceding assessments are condensed as below: i) Despite the precision of SM products varies by region, the majority of them have proven effective in capturing seasonal fluctuations of SM observations (Zeng et al., 2022 ). ii) Satellite-based products derived from L-band TB measurements generally perform better than those retrieved from TB measurements at higher-frequency bands (Chen et al., 2017 ). iii) Most of the model-based products regularly overestimate SM in the cold season and underperform in relatively arid regions (Zhang et al. 2022 ). However, it is worth mentioning that most of the previous work was concentrated on evaluating surface SM products for short-term periods (∼5 years) on the TP, while the assessment of SM products either at subsurface layers (e.g., root zone) or for an extended period is rare. Additionally, some newly developed products such as SMOSMAP (Li et al., 2022 ), NNsm (Yao et al., 2021 ), ESA CCI_v7.1, and SoMo have not yet been evaluated on the TP. Unlike the model-based products which can provide SM data at vaious depths, the satellite-based products are only available for surface SM, due to limited penetrating capability of current microwave satellites (generally less than 5 cm) (Zheng et al., 2021, 2019 ). Therefore, multiple approaches have been suggested to estimate subsurface SM based on the satellite-based surface SM, including phsically-based methods like the Soil Moisture Analytical Relationship (SMAR) model (Manfreda et al., 2014 ), empirical approaches like the exponential filter (ExpF) (Albergel et al., 2008 ), statistical approaches such as the principle of maximum entropy (POME) (Singh, 2010 ) and the cumulative distribution function (CDF) matching (Tian et al., 2020 ), data-driven approaches like the artificial neural network (ANN) (Kornelsen and Coulibaly, 2014 ), and data assimilation methods allowing to update model simulated SM as adopted by SMAP (Reichle et al., 2021 ). The selection of approaches for regional-scale applications should consider the amount of prior information and input data, particularly in data-sparse areas like the TP. Therefore, the ExpF method, which requires minimum inputs, is the most widely adopted method for regional-scale applications among the existing methods (Ford et al., 2014 ). For instance, Grillakis et al. (2021)  estimated subsurface SM worldwide based on ESA CCI surface SM data using the ExpF method combined with ANN technique. Tian et al. (2022)  predicted subsurface SM using the ExpF method combined with random forest technique based on surface SM observations collected from over 2000 stations across China. Tian et al. (2020)  used surface SM observations over three years (2014–2016) from the Qilian Monuntains on the TP to estimate subsurface SM using the ExpF method. However, the effectiveness of ExpF in estimating SM profile across different climatic zones of the TP over a long period has not been comprehensively assessed, hindered by the absence of long-term surface and subsurface SM observations. This research aims to comprehensively evaluate the accuracy of commonly used surface and subsurface SM products using a 10-year SM profile dataset on the TP, and to investigate the potential of ExpF method for estimating subsurface SM at regional scale. To this end, 12 satellite-based and 10 model-based SM products are firstly evaluated using a 10-year SM profile dataset produced by Zhang et al. (2022)  utilizing SM observations collected from a TP observatory (Tibet-Obs) (Su et al., 2011 ). The surface SM from outperforming satellite-based products are then employed to predict subsurface SM using the ExpF approach over distinct climatic zones, and the precision of subsurface SM estimations is further assessed utilizing SM observations. Additionally, the potential of model-based SM profile data improvement utilizing the satellite-based surface SM in conjunction with both CDF matching and ExpF methods is explored and discussed. The following is an overview of the paper structure. Section 2  introduces the long-term observed SM profile data and the selected multi-source SM products. Section 3  depicts the methodologies implemented for this research including data preprocessing, evaluation metrics, trend test, and subsurface SM estimate methods. Section 4  exhibits the evaluations of selected model- and satellite-based SM products, alongside the ExpF method. Section 5  discusses the potential of improving the model-based SM profile data utilizing satellite-based surface SM in combination with CDF matching and ExpF methods. Section 6  summarizes the primary findings.  2 Data 2.1 In situ SM profile data Tibet-Obs was founded in 2008 with the primary objective of calibrating and validating models and products (Su et al., 2011 ). It comprises four monitoring networks, including Maqu, Naqu, Shiquanhe, and Ali, covering various climatic regions across the TP (Fig. 1  a). Recently, Zhang et al. (2022)  developed a long-term upscaled SM dataset based on observations collected from sites with the longest SM records in these monitoring networks, which is accessible at doi: 10.4121/20141567.v1  (Accessed 22 June 2024). The SM datasets from two networks (i.e., Maqu and Shiquanhe) are utilized in this study for assessing the multisource surface and subsurface SM products. Brief descriptions of the two networks are given below, with more detailed information available in Zhang et al. (2021, 2022) . 2.1.1 Maqu monitoring network The Maqu monitoring network is situated at the northeastern part of TP, specifically within the coordinates 33.50°-34.25°N and 101.70°-102.70°E as depicted in Fig. 1 b. The local climatic condition is classified as cold-humid, featuring an averaged air temperature of around 1.2 ℃ and an annual precipitation of approximately 600 mm. The predominant land cover is characterized by grassland, with silt loam being the prevalent soil type. The Maqu network consists of 26 SM monitoring sites in total during the period between 2008 and 2019, while several of them have been damaged. The Decagon probes (e.g., 5TM) were positioned at various depths, i.e., 5, 10, 20, 40, and 80 cm, to measure SM with a 15-minute time interval. The SM observations at 10 and 80 cm were not adopted due to discontinuity found in the collected measurements at 10 cm and much less available sites measuring SM at 80 cm, respectively (Zhang et al., 2022 ). The daily upscaled SM profile data between 1 January 2010 and 31 December 2019 at depths of 5, 20, and 40 cm is adopted in this research.  2.1.2 Shiquanhe monitoring network The Shiquanhe monitoring network is situated at the western part of TP, specifically within the coordinates 32.36°–32.76°N and 79.75°-80.25°E as presented in Fig. 1 c. The local climatic condition is classified as cold-arid, featuring an average air temperature of around 7.0 ℃ and an annual precipitation of approximately 100 mm. The predominant land cover is characterized by bare ground, with sand being the prevalent soil type. The Shiquanhe network comprises 21 SM monitoring sites in total during the period between 2010 and 2019, while several of them have been damaged as the similar situation with the Maqu network. The Decagon probes were positioned at various depths of 5, 10, 20, 40, and 60 cm to measure SM with a 15-minute time interval. The measurements at 60 cm were not used for the upscaling due to much less available sites measuring SM at this depth (Zhang et al., 2022 ). The daily upscaled SM data between 1 January 2011 and 31 December 2019 at depths of 5, 20, and 40 cm is adopted in this research.   2.2 Satellite-based surface SM datasets 12 Satellite-based surface SM datasets are selected in this study for the assessment, which were mainly produced based on the satellite microwave measurements at different frequencies like ASCAT, AMSR2, SMOS, and SMAP or using multiple satellite measurements such as SMOSMAP, NNsm, and ESA CCI. The fundamental information of the selected satellite-based surface SM datasets is summarized in Table 1  , and the dataset access links are listed in the Appendix . Brief descriptions of these satellite measurements and corresponding SM products are given below 2.2.1 AMSR2 surface SM datasets Succeeding the AMSR-E instrument, AMSR2 was launched on 18 May 2012 onboard the satellite of Global Change Observation Mission 1-Water (GCOM-W1). It collects TB measurements from seven frequency bands in ascending and descending orbits, which scans the Earth every two days and passes over the equator at 13:30 and 1:30 (Parinussa et al., 2015 ). Two primary products are generated from AMSR2 TB measurements, namely Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) (Comiso and Cho, 2013 ) and Land Parameter Retrieval Model (LPRM) (Owe et al., 2008 ). The LPRM AMSR2 L3 daily 10 km surface SM product (V001) employed in this research is produced using the LPRM based on the AMSR2 TB measurements at two different frequencies, i.e., X-band (10.7 GHz) and C-band (6.9 GHz), which, thus, includes two different datasets: LPRM AMSR2_X and LPRM AMSR2_C. While the JAXA AMSR2 L3 daily 10 km surface SM product is produced employing the lookup table algorithm based on the AMSR2 TB measurements at X-band (10.7 GHz), hereafter JAXA AMSR2 which is also utilized in this research.  2.2.2 SMOS surface SM datasets The ESA’s SMOS satellite was launched to make global observations of SM over land and salinity over oceans on 2 November 2009. It collects TB measurements at L-band (1.4 GHz) in both ascending and descending orbits, covering the Earth every three days and passing over the equator at 6:00 and 18:00 (Kerr et al., 2012 ). The SMOS INRA-CESBIO SM product (SMOS-IC) with a grid resolution of 0.25° is adopted in this research, which is produced using the L-band Microwave Emission of the Biosphere model (L-MEB) (Wigneron et al., 2007, 2018 ) relying on the SMOS TB measurements.  2.2.3 SMAP surface SM datasets The NASA’s SMAP satellite equipped with a radiometer and a radar onboard to measure global SM was launched on 31 January 2015. The radiometer collects TB measurements at L-band (1.4 GHz) in ascending and descending orbits, which covers the Earth every 2–3 days and passes over the equator at 18:00 and 6:00 (O'Neill et al., 2015). In this research, the Enhanced Radiometer L3 daily 9 km product (Version 5, hereafter SMAP_L3) is employed, including two sets of datasets generated using the single channel algorithm at vertical polarization (SCA-V) and the dual channel algorithm (DCA), respectively. DCA is the new baseline algorithm in the latest version of SMAP_L3 product (O'Neill et al., 2021 ), while SCA-V initially served as the postlaunch baseline algorithm from 2015 to 2021 and was demonstrated better performances than DCA in certain previous assessments (Chan et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2018b; Chaubell et al., 2020 ).  2.2.4 SMOSMAP surface SM dataset The SMOSMAP is a global long-term (2010–2020) L-band SM product generated by Li et al. (2022)  boasting a 0.25° grid resolution. It is produced employing a mono-angular retrieval algorithm combining the L-MEB model based on merged L-band TB data, which is harmonized by the fitted TB measurements at the incidence angle of 40° from SMOS and the monthly linearly rescaled TB measurements from SMAP. The dataset can be downloaded through making application to the author, and for more details can be referred to Li et al. (2022) .  2.2.5 Nnsm surface SM dataset The NNsm is a global long-term (2002–2020) SM product generated by Yao et al. (2021)  boasting a 36 km grid resolution. It is produced employing the ANN algorithm to extend characteristics of the SMAP surface SM data to the merged TB data from AMSR-E/2, which is created by using a linear regression model to rescale the AMSR-E TB measurements to the AMSR2 TB measurements.  2.2.6 ASCAT surface SM datasets The ASCAT instruments were launched respectively onboard the satellites of EUMETSAT MetOp-A and MetOp-B on 16 October 2006 and 6 September 2012. They collect backscatter data at C-band (5.255 GHz) in ascending and descending orbits, covering the Earth every two days and passing over the equator at 21:30 and 9:30. The ASCAT H119 SM product with a 12.5 km sampling resolution is utilized for this research, which is produced by employing a change detection approach to covert the backscatter data into relative SM values ranging from 0 to 1 (Bartalis et al. 2007 ).  2.2.7 ESA CCI surface SM datasets As the part of the ESA’s programme on Global Monitoring of Essential Climate Variables (ECV), the SM CCI project was launched in 2010 and provides updated SM products every year. The SM CCI project comprises three separate products, namely the passive-microwave product (CCI_P), the active-microwave product (CCI_A), and the combined product (CCI_C). All three products are produced by combining multiple-source SM data using a weighted average method, boasting a 0.25°grid resolution (Gruber et al., 2019 ). Specifically, the input SM data for the CCI_A product is obtained from external operational sources like the SCAT and ASCAT SM datasets, while the input SM data for the CCI_P product is processed by LPRM algorithm based on the TB measurements derived from radiometer instruments such as AMSR2, TMI, WindSat, SMOS, Fengyun, GPM, and SMAP. The CCI_C product is then produced by merging the harmonized CCI_A and CCI_P products, which have been rescaled against the GLDAS Noah SM dataset. In this study, two versions of the product are employed, i.e., v5.3 and v7.1. The selection of these two versions relies on ESA CCI_v7.1 being the latest public release while ESA CCI_v5.3 demonstrating higher accuracy in assessments conducted on the TP. The major changes from ESA CCI_v5.3 to ESA CCI_v7.1 include the following key points: i) addition of the TB measurements from FY-3B/3C/3D and GPM instruments for the CCI_P SM product, ii) inclusion of both day-time and night-time TB measurements for the CCI_P SM product, iii) an updated LPRM algorithm for the CCI_P SM product that improves model parametrization for TB data at C-, X-, and Ku-bands, iv) inclusion of flagging for snow conditions and barren ground, and v) inclusion of an updated ASCAT SM dataset for the CCI_A SM product that includes improvements towards vegetation correction and snow/frozen flagging.   2.3 Model-based surface and subsurface SM products In this research, we assess 10 model-based products containing both surface and subsurface SM data, which can be categorized into three groups: the products produced using stand-alone LSMs such as GLDAS-2.1 CLSM, Noah, VIC, and ERA5-land; the products generated by LSMs embedded in data assimilation systems like ERA5, GLEAM, MERRA-2, and SMAP_L4; and the products produced using machine learning techniques like SoMo. Table 2   provides the primary information of these model-based SM products, brief descriptions are summarized below, and their access links are listed in the Appendix . 2.3.1 ERA5 and ERA5-land SM products ERA5 represents the 5th version of ECMWF atmosphere reanalysis product, succeeding the ERA-Interim product. The product amalgamates extensive historical data  employing the 4D-Var assimilation approach within ECMWF’s integrated forecast system (Hersbach et al. 2020 ), providing global hourly estimates of land and atmospheric variables with a 0.25° grid resolution. The SM simulations within layers of 0–7, 7–28, and 28–100 cm from ERA5 are utilized in this research. ERA5-land represents a reproduction of the terrestrial module within ERA5, generated through the hydro-tiled ECMWF Scheme for Surface Exchanges over Land model (H-TESSEL) (Balsamo et al., 2009 ). This model is driven by the atmospheric data obtained from ERA5, to offer global hourly SM estimates with a 0.1° grid resolution (Muñoz Sabater et al., 2021 ). The SM simulations within layers of 0–7, 7–28, and 28–100 cm from ERA5-land are utilized in this research.  2.3.2 GLDAS SM products GLDAS represents a global modelling and assimilation system designed to generate variables of terrestrial state and flux, which is jointly developed by the NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and the NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Prediction (Rodell et al., 2004 ). For this research, three products generated by distinct models integrated within the GLDAS-2.1′s land information system are employed (hereafter GLDAS CLSM, Noah, and VIC). They are driven by the same atmospheric data derived from a combination of simulations and observations, without data assimilation. It should be noted that the three GLDAS products only provide total soil water content simulations (Personal communication with GES DISC User Services). GLDAS CLSM is produced utilizing Catchment-F2.5 LSM, providing global 3-hour SM estimates with a grid resolution of 1.0° (Li et al., 2020 ). The SM simulations within layers of 0–2 and 0–100 cm from GLDAS CLSM are employed in this research. GLDAS Noah is produced utilizing Noah LSM, providing global 3-hour SM estimates with a grid resolution of 0.25° (Beaudoing and Rodell 2020a ). The SM simulations within layers of 0–10, 10–40, and 40–100 cm from GLDAS Noah are employed in this research. GLDAS VIC is produced utilizing VIC 4.1.2 LSM, providing global 3-hour SM estimates with a grid resolution of 1.0° (Beaudoing and Rodell 2020b ). The SM simulations within layers of 0–30 and 30–130 cm from GLDAS VIC are employed in this research, and the specific thickness of soil layers per region can be found by visiting https://ldas.gsfc.nasa.gov/gldas/specifications  (Accessed 22 June 2024).  2.3.3 MERRA-2 SM product MERRA-2 represents the most recent atmospheric reanalysis product developed by the NASA’s Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO), succeeding the original MERRA product with improvements towards both model parameterization and data assimilation system (Gelaro et al., 2017 ). The MERRA-2 SM product is produced utilizing the CLSM embedded in the Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS-5) version 5.12.4, offering global daily SM estimates with a 0.5°×0.625° grid resolution. The SM simulations within layers of 0–5 and 0–100 cm from MERRA-2 are employed in this research, and the specific thickness of soil layers per region is available at https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/ datasets/M2C0NXLND_5.12.4/summary  (Accessed 22 June 2024).  2.3.4 SMAP_L4 SM product The SMAP Level-4 product (hereafter SMAP_L4) is generated using the CLSM embedded in the GEOS-5 with data assimilation of TB measurements from SMAP, offering global 3-hour SM estimates with a 9 km grid resolution (Reichle et al., 2014 ; 2021). The SM simulations within layers of 0–5 and 0–100 cm from SMAP_L4 are used in this study.  2.3.5 GLEAM v3 SM products GLEAM v3 represents the third version of GLEAM developed by Miralles et al. (2011) , which incorporates a range of algorithms designed to independently calculate different aspects of terrestrial evaporation. The GLEAM v3 SM product is produced using a soil module driven by precipitation observations, with data assimilation of surface SM data from satellite using the Newtonian nudging algorithm (Martens et al., 2016, 2017 ), offering daily SM estimates with a 0.25°grid resolution. The GLEAM v3 SM product consists of two datasets, namely GLEAM v3a and GLEAM v3b, driven by different meteorological forcing data. Specifically, GLEAM v3a is driven by atmospheric data from satellite-based measurements, while GLEAM v3b is driven by atmospheric data that combines both satellite- and model-based data. The SM simulations within layers of 0–10 and 10–100 cm from both GLEAM v3.6a and v3.6b are utilized in this research.  2.3.6 SoMo SM product The SoMo is a global long-term (2000–2020) SM product developed by Sungmin and Orth (2020) that offers daily SM estimates boasting a 0.25° grid resolution. It is produced utilizing the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model, trained to predict spatiotemporal variations in daily SM based on ground observations from over 1000 monitoring sites worldwide. The SM simulations within layers of 0–10, 10–30, and 30–50 cm from SoMo are utilized in this research.    3 Methodology The procedure of this study consists of four primary steps, outlined as below: Step 1: 12 satellite-based surface SM datasets are assessed using upscaled SM observations through statistical analysis to determine the outperforming satellite-based dataset. Step 2: The outperforming satellite-based surface SM data is employed to estimate subsurface SM using the ExpF method, to evaluate the efficacy of the ExpF approach in distinct climatic regions on the TP. Step 3: 10 model-based surface and subsurface SM datasets are evaluated through statistical analysis and trend tests based on upscaled SM observations to identify the outperforming model-based products. Step 4: The surface SM from the selected model-based products is further rescaled incorporating the CDF matching method, with the outperforming satellite-based surface SM as the reference data, and the rescaled surface SM is then employed to estimate subsurface SM using the ExpF method. This step aims to investigate the potential for improving model-based SM profile data by leveraging satellite-based surface SM data in combination with both CDF matching and ExpF methods. The detailed descriptions of data pre-processing procedure, the ExpF and CDF matching methods, the statistical indicators, and the trend analysis approach are provided in the following subsections. 3.1 Pre-processing of SM products In order to achieve an objective evaluation of multi-source model- and satellite-based SM products against SM observations, several pre-processing procedures are essential. Firstly, the units of the SM data must be standardized to ensure consistency across various datasets. Secondly, the time interval and coverage period must be uniformized to facilitate accurate comparisons. Thirdly, the pixels and grids that cover the in situ network must be identified to ensure that the correct regional data is being compared. Finally, the model-based SM estimates must be matched to the depths of the SM observations. To accomplish the first objective, we convert the SM data unit from % to m3  m−3  using Eq. (1)  for the ASCAT and CCI_A datasets, and convert the SM data unit from kg m−2  to m3  m−3  using Eq. (2)  for the GLDAS CLSM, Noah, and VIC products. The units of SM observations and all other SM products are already in m3  m−3 .(1) θ = θ sat   × W     (2) θ = s w c / ( Δ Z × ρ H 2  O   )     Here, θ    refers to SM, θ sat      denotes soil porosity (m3  m−3 ), W    denotes soil wetness (%), swc    refers to soil water content (kg m−2 ), Δ Z    denotes layer thickness (m), and ρ H 2  O      denotes liquid water density (kg m−3 ). To achieve the second objective, the single SM value per day derived from the satellite-based product is regarded as the daily SM, and the hourly or 3 h SM estimates from the model-based product are averaged to daily SM. The evaluation duration covers between 1 January 2010 and 31 December 2019, and the months from May to October are defined as the warm season and the remaining months considered as the cold season. Additionally, the SM data in cold seasons derived from ERA5, ERA5-land, GLDAS CLSM, Noah, and VIC are excluded in assessments as their SM encompasses both ice and liquid content, while the SM observations from in situ monitoring sites only contain liquid content. To accomplish the third objective, the satellite pixels and model grids located within the monitoring network areas are chosen for each product. If the original spatial resolution of a product is larger than 0.25°×0.25°, the resolution is downscaled to a 0.25° grid through bilinear interpolation. The average SM of the pixels or grids that fall within the in situ network areas is then calculated and considered as the regional-scale SM for assessments in this study. The corresponding scope of each product is presented in Fig. 1 . To resample SM estimates at depths of 5, 20, and 40 cm, we compared two interpolation methods commonly employed in prior research (Gao et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022 ): depth-weighted and linear interpolations. The result indicated a notable similarity in the performance of both methods (Figure is not shown). In this study, we adopted the linear interpolation method to fully leverage the valid in situ measurements at each depth. This approach assumes that the SM value at the midpoint of each modelling layer represents the SM within this layer, and relevant computations can refer to Zhang et al. (2022) .  3.2 Exponential filter method ExpF is an empirical approach proposed by Wagner et al. (1999)  utilized for estimating subsurface SM from surface SM data. First of all, the predictability of subsurface SM based on surface SM should be demonstrated by cross-correlation analysis. The cross-correlation, also known as cross-covariance, is a statistical indicator for measuring the similarity between different data series. For this research, the lagged cross-correlation coefficient (Lag-R) is employed to gauge the coupling strength between surface SM (i.e. at depth 5 cm) and subsurface SM (e.g., at depths of 20 and 40 cm). The lag time is set between 0 and 30 days, and the maximum Lag-R value and its corresponding lag time is calculated to determine the strongest association between two SM time series. A higher maximum Lag-R value signifies a more robust connection between these two SM time series, suggesting a higher feasibility of using ExpF method to predict subsurface SM via surface SM (Mahmood and Hubbard, 2007 ). The ExpF method assumes that surface soil water index (SWI) time series provides an indication about the drying and wetting tendency of the soil profile, while the SM integrated over the deeper layer exhibits less variability compared to those observed in the surface layer. A filter is then required to smooth the SWI time series to reproduce the tendency in the deeper layer. Accordingly, Wagner et al. (1999)  proposed the straightforward two-layer water budget structure comprising surface and second layers to define a low-pass filter, where the second layer is treated as a reservoir that only exchanges water with the surface layer. Given these assumptions, the equation of water budget at the second layer is formulated as follows:(3) Δ Z dW  dt   = C × W s  - W        where W s     and W    represents the soil wetness of surface and second layer respectively, t    denotes the time, Δ Z    denotes the distance from the surface to the second layer, and C  represents a pseudo-diffusive parameter. Setting T = Δ Z / C    gives the integration of Eq. It can be thought of as a surrogate parameter that combines the influences of soil texture, hydraulic parameters, and layer thickness on SM, although it does not account for certain processes such as transpiration. (2011) , and Zeng et al. (2016) . The key idea behind this approach is to adjust biased SM data (θ b    ) by matching its CDF to that of the reference SM data (θ r    ). The matching is achieved by solving Eq. (11) , which makes the CDF of updated biased SM data (θ u    ) infinitely close to that of θ r    . The θ u     is then specifically obtained from Eq. It should be mentioned that the KGE requires an equal number of data points for the estimated and observed SM time series, which is not suitable for satellite-based SM data assessment in this study.  3.5 Mann-Kendall trend test The Mann-Kendall trend test was proposed by Mann (1945)  and has been widely employed to detect monotonic trend for SM time series (Albergel et al., 2013; Cheng et al., 2019 ). Herein, the trend test is utilized to examine the existence of trends in the SM time series during approximately 10 years for distinct periods: the entire year, warm seasons, and cold seasons. At first, the numbers of data points from the ground observations and model-based SM estimates are standardized to ensure data consistency. The assessments include both ascending (A) and descending (D) datasets of each product, as well as daily composite products like SMOSMAP, NNsm, and ESA CCI. Each subplot also provides the number of data points (N), bias, RMSD, ubRMSD, and R for each dataset. The LPRM SM datasets retrieved from C- and X-band TB measurements of AMSR2 show similar performance. The descending datasets generally outperform the ascending datasets since the LPRM algorithm assumes an equivalence between vegetation temperature (Tv ) and soil temperature (Ts ), which is often not true for daytime data (i.e., ascending data at 13:30). It is noted that the LPRM product tends to overestimate SM especially under wet conditions (i.e., in situ SM exceeds 0.3 m3/m−3 (−|-)), which results in larger dynamic ranges of SM aligning with findings from other regions of the TP such as Naqu and Pali (Chen et al., 2013; Zeng et al., 2022 ). On the contrary, both ascending and descending SM datasets from JAXA show significant underestimations and smaller dynamic ranges of SM, resulting in high bias and low R values. The inferior performance of JAXA has been previously noted in many regions (Bindlish et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2022 ), and Liu et al. (2019)  attributed the marked underestimation to the failure of using polarization and soil wetness indexes to eliminate the surface temperature effect on SM retrieval, which is a fundamental assumption in the JAXA algorithm. In addition, the look-up table adopted in JAXA was calibrated in Mongolia, which is an arid region (Fujii et al., 2009 ). Both ascending and descending SM datasets from SMOS-IC and SMAP_L3 exhibit comparable performance, with SMAP_L3 generally outperforming SMOS-IC with lower RMSD and ubRMSD values. This can be attributed to SMOS being more sensitive to radio frequency interference (RFI) compared to SMAP (Dente et al., 2012 ) that is equipped with improved RFI filtering technique (Bindlish et al., 2016 ). Another possible attribution is that the algorithm of SMOS-IC accounts for multi-angular (between 20° and 55°) TB measurements, while SMAP_L3 directly measures TB at a single angular (40°) (Li et al., 2021 ), resulting in larger uncertainties of SM retrievals from SMOS-IC. In addition, comparisons between the SMAP_L3 products generated by two different algorithms demonstrate that DCA performs slightly better than SCA-V, evidenced by achieving lower values of RMSD and ubRMSD. This finding supports the implementation of DCA as the baseline algorithm due to its improved SM retrieval performance as reported by O'Neill et al. (2021) . Considering these issues with SMOS aforementioned, the SMOSMAP product was developed by combining TB measurements from both SMOS and SMAP to generate a more reliable longer-term SM product. As expected, the assessment results indicate that SMOSMAP significantly outperforms SMOS-IC, which is consist with the report in Li et al. (2022b). Analogously, NNsm is another combined SM product that uses an ANN training approach to extend the advantages of the SMAP SM data to the AMSR-E/2 product. Similar to SMOSMAP, the NNsm product performs better than both LPRM and JAXA products derived from AMSR2. ESA CCI is another merged product that is undergoing continuous improvements, and we assessed versions 4.4, 5.3, 6.1, and 7.1 of the ESA CCI product but only presents here the results of the latest and best-performing versions, i.e., v7.1 and v5.3. The results reveal that CCI_P v5.3 performs comparably to SMAP_L3, with an ubRMSD at 0.064 m3/m−3 (−|-) and an R value at 0.76. This indicates a significant improvement over CCI_P v4.4, which yielded an ubRMSD at 0.083 m3/m−3 (−|-) and an R value at 0.43 as reported in a prior research (Cheng et al., 2019 ). The inclusion of SMAP data is a primary factor contributing to the improved performance of CCI_P v5.3 compared to previous versions. However, the results suggest that CCI_P v7.1 performs worse than CCP v5.3 as indicated by larger bias and RMSD values. This could be attributed to the additional inclusion of GPM and FengYun data, which collect microwave data at high-frequency bands that is more affected by vegetation. Additionally, the inclusion of the daytime dataset is another attribution to the inferior performance of CCI_P v7.1, because Ts  and Tv  from the daytime dataset are usually not in equilibrium which contradicts the assumption of the LPRM algorithm. While the preceding paragraphs focus on evaluating passive-microwave products, this study also evaluates the products derived from active microwave measurements, such as ASCAT and CCI_A. The results indicate that CCI_A v7.1 exhibits similar performance to ASCAT, with both products underestimating SM under dry conditions (i.e., in situ SM is below 0.3 m3/m−3 (−|-)) as also reported by Su et al. (2011) . This comparable performance may be ascribed to the utilization of the latest ASCAT descending SM dataset (H119) as the primary input data for CCI_A v7.1. However, CCI_A v5.3, which is based on the ASCAT H115 SM dataset, does not exhibit significant underestimation. We thus compared SM derived from the ASCAT H115 and H119 datasets, and found that the H119 dataset obviously underestimates SM in dry conditions during warm seasons compared to the H115 dataset (Figure is not shown). This discrepancy is possibly due to the change of H119 retrieval algorithm, which introduces spatial-variable crossover angles affecting the calculation of dry and wet backscatter references (Hahn et al., 2021 ). In contrast, both versions 5.3 and 7.1 of CCI_C, a product combining both passive- and active-microwave datasets, exhibit similar performance. Notably, their performance is also comparable to that of CCI_C v4.4 reported by Cheng et al. (2019) . This is because all versions of CCI_C use the GLDAS Noah SM product as a reference to rescale the input SM data. As a result, CCI_C SM data is always within the dynamic range of SM from GLDAS Noah, which also attenuates the features of SM data from various satellite-based products. As expected, the CCI_C datasets are likely to inherit the deficiencies of the GLDAS Noah product, which underestimates SM under wet conditions.  4.1.2 Evaluation metrics for the Shiquanhe network Fig. 3   presents scatterplots comparing SM observations at 5 cm and satellite-based surface SM estimates for the Shiquanhe network, covering the period from 1 January 2011 to 31 December 2019.
