Both LPRM and JAXA SM datasets retrieved from the AMSR2 TB measurements produce a significantly larger dynamic range than that of in situ SM measurements, leading to obvious overestimations under wet conditions (i.e., in situ SM exceeds 0.1 m3  m−3 ). The deviation may be attributed to the utilization of constant roughness parameters in both LPRM and JAXA products, which is not appropriate for the TP considering the significant variability of the roughness (Su et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2018c ). It is evident that the performance of JAXA is superior in the arid Shiquanhe region compared to the humid Maqu region. Similarly, the SMOS-IC datasets also tend to overestimate SM compared to ground observations. This finding aligns with Kerr et al. (2016) , which reported that the utilization of the Mironov model in the SMOS product generally results in higher SM values on a global scale, particularly in dry areas. In contrast, both the SMAP_L3 SCA-V and DCA products demonstrate better performance as evidenced by lower ubRMSD and higher R values. It is noted that SCA-V performs better than DCA which is contrary to the finding obtained for the Maqu network, which aligns with the assessment result in Zheng et al. (2018b)  indicating that the overestimation results from the inappropriate representation of surface roughness. As in the Maqu network, the merged products, SMOSMAP and NNsm, also demonstrate improved performance compared to the SMOS-IC and LPRM/JAXA datasets, respectively. Particularly, the NNsm product shows comparable performance with SMAP_L3 datasets, with an ubRMSD at 0.025 m3  m−3  and an R value at 0.66. The CCI_P v5.3 product demonstrates enhanced performance in the Shiquanhe network compared to CCI_P v4.4 as reported by Cheng et al. (2019) , due to the inclusion of the SMAP SM data. However, it still exhibits notable overestimations, which can be attributed to characteristics of the SM datasets derived from AMSR2 and SMOS. Unlike the inferior performance of CCI_P v7.1 compared to CCI_P v5.3 for the Maqu network, their performance is comparable for the Shiquanhe network. This could be due to the dominance of barren ground in the Shiquanhe network area, resulting in minimal vegetation impact on both TB measurements at high-frequency bands and thermal equilibrium for the daytime datasets. It should be noted that the improved flagging of barren ground in CCI_P v7.1 reduces the data points from 792 (CCI_P v5.3) to 239, yielding lower ubRMSD at 0.033 m3  m−3  (against 0.055 m3  m−3 ). All the active-microwave SM products (i.e., ASCAT and CCI_A) show weak correlations with SM observations for Shiquanhe, which could be explained by the occurrence of anomalous ASCAT signals in arid regions caused by underground scattering (Wagner et al., 2022 ). The CCI_C product also performs similarly across different versions due to the limitation imposed by the GLDAS Noah product, showing a larger dynamic range and an overall overestimation compared to the SM observations as the CCI_P products.  4.1.3 Time series analysis The assessment results for both networks indicate that the SMAP_L3 products outperform other satellite-based products in both humid and arid regions. Specifically, DCA demonstrates superior performance in the humid Maqu region, while SCA-V shows better performance in the arid Shiquanhe region. Among all the SMAP_L3 datasets, the ascending dataset using SCA-V (SMAP_L3_SCA_Asc) delivers the best overall performance for both networks, achieving ubRMSD values at 0.061 and 0.018 m3  m−3 , as well as R values at 0.82 and 0.69 for Maqu and Shiquanhe, respectively. Thus, the SMAP_L3_SCA_Asc dataset is chosen for further analysis in this research. However, it should be mentioned that SMAP_L3 has a constrained temporal coverage, starting from April 2015. Consequently, the further analysis also includes the NNsm product, which performs similarly to SMAP_L3 in both regions and covers a long-term period. Fig. 4  a presents the SM time series from the SMAP_L3_SCA_Asc and NNsm datasets compared to the upscaled SM observations for the Maqu network, covering the period from 1 January 2010 to 31 December 2019. The observed SM time series exhibits a seasonal pattern characterized by high values in summer attributed to rainfall while low values in winter attributed to soil freezing. Both SMAP_L3_SCA_Asc and NNsm SM datasets capture the temporal fluctuations of SM observations well, with high R values at 0.82 and 0.72. SMAP_L3_SCA_Asc slightly overestimates SM in summer due to inappropriate parameterizations of surface roughness and vegetation optical depth as highlighted by Zheng et al. (2018c) . The 9-month temporal gap between October 2011 and June 2012 noted for the NNsm is caused by the time gap between AMSR2 and AMSR-E satellites, and the SM time series of NNsm shows a systematic underestimation before October 2011 when TB data are collected from AMSR-E. Since the SM data from SMAP_L3 serves as the training target of the NNsm product, the statistical indicators and bias characteristics of the SM time series from NNsm is similar to those of SMAP_L3. Fig. 4 b shows the SM time series from SMAP_L3_SCA_Asc and NNsm compared to the upscaled SM observations for the Shiquanhe network, covering the period from 1 January 2011 to 31 December 2019. Both SMAP_L3_SCA_Asc and NNsm have filtered extremely low SM values under dry conditions, leading to less effective data points compared to those of Maqu network. However, the remaining data generally agrees well with SM observations, yielding the ubRMSD values of 0.018 and 0.025 m3  m−3 , both of which meet the specified criteria of 0.04 m3  m−3 .   4.2 Evaluation of ExpF method in estimating subsurface SM based on satellite-based surface SM data 4.2.1 Maqu network Fig. 5  a and 5b present the cross-correlation results between surface SM at 5 cm and subsurface SM at depths of 20 and 40 cm obtained from the upscaled SM observations for the Maqu network. The results indicate a strong connection between surface and subsurface at both depths, with the highest Lag-R values being 0.92 and 0.81. This suggests that surface SM can be utilized to predict subsurface SM in the Maqu network region. As such, the ExpF method is then employed using surface SM data obtained from SMAP_L3_SCA_Asc and NNsm to estimate subsurface SM. The network-average Topt  parameters for the SM data at 20 and 40 cm are determined by in situ measurements, with the respective values of 9 and 12 days. Fig. 6  a and 6b present the time series of subsurface SM estimates at depths of 20 and 40 cm using the ExpF method based on surface SM from SMAP_L3_SCA_Asc (hereafter “SMAP_ExpF”) and NNsm (hereafter “NNsm_ExpF”) for the Maqu network. The statistical indicators including bias, RMSD, ubRMSD, and R for SMAP_ExpF and NNsm_ExpF against SM observations are also presented in the figures. The results reveal that the accuracy of SMAP_ExpF at both depths is reliable, with low ubRMSD values at 0.045 and 0.025 m3  m−3 , as well as high R values around 0.80. While the accuracy of NNsm_ExpF is slightly inferior to that of SMAP_ExpF, it still yields high R values around 0.78 and acceptable ubRMSD values at 0.052 and 0.037 m3  m−3 . It is noted that both SMAP_ExpF and NNsm_ExpF agree well with SM observations during cold seasons but exhibit slight underestimations during warm seasons, which decreases with depth.  4.2.2 Shiquanhe network Fig. 5 c and d show the cross-correlation results for the Shiquanhe network, with the highest Lag-R values being 0.79 and 0.64. The results suggest that the surface SM holds predictive ability for subsurface SM in the Shiquanhe network area as well. The network-average Topt  parameters for the SM data at 20 and 40 cm are 5 and 10 days, respectively. Fig. 6 c and 6d present the SM time series of SMAP_ExpF and NNsm_ExpF at depths of 20 and 40 cm for the Shiquanhe network. As expected, correlations between estimated and observed subsurface SM time series for the Shiquanhe network are weaker than those for the Maqu network, which is in line with their respective coupling strengths between surface and subsurface SM observations. SMAP_ExpF can generally capture the temporal dynamics of SM observations and has acceptable accuracy at both depths, yielding R values at 0.53 and 0.47 alongside ubRMSD values at 0.017 and 0.016 m3  m−3 . NNsm_ExpF performs comparably to SMAP_ExpF except for data-deficient period, with ubRMSD values of 0.019 and 0.018 m3  m−3  for 20 and 40 cm, respectively. In summary, the results indicate that the ExpF method, based on surface SM data from both SMAP_L3_SCA_Asc and NNsm, is able to produce reliable subsurface SM estimates in both network regions. While SMAP_ExpF offers higher accuracy, NNsm_ExpF provides extended period of SM estimates. Additionally, it is noted that there is no notable difference in the accuracy of estimated SM at different depths (20 and 40 cm) for both networks.   4.3 Evaluation of model-based surface and subsurface SM products 4.3.1 Evaluation metrics for the Maqu network Fig. 7  a compares the KGE scores for SM estimates at depths of 5, 20, and 40 cm derived from 10 model-based products during both warm and cold seasons for the Maqu network, covering the duration from 1 January 2010 to 31 December 2019. As noted in Section 3.1 , SM estimates for the cold season from ERA5, ERA5-land, GLDAS CLSM, Noah, and VIC are not included in the assessments. The KGE scores indicate that ERA5 performs superior than other SM products at depths of 5 and 20 cm during warm seasons, followed by ERA5-land with slightly inferiority, but the performance of ERA5 and ERA5-land is comparable to each other at 40 cm. This is the first comparison between the two products for subsurface layers in Asia, but a similar finding has been reported for North America by Muñoz-Sabater et al. (2021), and the better performance of the ERA5 SM product for 5 and 20 cm is likely attributed to its usage of data assimilation (Cao et al., 2020 ). Although GLEAM_v3.6a also adopts meteorological forcing data from ERA5, such as net radiation and air temperature (Martens et al., 2020 ), it performs worse than ERA5 and ERA5-land at all depths due to using a different model. On the other hand, GLEAM_v3.6b shows improved performance compared to GLEAM_v3.6a during both warm and cold seasons, achieved through the utilization of satellite-based meteorological data (Martens et al., 2017 ). The CLSM, VIC, and Noah models operate on the same atmospheric forcing data within the GLDAS data archive, but they exhibit different performance. For the warm season, GLDAS CLSM performs worse than other two products at all three depths. GLDAS VIC performs better than GLDAS Noah at the depth of 5 cm, while GLDAS Noah provides better SM estimates at 20 and 40 cm, which is consist with the finding of Bi et al. (2016) . Even though both SMAP_L4 and MERRA-2 adopt the same LSM as GLDAS CLSM, the inclusion of the data assimilation in their modelling system results in improved accuracy of SM estimates, as indicated by higher KGE scores for every depth. SMAP_L4 outperforms other SM products at 5 and 40 cm during warm seasons, while MERRA-2 show slightly inferiority compared to SMAP_L4, resulting from the assimilation of L-band TB data as well as implementation of improved model parameterizations by SMAP_L4 as reported in Reichle et al. (2017) . The SoMo product outperforms most of other SM products during cold seasons, as indicated by higher KGE scores for every depth. However, for the warm season, SoMo demonstrates inferior performance compared to ERA5, ERA5-land, and SMAP_L4 at all three depths. SoMo is trained using a target dataset which captures the temporal variation of SM observations and keeps consistent with the ERA5 SM product regarding mean value and standard deviation (Sungmin and Orth, 2021 ). As such, the inferiority of SoMo may be attributed to the inclusion of ice content in the ERA5 SM product, resulting in an overestimation of the average value of the target SM data used in LSTM training.  4.3.2 Evaluation metrics for the Shiquanhe network Fig. 7 b compares the KGE scores for SM estimates at depths of 5, 20, and 40 cm derived from 10 model-based products for the Shiquanhe network, during the period from 1 January 2011 to 31 December 2019. As the Maqu network, SM estimates for the cold season from ERA5, ERA5-land, GLDAS CLSM, and GLDAS VIC are not included in the assessments. The KGE scores indicate that SMAP_L4 performs best among all SM products at each depth during both warm and cold seasons, likely due to assimilation of L-band TB measurements (Reichle et al., 2017 ), aligning with the finding of the SMAP_L3 surface SM data (see Section 4.1.2 ). Although MERRA-2 exhibits inferior performance than SMAP_L4 as the Maqu network, it generally outperforms most of other SM products especially in cold seasons. Both SMAP_L4 and MERRA-2 perform better than GLDAS CLSM, but CLSM provides better SM estimates at each depth among three GLDAS products in warm seasons. ERA5 performs better than ERA5-land at depths of 5 and 20 cm, with comparable performance at the depth of 40 cm, which aligns with the findings for the Maqu network. In contrast, GLEAM_v3.6a consistently performs better than GLEAM_v3.6b at all depths during cold seasons, while showing comparable performance during warm seasons. The performance of SoMo is at a moderate level among all products because of the fact that SM observations used in the target dataset for its model training do not cover the arid climatic region. Overall, KGE scores of model-based products for the Shiquanhe network are significantly lower than those for Maqu except for the SMAP_L4 product, indicating that model-based products generally exhibit higher accuracy in the humid zone than the arid zone. Additionally, KGE scores of these SM products also demonstrate a superior performance during warm seasons compared to cold seasons. However, the accuracy of SM estimates does not show a clear tendency with varying depths. SMAP_L4 generally outperforms most of other products in both network regions during both warm and cold seasons, while other products exhibit different performance by region and season. During the warm season, ERA5 and ERA5-land generally show better performance in Maqu followed by SoMo, while GLEAM_v3.6b and MERRA-2 outperform in Shiquanhe. During the cold season, SoMo shows higher accuracy at every depth in the Maqu network region, while MERRA-2 outperforms in the Shiquanhe network region. Therefore, three model-based SM products, namely SMAP_L4, GLEAM_v3.6b, and SoMo, are selected for further time series analysis and trend test in the following subsection.  4.3.3 Time series analysis and Mann Kendall trend test The left panel of Fig. 8   exhibits the SM time series derived from SMAP_L4, GLEAM_v3.6b, and SoMo compared to the upscaled SM observations at depths of 5, 20, and 40 cm for the Maqu network, covering the duration from 1 January 2010 to 31 December 2019. While all three model-based SM products are able to replicate the seasonal pattern of SM observations well, they produce smaller dynamic ranges of SM at all three depths and exhibit different accuracy by season. In the cold season, all products overestimate SM at every depth to different degrees that may be attributed to the failure of the parameterization in adequately describing the freezing-thawing process on the TP. In the warm season, SoMo significantly outperforms other two products at 5 and 20 cm, while underperforming at the depth of 40 cm with obvious overestimations. In contrast, GLEAM_v3.6b and SMAP_L4 underestimate SM at 5 and 20 cm as the influence of organic content within the Tibetan soil layer on hydraulic properties is ignored (Zheng et al., 2015a ). The right panel of Fig. 8  exhibits the outcomes of Mann Kendall trend analysis for the 10-year (2010–2019) SM time series of ground observations and three model-based products at three depths for warm seasons, cold seasons, and the entire year, respectively. Herein a monotonous trend can be identified when the absolute value of the Z statistic exceeds 1.96, accompanied by the corresponding Sen’s slope estimate. The results for SM observations at 40 cm and the SM estimates from SMAP_L4 are not shown due to insufficient data. At depths of 5 and 20 cm, all model-based SM time series show no monotonous trend for warm seasons, which aligns with the SM observations. However, none of the mode-based SM time series is able to replicate the drying trend of observed SM time series during cold seasons and the entire year. At the depth of 40 cm, GLEAM_v3.6b demonstrates a wetting trend during warm seasons and for the entire year, whereas SoMo shows no significant trend. The left panel of Fig. 9   exhibits the SM time series obtained from the three model-based products and the upscaled SM observations at depths of 5, 20, and 40 cm for the Shiquanhe network, covering the duration from 1 January 2011 to 31 December 2019. The results appear that SMAP_L4 is able to replicate temporal dynamics of SM observations well at every depth, while other two model-based products significantly overestimate SM at all three depths and produce larger dynamic ranges to different degrees. The higher accuracy of SM estimates from SMAP_L4 could be attributed to the assimilation of L-band TB measurements (Reichle et al., 2017 ), while the overestimations noted for other two model-based SM products are primarily due to overestimation of precipitation by the adopted meteorological forcing datasets (Zhang et al., 2022 ). The right panel of Fig. 9  exhibits the results of the Mann Kendall trend analysis and Sen’s slope estimate for the 9-year (2011–2019) SM time series of ground observations, GLEAM_v3.6b, and SoMo. At depths of 5 and 20 cm, the observed SM time series shows no significant trend during both warm and cold seasons, alongside for the full year. While both GLEAM_v3.6b and SoMo are able to replicate the trend of observed SM time series during warm seasons, they exhibit a drying trend during cold seasons and the entire year. At the depth of 40 cm, both GLEAM_v3.6b and SoMo exhibit a drying trend during cold seasons and for the entire year, with SoMo maintaining this drying trend during warm seasons whereas GLEAM_v3.6b showing no significant trend.    5 Discussion The assessment results of this study presented in previous sections reveal that the outperforming satellite-based products generally provide more accurate surface SM estimates than the outperforming model-based products on the TP. On the other hand, current model-based products generally exhibit higher accuracy in estimating surface SM compared to subsurface SM, as well as present better performance during warm seasons compared to cold seasons. Since the reliability of the ExpF approach in estimating subsurface SM has been evaluated in both network areas, we thus discuss here the possibility of updating the selected model-based SM estimates simultaneously using both CDF matching and ExpF methods in combination with the outperforming satellites-based surface SM data. Specifically, surface SM estimates from SMAP_L4, GLEAM_v3.6b, and SoMo are firstly rescaled utilizing the CDF matching method to the selected satellite-based SM data, i.e. SMAP_L3_SCA_Asc. The rescaled surface SM estimates are then used to estimate subsurface SM employing the ExpF method, whereby the required parameters of Topt  for each product are determined by original model-based surface and subsurface SM data. Eventually, the updated surface and subsurface SM estimates of these three products are assessed using SM observations, and their performance metrics are compared against those of corresponding original products. Fig. 10   compares the KGE scores for updated and original SM estimates at depths of 5, 20, and 40 cm from these three model-based products for both networks. In general, the updated SM estimates for all three products perform better than their original SM estimates at each depth in both network areas during the warm and cold seasons, except for the SMAP_L4 product for 5 cm and the GLEAM_v3.6b product for 40 cm in the Maqu area during warm seasons. Notably, the updated SM estimates of SoMo (SoMo_Update) exhibit the best performance at every depth in both network areas during both warm and cold seasons. Furthermore, Fig. 11   presents the time series of updated and original SM estimates from SoMo compared to SM observations at depths of 5, 20, and 40 cm for both networks. For the Maqu network, SoMo_Update shows markedly higher accuracy compared to the original dataset especially for subsurface SM and during cold seasons. SoMo_Update slightly overestimates surface SM during warm seasons due to the bias noted for the SMAP_L3_SCA_Asc dataset (see Section 4.1.3 ), which is used as the reference surface SM data for rescaling. For the Shiquanhe network, SoMo_Update also significantly improves the overestimations noted for the original SM estimates. The results reveal that the updated SM estimates for model-based products using the outperforming satellite-based surface SM data combined with CDF matching and ExpF methods are satisfactory in both network areas, which opens up a new possibility in improving the model-based SM profile data across the TP.  6 Conclusion This study comprehensively assess the performance of commonly used surface and subsurface SM products using long-term SM observations on the TP, and investigates the ability of the ExpF approach in estimating subsurface SM on regional-scale on the TP. Specifically, 12 satellite-based and 10 model-based SM products, along with subsurface SM estimates using the ExpF method based on the outperforming satellite-based surface SM products are evaluated against SM observations at depths of 5, 20, and 40 cm. The SM observations are collected over a 10-year period from two monitoring networks on the TP, i.e., Maqu and Shiquanhe, which are located in a humid region mostly covered by grassland and an arid region mainly covered by bare ground, respectively. Furthermore, the potential of using the satellite-based surface SM data in combination with CDF matching and ExpF methods to enhance the model-based SM profile data is explored. The assessments of satellite-based SM products indicate that surface SM retrievals from C- and X-band TB measurements (i.e., LPRM and JAXA AMSR2) generally show poorer performance compared to those from L-band TB measurements (i.e., SMAP and SMOS). Among all the products, SMAP_L3 provides the best surface SM retrievals for both networks, with the SCA-V and DCA products performing better in the arid and humid areas, respectively. As a result, the harmonized products produced based on the SMAP data (i.e., SMOSMAP and NNsm) provide enhanced accuracy compared to the SMOS-IC and LPRM/JAXA AMSR2 products. Surprisingly, the latest version (v7.1) of both CCI_P and CCI_A products shows degraded performance compared to its predecessor (v5.3) in both networks, as evidenced by larger values of biases and RMSD. The latest CCI_P product includes the usage of TB data from GPM and FengYun satellite operated at high-frequency bands as well as from daytime dataset, while the latest CCI_A product adopts the ASCAT H119 descending dataset, all of which may bring additional uncertainties and lead to potential deficiency. The evaluations of model-based SM products show that the majority of model-based SM simulations exhibit higher accuracy (i.e. higher KGE scores) in the humid area compared to the arid area, and generally perform better during the warm season in comparison to the cold season. In addition, most of the model-based products exhibit superior performance in estimating surface SM compared to subsurface SM. Among all the products, SMAP_L4 provides relatively more accurate SM profiles estimates in both regions because of the assimilation of L-band TB data. Additionally, the validation of subsurface SM estimates using the ExpF method based on the outperforming satellite-based surface SM data (i.e., SMAP_L3 and NNsm) suggests that the method is capable of estimating reliable subsurface SM in both regions. There is no notable difference in the accuracy of subsurface SM estimates between 20 and 40 cm. Moreover, the updated SM estimates of selected model-based products, which are produced using both CDF matching and ExpF methods in combination with the outperforming satellite-based surface SM data (i.e. SMAP_L3), exhibits significantly higher accuracy than the original SM estimates at every depth in both regions. In summary, this research has demonstrated the superiority of employing the L-band TB measurements especially from SMAP to generate surface SM data and constrain the model-based surface and subsurface SM simulations via data assimilation on both humid and arid regions over the TP. Besides the usage of data assimilation method, employing the outperforming satellite-based surface SM data in combination with both CDF matching and ExpF methods also leads to improved model-based SM profile data. It opens up a new possibility in enhancing accuracy of the model-based SM profile data across the TP in the future.
1 Introduction As a kind of natural carbon source and sink, wetlands are the main forces to achieve carbon sequestration and emission reduction in the ecosystem (Bao et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2024 ). A specific subset, peatland, covers 3 % of the earth's landmass (Evans, 2013 ) and hosts 550 Pg or about 20–30 % of global soil organic carbon reserves (Jackson et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2010 ). Peatlands play a major part in the global carbon cycle because they are active sites for the exchange of carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor between the surface and the atmosphere (Koebsch et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022c; Peng et al., 2019; Pullens et al., 2016 ). Peatlands provide irreplaceable ecological roles, yet they are also delicate and fragile ecosystems (Andersen et al., 2017; Anderson et al., 2003 ). The distinct hydrological characteristics inherent to peatlands serve as a critical foundation for their capacity to sustain carbon sequestration (Loisel and Gallego-Sala, 2022 ). The peatland ecosystem faces threats due to global warming, which also disrupts the water and carbon cycles (Leifeld et al., 2019; Turetsky et al., 2020 ). This variation impacts the hydrological process in the relevant region in addition to altering the exchanges of greenhouse gases. Consequently, it is crucial to monitor carbon and water vapor fluxes as well as associated meteorological and hydrological variables over an extended period in peatland ecosystems. The eddy covariance technology is widely used for carbon and water vapor fluxes monitoring (Liu et al., 2021; Sakabe et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2024 ). The eddy covariance system can concurrently gather a large number of environmental factors data and enable long-term continuous in-situ measurement of carbon and water vapor fluxes over a period of half an hour (Polonik et al., 2019 ). Currently, perennial monitoring is now primarily concerned with the ecosystems of river basins, grasslands, forests, and farmlands (Ahirwal et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2018; Ouyang et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2020 ), with subalpine peatland ecosystems in subtropics receiving less attention. Furthermore, prior research has focused mostly on carbon fluxes (Deshmukh et al., 2021; Lund et al., 2009 ), whereas studies on water vapor flux have been conducted in peatlands very infrequently. In addition, pertinent studies have concentrated on evapotranspiration (ET), encompassing plant transpiration and surface evaporation, which is a significant element of water vapor flux (Ponce-Campos et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2024 ) and a key component of water budget (Du et al., 2021; Keenan et al., 2013 ). Nevertheless, despite the use of several models and micrometeorological methodologies, water vapor investigation employing eddy covariance typically limits itself to evapotranspiration measurement and division owing to surface intricacy and variety of study regions (Klosterhalfen et al., 2019; Perez-Priego et al., 2018 ). In contrast to ET, water vapor flux accounts for H2 O exchanges in multiple directions. Furthermore, data processing techniques and in-situ continuous monitoring technologies have developed to the point where continuous and reliable data can be collected (Aubinet et al., 2012; Cao et al., 2016 ). However, long-term research on water vapor fluxes as well as their connections to carbon fluxes, especially for subalpine peatlands in subtropics based on in-suit observation, has not been documented. Comprehensive investigations in the aforementioned fields can not only compensate for the defects of carbon and water vapor monitoring in subtropical regions, but they can also supply vital data support for exploring the regularity and mechanism of the carbon and water cycle in peatlands. Carbon fluxes in wetland systems are reported to be regulated by multiple environmental factors, such as temperature, precipitation, and plant cover (Liu et al., 2021; Xiao et al., 2013 ), while less research on water vapor flux. Prior findings indicate that there is geographical heterogeneity in the carbon flux regulation mechanism (Griffis et al., 2020; Parmentier et al., 2009 ). Moreover, temperature changes in different seasons have distinct effects on carbon and water vapor flux variations. High temperatures in early spring extend the growing season and encourage the storage of carbon and water, whereas high temperatures in the summer hurt the carbon and water status of the ecosystem (Gu et al., 2022; Li et al., 2021; Seyednasrollah et al., 2020; Vermeire et al., 2008; Walker et al., 2015; Xie et al., 2018 ). It is implied that the dynamics of the carbon and water vapor fluxes may be regulated by environmental factors with temporal heterogeneity. Consequently, investigation into the mechanisms governing the fluxes of water vapor and carbon in subalpine peatlands in subtropics across a range of temporal scales is imperative. Hence, the Dajiuhu peatland was chosen as our study location and in-situ ecological monitoring was conducted using the eddy covariance tower. Over the course of seven years, fluxes of carbon and water vapor as well as meteorological and hydrological indices were collected. We separated all data into different periods, daytime and nighttime in the growing and non-growing seasons. Supplemented with analysis methods, the following objectives are expected to be achieved: (a) quantify the diurnal and seasonal patterns of CO2  and water vapor fluxes in the Dajiuhu peatland; (b) explore the relationship between CO2  flux and water vapor flux in the Dajiuhu peatland during different periods; (c) identify the primary environmental factors controlling CO2  and water vapor flux in the Dajiuhu peatland at daytime and nighttime in the growing and non-growing season, as well as obtain the indicators of carbon and water vapor flux variations.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study site description Our research was conducted in the Dajiuhu peatland (31°28′44.45″N, 110°00′14.61″E), the oldest, most typical, and well-preserved Sphagnum  bog. The Dajiuhu peatland, a part of the Dajiuhu National Wetland Park, is located in Shennongjia, northwest part of Hubei province, China (Fig. S1 ). In the middle of the wetland runs a small stream that connects nine lakes, and our study area is near the third lake. With an average elevation of 1730 m, the Dajiuhu wetland is acknowledged as a subalpine basin. Subalpine mountains, rising to elevations of 2200–2800 m, around it. There is no surface river drainage or influx of foreign rivers across the entire area; in other words, water originates from precipitation and exits underground. The Dajiuhu peatland, in the core area of the wetland, has a peat layer with an average thickness of 1.8 m and a maximum thickness of 3.6 m. This area is characterized by a subtropical monsoon climate, being wet and warm in summer, and drier and milder in winter, which has remarkable seasonal variation, of which the average temperature is 7.2℃. Precipitation in the Dajiuhu peatland mostly falls between May and September, with an approximate yearly total of 1550 mm (Liu et al., 2022b ). As to natural vegetation, Sphagnum palustre  is the principal species, and herbaceous plants including Carex argyi , Juncus effusus , and Festuca rubra  are also discovered.  2.2 Data source In-suit measurement was achieved by the eddy covariance system. Since August 2015, we have been measuring climatic conditions and the net ecosystem exchanges of carbon dioxide and water vapor between the surface and atmosphere by installing a 4-meter flux tower in the middle of the targeted peatland. Our eddy covariance measurement tower is mainly comprised of a 3D sonic anemometer (CAST3, LI-COR, USA), an open-path CO2 /H2 O monitor ((LI-7500, LI-COR, USA), wind sensor (A100R, Campbell, USA). Bio-meteorological auxiliary sensor (HMP155, Vaisala, Finland) was utilized to record air temperature (Ta) and RH. Precipitation (Prcp) was detected by tipping bucket rain gauge (TR-525USW, Campbell, USA). Moreover, multiple meteorological sensors were used to measure photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD) (LI-190SB, Campbell, USA), Rn (CNR4, Kipp&Zonen, Netherlands), soil temperature (Ts) at 10, 20 and 30 cm below the surface (TM-L10, LI-COR, USA), and soil water content (SWC) at 10, 20 and 30 cm below the surface (CS616, Campbell, USA). Using RH and Ta, the vapor pressure deficit (VPD) was calculated. Relevant data were captured by the Sutron (Sutron, USA) data collector. Fluxes raw data were monitored at 10 Hz, and meteorological data were measured at 1 Hz. Fluxes and meteorological data were recorded with an interval of 30 min. Unfortunately, entire water vapor fluxes data for the period of December 2019 to June 2020 was lacking due to data processing failure. Therefore, CO2  fluxes were also removed in the corresponding period. Moreover, some meteorological parameters were obtained from external weather stations.  2.3 Carbon dioxide and water vapor fluxes data process Four times a year, raw data was gathered using an external hard drive. The half-hourly original data were preprocessed by the EddyPro system (v.7.0.6, LI-COR, USA) and added quality control treatment thereafter. The steps for removing data were as follows: (1) Quality assurance and quality control filters applied to the data. The quality control policy, which employs a combined flag system, is described in the documentation of the Eddy Covariance software package TK2 (Mauder and Foken, 2011 ). This policy is widely used and served as the standard for the CarboEurope-IP project (https://www.copernicus.eu/en/carbo-europe-ip ). Under this system, fluxes with a value of “0” are the highest quality, fluxes with a value of “1” are suitable for general analysis, and fluxes with a value of “2” are defined as low quality. In this investigation, data with a flat “2” were eliminated from the dataset; (2) Data with precipitation in the same period were removed; (3) The moving-point test (MPT) in TOVI software was used to determine the friction velocity (u*) threshold. Data in this investigation were excluded if the u* criterion was less than 0.15 m/s; (4) The footprint analysis was conducted using a two-dimensional model (Kljun et al., 2004 ). The data beyond the region of interest after footprint flux allocation analysis were eliminated; (5) Outliers based on prior experience (NEE < −40 μmol m−2  s−1  or NEE > 40 μmol m−2  s−1 ; H2 O < −10 mmol m−2  s−1  or H2 O > 10 mmol m−2  s−1 ) were removed. After every round of filtering and data exclusion, more than 35 % of the data was kept. We address gaps in half-hourly data that passed the quality control process by multiple methods. Linear interpolation was used to fill in data gaps that lasted less than 2 h. Regarding data gaps of more than 2 h for meteorological parameters and fluxes, the REddyProcWeb online tool procedure (https://bgc.iwww.mpg.de/5622399/REddyProc ), launched by Max Plank Institute for Biogeochemistry, was applied for gap-filling. The “REddyProc” package in R, which provides standardized procedures for processing the eddy covariance data, served as the model for the creation of the REddyProcWeb web application. The look-up table (LUT) and mean diurnal course (MDC) methods integrated into the marginal distribution sampling (MDS) method found in the "REddyProc" package to perform interpolation based on the temporal autocorrelation of flux data and the covariation between flux data and meteorological parameters. The environmental variables, including Ts, Ta, PPFD, RH, and VPD, were utilized. NEE and H2 O flux data were processed with the same approach. Half-hourly gap-filled NEE were further split into total ecosystem respiration (Reco) and gross primary production (GPP) by night-time partitioning algorithm (Reichstein et al., 2005 ). Water usage efficiency (WUE) is the ecosystem-level ratio of carbon gain to water loss (Ponton et al., 2006 ). The ecological WUE was established in this manner:WUE = GPP  ET         2.4 Water table depth data acquisition and periods division From January 2019, we implemented WTD equipment (levelogger M20, Solinst, Canada) at the center of our study area. This apparatus can measure absolute pressure, which includes air and water pressure. Subsequently, the absolute pressure data is meticulously processed using Solinst Levelogger software to accurately derive the corresponding water table depths, with a precision level of ±1 cm. We conducted an analysis of climatic and hydrological parameters, CO2  and H2 O fluxes during a seven-year period, spanning from January 2016 to December 2022. Based on cumulative daily CO2  adsorption, the periods in the Dajiuhu peatland were divided into the growing season (GS) and the non-growing season (NGS) using the Growth/Sigmoid Logistic function in Origin (v.2022b, OriginLab, USA). The times at which the cumulative value of CO2  reaches 20 % and 80 % of the total cumulative value, respectively, are denoted by the symbols EC20 and EC80. The EC20 and EC80 points on the fitted curves marked the beginning and end of the growing season. We designated the period from May to September as the growing season and the remaining months of the year as the non-growing season based on the results. Based on PPFD results, a day was divided into day and night segments for additional analysis. When PPFD > 0, appropriate data sets were summarized in the daytime group, and the rest were in the nighttime group.  2.5 Statistical analysis Spearman’s rank correlation analyses were carried out to examine the relationship between CO2 , H2 O fluxes, and meteorological and hydrological factors throughout different periods based on half-hourly data using SPSS 18.0 (IBM SPSS Statistics). Using the R software packages “randomForest” and “rfPermute”, we performed random forest analyses to explore the significance of various environmental factors’ effects on fluxes fluctuations. K-fold cross-validation was accomplished by “caret” packages. Grouped bubble plots were created using the R software packages “ggplot2”, “dplyr”, and “base” to display the results. Linear and non-linear regression among CO2  and H2 O as well as fluxes and WTD were implemented in Origin software. Hysteresis between abiotic parameters and fluxes were plotted in Origin using seven-year averaged data at various times of the day.   3 Results 3.1 Meteorological and hydrological conditions in the Dajiuhu peatland  Fig. 1  exhibited daily dynamics of meteorological and hydrological parameters from 2016 to 2022 in the Dajiuhu peatland, with corresponding statistics set out in Table S1 . Around July and August, Ts and Ta peaked, whereas around January and February, they fell to the lowest level (Fig. 1 a). During the research period, the Rn maxima varied from 218.45 to 245.99 W m−2 , and they all appeared in July of the growing season (Fig. 1 b). In addition, the growing seasons yielded the highest PPFD values, which ranged from 369.68 to 672.98 mol m−2  s−1  (Table S1 ). Over a period of seven years, the SWC peaks varied from 62.92 % to 73.42 %, while the lowest values were between 44.23 % and 59.23 % (Fig. 1 c, Table S1 ). Most of the SWC peaks appeared in the non-growing season, while SWC minimum values were discovered in the growing season. July and August had the lowest recorded water table depths (Fig. 1 d). Moreover, meteorological and hydrological conditions showed obvious seasonal diurnal patterns (Table S2 ). We observed higher mean Rn, ET, Ta, Ts, and lower WTD in the growing season than in the non-growing season. In contrast, the average values of RH and SWC barely changed between the two periods. Except Ts, SWC, and WTD, there were notable variations in Rn, ET, Ta, VPD, RH, and PPFD during daytime and nighttime in both growing and non-growing seasons. From 2016–2022, the corresponding annual precipitations amounts were 1427.72, 1663.66, 1533.44, 945.20, 1702.01, 1928.40, and 1113.30 mm. The growing season was when the majority of evapotranspiration and precipitation were recorded (Fig. S2 ).  3.2 Characteristic of CO2  and H2 O fluxes Daily variations of CO2  and H2 O fluxes from 2016 to 2022 were exhibited in  Fig. 2 . Depending on the year, the Dajiuhu peatland may serve as a source or a sink. The corresponding annual NEE values were 121.00, −165.74, −239.23, −5.93, −66.29, −368.82, and 8.84 g C m−2  yr−1  (Table S3 ). The daily NEE fluxes down to peaks in May, June, and July (Fig. 2 a). The growing season saw the appearance of the greatest Reco levels. During the months of June, July, and August, the GPP changes reached their lowest points. In addition, the Dajiuhu peatland served as a permanent source of water vapor fluxes. From 2016–2022, yearly H2 O fluxes were 698.02, 784.24, 792.26, 582.97, 363.43, 635.83, and 601.76 kg yr−1 , correspondingly. The greatest H2 O fluxes were detected in July (Fig. 2 b). Additionally, NEE and H2 O fluxes presented distinct seasonal and diel patterns ( Fig. 3 ), and annual mean values of the half-hourly NEE and H2 O fluxes during various periods were displayed in Table S4 . During the growing season, NEE was lower during the day than they were during the non-growing season; however, at night, the opposite occurred (Fig. 3 ab). Furthermore, higher H2 O fluxes were discovered during the growing season, and H2 O fluxes always had their greatest values in the daytime (Fig. 3 cd). The daily variation tendency of NEE showed a “U” shape, while the daily H2 O fluxes over a seven-year period showed an inverted “U” shape, according to Fig. 3ef. From 2016–2022, the daily minimum values of NEE were −3.64, −4.02, −3.91, −4.14, −4.11, −3.13, and −3.17 μmol m−2  s−1 , and the daily maximum H2 O fluxes were 3.46, 3.65, 3.39, 2.97, 4.30, 3.03, and 3.39 mmol m−2  s−1 , respectively. NEE troughs and H2 O maxima occurred every day between 12:00–13:30.  3.3 Relationships between NEE and H2 O fluxes During the growth and non-growing seasons of each year, the correlations between NEE and H2 O fluxes were investigated both in daytime and nighttime. Linear or non-linear relationships were found in the daytime ( Fig. 4 ), while nighttime relationships were irregular (Fig. S3 ). Correlations and values of adjusted R-square were displayed in Fig. 4 , and Table S5  provided a summary of significant values. During the growing season, NEE values, the majority of which were negative, actually decreased as H2 O fluxes rose. Namely, NEE negatively related to H2 O fluxes with a correlation of −0.64, −0.69, −0.65, −0.53, −0.43, and −0.56 for six years (2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2021, and 2022), respectively. Cubic polynomials might be used to mimic the interactions between NEE and H2 O fluxes during the non-growing season; all of the results were highly significant. Moreover, we examined WUE in the Dajiuhu peatland (Fig. S4 ). For the year of 2016 through 2019 and 2022, the mean annual WUE was, respectively, 1.42, 1.93, 1.99, 2.77, and 1.33 g C kg−1  H2 O (Table S3 ). The WUE averages for the growing and non-growing seasons were 2.24 and 1.61 g C kg−1  H2 O, respectively.  3.4 Influential factors of CO2  and H2 O fluxes To assess the abiological associations between various environmental parameters and changes in CO2  and H2 O fluxes, we employed random forest analyses and correlation analyses ( Fig. 5 ). The random forest models were assessed using K-fold cross-validation (Fig. S5 ). Table S6  presented the correlation analysis results. Meteorological parameters accounted for 65.33 %, 39.24 %, 41.83 %, and 13.41 % of the variability in NEE, and 62.46 %, 22.56 %, 68.87 %, and 42.87 % of the variability in H2 O fluxes, during daytime and nighttime across both growing and non-growing seasons, respectively (Fig. 5 , Table S7 ). At daytime, RH and WTD were positively related to NEE, whereas had negative correlations with H2 O fluxes during the growing season. When it came to the non-growing season, ET was a reliable and consistent predictor. Ta had a strong correlation with changes in NEE at nighttime and with ET and VPD for H2 O fluxes. Most of the time, Rn, Ts, and Ta were important abiotic parameters for forecasting changes in NEE fluxes; however, these variables had no bearing on water vapor fluxes. We discovered that VPD and ET were strong, favorable environmental determinants for fluctuations of water vapor fluxes. Relevant investigations using data across the entire period demonstrated the significance of ET, Ta, Ts, and WTD in NEE flux variations; only ET was identified as a major factor affecting water vapor fluxes over the whole time. Table S8  and Table S9  contained a list of pertinent outcomes. Results of non-linear fit between monthly NEE, H2 O fluxes, and WTD in the growing and non-growing season suggested that water table depths of around 15 and 30 cm were important water levels in the Dajiuhu peatland ( Fig. 6 , Table S10 ), especially for carbon sequestration. In the growing season, the positive value of NEE emerged when WTD dropped to 32 cm. In the non-growing season, as WTD varied by about 14 cm, negative values of NEE appeared.  3.5 Hysteresis loops description Using seven-year mean data at various times of day for both growing and non-growing seasons, typical hysteresis loops involving NEE, H2 O fluxes, and Ts, Ta, and VPD were found ( Fig. 7 ). Diel phase analyses demonstrated that the hysteresis loops in the growing and non-growing seasons varied significantly in intensity. The region enclosed by a loop signified the magnitude of hysteresis, which was higher during the growing season. Diel phases of NEE and Ta generated counterclockwise patterns, while hysteresis between H2 O fluxes and Ta was clockwise (Fig. 7 ab). Overall, diel phases between NEE, H2 O fluxes, and Ta followed comparable patterns in the two periods. NEE and H2 O fluxes changed slightly with Ta at nighttime (from 20:00–6:00) in both seasons. During the daytime, NEE decreased to a minimum at around midday and then climbed as Ta rose. Precisely, NEE was higher in the afternoon than in the morning under the same air temperature, while H2 O flux was the opposite. In addition, a similar variation pattern to that observed in hysteresis between NEE, H2 O fluxes, and Ta was also discovered in loops between NEE, H2 O fluxes, and VPD (Fig. 7ef). The clockwise loop between NEE and Ts and the counterclockwise loop between H2 O flux and Ts both differed in shape between the growing and non-growing seasons (Fig. 7 cd)·H2 O fluxes increased gradually, peaked at 4.90 mmol m−2  s−1  around 13:00, and then declined to the minimum (almost 0.5 mmol m−2  s−1 ) at approximately 20:00. Around midday, NEE reached a minimum of −7.03 μmol m−2  s−1 , after which it rapidly increased. At the same soil temperature, NEE was higher whereas H2 O flux was lower in the afternoon than in the morning.   4 Discussion 4.1 Water vapor and CO2  fluxes Characterization in the Dajiuhu peatland The Dajiuhu peatland, being a reliable water vapor source, exhibited greater strength in water vapor emission, when compared to the Riganqiao alpine peatland (Liu et al., 2022c ). This suggested a more substantial influence on localized climate change (Li et al., 2006 ). Missing data was the reason given for the yearly water vapor flux value drop that was discovered in 2020. Besides, the Dajiuhu peatland served as a CO2  sink throughout a seven-year period. Past study has domonstrated that anomalies in precipitation during the initial stages of the growing season will have a profound impact on CO2  fluxes all year long (Barel et al., 2021 ). Thus, we conjectured that the Dajiuhu peatland turned into a source of CO2  as a result of less precipitation in May at the start of the growth season in 2016. Furthermore, the whole Yangtze River Basin had an uncommon intense drought episode in 2022 that lasted from June to September (Duan et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2023 ). This event was characterized by precipitation levels during this period reaching their lowest in 61 years (Shu et al., 2022 ). Our analysis found that yearly NEE and precipitation had a negative association for the whole study period (Fig. S6 ). This observation was consistent with phenomena previously documented within forest ecosystems (Chatterjee et al., 2018 ). Consequently, the diminished yearly precipitation in 2022 attenuated the carbon sink function of the Dajiuhu peatland. Our research demonstrated that, in contrast to water vapor source-sink functions, the carbon source-sink function of the Dajiuhu peatland was more vulnerable to qualitative changes brought on by extreme climate events.  4.2 Water vapor and CO2  flux relationships Higher WUE during the growing season indicated that more CO2  was sequestered than during the non-growing season (Xing et al., 2023 ). Consistent with earlier researches (Liu et al., 2022c, 2014; Niu et al., 2016 ), the Dajiuhu peatland exhibited noteworthy changes in both CO2  and H2 O fluxes during the daytime, with an extreme value noted between 12:00 and 13:30. There were discernible linear negative correlations between NEE and H2 O flux (Wang et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2013 ). This implyed that enhanced transpiration by peatland vegetation could further facilitate CO2  absorption during the growing season. However, it’s worth noting that this phenomenon was confined to daytime observations within our research area. Additionally, prior research has shown an exponential relationship between carbon and water vapor fluxes in sandy settings, which are predominantly governed by shrub species (Zhang et al., 2024 ). The disparity between our investigation and those pertaining to sandy terrain highlighted the important regulating role that vegetation has on carbon-water dynamics in different ecosystems. During the daylight hours of the non-growing season, the relationship between NEE and H2 O adhered to a Cubic polynomial model, indicating a more intricate interplay in carbon and water vapor exchanges occurring within this period. In the Zoige peatland, negative linear correlations persisted between NEE and H2 O fluxes in the non-growing season (Liu et al., 2022c ). This discrepancy suggested the necessity to conduct research on the coupling of carbon and water vapor fluxes in peatlands considering distinct temporal periods, aligning with specific research objectives. Furthermore, the nocturnal characterization of the carbon-water coupling, both within and beyond the growing season, presented a computational challenge for mathematical models (Lv et al., 2024 ), mirroring our research findings. In the Dajiuhu peatland, nighttime variations for both CO2  and H2 O fluxes are less well explained by meteorological conditions. These findings emphasized the imperative to avoid exclusive reliance on meteorological factors. The processes of greenhouse gas (GHG) production, translocation, and assimilation are mediated by a variety of environmental components, including water, nutrients, and overlaying vegetation (Bubier et al., 2003 ; Chapin et al., 2004 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ). In order to fill in the current knowledge gaps regarding the regulatory mechanisms controlling nocturnal carbon and water vapor exchanges in peatland ecosystems, a thorough examination of the previously described components was essential.  4.3 Indicative factors of CO2  and H2 O fluxes in the Dajiuhu peatland Our comprehensive investigation revealed that the main factors influencing CO2  fluxes in the Dajiuhu peatland were ET, WTD, Ts, and Ta. Significantly, ET emerged as a crucial determinant influencing variations in water vapor fluxes, highlighting its critical function in the hydrological dynamics of this ecosystem. The escalation of ET, triggered by global warming (Helbig et al., 2020; Humphreys et al., 2006 ), was poised to exert profound impacts on the carbon and water cycles within the Dajiuhu peatland. Moreover, water vapor flux in the Dajiuhu peatland was more responsive to hydrological and thermal parameters, specifically VPD and ET, while NEE was more sensitive to radiative and thermal conditions, such as Rn, Ts, and Ta. Likewise, in Zoige peatland, hydrological conditions alongside temperature exerted a significant influence on seasonal changes in water vapor fluxes throughout both the growing and non-growing seasons (Liu et al., 2022c ). RH and WTD functioned as co-regulating factors affecting both NEE and water vapor fluxes in the daytime during the growing season. Some studies indicate that NEE is not controlled by WTD (Parmentier et al., 2009 ), while others imply that WTD has a regulatory impact on NEE (Aslan-Sungur et al., 2016; McDonald et al., 2023; Yan et al., 2023 ). By controlling the existence of anoxic conditions within the soil environment, the water status of peatlands assume a crucial role in influencing CO2  exchange dynamics (Laiho, 2006; Taillardat et al., 2022 ). Based on half-hourly recorded data, we found a linear correlation between NEE, water vapor fluxes, and WTD. Furthermore, a WTD of 30 cm appeared as a key threshold throughout the growing season in the Dajiuhu peatland, according to monthly polynomial curve fitting analyses. This finding corroborated the evidence presented in the preceding research (Liu et al., 2022a ). Continuous decline beyond this threshold might precipitate a shift in ecological function, transitioning from CO2  sink to source. During the non-growing season, carbon sequestration was observed when WTD ranged from approximately 14 cm. The discoveries mentioned above underscored the necessity of conducting ecological research on a variety of time scales since they conveyed diverse implications. Studies have established that hydrological conditions control evapotranspiration (Driesen et al., 2020; Sonnentag et al., 2010; Volik et al., 2021 ). Additionally, we found that water vapor fluxes and WTD positively correlated in our investigation. Consequently, water vapor flux could be regarded as a comprehensive indicator reflecting the hydrological changes and overall hydrological function of the Dajiuhu peatland. Conclusions on how RH affected water vapor fluxes were likewise not entirely consistent. Prior study has shown that RH exerted a more pronounced influence on water vapor flux regulation compared to temperature (Xiao et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, a study (Liu et al., 2022c ) discovered a modest association between H2 O fluxes and RH. RH was identified as a critical regulating component for H2 O fluxes in our current investigation. The disparity was ascribed to different regional climates. The environment in the Dajiuhu peatland usually remained reasonably humid, with RH varying over a period of seven years from 64.47 % to 87.99 %. Additionally, RH exhibited notable fluctuations throughout the course of the year. In wetlands where reeds predominate, it was previously discovered that RH and CO2  fluxes were negatively associated (Jia et al., 2017; Li et al., 2016; Vázquez-Lule and Vargas, 2021 ). Reduced RH created circumstances of water stress, which in turn caused stomatal closure in other ecosystems (Bauer et al., 2013; Buckley, 2019 ), hence diminishing CO2  absorption. However, in our study area, a contrasting scenario was observed. The NEE direction was primarily governed by GPP rather than Reco in the Dajiuhu peatland (Fig. S7 ). Our observations showed significant positive associations between RH and GPP (Fig. S8 ). Elevated RH was observed to be positively related to precipitation and have a negative correlation with PPFD. Due to the decreased PPFD resulting from the increased cloud cover brought on by precipitation, rainfall events may cause a decline in GPP (Ouyang et al., 2021; Saunders et al., 2014 ). Low GPP led to increased CO2  emission.  4.4 Diel rhythms/phase analysis Numerous environmental conditions in peatlands influence carbon and water vapor fluxes, and each of these components has distinct rhythmic changes (Gentine et al., 2019 ). These fluxes also display seasonal and diel fluctuations. Hysteresis loops are caused by an inability of flux changes and ambient component rhythmicities to synchronize (Niu et al., 2011 ). In the Dajiuhu peatland, typical hysteresis between NEE, H2 O fluxes, and Ts, Ta, and VPD were observed. During the nighttime, various environmental factors undergo less conspicuous changes; consequently, diel patterns are more pronounced during the daytime, whereas the nocturnal patterns appear more disorderly. Hysteresis loops are used to monitor how plants interact with their surroundings (Lin et al., 2019 ). In forest and agricultural ecosystems, a hysteresis phenomenon is observed between VPD and net ecosystem productivity (Xing et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2022 ). Similar hysteresis loops between NEE and VPD as well as Ta appeared in our research region, displaying that net ecosystem production is often higher in the morning than in the afternoon. The elevated stomatal conductance of plant leaves in the morning has been linked to the observed fluctuations in net ecosystem productivity. Nevertheless, in our study area, where Sphagnum  dominates, its unique structure features pseudo-stomata in its sporophytes. Due to their inability to open and close, these pseudo-stomata lack the functioning mechanism of traditional stomata (Duckett et al., 2009; Merced, 2015 ). As a result, we proposed that the primary biological factor responsible for the observed hysteresis effect in the Dajiuhu subalpine peatland was herbaceous plants rather than moss. Hysteresis between fluxes and environmental factors varies among biomes and climat, as previous studies have demonstrated (Xu et al., 2022; Xu, 2022 ). Our research revealed that hystereses in subalpine peatland experienced seasonal variation. The larger enclosed area of the hysteresis was observed illustrating stronger relationships between CO2 , water vapor fluxes, and Ts, Ta, and VPD in the growing season suggesting that environmental factors other than Ts, Ta, and VPD become stronger in influencing the fluxes in this period (Cui et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, the resultant hysteresis loops prove the existence of limiting factors (Niu et al., 2011 ). Accumulated radiation and soil water content attributed to the hysteresis reactions of CO2  fluxes. Considering the collective evidence, in this current study, we speculated that lower Rn led to the smaller magnitude of hysteresis loops of NEE and Ts, Ta, and VPD during the non-growing season, when soil moisture level was adequate in the Dajiuhu peatland (Table S2 ). The simulation of fluxes in models faces challenges due to the hysteresis effects, as highlighted in previous studies (Cui et al., 2020; Matheny et al., 2014a; Renner et al., 2019 ). Rn therefore becomes a meteorological element that needs careful attention when building a model for carbon fluxes in subalpine peatlands in subtropics. A number of studies have examined the dynamics of hysteresis between evapotranspiration and abiotic variables, suggesting that soil hydraulic conductivity, closely related to the WTD (Pirastru et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023 ), is a primary factor in the formation of hysteresis loop (Matheny et al., 2014b; O'Grady et al., 1999 ). The direction, shape, and size of clockwise hysteresis loops between evaporation and VPD, Ta, and Ts vary in response to variations in water level (Cui et al., 2020 ). Stronger relationships displayed in hysteresis dynamics between water vapor fluxes and VPD, Ts, and Ta in the growing season, during in which WTD decreased, underscored the substantive impact of WTD.   5 Conclusion In this study, over the course of seven years, fluxes of carbon and water vapor as well as meteorological and hydrological indices were collected in the Dajiuhu peatland using the eddy covariance tower. All data were seperated into different periods, daytime and nighttime in the growing and non-growing seasons for further analyses. The key results are as follows:(1) The Dajiuhu peatland served as a CO2  sink, its stability was noted to be comparatively lower, rendering it susceptible to the effects of extreme weather events. Concurrently, it served as a reliable and stable source of H2 O·H2 O fluxes could be considered as a comprehensive indicator reflecting the hydrological changes and overall hydrological function of the Dajiuhu peatland.  (2) Elevated levels of CO2  uptake and H2 O release were documented during the growing season compared to the non-growing season. Furthermore, heightened rates of CO2  uptake and H2 O release were observed during daytime intervals as opposed to nighttime periods. In our investigation into the daytime carbon-water coupling, we noted a pronounced negative correlation during the growing season, whereas a trinomial relationship characterized the non-growing season; however, no conspicuous correlation was discerned during nighttime.  (3) RH, WTD, and ET emerged as pivotal meteorological parameters influencing the carbon-water coupling. Pronounced hysteresis loops manifested between CO2 , H2 O, and key environmental variables including Ta, Ts, and VPD. Notably, there was a noticeable increase in the hysteresis loop area in the growth season as opposed to the non-growing season. Rn was identified as the principal factor influencing the seasonal variations in hysteresis loops associated with NEE, whereas WTD was found to be the primary determinant driving the seasonal fluctuations in hysteresis loops related to H2 O fluxes.    The findings underscored the relationship between CO2  flux and water vapor flux as well as their primary influential environmental factors in the Dajiuhu subalpine peatland during different periods over a long period. These results underscored the imperative for ecological research to be undertaken across diverse temporal scales. Furthermore, they furnished empirical support for the sustainable management of carbon and water resources in subalpine peatlands.
1 Introduction Endorheic basin is a unique landscapes defined by closed hydrological systems, where land-locked watershed has no outflow beyond its boundaries. Within this basin, an endorheic lake, also referred to as sink or terminal lake, accumulates and maintains water volume through a balance of the inflow from rivers and precipitation to the loss of evaporation from the lake surface (Wang et al., 2018 ). This balance is vulnerable to disruptions from human activities, climate variations, and droughts, which can lead to rapid fluctuations in the total volume of these water bodies (Yapiyev et al., 2019 ). Such disturbances often result in significant environmental challenges and disasters in the riparian areas (Hassani et al., 2020; Szumińska et al., 2020 ). Examples of large-scale volume changes in endorheic lakes include the Aral Sea in Central Asia (Glantz, 2007 ), Urmia Lake in Middle East Asia (Dehghanipour et al., 2020; Schulz et al., 2020 ), and Lake Chad in Africa (Carmouze et al., 1983; Policelli et al., 2019 ). The impact of these volume changes extends beyond the lake vicinity, affecting surrounding ecosystems, water quality, marine navigation, and microclimates. Significant variations in the water level can act as indicators of climate change and highlight the impact of anthropogenic activities in an area (Rodionov, 1994; Williamson et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2021b ). For example, the Aral Sea, once the fourth-largest lake in the world, has almost disappeared, transforming the landscape into a desert and profoundly affecting local populations (Glantz, 2007; Micklin, 2000 ). Lake Urmia has been shrinking for a long time posing a significant threat of converting large areas into salt marshes (AghaKouchak et al., 2015; Hassanzadeh et al., 2012 ). The long-term trends and the short-term variability of climate have also significantly affected the status of Lake Turkana and Hayk Basin in East Africa (Mewded et al., 2022; Worku et al., 2014 ). Conversely, increased water levels have been reported in the Tibetan Plateau (Yao et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2021a; Zhang et al., 2017, 2011 ). Understanding the complexity of these systems requires a thorough examination of various factors, including climate change, human activities, and hydrological processes within the basin (Wine and Laronne, 2020; Yapiyev et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021b ). Such assessments are crucial not only for advancing hydrological research but also for informing critical environmental conservation and disaster prevention efforts (Hassani et al., 2020; Yapiyev et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021c ). The Aral Sea, the target of this research, is a dramatic illustration of human activities' impact on endorheic lake water balance. Irrigation expansion, in the latter half of the 20th century, has consumed approximately 84–90 % of the water resources in the basin for agriculture (AQUASTAT, 2019 ), triggering a significant decline in the sea's volume (Abdullaev et al., 2009; Hu et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2021; Raskin et al., 1992; Hamidov et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020 ). As a result, its volume shrank from 1,093.0 Gt in 1960 to 98.1 Gt in 2010 (Gaybullaev et al., 2012a ), 90 % reduction within 50 years. This decline led to the collapse of unique ecosystems and fisheries developed in and around the lake, alongside altering the surrounding climate (Kholmatjanov et al., 2020; Small et al., 2001 ). These large-scale environmental changes associated with the shrinking of the Aral Sea are called the “tragedy of the Aral Sea” and are widely recognized as one of the most severe crises of the 20th century (Glantz, 2007; Micklin, 2007, 2000 ). Moreover, the effects of climate change, evidenced by glacier shrinkage and increased temperatures, have further exacerbated the shrinking of the lake (Farinotti et al., 2015; Unger-Shayesteh et al., 2013; Zemp et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Touge et al., 2015b; Yang et al., 2020 ). Numerous studies have attempted to define drivers behind water level changes in endorheic lakes, addressing mainly climate change and human interventions (Alifujiang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2022; Schulz et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Bagheri et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2019 ). While traditional statistical approaches and satellite-based modeling techniques have been useful for reproducing the past, they cannot comprehensively analyze future climate change and quantify human activity impacts. Physically based terrestrial water circulation models have been widely applied at various scales and offer promising results addressing these limitations, allowing the integration of climate change scenarios and human activity projections (Archfield et al., 2015; Decharme et al., 2019; Döll and Siebert, 2002; Hanasaki et al., 2008; Nitta et al., 2020; van den Hurk et al., 2011 ). However, modeling the water balance of endorheic basins presents unique challenges, particularly in accurately representing the various human water consumption patterns, especially irrigation. Physical models often consider irrigation water consumption, typically calculated by multiplying the water requirement for crops by the irrigation efficiency. While some studies focus on the basin-wide agricultural water consumption, considering irrigation and non-irrigation water demand in the past (Hassani et al., 2020, Kharel and Kirilenko, 2018, 2015 ), very few address large basins’ complex irrigation schemes (Elguindi and Giorgi, 2006a, 2006b ). This research aims to bridge these gaps by developing a comprehensive terrestrial water circulation model for the endorheic lake systems. Through the integration of an endorheic lake budget model, the study provides a robust framework for verifying basin-scale water balance and quantifying the diverse impacts of human water consumption, including irrigation demands, efficiency losses, and diverted drainage water with insights into the complex interactions shaping the future of endorheic basins and their ecosystems. Human impact components extend beyond the required water for crop growth, as various factors have contributed to the shrinkage of the Aral Sea. First, the irrigation water required for agriculture connected to the expansion of the irrigation areas, increasing from 50,000 km2  in 1960 to 79,500 km2  in 1999 (Orlovsky et al., 2001 ). This expansion was primarily diverted to cultivating cotton and wheat on large farms requiring substantial amounts of water for irrigation. Second, it includes water loss due to low irrigation efficiency through traditional furrow irrigation, which can be split into two types: (a) application efficiency: water consumed for plant growth over total supplied water to the farm, leading to losses through evaporation and infiltration into subsurface layers; and (b) conveyance efficiency, related to losses in the canals network, which has expanded extensively to approximately 323,200 km in the basin. The lack of lining and inadequate maintenance exacerbate seepage losses during water transportation (Orlovsky et al., 2001 ). Third, a considerable volume of the drainage water is redirected to newly formed terminal lakes within the irrigated region and does not discharge to the sea (Conrad et al., 2016; Rosen et al., 2018 ). This diversion is related to the geological structure of the basin, where drainage water easily flows to the surrounding depression. And water quality control measures; drainage water is intentionally diverted from the river due to its high salinity level. Notably, creating an endorheic sub-basin as the case of Lake Sarygamysh, which has expanded since the 1960 s due to irrigation drainage from the lower Amu Darya region (Liu et al., 2019 ). Fourth, a significant quantity of water is withdrawn from the Amu Darya outside the Aral Sea watershed, with the Karakum Canal, the longest canal in the world, as a main example. These diversions further contribute to the diminishing water supply within the Aral Sea Basin. In the Aral Sea Basin, each of the outlined water consumption cases significantly impacts the water balance in the basin. Most of the studies address only partial aspects of them or each case separately. For example, the difference in the actual evapotranspiration in the Aral Sea Basin under hypothetical scenarios of irrigation and climate change was calculated (Shibuo et al., 2007 ), reproduction of the historical water balance in the Aral Sea Basin was attempted (Kobayashi et al., 2022; Touge et al., 2013 ), and future projection was performed using various GCM ensembles (Jarsjö et al., 2012 ), although focusing on specific water loss components. In contrast, this study, reconstructs the historical water balance of the entire basin, taking into account various types of human water consumption. The unique hydrological characteristics inherent to endorheic basins, notably observed in the fluctuations of sink lake levels, serve as pivotal benchmarks for validating our model both for the overall volume and constituent components of the basin's water balance. Therefore, our approach integrates a terrestrial water circulation model with an endorheic lake budget model to achieve three main objectives: (i) to develop a comprehensive framework for quantifying basin-scale water balance dynamics; (ii) to validate historical changes in the Aral Sea by reproducing observed fluctuations of the lake surface area; (iii) to quantify various forms of human water consumption over time. Specifically, water consumption is related to irrigation requirements for crops, irrigation efficiency, drainage discharged into the terminal lakes, and water withdrawn outside the basin. Thus, the model can ensure the rationality of the water balance of the entire watershed, especially in parts of water consumption cases and quantitatively measures human activity’s impact on the ecosystems in endorheic basins.  2 Methodology and target area 2.1 Target area The study area focuses on the whole Aral Sea drainage basin (Fig. 1  ). The Aral Sea functions as a terminal lake that accumulates all the surface water inflows. However, several watersheds within the basin were ignored; these include the Karakum Canal, Lake Sarygamysh, and the central Kyzylkum Desert. The Karakum Canal, the longest irrigation canal in the world, diverts water from the Amu Darya River to supply water to Turkmenistan. Lake Sarygamysh acts as a sink lake collecting drainage waters from the lower Amu Darya River region, and has been expanding as a result of it. These two watersheds are considered withdrawals to the outside of the basin. The center of the Kyzylkum Desert is a large depression located between the Amu Darya River Basin and the Syr Darya River Basin. Surface water within this depression does not contribute to the Aral Sea Basin, and therefore considered an external watershed for the purpose of this study.  2.2 Terrestrial water circulation model The main goals of the terrestrial water circulation model developed in this study were as follows: (i) quantify the inflow to the Aral Sea by simulating the hydrological cycle across the entire basin, (ii) incorporate all water consumption processes, and (iii) dynamically represent the expansion and shrinkage of the Aral Sea (detailed work flow is shown in Fig. 2  ). The model is based on the simple biosphere model, including the urban canopy (SiBUC), a land surface model capable of simulating irrigation practices across diverse land cover types, including water bodies (Tanaka, 2005 ). In this research, basically all water consumption is related to irrigation. This water consumption is initially routed to the agricultural fields as irrigation water and calculated by an irrigation scheme in SiBUC. Historical data on irrigated area serves as input for land cover classification. Improvements in irrigation efficiency in the analyzed period were also considered. Secondly, the model accounts for the contribution of irrigation drainage to the terminal lakes within the basin. The inflow was estimated as the amount of water required to maintain the lake's surface area, effectively compensating for evaporative losses. The land cover classification includes the water surface area of the terminal lake, and evaporation was estimated using the water body submodel in SiBUC. Additionally, water withdrawals directed outside of the basin were considered based on local statistical data. Total basin water resources are calculated as the sum of runoff in all grids. The inflow of water into the Aral Sea is then calculated as a difference in the available water resources and total water consumption for the entire basin. Accordingly, the resultant inflow was utilized in the endorheic lake budget model computation. The water body submodel calculated evaporation from the Aral Sea surface, and the resulting sea area was updated and reflected in the land cover condition in the following year. The analysis was conducted over 50 years, from 1961 to 2010, due to the availability of input data. The mountainous areas that supply most water resources have complex elevation distributions, while the downstream irrigated regions with the highest water demand have complex land cover distributions. Therefore, to capture these spatial disparities in high-resolution land cover and elevation distributions for water supply and demand, a high-resolution model with a 1 km mesh was used. This modeling framework offers a distinct advantage, the ability to validate the long-term and basin-scale water balance through changes observed in the endorheic lake (Aral Sea). In developing countries, limitations often exist regarding long-term hydrological data. Verifying the water balance of the endorheic lake thus becomes a valuable tool for understanding local hydrological processes. The validation process prioritized specific aspects of the model results with the following importance. Firstly, basin-scale and long-term water balance of components as estimated from the shrinkage of the Aral Sea. Secondly, the regional water balance for the catchment area of each discharge observation station. Thirdly, point-based validation of input data such as precipitation and temperature. Although a regional breakdown might reveal areas of overestimation or underestimation, the basin-scale, long-term water balance, as evidenced by matching the shrinking Aral Sea area, can be reliably approximated. As is common in studies focusing on developing countries, the analysis relies on readily available global datasets, which may have uncertainties. However, the primary focus is quantifying water consumption, as it has the greatest impact on long-term changes to the basin water balance, rather than achieving perfect accuracy in each individual dataset. Obtaining comprehensive validation data can be a significant challenge, particularly across different countries with an interest in reducing their technical water usage. Therefore, this study prioritized the development of a model that achieves a high degree of agreement with all available data. This approach acknowledges the limitations of validation data and emphasizes the model's ability to consistently perform on the existing datasets. 2.2.1 Land surface model SiBUC The land surface model SiBUC performs a vertical one-dimensional water-energy balance analysis for each mesh (Tanaka, 2005 ). SiBUC was developed based on the Simple Biosphere model (SiB) (Sellers et al., 1986 ). It is characterized by its ability to include irrigation in agricultural land and physical processes in urban areas and water bodies. SiBUC is divided into three submodels: green area, water body, and urban area. The green area submodel includes 10 types of natural vegetation and 5 types of irrigated crops. In addition, SiBUC employs a mosaic scheme to account for mixed land cover conditions within a mesh. The mosaic scheme calculates the surface fluxes for all land cover types individually within a mesh and takes a weighted average of the fluxes according to the land cover fraction to obtain the surface fluxes for the mesh. The model also considers various hydrological processes in this target area, including snow accumulation and snowmelt in mountainous regions, and irrigation practices in arid regions; the performance has been validated in various areas.
