For example, the global validation of river flow and irrigation water requirements (Kotsuki et al., 2012 ), accurate simulation of snow depth in areas with heavy snowfall (Sadyrov et al., 2024; Watanabe et al., 2020 ), the evaluation of drought conditions in rice paddy areas (Kotsuki and Tanaka, 2013 ), the validation of soil moisture in temperate humid regions (Shi et al., 2022 ), and assessment of climate change impacts on water resources and irrigation water demand in arid regions (Fujihara et al., 2008 ). Even in developing countries, where restrict inputs to globally available datasets, the model has demonstrated adequate accuracies for achieving research objectives. This is particularly advantageous in the context of endorheic lake basins, where land cover characteristics of irrigated areas and water bodies have a significant influence on water balance analysis. The SiBUC model's strength is its ability to account for these factors within the modeling framework. In the green area submodel, the SiBUC calculates the vertical water balance as the following equation at each mesh separately.(1) Runoff = Q s + Q s b = P r e c - E T - Δ s w e - Δ s m + W i n     where Runoff   , Prec   , ET   , Win    are runoff, precipitation, evapotranspiration, and supplied irrigation water, respectively. Δ s w e    and Δ s m    are changes in snow water equivalent and soil moisture, respectively, which are changes in storage in the mesh. Runoff    includes surface runoff Qs    and base flow Qsb    flowing outside of the mesh, which is regarded as a water resource from the mesh. The three soil layers represent the vertical infiltration process and the base flow Qsb    as infiltration from the lowest layer.  2.2.2 Irrigation scheme The irrigation scheme is a part of the green area submodel, where irrigated farms are included as land cover types. Minimum soil moisture is set for each crop type in the crop calendar. When soil moisture falls below this predefined threshold in a particular grid cell, irrigation water is directly applied to the soil layer. The total growing period for each crop is estimated for each mesh based on the variation in the leaf area index (LAI), and the period is divided into five stages using the percentage of the period specified for each crop (Kotsuki and Tanaka, 2015 ). The minimum soil moisture thresholds and other relevant variables were established based on field observations performed in Syrdarya Province in Uzbekistan from 2011 to 2014 (Touge et al., 2015a ).  2.2.3 Water balance analysis After SiBUC performed one-dimensional vertical calculations at each grid, the runoff was accumulated to calculate the river discharge and inflows to the Aral Sea. The time for horizontal water movement was regarded as negligible in this study because the monthly and annual summation of the flow was sufficient for the water balance of an endorheic lake. Therefore, river discharge and inflow into the Aral Sea were calculated as the sum of the water balance in the upstream grids during the analysis period. The equation (1)  calculates the water balance in each mesh, and the following formula aggregates results in all mesh and calculates the total water balance in the whole basin:(2) Q = ∑ Q s + Q s b    - ∑ Win  γ  - ∑ Evap  wb   - WD  out       where Q    is the river discharge or inflow to the Aral Sea. Evap  wb      is the evaporation only from the water bodies other than the Aral Sea calculated by SiBUC at each mesh. γ    is the irrigation efficiency, and WD  out      is the water withdrawal outside the basin. Win    is calculated by the irrigation scheme in 2.2.2 and regarded as a minimum required water for crop growth. The original irrigation scheme assumed optimal water operation, where the minimum required water is supplied directly to the root zone. However, the actual irrigation water consumption was determined through irrigation efficiency estimates taken from the river. Therefore, the transportation efficiency in the canals and the application efficiency in the irrigated farms were considered in this research, described as γ    in equation (2) . Transportation efficiency is the water lost by evaporation and infiltration in the canals when water is conveyed from rivers to agricultural lands (Howell, 2003 ). It has been reported that the transportation efficiency in the Aral Sea Basin is low, at approximately 55 % (Martius et al., 2009 ), due to the large proportion of widely distributed unlined canals (Bekchanov et al., 2010; Orlovsky et al., 2001 ). The application efficiency is the amount of water used for crop growth (transpiration) divided by the water provided for irrigation to farmland. In the Aral Sea Basin, furrow irrigation is the dominant irrigation method, accounting for 95 % of all irrigation techniques (FAO, 1997 ). Although furrow irrigation is a relatively inexpensive method, it requires a sufficient amount of water to be supplied to the farmland, almost flooding the field (Abdullaev et al., 2007; Horst et al., 2005; Saiko and Zonn, 2000 ). Water loss is high due to evaporation from the surface and infiltration into the deeper soil layers, which results in low application efficiency, high groundwater levels, waterlogging, and salinization of soil and water. These conditions can reduce crop yield and increase water requirements in the future. The irrigation efficiencies that the physical model cannot calculate were considered by statistics and reported data in Section 3.3.2 . Evap  wb      is a term to account for the water loss flowing into water bodies other than the Aral Sea. Due to the flat topography of the region, there are numerous natural and man-made lakes. Additionally, a large amount of drainage water is wasted intentionally, especially in the lower Amu Darya River Basin. Since a large share of irrigated land is affected by salinization, the drainage water is also highly salinized. Therefore, to control the salinity level of river water, the locals intentionally divert drainage to the surrounding depression, creating terminal lakes. The Lake Sarygamysh serves as the most prominent example of this strategy. The existence of these terminal lakes suggests the presence of sufficient inflows to compensate for the high surface evaporation rates they experience. Consequently, evaporation from these terminal lakes is calculated for each mesh using SiBUC water body sub-model. The resulting evaporative water loss is then subtracted from the basin water balance in equation (2) . If a terminal lake is too small for inclusion in the lake database described in section 3.3.2 , the associated water loss is considered negligible and disregarded. A detailed description of the values and dataset will be given in Section 3.3 . It is important to acknowledge that existing reports and statistics are insufficient to determine the precise amount of irrigation water consumption nor water discharge to the terminal lakes, including the Aral Sea itself. Therefore, several assumptions are necessary. The validity of these assumptions is supported through validation and verification that examines the basin's overall water balance and historical water level change in the Aral Sea. While individual water consumption values can’t be precisely determined, the total values can be verified, ensuring the overall calculation remains reasonable.  2.2.4 The Aral Sea budget model (Endorheic lake budget model) The Aral Sea budget model calculates the Aral Sea volume, area, and water level changes based on the water balance of the entire basin as the input. Δ S    is the change in water storage of the Aral Sea and is calculated by the following equation:(3) Δ S = Q + P r e c - E v a p    Aral       where Q    is the inflow to the Aral Sea calculated by Equation (2) , and P r e c - E v a p    Aral      is the difference between precipitation and evaporation in the Aral Sea. The change in water storage in the Aral Sea was calculated based on the water balance results determined for the entire basin. Equation (3)  was used for the calculation at the end of each year, and the Aral Sea area was updated based on Δ S    to reflect the land cover condition in the following year. The bathymetry data described in Section 3.4  were utilized to estimate the Aral Sea area from Δ S    by assuming the grids below a specific elevation as the water body. The Aral Sea area is calculated at the same spatial resolution as the bathymetry data, but the land surface analysis in SiBUC requires upscaling to 1 km resolution. Therefore, after determining the sea area, land cover fractions are recalculated, and the mosaic scheme accounts for changes in evaporation due to changes in the area of the water body. For the initial condition of the Aral Sea budget model, the reported surface elevation in 1960 was used. Additionally, the model considered the division forming the north side and south side of the Aral Sea in 1985. After that, the Amu Darya River was assumed to flow into the South Aral Sea, while the Syr Darya River was assumed to flow into the North Aral Sea. If the calculated water level in the North Aral Sea exceeded the level at the time of the split, the higher water level was assumed to flow into the South Aral Sea. This calculation flow helps the model to calculate the equilibrium between the water balance of the entire basin and that of the endorheic lake surface.    3 Calculation settings This section details the calculation settings used in this research. 3.1 Meteorological forcing SiBUC requires seven meteorological forcing variables, including precipitation, air temperature, specific humidity, air pressure, downward shortwave radiation, downward longwave radiation, and wind speed. Since available meteorological observation data is limited in the basin, reanalysis products were used for modeling. Verification of the accuracy of these datasets using local observations can be challenging, and the level of accuracy can vary depending on the chosen reanalysis product. To address this, local observations were employed to verify the accuracy of all reanalysis datasets. In this research, the Global Soil Wetness Project Phase 3 (GSWP3) forcing data was utilized to show the best performance from other available global datasets. GSWP3 offers a reanalysis dataset from 1901 to 2010, with a spatial resolution of 0.5° and a temporal resolution of one day (Kim, 2017 ). The detailed results of reanalysis products compared to ground observation are given in Appendix A . Based on this verification, GSWP3 has shown the highest accuracy compared to other reanalysis datasets. 3.1.1 Spatial downscaling method Since SiBUC calculates output hourly and the calculation grid resolution is 30 s, temporal and spatial downscaling was performed. Spatial downscaling was performed for each calculation mesh by the inverse distance weight (IDW) using the 4 nearest meshes from GSWP3. The elevation dependencies of air temperature and air pressure were considered to be 0.006 °C/m and 0.1 hPa/m, respectively. Additionally, since longwave radiation depends on air temperature, the relationship between longwave radiation and elevation was determined. From Stefan-Boltzmann's equation, the relationship between air temperature T    and longwave radiation L    is expressed as follows:(4) L = σ T  4      (5) ∂ L  ∂ T   = 4 σ T  3      where σ    is the Stefan-Boltzmann coefficient. The relationship between longwave radiation L    and elevation z    is as follows:(6) ∂ L  ∂ z   = ∂ L  ∂ T   dT  dz   = 4 σ T  3  dT  dz        Since ∂ T  ∂ z      was determined as described above, the elevation dependency of longwave radiation can be obtained by Equation (6) .  3.1.2 Temporal downscaling method Among the seven meteorological forcing variables, specific humidity, wind speed, and air pressure were assumed to be constant over a single day, while the other meteorological values were temporally downscaled to one-hour data as follows. Daily precipitation from GSWP3 was downscaled into hourly data based on the averaged diurnal distribution calculated from the Global Satellite Mapping of Precipitation (GSMaP) (Kubota et al., 2020 ). First, to obtain the averaged diurnal distribution for each month, hourly precipitation data from GSMaP were summed monthly for each hour of the day from 1998 to 2006. This was regarded as the average diurnal distribution, and then daily precipitation obtained by GSWP3 was allocated for each hour according to the distribution. For the air temperature, since GSWP3 provides daily maximum, daily minimum, and daily average values, the air temperature was interpolated based on the in-situ observation data at Muynaq, located in the South Aral Sea. The authors observed these data from August 2019 to June 2020. The corrections were made for each month according to Equation (7) . Since no data was available for July, the average of June and August was utilized.(7) α h    = 1 D  ∑ d = 1  D  T  obs   h , d    - T min  obs   ( h )   T max  obs   ( h )  - T min  obs   ( h )        where h    is the hour within a day, d    is the date within a month, D    is the total days in the month, α ( h )    is the correction value, T ( h , d )    is the observed temperature, the superscript obs    indicates the observed data and the subscripts min    and max    indicate the daily minimum and daily maximum, respectively. Using the correction value, the hourly temperature data were corrected using the following equation:(8) T ( h , d )  = T max  data   ( d )  - T min  data   ( d )     × α ( h )  + T min  data   ( d )      where T ( h , d )    is the temperature value utilized by the model, and the superscript data    indicates the GSWP3 dataset. The shortwave radiation was downscaled from the daily mean shortwave radiation in GSWP3. It was allocated by the cosine of the hourly solar zenith angle (Monteith and Unsworth, 1990 ), while negatives were treated as zero.   3.2 Land surface parameters Global Land Cover Characterization (GLCC) version 1 is global 1 km resolution data published by the United States Geological Survey (USGS), and these data are classified into 24 categories. The land cover types were reclassified into the defined classification in SiBUC. GLCC was also utilized to obtain glacier distribution in the mountainous zone to consider the glacial meltwater and snowmelt feeding upstream rivers. GLCC was used to determine the area fraction of natural vegetation, and land cover conditions were modified to account for historical development in the irrigated land, which is explained in 3.3.1. Since the SiBUC calculation requires the land cover fraction for its mosaic scheme, these land cover datasets were converted into fractions for each grid. A global surface parameters database (ECOCLIMAP) version 1 with a 1 km resolution was utilized for other land surface parameters, including soil and vegetation property (Faroux et al., 2013 ). ECOCLIMAP is based on a combination of 15 land covers and 16 climate datasets to create an ecosystem map and a dataset of vegetation and soil properties at a 1 km resolution, using statistical and satellite data for 125 major ecosystems of the globe.  3.3 Human activities 3.3.1 Historical changes in irrigated area The increase in water demand due to the historical expansion of irrigated land was reflected by revising the land cover data annually. The global irrigated land distribution dataset and local reports were fully utilized to reproduce their spatiotemporal distribution as follows. The Global Monthly Irrigated and Rainfed Crop Areas for the year 2000 (MIRCA2000) database was used for the irrigated land distribution (Portmann et al., 2010 ). It provides 26 classifications of irrigated and rainfed cropland at a 5-minute resolution. Additionally, to account for past irrigation development in this spatial distribution, land cover data from phase 3a of the Inter-Sectoral Impact Model Intercomparison Project (ISIMIP3a) was utilized (ISIMIP, 2023 ). The expansion rate of the irrigated area from 2000 was calculated annually at each 0.5° mesh. The ISIMIP3a data for each year were uniformly adjusted for the entire basin so that the sum of the irrigated area by crop for the entire basin matched the report by Aus der Beek et al. (2011)  (Table 1  ). The originally reported values were for various crop types but were reclassified as cotton, winter wheat, and others as the major crops in the Aral Sea Basin. Fodder, which had a larger area in the original report, was divided into cotton and winter wheat at 50 % each. It is because about 43 % of the cultivated land in Uzbekistan is cotton, and about 37 % is grains (including wheat) in 2013, and cotton and wheat are actually used as fodder (Notenbaert and van der Hoek, 2021 ). Other crops were assigned to others. The fraction of the irrigated area was changed based on the total annual irrigated area. The land covers other than the irrigated farms were uniformly modified to make the sum of the land cover rates into a grid equal to 1. However, the urban area and water bodies were fixed since they should remain unaffected by irrigated land expansion. Fig. 3   shows the estimated irrigated area distribution in 1961 and 2010. The data show that the irrigated area increased significantly in the main irrigated areas in the watershed, such as the lower Syr Darya River Basin and Karakalpakstan region.  3.3.2 Water outflow to terminal lakes and outside the basin A critical aspect of reproducing the shrinkage of the Aral Sea, a primary objective of this study, involves accounting for the volume of water existing in the basin through pathways other than the Aral Sea itself. Equation (2)  includes this term as WD  out     , which represents amount of water withdrawn outside the basin. Since the physical model cannot directly simulate water demand outside the watershed, this value is estimated based on reported data. Another term Evap  wb      in Equation (2) , which is the amount of evaporation from water bodies within the watershed, excluding the Aral Sea. This term specifically addresses the terminal lakes formed by irrigation drainage. The calculation involves summing the evaporation rates from water bodies, as water flowing into the terminal lake does not return to the river system and is ultimately lost through evaporation. Strictly in water balance, it is necessary to consider changes in lake volume, however, most terminal lakes in this region are situated on flat plains, resulting in the reservoir volumes that are considered negligible compared to the volume of the Aral Sea. The distribution of water bodies in the basin was from Global Lakes and Wetlands Database Level 3 (GLWD3), including terminal lakes and wetlands at a 30-second resolution. The GLWD3 was made based on available maps and information through the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) partnership. Although the historical change in the water body was not considered, the change in the Aydar Arnasay Lakes System (AALS) area was considered. It is located in the middle stream of the Syr Darya River Basin and is mainly fed by emergency outflows from the Chardara Reservoir. The AALS has expanded since 1969 and has an area of about 4,000 km2  (Kulmatov et al., 2021, 2013 ). The change in the water body was estimated by the normalized difference water index (NDWI) of Landsat (Gao, 1996 ). The NDWI threshold that separates water bodies from the land was given to match the reported historical water surface area. The Karakum Canal, under operation since 1954 (Table 2  ), reportedly withdrew 12.9 Gt of water in 1995 (Hannan and O’Hara, 1998 ), but the official detailed information is limited. To address this limitation, an estimation approach was adopted, assuming a constant ratio between irrigated area and water withdrawal over time. This ratio was established based on the reported values of 12.9 Gt of water supplied to 9,720 km2  of irrigated area in 2000 (Hannan and O’Hara, 1998 ). Given the changes in irrigated area documented in Table 2 , linear interpolation was employed to estimate the historical expansion of irrigated land on an annual basis (Fig. 4  ). This facilitated the estimation of water withdrawals throughout the historical period using the established ratio. Lake Sarygamysh serves as a unique example of a terminal lake formed by irrigation drainage discharged from the lower Amu Darya River. Although it receives inflows from the Aral Sea Basin, its location falls outside the Aral Sea catchment area, as shown in Fig. 1 . Therefore, it cannot be calculated using Evap  wb     , the amount was estimated as a separate endorheic lake budget model and added to WD  out     . Water withdrawal into Lake Sarygamysh was estimated by a water balance analysis, similar to the methodology applied for the Aral Sea Basin Equation (2) and (3) . As an endorheic lake with a substantial surface area (4,000 km2 ) and a volume (70 Gt) (Liu et al., 2019 ), it needs an inflow of water to compensate for evaporative losses from its surface to maintain its area extent. Furthermore, since the lake has been expanding, the water balance analysis must account for this ongoing inflow (Liu et al., 2019 ). Therefore, the amount of water was estimated according to the following equation, considering the water balance the water balance within Lake Sarygamysh Basin:(9) Δ V  LS   = P r e c - E v a p    LS   + Q LS   + WD  LS       where subscript LS    indicates Lake Sarygamysh, Δ V    is the change in lake volume, P r e c - E v a p      is the precipitation minus evaporation on the lake surface, and Q    is the water inflow due to water balance only within the Lake Sarygamysh Basin of 94,188 km2 . And WD  LS      represents the amount of water withdrawn from the Amu Darya River Basin. This calculation requires the lake area and water level changes for each year. Lake area data from 1972 to 2010 was obtained by isolating Lake Sarygamysh from the Landsat satellite imagery using the NDWI (Gao, 1996 ). Unfortunately, Landsat data is available only from 1972, while documented inflows into Lake Sarygamysh began in 1961 (Orlovsky et al., 2012 ). To address this data gap, the lake area WD  LS      for 1961–1971 was assumed to be 0. Water level changes were obtained from the Sensor Data Storage System (SDSS) only from 1993 onward. Therefore, the water level before 1993 was assumed to be consistent with the trend during the period of 1992 ∼ 2000 and was supplemented by linear extrapolation (Fig. 4 ).  3.3.3 Historical change in irrigation efficiency The average irrigation efficiency in the Aral Sea Basin increased from 0.5 in 1960 to approximately 0.7 in 2000 (Cai and McKinney, 1999; Dukhovny, 2003; Dukhovny et al., 2007; McKinney et al., 1999; Saiko and Zonn, 2000 ). Therefore, country-based irrigation efficiency data was utilized (Aus der Beek et al., 2011 ). Since the data are available every five years, they were linearly interpolated into annual data. And since there is no data for 1970–1985, the average of 1965 and 1990 was uniformly applied. And in Afghanistan, data was available only in 2000, the value was uniformly applied for the entire period. The estimated changes in irrigation efficiency are shown in Fig. 5  .   3.4 Bathymetry of the Aral Sea The generation of the Aral Sea’s bathymetry data is based on elevation data derived from the ASTER-GDEM version 3 at 1-second resolution (NASA, 2019 ). ASTER-GDEM is a global product jointly released by METI and NASA, proved suitable for bathymetric representation since the exposed seabed of the Aral Sea is now accessible for observation. However, ASTER-GDEM observation started around 2000 before the East Aral Sea had fully shrunk. Consequently, the bathymetry data for this region was not employed in this study. Instead, we utilized publicly available bathymetry data (Singh and Seitz, 2015 ). A potential limitation of the original bathymetry data arises from its 1 m height resolution. This resolution might not have captured small elevation variations between grid cells. The former seabed of the Aral Sea is known to be relatively flat. Therefore, using 1-m vertical resolution bathymetry resulted in many grids with the same elevation values. This, in turn, would have caused sudden and discontinuous changes in the calculated Aral Sea surface area response to the volume fluctuations. Since a core objective of this study aimed to show the equilibrium between the inflow to the Aral Sea and the evaporation from the lake surface shown in Equation (3) , it was necessary to achieve continuous representation of the increasing in evaporation with the change in the surface area. Therefore, the bathymetry was modified to reflect differences in elevation of less than 1 m. First, grids with the same elevation value were ranked according to their distance from the center point of the Aral Sea, and elevation values were calculated for each grid using Equation (10) :(10) Al t i  = A l t 0 i  + i N  + h     where i    is the rank, Alt  i     is the elevation value at the target mesh with the rank of i   , A l t 0  i     is the original elevation data, N    is the total number of the same elevation value meshes, and h    is a value uniformly added to satisfy the relationship between the water surface level, area, and volume with the reported value.   4 Results and data 4.1 Water consumption for irrigation Fig. 6   shows the breakdown of each irrigation water consumption within the basin. The “Crop requirement” component is the optimal irrigation water demand for each grid cell, estimated using the irrigation scheme of SiBUC. “Water loss for irrigation” component is related to the application efficiency within the farmland and the conveyance efficiency in the canal. The analysis shows an overall improvement in irrigation efficiency across the basin from 49 % in 1961 to 61.6 % in 2010 on average, particularly in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. Although irrigation efficiency differs even within the same country, the actual irrigation efficiency is determined by several factors including weather, soil properties, and agricultural infrastructure. Since the ways of improvement for application and conveyance efficiency differ significantly, it would be necessary to estimate water losses separately based on more detailed hydrological observation data. The long-term average lasts 10 years, the amount of water withdrawn into the Karakum Canal and Lake Sarygamysh was about 9.4 Gt/yr and 6.5 Gt/yr, respectively. While these values appear relatively small compared to the total irrigation water requirement of 81 Gt/yr, they collectively account for 19.6 % of total demand. Considering that the evaporation from the Aral Sea was less than 30 Gt/yr during this period, the impact of these withdrawals on the growth of the endorheic lake has been substantial.  4.2 River discharge and water inflow to the Aral Sea River discharge was calculated by running a water balance analysis using Equation (2)  for the entire watershed upstream of the observation point shown in Fig. 7  . The observed river flow data were the monthly averages obtained from UzHydromet. The period of the observation data was from 2000 to 2020, and data from four stations, one in the Syr Darya River (Chinaz) and three in the Amu Darya River (Darganata, Tuyamuyun, and Kipchak), were utilized (the location of each station is shown in Fig. 1 ). Chinaz station is located in the middle stream before the Syr Darya River flows into the Chardara Reservoir. Three stations in the Amu Darya River are located downstream from the Karakum Canal, and only Tuyamuyun and Kipchak stations are downstream from the intake point for the Lake Sarygamysh Basin through the irrigation canal extending from the Tuyamuyun Reservoir. These effects of water withdrawal are considered in the external term WD  out      in Equation (2) . The catchment areas of each observation station were estimated from HydroBASINS in HydroSHEDS. The calculation was accurate at Chinaz, located in the middle reaches of the Syr Darya River. It was slightly overestimated in the wet year and underestimated in the dry year. However, the values at the river discharge stations at Darganata, Tuyamuyun, and Kipchak, located downstream of the Amu Darya River, were overestimated. Nevertheless, their flow patterns matched those of the observations, while overestimations for some years were twice as large in absolute value. One possible reason for such an overestimation could be a larger share of the Karakum Canal withdrawal than that considered in this research and the difference in irrigation efficiency within a country. Although there were some differences in the accuracy between the Amu Darya River and the Syr Darya River, the river flow and trend were generally well reproduced. Fig. 8   shows the annual water inflow to the Aral Sea from two main rivers. Data from the Scientific-Information Center of the Interstate Commission for Water Coordination of Central Asia (SIC ICWC) website CAWater-info.net  were used for the reported values (http://www.cawater-info.net/aral/data/index_e.htm ). Since there are two types of time series data with different periods in the CAwater-info, both are shown in the figure. Model calculations tended to overestimate the reported values and showed large interannual variability. The inflow from the Amu Darya River was represented better than the inflow from the Syr Darya River, which was greatly overestimated in some years. Considering the water inflow to AALS during the heavy flood in 1969, 21 Gt of water was subtracted based on the reported value (Kulmatov et al., 2013; Rakhmatov et al., 2020 ). However, the river inflow was still overestimated, therefore, there should be other water loss due to flooding in the plain and inflowing to other depressions during the flood. Another reason could be dam operation in the upstream area. The total storage capacity of large dams in the Syr Darya River is approximately 38 Gt on average (Crétaux et al., 2015 ). This is large enough to store water from flood years for use in drought years and erase the interannual variation in the Syr Darya River inflow. Moreover, the river inflow has bottomed out in some years, indicating there was a significant fluctuation of the river inflow. Compared to the overestimation of river discharge at the middle stream of the Amu Darya River shown in Fig. 7 , the inflow from the Amu Darya River did not show this trend. Therefore, the water consumption downstream of the Amu Darya River Basin would be overestimated. Regarding irrigation efficiency given uniformly by country, although it might be lower downstream under highly arid climates, the other factors that overestimate water requirement downstream would be more influential.  4.3 Long-term changes in the annual water balance This section summarizes the results of the basin water balance calculations. Fig. 9   shows the long-term variation of the total runoff and total water consumption for irrigation in the Aral Sea catchment. The long-term average of total runoff during the analysis period was 127 Gt, which agrees with the reported value of 133 Gt (Micklin, 2014 ). It tended to be high in the 1960 s, but then there was almost no long-term trend, and anomalies during the 1969 flood year and the 2000 and 2001 drought years were well represented. Total water consumption for irrigation showed an increasing trend from 1961 to around 1990, reflecting many factors described above. After 1990, there was almost no increase in water consumption, although there was a slight increase in irrigated areas as shown in Table 1 . This is thought to be due to the effect of improved irrigation efficiency after the increase in irrigated area subsided. This trend is similar to the results of Aus der Beek et al. (2011) , and captures the changes in irrigated agriculture in the watershed. Moreover, the model has limitations in describing the drought effect. For example, 2000 was a record-breaking drought year, and the Aral Sea inflow from 2000 to 2001 dropped to 2 km3  (Micklin, 2016 ). The farmlands downstream could not receive the required amount of irrigation water. However, in the analysis, regardless of the drought year, the calculated water consumption was even more than the total runoff. The irrigation water requirement was overestimated at that time. Table 3   summarizes the long-term changes in the estimated total water consumption and reported irrigation water requirement. The water consumption includes all components shown in Fig. 6 . It was underestimated by about 20 % until the 1990 s and by about 5 % after 2000. There would be other water consumption in the basin, for example, leaching was not represented in the present irrigation scheme, and this could be a possible cause of underestimation during the entire analysis period. Additionally, the reported values are sometimes roughly estimated, and some imprecision of the reported values should be noted (Aus der Beek et al., 2011; Lipovsky, 1995 ). One way to verify the credibility of the reported values is to check whether irrigation is actually being conducted using Landsat or other methods.  4.4 Historical change in the Aral Sea The calculated historical water balance of the Aral Sea was compared with the reported values (Fig. 10  ) (Gaybullaev et al., 2012b ; SIC ICWC, 2023 ). Overall, the estimated evaporation rates calculated from the Aral Sea exhibited good agreement with observed data, although there was a slight overestimation. This decrease in evaporation reflects a decrease in the surface area of the Aral Sea over the study period. The calculated total inflow values closely mirrored the trend observed for the Amu Darya River shown in Fig. 10 (a), indicating that the annual variation was correct, although it was overestimated overall. The main factor of the overestimation was probably the same as in Section 4.2  when examining the river discharge. Furthermore, the annual water balance analysis did not account for dam operation, which can adjust water storage based on seasonal variations of wet and dry years. This could be one another contributing factor to the larger annual fluctuations observed in the modeled results. Additionally, the model did not incorporate regulations governing water use during dry and wet years (e.g., water conservation during droughts and increased water use during floods). Fig. 10 (b) shows a comparison of the modeled Aral Sea volume changes with those reported by CAWater-info.net  (SIC ICWC). The comparison shows an underestimation trend until 1987, followed by an overestimation afterward. The large fluctuations observed in the modeled river inflow (as discussed in Section 4.2 ) also contribute to this pattern. Specifically, the model simulates sudden increases in water level during high rainfall years (e.g., 1968 and 1986), reflecting rapid water volume recovery. The overestimation observed after 1987 can likely be attributed to the aforementioned overestimation of river inflow. Similarly, trends are evident when comparing the modeled Aral Sea area and water level with reported values from CAWater-info.net  (SIC ICWC) in Fig. 10 (c, d). The modeled area was calculated by aggregating all parts of the Aral Sea after the division of the sea into two parts. The water level results for both parts of the sea were overestimated after 1987 (Fig. 10 (b)). When the model overestimates the inflow from the Syr Darya River after 1987, excess water overflowed to the South Aral Sea. Given the flat bathymetry of the South Aral Sea, this leads to an overestimation of its surface area. Finally, Fig. 11   shows the change in the analyzed water surface area in the Aral Sea. The drastic changes in the Aral Sea surface were well reproduced over a period longer than 50 years. The distribution map is consistent with other studies that have shown the process of shrinkage of the Aral Sea (Bekchanov et al., 2017; Tanaka et al., 2024 ). Regarding Figs. 10 and 11 , it was noteworthy that this long-term desiccation was calculated by the basin water balance considering various human water consumption components throughout the Aral Sea Basin. In Fig. 11 , the water surface area each year was also estimated based on the reported elevation of the water surface and shown as a contour. The difference between the estimated and reported areas was small until the 1990 s but larger after 2000. The difference after 2000 would be because the water distributing operation within the Aral Sea was not well described in the Aral Sea budget model and because the flat topography of the former Aral Sea makes the estimation of the water surface area sensitive to slight differences in water surface elevation.   5 Discussion The application of the endorheic lake model framework demonstrated in the Aral Sea case serves as a valuable tool for understanding the lake surface fluctuation. This framework relies on the principles of the water balance expressed in equation (3) . This equation incorporates two key factors: the volume of water flowing into the lake and the net difference between precipitation and evaporation P r e c - E v a p    Aral      occurring over the lake's surface. When these two factors are in equilibrium, the lake level remains stable. However, human activities and climate change can disrupt this equilibrium, altering inflow volumes and driving the lake toward a new equilibrium state. In this context, the term P r e c - E v a p    Aral      can be interpreted as the volume of water required to maintain the lake level at equilibrium for a specific period. Table 4   shows the decade average of human water consumption and P r e c - E v a p    Aral      for the whole analysis period. The results showed the significant influence of various human water consumption practices on the Aral Sea's equilibrium states. For example, the inflow to Lake Sarygamysh is 6.5 Gt/yr, which accounts for 30.1 % of the P r e c - E v a p    Aral     , indicating that the Aral Sea water balance would be affected by as much as 30 % if it is not considered. Notably, these impacts have increased after 1990, while the area of the Aral Sea has decreased. It indicates that when the area of endorheic lakes is small, the required accuracy of water balance should be higher because the ratio is also relatively higher. The long-term desiccation of the Aral Sea was successfully reproduced based on the simulated water balance of the entire watershed. This approach aggregates various hydrological processes within the basin and considers the Aral Sea as the ultimate destination for all water. Table 4  highlights this sensitivity, demonstrating how even seemingly minor water consumption within the basin can significantly impact the Aral Sea's volume. Consequently, achieving high accuracy for all flow rates depicted in Fig. 2  is crucial for robust modeling. Unfortunately, accurate records were rarely available over the past 50 years, i.e., from 1961 to 2010. Therefore, this study employed a combination of available physical methods and statistical data to quantify human water impact and reproduce an endorheic lake. While the analysis successfully captured the long-term desiccation process, several limitations contributed to inaccuracies. In particular, the modeled water volume exhibited both overestimation and significant variability. The first reason is related to the hypothesis of the basin water balance, which assumes that all of the Q  calculated by Equation (2)  flows into the Aral Sea. However, this may not always hold true. There may be cases where the upstream areas are flooded and do not reach the Aral Sea in wet years, or diverted water volumes are higher than reported. An example is AALS, where drainage water flows from the Chardara Reservoir to a lake depression instead of reaching the Aral Sea (Rakhmatov et al., 2020 ). Accounting for such upstream flooding events in wet years could partially improve the accuracy of modeled inflow variations. Additionally, the analysis could not consider water inflow to small terminal drainage lakes. Although terminal lakes made by irrigation drainage were considered using the land cover dataset and water body submodel, lakes smaller than the GLWD3 dataset could not be considered in the analysis. The second limitation concerns the overestimation of river discharge at three Amu Darya River stations, as shown in Figs. 7 and 8 . These stations are located downstream from the intake point of the Karakum Canal and approach the Turkmenistan border. Regarding the Karakum Canal, the water withdrawal outside the basin was based on the reported value of 12.9 Gt annually, which was considered in the external term WD  out      in Equation (2)  in this research. However, the value has shown discrepancies across various sources (Aus der Beek et al., 2011 ). A treaty between Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan established a limit on the annual volume of water diverted to 18 Gt (Wegerich, 2008 ). Therefore, the amount of water withdrawn outside the basin would be underestimated. Additionally, water withdrawals from canals other than the Karakum Canal, Bukhara Channel, and Kashkadarya Channel were not considered. Although the Bukhara and Kashkadarya Channels withdraw water from the Amu Darya River, this water is subsequently used for irrigating areas that are inside the Aral Sea Basin in the scheme. Finally, the analysis did not account for industrial and municipal water use in the basin. This sector was reported to account for 8–10 % of the total water resources in the basin, but data are available only for the last decade (AQUASTAT, 2013 ). The various water uses related to irrigation could also be an important reason. In the present study, irrigation efficiency should not be uniform in the country, and the efficiency would tend to be lower in drier regions due to higher evaporation intensity and in the sandy region of soil due to higher infiltration. Results of Figs. 7 and 8  suggest that irrigation requirements in the lower Amu Darya River Basin are rather overestimated, the overestimation in this area of intense aridity would be even larger if the national distribution of irrigation efficiency is considered. However, it still needs improvement along with the accuracy of other water consumption estimates. In addition, the irrigated lands in the Aral Sea Basin have been seriously affected by salt accumulation in recent years (Toderich et al., 2008 ). More water is therefore required for leaching before the irrigation season in irrigated lands with severe salt accumulation. This study, however, did not consider the leaching water and may have underestimated the amount of water consumption in irrigation. Furthermore, irrigation water operation depends on soil moisture and a threshold in the irrigation scheme in SiBUC; however, irrigation water is applied more in high rainfall years and less in drought years. The analysis identifies water diversion outside of the Aral Sea Basin to be used mainly for irrigation purposes as the primary reason behind its disappearance. This diversion includes the strategic flow routing to terminal lakes to capture drainage water and reduce salinization in pursuit of water quality in the downstream as well as direct water diversion outside the basin. Examples include Lake Sarygamysh and the Karakum Canal, Karshi channel and Bukhara channel. The recent construction of the Kosh-tepa Canal in Afghanistan presents a potential future issue in this context. It is also important to point out the situation between the North and South Aral Sea as more nuanced than perceived. While the North Aral Sea is portrayed as experiencing a temporary restoration compared to the South's dire situation, a closer look reveals a more complex reality. The Syr Darya River Basin, feeding the North Aral Sea has a single big water diversion project in the Aral Alps Lowland System (AALS). In contrast, the Amu Darya basin, supplying the South Aral Sea, includes several examples as listed above. These factors have transformed the Aral Sea Basin to its current condition. Finally, the runoff process in SiBUC immediately discharged the excess water as surface runoff when the surface water volume exceeded a threshold value. This may have overestimated the amount of runoff, especially when rainfall intensity is high. The accuracy of river discharge tended to deteriorate in dry areas (Kotsuki et al., 2012 ). The accuracy of the global precipitation dataset used in this study is also important because meteorological observation networks are often inadequate in arid regions. There are indeed large differences among the datasets, and accuracy is especially important in mountainous areas, which provide most of the water resources in this basin.  6 Conclusion This study successfully reproduced the shrinkage of an endorheic lake considering various water consumption, and the following results were obtained. The dramatic desiccation of the Aral Sea over the past 50 years was reproduced in the framework through the integration of a basin-scale terrestrial water circulation model and an endorheic lake budget model. The strength of this approach lies in SiBUC's ability to physically represent irrigated areas and water bodies – crucial factors driving Aral Sea desiccation. By leveraging both physical methods and statistical data, the model effectively captures the combined effects of various hydrological processes occurring throughout the entire basin. The Aral Sea is a typical endorheic lake is highly sensitive to human activities, which have directly caused its disappearance. Application of this framework can consider various human water consumption as key hydrological components. Calculated results show that the water requirements for agricultural land were 39.0 Gt/yr, water loss due to irrigation efficiency 26.3 Gt/yr, water withdrawal to the Karakum Canal 9.4 Gt/yr, and drainage to Lake Sarygamysh equal to 6.5 Gt/yr in average from 2001 to 2010. When compared to average evaporation minus precipitation over the Aral Sea (21.5 Gt/yr from 2001 to 2010), it becomes evident that each of these human water consumption factors significantly impacts the equilibrium state of this endorheic lake. Notably, the endorheic lakes' changes were quantitatively visualized in terms of past water balance changes. In addition to river discharge, which is generally utilized to validate the hydrological analysis, this approach offers the long-term changes in the basin-scale water balance variations. The model successfully captures the aggregate effects of hydrological processes within the entire Aral Sea Basin, including historical trends in diverse water consumption patterns. Application of the same framework to Lake Sarygamysh, as a part of the water consumption, provides an estimation of discharge outside of the Aral Sea Basin. Endorheic lakes hold significant social and ecological importance due to their significant environmental and disaster risk implications on the surroundings. However, they also present unique scientific challenges in terms of elucidating the complex hydrological processes occurring within a watershed. The model incorporates key physical processes that represent the equilibrium state between river inflow and surface evaporation (through lake area reduction) for endorheic lakes. This allows for addressing both future projections and hypothetical scenarios. The equilibrium states, determined by basin water balance, would shift; therefore, the framework will also be useful as a quantitative estimation method for envisioning the surrounding environment and disasters. Extending the analysis period and applying it to various calculation conditions are expected in future studies. The successful simulation of this endorheic lake's equilibrium state dynamics across the entire Aral Sea Basin underscores a critical feature of such inland bodies of water – their dependence on both climatic and basin-specific water use patterns. The framework developed in this study can potentially be applied to other endorheic lakes. A valuable future direction would be to explore and clarify the key differences between endorheic lakes and other lake types.
1 Introduction The role of the forest on meteorological and hydrological processes has been gaining public attention for over two centuries (Andreassian, 2004 ). Scientific investigation on how forests modulate hydrologic responses was initiated early in the 1900 s (Hibbert, 1965 ), with the paired-watershed approach being used to assess the impact of the two main forest treatments, afforestation and deforestation (Van Loon, et al., 2019 ). The first paired-watershed approach was recognized to be the Wagon Wheel Gap study on two small catchments in the Colorado Rockies to investigate the forest influence on streamflow (Hibbert, 1965 ). This led to a number of similar studies by forest hydrologists throughout the twentieth century (Bosch & Hewlett, 1982; Andreassian, 2004; Brown, et al., 2005; Andréassian, et al., 2012 ), with most applications aiming to quantitatively measure changes to water yield and flood peaks due to land cover alterations (Van Loon, et al., 2019 ). A paired-watershed experimental design involves selecting two paired watersheds with similar characteristics, i.e., size, morphology, geology, climate, and land cover (Andreassian, 2004 ), which are well instrumented to quantify changes in hydrologic fluxes. The paired-watershed experiment (PWE) applies treatments such as deforestation (or afforestation) to be tested on one watershed, referred to as a treatment watershed. This treatment watershed is compared to a control watershed (without the treatments) to test changes in a target variable (watershed runoff). The paired watersheds are generally located adjacent to ensure higher similarity in climate inputs and watershed properties (Van Loon, et al., 2019 ). Watershed sizes are mostly a few km2  or smaller (Andréassian, et al., 2012 ) where the experimental manipulation of vegetation is feasible (Siriwardena, et al., 2006 ). The chronological observation matching of the paired catchments is considered necessary to ensure that the runoff is generated from almost identical inputs among the paired watersheds (Brown, et al., 2005; Van Loon, et al., 2019 ). After a calibration period of 3 to 10 years to assess similarity across the paired watershed responses to climate inputs, one of the watersheds is disturbed and subsequent responses compared with the other undisturbed (control) watershed being used as a reference (Andréassian, et al., 2012 ). The calibration period before the application of the treatment is used to show the inherent difference of two watersheds. As shown in Fig. 1  , the inherent difference of the calibration period is considered when the treatment impact is analyzed to estimate how much difference of the runoff measured after the treatment is actually from the treatment applied. The change that is observed after the treatment in comparison to the calibration period is analyzed to test the treatment impact (the right panel of Fig. 1 ). Further details for the paired-watershed experiment design can be found in Van Loon et al. (2019) . Paired-watershed studies in many places around the globe have shown that deforestation can increase water yield and flood peaks (of small-scale catchments) (Andreassian, 2004 ). However, the experiment results have been highly variable and at times unpredictable, especially for change in flood peaks (Hibbert, 1965; Andreassian, 2004 ). Reported results from thirty-nine studies (Hibbert, 1965 ) showed extremely varied annual water yield increases from 34 mm (in water depth unit which is runoff volume divided by watershed area) to higher than 450 mm in a five-year response after complete deforestation. The variability of flood peak increase is larger than the annual water yield (Troendle & King, 1985 ), however, also with reversed direction (i.e., a treatment (deforested) catchment showing lower peaks than a control (forested) paired catchment) (Andreassian, 2004 ). This high variability has made it difficult to make conclusive reasoning from the experiment results (Andreassian, 2004 ). As noted in some studies, such variability in the results could be attributed to the fact that the system states (e.g., soil moisture and groundwater) of an experimented watershed are not constant during the experiment period, and different watershed response and treatment impact could ensue. At Coweeta 37 catchment with 100 % clearcut treatment in North Carolina, USA, water yield increase in May and June (considered to be the dry months of the 1964 growing season) was unrecognizable (Hibbert, 1965 ). However, in September and October the increase was large, possibly from the heavy storm flushing out the evapotranspiration savings of the treatment watershed during the growing season (Hibbert, 1965 ). As another example, in the Hubbard Brook Experimental Forests, flood peaks increased by 15–60 % from cutting during the growing season but decreased by 2–40 % during the dormant season. This is presumably because during the dormant season, snowmelt starts earlier at the treatment (deforested) watersheds, mitigating its peak runoff in comparison to the control watershed (Hornbeck, et al., 1997; Andreassian, 2004 ). Ruprecht and Schofield (1989)  and SCRLUWS (1987)  noted the effect of the groundwater state on the treatment impact using the cases of paired-watershed experiments in south-eastern Australia. At Wights watershed with 100 % forest clearance during 1976 and 1977, a sudden streamflow increase (up to 10 % rainfall) was observed in 1977, which was attributed to interception loss (up to 13 % rainfall) of the watershed (Ruprecht & Schofield, 1989 ). The streamflow in the following years continued to increase (up to 30 % rainfall) until a new hydrological equilibrium for groundwater state was reached around 1984 (Ruprecht & Schofield, 1989 ). Comparison to other research watersheds in that region indicated that the main increase of streamflow can happen when and where the state of the groundwater level is higher and elevated to the surface at times. The results from the natural watershed experiments have shown recognizable variability (Hibbert, 1965; Andreassian, 2004 ). Although some studies noted watershed system states to cause the variability in the results, there has not been a systematic analysis framework to explicitly consider the effect of the watershed system states in the test of the treatment impact. Therefore, assuming that the watershed states can affect the treatment impact of the paired-watershed experiment, this study suggests the framework, called state-controlled hypothesis test, setting the state variables as control variables and testing the treatment impact in each controlled state condition. The data of the pre-existing paired-watershed experiment used in this study is explained in Section 2 , and in Section 3 , the analysis method called the state-controlled test is explained considering the data and paired-watersheds applied in this study. In Section 4 , the data of the pre-existing experiment is analyzed via the state-controlled test to demonstrate if the result variability can be reduced, and new insight be obtained via the state-controlled test of the paired-watershed experiment. In Section 5 and 6 , we discuss the necessity of the state-controlled test in watershed experiments and the importance the experimenter's experience and perception for a target watershed hold in real applications.  2 Study site and data In this study, we will re-evaluate data from a pre-existing paired watershed experiment data based on Wights (treatment) and Salmon (control) watersheds (Ruprecht & Schofield, 1989 ). Wights and Salmon watersheds are located southwest of the Collie River basin in Western Australia (Fig. 2  (a)). The experiment was originally designed to test deforestation impact on streamflow generation. The first treatment was the 100 % forest clearing and changing into pasture for the catchment area of 0.94 km2  during 1976 and 1977. In the middle of 1980, the second treatment of the surface disturbance involving the tree stump removal, pinwheel-raking, bulldozer-levelling, and ploughing was applied. During the entire experiment period, Salmon watershed located next to Wights remained in a forested condition. The forest in this region was dominated by Jarrah (Eucalyptus marginate ) and sub-dominated by marri (E. calophylla ) and bull banksia (Banksia grandis ). The changes in the interception and evapotranspiration (excluding the interception) estimated by Williamson et al. (1987) after the deforestation and agricultural development was 13 % and 15 % of rainfall respectively. The soils were gravelly and sandy laterites overlying a kaolinitic clay, with the granitic basement lying 30 m beneath the surface. The watersheds belong to a Mediterranean climate of cool and wet winters (from June to August) and dry summers (from December to February) with average annual rainfall of 1200 mm. The highest annual rainfall occurred in 1974 (1326 mm) and 1981 (1347 mm) and rainfall lower than 1000 mm in 1976 ∼ 1979 and 1982. The streamflow was found to be generated dominantly by throughflow from perched, shallow groundwater system before deforestation. The hydrological impact of this paired-watershed experiment was originally studied and published by Ruprecht and Schofild (1989), providing further details for the experiment design and hydrological process changes on the water yield aspect. The data from these experiment watersheds are used in this study as the first case study of a state-controlled hypothesis test because of its 100 % treatment and relatively higher annual rainfall and groundwater level, providing higher observable impact on runoff. Three periods of the experiment that can be differentiated based on the two treatment cases are the calibration period from 1974 to 1976 before the application of the first treatment, the treatment period 1 from 1977 to 1979 after the forest clearing during 1976 and 1977, and the treatment period 2 from 1981 to 1984 (Fig. 2 (b)) after the additional surface disturbance in 1980. Since the second treatment of the surface disturbance was in the middle of 1980, this year is not included in the second treatment period (1981–1984) for the clarity of the analysis. As noted by Ruprecht and Schofild (1989), the groundwater discharge area in Wights watershed was gradually increased after the treatment, and thus, difference between treatment period 1 and 2 would be able to demonstrate the effect of deforestation and higher groundwater level on daily runoff. During the calibration period (the left panel (1974–1976) of Fig. 2 (b)), similar daily runoff was observed from both catchments forested – slight difference was observed, with treatment watershed runoff relatively lower than those of the control watershed when the control watershed runoff exceeded 4 mm. After the 1977 forest clearing, the runoff of the treatment watershed was higher overall than the control catchment. As the middle panel (1977–1979 after the first treatment) of Fig. 2 (b) shows, there is high variability in the results even with no measurable changes, meaning that the two watersheds have similar runoff relations as the calibration period. After the second treatment in 1980, further increase in runoff was observed in the treatment watershed but still with high variability (the right panel (1981–1984) of Fig. 2 (b)). As noted in the previous studies for the paired-watershed experiments, this paired watersheds in south-east Australia also showed similar high variability in the results. Ruprecht and Schofield (1989)  analyzed annual water yield. The present study extends the analysis to daily time scales that have relatively higher variability. This serves to demonstrate the influence of states on the variability, propose methodology to disentangle its influence and reduce the variability, and understand changing treatment impact under each controlled state. In Section 3 , we introduce a new method for hypothesis testing such paired catchment experiments. We then use this method on the daily runoff data in Fig. 2 (b) to assess how the variability in ensuing results can be reduced.  3 Methodology 3.1 State-controlled hypothesis test This study argues that the high variability in Fig. 2  is a result of the changing watershed states. Each result of the PWE can be from markedly different states such as high or low groundwater levels, and the measured impact can be recognizably different. An approach that controls the watershed system states is necessary to reduce the variability in the paired-watershed testing procedure. This study proposes a state-controlled test in which the PWE is tested under each controlled watershed state as Fig. 3   shows. The PWE results are categorized and retrieved according to control variables (watershed state variables), and the treatment impact is tested for each and every category and gradually generalized. Reference modelling is applied in this study to describe the watershed system and simulate the system states used as the control variables. This simulated system states represent the surrogate variables of actual states that can be applied when the actual state variables are not available. According to Beven (2014), environmental modelling can be differentiated into perceptual, conceptual, and procedural modelling that represent the target environmental system with the different level of details and languages (e.g. mathematical and programming language). Any type of environmental model can be utilized if they can provide necessary level of details for the watershed system states. In this study, we apply perceptual modelling to the state-controlled hypothesis test of the PWE for its simplicity in application and interpretation as follows.  3.2 Reference modelling and state-controlled categorization The reference model this study applies to simulate the states of the control catchment is the perceptual model with the commonly recognized components of quickflow and baseflow (Fig. 4  ). In this study, the quickflow process is defined to be the rainfall P t     (this state will be denoted by P quick , t      in the following sections) contributing to runoff Q t     at the watershed outlet with zero-time lag in the daily time step. The runoff generation with longer time lag, meaning Q t     from rainfall P t - i      with i ≥ 1    is defined to be the baseflow considering the size of the experiment watersheds is smaller than 1 km2 . To separate the effect of relatively slower baseflow with deeper groundwater process, the runoff generation with time lags longer than 10 days is also differentiated in this study. According to Johnston (1987)  and Ruprecht and Schofield (1989) , Wights watershed has a perched shallow groundwater with rapid recharge at localized sites, and the infiltrated water without deep-rooted trees to extract water via transpiration eventually recharges the deep groundwater. The baseflow and deeper baseflow states with days and months time-lags are used as the surrogate variables for the perched shallow groundwater and deep groundwater respectively. The rainfall P t     with zero-time lag is used as the surrogate of the quickflow state, and the rainfall with 1 to 9 days-time lags (P t - 1   + P t - 2   ⋯ + P t - 9     / 9 = P base , t     ) is used to represent the baseflow state as described in Fig. 4 . For time lags longer than 10 days, the number of days of rainfall (∑ i = 10  60  I P t - i   > 0     = P d - b a s e , t      where I P t - i   > 0        is the indicator function that is 1 if the condition P t - i   > 0    is true) is counted instead. It is assumed that the number of days of rainfall occurrence is more related to the deeper baseflow state than the rainfall intensity. This means that the temporal persistence of daily rainfall occurrence may represent the recharge to deeper baseflow better than rainfall intensity since only limited amounts of rainfall can infiltrate and percolate to underground deeper flow. The categorization thresholds of the control variables are set to differentiate high and low state. The states are categorized using a 4 mm threshold for both quick and baseflow and 40 days for the deeper baseflow as shown in Fig. 5  , where every category has an enough amount of data for the analysis. This would be one of the general and basic perceptions for the watershed system, and gradually more detailed and complex models with more specified categorization can be developed and utilized as the reference model as we understand better the target system via the model-based state-controlled test. This iterative procedure can be understood as a way to gain information (and further understanding) from the experiment on top of current understanding (the reference model) for the target system.   4 Results The observations of the paired-watershed experiment from control (Salmon) and treatment (Wights) watersheds in southeastern Australia are categorized according to the state categories in Fig. 5 . Via state-controlled test, analyzing the experiment results based on the current level of understanding (the reference model) for the target system, this study attempts to explain that the high variability of the PWE results can instead provide further understanding for treatment impacts rather than hindering the experiment analysis. 4.1 Watershed processes with low rainfall-quickflow state Results from the state controlled paired-watershed experiments are presented in Fig. 6  . At first, the categories with low quickflow states, meaning the watershed processes when daily runoff is generated with no or low rainfall P  q u i c k , t      (0 to 4 mm) contributing to quickflow, are analyzed. Key observations from this analysis are (the abbreviation Q, B, D in parentheses represents the quickflow, baseflow, and deeper baseflow, and the subscript H and L the high and low states respectively): (QL , BH , DH )  With low quickflow state P quick , t     , almost no change is apparent (Fig. 6 (a)) when rainfall P base , t      and P d - b a s e , t      contributing to both shallow and deeper baseflow are high. The higher amount of rainfall P base , t      and P d - b a s e , t      can refill more the forest evapotranspiration loss of underground water storages for the control (forested) watershed, and the difference from the treatment (deforested) watershed is observed to be relatively smaller than other state categories. (QL , BH , DL )  When the rainfall P d - b a s e , t      contributing the deeper baseflow changes to low state (Fig. 6 (b)) while other states P quick , t      and P base , t      are the same as above, the treatment impact starts to appear, the treatment watershed having higher runoff than the control watershed. The low precedent rainfall state (P d - b a s e , t   ≤ 40 d a y s   ) could compensate less the forest evapotranspiration of the control watershed while the treatment watershed having no forest evapotranspiration loss. (QL , BL , DH )  When the rainfall state P base , t      contributing to the baseflow state is low instead while the rainfall state P d - b a s e , t      to the deeper baseflow is high (Fig. 6 (c)), only mild increase of the streamflow generation is observed in the treatment case 1 (the forest clearing and changing into pasture) but recognizable increase in the treatment case 2 (the additional surface disturbance and deep (permanent) groundwater level increase). This indicates that treatment (deforestation) impact by the shallow baseflow (or subsurface flow) process is relatively minor until the deep permanent groundwater level increase affecting the subsurface flow. More details for the deep permanent groundwater level change after the treatment can be found in Ruprecht and Schofield (1989) . (QL , BL , DL )  For the low rainfall state P quick , t      to quickflow, the highest change in the daily streamflow generation is observed when both P base      and P d - b a s e , t      are low (Fig. 6 (d)) with low rainfall infiltrating and percolating to baseflow and deeper groundwater flow. The lower evapotranspiration loss of water in the deforested treatment catchment could have higher baseflow and deeper groundwater flow states than the forested control catchment with low rainfall P base      and P d - b a s e      to compensate the forest evapotranspiration. These results for low quickflow state indicate that the treatment (deforestation) impact can appear when the precedent rainfall is not enough to refill the loss of the forest evapotranspiration in the control watershed. The underground stores of water for the baseflow are limited for its storage capacity, and thus, the difference in the baseflow amount of the control and treatment watershed could be recognizable when the forecast evapotranspiration of the control watershed is higher than the precedent rainfall that can refill the stores.  4.2 Watershed processes with high quick flow A larger runoff increase in the treatment watershed is observed for the high quickflow state, observable in Fig. 6 (e-h) when compared to Fig. 6 (a-d) for the low quickflow state. Key observations from this assessment are as follows: (QH , BH , DH )  For the high quickflow state P quick , t     , certain runoff change in the treatment watershed is observed even when the precedent rainfall P base , t      and P d - b a s e , t      to the baseflow states are high as Fig. 6 (e) shows – with the low P quick , t      instead, the high P base , t      and P d - b a s e , t      in Fig. 6 (a) showed no difference between the control and treatment watershed runoff values. The difference of the two watersheds for the high rainfall state P quick , t      could be attributed to the forest interception loss, the amount of rainfall that is intercepted by the leaves of trees and fallen leaves before reaching ground surface and does not contribute to the runoff.- To see the effect of the higher rainfall intensity of P quick , t      to the treatment impact (presumably causing different forest interception loss), the category is again divided into three categories (5  m m < P quick , t   ≤ 10  m m   , 10  m m < P quick , t   ≤ 25  m m   , and 25  m m < P quick , t     ) as shown in Fig. 7  . Although there are not many data points in each category, it shows a recognizable trend that the higher the rainfall state P quick , t     , the larger the difference between the control and treatment watersheds is.    (QH , BL , DL )  When the precedent rainfall (P base , t      and P d - b a s e , t     ) to baseflow and deeper baseflow becomes low instead, the high rainfall state P quick , t      to quickflow is observed to have even higher difference in the daily streamflow generation as shown in Fig. 6 (h) (in comparison to Fig. 6 (e)). We can see the gradual addition of the deforestation treatment impact, comparing Fig. 6 (a) (the state demonstrating no difference), Fig. 6 (e) (the difference due to the high P quick , t      state), Fig. 6 (h) (the difference due to both the high P quick , t      state and the low P base , t      and P d - b a s e , t      states), presumably due to the interception loss in Fig. 6 (e) and both the interception and evapotranspiration loss Fig. 6 (h). (QH , BH , DL  & QH , BL , DH )  There are still higher variability when the state of the rainfall P d - b a s e , t      contributing to deeper baseflow is low while the other states P quick , t      and P base , t      are high or when the state of the rainfall P base , t      contributing to baseflow is low while the other states P quick , t      and P d - b a s e , t      are high. It is expected that there are still various possible interactions between the baseflow and deeper baseflow processes when they belong to the different states (e.g., the high P base , t      and low P d - b a s e , t      states).  4.3 Treatment impact for larger quickflow state To see the treatment impact of the higher P quick , t      under various precedent rainfall states, the runoff response of P quick , t      larger than 20 mm is compared for the different combinations of precedent rainfall state P base , t      and P d - b a s e , t      for the baseflow and deeper baseflow states in Fig. 8  . The treatment subgroups 1 and 2 are not separated and threshold 20 mm is applied to have sufficient data points for all combinations of the precedent rainfall states. To see the change in the difference of two watersheds after the treatment, the reference period is firstly analyzed, which is marked with gray color shapes in Fig. 8 . The gray color filled marks of the reference period show that two watersheds under this high deeper baseflow state have very similar runoff generation before the treatment. However, when the deeper baseflow state becomes low instead, certain difference appears in the runoff generation of two watersheds, the treatment watershed showing lower runoff generation than the control watershed especially for the high baseflow state as the gray-color-line marks show. Therefore, this inherent difference of two watershed will be considered in the treatment impact analysis that follows. The treatment period with the quickflow state higher than 20 mm is marked with orange-colored markers in Fig. 8 . For the high quickflow state, the recognizable runoff increase of the treatment watershed is observed for all combinations of the baseflow and deeper baseflow states. The runoff increase due to the treatment becomes distinctively higher when the deeper baseflow state is in its low state as the orange-color-line marks (both circles and triangles) shows in comparison to orange-color-filled marks for the high deeper baseflow state. Actual treatment impact under this condition can be larger than the difference measured since the treatment watershed before the treatment (gray-color-line marks in Fig. 8 ) has the lower runoff generation than the control watershed for this category as explained before. In Fig. 7 , showing the effect of different rainfall intensity P quick , t      of the quickflow state, it was shown that the higher rainfall intensity can cause the larger treatment impact (the increase of the runoff due to the deforestation). In Fig. 8 , it is shown that the treatment impact can be more significant for the runoff generation with lower precedent rainfall.   5 Discussion From the review of the paired-watershed studies during last century (Andreassian, 2004 ), it was noted that the effect of forest on peak runoff is highly variable (more than (annual) water yield), and that the impact of deforestation on floods can be inclined to be due to exploitation (e.g. urbanization decreasing infiltration rate) rather than the loss of forest canopy itself. However, via the application of the state-controlled test to the paired-watershed experiments in southeast Australia, the high variability of the experiment results on daily runoff can now inform us that the loss of the forest canopy (Eucalyptus marginate ) can itself increase watershed runoff as shown in the results of Section 4 . The higher the rainfall intensity is, the larger the watershed runoff increases probably due to the lower interception loss of the deforested treatment watershed (Fig. 7 ). When the antecedent rainfall is relatively lower, the treatment watershed shows the additional runoff increase (Fig. 8 ). The rationale is that the higher evapotranspiration of the control watershed forest can limit the accumulation of the groundwater storage under the low antecedent rainfall condition more than the treatment (deforested) watershed. Almost no change in the treatment watershed is observed when the rainfall intensity is less than a few mm/day while the antecedent rainfall is higher enough to recharge the groundwater storage for both of the control and treatment watersheds (Fig. 6 (a)). The application of the state-controlled test in this study shows that the state-based reasoning of the high variability of the experiment results can provide further detailed understanding. The application to one of the paired watersheds (Wights and Salmon) in southeast Australia shows how forest loss can increase watershed runoff in various watershed states of that specific site. To generalize the understanding, the method would need to be applied to the paired-watershed experiments around Australia and the globe. The results of the state-controlled test would be different among sites according to a case specific reference model (developed by different focus and understanding for experimental sites in question), dominant watershed processes, watershed structures, and so on. Sharing the details about the reference models and watershed characteristics, the state variables that can differentiate and categorize the watershed characteristics among multiple sites could be found, and gradually more general conclusions obtained via the state-based reasoning.  6 Conclusions Paired-watershed experiments have been conducted for more than a century, but their results have been highly variable and often unpredictable, limiting the information that could be gained. Although paired-watershed experiments have gradually improved their consideration of treatment conditions and dependent variables, the issue of variability has not been resolved (Hibbert, 1965; Bosch & Hewlett, 1982; Andreassian, 2004; Brown, et al., 2005 ). This study suggests that the variability in the results of the paired-watershed experiments originates from the fact that the paired-watershed experiment is not a state controlled watershed experiment, with the control variables changing notably during the experiment. The solution this study tested is to set control variables using a reference modeling framework. The reference watershed model is used to distinguish and categorize the watershed system states via setting its state variables as control variables for the experiment. The treatment impact of the (natural) paired-watershed experiment can be tested for each and every categorized state and gradually generalized to understand the treatment impact under complex and dynamic natural system. This could be a way to gain information (and further understanding) from the experiment on top of current understanding (the reference model) for the target system. The application of the reference modeling and state-controlled test in the paired-watershed experiment shows that the variability of the pre-existing experiment results can instead provide detailed information how the various treatment impact can happen according to the different watershed states. It is found from the pre-existing paired-watershed experiment in southeast Australia that deforestation can cause higher impact (the runoff increase) with higher quickflow (from higher rainfall intensity) and lower baseflow (from lower precedent rainfall) states (Fig. 6 (h)). For the watershed experimented, the highest peaks during 8 years observation after the treatment (deforestation) occurred under this condition. The value of catchment scale experiments may not have been fully appreciated since it was too costly and unrepresentative (Neary, 2016 ) while the results were highly variable and often unpredictable (Hibbert, 1965; Andreassian, 2004 ). However, as the results of this study demonstrate, the data of the experimental catchments contains further detailed valuable information than reported in the past studies.
