What is necessary after the catchment experiment during last century would be to develop more tailored data-mining approaches for the natural paired-watershed experiments as suggested in this study. The present study proposes the framework of the state-controlled test with the perceptual reference modeling and categorization of state variables. The control of watershed states to reduce the variability of experiment results is dependent on how the reference model can describe the naturally changing system states. Further studies for developing reference models, optimizing state variables, and utilizing diverse data-mining tools are necessary to maximize the information that can be obtained from the PWE. The state-controlled test based on the reference modeling depends on the understanding of the analyzers (to develop the reference model). Different reference models from the different focus and understanding may be able to induce different information from the same experiment data. Sharing pre-existing PWE experiment data would be important to allow a diverse range of (interdisciplinary) researchers to gain as much diverse further information from the PWE data via different perception (and reference modelling) and control of a target system.
1 Introduction Impervious surfaces cause increased stormwater runoff, which rapidly transports sediments, trash, and pollutants from surfaces to natural waterways. This induces problems such as flooding, combined sewer overflows (CSOs), and increased contaminant concentrations to nearby water bodies (Lowe et al., 2013 ). As urbanization continues to increase impervious surface area, stormwater runoff is of growing concern (ASCE, 2021 ). To combat this, cities and municipalities have been investing more in green stormwater infrastructure (GSI), also known as low impact development (LID), stormwater management practice (SMP), or best management practice (BMP) (Debbage et al., 2017 ), particularly in response to funding mechanisms such as the 2019 U.S. Water Infrastructure Improvement Act (Office of the Federal Register, National Archives and Records Administration, 2019 ). Unlike the more traditional “gray” infrastructure such as gutters, pipes, and tunnels that have been used to transport stormwater, GSI is a nature-based solution to stormwater runoff on site. While the primary motivation for GSI installation in the U.S. has been in response to water quality legislation (i.e., the Clean Water Act), volume has often been considered a surrogate for design and inspection purposes based on the assumption that the quality and quantity of stormwater are directly related (Bell et al., 2019; McPhillips and Matsler, 2018 ). Consequently, multiple studies have shown GSI installations to improve runoff retention, downstream water quality, and CSO releases (Ando and Netusil, 2018; Holt et al., 2022; Hunt et al., 2008; Landauer et al., 2019; Shafique, 2017 ). With the growing popularity of GSI implementation, there has been an exponentially increasing number of GSI-focused studies (Wang et al., 2023 ). Many of these studies have reported on the potential of GSI in affecting hydrology of watersheds and/or alleviating CSOs (Autixier et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2019; Ghodsi et al., 2021; Li et al., 2019b; Lucas and Sample, 2015; Towsif Khan et al., 2020 ). Avellaneda et al. (2017)  used EPA’s Stormwater Management Model (SWMM) to evaluate the cumulative hydrologic performance of GSI and found significant decreases in discharge magnitude for return periods lower than five years. Another study using SWMM showed considerable reductions in CSOs in urban areas by using GSI, and reported that the ability of GSI to attenuate CSOs during rainfall events of varying intensity and duration varied by GSI type (Joshi et al., 2021 ). A different SWMM model study assessing GSI performance on CSOs in highly developed urban areas found that GSI would be an effective CSO control due to its successful reductions in peak flows and volumes, but only for low-intensity, short-duration storm events (Tao et al., 2017 ). While the impact of GSI on surface water hydrology has been shown to be effective at the site or small subdivision scale in both modelling and empirical studies, its performance at the catchment level has been less clear in empirical studies (Baker et al., 2022; Jefferson et al., 2017; Oswald et al., 2023; Prudencio and Null, 2018 ). Of the relatively few GSI studies in large (e.g., on the order of tens of square kilometers, or larger than a subdivision scale) urban watersheds, the results have been mixed. Results from previous studies suggest that smaller watersheds are more likely to see significant changes in streamflow from GSI installations than larger watersheds, although that may be attributed to the limited instances of significant GSI implementation in larger watersheds (Bedan and Clausen, 2009; Boening-Ulman et al., 2022; Hood et al., 2007; Hopkins et al., 2020; Jarden et al., 2016; Loperfido et al., 2014; Page et al., 2015a, 2015b; Pennino et al., 2016; Woznicki et al., 2018 ). Some studies identified significant effects from installed GSI at the neighborhood scale but not at the catchment scale (Mayer et al., 2012; Shuster and Rhea, 2013 ). A threshold value where GSI is likely to significantly alter watershed hydrology was also not established. A study of GSI impact at the watershed scale qualified watersheds with GSI controlling 5 % or greater of the drainage area as “high GSI” and found small but significant and positive changes in hydrology (Pennino et al., 2016 ). Due to the limited results on the impact of GSI on water quantity at the watershed level, and variability of the results, further understanding and quantification of how GSI affect runoff and discharge for the drainage basin remain a clear research need (Conley et al., 2022; Golden and Hoghooghi, 2018 ). Philadelphia is one of over 700 municipalities in the United States with complex, rapidly aging combined sewer systems (United States Government Accountability Office, 2023 ). Around 60 % of the city is still served by combined sewers, and the annual CSO discharge volume was estimated to be approximately 49.2 billion liters (13 billion gallons) as of 2011 (Philadelphia Water Department, 2023 ). Consequently, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) required Philadelphia to reduce its CSOs to meet the requirements outlined in the Clean Water Act and the 1994 National Combined Sewer Overflow Policy. In response to the Administrative Order for Compliance on Consent from EPA, the Philadelphia Water Department (PWD) established the Green City, Clean Waters (GCCW) program in 2011, a 25-year plan to reduce the annual CSOs to 30.3 billion liters (8 billion gallons) per year (Philadelphia Water Department, 2011 ). This long-term control plan proposed to control runoff from 40.5 km2  (10,000 acres) and capture 85 % of existing CSOs by replacing at least one-third of impervious surfaces with GSI and green space. This was the first ever plan submitted to the EPA that did not propose adding new gray infrastructure and treatment plants but almost entirely relied on GSI to preliminarily limit the volume of stormwater entering combined sewers (Fitzgerald and Laufer, 2017 ). As of December 2021, based on PWD’s definition of a greened acre, where one greened acre equates to 102,804 liters (27,158 gallons) of managed stormwater, the GSI in Philadelphia was able to handle 226 billion liters (59.6 million gallons) of stormwater. By this time, PWD also reported outperforming its 10-year annual overflow reduction goal of 7.74 billion liters (2.04 billion gallons) by annually reducing 11.6 billion liters (3.08 billion gallons) (The City of Philadelphia Water Department, 2022a ). One of the ways PWD has grouped their GSI projects is by GSI function. Their major GSI categories include curb bump-outs, drainage wells, infiltration / storage trenches, planters, rain gardens, swales, and tree trenches (The City of Philadelphia Water Department, 2022b ). GSI is defined by its reliance on functions such as storage, infiltration, and evapotranspiration to reduce stormwater, but each GSI type has their own advantages and disadvantages and varying hydrological impacts (Office of the Federal Register, National Archives and Records Administration, 2019 ). While GSI performance is highly variable by factors such as GSI design and distribution, and rainfall characteristics, some generalizations can be made by GSI type (Fahy and Chang, 2019; Li et al., 2019a ). For instance, bioretention systems, or rain gardens and bioinfiltration systems, are depressions containing plantings designed to receive stormwater runoff and are composed of vegetation, filter media, storage, and optional underdrains that the runoff is to be filtered through (U.S. EPA, 2015 ). Bioretention practices are associated with peak outflow reductions of 24 to 96 % and considered widely applicable and effective, but they typically have smaller footprints and are used to treat small (under 0.02 km2 ) drainage areas (Li et al., 2019a; Office of Water U.S. EPA, 2021a ). On the other hand, green roofs are roofs covered by growing media and vegetation to allow infiltration and evapotranspiration of rainwater. While they are an ideal alternative for urban areas with limited land available, they can be relatively capital intensive (Office of Water U.S. EPA, 2021b ). The treatment area of a green roof is limited to the area of the roof but has been shown to significantly reduce peak flow of most rainfall – runoff and is associated with 5 to 99.9 % peak attenuation (Li et al., 2019a ). Finally, permeable pavements maintain the functionality of impervious surfaces but allow water to infiltrate through the pavement and can be helpful in developed areas with limited open space. They are considered inappropriate for stormwater hot spots, or areas with high levels of stormwater pollutants, and are generally effective at reducing stormwater, but their performance is particularly sensitive to surrounding environmental conditions (i.e. infiltration rate of surrounding soils) (Office of Water U.S. EPA, 2021c ). Permeable pavements have been associated with 37.9 to 54.2 % reductions in peak flow (Li et al., 2019a ). While these observations about peak attenuations associated with GSI type are helpful, they are also site specific and their performance can vary when assessed at the watershed level. Studies have shown that there are optimal combinations of GSI to enhance reduction effectiveness, and applying comprehensive and diverse varieties of GSI can increase peak discharge reductions, but the optimal combination varies by location and characteristics of each area (Li et al., 2019a ). There are currently no comprehensive performance goals or measures regarding the long-term control plans submitted to EPA such as GCCW, making it difficult to assess the effectiveness or track the progress of the plans submitted to control CSOs (United States Government Accountability Office, 2023 ). As CSOs are expected to remain a pressing concern in the face of aging infrastructure and climate change, methods to quantify the efficacy of plans to combat CSOs, such as GCCW, are essential. Currently, over a decade into the pioneering GCCW program of Philadelphia, the objective of this study was to assess whether changes due to GCCW GSI installations could be observed in a local watershed’s hydrologic response.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Study area Most of Philadelphia’s original streams are buried under combined sewer systems. As of 2023, there were 164 combined sewer outfalls (Philadelphia Water Department, n.d .). Fig. 1   shows combined sewer outfalls and service areas within the city boundary. The increase in GSI implementation in combined sewer areas was notable. From publicly available data with reported installation years, there were 49 GSI installations in Philadelphia in 2006 and 627 GSI installations by 2011. Following the implementation of GCCW program in 2011, there were at least 4,648 GSI installations by 2023. All of these numbers were from the map in Fig. 1 , which was built using layers from OpenDataPhilly, an open data catalogue (OpenDataPhilly, 2019, 2016a, 2016b, 2014 ). The area of interest in this study, shown as the map inset on Fig. 1 , is the stretch of stream between two USGS gages. The gages are located within the Tookany / Tacony – Frankford (TTF) watershed, one of five major watersheds in Philadelphia. The TTF watershed has an area of 85.37 km2  (32.96 mi2 ) (Borton-Lawson Engineering, INC., 2008 ). Approximately 48 % of the watershed is impervious, and based on the greened acres of the GSI projects within the watershed, it can be estimated that 4.7 % of the impervious area, or 2.3 % of the total area in the TTF watershed is being treated by the GSI installed so far under GCCW (see Appendix A for more information) (Borton-Lawson Engineering, INC., 2008; Philadelphia Water Department, 2009, 2005; Philadelphia Water Department, n.d; The City of Philadelphia Water Department, 2022c, 2022b ). For context, estimated impervious area treated by GSI (4.7 %) is only a fraction of the GCCW goal of one-third (33 %) treated impervious area. Despite this, the current analysis endeavored to assess the hydrological response at a stream gage using publicly available streamflow and rainfall data with the hypothesis that even if statistically significant results are not observed, the methodology could be used in future years to continue assessment as more GSI projects are implemented. The TTF watershed discharges to the Delaware River and is comprised of three linked stream segments. Its headwaters are in Tookany Creek in Montgomery County, which drains into Tacony Creek as the water enters Philadelphia at Cheltenham Avenue, and then finally becomes Frankford Creek when it merges with Wingohocking Creek in Juniata Park (Philadelphia Water Department, 2005 ). The upstream gage, which is outside of Philadelphia, is USGS Gage 01467086 Tacony Creek above Adams Avenue with a drainage area of 43.3 km2  (16.7 mi2 ). The downstream gage is USGS Gage 01467087 Frankford Creek at Castor Avenue in Philadelphia with a drainage area of 78.7 km2  (30.4 mi2 ). There are 5.2 stream km (3.2 stream mi) between the two gages. Thirteen sewersheds serviced by combined sewers discharge into the stream between the gages, making this portion of the stream vulnerable to CSOs. The problem is further exacerbated downstream, where there are additional combined sewer outfalls downstream of USGS Gage 01467087. There were no notable datum changes reported for either stream gage (“Frankford Creek at Castor Ave, Philadelphia, PA,” n.d.; “Tacony Creek ab Adams Avenue, Philadelphia, PA,” n.d. ).  2.2 Period of study A hydrologic response analysis was conducted by comparing the peak flow rates observed at the two USGS gages before and after implementation of GCCW. To temporally compare the data, a “Before” period representing stream response prior to GCCW and the corresponding GSI installations, and an “After” period to evaluate the hydrologic response to GSI installations were selected. The before period was from fiscal year 2007 to 2011 (July 1, 2006 to June 30, 2011), and the after period from fiscal year 2017 to 2021 (July 1, 2016 to June 30, 2021). Fiscal years were chosen since PWD releases annual reports on combined sewer and stormwater management programs with a reporting period of a fiscal year. Five-year periods were chosen as it was the largest possible duration that could be studied for the before period based on available data; the period of record at USGS gage 01467086 begins in October 2005, and GCCW was adopted in 2011. Table 1   indicates the number of GSI with known installation years that were present within the 13 sewersheds of interest during the period of study. A substantial increase in GSI was noted between and within the periods. Including GSI without known installation years, there was a total of 547 GSI within the study area. Of those GSI, 375 had listed installation dates and they are shown below. Using the web-based modeling app Model My Watershed, land use analysis was conducted to ensure that there were minimal changes in urban growth in the watershed during the two study periods (see Appendix B for more information) (Stroud Water Research Center, n.d. ). Although changes to the land cover were relatively small during this time period (2006–2019), trends showed a loss of undeveloped land (i.e., open space and deciduous forest), with increases in land development (i.e., medium and high intensity development) (Table B1 ). This type of land change trend, from undeveloped to medium and high developed land, would generally be associated with higher volumes of runoff.  2.3 Rain event selection To assess hydrologic responses to precipitation events, rain events in the before and after periods were identified where dry periods exceeding six hours were considered separate rain events and cumulative precipitation during the event must have exceeded 0.64 cm (0.25 in) to qualify as a rain event. Within the identified precipitation events, events that met the following storm criteria were selected to be studied. The cumulative precipitation during the event had to be between 1.02 to 2.8 cm (0.4 to 1.1 in), as GSI is typically designed to target these smaller, more frequent storms, and GCCW aims to manage the first inch of stormwater on site (Fitzgerald and Laufer, 2017; Philadelphia Water Department, 2009 ). Events with precipitation 24 h preceding it, or snow 24 h prior to or on day of were excluded, as there may have been water from previous events remaining in the watershed that could affect hydrologic response (Singh, 1997 ). Storm events that met all criteria were identified using 1-hour increment precipitation data recorded by the Pennsylvania State Climatologist at the Northeast Philadelphia Airport, located 9.5 km (5.9 mi) and 10 km (6.2 mi) respectively from the upstream and downstream gages (“Frankford Creek at Castor Ave, Philadelphia, PA,” n.d.; “Pennsylvania State Climatologist,” n.d.; “Tacony Creek ab Adams Avenue, Philadelphia, PA,” n.d. ). Snowfall data from Automated Surface Observing Systems was also used for rain event selection (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, 2022 ). There were 188 and 123 events, respectively, in the before and after periods that fell within 1.02 to 2.8 cm of precipitation. After removing events where there was precipitation within 24 hours of the event, 95 events in the before and 87 events in the after period remained. Finally, after removing events with snow, a total of 167 storm events of interest were identified: 89 events from the before period, and 78 events from the after period. Table B2  contains the complete list of precipitation events used in the study. As shown in the boxplots in Fig. 2  , and based on Wilcoxon Rank Sukenvm tests with a significance level of 0.05, storm events in the before and after period were not statistically significantly different between the two periods in event depth (p  = 0.57), event intensity (p  = 0.82), and preceding dry time (p  = 0.52). This helped minimize the possibility that differences in hydrological response between the before and after periods were from differences in the precipitation events being compared.  2.4 Hydrological response Using USGS gage data, which recorded discharge in 15-minute increments, hydrographs were generated for the 167 qualifying storm events. Fig. 3   is one of the hydrographs that was generated and a good representation of typical storm event response. The downstream hydrograph at Frankford Creek frequently saw multiple peaks. The first peak often occurred before the upstream peak at Tacony Creek and since this area is within urban Philadelphia, it was likely due to runoff from nearby impervious surfaces that entered Frankford Creek shortly after precipitation began. Accordingly, this response was referred to as the “urban contribution peak.” The second peak in the downstream hydrograph, which was more likely due to the storm pulse moving through the stream, was referred to as the downstream peak. While all three discharge peaks – upstream, urban contribution, and downstream – were examined in the study, the urban contribution peaks were of primary interest. The primary objective of the GCCW program was to limit CSOs by reducing runoff. As baseflow plays a more significant role in the upstream and downstream peaks, and lowering total flow was not a goal, although a possible byproduct of GCCW, urban contribution peak was used as a performance indicator when evaluating possible watershed-level effects of GCCW. The nonparametric Mann-Kendall test was used to assess time series trends across the before and after periods (Helsel et al., 2020; Hopkins et al., 2022 ). Upon examining the 167 hydrographs, a system of flags was developed to remove precipitation events where the urban contribution peak could not be identified. This left a total of 159 events of interest, including 85 events from the before period and 74 events from the after period, where urban contribution peaks were manually identified and used for analysis. Of the 159 events remaining, there were events where upstream and downstream peaks could not be identified, leaving 69 events from the before period and 50 events from the after period. The utilized system of flags and how each of the hydrographs were flagged are in Table B3  and Table B2 .  2.5 Flood discharge and exceedance probability Gage heights of interest, including the action stage and various flood stages, were provided by the National Weather Service (NWS) at the downstream gage, USGS Gage 01467087 (Frankford Creek at Castor Ave). By pairing 15-min increment gage height data with discharge data from the gage, a rating curve was generated (Fig. B1 ). The rating curve was used to relate the notable gage heights to corresponding flow rates, as summarized below in Table 2  . The NWS defines action stage as when mitigation measures are required for potentially significant hydrologic activity. The flood stage is when water surface levels became a hazard, while moderate flood stage refer to some inundation of structures and roads by the stream. Major flood stage refers to extensive inundation of structures and roads (US Department of Commerce, n.d. ). The Weibull Formula, as shown below as Eq. 1, was used to assign plotting positions to urban contribution peak discharge values from events of interest in the before period, and after period, respectively (Mays, 2019 ). Using the plotting positions, flow magnitude was related to an empirical exceedance probability (P ), where m  is rank (1 is highest discharge) and n  is number of observations.(1) W e i b u l l  F o r m u l a :  P = m n + 1        Probability distribution fitting was performed to assess the difference between flood frequency in the before and after periods. The log-Pearson Type III distribution is commonly used in hydrologic analysis, particularly development of flood frequency curves (England et al., 2019 ). Using the method of moments approach on log-transformed observed peak flow values, the location (τ), shape (α), and scale (β) parameters were estimated. The distribution fit was assessed using root mean square error (RMSE) in the before and after periods. Once the two fitted log-Pearson Type III distributions were established, the nonparametric two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test with a significance level of 0.05 was performed to test whether the before and after distributions come from the same distribution (Massey, 1951; Ridolfi et al., 2020 ).   3 Results 3.1 Temporal changes in peak discharge As shown below in Fig. 4  , boxplots of the peak flows in the before and after periods were generated, and the Wilcoxon Rank Sum Test conducted to check for statistically significant differences between the two periods. Based on the boxplot, the upstream and downstream peaks are similar to each other in both periods, providing more support that the stream pulse was properly identified, and that there was minimal attenuation between the upstream and downstream gages. Comparing the two periods, the median urban contribution peak flow increased but the number of outliers decreased in the after period. A wider spread of upstream and downstream peak values in the after period was also observed. However, p-values from the Wilcoxon Rank Sum Test comparing peak discharge between the two periods (p  = 0.27 for urban contribution) revealed that there was insufficient evidence to suggest a significant difference between the peaks in the before and after periods. Fig. 5   shows the urban contribution peaks in the before and after periods in a time series. Mann-Kendall results (p  = 0.52 for the before period, p  = 0.82 for the after period) indicated an absence of a statistically significant trend in the before and after periods. Moving averages of urban contribution peaks were calculated and plotted against time to aid in visualizing the data (Fig. 5 ). Although there is no statistically significant change in peaks, any iteration of creating a moving average of the peaks indicated a reduction between the before and after periods. As seventeen was the mean number of identified storms of interest in a year, moving averages were generated for both periods by averaging seventeen peaks and four peaks to represent each year and each of the seasons. While using the larger averages smoothed the trends (solid gray lines in Fig. 5 ), using smaller averages captured temporal fluctuations (solid black lines in Fig. 5 ), likely due to factors such as seasonality and the stochasticity of precipitation.  3.2 Exceedance probability of flooding The exceedance probability of different flood stages defined by NWS was identified using the flood frequency plot (Fig. 6   and Table 3  ) generated by the Weibull plotting position (observed) and Log-Pearson Type III distribution (fitted). The fitted log-Pearson Type III distributions had RSME values of 0.031 and 0.022 for the before and after periods, respectively, which indicates the distribution was suitable for the observed data in both periods. Based on the two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, the null hypothesis was rejected (p  < 2.2e-16), indicating that the fitted log-Pearson Type III distributions are not considered to be from the same distribution. The likelihood of experiencing of peak flow reaching or exceeding flood stage (131.4 cms) more than halved in the after period (1.7 %) compared to the before period (4.6 %) based on the fitted Log-Pearson Type III distributions. The action stage saw the smallest difference in probability between the two periods and as the severity of the flood increased so did the reduction in probability of occurrence between the periods. The reduction in exceedance probability quantitatively demonstrates that GSI was effective in suppressing the urban contribution peak flows for the studied storms to reduce flooding likelihood.   4 Discussion The analysis results reflected the complexity in assessing urban streams and their interactions with GSI and the stochastic nature of what GSI receives – namely, precipitation, prior conditions of GSI, and the amount of GSI capture of the total area. Visual assessments from this analysis (Fig. 5  scatter plots and Fig. 6  flood frequency plot) demonstrate the potential effect the GSI installations from the GCCW program may have on reducing urban contribution peak flows. Meanwhile, boxplots (Fig. 4 ) and associated statistical tests indicate no statistically significant difference in peak flows between the before and after period. Although this may initially appear inconsistent with previous studies’ connecting GSI with peak flow reduction, these results were not surprising due to the limited quantity of the area controlled by GSI, and variability of the factors such as rainfall at play (Ando and Netusil, 2018; Boening-Ulman et al., 2022; Holt et al., 2022; Jarden et al., 2016; Landauer et al., 2019; Pennino et al., 2016; Shafique, 2017; Yang and Li, 2013 ). Other studies have completed similar analyses (Palla and Gnecco, 2015; Pennino et al., 2016 ), but none of the empirical studies have assessed hydrology at the watershed scale nor assessed such large watersheds. 4.1 Insignificant peak attenuation Despite GSI’s known benefit of reducing runoff volumes and peak flows, it was reasonable that there were no significant changes in peak flows for the studied periods. Miller et al. (2021)  had previously found that managing percent impervious cover is more effective at attenuating urban hydrographs in traditional stormwater management, and it has been theorized that a substantial portion of the impervious area must be treated by GSI to notice a difference in the watershed hydrology. While consensus on a threshold value for percent coverage by GSI has not been established, studies suggest this is easier to accomplish for smaller watersheds than for larger ones, like the area of interest in this study. Although Philadelphia is in progress of meeting its goals with GCCW, it is possible that the resulting 4.7 % of the impervious area treated by GSI in the study area of interest is insufficient to cause significant observable changes in the hydrologic response of the watershed. For instance, a modeling study by Palla and Gnecco (2015)  found a 5 % reduction in effective impervious area to result in only a 3 % reduction in peak flow. Consequently, the remaining percent impervious cover disconnected from GSI may still be dominating the hydrologic response in the TTF watershed. Regardless, this does not suggest that the program is ineffective in meeting its CSO reduction targets, and hydrologic changes are likely to become more prominent as the program continues. The slight increases in urbanization noted during land cover analysis where there was more removal than increase of green space would typically be associated with consequent increases in runoff and peak severity. However, the manner of implementation of GSI through the study periods may have aided the lack of significant changes in aggregated peak flows.  4.2 Temporal dynamics of GSI interactions Considering results from previous works and the complex results from the study, the limitation of studying the effects of GSI from GCCW in a discrete rather than continuous fashion was considered. As of 2021, Philadelphia, despite having met the 10-year goals of GCCW, was less than halfway through the program. Consequently, since the implementation of GCCW in 2011, and entirety of the after period, there has been significant growth of GSI in Philadelphia, including the area of interest. In the after period, there was an average increase of 39 known GSI installations per year. Even throughout the before period, prior to GCCW, the average increase of known GSI was 11 per year. As described in Section 2.2 , the study periods were selected to maximize usage of data prior to GCCW and to capture the most recent and therefore most significant impacts of GCCW. In reality the amount of and consequently the capacity of GSI in the study area were dynamic. Fig. 4  with the moving averages and Fig. 6  flood frequency plot were reflective of the dynamic scenario; when peak flow values were examined against time or plotting positions, reductions were observed. While changes in urban contribution peaks towards the end of the after period may have been significant compared to the peaks towards the beginning of the before period, aggregating the peaks for the before and after periods in the boxplots likely muted such changes. The innate randomness associated with precipitation makes it difficult to isolate the impact of GSI implementations. Rainfall can also be highly variable when moving across a watershed depending on the type of weather event, and spatial variability can also affect hydrologic response. Another consideration is that while the storms included in the study had a preceding dry time exceeding 24 hours to isolate the hydrologic response of the storm being examined, this may not have been enough time for GSI to regain its design capacity, lowering its performance during certain events. PWD’s performance assessments of GCCW found most of their surface GSI to drain within 12 hours, and subsurface GSI to drain down within 48 hours of the storm ending for 94 % of observed events (The City of Philadelphia Water Department, 2022a ). As the interquartile range of observed drain down times for subsurface systems fell between 2 and 16 hours, using a preceding dry time of 24 hours for the study should have been sufficient for most scenarios, but may have been insufficient for certain events. Regardless, it is important to keep in mind that the lack of statistically significant peak flow reductions for the amount of GSI in the study area do not imply that the installed GSI are ineffective nor that the goals of the GCCW are not being met since this study did not assess CSOs themselves. It may be difficult to capture statistical significance of highly dynamic environments when there is subjectiveness built into the null hypothesis (Cohn and Lins, 2005 ).  4.3 Study limitations Analyzing the relationship between total precipitation depth and corresponding responses in peak flow was complicated by the spatial difference between the rain gage and stream gage. Northeast Philadelphia Airport was the closest airport located to the two USGS stream gages of interest. However, as precipitation can vary greatly spatially, even by a few miles, there was likely some disconnect between the precipitation depths used in the study and experienced on site. The largest differences between the data used for analysis and observed precipitation on site was likely during the warm season, when convection is the most common cause of precipitation, which tends to be highly localized. Precipitation is generally more spatially uniform in the cold season. This may have explained the outlier in Fig. 5  where flow neared 142 cms (5000 cfs) for a precipitation event yielding 1.1 cm (0.42 in) of rain in June 2021; the precipitation and consequent runoff into the stream was likely greater than the 1.1 cm (0.42 in) observed at the airport. Additionally, rainfall intensity is another variable that can cause variations in hydrologic response. While there were no significant changes in the distribution of rainfall intensity for the two periods of interest, hydrologic response was not assessed against rainfall intensity. By temporally comparing peak flows to assess GSI influence on urban streams, the results of the study may have also been complicated by annual wetness or dryness, and consequent changes in baseflow. As seen with the moving averages in Fig. 5 , there were fluctuations in peak discharges, likely due to seasonality. Although general seasonal trends and variability was reflected in both periods as the same lengths of study (5 years) were used for the before and after periods, the yearly differences in overall precipitation were not as well accounted for. While the baseflow of the streams in the before and after periods should have remained relatively similar to each other, the analysis may be influenced by the annual meteorological conditions. Another consideration to note was that identifying stream pulses and peaks of hydrographs with actual data occasionally required interpretation. While there is reasonable confidence with the identified peaks, and the boxplots in Fig. 5  support the accuracy of selected peaks, hydrological interactions in nature are inherently complex. Table B2  and Table B3  are provided for transparency in how the hydrographs were assessed. Finally, the amount of publicly available data regarding GSI projects installed in Philadelphia was a study limitation. PWD provided the greened acres associated with each GSI project and defined greened acre as equivalent to an inch of managed stormwater from an acre of drainage area. Through their reported greened acres, the amount of impervious area being treated by GSI could be estimated in Section 2.1 . However, as greened acres is not a metric that is widely used in the field and GSI is commonly designed to handle 3.81 cm (1.5 in) of rain, it was a limited substitution for the drainage or treatment areas associated with each GSI project (Amur et al., 2022; Boston Water and Sewer Commission, 2024 ; NJ DEP, 2023; Philadelphia Water Department, 2021 ). The type and drainage area of GSI are critical parameters in quantifying GSI, and particularly as larger scale GSI projects become more common, it would be advisable for entities to make such parameters publicly available for accurate assessments and deeper understanding of GSI impact.   5 Conclusion A stretch of the Tacony-Frankford Creek and its peak flows upstream, downstream, and due to urban contribution before and after GSI installations from Philadelphia's Green City, Clean Waters program were assessed for changes in hydrologic response. It is important to note that the analysis presented here did not assess the target of the GCCW program, i.e., CSO reduction, but rather investigated whether the GSI installed as a result of GCCW has had an observable impact on urban stream peak flows. While there was no observed statistically significant change in the distribution of peak flows when they were temporally aggregated, a significant change in probability of exceeding flood stages was observed following the GSI implementations. These results reflected the complexity in assessing urban streams in larger watersheds and their interactions with GSI and the stochastic nature of what GSI receives − precipitation and meteorological conditions. The impact of GSI becomes more difficult to trace in larger watersheds, where it becomes more challenging to have enough GSI to alter peak streamflow. Hydrologic response alone was insufficient to fully capture the nuanced relationships at hand, but that does not indicate that the GSI implemented for GCCW has had no consequence. Studies have shown the broad impacts GSI can have on stormwater management and beyond, e.g., heat mitigation, however, the metrics for assessing the many benefits and challenges of these systems remain elusive. It remains essential to continue to study and assess GCCW, particularly as the concentration of GSI continue to increase under the program. As the first stormwater control plan to rely so heavily on GSI, GCCW has the potential to serve as a guideline for future urban stormwater management, and a thorough understanding of the impact GSI has on the hydrology of the watershed is needed for effective application moving forward.
1 Introduction Seawater intrusion (SWI) driven by over-exploitation and climate change has deteriorated groundwater quality (Hesamfar et al., 2023; Ketabchi et al., 2016; Taylor et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2022 ). Previous studies have shown that subsurface physical barriers, such as subsurface dams or cutoff walls are commonly used to prevent seawater intrusion in coastal regions (Abdoulhalik et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2023 ). Consequently, a large body of residual saltwater will be trapped upstream behind subsurface dams, which has adverse effect on fresh groundwater exploitation (Luyun et al., 2009; Yin et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2021 ). To accelerate residual saltwater scavenging remaining in the upstream aquifer of a subsurface dam, hydraulic barriers are effective for coastal aquifer remediation design. However, many parameters including extraction/injection rates or positions are imperative to be optimized given the complexity of the system. This process encounters a major obstacle because it involves numerically complicated groundwater models and high-dimensional decision variables, which limit their applications to optimization problems (Chen et al., 2022; Jiang and Na, 2020; Saad et al., 2022; Vali et al., 2021 ). A complete optimization process must repetitively invoke intensive numerical models and thereby yields a prohibitive computational burden (Chen et al., 2017 ). To overcome this drawback, surrogate models are low-computational-cost approximation models to emulate key characteristics of actual simulation models and thus aid convergence of the optimization procedure (Asher et al., 2015; Luo et al., 2023; Razavi et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2022 ). Data-driven machine learning models are widely utilized to replace high-fidelity numerical simulation models and have found fertile ground in the domain of water resources and environment (Garzón et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2022; Shaw et al., 2017; Tsoukalas et al., 2016 ). For instance, Yazdi and Neyshabouri (2014)  introduced a framework to solve high-dimensional problems for optimizing flood control detention dams. Guo et al. (2019)  integrated Kriging and mixed-integer nonlinear programming to identify groundwater pollution source. To efficiently calibrate agricultural hydrological models on a limited budget, Xi et al. (2017)  used sparse-grid based surrogates in a globally optimization procedure. Especially, most commonly-used surrogate models spanning over the groundwater decision-making field include evolutionary polynomial regression (Giustolisi et al., 2008; Hussain et al., 2015 ), artificial neural network (Kim et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2023; Yin and Tsai, 2018 ), radial basis function (Pang and Shoemaker, 2023; Wu et al., 2022 ), support vector machine (Lal and Datta, 2019; Yin et al., 2022 ) and Kriging (Luo et al., 2019 ). No method is universally superior and each surrogate model has its limitation under different situations. So, many studies have selected multiple machine learning models for comparative research or established ensemble models (Yin et al., 2024 ). Furthermore, due to existence of surrogate approximation errors (i.e., the differences between numerical model and surrogate model outputs), embedding surrogate models into optimization will introduce bias (Zhang et al., 2020 ). The accumulated errors of forecasting may mislead optimization and result in infeasible solutions. A highly potential approach to make up for surrogate errors and enhance optimality is to innovate adaptive surrogate models in optimization (Christelis et al., 2023; Forrester and Keane, 2009; Xu et al., 2012; Yan and Minsker, 2006 ). Actually, surrogate modeling can be roughly divided into two types, namely non-adaptive and adaptive modeling. For non-adaptive modeling, samples are pre-specified to conduct one-shot training and build surrogate models, which then substitute an expensive-cost numerical model for function evaluations (Jiang and Na, 2020; Razavi et al., 2012 ). A potential drawback of the non-adaptive modeling is that one-shot trained surrogate models probably cannot accurately represent potential relationships across inputs and outputs of an original system. On the other hand, adaptive modeling allows online frameworks to iteratively update surrogate models during the optimization process. The basic idea of adaptive modeling is to continuously update training data and retrain surrogate models in certain regions (Yondo et al., 2018 ). The adaptively retrained surrogate models can achieve more accurate predictions in the vicinity of optimal solutions and prevent evolutionary search from falling into local optima (Jin, 2011; Luo et al., 2020; Song et al., 2018 ). Generally, there are three types of adaptive sampling techniques: global adaptive sampling (Mo et al., 2017 ), local adaptive sampling (Luo et al., 2020 ), and a balance of global and local adaptive sampling. For example, Wu et al. (2022)  presented an adaptive switching technique to resolve a global optimization algorithm, where radial basis functions and Kriging with highest global prediction accuracy were employed as available surrogates. Results from benchmark cases proved more availability and effectiveness, but lack demonstration to more practical groundwater multiobjective optimization designs. Most real-world engineering applications contain multiple conflicts or independent factors (Deb et al., 2018 ). Therefore, high-performance but flexible surrogate methods are demanded to handle high-dimensional and computationally intensive optimization problems. Unlike major existing frameworks using pre-determined non-adaptive models, so far, the adaptive modeling framework is still relatively limited even though it has significant advantages of obtaining relevant information from previous iterations. Our previous study (Yin et al., 2023 ) found that pumping saltwater initially and then shifting to inject freshwater using a dual well were able to significantly improve aquifer desalination efficiency. To this regard, the proposed methodology is demonstrated to seek optimal extraction and injection strategies for scavenging residual saltwater in an upstream aquifer of a subsurface dam (Fig. 1  ). Two conflicting objectives of minimizing the total extraction and injection rates as well as maximizing saltwater removal effectiveness are considered in the study. More important, an adaptive modeling algorithm is newly incorporated to iteratively retrain those poorly-performed machine learning models. Optimal strategies obtained from machine learning surrogate based frameworks are compared against those from the physically based seawater intrusion model, and are finally verified using the high-fidelity numerical model. This study aims to (1) propose a novel adaptive machine learning surrogate based multiobjective optimization method for coastal aquifer desalination, (2) strike a balance among easing computational burden, inhibiting error accumulation of forecasting as well as enhancing convergence to true Pareto optimal solutions, and (3) test its robustness on different seawater intrusion remediation scenarios to obtain optimum extraction/injection rates for a dual well through a constrained multi-objective framework.  2 Methods 2.1 Physically based seawater intrusion model A physically based density-dependent saltwater intrusion model is developed using SEAWAT_V4 (Langevin et al., 2008 ), coupling groundwater flow model MODFLOW (Harbaugh et al., 2000 ) with solute transport model MT3DMS (Zheng and Wang, 1999 ). The model development is implemented using the Flopy package in Python environment (Bakker et al., 2016 ). As depicted in Fig. 1 a, the model is a two-dimensional unconfined homogeneous aquifer with a length of 1.20 m and a thickness of 0.35 m. Considering the grid Péclet number (Voss and Souza, 1987 ), the discretized grid resolution is 0.5 cm by 0.5 cm. For boundary conditions, the lower part of the numerical model is defined as no-flow boundary condition. The left hydrostatic boundary represents a coastline with a constant head of 0.346 m, and the concentration is set to 35 g/L corresponding to a saltwater density of approximately 1025 kg/m3 . The right inland boundary is considered as a constant freshwater head of 0.358 m with 0 concentration and density of 1000 kg/m3 . A subsurface dam is installed at 0.35 m away from the coastline being as an impermeable physical barrier to control seawater intrusion as well as increase the amount of underground freshwater resources. However, the issue is that a large body of residual saltwater will be trapped at the landside of a subsurface dam. To accelerate removal of residual saltwater, a dual well is installed to extract saltwater or inject freshwater at a distance of 0.16 m away from the dam. Six monitoring wells (M1-M6) are selected to gauge the salinity reduction. Model parameters for the numerical simulations are adjusted using measured values from the laboratory experiment, as given in Table 1  . More details of the model can be found from Yin et al. (2023) .  2.2 Data generation A uniformly distributed input–output dataset is required to construct machine learning models that can well represent the original response surface. The time-varying extraction/injection rates of a dual well are inputs to the numerical simulation model and represent decision variables. Outputs are the resulting chloride concentration at different monitoring well locations or salinity mass at the landside of the subsurface dam. To produce the most uniformly scattered inputs in a multi-dimensional decision space, a Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) approach is employed to generate independent training and validation input data. A maximum minimum distance criterion is adopted to maximize the minimum distance between samples. The LHS divides cumulative distribution of each input variable into a number of equiprobable intervals, which boasts a stratified sampling technique with excellent space-filling properties on individual dimensions (Aitken et al., 2022; Beevers et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2019 ). Subsequently, the sampled extraction and injection rates serve as inputs to a physically based SEAWAT model and yield outputs (chloride concentration and salinity mass). This study generates 400 training samples and 50 independent validation samples on high performance computing, which are sufficiently large to guarantee model performance.  2.3 Machine learning modeling In this study, three different machine learning models are considered including artificial neural network, Gaussian process, and response surface regression. A typical artificial neural network (ANN) is adopted whose architecture comprises three layers: input, hidden, and output layers. Each layer is equipped with neurons, and the neurons of adjacent layers are fully interconnected. The architecture of ANN is illustrated in Fig. 2  . Gaussian process (GP) is a non-parametric approach that can capture non-linear mappings or relationships across inputs and outputs of a system. GP is a powerful regression technique (Luo et al., 2022; Rajabi and Ketabchi, 2017; Saad et al., 2022 ) for a wide range of application domain, such as time-series predictions (Brahim-Belhouari and Bermak, 2004; Raghavendra and Deka, 2016; Sun et al., 2014 ) and groundwater level predictions (Kumar et al., 2020; Tao et al., 2022; Varouchakis et al., 2022 ). Response surface regression (RSR) models are valuable statistical tools used to capture the underlying relationship between a response variable (such as chloride concentration or salinity mass) and multiple explanatory variables (such as time-varying extraction and injection rates). A third-order polynomial function is employed as the response surface regression model. Mathematical descriptions of the three surrogate models are provided in the Appendix. Predicting performance of the developed machine learning models is evaluated using criteria including the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency coefficient (NSE), the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) and the root mean square error (RMSE). Mathematical expressions of these performance metrics are respectively given by:(1) NSE = 1 - ∑ n = 1  N  ( f ∼   ( n )   - f  ( n )   )  2   ∑ n = 1  N  ( f ∼   ( n )   - f  ¯    ( n )   )  2        (2) MAPE = 1 N  ∑ n = 1  N  f ∼   ( n )   - f  ( n )    f ∼   ( n )          (3) RMSE = 1 N  ∑ n = 1  N  ( f ∼   ( n )   - f  ( n )   )  2        where N   is the sample size; f  ( n )     is predicted chloride concentration (or salinity mass) from the surrogate model; f ∼   ( n )     is the chloride concentration (or salinity mass)simulated from the physically based the SEAWAT model; and f  ¯    ( n )     is the mean chloride concentration (or salinity mass) of all samples from the SEAWAT model.  2.4 Optimization model 2.4.1 Bi-objective desalination problem set-up In this study, two conflicting objectives are proposed to deal with upstream aquifer desalination behind a subsurface dam in a coastal region. The first objective aims to minimize the total extraction and injection rates to save energy. The second objective is to maximize effectiveness of residual saltwater removal from the aquifer, which is quantified by reduction of salinity mass at the end of management period. The objectives are formulated by:(4) min F 1  = ∑ t = 1  t  Q t    + ∑ t + 1  T  I t      (5) max F 2  = mass  ini   - mass  end     / mass  ini     × 100 %     where F 1    is the first objective function indicating total extraction and injection rates for water demands; Q t    and I t    are the extraction or injection rate at the t  th     stress period for the dual well; F 2    is the second objective function quantifying the removal extent of residual saltwater expressed by percentage of salinity mass decrease at the end of the management period. mass  ini     and mass  end     are the total salinity mass in the upstream region behind the subsurface dam at the beginning and end of the management period, respectively. A set of imposed constraints is needed to ensure that chloride concentrations at the monitoring well locations remain within prescribed limits. Specifically, stringent measures are in place to ensure that chloride concentrations do not surpass the lower limit of 17.5 g/L, corresponding to the 50 % isoline in this study.(6) C k  ≤ C max       (7) Q min   ≤ Q t  ≤ Q max       (8) I min   ≤ I t  ≤ I max       (9) ∑ t = 1  T  I t  ≤ I sum       where C k    is chloride concentration at k  th     monitoring well; C max     is a maximum permissible chloride concentration constraint at monitoring well locations; Eq. (7) and (8)  give a set of bound constraints, representing the extraction or injection capacity must be within specified lower and upper bounds (Q min    , Q max    ) and (I min    , I max    ), respectively; Eq. (9)  indicates that the total injection rate must be less than a prescribed maximum available water supply I sum    .  2.4.2 Integrating adaptive surrogate with multiobjective genetic algorithm The proposed methodology integrates data-driven machine learning models with a Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) to solve a multiobjective aquifer remediation problem (Deb et al., 2002 ). Traditionally, the offline framework is adopted to seek promising Pareto optimal solutions, where machine learning models are trained using prespecified samples. Then, one-shot trained surrogate models would be called iteratively to evaluate offspring populations from NSGA-II until convergence. However, some poorly-performed surrogate models accumulate errors of prediction, which thereby mislead optimization and exhibit suboptimal or false optima. To overcome this issue, this study further introduces an adaptive modeling approach to iteratively renew model predictions during the evolutionary search and accelerate convergence towards to a true Pareto front. As illustrated in Fig. 3  , the adaptive modeling approach consists of two main parts: the optimization and adaptive training modules. In a detail, surrogate models obtain possible optimal solutions assisted by some sampling criteria during iterative epochs. Afterwards, those possible optimal solutions with largest crowding distances are selected to rerun the numerical model and obtain input–output data. Finally, the newly added data would merge with old data to retrain surrogate models at the beginning of next cycle. In such a way, surrogate models can approximate the response surface of the original model more accurately and make useful predictions, which will assist convergence towards optimum. The adaptive training module is terminated until a given stopping criterion is fulfilled. This way, thereby, can maximize profit from the surrogate technique and reduce more computation requirements than offline algorithms. Two metrics, namely Inverted Generational Distance (IGD) and Hypervolume (HV) are quantified to evaluate convergence and diversity of the optimization framework. IGD (Coello Coello and Reyes Sierra, 2004 ) measures how close the current non-dominated front is to the true Pareto front, and HV (Zitzler and Thiele, 1999 ) describes convergence and diversity of Pareto optimal solutions. Taking a two-objective minimization problem as an example, its schematic diagram is shown in Fig. 4  a. The IGD metric is formulated as:(10) I G D P  ref   , P   = ∑ v ∈ P  ref     d i s ( υ , P )   P  ref          where P  ref     is the reference Pareto set that covers a true Pareto front; P   is the approximate Pareto set at the each iteration; dis ( υ , P )    is the minimum Euclidean distance between υ   and solutions in set P  ; and P  ref       is the number of Pareto optimal solutions in P  ref    . The advantage of IGD lies in that it combines the measure of proximity and diversity into a single performance metric, which is very useful for comparison of many solutions from different kinds of algorithms. The smaller the IGD value, the better the obtained Pareto optimal solutions. The HV metric is formulated as:(11) H V P   = δ ( ∪ i = 1  P    μ i  )      where P   denotes an approximate Pareto set; δ   denotes the Lebesgue measure to calculate volume; μ i    is the hypervolume of the i  th     approximate Pareto solution with respect to the reference point, as indicated by the shaded area in Fig. 4 b. The strength of HV is a monotonically increasing relationship between the indicator value and Pareto dominance. Hence, a higher value of HV indicates better-obtained solutions.  2.4.3 Pareto strategies verification The Pareto optimal pumping and injection strategies obtained from the optimization model are fed back into the physically based seawater intrusion model to verify if constraints are met or not. Considering uncertainty from surrogate models, the differences between chloride concentrations predicted from surrogate models and those simulated from the solute transport model are calculated in case that constraints are not satisfied. A flowchart of the work is presented in Fig. 5  , which involves machine learning model development and aquifer desalination optimization design.    3 Numerical application The applicability and effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated by seawater intrusion remediation in a coastal aquifer where a large quantity of saltwater remained at the landside of a subsurface dam. The method focuses on improving prediction accuracy of surrogate models and obtaining more reliable optimal solutions. In addition, due to lack of sufficient monitoring data, the accuracy of the field-scale numerical models cannot be guaranteed. So, the laboratory-scale numerical model is developed and well calibrated by experimental data. As depicted in Fig. 1 b, a dual well is installed to extract saltwater during an initial period and switch to inject freshwater when the toe of residual saltwater (50 % isoline) retreats to the position of the dual well (Yin et al., 2023 ). Decision variables corresponding to time-varying extraction and injection rates are to be determined during the remediation period. The salinity transport is strictly gauged using six monitoring wells. The extraction rates are bounded by the lower and upper limits of −0.4 cm3 /s and 0 cm3 /s, respectively, and the injection rates are constrained within the lower and upper limits of 0 cm3 /s and 0.4 cm3 /s, respectively. Meanwhile, a prescribed maximum water supply is set to 0.6 cm3 /s indicating freshwater availability. To construct machine learning models, we adopt the Latin hypercube sampling technique to generate extraction and injection rates, and then put into the seawater intrusion model to obtain resulting chloride concentration and salinity mass. 400 training samples are prepared to build three different types of machine learning models (ANN, GP and RSR) at the six monitoring locations. All the model performance is validated through 50 independent validation samples. To inhibit error accumulation of forecasting and correctly converge to a true Pareto front, the newly developed adaptive modeling algorithm is initiated to retrain those poorly-performed machine learning surrogates during the evolutionary search. In this study, the population size is identically set to 200, and the NSGA-II is utilized to solve a bi-objective management problem. Especially for the adaptive training, an initial population size of 150 is used. Five individuals with the largest crowding distances are selected from each of the first 50 generations until the training data size reaches 400. The machine learning model development as well as the optimization are implemented in Python programming.  4 Results and discussion 4.1 Evaluation of one-shot trained model performance Predictive performance of the developed machine learning models over validation data is depicted in Fig. 6  . Calculation of three statistical metrics (Table 2  ) indicates that they generally prove good fitting criterion. After being trained, most one-shot trained machine learning models have NSE greater than 0.98, MAPE less than 0.025, and RMSE less than 0.30, except for models at M6. This indicates that predicted chloride concentrations at the six monitoring sites have strong agreement with those from the SEAWAT model. Thus, the developed three surrogate models all have potential to predict the nonlinear behavior of SWI model. But in more detailed comparison, chloride concentrations predicted from the RSR model at M6 do not fit the existing data very well. This is because the model built with pre-specified 400 training samples might miss certain regions of the original response surface, and cannot accurately represent potential relationship between the original SEAWAT model and the interesting regions of decision variables. In fact, there is no specific surrogate model clearly superior to the rest ones. The salinity mass at the landside of the subsurface dam is more rewarding but difficult to predict. Fig. 7  a-7c demonstrate performance of three one-shot trained machine learning models (ANN, GP and RSR) for predicting salinity mass. In this study, all the machine learning models have NSE higher than 0.99, MAPE less than 0.0039, RMSE less than 0.02. This study also calculates errors between predicted and simulated salinity mass. Distribution of the absolute errors is illustrated using box plot in Fig. 7 d. The median error of the GP model is smaller than that of the ANN model and RSR model, suggesting that GP outperforms the other two. However, as the nonlinearity of the SWI model increases, predictive performance of all surrogate models will definitely degrade. Thus, an adaptive training algorithm is proposed to add samples near potential optimal solutions and improve local predictive performance of surrogate models.  4.2 Pareto optimal solutions of aquifer desalination In this study, the NSGA-II adopts 150 generations to find converged Pareto optimal solutions with a uniform population size of 200. For the sake of clarity, we incorporate NSGA-II with different one-shot trained machine learning surrogate models (ANN-NSGA-II, GP-NSGA-II, and RSR-NSGA-II) as well as the original SEAWAT model (SEAWAT-NSGA-II). Fig. 8   shows Pareto fronts obtained from the four cases. For comparison, the true Pareto front achieved by SEAWAT-NSGA-II (black triangles in Fig. 8 ) is considered as reference and compared with those from machine learning surrogate based frameworks. The majority of solutions obtained by ANN-NSGA-II (red circles in Fig. 8 ) and GP-NSGA-II (blue squares in Fig. 8 ) are equally optimal in quality compared against those obtained by SEAWAT-NSGA-II. The two cases exhibit a good job in achieving convergence with extremely high computing efficiency. They can effectively cover the region with total extraction and injection rates from 1.1 cm3 /s to 1.9 cm3 /s. Table 3   summarizes statistical results of IGD and HV obtained by all comparable algorithms. Among the three machine learning based optimization algorithms, GP-NSGA-II shows the best performance, implying that GP-NSGA-II can obtain promising solutions with limited numbers of function executions. However, the average quality of Pareto optimal solutions from RSR-NSGA-II (green diamonds in Fig. 8 ) is not equally superior. It cannot well capture the region with the total extraction and injection rate below 1.14 cm3 /s and above 1.72 cm3 /s. Especially at the later stage, the Pareto front of RSR-NSGA-II is deviated from the true Pareto front, as marked in the shaded area of Fig. 8 . The failure is because the RSR model developed in an off-line way may miss the locally important region and cannot well represent the entire decision space. Since the presence of the constraints complicates exploration of the optimal search space, any poor predictions would have adverse effect on the optimality. According to the previous results, the one-shot trained RSR model at M6 performs inferior relative to others and might increase risk to false optima. To overcome this type of imprecision issue, it is worthwhile finding ways to improve the search procedure and ensure convergence towards the true Pareto front.  4.3 Advancement of adaptive training algorithm As mentioned above, the one-shot trained RSR surrogate model suffers from potential inaccuracy for evaluating objective and constraint functions, which may induce infeasible solutions. Instead, this study retrains the RSR model by adding new data from an approximate Pareto set of each iteration, and then adaptively alleviates error accumulation of the one-shot trained model. Practically, the Pareto front derived from adaptive-RSR-NSGA-II (see red dots in Fig. 9  a) exhibits the best-known approximation of the true Pareto front. Meanwhile, the proposed method generates a more diverse Pareto front than that from ANN-NSGA-II, GP-NSGA-II. Embedding the adaptive surrogate model within optimization helps the algorithm escape from possible divergence or local optima. This stands on the fact that more valuable samples are provided by possible optimal solutions. These samples enhance prediction ability of the RSR model to attain higher fidelity level. Not surprisingly, the extent of improvement becomes progressively less obvious at a later period of evolutionary search when sufficient samples are generated for retraining the surrogate model. The above analysis indicates adaptive machine learning surrogate based multiobjective optimization has potential and effectiveness in resolving coastal groundwater dynamic management problems. To measure performance of the improved adaptive algorithm, an IGD metric in Eq. (10)  and a HV metric in Eq. (11)  are quantified. Fig. 9 b describes evolutions of the approximate solution quality from different frameworks over the number of generations. With regard to the IGD metric, three cases (RSR-NSGA-II, SEAWAT-NSGA-II and adaptive-RSR-NSGA-II) reach almost same convergence speed during initial generations. Afterwards, adaptive-RSR-NSGA-II converges faster after 10 generations and reaches an approximate speed of SEAWAT-NSGA-II during the middle generations, while the non-adaptive RSR-NSGA-II case is slightly slower. With respect to HV, convergence of adaptive-RSR-NSGA-II surpasses one-shot RSR-NSGA-II with higher HV values. Overall, the two metrics support the view that adaptive-RSR-NSGA-II can achieve better convergence and more diverse solutions than those from non-adaptive RSR-NSGA-II due to adaptive training. With regard to computing budget (see Table 4  ), the SEAWAT-NSGA-II requires 52.98 h, consuming 15,100 SEAWAT model runs for function evaluations on a desktop PC equipped with a 2.5 GHz Intel i7 processor and 16 GB of RAM. By contrast, offline surrogate based optimization requires 2.23 h with 400 SEAWAT model runs for data generation. The number of calls to SEAWAT models is reduced by 97.4 %. The adaptive-RSR-NSGA-II takes about 2.44 h to get the best-known non-dominant solutions since the RSR model needs to be adaptively retrained during optimization. We can confirm that using surrogate based method achieves substantial computational saving up to 95 %. Particularly, adaptive surrogate based evolutionary algorithms ensures the reliability of solutions while maintaining computational efficiency. This is especially appealing to large-scale groundwater remediation designs involved with numerically complicated simulation models.  4.4 Verification of residual saltwater scavenging effect Once Pareto optimal extraction and injection rates were identified, they should be verified via the SEAWAT model. Fig. 10   shows distribution of chloride concentration and velocity field through the SEAWAT model at the end of remediation period, where A, B and C represent three strategies in Fig. 8 . Also, Fig. 10 d depicts leading edges of chloride concentration with 50 % isolines, namely 17.5 g/L. The total extraction and injection rates of the three typical remediation strategies in Fig. 8  are 1.921 cm3 /s, 1.518 cm3 /s and 1.223 cm3 /s, respectively. Detailed optimal extraction-injection schedules during the remediation period are illustrated in Fig. 11  . In the absence of any remediation design, the initial saltwater plume is previously illustrated in Fig. 1 b, with a saltwater wedge toe location at 59 cm away from the coastline (baseline case). Once installing a subsurface dam, residual saltwater starts to retreat seaward in a very slow speed, and additional hydraulic control strategies would accelerate scavenging of residual saltwater (Yin et al., 2023 ). Especially, the salt plume is remarkably retreated with implementation of the optimal strategies. Compared to an initial baseline case, desalination effect using Strategy A performs much better in terms of the saltwater wedge toe location and salinity mass. The length of the saltwater wedge is decreased by 44.9 % while the salinity mass is reduced up to 54.4 %. Also, the area of saltwater intrusion surrounded by 50 % isolines is more narrowed using Strategy A. From this perspective, seawater intrusion could be more alleviated with extracting more saltwater and inject more freshwater. The Pareto fronts provide a wide spread of solutions for decision makers. Groundwater managers can select a prescribed solution to implement based on comprehensive economic and environmental benefits. There are tradeoffs between the two conflicting objectives which render the fronts to be convex. In general, there is an overall opposite trend between two objectives, meaning that any improvement in one objective requires a corresponding decline in the other objective. For example, if groundwater managers aim to remove more residual saltwater behind the subsurface dam, they must allow more saltwater extraction and freshwater injection.   5 Conclusions Data-driven machine learning approaches are promising to substitute expensive-cost groundwater numerical models within optimization. However, error of forecasting may be accumulated and cause adverse effect on the optimization reliability and accuracy. In this study, a novel adaptive machine learning surrogate multiobjective optimization method was proposed for seeking optimal strategies of aquifer desalination. The new method can improve the fitting accuracy of surrogate models to simulation models without significantly increasing the number of samples. Besides, the applicability and effectiveness of the new method were demonstrated through coastal groundwater remediation design, where a subsurface dam combined with saltwater extraction and freshwater injection was utilized to remove residual saltwater. Main conclusions from the study are drawn as follows:1. The majority of one-shot trained machine learning models can accurately capture underlying functional relationships among original model outputs and inputs within regions of interest, which render predicted chloride concentration or salinity mass to agree well with those from the SEAWAT simulation model. However, some specific ML models (such as the RSR model in the study) may accumulate prediction errors and miss certain areas in the original response surface, leading to a decrease in the reliability of the Pareto solutions.  2. The IGD and HV indicate that the adaptive training algorithm can remarkably enhance the search capability using valuable samples from iterations. Embedding the adaptive RSR model into optimization exhibits best-known approximation of the true Pareto front, and ensures the algorithm to escape from possible divergence, which is better than the quality of solutions gained by non-adaptive RSR-NSGA-II.  3. A wide spread of Pareto optimal extraction-injection schedules are derived for groundwater managers based on availability of groundwater resources and environmental impacts. The solutions are found equally optimal in quality compared with those from SEAWAT-NSGA-II while achieving substantial computational saving up to 95 %. The high computing efficiency is attributed to the significantly reduced number of original model evaluations that consume most time.  4. With implementation of the obtained nondominated strategies, seawater intrusion could be more effectively alleviated using a subsurface dam in conjunction with saltwater extraction and freshwater injection. Also, the choice of a dual well system can be quite favorable in achieving the goal of rapidly scavenging residual saltwater remained upstream behind a subsurface dam.    Although the proposed method can achieve desirable accuracy with greatly enhanced computing efficiency, multiple complex physical and chemical processes could generate more sophisticated seawater intrusion models with complicated response relationships. Such complicated response relationships probably result in inaccuracy of surrogates or inapplicability of proposed algorithm. Future research needs to demonstrate practicability in field-scale optimization design with consideration of more conflicting objectives. In addition, coastal aquifer management should not only consider controlling seawater intrusion, but also removing land-sourced pollutants. While being tested and applied to remove saltwater and reduce salinization in a coastal aquifer, the methodology is highly applicable to the regions with abundant land-sourced pollutants.
1 Introduction In the context to the response of aquifer systems to seismic perturbations, the aquifer and confining layer such as clay are often considered hydraulically independent. This assumption ignores the hydraulic interplay between the two compartments but conveniently focuses on analyzing the hydraulic responses of the aquifer induced by earthquakes. However, this may not be a fully accurate assumption, considering that clay layers, despite their low permeability properties, might not be completely impermeable (Zhou et al. 2008; Gimmi and Churakov 2019; Yoshikawa et al. 2016 ). For instance, in the context of carbon dioxide storage and oil/gas production, one significant concern is water infiltrating into the confining clay layer because of increasing fluid pressure in the target layer (Aminu et al. 2017; Karpiński and Szkodo 2015 ). However, although seismic perturbations have also been shown to generate significant excess pore pressures in aquifers (Wang et al. 2001; Cox et al. 2012; Liao et al. 2021 ), few studies have investigated the potential for seismically-induced water flow from aquifers into confining clay layers. Groundwater flow into confining clays implies vertical flow behavior following earthquakes. Current interpretations for seismically-induced cross-formation vertical groundwater flow and subsequent hydraulic responses are mainly based on two models, i.e., (1) vertical flow in unconfined aquifers (Mohr et al. 2015; Mohr et al. 2017; Breen et al. 2020; Wang et al. 2004; Rojstaczer et al. 1995 ) and (2) vertical flow in leaky aquifers (Wang et al. 2016; Shi and Wang 2016; Yang et al. 2021 ). A conceptual graph of these two models is illustrated in Fig. 1  . In the first model, it is assumed that in homogeneous unconfined aquifers groundwater flows vertically between the phreatic and vadose zones. In the second model, the behavior of seismically-induced vertical flow crossing aquitards essentially follows the assumptions of the analytical solution of Hantush and Jacob (Hantush and Jacob 1955 ), i.e., the aquitard is permeable only in vertical direction and its storage capability can be neglected. Ignoring the storage capacity of the aquitard implies that water can flow through the aquitard immediately without any interaction. In fact, the clay layers exhibit both sealing properties and possess permeability and water storage capacity (Gimmi and Churakov 2019; Liu and Birkholzer 2012; Liu et al. 2012 ). However, the absence of the clay layer or the neglected water storage capacity of the clay layer in the above models make both of them cannot deal with the issue of the hydraulic interplay between aquifer and clay layer caused by earthquakes and the resulting hydraulic responses. Neglecting groundwater flow into clay or the effect of the hydraulic properties of the clay may lead to incomplete analysis of the seismically-induced hydraulic response of the aquifer system. Furthermore, for clay layers, the inflow of additional water could possibly generate excess pore pressure in clay pores, and the effective stress (total stress minus pore water pressure) decreases, reducing the strength of the clays (Andersen et al. 1980; Yasuhara 1995 ). Consequently, the clay layer will become more shear-sensitive and prone to failure during earthquakes. Once the clay layer is damaged, its ability to confine groundwater is compromised, which in turn affects the hydraulic response of the aquifer to seismic events. Additionally, there are potential implications for the integrity of subsurface storage (produced water, CO2 , H2 ) and surface engineering projects. Thus, it is also important to consider the impact of water inflow induced by earthquakes on the pressure evolution within the clay layer. Here, we aim at the investigation of the mechanism of seismically-induced water flow into clays and the resulting hydraulic responses employing experimental and numerical simulation methods. The experiments consist of subjecting representative aquifer-clay systems (sand-box) to controlled shaking monitoring the corresponding water level and pore pressure changes. The experimental observations assist in understanding and characterizing the hydraulic response of the aquifer-clay system. Then, a numerical model is being developed to quantitatively investigate pore pressure evolution in the aquifer-clay system due to shaking-induced water flow into the clay considering the multi-factorial effects. The numerical simulations allow us to model and analyze the complex flow behavior in a heterogenous soil system, as well as the influence of varying hydraulic properties of different soil layers. By improving our understanding of the phenomenon of water flow into confining clays, we contribute to a better assessment of the hydraulic response of aquifer-clay systems and a better understanding of the role of hydromechanical processes in clay layers initiated by earthquakes.  2 Experimental setup and procedure The experimental setup of this study was designed based on the understanding we gained from our previous work (Gu et al. 2021 ). Compared to previous experimental apparatus, we improved the model box to achieve better aquifer confinement (see Fig. S1  and related notes in the supporting information  for model box improvements). Also, the purpose of the present study is more specific than before, mainly to investigate the seismically-induced groundwater flow into the clay layer, as well as related hydraulic responses. Therefore, modifications were made to the experimental conditions and procedures, as described later in this section.
