In this study, we designed a physical model representing a confined aquifer system consisting of saturated unconsolidated sand, overlying saturated clays and monitoring wells. Data acquisition sensors (a pressure sensor, accelerometers and water level meters) were installed in both the sand layer and wells to monitor the hydro-mechanical behavior of the system during the experiment. To establish initial hydraulic conditions, we implemented an external water injection system. This system ascertained controlled inflow of water into the sand layer after filling the model box to achieve the desired pressure head. A shaking table was employed to impose dynamic loading to the physical sand box. The shaking table can move controlled and vibrates in a single horizontal direction (x or y direction). Maximum displacement of the table is ± 0.20 m in the x- direction and ± 0.15 m in the y- direction. Fig. 2   presents a schematic view of the experimental setup. 2.1 Physical model and measurements As shown in Fig. 2  the physical sand box model used in the experiment measures 2.0 × 1.0 × 1.3 m3 . It was constructed using rigid and high-strength steel materials to ensure stability and resistance against deformation under dynamic loading conditions and internal pressure. The walls of the model box could be considered as the impermeable boundaries. Within the model box, three monitoring wells were pre-installed. These two-meter-high wells had a screen length of 0.8 m at the bottom and radius of 0.05 m. Water levels in three wells were recorded using the piezometric sensors (Solinist Levelogger 5) with a resolution of 2.5 × 10-3  m and a sampling rate of 8 samples/s. The model box was filled with uniform sand, with an average grain diameter of 0.45 mm up to a thickness of 0.8 m, matching the length of the well screens. This allowed water to enter the wells through the entire thickness of the sand layer. To fill the sand, fill the water in the tank first and then place the sand under water to ensure that the sand layer was fully saturated. During the sand filling process, multiple data sensors were placed within the sand layer. Near the screen of well No. 2, three accelerometers (Boyuan 941B, resolution: 5 × 10-6  m/s2 , sampling rate: 256 samples/s) and a pore pressure sensor (HRCT HC-25, accuracy: 0.04 kPa, sampling rate: 256 samples/s) were installed. The accelerometers were positioned at levels of 0 cm, 40 cm, and 80 cm measured from the bottom. The pore pressure sensor was placed within the sand layer 40 cm above the bottom. A layer of clay, with a thickness of 0.5 m, was placed on top of the sand layer. Both the sand and clay layers were carefully filled to achieve the desired thickness and homogeneity for the experiment. The wet densities of the sand layer and the clay layer were 2.3 g/cm3  and 1.857 g/cm3 , respectively.  2.2 The hydraulic conditions After placing the sand and clay layer in the model box, hydraulic boundary conditions were set by two water tanks either side unit with a constant head at 1.1 m (as shown in Fig. 2 ). To achieve the initial hydraulic conditions, we used an external water supply unit to inject water into the sand layer to increase the pressure head as follows:(1) The external water inlet, as well as the two air vents on the water tanks, and the influent switch were opened. The two vents were set up to check the saturated condition of the sand layer. After the water injection was started, water escaped at both air vents, proving that the sand layer was saturated. At this point, both air vents were closed, and water injection continued to increase the pressure head within the sand layer.  (2) The water level data in the wells were monitored continuously using piezometric water level meters. When the water levels in all three wells reached 1.1 m, we assumed the sand layer to be fully saturated and confined with a pressure head of 1.1 m. At this stage, the influent switch on the model box, as well as the water inlet, were turned off. So far, the water injection was completed and the water injection unit was then removed.    This process ensured that the sand layer in the model box was fully saturated and confined at a defined pressure head before the experiments were conducted. Given that water in the aquifer cannot freely drain or dissipate during earthquakes, our experiments were conducted for undrained conditions. This involved to keep on both water tanks the inlet and outlet valves closed throughout the experiment. By maintaining these undrained conditions, we were able to create a more realistic representation of the seismically-induced mechanical behavior of soil and water in aquifers.  2.3 Experimental implementation After ensuring steady state hydraulic conditions, we started the shaking table to a pre-shake for ∼ 60 s. This pre-shaking was designed to assist in displacing trapped gas and consolidate the aquifer material. Afterwards, we allowed the sand box model to settle for ca. 12 h. This settling period allowed the system to equilibrate (e.g., temperature stabilization, redistribution of the sand particles, re-establishment of the water table, and removal of any residual gas bubbles). Prior to the start of the experiment, we observed that there was no water leakage or uncontrolled infiltration visible at the surface of the clay layer, indicating that it was intact and ascertained confinement. Then, we proceeded with the actual experiment and data recording. The dynamic loading scheme for our experiment was to impose sinusoidal waves on the physical model four times through the shaking table. The sinusoidal wave frequency of all four shock inputs was 0.5 Hz, the input acceleration of shocks S1-S3 was 0.1 g, and the input acceleration of shock S4 was 0.06 g (g denotes the acceleration of gravity, 1 g= ∼9.8 m/s2 ). The duration of the four shocks was 66, 63, 63 and 64 s respectively. Peak accelerations used in the analyses were recorded by the accelerometer in the intermediate sand layer (A2 in Fig. 2 ), considering the reflection effect of the waves by the rigid model box and the superposition of the waves. The acceleration waveforms recorded by A2 and the results of spectral analysis are shown in Fig. 3  . It can be found that the main frequency of all waves is 0.5 Hz, consistent with the input. After each loading cycle, the physical model was allowed to settle for ∼ 3 h before the subsequent loading sequence. The characteristics of the dynamic loading conditions are summarized in Table 1  .   3 Experimental results and discussion 3.1 Pore pressure and water level responses to shaking Pore pressure recorded by the pressure sensor in the sand layer and the water level obtained from well No.2 are displayed in Fig. 4  . Shocks S1, S2, and S3 caused co-shaking step-like pressure increases followed by post-shaking pore pressure dissipation. The generated excess pore pressure values for shocks S1, S2, and S3 were 0.55 kPa, 0.07 kPa, and 0.28 kPa, respectively. After the shaking events pore pressures gradually decreased by 0.27 kPa, 0.06 kPa, and 0.25 kPa over a period of ca. 3 h, respectively. In contrast, shock S4 did not cause a significant increase in pore pressure, instead pore pressure continued to decline to −0.30 kPa following the trend already observed after shock S3. With respect to the water level responses, three types of change patterns were observed. Shock S1 resulted in co-shaking step rise followed by a gradual decrease after shaking. Shocks S2 and S3 caused a step drop-rise pattern in water level during the shakings, followed by a gradual decrease after shakings; while shock 4 did not generate the significant response in water level, instead, the water level consistently decreased with time. For the amplitude of water level changes, the co-shaking water level rises due to the four shocks were 3.81 cm, 0.55 cm, 2.14 cm, and ∼ 0 cm, respectively. In the post-shaking stages, the water level gradually decreased by 2.99 cm, 2.69 cm, 1.71 cm, and 1.33 cm after the four shocks, respectively. Our experiment results of water level changes corroborate with many previous field observations in porous media aquifers on alluvial plains, e.g. Wang et al. (2001), Cox et al. (2012) . However, most of these past field researches focused solely on seismically-induced water level changes due to the challenges associated with pore pressure measurements in the field. Our detailed records of both the pore pressure and water level, and their clear correspondence, helps to enhance the understanding of the relationship between both aspects in the aquifer following earthquakes. This provides an important basis for analyzing the mechanisms of seismically-induced water level changes.  3.2 Mechanisms for pore pressure and water level responses 3.2.1 Co-shaking pore pressure and water level changes The co-seismic water level responses reflect the stress–strain process of the aquifer under dynamic stress perturbations. A shear strain amplitude of 10-4  is tested as the critical threshold for irreversible plastic deformation and excess pore pressure generation in aquifers subjected to dynamic loading (Dobry et al. 1982 ). And the shear strain of a sand layer can be deduced from the history of horizontal acceleration as in Eq. (1)  (Zeghal and Elgamal 1994 ),(1) γ z i     = u i + 1   - u i    z i  - z i - 1    z i + 1   - z i    + u i  - u i - 1      z i + 1   - z i   z i  - z i - 1        / ( z i + 1   - z i - 1   )      Here the ui  is displacement history obtained by integrating twice the acceleration, then based on the displacements ui+1 , ui  and ui-1  of the three adjacent accelerometers in the saturated sand, the shear strain at depth zi  can be calculated. By applying Eq. (1) , the peak shear strain induced by the four shocks in this experiment were determined as 4.01 × 10−4 , 2.18 × 10−4 , 4.23 × 10−4 , and 2.36 × 10−5 , respectively. It can be found that the strain levels from shocks S1, S2, and S3 surpassed the critical threshold for irreversible plastic deformation, whereas shock S4 did not (Fig. 5  ). Therefore, we attribute the co-shaking water level step-rises to the sand layer undrained consolidation. When an earthquake occurs, the seismic stresses cause the soil particles in the unconsolidated aquifer to undergo rapid compression. As the soil particles are compressed, they come into closer contact with each other. The increased contact between soil particles hinders the drainage of water from the pore spaces, leading to trapped water and the development of excess pore pressure. The excess pore pressure leads to a synchronous rise in the water level in the observation wells during the earthquake due to the limited drainage escape routes. The strain generated by shocks S1, S2, and S3 exceeded the consolidation threshold of the sand, leading to step-rise in pore pressure and water level. However, shock S4 did not reach the consolidation threshold, resulting in no significant response in pore pressure or water level during the shaking. Additionally, shocks S2 and S3 also caused a minor drop in water level before the rise, which we attribute to a transient shear expansion of the sand layer, similar to what we observed in a previous experiment (Gu et al. 2021 ). The undrained consolidation is the predominant mechanism to explain the step rise in water level due to earthquakes in unconsolidated aquifers (Wang et al. 2001; Cox et al. 2012; Liao et al. 2021 ), and here we managed to find evidence for this particular mechanism. Measurement at the experimental site also provides evidence of sand consolidation, because the surface of the clay/sand contact settled by an average of approximately 3.5 cm averaged for the entire experiment. Assuming the clay layer and sand grains to be incompressible, the observed settlement of the sand layer by 3.5 cm, along with the dimensions of the physical model, enables us to estimate a decrease in porosity of approximately 4 % in the sand layer following the experiment. Notably, the calculated porosity reduction is larger than the theoretical value of 0.1 % to 0.01 % calculated by Wang et al. (2001)  for a porosity decrease in a Taiwanese alluvial fan after the Chi-Chi earthquake. We hypothesize that the discrepancy between the experimentally calculated porosity reductions and that obtained from field studies may arise from the physical model dimensions and bounded walls. Unlike in an infinitely extended field aquifer, the boundaries of the experimental model are constrained and reflect the dynamic stress-induced particle rolling, resulting in more pronounced consolidation and in a larger decrease in porosity.  3.2.2 Post-shaking pore pressure and water level changes The post-seismic water level changes reveal the mechanism of the dissipation of the co-seismic hydrological perturbations (Wang et al. 2004 ) and may reflect the distinct groundwater flow patterns after shaking. In all scenarios, the water levels in well No.2 showed sustained declines after the shaking experiments. We further examine the final water levels of the three wells at the end of entire experiment. We notice that the water levels in wells No.1, No.2, and No.3 decreased by 2.3 cm, 4.3 cm, and 3.1 cm, respectively, compared to the initial conditions (see Fig. S2  in supporting information ). The final water levels in all three wells were lower than the initial water levels implying that the sustained post-shaking declines resulted in water volume reduction in the sand layer. Given that our model is well-sealed under undrained flow condition, a mechanism is needed to explain the post-shaking water flow behavior and the movement of water in the sand layer. With lateral water flow experimentally restricted after the shakings, we infer that the pore water of sand layer flow upward into the clay layer as a potential mechanism causing the decline in water level. As stated in the introduction, the consolidation-generated excess pore pressure in the sand layer may force water to flow across the sand-clay interface and produce the hydraulic interactions with the overlying clays. Moreover, the clay minerals have a high affinity for water, potentially storing water flowing into the clay layer. In the absence of other recharge sources, this vertical flow can reduce the water content in the sand layer, leading to a post-shaking decrease in pore pressure in the sand layer and eventually a decrease in the water level in the observation well.   3.3 Limitations of experimental study This experimental study provides evidence for the relevant processes during the undrained consolidation of an aquifer system, thus elucidating the dominant hydromechanical mechanisms. Subsequently, while post-shaking water flow into the clay layer has been identified based on water level drops in well, this explanation remains qualitative and requires more evidence for support. For example, pressure changes in the clay layer to demonstrate water flow into the clays, were not recorded in our experiments. Another difficulty of the experimental study for post-seismic hydrological response is that the experimental results are conducted under a specific condition, whereas at field scale, post-seismic groundwater flow is usually affected by a variety of influencing factors, resulting in different and sometimes contradictory types of post-seismic hydrological responses (Wang et al., 2004 ). Therefore, it may not be possible to find the respective counterpart process in the field to validate the experimental results. Instead, in the following, we employ numerical modelling techniques to further investigate the mechanism of shaking-induced water flowing into the clay layer. Numerical methods can effectively investigate complex groundwater flow processes in heterogeneous soils, allowing us to quantitatively examine shaking-induced water flow into the clay layer and analyze the evolution of pore pressures in clay and sand layers, as well as to assess the influence of multiple factors on this process.   4 Numerical simulation and discussion 4.1 Model setup A two-dimensional finite element model is developed using the COMSOL Multiphysics 6.1 program (Fig. 6  ). The model is divided into two layers, the lower layer is considered to be a saturated sand layer and the upper layer is defined as saturated clay layer, representing the materials used in the experiment. In our numerical model the observation wells are not considered as a separate entity due to the complex nature of borehole effects and flow regime changes adjacent to the observation well. We analyze the hydraulic behavior of the model through changes in pressure in the sand and clay layers. 4.1.1 Governing equations The numerical model incorporates the dimensions of the experimental setup, where L represents the width of the setup, Ds  represents the thickness of the sand layer, and Dc  represents the thickness of the confining clay layer. Water flow in sand and clay layers follow Darcy’s law formulated as,(2) S ss   ∂ h s  x , t     ∂ t   = ∇ ∙ K s  ∇ h s  x , t       + q     (3) S sc   ∂ h c  x , t     ∂ t   = ∇ ∙ K c  ∇ h c  x , t       + q     where Sss  and Ks  are the specific storage and hydraulic conductivity of sand, respectively; hs (x, t) is the transient groundwater head of sand layer. Ssc  and Kc  are the specific storage and hydraulic conductivity of clay, respectively; hc (x, t) is the transient groundwater head of clay layer. ∇ is a vector of spatial coordinates and q is the hydraulic source term. The geometric and empirical hydraulic parameters (Fetter and Kreamer 2021; Carsel and Parrish 1988; Domenico and Mifflin 1965 ) used in the the model are listed in Table 2  .  4.1.2 Initial and boundary conditions The bottom boundaries are defined differently in the co-shaking and post-shaking simulation scenarios. In the co-shaking stage (1–60 s), to apply a pressure perturbation through the bottom, Γ1  is defined as the pressure boundary with a pressure step function as,p = ρghs (x, t) + pstep (t)  on Γ1  (4)   where pstep (t) denotes the pressure step function, which can be invoked from COMSOL with customized amplitude and duration, as shown in Fig. 6 . In the post-shaking stage (after 60 s), the bottom boundary (Γ1) is defined as a no-flow boundary. A pressure continuity condition is assigned at the sand-clay interface (Γ4 ) to couple the flow between the sand and clay layers as,hs  (x, t)  = hc  (x, t)  on Γ4  (5)    For the other boundaries, all are defined as no-flow boundaries according to the experimental conditions.   4.2 Model verification and interpretation under experimental conditions First, we test model performance by comparing the experimentally recorded and numerically simulated pore pressure evolutions in the sand layer. Four pressure perturbations are applied on the bottom boundary (Γ1 in Fig. 6 ) with the same magnitudes as the pressure changes due to the four shocks in the experiment. To capture the pressure change in the sand layer, an observation point (Obs 1 in Fig. 6 ) is arranged, which matches the location of the pressure sensor in the experimental setup. Fig. 7   shows numerical simulations of pore pressure changes against the experimental records, proving the reliability of our numerical model. The numerical simulation reveals the dynamics of pore pressure within the clay layer. As depicted in Fig. 8  , at the observation point in the clay layer (Obs 2 in Fig. 6 ), the pore pressures remain relatively stable during the shaking process (0- ca. 60 s) and early post-shaking stage (before ca.1000 s). This reflects the clay material's effective sealing property, which impedes the transient vertical pressure transmission developed in the underlying sand layer. Following that (after ca.1000 s), gradual increases in the pore pressures of the clay layer are observed. The pore pressures eventually augment by 90 Pa, 24 Pa, 51 Pa, and 52 Pa in the four given scenarios. These findings quantitatively support our hypothesis that the excess pore pressure generated by the shaking forces the water upwards from the sand layer into the confining clay layer, thereby reducing sand layer's pore pressure and increasing clay layer's pore pressure.  4.3 Sensitivity analysis and model application The numerical simulation results under experimental conditions have validated the model's performance, demonstrating the behavior of water flowing from the aquifer to the confining clay layer due to shakings. Further, we aim to apply this model to test the mechanism of seismically-induced groundwater flow into confining clays under field conditions, and evaluate the sensitivity of the primary influencing factors in this process. Accordingly, we introduce the following modifications to our model: (1) we incorporate a flow system within the model to simulate field seepage conditions. The aquifer is postulated as homogeneous isotropic and laterally unbounded. The left and right boundaries of the sand layer (Γ2 and Γ3 in Fig. 6 ) are adjusted to incorporate fixed head boundary conditions at an infinite horizon. These conditions are based on a subsequently determined average hydraulic gradient (0.001), derived from the specified fixed head values. The remaining boundary conditions are left at default settings. (2) At the field scale, earthquake can cause significant increases in water level, sometimes reaching several meters (Wang et al. 2001; Wang and Chia 2008; Weaver et al. 2019; Cox et al. 2012 ). Should the head loss effect at the observation well be neglected, a several-meter rise in water level is equivalent to an increase in pressure of the order of tens of kilopascal in the sediments. Therefore, in the scenario investigating the response of the drained aquifer system to seismic perturbation, we imposed a pressure perturbation of 20 kPa. (3) The simulation of post-shaking stage is allowed to run long enough (24 h) that the system can reach a quasi-steady state after shaking. Considering the permeability of the groundwater system are the factors that dominate groundwater flow and the dissipation of hydrologic perturbations in natural system (Wang et al. 2004 ), the effects of the sand layer hydraulic conductivity (Ks ) and clay layer hydraulic conductivity (Kc ) on pore pressure evolutions in the sand and clay layers due to shaking-induced water flowing into the clay layer under drained conditions are examined in our numerical model. The values of Ks  and Kc  are adopted from the range of empirical parameters of hydraulic conductivities for sands and clays, with Ks  being 10-3 , 10-4 , and 10-5  m/s, and Kc  being 10-8 , 10-9 , and 10-10  m/s in the tests. The other physical and hydraulic parameters of the model adopt the default settings as shown in Table 2 . Fig. 9   shows the shaking-induced pore pressure changes in both sand and clay layers under drained conditions. We find that the pore pressure change in the sand layer is mainly affected by Ks , while it is not sensitive to Kc . With increasing Ks , the co-shaking rise amplitude and the post-shaking dissipation rate of the pore pressure in sand layer increases. This suggests that horizontal water flow dominates the post-shaking pore pressure dissipation in the sand layer for drained conditions. The evolution in post-shaking pore pressure in the clay layer is influenced by the joint effects of Kc  and Ks . Fig. 10   further examines the post-shaking peak pore pressure changes in the clay layer for different scenarios, referred to as Pp . When Kc  takes on a relatively small value (10-10  m/s), no significant pore pressure changes are detected (Pp = ∼0) in all related scenarios. This is due to the low permeability of the clay layer which acts as a hydraulic barrier, preventing water flow from the sand layer. As Kc  increases, water from the sand layer can flow into the clay layer after shaking, leading to the manifestation of the effects of Ks . When Kc  = 10-9  m/s, the decreasing Ks  leads to larger values of Pp  in the clay layer. This is linked to the low permeability of the sand layer that blocks lateral pressure dissipation and forces excess pore water to flow into the lower pressure clay layer. If Kc  rises to 10-8  m/s, all considered scenarios display an increase and subsequent decrease in pore pressure (see Fig. 9 ), with a higher Pp  compared to Kc  at 10-9  m/s (see Fig. 10 ). This is attributed to the higher Kc  facilitating more free water flow through the clay layer, causing an initial rise and subsequent drop in pore pressure after shaking. It is noted that when Kc  of the sand-clay system is relatively large (10-8  m/s) and the Ks  is relatively small (10-5  m/s), shaking-induced water flow into the clay layer is slowed down for an extended period with the consequence of a persistent excess pore pressure in the clay layer (see Fig. 9 ). At the field scale, the alteration of seismically-induced groundwater flow may be influenced by a combination of one or several of these factors, resulting in distinct hydraulic responses. Neglecting the behavior of seismically-induced groundwater flow into clays may lead to inaccurate analysis of the hydraulic responses, especially for aquifers with low permeability or where lateral flow is blocked after the earthquake. On the other hand, the effect of seismically-induced water flow into clay layers can have significant consequences for their geomechanical stability. When water infiltrates the clay matrix, it leads to changes in its properties. The influx of water may cause fine fissures in a clay layer to expand and increase in volume (Nachum et al. 2020 ). This expansion can lead to a decrease in shear strength, which can further deteriorate the stability of clay particles during earthquakes (Xie et al. 2023 ). It has also been demonstrated that the crack may propagate in clay with increasing water content (Zhang and Song 2023 ). Given the potential consequences of clay layer rupture, including risks of contaminant leakage and the adverse effects on the stability of surface constructions, accurate assessment of seismically-induced water flow into clay layers is also of practical importance.   5 Conclusion In this study, we combine experimental and numerical simulation methods to investigate the mechanism of seismically-induced water flow into confining clay layers. The following conclusions are obtained: Through experimental study, we quantitatively demonstrate that shaking causes undrained consolidation of loose saturated sands, resulting in measurable sand settlement, generation of excess pore pressure within the sand layer, and co-shaking water level step-like rise in well. Moreover, through the sustained post-shaking water level drop under undrained experimental conditions, we identify that water in the sand layer may flow upward into the clay layer driven by shaking-induced excess pore pressure. We further develop a numerical model to quantitatively examine the mechanism of shaking-induced water flow into overlying clays. The numerical results under experimental conditions indicate that shaking leads to water flow from the aquifer into the clay layer which, in turn, affects the pressure changes in both layers. We proceed to extend the numerical model to natural seepage conditions. We evaluate the effects of the permeability of the sand and clay layers on the evolution of the pore pressures in the sand and clay layers due to seismically-induced water flow into the clay layer. The results show that the pore pressure change in the sand layer is primarily affected by the hydraulic conductivity of the sand, while the post-shaking pore pressure change in the clay layer is influenced by the combined effect of hydraulic conductivities of both layers. In general, elevated sand layer hydraulic conductivity prompts the excess pore pressure lateral dissipation after shaking, decreasing pore water flux into the clay layer; while elevated clay layer’s hydraulic conductivity facilitates the water flowing into the clay layer, leading to the greater pore pressure changes in the clay layer. In conclusion, our research introduces a novel mechanism regarding the seismically-induced hydraulic interplay between the aquifer and the confining clay layer. This mechanism is quantitatively verified and evaluated using a combined approach of experimental studies and numerical simulations. The findings, on the one hand, provide a more precise framework for analyzing the hydrological response induced by earthquakes at the field scale. On the other hand, they offer useful insights for assessing the stability of the confined aquifer system following earthquakes.
1 Introduction Due to climate warming and rapid urbanization, the rate of water circulation has accelerated and the stability of the water circulation system has decreased (Sun et al., 2015; McColl et al., 2022 ), resulting in uneven spatiotemporal distribution of water resources and increase in frequencies of extreme climate and/or hydrological events in regions and even globally (Cui et al., 2022; Chagas et al., 2022 ). Human society is facing the serious impact of increasingly frequent extreme weather and hydrological events such as droughts and floods (Stuart-Smith et al., 2021 ). According to global climate-related disaster statistics released by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) in 2015, floods events accounted for 43 % of disaster from 1995 to 2015, affecting 2.3 billion people worldwide. In the past three decades, 37 % of the European Union’s territory has suffered serious drought, affecting more than 100 million people and causing a series of socio-economic losses and ecosystem damage (Gudmundsson and Seneviratne, 2016 ). In addition, the 24 drought events that occurred in the United States from 1980 to 2017 resulted in nearly 3000 deaths and a total economic loss of $232.5 billion (Smith, 2018 ). Therefore, the Intergovernmental Hydrological Program (IHP) has specifically developed a strategic plan with the theme of Water Security: Responses to local, regional, and global challenges (IHP-VIII, 2014–2021) to address the increasing water security issues caused by extreme meteorological and hydrological events (Donoso et al., 2012 ). Abnormal changes in precipitation are the main cause of flood and drought disasters (Nakayama and Shankman, 2013 ), especially changes in precipitation patterns or fluctuations in intensity, which often lead to the extreme hydrological events (Zhang and Wang, 2007 ). Drought-flood alternation (DFA) event is sub-seasonal precipitation anomaly, which can lead to a compound disaster, with droughts and floods occurring successively and experiencing a transition from drought to flood or from flood to drought (Wu et al., 2006; Shen et al., 2012 ). Therefore, DFA event has a more serious impact and damage on agricultural production, ecology and environment (He and Sheffield, 2020; Chen et al., 2020a; Handwerger et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022; Qiao et al., 2022b; Wang et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023 ). More importantly, many observations since 2000 have confirmed that frequency and intensity of extreme precipitation and DFA events were increasing in many regions (IPCC, 2014 ). Fully recognizing the spatiotemporal patterns and changing characteristics of DFA is essential for establishing appropriate and innovative disaster reduction strategies (Ji et al., 2018 ), and also is an important part of disaster prevention in the context of global warming (Li et al., 2017a ). DFA event is common worldwide and has gained extensive attention from the governments, the public and scholars, and numerous studies regarding DFA have been conducted in the last decade (Yoon et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020a; Shi et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2021; Qiao et al., 2022a,b; Jiang et al., 2023 ). For instance, Wu et al. (2006)  and Shan et al. (2018)  suggested a quantitative indicator to identify DFA events in the Yangtze River basin based on summer precipitation anomalies. Cheng et al. (2012)  and Li et al. (2022)  explored the spatiotemporal distribution and intensity changes of DFA events in Huai River Basin (China) considering their differences in summer precipitation. Wang et al. (2020)  analyzed the spatiotemporal distribution, trend, intensity, and periodic changes of DFA in Poyang Lake Basin during 1960–2012. Shi et al. (2021)  examined the dynamic changes of DFA in Wei River catchment of northern China from 1960 to 2010, and further analyzed their possible driving forces in a changing environment. Yang et al. (2019a) and (2019b)  and Zhang et al. (2008)  have analyzed DFA events on a shorter time scale (7-day or 10-day). On a national scale, Qiao et al., (2022a and 2022b ) analyzed the spatiotemporal pattern changes in frequency, duration and severity of DFA events in Mainland China during 1980–2019. Moreover, Chen et al. (2020b) , Jiang et al., (2023)  and Wang et al. (2023)  projected the trends of DFA under future climate change, and assessed whether future DFA events would become more severe in terms of frequency, area and intensity under climate change scenarios. However, the precipitation data based on traditional rain gauges have inherent limitations (sparse stations or non-existent) in many remote and developing regions of the world (Ghile et al., 2010 ). Their point measurements and limited sampling areas make it difficult to accurately describe the changes in spatiotemporal patterns of DFA events, and it is also difficult to identify areas susceptible to DFA and key regions with higher risk of flood/drought disasters on a large scale (Li et al., 2017a ). On the other hand, rapid development in satellite technology has enabled remote sensing observations to have higher temporal and spatial resolution, meanwhile, the corresponding integrated multi-satellite retrieval algorithms for precipitation have significantly improved the accuracies of satellite-based precipitation products (SPPs) (Stisen and Sandholt, 2010; Li et al., 2014, 2022 ). Some SPPs, i.e., TRMM (Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission) and GPM (Global Precipitation Measurement), can provide reliable precipitation estimates over a wide area with high temporal/spatial resolution, and are considered the good alternative to traditional gauges data (Hou et al., 2014; Skofronick-Jackson et al., 2017; Huffman et al., 2018; Li et al., 2022 ). High-resolution SPPs have been widely applied in the fields of drought/flood monitoring (Duan et al., 2016; Zambrano et al., 2017 ), extreme precipitation analysis (Yi et al., 2018; Fang et al., 2019 ), rainfall characteristics (Fu et al., 2018 ) and hydrological modeling (Yang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2020 ), and it also has inherent advantages and great potential in large-scale describing of DFA. Therefore, the objectives of the study are: (1) assess the suitability of high-resolution SPPs, i.e., the Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (IMERG), for identifying and quantifying the DFA; and (2) investigate their spatiotemporal distribution patterns of frequencies and intensities of DFA events at various time scales in a humid subtropical basin in China. By doing so, the drought-flood alternation index at 1-month, 3-month and 6-month scales are calculated respectively and different statistical measures are investigated. This study can provide useful reference for application of high-resolution SPPs in identifying and quantifying the DFA at large-scale.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area Poyang Lake basin is located on the south bank of the middle reach of Yangtze River, China, with the drainage area of 162200 km2  (Li et al., 2017a, 2023a ). There are five major tributaries in the basin, including Xiushui River, Ganjiang River, Fuhe River, Xinjiang River and Raohe River ( Fig. 1 ). The runoff from the basin flows into China’s largest freshwater lake, Poyang Lake, and finally discharges into the Yangtze River through Hukou. Poyang Lake basin belongs to a subtropical humid monsoon climate, with an annual precipitation of 1400–1900 mm and an average of 1675 mm. Fig. 1 c shows the distribution of average monthly rainfall at 76 rain gauges in Poyang Lake basin from 1960 to 2019. The precipitation in each season is uneven, with only 25 % of the annual precipitation during the dry season (October-February of next year) (Li et al., 2016, 2017b ); The precipitation increases sharply from March to June, accounting for approximately 55 % of annual precipitation (Fig. 1 c), and the precipitation is relatively concentrated during this period, often leading to floods and waterlogging disasters (Wang et al., 2023 ). Correspondingly, the annual variation process of water level at different stations in Poyang Lake is shown in Fig. 1 d. The terrain of Poyang Lake basin shows a pattern of higher in the south and lower in the north, topography varies from mountainous areas to alluvial plains in the lower reaches of five major rivers. The soil types in the basin mainly include red soil, yellow soil, purple soil, tidal soil, mountain yellow brown soil, mountain meadow soil, and paddy soil (Ye et al., 2013 ). Red soil is the most widely distributed and extensive zonal soil in the basin (accounting for approximately 56 % of the total area), with low infiltration rate and susceptibility to heavy rainfall erosion (Li et al., 2020 ), followed by yellow soil (Ye et al., 2013 ).  2.2 Data The GPM project, as the successor of TRMM, was commenced in 2014 and aimed to produce a new generation of SPPs with higher accuracy and temporal/spatial resolution (Hou et al., 2014 ). IMERG adopts a unified algorithm that combines information from many passive microwave instruments in the GPM constellation and can provide precipitation products with 0.5-hour temporal resolution, 0.1°×0.1° spatial resolution and a spatial coverage area of 60° S−60° N (Huffman et al., 2018 ). More importantly, in the latest version 06 of IMERG, the algorithm integrated early precipitation products produced during TRMM satellite operation (2000–2015) and recent precipitation estimates collected during GPM satellite operation (2014-present) (Huffman et al., 2018 ). The IMERG series has three versions, including the near real-time “early” and “late” run data sets, and the post real-time “final” run data sets (Chen et al., 2021 ). In this study, the daily IMERG V06 Final products from June 1, 2000 to December 31, 2019 were selected after considering the length of rain-gauge data to identify and quantify the DFA events. These products can be downloaded freely from the NASA (National Aeronautics and Space Administration) website. Additionally, daily rainfall observed at 76 rain gauges in Poyang Lake basin from June 1, 2000 to December 31, 2019 were collected from the National Meteorological Information Center, China (NMIC) (http://data.cma.cn ) to evaluate and validate the performance of IMERG products. These data have been widely used in various hydrological and hydrodynamic modeling of Poyang Lake in previous studies (Li et al., 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023a,b; Wang et al., 2020, 2023; Xu et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2023 ) and the qualities of the data have been tested and reliable.  2.3 Drought-flood alternation index (DFAI) DFAI has been widely used for quantitative research on DFA phenomena in the fields of meteorology and hydrology (Wu et al., 2006; Li and Ye, 2015; Shan et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2023 ). Therefore, DFAI was used to identify and quantify DFA events at different time scales (1-month, 3-month, and 6-month scales) in this study. DFAI was calculated as follows (Wu et al., 2006 ):(1) DFAI = ( NP  i + 1   − NP  i   ) × ( NP  i + 1      + NP  i      ) × α  − NP  i + 1   + NP  i            (2) NP  i   = P  i   − P  ¯     / σ       where P i   is the rainfall in period i ; P  ¯    is the average and σ  is standard error of P i  ; NP i   and NP i +1  are normalized rainfall for period i  and i +1, respectively; α  is an empirical parameter reflecting the characteristics of rainfall in the basin. Wang et al. (2020)  compared and analyzed the sensitivity of the value of α  and concluded that a value of 1.8 is suitable in the Poyang Lake Basin. According to Wu et al. (2006) , (NP i +1 -NP i  ) denotes the intensity of DFAA event, (|NP i +1 |+|NP i  |) represents the intensity of drought/flood, and the item α  − NP  i + 1   + NP  i          is a weight coefficient to avoid persistent drought or flood in consecutive research periods and enhance the weight of DFA events (Wu et al., 2006 ). Meanwhile, it is regarded as normal if DFAI is between −1.0 and 1.0, DFAI >1.0 indicates a drought-to-flood event (DTF), and DFAI <-1.0 indicates a flood-to-drought event (FTD). In addition, the absolute value of DFAI represents the intensity of DFA events, meaning that the larger the values, the stronger the intensity. The intensity of DFA events was divided into three types according to DFAI ( Table 1 ).  2.4 Performance evaluation indexes To demonstrate the performance of IMERG products in calculating the DFAI, several statistical indexes, including the frequency bias index (FBI), false alarm ratio (FAR), probability of detection (POD), and equitable threat score (ETS), were adopted to compare and quantitatively evaluate the results from IMERG products with that from traditional rain gauges data. These indexes were obtained based on a 2×2 contingency table with different DFAI threshold as follows (Wilks, 2006 ):(3) FBI = a + b    / a + c          (4) FAR = b  / a + b          (5) POD = a  / a + c          (6) ETS = a − H  e      / a + b + c − H  e            (7) H  e   = a + b    a + c     / N       where a  represents the number of DFAI correctly estimated by the IMERG products; b  is the number of false detections; c  represents the omitted signals by the IMERG products; and N  represents the total number of DFAI. Generally, FBI indicates that IMERG products overestimates (FBI>1) or underestimates (FBI<1) the DFAI under a specific threshold; FAR provides the fraction of false alarms in DFAI; POD represents the proportion of correctly estimated DFAI, and ETS is generally used to reflect overall performance (Wilks, 2006 ). In this study, these indexes were calculated at DFAI thresholds of −3.0, −2.0, −1.0, 0, 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0, respectively.   3 Results 3.1 Evaluation of IMERG products for DFA events  Fig. 2  shows the scatter plots of the DFAI estimated from IMERG product and the gauges rainfall, and comparison is made for the whole basin and five sub-catchments. The good linear relationships between DFAI estimated from IMERG product and that from the rain-gauges data were presented at 1-month scale, with the R2  of 0.72–0.85 for five sub-catchments and 0.76 for the whole basin. At 3-month scale, the R2  was 0.34 for the whole basin and ranged between 0.33 for Ganjiang and Raohe sub-catchments and 0.40 for Xinjiang sub-catchment. However, the R2  values were very low at 6-month scale, regardless of the whole basin or five sub-catchments, indicating that IMERG products cannot capture the changes of DFAI well at 6-month scale. In addition, the accuracy of IMERG product for quantifying the DFA was further evaluated by FBI, FAR, POD, and ETS.  Fig. 3  shows the changes at different thresholds on three different time scales. It is seen that IMERG products tended to overestimate the DFAI at a large threshold (>1.0), especially on 6-month scale, with the FBI greater than 2. Meanwhile, IMERG products performed best at 1-month scale, with the FBI changing around 1 for different thresholds. Moreover, the FAR increased from 0 to 0.45–0.89 and POD decreased from 0.88–0.97 to 0.4–0.53 when the threshold increased from −3.0 to 3.0. These changes indicated that the ability of IMERG products to describe DFAI weakened at larger thresholds. Overall, IMERG products performed best in quantifying the DFA at 1-month scale (with the highest ETS score), but worst at 6-month scale (with the lowest ETS score).  3.2 Frequency characteristics of DFA events  Fig. 4  presents the intra-annual distributions of occurrence frequency of DTF and FTD events. The seasonal distributions of both DTF and FTD events in Poyang Lake basin were very uneven throughout the year. DTF events mainly occurred from March to June (with an average of more than 3 times), while FTD events mainly occurred during July-September at 1-month scale, especially with the highest frequency in July (nearly 8 times). Moreover, the seasonal heterogeneity of DFA events was more significant at 3-month and 6-month scales. DTF events were concentrated in the first half of year, with the highest frequency occurring from February to May, while FTD events mainly occurred in the second half of year, especially from July to October. These distribution characteristics of DFA events were closely related to the seasonal uneven distribution of rainfall in Poyang Lake basin.  Fig. 5  shows the spatial distributions of occurrence frequencies of DFA events. It is found that both DTF and FTD events exhibited significant spatial differences in frequency of occurrence at 1-month scale across the Poyang Lake basin. The DFA events were most frequent in Ganjiang sub-catchment and the lake area in the northern part of the basin, with an average frequency of more than 43.1 times. Among them, the lake area was mainly dominated by DTF events, while the Ganjiang sub-catchment was mainly dominated by FTD events (with an average frequency of 22.3 times) ( Table 2 ). The spatial heterogeneity of DFA events was more significant at 3-month and 6-month scales, with both DTF and FTD events having the largest frequency in the southern part of the Ganjiang sub-catchment and the lowest frequency in the Fuhe and Xiushui sub-catchments. Subsequently, the area distribution of DTF and FTD events at different occurrence frequencies are shown in  Fig. 6 . It is seen that the frequencies of DTF events occurring in Poyang Lake Basin was about 15–29 times at 1-month scale, among which the areas with 20 and 21 DTF events were the largest, accounting for 18.7 % and 17.9 % of the total area, respectively. In terms of accumulated area, 72.1 % and 8.4 % of the Poyang Lake basin experienced more than 20 and 25 DTF events during the period of 2000–2019, respectively. FTD events presented a similar area distribution characteristic. The area with more than 20 FTD events accounted for 70.7 % of the total area, and as many as 10.3 % of the basin experienced more than 25 FTD events. Furthermore, 1.6 % of the areas experienced more than 27 FTD events. For 3-month and 6-month scales, the area-frequency curves of both DTF and FTD events generally exhibited a similar distribution, except that the occurrence frequency ranges were 35–53 and 51–80 times, respectively.  3.3 Intensity characteristics of DFA events The spatial distributions of mild, moderate, and severe DTF and FTD events at different time scales are shown in   Figs. 7 and 8 , respectively. It is found that the occurrence of mild, moderate and severe DTF events in Poyang Lake basin showed great spatial differences at 1-month scale. The mild DTF events mainly occurred in the northern area of the basin, especially in Xiushui and Xinjiang sub-catchments with the highest frequency (averaging over 16.0 times). However, the severe DTF events mainly occurred in the southern area of the basin, especially in Ganjiang sub-catchment with a frequency of even more than 5 times (Fig. 7 ). Moreover, at 3-month and 6-month scales, the mild, moderate and severe DTF events also exhibited significant spatial heterogeneity. In addition to the southern part of the basin being a high-risk area for DTF events, the frequencies were also high in the northeastern region of the basin (including the Raohe and Xinjiang sub-catchments), especially the mild DTF events. Similarly, the mild, moderate and severe FTD events in the basin also exhibited significant spatial heterogeneity (Fig. 8 ). The mild FTD events mainly presented in the northern areas of the basin, except for the Xinjiang sub-catchment with a low frequency of 9.5 times, while the severe FTD events still occurred more frequently in the southern area of the basin, although Raohe and Xinjiang sub-catchments were high-risk areas for severe FTD events at 3-month scale. In addition,  Fig. 9  shows a comparison of frequencies of mild, moderate, and severe DTF and FTD events at different time scales in each sub-catchment. It is found that, although the frequencies of mild FTD events were lower than that of mild DTF events at 1-month scale, the frequencies of moderate and severe FTD events were higher than their counterpart, especially severe FTD events. Similar findings also existed at 3-month scale, especially in the Fuhe and Xinjiang sub-catchments, where the frequencies of severe FTD events were almost twice that of severe DTF events. Subsequently,  Fig. 10  shows the area distribution of DTF and FTD events with different intensities. It is seen that 97.4 % of the basin experienced more than 10 mild DTF events, 53.1 % of the areas experienced more than 15, and 6.6 % of the areas experienced even more than 20 mild DTF events at 1-month scale. Moreover, more than half of the basin experienced at least 3 moderate DTF events (57.0 %) and severe DTF events (55.7 %), and even 11.1 % and 10.9 % of the basin experienced 6 or more moderate and severe DTF events (Fig. 10 a). Correspondingly, the area with 10, 15 and 20 mild FTD events accounted for 74.4 %, 21.8 % and 0.06 % of the total area, respectively. In addition, as high as 82.8 % and 92.8 % of the basin experienced at least 3 moderate and severe FTD events, 23.8 % and 34.3 % of the basin experienced more than 6 moderate and severe FTD events, and even 5.1 % of the basin experienced more than 9 severe FTD events (Fig. 10 b). Overall, although the area of mild DTF events was larger than that of mild FTD events, the moderate and severe FTD events covered the much larger area than that of DTF events. Similar findings had also been made at 3-month and 6-month scales.  3.4 Interannual variation characteristics of DFA events Variations of the average area of DTF and FTD events (including mild, moderate and severe events) that occurred in Poyang Lake basin from 2000 to 2019 are shown in  Fig. 11 . The average area ranged from 3.4 % of the basin in 2004 to 14.5 % in 2000 for DTF events, and from 2.7 % in 2009 to 16.0 % in 2000 for FTD events at 1-month scale. The total area affected by DTF and FTD events showed a long-term downward trend during 2000–2019 (Fig. 11 a), however, the impact area of both severe DTF and severe FTD events presented a long-term upward trend, especially the severe DTF events (Fig. 11 b). At 3-month scale, the average area varied between 4.2 % of the basin in 2007 and 25.9 % in 2011 for DTF events, and between 8.3 % in 2007 to 25.5 % in 2010 for FTD events. The total area of DTF and FTD events still presented a long-term downward trend (Fig. 11 c). At the same time, both severe DTF and FTD events were covering increasingly large areas in Poyang Lake basin (Fig. 11 d). The annual area of DFA events also presented a similar long-term trend at 6-month scales. Fig. 11  indicated that although the total area affected by DFA events was decreasing, the coverages of severe DTF and severe FTD events were gradually expanding in Poyang Lake basin.   4 Discussion 4.1 Influencing factors of DFA events Climate change and abnormal atmospheric circulation were important factors affecting the spatiotemporal distribution and trend of DFA events in the basin (Chen et al., 2020b; Wang et al., 2023 ). The uneven seasonal distribution of precipitation within a year and frequent extreme precipitation were more likely to trigger DFA events (Li et al., 2017a ). Poyang Lake basin located in the subtropical monsoon region and was strongly influenced by the East Asian monsoon, resulting in significant seasonal and spatial variations in precipitation (Ye et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017a,b ). Monsoons transported a large amount of atmospheric moisture from the western Pacific to South China, and brought more heavy rainfall to the local area (Gao and Xie, 2016 ). Zhang et al. (2016)  found that the spatiotemporal patterns of extreme precipitation in Poyang Lake basin were strongly influenced by the propagation of monsoon activities. The southeast monsoon affected the precipitation changes in May and propagated northward from June to early July. Then, the monsoon began to move southward after August and dissipated from South China in October. Moreover, the weakening of the East Asian monsoon would limit its northward expansion and prolong the rainy season in South China. The studies of Zou and Ren (2015) , Ding et al. (2008)  and Ren et al. (2013)  also provided similar results, suggesting that the East Asian monsoon had a great impact on summer extreme precipitation in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River. The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) was another important factor that may lead to changes and trends in DFA events (Wang et al., 2023 ). Numerous studies on ENSO had confirmed the significant climatic connection between extreme precipitation and the warm and/or cold stages of Southern Oscillation (corresponding to El Niño and La Niña, respectively) in many regions (Xiao et al., 2015; Shan et al., 2018 ). Duan et al. (2017)  revealed that warm ENSO episodes could increase the moisture content and water vapor flux, thereby increasing the likelihood of extreme precipitation in South China. Zhang et al. (2014)  pointed out that extreme precipitation was mainly affected by ENSO events with 1-year time lag and the occurrence of ENSO events could significantly increase the variability of summer extreme precipitation in Poyang Lake basin. In addition, previous studies revealed that DFA in Poyang Lake basin was also related to effects of North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) (Linderholm et al., 2011 ), Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) (Yuan et al., 2008 ), and Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) (Chen et al., 2013 ), although these effects were complex in terms of seasonal variation and intensity (Xiao et al., 2015 ).  4.2 Suitability of IMERG product for identifying DFA IMERG product has different accuracies in identifying DFA events in Poyang Lake Basin at 1-month, 3-month and 6-month scales. Figs. 2 and 3  indicated that IMERG performed well at 1-month scale, but overestimated the DFAI at 3-month and 6-month scales. This is, on one hand, mainly related to the accuracy of the IMERG product. The study of Li et al. (2022)  revealed that IMERG had a significant error in estimating heavy rainfall. At a long time scale, this error is gradually accumulated and amplified, leading to great deviations in DFAI. On the other hand, α  is an important empirical parameter in the formula for calculating DFAI, and its value is related to the time scale of the study and the climate and catchment characteristics (Wu et al., 2006 ). Wu et al. (2006)  took a value of 1.8 for α when studying the summer long-cycle DFA phenomenon in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River. The same value was also used in the studies of Cui et al. (2022) , Shi et al. (2021)  and Yang et al. (2019a,b) . However, Zhang et al. (2012)  studied the DFA based on runoff in the Huai River Basin during rainy season, with a α value of 1.8 for long-cycle runoff DFA and 3.2 for short-cycle runoff DFA. Shan et al. (2018)  improved the calculation formula proposed by Wu et al. (2006)  and recommended the range from 1.0 to 1.4 as the reasonable domain for parameter α. Wang et al. (2020)  specifically analyzed the sensitivity of parameter α when studying the DFA events based on runoff in Poyang Lake Basin and compared the effects of α values of 1.3, 1.5, 1.8, 2.0 and 3.2 on the results. A value of 1.8 was adopted in this study according to most previous studies, which may not be suitable for calculating DFAI at a long-time scale, resulting in great uncertainty for IMERG product in identifying DFA at 3-month and 6-month scales. Further studies would be enhanced by investigating the relationship between α  and time scale and climate, and using different α  values for DFAI calculation at different time scales.  4.3 Hydrological and ecological implications of DFA Climate warming could lead to more heavy rainfall and was more likely to trigger floods or drought events. Especially, changes in precipitation patterns or fluctuations in precipitation intensity were often the important causes of regional extreme hydrological events (Lehner et al., 2006; Zhang and Wang, 2007 ). This study revealed that although the total area affected by DFA events was decreasing, the coverages of severe DTF and severe FTD events were gradually expanding in Poyang Lake basin. These changes meant that the likelihood of severe flood/drought in Poyang Lake basin was increasing. Zhang et al. (2016), (2019)  also found the similar results, and they pointed out that both the intensity of heavy rainfall and the area affected by extreme precipitation events showed the increasing trends in Poyang Lake basin. Moreover, Lei et al. (2021)  analyzed the spatiotemporal variation of extreme precipitation and detected their non-stationary characteristics in Poyang Lake basin. They believed that extreme precipitation during flood season was usually more likely to cause flooding, while in non-flood season, drought events may occur once the precipitation fell below the mean climatology. In a word, these changes in DFA and extreme precipitation meant that the flood control and drought reduction management should be further strengthened to address the severe water security issues in Poyang Lake basin (Wang et al., 2023 ). Moreover, the Poyang Lake floodplain was an internationally important wetland, with a rich variety of wetland plant species (Han et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2010 ). The wetland ecosystem was extremely sensitive to changes in the hydrological condition of the five rivers and lakes in the basin (Li et al., 2023a,b; Ye et al., 2023 ). Previous studies have found that continuous low water levels had caused wetland vegetation to exhibit a trend of xerophilization and a decrease in productivity (Yu et al., 2011 ). The decline in lake level and decrease in duration of high water-levels in Poyang Lake had led to early exposure of high-level floodplains, resulting in a decrease in soil moisture content and fragmentation of wetland area. The plants in Poyang Lake wetland showed an obvious trend of dwarfing and xerophilization, and even some hygrophytes were replaced by xerophyte as new dominant species (Hu et al., 2010 ). At the same time, the distribution area of Carex cinerascens community continuously expanded towards the center of the lake and occupied the area of submerged plants (Hu et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2023 ). In addition, the Poyang Lake wetland had many shallow sub lakes, and their hydrological conditions and wetland plant phenological characteristics were suitable for the feeding needs of waterbirds, making them the main habitats for a large number of waterbirds, especially overwintering birds (Li et al., 2023a ). The intensification of DFA events had a great impact on the hydrological conditions of these shallow sub lakes and their hydrological connectivity with the main lake body or surrounding water systems. Therefore, the changes in DFA events not only affected the succession and spatial patterns of wetland plants, but also the distribution and quality of waterbird habitats in Poyang Lake wetland. Therefore, it is recommended that local governments strengthen real-time monitoring of rainfall and water conditions, improve prediction accuracy and accurately predict the coverage, development process and intensity of extreme floods or droughts. This has become an inevitable requirement for dealing with floods, droughts and DFA events in Poyang Lake Basin. Moreover, there are as many as 10,798 reservoirs in Poyang Lake basin, with a total storage capacity of 32.8×109  m3  (Department of Water Resources of Jiangxi Province, 2009 ). These reservoirs should be fully utilized to intercept floods during the flood season and release water for downstream replenishment during the dry season (Li et al., 2023a ). At the same time, it is necessary to strengthen the joint operation of reservoir groups, including hundreds of large and medium-sized reservoirs in the local basin and large reservoir in the Yangtze River main stream (the Three Gorges Reservoir), to improve the level of water resource optimization and management in the Poyang Lake area. In addition, the Poyang Lake water control project has also been proposed to effectively prevent floods, reduce the impact of drought and DFA events (Yao et al., 2022 ). However, this project may bring new serious ecological impacts, especially on wetland plants and migratory bird habitats (Chen et al., 2020c; Yao et al., 2021 ). So, the construction of this project needs to be very cautious.   5 Conclusions This study evaluated the suitability of high-resolution SPPs (IMERG) for identifying and quantifying the DFA and investigated the spatiotemporal distribution patterns of frequencies and intensities of DFA events at 1-month, 3-month and 6-month scales in Poyang Lake basin. Major results demonstrated that IMERG product could effectively estimate the DFAI at 1-month scale, with high consistency with the results based on traditional gauges rainfall, and could identify the frequency and intensity characteristics of DTF and FTD events. However, its performance was not very satisfactory at 3-month and 6-month scales. In intra-annual distribution, DTF events were inclined to occur during from March to June, while FTD events from July to September at 1-month scale. And at 3-month and 6-month scales, DTF events generally occurred in the first half of the year, while FTD events appeared in the second half of the year. Moreover, frequencies and intensities of both DTF and FTD exhibited significant spatial heterogeneity. The lake area was mainly affected by DTF events (with a frequency of more than 23 times), while the Ganjiang sub-catchment was mainly affected by FTD events, with an average frequency of 22.3 times. The severe DTF and FTD events were inclined to occur in the southern area of the basin, especially in Ganjiang sub-catchment. Meanwhile, the northeast region of the basin (including the Raohe and Xinjiang sub-catchments) was also a high-risk area for DFA at 3-month scale, with a higher frequency of severe DTF and FTD events. Furthermore, although the total area affected by DTF and FTD events showed a long-term decreasing trend from 2000 to 2019, the area affected by both severe DTF and severe FTD events presented an upward trend in Poyang Lake basin. These changes in DFA indicated that water and ecological security in Poyang Lake basin were facing increasing challenges, and further efforts were needed to strengthen the flood control and drought reduction management in his area.
1 Introduction Soil surface evaporation plays a pivotal role in the terrestrial water cycle. Estimates indicate that evaporation losses from terrestrial environments account for approximately 20–40 % of the global evapotranspiration (Schlesinger and Jasechko, 2014 ). Moreover, over half of these losses result from soil water (SW) evaporation (Good et al., 2015 ), which significantly influences water utilization in terrestrial ecosystems (Kool et al., 2014 ). Unproductive SW loss due to evaporation is influenced by environmental factors such as local vegetation, topography, and soil properties (Brutsaert, 2014; Aouade et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2022 ), and plays a role in climate regulation (Hirschi et al., 2011 ). Most studies conducted to date have focused on conventional ecosystems, such as forests (Burchard-Levine et al., 2022 ), grasslands (Yepez et al., 2005; Robertson and Gazis, 2006 ), and croplands (Wen et al., 2016 ), on relatively flat surfaces (Sun et al., 2014; Xue et al., 2023 ). However, the mechanisms of soil evaporation in marginal or extreme environments are not fully understood, especially in alpine mountains where soil evaporation exhibits strong spatial heterogeneity. Field observation and simulation experiments in such areas are challenging and uncertain due to the constraints of the high alpine and complex surface environments. These limitations hinder a comprehensive understanding of soil evaporation patterns and their potential impacts on regional ecosystems, agriculture, and water management (Zimmermann et al., 1966 ). To date, there has been considerable interest among scholars in the realm of soil evaporation monitoring innovations. Obtaining high-precision, large-scale soil evaporation data remains challenging. Traditional methods of soil evaporation monitoring predominantly encompass in situ observations and remote sensing model estimations. Long-term in situ observations, including techniques such as the Bowen ratio, eddy covariance, and lysimeter, facilitate the separation of soil evaporation from vegetation transpiration at both plot and ecosystem scales (Lawrence et al., 2007; Jiang et al., 2022 ), ensuring precise and timely data acquisition. However, the substantial expenses associated with field installations and the regular maintenance of instruments pose significant challenges, particularly in remote areas. Meanwhile, model estimation, leveraging remote sensing data, often integrates MODIS data with the Penman–Monteith equation. This approach enables the indirect measurement of surface evaporation at regional (Cleugh et al., 2007 ) or global (Miralles et al., 2011 ) scales. Nevertheless, the reliability of these estimations remains uncertain owing to the heterogeneity and complexity of near-surface environmental conditions (Yang et al., 2022 ). Few models can provide precise estimates of soil evaporation beneath the canopy, results tend to overestimate the values (Xiang, 2021 ). Contrarily, stable isotope tracer techniques provide a promising alternative. They boast high accuracy and sensitivity, are applicable over a wide spatial range, and enable the sampling of large areas. Thus, these techniques play a crucial role in studies focusing on water movement and flux (Gazis and Feng, 2004; Quade et al., 2018 ). In recent years, numerous success stories that demonstrate the efficacy of stable isotope techniques have emerged. For instance, Kleine et al. (2020)  used hydrogen and oxygen stable isotopes to deepen our understanding of soil evaporation in forest land and grassland within catchment areas. Similarly, Al-Oqaili et al. (2020)  evaluated evaporation losses in semiarid agricultural lands using stable isotope techniques. Long-term monitoring results indicate that evaporation induces the following alterations in soil stable isotopes: 1) enrichment of SW hydrogen and oxygen isotopes in the surface layer, and 2) deviation of the stable isotope composition of SW away from the local meteoric water line (LMWL) (Sprenger et al., 2016 ). Previous studies have employed these “variations” to characterize soil evaporation patterns. While the evaporation intensity can be readily discerned from variations in SW evaporation line slopes (Rothfuss and Brüggemann, 2015; Deng et al., 2017 ), the slope fails to accurately quantify evaporation capacity as the slopes are only moderated by evaporative fractionation coefficients (Gibson et al., 2008 ). Recent perspectives have contended that line–conditioned excess (lc-excess) and deuterium excess (d-excess), determined by evaporation fractionation factors and residual SW storage, provide enhanced validity in characterizing soil evaporation (Rothfuss and Brüggemann, 2015; Hasselquist et al., 2018 ). Moreover, lc-excess values are preferable over d-excess values for indicating the presence of the evaporative fractionation signal (Landwehr and Coplen, 2006 ). The lc-excess value is commonly used as a qualitative indicator of evaporation intensity (Wei et al., 2021 ). The Craig-Gordon model (Craig and Gordon, 1965 ), along with the isotope mass balance equation (Gonfiantini, 1986 ), enhances the quantification of soil evaporation losses. Because of the influence of local environmental factors such as precipitation, temperature (Sprenger et al., 2017b ), relative humidity (Lyu et al., 2021 ), vegetation cover (Sternberg, 1988; Sprenger et al., 2017a; 2018 ), and other local environmental factors, SW stable isotopes exhibit substantial spatial and temporal variabilities across plot (Raz–Yaseef et al., 2010; Goldsmith et al., 2019 ), slope (Liu et al., 2022 ), watershed (Zhang et al., 2021 ), and regional (Lyu et al., 2021 ) scales. The extent of soil evaporation, as characterized by lc-excess values derived from SW stable isotopes, exhibits a distinct spatial pattern of variation (Oerter and Bowen, 2019; Liu et al., 2022 ). At present, the majority of studies mainly focus on multiple soil sampling of plots, with limited attention to the representativeness of soil plots at the watershed or regional scale (Evaristo et al., 2015 ), this increases the unreliability of related assessments (Liu et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, research regarding the influence of these factors on lc-excess values at the watershed or broader scales remains constrained, particularly in alpine mountain regions characterized by diverse land use types. Hence, it is necessary to conduct a comprehensive study that integrates isotopic methodologies with various environmental variables, encompassing meteorological, topographic, vegetation, and soil factors, to scrutinize the factors influencing soil evaporation characteristics and spatial patterns. The Qilian Mountains, located in the northeastern of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, feature diverse surface types and intricate subsurface conditions. Previous studies on soil evaporation mainly relied on site-based data collection (Zhang et al., 2003, Tian et al., 2011, Zhang et al., 2015, Wen et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2021; Yong et al., 2020 ) and model simulations with remotely sensed data (Song et al., 2022 ). However, these studies have mainly concentrated on individual ecosystems in or around the Heihe River Basin (HRB), and did not comprehensively compare and evaluate different ecosystems in the source region during the same period. Based on these considerations, this study investigations soil evaporation in the Heihe River source area. The primary objectives of this study are as follows: (1) analyze the spatial variation patterns of SW stable isotopes and lc-excess values; (2) estimate and compare the soil evaporation losses under different land use types; and (3) demonstrate how climate, soil properties, topography, and vegetation factors collectively influence soil evaporation in the Heihe River source area and within various land use types, and identify the key factors. These findings can indicate the criticality and importance of the Qilian Mountains in the water cycle process and provide a scientific basis for the construction of watershed hydrological models and assessment of water balance.  2 Research methods 2.1 Study area The Heihe River source area, a vital segment of the Qilian Mountain National Park in Qinghai, serves as a crucial water reservoir and natural vegetative barrier in northwest China. Spanning an altitude range of 2284–5203 m, this region features a plateau continental climate, with precipitation primarily occurring from May to September, peaking in July and August. The land use types include forests, shrublands, grasslands, and croplands. The dominant plant floras include conifers such as Picea crassifolia  and Sabina przewalskii , alongside shrubs such as Potentilla fruticosa , Salix oritrepha  schneid, and Caragana jubata . Herbaceous species, such as Kobresia pygmaea , Agropyron cristata , and Stipa krylovii  are also prevalent. The Heihe River divides into two branches, namely, the west branch, constituting the main stream, and the Toler River originating from the southern foot of Toler Mountain. In the upper reaches, the east branch bifurcates into the east fork, stemming from Jinyangling’s eight treasure river, and the west fork, sourced from the Yeniugou River on the main peak of the eastern Qilian Mountains. These branches converge at Huangzang temple in Qilian County, ultimately flowing out of the mountains at Yingluoxia.  2.2 Sampling design and data processing Precipitation and soil samples were mainly collected from 13 August to 20 August in 2018 and 10 August to 19 August in 2019. A total of 8 event-scale samples (precipitation >2 mm) were gathered, mostly through random sampling, using rainfall buckets. The samples were sealed in 60 mL polyethylene bottles with parafilm within and around the study area ( Fig. 1 a). During the peak growing season, soil samples were collected from multiple plots established in each land use type (cropland, grassland, forest land, and shrubland) on a regional scale. The average elevations of the sampling sites were as follows: grassland (3398 ± 334.89 m) > shrubland (3272 ± 201.46 m) > forest land (3104 ± 100.54 m) > cropland (2838 ± 133.71 m). Specifically, the sampling sites for forested areas and croplands were situated near the town of Qilian County (Fig. 1 a, b). Samples from grassland were collected within the elevation range of 2744–3961 m (Fig. 1 b). Soil samples were collected using soil auger at 10 cm intervals and sealed in 10 mL brown glass bottles with a parafilm sealing film, leading to the collection of a total of 540 samples. A total of 36 sampling sites were established in grasslands, and 8 sites each in woodlands, shrublands, and croplands, most of the samples were collected at a 50 cm depth. Moreover, two replicates were collected from each sample site, one for measuring the hydrogen and oxygen stable isotope values and one for the soil water content (SWC) determination. Groundwater was collected using mainly by a bucket or a sump pump, and spring water was collected at the spring outcrop in front of the mountain, with a total of 28 samples collected (Fig. 1 a). At the same time, handheld GPS was used to record the elevation, latitude and longitude of the sampling points. During the sampling period, all samples were refrigerated at a temperature below 4°C without evaporation. SW was extracted using a LI-2000 plant-soil moisture vacuum distillation system, with an extraction time of 2–3 h depending on the SWC. The precipitation and SW samples were filtered through a 0.22 μm filter membrane and measured using a liquid water isotope analyzer (IWA-35EP, USA). The measuring errors of δD and δ18 O were below 1 ‰ and 0.2 ‰, respectively. The results were expressed to Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water (VSMOW) (Craig, 1961 ).  2.3 Sources of auxiliary indicators Considering the significant elevation span of the sample site distribution, climate (relative humidity [RH], air temperature [TMP], precipitation [PRE], land surface temperature [LST], wind speed [WS], aridity index [AI], potential evapotranspiration [PET], and net surface solar radiation [SSR]), topographic (digital elevation model [DEM], slope [SLP], and aspect [ASP]), vegetation (normalized difference vegetation index [NDVI] and land use type [LUT]), and soil (SWC, soil bulk density [SD]) variables were selected to assess the influence degree of these factors on SW lc-excess values. Climate conditions, including precipitation, temperature, wind speed and relative humidity, can affect soil evaporation by altering the supply of moisture and energy to change soil evaporation (Fu et al., 2022 ). Meteorological data, including RH, TMP, PRE, WS, were accessed from the National Earth System Science Data Center (http://www.geodata.cn/ ). LST data were downloaded from the Geospatial Data Cloud site (http://www.gscloud.cn ) and PET data from the National Tibetan Plateau Data Center (http://data.tpdc.ac.cn ). Moreover, SSR data were obtained from the ERA5 dataset (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/#!/search?text=ERA5&type=dataset ) at a spatial resolution of 0.05° × 0.05° (Wang, 2021 ). Arora (2002)  proposed a formula for the AI to characterize the balance between atmospheric demand and water supply. These data were obtained mainly from the month before the sampling to analyze soil evaporation over a period of time. Vegetation factors and soil properties influence soil evaporation by altering the water and heat transfer processes (Su et al., 2023 ). Land use type (LUT) at a spatial resolution of 10 m (Gong et al., 2019 ), accessed from http://data.ess.tsinghua.edu.cn . The NDVI was utilized to assess the spatial distribution of vegetation, which serves as a remarkable indicator characterizing vegetation growth status (Jia et al., 2004 ). The NDVI data were derived from MOD13Q1 (MODIS) products with a spatial resolution of 1 km. SWC and SD affect the storage of SW and the extent of water vapor diffusion (Lyu et al., 2021 ). These parameters were determined using the differences in the mass of the soil samples before and after drying treatment at a constant temperature (105 °C). Soil water content was calculated as SWC (%) = (F –D )/D , where F and D  denote the fresh and dry weights, respectively. Topographical factors can indirectly influence soil evaporation by affecting environment factors such as climate and vegetation factors (McVicar et al., 2007 ). DEM data (30 m × 30 m) were downloaded from the Geospatial Data Cloud site (http://www.gscloud.cn ), providing information on elevation, slope gradient, and aspect information. The detailed descriptions and sources of the above data are shown in Table S1 .  2.4 Analysis methods 2.4.1 Calculation of soil water evaporation line (SEL) The soil water evaporation line (SEL) is determined by establishing a linear relationship between the SW δD and δ18 O values for various land use types (Allison, 1982 ):(1) δ D = a × δ  18   O + b     where a  and b  denote the slope and intercept of SEL, respectively.  2.4.2 Calculation and indication of deuterium excess (d-excess) and line–conditioned excess (lc-excess) Lc-excess and d-excess was calculated to characterize the strength of evaporative fractionation. D-excess was proposed by Dansgaard (1964) . A gradual decrease in lc-excess (or d-excess) values corresponds to an increase in soil evaporation level. The lc-excess and d-excess values were calculated as follows (Landwehr and Coplen, 2006 ):(2) d − e x c e s s = δ D − 8 × δ  18   O     (3) l c − e x c e s s = δ D − ( m  L   × δ  18   O + n  L    )      where m  L    denotes the slope of LMWL; n  L    , the intercept; and δD  and δ 18 O , the isotope ratios of hydrogen and oxygen in diverse water sources.  2.4.3 Quantification of soil evaporation losses The calculation of evaporative losses was based on the Craig-Gordon model (Craig and Gordon, 1965 ), which has been reformulated (Gonfiantini, 1986 ), as described by Fellman et al. The δD or δ18 O value of the initial water source, denoted as δ  p    , was determined by computing the intercept at the intersection point between the local meteoric water line (LMWL) and the SEL (Javaux et al., 2016 ) in the Heihe River source areas.
