Because of the limited number of precipitation sampling, we considered the previously established relationship between the isotopic composition of precipitation, longitude, and altitude during the same sampling period in the southern slope region of Qilian Mountains (δ18 O = 0.395 * longitude – 0.003 * altitude – 37.14 (R² = 0.88), δD = 3.683 * longitude – 0.018 * altitude – 362.373 (R² = 0.81)), simulating isotopic values of precipitation at each sampling point. The value of x  varies between 0.6 and 1, contingent upon the difference between the calculated LEL measurement and the estimated value. Calculations for all the aforementioned formulas were performed using Hydrocalculator  (Skrzypek et al., 2015 ) (http://hydrocalculator.gskrzypek.com ), yielding two sets of outcomes: one with x  set to 1 and the other with adjusted x  values. Finally, due to the sensitivity of the soil evaporation results to parameter variations, based on a grassland dataset, we conducted a sensitivity analysis on the input data as a case study.  2.4.4 Factor analysis based on Geodetector and redundancy analysis Geodetector is a tool for analyzing spatial stratified heterogeneity. It is mainly used to evaluate the explanatory power of a single factors and paired factors on the spatial variation of lc-excess values. The interaction detection quantifies the explanatory capacity of the novel factor layer generated by spatially overlaying two pre-existing factor layers, and the results were quantified by q values. The calculation is as follows (Wang and Xu, 2017 ):(9) q = 1 − 1 N σ  2    ∑ z = 1  L  N  z   σ  2  z       Where q  is the explanatory power; L  , the stratification of environmental factors; N  andN  z    , the number of the entire area and the z layer; σ  2   andσ  2  z   , the variances of the values of the dependent variables in the study area and the z layer. The Geodetector model mainly analyzes discrete variables, matching variable X (impact factors) and variable Y (lc-excess). and Geodetector was run through the “GD package” in the R software to maximize the acquisition of q values. This model is widely employed in various fields, including ecology (Shen et al., 2015; Han et al., 2021 ), plants (Li et al., 2022 ) and land use (Ren et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2022 ). Redundancy analysis (RDA) was employed to analyze the constraints in the relationship between lc-excess, d-excess, and environmental factors. The selection of RDA for ranking purposes and the application of the Monte Carlo test were aimed at assessing the significance of environmental factors in the spatial variations of the lc-excess and d-excess values following trend analysis. In additional, the effects of climate, soil, vegetation, and topographic factors on the similarity in the spatial distribution of the SW lc-excess values were quantitatively evaluated through variance partitioning analysis (VPA). VPA involved a forward selection method combined with R software to gradually eliminate factors with low correlation with lc-excess values, followed by replacement tests.  2.4.5 Statistical analysis SW and precipitation samples were collected in 2018 and 2019, respectively. Significance analysis was conducted using the Origin 2024 software to compare interannual and inter land use type differences in soil and precipitation isotopes. This was done to enhance the representativeness of the subsequent indications of SW evaporation.    3 Results 3.1 Stable isotopic compositions and lc-excess values of various water bodies The SW stable isotopic compositions in 2018 exhibited depletion compared with those in 2019, with average δ18 O values of −7.33 ‰ and −7.08 ‰ and average δD values of −50.92 ‰ and −48.57 ‰, respectively. There were no significant interannual differences in SW stable isotopes (P  > 0.05). The SEL in the Heihe River source area was expressed as δD = 6.03δ18 O–6.6 (R2  = 0.95, P  < 0.01). The range in SW δ18 O spanned −13.00 ‰ to −0.33 ‰, with a mean of −7.28 %, whereas the δD value ranged from −92.16 ‰ to −18.67 ‰, with a mean of −50.83 ‰. Precipitation exhibited a wider range of values than SW, with mean values of −7.60 ‰ for δ18 O and −47.55 ‰ for δD. Groundwater isotopes exhibited a low and steady variation. Across all soil layers, the δD and δ18 O values of SW initially increased and then decreased with soil depth, with significant enrichment observed at a 25 cm depth. The lc-excess values gradually increased from −10 ‰ to −7.08 ‰ with increasing soil depth ( Table 1 ). The mean values of SW stable isotopes were compared across four land use types, suggesting enrichment for cropland and depletion for shrubs, which are likely related to soil porosity and root distribution. SW stable isotope composition under all land use types lay below the LMWL ( Fig. 2 ), with shrubland exhibiting the smallest deviation, followed by forest land, cropland, and grassland. The slope and intercept of SEL under different land use types showed a similar trend, with larger slopes corresponding to larger intercepts. In additional, the lc-excess values were consistently above −10 ‰.  3.2 Spatial variation patterns of oxygen stable isotope and lc-excess values in SW The SW δ18 O values exhibited a pattern of gradual increase followed by a decrease from the southeast to the northwest. In the midwest region, the δ18 O values were significantly elevated, whereas in the northwest and eastern regions, the values were lower (Fig. S1 ). The high-value area is the downstream of Yeniugou River and Babao River, whereas the low-value area is located in the upper reaches of rivers with higher elevation. The spatial variation of SW isotope values from the surface to the deeper layers exhibited a depletion trend, unlike the spatial distribution of lc-excess values ( Fig. 3 ).  Fig. 4  depicted the vertical variation of SW stable isotopes under different land use types. Beneath forest land, the isotopic composition in surface soil exhibited a decreasing trend, with an inflection point observed at 10–20 cm, followed by enrichment of heavy isotopes in deeper layers. Conversely, the surface isotopes in the other three land use types showed varying degrees of increase, with an inflection point at the 20–30 cm soil layer, gradually depleting SW heavy isotopes in deeper layers, eventually reaching relative stability.  3.3 Evaporation estimates and sensitivity analysis We estimated the SW evaporation losses for different land use types ( Fig. 5 a) and compared with the corresponding lc-excess values (Fig. 5 b). The ranking of soil evaporation losses across land use types was cropland > grassland > forest land > shrubland, based on x = 1 and 0.6 ≤  x ≤  0.67 (Table S2 ). The SW lc-excess values ranked as shrubland > cropland > forest land > grassland (Fig. 5 b). Although cropland exhibited the highest lc-excess values, its corresponding evaporation losses were not the lowest (Fig. 5 a, b). From the perspective of soil layers, soil evaporation generally showed a decreasing trend with increasing depth (Fig. 5 a), whereas the lc-excess values exhibited a gradually increasing trend (Fig. 5 b). The computed results were subjected to sensitivity analysis (Table S3 ). It can be observed that the soil evaporation losses exhibited low sensitivity to TMP variations. When x  = 1, TMP increases of 1°C and 5°C led to ∼0.14 % and ∼0.31 % changes in f  (δ18 O) and ∼0.19 % and ∼0.95 % changes in f  (δD). When considering the adjusted x  values (0.6 ≤ x  ≤ 0.61), TMP increases of 1°C and 5°C led to ∼0.07 % and ∼0.35 % changes in f  (δ18 O) and ∼0.16 % and ∼0.81 % changes in f  (δD). However, RH exerted a substantial impact on soil evaporation losses. When based on x  = 1 and the adjusted x  values, a 10 % change in RH ultimately resulted in ∼2.64 % and ∼3.67 % changes in f . TMP and RH data were extracted from remote sensing imagery, and the isotopic composition of precipitation at each sampling point was obtained through linear regression. The variability of these parameters contributes to the uncertainty in the estimation of soil evaporation losses.  3.4 Influencing factors of SW lc-excess values Factor analysis was conducted to assess the spatial distribution of lc-excess values across soil layers in the Heihe River source area. The high q values of NDVI, RH, SWC, and TMP were identified as the primary influencing factors of lc-excess values, as shown in Fig. S2 . Surface (0–20 cm) lc-excess values were mainly influenced by TMP, PET, and LST (Fig. S2a , b), whereas deeper soil layers (30–50 cm) were influenced by NDVI, RH, TMP, and SWC (Fig. S2c -e). The influence of NDVI on the SW lc-excess values increased with soil depth, whereas the influence of TMP remained stable. SW lc-excess values were influenced by multiple factors, and a single factor may not sufficiently explain the variations in the Heihe River source area. The results indicated that interactions between various factors significantly enhance understanding of lc-excess values, both in bivariate and nonlinear aspects. The paired factors with the highest enhancement effect at different soil depths were as follows: the interaction value of WS∩BDA reached 0.75 followed by SLP∩LAT (q = 0.64) for the 0–10 cm soil layer (Fig. S2a ); 0.67 for LST∩SWCB followed by PET∩SWCB (q = 0.66) for the 10–20 cm soil layer (Fig. S2b ); 0.75 and 0.71 for RH∩SWCC and RH∩AI for the 20–30 cm soil layer, respectively; and 0.71 (Fig. S2c ) for the 30–40 cm soil layer; the interaction value of RH∩AI reached 0.83, followed by RH∩BDD and LST∩BDD (q = 0.81) (Fig. S2d ). For the 40–50 cm soil layer, the interaction values of LAT∩SWCE and LAT∩DEM reached 0.85 and 0.8, respectively (Fig. S2e ). As regards SW lc-excess mean value (Fig. S2f ), NDVI emerges as the main driving factor with the most significant explanatory capability for soil evaporation (q = 0.54). Nevertheless, the maximum contribution of the interaction between NDVI and other influencing factors such as SWC reached only 72 %, falling short of the 82 % contribution attributed to the interaction between LST (q = 0.23) and SWC (q = 0.43). This result indicated that while each influence factor may have limited explanatory power, their interactions substantially amplify the spatial impact on soil evaporation. Furthermore, RDA analysis was conducted to detect spatial variations in lc-excess values. The key explanatory factors varied for different land use types, with the SWC (68 %, p  = 0.014) being significant in forest land (Fig. S3a ), PRE (73.3 %, p  = 0.008) and LST (16.3 %, p  = 0.03) in shrubland (Fig. S3b ), TMP (23.2 %, p  = 0.01) and SWC (14.2 %, p  = 0.02) in grassland (Fig. S3c ), and AI (45 %, p  = 0.004) and ASP (44.6 %, p  = 0.07) in cropland (Fig. S3d ). The analysis revealed negative correlations between lc-excess (or d-excess) and PET, TMP, AI, and LST but positive correlations with DEM, SWC, RH, NDVI, ASP, WS, and LUT in the source area (Fig. S3e ). The VPA analysis identified the contributions of different sets of environmental factors to the spatial variation of lc-excess values ( Fig. 6 ), with 60.17 % attributed to the source area, 92.46 % to forested areas, 99.57 % to shrublands, 50.67 % to grasslands, and 88.44 % to croplands. Specifically, soil (SWC and BD) and climate (RH and LST) mainly explained the spatial variation of the SW lc-excess values in grassland (Fig. 6 d). Soil (SWC, BD) in forest land (Fig. 6 b), whereas climatic factors in shrubland (Fig. 6 c). Topographic (ASP) and climate factors (AI and RH) in cropland (Fig. 6 e).   4 Discussion 4.1 Spatial patterns of SW stable isotopes and soil evaporation Enrichment patterns of δ18 O values and dilution patterns of lc-excess at low elevations in the source area (Fig. S1a nd Fig. 3 ). This can be attributed to the intense evaporation of the soil. Similar findings were evident in research conducted by Sprenger et al. (2017a)  and Yong et al. (2020) . However, the spatial heterogeneity of the lc-excess values in shallow SW at the hillslope scale was not considered to be the main factor contributing to the variability of δD values. this inconsistency may have stemmed from variations in SW mixing across different seasons and study scales (Liu et al., 2022 ). Consequently, a comprehensive large-scale sample collection is indispensable for the regional-scale investigations of soil evaporation. The lc-excess values at nearly all soil sampling depth were below 0 in Heihe River source area, indicating a signal related to soil evaporation fractionation. Similar findings were reported by McCutcheon et al. (2016)  in a high-latitude northern environment, where the SW fractionation signal extended to a 70 cm depth. Conversely, Sprenger et al. (2017a)  found that soil evaporation may be limited to the upper 15 cm. In humid regions, soil evaporation fractionation signals mainly occur in the topsoil, whereas arid environments shift the evaporation signal to deeper soil layers (Barnes and Allison, 1988; Sprenger et al., 2016 ). The fluctuation range of precipitation isotope values was broader than that of SW, and the mean isotopic values at the soil surface were closer to the mean precipitation isotope values (Table 1 ). These findings suggested that SW recharge was influenced not only by precipitation but also by soil evaporation, and pre-precipitation mixing (Tang and Feng, 2001 ). Moreover, the groundwater δ18 O values ranged from −9.59 ‰ to −6.66 ‰, whereas the δD values ranged from −57.82 ‰ to −40.06 ‰; the groundwater line intersects with the atmospheric precipitation line (Fig. S4a ). This is consistent with the findings of Li et al. (2019) , who noted that the inland groundwater in Central Asia originates from precipitation. The SW isotopic compositions at a depth of 40–50 cm closely resembled the LMWL, with δD and δ18 O values ranging from −92.16 ‰ to −25.41 ‰ and −13.00 ‰ to −1.00 ‰, respectively (Table 1 ). Considering that groundwater is buried at depths ranging from 10 to 90 m (Liu et al., 2000 ), it is apparent that groundwater has a minimal contribution to SW recharge. To some extent, the lc-excess values can characterize soil evaporation, when SW δD and δ18 O deviated from the LMWL and the SW is recharged by precipitation other than other water bodies (Zhan et al., 2019 ). Therefore, soil evaporation signals as characterized by lc-excess values can reach 50 cm below the surface. The δ18 O and SW lc-excess values in the 0–30 cm of the Heihe River source area showed significant fluctuations (Fig. 4  and Fig. 5 ) and deviated from the LMWL (Fig. S4a ) compared to deeper soil depths (30–50 cm). Moreover, the higher SW δD and δ18 O values were found in the deeper soil layers (40–50 cm) of forest land than those in the surface soils (Fig. 4 ). The SW stable isotope composition from shrubland, grassland, and cropland all exhibited a distinct transition point in the 20–30 cm layer (Fig. 4 ). These finding indicated that precipitation infiltration drives the downward movement of mixed water. These results aligned with the vertical distribution patterns of SW stable hydrogen isotopes was observed by Brunel et al. (1997) and Chen et al. (2009) , confirming the presence of piston flow (Gazis and Feng, 2004 ). A common observation across these studies was the remarkable variation in soil hydrogen and oxygen isotope compositions with depth, with vegetation cover and anthropogenic factors collectively decreasing the rate of precipitation infiltration. Considering the lc-excess values across different land use types at various depths, a decrease was observed in the 30–40 cm soil layer under conifer trees and shrubs. Conversely, grassland exhibited a decreasing trend mainly in the 0–20 cm layer, possibly due to the distribution of plant roots. The root system extended from 0 to 60 cm in forest land (Zhu et al., 2022 ) and from 0 to 40 cm in shrubland (Liu et al., 2008 ). Herbaceous plants have their root systems predominantly located at depths greater than 20 cm below the surface (Rodriguez-Iturbe et al., 2001 ), characterized by staggered and densely distributed root growth contributing to water retention. Similar observations were obtained in the Qilian Mountains (Gui et al., 2023 ), where a higher evapotranspiration rate within the plant’s water supply layer led to even more negative values.  4.2 Comparison of soil evaporation loss under different land use types By comparing soil evaporation loss with SW lc-excess values in different land use types, we found that cropland exhibited the highest soil evaporation loss, which may be due to the amplification of the evapotranspiration capacity of crops during the rainy season (Liao et al., 2021 ). However, its corresponding lc-excess value was not the lowest. This discrepancy may be attributed to the dilution of the soil evaporation fractionation effect by precipitation inputs, leading to an increase in lc-excess value. Generally, SW lc-excess values are used to represent soil evaporation intensity, reflecting cumulative soil evaporation loss over an extended period (Sprenger et al., 2016, 2017a ). Lyu and Wang (2021)  found rainfall on the sampling day and the infiltration of upper SW with low lc-excess values may affect the ability of lc-excess to indicate soil evaporation. Existing researches also confirmed that soil evaporation loss and soil evaporation intensity can be inconsistent under certain conditions. Sprenger et al. (2018)  noted that instantaneous SWC, soil evaporation, and precipitation inputs can disrupt the linear relationship between soil evaporation and SW lc-excess values (Sprenger et al., 2017a ). Che et al. (2020)  found that increased SW lc-excess values were related to precipitation infiltration. Hervé-Fernández et al. (2016)  found that during the rainy season in south-central Chile, SW lc-excess values increased and approached zero due to the input of unfractionated precipitation. These cases highlight the sensitivity of SW lc-excess values to external factors like precipitation inputs. Therefore, when using lc-excess values to represent evaporation intensity, it is crucial to consider the weather conditions during the sampling period, especially in cropland areas that are subject to human disturbance and loose soil conditions (Liu et al., 2021 ). The soil evaporation losses in the order of cropland, grassland, forest land, and shrubland. Previous research in the HRB has also reported higher soil evaporation in cropland compared to grassland and forest land (Wang et al., 2021 ), corroborating our findings. Xu et al. (2021)  estimated daily soil evaporation rates in the HRB, finding that cropland was dominated by maize exhibited the highest soil evaporation (1.72 mm/day), followed by alpine meadows (1.58 mm/day), with shrubs (0.97 mm/day) slightly exceeding forest land (0.88 mm/day). To explain the lower soil evaporation loss in shrubland compared to forest land in this study, several reasons were provided. Firstly, during the growing season, the leaf area index for the major vegetation types ranks as follows: shrubland (1.1) > coniferous forest (0.9) > grassland and meadow (0.8) > sparse alpine vegetation (0.3), peaking at 3200 m altitude (Liu et al., 2017 ), which inhibited soil evaporation in the shrubland (Jiang et al., 2022 ). Secondly, rainfall during the wet season may affect RH under specific conditions, thereby influencing soil evaporation losses. Shrubland is distributed at a higher elevation (3271.5 m) compared to coniferous forest (3103.65 m). During the study period, the average rainfall in the shrubland (128.33 mm) exceeded that in the forest land (122.28 mm), and the RH in the shrubland (73.10 %) was significantly higher than in the forest areas (69.12 %). The dense canopy cover, higher PRE, and RH in shrubland areas suggested a weaker exchange of soil moisture with atmospheric vapor, thereby reducing soil evaporation losses. This relationship between high atmospheric humidity and reduced soil water evaporation has also been documented by Sprenger et al. (2018)  and Zhang et al. (2011) . Similarly, Yong et al. (2020)  reported higher soil evaporation losses in subalpine shrubland (20–30 %) in the foothill areas compared to spruce forests on the hillside (10–15 %) and alpine meadow at the mountain top (15–20 %) in the Xiying River Basin on the northern slope of the Qilian Mountains. Additionally, our results showed that soil evaporation losses in grassland are close to those in forest areas, consistent with Yong et al. (2020) . Grassland covered a wide area, and soil samples were collected from the entire source region of the Heihe River (Fig. 1 b). The extent of soil evaporation loss in different grassland regions varied due to influences such as vegetation cover (Zhang et al., 2022 ), climate (Lyu et al., 2021 ), and altitudinal gradients (Ding et al., 2024 ). In contrast, forest distribution is more concentrated, primarily around the Qilian County (Fig. 1 b), with soil evaporation less affected by elevation and terrain differences. Consequently, this study reflected the overall soil evaporation loss, thus diminishing the extremities soil evaporation losses in grassland.  4.3 Influence of climate, soil, topography, and vegetation on soil evaporation The SW lc-excess values primarily depend on NDVI in the Heihe River source area, with pNDVI  = 0.54 (Fig. S2f ). This phenomenon could be attributed to the influence of vegetation cover on soil-atmosphere moisture exchange (Rothfuss and Brüggemann, 2015; Che et al., 2020; Han et al., 2023 ). The positive correlation between the NDVI values and lc-excess values indicates that areas with better vegetation cover experience lower demand for soil evaporation (Fig. S3e ). Moreover, previous research has suggested that NDVI initially increases and then decreases with altitude, reaching a peak value between 3000 and 3300 m (Yuan et al., 2021 ). Forest land and shrubland areas with higher NDVI value exhibited the lower soil evaporation losses than cropland and grassland. A global meta-analysis highlighted the importance of soil moisture in controlling soil evaporation, with surface soil moisture availability being a key factor (Sun et al., 2019 ). Apart from SWC (pSWC  = 0.43), TMP (pTMP  = 0.35) also played a secondary role, as supported by Zhu et al. (2022) . SWC and TMP were also key factors affecting soil evaporation for grassland (Fig. S3c ). With increasing altitude, TMP decreases and SWC rises, lc-excess value increases (Fig. S3c , e). Notably, SWC and lc-excess showed a positive correlation. This contradicts the findings from site-scale studies, where higher SW availability resulted in stronger soil evaporation in shrub (Cavanaugh et al., 2011 ), pine forest (Raz-Yaseef et al., 2010 ), and eucalyptus forest (Mitchell et al., 2009 ). This suggests the limitations in the application of site-scale knowledge in understanding regional-scale processes. Additionally, environmental factors influencing soil evaporation shifted with varying soil depths (Xiang, 2021 ). Deeper soil evaporation was more strongly influenced by NDVI compared with topsoil, possibly due to the buffering effects of upper soil layers on climate factors like LST (Yang et al., 2015 ). In forest land, soil factors played a significant role in influencing soil evaporation (Fig. 6 b). SWC emerged as the primary controlling factor (Fig. S3a ) and showed a positive correlation with SW lc-excess values. This is attributed to the reduction in equilibrium fractionation during soil evaporation due to the soil tension effect as soil moisture increases, and the decreased water supply for soil evaporation caused by vegetation transpiration. Lyu and Wang (2021)  reported similar findings in the forest areas. Soil evaporation in cropland was notably influenced by the AI and ASP (Fig. S3d ). Primary crops such as barley and rapeseed are planted on sunny and shaded slopes, respectively, in croplands, aligning with the growth preferences of these plants. Cropland had the lowest SWC compared to the other three land use types (Fig. S4b ). Furthermore, the higher evaporation losses in areas with a higher AI, which may further lead to water shortages for crops during growth (Jiao et al., 2023 ). The soil evaporation was primarily controlled by PRE and LST in shrubland. PRE was negatively correlated with lc-excess values, consistent with the findings of Hasselquist et al. (2018) . Shrubland had a higher leaf area index and intercepted precipitation, leading to an increase in SW lc-excess values. Additionally, the higher LST result in stronger energy flux between the surface soil and the atmosphere (Song et al., 2022 ), also negatively correlating with lc-excess values.  4.4 Limitations and future perspectives This study has revealed spatial variations and key influencing factors of soil evaporation. However, when using SW lc-excess values to represent evaporation intensity, it is essential to consider the weather conditions during the sampling period, particularly for croplands with loose soils that are highly susceptible to precipitation infiltration. Moreover, the quantitative assessment methods for regional soil evaporation based on sample collection are limited. Soil evaporation losses are closely associated with temperature and RH, thus reflecting conditions during the study period only. In addition, obtaining empirical data in mountain regions is challenging. Using remote sensing data (such as TMP and RH) and δA  data corrected by LEL increases uncertainties in the estimates. Nevertheless, soil evaporation calculations using Hydrolcalculator  are still considered to be among the most reliable for estimating under-canopy soil evaporation (Skrzypek et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2021 ). The identified key factors through VPA cannot account for 50.67 % and 11.56 % of the variations in grassland and cropland, respectively (Fig. 6 d, e), highlighting the need for a more comprehensive selection. Factors affecting soil evaporation are complex, encompassing precipitation, air temperature, groundwater depth, soil temperature and texture, and vegetation greenery (Or et al., 2013; Gaj and McDonnell, 2019; Jiang et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2024 ). Human-induced disturbances, particularly in croplands, also play a significant role (Wang et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2021 ). The rapid development of animal husbandry and tourism has led to changes in soil texture and porosity due to grazing and trampling (Sirimarco et al., 2023 ), resulting in higher soil consolidation (Chyba et al., 2014 ), which affects the SW evaporation dynamics (Wang et al., 2015 ). Future research should scientifically select representative environmental variables, such as soil temperature and vegetation cover, to improve the explanatory power for soil evaporation. Observational data with higher spatial and temporal resolutions are crucial for assessing accuracy and reliability. Furthermore, model integration is essential for estimating soil evaporation losses and identifying the main controlling factors. Integration with relevant expert knowledge is essential for fostering a deeper understanding of soil moisture variation patterns.   5 Conclusion This study elucidated the spatial variation characteristics of soil evaporation in the Heihe River headwaters area and evaporation losses across different land use types, demonstrating the soil evaporation patterns and influencing factors in alpine mountains at the regional scale. The results indicated a gradual increase and then a decrease in soil evaporation from the southeast to the northwest, with NDVI acting as the priority controlling factor. Soil evaporation decreased with an increase in soil depth, and evaporation signals did not disappear within 50 cm. Among the land use types, croplands and grasslands experienced higher evaporation losses than forest lands and shrublands, with PRE and SWC mainly controlling shrublands and forest lands whereas TMP and SWC influencing grasslands. The AI and ASP positively affected soil evaporation in croplands. However, several limitations (or future research directions) still existed in the study. Firstly, soil evaporation estimation only reflected conditions during specific sampling periods and might not have captured temporal variation. Secondly, high-resolution observational data, including TMP, RH, and isotopic values of moisture in ambient air, are still needed to enhance calculation accuracy and assess soil evaporation at various spatial and temporal scales. Thirdly, scientifically selected environmental variables were crucial for identifying the main controlling factors of soil evaporation. Nevertheless, these findings suggested better management strategies that, continuous long-term drought monitoring and investment in water-saving technology research were essential to prevent drought-induced water scarcity for crop growth, especially for farmland with high evaporation losses. Ensuring the vitality and sustainability of grasslands and forest lands requires the maintenance of forest vegetation and strengthening of forest management. Moreover, implementing appropriate grazing management measures, such as artificial grass planting and rest-grazing management, was indispensable for preserving the health and density of grasslands. 1 Introduction Floods are severe natural disaster caused by heavy precipitation, rapid melt of ice and snow, storm surges, and other natural factors. In terms of frequency of occurrence and extent of impact, floods have consistently been the most wide-reaching disaster affecting human society (Mondal et al., 2023; Shah et al., 2020 ). According to statistics, flood disasters accounted for 44.28 % among various natural disaster events worldwide from 2000 to 2019, the population affected by floods comprise 41 % of the total affected population, making floods the most prevalent type of natural disaster (CRED and UNISDR, 2020 ). Moreover, with the ongoing changes in global climate, the frequency of various extreme weather events, particularly heavy rainfall, is continually increasing (Hallegatte et al., 2013; Shrestha et al., 2023 ). This further escalates the threat of flood disasters (Hirabayashi et al., 2013 ). Although flood disasters are typically challenging to fully mitigate (Puzyreva and de Vries, 2021 ), they can be partially mitigated by implementing strategies such as classifying floods based on their risk level, educating the public about flood disasters, optimizing evacuation routes, and utilizing numerical modeling to predict floods (Cai et al., 2019; Jia et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2023 ). Among these, flood numerical modeling largely entails collecting hydrological, meteorological, and underlying surface data in the study area, and then developing appropriate numerical models. Following the calibration of parameters, it is possible to retrospectively assess past floods in the region or predict future flood episodes. This improves the ability to forecast floods, hence decreasing the range of hazards connected with them (Zang et al., 2022 ). Presently, the predominant numerical models employed for simulating floods mostly consist of hydrological models and hydrodynamic models. Hydrological models require more parametric analysis and are generally appropriate for simulating rainfall-flood processes on a larger scale (Felder et al., 2017; Wen et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2013 ). Although they are generally effective, these systems may have difficulties in acquiring vital data, such as water depth and flow velocity in specific critical zones, which are essential factors for evaluating flood hazards. On the other hand, hydrodynamic models are commonly used to simulate flood processes on a smaller scale. They can accurately provide hydraulic elements, such as the water depth and velocity, at any location within the area. However, utilization of high-precision DEM data is essential for their operation, but acquiring such data might be difficult. Additionally, when employed for calculations on a larger scale, they encounter efficiency obstacles (Li et al., 2023; Moghim et al., 2023 ). Therefore, coupling these two models to simulate large-scale flood issues has become a research hotspot in recent years, with numerous scholars have conducted related studies (Cheng et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2012; Mignot and Dewals, 2022; Munar et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2022 ). Narrow-valley cities are widely distributed in the Loess Plateau region of northern China. The presence of extensive soil erosion has resulted in the formation of rough terrain, marked by the presence of numerous gullies and broken surfaces (Yu et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2022 ). Compared to towns and rural areas, urban areas often have higher population and economic density, along with a large amount of infrastructure. As a result, cities are more vulnerable to experiencing higher levels of damage in the case of a flood disaster (Luo et al., 2022 ). This characteristic is particularly evident in towns with narrow valleys, as a significant portion of their metropolitan areas are located on flat river terrace. These terraces tend to have dense populations and high level of economic activity. Additionally, the close proximity of urban areas to watercourses, floods in these watercourses are more likely to impact the regular operation of the city. The specific arrangement of the city not only results in unique flood characteristics but also places greater requirements on flood control measures within the city. This study selected a representative narrow-valley city located on the Loess Plateau in northern China as a case study. A hydrodynamic-hydrological coupling model was employed for modeling purposes. Evaluation indicators such as flood inundated area, disaster losses, duration of inundation, and the volume of overbank flow were chosen. The study analyzed the disaster characteristics of floods in narrow-valley cities and assessed the flood control effects of different flood control measures and their combinations. The remaining sections of this paper are as follows: Section 2  provides an introduction to the research background. Section 3  mainly introduces the hydrological model, hydrodynamic model, their coupling method, as well as the acquisition of rainfall data and the calculation method for flood disaster losses. Section 4  presents and analyzes the simulation results. Section 5  discusses the analysis of the results. Finally, Section 6  draws concise conclusions. The results of this study can be used as a valuable reference for flood modeling in narrow-valley urban areas, thereby enhancing the comprehension of flood characteristics and the development of effective prevention and control strategies in such cities.  2 Study area and data sets The study area selected in this paper is located in a basin of the Loess Plateau in northern Shaanxi Province, China. The location map is shown in Fig. 1  . The topography within the study area primarily consists of mountains, valleys, urban areas, and river channels, with specific land cover including buildings, roads, and vegetation. The river section within the urban area represents a typical narrow-valley type, with a width ranging between 100 m and 145 m, and a longitudinal slope of approximately 0.002. This area exemplifies a typical narrow-valley urban area in the gully region. To mitigate the flood damage caused by this mode of urban development, local authorities want to deploy various flood mitigation measures along the river. Fig. 2   depicts the DEM (Digital Elevation Model) map of this basin. Upon evaluating the flooding composition of the local urban areas, it becomes apparent that when rainfall occurs in this basin, the flooding mostly consists of two components: (1) The inflow from the upper reaches of the main river stream (depicted in pink in the Fig. 2 , accounting for 70 % of the entire upstream). (2) The local inflow from the upstream section of the urban area (shown in green in Fig. 2 , accounting for the remaining 30 % of the entire upstream). To effectively control the flow from these two sources, the proposal is to construct two reservoirs in the upstream area, distant from the city. Additionally, a flood diversion channel is planned at the river bend before it reaches the city, along with dredging the river in the urban section and raising the embankment. However, the efficacy of these strategies in enhancing local flood protection and reducing flood damage remains uncertain. Therefore, conducting precise simulations of local flood processes and assessing the impacts of various flood control measures are crucial to mitigating local flood disasters and guiding project construction. As mentioned in the introduction, the commonly used modeling methods currently include hydrological models and hydrodynamic models, each with its own advantages and disadvantages. Therefore, establishing a rational flood model based on the geomorphological features of the watershed is pivotal to addressing this issue. When analyzing the DEM map in Fig. 2 , it is evident that most areas of the basin are mountainous and consist of gullies, which are largely uninhabited. Rainfall runoff in these areas will flow into the adjacent gullies, subsequently discharging to the downstream outlet and entering the main river. In these areas, the dynamic process of surface water is less important, with the discharge process of the gully outlet being the primary consideration. Therefore, a hydrological model is highly suitable for modeling. This approach ensures accurate discharge while reducing the computational workload. Conversely, the urban area on the valley terrace has a concentrated population and economy, making it susceptible to flooding from the river's floodplain. Consequently, the surface hydraulic factor holds significant importance, necessitating the adoption of a hydrodynamic model to simulate the flood evolution and inundation process in this region. We introduced a coupling approach to integrate the hydrological and hydrodynamic models after applying them separately to simulate mountainous and urban regions. The detailed description of this specific method is provided in Section 3 . The validity of the coupled model was assessed by comparing it with actual flood processes. Subsequently, the validated model was used to simulate and analyze flood processes in the basin.  3 Materials and methods In this paper, we construct a set of hydrodynamic-hydrological coupling models with better applicability in view of the geomorphological features mentioned in the context of the study. This section mainly introduces the principles and solutions of the hydrologic model and the hydrodynamic model and how to coupling the models. 3.1 Hydrological model The hydrological calculation module in this paper employs a distributed hydrological model. The basic spatial unit for basin runoff calculation is the catchment sub-area. Generally, the catchment area is divided into several sub-areas, and the runoff process is calculated separately based on the characteristics of each sub-area. Finally, the outflows from each sub-area are superimposed using flow routing methods. In the calculation process of the hydrological model, rainfall, evaporation, and infiltration are initially computed based on the characteristic parameters of the sub-catchment area. After runoff calculation, surface runoff is obtained. Subsequently, a nonlinear reservoir method is applied for basin routing calculation. To accommodate the calculation of different characteristic sub-catchment areas, the model divides the underlying surface of each sub-area into three parts: a permeable area, an impermeable area with depressions capable of storage, and an impermeable area without depressions for storage. The model calculates runoff separately from the three types of surfaces. The runoff hydrograph for the catchment sub-area is then obtained through area-weighted aggregation. The calculation of the infiltration process in the hydrological model employs the Horton infiltration model. The model employs the nonlinear reservoir method to simultaneously solve the Manning's equation and the continuity equation for each sub-area. The continuity equation is given by:(1) d v  d t   = A d d  d t   = A i - Q      In the equation, V = A × d , represents the total volume of the sub-watershed, m3 ; A  is the area of the sub-watershed, m2 ; d  is the water depth, m; t  stands for time, s; i  denotes net rainfall intensity, which indicates the difference between rainfall intensity and the intensities of evaporation and infiltration, mm/s. Q  represents the discharge at the outlet of the sub-watershed, m3 /s. Calculating the discharge at the outlet using the Manning's formula:(2) Q = 1.49 × W n  ( d - d p  )  5 3   S 1 2        In the equation, W  represents the width of the sub-watershed in meters, m; n  is the Manning coefficient of the sub-watershed; dp  stands for the detention depth in meters, m; S  denotes the slope.  3.2 Hydrodynamic model In this paper, a one-dimensional river network hydrodynamic model is employed to calculate the river flow. In the computations, the second-order accuracy in both time and space is ensured using the Runge-Kutta method and the MUSCL scheme. In the model coupling diagram shown in Fig. 3  , the green area represents a mountainous region, which is modeled using a hydrological model. A hydrodynamic model models the urban area, represented by the blue area in the diagram. The blue polyline represents the main confluence paths in the basin as determined by hydrological analysis, whereas the pink areas represent the main channels in the hydrodynamic model. The primary modeling procedure in this research is outlined as follows: (1) Initially, hydrological analysis is performed on the watershed using DEM data. Hydrological analysis methods are used to identify the main gullies and streams in the watershed, along with the locations of nodes where gullies converge into the main streams. (2) Establishing the computational bounds and delineating the regions for both the hydrological and hydrodynamic models. (3) The hydrological model directs the runoff flow into the flow channels of the hydrodynamic model by using the nodes where gullies converge into the main streams as coupling nodes. (4) The hydrodynamic model is employed to simulate the progression and inundation process of floods within urban areas, therefore determining the regions impacted by the floods. The digital elevation model (DEM) used in this study was obtained by interpolating the elevation data measured in 2021, and the grid size of the DEM is 5 m * 5 m. During each time step, the hydrological and hydrodynamic models are computed independently before exchanging information at the coupling node. The hydrological model calculates the flow process at the outlet of the gully, while the hydrodynamic model captures the flow evolution on the surface of a specific area. The specific calculation method for water exchange can be found in the research conducted by Li et al. (2022) , which offers comprehensive elucidations of the exchange procedure and the corresponding functions used. The hydrological model includes externally callable interface functions, such as data extraction and water exchange functions, which enable the coupling of models. These functions can be accessed by calling the DLL (Dynamic Link Library) of the hydrologic model in the code of the hydrodynamic model. The implementation of reservoir measures in the model is as follows: the shape of the reservoir was defined according to the water level-storage capacity curve from the reservoir data. The regulation effect of the reservoir on floods was realized by setting the water level-discharge curve for various return periods in the model, according to the design standards of the reservoir. This process alters the flood of the downstream channel due to the regulation of the reservoir. The diversion channel was set in the hydrodynamic model and implemented using an inner boundary method. The grid at the entrance of the diversion channel was designated as the inflow grid, and the grid at the outlet was designated as the outflow grid. This configuration allows water to flow directly from the entrance to the downstream outlet, bypassing the urban area and achieving flood control.  3.4 Generation of rainfall files for different recurrence periods The hydrodynamic-hydrological coupling model, as described in this study, is driven by rainfall data (Barbero et al., 2022 ). In order to obtain the 24-hour design rainfall pattern for different recurrence periods in the local area, daily precipitation data from 1951 to 2017, spanning a total of 67 years, was collected. The collected precipitation data was subjected to assessments to ensure its reliability, representativeness, and consistency. The annual maximum daily rainfall amounts were extracted as shown in Fig. 4  . Table 1   presents the results of a fitting process using the P-III curve to derive the 24-hour design rainfall for various recurrence periods, based on the collected actual rainfall data. Afterwards, specific 24-hour rainfall occurrences were selected from the actual sequence. The events were then scaled at different recurrence periods using the design rainfall as a benchmark, resulting in the creation of designed rainfall processes for different recurrence periods, as illustrated in Fig. 5  .  3.5 Flood disaster loss assessment methods This research evaluates the impact of floods by employing a range of indicators, as indicated earlier. This section primarily introduces the subsequent methods for calculating flood disaster losses. The evaluation of flood damage can be categorized into two main components: direct economic losses and indirect economic losses. Direct economic losses mainly involve damage to local homes, indoor properties, and farmland caused by flooding. Indirect economic losses mostly arise from secondary hazards, such as power and communication disruptions caused by flooding (Duan et al., 2022; Fuchs et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019 ). While calculating indirect losses is crucial in the comprehensive assessment of flood disasters, acquiring data for computing indirect losses presents challenges. This paper primarily focuses on studying the direct impact of floods on urban areas, as well as how various flood control measures can reduce this direct impact. Therefore, this article primarily focuses on calculating the direct economic losses caused by flooding. The key to calculating direct economic losses is to evaluate the rate of property loss for houses and indoor properties at different levels of inundation, determine the relationship between inundation depth and property loss rate, and then calculate the losses based on the results of the coupled model. We combined the previous research by scholars with our own investigation to obtain the rates of property damage for houses and indoor properties. The relationship between inundation depth and the rate of loss is depicted in Fig. 6   (Fan and Jiang, 2000; Yu, 2007 ). The specific formulas for calculating losses are outlined in Eqs.
