Fig. 7   displays the simulation results for the two floods, which are accompanied by river flow monitoring data. It can be observed that the river flow process simulated by the hydrodynamic-hydrological coupling model aligns well with the measured process. The NSE (Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency) values for the two floods are 0.859 and 0.929, both beyond the threshold of 0.5. This indicates that the constructed model is accurate and reasonable. However, a comparison between the simulated and measured flood processes also reveals that the measured flood process experiences faster rise and recession, with sharper and narrower flood peaks. In contrast, the simulated flood process exhibits a more gradual rise and recession. The observed discrepancies may arise multiple causes acting together, such as alterations in channel cross-sections caused by urban development over time, changes in bed roughness resulting from variations in underlying surface conditions, and other associated complexity. These factors contribute to a complex process. Despite the challenge of fully capturing real-world changes based on existing data and adjusting parameters within the current model, the model's ability to accurately depict local flood processes is apparent from the NSE values obtained from two flood events.  4.2 Flood disaster characteristics of narrow-valley city The flood processes and control modes in the narrow-valley city exhibit significant distinctions in comparison to other regions. Fig. 8   illustrates flood inundation scenarios for various recurrence intervals. The close closeness of these cities to rivers makes them vulnerable to frequent floods, which directly endanger the central portion of the city when it becomes flooded. Conversely, when facing floods with longer recurrence periods, the limited development space within the city leads to extensive inundation, lacking sufficient room for further propagation. This results in the flooding of nearly all river terraces and generates extremely high water depths, leading to severe disasters. It can be concluded that these types of cities exhibit a higher propensity to causing disasters when facing floods of the same magnitude compared to other regions. From the inundated area and depth depicted in Fig. 9  , it is evident that when the recurrence time increases, the pace at which the inundated area expands reduces progressively. This phenomenon is particularly prominent for recurrence periods exceeding 200 years, where the growth rate of inundated areas levels off noticeably, approaching a maximum value. This indicates that virtually all urban areas (river terraces) have already been inundated. However, due to the increasing magnitude of floods with higher recurrence periods, the water depth in the urban area continues to exhibit a rapid upward trend. This is because floodwaters that have breached the levees have no other outlet and continue to converge within the urban area. The inundation schematics in Fig. 8  visually confirm this. Once the recurrence periods beyond 200 years, there is minimal observable alteration in the inundated area, except for a consistent rise in water depth.  4.3 Analysis of flood disaster in different recurrence periods The simulation demonstrates a close correlation between flood severity and the recurrence period of rainfall. Fig. 10   illustrates the flow processes at the entrance of the urban river section under different recurrence period rainfall conditions. It is clear that when the recurrence period of rainfall increases, both the total rainfall and peak rainfall increase, resulting in an elevated flood peak. The reduced lag time between the flood peak and rainfall peak, as well as higher peak values and earlier occurrence times, significantly escalate the risk of the flood. However, relying solely on the peak flow rate to assess the severity of a flood is not comprehensive. Therefore, indicators such as inundated area and economic losses resulting from the flood are selected for evaluating flood severity (the calculation of inundated area excludes the area within the levees). Table 3   presents the inundated area, economic losses, and floodplain volume in the urban area under different recurrence period rainfall. When the recurrence period exceeds 20 years, the inundated area caused by floods significantly increases, subsequently leading to an increase in economic losses. Furthermore, the simulation reveals the following patterns: The depth and area of inundation in urban upstream, middle, and downstream areas increase with a higher recurrence period. However, the impact on the affected area in the upstream region is more sensitive to peak flow rates. This is because floods spread out from the river channel in the upstream area, reducing the flood peak flow rate and causing a decrease in flow entering the middle and downstream areas. This makes it more difficult for the floods to breach the levees. As shown in Fig. 8 , during a 20-year recurrence period of flood event, inundation occurs only in certain upstream areas. As the recurrence period increases, middle and downstream areas gradually experience inundation, and it is only when the flood recurrence period exceeds a hundred years that significant inundation occurs in the downstream area, aligning with the aforementioned pattern in order to confirm this pattern, as shown in Fig. 11  , eight representative locations on both sides of the urban river section in upstream, middle, and downstream areas (mainly schools, hospitals, government institutions, and other key sites) were selected. The maximum inundation depth and duration greater than 0.1 m during the entire flood process were extracted, and the averages for upstream, middle, and downstream areas were calculated individually. These averages serve as indicators of the area’s overall inundation situation. Fig. 12   displays the average inundation depth and duration in the upstream, middle, and downstream areas. It is evident that the average inundation depth in the upstream area significantly increases with an increase in the recurrence period. In contrast, in the middle and downstream areas, the increase is relatively small, with average depths noticeably lower than in the upstream area. Another pattern is observed in the inundation duration at various locations, revealing the flood disaster characteristics of narrow-valley cities. When the flood recurrence period is less than 30 years, the selected typical locations experience minimal inundation depth and duration due to the limited extent of overbank flow. However, floods with a recurrence period exceeding 30 years occur generate overbank flow. Due to the unique topography of these narrow-valley cities, the overbank flood rapidly inundates the entire river terrace, extending to the base of the mountain. This leads to a reduction in the increasing trend of inundation duration with larger recurrence periods. Additionally, while there is a significant difference in inundation depth, the average inundation duration at upstream, middle, and downstream locations shows little variation across different recurrence periods. This is because once overbank flooding occurs in narrow-valley cities and exceeds the flood control standards, there is no outlet for the excess water until after the flood peak has passed and re-enters the river channel. Thus, within the same flood event, the typical locations in upstream, middle, and downstream areas experience similar inundation durations, with slightly shorter durations in the middle and downstream areas compared to the upstream area.  4.4 Effects analysis of single flood control measures As mentioned in the introduction, the catastrophic floods in the local area are primarily consist of three elements. Management of these three constituent components should be the focus of efforts to address the flood control issue in the area. Specifically, reservoir construction, diversion channels, and river channel dredging will be employed to control each of these elements. The reservoir’s primarily function is to regulate the inflow from the main upstream tributaries. Diversion channels serve to control the inflow from the large upstream areas in the urban region, while dredging of the urban section of the river channel primary aimed at ensuring the channel's flood-carrying capacity and preventing stagnant water in the urban section. Using the hydrodynamic-hydrological coupling model mentioned in the previous section, simulations will be conducted for scenarios involving these individual facilities. Fig. 13  (a) to (c), respectively, depict the peak inundated area, economic losses, and inundation volume. They also illustrate the reduction rates for each measure compared to the current situation for floods with different recurrence periods. Fig. 13 (a) illustrates significant variations in the flood control effectiveness of different flood control measures. Among them, the river channel dredging measure exhibits the poorest performance in controlling floods across different recurrence periods. While it shows a relatively high reduction rate in inundated areas (over 60 %) for floods with a recurrence period less than 30 years, this reduction rate consistently falls below 30 % for floods with a recurrence period exceeding 30 years. For floods with a 200-year recurrence period, the reduction rate drops to less than 10 %, indicating a substantial loss of flood control capacity. The diversion channel measure offers superior flood control compared to river channel dredging, but its effectiveness diminishes with an increase in flood recurrence periods. It is noteworthy that the diversion channel measure demonstrates a noticeable increase in the reduction rate of inundated areas when facing floods with a recurrence period of 100 years, followed by a sharp decline. This phenomenon can be attributed to the design standards of the local diversion channels. According to these standards, diversion channels operate at full capacity only when upstream inflows reach the 100-year recurrence period criteria. Below this standard, they operate at partial capacity. When floods exceed the 100-year recurrence period, the diversion channels can no longer control the floods beyond their designed capacity. Therefore, the diversion channel measure only achieves a reduction rate of 13.15 % in the inundated area when facing a flood with a recurrence period of 200 years. The reservoir measure is the most efficient flood control measure of the three options. Under the simulated conditions of various flood recurrence periods in this study, the reduction rate in inundated area achieved by the reservoir measure consistently exceeds 40 %. While its flood control effectiveness is comparable to the diversion channel measure for recurrence periods less than 50 years, the reservoir measure outperforms significantly as the recurrence period increases. For instance, even with a flood recurrence period of 200 years, the reservoir measure still achieves a reduction rate of 46.36 % in the inundated area, maintaining a high level of flood control effectiveness.  4.5 Effects analysis of combination of flood control measures Based on the simulation results and previous analysis, it is evident that employing individual flood control measures can effectively manage the various components of floods. However, when the entire watershed experiences significant rainfall, several components of urban catastrophic floods occur simultaneously. Relying on individual measures proves challenging for achieving effective flood control, particularly for events with long recurrence periods. As outlined in Section 4.4 , the reduction rates of various flood disaster indicators from individual measures generally exhibit a decreasing trend with an increase in recurrence periods. When facing a flood with a recurrence period of 200 years, the reduction rates for the inundated area achieved by the reservoir, diversion channel, and river channel dredging measures have decreased to 46.36 %, 13.15 %, and 9.44 %, respectively. As shown in Fig. 13 (a), this indicates that there still exists a large extent of inundation, which falls short of meeting flood control requirements. Therefore, considering the combination of the aforementioned individual measures, i.e., simultaneously employing two flood control measures, we will examine the reduction in various disaster indicators brought about by the combination of flood control facilities. We will analyze the similarities and differences between the effectiveness of combined flood control measures and individual flood control measures. Table 4   lists the different combinations of flood control measures. Looking at the changes in inundated area from Fig. 14  (a), it is evident that for each recurrence period, the flood control effectiveness of any combination of two flood control measures is significantly superior to the effectiveness of individual measures. For instance, Combination 1, which consists of diversion channels and river channel dredging measures, exhibits a reduction rate in inundated area of only 21.07 % for floods with a recurrence period of 200 years due to the relatively weaker flood control capacities of these measures. However, for other recurrence periods, the reduction rates in inundated areas exceed 50 %, maintaining a consistently high level and showing a marked improvement compared to individual measures. Combination 2, comprising reservoir and river channel dredging measures, follows a trend in inundated area reduction similar to that of the individual reservoir measure. This is because measures like river channel dredging, which involve modifications, have a smaller flood control capacity compared to large-scale flood control facilities like reservoirs. However, due to the enhanced flow capacity of the urban section of the river channel brought about by the river channel dredging measure, there is an increase in the reduction rate in the inundated area compared to the individual reservoir measure for various recurrence periods. Combination 3, which combines reservoir and diversion channel measures, demonstrates outstanding flood control effectiveness. When facing floods with a recurrence period of less than 100 years, the reduction rate in the inundated area consistently exceeds 80 % (approaching 100 % for recurrence periods less than 30 years). Even when encountering a flood with a recurrence period of 200 years, the reduction rate in the inundated area is 77.38 %, remaining at a high level. This significantly reduces flood disasters in the area. As analyzed earlier, this phenomenon is attributed to the reservoir and diversion channel measures controlling the inflow from major tributaries upstream as well as the local inflow from the reservoir downstream to the entrance of the urban area. While the urban section of the river also experiences some inflow from tributaries and local inflow, these are of smaller magnitude. The vast majority of catastrophic floods are primarily caused by the inflow from major upstream tributaries and local inflow, both of which are effectively controlled by reservoir and diversion channel measures. Therefore, they maintain excellent flood control effectiveness across various recurrence periods.   5 Discussions 5.1 Hydrodynamic-hydrological coupling model Amid frequent global extreme natural disasters, watershed-scale flood disasters have gained increasing attention. Consequently, there has been notable development and application of various flood simulation models. These include hydrological, hydrodynamic, and coupled hydrodynamic-hydrological models. Hydrological models focus on large watersheds, offering quick simulations of main drainage paths but may lack accuracy in certain critical areas. Hydrodynamic models, designed for smaller areas, demand high-quality data but accurately depict the hydraulic characteristics. Yet they encounter efficiency challenges with large watersheds. To address the limitations of both models—computational accuracy in hydrological models, data requirements in hydrodynamic models, and efficiency in large-scale calculations—this study couples them. For instance, this study employs a coupled hydrodynamic-hydrological model in a narrow-valley urban watershed with varied terrains (mountainous and urban river valleys). It employs detailed hydrodynamic simulations in urban river valley areas, crucial for understanding surface water dynamics and specific inundation zones. Meanwhile, less critical hilly areas of the mountains utilize hydrological models to capture runoff processes. These models interconnect via a one-dimensional hydrodynamic model, reducing the computational grid in hydrodynamic simulations while ensuring accuracy and higher computational efficiency.  5.2 Flood disaster characteristics of narrow valley city Floods in narrow valley cities differ significantly from those in plain regions. Firstly, in these terrains, floods can result in more severe damage to urban areas. With a narrow layout, even smaller floods can immediately threaten the city once the water overflows embankments. During larger floods, due to limited space on river valley terraces, excess water inundates the urban area, resulting in significant water depths, which is less common in plains where floods have more space to spread. Secondly, in narrow valley cities, the inundation process correlates with urban spatial positioning. Flood severity tends to be higher in the upper urban reaches, gradually diminishing downstream. This pattern, evident in the Section 4.3  analysis, stems from the topography. These cities align along the main river, forming a narrow strip distinctly divided into upper, middle, and lower reaches. The larger floods initially spill over the embankments, inundating the upstream urban areas while simultaneously reducing the peak flow. As the flood progresses downstream, the peak gradually diminishes, alleviating hazards for the downstream urban areas. This analysis emphasizes that flood control strategies in such areas shouldn't rely solely on short-term solutions like levee elevation, which could pose risks downstream. Instead, the key to effectively preventing and controlling floods is to comprehensively consider local topographical features and establish an integrated flood control system.  5.3 Suggestions for urban flood control in the study area In the Section 2 , we analyzed the components of the floods in the region and identified three main parts. To mitigate flood disasters, efforts should focus on controlling these three components of floods. We found significant differences in the flood reduction capabilities of different flood control measures. When these flood control measures are combined pairwise, the effectiveness of any two engineering measures is notably better than individual measures. Among different combinations, the combination of reservoirs and flood diversion channels has the best flood control effect. This phenomenon, to some extent, illustrates that the catastrophic floods in this river are primarily composed of the convergence of large upstream tributaries and local inflow in the urban upstream area. Therefore, in the construction of flood control projects in such narrow valley cities, particular attention should be given to the upstream runoff. Large-scale flood control facilities like reservoirs and diversion channels can be constructed farther away from the urban areas in the upstream region to regulate this portion of the flow. In addition, when dealing with small floods, employing local measures such as dredging river channels and raising embankments plays a role in ensuring the hydraulic capacity of the rivers. Considering that their construction costs are usually relatively low, these measures can be considered as flood prevention options.   6 Conclusions The study employed a hydrodynamic-hydrological coupling model to simulate flood processes in a narrow-valley urban area and analyzed its flood control strategies. A typical narrow-valley urban area in northern China was chosen as a case study to demonstrate the model's suitability. The study investigated flood characteristics for different recurrence periods and evaluated the effectiveness of various flood control measures. The conclusions are as follows: (1) The hydrodynamic-hydrological coupling model effectively simulates floods in narrow-valley cities, validated with NSE values of 0.859 and 0.929 from two actual flood events, showing strong simulation performance. (2) Flood characteristics in narrow-valley cities differ from those in plain areas, mainly in post-inundation flood evolution and spatial disparities due to elongated topography. (3) Flood control measures vary in effectiveness, decreasing with higher recurrence periods. Reservoirs are most effective, followed by flood diversion channels and river channel dredging, reducing inundated areas by 46.36 %, 13.15 %, and 9.44 % respectively during a 200-year flood event. (4) Combining multiple flood control measures is more effective than individual approaches. Integrating reservoirs and flood diversion channels reduces inundated areas by 77.38 % during a 200-year flood event, indicating upstream activities significantly contribute to catastrophic floods. This research offers a modeling approach for simulating floods in narrow-valley cities and provides valuable insights for planning and designing flood control infrastructure.
1 Introduction Groundwater is the primary source of water for billions of people worldwide (Alley et al., 2002; Amanambu et al., 2020; Velis et al., 2017 ); it is used for drinking, food production, and industrial processing; and it is also critical to the health of ecosystems, such as wetlands and rivers (Scanlon et al., 2023 ). Most of the world's arid regions are entirely dependent on groundwater, and as an increasing number of water resources are polluted, overexploited and depleted, water scarcity poses a serious threat to ecosystems and the sustainable development of human societies (Dolan et al., 2021 ). Currently, more than half of all groundwater systems are experiencing overexploitation; groundwater levels in some countries are declining at a very dangerous rate (Famiglietti and Ferguson, 2021; Taucare et al., 2024; Udimal et al., 2017 ), and studies indicate that the rate of groundwater depletion is accelerating worldwide (Doell et al., 2014 ). Groundwater drought is defined as a sustained decrease in the groundwater level and a reduction in the flow of streams and wetlands into groundwater due to meteorological drought and groundwater exploitation, resulting in below-average groundwater availability (Gullacher et al., 2023; Van Lanen and Peters, 2000 ). Groundwater drought threatens human security by triggering many disasters, such as ground subsidence, seawater intrusion, desertification and wetland degradation (Herrera-Garcia et al., 2021 ). There are two common methods for determining groundwater drought; one is the threshold level approach based on long time series of groundwater levels (Van Lanen et al., 2013; Van Loon and Laaha, 2015 ) and the run theory approach, which uses standardized drought indices, such as the drought index based on groundwater storage anomalies (Liu et al., 2023b; Song et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2022 ) and the standardized groundwater level index (Gu et al., 2020a, 2020b; Guo et al., 2021 ). Meteorological drought often drives other types of drought (Li et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2019 ), and previous research has focused primarily on the propagation characteristics between meteorological drought and hydrological drought or agricultural drought. In recent years, the relationship between meteorological drought and groundwater drought has become a popular research topic. Han et al. (2021)  proposed a probabilistic framework to determine the propagation threshold from meteorological drought to groundwater drought based on copula theory and the Bayesian approach and analysed the influencing factors; the results showed that soil evaporation and catchment elevation were the main factors influencing the threshold. Groundwater is less sensitive to meteorological changes because of its storage conditions. The presence of vegetation, soil, rocks, etc., also contributes to slowing the dynamics of the groundwater level and storage (Van Lanen and Peters, 2000; Wossenyeleh et al., 2020 ), so many scholars have focused on the propagation time of groundwater drought (Gong et al., 2023; Peters et al., 2006; Tallaksen et al., 2009 ). Liu et al. (2023a)  investigated the propagation time between four drought types on a global scale by calculating Pearson's correlation coefficients based on the SPI, SSI, SRI, and GDI and found significant regional differences in propagation characteristics. The propagation from meteorological to groundwater drought also varies significantly on seasonal scales. Zhao et al. (2022)  evaluated the drought propagation time in the North China Plain using the directed information transfer index (DITI), which showed that the propagation time is long in winter and short in summer. Although the above studies provide valuable insights into the mechanisms and characteristics of drought propagation, most of them are based on large spatial and temporal scales, ignoring the differences in the evolution of drought processes at the monthly scale and the characteristics of basins. The relationship between groundwater and vegetation is complex and involves a dynamic balance between groundwater, soil, and vegetation. The correlation between the NDVI and groundwater depth and precipitation suggests that groundwater can buffer the effects of drought events on vegetation (Deng et al., 2022 ). The drought resistance of different types of vegetation also varies; for example, in subtropical regions, forests and agricultural land are more susceptible to drought than is grassland (Liao et al., 2023 ). Miguez-Macho and Fan (2021)  evaluated plant utilization of four types of water sources at different spatial and temporal scales and reported that globally, 29 % of plant transpiration globally relies on groundwater and past precipitation stored in unsaturated soils. These studies have revealed the mechanisms of vegetation and groundwater interactions, providing a strong basis for future research. However, there is still a lack of clarity regarding the mutual feedback between groundwater drought characteristics and vegetation, particularly for the differences between crops and natural vegetation. The Sanjiang Plain is a significant agricultural reclamation area in China. In the past few decades, with the continuous expansion of groundwater irrigation areas (Zhang et al., 2023 ), the original natural environment, which was dominated by forests, grasslands and wetlands, has been largely replaced by an artificial ecological environment dominated by farmland, a typical coupled system of ecological and arable land. The backwards surface water deployment facilities in the study area have led to the excessive exploitation and utilization of groundwater resources (Sun et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2016b ), which has seriously constrained the stable and sustainable development of local agriculture and weakened groundwater recharge to wetlands, resulting in further shrinkage of wetland areas (Zou et al., 2018 ). Although the annual precipitation in the Sanjiang Plain is relatively abundant, there is significant seasonal variation. Due to climate change, extreme weather events are occurring frequently (Ling et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2016 ), exacerbating the water resource crisis in the region, and seasonal droughts are of particular concern (Pei et al., 2024 ). The formation and evolution of groundwater droughts in the Sanjiang Plain are poorly understood, which hinders the effective utilization and management of groundwater, as well as the protection of wetlands and forests. To address the above research gaps, this study used the standardized groundwater drought index (SGDI) to evaluate the spatial and temporal characteristics of groundwater drought in a representative region of the Sanjiang Plain, considering both irrigated areas and nonirrigated areas as well as irrigated and non-irrigated periods. The potential relationship between groundwater drought and vegetation was explored from an interaction perspective, and the multiple timescale correlations between the different influencing factors and the SGDI were quantitatively revealed based on wavelet coherence analysis (WTC). On this basis, we determined the propagation time from meteorological to groundwater drought and the propagation thresholds of different drought levels and their influencing factors.  2 Study area and data 2.1 Study area The study area is in the high-latitude region of northeastern China, the core of the Sanjiang Plain ( Fig. 1 ), which slopes gently from the southwest to the northeast and has an elevation range of 34–100 m. The region has a temperate monsoon climate, with an average annual temperature of 2.8°C and annual precipitation ranging from 450 to 650 mm. Approximately 60 % of the year's precipitation occurs from June to August, and there are approximately 2400 to 2500 sunshine hours annually. The aquifer structure in the study area is single, and there are loose sediments, such as sand and gravel of the fourth system, accumulated with a thickness of more than 200 m. The pore water of loose rocks has a thick and stable aquifer, which is the main object of groundwater exploitation and utilization. The proportion of groundwater supply to the total water supply in the study area is more than 40 %. Precipitation infiltration is the most important recharge mode for loose rock pore water in the study area, and irrigation infiltration and lateral runoff recharge are also important components of groundwater recharge. Groundwater discharge is dominated by artificial exploitation, while lateral runoff and a small amount of evaporation also exist. The study area is a major agricultural reclamation area in China; it is a major commercial grain production hub for wheat, soybeans, corn and rice, and it contains several large irrigation districts. Groundwater used for irrigation accounts for 85–95 % of the total regional groundwater consumption. The expansion of paddy fields has led to a significant increase in groundwater exploitation, resulting in a disruption of the dynamic balance of groundwater resources.  2.2 Data preparation Groundwater level data from 2000 to 2016 were provided by the Songliao River Water Resources Commission of Ministry of Water Resources. Precipitation (P) and air temperature (T) data measured monthly were obtained from the China Meteorological Service Network (https://data.cma.cn/ ). The NDVI, potential evapotranspiration (PET) and snow depth (SD) data were obtained from the National Tibetan Plateau Data Center (http://data.tpdc.ac.cn ). Soil moisture (SM) data can be accessed at https://www.scidb.cn/en . The NDVI data have a spatial resolution of 250 m and were generated using the maximum-value composite method. The data is based on the MOD13Q1 product from the Aqua/Terra-MODIS satellite sensor and land-use data, generated through the processes of smoothing and denoising with an S-G filter, retaining high-quality pixels and performing China-wide stitching. The snow depth data were derived from the inversion of SMMR and SSM/I remote sensing data, as well as the snow depth data recorded by the China National Meteorological Station (CNMS), using the improved Chang snow algorithm (Chang et al., 1987 ), with a spatial resolution of 0.25°.   3 Methods 3.1 Drought analysis 3.1.1 Standardized drought indices Using the SPI to characterize meteorological drought, the index was first proposed by American scholars (Mckee et al., 1993 ). It has the advantage of multiple time scales, and it can better reflect the drought characteristics of a certain region; additionally, it has been widely used in drought monitoring and other fields. To identify meteorological drought events using the SPI, the first step is to calculate the gamma distribution probability of precipitation over a specific period and subsequently normalize it. Finally, the drought and flood levels are classified according to the normal distribution curve of the SPI based on the established criteria. The SPI can be calculated as follows:(1) S P I = S t − ( c  2   t + c  1   ) t + c  0    ( ( d  3   t + d  2    )  t + d  1    )  t + 1   ,  t = ln  1 G ( x )  2          where t  is the precipitation distribution probability associated with the gamma function, x  is the sample of precipitation data, and S  is the positive or negative coefficient of probability density. Meteorological drought levels are defined as follows: extreme drought (SPI≤-2), severe drought (-2<SPI≤-1.5), moderate drought (-1.5<SPI≤-1), and light drought (-1<SPI≤-0.5). The standardized groundwater drought index is a nonparametric standardized drought indicator used to assess the drought status of groundwater resources. The extent of groundwater drought was quantified by comparing observed groundwater levels to long-term average levels. The calculation process is similar to that of the SPI and involves normalizing the groundwater level and dividing the difference between the water level and its long-term average by the standard deviation (detailed description in (Bloomfield and Marchant, 2013 ; Kubicz and Bak, 2019 )). The groundwater drought levels were defined as follows: extreme drought (SGDI≤-1.6), severe drought (-1.6<SGDI≤-1.3), moderate drought (-1.3<SGDI≤-0.8), and light drought (-0.8<SGDI≤-0.5) (Zhao et al., 2017 ).  3.1.2 Drought identification and characteristics Run theory is usually used to identify disaster events, and its advantage is that it can automate the identification of disaster events, avoiding the subjectivity and uncertainty of manual judgement (Jin et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2023b ). A disaster event is considered to have occurred when the disaster index falls below a specific threshold and the duration exceeds a specific length. This study defines a drought event based on two criteria. First, the SGDI must be consistently less than 0 for at least 2 months. Second, the minimum SGDI must be less than −0.5. If the interval between two adjacent drought events is one month and the drought index value of that month is less than 0, then these two drought events are combined. The quantification of drought characteristics based on the run theory includes drought duration (DD), drought severity (DS), and drought intensity (DI). Drought duration is defined as the number of months between the start and end of a drought. Drought severity is determined by the absolute value of the cumulative SGDI value during the drought event period, while drought intensity is calculated as the average of the SGDI values during the period, i.e., the ratio of drought severity to drought duration, which is expressed as follows:(3) D S = ∑ i = 1  D D   | S G D I  i    |  D I = ∑  i = 1  D D   | S G D I  i    |   D D         3.1.3 Drought propagation time and threshold The SGDI based on groundwater level can characterize groundwater dynamics, and a comparison with the SPI captures the time required for water deficit due to reduced precipitation to be transferred to the aquifer through the hydrologic cycle. The time scale of SPI-n corresponding to the highest Pearson correlation coefficient between the 1- to 24-month scale SPI (SPI-1, SPI-2…, SPI-24) and the 1-month scale SGDI is the time of drought propagation (n). Based on drought propagation time, a regression model is constructed to fit the SPI-n and SGDI corresponding to propagation time n. In the fitting relationship, the SPI-n value corresponding to the SGDI under different degrees of drought is the propagation threshold from meteorological drought to groundwater drought.   3.2 Quantification of impact factors The geodetector method (GDM) can quantitatively assessing the spatial variability of geographic factors and conducting driving mechanism analysis (Wang and Xu, 2017 ). Its calculation principle is based on information entropy theory and multiple regression analysis to determine the degree of influence and interaction relationship of each factor on the research object (Wang et al., 2010 ). In this study, factor detection and interaction detection are used to analyse the drivers of spatial divergence in drought propagation time and threshold: Factor detection: To measure the explanatory power of driver X  on the spatial divergence of drought propagation characteristics, we quantified the relative importance of each driver using the q value, expressed as follows:(4) q = 1 − ∑  h = 1  L   N  h   σ  h  2     N σ  2    = 1 − S S W  S S T       where the value range of q  is [0,1], and the larger its value is, the stronger the explanatory power is; L  is the number of strata of the driving factor X ; N h   and N  denote the number of sample units in the stratum h  and the entire region, respectively; σ  h  2     and σ  2     are the variances in the propagation time (threshold) in the stratum h  and the entire region, respectively; and SSW  and SST  are the sum of within-strata variance and the total variance in the entire region, respectively. Interaction detection: To explore whether the interaction between the two of the driving factors enhances or diminishes the explanatory power of the dependent variable or whether the effects of the two factors are independent of each other. For classification of interactions and further interpretation of this method, please refer to (Wang et al., 2010, 2016a ).  3.3 Wavelet coherence (WTC) Wavelet coherence is a method used to analyse the correlation between two time series. It is based on the wavelet transform, which decomposes the time series into frequency components at different scales and calculates the coherence between these frequency components (Labat, 2005; Qian et al., 2014 ). This study applied the WTC to demonstrate the correlation between SGDI and dynamic influences in the time-frequency domain. The wavelet coherence coefficients are equivalent to the local correlation coefficients in the time-frequency domain, which can be calculated from the wavelet coherence spectrum, as expressed in Eq. Fig. 2 a shows that groundwater droughts in the nonirrigated area were sporadic during the study period, with the three main drought events occurring in June 2001, July 2007, and August 2011 ( Table 1 ). To further verify the reliability of the results, we compared the SPI with the SGDI in the nonirrigated area, because the occurrence and development of droughts have a lag; therefore, we selected the SPI-3, which can reflect the seasonality of precipitation, for meteorological drought analysis (Ashraf and Routray, 2015 ) (Fig. 2 c). Groundwater droughts in the nonirrigated area coincide with meteorological droughts, while the interannual variation in the SGDI is smoother than that in the SPI, which indirectly confirms that groundwater drought mainly occurs due to meteorological causes in areas unaffected by groundwater exploitation and shows that the SGDI can effectively identify and capture groundwater drought. Groundwater drought events in irrigated area are concentrated after 2008 (Fig. 2 b), and there is a trend of increasing DD, DS, and DI over time, which is associated with the expansion of paddy fields and increased intensity of agricultural production in the study area (Huang et al., 2023 ). It is to be noted that the results of drought event identification should not be used as a criterion for evaluating the groundwater level conditions in these two areas. The SGDI describes only the degree to which the groundwater level deviates from the long-term average level. For irrigated area, the average groundwater level is lower than that of nonirrigated area; therefore, even if there were instances of irrigated area having a groundwater level lower than that of nonirrigated area before 2008, this does not necessarily indicate that there was a groundwater drought in irrigated area.  4.2 Spatiotemporal dynamics of the SGDI The temporal variation in the SGDI can reveal the abundance and depletion status of groundwater resources during different periods but fails to reveal its spatial distribution pattern; therefore, we spatially calculated the interannual rate of change in the SGDI from 2001–2016 ( Fig. 3 a). During the study period, most of the areas exhibited an "extremely significant decrease" (approximately 34.34 %), which was concentrated in the central and eastern parts of the basin, followed by 24.13 % of the areas with a "slight decrease". In addition, plant growth is significantly impacted by groundwater (Barbeta and Penuelas, 2017; Hayashi and Rosenberry, 2002 ). The depth of groundwater plays a crucial role in determining the distribution and growth of vegetation by affecting the dynamics of soil water and other factors (Glanville et al., 2023 ). Fig. 3 b displays the interannual variability in the NDVI throughout the study period. Over 70 % of the area exhibited a decreasing trend, of which 47.38 % showed a slight decrease. In areas less affected by agricultural production activities, both the SGDI and NDVI exhibited increasing trends, and the percentages of areas with increasing trends were 30.7 % and 26.7 %, respectively. This result suggests that an increase in groundwater levels has a positive impact on vegetation growth. The decreases in the SGDI and NDVI were concentrated in irrigated area. Although the presence of crops in irrigated areas increases the NDVI, the high latitude of the study area limits the time of year suitable for agriculture compared to the longer natural vegetation growth cycle in the nonirrigated area, resulting in a decrease in the mean annual NDVI in the irrigated area. Fig. S1 shows the spatial distribution of the SGDI for each year. During the period 2001–2009, the groundwater level showed an overall decreasing trend, which was related to the wetland development promoted by the local government (Liu et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2023c ), leading to the loss of the protective effect of the wetland on the groundwater and exacerbated the demand for groundwater for production and living. In some areas, the groundwater level rose after 2010, due to the implementation of the national ecological protection policy, which included converting farmland to forest and wetland (Li, 2004 ), etc. However, afterwards, as the density of the cultivated land and the intensity of the production bounced back to increase (Ning et al., 2024; Kang et al., 2024 ), the exploitation and utilization of the groundwater within the farmlands continued to increase, which affected the groundwater level of the irrigated areas and their surroundings to varying degrees.  4.3 Propagation characteristics from meteorological drought to groundwater drought 4.3.1 Propagation time By analysing the correlation between the SGDI and SPI at the monthly scale, the propagation characteristics from meteorological drought to groundwater drought in the irrigated area and nonirrigated area were revealed, and the results are shown in  Fig. 4 . There were seasonal differences in drought propagation, with the highest correlation coefficient occurring in the summer. The average propagation time of meteorological drought to groundwater drought is longer than that to other drought types due to the complex process of groundwater level response to precipitation (Liu et al., 2023a ); with precipitation first replenishing the soil layer above the groundwater surface and recharging the groundwater mainly through leakage from ditches, pits and depressions where runoff is pooled (Huang et al., 2015, 2017 ). The average drought propagation time is shortest during the summer (6 months), followed by autumn and spring (12.5 and 13.9 months, respectively), and longest during the winter (18.2 months), which is generally consistent with the findings of (Geyaert et al., 2018; Han et al., 2019 ). With abundant precipitation and sufficient soil moisture in summer, the intensity of infiltration depends mainly on the intensity of precipitation; i.e., the water table responds quickly to precipitation. While spring and autumn are in a period of precipitation deficit, coupled with the absorption of soil water by vegetation, most of the precipitation directly replenishes soil water, which prolongs the response time of groundwater drought to meteorological drought prolonged. In winter, under extremely low temperatures and in the presence of frozen soil, there is a long time lag in the impact of snowmelt on the groundwater level. The drought propagation times in spring, summer, autumn and winter are 12.7, 7, 11.7 and 18.7 months, respectively, in the nonirrigated area and 15, 5, 13.3 and 17.7 months, respectively, in the irrigated area. During the summer, drought propagates more quickly in irrigated areas than in nonirrigated areas. The study area experiences its main irrigation period during the summer, which keeps soil moisture levels higher. This finding suggests that exploiting groundwater during times of abundant water can accelerate the spread of drought between meteorology and groundwater. This is not only related to the fact that exploitation alters the surface water-groundwater cycle (Leng et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2023 ), but also because a meteorological drought during this period would increase the dependence on groundwater for irrigation, which could lead to more severe groundwater droughts. In contrast, during spring and autumn, drought propagated more slowly in the irrigated area than in the nonirrigated area. The study area is characterized by a continental monsoon climate, where annual precipitation is unevenly distributed and inadequate to maintain soil moisture saturation in spring and autumn compared to summer. Due to groundwater exploitation, the average groundwater level in irrigated area is lower than that in nonirrigated area, weakening the direct hydraulic connection between groundwater and surface water, which essentially enhances the sensitivity of surface soil moisture to precipitation (Han et al., 2021; Leung et al., 2011 ) and serves as a buffer against drought propagation.  4.3.2 Propagation threshold To improve the understanding of drought processes for effective response and early warning, it is necessary to study drought propagation quantitatively to understand what level of meteorological drought can trigger groundwater drought.  Fig. 5  displays the spatial distribution of propagation thresholds from meteorological drought to light, moderate, and severe groundwater drought during the spring, summer, and autumn seasons (winter is excluded due to snowfall and frozen soil in the study area). Lower values (lower SPI values and redder pixel color) indicate that a higher level of meteorological drought is required to trigger an equivalent groundwater drought; i.e., the groundwater system is more resilient to drought. A null value means that meteorological drought is not capable of triggering a groundwater drought at that level. The mean values of meteorological drought thresholds for triggering light groundwater drought in spring, summer, and autumn are −1.42, −1.57, and −1.43, respectively. Additionally, for moderate groundwater drought, 92.2 %, 68.6 %, and 84.8 % of the area can be triggered by meteorological drought during the three seasons, and for severe groundwater drought, these percentages are 20.5 %, 12.4 %, and 12.4 %, respectively. This finding suggests that the groundwater system is most resilient to drought in summer, followed by autumn and spring, due to the highest precipitation in summer as well as soil moisture memory (SMM) (Martinez-de la Torre and Miguez-Macho, 2019 ): for autumn, wet summer conditions buffer the effects of drought, whereas for spring, dry winter conditions lead to delays in recovery from drought. Under light and moderate groundwater drought scenarios, red pixels and null pixels are concentrated in the irrigated area, indicating that groundwater in the irrigated area is more resistant to meteorological drought, whereas the nonirrigated area is more susceptible to meteorological drought, which may be related to land air interactions. Soil plays a crucial role in the connection between precipitation and groundwater. SM variability regulates water and heat fluxes at the surface, which in turn affects air temperature and humidity (Dirmeyer et al., 2012; Hsu and Dirmeyer, 2023 ). At lower soil moisture levels, the relationship between SM and latent heat fluxes becomes decoupled, shifting from a strong correlation to a moisture-limited relationship (Santanello et al., 2007; Seneviratne et al., 2006 ). Excess surface energy leads to an increase in sensible heat fluxes, exacerbating near-surface atmospheric temperatures, which further worsens the reduction in SM (Qiao et al., 2023 ). Similarly, if the SM is greater, there is an inhibitory effect on the increase in drought according to the feedback mechanism. That is, temporally, SM is greater in summer; spatially, the exploitation of groundwater for irrigation in the irrigated area not only affects the water table but also keeps SM in a wet state through irrigation return flow (Fig. S2) (de Graaf et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2021 ). As a result, irrigated areas are more likely to maintain this relatively wet environment and are less susceptible to meteorological drought. Notably, this does not mean that groundwater drought does not easily occur in irrigated areas. The occurrence of groundwater drought events is determined by a combination of factors, and precipitation is only one of the main controlling factors when anthropogenic or other natural factors interfere with groundwater drought may still occur in a more serious way.   4.4 Factors influencing drought propagation characteristics As the process of drought propagation is influenced by multiple factors, it is crucial to examine the explanatory power of each factor on the propagation time and threshold. This will aid in understanding the mechanism of changes in drought propagation. The study considered the NDVI, precipitation, soil moisture, air temperature, potential evapotranspiration, and snow depth as influencing factors. The explanatory power of a single factor on the dependent variable and the effect of the interaction of two factors on the dependent variable are measured using the GDM. Compared to traditional geographically weighted regression methods, the GDM can effectively avoid the problem of possible multicollinearity among independent variables.  Fig. 6  demonstrates the extent to which each factor influences the propagation time and threshold in spring, summer and autumn. In terms of propagation time, PET and SD had the greatest influence in spring, contributing 46.9 % and 40.6 %, respectively. In autumn, SM, P and SD all had some influence, contributing 33.1 %, 30.4 % and 30.0 %, respectively; in summer, the largest driver was PET (55.6 %), followed by SM (36.2 %) and T (31.5 %). For the propagation threshold, the factors with the greatest influence in spring, autumn, and summer were P (37.4 %), SD (44.0 %), and T (32.4 %), respectively. The propagation of drought is influenced by a single factor as well as by a combination of factors. The interaction detection model generated 15 (10 in summer) combinations of q values based on 6 (5 in summer) independent variables, and the interaction detection results were all of the enhancement type, indicating that the influences of the factors are not independent and that the factors have synergistic effects on each other. The interactions between the factors are dominated by nonlinear enhancement ( Fig. 7 ), except for the summer propagation time, which mostly exhibits bivariate enhancement (SM∩PET, T, P; PET∩T, P; T∩P; P∩NDVI). The most explanatory interaction group is circled in red, where the most frequent influence factor is the NDVI, which is different from the factor detection results. In summer, for example, the explanatory power of the NDVI and SM for the propagation threshold was 23.3 % and 13.6 %, respectively. However, the combined effect of NDVI∩SM had the largest explanatory power (88.2 %) among all the interaction groups, indicating that it could sufficiently account for the variations in the propagation threshold. Most of the factors interacting with the NDVI, SD, and PET had greater explanatory power for the drought propagation variables. Specifically, for propagation time, the combinations that interacted with PET in the spring and summer and with NDVI in the autumn had the strongest explanatory power; for propagation threshold, the combinations that interacted with SD in the spring and autumn and with the NDVI in the summer had the strongest explanatory power.   5 Discussion 5.1 Correlation analysis between groundwater drought and vegetation Drought is a limiting factor for plant transpiration and photosynthesis and affects the distribution and structure of vegetation (Xu and Su, 2019 ). In addition, vegetation, as a primary producer of ecosystems, plays a key role in global climate change, material exchange and energy transfer between ecosystems (Fabricante et al., 2009 ). In the study area, the dry and wet seasons are distinct, and since precipitation is inadequate to meet the needs of plant growth, groundwater plays a crucial role in the regional ecological environment (Chan et al., 2021 ). The results of the previous section showed that the NDVI is an essential factor affecting the drought propagation process. To explore the relationship between groundwater drought and vegetation, we conducted a monthly spatial correlation analysis between the SGDI and NDVI, and only April to October was selected due to snow cover or no vegetation from November to March of the subsequent year. As shown in  Fig. 8 , the correlation between the SGDI and NDVI varied significantly across different months. In irrigated area, the NDVI gradually increased, peaked (in August) and then gradually decreased throughout the whole crop reproductive period (from April to October) (Fig. S3) (Huang et al., 2013 ). The SGDI and NDVI were positively correlated from April to June. The study area mainly includes annual crops, which have a low water requirement at the beginning of the growing season and a small crop coefficient (Kc ), which gradually increases as the crop grows and may decrease as the crop matures (Gao et al., 2019; Jia et al., 2019 ). Thus, during this period, precipitation is nearly sufficient to ensure crop growth, and at the same time, the soil moisture and groundwater level gradually increase. After June, the correlation between the SGDI and NDVI gradually became negative, with the level and range of negative correlations reaching their maximum in August. On the one hand, higher temperatures promote an increase in the vapour pressure deficit (VPD), which in turn increases evaporative loss at the surface (Fig. S4), leading to an increase in the soil moisture deficit (Hosseinzadehtalaei et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2023 ); on the other hand, crop growth enters the middle and late stages, and water demand increases so that despite the increase in precipitation, there is still a need to exploit groundwater, during which the NDVI increases at the expense of lowering the groundwater level. The correlation between the SGDI and NDVI in the nonirrigated area underwent a transition from negative to positive to negative. The Sanjiang Plain is a key national ecological area. However, due to the impacts of long-term agricultural reclamation and urbanization, the wetland area has decreased by more than 70 %, leading to a decline in biodiversity and loss of various ecological functions (Luo et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2010 ). To protect and restore the ecology and promote the virtuous cycle of the regional ecosystem, the Sanjiang Plain has implemented projects, such as wetland restoration and artificial afforestation (Xiang et al., 2020 ); thus, there are both natural and artificial forests and wetlands in the nonirrigated area. It is well recognized that forests consume more water than crops do, and evapotranspiration is greater for forests than for crops. (Scanlon et al., 2007; Teuling et al., 2019 ). Additionally, the water demand of wetlands, including water surface evaporation as well as vegetation and biohabitat water demand, is greater than that of cropland in the study area (Du et al., 2010 ). There is less precipitation in spring and autumn, so the vegetation in the nonirrigated area needs to consume groundwater for growth, which results in a negative correlation between the NDVI and SGDI. The ecological benefits of converting cropland to forestland are controversial (Sun et al., 2023a ), and several studies have shown that high evapotranspiration from forests reduces groundwater while decreasing SM (Jobbágy and Jackson, 2004; Schwaerzel et al., 2020 ). Han et al. (2020)  analysed a vegetation restoration programme on the Loess Plateau, a typical arid region of China; the results indicated that groundwater storage decreased significantly during the period of rapid growth of the NDVI, and there was no significant change in groundwater storage in the area where the NDVI was high. Sun et al. (2006)  assessed the reduction in water yield resulting from afforestation in various geographic regions of mainland China. The study showed that the rate of reduction in water production varied from approximately 50 % in the semiarid region of northern China to approximately 30 % in the tropical southern region. However, it has also been shown that in humid areas, forest restoration can improve soil structure to enhance infiltration and groundwater recharge and contribute to water source conservation (Zhou et al., 2015 ). Our study revealed the relationships between crops and natural vegetation and the SGDI and showed that the correlation between groundwater drought and the NDVI varied widely at monthly and seasonal scales and between irrigated area and nonirrigated area due to groundwater exploitation and crop irrigation, as well as differences in plant physiology between crops and natural vegetation. This finding means that the planning and utilization of groundwater resources as well as the implementation of ecological restoration projects, such as afforestation, need to be considered more finely at smaller temporal and spatial scales, which may require exploring the specific processes of evapotranspiration of soil moisture and groundwater recharge and depletion in both irrigated areas and nonirrigated areas.  5.2 Multiple timescale correlations between the SGDI and influencing factors The multiscale correlation characteristics of the SGDI and dynamic factors, such as the NDVI, were further analysed using the WTC, and the results are shown in  Fig. 9 . The colour scale bar on the right indicates the coherence of the two time series, and the arrows pointing to the right and left in the significant domain indicate the positive and negative correlation of the same phase, respectively. The degree of influence of each factor on the SGDI at different scales was assessed through the percentage area of significant coherence (PASC), which was calculated by dividing the area of coherence that passed the 95 % significance level test by the area of the whole time–frequency domain.  Table 2  calculates and summarizes the significant period, lag time, and PASC between the SGDI and the influencing factors. There was a significant correlation in the time-frequency domain between each factor and the SGDI in the nonirrigated area. Taking Fig. 9 a as an example, there was a statistically significant correlation between the SGDI and NDVI from April 2006 to June 2011, which was reflected in approximately 46–66 months. The phase angle indicated a lag time of approximately 33.72 months for the response of the SGDI to the NDVI. Additionally, the WTC spectra revealed a significant period (29–63 months) from April 2004 to November 2013, with an average phase difference of 6.8°, indicating that the SGDI changes lagged the SM changes by 0.85 months. The factor with the longest lag was SD (approximately 55.03 months), which had a continuous significant domain for periods of 49–67 months from October 2006 to May 2011. Among all the factors, the SGDI had the fastest response to soil moisture changes followed by precipitation. Understanding the water transfer pattern of the groundwater soil-vegetation-atmosphere system (GSVAS) is crucial for understanding drought formation (Nigatu et al., 2022; Rodriguez-Iturbe, 2000 ), and the soil, which is closest to the groundwater and has the closest water transfer relationship, must have strong explanatory power for groundwater drought in terms of its water content (Green et al., 2011 ). On the other hand, SM also plays an important role in drought recovery, and studies have shown that SM before the growing season determines the effects of drought (Lu et al., 2021 ). Yao et al. (2023)  found that SM is the most important environmental factor affecting the recovery time of ecosystems after they experiencing drought. In the irrigated area, there were no significant domains in the WTC except for the NDVI and SD; although the strong energy domains of the NDVI and SD were mostly located outside the significant area, they indicate the potential for a longer period. Moreover, the significant periods of SM, P and PET between 3 and 9 months dominated different periods of the study period, i.e., January 2003 to February 2005, August 2010 to October 2011, August 2004 to September 2005, and August 2006 to October 2007, which indicates that the dominance of each factor may change. The response of the groundwater level to external factors is dominated by a 12-month annual period (Tremblay et al., 2011; Yin et al., 2023 ), whereas the response of the SGDI to external factors is characterized by intermittent, discontinuous periods of less than 8 months and continuous periods of greater than 30 months, suggesting a combination of sudden and potentially long-term variability in groundwater drought events. Compared to the annual period characteristic between precipitation and groundwater levels, this result is likely indicative of groundwater drought events controlled by long periods of climate change on the one hand, in this case characterized by a 3-year or even longer period response, and on the other hand by short-term emergencies, such as extreme droughts and groundwater exploitation, etc. (Kaur et al., 2022; Shahid and Hazarika, 2010; Zhang et al., 2021 ). Compared to the WTC, the MWC has more regions of energy oscillations under the combination of multiple factors (Hu and Si, 2016 ). An additional factor is considered significant if it results in at least a 5 % increase in PASC (Hu et al., 2017 ). Fig. S5 and Table S1 present the MWC and PASC results for the combinations of the two influencing factors, and of all the two-factor combinations, SM and PET best explained the changes in the SGDI in nonirrigated area, followed by SM and T and SM and P, which had PASC values greater than 30 %. T and P can explain the variation in SM to some extent (Holsten et al., 2009 ). Feng and Liu (2015)  reported that the absolute contribution of air temperature is greater than that of precipitation and that air temperature is responsible for soil moisture surpluses or deficits by affecting evapotranspiration. Moreover, the transition of evapotranspiration between energy limitation and moisture limitation is governed mainly by the effective soil moisture (Dong et al., 2022; Feldman et al., 2019 ). SM and NDVI were the best combination for explaining the variation in the SGDI in irrigated area. In terms of changes in PASC, in nonirrigated area PASC increased in all combinations of factors except the NDVI and T, and SM and SD, and in irrigated area except the NDVI and P, SM and SD, SM and P, SD and P, and PET and P. All these combinations increased by more than 5 %, suggesting that the combined effects of the factors are synergistic in explaining the dynamics of groundwater drought at multiple scales. The increase in the PASC for the two-factor combination could be attributed to oscillations with periods of less than eight months (Fig. 9 ), where the combination of the two factors explains more of the SGDI variation than any single factor (Su et al., 2019 ). In order to ensure the sustainable development and utilization of groundwater resources in the Sanjiang Plain, it is recommended that some measures be taken, including developing the water quantity and level control indexes of groundwater and the annual groundwater exploitation plan in each irrigated area, controlling the scale of farmland irrigation, optimizing the spatial distribution of paddy fields and drylands, speeding up the construction of the regional water transfer project, and improving the dynamic monitoring network of groundwater in order to carry out the refined groundwater management. The Sanjiang Plain has undergone four large-scale reclamation activities since 1949 (Yan et al., 2002 ), resulting in significant changes in the utilization patterns of paddy fields, drylands, and wetlands. These changes have altered the land air energy balance and water and material exchange processes, impacted the climate at both local and regional scales, and further impacted the recharge/discharge balance of groundwater, increasing the vulnerability of groundwater to drought (Ling et al., 2023 ). This study focused on the differences in groundwater drought characteristics and drought propagation processes between irrigated and nonirrigated areas at annual, seasonal, and monthly scales, which can assist local water resource management authorities in rationalizing the use and spatial-temporal allocation of groundwater. It is undeniable that investigating the influencing factors in this study considered only the dynamic factors; however, importantly, static factors, such as soil and rock properties, aquifer thickness, and other topographic and geological conditions, also significantly influence the dynamics of the groundwater system. Scholars have researched this topic and found that different types of droughts respond differently to climate inputs due to variations in basin characteristics (Ding et al., 2021; Van Loon and Laaha, 2015 ), and that even the same degree of meteorological drought may result in different degrees of groundwater drought. It is recommended that future studies consider both dynamic and static factors together and that the effect of coupling between factors on drought propagation be further investigated. In summary, despite these shortcomings and the limited time series of groundwater level data, the reliability of the results on groundwater drought characteristics and propagation patterns in this study remains unaffected. More importantly, our study's primary objective is to reveal the evolution and propagation mechanisms of groundwater droughts, particularly in complex ecosystems comprising cultivated land and seminatural habitats, such as the Sanjiang Plain.   6 Conclusion In this study, the SGDI was calculated based on groundwater level data to identify groundwater drought events in the nonirrigated area and irrigated area. The groundwater drought events in the nonirrigated area were scattered throughout the study period, whereas in the irrigated area, they were concentrated after 2008 and increased in duration, severity and intensity over time. By calculating the correlation coefficients between the SGDI and SPI at different time scales to determine the propagation time from meteorological drought to groundwater drought, the results reveal significant seasonal differences, with the propagation time being greatest in summer (6 months), followed by autumn (12.5 months), spring (13.9 months) and winter (18.2 months). Due to differences in soil moisture, the drought propagation time was shorter in the irrigated area than in the nonirrigated area in summer and longer in spring and autumn than in the nonirrigated area. The drought propagation threshold results indicated that the groundwater system was most resistant to drought in summer, followed by autumn and spring, and spatially nonirrigated area was more vulnerable to meteorological drought. The factors that best explain changes in propagation time and threshold vary by season. The comprehensive effects of two factors were manifested as nonlinear enhancements, among which the combination of factors interacting with the NDVI, SD and PET had a stronger explanatory power for drought propagation variables. Due to the presence of irrigation and differences in plant physiology between crops and natural vegetation, in irrigated area, the SGDI and NDVI were positively correlated from April to June and then negatively correlated, whereas in nonirrigated area, the SGDI and NDVI underwent a process of shifting from negative to positive to negative correlation. There were continuous significant domains on the wavelet coherence spectrum between each influencing factor and the SGDI in the nonirrigated area, with soil moisture contributing the most, whereas there were no significant domains in the irrigated area except for the NDVI and snow depth. Under the combined effect of long-term climatic conditions and short-term events, there was a discontinuous response of less than 8 months and a continuous response of more than 30 months between the SGDI and external factors. This study enhances the understanding of the differences in groundwater drought characteristics between irrigated areas and nonirrigated areas and provides valuable insights into the mechanisms of drought propagation in the GSVAS.
1 Introduction The East Africa Rift System (EARS) is the most extensive and densely faulted continental rift that extends from the Middle East southward to the African continent (Gregory, 1968). This region has garnered increasing media attention due to the sudden appearance of the large crack of several kilometers, making the area a typical site for investigating dynamic processes leading to continental dislocation and the break-up of the African plate into two, the Nubian and Somali plates (Khaffou et al., 2023 ). This situation makes the EARS a living test room for studying the early stages of continental breakup. In Kenya, the crack damaged communities, railways, culverts, and highways to differing degrees (Jia et al., 2023 ). Apart from the observed crack, contrasting morphological changes and lake water level fluctuations are taking place in the region’s lakes. For instance, Lake Nakuru in Kenya expanded by 24.48 km2  (76.98 %) in just four years between January 2010 and December 2014 (Obando et al., 2016 ), while Lake Abijata in Ethiopia shrunk by 66.6 km2  between 1972 and 2015 (Hailu and Girma, 2019 ). These divergent happenings make the region a discussion hotspot of the academia, media, decision-makers, and others. Despite the changing lake morphology, there are a lot of disorganized and even contradicting publications on the status of water level fluctuation and the spatiotemporal pattern of Rift Valley lakes morphology. This situation calls for comprehensive action to ensure the sustainable utilization of the EKRV lakes and their watersheds. Thus, it is important to investigate the trend in water level fluctuation using up-to-date data on the spatiotemporal coverage of the lakes that are experiencing remarkable changes in their size and the driving forces. In this review, we investigated the trends in Lake water level fluctuations and the underlying causes for the shrinking and expanding lakes in Ethiopia and Kenya. The objective is to shed light on these trends and their underlying causes to the academia and decision-makers. We intend to reveal the roles of anthropogenic and natural factors for the observed changes in the morphology of the lakes and reveal the gaps in the so-far research related to the fluctuations and their consequences on the fragile nature of resources in the Rift Valley. Research articles related to the lake level fluctuations, land use land cover change (LULCC), and their concomitant impacts on the spatiotemporal trends of Lake water level changes were collected and analyzed. We attempted to integrate the vast majority of literature on the trends in the fluctuation of water level of eight lakes located in the Ethiopian and Kenyan Rift Valley areas: Lakes Baringo, Bogoria, Turkana, and Nakuru from Kenya and Lakes Abijata, Beseka, Ziway, and Hawassa from Ethiopia.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The study area extends from the boundary of Ethiopia in the northeast to the southern boundary of Kenya bounded between 14.760  & –5.330  latitudes and 39.820  & 38.900  longitudes as displayed in  Fig. 1 . It is characterized by a chain of lakes–nested in echelon fashion; streams and wetlands of various sizes and ecological settings (Alemayehu et al., 2006 ). In its Ethiopian portion, the region consists of Abaya, Chamo, Shala, Ziway, Langano, Abijata, Chitu, Beseka (Basaka), Afdera, Chew Bahir, Hawassa, and a group of Afambo-Abhe Lakes. Similarly, the Kenyan rift system is home to Lakes Elementaita, Nakuru, Bogoria, Baringo, Logipi, Turkana, Magadi, Naivasha, and Solai. The Ethiopian Rift Valley Lakes are physically arranged in a NE–SW direction from the Danakil Depression to Chew Bahir, bisecting the Ethiopian highlands into two. Some of these lakes are freshwater eco-regions of great biodiversity, while others are saline-alkaline “soda lakes” supporting highly specialized and a wide variety of flora and fauna. The rift valley lakes in Ethiopia are divided into three lots; the northern, central, and southern portions owing to their complex structural features (Jansen et al., 2007 ). The northern rift system ranges from Afar to Adama (consisting of the Afar triangle up to Lake Beseka). The central rift valley (CRV) system ranges from Adama to Hawassa and is characterized by tectonically controlled endorheic basin features consisting of a chain of four hydrologically interconnected lakes; Lakes Ziway, Abijata, Langano, and Shala. The southern rift system ranges from Hawassa to Chew Bahir encompassing the Hawassa, Abaya, Chamo, and Chew-Bahir Lakes (Legesse et al., 2004; Ayenew, 2004; Bedru Sherefa Muzein, 2006 ). The Kenyan rift consists of three basins namely, the Turkana Basin which consists of Lake Turkana and Lake Logipi, the Dome Basins containing Lakes Naivasha, Oloidien, Elmenteita, Nakuru, Bogoria, Baringo, Solai, Ol’ Bolossat, and the Lake Magadi Basin containing Lake Magadi and Ewaso Narok South Wetland swamp (Government of Kenya, and UNDP. 2021 ). The climate in the Ethiopian Rift Valley area is diverse and ranges from hot and arid to cool and humid with distinct wet and dry seasons. It is sub-humid and semi-arid close to the Kenyan border and arid in Afar. The Ethiopian Rift region consists of Dalol Depression, one of the hottest places on Earth, has an average annual temperature of around 500  C (Ayenew, 2007 ). The climate of the Kenyan Rift Valley lakes area varies from semi-arid (around Lake Turkana and Lake Magadi) to sub-humid. The Lakes Baringo, Bogoria, Nakuru, and Naivasha lie within the arid and semi-arid northern part of the central Rift Valley in Kenya (Kiage et al., 2007 ). Rainfall is low on the rift floor where it annually averages about 700 mm but is mostly greater than 2500 mm in the adjacent highlands (Kiage et al., 2007 ).  2.2 Methods Most of the published articles used in this review work were collected from online sources such as Google Search, Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, Research-Gate, and Science Citation Index Expanded (SCIE) bibliographic database. Some of the articles that were not available online were supplied by the authors on request. The literature search process was conducted by targeting scientific articles about the EAR lakes found in Ethiopia and Kenya published in English language in peer-reviewed journals. A three-step search strategy was used to develop a collection of documents. While the first strategy involves searching for articles based on their study area, the second and third strategies encompass thematic relevance and the names of renowned authors, respectively. Search terms including “East African Rift,” “Ethiopian Rift Valley Lakes,” “Kenyan Rift Valley Lakes,” “Central Rift Valley Lakes,” “Main Ethiopian Rift,” “Climate Change in the Rift Valley Lakes Areas,” and “LULCC in the Rift Valley Lakes Areas,” and name of lakes in the rift system were used to locate publications related to the topics under consideration. Until the last search date 31 May 2024, a total of 362 journal articles, book chapters, reports, and PhD theses were collected. These documents were reduced to 236 to establish our database for further analyses using inclusion criteria. The exclusion criteria include study area and research focus (dropped 47 articles), originality of articles (dropped 35 articles), self-produced primary data (dropped 15 articles), and publishing in reputable peer-reviewed journals (dropped 29 articles). Thus, the exclusion criteria dropped 126 documents leaving 236 documents for further careful reading, comparison, interpretation, and checked for their complementarity. Finally, results were presented, narrated, and discussed.   3 Results 3.1 Overview of Lake Level Fluctuation in Selected Rift Valley Lakes of Kenya Though Kenya is known for the utilization of its rift valley lakes for diverse socio-economic purposes, the lakes have been experiencing extraordinary rises in their water levels since 2010 (Okech et al., 2019; Aloo, 2002; Britton et al., 2007 ) nonetheless the phenomenon was not new to these lakes (Muita et al., 2021 ). Previous records of lake levels in Kenya show a significant rise in the levels and flooding of the mudflats and ring of acacia forest around the lakes in 1901 and 1963 (Obando et al., 2016 ). The current flooding being witnessed suggests a return of a 50-year cyclic climatic event. Recently, significant scientific considerations have started to be given to lake levels, including the detailed long-term metaphors of the negative socio-economic consequences was given considerations lately (Herrnegger et al., 2021 ). Intense country-wide media coverage due to increased water levels has provoked public debates on the potential causes, with expert opinions divided along potential geological, anthropogenic, and hydro-climatic influences (Herrnegger et al., 2021 ). According to the assumption of the potential geological process, it is argued that the affected rift valley lakes are located in a geologically active zone and lie in a closed basin without surface outlets. Consequently, the recent movement of tectonic plates in the region could have caused decrease in underground permeability, thereby decreasing sub-terranean outflow or seepage (Herrnegger et al., 2021 ). On the other hand, anthropogenic pushing factors such as LULCC and degradation of the catchment areas are considered possible causes for the lake level rise. Under this assumption, it is argued that the lower permeability of the subterranean pathways may have been worsened in one way or another by the potential sealing and clogging of the underground water paths as a result of amassed sediment loads from the nearby degraded catchments as a result of LULCC.
