In general, less infiltration and higher surface runoff are the results of LULCC, thereby accelerating surface runoff and peak discharges on shorter time scales (Guzha et al., 2018 ). This in turn affects the overall water balance on a longer time scale through decreased actual evapotranspiration (Andréassian, 2004 ). Because precipitation and actual evapotranspiration determine the atmospheric boundary conditions, they are important hydro-climatic drivers and elements of the water balance (Herrnegger et al., 2021 ). Thus, a divergence of inflow, on-lake precipitation, and/or real evapotranspiration from a magnitude that would produce equilibrium in the lake water levels can also account for rising water levels. If the lake surfaces are in equilibrium, it would make sense to have higher rainfall values and/or lower actual evapotranspiration in comparison to the mean values (Herrnegger et al., 2021 ). Lake water balance variations are responses to the potential changes in the watershed as well as the lake itself. Whatever the cause for the lake water level changes is – Kiage and Douglas, (2020)  argue that all the above can potentially play a role in the lake level fluctuations – a quantifiable magnitude can be derived by analyzing changes in lake volume, since they constitute an integrated catchment response. Changes in lake volume reflect potential influences due to deviations from an equilibrium regarding inflow and outflow, LULCC, or hydro-climatic changes. In general, the increases in lake level and consequent inundations of the riparian areas have had significant negative impacts on the socio-economic activities and livelihoods of citizens (Onywere et al., 2013 ). For this review, we explore the changes observed in Lakes Baringo, Bogoria, Nakuru, and Turkana in detail because they provide habitats for bird wildlife and are important economically for the fishing industry, drinking and irrigation water, and as major tourist attractions beyond their ecological significance.  3.2 Lake Baringo Lake Baringo is Kenya’s tropical third-largest freshwater lake despite a lack of surface outlet, shallow depth, and high net evaporation. It is located at 0°30’N to 0°45’N latitude, and 36°00’E to 36°10’E longitude approximately 60 km north of the equator at an altitude of 975 m a.s.l (Obando et al., 2016 ). The total catchment area of the lake is 6820 km2  that includes a large part of the western escarpment of the Kenyan rift valley, where most of the water is derived from and with annual rainfall ranging from about 600 mm to 1500 mm. Lake Baringo is an endorheic and holomictic lake (have a uniform temperature and density from surface to bottom at a specific time during the year, which allows the lake waters to mix in the absence of stratification). It occupies the eastern end of a half-graben depression in the central Kenya Rift Valley (IUCN, 2014; Renaut et al., 2017 ). The lake has no observable outlet but it is believed to have an underground seepage through lake sediments into the faulted volcanic bedrock that maintains its freshness by losing approximately 108 m3 /year (Dunkley PN et al., 1993 ). The lake is near the saline Lake Bogoria and it is fed by Ol Arabel, Makutan, Endao, and Chemeron seasonal streams and Molo and Perkerra perennial rivers (Odada et al., 2006 ). The perennial rivers reach the lake directly through surface recharge and bringing in a large amount of sediment load. Molo River collects water from the Mau Escarpment as far south as Elburgon Forest and is structurally controlled, following the troughs between the fault scarps or the base of the fault scarps in its flow northward (Hinckley et al., 2014; Herrnegger et al., 2021; Githaiga et al., 2021 ). In the recent past, while the Molo River displayed drying up towards the lake during the dry spell of each year due to several upstream impoundments to supply irrigation water, the down-flow of Endau stream was seriously affected by upstream construction of the Kiriandich Dam (Nyakeya et al., 2020 ). Lake Baringo is home to seven freshwater fish large populations of hippos, snakes, crocodiles, and over 500 avifaunal species that makes it a wetland of international importance and gazette as a Ramsar site in the year 2002 (Olago et al., 2009; Herrnegger et al., 2021 ). Lake Baringo’s Ramsar-designated water body has been facing myriad environmental challenges attributable to anthropogenic activities, thereby being an ecosystem under perturbation (Nyakeya et al., 2020 ). While Lake Baringo is located in a semi-arid climatic zone, its catchment covers a range of climatic zones, from semi-arid through semi-humid and sub-humid, to a small portion in the humid zone (Walumona et al., 2021 ), with unpredictable timing of dry and wet seasonality (Butzer, 1970; Hopson, 1982 ). The daytime temperatures vary from 16.7°C during the cold months of June and July to 33.8°C during the warmer months of January to March (Muita et al., 2021 ). The dry season usually extends from September to February while the wet season occurs between March and August (Odada et al., 2006 ). Though the majority of the catchment of Lake Baringo is comprised of vast plains and steep slopes, making it highly susceptible to erosion and sedimentation (Omweno Job. et al., 2021 ), it is home to a native variety of acacias and foreign invasive species, including Prosopis juliflora (Odada et al., 2006 ). Thus, the watershed has been suffering from soil erosion, sedimentation, and water pollution (Olago et al., 2009; Avery, 2010; Herrnegger et al., 2021 ). This condition favors the characterization of the lake by its high turbidity that is caused by the erosion of fine volcanic soils as a result of the anthropogenic activities associated with land and water use rights in the upper catchments in the basin (Omondi, et al., 2014 ). Seven islands are located in the lake, the largest being the volcanic Kokwa Island, from which several hot springs discharge into the lake (Cĺement et al., 2003 ). The lake is a source of water and provides livelihoods (mainly fishing) for the Icchamus, Tugen, Pokot, and Turkana communities, among others (Nyakeya et al., 2020 ). The lake has a shallow varying bathymetry which has reportedly declined since 1972 due to observable impacts of siltation, evaporation, and diversion of inflowing rivers (Avery, 2010; Feibel, 2011 ). Thus, Lake Baringo has a long history of water level fluctuation as a result of unpredictable rainfall patterns (Kassilly, 2002 ), and because of marked increases in anthropogenic activities (river impoundment, sand harvesting, and irrigation for flower farms and personal farms) in its catchments (Yuretich, 1979; Raini, 2009; Funk et al., 2015 ). The lake was initially been characterized as a very shallow water body with an average depth of 2.5 m (Britton et al., 2007 ) until approximately the year 2010 when the depth changes commenced (Nyakeya et al., 2020 ). According to the analysis of records by Odada et al., (2006) , between 1969 and 1972 the average depth of Lake Baringo was 8 m, while in early 2003, before the onset of the long rains, the average depth was 1.7 m. The average depth in 2006 increased to 2.5 m, with the deepest end of the lake being 3.5 m, where the increase in water depth was the result of the prolonged long rains during 2003, especially in the humid upper catchments (Odada et al., 2006 ). Due to heavy rains experienced since 2011 in the eastern African region, the lake water surface increased dramatically from nearly 135 km2  in 2010 (Omondi, et al., 2014 ) to 193 km2  in 2016 (Britton et al., 2007; Okech et al., 2019 ) and then to more than 250 km2  in 2020 (Nyakeya et al., 2020 ) as shown in  Table 1 . The rise in the water level of Lake Baringo is accompanied by improved lake depth from an average of 2.5 m in 2003–10.5 m in 2020 (Nyakeya et al., 2020 ). The lake submerged the fringe biodiversity and most buildings (including the Department of Fisheries, the fish store, several hotels such as Lake Baringo Block Hotel, Highland Camp, part of Soi Lodge, Roberts Camp, and the County Council of Baringo Reptile Center). As a result of this, there is an elevated risk of water-related and waterborne diseases (Omweno Job O. et al., 2021 ). Due to its geomorphic structure, Lake Baringo’s neighborhood is the worst affected area in the Rift Valley lakes than all the lakes showing similar trends in terms of the size of the affected human population (Britton et al., 2007; Hinckley et al., 2014; Herrnegger et al., 2021 ). In Baringo, the spread of the floodwaters submerged entire villages, displacing the communities and their livestock accompanied by a general loss of livelihoods for the local communities. At least eight schools in the villages, along with settlements and health care centers, were submerged. It is estimated that more than 1250 pupils were affected by the engulfment of classrooms (Obando et al., 2016 ). It is estimated that 617.40 km2  of pasture and browsing lands, with the capacity to support up to 38,588 livestock units, were submerged by the floods (Obando et al., 2016 ). Moreover, the flooding put extra tension on the nearby area, which could lead to conflicts between people and wildlife and jeopardize the socioeconomic activities that provide a living for the community (Obando et al., 2016 ). In recent years, the catchment of Lake Baringo has been threatened by increasing pressure from climate change (increase in rainfall), rapid population growth, and LULCC (Omondi et al., (2016) ; Obando et al., 2016 ). According to reports from Obando et al., (2016) , the natural forest cover of the catchment of Lake Baringo that regulates rainfall patterns, sediment regime, flooding, and sustains the groundwater recharge decreased from 829 km2  to 417 km2  between 1976 and 2006. Similarly, the report on the assessment of land cover conducted between 2000 and 2018 by the Government of Kenya & UNDP, (2021) revealed that forest cover that was 563.7 km2  in 2000 increased to 769.6 km2  in 2014 and finally declined to 513.9 km2  in 2018. Conversely, cropland increased that was only 1652.6 km2  in 2000 and grew to 2175.3 km2  in 2018. An increase in cropland indicates that more vegetation is converted to farmland and the increase in wetland signifies the increase in water levels of the lakes within the catchment.  3.3 Lake Bogoria Lake Bogoria is a narrow, saline and alkaline closed basin lake that occupies a deep half-graben depression and extends from 0°10’N to 0°20’N and 36°04’E to 36°26’E, at an elevation of 992 m a.s.l. It is located some 20 km due south of Lake Baringo separated by the Loboi plain which constitutes a drainage divide that rises to about 1000 m a.s.l. (Onywere et al., 2013 ). It is located in the Kenyan CRV fed partly by ∼ 200 hot alkaline springs located in three groups along its margins (Renaut et al., 2017 ). The lake is lying in a trough formed between a fault fragmented, eastward sloping Kipngatip plateau of phonolite lava to its west, and Lake Bogoria fault scarp immediately to its east (Obando et al., 2016 ). The endorheic basin of Lake Bogoria influences its salinity and alkalinity that is exacerbated by inflow from saline hot springs and high evaporation rates that exceed precipitation. In 1970, Lake Bogoria was first declared a national reserve because of its scenery, hydrologic features, and biodiversity (large number of bird species, buffalo, baboon, caracal, cheetah, spotted hyena, warthog, impala, zebra, etc.) (Obando et al., 2016 ). The status was later changed to a National Park in 1990 and subsequently designated as a Wetland of International Importance under the Ramsar Convention in 2001 (Agembe et al., 2018 ). At present, the catchment of Lake Bogoria is around 1060 km2  which lies within Lake Bogoria National Park. Around Lake Bogoria, the terrestrial vegetation is primarily composed of thorny bushland composed of Acacia spp., Balanites, and Commiphora, with pockets of riverine woodland consisting of Ficus capensis, Acacia tortilis, and Acacia xanthophloea (Wetang’ula et al., 2013 ). The hydrology of Lake Bogoria is primarily influenced by the inflows from several springs, most of which emerge along the N-S fissures at the shores of the lake. The springs include the Sandai, Loboi, Waseges, and Emsoss Rivers flowing in from the north of the lake during the wet season (April to August), discharges from the lake floor, and approximately 200 alkaline hot springs nearby. Emsoss warm spring flows in from the south through fissures in the Emsoss escarpment (Obando et al., 2016 ). The larger part of the Bogoria drainage area, 1075.5 km2 , is occupied by the Waseges River (Onywere et al., 2013 ). Lake Bogoria has the highest concentration of geysers in Africa (IUCN, 2014). With a high rate of evapotranspiration at 1500 mm per day, Lake Bogoria is situated in a semi-arid zone in an area that receives about 50 mm of rainfall per month and 400–600 mm of precipitation annually lacking a known surface outflow (Agembe et al., 2018). During the April to August wet season, the increased flow from the catchment coupled with geysers along the banks of Lake Bogoria raises the water level which subsequently declines from December to March. Lake Bogoria, a major tourist destination due to its famous boiling springs and millions of flamingos, lost most of its hot springs to the floods and all geysers have been suppressed (Government of Kenya & UNDP, 2021). Moreover, there is renewed concern that the alkaline lake will overflow and merge with the freshwater Lake Baringo, thereby causing severe cross-contamination (Githaiga et al., 2021 ). The report prepared by the Government of Kenya & UNDP, (2021) revealed that the land cover of Lake Bogoria catchment showed an increasing trend in its forest cover from 26.5 km2  to 38.7 km2 ; cropland from 361.9 km2  to 416.5 km2 ; and water body & wetland from 39.1 km2  to 49.4 km2  between 2000 & 2018.  Fig. 2  displays the mean surface area of Lake Bogoria from 1984 to 2020. The surface area of the lake increased to 40.50 km2  in 2015 and remained mostly above 34 km2  since 2010. The overall increase in the size of Lake Bogoria between 1984 and 2020 is 11.11 km2 . The suppressed increase in Lake Bogoria's surface area is related to the steeper topography of the surrounding area when compared to the other lakes. The lake occupies a deep and, somewhat, narrow depression which experienced a rise in lake level but was accompanied by limited expansion in surface area when compared to the shallow depressions occupied by the other lakes (Herrnegger et al., 2021 ). In Lake Bogoria the communities living along the northern shore of the lake within the River Waseges floodplain were displaced and flooding also resulted in drowning or migration of land-based invertebrate and vertebrate animal species to the drier surrounding areas. There was also a change in the water quality, in particular a decrease in salinity thereby affecting the flamingo population.  3.4 Lake Nakuru Lake Nakuru is a shallow, alkaline, and saline lake that extends from 0°18’S to 0°24’S and 36°03’E to 36° 07’E. It is located within an endorheic basin characterized by its hyper-salinity (Onywere et al., 2013 ). The lake is located 53 km from the southern edge of Lake Bogoria at an elevation of 1754 m a.s.l. Lake Nakuru lies in a graben between the Lion Hill fracture zone in the east and a series of east downthrown step-fault scarps leading to the Mau Escarpment to the west (Hinckley et al., 2014; Herrnegger et al., 2021 ). Its catchment covers a total area of 1471 km2  with daily temperatures that range between 9.4°C during the cold months and 26.8°C during the warmer months (Muita et al., 2021 ). The wet season in the region falls between April and August, while the dry season occurs between October and March with mean annual rainfall is 95.1 mm (Agembe et al., 2018). In addition to precipitation, Lake Nakuru is fed by the effluent of the nearby Nakuru City sewerage treatment system, Baharini spring on its eastern shoreline, and seasonal surface streams Njoro, Nderit, Makalia, Enderit, and Lamudhiak, originating from the Eastern Mau Forest (Avery, 2013; Zaniolo et al., 2021 ). The rest of the drainages rising from Eburru, Bahati, and the rest of the Mau escarpment, carry runoff only during prolonged rainfall but never reach the lake using surface recharge. Lake Nakuru is part of Lake Nakuru National Park known for its highest biodiversity in Kenya. It is home to a large population of Lesser Flamingos described as “the world’s greatest ornithological spectacle” with over 450 species of birds, 50 species of mammals 300 species of plants, and 70 species of waterfowl and water-related birds (Government of Kenya & UNDP, 2021). Each year the resident bird life of the park is enriched by the presence of several species of Palearctic waders that use the lake as a staging ground during their winter migration down the Rift Valley flyway. The lake has faced major ecological restructuring as a result of flooding. The area of Lake Nakuru is a protected area under the Ramsar Convention on wetlands. The area has been designated as a Bird Sanctuary since 1960, declared a National Park in 1968, as well as the first rhino sanctuary and the first Ramsar Site in Kenya in 1987 and 1990, respectively (Government of Kenya & UNDP, 2021). It was identified as an Important Bird Area in 1999, and lastly in 2011, it was designated as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO (Agembe et al., 2018). Since this is a shallow lake it shows rapid fluctuation in size/area where its water is greatly reduced during a prolonged drought that will be fed only from sewage water from the Nakuru sewage treatment works and perennial small springs off Lion Hill (Hinckley et al., 2014; Herrnegger et al., 2021 ). Lake Nakuru undergoes major fluctuations, sometimes drying up completely in 1995 and 1996, resulting in most birds disappearing and tourism being greatly diminished (Haack and Messina, 2009; Spruill, 2019 ). Following extreme El Niño-driven flooding in 1997 and 1998, the lake levels rebounded (Kimaru et al., 2019 ) and have shown an increase in water levels since 2011 (Onywere et al., 2013 ). This resulted in an increase in its flood area from a low area of 31.8 km2  in January 2010 to a high of 54.67 km2  in September 2013, corresponding to a 22.87 km2  increase in area. Lake Nakuru is the first of Kenyan rift valley lakes to burst its bank since the short rains of September 2010 (Onywere et al., 2013 ). The lake has swollen submerging old buildings, grazing and farm lands, and the Nakuru sewerage treatment works. The rising levels of the lake coincide with the increase in rainfall in the catchment areas, with sharp increases in the surface area observed in 2014 and 2020 (Government of Kenya & UNDP, 2021). Apart from the impact on the livelihoods of multitudes of local community members, there are reports of risks of attacks by snakes and crocodiles and a high risk of contracting waterborne diseases due to the submersion of public utilities like sewage treatment plants, transport infrastructure in the park, the tourism, the park main gate, and other sanitation units. According to the report of the Government of Kenya & UNDP, (2021), the land cover change trend within the catchment of Lake Nakuru depicts that forest cover decreased from 192.5 km2  to 174.8 km2 , while cropland and wetland increased from 803.7 km2  and 58.73 km2  to 1059.5 km2  and 75.16 km2  respectively between the year 2000 and 2018. The decrease in forest cover may be attributed to the conversion of forest to cropland which is evinced by a steady increase in cropland. The increase in wetlands conversely is an indication of rising levels of water in Lake Nakuru.  Fig. 3  describes the mean surface area of Lake Nakuru between 1984 and 2021. In just 11 years, between 1984 and 1995 the size of Lake Nakuru decreased by 7.90 km2  and remained low until after 2010 when it increased from 38.86 km2  to 54.40 km2  in 2015. In 1995, the lake showed its lowest areal extent of 33.10 km2 . Between 1995 and 2021, the lake showed an increase in size by 34.90 km2 . While changes in lake water levels between 2010 and 2021 depict overflows submerging an estimated area of 29.14 km2 , the lake experienced an overall increase in size of 27.00 km2  between 1984 and 2021. Thus, the 27.00 km2  neighboring area of Lake Nakuru is inundated by the rising water level.  3.5 Lake Turkana Lake Turkana is the fourth largest lake in Africa, the world’s largest alkaline lake, the world's largest desert lake, and the largest endorheic lake located in the arid region of EARS with a unique ecosystem (Ayenew, 2002a; Moses et al., 2011; Hairston and Fussmann, 2002 ). It loses water mainly through a strong evaporation rate estimated to be around 7 mm/day (Hairston and Fussmann, 2002; Abebe et al., 2018 ). It is located in the arid northwestern part of Kenya at about 4°39'13.55'' N and 36°10'12.20" E. Most of the lake lies in Kenya, but part of the Omo River that supplies water to the lake delta lies in the southwestern part of Ethiopia (Odada et al., 2003 ). Lake Turkana is characterized by an elongated shape oriented north-south, with a distance between the north shore and the south shore of about 200 km and a maximum width of about 40 km. The lake's surface area is about 7000 km2  and the catchment area is 131,000 km2  (Feibel, 2011 ). The wet season in the Lake Turkana basin is from April to October, with peak rainfall typically seen in April (Funk et al., 2015 ). However, it should be noted that rainfall patterns differ substantially across the basin from the tropical, humid climate in the Ethiopian highlands in the north to the hot, arid semi-desert climate in the south. Despite being a key stop-over site for birds on passage, Lake Turkana is home to 84 water-bird species, including 34 Palearctic migrants, and a breeding ground for at least 23 species of birds (Government of Kenya & UNDP, 2021). Thus, the lake is a unique ecosystem in the northern portion of the Kenyan Rift Valley. The catchment of Lake Turkana covers an arid region and is fed by Turkwel and Kerio Rivers from the South–West, and the Omo River from the North. Turkwel and Kerio rivers have their sources in the Cherangany Hills forest reserves. Omo River (acts as the Turkana’s “umbilical cord”) provides about 90 % of the lake inflow emanating from Ethiopian highlands with plentiful rainfall (Hairston and Fussmann, 2002; Legesse et al., 2002; Ayenew, 2002a ). As a result, the lake’s water level fluctuations are almost entirely caused by variations in rainfall over the Ethiopian highlands. Due to its restricted basin character, arid surroundings, and heavy reliance on the Omo River for its intake, Lake Turkana is a highly pulsed, changeable system despite its large size (Ojwang et al., 2016 ). As a result, the lake is occasionally referred to as an "amplifier lake," that is, it "amplifies" climatic variations. The hydrological characteristics of the basin's river discharge into Lake Turkana have long been progressively changing with increasing anthropogenic pressure (Woodroofe, Richard, and Associates, 1996 ). Since 2015, the lake inflow cycles have been permanently altered by the upstream developments on the Omo River (Avery and Tebbs, 2018 ). Thus, the dynamics in the watershed of Lake Turkana have been modified in the last decades by the construction of a cascade of dams within the Omo basin (Avery, 2012 ). According to the prediction of Hairston and Fussmann, (2002) ; Abebe et al., (2018) ; Belete et al., (2016) , the development efforts in the Omo–Gibe basin is accompanied by a drop in the water level of Lake Turkana by 20 m. The filling of the Gibe III reservoir (located more than 380 km away from the lake) alone would cause a 2 m drop in Lake Turkana’s surface level. Apart from this drop in water level, since the dam’s completion in 2015, there have been reports that the regulation of flow from the dam has “eliminated the annual flood pulses of the Omo River” (Hodbod et al., 2019 ). There are conflicting reports concerning this drop in the lake water level and the development efforts in the upper most catchment of the lake in Ethiopia. On the one hand, although Zaniolo et al., (2021)  reported that the filling process of the Gibe III dam was accompanied by drop of the water level of Lake Turkana by 1.7 m, historical lake level studies reveal contradicting results. According to Haack and Messina, (2009) , the historical lake level studies conducted between 1973 and 1989 indicated around 10 m drop in the water level of the lake. This drop allowed the formation of a large wetland and an estuary at the lake inlet. According to the findings of Spruill, (2019) , a decreasing and an increasing water surface elevation was noted for Lake Turkana between 2000 and 2014. The decreasing trend was recorded between 2000 and 2006 where the water surface elevation decreased from an annual average of 364.05 m in 2000 to an annual average of 361.83 m in 2006. Conversely, the increasing water surface elevation was observed from 2006 to 2014 where the annual average increased from 361.83 m to an annual average of 364.51 m in 2014. Before the filling of the Gibe III reservoir commenced, these data show a pattern of annual peak lake surface elevations between September and November for most years. Exceptions include 2002 and 2009, which saw negligible peaks during these months. During the filling of the reservoir, there was a cessation of annual peaks and a general decline in lake surface elevation from early 2015 to mid-2017 (Spruill, 2019 ). From mid-2017 through 2018, lake levels were on the rise and began to display annual peaks, albeit less pronounced than pre-dam conditions. The 18-year change in lake volume variations for Lake Turkana sums to +1.06 km3 , indicating the lake has had a net increase in volume since 2000. Between the years 2000–2014 (before the filling of the Gibe III reservoir) there was an overall increase in the volume of Lake Turkana by 1.36 km3  (Spruill, 2019 ). Moreover, during the reservoir filling period (2015–2018), Lake Turkana experienced an overall decrease of 0.30 km3  in volume. The years 2007, 2010, and 2013, are noted with a volume increase of 9.46 km3 , 6.81 km3 , and 5.60 km3 , respectively, since these are the wettest years (Spruill, 2019 ). The three driest years were 2002, 2009, and 2015, with a volume decrease of 7.65 km3 , 9.54 km3 , and 10.37 km3 , respectively (Spruill, 2019 ). The effects of the Gibe III Dam construction on Lake Turkana that was assessed by Spruill, (2019)  revealed that the magnitude of seasonal floods used to occur from August to October before the construction of the dam was reduced by half and occurred approximately four months earlier. Likewise, periods of negative volume variation were also smaller in magnitude, indicating the dam had a moderating effect on Lake Turkana water levels. In general, the trends in the water level fluctuation of Lake Turkana contradict the forecasted negative impacts of the ongoing water resources projects being carried along the Omo River in Ethiopia, which is considered the main water source for the lake (Avery and Tebbs, 2018 ). The substantial increase in water levels is affecting the local communities (Ojwang et al., 2016 ). The size of Lake Turkana between 2010 and 2020 is displayed in  Table 2  below. When it comes to the assessment of land cover change of the watershed of Lake Turkana between 2000 and 2018, the report compiled by the Government of Kenya & UNDP, (2021) demonstrates that forest cover slightly decreased while cropland and wetland steadily increased. Forest cover decreased from 3762.6 km2  in 2000–3272.9 km2  in 2018 and cropland steady increase from 256.5 km2  in 2000–978.3 km2  in 2018. Wetland also increased from 7358.43 km2  to 7431.45 km2 . This signifies that there was conversion of forest to cropland and that the lakes within the catchment expanded hence decreasing the size of grassland. In general, the investigation on the rise in the water level of the four lakes in the Kenyan Rift Valley has had significant detrimental effects on the ecosystems, biodiversity, human settlements, agricultural and grazing land, infrastructure, and affect economic activities. The loss of biodiversity, especially of acacia trees and other vegetation due to submergence has implications for ecosystem health. Elevated risk from malaria and waterborne diseases has implications for the health of local populations who are also affected by contamination of lake waters and borehole water. Possible snakebites and crocodile attacks are the most eminent effects displayed by the community members (Obando et al., 2016 ).  3.6 Overview of Lake Level Fluctuation in Selected Ethiopian Rift Valley Lakes Recently, the lakes that are situated in terminal positions in the Ethiopian rift, have witnessed major lake water level fluctuations. For instance, until the mid-1970s before irrigation activities started in the Ziway area, Lake Ziway continued to maintain its natural fluctuation pattern. Similarly, before the establishment of the Abijata Soda Ash Factory in the mid-1980s, Lake Abijata was able to maintain a natural balance between inflow and evaporation without any human interference (Seyoum et al., 2015; Dinka, 2012 ). Due to anthropogenic economic activities such as expansion of irrigation agriculture, industrial lake water use, land degradation, and neo-tectonic movements, the lakes’ water level has been rapidly declining in some of the rift valley lakes (Ayenew, 2007 ). On the contrary, the irrigation return flows have been blamed for the observed extraordinary expansion of Lake Beseka since the late 1960s (Ayenew, 2011 ). Similar to the discussion made for the Kenyan Rift Valley Lakes, four Ethiopian Rift Valley Lakes: Lake Abijata, Lake Ziway, Lake Beseka, and Lake Hawassa were selected for the investigation of the shrinking and expanding patterns owing to their ecological significance, economic importance, and the observed contrasting responses to anthropogenic factors.  3.7 Lake Abijata Lake Abijata is an alkaline and saline closed-basin terminal lake that is located at 7°36'59.99" N 38°35'59.99" E. The main water inputs into the lake come from the Horekelo and Bulbula Rivers, direct precipitation, and groundwater recharge. While the Bulbula River connects Lake Ziway and Lake Abijata, the Horekelo River connects Lake Langano and Lake Abijata. Thus, Lake Abijata is a terminal lake connected to two different lakes through two rivers. Owing to its terminal position in the drainage area and its shallow depth, Lake Abijata is especially susceptible to climate change and LULCC in its catchment (Vilalta, 2010; Belay et al., 2019 ). Since the mid-1980s Lake Abijata’s water level has been in almost constant decline, which is unparalleled by the pattern of rainfall records that did not show a declining trend, indicating that the anthropogenic water abstractions could be the main cause for the lake level decline (Ayenew, 2002b; Hengsdijk and Jansen, 2006 ). Studies conducted by Goerner et al., (2009) ; Desta and Fetene, (2020) ; Muita et al., (2021) ; Billi, (2015) ; and Dinka, (2020)  disclosed that the spatial coverage of Lake Abijata has been decreasing rapidly over time due to the recent development schemes, such as pumping of water from the lake for soda extraction, and the utilization of water from feeder rivers and Lake Ziway for irrigation. The rapid decline of the lake is correlated with the increase in salinity of the lake water increased from 8.1 to 26 mg/L, the pH varied between 9.5 and 10.1, and alkalinity changed from 80 to 326 mg/L (Ayenew, 2002b ). The increase in the ionic species could be the result of the loss of water. According to Legesse et al., (2004) , the size/area of Lake Abijata decreased from 202 km2  in 1970–153 km2  in 1990. Hence, Lake Abijata has receded 3 km from the pumping station of the soda ash factory which has slowed down the factory’s production because of the loss of water from the lake. Similarly, Seyoum et al., (2015)  reported that Lake Abijata lost 6.5 m height between 1985 and 2006, and 70 % (∼4.5 m) of the loss has been attributed to human-induced causes whereas the remaining 30 % is related to natural climate variability. This means the lake has lost approximately 36 km2  (35 %) of inundated area since 1985. According to Belete et al., (2016) , the water level of Lake Abijata has decreased in size by 25 % between 1980 and 2010 due to decrease in the level of Lake Ziway and intensive withdrawal of water from Lake Abijata for soda ash production. Ayenew, (2007) , reported that until 2007 the shoreline of Lake Abijata located closer to the soda ash plant had receded by 1.3 km from the 1980s position. On the other hand, Hailu & Girma, (2019), reported that Lake Abijata shrunk in its area coverage from 198.4 km2  in 1972–131.8 km2  in 2015 a decrease in size of 66.6 km2 . Although there are slight differences in the reported data by these researchers, there are some important overlaps of observations in the reported results. The difference in the reported values might be because of the base year difference. For instance, Legesse et al., (2004)  used 1970 as the base year, which was ten years before the industrial water abstraction started. On the other hand, Seyoum et al., (2015) , used 1985 as a base year which is five years after the industrial water abstraction started. Even though these differences in the reported values exist, the lake's size at the beginning of the 1970s (in 1972 and 1973) was roughly closer to 200 km2  crudely declined to 130.98 km2  in 2018, a decrease of 69.02 km2  in nearly half a century as can be witnessed from  Fig. 4 . According to this observation, Lake Abijata showed a continuous decline in its area coverage between 1984 and 2018 as was expected from the anthropogenic activities taking place in its watershed and the direct abstraction of water from the lake and its tributaries. The area exploded and reached as large as 140.19 km2  in 2020 due to the heavy rainfall and its accompanied flooding in the watershed of the lake. The assessment conducted by Hamera et al., (2017)  on the LULC dynamics from 1973 to 2016 and its impact on biodiversity resources in the Abijata–Shala National Park, revealed that cultivated land and grazing land increased by 14.89 % and 14.1 % respectively, while water bodies and the acacia woodland areas decreased by 15.51 % and 8.86 %, respectively. Concerning the fluctuation of the water level of Lake Abijata two things should be carefully noted. The first one is the water level of Lake Abijata closely follows the trends in the water level of Lake Ziway, with an average lag time of about 20 days (Ayenew, 2003 ). Thus, the decline in the water level of Lake Ziway is accompanied by a decrease in outflow into the Bulbula River which causes a decrease in the inflow of water into Lake Abijata (Krienitz et al., 2016 ; Dunkley et al., 1993). The second area to focus on is more serious where many researchers predict that, if business continues as usual in the CRV, Lake Abijata could dry up completely in the next 20 – 50 years (Jansen et al., 2007 ). Lake Abijata is a shallow and vulnerable lake whose decline in the water level alters the physico-chemical and biological conditions of the lake, affecting the fauna and flora of the lake and its overall ecosystem services.  3.8 Lake Beseka (Basaka) Lake Beseka is one of the volcanically dammed endorheic lakes located at 80 51.5’N latitude, 390 51.5’E longitude within the tectonically active Ethiopian northern rift portion near the Afar triangle in the middle of Awash Basin on Metahara plain (Dinka et al., 2014; Kedirkan, 2019; Dinka and Klik, 2019; Desta and Fetene, 2020 ). The topographic nature of the watershed is characterized by diverse relief displacement including undulating plateaus, narrow valleys, and flat plains with elevations ranging from 940 m to 1872 m a.s.l. that falls within warm & semiarid agro-climatic zone (Belay et al., 2019 ). Unlike other Rift Valley lake watersheds, the catchment of Lake Beseka does not contain perennial river that drains into the lake, except for seasonal floods in the wet season, in addition to excess irrigation drainage and groundwater inflow (Gichamo et al., 2022 ). The lake was essentially a surface pond of about 2.7 km2  to 3 km2  total surface area in the late 1950s and early 1960s before the establishment of Metahara Sugar Estate (Jansen et al., 2007; Dinka and Klik, 2019 ). Lake Beseka has a high level of salinity, alkalinity, and fluoride concentration with no surface outflow until the 2007 intervention was launched due to its violent expansion over half a century (Kebede and Zewdu, 2019; Kiage and Douglas, 2020 ). In contrast to many East African terminal lakes, despite the aridity of the rift valley, Lake Beseka is exceptionally the only lake that has extremely expanded at an alarming rate in surface area and volume over the last decades (Dinka and Klik, 2019; Elizabeth et al., 1994 ). Although the starting time of expansion is not exactly known, most previous studies tend to agree that the problem started in the late 1960s and early 1970s when the Metahara mechanized farm was started to be irrigated for the cultivation of cotton and citric fruits that later on shifted to sugarcane development (Jansen et al., 2007; Desta and Fetene, 2020; Kedirkan, 2019; Dinka and Klik, 2019; Kebede and Zewdu, 2019 ). Lake Beseka expanded enormously between 1973 and 2010 comprising about 53 % lake area and 46 % of its volume (Dinka, 2012 ). During this period forested lands in the lake’s watershed were changed to irrigated farmlands consuming significant quantities of water. Cognizant of the potentially damaging effects of the rise in the level of the lake, the Ministry of Water Resources initiated the proportional mixing of the lake water with the Awash River in 2007 (Dinka, 2012 ). The mixing was accompanied by minor calming of the lake level rise that did not bring about substantial lake level stabilization. Various hypotheses have been proposed to explain the aggressive expansion of Lake Beseka. While some scholars claim to relate the expansion of the lake with the establishment of irrigation schemes in the area and leakage from the Awash River favoring groundwater discharge, others argue that the hot springs around the lake and recharge from irrigation runoff or their combinations cause the lake’s expansion (Desta and Fetene, 2020; Dinka and Klik, 2019; Wood and Talling, 1988; Beyene, 2007; Shishaye, 2015 ). Apart from the rough overlapping of the time of initiation of the commercial irrigation farms, it is also important to consider that the area is prone to different tectonic activities that might contribute to the expansion of the lake in some ways (Desta and Fetene, 2020; Dinka and Klik, 2019; Wood and Talling, 1988; Beyene, 2007; Shishaye, 2015 ). Conversely, some focus on the increased surface runoff, climate change, LULCC, geological changes happening in the Ethiopian Rift Valley, etc. as causes for the expansion of the lake (Wood and Talling, 1988; Teffera et al., 2018 ). Still, certain other researchers believe that the main changes in the water balance of Lake Beseka come from groundwater inputs, which are related to the recent increment of recharge from the nearby irrigation fields and due to the rise of the Awash River level after the construction of the Koka dam located some 152 km upstream (Jansen et al., 2007; Desta and Fetene, 2020 ). Before the construction of the Koka Dam, the Awash River sometimes ran dry between December and March. However, after the construction of the dam, there has been a fairly steady flow of the river throughout the year. The sustained flow of the Awash throughout the year has become a source of continuous indirect recharge to the groundwater of the area, ultimately feeding Lake Beseka which is located at a relatively lower topographic position (Ayenew, 2004 ). Apart from the issues related to irrigation return water and groundwater recharge, the LULCC analysis conducted by Dinka, (2012)  indicated that the watershed of Lake Beseka had experienced a drastic change in its LULC conditions over the last four to five decades because of the rapid increase in human settlement, deforestation, establishment of irrigation schemes, etc. Approximately, 189.24 km2  of forest and 47.30 km2  of grazing lands were devastated from 1973 to 2008; reducing the forest coverage from 42 % in the 1970s to only 6 % in the 2000s (Dinka, 2012 ). This phenomenon coincides with the period where about 70 % of the lake expansion was observed (Dinka et al., 2014 ). Moreover, Dinka and Klik, (2019) , estimated the effect of LULCC on surface (direct) runoff for the Lake Beseka catchment indicating about 86 % of forest coverage and 46 % of grasslands were lost between 1973–2015, which were shifted to open bushy woodlands, farms, lake water and wetlands. Although different hypotheses were proposed to explain the expansion of Lake Beseka, it was finally confirmed by Kebede and Zewdu, (2019)  that through the research conducted by using dual Radon and isotope analysis, the main source of water responsible for the expansion of the lake is the excess irrigation water joining the lake through subsurface flows. Different studies indicated that the expansion of the lake is challenging the socio-economics and environment of the region significantly (Dinka, 2017 ). Accordingly, Dinka, (2020) , reported that the substantial growth in lake size along with its saline content of the water causes multiple challenges to the Rift Valley and the Awash Basin communities. Moreover, Eleni, (2009)  described the situation as a natural disaster for the ecosystem of the region because the lake’s expansion has created an unstable transitional zone between the wetland and the nearby terrestrial ecosystem. The effort to protect the further expansion of the lake through controlled draining of it into Awash River is compounded by unprecedented consequences to the downstream communities (Dinka, 2020 ).  3.9 The Extent and Pattern of Expansion of Lake Beseka Wood and Talling, (1988) , initially reported the area coverage of Lake Beseka was 3.2 km2  around the year 1957. This reported value has been cited by different scholars until very recently without considering the changes taking place concerning the overall coverage of the lake. For instance, Elizabeth et al., (1994) ; Ayenew, (2004) ; Alemayehu et al., (2006) ; and Belete et al., (2016)  used this value as it is in their reports without considering the changes taking place over time. Although Wood and Talling, (1988)  reported the size of the lake to be 3.2 km2  in their 1988 article, Ayenew, (2004)  and Gulilat, 2000 as cited by Dinka, (2020)  reported that the area of the lake was only 3 km2  in 1957. The least reported size/area was 2.7 km2  as indicated by Dinka, (2012)  as an initial area of the lake in 1960. These reported sizes can be considered as starting values of Lake Beseka to evaluate its spatio-temporal expansion. In the so far assessment of published articles concerning the areal expansion of Lake Beseka, Ayenew, (2004) , Beyene, (2007) , Dinka, (2012) , and Gichamo et al., (2022)  extensively assessed and reported the spatio-temporal expansion of the lake from the late 1950s. The result of an assessment of the water level of Lake Beseka as reported by Ayenew, (2004)  and (Dinka, (2012)  is given in  Table 3 . The findings of Ayenew (2004)  and Dinka, (2012)  on the expansion of Lake Beseka demonstrate closer results. According to Ayenew, (2004) , the expansion of Lake Beseka showed a record high expansion (17.1 km2 ) in the 1970s (between 1972 and 1978), a few years after the commencement of irrigation in the area. In general, the lake expanded by 37.02 km2  between 1957 and 1998. According to Dinka, (2012) , a record-high expansion (19.3 km2 ) of the lake was noted between 1975 and 1986. The period between 2000 and 2010 is characterized by more or less the culmination of expansion of the lake, due to discharging of the lake water into Awash River. In general, the lake expanded by 45.8 km2  between 1960 and 2010. Taking the 3 km2  and 2.7 km2  as starting areal coverage of Lake Beseka, both researchers reported that the lake has expanded by 0.903 km2  per year and 0.916 km2  per year. Accordingly, while Ayenew, (2004)  reported the overall expansion of the lake to be 37.02 km2  in 41 years, Dinka, (2012)  indicated an overall expansion of 45.8 km2  in just half a century. This was about a 15-fold incremental area increase since 1960 accompanied by detrimental effects on the surrounding residential, ecological, hydrological, and infrastructural facilities (Ayenew and Tilahun, 2008 ).  Fig. 5  shows the aggressive expansion of Lake Beseka between 1973 and 2008 to establish an island (the white spot in the middle of C and D). In a conference poster Shishaye, (2015) , reported that the size of Lake Beseka raised to its highest level of 54 km2  in 2015. Similarly, Teffera et al., (2018)  revealed that the lake area that was approximately 11.7 km2  in 1972 rose to 41.1 km2  in 2005 that finally reached 46.7 km2  in 2017. According to this report, the lake has shown a total areal increment of about 35 km2  between 1972 and 2017 with expansion rate of 0.78 km2  each year. Very recently, Gichamo et al., (2022)  extended the study on the extent of expansion of Lake Beseka between the years 2007 and 2013. According to his finding, the surface area of the lake expanded by 1.47 km2 /year and expanded by 8.86 km2  in just six years to reach 54.49 km2 , which was approximately 18 times greater than the lake’s size in 1960 as shown in  Fig. 6 . These research reports reflect the severity of the flooding problem in the area as a function of the rising lake level because of the flat topography of the area surrounding the lake. If this condition of the lake is left unchecked, the terminal Beseka Lake might become an open system lake by joining the Awash River through its overflow causing a calamity to all downstream irrigation developments in the Awash River basin. Several studies have been conducted around Lake Beseka mainly focusing on the pattern of expansion of the lake and the LULCC on its watershed. According to Dinka, (2012) , the LULC pattern of the watershed of Lake Beseka experienced drastic changes over the last four to five decades because of rapid increases in human settlement, deforestation, the establishment of irrigation schemes, and the establishment of Awash National Park. Approximately 189.24 km2  of forest and 47.30 km2  of grazing lands were devastated between 1973 and 2008 (Dinka, 2012 ). At the same time, there was a shift in land cover from forests/woodlands to open woodlands, shrubs, and grazing lands. Recently, Dinka and Klik, (2019) , stated that the catchment of Lake Beseka experienced a significant LULC change, where about 86 % of forest coverage and 46 % of grasslands were lost between 1973 and 2015, which were shifted to open bushy woodlands, farms, lake water and wetlands as shown in  Fig. 7 . As can be witnessed from the Figure as reported by Dinka and Klik, (2019) , while farmland, lake area, wetland and bush land expanded, forest, grassland, and bushy woods declined. Lake area increased by 1.05 km2  each year reaching 51.0 km2  in 2015. Conversely, forest area declined by 4.52 km2  each year, reaching 21 km2  in 2015 from 211.0 km2  in 1973.  3.10 Lake Ziway Lake Ziway is an open lake located in the upstream portion of the Ethiopian CRV portion at 80 01’N and 380 47’E. The mean and maximum depths of the lake are about 2.5 m and 9 m, respectively. The main water inputs to Lake Ziway come from Katar River (from the western highlands) and Meki River (from the eastern mountains), and direct precipitation. The main outputs are evaporation, discharge via the Bulbula River, and groundwater leakage through faults and paleo-channels. The annual discharge of water from the lake is around 170 Mm3  (Getnet et al., 2014; Goshime et al., 2020 ) into Lake Abijata via Bulbula River. According to Ayenew, (2003) , hydro-chemical and isotopic evidence revealed that there is a southward groundwater migration from Ziway to Abijata. Since the early 1970s agricultural activities have massively intensified in the watershed of Lake Ziway where its forests and woodlands have been degraded leading to the subsequent siltation in the lake (Onywere et al., 2013; Kassilly, 2002; Dinka et al., 2014; Ibrahim, 2021; Belete, 2013 ). The intensification of large-scale irrigation in the watershed is achieved at the expense of water consumed from the lake and its main feeder rivers (Ayenew, 2002a ). The first reported size/area of Lake Ziway was 442 km2  that came from (Wood and Talling, 1988 ). Similar to that of the size of Lake Beseka, this reported value of the size of Lake Ziway kept on appearing in scientific articles until the second reported size/area of 440 km2  came from Ayenew and Legesse, (2007) . This reported size of Lake Ziway kept on appearing in scientific articles until 2016 as it was reported by Pascual-Ferrer et al., (2008) ; Seyoum et al., (2015) . According to Teklu et al., (2018) , the size of Lake Ziway was 434 km2  which is 8 km2  less than the size reported in 1998. Asfaw et al., (2020)  revealed that the water level reduction of 40 cm/annum, surface area shrinkage of 0.08 km2 /annum, and loss of water storage by about 20.4 Mm3 /annum. As a result, since 2009 the lake has lost 12.75 % of its water storage volume.  Table 4  below displays the output of the change in the size of Lake Ziway between 1985 and 2015. The watershed of Lake Ziway is bounded between 7°20′54″N and 8°25′56″N latitudes and 38°13′02″ E and 39°24′01″E longitudes that include the rift floor, two escarpment areas, two major river inlets and one river outlet encompassing 7300 km2  (Desta and Fetene, 2020 ). It is characterized by higher mountains at the periphery (along the southeastern and northwestern ridge) and predominantly flat landforms with elevations ranging from 1601 to 4213 m a.s.l. (Desta and Fetene, 2020 ). The slope classes in the watershed are spatially distributed along with elevation. Eighty-nine percent of the total watershed areas consist of < 30 % slopes, and the remaining > 30 % slopes (steep to very steep hills and mountains). Thus, the watershed of Lake Ziway is characterized by rugged terrain and geological and structural complexities in which the principal features in the rift margin are dominated by chains of mountains, step faults, horst-graben structures, and river channels (Mechal et al., 2022 ). The vegetation cover within the rift floor is characterized by Acacia spp. open woodland, with deciduous woodlands (composed of Olea europaea, Celtis, Dodonaea viscosa, and Euclea) on the escarpments. According to Vallet-Coulomb et al., (2001) , change in the LULC of the watershed of Lake Ziway began in the early 1970s. Thus, in the past 50 years, the watershed of Lake Ziway has been under progressive and intensive LULC changes. Different scholars reported their findings on the LULC change taking place within the Ziway-Shala sub-basin. For instance, Desta and Fetene, (2020) , reported that out of the eight land use classes they identified cultivated land, agroforestry and settlement expanded at the expense of woodlands for the study period from 1973 to 2018, where cultivated land increased by 15.45 km2  per year and woodland declined by 10.42 km2  per annum. Similarly, Bekele et al., (2019) , reported similar findings where the rate of loss of acacia woodland and gain by agricultural land was 12.69 km2  and 6.36 km2  per annum, respectively. Mechal et al., (2022)  reported that cultivated land increased from 2598.07 km2  to 3588.68 km2  for the period 1985 and 2020. Similarly, settlement increased from 365.00 km2  in 1985–1007.4 km2  in 2020. According to this finding, cultivated land and settlement expanded by 27 km2 /year and 1.8 km2 /year, respectively. The expansion of cultivated land and settlement in the watershed is at the expense of woodland diminished from 1718.42 km2  in 1985–219 km2  in 2020 with a negative annual rate change of 42.8 km2  per year. Studies conducted on the watershed of Lake Ziway by Omondi et al., (2016) ; Degife et al., (2019) ; Dessie, (2007) ; Muriithi, (2016) ; and Ibrahim, (2021)  revealed similar increasing trends for cultivated land and settlement while decreasing trend in forest, woodland, and grassland, although there are differences in the numerical values they reported. In general, the changes in the reported land use pattern of the watershed of Lake Ziway since 1973 confirmed that cultivated land, agroforestry, and settlement areas increase at the expense of forest land, woodlands, grazing land, bush/shrub-land, and water bodies and wetlands.  3.11 Lake Hawassa The Lake Hawassa basin represents a large collapsed caldera bordered by highlands to the north and east. The center of the caldera is occupied by Hawassa and Shallo (Cheleleka) lakes (Ayenew and GebreEgziabher, 2015 ). Lake Hawassa is an endorheic freshwater lake within the southern portion of the Ethiopian rift located between 60 59’3.91”–70 7’42.24”N latitude and 380 23’17.8”–380 28’52.9” E longitude. The elevation of the lake is 1680 m a.s.l., representing the culmination of the Ethiopian Rift floor level occupied by lakes (Ayenew and GebreEgziabher, 2015 ). The floor of the caldera is faulted and dotted by volcanic hills (Ayenew and GebreEgziabher, 2015 ). The input to the lake comes from rivers, direct precipitation, and groundwater. Usually, the overflow from the Shallo/Cheleleka wetland which is located about 6 km east of Lake Hawassa is the only perennial water source that drains into Lake Hawassa via the Tikur Wuha River. Chelelaka wetland receives water from Wedesa, Gomesho, Shenkora, Werka, Wesha, and Lango streams serves as a sediment trap, and transports the water and sediment to Lake Hawassa. Seasonal streams may also terminate in wide-open fractures before reaching the lake (Ayenew and GebreEgziabher, 2015 ). Lake Hawassa and its feeder Cheleleka have been subjected to natural and anthropogenic alterations. Thus, different scholars reported their findings concerning the lake size/area and volume at different times. Unlike the other lakes, there is no substantial abstraction of water, except for limited diversions for local irrigation from the Tikur-Wuha River. The water level of Lake Hawassa has been experiencing a progressive rise with an average rate of 4.9 cm/year between 1970 and 2010 (Hailu & Girma, 2019; Phiri et al., 2019 ). According to Abebe et al., (2018) , the surface area of Lake Hawassa increased by 7.5 % in 1999 and 3.2 % in 2011 from 1985, while the water volume decreased by 17 % between 1999 and 2011. Moreover, silt accumulated over more than 50 % of the bed surface causing a 4 % loss of the lake’s storage capacity. The sedimentation patterns identified may have been strongly impacted by anthropogenic activities including urbanization and farming practices located on the northern, eastern, and western sides of the lake watershed (Abebe et al., 2018 ). Similarly, Menberu et al., (2021)  reported the changes in surface area of Lake Hawassa over a period of 46 years (1973–2019). According to this report, there was a fast increase in the surface area of the lake from 1973 to 2002 by about 7.89 km2  in 29, accompanied by a gradual increase of surface area up to the year 2010 and finally, a rapid increase. In general, the the surface area of the lake increased by 11.28 % over 46 years between 1973 and 2019 as shown in  Fig. 8 . According to the findings of Menberu et al., (2021) , the discharge from Tikur-Wuha River along with the sediment into Lake Hawassa is the culprit for the increased surface area of the Lake as well as the cause for reduction in the lake depth. This situation urges for the investigation of the changes taking place in the watershed of the lake. The watershed of Lake Hawassa consists of important ecosystems is about 1435.61 km2  located in an old caldera in a closed drainage system, approximately between 60 45'N and 70 15'N Latitude and 380 15'E and 380 45'E Longitude. The formation of the watershed is attributed to intensive tectonic activity which is related to the formation of the main Ethiopian rift system (Degife et al., 2019 ). The dominant landscapes characterizing the watershed are the volcanic mountains forming the surrounding escarpments and flat plains lying at the foothills of the mountains. In terms of elevation, the watershed ranges from 1680 to 2970 m a.s.l. Thus, the topographical characteristics include inter alia, flat plains, gentle slopes to dissected escarpments, mountainous regions, and hilly surfaces (Degife et al., 2021 ). The central part of the watershed is characterized by low-lying plains. The area between the low-lying plains and the top of the escarpments is characterized by steep slopes. There are several urban centers in the watershed, with Hawassa City being one of the biggest. The dominant economic activity in the watershed was agriculture, which was characterized by subsistence-level mixed cropping with some commercial farming and livestock production (Degife et al., 2021 ). The eastern part of the watershed is a “Moist Woina Dega” (moist mid-highland), and a montane forest composed of Podocarpus falcatus and Juniperus procera is dominant (Degife et al., 2019 ).The western part of the “Dry Woina Dega” (dry mid-highland) harbors shrubs and acacia woodland (Dessie, 2007 ). The rainfall within the watershed amount differs between the drier western escarpments, which receive 900 mm a year, and the wetter eastern escarpments, which receive 1200 mm. The mean annual temperature in the foothills varies from 170  C to 190  C (Degife et al., 2019 ). Studies on LULC change conducted in the watershed of Lake Hawassa and the CRV might help to explain the causes for the expansion of Lake Hawassa. Taking this into consideration, Elias et al., (2019) , conducted an overall assessment of LULC change taking place in the CRV from 1985 to 2015 & revealed that settlement area increased by 223.77 km2 , while large-scale farming expanded by 203.31 km2 , and woodland and forest decreased by 335.42 km2 . Similarly, Mekuria et al., (2021)  reported that farmlands, bare lands, and settlement areas showed positive changes, while forest, grasslands, shrub-lands and waterbodies showed negative changes between 1973 and 2020 where agricultural lands expanded at the expense of grassland, forestland, and shrub-land. Accordingly, 2044.91 km2  of grassland, 5568.34 km2  of forestland, and 2614.12 km2  of shrub-land are lost in just half a century. Generally speaking, while forestland, grassland, shrub-land, and water body declined by 68.0 %, 68.8 %, 82.3 & 8.5, respectively, farmland, bare land, & settlement increased by 350.1 %, 1813.5 %, and 696.8 % respectively.  Table 5  shows the details of LULC change in the CRV for 47 years. These changes have serious ecological consequences apart from their social and economic improvement. In similar track record, Gebreslassie, (2014) Seifu et al., (2019) , Desta and Fetene, (2020) , and Ayalew et al., (2022)  revealed comparable trends in the LULC changes in the CRV and their deriving forces. These scholars revealed that the driving forces for the LULC change in the Ethiopian Rift Valley system are enhanced socio-economic development, population increase, and human pressures on agricultural lands.   4 Discussion The study of lake morphology is important to lake management professionals in making the right decisions for sustaining and protecting lakes. In this review, we summarized data collected over more than five decades for EARS lakes that show contradicting variations in their water level and its concomitant effects. According to our findings, the water levels of Lakes Abijata and Ziway in Ethiopia are dropping while Lake Beseka and Lake Hawassa in Ethiopia and Lake Baringo and Lake Bogoria in Kenya are rising at worrisome rates. While the lakes in the Kenyan Rift Valley are tectonic in origin where water is tapped in the down-faulted valleys (Obando et al., 2016 ), the Ethiopian Rift Valley Lakes are the results of volcano-tectonic structural depressions that became sites for many rift valley lakes (Ayenew, 2002b ). These lakes and their associated wetlands play significant roles in the maintenance of aquatic biodiversity and ecosystem function; climate modulation; provision of ecosystem goods and services; flood regulation; water quality regulation; and groundwater recharge. Moreover, the EARS lakes form an important migration route for Arctic and Palaearctic birds during the winter season in the northern hemisphere (Ayenew, 2004; Ayenew, 2007 ; Government of Kenya & UNDP, 2021). For instance, the muddy shore of Lake Abijata and Lake Baringo support a wealth of bird life unequaled over perhaps the whole of Africa (Burnett and Rowntree, 1990; Ayenew, 2004 ). Lakes Baringo, Bogoria, Naivasha, and Nakuru are internationally recognized as Ramsar sites due to their significant biodiversity. Three of the lakes, Bogoria, Naivasha, and Nakuru, are incorporated within national parks and are well-known tourist destinations in Kenya (Obando et al., 2016 ). Lake Baringo also attracts a significant number of tourists despite it not being a reserve. The increment in surface extent of the Kenyan Rift Valley lakes was substantially noted from 2018 to 2020. The real causes for the expansion of these lakes are still not certain despite the suggestive correlation with the increased rainfall over the lake catchments. A detailed investigation into the lake water balances, the role of climatology, LULCC in the watershed of the lakes, land degradation, and sediment yield into the lakes from the catchment as well as the role of geological activities including the status of the many geological faults and fissures in the region are key in understanding the underlying factors for the fluctuations. On the other hand, the shrinking and expansion of lakes in Ethiopia's Rift Valley are more related to anthropogenic forces and LULCC. The unprecedented increase in water levels in lakes inundates entire villages causing serious environmental and social harm that disrupts the livelihoods of local communities by uprooting thousands of people, damaging biodiversity, and destroying lake ecosystems. Short- and medium-term effects include extensive property loss, infrastructure damage such as roads, railways, and buildings, and sewer damage. The review revealed that this is a good indication that the health of the rift lakes has been under immense influence from extensive anthropogenic and naturally occurring pushing factors. The study contributes to knowledge by documenting changes in lake levels. The long-term management of the lakes needs to take into account the dynamic nature of water resources over time and the need for flexible management systems that consider the resource base. Given that the Rift Valley lakes are influenced by tectonics, there are possibilities that there could be an influx of geothermal water also contributing to an increase in the lake levels and this needs to be further investigated including the impacts from contaminated surface water and groundwater by use of geochemical methods. For the last five decades, the Ethiopian CRV region has been the focus of large-scale irrigation developments industrial expansion, and other anthropogenic activities that withdraw considerable amounts of water from the lakes and their tributary rivers. This situation puts immense pressure on the existing forests, grasslands, water bodies, and woodlands. These anthropogenic forces are the possible culprits for the fluctuations in the lake water levels, hydrodynamics, and increased salinity in the lakes as they are frequently carried out without a fundamental understanding of the intricate hydrological, and hydrogeological features, and the fragile nature of the Rift Valley’s ecosystem. This does not mean that the anthropogenic pushing factors are the only reasons for the observed fluctuations. Climate change is expected to contribute its share for the observed changes that needs to be assessed deeply using state-of-the-art technologies. Throughout the analyses of the collected articles, we were unable to get any kind of evidence that attempted to link the lake water level fluctuation with the dynamic processes leading to continental breakup in the East African continent. Thus, we suggest investigating the possible link of the continental movement with the shrinkage or expansion of the lakes in the future. Finally, we believe that this is the right moment to exert multidisciplinary and concerted efforts to at least halt further expansion and shrinking of the lakes to avoid the approaching apocalypse of lake resources and related loss of their important services.  5 Conclusions Lakes play significant roles as essential components of biogeochemical processes and suppliers of vital ecosystem services. Thus, the shrinking and expansion of lakes can cause serious ecological and environmental disasters. There are limited research articles that attempt to highlight the significant roles that lakes can play as integral parts of biogeochemical processes and suppliers of vital ecosystem services along with the loss of carbon with their shrinkage or expansion. From the pattern of trends of anthropogenic activities in the EKR valley region greater demand for lake and river water resources is expected, besides the predictable rise in temperatures and flooding related to climate change. These situations put the Rift Valley lakes in grave danger exposing the surrounding regions to diverse consequences that might threaten human health from aggravated shrinkage, expansion, and deteriorating water quality. Despite the fluctuations in the water level of lakes in the rift region, there are no sufficient accounts of how these fluctuations have affected the water quality parameters and ecological functions. Thus, this is high time to halt and think about the health of the Rift Valley lakes and their ecosystem services by the academia and decision makers and get prepared to shape the issue of shrinking and expanding lakes to get global attention. Finally, the linkage between the lake level fluctuation and climate change, lake biogeochemistry, macro- and micro-faunal ecology, and effects on neighboring communities, dwindling resource availability (such as fishery), socio-political pressures, ecological degradation within the lakes and beyond are areas that need to be given due attention in the future.
1 Introduction Phosphorus (P) loss during agricultural production is widely recognized as a substantial contributor to agricultural non-point source pollution (Liu et al., 2012 ). As the primary limiting factor for aquatic plant growth (Bertol et al., 2010 ), even low P concentrations (0.05–0.10 mg L−1 ) can result in algal blooms in freshwater (Shigaki et al., 2007 ). According to the Bulletin of the Second National Census of Pollution Sources, agricultural discharges of total phosphorus (TP) accounted for 67.2 % of water pollutants in China (MEEC, 2020 ). P transport in runoff occurs in two distinct forms: particulate phosphorus (PP) and dissolved phosphorus (DP). PP is typically adsorbed onto soil particles and organic matter and lost via soil erosion (Ross et al., 2022 ). In contrast, DP is primarily lost via desorption and dissolution (Sharma et al., 2017 ). Runoff serves as the primary transport pathway for non-point source pollution, facilitating the movement of nutrients, such as DP and PP, from agricultural fields to adjacent water bodies. This process, leads to eutrophication, biodiversity loss, and environmental degradation within aquatic systems (Peuelas and Sardans, 2022; Ma et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2017 ). Therefore, quantifying the TP, DP, and PP fractions in runoff is of great significance in controlling P source loss and transport. Non-point source pollution due to nutrient loss from agricultural land is a major hazard in the Three Gorges watershed (Zhang et al., 2017 ). Various factors (e.g., rainfall, runoff, and soil cultivation) influence this process (Liu et al., 2014a ). Fertilizer application has been shown to significantly impact soil P accumulation, transformation processes, and hydrological properties (Hua and Zhu, 2020 ). This is because continued application of mineral fertilizers and manures may exceed the capacity of crops to absorb P, leading to P accumulation in the soil and subsequent migration via runoff. Organic fertilizer is a viable alternative to chemical fertilizers in agricultural applications because of its rich nutrient content, which has the potential to improve the physical and chemical properties of the soil (Lourenzi et al., 2021 ). By gradually releasing nutrients, this approach also mitigates the environmental pollution associated with the rapid effect of chemical fertilizers and their low utilization efficiencies (Zhou, 2023 ). Zhang et al. (2021)  revealed that the continuous application of organic fertilizers reduces the loss of TP in runoff. However, a large body of research has demonstrated that the persistent and prolonged application of organic fertilizers increases N and P losses in surface runoff (Lourenzi et al., 2021; Zanon et al., 2020 ). Therefore, characterizing P concentrations and losses in runoff under various long-term fertilization scenarios is of great importance in assessing the environmental impacts of P losses via runoff. The Sichuan Basin holds considerable agricultural significance within the upper reaches of the Yangtze River. It is considered an important arable land in the humid subtropical region of China, with an area of approximately 300,000 km2 , which accounts for 7 % of the total arable land in the country (Li et al., 1991 ). The region relies on rain-fed agriculture for over 65 % of its land area that most of the farmland is cultivated on slopes, and the rainy season has a prolonged duration (Zhu et al., 2009 ). Rainfall, as the primary driver of surface runoff, is a primary factor influencing nutrient loss (Liu et al., 2014b ). Consequently, these soils exhibit susceptibility to the effects of rainfall and cultivation, thereby leading to P losses and subsequent widespread environmental pollution. In contrast, previous research has focused on short-term experimental studies and simulated rainfall experiments. For instance, a 2-year study found that the application of organic fertilizers, as opposed to conventional fertilizers, was effective in reducing P losses in surface runoff across different rainfall scenarios (Liu et al., 2012 ). During a 1.5-year continuous monitoring period of a subtropical double rice system with various fertilizer application rates, Liu et al. (2020)  discovered that during this time, both the concentration and runoff loss of P increased significantly with increasing fertilizer application rates. Wang et al. (2013)  found that surface application of fertilizer and an increase in the amount of fertilizer applied increased the loss of P via runoff under simulated rainfall conditions. Although a substantial amount of research has been conducted on the characterization of P loss under rainfall conditions, long-term experimental studies of monitored rainfall in the field are still required to substantiate the findings. This study reports the characteristics of runoff depths, sediment, and P loss via runoff from agricultural fields under various fertilizer application conditions for 120 rainfall events over a 15-year period from 2008 to 2022. The objectives of this study were as follows: (1) to quantify the concentrations and amounts of TP, DP, and PP that are lost in surface runoff and (2) to evaluate the interrelationships between runoff depth, sediment yield, and P concentration and loss.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The field experiments were conducted at Southwest University experimental station for soil and water conservation exploration in the Chongqing Municipality (106°24′20″ E, 29°48′42″ N) ( Fig. 1 ). The study site is located in the Yangtze River Basin, which is a typical rice-wheat crop rotation region in China characterized by the following: a subtropical monsoon climate, mean annual temperature of 18.6ºC, a mean annual precipitation rate of 1153 mm over a 15-year (2008–2022) period ( Fig. 2 ), mean relative humidity of 80.6 %, and mean frost-free period of 340 d. The soils in the study area are classified as purple in the Chinese soil classification and Entisols in the U.S. soil classification (Liu et al., 2009 ). The following major soil properties were determined from top layer samples at a depth of 0–20 cm: pH = 8.16, organic matter content = 8.75 g kg−1 , total P = 0.68 g kg−1 , available P = 18.29 mg kg−1 . The main crops grown in the region are winter wheat (Triticum aestivum  L.) and summer corn (Zea mays  L.).  2.2 Experimental design Runoff plots (length: 8 m × width: 4 m) were constructed on 15° slopes in 2008 and rainfall and nutrient losses were subsequently monitored (Fig. 1 ). All three replicate treatments included the following: (1) CK: no fertilizer with downslope cultivation, (2) T1: chemical fertilizer application with downslope cultivation, (3) T2: manure and chemical fertilizer combined with downslope cultivation, (4) T3: 1.5-fold chemical fertilizer application with downslope cultivation, (5) T4: chemical fertilizer application with contour cultivation. The contour cultivation for T4 was characterized by a ridge height of 5–8 cm, a width of 40–50 cm, and a distance of 40 cm from the ridge. The crop rotation system consisted of a double-season wheat-corn rotation. Yumai 7 (Triticum aestivum  L.) and Zhongnuo 39 (Zea mays  L.) were used as winter wheat and summer maize, respectively. Wheat was sown in mid-November to early December and harvested in mid-May. Maize was transplanted in early to mid-April and harvested in late July. The experimental area utilized rain-fed agriculture without irrigation because precipitation usually provides sufficient water for the normal growth of wheat and maize in this region. Winter wheat was fertilized before sowing, followed by supplementary fertilizer application in January–February of the following year. Maize was fertilized prior to transplanting, and supplementary fertilizer was applied in May. The application of fertilizer was performed by spreading. Urea, calcium superphosphate, and potassium chloride were used for nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium fertilizers, respectively. Urea contained N ≥ 46.4 %, superphosphate contained P2 O5  ≥ 12 %, and potassium chloride contained K2 O ≥ 60 %. The organic fertilizer was farm manure (pig feces and urine), comprising the following elements: C (4.31 %), N (0.24 %), P2 O5  (0.17 %), and K2 O (0.21 %).   Table 1  presents plot information and agricultural fertilizer management data.  2.3 Sample collection and analysis Miniature weather stations were installed in the experimental area to record each rainfall event. Following each runoff event, the runoff volume from the plots was manually recorded, and the ratio of runoff volume to plot area was subsequently calculated to derive the runoff depth (mm). In addition, water samples were collected from the runoff plots by thoroughly mixing the water with a clean bamboo pole to determine the concentrations of total N (TN), total dissolved N (TDN), TP, and DP. Samples (500 ml) were taken and promptly stored in a laboratory refrigerator at 4 °C after collection. The TP and DP concentrations of unfiltered runoff water samples were determined prior to and following filtration with a 0.45 μm membrane; the PP concentration was calculated as the discrepancy between TP and DP (Uusitalo et al., 2000 ). The TP and DP concentrations were determined using the potassium persulfate-molybdenum blue colorimetric method (SEPAC, 1997 ). After vigorously shaking the mixed samples, 100 ml was transferred to a beaker and dried at 105 °C in an oven. Following the weighing of samples, the sediment concentration was calculated. Sediment yield for each plot was calculated by multiplying the runoff volume by the sediment concentration. As per the China National Standard (General Administration of Quality Supervision, 2012 ), rainfall is categorized according to the amount of rainfall: light rain (< 9.9 mm), moderate rain (10–24.9 mm), heavy rain (25.0–49.9 mm), rainstorm (50.0–99.9 mm), and large rainstorm (100–249.9 mm), extreme rainstorm (> 250 mm). A total of 120 runoff-producing rainfall events that occurred between 2008 and 2022 were selected for this study ( Fig. 3 ). In addition, rainfall ranged from 10.7 to 222.5 mm. These rainfall events that produced runoff could be categorized into the following categories: 23 moderate rainfall events, 50 heavy rainfall events, 32 rainstorms, and 15 large rainstorms. These categories accounted for 19.2 %, 41.7 %, 26.6 %, and 12.5 % of the total runoff events, respectively.  2.4 Data analysis The Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) test was used to test the normality of variables, whereas the log10  transformation was conducted when the data deviated from a normal distribution. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and Tukey's test were used to detect differences in runoff depths, sediment yield, and P concentration and loss between rainfall and treatments. In addition, a linear fit model was used to simulate the relationship between runoff depth, sediment yield, and P concentration and loss. A p -value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses of the results were conducted using IBM SPSS 25.0. Figures were compiled using Origin 2021.   3 Results 3.1 Runoff depth and sediment Runoff depths for each treatment were greatest during large rainstorms, ranging from 21.5 % to 252.4 % higher than those during other rainfall categories ( Fig. 4 a). Across all rainfall categories, runoff depths of the CK treatment were significantly higher (i.e, 18.1–87.3 %) than those of the fertilized treatments (T1, T2, T3, and T4). The lowest runoff depth was observed in the T4 treatment (Fig. 4 a). There were no significant differences in sediment concentration and yield among rainfall categories in all treatments (Fig. 4 b, c). Among the five treatments, sediment concentration and yield were significantly higher (i.e., 143.3 % and 382.3 %, respectively) in the CK treatment than those in the T4 treatment during heavy rain (Fig. 4 b, c).  3.2 Runoff P concentration The CK treatment produced significantly higher TP concentrations (i.e., 77.5 %) in runoff during the heavy rain than during the large rainstorm, whereas the remaining four treatments did not vary significantly across rainfall categories ( Fig. 5 a). In addition, T2 produced the highest runoff TP concentration during heavy rain, which was significantly higher (i.e., 41.3 %) than that of CK. The treatments did not differ significantly across the remaining rainfall categories (Fig. 5 a). The lowest concentrations of runoff DP were observed in the large rainstorms, which were significantly lower (i.e., 15.8–69.0 %) than the rainstorms, heavy rain, and moderate rain categories (Fig. 5 b). There were no significant differences among the five treatments for rainstorms and large rainstorms (Fig. 5 b).
