However, concentrations of runoff DP in CK were significantly lower (i.e., 40.2 % and 35.2 %, respectively) than those in T4 for moderate rain and heavy rain, respectively (Fig. 5 b). The PP concentrations in runoff from both the T2 and T4 treatments were not significantly different across rainfall categories (Fig. 5 c). Concentrations of PP in runoff from the CK during the large rainstorm were significantly lower (i.e., 40.6 %) than those during the rainstorm (Fig. 5 c). Moreover, there were no significant differences in PP concentrations in the runoff between treatments across different rainfall categories (Fig. 5 c).  3.3 Runoff P loss The TP loss was significantly lower (i.e., 58.5–73.1 % and 44.2–69.2 %, respectively) during moderate and heavy rain than that during the large rainstorm ( Fig. 6 a). There was no significant difference in TP losses across all treatments in moderate rain, heavy rain, and large rainstorms (Fig. 6 a). In contrast, TP loss in the CK treatment during heavy rain was significantly higher (i.e., 63.1 %) than that in the T4 treatment (Fig. 6 a). The DP loss for CK and T4 were not significantly different across rainfall categories, but T2 was significantly lower for both moderate and heavy rain than for rainstorms (53.2 % and 40.0 %, respectively) and large rainstorms (52.8 % and 39.4 %, respectively) (Fig. 6 b). The DP loss was not significantly different among treatments during moderate rain, rainstorms, and large rainstorms. Moreover, T3 was significantly higher (i.e., 31.1 % and 31.6 %) than T2 and CK during heavy rain (Fig. 6 b). The PP loss was significantly higher in T1, T2, T3, and T4 treatments during large rainstorms than during rainstorms (20.2–143.1 %), heavy rain (102.6–275.5 %), and moderate rain (232.9–473.4 %) (Fig. 6 c). PP loss was significantly higher for CK during rainstorms and large rainstorms than during moderate and heavy rain. The PP loss was not significantly different across treatments during moderate rain, heavy rain, and large rainstorms (Fig. 6 c). Additionally, T4 was significantly lower (i.e., 60.0 %) than CK during rainstorms (Fig. 6 c).  3.4 Relationship between runoff depth, sediment, and runoff phosphorus Runoff depth showed a significant linear relationship with TP loss, PP loss, and DP concentration (p  = 0.000) ( Fig. 7 b;  Fig. 8 a, c). However, the runoff depth had no significant linear correlation with DP loss, TP concentration, and PP concentration (p  = 0.058–0.814) (Fig. 7 a, c; Fig. 8 b). The sediment concentration was not significantly correlated with TP concentration, DP concentration, and PP concentration (p  = 0.507–0.932) (Fig. 7 d, e, f). The sediment yield was not significantly correlated with TP loss, DP loss, and PP loss (p  = 0.606–0.949) (Fig. 8 d, e, f).   4 Discussion 4.1 Characterization of runoff depth and sediment Our study revealed that the runoff depth increased significantly with rainfall. This could be because moderate rain is of low intensity. In contrast, heavy rain is more intense and destructive to the soil surface (Meng et al., 2021 ), potentially resulting in increased runoff depths. Moreover, the runoff depth produced by the fertilized treatment was less than that of the unfertilized treatment (Fig. 4 ). These findings were consistent with those of Du et al. (2021) , who reported that fertilizer application on sloping cropland in Sichuan effectively reduced the runoff depth. Because of the low nutrient content of soils in the unfertilized treatment, the formation of a soil microcrust is promoted, reducing infiltration and exacerbating runoff formation, which can be mitigated by fertilizer application (Lasanta et al., 2000 ). The sediment concentration exhibited distinct responses to the rainfall categories in comparison to the runoff depths. We found that heavy rains had higher sediment concentrations than large rainstorms (Fig. 4 ). In general, sediment concentration increases with rainfall intensity and volume. However, numerous studies have shown that other factors influence sediment concentration. For example, Defersha and Melesse (2012)  demonstrated that soil type and moisture content dominate sediment yield and concentration. In a study on rangelands, Wei et al. (2009)  established that increased runoff depth result in decreased sediment concentration. Sediment concentration was affected by subsurface soil water pressure and surface confinement under simulated rainfall conditions (Römkens et al., 2002 ). Our study found that contour cultivation yielded lower sediment concentrations than downslope cultivation during moderate rain, heavy rain, and rainstorms. Conversely, downslope cultivation had lower sediment concentrations than contour cultivation during large rainstorms (Fig. 4 ). In general, contour ridges increase ground roughness, increase water infiltration, and reduce runoff-transported sediments (Li et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2015 ). However, because of the high rainfall volume and the high kinetic energy of the raindrops during large rainstorm conditions, localized contour ridges are destroyed, and ridge collapses may even occur, which provides a rich source of sediment loss (Xu et al., 2018 ). In a simulated rainfall experiment by Liu et al. (2014a) , the peak sediment concentration loss following contour ridge collapse was 40 times higher than that before the collapse.  4.2 Characterization of runoff P concentration There were no significant differences in TP concentrations via runoff during each rainfall category. In a 20-year study in Canada, Liu et al. (2019)  discovered that reduced rainfall similarly had no significant impact on P concentrations in rainfall runoff. In addition, we found that TP concentrations in runoff were higher in the organic fertilizer-chemical fertilizer application treatment than those in the chemical fertilizer application treatment (Fig. 5 ). Zanon et al. (2020)  identified a similar phenomenon in which the long-term application of organic fertilizer resulted in increased TP concentration in runoff. Wang et al. (2012)  observed that when organic and chemical fertilizers were combinedly applied in soils, the TP concentration in runoff escalated concurrently with the augmented application rates of organic fertilizer. This phenomenon may be attributable to the organic acids presented in organic manure impeding the adsorption pathway of P to the soil (Bertol et al., 2010 ). Alternatively, it may be the result of organic manure particulate matter obstructing soil pore space, thereby causing a soil surface closure and subsequent high P concentrations in runoff (Hooda et al., 2000; Gilley et al., 2007 ). In contrast to TP concentrations in runoff, DP concentrations in runoff were lower than in other rainfall categories during large rainstorms (Fig. 5 ). This may be because of the high runoff volume generated by large rainstorms, which dilutes the concentration of DP. The significant negative linear correlation between runoff depth and DP concentration verified this result. In addition, soil water content and infiltration ability could influence DP concentration in runoff (Nash et al., 2021 ). Sharpley et al. (1981)  attributed a decrease in soluble P concentration to the reabsorption of sediment during soil erosion. In a study on the effect of different crop rotation systems and fertilization treatments on runoff, Li et al. (2021)  discovered that the application of chemical fertilizers, organic fertilizers, and fertilizer blends had little effect on DP concentrations in runoff. However, DP concentrations in runoff were lower in the organic fertilizer-chemical fertilizer combined treatment than those in the chemical fertilizer application treatments. The water-soluble P content of chemical fertilizers is higher than that of organic fertilizers (Bertol et al., 2010 ), and it is more likely to be lost in runoff, thereby causing pollution of downstream water bodies. PP concentrations in runoff were higher during heavy rain, rainstorms, and large rainstorms than during moderate rain (Fig. 5 ). Higher sediment yields are generated during heavy rain, rainstorms, and large rainstorms, which transport more PP. Concurrently, sediment transport caused by rainfall exacerbates the transport and enrichment of PP in the runoff (Stutter et al., 2008 ). Concentrations of PP in runoff were higher in the organic fertilizer-chemical fertilizer application treatment than those in the chemical fertilizer application treatment. Bertol et al. (2010)  revealed similar results in a study evaluating P losses in field experiments with varying chemical and organic fertilizer applications. Applying organic fertilizers changes the soil chemistry and promotes the release of organic and inorganic P fractions from the soil (Hua and Zhu, 2020 ), thereby increasing the concentration of PP in runoff.  4.3 Characterization of runoff P loss Nutrient losses in runoff are influenced by factors such as the timing of fertilizer application, rainfall, and nutrient concentrations (Gilley et al., 2012 ). Moreover, the effect of runoff volume plays a dominant role in nutrient loss (Zhang et al., 2016 ). In this study, TP and PP losses were significantly higher during heavy and heavy storms than during heavy and moderate rainfall events (Fig. 6 ). This result is corroborated by Liu et al. (2002) . Large rainstorms produced high runoff depths (Fig. 4 ). At the same time, runoff depths were significantly and positively correlated with TP loss and PP loss (Fig. 8 ), supporting the dominant role of runoff depth in nutrient loss. Our study showed that the loss characteristics of TP and PP exhibited the same trend, which indicated that PP loss accounted for the majority of TP loss. The study by Wu et al. (2021)  found similar results. DP mainly originates from fertilizers, which are easily absorbed and utilized by plants and, simultaneously, easily lost through surface runoff (Ross et al., 2022 ). The higher the fertilization rate, the greater the DP loss (Wang et al., 2012; Cui et al., 2020 ). P loss decreases with rainfall duration, and the timing of fertilizer application and initial rainfall is crucial for DP loss because of the filtering effect of P loss by the root system of the cultivated crop (Gao et al., 2009 ). Our study found that the unfertilized treatment had lower DP losses than those observed in the other fertilized treatments (Fig. 6 ). This could be because more rainfall events occurred shortly after fertilizer application. Our study of DP concentrations in runoff confirms this result (Fig. 5 ). Wang et al. (2014)  showed that runoff depth and sediment load were highly correlated with DP loss; however, our study found neither of these significantly correlated with DP loss. This observed phenomenon may be attributed to the fact that DP loss in runoff was primarily influenced by rainfall intensity. This assertion was corroborated by Wu et al. (2018) , indicating that under conditions of low rainfall intensity, P loss predominantly occurs in a dissolved state, while under high rainfall intensity, P loss manifests in various other forms. The loss of PP in runoff was lower in the unfertilized treatment than in the fertilized treatments during large rainstorms, whereas the results were reversed during other rainfall categories (Fig. 6 ). Fertilizer application treatments during large rainstorms produced high sediment yield (Fig. 4 ), resulting in the migration of P-rich sediment and fertilizer particles on the soil surface (Bertol et al., 2010 ). Concurrently, large rainstorms imparts significant kinetic energy to its raindrops, leading to soil splash and associated PP loss (Wu et al., 2013 ). Contour cultivation can reduce runoff volume during rainstorm conditions by reducing slope length and the associated N and P losses in runoff by reducing sediment content (Guo et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2015 ). This is supported by our findings that PP loss was lower in contour cultivation than in downslope cultivation during moderate rain, heavy rain, and rainstorm conditions. At the watershed scale, Li et al. (2015)  established a power function relationship between sediment yield and PP loss. They were able to estimate PP by utilizing rainfall kinetic energy, runoff, and sediment yield from rainfall events. We discovered a significant positive correlation between runoff depths and PP losses. However, there was no significant correlation between sediment yield and PP loss (Fig. 8 ). This phenomenon could potentially be attributed to the decoupling of the relationship between PP loss and sediment yield, which was caused by the intricate nature of the purple soil zone region and the uncertainty of regional rainfall. Currently, there exists uncertainty regarding the use of sediment yield as a means to estimate PP loss; therefore, a combination of factors such as runoff depth and sediment yield needs to be considered.   5 Conclusion Following long-term rainfall monitoring of runoff P loss characteristics in response to different fertilization treatments from 2008 to 2022, we found that the runoff depth increased with rainfall and was lower in the fertilized treatment than in the unfertilized treatment. The loss characteristics of TP and PP exhibited similarities, indicating that the main form of P loss from runoff originating from arable land on slopes with purple soil is PP. DP loss in runoff was lower in the combined organic and chemical fertilizer application treatments than in the chemical fertilizer application treatment. Contour cultivation mitigated soil erosion and reduced P loss from rainfall during moderate rain, heavy rain, and rainstorm conditions. We discovered a significant correlation between PP loss and runoff depths. However, there was no significant correlation between PP loss and sediment yield. This indicates that the prediction of PP necessitates the consideration of various factors, such as runoff depth and sediment yield. The utilization of chemical fertilizers on sloping cropland worldwide has led to a significant increase in runoff. The diverse characteristics of P loss in runoff on sloping croplands can be regulated by variable rainfall categories. Therefore, our study establishes a foundation for accurately describing and assessing P loss via runoff in agricultural slope croplands, and has valuable implications for managing non-point source pollution resulting from P loss.
1 Introduction Evaporation is an important component of the hydrologic cycle, water resources evaluation and meteorological science (Dong et al., 2021 ). Water shortage has become a problem worldwide and evaporation is the primary loss of water from agricultural soil and reservoirs, especially in arid and semi-arid areas (Aghelpour et al., 2022 ). Loss of water due to evaporation covers 61 % of the precipitation worldwide (Kushwaha et al., 2021 ). Therefore, accurate estimation of evaporation is significantly vital for many purposes including irrigation scheduling, water resources and hydrology management, water allocation and agricultural activities, particularly in areas where water resource is limited (Malik et al., 2020; Shiri et al., 2019; Zhao and Gao, 2019 ). However, the complicated interaction between atmospheric and land components makes evaporation a challenging phenomenon to effectively and accurately represent (Chang et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2021 ). It exhibits intricate and non-linear behavior, affected by a spectrum of climatological factors, including sunshine hour, wind speed, temperature and relative humidity (Aghelpour et al., 2022 ). Generally, evaporation measurements are categorized as direct (e.g., pan evaporimeter) and indirect measurements (using semi-empirical and empirical equations) (Aghelpour et al., 2022; Novotná et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019 ). Even though realistic evaporation measurement can be obtained using a pan evaporimeter, it is highly costly (maintenance and initial cost), time-consuming, and susceptible to different sources of errors such as heavy rain, strong winds, animal activity in the vicinity of the pan and pan size (Dong et al., 2021; Ghorbani et al., 2017; Kushwaha et al., 2021; Malik et al., 2020 ). The application of empirical equations for the estimation of evaporation, on the other hand, is often limited because of their requirement for sophisticated and reliable climatic data which is not easily available in most areas (Dong et al., 2021; Malik et al., 2020 ). Thus, the application of reliable and robust intelligence algorithms is a hot research area in the field of hydro-climatology (Yaseen, 2023 ). Considering the drawbacks of both the direct and indirect measurement of evaporation, machine learning (ML) approaches are becoming the best alternative which can effectively handle the nonlinear and randomness of the evaporation process using easily measurable climatic variables (Malik et al., 2021 ). The ML-based approaches for hydro-environmental process modeling generally yield reliable predictive accuracy, require fewer input variables, and have a simple structure and fast convergence time (Gelete, 2023a ). Nowadays, several ML models have been employed for the estimation of Epan  such as support vector machine (SVM) (El Bilali et al., 2023; Keshtegar et al., 2019; Kushwaha et al., 2021; Malik et al., 2021 ), adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) (Adnan et al., 2019; Adnan et al., 2019; Moghaddamnia et al., 2009 ), gaussian processing regression (GPR) (Al Sudani and Salem, 2022; Shabani et al., 2020a,b ), extreme learning machine (ELM) (Qian et al., 2021; Sebbar et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2020a,b ), multilayer perceptron (MLP) (Aghelpour et al., 2022; Ghorbani et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017 ), artificial neural networks (ANNs) (Ahi et al., 2023; Al-Mukhtar, 2021 ) and show reliable performance. In addition to the above ML models, deep learning models such as the LSTM model are becoming popular in hydrologic process modeling. The LSTM model resolves the gradients vanishing and exploding problem of recurrent neural networks (RNN) (Yin et al., 2021 ). For different hydrologic problems such as Epan  modeling (Majhi et al., 2020 ), streamflow modeling (Rahimzad et al., 2021 ), estimation of reference evapotranspiration (Ferreira and da Cunha, 2020 ), and suspended sediment load (Gelete, 2023a ), the LSTM model was successfully implemented. Fig. 1   presents the literature of the established ML versions for Epan  where more comprehensively the exhibited previous studies can be understood. Of recently developed methodologies, several ensemble learning algorithms were adopted as key tools for modeling hydrological problems (Abed et al., 2022a–c; Sharafati et al., 2020a,b; Tausif et al., 2023 ). According to Lu et al. (2018) , the ensemble algorithms have greater computational efficiency and are simple and highly performing models for complex problems. Generally, the ensemble algorithm namely boosting and bagging approaches are intended to alleviate the weakness of poor predictors (Erdal and Karakurt, 2013 ). In several hydrologic problem investigation studies, two efficient ensemble models; the RF and BRT are employed. The RF model when applied for pan evaporation estimation showed reliable estimation performance (Al Sudani & Salem, 2022; Wang et al., 2023a,b ). Although the BRT model has never been used before to predict Epan , it has demonstrated a reliable accuracy in several hydrologic processes modeling such as rainfall-runoff (Gelete, 2023b ), reference evapotranspiration (Malik et al., 2022a,b ), traffic noise modeling (Umar et al., 2023 ) and flood susceptibility mapping (Abed et al., 2022a–c ). Nonlinear system identification (NSI) models are the other ML tools gaining popularity in the field of hydrology and environment. The Hammerstein-Wiener (HW) model is among the NSI models gaining popularity in different fields (Gelete, 2023b ). Even though the HW model has not been tested for Epan  estimation, it has demonstrated a superior predictive power in different hydrologic fields such as suspended sediment load (Gelete, 2023a ), rainfall prediction (Pham et al., 2019 ), concentration of dissolved oxygen (Abba et al., 2020 ) and runoff modeling (Gelete, 2023b ). It is clear from the previously mentioned studies that several ML models were utilized for Epan  modeling and showed superiority over empirical and regression models (Majhi et al., 2020 ). Despite the increasing popularity and usefulness, the prediction accuracy of some of these ML models remains compromised by varying degrees of inadequacy and imprecision, especially when used in highly non-stationary processes (Pham et al., 2019 ). It is also clear that there is no one predictive model that is guaranteed to yield superior performance for all dataset types and in all catchments (Nourani et al., 2021a,b ). Model hybridization can therefore alleviate the constraints of single models in the prediction of complicated and nonstationary hydrologic problems (Sharghi et al., 2018 ). As a result, numerous hybrid models have been utilized by different research for hydro-climatic prediction. For instance, Liu et al. (2012)  designed a hybrid of Autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) with Kalman Filter (KF) and ANN for the prediction of wind speed and concluded that the hybrid models excelled the base models. For rainfall prediction, Pham et al. (2019)  combined ARIMA with Neuro-fuzzy (NF), Least-squares SVM (LSSVM), HW and MLP and they discovered that the ARIMA-HW and ARIMA-NF models produced better modeling result than the base models. Umar et al. (2023)  also utilized the conjugation of the multilinear regression (MLR) model with GPR, BRT, ANN and SVM models for traffic noise modeling. The result of this study revealed that the MLR-GPR model provides better prediction results than single models and the other hybrid models. Dong et al. (2021)  developed hybrid of CatBoost with bat algorithm (Bat-CB) for pan evaporation modeling and compared with RF and CatBoost models and the finding of the study revealed the hybrid Bat-CB model provided enhanced result. Nevertheless, to the best of our information, there is no published research that developed a hybrid of SWLR with deep learning model (LSTM), ensemble tree model (RF and BRT) and nonlinear system identification model (HW) in hydrology in general, particularly in Epan  estimation. Additionally, there is no previous study which have used HW and BRT models in Epan  estimation. Consequently, the main aim of this study was: 1) to investigate the performance of different powerful models such as HW, BRT, SWLR, LSTM and RF for Epan  modeling under the first scenario and 2) to develop a hybrid learning technique by combining the classical linear SWLR model and robust nonlinear ML models (SWLR-LSTM, SWLR-HW, SWLR-BRT and SWLR-RF) to capitalize on the strength of both nonlinear and linear pattern handling capabilities of the models under the second scenario. Before modeling using individual models (scenario 1), sensitivity analysis using correlation and RF-based single input–output technique was conducted to determine the most significant input feature that affects the Epan . The novelty of the current study includes several essential components. It is the first study to investigate the performance of HW, SWLR and BRT models for Epan  estimation. Also, only a limited number of research had studied the application of deep learning (LSTM) and ensemble models (e.g., RF) in Epan  estimation; however, the ML model’s performance is greatly influenced by the type of the used data and their accuracy differs if the datasets is changed. Hence, more research is necessitated to create a superior predictive ML model over the other tools for daily Epan  modeling. Additionally, most of the single models employed in the present study are comparatively new to the Epan  modeling. Also, there is lack research that compares the predictive accuracy of deep learning (e.g., LSTM), ensemble tree (RF and BRT), nonlinear system identification (HW) and regression (e.g., SWLR) models in the field of hydrology particularly for evaporation modeling. As a stochastic process, there could be both linear and nonlinear association between the input parameter and Epan . Because of this complex characteristic, it might be inappropriate to use only linear models (e.g., SWLR). Even though the nonlinear ML models (BRT, RF, HW and LSTM) are powerful tools, their performance is not superior under all conditions due to different factors and may introduce errors, especially in estimation data exhibiting a linear pattern. One way to improve the modeling accuracy is therefore to develop a hybrid model. Therefore, the present study, for the first time, developed linear-nonlinear hybrid models including SWLR-LSTM, SWLR-HW, SWLR-RF and SWLR-BRT models for Epan  modeling and compared their performance against individual models. There is no study before that used a linear-nonlinear hybrid model in Epan  estimation. This study applied a unique model combination that has never been documented in the Evaporation estimation. For example, conjugating SWLR with the HW model enhances the ability of the models to capture the linear pattern (by SWLR) and to better handle non-linear relationships between input features and Epan rates (because of the strong nonlinear identification ability of HW) and leads improved modeling results. Similarly, the hybridization of SWLR and LSTM increases the capability of the models to effectively capture both the linear association and complex nonlinear temporal dependency in the dataset, which is especially important in time-series estimation such as pan-evaporation studies. Also, integrating SWLR with ensemble tree models (RF and BRT) benefits from the simplicity and strong linear trend-capturing ability of SWLR and the strong predictive power of the ensemble models leading most accurate overall Epan  estimation.  2 Case study description 2.1 Study area The research is conducted in the Lake Hawassa watershed which is among the sub-watersheds of the Ethiopian Rift Valley basin. Geographically, the study area is situated between 6°45′ to 7°15′ North, and 38°15′ to 38°45′East (Fig. 2  ). Lake Hawassa catchment covers an area of 1461 Km2  and is located in the Oromia and Sidama regional states (Lencha et al., 2022 ). The elevation of the watershed varies between 1624 and 2980 m above mean sea level. The slope of the major part of the catchment is from flat to gentle with undulating topography and the eastern part is surrounded by steep escarpments of mountains (Alehu and Bitana, 2023 ). The climatic condition of the Lake Hawassa watershed is dominantly dry sub-humid with annual mean temperature of 19.5 °C and rainfall of 990 mm. Rain feed agricultural production is the primary source of livelihood in the catchment. The study watershed comprises three different seasons according to Ethiopian local seasons considering the rainfall distribution such as Bega (dry season) from October to January, Belg (short rainy season) extending from February to May and Kiremt (min rainy season) from June to September.  2.2 Data used The climate data for the Lake Hawassa catchment for 14 years (2003 to 2016) was obtained from the Ethiopia Meteorological Agency. The data collected includes: sunshine hour (SSH), Epan , minimum temperature (Tmin ), wind speed (WS), relative humidity (RH) and maximum temperature (Tmax ). In the study area, there is only one station with a complete Epan  measurement and other climatic variables (Fig. 2 ). From the whole dataset, 70 % (2003–2012) was used for model calibration and the remaining 30 % (2013–2016) for model validation. The statistics of the weather variables including maximum (Xmax ), minimum (Xmin ), standard deviation (XSd ), average (Xmean ), skewness (XSk ) and coefficient of variation (Xcv ) values are presented in Table 1  . Normalization of both input features and output variable, as an important task in ML model development, was performed to improve the data integration. In this process, the dataset (both input and target parameters) was transformed between 0 and 1. According to Nourani et al. (2019) , normalizing data helps to make sure all values receive equal attention, improves modeling performance and avoids the smallest values from being dominated by the largest values. Normalization of the data was performed as follows:(1) Y = X i  - X min    X max   - X min         where Xi  , Xmin  , Y  and Xmax   denote the measured data, minimum value, normalized value and maximum values, respectively.   3 Applied machine learning models This study was conducted in three steps as shown in Fig. 3  . First, the most significant input feature selection was conducted using RF-based single input–output and linear Pearson correlation methods. Afterwards, five different single models including LSTM, BRT RF, HW and SWLR were developed to predict the Epan  using different input combinations. Finally, novel linear and nonlinear hybrid models were employed by integrating the best result of the linear SWLR with the four nonlinear ML models (LSTM, RF, BRT and HW). The estimation performance of hybrid and individual models was then compared using different visual and statistical performance metrics. 3.1 Random forest (RF) RF is a supervised ML modeling tool that utilizes the ensemble technique for both regression and classification procedures (Sharafati et al., 2020a,b ). It uses the bootstrap and bagging ensemble techniques. As a tree-based ensemble ML algorithm, in the RF model, decision trees (DT) are used as base learners and individual trees depend on a set of random parameters (Zounemat-Kermani et al., 2021a,b ). Each tree is created from the primary data using bootstrap sampling. The building process of trees is performed parallelly where tree growing is conducted without interaction (Weiqi et al., 2022 ). Therefore, the estimation output value is then obtained by averaging the estimation value of each tree (Ren et al., 2021 ) as shown in Appendix A . Like other ensemble tree algorithms, RF is a meta -estimator that combines the output of several estimations obtained by each decision tree into a single ensemble estimation (Sharafati et al., 2020a,b ). Hence, this model is preferred over a single DT as it reduces the problem of overfitting by averaging the output. According to Zounemat-Kermani et al. (2021a,b ), RF modeling process follows four steps. The first step involves selecting bootstrap samples from the training dataset. In the second stage, a DT is created from each sample and their estimation output is then obtained. Afterwards, a voting step is performed for each ‘DT’s estimation result. Finally, the most accurate predictive mode is selected as the most modeling result. RF has been successfully applied and provides reliable results in the field of hydrology (AlDahoul et al., 2022; Hanoon et al., 2022; Sahour et al., 2021 ). In this study, the hyperparameters of RF such as maximum depth and number of trees were tuned to find their optimal values which can provide the best fit between measured and computed Epan . For this purpose, orange data mining software was to develop the RF model.  3.2 Boosted regression tree (BRT) BRT is a unique model used for both classification and regression purposes which is the combination of ML and statistical technique (Umar et al., 2023 ). BRT model is among the different methods for enhancing the predictive accuracy of models through an ensemble of multiple independent models (Malik et al., 2022a,b ). The BRT model combines the collective power of regression and boosting algorithms to improve model performance while reducing model variance (Aertsen et al., 2010 ). By leveraging each algorithm’s strength, the BRT model achieves superior predictive performance. Boosting is a robust ensemble technique that improves model accuracy by iteratively integrating weak learners, often DT, into a powerful predictive model. This sequential process involves fitting new trees to the residual errors (RE) of the existing ensemble tree, efficiently decreasing the overall modeling error and enhancing the model's generalization ability (Aertsen et al., 2010 ). BRT creates the initial tree from the entire training dataset. The subsequent trees are then created using the remaining data that was not used for the previous tree (Elith et al., 2008 ).This technique ensures that each tree focuses on different aspects of the data, leading to a more robust and comprehensive model. The advantage of the BRT model includes the information in DTs are easy to visualize, insensitive to outliers, having quick convergence time and less prone to overfitting (Malik et al., 2022a,b; Umar et al., 2023 ). Although it has not been applied before for Epan  estimation it has shown its superiority in other fields (Aertsen et al., 2010; Gelete, 2023b; Youssef et al., 2016 ). The MATLAB environment’s (2021a version) regression learner was used to develop the BRT model for the present study. The overall architecture of the BRT is indicated in Appendix B .  3.3 Hammerstein-Weiner mode (HW) The other nonlinear ML algorithm for the identification of nonlinear systems is the HW model (Pham et al., 2019 ). Appendix C  depicts the structure of the HW model that involves a series of interlinked dynamic blocks which are both nonlinear and linear. The HW model captures the important knowledge concerning the characteristics of the process and enables adjustable parameterization making it an appropriate tool to be used as both a grey-box and black-box model in complex phenomena modeling (Gaya et al., 2017 ). Ghali et al. (2020)  stated that due to the HW model being able to consider both the linearity and nonlinearity aspects of the dataset, it can give reliable estimation performance in many applications than linear models (e.g., MLR) and nonlinear models (e.g., ANNs). Several studies have successfully utilized this model, which performs reliably (Abba et al., 2019; Abba et al., 2019; Gelete, 2023b ). The following is the description of the process in the HW model structure (Pham et al., 2019 ): The nonlinear function changing the input data is described as follows:(2) w ( t )  = f ( u t    )       The linear transfer function is expressed as:(3) x ( t ) = w ( t ) B / F     where: x(t) and w(t) represent the variables defining the linear block’s input and output, respectively. Also, h and f in the HW model structure acts on the linear block’s output and input ports (Pham et al., 2019 ).  3.4 Long short‑term memory (LSTM) An advanced version of the RNN model, the LSTM model is designed to regulate and store information across time (Koch and Schneider, 2022 ). Due to this, the LSTM model is appropriate for learning memory effect and long-term dependencies (Fayer et al., 2023 ). The LSTM model is capable of reconstructing gradient vanishing in the analysis of lengthier time series due to its ability to evaluate long-term data based on pre-served memory (Elsayed et al., 2023 ). A detailed description of the LSTM model was presented by Kratzert et al.(2018) . The LSTM model structure (Appendix D ) contains different gates namely input gate (it ), hidden state (ht ), forget gate (ft ), cell state (C  ¯   t  )     and output gate (Ot ) (Ferreira & da Cunha (2020 ). In this model, the information of the preceding time (t-1, t-2…) is taken into account during the processing of the input data at present (t) (Ferreira and da Cunha, 2020 ). The LSTM model structure is mathematically described as follows (Kisi et al., 2022 ):(4) i t  = σ W i  . ( h t - 1   , X t  )  + b i         (5) f t  = σ W f  . ( h t - 1   , X t )  + b f         (6) O t  = σ W 0  . ( h  t - 1   , x t  ) +  b o         (7) C  ¯   t  = t a n h W c  . ( h t - 1   , X t  )  + b c         (8) C t  = ( f  t  C t - 1   ) +  i t  C  ¯   t      (9) h t  = O t  t a n h C t         where Wi  , Wf  , Wc   and Wo   represent the weights of the input, forget, cell and output gates respectively. bi  , bf  , bc   and bo   denote the biases of it , f t , C  ¯   t     and Ot , respectively. Whereas, the σ  and tanh    designates the hyperbolic sigmoid and tangent activation functions, respectively. In the current study, MATLAB code was used to develop the LSTM model. Also, Ct-1   and Ht-1  are the cell unit and hidden state output at the previous time, respectively and Ct   represents the memory cell at the present time.  3.5 Stepwise linear regression (SWLR) The regression models are among the widely applied techniques used for describing the association between the target and independent variables (Umar et al., 2022 ). Among the different regression analysis tools, the SWLR model was used in the current study due to its simplicity and performance in different studies (Wu et al., 2020a,b; Yasar et al., 2012 ). The SWLR model is expressed as (Wu et al., 2020a,b ):(10) y = c 0  + c 1  x 1  + c 2  x 2  + ⋯ c i  x i      where y  is the target variable, ci  is the regression constant for the ith   input parameter and xi   represents the ith   input parameter. A comprehensive description of the SWLR model and its underlying theoretical concepts are provided (Wu et al., 2020a,b ).  3.6 Hybrid machine learning models development In various real-world problems, such as the estimation of Epan,  a nonlinear and linear association may exist between the input features and output variable (Epan ). Due to this complex behavior, it may not be adequate to apply only classical linear models (e.g. SWLR) for such a process. In contrast, nonlinear models (such as ML-based models), offer the benefit of modeling complex processes effectively. However, their performance is not appropriate in all conditions, and they may introduce inaccuracies, especially when modeling data exhibiting a linear pattern (Umar et al., 2023 ). Also, there is indeed no one modeling tool providing better estimation performance for all types of datasets and catchments. Furthermore, several studies have revealed that different models may provide varied modeling results using the same dataset. It is very challenging to completely understand the properties of data in a real problem. Therefore, utilizing hybrid models is an appropriate approach for robust estimation performance as an amalgamation of multiple models helps in capturing diverse aspects of the data (Nourani et al., 2011 ). The new approach is to explore hybrid models that are important to capture both linear and nonlinear associations between the predictor and output variable. Therefore, in the present study, five different individual ML-based models such as HW, LSTM, SWLR, RF and BRT models were employed for Epan  estimation. Afterward, a hybrid model was developed by combining the linear SWLR model with nonlinear deep learning (SWLR-LSTM), ensemble tree (SWLR-BRT and SWLR-RF) and nonlinear system identification model (SWLR-HW) to benefit from the strength and unique feature of both the SWLR and ML-based models in capturing different patterns. The nonlinear and linear patterns were modeled separately using different models and the predicted results were then combined to increase the overall estimation performance. According to Zhang (2003) , time series problems have both nonlinear component and linear autocorrelation structures. Thus, the two components are defined as:(11) y i  = N i  + L i      where y i     represents the observed Epan  and N i     and L i     and nonlinear and linear elements of Epan , respectively. The linear and nonlinear elements should be predicted from the data. In the current study, hybrid models were developed in three steps. In the first stage, SWLR was trained to generate the best linear fitted values. Then, the error (residual) of the SWLR model was computed as follows:(12) r i  = y i  - L ^  i      where r i     is residual (error) and L ^  i     is the predicted Epan  values by the linear SWLR model. Second, the residual that only comprises the nonlinear pattern of Epan  which was not effectively handled by SWLR, went through (predicted by) the nonlinear kernel of ML-based models (LSTM, HW, BRT and RF) to capture the data’s nonlinear pattern. In the last (third) step, the output of nonlinear ML models was aggregated with the predicted result of the linear SWLR model obtained in the first step to get the Epan  estimation result using hybrid models as follows:(13) y ^  i  = L ^  i  + r ^  i      where y ^  i     is the predicted Epan  value, r ^  i     is the predicted residual value obtained by ML (nonlinear) models. The linear-nonlinear hybrid model development process is developed for the current study as shown in Fig. 4  .  3.7 Model’s accuracy evaluation The accuracy of hydro-climatological models needs be evaluated in both model calibration and verification periods. According to Nourani et al. (2021a,b ), estimation performance evaluation metrics should include a minimum of one statistical error and one goodness-of-fit index. Therefore, percent bias (PBIAS), Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), index of agreement (IA ), Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE), root mean square error (RMSE) and coefficient of determination (R2 ) were employed in this study to assess model performance. The NSE value varies between negative infinity and 1, and assesses the degree match between the measured and predicted Epan  values. A perfect agreement, indicating an accurate estimation result, is achieved at the NSE value of one. A more accurate estimation result is obtained when the NSE value is close to 1. The RMSE has values between 0 to positive infinity, with a value of 0 indicating a perfect model. The other error metric, the Pbias, measures the tendency of the developed hybrid and single models to underestimate or overestimate the observed Epan  values. A negative and positive Pbias value indicates underestimation and overestimation of the measured values, respectively and a perfect model gives a Pbias value of 0 (Jimeno-Sáez et al., 2018 ). The R2  metrics determine the association between the observed and predicted Epan  and a better fit is obtained when its values are close to 1. The used accuracy measures (metrics) were calculated as (Moriasi et al., 2015; Karbasi et al., 2024 ):(14) P B I A S = ∑ i  n  ( Ob  i  - Pr  i  )  100  ∑ i  n  Ob  i       - ∞ ≤  P B A S  < ∞     (15) RMSE = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  Ob  i  - Pr  i     2    0  ≤  R M S E  <  ∞     (16) R  2  = ∑ i = 1  n  ( O b  i  - O b  i   ¯   )  ( Pr  i  - P r  i   ¯   )     2  ∑ i = 1  N    Ob  i  - P r  i   ¯      2  ∑ i - 1  n  ( Pr  i  - P r  i   ¯   )  2    0  ≤  R 2  <  1     (17) NSE = 1 - ∑ i = 1  N  Ob  i  - Pr  i     2   ∑ i = 1  N  Ob  i  - O b  i   ¯      2    -  ∞  <  N S E  ≤  1     (18) KGE = 1 - R - 1    2  + α - 1    2  + β - 1    2    -  ∞  <  K G E  ≤  1     (19) I A  = 1 - ∑ i = 1  N  Pr  i  - Ob  i     2   ∑ i = 1  N  Pr  i  - Ob  i   ¯     + Ob  i  - Ob  i   ¯         2       0  ≤  I A  <  1     where Ob  i     and Pr  i     represents the actual and predicted Epan  values; Ob  i   ¯      and Pr  i   ¯      are the average values of observed and predicted Epan,  respectively while N is the size of the data. α represents the relative standard deviation of the predicted and observed Epan . β  denotes the ratio between the mean predicted and observed Epan  values and R is the correlation coefficient.   4 Results and discussions The results of the sensitivity analysis, individual and hybrid models are presented and discussed in the following subsections. 4.1 Input variable selection Prior to model development, it is crucial to determine the influence of each input variable on the target variable using different sensitivity analysis techniques. Different studies have used various input selection and ranking methods. This method includes a linear Pearson correlation method (Abed et al., 2023), a single input–output neural network approach (Nourani et al., 2021a,b ), mutual information (Umar et al., 2023 ) and an improved gamma test for feature selection(Ghanbari-Adivi et al., 2022 ). Significant Input feature selection and ranking in this study was conducted using an RF-based method and input variables were ranked based on their validation phase NSE values as shown in Table 1 . In this approach, each input variable was imposed on the RF model separately one by one to predict the target variable (i.e., Epan ). Then the validation period NSE value of the RF model results for each input was computed to determine their significance without considering the influence of other inputs. The input variable providing the highest NSE value was ranked first, and its importance (rank) decreased as the NSE value was reduced. The results of the RF-based input selection results are presented in Table 2  . As shown in Table 2  the RH was found to be the most relevant input that affects the Epan  in the study area followed by Tmax  and SSH as the second and third sensitive input features, respectively. The WS which gives the smallest NSE values was identified as the least important input parameter. The dominant influence of RH in this study is not surprising as it directly reflects the capacity of the air to hold moisture and hence influences the evaporation rate. Similarly, Tmax heats the surrounding air and helps the conversion of liquid water into vapor, leading to increased evaporation. The feature selection result of this study was in agreement with the findings by Abed et al. (2022a–c , 2023), Kushwaha et al. (2021)  and Novotná et al. (2022 ). Pearson correlation (r) as linear correlation analysis was also used to determine the linear relationship between the Epan  with the independent variables. The results are shown in Table 3  . As can be inferred from the table, linear sensitivity analysis (r) provides similar input variables ranking confirming the nonlinear RF-based sensitivity analysis. After ranking the input features based on their relevance, five different input combinations were created, and RH is included in all input combinations as it is the most important feature:(18) M 1 = f R H , T max ,   S S H , T min   , W S        (29) M 2 = f R H , T max ,   S S H , T min          (20) M 3 = f R H , T max ,   S S H        (21) M 4 = f R H , T max          (22) M 5 = f R H        where M1 to M5 denotes the different input combinations created and f  is to represent the functions related to input parameters. The removal of the input parameters from the preceding input combination is based on their relative importance shown in the sensitivity analysis.  4.2 Results of the single models In this section, the predictive performance of the base models such as SWLR, HW, LSTM, BRT and RF models for Epan  modeling was discussed. The proposed individual models were calibrated and validated for each input combination separately and their accuracy was evaluated using Pbias, NSE, RMSE, and R2  values as shown in Table 4  . The MATLAB environment was utilized for the development of all models except for the RF model where orange data mining software was utilized to develop it. As shown in Table 4 , each model provides the best result when all the input features are included in the input combination (M1). Table 4  demonstrates that the performance of the employed models deteriorated as more input parameters were excluded from the preceding input combinations. A substantial performance decline was observed for each model from M1 to M5. For instance, the validation period NSE value of M2 (without WS) decreased compared to M1 (with all inputs) by 2.344 %, 0.375 %, 1.546 %, 4.714 %, and 0.533 % for SWLR, HW, LSTM, BRT, and RF models, respectively. Similarly, the validation phase NSE value of M3 (without Tmin  and WS) compared to M1 was reduced by 2.734 %, 3.371 %, 7.25327 %, 6.734 %, and 7.135 % for SWLR, HW, LSTM, BRT, and RF models, respectively. The accuracy of SWLR, HW, BRT, RF and LSTM models also decreased by 4.167 %, 4.869 %, 12.346 %, 10.863 % and 9.394 %, respectively, based on the validation stage NSE value from M1 to M3. A notable validation period NSE value reduction was also observed from M1 to M5 for RF, BRT, LSTM, HW, and SWLR models, reaching up to 12.5 %, 9.488 %, 12.485 %, 15.264 %, and 19.489 %, respectively. As stated above, the best results of each model were achieved using input combination 1(M1). Therefore, the discussion in this section is based on the results of each model for M1. As can be depicted from Table 4 , all the models led to acceptable results, however, the ensemble tree models (RF and BRT) outperformed all the other models by giving smaller Pbias and RMSE values and higher R2  and NSE values. The RF model provides better performance, followed by the BRT, LSTM, HW, and SWLR models, respectively in their order of predictive accuracy. The RF-M1 model demonstrated the most accurate estimation results compared to the other competing individual models with calibration phase NSE, Pbias, RMSE and R2  values of 0.966, 0.495 %, 0.384 mm/day and 0.967, respectively. In the validation phase, NSE, Pbias, RMSE and R2  values of the RF-M1 model were 0.939, −1.193 %, 0.403 mm/day and 0.94, respectively. The superior performance of the RF model is not surprising and according to Abba et al. (2020 ), the remarkable predictive performance of the RF model is because of its ability to successfully ensemble different decision trees through a randomization process. This approach leads to robust modeling obtained by averaging the results of individual decision trees. The second best Epan  estimation performance was obtained from the BRT-M1 model with the calibration and validation period R2 , Pbias, RMSE and NSE values as 0.926 and 0.894, 0.874 % and −2.293 %, 0.562 mm/day and 0.645 mm/day, and 0.931 and 0.891, respectively. The BRT model led to a better estimation result than LSTM, HW and the linear SWLR models in both validation and calibration periods. Its superior accuracy could be due to it ensembles multiple regression learners using the boosting method which in turn makes this model a powerful tool to handle nonlinear relationships (Umar et al., 2023 ). This synergistic method makes the BRT model a powerful tool for modeling intricate data patterns and making highly accurate estimations. Although the current research is the first to utilize the BRT model in Epan  estimation, similar results where the BRT model outperformed other ML models were reported in traffic noise modeling (Umar et al., 2023 ). The deep learning LSTM-M1 models show the third estimation accuracy by outperforming the HW and SWLR models with the validation phase R2 , Pbias, RMSE and NSE values of 0.844, 1.731 %, 0.78 mm/day and 0.841, respectively. The nonlinear system identification model, HW model also shows reliable Epan  estimation performance although it was outperformed by the ensemble tree (BRT and RF) and deep learning (LSTM) models. The HW-M1 model provides the calibration and validation phase values of R2 , Pbias, NSE and RMSE as 0.865 and 0.801, 0.393 % and 0.444 %, 0.77 mm/day and 0.872 mm/day, and 0.861 and 0.801, respectively. The SWLR model yielded the worst accuracy with the validation stage values of R2 , Pbias, RMSE and NSE as 0.775, −1.403 %, 0.952 mm/day and 0.768, respectively. Comparing the nonlinear ML model’s performance with the linear SWLR model, the RF model has enhanced the modeling accuracy of SWLR by reducing the error (RMSE) by 49.265 % during the validation stage, BRT by 32.248 %, LSTM up to 18.067 % and the HW model reduced the error (RMSE value) of the linear SWLR model by 8.404 %. Similarly, the quantitative observations with regard to the NSE value, the results demonstrated that the RF, BRT, LSTM and HW model improved the estimation accuracy of the linear SWLR model by 22.266 %, 16.016 %, 9.505 % and 4.297 %, respectively in the validation stage. The best single model, the RF model, improved the performance of SWLR, HW, LSTM and BRT in terms of the validation phase RMSE by 49.265 %, 44.61 %, 38.077 % and 25.116 %, respectively. All the individual models gave positive Pbias values in the calibration phase which based on Moriasi et al. (2007)  guideline is an underestimation of the actual Epan  value by the employed models. During the validation phase, the RF-M1, BRT-M1 and SWLR-M1 models led to negative Pbias values which indicate overestimation. According to Tibangayuka et al. (2022) , the accuracy of the hydro-climate model is good when their RMSE value is smaller than half of the observed data’s standard deviation. In this context, all the single models led to good estimation results except the SWLR model. The superiority of the RF model was reported in the study that compares different ensemble tree models for flood susceptibility by Abed et al. (2022a–c ) and in the study that compares BRT and RF for landslide susceptibility mapping (Abed et al., 2022a–c ). Ayana et al. (2023)  also compared deep learning models with RF and found that RF outperformed the LSTM model although it was outperformed by other deep learning. The RF model also outperformed LSTM in wind pressure modeling (Li et al., 2022 ). According to Moriasi et al. (2015) , to have a comprehensive and robust comparison in hydrologic process estimation, both visual and statistical performance measures should be used. In this regard, the current study used scatter plots, boxplots, radar charts, time series and Taylor diagrams to examine the performance of the utilized hybrid and individual models to predict Epan . It should be noted that the visual comparison (graphs) presented here are only for the best result of each model (i.e., M1). The time series and scatter graph between the observed Epan  and computed Epan  in the validation stage are shown in Fig. 5  . As can be depicted from Fig. 5 g and i, the ensemble models (RF and BRT) provide better estimation accuracy as the data points are less scattered and closer to the 1:1 diagonal line than the other models. The least accurate performance is shown by the SWLR model (Fig. 5 a and b) as the data points are more scattered and deviate from the 1:1 line. The scatter plot of the LSTM (Fig. 5 e) and HW (Fig. 5 c) indicate better accuracy compared to the linear SWLR model although the data points are scattered particularly in the medium and large Epan  values. Fig. 5  also shows the time series observed and predicted Epan  by individual models. As shown in the figure, all the nonlinear models simulated the trend of the observed value fairly even though the best agreement was observed between RF and actual Epan value. As shown in Fig. 5 j, the RF model exhibits a highly congruent pattern with the observed Epan  time series. This strong correspondence stands as a remarkable achievement of the RF compared to the performance exhibited by the other competing models. The time series of SWLR (Fig. 5 b), HW (Fig. 5 d) and LSTM (Fig. 5 f) models showed noise and deviations from the actual time series values. The models led to different estimation performances at different points in the time series. For example, the minimum observed Epan  value during the validation period (2013–2016) was 0.5 mm/day occurred on August 9, 2016, while the modeled Epan  by BRT, RF, HW, SWLR and LSTM was 1.53 mm/day, 1.107 mm/day, 1.07 mm/day, 1.502 mm/day and 1.772 mm/day, respectively. This indicates even though all the models overestimated the minimum Epan  value, the least accurate nonlinear model (HW) gave the closest predicted value to the actual Epan . Besides the scatter plot, the stability of single models was evaluated through a radar chart as shown in Fig. 6  . The estimation result of a model is considered stable when its NSE value percentage variation between the calibration and validation period is less than 5 % (Umar et al., 2022 ). In this regard deep learning LSTM and ensemble tree (RF and BRT) models gave stable estimation results. The HW and SWLR model’s estimation results were not stable as the difference was greater than 5 %. Radar plot was successfully used for model stability and accuracy comparison in different studies (Gelete, 2023a; Pham et al., 2019; Umar et al., 2022 ). The predictive performance of single models was evaluated using boxplot, another visualization. The agreement between the observed Epan  values and predicted value using the single models during the validation stage was assessed using interquartile range (IQR) and various quartiles using boxplots as shown in Fig. 7  . As shown in Fig. 7 , the median (Q50% ) of observed Epan  was 4 mm/day while the computed values by BRT, RF, HW, SWLR and LSTM were 3.964 mm/day, 3.914 mm/day, 3.754 mm/day, 3.813 mm/day and 3.708 mm/day, respectively. This indicates that the BRT outperforms other models, while RF and SWLR gave the second and third closest median value to the observed Q50%  value. Regarding IQR value, the RF model (IQR = 2.85 mm/day) shows consistent results with the observed Epan  (IQR = 2.8 mm/day). Boxplot was successfully utilized for model accuracy comparison by different studies in various fields (Nourani et al., 2021a,b; Sharafati et al., 2020a,b ). From the time series and box plot analysis, it can be seen that different models provided different predictive results for the same type of data. At some points in the time series, even the least accurate linear model (SWLR) gave the closest estimation result to the nonlinear models. Therefore, it is clear that better predictive performance could be attained by employing hybrid models to capitalize on the strength of each single model. To this end, this study developed linear-nonlinear hybrid models for the first time in the Epan  estimation using.  4.3 Results of the hybrid models To enhance the predictive accuracy of the individual models employed in the first strategy, four distinct linear-nonlinear hybrid models were developed in strategy two. Like the individual models, the predictive accuracy of the employed hybrid models (i.e., SWLR-RF, SWLR-BRT, SWLR-LSTM and SWLR-HW) was assessed and compared using R2 , Pbias, RMSE and NSE, and the performance comparison result is shown in Table 5  . Table 5  depicts the superior predictive performance of the linear-nonlinear hybrid models compared to the individual models. The hybrid models showed a notable enhancement in the performance of Epan  estimation. The results of the current study are supported by the findings of studies conducted by Gelete (2023a), Ghorbani et al. (2017 ) and Malik et al. (2021 ). As depicted in the table, the best performance with the lowest RMSE and Pbias and highest NSE and R2  value was obtained from the SWLR-RF. The SWLR-BRT model led to the second accurate performance followed by SWLR-LSTM and SWLR-HW, respectively. The SWLR-RF model provided R2  = 0.985 and 0.973, NSE = 0.983 and 0.972, RMSE = 0.272 mm/day and 0.326 mm/day, and Pbias = 0.5 % and −1.249 %, respectively during the calibration and validation phases. The performance evaluation result (Table 5 ) clearly shows the efficiency of the hybrid models in enhancing the accuracy of single nonlinear and linear models. This substantial enhancement in estimation accuracy underscores the synergistic power of combining linear and nonlinear approaches (Pham et al., 2019 ). The best hybrid model, SWLR-RF, increased the accuracy of single models concerning the NSE values of SWLR, HW, LSTM, BRT and RF by 26.563 %, 21.348 %, 15.577 %, 9.091 % and 3.514 %, respectively during the validation stage. Based on the validation phase RMSE values, the SWLR-RF improved the performance of the nonlinear HW, LSTM, BRT and RF by 62.615 %, 58.205 %, 49.457 % and 32.505 %, respectively and linear SWLR by 66.87 %. The hybrid SWLR-RF model also improved the single models in terms of R2  between 3.511 % and 25.548 % and Pbias by 4.694 % and 60.699 %. This indicates for the Epan  estimation, the powerful nonlinear ML-based models provide improved results when integrated with the linear model. The second-best predictive performance was obtained by SWLR-BRT with validation period Pbias, RMSE, R2  and NSE values of −1.963 %, 0.94, 0.486 mm/day and 0.938, respectively. The SWLR-BRT model improved the accuracy of the single SWLR, HW, LSTM, BRT and RF models in terms of validation period RMSE value by 50.61 %, 44.266 %, 37.692 %, 24.651 % and 0.6211 %, respectively. Among the hybrid models, the third best predictive result was obtained from the SWLR-LSTM with the validation period Pbias, RMSE, R2  and NSE values of −2.242 %, 0.646 mm/day,0.899 and 0.891, respectively. It increased the validation phase performance of SWLR, HW and LSTM models, respectively by 16 %, 12.235 % and 6.517 % in terms of R2 , and 34.35 %, 25.917 % and 17.18 % in terms of RMSE value and 16.016 %, 11.236 % and 5.945 % in terms of NSE value. The SWLR-LSTM model performs less than the single ensemble regression tree (RF and BRT) models. This could be the strength of ensemble tree models as a combination of multiple regression trees to handle the complex Epan  more than the combined SWLR and LSTM model. The least accurate modeling result among the hybrid models was obtained from the SWLR-HW model with R2 , Pbias, RMSE, and NSE values of 0.882, −2.878 %, 0.691 mm/day and 0.875, respectively during the validation stage. The lowest accuracy of the SWLR-HW model could be because of the weak performance of the HW model compared to the other single nonlinear models. All the hybrid models yielded negative Pbias values during the validation phase which is an indication of overestimation according to Moriasi et al. (2015)  guideline. The estimation results of the hybrid models were further compared with the findings of previous studies in the literature. Umar et al. (2023)  recommended the use of goodness-fit metrics instead of error indicators to make comparison with previous study as the data range varies. In the study carried out in northern India, hybrid SVR-SSA predicted the Epan  with an NSE value of 0.861 (Malik et al., 2021 ). An other study by Lu et al. (2018)  also reported a validation period value of NSE = 0.81 and R2  = 0.81 using gradient boosted decision tree in the study conducted in China for Epan  estimation. The Epan  estimation study by Keshtegar et al. (2019)  also revealed NSE = 0.97 using the best model (SVR-RSM). Malik et al. (2022a,b ) in their model comparison study between boosted machine and deep learning (DL) obtained the NSE = 0.8344 from DL models. The best hybrid models, NCA-LSTM (Jayasinghe et al., 2022 ) and MLP-FFA (Ghorbani et al., 2017 ) provided NSE values of 0.846 and 0.922, respectively. Compared to these studies, the best hybrid model of the present study (SWLR-RF) led to the highest NSE = 0.972 in the validation stage. Thus, this model can be used to predict Epan  reliably and accurately with a higher stability. Besides statistical metrics, the performance of the hybrid models during the validation period was evaluated through different graphs (Fig. 8  ). As depicted in Fig. 8 , the hybrid of the linear model (SWLR) with ensemble tree models (i.e., SWLR-RF and SWLR-BRT) demonstrated a better match with the actual Epan  values than the other hybrid models. In the SWLR-RF model, the values are closer to the 1:1 diagonal line and each other (Fig. 8 g) and the time series had better agreement with the observed time series (Fig. 8 h). The second-best agreement between predicted and observed Epan  values was observed from the SWLR-BRT model (Fig. 8 e and f) and the SWLR-LSTM model showed the third-best estimation performance. In the least accurate SWLR-HW model, the data points were more scattered (Fig. 8 a) and its time series had some deviations from the actual time series (Fig. 8 b). The predictive stability and accurateness of the hybrid models were also evaluated through a radar chart as shown in Fig. 9  . All the developed hybrid models led to a stable model in terms of all the performance indicators according to Umar et al. (2022)  suggestion, as the percentage difference between the calibration and validation values of R2 , NSE and RMSE values were <5 % for all models. The variation of observed Epan  against the predicted value obtained by hybrid models was also evaluated via boxplots using IQR and multiple quartiles (Q75% , median and Q25% ) as shown in Fig. 10  . The most consistent estimation output was between the SWLR-RF (median = 3.948 mm/day and IQR = 2.826 mm/day) and observed Epan  (median = 4 mm/day and IQR = 2.8 mm/day). The IQR values for the SWLR-BRT, SWLR-LSTM and SWLR-HW models were 2.886 mm/day, 2.949 mm/day and 2.939 mm/day, respectively. As shown in Fig. 10 , the minimum observed Epan  value (0.5 mm/day) was better predicted by the SWLR-BRT model (0.52 mm/day) compared to the other models. The performance of the individual and hybrid models was also evaluated and compared graphically using the Taylor diagram (Fig. 11  ). Taylor diagram is an important graph for visualizing model accuracy as it can show different statistical indices together in one graph (Taylor, 2001 ). As shown in Fig. 11 a, the RF model performed better than the other single models with correlation coefficient (r) and standard deviation (SD) of 0.969 and 1.919, respectively, while the least performing model was SWLR with r value of 0.886. The linear-nonlinear hybrid SWLR-RF model was the best model of the other hybrid and single models with an r-value of 0.986 (Fig. 11 b). The highest performance of SWLR-RF is shown in the figure as its value was close to the observed value and the highest r value than the other models. Taylor diagram was effectively been utilized to compare model accuracy by various studies (Abd-Elaty et al., 2023; Kushwaha et al., 2021; Malik et al., 2022a,b ).  4.4 Generalization feasibility investigation In the domain of applied ML models for solving hydrological processes, the question always raises that, what is the degree of the generalization feasibility of the established models? Hence, the current adopted methodology was tested on several datasets presenting different climatic variability collected from the literature. The quantitative results are presented in Table 6   for the investigated dataset. For this purpose, datasets were collected for Turkey (Siirt Station) (Ghaemi et al., 2019 ), Iran (Manjil, Yazd, and Ahvaz stations) (Ghorbani et al., 2017; Karbasi et al., 2024 ) and Morocco (Sidi Mohammed Ben Abdellah station) (El Bilali et al., 2023 ). As per the presented modeling results, the developed hybrid ML model revealed superior results to the standalone ML models. In harmony with the investigated case study of Lake Hawassa station, the RF model showed a superior modeling performance compared to the other standalone models in all stations. The RF model gave the validation phase NSE values of 0.976, 0.977, 0.936, 0.93 and 0.903 for Manjil, Siirt, Yazd, Ahvaz, and Sidi Mohammed Ben Abdellah stations, respectively. The hybrid models in the case studies on different regions also improved the performance of the standalone models. The best linear-nonlinear hybrid model (SWLR-RF) improved the performance of single models based on the verification stage NSE value by 0.72 %–21.33 % for Manjil station, 0.717 %–25.19 % for Siirt station, 4.7 %–35.172 % for Yazd station, 4.41 %–24.487 % for Ahvaz station, and 7.97 %–24.521 % for Sidi Mohammed Ben Abdellah station. Based on the obtained modeling results, the proposed methodology approved its feasibility as a robust and reliable ML model for Epan  estimation. This is an essential step (Step 3) in the development of intelligent expert systems for crops, agriculture, and irrigation-related activities.   5 Conclusions and recommendations In this study, the estimation accuracy of various ML models including SWLR, HW, LSTM, BRT and RF were compared for Epan  estimation. Prior to model development, sensitivity analysis was conducted and RH, Tmax  and SSH were found to be the first, second and third most relevant input parameters. The modeling results were assessed using Pbias, R2 , RMSE and NSE as well as various visual performance evaluation methods. Overall, the results obtained from the individual models showed the better power of the nonlinear models, particularly RF model. The RF model yielded the validation phase R2 , Pbias, RMSE, and NSE values of 0.94, −1.193 %, 0.483 mm/day and 0.939, respectively. It improved the performance of the linear SWLR model by 49.265 % and the other nonlinear models by between 25.116 % and 49.265 % in terms of validation phase RMSE value. Afterward, a hybrid model was developed by integrating the linear SWLR and nonlinear models (SWLR-HW, SWLR-LSTM, SWLR-BRT and SWLR-RF) to enhance the overall estimation accuracy by capitalizing both the nonlinear and linear pattern-capturing ability of each model. Accuracy assessment using statistical and graphical metrics revealed that the hybrid models consistently outperformed their single-model counterparts, with the hierarchical order of SWLR-RF > SWLR-BRT > SWLR-LSTM > SWLR-HW. The hybrid SWLR-RF model improved the accuracy of the linear SWLR and nonlinear single models in terms of validation phase NSE value by 26.563 % and 3.514 % to 21.348 %, and in terms of RMSE value by 66.87 % and 32.505 % to 58.205 %, respectively. This indicates that for Epan  estimation, powerful nonlinear models could provide better estimation results when hybridized with linear models. In conclusion, the proposed hybrid model stands as a valuable tool for water engineers engaged in decision-making processes regarding irrigation scheduling, agronomy, and water allocation within the Lake Hawassa catchment, Ethiopia. It is suggested that future studies can be adopted to test the feasibility of the proposed hybrid model to be integrated with a federated learning strategy where a centralized modeling phase to be incorporated for online learning. It is also suggested that future studies can test the potential of hybridizing linear models with nonlinear models optimized with nature-inspired algorithms optimization to improve the prediction accuracy. This can essentially contribute to smart agriculture management as Epan  is an important weather parameter to be identified, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions.
