After this large pulse of 4 He enters the river, the concentration decreases steadily along the next 18 km, though at the end of the study reach the concentration is still above atmospheric equilibrium (Fig. 5 ). This substantial pulse of 4 He and long-lived anomaly is likely the first such dataset described in the literature. The extended pulse of 4 He in the Colorado River (Fig. 5 ) compared to the Virgin River (Fig. 3 ) could be caused by sustained groundwater discharge to the Colorado River or slower degassing in the Colorado River owing to the greater water column depth than the Virgin River. Helium mass-balance model results for the Colorado River (Fig. 6  ) indicate that both models of spatially variable and homogeneous 4 He in groundwater generally match the overall pattern observed in the longitudinal profile of 4 He in the river, with the exception of the distance over which the initial pulse of 4 He is observed and the maximum values. Measurements indicate that 4 He concentrations increase along approximately 1 km whereas the model simulations require approximately 2.5 km to increase from atmospheric equilibrium to peak concentrations. This lag effect could be caused by the model discretization or by the treatment of boundary conditions such as k, A, and d in a homogeneous manner within the model. Sensitivity analysis using variable discretization (Δx in Eq. (1)  indicated that the model was relatively insensitive to discretization. Model runs using both 1,000 cells and 100,000 cells illustrated that in both cases a lag existed in the simulated 4 He, though the model with more cells required substantially longer runtimes. The 4 He mass-balance equation (Eq. (1)  requires estimates of river depth and width, which in turn dictate velocity through integration with discharge. Width was assigned based on data from SWOT (Altenau et al., 2021 ), but a single depth value was estimated for the entire study reach. It is possible that more granular definition of river depth, and therefore velocity, from observations along the study section could improve model fit, particularly around the initial pulse of 4 He. Simulated qgi  values differ substantially between the spatially variable and homogeneous models. Both sets of simulations indicate substantial groundwater discharge at approximately 5,000 m, approximately coincident with and slightly upstream from the pulse of observed 4 He in the river. Downstream from 5,000 m, the simulated groundwater discharge in the models diverges, with the spatially variable model indicating multiple zones of increased groundwater discharge at approximately 7,000 to 9,000 m and 13,000 to 15,000 m whereas groundwater discharge in the homogeneous model decreases throughout the remainder of the stream reach. The most pronounced difference between the models occurs at the downstream end of the reach where simulated groundwater discharge in the spatially variable 4 He model increases by two orders of magnitude. This increase in simulated groundwater discharge is caused by the inclusion of the sample from South Canyon Hot Springs in the model inputs. This hot spring is located approximately 1,000 m from the river (site S6 on Fig. 1 ) and has substantially lower 4 He concentrations than other hot springs occurring immediately adjacent to or within the Colorado River (Table 1 ). Although this spring represents local geothermal discharge, based on the difference in geochemical composition, it is unlikely that it represents discharge from the same geothermal upwelling zone that discharges directly to the Colorado River in the Glenwood Springs area. The differences in model output depending on which springs are considered in model inputs illustrates the importance of collecting spatially distributed information on groundwater inflows, specifically the 4 He content and spring discharge estimates (if available). Simulated groundwater discharge also increases slightly in the vicinity of the West Glenwood Fault, similar to the simulation of the Virgin River near the Hurricane Fault. Results from both study areas therefore demonstrate the utility of the portable mass spectrometer and mass-balance model methods in understanding structural controls on geothermal groundwater discharge.   4 Discussion 4.1 Identifying and quantifying deep groundwater discharge. Recent research has indicated that groundwater discharge to streams may be dominated by groundwater sourced from relatively shallow depths (<500 m; Ferguson et al., 2023 ). These estimates are corroborated by observation of shallow active groundwater circulation in mountain watersheds dominated by sedimentary lithologies (10 s of m; Manning et al., 2020 ). Despite the possibility that global groundwater discharge to streams may be dominated by shallow groundwater, the discharge of old, deep groundwater within geothermal systems and highly incised mountainous terrain has been well established (Diamond et al., 2018; Gleeson and Manning, 2008; McIntosh and Ferguson, 2021 ). In some instances, groundwater discharge from deep systems contributes substantial solute loads to receiving water bodies (Mast and Terry, 2019; Wood et al., 2023 ), potentially causing ecological harm and degrading water quality. The somewhat contradictory nature of the established knowledge of deep groundwater circulation and discharge with small estimates of global deep discharge volumes may be due to the difficulty of observing deep groundwater flow paths (Condon et al., 2020 )), and the difficulty and complexity of quantifying the discharge of old groundwater to surface waters (Bourke et al., 2014 ). Differential gaging (Chafin and Butler, 2002 ), specific conductance mass balance (Rumsey et al., 2015 ), or stable isotopes (Tuttle and Grauch, 2009 ) each provide methods by which to estimate deep groundwater inputs (if appropriate endmembers may be estimated), but these methods generally have high uncertainty or require complex laboratory analyses. Smerdon and Gardner (2022)  recently illustrated the utility of environmental tracer (noble gas, 3 H, etc.) sampling of river waters for hydrologic investigation of large areas. Application of the portable mass spectrometer extends this methodology. The ability of river-borne portable mass spectrometer measurements to identify deep groundwater discharge with elevated He, in this study manifesting as geothermal inflows, with high spatial precision is observed in both the Virgin (Fig. 3 ) and Colorado (Fig. 5 ) Rivers. The approach is scalable over multiple orders of magnitude in river discharge, with the discharge of the Virgin River upstream from the geothermal inputs being approximately 150 L/s, whereas the Colorado River discharge was approximately 39,700 L/s (U.S. Geological Survey, 2024). This approach allowed for more than 50 noble gas measurements to be made in both river systems (with study reaches ranging from 3 km to 25 km), a dataset that would be logistically difficult for most studies using standard copper tube or diffusion samplers collected for laboratory analysis unless precise locations of step changes in He content of river water could be known apriori. These datasets illustrate the high degree of spatial variability in noble gas compositions of river water receiving geothermal inputs, a pattern that would most likely not be observable with less spatially robust data. In particular, the ability of the portable mass spectrometer to define spatial variability means that the method shows promise for reconnaissance studies of large watersheds (e.g., Smerdon and Gardner, 2022 ). It is also possible that specific conductance or temperature could be used to identify groundwater discharge zones (Cook, 2013 ), but because these tracers are more conservatively transported in the surface water than the degassing He, it is unlikely that high-resolution identification of specific groundwater discharge zones, such as those observed in the Virgin River, could be uniquely identified. The nature of the identified geothermal discharge zones is also of note. In both the Virgin River and Colorado River, 4 He anomalies manifested both as broad zones that were apparently unrelated to geologic structures and also as focused anomalies that occurred in close proximity to mapped faults. In some respects, the geothermal discharge along faults could be considered discrete discharge zones because discharge is focused along discrete physical features. In the hydrologic sense however, these discharge zones are still diffuse because geothermal water discharges across large areas of the riverbed, as verified by field observations that show bubble formation and thermal anomalies over zones that are multiple meters in length. The portable mass spectrometer is able to detect 4 He anomalies from both discrete spring discharges along the edges of the river and from diffuse zones along the riverbed. Mass-balance model simulations were used to quantify groundwater discharge to both the Virgin and Colorado Rivers. The models represent the spatially variable patterns of 4 He in both river systems relatively well (as illustrated by the overlap of 95 % confidence intervals with data points). However, the models were unable to reproduce rapid increases in 4 He increases at the upstream end of both study reaches where large discrete springs are known to contribute geothermal water. Simulated groundwater discharges in both study reaches correspond broadly to known or hypothesized structural conduits for groundwater flow. With this knowledge of the general locations of geothermal discharge points, the portable mass spectrometer could be reused on a finer spatial scale to map localized discharge zones along these faults. These results corroborate previous applications (Beisner et al., 2018; Gardner and Susong, 2019; Smerdon and Gardner, 2022 ) of the mass-balance modeling methodology being appropriate for estimation of diffuse deep groundwater discharge to streams where there is uncertainty in model parameters. It is noteworthy that the model results are sensitive to the product of groundwater discharge (qgi ) and groundwater concentration (Cgw , see Eq. (1) ) and that recasting the results in combined discharge-concentration space could be used to further explore model uncertainty, where spatially distributed groundwater concentration data are available. In addition to precise spatial identification of discharge zones, the high-resolution sampling also likely reduces the error in groundwater inflow estimates derived from the He mass-balance model. Cook (2013)  derives relations between sample spacing and groundwater discharge uncertainty, with results indicating that inflow estimates have greater error at greater sample spacings. Most longitudinal studies of dissolved gases in rivers use sample spacings of multiple kilometers (Beisner et al., 2018; Cook, 2013; Gardner et al., 2011; Smerdon and Gardner, 2022 ). Utilizing the portable mass spectrometer allows sample spacings on the order of 10 s to 100 s of meters, even for long study reaches, which likely reduces the uncertainty of groundwater discharge estimates.  4.2 Applicability and possibilities for additional studies The ability of both models to fit abrupt increases in observed 4 He concentrations could be improved by additional data collection in the field. The mass-balance model uses the geometry of the river in model inputs, namely depth, width, and discharge. These values are used to define the velocity field for the river which in turn is used in the calculation of k (Raymond et al., 2012 ). The mass-balance model treats these properties as homogeneous along the study reach, which may not accurately reflect longitudinal variations along the river. In this study, these attributes were estimated using satellite imagery and several field measurements. Additional applications could measure these properties at a given interval, such as each time the portable mass spectrometer begins a measurement. This could result in a more detailed input dataset which could represent the true geometry of the river channel and possibly improve model fit. Misfits in the simulations could be improved by evaluating longitudinal and transverse mixing in the vicinity of 4 He inputs to quantify if the approach of measuring dissolved gases in the center of the channel is appropriate or introduces bias. Cross sections of field parameters (such as specific conductance and temperature) could be combined with measurements of noble gases across the rivers to understand if the assumption of fully mixed conditions is met. In addition to measurements of noble gases across the river, measurements of river water directly in zones of groundwater discharge could be made using the portable mass spectrometer. In this study, measurements were made in the well-mixed river and in discrete spring pools. Including measurements of the river directly adjacent to the diffuse riverbed discharge zones could provide data on the 4 He composition of river water prior to mixing. Although these data would not be used for the model, because the modeling approach assumes mixing, the river composition immediately following groundwater discharge could be useful for further constraining potential spatial variation in groundwater compositions. Model fit could also be improved by adding additional tracers of groundwater discharge to the model inversion process. For example, Rn is a useful tracer of total groundwater discharge (Adyasari et al., 2023; Avery et al., 2018 ) whereas 4 He in these study areas was a tracer of old groundwater discharge specifically because old groundwater has elevated 4 He content (Kulongoski et al., 2008 ). Adding Rn data collection using portable instruments (Dimova et al., 2009 ) could provide another dataset to include in the model inversion and fitting process; and therefore may improve the simulated fits to the observations (Beisner et al., 2018 ). Including measurement of spring discharge from discrete locations along a study reach could also assist in constraining groundwater discharge measurements at specific points in space, potentially providing information useful in evaluating simulated groundwater discharge profiles (i.e., Fig. 4 ; Fig. 6 ). Comparison of model simulations using spatially variable and homogeneous groundwater compositions illustrates the importance of collecting spatially distributed data to represent the groundwater endmember, if locations to collect such data are available. The high spatial variability in the Glenwood Springs geothermal system discharging to the Colorado River compared to the relatively homogeneous noble-gas composition of the Pah Tempe geothermal system discharging to the Virgin River indicates that uncertainty of the estimated groundwater discharge volumes could be increased in locations with more variable groundwater endmembers. Increasing uncertainty due to spatial heterogeneity is consistent with previous work by Atkinson et al. (2014) , which underscores that spatially distributed data need to be collected if quantification of groundwater discharge is a primary goal of studies. Alternatively, if only the spatial location of discharging groundwater is of interest, then fewer spatially distributed groundwater endmember compositions would be necessary. Although this study directly identifies the presence of deep groundwater discharge to both the Virgin and Colorado Rivers and estimates the discharge quantity, the age of the discharging groundwater was not addressed. Recent studies utilizing distributed samples of environmental tracers in streams (Beisner et al., 2018; Smerdon and Gardner, 2022 ), with larger spatial gaps between samples than the current study, illustrate that the age of discharge groundwater may vary substantially along a river reach. Spatially variable groundwater ages may influence the sustainability of streamflow where streams are groundwater supported (Gleeson and Richter, 2017 ). The portable noble gas mass spectrometer could be combined with sampling of environmental tracers such as 3 H, CFCs, and SF6  to quantify both groundwater discharge volumes and the age of the discharging groundwater (i.e., Smerdon and Gardner, 2022 ). Inclusion of tracers of old groundwater (4 He, 81 Kr, 14 C) could be combined with tracers of young groundwater (3 H, SF6 , 39 Ar) to more fully understand distributions of groundwater ages in watersheds where the combined tools of discrete samples and continuous profiling using the portable mass spectrometer were applied. In the Virgin River and Colorado River study areas, the discharging deep groundwater is of geothermal origin, and unique estimates of residence times of geothermal water are difficult to quantify given the complexity of geochemical reactions within the reservoir (Qiu et al., 2018; Stefánsson et al., 2019 ). Although constraining watershed-scale residence times in these settings may be complex given the geothermal systems, the approach of combining high-resolution noble gas measurements with discrete samples of other environmental tracers could be utilized in watersheds with old, non-geothermal groundwater upwelling such as the Paradox Valley of Colorado (Mast and Terry, 2019 ). As described by previous studies utilizing noble gases as tracers of groundwater/surface-water interactions, one of the primary unknowns in the mass-balance model is the gas exchange velocity, k (Beisner et al., 2018; Gleeson et al., 2018 ). Some studies directly quantify k for specific study reaches using gas injection approaches (Avery et al., 2018 ) or estimate via modeling of multiple tracers simultaneously (Gleeson et al., 2018 ). Approaches to directly estimate k for specific study reaches could be expanded through use of the portable mass spectrometer. One option to estimate gas exchange velocity is to log dissolved oxygen for several days at one or two sites along the stream reach and fit a similar gas exchange and stream metabolism model after Hall et al. (2016) . Another potential experiment to derive site-specific k values could be to pair the portable mass spectrometer with a continuous dye-tracer injection test. Given appropriate considerations for dye mass balance (Runkel, 2015 ), spatially distributed measurements of dye concentrations could be used to quantify diffuse inflows with relatively low uncertainty because the influent groundwater is known to have a dye concentration of zero. Noble gas concentration observations made with the portable mass spectrometer could then be used with the modeling approach described herein to match the groundwater discharge measured using dye dilution, making the k values the objective of the iterative approach. Another approach to estimate k values could be made by injecting a noble gas species known to be absent from diffuse discharge, such as Ar or Kr in the river reaches within this study. Simultaneous measurement of the loss of injected gas through degassing with gases derived from deep groundwater discharge (He) could allow the gas exchange behavior of both gases to be estimated using the equations in Raymond et al. (2012) . It may be beneficial to include gases with substantially different masses (such as He and Kr) because this may allow for differences in gas exchange behavior to be quantified with higher precision. Finally, if groundwater inflow were known apriori to be zero within a specific stream reach using other methodologies, then the term qgi  in Eq. (1)  could be eliminated, allowing direct calculation of k with spatially distributed longitudinal datasets. It is noteworthy that each of these potential approaches could quantify spatial changes in k, which is presently unaddressed in the literature. It is also useful to consider the applicability of the methodology to rivers of variable size and with different 4 He sources. Streamflow of the rivers considered in this study ranged over several orders of magnitude (150 L/s in the Virgin River and 39,700 L/s in the Colorado River). These rivers are relatively small compared with other rivers in North America and around the world that may be experiencing inflow of old groundwater. For instance, low-flow discharge of the Columbia River in the northwestern United States is approximately 3 x 106  L/s (U.S. Geological Survey, 2024), multiple orders of magnitude larger than the Colorado River. Groundwater in the Columbia River basalt aquifers can have terrigenic 4 He concentrations up to 2.5 x 10-6  cm3 STP/g (Johnson et al., 2024 ). If the dynamics of groundwater discharge and air–water exchange were similar between the Columbia River and the Colorado River, then the hypothetical river 4 He concentration could be considered by simple dilution. Observed 4 He in the Colorado River reaches 11.25 times the concentration of air equilibrated water (Fig. 5 ). Dilution of this signal by the approximate greater discharge in the Columbia River versus the Colorado River indicates that 4 He concentrations in the Columbia could be expected to be up to 15 % greater than atmospheric equilibrium. Given that the analytical uncertainty of the portable mass spectrometer is 1 to 3 % (Brennwald et al., 2016 ), it is possible that the signal of discharging groundwater could be uniquely identified even in a river as large as the Columbia. These calculations incorporate several simplifying factors, such as the exact dynamics of groundwater discharge, the 4 He content of the discharging groundwater, and gas exchange with the atmosphere, which are likely to differ between different river systems. Nevertheless, the method could be viable across large ranges in river dynamics and groundwater inflow regimes.   5 Conclusions Groundwater discharge to streams is a critical control on streamflow generation, water temperature variability, and solute budgets. Recent investigations suggest that most groundwater discharge to streams is young (Ferguson et al., 2023; Jasechko et al., 2016 ), yet the discharge of old groundwater with high solute concentrations is important from a global mass balance perspective (Mayfield et al., 2021; Wood et al., 2023 ) and for watershed-scale processes (Frisbee et al., 2017; Mast and Terry, 2019 ). Diffuse discharge of groundwater, particularly old groundwater, is commonly difficult and costly to quantify (Bourke et al., 2014; Smerdon and Gardner, 2022 ). In this study, a portable mass spectrometer was used to measure 4 He concentrations in the Virgin River and Colorado River, both of which have geothermal inputs that increase salinity (degrading water quality) and cause substantial economic damage (Miller et al., 2017). Longitudinal profiles of 4 He concentrations with high spatial resolution were used in an inverse mass-balance modeling approach to estimate the total groundwater discharge to both reaches. Longitudinal profiles of 4 He in both rivers indicate substantial 4 He influx leading to river concentrations enriched multiple orders of magnitude greater than the atmosphere for hundreds of meters in the Virgin River to more than 10 km in the Colorado River. Large fluctuations in 4 He concentrations along short distances in the Virgin River near Pah Tempe springs illustrate concentrated groundwater discharge zones and relatively rapid degassing of 4 He to the atmosphere. Contrastingly, the Colorado River near Glenwood Springs is characterized by one substantial pulse of 4 He that is maintained downstream. This pattern is more characteristic of broad groundwater discharge zones and slower degassing likely linked to the deeper water column in the Colorado River. Comparison of observed and simulated profiles of 4 He illustrate that although the mass-balance model is robust for estimating groundwater discharge and for evaluating gas exchange dynamics, additional field data collection could improve model fits. Collection of river geometry measurements coincident with noble gas data could constrain the channel dimensions throughout the study reach, thereby potentially improving model fit through more detailed definition of boundary conditions. Additionally, collecting spatially distributed Rn, 3 H, and CFC data could provide another dataset for inclusion in the inversion process and allow spatially variable groundwater ages to be estimated. Finally, the portable mass spectrometer shows promise for use in direct quantification of gas exchange rates using field experiments where other quantities in the mass-balance model can be directly quantified.
1 Introduction Water, land, and grain are fundamental resources for human survival and development (Chiarelli et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2024 ). However, with rapid population growth and land use changes, the efficiency of utilization and distribution patterns of water, land, and grain resources will have a significant impact on regional sustainable development (Shu et al., 2024 ). In recent years, the nexus approach has been applied to obtain a comprehensive and systems-oriented perspective in the field of regional resources and development (Akbar et al., 2023 ). The water − land − grain nexus has gradually expanded to encompass the broader correlation between natural and socio-economic systems. Additionally, concepts such as ecosystem services, sustainable development, climate change, and adaptive management have been introduced to conduct research on the trade-off and synergy of multi-factor systems (Keson et al., 2023; Ngarava, 2023; Yuan et al., 2023 ). In this context, the water − land − grain nexus requires more attention (Fig. 1  ). From the perspective of water resource utilization, the utilization efficiency of irrigation water and effective precipitation has become an important research direction for farmland utilization and grain production (Buttinelli et al., 2024 ). Many studies have evaluated irrigation water use and the effective precipitation of crops at multiple spatial scales, such as global, national, regional, and farm levels (Liu et al., 2023 ). However, with the increase in demand for grain, the decline in agricultural productivity and grain production, coupled with the uncertainty of precipitation, has intensified regional water resource shortages (Zhang et al., 2024 ). Therefore, previous studies have mainly explored the utilization of arable land and grain security in the context of water scarcity from the perspectives of irrigation water use and effective precipitation (Cui et al., 2022 ). For example, Yang et al. (2022)  analyzed the matching characteristics of agricultural water and land resources in the North China Plain, and revealed the development direction of irrigation agriculture in the future and the suitable planting layout of winter wheat. Ti et al. (2021)  conducted a large-scale household survey in the North China Plain to assess the possible impact of the World Food Programme on groundwater and food security. From the perspective of farmland utilization, improving farmland utilization efficiency in water scarce regions is also an important means to achieve sustainable agricultural development (Li et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023 ). In addition to variety, fertilization, and agricultural technology, expanding the irrigation area and improving irrigation technology are important measures to increase grain yield (Li et al., 2024). In the context of water scarcity, the relationship between water resources and grain production has become the main focus of research. Previous studies have conducted extensive and multi-scale assessments of irrigation water demand, consumption, and efficiency, providing important information for assessing the water grain relationship and decision-making in irrigation management (Yang et al., 2023 ). From the perspective of grain production, water and arable land are important resources for crop cultivation and grain production. Against the backdrop of population growth and urban development, the uncertainty of arable land availability and water supply is increasing (Chai et al., 2019 ). The future world needs to utilize limited water and land resources to produce more grain, especially in densely populated regions. From studies of the water − land − grain nexus, research in this field has evolved through a development process from a single element centered on water, land, and grain (Ma et al., 2019; Wang et al.; 2013; Yuan et al., 2014 ), to a binary relationship between water-land, water-grain, and grain-land (Li et al., 2024), and finally to the development of the water − land − grain nexus relationship (Cao et al., 2023 ). The specific content of these studies includes: a single element analysis of water resources, land resources, and grain production (Fang et al., 2024 ); analyses of the interrelationships within the water − land − grain system (Shu et al., 2024 ); construction of the concept of linkage relationships (Feng et al., 2023 ); trade-offs and synergistic effects among factors (Bai et al., 2024a,b ); impacts of climate change (Wang et al., 2024a,b ); impacts of trade flows (Bai et al., 2024a,b ) and ecosystem services (Wang et al., 2024a,b ); and an interactive comparison of coupled models (Sun et al., 2024 ). Studies of water resource utilization in the study area have shown that due to the lack of surface water resources in the North China Plain (NCP), groundwater has become the main source of agricultural irrigation (Yang et al., 2022 ). Long term excessive extraction of groundwater to maintain a high-intensity planting system has led to a continuous decline in groundwater levels (Li and Ren, 2023 ). The urban groundwater level in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region has decreased by 20 − 40 m in the past 30 years (Zhong et al., 2019 ). This decline can be attributed to the combined effects of population growth and urbanization; domestic, industrial, and ecological water requirements; and high-water-consumption agricultural planting structures. Under these conditions, the conflicts between water, land-use, and grain have become increasingly acute. At the same time, under the influence of land use and climate change, the total amount of water resources in the basin is continuously decreasing (Ti et al., 2021 ). Located in the north of the NCP, the Daqing River Basin (DRB) is a region with one of the most strained human − water relationships in China (Meng et al., 2012; Yang et al. 2009; Zeng et al. 2019; Zhong et al. 2019 ). The natural water production in this basin is much lower than the water consumption. In addition to the region's own water production, the current water supply of the DRB also includes inter-basin water diversions from the Yangtze River (South-to-North Water Diversion Project) and the Yellow River (Yellow River-to-Baiyangdian Water Transfer Project). The scarcity of water resources in the DRB has led to its dependence on external water transfers, although inter-basin water replenishment schemes are uncommon both in China and globally. There are several shortcomings in the existing research. First, the current macro level research on water resource utilization is mainly based on point data rather than surface data. Most studies have analyzed the effective precipitation and irrigation water demand of crops, while the spatial pattern of water resource utilization at the grid scale has not been investigated. Second, previous studies have often assumed that the water resources in the study area are static, while ignoring the significant impact of large-scale inter-basin water transfer on regional water resource utilization. Third, the current research lacks a spatial perspective to explain how to balance the relationship between water resource utilization and grain production. Based on these issues arising from previous studies, there were four main issues that this study addressed. First, a water yield module based on the InVEST model was used to calculate the natural water production of the DRB on a 30 m grid scale. Second, based on the crop spatial distribution data, the spatial distribution pattern of crop water demand, effective precipitation, and irrigation water demand were calculated at a 30 m grid scale. Third, the current balance of water resource utilization in the DRB was analyzed from the perspectives of supply and demand. Fourth, under the premise of considering inter-basin water transfer, different balancing schemes for future water resource supply and grain production were proposed from the perspective of the spatial pattern. There were three main contributions of this study. (1) The DRB is the region of China with the most severe strain on the human − water relationship, the most inter-basin water transfer, and is a key area for coordinated development in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region. The study area’s representativeness provides an important reference for regions with the most significant conflicts within the human − water − land − grain nexus. (2) The research method was based on the calculation and simulation of raster data, which resulted in more detailed and objective results than the evaluation of traditional agricultural experimental stations using points instead of surfaces. (3) Suggestions for the optimization of the water resource quantity were made, but a balanced plan between water resource utilization and grain production was also developed from the perspective of the spatial pattern. This will be an important reference for optimizing water resource management in water scarce regions in the future.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Study area Located in the north of the NCP (113° 39′E−117°86′E, 38°23′N−40°09′N), the DRB is one of the nine major tributaries in the Haihe River Basin. It spans the four provincial administrative regions of Shanxi, Hebei, Beijing, and Tianjin, with a drainage area of approximately 43,060 km2 . The average annual precipitation in the DRB is 506.7 mm, which is unevenly distributed throughout the year. In 2020, the total population of the basin was approximately 27.61 × 106 , and there was approximately 2.08 × 106  hm2  of arable land in the basin. The main crops planted are winter wheat, spring maize, and summer maize, with a winter wheat − summer maize rotation. The total grain production (referring only to wheat and maize, which accounts for about 95 % of the total grain production in the DRB) is 12.33 × 106  t, with a per capita grain allocation of 447 kg. During the water sensitive period of winter wheat growth and development (April − May), the effective rainfall is much lower than the growth in water demand (Li et al., 2021 ). The growing season of summer maize (June − September) is the main rainy season in the DRB, when 80 % of the total annual rainfall is received. Natural rainfall can meet the water resource demand for summer maize. Faced with a serious water scarcity problem, the Chinese government has introduced a series of relevant policies in recent years, with the aim of reducing the winter wheat planting area in regions with severe groundwater overexploitation. This would alleviate the human − water conflict in the DRB (Wang et al., 2016 ).  2.2 Materials (1) Remote sensing data. Landsat 8-OLI remote sensing images were used for a land use classification in the study area. The image data was sourced from the United States Geological Survey (https://glovis.usgs.gov/app ), with a spatial resolution of 30 m. The cloud cover of the selected images in this paper was < 1 %. A total of 13 images were used, and their acquisition dates and path/row numbers are given in Table 1  . (2) Meteorological data. Daily average precipitation data and evapotranspiration data from 27 meteorological stations in the DRB for 30 years (1981 − 2010) were sourced from the National Meteorological Information Center (https://www.nmic.cn ). Grid data with a spatial resolution of 30 m was obtained through a Kriging interpolation on the ArcGIS 10.8 platform. The 1981 − 2010 data is the latest dataset product of the National Meteorological Information Center, with the most recent and comprehensive collection of meteorological data, including a wide coverage of meteorological stations. Although the data after 2010 would obviously be more recent, continuous meteorological data in the DRB for this period was only available from a few stations. Its use would therefore seriously affect the spatial interpolation accuracy of meteorological data. (3) Statistical data. The population and grain yield data were sourced from the statistical yearbooks of Hebei, Shanxi, Beijing, and Tianjin. The water resource data was mainly obtained from the water resource bulletins of the four provinces, The Water Resources Bulletin of the Haihe River Basin, and the Hydrological Yearbook of the People's Republic of China-Hydrological Data of the Haihe River Basin. (4) Other data. Digital elevation model data and soil data were obtained from the Resource and Environmental Science Data Center of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (https://www.resdc.cn ). The spatial resolution of the digital elevation model data was 30 m, and it was used to construct the vector boundary of the study area and conduct a basin analysis. Soil data included attributes such as soil type, soil texture, and organic matter content, with a spatial resolution of 1 km. This data was used to calculate the effective soil moisture content.  2.3 Methods 2.3.1 Remote sensing identification of land use and the major crops 1) Data preprocessing. Preprocessing of the remote sensing images of the DRB was conducted using the ENVI 5.2 software platform. This mainly involved geometric correction, radiometric correction, splicing, clipping, and image enhancement. The land use classification system was divided into six categories: farmland, forest land, grassland, water bodies, built-up land, and bare land.  2) Remote sensing image features. The Maximum Likelihood Method was used in supervised classification algorithms to select six land use classification samples from Landsat OLI and interpret the land use distribution in 2020. The images were used to calculate the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and the temporal variation curves of the NDVI were plotted for different crops as a reference for crop classification. The NDVI was calculated as follows:   （1） NDVI = R NIR   - R RED      R NIR   + R RED            where RNIR   and RRED   represent the reflectance values in the near-infrared and red light bands, respectively. In Landsat OLI remote sensing images, the RNIR   and RRED   are Band 5 and Band 4, respectively. The NDVI not only improves the ability to recognize the soil background, but also weakens the influence of terrain shadows and the atmosphere, therefore indicating the growth status of vegetation.3) Time window. The crop phenological calendar provides the basis for selecting the optimal timing for crop identification. Based on the phenological calendar of the DRB, the time windows of winter wheat, summer maize, and spring maize, were selected to extract planting information for different crops. For example, from mid-March to early April, crops such as maize and cotton were not yet been sown, and there was a significant difference in the NDVI between winter wheat and other crops. Therefore, this time period was the best time window for extracting winter wheat.  4) Determine the threshold. Based on the ENVI 5.2 and ArcGIS 10.8 platforms, the NDVI differences of different crops were analyzed, appropriate thresholds were set, crops were recognized and extracted, and Google Earth high-resolution images were used to correct and verify the accuracy of the classified land types.     2.3.2 Water yield estimation The InVEST model water yield evaluation module has been widely used for water yield estimations at different research scales in various regions (Yang et al., 2019 ). Its core algorithm uses the principle of water balance combined with terrain, climate, soil, and land use data to calculate and summarize the water yield of each grid in the basin. The water yield is the precipitation of each grid in the watershed minus the actual evapotranspiration (Sharp et al., 2015 ), including surface runoff and infiltration. It is calculated as follows:（2） Y xj   = P x  - AET  xj        where Yxj   is the annual water yield; Px   is the annual average precipitation of grid x; and AETxj   is the annual average evapotranspiration of grid x in land type j. All units are mm.  2.3.3 Crop water consumption The water consumption of crops can be calculated by the irrigation water demand and effective precipitation during the crop growth period. It is calculated as follows:（3） W i , v e g   = W i , i r r   + W i , p r e        where Wi,veg   is the total water consumption of crop i  during its growth period; and Wi,irr   and Wi,pre   are the irrigation water volume and effective precipitation of crop i  during its growth period, respectively. All units are mm. To determine water consumption during crop growth, the crop coefficient method recommended by FAO 56 is widely adopted due to its advantages of easy data acquisition and high level of accuracy (Allen et al., 1998 ). The formula is:（4） W i , v e g   = ET  0  × K c , i        where ET0   is the potential evapotranspiration, which can be calculated using formula (5); and Kc,i   is the crop coefficient of the i  crop. The Kc,i   for winter wheat, spring maize, and summer maize in this study are 0.90, 0.87, and 0.87, respectively. The formula for calculating potential evapotranspiration (the Penman-Monteith equation) (Allen et al., 1994 ) is as follows:（5） ET  0  = 0.408 Δ R n  - G    + γ 900 273 + T   u 2  e a  - e d      Δ + γ 1 + 0.34 u 2            where ET0   is the potential evapotranspiration, unit: mm; Δ is the slope of the saturated water pressure and temperature curve, unit: kPa/℃; Rn   and G  are the net radiation and soil heat flux, respectively, unit: MJ/m 2 ;γ  is the psychrometric constant, unit: kPa/℃; T  is the daily average temperature, unit: ℃; u2   is the daily average wind speed at a height of 2 m, unit: m/s; and ea   and ed   are the saturated water pressure and actual atmospheric water pressure, respectively, unit: kPa. Only effective precipitation can be used for crop growth. The daily effective precipitation method proposed by Liu et al. (2005)  was applied as follows:（6） P i , e f f   = P , P ≤ E T    E T , P > E T              where Pi,eff   is the effective precipitation; and P  and ET  are the ten-day precipitation and the actual evapotranspiration of crops, respectively, unit: mm.    3 Results 3.1 Land use and crop planting patterns Land use types were divided into six categories: farmland, forest land, grassland, water bodies, built-up land, and bare land, with areas of 20,799, 12,770, 2444, 500, 4467, and 702 km2 , which accounted for 49.9 %, 30.6 %, 5.9 %, 1.2 %, 10.7 %, and 1.7 % of the total area, respectively (Fig. 2  a). Farmland was the main land use in the DRB, accounting for nearly half of the total basin area. The planting area of winter wheat in the DRB was 645,500 hm2 , summer maize was 881,800 hm2 , and spring maize was 554,000 hm2  (Fig. 2 b). The winter wheat − summer maize rotation covered an area of 610,000 hm2 , which was mainly distributed in the plain area bordering the Taihang Mountains. The average annual temperature in the Taihang Mountains is relatively low, with the severe winter temperatures making it unsuitable for growing winter wheat. The main crop in this area was spring maize.  3.2 Annual average water yield Based on the InVEST model's water yield evaluation function, the annual average water yield of the DRB under natural conditions was 3.47 × 109  m3 (total natural water resources). The average runoff depth was 83 mm (Fig. 2 c). From the perspective of the spatial pattern, the water yield in the western mountainous regions was relatively low, with an average runoff depth largely below 50 mm. This was mainly because there were more forests in the upstream region, with strong evapotranspiration and relatively little precipitation. The central mountainous plain had a higher water yield, with an average runoff depth of 80 − 100 mm. The main reason is that the rainfall in this region was higher, while the actual evapotranspiration was lower. The evapotranspiration coefficients of built-up and bare land were relatively low, resulting in a high water yield.  3.3 Crop water consumption 3.3.1 Effective rainfall and irrigation water demand The spatial differences in irrigation water demand during different crop growth periods in the DRB were significant, and the spatial trend revealed a gradually increasing trend from west to east. During the growth period of winter wheat, the average annual effective precipitation was 110 − 150 mm, with an average of 135 mm (Fig. 3  b), and the average irrigation water demand was approximately 285 mm. The average annual precipitation during the growth period of summer maize was 250 to 290 mm, with an average of 272 mm (Fig. 3 d), and the average irrigation water demand was only 20 mm. The average effective precipitation during the growth period of spring maize was 310 − 410 mm, with an average of 359 mm (Fig. 3 c), and the average irrigation water demand was approximately 73 mm. The effective rainfall in the rotation area of winter wheat and summer maize was 390 − 430 mm, with an average of 409 mm (Fig. 3 a), and an average irrigation water requirement of approximately 301 mm. Based on the farmland situation in 2020, the total irrigation water demand in the DRB was 2.43 × 109  m3 , i.e., about 70 % of the total natural water resource. The irrigation water demands for winter wheat, summer maize, and spring maize were 1.84 × 109  m3 , 1.80 × 108  m3 , and 4.10 × 108  m3 , accounting for 75.7 %, 7.4 %, and 16.9 % of the total irrigation water demand respectively (Table 2  ) (Fig. 4  ).  3.3.2 Water consumption of crops during the growth period There were significant differences in water consumption among the different crops in the DRB. The water consumption of winter wheat during its annual growth period was 360 − 490 mm, with an average of 420 mm. The water consumption during the annual growth period of summer maize was 250 − 350 mm, with an average of 292 mm. The water consumption during the annual growth period of spring maize was 380 − 520 mm, with an average of 420 mm. Under a single cropping a year (only spring corn and idle land consume water), the average annual water consumption was 589 mm. Under the double cropping a year (winter wheat − summer corn rotation), the average annual water consumption was 699 mm. Under a three crops over two years system (winter wheat, summer maize, spring maize), the average annual water consumption was 644 mm (Fig. 5  ). During the growth period of each crop, the overall water demand was lower in mountainous regions than in plain regions, with a gradually increasing trend from west to east. The lowest water demand of crops occurred in the northwest and southwest of the basin, while the highest water demand of crops occurred in Tianjin city downstream of the basin.   3.4 Analysis of the supply–demand balance of water resources In 2020, the per capita water consumption in the DRB was approximately 223 m3 , with the values for agriculture, industry, domestic, and ecological requirements being 119, 26, 43, and 35 m3 , which accounted for 53.4 %, 11.7 %, 19.3 %, and 15.7 % of the total, respectively. According to the analysis of the water supply and demand structure (Fig. 6  ), the total water consumption in the DRB was currently 6.16 × 109  m3 , with the water supply sources including natural water resources of 3.47 × 109  m3 , water diversion of 1.64 × 109  m3 , and 3.3 × 108  m3  of other sources, resulting in a water supply shortfall of approximately 7.20 × 109  m3 . The water supply gap was mainly supplemented by the overexploitation of groundwater. Therefore, in the current and future development plans of the DRB, it will be necessary to gradually increase the amount of inter-basin water transfer and appropriately increase the proportion of unconventional water uses, such as sewage treatment and reuse, to protect the ecological conditions in regions where groundwater is overexploited. According to the urban planning of Hebei Province, Tianjin City, and Beijing City, the water resource demand in the DRB depends on the future population growth, economic development, and grain security standards (An et al., 2019; People's Government of Beijing Municipality, 2017; Hebei Provincial Department of Housing and Urban Rural Development, 2017). Therefore, according to existing development models and inertia, the future water resource demand largely depends on agricultural, industrial, and domestic water, as well as water required for ecological needs. According to the development plans of the various provinces in the DRB, the population will reach approximately 3.4 × 107  by 2030, and water security will become a serious issue for the DRB. Except for agricultural water consumption, the per capita comprehensive water consumption in the DRB was 104 m3 . At this level of consumption, an additional 6.60 × 107  m3  will be required to meet the domestic, ecological, and industrial water requirements of the increased population of the DRB by 2030. If this problem is to be solved from within the basin, it means expanding the fallow winter wheat area by approximately 2.33 × 105  hm2 . At this time, the per capita grain allocation is only 340 kg, far below the safety level of 400 kg (Ma et al., 2009). Therefore, if the current development inertia is maintained, the DRB will face the dual pressures of water resource and grain security by 2030. There is an urgent need to balance the relationship between water resource utilization and grain production and make appropriate policy arrangements.  3.5 Current trade-offs and future evolution of the water − land − grain system Due to the lack of surface water resources in the NCP, groundwater has become the main source of agricultural irrigation (Gao et al., 2015 ). Long term overexploitation of groundwater to maintain a high-intensity planting system has led to a continuous decline of the groundwater level, especially in the areas of the DRB located in the north of the NCP (Zhao et al., 2018 ). There is a need to an alleviate the conflict between water resources and grain production in the DRB. Adjusting the planting structure and reducing the planted area of high water demand crops are considered effective measures to reduce water resource consumption (Li et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2018 ). Since 2014, China and Hebei Province have allocated more than 7 billion yuan annually for establishing fallow areas and crop rotation, as well as monoculture subsidies. These measures have achieved good results in alleviating water resource pressure and restoring groundwater funnel regions. The construction and development of Xiong'an New Area also relies on the effective use of water resources. The guarantee and sustainable utilization of water resources is a key factor affecting the future construction and development of Xiong'an New Area. Additionally, to alleviate water scarcity, China has implemented the South to North Water Diversion Project, which is expected to replace about 4 billion m3  of the groundwater overdraft in the NCP by 2025 (Yao et al., 2019 ). However, even with the completion of the middle line of the South to North Water Diversion Project in 2014, there is still significant potential for improvement in water diversion capacity (Wang et al., 2019 ). Therefore, how to more effectively implement water diversion projects and improve the efficiency of water resource utilization is also an important issue for the optimal management of water resources in the DRB. Clearly quantifying the irrigation water consumption in future agricultural production planning is critical for the comprehensive sustainable management of water resources in the DRB. Grain and water security are two key issues in the DRB. From the perspective of the coordinated development of Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei and the strategic positioning of Xiong'an New Area, water security takes priority over grain security. There is a particular need to control agricultural irrigation water use and reduce groundwater overexploitation. Grain security can be achieved through the grain trade and macroeconomic regulation. In this context, an optimization plan was proposed for the agricultural planting structure in the DRB by balancing the current and future water − land − grain nexus. In 2020, the groundwater overexploitation in the DRB was approximately 7.20 × 108  m3 , which was equivalent to the irrigation water requirement for planting approximately 2.53 × 105  hm2  of winter wheat. Under the current water resource supply structure, to control groundwater overexploitation, the DRB should continue to expand the fallow area of winter wheat or increase inter-basin water diversion to restore groundwater levels. The potential fallow area was located east of the 294 mm contour line under the winter wheat irrigation water demand (Fig. 7  a). If the water supply from inter-basin diversion or regeneration increased, the fallow area of winter wheat could be appropriately reduced. The potential fallow areas were located southeast of the 299 mm contour line in Fig. 7 a with an increase of 2.0 × 108  m3  in water supply, or southeast of the 310 mm contour line with an increase of 5 × 108  m3  in water supply. By 2030, under the premise of not overexploiting groundwater, the DRB will require an increase of approximately 1.38 × 109  m3  to meet its domestic, industrial, and ecological water use requirements. This increase in water resources is equivalent to a doubling of the current water diversion in the DRB. Continuing to expand the fallow area of winter wheat is also a policy choice that could alleviate future water resource pressures. If the inter-basin water transfer is not increased, it will require an additional 4.73 × 105  hm2  of fallow winter wheat area to meet the water resource demand of the basin, which will in turn lead to a 23 % decrease in grain production. The potential fallow area is currently located southeast of the 269 mm contour line for the winter wheat irrigation water demand (Fig. 7 b), and the winter wheat planting area that can be preserved only includes a portion of the plain bordering the Taihang Mountains. Similarly, if the water supply from inter-basin water transfer or recycled water is increased, the fallow area of winter wheat could be appropriately reduced. The potential fallow areas were located southeast of the 290 mm contour line in Fig. 7 b with an increase of 5.0 × 108  m3  in the water supply, or southeast of the 300 mm contour line with an increase of 1 × 109  m3  in water supply.   4 Discussion 4.1 Water yield accuracy Accurately estimating the total amount of water resources in a basin is crucial for comprehensive water resource management. This study used the InVEST model to estimate the water yield of the DRB. The results showed that the average total annual water yield of the DRB under natural conditions was approximately 3.47 billion m3 , and the average runoff depth was about 83 mm. Bai et al. (2013)  used the InVEST model to calculate the water production of the Baiyangdian Basin to be approximately 3.12 billion m3 , which was similar to the results of this study. Although the InVEST model has been widely applied in ecosystem evaluation, there may still be a certain degree of uncertainty in its water production module when simulating the water balance under complex land use patterns (Zhao et al., 2019 ).  4.2 Crop irrigation water demand accuracy Against the backdrop of the increasingly severe agricultural water crisis, researchers have conducted extensive research on the water requirements for winter wheat, summer corn, and spring corn cultivation. The present study found that the average annual water demand for winter wheat during its growth period in the DRB was 420 mm, and the average irrigation water demand was approximately 285 mm. The average annual water demand during the growth period of summer maize was 282 mm, and the average irrigation water demand was only 20 mm. The average annual water demand during the growth period of spring maize was 420 mm, and the average irrigation water demand was approximately 73 mm. These values were similar to those reported by Wang et al. (2013)  and Liu et al. (2005) , but slightly lower than the results reported by Cao et al. (2018)  for crop water demand in Baoding City, and higher than the results reported by Yu et al. (2018)  for the winter wheat growth period water demand in Tianjin City. In this and previous studies of irrigation water demand, the crop coefficient method was used. The main factor that affects the results, in addition to the length of time selected for meteorological data, is the calculation of effective precipitation. The most accurate way of calculating the effective precipitation during the crop growth period is the water balance method, which requires the precipitation and evapotranspiration of each period (1 − 5 days), as well as the measured values of soil water storage at the beginning of the period and the maximum water storage, which is difficult to obtain in practical operation. In this study, the chosen method for calculating effective precipitation calculation method utilized a ten-day period. This approach not only met the accuracy requirement, but also ensured the original data's availability and operability. Additionally, the crop water demand, effective precipitation, and irrigation water demand in this study were all calculated based on spatial grid crop sowing data, which is a more objective approach than the “point to surface” evaluation that is traditionally adopted in agricultural experimental stations.  4.3 Impact of planting structure adjustments on the water − land − grain system Adjusting the planting structure and reducing the planting area of high water consuming crops are effective means to alleviate the conflict between water resources and grain production in the DRB. Since 2014, China and Hebei Province have allocated more than 7 billion yuan annually for fallow and crop rotation, as well as monoculture subsidies. These measures have been effective in alleviating water resource pressure and restoring groundwater funnel regions. The impact of winter wheat fallow potential on grain production was estimated based on the winter wheat fallow policy in the DRB. If the fallow potential of the winter wheat planting area was calculated based on a per capita grain allocation of 400 kg, there would be 2.16 × 105  hm2  of fallow area for winter wheat, which could save 6.20 × 108  m2  of irrigation water (Fig. 8  ). When winter wheat was completely fallow in the basin, a total of 1.84 × 109  m2  of irrigation water could be saved, accounting for 53 % of the total natural water resources in the basin. However, under these conditions the grain production capacity of the DRB decreased by 31 %. When all the winter wheat planting regions were converted into three crops (winter wheat, summer maize, and spring maize) over two years, an annual irrigation water saving of 7.50 × 108  m2  could be achieved, which accounted for 22 % of the total natural water resources in the basin. However, the average annual grain production capacity decreased by 12 % under these conditions. When all winter wheat planting regions (including the winter wheat − summer maize rotation) were converted into spring maize for a single cropping each year, 1.52 × 109  m2  of irrigation water was saved, accounting for 44 % of the total natural water resources in the DRB. Under these conditions the grain production capacity decreased by 24 %. In future fallow planning, the winter wheat planting regions in counties with a high water demand in the southeast of Baiyangdian should be compressed. Additionally, the current winter wheat − summer maize rotation area should be gradually converted to a three crops over two years system (winter wheat − summer maize-spring maize) or a single cropping each year (spring maize). These actions would alleviate the water resource pressure in this region.  4.4 Agricultural irrigation efficiency and water-saving potential Improving agricultural irrigation efficiency is also an effective way to alleviate the shortage of water resources in the DRB. Currently, the traditional methods of flood irrigation or local sprinkler irrigation are used for farmland irrigation in the DRB. Previous experimental results obtained for the different irrigation methods for wheat and maize in the DRB (Gao et al., 2015; Ren et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2018 ) were used to evaluate the irrigation water demand, water-saving potential, and relative production of crops under different irrigation methods (Fig. 9  ). Drip irrigation had the best water-saving and increased crop production potential, with a reduction in the agricultural irrigation water and arable land resources used to meet grain demand. However, the adoption of this system would lead to increased costs for agricultural production facilities. The costs of sprinkler irrigation and micro-spray irrigation are relatively low, and their water-saving ability and grain production have also been significantly improved over time. The development of efficient water-saving irrigation technology is clearly of great significance for the sustainable development of agriculture in the DRB. Unfortunately, in addition to being constrained by the existing agricultural scale, infrastructure, and technological conditions, farmers producing the low value-added wheat and maize crops often cannot afford the high production costs associated with water-saving irrigation methods such as drip irrigation and micro spraying. Therefore, in the future development of agriculture in the DRB, there should be a focus on developing large-scale agricultural systems, promoting efficient water-saving irrigation, and increasing financial subsidies for green agriculture. To alleviate water scarcity, China has implemented the South-to-North Water Diversion Project. By 2025, the overexploitation of groundwater in the NCP (about 4.0 × 109  m3 ) is expected to have been halted due to water delivered by the South to North Water Diversion Project (Yao et al., 2019 ). However, even after the completion of the middle line of the South to North Water Diversion Project in 2014, there is still significant potential for further improvement in water diversion capacity (Wang et al., 2019 ). Therefore, the effective implementation of water diversion projects and improvements in the efficiency of water resource utilization are also important optimization options for the comprehensive management of water resources in the DRB.   5 Conclusions This study explored the crop planting pattern and the relationship between water supply and demand in the DRB in the NCP of China, and analyzed the current trade-off and future evolution characteristics of the water − land − grain system. The results showed that the average annual water yield in the DRB was approximately 3.47 × 109  m3 . The total irrigation water demand for winter wheat, summer maize, and spring maize was 2.43 × 109  m3 , accounting for approximately 70 % of the total natural water resources in the DRB. Excessive water consumption in agricultural irrigation was the main factor causing strain on water resources in the DRB. Based on the grain security standard of 400 kg per capita grain allocation, the DRB can currently achieve self-sufficiency in grain. By 2030, the DRB will face the dual pressures of water and grain security. The overexploitation of groundwater in the DRB is severe, and the irrigation water saved by the existing local fallow measures only accounts for 7 % of the current extraction. To achieve a balance between the supply and demand of water resources and avoid overexploitation of groundwater, it is necessary to expand the fallow area in the southeastern plain region of Baiyangdian by approximately 2.53 × 105  hm2 , or increase the inter-basin water diversion by approximately 7.20 × 109  m3 . By 2030, the water resource gap in the DRB will reach 1.38 × 109  m3 . Measures such as increasing inter-basin water transfer and increasing the fallow area of winter wheat must be taken to alleviate the water − grain conflict. This study provides important references for the allocation of water resources in water deficient regions and the sustainable development of grain production.
