1 Introduction Karst systems are known as complex media hosting a combination of primary (matrix), secondary (fracture), and tertiary (dissolution) porosity and permeability, with one component typically dominating in natural aquifers (White and White, 2005; Palmer, 2007 ). These aquifers are significantly distinct from granular and fractured-rock aquifers in terms of physical properties (e.g., effective porosity, homogeneity, isotropy, and storage) and hydrodynamic characteristics (e.g., flow rate, velocity, and flow regime) (ASTM, 1998; Mohammadi et al., 2019 ). Karst aquifers predominantly develop in carbonate rock due to the gradual dissolution by CO2 -rich water, forming intricate networks of conduits and caves (Bakalowicz, 2005; Fandel et al., 2020 ). Fracture networks and bedding planes represent major inception horizon zones that provide the framework for karstification processes, which leads to the development of a dissolution conduit network (Gill et al., 2021 ). Generally, the conduit network within karst aquifers typically exhibits fast and turbulent groundwater flow, contrasting with the slow and laminar movement in the surrounding porous, fissured, and fractured settings. (Hartmann et al., 2014; Şen et al., 2020; Olarinoye et al., 2022 ). Two end-members of the flow system have been identified in well-developed karst aquifers, representing a very heterogeneous mature karst system with high flow velocities in channels and low flow velocities in the fissure system (Clemens et al., 1997 ). Fundamental distinctions in hydraulic behavior between karst and fractured-rock systems can be demonstrated based on their heterogeneity grade (Kovács, 2003; Kovács et al., 2005 ). The degree of karst development in soluble rocks is influenced by various factors, such as lithological characteristics, layers thickness, tectonics (i.e., fractures and faults), relief, and precipitation, etc. (White, 1988; Parise et al., 2015a, 2018 ). Understanding the degree of karst aquifer development is crucial as it can indicate flow depletion patterns (Naufal et al., 2020 ). The fluid flow in the fractured-rock aquifers is controlled by a network of interconnected conductive fractures (Parashar and Reeves, 2011 ), while in karstic aquifers, highly transmissive conduits are formed by the dissolution of separate passages along structures such as fractures and bedding planes, leading to highly heterogeneous fluid flow (Aliouache et al., 2019 ). The extreme spatial heterogeneity strongly influences the hydraulic behavior of karst aquifers (Pardo-Igúzquiza et al., 2012 ), impacting the shape of spring hydrograph due to significant differences in conduit and fracture apertures (Mayaud et al., 2014 ). Although karst aquifers exhibit a wide range of hydraulic flow conditions, these can be classified into two end-members: slow flow within fissures and intergranular pores, and fast flow within the conduit network. (Atkinson, 1985; White, 2002 ). The concept of a fractured-rock and karst aquifer was first introduced by Atkinson and Smart (1979)  for conditions where turbulent flow occurs in a network of joints and bedding planes that have been widened by dissolution to an aperture of about 10 cm. These aquifers are of interest not only as freshwater sources (Stevanović, 2018, 2019 ) but also in construction projects (Milanović, 1981, 2000, 2002; Karay and Hajnal, 2015; Parise et al., 2015b ). Extensive research has been conducted on fractured-rock and karst aquifers by various researchers, including Keeler (1997), Siemers and Dreybrodt (1998), Kaufmann and Braun (2000), Kovács (2003), Kovács et al. (2005), Taylor and Greene (2008), Colombo et al. (2012), Kaufmann (2016)  and Wang et al. (2017) . Comprehension of the hydrological behavior of fractured-rock and karst aquifers requires multi-disciplinary approaches involving surface hydrology, hydrogeology, geochemistry, etc. (Jourde et al., 2018 ). Determining the catchment area and conduit network geometry are crucial steps in understanding the hydrogeology and hydraulics of karst aquifers (Goldscheider and Drew, 2007; Malard et al., 2015 ). Conventional methods for studying fractured-rock and karst aquifers include spectral and correlation analysis, tracer tests, pumping tests, chemographs and stable isotopes analysis, well and spring hydrograph analysis, and numerical and physical models ( Angelini, 1997; Smart, 1988; Peely et al., 2021; Thrailkill, 1988; Nassimi and Mohammadi, 2018; Aquilina et al., 2005; Hillebrand et al., 2013; Shevenell, 1996; Mohammadi and Shoja, 2014; Eisenlohr et al., 1997; Mohammadi et al., 2021; Leins et al., 2023; Liso et al., 2023 ). Due to the heterogeneity of karst aquifers, generalizing the information obtained from tracer and pumping tests to the entire aquifer may lead to a misinterpretation of the conditions governing the aquifer. The spring hydrograph, and particularly its recession part, reflects the response of the whole aquifer to rainfall and recharge events and enables a better understanding of the hydrogeology and hydraulics of the karst aquifer (Padilla et al., 1994 ). A more accurate understanding of the karst hydro-system requires using a combination of direct and indirect methods (Assari and Mohammadi, 2017 ). Many karst terrains crop out in Iran, especially in the Zagros region. Among the several limestone aquifers in the Zagros zone, the Asmari and Sarvak Limestone aquifers are well known. These aquifers have been known and studied mainly as developed karst (Karimi et al., 2005; Ashjari and Raeisi, 2006; Moradi et al., 2018 . Some of these aquifers have been recognized as fractured-rock and karst aquifers (Adinehvand and Raeisi, 2018; Adinehvand et al., 2020 ). The Sarvak Formation is a thick carbonate stratigraphic member of the Bangestan group, deposited in the Zagros region and the southern margin of the Neotitis (Aveili, 2016 ). It is one of the most important karst formations in the Zagros Mountain range, and its aquifer supplies numerous large springs (Dashti Barmaki et al., 2019 ). The study area is located on the Sarvak Limestone Formation in the folded zone of the Zagros Mountain ranges. Bakhtiari Dam, a 275 m high double-curvature concrete arch that will be one of the highest of its kind in the world (Haftani et al., 2013 ), is planned to be constructed in the study area. Understanding the degree of karst development of the Sarvak Limestone Aquifer (SLA) is of great importance due to the multiple and successive thin limestone layers of the Sarvak Formation and the emergence of the large spring Pelle Khan (with a flow rate of 50 to 1800 l/s) downstream of the Bakhtiari Dam reservoir. The aims of this study include a comprehensive characterization of SLA and an investigation of its karst development potential by integrating the results of geological investigations, hydrogeological analyses, hydrochemical and isotopic evaluations, and dye tracer tests. Through this approach, we aim to elucidate the intricate nature of SLA, delineating its lithological and structural characteristics, and discerning its hydrogeological properties, such as pressure test responses, groundwater level fluctuations, and spring discharge patterns. We endeavor to conceptualize a comprehensive model of groundwater flow within SLA. Additionally, we seek to determine the direction and velocity of groundwater movement, characterize the flow regime within the aquifer, and elucidating the factors governing the spatial and temporal variability of hydrochemical and isotopic compositions.  2 Materials and methods In this section, a detailed overview of the available materials and methods is provided. The approach is structured to ensure a comprehensive understanding of the case study area, including its geological and hydrogeological characteristics. We also elaborate on the types of data collected, the measurement techniques employed, and the analytical methods used to interpret the data. The materials used in this study include geological maps, hydrogeological data, and various measurement instruments essential for data collection. The methods encompass both fieldwork and laboratory analyses to ensure accurate and reliable results. 2.1 Case study The study area is a part of the Zagros Region (MSJV, 2015 ), and located at the Bakhtiari Dam site (Fig. 1  ) which is being investigated and is under construction with a designed reservoir volume of 4800 MCM (MPJV, 2018 ). The catchment area of the Bakhtiari River (B-R) at the dam site is about 6,500 km2 , and its average and maximum elevations are 2,212 and 4,080 m above sea level (asl), respectively. The average annual rainfall is 1116.8 mm, and the mean discharge of the river is 1.45 × 105  l/s. Downstream of the dam site, the Bakhtiari River joins the Sezar River to form the headwaters of the Dez River. From a geomorphological standpoint, the dam site is located in a narrow gorge 35 m-wide at the river bed. A major perennial karst spring (Pelle Khan Spring: P-Kh-S) emerges downstream of the dam site and is the source of drinking water for several villages.  2.2 Geological setting This section outlines the geological characteristics of the study area, which are crucial for understanding its hydrogeological properties. The geological setting encompasses various aspects such as lithostratigraphy and structural geology, both of which play significant roles in influencing groundwater flow and storage. Detailed knowledge of the geological setting provides a foundation for interpreting hydrogeological data and developing conceptual models of groundwater systems. The lithostratigraphic framework describes the different rock layers and their spatial distribution, which is essential for identifying aquifers and confining units. Structural geology, on the other hand, examines the deformation features such as faults and folds that can impact groundwater movement. 2.2.1 Lithostratigraphy According to the geological maps (Figs. 2 and 3   a), the study area is covered by Garau (Gr), Sarvak (Sv1-7), and Gurpi (Gu) formations. Garau Formation (Lower to Middle Cretaceous), with a thickness of 823 m, mainly consists of shale and limestone layers and crops out in low-elevation areas of the Giriveh Anticline. The limestone layers of the Sarvak Formation are the most important rock units in the study area: this formation, between the Garau (at the bottom) and Gurpi (at the top) formations, is categorized as part of the Bangestan Group of Middle Cretaceous age (MSJV, 2017 ). The Sarvak Formation in this area is divided into seven distinct units, numbered from Sv1 to Sv7. This differentiation is mainly based on the presence or absence of marl and shale interbeds and their thickness and on the silica contents (BJVC, 2009b ). The stratigraphical characters of the different units of the Sarvak Formation are listed in Table 1  . The Gurpi Formation (Upper Cretaceous) is comprised of shales and marls with limestone intercalations and has low permeability.  2.2.2 Structural geology The study area is part of the Giriveh-Siah Kuh Duplex-Anticline folded structure. The Giriveh Anticline is thrust by the high-angle reverse fault F1 over the Siah Kuh Anticline, where the dam axis is placed. The Bakhtiari River intersects the northwestern flank of this anticline upstream of the dam gorge. The flanks of the anticline consist of the Sarvak Formation (Sv1–Sv7), whereas its core is in the Garau Formation. Due to the folding of the duplex structure, the Siah Kuh Structure developed as an asymmetrical anticline. The dip angle of its axial plane varies between 60° and 90° to the northeast. Thrusting of the Giriveh Structure over the Siah Kuh Structure along the F1 fault resulted in drag folds in the hanging wall (Garau Formation layers) and chevron fold in the footwall in the Sv3 unit (BJVC, 2010; MPJV, 2018 ). The orientation of all surveyed bedding planes at the dam site indicates that the southwestern limb dips 75° towards the SW (215°), while the northeastern limb dips 50° toward NE (30°) (BJVC, 2009a ). Four major fault systems (F1 to F4) are in the study area (BJVC, 2009b ). The strike of the F1 fault plane is NW−SE with a dip direction towards NE. The dip of the F1 plane moderates gradually upwards. The F2 fault is located adjacent to the boundary between Sv6 and Sv7, about 600 m downstream of the dam site. The F2 is a subvertical NW-SE trending fault with a direction approximately perpendicular to the river, and the fault extends for a long distance on both sides of the river (about 15 km). Field observations and findings from the cores of boreholes indicate that the fault splits into two parallel branches (approximately 30 − 40 m apart and hidden below overburden material). The strike of F3 is NW−SE; the dip of its plane is gentle (less than 10° to 30°) in the upper and lower parts, and steep (more than 60°) in the middle part. Displacements in Saravak Formation units are readily evident along the F3 fault on both sides of the Bakhtiari River (Fig. 3 a). Field observations indicate that F1 and F3 faults merge at the crest of Siah Kuh Anticline on the right side; F1 and F3 show the same displacement direction and therefore have to be considered as the same structure (F1 − F3 fault system). The F4 fault with the SW−NE strike was traced about 1.5 km downstream of the dam site and in the vicinity of Pelle Khan Spring (Fig. 3 a). Its location from the river bed to the F2 fault has been identified and confirmed. In the study area, three sets of joints J1, J2, and J3 can be seen, their maximum aperture is 5 mm, and some of them are filled with calcite (MPJV, 2018 ). Some of the Sarvak Formation layers have locally been folded in the southwestern flank of the Siah Kuh Anticline. These areas are mostly found in the Sv3 unit in the downstream limb of the anticline and Sv7 unit on both riverbanks (Parts of the Sv7 unit near the Pelle Khan Spring) indicated as Kink Band Zones in the geology map (Fig. 3 a). Parts of the marly limestone and siliceous limestone layers of Sv3 in the western flank of the Siah Kuh Anticline are folded in both abutments, around the anticlinal axial plane. These areas are very heterogeneous, messy structures that affect a small part of the Sv2 unit. This disturbed zone is located directly at the contact of Sv3 to the F1 − F3 fault system, the so-called Chevron Fold Zone (Fig. 3 a) (BJVC, 2009a; MPJV, 2018 ).   2.3 Hydrogeological framework The Sarvak Limestone Aquifer is the main aquifer system in the study area. The Bakhtiari River flows over it, and a potential hydraulic connection with the SLA is expected. Recharge of the aquifer occurs as slow percolation, mainly due to rainfall. Surficial point-recharge features (i.e., sinkholes, dolines, and shafts) are not evident in the study areas suggesting limited concentrated recharge occurrences. In the wet season, the flow direction is usually from the aquifer towards the Bakhtiari River, but during the dry season, the direction is reversed, with the river feeding the SLA. Moreover, a wide range of preferential flow paths, as a result of numerous fault and joint systems, are responsible for conveying the groundwater flow. The Pelle Khan Spring is the main discharging point of the SLA. Permeability of Sv1 is considered to be very low, but despite this, a few seasonal low-discharge springs (<1 l/s) emerge along the boundary with the underlying impermeable Garau Formation. Sv2 unit is a marly limestone, with open joints potentially enlarged by dissolution processes. In the Sv3 unit, due to the presence of interbedded siliceous limestone, there is no dissolution potential, but some solutional features like honeycombs, called alveolarization, were reported (BJVC, 2009b ). In the Sv4 unit, significant dissolution occurred at the contact between the marlstones and the pure limestones. Due to the lack of clay or shale in the Sv5 unit, dissolution features are usually observed in this unit. In general, more dissolution features have been reported from Sv4 to Sv6 than other units. On the other hand, the Sv7 unit has meager dissolution potential due to the shaley impurities. Despite the difference and variety of dissolution evidence and lithological characters of the seven units of the Sarvak Formation, overall, this can be considered a calcareous aquifer system. In most regions of Iran, karst has been well developed through the Sarvak Formation (Raeisi and Stevanovic, 2010; Karimi Vardanjani et al., 2017; Mohammadi et al., 2018; Saberi Mehr and Raeisi, 2019; Nassery et al., 2021; Geravand et al., 2022 ). In contrast, the lack of widespread surface karst features in the study area indicates the SLA was mainly affected by intensive tectonic events. The core of thrust faults usually represents the area of greatest strain, characterized by severely deformed materials that significantly decrease both porosity and permeability in comparison to the surrounding damage zone and primary rock (Chester and Logan, 1986; Forster and Evans, 1991; Antonellini et al., 1994; Goddard and Evans, 1995; Billi et al., 2003; Adinehvand and Raeisi, 2018 ). In the cases where brittle rocks are present, numerous fractures and joints are produced in the damage zone, resulting in the possibility of the formation of fractured-rock aquifers (Chester and Logan, 1986; Forster and Evans, 1991; Caine et al., 1996; Isaacs et al., 2007; Bense et al., 2013; Adinehvand and Raeisi, 2018; Leah et al., 2018 ). The high frequency of joints in the study area implies that SLA can be categorized as a fractured-rock and karst aquifer rather than a well-developed karst aquifer. This aquifer stores less water in the rock matrix, which gradually discharges into the joint system. More than ninety percent (90–95 %) of the bedding planes and joints have apertures of less than one millimeter (Haftani et al., 2013 ). The remained discontinuities (less than 10 %) are responsible for local preferential flow paths. Therefore, the SLA in the study area can be considered a fractured-rock and karst aquifer with subordinate presence of karst conduits along its main discontinuities. The only permanent spring in the study area is the Pelle Khan Spring, discharging from the Sv7 unit into the left bank of the Bakhtiari River (Fig. 3 a). The precise amount of the discharge of the Pelle Khan Spring remains unknown because part of the spring water emerges in the river bed. However, based on available field measurements, discharge of the Pelle Khan Spring varies from 50 to about 1800 l/s (WET, 2005 ), reaching its highest value in the middle of the spring season and decreasing sharply in a short period (Fig. 4  ). A catchments area of 109 km2  was estimated for the Pelle Khan Spring based on the water balance calculation. According to outcrops of the Sarvak Formation (Fig. 2 ) and assuming the topographic condition, it seems that a small part of the estimated catchment area (less than 10 %) belongs to the study area around the Bakhtiari Dam site. Therefore, based on the computation of the water balance, the annual discharge volume of Pelle Khan Spring is not supplied by the SLA in the study area but depends on the outcrops of Sarvak Formation in the south-east sector of the F4 fault (Fig. 2 ).  2.4 Available data, measurements, and analysis A wide range of data and measurements, including the results of four tracing tests, 1406 Lugeon tests, water-table measurements in 40 boreholes, spring discharges, river-level measurements, and hydrochemical isotope analyses, were used in this research. The general characteristics of the four dye tracing tests are given in Table 2  . The first and second tests were conducted to investigate the role of the F4 fault in conveying groundwater toward the Pelle Khan Spring and the karst development around the designed Bakhtiari Dam site, respectively (Fig. 5  ) (MSJV, 2015 ). Hydraulic connectivity between upstream and downstream areas of the dam axis, as well as the contribution of the dam construction area in supplying the discharge of Pelle Khan spring, were investigated through the execution of the third and fourth tracing tests (Fig. 5 ) (MPJV, 2020 ). To analyze the rock permeability and flow regime, 1406 water pressure tests (Lugeon test) were performed in 77 boreholes with a wide depth range of 25–310 m (average depth of 104.5 m). Considering the geotechnical conditions in the different boreholes, the length of the Lugeon test intervals varied from 2 to 5 m (BJVC, 2009a ). Field measurements and laboratory analyses were done at different sampling points, including river sections, observation wells, and Pelle Khan Spring, to measure water level fluctuations, spring discharge volumes, and hydrochemical and isotopic sampling. The groundwater level in 40 boreholes and the river level in four sections of the Bakhtiari River were bi-weekly measured with a gauge from 12/4/2018 to 7/28/2022 (Table 3  ). During the third and fourth tracing events (5/16/2021 to 2/17/2022), water levels were not measured due to the unavailability of separate depth gauges for each borehole. Additionally, tracing protocols prevented the use of a common depth gauge for all boreholes. Discharge of Pelle Khan Spring was measured from 5/17/2004 to 3/2/2005 (Fig. 4 ) (WET, 2005 ). Hydrochemical sampling of different water sources was done in two wet (5/12/2019) and dry (10/12/2019) seasons (Table 3 ), and the amounts of the main ions and physico-chemical properties of water (T, pH, EC, TDS, etc.) were measured in the hydrochemistry laboratory at the Shiraz University. In order to ensure precise analysis of the concentrations of total cations and anions, the Charge Balance Error (CBE) was calculated using the equation presented by Domenico and Schwartz (1997) . The calculated CBE was found to be within the acceptable range (±5%). Isotopic sampling (Oxygen-18 and Deuterium) was performed in wet (4/13/2019) and dry (10/12/2019) seasons at several points (Table 3 ), and the samples were sent to the Hydroisotop GmbH laboratory in Germany for analysis.   3 Results and discussion This section presents the findings of the study and integrates them with a comprehensive discussion of their implications. The hydrodynamic characteristics of the SLA, the general groundwater flow direction, and the hydrochemical and isotope signatures observed in the study area are systematically analyzed. These results are critical for understanding the behavior of the SLA as a fractured-rock and karst aquifer. The discussion also introduces the conceptual hydrogeological model of the SLA, highlighting the interactions between geological formations and groundwater flow. By synthesizing the results, we provide insights into the hydrogeological processes governing the SLA. 3.1 Hydrodynamic characteristics of the SLA Geologically, the SLA units react differently to tectonic forces, degree of weathering, and dissolution process, so SLA can be considered a highly heterogeneous media. The Lugeon tests also reveal a broad range of variation (Quiñones-Rozo, 2010 ): the Sv1, Sv5, and Sv6 units mainly (at least in 88 % of the tests) show low to medium hydraulic conductivity, whereas the Sv2, Sv3, Sv4, and Sv7 units have low to high hydraulic conductivity (Table 4  ). As regards Sv4 is more siliceous, thus behaving more brittle than Sv1 to Sv3, it is distinguished as more permeable than Sv1 to Sv3. The wide range of hydraulic conductivity in the Sarvak units (Table 4 ) indicates a mixed regime of groundwater flow, ranging from slow to fast. Also, the analysis of the results of four tracing tests shows the existence of some channels with fast flow in the study area. According to previous studies, the velocities range of fast flow in carbonate aquifers is usually 0.01–1 m/s, while the maximum Darcian velocity for slow groundwater flow is calculated as 1.97 × 10−3  m/s (Gale, 1984 ). In the first tracing test, the groundwater velocity was estimated to range from a minimum of 6.94 × 10−5  m/s (B419 borehole) to a maximum of 6.5 × 10−3  m/s in Pelle Khan Spring. The computed groundwater velocity was relatively higher in the Pelle Khan Spring because the injection borehole (B421) was located on the F4 fault, which functions as a conduit facilitating groundwater flow towards the Pelle Khan Spring. In the second tracing test, the minimum and maximum groundwater velocity were computed in GL423 (2.75 × 10−5  m/s) and Pelle Khan Spring (1.4 × 10−3  m/s), respectively. The movement of the tracer at a velocity of 1.4 × 10−3  m/s toward the Pelle Khan Spring confirms the existence of fast flow in this area, related to the role of the F4 fault in transferring groundwater to the spring. In the other dye detection points (B415, B416, GL409, and GL423), the maximum velocity of groundwater was estimated to be 9.9 × 10−4  m/s. Groundwater velocities on the right and left banks of the Bakhtiari River were estimated to be 1.37 × 10−4  m/s and 3.2 × 10−5  m/s, respectively based on the third and fourth tracing tests. In general, the results of the tracing tests confirm the occurrence of higher velocities along the discontinuities especially major fault systems, where it is possible to develop preferential flow paths. The critical velocity at which laminar flow transitions into turbulent flow is typically identified using the Reynold’s number (Re ) (Ford and Williams, 2007 ). The Reynold’s number is expressed by the following equation:(1) R e  = Vd  â ± ±       in the equation, V  is the mean flow velocity, d  is a characteristic length (conduit diameter or fissure aperture), and ⱱ  is the kinematic viscosity. The critical Reynolds numbers for carbonate aquifers fall between those of granular aquifers and straight manufactured pipes, ranging from 100 to 1000 (Worthington and Soley, 2017 ). By calculating the Reynold’s number based on the velocities obtained from the tracing tests, it is determined that the flow in the study area is predominantly laminar (Table 5  ). However, exceptions exist, notably in the area between injection borehole B29 and Pelle Khan Spring, where groundwater may flow along bedding planes, and in the vicinity of the F4 fault, where turbulent flow is observed. These instances suggest the development of karst conduits in these pathways. A part of the discharge of Pelle Khan Spring emerges below the water level of the Bakhtiari River, making it difficult to obtain precise and regular measurements of the spring flow rate. Despite this challenge, variations in the water level at Borehole TR13 (Fig. 5 ), situated upstream and near the spring outlet, have been monitored. An attempt has been made to obtain useful information about the flow release pattern in the SLA through well hydrograph analysis. By plotting the natural logarithm of water level changes vs. time, two segments of the recession curve of the TR13 hydrograph were determined (Fig. 6  ). The slope of each segment of the recession curve is computed by the following equation (Moore, 1992; Shevenell, 1996; Kovács et al., 2015 ).(2) α = l n H 1  / H 2     ( t 2  - t 1  )       H  , is the water level change, α   is the recession coefficient, and t   is time. A singular slope of recession curve indicates drainage solely from the lower transmissivity matrix. On the other hand, recession curves with two slopes feature an extra, quicker response segment that signifies drainage from the fractures with higher transmissivity and lower specific yield (S y   ) (Shevenell, 1996 ). Despite the proximity of borehole TR13 to the outlet of the Pelle Khan spring, the high heterogeneity within the fractured-rock and karst aquifer means that this borehole may not intersect the main conduit feeding the spring, exhibiting a distinct drainage pattern. The two-segment recession observed in the TR13 hydrograph, characterized by relatively low slopes (Fig. 6 ), is not indicative of drainage from a major karst conduit. Instead, this hydrograph shape might result from the influence of a grid-like conduit pattern.  3.2 General groundwater flow direction Based on water level measurements in 40 observation wells and 4 sections of the Bakhtiari River, the temporal and spatial pattern of groundwater flow in the SLA has been reconstructed. The available data allowed us to identify an almost identical pattern of the general flow direction in the SLA, as shown in Fig. 7  . To investigate the time changes in the water level and the relation between SLA and the river, the hydrograph of the observation wells has been drawn relative to the nearest river level (Fig. 8  a–d). The Bakhtiari River in the study area is the erosion base level and controls the groundwater flow. Comparing the time series of the water level in the boreholes with the nearest gauge from the Bakhtiari River (Fig. 8 a–d) shows that the flow direction changes along the river and during the wet and dry seasons. The infiltration rate from rainfall through the different units of the Sarvak Formation is non-uniform along the river due to the permeability and connectivity of the fracture network hosted within SLA. There are contrasting outcomes about the flow direction: on the right side of the Bakhtiari River, close to the river gauge 1 (R1 in Fig. 7 ), the groundwater flow is from the SLA to the river most of the year. Near gauge R2, in four cases out of the eight boreholes, the direction of groundwater flow is the opposite, but during the flood season, the flow reverses. Considering that the groundwater level of some boreholes (e.g., TR3, B403, and TBH2 in Fig. 8 a and b) is noticeably higher than the river level, the general flow direction in those areas is from the SLA to the river. On the left side, in about all investigated boreholes, the direction of groundwater flow is usually from the river to the SLA, but in some of them, the flow is reversed during the flood season. Drawing the equipotential map in both wet and dry seasons shows that the general direction of the groundwater flow is from the upstream of the dam axis to the downstream (Fig. 7 ). The occurrence of exchange flow between the aquifer and both sides of the river can also be inferred.  3.3 Hydrochemical and isotopic signatures The results of hydrochemical analysis show that EC, as a representative of the total solutes in the water sample, exhibits few changes across the sampling points (Table 6  ). Generally, the EC value is less than 1000 μs/cm in the sampling points, which indicates fresh water. Fig. 9   shows the Piper diagram, where wet and dry seasons were marked in the different sampling points. Most of the samples have calcium-magnesium bicarbonate water type, but the water from the observation wells shows an increase in the relative concentration of sulfate, chlorine, and magnesium ions (Fig. 9 ). The lack of substantial changes in the concentration of dissolved solutes in the samples in both wet and dry seasons indicate the presence of slow flow in the SLA domain. The saturation indices (SI) for calcite and dolomite exceeding 1 indicate that the groundwater within the SLA has a relatively prolonged residence time, sufficient to achieve equilibrium and saturation conditions. This finding is consistent with the expected characteristics of a slow flow regime, as illustrated in Fig. 10  . The similarity of the chemical composition between the different water sources (e.g., Bakhtiari River, observation wells of the SLA, and Pelle Khan Spring) is indicative of the hydraulic connection between the Bakhtiari River and SLA. The magnesium ion (Mg2+ ) is a useful indicator for determining the residence time of water in carbonate aquifers due to the slower dissolution kinetics of dolomite compared to calcite (Bicalho, 2010 ). The (Mg2+ /Ca2+ ) index serves as a valuable parameter capable of indicating the relative distribution of calcite and dolomite within carbonate rock through which groundwater has passed (White, 1988; Vu et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2023 ). The dissolution of dolomite is indicated by a ratio of equivalent concentrations (Mg2+ /Ca2+ ) = 1, while the dissolution of pure calcite is represented by a ratio (Mg2+ /Ca2+ ) = 0. Alternatively, a ratio of (Mg2+ /Ca2+ ) = 0.5 signifies the equilibrium of water with both calcite and dolomite (Vu et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2023 ). The low Mg2+ /Ca2+  ratio in the water samples during the wet season can be attributed to the rapid movement of water from rainfall through fractures in the vadose zone (i.e. short residence time) (Fig. 11  ). Conversely, in the dry season, the slower water movement, attributed to the gradual drainage of the rock matrix and fractures with lower permeability, prolongs the duration of water–rock interaction. Consequently, the ratio of Mg2+ /Ca2+  increases. To classify the isotopic composition of water samples and to identify the relationship between different water sources, the isotopic composition of water samples is shown in Table 7   and plotted in Fig. 12   relative to the Mediterranean Meteoric Water Line (MMWL) and the South Zagros Meteoric Water Line (SZ-MWL) (Heydarizad et al., 2019 ). The samples plotted close to the SZ-MWL (Fig. 12 ) and are distributed around the atmospheric water line in both wet and dry seasons reflecting an atmospheric origin. In addition, no significant effect of evaporation and deviation from the atmospheric water line is observed. The slight disparity in isotopic content observed in groundwater samples between wet and dry seasons suggests a slow flow regime characterized by low groundwater velocity and probably the absence of developed karst conduits in the SLA. The isotopic composition of the samples from the left bank (e.g., GL409 and GL423) and the Pelle Khan Spring are very similar, which can indicate the supply of part of the spring discharge from the left bank of SLA. The relative difference in the isotopic composition of water samples from the right bank and the Pelle Khan Spring (e.g., B210 and DL1R1) suggests a lack of direct hydraulic connectivity with the Pelle Khan Spring. Additionally, the distinct isotopic composition between the Pelle Khan Spring and the Bakhtiari River underscores the minimal contribution of the river to the spring discharge. The isotopic composition of the boreholes on the left bank (GL423 and GL409) and DL1R1 on the right bank is similar to the Bakhtiari River in the dry season, suggesting river water flows toward the SLA (Fig. 12 ). The lack of resemblance in the isotopic composition of borehole B210 and the river can be considered a sign of no flow from the river toward this borehole.  3.4 Introducing the SLA as a fractured-rock and karst aquifer The study area has experienced a long tectonic history, forming a narrow valley produced by the erosional activity of the Bakhtiari River. In the following paragraphs, SLA is examined in terms of the role of the Baktiari River on groundwater flow, characteristics of karst development, and pieces of evidence of the dominant slow flow regime through the fracture-rock-bedding plane network. The Bakhtiari River acts as the erosion base level and controls the groundwater flow in the SLA, mainly flowing toward the river but also in the reverse direction in some sectors. Irrespective of the borehole locations, the excavated Sarvak unit, the depth of excavation below the river level, and the thickness of the overburden at the boreholes, the difference in water level across the SLA amounts to approximately one meter (Fig. 13  ). Additionally, the water level in the SLA fluctuates less than one meter compared to the river level for most of the year. Water levels in boreholes with an overburden from 5 m to 200 m are similar, indicating some degree of dissolution in the overburden limestones and epikarst. The thickness of the limestone layers in the SLA does not exceed 0.2 m, thus the formation of notable karst features, including major conduits, is generally constrained. The presence of impurities within the limestone layers, including clay and thin silica strata, has inhibited the progression of the dissolution process. Available data from the borehole logs provides evidence of the dissolution process on the joint surface and vugs (e.g., at units Sv2–Sv7) and small karst cavities (e.g., at units Sv3–Sv7). As explained in the geological setting of the study area, two parallel thrust faults, numerous joint sets, and fractures are created parallel to the thrust faults, which probably continue to a great depth (Adinehvand and Raeisi, 2018 ). The thrust faults (e.g., F1 and F3) caused substantial displacements in the SLA limestones, likely producing a network of joints acting as a major media in water storage and transfer. The conventional mechanism for the development of karst aquifers includes the recharge and storage of rainfall in the released joints and weathered part of the epikarst and the flow through the major joints at depths within the saturated zone of the aquifer (Palmer 1991, 2007; Ford and Williams, 2007 ). The dissolution process causes an enlargement of the major joints to form karst conduits; consequently, larger conduits are gradually developed at the intersection of joints/faults/bedding planes. In the study area, the dissolution process is driven not only by rainfall but also by exchange flows with the river. The extensive network of joints and fractures provides abundant surfaces for rainfall infiltration, which prevents the accumulation of recharged water within a master joint and the formation of concentrated channel flow of a typical karst aquifer. As a result, rainwater penetrates through extensive networks of deep joints, potentially enlarging them and creating isolated conduits. However, this process offers little opportunity for the formation of major conduits capable of concentrating groundwater flow. The exchange flow between the SLA and the river water as the base level of erosion caused local dissolution in the network of joints and bedding planes. Various geological characteristics observed in the SLA, including numerous stratification boundaries, thin limestone layers with interbedded siliceous and marl impurities, widespread joints and fractures, and the absence of significant point recharge sites, suggest a complex hydrogeological setting. These features, along with the exchange flow between the SLA and the Bakhtiari River serving as the base level of erosion, indicate a fractured-rock and karst aquifer system. Despite the identification of some dissolutional features and fast flow pathways, the evidence does not support the existence of a well-developed karst system. Instead, the slow flow regime in many parts of the SLA, as evidenced by low spatial and temporal fluctuations in groundwater levels and negligible seasonal variations in hydrochemical and isotopic composition, suggests a system characterized by low velocity and long residence time for groundwater. Further research and analysis are warranted to refine our understanding of the hydrogeological processes at play in the SLA.  3.5 Conceptual hydrogeological model of the SLA The Sarvak Formation is defined as an integrated fractured-rock and karst aquifer bounded by the impermeable Garau Formation, the Bakhtiari River, and the F3 and F4 fault systems (Fig. 14  ). Although slow percolation from rainfall mainly occurs in the SLA catchment, the exchange flow between the SLA and the Bakhtiari River partially provides local recharge to some of its sectors. Available results from four dye tracing tests and hydrogeological evidence (Tables 2 and 5 ) suggest that the infiltrating water is transferred slowly through the joint sets and generally conducted through the bedding planes and major faults to move finally toward the Pelle Khan Spring as the main discharging point. The network of joints and multiple beddings prevents the development of channelized flow and karst conduit. However, the F4 fault demonstrated a role in the major flow path of Pelle Khan Spring, acting as a fast flow path (Fig. 14 ).   4 Conclusion An integrated approach, incorporating geological studies (lithological and structural characters), hydrogeological analysis (pressure test, water table variations, and spring discharge measurements), as well as hydrochemical and isotopic signature, alongside dye tracer test results, has been employed to characterize the Sarvak limestone aquifer (SLA) as a part of the under-construction Bakhtiari Dam site. Although the Sarvak limestone formation is potentially susceptible to high dissolution and is known as a karst aquifer in the Zagros zone, the unique hydrogeological condition of the study area prevented the formation of a well-developed karst aquifer. The intersection of intensive faults and joint systems with abundant bedding-plane boundaries, small thickness of limestone layers, and frequent impurities of silica and marl are the major obstacles to developing karst conduits in the SLA. Moreover, numerous joint sets and fractured zones in the vicinity of thrust faults prevent the concentrated flow paths and the development of karst channels. Despite the vast difference in the units of the Sarvak Formation in terms of lithology and permeability, they have formed a unique aquifer, hydraulically connected with the Bakhtiari River as the base of erosion. Evidence such as slight temporal and spatial variation in groundwater level, lack of severe changes in the hydrochemical and isotopic composition of groundwater samples, and the supersaturated state of groundwater with calcite and dolomite suggested a slow flow regime characterized by low groundwater velocity and long residence time in SLA. Moreover, the velocities obtained from the tracing tests were generally low across most paths, indicating a laminar flow regime in the region. Overall, the behavior of SLA is similar to a fractured-rock aquifer, in which water is transferred through a network of joints, only locally enlarged by dissolution, but without indications of developed major conduits. The presence of Pelle Khan karst spring downstream of the study area does not contradict the assertion of weak karst development in this part of the SLA, because only a small portion of the spring's catchment area is within the studied dam area. The results demonstrate that despite the high solubility of carbonate rocks, their karst development may not be considerable and under the influence of extensive joint networks, show a behavior similar to the fractured-rock aquifers. While localized development of karst conduits is possible in such aquifers, overall, the high-density fracture and joint system plays a predominant role in controlling fluid flow dynamics.
1 Introduction With global climate change, extreme weather events and natural hazards presented increasing trends, often linked to global warming (Berg and McColl, 2021; Yuan et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024a ). Drought disasters were recognized as significant environmental hazards (Mishra and Singh, 2010 ), capable of causing substantial economic losses worldwide (Wilhite et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2020 ). Many studies have consistently demonstrated an increasing trend in drought intensity and frequency (Cook et al., 2018; Pokhrel et al., 2021 ), potentially leading to even more significant losses in the future (Hasegawa et al., 2021 ). Given China's diverse climates, topographies, and vegetation types (Ding et al., 2021b; He et al., 2017 ), understanding the factors influencing drought, including climate, topography, and vegetation (Han et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2018a ), and their varied impacts across different regions remain a challenge (Wang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2022 ). Hence, this study investigated how various factors contribute to drought in China. Drawing upon the categorization by Mishra and Singh (2010) , drought was commonly classified into meteorological, agricultural, hydrological, and socioeconomic types (Cai et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2018; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020 ). Meteorological drought typically arises from a lack of PRE over a region (Mishra and Singh, 2010 ), while hydrological drought is linked to surface and subsurface water resources and runoff (Mishra and Singh, 2010 ). Agricultural drought could be explained as declining and maintaining a low level over time (Sun et al., 2023 ). Socioeconomic drought encompassed the economic, social, and environmental impacted resulting from a period of drought or inadequate water resources (Shi et al., 2018 ). Drought conditions were often characterized using drought indices (Mishra and Singh, 2010; Wang et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2021 ), with meteorological, hydrological, and agricultural drought typically assessed using the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), Standardized Runoff Index (SRI), and Standardized Soil Moisture Index (SSMI) (Han et al., 2021; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2021 ). Drought studies have widely used these indices (Mishra and Singh, 2010; Xu et al., 2018 ). Numerous studies have investigated the influencing factors of drought (Ding et al., 2021a; Zhang et al., 2022 ). For example, Zhang et al. (2022)  found that agricultural drought in eastern China was mainly influenced by soil moisture (SM) and temperature. Huang et al. (2015)  suggested that large-scale atmospheric circulation and local landscape conditions impacted the propagation from agricultural to meteorological drought in the Weihe River Basin of China. Ding et al. (2021a)  analyzed the relative importance of evapotranspiration (ET), precipitation (PRE), and SM in hydrological and agricultural drought in China. Swain et al. (2022)  investigated hydroclimatic, physiographic, and socioeconomic factors affecting comprehensive drought in the Narmada River Basin of India. These influencing factors can be categorized into direct and indirect factors affecting drought (Guo et al., 2023 ). Direct driving factors were variables used directly for drought evaluation and monitoring (Zhang et al., 2022 ), while indirect driving factors indirectly influence the variables used for drought evaluation (Nanzad et al., 2019 ). For example, PRE and ET were direct driving factors used to evaluate and monitor meteorological drought (Sun et al., 2023 ), while specific humidity, SM, and temperature can influence PRE and ET, thereby indirectly affecting meteorological drought (Wei et al., 2024 ). Moreover, some driving factors exhibited dynamic changes, such as TEM, SM, and PRE (Huang et al., 2015; Mishra and Singh, 2010; Swain et al., 2022 ). The degree of influence of driving factors might dynamically change over time, depending on the dynamic nature of these factors. Therefore, this study was essential to quantify the dynamic impact of both direct and indirect driving factors on different types of droughts. Previous studies have primarily focused on various aspects of drought, including drought propagation (Ding et al., 2021b ), drought characteristics (Yao et al., 2018a ), and the impact and risk of drought disasters (Hasegawa et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2022 ). Understanding the essence and mechanisms of drought change can be achieved through investigating its driving factors (Ding et al., 2021a; Huang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2022 ). Several methods, such as Lindeman–Merenda–Gold, correlation coefficient, and wavelet analysis, have been used to quantify the impact degree of factors on drought in previous studies (Ding et al., 2021a; Huang et al., 2015; Nanzad et al., 2019 ). However, both correlation coefficient and wavelet analysis methods had limitations in providing the relative importance of multiple factors to drought (Huang et al., 2015; Puth et al., 2015 ). The Lindeman–Merenda–Gold method faced challenges in accurately quantifying the degree of impact of factors in the presence of multicollinearity (Gromping, 2006; Hu et al., 2022 ). Advanced techniques, such as Random Forest, offered a solution to these issues by accurately determining the relative importance of various influencing factors on drought (Breiman, 2001; Wei et al., 2024 ). Additionally, using regional averages to represent characteristics of entire regions might overlook spatial differences in factors and drought, thereby hindering comparisons of factors driving drought changes (Wei et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2023 ). Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the relative importance of driving factors to drought using the advanced Random Forest method and grid cells as spatial units in China. Energy played a crucial role in driving water movement in the soil–plant–atmosphere continuum system (Xun et al., 2022 ). Meanwhile, drought was influenced by various factors (Mishra and Singh, 2010; Swain et al., 2022 ). We hypothesized that the relative importance of driving factors might dynamically change with climate change over time. Therefore, this study sought to verify this hypothesis using extensive time series data. The primary objectives of this study were as follows: (1) to evaluate the accuracy and reliability of the drought monitoring variables provided by reanalysis data. (2) to reveal the relative importance of direct and indirect driving factors for different types of droughts and to investigate spatial differences in the relative importance of driving factors across different regions. (3) to investigate the dynamic change characteristics of the relative importance of driving factors with climate change. This study aimed to expand the current understanding of the formation and evolution of drought phenomena. Furthermore, by elucidating the spatiotemporal dynamics of key climatic drivers, this research aimed to provide an enhanced scientific basis for drought monitoring and prediction. The insights gained might inform the development of targeted adaptation strategies to build resilience against future droughts exacerbated by climate change.  2 Data and methods 2.1 Study area China is located in East Asia, spanning from 3°51′N to 53°33′N latitude and 73°29′E to 135°04′E longitude, covering an approximate land area of 9.63 million km2  (Ding et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2018b ). Generally, In China, the three-terrace topography generally refers to the division of the landscape based on elevation and topography from west to east (Yao et al., 2018b ), as shown in Fig. 1  a. The first level of terrace topography primarily includes the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and the Qaidam Basin. The first level of terrace topography boasts an average elevation of approximately 4,000 m (Zhang et al., 2023 ). Numerous rivers originate from the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, including the Brahmaputra River, Nu River, and Jinsha River. Additionally, the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers also find their sources in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (Li et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023 ). The second level of terrace topography predominantly comprises the Inner Mongolia Plateau, Loess Plateau, Alxa Plateau, Yun-Gui Plateau, Dzungaria Basin, Sichuan Basin, and Tarim Basin. The average elevation of the second level of terrace topography ranges between 1,000 and 2,000 m (Ding et al., 2021c ). The primary rivers within this level comprise the upstream Yangtze River, midstream Yellow River, and upstream Pearl River. The third level of terrace topography primarily consists of the Northeast Plain, North China Plain, and Middle-Lower Yangtze Plain. The average elevation of the third level of terrace topography ranges between 200 and 1,000 m (Koch et al., 2020 ). The main mountain ranges include the Greater and Lesser Khingan Mountains, Changbai Mountains, and Southeast Hills. The primary rivers include the downstream sections of the Yangtze River, Yellow River, and Pearl River, as depicted in Fig. 1 a. The study areas' subregions were delineated based on climatic, vegetation, land cover, and topographic characteristics (Sun et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2018a; Yao et al., 2018b ), as detailed in Table 1  . Subregion 1 had a large desert area and was located in the temperate zone of China. Subregion 1 was defined as the temperate and warm-temperate desert of northwest China (Liu et al., 2023b ). Subregion 1 mainly included the Alxa Plateau, Dzungaria Basin, and Tarim Basin. Subregion 2 had a large area of grassland and was located in the temperate zone of China (Cai et al., 2021 ). Subregion 2 was defined as the temperate grassland of Inner Mongolia. Subregion 3 exhibited extensive subhumid and warm-temperate climate characteristics. Subregion 3 was defined as the temperate humid and sub-humid northeast China. Both subregion 4 and subregion 5 were situated within subtropical climate zones (Koch et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020 ). Subregion 4 was defined as the warm-temperate humid and sub-humid north China. Subregion 5 was defined as the subtropical humid central and south China. The Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau and Qaidam Basin were combined into subregion 6 which was defined as the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau. Subregion 7 had tropical humid climate characteristics (Zhou et al., 2021 ) and it was defined as the tropical humid south China, as shown in Fig. 1 b.  2.2 Datasets 2.2.1 Observation and simulation data Meteorological observation data were acquired from the National Meteorological Information Centre, utilizing data from 826 meteorological stations within the study zones (https://data.cma.cn/en ). Meteorological observation data comprised daily measurements of precipitation (PRE), temperature (TEM), near surface wind speed (WS), relative humidity, and duration of sunshine, derived from station observations. The meteorological observation data encompassed daily records from stations spanning the period from 1961 to 2017. These data were utilized to calculate potential evapotranspiration (PET) using the Penman–Monteith method in this study (Allen et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2021 ). The computed PET values from the observation data were employed to evaluate and compare the performance of the reanalysis product dataset. Meteorological observation data have been widely utilized in various studies, including research on precipitation (Yao et al., 2018b ) and drought characteristics (Sun et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2018 ). Soil moisture (SM) observation data were obtained from the Hydrological Monitor and Forecast Center, Ministry of Water Resources of the People's Republic of China. SM observation data were compiled and organized by Wang and Shi (2021) . The observational SM dataset provided monthly SM observation data in different layers of depth (10 cm, 20 cm, 50 cm, 70 cm, and 100 cm) from 732 observation sites across China spanning the period from 1992 to 2013. The observational SM dataset employed the gravimetric method (Zhou et al., 2023a ) to measure SM in the study areas. The SM dataset was used to compare and evaluate the performance of the reanalysis product dataset in this study. The Land-Climate Dynamics group of the Institute for Atmospheric and Climate Science developed the runoff dataset with Global Runoff Reconstruction (GRUN 1.0) (Ghiggi et al., 2019 ). This study used the GRUN dataset to compare runoff with ERA-5. GRUN could provide runoff data globally from 1902 to 2014 with monthly and 0.5°×0.5° spatiotemporal resolution. This observational runoff data was obtained from 35,002 streamflow stations worldwide. The GRUN dataset was selected as spatiotemporally continuous observation runoff data, which is challenging to obtain in this study area (Ding et al., 2021b ). GRUN has also been widely utilized in numerous related studies (Ding et al., 2021a; Ding et al., 2021b ).  2.2.2 Reanalysis product dataset ERA5 was the fifth-generation product of atmospheric reanalysis for the global climate, provided by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (Jiang et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2021 ). ERA5 provided monthly PRE, PET, SM, RO, bare soil evapotranspiration (BSET), vegetation canopy evapotranspiration (VCET), subsurface runoff (SUBRO), surface runoff (SURRO), Temperature (TEM), Near surface wind speed (WS), and Soil moisture (SM) data over China. The corresponding full names and abbreviations of variable can be referred to Table 2  . The ERA5 dataset had a spatial resolution of 0.1° × 0.1° grid cells and a monthly temporal resolution. The ERA5 reanalysis dataset covers the time series from 1950 to 2022, combining weather model simulations with observational data from satellites and ground sensors. (Jiang et al., 2023 ) (https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/CKB/ERA5-Land ). The PRE, TEM, and WS from ERA5 were obtained through observations from radar, satellites, and rain gauges. The SM data in ERA5 was derived from the uppermost soil layer, integrating satellite observations and meteorological constraints such as temperature and humidity during the data production process. (Luo et al., 2021 ). ERA5 data have been widely used in related studies (Wu et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2021 ). In this study, ERA5 data offered higher-quality, spatiotemporally continuous datasets compared to station data, facilitating a more comprehensive investigation into drought characteristics (Zhou et al., 2021 ). Specific humidity (SH) was provided by Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS). Noah Land Surface Model L4 drove and produced 0.25° × 0.25° grid cells of spatial resolution and a monthly temporal resolution. We used bilinear interpolation method to change spatial resolution into 0.1° × 0.1° grid cells (Wang et al., 2018 ). GLDAS dataset have also been widely used in related studies (Han et al., 2023; Koch et al., 2020 ).   2.3 Methodology 2.3.1 Drought index In this study, meteorological drought, hydrological drought, and agricultural drought were characterized using the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) (Ding et al., 2021a ), Standardized Runoff Index (SRI) (Li et al., 2020 ), and Standardized Soil Moisture Index (SSMI) (Han et al., 2021 ). The SPEI, derived from the water deficit calculated using the water balance equation (PRE-PET) over a defined period (Ding et al., 2021a; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2014 ), used PRE and PET as drought monitoring variables for meteorological drought. The PET, estimated using the Penman-Monteith method based on meteorological observation data, was used to compute the SPEI in this study (Allen et al., 2006 ). The SPEI, obtained through a log-logistic probability distribution of the water deficit difference between PRE and PET, was well-established in drought-related research, with detailed grading explained by various studies (Ding et al., 2021a; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2014; Yao et al., 2018a ). The SRI, calculated from runoff (RO) time series, was subjected to a log-normal distribution. In this context, RO served as the drought monitoring variable for hydrological drought. Similar to the SPEI, the SRI has been widely used in drought-related studies, with detailed grading explained in several investigations (Ding et al., 2021b; Zhou et al., 2023b; Zhou et al., 2021 ). In many studies, SRI was used to investigate drought propagation (Ding et al., 2021b ), drought risk evaluation (Zhou et al., 2023b ), and analysis of drought change trends (Ding et al., 2021a ). The SSMI was derived from the SM time series (Han et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2017 ). In this study, the uppermost-layer SM from ERA5 was used for SSMI computation due to its reliance on satellite and ground observations, which potentially offer greater reliability and accuracy compared to the deep soil simulating SM of ERA5 (Jiang et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023b ). SM was defined as the drought monitoring variable for agricultural drought:(1) S S M I = S M - S M  ¯    σ      where SM was the time series of soil moisture in a period. S M  ¯      and σ    were the average value and standard deviation of the time series of soil moisture, respectively.  2.3.2 Classification of direct and indirect driving factors Based on the hydrological cycle processes, we categorized the direct and indirect driving factors of various droughts, as illustrated in Table 2 . Meteorological drought was evaluated using PRE and evapotranspiration (Wang et al., 2023a ). In this study, PRE, bare soil evapotranspiration (BSET), and vegetation canopy evapotranspiration (VCET) were identified as direct driving factors for meteorological drought (Yang et al., 2021 ). Consequently, PRE, BSET, and VCET were classified as direct driving factors for meteorological drought. Furthermore, temperature (TEM), specific humidity (SH), near-surface wind speed (WS), and SM were recognized as indirect driving factors, as they influence evapotranspiration, thereby affecting meteorological drought (Yang et al., 2021 ). Hydrological drought was computed using RO (Zhou et al., 2021 ), making subsurface runoff (SUBRO) and surface runoff (SURRO) direct driving factors for hydrological drought. PRE is the primary water source for both RO and SM (Zhang et al., 2019 ). Moreover, BSET, VCET, TEM, SH, WS, and SM influence evapotranspiration, affecting shallow SM and subsequently impacting hydrological drought. The fluctuation in SM directly impacts water movement in the soil, such as infiltration and SURRO, thereby influencing the process of RO generation (Luo et al., 2021 ). Consequently, PRE, BSET, VCET, TEM, SH, WS, and SM were categorized as indirect driving factors for hydrological drought. Agricultural drought was evaluated using SM (Wu et al., 2023 ). PRE, BSET, VCET, TEM, SH, and WS were identified as indirect driving factors for agricultural drought, influencing water input and output. Thus, PRE, BSET, VCET, TEM, SH, and WS were classified as indirect driving factors for agricultural drought. Many studies have divided long time series into multiple periods to investigate changes in specific patterns (Ding et al., 2021c; Wu et al., 2023 ). In this study, we aim to divide the long time series into multiple periods to explore the dynamic changes in the influence of driving factors on drought. Nanzad et al. (2019)  used data from 2000 to 2016 to examine the relationship between vegetation drought monitoring and climate factors. A dataset spanning over ten years may reveal the relationship between driving factors and the trend of drought variations during that period (Han et al., 2023; Nanzad et al., 2019 ). Therefore, we divided the time into different segments with a timestep of fifteen years, resulting in five periods: Period I (1950–1964), Period II (1965–1979), Period III (1980–1994), Period IV (1995–2008), and Period V (2009–2022). Each time spans more than ten years, enabling examining the impact of driving factors on drought.  2.3.3 Random Forest method Random Forest is an ensemble learning algorithm (Breiman, 2001; Han et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023a; Wei et al., 2024 ). Breiman (2001)  elucidated that the framework of a Random Forest comprises a combination of tree predictors, with each tree depending on the values of a random vector and sharing the same distribution within the forest. The generalization error of a forest of tree classifiers is influenced by both the strength of the individual trees and the correlation among them. The Random Forest algorithm employs bootstrap aggregating and the random subspace method to select samples and features (Wei et al., 2024 ). When constructing the decision tree, each node randomly selects and splits the feature subset based on the optimal feature subset (Wei et al., 2024 ). Random Forest finds application in prediction (Breiman, 2001; Liu et al., 2023a ) and determining variable weights (Han et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2024 ). In this study, we used the Random Forest method to assess the degree of relative importance of the driving factors (RID) in drought. The weight of each driving factor was calculated using the Random Forest method (Han et al., 2023 ), with the weighting proportion of each driving factor contributing to the aggregate weighting defined as RID in this study (Ding et al., 2021b ). We will compare RID of each grid's driving factors; the driving factor with the highest RID will be designated as the primary driver factor.  2.3.4 Statistical metrics In this study, the correlation coefficient and Normalized Root Mean Squared Error (NRMSE) was used to evaluate the performance of ERA5 (Jiang et al., 2023 ). The correlation coefficient and NRMSE were widely employed to evaluate simulation results of model and product datasets, such as Jiang et al. (2023)  and Yang et al. (2021) . The least squares method was used to fit the slope and analyze the changing trend of the driving factors (Ding et al., 2020 ).(2) N R M S E = ∑ i = 1  n  ( P i  - O i  )  2   n    · 1 O avg        Where Pi   and Oi   were the i th predicted and observed values, respectively, Oavg   was the observed mean value, and n was the number of time scales.    3 Results 3.1 Statistical assessment and trend analysis of drought monitoring variables 3.1.1 Statistical assessment of ERA5 The accuracy and reliability of PRE, PET, SM, and RO were evaluated by observational data. Several studies have also evaluated product data performance in China (Jiang et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2023 ). Some studies have indicated that ERA5 PRE products exhibit relatively poor performance in daily and extreme precipitation compared to alternative PRE products, such as Integrated Multi-satellite Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement, Climate Prediction Center, and Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission Multi-Satellite Precipitation Analysis (Jiang et al., 2023 ). However, ERA5 PRE products have performed similarly to simulating monthly PRE with the products above (Jiang et al., 2023 ). Since this study used monthly PRE products from ERA5, the relatively poor performance of ERA5 in daily and extreme PRE might have a minimal impact on investigating drought monitoring variables. Guo et al. (2022)  highlighted the value levels and spatial characteristics of monthly ET biases among different products across China, consistent with the results of ERA5 in this study. Yu et al. (2023)  demonstrated that the SM products of ERA5 exhibited superior performance and greater potential than many products for application in Central Asia. Figs. 2 and 4  illustrate that drought monitoring variables displayed lower bias levels in the study zones. Moreover, this study primarily focuses on dynamic changes in drought monitoring variables, where the correlation coefficient may be more critical than the Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE) (Ding et al., 2021b; Zhou et al., 2021 ). From Figs. 3 and 4 , we observe that the correlation coefficient also demonstrated higher levels within the study zones. Furthermore, ERA5 boasted higher spatial resolution, better spatiotemporal continuity, and an updated status of the latest available data (Jiang et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2023b ). Therefore, ERA5 proves to be a highly suitable data product for this study. The ERA5 product dataset typically acquires observational data from satellites, sensors, and ground measurement equipment (Jiang et al., 2023 ). Various interpolation algorithms and models have been used to fill the missing values of global spatiotemporal observations in grid cells (Guo et al., 2022; Qian et al., 2023 ). Observational data from ground measurement equipment are used to correct biases between simulation and ground observation results (Jiang et al., 2021 ). Hence, biases in ERA5 products' drought monitoring variables could stem from observational equipment, simulation methods, and the quality of simulation result correction (Qian et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2023 ). From Fig. 4 , we observe that PRE and SM in subregion 7 exhibit more significant biases than in other subregions. Arid climates and extensive desert areas may impact ERA5 simulations and satellite observations, respectively (Ding et al., 2021b; Yao et al., 2018b ). Additionally, Fig. 4 d illustrates that SM and RO display more significant biases in subregion 6 than in the other subregions. Glacier melting snow and permafrost may affect the accuracy of simulations in subregion 6 (Wang et al., 2023b ). Moreover, the limited number of ground-observation stations may not provide sufficient data to correct simulation results in subregion 6 (Jiang et al., 2021 ).  4.2 Spatial differences of driving factors impacting the different types of droughts Our investigation primarily delved into analyzing the importance of various driving factors for drought across each grid cell building based on the findings presented in Section 3.2 . Our study revealed that BSET and PRE exhibited higher importance for meteorological drought in subregions 1, 2, 3, and 6, as depicted in Fig. 7 . Feng et al. (2024)  identified that arid-semiarid regions in China predominantly encompassed northwestern China, the Inner Mongolian Plateau, the North China Plain, the Northeast Plain, and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, which largely overlap with subregions 1, 2, 3, and 6 (Feng et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2018b ). Consequently, BSET and PRE may demonstrate greater significance for meteorological drought in regions characterized by arid-semiarid conditions. Additionally, we observed that BSET played a primary role in meteorological drought within sparse grassland and desert areas of subregions 1 and 6 (Ding et al., 2022; He et al., 2017 ). Lower vegetation canopy coverage in these regions may limit the influence and importance of VCET for meteorological drought. Consistent with Zhuang et al. (2024)  observations, our study suggests that soil evaporation has a more significant contribution than vegetation evaporation to ET, particularly in regions such as the Three Rivers Source region of the Tibetan Plateau. Additionally, VCET displayed higher importance for meteorological drought in subregions 3, 5, and 7, potentially influenced by high vegetation canopy coverage and adequate precipitation promoting VCET while limiting the significance of PRE (Ma et al., 2023; Sahaar and Niemann, 2020 ). Human irrigation practices may also restrict the importance of PRE for meteorological drought in the North China Plain, as suggested by research from Koch et al. (2020)  and Xu et al. (2023) . Our study also investigated the importance of indirect driving factors on meteorological drought. We found that SM and VCET were the primary driving factors for meteorological drought in southern China, potentially influenced by vegetation coverage and maximum rooting depth (Sahaar and Niemann, 2020 ). Generally, SM levels were higher in southern China than in the north (Cai et al., 2021; Wang and Shi, 2021 ), and VCET might be influenced by SM in regions with high vegetation coverage, thus playing a significant role in meteorological drought (Ma et al., 2023 ). Additionally, our findings revealed PRE as the primary driving factor in northwestern and southern China. At the same time, SM exhibited primary importance in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, eastern Inner Mongolian Plateau, and northeastern China. These spatial patterns align with the arid, humid, and semiarid characteristics of these regions (Feng et al., 2024; Li et al., 2017 ). Moreover, our investigation identified BSET, VCET, and TEM as primary driving factors influencing agricultural drought across most regions of China. These factors play crucial roles in ET processes (Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2019 ), consistent with the findings of Guo et al. (2023) . Furthermore, our study corroborates the dominant role of PRE in agricultural drought in northwestern China, as highlighted by Guo et al. (2023) . In terms of drought propagation, our findings suggest that meteorological drought may influence the propagation of agricultural and hydrological drought through water input and output processes. TEM, PRE, and SM play significant roles in controlling the input, output, and terrestrial water storage, respectively, impacting the propagation from meteorological to agricultural and hydrological drought across China. These conclusions align with previous studies (Ding et al., 2021a; Han et al., 2023; Li et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024b ). Furthermore, as detailed in Section 3.3 , the RID of direct and indirect driving factors exhibited spatiotemporal dynamic changes concerning drought across different subregions. As a complex system, climate change, the hydrological cycle, and human activities have impacted drought over a long time series and in large regions (Abbott et al., 2019; Pokhrel et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2023 ). Our study found that the RID of driving factors demonstrated dynamic changes across different periods and subregions. Changes in certain driving factors within the complex drought system can impact and alter other driving factors, resulting in dynamic changes in RID (Pokhrel et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2023b ). For instance, the relationship between certain driving factors exhibited negative dynamic changes, such as PRE and BSET for meteorological drought in subregion 3, TEM and SM for meteorological drought in subregion 2, and PRE and SM for hydrological drought in subregions 1 and 2.  4.3 Limitations and prospects In this study, our work has some limitations. We used ERA5 and GLDAS reanalysis datasets to investigate the mechanisms and degrees of driving factors affecting different droughts. We used reanalysis datasets due to the challenge of acquiring station observation data that could adequately meet the high spatial resolution requirements of our research. Many studies have also used reanalysis datasets to evaluate and monitor drought (Cai et al., 2021; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2022 ). Additionally, we used station observation data to evaluate the accuracy and reliability of the reanalysis datasets. However, while river discharge was monitored by some hydrological stations (Zheng et al., 2019 ), RO change was observed by very limited ground monitoring data. Therefore, we compared RO between the GRUN and ERA5 datasets. RO data in this study limited the reliability of hydrological drought assessment. As stated in the introduction, the research thoroughly investigated the dynamic impact of driving factors on drought. However, the study did not investigate the degree of impact of certain dynamic driving factors, such as atmospheric circulation factors (Guo et al., 2023 ). Atmospheric circulation may influence droughts with teleconnection patterns (Ding et al., 2021b ). The relationship between atmospheric circulation factors and drought could be an interesting area for future research. Furthermore, this study did not analyze the roles and effects of driving factors in the process of drought propagation (Guo et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024b; Zhou et al., 2023b ). Exploring causal relationships could enhance our understanding of the mechanisms behind drought propagation involving driving factors. This area holds potential as an intriguing avenue for future research. Moreover, field observations and validation experiments in small-scale areas help enhance the reliability of analysis results in more significant regions (Allen et al., 2006; Sahaar and Niemann, 2020 ). However, this study lacks field observation experiments to validate conclusions at a large regional scale. Therefore, it is necessary to supplement field observation experiments to validate and improve the reliability of the research results in future studies.   5 Conclusions This study investigated the spatial distribution and dynamic changes of RID of driving factors associated with various types of droughts using ERA5 data from 1950 to 2020. The performance of ERA5 drought monitoring variables was evaluated, and their change trends were analyzed across China. Meteorological, hydrological, and agricultural droughts were described using the SPEI, SRI, and SSMI. The Random Forest method was employed to quantify the RID of driving factors to droughts. Simulation results were evaluated using the correlation coefficient and NRMSE. Additionally, the importance of direct and indirect driving factors was analyzed for spatial distribution characteristics and differences in subregions across China. The main findings were as follows:(1) The drought monitoring variables of ERA5 demonstrated great performance compared to observational data across the study zones. However, drought monitoring variables exhibited relatively poor performance in subregion 1, with the SM correlation coefficient showing a lower level than other drought monitoring variables across China. PRE and RO exhibited similar spatial distribution characteristics of change tendency across China.  (2) In subregions 1, 2, and 3, BSET and PRE had higher RID for meteorological drought, while SUBRO exhibited higher RID in influencing subregions 3, 4, and 5, and SURRO showed higher RID in influencing subregion 1. BSET and PRE played crucial roles in meteorological drought in northern China, while VCET was essential in hydrological drought in southern China and the North China Plain. For meteorological drought, a significant proportion of areas had SM and TEM as primary driving factors. In contrast, areas with PRE and TEM as primary driving factors for agricultural drought were relatively large. Similarly, areas with PRE and SM as primary driving factors for hydrological drought were relatively large across China.  (3) The RID of direct and indirect driving factors demonstrates dynamic changes across various drought types in different subregions of China. In most subregions, contrasting dynamic changes between PRE and BSET were observed for meteorological drought. Meanwhile, the RID of WS showed a lower level for hydrological drought across various subregions. Different indirect driving factors exhibited similar RID for agricultural drought in various subregions.
1 Introduction Water quality prediction can provide early warnings and assess the impact of various factors on a river’s water quality (Visser et al., 2022 ). This allows decision-makers to take effective measures to mitigate pollution in advance, make rational water resource decisions, and evaluate the risks of strategies (Pathak et al., 2021 ). Especially in river delta areas with intensive human activities, concentrative urban agglomeration, rich industries, and large pollutant emissions, the impacts of climate changes and human activities on water quality are extremely complicated. Also, various influencing factors have complex interrelationships, which further affect water quality and pose significant challenges to water environmental management (Romic et al., 2020 ). Therefore, accurate water quality prediction can be an effective tool to quantify the interaction of these factors and provide adaptive measures for decision-makers (Fu et al., 2020; Maguire et al., 2016 ). Existing water quality prediction approaches mainly include water quality simulation models such as environmental fluid dynamics code (EFDC) (Irby et al., 2016; Vincon-Leite and Casenave, 2019 ), and data-driven models such as long short-term memory (LSTM) (Liang et al., 2020; Wan et al., 2022 ). Recently, the data-driven model has become a popular method due to its high efficiency and low computational requirements. Many scholars have made attempts and obtained satisfactory prediction results (Xiong et al., 2022; Zanoni et al., 2022 ). Data-driven models require many long-time series water quality monitoring data. Changes in several variables do not reflect the influence of human activities and climate change on the migration mechanism of water quality in rivers. The prediction results make it difficult to provide adaptive measures for water quality management. Water quality simulation models can address these problems (Noori et al., 2020; Zou et al., 2014 ), which is applicable in practice (Peng et al., 2020 ).
