However, in real rivers, it is difficult to monitor pollution sources due to the randomness and complexity of enterprise emissions (Ahmed et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2023 ). Accordingly, the pollution sources with uncertainty cannot be accurately obtained (Tan et al., 2011 ). Meanwhile, simulation models encounter uncertainty in parameter estimation during the calibration and validation process (Park et al., 2020 ). This makes it challenging for models to obtain accurate predictions. To address the issue of insufficient data, previous scholars have developed inverse methods to identify the parameters of the model and pollution sources, including groundwater (Boano et al., 2005; Michalak and Kitanidis, 2003; Neupauer et al., 2000 ), conventional pollution (Liang et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2014 ), and sudden pollution (Shao et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2019a; Zeunert and Meon, 2020 ). Among them, the integration of inverse methods, water quality models, and Bayesian inferential methods has become an effective approach for its capability to predict the frequency, which has provided more information on uncertainty. These methods combine existing expert knowledge and experience through prior distributions to produce more accurate estimates (Neuman et al., 2012 ). For example, Liu et al. (2008b)  used Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) in the distributed-source model to backward estimate first-order decay rate (ki  ) and annual pollutant loading for biological oxygen demand (BOD) and ammonia (NH4 + ). Zhao et al. (2014)  reversely estimated seasonal loading and decay rate (k ) for ammonia by combining MCMC with an ordinary one-dimensional water quality model. Shao et al. (2021)  developed a stochastic source identification model that couples Bayesian inference with SWMM to identify the unknown source parameters in an instantaneous dumping event. However, these methods are inadequate for decision-makers to devise countermeasures swiftly, because the computational costs and durations are excessively protracted, and the intricate mechanistic processes of river networks are not fully captured. Their detailed advantages and disadvantages are shown in Table 1  . Efficient and practical methods to address the above deficiencies still relatively few. Among them, MCMC requires the construction of a Markov chain to obtain a stable posterior probability of sample convergence, which tends to consume more computational resources, especially when combined with complex models such as SWMM. The concept of GLUE in Bayesian methods is relatively simplicity, which defines a likelihood objective function and avoids complex integration operations to calculate the posterior distribution of parameters (Thorndahl et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2020 ). This approach requires minimal modeling skills and is easy to implement (Dotto et al., 2012; Reynolds et al., 2017 ). Additionally, the water quality analysis simulation program (WASP) can simulate the impacts of human activities and climate change on multiple indicators by considering the processes and interactions of pollutants (Chueh et al., 2021; Liang et al., 2015 ). It is more suitable than ordinary one-dimensional models to simulate river network areas with poor exchangeability, weak self-cleaning ability, and severe water pollution (Zhao et al., 2014 ). Compared to complicated models (e.g., SWMM and EFDC), it requires less data (e. g, topographic map) and is more convenient to operate (Bouchard et al., 2017; Lai et al., 2011 ). Therefore, to address the limitations, combining WASP, general likelihood uncertainty estimation (GLUE), and inverse method into multiple parameters and pollution sources inverse estimation method (MPSIE), which can not only quantify the uncertainty range of parameters, but also provide efficient calculations considering complex nonlinear mechanisms processes. It has the advantage of effectively revealing the main driving factors of complex river systems and dealing with uncertainty under limited data, which can improve the reliability of predictions. Moreover, the water quality process with intensive human activities is strongly influenced by multiple factors such as water projects, pollution emissions, and climate change. Many scholars have demonstrated these impacts using water quality simulation models (Noori et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2019 ). For example, Liu et al. (2014)  analyzed the water quality effects of driving forces, including watershed nutrient loading, flow of water diversion projects, and lake water level. Zou et al. (2014)  proved that the water quality response to water diversion demonstrates clear spatial and temporal variabilities. Zeng et al. (2020)  designed the impact of factors including the point source, the non-point source, and water transfer. However, previous studies focused on water quality response to water diversions which have been constructed to transfer clean water to rivers (Tang et al., 2021; Xiao et al., 2021; Zeng et al., 2015; Zou et al., 2014 ). Studies on the impacts of multiple water intakes (WIs) on river networks are relatively slim. The way people draw water from rivers, such as the South-to-North Water Diversion Project (Wang et al., 2016 ), has not only reduced the water volume but also affected the water quality of the river. Thus, WIs have a greater impact on rivers than water diversions. It is necessary to assess whether adjusting multiple WIs has a positive or negative impact. Additionally, the combined impacts of WIs, human pollution sources, and climate changes under uncertainty on the water quality of river networks remain much unclear. Understanding the impacts is important to help obtain practical management measures. However, the previous uncertainty prediction models only forecasted the probabilities of water quality separately, without considering the impact of future climate change uncertainty (Guo et al., 2022; Peng et al., 2020 ). Climate change-induced streamflow prediction is subject to significant uncertainty of randomness, which can greatly affect simulation output of water quality prediction (Mailhot and Duchesne, 2010; Xu et al., 2020; Zahraeifard and Deng, 2012 ). It is important to quantify these to achieve reliable medium and short-term predictions. Compared to the long-term result of general circulation models (GCMs), the Markov-Chain (MC) model can analyze runoff sequence data to calculate the interval values and their corresponding probability, rather than specific values, which could improve the credibility (Jin et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022b ). Additionally, the algorithm is simple with high accuracy. Therefore, to gain reliable predictions and efficient improvement measures, this is the first attempt based on the MPSIE method to combine MC to form a multi-scenario ensemble water quality prediction (MEWQP) approach. Particularly water resources system in the Downstream and Delta of Dongjiang River (DSDDR) Basin is the primary source for the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA) (Huang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022a ). Due to intensive human sewage activities and concentrated WIs, this is an application case. MEWQP will enhance its water quality, and obtain more clean water resources. It thus has important theoretical and practical significance to promote the sustainable development of GBA. This research aims to develop a water quality prediction approach from a multi-factor perspective under uncertainty. The innovations of this research are: 1) develop an efficient water quality prediction approach (MEWQP) by combining MC based on MPSIE to improve the reliability of the model; 2) quantify the combined and individual impacts of multiple factors; 3) identify the optimal scheme of WIs, which improve the water quality of DSDDR. The methods could help decision-makers better understand the potential effects of these factors and seek adaptive measures for water quality management.  2 Materials 2.1 Overview of the studying area The study area (DSDDR) is shown in Fig. 1  . Due to the prosperous industry and concentrated population (Jiang et al., 2016 ), its industrial and domestic pollution sources are multi-point existence. Generally, the pollution level is moderately high, resulting in DSDDR being the most polluted place in the Dongjiang River (DJR) Basin (Sun et al., 2016 ). Although the local Ecological Environment Bureau has carried out strict law enforcement, the practice of stealing and leaking discharge is still repeated. It is difficult to find out the exact input ones. Ecological Environment Bureau can only obtain the minimum emission data, so there is obvious uncertainty in it. In addition, it is densely covered with lots of WIs supporting core cities in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA), such as Hong Kong, Dongguan, Shenzhen, and Guangzhou. The water resources supply the production, living, and ecological water consumption for nearly 40 million people. Deterioration of water quality can directly affect GBA’s water safety. The area is crisscrossed by river networks, and polluted water will further deteriorate under climate change (Che et al., 2019 ). The monitoring data shows that the pollution is serious in the flood season. Drinking water sources of Dongguan are classified into three types of water quality. Sixty percent of Guangzhou's drinking water sources are also Class III. Water quality indicators including BOD5 , NH3 -N, and DO in some months even exceed Class III. As a result, high-quality drinking water sources in this area are insufficient, leading to serious quality-induced water shortage (Long. et al., 2019 ; Huang et al., 2024 ). Water security faces severe challenges, which would restrict the stable socio-economic development of GBA. Therefore, the problems of DSDDR to be urgently solved are as: (1) how to make the water quality model reliable using limited data under uncertainty? (2) how to accurately predict water quality considering human activities and climate changes? (3) what are the combined impacts of multiple factors, and what are individual impacts? (4) what is the best scheme of WIs with the least impact on water quality and quantity?  2.2 Sub-basins and river segments division In DSDDR, downstream is about 44 km length from the intake of Tonghu Water Supply Plant (WSP) in Huicheng District, Huizhou City to Shilong Town, Dongguan City. Downstream flows into the Delta from Shilong Town, which is divided into North Main Stream and South Tributary. The North Main Stream has tributaries namely Shahe, Libo, Zengjiang, Xifu, Yayao, and small surge rivers. It also has three tributaries flowing out. For instance, the Huangchong River flows out from it in Huangchong Town. It is then divided into Daoyunhai Waterway and Hengyong River in Doulang Town, Dongguan. At last, it flows into Shiziyang (ocean) in Dasheng Village, with a length of about 38 km. The South Tributary flows through Shijie Town and the downtown of Dongguan City. Then it is separated into Dongguan Waterway and Zhongtang Waterway. It also flows into Shiziyang at Shatian Town, with a length of about 39.5 km. DSDDR is divided into five sub-basins according to the different flow levels, including the Mainstream, North Main Stream, South Tributary, Dongguan Waterway, and Zhongtang Waterway. As shown in Fig. 2  , five sub-basins are separated into 17 river segments (S1 to 17) based on WIs and monitoring points.  2.3 Data collection Table S1  shows basic information about 17 river segments required for WASP. Among them, the length, width, and depth of each segment were extracted from Google Earth. The roughness coefficients were available from previous studies in relevant literature (Jiang et al., 2016; Ni et al., 2018 ). Initial pollution source in 2016–2017 and monthly average values of BOD5 , NH3 -N, and DO at 17 monitoring points provided by the local Ecological Environment Bureau. The meteorological data from 2016 to 2017, such as solar radiation, temperature, and wind speed, were downloaded from the National Meteorological Science Data Center (http://data.cma.cn/ ). The streamflow data includes the 64-year data of Boluo and Qilin Hydrologic Station, which were obtained through the local Water Authority. The flow data of WIs from 2016 to 2025 was also provided by them. In five sub-basins, the streamflow of Boluo Hydrologic Station is adopted for the mainstream. Then streamflow of the North Main Stream and South Tributary is calculated through the diversion ratio of mainstream. Numerous tributaries flow into the North Main Stream, all of which are located near Zengjiang River (ZJR). The streamflow of tributaries can be calculated by using the hydrological analogy method (Wang et al., 2014 ). Also, the streamflow of tributaries separated from the north mainstream can be calculated by their respective diversion ratio.   3 Methodology To overcome the limited data making the model reliable, MEWQP can not only quantify the impacts of multiple key factors under uncertainty on water quality, but also identify the optimal mode of WIs. Firstly, combining GLUE, and WASP with inverse methods to develop MPSIE under uncertainty. Secondly, using MC to predict 6 flows affected by climate change. Thirdly, setting up multiple prediction scenarios. Fourthly, evaluating the comprehensive impacts of these multiple factors to obtain the optimized scheme of WIs, and calculating their contributions. Fig. 3   shows the framework of MEWQP approach in detail. 3.1 WASP model The latest version of the water quality simulation model is WASP8 developed by USEPA. It can effectively simulate the one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and three-dimensional hydrological dynamics of rivers, as well as the migration and transformation characteristics of water pollutants (Bouchard et al., 2017 ). DSDDR Basin belongs to medium-sized rivers, which is suitable for simulation analysis of a one-dimensional water quality model. The basic equation is the governing mass-balance equation, which can be used to fully describe the changes of any flow quality parameters with space and time (Liang et al., 2015 ). Water quality concentration C (mg/L) can be expressed by the following equation:(1a) ∂ C  ∂ t   = - ∂ ∂ t   ( U x  C )  - ∂ ∂ y   ( U y  C )  + ∂ ∂ x   ( E x  ∂ C  ∂ x   )  + ∂ ∂ y   ( E y  ∂ C  ∂ y   )  + ∂ C  ∂ z   ( E z ∂ c  ∂ z   )  + S L  + S B  + S K      where t  is time step (s); U x   , U y   , and U z    are the longitudinal, horizontal, and vertical velocity of water body (m/s), respectively; E x   ,E y   , and E z    are the longitudinal, horizontal, and vertical diffusion coefficient of water body (m2 /s); S L    refers to point source and non-point source pollution (g/m3 ·d); S B    is load rate, including upstream, downstream, bottom, and atmospheric environment (g/m3 ∙d); S K    is total kinetic transformation rate (g/m3 ·d). By integrating y and z of the previous formula (1a), a one-dimensional water quality balance equation can be formulated (Ambrose, 1993; Peng et al., 2010 )(1b) ∂ ( A C )  ∂ t   = ∂ ∂ x   ( - U x  A C + E x  A ∂ C  ∂ x   )  + A ( S L  + S B  )  + A S K      where A is the cross-sectional area of the water body after simulation, and other contents are the same as the above formula (1a). In the EUTRO model, the calculation of water quality components such as BOD5 , NH3 -N, and DO not only follows the conservation of mass in the formula (1b), but also has its mechanism process (Akomeah et al., 2019 ).  3.2 Parameters and pollution sources estimation method Firstly, we used the monitoring data of 2016 for calibration. GLUE was used to obtain uncertainty ranges and optimal values of parameters for three indicators in WASP model. The most likely monthly pollution sources for BOD5  and NH3 -N to be imported into each river segment in 2016 were calculated by using the reverse method. Secondly, we input the optimal parameter values of BOD5  and NH3 -N determined into WASP and verified them with the monitoring data in 2017. Then we adjusted the monthly pollution source of BOD5  and NH3 -N for each river segment in 2017. Finally, DO can be used to verify the parameters and pollution sources. The detailed steps are as follows: (i) importing the preliminary pollution source, WIs, and basic data of each river segment in WASP. To save the calculation cost, the most sensitive parameters of these indicators were found by trial calculation. The default values were used for other insensitive parameters; (ii) the prior distribution is uniform by default according to GLUE (Beven and Binley, 2006 ). We used Monte Carlo technology in MATLAB to sample the most sensitive parameters of indicators, such as Decay Rate Constant (Kd  ) (0–0.5), Nitrification Rate Constant (K12  ) (0–10), and Reaeration Rate (K2  ) (0–10). The specific codes are provided in the Supplementary Material ; (iii) analyzing monitoring values of BOD5  and NH3 -N, and selecting their decreased monitoring values. At the same time, we imported the sampling values of K12   and Kd   into WASP to obtain the simulation values. Then we compared the simulated values with those measured values for BOD5  and NH3 -N, and calculated the corresponding likelihood values by(2a) L ( θ )  = 1 - 1 M  ∑ m = 1  M  H m  - Q m     Q m   , m = 1 , 2 … n     where H m    is the simulated value for BOD5  and NH3 -N; Q m    is the observed value for BOD5  and NH3 -N; m  is the number of reduced water quality per month in each river segment. (iv) setting threshold Θ to identify the behavioral parameter set by L ( θ ) ≥ Θ    and the non-behavioral parameter set by L ( θ ) < Θ   (Dai et al., 2018 ). Likelihood thresholds of Kd   and K12   were set to 0.94 and 0.85, respectively. After we retain the parameter value that conforms to the likelihood value. Then the optimal value and uncertainty range of parameters corresponding to the highest likelihood value were obtained. (v) inputting the optimal values of Kd   and K12   in WASP to gain simulated values. By calculating the minimum Mean Absolute Relative Error (MARE) between all analog and monitoring values, the input of pollution sources can be adjusted. The formula of MARE can be described as:(2b) ε = 1 K  ∑ k = 1  K  1 T  ∑ t = 1  N  H t  - Q t     Q t       where H t    and Q t    are monthly simulated and observed values for BOD5  and NH3 -N in each river segment; t  represents the number of months; K  represents the number of river segments. (vi) importing the sampling value of parameter K2   in DO to run WASP, also setting a likelihood threshold of 0.84 to reject the non-behavioral simulations. We then obtain the optimal parameter value and uncertainty range of K2   corresponding to the highest likelihood value. The likelihood value can be calculated by(2c) L ( θ )  = 1 - 1 J  ∑ j = 1  j  1 T  ∑ t = 1  T  H t  - Q t     Q t       where H t    and Q t    are monthly simulated and observed values for DO in each river segment; t  is the number of months; j  is the number of river segments. (vii) validating with the monitoring data in 2017. We imported the optimal parameter values obtained from the calibration and the pollution source data in 2017 from the preliminary survey into WASP. To begin with, we used the observed values of BOD5  and NH3 -N to verify the parameters of Kd   and K12  . Then we minimized MARE (Eq.(2b)) between the simulation and the monitoring values to adjust the pollution source. Finally, the simulated values of DO were compared with the measured values to verify the pollution source and parameter K2  . The multiple WASP files that match the likelihood value parameter values can be found in the available online (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/374902072_water_quality_analysis_simulation_programming_for_research_of_a_multi-scenario_water_quality_prediction_approach ).  3.3 Markov-Chain model The concept of the Markov process was proposed by Andrey Markov at the end of the 19th century (Markov, 1906 ). Markov-Chain model can well reflect such randomness, so it can be used for streamflow prediction analysis (Prairie et al., 2008 ). We divided the monthly average streamflow into different levels (wet, normal, and dry). It has covered the maximum flow (flood period) and minimum flow (drought period) caused by extreme climate in the past 64 years. The specific steps for streamflow prediction can be found in the Supplementary Material .  3.4 Scenario design In this research, there are mainly three types of scenarios. The first one is four WIs scenarios. The water withdrawal and the number of WIs in 2016–2017 are represented by W1. According to the Water Supply Security Plan of the local water authority, schemes of WIs in 2024 and 2025 are set as W2 and W3, respectively. The scenario of non-water intakes is denoted by W4. Table S2  and Figs. S1-S3  show the differences from W1 to W3. In W2, several small WSP would be closed. Some large intakes would take more water and some less. The intake of the fourth WSP would be moved from S16 of the Zhongtang Waterway to S7 of the Southern tributary. There will be more water withdrawal in 2024 than in 2016 in the study area. Water withdrawal in 2025 would be reduced, and the small intake would be further closed. The second one is three input pollution source scenarios. That in 2016 and 2017 are set to P1 and P2, respectively. Non-pollution source scenario is designed as P3. The third one is the six streamflow scenarios predicted by the Markov-Chain. The streamflow is divided into corresponding interval values of wet, normal, and dry periods. The upper and lower limits of the above three periods are set as HU, HL, MU, ML, LU, and LL scenarios, respectively. Among them, HU and LL represent periods of extreme rainfall and drought, respectively. Because P3 is used to verify the reduction of sewage quality without pollution sources. Moreover, under P3 the difference between intake and non-withdraw is not apparent, so scenarios of W2 and W3 are not simulated. Therefore, by combining 4 WIs schemes, 3 pollution sources, and 6 streamflow scenarios, there will be 60 assessment scenarios in total. Besides, the streamflow in 2016 under non-water intakes is set as the baseline scenario (BS).   4 Results and discussions 4.1 Parameters and pollution sources estimation The most sensitive parameters for three water quality indicators (BOD5 , NH3 -N, and DO) including Kd  , K12  , and K2   were selected through trial analysis and relevant literature (Li et al., 2021; Pei et al., 2020; Yu, 2007 ). Fig. 4   shows the uncertainty range, optimal value for behavioral parameter sets, and their corresponding likelihood value, respectively. The three parameters have obvious peaks. The range of Kd  , K12  , and K2   conforming to the likelihood behavior are [0.31, 0.49], [3.71, 5.61], and [2.08, 4.45], respectively. Their optimal parameter values are 0.38, 4.56, and 3.01. The maximum likelihood values corresponding to the optimal values of the three parameters are 0.944, 0.913, and 0.844, respectively. Fig. 5   shows the posterior distribution of the three parameters. They have changed from the previous uniform distribution to an approximate normal distribution. Tables S3-S4  show the most likely pollution sources of NH3 -N and BOD5  from 2016 to 2017 corresponding to the optimal parameters. Fig. 6   shows the comparison between the measured and the simulated values during the calibration period in 2016. MARE of calibrated BOD5 , NH3 -N, and DO are 5.87 %, 9.19 %, and 15.25 %, respectively. Then during the validation, we verified the calibration parameters and estimated the pollution source in 2017. Fig. S4  shows the comparison during the validation period. MARE of BOD5 , NH3 -N, and DO are 11.61 %, 10.78 %, and 16.55 %, respectively. According to relevant literature (Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2016 ), relative errors of three water quality indicators are all within 20 %, and there were both have good fitting effects in the calibration and validation period. Before the use of MPSIE, the difference between the simulated and measured values for DO was more than 20 %. Many previous studies (Azaïez et al., 2014 ; Belgacem et al., 2016; Long, 2020 ) used the relationship between DO and BOD5  to calculate the number of pollution sources, and many studies (Gomolka et al., 2020; Gupta et al., 2005; Zurita et al., 2021 ) demonstrated that DO is jointly affected by BOD5  and NH3 -N. The above results demonstrate that the parameters and pollution sources can be estimated at the same time. MPSIE not only allows WASP model to be used to robustly predict the water quality in DSDDR with limited data, also can be applied in other watersheds.  4.2 Streamflow prediction affected by climate change Table 2   shows the monthly interval streamflow of the two basins in the wet, normal, and dry periods after division, according to the relevant standards of the Code for Hydrologic Information Prediction (GB/T 22482–2008) (Wang., 2018 ). The probability corresponding to the streamflow from 2022 to 2025 is shown in Fig. 7  . We can find that except for January and February, the prediction results of DJR in most months of 2022 to 2025 would be the most likely in the dry period. As a tributary of DJR, ZJR would still have the highest probability of drought except in June and December (Fig. 7 b). On the contrary, the probability of a normal period would be the lowest in all results. This shows that the mainstream and tributaries of DJR will encounter more extreme weather in the future. The latest research (Liu et al., 2023; Zhai et al., 2016 ) indicates that under future climate warming scenarios, compared to the past baseline period, the runoff in DJR will increase during the wet period and decrease during the dry period. As far as we know, the period 2021–2022 has already experienced the biggest drought in 60 years (Yang et al., 2023 ). Besides, with the increase of years, the probability of prediction will become more and more stable (Li et al., 2022b ). For example, in Fig. 7 a, from 2023 to 2025 that of wet, normal, and dry periods in January would be 0.36, 0.36, and 0.28, respectively. This result is consistent with the characteristics of the Markov method and tends to be stable (Cai et al., 2021 ).  4.3 Water quality prediction under multiple scenarios 4.3.1 Temporal changes in water quality The monthly water quality predictions from 2022 to 2025 under the four WIS (W1 to W4), pollution scenarios (P1), and extreme flows (LL) are presented in Fig. S5 . We find that under the same pollution sources, flow levels, and WIs, the results over the years are consistently similar. From Fig. 8   (S1-6) and Fig. S6  (S7-17), the temporal trend of three water quality indicators would be diverse in 2025 under historical WIs (W1). In Fig. 8 a and Fig. S6 a, the temporal trend of BOD5  is obvious differences. In sum, under P1 and W1, BOD5  in the whole study area would decline in February, rise in March, decrease in April, increase in May, decline from June to August, rise from September to October, decline in November, and rise in December. From Fig. 8 b and Fig. S6 b, we also can find distinct time variations of NH3 -N. In Fig. 8 c and Fig. S6 c, the temporal trend in DO also would be reversed to that of BOD5  and NH3 -N. Among them, DO Would be more affected by NH3 -N. For example, in the mainstream, DO at S1 would be the lowest in January, and raised to the highest in April. The range would vary between 1.61 and 8.3 mg/L. While NH3 -N at S1 in the lowest and highest months would be the contrary. When NH3 -N would not be high, DO would be affected by BOD5 . Previous studies (Wu et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2015; Zhong et al., 2021 ) also demonstrated that the changing trend of DO is opposite to that of BOD5  and NH3 -N. In Fig. 8  and Fig. S6 , water quality under non-water intake scenario (W4) would have remarkable inter-month variability, also a significant reduction of concentration. This phenomenon is consistent with previous studies. For example, Wang et al. (2016)  found that the water intake of the South to North Water Diversion Project worsened the water quality of the Hanjiang River. Seo and Song (2011)  reported that there is a significant change in BOD5  when considering water intake. Due to the difference in the impact of WIs, we could divide all segments into three types. The first type is that the concentration would be lower, and the temporal trend would be generally like historical WIs scenario. For example, the time variation of BOD5  at S1-3, S8-9, and S13 would belong to the first type. The second type is that the time trend would have a slight change. For BOD5 , the highest concentrations of S4-6 would occur in December. The third type is that the time trend and concentration reduction would be both significant. For example, the trend of Dongguan Waterway (S15-17) and Zhongtang Waterway (S7 and S14) would change in the same months. Comparing Fig. 8  and Fig. S6  (P1) with Fig. S7  (P2), under the situation P2, except that the concentration of S13 would be higher than that of P1, those in other segments will decrease. It indicates that the pollution sources of 16 segments in 2017 have been controlled and are gradually reduced. Moreover, although the temporal trend of water quality for each segment would be varied under scenario P2, each index in the whole study area would conform to its time variation law. Xiao et al. (2015)  also proved that the impact of changing pollution sources on water intake is obvious.  4.3.2 Spatial changes in water quality In Fig. 9   (January to June) and Fig. S8  (July to December), the water quality prediction demonstrates significant spatial variability and the migration law of the river under the combined influence of multiple factors. For example, BOD5  in January would vary between 4.39–28.89 mg/L for all segments under historical WIs (W1) and minimum flow level (LL). When the river from the mainstream to the north mainstream, it would be increased by 1.24 mg/L. Therefore, we can see the main migration law of BOD5  is as follows. After the mainstream is divided into north and south tributaries in Shilong Town, the pollution will become more serious. In the South Tributary, the concentration would rise suddenly in S6, then it would decrease slightly flowing into the Zhongtang Waterway and Dongguan Waterway. Compared with BOD5 , the migration law of NH3 -N (Fig. 9 b and Fig. S8 b) would be similar. For instance, in March, NH3 -N at S7 would be raised by 1 mg/L. Fig. 9 c and Fig. S8 c also show prominent spatial variability of DO. For example, in April, it would rise to the highest in S1-3, fall in S4-10, rise in S11-12, drop to the lowest in S13, and rise in S14-17. This change trend would be mainly reversed to that of NH3 -N, except at S7 and S15 would be contrary for BOD5 . Bai et al. (2019)  also reported similar spatial variation patterns from upstream to downstream of DSDDR. Besides, by comparing Fig. 9  and Fig. S8  with Fig. S9 , the spatial migration law in the P2 scenario would be the same as that in P1. Fig. 9  and Fig. S8  also show water quality response would have obvious spatial variability after non-water intake situations (W4). Previous research by Wang et al. (2016)  showed that after water intake, the spatial concentration of pollutants in rivers increases from upstream to downstream. The latest research by Luan et al. (2024)  illustrates the spatial trend of water quality changes in rivers affected by different drainage strategies. We found that in several months, the water quality of the mainstream would become worse than that of the north and south tributaries. For instance, in January, BOD5  at S1 would be 6.92 mg/L. Then in the South Tributary and North Main Stream, it would be reduced by 2.1 mg/L at S6 and by 2.69 mg/L at S13, respectively. However, the spatial change trend without WIs would be more obvious for NH3 -N. For example, NH3 -N in May would be a downward trend from S2 to S7. For DO, it would have an obvious response to spatial changes in Fig. 9 c and Fig. S8 c.  4.3.3 Climate change in water quality Monthly water quality prediction under 6 flows caused by climate change is shown in Fig. 10   and Fig. S10  under the pollution (P1) and historical WIs (W1) scenarios. We can see that it would be improved significantly with the increase in flow (Leveque et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2019b ). However, we can note that a special case is that it would slightly deteriorate with the increase in flow. For instance, NH3 -N also at S1 in April, May, June, July, August, and November would be raised by 0.02, 0.01, 0.09, 0.06, 0.07, and 0.03 mg/L respectively. This is because these segments have no pollution source in some months. To verify the reason, we set up simulation scenarios of non-pollution sources (P3) under multiple flow levels. As shown in Fig. 11  , water quality would deteriorate with the increase of flow. Moreover, with the migration of the river, water quality from the mainstream to the tributaries would continue to improve. This result also verifies that MPSIE method is reasonable. The above results like previous studies, show that the impact of increased flow on different river segments is complex. For example, Xiao et al. (2015)  pointed out that as the flow rate increases, the water quality will improve, but it is not the best under the maximum flow rate. Zhong et al. (2021)  indicated that a negative relation exists between DO concentration in the Yongjiang River and the releasing discharge of the Laokou hydro project. Jiang et al. (2016)  also found that with the increase in the discharged flow from the Dongjiang Hydro-Project, the peak concentration of NH3 -N decreased significantly, and the improvement of water quality at the intake of the Dongshen Water Supply Project was remarkable. Fig. S11  shows that water quality without intake (W4) would become better with the flow increases. From Fig. S11 , we also can observe the results of baseline (in 2016) indicate that 2016 was an extremely wet year, and pollution emissions in the wet year were relatively large. In addition, in Fig. 10  and Fig. S10-S11 , under different scenarios of WIs water quality would have visible time changes. Furthermore, the spatial change in it caused by weather would be more apparent under non-water withdraws (W4) compared to historical conditions (W1). Taking BOD5  as an example, from Fig. 12  , under scenario W4 the maximum value for the south tributaries in many months (May, August, and October) would be lower than that of the mainstream with the increase of flows. But under historical water withdraws (W1), BOD5  only in January and February would have spatial change. Wang et al. (2016)  also found that with the water flow rate decreasing, water quality will stay in a worse state than previously suspected. Ortiz-Lopez et al. (2023)  showed that river flow presented a very strong correlation with raw water quality. Panton et al. (2020)  also found that terrestrially-derived dissolved organic carbon concentrations increased with increased river flow rates. Jiao et al. (2021)  and Woo et al. (2021)  reported that with the increase in water diversion, the runoff of mainstream rivers will increase, and the ecological environment will be improved.  4.3.4 Impacts of water intakes in water quality As shown in Table S5 and S6 , we calculated the corresponding annual changes of three indicators under different flows and pollution source scenarios compared with the non-intake. All indicators would have significant responses to WIs. The change of them would be the highest at low flows. For example, under W1 and P1 conditions, the average annual change of BOD5  for all segments would be between 0.92 to 10.72 mg/L from high to low flows. That of NH3 -N and DO would be between 0.27 to 6.25 mg/L and −1.08 to −3.1 mg/L, respectively. Previous studies (Luan et al., 2024; Seo and Song, 2011; Wang et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2020 ) also shown that the CODMn , NH3 -N, DO, BOD5 , and TP concentration of the whole stream generally increases after the projects. Overall, the annual average change in all indicators shows that the order of impact on WIs would be W3 > W2 > W1. For instance, under P2 and ML, that of BOD5  (Table S6 b) for all segments in W1, W2, and W3 would be 1.68, 1.5, and 1.43 mg/L respectively. That of NH3 -N would be 0.82, 0.74, and 0.67 mg/L respectively. That of DO would be −2.1, −1.8, and −1.64 mg/L respectively. Therefore, considering that DO is affected by NH3 -N and BOD5 , as well as pollution sources and flows. Especially its data intuitively reflects the changes after water intake. We were consistent with previous studies in choosing DO as a comprehensive indicator to calculate its annual average change rate compared with non-water intakes (Xiao et al., 2015; Zhong et al., 2021 ). As shown in Fig. 13  , the water intake would have the greatest impact on S13, and the lowest impact on S1. Besides, water quality can be improved by altering the mode of WIs without changing the total intake flow. For example, W3 in the mainstream is to shut down the four small WSP from S2 to S4, and increase the water intake flow of large WSP such as the Third WSP in Qiaotou Town at S2 and the WSP in Shipai Town at S4. The total intake flow of the mainstream under W3 would still be slightly greater than W2. While change at S4 under W3 would be less than or equal to W2. Luan et al. (2024)  also illustrated that the diversion flows under scenarios C1 and C2 were lower than those under other scenarios, but provided the greatest water quality improvement effect. Liu et al. (2012)  also reported that when the pumped streamflow into the upper Foshan River (Shakou pump) is ≤   10 m3 /s, with the increase of intake from the Shiken pumping station, the water quality of the Jiebian section deteriorates. In general, under any scenarios including combined impacts of climate change and pollution sources the average change rate of DO in W1, W2, and W3 would be −31 %, −27 %, and −25 %, respectively. While the order of intake flow would be W2 > W1 > W3. Therefore, W3 would be the optimal scenario of WIs, followed by W2 and W1. This shows that the water quality can be improved by closing the small WIs and increasing the water volume of large intakes. And further reducing the overall intake flow will significantly improve the water quality. Our research demonstrates that water quality can be improved as the intake flow decreases, and can be enhanced by changing the intake mode without changing the flow rate. This is a practical suggestion for decision-makers. Previous studies by Dehbalaei and Javan (2018)  found that a combination of 50 % surface water withdrawal and 50 % bottom withdrawal was the best scenario because of improving eutrophication and weakening dissolved oxygen in the Ilam reservoir. This also indicates that changing the intake model and quantity can improve water quality. Furthermore, the impact on water quality is the smallest under non-pollution source scenario (P3). Thus, in agreement with previous studies, the impact of pollution sources is the largest (Cho and Lee, 2015; Dehbalaei and Javan, 2018; Liu et al., 2014; Xiao et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2020 ). Then we compared the impacts of climate change and WIs under the same scenario of pollution sources. We subtracted the annual mean concentrations under future flows (W4, LL, LU, ML, MU, and HL) and baseline from the historical conditions (W1 and flow levels in 2016), respectively. Meanwhile, 17 segments and their average values (Table S7 ) were calculated. Under the historical flow scenario and non-water intakes (W4), compared to the historical intake (W1), BOD5 , NH3 -N, and DO in the whole area would be improved by 0.93, 0.31, and 0.81 mg/L, respectively. However, under the flow scenario HL and W1, BOD5 , NH3 -N, and DO would be deteriorated by 1.6, 0.48, and 1.51 mg/L, respectively. The results show that the effect of climate change is greater than that of WIs under the same pollution source (Liu et al., 2014; Zou et al., 2014 ). Particularly during periods of extreme drought, concentrations will increase the most. Moreover, in several segments, the effect of WIs can offset the impact of climate change. For example, the mitigation rates of NH3 -N in segments including S2-4 and S16-17 to climate change under LU would be 39 %, 47 %, 9 %, 9 %, and 8 %, respectively. Especially in flows MU and HL, NH3 -N in 10 river segments (S2-5, S7-8, and S14-17) reflects that the influence of WIs can compensate for the impact of climate change. That of BOD5  at S5 under ML would be 22 %. That of DO at S2 and S16 under LU would be 16 % and 7 %, respectively. Similarly, previous studies by Liu et al. (2012)  also found that the optimal water diversion scheme after inputting fresh water can improve downstream water quality during the dry season.  4.3.5 Universal application River networks are heavily populated and industrialized areas, both domestically and internationally. As a result, the water quality of rivers is easily polluted by domestic sewage and industrial waste. Additionally, a larger population has a greater water demand, leading to a dense distribution of WIs in the river network (Bai et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2008a; Sun et al., 2012 ). The impact of these multiple WIs on water quantity is well known to significantly reduce river flow (Wu et al., 2023 ). Previous studies have only focused on the impact of individual WIs or large-scale water diversion projects on water quality (Sun et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2015 ), while the combined impact of climate change and pollution sources on the water quality of the entire river network has been overlooked. The method developed in this research also can be efficiently applied in the Yellow River Delta, Yangtze River Delta (Yu et al., 2023 ), the Pearl River Delta (Luan et al., 2024 ) in China, as well as in urban river network areas abroad such as the San Francisco Bay-Delta (Martyr-Koller et al., 2017 ), Vietnam Red River Delta (Hien et al., 2023 ), Bangladesh River Network (Islam et al., 2020 ), and Korean urban rivers (Kim et al., 2016; Seo and Song, 2011 ). WIs can even cause interruptions in rivers during dry seasons (Harlan et al., 2021 ), and water resource issues can become a significant factor that restricts economic and social development. The management of multiple WIs is urgently valued by managers due to the inevitability of water intake in urban river networks. Additionally, due to the influx of many pollution sources and sudden water pollution incidents, it is difficult to estimate the pollution sources of the river network (Wang et al., 2019a ). Therefore, the method developed has universal applicability and can solve the problems existing in most river networks (Huang et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2016 ).    5 Conclusions In this research, firstly, the multiple parameters and pollution sources inverse estimation method namely MPSIE has been proposed to make the water quality simulation model reliable under uncertainty. Then, a multi-scenario ensemble water quality prediction (MEWQP) approach was developed by combining MC to reveal the scientific relevance of this study is the migration law and main driving mechanisms of water quality on river networks under multiple factors such as WIs, human pollution sources, and climate change. MEWQP has the following advantages: (1) efficiently estimate optimal parameters and pollution sources for BOD5 , NH3 -N, and DO to address sparse data of boundary conditions; (2) enhance the predictive capacity of model; (3) evaluate the independent and combined impacts of multiple factors; (4) identify the optimized schemes of WIs. The results indicate that: (i) the annual average value of DO in the whole study area under the pollution source scenario would be improved by 31 % without WIs; (ii) the order of individual impacts is that pollution sources have the greatest impact, followed by climate change, and then WIs; (iii) under non-water intakes (W4) NH3 -N in segments including S2-4 and S16-17 to the impacts of climate change under LU would be improved by 39 %, 47 %, 9 %, 9 %, and 8 %, respectively; (iv) considering the comprehensive impact of pollution sources and climate change, the optimal order of WIs is W3, W2, and W1, respectively. Based on the results, decision-makers should close small WIs and increase the water volume of larger WIs to improve water quality. Additionally, reducing the total flow of WIs will have a significant positive impact on water quality. Therefore, decision-makers should continue to control pollution sources and strengthen the management of WIs. Suspending intake can improve the water quality of river, particularly during periods of extreme dryness when pollution sources remain unchanged. This method provides optimized schemes of WIs and effective management measures, which help to improve water quality in 5 cities (e.g., Hong Kong, Huizhou, Dongguan, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen), also promotes the sustainable development of GBA. Therefore, the method developed provides theoretical and methodological support for water environment management that eliminates urban black and odorous water bodies. It also can conduct efficient water management scenario analysis when facing increasingly complex drinking water problems, ensuring river water safety. In the future scope, the method can be applied to other urban river networks to explore the movement of pollutants under external factors. It also can be used for sudden environmental incidents and traceability of water pollution, providing useful tools to evaluate alternative watershed management plans. Moreover, due to the limitation of the model, this article does not consider the impact of rainfall on climate change. Hydrological mechanism models such as soil and water assessment tool (SWAT) and GCMs can be further coupled with water quality models to refine the long-term impact of water quality.
1 Introduction Field and budgetary constraints often limit the direct measurement of soil hydraulic properties, even though they are essential for various studies related to water and solute movement (Schaap et al., 1998 ). Pedotransfer functions (PTFs) have been formulated to predict these properties from readily available soil parameters (Wösten et al., 2001 ). Typical inputs for PTFs include soil texture or particle size distribution (PSD), organic carbon content (OC), and bulk density (BD) (Bouma, 1989; Vereecken, 1995 ). While they could predict certain soil hydraulic properties to a level that is acceptable in many applications, their oversimplified models and limited input features prevent them from accurately conveying the relationships between structure and function of soil pore space (Pachepsky et al., 2006 ). Therefore, it’s imperative to explore additional variables and methodologies to address these shortcomings (Van Looy et al., 2017 ). On the one hand, soil horizon and land cover class, two easily accessible (categorical) variables, may offer potential solutions to alleviate this inherent limitation of PTF. Soil horizons impact the movement of moisture and solutes at varying depths (Wösten et al., 1999; Kutílek, 2004 ). Structural changes in soil from the surface to deeper layers, such as differences in pore size distribution and OC, can lead to significant disparities in soil hydraulic properties in the vertical direction (Kay and VandenBygaart, 2002 ). Moreover, such soil heterogeneity might be amplified in different land cover types, affecting the accuracy, robustness, and extrapolation capabilities of developed PTFs (Van Looy et al., 2017 ). Land cover classification serves as a window to reveal the interactions between the soil and the overlying vegetation and surface features, which might influence the dynamics of infiltration, retention, and percolation in the soil, potentially altering the hydrological responses and overarching processes within the ecosystem (te Wierik et al., 2021; Bormann and Klaassen, 2008 ). For instance, cropland soils face periodic compaction, altering soil structure and water retention during agricultural activities, while forest soils may exhibit diverse hydrological patterns due to root distribution and litter deposition (Lin et al., 2022; Van Looy et al., 2017 ). The integration of land cover and soil horizons has been verified to improve the precision of developed PTFs when predicting OC in subsurface horizons of European soils (Fernández-Ugalde and Tóth, 2017 ), while studies applying these variables to the development of PTFs for soil hydraulic properties remains limited. On the other hand, various machine learning models, such as multiple linear regression (MLR), support vector machines (SVM), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), and artificial neural networks have been utilized to identify the linear and non-linear correlations between soil hydraulic properties and soil features (Al-Anazi and Gates, 2010; Botula et al., 2013; Khlosi et al., 2016; Nemes et al., 2006; Nguyen et al., 2015; Pachepsky et al., 1996 ). To improve the accuracy and robustness of PTFs while mitigating overfitting, ensemble learning algorithms have garnered growing attention among researchers. In the realm of developing PTFs, various ensemble learning techniques, such as Cubist, Bagging, and Boosting, have been employed (Xiao et al., 2022 ). Cubist enhances predictive accuracy by combining multiple regression trees, while Bagging reduces variance by generating multiple independent models from repeated data sampling, and Boosting iteratively refines models to correct preceding errors, enhancing overall accuracy (Szatmári et al., 2023; Bühlmann, 2012; Mienye and Sun, 2022; Zounemat-Kermani et al., 2021 ). Stacking ensemble learning instead, which replaces original dataset inputs with predictions from ensemble members and uses a meta -classifier to combine them, effectively leverages the strengths of various models (Wolpert, 1992; Gomes et al., 2017 ). Stacking ensemble learning has demonstrated strong performance in regression problems related to surface hydrological processes, medicine and finance (Zounemat-Kermani et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2019; Ribeiro and dos Santos Coelho, 2020 ), but its application in PTF development remains unexplored. While ensemble models excel in predictive power, they often compromise on interpretability, which is especially crucial in sectors like soil hydrology and environmental science (Bouma et al., 2022 ). Advances in interpretative techniques, notably the use of a SHAP value (SHapley Additive exPlanations), are progressively addressing this transparency concern in complex models (Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Shapley, 1953 ). This study aims to investigate the potential of various ensemble learning techniques, with an emphasis on Stacking, in developing PTFs for soil hydraulic properties. We incorporated two readily accessible (categorical) features, soil horizon and land cover class, in addition to the ‘traditional’ variables (particle size distribution, organic carbon content, bulk density, CaCO3 , pH, and cation exchange capacity) to better learn complex soil property interactions. Both direct dataset division and one-hot encoding (OHE) were employed to preprocess categorical data, for striking a balance between maintaining sufficient sample representation and mitigating potential issues from numerical hierarchies. Furthermore, the SHAP value was employed to quantify the feature importance. To test our methodology, we employed the European Hydropedological Data Inventory (EU-HYDI) database (Weynants et al., 2013 ). We hope this study serves as a valuable reference for soil hydrological, ecological and climatological modeling communities, among others.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Dataset The European Hydropedological Data Inventory (EU-HYDI) dataset (Weynants et al., 2013 ) was compiled to establish PTFs of European soil hydraulic properties. It contains 6014 sampling sites and 18,682 samples from 18 countries with contributions from 29 institutions. It aggregates European soil data, including soil physical, chemical, and hydraulic properties, along with geographical, stratification, and land cover details. During the data preparation phase in this study, samples without recorded location information were eliminated, resulting in a total of 5812 remaining sites (Fig. 1  ). In this study, we developed point predictions of soil hydraulic PTFs, including saturated hydraulic conductivity (KS  cm day−1  ), saturated water content (θS  cm3  cm−3  ), water content at field capacity (θFC  cm3  cm−3  ), water content at wilting point (θWP  cm3  cm−3  ) and available water capacity (θAWC  cm3  cm−3  ). The logarithm of saturated hydraulic conductivity (log10  KS  ) was used to address skewness in the data distribution (Tietje and Hennings, 1996; Tóth et al., 2015 ). Available water capacity is defined as the difference between the amount of soil water content at field capacity and the amount at wilting point (Veihmeyer and Hendrickson, 1927 ). Field capacity was taken at the commonly used matric potential of −330 hPa, and the wilting point was assessed at −15000 hPa. To facilitate a direct comparison of model performance, the study utilized the same dataset and feature combination strategies (Table 1  ) as Tóth et al. (2015) . These feature combinations are commonly used in current PTF research and have been validated for their effectiveness in predicting soil properties, and they are also commonly collected indicators in soil data acquisition (Vereecken et al., 1989; Wösten et al., 2001 ).  2.2 Soil horizon designations The EU-HYDI dataset uses the uppercase letters H, O, A, E, B, C, and R to distinguish distinct soil master horizons and layers. Among these, H and O refer to layers dominated by organic material, and A refers to mineral horizons formed at the surface or below an O horizon (FAO, 1998 ). This study employed a total of 4308 topsoil samples and 14,374 subsoil samples. The topsoil samples were categorized as the transitional horizons of A that start at a depth of 0 cm, as well as H, O, and A horizons. Should the dataset lack specific horizon designation, layers at the top depth of 0 cm or samples drawn entirely from the 0–30 cm depth and with their top within the 0–5 cm depth, were also treated as topsoil representatives. All other samples were categorized as subsoil samples. The approach to soil stratification, founded on horizon nomenclature and depth of sampling, aligns with the methodology implemented by Tóth et al. (2015) .  2.3 Land cover classification The EU-HYDI dataset only provides land cover classification (LCC) information for a total of 2658 sampling points. It uses the classification standards of the Land Use/Cover Area Frame Survey (LUCAS), which divides land use and cover area into eight major categories: artificial land, cropland, woodland, shrubland, grassland, bare land, water, and wetland. Considering that most of the samples with missing land cover information were collected predominantly in the 1990 s, we used the CORINE Land Cover (CLC) inventory (with a resolution of 100 m) to supplement the missing part. The dataset was obtained from the Google Earth Engine (GEE) platform (COPERNICUS/CORINE/V20/100m). The appropriate dataset was selected based on the time period covered by each CLC asset: 1990 asset (covered 1989–1998), 2000 asset (covered 1999–2001), 2006 asset (covered 2005–2007) and 2012 asset (covered 2011–2012). This process supplemented LCC information for an additional 754 sampling points.  2.4 Machine learning algorithms In comparing the performances of various machine learning models for constructing PTFs, models spanning the major categories of machine learning algorithms were chosen, and the optimal model was identified based on the comparative performance of these selected algorithms. Detailed descriptions and rationales for selecting each model are as follows:1) Linear models: These include multiple linear regression (LR) and ridge regression (RR). Multiple linear regression is preferred for its interpretability but is vulnerable to multicollinearity. Ridge regression, on the other hand, employs L2 regularization to mitigate overfitting and reduce the effects of multicollinearity, but it cannot completely eliminate them and still poses risks to interpretability (Picciafuoco et al., 2019 ).  2) Instance-based models: K-nearest neighbors (KNN) and support vector regression (SVR) were selected because they excel in identifying local soil data trends, deciding based on similarities among data points, and processing varied soil data without adhering to rigid parametric prerequisites (Al-Anazi and Gates, 2010; Lamorski et al., 2008; Nemes et al., 2006 ).  3) Neural network model: The multilayer perceptron (MLP) was adopted for producing PTFs due to its ability to model complex non-linear relationships, extract hierarchical features through its layered architecture, and customize its structure for specific dataset needs, making it apt for the intricate patterns in soil data (Schaap et al., 1998; Singh et al., 2022 ).  4) Bagging ensemble models: Random forest (RF) and extremely randomized trees (ET) operate by training on different subsets of data to reduce variance, ensuring stability in PTFs across diverse soil datasets (Szabó et al., 2019 ). These models benefit from parallel training and excel at capturing complex soil data relationships by aggregating predictions.  5) Boosting ensemble models: Gradient boosting (GB), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) and adaptive boosting (AdaBoost) all enhance the performance by sequentially adding new models to the ensemble, effectively transforming weak learners into strong ones, and aiming to reduce both bias and variance in the development of PTFs (Zounemat-Kermani et al., 2021 ). While adaptive boosting focuses on adjusting weights of misclassified instances, gradient boosting and extreme gradient boosting aim to correct residuals of previous models. Notably, extreme gradient boosting refines its predictions by incorporating L1 and L2 regularization during model training, which helps prevent overfitting and enhances generalization.  6) Stacking ensemble models: In a stacking ensemble model, multiple base models are trained and then integrated into a meta -model to boost prediction accuracy, often reducing bias and outperforming individual algorithms (Wolpert, 1992; Chatzimparmpas et al., 2021 ). For PTFs, stacking may harness the predictive power of diverse algorithms, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of soil data patterns.    In this study, the above-mentioned 10 models were designated as base models, while each was also used in rotation as a meta -model, forming a total of 10 stacking model combinations. Detailed information on the models and the parameters used in this study are provided in Supplementary Material S2 . This approach aimed at finding the optimal combination of base and meta -models for constructing soil hydraulic PTFs, and the risk of overfitting was mitigated through 5-fold cross-validation. A total of 20 distinct machine learning models were thus employed in PTF construction. This diverse methodological approach ensured an exhaustive exploration of the dataset. Given the unique capabilities of each model, it enables a nuanced understanding of the data, ensuring the identification of models best suited to address the intricacies inherent in the dataset. The specific procedures used are as follows:1) Data cleaning: Entries having null values in both predictor and variables were systematically removed.  2) Collinearity assessment: Through the variance inflation factor (VIF), multicollinearity among features was evaluated:   (1) VIF  j  = 1 1 - R j  2    #          where, R j  2    is unadjusted coefficient of determination for regressing the j th independent variable on the remaining ones. Features with a VIF>10 indicate strong multicollinearity (O’brien, 2007 ). As a result, only 18 models were ultimately included in the accuracy evaluation, excluding linear models sensitive to collinearity (Picciafuoco et al., 2019 ). The calculated VIF results are provided in Supplementary Material S1 . In each test condition, multicollinearity is present in all feature combinations except for the combination of PSD and OC.3) Feature engineering: Categorical variables underwent one-hot encoding (OHE) to transform them into a format compatible with machine learning algorithms, while remaining variables were standardized. In OHE, each unique object is represented using binary vectors where only one bit is set to 1, and the rest are set to 0 (Xiang et al., 2023 ).  4) Training and validation: A 5-fold cross-validation strategy was employed to ensure robustness and generalizability of the model’s performance by reducing the bias associated with reliance on a single training/test split (Rodriguez et al., 2010; Pachepsky and Rawls, 1999 ), with a consistent random seed ensuring reproducibility and fairness across runs. Each model was trained and evaluated, with performance metrics including root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and the R2  score being computed:   (2) RMSE = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  y i  - y ^     2    #         (3) MAE = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  y i  - y ^    #         (4) R  2  = 1 - ∑ y i  - y ^     2   ∑ y i  - y  ¯      2    #         where, y i    is the actual value, and y ^    is the predicted value. Among them, RMSE was the primary evaluation metric. When RMSE values were identical, R2  and MAE were used in succession to determine the best model.  2.5 Feature importance To understand the influence of individual features on our model’s predictions, we employed SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values, a method grounded in game theory and rooted in the Shapley values concept (Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Shapley, 1953 ). These values quantify the impact of each feature relative to a baseline, revealing its effect on the prediction. A positive SHAP value indicates that the feature contributes to increasing the prediction value, while a negative value indicates that the feature contributes to decreasing the prediction value. To visualize the contributions and importance of features, we utilized SHAP summary plots, offering a holistic view of the model’s decision-making process.  2.6 Data analysis The data utilized in this study is fully accessible to the participants (including the corresponding author of this article) that contributed to the EU-HYDI initiative and the Joint Research Centre of the European Union (Weynants et al., 2013 ). All computational analyses were conducted using Python version 3.10. Key libraries employed for data processing and analysis included scikit-learn, xgboost and SHAP (Pedregosa et al., 2011; Chen and Guestrin, 2016; Lundberg and Lee, 2017 ). The source code associated with this research has been made publicly available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.25151705 . Geospatial analysis and mapping were performed using ArcGIS version 10.4 (Esri, Redlands, CA, USA).   3 Results 3.1 The performance of ensemble learning models In the development of PTFs in this study, a rigorous evaluation was undertaken spanning diverse feature combinations and modeling techniques. By systematically assessing five target variables across six different feature combinations, and testing them against 20 distinct models, we appraised a total of 600 scenarios. The optimal feature and model combinations for predicting each target variable are shown in Table 2  . Each table entry represents the highest-performing PTF among the combinations tested. All other PTF results are available in the Supplementary Material  (S1). The results revealed distinct patterns in the best performing models and feature combinations for predicting KS   and θS  , with the stacking model demonstrating particularly exceptional performance. For both targets, the features of PSD, OC, and BD were most influential, achieving an RMSE as low as 0.841 log10  cm d−1  for log10 KS   and 0.027 cm3  cm−3  for θS  , and an equally low MAE of log10  0.645 cm d−1  for log10 KS   and 0.018 cm3  cm−3  for θS  . The robustness of the model is further emphasized by the R2  values being as high as 0.869 when predicting θS   using the above-mentioned feature set. The R2  of the log10 KS   PTF remained, however, low (and was not higher than 0.258). For predicting θFC , θWP   and θAWC  , the Bagging ensemble learning model, ET, was identified as the optimal choice. Across these three target variables, various combinations of features, especially PSD, OC, BD, and chemical features (containing CaCO3 , pH and CEC), delivered optimal performances in terms of RMSE, MAE and R2  value. Compared to the results of for example the multilayer perceptron model, the RMSE and MAE for predicting θFC   were reduced by up to 21.8 % and 24.4 %, respectively, while the R2  for predicting θAWC   saw a significant increase of 294.6 %.  3.2 The contribution of soil horizons on PTF improvement To evaluate the applicability of soil horizons in PTF development, five target variables were assessed across six feature combinations and tested against 20 models using three stratification strategies: stratification of soil horizons (HOR) using OHE (OHE-SH), separate PTF for topsoil, and separate PTF for subsoil. Table 3   shows the optimal model and feature combinations for predicting each target variable under each soil stratification strategy Each table entry represents the highest-performing PTF among the combinations tested. All other PTF results are available in Supplementary Material  (S1). Ensemble learning techniques, particularly the stacking and Bagging models, consistently stood out for their accuracy among the 20 models. Compared to the PTFs that did not consider stratification (Table 2 ), the inclusion of the HOR feature did not yield significant improvements in prediction accuracy. Creating separate PTFs for topsoil and subsoil even led to reduced model accuracy, with MAE increasing by up to 17.4 % and R2  reducing by as much as 60.5 % in the prediction of θs   and KS  , respectively, under topsoil stratification. In predicting θFC , θWP   and θAWC  , topsoil-stratified PTFs exhibited improved RMSE and MAE over non-stratified and OHE-SH stratified, but with a 6.1 % to 26.0 % decrease in R2 , indicating enhanced average accuracy, but reduced capability in capturing the full variability of soil properties. On the other hand, accounting for soil stratification by using OHE-SH or targeting on the subsoil did not result in better PTFs. On the contrary, subsoil PTFs now performed worse, and the higher performance of topsoil PTFs seems to be offset by the lower performance of the subsoil PTFs.  3.3 The contribution of land cover classes on PTF improvement In the quest to further optimize the predictive accuracy of PTFs, our analysis revealed interplays between feature sets, models, and LCC. Table 4   shows the optimal combinations of feature sets and models, which contain five target variables, 12 feature combinations (with and without HOR), and 20 models, tested under four LCC strategies. All results can be found in Supplementary Material  (S1). Models that employed the OHE-LCC strategy, especially with the ET model, consistently outperformed, signifying the prowess of this approach. However, under the same classification conditions, as with the previous results (Table 3 ), the inclusion of the HOR variable did not substantially enhance model accuracy. For the prediction of KS  , the PTFs that considered LCC exhibited a remarkable improvement compared to those without accounting for LCC (Table 2  without HOR and Table 3  with HOR), with reductions in RMSE and MAE by as much as 33.4 % and 35.2 % (in grassland classification), respectively, highlighting the unique soil properties associated with specific land cover. Under the consideration of LCC, the combination of PSD, OC, and BD features with the stacking model consistently demonstrated superior performance in predicting θS   for cropland, grassland, and OHE-LCC group. Such results show the pivotal relationship between individual land cover types and their intrinsic soil water retention properties. However, relative to PTFs without LCC consideration, the prediction accuracy for θS   in cropland slightly decreases, with increases in RMSE and MAE < 0.01 cm3  cm−3 , and decreases in R2  < 0.1. To predict θFC , θWP   and θAWC  , the models’ performances are relatively consistent, and the synergy of LCC and ensemble learning models, especially ET model, remains evident. The OHE-LCC and cropland group benefited from the inclusion of soil chemical features (including CaCO3 , CEC and pH), enhancing the PTFs' accuracy, with the combination including the HOR improving the R2  of predicted θAWC   by up to 30.4 %, compared to PTFs without considering LCC. For grassland predictions, the incorporation of LCC significantly improved accuracy across all target variables, and when considering HOR, the most significant gain was observed in θAWC   predictions, with RMSE and MAE being reduced by up to 41.8 % and 38.3 %, and R2  increased by up to 55.4 %. This trend fortifies the notion that a specific LCC can provide nuanced insights into the soil’s behavior under varying moisture conditions. For woodland, however, the inclusion of LCC did not yield the same level of predictive improvement as seen in other land covers.  3.4 Feature importance When assessing the model’s feature importance through SHAP values, distinct patterns emerged indicating the varying impact of different soil characteristics on the prediction of the five soil hydraulic parameters within the dataset. The summary plots for three categories: non-stratified (Table 2 ), OHE-SH (Table 3 ), and OHE-LCC (with HOR, Table 4 ) are presented in Fig. 2  . The SHAP summary plot visualizes the influence of individual features within a model on its predictive outcomes. Positioned horizontally, the points signify the strength and polarity of the impact: leftward for a negative effect on the predicted value, rightward for a positive one. The vertical layout ranks features by their predictive potency, topmost being the most pivotal. A gradient from blue to red colors the points, correlating to the actual feature values—blue for lower, red for higher. Take Sand in Fig. 2 (a): as its feature value ascends towards red, its SHAP values climb, hinting that more Sand may raise the KS  . In contrast, scanty Sand, shown by blue points veering left, corresponds to negative SHAP values, indicating that the predictions decrease compared to the baseline when there is little sand present. For KS   and θS  , the predominance of BD and PSD in the non-stratified group (Fig. 2  a and d) suggests their direct correlation with the soil’s inherent structure and its effect on transmission and retention of water. Regarding θFC   and θWP   (Fig. 2  g, h, j and k),  the PSD and CEC were predominant. An increase in clay content positively influenced both θFC   and θWP   which can be attributed to the water adsorption capabilities of finer and charged soil particles. In the case of θAWC   (Fig. 2  m and n), the emergence of PSD and CaCO3  as the primary determinants underscores the chemical-physical interplay within the soil matrix that affects water availability. The influence of CaCO3  on water retention and release patterns arises through its effects on soil structure and porosity, which in turn may affect θAWC  . Soil horizons (Fig. 2 , OHE-SH group) exhibit varied influences on hydrological properties. For KS   and θS  , the topsoil horizon (red dots) typically exerts a greater impact due to its looser structure and higher porosity, facilitating water infiltration and storage. Conversely, the influence of the subsoil (blue dots) is often less significant, possibly due to its denser composition. Regarding θFC   and θAWC  , soil horizons present a complex pattern of influence without a consistent trend, highlighting the variability in the soil’s water retention capabilities. This diversity emphasizes the need to integrate soil stratification into predictive models to accurately capture the subtle effects on soil–water dynamics. When LCC was incorporated into the model (Fig. 2  OHE-LCC with HOR group), a noticeable shift in the SHAP values across all features was observed. Specifically, for every target variable, high feature values consistently exhibited a positive influence, contrasting with models that did not include LCC. This issue is generally not attributable to the SHAP methodology itself but rather to the complexities of the data and model. These counter-intuitive results are likely due to multicollinearity introduced by LCC, which impairs model interpretability. The SHAP summary plots for the OHE-LCC (without HOR) group are provided in Supplementary Material S2 Fig. 2 , where a similar pattern is discernible. Fig. 3   shows the SHAP summary plots for the PTFs with the HOR feature for cropland, woodland, and grassland as presented in Tab. 4. Results without the HOR feature are shown in Supplementary Material S2 Fig. 3 . The SHAP summary plots clearly underscore the importance of physical indicators, with high sand content invariably associated with increased predictions of KS   across all land uses. In woodlands, the effect of BD on KS   and θS   is minimal, suggesting its limited predictive power in these contexts. For θFC  , θWP  , and θAWC  , woodland models continue to be driven by physical properties, whereas cropland models experience a notable prediction accuracy boost from chemical properties. CEC particularly stands out, with its higher values significantly raising θFC   and θWP  , predictions in croplands. However, the limited availability of woodland samples with chemical indicators in the EU-HYDI dataset precludes the inclusion of these factors in our woodland model analyses. In grasslands, PSD emerges as a more influential predictor for θFC   and θWP   than chemical indicators. Meanwhile, CaCO3  is identified as a key factor in the estimation of θAWC   within both cropland and grassland. Integrating HOR substantially improves the precision of KS , θS  , θFC   and θWP  , predictions for all land uses, with the greatest impact observed in cropland, indicating the critical role of soil layer attributes in these models.   4 Discussion 4.1 Performance of ensemble learning in developing PTFs This study compared the performance of 20 models across combinations of six common features, while also considering soil stratification and land cover, resulting in the training of a total of 6,320 models. The rigorous evaluation undertaken showcased the nuances of diverse feature combinations and modeling techniques, and the notable performance of ensemble techniques in this complex scenario highlights their potential in capturing the intricacies inherent to soil properties. Among the ensemble techniques, stacking and ET models prominently stood out. The stacking model’s success in predicting KS   and θS   can be attributed to its ability to combine predictions from multiple models, blending the strengths of individual models while offsetting their weaknesses (Chatzimparmpas et al., 2021; Wolpert, 1992 ). By achieving an RMSE as low as 0.841 log10  cm d−1  for log10 KS   and 0.027 cm3  cm−3  for θS  , 0.039 cm3  cm−3  for θFC  , 0.040 cm3  cm−3  for θWP   (Table 3 ), it aptly demonstrates its competence in representing the dataset’s diverse soil attributes. For comparison, in the benchmark study by Tóth et al. (2015) , who also considered soil stratification and applied linear regression and regression tree prediction methods using the EU-HYDI dataset (as in our study), best RMSE values for the above target parameters were 0.90 log10  cm d−1 , 0.020 cm3  cm−3 , 0.058 cm3  cm−3  and 0.043 cm3  cm−3 . Significantly, our model shows a 33.33 % improvement in predicting θFC  , underlining its enhanced efficacy in the mid-range soil moisture region where PTFs typically demonstrate lower performance (Vereecken et al., 2010 ). While a robust base model may excel in specific scenarios, increasing the variety of base models in a stacking ensemble tends to provide more consistent and reliable performance over the long term (Hagedorn et al., 2005; Zhang and Schaap, 2019; Džeroski and Ženko, 2004 ). For instance, the ET model, like the stacking model, which was seldom used for developing PTFs, consistently excelled in predicting θFC , θWP   and θAWC  . Compared to the commonly used random forest models in PTF development, the ET model randomly selects a set of split points and then chooses the split that minimizes impurity, and requires less parameter tuning, while often delivering higher computational efficiency and a lower risk of overfitting (Geurts et al., 2006; Biau and Scornet, 2016 ). It adeptly captures complex non-linear soil property relationships and is scale-invariant, seamlessly accommodating variables of different scales (such as sand/clay content and topsoil/subsoil distinctions) without extensive preprocessing (Hothorn et al., 2006; Van Looy et al., 2017 ). Therefore, ET could be a robust, versatile choice for tackling the complexities in PTF development. Ensemble techniques, like the stacking model used in this study with 10 distinct base models, offer significant predictive advantages by leveraging the strengths of individual models and offsetting their weaknesses (Wolpert, 1992; Díez-Pastor et al., 2015; Matloob et al., 2021 ). They inherently resist overfitting, a crucial benefit especially in complex PTF landscapes. Additionally, as expected, linear models, when used as meta -models in the stacking method, demonstrated superior performance, suggesting they effectively discern relationships among base model outputs (Džeroski and Ženko, 2004; Tao et al., 2023; Ženko and Džeroski, 2002 ). While theoretically, diverse models can boost accuracy, the practical development of stacking models is intricate due to multiple algorithm choices and their configurations (Chatzimparmpas et al., 2021 ). This study encompassed a wide range of machine learning methods and feature combinations to provide a comprehensive overview of their relative strengths and weaknesses in PTF development, aiming to identify potential directions for future research and applications, rather than optimizing each individual model’s performance. Therefore, manually setting hyperparameters was a strategic choice, as fully optimizing them for all models would have required over a decade of computational time, although this may have led to suboptimal performance for some models like multilayer perceptron. Despite this, the results demonstrated significant accuracy improvements compared to previous studies (Tóth et al., 2015 ). If each base model were optimized for hyperparameters to achieve high accuracy, the stacking model would likely combine the strengths of multiple high-performance models, reducing the bias and variance of individual models, thereby further enhancing overall model performance. Future research could focus on optimizing the hyperparameters of each base model to fully leverage the potential of stacking and other ensemble techniques in PTF development. This could involve advanced automated hyperparameter tuning algorithms, such as grid search and random search.
