Additionally, integrating more diverse machine learning models and feature engineering methods could further enhance predictive accuracy and robustness.  4.2 Feature importance in PTFs development Developing PTFs requires understanding of the intricate interactions between soil physicochemical and hydraulic properties. Through SHAP values, one can quantitatively analyze the influence of these features within PTFs derived from machine learning (Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Shapley, 1953 ). As expected, PSD shows rather high SHAP values in the KS   and θS   PTFs, which may be due to its direct impact on soil porosity and permeability, its integral role in representing soil structure and composition, and the varied and significant data representation of PSD across the dataset (Alaoui et al., 2011 ). With most of the samples in the EU-HYDI dataset being sourced from croplands, especially from corn and wheat fields, they show a wide variety in the degree of soil compaction, resulting from frequent mechanical tillage and other farming operations. This generally leads to increased BD values, subsequently reducing the soil’s KS   and θS   in the non-stratified group (Lin et al., 2022; Alaoui et al., 2011 ). Despite feature combinations including BD achieving higher predictive accuracy, the inclusion of HOR features often resulted in the lowest absolute SHAP values for BD when predicting θS  , θFC  , θWP   and θAWC  , which corroborates the conjectures made by Tóth et al. (2015) . This phenomenon may stem from multicollinearity (VIF > 10) between BD and features other than PSD. When HOR is introduced into the model, it would provide overlapping or more distinct information compared to BD and exhibit significant interactions with other features, thereby reducing the relative importance of BD in the predictive model (Hartemink et al., 2020 ). On the other hand, soil chemical properties not only emerged as key features in improving PTF accuracy for θFC , θWP   and θAWC  , but also highlighted the essential role of differentiating chemical interactions across varied land covers. Particularly, in croplands, plant root exudates could boost the soil cation adsorption capacity, reflected by a high SHAP value for CEC, which in turn affects θFC   and θWP  . A high CEC allows the soil to hold more nutrients and retain moisture effectively, benefiting plant growth and reducing the risk of nutrient leaching (Mensah, 2015 ). Inclusion of soil chemical indicators also led to heightened prediction accuracy for grassland soil hydraulic properties. Grassland soils, with their inherent stability and uniformity, offer a clearer correlation between chemical indicators and hydraulic properties compared to frequently intervened croplands or complex forest ecosystems. Considering that most grassland samples in the EU-HYDI dataset come from pastures, grazing activities may lead to decreased total porosity, air capacity, and saturated moisture content, while simultaneously increasing soil pH and CEC (Zhang et al., 2019 ). Elevated pH and CEC can improve soil water retention by enhancing colloidal stability and increasing the soil’s ability to hold essential cations, respectively (Delgado and Gómez, 2016 ). This, in turn, impacts θFC , θWP   and θAWC  , which could explain its high SHAP values in our results. However, Tóth et al. (2015)  found that chemical features like CEC, CaCO3 , and pH did not improve θFC   and θWP   predictions significantly. This variation from our findings could be due to the enhanced capabilities of ensemble learning, which might better capture the nuanced interactions between soil properties. Regarding the impact of soil stratification on the prediction of soil hydraulic parameters, the findings present two distinct trends. For predicting KS   and θS  , models that incorporated soil stratification did not substantially surpass those that overlooked it. This might be attributed to the fact that while these parameters are largely influenced by subsoil characteristics like macro-porosity and deep root distribution, which are less sensitive to the fine-scale variations captured by soil stratification, they are nonetheless strongly impacted by BD, OC and LCC (Jarvis et al., 2013; Dexter et al., 2004; Kay and VandenBygaart, 2002 ). Additionally, the measurement techniques for KS   and θS   may not capture the fine-scale variations that soil stratification addresses, thereby limiting the predictive benefits of incorporating stratification. Although incorporating soil stratification might not significantly improve the prediction accuracy, it adds depth to model interpretability by distinguishing between these distinct soil layers. Furthermore, the pronounced feature importance of HOR in SHAP value calculations suggests the model recognizes the inherent disparities between topsoil and subsoil. These differences, accentuated by various land cover types, underscore soil stratification’s role as a crucial factor in distinguishing soil properties and hydraulic behaviors (Yu et al., 2015 ). In summary, while the addition of soil stratification may not notably enhance prediction accuracy for certain parameters, it enriches model interpretability by highlighting the unique properties and behaviors across soil horizons, potentially even serving as a proxy for other unincorporated soil properties.  4.3 Influence of LCC strategies on PTF development Two methods are adopted to process LCC information in our study. One-hot encoding (OHE) is primarily used in machine learning and deep learning models for handling categorical variables, particularly in fields like natural language processing and land cover classification (Kuo et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2016 ). In our study, applying one-hot encoding for LCC ensured a robust sample size for PTF development and notably enhanced prediction accuracy by delineating the distinct soil attributes and hydraulic behaviors associated with various land covers. Compared to the group without LCC consideration, this approach reduced RMSE by 23.6 % and MAE by 25.9 % in predicting KS  , and increased R2  by 30.3 % in predicting θAWC  . However, according to the SHAP values (Fig. 2 , OHE-LCC group), several counter-intuitive results arose, such as higher values of clay content and sand content consistently leading to elevated predictions across all target variables. This deviates from traditional soil science principles, but these outcomes still revealed the intricate interplay among soil, water, and vegetation interactions (Pham et al., 2023 ). As a tool for interpreting machine learning model outputs, SHAP values sometimes produce counter-intuitive results. This issue is generally not attributable to the SHAP methodology itself but rather to the complexities of the data and model. In our study, these counter-intuitive results are likely due to multicollinearity introduced by LCC, which impairs model interpretability. Upon examining the VIF values (S1) for all the models with optimal predictive accuracy, we found that the VIF values for cropland and grassland in the OHE-LCC features frequently exceeded 10. In particular, the VIF values for cropland exceeded 60 when soil chemical indicators were included, indicating significant multicollinearity. One reason for this could be that one-hot encoding transforms each category into an independent binary feature, which avoids assumptions about the order of categorical data but increases the dimensionality of the input data. This may amplify the relationships between categorical features and soil physicochemical properties, leading to multicollinearity. Additionally, the EU-HYDI dataset consists of soil data provided by various European countries, where the soil characteristics of cropland and grassland are uniquely influenced by differing agricultural practices and natural conditions. When land use types are included as input alongside soil physical and chemical characteristics, these regional correlations may further exacerbate multicollinearity. When datasets were segmented based on LCC (Fig. 3 ), and PTFs were tailored for each category, these anomalies vanished, confirming our hypothesis. While multicollinearity issues persisted among feature variables, the segmented models effectively captured the complex relationships, resulting in outcomes consistent with established soil science principles. The segmentation reduced the complexity of interactions between different LCCs, minimized feature overlap and correlation, and mitigated regional correlations, thereby diminishing the impact of multicollinearity. This method bolsters interpretability and ensures accuracy, but it also results in using fewer samples, possibly impacting the robustness of specialized models. Compared to the non-classified group, the R2  for predicting KS   in cropland decreased by up to 19.7 %, and for predicting θAWC   in woodland, it decreased by as much as 17.0 %. However, for grassland predictions, the incorporation of LCC significantly improved the accuracy across all target variables, and when considering HOR, the most significant gain was observed in θAWC   predictions, with RMSE and MAE were reduced by up to 41.8 % and 38.8 %, and R2  increased by up to 55.4 %. Therefore, a trade-off is needed between enhancing model interpretability and robustness at the cost of sample size and improving accuracy at the expense of interpretability.   5 Conclusion This study aimed at testing various machine learning strategies and the contribution of different predictor features in developing robust and high-precision PTFs. The success of these models, especially in contexts where they have been less commonly applied, opens new avenues for soil property prediction. The Stacking model’s integration of multiple models' strengths and the ET model’s ability to navigate complex nonlinear relationships exemplify the potential of these techniques in soil science. To address interpretability issues in ensemble models, the study employed SHAP values to clarify feature importance in PTF development. While KS   and θS   were mainly influenced by PSD and BD, soil chemical features (including CaCO3, CEC, and pH) played a key role in the predictive accuracy of θFC , θWP   and θAWC  , especially under different LCC. However, when OHE was applied to encode LCC, the SHAP values struggled to provide accurate interpretations of the model, leading to some counterintuitive results. Thus, a trade-off between enhancing model interpretability and robustness at the expense of sample size and improving accuracy at the expense of interpretability needs to be considered. Conversely, while soil stratification may not markedly improve the predictive precision in developing PTFs, the emphasized feature importance of HOR in SHAP value analysis suggests that the model recognizes the intrinsic disparities between topsoil and subsoil. Meanwhile, these distinctions, further highlighted by various land cover types, not only underscore the pivotal role of soil stratification in differentiating soil properties and hydraulic behaviors but also add a crucial layer of complexity to the study, offering deeper insights into the effects of different soil layers. This study elucidated the potential of ensemble learning in the development of high-precision PTFs soil hydraulics, as well as the feasibility of using SHAP values for model interpretability, hoping to offer a new perspective and methodology to tackle the challenges of predicting hydraulic properties.
1 Introduction Chinese cities have witnessed an increasing frequency of pluvial floods in recent years, driven by the profound impacts of climate change (H. Shang et al., 2019; W. Zhang et al., 2021 ). According to a 2023 announcement by the Ministry of Emergency Management of the People’s Republic of China (2024) , approximately 52.789 million people were affected by flood disasters throughout the year. Old urban areas, characterized by complex land use and inadequate infrastructure, exhibit high vulnerability to pluvial floods (Francipane et al., 2021; Zhang R. et al., 2019 ). In 2023, old communities in cities such as Guilin, Guangxi (late May), Baojing, Hunan (late June), Xianning, Hubei (mid-July), and Xiamen, Fujian (early September) experienced severe pluvial floods, necessitating large-scale emergency operations involving rescuers and lifeboats to save affected residents (Fig. 1  ). Optimizing stormwater systems in these old communities has emerged as a critical imperative for effectively addressing precipitation extremes (Shang L. et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023 ). However, the transformation of Sponge Cities in old neighborhoods faces numerous challenges. First, the design criteria governing drainage pipe networks in these areas generally fall short of optimal standards (H. Wang et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2023 ). Additionally, old urban areas have limited green spaces, and passive sponge facilities inherently exhibit limitations in mitigating runoff peaks during torrential downpours (Chan et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2019; Mei et al., 2018, 2018; Song et al., 2021; Yin et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, the planning of sponge facilities should balance the socializing, sports, and recreational needs of residents to increase spatial equity (Gu et al., 2022 ; R. Wang et al., 2022 ). Given these constraints, promoting the spatial configuration of multi-functional infrastructures in old urban areas has become crucial for enhancing flood resilience. In April 2023, the Chinese government proposed integrating dual-use public infrastructures in megacities to serve both regular and emergency purposes. For flood-related emergencies, this initiative focuses on harnessing the potential functionality of plazas, sports fields, and similar public spaces as temporary flood detention ponds (Netzel et al., 2021 ). In urban design disciplines, dual-use public spaces for flood detention have a historical precedent, exemplified by the renowned Water Plaza in Rotterdam, Netherlands (Biesbroek et al., 2014 ). Similarly, Washington Park in Illinois, USA repurposed soccer fields as storage ponds, resulting in investment savings of $5 million (Jackson, 2010 ). Rouault et al. (2023)  have documented cases of multifunctional sports facilities, a stormwater playground, and a public park in Hamburg, Germany as well. The proactive approach of “dual-use transformation” offers significant advantages in efficient space utilization, making water plazas particularly suitable for flood management in the complex environments of old communities. However, the implementation of this commendable approach faces obstacles due to unclear managerial rules and obligations (Naughton et al., 2021 ). Manual operations may further exacerbate these challenges by increasing costs and risks. Additionally, prolonged detention of runoff, even in automated systems, poses potential hazards. Such detention not only endangers pedestrian safety but also raises health concerns, as stagnant water may harbor pathogenic bacteria (Sales-Ortells & Medema, 2015 ). Given these gaps, real-time control (RTC) solutions emerge as a promising avenue to address the complexities of managing water plazas. Related RTC applications in stormwater systems aim to mitigate combined sewer overflow (CSO) occurrences and peak runoff during storm events (Lund et al., 2018; Shishegar et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2021 ). RTC of drainage pipes and nodes minimizes overflow risks by predicting and adjusting available storage volume using Rule-Based Control (RBC) or Model Predictive Control (MPC) algorithms (Beeneken et al., 2013; Löwe et al., 2016; Pleau et al., 2005; Weyand, 2002 ). However, constraints persist even with real-time optimization due to the limited design capacities of existing pipe networks (Garofalo et al., 2017 ). To address this limitation, RTC applications have been progressively extended since 2018 to include more prototypes of smart stormwater infrastructures. These include road storage units with smart inlets (Kändler et al., 2020, 2022; Lund et al., 2019 ), smart detention basins (Bilodeau et al., 2018; Shishegar et al., 2019, 2021; Zhou et al., 2023 ), smart rain barrels (Oberascher et al., 2019, 2021; Xu et al., 2022 ), smart blue-green roofs (Busker et al., 2022; Cristiano et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024 ), and smart tanks (Li & Burian, 2023; Sun et al., 2023 ). Table 1   presents a compendium of studies published since 2018, offering a comparison of pivotal RTC metrics such as scale, 1D/2D platform, algorithms, prototype design, resilience contribution, dynamic flood patterns, and multi-horizon comparisons. This comparison elucidates current gaps in the following three aspects:(1) Lack of Dual-Use Mechanisms.  Previous RTC prototypes primarily focus on retrofitting existing types of stormwater infrastructure, showing a significant lack of integration of dual-use public spaces to enhance storage volume. Moreover, effective utilization of temporary detention spaces necessitates a thorough interdisciplinary approach that utilizes spatial configuration and 3D modeling in urban design disciplines (Biesbroek et al., 2014; Souza, 2022 ).  (2) 1D Modeling Limitations.  The prevalent use of the 1D SWMM model for developing RTC algorithms has failed to accurately capture the dynamics of pluvial flood patterns during torrential events (Jean et al., 2022; Li & Burian, 2023; Liang et al., 2021; Sadler et al., 2019 ). The 1D approach is unable to effectively integrate 2D elements with hypsographic data into the RTC framework, resulting in a disconnect between hydrological analysis and spatial terrain design (Henonin et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2023 ).  (3) Lack of Resilience Contribution Analysis.  Previous RTC studies have rarely systematically described the resistance and recovery processes of stormwater systems during extreme precipitation events (Casal-Campos et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2017 ). This lack of system performance assessment makes it challenging to determine the overall contribution of RTC to urban flood resilience (Li & Burian, 2023; Mugume et al., 2015 ). Additionally, previous research has not included multi-horizon comparisons, making it difficult to provide reasonable recommendations on response times for urban emergency and water management departments.    To address the aforementioned gaps, this paper advances a solution in the form of a Smart Water Plaza (SWP) system, aimed at integrating predictive control and dual-use public spaces in old urban areas. SWPs utilize enclosed plazas, sports fields, or parking lots to mitigate downstream flooding by restraining discharges at staggered intervals during peak storm hours (Fig. 1 ). This empirical research aims to achieve the following objectives: (1) providing a systematic method for recognizing and organizing two SWP prototypes in high-risk old communities; (2) proposing a 2D-1D MPC algorithm using InfoWorks ICM, detailing the optimization procedure, modeling conditions, and evaluation criteria; (3) analyzing the effectiveness of SWPs in enhancing flood resilience through system performance curves and dynamic flood pattern diagrams; and (4) comparing the impact of various forecast horizons on the efficiency of SWPs. The overall methodology aims to comprehensively demonstrate the potential of SWPs to manage pluvial floods. This offers valuable insights for urban designers, hydrological engineers, and decision-makers when planning multi-use public spaces as part of urban renewal efforts.  2 The Smart Water Plaza (SWP) system 2.1 Two SWP prototypes 2.1.1 In-situ detention units The SWP system encompasses two distinct types of units. An in-situ detention unit (Fig. 2  ) temporarily manages runoff from the individual catchment in which it is located. Runoff may originate not solely from the plaza itself but also from a broader area within the same catchment. When designing this unit, it is unnecessary to allocate the entire plaza for runoff storage. Instead, a designated storage zone is established, with storage depths varying between 0.1 m and 1.2 m at the lowest point. This requires a clearly defined enclosure and the renovation of water-retaining structures at the periphery. Low walls, steps, or ramps can define storage zones while maintaining unobstructed regular access. For RTC operations, an automatic valve is installed at the outlet, and an overflow well is essential to prevent water levels from exceeding the storage capacity. Fig. 2  illustrates the conversion of a landscaped plaza into an in-situ detention unit as an example.  2.1.2 Runoff-receiving units A runoff-receiving unit utilizes sunken sports fields or lawns to accommodate runoff from multiple adjacent catchments through pipes or channels (Fig. 3  ). The unit relies on topographical elevation and gravitational forces to orchestrate the trajectory of the runoff. Therefore, it is regulated by both inlet and outlet valves. When designing this unit, the designer should first ascertain the storage zone, maximum depth (not exceeding 1.2 m), and runoff inlets. The flow in the surrounding pipes can be determined from monitored data or pre-simulations, which helps in selecting inlets to ensure that diverted runoff aligns with storage capacity. The outlet valve operates in inverse synchronization with the inlet valve to maintain balanced flow dynamics. Additionally, the unit is designed with an overflow mechanism to guarantee safety. Fig. 3  exemplifies the spatial design of a sunken athletic field, supplemented by a detailed sectional view.   2.2 Case study 2.2.1 The study area The study area, Wangchengpo, is located in the Yuelu District of Changsha, China, covering approximately 4.5 km2  (Fig. 4  a). The boundaries were delineated by overlaying administrative demarcations and watershed borders. Comprising ten old communities, all constructed before the year 2000, this neighborhood is home to approximately 140,000 residents. The cumulative pluvial flood risk across the site is significant. The drainage network was engineered based on a 1-year return period, with runoff accumulation potentially exceeding 0.5 m at the Leifeng Road Interchange and the Fenglin 2nd Road Interchange during storm events. Additionally, the Jiantang Community is notably vulnerable, having experienced numerous incidents of flooded parking garages in recent years. An Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) was employed to acquire an orthographic map and a digital surface model (DSM), achieving a high resolution within 0.1 m. Manhole and conduit data were sourced from the “Flood Control and Drainage Planning” document, courtesy of the Changsha Planning & Design Survey Research Institute. Several manhole locations were further verified during the site investigation phase.  2.2.2 SWP system layout To identify potential SWPs in the community's public spaces, four evaluation indicators were employed: average slope, distance to observed flood points, distance to drainage nodes, and distance to surface runoff pathways. Mapping was conducted using the ArcGIS platform, where buffer zones were established, and a spatial overlay analysis of the four equally weighted indicators was performed. Fig. 4 b illustrates the results of this potential evaluation. The study then scaled down to each site to assess whether the plazas could meet the diversion criteria for runoff-receiving units or should only function as in-situ detention units. Additionally, a terrain renovation design was conducted to facilitate the determination of the precise locations and volumetric capacities of storage zones within the units. Following the spatial configuration, 34 plazas were designated as in-situ detention units, and three plazas were identified as runoff-receiving units (Table 2  ). Fig. 5  a presents the overall layout. The cumulative area of the SWP system is 0.23 km2 , representing 5 % of the study area, with the actual area functioning as storage zones being 0.06 km2 . The land serving as the source of regulated runoff comprises 22 % of the study area, and the maximum storage capacity of the SWPs is estimated to be 43,100 m3 .  2.2.3 2D-1D baseline model A hydrodynamic model was developed using InfoWorks ICM for evaluating SWPs’ performance in pluvial flood control. The adopted 2D-1D approach departs from the conventional 1D or 1D-2D approach that computes runoff generation based on artificially designated 1D catchments. Instead, this approach involves the direct application of rainfall onto a 2D grid, allowing runoff to navigate through variable elevation zones and ultimately converge at 1D nodes (Henonin et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2023 ). The 2D-1D approach necessitates high-resolution spatial data, thereby providing a more precise description of SWP terrain design and dynamic flood patterns. The procedures for model establishment (Fig. 5 b) are as follows:(1) 3D Model Reconstruction.  The high-precision DSM was initially modified by excluding interferences from canopy trees and viaducts using supervised segmentation in ArcGIS. The raster was then resampled as a 1 m point cloud and reloaded into Rhino 7.0. Leveraging the robust meshing tools of Rhino 7.0, this phase involved a thorough 3D reconstruction process to accurately represent the terrain variations of SWPs. Elevation points, accurate to 1 m, were extracted from the 3D model. The refined data, encompassing buildings, green spaces, roads, and the drainage network, was integrated into the InfoWorks ICM platform.  (2) 2D-1D Configurations . The platform facilitated the convergence of runoff from 2D grids into 1D nodes or its accumulation by delineating roughness, infiltration, and hydraulic zones, based on terrain circumstances. The average size of the 2D mesh within InfoWorks ICM was set at 20 m2 . This study integrated 2D walls into the model to serve as water-retaining structures for the SWPs. The inlet and outlet pipes connecting the SWPs were configured as variable links, enhancing adaptability. The valve node was designed to match the diameter of the associated variable link, ensuring congruence, with an opening rate set at 0.02 m/s.  (3) Calibration and Validation.  Two rainfall events in 2023 were used for calibrating and validating the 2D-1D model. A portable ultrasonic level sensor was used to measure the water depth at a flood-prone spot in the Jiantang community. Beijing AQUAROOT Environmental Technology (Changsha) Co. assisted in collecting the data at 10-minute intervals. Precipitation data were acquired via an automated weather station located near the site, with measurements taken at 5-minute intervals. Indicators of the coefficient of determination (R2  ) and Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency coefficient (NSE ) were quantitatively assessed, yielding validation values of 0.749 and 0.831, respectively, thereby demonstrating the model's validity.    The calibrated 2D-1D model provided a robust foundation for algorithm programming, scenario reconstruction, and multi-horizon analysis of the SWPs. More detailed comparisons between the 1D, 1D-2D, and 2D-1D models, along with calibration figures, are provided in the supplementary materials .    3 Control methodology 3.1 Predictive control algorithms The algorithm executes control based on forecasted rainfall and discriminative rules. The fundamental principle is to select the optimal control command C    from possible options during each control horizon τ    to achieve effective pluvial flood mitigation with minimal activation of SWPs. A pre-simulation identified the most severely affected flooding point, Node 0 (Fig. 5 a), characterized by the highest flood depth and the longest duration. Flood depth at Node 0 is monitored and simulated to predict the real-time control effects. Three control horizons—5, 30, and 60 minutes—were compared to assess the impact of control frequency on overall performance. At the beginning of horizon τ   , the input parameter R  τ      is defined as the total expected rainfall in this subsequent horizon. The algorithm activates SWP units 1 to n    by determining whether the current/predicted water level h  0 , τ     ,h  0 , τ + 1      at Node 0 exceeds its ground level H  0     , forming a command array C = [ δ  1   , δ  2   , … … , δ  n   ]    (Default C = [ 0 , 0 , … … , 0 ]   ). h  0 , τ      is obtained directly by a level sensor and the algorithm utilizes the 2D-1D baseline model to simulate h  0 , τ + 1      with R  τ      and C    (Eq. If no flood is detected, the algorithm inputs R  τ      and Default C    to simulate h  0 , τ + 1      using the 2D-1D model. If h  0 , τ + 1   ⩽ H  0     , then no units should be activated, maintaining the default state. If all planned SWPs were controlled individually, 237  commands would need to be simulated at a single horizon, far exceeding RTC requirements. Therefore, it is necessary to uniformly control certain units to maintain efficiency. In this study, each runoff-receiving unit was autonomously controlled, while all in-situ detention units were collectively regarded as a unified entity with a consistent state. Consequently, n    in this study was set as 4 instead of 37, and the maximum C    needed to be simulated simultaneously was 16. It is important to emphasize that uniformly controlling in-situ storage units, which utilize more spaces to achieve staggered discharge, does not diminish the effectiveness of flood control, although it may affect larger urban functional areas. The consistency of the forecasted and control horizons is also crucial to highlight. In prior research on smart detention basins (Zhou et al., 2023 ), a control horizon of 5 minutes was implemented, with a forecast horizon of 90 minutes. The measure was adopted to ensure that the basins could be emptied in advance. As the SWP units do not require pre-empty operations, they can maintain consistent forecasted and control horizons, which further helps reduce computational consumption.  3.2 Modeling approaches 3.2.1 Control programming The programming of the control algorithm was executed with InfoWorks ICM Exchange, leveraging its inherent RTC editor and Ruby scripting capabilities. The process involves several steps:(1) Initialization of Variables and Rules . Utilizing the RTC editor, this step involved the establishment of global variables, including R  τ      and h  0 , τ     . Variable links were configured with the internal variable δ  n      for each SWP unit. Variables and forecasted rainfall inputs were integrated to form control rules.  (2) Ruby Scripts . Scripts were implemented to streamline the filtering procedures of the optimal solution within a single horizon.  (3) Rolling Horizon Simulation.  After execution, the model used the results from the previous horizon as the initial conditions for the subsequent one, thus enabling a continuous, rolling horizon simulation until the completion of the process.  (4) Results Exportation and Comparative Analysis . Upon completion, the results were exported to the ArcGIS platform for advanced visualization. A comparative analysis was conducted on data derived from different simulated scenarios.     3.2.2 Modelling conditions This research presents a comparative analysis of four distinct control scenarios: a static scenario, and SWP implementations with 5, 30, and 60-minute intervals. Given the challenges associated with securing high-precision real data, this study first employed the storm formula of Changsha (supplementary material s) to generate four 180-minute design rainstorms corresponding to 5, 10, 20, and 100-year return periods. Design events, modeled after the Chicago pattern, primarily served to evaluate the resilience contribution of the SWP system. Recognizing the limitations of design events in replicating peak fluctuation processes, the study additionally incorporated an actual rainfall event on August 25, 2021 (16 h, 137 mm) to visualize the flood pattern dynamics of SWPs during multi-peak events. A key assumption was made regarding the rainfall inputs, postulating them to be 100 % accurate, thereby deliberately overlooking potential distortions caused by nowcasting errors. The ambient rainfall inputs were characterized by a 5-minute interval, while forecasted rainfall inputs were categorized into 5, 30, and 60-minute intervals.   3.3 Evaluation metrics 3.3.1 Failure curves for design events System performance curves serve as a pivotal tool for evaluating the flood resilience of stormwater systems (Guptha et al., 2022; Li & Burian, 2023; Mugume et al., 2015 ). This approach was employed to assess the resilience improvements contributed by SWPs under design rainfall with multiple return periods. According to Chinese flooding standards, manholes with a water depth exceeding 0.15 m for at least 30 minutes are designated as failed nodes.
