The research utilized depth visualizations at 0.3 m intervals, designating any depth exceeding 0.6 m as high risk. In conjunction with flood dynamics, the study further quantified three indicators to evaluate the flood mitigation contributed by SWPs:(1) Uncontrolled Flooded Area.  This metric calculates the mesh area where the water depth surpasses 0.15 m on ArcGIS, excluding the storage zones within the SWPs.  (2) High-Risk Zones.  This index quantifies the mesh area with water depth exceeding 0.6 m outside the confines of SWPs.  (3) Variation in Water Depth at Node 0 . This measure evaluates the efficacy of the SWP in reducing the peak water depth at the monitored Node 0, considering both the magnitude and duration.       4 Results and analysis 4.1 Failure curves in SWP scenarios Table 3   elucidates the reduction in failed nodes and the resilience contributions attributed to SWP scenarios. Overall, the results indicate that SWPs can enhance the operational efficiency of the stormwater system under various return periods. However, it is observed that the regulatory impact progressively diminishes as the return period increases. Moreover, the efficacy of SWPs is influenced by the control horizon as well. The most notable outcomes were achieved when the SWPs were regulated with a 5-minute horizon. This scenario resulted in a reduction of the maximum failed nodes r  f n      by 24.0 %, 19.7 %, 18.6 %, and 14 % for 5, 10, 20, and 100-year return period events, respectively. Correspondingly, it manifested a resilience contribution index RCI    of 38.3 %, 15.3 %, 14.1 %, and 8.6 %. Further insights from multi-horizon comparisons indicate an inverse relationship between the frequency of control horizons and flood mitigation effectiveness. Fig. 7   delineates the failure curves F ( τ )    of SWP scenarios. The analysis reveals that SWPs prolong the recovery time of the stormwater system by approximately 1.5 to 3 hours in comparison to the static scenario, aligning with the principles of the staggered discharge strategy. A noteworthy observation was the minor fluctuations in the SWP’s recovery phase. This phenomenon can be primarily attributed to the predictive control enacted at 30 and 60 minutes, which may facilitate rapid runoff discharge, consequently leading to a marginal resurgence of flooding at certain nodes. Conversely, the control at a finer resolution of 5 minutes, marked by its enhanced precision, effectively precluded such performance oscillations.  4.2 Flood dynamics in SWP scenarios The actual event occurring on August 25, 2021, has been chosen for a comprehensive analysis and visualization of the SWPs’ efficacy under multi-peak rainfall events. The findings (Table 4  ) indicate that SWP scenarios collectively contributed to a reduction in uncontrolled flooded areas within the community, ranging from 46 % to 48 %. Notably, the diminution rate in areas categorized as high-risk fluctuated between 35 % and 45 %. Subsequent analysis of Node 0 revealed that the peak water depth in the static scenario reached as high as 1.1 m, persisting for 8 hours. In contrast, three SWP scenarios resulted in a notable reduction in the maximum water depth, confined to between 0.6 and 0.8 m, with the duration curtailed to 4 to 6 hours (Fig. 8  ). Consistent with the findings in the preceding section, the 30- and 60-minute SWP scenarios exhibited brief periods of ponding during the recovery phase. This occurrence was primarily due to the expedited discharge from the plazas. Fig. 8  highlights these transient fluctuations with red arrows, pinpointing the instances of short-term water depth variation. Fig. 9   meticulously illustrates the flood dynamics throughout the study area over an 8-hour period from 10:00 to 17:00. The variograms presented offer compelling evidence to support the capacity of the SWPs to effectively accommodate storms characterized by multiple peak fluctuations.   5 Discussions 5.1 Major innovations This modeling-based study provides evidence and illustrates the viability of dual-use Smart Water Plazas (SWPs) in effectively enhancing community-level flood resilience. Compared to published smart RTC prototypes, SWPs proactive manage public spaces for temporary flood detention, instead of traditional facilities such as pipes, detention basins, or tanks, significantly expanding valuable emergency spaces in old neighborhoods. Therefore, the unique attribute lies in their ability to improve resilience without necessitating a renovation of existing drainage pipe networks. Although RTC technologies have reached a stage of relative maturity, the novelty of this research is primarily manifested in the following two aspects. 5.1.1 Improvements in MPC modeling and temporal analysis This article systematically elucidates a practical spatial realization of MPC systems. Previous studies using 1D platforms frequently relied on oversimplified site descriptions or hypothetical settings, failing to accurately reflect the complexities of real-world implementations. This study addresses the disconnect between theoretical hydrological analysis and spatial design by programming control algorithms on a 2D-1D model. Derived from high-precision DSM and Rhino 3D models, this approach offers higher complexity and fidelity to real urban spaces. It can directly reflect terrain configurations and verify their suitability for temporary flood detention. By integrating Rhino, InfoWorks ICM, and ArcGIS, urban designers, and hydrological engineers can better collaborate using this 2D-1D workflow to harness the disaster prevention potential of urban public spaces. This study also conducted secondary development of MPC control scripts, introducing an effective filtering procedure. The MPC workload involved in multi-horizon comparisons is noteworthy. The results indicate that coarser intervals may facilitate the rapid discharge of temporary detention runoff, potentially leading to flood resurgence at certain nodes. Additionally, this study systematically analyzes the contribution of SWPs to the resilience of urban stormwater systems using failure curves, forming a robust system of temporal analysis. Furthermore, the study demonstrates dynamic flood patterns during multi-peak rainfall events. Previous research has primarily focused on CSO and peak runoff reduction, with few studies supporting real-time extraction of high-risk zones using MPC. In summary, the 2D-1D MPC adapts well to the complex land use in urban planning. Multi-horizon comparisons, failure curves, and flood variograms demonstrate core characteristics of the short-term responses in urban hydrology.  5.1.2 High applicability in sponge city transformation and urban renewal SWPs leverage the disaster mitigation potential inherent in surface public spaces, demonstrating the potential to reduce the costs of renovating drainage pipe networks. Moreover, SWPs exhibit high applicability in high-density old communities, where the expansion of sponge facilities is often constrained by complex land use. Our case study indicates that the proposed prototypes adapt well to various plazas, sports fields, or parking lots with different terrains, while high-precision control horizons effectively respond to varying rainfall fluctuations. Given that there are approximately 160,000 old residential communities nationwide, with more than 42 million households, SWPs present a broad range of application scenarios across China. China has entered a new era of comprehensive sponge city construction. However, the traditional planning method of annual runoff volume decomposition is inadequate for adapting to future precipitation extremes. This study innovatively integrates a dynamic time sequence into static sponge city planning methodologies, thereby enhancing adaptability. This integration represents an evolution from a passive process, traditionally focused on risk assessment, sponge facilities, and pipe maintenance, to an active renewal characterized by predictive control. This new approach can support old communities in seeking national funding for Sponge City transformation and acquiring social capital for urban renewal. Despite historically modest levels of automation within stormwater systems in China, there is a noticeable and progressive trend towards increased RTC. The recent release of the “Technical Standard for RTC of Urban Drainage Systems (Draft)” by the China Urban Water Supply and Drainage Association in November 2023 provides a standard basis for SWPs. This document signifies a collective recognition within the industry of the importance of smart stormwater infrastructure.   5.2 Limitations and future works 5.2.1 Control uncertainty and operational efficiency The algorithm hinges on a 2D-1D model to enable comparative assessments of potential solutions. Nevertheless, the absence of a 100 % accurate digital twin introduces certain ambiguous processes within the framework. Firstly, the parameters governing drainage pipe networks and surface runoff processes are subject to inherent deviations. Secondly, the hydraulic characteristics of valves are derived from commonly used values, leading to discrepancies in real-world applications. Furthermore, this research assumes accurate rainfall predictions and does not explicitly tackle the issue of data faults in practical settings. At present, meteorological products in China can provide one-hour nowcasting data, which falls short of the 5-minute resolution mandated by the UK (Pulkkinen et al., 2019; Ravuri et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2020 ). All these aspects warrant detailed examination in future explorations. A 2D-1D model necessitates extensive data preparation and significant computational power. Although effective for assessing SWPs, this approach poses challenges in real-world scheduling applications due to its slow computation rate. Deep learning (DL), a “model-free” method, can alleviate the computation burden of MPC through offline training. Luo et al. (2023)  observed that the DL-based surrogate model effectively matched the mechanism model, reducing the computational time by 99.1 %. Bowes et al. (2020)  conducted a comparative analysis of MPC and DL, which demonstrated a significant speed improvement of 88 times. Saliba et al. (2020)  emphasized that DL can provide stability by effectively handling faults in prediction. Hence, future research efforts could focus on training a DL-based surrogate model using the 2D-1D model for practical deployments. Additionally, due to the large number of SWPs planned, the total number of control arrays in the filtering procedures was simplified in this study. By leveraging the rapid computation capabilities of DL, future research will be able to compare more arrays within one horizon, thereby significantly enhancing the accuracy of predictive control.  5.2.2 Promotion challenges and cost-benefit analysis Although the SWP prototype identification and control algorithm proposed demonstrates a degree of generalizability, the paper presents findings based on a single climate zone and a single city. The effectiveness of SWPs is highly dependent on the availability of public spaces, and their performance in cities with different climate zones requires further analysis and validation. Additionally, this paper primarily focuses on old urban areas and does not sufficiently address the necessity and potential benefits of planning SWPs in regions with relatively well-developed drainage networks. Within China's top-down Sponge City planning framework, project managers are typically not mandated to implement dual-use public infrastructures, as long as the site's total annual runoff control rate aligns with stipulated standards. Therefore, the potential funding sources for SWPs remain unclear. Moreover, cost-benefits associated with the SWP's space renovation, equipment arrangement, operations, and maintenance require further investigation. The SWP proposal is a typical community-based flood preparedness plan that necessitates considerable public awareness (Pradhananga & Davenport, 2017; Šakić Trogrlić et al., 2018 ). Hence, the exploration of effective strategies to motivate broader stakeholder engagement in pluvial flood control becomes imperative (Wolff, 2021 ). Future research should explore stakeholder engagement to facilitate this participation.    6 Conclusions The integration of dual-use public spaces stands at the forefront of urban planning initiatives for mitigating the repercussions of natural disasters. This research introduces an enhanced Smart Water Plaza system, engineered with predictive control to effectively alleviate pluvial floods. A high-risk old community in Changsha, China has been selected for this empirical investigation. The study establishes two distinct types of SWP units based on spatial mapping, potential analysis, and terrain design. A pivotal component of the system is the implementation of a 2D-1D MPC algorithm guided by forecasted rainfall at three intervals. The study conducts a thorough evaluation of the SWP system's performance under various design rainfalls and during an actual event. The main findings are as follows:(1) SWPs achieve an obvious resilience contribution index for the current stormwater system, with a range of 9 % to 38 % for storms with return periods of 5 to 100 years.  (2) Results of an actual event highlight a reduction in uncontrolled flooded areas, ranging between 46 % and 48 %, utilizing SWPs, which constitute only 5 % of the studied old urban area.  (3) The effectiveness of SWPs is influenced by the accuracy of the control horizon. Lower control precision at 30 and 60 minutes might lead to temporary flooding during the system's recovery phase, which can be prevented by using a 5-minute control horizon.    The results underscore an enhanced flood resilience in old communities brought by smart multifunctional landscapes. The SWP proposal demonstrates a strong response to China’s cutting-edge initiative of promoting dual-use public infrastructure for regular and emergency situations. Future research should consider developing surrogate models to improve computational efficiency. Additionally, efforts should be directed toward exploring community-based flood preparedness and public willingness to participate. While this work primarily focuses on the implementation of SWPs in old urban areas, future studies should evaluate the performance of SWPs across a broader range of urban environments, considering different climatic conditions and infrastructure states.
1 Introduction Water resources management and flood mitigation are crucial issues in hydrological analysis, particularly in regions where floods are prevalent. The flow coefficient is a fundamental parameter in the hydrological analysis to estimate the river’s discharge and flood potential (Burch et al., 1987 ). Accurate estimation of the flow coefficient is essential in mitigating flood-related damages (Savenije, 1996 ), administering flood alert mechanisms, and regulating water discharge. However, determining the flow coefficient accurately is a challenging task due to the need for a comprehensive understanding of various factors such as the hydrology, climate, topography, and soil characteristics of the river basin (McNamara et al., 1988; Bayazit, 1999 ). A hydrological analysis is critical in managing water resources and mitigating flood damages in regions prone to floods. In hydrological study, an accurate calculation of the flow coefficient is critical, and various methods have been developed to estimate it (Blume et al., 2007; Abrahart and See, 2000 ). Statistical, empirical, and machine-learning techniques have been used to estimate the flow coefficient with varying degrees of success (Azari et al., 2022; Ali et al., 2022 ). In recent years, machine learning techniques have gained popularity in hydrological analysis due to their ability to model complex relationships and handle large datasets. ANFIS, SMRGT, and ANN are three machine-learning techniques used to estimate the flow coefficient with varying degrees of success. ANFIS is a hybrid method that combines fuzzy logic and neural networks to create a model that can handle uncertainties and non-linearity in the data (Hsu et al., 2002; Riad et al., 2004; Mazvimavi et al., 2005 ). SMRGT is a rule-based method that uses simple membership functions to create rules representing the relationship between input and output variables. ANN is a neural network-based method that can model complex relationships between input and output variables (Shamseldin, 1997; Zealand et al., 1999 ). The cities emphasize the precise computation of flow coefficients within regions that collect rainfall and have even developed tables for flow coefficients. The compelling study of the coefficient is a highly complex operation due to many influencing variables (Lallam et al., 2018 ). A range of methodologies has been documented in the literature for flow coefficient modelling, including statistical, empirical, and machine-learning techniques (Blume et al., 2007 ). However, most of these methods rely on opaque techniques that need more generalizability, making it challenging to apply them to other study regions (Zounemat-Kermani et al., 2021; Gandomi et al., 2021; Kashani et al., 2021 ). Modelling techniques are categorized as empirical, conceptual, or physically based models. Empirical models use pre-existing data and are referred to as data-driven models (Hsu et al., 1995; Zealand et al., 1999 ). Conceptual models use semi-empirical equations and physical data to calibrate the model. Physically based models offer a more authentic approach to modelling by mathematically representing the actual phenomenon but are limited by their complexity and computational cost (Uvo and Tolle, 2000; Anmala et al., 2000; Abrahart and See, 2000 ). Empirical models, such as Fuzzy Inference Systems and Artificial Neural Network models, have become increasingly popular. Recent studies (Riad et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2017 ) employed both empirical and physically based methods to predict flow coefficient, with empirical models being widely utilized to describe complicated interconnections in a variety of hydrology parameters, such as rainfall-runoff prediction and stream flow prediction. Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) and fuzzy logic have emerged as promising alternatives for flow coefficient estimation in hydrological analysis. ANNs were developed in the 1940 s as a computational model based on the structure and operation of the human brain (Toprak, 2009; Coskun, 2014 ). ANNs can model complex relationships between input and output variables and handle large datasets. On the other hand, fuzzy logic was introduced by Zadeh in 1965 and gained popularity in engineering and management for addressing forecasting and planning challenges (Yalaz and Atay, 2016 ). Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have emerged as a highly effective method for modelling hydrological phenomena related to rainfall-runoff processes (ASCETask CommitteeI, 2000; ASCETask CommitteeII, 2000 ). Compared to traditional modelling approaches, ANNs have demonstrated a higher level of efficacy (Halff and Halff Azmoodeh, 1993 ). Previous studies (Kaltech, 2008; Smith and Eli, 1995 ) have created three-layer feed-forward ANNs that employ rainfall hydrographs as input and output hydrographs, expanding the scope of potential ANNs applications in rainfall–runoff analysis. Several studies (Hsu et al., 2002; Zealand et al., 1999; Tokar and Johnson, 1999 ) have employed ANNs for runoff modelling due to the compatibility of the phenomenon of rainfall-runoff with ANNs. The Adaptive Neural Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) was proposed as a fusion of ANNs and fuzzy systems (Ghose et al., 2013; Suparta and Samah, 2020; Razali et al., 2020; Nath et al., 2019; Jang, 1993 ) which allows the system to acquire knowledge from ambiguous input data and expedite the process of drawing conclusions. ANFIS can effectively utilize the self-learning and memory capabilities of ANNs, resulting in a more sustainable training process (Huang et al., 2017 ). The Adaptive Neural Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) was proposed by Jang in 1993, which integrates the capabilities of ANNs and fuzzy logic (Sevgin and Toprak, 2019 ). The ANFIS methodology combines the ANN’s learning capabilities to derive fuzzy if-then rules that exhibit suitable membership functions. This integration enables the system to acquire knowledge from ambiguous input data and expedites conclusion. Additionally, ANFIS can effectively utilize neural networks’ self-learning and memory capabilities, resulting in a more sustainable training process (Unes et al., 2020 ). ANFIS has been used in various applications of hydrological analysis, including flow coefficient estimation (Kashani et al., 2021; Jang, 1993 ). In 2009, Toprak developed the Simple Membership Functions and the Fuzzy Rules Generation Technique (SMRGT), which is a novel approach that considers physical causality and aims to aid individuals in determining the appropriate quantity, structure, and rationale of membership functions and fuzzy rules for a given fuzzy set. The Fuzzy SMRGT technique utilizes uncomplicated membership functions (MFs) and fuzzy rules (FRs) to produce precise forecasts by leveraging expert knowledge and accessible data (Toprak, 2009 ). This approach improves interpretability compared to other fuzzy methods, facilitating domain experts’ comprehension and customization of the model (Coskun, 2014; Yalaz and Atay, 2016 ). The SMRGT technique has been employed in various applications, including simulating flow discharge in open canals (Toprak, 2017 ), assessing losses in drinking water networks (Unes et al., 2020 ), assessing water surface profiles in open channels (Toprak, 2017 ), and categorizing floors regarding their seismic properties, and estimating the flow rate of a river using different models (Altas et al., 2017 ). Toprak investigated the SMRGT approach’s strengths, limitations, and actual implementation (Toprak, 2017 ). The ANFIS and other fuzzy systems lack a conclusive method for determining the number of fuzzy rules and membership functions necessary for each rule, in addition to lacking a learning algorithm to improve the precision of the matrix factorization process by limiting output error. In the recent literature (Vojtek et al., 2023; Akay, 2021; Arora et al., 2021 ), there has been a growing interest in implementing a combination of MCDM methods and metaheuristics with machine learning techniques for various applications. One noteworthy application is the estimation of the flow coefficient in river basins, which plays a crucial role in water resource management. Specifically, researchers have explored the implementation of Fuzzy Set Theory, Self-Organizing Map (SOM) Neural Networks, and Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference Systems (ANFIS) for flow coefficient estimation. The integration of Fuzzy SMRGT (Simple Multi-Attribute Rating Technique) with machine learning approaches like ANNs (Artificial Neural Networks) and ANFIS has shown promising results in improving the accuracy and reliability of flow coefficient estimation (Akay, 2021 ). Fuzzy SMRGT allows decision-makers to handle the inherent uncertainty and imprecision associated with river basin flow coefficient data. By combining this method with ANN and ANFIS, researchers have been able to capture the complex relationships between input variables and flow coefficient values, resulting in more accurate estimations (Butt et al., 2023 ). Moreover, the application of metaheuristic algorithms, such as genetic algorithms and particle swarm optimization, has been explored to optimize the parameters of the ANN and ANFIS models (Arora et al., 2021; Butt et al., 2023 ). These metaheuristics help in finding the optimal configuration of the models, enhancing their performance and convergence speed. The integration of MCDM methods, metaheuristics, and machine learning techniques for flow coefficient estimation in river basins presents a promising approach. The combination of Fuzzy SMRGT, ANN, and ANFIS allows for improved decision-making in water resource management by providing more accurate estimations of flow coefficients. The incorporation of metaheuristic algorithms further enhances the performance of the models (Butt et al., 2023 ). Therefore, this research aims to compare three distinct methodologies, namely ANFIS, SMRGT, and ANN, to determine the flow coefficient in Antalya’s Aksu River Basin. The study region was selected due to its high potential for floods and the importance of accurate flow coefficient estimation in managing water resources and mitigating flood damages. The models were developed using various data, including precipitation, temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, land use, and soil properties, tailored to the particular study region. The research carried out a comparative examination of the outcomes, considering diverse performance metrics of the model, such as MAE, NSE, RMSE, and R2. The study’s findings will contribute to more accurate flood prediction, water resource management, and flood mitigation strategies, benefiting the residents and stakeholders in the Aksu River Basin and potentially other flood-prone regions. Additionally, the innovative modeling techniques employed in this study serve as a foundation for future research in other river basins facing similar challenges. The objective of the study is to apply and compare the performance of three well-established methodologies, namely Fuzzy SMRGT, ANN, and ANFIS, for accurately estimating flow coefficients in the Antalya River Basin, and to evaluate the suitability of these methodologies in a real-world river basin context, considering factors such as data availability, basin characteristics, and modeling requirements. Previous studies (Smith and Eli, 1995; Jang, 1993; Abrahart and See, 2000 ) have primarily relied on traditional statistical approaches, which not adequately capture the complex nonlinear patterns exhibited by flow data. By introducing these advanced modeling techniques, this research attempts to overcome established approaches’ shortcomings and provide more accurate estimations of flow coefficients. The innovative contribution of this study lies in its integration of fuzzy logic, genetic training, neural networks, and adaptive inference systems. This approach considers uncertainties and linguistic variables associated with flow coefficient estimation, which need to be adequately addressed in previous studies. Furthermore, incorporating ANN and ANFIS models enables the capturing of nonlinear relationships, resulting in improved accuracy. Fuzzy SMRGT models provide a robust framework for handling uncertainty and variability in the Antalya River Basin context. Additionally, the innovative modeling techniques employed in this study serve as a foundation for future research in other river basins facing similar challenges. The implementation of Fuzzy SMRGT, ANN, and ANFIS approaches for flow coefficient estimation in the Antalya River Basin has certain limitations that should be considered; the accessibility and quality of data are critical factors in estimating accuracy Limited or unreliable data for critical variables hinder the model’s performance. The model’s applicability to other river basins varies due to differences in hydrological characteristics and environmental factors. Factors such as varying flow patterns, land use, and water management practices significantly impact the model’s effectiveness in different contexts. The calibration and validation of the model are essential to ensure reliable results, as improper parameterization or validation processes lead to biased estimations. Furthermore, the inherent uncertainties and assumptions associated with the models should be acknowledged, as they influence the reliability of the estimations. Despite these limitations, integrating Fuzzy SMRGT, ANN, and ANFIS approaches improve flow coefficient estimation in the Antalya River Basin and other similar river basins facing similar challenges. Further research and validation in different geographical contexts are necessary to assess this approach’s applicability and effectiveness. The research compares three distinct methodologies, namely ANFIS, SMRGT, and ANN, for estimating the flow coefficient in Antalya’s Aksu River Basin. Acknowledging the models’ limitations and their broader applicability is crucial. One limitation is that the comparison of methodologies is confined to the specific study region of Antalya’s Aksu River Basin. The hydrological characteristics of different regions vary, and therefore, the performance of these models differs in other geographic locations. To apply the findings to other river basins, it is necessary to consider those regions’ unique environmental and hydrological conditions. Moreover, the reliability and accuracy of the model’s quality and availability of input data are crucial. The study utilizes diverse data sets, including precipitation, temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, land use, and soil properties, which were explicitly tailored to the Aksu River basin. However, in regions where data availability or quality is different, the performance of these models needs to be improved. Additionally, while the study employs quantitative performance metrics such as MAE, NSE, RMSE, and R2 to compare the models, other factors like interpretability, computational efficiency, and ease of implementation are also considered in practical applications. The current research presents a novel approach utilizing an Artificial Neural Network (ANN), Adaptive Neural Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS), Simple Membership functions, and fuzzy Rules Generation Techniques (SMRGT) models to describe the nonlinear connection between influencing factors and flow coefficients properly. In addition, empirical measurements and comparison analysis are included in the study to support the proposed model. Relying exclusively on climate, topography, and soil characteristics of the river basin as input and subsequently evaluating the effectiveness of the employed methodology about its predictive aptitude. Another objective of this investigation is to present a novel approach, Fuzzy SMRGT, which precisely assesses the river flow coefficient.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area and data used In this study, the case study is Aksu River Basin, which is a sub-basin located within the Antalya Basin in Turkey. The geographical location is delineated located between approximately 36.75° N to 37.25° N latitude and 30.5° E to 31.5° E longitude, as depicted in Fig. 1  . The Aksu River Basin is located in the Taurus Mountains, which is a mountain range in southern Turkey. The Aksu River originates from the Toros Mountains. The climate in the Aksu River Basin is typically Mediterranean, which is characterized by hot and dry summers and mild and rainy winters. The average annual precipitation in Antalya, which is the closest major city to the Aksu River Basin, is around 1000 mm (https://www.mgm.gov.tr/eng/forecast-cities.aspx  (last access 6 July 2023)). The Aksu River Basin is located in the southern part of Turkey, in the province of Antalya. The elevation of the gauge in the Aksu River Basin between approximately 0 m (at sea level) to around 2000 m in the upper reaches of the basin, where the Taurus Mountains are located. Based on extensive research conducted on the river’s hydrodynamics over an extended period, it has been determined that the Aksu exhibits an average annual discharge of 94.98 hm3 . The present investigation employed a comprehensive dataset encompassing precipitation, temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, slope, soil type, and land use data of the Aksu River Basin spanning a considerable timeframe from 1990 to 2020. The weather data were obtained from the Turkish government’s recognized meteorological service. The classification of land use comprises five distinct categories, namely natural and forestry regions, pasture-low agricultural areas, wetland regions, high agricultural areas, and residential and industrial zones. The employment of impermeable materials such as asphalt, parquet, and concrete in residential areas results in an increase in the amount of precipitation that reaches the flow. The Turkish State Hydraulic Works (DSI) is responsible for the development and management of Turkey’s water resources, including rivers and watersheds. They have a high-resolution DEM of the Aksu River Basin that is available for use. The maximum yearly flow values of station 9–34, the basin’s sole flow monitoring station operated by The State Hydraulic Works, were used. The station has an annual mean flow value of 4.19 m3/s (Baykal et al., 2022 ). The study area encompasses a diverse range of soil types, each exhibiting unique permeability and aeration characteristics resulting from polarization, exhibiting varying responses to and magnitudes of flood events. Within this particular context, it observed that the regions that possess the highest potential for risk bearing are those that are characterized by Alluvial, Chestnut, Terra Rossa, and Terra fusca soil. These specific soil categories are particularly abundant in the geographical area that surrounds the Aksu River Basin. The study has employed various measurement techniques to collect data related to flow coefficients in the Antalya River Basin. Techniques include stream flow gauging stations (Antalya River Basin station), where water flow rates are directly measured using flow meters or velocity-area methods. Remote sensing techniques such as satellite imagery or aerial photography also have been utilized to obtain information on river width, depth, and surface characteristics (Turkish Meteorological Service). In the context of Fuzzy SMRGT, ANN, and ANFIS models, calibration is performed by optimizing the model parameters using appropriate optimization algorithms, genetic algorithms involve the use of genetic operators such as crossover, and selection to search for optimal solutions in a population-based manner. This involves adjusting membership functions, rule bases, activation functions, or connection weights to improve the model’s performance and achieve a better match with measured flow coefficients. The calibration process involves dividing the available data into calibration and validation periods. The calibration period is used to estimate the model parameters, while the validation period is used to assess the model’s performance in an independent time frame.  2.2 Artificial Neural Network (ANN) The Artificial Neural Network (ANN) is formed up of neurons that are replicas of their biological counterparts. The neurons possess the ability to acquire knowledge and can be instructed to execute operations such as recognizing patterns, categorizing information, and forecasting forthcoming occurrences (Clair and Ehrman, 1998 ). Typically, a network of this nature is composed of multiple layers that are sequentially arranged. Each layer has one or more neurons that have the same pattern of connections as the neurons in the other layer(s) (Shamseldin, 1997 ). The first and final layers of neural networks are allocated for input and output variables, respectively. The hidden layer is the term used to describe the intervening layers, which may consist of one or multiple layers, contingent upon the intricacy of the problem at hand. The process of adjusting the weights of a neuron is automated through network training, which follows a predetermined learning rule. This continues until the network is able to accurately replicate past data or complete the intended task, as noted by (Shamseldin, 1997; Zealand et al., 1999; Furundzic, 1997 ). Neuron transfer functions, which are mathematical functions, are used to convert each neuron’s input into output. The log-sigmoid transfer function is commonly used in the context of hidden layer neurons, especially in conjunction with the back-propagation method (see Fig. 2  ) (Neural Network, 2002 ). The current investigation employed the back-propagation (BP) algorithm for training, utilizing the Levenberg–Marquardt optimization technique. The input data are fed into the network, and the output is calculated using the current weights of the connections between neurons (Neural Network, 2002 ). The error between the predicted output and the actual output is calculated using a cost function, such as mean squared error. According to Najjar and Ali’s study (Najjar and Ali, 1998 ), this particular optimization technique is purported to possess greater efficacy than traditional gradient descent techniques. The study’s findings indicated that the Marquardt algorithm exhibits a high level of efficiency in the training of neural networks that possess a relatively small number of weights, typically numbering in the hundreds. Despite the higher computing needs associated with repeated Marquardt method functioning, its efficacy is superior. This is especially true when a high level of precision is required. The present investigation utilized the Artificial Neural Network (ANN) methodology to forecast the flow coefficient, employing MATLAB software. The Artificial Neural Network (ANN) models were constructed utilizing an input layer comprising four neurons representing precipitation, temperature, humidity, and wind speed. A single hidden layer was employed, comprising 20 neurons. The determination of the optimal number of neurons in the hidden layer was achieved through a process of trial and error. The output layer consists of a solitary neuron that functions to forecast the flow coefficient. Three ANN models were conducted using Levenberg-Marquardt back-propagation training algorithms called the TRAINLM function in MATLAB. The Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm is a modified iteration scheme of the Gauss-Newton method, as elaborated in references (Hagan and Menhaj, 1994; Reynaldi et al., 2012 ). The initial model, designated as ANN-1, underwent training utilizing two sets of inputs, namely temperature and wind speed. The subsequent model, ANN-2, was trained to utilize a set of three inputs, namely precipitation, temperature, and humidity. The third model denoted as ANN-3, was trained to utilize four inputs: precipitation, temperature, wind speed, and humidity. The artificial neural network (ANN) model underwent training using a dataset of 16 years of meteorological observations. The dataset was partitioned into three subsets, with 70 % of the data allocated for the training stage, 15 % allocated for the validation stage, and the remaining 15 % allocated for the test stage. The Min-Max scaling method standardized the training, test, and validation datasets.  2.3 Adaptive Neural fuzzy Inference system Fuzzy neural networks represent a class of connectionist models that amalgamate the principles of neural networks and fuzzy logic. ANFIS training makes use of neural networks, with their structures interpreted as a set of fuzzy rules, notably the Takagi-Sugeno-Kang rule set (TSK) (Takagi and Sugeno, 1985 ) fuzzy rules. According to Jang (Jang, 1993 ), fuzzy rules can be considered logical statements that can be used for the purpose of derivation. The procedure for performing this derivation is usually referred to as the inference procedure, as stated by (Jang, 1993 ). The ANFIS model includes a linear combination of input variables that act as preconditions for the subsequent component of each rule, as well as a constant term. The ultimate output is determined by taking a weighted average of each rule’s output. As an example, if the Fuzzy Inference System being analyzed consists of a rule base comprising of two if-then rules following the Takagi-Sugeno-Kang (TSK) (Takagi and Sugeno, 1985 ) model, TSK fuzzy rules with two input variables, x and y, and one output variable, f, can be represented as:(1) R 1 : I F  x  i s  A  1    a n d  y  i s  B  1   , T H E N  f  1   = p  1   x + q  1   y + r  1       (2) R 2 : I F  x  i s  A  2    a n d  y  i s  B  2   ,  T H E N  f  2   = p  2   x + q  2   y + r  2       where fi is the output and pi, qi, and ri are the ith rule’s subsequent parameters (Agbaogun et al., 2021 ). According to (Jang, 1993 ), the linguistic identifiers Ai and Bi are distinguished by their membership function parameters, which are predicated parameters and denoted as fuzzy sets. The current computation involves calculating the inferred output, which is represented as y*:(3) y ∗  = f =  ( f 1 W 1 +  f 2 W 2 )  W 1 +  W 2   =  W   ¯   f 1 +  W   ¯   f 2      Fig. 3   depicts the ANFIS architecture, which typically consists of five distinct layers: the fuzzification layer, the product layer, the normalized layer, the defuzzification layer, and the output layer. This framework was initially proposed by (Jang, 1993 ). The layers in question have distinct functions and comprise multiple nodes, each characterized by its node function. These functions may include adaptive nodes, which allow for adjustable parameters within the system, or fixed nodes, which pertain to nonadjustable parameters (Jang, 1993 ). The ANFIS training algorithm adopts a hybrid approach that combines the back-propagation gradient descent algorithm and the least square method to acquire information and discover patterns in the training dataset. Following that, a distinct dataset (the test dataset) is used to assess the overall generalizability of the resulting systems. Additional information regarding the theoretical underpinnings and practical implementations of fuzzy set theory, as well as the architecture of Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference Systems (ANFISs), can be located in scholarly works such as (Takagi and Sugeno, 1985; Agbaogun et al., 2021 ). 2.3.1 Artificial Neural Network (ANN) model Artificial Neural Networks are systems formed up of process fragments that are coupled to one another using variable weights. The feed-forward back-propagation ANN model, which operates on the principle of error back-propagation, is the most widely used Artificial Neural Network (ANN) approach. An Artificial NeuralNetwork cell is made up of five major components: the input layer, variable weight multipliers, total function, activation function, and output layer. The present investigation in Fig. 1  employed three distinct input combinations for the ANN method. Specifically, the initial model (ANFIS-1) incorporated temperature (T) and wind speed (Ws) as the input variables. The second model, ANFIS-2, incorporated precipitation (P), temperature (T), and relative humidity (Rh) as input variables. In the third model, the input variables comprised precipitation (P), temperature (T), relative humidity (Rh), and wind speed (Ws). The bias multiplied by the input values and weighted averages (w) yields the output estimation values for ANN. These are coefficient values that express how the prior input data affected the treated element. The output (flow coefficient) was consistent across all models. During the training and testing stages, a range of 60–40 % was utilized as it yielded precise outcomes. Training is conducted using a membership function such as the Gaussian membership function (gaussmf), while the test stage is conducted using generalized bell membership functions (gbellmf), with a Grid partition section of 50 iterations. The 15-year monthly data were used. Following this, a fuzzy inference system (FIS) is developed and tested, which is capable of producing MSE and MARE. To reduce the computational load caused by excessive preprocessing, the data is normalized to ensure that their values fall within the range of 0 to 1. This is accomplished by using the following equation:(4) Xnor . = X - X m a x  Xmin - X m a x       where Xnor.   is the normalized data, x is the original data, Xmin  , and Xmax   are the minimum and maximum values of the original data, respectively.   2.4 The Simple membership functions and fuzzy rules Generation techniques (SMRGT) The SMRGT method was proposed by (Toprak, 2009 ) to aid those who experience challenges in ascertaining the quantity, configuration, and reasoning of the membership functions and fuzzy rules within a given fuzzy system. SMRGT is a method used in fuzzy logic systems to generate fuzzy rules based on data inputs and outputs. SMRGT is a simple and intuitive method that does not require extensive knowledge of the system being modelled; this method involves two main steps: membership function design and fuzzy rule generation. The novel fuzzy methodology relies exclusively on a limited set of key numerical values for all membership functions pertaining to the input and output variables. The primary numerical values were determined through the utilization of MF geometry, including triangular and trapezoidal shapes, as well as defuzzification techniques such as centroid and maximum membership degree. The following content presents a structured plan of the algorithm and methodology that serves as the foundation for the suggested approach:i Determine the factors that are independent that influence the dependent variable in the current event. In a fuzzy system, the independent variables act as inputs, while the dependent variable(s) function as outputs. The present investigation consists of 5 models with different combinations of the inputs variable. The 1st model (SMRGT-1) employed temperature (T) and wind speed (Ws) as inputs, the 2nd model (SMRGT-2) employed precipitation (P), temperature (T), and relative humidity (Rh) as inputs, the 3rd model (SMRGT-3) employed precipitation (P), land use (LU), and soil permeability (Sp) as inputs, the 4th model (SMRGT-4) used land use (LU), and slope (S) as inputs, the last model (SMRGT-5) used precipitation (P), temperature (T), and relative humidity (Rh), slope (S), and land use (LU) as inputs. At the same time, the dependent outcome is represented by the flow coefficient for all models  ii Specify the variability domain, which includes limits on input and output variables. Upon analysis of the data gathered from the designated study region, it was determined that the precipitation ranges exhibited a minimum and maximum value of (200–2000) mm, land use (0–100)%, temperature (0–50) °C, wind speed (0–10) m/s, relative humidity (0–100)%, slope (0–90)°, and soil permeability (0–100), respectively  iii Choose the shape of the membership function (MF), such as triangular, trapezoidal, etc., as per the suggestion put by (Toprak, 2009 ). The utilization of triangular was preferred in models (SMRGT-1, SMRGT-2, SMRGT-4, and SMRGT-5), while trapezoidal membership functions were prioritized in model SMRGT-3. For each independent variable, the number of membership functions must be determined, with a minimum allocation of three MFs. The present study involves the construction of membership functions for each independent variable, comprising five distinct fuzzy sets denoted as (Very low (VL), low (L), medium (M), high (H), and very high (VH)), while only for SMRGT-1 they were very very low (VVL)Very low (VL), low (L), medium (M), high (H), very high (VH), and very high (VVH))  iv The values of the independent variables were determined by assigning key values (K1, K2, K3, K4, and K5), the unit width (UW), the core value (Ci), the number of right-angled triangles (nu), and the expanded base width (EUW) to them (see Fig. 4  ). It should be mentioned that the number of key values corresponds to the number of membership functions for each independent variable. The determinant values provided above are used as inputs to the fuzzy model. Valid inputs for the fuzzy model are data supplied within the range of the first and last membership functions for each variable. In this particular case of NSE, a value of 1 indicates that the modelled and observed values correlate entirely, whereas a value of 0 shows that the model predictions are as precise as the mean of the actual values. When the NSE value is negative, it indicates that the model is not as effective in prediction as the mean of the observed values. Equations (14)–(16)  explicitly specify the aforementioned parameters. As a result, it is preferable for models to have mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean square error (RMSE) values of zero. The coefficient of determination refers to the proportion of the total variance explained by the regression line in a linear regression model. The determination coefficient (R2 ) of a regression line representing the mean value of a given dataset is zero, but a great model has an R2  value of one.(14) MAE = 1 n  ∑ 1  n  C i  -  C p        (15) RMSE = 1 n  ∑ 1  n  ( C i - C p )  2        (16) NSE = 1 - ∑  1  n   C i - C p    2    ∑  1  n   C i - A ¯     2         where Ci  represents the actual data, Cp  represents the predicted data, and A (bar) represents the mean value of the actual data.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 LMBP-ANN Using artificial intelligence techniques, this study aimed to determine the flow coefficient of the Aksu River Basin in Antalya, Turkey, including Fuzzy SMRGT, ANN, and ANFIS approaches, as well as Multi Linear Regression methods. To evaluate the success of the models, mean absolute error (MAE), mean squared error (RMSE), coefficient of determination (R2 ), and Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) metrics were used, as described in Equations (14)–(16)  (Hahs-Vaughn, 2016 ). The study presented a case study where three different input combinations of neural network models were assessed to forecast the flow coefficient of the Aksu River Basin. Monthly climate data from 15 years (2005–2020) were selected for this study, and three Levenberg-Marquardt back-propagation (LMBP-NN) training algorithm functions in MATLAB were employed to determine the effect of individual parameters on output, following the selection of suitable input combinations. The optimal input combination was selected based on the minimum score of (MAE, RMSE) and maximum score of (R2 , NSE). The study summarized the input parameters for the three models and their performance assessment criteria in Table 1  . The correlation coefficient (R2 ) between the observed and predicted flow coefficient was evaluated for each model, with ANN − 1 (comprised of two input parameters) producing values of 0.723, 0.053, 0.098, and 0.515 for training, validation, test, and all data, respectively. For ANN–2 (comprised of three input parameters), the values were 0.837, 0.779, 0.684, and 0.76 for training, validation, test, and all data, respectively. Meanwhile, for ANN–3 (comprised of four input parameters), the values were 0.889, 0.869, 0.803, and 0.876 for training, validation, test, and all data, respectively. It is seen that the parameters (precipitation, temperature, humidity, and wind speed) altogether have a significant effect on output (C). The plot of observed and predicted data for ANN-3 showed an excellent similarity (Figs. 6–8    ). Therefore, it is considered the best input combination for the ANN models and was considered for flow coefficient prediction in the Aksu River Basin.  3.2 ANFIS The ANFIS analysis used Gaussian membership functions for training and generalized bell membership functions (gbellmf) for testing, as well as the grid division section with 50 iterations, assuming linear output. The dataset was divided into two distinct phases, namely the training and testing phases, with a 60–40 % split. The outputs of the ANFIS technique were shown using scatter plots. The coefficient of determination for each training, testing, and all data points was calculated to be (R2 :0.993, R2 :0.561, and R2 :0.863) for ANFIS–1, (R2 :0.893, R2 :0.66, and R2 :0.801) for ANFIS–2, and (R2 :1, R2 :0.935, and R2 :0.974) for ANFIS–3, as shown in Figs. 9–11    . The results of the ANFIS–1 and ANFIS–2 models showed that the predicted data differed significantly from the actual values; however, the ANFIS–3 model showed a robust correlation between the actual and anticipated data, as seen in the figures below. All data points in the ANFIS–3 model scatter plots are quite close to the (1:1) line of agreement. The statistical parameters for ANFIS-based prediction are given in Table 2  . ANFIS–1 and ANFIS–2 models exhibit more significant error rates than ANFIS–3 and poorer NSE and R2  values when the RMSE and MAE criteria are used. The results of the ANFIS–3 model demonstrated that the Adaptive Neural Fuzzy Inference System method could be successfully applied to establish accurate and reliable flow coefficient prediction. It is very clear from the ANN and ANFIS model result that neural network models are becoming significantly more accurate as the number of inputs to the model increases. A low correlation coefficient indicates a weak linear relationship between the inputs and the target variable (Hahs-Vaughn, 2016 ). In this case, the inputs may not contain enough information or exhibit a strong enough pattern to predict the target variable accurately. The model’s inability to capture this weak relationship can lead to high prediction errors. Moreover, neural networks are capable of learning complex patterns and relationships in data. However, with only two inputs, the model may struggle to represent and learn the underlying structure of the data accurately. The limited complexity of the model can result in high errors as it fails to capture the non-linear relationships or dependencies between the inputs and the target variable (Hahs-Vaughn, 2016 ).  3.3 SMRGT The Mamdani approach was used as the fuzzy inference mechanism in the SMRGT framework, and the centroid technique was used as the defuzzification process. The centroid technique appears to be more suited for fuzzy SMRGT, according to (Toprak, 2009 ). In order to develop the membership functions for each independent variable, a large number of membership functions were generated and assigned significant values to each MF. The estimated key values for all input combinations are shown in Table 3  . These values are the model’s inputs. The minimum and maximum value ranges of the flow coefficient are traditionally thought to be 0 and 1, respectively. Figs. 12 and 13    depicts the results of the Simple Membership functions and fuzzy Rules Generation Technique (SMRGT) model for flow coefficient estimate. Upon examination of the figures, it was observed that the forecasted values yielded outcomes that were more proximate to the actual values almost in all combinations. The regression line of the scatter plot intersects the horizontal axis at a 45-degree angle, suggesting that the model produces inconsistent estimates that deviate from the actual data. In other words, the model exhibits a lack of tendency to either overestimate or underestimate the data, thereby indicating its reliability and accuracy (Toprak, 2009; Sevgin and Toprak, 2019; Bayri, 2018 ). The models’ statistical criteria were assessed and computed using the approach described in the preceding section. Based on the parameters of RMSE, MAE, and R2 , the assessment found that the SMRGT framework produced the best results. Table 4   presents a summary of the statistical results. The obtained correlation coefficients for SMRGT–1, SMRGT–2, SMRGT–3, SMRGT–4, and SMRGT–5 were 0.99, 0.963, 0.976, 0.98, and 0.983, respectively. Table 1  indicates that the SMRGT model performed better than the other models employed in this investigation. Upon comparison with all other models, it is evident that the SMRGT model exhibited the least error rates in terms of both root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) while also displaying the highest correlation because physics-based models have the advantage of being able to function effectively with lesser quantities of data in comparison to solely data-driven approaches. This is due to their utilization of fundamental physical principles to formulate predictions and compensate for potential data sparsity. Through the integration of physical laws, these models possess the capability to extrapolate and interpolate the system’s behavior, thereby mitigating the necessity for copious amounts of training data. Furthermore, it pertains to their robustness, which refers to their capacity to perform effectively in the face of noise, uncertainties, or perturbations. The SMRGT approach provides a notable level of interpretability due to its reliance on precisely defined fuzzy rules and expert knowledge. Monthly data sets from the Aksu River basin in Antalya, Turkey, were utilized for this investigation. The study’s findings indicate that the SMRGT model exhibited superior performance based on the statistical parameters and correlation coefficients in the context of non-linear modeling. Moreover, it was observed that the ANFIS-3 model exhibited superior performance in comparison to the Artificial Neural Network (ANN) models. The study provides a comprehensive comparative analysis of three methodologies, namely Fuzzy SMRGT, ANN, and ANFIS, for estimating the flow coefficient in the Antalya River Basin. Through rigorous evaluation of their performance, strengths, and weaknesses, this study aims to identify the most effective methodology or combinations of methodologies. The implementation of Fuzzy SMRGT, ANN, and ANFIS models for flow coefficient estimation in the Antalya River Basin has yielded significant findings and led to specific conclusions. A comprehensive comparative analysis of the models was conducted, evaluating their performance in terms of accuracy and reliability. The Fuzzy SMRGT model emerged as the superior approach, outperforming both ANN and ANFIS models in capturing the complex nonlinear patterns and uncertainties associated with flow coefficient estimation. This finding highlights the effectiveness of the proposed approach in enhancing estimation accuracy. Additionally, the integration of fuzzy logic, genetic training, neural networks, and adaptive inference systems enabled the models to handle uncertainty robustly. The models considered linguistic variables and uncertainties, leading to more comprehensive and reliable estimations. The best input performance metrics model was found by applying a minimum score of (MAE, RMSE) and a maximum score of (R2, NSE). The ANN-3 model has the best statistical performance. This model has the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) values among the three models, indicating that it has the most negligible average difference between observed and predicted values. In addition, the ANN-3 model has the highest Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) and correlation coefficient (R2) values, suggesting that it has the best overall fit to the data. The ANN-3 model uses a combination of four input variables (T, Rh, P, and Ws), which provides a more comprehensive representation of the factors affecting flow than the other models with fewer input variables. The superior performance of the ANN-3 model may also be due to the use of the Levenberg-Marquardt back-propagation (LMBP-NN) training algorithm, which is known for its ability to quickly converge to a solution and avoid becoming stuck in local minima. The ANFIS-3 model based on performance metrics has the best statistical performance. This model has the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) values among the three models, indicating that it has the most negligible average difference between observed and predicted values. In addition, the ANFIS-3 model has the highest Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) and correlation coefficient (R2) values for both the training and test datasets, suggesting that it has the best overall fit to the data, with the lowest MAE and RMSE values for both the training and test datasets, Suggesting that it has the best overall fit to the data. The fuzzy logic theory has the potential to evaluate traditional systems with relatively moderate levels of complexity and no significant uncertainties or problems. The ANFIS and SMRGT fuzzy approaches have been widely used in a variety of hydrological applications. The ANFIS approach is based on adaptable neural networks and fuzzy inference systems, which can effectively manage complex and non-linear data connections. The SMRGT approach, on the other hand, employs simple membership functions and fuzzy rules to recognize ambiguous and imprecise information features. The choice of a method is determined by the specific characteristics of the river basin and the data available, as each method has advantages and limitations. Both approaches have shown promising results in accurately estimating the flow coefficient. SMRGT’s results, on the other hand, outperformed ANFIS. The scatter plot, high coefficient of determination, and low MAE and RMSE values demonstrate the SMRGT model’s neutrality and linearity. These findings suggest that the model is reliable, exact, and appropriate for flow coefficient calculations, a critical parameter in hydrological modelling and water resource management, and that further research is required.
1 Introduction Multiphase fluid flow in porous media presents persistent engineering challenges across various fields, such as oil and gas recovery (Shen et al., 2009 ), groundwater management (Essaid et al., 2015 ), carbon dioxide sequestration (Abidoye et al., 2015 ) and soil physics (Farthing & Ogden, 2017 ). These challenges have led to increased research attention and allocation of resources towards studying the characteristics of multiphase flow. Starting with the instantaneous and local fluid mechanics equations and the interfacial jump conditions, macroscopic averaging methods are utilized to obtain multiphase models that describe the variation of macroscopic parameters like capillary pressure (Pc  ), relative permeability (kw  ) and saturation (Sw  ) in multiphase flow (Lenhard & Parker, 1987; Parker et al., 1987 ). One notable approach for describing soil hydraulic properties is the composite parametric kw −Sw −Pc   model (Van Genuchten, 1980 ). Constitutive models, which depend on the historical changes in fluid saturation (i.e kw   (Sw  ) or Pc   (Sw  )), are commonly associated with hydraulic hysteresis phenomena. It is recognized that the process of macroscopic averaging leads to the loss of microscale flow dynamic information. From a pore scale perspective, the non-wetting phase (NWP) first reaches the critical capillary pressure of larger pores during drainage. However, due to the presence of smaller surrounding pores and poor pore connectivity, a portion of the wetting phase (WP) may be trapped within the pores. Conversely, the WP tends to preferentially fill smaller pores. Therefore, the capillary pressure threshold for drainage is different from that for imbibition, hydraulic hysteresis can be generated by the succession of pore throats and pore bodies (Soldi et al., 2017; 2022 ). Additionally, Due to factors such as snap-off, the WP may not fully occupy all voids during the imbibition process (Andrew et al., 2015; Blunt, 2017; Pickell et al., 1966 ). Displacement patterns at the pore scale, which vary over time, govern the properties observed at the continuum scale and are responsible for the occurrence of capillary pressure hysteresis (Cihan et al., 2014; Haines, 1930; Hilfer, 2006a;b ). Therefore, it is now recognized that the fluid historical topological configuration during the processes should be considered as an additional state variable to eliminate the hydraulic hysteresis (Hassanizadeh & Gray, 1993; Held & Celia, 2001; Joekar-Niasar et al., 2008; Reeves & Celia, 1996 ). Traditional methods lack the ability to accurately monitor in situ fluid motion and internal phase interactions due to their limited spatial and temporal resolution. As an emerging technique, microfluidics facilitates high-resolution visualization of pore-scale fluid behaviors (Avraam & Payatakes, 1995; Reynolds et al., 2017; Rücker et al., 2015; Schlüter et al., 2016 ). Numerous displacement experiments using microfluidic porous media chips have revealed varying displacement patterns under different capillary numbers (Ca ) and wetting conditions (Hu et al., 2019; Lenormand et al., 1988; Qiu et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2016 ). The hysteresis behaviors kw   (Sw  ) and Pc   (Sw  ) have been examined through image analysis (Chen et al., 2007; Cheng et al., 2004; Pyrak-Nolte et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2021 ). Water plays a crucial role as a carrier in solute diffusion in unsaturated soil environments. The diffusion coefficient in unsaturated soil has been commonly expressed as a monotonically increasing function of water content, as the decreasing water content leads to more tortuous diffusive paths (Chou et al., 2012; Revil & Jougnot, 2008; Šimůnek et al., 2022 ). To characterize the diffusion coefficient of porous media, Dp  , we introduced the diffusive tortuosity(τd  ). τd   is sometimes defined as the diffusion coefficient of solute in free fluid, Dm  , relative to Dp  , i.e. τd   = Dm  /Dp   (Clennell, 1997; Satterfield & Sherwood, 1963; Shen & Chen, 2007 ). In a more rudimentary definition, τd   can be expressed as the square of the ratio of the average diffusion path length of the solute to the straight-line distance (Carman, 1956; Ghanbarian et al., 2013 ). It remains unclear how the different configurations of pore water impact the unsaturated diffusion during drainage and imbibition. A physically consistent and adequate description of tortuosity related to the underlying displacement physical processes would improve knowledge of solute transport in unsaturated flow. In this study, we employed microfluidic experiments to investigate the effects of historical changes of pore water configuration on unsaturated diffusion. We conducted investigations of hydraulic hysteresis at various Ca  through the implementation of cyclic water–air displacement and image analyses. Subsequently, we examined the unsaturated diffusion coefficients during the drainage-imbibition loop.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Micromodel design and size of Representative-Element-Volume (REV) The micromodel utilized in this study consisted of randomly distributed cylindrical obstacles ranging from 100 μm to 600 μm in size, with a minimum spacing of 20 μm between two cylinders. The pore size distribution was analyzed following the method described Rabbani et al (2014) . The mean pore size was approximately 63.68 μm, as shown in Fig. 1  b). The porosity of the micromodel was measured to be 43.27 %. The overall dimensions of the micromodel were 30.72 × 20.48 mm2 , and it had a uniform internal depth of 20 μm. These dimensions were chosen to ensure complete drainage and imbibition cycles within the micromodel. To investigate the fluid properties at the Representative-Element-Volume (REV) scale, 61 sub-samples were cropped, with sizes increasing from 75 to 4575 pixels along the x-axis and 50 to 3050 pixels along the y-axis. The REV size was determined based on analyses of porosity and absolute permeability. In order to maintain consistency, the sample size was systematically varied while keeping the top left diagonal point of the sample fixed. Porosity was calculated using image binarization, where pores and solids were represented by 0 and 1 in the matrix, respectively. This allowed us to determine the percentage of the image occupied by 0 elements, which quantified the porosity. Absolute permeability was computed using a pore network model (Qu et al., 2023, 2024 ), where network was generated using a maximum ball based algorithm (Dong & Blunt, 2009 ). The value of property within a 10 % variation of the value at the largest scale can be considered convergent. Our investigation revealed that both porosity and absolute permeability demonstrated similar REV levels, as depicted in Fig. 2  . The for porosity reached the desired level when the sub-sample size was (350, 525) pixels, while the absolute permeability required (650, 975) pixels. To meet the scale requirements, a sample size larger than or equal to the critical size is necessary. In particularly, when analyzing unsaturated images on the REV scale in Section 3.2, we chose (700, 1050) pixels as appropriate scale to facilitate the computation and alleviate the effect of a larger REV scale for the saturation condition. And the required length is approximately (4.65, 6.98) mm, with 73.0 mean pore size units in the y -axis direction and 109.6 units in the x -axis direction. Also, to measure the absolute permeability of the whole chip, we used the pump to inject a constant flow into the chip and connected a pressure sensor (FluidicLab PS5) at the inlet to record the pressure. The absolute permeability calculated by Darcy’s law is approximately 2.01 × 10−12  m2 , which matches the convergent permeability (2.26 × 10−12  m2 ) well. Detailed calculations can be found in SI. Due to the distortion effects caused by the camera lens, we cropped the pixels along the upper and lower boundaries of the images to ensure that no impact was introduced in subsequent calculations. For the entire micromodel (i.e. REV1 ), we obtained samples at 2805 pixels along the y -axis direction and 4608 pixels along the x -axis direction. It should be emphasized that there may be slight fluctuations in the pixels' x -direction between different sets, but these do not impact the outcomes.  2.2 Experimental setup The experimental setup, as depicted in Fig. 3  , consisted of a visualization system and flow control components. A CMOS camera (Hikrobot MV-CE200-10UC) and a magnifying lens (Hikrobot FM110-04X20G f/1.8–135 mm) were used to monitor the glass microfluidics, while a high-precision syringe pump (CchipP01-B) controlled the imbibition and drainage processes. The camera had a maximum resolution of 5,472 × 3,648 pixels, and the magnifying lens was positioned as close as possible to the micromodel to capture the entire pattern within the image. Initially, the micromodel was fully saturated with a 10 g/L methyl blue solution, serving as the wetting phase (WP), with a contact angle of 42.22°. Subsequently, air, acting as the non-wetting phase (NWP), was sucked into the micromodel at a constant rate (drainage process), which was stopped once the air reached the pattern boundary. Immediately after, the solution was injected from the other side at the same rate (imbibition process). The viscosities of the WP and NWP were 1.83 × 10−2  and 5.93 mPa·s, respectively, with an interfacial tension of 74.5 mN/m. The viscosity of the methyl blue solution was measured using a rheometer (Anton Paar MCR302), while the contact angle and surface tension were determined using a contact angle surface tension measurement instrument (Dropmeter 100P). The injection rates (Q ) ranged from 5 to 500 μL/hr, corresponding to Ca  in the range of 6.33 × 10−8  to 6.33 × 10−6  during imbibition and 1.95 × 10−10  to 1.95 × 10−8  during drainage, which are sufficiently small to ensure a quasi-static system (Hu et al., 2019; Karadimitriou et al., 2014 ).(1) Ca = v i  μ i   σ      (2) v i  = Q A · ϕ       where vi   [LT−1 ] and μi   [ L−1 MT−1 ] represents the apparent velocity and viscosity of the invading phase fluid, σ  [MT−2 ] is the interfacial tension between fluids, and A  [L2 ] is the cross-sectional area through which the fluid enters. Images were recorded at intervals of half a second to a second, with shorter intervals for higher injection rates. The experiments were conducted at a temperature of 25 °C and atmospheric pressure. The recorded images were then processed to extract fluid saturation, fluid spatial distribution, and averaged capillary pressure.  2.3 Image processing and data analysis The images underwent pre-processing using ImageJ  software, including batch rotation and cropping. The dimensions of each pixel are approximately 6.65 µm. It was observed that even the smallest pores could occupy approximately 3 pixels. We first binarized the saturated images to extract a patterned mask (Fig. 4  a), and superimposed the mask on the unsaturated images as shown in Fig. 4 c. Then we subtracted these images from the masked saturated images to extract the shape of the NWP, and detected the fluid–fluid interface (i.e. the yellow line segment in Fig. 4 d) and the fluid–solid interface (the red line segment in Fig. 4 d) by Canny edge detection (Canny, 1986 ). Previous studies have demonstrated that fluid behavior under our experiment conditions (i.e., the range of Ca ) was predominantly governed by capillary forces with negligible viscous forces. This implies that the interfacial pressure is approximately equal to the capillary pressure (Godinez-Brizuela et al., 2017 ). Based on this understanding, our approach was on detecting the fluid interface, calculating Sw  , Pc  , and interfacial area (awn  ). A tortuosity factor, τ  (Sw  ), is usually proposed to account for the reduced cross-sectional area and longer pathway in diffusion in unsaturated media (Jury & Horton, 2004 ):(9) D ( S w  )  = D m  τ ( S w  )        where Dm   [L2 T−1 ] refers to the molecular diffusion coefficient (Fu et al., 2021 ; L. Shen & Chen, 2007 ). It should be noted that, there are different definitions for tortuosity (Fu et al., 2021; Ghanbarian et al., 2013 ). In a more mechanistic manner, the constrictivity was proposed to characterize the cross section of a segment varies over its length, while the tortuosity is related to the angle between the main diffusion path and the concentration gradient (Rembert et al., 2020; van Brakel & Heertjes, 1974 ). However, in this study, we calculated the tortuosity factor, τ  (Sw  ), through random walk simulation using the python package Pytrax (Tranter et al., 2019 ). The constrictivity and tortuosity mentioned above have been incorporated along to consider in calculating τ  (Sw  ). Specifically, we utilized the Mean Square Displacement (MSD) of random walkers for this purpose. Theoretically, with a sufficiently large number of walkers (nw ), the walking trace can comprehensively cover the accessible space and accurately quantify the complex spatial structure. Therefore, in the following discussions, the constrictivity is omitted and τ  (Sw  ) takes account for the comprehensive effect of cross section area varies and diffusion pathway. Prior to the calculation, the images were preprocessed into binary images, with the water, air, and solid phases separated. The air phase was treated as part of the solid phase. The space occupied by water serves as the accessible region for the walkers. A designated nw  were randomly assigned different starting positions within the wetting phase at t  = 0, and a specified number of steps (nt ) were taken by each walker in parallel. Then, each walker randomly chooses one of its neighboring orthogonal-directional voxels as its possible position at the next time step. If the selected voxel belongs to the pore phase, the walker moved to the new position. When encountering the air phase or solids, the walkers were reflected back and stayed at the current location. In the absence of advection, the MSD of all random walkers is a function of time step with the random walking procedure repeated. MSD is described in two dimensions as:(10) MSD = ∫ - ∞  ∞  x  2  p ( x , t )  d x = ∫ - ∞  ∞  ( x 1 2  + x 2 2  )  p ( x , t )  d x 1  d x 2     where p  (x , t ) is the Gaussian distribution of walker position. Then τ  (Sw  ) in the algorithm is defined as the ratio of MSD in free space (MSD f  ) and porous media (MSDp ), and MSD f   increases linearly proportional to time, i.e. MSD f   = t . This is primarily because, at a viscosity ratio of Ϻ  ≈-2, these flow rates result in non-wetting phase (NWP) exhibiting predominantly finger-like flow patterns, such as capillary fingering and viscous fingering. All images demonstrate similar patterns under three flow rates. This phenomenon primarily stemmed from the heterogeneities of capillary, with lower values in the left bottom section. 3.1 Hydraulic hysteresis We provide the results for the average capillary pressure (Pc  ) and interfacial area (awn  ) as a function of saturation (Sw  ) for the six flow rates. In order for air to enter the chip during the initial drainage process, a critical value of Pc   must be surpassed, resulting in a rapid increase. Notably, there is a clear trend indicating that Pc   decreases during drainage as the flow rate increases. To quantify this hysteresis, we interpolated Pc   −Sw   for both drainage and imbibition processes. Then we calculated the maximum difference at the same saturation (i.e., ΔPc  max ). As shown in Fig. 6  , ΔPc  max  exhibited at saturation of 0.83, 0.78, 0.81, 0.72, 0.80, 0.82, respectively, nearly at the maximum saturation during each imbibition. Our observations indicate that as drainage capillary number (Ca ) increased, the capillary pressure hysteresis between drainage and imbibition became less pronounced. These findings align with those reported by Karadimitriou et al. (2014) . For awn  -Sw   relationship, we observed a linear variation in awn   with respect to Sw   during drainage. Additionally, growing inclination was observed in the slope of awn  −Sw   as the drainage Ca  increases, which aligns with previous findings (Dastjerdi et al., 2023 ). This suggests that higher Ca  values correspond to larger awn   at the same Sw   due to the increased prominence of the fractal nature of the NWP. The almost linear variation in awn   with respect to Sw   during drainage is consistent with the phase diagram proposed by Lenormand et al. (1988) , which suggests that an increase in Ca  causes the NWP to transition from capillary fingering to viscous fingering. Higher Ca  is associated with a greater number of minor phases with large specific surface areas (Cheng et al., 2004 ), including disconnected air and water phases. awn   does not change linearly with saturation during imbibition. The fragmentation of air by water lead to an increase in awn   firstly. As water continues to invade, awn   inevitably decreases due to the reduction in air saturation. In a similar manner as ΔPc  max , we investigated the maximum difference in awn   (Δawn max  ). Naturally, a similar hysteresis trend in Pc  -Sw   is captured in the awn  -Sw   relationship (Fig. 6 d). Δawn max   in each corresponding Sw   range from 0.70 to 0.83, with values of 0.83, 0.72, 0.81, 0.74, 0.70 and 0.81, respectively.  3.2 Diffusion hysteresis Importantly, our study explores the relationship between unsaturated diffusion coefficient (D ) and water saturation (Sw  ) in drainage and imbibition processes. Fig. 7   shows that, at the same saturation levels, D  during drainage were larger than during imbibition, indicating hysteresis behavior. Although diffusion hysteresis has not been explicitly discussed previously, some relevant studies were implemented regarding wetting-phase connectivity during two-phase displacement loops (Schlüter et al., 2016 ). It has been shown that a higher number of redundant loops around grains and non-wetting phase fingers were produced during drainage. As main imbibition proceeded, the air was disrupted as water clusters reconnected, the loops reduce lead to lower connectivity than drainage at the same saturation. We fitted a quadratic function for the D -Sw   relationship, with a coefficient of determination (R2  ) above 0.90. Then we took the maximum difference between the fitted values for the two processes, i.e., the magnitude of diffusion hysteresis (ΔDmax  ), to quantify diffusion hysteresis. The saturation for ΔDmax   was 0.83, 0.73, 0.79, 0.77, 0.78, and 0.80 for each flow rate, which closely matched the saturation values for ΔPc max   and Δawn max   in hydraulic hysteresis.
