Fig. 7 b shows a decreasing response of D  as Ca  decreases. Overall, ΔDmax   ranges from approximately 6.10 % to 9.48 %. To gain insights of the influence of residual saturation (Srw  ) on diffusion hysteresis, we also conducted an analysis at a smaller scale of 700 pixels × 1050 pixels (i.e., REV2 ), which was 1/16 of the chip size but still satisfied the REV requirement (i.e., the size should be larger than or equal to 650 pixels × 975 pixels). By doing so, the heterogeneity of residual water phase caused by capillary fingerings could be better resolved. Furthermore, this allowed us to collect 16 times the amount data compared to analyzing the entire chip. Fig. 8   illustrates the relationship between D  and Sw   at the given scale positions of the micromodel with the injection rate Q =100 μL/hr. The D -Sw   diagrams for other flow rates can be found in the Supplementary Information  (Figure S2-S6 ). Diffusion hysteresis was observed in almost all diagrams. The results also provide us with insights into the hysteresis relationships for different Srw  . We have thoroughly examined the results for the subsections across all flow rates, as presented in Fig. 9  . It also illustrates that the blue data points, corresponding to lower Ca  values, are concentrated in the highly Srw   range (0.6–1.0), whereas the red data points, corresponding to larger Ca  values, exhibit a more dispersed distribution. This difference suggests that lower Ca  values resulted in an incomplete flow pattern and an increased Srw   due to the formation of capillary fingers. The hysteresis effect became more noticeable as Srw   decreased. Furthermore, a larger Ca  value led to a smaller rate of change of ΔDmax  −Srw   (Fig. 9 b). This finding provides additional support for the previous conclusion that a lower flow rate resulted in more pronounced diffusion hysteresis.  3.3 Modeling of diffusion coefficient with saturation and capillary pressure To eliminate hydraulic hysteresis, Hassanizadeh and Gray (1993)  introduced awn   as an additional state variable, i.e., formulating Pc   as a function of both Sw   and awn  . The underlying assumption is that there exists a unique three-dimensional (3D) surface defined by these three variables. However, researchers soon discovered that this 3D surface is not unique (Reeves & Celia, 1996 ). This led to the proposition to replace Pc   (Sw  , awn  ) with a relationship: awn   (Sw  , Pc  ) (Held & Celia, 2001; Joekar-Niasar et al., 2008 ). Since then, numerous studies from both experimental and modeling perspectives have provided evidence that the surface awn  (Sw  , Pc  ) could reduce the hysteresis behavior of Pc   (Sw  ) curve in imbibition and drainage with a quadratic polynomial relationship (Chen et al., 2007; Cheng et al., 2004; Li et al., 2018; 2019; McClure et al., 2020; Pyrak-Nolte et al., 2008; Yan et al., 2022 ). A recent work have shown that some parameters of topological characteristics, such as connectivity, also exhibited good fitting relationships by incorporating Sw   and Pc   (Schlüter et al., 2016 ). Inspired by the previous studies, we established a D  (Sw  , Pc  ) surface using all the data from both drainage and imbibition for the flow rate of Q =100 μL/hr at the REV2  scale, as depicted in Figure S7 d. We fitted a quadratic polynomial against to the data (R2  = 0.9927), as shown below and the fitting parameters are displayed in Table 1  .(12) D ( S w  , P c  )  = b 00  + b 10  ∗ S w  + b 01  ∗ P c  + b 20  ∗ S w 2  + b 11  ∗ S w  ∗ P c  + b 02  ∗ P c 2       The uniqueness of D  (Sw  , Pc  ) surface greatly reduced the hysteresis which exists in both P c  (Sw  ) and D  (Sw  ) curves, making it possible to accurately predict the diffusion coefficient during the loop through Sw   and Pc  . For the other Ca , we examined the fitting results under other injection rates, the R2  values all exceeded 0.98 (Figure S7 ). To test the predicting ability of this model, the data sets obtained under changed flow rates conditions (Q =5, 25, 50, 200, 500 μL/hr) at the same scale were used to validate the model. The experimental values closely aligned with the predicted ones within a 1:1 line (Fig. 10  ). Additionally, the data from each flow rate were fitted separately to predict the other groups. We conducted an examination on the root mean square error (RMSE) for models (Table S2 ). This result confirms the validity of using Pc   and Sw   as independent variables to predict D  at the same scale. By considering that the measurements of Pc   and Sw   are relatively more convenient to obtain, this model demonstrates a promising potential for predicting diffusion in unsaturated porous media. Future iterations of the model should incorporate parameters such as the Ca , pore size, fluid viscosity, and other pertinent factors, which are critical for enhancing its generalizability across different conditions. To comprehensively validate and refine the model, it is imperative to conduct systematic experiments varying these parameters and perform extensive numerical simulations. Such investigations will provide deeper insights into the interplay between these factors and help in developing a robust, generalizable model.   4 Conclusion The extensive study of hydraulic hysteresis in unsaturated porous media during drainage and imbibition cycles is well-documented, yet the impact of historical changes on solute diffusion remains unexplored. Our research aims to investigate diffusion hysteresis in unsaturated porous media by conducting air–water displacement experiments in a micromodel. Hysteresis was measured by determining saturation (Sw  ), capillary pressure (Pc  ), interfacial area (awn  ), and the diffusion coefficient (D ) of the water phase from the obtained images. Our study revealed a hysteresis between D  and Sw   during the drainage and imbibition processes. Notably, D  was found to reduce by 6.10 %–9.48 %during the imbibition process compared to drainage. This novel finding, unreported in existing literature, implies that the historical changes involved influences unsaturated diffusion. Furthermore, the magnitude of D  hysteresis diminished with the capillary number (Ca ) and showed a negative correlation with residual saturation (Srw  ). Finally, we have established a quadratic polynomial model that accurately predicts D  by incorporating Sw   and Pc  , effectively eliminating the diffusion hysteresis. By considering the important role of diffusion in both natural processes and engineering applications, the findings presented in this study provide valuable insights into predicting and understanding solute transport in unsaturated porous media. We have also recognized that our simulation of diffusion coefficient is constrained to 2D directions, and the experimental system is analogous to a 2D system. In the future, a more thorough investigation may be implemented using 3D porous structures and non-intrusive imaging techniques.
1 Introduction Aquatic ecosystems, which support over 10 % of all known species, are among the most biodiverse environments on earth (Cumberlidge et al., 2009; Song et al., 2023 ). Large riverine ecosystems contribute substantial amounts of carbon and nutrients to oceans, establishing crucial links between freshwater, terrestrial, and marine ecosystems, providing vital ecological services (Palmer and Ruhi, 2019 ). Monitoring and assessing the spatiotemporal dynamics of key biotic components within riverine ecosystems are essential for evaluating river network health, representing an important facet of water ecology research (Sprong et al., 2020 ). Plankton communities, predominantly composed of phytoplankton and zooplankton, shape the biological structure of riverine ecosystems and act as principal drivers of biogeochemical cycling (Junger et al., 2023 ). The composition of plankton communities is highly responsive to complex environmental changes, making them essential indicators for evaluating the ecological health of freshwater ecosystems due to their short reproductive cycle, widespread distribution, and ease of collection (Li et al., 2020a, 2020b; Zhang et al., 2023a ). Additionally, structural variations in plankton directly affect the upper food chain and ecosystem stability (Moellmann and Diekmann, 2012 ). Understanding the spatiotemporal patterns of plankton communities and the mechanisms driving their assembly is crucial for maintaining the stability of aquatic ecosystems. The core of community ecology lies in comprehending spatiotemporal patterns in community composition and their underlying driving mechanisms. Distance-decay relationships (DDRs) represent well-established biogeographical patterns in characterizing the spatial distribution of biological communities, primarily involving the study of geographic and environmental distances (Yang et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2020 ). Two fundamental processes, species sorting (environmental filtering) and dispersal limitation, determine the patterns of community DDRs at large spatial scales (Hanson et al., 2012 ). Comparing DDRs between biological communities and geographic/environmental distances help shed light on the potential driving forces of community construction (Yang et al., 2023 ). While DDRs have been widely adopted to explore the biogeographic distribution patterns of diverse biomes mainly microorganisms or macroorganisms (Liu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023b ) at local (Odriozola et al., 2023 ), regional (Feng et al., 2023 ), and even continental scales (Zhang et al., 2022b ), the biogeographic patterns of riverine plankton have not received sufficient attention. Although a few publications have demonstrated the distinct spatial distribution patterns of plankton in reservoirs (Jin et al., 2022 ) and coastal waters (Liu et al., 2022 ), the biogeographic patterns of plankton distribution in different water bodies within large-scale watersheds remain unclear. Community assembly, which is crucial for explaining species coexistence and diversity maintenance, involves deterministic (e.g., niche differentiation) and stochastic (e.g., dispersal limitation) processes proposed by ecological niche theory and neutrality theory, respectively (Hu et al, 2023; Ning et al., 2020 ). Existing research has recognized that both deterministic and stochastic processes contribute to community assembly, proving to be compatible and complementary (Cheng et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023b ). Therefore, it is essential to probe the importance of these processes in community assembly. To quantify the relative significance of ecological niche differentiation and dispersal limitation in community assembly, a dispersal-niche continuum index (DNCI) based on PER-SIMPER has been proposed (Vilmi et al., 2021 ). This DNCI has been applied to investigate the community assembly of flea, small mammals, and plankton (Gibert et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023a ). The roles of niche differentiation and dispersal in plankton community assembly are closely associated with spatial scale, habitat type, and dispersal capabilities of organisms (Rusanov et al., 2022 ). While it has been demonstrated that dispersal plays a major role in constructing plankton communities in a freshwater reservoir and varies seasonally (Liu et al., 2023a ), the impact of seasonal fluctuations in species composition and environmental conditions in large-scale watersheds on community assembly remains unknown. The Yellow River Basin, the world’s fifth-longest river, is renowned for its high sediment content (Ding et al., 2022b; Mu et al., 2012 ) and traverses the ecologically fragile Tibetan Plateau, Inner Mongolian Plateau, Loess Plateau, and North China Plain, showcasing extremely complex geomorphic features (He et al., 2011 ). The exceptionally high sediment content in the Yellow River, coupled with severe siltation and unpredictable course shifts, renders the ecological environment highly sensitive and vulnerable (Ding et al., 2022a ; Jiang et al., 2020 ). Moreover, extensive hydraulic projects, particularly man-made reservoirs, have fragmented the river, disrupted water resource distribution, and disturbed natural biogeochemical cycles, further affecting the seasonal distribution of plankton communities (Ding et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022a, 2022b ). In this study, we investigated the structure characteristics, biogeographic patterns, environmental responses, and community assembly of plankton communities in different water bodies (free-flowing river and reservoir sections) of the Yellow River during two seasons (spring and summer). This study aimed to elucidate: (1) the spatiotemporal distribution patterns of the plankton communities; (2) the biogeographic patterns of the plankton communities, especially in different water bodies; (3) the contributions of ecological niche differentiation and dispersal limitation to plankton community assembly. This study enhances our comprehensive understanding of the interactions between aquatic communities and environmental variables in large-scale rivers, which is essential for the rational protection and restoration of the environmental status and biological resources of heavily sediment-laden rivers.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area and sampling sites The Yellow River (32°10′ N-41°50′ N and 95°53′ E-119°10′ E) is the second-longest river in China, originating from the Bayan Hara mountains in Qinghai Province and spanning approximately 5464 km. The study area extends from Gonghe County, Qinghai Province (west) to Lijin County, Shandong Province (east), encompassing the upper, middle, and lower reaches of the mainstream of the Yellow River (Fig. 1  ). Sampling was conducted twice during March-April (spring, dry season) and July-August (summer, wet season) of 2023. Surface water (depth, 0.5 m), sediments, and plankton samples were collected from 18 free-flowing river sites and 14 reservoir sites (Table S1 ), with sampling sites set according to the requirements of “Technical specifications for freshwater plankton surveys”. Sampling sites should be randomized and evenly distributed. The selection of typical sites should consider the distribution, mixing degree, and water quality heterogeneity, while avoiding areas of strong anthropogenic interference, such as pollution sources. Six major reservoirs (Longyangxia, Liujiaxia, Qingtongxia, Wanjiazhai, Sanmenxia, and Xiaolangdi) were investigated and sampling sections were set up according to reservoir capacity (H: head section; M: center section; T: tail section).  2.2 Determination of environmental variables In-situ water quality variables, including water temperature (WT, °C), total dissolved solids (TDS, mg L−1 ), pH, electrical conductivity (EC, μS cm−1 ), salinity (SAL, ng/L), and dissolved oxygen (DO, mg L−1 ), were measured using a Pro Plus Multi-Parameter Water Quality Meter (YSI). At each site, 2 L of surface water was collected, sealed, and stored at 4 °C in the dark, then sent to the laboratory within 24 h to measure chemical oxygen demand (COD, mg L−1 ), total phosphorus (TP, mg L−1 ), phosphate (PO4 3− , mg L−1 ), total nitrogen (TN, mg L−1 ), ammonia nitrogen (NH4 + , mg L−1 ), and nitrate (NO3 – , mg L−1 ). These parameters were analyzed according to “Environment Quality Standards for Surface Water” (Yang et al., 2023 ). Another 5 L of surface water was collected and filtered across a 0.45 μm mixed cellulose membrane (Merck Millipore, USA) using a vacuum filtration unit, and the membrane was collected to determine the total suspended sediment (TSS) concentration by gravimetric method. Surface sediments (0–10 cm) were sampled with a Peterson dredge, transported to the laboratory at 4 °C in the dark, freeze-dried, ground, and sieved to measure the organic matter content (SOM) and particle size distribution (PSD). SOM content was measured by burning sediments at 550 °C for 4 h to determine weight loss after combustion (Lee et al., 2021 ). Sediment PSD was measured with a laser particle sizer (LA-960, Horiba, Japan) and classified as clay (<0.004 mm), silt (0.004–0.067 mm), and sand (0.067–2.00 mm). Geographic variables including longitude, latitude, and elevation were recorded using OWI interactive map software (V9.9.1).  2.3 Collection, identification, and enumeration of plankton communities Qualitative and quantitative samples of phytoplankton and zooplankton were collected at each site. Qualitative samples were collected using a NO. 25 plankton net (sieve aperture: 0.064 mm) for phytoplankton and a NO. 13 plankton net (sieve aperture: 0.112 mm) for zooplankton. These plankton nets were gently towed back and forth from the surface to a depth of 0.5 m at a speed of 20–30 cm/s for approximately 1–3 min. In deeper water columns exceeding 3 m, sampling was conducted from mixed upper, middle, and lower strata. Subsequently, the plankton net was lifted to drain water, and the concentrated qualitative samples were stored in 100 mL sample bottles. Inorganic Lugol’s iodine was added for phytoplankton preservation and formaldehyde solution was added for zooplankton preservation. Taxonomic identification of qualitative samples was conducted at species level based on “Atlas of Freshwater Microorganisms (Zhou and Chen, 2010 ) and “Descriptions of Freshwater Organisms in China (Han and Shu, 1995 ). For quantitative phytoplankton samples, 1 L of water was collected with a 1 L organic glass hydrophore, fixed with Lugol’s iodine, and allowed to stand for 24 h to facilitate precipitation. After decanting the supernatant, the remaining precipitate (20–25 mL) was transferred to a 50 mL sample bottle. The concentrated samples were shaken well, and 0.1 mL was aspirated to the 0.1-mL counter box for species-level cell counts under a perioptometry. Protozoa and rotifers were counted from the phytoplankton samples, with counts performed using 0.1 mL and 1 mL whole piece from the concentrated 30 mL sample, respectively. Cladocera and copepoda were quantified by filtering 20 L of water using a NO. 13 plankton net, preserved with formaldehyde solution, and counted with a 1 mL counter box. The average values of three parallel experiments were taken to calculate the density and biomass of the plankton samples. All identifications were conducted by Qingdao Zhengke Aquatic Biological Inspection Co., using the optical microscope (Olympus-CX31).  2.4 Data visualization and statistical analyses 2.4.1 Community diversity indices calculation To quantify the alpha diversity of the phytoplankton and zooplankton at each sampling site, Shnnon-Wiener’s diversity index (H' ) (Shannon, 1997 ), Margalef’s richness index (D ), and Pielou’s evenness index (J ) (Pielou, 1966 ) were calculated as follows:(1) Shannon - W i e n e r  i n d e x  ( H ' )   =  - ∑  i =1  S   N  i   N   ln N  i   N     (2) Margale f  '   s  r i c h n e s s  i n d e x  ( D )   = S - 1  lnN     (3) Pielo u  '   s  e v e n n e s s  i n d e x  ( J )   = ( S - 1)  lnN     where Ni   and N  are the number of genus i and the total number of all kinds of genus within the sample, S  is the number of species. Based on three diversity indices, the biological assessment of water quality was conducted (S5, Fig. S1 ).  2.4.2 Spatiotemporal differentiation of environmental variables and plankton Significant pairwise differences of environmental variables were conducted using one-way ANOVA followed by post-hoc Bonferroni tests, and only environmental factors with significant spatiotemporal differences (p  < 0.05) were visualized using box plots in GraphPad Prism 9.5. Non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) and analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) were performed using the “vegan” package in R 4.2.1 to investigate the spatiotemporal differences in plankton communities. Community distance-decay analysis was conducted to explore the relationships between geographic/environmental distance and community dissimilarities, performed using the “geosphere” and “vegan” packages. Principal coordinate analysis of neighbor matrices (PCNM) was employed to construct spatial variables based on the latitude and longitude coordinates of each sampling site. To identify the explanation of geographic, environmental, and altitudinal factors to the spatiotemporal patterns of plankton, variation partitioning analysis (VPA) was implemented using the “vegan” package.  2.4.3 Correlation analysis and driving mechanism of community construction The Mantel’s test based on Pearson’s correlation was performed using the “linkET” package to investigate the possible relationships between environmental factors and plankton community structure. Community assembly is considered as an outcome of multiple intertwined processes, including deterministic (niche-based), stochastic (dispersal-based) processes, and phylogeography (D'Amen et al., 2018; Wen et al., 2022 ). The niche breadth of plankton was measured based on the range and dispersion of individuals over the resource date (Feinsinger et al., 1981 ), using the “spaa” package. One-way ANOVA was conducted to evaluate the differences in niche breadth between communities. Based on the niche- and dispersal-controlled models, PER-SIMPER and dispersal-niche continuum index (DNCI) were derived to reveal the driving mechanisms behind dissimilarities in species composition among different communities (Vilmi et al., 2021 ), and they were conducted using the “DNCImper” package.    3 Results 3.1 Spatiotemporal patterns of environmental variables Table S2  summarizes the measured environmental factors, and Fig. 2   shows those exhibiting significant spatiotemporal differences. Seasonal variations in WT, DO, COD, and TP were statistically significant in both river and reservoir sections (p  < 0.05). The summer season was characterized by higher WT and TP levels, and lower DO and COD levels. In river sections, the concentration of PO4 3−  was significantly higher in summer compared to spring. Furthermore, the TSS levels in the reservoirs were lower than those in the river sections during the spring season, and this discrepancy was consistent for TDS levels in both spring and summer (Fig. 2 C and 2H).  3.2 Diversity and composition of plankton communities As shown in Fig. 3  A, both the Shannon-Wiener diversity index (H’ ) and Pielou’s evenness index (J ) of phytoplankton exhibited significant seasonal variations in river sections (p  < 0.001), with higher values observed during summer. Notably, the Shannon-Wiener diversity index in river sections was significantly higher than that in reservoir areas during summer (p  < 0.01). For the zooplankton community, both the Shannon-Wiener diversity and Margalef’s richness indices were significantly higher during summer compared to spring in both the river and reservoir sections (Fig. 3 B) (p  < 0.01). The higher diversity indices during summer suggest improved water quality conditions, characterized by a higher proportion of moderately/lightly polluted sample sites (based on H’ ) or even predominantly unpolluted sites (based on J ) (S5, Fig. S1 ). During spring months, five phytoplankton phyla were detected in the Yellow River, including Cyanophyta, Bacillariophyta, Chlorophyta, Cryptophyta, and Dinophyta, with Bacillariophyta (relative abundance of 29.2–100 %) prevailing as the dominant species (Fig. 3 C). At the species level, Bacillariophyta primarily consisted of Asterionella formosa  and Synedra acus  during spring (Fig. S2 A). Apart from the above phyla, Chrysophyta and Euglenophyta were observed in summer. The phytoplankton communities in river sections were all dominated by Bacillariophyta, with relative abundance ranging from 37.9 % to 100 %. Contrastingly, in the upstream LYX and LJX reservoir, Chrysophyta (Dinobryon divergens ) emerged as the dominant phylum, with relative abundance varying from 35.7 % to 70.6 % (Fig. 3 C and Fig. S2 B). Additionally, the relative abundance of Chlorophyta increased at most sampling sites during summer. Apart from taxonomic composition, phytoplankton were categorized into functional groups, yielding a total of 21 groups (Table S3 ). During spring, functional groups C and D were predominant (Fig. S3 A). However, in summer, distinct differences emerged among water bodies, with groups X1, Q, and TB  dominating in river reaches, and groups E, F, and P prevailing in reservoirs (Fig. S3 B). Regarding zooplankton, Rotifera, Cladocera, and Copepoda were identified as the primary components (Fig. 3 D). During spring, Rotifera asserted absolute dominance in both river and reservoir sections, with a relative abundance ranging from 33.3 % to 100 %, and the dominant species being Polyarthra trigla  and Keratella. cochlearis  (Fig. S4  A). The relative abundance of Cladocera and Copepoda increased significantly in summer, with Copepoda exhibiting a higher abundance in river sections compared to reservoirs. The increased abundance of Cladocera during summer was attributed to the increased density of Bosmina longirostris , while the increase in the abundance of Copepoda was attributed to the increased abundance of Copepod nauplii  at the species level (Fig. S4 B). Zooplankton were categorized into 6 functional groups according to body size and feeding habits (Table S4 ). During spring, RF and RC were prevalent across most of the sampling sites (Fig. S5  A), whereas the proportion of SCF notably increased during summer (Fig. S5 B).  3.3 Biogeographic analysis of plankton communities The diversity indices revealed significant seasonal variations in both phytoplankton and zooplankton communities, with phytoplankton exhibiting differentiation in different water bodies during summer. The NMDS plots and ANOSIM based on Bray-Curtis distance demonstrated significant differences in phytoplankton and zooplankton communities among the four groups, with phytoplankton showing higher dissimilarities than zooplankton (phytoplankton: R =0.44, p  < 0.001; zooplankton: R =0.32, p  < 0.001) (Fig. 4 A and 4B, Fig. S6 ). To probe the potential factors driving the variability in plankton communities, we conducted biogeographic analysis, which is fundamental for studying the spatiotemporal pattern of biodiversity and the mechanisms of diversity maintenance. Distance-decay relationships, a prominent biogeographic model, explore the relationships between regional geographic distance (stochastic processes) and local environmental distance (deterministic processes) with community dissimilarities (Hu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023b ). Across all sampling sites, phytoplankton and zooplankton community dissimilarities significantly increased with geographical distance in summer (p  < 0.001) (Fig. 4 C and 4D), with a stronger distance-decay effect observed for phytoplankton than zooplankton communities (higher R2  value for phytoplankton). In spring, significant relationships between community dissimilarities and geographic distance were only observed in river sections (Fig. S7 A and S7B) (p  < 0.01). Furthermore, as illustrated in Fig. 4 E and 4F, the Bray-Curtis dissimilarities of phytoplankton and zooplankton communities were significantly correlated with environmental distance (based on Euclidean distance) in both spring and summer across all sampling sites (p  < 0.05).  3.4 Relationship between plankton communities and environmental factors Although DDRs revealed a correlation between plankton community heterogeneity and both geographic and environmental distances, variance partitioning analysis (VPA) underscored the predominant influence of environmental factors on plankton communities compared to geographic and elevational variables (Fig. S8 ). We further explored the relationships between plankton communities and environmental factors using Mantel’s test, as shown in Fig. 5 . In spring, pH and DO were significantly associated with phytoplankton (p  < 0.01) and zooplankton (p  < 0.05) composition, respectively (Fig. 5 A). While in summer, five environmental variables (EC, TDS, SAL, SOM, and the proportion of Clay) exhibited significant correlations with phytoplankton community (p  < 0.01) (Fig. 5 C). For zooplankton, WT, DO, EC, and COD were the dominant environmental factors significantly shaping its composition. A correlation analysis was conducted between plankton phyla and environmental factors to discern the effects of environmental factors on plankton community structure. In spring, the abundance of phytoplankton phyla Cyanophyta and Bacillariophyta displayed positive and negative correlations with TSS, respectively (Fig. 5 B). Within the zooplankton community, only Cladocera density exhibited a significantly positive correlation with NH4 + , EC, and WT (p  < 0.05). In summer, WT, EC, TDS, and SAL were significantly positively correlated with the abundance of Chlorophyta but negatively correlated with that of Dinophyta and Chrysophyta (Fig. 5 D) (p  < 0.05). Sediment properties, including SOM, Clay, and Silt proportions were significantly negatively correlated with Cryptophyta abundance (p  < 0.05). Regarding zooplankton, the abundance of Rotifera exhibited a significant positive association with DO and pH but was negatively related to WT (p  < 0.05). Copepoda abundance displayed a significant positive correlation with NH4 +  and TSS but a negative association with TP and DO (p  < 0.05). Additionally, the response of phytoplankton functional groups to environment variables was analyzed, revealing that DO, COD, TP, PO4 3−  and TSS were the primary factors influencing their distribution in spring (Fig. S9 A). In summer, factors such as EC, TDS, and TN also contributed to their distribution (Fig. S9 B). For zooplankton, DO, WT, and EC were the primary factors in spring, while COD, TN, and TP also played a role in summer (Fig. S9 ).  3.5 Driving mechanisms of plankton community assembly To gain deeper insights into the structural variations within phytoplankton and zooplankton communities, we calculated the niche breadths of communities for each sample. As shown in Fig. 6  A and 6B, no significant seasonal variations were observed in the niche breadths of plankton communities. The PER-SIMPER analysis unveiled that niche- and dispersal-controlled processes collectively shaped plankton communities in both seasons, as the E value (Log of the sum of square deviations with empirical profile) of the “Niche + Dispersal” process was the lowest (Fig. 6 C, 6D, 6E, and 6F). In spring, both phytoplankton and zooplankton communities possessed a lower E value at niche models, suggesting that the potential of niche differentiation played a more robust role in community assembly compared to dispersal limitation. Additionally, zooplankton had a higher DNCI value than phytoplankton in spring, indicating that niche processes exerted a more dominant influence on the assembly of zooplankton compared to phytoplankton. In summer, the phytoplankton community assembly shifted towards a stronger influence of dispersal limitation compared to niche-based processes (Fig. 6 D). Furthermore, a neutral model was adopted to analyze the community assembly, and the low migration rate (m) (3.08–9.09 × 10−5 ) reflected that the stochastic processes contribute less to plankton community assembly both in spring and summer (S14, Fig. S10 ).   4 Discussion 4.1 Spatiotemporal dynamics of plankton communities Monitoring the spatiotemporal dynamics of plankton is imperative for comprehending the functionality of aquatic ecosystems, as well as their interaction and evolution in response to environmental variations (Kaneko et al., 2023 ). This study revealed significant temporal variations in plankton community structure (Fig. 3 A, 3B, 4A, and 4B), with higher diversity and total density observed in summer. Seasonal fluctuations of plankton have also been observed in freshwater reservoirs (Liu et al., 2023a ) and lakes. Seasonal variations in WT and nutrient levels were likewise critical factors affecting plankton diversity and abundance (Staley et al., 2015 ). The average WT of the river and reservoir sections in summer was 25.42 °C and 23.18 °C, respectively (Table S2 ), falling within the optimal temperature range for most organisms, promoting plankton growth and reproduction (Zhou et al., 2023 ). Meanwhile, phosphorus nutrient level was significantly higher in summer than in spring (Fig. 2 ), contributing to plankton growth and metabolism. The prevalence of Bacillariophyta in the phytoplankton community of the Yellow River was attributed to its adaptability to heavily sediment-laden environments (Stevic et al., 2013 ), as previously reported (Ding et al., 2022b ). A certain proportion of Cyanophyta, primarily Oscillatoria  and Lyngbya , were observed in some free-flowing river sections (e.g., LZ, SZS, LM) (Fig. 3 C and Fig. S2 ). These Cyanophyta genera typically inhabit environments that are easily disturbed and rich in organic matter. This phenomenon, as also observed in Ding et al. (2022a) , might be linked to the intensity of human activities surrounding the monitored section. The substantial increase in abundance and dominance of Chrysophyta (mainly Dinobryon ) in high-altitude reservoirs during summer was linked to its preference for clean water bodies (Korneva and Solovyeva, 2017 ). Dinobryon , was the main component of Chrysophyta, is known to thrive in environments with low nutrient levels and organic matter (Wang et al., 2023 ). We also observed a significant negative correlation between Chrysophyta and COD (Fig. 5 D). Notably, the LYX and LJX reservoirs are located at the most upstream locations among the sampling sites, with cleaner water conditions and low COD levels, contributing to a substantial increase in the abundance of Chrysophyta. For zooplankton, the dominance of Rotifera was due to their diverse feeding habits, high reproductive rate, and environmental adaptability (Shen et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2021 ). The growth of Bosmina longirostris  was reported to be stimulated under warming and eutrophic conditions (Li et al., 2016 ), potentially explaining its increased abundance during summer. Distinct plankton community composition was observed in free-flowing river sections (lotic ecosystems) and reservoirs (lentic ecosystems). Different hydrological characteristics in free-flowing rivers and reservoirs shaped distinctive responses of plankton (Ding et al., 2022b ). The interception and enrichment of reservoir dams on nutrients contributed to higher plankton abundance (Yang et al., 2017 ). In this study, only TDS and TSS contents exhibited significant differences in rivers and reservoirs. Faster currents and higher TSS in free-flowing river sections may limit plankton growth due to water disturbance and low light intensity (Wehr and Descy, 1998 ). Conversely, the extended retention time and slower flow velocity in reservoirs facilitate the settlement of suspended sediment, which contributes to higher transparency and favors phytoplankton photosynthesis. This stable environment in reservoirs supports plankton growth and renders them more sensitive to environmental changes (Naselli-Flores and Barone, 2000 ). These intricate interactions and influencing factors culminate in variations in plankton structure between the two water bodies. Within the reservoir, the total density of phytoplankton exhibited an increasing trend from the tail to the head of LYX reservoir in summer, mainly due to the slow flow of the water body over an extended period. The head of the reservoir was closer to the lake habitat, which had the highest existing phytoplankton density. In contrast, for the XLD reservoir, which is irregularly regulated, the total plankton density showed fluctuations, likely due to the unstable water environment. Additionally, the plankton density at the downstream sites of XLD reservoir was lower than that in the reservoir, possibly due to the strong turbulence, high sediment content, and the homogenization of plankton habitats resulting from water-sediment regulation (Hou et al., 2021 ). Furthermore, we observed prevalent positive interactions between phytoplankton and zooplankton functional groups across different seasons. For instance, notable positive correlations were found between the densities of zooplankton filter feeders (RF, MCF, and SCF) and those of phytoplankton functional groups A, C, and J during spring (Fig. S11 A). Similarly, in summer, positive correlations were observed between zooplankton LCF density and phytoplankton functional group J, H1, X2, and Z densities (Fig. S11 B). The dominant LCF identified in this study were Copepods that primarily feed on algae, bacteria, and organic matter. Concurrently, phytoplankton functional group J, predominantly composed of Chlorophyta, exhibited a significant positive correlation with LCF density. In summer, both Copepods and Chlorophyta exhibited increased relative abundance, suggesting a potential predation dynamic between them contributing to the synchronized increase.  4.2 Biogeographic patterns of plankton communities Distance-decay relationships (DDRs) are widely used to characterize biogeographic patterns, elucidating how community dissimilarities fluctuate with spatial and environmental changes (Li et al., 2022a, 2022b ; Zhang et al., 2023c). Consistent with previous studies (Jin et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023b ), substantial DDRs were observed between plankton dissimilarities and geographic distance, with correlation varying across seasons. Both geographic and environmental distances had an effect on plankton community heterogeneity in summer (Fig. 4 ), suggesting that community assembly is controlled by a combination of environmental filtering and dispersal limitation, as observed in prokaryotic communities in the Yangtze River (Hu et al., 2023 ). In spring, significant DDRs between environmental distance and plankton community dissimilarities indicated a more substantial contribution of environmental filtering to the variations in plankton community assembly. Previous studies recognized that the decisive effects of environmental factors such as water quality and climate conditions on plankton composition (Huszar et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019 ), as indicated by the significant DDRs between environmental distance and community dissimilarities in this study. Additionally, DDRs between environmental distance and phytoplankton community dissimilarities were more pronounced in summer than spring, likely attributed to the more diverse functional groups during summer, which are more indicative of environmental heterogeneity and more responsive to environmental fluctuations (Ding et al., 2022b ) (Fig. S9 ). Regarding different water bodies, phytoplankton heterogeneity between reservoirs was significantly affected by geographic and environmental distances only during summer months (Fig. S7 ). In contrast, the dissimilarities of both phytoplankton and zooplankton between free-flowing river sections were influenced by spatial and environmental factors in both seasons. The divergence in DDRs patterns between river and reservoir sections stemmed from two main reasons. One was that the beta diversity between reservoir sections was lower than that in river sections (Fig. S5 ); the other was that initial community similarities were high in adjacent river sections, which typically leads to more pronounced DDRs (Jin et al., 2022; Soininen et al., 2011 ).  4.3 Effects of environmental variables on plankton communities Environmental filtering emerged as a key determinant of the spatiotemporal differences in plankton community composition, as revealed by DDRs and VPA analyses. In this study, water quality emerges as a dominate driver of plankton community structure. During spring, DO and pH were the primary environmental attributes that significantly affected phytoplankton and zooplankton composition, respectively. DO was recognized as a key factor influencing plankton taxa due to its effect on their activity, exerting specific selection on different plankton taxa (Zhang et al., 2022c ). Meanwhile, pH could alter the nutrient uptake of aquatic organisms through effects on enzyme synthesis and cellular osmotic pressure, thereby influencing their growth and metabolism (Santini et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023 ). The abundance of Cyanophyta and Bacillariophyta exhibited significant correlations with TSS, indicating their sensitivity to suspended sediment content during spring. TSS was also significantly associated with the abundance of phytoplankton functional groups MP and Z. The effect of TSS on phytoplankton community was identified as a nondeterministic process that could either promote or inhibit them, as indicated in this study. TSS is primarily generated by sediment resuspension, a process that releases nutrients and thus increases phytoplankton primary productivity (Wei et al., 2020 ). Meanwhile, increased TSS concentration could reduce water transparency, thus restricting phytoplankton photosynthesis and growth (Li et al., 2018 ). During summer months, WT, DO, EC, COD, and the proportion of clay emerged as the most important factors affecting zooplankton and phytoplankton communities. WT plays a critical role in driving phytoplankton metabolism, including photosynthesis, cell division, and nutrient uptake (Li et al., 2023 ), and it was positively correlated with Chlorophyta density in summer (Fig. 5 D), possibly due to that higher temperature was favorable for the growth of Chlorophyta (Alam et al., 2001 ). EC reflects the total concentrations of various ions in the water body, which could affect the plankton communities by altering the trophic structure (Zheng et al., 2018 ). In this study, EC exhibited a notable increase in river sections during summer, primarily attributed to anthropogenic discharges and river runoff inputs (Teittinen et al., 2017 ). The heightened frequency of precipitation during this season may lead to increased runoff inputs into rivers and subsequent increased EC levels. Plankton functional groups were correlated with nutrients (e.g., TP, TN) (Fig. S9 ), suggesting that they are more sensitive to nutrient availability and are affected by the effectiveness of resource use (Oleksy et al., 2020 ). Additionally, sediment characteristics (SOM and PSD) also exerted a significant effect on plankton composition. Organic matter derived from surrounding land or aquatic organisms plays an important role in carbon cycling, aquatic organism distribution, and water quality (Li et al., 2020a, 2020b ). Through interactions with microalgae, sediment clays could mediate aquatic biological and physicochemical processes, thereby affecting the growth of phytoplankton and the feeding behavior of zooplankton (Ho et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, land use, surface runoff, and other factors can also indirectly affect plankton community structure through their coupling with water quality. For instance, during summer, elevated rainfall augments surface runoff, thereby intensifying EC and TP concentrations in the water bodies. These fluctuations influence plankton activities, including growth and metabolism (Zhang et al., 2018 ). Likewise, land use, serving as a spatial reflection of human activities, significantly affects water quality (Zhang et al., 2022a ), indirectly shaping the plankton community by altering nutrient concentrations and reducing water transparency. Previous studies have reported a positive correlation between cultivated area and nutrient levels in the Yellow River, further impacting the community structure of eukaryotic phytoplankton (Han et al., 2024 ).  4.4 Assembly processes of plankton communities Deterministic and stochastic processes were identified as the primary drivers of community assembly, with the former assumed to be more affected by ecological niche-based environmental filtering, and the latter considered to be shaped by stochastic processes such as dispersal limitation and ecological drift (Liu et al., 2023a ). Phytoplankton and zooplankton community assembly were primarily driven by a combination of niche differentiation and dispersal limitation during both spring and summer months. Comparing niche-based deterministic processes with dispersal limitation, niche differentiation played a more dominant role in community assembly, particularly during spring. Different from previous studies where stochastic processes dominated in phytoplankton community assembly (Yi et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2021 ), phytoplankton and zooplankton communities were more driven by niche differentiation in spring, possibly due to relatively slow water velocity during spring, which could inhibit dispersal (Song et al., 2022 ). Lower taxonomic and functional diversity of plankton communities during spring led to increased sensitivity to environmental changes and more pronounced driving force of ecological niche differentiation. Furthermore, investigations have indicated that eukaryotic plankton, with more cellular structures, exhibit a broader response to environmental heterogeneity and are more affected by deterministic process (Logares et al., 2018 ). The driving effect of dispersal limitation on community assembly intensified (revealed by DNCI index and neutral model) and exceeded niche differentiation in phytoplankton community assembly during summer (Fig. 6 D). This indicates that spatial factors had a more pronounced impact on phytoplankton composition in summer, aligning with the results of distance-decay analysis (Fig. 4 C). These above findings align with prior studies focusing on the community assembly of phytoplankton in Lake Wuchang and Lake Changhu in the Yangtze River Basin, where spatial factors dominated in the wet season, while environmental variables were the primary driving force in the dry season, (Guo et al., 2019; Meng et al., 2023 ). However, for zooplankton, ecological niche differentiation remained the dominant force in community assembly. The divergent community constructions of phytoplankton and zooplankton in summer followed the “size-plasticity” hypothesis, i.e., smaller species (phytoplankton) were more susceptible to dispersal limitation due to their higher diversity and environmental tolerance in the habitat compared to larger species (zooplankton) (Farjalla et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2021 ). Interestingly, DNCI analysis found that ecological niche processes dominated the plankton community assembly in the Yellow River. However, VPA analysis revealed that environmental and spatial factors explained a smaller portion of the plankton community variation during summer. In summer, hydrological variables such as water velocity, water surface width, and water inflow among sampling sites varies due to increased rainfall and reservoir regulation (e.g., XLD reservoir) (Hou et al., 2021 ). These factors were previously reported to affect the community structure and construction of plankton communities (Lu et al., 2020 ), they may also play a role in shaping plankton community structure in this study, which warrants further investigation.   5 Conclusions In this study, we analyzed the structural characteristics of plankton communities in different water bodies within the Yellow River Basin, where Bacillariophyta and Rotifera dominated the phytoplankton and zooplankton communities at the majority of sampling sites, respectively. Biogeographic patterns of plankton communities were unveiled using the distance-decay relationships (DDRs), revealing a season-independent significant correlation between environmental distance and community heterogeneity, while geographic distance had a pronounced effect on phytoplankton composition during summer. Notably, DDRs were stronger between free-flowing river sections than between reservoirs. In spring, DO and pH were the pivotal environmental variables affecting the distribution of plankton communities, while in summer, WT, EC, COD, and SOM played dominant roles. Nutrients including TP, TN, and COD significantly altered the composition of plankton functional groups. Ecological niche differentiation and dispersal limitation jointly drove the construction of plankton communities in the Yellow River. Among them, the deterministic process represented by niche differentiation dominated plankton community assembly in spring, while in summer, phytoplankton community was more driven by dispersal limitation. This study deepens our comprehension of plankton distribution and community assembly in both lentic and lotic water bodies across large-scale river basins, laying the groundwork for further insights into the water ecological health of the Yellow River Basin.
1 Introduction The current flood frequency analysis (FFA) paradigm mainly involves fitting a parametric probability model to annual maximum (AM) discharge records. A broad consensus has developed over the choice of the most appropriate parametric models with the three-parameter Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) and Log Pearson III (LP3) models seeing widespread usage (Stedinger et al., 1993; Vogel and Wilson, 1996 ). However, there would be few, if any, who would argue that these models represent the true AM flood distribution, at best they represent an approximation. It is, therefore, not uncommon to find these models fail to achieve a good fit over the whole frequency range. The issue of lack-of-fit has raised concerns about the relevance of the smallest AM floods to the estimation of large flood risk (Cohn et al., 2013 ). The fundamental concern was expressed by Klemeš (1986, pp. 183S–184S) : “For it is by no means hydrologically obvious why the regime of the highest floods should be affected by the regime of flows in years when no floods occur, why the probability of a severe storm hitting this basin should depend on the accumulation of snow in the few driest winters”. Recently Lamontagne et al. (2016)  observed that: “Annual maximum flood records may contain observations dominated by different physical processes, and we should not extrapolate the distribution of the largest floods from the distribution of small floods, when small floods are likely due to different processes”. Turning to the lack-of-fit issue, they identified two broad strategies to address lack-of-fit. The first retains the three-parameter probability model but adopts estimators that put emphasis on the largest flood observations at the expense of the smaller floods. The second uses a more flexible probability model with the intent of producing a better fit and so obviating the need to weight more heavily larger flood observations. The first strategy has been the focus of a concerted research effort in recent years with one approach adopted in national guidelines. This approach relies on identifying potentially influential low flows (PILFs) and censoring them when estimating the probability model parameters. In the context of the LP3 distribution, Bulletin 17C (England et al., 2019 ) has adopted the multiple Grubbs-Beck test for identifying PILFs and censoring them using the EMA estimator (Cohn et al., 1997; Griffis et al., 2004 ). Likewise Australian Rainfall and Runoff (Ball et al., 2019 ) recommends the multiple Grubbs-Beck test for identifying PILFs which are treated as censored observations in a Bayesian framework. Another approach uses LH moments (Wang, 1997 ) which generalize L-moments using higher-order statistics that emphasize the upper part of the distribution. The second strategy, the focus of this paper, is motivated by the mounting evidence that different physical mechanisms are responsible for producing AM floods and hence the flood record contains samples from multiple populations (Alila and Mtiraoui, 2002; Barth et al., 2019 ). The parametric modelling of multiple populations in flood records has been largely implemented using mixture distributions (recent examples include Barth et al., 2019; Iacobellis et al., 2011; Kjeldsen et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2015 ). Mixture distributions provide more flexibility in fitting AM series than three-parameter distributions at the expense of a higher number of parameters requiring inference and, in turn, an increase in uncertainty of high quantile estimates. Waylen et al. (1993)  note that mixture distributions can be represented as finite additive or compound models. The most common FFA applications of mixture distributions use an additive mixture of two populations with each population represented by a two or three-parameter distribution. Allowing for the mixture weight, the number of parameters can range from five to seven. The application of mixture distributions in FFA has been limited by the need for long AM records (Alila and Mtiraoui, 2002 ). When stratification of AM records is possible using independent information, the need for long AM records is reduced. In such cases, two- or three-parameter distributions can be fitted to the stratified records (Barth et al., 2019; Franks and Kuczera, 2002; Kiem et al., 2003; Micevski et al., 2006; Webb and Betancourt, 1992; Yan et al., 2019 ). It is noted that Bulletin 17C does not discourage use of well-constructed stratified records. Nonetheless, while the ability to stratify samples reduces the need for long AM records, the stratified samples need to be sufficiently long to identify the individual populations. Despite the issue of overparameterization and identification of populations, there has only been limited assessment of uncertainty in the parameters of mixture distributions (e.g., Evin et al., 2011; Grego and Yates, 2010; Yan et al., 2019 ). Evin et al. (2011)  used a Gibbs sampler to infer the Bayesian posterior distribution. Yan et al. (2019)  coupled the parametric bootstrap with maximum likelihood estimators to approximate the sampling distributions and found this procedure was not robust. To our knowledge, there has been no comprehensive assessment of uncertainty in FFA mixture models and the relationship between identifiability and record length. The current practice of applying mixture distributions only in cases with long AM records or with shorter AM records when independent information permits stratification, leaves open two mutually related questions: how useful are short to moderate AM records and how robust are current estimation procedures when one population is dominant resulting in poor identifiability of the other population, a situation referred to as degeneracy ? These questions were investigated by Zheng and Frey (2004)  who considered a two-population additive mixture model. They examined the influence of the weight, sample size and degree of separation between populations on identifiability. They found in cases of limited separation between populations, the parametric bootstrap using maximum likelihood estimators could fail and recommended use of a single population. Within the framework of mixture models, compound models have received far less attention than additive ones. They offer a compromise between the flexibility offered by two different populations and the advantage of a more parsimonious distribution. In return for a reduction in flexibility, compound models offer the prospect of reducing or even eliminating the reliance on stratifying AM records into two populations. In summary, the mixture distribution approach requires adopting probability models with four or more parameters to provide the additional degrees of freedom to improve model fit. If well chosen, such models may avoid the need to identify and manage PILFs. They may also offer the opportunity to explicitly represent the contribution of different physical processes to AM floods and thus provide a stronger foundation for extrapolation. However, the issue of degeneracy and availability of adequate records present a significant barrier to adoption. Several compound models have been proposed in the literature, among which there is the Two Component Extreme Value (TCEV) distribution, developed by Rossi et al. (1984) . Exploiting the theory of exact distribution of extremes (Todorovic, 1970, 1978 ), TCEV represents the exact distribution of extremes arising from a mixture of exponential exceedances. With four parameters, TCEV is more parsimonious than additive mixture models using two- or three-parameter components. The purpose of this paper is twofold. The first is to develop an inference scheme for TCEV that robustly deals with degeneracy and its impact on parameter identifiability. The second is to assess the potential of TCEV in at-site applications using short to long AM records with particular focus on goodness of fit and understanding how degeneracy impacts on parameter and high quantile uncertainty. Section 2  of this paper describes the TCEV model and reviews approaches used to estimate its parameters. It then develops a Markov chain sampling implementation of the Bayesian framework for at-site analysis. It proposes parameterizations to manage and diagnostics to identify degeneracy and illustrates their application. This represents the first comprehensive treatment of identifiability in mixture distributions. Section 3  explores the potential of Bayesian TCEV using a case study based in eastern Australia focusing on catchments with long (70 or more years) records. It compares implementation of the TCEV and LP3-PILF approaches for these catchments, first using the full records and then shorter records. The comparison focuses on goodness of fit and extrapolative quantile uncertainty. The paper ends with a critical discussion of the findings and future directions.  2 Robust inference of TCEV parameters using annual maximum data This section presents and illustrates a Bayesian framework for inferring TCEV parameters that robustly handles degeneracy which arises when the parameters of one component are poorly identified. To our knowledge, this is the first rigorous treatment of identifiability in flood frequency mixture models with four or more parameters. It makes possible the application of TCEV to sites with records much shorter than the long records typically used with the additive mixture flood models and the robust quantification of quantile uncertainty for magnitudes beyond the observed data. 2.1 Conceptual foundation The TCEV model is a compound mixture model. It assumes there are two processes contributing to the annual maximum flood. However, unlike additive mixture models, there is no explicit assignment of weight to the probability models associated with each process. The conceptual framework underpinning TCEV assumes in any year that each flood process i    (i = 1 , 2    ) generates a random number of events whose number is sampled from a Poisson distribution with parameter λ i     (mean number of events in a year) and whose peak flow is sampled from an exponential distribution with parameter θ i     (mean peak flow). Rossi et al. (1984)  showed the distribution of annual maximum floods q  resulting from these two processes is:[1] F q | Θ    = exp - λ  1   e  - q  θ  1       - λ  2   e  - q  θ  2           q > 0   exp - λ  1   - λ  2       q = 0   0  q < 0          where Θ  T   = λ  1   ,  θ  1   ,  λ  2   ,  θ  2         with λ 1  , λ 2  ≥ 0    and  θ  1  , θ 2  > 0   . Two important tail behaviors of the TCEV need to be highlighted. First, the right tail of the TCEV converges to a Gumbel distribution,[2] F q | Θ    →  q → ∞   exp - λ  r   e  - q / θ  r         ,     r = arg max  i   θ  i   , i = 1 , 2        Given the primary interest in FFA is estimation of the right tail, the identifiability of the right-tail component parameters λ r     and θ r     and the goodness-of-fit to the right tail are key considerations. Second, there is a finite probability that neither process generates an event in a year resulting in a zero annual maximum flood. This may be useful in applications involving arid and semi-arid catchments where flows are ephemeral. However, this means F q | Θ       is not differentiable at q  = 0 requiring the probability density function to be expressed as a generalized probability density[3] f ( q | Θ )  = λ 1  θ 1   exp - q θ 1      + λ 2  θ 2   exp - q θ 2        F ( q | Θ )    q > 0    exp - λ 1  - λ 2       q = 0    0   q < 0               2.2 Bayesian framework Estimation of TCEV parameters has been largely confined to regionalization applications using maximum likelihood and L-moments. Mindful of their experience with Italian data where the largest annual maximum floods were represented by an “outlier” component, Rossi et al. (1984)  commented “when the four parameters of the TCEV distribution are estimated from a single AFS, the uncertainty is great, particularly as regard the parameters of the outlying component ”. However, the right-tail component does not necessarily have to be an “outlier”. Connell and Pearson (2001)  applied TCEV to sites in New Zealand and found distinct dog-leg signatures in Gumbel frequency plots, a clear sign that both components are well-identified. Totaro et al. (2024)  applied TCEV to long-record sites in eastern Australia where flood regime is linked with decadal-scale climatic phenomena (Erskine and Warner, 1988; Franks and Kuczera, 2002; Micevski et al., 2006 ). Like Connell and Pearson (2001)  they found both TCEV components were well identified. TCEV was also applied to the seasonal components of AM flood series (Strupczewski et al., 2012 ). To date, most of TCEV applications have used either maximum likelihood (ML) or L-moments to fit parameters. The ML method developed by Rossi et al. (1984)  and modified by Fiorentino et al. (1987)  uses the method of successive approximations to solve the nonlinear equations obtained by setting the derivative of the log-likelihood function to zero. A limitation of this ML approach is that AM records must be strictly positive. Arnell and Beran (1988)  investigated an alternative approach using L-moments estimators. In synthetic experiments they found the L-moments estimators failed to reach a solution in a significant proportion of cases (41 % for the UK-based parent and 9 % for the Italian-based parent), while ML found a solution in all cases. They concluded that the failure of the L-moments procedure was due to the limited range of L-skew and L-kurtosis covered by the TCEV distribution. In view of the concern about the robustness of L-moments estimators, the Bayesian framework was chosen to infer TCEV parameters. Marin et al. (2005)  summarize the literature on Bayesian approaches to mixture distributions which have identifiability issues similar to TCEV. Their work suggests that with care, Markov chain sampling of the posterior distribution offers a robust tool to evaluate uncertainty about TCEV parameters even in the case of degeneracy. A key step in Bayesian inference is the evaluation of the posterior distribution (Gelman et al., 1995 )[4] p Φ | D    = p D | Φ    p Φ    p D         where Φ    represents some transformation of the native TCEV parameters Θ   , D    represents the data used to update the prior density p Φ     , p D | Φ       represents the likelihood function which assigns a data-based weight to the prior, and p ( D  )    is a normalizing constant independent of Θ   . A problem peculiar to mixture distributions (Evin et al., 2011; Marin et al., 2005 ) also arises for TCEV. If the component indices 1  and 2  are swapped, the distribution function F q | Θ       and density f q | Θ       remain unchanged. To avoid computing a posterior distribution having two regions, one a perfect copy of the other, an additional constraint θ 1  < θ 2     is imposed. This means that component 2  will describe the right tail behavior of the TCEV. While the imposition of the constraint θ 1  < θ 2     is well founded in the case of TCEV, Marin et al. (2005)  note that imposing constraints on location parameters for mixture distributions with more than two populations can be problematic. If the TCEV were generalized to three or more components, a different strategy would be required to deal with the issue of invariance of F q | Θ       under permutation of component indices. Samples from the posterior are drawn using a Metropolis-Hasting sampler (Gelman et al., 1995 ). The sampling involves the following steps:1) Find the maximum posterior estimate Θ ^     using the Shuffled Complex Evolution optimization algorithm (Duan et al., 1993 ) to maximize the log-posterior.  2) Estimate the posterior covariance Σ ^      by computing the Hessian of the log-posterior at Θ ^     using central differences. If this fails, assign an identity matrix to the covariance.  3) Generate multiple Metropolis-Hastings chains using a multivariate normal proposal with covariance Σ  P     : i. Burn-in phase: Starting at Θ ^     with Σ  P   = Σ ^  ,    update Σ  P      at specified intervals using generated samples and adjust the covariance scaling factor with the goal of achieving an acceptance rate in a target range.  ii. Production phase: Generate a specified number of samples using the Σ  P      tuned in the burn-in phase.     4) Compute Gelman-Rubin statistic to assess the mixing of chains.  5) If the maximum Gelman-Rubin statistic< 1.01, stop. Otherwise go to step 3 and rerun with an increased number of samples.    For well-identified posteriors, 60,000 production samples were found more than adequate with run times of the order of 10 s on an Intel I7 processor. For degenerate posteriors, the number of samples was increased by a factor up to 5 to allow the sampler to visit the entire posterior domain.  2.3 Degeneracy In mixture distributions, degeneracy occurs when one or more weights approach zero making the affected populations unidentifiable. With TCEV, a similar form of degeneracy can arise. The annual maximum is the largest of the peaks generated by two independent component processes. If one component produces all the annual maximum peaks, the other component is unidentifiable. Degeneracy can occur in two ways:1) Component degeneracy occurs when the contribution of component i  to F ( q | Θ )    vanishes for all q  in the data D  : this condition arises when λ i  exp - q θ i      → 0    for all q ∈ D    . Either θ i  → 0    or λ i  → 0    will satisfy this condition.  2) Gumbel degeneracy occurs when both components become identical: This condition arises when | λ  1  - λ 2  | → 0     and θ 1  - θ 2    → 0 .    The location constraint θ 1  < θ 2     forces this condition to manifest itself as component 1  vanishing.     2.4 Identifying degeneracy When degeneracy occurs, the data D   does not contain enough information to meaningfully identify the two components of the TCEV. At best, there may be useful information about the dominant component and little (or none) about the degenerate component. It is therefore essential that such a circumstance be clearly identified and managed. The robustness of the Metropolis-Hasting sampler can be enhanced by selecting a transformation Θ → Φ    which allows the multivariate normal proposal to efficiently sample feasible parameters over the posterior domain. In the presence of degeneracy, the posterior is expected to have significant density close to zero for one or both of the degenerate-component parameters. This suggests that a log transformation be used, namely Φ  k   = log  e   Θ  k     , k = 1 , . . , 4   . As the degenerate component parameters θ → 0 , λ → 0   , the parameters in the posterior domain log e  θ → - ∞ , log e  λ → - ∞ .    Such a domain ideally suits the unbounded multivariate normal proposal used in the Metropolis-Hastings sampler. To further improve the performance of the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm in cases of degeneracy, a weak prior is specified. For log e  θ i     and log e  λ i  ,    the prior is uniform bounded by −5 and 15. This prior has effectively no influence on the posterior for well-identified cases in this study but limits the feasible domain in degenerate cases. Of particular importance is the lower bound of −5. This bound would only be active in cases of degeneracy and prevents the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm from sampling values of θ i     and λ i     infinitesimally close to zero, a domain of no practical relevance. 2.4.1 Posterior degeneracy diagnostics The posterior has distinctly different signatures when a TCEV component is well identified and when it is degenerate. When both components are well identified, the posterior can be approximated by a multivariate normal distribution, which is the asymptotic form of the posterior. In the case of degeneracy, the multivariate normal signature is absent. It is replaced by large regions of near-uniform density where the degenerate component parameters ensure the component has near-zero probability of contributing to the annual maximum. In addition to study of the posterior, it is useful to compute diagnostics that alert to the presence of degeneracy. We present two posterior diagnostic measures for identifying degeneracy and a discussion of their use. We note that Strupczewski et al. (2012)  assessed the contribution of seasonal components to AM quantile uncertainty in their investigation of a two-season TCEV model. The first diagnostic is based on the strength of the contribution of component 2 to F q | Θ      [5] Ψ  2   Θ , q    = λ  2   exp - q θ  2        λ  1   exp - q θ  1       + λ  2   exp - q θ  2             Frequency plots of Ψ  2   Θ , q       for a range of q  evaluated over the posterior can be used to assess the strength of component 2.  When both components are well identified, one expects to see the strength Ψ  2   Θ , q       vary from 0 to 1 over the range of q.  Furthermore, Ψ  2   Θ , q       helps identify the flow beyond which the right tail of the TCEV is described by a Gumbel distribution. The second diagnostic is the probability that an annual maximum is produced by component 2. Beran et al. (1986)  show that the probability of the annual maximum produced by component 2 is[6] P  2   Θ   = - λ  ∗    θ  ∗     ∑  j = 0  ∞   - 1    j    j !   λ  ∗  j   Γ j + 1  θ  ∗           where θ ∗   = θ 2  θ 1      and λ ∗   = λ 2  λ 1  1 / θ ∗        . This diagnostic is useful because it is independent of q  and therefore can be used to obtain the expected number of annual maxima in a sample produced by each component.  2.4.2 Degeneracy signatures Two synthetic cases are presented to illustrate the posterior signatures associated with degeneracy. Case 1: Gumbel degeneracy  This case involves a sample of 100 generated by a Gumbel distribution with true parameters log e  λ = 1.39    and log e  θ = 2.71 .   Fig. 1   shows the posterior parameter plot. The plots for log e  λ 2     and log e  θ 2     show the signature of well-identified parameters, the plots exhibit Gaussian-like behavior with bell-shaped densities (which overlap with the true parameters) and elliptically-shaped 2-d frequency plots. In contrast, the plots for log e  λ 1     and log e  θ 1     show a typical degeneracy signature. The 2-d frequency plots for log e  λ 1     and log e  θ 1     show a wide low-density coverage with all points within this domain corresponding to pairs of log e  λ 1     and log e  θ 1     which result in near-zero strength for component 1  for all flows in the record. The densities of log e  λ 1     and log e  θ 1     are skewed and have large standard deviations. Finally, the 2-d frequency plots between components 1 and 2 are indicative of no interaction between the parameters of components 1 and 2. Fig. 2   shows the posterior strength of component 2 for floods with Annual Exceedance Probabilities (AEPs) ranging from 1 in 1.01 to 1 in 100. The dominance of component 2 is unequivocal. This is confirmed by Fig. 3   which shows that posterior probability of the annual maximum produced by component 2 is virtually one. Case 2: Component degeneracy  In the case of Gumbel degeneracy, the degeneracy will arise regardless of sample size. The more likely form of degeneracy arises when P  2   Θ   → 1   . As the dominant component probability approaches 1 and the sample size decreases, the chance that the record contains annual maxima produced by the dominated component decreases ultimately leading to degeneracy. Fig. 4    to Fig. 6   show the posterior parameter plot and degeneracy diagnostic plots for a 100-year synthetic record generated by a TCEV distribution with parameters matching those fitted to the Barron River at Picnic Crossing site considered in Section 3 . The posterior plot in Fig. 4  shows the signature of well-identified components with Gaussian-like behaviour. Fig. 5  shows that component 2 becomes dominant for flows with AEP less than 1 in 2, while Fig. 6  shows the expected probability of component 2 producing an annual maximum is 62.8% with the probability ranging from 30% to 90%. The posterior plots are repeated in Fig. 7    to Fig. 9   using the first 25 years of the synthetic record. Given that component 2 has an expected 69.9% chance of producing an annual maximum, one would expect on average in a sample of 25, 17 samples from component 2 and 8 from component 1. The posterior parameter plot in Fig. 7  shows that component-2 parameters are well-identified and consistent with those in Fig. 4 . However, the component 1 plots suggest there is limited information about the parameters. The posterior density of log e  θ 1     is bimodal with the right mode close to the posterior mean in Fig. 4 . The 2-d frequency plot for log e  λ 1     and log e  θ 1     shows a narrow-curved region of high density bordering a large region of low density. Fig. 8  shows that component 2 is largely dominant for flows with AEP less than 1 in 1.10, which accounts for over 90 % of the record. Fig. 9  confirms the overall dominance of component 2. The posterior plots show that, while there is useful inference of component-2 parameters, there is limited and difficult-to-interpret information about component 1.    3 Comparative case study evaluating goodness-of-fit and predictive uncertainty With a robust inference framework in place for the TCEV, the goal of this section is to explore its practical potential in at-site analysis. This will be done by comparing TCEV against LP3 in a case study involving 31 catchments from eastern Australia. The LP3 analysis, referred to as LP3-PILF, uses the procedure recommended in Australian Rainfall and Runoff (Ball et al., 2019 ) which involves identification of PILFs using the multiple Grubbs-Beck test followed by Bayesian censoring. There are two parts to the case study: the first compares TCEV and LP3 for long records of at least 70 years, the second repeats the comparison using split samples. 3.1 Selection of sites The sites used in the case study were taken from the P5 database used to develop regional frequency methods in Australian Rainfall and Runoff (Ball et al., 2019 ). All sites from NSW and Queensland that had 70 or more years were selected. The rationale for this cutoff was to maximize the chance of identifying two TCEV components in the full record. Table 1   summarizes the key characteristics of the 31 sites. Catchment areas range from 16 to 2972 km2  and record lengths from 70 to 101 years. Fig. 10   shows the location of the catchments which shows the sites cluster in four regions.  3.2 Full record analysis The section compares the performance of TCEV and LP3-PILF using the full records. Because these record lengths are representative of the longest available, they showcase outcomes least affected by sampling variability. The first part focuses on a qualitative assessment of TCEV and LP3 goodness-of-fit and predictive uncertainty for high quantiles. The second focuses on the identifiability of TCEV parameters. 3.2.1 Comparison of TCEV and LP3-PILF goodness-of-fit and predictive uncertainty The comparison focusses assessment of goodness-of-fit and right tail quantile uncertainty. We use frequency plots to qualitatively assess goodness-of-fit. Following a scheme similar to that of Barth et al. (2019) , we use normalized confidence intervals , defined as the ratio of the 95% confidence interval and the expected probability quantile to report predictive uncertainty. Mindful that plotting positions are correlated, we also use the number of outlying observations, defined as observations lying outside the 95% quantile confidence limits, as a guide of misfit. We stress that comparison of TCEV and LP3-PILF fits cannot be done using traditional goodness-of-fit metrics such as Akaike or Bayesian Information Criteria, because the information used in fitting differs (TCEV is fitted to all the data while LP3 is fitted to a subset of the data). By way of illustration, consider Fig. 11   which shows the LP3 and TCEV frequency plots for site 31. The plots use an AEP Gumbel scale up to the 1 in 200 AEP and have identical vertical scales. For a given AEP, the uncertainty in the quantiles is expressed by 95% confidence limits (or more accurately, credible limits). Censoring of PILFs is denoted by a square box located at the censoring threshold. For both TCEV and LP3 all observations lie within the 95% confidence limits with the principal differences occurring in the way the distributions fit the right tail - LP3 overshoots the top 4 ranked flows, while TCEV undershoots the rank 2–4 flows but matches the rank 1 flow. Both distributions are judged as fitting the data satisfactorily. The most obvious difference between the plots is the width of the 95% confidence intervals with TCEV exhibiting relatively narrow intervals at high quantiles which contrast with the rapidly widening intervals for LP3. This result is typical for the large majority of LP3 and TCEV site comparisons. The LP3 was judged to fit all the sites satisfactorily in the sense the 95 % confidence limits largely contained the observations. In contrast for TCEV, it was found at several sites that a larger than expected number of observations were outside the 95% confidence limits. Table 2   reports the number of observations lying outside the 95% confidence limits for each site. For LP3, only six sites had outlying observations with a maximum of 3. In the case of TCEV, sixteen sites had outlying observations with five sites having 4 or more flows lying outside the 95% limits. Table 2  also reports the percentage of flows identified as PILFs and censored in the LP3 fit. By censoring PILFs, LP3 is being preferentially fitted to the larger flows. As shown in Table 2 , one or more PILFs were identified in twenty sites (out of 31) with sixteen sites having ≥   30% PILFs and nine sites with ≥   40% PILFs. As a practical consequence, LP3 has three parameters to fit in many cases to the top 50–75% of the data while TCEV has to fit the whole series. This observation also supports the fairness of the proposed comparison. An example of a site with significant outlying observations in the TCEV fit is site 29, Boorowa River at Prossers Crossing. Fig. 12   shows the TCEV and LP3 frequency plots for this site. TCEV has six outlying observations - three lie close to the confidence limits, while the other three correspond to the top three ranked flows which lie well above the upper confidence limit. In contrast, LP3 has no observations lying outside the limits, though 29% of the original observations were censored. Both the LP3 and TCEV fits overshoot the flows between 1 in 10 and 1 in 5 AEP. However, LP3 has more flexibility to follow the path of the top ranked flows than TCEV but this comes at the price of significantly inflated confidence intervals. In summary, the comparison of LP3 and TCEV fits suggests there is little practical difference for the bulk of the sites. There were, however, about five sites where LP3 better fitted the highest-ranking flows in the sense of observations lying within the 95 % confidence limits.
