This is in part attributed to the censoring of PILFs which allows more flexibility fitting the right-hand tail but, more likely, is due to the fact the LP3-PILF 95% confidence intervals are much wider than the TCEV intervals for high quantiles. This is clearly demonstrated in Fig. 13   which shows a scatter plot of normalized confidence intervals for 1 in 50 and 1 in 100 AEP quantiles. Using the 1:1 red line as a reference, it can be seen that the LP3 normalized quantile uncertainty is roughly double that of TCEV.  3.2.2 TCEV parameter identifiability The identifiability of the TCEV parameters was assessed studying the posterior parameter and degeneracy diagnostic plots. An example of degeneracy is shown for site 11, Barnard River at Barry. Fig. 14   shows the TCEV frequency plot and the parameter posterior. While the fit is satisfactory and the high quantile confidence intervals much smaller than the LP3 intervals, the posterior exhibits a complex degeneracy signature. The posterior of component 2 is uni-modal but heavily skewed. The posterior of l n ( θ 1  )    is bimodal. This bimodality is very evident in the 2-d frequency plots involving l n ( θ 1  )    and the component-2 parameters. The 2-d frequency plots involving l n ( λ 1  )    and the component-2 parameters have the characteristic L-shape consistent with degeneracy. The component 1 standard deviations are about 6 times greater than their component-2 counterparts. The practical focus is identification of the right tail of the TCEV. In this regard, two items of information are particularly relevant, the posterior of the component-2 parameters and the AEP beyond which component 2 dominates the right tail of the TCEV. Four figures are used to summarize the identifiability issue across the 31 sites. Fig. 15   shows for each site the posterior mean with standard deviation error bars for l n ( θ )   , while Fig. 16   does so for ln λ      . Fig. 17   shows for each site the posterior mean with standard deviation error bars of the component-2 strength for AEPs 1 in 2, 1 in 5 and 1 in 10 as well as 1 - P  2   Θ     . Fig. 18   offers a different perspective showing box plots of the component-2 strength posterior means for AEPs from 1 in 1.01 to 1 in 100. These figures offer the following insights:1) The AM records contain more samples from component 2 than 1. Fig. 18  shows the transition from component 1 to component 2 occurs in the AEP range 1 in 1.01 to 1 in 2. This is consistent with the posterior mean of P 2  ( Θ )     lying above 0.5 for all but four sites.  2) For all sites, the component-2 posteriors are well identified with Gaussian-like behavior. Fig. 15  and Fig. 16  show that the component-2 parameters have much tighter standard deviations than their component-1 counterparts. This is attributed to the greater number of samples in the AM records arising from component 2.  3) Unlike component 2, the uncertainty in the component-1 parameters exhibits much more variability. The posterior standard deviations range from small values comparable to component 2 to large values associated with degeneracy. When degeneracy occurs, the posterior standard deviations of both component-1 parameters are large.  4) Component 2 is dominant for quantiles with AEPs less than 1 in 5 meaning the right tail closely follows a Gumbel distribution for AEPs less than 1 in 5. Fig. 17  shows that for an AEP of 1 in 5, the expected strength of component 2 is greater than 0.9 for all but two sites. For an AEP of 1 in 10, only one site has an expected strength less than 0.95. The tight confidence limits for high quantiles arise from the fact that well over half of the AM record is available to identify the component-2 parameters, which define the right-tail Gumbel distribution.      3.3 Split-sample analysis The goal of this section is to assess the identifiability of TCEV parameters when fitted to records short to moderate in length. Such records are obtained by splitting site records in two and four nonoverlapping sub-samples. The results are reported here for the same three sites used in the previous section, sites 11, 29 and 31. Fig. 19   shows plots of posterior mean and two standard deviation bars for the TCEV parameters at three sites for all sample combinations. The leftmost sample is the full record. As expected, uncertainty increases with decreasing sample size. Nonetheless, the component-2 parameters remain well-identified. In contrast, the component 1 parameters are subject to much more uncertainty and in many cases are poorly identified. Their posteriors are often bimodal with complex non-Gaussian signatures. This poor identifiability is consistent with low values of 1 - P  2  ( Θ )    , shown in Fig. 20  , which indicates only a small number of AM come from component 1 in all cases except one. The exception occurs for the fourth split sample of site 29, where component 2 is dominated by component 1. Likewise, the component-2 strength plots show that component 2 is dominant for all AEPs lower than 1 in 2. As before, the confidence limits for TCEV are much narrower than LP3-PILF due to convergence of the TCEV right tail to a Gumbel distribution. However, due to the increased quantile uncertainty, only a limited number of observations lie outside the TCEV confidence limits. These results are not reported here because they are consistent with those of the previous section.  3.4 Discussion The purpose of the case study was to empirically assess the practical potential of TCEV in at-site FFA. In assessing its potential, two questions need to be answered. The first is whether the TCEV inference framework is robust. Clearly, without a reliable inference framework, there is little prospect of practical application. The Bayesian framework presented in Section 2  proved to be robust in the case study in the sense that the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm produced chains that adequately mixed in all cases including a significant number involving degeneracy. The degenerate posteriors were found to have quite complex signatures (including bi-modality and non-linear interaction) which are very different to the Gaussian signature expected in large samples. While there is no guarantee the Bayesian framework will be robust in application to other catchments, the widespread usage and success of Markov chain sampling in Bayesian computation suggests it is reasonable to expect similar performance elsewhere. The second question is whether TCEV produces FFA outcomes that are unambiguously better than existing methods. Unlike the first question, this one is more difficult to answer with confidence. The ultimate practical goal of FFA is to estimate high flow quantiles as accurately as possible - ideally the quantile estimates should be unbiased and have narrow confidence intervals. The case study compared the performance of TCEV against the LP3-PILF approach. The first part of the case study focused on long records as they provide the best opportunity to assess goodness-of-fit. Overall, there is little practical difference in the LP3-PILF and TCEV fits. If one uses the number of observations lying outside 95 % confidence limits as a measure of misfit, then LP3-PILF fits would be judged to be better - TCEV has five sites with 4 or more observations lying outside 95 % confidence intervals, while LP3-PILF has six sites with outlying observations with a maximum of 3. While this result may be due to censoring of PILFs which allow LP3 to better fit the right tail, it is more likely a consequence of LP3-PILF having much wider confidence intervals than TCEV for high quantiles. The main difference to emerge is the consistently narrower confidence intervals produced by TCEV. This result runs counter to the expectation that flood probability models with more parameters are subject to greater extrapolative uncertainty. However, as the case study shows this may not always be the case. In the case study, component 2 produced more annual maximum samples than component 1. This resulted in component-2 parameters being well-identified in all cases including records of the order of 20 years. Because the right tail of the TCEV approaches a Gumbel distribution as component 2 becomes dominant, the confidence intervals for high quantiles will be tighter compared to LP3-PILF whose right-tail behavior is quite sensitive to uncertainty in the skew parameter. Which high-quantile confidence intervals, those produced by TCEV or LP3-PILF, better represent the true uncertainty? While it is beyond the scope of this study to seek an answer to this question, it is worth noting some of the awkward issues that need to be confronted. Given that goodness-of-fit assessment is limited by historical record lengths, the credibility of extrapolation becomes central to this question. To our knowledge, there is no known physical justification for LP3 as a model of flood frequency. The skew parameter can be thought of as a fitting device to allow curvature in the log-normal probability domain. On the other hand, TCEV has a physical foundation in so far that annual maxima are sampled from flow events generated by two independent processes. Totaro et al. (2024)  provided a theoretical framework supported by physical evidence for justifying the application of TCEV distribution in eastern Australia. Extrapolation of the TCEV rests on the assumption that its right tail is sampled from events whose peaks are exponentially distributed and whose number is Poisson distributed. In principle, these are testable hypotheses using data other than AM. The fact that both TCEV components were identifiable in the majority of the long records in the case study (see Figs. 15 and 16 ) suggests that AM flows with AEP greater than 1 in 2 may be the product of processes different to those producing the rarer flows. Again, in principle, this is a testable hypothesis using data other than AM. Two probabilistic approaches have been proffered as providing a plausible foundation for extrapolation. One is based on the theory of asymptotic distributions of extremes, the other on the theory of exact distributions. Each approach makes assumptions which must be validated if the approach is to provide a credible basis for extrapolation. If the number of independent events in a year is insufficient to ensure convergence, the asymptotic distributions approach is incapable of providing a credible basis for extrapolation. In a similar vein, the lack of knowledge about the true underlying distribution of event exceedances (Koutsoyiannis, 2004; Lombardo et al., 2019 ) undermines the extrapolative credibility of the exact distributions approach. However, the exact distributions approach is open to refinement. The challenge is to make the best use of our accumulated knowledge on the physics of floods and the extensive data on floods to identify with more confidence the underlying event exceedance distribution. We are of the view that the growing evidence of multiple flood populations and the derived distribution framework (Eagleson, 1972 ) will contribute to the refinement. The Bayesian scheme for inferring TCEV parameters can exploit additional sources of information (e.g., historical or pre-gauged information) which can lead to significant reductions in quantile uncertainty. Viglione et al. (2013)  highlight the versatility of Bayesian inference in using spatial, temporal and causal information in flood frequency hydrology. The use of historical information has received considerable attention in the literature (see, Stedinger and Cohn, 1986; Reis and Stedinger, 2005; Kjeldsen et al., 2014 ), to the point that its use has been incorporated in national flood frequency guidelines (e.g., Bulletin 17C, England et al., 2019 ; Australian Rainfall and Runoff, Ball et al., 2019 ). Furthermore, the physical basis underlying the derivation of the TCEV distribution supported by physical arguments for the case study of Eastern Australia (Totaro et al., 2024 ), offers the prospect of developing regional relationships that may lead to further reduction in quantile uncertainty. While this study has presented empirical evidence to suggest that the TCEV has practical potential in at-site FFA, it is important to stress the tentative nature of this conclusion. The case study is representative of four clusters of catchments in eastern Australia with areas up to about 1000 km2 . The success of TCEV rests on the identifiability of the right-tail component. In this case study, more than half of the AM records were produced by the right-tail component so its two parameters were identifiable even using short records. In other regions, the right-tail component may be dominated by the left-tail component. How TCEV compares with LP3-PILF or other approaches in such regions needs to be investigated.   4 Conclusions The issue of lack-of-fit in AM flood series can be tackled by censoring PILFs when fitting three-parameter probability models. An alternative and less-studied approach is to apply mixture probability models which offer greater flexibility to fit AM series. Mixture models may be additive or compound with compound models being more parsimonious. This study investigated the potential of using the four-parameter TCEV compound model in at-site flood frequency analysis. The conceptual foundation of TCEV relies on two independent processes contributing to AM floods. If one process dominates, degeneracy arises with the parameters of the other process not being identifiable. For this reason, a robust inference of TCEV parameters is required. This study produced two significant outcomes. The first addressed the issue of robust inference of TCEV parameters. Given L-moment estimation has been found to be questionable for TCEV, a Bayesian framework using Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling was developed. It produced new insight into the nature of degeneracy associated with TCEV. In particular, the posterior signatures for well-posed and degenerate cases were described. It was found that the signatures in degenerate cases were quite complex. To aid assessment of such degeneracy, two new posterior diagnostics based on the strength of the TCEV components were developed. This work represents the first known comprehensive assessment of identifiability in FFA using mixture models with four or more parameters. In the still wide-open field of model selection, the Bayesian framework and tools developed in this study offer interesting perspectives for further methodological developments in the comparison between different types of heavy tailed distributions, not excluding mixture distributions. Armed with a robust inference framework, the study evaluated the potential of TCEV using a case study based on 31 catchments in eastern Australia with record lengths 70 or more years. The evaluation involved comparing TCEV fit and high quantile uncertainty against the LP3-PILF approach recommended in Australian Rainfall and Runoff (Ball et al., 2019 ). The second significant outcome showed that, at least for the case study, the TCEV distribution is a suitable choice for at-site flood frequency analysis. TCEV was shown to deal with the dog-leg signatures encountered in the flood frequency plots. Overall, there appears to be no clear difference in goodness-of-fit between TCEV and LP3-PILF. Unlike LP3-PILF, TCEV was sufficiently flexible to fit all AM data without the need to censor low flows. However, and contrary to the expectation that more parameters lead to greater high quantile uncertainty, TCEV produced consistently narrower high quantile confidence intervals than LP3-PILF. It was found that TCEV extrapolative uncertainty depends on the number of AM floods in the record being generated by the right-tail component process. While more case studies in different regions using the TCEV Bayesian framework are needed, this study has demonstrated that TCEV can produce fits comparable to LP3-PILF with significantly narrower high quantile confidence intervals. This study does raise a significant and difficult-to-answer question, which high-quantile confidence intervals, those produced by TCEV or LP3-PILF, better represent the true uncertainty? While it is unlikely this is a genuinely binary choice, the question deserves serious consideration. Goodness-of-fit is a necessary but not sufficient criterion for selecting the probability model that best represents flood frequency. The path to sufficiency will likely require probability models to better reflect the physical basis of AM floods.
1 Introduction Nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) losses via runoff from sloping croplands are important environmental factors that lead to soil fertility loss and downstream water quality degradation (Udawatta et al., 2006; Cherobim et al., 2017 ). Due to the different forms of N and P elements transported via runoff, the total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP) in runoff comprise dissolved nitrogen (DN), dissolved phosphorus (DP), particulate nitrogen (PN), and particulate phosphorus (PP) forms, which respond differently to rainfall runoff (Liu et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2022 ). The concentrations and losses of N and P in runoff in different forms have attracted considerable attention when assessing the impacts of N and P in runoff on the soil nutrient budget and water eutrophication (Bah et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020 ). The stoichiometric ratios of various forms of N and P in runoff have rarely been studied, including TN:TP, DN:DP, and PN:PP which are key variables reflecting the nutrient balance in runoff water, though the stoichiometric characteristics of N and P have been strongly emphasized in studies of various soil and aquatic ecosystems (Jarvie et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021 ). Therefore, given the increasing frequency and intensity of human activities and climate change, further study of changing N and P concentrations, losses, and stoichiometry in runoff in sloping croplands is important to promote sustainable soil fertility and water quality management. Rainfall primarily drives runoff production and plays a key role in nutrient loss via runoff in sloping croplands (Huang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022 ). Previous studies have shown that different categories of rainfall amount have distinct effects on the runoff concentration and loss of soil nutrient (Li et al., 2022 ). Smith et al. (2007)  observed that low rainfall amounts can increase nutrient concentration in runoff compared to high rainfall amounts because of rainfall-runoff events after fertilization applications. Liu et al. (2024)  found that the concentration and loss of N in runoff were significant higher in large rainstorm than in other rainfall events. To date, studies of the concentrations, losses, and stoichiometry of different forms of N and P under multiple rainfall amount categories are still limited. Chemical fertilizers have played an important role in improving soil fertility and crop production to satisfy the rapid population growth worldwide over the past few decades (Rose et al., 2014; Sane et al., 2021 ). However, excessive chemical fertilizers accumulate in soils due to blind fertilizer applications. This does not directly promote fertilizer use efficiency but increases N and P losses via runoff (Smith et al., 2007; Cui et al., 2020; Hua and Zhu, 2020 ). In recent years, manure has been globally applied to many sloping croplands as an environmentally sustainable strategy (Hati et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2020 ). Compared to chemical fertilizers, the application of manure and its combination with chemical fertilizers can significantly improve soil properties and crop productivity (Zhang et al., 2009; Dhiman et al., 2019 ) and reduce N and P losses via runoff (Tomer et al., 2016; Li et al., 2022 ). However, some studies have determined that the independent use of manure and/or its combination with chemical fertilizers increased N and P losses by runoff due to the progressive saturation of soil element sorption capacities (Yan et al., 2017; Zanon et al., 2020 ). More data is needed to interpret the effects of manure and chemical fertilizers on N and P losses via runoff from sloping croplands conclusively. Straw return has been widely applied to sloping croplands to reduce runoff and soil loss by improving soil properties, increasing surface roughness and runoff infiltration, and dissipating raindrop energy (García-Orenes et al., 2009; Jing et al., 2022 ). Recently, studies have reported the negative effects of straw return on soil properties as well as losses of soil and nutrient, which increases concerns on the utilizability of straw return globally. For instance, Liang et al. (2023)  reported that straw return can exacerbate soil acidification in major Chinese croplands due to increased leaching of soil base cations. Rahma et al. (2017)  suggested that returned straw enhances rill erosion and exacerbates soil loss under certain extreme rainfall conditions. Park et al. (2021)  observed an increased dissolved organic carbon loss via runoff under rice straw return because the returned straw materials contributed to the nutrient source. Liu et al. (2024)  observed larger N loss with straw return relative to the N loss without straw return under the heavy rain. These inconsistent results indicated that the effects of straw return on runoff reduction and nutrient loss remain unclear (Li et al., 2019a; Zhang et al., 2021 ). Therefore, further characterization is required for the response of N and P characteristics, including concentrations, losses, and stoichiometry, in runoff to the integrated use of fertilization and straw return to optimize agricultural management strategies in sloping croplands. In this study, a three-year dataset recording multiple natural rainfall events from 2019 to 2021 was used to determine the changes in N and P of runoff as affected by local traditional fertilization (control, CK), multisource fertilization (T1), and the combination of T1 with straw return (T2) under different rainfall amount categories in a representative sloping cropland subjected to natural rainfall events. The response of N and P concentrations, losses, and their paired stoichiometries in runoff to rainfall amount category, multisource fertilization and straw return were particularly examined. The specific objectives of this study were to (1) determine the runoff characteristics and the concentrations, losses, and stoichiometry of TN, DN, PN, TP, DP, and PP as affected by the CK, T1, and T2 under different rainfall categories; and (2) quantify the relationships between rainfall amount, runoff depth, and the N and P variables.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area This study was conducted at a field base monitoring N and P losses in sloping croplands in Xinglong Town, Yubei District, Chongqing Municipality, Southwestern China (106°45′22″E, 29°54′46″N). The site has a subtropical monsoon climate, with an average annual rainfall of 1189.5 mm, mainly occurring from May to October, an average annual temperature of 17 °C, an average annual sunshine duration of 1229.3 h, and an average annual frost-free period of 319 days. The overlying soils were purple soil per the Chinese soil taxonomic classification, which is equivalent to Entisols in the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) taxonomy (Liu et al., 2009 ). A preliminary survey before the initiation of monitoring experiments obtained the soil properties within the 0–20 cm soil depth: sand 18.6 %, silt 57.2 %, clay 24.2 %, soil bulk density 1.34 g cm−3 , pH 5.89, organic matter content 11.19 g kg−1 , TN content 0.73 g kg−1 , TP content 0.34 g kg−1 , nitrate nitrogen content 3.44 mg kg−1 , ammonium nitrogen content 9.56 mg kg−1 , and Olsen-phosphorus 30.07 mg kg−1 . The prevailing vegetation was evergreen broad-leaved forests, such as Pinus Massoniana  (Lamb.), Quercus Fabri  (Hance.), and Cupressus funebris  (Endl.). The common crops on the sloping cropland were predominantly radish (Raphanus sativus  L.) and corn (Zea mays  L.). Irrigation management was not conducted during the experimental period as rain-fed farming is a common agricultural management practice in the region (Wang and Zhu, 2011 ).  2.2 Experiment design To determine the characteristics of N and P in runoff when subjected to CK, T1, and T2 under different natural rainfall events, nine parallel runoff plots (8 m × 3 m) were constructed on a purple soil sloping cropland with a slope gradient of 5° (Fig. 1  ). Combined with the prevailing rotation of winter radish and summer maize in the study area, three treatments, including local traditional fertilization (control, CK) (pig manure in radish season, and pig manure + compound chemical fertilizer in maize season), T1 (pig manure + artificial organic fertilizer in radish season, and pig manure + compound chemical fertilizer + artificial organic fertilizer in maize season), and T2 (T1 + straw return in both radish and maize seasons), were randomly applied on those plots, and each experimental scenario had three replications. All runoff plots were separated by concrete brick walls to eliminate potential substrate interactions. A T-shaped trough was equipped at the lower end of each plot to concentrate the surface runoff produced by rainfall events into the terminal water collection tank with a volume of 2.94 m3  (3 m × 1.4 m × 0.7 m). An aluminum panel was set above each tank to avoid rainwater interference with the runoff volume. A rotation of winter radish and summer maize was adopted in each plot for each treatment. Winter radishes were planted in late October using hole sowing with a spacing of 60 cm × 20 cm and harvested in early February of the following year. Summer maize was sown in early April on flat croplands adjacent to the plots in early March, with a plant spacing of 60 cm × 40 cm, and harvested in late June, then remained fallow until the next radish growing season. Nevertheless, multisource fertilization differed between the winter radish and summer maize seasons. Twice fertilization was used in the radish season: basal fertilizer was applied before sowing, and topdressing fertilizer was applied in early December. During the maize season, a single basal fertilization treatment was applied before transplanting. The types of fertilizers applied to the cropping system included pig manure (moisture 90 %, 0.5 % N, 1.1 % P2 O5 , and 0.7 % K2 O), artificial organic fertilizer (moisture 2 %, 15 % N, 7 % P2 O5 , and 13 % K2 O), and compound chemical fertilizer (moisture 2 %, 15 % N, 15 % P2 O5 , and 15 % K2 O). The nutrient inputs for CK, T1, and T2 treatments are listed in Table 1  . The fertilizers applied for T1 and T2 were the same in both radish and maize seasons. T2 included additional straw return, and the harvested cornstalk (average rate 2.0 ± 0.15 kg m−2 ) was returned immediately to the plots as mulch.  2.3 Sampling strategy and measurements During 2019–2021, rainfall was recorded using a rain gauge installed near the cropland (within approximately 200 m) of the experimental plots. Runoff volume was measured for each rainfall event in each collection tank. Runoff samples were collected at different depths from the tank using two prewashed polyethylene bottles (approximately 500 ml for each) after mixing thoroughly, and the remaining runoff in the tank was cleaned. Those runoff samples were delivered to the laboratory within 2 h, and kept in a 4 °C refrigerator for further analysis. In the laboratory, the content of one sample bottle was used to separate the sediment from the runoff, and obtain an accurate runoff water volume. The content of the second sample bottle was divided into two portions: one was unfiltered to determine the total nitrogen concentration (TNc) and total phosphorus concentration (TPc); the other was filtered through 0.45 μm water filtration membranes to measure the dissolved nitrogen concentration (DNc) and dissolved phosphorus concentration (DPc). TNc and DNc were determined using alkaline potassium persulfate digestion ultraviolet spectrophotometry, and TPc and DPc were analyzed using the potassium persulfate molybdenum blue colorimetric method. The particulate nitrogen concentration (PNc) and particulate phosphorus concentration (PPc) were calculated by subtracting the DNc and DPc from the corresponding TNc and TPc, respectively (Liu et al., 2012 ). All measurements were conducted within 24 h, per standard Chinese protocols (SEPAC, 1997 ).  2.4 Rainfall amount categories and data calculation To determine the effects of different rainfall amount categories on N and P characteristics in runoff, rainfall events producing runoff were grouped into light rain (LTR, < 9.9 mm), moderate rain (MR, 10–24.9 mm), heavy rain (HR, 25–49.9 mm), rainstorms (RS, 50–99.9 mm), and large rainstorms (LR, > 100 mm), according to the rainfall amount within 24 h following the China National Standard GB/T 28592-2012 (GAQS and IQPPC, 2012 ). During 2019–2021, 22 rainfall events producing runoff were recorded (Fig. 2  ). The maximum rainfall was recorded on July 8, 2021 (125.1 mm), and the minimum rainfall was observed on May 13, 2019 (15 mm). The average rainfall of the 22 events was 67.6 ± 26.8 mm, and the cumulative rainfall was 1486 mm. Additionally, the 22 rainfall events were grouped into 1 MR (15 mm), 4 HRs (39.3 ± 7.6 mm), 15 RSs (72.5 ± 17.3 mm), and 2 LRs (112.9 ± 17.3 mm), accounting for 4.5 %, 18.2 %, 68.2 %, and 9.1 % of those rainfall events, respectively. To interpret the runoff characteristics, runoff depth was calculated using Equation (1) :(1) RD  ij   = Q Tij   × Q  bij    A × V       where RDij   is the runoff depth (mm) with the subscripts indicating the i th runoff event and j th plot; QTij   is the runoff volume in the tank (L); Qbij   is the runoff water volume (L); A  is the area of the plot (m2 ); and V  is the volume of the bottle (L). The loss of TN (TNl), TP (TPl), DN (DNl), DP (DPl), PN (PNl), and PP (PPl) was obtained using Equations (2)–(5) , respectively:(2) TL  ij   = TC  ij   × Q  Tij    A × 100       (3) DL  ij   = D C ij   × Q Tij   × Q bij    V × A × 100       (4) PC  ij   = TC  ij   - DC  ij       (5) PL  ij   = TL  ij   - DL  ij       where TLij   is the TNl and TPl (kg ha−1 ) with the subscripts indicating the i th runoff event and j th plot; TCij   is the TNc and TPc (mg L− 1 ); DLij   is the DNl and DPl (kg ha−1 ); DCij   is the DNc and DPc (mg L− 1 ); PCij   is the PNc and PPc (mg L− 1 ); and PLij   is the PNl and PPl (kg ha−1 ).  2.5 Statistical analysis The Shapiro-Wilk test was used to test the normality of the variables, and the log10 -transformation was conducted when the data was not normally distributed. One-way analysis of variance with Tukey’s HSD post hoc test was conducted to determine the effects of rainfall amount categories and agricultural treatments on runoff depth; the concentrations and losses of TN, DN, PN, TP, DP, and PP; and the stoichiometric ratios of TN:TP, DN:DP, and PN:PP. Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was used to coordinate the correlations among study variables. Simple regression analysis was used to explore the relationships between runoff depth and different forms of N and P losses. A value of p  < 0.05 was regarded as a statistically significant difference in this study. All statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 22.0. All figures, except Fig. 1 , were generated using SigmaPlot 12.5.   3 Results 3.1 Runoff depth Runoff depth varied significantly among the different rainfall amount categories (p  < 0.05) and was highest for the RS group. Runoff depth for the RS group was 191.1 %, 178.7 %, and 6.5 % higher than those for the MR, HR, and LR groups, respectively (Table 2  ). Runoff depth was not significantly different among three treatments (i.e., CK, T1, and T2) with p  > 0.05 (Table 2 ), but was significantly higher in RS and LR compared to MR and HR within CK, T1, and T2, respectively (p  < 0.05) (Fig. 3  a).  3.2 N and P concentrations in runoff The TNc was not significantly different among the rainfall amount categories or the three treatments (p  > 0.05) (Table 2 ). However, TNc was the highest in the MR in the T1 and T2 (p  < 0.05), showing 63 %, 115.2 %, and 122.3 % higher than that in the HR, RS, and LR in T1, and 66 %, 103.5 %, and 146.6 % in T2 (Fig. 4  a). The DNc was not significantly different among the rainfall amount categories and three treatments (Table 2 ). The DNc was the highest for MR at T1, showing 88.9 %, 102.4 %, and 163.3 % for HR, RS, and LR, respectively (p  < 0.05) (Fig. 4 b). The PNc was 56.2 %, 135.5 %, and 64.8 % higher in the MR than that in the HR, RS, and LR (p  < 0.05) (Table 2 ). In contrast, PNc did not vary significantly among the treatments (p  > 0.05) (Table 2 ), and was significantly higher for MR than for the other rainfall amount categories in T2 (p  < 0.05) (Fig. 4 c). The TPc was the highest for the LR group (115.8 %, 70.8 %, and 32.3 % higher than for the MR, HR, and RS groups, respectively; p  < 0.05) (Table 2 ). The TPc was not significantly different among the three treatments (p  > 0.05) (Table 2 ), but varied significantly among rainfall amount categories in the CK (p  < 0.05) (Fig. 4 d). The DPc was also the highest for the LR group, 357.1 %, 128.6 %, and 60 % higher than for the MR, HR, and RS groups, respectively (p  < 0.05) (Table 2 ). The DPc did not vary significantly among the three treatments (p  > 0.05) (Table 2 ), but increased significantly from MR to LR in CK, T1, and T2 (p  < 0.05) (Fig. 4 e). The PPc did not vary significantly among the rainfall amount categories and treatments (p  > 0.05) (Table 2 ), and was not significantly different according to the rainfall amount category in each treatment (p  > 0.05) (Fig. 4 f).  3.3 N and P losses in runoff The TNl did not vary significantly among the rainfall amount categories or the three treatments (p  > 0.05) (Table 2 ), and was not significantly affected by the rainfall amount category in each treatment (p  > 0.05) (Fig. 5  a). The DNl was the highest for RS, with 184 %, 255 %, and 31.5 % higher values than those in MR, HR, and LR, respectively (p  < 0.05) (Table 2 ). The DNl was not notably affected by the treatments (p  > 0.05) (Table 2 ), but was significantly higher in RS than in the other rainfall amount categories for all three agricultural practices CK, T1, and T2 (p  < 0.05) (Fig. 5 b). The PNl was the highest for the LR group, which was 100 %, 192.3 %, and 46.2 % higher than for the MR, HR, and RS groups, respectively (p  < 0.05) (Table 2 ). The PNl was not significantly affected by the treatments (p  > 0.05) (Table 2 ), and did not vary significantly among the rainfall amount categories within each treatment (p  > 0.05) (Fig. 5 c). The TPl was the highest in LR, which was 400 %, 400 %, and 25 % higher than in MR, HR, and RS, respectively (p  < 0.05) (Table 2 ). The TPl did not significantly differ among the three treatments (p  > 0.05) (Table 2 ), and varied significantly among rainfall amount categories in the CK (p  < 0.05) (Fig. 5 d). The DPl was 1233 %, 300 %, and 100 % higher for the LR group than for the MR, HR, and RS groups, respectively (p  < 0.05) (Table 2 ). The DPl did not vary significantly among the three treatments (p  > 0.05) (Table 2 ), and consistently increased significantly from MR to LR in each treatment (p  < 0.05) (Fig. 5 e). The PPl was the highest in RS and was consistently 100 % higher than that in the other rainfall amount categories (p  < 0.05) (Table 2 ). The PPl was not significantly different in the three treatments (p  > 0.05) (Table 2 ) or rainfall amount categories within each treatment (p  > 0.05) (Fig. 5 f).  3.4 N and P stoichiometry in runoff The TN:TP ratio was higher for the MR group (69.8 %, 78.1 %, and 265.6 %, respectively) than for the HR, RS, and LR groups (p  < 0.05) (Table 2 ). The TN:TP ratio was highest in T1, followed by T2, and lowest in CK (p  < 0.05) (Table 2 ), and decreased significantly from MR to LR in T1 (p  < 0.05) (Fig. 6  a). The DN:DP ratio was the highest for the MR group, being 204 %, 164.9 %, and 835.9 % higher than for the HR, RS, and LR groups, respectively (p  < 0.05) (Table 2 ). The DN:DP ratio was not significantly affected by the treatments (p  < 0.05) (Table 2 ), and was the highest for the MR in the CK and T1 (p  < 0.05) (Fig. 6 b). The PN:PP ratio was not significantly affected by the rainfall amount category, but varied significantly among the treatments, with the highest in T1 (p  < 0.05) (Table 2 ). The PN:PP ratio did not vary significantly among the rainfall amount categories for any treatment (p  > 0.05) (Fig. 6 c).  3.5 Relationships between rainfall amount, runoff, and N and P traits Spearman’s rank correlation analysis showed that the rainfall amount and runoff depth were significantly correlated with N and P losses, in particular runoff depth (Table 3  ). The regression analysis indicated that the significant relationships between runoff depth and losses of N and P in runoff were better described by a linear function for each treatment (Table 4  ).   4 Discussion 4.1 Response of runoff depth to rainfall amount category, multisource fertilization, and straw return Our results showed the highest runoff depth during RS, which was similar to that during LR, but significantly higher than that during MR and HR (Table 2 , Fig. 3 ). This result was consistent with previous discoveries (Ramos and Martínez-Casasnovas, 2006; Meng et al., 2021 ). An et al. (2023)  reported that rainstorms produced the largest runoff depth, accounting for 36.8 %–39.3 % of the total runoff in sweet potato and peanut contour ridges in the rocky mountain areas of Northern China. Li et al. (2022)  suggested that large rainfall amounts related to rainstorms and large rainstorms generated higher runoff depths in long-term fertilized purple soil sloping croplands. This is because that high rainfall amounts in rainstorms and large rainstorms can cause soil saturation and sealing during a relatively short period, leading to a higher runoff depth than lower rainfall amounts in moderate and heavy rains (Jia et al., 2007 ). Compared to CK, T1 and T2 reduced runoff depth though these reductions were not statistically significant (Table 2 ). These outcomes are similar to previous reports by Bah et al. (2020) , who observed that organic manure and its combination with crop residues reduced the discharge of overland flow and interflow compared to chemical fertilizers, and these changes did not vary significantly. In general, fertilization can improve soil structure and physical properties (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2010; Dhiman et al., 2019 ), leading to increased water infiltration and reduced runoff production (Gilley and Risse, 2000; Tomer et al., 2016 ). Fertilization can also augment crop biomass and vegetation coverage (Hati et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2009 ), which increases rainfall interception and the dissipation of raindrop kinetic energy and decreases runoff loss (Marques et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2016 ). The above outcomes imply that the improvement of soil properties, crop biomass, and vegetation coverage as affected by multisource fertilization can contribute largely to the reduction of runoff depth. Returned straw materials can increase the interception and infiltration of rainfall water to reduce runoff production in immediate or short-term applications (Prosdocimi et al., 2016 ), and improve the water storage capacity (Dong et al., 2019 ) and soil structure (Jordán et al., 2010 ) to reduce runoff loss in long-term applications. However, straw return can direct runoff water along the length of the straw materials to the outlet (Rahma et al., 2017 ), thereby increasing runoff loss. Li et al. (2019b)  suggested that compared to bare slope, the immediate straw return elevated the runoff rate because the straw materials intensified the concentrated runoff flow, leading to raised runoff depth in the hillslope, southwest China. In this study, the non-significant changes in runoff depth were possible because the T1 and T2 were not able to improve the soil physicochemical properties effectively, which play a key role in altering runoff production in the three-year monitoring experiments. This is favored by Zanon et al. (2020)  who pointed out that the long-term manure application and straw return were not capable of reducing runoff loss in heavy rainfall due to the lack of significant improvement in soil properties. These outcomes suggest that the applications of T1 and T2 have great potential for decreasing runoff depth.  4.2 Response of N and P concentrations and losses in runoff to rainfall amount category, multisource fertilization, and straw return Although the concentrations of TN, DN, and PN did not vary significantly among the different rainfall amount categories, relatively higher TNc and DNc and lower PNc in runoff were found in MR, in which the TPc and DPc were significantly higher than those in other rainfall amount categories (Table 2 , Fig. 4 ). Similar discoveries were presented in previous studies showing that moderate rain was capable of producing higher nitrate nitrogen concentration in runoff (Li et al., 2022 ). Additionally, higher TPc and DPc in runoff could result from large rainstorms (Huang et al., 2020 ). The timing of fertilization is possibly answerable for higher N and P concentrations in runoff under low rainfall amounts (Sharpley, 1997; Jung et al., 2015 ). Wang and Zhu (2011)  detected higher nitrate nitrogen concentration in runoff when rainfall occurred after fertilization in a hilly area of purple soil in China. Li et al. (2020)  observed high DN and DP concentrations in runoff after fertilization in a watershed in China that was dominated by sugarcane growth. These discoveries highlight the importance of rational fertilization timing in reducing N and P concentrations in runoff (Cherobim et al., 2017; Li et al., 2022 ). The concentrations of TN, DN, PN, TP, DP, and PP were marginally higher with T1 and T2 than with CK (Table 2 , Fig. 4 ). This outcome implies that manure, chemical fertilizers, artificial organic fertilizers, and their combination with straw return have the potential to increase N and P concentrations in runoff, which is sustained by previous discoveries (Cui et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020 ). This is probably because that T1 and T2 increase soil N and P retention, which contributes substantial N and P substances to runoff water (Huang et al., 2020; Zanon et al., 2020 ). Lourenzi et al. (2021)  reported that fertilization applied successively or excessively caused nutrient (especially P) accumulations on the surface soil layer and raised their losses via runoff. However, the opposite discovery was detected by Eghball et al. (2002)  who found that long-term manure application did not markedly influence N and P concentrations in runoff. The changes in solute (e.g., N and P) concentration in runoff are regulated by the features of solute and runoff flow, and need further elucidation (Moatar et al., 2017 ). In addition, average concentrations of TN (6.88 mg L-1 ) and TP (0.31 mg L-1 ) in runoff across all treatments exceeded the threshold value of surface water quality standards (TN 2.0 mg L-1  for grade V and TP 0.3 mg L-1  for grade IV) in China (Tan et al., 2015 ). This indicates the need for effective measures to minimize N and P concentrations in runoff and avoid potential water quality degradation in downstream aquatic ecosystems. The DN, PN, TP, DP, and PP losses were similar to the changes in runoff depth among the different rainfall amount categories, with significantly higher values for RS and LR (Table 2 , Fig. 5 ). These discoveries are also approved by the relationships between runoff depth and runoff losses of the N and P variables in this study, implying that N and P losses are predominantly regulated via runoff generation (Udawatta et al., 2006; An et al., 2023 ). Liu et al. (2024)  investigated the N loss characteristics related to N concentration and runoff depth under different categories of rainfall amount, and suggested that N loss was mostly dependent on the runoff rather than N concentration. The T1 and T2 did not significantly augment the losses of TN, DN, PN, TP, DP, and PP compared to CK (Table 2 , Fig. 5 ). The similar outcomes were found in Liu et al. (2020) . Wang et al. (2022)  observed that the losses of TN, DN, TP, DP, and PP by runoff did not alter significantly between reduced chemical fertilizer plus manure and straw return plus chemical and organic fertilizers at the same rate in a fava bean and rice rotation. However, under the wheat and maize rotations in the purple soil sloping croplands, Bah et al. (2020)  found significant reductions in the losses of TN, PN, TP, and PP via runoff under organic manure combined with chemical fertilizer and crop residues combined with chemical fertilizer, compared to chemical fertilizer alone. The antecedent soil moisture and vegetation coverage as affected by multisource fertilization and straw return are answerable for the different outcomes (Udawatta et al., 2006; Van Verseveld et al., 2009 ) and jointly determine the losses of N and P via runoff. Cheng et al. (2021)  demonstrated that antecedent soil moisture significantly affected the losses of N and P during the soil erosion process, due mostly to the shifts in runoff dynamics under different levels of antecedent soil moisture. Huo et al. (2021)  detected the nonlinear relationships between nutrient loss and vegetation coverage, and suggested that 60 % vegetation coverage presented lowest soil nutrient loss. In addition, our results showed that DN and DP losses accounting for 70.5 % and 59.8 % of TN and TP losses across all treatments, respectively (Table 2 ). This corresponds to findings by Wang et al. (2022) , who reported higher losses of DN and DP than those of PN and PP in a fava bean and rice rotation. However, this was inconsistent with the N and P losses via surface runoff under wheat and maize rotations (Bah et al., 2020 ), which showed higher proportions of DN and PP losses in the total losses of TN and TP. With manure application time, Cherobim et al. (2017)  observed gradually reduced proportions of PP losses on the TP. Lourenzi et al. (2021)  found that DP loss exceeded PP loss via runoff in untilled soil subjected to successive organic waste and mineral fertilizer applications. These discoveries are likely due to the low sediment yield from runoff, thus producing a low associated PP loss (Zanon et al., 2020 ).  4.3 Response of N and P stoichiometry in runoff to rainfall amount category, multisource fertilization, and straw return The TN:TP and DN:DP in runoff were significantly higher in MR than in the other rainfall amount categories, whereas PN:PP did not differ significantly by rainfall amount category (Table 2 , Fig. 6 ), implying that DN was more easily transported via runoff than DP under low rainfall amounts. This discovery also suggests that the DN and DP lost via runoff contributed to the losses of TN and TP. The T1 and T2 increased TN:TP, DN:DP, and PN:PP relative to CK (Table 2 , Fig. 6 ). Wang et al. (2022)  reported similar findings, with a higher TN:TP ratio in runoff in the combination of manure and chemical fertilizers and straw return than in chemical fertilizer plus manure and reduced fertilizer combined with manure. Zhang et al. (2023)  found that the TN:TP ratio in runoff was significantly lower in plots with fertilizers and contour cultivation than in plots with no fertilizers and downslope cultivation on a purple soil sloping cropland. They also suggested that the combination of manure and chemical fertilizers did not significantly change the TN:TP ratio in runoff compared to the same or increased chemical fertilizers. This is likely due to the changes in fertilizer sources and straw return, which can cause different microbial activities in soils, altering the runoff stoichiometric ratios of N and P in different forms (Wang et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021 ). The TN:TP (77 ± 79), DN:DP (109 ± 149), and PN:PP (59 ± 60) in runoff across all treatments were higher than those reported by Bah et al. (2020) , showing that the average TN:TP (12 ± 4), DN:DP (51 ± 27), and PN:PP (8 ± 3) in the surface runoff influenced by the applications of manure, chemical fertilizers, and crop residues on the purple soil sloping croplands. The larger N:P ratio in runoff is attributed to a greater soil N than soil P, which is readily transported via runoff. These discoveries attest the effectiveness of T1 and T2 in improving soil N and P retention and lowering sediment yield driven by rainfall runoff. These results also imply that the stoichiometric potential for P depletion in runoff is affected by T1 and T2 (Smith et al., 2017 ).  4.4 Implications Our results indicated that runoff depth exhibited better relationships with the losses of TN, DN, PN, TP, DP, and PP in different treatments compared to rainfall amount (Tables 3 and 4 ). Thus, runoff depth should be considered an important parameter and incorporated into the prediction model for N and P losses via runoff (Schlesinger et al., 2000; Li et al., 2022 ). The T1 and T2 seemed to decrease runoff production but increased N and P losses in this study. Prolonged observations are required to identify the responses of N and P dynamics in runoff to the treatments under natural rainfall events in the study area, which will contribute to the identification of effective agricultural management practices for rain-fed sloping croplands. Further, previous evidence shown that N and P concentrations in runoff significantly elevated when N and P sources were applied just before rainfall events (Sharpley, 1997; Eghball et al., 2002 ). Therefore, possible increases in N and P losses for early runoff events after the application of fertilizers, including manure, artificial organic fertilizers, and compound chemical fertilizers should be investigated (Smith et al., 2007; Zanon et al., 2020 ). To minimize N and P losses via runoff due to fertilization timing and rates, using weather forecasts to inform decisions about when to apply fertilizers and the preset fertilizer rate based on soil nutrient levels is highly recommended (Lourenzi et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022 ). In addition, immediate straw return has the potential to induce greater soil loss during extreme rainstorms, increasing concerns about N and P losses by runoff (Rahma et al., 2017 ). Further investigation is required to determine a rational straw return rate to decrease the loss of soil nutrients via runoff under variable extreme rainfall conditions and site-specific soil environments (Janeau et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021 ).   5 Conclusion Higher runoff depths, and TPc and DPc values were found in rainstorms and large rainstorms, whereas the highest PNc was observed in moderate rainfall. These results favor higher losses of PN, TP, DP, and PP via runoff during rainstorms and large rainstorms. The runoff depth was slightly reduced by 4.2 % and 12.7 % in multisource fertilization and the combination of multisource fertilization and straw return, respectively, in comparison to CK. The concentrations and losses of N and P in runoff marginally elevated in multisource fertilization and the combination of multisource fertilization and straw return relative to CK. The DN and DP losses dominated the TN and TP losses via runoff. Higher TN:TP ratios in runoff across all treatments relative to the Redfield ratio implied a stoichiometric potential for P depletion in the runoff. These results indicated that multisource fertilization and the combination of multisource fertilization and straw return had the potential to decrease runoff production but raised the risk of dissolved nutrient loss via runoff. Notably, these results also reflected the importance of long-term monitoring experiments under natural rainfall events in assessing the feasibility of reducing nutrient loss via runoff using prevailing agricultural practices. Our results are valuable for optimizing control measures for N and P losses via runoff in sloping croplands under intense human activity and climate change.
1 Introduction Drought, as a natural climatic phenomenon, occurs in every hydro-climatic region. It can be defined as a climatic condition experiencing a prolonged shortage in water supply resulting from insufficient precipitations, particularly prevalent in arid or semi-arid regions where the rainfall pattern exhibits high variability (Glantz, 2003 ). Drought can recur as a phenomenon, becoming a major concern when it reaches a threshold that stresses a number of agricultural, ecological, hydrological, and biophysical processes with socio-economic implications (Wilhite and Glantz, 1985 ). The complexity of drought is heightened by a sequence of processes that unfolds in a cascading manner, leading to challenges to the scientific community in uniformly quantifying drought across disciplines (Tramblay et al., 2020 ). In order to quantify these drought phenomena, and investigate their interannual and regional variability as well as the impacts of climate change, a set of precipitation-based indices have been proposed for IPCC reports (Gutiérrez et al., 2021; Han and Singh, 2023; Lee et al., 2023; Pachauri et al., 2014 ) and implemented in the Rclimdex tools (Shrestha et al., 2017; Zhang and Yang, 2004 ). They mostly refer to yearly information on precipitation amounts, dry spells, and occurrences of extreme precipitation events (Meteorological indices). In a more integrative way, the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), a widely used drought index relying solely on precipitation data, has emerged as a main tool in operational drought monitoring. Introduced by McKee et al (1993)  and further elaborated by Edwards and McKee (1997) , the SPI assesses monthly precipitation anomalies at a specific location by comparing observed total precipitation levels over a defined accumulation period (e.g., 1, 3, 12, or 48 months) with the long-term historical rainfall data for that corresponding period. More recently, Vicente-Serrano et al (2010)  combined Potential Evapotranspiration (PET) and SPI into the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI). Beside the direct use of these indices for agro-ecological assessments (Gao et al., 2018; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2012; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2014 ), recent studies could derive additional features such as drought onset, offset, peak drought month, and intensification rate as key drivers of agro-ecosystems functioning (Beyene et al., 2023; Fung et al., 2020; Iglesias et al., 2022; Mathbout et al., 2021; Rahmat et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2021; Yoo et al., 2022 ). We could, however, deplore an intrinsic lack of temporal precision on a monthly time resolution. Nevertheless, these recent studies highlight the multifaceted nature of drought events and their intricated implications (Beyene et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2018 ), so that a single drought index appears insufficient to cover all drought impact assessments (Zargar et al., 2011 ). Daily soil water balance models, simulating a temporal information on soil water content (mm/day), could provide a more detailed and dynamic picture of drought compared to monthly or seasonal indices, including rainfall pulses or deep drainage during extreme events when rainfall inputs exceed the capacity of soil to retain this water (Deo et al., 2017; Lu et al., 2014 ). Empirical soil water budget models as, among others, the Keetch-Byram Drought Index (Keetch and Byram, 1968 ), are tailored to reflect the impact of daily meteorological anomalies on soil water loss (further called water depletion measured in mm/day), relying on precipitation data and accounting for water that integrates soil layers (i.e., upper and duff soil layers). Based on this daily soil water content (or desiccation to field capacity defining the daily drought intensity), already standard yearly integration of drought features can be implemented more precisely as severity, duration, and timing (onset and offset), more readily usable than the raw meteorological measures used for their calculation (Zargar et al., 2011 ). Drought onset can be defined by the day when soil water content falls below a threshold, while drought offsets is determined when a large amount of rainfall increment to the hydrological cycle will replenish soil moisture above that threshold, with drought duration and severity directly derived from these timings (Liu et al., 2021; Tsakiris et al., 2007; Yoo et al., 2022; Zargar et al., 2011 ). Heretofore, a comprehensive understanding of a drought event and its associated impacts on agriculture and ecosystems, entails multiple facets of the soil water content dynamic across the dry period, surpassing the confines of a singular drought feature (Beyene et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2018 ). Yet, to date, this domain is comparatively underexplored, presenting an ongoing frontier for exploration and there are currently only few attempts having targeted the characterization of yearly drought features through a daily measured or simulated water balance (Deo et al., 2017; Hunt et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2011; Lu, 2009; Lu et al., 2014; Ruffault et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2022; Zribi et al., 2016 ), yet no consensus on a generic tool to generate these features has been proposed. Accordingly, this study aims at presenting DFEAT, an automated tool for drought features identification, designed to discern and extract a set of yearly drought features derived from a daily soil water desiccation time series. We have tested this tool with the Keetch-Byram drought index over Lebanon, a Mediterranean drought-prone region covering a climate gradient from Mediterranean sub-humid to arid and present here its application, genericity, and sensitivity to climate uncertainty.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area Lebanon is located on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean Sea (Fig. 1  a), covering an area of 10,452 km2  between 33°–35°N and 35°–37°E (Shaban, 2020 ). Lebanon hosts a harsh topography providing various microclimates from Mediterranean to arid, representative of the whole Mediterranean basin. Three major geomorphological features exist (Fig. 1 b). The Anti-Lebanon mountain chain runs North/South parallel to the Mount-Lebanon chain and the Mediterranean coast, separated by the agricultural Bekaa Plain. The two parallel mountain ridges of Lebanon, which overlook the Mediterranean Sea, serve as a meteorological barrier. This barrier intercepts the cold air masses originating from the Mediterranean sea and causes them to condense into rain and snow (Shaban et al., 2019 ). Accordingly, this topographic complexity of mountainous regions across the country results in a high spatial variability in precipitation (Jomaa et al., 2019 ), with high annual rainfall amounts occurring on the high mountainous regions (>1200 mm) and predominant semi-humid to humid climate in the coastal zone (around 800 mm) (Fig. 1 a). Arid-climate is located in the Northeastern part of Lebanon (Shaban et al., 2019 ) with annual rainfall amounts being lower than 600 mm. Under a typical Mediterranean climate with four distinct seasons, warm and dry summer and wet winter, the rainfall pattern follows a seasonal distribution, primarily occurring between the months of October and March (Kobrossi et al., 2021 ). The four consecutive months, June to September, constitute the warmest period of the year and experience relatively low levels of precipitation. The average winter temperature is 13 °C on the coast, decreasing with altitude. In summer, the average temperature is 29 °C (Shaban, 2020 ).  2.2 Meteorological data We used the daily ERA5-Land dataset over the period 1960–2020. ERA5-Land is an open-source climatic dataset with a global spatial resolution of 9 km, simulated hourly by global high-resolution numerical integrations of the ECMWF land surface model driven by the downscaled meteorological forcing from the ERA5 climate reanalysis, including an elevation correction for the thermodynamic near-surface state (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021 ). ERA5-Land data, offering the finest resolution with the open-source climate data, have been widely used in climate impact research and have been locally acknowledged for their good performance (Gatien et al., 2023; Gomis-Cebolla et al., 2023 ). For our study, the climatic variables downloaded all over Lebanon were air temperature (K) at 2 m and total precipitation (m) for the selected time period. However, ERA5-Land data are unavailable for certain pixels near the coastal zones, as ERA5-Land relies on a network of observations and satellite data, and in some instances, these sources may not provide adequate coverage or resolution near coastlines.  2.3 Keetch-Byram drought index (KBDI) The Keetch-Byram drought index (KBDI, Keetch and Byram, 1968 ) is an indicator of soil water deficit to field capacity (i.e., maximum amount of water that a soil can hold after draining and measured in mm) based on a simplified water-balance model simulating daily soil water loss per day. The index is widely used in wildfire monitoring (Ainuddin and Ampun, 2008; Brown et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2010; Varol and Ertuğrul, 2016 ) through the flammability of organic materials within the ground (Novitasari et al., 2019 ), fire management (Dimitrakopoulos and Bemmerzouk, 2003; Ganatsas et al., 2011 ), and fire hazard prediction (Hamadeh et al., 2015; Nogueira et al., 2017; Zhao and Liu, 2021 ). In addition, it was used in climate change (Gannon and Steinberg, 2021 ) and agricultural research studies (Salehnia et al., 2018 ). The index calculation requires few meteorological data: daily maximum temperature (Tmax), daily precipitation (P), and the mean annual precipitation data (Py). It is a cumulative index of the litter and duff layer desiccation, calculated as a balance between soil water input from effective precipitation (Eq. (1) ) and an empirical model that approximates the actual evapotranspiration from daily soil desiccation (Eq. (2) ) and temperature-based evaporative demand (i.e., PET) (Liu et al., 2010 ) (Eqs. (3) , (4)). We define here soil desiccation as the soil water deficit to field capacity and soil water depletion as the daily soil water loss based on Zhang et al (2023) . Note that in KBDI initial document (Keetch and Byram, 1968 ), you will find soil depletion defined as our soil desiccation, a concept that was not fully standardized at the time. The KBDI initial version assumes that the field capacity of the upper soil/duff layer is 8 in. (203 mm), a strong assumption as this field capacity is not always true, since it depends on soil texture and depth, but kind of a fair value within the superficial rocky soils observed in Mediterranean ecosystems (Ganatsas et al., 2011; Häusler et al., 2019; Pellizzaro et al., 2007; Ruffault et al., 2013; Zribi et al., 2016 ). In Equation (3) , soil moisture is assumed to saturate at 8 in. and the KBDI values are then constrained to a maximum value of 800 (unit: 0.01 in.).
