Estimation of global warming potentials   To better assess the contribution of GHGs emission from Honghu Lake to global warming, the Global Warming Potential (GWP) of GHGs was calculated, as shown in the following formulas:(5) GWP = F × n      In the formula, GWP  represents the global warming potential of GHGs (mg m−2  d−1 ); F  is the water–air interface flux of GHGs (mg m−2  d−1 ); n  is the corresponding GWP  value of the GHGs. Hydrochemical analysis   Hydrochemical indicators help reveal the nutrient cycling and biogeochemical processes within lake ecosystems, directly impacting the production and emission of GHGs. Before the analysis of the total carbon (TC), total nitrogen (TN), DIC, and DOC, water samples were filtered through a 0.45 μm membrane filter (MILLIPORE, USA). TC, TN, and DOC concentrations were immediately measured using a TOC analyzer (Shimadzu TOC-V CPH, Japan). Ammonium nitrogen (NH4 + -N) and nitrate nitrogen (NO3 - -N) were determined using a UV–Visible spectrophotometer (HACH DR6000, USA) in accordance with national standards HJ 535-2009 and HJ/T 346-2007. Excitation-emission matrices (EEMs) were obtained using a fluorescence spectrophotometer (Agilent Cary Eclipse, USA). The excitation wavelength ranged from 200 to 450 nm with a step of 5 nm; emission wavelengths ranged from 250 to 600 nm with a step of 2 nm. The scanning rate was 1200 nm min−1 . Parallel factor analysis.   Parallel factor analysis (PARAFAC) of the three-dimensional fluorescence spectroscopy data was performed using the DOMFluor toolbox in MATLAB R2020b. Over the past decade, PARAFAC has been commonly used to interpret EEMs data and identify organic matter types in DOM fluorescence groups (Stedmon et al., 2003; Stedmon and Markager, 2005 ).  2.4 Quantification of groundwater discharges 222 Rn is a radioactive substance with a relatively short half-life (about 3.8 days). Variations in the 222 Rn concentration can indicate the degree of exchange between groundwater and lake water. If the 222 Rn concentration in lake water is relatively high, it usually indicates a significant amount of groundwater discharging into the lake. Therefore, current study utilizes a steady state 222 Rn mass balance model to quantify the groundwater discharge at the lake bottom (Adyasari et al., 2023 ). The model identifies all possible sources (inputs) and sinks (outputs) of 222 Rn and assumes that the missing radon in the balance model is provided by groundwater discharge, while quantifying them. In the general 222 Rn mass balance model, groundwater input, sediment release, and radium decay are considered as sources of 222 Rn in lake water, while atmospheric diffusion and radioactive decay of radon in lake water are considered as sinks, as shown below:(6) F adv  + F diff  + λ Rn  I Ra  = λ Rn  I Rn  + F atm       In the formula, Fadv   represents the advective radon fluxes from the sediment (Bq m−2  d−1 ); Fdiff   represents the diffusive radon fluxes from the sediment (Bq m−2  d−1 ); λRn IRa   represents the decay of 226 Ra dissolved in the water (Bq m−2  d−1 ); IRa   represents the 226 Ra inventory (radium concentration × water depth; Bq m−2 ); λRn IRn   represents decay (Bq m−2  d−1 ); Fatm   represents radon degassing to the atmosphere (Bq m−2  d−1 ). In our study, we assumed that the primary source of radon is from groundwater discharge, consistent with existing research findings (Jiang et al., 2023; Sadat-Noori et al., 2021 ). Additionally, previous studies have also reported sediment diffusion and 226 Ra as minor components in the radon mass balance of lakes receiving groundwater discharge (Burnett et al., 2003; Perkins et al., 2015; Sadat-Noori et al., 2016; Tait et al., 2013 ). The groundwater discharge rate can be expressed as (Jiang et al., 2023 ):(7) V = F adv   C gw         In this equation, V  is the groundwater discharge rate (mm d−1 ), Cgw   is the 222 Rn concentration in groundwater (Bq m−3 ). Radon escape at the water–air interface is usually the main reason for the significant decrease in radon levels in surface water. The rate of this process is influenced by the efficiency of turbulent transfer and molecular diffusion caused by the concentration difference at the water–air interface, and its estimation can be conducted as follows:(8) F atm  = k C w  - α C air          In this equation, Cw   and Cair   represent the concentrations of radon in water and air (Bq m−3 ), respectively; α  is the radon partition coefficient reflecting the water–air distribution, which varies with temperature; and k  is the transfer rate of radon (cm h−1 ). This transfer rate can be estimated using an empirical formula proposed by MacIntyre (1995)  for lakes, which considers the influence of wind speed (v ; in m s−1 ) and Schmidt number (Sc ; dimensionless). By this method, our model effectively corrects for the impact of temperature and wind speed on 222 Rn concentration measurements, enhancing the accuracy of the tracer assessment.(9) α = 0.105 + 0.405 × e - 0.0502 × [ T - 273.15 ]       (10) k 600  = 0.45 v 10    1.6   Sc  600    - 2 / 3  or   - 1 / 2        In formula (10), Sc−2/3  is used at wind speeds below 3 m s−1 , and Sc−1/2  is used at wind speeds above 3 m s−1 . To compare the Schmidt numbers of different gases, the actual value of Sc is divided by the Schmidt number of CO2  at 20 °C, which is 600. The subscript “600” in k600 indicates this standardization. Sc can be estimated using the empirical formula provided by Wanninkhof (1992) :(11) Sc = A - B t + C t 2  - D t 3       In this formula, t  represents the water temperature (°C); Parameters A, B, C, and D are the coefficients for the least-squares third-order polynomial fit of the Schmidt number versus temperature (Wanninkhof, 1992 ). Based on the above calculations, the GHGs fluxes from groundwater to the lake were calculated as (Jiang et al., 2023 ):(12) F GHGs   = V × C GHGs        In this formula, V  represents the groundwater discharge rate (mm d−1 ); CGHGs   is the concentration of GHGs in groundwater (mg m−3 ).  2.5 Statistical analysis Redundancy Analysis (RDA) was conducted using the 'vegan' package (version 2.5–7) in R software version 3.6.3. Pearson correlation analysis was selected for execution, utilizing version 26.0 of the SPSS statistical software suite, considering the study encompasses 80 samples which conform to a normal distribution. Spatial maps were generated by interpolating point data in Arc GIS 10.4. The Inverse Distance Weighted (IDW) model was used for interpolation, as it outperforms other interpolation models like kriging, co-kriging, and thin plate splines (Sadat-Noori et al., 2021 ).   3 Results 3.1 Dissolved GHGs and 222 Rn in surface water In Honghu Lake, the seasonal and spatial distribution patterns of the four gases exhibited notable variations (Fig. 2  ). Overall, the concentration of 222 Rn in Honghu Lake was highest in winter and lowest in summer. In winter, the high levels of 222 Rn in the southeastern region formed a significant concentration peak, far exceeding the average of other regions at 185 ± 13.9 Bq m−3 , indicating strong groundwater activity in this area. In contrast, CH4  reached its highest concentrations in the southeastern regions of the lake in summer, with the maximum average value being 12.66 ± 1.53 mg m−3 . The spatial and temporal patterns of dissolved CO2  concentrations in the lake varied greatly. The southern edge of the lake recorded exceptionally high levels in autumn, averaging a peak concentration of 1525.21 ± 218.68 mg m−3 . This is in great contrast to other seasons and areas, such as the average spring concentration of 464.28 ± 39.49 mg m−3 . The distribution of N2 O across the area was relatively consistent, with seasonal average concentrations ranging from 0.38 ± 0.03 mg m−3  and 0.46 ± 0.03 mg m−3 . However, notable hotspots of elevated concentrations were observed in the southwestern section of the lake in spring, where levels peaked at 0.68 ± 0.03 mg m−3 .  3.2 GHGs emission fluxes Fig. 3   represents the monthly and seasonal variations in the characteristics of the emission fluxes of three GHGs measured during the sampling period. All observations were set up with three replicates to ensure the reliability of the samples. CH4 , CO2  and N2 O showed significant variations in trends over the eight-month monitoring period. CH4  emissions peaked in August and July, at 77.8 ± 16.9 mg m−2  d−1  and 66.7 ± 170 mg m−2  d−1  respectively, with the lowest emission in May at 4.09 ± 1.45 mg m−2  d−1 . In contrast, CO2  emissions fluctuated significantly throughout the year, reaching their monthly average maximum of 1.25 × 103  ± 294 mg m−2  d−1  in September and the minimum of −314 ± 200 mg m−2  d−1  in July, likely linked to the growth cycle of vegetation and seasonal changes in microbial activity. N2 O emissions were comparatively stable, with higher emissions in summer at 0.523 ± 0.151 mg m−2  d−1  and the lowest in winter at −0.026 ± 0.104 mg m−2  d−1 , reflecting the seasonal modulation of microbial nitrification. Seasonally, the emission patterns of all three gases showed periodic patterns corresponding to seasonal changes, although peak values occurred in different seasons. CH4  (58.6 ± 8.84 mg m−2  d−1 ) and N2 O (0.523 ± 0.147 mg m−2  d−1 ) had their highest average emissions in summer, while CO2  peaked in autumn (907 ± 155 mg m−2  d−1 ). Anomalies identified in Fig. 3  indicate short-term, high-intensity GHGs emissions, possibly suggesting the presence of sporadic events or non-periodic emission sources, such as occasional increases in groundwater discharge from the lakebed or significant releases of domestic and industrial pollutants. However, the results show that despite fluctuations, the emissions of the three GHGs still revolve around their mean values (CH4 : 31.1 ± 4.88 mg m−2  d−1 ; CO2 : 386 ± 90.7 mg m−2  d−1 ; N2 O: 0.327 ± 0.072 mg m−2  d−1 ), reflecting a normal or stable pattern in the temporal variation characteristics of GHGs emissions from Honghu Lake. To evaluate the specific impact of GHGs from Honghu Lake on global warming, we calculated the GWP over 20 and 100 years (Fig. 4  ). In the 20-year time frame, the GWPs of CH4 , CO2 , and N2 O are 82.2 %, 14.2 %, and 3.58 % respectively. Over 100 years, these figures change to 62.2 %, 30.9 %, and 6.91 %, where CH4  becoming the potentially major GHGs.  3.3 Water chemical variations between lake and groundwater We examined the variations in the water chemistry parameters between surface water and groundwater, as illustrated in Fig. 5  . The average concentration of 222 Rn in groundwater was 6232 ± 310 Bq m−3 , 59 times that of surface water. The average concentrations of CH4 , CO2 , and N2 O in groundwater were 12.1 ± 0.584 mg m−3 , 5720 ± 421 mg m−3 , and 1.04 ± 0.057 mg m−3 , respectively, which were 2.1, 12, and 2.4 times of the average concentrations in surface water. The average concentration of DOC in groundwater (3.02 ± 0.215 mg L−1 ) was 0.65 times lower, while the average DIC concentration (96.3 ± 5.40 mg L−1 ) was 3.0 times higher than in surface water. The average TC concentration in groundwater (99.3 ± 5.41 mg L−1 ) was 2.7 times that of surface water. The concentrations of NH4 + -N (0.364 ± 0.065 mg L−1 ), NO3 - -N (0.682 ± 0.088 mg L−1 ), and TN (3.18 ± 0.435 mg L−1 ) in groundwater were 1.4, 10, and 5.4 times, respectively, the average values in surface water. The average pH in groundwater (6.69 ± 0.053) and DO concentration (4.53 ± 0.221 mg L−1 ) were lower than those in surface water. The average EC value of groundwater was 429 ± 11.2 μS cm−1 , slightly lower (0.9 times) than that of surface water. Physicochemical variations   Here, we monitored the pH, DO concentration, EC, and Tw in the surface water and groundwater of Honghu Lake across the year (Fig. 6  ), to assess the potential impact of groundwater on GHGs emissions. The pH value of surface water reached its highest in summer, with an average of 8.58 ± 0.078, peaking in July at 8.91 ± 0.103, and the lowest in winter, at 7.58 ± 0.107. Correspondingly, the pH value of groundwater showed less variation in all seasons, indicating a more stable buffering capacity. The DO content was lowest in the surface water during summer, averaging 7.13 ± 0.323 mg L−1 . Groundwater DO content showed smaller seasonal variations, reflecting its relatively isolated environmental characteristics. EC data indicated that surface water reached its highest value in summer, averaging 504 ± 9.68 μS cm−1 , peaking in August at 517 ± 16.4 μS cm−1  within the summer season. Groundwater EC values decreased slightly in winter, but the overall variation was smaller than in surface water. Tw varied significantly with the seasons, with surface water being hottest in summer, averaging 29.6 ± 0.582 °C, peaking in July at 32.5 ± 0.543 °C. Groundwater temperature fluctuated less, showing its thermal stability. Carbon and nitrogen variations   To gain a deeper understanding of the carbon and nitrogen cycles and their environmental impacts in surface and groundwater sources, we compared and analyzed the concentrations of carbon and nitrogen in surface water and groundwater, including DOC, dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), TC, NH4 + -N, NO3 - -N, TN, as shown in Fig. 7  . Although the concentrations of DIC and TC fluctuated, they were relatively stable compared to DOC, with seasonal averages ranging from 15.8–35.5 mg L−1 , 20.7–40.4 mg L−1  and 3.93–5.72 mg L−1 , respectively. This suggests that in Honghu Lake, biogenic organic matter is the main driver of DOC concentration changes, while DIC and TC may be more influenced by geological background and atmospheric inputs. Compared to surface water, the concentrations of DOC, DIC, and TC in groundwater showed significant stability, indicating that groundwater contributes consistently to the lake's carbon cycle and could be a stable carbon source. The seasonal average concentrations for groundwater were 2.76–3.26 mg L−1 , 93.5–97.8 mg L−1  and 96.2–101 mg L−1  respectively. During the study period, we observed that the concentrations of NH4 + -N, NO3 - -N, and TN in surface water samples were relatively stable, with average values of 0.264 ± 0.032 mg L−1 , 0.068 ± 0.009 mg L−1 , and 0.588 ± 0.035 mg L−1 , respectively. In contrast, groundwater samples showed noticeable fluctuations in nitrogen content, with the highest monthly average values of NH4 + -N, NO3 - -N, and TN appearing in July and April, reaching 0.866 ± 0.133 mg L−1 , 0.986 ± 0.404 mg L−1 , and 4.62 ± 0.956 mg L−1 , respectively. These fluctuations may reflect the different hydrogeological conditions encountered by groundwater during its flow, as well as the impacts of seasonal hydrological events or human activities. The results emphasize the need to consider the different dynamics of groundwater and surface water and their distinct contributions to water chemistry when studying lake water quality and GHGs emissions. Redundancy analysis   The associations between environmental variables and the samples gathered in various seasons were graphically illustrated using Redundancy Analysis (RDA), with the results presented in Fig. 8  . RDA is distinct from Principal Component Analysis (PCA) in that RDA is a form of constrained ordination technique which incorporates external environmental variables to explain the variation in the species data. Unlike PCA, which is an unconstrained technique and does not consider such external information, RDA integrates the influence of environmental variables to identify the main directions of variability that are directly related to these explanatory variables (Zuur et al., 2007 ). The axes in RDA are analogous to principal components, but they are derived from a combination of the GHGs data and their relationship with the environmental variables. In our study, the first two RDA axes explain more than 30 % of the variance, which suggests a relatively close relationship between environmental conditions and the observed patterns in the GHGs data. Parallel factor analysis   Fig. 9   and Fig. 10   present the organic matter components in water samples from Honghu Lake analyzed using Parallel Factor Analysis observing their variations across different seasons. Based on the excitation and emission wavelength ranges of the samples, the main organic matter components in Honghu Lake were identified as humic substances. To assess the identified components, we consulted the OpenFluor database (https://openfluor.lablicate.com ). This digital platform facilitates comparison with previously identified and characterized PARAFAC models in DOM studies. The results are presented in Table 2  . Component C1 (Ex:230 (310); Em: 410) mainly originates from human activities, such as agricultural drainage and urban wastewater discharge. Component C2 (Ex:260 (355); Em: 460) is mainly derived from terrestrial sources, reflecting the natural input of plant residues and soil organic matter, which may enter the lake via runoff. Component C3 (Ex:240 (330); Em: 450) primarily originates from environmentally stressed areas, potentially from overdeveloped land, polluted watersheds, or other areas under environmental stress conditions. Fig. 8  shows that the Component C1 is the most abundant organic matter in all seasons, with its abundance gradually increasing from 49 % in summer to 55 % in winter, then slightly decreasing to 54 % in spring. This sustained high abundance may indicate the significant contribution of wastewater discharge to the lake's organic matter. In contrast, the abundances of Components C2 and C3 are lower and show relatively stable seasonal variations, with C2 fluctuating between 26 % and 29 %, and C3 between 20 % and 23 %. Although Component C2 is less abundant than C1, the Terr-Humic Fraction is a key bridge connecting terrestrial ecosystems with the lake's carbon cycle. C2 shows a seasonal trend similar to the intensity of groundwater discharge. This suggests that groundwater flow may facilitate the transfer of the organic matter from soil layers and underground sediments to the lake, especially during seasons with less precipitation and reduced surface runoff, making this pathway particularly important.  3.4 Quantification of groundwater discharge fluxes A steady-state radon mass balance model indicates that groundwater discharges into the lake at a rate of 8.19 ± 0.471 mm d−1  (Table 3   and Table 4  ), with the daily groundwater discharge volume accounting for 0.649 % of the total lake volume. Fig. 11   shows the temporal distribution characteristics of 222 Rn concentration in surface water and groundwater discharge flux at the lake bottom. The concentration is lowest in summer at 54.0 ± 5.68 Bq m−3  and gradually increases with the seasons, peaking in winter at 117 ± 12.9 Bq m−3 . Afterward, the concentration begins to decline, decreasing into the spring. The groundwater discharge flux also shows its highest value in winter at 9.79 ± 1.57 mm d−1 , subsequently dropping to its lowest in spring at 6.98 ± 0.775 mm d−1 . The emission fluxes of CH4 , CO2 , and N2 O from the lake caused by groundwater were 0.099 ± 0.004mg m−2  d−1  CH4 , 46.9 ± 3.08mg m−2  d−1  CO2  and 0.008 ± 0.0004 mg m−2  d−1  N2 O.   4 Discussion 4.1 Shallow lakes as sources of GHGs to the atmosphere Shallow lakes produce a large amount of GHGs including CO2  and CH4  via anaerobic degradation of organic carbon and, thus, are regarded as a major driver of climate warming (Duan et al., 2023 ). In the case of the large shallow lake, Honghu Lake, the CH4  and N2 O emission fluxes were needed to be converted into CO2  equivalents for an assessment over 20-year and 100-year time frames. According to the IPCC Fourth Assessment Report, the global warming potential of CH4  is about 72 times (20-year frame) and 25 times (100-year frame) that of CO2 , while for N2 O, it is about 289 times and 298 times respectively (Change, 2007 ). Our results show that, in Honghu Lake, on both 20-year and 100-year time scales, CH4  contributes the most to the GHGs emissions, accounting for as high as 82.2 % and 62.2 % respectively, while N2 O contributes the least, only about 3.6 % and 6.9 %. Although there have been studies reporting different proportions of CO2  emissions from lakes to the atmosphere (Li et al., 2022; Sadat-Noori et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2023 ), our study suggests that the proportion of CO2  from Honghu Lake is relatively low. This phenomenon may be attributed to the year-round data on lake GHGs emissions that we adopted (Fig. 3 ), coupled with the strong photosynthesis in Honghu Lake that to some extent suppresses CO2  emissions (Huotari et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2017 ). Additionally, the shallow depth of Honghu Lake means that CH4  produced in the sediments has less chance of being oxidized before it reaches the water–air interface (Davidson et al., 2015 ), resulting in higher CH4  emissions. It is important to note that calculating both the 20-year and 100-year GWP for short-lived GHGs like CH4  is crucial because both time frames would offer a more comprehensive perspective on the impact of different GHGs over varying time scales of climate warming (Lynch et al., 2020 ). For instance, CH4  has an atmospheric lifetime of about 10 years, which is much shorter than the CO2  which has a century scale lifetime (Meinshausen and Nicholls, 2022 ). Therefore, the 20-year GWP better captures the short-term warming effect of CH4 , while the 100-year assessment of the GHGs provides nature of long-term climate impact on planet Earth. This distinction would be particularly vital when formulating the effective strategies for climate change mitigation. Overall, as a large shallow eutrophic lake, Honghu Lake shows a relatively normal stable emission pattern throughout the year (Natchimuthu et al., 2016 ). However, it is worth noting that Honghu Lake is a net source of atmospheric CH4  throughout the year (Fig. 3 ). Studies such as Zhou et al. (2020)  suggest that CH4  emission fluxes may vary among lakes with different trophic states in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River. Our data shows that CH4  emission flux from Honghu Lake is an order of magnitude higher than that of the eutrophic lakes (average: 0.1 mg m−2  h−1 ), which is comparable to the middle-eutrophic lakes (average: 4.4 mg m−2  h−1 ), but much lower than the hyper-eutrophic lakes (average: 12 mg m−2  h−1 ). Although recent comprehensive nutrient state indices for Honghu Lake have shown an improvement from moderate to mild eutrophication (Zhou et al., 2020 ), the CH4  emission flux from the lake still indicates a moderately eutrophic state. This mismatch between water quality and CH4  emission flux may be related to the shallow depth of Honghu Lake, with an average depth of about 1.35 m (Yang et al., 2015 ). Xun et al. (2024)  pointed out that shallow lakes and shallow areas of lakes emit more CH4  than deeper areas, and the variability of water depth in response to temperature changes interacts with temporal variability, making shallow areas more sensitive to temperature changes. In addition, shallow lakes are conducive for submerged macrophyte growth, vegetation decomposition and soil carbon and nitrogen storage and emission (Zhang et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2022 ). In this study, we observed distinct seasonal variations in the GHGs emissions from Honghu Lake, with CH4  and N2 O peaking in summer and CO2  emissions being highest in autumn (Fig. 3 ). Analysis, including relevant analysis (Table S1 ) and RDA analysis (Fig. 8 ), suggests that temperature is one of the key factors influencing the CH4  and N2 O emissions. Additionally, our data indicate that groundwater discharge significantly contributes to the lake's CO2  emissions (Table 4 ). As the frequency of extreme weather events increases with climate change, fluctuations in lake water levels may intensify (Bai et al., 2024 ), potentially enhancing the exchange between the lake and groundwater, which could further increase the lake's CO2  emissions. An increase in GHGs emissions could have a positive feedback effect on climate change by amplifying the greenhouse effect in the atmosphere (Rõõm et al., 2014 ). In particular, CH4  due to its potent greenhouse effect (Fig. 4 ), can have a significant impact on regional and even global climate, even with relatively low emissions. Therefore, this study not only quantitatively analyzed the contribution of the three main GHGs of Honghu Lake to global warming over different time scales but also emphasized the importance of research in mechanisms behind the GHGs emissions from large shallow eutrophic lakes. Such understanding would be significant for water resource managers of shallow lakes including Honghu Lake in China in formulating management targets and restoration measures to mitigate the global warming effect.  4.2 Driving forces of groundwater discharge High surface water radon concentrations indicate the presence of groundwater discharge in lakes, a fact confirmed by the results of the 222 Rn mass balance model (Fig. 11 ). Xing et al. (2020)  used hydrochemical isotopic and groundwater age to reveal the flow direction of groundwater in the Jianghan Plain, which is consistent with the surface topography. Moreover, from June 2022 to May 2023, the average water level of Honghu Lake was 24.50 m, based on data from the Wagouzui station. The average elevation of the groundwater table in the wells during the sampling period was 26.33 m. The groundwater level was 1.83 m above the lake level. In the summer, when precipitation is higher, the water level of Honghu Lake ranged from 24.23 − 25.48 m, with an average of 25.00 m, while the groundwater table in the wells ranged from 26.05 − 27.31 m, averaging at 26.59 m. The groundwater level was higher than the lake level by 1.1–2.3 m. These results indicate that Honghu Lake is replenished by groundwater. Thus, due to the hydraulic head difference (Sun et al., 2022 ), groundwater is able to discharge into the lake. The similarity in the fluctuating trends of groundwater and 222 Rn concentrations within the one-year observation period suggests that 222 Rn concentration strongly supports the groundwater discharge and dynamics. Although winter and summer witnessed the highest and lowest 222 Rn concentrations with maximal winter groundwater discharge flux, there were no obvious correlations between them, suggesting that the climatic factors such as temperature and rainfall across the season may have played a significant role. In summer, the high temperature of the lake increases the diffusion rate of 222 Rn from water to the atmosphere (Adyasari et al., 2023 ). Additionally, surface water levels may rise due to heavy rainfall events, and the rainwater typically has lower 222 Rn concentrations, near zero, leading to an overall reduction in lake radon levels (Qin et al., 2021 ). However, due to the flash drought in the summer of 2023, the overall water level of the lake decreased (Gao et al., 2024 ), and the groundwater may have responded slowly to the flash droughts and high temperatures (Jiang et al., 2023 ). This could have increased the difference between the groundwater and surface water levels, causing the hydraulic gradient between the surface water and groundwater of Honghu Lake to be higher in summer than in autumn. Such phenomenon could have been fundamental to the groundwater dynamics in Honghu Lake. For instance, a higher groundwater discharge in certain summer months, such as August, compared to autumn, resulted in different temporal characteristics of groundwater discharge flux and 222 Rn (Fig. 11 ). An increased 222 Rn concentration and groundwater discharge flux to the lake in winter could have been the result of the positive hydraulic gradient in Honghu Lake as well as the reduced water temperature slowing down the escape of 222 Rn (Kishel and Gerla, 2002 ). For instance, a recent study reported that groundwater discharge fluxes in subtropical floodplain lakes in China during winter were twice as high as in summer (Jiang et al., 2023 ). There may be a little or more effect on Honghu lake, in spring, however, the impact of snowmelt and precipitation-induced surface runoff on lake levels may decrease the hydraulic gradient between groundwater and the lake, consequently reducing the groundwater discharge flux (Seyfried et al., 2009 ). This study reveals the driving mechanisms of seasonal hydraulic gradients on groundwater discharge from the lakebed. The influence of surface water may be dominant in summer and spring, while the contribution of groundwater may be more significant in autumn and winter (Fig. 11 ). The 222 Rn concentration serves as a tracer for reflecting the contribution of groundwater to the lake, as well as the growing influence of climatic factors such as temperature and rainfall pattern in the lake convective mixing and radon emissions in Honghu Lake.  4.3 Multifactorial drivers of lake GHGs emission dynamics The redundancy analysis (RDA) ordination with relatively higher proportions of the total variation demonstrated by axis 1 (18.9 %) and axis 2 (11.7 %) suggests the influence of season on CH4 , CO2 , and N2 O emissions and their relationships with environmental factors in Honghu Lake. DOC and 222 Rn are identified as the two prominent factors in the RDA, related to CO2  emissions, indicating that CO2  emissions are influenced by DOC and groundwater discharge (Fig. 8 ), although the strength of these relationships is moderate, as evidenced by the positive correlations (Table S1 ) between CO2  and 222 Rn (R=0.30, p < 0.01) and CO2  and DOC (R=0.24, p < 0.05). The stronger correlation between 222 Rn and DOC (R=0.36, p < 0.01) suggests the presence of dissolved CO2  in the groundwater system of Honghu Lake, which may contribute to CO2  emissions during periods of groundwater discharge. The mechanisms of CO2  emissions may be both: 1) by directly emitting the dissolved CO2  to lake surface water, and 2) by indirectly via the discharge of DOC then to be converted into CO2  (Sadat-Noori et al., 2021 ). The CO2  emissions related to groundwater DOC are reported by rapid urbanization and global warming (McDonough et al., 2020 ), where the increase in groundwater DOC often enhances inorganic carbon (DIC and CO2 ) flux through mineralization and dissolution of carbonate minerals in the groundwater system (Duvert et al., 2019 ). The direct input of DOC by groundwater can also promote carbon respiration within the lake system (Maher et al., 2015 ), causing surface water CO2  supersaturation and its emission to the atmosphere through the water–air interface (Dong et al., 2012 ). Contrary to the expected positive association, the negative relationship (Table S1 ) between CO2  and water temperature (R=-0.39, p < 0.01) as well as between CO2  and TN (R=-0.32, p < 0.01) suggests that higher temperatures and nutrient levels may not necessarily augment CO2  emissions as previously believed. Instead, these conditions could facilitate processes that sequester CO2 , potentially through enhanced photosynthetic activity or the stimulation of microbial communities that preferentially consume CO2  (Lu et al., 2022 ), such as the chemoautotrophic bacteria, which convert inorganic carbon (like CO2 ) into organic matter using energy derived from chemical reactions (Alfreider et al., 2017 ). In the case of a lake like Honghu, its modest average depth of 1.35 m allows for higher water temperatures and increased light penetration, which are conducive to photosynthesis. This, in turn, leads to an enhanced fixation of CO2  (Zhou et al., 2023 ). In addition, fluctuations in nutrient levels affect the balance between lake productivity and respiration (Li et al., 2021 ). When the rate of photosynthesis exceeds the rate of respiration, less CO2  is produced. An increase in nutrients promotes the growth of phytoplankton and aquatic plants, which absorb CO2  from the water through photosynthesis and convert it into organic matter, thus lowering the CO2  concentration in the water body. Study by Sun et al. (2021a)  on Wulan Suhai Lake, a eutrophic shallow lake in the arid region of northern China, also showed that elevated nutrient levels suppress the lake's CO2  emissions. This indicates a multifaceted interaction where CO2  emissions are influenced not only by DOC and groundwater discharge but also by the physicochemical parameters of the lake, such as temperature and nutrient availability. Our analysis reveals a modest but notable positive correlation (Table S1 ) between CH4  emissions and temperature (R=0.26, p < 0.05), suggesting that warmer conditions may enhance the metabolic rates and activity of methanogenic bacteria. This, in turn, could accelerate the decomposition of organic matter, leading to increased CH4  production (Keller et al., 2020 ). Additionally, our findings highlight a positive relationship (Table S1 ) between CH4  emissions and pH (R=0.22, p < 0.05). The impact of pH on CH4  primarily manifests in promoting microbial activity and enhancing the availability of organic matter. Typically, a neutral to slightly alkaline environment (pH 7–8) is considered optimal for the survival of most methanogenic microorganisms (Davidson et al., 2015; DelSontro et al., 2018 ). As the pH of the lake increases, it may stimulate the growth and activity of these methanogenic microbes, thereby increasing the production and emission of CH4 . In contrast, we observed a strong negative correlation (Table S1 ) between CH4  emissions and DO (R=-0.42, p < 0.01), underscoring the critical inhibitory role of oxygen on methanogenic processes. CH4  is predominantly generated under anaerobic conditions (Buan, 2018 ), and thus, elevated DO levels can significantly suppress CH4  formation. The results indicate that the influence of groundwater discharge on CH4  emissions in Honghu Lake is relatively minimal. CH4  emissions are primarily governed by internal processes within the lake and are significantly influenced by environmental factors; temperature and pH positively correlate with CH4  emissions, while DO concentration is a key limiting factor. These elements interact complexally within the lake ecosystem to affect the metabolic rates and activity of methanogenic bacteria, substrate availability for methanogenesis, and the anaerobic conditions necessary for CH4  production. Hence, while groundwater discharge contributes to the lake's hydrological and chemical inputs (Meinikmann et al., 2015 ), its direct role in modulating CH4  emissions is considerably less pronounced than the internal dynamics and environmental conditions of the lake itself. In Honghu Lake, the observed positive correlation (Table S1 ) between N2 O emissions and water temperature (R=0.23, p < 0.05) as well as between N2 O and NH4 + -N concentrations (R=0.28, p < 0.05) highlights the intricate dynamics of nitrogen cycling within the lake ecosystem. The pivotal roles of both abiotic factors, exemplified by temperature, and biotic factors, represented by nutrient availability, in the modulation of N2 O production and release are thus highlighted. The increase in water temperature accelerates the metabolic processes of denitrifying bacteria, thereby enhancing denitrification and facilitating the production and emission of N2 O. This observation is congruent with the research conducted by Liu et al. (2018) , which explored N2 O fluxes within Lake Taihu, a large shallow eutrophic lake in Eastern China, revealing a robust correlation between N2 O emissions and water temperature. Similarly, the role of NH4 + -N as a substrate in the nitrification process is crucial, and its concentration level determines the production of N2 O. This is supported by research conducted by Bianchi and Lefevre (1999)  on the natural conditions of nitrification in the Rhone River Delta, where the availability of NH4 + -N accounted for 74 % of the variance in nitrification rates. Our research reveals the comprehensive impact of temperature and nutrient dynamics on the nitrogen cycling in Honghu Lake, emphasizing the critical role of environmental factors in regulating greenhouse gas emissions within freshwater ecosystems. Although in Honghu Lake, our correlational analysis did not identify a direct relationship between groundwater discharge and N2 O emissions, the monitoring of groundwater nutrient dynamics showed that, compared to surface water, groundwater contains higher concentrations of nutrients (Fig. 5  and Fig. 7 ). This suggests that globally, groundwater cannot be overlooked in understanding the functioning of lake ecosystems and their role in the global GHGs balance.  4.4 The contribution of groundwater to lake GHGs emission fluxes Groundwater is a potential source of GHGs for lakes, as our results for Honghu Lake show that the groundwater contains high concentrations of dissolved CH4 , CO2 , and N2 O (Fig. 5 ). We adopted 222 Rn mass balance model for groundwater contributions to the GHGs emissions in Honghu Lake, as 222 Rn mass balance model potentially quantifies the GHGs emissions to the lake by combining the groundwater discharge with the dissolved GHGs in the groundwater system (Bartosiewicz et al., 2015; Li et al., 2018; Sadat-Noori et al., 2021 ). In our study, the proportions of CH4 , CO2 , and N2 O derived from groundwater in the total GHGs emission fluxes at the lake's water–air interface are approximately 0.318 %, 12.1 %, and 2.59 %, respectively, detailed in Table 4 . The impact of Honghu Lake's groundwater on GHGs emissions has not been underestimated, it's actually lower than that in comparable studies (Table 5  ). For instance, Sadat-Noori et al. (2021)  found groundwater contributions to atmospheric CO2  and CH4  emissions to be 25 % and 13 %, respectively, in a Sydney Lake, while Perkins et al. (2015)  observed that groundwater flux constituted about 55 ± 50 % of Lake Ainsworth's volume, with 13 ± 25 % of CO2  emissions stemming from groundwater seepage. Einarsdottir et al. (2017)  found that groundwater accounted for 96 % of the total CH4  load in a lake in the northern Baltic Sea. The small contribution of groundwater to GHGs emissions in Honghu Lake can be attributed to two main factors. Firstly, the discharge rate of groundwater in Honghu Lake was relatively low, at only 8.19 mm d−1 . This stands in contrast to other studies, such as the 160 ± 100 mm d−1  reported by Sadat-Noori et al. (2021) , 43 ± 20 mm d−1  reported by Dabrowski et al. (2020) , and an average rate of 61 mm d−1  reported by Sun et al. (2022) . The lowest of these rates is 5 times higher than that of Honghu Lake, while the highest is 20 times greater. Despite these notable differences in discharge rates, it is crucial to recognize that groundwater still accounts for 12 % of the lake's CO2  emissions, underscoring the vital yet underappreciated role of groundwater in the ecosystem's carbon dynamics. Furthermore, Honghu Lake is significantly affected by human activities. Our research indicates that the primary source of DOM in Honghu Lake stems from human activity and the humic substances from sewage discharge (Fig. 10 ). This external input reduces the contribution of natural groundwater to the lake's GHGs emissions, highlighting the complex interaction between anthropogenic impacts and natural processes. The low discharge rate of groundwater can be attributed to the location of Honghu Lake on the Han River Plain, characterized by a minimal hydraulic gradient between surface water and groundwater (Burnett and Dulaiova, 2003 ).  4.5 Limitations and uncertainty analysis In this study, we quantified the seasonal dynamics of GHGs and groundwater discharge fluxes in Honghu Lake over a year by observing the concentrations of 222 Rn in lake water and groundwater, based on a mass balance model. Using 222 Rn as the sole tracer to represent groundwater over a year is practical due to its utility, offering a simplified yet reasonable method for quantifying groundwater. However, this assumption does not apply to situations where there are significant short-term changes in lake water storage, such as before and after flood events, as these processes can lead to an imbalanced distribution of 222 Rn between lake water and groundwater. For cases with significant changes in lake water storage, it is necessary to combine 222 Rn tracing with other tracers, such as δ18 O and δ2 H (Qin et al., 2021 ). Additionally, we have selected three groundwater sites and ten surface water sites around Honghu Lake, each situated in a different area of the lake. Increasing the number of lake water and groundwater sampling sites could more accurately define the groundwater end-member, however, it is challenging due to the limited number of accessible monitoring wells. The limited number of sampling sites may result in some uncertainties of the results. Future studies could consider increasing the sample size and monitoring points to clarify the spatial heterogeneity and uncertainty of GHGs coupled with groundwater discharge within the water body. In general, the groundwater end-member is considered the main source of uncertainty in assessing groundwater discharge (Wang et al., 2021b; Sadat-Noori et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2022 ). In this study, if we assign an uncertainty of 50 % to 222 Rn activity in the groundwater end-member, the groundwater discharge flux would have a variation of 33 % to 100 %. Atmospheric evasion is the primary sink for 222 Rn in Honghu Lake, accounting for 77 % of the total loss (Table 3 ). The uncertainty in atmospheric evasion losses primarily results from wind speed. An increase of 1 m s−1  (32 %) in wind speed would cause a 56 % increase in atmospheric evasion losses and a consequent 42 % change in the final groundwater discharge flux. Decay losses account for 23 % of total losses and are related to the 222 Rn inventory, with errors mainly from measurement inaccuracies of 222 Rn. If we assign an uncertainty of 50 % to 222 Rn activity in the surface water, decay losses would correspondingly change by 50 %. It would result in a 52 % change in atmospheric evasion and a 52 % change in groundwater discharge flux. Overall, these analyses indicate that the activities of 222 Rn in groundwater and surface water end-members, as well as wind speed, are the main sources of uncertainty in groundwater discharge. In addition, the uncertainty in GHGs fluxes mainly arises from the measurement of GHGs concentrations and the parameters used in calculations, such as air pressure and temperature. An increase of 50 % in the measured concentrations of GHGs would also increase their flux values by 50 %, representing the greatest source of uncertainty. A 1 kPa error in ground-level air pressure and a 1 °C error in temperature could potentially change the GHGs fluxes by 1 % and 0.3 %, respectively. These uncertainties indicate the importance of selecting representative observation sites for assessing GHGs fluxes.   5 Conclusions Our study investigated the multifaceted driving mechanisms behind GHGs emissions from lakes, emphasizing the combined role of groundwater discharge and lake ecological dynamics. The findings revealed significant seasonal variations in GHGs emissions from Honghu Lake, with CH4  and N2 O emissions peaking during summer, while CO2  emissions were higher in autumn. Compared to CH4  and N2 O, groundwater has a relatively greater impact on lake CO2  emissions, with the daily CO2  contribution from groundwater discharge comprising 12.1 % of the total CO2  emissions at the lake's water–air interface. The enhanced contribution of groundwater discharge to CO2  emissions was primarily due to its transport of DOC and high concentrations of CO2  to the lake. However, the contribution of quantitative groundwater discharge to CH4  and N2 O emissions was relatively low, and no direct correlation between groundwater and these emissions was found. The influences of groundwater discharge on CH4  and N2 O emissions were relatively minor, primarily driven by lake ecological processes. CH4  emissions were controlled by the metabolic rate and activity of methanogenic bacteria, the availability of substrates for methanogenesis, and the anaerobic conditions required for CH4  production. In contrast, N2 O emissions were mainly influenced by temperature and nutrient dynamics. This suggests that while the impact of groundwater on CH4  and N2 O emissions is less pronounced than that of the lake's ecological factors, its effect on CO2  emissions is more substantial than these ecological factors. Overall, the results underscore the need to consider both groundwater discharge and environmental factors when assessing GHGs emissions from lakes. Although groundwater discharge played a critical role only in the emissions of CO2 , it still revealed groundwater discharge as an important, previously overlooked source of carbon and nutrients to lakes over the long term. These insights not only enrich our understanding of the mechanisms behind lake GHGs emissions but also provide a scientific basis for developing effective lake management and GHGs reduction strategies. As climate change and human activities intensify, in-depth research on groundwater GHGs emissions will be crucial for the future health of lake ecosystems and the accurate assessment of the global greenhouse gas budget.
1 Introduction Groundwater, constituting a vital portion of freshwater resources, accounts for approximately a quarter to a third of total freshwater withdrawals, meeting agricultural, domestic, and industrial water needs (Jyolsna et al., 2021; Shamsudduha and Taylor, 2020 ). The escalating population growth and economic development have triggered a surge in groundwater abstraction, resulting in a range of severe challenges, including continuous declines in groundwater levels, deterioration of water quality, desiccation of wetlands and rivers, and land subsidence (Chen et al., 2019; Gong et al., 2018; Scanlon et al., 2012 ). Groundwater is crucial for nearly half of global irrigation water use (Table 1  ), particularly in high-reliance regions such as South Asia and the Middle East, where effective monitoring and management of groundwater resources are imperative to advert depletion of water resources (Siebert et al., 2010 ). In contrast, sub-Saharan Africa exhibits lower dependence on groundwater, with only 6 % of the irrigation area utilizing groundwater and 7 % of the total water use sourced from groundwater. Nonetheless, groundwater reservoirs in sub-Saharan Africa hold substantial potential for effective management and utilization. Traditional groundwater monitoring primarily relies on networks of observation wells. However, this approach has notable limitations, including limited coverage, challenging maintenance, and obstacles to data sharing (Miro and Famiglietti, 2018; Pascal et al., 2022 ). The launch of the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) satellites in 2002, and its follow-on mission, GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO), in 2018, revolutionized groundwater monitoring on a global scale by detecting gravity variations. However, applying GRACE data to a local scale requires spatial downscaling due to the native resolution of GRACE being only approximately 90,000 km2  (about 3° × 3°) (Vishwakarma et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021 ). GRACE downscaling methods can be categorized into two categories: model-based downscaling (or dynamic downscaling) and data-based downscaling (or statistical downscaling) (Pascal et al., 2022 ). Model-based downscaling methods integrate GRACE data into land surface models, hydrological models, or groundwater models based on physical processes, enabling the simulation of terrestrial water storage anomaly (TWSA) and groundwater storage anomaly (GWSA) at higher spatial resolution. Despite their clear physical interpretations, these methods require extensive data and computation and are constrained by model parameters and process expression (Jyolsna et al., 2021; Pascal et al., 2022 ). In contrast, statistical downscaling methods offer a simpler framework and require less data. These methods operate under the basic assumption that the relationships between TWSA/GWSA and other hydrological variables remain consistent across different spatial resolutions. Initially established relationships between TWSA/GWSA and other hydrological variables at the original spatial resolution are leveraged, and high-resolution data are utilized as input to derive downscaled TWSA/GWSA data. Commonly employed statistical methods include multiple linear regression (MLR), artificial neural networks (ANN), and Random Forests (RF) models. RF models, in particular, have the capability to handle multiple input variables simultaneously and exhibit reduced susceptibility to overfitting compared to other methods commonly used in hydrological research (Abowarda et al., 2021; Breiman, 2001; Long et al., 2019; Tyralis et al., 2019 ). Several recently published studies on GRACE downscaling are shown in Table 2  , predominantly conducted at regional scales. Jyolsna et al. (2021)  utilized MLR and RF techniques to downscaling 1° (approximately 110 km) gridded GWSA to 0.25° (approximately 27 km) over four major aquifer systems in India, achieving a close agreement between GRACE-derived groundwater levels and measurements for three of the four basins. Miro and Famiglietti (2018)  employed an ANN model to downscale GWSA to a high resolution (approximately 4 km) over California’s Central Valley. Chen et al. (2019)  utilized the RF method to downscale GWSA from 1° and to 0.25° over the northeast of Mainland China. Zuo et al. (2021)  conducted downscaling based on RF to obtain high-resolution GWSA (1 km) over the Tarim River basin in Northwest China. Pascal et al. (2022)  downscaled GWSA data from 3° to 0.5° using the RF algorithm over a fractured crystalline aquifer in South India. Overall, the majority of GWSA downscaling studies have been conducted at local scales within specific regions, with only a few extending to larger study areas. Zhang et al. (2021)  conducted GWSA downscaling on a national scale; however, their input data were confined to China rather than the boundaries of aquifers or river basins. Vishwakarma et al. (2021)  produced a 0.5° downscaled TWSA on a global scale; however, their results were not validated with in-situ observation data. This study focuses on proposing a novel method for spatial downscaling of GRACE data based on the RF algorithm. GRACE data for sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia were downscaled to enhance our understanding of spatiotemporal variability in finer-scale groundwater storage, which could inform local water management efforts. The Middle East and South Asia face issues of groundwater depletion (Rodell et al., 2018 ), whereas groundwater resources are relatively abundant in sub-Saharan Africa. The selection of these diverse regions ensures the applicability of our downscaling method to even larger scale, considering the varying conditions in groundwater distribution. We employed the RF algorithm to downscale GWSA across continental scales, enhancing the spatial resolution of GRACE GWSA from 3° to 0.25°. In addition, we conducted model training and validation separately for different aquifers in the study regions to ensure that the downscaling method can be applied to study areas in different environments. We utilized different combinations of predictor variables, including accumulated hydrological fluxes, to enhance the accuracy and reliability of the downscaled TWSA. These measures ensure the accuracy and broad applicability of our method compared with previous studies. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2  provides an overview of the study regions and the related data used. Section 3  details the methodology, including the development of RF models to downscale TWSA, the separation of the GWSA signal from the downscaled TWSA, and the metrics used to evaluate the RF models and downscaled GWSA. Section 4  presents the downscaled TWSA and GWSA, model accuracies, and validation results based on in-situ observations. Section 5  discusses the uncertainty in the downscaled data, the relationship between trend, seasonality, and reminder of downscaled GWSA, and hydrological fluxes, including precipitation and evapotranspiration (ET), and the groundwater reliance of different countries in the study regions. Section 6  concludes by summarizing the key results of the study.  2 Study region and data 2.1 Study regions This study spans across three regions, sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia, as illustrated in Fig. 1  . The selection of these regions is motivated by their distinct characteristics in groundwater dynamics and their significance in regional water resource management. Particularly, South Asia and the Middle East exhibit a pronounced reliance on groundwater resources, as evidenced by data in Table 1 . Alarming trends of groundwater depletion are particularly evident in these regions, with India serving as a typical example. Rodell et al. (2018)  revealed a concerning decline in GRACE-derived TWSA in North India, amounting to −19.2 ± 1.1 Gt/yr from April 2002 to March 2016. A substantial portion (45 %) of this affected area is dedicated to irrigation, a key factor fueling the depletion in water storage. The intensive extraction of groundwater for irrigation, particularly in semi-arid climates, has led to a critical depletion of groundwater levels. This phenomenon is exacerbated in East India, where a combination of intense irrigation practices and reduced precipitation during the monsoon season has contributed to a significant decline in TWS (Rodell et al., 2018 ). Similarly, regions such as Northwest Saudi Arabia and the Northern Middle East manifest noteworthy trends in decreasing TWS, with rates of −10.5 ± 1.5 Gt/yr and −32.1 ± 1.5 Gt/yr, respectively. The primary drivers behind these declines are drought conditions, amplifying the demand for groundwater and resulting in a reduction of GWS in these areas (Rodell et al., 2018 ). Given these circumstances, effective groundwater monitoring and management emerge as imperative measures to avert the peril of overexploitation. In contrast, numerous areas within sub-Saharan Africa exhibit a positive trajectory, witnessing rises in groundwater levels during recent years (Cuthbert et al., 2019 ). This region presents an untapped reservoir of groundwater potential, capable of fostering sustainable development and acting as a resilient buffer against the vagaries of climate variability.  2.2 Data Here, three GRACE mascon products obtained from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), Center for Space Research (CSR), and Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) were utilized as the objective variables for the modeling process. The optimization of the model involved the inclusion of eight hydrological variables as predictors. These variables encompassed three key hydrological fluxes: precipitation, evapotranspiration (ET), and runoff, along with their accumulations. Furthermore, soil moisture (SM) and the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) were integrated into the modeling process as essential predictor variables. For a comprehensive understanding of the data utilized in developing the RF models, please refer to Table 3  , which provides detailed information on the various datasets employed. 2.2.1 Grace-derived terrestrial water storage anomalies Here, we utilized three GRACE RL06 mascon products from JPL, CSR, and GSFC. The preference for the mascon solution over spherical harmonics is justified by its inherent advantages (Scanlon et al., 2016 ). The utilization of location-dependent mascon parameters facilitates a more straightforward constraint application based on a priori information (Luthcke et al., 2006 ). Moreover, mascon solutions exhibit resilience against signal leakage, eliminating the need for de-striping or filtering during postprocessing (Humphrey et al., 2023 ). The three selected mascon products form an ensemble, demonstrating comparable reliability. This ensemble approach is instrumental in assessing the uncertainty associated with downscaled TWSA and GWSA. For the computation of TWSA, a straightforward deduction involved subtracting the long-term mean TWS during a baseline period (2004–2009). The three mascon products are formatted on a monthly basis with a nominal spatial resolution of 0.25° or 0.5° and a native spatial resolution of approximately 3° × 3°. In instances of missing data, a linear interpolation method was applied, except for the temporal gap spanning from July 2017 to May 2018 between the GRACE and GRACE-FO missions.  2.2.2 Predict variables In our predictive modeling of high-resolution TWSA, we incorporated hydrological and vegetation data to consider various influential factors. Three essential fluxes–precipitation (P), evapotranspiration (ET), and runoff (Q)–were selected as critical predictors for TWSA based on the water balance equation in an aquifer. Additionally, to capture the nuanced soil and vegetation conditions, we included SM and NDVI in our model. All input data have spatial resolutions equal to or higher than 0.25° and temporal resolutions equal to or higher than one month. ET data were obtained from the Global Land Evaporation Amsterdam Model (GLEAM, https://www.gleam.eu ). We utilized the GLEAM v3.6b monthly product with a 0.25° spatial resolution as a predictor. GLEAM algorithms utilize multiple satellite observations of climatic and environmental variables to estimate ET components separately, optimizing ET retrieval (Martens et al., 2017; Miralles et al., 2011 ). Monthly precipitation data were acquired from the Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (IMERG, https://gpm.nasa.gov/data/imerg ). We utilized the monthly 0.1° IMERG v07 product (Huffman et al., 2019 ). The IMERG algorithm derives global precipitation based on the Global Precipitation Measurement Mission (GPM) satellite constellation, incorporating passive microwave (PMW) and infrared (IR) satellite data. IMERG v07 final run data also integrate precipitation gauge data to rectify inherent bias in satellite precipitation estimates. For daily runoff and root zone soil moisture, we employed the Catchment Land Surface Model (CLSM) of the Global Land Data Assimilation System Version 2.2 (GLDAS-2.2, https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov ). GLDAS-2.2 CLSM provides 0.25° daily products including data assimilation from GRACE from 2003 to present. Consequently, TWSA in this dataset closely aligns with GRACE TWSA (our objective variable), rendering it suitable to use SM from GLDAS-2.2 CLSM as predictors. The root zone soil moisture of CLSM spans a soil depth range from 0 to 100 cm. NDVI data were sourced from the MODerate resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) dataset. We utilized monthly 0.05° MODIS data from Terra (MOD13Q1) and Aqua (MYD13Q1) satellites, computing the averaged value of these datasets to incorporate NDVI as a predictor. Inclusion of NDVI accounted for potential vegetation impacts on GWS (Koirala et al., 2017 ).  2.2.3 Other data In validation process for downscaled GRACE data, we utilized in-situ observed groundwater levels obtained from 29,513 wells in India, sourced from the Indian Water Resources Information System (https://indiawris.gov.in/wris/#/groundWater ). The observation dataset covers the period from May 1996 to January 2017, with measurements taken at three-month intervals to capture dynamic groundwater fluctuations. These wells were classified as either dug wells (shallower) or bore wells (deeper), considering the distinct characteristics of each type of well. To ensure comprehensive validation, downscaled TWSA was separately validated against groundwater levels from each well type. To isolate GWSA from TWSA, we incorporated SM data from GLDAS-2.2 Noah into our analysis. This integration aimed to minimize uncertainties in downscaled GWSA by leveraging additional information on soil moisture dynamics. Additionally, to enhance our analysis, we introduced a land mask derived from the MODIS Land Cover dataset (MCD12C1, https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/products/mcd12c1v061/ ). This mask effectively excluded variables over water areas, such as ocean surfaces and lakes, refining our analysis and ensuring its accuracy.    3 Methodology 3.1 Overall framework Here, we employed RF models to downscale GRACE data from a coarse resolution of 3° to a finer resolution of 0.25°. The development of the downscaling model involved establishing a statistical relationship between GRACE derived TWSA and independent variables at the initial coarse resolution (3°) through the training of RF models. The underlying assumption was that this relationship remains consistent across different resolutions, allowing the model to be applied to fine-resolution predictors to generate predicted TWSA at a higher resolution (0.25°). The intricacies of our model design are illustrated in Fig. 2  . Overall, there are four major steps in our study.(1) Data preprocessing: Prior to downscaling, preprocessing of both the target variable (TWSA) and predictors, including precipitation, ET, runoff, SM, NDVI, and accumulated fluxes, was essential. Given the spatial correlation inherent in GRACE mascon products, despite being provided at high resolutions (0.25° or 0.5°), they must be aggregated to the native resolution (3° × 3°) of GRACE. All predictors were similarly aggregated to the training resolution (3° × 3°, 1 month) and target resolution (0.25° × 0.25°, 1 month) for RF model training and GRACE downscaling. Additionally, accumulated precipitation, runoff, and ET were derived by summarizing the monthly fluxes from February 2003 to the target month, contributing to the comprehensive data preprocessing phase.  (2) Model training: Utilizing RF models, we endeavored to capture the statistical relationship between predictors and TWSA on the low-resolution scale (3° × 3°). Distinct models for each aquifer within the study area were developed, excluding several smaller aquifers, to downscale TWSA over different geological conditions. In cases where small aquifers lacked a corresponding GRACE grid cell, we employed RF models from the nearest GRACE grid cell for reliable TWSA downscaling.  (3) TWSA Downscaling: After training the RF models, high-spatial-resolution data were input to derive TWSA in 0.25° grid cells. This process involved calculating coarse residuals by subtracting the TWSA of the 3° aggregated model simulation from the 3° GRACE-derived TWSA. To refine the spatial representation, these coarse residuals were resampled to a finer 0.25° resolution using Kriging interpolation. The final downscaled TWSA was then generated by subtracting the 0.25° residuals from the model derived TWSA, a procedure known as additive correction. This correction ensured mass consistency in 3° grid cells, thereby enhancing the reliability of the downscaled TWSA.  (4) Signal separation and validation: The separation of GWSA from TWSA was achieved by subtracting other components of TWS, with particular emphasis placed on SM derived from the GLDAS CLSM and Noah in this study. The performance of the RF models was systematically evaluated through both the training and validation sets, randomly abstracted from the inputs at rates of 70 % and 30 %. The downscaled GWSA was validated against in-situ observed groundwater levels from dug and bore wells across India. This comprehensive validation process ensures the robustness and accuracy of the downscaled TWSA and GWSA, providing a reliable foundation for subsequent analyses and applications.     3.2 Terrestrial water storage anomaly downscaling The downscaling of TWSA was accomplished utilizing the RF algorithm, selected for its versatility and robust performance in supervised statistical machine learning tasks, including regression problems (Svetnik et al., 2003 ). Originating as a classification and regression tool, the RF algorithm operates by randomly selecting subsets from training samples via bootstrap resampling, generating multiple decision trees collectively forming a “forest”. The predictions of these trees are then aggregated through voting or averaging, depending on the task at hand. One notable strength of RF lies in its ability to mitigate overfitting, particularly when compared to other machine learning algorithms such as ANN (Cutler et al., 2012 ). This characteristic proves advantageous when dealing with various input variables and limited training samples. The bootstrap resampling feature of RF enables efficient handling of datasets with small sample sizes. RF’s capacity to achieve low-overfitting performance and adaptability to diverse input variables renders it a particularly suitable choice for TWSA downscaling. RF models were individually constructed for each aquifer to ensure the unique relationships between predictors and the target variable, TWSA, specific to hydrological dynamics and geological conditions of each aquifer. Four variable combinations of predictors were considered for RF model construction based on the training set (70 % of the samples). The performances of these models were rigorously assessed using both the training and validation sets (30 % of the samples), with results summarized in Table 4  . Before calibrating the RF model, the hyperparameter MinLeafSzie (the minimum number of leaf node observations) was optimized. For each aquifer, ensembled TWSA products and predictor variables were used to optimize the MinLeafSzie. Training 50 trees with MinLeafSize values ranging from 5, 10, 15, 20, to 25, 70 % of the samples were employed, while RMSE of the remained 30 % samples was utilized to select the optimal MinLeafSize. Both the training and validation datasets were randomly selected in temporal and spatial dimensions. An initial assessment, considering only ET, precipitation, and runoff as predictors, revealed a relatively poor performance of the RF model. However, the inclusion of SM and NDVI significantly enhanced model performance, indicating their positive influence on TWSA prediction. Additionally, recognizing the impact of accumulated fluxes on the state variable (TWS) within a given period (Li et al., 2022 ) as illustrated in Eq. The RF model reaches the optimal state when accumulated fluxes (i.e., Pacc , ETacc , and Qacc ) were also taken into consideration. Therefore, the fourth combination was chosen in this study at the beginning of model optimization. Here, the RF algorithm was implemented using the TreeBagger function in MATLAB. Two critical hyper-parameters, namely the number of regression trees grown and MinLeafSzie, played pivotal roles in shaping the model's performance. Typically, increasing the number of regression trees grown enhances model performance, albeit with a potential increase in computational costs. Following a trial-and-error procedure, the number of regression trees grown was set to 50 for this study, striking a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. To evaluate the predictive ability of the predictors, samples not used for model training in the training set, known as out-of-bag (OOB) observations, were leveraged. The importance of each predictor was estimated through permutation feature selection (PFS). PFS measures how model performance degrades when the statistical relationship is established by a model that excludes a given predictor (Breiman 2001; Mecikalski et al., 2021 ). This procedure resulted in the identification of the four most important variables in each model. Finally, the models were retrained using the new combination of predictors, incorporating the four most important ones. The additive correction process ensures mass consistency within each 3° × 3° grid cell before and after the TWSA downscaling process.  3.3 Groundwater storage signal separation TWS serves as a comprehensive measure encompassing all water storage on the land surface and subsurface, including surface soil moisture, root zone soil moisture, groundwater, snow, ice, water stored in vegetation, and river and lake water (Girotto and Rodell 2019 ). The composition of TWS can be simplified into the following equation:(7) Δ T W S = Δ G W S + Δ S M S + Δ S W S , #         where SMS  represents soil moisture storage and SWS  represents surface water storage. Δ  denotes the anomalies relative to a baseline period (2004–2009). In practice terms, changes in surface water storage are typically much smaller than those in GWS. Therefore, for simplicity, ΔSWS  is often considered negligible compared to ΔGWS  (Yang et al., 2022 ). Based on this assumption, GWSA was separated by subtracting the SMS anomaly (SMSA) from TWSA as follows:(8) GWSA = T W S A - S M S A . #         To characterize the uncertainty in GWSA, we utilized three TWSA products and two SMS products (i.e., soil moisture estimates provided by GLDAS-2.2 CLSM and Noah) to derive GWSA from downscaled GRACE data. Here, we considered only SMS with a soil layer depth of less than 100 cm in the two models. By combining the three TWS products with two SMS products, six GWSA outputs were obtained. The standard deviation (SD) of GWSA was calculated as follows:(9) σ GSWA   = 1 6  ∑ i = 1  6  G W S A i  - ∑ i = 1  6  GWS A i   6     2    . #         The SD computed from the six GWSA outputs serves as a metric to characterize the uncertainty inherent in the GWSA results. A higher SD indicates greater variability or dispersion among the different GWSA estimates, reflecting the range of potential values and emphasizing the uncertainty associated with the estimation process. To enhance the robustness of the results, an averaged GWSA output was generated. This average consolidates information from the various GWSA estimates, providing a more stable and representative value.   4 Results 4.1 Downscaled terrestrial water storage anomalies The performance of the RF models plays a crucial role in determining the accuracy of TWSA downscaling, as illustrated by the performance metrics and variable importance depicted in Fig. 3  . Our developed models exhibit accuracy on the validation sets comparable to that of existing studies shown, as shown in Table 2 , while demonstrating higher accuracy on the training sets, indicating their superior performance. Notably, all median values of predictor importance are positive, emphasizing the necessity of all variables in the downscaling process. Hydrological fluxes, as fundamental components of the water balance, play a pivotal role in predicting TWSA. Interestingly, accumulated fluxes emerge as particularly important predictors, highlighting their direct and substantial influence on TWSA, as outlined in Eq. (1) . Additionally, SM and NDVI also play significant roles in TWSA prediction. SM, being a vital constituent of TWS, exerts a considerable impact on TWS changes, as observed in regions like West Africa (Jung et al., 2019 ). Meanwhile, NDVI, serving as an indicator of vegetation growth status, exhibits a close association with TWS, a relationship supported by prior studies (A et al., 2015; Ndehedehe et al., 2019 ). Compared to the original 3° GRACE TWSA, downscaled data exhibit superior capabilities in characterizing spatial variability and trends in TWSA, offering more intricate details. The distributions of both the original and downscaled TWSA for a selected month (May 2011) are presented in Fig. 4  a–b. Despite the overall agreement between the downscaled and original data owing to residual correction, the downscaled data surpass in revealing finer details and effectively pinpointing locations with extreme TWSA values. The enhanced spatial resolution in the downscaled data can be attributed to variations in TWSA downscaling outcomes arising from diverse input data (i.e., precipitation, ET, runoff, SM, and NDVI) within the same aquifer. Additionally, distinctions in TWSA distribution between different aquifers contribute to the improved delineation of spatial details. For instance, the downscaled data clearly illustrate the non-continuous distribution of TWSA in the vicinity of the downstream of the Nile River and the surrounding desert region. To better illustrate the enhancement in spatial details introduced by downscaling, we conducted a comparative analysis between our downscaled results and linearly interpolated TWSA data over the Congo basin aquifer, presented in Fig. 4 e–g. The spatial interpolation algorithm employed for linear interpolation utilized information solely from low-resolution TWSA data, assuming a regular spatial variation of TWSA signals. It operated under the assumption that the TWSA value at each 3° grid cell represented the actual TWSA value at the center of the grid cell, resulting in spatial details of limited clarity and an inability to provide a valid high-resolution reference. While both downscaled TWSA and linearly interpolated TWSA yield products with a spatial resolution of 0.25°, the downscaled TWSA derived from the RF model demonstrates greater reliability in capturing spatial features within 3° × 3° grid cells compared with linearly interpolated results. This is achieved by leveraging information from other related high-resolution datasets during the downscaling process. For instance, grid-cell values of downscaled TWSA through linear interpolation in the Congo basin aquifer may be influenced by TWSA data from outside of the aquifer, potentially overlooking distinct features of TWSA between adjacent aquifers. Similarly, during the training of the RF model corresponding to the Conga basin aquifer, information from adjacent aquifers was unavoidably utilized due to the 3° × 3° grid cells spanning two or more aquifers. However, when downscaling TWSA within the Congo basin aquifer using RF models, 0.25° × 0.25° gridded predictor values were specifically employed to mitigate the impact from adjacent aquifers. This meticulous approach ensures that downscaled data by RF models accurately reflect differences in TWSA variability within distinct aquifers. We further examined trends in both the original and downscaled TWSA ensembles across the study regions, as illustrated in Fig. 4 c–d. Results reveal a significant decrease in TWS over North India and the Middle East, whereas most aquifers in Central Africa exhibit increased TWS, particularly in the vicinity of Lake Victoria. Notably, the downscaled data not only capture these TWSA trends but also show better performance in identifying grid cells with significant trends in TWSA. Detailed analysis of the downscaled data exposes grid cells with the most pronounced trends, showing the steepest decline in TWS in the northwest of India at −7.36 cm/yr and the sharpest increase in West Africa at 5.19 cm/yr. In comparison, the original TWSA highlights the largest decrease and increase values at −5.93 cm/yr and 4.47 cm/yr, respectively. This disparity underscores that downscaled data provide a more nuanced depiction of regions undergoing substantial changes in TWS, offering a superior assessment of the TWS change rate. Moreover, the downscaled data effectively characterize differences in TWS trends between aquifers. This capability enhances the utility of downscaled information in discerning regional variations and facilitates a more comprehensive understanding of the intricate dynamics of TWS.  4.2 Downscaled groundwater storage anomalies Downscaled GWSA can be derived from downscaled TWSA through signal separation, as detailed in Section 3.3 . Results reveal that the distributions of GWSA may exhibit slight differences compared with TWSA in a given month, as illustrated in Fig. 4 a–b and Fig. 5  a–b. These differences arise because of the subtraction of SMSA. Trends observed in GWSA across the study regions also follow a pattern similar to that of TWSA, as depicted in Fig. 4 c–d and Fig. 5 c–d. This similarity is attributed to the mainly seasonal nature of SMSA variability, which does not significantly impact the long-term trends of TWSA over approximately 20 years of the study period. Highlighting the significance of data downscaling, the maximum rate of decline in GWS within a 0.25° grid cell was recorded at −7.30 cm/yr (compared to −5.85 cm/yr in the original GWSA dataset), notably observed in North India. Once again, this underscores the crucial role of data downscaling in accurately estimating extreme changes in GWSA. Furthermore, GWSA time series for 14 representative aquifers were estimated using downscaled GWSA. Location information on these 14 major aquifers in the study regions, along with the changes in downscaled GWSA and its uncertainty, are presented in Fig. 6  . The 14 major aquifers consist of two in the Middle East, two in South Asia, and ten in sub-Saharan Africa. Each small subplot in Fig. 6  illustrates the change in downscaled GWSA (blue line), its linear trend (red dashed line), and the uncertainty in downscaled GWSA estimated by the SD of the six GWSA outputs (blue area) within a major aquifer. Results reveal an increasing trend in GWSA for major aquifers in sub-Saharan Africa, while major aquifers in the Middle East and South Asia undergo a decrease. Notably, among these major aquifers, the Ganges-Brahmaputra basin exhibits the most significant decline in GWSA at a rate of −1.76 cm/yr, equivalent to −5.41 km3 /yr. Similarly, the Indus basin, another major aquifer in South Asia, demonstrates a noteworthy decreasing trend in GWSA (−1.35 cm/yr, or −8.32 km3 /yr). The principal drivers for the decline in GWSA in these regions, including the Middle East, are irrigation with groundwater and reduced precipitation (Rodell et al., 2018 ). For instance, Joodaki et al. (2014)  estimated that over half of the groundwater loss in Iran was attributed to human withdrawals during 2003–2012 by leveraging GRACE data, land surface models, and well observation. Additionally, disparities in water resource management policies for transboundary aquifers may further contribute to unjustified groundwater withdrawals in the Tigris-Euphrates-Western Iran region (Voss et al., 2013 ). In some aquifers, GWSA did not exhibit a consistent upward or downward trend. Particularly, GWSA of the Upper Kalahari-Cuvelai-Upper Zambezi basin in Southern Africa initially increased from 2002 to 2012, followed by a decline until 2019. In the recent two years, GWSA in this basin has shown signs of an increasing trend once again. For analogous aquifers in sub-Saharan Africa, variations in precipitation primarily account for TWS changes (Rodell et al., 2018 ). The frequency of groundwater recharge from precipitation is determined by aridity levels and the type and sensitivity of the recharge relationships are further shaped by local hydrogeology. As aridity increases from humid to arid, the frequency of groundwater recharge tends to decrease, shifting from annual or seasonal patterns to episodic occurrences (Cuthbert et al., 2019 ). Some aquifers exhibit notable seasonal variations in GWSA, while others do not, a phenomenon likely associated with the diverse seasonal patterns of precipitation and hydrogeological factors across different aquifers. It is important to note that the 14 major aquifers considered in this analysis do not include basins with significant changes in lake water storage around Lake Victoria in East Africa. Therefore, when analyzing changes in GWSA in basins with large lakes, further consideration needs to be given to the impact of surface water storage changes on GWSA signal separation (Nanteza et al., 2016 ).
