This factor is crucial for a more comprehensive understanding of the dynamics influencing GWSA in regions with significant surface water bodies.  4.3 Validation of downscaled terrestrial water storage anomalies The validation of downscaled TWSA involved the utilization of monthly well water level observations in India, spanning from February 2003 to January 2017, with a three-month time interval. These observational data were obtained from the Indian Water Resources Information System, encompassing both dug well and bore well observations. Dug wells, characterized by their generally shallow depths, serve as indicators of changes in shallow groundwater aquifers, whereas bore wells, typically drilled to deeper depths, are representative of changes in relatively deep groundwater aquifers. To ensure the reliability of the analysis, well data with fewer than ten observations during our study period were excluded. Spearman’s CC was calculated to assess the correlation between the well water levels and TWSA data, considering the challenge of directly comparing these two datasets. The comparison between GRACE TWSA, downscaled TWSA, and the observed well water level is illustrated in Fig. 7  . The validation results indicate that 90 % and 95 % of the CC values between downscaled TWSA and observations from dug and bore wells, respectively, are positive. Overall, the correlation between TWSA derived from downscaled GRACE data is relatively higher with bore well observations compared to dug well observations. This heightened correlation with bore well observations can be attributed to their greater depth, enabling them to capture variations in GWS from both shallow and deep layers of the aquifers, which aligns more closely with the observations made by gravity satellites. There is not a significant difference in the CC values before and after downscaling, whether in dug wells or bore wells (Fig. 7  a–d). However, there is a negative correlation between the difference in CC before and after downscaling (CCRF, dug  − CCGRACE, dug  and CCRF, bore  − CCGRACE, bore ) and the CC before downscaling (CCGRACE, dug  and CCGRACE, bore ) in both dug and bore wells (Fig. 7  e–f). This suggests that in regions with spatial heterogeneity in groundwater changes, where there are low CC values between GRACE TWSA and in-situ well observations, downscaled data can enhance the correlation between remote sensing TWSA and well measurement data, thereby better reflecting detailed TWSA changes. It is noteworthy that some well observations exhibit negative CC values correlated with downscaled TWSA. This discrepancy may be linked to small aquifers that were not considered during RF model training. In such cases, downscaled TWSA was derived using RF models trained in adjacent larger aquifers. Additionally, the difference between GRACE-derived TWSA and well observations can be influenced by uncertainty in GRACE observations. Despite the application of the Coastal Resolution Improvement (CRI) filter to the JPL TWSA mascon dataset to mitigate land/ocean leakage errors, residual signal leakage errors of approximately 1 cm persisted in non-ice-covered regions (Wiese et al., 2016 ).   5 Discussion 5.1 Uncertainty in downscaled data We quantified the uncertainties in TWSA and GWSA by calculating the SD among three GRACE TWSA products and six GWSA outputs. To evaluate the influence of these uncertainties on the estimated trends in TWSA and GWSA, we took an additional step of normalizing the SD of TWSA and GWSA. This normalization was achieved by dividing the SD values by the respective maximum and minimum values of TWSA and GWSA during the study period, as expressed in Equation (10) .(10) σ TWSA / G W S A , N   = σ  ¯   TWSA / G W S A   m a x T W S A t  / G W S A t    - m i n T W S A t  / G W S A t      , #         where σTWSA/GWSA,N   represents the normalized SD of TWSA or GWSA, σ  ¯   TWSA / G W S A     represents the temporal averaged SD of TWSA or GWSA; and TWSAt /GWSAt   represents the time series of TWSA o r GWSA ensembles. The absolute SD and normalized SD of original TWSA are shown in Fig. 8  a–b. The results indicate that the absolute SD values of TWSA tend to be higher in regions characterized by significant TWSA trends. However, the normalized SD values are generally low in regions with notable trends in TWSA. This observation suggests that the SD of TWSA does not significantly impact our evaluation of significant trends in TWSA. The spatial distribution of the absolute SD and the normalized SD of GWSA are depicted in Fig. 8 c–d. Notably, both the uncertainties in GWSA and TWSA exhibit similar spatial distributions across the study regions, indicating that the uncertainties in downscaled GWSA results primarily stem from discrepancies among different GRACE TWSA products. Furthermore, due to the introduced uncertainties from the downscaling process and signal separation, the mean SD of GWSA (2.57 cm) is relatively higher than that of TWSA (2.17 cm). Across the majority of grid cells, SD values of downscaled GWSA are lower than 5 cm, with the median value being 2.46 cm across our study regions. This magnitude aligns well with the RMSE of the RF models, indicating that the error introduced by the downscaling model falls within the same range as the differences among GRACE GWSA outputs. This alignment underscores the acceptable performance of the RF model in reproducing GWSA. Grid cells exhibiting insignificant or small GWSA trends display relatively higher normalized uncertainties, suggesting that our downscaled GWSA output maintains sufficient accuracy to discern and evaluate significant changes in GWSA across the study regions. Comparison with previous studies (Table 2 ), our method achieves a relatively advanced level of accuracy and covers a larger spatial range. This is mostly due to two reasons. First, we trained different RF models for different aquifers, enabling the method to be applied to regions with diverse environments. Second, by introducing cumulative fluxes as predictive variables, we can consider the constraints of water balance on the downscaled TWSA results.  5.2 Correlation between downscaled groundwater storage anomalies and hydrological fluxes To attribute GWSA changes in various regions, we conducted an analysis of the correlation between GWSA and two primary hydrological fluxes: precipitation and ET. To assess the correlation in various time phases, we employed the Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS (STL) algorithm (Cleveland et al., 1990 ) to decompose downscaled GWSA, precipitation, and ET time series into three additive components (i.e., long-term trend, seasonal variation, and reminder). Prior to the time series decomposition, gaps between GRACE and GRACE-FO derived GWSA were interpolated using the Singular Spectrum Analysis (SSA) algorithm, which has been shown to be suitable for filling GRACE data gaps (Vautard et al., 1992; Yi and Sneeuw 2021 ). The relationships between the long-term trend, seasonal variation, and remainder of monthly GWSA and monthly precipitation and ET are illustrated in Fig. 9  . This approach enables a nuanced understanding of the interdependencies among different components of GWSA and hydrological variables over time. Overall, GWSA demonstrates a stronger correlation with ET compared to precipitation across our study regions for all three components: long-term trend, seasonal variation, and remainder. This suggests that GWSA responds more directly to changes in ET than to precipitation over the study region. Groundwater storage exerts a substantial influence on ET through factors such as irrigation and the intricate connection between groundwater and soil moisture (Chen et al., 2018; Condon et al., 2020; Douville et al., 2021 ). Among the three temporal components, the seasonal terms of GWSA and hydrological fluxes exhibit the most significant correlation (whether positive or negative) in most regions, owing to their regular seasonal variations. Regions near the equator, such as Middle Africa and South India, undergo strong seasonal variations in precipitation and ET due to the monsoon climate. However, there is little significant positive correlation between the seasonal variations of GWSA and precipitation in these areas, which may be attributed to the time lag associated with groundwater recharge from precipitation. Additionally, precipitation does not consistently contribute to groundwater recharge, leading to instances where peaks in seasonal fluctuations of groundwater do not align with peaks in precipitation (Cuthbert et al., 2019 ). In the Middle East, where groundwater is a predominant source for irrigation, seasonal variations of GWSA and ET display a strong positive correlation. High seasonal GWSA during the irrigation season can facilitate the availability of water withdrawal for irrigation, resulting in an increase in ET during the corresponding season and leading to the observed positive correlation. In addition to anthropogenic groundwater withdrawal, processes such as phreatic ET can also lead to the strong relationship between seasonal variations of GWSA and ET. When vegetation transpiration and soil moisture evaporation deplete water in the soil, shallow groundwater can replenish the soil moisture through capillary rise of the soil. Previous studies have shown that shallower groundwater table depth results in higher phreatic ET (Johnson et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2022 ). Thus, for sub-Saharan Africa characterized by shallow groundwater table depth (Fan et al., 2013 ), the significance of phreatic ET accentuates the positive correlation between seasonal variations of GWSA and ET. This observation further underscores the intricate relationship between GWSA and ET, highlighting the relevance of GWSA in influencing regional hydrological dynamics. Regarding long-term trends and remainder terms, GWSA also exhibits a significant correlation with ET in more areas compared to precipitation. In Northwest India and Pakistan, irrigation with groundwater and precipitation decrease led to a significant decline in GWS (Rodell et al., 2018 ), while ET showed a significant upward trend (Pan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2016 ), establishing a marked negative correlation between the long-term trends of GWSA and ET. In contrast, in South India, GWSA shows a long-term increase trend due to precipitation increase and groundwater policy change, such as reduction in electricity subsidies for groundwater extraction, which shows similarity to the causes of GWSA increase observed in the North China Plain following the South-to-North Water Diversion (Dangar et al., 2021; Long et al., 2020; Rodell et al., 2018; Shah et al., 2012 ), resulting in positive correlations between GWSA and ET as well as GWSA and precipitation in the long run. The substantial correlation between GWSA and ET elucidates why ET and accumulated ET serve as indispensable predictor variables in the developed RF models.  5.3 Reliance on groundwater at the national scale To evaluate the uncertainty surrounding groundwater resource availability, it is imperative to pinpoint regions where groundwater is currently essential or projected to become increasingly vital for industrial, agricultural, and domestic water needs. To achieve this, we utilized annual data on fresh groundwater withdrawal and total freshwater withdrawal for countries within our study regions spanning from 2003 to 2019, sourced from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). We integrated four metrics to characterize the reliance on groundwater in the studied countries. Firstly, the trend in GWS change derived from downscaled GWSA ensembles (Fig. 10  a) provides insight into how groundwater availability evolved over time. Secondly, the trend in groundwater withdrawal amount (Fig. 10 b) assesses the quantitative changes in groundwater extraction, offering a measure of the actual amount of groundwater withdrawn. Thirdly, the mean proportion of groundwater withdrawal in total water withdrawal during 2003–2019 (Fig. 10 c) indicates the significance of groundwater in the overall water supply. Lastly, the trend in the proportion of groundwater withdrawal in total water withdrawal during 2003–2019 (Fig. 10 d) examines whether reliance on groundwater was increasing or decreasing. By amalgamating these metrics, we obtain a comprehensive characterization of the reliance on groundwater resources in the studied countries, considering both the quantitative aspects of groundwater withdrawal and the trends in groundwater storage derived from downscaled GWSA ensembles. This information is invaluable for understanding the dynamics of groundwater usage and for formulating strategies to manage and sustain these critical water resources. Against the backdrop of groundwater depletion, India has witnessed an increasing trend in groundwater withdrawal (1.24 km3 /yr2 ), showing a pronounced dependence on groundwater resources. This escalating reliance raises substantial concerns regarding future groundwater availability. Immediate regulatory interventions are imperative to address the unsustainable groundwater withdrawal practices in this region. Similarly, countries in the Middle East, including Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Iran, have consistently showed a significant proportion of groundwater withdrawal relative to total water withdrawal. Despite experiencing a slight decline in GWS, the diminishing groundwater resources in these regions may become increasingly conspicuous in the years ahead. The substantial proportion of groundwater withdrawal underscores the potential challenges in sustaining groundwater availability in these areas. Zimbabwe presents another noteworthy case, demonstrating a progressively intensifying reliance on groundwater. With a notable increasing trend in the proportion of groundwater withdrawal (1.5 %/yr), there is a pressing need for enhanced groundwater management efforts to mitigate dependence on groundwater in the foreseeable future.  5.4 Comparison with linear regressions Two linear statistical methods, multiple linear regression (MLR) and partial least squares (PLS) regression, were further investigated and compared with the non-linear RF algorithm. MLR assumes a linear correlation between predictors and the predictand (TWSA), as described by the equation:(11) Y = β X + β 0  + ε , #         where Y   represents the predicted vector (time series of TWSA), X   is an n ×  8 matrix of the time series of eight predictors where n  is the length of the time series of TWSA, β   and β 0  are parameters to be regressed, and ε  is the residual. In contrast, PLS is a method for constructing predictive models when predictors are highly collinear, achieved by extracting latent factors from predictors (Höskuldsson 1988; Vishwakarma et al., 2021 ). The input variables for both MLR and PLS were standardized to maintain consistent statistical parameters, and both models were trained and validated using the same approach outlined in Section 3.2 . Notably, various numbers of components for PLS were tested, and the configuration resulting in the lowest RMSE in the validation set was chosen for each aquifer, ensuring optimal performance of the linear models in capturing the relationships between predictors and TWSA across diverse aquifers. Results indicate that the performance of MLR and PLS is comparable in TWSA downscaling, as depicted in Fig. 11  . However, both MLR and PLS exhibit overall lower performance compared to RF models (as shown in Fig. 3 ). This disparity can be attributed to the RF models' ability to capture the non-linear relationship between predictor variables and TWSA. While PLS can extract latent factors from predictors, its reliance on linear transformations to reorganize the predictors and fit the regression results in only marginal improvements in the accuracy of TWSA downscaling. The inherent limitation of linearity in MLR and PLS methods impedes their capacity to effectively capture complex non-linear relationships present in the data, leading to a performance gap when compared to the RF models. These findings underscore the advantage of utilizing non-linear methods, such as RF, particularly in scenarios where the relationships are intricate and non-linear.   6 Conclusion This study aims to downscale GRACE data from 3° to 0.25° in sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia, utilizing the RF algorithm with precipitation, ET, runoff, NDVI, and SM data to accurately downscale TWSA and GWSA derived from GRACE and GLDAS dataset over the study regions. The major findings of this study are summarized as follows.1. RF models demonstrate high accuracy in downscaling GRACE data, achieving CC values exceeding 0.92 for training sets and 0.85 for validation sets on average across the 114 aquifers within the study regions. Incorporating accumulated hydrologic fluxes during model optimization enhances model reliability. Moreover, downscaled GWSA aligns well with in-situ observations, exhibiting positive Spearman’ CC of 90 % for dug wells and 95 % for bore wells.  2. Uncertainties in TWSA and GWSA were assessed using various GRACE solutions and GLDAS products. Regions with extreme TWSA and GWSA changes exhibit large SD in TWSA and GWSA. However, the normalized SD values of TWSA and GWSA are comparatively lower. The uncertainty introduced by downscaling and signal separation contributes to a higher SD of GWSA compared to TWSA.  3. Correlation between the long-term trend, seasonality, and remainder of GWSA and precipitation as well as ET reveals that the correlation between GWSA and ET is stronger than that between GWSA and precipitation, suggesting a robust connection between groundwater change and ET across the study regions.  4. In conjunction with annual water withdrawal data, the downscaled GWSA was employed to identify countries with a high reliance on groundwater resources in the study regions. The analysis detected a significant dependence on groundwater resources in India, the Middle East, and Zimbabwe.    Overall, the developed downscaling method enhances the spatial resolution of GRACE-derived TWSA and GWSA over sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia. This method may also be applicable on a global scale. Downscaled TWSA and GWSA offer valuable support for other high-resolution hydrological studies and serve as a reference for formulating local groundwater management strategies.
1 Introduction Over the years, hydrological modeling has gone through numerous methodological developments targeting improved streamflow prediction for sustainable decision-making in water infrastructure planning and management. The recurring instances of floods and droughts pose a menace that necessitates robust streamflow prediction to meet the various aggressive demands of society on a sustainable basis. However, developing streamflow prediction systems is challenging because of the complex and ever-changing nature of runoff due to climate variability patterns globally, which is influenced by erroneous precipitation (rain as well as snow) patterns, local micrometeorological conditions (soil moisture, soil temperature, and snow budget), evapotranspiration, and dynamics of land use & morphological features of catchment over time and across regions. As a result, there has been significant interest among researchers and policymakers globally in the prediction of proficient streamflow models at monthly and/ or daily intervals in the past few decades (Rasouli et al., 2012; Mushtaq et al., 2022 ). Typically streamflow prediction models are categorized into physical-based and data-driven models (He et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2015; Kratzert et al., 2019 ). Physical-based models have their strength in integrating the process-driven complexities of the hydrological cycle, taking the conservation of mass, momentum, and energy into consideration, which gives confidence to the researchers in decision-making (Toth and Brath, 2007; Zhang et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2020 ). The physically-based models are prone to prediction uncertainty when subjected to the non-availability of different datasets, indicating their weakness in conceptualizing the physical process with limited parameters. This shortcoming of the physical-based model limits its transferability (Yadav et al., 2007; Parajka et al., 2013; Samaniego et al., 2017 ). On the contrary, machine learning (ML) algorithms are data-driven and predict the streamflow using historical hydro-climatological data, without necessitating the hydromorphologic information of the basin. Currently, there exists remarkable advancement in the application of ML-based models in water resources development and management. ML is useful for addressing the challenges presented by climate change and the escalating impact of human activities on the environment because of its capability to capture the complex non-linearity in natural hydrological processes (Toth and Brath, 2007; Yang et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2021 ). However, the efficacy of these approaches largely depends on the data quality, as the data with measurement uncertainty may lower the reliability of the model (Gharib and Davies, 2021 ). Moreover, these ML-based models are entirely dependent on the time-series streamflow observation data whose frequencies for each category of flow (low, medium, and high flows) are not uniformly distributed. Each flow category has a different runoff mechanism based on its characteristics. Eventually, predictions based on such models depreciate proficiency since each flow regime participates differently during training (Yang et al., 2019 ). The erroneous training process is most common for high-flow regimes due to the lack of a sufficient number of instances in the time series (Sudheer et al., 2003 ; C. L. Wu et al., 2009 ). There are several ML algorithms used for predicting streamflow. These prediction models differ from others in input feature selection as well as approaches for their optimal number of feature selections. Input variables for the streamflow prediction model include both endogenous and exogenous variables. The endogenous variable is a variable that is explained by other variables within a model e.g., prior streamflow data; on the contrary exogenous ones are not explained by other variables within a model e.g., climatic variables, LULC, and soil. Various ML models were used: support vector machines (SVM) and auto-regressive integrated moving average [ARIMA; Maity et al., (2010) ]; artificial neural network (ANN) and adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system [ANFIS; He et al., (2014) ]; classification and regression trees and ensembled bagged regression trees [BRTs; Erdal and Karakurt (2013) ] to predict daily and monthly streamflow based on endogenous input variables, specifically antecedent flows. Whereas, significant studies consider both endogenous as well as exogenous input variables conducted on predicting streamflows. Adnan et al. (2019  ; 2020)  evaluated the performance of four different models, namely optimally pruning extreme learning machine (OP-ELM), least square support vector machine (LSSVM), multivariate adaptive regression lines (MARS), and M5 model tree (M5Tree) using precipitation, temperature, and streamflow data in two different watersheds. The results showed that OP-ELM performed better in the Yangtze River watershed, in China, while MARS performed better in the Swat Watershed, in Pakistan. The afore-discussed literature indicated that the performance of any specific ML algorithm, and a specific input feature variable cannot be generalized for every study area and dataset. Some studies have focused on relevant atmospheric, hydro-meteorological, and surface variables in relation to streamflow generation processes by employing random forest [RF; Hagen et al., (2021) ], ANN (Yang et al., 2020 ), and long short-term models LSTM (Yin et al., 2021 ). Rasouli et al. (2012)  considered a wide range of exogenous variables including climate indices and local hydrometeorological input variables to forecast streamflows at lead times using Bayesian neural network (BNN), gaussian process (GP), SVR, and multiple linear regressor (MLR). Moreover, ML algorithms were also employed to generate synthetic daily, 10-day, and monthly streamflow simulations proposed by Jia et al., (2022)  employing the k-means algorithm, expectation-maximization, and information criteria. A non-exhaustive review of streamflow predictions using these algorithms is presented in  Table 1 . Recent literature suggests that ML-based models often face challenges in predicting a generalizable estimate because of the erroneous variable selection process, resubstituting validation, and inconsistent validation processes for different algorithms (Gharib and Davies, 2021 ). Generally, hydrological processes provoke more uncertainty than the uncertainty in the model, which may not emulate well, irrespective of the best set of predictors being obtained from the training set. Such selection often suggests a few redundant variables adding noise to the model and affecting the performance of generalizable estimates (Quilty and Adamowski, 2020; Schmidt et al., 2020 ). Additionally, the most common methodological miscalculation in the ML-based modeling process made by past studies is testing the trained model with the same set used to train the model, which commonly refers to resubstituting validation. Furthermore, the k-fold cross-validation method emerges as the best-suitable technique to ensure the validation set does not cross over in successive iterations (Jena et al., 2021 ). Therefore, the test set should be kept aside from this technique to ensure the generalizable estimate, prevent overfitting in the model, and ultimately come up with a 3-step (training, validation, and testing) hold-out method (Solomatine and Ostfeld, 2008; Wu et al., 2013; Raschka, 2020 ). Another drawback that reveals the performance estimation bias of the model, is due to inconsistencies involved in cross-validation and resampling among different algorithms. Error metrics-based comparison may not suggest the best choice among these algorithms, as the best ML-based model results in a vague prediction (Quilty and Adamowski, 2018; Gharib and Davies, 2021 ). From the literature, it was also observed that the input feature selection for model construction includes both endogenous and exogenous input variables. However, the majority of research incorporates rainfall and temperature as variables, while a very smaller subset also includes potential evapotranspiration as an additional exogenous variable. It is evident from physical distributed models that runoff regimes have a positive correlation with land use patterns. We believe the slow-changing impact of land use class over the years, and static basin physiographic variables across basins will have a strong influence on runoff regimes, and machine learning algorithms at current capacities will grasp these patterns and enhance the model development for prediction systems. The known fact is that increasing the number of input feature variables in a dataset introduces noise and hinders generalization. Therefore, the study also aims to examine whether incorporating input feature variables related to land use dynamics will improve the accuracy, or if it will fail to generalize. Moreover, from the literature, it was found that very few streamflow prediction models have been developed for agricultural-dominated tropical watersheds having data scarcity. So, this work focuses on predicting streamflow in agricultural-dominated tropical watersheds using widely used regression algorithms such as ANN, SVR, M5P, REPTree, RT, and RF. This study also proposes a two-stage framework in the model training and testing phases to select optimal feature selection and, subsequently develop a robust ML-based streamflow prediction model, that overcomes the pitfalls of ML model development mentioned earlier, and ensures generalizability in its performance. The overarching objectives of this streamflow prediction study are: (1) to carry specific preprocessing to the input variable and select a proficient ML algorithm; (2) to select the optimal hierarchical predictor set through a hybrid input feature selection algorithm; and (3) to develop a robust and reliable ML-based model for daily streamflow prediction.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The study area, the Rana watershed, is located in the lower-middle reach of the Mahanadi River basin in the state of Odisha, India ( Fig. 1 ). The Rana watershed extends from 20.11˚ N to 20.41˚ N latitudes and from 85.39˚ E to 85.63˚ E longitudes, bounded by hills on the east and west, and the Mahanadi River on the north side. The total drainage area of the watershed is 496 km2,  with the longest flow path of this watershed being about 25 km. Topographically, this watershed slopes moderately (up to 8 %) from south to north, with a greater slope of approximately 22 % having hillocks and drainage channels in lateritic uplands (Jena et al., 2021 ). The average annual rainfall received by the region is around 1451 mm, out of which 70 % is received during July to October (Jena et al., 2020 ). Our motivation for selecting this study area was that the watershed is an agricultural-dominated watershed with more than three-quarters of the area as agricultural land, which was inline with the overarching objective of this study. The monitoring activity conducted by the authors and the availability of the data also regulated the selection of this watershed. Moreover, it is located in the lower-middle reach of the Mahandi River, a major river basin in Eastern India. Major hydrological findings from this study area could be utmost insights for the prediction of hydrological processes in adjacent as well as similar hydro-climatic watersheds.  2.2 Data Soil textural information for the study watershed was obtained from Jena et al., (2021) . It was found that 5 USDA soil classes exist in the study area, with the majority of the soil identified as a sandy loam (40.9 %) followed by loam (30.9 %), silty loam (19 %), silty clay loam (8.8 %) and sand (0.4 %). This study collected LULC data for the year 2002 on a scale of 1: 50000 obtained from the Odisha Space Application Centre (ORSAC), and LULC at a spatial resolution of 53 m × 53 m for the years 2005, 2010, and 2015 obtained from the National Remote Sensing Centre, Hyderabad, India. The LULC classes found in the Rana watershed are dense forest (∼9.74 %), shrub forest (∼0.02 %), agricultural land (∼76.13 %), wasteland (∼5.34 %), water bodies (∼3.20 %), and built–up areas (∼5.57 %), making it agriculture dominant watershed (Fig. 1 ). The watershed's digital elevation model (DEM) was extracted from the Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer (ASTER) data at 30 m × 30 m spatial resolution downloaded from the United States Geological Survey (USGS) public database (https://earthexplorer.usgs.gov/ ). The slope map generated was classified into five subgroups: 0 % – 5.04 %, 5.05 % – 9.62 %, 9.63 % – 16.81 %, 16.82 % – 33.74 %, and 33.75 % – 140.75 %. The spatial datasets used in this study with varying spatial resolution and formats were then converted into raster format with a pixel size of 53 m × 53 m to unify the spatial inputs for the model training. The streamflow data at the outlet, just before the confluence of Mahanadi and tributary Rana (the blue triangle in Fig. 1 ) was monitored daily between 2014 and 2016 by the authors, and additional measurements from 1997 to 2014 were collected from the Central Water Commission, India. Table S1  shows the descriptive statistics of the discharge dataset of 20 years, which were separated into small (0–12.17 m3 /sec), medium (12.17–42.47 m3 /sec), large (42.47–70.66 m3 /sec), and extraordinarily large (>70.66 m3 /sec) flows based on 80th, 95th, and 98th percentile flow frequencies (Sun et al., 2008 ). The box plot in  Fig. 2  shows the median, interquartile range, and outliers for different classes of flows in which extraordinarily large flows show few events of abnormal discharges.  Fig. 3  and Figure S1-S4 , respectively show the yearly and monthly composition of flow stacked charts which visualize the frequency distribution according to the classes of flows. The monthly composition depicts the ephemeral nature of the stream (Figure S1-S4 ). Fig. 3  shows that 1999 was a dry year, except that the ephemeral streams possessed mostly medium flow in the study period. The daily meteorological parameters, namely maximum and minimum temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, solar radiation, and rainfall were obtained from an automatic weather station (AWS) installed in the study watershed at the location marked with a red square in Fig. 1 . The descriptive statistics on different weather parameters presenting the watershed characteristics are listed in Tables S2  & S3. The skewness of the rainfall dataset is very high, representing the uneven distribution of rainfall. The high kurtosis associated with the rainfall dataset reflects the existence of outliers in the rainfall dataset. Furthermore, PET is also a significant variable for streamflow modeling and studies can be found that performed streamflow simulations at daily time steps incorporating Penman-Monteith Equations (Penman monteith, 1963 ) for accurate streamflow prediction (Ellenburg et al., 2018 ). In this study, the daily PET was computed using the FAO Penman-Monteith method using the following equations (Cai et al., 2007; Rao et al., 2012 ):(1) R  n   = R  ns   − R  nl       (2) R  ns   = 1 − α    R  s       (3) R  nl   = σ T  max  4   + T  min  4    2      0.34 − 0.14 ⅇ      1.35 R  s    R  so     − 0.35        (4) R  h   = ⅇ  e  s     × 100     where R n   is the net radiation; R ns   is the net shortwave radiation (MJ m−2 day−1 ) obtained from Eq. 2  considering albedo (α ) of surface as 0.26 and R s   is the average solar insolation incident on a horizontal surface (MJ m−2 day−1 ) obtained from automatic weather station (AWS) installed in the watershed; Rnl  is the net longwave radiation (MJ m−2  day−1 ) obtained from Eq. 3 ; σ   is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant for a day (4.903 ×10–9 MJ K−4 m−2 day−1 ); Tmax  and Tmin  are the maximum and minimum temperature in Kelvin, R so   is the average top of the atmosphere solar insolation (MJ m−2 day−1 ), and e is the actual vapor pressure, that can be computed from the saturation vapor pressure es  using Eq. 4, by  knowing relative humidity Rh  values collected from the AWS. The extreme minimum and maximum values of rainfall and PET of the testing dataset were within that of the training dataset envisaging appropriate model development and testing (Kişi and Aytek, 2013 ). Various point scale observed and derived datasets (i.e., rainfall, potential evapotranspiration, and streamflow) collected from different sources were preprocessed at daily temporal resolution. The spatial resolution was unified by converting and resampling the spatial datasets (i.e., soil texture, slope, and LULC) to the required format and resolution using Arc GIS 10.2. The unit of the data was made consistent throughout the following SI units. The study also evaluated the descriptive statistics of the time series data to evaluate the quality of the data and the influence of the outliers in the dataset. The quality and consistency verification was challenging because of the data-scares nature of the region. However, before applying the dataset for model development, internal consistency detection tests and basic integrity checks were conducted for the temporal dataset obtained from AWS. Internal consistency check involves the check on temporal variation: for instance, identifying the days with maximum temperature lesser than minimum temperature; basic integrity checks by identifying outliers, descriptive statistics (Table S2  & S3), and negative precipitation values (Hunziker et al., 2018; Adeyeri et al., 2022 ). The inconsistencies and missing data found were inspected and corrected as per norms of climatological practices suggested by (WMO, 2018 ) by calculation of monthly and yearly means and sums. The estimated yearly sum of potential evapotranspiration was validated with the earlier studies under Indian conditions conducted by the Central Research Institute for Dryland Agriculture (CRIDA), Hyderabad, India through spatial variation presented using isolines (Rao et al., 2012 ).  2.3 Machine learning algorithms The selection of machine learning techniques for streamflow prediction in this study was based on the historical evolution, popularity, and diversity of machine learning, encompassing traditional neural networks to modern ensemble models. The Weka 3.8.6 (Khosravi et al., 2021 ) and Python codes (Abbas et al., 2022 ) were used to implement six ML algorithms, two classical algorithms: ANN, and SVR; three decision tree algorithms: M5P, REPTree, and RT; and an ensembled model: RF in this study. The efficacy of ML algorithms was improved using the two-fold framework proposed in this study ( Fig. 4 ). The following sections provide a detailed description of each algorithm for streamflow prediction: 2.3.1 Artificial neural networks ANN functions analogous to biological neural networks of the human brain (Haykin, 1998 ). Typically, neural networks are defined by their architecture, which describes the arrangement of connections between nodes, the mechanism for calculating the weights of these connections, and the activation function. This study uses the popular feed-forward backpropagation to learn a multi-layer perceptron by normalizing the input data between –1 and +1, and finally, the outputs gets scaled back to the original range. The feed-forward design alone facilitates the flow of data solely from the inputs to the outputs. The backpropagation technique calculates the gradient of the loss function with respect to all the variables and parameters in the network. These derivatives are then used to update the weight and bias parameters (Kasiviswanathan and Sudheer, 2017 ). The multilayer perceptron can be mathematically represented as:(5) Y  k   = σ  k   ∑ j = 1  m   w  kj   σ  j   ∑ i = 1  n   w  ij    X  i   +  b  j      +  b  k            This study used a 4-layer network architecture, consisting first layer as the input layer, two hidden layers, and a fourth layer as the output layer, and the sigmoid function as the activation function and formulated as in Eq. 6  (Cheng et al., 2020 ). The variable Xi  represents the input value at neuron i, whereas Yk  represents the output value at neuron k. The activation function for the hidden layer is denoted by σ  k    , while the activation function for the output layer is denoted by σ  j    , m and n represent the number of neurons in the input and hidden layers, respectively. wij  denotes the weight connecting input neuron i and hidden neuron j, while wkj  represents the weight connecting hidden neuron j and output neuron k. bj  and bk  refer to the biases of the jth  neuron in the hidden layer and kth  neuron in the output layer, respectively.(6) F a    = 1  1 + exp  − a               Consequently, the final weights and biases are acquired by minimizing the subsequent objective function as follows:(7) Obj w  ij   , b  j   , w  jk   , b  k      = ∑ i = 1  n    ∑ i = 1  n      X  n , m   − X ′  n , m   w  ij   , b  j   , w  jk   , b  k         2        where X and X′ are observed and predicted variables, respectively. This algorithm was optimized by a grid-search technique, that used several combinations of the provided hyperparameters and their respective values to compute the performance for each combination. ANN limits its applicability due to its “black box” nature that lacks transparency, proneness to overfitting, and the empirical nature of model development. This study employed k-fold cross-validation to mitigate the issue of overfitting.  2.3.2 Support vector regression SVR is an adaptation of classical SVM, under the criteria of supervised statistical learning method that assumes non-parametric, no knowledge in the joint distribution of input and output variables exists, and seeks a probable correlation between them (Cortes and Vapnik, 1995 ). The SVM transforms the input dataset into a feature space with a greater dimensionality than the original input space. This increased dimensionality simplifies the hidden decision boundary (hyperplane) within a feature space. The SVR problem was defined as follows (Maity et al., 2010 ): Considering a training set x  i  ′     y  i      ⅈ = 1  N    , in which xi  ε Rp  represents p dimensional input vector and yi  ε R is scalar measured output, which represents the system output. The goal is to construct a function y = f(x) which represents the dependence of the output yi  on the input xi . The form of this function is(8) y = w  T   ϕ x    + b     where w is known as the weight vector and b the bias, ϕ i    denotes a nonlinear transfer function that maps the input vectors into a high-dimensional feature space in which theoretically a simple linear regression can cope with the complex nonlinear regression of the input space. Unlike classification problems, typical regression problems do not allow decision boundaries to be divided into distinct (straight) decision boundaries, rather hyperplane is defined as a regression curve which limits its applicability. Hence, kernel functions emerge as non-linear terms that appear in regression problems which assist in transforming the data and projecting onto a new space where the differences are more apparent. In this study, we used the radial basis function kernel (RBF), also known as the Gaussian function can be defined as(9) K x , x  i  ̇       = exp − x − x  i      2 σ  2            where, σ is the kernel function parameter of the RBF kernel. Vapnik (1999)  suggested the use of sequential minimal optimization for regression (SMO-reg) of ε-insensitive loss function where the error is not penalized as long as it is less than ε. Using this error function together with a complexity parameter C, the optimization problem is solved by the support vector machine (Shevade et al., 2000; He et al., 2014 ):(10) Minimize : 1  2   w    2   + C ∑ i  N   ξ + ξ  i  *              Such that wi  * ϕ(xi ) + bi -di  ≤ ԑ + ξi *, i = 1,2,3…N yi  - wi  *ϕ(xi ) + bi  ≤ ԑ + ξi , i = 1,2,3…N ξi,  ξi *, i = 1,2,3…N where ξi  and ξi *are slack variables that penalize training errors by the loss function over the error tolerance ξ and C is a positive trade-off parameter that determines the degree of the empirical error in the optimization problem. The hyperparameters employed for this algorithm were RBF kernel hyperparameter σ, complexity parameter C, error tolerance set as 0.001, and epsilon set as 1.0E-12. This study employed a grid-search algorithm to refine the two hyperparameters (C, σ) using cross-validation on the training set to determine the best hyperparameter setting.  2.3.3 M5Prime tree M5 Tree is a type of supervised machine learning algorithm that falls under the genre of decision trees, composed of decision nodes that are connected to other decision nodes or leaf nodes, forming a tree-like structure with trucks connected by branches. These Model trees extend the concept of regression trees by including regression functions in their leaves. Accordingly, continuous non-linear numerical complexities can be transformed into piece-wise linear functions that are linear in different intervals. The M5Prime algorithm is a reconstruction of the M5 algorithm for inducing trees of regression models (Quinlan, 1992 ). The process of constructing an M5P Tree has a couple of stages: (i) a decision tree is created using a split criterion; and (ii) the model tree is designed by pruning the excessively growing tree, which is susceptible to overfitting (Singh et al., 2010 ). It uses a divergence metric called “standard deviation reduction” (SDR) as a split criterion for producing a decision-based regression tree (Pal and Deswal, 2009; Ghasemi et al., 2018; Adnan et al., 2019 ). Considering a set of S training instances with independent variables as input and dependent target variable. These independent variables can be either presented as the leaf, or they can split into subsets using aforesaid SDR, and the standard deviation of instances reaching at each node is denoted as ‘sd’. Si  is represented as a subset of instances ith  outcome of the potential set. Therefore, the SDR is the method used to calculate the anticipated decrease in the standard deviation.(11) SDR = sd S    − ∑ S  i      S      sd S  i           The algorithm was followed by pruning and smoothening to cater to decreased error estimates E’ at each node and to compensate for the acute discontinuity that appears obligatory between adjacent linear sets at the leaves of a pruned tree (Quinlan, 1992 ).(12) E ′ = nf + ka  n + k       where, a is the predicted value at S; n is the no of training instances reached at Si ; f is the predicted value at Si ; k is the smoothening constant. Hyperparameters involved in the M5Prime algorithm were maximum depth, the minimum number of leaves, and a specific smoothing constant from Eq. 12 . The optimal combination of hyperparameters and their values were found using a grid search algorithm using 10-fold cross-validation through the training dataset.  2.3.4 Reduced error pruning tree The REPTree is a hybrid approach of reduced error pruning (REP) and DT, that stands as a fast decision tree learner that works on information gain or reducing the variance as splitting criteria, and it does pruning based on the entropy or mean square error on the predictions made by the tree. The process was recursively repeated to interpret and prune the tree by contemplating it against already established trees. This process was repeated for several specific depths of the trees to converge to the stopping criteria (Joseph and Ravichandran, 2012 ; Chen et al., 2019 ; Khosravi et al., 2018 ). Decision trees are built by searching for the input variable with the highest Gain Ratio denoted as GR(x,Z)(13) GR x , Z    = Entropy Z    − ∑ i = 1  n   Z  i      Z      Entropy Z  i        − ∑ i = 1  n   Z  i      Z      logbase 2 Z  i      Z              where, x is the attribute to training dataset Z with subset Zi , i = 1,2,3,…,n. The hyperparameters involved in the REPTree algorithm for this study were maximum depth, and threshold entropy value, which can be present for splitting to be performed in the regression trees. The optimal combination of maximum depth, threshold entropy, and the number of nodes was obtained from the grid search algorithm and the optimum values were selected by carrying out a 10-fold cross-validation.  2.3.5 Random tree The RT algorithm is positioned between a basic decision tree and an RF in terms of complexity (Pal and Singha, 2022; Karaman and Frazzoli, 2011 ). The RT model was constructed using prediction trees. This algorithm involves a random number of trees with a significant depth, allowing for the selection of the most crucial votes from a range of trees with ‘x’ randomly chosen independent variables in each iteration (Pal and Singha, 2022; Xu et al., 2019 ). This algorithm does not prune and only allows the estimation of class probabilities of hold-out-set. The hyperparameters involved in the RT for this study involve ‘x’ value and maximum depth. The optimal combination of hyperparameters obtained from the grid search algorithm and a suitable value for each hyperparameter were assigned by performing 10-fold cross-validation.  2.3.6 Random forest The RF algorithm was developed by Breiman (2001) . It is a non-parametric and quasi-unsupervised method that belongs to the decision tree genus. This technique is widely used in machine learning for conducting "tree-based learning". It combines two operations: (i) makes the array of all the recommended places (bootstrapping) which ensures different sizes and combinations of attributes; and (ii) does the voting process to select the best place (aggregation). The whole process of getting the recommendation and selecting the best place is generalized as a “bagging” process. It exhibits optimal performance when the number of observations surpasses the number of variables. An advantage of applying algorithms is their ability to provide an internal unbiased estimate of generalization error as the process of developing a forest continues. RF algorithm creates a collection of decision trees by randomly selecting instances and attributes, known to be an ensemble model. These models are then combined to make predictions, resulting in improved efficiency (Tahmasebi et al., 2020 ). Therefore, the forecast for a test or fresh data point xˈ may ultimately be derived as:(14) f  ′   = 1  B   ∑ b = 1  B   f  b   x  1           where f ’b  is the regression tree on the bth  sample (Xb  and Yb ) out of the total B bootstrapped samples from original training data X = {xi , i= 1,…,n} and Y = { yi , i = 1,…,n}. This bagging is much more efficient in dealing with bias-variance trade-offs and reduces the variance of a prediction model, certainly overfitting. Further, it efficiently generates rankings of variable significance based on the importance in regression model training (Mushtaq et al., 2022 ). Hyperparameters involved were maximum depth and the number of estimators, which suggest a stopping criteria to choose the best set of attributes and also can compute the importance of each attribute contributing to the target attribute (Oppel and Schumann, 2020; Hagen et al., 2021 ). To obtain a generalized outcome from this algorithm, a combination of hyperparameters was obtained by carrying out a grid search algorithm, while training the dataset using 10-fold cross-validation.   2.4 Model performance evaluation The evaluation criteria selected to compare algorithms and measure the prediction skill of the models were mean absolute error (MAE): examines the linear scoring principle and computes the average magnitude of the error irrespective of its direction, root mean square error (RMSE): examines how the dispersion of differences between measured and expected data occurs, coefficient of determination (R2 ): examines the differences between the mean and variation of measured and estimated values, and Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE: Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ): examines model validation, its dimensional form allows the comparison of performances in different periods. The expressions for MAE, RMSE, R2 , and NSE are(15) MAE =  1  N   ∑ i = 1  N   h  si   − h  oi          (16) RMSE = ∑ i = 1  N   h  si   − h  oi      2     N         (17)  R  2   =  ∑ i = 1  N   h  oi   − h  o    ̅     h  si   − h  s    ̅         2    ∑ i = 1  N   h  oi   − h  o    ̅     2    ∑ i = 1  N   h  si   − h  s    ̅     2          (18) NSE = 1 − ∑ i = 1  N   h  oi   − h  si      2     ∑ i = 1  N   h  oi   − h  o    ̅     2          where hoi  is the observed streamflow discharge at test locations; hsi  is the predicted streamflow discharge obtained from the model algorithm; h  0    ̅    is the mean of observed streamflow discharge; h  s    ̅    is the mean of predicted streamflow discharge; N is the number of observations. The best fit between the observed and predicted streamflow discharge under ideal conditions would yield an MAE and RMSE value equal to zero, whereas R2  and NSE values equal one. Moreover, NSE values between 0.0 and 1.0 are generally considered acceptable performance levels. In contrast, a negative NSE value indicates that the mean observed value is a better predictor than the simulated value (Moriasi et al., 2007 ). Additionally, the final model performance of the proposed prediction system was also evaluated using the Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE), a goodness-of-fit indicator that is popular in hydrology (Gupta et al., 2009; Clark et al., 2021 ):(19) KGE = r − 1    2   + α − 1    2   + β − 1    2         where r is the linear correlation between observed and predicted, α is a measure of variability error, and β is the bias term.  2.5 Methodological framework 2.5.1 Resampling dataset Twenty years (1997–2016) of hydroclimatic parameter time series and basin-level physiographic datasets were split into a training set (1997–2012) and a testing set (2013–2016). The training set was used for hyperparameter tuning using 10-fold cross-validation. The cross-validation technique was only applied to the training set (1997–2012) in this study, and the performance of different algorithms was compared (Gharib and Davies, 2021 ). The test data were excluded from cross-validation to prevent any possible sharing of statistical parameters between the training and testing datasets, meaning that the model testing was completely unaffected by the training dataset.  2.5.2 Hierarchical predictor selection The fundamental requirement of enhancing the prediction skill is to select the most pertinent predictors from the available predictors. Possible over/underfitting can impact prediction performance due to the existence of noisy and irrelevant data. A new two-stage approach was framed in the study for input predictor/ feature selection to resolve the issue mentioned above. Historically, the filter, wrapper, and embedded methods were employed by studies for predictor selection (Lin et al., 2014; Rodriguez-Galiano et al., 2018; Jena et al., 2021 ). In this study, we conducted the predictor selection using a hybrid wrapper embedded technique to help build a more generalized ML-based model. In stage one, the primary objective was to select the most suitable machine learning algorithm out of six alternatives and conduct predictor selection. The k-fold cross-validation technique was carried out, where k = 10 (tenfold cross-validation) was chosen. Initially, HIDs were developed by the forward selection or backward elimination of predictors under the wrapper method. These HIDs were combinations of relatively slow-changing spatial variables, and highly dynamic temporal predictors, that capture both conditional influences (HID 1 to HID 25) as well as marginal influences (HID 26 TO HID 30) on the predictand ( Table 2 ). Relatively less dynamic predictors such as LULC, slope, and soil were included in this framework to incorporate any regionalized information from the multiple watersheds in an area that could constrain the ensemble prediction systems (Yadav et al., 2007 ). The performance of the ML-based streamflow prediction algorithms based on different HIDs was evaluated using four goodness-of-fit criteria described in the subsequent section. Based on the metrics values, the HIDs were later partitioned into groups that can be interpreted as ‘good,’ moderate,’ and ‘poor’ using a k-means clustering algorithm (Solomatine and Shrestha, 2009; Jena et al., 2021 ). The performance of six ML algorithms for ‘good cluster’ HIDs was used for algorithm selection for model development. Subsequently, the embedded method was used for ranking the predictors for all ‘good cluster’ HIDs by assessing importance calculated based on mean decrease impurity using Eq. 20  (Breiman, 2001; Louppe et al., 2013 ):(20) Imp X  m      = 1  N  t     ∑ T   ∑ t ϵ T : v st    = Xm   P t    Δ ⅈ st , t          where X m   is the importance of predictor for predicting Y  by adding up the weighted impurity decreases P(t) Δi (st, t)  for all the nodes t  where X m  is  used, averaged over all N t   trees in the forest; P(t)  is the proportion of N/N t   of reaching t,  and v(st)  is the variable used in the split ‘st’.  The predictors were ranked from 1 to n (high to low), where “n” is the number of predictors in a particular HID. A rank frequency matrix was created to assess predictors' suitability based on the number of times each predictor was assigned to a corresponding rank. In this study, we adopted the hybrid wrapper-embedded predictor selection algorithm to select the model with the optimal number of relevant predictors, named ‘HID-P,’ with the highest prediction skill (Jena et al., 2021 ). The predictor selection criteria considered for stage 1 to select the predictors were: the predictors were selected (a) those having higher frequencies for getting assigned to the ranks between 1 and 5, and (b) predictors possessing ≥50 % of the total instances of appearance in ‘good’ HIDs within ranks 1–5. In the second stage of this framework, we conducted a lag analysis of the temporal dataset: rainfall, PET, and discharge time-series data at the daily time step. Maximum up to two days lag associated hydroclimatic variables and runoff were considered. Nine combinations (HIDs) of lag-associated predictors were developed ( Table 3 ). These combinations of predictors were subsets constructed to have the inferences on each training iteration by adding or removing the predictors from the whole predictor set. Now, each HID undergoes 10-fold cross-validation employing only the model selected in Stage 1. Then, the hybrid wrapper-embedded technique with a rank frequency matrix, similar to the Stage 1 was deployed for predictor selection to obtain the potential lag-associated predictors using the algorithm as follows. The predictor selection criteria considered for Stage 2 were: the predictors were selected (a) those having higher frequencies for getting assigned to the ranks between 1 and 3, and (b) predictors possessing ≥50 % of the total instances of appearance in ranks 1–3. Additionally, the significant lagged streamflow variable was also included in the feature selection set, considering the Partial Auto Correlation Factor (PACF) analysis (He et al., 2014 ). This factor is a statistical metric used to identify patterns in streamflow and examine how strongly each observation is correlated to its past observation at specific time lags while controlling the influence of other intermediate lags. Such analysis also reveals if there exist any systematic changes in streamflow patterns over time. PACF was employed in this study for capturing the temporal dynamics of the hydrological process aiding in improved prediction proficiency of the model. Moreover, using the categorization approach mentioned in Section 2.2 , the lagged streamflow predictors were categorized into low, medium, high, and extraordinary flows. This categorization helps identify each flow category's flow regime and train the model based on the underlying runoff generation mechanisms. Defining the flow regimes based on categorization could reduce prediction uncertainties and enhance ML-based hydrological models' proficiency (Sivapragasam and Liong, 2005 ). In the last step, the identified supreme pertinent predictors (HID-SPP): pertinent predictors from both stages, significantly lagged streamflow, and its categorized flow regime were used for ML-based model training and testing.    3 Results 3.1 Algorithm section This study conducted consistent resampling and cross-validation across different algorithms under consideration to ensure unbiased performance evaluation of the model. All the HIDs presented in Table 2  were used for 10-fold cross-validation for the training data using the six algorithms: ANN, SVR, M5P, REPTree, RT, and RF. The performance evaluation results (RMSE, MAE, R2 , and NSE) are presented in Figure S5 . It was found that RF outperformed the rest of the algorithms throughout. The second best algorithm was the REP Tree, with slightly different values of RMSE compared to that of RF, while MAE, R2 , and NSE values were not in a similar range as that of RF. Hence, the RF algorithm was selected for developing the streamflow prediction model in this study. The significance of each predictor and its influence on either inclusion or exclusion is discussed in the next section.  3.2 Predictor selection Based on the performance metrics values, the HIDs were further clustered into three clusters, “good,” “moderate,” and “poor” HIDs, using the k-means clustering algorithm, resulting in 16, 7, 7 “good,” “moderate” and “poor” HIDs, respectively. The “good” HIDs are presented in  Fig. 5 , which depicts most good clustered HIDs are of conditional influences on the predictand than marginal influence, except the case of the marginal influence of potential evapotranspiration on the streamflow in the hierarchy set HID-27. Moreover, it was observed that there is scope for improving the performance of prediction models through the methodologies described targeting a generalizable streamflow prediction model development. Further, the influence of the relative importance of the predictors was examined using the rank frequency matrix. Table S4  indicates the results of ranking predictors based on their importance and was used for eliminating redundant predictors using the embedded technique using mean decrease impurity calculated using Eq. 20 . This approach restraints the uncertainty caused by input feature selection to a great extent that ensures eliminating the redundant predictor to be included in model development. The eight pertinent predictors selected in Stage 1 were PET, LULC (built-up area, agricultural land, dense forest, shrub forest, wasteland, water bodies), and rainfall, as they had a higher frequency of ranks in the range 1–5. The number of instances each selected predictor appeared within rank five was more than or equal to 50 % of the total number of times it appeared in 16 “good” HIDs. For instance, PET was selected as a predictor as it possessed higher frequencies, i.e., 8, 1, 1, 0, and 1 of getting assigned to the ranks 1–5, and it has appeared 11 times out of a total of 16 appearances (greater than 50 %) in good clustered HIDs. Similarly, soil texture ‘Loam’ having frequencies 1, 1, 1 acquired ranks 3, 4, and 5, respectively, satisfying criteria (a); but failed to satisfy criteria (b) because only three out of a total of 8 appearances which is 37.5 % of the times it appeared within rank 5. Thus, these eight predictors involving PET, land use classes, and rainfall were selected as HID-P   in stage 1. This result was attributed to the temporal variations in these predictors, leaning towards the regimes of streamflow. Subsequently, analysis in Stage 2 was performed as described in Section 2.5 . Table 3  shows the considered combinations of lagged predictors and nine created hierarchies of Stage 2. The hybrid wrapper-embedded technique and rank frequency matrix were applied as in Stage 1, employing 10-fold cross-validation with the RF algorithm. Based on the predictor selection criteria for Stage 2, three predictors: rainfall considering two-day lags (Pt-1  & Pt-2 ) and PET considering one-day lag (PETt-1 ), were selected, as they have a higher frequency of rank assignment below 3. The number of instances each selected predictor appeared within rank three was more than or equal to 50 % of the total number of times it appeared. Table S5  shows the significance of the time of concentration in streamflow generation to rainfall and potential evapotranspiration predictors considering the lag episodes that two-day lag rainfall (Pt-1  & Pt-2 ) and one-day lag PET (PETt-1 ) was more effective than considering the rainfall and PET without lag. Further, significant lag for streamflow was obtained to augment and enhance the prediction proficiency. PACF was computed in a Python environment importing ‘plot_pacf’ from ‘statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots’ package. As seen in  Fig. 6 , one-day lagged streamflow can enhance the prediction. Therefore, LULC classes, rainfall with two-day lags (Pt-2  & Pt-1 ), PET with one-day lag (PETt-1 ), and streamflow with one-day lag (Qt-1 ) and its flow categorization based on reference percentile were packaged to build HID-SPP  .  3.3 Streamflow prediction using RF with HID-SPP The best-performing model for streamflow prediction with HID-SPP obtained from the two-stage analysis utilized six LULC classes (built-up areas, agricultural land, dense forest, shrub forest, wasteland, waterbodies), Pt-2,  Pt-1 , PETt-1 , and Qt-1 . Subsequently, the observed daily streamflows of sixteen years (1997–2012) were used to train the RF algorithm. The RMSE, MAE, R2 , NSE, and KGE values during training of the algorithm, were found to be 3.584, 0.753, 0.973,0.972, and 0.96, respectively. The scatter plot shown in  Fig. 7 (a) depicts that the model has a higher accuracy for predicting the streamflow values less than 150 m3 /sec, while slight discrepancies exist for the values greater than 150 m3 /sec. Only a fraction of peak flows (classified as ‘extraordinary’ in Section 3.1  and Fig. 2 ) showed depreciating the model performance. This could be attributed to the existence of outliers as well as insufficient instances in the extraordinary flow regimes that deviated from the performance as compared to other flow regimes. Altogether, the performance suggests overall superior accuracy of the model developed using RF. The trained model named “stRFlow ” was then tested (hold-out set) using the daily streamflow dataset of 4 years (2013–2016) with HID-SPP predictors. Results obtained for RMSE, MAE, R2 , NSE, and KGE while testing were found to be 10.50, 2.82, 0.855, 0.851, and 0.92 respectively. The scatter plot presented in Fig. 7 (b) suggests that the model performed well in all categories, but there exists feeble overprediction and underprediction in the extraordinary flow category (above 98th reference percentile) of instances below and above 150 m3 /sec due to a lack of cases sufficient for training. It is evident from the scatter plots of the training and testing of “stRFlow ” that the streamflow prediction model could produce reliably accurate streamflow prediction with a pertinent predictor dataset. The “stRFlow ” was trained and tested using a dataset with a wide range of inherent variability in predictors, which supports its generalizable application in daily stochastic streamflow prediction.   4 Discussion The ML algorithm RF favors the applicability to grasp the most pertaining input variables for the prediction model over other algorithms. Nevertheless, the performance of the REPTree model, which was the second-best algorithm, was also commendable in Stage 1. This can be attributed to the building procedure, which involves employing variance reduction “Information Gain Ratio” to create balanced tree splits and recursively pruning the tree by comparing it to previously built trees. It should be noted that if REPTree were to be identified as the best ML algorithm, the method used to rate its relative performance would differ from the mean decrease impurity technique. In Stage 2, the temporal lag variable undergoes lag episode pattern recognition, which exhibits reduced noise. This was the reason for keeping the component of ML algorithm selection was deliberately chosen in stage 1, to obtain a generalizable estimate that prevents overfitting, even in the presence of noise that eliminates other underperforming ML algorithms. This pertains to the subpar performance exhibited by certain algorithms. We also emphasize an additional feature in this study, which involves including a categorization strategy for continuous significant lag flow values into the model as category flow regimes. This allows the model to learn based on the distinct runoff mechanisms associated with each flow regime. In situations apart from the one described in this article, it is possible to encounter multiple episodes of significant lag in streamflow, from an auto-correlation technique. In such cases, alternative learning techniques must be used to provide input for the categorical flow regime. Therefore, there were a quite few constraints of this two-stage framework workflow that can be integrated with alternate techniques. However, this approach can serve as a global workflow for determining the optimal number of input feature selections for model construction. This study emphasizes the need for extended evaluation with multiple feature selections from varying climatic and hydrological settings to state “stRFlow ” as a generalizable streamflow prediction model. There are several past studies have considered the lagged rainfall, lagged PET, humidity, temperature, and streamflow for making daily or monthly streamflow predictions (He et al., 2014; Adnan et al., 2019, 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Cheng et al., 2020 ). In this study, in addition to temporal lagged predictors, LULC dynamics were considered to enhance the prediction proficiency of the model. In contrast, considering only the temporal lagged predictor in this study area, the model results in training were indistinguishable— comparison based on “the Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE)”— but the model depreciates its performance in testing as shown in Figure S6 and S7 . Evaluation of enhancement to predictive model is measured considering performance indicator, KGE found to increase from 0.86 to 0.92 in the hold-out set, which is now evident that data requirement including extensive dataset considering relatively slow-changing spatial watershed characteristics (dynamics of LULC) can enhance the prediction and improve the applicability of ML-based hydrological models which is in line with the perspective of Yang et al. (2020) . However, most streamflow prediction systems’ performance progressively declined in near-future years due to uncertainty in runoff mechanism processes. Therefore, integrating LULC dynamics in the model development, as an input feature can augment to a great extent to the prediction system upto a decade without affecting its proficiency. Hence, the current version is a suitable alternative tool to cumbersome physical-based models for scientists with similar hydrological conditions in agricultural-dominated watersheds by acquiring easily available spatiotemporal satellite-based estimates of the chosen meteorological parameters in this study, subjected to uncertainities due scale gap effects in temporal predictors for larger study areas. The framework developed can be adapted globally to make streamflow prediction accurate and cost-effective.  5 Conclusions This study attempted to predict streamflow by leveraging several ML algorithms. ML techniques often encounter pitfalls where they initially perform well during training but eventually fail to produce reliable predictions in testing. Here, the authors have presented a two-stage methodological framework for selecting the optimal input variables for generalized model development to predict streamflows. The key conclusions are listed as follows:I. The ensemble training-based RF algorithm outperformed the other ML algorithms for the study region with the current set of data by consistently producing reliable goodness-of-fit metrics.  II. Optimal input variables of rainfall and PET for preceding time steps are found to be more effective for current streamflow prediction; hence Stage 2 component in the framework enables decreased noise and is found to be a significant leap for model development without overfitting.  III. Partitioning continuous streamflows of significant lag episodes into regimes of categorical runoff mechanism helps the model to train efficiently and reduce the uncertainties in the testing phase.  IV. Consequently, the hybrid wrapper-embedded technique becomes a robust tool for selecting the optimal number of input variables in the model development. The deduced pertinent predictor set for this study was HID-SPP with six LULC classes (built-up areas, agricultural land, dense forest, shrub forest, wasteland, waterbodies), Pt-2,  Pt-1 , PETt-1 , and Qt-1 .  V. Input variables with slow-changing dynamics of land use along with optimal temporal variables proved to be augmenting, and generalizing the model prediction as compared with input feature selection of temporal variables alone. This shows the model grasping the important patterns causing streamflow generation.  VI. The developed model using the RF algorithm, “stRFlow”  model trained and tested proficiently using a wide range of inherent variability in predictors, which supports its generalizable application in streamflow prediction in agricultural-dominated tropical watersheds. The current version is a suitable alternative tool to cumbersome physical-based models for scientists with similar hydrological conditions by acquiring easily available spatiotemporal satellite-based estimates of the chosen meteorological parameters in this study.    This framework could be a stepping stone in line with research, development, and near real to real-time watershed management. The future research on this two-step framework is to constrain the ensemble prediction systems at any ungauged site based on the regionalized information from the multiple region-specific watersheds. This information includes the relatively slow-changing spatial predictors based on the watershed characteristics and its response behavior towards the streamflow, which will lead to improved trade-offs between physical and ML-based models. 1 Introduction Droughts are typically classified into four categories: meteorological, agricultural, hydrological, and socioeconomic (Mishra and Singh, 2010; Wilhite and Glantz, 1987 ). Meteorological drought entails a prolonged precipitation deficit over a wide area for an extended period. Agricultural drought occurs when soil moisture deficit hampers crop and vegetation growth, driven by meteorological drought. Hydrological drought occurs when the hydrological system experiences a water shortage, usually following several months of meteorological drought, leading to unusually low streamflow in rivers and depleted water levels in lakes, reservoirs, and groundwater. The consequences of such droughts can be severe, affecting ecological systems and economic sectors across vast areas for extended periods, triggering water and energy insecurity often ranging from months to years. The impacts of drought can be far-reaching, affecting crop irrigation, waterborne transportation, hydropower generation, drinking water supply and water quality, among others (Van Loon, 2015 ). Brazil has experienced severe droughts during the first two decades of the 21st century, impacting both socioeconomic sectors and ecological systems (Anderson et al., 2018; Aragão et al., 2018; Brito et al., 2018; Coelho et al., 2016; Cuartas et al., 2022; Cunha et al., 2019, 2018; Deusdará-Leal et al., 2020; V. R. Fernandes et al., 2021; Marengo et al., 2008, 2015, 2021; Nobre et al., 2016; Tomasella et al., 2011 ). However, in the latest decade, it has faced droughts in almost all country regions (Cunha et al., 2019 ), and in the latest years, drought events have occurred concomitantly in the Southeast, Mid-West and South regions (Cuartas et al., 2022 ). One of the most impacted basins was the Paraná River Basin (Naumann et al., 2021 ; Cuartas et al., 2022 ) since it drains those three regions. This basin is the major hub for hydropower generation, with a total of 87 hydropower plants (Rafee et al., 2019 ), with a significant share originating from it; 35 % of the total hydropower generation in Brazil. According to WMO (2021) , in the last decade, the most expensive disaster recorded in South America was the drought in the Southeast region of Brazil in 2014/15, which accumulated losses of more than US$5 billion. The impacts of climate variability, along with the need for mitigation and adaptation to climate change, have led to new demands for climate services that can provide relevant information to decision-makers (Findlater et al., 2021 ). This study filled the gap of producing high-quality climate information based on an understanding of the needs and perspectives of stakeholders associated with the Brazilian hydroelectric sector, who actively participated in the design process of the new tools to be implemented. It was developed in collaboration with the Drought Information System for Southern South America (SISSA), supported by the EUROCLIMA+ program. Its goal is to assist in improving water resources management strategies, aiming to contribute to sustainability and energy security of Brazil and southern South America during future drought events. The most common information used to monitor and characterize drought events are drought indices. Most studies employ univariate indices such as the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) (McKee et al., 1993 ) being the most widely used, and recommended by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the Global Water Partnership (GWP) (2016) , Soil Moisture Deficit Index (SMDI) (Narasimhan and Srinivasan, 2005 ), Standardized Streamflow Index (SSFI) (Modarres, 2007 ), among others. However, it is essential to recognize that hydrometeorological processes are inherently multivariate in nature, resulting from the spatial-temporal interactions among various hydrological, meteorological, climatological, and anthropogenic factors (Hao and AghaKouchak, 2013; Mishra and Singh, 2011, 2010; Van Loon, 2015; Van Loon et al., 2019 ). Consequently, univariate indices may offer a limited comprehension and understanding of drought (Liu et al., 2019; Nikravesh et al., 2020; Shiau, 2006 ). Several studies have emphasized the need for a multivariate approach to analyze and model drought events accurately (Hao and AghaKouchak, 2013; Liu et al., 2019; Nikravesh et al., 2020 ). To account for the interaction between various hydrometeorological variables, several indices have been developed, including the Aridity Anomaly Index (AAI), Drought Reconnaissance Index (DRI), Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI), Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), Soil Moisture Anomaly (SMA), and Palmer Hydrological Drought Index (PHDI) (World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and Global Water Partnership (GWP), 2016 ). However, calculating these indices can be challenging due to incomplete or unavailable input data in some regions. Additionally, real-time data availability is often lacking for drought monitoring purposes. Some indices also rely on potential evapotranspiration time series, which may have uncertainties related to the estimation method. Furthermore, some indices are not suitable for long-term or multi-seasonal events. In this context, the Copula theory emerges as a valuable alternative for generating multivariate indices. While extensively used in financial and insurance sectors (Mendes and Souza, 2004 ), its application in environmental sciences is a relatively recent development (Tootoonchi et al., 2022 ). A copula is a mathematical function that combines dependent variables through their individual marginal distribution functions to construct a joint distribution function. Previous studies, such as Hao and AghaKouchak (2013)  and Nikravesh et al. (2020) , have utilized copulas to estimate two-variate indices. The first study used precipitation and soil moisture to characterize drought conditions in California and North Carolina, USA. The second study used precipitation and streamflow data to analyze drought frequency in two small basins in Iran; the Rasht (77.11 km  2    ) and Urmia (117.68 km  2     ) basins. The results of these studies demonstrated the suitability of considering at least two variables in one index for characterizing and assessing drought events effectively. Therefore, we estimated the Two-variate Standardized Index (TSI) for the Paraná River Basin by using precipitation and streamflow that are often available data, and commonly used by the hydropower sector.
