(2) Theil-Sen Median and Mann-Kendall Based on the long time-series of TWS from 1861 to 2099, we calculate the σ TWS  2    time series using a moving window, with a window-length of 30 years and a window-interval of one year. The Theil-Sen Median method is used to calculate the trend of σ TWS  2    time series and the Mann-Kendall method is used to test the significance (Mann, 1945 ). The trend (β  ) is calculated as (Burn and Hag Elnur, 2002 ),(13) β = median x j  - x i   j - i     ∀ i < j     where x i    and x j    denote values at positions i  and j  in the σ TWS  2    time series, respectively.    3 Results 3.1 Trends of interannual variability in TWS during 1861-2099 Based on the TWS data from the ISIMIP2b during 1861–2099, we calculate the time series of σ TWS  2    every 30 years using a moving window of one year. The trends of σ TWS  2    time series for different scenarios (PIC; HIST and RCP2.6; HIST and RCP6.0 scenarios) are obtained based on Theil-Sen Median and Mann-Kendall methods (Fig. 1  ). Results generally show a slight increase of σ TWS  2    in most regions in the future, with a strong increasing trend of σ TWS  2    in parts of Amazon, India, and North China Plain (Fig. 1 a-c). Under the PIC scenario, the proportion of land areas for (significant) increase and decrease of σ TWS  2    is similar, both being around (37 %) 50 %, indicating limited influences of anthropogenic activities and land use changes on future σ TWS  2    trends (Fig. 1 d). While for HIST and RCP2.6, as well as HIST and RCP6.0 scenarios, around 60 % (50 %) of the land areas are expected to have (significant) increasing trends of σ TWS  2    in the future (Fig. 1 e, f). In general, under the RCP scenarios, more land areas are projected to have increasing trends of future σ TWS  2    relative to the PIC scenario, indicating drastic future TWS variations in more areas caused by climate change.  3.2 Changes of interannual variability in TWS in historical and future periods Fig. 2   shows σ TWS  2    in historical (1976–2005) and future (2070–2099) periods under different scenarios. The spatial patterns of σ TWS  2    in historical and future periods are similar in most regions, showing high σ TWS  2    in the Amazon, India, parts of the United States and North China Plain, indicating more drastic interannual fluctuation of the TWS in these regions (Fig. 2 a-e). In addition, there is also strong interannual variability in TWS in central Asia and Europe, eastern coast of North America, parts of Africa and Australia, and most of South America in these two periods (Fig. 2 a-e). Fig. 2 f shows the probability density distribution of the σ TWS  2    for all grid cells across the global land in different periods and scenarios. The probability curves for σ TWS  2    in PIC scenario show similarities between historical and future periods, indicating little impact from anthropogenic activities and land use changes which agrees with the results of trend analysis in Section 3.1 . For the HIST, RCP2.6, and RCP6.0 scenarios, the probability curves of σ TWS  2    show clear divergence with more large σ TWS  2    values but fewer small values in future RCP2.6 and (particularly) RCP6.0 scenarios than HIST scenario. We further quantify σ TWS  2    changes under future (PIC, RCP2.6, and RCP6.0 scenarios; 2070–2099) relative to historical period (HIST scenario; 1976–2005), and analyze significance of the changes (see Section 2.2.1  in detail) (Fig. 3  a-c). Results show that strong increase of future σ TWS  2    in India, North China Plain, parts of central Africa, and southeast United States. Coversely, future σ TWS  2    is also expected to decrease in a few regions, e.g., parts of North America and Europe, south of South America, and most of Australia (especially in RCP2.6 and RCP6.0 scenarios). Fig. 3 d shows statistical results of proportion of land areas for the σ TWS  2    changes in different scenarios. Comparing the σ TWS  2    changes under different future scenarios relative to the historical peroid reveals that σ TWS  2    is projected to increase across most land areas in the future, especially with a dramatic increase of land proportion of σ TWS  2    with more than 4,000 mm2 · yr−2  from 5.21 % in the PIC to 6.61 % and 9.44 % in the RCP2.6, and RCP6.0 scenarios. The detailed proportion of land areas for future σ TWS  2    (significant) change relative to the historical period is shown in Table S2 . Result shows that from PIC to RCP2.6 and RCP6.0 scenarios, there is more proportion of land areas with significant σ TWS  2    increase, indicating a general increase of σ TWS  2    under warming. These findings underscore a general shift of the σ TWS  2    to stronger variability in more areas in the future driven by climate change.  3.3 Contribution of TWS components to interannual variability in TWS 3.3.1 Decomposition of interannual variability in TWS We use the WaterGAP2 model which contains five detailed TWS components (i.e., water stored in canopies CW , groundwater GW , soil moisture SM , surface water SW , and snow water equivalent SWE ) to decompose the σ TWS  2    into variances of these components and their covariances (i.e., σ CW  2   , σ GW  2   , σ SM  2   , σ SW  2   , σ SWE  2   , and T Cov    ) (Eq. 2). Variabilities of TWS components for different scenarios in historical and future periods are shown in Figs. S2-S3 . In general, the interannual variability (IAV) of CW  (σ CW  2   ) is small in both historical and future periods  (Figs. S2 a and S3a-c), while GW  has strong interannual variability (σ GW  2   ) in the Amazon region and Southern Asia (Figs. S2 b and S3d-f). The regions with strong interannual variability in SM  (σ SM  2   ) are concentrated in parts of the United States, South America, and northern Europe (Figs. S2 c and S3g-i). The SW  has strong interannual variability (σ SW  2   ) in northern North America (Figs. S2 d and S3j-l), while the large IAV of SWE  (σ SWE  2   ) is mainly located at high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere (Figs. S2 e and S3m-o). In addition, the covariance component Tcov   is also large in some regions, e.g., South and North America, and Southeast Asia (Figs. S2 f and S3p-r). Contribution (Cx   in Eq. 4) of each TWS component to the σ TWS  2    in historical period (HIST scenario; 1976–2005) is shown in Fig. 4  , and in future period (PIC, RCP2.6, and RCP6.0 scenarios; 2070–2099) are shown in Fig. S4 . The Cx   for each TWS component has similar spatial patterns for different scenarios in both historical and future periods in most regions. Specifically, large contribution from σ GW  2    to the σ TWS  2    (CGW  ) is generally located in the regions between latitudes of 30°S ∼ 30°N, especially in India, northern Africa, and parts of the North China Plain, with very few contribution from σ CW  2    (CCW  ) (Fig. 4 a, b). The σ SM  2    shows strong contribution (CSM  ) to σ TWS  2    in western United States and Europe (Fig. 4 c). While the σ SW  2    has strong influence (CSW  ) on σ TWS  2    in Canada, parts of northern Africa and West Siberian Plain (Fig. 4 d). At high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere, the σ SWE  2    shows strong influence (CSWE  ) on σ TWS  2   , especially northwest North America, parts of Tibetan Plateau, and the northern edge of Asia (Fig. 4 e). Additionally, the covariance (Tcov  ) generally has a positive contribution to σ TWS  2    in most regions over land (Fig. 4 f). We further compare changes in contribution from each TWS component to σ TWS  2    in future scenarios (PIC, RCP2.6 and RCP6.0; 2070-2099) relative to the historical period (HIST; 1976-2005). This comparison is based on the difference in contribution of each TWS component to σ TWS  2    between future and historical periods, represented as ΔCx   in Figs. 5–6   . Contribution change of σ CW  2    to σ TWS  2    (ΔCCW  ) is very small, with ΔCCW   less than 0.05 % in most regions (Fig. 5 a). In general, the σ GW  2    and σ SW  2    contribute more to σ TWS  2    under future warming, with positive ΔCGW   and ΔCSW   in most land areas (Fig. 5 b, d). While for σ SWE  2    in most regions, its contribution to σ TWS  2    shows a decrease in future scenarios, indicating a shift in the influence of σ SWE  2    on σ TWS  2    to other components (Fig. 5 e). For example, dominance of σ SWE  2    on σ TWS  2    in western United States is generally transformed to σ SM  2   , while in the Tibetan Plateau and Western Siberian Plain regions, the dominance of σ SWE  2    is mainly transformed to σ SW  2    (Fig. 6 ). Moreover, the contribution of σ GW  2    to σ TWS  2    is expected to increase in most of Europe, especially under RCP6.0 scenario (Fig. 6 f). In terms of σ SM  2    and Tcov  , there are limited changes in their contribution to σ TWS  2    in the future relative to historical period (Fig. 5 c, f). We further demonstrate spatial pattern of major TWS components influencing the σ TWS  2    in historical and future periods under various scenarios (Fig. S5 ). The primary influencing components on the σ TWS  2    show similar global patterns under four scenarios but differ in some regions, for instance, from PIC to RCP2.6 and RCP6.0 scenarios, interannual variability in TWS is affected by σ SWE  2    (σ SW  2   ) in fewer (more) areas of the Tibetan Plateau, while σ TWS  2    in the western United States is found affected by σ SM  2    in more areas, which is consistent with results in Fig. 6 .  3.3.2 Attribution of changes in interannual variability of TWS Fig. 7   shows that the changes in interannual variability (IAV) of TWS components (Δ σ SW  2    , Δ σ CW  2    , Δ σ GW  2    , Δ σ SWE  2    , Δ σ SM  2     and Δ T cov    , Eq. 5) using the WaterGAP2 model datasets under future (PIC, RCP2.6 and RCP6.0 scenarios; 2070–2099) relative to the historical period (HIST scenario; 1976–2005). There is little change of σ CW  2    in the future compared with other components (Fig. 7 a-c). The σ GW  2    shows a strong increase in India and a few parts of North America (Fig. 7 d-f). The σ SM  2    generally decreases over land, particularly in parts of Europe (Fig. 7  g-i). Changes in σ SW  2    are strong in most regions with prominent decreases in Canada, and most of Asia and Europe (Fig. 7 j-l). The σ SWE  2    shows a decrease in most regions especially at high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere (Fig. 7 m-o). Contribution (E Δ x   in Eq. 8) of changes in IAV of TWS components (Δ σ CW  2    , Δ σ GW  2    , Δ σ SM  2    , Δ σ SW  2    , Δ σ SWE  2    , and Δ T cov    ) to Δ σ TWS  2     in different scenarios are explored, with the σ TWS  2    increasing and decreasing areas separately shown in Figs. 8–9   . In general, the Δ σ CW  2     has minimal impact on Δ σ TWS  2     (E Δ CW  ; Figs. 8 a-c and 9a-c). The Δ σ GW  2     contributes more to the σ TWS  2    increase than the decrease, with high positive Δ σ GW  2     (E Δ GW   > 50 %) in India, Middle East and northern Africa (Figs. 8 d-f and 9d-f). The Δ σ SM  2     makes large contribution to σ TWS  2    decrease in parts of Europe (E Δ SM  ; Fig. 9  g-i), while the Δ σ SW  2     contributes notably to the σ TWS  2    decrease in Canada (E Δ SW  ; Fig. 9 j-l). The Δ σ SWE  2     generally shows influence on Δ σ TWS  2     at high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere (E Δ SWE  ; Figs. 8  m-o and 9 m-o), with a strong contribution to the σ TWS  2    increase at the northern edge of Asia (E Δ SWE   > 75 %). The probability distribution of contribution for the IAV changes in TWS components to Δ σ TWS  2     across the global land and the dominant components leading to Δ σ TWS  2     in different scenarios are summarized in Figs. S6-S7 , which generally show more positive contribution of TWS components to Δ σ TWS  2    . Results of dominant components also agree with those in Figs. 8–9 , e.g., future σ TWS  2    increase in northern Africa is mainly due to variations in σ GW 2    and σ SM 2   , while the dramatic σ TWS  2    increase in India is primarily from variation in σ GW 2    (Fig. S6 d-f).    4 Discussion Though various studies have explored the historical mean, trend and seasonal cycle of TWS (Shen et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022a ), in this study, we focus on the long-term interannual variability in TWS (σ TWS  2   ). We find that the σ TWS  2    is expected to intensify in most regions in the future, especially in parts of Amazon, India and North China Plain, driven primarily by climate change rather than anthropogenic activities and land use changes. This finding extends previous studies showing a close relationship between TWS variation and global warming, e.g., Humphrey et al. (2018)  and Pokhrel et al. (2021) . These results suggest a potentially more unstable state of available terrestrial water resources in the future, with an increased risk of water shortages and floods in more regions. Though studies based on observations have highlighted strong impacts of anthropogenic activities on short-term variation of regional TWS (An et al., 2021 ), the results of this study reveal the primary influence of climate change on long-term variability in TWS. From a hydrologic cycle perspective, these long-term variability of TWS may result from dramatic global and regional changes in water cycle components, e.g., precipitation, evapotranspiration, and runoff, driven by global warming (Wang et al., 2022b; Zhang et al., 2019 ). Several studies have tried to divide TWS into two different components, i.e., soil water and snow water equivalent, using datasets from Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (e.g. Jensen et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2015 ). In this study, by decomposing the σ TWS  2    into five TWS components (i.e., canopy water, groundwater, soil moisture, surface water, and snow water equivalent) based on the variance decomposition method using the ISIMIP2b dataset, we find that the interannual variability of groundwater (σ GW  2   ) is an important component of the σ TWS  2    in some regions, such as India, which agrees with previous studies showing impact of groundwater depletion on the TWS in populous and arid regions (Chen et al., 2014 ). Moreover, we find that σ GW  2    in the North China Plain strongly influences σ TWS  2   . Previous studies have indicated gradual exhaustion of groundwater due to irrigation activities in the North China Plain (Chen, 2010 ), which could result in strong variability of the TWS in these regions. The interannual variability of surface water (σ SW  2   ) dominates σ TWS  2    in some regions, such as Canada, parts of northern Africa and West Siberian Plain. Recent studies have shown a rapid decline of surface water in Canada and attributed to the changes in lake level and area (Woolway et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2022 ), which likely contributes to TWS fluctuation. Notably, our findings suggest that dominance of σ SW  2    will strengthen further in the future with the intensification of climate change in the West Siberian Plain. The interannual variability of snow water equivalent (σ SWE  2   ) is found as the primary component of σ TWS  2    at high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere, especially in western North America and Tibetan Plateau. That is supportive of conclusions clarifying importance of snow and ice for future TWS change at high latitudes using model simulations (Li et al., 2023 ). In this study, we further investigated changes of σ SWE  2    contributing to the σ TWS  2    under climate change. By comparison of contribution from the interannual variability of TWS components to the σ TWS  2    in historical and future periods, result shows that contribution of σ SWE  2    (σ SM  2    and σ SW  2   ) on σ TWS  2    will decrease (increase) in more land areas under warming. It means that impact of σ SWE  2    on TWS variability will transform gradually to other components in the future, with weakened (strengthened) impacts from σ SWE  2    (other components). That may be caused by less regional snowfall (shifted precipitation phases with more water in liquid instead of solid form) and increased snowmelt under warming, making solid water storage (SWE ) change to liquid water (SM  and SW ) (Ombadi et al., 2023; Rhoades et al., 2022 ). Tao et al. (2020)  have also identified strong correlation between TWS variation and temperature change in the subarctic region. The above results imply importance of process and mechanism of water phase shift (e.g., precipitation phase shifting and snow-melting) on the σ TWS  2    under climate change. The important role of liquid water in TWS is expected to change in snowpack areas of the Northern Hemisphere (Getirana et al., 2017; Trautmann et al., 2018 ). With higher frequency of extremely high temperature under global warming (Qin et al., 2023 ), we presume that future TWS could be more influenced by liquid rather than solid water in some specific areas with snowpack. For instance, future contribution of σ SWE  2    to σ TWS  2    has been found to significantly decrease with enhanced contribution from soil moisture (σ SM  2   ) in western United States. This may be relevant to the arid environment in this region which makes melting snow and liquid water from the ground and atmosphere primarily convert to soil water (Borsa et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019 ). Moreover, the dominance of σ SWE  2    on σ TWS  2    in the Tibetan Plateau is projected to transform into surface water (σ SW  2   ) in the future. Glacier depletion by melting is generally considered to be the main cause of the dramatic changes in TWS, with expansion of lakes and reservoirs also showing strong impacts in this region (Matsuo and Heki, 2010; Li et al., 2022 ). This transformation in the form of TWS could severely affect the availability of water downstream for snowmelt irrigation as well as raise the risk of glacier avalanches (Biemans et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2019 ). Of course, limited available hydrologic modeling data in this study may lead to uncertainties of the results, and we expect more hydrological model simulations of detailed TWS components to provide support for attribution of the σ TWS  2    and its variations in the future. The findings of this study offer practical insights that could benefit hydrological disaster prevention and water resources management in several ways. For instance, with a generally increasing variability of TWS in the future, improvement of flood control and drought relief standards in rivers and reservoirs seems necessary to mitigate impacts of more risky hydrological disasters. Furthermore, divergent influences of the TWS components on TWS variability and its change in the future also have important implications for the formulation and implementation of water resources management strategies. It suggests that tailored strategies will be necessary to address potential water crisis in various regions under changing environmental conditions. For example, in regions where dramatic TWS changes are mainly caused by groundwater and surface water (e.g., the Northern China Plain and Canada), it is essential to raise public awareness about the over-exploitation of water resources (Shumilova et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2021 ). In regions with high impacts of snow water equivalent (e.g., the Tibetan Plateau), more focus is suggested to put on impacts of water supply and hydrological risks in downstream areas, which are relevant to lake expansion and alpine snowmelt triggered by drastic water phase shifts from upstream under warming (Li et al., 2022 ).  5 Conclusions In this study, we adopt hydrological simulations to investigate the interannual variability of TWS (σ TWS  2   ), focusing on its long-term trends, changes between historical (HIST; 1976–2005) and future (PIC, RCP2.6, RCP6.0; 2070–2099) periods and attribution to interannual variability of TWS components. Results show that σ TWS  2    is projected to increase in most land areas in the future (RCP2.6 and RCP6.0) compared to historical period, especially in parts of Amazon, India, and North China Plain. By comparing the historical and future σ TWS  2    in different scenarios, it is shown that σ TWS  2    changes (Δ σ TWS  2    ) are mainly influenced by climate change with more proportion of land areas having dramatic σ TWS  2    increase under warming. For instance, the proportion of land areas with future σ TWS  2    increase of more than 4,000 mm2 · yr−2  from 5.21 % in the PIC to 6.61 % and 9.44 % in the RCP2.6, and RCP6.0 scenarios respectively. The σ TWS  2    and its future changes are shown dominated by divergent TWS components in different regions. Influence of the σ SWE  2    on σ TWS  2    in the future is shown to be weakened, while impacts from some other components (e.g., surface water and groundwater) are shown to be strengthened. For instance, in the Tibetan Plateau region and western United States, impact of future σ SW  2    and σ SM  2    on σ TWS  2    is shown to be more prominent with a decreasing influence of σ SWE  2   . Moreover, changes of future σ TWS  2    (Δ σ TWS  2    ) are shown influenced by changes in interannual variability for divergent TWS components in different regions. For instance, increases of future σ TWS  2    in India and northern Africa are strongly affected by Δ σ GW  2    , while decreases of future σ TWS  2    in parts of Canada are primarily influenced by Δ σ SW  2    . The findings of this study suggest stronger interannual fluctuation of future TWS due to climate change with higher risks of water storage availability faced by most land areas in the future and clarify different contribution of each TWS component, which is helpful to rational utilization of water resources as well as understanding of hydrological extremes.
1 Introduction Over 50 % of the world’s population lives in urban areas, and this proportion will increase to 68 % by 2050 (UN, 2019 ). Along with climate change and the increase in impervious surfaces, urbanization has significantly altered surface physical characteristics and the natural water cycle, increased the frequency of urban flooding, and decreased the water quality (Chen et al., 2022; Ferrer et al., 2018; Schneider, 1975; Yang et al., 2021a ). Globally, the total urban area exposed to flooding continues to increase, particularly in developing countries (Berndtsson et al., 2019; Cao et al., 2022; Jongman, 2018 ). According to the China Floods and Droughts Disasters Bullet in 2019, an average of 158 cities in China experienced flood disasters between 2008 and 2018, resulting in serious economic losses and casualties. To tackle urban flooding and related water management issues, the construction of Sponge City was formally put forward in 2013 in China, which aims to achieve better stormwater management and control through gray and green facilities (Chan et al., 2018; Xia et al., 2017 ). Conventional stormwater measures, which prioritize flood mitigation and shield cities from gray infrastructure such as storm sewers, pipes and retention basins, cannot manage the increase in flow and ensure system resilience due to the impact of climate change (Chen et al., 2021; Depietri and McPhearson, 2017; Valipour et al., 2020 ). In contrast, green infrastructures that mimic the hydrological processes of a natural watershed can reduce the risk of floods and water deterioration at the source (Eakin et al., 2022; Li et al., 2020 ). Common green infrastructures, such as permeable roads, rain gardens, green roofs, and constructed wetlands, are applied individually or in groups at the urban scale (Arthur and Hack, 2022; Chatzimentor et al., 2020; Lourdes et al., 2022 ). Green infrastructure can significantly reduce flood damage and improve the storage capacity and water quality (Hamel and Tan, 2022; Lee et al., 2021; Li et al., 2020; Masterson et al., 2019 ). Moreover, the low cost and ease of renovation and upgrading of green infrastructures have attracted increasing attention (Heidari et al., 2023 ). A cost-combined life cycle assessment indicated that the coupled system yielded higher environmental benefits during the construction phase (Xu et al., 2021 ). The combination of gray and green infrastructure could improve urban resilience in stormwater management (Li et al., 2023; Staddon et al., 2018; Tansar et al., 2023 ). Field studies, rational methods and models such as the Storm Water Management Model (SWMM) (Cipolla et al., 2016; Hamouz and Muthanna, 2019 ), MIKE Urban (Zölch et al., 2017 ), and InfoWorks ICM (Fan et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2023 ) have commonly been employed for designing gray–green infrastructure and obtaining optimal solutions of their combinations (Duarte Lopes and Barbosa Lima da Silva, 2021; Wang et al., 2022 ). The optimization layout of gray and green infrastructures is influenced by multiple factors. Fan et al. (2022)  used hydraulic and water quality models to analyze the hydrological and pollution reduction effects of complex factors on outfalls and storage. They found that the location of green infrastructure installation is a key factor affecting the reduction in overflow runoff and pollution. The spatial distribution of different green infrastructure will affect the flow distribution into the pipeline network nodes, thereby changing the spatiotemporal conditions of water inflow (Hung et al., 2020; Torres et al., 2021 ). In addition, rainfall patterns and connection modes of gray–green system have received increasing attention, especially for certain types of rainfall events (Han et al., 2022; Shojaeizadeh et al., 2021 ). The confluence connection mode between green infrastructure and pipeline network affects the process curve of rainwater runoff and pollutant load, leading to different performance of urban drainage systems (Zeng et al., 2019 ). Therefore, design and optimization of gray-green system based solely on individual factors is insufficient for effectively addressing the complex issues of stormwater runoff and pollution (Yang et al., 2021b ). The synergistic effects of various factors on optimized strategies involving gray–green system for improving stormwater management should be examined further. Optimizing the layout of gray-green system considering location and confluence connection is of great significance to building a more efficient urban stormwater management system. Resilience has grown exponentially since Holling first introduced this concept in 1973 as part of ecosystem research (Holling, 1973; Joyce et al., 2017 ). In particular, in regard to drainage infrastructures, resilience is generally used to characterize the ability of such a system to absorb and recover from disturbances, such as increased flooding and water deterioration associated with climate change and rapid urbanization (Akter et al., 2021; Dong et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2020 ). Reasonable and comprehensive resilience indicators are needed for different scenarios to depict the functional status and optimally design gray–green infrastructures. The peak flow, runoff coefficient, overflow, and runoff reduction have typically been considered in previous studies (Palermo et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2023 ). Joyce et al. (2017)  developed a multiscale modeling platform and used peak inflow reduction as a quantitative resilience indicator to assess gray–green drainage resilience in response to coastal flood hazards for 2030. The results confirmed that LID can offer increased resilience via peak outflow reduction. In addition, Tansar et al. (2023)  used resilience, reliability, and sustainability as urban drainage system performance indicators and confirmed that green infrastructure shows better than gray infrastructure. Wang et al. (2019)  defined a resilience metric as the ratio of the number of unflooded grid cells to the total grid cell number in an urban drainage catchment to assess urban flood resilience. Engineering, environmental, social, and economic aspects were also considered in a resilience-driven evaluation model to provide optimized solutions for urban planning (McClymont et al., 2020 ). Resilience assessment has been proven to help develop effective adaptation strategies to enhance the resilience of urban stormwater management. However, there are still research gaps in the reasonable and integrated selection of resilience indicators, especially when considering the management in both water quality and water quantity. The resilience value not only indicates the stormwater management capabilities of gray-green system, but also reflects the severity of a certain rainfall event. Therefore, further exploration is also needed on how to assess the risk of rainfall events based on resilience values. Regarding the abovementioned research limitations, in this study, we propose an integrated framework based on the resilience index. Four sub-indicators, including reliability, bearing capacity, recovery speed and recovery capacity, are considered in the evaluation framework to reflect the water quality and quantity management capability of the system. Furthermore, a bivariate copula joint distribution function is constructed to conduct risk assessment of rainfall events based on corresponding resilience values. Scenario analysis is conducted in a typical urban catchment area, Beijing, China. The optimization layout strategies of gray-green infrastructures considering both location and confluence mode are revealed by comparing the resilience values and risk assessment results under different rainfall events. This study seeks to answer two questions:1) how does the resilience of gray–green systems differ when both water quality and quantity issues are considered?  2) what layout strategy of gray–green infrastructures could contribute to the resilience of urban stormwater management?    This study can provide evidence to support decision-making for sustainable urban stormwater management, particularly in an era of climate change and rapid urbanization.  2 Methodology 2.1 Study area The Future Science City located in northern Beijing, China, covers an area of approximately 4.6 km2  and includes roofs, roads (including pavements, asphalt roads and intracommunity roads), and green spaces (such as green belts and other green land). The average temperature ranges from 11-13 °C, and annual rainfall ranges from 500-600 mm, 80 % of which falls between June and August. As shown in Fig. 1  , the catchment area encompasses a separate sewage system that includes 791 junctions and 5 outfalls. A total of eight rainfall events—three light, two moderate, and three heavy rain events—were recorded in June and July 2021. Rainfall data were obtained from a WatchDog 2000 series weather station. An automatic logging flow meter (FL900, HACH, USA) was installed to record the continuous runoff flow during each rainfall event at 5-min intervals. Water quality samples were collected manually using 2-L plastic bottles at intervals of 5–30 min. The spectrophotometric salicylic acid method, chromate method, and gravimetric method were used to analyze the ammonia nitrogen (NH3 -N), total phosphorus (TP), chemical oxygen demand (COD) and suspended solids (SSs), respectively. Hourly rainfall data from 2010 to 2019 were collected from the National Basic Meteorological Station-Beijing Southern Suburb Observatory (54511). In addition to the return period, considering the differences in multiple rainfall events, a total of 631 rainfall events were extracted (the interval between two rainfall events should be greater than 10 h) and used in the simulations, of which 608 rainfall events exceeded 0.1 mm (Hung et al., 2020 ). As shown in Fig. S1 , rainfall variables, including annual rainfall, average rainfall per occurrence, number of annual rainfall fields, typical dry days at the early stages, average rainfall duration per occurrence, and average rainfall intensity per occurrence, were all subjected to autocorrelation analysis. The changes in these variables over the past decade are shown in Fig. S2 . The results of quantitative trend analysis of these variables using the Mann–Kendall nonparametric trend test are listed in Table S1 .  2.2 Design and setup of the comprehensive assessment method Resilience has been widely used to evaluate the stormwater control capability of gray–green systems (Andersson et al., 2022; Fu et al., 2021; Reckner and Tien, 2023; Zuniga-Teran et al., 2020 ). In this study, an integrated resilience assessment method for assessing the capability and effectiveness of gray–green infrastructures for stormwater management is proposed, as shown in Fig. 2  . The reliability, bearing capacity, recovery speed and recovery capacity are considered to construct a resilience index. The curve of event mean concentrations (EMCs) was used to characterize the water quality management capability. According to the Beijing municipal standard (Integrated discharge standard of water pollutants; DB 11/307-2013), the Class B emission limit value discharged into surface water bodies is adopted as the standard line to determine whether the concentration exhibited exceedance. The COD, TP, SS and NH3 -N limits are 30 mg/L, 0.3 mg/L, 10 mg/L and 1.5 mg/L, respectively. Regarding the water quantity curve, the runoff control resilience was calculated based on the runoff discharge curve. The resilience of waterlogging control was calculated based on the waterlogging area curve. The real-time pollutant concentration curve and runoff curve were obtained based on the SWMM simulation results, and the real-time waterlogging area was obtained based on the two-dimensional simulation results of InfoWorks ICM. The hazard degree and probability are characterized by the overall resilience values and the return period of rainfall events, respectively. The resilience index is designed considering water quantity control (runoff and waterlogging) and water quality control (COD, SS TP, and NH3 -N levels). The average resilience value of the four pollutants is regarded as the comprehensive water quality control resilience value. The SWMM coupled with the ICM model aims to simulate runoff processes, water quality changes, and waterlogging processes during rainfall events. A copula joint probability distribution function is constructed, with rainfall and rainfall duration as risk distribution variables of the water quantity, and the antecedent dry days and rainfall intensity as risk distribution variables of the water quality. The risk level is divided by the resilience value, and the return period is calculated based on the joint probability distribution function. Resilience is characterized by four sub indicators: reliability, loading capacity, recovery speed, and recovery capacity. The definitions are given below.• Reliability  (R1  ) is the capacity of gray–green system to maintain a normal performance when faced with rainfall disturbances;  • Loading capacity  (R2  ) is the capacity of gray–green system to reduce damage after rainfall disturbances and is expressed in terms of the maximum waterlogging area, peak runoff, and maximum pollution load;  • Recovery speed  (R3  ) is the capacity of gray–green system to recover to a normal state after a disturbance, as reflected by the rate of reduction in the waterlogging area, absorption of total rainwater, and reduction in the pollutant concentration;  • Recovery capacity  (R4  ) is the capacity of gray–green system to recover to a state free from the influence of rain. The value is set to 1 to indicate that runoff and pollution cease following the end of rainfall.    All the indicators are calculated, as provided in Table 1  . It should be noted that the preset weight of each sub indicator (i1   ∼ i4  ) in this study is 0.25. In actual urban stormwater management situation, the weight of each indicator needs to be adjusted by the manager according to the objectives and actual situation in a reasonable manner.  2.3 Risk assessment method based on Copula-based joint distribution function In this study, a risk assessment method based on bivariate copula joint distribution function is constructed to identify the risk boundary and to characterize the response of gray–green systems to different rainfall events. Firstly, rainfall events are classified into risk-free, low-risk, and high-risk categories based on resilience values obtained under specific scenarios. Secondly, the rainfall events on the risk-free boundary and high-low risk boundary are identified risk boundary events and fitted. The characteristic values of risk boundary events (rainfall duration, precipitation, antecedent dry days and rainfall intensity) are then used to build bivariate copula joint distribution functions. In order to quantify the risk boundaries of the system in stormwater risk control under a certain scenario, the return period (RP ) is defined and calculated based on the obtained bivariate copula joint distribution function. The RP  under a certain scenario represents the time interval between repeated occurrences of risk boundary events. The larger the RP  is, the greater the ability of gray–green system to mitigate stormwater risk. Detailed processes are described as follows. The function construction process involves determining, fitting and optimizing random variables and their marginal distributions, and deriving a joint probability distribution. Bivariate copula functions of 1) the water quantity vs. rainfall duration and precipitation and 2) the water quality vs. antecedent dry days and rainfall intensity were constructed. According to the skewness and kurtosis of variables including rainfall duration, precipitation, antecedent dry days and rainfall intensity as described in Table S2 , the tail of the edge distribution of each variable is obviously asymmetric. Therefore, the Archimedean copula function is chosen for fitting, which provides numerous and sophisticated functions for analyzing the relationships between the individual elements of a hydrological cycle (Bačová Mitková et al., 2023; Bezak et al., 2016 ). The commonly used Archimedean Copula functions include Gumbel Copula, Clayton Copula, and Frank Copula (Nelsen, 2006 ). The corresponding functions are as follows:(1) C  Gu   u , υ ; θ    = e x p - - l n u    θ  + - l n υ    θ     1 θ      , θ ∈ 1 , ∞        (2) C  cl   u , υ ; θ    = m a x u  θ  + υ  θ  - 1    1 θ      , θ ∈ 0 , ∞        (3) C  F r u , υ ; θ      = - 1 θ  l n 1 + e x p - θ u    - 1   e x p - θ υ    - 1     e x p - θ    - 1        , θ ≠ 0     where u  and v  denote the two-variable marginal distribution functions, and θ  is a dimensionless parameter of copula functions. Using Euclidean distance as the index, the fitting goodness of the above three Archimedean Copula functions are compared. According to the fitting results in Table S3 , the Clayton copula (Eq. (2) ) with the smallest square Euclidean distance (the average distance between the two groups of variables is 0.17 and 0.07) is selected in this study. Based on the obtained bivariate joint distribution function, the probability P  of a certain rainfall event exceeding the two parameters (ADD  and INT ; or PRE  and DUR ) and RP  of the risk boundary rainfall events can be calculated as follows:(4) P A D D , I N T    = 1 - C  Cl   ( u , v ; θ )  ADD + I N T       (5) P P R E , D U R    = 1 - C  Cl   ( u , v ; θ )  PRE + D U R       (6) RP = 1 / P     where ADD  denotes the antecedent dry days, INT  is the rainfall intensity, PRE  is the precipitation, and DUR  is the rainfall duration.  2.4 Integration and setup of the SWMM-ICM model The SWMM developed by the US Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) is widely used in the implementation of urban low impact development (LID) measures due to its excellent simulation performance (Bai et al., 2018; Lisenbee et al., 2022; Rossman, 2010 ). In this study, the SWMM (2017 version) was used to calculate surface runoff and nonpoint source pollution loads during rainstorm events and to simulate and optimize rainwater management measures. The catchment area was delineated according to the digital elevation model (DEM) through ArcGIS 10.2 software, and the Thiessen polygon function was used to delineate the pipe network layer. To better characterize the impact of the underlying surface on the hydrological path, the sub watershed was further delineated by referring to the land use and digital image map layers. As shown in Fig. 1 (a), a total of 4155 sub watersheds representing homogeneous sub-watersheds (individual land uses) were obtained, 1824 of which were impermeable areas. The area of these sub watersheds varied between 0.001 and 10.3 ha. To calibrate the SWMM, the sensitivity-based radio tuning calibration (SRTC) tool was used to determine the parameter sensitivity according to Eqs. (7) and (8) .(7) V low   = V initial   1 + V f        (8) V high   = V initial   × 1 + V f          where V initial      is the initial value of the calibrated parameter, V f     is the uncertainty value, and V low      and V high      are the lower and upper limits of the calibrated parameter, respectively. The initial values of the calibrated parameters were set with reference to relevant studies (Hou et al., 2020; Lopes and da Silva, 2021; Zhang and Chui, 2020 ). The Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) and Pearson correlation coefficient (R2 ) were used to assess the goodness of fit. In this study, the R2  and NSE values during calibration and validation were above 0.87 and 0.74, respectively, indicating acceptable results. Fig. 3   shows the simulation and observation hydrological results for the different rainfall events. The information of the 8 monitored rainfall events is provided in Table S4 . The calibration and validation results of pollutants are provided in Table S5 . The observation and simulation processes of pollutants for the different rainfall events are provided in Figs. S4–S7 . The calibration results of the main parameters of the SWMM are provided in Table S6 . Although the SWMM can extract flood processes from overflow inspection wells, it cannot directly calculate the two-dimensional flooding process of surface water. The use of the SWMM alone does not allow for the characterization of surface waterlogging or water accumulation due to surface ponding. Therefore, the two-dimensional (2D) simulation module of InfoWorks ICM was utilized to simulate the waterlogging risk (Liu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2022 ). High-precision DEM data are needed to create ground TIN models for 2D waterlogging modeling. Therefore, based on the DEM of the inspection wells in the study area, the required DEM data were obtained using the inverse distance weight interpolation (IDW) method in ArcGIS. A 2D simulation polygon within the scope of the TIN was created, and the building area was defined as a blank area to prevent runoff from flowing in. The polygons were gridded and subjected to 2D calculation to obtain a waterlogging area versus time curve. The rainfall amount corresponding to the design standards of the pipeline network was selected, and the comprehensive resilience index of waterlogging control was calculated. The 631 rainfall events were employed for simulation, and comprehensive indicators of the water quantity and water quality control were calculated. The average value of all the indicators was used to assess the joint risk.  2.5 Scenario design Previous research has indicated that the location of green infrastructure is a key factor affecting the gray–green system (Ncube and Arthur, 2021 ). In this study, the locations of gray and green facilities constitute the basis for scenario setting. Considering the effect of location on the gray–green system, for each node, the corresponding rainwater dissipation time is calculated (the time required for rainwater to flow from the node to the outlet, which is used to characterize the position of the node in the pipe network). The green infrastructures where runoff flows into the node correspond to this location parameter. The location attribute division results of the inspection wells and the potential renovation catchment area are shown in Fig. 1 (b). Under the specific scenarios, the study area was first divided into upstream, middle, and downstream sections according to the location of the rainwater well nodes. Based on the planning documents of the study area, green roofs, permeable pavement and bioretention cells were selected for optimizing the original roofs, road and pavement, and bare land, respectively. The confluence path was divided into direct and indirect impervious surface confluence paths. In the direct mode, runoff flows directly into the pipe network. In the indirect mode, runoff flows from the impermeable surface through the permeable surface before flowing into the pipe network. Based on the above rules, the details of the available area for reconstructing each land type are provided in the Tables S7 and S8 , and Fig. S8 . All kinds of green infrastructures were set to provide the same renovation area to ensure comparability between all scenarios. Specifically, based on the above calculation results, the minimum area of each land type was chosen as the corresponding area of green infrastructure to calculate the renovation area ratio of the different land types under each renovation scenario. A total of eight scenarios were set, as defined in Table 2  .   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Resilience under the various gray–green system scenarios In this study, hourly data for the 631 rainfall events from 2010 to 2019 were collected and used for the simulations of the study catchment. The resilience values of water quality and water quantity under different rainfall events were calculated based on the method described in Section 2.2 . The average resilience value of 613 events is used to indicate the stormwater management capability of the gray-green system in a certain scenario. The resilience distribution of the water quality and quantity under different scenarios were shown in Fig. 4  . Compared with the baseline scenario, the water quality resilience of gray–green system after green infrastructure renovation under all the scenarios improved by 1 % to 4 %, and the water quantity resilience improved by 0.04 % to 0.3 %. Specifically, under the baseline scenario, the value of water quantity resilience in Fig. 4 (j)–(l) is 0.9279, and the corresponding values are 0.9303, 0.9289, and 0.9293 under Scenarios 3, 2 and 1, respectively. Under Scenarios 6, 5 and 4, the values of resilience are 0.9297, 0.9276, and 0.9283, respectively, while the values under Scenarios 7 and 8 are 0.9293 and 0.9284, respectively. Regarding the water quality resilience shown in Fig. 4 (a)–(f), the value is 0.7282 under the baseline scenario, with the values under Scenarios 3, 2 and 1 reaching 0.7478, 0.7586, and 0.7601, respectively. Under Scenarios 6, 5 and 4, the values are 0.7363, 0.7370, and 0.7346, respectively. The values under Scenarios 7 and 8 are 0.7605 and 0.7408, respectively. Compared with the baseline scenario which indicates the current status of the study area, the renovation of green infrastructure could improve the resilience of the system, promoting the reduction in stormwater runoff, peak flow, and pollution by increasing retention and infiltration (Chen et al., 2021; Moser and Avery, 2021; Wang et al., 2021 ). From the perspective of the extent of resilience enhancement in gray-green systems after renovation, both the current conditions of the study area and the weight of the four indicators will have an impact on the resilience value to some extent. In this case study, the area is a newly developed district with a relatively well-established gray-green infrastructure base, which has fewer issues with water risk compared with old district. The proposed resilience index integrates reliability, bearing capacity, recovery speed, and recovery capacity. Each of the four indicators was assigned a weight of 0.25 for easier to quantitatively sort. In practice, weights should be adjusted according to the preferences of decision-makers and regional characteristics. Both these factors may result in a small increase in resilience index observed in this case study. Nevertheless, the comprehensiveness of the proposed resilience index framework suggests that even these slight enhancements in resilience can still demonstrate the important role that gray-green system play in water quality control than water quantity in highly urbanized watersheds, as depicted in Fig. 4 . This is consistent with previous research findings (Reisinger et al., 2019 ). An appropriate layout of gray–green system could lead to many efforts focused on reducing pollutant export from the landscape before it enters the aquatic network. These efforts are vital for enhancing pollutant retention and the overall urban stormwater quality. The confluence mode and relative location of gray and green infrastructures are two nonnegligible factors in optimizing stormwater management. As shown in Fig. 4 (c)–(f) and (i)–(l), the catchment area adopting the direct confluence mode is a hotspot for system renovation to achieve better effects on water quality control. Under direct confluence, the resilience of water quality management ranges from 0.7478 to 0.7605, which is greater than that under indirect confluence (0.7346 to 0.7408). The relative location of gray and green infrastructures also plays a key role in risk control, as shown in Fig. 4 (a), (b), (g) and (h). In particular, for direct confluence catchments, the average renovation strategy is more effective (with a resilience of 0.7605) than other strategies for controlling water quality (with a resilience of 0.7478, 0.7586 and 0.7601, respectively). In contrast to runoff control, pollutant abatement involves building-up, washing-off, and discharging processes (Wijesiri et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2021b ). Therefore, relevant factors such as location, confluence mode, layout, hydrological pattern, and parameter settings are nonnegotiable for risk control. For runoff control, different from water quality control strategies, the direct confluence and downstream strategy is suggested for gray-green system renovation. Previous researches also confirmed that the relative location of gray-green system leads to disparate performance on water quantity and quality control. Fan et al. (2022)  used runoff control rate and pollution reduction rate as the variables to characterize the effect of LIDs practice implementation. They think that the downstream installed location is a better choice for pollution and runoff control. Zeng et al. (2019)  discussed the synergistic effects of gray-green system on the social, environmental, and technological performance. Performance indices including total amount of flooding, total amount of Combined sewer overflow and total shock amount to wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) were selected to evaluate the performance. LIDs facilities placed in the upstream or near to the WWTP are optimal solutions. It can be seen that the selection of indicators will lead to certain differences in optimization strategies suggestions, especially when considering water quality and quantity simultaneously. In highly urbanized areas, evaluating gray-green system with reasonable indicators is the key to addressing complex water issues. The resilience evaluation framework, which integrates for sub indicators including reliability, bearing capacity, recovery speed and recovery capacity, can provide a more comprehensive consideration for the system optimization. Moreover, there is a game relationship among the strategies. The weight value of sub indicators can be adjusted accordingly based on the preference of decision makers. According to the shape of the probability density, the water quantity and water quality resilience distributions exhibit a bimodal pattern, with the water quality resilience peaks ranging from 0.40 to 0.60 and from 0.70 to 0.90 and the water quantity resilience peaks ranging from 0.90 to 0.93 and from 0.97 to 1.00. The features of the rainfall events that correspond to the peak interval deserve close attention in the design process.  3.2 Risk assessment of gray–green scenarios The resilience values of 631 rainfall events obtained from Section 3.1  indicate the stormwater management capabilities of gray-green system, and also reflect the severity of a certain risk event (i.e., rainfall event). The risk categories of rainfall events were classified based on the resilience values of the water quantity and quality. The larger the return period corresponding to the risk boundary is, the greater the ability of the study area to mitigate rainfall runoff and nonpoint source pollution interference. As shown by the shape of the probability density curve in Fig. 4 , the rainfall events corresponding to the turning points should be carefully considered in the planning and design process. From a probability perspective, they represent the key rainfall events that determine the system performance and must be addressed. Fig. 4  shows that a value of approximately 0.70 is an obvious dividing point for water quality resilience. Based on this value, rainfall events are categorized into three parts in this paper. For events with a water quality resilience of 1.00, no risk of exceeding the water quality standard is defined. A resilience value between 0.70 and 1.00 is defined as these events exhibiting a low risk of exceeding water quality standards. For a resilience less than 0.70, there is a high risk of the water quality exceeding the standards during such events. Similarly, for events with a water quantity resilience of 1.00, no water quantity risk is considered under the circumstances. A resilience between 0.90 and 1.00 is considered to indicate that such events exhibit a low water quantity risk. For a resilience less than 0.90, there is a high risk for water quantity. Therefore, the risk boundary rainfall events are identified and fitted as shown in Fig. 5  . According to the fitting results as show in Table S3 , the joint distribution function can be obtained as Eq. (9)  and Eq. (10) . The corresponding RP  of risk boundary events calculated based on Eqs. (4)–(6)  is shown in Fig. 5 .(9) C  Cl   ( u , v ; θ )  ADD + I N T   = m a x [ ( u ADD    1.7998   + v INT    1.7998   - 1 )  1 / 1.7998   ]      (10) C  Cl   ( u , v ; θ )  PRE + D U R   = m a x [ ( u PRE    4.3858   + v DUR    4.3858   - 1 )  1 / 4.3858   ]      where u ADD      and u PRE      are the marginal distribution functions of the antecedent dry days and precipitation, respectively; v INT      and v DUR      are the marginal distributions of the precipitation intensity and duration, respectively; and 1.7998 and 4.3858 are the parameter values estimated by the maximum likelihood method, dimensionless. The return period of the water quality control risk boundary ranges from 1.13 years (baseline scenario) to 1.14–1.17 years, and the return period of high- and low-risk boundary events ranges from 2.10 years (baseline scenario) to 2.23–2.58 years (Fig. 5 (a)–(h)). The system risk boundary shows an outward shift, suggesting that renovation enhances the gray–green system to better manage a wider range of rainfall events. Average renovation can reduce system risks, while direct renovation shifts the high-low risk boundaries of the system more outward. Regarding the water quantity control results shown in Fig. 5 (i)–(p), the return period of high- and low-risk boundary events increased from 3.21 years (baseline scenario) to a maximum of 3.69 years. In particular, under Scenario 1, improving the risk boundary was more effective.  3.3 Implications for varying conditions Green infrastructure, including vegetation- or sustainability-based practices, provides a high infiltration rate at the early stages of rainfall to reduce runoff and improve the water quality when the antecedent condition is not saturated (Dong et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019; Suresh et al., 2023 ). With increasing rainfall, gray infrastructures, including storm sewers, pipes, and retention basins, exhibit favorable performance in terms of the rapid discharge of runoff to alleviate urban waterlogging (Zhang et al., 2020 ). In this study, key factors, including rainfall amount, duration, intensity, and antecedent dry days, were considered to investigate the ability of gray–green system to control the water quality and quantity. According to the copula-based function described in Section 2.3 , the relationships between water quality resilience and antecedent dry days, and between water quality resilience and rainfall intensity are shown in Fig. 6   displayed by brown contours. Gray–green system is more effective at controlling water quality during rainfall events when there are a small number of antecedent dry days and low rainfall intensity. The peak value and the recovery duration time are shortened as shown in Fig. S3 (a) for shorter antecedent dry days circumstances. For longer antecedent dry days circumstances, more pollutants accumulate on the surface. Subsequent rainfall prompts the rapid mobilization of these accumulated pollutants, which are then transported into nearby water bodies via surface runoff, thus exacerbating water pollution. This scenario also puts higher requirements on the capabilities of urban stormwater management system (Wang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021c ). In the case of rainfall events with a large number of antecedent dry days and rainfall intensities, compared with baseline scenario, Scenarios 1 and 7 show better capabilities of gray–green system on water quality control. According to the rainfall trends in recent years (Figs. S1 and S2 ; Table S1 ), the antecedent dry days and rainfall intensity show increasing trends, especially the antecedent dry days. Therefore, when considering improving water quality management, Gray–green system utilizing direct confluence, and the downstream or the average layout are hot spots for future system improvement. As shown in Fig. 6  displayed by the blue contours, the relationship between water quantity resilience and rainfall duration also shows a similar pattern to that of water quality resilience. For events with less rainfall and shorter durations, gray–green system yields better effects. Based on the characteristics of rainfall events over the past decade (Figs. S1 and S2 ; Table S1 ), the precipitation and duration values of each event show an increasing trend. Therefore, within the context of climate change, current gray–green system poses potential risks in controlling the water quantity in the future. According to multiple nonlinear regression analysis, improvements in direct confluence connections in terms of runoff control could lead to better responses to such events. From a water quantity control perspective, direct confluence connections should therefore be emphasized when developing gray-green system. The reasonable selection of resilience indicators is crucial for the effective evaluation of gray-green systems. In previous studies, many performance indicators such as the loss in system functionality, flood duration, runoff control rate, and outlet peak flow, have been employed for the resilience evaluation (Guptha et al., 2022; Hua et al., 2020; Mugume et al., 2015; Tansar et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2020 ). However, when it comes to assessing the control ability on water quantity and quality risks simultaneously, the previously proposed frameworks appear inadequate and needs further improvement. In this study, the four sub indicators, including reliability, bearing capacity, recovery speed and recovery capacity, provide a comprehensive perspective to evaluate the system’s resilience under climate change. The proposed framework has flexibility and adaptability in future application. If necessary, the sub indicators can be separately compared and analyzed based on the preference of decision makers.   4 Conclusions In this study, an integrated method is proposed to evaluate the resilience of gray–green systems considering both water quality and quantity issues. Optimal schemes for assessing gray–green system in the study area are explored, with a focus on two factors: confluence mode and relative location. The results demonstrate that the proposed resilience index is feasible and effective for assessing water risk management in gray–green systems. Compared to those under the baseline scenario, after green infrastructure renovation, the water quality and water quantity resilience levels improved by 1–4 % and 0.04–0.3 %, respectively. To mitigate the ever-increasing water risks under climate change, gray–green system with direct confluence modes, and average or downstream renovation strategies are hot spots for system renovation. The results can be used as implications for the sustainable management of urban gray–green system. However, it should be noted that this study only focused on the regression relationships between rainfall and gray–green systems, and qualitative recommendations for gray–green system renovation were subsequently proposed. Considering future climate extremes is essential for upgrading gray–green systems, intensive research is needed on the quantitative optimization scheme of gray–green systems to address climate change. In terms of the application of the proposed resilience evaluation, the weight value should be adjusted appropriately based on regional characteristics. The selection of resilience risk thresholds can be improved based on local evaluation criteria to systematically evaluate the joint risk of the water quantity and quality.
1 Introduction The United States (US) Federal Government in the early 19th century began construction of dams and locks on America’s rivers (both mainstems and tributaries) to facilitate ship passage throughout the dry summer and fall months (Bonnet et al., 2015 ). After initial investments in riverine navigation infrastructure (e.g., mainstem locks and dams), investments by both local and federal authorities were made in other river control infrastructure, mostly on tributaries (e.g., multi-purpose reservoir projects that provide benefits for seasonal storage, low flow augmentation, flood control, water supply and hydropower generation) (Bonnet et al., 2015 ). There was a building boom in the first half of the 20th century through the 1960s, and by 1980 America had constructed almost 80% of all the river control infrastructure in its territories as of the last available infrastructure census (73,517 in place as of 2024) (NID, 2024 ). During the same period, stream gages were added to America’s rivers to measure flow, velocity and stage; however, as shown in Fig. 1 , only approximately 65% of these (out of a total of 8882 installed as of 2023) were constructed by 1970 (USGS, 2023 ). The installation of river control infrastructure has out-paced the installation of stream gages, with important consequences for the modern focus on natural and ecologically-sustainable flow regimes. We have sparse, and in many cases non-existent, records of natural river flow patterns, which are critical inputs for water management policies aimed at ecological well-being (e.g., Kastl et al., 2022; Morrisett et al., 2023 ) and/or distributional equity (e.g., Null et al., 2021 ). Records of natural flow are also critical inputs to economic policies, such as the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES), which permits an allocation of pollutant discharge as a function of river’s assimilating capacity as well as public vulnerability and public benefit offered by the pollution-producing activity (e.g., EPA, 2018a ). Low flow statistics are similarly embedded in the National Economic Development (NED) calculation reported by the US Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) when accounting for the value of their infrastructure (Bonnet et al., 2015 ) We cannot know what function the infrastructure performs (and therefore the value it adds) without understanding the condition of the river in its absence. In response, this paper demonstrates a method to decouple natural streamflow from the impacts (additive or subtractive) of river control infrastructure on such streamflow data.  The result of the decoupling is two distinct time series: one representing the observed record of streamflows, and one representing the counter-factual, or what would have been the observed record had the water control structures not been installed (i.e., the “naturalized” flow record). The methods available for estimation of naturalized streamflow regimes range from simple to complex, and include straightforward statistical transpositions, physically-based (or conceptual) hydrologic models, and machine learning algorithms. The methods have unique advantages and limitations, as described below. 1.1 Streamflow decoupling: Observations versus naturalized flows Our interest is in a method for estimation of naturalized flows intended for general application to a broad range of global river systems. We have therefore prioritized simplicity, with minimal data requirements. As is discussed in detail in the methods section, the method presented in this paper assumes the availability of the following data: streamflow, reservoir holdouts and topography. The cooperation of the local agency responsible for reservoir operation is valuable as a source of reservoir holdout data, but not essential, as time series of reservoir holdouts can be found as published datasets (e.g., Steyaert et al., 2022 ) or estimated using reservoir storage, which is derivable from satellite data (e.g., Khandelwal et al., 2022; Hao et al., 2024 ). To account for junction locations and flow lags relevant to a large river system, we combined a water balance method with basin re-scaling, and added a parsimonious flow routing algorithm. This technique accommodates missing records in the streamflow data, and is accurate throughout the flow regime (for low flows as well as high flows). Water balance methods such as those adopted here depend only on streamflow data. Some water balance methods remove anthropogenic impacts from observed flows algebraically (e.g., Wang et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2017 ) adding a time series of known withdrawals to the time series of downstream observed flows. In the case of a complex network of dammed rivers, however, the location of each junction of altered streamflow becomes important, as flow lags accumulate downstream (e.g., Champathong et al., 2020 ). When observations of natural conditions throughout the watershed prior to construction of the dam are unavailable, one way to estimate the condition of the river in its natural, uncontrolled state is to re-scale the streamflow downstream of the control structure to the uncontrolled streamflow upstream of the control structure. This method requires the availability of a time series of streamflow data of sufficient length both upstream and downstream of the dam, and it has limitations when applied to systems with multiple control structures and large distances (river water travel times) between the upstream and downstream comparison points. The method is appropriate when considering a single control structure, and when there is reason to believe that the flow downstream of the control point prior to installation of the control was highly correlated to the river flow upstream of the control point (i.e., there are no substantial withdrawals or tributaries in between) (Wang et al., 2017 ). In the case of a river basin with a single dam, assuming a sufficient record of streamflow data and ignoring climate non-stationarity, the estimation of natural river flow might be as straightforward as separation of streamflow observations pre- and post-installation of the dam (e.g., Li et al., 2020; Talukdar and Pal, 2019; Tian et al., 2019 ). The more river control structures exist in a river basin, the more difficult it is to decipher the portion of streamflow occurring naturally, and the portion contributed by reservoirs and diversions at any downstream point. In a large river basin with multiple water control structures, such as the one adopted as a case study in the analysis presented in this paper, a method is needed for incrementally decoupling the natural streamflow from each additional control point downstream along the flow path. The method adopted in this paper is empirical. Alternatively, model-based methods build on simulations of natural flow. Hydrologic models can incorporate information on rainfall, temperature, land use, soil type, slope, and other variables, to estimate natural streamflow time series using just the natural physical phenomena, assuming the availability of at least a few years of uncontrolled streamflow data by which to calibrate the model. When human-hydrologic models are employed that account for reservoir operations, the control components can be used for calibration and then statistically removed (e.g., Mahapatra and Jha, 2022 ). Alternatively, calibration can be performed using only uncontrolled gages to directly estimate the natural flow in uncontrolled portions of the river (e.g., Lin et al., 2019 ). Hydrologic modeling requires overlapping time series of a range of variables at the same temporal and spatial resolution, and becomes complex in large basins with multiple control points (Ray et al., 2019 ). Furthermore, the cascade of uncertainties throughout the modeling chain complicates the decoupling process when using hydrologic models (Wilby and Dessai, 2010 ). Machine learning models are a data-driven (i.e., empirical) alternative to process-based hydrologic models for streamflow estimation (e.g., de Sousa et al., 2023 ). Statistical streamflow estimation methods (e.g., Santos et al., 2019 ), or physically-based estimation methods (e.g., Yang et al., 2020 ), can be combined with machine learning for improved model performance. Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, for example, are able to account for snow and other long term storage (e.g., Kratzert et al., 2018 ). The same cascade of uncertainty that complicates hydrologic model interpretations applies to machine learning approaches (Nearing et al., 2016 ). In cases in which streamflow observations are available, techniques to estimate the naturalized flow based solely on historical observations, as presented in this paper, are more direct, and less subject to complex uncertainties.  1.2 The importance of seasonal and extreme low flow The flow regime of a river describes the seasonal pattern of periodic high flows and low flows (Poff et al., 1997 ). A river’s flow regime responds to seasonal patterns in precipitation, temperature (e.g., freezing, thawing, evapotranspiration rate), and other seasonal factors. Most global rivers demonstrate seasonality in flow regime (Floriancic et al., 2021 ). The focus of this paper is low flow (seasonal and extreme), which is critical to navigation, water quality, urban water security, agricultural irrigation, and ecological well-being. For navigation passage, each river requires a minimum stage, which is a function of ship hull design, target cargo weight, and the capacity of the available water control infrastructure (especially locks). The USACE maintains a minimum river stage of 9 ft at the locks, as mandated by Congress (USACE, 2023 ). Without a sufficient store of fresh water, the number of lockages that can be performed decreases, reducing the number of ships that can traverse the river (Vinke et al., 2022 ). The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) uses low flow thresholds to calculate each contaminant’s Total Maximum Daily Load (TMDL) for critical water quality events when the available dilution is low. The US EPA applies a variety of low flow variables (differing in period and frequency), such as 1Q10, 7Q10, 1B3, 4B3, depending on the level of concern associated with the contaminant and degree of exposure risk downstream (EPA, 1991, 2018b ). The 1Q10 is the lowest one-day average flow that occurs (on average) once every 10 years, the 7Q10 is the lowest 7-day average flow occurring (on average) once every 10 years. The 1B3 (4B3) is a biologically-based 1-day (4-day) average flow event, which occurs (on average) once every 3 years. For healthy river ecosystems, “the full range of natural intra- and inter-annual variation of hydrologic regimes” is needed to sustain the native biodiversity and integrity of aquatic ecosystems (Richter et al., 1997 ). Disruption of the natural patterns (e.g., magnitude, frequency, duration, variation) by dams or other river modifications can endanger many species (Carlisle et al., 2019 ). However, dams may help avoid the problem of insufficiency of river water at extreme low flow, which reduces the habitat of aquatic organisms, and constrains their life cycle events (e.g., spawning, migration) (e.g., Huang et al., 2019; Kastl et al., 2022 ). In sum, the impact of dams on river regime and ecosystem well-being is ambiguous, though in most cases deleterious. Most anthropogenic water demand is for agricultural irrigation, but urban centers require water security for drinking, bathing, sanitation (especially toilet flushing), washing (especially clothing), and food preparation, among other uses (Gleick, 1996 ). Scarcity of river water available for agricultural irrigation can decrease food production and increase the strain on limited groundwater reserves (e.g., Marston and Konar, 2017 ), ultimately resulting in difficult-to-reverse groundwater depletion (e.g., Scanlon et al., 2012 ). The allocation of water resources, especially during scarcity, is a complex, multidimensional problem (e.g., Berger et al., 2007; Berger, 2001 ). When scarce water is directed to one problem, scarcity often exacerbates in other locations, other sectors, and other populations (e.g., van Dijk et al., 2013 ). The effects of the drought can propagate through hydrological, ecological, economic, and social cycles, e.g., forest fires, tourism losses, stress on utilities, low nutrition, and generally diminished psychological well-being (van Dijk et al., 2013 ). In American applications, streamflow data and basin information (e.g., basin area, river reach lengths) are available from the USGS. Reservoir operation datasets are in many cases also available from the institutions or agencies responsible for the dams in question (Steyaert et al., 2022 ). The methodology presented here relies only on the availability of inflow and outflow time series from each reservoir. In the case of the Ohio River used for this study, USACE had estimated naturalized flow at critical junctures (described in greater detail in the Background Motivating the Case Study section below) as the amount of water that would have passed through tributaries in the absence of USACE infrastructure. The purpose of this paper is to estimate the degree to which existing water control infrastructure alters the low flow at critical points along a river mainstem, and at basin-scale. To do so, we developed a method for routing naturalized flow estimates from reservoir locations (typically on tributaries, and not on the river mainstem), to points of concern along the river mainstem, and to the basin outlet. In order to arrive at a methodology that can be applied to other river systems, we developed a simple water balance model built on the observed flow, reservoir inflows and outflows, basin area at points of interest along the river, and estimates of the lag in between. Because the concern of this present study was the low flow, to increase the accuracy for low flow estimation while also keeping the routing model as simple as possible, we introduced a coefficient that acts as a proxy for precipitation. The method presented here can be applied to any global river basin with similar data.  1.3 Background motivating the case study The Ohio River is the largest river by long-term average flow in the United States (Brooks et al., 2018 ); the lower Mississippi is mostly Ohio River water. It is 1579 km (981 miles) long, and a direct source of drinking water for more than five million people. The Ohio River Basin covers 528,000 square kilometers (204,000 square miles), including parts of 15 states, and houses more than 25 million people (ORF, 2023; USACE, 2020 ). The Ohio River is located in a region of relatively high annual average precipitation, with heavy spring rains coinciding with large-scale snow melt. Managers of the Ohio River therefore face regular challenges related to flooding (Zhu et al., 2020 ). It is also a highly industrialized basin with chronic water contamination events (Behzadi et al., 2022 ). Ohio River velocity is a good explanatory variable for its turbidity (Rahat et al., 2023 ), and therefore contaminants of other kinds (Rügner et al., 2019 ). The USACE Great Lakes and Ohio River Division (LRD) reports to Congress each year on flood damage reductions achieved, comparing computed naturalized flow and stage with historical stream gage observations. As part of this process, USACE LRD districts (e.g., Pittsburgh, Huntington, Louisville) provide LRD Division Headquarters in Cincinnati with computed naturalized flows from each major tributary to the Ohio River mainstem. Naturalized flows are estimated algebraically (see Methodology) by each district as what would have passed each day from tributaries in their jurisdiction to the Ohio River mainstem in the absence of USACE infrastructure. The primary sources of streamflow data used for this study were: USGS historical observed daily streamflow and basin properties (area and stream reach/network); and USACE historical observed daily streamflow, reservoirs hold-outs, and estimated naturalized streamflow over a 30-year historical period,1994–2023. USACE-generated naturalized flows were not available for the Ohio River mainstem. They are calculated by USACE district offices at dam locations within their jurisdictions. The USACE district offices provide naturalized flows to the regional office at tributary “hand-off points” substantially upstream of points of interest to this study. In order to estimate the naturalized flow along the river mainstem downstream, we developed a routing model capable of accumulating tributary and mainstem flows, with appropriate time lags, to points downstream. The routing model can also be used as a basic water balance model to combine changes to the streamflow from dams upstream, so that naturalized flow can be estimated at any point in the watershed.   2 Methodology This section presents a general methodology to quantify the impact of the water control infrastructure in low flow conditions, by comparing two time series of streamflow in multiple locations: observed and naturalized. There are many factors to be considered when estimating naturalized flows (Huang and Kadir, 2016 ). USACE protocols include measuring the natural flow upstream of the structure (if available), and estimating the change in storage volume using a stage-storage relationship derived from the bathymetric survey data. USACE sets daily reservoir outflow values at each dam, which are recorded. Dams’ “hold-outs” (Q  h , ⋅    ) are defined as the difference between the flow into and the flow out of the dam at any given day. Change in storage (Δ S  t     ) is divided by the time step (Δ t   ) to convert it into the holdouts in units of flow [volume/time]. When the hold-outs, Q  h     (positive or negative), are added to the observed dam/reservoir outflow, Q  o    , the result is the naturalized flow, Q  n    , for that river reach (see Eq. (1) ). Availability of any two of these 3 variables is the requirement for the method presented in this paper. The naturalized/observed flows are then routed through points downstream.
