Deep learning (DL) models have generally demonstrated superior performance compared to other ML models in hydrology and environmental disaster research such as groundwater level (GWL) (Wei et al., 2023 ), streamflow forecasting (Fang et al., 2024 ), river flood (Hosseiny, 2021 ), and flooding forecasting (Dtissibe et al., 2024 ). DL models such as gated recurrent unit (GRU), long short-term memory (LSTM) and transformer (TR) are considered powerful algorithms because these networks can analyze historical datasets and capture complex temporal dependencies to make accurate predictions about future values (Chenjia et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2024 ). A study by Wu et al. (2023)  revealed that GRU and LSTM outperformed support vector machines and ANN in predicting hourly GWL in China. Fang et al. (2024)  stated that the TR models accurately provided excellent results for multistep-ahead streamflow forecasting in mainland China. A study by Dtissibe et al. (2024)  showed that the LSTM and CNN models outperformed the classical ANN model for flood forecasting in Cameroon. While standalone SL and DL models have demonstrated promise in the water resources domain, their performance could be enhanced by hybridizing or combining them with other algorithms (Elzain et al., 2021 ; Tao et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2024; Boo et al., 2024 ). This becomes especially relevant when dealing with the highly non-linear and non-stationary properties of water level fluctuations, which pose significant challenges for standalone ML and DL models (Li et al., 2023; Cui et al., 2024 ). Several research studies have applied hybrid DL and SL with other models for forecasting river water level (Li et al., 2023 ), GWL (Cui et al., 2024 ), lake water levels (Tan et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2024 ), and flood susceptibility (Ha et al., 2021 ). All the above-mentioned studies confirmed that the combined or hybrid models are effective and accurate tools in hydrological research. Despite advancements in water level and flood forecasting methodologies, the rolling forecasting method, where forecasts are continuously updated based on new data, is not yet widely used in hydrological forecasting practices. While techniques such as wavelet transformations have shown promise in improving forecasting accuracy, the implementation of rolling forecasting for water level or flood prediction remains underexplored. However, this approach has the potential to provide dynamic and real-time insights into groundwater behavior, warranting further investigation and integration into water-level forecasting frameworks. In this study, we used for the first time the rolling forecasting method alongside SL and DL models. Our research contributes to the state-of-the-art by utilizing SL (CBR, XGB, LGBM), DL (LSTM, GRU, TR), and their stacked models to forecast WTR in arid regions. In this research, we propose a novel two-level modeling approach. We used the predictive results of SL and DL at level 1 as input for the level 2 modeling strategy to produce stacked SL and DL models. Our contributions encompass: applying SL and DL novel models for the first time and introducing innovative modeling strategies to forecast WTR in arid regions. Additionally, we incorporated rolling forecasting alongside modeling at two levels to enhance model performance and accuracy. Therefore, the objectives of this paper are to (i) evaluate the performance and accuracy of various SL and DL models and their stacked model at two levels to forecast the WTR for one, two, and three-week ahead, and (ii) identify the most accurate, robust, reliable, stable, efficient, and time-effective algorithms for forecasting WTR.  2 Study area and data The study area is located in the Muscat Governorate, Oman (Fig. 1  a ). Muscat exhibits a complex geology and topography, characterized by systems of wadis, mountains, and a coastal plain piedmont. The main urban area is constructed along a coastal plain surrounded by a chain of relatively high, elevated mountains. This area has a distinct drainage pattern and contains several catchments, including Wadi Aday, Mayh, and Al-Ansab. The annual groundwater recharge for the Muscat region is estimated at 17.14 Mm3 /year (MacDonald M, 2013 ). Currently, the primary sources of groundwater are extensive alluvial aquifers located on both the eastern and western sides of the Hajar Mountains (MacDonald M, 2013 ). The study area has an arid climate, with average monthly temperatures reaching 29 °C in June, the hottest month, and dropping to 17 °C in January, the coldest month (McDonald, 2013 ). The average annual rainfall is 77.75 mm (McDonald, 2013 ). A minimum rainfall threshold of 50 mm per year across the catchment area results in a catchment runoff of 18.1 mm3 /year. Significant water loss occurs through evaporation, surface ponding, the vadose zone, and alluvium near the ground surface (McDonald, 2013 ). Jones (1978)  estimated that 20 % of rainfall becomes runoff, while the remaining 80 % is lost through evaporation and recharge. WTR in some areas in Muscat is evident from scattered monitoring records, the presence of ponds and lagoons, water rising in excavations, and damage to structures (Al-Battashi et al., 2022 ). However, there are many other factors that may play a significant role in this phenomenon, including sewage water, losses from the public network, and the geological setting of different rock types (Selim et al., 2014 ). A study by Kacimov et al. (2019a, 2019b)  indicates that the reasons for WTR in Muscat regions are both natural and anthropogenic. Anthropogenic causes include (i) leaks from the public water network, (ii) extensive urbanization that covers ground surfaces, (iii) cessation of water abstraction, and (iv) blocking of drainage systems in urban areas. On the other hand, natural causes include (i) seawater acting as a hydraulic barrier, preventing further downstream flow, although not directly contributing to the WTR, and (ii) recharge following natural storm events such as Gonu and Phet, which has proven effective. The Wadi Al-Ansab catchment, where the WTR phenomenon was observed and monitored (Fig. 2  ), is about 143 km2  (Colquhoun, 1976 ). The thickness of the major aquifer unit in this catchment remains unknown, although estimates suggest it extends to a depth of 600 m (Jones, 1978 ). Aquifer systems in the Al-Ansab area comprise a 20 m thick outwash fan, poor quality ophiolite, Hajar Supergroup, and Tertiary units, which constitute the primary aquifer sources. Pumping tests conducted by Colquhoun (1976), Jones (1978) , and McDonald (1989)  on old and new well fields yielded an average discharge of 410 m3 /day, with yields ranging from 0.17 l/s to 1.9 l/s. Transmissivity ranges from 0.1 to 115 m2 /day, with a storage coefficient of 0.002. In this study, two piezometers were drilled in the Al-Ansab area to investigate the shallow subsurface and monitor hydrochemical and hydrological parameters. Only one well has been used for modeling in this study. Dataloggers have been deployed in the two piezometers in Al-Ansab from October 27, 2017, to January 2019. Head, EC, and temperature were recorded every half an hour. The long-term record of these two piezometers was analyzed for head changes. Core samples were collected for each 1 m depth. 10 m intervals were assessed for each well. A pumping test was conducted to analyze the hydraulic properties of the subsurface material and to assess the response of water to pumping. During the test, the well dried out after about 5 min of pumping (0.3 l/sec.) and recovers within a half hour. The total volume of water discharged from the well is approximately 100 L pumped in about 300 s. estimated K value is in the range of 10-6  to 10-7  m/sec. The upper 2–3 m are more permeable as they are composed of loose gravel. In this research, a total of 19,465 measurements, recorded every half hour from December 2017 to January 2019 in the Wadi Al-Ansab plain, were used. The datasets were split into two subsets for model development: the first 11 months (90 % of the total dataset) were used for training, and the remaining data from the last month (10 % of the total dataset) were used for testing. The WTR dataset covered three seasons: Winter-1, Summer, and Winter-2. Descriptive statistics from different seasons (Dec. 2017 to Jan. 2019) and groundwater quality parameters of the WTR in the study area are shown in Tables S1 and S2, respectively.  3 Materials and methods In this research, various types of SL and DL models were applied for forecasting WTR. The following section will briefly describe the model’s theory and applications. The methodology flow chart is shown in Fig. 3  .  3.1 Level −1 of modeling − shallow learning (SL) models (individual models) 3.1.1 CatBoost regressor (CBR) CBR is a gradient boosting algorithm developed by Yandex, 2017 that is specifically designed for handling categorical variables in machine learning tasks. It utilizes an innovative technique called ordered boosting, which optimizes the tree structure during the training process to reduce overfitting and improve model performance. One of the key features of CBR is its ability to handle categorical variables effectively without the need for extensive preprocessing. It internally converts categorical features into numerical representations using various encoding techniques, thereby simplifying the modeling process. CBR also incorporates advanced techniques for handling missing data, such as gradient-based imputation, which helps improve model robustness in the presence of incomplete or noisy data. More information about the CBR model can be found in Huang et al. (2019) .  3.1.2 XGBoost (XGB) regressor XGB is a popular ML algorithm developed by Chen and Guestrin, (2016)  renowned for its efficiency and effectiveness in regression tasks. XGB builds an ensemble of decision trees sequentially, where each subsequent tree corrects the errors made by the previous ones. This iterative process allows XGB to gradually improve its predictive performance with each new tree added to the ensemble. XGB lies in its ability to handle complex datasets with high-dimensional features and nonlinear relationships effectively. It incorporates regularization techniques to prevent overfitting and model complexity, such as shrinkage (learning rate) and tree pruning. More information about the XGB model can be found in Niazkar et al. (2024) .  3.1.3 LightGBM (LGBM) regressor LGBM, is a ML algorithm developed by Microsoft that belongs to the family of gradient boosting algorithms. Unlike traditional decision tree algorithms that grow trees level-wise, LGBM employs a leaf-wise growth strategy. This means that instead of splitting nodes sequentially, LGBM selects the leaf with the maximum delta loss to split at each step, resulting in a more efficient use of computational resources. Additionally, LGBM incorporates advanced regularization techniques to prevent overfitting and improve generalization performance. It is specifically designed to optimize training speed and efficiency while maintaining high predictive accuracy, making it particularly suitable for large-scale datasets and time-sensitive applications. These techniques include regularization on leaf-wise tree growth, feature fraction, and early stopping criteria. More information about the LGBM model can be found in Ke et al. (2017) .   3.2 Deep learning (DL) models 3.2.1 Long Short-Term memory (LSTM) LSTM is a type of recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture that is well-suited for processing and predicting sequences of data developed by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) . LSTM networks are designed to overcome the limitations of traditional RNNs in capturing long-term dependencies in sequential data (Bowes et al., 2019 ). LSTM networks consist of units called memory cells, which can maintain their state over extended periods. Each cell comprises three main components: an input gate, a forget gate, and an output gate. These gates regulate the flow of information into, within, and out of the cell, allowing the network to learn which information to retain, update, or discard. This makes LSTM useful for tasks involving time series forecasting, where capturing temporal dependencies is crucial for accurate predictions. More details about the LSTM model can be found in Lindemann et al. (2021) .  3.2.2 Gated recurrent unit (GRU) GRU is another type of RNN architecture developed by Cho et al. (2014) , similar to LSTM, designed to model and predict sequential data. GRU networks address some of the limitations of traditional RNNs, such as vanishing gradient problems, by introducing gating mechanisms that regulate the flow of information within the network. GRUs simplify the LSTM architecture by combining the forget and input gates into a single update gate and using a reset gate. The update gate controls the amount of past information to pass along to the future, while the reset gate determines how much of the past information to forget. Unlike LSTM, GRU has a simpler architecture with fewer parameters, making it computationally more efficient and faster to train. GRU is particularly useful for tasks involving time series forecasting, where capturing long-term dependencies is crucial for accurate predictions, and computational efficiency is desirable for handling large datasets. More information about the GRU model can be found in Niu et al. (2023) .  3.2.3 Transformer (TR) The Transformer is a DL model architecture proposed in the paper by Vaswani et al. (2017) . Unlike traditional RNNs or CNNs, the TR architecture relies solely on self-attention mechanisms without recurrence or convolutions, making it highly parallelizable and efficient for processing sequences of data. The TR architecture consists of multiple layers of self-attention modules, known as encoder and decoder layers. The encoder processes the input sequence, while the decoder generates the output sequence. Each layer in the TR contains multiple self-attention heads, allowing the model to attend to different parts of the input sequence simultaneously and capture diverse patterns and relationships. The TR architecture has achieved state-of-the-art performance on various NLP tasks (Singh et al., 2021 ), surpassing traditional recurrent and convolutional architectures. TR represents an important DL model in recent water resources applications due to its scalability, efficiency, and ability to capture long-range dependencies, which have made it a foundational model in the field of DL (Wei et al., 2023 ; Sun et al., 2024 ). More information about the TR model can be found in Lin et al., 2022 .   3.3 Level 2 of modeling (Stacked models) Stacking, also known as weighted average for the predictions of the models, is a powerful ensemble technique utilized in machine learning. It involves combining the predictions of multiple individual models to create a more robust and accurate final prediction. In stacking, the predictions generated by each base model are used as input features for a meta -model, which then produces the final prediction. This meta -model learns how to best combine the predictions of the base models, assigning weights to each model's prediction based on its performance. Stacking is particularly effective when the individual base models have diverse strengths and weaknesses, as it leverages the collective intelligence of multiple models to improve overall performance. By blending the predictions of various models, stacking can mitigate the impact of errors in individual models and yield more reliable forecasts.  3.4 Feature engineering Feature engineering (FE) is a fundamental aspect of data preprocessing in time series analysis, particularly in forecasting task (Vouk et al., 2023 ). Lag, difference (diff), and aggregate transformations are common techniques used in FE to extract valuable information from time series data (Elzain et al., 2024a; Boo et al., 2024 ). Lag transformation involves creating new features by shifting the values of a time series variable forward or backward in time. Difference transformation calculates the difference between consecutive observations of a time series variable. Both lag and difference transformations are essential techniques in FE for time series analysis (Tao et al., 2022; Boo et al., 2024; Elzain et al., 2024a ). They help transform raw time series data into informative features that can be used for forecasting, anomaly detection, and other predictive modeling tasks (Elzain et al., 2024a ). Aggregate transformation refers to creating new features from the original time series data by aggregating values over specific time windows. Aggregate data can capture trends and patterns that may not be apparent from the raw data. Aggregation helps smooth out noise, summarize the data, and highlight important temporal structures (Elzain et al., 2024a ).  3.5 Rolling forecasting technique Rolling forecasting, also known as rolling window forecasting or moving window forecasting, is a technique used in time series analysis to make predictions for future time points by repeatedly updating the forecasting model as new data becomes available (Liu et al., 2021 ). In rolling forecasting, a fixed-size window of historical data is used to train the forecasting model, and predictions are made for the next time point. After making a prediction, the window is shifted forward by one time step, incorporating the latest observed data point while discarding the oldest one. This process is repeated iteratively until predictions are made for all desired future time points. One advantage of rolling forecasting is that it allows the forecasting model to adapt and capture changes in the underlying patterns or trends of the time series over time. By continuously updating the model with new data, rolling forecasting can provide more accurate and up-to-date predictions compared to static forecasting methods (Maltare et al., 2022 ).  3.6 Shapley additive exPlanations (SHAP) model ‘ SHAP is a powerful technique used for interpreting ML models (Elzain et al., 2024a ). It provides insights into the importance and impact of each feature on the model's predictions. The SHAP values are based on game theory concepts and offer a principled way to attribute the contribution of each feature to the final prediction. This allows users to understand the underlying mechanisms driving the model's decisions. SHAP can handle complex models, including ensemble models and deep learning architectures. It provides both local and global explanations, allowing users to interpret individual predictions as well as overall model behavior (El Bilali et al., 2023 ).  3.7 Data management for the modeling 3.7.1 Modeling preprocessing Before modeling, the time series WTR was analyzed using histograms and box plots to understand the data distribution, identify outliers, assess data quality, and inform feature engineering. This process resulted in more accurate and reliable WTR predictions. Furthermore, we utilized decomposition analysis to identify long and short patterns in different seasons and distinguish between actual shifts in the data and random fluctuations for enhancing the accuracy and reliability of the models. In our preprocessing for modeling, the input data were derived from feature engineering of historical WTR, such as lags, differences, and aggregated datasets. Groundwater systems have memory due to the slow movement of water through the subsurface. Hence, current groundwater levels are influenced by the levels in previous time steps. In this research, we derived the lag values of the WTR at previous time steps (e.g., WT R t - 1   , W T R t - 2   , ⋯ W T R t - n     ) to provide the model with the historical context necessary for accurate WTR forecasting. The derived lag feature intervals were chosen for two goals: (i) hourly lags for capturing WTR short-term dependencies (e.g., 1-hour, 2-hour, up to 24-hour lags); (ii) daily (e.g., 1-day, 2-days, …n-days) and weekly lags (e.g., 1-week, 2-weeks, …n-weeks) for capturing longer-term trends and periodic cycles, respectively. Lag features are important for capturing such temporal dependencies in the WTR data. Besides raw lag values, differences between consecutive lags (e.g., WT R t - 1   - W T R t - 2     ) and aggregate statistics (e.g., average WTR level) were derived over a forecasting window such as time of the day and season to provide additional context.  3.7.2 Selection of input data The selection of the best input variables is important in time series forecasting models. The irrelevant or redundant variables in forecasting can lead to model complexity and cost associated with data acquisition (Boo et al., 2024 ). While there is no rule of thumb to choose the suitable lag times for input variables in forecasting, careful consideration and empirical validation are imperative to ascertain optimal input configurations (Barzegar et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2022; Uc-Castillo et al., 2023; Boo et al., 2024 ). Through a trial-and-error approach, it was determined that all lagged, differences and aggregates inputs datasets were utilized in the final modeling phase. By incorporating all lagged input data into the model, we captured the comprehensive temporal dependencies and patterns present in the dataset, thereby enhancing our model's forecasting accuracy and reliability.  3.7.3 Data splitting We used an expanding time series split approach, covering 13 months, to divide the data into training, validation, and testing sets. In this approach, the training folds represent all past data, while each validation fold represents the subsequent sequential period (week/weeks). As the model is processed through the folds, the training data progressively expands. The final month of the dataset was used for testing. Therefore, the split ratio of training to testing was 90:10, based on the trial-and-error method. We considered three-time variants for the forecasting process: 1 week, 2 weeks, and 3 weeks. Each variant involves training the model on past data and making predictions incrementally, according to the specified period (one, two, or three weeks at a time). The forecasting window, which determines the duration for which predictions were made, significantly impacts the number of steps ahead for forecasting.  3.7.4 Rolling forecasting In rolling forecasting, the model predicted one step ahead (e.g., one-hour WTR) for each fold, then updated the feature inputs (e.g., lagged values, differences) based on these predictions. This process was repeated until the entire period of the fold was forecasted (e.g., a week), at which point the feature values were reset to the actual values. By resetting the feature values to the actual observation at the beginning of each new fold and not carrying the predictions from one-fold to the next, the methodology simulates real-world forecasting scenarios for each period. This separation ensures that each prediction phase starts with a clean state, relying only on real data up to that point.  3.7.5 Application of SL and DL at two level of modeling We implemented three SL (CBR, XGB, LGBM) and DL (LSTM, GRU, TR) models for forecasting WTR at level 1 of modeling. At level 2, we stacked the outputs of each SL and DL model using the weighted average method. Besides the SL and DL models, we utilized a rolling forecast approach, continuously updating the models with new feature data. The hyperparameters were tuned using Optuna for Bayesian optimization. The value of the best hyperparameters is shown in Table 1   and their explanations are as follows: Shallow Learning Models:• Max Depth: refers to the maximum depth of the tree. Deeper trees can learn more complex patterns.  • N Estimators: indicates the number of trees in the ensemble. More trees can improve the model's accuracy but may also increase computational demand.  • Reg Lambda: the regularization term on weights (L2 regularization), which can help prevent overfitting by penalizing large weights.  • Col Sample by Tree: this is the subsample ratio of columns when constructing each tree. Subsampling occurs once for every tree constructed.  • Num Leaves: specifies the maximum number of leaves in LGBM.  • Subsample: denotes the fraction of samples to be used for fitting the individual base learners. Less than 1.0 can lead to faster training times and reduce overfitting.  • Learning Rate: controls the contribution of each tree in the ensemble. A lower rate requires more trees but can lead to better generalization.    Deep Learning Models:• LSTM/GRU Units: refers to the number of units in LSTM or GRU layers which help the model in learning dependencies in sequence data.  • Dense Units: these are units in fully connected layers that process features derived from previous layers. The configuration 32,16,8,16 shows a progressively narrowing network.  • Feedforward Dimension: used in Transformers to specify the size of the inner layer of feedforward networks.  • Attention Heads: in TR model, this specifies the number of attention heads, allowing the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces.  • Optimizer: all hybrid models use AdamW, a variant of the Adam optimizer that includes a correction factor to the update rule to better handle sparse gradients and improve generalization.    The experiments were conducted on a Kaggle notebook environment utilizing an Nvidia P100 GPU and 30 GB of RAM. The code utilizes the Python programming language, with libraries such as TensorFlow for building and training neural network models, and scikit-learn for data preprocessing and model evaluation.  3.7.6 Interpretability of feature importance Feature importance was performed using SHAP analysis to assess the importance of each feature, with the outcome indicating that almost all features are useful, reinforcing their inclusion in the model. The SHAP approach proves particularly beneficial in comprehending the influence of input variables on model simulations, as evidenced by recent studies (Chidepudi et al., 2023 ; Elzain et al., 2024a; Cui et al., 2024 ). For instance, Liu et al. (2022)  utilized the SHAP technique to interpret ML models for near-term GWL simulations. The analysis of SHAP values was based on SL models.   3.8 Models evaluation accuracy To evaluate the model accuracy of various models used in this study, we conducted two statistical metrics such as Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) and the Ratio of Root Mean Square Error to Standard Deviation of Measured Data (RSR). The NSE and RSR have been commonly used in different studies in hydrology such as groundwater level (Boo et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2024 ), reference evapotranspiration modeling (Elzain et al., 2024a ), runoff forecasting (Zhang et al., 2022 ), and water lake predictions (Nhu et al., 2020 ).
