During the first winter, there is a noticeable gradual increase in the WTR. In contrast, the summer period exhibits consistency and no major rise in the water table trend was observed. However, the WTR increased again in the second winter period and the water level shows a rising trend. The second winter displays a pattern similar to the first. In the past decade, Muscat governorate has witnessed alternating prolonged periods of severe drought interrupted by short periods of anomalous rainfall. The area has experienced two major cyclones with heavy rainfall exceeding 800 mm/day (Abdalla and Al Abri, 2011; Helmi, 2012 ). These two exceptional pluvial events in addition to the city expansion and urbanization and the availability of domestic water through a modern network can be the main causes of the rising water level in Muscat area. The histogram (Fig. 4 b ) demonstrates the consistency of WTR fluctuations during the summer, which shows a unimodal distribution. In contrast, the two winter seasons exhibit nonsymmetric bimodal distributions, and the left-skewed distribution (negatively skewed) indicates two events in this period. The box plot (Fig. 4 c ) shows that the data for winter 1 and 2 fall in the upper quartile of the box plot area, whereas the summer data is relatively located around the mean. In the first and second winters, respectively, 25 % of the data are above 605, indicating higher WTR compared to summer, which is mainly observed at 600 cm. For high resolution visualization of data, selected representative short periods from different seasons were presented (Fig. 5  a-c ). These plots reveal a distinct pattern in WTR, characterized by high peaks during midnights (00:00 AM–6:00 AM) and middays (12:00 PM–6:00 PM). These fluctuations might be closely linked to the operation of public water network (PWN) where the policy mandates keeping a constant pressure throughout the day. However, the low peaks were observed between (6:00 AM-12:00 PM) and (6:00 AM − 00:00 AM). These low peaks are due to an increase in water usage by locals, resulting in higher demand and subsequently lowering water table levels. In other words, the observed high-water level is associated with the low demand periods, whereas the low WTR is associated with the high demand periods. This systematic and periodicity trend in WTR strongly suggests the need for adjustments in the pressure regulation (variance in the pressure) of the PWN to ensure a more balanced and consistent distribution of water throughout the day. The observed lowered water levels during the mornings and evenings highlight the dynamic nature of water demand and the importance of effective management strategies within the PWN to ensure adequate supply and distribution of water resources. Fig. S1   shows the seasonal decomposition of WTR in different seasons. The winter seasons exhibit higher variability and a noticeable rising trend in the water table compared to the summer season. This can be attributed to higher precipitation rates and lower evapotranspiration during winter, which leads to an increased WTR amount. In contrast, the WTR trend in the summer season appears to be relatively stable with minor fluctuations and there is no significant upward or downward trend observed. This stability suggests that in summer, the WTR was maintained with minor variations. It is observed that all seasons show regular periodic fluctuations. There are some hourly seasonal patterns, as evident from the periodicity in the seasonal component. This confirms our observations in Fig. 5  which suggests that the seasonality period is 12 h.  4.2 Performance of forecasting models The results obtained from the multi-step ahead forecasting of WTR during the training, testing, and forecasting periods are visually presented in Fig. 6  a-i . In week 1 forecasting ahead, SL models (Fig. 6 a ) exhibited good performance in capturing the high and low peaks of the actual WTR trend. The LGBM model demonstrates superiority compared to CBR and XGB in both training and testing. In contrast, DL models (Fig. 6 b ) were unable to capture the dynamic fluctuations of WTR, especially during the earlier part of the training period, where a significant shift between the predicted and actual WTR was observed. The GRU demonstrated relatively good performance predictability during the training and testing phases in fitting actual WTR compared to LSTM and TR models. Additionally, the stacked SL and DL models (i.e., level 2 of modeling) (Fig. 6 c ) outperformed the standalone SL and DL models, respectively. This improvement was visually observed when the over/underestimation of standalone SL and DL models in level 1 was relatively diminished, allowing stacked models to better capture the actual trend of WTR. In the week 2 forecasting ahead, SL models ( Fig. 6 d)  tend to either underestimate or overestimate the predicted values of WTR compared to their performance in week-1 during the training and testing periods. Similarly, DL prediction models ( Fig. 6 e)  exhibit lower performance in capturing the changing behavior of actual WTR to a higher degree compared to DL predictions in week 1. However, the visual performance of stacked SL and DL models ( Fig. 6 f)  outperforms individual SL and DL models, but still falls short in capturing the changes in WTR levels compared to the stacked SL and DL models in week 1 ahead forecasting. In the week 3 forecasting ahead, both SL and DL models ( Fig. 6 g, h)  exhibit poorer performance predictability during both training and testing phases, resulting in nonrealistic results during the forecasting periods compared to week 1 and 2 forecasting. As a consequence, the forecasts produced by both SL and DL models deviate significantly from the actual WTR observations, leading to less reliable predictions in comparison to the stacked DL and SL models.  4.3 Accuracy of forecasting models Table 2  a and b  show that the forecasting accuracy varied across different time steps in the training and testing periods. In the training and testing datasets, the one-week ahead forecasting consistently yielded more accurate results, characterized by higher NSE and lower RSR values, compared to the two- and three-weeks ahead forecast across all modeling levels. The accuracy of the model’s evaluation is based on testing data because it provides an unbiased and accurate assessment of the model's performance based on unseen data (Elzain et al., 2024a ). Fig. 7   shows that the error increases as the number of steps ahead (window of forecasting) increases, while the accuracy increased toward the stacked model direction of SL and DL models at level 2 of modeling. At level 1 of modeling, in the testing data, when comparing SL models with DL models, SL models consistently outperformed DL models in terms of both NSE and RSR metrics across all forecast time steps except for the GRU model in the one week ahead. However, at level 2 of modeling, where DL and SL models were stacked each one at a time, we observed a notable improvement in the overall forecasting accuracy. The improvement percentage of all forecast time steps is shown in Table S1  .  For example, in the week one ahead forecasting, the improvement percentages of the stacked SL model compared to CBR, XGB, and LGBM models were 32.80 %, 31.79 %, and 30.77 % reduction in RSR, respectively. Meanwhile, the improvement percentages of the stacked DL model in comparison to LSTM, TR, and GRU were 41.17 %, 8.71 %, and 4.61 % reduction in RSR, respectively.  4.4 Contribution of the SL and DL in the stacking models Fig. 8   illustrates the contributions of SL (LGBM, XGB, CBR) and DL (GRU, LSTM, TR) models to the ensemble stacking models, measured by the absolute coefficient value. This value indicates the magnitude of the relative influence of each model, thereby assessing their importance within the stacked models. As the forecasting window extends from one week to three weeks ahead, the contribution of LGBM and GRU models decreased over time, resulting in reduced absolute coefficient values for SL and DL, respectively. In contrast, the XGB, TR, LSTM contributions to the stacking models increased as the forecasting window extended. While the CBR increased its contribution to the stacking models in the first and second weeks ahead, it decreased in the third week.  4.5 Stability of the models Table 3   illustrates the percentage change of testing over training periods for all models used in the study area. The results show the variations in the percentage change of RSR values between the testing and training datasets across forecasting periods. A minimal variation percentage in the performance metric between the training and testing phases indicates a high level of model stability. (Fan et al., 2018). We can observe that the SL models exhibit higher stability compared to the DL models in one-week-ahead forecasting at level 1 of modeling, while variability is observed in the models for other forecasting periods in the second and third weeks ahead forecasting. The performance stability indicates that the stacked SL and DL models at level 2 of modeling exhibit higher stability in comparison with individual SL and DL models at level 1 of modeling. However, it is noteworthy that the stacked models demonstrated satisfactory stability in their modeling, with a percentage increase in testing RSR values of less than 12 %.  4.6 Time execution of the models Fig. 9   shows that the average computational cost associated with DL models (GRU, LSTM, TR) is notably higher when compared to that of their SL models (LGBM, XGB, CBR). As a result, the training and testing periods for DL and stacked DL models tend to be more time-consuming compared to SL and their stacked models. Despite the longer computational time required by DL models, their enhanced complexity often leads to improved performance and more realistic results, particularly in tasks such as future forecasting.  4.7 Model interpretability of input features using SHAP method Fig. 10   shows the identification of the most influential features for accurate WTR in different time-step forecasting. The variations in feature importance reflect the model’s capability to adaptively select the most relevant temporal dependencies. Fig. 10  illustrates that shorter lags capture immediate, short-term effects that are crucial for making accurate predictions, while longer lags and statistical aggregations assist in identifying long-term effects and seasonal trends. The model dynamically prioritized features that provided the strongest predictive power for the current state of the WTR. It is trained on past weeks’ data to predict future weeks, and each time it is fitted, it identifies the optimal features.   5 Discussion 5.1 Data analysis as modeling pre-processing for WTR Analyzing data distribution and conducting statistical analysis provides insights into the underlying patterns and trends in the time series data. Figs. 4 and 5  present similarities and differences in patterns between winters 1 and 2 as well as the summer, which helped in selecting the appropriate models for this study. The short-term dynamic and systematic patterns presented in Fig. 5  seem to be influenced by anthropogenic factors. On the other hand, some of the data in different seasons show a different pattern, in contrast to Fig. 5 , due to the contribution of various factors such as the evapotranspiration effect, changes in temperature, precipitation, and/or other natural factors. The observations from a statistical and data distribution perspective have been confirmed by Fig. S1  , showing seasonal, trend, and residual components of different seasons in the study area. Therefore, the dynamics of WTR in arid regions include seasonal variations, short-term trends, long-term trends, and the potential impacts of climate change should be carefully considered before model selection. The authors believe that understanding time-series data is vital for selecting appropriate an approach with AI and ML models that can effectively forecast water table dynamics in arid regions with changeable and harsh climates.  5.2 Models input Accurate forecasting of dynamic water table fluctuations depends on the types and availability of data that significantly impact the output (Boo et al., 2024 ). Selecting lag features from historical data can be crucial for forecasting tasks in hydrological studies such as GWL, water lake forecasting, and river forecasting (Tao et al., 2022; Uc-Castillo et al., 2023 ). For example, an extensive review by Rajaee et al. (2019)  and Boo et al. (2024)  found that antecedent GWL was among the top, followed by P and T, as frequently used model inputs. Lag features represent the historical values of the dynamic water table at previous time steps, allowing the model to capture the delayed effects of WTR and incorporate them into the forecasting process. In our study, we believe that antecedent WTR (i.e., lag) is suitable for forecasting WTR, which aligns with other research such as GWL (Boo et al., 2024; Tao et al., 2022 ), especially in arid regions with limited or rare rainfall.  5.3 Performance, accuracy and models contribution at two level of WTR modeling Model predictability and performance capabilities in time-series data depend on the model structures, the size, and the long seasonality of data (Tao et al., 2022 ). Recent studies (Yang and Zhang, 2022; Wu et al., 2023; Boo et al., 2024 ) show that the DL models were superior to SL models in the training and testing datasets. In our study, the superiority of SL GBMs over DL models, especially in the training period (winter 1, summer and two months of winter 2), was notable, while GRU outperformed all models in the testing phase (last month of winter 2) only in the one week ahead forecasting time. The superiority of GBMs is due to their effectiveness in handling small data in a shorter period of time and therefore reducing the overfitting, bias, and variance of the model (Saber et al. (2022 ). In contrast, DL models require a large amount of data, very long-term seasonal trends (a long history of different seasons), and variability of data. The analysis also revealed that forecasts for the one week ahead (Figs. 6-7 and Table 2 ) were the most accurate and promising, compared to predictions for the second and third weeks ahead. This trend was consistent across both individual and stacked models. This is due to the accumulation of errors over time, the overfitting problem, model complexity, and data variability. The SL models experience sharp drawdowns in all forecasting periods, while DL models show relatively gentle drawdowns, reflecting a period of gentle recession. The DL model relatively mimics the actual gentle recession of groundwater after heavy precipitation in the winter 2, while the SL model declines due to the simple structure of SL models compared to DL models. However, DL models require more time and a large amount of data to be well-trained. These findings underscore the challenges associated with longer forecasting horizons and emphasize the importance of continuously monitoring and adjusting the forecasting models to maintain excellent performance and reliability over extended periods. In our analysis, the integration of each SL and DL model through a stacking approach demonstrated superior performance compared to individual standalone SL (LGBM, XDB, CBR) and DL (GRU, LSTM, TR) models. Specifically, the stacking SL and DL models significantly improved the accuracy and stability of the WTR forecasts. The improvement percentage in Table S3  suggests that stacking DL and SL models allowed us to leverage the strengths of individual models, resulting in enhanced predictive performance. Our findings confirm other research by Elzain et al. (2023) and Elzain et al. (2024) that level 2 modeling can extract more information and therefore increase predictive accuracy compared to level 1 modeling. Furthermore, the implementation of the rolling forecasting technique alongside the models was crucial in achieving our results. Rolling forecasting, which involves continuously updating the model with new data, enhanced the predictions and minimized data leakage (Henttu-Aho et al., 2018 ). Among the various models evaluated, the combination of SL and DL models through stacking emerged as the most effective strategy. This approach not only exhibited superior performance but also maintained good accuracy and stability in forecasting WTR. The findings highlight the importance of utilizing a hybrid model approach alongside rolling forecasting to achieve optimal forecasting outcomes. Despite the increased variability observed in longer-term forecasts, the stacking approach consistently enhanced the accuracy and stability of predictions. These results underscore the importance of considering different forecasting horizons and continuously refining models to ensure reliable and timely insights for WTR forecasting. The study provides insights into model complexity versus predictive accuracy and guides model selection for different forecasting periods. Ultimately, it advances the understanding of SL and DL techniques in hydrogeological forecasting for sustainable water management.  5.4 SL and DL contribution to the stacked models Identifying the relative importance or influence of each model in the stacked ensemble is essential to understanding the ability of each model to perform accurately in short- and long-term dependencies and therefore to increase accuracy. In the one week ahead (Fig. 8 ), the LGBM and GRU models play a crucial role in the predictive accuracy of the stacked ensemble, as seen by their high absolute coefficient values. However, as the forecast horizon extends to two and three weeks ahead, the LGBM and GRU influence decreases. This trend suggests that LGBM and GRU are effective for short-term predictions. In the two and three weeks ahead forecasts, XGB, TR and LSTM models may capture longer-term dependencies more effectively, thus contributing more significantly to the model’s performance in later weeks.  5.5 Stability and time execution The stability of ML and AI models is important for accurate hydrological forecasting (Fan et al., 2018). In this study, high model stability is relatively consistent with high modeling accuracy, especially in the stacked models at level 2 (Table 3 ). For example, the stacked SL and DL models demonstrated greater stability (evidenced by the smallest percentage increase in testing RSR) in level 2 of modeling compared to the individual SL and DL models. The computational time of models is a crucial factor in their deployment (Tejada et al., 2022 ). Our findings showed that the DL models (Fig. 9 ) and their stacked model required considerably more average time to converge compared to the SL models and their stacked model. The increased computational cost of DL models can be attributed to the increased complexity inherent in DL algorithms, which require more computations during both the training and testing phases. DL models typically involve deeper architectures with numerous layers, which necessitate additional computational resources to process the data and optimize the model parameters.  5.6 Interpretability of feature importance using SHAP technique SHAP illustration (Fig. 10 ) shows the feature importance after the model has been trained on a significant portion of the training data, showcasing a blend of short- and long-term patterns. This initial insight is derived by examining the overall importance of the features. Regarding the order of importance, lag features are typically highly correlated, especially when they originate from periods close to each other. Consequently, the model might assign importance to one of these features while considering others as redundant. The selected feature provides essential information to capture the primary patterns in the data. While additional correlated features also hold significant value close to that of the selected feature, they offer minimal incremental value due to their high correlation. As a result, these additional features receive lower importance scores. This explanation clarifies why certain lags display greater importance while others, despite being within the same temporal range, appear less significant. Moreover, based on Fig. 5 , there seems to be hourly seasonal patterns occurring every 12 h. Therefore, we should interpret the importance of lags not only in terms of the similarity between the current day’s WTR value and previous days’ WTR values but also in terms of the similarity between the current time of day’s WTR value and the previous days’ time of day WTR values. This suggests that the model might be identifying noticeable hourly-based patterns from previous days. Such an interpretation helps clarify why, in some cases (e.g., in the mentioned plot), certain lags with larger values could have higher importance than lags with smaller values.   6 Research limitations, recommendations, and future direction for WTR modeling Despite the shorter time span of the dataset, we utilized high-resolution hourly measurement datasets to enhance the detail of our analysis. The hourly measurements with a 30-minute interval for 13 months (19,465 dataset) allowed us to identify daily and weekly patterns within each season. The high temporal resolution compensates for the shorter overall duration by capturing fine-scale variations and trends. While the SL and DL models demonstrated satisfactory and promising outcomes in forecasting WTR with the available time series data, the study is limited by the data capturing different seasons in only 14 months. This limited seasonal representation restricts the models’ ability to fully capture the long-term seasonal variations and hydrological dynamics that influence WTR. The authors believe that increasing the dataset to include multiple seasonal cycles in several years will provide a more robust foundation for these models, allowing them to better forecast the complexities and variabilities in WTR across different climatic conditions. While acquiring data over multiple seasons is important for increasing data confidence, it is impractical for the current study due to limited funding and project duration. We highly recommend that future studies in the region build on this work to improve data acquisition and certainty. Boo et al. (2024)  highlighted that its essential to not only include an adequate amount of data, but also carefully assess its relevance and accuracy. If necessary, the training database should be reduced to ensure that the data accurately represents current conditions. Based on the systematic pattern observed with high WTR (Fig. 5 ) during midnights (00:00 AM-6:00 AM) and middays (12:00 PM-6:00 PM), which may be attributed to anthropogenic factors such as leaks from the PWN, we recommend integrating real-time AI models with pressure sensor control systems and the Internet of Things (IoT). This integration would allow for the dynamic adjustment of pressure settings during periods of low water demand (i.e., when WTR is high). This study presents the first report on forecasting WTR or groundwater flooding using several SL and DL models, as well as their stacked models. It establishes a baseline for future global research in the area of WTR research using AI models. For future directions, we recommend exploring different structures of ML and AI models, including hybrid approaches (i.e., combining SL and DL with wavelet transformation and evolutionary algorithms). Also, novel approaches such as combining numerical models with AI are needed to predict or forecast accurate WTR worldwide.  7 Conclusion Accurate forecasting of WTR in arid regions with limited water resources is important for understanding groundwater dynamics, managing water resources, and mitigating potential hazards such as groundwater flooding or soil salinization. This study used an innovative approach for forecasting WTR at two levels of modeling strategy for several weeks step-ahead. Several individual SL (CBR, XGB, LGBM) and DL models (LSTM, GRU, TR), along with their stacked models, were implemented and evaluated.• At all levels of the modeling strategy, the one-week step-ahead was accurate in producing results for both the training and testing periods. Additionally, at level 1, the SL models outperformed the DL models in the training datasets. However, the GRU showed superior accuracy in the testing phase among all models, with low RSR and high NSE values. In contrast, the two and three-step-ahead WTR forecasts exhibited low predictive accuracy due to the accumulation of errors over time.  • At level 2 of the modeling strategy, the ensemble stacked SL and DL model yielded superior results in terms of accuracy measurements. It improved the overall performance of the model by extracting more information and leveraging the strengths of the standalone SL and DL models. Therefore, it was capable of capturing complex short- and long-term temporal patterns of WTR fluctuations.  • It’s observed that DL models and their stacked model require more time to converge during the modeling process compared to SL models. Interestingly, the stacking SL and DL models at level 2 show significant stability (the smallest percentage increase in testing RSR) compared to the individual SL and DL models in all forecasting step-ahead windows.  • The stacked SL and DL models show promise as an effective tool for forecasting hourly WTR on a global scale. Stacked models can be confidently used to predict WTR in arid areas for a reasonable period of weeks. This period can be extended with additional data collection in different seasons for long-term model improvements.
1 Introduction The dynamics of water bodies are critical variables for both humanity and the ecological system (Revenga et al., 2000; Vorosmarty et al., 2010 ). Surface water has multiple purposes, including drinking, irrigation, power generation, transportation, and industry (Shiklomanov, 2000; Vorosmarty et al., 2000 ). These changing water conditions present both opportunities and risks for humans and the environment, hence the study of water body dynamics has garnered much attention (Haddeland et al., 2014; Vorosmarty et al., 2000; Wada et al., 2016 ). As climate change and human interventions continue to alter water regimes, interdisciplinary research becomes indispensable in adapting to these changes for a sustainable future (Busker et al., 2019; Karpatne et al., 2016; Milly et al., 2005 ). The utilization of remote sensing technology has enabled the frequent production of updated maps of water bodies (Fisher et al., 2016; Ling et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022 ). To construct global and regional surface water dynamics, significant efforts have been made, resulting in the derivation of various datasets. For instance, Prigent et al. (2012)  developed a monthly global dataset of surface water extent and dynamics by leveraging multi-satellite observations at a coarse spatial resolution of 0.25°, covering the period between 1993 and 2007. Yamazaki et al. (2015)  utilized Landsat satellite imagery at 5- to 10-year intervals to generate global water body seasonality maps at a resolution of 3 arc-seconds (∼90 m). Mueller et al. (2016) , on the other hand, used 27 years of satellite imagery spanning 1987–2014 to map the seasonality and changes of surface water across Australia. Meanwhile, Yang et al. (2020)  constructed monthly water body extent estimates for France, with a resolution of 10 m, using Sentinel-2 imagery between 2017 and 2019. Bonnema et al. (2022)  estimated the changes in surface area of a group of the largest lakes and reservoirs on the planet by employing Sentinel-1 radar observations. Based on remote sensing data, there are also studies that have emphasized mapping the expansion of lakes, highlighting the evolving nature of vast water bodies and underscores the invaluable role of satellite data in water resource management for decision-makers (Deoli et al., 2021; Deoli et al., 2022 ). Among the datasets available, the European Commission's JRC GSW (Table 1  ) dataset stands out for its extensive temporal and comprehensive spatial coverage (Pekel et al., 2016 ). The JRC GSW dataset is a vital resource for numerous studies examining changes in water bodies, serving as a critical reference. For example, researchers have utilized the JRC GSW dataset to investigate the global distribution and trajectory of tidal flats (Murray et al., 2019 ), refine estimates of carbon flux (Mendonça et al., 2017 ), and analyze the global methane budget (Saunois et al., 2020 ). Thus, the JRC GSW dataset plays a crucial role in advancing the understanding of the planet's water resources. In practice, however, despite its unmatched resolution and timeline, the JRC GSW dataset suffers from significant data gaps which impede its full potential, given detecting water bodies using Landsat imagery is challenging due to several factors. These include the unavailability of Landsat data, complex water spectrals, and various types of interference such as cloud cover, cloud shadows, and terrain shadows (Feng et al., 2016; McFeeters, 1996; Xu, 2006 ). Additionally, the failure of the Scan Line Corrector (SLC) on Landsat-7 can also hamper the accuracy of water body detection (Lillesand et al., 2015; Scaramuzza and Barsi, 2005 ). This can lead to gap areas in the resulting water maps. Approximately one-third of the JRC GSW dataset was marked as “No observations” (Mullen et al., 2021 ), which poses a significant challenge for subsequent studies and applications (Donchyts et al., 2016; Hansen et al., 2013 ). To ensure the quality of the dataset, many studies have opted to discard contaminated images. Specifically, images are excluded from analysis if their level of contamination exceeds a predetermined threshold. However, this approach has a greater impact on regions with high levels of contamination, such as frequently cloud-covered areas or those affected by SLC errors of Landsat 7, leading to a considerable reduction in the number of usable images. Many studies have also chosen to use data synthesized from multiple periods for analysis, which, however, can lead to temporal inaccuracies (Zhu and Woodcock, 2014 ). Addressing the data gaps in the JRC GSW dataset is of paramount importance for its practical use and for achieving a holistic product. One potential approach to achieve this goal is by restoring the surface reflectance of gap areas and then identifying water bodies from the restored reflectance (Gao et al., 2006 ). While various methods have been proposed to replace the reflectance of an gap pixel using neighboring pixels (Cheng et al., 2014; Gómez et al., 2016 ) or multi-temporal images (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu and Woodcock, 2014 ), these approaches may not accurately estimate reflectance in areas with rapid land cover changes (Li et al., 2021 ). The reflectivity-based method also requires a significant allocation of computational resources, making it unsuitable for this study, given its global scope. Instead of directly filling gap areas in the dataset using reflectance imagery, it has been demonstrated that it is more beneficial to use the spatial–temporal correlation of water bodies based on the time series of classified water maps to fill the gap areas. The distribution of water bodies is often determined by topographic conditions, resulting in spatial and temporal correlation (Birkett et al., 2002; Sorensen and Seibert, 2007 ). Various techniques have been proposed to fill gap areas by analyzing the classification results. One such method is designed specifically for lakes and reservoirs (Yao et al., 2019; Zhao and Gao, 2018 ). This approach estimates the inundation status of gap pixels by considering the historical occurrence of water bodies and the current inundation status of neighboring pixels. However, this approach has not been validated for other types of water bodies. Mullen et al. (2021)  and Bai et al. (2023)  used pixel-wise features as predictors and trained supervised classifiers (Random Forest and Naive Bayes) to fill in the gaps. However, these methods do not fully utilize spatio-temporal information as they rely on point-wise features, and the relatively simplistic models cannot accurately represent the complex correlation of the features. Breaking away from traditional methods, this study introduces a novel approach to address the data gaps in the JRC GSW dataset. Instead of directly filling gap areas using reflectance imagery, this study leverages the spatial–temporal correlation of water bodies based on the time series of classified water maps to fill the gaps. This method capitalizes on the intrinsic topographic conditions which dictate the spatial and temporal correlation of water bodies. Existing techniques, though valuable, have not tapped into the full potential of spatio-temporal data (Zhao and Gao, 2018 ). In contrast, deep learning (DL) methods, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have shown immense promise in capturing intricate spatio-temporal patterns from data (Jing and Tian, 2020; Moortgat et al., 2022 ). In essence, CNNs are a type of machine learning model designed to process data with grid-like topology, such as images, making them particularly adept at discerning patterns in spatial data over time. This study proposes a novel self-supervised DL method specifically designed to fill gap data in seasonal water areas of the JRC GSW dataset. Differing from traditional approaches, the proposed method involves generating high-quality training data from the unlabeled JRC GSW dataset and harnessing the power of advanced DL techniques to model the dynamics of water bodies. To put it simply, instead of relying on labeled data where each data point is paired with its correct outcome (as in traditional machine learning), the proposed method uses the inherent structure of the data to teach the model. The exceptional accuracy of JRC GSW data leads to a low noise level of data, enabling the use of self-supervised learning, which allows models to gain knowledge from data without explicit labels, thereby improving their adaptability and generalization capabilities across various situations (He et al., 2022; He et al., 2020; Jing and Tian, 2020 ). By innovatively merging self-supervised learning with state-of-the-art DL techniques, this work sets a benchmark for future studies in modeling and understanding water body dynamics. The primary objectives of this study are to: (1) introduce a self-supervised DL method tailored for addressing data gaps in the JRC GSW dataset, particularly in seasonal water areas. (2) evaluate the performance of the proposed method using simulated validation data. (3) highlight the practical implications and significance of the improved dataset.  2 Data 2.1 Monthly water history and water occurrence map from JRC GSW 2.1.1 JRC GSW monthly water history The JRC GSW (v1.4) monthly water history is a highly accurate and reliable dataset that is produced using techniques including expert systems, visual analytics, and evidential reasoning (Pekel et al., 2016 ). To categorize each pixel in the dataset as water, land, or an observation gap, the expert system relies on a range of multispectral and multitemporal attributes from the Landsat archive as well as supplementary data layers such as Digital Elevation Models (DEMs), glacier data, urban areas data, and lava masks. However, it is estimated that approximately one-third of the JRC GSW data are data gaps (Mullen et al., 2021 ). The primary reasons for these gaps are geographic and temporal discontinuities within the Landsat archive itself (Pekel et al., 2016 ). This includes a lack of Landsat data for certain locations or time periods, as well as poor quality or unusable data resulting from issues such as cloud cover or sensor-related problems. These factors are responsible for most of the gap data in the JRC GSW monthly water history.  2.1.2 Occurrence map and distribution of water occurrence frequency for seasonal water In this study, the JRC GSW occurrence map is utilized to assist in model training and validation. The occurrence map is a product that captures the frequency of surface water occurrence between 1984 and 2021, providing information on overall water dynamics. This was achieved by summing water detections and valid observations for each month from March 1984 to December 2021 and then averaging the results to give the long-term overall surface water occurrence. The resulting map shows the areas where water was present frequently and less frequently. Fig. 1   illustrates the estimated probability distribution of water occurrence frequency for seasonal water. This was achieved this by randomly sampling 10,000 pixels from each of the 1 × 1 degree water occurrence maps provided by JRC GSW within the maximum water extent, excluding pixels with an occurrence of 1.0. The distribution of occurrence frequency for seasonal water is highly skewed towards high frequency. In the range of 0–1, a seasonal water pixel has an 80.58 % chance of being water. Whereas, in the range of 0–0.93 of frequency, a seasonal water pixel is equally likely to be land or water. The above analysis highlights the necessity of distinct validation processes for seasonal  water bodies in gap-filling methodologies. This is due to the disproportionate distribution of water occurrence probabilities (Fig. 1 ), which are heavily skewed towards permanent bodies or those with high occurrence probabilities. While filling data gaps in areas of permanent or high-probability water is relatively straightforward, it is crucial to address seasonal water bodies. These bodies are key indicators of fluctuating water area dynamics and thus, filling their data gaps is of utmost importance (Pekel et al., 2016 ).   2.2 Sentinel-2 data To validate the gap-filled dataset, 84 locations were randomly selected worldwide (Fig. 2  ). Cloud-free Sentinel-2 top-of-atmosphere images were acquired through Google Earth Engine. These images have an average size of 10,227 km2 . These locations were filtered from a pool of 132 sites because not all data from the JRC GSW in the same month were cloud-contaminated and thus could not be used for validation. For each location, monthly composite cloud-free Sentinel-2 data was downloaded for all dates ranging from 2016 to 2021. This resulted in 639 cloud-free Sentinel-2 images that had JRC GSW partial data gap. The mean fraction of pixels that are gaps in JRC GSW but valid in Sentinel-2 was 47.19 %, which represents the contamination rate.  2.3 Reservoir water levels data To ensure the reliability of the gap-filled dataset over an extended period, additional testing was carried out to assess the model's performance. Four sets of recorded reservoir water level data from 1992 to 2020, obtained from G-REALM (https://ipad.fas.usda.gov/cropexplorer/global_reservoir ) were utilized to conduct this validation.   3 Methods The proposed method aims to fill gap areas in the JRC GSW dataset by leveraging DL to recognize spatio-temporal patterns in water bodies (Fig. 3  ). Areas with occurrence frequency were designated of 1 and 0, respectively, as water and land. Then, a self-supervised training dataset was constructed using valid (non-gap) JRC GSW images and balance it based on water area ratios, mean water occurrence, and months of the target image. Images that only contain permanent water or land pixels were filtered out. A U-Net convolutional neural network (Ronneberger et al., 2015 ) is used as the model architecture. A custom loss function was used that takes into account the varying water area ratios and the number of land and water pixels in the label. Finally, the gap-filled dataset was generated by breaking down the maximum water extent into 256 × 256 pixel blocks with an overlap and filling in any seasonal water gap areas using the trained model. The accuracy of the gap-filling method was assessed using simulated JRC GSW data, as well as cloud-free Sentinel-2 data reservoir water levels. The approach to the data preparation ensures robustness against overfitting and enhanced generalizability. By utilizing a vast dataset, this study aims to capture a wide spectrum of real-world scenarios. The proposed methodologies, including the use of dropout layers and batch normalization, further assist in refining the model's adaptability. 3.1 Constructing the self-supervised training dataset To generate training data for a DL model that fills gap areas in water maps using JRC GSW monthly records, a valid JRC GSW image was first selected but mask some of its pixels as model input. The unmasked JRC GSW image is then used as the label (Fig. 4  ). The time series monthly records before and after the selected image are used as model input. Due to the use of time series images as model input, there is a large computational requirement, and so the image size for model input is constrained to be 256 × 256 × N, where N is the sum of the number of input months and two additional maps: the occurrence map and the target month image. The selection of the number of input months is discussed in Section 5.1 . Using self-supervised training allows for a large amount of training data to be generated, which is critical for sufficiently training the DL model. This allows the model to accommodate different scenarios, including different water changing patterns and different levels of gap densities. In order to effectively train the model, having a balanced dataset is critical, since the distribution of occurrence frequency for seasonal water is highly imbalanced (Fig. 1 ). It has been empirically found that random sampling without considering the balancing problem of the dataset results in poor gap-filling performance. The first factor causing data imbalance is water occurrence frequency. Random sampling around the globe within the maximum water extent would cause a significant portion of sampled images (256 × 256) to only contain permanent water (occurrence for all pixels is 1). Such images can be quite easily found in areas with large reservoirs or near the shoreline. These images are not very useful for model training, as the most critical part of water maps gap filling is the filling of seasonal water bodies (occurrence between 0 and 1). Therefore, as a first step in balancing the training data, images with only permanent water or permanent land pixels were filtered out (Fig. 4 ). This process generated approximately 275,000 images for model training. A large number of valid images that contain seasonal water for model training have been identified. However, it has been noticed that the ratio of water areas (areas where occurrence > 0) to the overall image area (256 × 256) is not evenly distributed among the training images (Fig. 5  a). This could pose a challenge to model's ability to fill gaps in different-sized water bodies. The data imbalance is also related to the mean water occurrence and the temporal location of the target image (Fig. 5 b, c). The imbalance can be attributed to several factors. Firstly, seasonal water bodies tend to have a higher occurrence frequency (Fig. 1 ). Additionally, valid observations were more frequently obtained during the summer season, whereas the winter season were often hindered by the unavailability of Landsat data. Moreover, the majority of water bodies are distributed in the northern hemisphere, further exacerbating the uneven distribution. It is critical to address the above-mentioned imbalance issues, as it is desired that the trained model to be able to fill water with different occurrence frequency, different water body sizes, and at different months (temporal locations). To do so, the training images were classified into 360 categories. For water area ratios (number of pixels with occurrence > 0 divided by 256 × 256), there are six categories: 0–0.2, 0.2–0.4, 0.4–0.6, 0.6–0.8, 0.8–1.0, and 1.0. For mean water occurrence of the image, there are five categories: 0–0.2, 0.2–0.4, 0.4–0.6, 0.6–0.8, 0.8–1.0. For months of the target image, there are 12 categories of 12 months from Jan to Dec. During training, for selecting a training sample, the probability for sampling different categories was normalized by logarithm (Fig. 5 ). Then, the generated combination of categories (e.g., water area ratio = 0.1, mean occurrence = 0.8, month = Feb) is used to select an image from the 360 pools of training data. This process ensures that the data used for model training is balanced in terms of the water area ratio, water occurrence frequency, and temporal location.  3.2 Deep learning model and training settings In this study, a CNN was used with a U-Net (Ronneberger et al., 2015 ) architecture containing approximately 30 million parameters. The model's capabilities were further enhanced using gated convolution and ConvNext block (Liu et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2019 ). Gated convolution is a technique commonly used in image inpainting tasks in computer vision. It allows the model to disregard less important features at each layer, effectively dealing with large amounts of data gaps in the input time series. The ConvNext block has a superior representation power compared to commonly used blocks like ResNet and VGGNet. Widely accepted practices like learning rate decay, dropout, and layer norms are used to boost model convergence. The loss function was designed to account for the varying water area ratios that may exist in a given training batch (Fig. 5 ). Additionally, the loss function considers the number of land and water pixels in the label, and the loss is only calculated for seasonal water areas:(1) Loss = - 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  ∑ j = 1  H × W   m ij   w pos  l ij   log p ij     + w neg  1 - l ij      log 1 - p ij               where N   is the number of images, H   and W   are the height and width of the images, respectively. m ij     is the binary mask value at pixel ( i , j )    indicating pixels that are gap in the input, but valid in the label, the occurrence frequency of these pixels falls between 0 and 1, l ij     is the label value at pixel ( i , j )   , and p ij     is the predicted value at pixel ( i , j )   . The weight for positive is denoted as w pos    = 0.7   , and the weight for negative is w neg    = 1.3   . The summation of loss is only performed on pixels with a positive value on the binary mask image. To balance the weight of water (positive) and land (negative), we calculate the total number of pixels for both from the training dataset and determine the weights. The final loss value is averaged at the image level rather than the pixel level. This approach ensures that the model is not biased towards specific images. If the loss were averaged at the pixel level, images with a large water area ratio would dominate the training as they have far more pixels for calculating loss than other images. Different images in the same training batch have a different number of pixels for calculating loss. The proposed model requires a time series input of 256 × 256 × 122, which corresponds to a 10-year period, and includes an occurrence map and a masked target image (Fig. 6  a). Since input data was already confined within a (0,1) range, model input didn't necessitate any normalization. In cases where the target month lacks sufficient data from the 5-year period before or after it, particularly for years prior to 1989 or after 2016, the incomplete half of the time series is padded with zeros to ensure a 5-year span. This approach guarantees that the model can handle gap data effectively by leveraging both forward and backward information to fill the gaps based on the spatio-temporal patterns of seasonal water. Model training and inference is implemented in Python (with PyTorch library). The model was trained using the AdamW optimizer, which implements an adaptive learning rate, with a base learning rate of 3e-4 and a cosine decay learning rate schedule. The training was performed with a batch size of 32 using mixed precision on an Nvidia RTX 4090 with 24 GB of memory. It is found that training for approximately 16 h was sufficient for performance convergence on the separate development dataset (Fig. 6 b). To produce the gap-filled dataset, the maximum water extent from JRC GSW was divided into blocks of size 256 × 256 with a 10-pixel overlap with adjacent blocks. The overlapping of the divided blocks prevents undesirable artifacts that may occur at the image boundary. Since the model is only trained to fill seasonal water, permanent water filling is accomplished by designating pixels with a water occurrence frequency of 1.0 as water. It is noteworthy that while specific image processing techniques like random cropping might slightly extend the computational timeline, they are intrinsically incorporated on-the-fly during training, ensuring an effective integration. However, the broader scope of global dataset filling is indeed a more time-intensive endeavor. As a detailed example, an expanse measuring 140 km2  is anticipated to take a span of 10–30 min for comprehensive filling. External variables, notably I/O speed, may further modulate these time estimates.  3.3 Validation method Three validation methods have been developed for assessing the quality of the proposed gap-filling method, with a particular focus on its performance on seasonal water pixels (which have an occurrence frequency between 0 and 1). The first method involves generating validation data from JRC GSW in different areas that were not included in the training data. The second method involves identifying cloud-free Sentinel-2 images during months when the JRC GSW has partial contaminations. The third method use reservoir water levels data to evaluate the quality of the gap-filled dataset over a long time series. To evaluate the performance of the proposed method on simulated JRC GSW data, valid pixels on the JRC GSW image (256 × 256) were masked out and compare the gap-filled image with the unmasked image only for seasonal water areas. This process was performed on 10,000 simulated images to obtain a representative evaluation result (Fig. 7  ). F1 score is calculated for both land and water:(2) F 1  = 2 precision × recall  precision + recall   = 2 tp  2 tp + fp + fn        The reason for employing the F1 score in the evaluation is due to its ability to provide a balanced measure between precision and recall. In scenarios where class imbalance is prevalent, accuracy might not provide a complete picture of model performance. In an imbalanced binary classification scenario, having a high F1 score for both categories (positive and negative) indicates that the model is performing well in identifying both the minority and majority classes. The F1 score is calculated at the image level and then averaged to prevent images with large water areas from dominating the validation result. To evaluate the performance of the proposed method on cloud-free Sentinel-2 data, a similar procedure as that used in (Pekel et al., 2016 ) (Fig. 8  ) was followed. To estimate omission error, random water pixels were identified from Sentinel-2 images and extract the corresponding pixel on the gap-filled image produced by the trained model. If the pixels filled by the model are land (FN), then they contribute to the omission error. To estimate commission error, pixels that have been filled as water from the gap-filled image were identified, and then we determine if the corresponding pixels on Sentinel-2 are also water (TP). If they are not (FP), then they contribute to the commission error. Validation was performed on 3,632 pixels that were initially gaps in the JRC GSW monthly water history and have an occurrence frequency between 0 and 1, i.e., seasonal water areas. To evaluate the precision and recall of land, the same process is repeated. The coefficient of determination (R2 ) was calculated between the gap-filled water area time series and the documented water level. This allowed to assess the quality of the dataset and its ability to accurately reflect reservoir water levels over time.   4 Results 4.1 Validation with simulated JRC GSW data Based on the evaluation of simulated JRC GSW data, the trained model achieved an F1 score of 0.83 for water and 0.74 for land, with an occurrence range of 0 to 1 (Table 2  ), and are associated with TP=7,302,817, TN=4,487,273, FP=717,045, FN=2,274,470. To validate the model, random masks were used from various locations, resulting in an average of 45 % valid observations. Masking is only performed for the target month. Since the masking process involves randomly selecting from the JRC GSW, this level of masking closely resembles the actual gap-filling tasks for JRC GSW. At this level of masking, the proposed method is capable of generating a reasonable F1 score for both the majority and minority classes at an image level of size 256 × 256 (rather than pixel level). In order to assess the model's performance under more difficult conditions, its accuracy on pixels with an occurrence range between 0 and 0.93 was evaluated. The F1 score for both water and land was 0.74 in this case. The number of water and land pixels in the validation dataset was identical within this range (Section 2.1.2 ). As a result, the accuracy score of 0.84 at this range can be considered a reliable indicator of the model's performance. Remarkably, the model can accurately perform gap-filling using only ∼ 2 % of valid observations, which demonstrates its robustness (Table 2 ). Fig. 9   showcases successful examples of gap-filling in both seasonal water and land. The model accurately fills in the gap of seasonal areas. Permanent water or land is not displayed in the gap-filled image and JRC GSW to highlight the appearance of seasonal water or land.  4.2 Validation with independent reference The average performance of gap filling for water in the Sentinel-2 evaluation yielded an F1 score of 0.74. This score is quite strong considering that only seasonal areas were involved in the validation process. However, the score is slightly lower than the result obtained from the simulated JRC GSW data. This is partially due to the inherent detection errors present in JRC GSW (Fig. 10  ), which can result in lower accuracy in certain scenarios. The data quality of JRC GSW has an impact on the model's performance, particularly in the detection of water in complex scenarios involving snow, ice, and water with complex colors. The accuracy of JRC GSW at water boundaries has been reported to be lower as well (Pickens et al., 2020 ). One possible explanation for the performance drop on Sentinel-2 could be the difference in observation times between Sentinel-2 and Landsat. This difference could result in varying water extents, which may affect the accuracy of model predictions based on observed Landsat extent. The performance drop of the Sentinel-2 evaluation can also be attributed to the inclusion of more winter examples in the validation, and the quality of JRC GSW tends to be lower during this season. During this season, there is a greater likelihood of overlapping dates between data gaps in JRC GSW and cloud-free Sentinel-2 images, as Landsat is less available during this season. The evaluation of reservoir water levels indicates that the gap-filled water area time series is more accurate than the raw JRC GSW area time series (Fig. 11  ). The raw JRC GSW area time series shows poor correlation with water levels data due to contamination. However, it should be noted that Fig. 11  only demonstrates successful examples of regressing areas to water levels. In many cases, the reservoir area and water levels do not fit well to a linear regression model. Nevertheless, Fig. 11  demonstrates that the gap-filled dataset generally provides a more accurate representation of the reservoir water area time-series. These findings suggest that using the gap-filled data will enhance the precision of analysis and contribute to more reliable results.   5 Discussion 5.1 Evaluating the impact of temporal input length Using the entire JRC GSW time series (1984–2021) may not be necessary for gap-filling. This is because remote temporal dependency is likely weak, and including such data significantly increases the computational stress when performing global data filling. To help determine the optimal temporal length of input (i.e., N-2 in the input data shape N×256 × 256), integrated gradients was utilized. This neural network interpretation algorithm allowed to assess the sensitivity of the model output to inputs at different time steps, thereby enabling to select the most effective temporal length without compromising the effectiveness. Integrated gradients can evaluate the contribution of different input components to the prediction, or the sensitivity of the output to different input components (Sundararajan et al., 2017 ). Denote the function for predicting a single pixel as F : R  m × n × n   → R   , where x ∈ R  m × n × n      is the input and x  ′  ∈ R  m × n × n      is the baseline, typically a zero matrix. Integrated Gradients calculate the integral of gradients of a neuron to the input along the path from a given baseline to the input. That is, the attribution of each input to the output is calculated by observing the changes of output when input shifts from a baseline to the actual value:(3) I i approx   x   : = x i  - x i ′   m  ∑ k = 1  m  ∂ F x ∼     ∂ x ∼  i       x ∼  = x ′  + k m  x - x ′           where x i    is the i  -th input, a scalar. m   is the number of steps used to approximate the integral, which is 20 based on the recommendation. The degree of dependence on different point-in-time inputs is assessed when reconstructing a given sample, by aggregating attributions of input pixels at the same time step spatially. This method allows to evaluate the model's dependence on different time points of the input by training it with the full length of the temporal input. The attribution results indicate that remote temporal locations have minimal impact on the model's inference (Fig. 12  ). Therefore, a long temporal dependency is not necessary for filling gap pixels in seasonal water areas. Fig. 12  provides an example in which each image corresponds to a target time point. As the target time point shifts, the model's attention to the input at different time points also shifts. The model is sensitive not only to the target time point but also to the information preceding and following it. Information closer to the target time point is given greater weight. It is argued that a model input length of 10 years was optimal after observing the attribution results of different time step inputs.  5.2 The role of spatial cues in gap-filling accuracy The precision of gap-filling is heavily influenced by the accessibility of information within the same region and time frame. The emergence or recession of seasonal water pixels offers the most valuable data for gap-filling. In cases where there is a significant amount of information in seasonal water areas, achieving high accuracy in gap-filling becomes more feasible, leading to clear and precise water boundaries. As the available information diminishes, gap-filling becomes increasingly challenging. In extreme cases where no seasonal water pixels are observed, the model has been specifically trained to address such areas using only temporal information. This was accomplished by incorporating fully masked images into the training dataset. However, it is crucial to recognize that expecting high accuracy in fully masked images may not be practical. This limitation arises because the model is devoid of spatial cues and must rely exclusively on temporal cues to fill in the gaps. The validation results indicate that even with a high level of masking (e.g., >98 %), gap-filling performance remains robust, yielding F1 scores of 0.8 for water and 0.72 for land. However, the performance significantly declines when dealing with fully masked images.  5.3 Quality control and data uncertainty To address dataset uncertainty, a binary quality score is assigned to each 256 × 256 gap-filled block. The binary mask is positive when the 256 × 256 block has at least 2 % valid observations within the seasonal water areas and negative otherwise. This threshold was chosen based on the validation at this high masking level (Section 4.1 ). Although some areas with a high fraction of gap observations (>98 %) may not have been addressed, the proposed approach has significantly improved the amount of usable information compared to the raw JRC GSW data before filling the gap areas. By identifying the spatial and temporal locations of these low-quality fillings through the proposed quality score, data uncertainty in the proposed dataset has been substantially reduced. As the demand for precision in hydrological and climatological models grows, refining the approach to uncertainty is essential. Future endeavors might focus on developing probabilistic models or Bayesian networks to provide a more detailed representation of uncertainty, moving beyond binary quality scores to offer a spectrum of confidence levels for each filled block. It is essential to acknowledge that the high latitudes of the northern hemisphere pose a significant challenge due to the brief observation season, low solar zenith angles, and a scarce archive of data above 78° N (Pekel et al., 2016 ). As a result, filling gaps in data for these months becomes problematic, given the limited availability of observed information for those months across various years. Ensuring consistency in the time periods being compared across different years is vital for successful spatiotemporal gap-filling. Consequently, the effectiveness of gap-filling efforts in these regions remains notably inadequate which should be addressed in future research. The primary limitation stems from the inherent data uncertainties in the JRC GSW dataset. The spectral properties of water can vary significantly due to factors like chlorophyll concentration, total suspended solids, and colored dissolved organic matter, leading to uncertainties in water detection. The JRC GSW dataset's accuracy is also affected by the limited temporal resolution of the Landsat satellite, which can result in the underestimation of the extent of ephemeral flood processes. This, in turn, can impact the accuracy of the proposed gap-filled dataset, as the model is trained on the assumption that the maximum water body boundary in the JRC GSW represents the actual maximum boundary of water bodies on earth. Our method leverages the spatial–temporal correlation of water bodies, which is often determined by topographic conditions resulting in predictable spatial and temporal patterns. The simulated labels are generated based on these intrinsic correlations, which helps the model to learn and predict the dynamics of water bodies effectively. However, we recognize that relying on simulated labels to train our model might introduce certain biases and assumptions, potentially affecting the model’s performance and generalizability. While simulated labels provide a practical means to generate a large volume of training data, they inherently carry assumptions about the data generation process that may not fully capture the complexities of real-world observations. For instance, if the simulation process consistently underestimates the variability of seasonal water bodies, the model trained on such data might perform well on simulated validation sets but poorly on actual, more variable conditions. This could lead to overfitting to the specific patterns present in the simulated data.   6 Conclusions The study presented a novel self-supervised learning method tailored for addressing data gaps in the JRC GSW dataset, with particular emphasis on seasonal water areas. Achieving an F1 score of 0.83 for water and 0.75 for land by leveraging the spatio-temporal dynamics of water bodies. The research underscores the potential of self-supervised deep learning in geospatial data analysis. However, challenges persist, particularly in the high latitudes of the northern hemisphere, where data limitations compromise effective gap-filling. Additionally, inherent data uncertainties in the JRC GSW dataset, influenced by factors like spectral properties of water and limited temporal resolution of the Landsat satellite, could impact the accuracy of the gap-filled dataset. Future research can overcome the challenges and limitations in addressing data gaps in high latitudes by integrating data from multiple sensors, including optical, radar, and thermal satellites, can mitigate the limitations of any single data source. For instance, radar data can penetrate clouds and provide observations in conditions where optical sensors cannot. By addressing these challenges, future research can provide a more accurate and reliable representation of global water dynamics, particularly in underrepresented high-latitude regions.
1 Introduction Characterization of aquifer hydraulic properties plays a vital role in managing and protecting groundwater resources. These properties vary spatially at multiple scales, and direct measurements (Berg and Illman, 2011; Kontopoulos et al., 2020; McPhee et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2005 ) of these aquifer properties (e.g., hydraulic conductivity) are always limited due to the high cost. As a result, inverse approaches arise to estimate and map spatially varying properties through less costly measurements such as hydraulic heads or tracer concentrations (Carrera et al., 2005 ). All hydraulic tests (i.e., the classic aquifer test using Theis or Jacob’s solution) to derive aquifer properties are inverse modeling. Generally, inversion methods for this purpose include direct (Irsa and Zhang, 2012; Sagar et al., 1975 ) and indirect approaches. For instance, when solving a quadratic equation, the direct method involves using the discriminant without any iteration process, while the indirect method requires defining and minimizing an objective function that involves an iteration process (Weglein, 2017 ). Using a data assimilation (DA) framework is the most dominant method among the indirect methods. A DA-based framework usually consists of three components: (a) a hydraulic parameterized model representing the subsurface structure; (b) a forward model linking the hydraulic parameter inputs to the dynamic response (e.g., hydraulic head or solute concentration); and (c) a DA algorithm for parameter estimation (Linde et al., 2015 ). The classical geostatistical groundwater inversion algorithms Quasi-Linear Geostatistical Approach (QLGA) (Kitanidis, 1995 ), and the Successive Linear Estimator (SLE) (Yeh et al., 1996 ) used the DA framework. They consider the inverse problem a stochastic estimation problem: assuming the parameters are stochastic fields characterized by mean, variance, and covariance, representing prior information about the parameter’s variability and geologic structure. Then they incorporate head data for inversion. Many have proposed different inverse methods but ignore the issue associated with ill posedness of the inverse problem (Mao et al., 2013 ). Of course, collecting a large number of spatial observed data and reducing the dimension of model parameters are the ways of balancing the numbers of data and unknowns (Zhou et al., 2014 ). Collecting more data on hydrogeology problems is impractical due to high costs and technological limitations. On the other hand, reducing the parameter dimensionality leads to the representativeness issues of the estimated parameters (Wu et al., 2005 ), and creating effective parameters with artifacts (e.g., anisotropy, non-Fickian dispersion, and others) due to omitting detailed heterogeneities as discussed in (Wu et al., 2005; Yeh et al., 2015, 2023 ). To mitigate the inherent ill-posed nature of inversion problems in high-resolution characterization, incorporating additional datasets with non-redundant heterogeneity information and using a highly parameterized geostatistical model are promising. Hydraulic Tomography (HT) has been developed recently (e.g., Yeh and Liu, 2000 ) as a cost-effective method to characterize the spatial distribution of geological media properties. Its effectiveness has been widely demonstrated in numerical simulations (Wen et al., 2020 ), sandbox experiments (Illman et al., 2008, 2007 ; Wang et al., 2023a ), and field tests (Berg and Illman, 2013; Chen et al., 2019; Luo et al., 2022; Tong et al., 2021 ). HT is an extension of common sense: viewing an object from different angles and perspectives to gain details of the object. HT changes the pumping location in a well field and collects head changes in other wells. The recorded head data represent images of the aquifer heterogeneity from different perspectives: nonredundant information about the heterogeneity (Zha et al., 2018 ). After collecting many nonredundant images, HT interprets them using an inverse model for hydraulic parameter distributions in space. Highly-parameterized geostatistical inversion approaches have shown good promise in HT surveys (Cardiff et al., 2009; Cardiff & Barrash, 2011; Li et al., 2005; Xiang et al., 2009; Zha et al., 2018; Zhu & Yeh, 2005 ). Integrating hydraulic tomography inversion algorithms (e.g. QLGA and SLE) with a dimensionality reduction method can streamline the inversion process (Kitanidis and Lee, 2014; Zha et al., 2018 ). By leveraging their powerful nonlinear fitting and feature learning capabilities, deep learning (DL) methods have widely been applied in solving inverse problems. In DA framework, DL-based methods are usually used to enhance parameterized model identification and time-consuming forward simulation (Zhan et al., 2022 ). For example, to improve the hydraulicparameterized model, Laloy et al. (2019, 2018, 2017)  used variational autoencoder (VAE) and Spatial Generative Adversarial Network (SGAN) to generate geostatistical realizations. Both networks build a low-dimensional representation of the parameter field. Similarly, Mo et al. (2019)  employed a deep autoregressive neural network, which uses the spatially correlated hydraulic conductivity (K   ) field and the pollutant concentration snapshot at time t    as inputs to predict the distribution of pollutants at time t + 1   . Mo et al. (2020) , using an effective parameterized model and surrogate modeling technique, developed a convolutional adversarial autoencoder (CAAE) network to parameterize parameter fields and embed this network into the DL surrogate model. They applied this method to solve an inversion problem to estimate non-Gaussian hydraulic conductivity fields. Zhang et al. (2018)  applied DL to enhance the performance of a traditional DA method, the Ensemble Smoother (ES). Wang et al. (2021a)  pointed out that various optimization algorithms can be utilized as a new inversion method following a DL surrogate. Unlike traditional DA methods, Jardani et al. (2022)  used an encoder-decoder structure to directly learn the inverse operator from the hydraulic head responses to the hydraulic transmissivity fields. However, the data availability for groundwater inverse problems is sparse and limited, which limits the performance of DL methods that rely on big data. A theory-driven model (Moharir et al., 2017 ) with good interpretability is one possible way to deal with sparse and noisy groundwater data. In recent years, hybrid modeling approaches integrating theory-driven and data-driven methods (Wang et al., 2020 ) have attracted tremendous attention (Reichstein et al., 2019 ). As one of the hybrid modeling approaches, physics-informed neural networks (PINN) (Raissi et al., 2019 ) allow deep learning to be used in forward models (Wang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022 ), and inverse problems (Bandai and Ghezzehei, 2022, 2021; Depina et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2023; He et al., 2020; Tartakovsky et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2023b ), and discovering new physical laws (Song et al., 2022 ). Likewise, PINN incorporates prior knowledge, including governing partial differential equations (PDE), boundary conditions, and engineering experience as regularizations into its loss function. Theory-guided Neural Network (TgNN) that imposes physical constraints has better extrapolation capabilities than a data-driven deep neural network (DNN) such that it builds a more physically correct surrogate (Wang et al., 2020 ). Tartakovsky et al. (2020)  applied PINN to solve groundwater inversion for the first time. He et al. (2020)  extended this method to assimilate multiphysics measurement and solved subsurface transport problems. Although PINN has been able to solve a wide variety of physical problems (Cai et al., 2021; Daolun et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2021; Shadab et al., 2021; Wang and Perdikaris, 2021; Wight and Zhao, 2021 ), many issues remain in solving inverse problems. First, DL methods require many direct observations to derive the smooth estimated parameter field during training, while traditional methods, such as QLGA, SLE, and most DA methods (Kang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018 ), do not have such requirements. Guo et al. (2023)  applied PINN to solve the HT inverse problem for the first time, but at least 61 direct transmissivity measurements in the domain were needed to ensure the stability and accuracy of the results. Wang et al. (2021a)  demonstrated that the performance of TgNN-geo is unsatisfactory without hydraulic conductivity measurements. Li and Tartakovsky (2022)  proposed the PI-CKL-NN method for parameter estimation, given sparse measurements of the parameters and state. Besides, Huang et al. (2021)  pointed out that partial differential equations with a point source, expressed as a Dirac delta function, are difficult to solve by PINN. Xu et al. (2021a, 2021b)  proposed a weak form TgNN (TgNN-wf) as a surrogate model to solve this problem but found it is difficult to train without hydraulic conductivity measurements when a single constant-rate pumping well is considered. As a result, Zhang et al. (2022)  approximated the Dirac delta function by a multi-dimensional Gaussian density function. Using the PINN method, this study aims to solve a 2-D groundwater inverse problem with various data collection scenarios. Our study focuses on Gaussian random fields (GRF) and uses Karhunen-Loeve expansion (KLE) to represent a GRF in order to reduce the number of parameters to be identified. It combines PINN and KLE to estimate the hydraulic conductivity field from the hydraulic head data without hydraulic conductivity measurements. In the base experiment, we used a DNN to approximate the water head field and incorporated prior geostatistical information by using truncated KLE. A penalty term is added to the loss function to impose an inner boundary condition (source term) constraint to ensure mass conservation in a predefined collocation region. We analyze the performance of our method and discuss the sources of error by using two custom reference indicators in the base experiment. Next, we explored the stability and convergence of the method. In natural gradient flow (NG) test example, we pay more attention to the effect of loss weight because it is conducive to training DNN to approximate the water head field when the variation of the hydraulic gradient is small. Hydraulic tomography (HT) test examples investigate the stability and convergence of the training under different pumping data conditions. Lastly, we evaluate the performance of our method under different scenarios of outer boundary conditions, including unknown and erroneous ones.  2 Models and method 2.1 Groundwater flow equations Under steady-state flow conditions in a heterogeneous and isotropic confined aquifer system, there is a general governing equation in the absence of the source term:(1) ∇ · ( K ( x ) ∇ u ( x ) ) = 0      where u    is the hydraulic head;K    is aquifer hydraulic conductivity, which is dependent on the position within a geologic formation; ∇    is the gradient operator;x = ( x , y )    is spatial coordinate. When a no-flow boundary condition is considered, q N  = 0   .  2.2 Karhunen-Loeve expansions This study uses the Karhunen-Loeve Expansion (KLE) method to generate random fields with a given covariance function. Specifically, this study considers Y ( x ) = ln [ K ( x ) ]    as a random process expressed by Eq. (7) :(7) Y ( x )  = Y  ¯   + Y Â ́   ( x )       where Y  ¯      is the mean of the random field, x = ( x , y )    is the spatial coordinate in a 2-D space, Y Â ́   ( x )     is considered to be a stochastic process. Because the covariance function C Y  ( x 1  , x 2  )     is bounded, symmetric, and positive definite, it can be decomposed into (Zhang and Lu, 2004 ):(8) C Y  ( x 1  , x 2  )  = ∑ n = 1  ∞  λ n  f n  ( s 1  )  f n  ( s 2  )       where λ n     and f n  ( x )     are eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, respectively. The eigenvalues are rearranged in nonincreasing order. The mean-removed stochastic process Y Â ́   ( x )     can be expanded in terms of f n  ( x )     as:(9) Y  ′  ( x )  = ∑ n = 1  ∞  ξ n  λ n    f n  ( x )       where ξ n     are orthogonal Gaussian random variables with zero mean. The expansion in Eq. (9)  is called the Karhunen–Loeve expansion. Eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of a covariance function can be solved from the following Fredholm equation:(10) ∫ D  C Y  ( x 1  , x 2  )  f ( x 1  )  d x 1  = λ f ( x 2  )       where x 1  = ( x 1  , y 1  )     and x 2  = ( x 2  , y 2  )     are two points in a 2-D space. For some special types of covariance functions, eigenvalues and eigenfunctions can be found analytically. For this study, we assume a covariance function C Y  ( x 1  , x 2  )  = σ Y  2  exp ( - x 1  - x 2     η x   - y 1  - y 2     η y   )     in a rectangular domain D    that has a length L x     in x    direction and L y     in y    direction. The variance of lnK    is σ Y  2     and the correlation lengths in x    and y    directions are η x     and η y    , respectively. Next, the following equations are solved for the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions:(11) λ n  = λ n  ( x )   λ n  ( y )       (12) f n  ( x )  = f n  x , y    = f n  ( x )   x    f n  ( y )   y         where x    and y    represent two directions, respectively. λ n  ( x )      and f n  ( x )   x       are the eigenvalues and eigenvectors in x    direction, respectively, which can be calculated by:(13) λ n  x     = 2 η x  σ Y  2   η x  2  w n  ( x )      2  + 1       (14) f n  x     x    = 1 η x  2  w n  ( x )      2  + 1   L x  / 2 + η x     η x  w n  x     cos w n  x     x    + sin w n  x     x           where w n  ( x )      are positive roots of the characteristic equation:(15) η x  w n  x     - 1   sin ( w n  x     L x  )  = 2 η x  w n  x     cos w n  x     L         Because the covariance function is separable, in y    direction, the eigenvalues λ n  y       , eigenvectors f n  y     y       and the positive roots w n  y        can also be obtained by Eq. (13) , (14) and (15). Finally, the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions are obtained by multiplying the values in both directions, as expressed in Eq. (11) and (12) . Usually, KLE is truncated according to the decaying of eigenvalues λ n    . For instance, if the summation of the first N kl      eigenvalues dominate the summation of all eigenvalues (i.e. Eq. (9) ), then only the first N kl      eigenvalues are kept.
