Thus, Y  ′     can be decomposed into a finite number of terms as follow:(16) Y  ′  ( x )  ≈ ∑ n = 1  N kl    ξ n  λ n    f n  x        where N kl      is the number of terms needed for a given accuracy of Eq. (16) . After λ n     and f n  x       (n = 1 , 2  , ⋯ , N  kl     ) are calculated, a realization of the parameter field can be obtained simply by independently sampling a certain number of values from the standard Gaussian distribution. For convenience, we call these random variables the KLE coefficients ξ n     (n = 1 , 2  , ⋯ , N  kl     ) in Eq. (16) . To measure how well the truncated KLE approximates the original covariance, a norm of the normalized cumulated eigenvalues β = ∑ i = 1  N kl    λ i  / ∑ i = 1  N M   λ i       is used. Typically, positive infinity is denoted by a sufficiently large integer N M    . A larger β    close to one indicates a higher accuracy of the truncated KLE.  2.3 KLE-PINN network architecture 2.3.1 Basic architecture Fig. 1  a illustrates a feedforward Deep Neural Network (DNN), a point-to-point mapping network consisting of one input layer, several hidden layers, and one output layer. Each layer is composed of a certain number of neurons. In Fig. 1 a, the number of neurons in the input layer is 2, i.e., the 2-D spatial coordinate ( x , y )   . The number of neurons in the output layer is 1, i.e., the hydraulic head value u    at the given spatial coordinate. The number of neurons in each hidden layer varies, depending on the difficulty of the nonlinear fitting problem. Fig. 1 b shows the basic architecture of our KLE-PINN approach for solving inverse problems. The approach constructs a DNN (Fig. 1 a) to fit a water head field since DNN has powerful nonlinear fitting capabilities. We must emphasize that our network is a point-to-point mapping network. It does not perform an image-to-image regression task that transforms the hydraulic conductivity field into the water head field. Therefore, when we are interested in the water head value u    at a certain point, we only need to input the coordinates x = ( x , y )    to the network. The fitted DNN result is denoted as NN ( x ; θ )    (see Eq. (18)). On the other hand, the values of hydraulic conductivity K    at given spatial locations are obtained via the KLE. According to Eq. (13) , (14), and (15), the eigenvalues λ n     and the positive roots of the characteristic equation w n     are related to the correlation length η    and the variance σ Y  2    , the prior information needed for the KLE-PINN method. Therefore, only the KLE coefficients ξ n     in Eq. (16)  determines the pattern of lnK    field. We calculate the eigenvalues λ n     and the positive roots of the characteristic equation w n     in advance and obtain f n  ( x )     based on the input ( x , y )   . Finally, we reconstruct the parameter field via Eq. (16) . Similarly, by inputting the spatial coordinates, the corresponding parameter values can be obtained. Through automatic differentiation (AD) (Baydin et al., 2018 ) in deep learning, we obtain the spatial first-order and second-order derivatives of the state u    and the parameter K   . Thus, we can further construct physical constraints to be incorporated into the training process. In summary, simultaneously training multiple DNNs allows us to fully leverage HT data, while incorporating the KLE reduces the number of model parameters. Both aspects improve the efficiency of the inverse problem solving.Before training, we need to prepare the training dataset, as shown in the purple box in Fig. 1 b. We refer to the observed data (i.e. the observed water head data) as labeled data as previous PINN works do. Besides, we need to know the values of Dirichlet BCs, and the pumping flow rate Q p     (Eq. (4) and (5) ). In addition, we expect the residuals of Neumann BCs and PDE to be 0 (Eq. (2) and (6) ). After training using this information, DNN is a nonlinear estimator and the KLE coefficients are optimized. The DNN and the truncated KLE (i.e. Eq. (16) ) with the optimized KLE coefficients can estimate the values of the state u    and the parameter K    at any location in the domain, respectively. Observed head data from different pumping tests (e.g., HT surveys) can be included in the training. Section 4.5  explores the relationship between the performance of our method and the number of pumping tests (N pt     ).  2.3.2 Loss function We approximate u ( x )    with DNNs and estimate K ( x )    via Eq. (18): u ( x )  ≈ u ^  ( x ; θ )  = N N ( x ; θ )     and K ( x )  ≈ K ^  ( x ; ξ )  = K L E K  ( x ; ξ )     (18) where θ    denotes the DNN parameters, including weights and biases (w    and b   ); ξ    denotes the finite number of the KLE coefficients. They are all trainable. This study minimizes a loss function consisting of five parts (Eqs. (19) to (23) , below) during training. Los s u     in Eq. (19)  represents the data mismatch between observed and predicted heads, u ob  ∗      and u ^  ( x i  u  ; θ )    , respectively, at N u     observation wells at ( x ob   , y ob   )   . Los s diri      in Eq. (20)  denotes the deviations from the specified or observed heads u diri  ∗      at the Dirichlet boundaries of the domain, while Los s neum      in Eq. (21)  quantifies the deviations of the predicted hydraulic head gradients at the Neumann boundaries where the flux is zero. N d     and N n     denote the number of collocation points where the Dirichlet and Neumann BCs need to enforce, respectively. In Eq. (22) , Los s pump      describes the discrepancies between the specified pumping rate and those from the specified number of collocation regions (N pump     ) that must satisfy the governing equation Eq. (3) and (4) . We defined that a collocation region is enclosed by N pc      collocation points. These points divide the outer boundary of the square collocation region into a finite number of line segments. By integrating these line segments, we obtain our estimated flow rate value Q ^  p     through the numerical summation method. If the value of head at the pumped well is known, Los s pump      can be treated as Los s diri     . Los s pde      in Eq. (23)  ensures that the number of collocation points N c     in the domain satisfy the governing equation Eq. (1) and (2) .(19) Los s u  = 1 N u   ∑ i = 1  N u   u ^  x i  u  ; θ    - u ob  ∗      2      (20) Los s diri   = 1 N d   ∑ i = 1  N d   u ^  x i  d  ; θ    - u diri  ∗      2      (21) Los s neum   = 1 N n   ∑ i = 1  N n   ∂ u ^  n  ( x i  n  ; θ )   ∂ n      2      (22) Los s pump   = 1 N pump    ∑ i = 1  N pump    Q ^  p  - Q p     2  = 1 N pump    ∑ i = 1  N pump    ∮ C  K ^  ( x i  pc   ; ξ )  ∂ u ^  ( x i  pc   ; θ )   ∂ n   M d s - Q p     2      (23) Los s pde   = 1 N c   ∑ i = 1  N c   ∇ · ( K ^  ( x i  c  ; ξ )  ∇ u ^  ( x i  c  ; θ )  )    2       The loss function of our method is the sum of the weighted loss terms:(24) Loss = λ u  L o s s u  + λ diri   L o s s diri   + λ neum   L o s s neum   + λ pump   L o s s pump   + λ pde   L o s s pde        where λ u    , λ diri     , λ neum     , λ pump     , and λ pde      are the weights of each residual term. These weights should balance different sources of residuals and are commonly chosen by trial and error (Xu et al., 2021b ). Based on Eq. (24) , the trainable parameters θ    and ξ    can be found by minimizing the loss function as follow:(25) θ ^  , ξ ^    = arg min  θ , ξ   L o s s ( θ , ξ )       It should be noted that it is possible to calculate the loss according to Eq. (24)  when having only one set of pumping test data, i.e., N pt   = 1   , where N pt      is the number of pumping tests. As the pumping well locations and the water head fields change, the location of collocation points and collocation region also shifts accordingly. We present more details about the case setting in Section 3.2 . Therefore, to estimate one parameter field, we can construct multiple DNNs that approximate the water head fields corresponding to different sets of pumping test data (N pt   > 1   ), and we obtain the total loss Los s total      as follow:(26) Los s total   = ∑ i = 1  N pt    L o s s i       We use a separate DNN for fitting each head field. The choice of the network architecture and the specific values of the hyperparameters have a significant impact on the results, as shown in Fig. s1  of the supplementary materials . Notice that the data mismatch requires inputs of observed head values (u ob  ∗     ) at given locations ( x ob   , y ob   )    (Eq. (19) ). To construct the physical constraints, the head values (u diri  ∗     ) at location ( x diri   , y diri   )    where the Dirichlet boundary is (Eq. (20) ) and the pumping rate Q p     at the pumping location ( x p  , y p  )    (Eq. (22) ) are required to be known. In Section 5 , we will discuss whether the outer BCs constraint can be missing or incorrect. The loss functions (Eqs. (19) to (23) ) are different constraints to train the network. Specifically, Los s u     constrains the DNN with the observed hydraulic heads at observation well locations. Los s diri      and Los s neum      ensure the Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions of the classical governing equation are met. The inner boundary condition in the aquifer domain (a pumping rate) is enforced by Los s pump     . Lastly, the regions without source/sink must abide by the conservation of mass and Darcy’s Law constraints, i.e. the groundwater flow PDE constraint (i.e., Los s pde     ).    3 Numerical experiments 3.1 Base experiment Two-dimensional steady-state flow experiments are examined. Using KLE and given spatial statistics, we generate one random lnK    field as a reference field to evaluate inversion accuracy for this base experiment. This reference lnK    field is used as input to MODFLOW to derive the head fields due to different pumping tests. The domain size is 1280 [L   ] × 1280 [L   ] and is uniformly discretized into 1024 × 1024 grids of 1.25 × 1.25 L   , where [L   ] is any consistent length unit. The use of truncated KLE generates each grid’s K    values. The correlation lengths in the x    and y    directions are set to 256 [L   ], i.e., η x  = η y  = 256 [ L ]    . The mean of lnK    is 0 and the variance σ Y  2     is 1. We set β = 80 %   , which leads to a good approximation accuracy. According to this setting, we calculate N kl   = 71   , that is, we need to optimize the KLE coefficients  ξ n     (n = 1 , 2  , ⋯ , 71   ). The reference lnK    field is shown in Fig. 2  a. With the given reference lnK    field, the flow problem is solved using the MODFLOW-2005 software (Harbaugh, 2005 ) with the assistance of the FloPy package in Python (Bakker et al., 2016 ). A pumping rate of Q p  = 100 [ L  3  ]  / [ T ]     is used, where [T   ] any consistent time unit. The top and bottom boundaries are impermeable (Neumann boundary) and the left and right boundaries are constant-head (Dirichlet boundary) with a head equal to 0.0. Fig. 2 b shows 49 wells (well id = 0 to 48), evenly distributed across the domain. Pumping tests are performed sequentially in five selected wells at the center (well id = 24) and corners (well id = 8, 12, 36, 40). For each pumping test event, water is withdrawn at a constant rate from one of the five wells, and hydraulic heads are observed from the rest 48 wells as indirect measurements, i.e. N u  = 48   .  3.2 KLE-PINN implementation Our DNN network, approximating the water head field, has 6 hidden layers, and each layer has 20 neurons with the Tanh activation function(Goodfellow et al., 2016 ). Results of our investigation prior to this study confirmed that such a DNN network was sufficient to capture nonlinear relationships, so the discussion of the structure and hyperparameters of the DNN are omitted here. Besides defining the loss function in section 2.3 , we must also specify the collocation points and regions where the physical constraints, including the BCs and PDE constraints, are enforced. For this purpose, we set 400 collocation points uniformly in the upper and the lower boundaries for imposing the Neumann BCs and 4000 collocation points uniformly in the left and the right boundaries for the Dirichlet BCs (red and blue points in Fig. 2 c), i.e. N n  = 400    and N d  = 4000   . For the PDE constraints on the non-pumping region, we also sample uniformly except in the relax region: a square area with a side length of 120[L], and the pumping well is at its center. The size of this area was determined through trial and error. We find that the size of relax region may affect the inversion results If the area is too small, PINN may be challenging to train, while the inversion accuracy may reduce if the area is too large with too few collocation points. See Fig. s2  in the supplementary materials . To balance the computational cost and inversion accuracy, we uniformly sample 64 collocation points in both x    and y    directions except the relax region. Finally, 3819 collocation points are chosen to enforce the PDE constraint (pink points in Fig. 2 c), i.e. N c  = 3819   . To impose inner BC, for simplicity, we define that a collocation region is the same as the relax region. Each side of this square collocation region is divided into six segments, so we get 24 collocation points for one collocation region (gray points in Fig. 2 c), i.e. N pump   = 1    and N pc   = 24   . It should be noted that we can set multiple collocation regions for mass conservation. The effects of the size of this region on the inversion are similar to the relax region.. If there is no Los s pump      though setting up the relax region, we find the estimated parameter filed deteriorate rapidly and are not reversible. Some methods have been proposed to adaptively optimize the loss weights and the distribution of collocation points during the training process (Lu et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2021b ; Wang et al., 2022; Xiang et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022 ). However, these methods do not perform consistently well for our problem, so we use the constant loss weights and fixed collocation points obtained by trial and error. We set the weights of each loss term as follows: λ u  = λ diri   = λ neum   = 1.0   , λ pde   = 0.01   , λ pump   = 0.001   . The iteration number for achieving convergence varies with the weights of each term of loss, the number and the distribution of measurements and collocation points, and so on. In this study, we observed that the required number of iterations for most simulations is between 300,000 and 500,000 (the value of the loss function is about 10e-3 to 10e-4 at this time). Therefore, we set a hard stop criterion of 300,000 iterations, that is, we stop the training after 300,000 iterations even if the full convergence is not met. An epoch refers to one iteration that calculates Los s total      and optimize the trainable parameters. Most PINN training uses two optimizers: Adam optimizer followed by L-BFGS-B optimizer. However, we find that the convergence is not significantly improved by using the L-BFGS-B optimizer. Therefore, we only keep the Adam optimizer with a learning rate l r  = 0.001   . In all our cases, the impact of data noise has not been considered. Our KLE-PINN is programmed in PyTorch 1.7.1 (Paszke et al., 2019 ). All of the tests are run on a single NVIDIA GEFORCE RTX 3070 processor. For additional details about the computation time, please see Tabel s1 in the supplementary materials .  3.3 Evaluation metrics for estimation accuracy After training, the predicted water head fields (N N  i    ) from DNNs are compared with the reference water head fields from MODFLOW, and the estimated lnK    (K L E l n K     ) with the reference lnK    field, generated by KLE. We utilize the relative L2  error to evaluate the accuracy of our training results. All solutions involved in calculating relative L2  errors are on a 1024 × 1024 uniform grid. The relative L2  error of u    (e u    ) and the relative error of lnK    (e ln K     ) for the entire domain are calculated by:(27) e u  = ‖ N  N  i  ( x )  - h   i  ( x )  ‖   2  2  ‖  h   i  ( x )  ‖   2  2   , x ∈ Ω     (28) e ln K   = ‖ K L  E l n K   ( x )  - l n K ( x )  ‖   2  2  ‖ l n K ( x ) ‖  2  2   , x ∈ Ω      where h   i     is one of the reference head fields and N N  i     is the predicted head via DNN, l n K    is the reference lnK    field and K L E l n K      is the estimated lnK    field via KLE. In addition, the coefficient of determination R  2     are used to evaluate the results:(29) R u  2  = 1 - ‖  h   i  ( x )  - N N  i  ( x )  ‖   2  2  ‖  h   i  ( x )  - μ h  i  ‖   2  2   , x ∈ Ω     (30) R ln K  2  = 1 - ‖ l n K ( x )  - K L  E l n K   ( x )  ‖   2  2  ‖ l n K ( x )  -  μ KLE   ‖   2  2   , x ∈ Ω     where μ h  i     and μ KLE      is the mean of one of the reference hydraulic head field and the mean of the reference lnK    field, respectively. Besides, we define two other metrics. They are e forward      and e coupling     , as shown in Fig. 3  . Assuming that we already know the reference lnK    field, we only need to solve the forward modeling using KLE-PINN. We still use a loss function consisting of Los s u    , Los s diri     , Los s neum     , Los s pump     , and Los s pde      to train the DNN exclusively. We refer to the solution obtained as N N forward  i    . e forward      is calculated by comparing it with h   i     from MODFLOW:(31) e forward   = ‖ N  N forward  i  ( x )  - h   i  ( x )  ‖   2  2  ‖  h   i  ( x )  ‖   2  2   , x ∈ Ω      Thus, e forward      is an indicator to measure the relative L2  error from KLE-PINN forward model for predicting water head field without any input K    error (Fig. 3 ). Similarly, we use the lnK    fields obtained from the KLE-PINN inverse model as the input to MODFLOW to simulate the water head fields. These water head fields h  coupling  i     consider the errors due to the estimated K    field from KLE-PINN inverse model without forward predicting error from DNN since these heads are calculated directly from MODFLOW. By comparing N N  i     and h  coupling  i    , we obtain the metric e coupling     :(32) e coupling   = ‖ N  N  i  ( x )  - h  coupling  i  ( x )  ‖   2  2  ‖  h  coupling  i  ( x )  ‖   2  2   , x ∈ Ω      This indicator measures forward predicting error from KLE-PINN during inversion, reflecting whether the state variable u  and the parameter K  are tightly coupled during the optimization process. e coupling      has two uses. First, numerically, we certainly hope that it is as small as possible, indicating that the forward model in KLE-PINN has sufficient accuracy. Second, e coupling      can be used to compare with e u    . If e coupling      is constitutes the major part of e u     (note e coupling      is not necessarily smaller than e u    ), it indicates that the coupling error is the main source of error in KLE-PINN forward/inverse modeling.   4 Results of numerical experiments In this section, we first analyze the results of our base experiment that assimilates only one set of pumping test data. Next, we investigate the impact of weight initialization and discuss the stability and convergence of this method using many realizations of the K    fields. Finally, we compare the results under natural gradient flow (NG) condition and hydraulic tomography (HT) condition with our base experiment. 4.1 The predicted head fields Fig. 4  a illustrates the contour maps of the predicted and reference water head fields (red dash-dotted, black dashed contour lines, respectively) of the five pumping tests, while the hexbin map (Fig. 4 b) compares their values statistically. A hexbin map is similar to a scatter plot, but it shows the density of data points in a given area using hexagonal bins. The color of each hexagonal bin represents the number of data points that fall within it. The black dashed line is a one-to-one relationship between the predicted and the reference heads, while the red dashed line is a linear regressed relationship between them. Table 1   lists the calculated evaluation metrics for the base experiment. All of the hexbin maps exhibit trailing shapes at the large drawdown indicating significant deviations near the pumping wells. This is attributed to the relax region for the governing equation on the non-pumping grid and a limited collocation region for the inner BC (pumping area), which means that we have given up on accurately predicting the water head field in areas with very large hydraulic gradients. This tradeoff makes training easier and less prone to significant degradation of inversion accuracy. In some of our preliminary tests, it can be stated that the results worsened as the collocation points are setting away from the pumping well location and N c     decrease. Thus, we have chosen a proper buffer zone around the pumping well by balancing the training effort and accuracy, analogous to the adaptive grids around the pumping well in MODFLOW simulations. After excluding predefined relax region, we find that only one test had an e u     about 11 % (well id = 40), while the rest of the tests had an e u     below 5 %. This is consistent with the visualization plots (the last row of Fig. 4 a), which show a significant deviation of the fitted water head field away from the pumping well location, especially in the area near the bottom right corner. Next, we calculate e forward      to prove that e u     is already low enough. For the KLE-PINN forward model, since we find the result have already converged after 100,000 epochs, we calculate the reference metric e forward      at that point. We find almost all of e u     and e forward      are numerically equivalent (Table 1 ). A large e forward      indicates a poor fit of the water head field after applying the KLE-PINN forward model, which makes the inversion more challenging (well id = 36 and 40 in the base experiment). For this reason, we pay close attention to the fit of the water head field. In general, e u     can be composed of several parts: 1) error due to data noise; 2) fitting error due to the limited fitting ability of DNNs; 3) error caused by the inaccuracy of lnK    and the coupling error during the coupling of the state variable and parameter; 4) the lack of proper physical constraints; 5) the numerical calculation error of PINN, such as the truncation error of tensor calculation in DL, etc (Jagtap et al., 2020 ). We are concerned about the impact of the fourth factor, assuming that any other errors are negligible. The ideal training result should show that u    and K    are highly correlated, according to classical groundwater flow principles. e coupling      is a good indicator for characterizing variable coupling relationships. The process of calculating this indicator can be viewed as feeding the same input to the PINN and the numerical model that get two different head fields respectively and we generally assume that there is no coupling error between these two variables in using the numerical model. In the base experiment, e coupling      varies numerically, with the lowest relative L2  error reaching 2.65 % and the highest 5.39 %. All relative L2  error values are small, indicating that the coupling relationship between the two variables is relatively close. This indicator is not perfect because we know that the optimization trends of the two variables are not perfectly synchronized, so the corresponding e coupling      also changes throughout the whole training process. It is just a reference value for the degree of coupling of the two variables. Moreover, the other sources of e u     cannot be ignored entirely.  4.2 The estimated l  n  K     field Fig. 5  a shows the estimated lnK    fields and Fig. 5 b presents hexbin maps of the reference lnK    compared to the estimates. Table 1  also shows the results of the estimated  l n K   . Compared with the reference lnK    field (Fig. 2 a), all of the estimations capture the main pattern of the reference field. The mean of e lnK      is 55.12 % and the mean R  2     coefficient is 0.6822. These results are acceptable, since e coupling      is quite low, which means the estimated lnK    field can map to the water head field accurately with negligible forward error. See the results when inaccurate prior information (variances and correlation lengths) is used in Fig. s4  of the supplementary materials .  4.3 The stability and convergence of the method In this section, e u     and e lnK      during training process are analyzed instead of the loss values. Because we find the loss function oscillates during the middle and late stages of training, which happened similarly in solid mechanics (Haghighat et al., 2021 ). Each loss term can be minimized to a small value at the end of the training. We notice that the major components of the weighted loss function are λ pde   L o s s pde      and λ u  L o s s u    , while other parts of the loss have a very small proportion. Analyzing these loss values may not reveal whether the training results are satisfactory. However, we aim to achieve a specific threshold for the loss function that incorporates physical constraints appropriately. 4.3.1 Effects of initialization This section investigates the effects of weight initialization and initial guesses of KLE coefficients on the robustness of our method by selecting five random seeds in KLE. Fig. 6  a and 6b shows the e u     and e lnK      during the training, respectively. Each blue dashed line represents one of the results from five random seeds, and the solid line is the mean of the five lines. The mean and standard deviation of e u     are 4.96 % and 0.21 %, respectively, while the mean and standard deviation of e lnK      are 52.49 % and 3.23 %, respectively. The smaller e u     shows that the weight initialization of the DNN has minimal effect on the fitting of the water head field. This result also demonstrates that obtaining a good fitting of the head field is easier than reconstructing the lnK    field. This finding is mainly due to the massive number of trainable parameters of the neural network, which means that the degree of freedom of the DNN is very high. On the contrary, the initial guess of the KLE coefficients has a more significant impact on the results because the degree of freedom of the parameter field is greatly reduced. The initial e lnK      lies around 100 %, but the final e lnK      are all acceptable. If our guess of the initial KLE coefficients is far from the reference value, our method has difficulty finding the exact solution, as indicated by the top blue dashed line in Fig. 6 b. Otherwise, the inversion benefits from a good initial guess (the blue dashed line at the bottom in Fig. 6 b).  4.3.2 More realizations ofK    In this section, we examine the performance of our method under another four realizations of lnK    field. All five realizations (including the base one) of lnK    field and their statistics are shown in Fig. 7  . The results of the five pumping tests (Section 3.2 ) in the five realizations of lnK    fields are summarized in Fig. 8   as a scatter plot, where the x-axis is e u     and the y-axis is e lnK     . We observe a significant increase in both the mean relative L2  error and the standard deviation of the relative L2  error in this case, compared to our base experiment. The mean of e lnK      rises from 55.12 % to 67.96 %, and the standard deviation increases from 4.60 % to 14.48 %, possibly due to unsatisfactory training results, as evidenced by the points far from the lower left corner of Fig. 8 . Generally speaking, most of the points are close to the origin at the lower left corner, indicating that most of the training results are satisfactory. On the other hand, an ill-posed inverse problem with insufficient information (Mao et al., 2013 ) is impossible to yield the actual K    field. In the scatter plot of Fig. 9  , the two solid green points at the top represent two inferior results of twenty-five trials. Even though the observed water head filed fitting is very satisfactory, the differences between the K    estimates and true ones are large. This issue also exists in the other inverse modeling methods. As elaborated in Yeh et al. (2015)  and (2023), an iill-posed inverse problem always leads to the ‘effective’ hydraulic properties that satisfy a given observed head field, but they are not the actual K    field. For this reason, collecting more indirect observations by adding more observation wells is necessary, which is costly in practice. Otherwise, as elaborated in Yeh et al. (2015)  and (2023): use common sense to collect nonredundant indirect data cost-effectively using multiple sets of pumping test data (HT survey), as verified in Section 4.5 . Moreover, incorporating a certain amount of direct observations into the model can enhance its accuracy (supplementary material s Fig. s4 ) and stabilize its training process, as other studies have already demonstrated.   4.4 Case NG (Natural gradient flow) This section examines the performance of our method using heads from a natural gradient flow (NG). The term Los s pump      is omitted from Los s total     . All wells are observation wells, i.e. N u  = 49   . We set the left boundary condition as a constant head condition with 10[L] and other conditions remain unchanged (Section 4.3.2 ). Since DNN performed poorly in nonlinear fields with significant gradient variations, DNN is more likely to fit the head field well in natural gradient flow without the point source/sink. To avoid overfitting due to the smoother state field, we train for only 10,000 epochs. The loss weight λ pde     , controlling the strength of the regularization penalty about the governing equation has a more significant impact in this case. The loss weight value λ pde      varying from 0.01 to 1.0 are tested to evaluate the effect on the performance. Fig. 9 a shows the performance of the predicted water head, indicating that the predicted head fields closely agree with the reference ones, while Fig. 9 b and 9c show the reference and estimated lnK    field, respectively. The statistical comparison between different λ pde      is shown in Fig. 9 d. The estimations capture the approximate pattern, and the inversion accuracy of the natural gradient flow can also be satisfactory (Fig. 9 c and 9d). However, the best result, in this case, is also slightly inferior to our base experiment. e u     is about 2 % in all three scenarios. The lowest e lnK      achieved in the best result is 73.4 % (λ pde   = 1.0   ). As λ pde      increases, e u     slightly decreases and e lnK      slightly increases. DNN with stronger regularization produces a more linear approximation of the water head field (the last row of Fig. 9 a), and the corresponding estimated lnK    field also shows a smoother pattern (the last row of Fig. 9 c).  4.5 Case HT (Hydraulic Tomography) With five sets of pumping test data, we select various combinations of data sets for training. For convenience, we define the scenario using multiple pumping test data as MPT and the cases using a single pumping test data as SPT. N pt      refers to the number of pumping tests. The results of the SPT have been discussed in Sections 4.1 and 4.2 . Fig. 10  a shows that e u     is smaller in most MPT scenarios than the corresponding SPT, although the relative L2  errors are of the same magnitude. Fig. 10 b shows that the estimated lnK    fields of MPT are always more accurate than the results from using SPT data. Specifically, e ln K      in MPT is always smaller than the smallest relative L2  error among all SPT scenarios. Comparing the decrease of e u     and e ln K     , the decrease of e u     is less significant. Fig. 10 c shows that the estimated lnK    using five data sets reveals more details of the reference lnK    field.sett. Fig. 11   further illustrates the advantages of using the HT survey by showing the changes in e ln K      using different numbers of pumping tests (i.e., N pt     =1, 2, 3, and 5) as a function of epochs during training. A dashed line with color is the behavior of e ln K      based on head data from each test: when N pt   = 1    (SPT), there are five red dashed lines; when N pt   = 2    (MPT), ten blue dashed lines, and when N pt   = 3    (MPT), four green dashed lines, and the corresponding colored solid lines are their mean. When N pt   = 5   , there is only one, which is its mean (the black solid line). The mean of e ln K      red solid line is the greatest, followed by the blue solid line, the green solid line, and the black solid line, respectively. This result confirms that the estimates are improved by fusing head data from the increase of N pt     . At the end of the training, the scattering and mean of e ln K      decreases as N pt      increases. Notes that the difference between N pt   = 3    and N pt   = 5    is marginal. The mean e ln K      decreases from 25.56 % to 22.02 %, a relatively small reduction, indicating further improvements with the increasing N pt      is unlikely because various facts, such as effects of ill-posed and e coupling     , are always present. Another way to evaluate whether the parameter fields are accurately estimated is to predict independent pumping test data, as shown in Fig. s4  of the supplementary materials . In this section, we conducted further testing on specific cases (N pt   = 1    and N pt   = 5   ) utilizing the ESMDA (Emerick and Reynolds, 2013 ), a widely used geostatistical inverse algorithm. Our testing employed a 64 × 64 grid, as a denser grid would have imposed a substantial computational overhead during the execution of the numerical forward model. Detailed configurations for the ESMDA implementation are outlined in Table s2  of the supplementary materials . The results indicate that the runtime of ESMDA, primarily influenced by the number of assimilations and ensemble size, is relatively brief. This model can solve this inverse problem from just a few minutes to about a half hour when using a CPU (Inter Core i7-10700). Nevertheless, the final estimations generated by ESMDA are not as accurate as those obtained through the KLE-PINN method (Table s2  and Fig. s6  of the supplementary materials ).   5 Effects of boundary conditions 5.1 Case with missing boundary conditions Specifying accurate BCs or their locations for field sites is difficult (Liu et al., 2020; Zha et al., 2014 ). Therefore, we set up this case without knowing the boundary conditions, which can be accomplished by removing Los s diri      and Los s neum      from Los s total      in our approach. Besides, the distribution of collocation points for Los s pde      is set in the area of well distribution. The reference case for investigation is the same as the case in Section 4.3.2  when well id = 24 (not HT). Fig. 12  a is the comparison of e ln K      and e u     between the baseline and the missing-BCs scenarios. Fig. 12 b is one of the visualizations of the predicted u    field, and Fig. 12 c is one of the visualizations of the estimated lnK    field. To better illustrate the inversion results, we have divided the domain into two parts for evaluation metrics calculation and visualization purposes: the center part, distributed with observation wells, and the edge part, without observation wells. We have adjusted the color bar to the same range for a better visual comparison. The results of the approximated head field close to the edge are worse in the Scenario without BCs. As shown in Fig. 12 a, the red points are positioned more toward the right than the light red data points. It means that e u    , which accounts explicitly for relative L2  errors near the boundaries, increase significantly. Other relative L2  errors did not change significantly, suggesting that our method can still effectively solve the inverse problem without boundary condition information. The constant head boundaries (the left and right boundaries) can even be roughly inferred (Fig. 12 b). This result is because our indirect measurements implicitly contain information about the BCs, so the predicted head field can be reasonably extrapolated through the limited indirect observations. As shown in Fig. 12 c, the estimated lnK    field has only mapped the approximate pattern, which was also reported by (Zha et al., 2014 ).  5.2 Case with wrong boundary conditions In this section, we intentionally used incorrect BCs information to test our method. We assigned the boundary conditions incorrectly, namely, a constant head boundary (head value is 0.0) at the top and bottom and a no-flow boundary at the left and right. The baseline is the same as in Section 4.3.2  when well id = 24 (not HT). Fig. 13  a is the statistical comparison of e u     and e ln K      between the baseline and the wrong-BCs scenario. Fig. 13 b is one of the visualizations of the predicted u    field, and Fig. 13 c is one of the visualizations of the estimated lnK    field. The accuracy of our parameter inversion method decreases a lot after being given the wrong BCs information because the incorrect information directly and severely impacts the fitting of the water head field. As shown in Fig. 13 b, the DNN tends to fit the upper and lower boundaries as constant head boundaries and the left and right boundaries as impermeable due to the incorrect boundary condition information. When there is conflicting information instead of lacking information, parameter inversion will depend on the relative influence of the BCs constraint and the data mismatch. Our approach tries to satisfy both constraints. If the physical constraints of BCs have a strong effect, e u     at the edges is likely to be even great. As shown in Fig. 13 c, the estimated lnK    fields, both in the central region and near the edges, demonstrate notable disparities from the reference. Based on the above two cases, we still see the significant advantages of KLE-PINN in the unclear boundary conditions information. With unknown or inexact BCs, a good inversion result can be maintained by not using the BCs constraint entirely or reducing the impact of the BC constraint, such as reducing the weight λ diri      and λ neum     . The water head fitting was significantly better in the region where observation wells were distributed than in other regions. Therefore, the estimated lnK    field captures the main pattern of the spatial heterogeneity of the hydraulic conductivity. In contrast, the traditional inversion framework that relies on a finite element or finite difference groundwater model cannot separate the BC constraint from equation constraints, nor assign different fitting weights for them. For instance, in the SLE algorithm, a reliable forward model is typically employed to simulate the groundwater system. Boundary conditions, as one of the definite solution conditions, are indispensable. If the boundary conditions are omitted or incorrectly defined, it can lead to erroneous simulation results, no matter in conceptual analysis or numerical simulation (Franke and Reilly, 1987 ). However, our method demonstrates remarkable flexibility in dealing with this limitation because the inherent advantage lies in the separability of the physical constraint components.   6 Limitations of current work Many aspects of our study deserve to be further explored. Keeping the balance of each loss term is essential during training, which keeps the impact of regularizing physical constraints in a suitable range. The locations of collocation points, regions, and loss weights are fixed throughout the training process and do not adapt to the training conditions. Nevertheless, these settings achieve acceptable inversion performance. Specifically, the data mismatch is used as the main driving force to guide the training direction and keep the training stable, allowing the approximating of the head field to rely more on indirect observations. The physical constraints are only used as an auxiliary force. Future research can focus on improving the efficiency and stability of inversion. The use of the truncated KLE makes the inversion easier, but with the cost to be limited to the second-order stationary random field. The PINN method could be combined with other deep learning methods, such as GAN, to deal with more challenging reality (e.g., non-stationary random field). Lastly, while different inverse modeling approaches have different advantages, this study confirms common sense: collecting nonredundant data from different perspectives--tomography survey. Moreover, we promote exploiting natural events as hydrogeophysical tomographic surveys for basin-scale aquifers (Yeh et al., 2008 ).  7 Conclusions We apply the KLE-PINN method that combines PINN and KLE to solve inverse problems without direct measurements of hydraulic parameters. A finite number of KLE coefficients are set to be trainable to reconstruct the hydraulic conductivity field. Utilizing DNNs is to simulate the different head fields generated from a single pumping test, natural gradient flow (NG), and hydraulic tomography (HT) survey. In this study, our main contributions and discoveries are:(1) KLE-PINN can solve inverse problems under different data collection scenarios without direct measurement. Karhunen-Loeve expansions can play a role in smoothing hydraulic conductivity. Therefore, the performance is satisfactory even if hydraulic conductivity measurements are unavailable.  (2) Building upon our approach, we have the capability to disentangle the sources of error in the inversion problem. Our error analysis endeavors to quantitatively quantify the components of error. It is an initial exploration in this domain. Such error analysis also facilitates the comprehension of the behavior of PINN, thereby providing potential avenues for refining the model to achieve more accurate solutions.  (3) Our method verifies the superiority of utilizing multiple pumping test data (HT) over data from a single pumping test. With the constraint of more nonredundant observed head data, the convergence speed of training and the final convergence accuracy is improved, and the training instability is suppressed. However, we find the benefit of including more pumping tests with the same number of observation wells decreasing, indicative of non-uniqueness issues of ill-posed inverse problems.  (4) KLE-PINN can easily investigate cases where BCs are unknown. The inherent advantage of our method lies in the separability of the physical constraint components. It also shows that the location and type of possible boundaries can be roughly inferred from the inversion when missing BCs.
1 Introduction The stable isotopic method for investigating the hydrological cycle began in the 1960s, initiated by the pioneering works research of Craig (1961)  and Dansgaard (1964) . Stable water isotope analysis relies on interpreting isotope ratios (δ18 O, δ2 H) and deuterium excess (d-excess, d=δ2 H−8×δ18 O; Dansgaard, 1964 ), proving effective in identifying water origin, mixing processes, residence time, and flow paths (Dinçer et al., 1970; Kendall and McDonnell, 1993, 2012; Ingraham, 1998 ). The relationship between latitude, elevation, and temperature to stable water isotopes is well-established (Dansgaard, 1964; Friedman et al., 1964 ). These isotope ratios are widely used to investigate large-scale water cycles across surface water, groundwater, and precipitation compartments (Lambs, 2000; Dalai et al., 2002 ). Stable water isotopes within the same area's hydrological compartments can provide insights into infiltration contributions to subsurface aquifers (Krishnamurthy and Bhattacharya, 1991; Ingraham, 1998 ). With freshwater stress projected to rise in India, understanding water sources and processes is crucial for effective water management (Gupta and Deshpande, 2005 ). In India, extensive research has focused on larger river systems like the Ganges, Yamuna, and Indus, highlighting the spatial and temporal variations in stable isotopic ratios (Ramesh and Sarin, 1992; Pande et al., 2000; Dalai et al., 2002; Rai et al., 2016; Lone et al., 2022 ). Despite these extensive studies, there remains a research gap regarding the stable isotopic analysis of smaller river systems (drainage area < 10,000 km2 , Milliman and Syvitski, 1992 ; Milliman et al., 2017 ), particularly in the Western Ghats of Karnataka and Kerala. While some studies have effectively explained water cycle mechanisms using stable isotope ratios in this region (Tripti et al., 2013, 2016, 2019; Saranya et al., 2020 ), baseline studies on stable water isotopes are lacking for many west-flowing river systems in the Western Ghats. Most of the rivers in the region are highly regulated through damming. Notwithstanding this, the aspect of damming is seldom considered. As rivers act as important sources of water, numerous dams have been built across rivers for the past century for various purposes such as electricity, irrigation, and recreation (Tahmiscioğlu et al., 2007; Poff and Schmidt, 2016; Maavara et al., 2020 ). These infrastructures have significantly altered the natural flow of rivers globally, with approximately 66 % of rivers' natural flow being restricted by dams and reservoirs (Zhang et al., 2019; Maavara et al., 2020 ). This alteration has prompted extensive research into their impacts on the hydrological cycle. One notable impact is reservoir-based evaporation. Reservoir-based evaporation has caused 5 % additional water loss in global river water flow (Shiklomanov, 2000; Lehner et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2021 ). Especially in seasonal rivers, dam construction significantly alters the hydrodynamics of river catchments. Understanding the effect of the dams in hydrological cycles largely includes studies on dam-induced evaporation and groundwater-surface water interactions within the dam area. Globally, such studies have been more focused on larger river systems (Marengo, 2006 ; Bastawesy et al., 2015 ; Négrel et al., 2016 ; Vanplantinga et al., 2017 ; Wang et al., 2019 ; Jiang et al., 2021 ). Nonetheless, even in small river systems, the local climate can be affected by damming, where evaporated local moisture from reservoirs can create a pseudo-elevation effect (Saranya et al., 2021 ). A noteworthy study in the Western Ghats rivers of Kerala has highlighted the impact of reservoirs and drought on water cycles, emphasizing the need to consider the damming effect in river catchment studies (Saranya et al., 2020 ). To address this research gap, we selected a small Western Ghat river with two dams across its length. A huge reservoir situated within the catchment covers 65 % of the whole catchment area (Durbude and Purandara, 2005 ). The present study aims to understand i) the seasonal and temporal variations in isotopic signatures, ii) the interaction between groundwater, river water, and rainwater in the catchment, iii) the effect of elevation on isotopic signatures, and finally, iv) address the impact of damming on the water cycle process in the catchment. By focusing on these aspects, this study seeks to contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of hydrological processes in small river systems, addressing the significant yet often overlooked impacts of dam construction.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The Sharavati river basin covers an area of about 3040 km², and the river originates at Ambutheertha, at an elevation of 656 m above mean sea level (amsl). It traverses through two districts of Karnataka (Shimoga and Uttara Kannada) before debouching to the Arabian Sea ( Fig. 1 ). Stretching over 128 km, the river is one of the important rivers of the Western Ghats system. The annual rainfall ranges from 2000 to 4000 mm in the catchment. Notable tributaries include Nandihole, Harlihole, Mavinahole, Nagodihole, and Haridhravdhi (Ramachandra et al., 2012, 2017 ; Water Resources Department, Karnataka, 2019; Amrish et al., 2022 ). Unlike other west-flowing rivers in Karnataka, the downstream section of the Sharavati river remains relatively untouched by human activities (Amrutha et al., 2023 ). The predominant rocks in the basin are Peninsular gneiss, laterite, schist, and greywacke (Bhukosh, ). These units of rocks are mainly from the Bababudhan, Chithradurga, and Peninsular Gneisic Complex group of rocks (Fig.S2). Two major dams, the Linganamakki Reservoir and the Gersoppa Dam, are situated within the Sharavati river catchment.  2.1.1 Linganamakki reservoir Linganamakki Reservoir is an earthen dam with a maximum height of 51.8 m (Setty and Rau, 1967 ). The dam is situated in the midstream of the Sharavati river (Fig. 1 ). The dam's catchment area is about 1992 km2 , which is 65 % of the total basin area of the river basin (Durbude and Purandara, 2005 ).  2.1.2 Gersoppa dam Gersoppa Dam is situated downstream of the Sharavati river (Fig. 1 ). The dam has been functional since 2001 (Ramachandra et al., 2017 ). The discharge rate from the dam is estimated as 3.4 km3 /y (Karnataka Power Corporation, 2020; Amrish et al., 2022 ).   2.2 Evaluation of seasonal and spatial variation in isotope signatures River water, groundwater, and rainwater samples were collected seasonally from the Sharavati river catchment. The surface and groundwater samples were collected from the source to the mouth of the river (Fig. 1 ). Forty-two surface water samples were collected for four seasons (Pre-monsoon 2019, monsoon 2019, post-monsoon 2019, and post-monsoon 2018). Twenty-nine groundwater samples were collected for three seasons (Pre-monsoon 2019, monsoon 2019, post-monsoon 2019-  Table.1  and Table. S2 ). The major rainfall events happened during the time of sampling were sampled from Gersoppa (R8) during monsoon season. Samples were collected in 30 ml LDPE (Low-Density Polyethylene) bottles and glass bottles by filling them to the brim. The sample bottles for isotopic analysis were then tightly sealed using parafilm tapes (to avoid evaporative fractionation) and kept under ambient temperature until the measurements. Basic parameters were measured in situ using the Hach multi-parameter kit. Isotopic measurements were made at the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad, India. The stable water isotopic ratios have been measured using an isotope ratio mass spectrometer (Delta V plus Thermo Scientific). The method followed was the standard gas equilibration method. For the δ18 O and δ2 H measurements, 300 μL of water was equilibrated with CO2  (or H2 ) for 16 hours (or 1 hour), after which the equilibrated gas was analyzed for its isotopic ratio of 18 O/16 O (or 2 H/1 H) (Lone et al., 2022 ) The analytical results were reported as delta (δ) values relative to Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water (V-SMOW).δ18 O, δ2 H= [(Rample /RSMOW )-1]x 1000(a)    Rsample  is the ratio of the heavy to light isotope in the sample and RSMOW  is the ratio of the heavy to light isotope in the Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water.  2.3 Assessment of interaction between groundwater, surface water and rainwater The seasonal isotopic signatures of surface water, groundwater, and rainwater were plotted in a cross plot of δ18 O vs δ2 H to assess the interaction of these compartments in the hydrological cycle. The global, local meteoritic water lines and local evaporative lines were also plotted in the same figure. The Global Meteoritic Water Line (GMWL,Craig ,1961)  was plotted using the regression line equation (b).δ2 H=8 × δ18 O+10(b)    The Local Meteoric Water Line (LMWL) was adopted from Kumar et al., (2010) . As a water pool evaporates, its isotopic composition changes due to kinetic fractionation and deviates from the LMWL along an Evaporation Line (EL) with a lower slope (Clark and Fritz, 1997 ). Thus, the EL is determined by extrapolating the regression line that connects the water samples with a lower slope to LMWL.  2.4 Estimation of elevation effect, d-excess, line conditioned excess and evaporative loss from reservoirs 2.4.1 Quantification of elevation effect in the catchment The elevation effect in the catchment was quantified using the simple linear regression method. The statistical analysis was performed in Microsoft Excel 365. The dependent variable was the δ18 O value, and the independent variable was elevation. The elevation effect was calculated for 100 m per elevation.  2.4.2 Estimation of d-excess and line-conditioned excess The d-excess is a function of the isotopic compositions of oxygen (δ18 O) and hydrogen (δ2 H) in water (Dansgaard, 1964 ). This was calculated based on the formula (c).d-excess = δ2 H − 8 × δ18 O(c)    The d-excess parameter was initially developed to understand the deviation of precipitation from the global linear relationship of δ2 H = 8 × δ18 O+10. Thus, the d-excess is traditionally used to contain the moisture source (Gat and Carmi, 1970; Celle-Jeanton et al., 2001 ), raindrop evaporation below the cloud base in the unsaturated air column, or precipitation formation under supersaturated conditions (Araguás-Araguás et al., 1998; Rozanski et al., 1993 ). d-excess in surface water bodies can indicate the evaporation processes and mixing of water from different sources (Gonfiantini, 1986 ). However, the d-excess estimated using the slope and intercept value of the GMWL may not be suitable for understanding the local hydrometeorological processes of a region depending on the deviation of LMWL from the GMWL. Landwehr and Coplen, (2006)  developed a new parameter (line conditioned excess) to accommodate the deviation of LMWL from GMWL.lc-excess= δ2 H- a x δ18 O-b(d)    where 'a' and 'b' are the slope and intercept of the LMWL, respectively. The lc-excess parameter is utilized in the current study to understand the evaporation signatures as the local meteoric water line deviates from the GMWL regarding both the slope and intercept (δ2 H = 7.78×δ18 O+11.32, Kumar et al., 2010 ). A negative lc-excess value denotes the deviation of the water sample from the LMWL due to evaporative fractionation.  2.4.3 Estimation of evaporative loss from reservoirs The evaporative loss ratio from the reservoirs is estimated using the Hydrocalculator, which facilitates the simpler estimation using the stable isotope data following the equation (Skrzypek et al., 2015 ); f =  1 − ( δ − δ  *   )  ( δ  0   − δ  *   )        1 / m     Here, f  is the evaporation loss ratio, δ is the measured δ18 O and δ2 H for the reservoir water, and δ 0   is the isotopic signature in the stream water before the impediment with the reservoir, δ* is the limiting isotopic enrichment factor, and m is the enrichment slope (Welhan and Fritz, 1977 ). The rainfall isotopic composition was derived from the intersection point of the local evaporation line (LEL) to the local meteoric water line (LMWL).    3 Results and discussions The stable isotopic ratios of oxygen and hydrogen (δ18 O and δ2 H values) in river water and groundwater samples of the catchment are given in the Table 1. , along with some basic physico-chemical parameters, and the rainwater isotopic composition is provided separately in  Table 2 . The average pH of the river water was 6.86, and the groundwater was 6.09. Groundwater is more acidic compared to river water. This might be due to the strong interaction of the rocks (peninsular gneiss, laterite, schist, and greywacke) with the aquifers compared to the rivers (Appelo and Postma, 2005 ). The increase in acidic nature (5.72) observed in the monsoon season of the groundwater indicates the impact of precipitation along with the rock-water interactions. The average groundwater EC was 130.47 µS/cm, and river water was 85.28 µS/cm. The slightly high EC in groundwater might be due to the leaching of more ions from the aquifer systems. The higher concentration of ions in groundwater compared to river water in the river catchment substantiates this observation. The lowest pH (4.9) in groundwater is observed at Tumari (GW5), and the highest pH was recorded at Jog fall (GW8) during the pre-monsoon season. In the river water samples, pH ranged between 5.7 and 7.54. The lowest EC observed for groundwater was 28.9 µS/cm at Tumari (GW5); for river water, 14.46 µS/cm at Shamsi (R11). Even though the average groundwater EC (130.47 µS/cm) was slightly higher than river water EC, the physico-chemical parameters are more or less similar. It is evident from the EC and other physico-chemical parameter values that groundwater and river water compartments interact spatially and temporally, thus shaping the local hydrological cycle. 3.1 Temporal and spatial variations of δ18 O and δ2 H in river water and groundwater of the catchment River water samples showed greater variations compared to groundwater signals both spatially and temporally (      Figs. 3 to 8 ), which is observed elsewhere (Gupta et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2014 ). Surface water samples are more prone to evaporation than groundwater samples because of their exposure to the atmosphere, and they readily undergo more kinetic fractionation than groundwater samples (Manu et al., 2023 ). Spatially, river water samples for δ18 O and δ2 H were high in the midstream region of the catchment during the pre-monsoon season. Due to the heavy seasonal rainfall, significant spatial variations were not observed during the monsoon season in the catchment. The location R4 in pre-monsoon 2019 showed the catchment's highest δ18 O value (1.2 ‰). In a river system like Sharavati, where the Linganamakki reservoir exists, the surface water is more vulnerable to evaporation, especially the sampling point within the reservoir (Li et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019 ). The location R4 was situated in the Linganamakki reservoir (Figs. 6 to 8 ). However, Groundwater sample GW8 (downstream), in pre-monsoon season 2019, documented δ18 O of 0.07 ‰ (Fig. 6 ), which is an outlier compared to the rest of the groundwater samples in the catchment. The location GW8 (Fig. 1 ) has numerous N-S trending faults (Subramanian and Ramesh, 2009 ; Kale, 2010 ), which might have facilitated the seepage of evaporated water from the Linganamakki reservoir. Seasonally, river water samples have shown variations in δ18 O values. The pre-monsoon samples were slightly enriched in heavier isotopes. The prevailing climatic conditions (Figs. 2 and 5 ) during the pre-monsoon of 2019 might have contributed to the observed increase in evaporation of surface water, resulting in the enrichment of heavier isotopes. The location Gersoppa LTM (R9) recorded the lowest δ18 O values (-3.6 ‰). The combination of the physiographic setting and the Linganamakki Reservoir, which acts as a water barrier, significantly facilitates Mavinahole (R4) in experiencing greater evaporative loss. The majority of Western Ghat rivers are heavily regulated by dams on their river course. The construction of dams has changed the water cycling in river basins across the globe (Wildi, 2010; Luo et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, the monsoon season samples were depleted in δ18 O with an average of −1.7 ‰ (Fig. 3 ). The lower value of δ18 O recorded during the monsoon season can be attributed to the dilution effect exerted by the intense monsoon rainfall (Fig. 7 ). The δ2 H values in groundwater and river water samples have shown a similar trend as δ18 O. The Mavinahole (R4) showed the highest δ2 H (11.5 ‰) composition (Fig. 4 ) in river water, and it was the same location where the highest δ18 O was observed. Similarly, the lowest δ2 H in river water samples (-18.6 ‰) was recorded at the same location (Gersoppa LTM-R9) where the lowest δ18 O was observed (Fig. 4 ).  3.2 Interaction of groundwater, surface water and rainwater and source identification The hydrological cycle of a watershed is highly significant because of its potential role in controlling the ecological and social aspects of the catchment. In the current study, most of the river and groundwater samples were clustered around the same region in the cross-plot (Fig. 7 ). However, the pre-monsoon season's surface water and groundwater samples fell away from the cluster of samples. The general trend of clustering of the plot refers to the humid vapour source in the catchment area (IAEA, 2000 ). Furthermore, the pre-monsoon samples of both river and groundwater represent more humid conditions and evaporative loss in the isotopic signals. The rainwater samples in the cross-plot exhibit low δ18 O values, forming a distinct cluster. This indicates that the particular events resulted from a depression/cyclone system (Good et al., 2014; Rahul et al., 2016; Saranya et al., 2018 ). The total rainfall in the 2019 monsoon reached approximately 4376 mm, marking a 44.72 % increase compared to the previous year's monsoon (Karnataka Power Corporation Limited, 2020; Amrutha et al., 2023 ). The rainwater samples were collected during one of the peak rain events of the monsoon season. The direct influence of rain has been observed in a river water sample collected soon after the event. This particular sample, Gersoppa_LTM (R9), fell close to the rainwater cluster in the Fig. 7 , indicating the direct influence of rain events. Overall, the basin's water source can be attributed to precipitation. Both groundwater and surface water were of meteoritic origin. This observation can be drawn from the cross plot of δ18 O and δ2 H, where the groundwater and river water samples fall close to LMWL (Saranya et al., 2020 ). Interestingly, the groundwater sample of Jog falls had evaporation signatures compared to the other samples. This could be due the recharging of surrounding aquifers through the local geological faults (Boulton et al., 2017; Olaka et al., 2022 ). Additionally, no visible correlation between well water depth and isotopic values was observed in groundwater samples (Fig. S3 ). Both river and groundwater samples showed similar isotopic signatures in monsoon seasons. Compared to post-monsoon 2018, the river water samples are more depleted in post-monsoon 2019. This could be due to the high amount of rain received during the previous monsoon (Fig. 2 ) and the damming effect. It is possible to draw a general conclusion that there is a contribution from river water to groundwater in monsoon seasons and in non-monsoon seasons, especially in pre-monsoon seasons groundwater to river water. The groundwater-surface water interaction model roughly (Fig. S1 ) gives an idea about the scenario. This is a general pattern of small Western Ghats rivers in Karnataka in monsoonal and non-monsoonal seasons (Tripti et al., 2016 ).  3.3 Elevation effect in the catchment The elevation effect on stable isotopic signatures is well-established (Clark and Fritz, 1997; Scholl et al., 2009 ). Elevation is one of the important factors that influence the spatial and temporal distribution of oxygen isotopes in precipitation (Song et al., 2020 ). The gradual decrease in the values of δ18 O in rainfall with the increase in the altitude is termed the altitude or elevation effect (Dansgaard, 1964; Friedman et al., 1964 ). A linear decrease in δ18 O with increasing altitude is observed in major rivers across the world (Poage and Chamberlain, 2001; Ramesh and Sarin, 1992 ). The effect of elevation on oxygen isotopes in a riverine system can be influenced by various factors such as precipitation, moisture source in higher altitudes, and temperature (Rozanski et al.,1992; Gat., 1996; Yao et al., 2013 ). The heavier 18 O gets depleted more easily compared to 16 O due to orographic levitation and cooling in precipitation (Yao et al., 2013 ). If the river is directly fed by precipitation, the reflection of the elevation effect will be observed in the surface water as well (Yao et al., 2013 ). Our results do not show a substantial variation of values of δ18 O with the altitude ( Table 3 ). Few other studies conducted from the Western Ghats region have observed similar observations (Tripti et al., 2016 ; Lambs et al., 2011 ; Tripti et al., 2019 ). Lamb et al., 2011 attributed the absence of a significant elevation effect to the role of mist formation at higher altitudes. The peaks up to 1900 m amsl in the Western Ghats region (Mullayanigiri) did not exhibit any elevation effect (Tripti et al., 2016 ), but Tripti et al. (2019)  observed a significant elevation effect for mountain belts with an altitude greater than 2050 m asl. The isotopic signature of the river water would likely be influenced by other factors such as local rainfall patterns, moisture sources, and evaporation processes within the river system (Gat et al., 1991 ; Rai et al., 2021 ). The evaporation affected the samples collected from the catchment during the pre-monsoon season. Hence, these samples were unevenly spread in the elevation Vs. δ18 O plot (Fig. 8 ). Monsoon samples are more appropriate considering the elevation effect in such basins with evaporation effect (Warrier and Babu et al., 2011; Warrier et al., 2016 ). During the monsoon season (monsoon_19), a significant elevation effect was noticed (Table3 ) with 0.05 ‰ variation in δ18 O per 100 m elevation in river water samples (Table3 ). This could be due to the SW monsoon air mass and its path in the Western Ghats (Saranya et al., 2021 ). Deshpande et al., (2003)  reported an elevation effect in the groundwater (0.4 ‰/100) in south India; however, no elevation effect in groundwater samples was noticed in our catchment. The Western Ghats (Sahyadri ) mountain range in the catchment has a relatively consistent altitude along its length. Therefore, the isotopic composition of precipitation and the subsequent river flow may not vary considerably with the elevation (Lambs et al., 2011; Tripti et al., 2016 ). The highest elevation at which samples were collected was 656 m amsl. The relatively constant altitude in the study area is the main reason for the absence of an elevation effect. Even though the catchment exhibits a gentle slope throughout the basin, a sudden abrupt change in the elevation gradient is observed in the downstream region because of the N-S trending faults of the Jog falls region due to the Western Ghats orogeny (Subramanian and Ramesh, 2009 ; Kale et al., 2010 ). Even this change did not bring any noticeable observation in δ 18 O with elevation.  3.4 Evaporation and damming effect in the catchment In a highly regulated catchment, damming of water significantly affects the evaporative signals. Processes such as evaporation and diffusions are always associated with kinetic fractionation. In water, the lighter isotope preferentially goes to the vapour phase, and the heavier stays in the liquid phase. The kinetic fractionation of water during evaporation is determined by meteorological factors such as humidity, salinity, and temperature (Gonfiantini et al., 2018 ). Specifically, relative humidity affects the isotopic composition of water vapour and rainfall. This will lead to a deviation of δ18 O and δ2 H from the global and local meteoritic water line (Craig, 1961; Horita et al., 2008 ). This deviation is expressed in terms of deuterium excess (d-excess). 3.4.1 Deuterium excess and line conditioned excess variability in the catchment and role of Western Ghats The mean d-excess value for groundwater samples was 9.7 ‰, whereas for river water samples it was 7.9 ‰. In arid areas characterized by low relative humidity, the d-excess is typically in high order (Clark and Fritz, 1997; IAEA, 2000 ). Conversely, in humid regions, the d-excess tends to be lower. In this study, the d-excess values were indicative of the hot and humid climatic conditions of the catchment area. The d-excess values in a humid tropical catchment (around 10 ‰) could be a indicative of the oceanic moisture source (Salati et., 1979 ; Ingraham and Taylor, 1991 ; Gat, 1996 ; Tripti et al., 2016 ). The highest d-excess (12.98 ‰) was observed at Jog falls (R8) in post-monsoon season 2020 (Fig. 6 ). A few locations showed high d-excess values (greater than 10 ‰) in the catchment. Compared to river water samples, more groundwater samples showed higher d- excess. About 78 % of post-monsoon-2020 groundwater samples exhibited high d-excess (Fig. 8 ) values and 50 % of monsoon 2019 samples showed a similar pattern. As mentioned, the river water samples had relatively low d-excess values. In pre-monsoon 2019, only one location (R8) had a d-excess value greater than ten ‰. The higher d-excess values could be due to the precipitation from recycled moisture and re-evaporated rainfall (Zhang et al., 2021 ). A novel parameter known as line conditioned excess (lc-excess), introduced by Landwehr and Coplen, 2006 , was employed to gain a better understanding of the effect kinetic fractionation on the hydrological processes. In the study area, the lc-excess values were mostly negative across all seasons, regardless of the water type. This suggests that the sampling points consistently fall below the LMWL (Landwehr and Coplen, 2006 ). The seasonal averages for groundwater samples were −3, −2, and −1 during pre-monsoon, post-monsoon, and monsoon seasons, respectively. Notably, the pre-monsoon season exhibited comparatively higher evaporation, while the post-monsoon lc-excess values approached zero, indicating low evaporation. For river water samples in pre-monsoon 2019, the lc-excess was more negative (lc-excess=-6). Among these samples, Gersoppa (R10) recorded the highest lc-excess values (-13), followed by Mavinahole (-10) in pre-monsoon 2019. The d-excess values also exhibited a similar trend, indicating a substantial amount of evaporation in these two regions, both of which are affected by the reservoir in the course of the river. Further details on the reservoir effect will be discussed in Section 3.4 . In monsoon 2019, post-monsoon 2019, and post-monsoon 2018, the lc-excess values were −2, −3, and −5, respectively. Notably, the location R10 showed particularly high lc-excess values in post-monsoon 2018 (-14). Irrespective of the seasons R10 was more prone to evaporation. The Western Ghats system acts as a barrier to the oceanic vapor carried by winds, thereby facilitating precipitation on the windward side of the mountain range. This system has a significance influence on the d-excess values within the catchment areas. Tripti et al. (2016)  reported an average d-excess of 19.05 ‰ in the Swarna basin, located approximately 100 km from the Sharavati River catchment. Further south, Warrier et al. (2016) observed an average d-excess of 10.6 ‰ in rainwater samples from Calicut, approximately 400 km away from the catchment. In the Western ghat system of Mumbai, Deshpande et al. (2003)  reported a lower average d-excess of 8.7 ‰. Saranya et al. (2021) , in their study of the Western Ghats in Kerala, suggested that the increase in d-excess values from lowland to highland stations could be attributed to the contribution of recycled precipitation and the barrier effect of the mountains on precipitation. In summary, the mountainous terrain of the Western Ghats, along with its misty conditions, facilitates water vapor recycling within its catchments, leading to elevated d-excess values.   3.4.2 Impact of dams in the catchment Large reservoirs, even small dams, have the potential to change the morphological and hydrological characteristics of a river (Bao et al., 2020; Song et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2021 ). In our catchment, the Linganamakki reservoir and Gersoppa dam play significant roles in the hydrological and morphological condition of the basin. The Linganamakki reservoir, situated in the midstream of the basin, influences about 65 % of the catchment area (Durbude and Purandara, 2005 ). It also exhibits considerable water level fluctuations between seasons (Table S1 ). Hence, it has a substantial impact on the hydrological cycle. The second dam, Gersoppa, is located downstream of the catchment and, though smaller in size, impacts the hydrological cycle ( Fig. 10 ). This influence is demonstrated in the stable isotope data. A river's flow regime, particularly in seasonal rivers, is significantly affected by damming (Jiang et al., 2021 ). Damming can impart lake-like characteristics to a river, resulting in the evaporation of surface water. This evaporation process is identified as a major factor contributing to climate change in terrestrial environments (Gibson et al., 2002 ). Within the Sharavati river catchment, the lc-excess values indicate that most groundwater and surface water samples have undergone evaporation. Notably, two river water locations, R4 and R10, during the pre-monsoon of 2019 (Fig. 1 ), showed high evaporative signals (lc-excess −10 and −13, respectively). The location Mavinahole (R4), which is in the midstream, serves as the only sampling point from the reservoir, exhibiting high evaporation signals likely due to the lake-like structure created by the Linganamakki dam in the main channel (Fig. 10 ). Reservoirs like this can transform a river into an elongated, narrow lake, resulting in increased evaporation (Jiang, 2021 ). Another location displaying a high evaporative signal was Gersoppa (R10). This location exhibited low lc-excess values even in post-monsoon 2018 (-14). Despite being situated downstream of the Gersoppa dam, R10 experienced high evaporative signals in both pre-monsoon 2019 and post-monsoon 2018. This can be attributed to the release of dammed water into the channel. Unlike Linganamakki, where the dam is also used as a reservoir to store water, the Gersoppa dam is primarily used for power generation (Karnataka Power Corporation Limited ). The dammed water from Gersoppa can reach downstream locations (R10), as evidenced by the stable isotope data. Unfortunately, due to accessibility constraints, collecting a water sample directly from the dam was not feasible. Even though the damming of water in river systems has yielded positive economic impacts, its negative effects on the hydrological and ecological aspects remain a subject of debate (Zhan et al., 2015 ). Dammed water facilitates the interaction of groundwater, a phenomenon not observed in rivers without dams, which typically show no significant effects of evaporation and limited interaction with surface water (Zhu, 2021 ). In our catchment, the relationship between groundwater and surface water could be attributed to the effects of damming (Ba et al., 2014; Rai et al., 2021 ).  3.4.3 Evaporative loss Evaporative loss during the pre-monsoon season from the Linganamakki reservoir was estimated at 10 %, while from the Gersoppa dam was 6 %. The pre-monsoon rainfall during the year 2019 was 73 % deficient than normal which led to this evaporative loss. The cross plot of δ18 O and δ2 H (Fig. 9 ) suggests that even the groundwater sampled closely from reservoirs was plotted along the local evaporation line, indicating recharge from the evaporated reservoir water. At the same time, the rest of the groundwater samples (located along higher elevations) inherited the isotopic signatures of the stream water. This sort of groundwater recharge by dam water is possible either due to a dam leakage or reservoir water discharge to the nearby area (Saranya et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2021 ). The increased water residence time due to river damming enhances evaporative loss, reducing stream discharge. Reservoir-based evaporation has caused a 5 % additional water loss in global river water flow (Shiklomanov, 2000; Lehner et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2021 ). In our catchment area, the reservoir-based evaporation loss is even higher because of prevailing climatic conditions. The annual evaporation volume from 721 reservoirs in the United States is equivalent to 93 % of the country's annual public water supply (Zhao and Gao, 2019 ), highlighting the significance of the cumulative effect of these dams. India ranks among the top five countries with the largest annual average reservoir evaporation volume (Tian et al., 2022 ). Therefore, understanding the dam-induced evaporation from the rivers of the Western Ghats is significant for getting a better understanding of the hydrological cycle. The groundwater sampling was conducted across a large spatial scale, the samples were significantly spaced apart and came from different geological formations. As a result, we couldn’t interpolate the groundwater contours. Additionally, logistical difficulties prevented us from obtaining more samples from the centre of the reservoirs. Future studies with finer resolution in the catchment area should improve the knowledge.    4 Conclusions The study achieved a basic understanding of the stable isotopic water characterization of the Sharavati river catchment. Groundwater samples exhibited lesser variations in stable water isotopic ratios than river water samples in the Sharavati river catchment, likely due to the evaporation effect in surface water samples compared to groundwater samples. Spatially, the midstream region, particularly within the Linganamakki reservoir (Mavinahole-R4), shows higher δ18 O and δ2 H values during the pre-monsoon season, which is due to the enhanced evaporation rate during the season. Subsequently, the fault systems in the region have facilitated groundwater recharge from the reservoir, thus substantiating the anomalously high δ18 O value in the downstream groundwater samples. Due to the heavy rainfall, spatially, monsoon season samples did not reflect significant variation in the isotopic signatures. Temporally, monsoon season samples display lower isotopic signatures that can be attributed to the dilution effect of intense rainfall. The pre-monsoon samples were enriched in heavier isotopes due to the increased evaporation under the prevailing climatic conditions. In addition to the drier climate in the pre-monsoon season, the damming effect led to increased evaporation in river water samples, resulting in highly enriched δ 18 O values. Most river and groundwater samples cluster around the same region in the cross-plot, indicating a humid vapor source in the catchment area. Surface water and pre-monsoon groundwater samples fall away from this cluster, reflecting more humid conditions and evaporative loss in their isotopic signals. Rainwater samples exhibit low δ18 O values, forming a distinct cluster that suggests they are influenced by depression/cyclone systems. The d-excess signals in the river catchment reflected the humid tropical climatic conditions. It can be concluded from the stable water isotope ratios that the monsoonal and post-monsoon river water have been sourced from precipitation. This is evidenced by the alignment of groundwater and river water samples close to the Local Meteoric Water Line (LMWL) in the δ18 O and δ2 H cross-plot. Furthermore, the groundwater contributed to surface water in pre-monsoon seasons. Specific locations, such as Sidyapura (R3) and Jog falls (R8), show interaction with groundwater during the pre-monsoon season, indicated by similar isotopic signatures. The elevation effect is well-established in major river systems. However, in the case of the Sharavati river catchment, such an elevation effect in the isotopic signal was absent. The isotopic signatures of river water are likely influenced by local rainfall patterns, moisture sources, and evaporation processes rather than elevation alone. The low elevation gradient compared to other mountain rivers and relatively gentle slope must have contributed to such an effect. Only monsoon river water samples showed a significant elevation effect, with a 0.05 ‰ variation in δ18 O per 100 m elevation, possibly due to the SW monsoon air mass movement. River damming significantly has an impact on the hydrological process. The Linganamakki reservoir influences about 65 % of the catchment area, and the Gersoppa dam, although smaller, also affects the hydrological cycle.
