Locations upstream and downstream of dams, such as Mavinahole (R4) and Gersoppa (R10), exhibit high evaporative signals, indicated by negative lc-excess values. This is due to the lake-like structure created by the Linganamakki Dam and the Gersoppa Dam. Groundwater samples near reservoirs showed isotopic signatures aligned with local evaporation lines, suggesting influence from reservoir water. lc-excess values were mainly negative, suggesting consistent evaporation across all seasons and water types, with pre-monsoon samples showing the highest evaporation rates. Evaporative loss from the Linganamakki reservoir was estimated at 10 %, and from the Gersoppa dam at 6 %. It's high time that the researchers treat the dammed rivers as long, narrow lakes as dammed river no longer behave as rivers. Our results impart the idea that we must consider a dammed river as a series of connected elongated narrow lakes. The perspective shift can enhance our understanding of hydrological processes better. Our study demands the need for more such studies in order to understand the impact of river damming, especially on small mountainous rivers.
1 Introduction Flow-vegetation-sediment interactions play an important role in the evolution of gently sloped landscapes (Lacy et al., 2021; Politti et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2022 ). A typical gently sloping landscape floodplain, for example, is a mudflat of inundation, deposition, exposure, and erosion, a transition zone between land and water, as well as areas with the most significant flow-vegetation-sediment interactions. Floodplains are defined in this paper as “a level area near a river channel, constructed by the river in the present climate and overflowed during moderate flow events”(Leopold, 1994 ), and recognized primarily on the basis of frequency of inundation, morphology, and vegetation type, which are inherently dynamic(Curran and Hession, 2013; Osterkamp and Hupp, 1984; Osterkamp and Hupp, 2010 ). Floodplains have many important economic and ecological functions, such as water purification, flood mitigation, erosion control, and provision of aquatic habitats (Havrdová et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022 ), and play an important role in the cycling of materials between the water and the land (Ang et al., 2022; Bourgoin et al., 2007 ). The main channel-floodplain ecosystem and geomorphologic evolution have undergone significant changes in recent years due to climate change and human activities, posing serious threats to the ecological functions of floodplains (Havrdová et al., 2023 ). Floodplain erosion and deposition are important processes affecting the evolution of floodplain ecosystems and landscapes, and turbidity currents are one of the main forms of erosion and deposition occurring on floodplains. Turbidity current refers to two or more different densities of fluids in contact with each other, due to the fluid suspended sediment and other particles caused by the density difference, so that one of the fluids can flow along the interface, and does not occur with the ambient fluid global mixing of the fluid, also called particle-laden gravity current. Turbidity currents are common in places such as river reservoirs, estuaries, and the deep sea, and are often thought to be caused by major external events such as landslides, storms, floods, or earthquakes. Notably, (Hizzett et al., 2018 ) were the first to indicate that the majority of turbidity currents in rivers are triggered by sediment deposition in surface river plumes rather than major external events. (Hage et al., 2019 ) suggest that turbidity currents are triggered once erosion of the flow occurs. This means that turbidity currents will be triggered on a larger scale and more frequently. Traditional research on turbidity currents has focused on transport from rivers and coasts to the deep sea, whereas turbidity currents at the scale of a composite cross-sectional river consisting of the main channel of a river and its floodplain have been less studied, ignoring the fact that turbidity currents also exist on floodplains, and we hope to complement the research gap in this area. Floodplains are highly susceptible to erosion because they contain large quantities of easily suspended sediments and are susceptible to turbidity currents caused by external forces such as fluctuating water levels, heavy rainfall, floods and landslides. Suspended sediment in floodplain turbidity currents is primarily originated from the beds or banks of rivers and their tributaries, or in off-channels within the catchment area, such as bare soil susceptible to erosion, which is a process controlled by various factors such as land use, soil type, and ground cover (Asadi et al., 2007; Wood, 1997 ). Because the sediment in turbidity currents is primarily suspended load, temporary deposition is prone to occur when the current momentum is weak (He and Walling, 1998 ). For this reason, temporary deposition of large amounts of suspended sediment in the floodplain makes it a potential source of erosion. In recent years, the construction and operation of large-scale water conservancy projects have resulted in the retention of large amounts of sediment in rivers, a significant reduction in sediment fluxes downstream of rivers, and the scouring of low-sediment-content streams that have increased the flood plain erosion possibilities(Li et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2015 ). Frequent fluctuations in water levels and flooding tend to cause severe erosion and gradual desertification of river floodplains (Pham and Bui, 2023 ). Notably, soil anti-erodibility and hydrodynamic conditions in floodplains are crucial factors determining the occurrence and intensity of erosion. Turbidity currents carry a large amount of sediment or suspended particles, and the influent flow velocity, sediment concentration, and particle size distribution are important parameters affecting their dynamics. The mechanism by which sediment particles denser than the ambient fluid overcome gravitational suspension determines the turbidity current dynamical state, which in turn constrains the form of transport of sediment particles and the range of particle sizes over which they can be transported, thus controlling the law of sediment transport in turbidity currents(Heerema et al., 2020 ). Coarser sediment particles tend to be deposited on the streambed, while finer sediment particles are more likely to remain in suspension as the turbidity current moves downstream. Changes in sediment content due to sediment deposition or erosion drive density differences in turbidity currents, altering their spatio-temporal evolution(Francisco et al., 2018 ). Thus, the spatio-temporal evolution of turbidity currents also depends on their particle size distribution, i.e., the ratio between the fine and coarse particles they carry. The study also focuses on the effect produced by the turbidity current particle size distribution. Usually, the presence of various types of vegetation on the floodplain increases the resistance to water flow and affects the turbidity state and its sediment movement processes, thus influencing the ecological function and geomorphologic evolution of the floodplain. The vegetation presence can substantially improve floodplain stability and stream health parameters (Gurnell et al., 2012 ). In floodplains with low-energy river ecosystems, vegetation gradually becomes the main driving force of the spatiotemporal evolution of water flow structure, sediment erosion and transport, and landscape patterns (Larsen, 2019 ),influencing floodplain sediment transport on a short time scale and river morphology on a long time scale. Studies of flow-vegetation-sediment interactions involve many traditional and emerging fields, including turbulence, ecological hydraulics, sediment transport, hydrogeomorphology, and soil and water conservation among others (Etminan et al., 2018; Graziano, 2018; Nepf, 1999; Singh Chauhan, 2009; Tanino et al., 2005 ). With advancement of theoretical modeling, numerical simulation, and flume experiments, the scope of vegetation flow studies has evolved to consider both the local scale and the plant scale (Huai et al., 2021 ). Such fine-scale studies allow the dissection of the interaction between water conveyance patterns and sediment transport patterns in the presence of vegetation. Flow through vegetated areas is affected by vegetation resistance resulting from physical obstructions imposed by vegetation structures (such as branches, leaves, stems, and roots), and shape drag arising from friction generated by the flow to cause a loss of momentum and capacity, which in turn affects the force of the flow to hold the sediment (Huai et al., 2021 ). Numerous studies have shown that aquatic vegetation supports stream ecological processes by altering velocity profiles, drag and turbulence characteristics, sediment and nutrient deposition patterns, and increasing flow resistance. Vegetation flow resistance is usually expressed by parameters such as overall roughness, friction coefficient, and drag coefficient derived from empirical or semi-empirical formulae, and is the most commonly used parameter for modeling the feedback of vegetation on hydraulics (Soler et al., 2021; Västilä and Järvelä, 2017; Zhang et al., 2020 ). Considering the complex geometrical structure of real vegetation, the vegetation model is usually simplified to an array of rigid cylinders with uniform diameters in experiments, and most of this type of simulated vegetation is used for parameter correction in empirical or semi-empirical formulae (El Allaoui et al., 2015; Liu and Nepf, 2016; Liu et al., 2021 ). Some research has provided a detailed overview of the physical and mathematical analysis of multiscale vegetation influencing flow, turbulence, and diffusion (Nepf, 2012; Vercruysse et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2015 ). Previous research has been mainly focused on the effects of vegetation characteristics such as vegetation height, density, patch length, and arrangement on water–sediment movement (Barcelona et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2018; Xu and Nepf, 2020; Zong and Nepf, 2010 ). However, the results of studies using rigid cylinder arrays are only applicable to rigid vegetation with less branching below the water surface, which has a large gap from the actual situation. As a matter of fact, the resistance to vegetation flow is highly variable both spatially and temporally due to the flexible stems and complex branching structures of most aquatic vegetation and the physiological changes in vegetation throughout the year (such as growth, defoliation, and decay) in the nature. These difficulties have attracted great research interests. For example, (Hu et al., 2018 ) found that the length of leaf blades has impacts on turbulence damping, which in turn affects the regional extent of sediment deposition. Mavrommatis and Christodoulou compared the water flow characteristics of three simulated vegetation to assess the effects of vegetation density, leaf morphology, and plant position in the array (Mavrommatis and Christodoulou, 2022 ). Zhao et al. considered vegetation patterns in numerical simulations and proposed the Karman coefficient applicable to complex vegetation patterns (Zhao et al., 2023 ). Recent research has shown that vegetation canopy morphology and structure are important determinants of the ability of vegetation to modify fluid structure and sediment transport (Box et al., 2019; Hu et al., 2018; Xu and Nepf, 2020 ). However, the physical mechanisms by which vegetation canopy morphology and structure affect flow dynamics and sediment transport have not been elucidated, and it remains experimentally difficult to simultaneously measure the flow velocity and sediment concentration within vegetation (Yang et al., 2023 ). Due to the lack of detailed experimental observations in close natural conditions, little is known about the evolution of turbidity currents in real vegetation patches. To make the simulation closer to the natural environment, we considered the unique characteristics of real vegetation species from the perspective of canopy morphology, took into account the differences in sediment size distribution caused by sediment erosion and deposition during the turbidity current movement in the floodplain. Turbidity dynamics characteristics and sediment deposition law of different sediment size distributions under the influence of vegetation canopy morphology and structure were investigated. The study reveals the turbidity currents evolution process which is more closely related to the floodplain ecosystem and provides reference for ecological restoration of the floodplain.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Flume set-up The experiments were conducted in a rectangular flat flume (450 cm long, 30 cm wide and 40 cm high) (Fig. 1  ). The side walls and bottom of the flume were made of methacrylate resin, which is colorless and transparent for easy viewing. The lock-exchange flume system consisted of a removable vertical gate that divides the flume into the storage section (150 cm) and the test section (300 cm). For each experimental run, once the sediment–water mixture was introduced into the storage section of the flume and well mixed with the rest of water therein, the lock gate was lifted to release it into the test section, where it flowed as a turbidity current. Fifteen sediment traps (ST0 to ST14) with a diameter of 4 cm and a height of 1.8 cm were placed at the flume bed, which were deployed to analyze the sediment deposited from the turbidity current as it travelled along the flume. The starting point (0 cm) for the movement of water containing sediment was at the gate. ST0 was placed at 20 cm to the left of the gate (−), and ST1 to ST14 were placed at 20 cm intervals in the test section to the right of the gate (+). PVC sheets were laid to fix the sediment traps and simulated vegetation. Measurements were made by a slide of two CCD high-resolution cameras mounted on a fixed tripod above the flume, and processed to obtain the running speed from the position and time of the current front run as determined from the video data.  2.2 Vegetation canopy Two kinds of simulated vegetation canopies with different morphological structures were used (Fig. 2  ). The two simulated vegetation were modeled based on the morphological characteristics of the natural plant Acorus  calamus L. and Abutilon theophrasti  Medicus, two common plant species in freshwater river floodplains. In this experiment, the leaf length–width ratio was used as a measure of the morphological characteristics of the canopy. The vegetation patches laid out by the two simulated vegetation are shown in Fig. 2 . The simulated vegetation represented by Acorus  calamus L. with a leaf length–width ratio of 18.15 represent a striped canopy morphology, and the vegetation patches composed of this plant were denoted as striped-leaf vegetation patches; while simulated vegetation represented by Abutilon theophrasti  Medicus with leaf length–width ratio of 1.47 represent a round canopy morphology, and the vegetation patches composed of this plant were denoted as round-leaf vegetation patches. Single simulated vegetation was arranged at the bottom of the flume according to the points generated by the random function to lay out randomly distributed vegetation patches (Pujol et al., 2013 ), and to ensure that the plant height and vertical arrangement of leaves of each plant within the patches were generally the same. The density of vegetation was quantified using their solid plant fraction (SPF), which is defined as the fraction of the bed area occupied by the vegetation stems (Serra et al., 2004 ),(1) SPF = 100 π N d / 2    2   A      In the formula, SPF is the vegetation density; N is the number of plants; d is the plant stem diameter, cm; and A is the area occupied by vegetation patches, cm2 . In this experiment, SPF was set at 1 %, 2 %, and 3 %, which correspond to 240, 300, and 360 obstacles m2 , respectively (Fig. 2 ). These correspond to dimensionless vegetation patch density (ad) of 0.01 to 0.1, which fall within the range observed in natural vegetation canopies (Bouma et al., 2007 ).  2.3 Sediment characteristics The flume was filled with water to a height H (9 cm, 12 cm, and 15 cm), and the lock gate was set to separate the two sections from each other. A volume of 3 L of water was taken from the storage section, and added with sediment, followed by vigorous stirring for five minutes to ensure full mixture of the particle suspension. The sediment–water mixture sample was then returned to the storage section and mixed with the remaining water therein, making an initial sediment concentration of C0  = 6 g/L (Soler et al., 2021 ). To better represent the non-spherical irregular natural characteristics of natural sediments, the experiments used sediments collected from the river diffuse beach of Liangzi Lake in Hubei Province. After removal of the debris such as leaves and roots from the sediment samples, the particles larger than 0.5 mm in size were removed by sieving through a screen and the remaining samples were used to configure three different particle size distributions of the same concentration turbidity current. The particle size distribution was determined using a LISST-100 particle size analyzer. The sediment was pre-treated before the measurement. Firstly, 2 ml of 30 % hydrogen peroxide was added to the collected sediment, and the water bath was heated until the organic matter was completely removed and the suspension was free of bubbles, followed by adjustment of pH value 7 after cooling. Next, centrifugation was used to remove the supernatant, and ultra-pure water was added according to a certain water-to-sediment ratio. Then, 0.5 ml of measurement sample was taken after shaking well. Finally, the sediment particle size distribution of the deposited sediment was analyzed by LISST-100 particle size analyzer. The sediment in the particle size range of 10–100 µm was classified as coarse-grained suspended sediment (fine to coarse silts and small sediment particles), which are weakly cohesive particles; and the sediment in the particle size range of 1–10 µm was classified as fine-grained suspended sediment (clays and very fine silts), which are very cohesive particles according to the classification of a previous study (Blott and Pye, 2012 ). The sediment samples were divided into S66% , S75% , and S82%  according to the initial percentage of coarse-grained suspended sediment. A few bulky particles quickly precipitated out from the turbidity current and were therefore not considered in the analysis.  2.4 Experimental parameters and runs Fifty-four lock-exchange experiments were conducted using turbidity currents configured by simulated vegetation with different leaf morphology characteristics, vegetation density, water depth, and sediment samples with different particle sizes. The test parameters are shown in Table 1  .   3 Results 3.1 Advance of the turbidity current To verify the evolution pattern of turbidity currents under different conditions, we analyzed the position of the front of turbidity current (x) evolution with time (t) (Fig. 3  ). At a water depth (H) of 9 cm, there was a strong feedback relationship between the vegetation conditions and the spatiotemporal evolution (velocity) of turbidity currents configured with three sediment samples (S66% , S75%  or S82% ) (Fig. 3 a). Turbidity currents configured with sediment samples S82%  evolved more slowly over time in patches with a vegetation density (SPF) of 3 %, reaching shorter x for the same t. The rate of the spatiotemporal evolution of turbidity currents was negatively correlated with the content of coarse-grained suspended sediment in the turbidity currents and the vegetation density. A comparison of vegetation with striped- and round-leaf canopy revealed that the turbidity current front evolved more slowly with time under striped-leaf canopy in most cases. The above law was also true for turbidity currents with water depths of 12 cm (Fig. 3 b) and 15 cm (Fig. 3 c). Fig. 3  also shows that the evolution of turbidity currents over time was accelerated with increasing water depth. Different degrees of vegetation inundation in turbidity currents at different water depths lead to changes in the effective flow blocking area, which in turn affects the evolution of turbidity currents. However, a few cases have arisen that do not fit the above pattern. For example, in Fig. 3 a1 and b3, after 200 s of turbidity current movement, the evolution rate of the striped vegetation with with a vegetation density (SPF) of 2 % is instead slower than SPF 3 %; in the striped-leaf canopy with a SPF 1 % in Fig. 3 a3 and b3, there is not a more pronounced tendency for the evolution rate to slow down with the increase in the content of coarse-grained suspended sediment as in the other runs. We attribute the above phenomena to two directions: 1) striped-leaf canopy are prone to morphological reconfiguration and are more unstable in the flow; 2) the process of sediment particle–particle collision with each other is more complicated in turbidity currents with different sediment size distributions. At present, the study of the physical mechanism of flexible blade water blocking and multi-grain turbidity current motion is still a black-box process, which should be strengthened in this direction in the future. To investigate the general law of the spatiotemporal evolution of turbidity currents, a state partitioning analysis was carried out on turbidity currents under all conditions(Huppert and Simpson, 2006; Marino et al., 2005; Maxworthy et al., 2002 ). At the beginning of the turbid current movement, there was a linear relationship between the non-dimensional position (x/H) and the non-dimensional time (g′/4H)1/2 ·t (Fig. 4  a):(2) x c  H  = 0.51 g  ′  4 H      1 / 2   t     Therefore, the turbidity current velocity is kept constant and its prediction equation is:(3) v c  = 0.51 g  ′  H  4     1 / 2        The turbidity current after the inertial regime was slowed down by the return flow of the environment fluid above. If there is an obstacle such as vegetation, it directly enters the drag-dominated regime, when the turbidity current evolution with time is more complicated. This is the same as the results of experiments carried out in rigid cylinder arrays(Soler et al., 2017; Zhang and Nepf, 2008; Zhang and Nepf, 2011 ), and is also similar to the results of the study of the turbidity evolution process in the lock-exchange experiment using simulated vegetation (Barcelona et al., 2018; Soler et al., 2021 ). The general law of the spatiotemporal evolution of turbidity currents has good applicability. We further studied the accuracy of predicted flow rates and their trends and explored the effect of changes in vegetation factors on predicted flow rates. The mean velocity of the turbidity current in the inertial regime vinertial  was calculated. The ratio of the mean velocity of turbidity current to its predicted velocity in the inertial regime (equation (2)  was plotted versus the fractional volume of the vegetation (ad) for all studied cases (Fig. 5  a). In the inertial regime, the ratio was found to be independent of ad with a mean value of 0.9923, which could be expected since this regime is dominated by the inertia of the flow. Turbidity currents in this regime are driven primarily by inertial forces and are temporarily undisturbed by vegetation resistance. In the drag-dominated regime, we calculated the mean velocity of the turbidity current in the first meter of this regime vdrag . The ratio of the mean velocity of turbidity current to the velocity predicted for this regime (equation (4) ) was also plotted versus ad (Fig. 5 b). In this case, the ratio rose following a power relationship of vdrag /k(q0 g′d/CDa φ)1/4 ·t−1/2  = 1.16(ad)0.15 . Based on the verified general law of the spatiotemporal evolution of turbidity currents, we then focused on the influence of two factors, plant leaf morphology and sediment particle size distribution, on the generation of turbidity currents.  3.2 Analysis of drag-dominated regime The results of the previous section show that vegetation conditions and sediment size distribution have certain degrees of influence on the evolution pattern of turbidity currents over time. First, the transition region for the three regimes of turbidity current was defined. The positions where transition of these regimes occurs are hereafter referred to as x = Lini  (where the inertial regime ends and the drag-dominated regime begins) and x  = Lend  (where the drag-dominated regime ends and the viscous regime begins) (Soler et al., 2021 ). Fig. 6   presents the trend of Lini  and Lend . The normalized turbidity current toe drag was calculated for Lini  and Lend  in each run. We investigated the relationship of the non-dimensional canopy drag force at each position CDa ax (CDa aLini  and CDa aLend ) in the transition zone with non-dimensional frontal canopy area aH, another vegetation-related independent variable, and the results are plotted in Fig. 6 . The aH value reflects the density of vegetation canopy in the water, with a lower value indicating a sparse vegetation canopy or shallower water depth. The existence of thresholds for aH can be seen in the figure. Both CDa aLini  and CDa aLend  of turbidity currents with three sediment particle size distribution varied linearly with aH at values below 0.63. The details are as follows:(a) sediment sample S66% ;    CDa aLini  = 16.1aH − 0.04 (r2  = 0.83; n = 14; p < 0.001) CDa aLend  = 34.38aH+0.004 (r2  = 0.87; n = 14; p < 0.001), respectively.(b) sediment sample S75%;    CDa aLini  = 14.3aH+0.37 (r2  = 0.81; n = 14; p < 0.001) CDa aLend  = 32.23aH+1.41 (r2  = 0.86; n = 14; p < 0.001), respectively.(c) sediment sample S82%;    CDa aLini  = 11.44aH+1.72 (r2  = 0.75; n = 12; p < 0.001) CDa aLend  = 22.38aH+5.45 (r2  = 0.79; n = 12; p < 0.001), respectively. When aH>0.63, both CDa aLini  and CDa aLend  were constant at turbidity current configured from sediment samples S66%  (CDa aLini  = 9.83, CDa aLend  = 24.41), S75%  (CDa aLini  = 10.36, CDa aLend  = 23.69), and S82%  (CDa aLini  = 8.98, CDa aLend  = 20.37), respectively. The drag force value at the beginning and end of the drag-dominated regime of the turbidity current generally remained constant. In addition, the CDa aLini  and CDa aLend  values differed for turbidity currents with three sediment particle size distributions. The range of the drag-dominated regime decreases slightly with increasing content of coarse-grained suspended sediment in the turbidity current.  3.3 Analysis of deposition flux To investigate the specific movement patterns of turbidity currents, sediment was collected at the same location for each set of experiments to analyze the sediment transport and deposition patterns of turbidity currents. The distribution of suspended sediment deposition along the direction of turbidity current movement is shown in Fig. 7  . The data support the inferred effect of leaf morphology on sediment deposition in different cases, and lay a basis for exploring the effect of leaf morphology characteristics on sediment transport and deposition patterns. The deposition flux (DF) represents the amount of sediment in the fluid that passes through a given cross-section per unit time, which is divided by the initial flux to obtain the non-dimensional DF (Soler et al., 2017 ). The amount of sediment deposited in a turbidity current was quantified using non-dimensional DF, with a higher value indicating more sediment in the cross-section fluid and a lower amount of deposited sediment. In all experiments, the non-dimensional DF reached the maximum at the location closest to the gate and the minimum at the tail end of the flume, showing an overall monotonically decreasing trend with distance from the gate. We further investigated the sediment deposition in turbidity currents in different water depths (Fig. 7 a), and found that the non-dimensional DF increased with increasing water depth. When the water depth increased, the vegetation changed from a non-inundated state to an inundated state, accompanied by an increase in the canopy blocking area, but the proportion of vegetation area in the flow cross-section gradually decreased, resulting in an increase in non-dimensional DF and a decrease in the amount of sediment deposited in the canopy. In addition to water depth or relative inundation of vegetation, vegetation density is also an important factor affecting the effectiveness of vegetation in blocking water and sediment. Increases in vegetation density in both striped-leaf and round-leaf canopy resulted in a decrease in non-dimensional DF and an increase in sediment deposition within the canopy (Fig. 7 b). Then, the deposition flux was determined to examine the effect of sediment particle size distribution and canopy morphology on turbidity currents. In the experiment with a water depth of 12 cm and a vegetation density of SPF=2% (Fig. 7 c), we observed that changes in turbidity current particle size distribution influenced the non-dimensional DF. Whether it is for striped-leaf or round-leaf canopy, turbidity current with S82%  showed the highest non-dimensional DF, as well as the most significant decreasing trend. There was a positive relationship between non-dimensional DF and coarse-grained suspended sediment content in turbidity currents, i.e., a higher non-dimensional DF in turbidity currents with a high content of coarse-grained suspended sediment indicates a smaller amount of sediment deposition and higher turbidity. These results indicated that the non-dimensional DF is not only affected by the vegetation conditions, but also closely related to the particle size distribution of turbidity currents. Under the same conditions, there was a significant difference in deposition flux between the strip-leaf and round-leaf canopy. In the striped-leaf canopy, the deposition flux of turbidity currents was smaller, which is more favorable for sediment deposition. Moreover, Fig. 7  shows that the non-dimensional DF always remains constant when the turbidity currents are in the inertial regime, and decreases significantly when the turbidity currents enter the drag-dominated regime. Thereforg flow-vegetation-sediment feedback mechanism is mainly manifested in the drag-dominae, the stronted regime. Fig. 8   shows the changing trend of non-dimensional DF ratio with respect to the vegetation canopy resistance exerted on the turbidity current front. The vegetation resistance exerted on the front during turbidity current movement along the flume is represented by CDa ax. The turbidity currents are in the inertial regime until CDa ax reaches a certain value (0.68 in the striped-leaf canopy and 0.53 in the round-leaf canopy), and the non-dimensional DF ratio generally remained constant, indicating that the turbidity currents can maintain their turbidity at this regime, which is similar to the results of a previous study (Soler et al., 2020 ). In the inertial regime, the non-dimensional DF ratio is independent of CDa ax, with values of 1 ± 0.1 regardless of canopy morphology. Upon entering the drag-dominated regime, the non-dimensional DF ratio decreases in a power law with increasing CDa ax, with slopes of –0.487 in the striped-leaf canopy and –0.27 in the round-leaf canopy. These results suggest that there is a strong feedback mechanism among vegetation canopy morphology, sediment particle size distribution, and sediment deposition in the drag-dominated regime under the test conditions.   4 Discussion 4.1 Evolutionary pattern of turbidity currents This study investigated the evolution of turbidity currents over time under the influence of vegetation density, leaf morphology, water depth, and sediment particle size distribution, and determined that the general laws for the spatiotemporal evolution of turbidity currents are applicable to this experiment. In the experiments, the evolution of turbidity currents over time mainly depends on the vegetation conditions (vegetation density, leaf morphology, inundation degree, and water depth), which is generally in agreement with the results of other studies (Barcelona et al., 2018; Han et al., 2021; Tanino et al., 2005 ). Vegetation influences the downstream flow field, increasing resistance to flow and reducing flow velocity. Turbidity currents were found to evolve more slowly over time in vegetation patches with striped-leaf canopy than in those with round-leaf canopy. Since the vegetation height was fixed in the experiment, different water depths generated different vegetation submergence situations (at a water depth H of 9 cm, the vegetation was not submerged, and at a water depth H of 15 cm, the vegetation was submerged). A higher vegetation density generally represents slower movement of turbidity currents along the flume, and the same results were obtained with different vegetation submergence levels. In this study, the setting of water depth can precisely reflect the change in vegetation from non-submerged to submerged state, and thus the change in canopy blocking area resulted in a change in the rate of spatiotemporal evolution of turbidity currents. The rate of spatiotemporal evolution of turbidity currents is negatively correlated to the content of coarse-grained suspended sediment in turbidity currents. It should be noted that not all runs in the experiment followed the above pattern. We consider that striped blades are prone to unstable morphological reconstruction in the fluid environment, and that sediment particles with different size distributions also show complex responses to the fluid environment, especially the collision process between particles of different sizes, which is still a black-box process in the physical analysis of this part of the process. Even though there are unanticipated experimental phenomena, it can still be determined that the spatiotemporal evolution pattern of turbidity currents is influenced by vegetation conditions and sediment particle size distribution. The resistance effect of vegetation on the flow was reconfirmed by quantitative experiments. Furthermore, the turbidity current movement process was divided into inertial regime and drag-dominated regime to be studied separately (Huppert and Simpson, 2006; Marino et al., 2005; Maxworthy et al., 2002; Zhang and Nepf, 2011 ). The results showed that the strong flow-vegetation-sediment feedback mechanism is mainly reflected in the drag-dominated regime.  4.2 Sediment transport and deposition In natural rivers and streams, there are spatial and temporal differences in sediment transport and deposition patterns or mechanisms. Vegetation regulates the basic sediment transport pattern of turbidity currents by altering their evolution over time. Sediment transport is essentially a process of interaction between turbulent diffusion and sediment gravity (Fukuda et al., 2023 ). Sediment transport capacity of turbidity currents in vegetated areas is reduced by momentum absorption of vegetation stems and canopy resistance. It also cuts off the convective channels of the ambient fluid, indirectly reducing the turbulence intensity at the turbidity current interface with the ambient fluid. The other part of turbulent kinetic energy is consumed to maintain the particles in suspension and lift them in turbulent mixing with the ambient fluid (Wells and Dorrell, 2021 ). Sediment transport and deposition in turbidity currents under different dynamical regimes, such as inertial regime, drag-dominated regime and its transition zone, were quantified by the non-dimensional canopy drag force at each position CDa ax and non-dimensional DF. The experiments showed that the sediment DF remained generally constant when the turbidity current was in the inertial regime in all runs. During turbulent diffusion, sediments migrate in two directions. The equilibrium is mainly due to the fact that the upward buoyant force on the sediment particles is equal to the downward gravitational force. In this regime, the amount of sediment entering the fluid equilibrates with the amount of deposited sediment. At this point, the turbidity current retains its mean velocity and turbulence intensity, as well as its mean density distribution in time and space. Therefore, the turbidity currents in different scenarios show a generally stable trend in DF in this regime. After the turbidity current enters the drag-dominated regime, the barrier effect of vegetation on flow and sediment is obviously enhanced. With increasing total volume of vegetation during turbidity current movement, the canopy blocking area gradually increases. Changes in vegetation conditions (density, inundation, and leaf morphology) also affect vegetation resistance by controlling the canopy blocking area, resulting in a greater reduction in turbidity current velocity than the increase in turbulence intensity, a decrease in overall kinetic energy, and a significant decrease in DF. Turbidity currents with the three sediment grain size distributions also showed differences in DF, and those with a higher content of coarse-grained suspended sediment had high DF. The inertia is different between coarse-grained suspended sediment and fine-grained suspended sediment (Landers and Sturm, 2013 ), which together with the relative motion of the surrounding fluid affects the particle turbulence effect within the wake flow. When the vegetation resistance is consistent, the coarse-grained suspended sediment has a higher inertia. The particles have a stronger ability to maintain their own motion than the fine-grained suspended sediment, and there is a larger relative motion with the surrounding fluid, which enhances the effect of particle turbulence within the wake flow, thereby increasing the DF. Overall, the turbidity current has a substantially reduced deposition flux in the drag-dominated regime, where sediment deposition occurs primarily. The location Lini  of the transition from the inertial regime to the drag-dominated regime and the location Lend  of the transition from the drag-dominated regime to the viscous regime of turbidity currents were investigated by CDa ax. The vegetation conditions were controlled to be consistent to ensure that the momentum absorption scale CDa a does not change, and the magnitude of CDa aLini  and CDa aLend  in the drag-dominated regime are mainly determined by Lini  and Lend . It was found that Lini  and Lend  of different dominated regimes decreased with increasing percentage of coarse-grained suspended sediment, and the range of drag-dominated regime also showed a slightly decreasing trend. The major areas of turbidity current deposition correspond to the drag-dominated regime in the kinetic partitioning. Hence, the turbidity current in the sediment sample S82%  distribution is significantly less extensively deposited in the vegetated patches compared with that in the sediment sample S66%  distribution. In other words, the increase in coarse-grained suspended sediment reduces the major deposition distance of the turbidity current. Combined with the analysis results of the evolution of turbidity currents over time, it can be speculated that the transport distance of turbidity currents in vegetation patches is limited by the increase in coarse-grained suspended sediment, but is promoted by a moderate increase in fine-grained suspended sediment. The interaction mechanism between turbulent currents and sediment in vegetated open channels is very complex(Xie et al., 2023 ). Turbidity currents configured with different sediment grain size distributions also showed different time evolution patterns and deposition mechanisms. Unexpectedly, turbidity currents with a high content of coarse-grained suspended sediment showed slower evolution with time, but had a higher sediment deposition flux and thereby lower sediment deposition, suggesting that the correlation between turbidity current momentum and sediment transport decreases under complex conditions.  4.3 Influence of vegetation canopy morphology and structure The role of vegetation canopy morphology and structure was fully considered in the lock-exchange flume experiment by varying the leaf morphology and vegetation density. The striped and rounded leaves of the experiment plants can represent the most common leaf morphology in the nature. As a result, the striped-leaf canopy led to slower evolution of turbidity currents over time and showed an overall better water-blocking effect. Vegetation exhibits dynamic changes in response to the flow field, a process called morphological reconfiguration, which changes the original plant posture and affects vegetation resistance by reducing the canopy blocking area (Miri et al., 2017 ). Aquatic vegetation with flexible branches and leaves is susceptible to morphological reconfiguration during water flow bending, and leaf morphology has a great impact on morphological reconfiguration (Caroppi and Järvelä, 2022 ). For turbidity currents in vegetation, dynamic reconfiguration of striped-leaf canopy and the round-leaf canopy induces differences in the evolution of turbidity currents over time and momentum exchange. Flexible leaves control the evolution of turbidity currents over time and the momentum exchange, and therefore may affect the transport and deposition of suspended sediment. To reveal the specific mechanisms by which canopy morphology influences sediment transport and deposition, we quantitatively investigated the sediment deposition in striped-leaf canopy and round-leaf canopy vegetation patches by involving various shapes of leaves and patches with different densities and degrees of inundation. The results showed that regardless of the density and inundation degree, the vegetation patches formed by the striped-leaf canopy always had lower non-dimensional DF, which is more favorable for sediment deposition. In addition, we found that turbidity currents in the inertial regime stabilized the non-dimensional DF in vegetation patches of both leaf morphologies, but non-dimensional DF in the drag-dominated regime showed a clear downward trend with the temporal evolution of turbidity currents, indicating that the drag-dominated regime has the strongest water flow-vegetation-sediment feedback mechanism, as well as the most significant effect of vegetation to block water and sediment. The transition zone among different regimes of turbidity currents is influenced by the parameter aH, which characterizes the density of vegetation in the water and water depth with a threshold value > 0.63. When aH<0.63, the values CDa aLini  and CDa aLend  at the location of state transition occurs increases linearly the with aH; when aH>0.63, CDa aLini  and CDa aLend  generally remain unchanged. The results indicated that both vegetation canopy morphology and structure are important factors controlling vegetation resistance and morphological reconfiguration, and vegetation leaf morphology is a key attribute influencing the flow and sediment barrier effect of vegetation. Thus, the effect of leaf morphology needs to be taken into account in the modeling of flow resistance. However, the reconfiguration of resistance generated by leaved plants cannot be reliably predicted by traditional empirical or semi-empirical models using such plant-scale bulk properties that are mainly controlled by the stem (Rubol et al., 2018 ). The spatiotemporal variability of vegetation (such as the growth process and wilting of leaves) and the dynamic reconfiguration of flexible vegetation leaves complicate the parameterization of vegetation resistance, which will be a challenge for future research. Through the study of turbidity dynamics and sediment movement in vegetation patches with different canopy morphologies, we found that vegetation with a striped-leaf canopy has a stronger water and sediment blocking effect, which is more conducive to reducing the erosion of suspended sediments with higher organic or nutrient content on the floodplain, and that a slower rate of turbidity evolution promotes the accumulation of nutrients on the floodplain, which in turn affects the ability of the vegetation to thrive. This also implies that the striped leaf canopy is dominant in the application of ecological restoration in floodplains. Different plant species slow down water flow and promote sediment deposition to different degrees (Przyborowski and Łoboda, 2021; Przyborowski et al., 2019 ), which leads to the heterogeneity of the floodplain in terms of the trend of geomorphologic evolution. A typical case study, (Zhang et al., 2016 ) investigated the effect of plant morphology on flow structure and concluded that suspended sediments are more likely to be deposited within the canopy of Vallisneria natans  compared to Potamogeton malaianus . Research on the effects of plant morphological characteristics on hydrodynamics and sediment deposition can gradually screen plant species with stronger water and sediment blocking effects, which is of great ecological significance for the evolution of floodplain landscapes and ecological restoration.   5 Conclusion Effects of vegetation on the evolution of turbidity currents and sediment transport processes have been well established in the research fields of hydrodynamics and river dynamics, and complete theoretical analyses have been carried out at both the monoculture and patch scales. However, research using rigid cylinder arrays to simplify vegetation patches is quite different from the natural situation, and can only provide limited guidance for practical applications such as soil and water conservation and ecological restoration in floodplains. To fill this research gap, this study considered the role of vegetation canopy morphology and structure. The hydrodynamics and sediment transport and depositional processes of turbidity currents in vegetation zones with different canopy morphologies were investigated using a lock-exchange experiment. Under the conditions of this experiment, the universal law of spatiotemporal evolution of turbidity currents in vegetation patches was still applicable under the experimental conditions. The present study suggests that the canopy structure of vegetation patches and the hydrodynamic characteristics together determine the transport of suspended sediment. In other words, the amount of sediment deposition or turbidity of turbidity currents depends on the vegetation structure, vegetation density, and leaf morphology (rounded and striped), as well as hydrodynamics (water depth and sediment particle size distribution in this study). In summary, this study verified the general law of the spatiotemporal evolution of turbidity currents in complex vegetation morphology. Leaf morphology is a key attribute affecting the water and sediment barrier effect of vegetation as it has important impacts on the range of turbulent regime and reconfiguration of vegetation morphology. Moreover, vegetation canopies with striped leaves have a stronger water and sediment barrier effect. The correlation between turbidity current momentum and sediment transport decreases under complex conditions, and coarse-grained suspended sediment (10–100 µm) content negatively affects the transport and major deposition distance of the turbidity current.
1 Introduction The development and management of river basin cities face many challenges, especially in responding to climate change and extreme weather events. With global warming, the frequency and intensity of extreme precipitation events are showing an upward trend, bringing more frequent and severe flooding disasters to river basin cities (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2023 ). The geographical location of river basin cities makes them particularly vulnerable to upstream flood events. The increase in impermeable surfaces in urbanisation has further intensified the risk of urban waterlogging (Marsooli et al., 2019; Huo et al., 2024 ). Furthermore, the socio-economic activities of basin cities are highly dependent on rivers and related water resources, such as fisheries and tourism. This makes rational and effective flood management crucial for the sustainable development of these cities (Luu et al., 2018 ). For example, from July 17 to 23, 2021, Zhengzhou City and surrounding areas experienced a rare persistent extreme precipitation. On July 20, the 24-hour rainfall in Zhengzhou City reached 617.1 mm, exceeding its annual average rainfall (Lu et al., 2024 ). The rainfall on this day far exceeded the precipitation record in Germany during the same period, becoming one of the most significant single-day rainfall events in China since meteorological records began. This flood caused severe flooding disasters in Zhengzhou and surrounding areas, with urban flooding occurring in many places (Yang et al., 2023 ). Subway lines were forced to shut down, and several subway cars were flooded, resulting in dozens of casualties. Roads and bridges were washed away, affecting millions of residents, many of whom were trapped at home or took refuge in temporary shelters. Power and communication facilities were damaged, affecting the progress of rescue work. The Zhengzhou flood disaster is a severe test of the city's ability to cope with extreme climate challenges and is a vital issue to consider in future urban planning and management (Guo et al., 2023 ). Accurately assessing the risk of compound disasters and scientifically formulating composite flood prevention decisions are essential for basin cities. Therefore, this study aims to explore the prediction of compound floods in basin cities under simulated extreme rainfall scenarios, to provide stronger support for disaster prevention and relief decision-making, to discuss risk assessment methods and urban planning and management strategies when basin cities face flood disasters, in order to propose comprehensive solutions to reduce the negative impacts of climate change on basin cities. A comprehensive approach based on disaster factors is used for composite flood simulation and impact analysis in a constantly changing environment. Previous studies have proposed various models, including empirical, stochastic, and mechanical (Khosravi et al, 2018 ). Empirical models, in particular, are mathematical methods based on measured data used to determine the relationships between variables. They are useful in quantifying disaster associations through regression analysis or correlation coefficients. For example, Grahn and Nyberg (2017)  assessed residential flood exposure and vulnerability in urban areas based on 49 rainfall events in Sweden that resulted in 2140 residential building insurance claims. They found that the duration of rainfall and the total amount of daily precipitation had a significant impact on estimating the extent of damage. Luu et al (2018)  studied the flood event in Gia Lai, Vietnam, 2013. The marked data included flood depth and duration, combined into a single map using a weighted linear combination method and integrated with GIS to generate flood hazard maps. This assessment method is common in early risk studies, with low requirements for the quality and accuracy of geographic data and simple calculations. However, it necessitates a long time series of basic hydrological observation data. The assessment conclusion reflects the overall flood disaster risk of the region, but it cannot display the spatial differences in risk. Index System Method: The index system method mainly starts from the elements that constitute flood risk, selects appropriate indicators according to certain principles, and assesses by constructing a comprehensive function of flood disaster risk (Udaleclarke et al., 2005 ). Zelenáková et al. (2015)  proposed a universally applicable method implemented in a GIS environment for determining areas at risk of flash floods caused by heavy rainfall. However, the selection of indicators might be biased or atypical due to limitations in data availability, making it unsuitable for risk assessment in areas smaller than urban scale and not fully reflecting the spatial distribution characteristics of disasters. The scenario simulation method primarily involves constructing urban stormwater models to simulate flood disasters under different scenarios and assessing the flood risk in the affected areas (Tabari, 2020 ). Baky et al (2020)  assessed flood disasters by integrating geographic information systems, hydrodynamic modelling, and necessary field information. They evaluated flood risk based on flood hazards and vulnerability indices, utilising the Delft3D model for two-dimensional flood flow simulation to calculate inundation depths in flood-prone areas. Their study found that flood risk can still vary even if the intensity of flood disasters remains unchanged. Erena et al. (2018)  conducted a study in Dire Dawa, Ethiopia, using the FLO-2D hydrodynamic model to identify villages vulnerable to flooding and create flood hazard maps. However, this method also has limitations, such as the requirement for high-quality regional baseline data, a complex assessment process, and unsuitability for large spatial scale regions. In watershed urban areas, when the intensity or cumulative amount of precipitation exceeds the capacity of the urban drainage system, it can lead to urban flooding. With the persistence of high-intensity rainfall and the increase in surface water accumulation, it becomes easy to hinder the normal operation of watershed cities, potentially resulting in significant economic losses and casualties. Faced with the increasingly severe issue of urban flooding in watershed cities, a wealth of practical experience has shown that solely relying on flood control and drainage engineering measures are insufficient to fully mitigate the impacts of flooding disasters (Yan et al., 2012 ). Therefore, during the early stage of disaster prevention, emphasis should be placed on the application of non-engineering measures, such as risk management of urban flash flood disasters, simulation, and early warning of urban flash floods, in order to avoid or minimise the losses incurred when flooding disasters occur (Huang and Li, 2021 ). Due to its simplicity and effectiveness, empirical models are widely used. Researchers can better understand various disasters and their complex interactions and impacts in a continuously changing environment by employing comprehensive analysis methods that consider disaster factors (Huo et al., 2021 ). However, the drawback of empirical models is their inability to extrapolate, and compared to statistical and numerical models, the application of empirical models is subject to certain limitations due to uncertainty. Random models are powerful tools for analysing relationships between multiple variables, especially in the context of extreme environmental events. Mechanistic models are mathematical modelling based on hydrological and hydraulic processes. These models can be divided into two categories: conceptual and physical. Conceptual models focus on the individual components of hydrological processes and integrate modules such as precipitation, runoff, evapotranspiration, infiltration, and routing to simulate flood inundation. Physical models attempt to simulate processes involving various physical parameters, including atmospheric, oceanic, climatic, and hydrological systems. The computational results of physical models have clear physical significance. Many studies utilise mechanistic models to simulate and analyse the impacts of compound floods. Traditional statistical and numerical models have been widely used to analyse the impacts of compound floods. However, to understand the complex mechanisms behind compound floods, it is necessary to employ multiple methods and conduct multi-process coupled simulations. This approach allows for the comprehensive assessment of the overall effects of atmospheric, riverine, and urban factors, thereby achieving a comprehensive interpretation of the effects of compound disasters (Tamm et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2024 ). Although there have been studies on the amplifying effect of extreme rainfall caused by climate change on watershed urban flooding disasters, research in this area remains insufficient. For example, Liu et al (2022a,b)  conducted a case study in Haikou City, China and found that future changes in rainfall combined with the urbanisation process will significantly increase the extent, depth, and duration of floods. They also concluded that the impact of rainfall changes on floods exceeds the sum of individual factors. Furthermore, Moftakhari et al. (2017)  utilised copula methods and bivariate dependence analysis to predict the increase in failure probabilities of coastal defenses in eight estuarine systems along the U.S. coast under different Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) for the years 2030 and 2050. Zhong et al. (2024)  explored the combined effects of multiple disaster factors under the environmental change of coastal cities based on Delft3D-FLOW and HEC-RAS hydrodynamic models. It showed that the impact of multiple disaster factors was more serious than that of single consistent disaster factors and precipitation was the main disaster factor in cities with strong coastal protection. Park and Lee (2020)  assessed the probability of coastal flooding risk under future rainfall scenarios in South Korea using machine learning algorithms. Xu et al. (2022)  applied the Delft3D-Flow model and copula functions to calculate compound flood risks in coastal areas. Despite these efforts, most studies are still limited to considering the impact of urbanisation, while research that comprehensively addresses watershed urbanisation, extreme rainfall, and urban drainage networks remains scarce. More research is needed to comprehensively assess and predict the multifactorial joint impacts of compound floods under climate change. This study considered these factors to assess the changes in extreme rainfall intensity under climate change and the impacts on watershed urban surfaces and urban drainage networks. It employed numerical analysis to construct an innovative integrated model called SWMM-LISFLOOD. This model considers the characteristics of watershed urban surfaces, rainfall scenarios, and urban flooding, allowing for a more comprehensive evaluation of the risk of compound floods under changing climatic conditions. The SWMM-LISFLOOD model simulates the process of watershed urban flooding disasters under the influence of extreme rainfall. In contrast, the SWMM model is employed to represent the boundaries of watershed urban surfaces, runoff, and rainfall, simulating the flooding of urban areas. The objectives of this study are as follows: (a) to establish a hydrodynamic simulation model for compound floods in watershed urban areas; (b) to simulate the changes in watershed urban flooding disasters induced by extreme rainfall under climate change scenarios in the study area; and (c) to analyse the inundation extent and spatial characteristics of extreme compound floods in watershed urban under different return periods of extreme rainfall.  2 Materials and methods The methodology framework is shown in Fig. 1  . Part I constructs a numerical model that can reflect the flooding process based on the basic data of the study area. Based on the constructed coupled model, Part II quantitatively analyses the impact of extreme rainfall and drainage network on urban flood disasters through scenario design. Part III analyses the urban flood risk by combining multiple methods. Following this, measures to mitigate regional flood risk are proposed through drainage capacity analysis. 2.1 Study area and data This article takes the urban area of Huyi District in Xi'an City, located in the Wei River basin of Shaanxi Province, which is a rapidly urbanising area, as the research subject. Huyi District is located in the southwestern part of Xi'an City, Shaanxi Province, China, in the middle of the Guanzhong Plain, belonging to the middle reaches of the Yellow River's Wei River basin, as shown in Fig. 2  (a). The range is 33°46′–34°16′ N, 108°22′–108°46′ E, and the altitude is 404.1–434.8 m. The southern part is the Qinling Mountains. The main urban area of Huyi District extends from Gucheng Road in the north to Lügong Road in the south, from Laoyu River in the west to Tanbin River in the east. The overall terrain is higher in the south and lower in the north, with gentle slopes and slight variation in ground elevation, ranging between 366 and 390 m. Huyi District is located in the warm temperate semi-humid continental monsoon climate zone, characterised by warm and humid weather, distinct seasons, hot and rainy summers, and cold and dry winters. Rainfall varies significantly with the seasons and is unevenly distributed, generally less in winter and moderate during the spring and autumn rainy seasons. The rainfall is concentrated around July to September, accounting for about 62–65 % of the annual rainfall, with an average annual rainfall of about 600 mm. The district covers a total area of 19.32 km2 , with residential, commercial, and industrial lands being the main types of construction land, and has a moderate population density. The drainage network in the region is representative and independent, comprising both old pipelines and those constructed in recent years, presenting a complex situation. The data required for modelling for the study area includes rainfall data, topographic data, drainage network data, land use data, etc. The rainfall data comes from a self-established meteorological station, and all stormwater simulations in this paper are based on individual rainfall events, so the water loss due to evapotranspiration can be ignored. The DEM data is sourced from the Geospatial Data Cloud platform of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (https://www.gscloud.cn/ ), with a spatial resolution of 30 m. The drainage network information comes from the municipal management office of Huyi District, with the main drainage pipes being circular. The land use data utilises the 10 m resolution land use data from Tsinghua University in 2017 (https://data.ess.tsinghua.edu.cn/fromglc102017v01.html ).  2.2 Models 2.2.1 SWMM The SWMM model was developed by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency in 1971 and has undergone multiple improvements and upgrades. The latest version is SWMM5.1, which can simulate surface runoff, one-dimensional hydraulic simulation of the pipe network, and water quality simulation. Among them, the surface runoff module can choose three methods (Horton, Green-Ampt, SCS runoff curve) to simulate the infiltration process, the surface runoff uses the nonlinear reservoir method, and the one-dimensional hydraulics of the pipe network can choose the kinematic wave or dynamic wave simulation. The SWMM model is well suited for simulating urban drainage systems and has the advantages of being simple, easy to use, and open source. It has been widely used in urban drainage systems.(1) ∂ A  ∂ t   + ∂ Q  ∂ x   = 0     (2) ∂ Q  ∂ t   + ∂ Q  2  A      ∂ x   + g A ∂ H  ∂ x   + g A S f  = 0     where x  is the distance, in meters (m), t  is the time, in seconds (s), A  is the cross-sectional area of the flow, in square meters (m2 ), Q  is the flow rate, in cubic meters per second (m3 /s), H  is the water head in the pipe, in meters (m), Sf   is the friction slope, and g  is the acceleration due to gravity, 10 m/s2 .  2.2.2 LISFLOOD-FP The LISFLOOD-FP is a grid-based flood inundation model developed by the University of Bristol, UK. It is a two-dimensional hydraulic model used to simulate flood inundation in complex terrain efficiently. The LISFLOOD-FP model conducts hydraulic simulations for two-dimensional floodplain areas based on the Digital Elevation Model (DEM), calculating flow balance for individual grid cells and considering water balance between adjacent grid cells.(3) dV  dt   = Q up   + Q down   + Q left   + Q right       (4) Q ij   = A ij   R ij   S ij  1 / 2    n      where V  represents the total flow of the grid cell; t  represents time; Q up   ,  Q down   ,  Q left   ,  Q right      represent the flow from the upstream, downstream, left, and right neighbouring grid cells, respectively; Q ij      represents the flow between the i th and j th grid cells; A ij      and R ij      represent the cross-sectional area and hydraulic radius at the interface between adjacent grid cells i  and j , respectively; S ij      represents the water surface slope between adjacent grid cells i  and j ; n  is Manning's coefficient.   2.3 Coupling of SWMM and LISFLOOD models The SWMM model has mature functionality for simulating conduit flow in drainage networks. However, it cannot simulate two-dimensional surface overflow and thus cannot provide information such as flood extent, water depth, and the flooding process. The advantage of the LISFLOOD-FP model lies in its ability to simulate the flood extent, water depth, and flooding process in urban areas based on the overflow process from overflow nodes (i.e., the relationship between flow rate and time) and urban topography. In the coupling process, the SWMM model provides the flow rates of overflow nodes, while the LISFLOOD-FP model further simulates the flood extent, water depth, and flooding process. This coupling method leverages the strengths of both models to conduct more realistic two-dimensional simulations of urban flooding caused by heavy rainfall. The coupling between the SWMM and LISFLOOD-FP models is one-way, where the SWMM model performs runoff and conduit flow calculations. In contrast, the LISFLOOD-FP model is used for two-dimensional surface inundation calculations. The key step in model coupling is to extract the overflow process from the SWMM model and the coordinates of overflow points and store them in the LISFLOOD-FP model's *.bdy and *.bei files. 2.3.1 Construction of the SWMM model First, the pipe network and manhole data are generalised, with less generalisation at the nodes prone to flooding, to obtain a more realistic overflow process. Secondly, the Thiessen polygon method is applied to generalise the sub-catchment areas, and topological checks are performed on the pipe network and node data. Finally, the model parameters are calculated. The generalisation of the pipe network and subdivision of sub-catchment areas are completed in ArcGIS, resulting in 180 nodes, 196 pipe segments, and 10 outfalls, as well as 190 sub-catchment areas, as shown in Fig. 2 (c) after generalisation. In this study, it is assumed that the river system can fully meet the drainage capacity of the drainage system. The outlets in the drainage system are free-flowing, with the outflow entering planned river systems such as Lao Yu River, Xu Jia River, and Tan Yu River, as well as drainage ditches on the west side of the railway.  2.3.2 Construction of the LISFLOOD-FP model The files required for the LISFLOOD-FP model include *.bdy, *.bci, *.ascii, and *.par. The time-varying boundary conditions file (.bdy) contains time boundary information, storing the flow rates obtained from SWMM for overflow nodes. The Boundary condition type file (.bci) is a coordinate boundary file that stores boundary coordinates and overflow node coordinates. The Digital Elevation Model file (.dem.ascii) specifies the digital elevation model used by the model, stored in ASCII format for the study area DEM. The Parameter file (.par) is the main file for model execution, containing empirical parameters, default values, and keywords to access the files as mentioned above.   2.4 Watershed trees and floods have the same origin Each component plays a different role in modern urban flood control and drainage systems. The small drainage system, also known as the urban sponge, is the first line of defense. It utilises facilities such as green spaces, permeable roads, and depressed squares to absorb and utilise rainwater to the maximum extent possible, reducing peak runoff and alleviating the risk of urban flooding. The large drainage system acts as the second line of defense, collecting surface runoff and conveying it to the urban river network. Excess rainwater is discharged promptly through facilities such as pipelines and pumping stations, lowering the water level in urban rivers. The river network system serves as the third line of defense, regulating urban rivers, reservoirs, lakes, and other water bodies to utilise flood resources, ensuring urban safety and ecological balance. The urban flood control and drainage system can be seen as a “basin tree” consisting of “land-pipe-river” components, as depicted in Fig. 3  , the schematic diagram of the structure of the modern urban flood control and drainage system “basin tree”. The accumulation of surface rainwater due to inadequate drainage, leading to disasters, is called “waterlogging,” while inundation caused by river overflow is termed “flooding.” The concept of “flood and waterlogging sharing the same origin” implies that the basin should be considered a whole entity in urban flood control planning, considering the rainfall-runoff situation across the entire watershed. Specifically:(1) There is a close relationship between the upper, middle, and lower reaches of urban river networks and between main and branch streams. Increased flow in the upper reaches can elevate water levels downstream, while higher water levels downstream can reduce the capacity for upstream flow to discharge, potentially causing upstream flooding.  (2) Ground surfaces, pipelines, and river channels are crucial in urban flood control. Fast surface drainage can increase pipeline flow, while slow drainage can lead to the accumulation of surface water. Rapid pipeline drainage can elevate river water levels, influencing pipeline drainage and potentially causing overflow, resulting in flooding. Due to the interconnection between river networks and pipeline networks within the watershed, flooding and waterlogging phenomena mutually influence each other in urban areas. The occurrence and propagation of flooding and waterlogging depend on natural factors, urban planning, and infrastructure construction.     2.5 Modification of HR threshold method for flood hazard index Based on the relevant experience in managing urban waterlogging risk in China, inundation depth and duration are two important factors to consider in waterlogging risk assessment. In the risk level assessment, the sensitivity coefficient of the target disaster-bearing body is introduced. We classify the sensitivity of different land uses according to their importance. We modify the Flood Hazard Risk Index (HR) threshold method from the UK (Ma, 2019 ) to simultaneously consider inundation depth (d ), inundation duration (T ) (unit: hours), and the sensitivity parameter of land use α ( 0 < α ≤ 1 )   . The modified formula for HR, denoted as HR  x    , is as follows:(5) HR  x  = α × d × T + 0.5    + d f         where d  represents the inundation depth in meters, T  denotes the duration of inundation in hours, d f     signifies the depth hazard parameter (d    ≤ 0.15 m, d f     = 0.5; d   ＞0.15 m, d f     = 1.0).  2.6 Rainstorm scenario design The common rainstorm process lines include the Chicago flow process line method, Huff method and Pilgrim and Cordery method, among which the Chicago rain type is suitable in China (Liu et al., 2023 ), and this paper adopts the Chicago rain pattern. According to the rainstorm data of Xi 'an, the rainstorm intensity formula of Xi 'an is as follows:(6) i = 13.26522 × ( 1 + 2.915 l g P )  ( t + 21.933 )  0.974        where P  is the current period (year); t  is rainfall duration (min); i  is the rainstorm intensity (mm/h), and the rain peak coefficient is 0.35481. The rainstorm process is designed for 2 h with a return period of 5a, 10a, 50a, 100a, 500a, and 1000a with a time step of 5 min.
