The calibration method for the rainfall-runoff model based on the comprehensive runoff coefficient first requires obtaining the runoff coefficient. The runoff coefficient is the ratio of runoff to rainfall in a specific drainage area and is generally influenced by the underlying surface conditions of the watershed. The study area is located in the central urban area of Huyi District, where the buildings are relatively dense, and the comprehensive runoff coefficient is 0.507. On September 11, 2023, rainfall was selected to calibrate the model parameters. The model's uncertain parameters were repeatedly adjusted, and the runoff coefficient simulated by the SWMM model was eventually found to be 0.507. The parameter adjustment details are shown in Table 1  . Based on the calibrated parameters, simulations were conducted for the dates 20230826, 20230919, and 20231004. The comprehensive runoff coefficients were calculated by averaging the runoff depths of each sub-catchment area and then dividing by the rainfall amount, as shown in Table 2  . The comprehensive runoff coefficients ranged from 0.459 to 0.554. The highest runoff coefficient occurred on 20230919 due to heavy rainfall and overflow in the drainage network, resulting in significant runoff.  3.1.2 SWMM-LISFLOOD coupling model verification According to the simulated inundation range based on the rainfall data from September 11, 2023, as shown in Fig. 2 (b), it was found that the points with severe flooding were mainly concentrated in Gucheng West Road, Dongjie, Meibeixi Road, and Dongcheng Road. At this time, the inundation area of the study area reached 0.208 km2 . The figure shows that positions in the study area with water depth exceeding 1 m are mainly concentrated near Gucheng West Road, Meibeixi Road, and Dongcheng Road, indicating the most severe flooding areas. Secondly, flooding is extensive in Dongjie, with water depth mostly below 1 m. Based on actual investigations and the information provided by the Huyi District Emergency Management Bureau, Gucheng West Road, Dongjie, Meibeilu, Dongcheng Road, and Zhaofeng East Road are all prone to flooding, which are the areas severely affected by inundation in the study area. Therefore, the two-dimensional simulation results of the coupled model can reflect the distribution of actual vulnerable points, indicating that the coupled model has good accuracy.   3.2 Node overflow analysis The SWMM model can simulate the operational status of drainage network nodes under rainfall events of different return periods. The overflow flow rate at the nodes increases with the overflow duration, as shown in Table 3  . The statistical results of overflow nodes under rainfall events of various return periods indicate that with the increase in the return period of rainfall, there is a noticeable upward trend in the number of overflow nodes, total overflow volume, and maximum overflow duration. In summary, surface runoff exceeds the outflow of the drainage network, leading to overflow at some nodes and resulting in surface water accumulation. As the return period increases, the overflow situation worsens. The overflowing manholes gradually increase, the overflow duration prolongs continuously, and the maximum overflow volume at each node increases. These factors mainly contribute to the increase in water accumulation volume and area in the study area. The total overflow volume increases from 74.353 × 106  L to 1157.132 × 106  L, and the maximum overflow duration increases from 1.05 h to 2.53 h. The number of overflowing nodes increases from 64 to 146, and the percentage of overflowing nodes increases from 36.57 % to 80.43 %.  3.3 Two-dimensional coupling submergence analysis Using the established urban stormwater flooding model, simulations of surface inundation conditions at different return periods were conducted at various nodes. Based on the LISFLOOD inundation calculation results and referencing GB 50014-2021 “Code for Design of Outdoor Drainage” and relevant literature, the inundation depths were categorised into four intervals: 0–0.2 m, 0.2–0.5 m, 0.5–1 m, and >1 m. The surface inundation depths and extents under different return periods are shown in Fig. 5  . The figure shows that the inundation areas under different return periods mainly occur in the northwest, northeast, and central parts of the study area. For example, areas such as Gu Cheng Xi Road, Dong Cheng Bei Road, Mei Bi Dong Road, Dong Jie, Ren Min Road, Mei Bi Dong Road underpass, Zhaofeng East Road underpass, Nan Yuan Hua Ting, Dong Cheng Hua Yuan, Price Inspection Compound, and Zhu Que Jin Yuan Community are heavily affected. This result may be attributed to several factors:(1) The southeastern part of the study area has higher terrain, while the northwest and northeast parts have lower terrain, making them prone to flood accumulation.  (2) The central area is primarily urban construction land with high impervious surface coverage, leading to poor water infiltration.  (3) Inadequate drainage capacity of the drainage network system in the study area results in the inability to promptly discharge excess floodwater, exacerbating the situation of surface inundation in some areas.    Specifically, under the 5–10-year return period conditions, inundation points are mainly located near Gu Cheng Road, Xi Yuan Road, Mei Bi Road, and Dong Jie, with severe inundation at the Mei Bi Road underpass. In the 50-year return period conditions, new inundation points include You Yi Road, Lu Gong Dong Road, Lao Bin Bei Road, and Bei Jie. In contrast, the original inundation areas still experience flooding, and the inundation area further expands. Under the 100-year return period conditions, new inundation points include Lou Jing Road and Gu Cheng Dong Road intersection, Zhaofeng Bridge Elementary School, Mei Bi Xi Road, and Zhan Hong Road intersection. New inundation points under the 500-year return period conditions include Lao Bin Nan Road and Dong Xin Road, Chao Yang Road and Zhaofeng Dong Road, and Hua Zhan Street. Under the 1000-year return period conditions, all pipelines are overloaded, with overflow points accounting for 83.43 %, and 25 % of the study area is submerged. Apart from the flood-prone areas, the inundation situation is also severe at Dong Cheng Nan Road, Dong Jie intersection, and Ren Min Road. Statistical analysis of the inundation depths corresponding to each inundation area interval and their proportion to the total inundation area are presented in Table 4  . It can be observed that under different return period scenarios, the inundation area gradually expands, with the proportion of the inundation area to the total study area being 3.48 %, 7.50 %, 14.85 %, 18.15 %, 25.15 %, and 27.71 % respectively. From the changes in inundation area corresponding to different water depths, it can be seen that under different return period conditions, the proportion of inundation area with depths below 0.2 m is above 55 %, indicating a relatively optimistic situation regarding inundation in the study area, with severe inundation mainly occurring in the aforementioned vulnerable points. However, with the change in the proportion of inundation area corresponding to different water depths, it is observed that as the return period increases, the proportion of inundation area with depths below 0.2 m gradually decreases, while the proportion of inundation area with depths above 0.2 m increases. Shallow inundation areas in the study area are gradually replaced by deeper water, indicating a less optimistic situation regarding inundation. Additionally, to improve the efficiency of the model calculations, this study simplified the drainage network model by simplifying some of the rainwater wells and branches. This simplification may result in the neglect of some nodes that originally overflowed, leading to an underestimation of simulated overflow or the omission of some actual inundation points. Therefore, the actual inundation situation in the study area may be more severe than the simulated results, necessitating attention to vulnerable areas and timely implementation of appropriate response measures.  3.4 Waterlogging risk level assessment results and analysis For the risk level distribution under different return periods, the process of risk level assessment based on inundation depth and duration directly utilises the simulated results of depth and duration for each grid in the 2D grid. Based on the partitioning rules, inundation risk levels are assessed. ArcGIS spatial overlay analysis is employed for the modified HR threshold method, incorporating a land-use layer for the area to obtain the land use of each 2D grid. This information is used to calculate the sensitivity parameter for each grid, resulting in the modified hazard index HR  x    , as shown in Fig. 6  . From the risk maps above, it can be observed that most areas belong to the categories of no risk and low risk, and as the return period increases, the high-risk areas also increase. Since the HR threshold method considers any inundation as posing a risk, all inundated areas are considered risk areas, with the proportion of risk areas to inundated areas being 100 %. The ranking of risk area ranges from low-risk area > high-risk area > extremely high-risk area > moderate-risk area. In terms of inundated areas, low-risk areas have the most significant proportion, accounting for over 70 %, while the area of moderate-risk zones is the most minor, less than 3.5 %. The area of high-risk zones is tiny, accounting for less than 12 %. Looking at the trend, as the rainfall increases, the proportion of low-risk areas gradually decreases while the proportion of moderate and high-risk areas increases. Overall, the proportion of low-risk areas is still significant, and with the increase in return period, the difference in proportion between moderate-risk and high-risk areas gradually decreases. This indicates that more inundated areas transition from moderate-risk to high-risk zones with increased rainfall. Regarding spatial distribution (as shown in Fig. 6 ), in the scenarios of 100-year, 500-year, and 1000-year return periods, the southeastern part of Huyi District shows relatively higher risk areas. It appears in patches, with small areas of high-risk zones in the northern part. The highest risk areas are observed in locations such as Gucheng West Road, Dongcheng Road, and Renmin Road, while areas such as Meibi Road and Loujing Road exhibit relatively high risk. Dongjie and Lvgong Roads also show high-risk areas, but their extent is relatively small.  3.5 Mitigation measures Existing research results show that drainage system is effective in reducing runoff (Zhao et al., 2024 ). At the same time, the analysis also shows that some drainage system in the study area has insufficient effective drainage capacity when the flood occurs, resulting in a long period of water retention and high flood risk. In order to confirm this hypothesis, the drainage capacity of the pipeline in the study area was analyzed. The SWMM model in the study area is composed of 5a, 10a, 50a, 100a, 500a and 1000a rainstorms during the return period, respectively (see Section 2.6  for the design of the rainstorms). Fig. 7   shows the spatial distribution of inundation networks under heavy rainfall in different return periods. In modern urban flood control and drainage systems, effectively coordinating small, large, and river network systems is crucial to ensuring urban flood safety and conserving water resources. Watershed flood control and drainage involve various engineering and management measures, which can be categorised into three main parts:(1) Small Drainage System    For implementing small drainage systems, consideration can be given to increasing the construction of green spaces and rain gardens in urban planning. In densely populated urban areas, green spaces and rain gardens can be added to construct urban sponges, maximising the absorption and filtration of rainwater. Suitable natural vegetation and permeable soil can be selected for urban green spaces to optimise rainwater infiltration. Permeable paving materials can be used for asphalt road surfaces with low permeability to improve the permeability of sidewalks, roads, and squares, thereby reducing surface runoff formation. Rain barrels can be installed in residential areas to achieve decentralised rainwater collection, laying the foundation for utilising unconventional water sources.(2) Large Drainage System    Effective implementation of the extensive drainage system requires the construction of advanced underground drainage networks. Near inspection wells where overflow frequently occurs on main roads or in neighbourhoods and near overloaded pipelines, an additional trunk pipeline can be installed on the other side of the road, or drainage zones can be redefined based on terrain to alleviate local drainage pressure, thereby increasing the drainage capacity of the local area. Rainwater detention facilities can be installed at underpasses or overpasses to prevent surface runoff from entering nearby drainage pipes directly. Additionally, installing drainage pumping stations is essential to improve drainage efficiency, especially in low-lying areas and areas prone to flooding.(3) River Network Drainage System    The construction of the river network system involves water resources regulation in the upstream watershed. In the upstream watershed, reservoirs and detention basins can be considered to regulate rainfall runoff and slow down the arrival time of flood peaks. Through scientific planning and design, the volume and flood discharge capacity of reservoirs can regulate rainfall runoff to some extent and delay the arrival time of flood peaks, effectively alleviating the pressure of downstream floods. Regarding urban rivers, river management and ecological restoration are long-term tasks. It is necessary to dredge the river, reshape the riverbed, and restore vegetation to improve the water capacity and flood resistance of the river and improve water quality and the ecological environment. The synergistic interaction among the small, large, and river network systems is vital to constructing an urban watershed flood control and drainage system. Through detailed planning, scientific design, and ongoing management, cities can effectively enhance their resilience to floods and waterlogging, achieving sustainable development and rational utilisation of water resources.   4 Discussion Traditional urban flood control and drainage methods typically adopt isolated approaches to address flood and waterlogging disasters, employing targeted measures. Waterlogging prevention often involves adjusting and enlarging pipe diameters, utilising overflow and storage, and increasing pipe sizes (Donratanapat et al., 2020; Rossi et al., 2022 ). However, local pumping measures are needed due to the high water levels in pipe drainage areas, which may cause water to exert buoyant force on the drainage system. For flood control, measures for river overflow usually include raising embankments, widening rivers, or utilising upstream reservoirs for flood storage (Pirone et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2024 ). However, this “floods for floods, waterlogging for waterlogging” approach has drawbacks as it fails to fully consider the interconnection and mutual transformation between urban flood and waterlogging disasters. When urban surface water accumulation leads to waterlogging, increasing the scale of drainage networks and strengthening end-point pumping can address local issues (Liu et al., 2022a,b ). However, as the scale of pipelines and pumping stations increases, the inflow into rivers will also increase, potentially causing river water levels to rise and triggering river overflow in other areas, leading to the “waterlogging-induced flooding” problem. On the other hand, when urban rivers overflow, raising embankments may cause river water levels to rise, which could affect the drainage effectiveness of the pipeline network, leading to the “flooding-induced waterlogging” problem. Therefore, traditional urban flood and waterlogging control methods have significant limitations, overlooking the close connection between small and extensive drainage systems and potentially transferring urban flood and waterlogging risks. This article, based on the concept of watershed tree construction, requires a change in perspective, starting from the perspective of the entire watershed, coordinating resources from upstream and downstream, left and right banks, and combining factors such as reservoirs, ponds, pipelines, and river channels to optimise the layout of watershed flood control projects. First, a comprehensive assessment of the defence capabilities of the existing watershed flood control system is conducted based on the urban flood control model. By analysing the distribution maps of pipeline fill levels, river water levels, ground elevations, and flood depths, a deeper understanding of the causes of watershed flood disasters can be gained. Further analysis is conducted on urban land use planning, renovation projects, surrounding environmental factors, and engineering experience. In cases where it is not feasible to directly increase the flood control standards of the mainstream and downstream branches on the right and left banks, measures such as digging reservoirs upstream, adding detention facilities combined with urban renewal, utilising existing ponds, and building wetland parks (flood storage areas) can be taken to attenuate floods and peak flows, systematically improving the watershed's defence standards. For situations where it is difficult to directly expand and upgrade pipelines, measures such as reducing river water levels by utilising upstream detention reservoirs and local tributary channel rectification can be implemented to reduce the water inflow and buoyancy effects at pipeline outlets, thereby systematically enhancing the pipeline's ability to cope with heavy rainstorms. For areas with low local terrain, elevation of platforms can be carried out in conjunction with urban renewal projects; in areas without such projects, pumping stations can be installed. Finally, based on the assessment results of the current flood control system's defence capabilities in the watershed, preliminary scales of engineering measures are proposed based on engineering experience. The effectiveness of planned projects can be evaluated using urban flood control models to analyse data such as watershed flood processes, water level changes, pipeline fill levels, flood depths, and ranges. If the planning objectives are not met, the layout and scale of the projects can be optimised and adjusted until satisfactory planning objectives are achieved. The viewpoints proposed in this article are similar to those proposed by Huang Guoru in the literature (Huang et al., 2019 ). However, they are more specific in terms of application and methods, especially in the urbanisation process of the middle reaches of the Yellow River. This approach to watershed flood control takes a more comprehensive consideration of the interrelationships between urban flood disasters, avoiding the limitations of traditional methods and offering a fundamental solution to urban flood disasters.  5 Conclusions In this study, the SWMM-LISFLOOD coupled model constructed based on the research area was utilised to investigate the impact of watershed urbanisation on different flood characteristics under various scenarios of extreme rainfall return periods. Additionally, by combining methods such as node overflow, water depth (WD) and hazard rating (HR), the flood risk in the research area was analysed. Subsequently, mitigation measures for regional flood risks were proposed. The main conclusions are as follows:(1) In urban flood control and prevention, attention should be paid to areas with low terrain, small pipe diameters, and extensive service ranges. With the increase in the return period of rainfall, the number of overflow nodes increased from 64 to 146, and the total overflow volume increased from 74.353 × 106  L to 1157.132 × 106  L. The maximum overflow duration also increased from 1.05 h to 2.53 h.  (2) The SWMM-LISFLOOD simulation demonstrates strong reliability for urban areas in the middle reaches of the Yellow River basin. In the flood risk assessment results, as the rainfall amount increases from a 5-year return period to a 50-year return period, the risk area in the research region increases from 3.48 % to 14.85 % With the increase in return period, the proportion of inundated areas with depths less than 0.2 m gradually decreases. In contrast, the proportion of inundated areas with depths greater than 1 m gradually increases, indicating that shallow water accumulation areas are gradually being replaced by deeper water, and internal flooding is becoming more severe. Areas with low terrain, small pipe diameters, and extensive service ranges have higher levels of risk.  (3) The duration significantly impacts flood risk in the research area. Considering longer durations typically increases one risk level, with the proportion of low-risk areas transforming into moderate risk and moderate-risk areas into high risk exceeding 90 %. The capacity of the drainage system falls within rainfall intervals occurring every 1–2 years. Under rainfall scenarios with return periods of 50 and 100 years, the main pipelines operate at overload for more than 3 h. Inadequate drainage capacity leading to prolonged water accumulation is the primary cause of flood risk in the research area.    Due to limited land space in watershed cities, there is notably insufficient space for upgrading urban rivers and drainage networks. Therefore, flood control project layout must consider economic and constraint principles. This paper proposes an urban flood simulation model that couples “ SWMM-LISFLOOD”. This study fully considers the interconnection of various urban drainage systems, as well as the relationship between upstream and downstream areas, main and tributary streams, under the holistic view of the watershed system. In conclusion, this paper proposes the concept of urban flood control and the corresponding urban flood simulation method, which can provide technical support for urban flood control and has promising prospects for widespread application.
1 Introduction Natural river systems are characterized by a substantial variability in streamwater discharge, marked by frequent, irregularly occurring peak flow events (Ceola et al., 2013; Trauth and Fleckenstein, 2017 ). This natural variability is caused by precipitation or snowmelt (McGlynn et al., 1999; Singh et al., 2020; Trauth and Fleckenstein, 2017 ). However, free-flowing rivers have become rare and are increasingly altered by anthropogenic activity. For instance, wastewater treatment plants (WWTP), hydropower plants (HPP), and dam operations often cause regular, daily oscillating fluctuations of discharge with a reduced peak flow compared to natural flow regimes (Hayes et al., 2022; Hucks Sawyer et al., 2009; Mueller et al., 2022a ). Rivers play an important role in the global carbon (C) cycle (Battin et al., 2009 ). Streams and rivers convert a substantial amount of terrestrial-derived C and emit ∼ 1.8 Pg C of carbon dioxide (CO2 ) annually (Raymond et al., 2013 ). This is the largest share of carbon emitted by inland waters which is estimated to 1.85 ± 0.5 Pg C per year (Regnier et al., 2022 ). In comparison, fossil fuel and industry emitted 9.3 Pg C annually average over the decade 2006–2015 (Le Quéré et al., 2016 ). CO2  emission flux measurements depend on gas transfer velocity (k) and CO2  concentration in the water column. The velocity of streamwater directly impacts k and thus underlines the importance of flow regimes. The CO2  in the streamwater originates from external sources such as groundwater (Amiotte-Suchet et al., 1999; Ge et al., 2021; Hope et al., 2004 ), or internal sources such as in-stream respiration (Finlay, 2003; Rasilo et al., 2017; Saccardi and Winnick, 2021 ). Notably, in-stream respiration was found to occur mainly in the streambed, particularly in the hyporheic zone (HZ) (Fellows et al., 2001; Naegeli and Uehlinger, 1997 ). The HZ is the area of the streambed where porewater flow paths originate and end within the water column (Boano et al., 2014 ). The HZ is characterized by intensive microbial activity, diverse microbial communities inhabiting the streambed, and a variety of redox conditions (Boano et al., 2014; Lewandowski et al., 2019; Mueller et al., 2022b ). The streambed interacts with the streamwater, which may exert shear stress that induces the movement of the sediments (Ahmerkamp et al., 2015 ). The movement of fine sediment grains often shapes the bed into repeating wave-like structures that are called bedforms (Kennedy, 1969 ). Bedforms may move downstream at a speed (i.e., celerity) that is mostly dictated by the size of the grains and the streamwater velocity (Ahmerkamp et al., 2015 ). The irregular shape of the bedforms creates hydraulic head variations at the stream-sediment interface (Boano et al., 2014 ). Such head variations drive a flux of streamwater through the streambed, which is referred to as hyporheic exchange flux (HEF). The occurrence of HEF due to the head distribution along the bedforms is often called ‘pumping’. Pumping controls the exchange process in non-moving bedforms and is characterized by downwelling and upwelling zones where advective transport moves water and solutes between the streamwater and pore water of the HZ (Boano et al., 2014 ). When bedforms are moving, pore water is released from the upstream face of the bedforms and at the same time streamwater gets trapped in the sediment at the downstream side of the bedforms. The HEF due to bed motion is termed ‘turnover’ (Elliott and Brooks, 1997a; Packman and Brooks, 2001 ). Pumping and turnover increase with increasing streamwater velocity and bedform celerity in non– and slow-moving sediments (Schulz et al., 2023 ), while under higher bedform celerities the relative contribution of pumping to HEF is reduced. Thus, changing streamwater velocities during flow events are expected to significantly affect bedform celerity and HEF, which in turn are expected to influence solute exchange and various biogeochemical processes in the streambed. Numerous studies have recognized the significance of dynamic streamwater flow for HEF (Boano et al., 2007; Singh et al., 2020, 2019 ) and biogeochemical processes within the HZ (Galloway et al., 2019; Hester et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2021b; Kaufman et al., 2017; Trauth and Fleckenstein, 2017 ). Nevertheless, most of the abovementioned studies focused on immobile streambeds despite the frequent occurrence of bedform motion in natural environments (Risse-Buhl et al., 2023 ). Several modeling and experimental studies attempted to quantify the effects of discrete, constant streamwater velocities and bedform celerities on processes such as O2  consumption rates (Ahmerkamp et al., 2017, 2015; De Falco et al., 2018; Wolke et al., 2019 ), microbial activity (Monterroso et al., 2024; Scheidweiler et al., 2021 ), transformation of nitrogen-containing compounds (Ahmerkamp et al., 2015; Kessler et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2019 ), N2 O production (Jiang et al., 2022 ), and other reaction rates (Santizo et al., 2022 ). To the best of our knowledge, the combined impact of dynamic flow regimes and bedform motion on biogeochemical processes has not been explored previously. Here, we present an experimental study providing new insights into CO2  production, as well as its retention in the HZ vs. release to the water column and ultimately to the atmosphere under both constant and dynamic flow regimes. The aim of this study was to quantify the effect of flow regimes on the dynamics of aerobic respiration and CO2  evasion during bed motion. To achieve our goal, we designed flume experiments with different flow regimes including constant discharge (C), sinusoidal flow (S), and a single peak flow event (F). These flow regimes represent natural events and human-altered flow conditions resulting from water resource management practices. We hypothesize that different flow regimes determine the zones of aerobic biogeochemical activity in the hyporheic zone and hence influence the distribution of O2  and CO2  concentrations in the streambed (H1). More specifically, we expect flow regimes to influence aerobic respiration (O2  consumption and DIC production) within the streambed in a way that O2  consumption and DIC production rates will follow the order: rates S > rates F > rates C (H2). This order is suggested as we expect non-linearly increasing respiration rates with increasing streamflow velocity (Schulz et al., 2023 ). Furthermore, variation of streamflow velocity and celerity may activate various sections of the streambed that are expected to produce overall higher respiration rates.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Experimental setup and study design The experiments were conducted in a 260-cm-long and 29-cm-wide recirculating indoor flume. Water and sediments were recirculated by a variable speed pump, while the discharge was measured with a magnetic flow meter located in the return pipe (SITRANS MAG 5100, Siemens, Germany). Natural sediment was collected from the upper 10 cm of the Yarqon Riverbed and placed in the flume to a depth of 17 cm. The collected sediment contained the natural microbial community, and no additional microorganisms were added to the flume. It is reasonable to assume that the microbial community near the water–sediment interface contained aerobic, anaerobic, and facultative bacteria. The sediment was characterized as medium sand (D50  = 0.27 mm) with a porosity of 0.37. The flume was filled with deionized water (DI) and sodium chloride (NaCl) was added to reach an electrical conductivity (EC) of approximately 1.5 mS cm−1 . The EC is slightly higher than that in the Yarqon but was essential to ensure the stability of the CO2  planar optodes. The water height above the sediment was 14 cm. The water was kept between 24.5 and 25 °C by driving water through a chiller (TR/TC 10, TECO Refrigeration Technologies, Ravenna, Italy). The flume was covered by black fabric to avoid photosynthesis and algal growth, and to protect the photosensitive planar optodes. Openings in the fabric ensured sufficient ventilation. More details concerning the setup were described in detail by Schulz et al. (2023) . Three flow regimes were tested in triplicate and included a constant flow regime (C), a sinusoidal flow regime (S), and a single peak flow event (F) (Fig. 1  a). We refer to the triplicates as “repeated measurements” (RM) since true replication is not feasible when conducting experiments at that scale (with one large flume), which is essential to produce the hydraulic conditions for the experiments. Therefore, the different flow conditions were applied consecutively. To overcome the potential effect of diminishing nutrients and substrates during the experiments on the reaction rates, and to make sure that there were no other systematic effects, we applied the flow conditions in an alternating order (RM I: C, S, F; RM II: S, C, F; RM III: F, S, C). Flow regimes were designed in a way to ensure that the same amount of water passed through the system over 24 h. The length of the experimental runs was 24 h, except for two of the RMs of flow regime C (Table S1 ). Different measurement lengths for C resulted from pump failures during the measurements and the fact that we did not observe significant dynamics during flow regime C. These reasons led to the decision of reducing the length of the experimental runs as the shorter measurement time was considered sufficient for data analysis. Prior to each experimental run, an adaptation time of 24 h was applied. The flow regime during the adaptation time was the same as during the experiments for flow regimes C and S. For flow regime F, a constant flow condition was used to mimic a typical flow regime prior to a flood event.  2.2 Flow regimes and automated flow control An automated flow control system was established through the utilization of a Campbell Scientific datalogger (CR1000) connected to an Encom EDS800 power inverter and to the centrifugal pump responsible for driving water through the flume. Additionally, the CR1000 was linked to the flow meter that measured the discharge. These connections enabled regulation of the speed of the pump via a Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) loop. The control system was programmed to modulate discharge following a sinusoidal and an exponential function, for flow regimes S and F, respectively. The streamwater velocity was calculated by dividing the discharge by the cross-sectional area of the water column (Schulz et al., 2023 ). The sinusoidal function had a period of 12 h and an amplitude of ± 9 cm s−1  around the mean of 21 cm s−1 . Sinusoidal flow regimes are often caused by WWTP and HPP operations that result in daily fluctuations (Mueller et al., 2022a ). A typical single peak flow event represents a flood-type flow that may occur due to intense rainfall or snow melt. The single peak flow event started at a discharge of 14 cm s−1  with a linear increase over one hour until reaching the peak discharge of 37 cm s−1 . The subsequent decline and tailing were calculated based on an exponential decline with a decay rate constant of −4.17 x 10-5  over 23 h. The flow was kept constant at 21 cm s−1  for flow regime C. The sinusoidal and flood-type flow regimes were based on actual flow patterns observed in the Erpe River (Germany) and the Yarqon River (Israel), respectively. However, the patterns of the different flow conditions are similar in other streams and rivers around the world.  2.3 Bedform celerity and hyporheic exchange flux The bedform celerities were calculated based on a power relationship (R2  = 0.94) between bedform celerities and streamwater velocities, with bedform celerity measurements conducted at discrete constant streamwater velocities (Schulz et al., 2023 ) (Fig. S1 a). We calculated HEF from an exponential relationship (R2  = 0.99) between discrete HEFs at various streamwater velocities from a prior study (Fig. S1 b) (Schulz et al., 2023 ).  2.4 Streamwater chemistry Water chemical conditions during the flume experiments were measured continuously using Aqualabo sensors for O2  (OPTOD), pH (PHEHT), turbidity (Champigny sur Marne, France), CO2  (eosGP, Eosense, Dartmouth, Canada). Data were collected and stored at a 1-minute interval using a CR1000 data logger (Campbell Scientific, USA). Electrical conductivity was measured daily to ensure stable EC values throughout all experimental runs using a handheld meter (WTW, Multi3420, Weilheim, Germany).  2.5 Solute Imaging A planar optode system was used to measure the spatial distribution of O2,  CO2  and pH at the sediment–water interface and in the HZ (VisiSensTD, Presens GmbH, Regensburg, Germany). Self-adhesive optodes (CO2 : SF-CD1R; O2 : SF-RPSU4, pH: SF-HP5R) were cut into 1-cm wide strips (0.5-cm wide for pH optodes). The optode strips were installed in vertical orientation in an alternating order along the inner side of the flume before packing it with sediment. The final area covered by the optodes was 15 x 11 cm. Results of pH optodes were not used in this study. Excitation light sources (VisiSensTD TD Big Area Imaging Kit, Presens GmbH, Regensburg, Germany) and optode camera were placed perpendicular to the optodes at a distance of 17 cm. The streambed-water interface was detected using an infrared (IR) camera module and IR-lights operated by a Raspberry Pi (Raspberry Pi 4 model b, Raspberry Pi foundation, United Kingdom). Optode excitation lights and IR-lights were switched on and off automatically to minimize light exposure of the photosensitive planar optodes. Planar optode data and IR images underwent several processing steps, including a distortion correction, geometrical transformations, and linear grid interpolation of missing data in between optode strips. Finally, they were matched to unified coordinates allowing the overlay of the sediment–water interface and the distribution of solutes in the hyporheic zone. More detailed information on the planar optode setup and image processing can be found in Schulz et al. (2023) . Planar CO2  optodes were calibrated weekly. Calibration curves were determined by bubbling CO2  gas into a calibration chamber for a short amount of time. The calibration chamber contained a piece of CO2  optode of the same batch as the optode installed in the flume and was exposed between calibration measurements to the same biogeochemical and physical conditions as the optodes in the flumes. The water in the calibration chamber was kept at 25 °C while it was continuously mixed by a magnetic stirrer. Concentrations were measured simultaneously with the CO2  optode and a CO2  sensor (eosGP, Eosense, Dartmouth Canada), while CO2  concentrations in the chamber decreased over time due to continuous outgassing. The calibration curve was fitted to a sigmoid function. Planar O2  optodes were calibrated daily by linear regression using a two-point calibration. This was done by setting a 20x20-pixel area of the optode that displayed surface water to be the 100 % air saturation calibration point. The 0 % air saturation calibration point was taken from an area of equal size in the lower part of the optode that was always anoxic. More information on calibration procedure was given by Schulz et al. (2023) . Optode images were taken at different sampling rates, which were on the one hand chosen to capture the movement of the bedforms while passing through the image frame. On the other hand, the different sampling measurement intervals helped to reduce the number of images as much as possible to protect the photosensitive optodes from photodegradation. Because of the high range of bedform celerities under flow regime F, the sampling rates changed throughout the experimental runs. Data of flow regime F was resampled to one data point per minute to obtain an equal sampling rate to be used during the analysis. Experimental runs of flow regime C RMs I and II did not cover the entire period of 24 h. Therefore, time series of RMs I and II were extrapolated to be able to integrate over 24 h. This was done by taking the arithmetic mean of the existing data due to the assumption that the system was at steady state during constant flow regimes. CO2  concentration images were converted to DIC images by accounting for alkalinity. DIC was computed using the Python tool PyCO2SYS version 1.8.1 Humphreys et al. (2022b)  developed by Humphreys et al. (2022a)  by taking into account the atmospheric and hydrostatic pressure, as well as concentrations of sulfate, phosphate, ammonia, calcium, fluoride, and salinity (input data in Table S2 ). Alkalinity was measured by titration with 0.01 M HCL (Metrohm, 775 Dosimat, Herisau, Switzerland). The DIC images that accounted for dissolved CO2 , bicarbonate, and carbonate, served as a basis a basis to calculate DIC production rates (Stumm & Morgan, 1996 ).  2.6 Respiration rates Respiration rates were calculated by Equations (1) and (2) .(1) R t , O 2   = F t , i n O 2     - F t , o u t  O 2     δ ∗ θ ∗ 24 h       (2) R t , D I C   = F t , o u t  DIC    - F t , i n  DIC     δ ∗ θ ∗ 24 h       where Rt   is the respiration rate at time t  (µmol L-1 h−1 ), Ft,in   and Ft,  out  are the fluxes into and out of the streambed (µmol cm−2  d-1 ), δ  is the mean penetration depth of the respective solutes (cm), and θ  is the porosity of the sediment.
