The Cohen’s d  or standardized mean difference is a common effect size to determine differences between groups (Hedderich and Sachs, 2016 ). Cohen’s d  is calculated by dividing the difference between means of groups (x ¯  1   a n d  x ¯  2  )   by the pooled standard deviation, sp   (Equation (4) ). sp   for unequal sample sizes is calculated using Equation (5) .(4) d = x  ¯   1  - x  ¯   2   s p       (5) s p  = n 1  - 1   ∗ s  1  2  + n 2  - 1   ∗ s  2  2   n 1  + n 2  - 2        where n  is the sample size and s  is the standard deviation of groups (1) and (2) . In cases where groups with RMs were compared, weighted means of RMs were used in Equation (4)  and standard deviations of RMs were averaged before applying Equation (5) . Cohen’s d values indicate how much groups differ from each other. A Cohen’s d  of 1 indicates that groups differ by 1 standard deviation. Commonly the strength of Cohen’s d  is given by 0.2 being a small, 0.5 a medium, and 0.8 and above being a large effect size (Hedderich and Sachs, 2016 ).   3 Results 3.1 Impacts of flow variation on streambed morphology and hyporheic exchange flows Three flow regimes were applied during the experiments by controlling the magnitude and timing of streamwater discharge. The experiments were designed in a way that the total volume of streamwater that was circulated through the system in 24 h was equal (720 m3 ) in order to have a common metric under all flow regimes. The changes in streamwater velocity influenced bedform celerity, HEF, microbial activity, and streamwater chemistry (Fig. 1 ). Streamwater velocity, bedform celerity, and HEF were positively correlated (Spearman‘s coefficients of 1) and showed similar patterns across the three flow regimes (Fig. 1 a-c). The streambed became stationary when flow conditions were below the critical shear velocity (flow regimes S and F in Fig. 1 b). The streambed was never stationary in flow regime C. Flow dynamics were also reflected in the physical and chemical properties of the streamwater. For example, turbidity and CO2 , produced by aerobic respiration, followed the fluctuating patterns of streamwater velocity but with a slight delay (Fig. 1 d and f). pH values dropped in accordance with increasing CO2  concentrations (Figure S2 ). O2  concentrations were fluctuating near saturation value (∼268 µmol/L) under all streamflow conditions, with variability mainly related to the ± 1 °C changes in temperature (Fig. 1 e). The distributions of streamwater velocity, bedform celerity, and HEF differed among the three flow regimes (Fig. 2  a). Medians for streamwater velocity, bedform celerity, and HEF were equal between flow regimes C and S and slightly lower for flow regime F. The range of data was the smallest for C and largest for F. The distributions of streamwater velocity for flow regime S were equally distributed around the median while skewed toward the low values for flow regime F. In contrast, the data distribution was heavily skewed to the lower values for the celerity and HEF for flow regimes S and F. Bedform celerity and HEF differed substantially between flow regime C and the other two, despite the similarity in streamwater velocities among groups (indicated by Cohen’s d values in Fig. 2 a). Finally, the total amount of water exchanged with the streambed was higher for S and F compared to C, although the total volume of streamwater that passed through the stream was the same for all flow regimes (Fig. 2 b).  3.2 Distributions of O2  and CO2  in the streambed The spatial distributions of O2  and CO2  in the streambed strongly depended on the hydrological conditions and associated bedform celerities (Fig. 3  ). CO2  concentrations in the upper fraction of the streambed were higher than streamwater concentrations when the bed was temporarily stationary regardless of the flow regime (e.g., Fig. 3 : S4, F1 & F4). In addition, curved distributions with pronounced anoxic chimneys of higher CO2  and lower O2  concentrations were observed when the streambed was stationary. Under these conditions, we observed smooth concentration gradients in the streambed from top to bottom. Slow-moving bedforms resulted in blurred O2  and CO2  chimneys, which traveled with the movement of the bedform (Fig. 3 : C1-C4, S2, F3; Movies S1-9). Also, the CO2  concentration in the moving fraction of the streambed was slightly higher than in streamwater. Under fast-moving bedforms (Fig. 3 : S3, F2), the concentrations of both gases were more homogeneous due to extensive mixing within the moving fraction of the bed. However, even under the fastest streamwater velocity, CO2  concentrations in the pore water of the moving fraction were slightly higher, and O2  concentrations were somewhat lower than streamwater concentrations. CO2  concentrations consistently increased with depth in the anoxic, non-moving fraction of the streambed under all flow conditions.  3.3 Dynamics of O2  and CO2  concentrations and respiration rates in the streambed The flow regimes influenced the O2  and CO2  concentrations within the oxic area of the streambed. Higher O2  concentrations were generally associated with lower CO2  concentrations and vice versa. Moreover, O2  concentrations typically increased with streamflow velocity, while CO2  concentrations decreased (Fig. 4  ). Small fluctuations in the concentrations were observed in flow regime C. In contrast, more substantial changes were observed during flow regimes S and F, where flow variability was higher. The strongest link between streamflow velocity and O2  and CO2  concentrations was observed during flow regime F. CO2  concentrations dropped, and O2  concentrations peaked during the initial flood peak of flow regime F. Afterwards, O2  concentrations continuously declined, and a continuous CO2  concentration build-up was observed during the tailing of the flood as the bedform celerity slowed down. DIC production rates were calculated after accounting for all inorganic carbon of the carbonate system by calculating DIC from the CO2  concentrations detected by the planar optodes. Both DIC production and O2  consumption rates increased with streamwater velocity and bedform celerity (Fig. 5  ). This is shown by relatively constant rates in flow regime C (Fig. 5 C). The respiration rates closely followed the dynamics of streamwater velocity in flow regimes S and F with very low respiration rates during stationary conditions (Fig. 5 S and F). The positive relationship differed from the relationships between streamwater velocity and CO2  and O2  mean concentrations, which decreased and increased, respectively (Fig. 4 ).  3.4 Comparison of respiration rates across flow regimes The highest respiration rates were found for flow regimes C, followed by flow regimes F and S. (Fig. 6  a and b). Effect sizes and percentage changes in medians determined for respiration rates supported these differences among flow regimes. The differences between the O2  consumption rates under the different flow regimes were less clear than those of the DIC production rates (Fig. 6 a and b). Respiration rates generally decreased as the experiment proceeded, with the highest respiration for repeated measurement I and the lowest for repeated measurement III. The total amount of O2  consumed and DIC produced within the 24 h of the experimental runs follow the trend of rates where C ≫ F ≥ S (Fig. 6 c). Overall, more O2  was consumed than DIC was produced, which translates to a respiratory quotient RQ lower than one.  3.5 Dynamics of CO2  evasion CO2  evasion rates from streamwater to the atmosphere followed the trends observed for streamwater velocity (Fig. 7  ). Evasion rates peaked slightly later than the streamwater velocity of flow regimes S and F (Fig. 7 a). The median and variability of CO2  evasion rates in flow regime C were substantially lower compared to the dynamic flow regimes S and F (Fig. 7 b). Comparison among flow regimes resulted in similar rates between the dynamic flow regimes S and F. Still, the evasion rates of both dynamic flow regimes were higher than the rates under flow regime C (indicated by Cohen’s d  values). These differences between flow regimes were also observed by looking at the overall amount of CO2  emitted from the streamwater (Fig. 7 c).   4 Discussion The aim of our study was to quantify the influence of different flow regimes on the dynamics of aerobic respiration and CO2  evasion to the atmosphere. To achieve this goal, we conducted flume experiments that encompass a constant, a sinusoidal, or a peak flow regime with conditions that combined sediment motion and stationary phases. To make the flow regimes comparable, an equal volume of streamwater was passed through the experimental system under the different flow regimes. 4.1 Dynamic flow regimes influence the distribution of O2  and CO2  in the streambed The distributions of O2  and CO2  concentrations in the sediment were influenced by the hydrological conditions of the various flow regimes and the resulting streambed morphodynamics thereby confirming the first hypothesis (H1). To clarify how morphodynamics affect solute distribution and reactions, we categorized the conditions into stationary (celerity = 0), slow-moving (0 < celerity > 0.13 m h−1 , which can be scaled to a movement of approximately one bedform length per hour), and fast-moving streambeds (celerity ≥ 0.13 m h−1 ). In stationary streambeds, the transport and distribution of solutes are determined by advective pumping, causing curved isolines in plots of concentration and spatially defined upwelling regions, i.e., “chimneys” (Fig. 3 : S4, F1 & F4; (Elliott and Brooks, 1997b; Precht et al., 2004; Schulz et al., 2023 )). Smooth concentration gradients were formed from top to bottom of the streambed, indicating hydrological connectivity between upper (moving) and lower (non-moving) fractions of the bed (Jiang et al., 2022; Schulz et al., 2023 ). Elevated dissolved CO2  concentrations were observed in the upper section of the bed compared to streamwater (Fig. 3 : S4, F1 & F4). This enrichment indicated that CO2  production in the streambed exceeded CO2  transport and created temporary storage of CO2  in the streambed (Ahmerkamp et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2022; Schulz et al., 2023 ). Fast-moving streambeds were characterized by fast celerity and rapid solute exchange between streamwater and streambed, which was dominated by turnover processes (Elliott and Brooks, 1997b, 1997a; Packman and Brooks, 2001 ). The flattening of flow paths and rapid mixing within the streambed led to a distinct sharp concentration gradient at the scour depth, between the moving and non-moving fractions of the bed (Fig. 3 : F2 & S3). The horizontal interface between a fast-moving layer above a non-moving streambed layer resulted in a redox seal (Precht et al., 2004 ). The elevated CO2  concentrations found in the moving fraction of the streambed (Fig. 3 : F2 & S3), even under fast-moving conditions, stems from aerobic respiration in the streambed and/or from the delivery of the stored CO2  from deeper streambed sections. The mechanism of CO2  transport from the deeper streambed towards the water column could be diffusion or bed scour. The scour depth of the sediment varies in time and depends on the bedform shape (Dallmann et al., 2020; Teitelbaum et al., 2021; Tonina et al., 2014 ). Deeper scour depths release CO2  from pore water that was once in the non-moving section of the streambed but were re-mobilized. Slow-moving sediments display the outcome of an interplay between advective pumping and turnover processes. Therefore, the isolines of solute concentrations were distorted from their characteristic curved shape under the stationary bed to a plume elongated in the direction of bedform movement. The elongated structure was particularly pronounced for O2  but less evident for CO2  concentrations (Fig. 3 : C1-C4, F3, S1 & S2). This is probably due to the lower resolution of the CO2  optodes (Schulz et al., 2023 ). The flow regimes S and F were characterized by relatively rapid shifts between stationary, slow-moving, and fast-moving bedforms compared to the constant conditions of slow-moving bedforms in the C regime. This can be observed in movies of bedform movement under all flow regimes (Movies S1 – S9). Our findings suggest that the O2  and CO2  distributions in the sediment at any given moment during the dynamic flow regimes depend also on the preceding hydrological conditions. Particularly the CO2  concentrations detected by the planar optodes seem to depend strongly on the aforegoing conditions in the streambed. For instance, in flow regime F (Fig. 3 : F1), the stationary sediment exhibits a well-defined curved distribution with distinct chimneys for both O2  and CO2  distributions. However, in Fig. 3 : F4, the characteristic distribution associated with advective pumping is already apparent in the oxygen distribution, while the CO2  concentration has not yet developed the characteristic pattern. This phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that prior to the peak flow in flow regime F, the streambed was stationary for 24 h. This extended period allowed enough time for CO2  accumulation to make the curved distribution strongly visible. After the flood peak, the curved distribution was probably developed but not visible due to the lower relative resolution of the CO2  optodes as compared to the O2  optode.  4.2 Mean concentrations and respiration rates in the streambed respond differently to changes in streamwater velocity The mean concentrations of O2  and CO2  in the oxic zone and the respiration rates in the streambed were clearly linked to the variations in streamwater velocity (Figs. 4 and 5 ). In general, the mean concentration of O2  increased, and the mean concentration of CO2  decreased with increasing streamwater velocity (Fig. 4 ). This is because increasing streamwater velocity is associated with increasing HEF, which in turn reduces the residence time of the porewater in the streambed. The increasing mean O2  concentrations in fast-moving bedforms do not necessarily translate into a decline in respiration rates, because of their dependency on HEF (Equations (1) and (2) ) that increased with celerity. O2  consumption and DIC production rates increased with streamwater velocity (Fig. 5 ). The highest rates were observed during the peak flow of flow regime F and the lowest rates under slow streamwater velocity when the streambed was stationary (i.e., under flow regimes S and F). These trends were similar to previous studies that measured (Schulz et al., 2023 ) and modeled (Kessler et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2019 ) how biogeochemical reaction rates are affected by celerity by applying discrete constant flow regimes and allowing time to reach steady-state conditions. Our observations suggest that the response time of microbial activity (i.e., respiration rate) to bedform celerity and associated HEF was relatively short, and the respiration rates under the dynamic flow conditions followed well the trends expected from discrete flow conditions (Schulz et al., 2023 ). The short response time is clearly seen by the synchronization between the rates and streamwater velocity, bedform celerity, and HEF (Fig. 5 ). A positive relationship between respiration rates and streamwater velocity within dynamic flow regimes was also found by Galloway et al. (2019), Jiang et al., (2021b) , and Trauth and Fleckenstein (2017) . Galloway et al. (2019)  and Jiang et al., (2021b)  report a delay between streamwater velocity and reaction rates under dynamic flow conditions, in contrast to our study. For instance, the study by Galloway et al. (2019)  is highly comparable to our study as it was conducted with sediment taken from the same location. However, because the entire flow regime consisted of non-moving bedforms and slow streamwater velocities (4 – 15 cm s−1 ) and HEF (2.5 – 7 cm d-1 ), the responses of O2  transport and distribution in porewater to changes in flow conditions were much slower than in our study.  4.3 Constant flow regimes produce more DIC than dynamic flow regimes The temporal dynamics of respiration rates clearly indicated that the highest potential for DIC production occurred under fast flow conditions and fast celerity. However, the distribution of production rates and the calculation of the 24-hrs cumulative production of DIC revealed that the highest production occurred under flow regime C, followed by flow regime F and S (C > F > S, Fig. 6 ). This finding contradicts the second part of the hypothesis (H2), which initially predicted the order S > F > C. It was anticipated that flow regime C would result in lower respiration rates due to lower HEF without any periods of high HEF compared to flow regimes S and F (Fig. 2 ), which was supported by the observed positive relationship between flow and respiration rates. However, the temporal distribution of flow conditions along flow regimes S and F resulted in a relatively prolonged duration where the streambed was stationary and thus exhibited particularly low respiration rates (Fig. 5 ). Therefore, the distribution of respiration over 24 h was primarily skewed towards the low values (Fig. 2 a and 6a and b). This behavior was consistent in all three RMs, despite the trend of reduction in the rates from RMs I to III due to the depletion of available nutrients over the course of the experiment. The increase in respiration rates from stationary to slow-moving bedforms was dramatic. In contrast, further increase in celerity led to a more gradual increase in respiration rates (Schulz et al., 2023 ), and thus the overall efficiency of flow regime C, with its slow but constant celerity, was the highest. However, it is important to note that the order of flow regimes is highly dependent on the velocity and celerity range chosen during the experimental design. This is especially true regarding the extent to which the bed remains stationary versus in motion. Changing flow conditions beyond those used in our experiment will require a study that combines the experiments with a numerical model that can capture flow, morphodynamics, and biogeochemical reactions. The finding again highlights how differently stationary streambeds behave from moving streambeds and that HEF is insufficient to predict respiration under dynamic flow conditions. This is especially important because most studies on biogeochemical processes in sandy streams have predominantly focused on stationary streambeds (Ping et al., 2022; Wolke et al., 2019 ), while bedform movement has been widely reported in geomorphic studies (Lichtman et al., 2018; Phillips et al., 2019 ). Furthermore, it appears that even slow-moving bedforms play a substantial role in hydrology in comparison to stationary streambeds and should be taken into consideration when studying biogeochemical processes in the hyporheic zone of streams and rivers. Estimation of bed movement is currently not widely available, but it is evident that many streambeds of lowland streams and rivers have slow-moving beds (Risse-Buhl et al., 2023 ). The sparse available information indicates that as much as 50 % of the sediments in lowland streams and rivers could be in motion at any given moment (Booker and Dunbar, 2008; Verzano et al., 2012 ). For example, about 16 % of all stream water courses in Germany have sandy sediments (Umweltbundesamt, 2014 ) and streamflow velocities that potentially move sediment.  4.4 Streambed movement enhances the release of CO2  into the atmosphere The fluctuations in streamwater CO2  concentrations (Fig. 1 ) and CO2  evasion rates (Fig. 7 a) demonstrated the strong connection with streamwater velocity. The increase of evasion with increasing streamwater velocity is straightforward and attributed to the increase of the gas transfer velocity with higher flow due to increased turbulence (Kokic et al., 2018; McDowell and Johnson, 2018; Raymond et al., 2012; Raymond and Cole, 2001; Tremblay, 2005 ). It is also expected that CO2  evasion will increase when CO2  concentrations in the streamwater are higher (Figs. 1 and 7 a). More unusual was to see that CO2  concentrations in streamwater increased during and after the peak in streamwater velocity (Fig. 1 ), even when respiration rates were already reduced (Fig. 5 ). Similarly, CO2  evasion lagged slightly behind the peak in flow regime F (Fig. 7 a), which was unexpected when considering the strong relationship between streamwater flow and the gas transfer velocity for CO2  (kCO2  ) (McDowell and Johnson, 2018; Raymond et al., 2012 ). The observed delay suggests that the CO2  in the streamwater column originates from the stored CO2  in the streambed that is released to the water column due to sediment motion. A substantial contribution of CO2  to the streamwater may be attributed to the release of stored CO2  from the deeper section of the bed, which is released during deep scour events. The comparison between the different flow regimes reveals a notable difference in the overall CO2  emitted between the two dynamic flow regimes, S and F, and the constant flow regime C (Fig. 7 b and c). This pattern aligns with the overall flux delivered through hyporheic exchange (Fig. 2 c) and deep scour events. This exemplifies that the overall CO2  evasion is the combined outcome of accelerating the production of CO2  and releasing accumulated CO2  during high flow events in the dynamic datasets.  4.5 Implications The flume experiments conducted in this study provided a realistic representation of field conditions and complemented previous studies on biogeochemical processes in moving streambeds, which were conducted under discrete flow conditions (Ahmerkamp et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2019 ). At the same time, the conditions in the flume experiments are simplified compared to natural conditions. Including complexities such as less uniform flow regimes, heterogeneous sediments, the presence of macrophytes, fluctuations in groundwater levels, and temperature variations, may lead to more realistic conditions but at the same time will probably hinder the identification of clear relationships. This is inherent to all laboratory experiments. We acknowledge that mesocosm experiments simplify field conditions but that is exactly the reason to conduct flume experiments. The main advantage of using flumes over other methods is the ability to control flow conditions and thus systematically investigate how flow conditions affect CO2  production and evasion. These experiments serve as complementary observations to field sites, where flow conditions are uncontrolled and detailed measurements of coupled CO2  production and evasion with bedform morphodynamics are challenging. As far as we know, there have been no studies under field conditions that included measurements on dynamic flow conditions, streambed morphodynamics, and CO2  production and evasion. The HZ with its steep redox gradients is a microbial habitat with a high diversity of microbial reactions (Lewandowski et al., 2019 ). The fluctuating stream flow conditions leading to permanent changes in sediment transport and hyporheic exchange also have a pronounced effect on the redox conditions within the sediment that are altered on short temporal scales (Boano et al., 2014; Lewandowski et al., 2019 ). The end products of the redox sequence include the GHGs CO2 , N2 O, and CH4  (Jiang et al., 2022; Mueller et al., 2022b ). The dynamics of CO2  production, storage and evasion described in the present study may also apply to other GHGs produced in streambeds (Jiang et al., 2022 ). These GHGs are formed at different bed depths of the streambed because their formation depends on the redox sequence as well as on the scour depth and stability of the streambed. The hydrological connectivity between the water column, the upper moving section of the streambed, and the immobile deeper sediment is influenced by dynamic flow conditions and has potentially far-reaching implications for CO2  emissions from streams and rivers (Ahmerkamp et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2021a ). We are not aware of any study that measured flow conditions, bed dynamics, and CO2  evasion. Therefore, it is unknown how this translates into estimates of annual CO2  emission or the pattern of CO2  evasion during a single peak flow or successive peak flow events (Singh et al., 2020 ). For instance, the supply of O2 , nutrients and dissolved organic matter (DOM) to distinct areas of the streambed is impacted by bedform movement. Also, the exchange and transport of produced gases abundant in the different zones of the streambed are strongly dependent on bedform celerity (Ahmerkamp et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2022; Schulz et al., 2023 ). Particularly important is the shift between stationary and slow-moving sediment conditions as well as peak flow events that can scour the bed and activate deeper sections of bed. Finally, it was shown here that bedform celerity controls HEF and is directly linked to respiration and CO2  evasion dynamics. It is apparent that streambed morphodynamics play an essential role in the aforementioned processes and need to be measured when studying biogeochemical reactions in streams and rivers with fine sediments. This was rarely done in the past. Floods have always been a focus when studying the hydrology of streams and gas evasion. Floods also have the potential to allocate a significant amount of sediment via fast-moving bedforms. However, it appears that slow-moving bedforms are particularly important for the overall respiration of the streambed. This is because slow-moving bedforms drive relatively fast reaction rates, especially when compared to stationary bed conditions (Schulz et al., 2023 ). It is likely that slow-moving bedforms are common, however, there is no global systematic information and statistics on sediment movement in stream and river networks.
1 Introduction Big data turns into information over complex systems as society develops its analytical vocation. In this context, anomaly detection is fundamental to transforming raw data into models describing the phenomena of interest. Anomalies, in the present work context, are defined as samples that present a significantly different behavior or pattern when compared to neighboring samples or sample universe. Hydrological time series can exhibit anomalies with distinct characteristics, which result from several causes, such as instrumentation and observation errors, equipment failures, and anthropogenic or natural changes in hydrological morphodynamics. Two terminology systems prevalent in academic literature will be adopted for this study due to their complementary nature and their apt delineation of notable characteristics of hydrological anomalies present in Brazilian data. Firstly, Crochemore et al. (2020)  emphasize heterogeneities, trends, outliers, and gaps. Heterogeneity refers to abrupt alterations in series because of natural or anthropogenic phenomena, such as shifts in river morphology following a storm or derivation from hydraulic works. Conversely, trends represent persistent characteristics with long duration attributed to morphodynamical evolution, human intervention, or gradual repositioning of measuring devices. Both trends and heterogeneities can manifest in streamflow time series in the absence of proper compensation for rating curve residuals. Alternatively, Chandola et al. (2009)  categorize anomalies into point-based, contextual, and collective. Point anomalies, or outliers, are high-frequency entities that deviate considerably from the sample pool or the immediate neighborhood. They became the focal point of much anomaly detection research based on statistical techniques. Contextual anomalies are instances that exhibit inconsistencies in behavior in relation to their neighbors. And lastly, collective anomalies present themselves as anomalous clusters that, within the context of the time series, appear as sequences of anomalous samples. In August 2020, Brazilian National Hydrometeorological Network (BHN), coordinated by the National Water and Basic Sanitation Agency (ANA), had 15,790 stage gauges, among them 6,813 were operated without telemetry, 5,365 were inoperative and 3,621 were telemetric gauges (ANA, 2020 ). In Brazil, where 40 % of its territorial extension is covered by the Amazon rainforest, there are important logistic challenges in operating a network of hydrologic gauges, either automated or not. The water stage is observed twice a day by riverside dwellers and months later collected by operating entities during streamflow measurement campaigns of those same stations, even in telemetric gauges. During the expected period of three months between technical visits, the observed time series may incorporate anomalies. This increases the chances and severity of observation errors, e.g., the so called “meter error” (when the observer, reading a gauge in centimeters, wrongly adds or subtracts a unit from the hundreds place), gauge displacements, subsampled observation, and low density of streamflow samples on high water stage. Consequently, artifacts of different characteristics such as gaps, high-frequency anomalies, inhomogeneity, and trends are present in the BHN time series of different regions. The inherent intricacies of BHN management are quantifiably delineated by Crochemore et al. (2020) , who scrutinized 36,652 flow data time series from a global cohort of 13 operators. Their examination sought key indicators such as data availability, outlier’s ratio within series, homogeneity, and trending patterns. Within BHN, they uncovered a 40–60 % availability of total data spanning 1961 to 2019, a prevalence of series marred by monthly gaps, an insignificant outlier’s ratio in the Amazon basin, and between 0.5 to 1.0 % in other Brazilian regions. Disparities were noted in mean annual data homogeneity across various regions, alongside identified trends in mean annual flows and specific months. In an international context, hydrometeorological networks in Africa and Asia were analogous to BHN, whereas data from North America, Europe, Russia, and Australia proved superior. Motivated by the findings of Crochemore et al. (2020) , the aim of the present study became to design and validate a model capable of detecting anomalies across various frequency bands, whether clustered or isolated, To accomplish this, multiresolution analysis will be coupled with the Generalized Extreme Studentized Deviate (GESD) to detect short time scale anomalies (one-day pulses), while Wavelet Coherence ((WTC) and Multi-wavelet Coherence (MWTC) will target longer time scale anomalies (above 16 days) present in network stage gauges. The model will enable a multivariate network analysis, leveraging the advantages of data availability and cross-referencing information from neighboring stations to detect anomalous artifacts. These two modules will constitute a pioneering ensemble named the Multiresolution Anomaly Detection System − MADE. In the proposed method, samples from contiguous series will be analyzed through oscillation modes confined to specific frequency bands, resulting in a more conditioned dispersion. Furthermore, modes within the same band tend to share common physical origins, enhancing the interpretability of anomaly detection. To showcase the scientific contributions of this approach, existing anomaly detection tools will be classified, and their key features highlighted. Subsequently, the new methodology will be presented, emphasizing its distinct advantages. After that, the innovative system will be validated by comparing its performance with three anomaly detection models based on approaches found in the literature. The first one is a state-of-the-art (SOTA) model based on Miau and Hsi (2020) , that detects anomalies by classifying the residuals from the regression of the target series using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) algorithms. The second applies k -Nearest Neighbor (k -NN) paired with neural network regression as presented by Yu et al. (2014)  and Hill and Minsker (2010) , a widespread approach. The third validation model uses Empirical Data Analytics (EDA) model coupled to clustering technics (Gu and Angelov, 2017 ). The models will be tested on two experiments with synthesized anomalies of low and high frequencies, enabling access to their real classification. This will facilitate the accurate estimation of the specificity, sensibility, and precision of the tools.  2 Related works A brief categorization and description of the primary techniques employed in the detection of hydrological data anomalies is provided, with an intent to highlight their disparities. Subsequently, this description will underscore the advantages of the proposed method, which will be validated using models from the various categories outlined henceforth. The classification adopted broadly follows the approach by Chandola et al. (2009) , dividing the techniques into statistical, clustering, nearest neighbor-based and spectral. Hodge and Austin (2004)  further subdivided the statistical techniques into parametric proximity-based, non-parametric, and semi-parametric − nuances of relevance to this study. There also exist techniques based on signal processing analysis (Barua and Alhajj, 2007; Rasheed et al., 2009 ), which are categorized here as spectral techniques. 2.1 Statistical techniques In the present work, statistical anomaly detection techniques are those that classify as anomalous samples with low probability to be generated from the statistical (parametric or non-parametric) model fitted to the given data universe. Conversely, normal instances occur in high probability regions of the fitted model. The classification is made by a statistical inference test. This group of techniques provides a statistical basis for classifying anomalies according to the confidence interval adopted. Thus, if the data distribution respects the statistical model assumptions, significance can be adjusted as in a decision-making process, leading to unsupervised classification of anomalies. Nevertheless, the statistical inference test considers the entire sample universe and is not able to detect contextual anomalies. Additionally, collective anomalies may not be statistically independent, contaminating the assumptions of the fitted model. Among one-dimensional parametric techniques, the GESD stands out because it deals with multiple outliers that end up masking each other in a univariate and approximately normal distributed data set. The process was described by Manoj and Kannan (2013)  who found that GESD was superior to the Grubbs test in detecting abnormalities in blood pressure data. GESD only requires the prior specification of the maximum number of outliers to be detected, r . The technique performs r  sequential tests, selecting and removing, each time, the sample with the largest absolute standard deviation. Another example of statistical approach is found in Kiang et al. (2018) , where an outlier detection parametric statistical technique was as part of a tool package used by the American Geological Survey − USGS, for flow time series analysis. Bae and Ji (2019)  detected outliers in water stage data based on the robust Median Absolute Deviation estimator – MAD, associated with a weighted moving average filter. The sensitivity of the outlier identification step using MAD was linked to the window size and the rejection criterion used in the modified Z  Test.  2.2 k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) techniques k -NN methods locally approximate functions to neighboring predictor samples. This provides the ability to fit these functions to local features and to model hydrologic time series non-stationarities. The selection of the vicinity samples to fit the models plays a similar role to the window size in a filtering technique. Thus, the phenomena that can be resolved are intrinsically related to the window size of the neighboring dataset. Although the implementation is easy, the computational cost grows significantly with the dimensionality. At first glance, the computational complexity of a k -NN model appears to be O (n 2 m ), where n  is the number of samples and m  is the dimensionality. But calculating metrics across all dimensions means that high dimensionality quickly exceeds such computational efforts. Moreover, when combining neural networks and k -NN, the cost will also increase with the number of parameters, depending on the adopted network architecture. Limiting the number of neighboring samples would make k -NN models fast and attractive to online anomaly detection. However, proximity-based techniques classify samples according to a pre-established norm and threshold that must be calibrated to proper anomaly detection. A sliding window regression model classified both future water stage and streamflow data of two important control sites of the upper and middle reaches of the Yellow River, in China (Yu et al., 2014 ). The model exhibited stable reciprocity relationships between sensitivity and specificity, compared to other models, such as Box-Plot, support vector machine (SVM), and median, with better average results. Similarly, an ARIMA multi-layer Perceptron artificial neural network detected anomalies in online wind data of Corpus Christ, Texas (Hill and Minsker, 2010 ). Ye et al. (2020)  implemented an ARIMA model with a sliding window (k -NN) coupled with a K -Means algorithm at a hydrologic time series of 70 gauges on the Chu River between 2015 and 2017. They outperformed an isolated ARIMA model and performed like Multivariate Adaptive Spline Regression models, considering sensitivity.  2.3 LSTM based techniques The use of LSTM algorithms in anomaly detection approaches, although considered state-of-the-art, is like the reviewed k -NN techniques in the sense they use target series regression to study the distribution of residuals in neighborhoods defined by sliding windows, for each sample. However, the regression would theoretically become less dependent on windows, given the LSTM's ability to maintain relationships of various scales over long periods. LSTMs detected anomalies in time series data from different areas (Malhotra et al., 2015; Malhotra et al., 2016 ). According to the authors, LSTM allowed for the detection of anomalies independent of window characteristics. However, the length of the windows used for sequence-to-sequence training not only limits the scales of relationships established by the LSTMs but also determines the number of dimensions to describe the probability distribution space of residuals. In Miau and Hsi (2020) , LSTM was used for anomaly detection in hydrological water stage.  2.4 Clustering techniques Empirical Data Analysis (EDA) identified anomalies via non-parametric estimators in synthetic data, and in other three benchmark datasets (Gu and Angelov, 2017 ). Firstly, EDA detected potential anomalies. Then, a partitioning procedure grouped the data in shape-free nonparametric data clouds and only samples that remained isolated were confirmed as anomalous. The multivariate and autonomous non-supervised technique was based on data characteristics. The method has the advantage of requiring no prior assumptions or knowledge about the data set, and it outperformed two other anomaly detection methods which were investigated by Gu and Angelov (2017) .  2.5 Multiresolution analysis-based techniques Multiresolution analysis-based techniques aim to correctly identify anomalous samples, by using both time and frequency as contextual attributes. The balance between temporal and frequency resolution (in the case of time series) allows for capturing low-frequency coarse information and high-frequency details. Multi resolution analysis using Wavelet Transform techniques has had many applications in recent years in several areas related to hydrology, meteorology, oceanography, and other geosciences (Labat et al. 2000a,b; Machiwal and Jha 2006; Labat 2008; He and Guan 2013; Nutz and Wolf 2014; Doucoure et al 2016; Han et al. 2017; Ciria et al. 2019 ). Barua and Alhajj (2007)  developed a sea surface temperature (SST) and rainfall data anomaly detection algorithm using the Daubechies-4 Fast Wavelet Transform (FWT). The anomalies were locally characterized by the difference between the modes of the same scale in the neighborhood. The results were not compared to other techniques. In anomaly detection, multiresolution analysis is the research base in different fields, (e.g., Zhang et al., 2008 , on internet traffic anomaly detection; Ando et al., 2013 , on numerical and sequential observation of behaviors, such as trajectories). However, the authors found no research applying multi-resolution analysis to river data networks in the present review. The present work addresses this subject, observing that it becomes increasingly relevant as many human interventions in the watersheds change water stage and discharge historical patterns (e.g., Han et al. 2021 ), not to mention climate change. Therefore, the present research constitutes an innovative application of multi-resolution analysis in the detection of anomalies of different scales in hydrological networks.   3 Methods The review and description of the methods by classification group made in the previous item will now allow the reader to understand the differences and advantages of the proposed method. Parametric statistics techniques have limitations regarding dimensionality. Additionally, such techniques compare the entire sample universe without multiresolution criteria, making it difficult to identify contextual anomalies. GESD stands out for robustly dealing with multiple outliers, which end up masking each other. However, GESD can only identify point anomalies. The nearest neighbor techniques and LSTM, on the other hand, could theoretically reduce the scope of the analysis, focusing on the surroundings by adopting an analysis window, which would bring computational gain. However, the choice of the analysis window implies the predefinition of the mathematical basis, harming the analysis of non-stationarity and non-linearities present in real signals. Nonlinearities potentially manifest themselves as modulations of frequency or amplitude, causing significant changes at intervals smaller than a characteristic period of the phenomena. In this context, a rigid mathematical basis, tied to a fixed filter width would need to be adapted to each case or even to certain portions of the signal. The EDA coupled with potentially anomalous samples clustering, allows multivariate applications, making them attractive for use in monitoring networks, where one or more stations would be used to perform the consistency of the target series. In addition, EDA showed versatility when autonomously tested on different data sets. But none of the revised tools can handle all the anomalies identified in BHN data. The detection of point, contextual and collective anomalies can be improved by using time and frequency as contextual attributes. In the present research, multiresolution analysis was used to detect anomalies in the raw water stage time series of the BHN. To this end, GESD detected short time anomalies on water stage wavelet faster modes (2-, 4-, and 8-days periods), while Wavelet Coherence (WTC) and Multiple Wavelet Coherence (MWTC) detected anomalies on periods above 16 days. 3.1 Method advantages– preconditioning Reviewed methods aim to identify anomalies in time series through the statistical distribution of the entire sample space (as in GUESD) or neighborhood (as in k -NN and LSTM). Even clustering methods do so from the entire sample universe. However, by comparing modes resulting from the discrete wavelet (at faster scales) and modes from the continuous wavelet (at slower scales), the proposed method preconditions the space. Fig. 1  (A) displays the scatter between the daily mean water stages time series from stations 22 and 24 (see numbering in Fig. 2  ), while part (B) corresponds to the scatter between the 16-day modes of these same stations. (B) has principal directions ratio about 25 % lesser than (A). The same comparison between normalized time series on (C) and normalized modes on (D) shows a reduction of 42 % on the ratio of principal components of normalized modes. Hence, besides conditioning the space, mode analysis improves normalization since each mode resembles a harmonic, having a zero mean with rare amplitudes greatly exceeding the standard deviation. Furthermore, (B) and (D) have improved covariance structures, as illustrated by the shapes of corresponding histograms plotted without axes labels in (C) and (D). Simpler covariances benefits parametric classification approach (e.g., fitting a normal distribution to the data). It also favors the direct application of the Mahalanobis distance, which requires an invertible covariance matrix with a simplistic structure. Non-parametric tool adjustments, like the One-Class SVM, would also perform better by modes. Finally, it is evident that the anomalous samples in (B) and (D) are aligned in a distinct principal direction, which is undoubtedly a significant contribution of the proposed approach.  3.2 Wavelet, WTC, and MWTC Wavelet is the theoretical basis of both WTC and MWTC. In the past, the Fourier-based techniques were supported by the stationarity and linearity hypothesis, compromising real-world signal analysis. Such methods tend to disperse energy through frequencies, causing poor spectral resolution, especially at low frequencies (Rao and Hsu, 2008 ). Furthermore, Fourier-based techniques do not integrate time and frequency domain analysis. Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) overcame stationarity limitations, but with resolution tied to a fixed-width filtering window (Pimentel, 2019 ). STFT can be considered a Wavelet particular case (Pinto, 2009 ). But Wavelet uses a base called mother Wavelet that can be deformed and translated, leading to a balance between time and frequency resolution. The mother wavelet does not need to be sinusoidal, unlike the Fourier Transform base. The Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) is defined as the convolution of the series with local Wavelets, according to equation (1) , where x (t ) is the time series, ψs   the Wavelet, and t  the time.(1) W x , ψ   s , t   = x ( t )  ∗ ψ s  t          The above convolution is defined in a time–frequency domain. The scale parameter s  manipulation deforms the base to balance time–frequency resolution. As a filtering operation, Wavelet exhibits a boundary effect varying according to filter width through scales. This effect is characterized by a region at the time–frequency scalogram known as the cone of influence. Let ψ t      the wavelet basis located at - T / 2 , T / 2    , and centered at t  = 0. The Wavelet Transform convolutes the signal with shifted and scaled wavelets 1 s  ψ t - τ  s      , located and centered at t  = τ . The scale parameterization distinguishes CWT from Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT). (2003) . To reveal spectral regions that are not merely coincidental coherent, WTC significance is estimated. More details on significance and smoothing in space and frequency can be seen in Torrence and Compo (1998) . Cross Wavelet Spectrum was used by Jevrejeva et al. (2003)  to establish Arctic Oscillation and Baltic Sea maximum ice covering connection. Labat (2010)  used the WTC and the Cross Wavelet Spectrum to establish connections between large-scale atmospheric and oceanographic data and estimated ocean discharge of main rivers in five continents (Amazonas, Orinoco, and Paraná rivers in South America). The study focused on interannual and decadal time scales. As WTC can be seen as a bivariate correlation coefficient, MWTC is a multivariate correlation coefficient. Hu and Si (2016)  presented a robust method for MWTC calculation tested in synthetic data sets resulting by the summation of five cosine waves with different scales. The method overperformed existing techniques by exhibiting spectral coherences in the interval [0,1] and not being limited to bivariate cases. The method was also tested on real-time series of free surface evaporation and other meteorological data in Shaanxi, China.  3.3 Long time scales and network multiresolution analysis Above certain scales, time series of contiguous stations show similarity translated into persistent spectral coherence regions in WTC scalograms. Spectral coherence drops point out possible anomalies, considering an adopted significance. Thus, grouping network contiguous stations is a pre-processing main task to identify anomalies. Contiguous stations located at the same river reach were grouped and MADE calculated WTC of their raw water stage time series two by two. Only pairs that presented similarity above a threshold (linear regression coefficient of determination was used) had WTC calculated. In stretches with tributaries, MWTC of the downstream station was evaluated, having all upstream contiguous tributaries as regressors. By posit, groups of contiguous stations at the same reach were classified as (type 0) and groups containing tributary rivers stations were classified as (type 1). Fig. 2  illustrates a single-line diagram with São Francisco River (SF) stations. Local identification numbers had been assigned to diagram stations. Two groups were marked: a green solid line encloses a group of contiguous stations with local numbers 22, 24, and 26, in the SF channel (type 0), while a dashed red line bounds another group with station 24 (on the SF channel) as MWTC target, and stations 22 (on the SF) and 23 (on the Urucuia river) as predictors. 3.3.1 WTC type 0 groups In type 0 groups, water stage time series pairs generated WTCs scalograms with predefined significance. Fig. 3   illustrates station 24 WTC scalograms (HIDROWEB/ANA code 44200000). SF contiguous stations were grouped three by three as described in Table 1  . Black solid lines in Fig. 3  encompass WTC regions above 50 % of significance. Reducing WTC significance would generate different anomaly detection scenarios, ignoring, for instance, subtle anomalies caused by incremental runoff effects between stations. Red rectangles cover sudden coherence decline regions, corresponding to potential anomalies. The four red rectangles in Fig. 3  corresponds to the four anomalous sections synthesized in the target series 24, as described in item 4. Black arrows in Fig. 3  scalograms represent the lag between signals through the scales of analysis and were defined in Grinsted, et al. (2004) . In the present methodology, the lags are used only as graphic elements illustrating the coherence between the signals, allowing the identification of regions with remarkable spectral coherence. Sudden angle changes would highlight anomalies. Vertical axes in Fig. 3  are dyadic timescales varying from 2 days to the maximum WTC period extracted from time series common lengths. Vertical axes markers, called octaves, were subdivided into a preset number of voices per octave for the WTC analysis. The greater the number of voices per octave, the better the continuous wavelet is solved, requiring, however, more computational effort. The present study adopted 12 voices per octave as standard, solving scalograms satisfactorily. Morlet was chosen as the mother-wavelet because it is the standard in both WTC and MWTC algorithms. Although using other wavelets might reveal unnoticed artifacts, this is not deemed a suitable validation strategy once Grinsted, et al. (2004)  chosen Morlet due to its excellent balance between time and frequency localization, enabling smooth, readable scalograms. Time series boundary effects are represented by translucent areas delimited by thin black lines in scalograms and are named cones of influence. Boundary effects occur in any averaging process because in such regions the lengths of the filters used extend outside the validity period of the analyzed series. Thus, series must be extended beyond filter length, (e.g., series limit mirroring). Elements at the cone of influence were not processed by WTC or MWTC. Fortunately, for the present analysis, the interest time range, under 90 days was not affected considerably by cones. Before analysis, two null matrices stacks P K × L × N     and M K × L × N     were computationally pre-allocated, where K   is the maximum number of voices among all the analyzed scalograms, L   is the maximum common length between WTC stations pairs and N  is the total number of stations. The total number of WTC analyzes (m  ) results from combining type 0 groups stations two by two. Each WTC analysis generated a matrix W k i  × l i    ( i = 1 : m )     with associated scalogram dimensions, being k i   , the number of WTC octaves multiplied by the pre-established number of voices per octave and l i   , the common length of series. W   was then converted into a binary matrix I k i  × l i     , with zero on elements with significant WTC, and one elsewhere. As each WTC involved two stations, the elements of each I k i  × l i    ( i = 1 : m )     were added at respective positions of two P K × L × N     layers. In the end, each P   element stored the number of low coherence incidences on respective k i  × l i     scalogram elements. In parallel, each M K × T × N     position counted the number of times the respective Δ k i  × Δ l i     elements were analyzed, excluding cones of influence and missing data gaps. As an example, coincident regions of low WTC were marked with red rectangles in Fig. 3 . Thus, after WTC analysis, respective elements value assumed four in P   and M   matrices of station 24.  3.3.2 MWTC type 1 groups Like WTC, MWTC was carried out by totalizing the number of times (excluding time series gaps and cone of influence) each discrete space element was evaluated in respective M   matrices and the number of low MWTC occurrences on respective P   matrices. However, on MWTC, only the downstream station at each type 1 group was targeted, having contiguous tributary stations as regressors.   3.3.3 Long time scales anomalies After WTC and MWTC, only the P   elements equal to respective M   elements were classified as anomalous, because they corresponded to time–frequency domain elements with no significant coherence compared to correspondent M   elements and assumed value 1, while other P   elements received 0. P   matrices were then transformed into vectors with length L  by summing up their lines. Station samples with corresponding P   elements greater than zero were finally classified as anomalous. Indeed, as the pairs of WTCs were compared, the matrix P   accumulated the number of times each of its time–frequency elements had coherence below the adopted significance, while M   accumulated the number of crossings of each corresponding element in the Scalograms. In the end, only elements with equal values in P   and M   were considered anomalous and assigned a value of 1. The sum (through the frequency band of blue rectangle) of the rows in each matrix in the P   stack (from 1 to N stations) that exceeded unity corresponded to the time positions of anomalous samples. Fig. 4  shows the MWTC of station 24 with predictors 22 and 23. Red rectangles marked four low coherence regions previously pointed out by WTC.  3.3.4 Long time scale pseudo-code Read data [dates , station 1 , …, station n ];  Read codes; # two columns matrix (local station codes × base general codes);
