GESD was chosen to detect short-time outliers because it is robust, deals with outliers that mask each other, and requires, as a parameter, only the maximum number r  of outliers to be detected. To favor high-frequency anomalous pulses detection, the DWT was previously applied to series, using the Symlets wavelet with two null moments as the mother wavelet and the mirroring technique to extend the contours. Only the fastest modes sum resulting from the DWT was submitted to GESD. 3.4.1 Short time scales pseudo-code Read data [dates , station 1 , …, station n ];  Read codes; # two columns matrix (local station codes × base general codes);  Enter the analysis band b ; # (for short time scales, use 2-days and 4-days modes);  Pre-allocate I  , with N   lines and L   columns;  For i = 1 : N    (WTCgroups)  x i  ← m o d e 1 + m o d e 2 ;    # Here, x i    without gaps, m o d e 1    and m o d e 2    are the 2-day and 4-days modes of x i   ;  x i  ← G E S D ( x i  )    ; # call GESD only for specific modes;  I i     receives the elements of x i    at corresponding positions, where anomalies are ones and normal samples are zeros  end       4 Case studies Two anomaly detection experiments were carried out separately in station 24 daily mean water stage time series. The first with synthetic anomalies scaled above 15 days and the second containing one-day synthetic anomalous pulses. Both experiments had positive labels only on synthetic anomalies, allowing specificity, sensitivity, and accuracy estimations. Specificity is the rate of proper non-anomalous classification, sensibility is the proportion of anomalies correctly classified, and accuracy is the rate of total samples correctly identified. The synthetized anomalies are described in items 4.3 and 4.4. 4.1 Models and scenarios The performances of MADE modules (long and short-time scale) were compared with a LSTM model, a k -NN model based on ANNs, and a third validation model called Autonomous Anomaly Detection (AAD), based on EDA coupled with grouping techniques to identify anomalies. Several scenarios were simulated to validate MADE in both experiments. 4.1.1 MADE scenarios The scenarios of MADE were built varying significance μ  of WTC and MWTC at low frequencies and r  parameter, proportional to the number of anomalies detected by GESD at high frequencies, r  = [0, 1].  4.1.2 LSTM scenarios The LSTM validation model took inspiration from the reviewed works (Malhotra et al., 2015; Malhotra et al., 2016; Miau and Hsi, 2020 ). Thus, in both the rapid-scale and slow-scale experiments, the target series from station 24 was regressed from series 22 and 26 using a sequence-to-sequence regression approach. First, the input and output series were divided into sliding sequences of size ΔT. Then, the test set T1 was created by setting aside all ΔT sequences containing synthetic anomalies. In this manner, each anomaly was contained in ΔT test sequences. Next, two anomaly-free validation sets, making up 15 % of the remaining sequences ΔT, were randomly selected without replacement. To avoid anomalies in the validation subsets V1 and V2, LSTM was trained using consisted time series. The first validation set, V1, was used to generalize the model composed of an LSTM layer, a fully connected layer, and a regression layer. The LSTM was trained via mini-batch learning, using the optimal batch sizes of 32, considering the best validation loss. After training, the LSTM residuals in V1 (a ΔT dimensional space, as each V1 sample was part of a ΔT sequence-to-sequence relationship) was used to calibrate a One-class SVM (Hayton, et al., 2007 ) model with an extremely low significance, so that the number of samples classified as anomalies in V1 were virtually null. Subsequently, the same SVM determined the false positive rates in V2 and true positive rates in T1. This approach was deemed more suitable than fitting a parametric distribution, given the expected complexity in the covariances as depicted in Fig. 1 .  4.1.3 k -NN scenarios The ANNs in k -NN model used to validate MADE regressed h 0 t + 1     (t  + 1 water stage) as a function of k  previous values of the target and predictors:(5) h ^  0  t + 1   = f J i  t    , i = 0 : n     where J i  t  = { h i  t - k + 1   , h i  t - k   , ⋯ , h  i  t  }    , h ^  0  t + 1     is the estimated value of h 0  t + 1     and i  = 0 corresponds to the k -nearest autoregression window. The k -NN model used autoregressive ANNs with external predictors, and a backpropagation training function with Bayesian regularization (MathWorks, 2022 ). The simulated networks exhibited satisfactory performance with ten neuron units in the intermediate layer. The model used a prediction interval λ  (a range of plausible values that the next value can assume) calculated from the autoregression window data to detect anomalies. On k -NN model, the scenarios were created varying window size and the significance μ of the predicted value to fall off λ , according to:(6) h ^  0  t + 1   ± t μ / 2 , k - 1   × s 1 + 1 k     ⏟  λ      where t μ / 2 , k - 1     is the p th percentile of a Student’s t -distribution with k -1 degrees of freedom, s  is the standard deviation of the model residual inside the window (Hill and Minsker, 2010 );  4.1.4 AAD scenarios The AAD model selected as potential anomalies the first half of 1 n  2     of the data samples ranked in ascending order of multimodal density and the same number of samples ranked in ascending order of weighted local unimodal density, as in Gu and Angelov (2017) . In this case, n   describes the probability of a data sample to be more than n σ    (number of standard deviations) away from the mean μ , as in Chebyshev inequality. Thus, the validation scenarios were constructed by varying n σ   . In the fast time scales experiment, the AAD scenarios simulated only the first two DWT modes of water stage time series.   4.2 Research site and data MADE was tested on stations located mostly in the middle SF physiographic region. São Francisco is the largest river that lies entirely within Brazil, spanning for five states. Fig. 5   illustrates the region of interest in the SF basin. The region exhibit a climatic transition between dry sub-humid tropical from Cerrado biome to semi-arid tropical Caatinga, with 600 to 1,400 mm average annual precipitation, 24 °C average temperature, and 1,300 mm average annual evapotranspiration. The rainy season occurs from November to March, coinciding with Brazilian summer. The dry season is from April to October, with scarce or nonexistent rainfall (ANA, 2004 ). The study conducted by the National Water Agency (ANA, 2018 ) reveals that the middle São Francisco River, particularly Paracatu sub-basin shown in Fig. 5 , possesses a significant aquifer zone with optimal porosity, primarily located on the left side of the upstream basin. This finding is based on an analysis of aquifer typologies within the crastic and crastic-fissural hydrogeological systems in the São Francisco Basin. In addition to this geological characteristic, the presence of the Três Marias reservoir further contributes to a well-regulated flow regime observed at station 44200000. The flow data indicates a consistent ratio of 2/3 between the 95th percentile streamflow and the average streamflow. Fig. AI.1 in Appendix I  (Pimentel, 2024 ) shows the percentile streamflow curves within September 1972 to December 2014 for the main monitoring stations, and August 1986 to December 2014 for the tributaries. Anomaly detection simulations targeted station HIDROWEB/ANA 44200000 daily raw water stage time series, in the SF channel. Stations 42210000, 43200000, 44290002, and 44500000, located in the SF channel, and stations 42980000, 43980002, and 44250000, located in tributaries, were compared on MADE. Only stations 43200000, 44290002, and 44200000 fed ANNs and LSTM models, considering common data length, low gap incidence, and multicollinearity remedy (caused by correlated regressors). MADE and AAD did not have such restrictions and used all available series, including tributaries.  4.3 Slow time-scale anomalies Four slow time scale anomalies were synthetized by reducing the water daily stage sampling period to a fortnight and interpolating the resulting data: two in dry seasons (03/01/1978 to 11/01/1978 and 02/01/1990 to 11/01/1990), and two in rain seasons (12/01/1983 to 07/01/1984 and 10/01/2009 to 05/01/2010). Such synthetic anomalies are collective and contextual because they constitute anomalous groups with different frequencies from the neighborhood. Figs. 7 and 8  illustrate experiment time series and slow time scale anomalies. The time series from the remaining stations simulated by MADE are shown in Figs. AI.2–AI.4 included in Appendix I of the Supplementary material  (Pimentel, 2024 ). There is a notable similarity between the SF time series, highlighting synthetic anomalies.  4.4 Fast time scale anomalies In the second experiment, anomalous pulses were added to water stage time series 44200000. To formulate the pulses, the time series was divided into quartiles. Daily variability was then calculated as the daily water stage derivative within each water stage quartile. Finally, we randomly added or subtracted 0.1 % of the largest variability of corresponding January 15th and July 15th levels in the samples of those days. Fig. 6   illustrates the original time series and two synthetic anomalies. In 07/15/1974, for instance, the original water stage, 318.0 cm, was in the second quartile [270.0, 330.0) cm, and we subtracted a 105.1 cm pulse, corresponding to 0.1 % of the second quartile variability. Further detailed examples of synthetic pulses added to the series 44200000 can be found in Figs. AI.5–AI.7 in Appendix I  (Pimentel, 2024 ). Synthetic pulses resulted in Contextual and isolated anomalies. Therefore, anomaly detection tools must be able to assess variability locally, a challenging task, especially in January, when summer rains produce peaks in the studied time series. The magnitude of synthetic anomalous pulses is considerably smaller than the standard deviation of series 44200000. Values exceeding three standard deviations are generally considered outliers.   5 Results In anomaly detection experiments, the predominance of negative over positive samples renders the use of accuracy as an evaluation metric less effective. In these contexts, models categorizing all samples as false can misleadingly exhibit high accuracy. Therefore, a balance between precision and sensitivity is deemed a more effective strategy for accurate anomaly detection. However, in the present study, two regression-based models (one with LSTM and the other with ANN) were employed. For regression models, precision cannot be directly assessed due to the intricacies of separating training, validation, and test datasets. The number of false negatives could only be indirectly estimated (labeled as FN*) from the false negative rate noted in the validation set. Accordingly, four metrics were chosen to evaluate model performance: specificity, sensitivity, accuracy, and precision. These measures, along with their incorporation into Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) and Precision-Recall Curves (PRC), offer comprehensive insights into the efficacy of the models in anomaly detection. Table 2   summarizes the specificity (SP), sensitivity (SS), Acuracy(A), and precision (P*) of most significant scenarios of raw water stage anomaly detection of station 44200000, on slow and short time scales, with the best results highlighted in bold face. The asterisk in P* indicates that for regression models, precision was derived from the estimation of false negatives during validation. On slow time scales, MADE exhibited 92.0 % sensitivity, considerably higher than the 79.2 % sensitivity of k -NN, with window size ΔT = 15 days and significance μ  = 5.0 %. Only AAD model specificity outperformed MADE, with standard deviation parameter n  = 9, although it showed insufficient 0.25 % sensitivity and 93.8 % accuracy. MADE scored highest accuracy. Considering sensitivity and specificity together, the best model was MADE (in bold) followed by LSTM with ΔT = 7 days. At slower scales, MADE exhibited a P* 90 % higher than the second-ranked LSTM. MADE succeeded in detecting high-frequency anomalous pulses as well, achieving almost 100 % specificity and accuracy, and 95.1 % sensitivity. k -NN model with ΔT = 10 days and μ  = 0.0005 % exhibited 100 % sensitivity but with lower 98.8 % specificity, resulting 98.8 % accuracy. In third place, LSTM model with ΔT = 3 days, scored 100 % sensitivity and 96.8 % specificity, resulting in 97.4 % accuracy. Still, given the imbalance between positive and negative classes, MADE's superiority stood out significantly in terms of P*, outperforming the second-place k -NN by 129 %. MADE superiority stood out graphically. Fig. 7   presents the results of simulations using various models for two segments of synthetic anomalies, covering drought seasons in 1978 and 1990 (dashed black lines). Meanwhile, Fig. 8   displays simulations for two segments of rainy seasons starting in the summers of 1983–1984 and 2009–2010. In these figures, the areas where low-frequency anomalies were introduced in the series 44200000 are marked by dashed black rectangles, while samples classified as positive by the models appear in red. MADE consistently identified those sections as anomalous, while classifying the remaining data as normal. LSTM and k -NN reached low A and P* with similar proportions of positive classifications inside and outside the anomalous regions. However, the AAD model exhibited good accuracy, but with low sensitivity and P*, except between October 2009 and April 2010 (Fig. 8 L). Another aspect graphically revealed in Figs. 7 and 8  is network effects on MADE, analyzing other stations within the same group (A to C), with 43200000 located upstream and 44290002 downstream. While LSTM and k -NN did not analyze any contiguous station, MADE identified their possible anomalous samples, such as the artifacts between January and April 1979 (Fig. 7 C), and between July and October 1984 (Fig. 8 C) at station 44290002, absent in upstream series and in downstream series. On AAD, besides, suspicious samples in one series were indiscriminately classified as anomalous in all series of the group. At high frequencies, Fig. 9   illustrated MADE advantages in the best scenarios results. Despite having a slightly lower sensitivity than k -NN, MADE exhibited higher specificity, with virtually no false positives, while k -NN scored 98.8 % specificity. In terms of absolute values, the higher specificity means that k -NN misclassified 266 over 15.157 normal samples as false positives against just 6 false positive of MADE. Despite the absence of false positives from LSTM in Fig. 9 , its performance in terms of estimated P* (derived from the false positive rate of the validation set) was significantly inferior. The best P* performance was achieved by MADE, 0.987, followed by k -NN with 0.431. Additional scenarios were simulated to plot the Receiving Operating Characteristics (ROC) curves of the classifiers. Fig. 10   illustrates both slow time (ST) and fast time (FT) scales ROC curves. In ST, MADE exhibited considerably larger area under the curve (AUC) than the other classifiers confirming its superiority in anomaly detection on time scales over 16 days. The other models behaved almost as random classifiers, with ROC curves close to the [0,0] [1,1] straight line. In FT, the higher imbalance between positives and negatives led to an apparent balancing of the AUC. Thus, MADE, k -NN with 10 days windows size, and LSTM, with 3 days sequence-to-sequence length had similar AUC, with superior specificity of MADE, leading to a more accurate classification as shown in Table 2 . AAD once again resembled a random classifier. On the other hand, the Precision-Recall Curves (PRC) better highlighted MADE superiority in both slow and fast scales, proving the system's capability to be fine-tuned under the specified conditions, as revealed by Fig. 11  .  6 Discussion Four Different models were evaluated in the experiments, and MADE demonstrated superior performance, particularly in the ST. The discrete wavelet in the FT and the continuous wavelet in the ST led to data evaluation in a preconditioned space with simpler covariance relationships. Additionally, the mode decomposition projected the anomalies in a principal direction distinct from the data pool. These findings suggest that this advantageous approach could potentially be incorporated into other techniques or enable distinct MADE formulations. Furthermore, the analysis of specific modes or frequency bands allows for exploring the relationships between phenomena and the forces that generate the various features present in the studied signal in a more phenomenological approach. Despite the discrete wavelet resolution limitations due to its dyadic time scale, it still provides approximations of the temporal scales of well-known hydrological events. For example, orographic rainfall or late afternoon rainfall in tropical regions can be partially captured on the two-day scale, while cold fronts in subtropical regions can be captured in the four-day and eight-day modes. Other phenomena, such as Madden-Julian oscillations, effects related to the lunar component of the tide, and seasonality, can also be observed at different scales. These findings are applicable to longer waves as well. Regarding suggested experiments, a complement to the technique involves using additional data to corroborate anomalies, however with some caveats. For example, when analyzing rainfall data and streamflow, their spectral coherence is influenced by the characteristics of the incremental basin. The basins filter rainfall events and reduce coherence at faster scales. Alternatively, the target streamflow or water stage can be regressed using rainfall and other climatic series, and the results can be compared to identify anomalies. When using the WTC and MWTC methods to detect anomalies, data cross-linking significantly influenced by external noise, such as hydraulic works or abrupt morphodynamic changes, should be avoided. Excessive noise can convert low coherence into a consistent pattern rather than an exception. One potential scenario worth exploring is the crossing of series from opposite sides of a dam, particularly in large hydroelectric power plants. As the reservoir comes into operation, a covariance shift occurs in the scalograms. Thus, one should expect both slow-time anomalies caused by the reservoir regulation effect and fast-time anomalies triggered by operational outflows from the dam. Therefore, it is crucial to consider these factors when interpreting the results. An alternative approach to address the high computational costs of WTC and MWTC in the ST experiment, is to first decompose the data with DWT and then measure the similarity between corresponding modes of the series. Subsequently, a non-parametric tool, such as One-class Support Vector Machine, can be employed to classify the statistical distribution of similarities. Another suggestion to enhance efficiency is to calibrate the classification tool, which may be the WTC, by discretely varying its significance from a value close to zero to a value near 100 %. This approach would enable the calculation of the probability P   of each sample to be anomalous, rather than relying on a predetermined threshold for binary classification. The resulting probability can be computed as be P = 1 - μ ^    , where μ ^    denotes the minimum significance of analysis at which the sample obtained an anomalous classification. Then, visualizing the time series with a color scale corresponding to the resulting sample probability vector, would allow for the intuitive selection of the threshold that balances both sensitivity and specificity. These proposed alternative approaches expand the scope of the research beyond its initial objectives. However, as MADE continues to evolve during scaled use at BHN, these perspectives may be explored in future investigations.  7 Conclusions The BHN has vast dimensions, and a significant portion of its territory is covered by the Amazon rainforest. Within this network, issues such as unreported downrsampling of water stage by observers and failures in isolated telemetric sensors, among other causes, lead to the introduction of anomalous artifacts in the temporal series, which can be difficult to detect using traditional methodologies. This study presented and validated the multi-resolution anomaly detection system (MADE) for evaluating hydrological time series in the time–frequency domain. MADE provides a multi-scale insight and allows for the simulation of various types of anomalies, whether point, contextual or collective. Additionally, MADE employs network multivariate analysis to group hydrologically similar stations, preventing the misclassification of artifacts present in more than one time series of the same group as anomalous. These characteristics, combined with the preconditioning of the sample space, contributed to the superior performance of MADE in two validation experiments. MADE utilized WTC and MWTC for long-term scales (>16 days) and DWT coupled with GESD for fast time scales, resulting in effective anomaly detection. In the slow time-scale anomaly detection experiment, MADE outperformed LSTM-based, k -NN-based, and AAD-based models. The anomalies were synthesized by the fortnight downsampling of originally daily data from station 44200000, in SF River. The downsampling triggered a drop in spectral coherence ranging from 2 to 64 days, as observed in Fig. 3  WTC scalograms, covering a wide range of real-world anomalies while excluding trends caused by gauge displacement and other slow effects, which can be compensated for during stage discharge fitting or easily identified through WTC or visual inspection of time series. ROC and PRC analysis revealed that both k -NN and AAD models performed at random chance levels for periods longer than 16 days, while MADE behaved similarly to an ideal classifier. MADE also outperformed other tools in detecting synthetic anomalous pulses added to the raw water stage time series of station 44200000. The multi-scale DWT analysis enhanced outlier identification through GESD, displaying high accuracy, specificity, sensitivity, and precision. Despite achieving the best sensitivity among k -NN models by correctly classifying all 82 anomalies as true positives, its specificity of 98.8 % resulted in 266 false positives out of 15,157 cases, whereas MADE misclassified only 6 normal samples. Therefore, MADE’s precision outperformed by 129 %. Dealing with a high number of false positives can render the task of data scientists infeasible, as it is challenging to distinguish neighboring samples without the multi-scale criteria provided by MADE. Moreover, ROC analysis revealed that MADE performed closely to an ideal classifier in the best scenarios. The superior results of MADE in detecting synthetic anomalies with challenging characteristics, expected in various real situations, validate the model for its application in the consistency of hydrological network data. However, like other models presented, MADE requires case-by-case calibration. The discussion emphasized some strategies to reduce computational costs for model validation. Furthermore, the good results obtained in downsampling anomaly detection suggest exploring the potential of MADE in detecting trends and non-homogeneities caused by gauge displacements or morphodynamic evolution of the gauge section. Finally, it is suggested to further investigate the anomaly detection capability of MADE in streamflow time series to mitigate issues related to inhomogeneity and trends, optimizing rating curve regression.
1 Introduction In recent decades, global urbanization has accelerated continuously. According to the World Cities Report 2022, the percentage of the global population living in the urban areas surged from 25 % to 50 % between 1950 and 2020, and its projection indicates that it will reach 58 % over the next 50 years (UN-Habitat, 2022 ). Moreover, this trend is taking place amidst an ongoing intensification of global climate change. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) reported that the average global surface temperature has risen by 1.09 °C during the decade of 2011–2020, relative to the period of 1850–1900 (IPCC, 2021 ). In face of rapidly increasing global urbanization and climate change, urban flooding has become an ever-more pressing issue, causing significant economic and human loss. Disturbingly, between 1980 and 2013, urban flooding disasters incurred over US$ 1 trillion in direct economic damage and claimed more than 220,000 lives worldwide (Winsemius et al., 2016 ). Furthermore, addressing water scarcity necessitates rainwater harvesting (Jamali et al., 2020; van Dijk et al., 2020 ). To optimize flood management in urban areas, the adoption of numerical models calibrated with multiple sources of data is essential for evaluating associated risks and designing effective prevention solutions (de Vitry and Leitão, 2020 ). The primary cause of urban flooding is extreme rainfall events. According to Muller et al. (2015) , rainfall intensity (RI) can differ significantly by as much as 30–50 % over a distance of 3–5 km, indicating a pronounced spatial variability. The distribution of rainfall across a region is influenced not only by topography and geomorphology, but also by the duration of the rainfall (Willems et al., 2012 ). Urban storms of short-duration (e.g., lasting less than three hours) exhibit a greater degree of spatial variability than their longer-duration counterparts, resulting in localized pockets of intense rainfall and more pronounced temporal heterogeneity, evidenced by steep rainfall process curves (Wasko and Sharma, 2015; Zheng et al., 2015 ). These spatial variations in the distribution of rainfall have significant impacts on urban hydrological and hydrodynamic processes, ultimately influencing the regional prevalence of urban flooding and contributing to severe events in specific localities (Rabiei et al., 2013 ). Schilling (1991)  found that in order to effectively simulate urban drainage systems, rainfall data with a high temporal resolution of 1 min and a spatial resolution of 1 km2  are highly essential. Moreover, Gires et al. (2012)  discovered that rainfall data with a spatial resolution of 1 km2  may cause significant errors in simulation results compared to data with a much higher spatial resolution of 125 m × 125 m. Therefore, to achieve accurate and timely simulation and prediction of urban hydrological responses and to enable effective prevention and mitigation of urban flooding, it is critical to have access to real-time rainfall data with high spatial and temporal resolutions. There are several methods available for measuring RI, including rainfall station monitoring (Villarini et al., 2008 ), ground-based radar measurement (Thorndahl et al., 2017 ), and satellite-based remote sensing (Yong et al., 2012 ). Regardless of the method used, careful consideration of factors such as cost, accuracy, and spatial and temporal resolution is necessary to ensure reliable and effective RI estimation. While the traditional method of rainfall station monitoring offers high accuracy and wide applicability, it requires a high-density rain gauge network and comes with a high cost of construction and maintenance (Sevruk, 2006 ). Regarding more advanced methods and technologies, radar is a highly valuable remote sensing tool widely utilized in hydrological and meteorological monitoring, and currently available ground-based radar systems offer a spatial and temporal accuracy of 1 km2  and 5 min, respectively (Borga et al., 2022 ). However, their calibration and validation still rely upon ground precipitation measurements, limiting the valid spatial coverage of radar rainfall measurements (Michaelides et al., 2009 ). Furthermore, various factors such as uneven vertical distribution of rainfall, anomalous electromagnetic wave propagation, and ground clutter often lead to large errors (da Silveira and Holt, 2001; Sasidharan et al., 2023 ). While satellite-based remote sensing solutions can provide RI estimates globally, their spatiotemporal resolution of data is not sufficiently high, with real-time RI estimation for urban grids still posing difficulties (Kidd and Levizzani, 2022; Yong et al., 2012; Zorzetto and Marani, 2019 ). Nonetheless, advances in radar- and satellite-based technologies hold immense potential for overcoming these limitations and providing researchers with more accurate and efficient tools for rainfall monitoring. The recent rapid development of Internet of Things (IoT) technology has led to an increasing use of new sources of data (Zheng et al., 2018 ). This approach involves distributed sensors collecting data and subsequently aggregating them with a high degree of accuracy. Among the technologies employed for rainfall monitoring, smart wipers in cars adjust their movement based on RI, and smart umbrellas infer RI from sound variation due to raindrop impacts (Hut et al., 2014; Rabiei et al., 2013 ). Moreover, microwave receivers can estimate raindrop size as a function of the attenuation of microwave communication signals coming from the ground and space (Van Leth et al., 2020 ). However, despite potential benefits, it still requires a large number of sensors and further refinement before these new technologies can be extensively used. One promising method for estimating RI with high spatiotemporal resolution is the use of image or video data from surveillance cameras. Garg and Nayar (2007)  were among the earliest to propose the idea of estimating RI from such data. Later, Allamano et al. (2015)  proposed the concept of “camera rain gauge” and developed an analytical method for estimating RI from image data. Recently, deep learning (DL) has been used in various fields of urban water management (Fu et al., 2022 ). Leveraging the ability of DL to perform feature extraction and function approximation, Zen et al. (2019)  developed a method based on convolutional neural network (CNN) to estimate RI in Singapore from a network of traffic cameras and rain gauges. More recently, Yin et al. (2023)  proposed a CNN-based approach called irCNN to estimate RI from rainfall images collected from cameras, and this was followed by a subsequent improvement where an image processing approach was employed to enhance irCNN in extracting raindrop information (Zheng et al., 2023 ); they reported good performances of RI estimation under both daytime and nighttime conditions. Other than the image-based approaches, Haurum et al. (2019)  and Wang et al. (2023)  respectively used 3D- and 1D-CNNs to extract information from surveillance video imagery. These two studies directly processed the video data to obtain continuous estimates of RI, and hence required huge computational resources and data for training. To address this issue, one can instead consider the video as time series of images, apply a CNN model to extract the image features, and then use a time series model (e.g., long short-term memory, LSTM) to predict the quantity of interest (McLaughlin et al., 2016 ). The CNN-LSTM architecture has a relatively small number of parameters, requires less training data, and thus can be trained much faster. Finally, one often-neglected matter is the quantification of uncertainty in the RI estimates. To effectively assess risks and control urban flooding, it is crucial to incorporate an analysis of the associated uncertainty (Beven and Hall, 2014 ). Therefore, a thorough consideration of the estimation uncertainty of RI is essential to make informed decisions. Here, we propose a DL approach based on the use of a CNN-LSTM model to estimate RI from video imagery. To quantify the uncertainty of the RI estimates, we introduce a Bayesian formulation that enables effective training of the CNN-LSTM model with variational inference (Graves, 2011; Li et al., 2021 ). In recent years, Bayesian DL has emerged as a powerful framework for addressing uncertainty and improving model robustness in machine learning tasks (Bharadiya, 2023 ). Unlike traditional DL methods that typically yield point estimates for predictions, Bayesian DL adopts a more probabilistic stance. It treats model parameters as random variables, learning their distributions rather than treating them as fixed values. This paradigm shift enables Bayesian DL to skillfully capture the innate uncertainty existing within both the dataset and the model itself—a capability particularly advantageous in hydrology, where precise risk assessment and informed decision-making are important (Bentivoglio et al., 2022; Li et al., 2021 ). The probabilistic nature of Bayesian DL naturally leads to improved generalization performance and reduced overfitting, which is essential for building robust prediction models (Wilson and Izmailov, 2020 ). In this work, we introduce the Bayesian CNN-LSTM model as a foundational tool to enhance the robustness and interpretability of RI estimation from video imagery. The main contributions of the present study are the development of the CNN-LSTM model for accurate estimation of RI from video data and the formulation of the Bayesian approach for reliable quantification of uncertainty. This can provide important data support for the near real-time management of urban floods. The present study marks a significant advancement over our prior work (Yin et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023 ). Yin et al. (2023)  first introduced the image-based rainfall CNN model, dubbed irCNN, for estimating RI from surveillance camera images captured during rainfall. To further enhance the performance of irCNN, Zheng et al. (2023)  proposed initially extracting raindrop information from the images before utilizing the irCNN model for RI prediction. However, both of these studies are limited to handling image data, rendering them unable to process video data properly. Consequently, there arises a discrepancy between the instantaneous RI estimated from a single image and the cumulative RI measured by a rain gauge. Additionally, the uncertainty of RI estimation is overlooked by Yin et al. (2023)  and Zheng et al. (2023) . Uncertainty estimation provides a measure of reliability in the rainfall estimates. This helps users understand the level of confidence associated with the provided rainfall data, allowing them to make informed decisions. Therefore, the CNN-LSTM model as well as the associated uncertainty quantification method proposed in the present study is innovative compared to our previous research and represents a significant progress in research areas of urban hydrology and flooding control. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2  introduces the theory and implementation details of the proposed approach. In Section 3 , we demonstrate the utility of our method using video data under various light-intensity conditions, including daytime, nighttime, early morning, and early evening. We validate our method through both random sampling and independent rainfall events and investigate the impact of LSTM network on the model performance. Finally, we conclude this work and discuss its limitations and possible ways to further improve our method’s performance in Section 4 .  2 Methodology Accurate RI estimation is crucial for precise urban flood modeling. The utilization of advanced RI estimation techniques imparts indispensable input to the model, thereby augmenting the authenticity of simulations and advancing the domains of flood prediction, mitigation, and overall urban resilience. The intrinsic connection between RI estimation and flood modeling underscores the imperative need to incorporate readily available data, highlighting its significance in fostering effective flood risk assessment within urban environments. To extract information regarding RI from video data, we deliberately choose the combination of ResNet (a widely used CNN model) and LSTM due to their established effectiveness in processing spatial and temporal information, respectively. This amalgamation resulted in the CNN-LSTM model, ideally suited for handling the rainfall video data in our research. Indeed, the design space for DL model structures is vast. For the CNN component alone, options such as ResNet, DenseNet, and Unet abound, while sequence data can be effectively processed using LSTM, gated recurrent unit, or transformer architectures. However, delving fully into the entire spectrum of potential model structures exceeds the scope of the current study. Fig. 1   illustrates the Bayesian DL approach used in this study for RI estimation from video imagery. This approach comprises two key components: the CNN and LSTM modules. The CNN part extracts relevant features from each frame of the rainfall video, while the LSTM network captures the temporal dependencies in the sequence of extracted features. The input to the CNN-LSTM coupling model is video with a sequence of rainfall images, X = x 1  , ⋯ , x T       , where x i     corresponds to the i   - th frame of the video. Each rainfall image is passed through the CNN model to extract a set of high-level features, h 1  , ⋯ , h T      . These features are then fed into the LSTM network to model the temporal dynamics of the rainfall process. The output of the LSTM network is the estimated RI value for the duration of the video clip. To quantify estimation uncertainty of the model, we utilize a Bayesian framework during training and inference of the CNN-LSTM model. This involves treating the model weights as random variables and using Bayesian inference to estimate their posterior distributions. We begin by placing a prior distribution over the model weights and leveraging observed rainfall data to refine our understanding of model weights through Bayes’ rule. By propagating (through the CNN-LSTM model) the posterior distribution of the weights into the estimated RI value, we can obtain estimates of both the mean (μ   ) and standard deviation (σ   )—and thereby the estimation uncertainty. This approach enables us to provide probabilistic RI predictions that consider both the inherent uncertainty in the model and variability in the data. It is noted here that rainfall distributions often exhibit a high degree of skewness, with lower amounts being more frequent. However, it’s crucial to clarify that the normal distribution assumption in our Bayesian DL model does not contradict this observation. Typically, a skewed distribution, such as the Gamma or Gumbel distribution, is employed to characterize RI for the entire rainfall event. In contrast, our method is tailored to predict RI from one-minute videos. Through the Bayesian approach, we compute both the mean and variance of the RI estimate for each one-minute period, rather than for the entire rainfall event directly. The adoption of the normal assumption is rooted in the central limit theorem and it gains widespread use in representing predictive uncertainty. This approach finds support in methodologies such as Gaussian process regression (Rasmussen and Nickisch, 2010 ) and Bayesian neural networks (Jospin et al., 2022 ). In summary, a CNN-LSTM model is used to estimate the spatiotemporal evolution of RI from a sequence of rainfall images (i.e., video imagery), and the use of a Bayesian framework enables probabilistic prediction of the RI while accounting for estimation uncertainty of the model. The architecture of the CNN-LSTM model and its probabilistic implementation are presented below. 2.1 Architecture of the CNN-LSTM model Our proposed CNN-LSTM coupling model combines a pre-trained ResNet34 image classification network, developed by He et al. (2016) , with two LSTM layers, as illustrated in Fig. 2  (c). The model takes a one-minute video clip (consisting of 60 frames) as input and outputs the estimate of cumulative RI (mm/min) during this time period. The input layer receives video image sequences with a size of 128 × 128 × 3 × 60, consisting of 60 image frames each having a size of 128 × 128 × 3. After passing through a sequence folding layer, the pretrained ResNet34 model extracts features from each frame, as shown in Fig. 2 (b), and gradually transits them to an output with a size of 1 × 1 × 512 through a series of operations, including 2-D convolution (Conv), batch normalization (BN), rectified linear unit (ReLU), and max-pooling (MP). To mitigate the vanishing gradient issue, we stack two types of residual blocks (the light green and light red blocks in Fig. 2 a, where the “⊕” symbol indicates addition) with the skip connection. To restore the sequence structure, a sequence unfolding layer is applied to the outputs, resulting in feature maps with a size of 1 × 1 × 512 × 60, followed by a flatten layer to reshape this to a 512 × 60 vector sequence. To perform regression on the resulting vector sequence, we add two LSTM layers, followed by two fully connected (FC) layers that compute the mean and standard deviation (sigma) of the RI estimate, respectively. The standard deviation represents the estimation uncertainty of the CNN-LSTM model, as discussed in the following section. For clarity, Fig. 2  uses different colors to represent the building blocks of the CNN-LSTM model. Here, Conv processes a 2-D image I    with a kernel K    in the following way (Goodfellow et al., 2016 ):(1) S i , j    = I ∗ K    i ,  j    = ∑ m  ∑ n  I m ,  n    K i - m ,  j - n    .     To stabilize learning, a BN operation is applied to each minibatch of activations H   :(2) H  '   = H - μ  B N    σ  B N     ,     where μ  B N      and σ  B N      are the mean and standard deviation of each unit, respectively. Note that ReLU is a non-linear activation function defined as the positive part of its input x    as f x    = max ( 0 ,  x )    , whereas MP replaces the outputs of a layer within a certain rectangular neighborhood with the maximum value. The LSTM network, originally proposed by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) , is adept at handling sequence data by maintaining an estimate of its hidden state through time (as shown in Fig. 3  ):(3) f  t   = σ W  f   x  t   + U  f   h  t - 1   + b  f      ,   i  t   = σ W  i   x  t   + U  i   h  t - 1   + b  i      ,   o  t   = σ W  o   x  t   + U  o   h  t - 1   + b  o      ,   g  t   = tanh W  g   x  t   + U  g   h  t - 1   + b  g      ,   c  t   = f  t   ⊗ c  t - 1   + i  t   ⊗ g  t   ,   h  t   = o  t   ⊗ t a n h c  t     ,        where x t     is the input, f t     is the activation of forget gate, i t     is the activation of input/update gate, o t     is the activation of output gate, h t     is the hidden state, g t     is the activation of cell input, c t     is the cell state, W   , U    and b    are the weight matrices and bias vectors, and ⊗    is the Hadamard product, respectively. As shown in Fig. 2 (c), the 60 sequencing frames with each being a size of 128 × 128 × 3 were taken as the input to the model. This is followed by applying the CNN (ResNet34) to extract the features from each frame. Since the measured RI was in one-min time resolution, the features of the total 60 sequence frames correspond to a single RI measurement. Therefore, the LSTM is subsequently employed to retain information over extended periods (multiple scenes) in order to capture intricate non-linear relationships among these sequencing frames. In computing science and engineering domain, combining a CNN with an LSTM is a typical manner to enable the classification of the video (McLaughlin et al., 2016 ). It’s worth noting that while the theory behind DL models may seem complex, constructing one using mature toolboxes like PyTorch based on Python or the Deep Learning Toolbox based on MATLAB is remarkably straightforward. For example, incorporating an LSTM layer can be achieved with just a single line of code. Additionally, mature CNN models like ResNet, DenseNet, and others can be readily downloaded from online repositories and applied with minimal adjustments. Therefore, readers unfamiliar with the theory can still easily begin using DL models.  2.2 Probabilistic deep learning with variational inference From the training dataset, D = X  1   , y  1     , ⋯ , X  N   , y  N           , we can build a mapping from the input X    (video clip) to the output y    (RI value) using the CNN-LSTM model described above. When training such models, it is traditional to search for the model weights w  ∗      that minimize the following loss function:(4) L  N  w ,  D    = - log p D | w    = - ∑ i  log p ( y i  | X i  , w )  .     To assess the estimation uncertainty of the model, a Bayesian approach can be adopted to obtain the posterior distribution of w   , i.e., p w | D ,  α      , depending on some parameters α   . This allows for uncertainty to be incorporated into the model, which can help to prevent overfitting. Due to the high complexity of the CNN-LSTM model, the posterior p w | D ,  α       cannot be analytically evaluated or efficiently sampled. We therefore use variational inference to approximate p w | D ,  α       with a variational distribution q w | β       that depends on some parameters β   .  Generally, q β      has a more tractable form than p α     . The target then becomes to find the optimal q β      instead of the optimal w   . This can be achieved by minimizing the following function (Graves, 2011 ):(5) F = E  w ∼ q β     L  N   w ,  D       + K L q β   ‖ p α      ,     where E  w ∼ q β     L  N   w ,  D          is an error loss term that measures the model’s estimation accuracy, and K L q β   ‖ p α         is a complexity loss term that measures the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between q β      and p α     . In practice, we define β = μ , σ       and q ∙ | β    = N μ , Σ      , where Σ = d i a g σ  1  2   , ⋯ , σ  d  2        . Via backpropagation, the gradient of F    with respect to β    can be evaluated and, using an adequate optimizer, an estimate of the optimal q β      can be found. For more details about variational inference, please see (Blundell et al., 2015; Graves, 2011; Li et al., 2021 ). In this work, the DL library PyVarInf  is used for the convenient implementation of variational inference in PyTorch .   3 Results and analysis To evaluate the performance of the proposed method, we analyzed a dataset of 36 rainfall events. These events were captured by a camera installed at the Zijingang Campus of Zhejiang University in Hangzhou, China (Fig. 4  a). More specifically, the video data was captured by this camera with a time period of 1,253 min between June and July 2020. The camera model is “DH-IPC-HFW12XYZC-ABCD”, which was manufactured by Dahua Technology. This camera was positioned on the roof of Anzhong Building within the Campus with an angle of 30° downward and southward (Fig. 4 b). The camera captured video imagery at a rate of one frame per second, with an original resolution of 1920 × 1080 × 3, where the channel number was 3. The camera primarily relied on natural light, with some additional artificial light from nearby municipal and automobile sources. To improve the video quality in the low-light scenario, the camera was operated in an infrared mode at night. Ground-truth RI values were obtained using an FRT SL3-1 double skip rain gauge, located approximately 160 m southeast of the camera (Fig. 4 a), with a measurement accuracy of 0.1 mm/min. The rainfall event with the highest average RI occurred on the night of July 2, 2020, with an RI of 0.84 mm/min and a duration of 29 min. The maximum instantaneous rainfall intensity was up to 2.6 mm/min, representing an extreme event. This dataset with 36 rainfall events provides a comprehensive and diverse range of RIs, durations, and light-intensity conditions (details are given in Table 1  ), representing typical rainfall events used for model development and evaluation. Our study encompasses four different image-brightness conditions, including daytime (6:00 AM–7:00 PM), nighttime (8:00 PM–5:00 AM), early morning (5:00 AM–6:00 AM), and early evening (7:00 PM–8:00 PM). Of these, early morning and early evening present particular challenges due to significant changes in brightness, making it difficult to accurately estimate RI using a single image. To evaluate the proposed approach, both random samples and independent rainfall events were utilized based on the aforementioned dataset, which contains a total of 1253 pairs of input–output data points that can be used for training and/or evaluation. Six performance evaluation metrics commonly used in hydrological analysis are employed, including error (Err, mm/min, ranging from −∞    to ∞   )(6) E r r = y i  - y ^  i  ,     relative absolute error (RAE, %, ranging from 0 to ∞   )(7) R A E = y ^  i  - y i     y i   ,     mean absolute percentage error (MAPE, %, ranging from 0 to ∞   )(8) M A P E = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  y ^  i  - y i   y i      ,     root-mean-square error (RMSE, mm/min, ranging from 0 to ∞   )(9) R M S E = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  y ^  i  - y i     2    ,     Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE, dimensionless, ranging from −∞    to 1)(10) N S E = 1 - ∑ i = 1  N  y ^  i  - y i     2   ∑ i = 1  N  μ o b s   - y i     2    ,     and Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE, dimensionless, ranging from −∞    to 1)(11) K G E = 1 - r - 1    2  + μ p r e d   μ o b s    - 1    2  + σ p r e d   σ o b s    - 1    2    ,     where y i     is the i   -th observation of RI, y ^  i     is the corresponding estimate provided by the CNN-LSTM model, r    is the Pearson correlation coefficient between observed and estimated RIs, μ o b s      and μ p r e d      are the mean values of the observed and estimated RIs, and σ o b s      and σ p r e d      are the standard deviations of the observed and estimated RIs, respectively. Here, E r r = 0   m m / m i n   , R A E = 0   %   , M A P E = 0   %   , R M S E = 0   m m / m i n   , N S E = 1    and K G E = 1    indicate the perfect data match. 3.1 Model evaluation using random sampling of rainfall data To evaluate the performance of the proposed approach, we first conducted tests using random sampling of rainfall data from the camera. Four different cases were established based on varying light-intensity conditions, as documented in Table 1 . Each case involved training the CNN-LSTM model with 80 % of the available data, while the remaining 20 % were reserved for evaluation. For instance, Case 1 encompassed rainfall videos lasting for 737 min in a daytime setting, with a total duration of 590 min randomly selected for training and the remaining 147 min dedicated to evaluation. The approach to random sampling in the training and evaluation of the CNN-LSTM model is designed to maintain model performance without compromising the inherent temporal dependencies within the data. To ensure consistency, we conducted three repetition runs for each case, which yielded comparable outcomes. For the purpose of demonstration, we present the results from a single typical run that effectively exhibits the performance of our proposed approach. Fig. 5   displays the evaluation results for Cases 1–4. Clearly, the CNN-LSTM model yields the best performance in the daytime condition of Case 1, with the smallest MAPE (12.18 %) and RMSE (0.04 mm/min). This is attributed to the clearer visibility of rains during the daytime, coupled with relatively consistent background in the video imagery. However, in the early morning/early evening scenes (Case 3), rapid changes in light intensity occur within a short period, resulting in a significantly varying background. Consequently, the performance of the model is the worst (MAPE=16.88 %). Even in the nighttime condition (Case 2), the accuracy of the model still exceeds that of Case 3, suggesting that the variations in background lighting may be more influential than light intensity. However, when all scenarios are combined into Case 4, where the data contains significantly varied background lighting, the model’s performance remains relatively consistent. This suggests that the model effectively leverages the abundance of training data to compensate for variations in light intensity. It’s worth noting that, as a DL model, the CNN-LSTM is heavily influenced by both the quality and quantity of the data available for training. Fig. 6   presents boxplots of the relative absolute error (RAE, %) and error (Err, mm/min) for all estimated RIs in Cases 1–4. To assess the model’s performance under different RIs, we have divided the data into six subgroups based on the values of observed RIs. The results suggest an inverted U-shaped relationship between RI and RAE, where RAE first increases and then decreases with increasing RI. On the other hand, the range of Err shows a clear positive trend with increasing RI values. These findings imply that while the relative error of the model’s estimates may decrease with increasing RI, the absolute error (i.e., the absolute of Err) is likely to increase. Interestingly, when handling the extreme rainfall events that can be of great interest, the model’s accuracy (both RAE and Err) is not significantly deteriorated compared to smaller rainfall events. We observe that under conditions with larger RIs, the raindrops tend to be more prominent in the video, which assists the CNN model in extracting high-level features more effectively. However, the frequencies of the extreme rainfall events are often lower than the small-moderate events, resulting in insufficient video data with high RI values for model training. This can inevitably affect the model’s performance. Therefore, if we are to train the model with a large volume of historical data that encompass diverse conditions and continuously refine it with new data using transfer learning (Zhuang et al., 2020 ), we can anticipate obtaining more reliable estimates of RI. This is a significant benefit of the proposed method for practical applications as the urban cameras are often intensively distributed.  3.2 Model evaluation using independent rainfall events In the previous section, we evaluated performance of the CNN-LSTM model using random sampling of rainfall data from a single camera and assessed estimation accuracy using various performance metrics. However, such an evaluation procedure is insufficient for three reasons. Firstly, the training and evaluation data were derived from the same rainfall events. To assess the robustness of the DL model, it is essential to test it with new (previously unseen) evaluation data. Secondly, we only considered the estimated mean when computing the performance metrics, neglecting the uncertainty of the estimates. Thirdly, we expect the proposed method can be eventually used for practical application and hence the RI estimates for the new events are the ultimate goal. To address these concerns, we further evaluate the performance of the method using a set of independent rainfall events. We expand our testing to three additional cases (i.e., Cases 5–7), each with three repetition runs for increased statistical significance. For each repetition run, we randomly select one rainfall event for evaluation and use the remaining events to train the CNN-LSTM model. Table 2   summarizes one of the repetition runs for Cases 5–7. For example, in Case 5, we randomly select Event 11 from a total of 21 daytime events and use the remaining 20 events for training. Similarly, Cases 6 and 7 follow similar setups for the nighttime and early morning/evening conditions, respectively. These additional cases enable us to gain a more comprehensive understanding on the effectiveness of our approach under various conditions. It should be highlighted that we only present one typical run results for illustration as the other runs show similar performance. In Fig. 7  , we compare the observations of RI and the predictions of RI obtained by the CNN-LSTM model, using scatter plots and performance metrics. The CNN-LSTM model shows the best overall performance in the daytime condition, as evidenced by having the smallest MAPE and largest NSE. However, the performance has slightly deteriorated compared to Cases 1–4. Specifically, using independent events for evaluation, the MAPE values become 14.51 %, 15.10 %, and 18.92 % for the daytime, nighttime, and early morning/evening conditions, respectively. These values are slightly larger than the respective values of 12.18 %, 15.93 %, and 16.88 % obtained using random sampling. This is because the evaluation data are completely new to the training data; but when validating the model using random data, some data from the same rainfall events can be used for model training and the remainder are used for evaluation. Even though, the performance of the proposed model in estimating RI for the independent rainfall events is not significantly deteriorated compared to that using random samples. These findings imply that the proposed method possesses a great generalizability and underscore the importance of collecting more data with significant variations in background lighting to further enhance the model’s performance and generalizability. Fig. 8   illustrates the relationship between RI and RAE/Err in Cases 5–7. As the independent rainfall event test is more challenging, the CNN-LSTM model produces higher RAE values (i.e., worse performance) compared to Cases 1–4 (random sampling test). However, we also observe that the mean values of RAE are very similar and do not show the inverted U-shape as depicted formerly in Fig. 6 (a). In Fig. 8 (b), we could observe a clear increasing trend of Err, indicating that the model tends to underestimate RI values for relatively heavy rainfalls. This observation provides valuable insights into the model’s limitations and thus highlights the need for further investigations to improve its performance under extreme rainfall conditions. Fig. 9   depicts the evolution of RI estimates over time for the three independent rainfall events of Cases 5–7. The purpose of this analysis is to evaluate the estimation uncertainty of the CNN-LSTM model. The blue bars in this figure represent RI observations obtained from a tipping-bucket rain gauge, while the red lines indicate the mean estimates provided by the proposed model. The light red areas illustrate the associated 95 % confidence intervals of uncertainty estimates (i.e., [μ  − 1.96σ , μ  + 1.96σ ], where μ    and σ    are the mean and standard deviation). It is evident from Fig. 9  that while there can be some deviations between the mean estimates and the actual observations of RI, these deviations fall within the 95 % confidence intervals. Such RI uncertainty estimates can be incorporated into hydrological or hydrodynamic models to facilitate probabilistic forecasting of urban flooding so that decision-makers can make properly informed decisions. Neglecting the uncertainty can lead to over-confident results that potentially bias decision-making towards sub-optimal or even wrong directions. Fig. 9  illustrates the performance of the CNN-LSTM model having two LSTM layers. However, it’s natural to question what happens if we add or remove part or all these LSTM layers, and how significant is the LSTM network to the model’s performance? Moreover, the metrics outlined in Eqs. (6)–(11) lack consideration for prediction uncertainty. To enhance the evaluation of various models’ performance, we adopt the Predictive Model Choice Criterion (PMCC) proposed in Gneiting and Raftery (2007) :(12) P M C C = ∑ i = 1  N  y ∼  i  - y i     2  + ∑ i = 1  N  σ i  2  ,      where y ∼  i     and σ i  2     denote the prediction mean and variance, respectively, while y i     represents the observed value of RI (i = 1 , ⋯ , N   ). Through incorporating prediction variance, this metric enriches the analysis, providing a more nuanced assessment of predictive performance. To investigate these issues, we conducted four tests wherein we reevaluated Case 6 with CNN-LSTM models having different numbers of LSTM layers. When the LSTM layers are absent, the CNN-LSTM model simplifies to the irCNN model utilized in our previous studies (Yin et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023 ). From Fig. 10  (a), we can see that when the LSTM layers are removed from the model, the prediction results diverge significantly from the observations, and there is a substantial increase in estimation uncertainty. On the other hand, with the inclusion of LSTM layers, the model’s performance is enhanced across all five metrics. These findings unequivocally validate the superiority of the proposed approach over our previous method based on irCNN. Moreover, the Bayesian CNN-LSTM model’s capacity to quantify uncertainty signifies a significant leap forward from our earlier research. Conversely, such improvements require greater computational resources (during training) and so an optimal balance between performance and effort is crucial in practical applications of this method.   4 Conclusions and remarks To mitigate the negative consequences of urban flooding, it is essential to obtain accurate and high-resolution spatiotemporal estimates of RI. The limitations of traditional methods of estimating RI can possibly be overcome via the use of video imagery recorded by city-wide surveillance cameras. Here, we propose and test a Bayesian DL approach that combines CNN and LSTM to estimate RI from video imagery, while also quantifies the associated estimation uncertainty. The approach uses a pretrained CNN model (ResNet34) to extract features from each frame of the video, followed by the LSTM network to process the sequence of high-level features and thereby estimate RI. A Bayesian framework, based on variational inference, is used to assess the uncertainty of the estimates. Evaluation of the method, using both random sampling and independent event testing, indicates that it performs less accurate under conditions when light intensity changes rapidly (such as during early morning/evening) compared to daytime and/or nighttime periods when the light intensity is relatively steady; we believe that this issue can be effectively resolved by increasing the quantity and diversity of training data. We also showed that the incorporation of LSTM network for temporal processing is an important component of the approach. In this work we obtained good results using two LSTM layers – while increasing this number could potentially enhance the model's performance, the marginal benefit of doing so must be balanced against the additional training effort required. Although the proposed approach of this study shows promise, several issues require careful attention for practical applications. Firstly, the use of video imagery from urban surveillance cameras may raise data-privacy challenges. A possible solution may adopt privacy-preserving DL (Tanuwidjaja et al., 2020 ). Secondly, although surveillance cameras provide high temporal resolution recording of rainfall and might be even more abundant than ground-based rainfall gauges, their spatial distribution throughout cities tends to be quite uneven according to most of current situations. To improve spatiotemporal estimation of RI, a promising strategy may be to combine different sources of RI estimates (including rain gauges, methods based on image/video, radar and remote sensing) using DL for multimodal data fusion (Gao et al., 2020 ). Thirdly, while the CNN-LSTM model performed satisfactorily according to this study, its architecture may not be optimal. Other DL models, such as those incorporating attention mechanisms (such as transformer networks) and reinforcement learning may produce better results and should therefore be explored. Finally, it is highlighted that the main aim of this study is to develop a new CNN-LSTM model to estimate RI based on the camera data, and hence the generalizability investigation is out of the scope. However, it is important to improve the model’s generalizability in future studies, possibly using the following options: (i) the model can be trained based on a diverse dataset representing different weather conditions and geo-climatology to ensure its effectiveness in various settings and scenarios during the practical implementations, (ii) we may identify some parameters that relate to local, observable characteristics (e.g., background lighting conditions, pointing angle, field of view) that could enable transferability of the model application to another camera, (iii) the proposed CNN-LSTM model can be trained using a quantitative RI estimate from a collocated pixel provided by a nearby radar, in addition to the camera data. It is noted that the proposed method is effective for video frames with rain available. However, the rain within a rainfall event may be intermittent and hence some camera frames may do not have rain features at the time without rain. For such circumstances, the proposed CNN-LSTM model may produce a low RI estimate for the frame with no rain. We acknowledge such frames can result in estimation errors, but at a low magnitude due to that a total of 60 sequencing frames were jointly used to enable the RI estimation. Nonetheless, a future study should be carried out to systematically explore the impacts of frames without rain on model’s accuracy as well as develop methods to address such an issue.
1 Introduction Geothermal resources have advantages in combating climate change, reducing environmental pollution, and energy restructuring due to their cleanliness, renewability, and stability. Geothermal resources have been used for power generation, heating, and other purposes in many countries around the world (Karlsdottir et al., 2020; Jolie et al., 2021 ). Geothermal resources can be categorized into two types according to the occurrence medium of the geothermal energy: hot dry rock type and hydrothermal type. Currently, the development and use of geothermal resources is dominated by the hydrothermal type. According to the reservoir temperature, geothermal resources can be categorized into low-temperature (<90 °C), medium-temperature (≥90 °C and < 150 °C), and high-temperature (≥150 °C) geothermal resources (Sun et al., 2024 ). High-temperature geothermal systems have a higher exploitation potential and scientific research value than medium- and low-temperature geothermal systems. If the heat source of a high-temperature geothermal system is a magma chamber, the system is classified as a magmatic geothermal system. Magmatic systems tend to have greater exploitation potentials, scientific research value, and economic and social benefits than geothermal systems with other heat source types. China’s high-temperature geothermal resources are mainly distributed in western Yunnan, western Sichuan, Tibet, and Taiwan (Liao and Zhao, 1999 ) and are a part of the Yunnan–Tibet geothermal belt. Some of the high-temperature geothermal systems in China have magmatic heat sources. However, many of these high-temperature geothermal systems, especially those in southern Tibet, have not been thoroughly investigated, and it is not clear whether their heat sources are magmatic or not, even though they are characterized by abundant surface hydrothermal manifestations. Thus, the characteristics of the heat sources in high-temperature geothermal systems in China require further exploration. Hydrogeochemical studies of geothermal water have been widely conducted to reveal the types of geothermal systems and properties of the heat sources. Guo (2020)  proposed a preliminary method for determining if a geothermal system has a magmatic heat source based on the surface hydrothermal manifestations and hydrochemical type of the system; however, further hydrochemical and isotopic analyses are needed to determine the properties of the heat source. Classic geothermometers based on the chemical composition of the geothermal water can be effective in assessing whether a hydrothermal geothermal system is a high-temperature system (Fournier, 1977; Arnórsson et al., 1983; Giggenbach et al., 1983; Fournier and Potter, 1979; Sanjuan et al., 2014; Kharaka et al., 1982; Fouillac and Michard, 1981; Michard, 1990; Verma and Santoyo, 1997 ). However, classic geothermometers cannot indicate whether the heat source is magma. Although the stable isotopes of hydrogen and oxygen can be used to indicate whether a high-temperature geothermal system is recharged by magmatic fluids (i.e., whether there is a magmatic heat source), these isotopes are easily affected by a variety of factors, such the cooling processes. Thus, if the stable isotopes of hydrogen and oxygen are to become an effective indicator, it is necessary to collect a variety of water samples and calculate the isotope compositions of the parent geothermal fluid, which are difficult tasks (Truesdell et al., 1977; Shoedarto et al. 2020; Pan et al., 2021 ). Geophysical survey methods have also been used to reveal the heat sources of geothermal systems (Yan et al., 2024 ). However, a single physical survey method cannot effectively reveal the properties of the heat source, and it is often necessary to integrate multiple geophysical survey methods to obtain a reliable conclusion, which is expensive. It can be seen that existing methods that can be used to reveal the properties of the heat source of geothermal systems are not universal and economical. Therefore, a new method that is economical and universal is needed to determine whether a high-temperature geothermal system has a magmatic heat source. In geothermal water, Cl, B, and Li are not easily affected by hydrogeochemical processes, except for solution filtration of the surrounding rocks. Thus, these elements have been widely used to reveal the genesis of geothermal water (Jackie et al., 2017; Negri et al., 2018; Daniele et al., 2020; Pasvanoğlu, 2020 ). For geothermal water with magmatic heat sources, the magmatic fluids can provide additional Cl, Li, and B to the geothermal water (Ellis and Mahon, 1964 ; Rodríguez et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2020 ). Thus, these three elements have the potential to indicate if a high-temperature geothermal resource has a magmatic heat source. However, based on our data for geothermal water samples, the Cl and B concentrations of some geothermal water with non-magmatic sources are significantly higher than those of geothermal water with magmatic sources (see Section 4.2 . for more details). This suggests that B and Cl cannot be generally used to determine the heat sources of hydrothermal geothermal systems. In contrast, the Li concentration of geothermal water with magmatic sources is generally significantly higher than those of geothermal water with non-magmatic sources (see Section 4.2 . for details). In addition, research has shown that the Li concentrations of sinters deposited by a hot springs can reflect the effect of magmatic fluids on geothermal water (Parnell and Armstrong, 2023 ). Thus, Li has the potential to be a general indicator of the heat-source properties of high-temperature hydrogeothermal systems. In this study, three groups of high-temperature geothermal waters with relatively close sampling sites, namely, Tengchong Rehai (RH) and Longling Banglazhang (BLZ) in Yunnan, Kangding (KD), and Batang (BT) in Sichuan, and Daggyai (DGJ) and Quzhuomu (QZM) in Tibet, were selected to compare the Li concentrations of the geothermal waters with magmatic (RH, KD, and DGJ) and (BLZ, BT, and QZM) non-magmatic heat sources and to analyze their differences. Based on the findings, we developed a new method with good generalizability to determine whether a high-temperature geothermal system has a magmatic heat source or not. These findings are of great significance for the exploration and use of high-temperature geothermal resources in China, especially those in the Yunnan–Tibet geothermal belt, and for the enrichment of lithium in geothermal water, which can act as a source of lithium (Dugamin Elza et al., 2011 ). The research questions in this study are shown in Fig. 1  , and the procedures of this study are shown in Fig. 2  . First, the geological background of each research object is introduced. Then, the influence of the magmatic fluids on the hydrogeochemical characteristics of the geothermal water is analyzed to determine whether lithium can be used to indicate the presence of magmatic heat sources in hydrothermal geothermal systems. Second, the differences in the Li enrichment mechanisms of non-magmatic geothermal water and magmatic geothermal water are analyzed. Third, it is verified again that lithium can be used to indicate whether a hydrothermal geothermal system has a magmatic heat source. Finally, a universal and economical method based on the Li concentration of geothermal water is proposed to determine whether a hydrothermal geothermal system has a magmatic heat source.  2 Geologic background (1) Rehai and Banglazhang    The RH geothermal system is located in Tengchong County, Yunnan Province, and has a total area of approximately 10 km2 . Based on geophysical, geochemical, and hydrogeochemical evidence, the heat source of the RH geothermal system is magma located at a depth of 7 km (Tong and Zhang, 1989; Shangguan, 2000; Bai et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2020 ). The geothermal waters are mainly exposed in the vicinity of the Liuhuangtang–Huangguajing and Zaohetang faults, and surface manifestations such as hot springs, boiling springs, fumaroles, and hydrothermal explosions, are abundant. The geothermal reservoir is hosted by the Yanshannian granite and Proterozoic metamorphic rocks, and the caprocks are composed of intensively altered conglomerate and sandstone (Table 1  ). The BLZ geothermal system is located in Longling County, Yunnan Province, and has a total area of approximately 0.2 km2 . The rock outcroppings in the study area include Holocene alluvium, Pliocene sandstone and gravelstone, Middle Devonian dolomite, Cambrian quartz sandstone and feldspar sandstone, and Middle Proterozoic biotite-plagioclase granulite and migmatitic granite. Magmatic rocks including Himalayan andesite, basalt, and Yanshanian granite are also present (Fig. 3  ). Although no boreholes have been drilled in BLZ, based on the surface geology, the host rocks of the BLZ system are likely Proterozoic metamorphic rocks (Table 1 ) according to the surface geology (Fig. 3 ) (Guo et al., 2017a ).(2) Kangding and Batang    The KD geothermal system is located in Kangding County, western Sichuan Province. Magmatic rocks including Presinian biotite granites are exposed in the west, and the Yanshannian granodiorites are exposed in the east. The exposed strata in the middle of the basin are mainly composed of unconsolidated sediments, sedimentary rocks (including slate and quartz schist), and metamorphic rocks (including crystalline limestone, marble, and phyllite) dating from the Quaternary to the Permian but excluding the Mesozoic. The rift basin is covered by Quaternary unconsolidated sediments with an average thickness of dozens of meters. The sediments are underlain by Permian sedimentary rocks and magmatic rocks (Guo et al., 2017b ). The BT geothermal system is located in Batang County in western Sichuan Province and is divided into two geothermal areas, Bogexi and Rekeng. Large-scale outcrops of limestone are distributed in the central region of the study area, and the geothermal waters within in the Bogexi study area are located at or close to the limestone stratum. The Rekeng geothermal area is located in the northeastern part of the study area, and the outcrops are mainly composed of Triassic strata. The Triassic strata are primarily composed of altered sandstone and phyllitic and sandy slate. In addition to the igneous rock, monzonite granite outcrops in the eastern part of the area. The Rekeng geothermal area is located in the contact region between the igneous rocks and sandstone, and the reservoirs are composed of granite (Table 1 ) (Li et al., 2019 ).(3) Daggyai and Quzhuomu    The DGJ geothermal area is located in Angren County and has abundant surface manifestations. Hydrogeochemical studies have revealed that the heat source of the DGJ geothermal system is magma (Liu et al., 2019 ), but geophysical investigations need to be applied for further verification. The geothermal reservoir is hosted by Cretaceous hornblende monzonite and biotite monzonite (Table 1 ), while the caprocks are Quaternary sediments and pyroxenites. The QZM geothermal area is located in Quzhuomu Village, Cuona County, Tibet. The basement of the QZM geothermal area is composed of Precambrian metamorphic rocks that are covered by Mesozoic to Eocene marine sediments and Oligocene to Holocene continental sediments. With increasing depth, the main stratigraphic units are Holocene alluvium, Early Cretaceous sandstone and dacite, Late Jurassic quartz sandstone and siltstone, Middle Jurassic lithic sandstone and amygdaloidal basalt, and Early Jurassic thick-layer limestone. In general, the lithology of reservoir is dominated by limestone along with sandstone and tourmaline-rich granite (Table 1 ). The caprocks are Quaternary sediments and travertine (Liu et al., 2019 ).  3 Sampling and methods In this study, all the data were collected from the literature, and the sampling and testing methods are described in the corresponding papers. Classic geothermometers including SiO2 , Na–K, K–Mg, and Na–Li geothermometers are described in this section to discuss the reservoir temperature and water–rock interactions. 3.1 Sampling and testing methods The hydrochemical and isotopic data for the geothermal water samples from RH, BLZ, KD, and BT were obtained from Wang et al. (2020), Guo et al. (2017a), Guo et al. (2017b) , and Li et al. (2019) , respectively. The resolution or accuracy of the data can be found in the cited literature. The data for DGJ and QZM were obtained from Liu et al. (2019) . The specific sampling and testing methods are described in these references. The hydrochemical and isotopic data for the surface waters and parent geothermal fluids in RH were obtained from Li et al. (2015) . The data on the atmospheric precipitation, shallow cold waters, and snowmelt waters in KD were obtained from Guo et al. (2017b) . The data for the parent geothermal fluids in KD were obtained from Li et al. (2018) . The hydrochemical and isotopic data for the surface water in DGJ were obtained from Liu (2018) . All of the data are presented in Tables 1S, 2S and 3S . Medium-alkaline and acidic geothermal waters are both exposed in the RH, KD, BT, and DGJ geothermal systems. However, due to the significant differences in the hydrochemical type and genesis of the medium-alkaline and acidic geothermal waters, we mainly discuss the medium-alkaline geothermal waters in this paper.  3.2 Analysis methods 3.2.1 Reservoir temperature We used SiO2 , Na–K, K–Mg, and Na–Li geothermometers to estimate the reservoir temperatures of the geothermal systems.
