The selection of the geothermometers is discussed in Section 5.2.2 .    4 Results In this section, the basic water chemistry characteristics, characterization of the Cl, B, and Li concentrations and characterization of the hydrogen and oxygen stable isotopes are described to discuss the differences in hydrogeochemical characteristics of the magmatic geothermal waters and non-magmatic geothermal waters. Then, the influence of the magmatic fluids on the hydrogeochemitry of the geothermal waters is determined and whether or not the Li concentration can be used to indicate the properties of heat sources is determined. 4.1 Basic water chemistry characteristics The RH geothermal waters are HCO3 -Cl-Na and HCO3 -Na-Cl hydrochemical types. The hydrochemical type of the BLZ geothermal waters is predominantly HCO3 -Na, it is HCO3 -SO4 -Na at BLZ02, BLZ03, and BLZ09. The hydrochemical type of the cold springs in the BLZ area is Ca-Mg-HCO3 . The hydrochemical type of the geothermal waters in Rengkeng in BT is predominantly HCO3 -Na, the hydrochemical type of Bogexi (BT1, BT2, and BT3) is HCO3 -Na-Ca, and the hydrochemical type of the cold spring in the BT area is HCO3 -SO4 -Ca-Mg. The hydrochemical type of the KD geothermal waters is mainly HCO3 -Cl-Na, while that of sample 15J43 is HCO3 -Ca-Na. The hydrochemical type of the river water is HCO3 -SO4 -Ca-Mg. The hydrochemical type of the geothermal waters in the DGJ area is HCO3 -Cl-Na, and the hydrochemical type of the river water in the DGJ area is HCO3 -Ca-Na. The hydrochemical type of the geothermal waters in the QZM area is SO4 -Cl-Ca-Na, the hydrochemical type of the river water in the QZM area is SO4 -HCO3 -Ca, and the hydrochemical type of the snowmelt water is Ca-HCO3 . The major cation in the geothermal waters with magmatic heat sources is Na, and the major anions are HCO3  and Cl. For the geothermal waters with non-magmatic heat sources, SO4  and/or Ca are the main ions. This is similar to those of the river water and cold springs. Ca and Mg are the characteristic cations in cold water, including cold springs, river water, and snowmelt water. Thus, Ca and Mg can serve as indicators of the mixing of geothermal and cold water.  4.2 Characterization of the Cl, B, and Li concentrations Cl, B, and Li are considered to be characteristic elements in geothermal water because of their conserved chemical properties. The Cl concentrations of the RH and KD geothermal waters (285–698 and 73.3–749.5 mg/L with average values of 446.13 and 510.45 mg/L, respectively) are generally significantly higher than those of the other geothermal waters due to filtration by the host rocks and recharge of magmatic fluids (Fig. 4  a). However, despite being recharged by magmatic fluids, the Cl concentration of the DGJ geothermal water (117.9–162.3 mg/L, average = 150.38 mg/L) is significantly lower than that of the QZM (173.5–385.2 mg/L, average = 268.39 mg/L). The geothermal reservoirs in QZM are marine sedimentary rocks and granites, and the dissolution of marine sedimentary rocks may provide a large amount of Cl to the QZM geothermal waters. Although the Cl concentrations of the DGJ geothermal waters are significantly lower than those of the QZM geothermal waters, the Cl concentrations of the DGJ waters are significantly higher than those of the BLZ and BT waters. The geothermal reservoirs for all of these systems are granites. Therefore, the larger Cl concentrations of the geothermal waters of DGJ are derived from magma. Overall, the concentrations of Cl in geothermal waters with magmatic heat sources are not always greater than that in geothermal waters with non-magmatic heat sources. Thus, Cl cannot be universally used to determine the heat sources of high-temperature hydrogeothermal systems. The B concentrations of the DGJ geothermal waters (72.8–106.9 mg/L, average = 97.98 mg/L) are significantly higher than those of the other geothermal waters (Fig. 4 b). After DGJ, the B concentrations of QZM are the next highest (21.9–44.6 mg/L, average = 31.3 mg/L). The B concentrations of the KD geothermal waters (0.3–2.2 mg/L, average = 1.41 mg/L) are generally lower than those of the BT geothermal waters (0.5–4.5 mg/L, average = 3.32 mg/L) even though the KD geothermal waters are recharged by magmatic water. The B concentrations of the RH geothermal waters (4.79–10.3 mg/L, average = 7.3 mg/L) are generally higher than those of the BLZ geothermal waters (0.86–3.7 mg/L, average = 2.95 mg/L). The B concentrations of the geothermal waters with magmatic heat sources are generally not higher than those of the geothermal waters with non-magmatic heat sources. Thus, as for Cl, B cannot be universally used to identify the heat sources of high–temperature hydrogeothermal systems. The characteristics of the Li are significantly different from those of Cl and B. In general, the Li concentrations of the geothermal waters with magmatic heat sources are significantly higher than those of the geothermal waters with non-magmatic sources (Fig. 4 c). The Li concentrations of the RH, KD, and DGJ geothermal waters range from 3.923 to 11.778, 1.2 to 8.5, and 3.7 to 5.9 mg/L, respectively, and most of the geothermal waters have Li concentrations of ≥5 mg/L or greater. Therefore, Li may be universally used to determine the heat sources of high-temperature hydrogeothermal systems. The Li concentrations of the non-magmatic geothermal waters are ≤4.9 mg/L. However, the Li concentrations of most of the magmatic geothermal waters are greater than 4.9 mg/L. Therefore, in order to exclude all of the geothermal waters with non-magma heat sources, we chose a lithium concentration of 5 mg/L as the threshold for distinguishing between magmatic and non-magmatic geothermal waters. 4.2.1 Characterization of hydrogen and oxygen stable isotopes Elevation affects the compositions of hydrogen and oxygen stable isotopes. Thus, the different elevations of the three groups of studied geothermal systems resulted in different stable isotope values and patterns. The δ2 H and δ18 O values of the RH and KD geothermal waters are generally higher than those of the BLZ and BT geothermal waters. In addition, the δ2 H and δ18 O values of the DGJ geothermal waters are generally lower than those of the QZM geothermal waters. Deuterium excess (d-excess = δ2 H − 8 × δ18 O) can reflect the water–rock interactions of groundwater as well as the influences of recharge sources on groundwater (Yin et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021 ). Therefore, we used the d-excess value to analyze the differences between the hydrogen and oxygen stable isotope compositions of the geothermal waters with magmatic and non-magmatic heat sources. Fig. 5   shows that the d-excess values of the magmatic geothermal waters were significantly lower than those of the non-magmatic geothermal waters in the same area, but their patterns were similar. Lower d-excess values indicate larger δ18 O values and stronger water–rock interactions. The geothermal waters with magmatic heat sources exhibit significant “δ18 O shift” due to their higher reservoir temperatures, stronger water–rock interactions, and the recharge by magmatic fluids (with relatively high δ2 H and δ18 O values), which decreased their d-excess values. The geothermal waters with non-magmatic heat sources have lower reservoir temperatures and are not recharged by magmatic fluids. Thus, they have relatively weak water–rock interactions, resulting in less δ18 O drift and a larger d-excess values.  4.2.2 Li concentration as an indicator of the heat source properties of geothermal water The reservoir temperature is an important parameter for evaluating whether a geothermal system is a high-temperature geothermal resource. Geothermal systems with magmatic heat sources in inland areas tend to produce many surface hydrothermal manifestations and to have reservoir temperatures greater than 150 °C. Thus, the reservoir temperature is the most basic condition for constraining the properties of the heat source of a geothermal resource. The analysis in Section 4.2  indicates that the Cl and B concentrations cannot be universally used to identify the type of heat source of a hydrogeothermal system, whereas the Li concentration has the potential to be a universal indicator. Therefore, we plotted the Li concentration versus the reservoir temperature calculated using the quartz geothermometer (the reasons for the selection of the quartz geothermometer are discussed in Section 4 ). In the plot of the reservoir temperature vs. Li concentration (Fig. 6  ), most of the data points for geothermal waters with magmatic heat sources plot in the region with reservoir temperatures of >150 °C and Li concentrations of >5 mg/L. Although two samples do not plot within this region, they plot very close to it. Only four samples plot far from this region and have Li concentrations of significantly less than 5 mg/L. Because their Li concentrations are <5 mg/L, it is apparent that none of the non-magmatic heat source geothermal waters that plot in the region with a reservoir temperatures of >150 °C and Li concentrations of >5 mg/L. Therefore, reservoir temperatures of >150 °C and Li concentrations of >5 mg/L may be universal indicators that can effectively indicate whether a high-temperature geothermal system has a magmatic heat source. To confirm these criteria, we discuss the Li enrichment mechanism of magmatic and non-magmatic geothermal waters and validate the Li concentration threshold using Li and SiO2  data for other magmatic geothermal waters in China.    5 Discussion In this section, the cooling processes experienced by the geothermal water and the water–rock interactions are discussed to reveal the the differences in the Li enrichment mechanisms of the magmatic geothermal waters and non-magmatic geothermal waters. In addition, an economical and universal method based on Li concentrations is proposed to indicate the properties of the heat sources of the hydrogeothermal systems. 5.1 Role of the cooling process in controlling the Li concentration Geothermal water undergoes cooling processes such as mixing, conduction cooling, and adiabatic cooling as it rises, resulting in changes in its chemical composition (Fournier, 1977 ). Since shallow cold groundwater and surface water usually have low Li concentrations under natural conditions, mixing with geothermal water will dilute the geothermal water, resulting in a decrease in the Li concentration. If conductive cooling occurs during the ascent of geothermal water, its heat will be transferred to the host rock, resulting in a decrease in the temperature of the reservoir. The dissolution of the host rock will gradually become weaker, resulting in a gradual decrease in the amount of Li that enters the geothermal water from the host rock. Thus, the Li concentration of the geothermal water increases but not significantly. During adiabatic cooling, geothermal waters boil as they rise to a depth near the surface. This concentrates the geothermal water, resulting in a significant increase in its Li concentration. The Cl–δ2 H diagram has been widely used to reveal the cooling processes of geothermal waters (Truesdell et al., 1977 ). As shown in Fig. 7  , the main cooling processes experienced by the geothermal waters with non-magmatic heat sources analyzed in this study are cold-water mixing and conductive cooling (Fig. 7 b, d and f). As a result, the exposed temperature was significantly lower than the local boiling point, and the Li concentrations were relatively low overall. For the geothermal waters with magmatic heat sources, the samples from RH and DGJ undergo cold-water mixing, conductive cooling, and adiabatic cooling (Fig. 7 a and e). In general, the Li concentrations of the adiabatically cooled geothermal waters are higher than those of the conductively cooled geothermal waters, and the mixed geothermal waters have the lowest Li concentrations. Except for the samples from KD, most of the geothermal waters with Li concentrations of >5 mg/L plot in the conductive cooling and adiabatic cooling regions. Although the main cooling process experienced by the KD geothermal waters is cold-water mixing (Fig. 7 c), their Li concentrations are still greater than 5 mg/L. The reasons for this are as follows. Magmatic fluids can provide a large amount of Li to geothermal waters. Furthermore, the magma chamber and magmatic fluids provide a large amount of additional thermal energy to geothermal waters, increasing the reservoir temperature and enhancing the water–rock interactions. These changes in turn lead to an increase in the Li concentrations in the geothermal waters via host rock dissolution. Therefore, even if a geothermal water with a magmatic heat source undergoes cold-water mixing during its ascent, its Li concentration can still exceed 5 mg/L. However, even if a geothermal water with a non-magmatic heat source only undergoes conductive cooling, its Li concentration will still be lower than 5 mg/L due to the absence of additional Li and heat provided by the lack of a magma chamber and magmatic fluids.  5.2 Water–rock interactions 5.2.1 Water–rock equilibria The Na–K–Mg ternary diagram presented in Fig. 8   shows that most of the geothermal waters with low Li concentrations plot in the immature water area, indicating a low degree of water–rock interaction. As discussed in Section 5.1 , due to the conductive cooling or cold-water mixing of these waters, they receive relatively little Li from the host rocks or are diluted by cold water with a low Li concentration. The geothermal waters with high Li concentrations mostly plot in the partially equilibrated water areas, indicating the occurrence of a high degree of water–rock interaction. These geothermal waters mainly experienced adiabatic or conductive cooling or a limited degree of mixing. As a result, these waters receive a relatively large amount of Li from the host rocks and are not strongly diluted by cold water with a low Li concentration. The plot of 10 Mg/(10 Mg + Ca) vs. 10 K/(10 K+Na) (Fig. 9  ) (Giggenbach, 1988 ) has been widely used to assess the equilibrium between water and rocks. As shown in Fig. 9 , none of the geothermal waters plot on or near the line of perfect equilibrium, indicating that equilibrium is not reached between the rocks and geothermal waters. However, the Li concentrations increase gradually moving from the Mg corner to the equilibrium line. Therefore, a higher degrees of water–rock interaction generally corresponded with higher Li concentrations in the geothermal waters.  5.2.2 Reservoir temperature The reservoir temperature, which is an important factor affecting the water–rock interactions, can be estimated using SiO2  and cation geothermometers. The geothermal waters in this study do not plot in full equilibrium area (Fig. 8 ), indicating that the cation geothermometers are not suitable for estimating their reservoir temperatures. The plot of log(Na/Li) vs. T(K) (Fig. 10  ) also shows that the geothermal waters deviate from the Na–Li geothermometer trends. Thus, the Na–Li geothermometers are not suitable for estimating their reservoir temperatures. During the migration of geothermal water, heat is gradually lost, and the cations will maintain the previous equilibrium or reach a re-equilibrium. Thus, when the geothermal water reaches the surface or a depth near the surface, the changes in the geothermal water temperature and cation ratio are not synchronized, and the ionic ratios will be retained at depth. Thus, it will not follow the trend of the Na–Li geothermometers completely. Rather, the Na–Li geothermometers can provide information for estimating the temperature of a deep reservoir. For example, the average deep reservoir temperatures of the RH and KD samples are calculated to be 322.3 °C and 287.5 °C, respectively, using the Na–Li geothermometers [lines (16) and (17)]. These temperatures are similar to the reservoir temperatures of the PGF calculated using the Fixed-Al and Cl-enthalpy graphical methods (336 °C and 260 °C, respectively). Similarly, the plot of log(SiO2 ) vs. 1000/T (Fig. 11  a) shows that most of the water samples do not plot above or near the SiO2  geothermometer line. The plot of log(SiO2 ) vs. log(K2 /Mg) (Fig. 11 b) shows that most of the water samples plot above or near the quartz and chalcedony geothermometer lines, suggesting that the SiO2  geothermometers can be used to estimate the reservoir temperatures of geothermal waters. The reservoir temperatures of some of the geothermal waters calculated using the chalcedony geothermometers are even lower than the exposed temperatures of the geothermal waters. Thus, in this study, the quartz geothermometers are chosen to calculate the reservoir temperatures of the geothermal waters in this study. It should be noted that because geothermal waters undergo various cooling processes during migration, which affect their SiO2  concentrations, most of the calculated reservoir temperatures are relatively shallow reservoir temperatures and do not represent deep reservoir temperatures. The plot of log(SiO2 ) vs. Li (Fig. 12  ) demonstrates that the Li concentration is strongly positively correlated with the reservoir temperature. A higher reservoir temperature corresponds to stronger water–rock interactions and the migration of a greater amount of Li extracted from the host rock to the geothermal water. For a geothermal system to be considered a high-temperature geothermal resource, its reservoir temperature must be greater than 150 °C. Regardless of the SiO2  geothermometers used to estimate the reservoir temperature, most of the geothermal waters in this study had reservoir temperatures of greater than 150 °C and Li concentrations of greater than 5 mg/L. These characteristics may be important features of the geothermal waters with magmatic heat sources.  5.2.3 Minerals in the host rocks The dissolution and alteration of minerals in the host rocks have important effects on the Li concentrations of the geothermal waters. The dissolution of Li-bearing minerals increases the Li concentration of the geothermal water. The adsorption and co-precipitation of alteration minerals formed at high temperatures can also significantly affect the Li concentration of geothermal water (Pogge von Strandmann et al., 2022; Sanjuan et al., 2022 ). Thus, it is important to know what minerals are the main sources of Li in geothermal water. Although it is not appropriate to utilize the Na–Li geothermometers to estimate the reservoir temperature, the lag in the relationship between the Na and Li molar ratios with respect to temperature can still provide useful information about the sources of the Li in geothermal water. The plot of log(Li) vs. log(Na) (Fig. 13  a) shows that most of the geothermal waters plot near lines (16), (17), and (18) for the Na–Li geothermometers (300 °C). The plot of log(Na/Li) vs. log(Na/K) (Fig. 13 b) shows that most of the geothermal waters with magmatic heat sources (RH, KD, and DGJ) and the QZM samples plot within a relatively concentrated area within the vicinity of lines (16) and (17) on the plot, indicating that these samples are in equilibrium with Na- and K- feldspars. Most of the Li-rich geothermal waters are affected by granite. Eqs. (16) and (17)  are based on data from geothermal waters with granite reservoir. The geothermometers corresponding to Eqs. (16) and (17)  are similar, and their thermodynamic equations can be expressed as follows (Michard, 1990 ):(19) NaAlSi 3  O 8  ( albite )  + Al 2  Si 2  O 5  ( OH )  4  ( kaolinite )  + Li   +     = LiAl 3  Si 3  O 10  ( OH )  2  ( Li - mica )  + 2 SiO  2  ( quartz )  + H 2  O + Na   +           It can be seen that Li-bearing mica in the host rocks is an important source of the Li in the magmatic geothermal waters, including geothermal waters in the QZM area which obtain Li from the host rocks. Although the data points for the waters with non-magmatic heat sources (BLZ and BT) deviate from lines (16) and (17) on the plot, the lithologies of their reservoirs are granites, and on the Na-Li plot, most of their data similarly plot near lines (16), (17), and (18) for the Na–Li geothermometers (300 °C). Thus, Li-bearing mica may also have been a major source of the Li in the BLZ and BT water samples. Octahedral clay alteration minerals produced by water–rock interactions are common in geothermal systems. Due to the similar ionic radii of Li and Mg, Li can displace Mg in the octahedral positions of silicates and other alteration minerals. Thus, the precipitation of these minerals can lead to a decrease in the Li concentration of geothermal water. In addition, Li can also be adsorbed by clay minerals such as mica, mixed-layer clay, and chlorite (illite), leading to a decrease in the Li concentration of the geothermal water and a low concentration of Li relative to Cl. On the plot of the Li concentration vs. The Cl concentration in Fig. 14  , all of the geothermal waters plot below the straight line corresponding to granite, indicating the Li concentration is low relative to the Cl concentration. This may be due to the incongruent dissolution (i.e., the preferential extraction of Cl relative to Li) of the host rocks or the removal of Li from the geothermal waters. For the magmatic geothermal waters, the samples deviate more from the straight line compared with the non-magmatic geothermal waters (except for QZM), which may be because the magmatic fluids provide more Cl relative to Li. In addition, as a result of the higher reservoir temperatures of the magmatic geothermal waters compared to the non-magmatic geothermal waters, the degree of mineral alteration is higher in the magmatic geothermal reservoirs, resulting in the removal of more Li. The QZM samples substantially deviate from the straight line corresponding to granite, which can be attributed to two factors. First, the marine carbonate rocks of the QZM reservoir provided Cl. Second, the relatively high temperature of the reservoir lead to the mineral alteration in the host rocks, resulting in the removal of Li from the geothermal waters. Therefore, the distribution of the QZM samples in Fig. 14  differs distinctly from those of BLZ and BT. The Cl–Li–B ternary diagram (Fig. 15  ) indicates the occurrence of a similar phenomenon. The distributions of the data points of the magmatic and non-magmatic geothermal waters differs significantly. The recharge of the RH and KD geothermal waters by magmatic fluids, which provided additional Cl and B, and the removal of Li from the geothermal waters resulted in the water samples gradually deviating from the rock area on the diagram. In contrast, the DGJ samples plot near the B apex due to recharge with high-B/Cl magmatic fluids. This suggests that DGJ is a relatively young system because B is usually more enriched in the early evolution of geothermal systems. The non-magmatic geothermal waters are mostly distributed near the rock area on the diagram (green area in Fig. 15 ), indicating that the Li, Cl, and B are mainly derived from leaching of the host rocks. The QZM samples deviate from the rock area and the Li apex on the diagram, and plot closer to the B apex. This can be attributed to the leaching of more B from the host rocks (tourmaline-rich granite) relative to Cl and Li. In conclusion, the dissolution of Li-bearing mica is an important source of the Li in geothermal waters, and a higher reservoir temperature generally promotes the leaching of Li from the host rocks into the geothermal water, thus increasing the Li concentration of the geothermal water. The replacement of Li with Mg in the octahedral clay alteration minerals and the adsorption of clay alteration minerals remove Li from the geothermal water, resulting in a decrease of Li concentration.  5.2.4 Validation of methods In Section 4.3.4, we suggested that a Li concentration of >5 mg/L may be a valid indicator of a high-temperature geothermal system with a magmatic heat source. To further validate this criterion, we obtained the SiO2  and Li concentrations of four magmatic geothermal waters: Yangbajing (YBJ) (Guo et al., 2007 ), Yangyi (YY) (Guo et al., 2009 ), Gudui (GD) (Wang and Zheng, 2019 ), and Gulu (GL) (Wang et al., 2018 ). The plot of Li concentration vs. log(SiO2 ) (Fig. 16  ) shows that most of the geothermal water samples haveLi concentrations of greater than 5 mg/L and reservoir temperatures of >150 °C (based on the quartz geothermometers). Although the reservoir temperatures of most of the GD geothermal waters were less than 150 °C due to cold-water mixing (Wang and Zheng, 2019 ), the Li concentrations was still significantly higher than 5 mg/L. Magmatic fluids provide a large amount of Li to geothermal water as well as a large amount of heat, which increases the reservoir temperature and promotes dissolution of the host rocks. As a result, Li is released from the rocks into the geothermal water, increasing the Li concentration. Although some of the geothermal waters are diluted by shallow cold water, their Li concentrations are still generally higher than those of non-magmatic geothermal waters, and most of their Li concentrations are still greater than 5 mg/L. If only water–rock interactions occur without magmatic fluid recharge, the Li concentration of the geothermal water will not reach 5 mg/L, even under high reservoir temperatures. Therefore, for high-temperature hydrogeothermal systems, we suggest that the properties of the heat source can be determined based on the Li concentration (Fig. 17  ) as follows: Step 1. Conduct field observations to assess the abundance of surface hydrothermal manifestations (e.g., hot springs, boiling springs, vents, and hydrothermal explosions). Step 2. Calculate the reservoir temperature using multiple geothermometers to determine whether the temperature is close to or greater than 150 °C. Step 3. Determine if the Li concentration is ≥5 mg/L. Only part of the geothermal water needs to meet this criterion for the Li concentration. If a hydrothermal geothermal system meets the above requirements, the hydrothermal geothermal system can be considered to have a magmatic heat source.    6 Conclusions • The main cation in the magmatic geothermal waters was Na, and the main anions were HCO3  and Cl. For the non-magmatic geothermal waters, the main anions were SO4  and Ca. Generally, the Li concentrations of the magmatic geothermal waters were significantly higher than those of the non-magmatic geothermal waters; but no similar relationship was found for the Cl and B concentrations. Most of the magmatic geothermal waters were characterized by reservoir temperatures of >150 °C and Li concentrations of >5 mg/L. The non-magmatic geothermal waters did not share these features.  • Magmatic fluids provide large amounts of Li and heat to geothermal water, thereby increasing the temperature of the reservoir, enhancing the water–rock interactions, and increasing the Li concentration resulting from dissolution of the host rock. Therefore, the magmatic geothermal waters in this study had Li concentrations of >5 mg/L and underwent the conductive and adiabatic cooling processes, except for the KD geothermal waters which undergoes cold-water mixing. In contrast, the non-magmatic geothermal waters mainly experienced cold-water mixing and conductive cooling.  • The geothermal waters all experienced incongruent dissolution, and Li-bearing mica was the main source of the Li that migrated from the host rocks into the geothermal waters. The degree of hydrothermal alteration was higher in the magmatic geothermal systems than in the non-magmatic geothermal systems, which caused more Li to be removed from the host rocks via the adsorption of octahedral silicate minerals.  • The Li concentrations and reservoir temperatures of the YBJ, YY, GD, and GL geothermal waters further demonstrate that the Li concentration can be used to reveal the heat source property (magmatic or non-magmatic) of a high-temperature hydrogeothermal system. Accordingly, in this study, we developed a generalized method based on the Li concentration of the geothermal water for determining whether or not a geothermal system has a magmatic heat source.  • Our method proposed for identifying the heat sources of hydrothermal geothermal systems has a better economy and universality compared to other methods, however, the calculation of the reservoir temperature in our method requires selecting appropriate geothermal thermometers or using other methods (such as the multi-mineral saturation index method or FixAl method) based on the geological background of the specific geothermal system, because the choice of the method of calculating the reservoir temperature directly determines the result of the reservoir temperature calculation, thereby affecting the result of this method.  • In future research, Li isotopes should be considered to further identify the differences in water–rock interactions in magmatic and non-magmatic hydrogeothermal systems.
1 Introduction Since the First Industrial Revolution, both the population and greenhouse gas emissions have significantly increased, exacerbating global warming (Liu et al., 2022 ). This has led to an increase in global average precipitation and more frequent extreme weather events (Huntington, 2006; Jiang et al., 2023 ). Consequently, flood disasters have become one of the most perilous natural occurrences (Camarasa-Belmonte, 2016; Hosseini et al., 2020 ), resulting in substantial economic losses in this century (Merz et al., 2021 ). According to disaster statistics, landslide disasters in China are primarily distributed in the mountainous areas of the southwest (Gan et al., 2018 ), particularly pronounced after strong earthquakes. This highlights the significant natural issue of sediment accumulation on mountain slopes caused by extreme weather events and earthquakes (Michalek et al., 2023 ). The continual accumulation of these materials in river channels due to rainfall and subsequent earthquakes exacerbates the severity of landslide disasters (Chen et al., 2022 ). These active sediments not only intensify secondary disasters such as debris flow and flash floods (Hooke, 2019 ) but also pose additional threats to personal and property safety (Li et al., 2021 ), further complicating the management of flood in mountain rivers (Vázquez-Tarrío et al., 2024 ). In mountainous regions, significant errors often arise in estimating sediment movement when using widely used formulas derived from the hydraulic resistance statistical model or the reference shear stress model (Einstein, 1950 ; Hag and Boss, 2018; Akers and White, 1973) due to inherent differences in bed slope and sediment transport mechanisms between mountain and lowland rivers (Lenzi et al., 2006; Yager et al., 2012 ). Thanks to advancements in numerical simulation technology, progress has been made in understanding sediment transport processes and related geomorphic dynamics (Kuriqi et al., 2020 ), enabling a deeper understanding of the timing of sediment output from landslides (Croissant et al., 2017 ) and its impact on flash flood processes (Yang et al., 2020 ). In reality, almost all soils are composed of sediment particles of varying sizes (Campmans and Wijnberg, 2022 ), resulting in highly complex geometrical shapes and particle size distributions of these sediments as they enter channels (Crosta et al., 2007 ). However, sediment transport models for mountain river systems frequently overlook the inherent particle size distribution characteristics of sediment, neglecting the unbalanced particle interactions between coarse and fine particles, which significantly impact the sediment transport process (Wyssmann et al., 2023 ). This oversight leads to inherent uncertainties in modeling sediment movement in unstable and non-uniform flows, posing a significant challenge to calculating sediment transport processes in mountain rivers (Lenzi et al., 2006 ). During the flow of sediment-particle mixtures, differences in their geometric sizes lead to particle sorting (Gray, 2018 ). Over time, this process leads to stratification and an uneven spatial distribution of particulate materials (Bancroft and Johnson, 2021 ). The research on particle size segregation in dense granular flows has been quite comprehensive (Frey et al., 2020 ). Savage and Lun (1988)  conducted experiments demonstrating clear segregation in the vertical direction during the sliding of initially mixed particles on steep slopes. Van Der Vaart et al. (2018)  elucidated the relationship between small particle concentration and bottom slip amount, emphasizing the crucial role of size-segregation wave structures in particle sorting. Hu et al. (2021)  utilized numerical simulations with various particle compositions to examine the impact mechanism of particle grading on the motion and accumulation process of debris avalanches, revealing that particle non-uniformity results in a stratified structure within debris avalanches. Jing et al. (2022)  developed an improved Stokes resistance model to quantify the resistance of invading particles in shear flow, clarifying the proportional relationship between different particle velocities and effective resistance. Edwards et al. (2023)  applied depth-averaged theory and a bimodal particle size segregation model to simulate self-channelizing flow fields continuously released from an inclined plane point source, elucidating the feedback effect of particle segregation on flow fields. In practical scenarios, granular flows are often either saturated with water (e.g., debris floods and debris flows) or completely submerged (e.g., submarine landslides and sediment flows) (Coussot and Meunier, 1996 ). In these dynamic processes, the interactions between solid particles and fluid play a crucial role in influencing particle dynamics and subsequent rearrangement (Iverson, 1997 ). Quantifying variations in particle segregation in dense granular flows under fluid action during flash flood processes poses significant challenges, where segregation is less apparent compared to dry flows due to factors such as sediment particle saturation, grain size distribution, and fluid characteristics (Major, 1997; Zhou et al., 2019; Zanuttigh and Ghilardi, 2010; Zhou et al., 2020 ). For instance, Ferdowsi et al. (2017)  conducted research on the impact of bedload transport and particle creep on riverbed armor development by focusing on the mechanism of particle segregation through experiments and numerical simulations. Zanuttigh and Ghilardi (2010)  investigated how particle–fluid segregation depends on average grain size and concluded that larger particles slow down segregation as they allow more fluid between voids, reducing particle collisions. Zhou et al. (2020)  demonstrated that changes in contact pressure gradient around particles under environmental fluid actions significantly affect vertical particle segregation behavior along with no influence from normal fluid drag. He et al. (2021)  conducted underwater collapse experiments using bidisperse granular deposits where they suggested that increased mobility may be attributed to small particles intercalating between voids of large particles leading to a transition from sliding friction to rolling friction. Cui et al. (2021)  investigated the combined effect of fluid viscosity and density on particle segregation behavior under varying flow conditions by exploring different parameters such as size and weight for submerged bimodal particles in plane shear flow revealing an increase in segregation rate with increasing density. These studies on segregation in particle–fluid mixtures primarily focus on evaluating various fluid effects on particle segregation. Although they effectively characterize the mechanisms of particle–fluid interaction and kinematic features, they do not provide a unified explanation for the mechanisms generated by sediment grading in coupled sediment-fluid motion. Furthermore, it is particularly noteworthy that these studies have not clearly elucidated how the inherent grading properties of sediment affect the sediment transport process, indicating a lack of a macroscopic view and holistic understanding of bed movement and sediment transport (Frey et al., 2020 ). Therefore, it is essential to assess the impact of sediment particle grading characteristics on sediment transport rates to improve predictions of segregation patterns of graded sediment particles in particle–fluid mixtures during flash floods and to better understand their contribution to the sediment transport process. The primary aim of this study is to evaluate the influence of sediment particle size grading characteristics on the transport process during flash floods. To achieve this, a CFD-DEM coupled model was utilized to investigate the movement of sediment accumulations from steep tributary in the channel under the influence of water flow. Following verification of the numerical scheme and establishment of credibility for the CFD-DEM model, nine simulation sets were designed to examine the impact of sediment coefficient of uniformity on its transport processes during flash flood event. The results of this study contribute to a deeper understanding of dynamics, transport processes, and mechanisms involved in sediment transport caused by landslide deposits in mountainous channels.  2 Method 2.1 Governing equations of fluid flow The movement of fluids is computed using the open-source software OpenFOAM in this study. The well-known volume-averaged governing equation (Anderson and Jackson, 1967 ) is employed to describe the phase motion of fluids, with its continuity equation form being:(1) ∂ α  f    ∂ t   + ∇ · α  f   u  f      = 0      In this equation, αf   represents the volume fraction of fluid in one fluid cell or the local porosity or particle porosity; t  is time; and u f   is the fluid velocity. The momentum equation for the fluid phase is:(2) ∂ ρ  f   α  f   u  f       ∂ t   + ∇ · ρ  f   α  f   u  f   u  f      = - α  f   ∇ p + α  f   ∇ · τ + α  f   ρ  f   g + f  f  i   ¯       In this equation, ρf   is the density of fluid, p  represents the fluid pressure; τ = μ  f   ∇ u  f   + ∇ u  f      T         is the fluid stress tensor, where μf   is the dynamic viscosity of fluid; g  is the gravitational acceleration; and f  f  i   ¯     is the average interaction force vector exerted by the particles on the fluid. It is noteworthy that the numerical implementation takes into account the turbulence closure and allows for the incorporation of various turbulence models (Jing et al., 2016 ). In the simulations conducted in this paper, the k  − ε  turbulence model was used. In this study, the Volume of Fluid (VOF) method was employed to couple the modeling of multiphase fluids. For one particular mesh cell, the volume fraction of water can be represented as α 1  (0 ≤ α 1  ≤ 1), while the volume fraction of air α 2  can be expressed as:(3) α 2  = 1 - α 1       Hence, 0 < α 1  < 1 indicates the existence of the free surface in this cell. The physical characteristics of the mixture, such as density (ρf  ) and viscosity (μf  ), can be linearized based on the parameters specific to water and air.(4) ρ f  = ρ 1  α 1  + ρ 2  α 2      (5) μ f  = μ 1  α 1  + μ 2  α 2      where, ρ 1  and ρ 2  represent the density of water and air, respectively; μ 1  and μ 2  represent the viscosity of water and air, respectively. The porosity in this three-phase system, comprising solid particles, water, and air, is as follows:(6) α f  = 1 - ∑ V pi   / V  c  = V 1  + V 2     / V c       where, Vpi   represents the volume of the i th particle, which is mapped from the DEM domain to the corresponding fluid cell; V 1  and V 2  represent the volumes of fluid 1 (water) and fluid 2 (air), respectively, while Vc   denotes the total volume of the cell. Phase fraction α 1  represents the volume fraction of fluid 1 relative to the total void volume (Vv   = V 1  + V 2 ), where α 1  = V 1  / (V 1  + V 2 ) and α 2  = V 2  / (V 1  + V 2 ). Thus, over the total volume Vc   it gives the locally averaged phase fraction, αf  α 1  = V 1  / Vc  , which is the quantity transported by VOF transport equation. Taking into account the fluid volume fraction αf  , the VOF transport equation is:(7) ∂ α  f   α  1       ∂ t   + ∇ · α  f   α  1   u  f      + ∇ · α  f   α  1   1 - α  1      u  r      = 0     where, u r   = u 1  – u 2  is the relative velocity referred to as compression velocity (Jing et al., 2016 ). The first and second terms on the left-hand side exhibit the same advection form as the continuity equation, indicating that in an incompressible fluid, mass conservation is synonymous with volume conservation, thereby defining the volume fraction. The third term ∇ · α  f   α  1   1 - α  1      u  r         is an additional factor that exclusively contributes to the computation at the free surface, facilitating its distinction (Zhao et al., 2016 ).  2.2 Governing equations of particle motion In this study, the discrete element method (DEM) is utilized to calculate particle motion. The particles experience gravity, inter-particle contact forces, and hydraulic forces during their movement. The governing equations for particle motion during the transport process follow Newton’s second law:(8) m i  d u p   dt   = f c  + f i f  + m i  g     (9) I  i   d ω  i    dt   = ∑  c   r  c   × f  c   + M  r       where mi   is the mass of particle i ; u p   is the velocity vector of particle i ; f c   is the force exerted on particle i  by the surrounding particles (contact force); f i f   is the particle–fluid interaction force acting on particle i  by the fluid phase; Ii   is the rotational inertia of particle i ; ω i   is the angular velocity of particle i 's motion; r c   is the vector from the center of mass of the particle to the contact point; M r   is the particle rolling resistance moment. The rolling resistant moment increases gradually from zero to the maximum value when two particles come into contact and rotate over each other (Belheine et al., 2009 ). The magnitude of elastic rolling moment (Mr  ) is proportional to the relative rotational angle, as calculated incrementally by equation (10) .(10) M r  = k r  · θ r L      where k r  = β K s  r 2     is the rolling stiffness with β  is a dimensionless coefficient used for the rolling stiffness, r  is the average particle radius at contact, Ks   is the shear stiffness, and θ r L     is the angular vector of the rolling part. The magnitude of the maximum rolling moment is defined as (Zhao 2017 ):(11) M  r , max   = η · r · F  n         where, η  is a dimensionless coefficient used for the plastic moment and F  n       represents the norm of the normal contact force.  2.3 Forces between particles and fluid The interaction forces between the fluid and the particles primarily consist of pressure gradient force, buoyancy force, viscous shear force, drag force, virtual mass force, Basset force, and lift force (Zhu et al., 2007 ). Virtual mass force arises when a solid body accelerates in a fluid. However, it is often overlooked in steady-state or low-acceleration scenarios because its effect is relatively small (Zhou et al., 2010 ). The Basset force arises in the context of unsteady fluid flow problems, particularly in cases involving objects oscillating or moving rapidly through a fluid. This force takes into account the history of motion, and its calculation can be complex and computationally intensive. In many practical scenarios, especially those involving relatively slow or steady motion, the effects of the Basset force are insignificant compared to other forces acting on the system (Nie et al., 2022 ). The lift force is generated perpendicular to the direction of fluid flow around an object. In many scenarios, particularly those involving objects moving at relatively low speeds or in situations where lift effects are minimal, the omission of lift force would not significantly impact the accuracy of the analysis. Another reason for choosing to disregard these forces is that they are typically difficult to calculate computationally, and there has been insufficient research to incorporate them into the CFD-DEM method (Schmeeckle, 2015 ). As a result, lift, Basset, and virtual mass forces are excluded from this paper’s calculation. Thus, in this computation, the interaction force acting on a single particle between particle and fluid can be written as:(12) f i , m  f  = f d , i   + f ∇ p , i   + f ν , i        The drag force f d , i      represents the flow resistance encountered between fluids and particles, which is related to the relative velocity between fluid and particles (u  p   - u  f     ). The pressure gradient force f ∇ p , i     , resulting from the fluid pressure difference, encompasses both buoyancy and accelerated pressure gradient forces in the fluid, defined as f ∇ p , i   = - V s , i   ∇ p   , where V s , i      denotes the particle's volume. The viscous shear force f ν , i     , induced by the fluid's shear stress or the deviatoric stress tensor, is defined as f  ν , i   = V  s , i   ∇ · τ   . The drag force analyzed in this study was determined using the empirical correlation formulated by Di Felice (1994) :(13) f d , i   = 1 2  C d  ρ f  π r 2  u p  - u f      u p  - u f      · n 1 - χ        In this context, n  is the porosity, which is numerically equal to αf  . C d  = 0.63 + 4.8 Re p - 0.5       2     denotes the drag coefficient between the particle and fluid. The Re p     term represents the particle Reynolds number, which is defined at the particle size level and calculated using Re p  = ρ f  d u p  - u f       / μ    , where d  is the particle diameter. Furthermore, χ = 3.7 - 0.65 exp - 1.5 - log 10  Re p       2   / 2        signifies the empirical correction factor. In the unresolved CFD-DEM method, when the particle size is close to or greater than the minimum fluid mesh size, the volume fraction occupied by the particle phase will be close to or even greater than the mesh volume (Cheng et al., 2018 ). This leads to a discontinuous porosity field in the fluid domain and makes numerical convergence difficult. Therefore, the CFD-DEM calculation employed the modified porosity model proposed by Jing et al. (2016)  to alleviate the constraints imposed by the size ratio of fluid units and particle diameters on the model configuration.  2.4 CFD–DEM model validation for sediment transport simulation The methodology of the coupled simulation computation and transfer process is outlined in Fig. 1  . Before the computation begins, the program reads a preprogrammed model that includes fluid grids and particle motion boundaries. During the DEM computation cycle, contact and overlap between particles are detected, and the force and momentum for each particle are calculated using the nonlinear Hertz-Mindlin contact model. The motion state of each particle is determined based on force and momentum according to Newton’s second law of motion. Following this, all particle velocities and positions are updated accordingly. Via the CFDEM coupling module (Goniva et al., 2010 ), all particle information is transferred to the CFD cycle for execution. The particles within each grid are identified, which allows for the determination of volume fraction and average particle velocity for that grid. In the CFD cycle calculation, the PISO algorithm is employed to solve the fluid flow. Simultaneously, the computation of fluid–solid interaction forces acting on individual particles takes place. All computed fluid forces acting on particles are then transferred back to DEM simulations for further analysis. Upon completion of all time calculations, the program prints comprehensive results. In the Discrete Element Method (DEM), the motion characteristics of granular materials are governed by the micromechanical parameters of particle contacts. Considering that the system’s energy dissipation primarily depends on key parameters like the friction coefficients, accurately determining these parameters in the DEM model is vital (Hu et al., 2021 ). Consequently, this study utilizes existing laboratory experiments by Lei et al. (2019)  for verification, focusing on the sediment deposition evolution in the water tank and the post-stabilization water depth changes along the path. We selected this experiment as the validation study for the following reasons: Firstly, the flume used in Lei et al.'s (2019)  experiment is significantly longer in the length direction than in the width direction. Secondly, our model investigates sediment movement under free surface flow conditions with shallow water depth, which aligns with the essential characteristics of our numerical model except for slope variations. Their study utilized a flume measuring 7.7 m in length and 0.2 m in width, featuring slopes of 5 % and 1 % (referenced in Fig. 2  a). The sediment entry point was positioned 0.6 m from the upstream water inlet. During the experiment, the flow rate was incrementally raised to a preset value of 1.6 L/s, followed by the addition of 0.5 kg of sediment (with particle sizes ranging from 3 mm to 10 mm, density of 2650 kg/m3 , and a total of 2226 particles in the DEM model) to the flume. Before the first addition of sediment, the water flow rate at the sediment addition location was approximately 0.83 m/s. This procedure of adding sediment was replicated seven times, spacing each sediment addition 30 s apart. Subsequently, after the sediment from each interval had settled, the location of the sediment accumulation front was documented. Following the addition of all sediment, alterations in the water level along the course were documented. For accurate simulation of particle motion, the boundaries of the DEM model and the particles themselves are constructed from the same material. In this validation model, a multiphase flow mass flow rate inlet is utilized at the fluid entrance to control the mass of fluid entering the tank. Meanwhile, the side walls are established as no-slip boundary conditions, and the outlet is designated as a free outflow. In the DEM model, all water channel boundaries are defined as fixed boundaries, while the exit is configured as an open boundary to allow particles to leave the channel. The contact between particles and boundaries is determined using the Hertz-Mindlin model. Numerical observations from the research problem indicate that a time step ratio of 1:100 is optimal for ensuring both accuracy and efficiency (Zhao et al., 2017 ). Fig. 2 b displays the fluid grid structure utilized for model validation, which extends along the path for 5 cm. For an accurate representation of the changes in the air–water interface, the grid is segmented vertically into 20 sections, spanning a total length of 10 cm. The grid expansion rate, defined as the ratio between the initial and final grid sizes, is set at 2. Considering that the friction coefficient of particles in the DEM model has a significant impact on their movement process, the value of the friction coefficient is determined by using the evolution process of the length of the deposit after the first addition of sediment in the experiment. As shown in Fig. 2 c, an increase in the sliding friction (Sf ) makes it more difficult for the sediment suddenly added to the trough to be washed away by the water flow, resulting in a slower growth of the simulated deposit length with Sf  = 0.8. Meanwhile, a smaller Sf allows the particles to form a compact deposit, so at 22 s in the simulations with Sf  = 0.1 and 0.2, the deposit length is significantly smaller than the experimental results. In Fig. 2 d, the development process of the deposit is illustrated under different rolling frictions (Rf ). As the Rf  increases, the energy consumed by the sediment particles during movement gradually increases, resulting in a deceleration of movement speed and a corresponding slowdown in deposit formation. Based on the above results, it is deemed more appropriate to use a Sf  of 0.4 and a Rf  of 0.1. According to the results of parameter sensitivity analysis, Table 1   presents a comprehensive list of the material properties employed in the simulation. Fig. 2 e illustrates the length of the downstream deposition body subsequent to each sediment addition. It is observed that as the number of sediment additions increases, the rate of sediment accumulation length development gradually diminishes. The sediment deposit led to a notable rise in the water level in the downstream flume, as depicted in Fig. 2 f. The correlation between the simulation and physical experimental results suggests that the numerical model employed in this study effectively represents the sediment movement process in a flume featuring a free water surface and shallow depth.  2.5 CFD-DEM model setup and test program Fig. 3  a presents a simplified schematic representation of the simulation model. Given the presence of sediment supply from mountain branch gullies, the simulation employs a non-variable slope flume model incorporating a branch gully. In this model, the main flume measures 10 cm in height, while the branch flume, 0.1 m wide with a 50 % slope and 0.56 m in length, connects to the main flume 2 m from the inlet. At the outset, a hexahedral region, measuring 0.26 m in length, 0.1 m in width, and 0.4 m in height, is set up at the upper part of the DEM model’s branch for particle generation. This hexahedral region is positioned 0.3 m away from the main flume. Particles are randomly generated within this area, without considering hydrodynamics. Under the influence of gravity and mutual collisions, particles dislodge from their initial positions. Refer to the grid scale and its relationship with particle size in the model verification case study in Section 2.4  to perform grid division. Along the longitudinal direction of the channel, the horizontal length of each grid is 5 cm, with a total of 154 grids. In the transverse direction of the channel, we divide the computational domain into 20 equal parts, with the length of each grid being 1 cm. In the vertical direction, we set 20 grid units, and the grid expansion rate is 2. Following natural compaction due to gravity, the hexahedral area is removed, allowing the particles to gravitationally slide down into the main flume. Upon entering the main flume, the sediment particles are impeded by the sidewalls, gradually decelerating to form a deposition body as shown in Fig. 3 b. A particle with a diameter of 4 mm belongs to the fine particles category, while particles ranging in size from 5 to 12 mm are classified as coarse particles. The particles are modeled as sphere with a density of 2650 kg/m3 . Variations in particle combinations used in the experiments range from 4-4 mm to 4–12 mm. Coefficient of uniformity (Cu ) describes the particle size distribution in the numerical simulation, as illustrated in Table 2  . The Cu  is calculated by d 60  / d 10 . Here, d 10  represents the particle diameter at which 10 % of the sample (by weight) is finer; d 60  represents the particle diameter at which 60 % of the sample (by weight) is finer. When all particles achieve stability, the upstream water tank commences water supply at a rate of 3.6 L/s, setting the system time to 0 s. The boundary conditions in the numerical model align with the boundary conditions used for model validation.   3 Results 3.1 General description of simulated phenomena Fig. 4   depicts the evolution of loose sediment particles under the influence of water flow. Within the Fig. 4 , the color red signifies coarser sediment particles, while the color blue denotes those with finer diameters. To ensure clarity in illustrating sediment particle movement, Fig. 4  intentionally omits the depiction of water motion. At t  = 3 s, the water flow approaches the position of the accumulated sediments without triggering their movement. With an increase in Cu  values, the coarser particles in the accumulation exhibit a greater tendency to move towards the opposite side of the branch flume. This occurs chiefly due to the rapid sorting of coarse and fine particles during sediment accumulation from landslides, where fine particles are deposited at the bottom and coarse particles rest at the top. Consequently, the coarse particles, being subjected to less friction, are more prone to being washed farther away. At t  = 5 s and t  = 7 s, the patterns distinctly show the movement of sediment particles following the wash by water. At t  = 5 s, while some sorting between coarse and fine particles is evident, it remains relatively minor. The front edge of the coarse sediment particles is only marginally ahead of that of the fine particles. This could originate from the coarse sediment particles being atop the accumulation, thereby moving first when water washes over it (analysis in Discussion 4.1). Another significant observation is that, with an increase in Cu  values, at t  = 7 s, the sorting degree between coarse and fine sediment particles becomes more pronounced. As depicted in Fig. 4 , at t  = 7 s, a substantial portion of the coarse particles has advanced ahead of the fine particles. This occurs as, following the accumulation movement, subsequent sediment particles entering the main gully continue to exhibit the layering of coarse particles on top and fine particles at the bottom. Therefore, when influenced by the water flow, these particles collectively move downstream, and the fine particles located underneath reduce the energy dissipation of the entire system due to frictional resistance (analysis in Discussion 4.2).  3.2 Movement process of sediment In the simulation, as sediment particles predominantly move along the x-axis (the channel direction), analyzing the variation in their longitudinal velocity is instrumental in understanding sediment transport dynamics. Fig. 5   captures the evolution of coarse particles and fine particles average velocity along the channel direction following the scouring by water flow. A significant difference is apparent in the velocity evolution of coarse versus fine sediment particles. In all simulations, the movement velocity of coarse sediment particles gradually increases before the 12 s. However, this velocity trend for coarse particles during this phase differs among different simulations. As the Cu  increases, the first 4 s show a rising trend in coarse sediment particle velocity, indicating a phase of rapid acceleration. Owing to the uniform and steep slope of the channel in our model, sediment begins to accelerate once it starts moving under the influence of the water flow. This phenomenon suggests that an increase in Cu  significantly enhances the transition from static to accelerated sediment movement. From 4 to 12 s, the velocity increase rate of coarse particles gradually declines, showing more consistency across simulations. During this stage, as coarse particles advance ahead of fine ones, the diminishing friction resistance effect from fine particles diminishes, leading to a reduced velocity increase rate. Moreover, as high-speed sediment particles exit the flume through the outlet, this further curbs the overall velocity increase. Subsequently, as coarse particles migrate to the outlet and exit the simulation area, their average velocity reaches a peak and then gradually diminishes to zero. For fine sediment particles, as some particles have not yet entered the flume at the beginning of their movement, and those already in the flume are mostly located under the accumulation, they are not driven by the sudden water flow to generate a significant increase in velocity. After a short period of movement, the fine particles primarily provide drag reduction for the coarse particles, and their own velocity increase is suppressed. As subsequent particles with low velocity enter the channel and when some particles leave through the outlet, this further leads to a relatively uniform change in the velocity increase of fine particles. During the movement of fine sediment particles, some are carried by the water flow near the sidewalls and proceed towards the outlet along the sidewalls. Given that the water flow near the sidewalls has a lower velocity, these sediment particles move slower and more steadily. This results in the velocity of the fine particles to gradually decrease and eventually stabilize after reaching the peak. Sorting during particle transport has a significant influence on downstream impacts and deposition patterns (Pudasaini and Fischer, 2020 ). Fig. 6   depicts the sorting evolution between coarse and fine particles throughout the sediment transport process. In this study, sorting is quantified by calculating the x-axis coordinate difference (channel direction) between the centers of coarse and fine particles, as shown in Fig. 6 a. The center of particles is representative of the average position of the coarse and fine particles located in the main channel. For each type of particle, the particles that have already entered the main channel are initially selected for calculation. Subsequently, the masses of these particles are added together to give the total mass Mp  . For each particle, its mass mi   is multiplied by its position ri   in the numerical model space to obtain the weighted position (m i  · r i    ), and then the weighted positions are added up to obtain the total weighted position (∑ i = 1  N  m i  · r i     ). Ultimately, the total weighted position is divided by the total mass to obtain the centers of each type of particle (CP , which equal to ∑ i = 1  N  m i  · r i    / M   ). It is evident that for each particle of the same size, the center of the particle is equal to the arithmetic mean of the positions of each particle. When sediment particles are laterally entered into the main channel, no sorting in the x-direction between coarse and fine particles is observed before the commencement of overall movement. Upon the arrival of upstream water flow, sediment particles are set in motion. To quantify this particle sorting phenomenon induced by water flow, we use the nondimensional degree of sorting (DS ) to represent the spatial position difference between coarse and fine particles. The definition of DS  is:(14) DS = C P c  - C P f   L      where, CPc   and CPf   represent the centers of coarse and fine sediment particles that have entered the channel, respectively; L  represents horizontal length of the channel, which is set to 7.7 m according to the model in this paper (shown in Fig. 3 ). Fig. 6 b illustrates the phenomenon of a gradually increasing sorting degree, coinciding with the emerging speed difference between coarse and fine particles. In general, with a gradual increase in Cu , influenced by the relative velocity changes between coarse and fine particles, the rate of increase in DS  also escalates. Across all simulations with varying Cu  values, the DS  peaks around 10 s, signifying the end of the slow speed increase phase for coarse particles. Although coarse particles in the main channel continue accelerating towards the outlet after 10 s, the exit of numerous front edge particles slows the movement of CPc  , leading to their eventual convergence with CPf   and a resultant decrease in DS . As sediment transport advances and most coarse particles exit, CPc   returns to zero, resulting in the DS  subsequently shifting to a negative value. Following the analysis of the temporal variation pattern of sorting, maximum DS  values from different simulations were extracted and plotted in Fig. 6 c. Observations indicate that with an increasing non-uniform coefficient Cu , the maximum value of DS  in the simulations progressively increases. Nonetheless, the magnitude of this increase diminishes with a higher Cu  and tends towards stabilization. This phenomenon is ascribed to the fact that with increasing Cu , the velocity difference between coarse and fine particles leads to larger DS  within the channel’s limited length. However, owing to the channel’s limited length, the velocity difference between coarse and fine particles cannot continually increase, resulting in a gradual decrease in the increment magnitude of the maximum DS  value. Sediment particles, once transported by water flow, form structures with interstitial volumes influenced by merging, collision, and separation during their movement. These dynamics, in turn, govern the structural formation of the sediment particles in motion (Goldhirsch, 2002 ). Fig. 7   demonstrates that sediment particles with varying Cu  values display marked differences in the distribution of angular velocities during movement. Fig. 7 a shows that in simulations with Cu  = 1, the difference of average angular velocity between surface and bottom particles is minimal, and the value of the average angular velocity is relatively low, suggesting an overall bulk sliding characteristic. As Cu  increases, coarse and fine particles start to sort during their accelerated downstream movement. Bottom particles display a significant increase in angular velocity, clearly differing from surface particles. In this scenario, coarser sediment particles on the surface predominantly move downstream by sliding and saltation, whereas finer particles at the bottom show more pronounced rolling, which greatly promotes the transport of sediment downstream. Fig. 7 b depicts the ratio of angular velocities between coarse and fine sediment particles during the transport process. Before  the water flow reaching the accumulation, coarser sediment particles, more prevalent on the surface, are less stable compared to the finer particles beneath. As a result, local and minute rolling of these particles may occur, contributing to a more stable accumulation structure. At t  = 3 s, as the water flow approaches the sediment accumulation, discrete sediment particles from upstream landslides initiate movement. In conjunction with Fig. 4 , it is evident that these discrete particles are predominantly fine. During this phase, as the sediment particles are discrete and lack a stable accumulation structure, they are rolled by the water flow, leading to a significant drop in the angular velocity ratio. When the water flow triggers the overall movement of the accumulation, surface coarse particles begin moving first, generating angular velocity and causing a slight increase in the angular velocity ratio between coarse and fine particles. Following this, with coarse particles continually accelerated by the fine sediment, the angular velocity ratio further declines. Moreover, Fig. 7 b clearly shows that after overall movement, the angular velocity ratio between coarse and fine particles generally decreases with increasing Cu , confirming the more pronounced rolling characteristics of fine particles.  3.3 Cross-Sectional sediment transport process In the model used in this study, both water flow and bed sediment particle movement show significant temporal and spatial variations. Therefore, this study analyzes changes in dimensionless mass and sediment transport rate, focusing on the probability of sediment presence at various channel locations over time. The dimensionless sediment transport rate at a cross-section represents the probability of sediment transit through that section at a specific dimensionless time, with dimensionless mass being the time integral of this probability. The formulas for calculating these dimensionless factors are as follows:(15) t ′  = t / H / g        (16) M ′  = Mc  / Mt       (17) M r ′  = d M ′   d t ′        (18) x ′  = x / L      where, t  denotes the actual simulation time; H  is the height differential between the upstream inlet and downstream outlet, measuring 0.385 m in this study; g  represents the gravitational acceleration, set at 9.81 m/s2 ; M ' denotes the dimensionless mass at a cross-section; Mc  represents the cumulative mass of sediment particles that have passed through the cross-section up to the current moment; Mt  is the total cumulative mass of sediment transited through the section over the simulation.; Mr ' signifies the dimensionless sediment transport rate at a cross-section; x ' represents the dimensionless distance along the channel; x  denotes the actual coordinate of the sediment measurement cross-section in the channel, measured in meters, m; L  represents the channel's total horizontal length, 7.7 m in this study. Given that the simulated data for cross-sectional sediment transport rates show features such as unimodality, skewness, and notable long-tail effects, the Weibull Probability Density Function (PDF) and Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) are utilized to model the cross-sectional sediment transport rates and cumulative sediment amounts (Nie et al., 2024 ). Furthermore, since sediment particles do not traverse the measurement section initially post-simulation start, the PDF and CDF of the Weibull distribution are appropriately adjusted. The adjusted PDF and CDF are presented in equations (19) and (20) .(19) M r ′  = 0  t ′  < c    λ t ′  - c     λ - 1    / η λ     exp - t ′  - c    / η     λ         t ′  ⩾ c             (20) M ′  = 0  t ′  < c    1 - exp - t ′  - c    / η     λ         t ′  ⩾ c              In this context, λ  represents the shape parameter; η  the scale parameter; and c  the time offset parameter of the transport process. All of these parameters are dimensionless. Model predictions, which are aligned with these parameters, along with the simulation results, are presented in Fig. 8  . For completely uniform sediment particles (Cu  = 1.0), these formulas accurately capture the unimodal and skewed characteristics of the sediment transport rate. During bidisperse sediment particle movement, with smaller Cu  values that indicate relatively uniform particle size distribution, the sediment transport rate process exhibits unimodal and skewed characteristics at different channel cross-sections. Therefore, applying equations (19) and (20)  to directly model the total sediment transport rate, comprising movement of both sediment particle types, retains considerable accuracy. Nonetheless, in simulations with larger Cu  values, which indicate a more uneven particle size distribution, the total sediment transport rate process undergoes changes. At smaller x ' values, which are closer to the confluence of the branch channel and main channel, the total sediment transport rate process still exhibits typical unimodal and skewed characteristics. As x ' increases, and there is a greater separation between coarse and fine particles, the total sediment transport rate process starts to resemble a bimodal distribution. Therefore, while direct fitting with equations (19) and (20)  accurately represents the rapid fluctuations in sediment transport rate, it does not fully capture intermediate process changes. In this study, we developed a methodological approach that separately fits the transport data of coarse and fine sediment particles during sediment transport and subsequently merges these results to outline variations in the sediment transport rate. While still based on equations (19) and (20) , this approach distinguishes itself by independently fitting coarse and fine sediment transport data and then integrating these findings using the mass proportions of each sediment type as weights in the formula. This provides a comprehensive depiction of the sediment transport process, reflective of particle composition. The methodologies are explained in equations (21) and (22) :(21) M r coarse + fine  ′  = w coarse  M r coarse ′  + w fine  M r fine ′      (22) M coarse + fine  ′  = w coarse  M coarse ′  + w fine  M fine ′       In these equations, ‘coarse’ and ‘fine’ subscripts in Mr ' and M ' represent, respectively, the transport process (Mr ') and cumulative mass process (M ') for coarse and fine sediment particles, derived from equations (19) and (20) . The terms w coarse  and w fine  indicate the mass proportions of coarse and fine sediment particles, respectively. Fig. 8 d1-F1 highlight the marked disparities in the transport processes of coarse (illustrated by the red line) and fine (blue line) sediment particles. The merged transport rates of both particle types (represented by the green line) exhibit significant congruence with the process ascertained through direct fitting (indicated by the purple line), and both correspond closely with the simulation results. The sorting phenomenon of sediments significantly influences these processes, notably causing the transport peak of coarse particles to precede that of fine particles. This temporal discrepancy between the two peaks increases progressively with the increase of x '. Moreover, the magnitude of these peaks exhibits a decrease in relation to the increase in x '. Fig. 8 d2-f2 clearly demonstrate that in the early stages of sediment transport, the transport rate is predominantly driven by coarse particles. Yet, as fine particles traverse the cross-section, the transport processes of both particle types converge, collectively sustaining the overall sediment transport rate and culminating in its peak. This is followed by a transition to a process that is increasingly dominated by fine particles as the transport of coarse particles concludes. (For interpretation of the references to color in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.) The increasing nonuniformity of sediment amplifies the differences in the transport processes between coarse and fine particles. This phenomenon is evident in the cumulative mass process, as shown in Fig. 8 g2-i2, where the overlap period between the transport processes of coarse and fine particles diminishes. This indicates a reduced duration for the shift from a coarse-particle-dominated to a fine-particle-dominated transport process, thus highlighting the segregation between these two processes. Furthermore, it is observed that this transition period further contracts with an increase in x '. This distinction, apparent in the overall sediment transport rate process, gives rise to the development of a double-peak phenomenon. As Fig. 8 i1 shows, the total sediment transport process line, resulting from the combination of the transport rates of coarse and fine particles, distinctively features a double peak.   4 Discussion 4.1 Mechanism of coarse particles initiating movement first The initiation of motion in coarse sediment particles is elucidated through an analysis of the forces exerted upon them. In their deposited state, these upper-layer coarse particles experience a gravitational force (F g ), a contact force (F c ) transmitted from the lower layer particles via the contact surface, and a frictional force (F f ) arising from potential relative motion. As floodwaters upstream meet this deposited sediment, which prompts the coarse particles to verge on a critical movement state, they further experience forces such as buoyancy (F b ) imparted by the water flow, alongside lift (F L ) and drag (F d ) forces (Deal et al., 2023 ). Within this framework, θ  represents the angle of the bed surface, while α  denotes the angle at the contact interface between the upper coarse particles and the lower fine particles. The force analysis is depicted in Fig. 9  . At this point, for coarse particles that are in a critical state of movement, the force equation along the direction of the contact surface is as follows:(23) F 1g  - F 1b     sin α + F 1d  cos α - θ     = F 1f  + F 1 L   sin a - θ          It can be inferred that when coarse particles start to move, the magnitude of the critical drag force F 1d  is:(24) F 1d  = F 1f  + F 1 L   sin a - θ     - F 1g  - F 1b      sin α     1 cos α - θ            For the sediment particles in the lower layer, in addition to the aforementioned forces, they are also subjected to the contact force F 1c ' and frictional force F 1f ', both transmitted through contact from the upper layer particles. When these lower layer sediment particles are in a critical state, about to initiate movement, the force balance equation along the direction of the fine particles at the riverbed contact surface is:(25) F 2 g   - F 2 b      sin θ + F 1 f  ′  cos α - θ     + F 2 d   = F 1 c  ′  sin α - θ     + F 2 f        At this point, the magnitude of the drag force F 2d  required to initiate sediment movement is:(26) F 2 d   = F 1 c  ′  sin α - θ     + F 2 f   - F 2 g   - F 2 b       sin θ - F 1 f  ′  cos α - θ         when θ  = α , the expressions for F 1d  and F 2d  can be simplified as follows:(27) F 1d  = F 1f  - F 1g  - F 1b      sin θ     (28) F 2 d   = F 2 f   - F 2 g   - F 2 b       sin θ - F 1 f  ′      where:(29) F 1f  = μ F 1 c   = μ F 1g  - F 1b     cos θ - F 1 L   - F 1 d   cos α - θ             (30) F 2f  = μ F 2 c   = μ F 2g  - F 2b     cos θ + F 1 c  ′  - F 2 L            In these equations, μ  represents the coefficient of sliding friction. Since the object of this study is a bidisperse particle system, the ratio of particle sizes between coarse particles and fine particles is Cu . Therefore, the critical drag force required to initiate the movement of sediment particles is:(32) F 1 d   = μ F 1g  - F 1b     cos θ     - F 1g  - F 1b      sin θ     (33) F 2d   = μ F 2g  - F 2b     cos θ     - F 2g  - F 2b      sin θ     = 1 C u 3    μ F 1g  - F 1b     cos θ     - 1 C u 3    F 1g  - F 1b      sin θ     = 1 C u 3    · F 1d           It can be observed that for both coarse and fine sediment particles, the critical drag force required to initiate movement is related to the submerged weight of the sediment particles and the angle of friction. Since the material of both coarse and fine sediment particles is the same, the angle of friction is identical for both. However, the difference in volume between the two causes the discrepancy between F 1d  and F 2d . However, before the initiation of sediment particle movement in the upper layer, the lower layer experiences a decelerated water flow velocity at that location due to the hiding effect exerted by the upper layer (McCarron et al., 2019 ). This not only causes u 1  to be less than u 2 , but also leads to a smaller Particle Reynolds number for the particles positioned in the lower layer, yielding a large Cd  (Cheng, 2009 ). Given these conditions, it becomes difficult for equation (36)  to hold true. Therefore, the sediment particles positioned above are more likely to move first.
