In the training step, many data-model pairs with response data as input are used to train the network by minimizing the difference ψ   between the output of the neural network m p  r  e      and corresponding training model m t  r  u  e      defined by(10) ψ  = Loss  ( m t  r  u  e    , m p  r  e    ) ,     where Loss  is the measure the difference of two vectors (e.g., root mean square error (RMSE)).   3 Method 3.1 Basic idea of the two-step strategy In this section, we will introduce a two-step strategy to obtain subsurface water content information from AMT data using DL methods, described in the flowchart of Fig. 1 . In the first step, we use a DL algorithm to obtain the subsurface resistivity distribution from AMT data and examine how different dataset combinations affect the DL inversion result. In the second step, we use another DL network to do subsurface structure zonation and apply the unit-specific petrophysical relationships to obtain the water content (Chen and Niu, 2022 ), which has been proven to be capable of reducing the uncertainty of water content estimation. In this first step, we design 3 AMT application scenarios as in the flowchart Fig. 1 : Case 1 only apparent resistivity is used to predict the subsurface resistivity model, which is typical in deep learning inversions (e.g., Liu et al., 2021 ); Case 2 both apparent resistivity and phase are considered; Case 3 apparent resistivity and phase, and models from the Bostick transformation (as an initial guess) are used as input. The reasons to select the three specific scenarios are that in most practical applications, it is common to utilize the apparent resistivity and/or phase to recover the 2D subsurface resistivity structure with or without the application of priors. Our three scenarios actually cover the most common practice in AMT inversion. For DL inversions, we aim to investigate how the inclusion of more data information with and without priors affects the inversion results, which is not examined in the literature. In the second step, we use resistivity models from inversion, and models from the Bostick transformation as input to predict the subsurface structure information. The inversion and structure information are handled in different U-Net-based networks. For convenience, we use Inv-U-Net and S-U-Net to represent the networks for inversion and handling structure information, respectively. The details of S-U-Net and Inv-U-Net will be introduced in the network design section.  3.2 Data generation For DL inversion, we have to generate the data ensemble consisting of pairs of resistivity models and corresponding response data (e.g., apparent resistivity and phase), which will be used to train Inv-U-Net. Here, we generated synthetic electrical resistivity models that are representative of hydrological targets. Model generation is considered as an important step for DL inversion since this determines the generalization of trained networks. Synthetic models are derived from the typical alluvial aquifer-aquitard complex model (Fetter, 2018; Xu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Hilton and Jasechko, 2023 ). In the system of alluvial aquifer-aquitard complexes, there are three main structures and Fig. 2  b shows a typical system of alluvial aquifer-aquitard complexes. The upper layer is the unconfined aquifer with relatively higher porosity and moderate water content. In the middle layer, there is a confined unit with relatively lower porosity and low water content. At the bottom, there is a confined aquifer with relatively higher porosity and high water content. Thus, the electrical resistivity in the confined and unconfined aquifers is generally low due to the higher water content, with higher resistivity for the middle confined unit. We introduce an additional blocky anomaly to create subsurface heterogeneity. As shown in Fig. 2 b, the typical model consists of two layers of alluvial deposit with the second layer partly eroded and one sandstone layer with rectangular anomaly embedded in this layer. Their resistivities and sizes are generated randomly from the ranges listed in Table 1   to diversely represent the typical practical hydrogeological structures. The ranges for all the parameters are conservatively given based on the work (Liu et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2020 ). Once we have generated numerous resistivity models, we need to carry out the forward modeling to generate the response data for each model. In this work, we calculate the response in terms of apparent resistivity and phase for transverse magnetic (TM) polarization. The 2D forward modeling is numerically carried out in ModEM using the finite-difference method (Kelbert et al., 2014 ). Though the region of interest is relatively small, to guarantee accuracy, we extend the computational domain in each direction to make sure that the boundary conditions applied are accurate, as shown in Fig. 2 a. In the study area, we use a uniform discretization in the y -direction, then stretch the grid to the boundary. In the z direction, a logarithmic discretization is applied and at least 5 discretization points are guaranteed for the smallest skin depth (calculated at the highest frequency and for a half-space model with the lowest possible resistivity considered in this work). The inversion model grid differs from the forward modeling grid and consists of resistivity parameters of the 40 ×   40 cells uniformly discretizing the target area with spacings of 125 m and 50 m in the y and z-directions, respectively. This leads to a dimension of 40 ×   40 for each synthetic resistivity model. 40 AMT stations are located at the surface with a spacing of 125 m, starting from the origin of the y-coordinate, as shown in Fig. 2 . 40 frequencies ranging from 4.7 Hz to 10,000 Hz are used, producing response data with a dimension of 40 ×   40 for each model. In this work, we randomly generate 16,000 synthetic resistivity models and calculate the response data set using the modeling code mentioned above, with 15,000 pairs for training, 500 pairs for validation and 1500 pairs for test. To model the real applications, 1 % to 3 % Gaussian errors are randomly generated and added to the synthetic response data to produce the training datasets. Specifically, for each model, a random number within the 1 % to 3 % range is generated and multiplied with the apparent resistivity and phase to determine the corresponding error standard deviations for each frequency. These standard deviations define Gaussian distributions, from which the apparent resistivity and phase errors are realized. Fig. 3  (a)-(c) shows three pairs of synthetic resistivity models and response data from the test pairs randomly generated during the data generation process. The details of synthetic response data can also be found in Figures S1  to S3. In the test datasets, we have added noise up to 10 % of random Gaussian errors to test the robustness of the networks. For one case, the corresponding Bostick transformed data together with response data are considered as inputs. For S-U-Net, the input data includes the inversion model and the Bostick transformed data. The output data (the boundary information) for S-U-Net is the model gradient, calculated numerically based on generated synthetic resistivity models. As an example, the last row of Fig. 3  shows the boundary information for the models shown in the first row of Fig. 3 .  3.3 Networks design As in the traditional deep learning inversion algorithm, we design the CNN architecture to perform the inversion and structure information extraction. The architectures of Inv-U-Net and S-U-Net are similar and modified from the 2D U-Net (Ronneberger et al., 2015 ) consisting of a U-shaped network, based on which Wu et al. (2020)  developed a deep learning algorithm for Paleokarst collapse feature segmentation. The major difference between Inv-U-Net and S-U-Net is the choice of the loss function. Loss function (its mathematical definition will be given later) is a mathematical formula that measures the difference between the expected outcomes and those produced by the network during training. The network is optimized by minimizing the loss function. The network architecture used in this work is shown in Fig. 4  , including a bottleneck at the center, a typical contracting network and a symmetric expansive network (Ronneberger et al., 2015 ). The bottleneck includes two 3 × 3 convolutional layers, each with 512 filters. Each convolutional layer is followed by a ReLU activation function f (x ) = max (0, x ) (Krizhevsky et al., 2017 ) to increase the network nonlinearity and a batch normalization layer to re-scale the data, making the training process robust and faster (Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015 ). Similar to the 3-D U-Net structure proposed by Wu et al. (2020) , the left contracting network contains three convolutional blocks with each block consisting of two 3 × 3 convolutional layers and a 2 × 2 pooling layer with strider 2. In each convolutional layer, the input is convolved with a number of filters (e.g., 64, 128 and 256 as shown in Fig. 2 ) to extract multiple features of the input data. Again, a ReLU activation function and a batch normalization layer are applied after each convolutional layer. The expansive network sequentially upsamples the reduced data features back to the original size of input data, also including three convolutional blocks. Each block has similar structures as in the left contracting network, for instance, including a ReLU activation function and a batch normalization layer after each convolutional layer. However, rather than using a pooling layer after each block, the expansive network applies a 2 × 2 upsampling operation with stride 2 from Pytorch (Paszke et al., 2017 ) and an additional concatenation layer to combine the features from the contracting network. The final output layer is a 1 × 1 × 1 convolutional layer followed by a sigmoid activation function f ( x )  = 1 1 + e  x       to generate values in the range [0, 1]. Activation function is a simple mathematical gate between the layers of a network that decides whether a neuron should be activated or not. The network is randomly initialized from a normal distribution for each parameter. In the training process, the network parameters are iteratively optimized with the Adam method (Kingma and Ba, 2014 ), during which the error between the outputs and the training resistivity models is minimized. For instance, the mean square error (MSE) between the outputs and the training resistivity models is used as the loss function for Inv-U-Net, defined by(11) L M S E   ( y i  T  , y i  P  )  = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  y i  T  - y i  P     2  ,     where y i  T    is the target output, y i  P    is the predicted output and N  is the size of the output data. In case 3, to add an initial model to constrain the inversion, we extend the loss function as(12) L M S E   ( y i  T  , y i  P  )  = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  y i  T  - y i  P     2  + α  1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  y i  B  - y i  P     2  ,     where y i  B    is the Bostick transformed model parameter and α   is the balance parameter (α = 0.01    in this work). This modification can be utilized to incorporate any prior information (e.g., available geophysical data) in DL inversion to avoid overfitting problems. The DL algorithm minimizes the misfit between the true and predicted model, and at the same time makes the prediction as close as possible to Bostick transformed resistivity. Their relative importance is controlled by the hyperparameter α. If α is too big, the misfit between the true and predicted model can be hardly decreased during the training; If α is too small, the misfit between the true and predicted model could dominate the training process and will produce some apparent artifacts. A proper choice of α is challenging. We run tests for different α and choose one to decrease the misfit efficiently and simultaneously give results as close to the Bostick transformed resistivity as possible, typically improving the overfitting problem during the training process. The structure extraction can be considered as an image segmentation problem and S-U-Net uses a loss function of binary cross-entropy (BCE), defined by(13) L B C E   ( y i  T  , y i  P  )  = - 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  y i  T  · l o g y i  P  + 1 - y i  T    · l o g 1 - y i  P      .      For this network, the accuracy is calculated by(14) A c c u r a c y = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  i = N   e y i T  , y i P    , e y i T  , y i P    = 1 ,  if  y i T  = [ y i P  ]    0 ,  if  y i T  ≠ [ y i P  ]      .    Since the output is a probability feature map, we need to transform it into a label map. We define[ y  i  P  ]     = 1 (referred as label 1) for the probability > 0.5, otherwise[ y i  P  ]    = 0 (referred as label 0). Label 1 donotes the existence of the structure boundary in the corresponding region while 0 means there is no structure boundary. It is common to train a network iteratively with a number of epochs. In each training epoch, the trained network is evaluated based on the calculated losses (and accuracies for S-U-Net) over both the training and validation data sets.  3.4 Networks evaluation The 15,000 training datasets are used to train the designed U-Net structure shown in Fig. 5  . In the training process, the networks are optimized with the Adam method (Kingma and Ba, 2014 ). For Inv-U-Net, 50 epochs are used in the training process with a batch size of 50. The initial learning rate is 0.0001. The Inv-U-Net weights are initialized from a normal distribution with a standard deviation of 0.02 before training. The network is trained for each of the three cases mentioned previously, with convergence information shown in Fig. 5  (a), (b) and (c). As shown in the figure, the MSE loss over training and validation data sets converges better as more information is included in the training process. With the addition of phase data, case 2 decreases the MSE losses over training and validation data sets after 50 epochs to respective 0.0031 and 0.0047 (against 0.0038 and 0.0057 for case 1). The further inclusion of initial model information in case 3 decreases the MSE losses further to 0.0015 and 0.0038, respectively, at convergence. From the results, we can find that more information included in the training process can always yield improvement on the numerical performance of the trained network. The numerical performance of our trained networks is examined further on the test dataset shown in Fig. 5  (d), (e), (f) and (g). Fig. 5  (d) shows the whisker plot for MSE over the test dataset for the three cases, which summarizes the statistical information (such as outliers, “minimum”, 75 % and 25 % quartiles, median, and “maximum” in this work) for MSE. When more data is included, the performance of the trained networks on the test data is improved. Similar results are also shown in the histograms of Fig. 5  (e)-(f). We also did a test on our Inv-U-Net with different noise levels, indicating that when the data noise is within 10 %, the DL inversion can still produce good results. For S-U-Net, A total of 15 epochs are applied to train the network iteratively at a learning rate of 0.0001. For each epoch, a batch size of 50 is used. Initial S-U-Net weights are randomly generated from a normal distribution with a standard deviation of 0.02 before training. The calculated accuracy and loss for each epoch during the training process for S-U-Net are shown in Fig. 6  . Fig. 6  (a) shows that the prediction accuracy on training and validation datasets increases to 96.4 % and 95.9 %, respectively, after 15 epochs. The BCE losses shown in Fig. 6  (b) for training and validation datasets gradually converge to 0.11 and 0.13, respectively. The convergence patterns of prediction accuracy and BCE loss on both training and validation datasets are consistent, indicating that the training process is not over-fitting. The trained network is then applied to the test dataset for structure information extraction. The statistics of BCE loss and accuracy are shown in Fig. 6  (c) and 6 (d). The histograms show that the accuracy peaks at around 96 % and the loss has the highest probability at about 0.1, indicating the good performance of our trained S-U-Net on the test dataset.   4 Applications and results 4.1 Synthetic examples In this subsection, we will examine the trained networks more closely based on three models from the test dataset shown in Fig. 3  for the three scenarios. The three models present three different typical shapes (left oblique, right oblique and no oblique) of the alluvial aquifer-aquitard complexes system. For the three scenarios, the DL inversion results are shown in Fig. 7   and traditional regularization inversion results are shown in supplementary material Figure S4 . The traditional regularization inversion uses a very small regularization parameter λ = 0.1 to avoid producing an oversmoothed model and better fit the data. The data misfits in the three models of traditional regularization inversion are all very small. The traditional inversion methods produce models with a dominant smooth structure and little boundary information. By comparison, the DL-based inversion method can recover most of the structure information of true models. The results from case 1 to case 3 show that further inclusion of more data information generally provides better inversion results. For the structure prediction as in Fig. 7 , the trained S-U-Net cannot recover accurate boundary structure information. However, it can generally reproduce the major structures in the model. This can be useful for subsurface structure zonation, based on which the unit-specific petrophysical relations can be applied to estimate the water content. To quantify the match between the inversion result y i  P    and the true model y i  T   , we define the R2 (coefficient of determination) regression score, calculated as(15) R 2  = ∑ ( y i P  - y i P  ¯  )  2   ∑ ( y i T  - y i P  ¯  )  2    ,    where y i  P   ¯     is the mean value of y i  P   . Besides R2, we also apply RMSE to quantify the misfit between the inverted model and the true model. Traditional inversion still has poor performance as indicated in the quantitative comparisons in Table 2  . As shown in Table 2 , the R2 results indicate that the inclusion of both apparent resistivity and phase data yields larger R2 and smaller RMSE values against the case that only apparent resistivity data is considered for all three models. The addition of initial models obtained from Bostick transformation of apparent resistivity and phase further increases the R2 value and decreases the RMSE value. This also indicates that our proposed data assimilation is effective and can be extended for other similar geophysical inversions.  4.2 Field example comparisons In this part, we apply the trained DL inversion networks, to carry out the inversion for field AMT data, collected from the northern Tibet plateau in Qinghai, China (Liu et al., 2021 ). The inversion of the data is used to delineate the hydrogeological characteristics (e.g., aquifer and aquitard) in this area and provides geophysical evidence for water resource exploitation and management. The study area is located on the northeast margin of the Qaidam Basin, which experienced strong neotectonics movement. The elevation map in Fig. 8   shows elevated terrain on both sides of our survey area. As shown in the figure, AMT data for 10 sites along one profile are collected. The nearby seismic survey (Xu et al., 2020 ) shows that the subsurface structure is intact with clear horizontal zonation and stratum structure. For comparison purposes, the NLCG inversion (Siripunvaraporn and Egbert, 2007 ), referred as traditional inversion in this work for convenience, is also carried out for this dataset and a small λ value is used to make sure the data information dominates the inversion process. The structure information applied is the same as in synthetic cases. In this inversion, we use AMT data at 10 stations from one survey line (Liu et al., 2021 ) with station spacing of 500 m. 40 frequencies are used, ranging from 4.7 Hz to 10,000 Hz. The dimensionality analysis based on the elliptic indicators of phase tensor (Caldwell et al., 2004 ) for this dataset shows that the underground structure of the survey area is likely to be one-dimensional (Liu et al., 2021 ; see Figure S5  in the supplement). The original data with a station spacing of 500 m are interpolated to produce data with a spacing of 125 m to match the 40 ×   40 input requirement for Inv-U-Net and S-U-Net. The transformed depth is up to 2 km depth. Since the region below 0.5 km is relatively homogenous, we just show the resistivity structure shallower than 0.5 km for better demonstration and better comparison with borehole results. The inversion results from both traditional and deep learning inversion are shown in Fig. 9 . In the traditional NLCG inversions, the effects of different initial models on the inversion results are examined. As shown in Fig. 9   (a) and (b), the application of different initial models leads to slightly different inversion results, particularly at the two ends of the profile. Due to the use of smooth constraints, for both cases, the smeared-out high resistivity boundary is one of the major features in the recovered models, which may not be real, especially for the case considered in this work (Xu et al., 2020 ). There are numerous small-scale structures in the shallow area, also probably caused by the enforced artificial constraints since the near-surface structure is generally uniform in the study area (Liu et al., 2021 ). For the DL inversion, the results are obtained for the three scenarios, shown in Fig. 9  (c), (d) and (e). They are generally consistent with the results from traditional NLCG inversions. However, the result from Inv-U-Net indicates a simpler resistivity structure with clear resistivity boundaries, which is more consistent with the sedimentary environment in this area (Liu et al., 2021 ). In contrast to the traditional NLCG inversion results, the shallow region from the deep-learning inversion is generally uniform. The fit of the predicted data from the inversion results and the corresponding measured data in terms of apparent resistivity and phase is shown in Fig. 10  . In general, the predicted data are all in good agreement with the measured data. The predicted data from the DL inversion has slightly poorer fitting with the measured data at several stations. It is understandable since the traditional inversion searches for a solution by directly minimizing the data fitting, weakly constrained by enforced artificial structure (e.g., smooth structure) in this paper. In the three DL inversions, we can find that the predicted data from case 3 are more comparable to the measured data while the fitting is poorer for case 1. We prefer the inverted result from case 3, which is used for later interpretation. There are two shallow boreholes, drilled at the locations of 1.5 km and 4.0 km, respectively, along this profile (referred to as borehole-1 (BH1) and borehole-2 (BH2), respectively, for convenience). The detailed drilling data of borehole borehole-1 and borehole-2 can be found in Figure S6 . For borehole-1, interbedded layers of sandy gravel and sandy gravel with mud are encountered from the ground surface to 80 m depth. A layer of silty gravel with sand is observed at depths ranging from 80 m to 84 m. Down to 121 m, a relatively uniform layer of sandy gravel was drilled (for more details please see Liu et al., 2021 ). Previous tests show that the resistivities for layers of sandy gravel and sandy gravel with mud are generally lower than that for the layer of silty gravel with sand (Xu et al., 2020 ). For borehole-2, a layer of sandy gravel with pebbles was drilled from the surface to 69 m depth, followed by a layer of sandy gravel with mud at depth ranging from 69 m to 95 m and a layer of Argillaceous gravel down to 150 m. The resistivity of the three layers becomes increasingly higher. All the inversion results, including traditional methods, match the major resistivity variation patterns obtained from the two boreholes. The DL inversion result captures the detailed structure variation better, for instance, the decrease of resistivity or the last layer of borehole-1.  4.3 Field water content estimation The resistivity model from DL for case 3 is used for water content estimation. For this purpose, we use S-U-Net to extract the boundary probability information from the inversion result, shown in Fig. 11   (a). Then, we label the boundary probability map with label 1 and label 0 based on the probability values mentioned previously. Based on the labeling map, we can extract zonation information, as illustrated in Fig. 11 (b). For comparison purposes, we also plot the geological units (Xu et al., 2020 ) and the DL inversion result from case 3 for this profile in Fig. 11  (b). For the shallow area, combining the inversion results with the borehole result, we consider the top layer as alluvial deposits, dominated by coarse gravels. The underlying layer with relatively higher resistivity consists of siltstone and mudstone. For the bottom layer, the higher porosity of sandstone lowers the resistivity of this layer. The deep groundwater is mostly saturated (depth > 20 m) (Fan et al., 2013) and we propose to use the saturated Archie’s law to estimate the water content of the subsurface. The saturated Archie’s law (Archie, 1942 ) defines(16) ρ = ρ w  ϕ - m   ,    where ρ   is the electrical resistivity, ρ w    is the electrical resistivity of water, ϕ   is the porosity and m   is the porosity exponent, commonly known as cementation exponent. Geochemical measurements show that the electrical resistivity of groundwater is around 20 Ω  m    (Kong et al., 2019 ). The cementation exponent is determined in former petrophysical laboratory work (e.g., Daily et al., 1992; Campanyà et al., 2015 ). Since the unit-specific petrophysical relations are applied, we need to determine the petrophysical parameter for each geological unit. In this study, we use m  ranging from 1.39 to 1.58 for the coarse gravel Alluvial fan (Daily et al., 1992 ). m  for the siltstone and mudstone is around 1.67 (Campanyà et al., 2015 ) and is in the range of 1.9 to 3.7 for sandstone (Rubin et al., 2006 ). Here due to the lack of local resistivity petrophysical test, we use m  with a large range to reduce the estimation bias with the uncertainty overestimated in the results. Thus, the results should fit the local geomaterial with potential overestimation of uncertainty. Then we utilize the range of unit-specific petrophysical parameters and use Monte Carlo (MC) simulation to estimate the porosity and its uncertainty. Since deep groundwater is saturated, the water content is approximately equal to the porosity. After 1000 MC simulations, we can obtain the subsurface water content and standard deviation of water content, as shown in Fig. 12  . The water content values in the alluvial deposits, which represent the shallowest structural unit as shown in Fig. 11 , range from 0.3 to 0.4. These values are consistent with previous soil moisture measurements conducted at nearby sites on the Tibetan Plateau, approximately 200 km south of our field site, where similar hydrometeorological conditions exist (Yang et al., 2003 ). From the water content distribution in Fig. 12  (a), it shows that the groundwater mostly concentrates at alluvial deposit fans and sandstone units. In the siltstone and mudstone layer, there are some weak zones at a horizontal distance of around 1 km, which may be considered as the preferential flow path for water interaction between coarse gravel Alluvial fan and the sandstone layer. The uncertainty of water content in the sandstone is large with some mean values of water content larger than 1, which means that the water content in the deep area is overestimated. Note that in Fig. 12 , to show the mean value distribution of water content better, we only set the colorbar for the values from 0 to 0.6. The overestimation of water content is typically caused by inappropriate use of petrophysical parameter range or high clay content in the deep area. Since a relatively conservative range for the petrophysical parameter is applied, this is likely caused by high clay content in the deep area, which is also observed in other regions of China (Guo et al., 2015 ).   5 Discussion Overall, the two-step strategy shows the potential ability to provide subsurface hydrologic information from AMT data. In this work, the traditional U-Net deep learning network is used to predict the subsurface resistivity and structure information from AMT data. Compared to the traditional regularization inversion method (e.g., NLCG used in this study), the DL inversion has several advantages, for instance, no smooth constraints are required, no need for calculation of sensitivity matrix. For DL inversion, once the network has been trained, the inversion can be done within a very short time. Subsequently, we will present a complete comparison between the calculation time for DL and NLCG. including the ability to do structure prediction, improved subsurface resistivity recovery without smooth regularization, and potentially reduced inversion time. The structure information and resistivity predictions were presented in previous sections, and here we will discuss inversion time. Both traditional inversion and DL inversion can be run on a personal computer equipped with a CPU and GPU (e.g., Intel i7-12700 k and NVIDIA RTX 3060 used in this study). NLCG (coded in Fortran) takes hours to search for an optimal solution each time with the CPU. DL inversion involves two main stages: training the neural network and performing the inversion. The training process can be easily done on a GPU, allowing for much faster calculations. 20 min are taken for the training phase. Once the network is trained, inverting new data to obtain subsurface models is almost instantaneous. In this stage of discussion, the data generation time is not included, which will be discussed later with transfer learning. The traditional U-Net network also faces some challenges and limitations such as training data generation and data dimension mismatch with field data. Based on the two-step strategy framework, we can also include other methods/datasets to extract hydrologic information from AMT data. For instance, for the step of inverting AMT data, we can also apply more advanced inversion technologies (e.g., blocky inversion and joint inversion) to obtain a good subsurface resistivity distribution (Blanchy et al., 2020; Linde and Doetsch, 2016 .). For the DL inversion, it is also beneficial to apply a transfer learning algorithm to save the time of data generation and network training for data outside the range of training/testing samples. For the step of extracting subsurface structure, except for the application of DL methods on AMT data, we can also utilize other sources of data (e.g., seismic). With the development of DL technology, it can be expected that both the resistivity and structure information can be extracted in one advanced multi-task network in the upcoming years.  6 Conclusion This paper proposes a two-step deep learning algorithm to improve the inversion of AMT data for deep groundwater aquifer characterization. In the first step, we develop a DL inversion network based on a U-shaped CNN network (Inv-U-Net) to predict subsurface resistivity from AMT data. We examine the performance of different networks trained by the inclusion of increasingly more data information (i.e., apparent resistivity, apparent resistivity and phase, and apparent resistivity, phase and initial resistivity model from the Bostick transformation). To include the Bostick transformed initial resistivity model in the DL network training process, we propose a modified loss function. In the second step, we use another similar network (S-U-Net) to extract subsurface structure information and then estimate subsurface water content based on the unit-specific petrophysical relations. Our test results on synthetic models show that the network performance improves with more information added in DL inversions. S-U-Net recovers the major structure of the subsurface, enabling us to do zonation and apply unit-specific petrophysical relations. To further examine the effectiveness of our proposed two-step strategy, we consider a field AMT hydrogeological investigation case from Qinghai, China. Compared with the traditional regularization inversion, our DL inversions produce more realistic inversion models, consistent with the geological information and borehole results. The S-U-Net successfully extracts the boundary information for the field data, together with the local geological information to delineate layers of alluvial deposits, siltstone and mudstone, and sandstone for the subsurface structure. Then the unit-specific petrophysical relations are applied to map subsurface water content distribution from the resistivity structure, with uncertainty generated from Monte Carlo simulations. The resulting water content distribution exhibits some notable hydrogeological features consistent with local geological information, for instance, the preferred flow path. However, in the deep region, our result exhibits unrealistically high water content, which may be caused by higher deep clay content at this location than we previously assumed.
1 Introduction Process-based models that solve partial differential equations for shallow surface water (de Saint-Venant, 1871 ) and variably saturated subsurface flow (Richards, 1931 ) provide invaluable insights into hydrological processes. However, the numerical solution of these governing equations is computationally demanding because non-linear surface and subsurface processes need to be solved at high spatial and temporal resolution using iterative time-stepping methods. Moreover, the inclusion of diverse data sources and inherent heterogeneity in the landscape properties add computational burden to the preparation of the model input. Computational demands have, therefore, limited the widespread application and adaptability of process-based models at watershed scales (Singh and Woolhiser, 2002; Wood et al., 2011; Bierkens et al., 2015 ). Advances in computing resources and evolving numerical methods aim to solve increasingly complex problems (e.g., Maxwell et al., 2014 ; Clark et al., 2011; Brookfiled et al., 2023 ). Computational requirements of watershed-scale models may also extend beyond the mere representation of complex physical processes required to understand, quantify, and reduce uncertainty (Liu and Gupta, 2007 ). Considerable efforts have been directed towards coupled model development (Shi et al., 2013; Shelia et al., 2018 ; Sophocleous et al., 1999; Wagner et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2013 ) that can simulate interactions between different hydrological processes, increasing the functionality and utility of the models by leveraging the capabilities of individual models. In addition, watershed-scale models need to consider optimization strategies for parameter identifiability and sensitivity analysis (Gupta & Razavi, 2017; Harada and Alba, 2020 ), adaptation of advanced data structures and assimilation techniques (Vrugt et al., 2005 ; Moradkhani et al. 2005 ), and model calibration (Razavi and Tolson, 2013; Zhang et al., 2009; Kan et al., 2019 ) . For example, large-scale watershed models (Shen & Phanikumar, 2010 ) are commonly used to sustainably manage water resources by studying resource allocation, reservoir operations, and infrastructure planning (e.g., Kurtz et al., 2017 ) to predict and design early warning systems in susceptible regions (e.g., Chen et al., 2017 ) for climate change adaptation and environmental protection. High computational demands frequently necessitate simplifying process representation such as preferential flow pathways (Tetzlaff et al., 2015 ), subsurface heterogeneity (Hartmann, 2016 ), etc in large watersheds and limit our ability to scrutinize behavior at specific locations. This research advances a novel computationally efficient watershed scale hydrologic modeling framework (e.g., Ajami et al., 2016 ). In particular, a hillslope scale surface–subsurface coupling framework developed by Chen et al. (2022)  is extended to the watershed scale. Chen et al. (2022)  externally coupled the KINEROS2 (K2) model (Goodrich et al., 2012 ), which solves the 1D kinematic wave equation for overland flow (Woolhiser et al., 1990 ), with the HYDRUS-1D (H1D) model (Šimůnek et al., 2005, 2016b ) that solves the Richards equation for the variably saturated subsurface flow using a boundary switching algorithm. H1D and K2 are well-tested, state-of-the-art models tailored to simulate specific hydrologic components (processes), often equipped with highly refined and sophisticated analysis tools to provide invaluable insights for targeted investigation. The overarching objective of coupling the H1D and K2 models is to develop a straightforward, accurate, and computationally efficient hydrologic model at the watershed scale, enabling accurate simulation of surface–subsurface hydrological processes at large scales. The computationally efficient watershed-scale model developed in this work is referred to as the H1DK2-WS model. The coupled model integrates specialized modeling and analysis capabilities of both H1D and K2 models while simulating hydrologic processes at the watershed scale. In this approach, each watershed is subdivided into a cascade of 1D overland-flow planes to route surface flow from hillslopes into channels and ultimately to the watershed outlet using K2. Each hillslope and channel reach are externally coupled to one or multiple vertical H1D soil columns in the subsurface, accommodating both homogeneous and heterogeneous systems. We assess the robustness and efficacy of the modeling approach through comparisons with benchmark simulations (Chen et al., 2022; Maxwell et al., 2014; Kollet and Maxwell, 2006 ) and evaluate the model's capability to replicate observed hydrographs from a small semi-arid watershed divided into 22 plane and channel elements within the Walnut Gulch Experimental Watershed WGEW (Goodrich et al. 2022; Moran et al. 2008 ) . The H1DK2-WS model can provide a comprehensive understanding of water fluxes and soil water dynamics across hydrologic components that require an in-depth and nuanced understanding of specific processes. For example, the model may be used to study the effectiveness of managed aquifer recharge (MAR) or changes in rechange due to factors like climate and land use. This model also enables adaptation to evolving conditions that standalone integrated models may struggle to achieve. Consequently, the H1DK2-WS model provides a valuable tool for researchers, watershed managers, and policymakers striving to quantify real-world conditions (e.g., soil moisture estimation, stream flow forecasting, and estimation of water fluxes and recharge) and to manage environmental resources effectively (urban storm management, land-use planning, water management, and conservation planning). However, it is also acknowledged that process-based models are resource-intensive and challenging to work with (Jajarmizad et al., 2012 ), and this sometimes makes them less flexible for site-specific and process-specific analyses.  2 Methods 2.1 Summary of K2 and H1D models The K2 model is an open-source code that solves the 1D kinematic wave equation for surface runoff at various spatial scales (Morris and Woolhiser, 1980 ). It includes the Parlange three-parameter equation for estimating infiltration amounts (Smith & Parlange, 1978 ). The kinematic wave equation in K2 is given as:(1) ∂ h  ∂ t   + α m h  m - 1   ∂ h  ∂ x   = q x , t   = P - F     where t  is time [T], x  is the distance along the slope direction [L], h  is the depth of surface water [L], and q  is the source and sink term [LT−1 ] represented as a function of precipitation (P ) [LT−1 ] and infiltration (F ) [LT−1 ] components. The parameters α   and m  are flow parameters related to surface roughness, flow regime, and slope. K2 has been applied to a wide array of hydrological and environmental problems (Goodrich et al., 2006; Goodrich et al., 2000 ). The Automated Geospatial Watershed Assessment (AGWA) tool (Miller et al., 2007 ; https://www.tucson.ars.ag.gov/agwa/  ) is a GIS-based hydrologic modeling tool (ArcGIS 10.x) that uses commonly available GIS data layers to efficiently processes necessary datasets that delineate watersheds, extract initial parameters from national databases, executes the model, and supports visualizing simulation results in the GIS. K2 includes well-structured workflow and analysis tools for event-scale runoff predictions (Goodrich et al., 1997 ) and uses precipitation data from various sources (Yatheendradas et al., 2005 ). A continuous version of K2 is now available that also includes the treatment of snowfall and melt. Hillslope model elements in K2 can be planar or curvilinear (especially important for erosion and sediment transport) and can become narrower or wider in the downslope direction. It has been successfully applied to assess the impacts of land use changes, urbanization, and green infrastructure (Hernandez et al., 1999 ; Kennedy et al., 2013 ; Korgaonkar et al., 2020 ), as well as the effects of wildfires on watershed responses (Sidman et al., 2015; Guertin et al., 2019 ). The model provides high-resolution spatially distributed simulation outputs across the study watershed at a 1-minute or user-defined time step. The H1D model is an open-source code that solves the Richards equation for saturated–unsaturated flow in porous media (Šimůnek et al., 2005, 2016b ). The Richards equation is given as:(2) ∂ θ  ∂ t   = ∂ ∂ z   K h   ∂ h  ∂ z   + K ( h )    - S h       where h  is the water pressure head [L], θ  is the volumetric water content [L3 L-3 ], z  is the spatial coordinate in the vertical direction [L] (positive upward), S  is the sink term [L3 L-3 T−1 ], and K  is the unsaturated hydraulic conductivity function [LT−1 ]. The HYDRUS models (Šimůnek et al., 2016a , 2024)  are among the most widely used numerical models for simulating various transport processes, such as water flow and heat and solute transport in variably saturated porous media (e.g., soils or the vadose zone). The HYDRUS software includes an interactive graphics-based interface for data preprocessing, soil profile discretization, and graphic presentation of the results. While HYDRUS-1D simulates flow and transport processes in one dimension and is a public domain software, HYDRUS (2D/3D) (and earlier HYDRUS-2D) extends the simulation capabilities to the second and third dimensions and is distributed commercially. There are many thousands of HYDRUS users worldwide, with many applications (also several thousand) appearing in peer-reviewed literature and many technical reports (Šimůnek et al., 2016b , 2024 ). This model provides a comprehensive grasp of water dynamics in diverse soil and geological conditions (Kornelsen & Coulibaly, 2014; Chen et al., 2014 ), enabling applications such as groundwater recharge estimation (Han et al., 2015; Tonkul et al., 2019 ).  2.2 Overview of the H1D-K2 coupling framework The hillslope H1D-K2 model (Chen et al., 2022 ) has undergone rigorous testing and evaluation across a wide range of scenarios, including various rainstorm events, different slopes, subsurface heterogeneity, and varying bottom boundary conditions (BCs). The workflow also includes simulation of flow processes, computing the water balance for each surface node along the single hillslope (plane element) at selected time steps to exchange the information between the H1D and K2 models. Its performance was then compared with the HYDRUS-2D model (Šimůnek et al., 2006; Šimůnek, 2015 ), serving as a benchmark for the evaluation. Results demonstrated that the coupled H1D-K2 model performs exceptionally well in reproducing hydrographs, surface water levels, soil moisture, and water balance component errors compared to the HYDRUS-2D model. The model also maintains high computational efficiency due to a dynamic time-step approach and a dimensionality reduction method where a single H1D soil profile represents an entire overland flow plane. The improvement in the computational time ranges from a factor of 1.3 to 10 to that of the HYDRUS-2D model (Chen et al., 2022 ). The watershed-scale coupling involves using a procedure initially designed for the single hillslope scale in Chen et al. (2022) . Expanding the H1D-K2 model to a watershed scale model (H1DK2-WS) involves dividing the watershed into a series of interconnected rectangular plane and channel elements. Each channel and plane element is associated with at least one H1D column to simulate water movement in the subsurface. The H1D column can be homogeneous or heterogeneous. The planes and channel elements have unique IDs, so their hierarchical connections with neighboring elements, upstream, lateral, and downstream, are maintained to describe the flow. The MATLAB (R2021b) code was derived from the hillslope scale and is designed to read and apply climate inputs to the unique element IDs (plane and channel). As described in the workflow (Fig. 1  ), the MATLAB script executes the H1D and K2 codes sequentially using a series of functions to simulate subsurface and overland flow processes, respectively. The H1D and K2 Fortran codes were modified to write temporary files to allow the exchange of information between K2 and H1D. The exchange of information between the two models occurs at different time scales. The H1D model runs at a coarser time scale, Δ t  hyd    , compared to the K2 model, which runs at a relatively finer resolution (Δ t  k 2    : K2 time step). The H1DK2-WS code first executes the H1D model for all elements (plane and channel) in the watershed and computes infiltration at the surface, soil moisture redistribution across the soil matrix, and recharge (outflow at the bottom of the soil column) at the Δ t  hyd     time step. H1DK2-WS then computes precipitation minus infiltration values at every sub-Δ t  hyd     time step (i.e., Δ t  k 2     equal to 1 min), at which K2 computes overland flow rates and surface water levels in each element. Δ t  k 2     and Δ t  hyd     are multiples of the total simulation time where Δ t  hyd     varies from 2 min to the maximum total simulation time depending on the model convergence and subsurface soil column resolution.(3) Δ t  hyd   = T o t a l _ S i m  time   / n k     where nk    is an integer number indicating the number of H1D runs for each watershed element. The Δ t  k 2     time step ranges from the sub-minute scale (usually a small simulation time step in K2 runs) to larger time steps that are a multiple of Δ t  hyd    . The key component in the H1DK2-WS code was the replacement of the Parlange infiltration equation (Parlange et al., 1982 ) by the Richards equation in the H1D model (Šimůnek et al., 2005 ). Instead of subtracting infiltration from surface water depth and precipitation input during flow routing, the H1DK2-WS model routes the rainfall minus infiltration amount, q rmi    , to compute runoff outflow at every 1-minute interval and water depth (h t     ) at every node in each element. The K2 code runs the routing scheme across the entire watershed at every K2 time step Δ t  k 2     between every simulation pause and start period Δ t  hyd    , in which the outflow rate from the upstream hillslope (plane element) at every time step is used as an inflow to the downstream plane or channel element in addition to the precipitation input. While executing the H1D and K2 codes and implementing the information exchange schemes, the H1DK2-WS model computes the water balance on the surface, which dictates the initial condition and infiltration rates to simulate flow for the next time step. In the interconnected K2 elements (plane and/or channel), outflow from upper hillslopes serves as an inflow for lower elements. Therefore, at every time step Δ t  k 2    , the inflow rate in the downstream plane or channel comprises both the outflow rate from upstream planes and q rmi    . The key functions in the exchange are the boundary condition switching function in the water balance analysis at every time step and the computation of the water depth across the hillslope (for details of the water balance and water depth analysis, see Supplementary Material  I ).  2.3 H1DK2-WS model setup Setting up the H1DK2-WS model involves creating inputs and domain representations for the K2 and H1D models. The model domains include the rectangular plane and channel elements, with associated parameter values describing the geometry, roughness, slope, soil hydraulic conductivity, and soil moisture at saturation and wilting points. It also consists of the corresponding geometry and properties of the soil columns of all the elements representing the subsurface structures. This process varies depending on the domains used in this study. These are:1. Hypothetical Domain: This includes simple geometric watersheds used in previous model development and evaluation studies. Model geometric domains and associated input files, parameters, and BCs are defined using information available in the literature.  2. Lucky Hills Domain: Lucky Hills is an experimental watershed within the WGEW in southeastern Arizona. Its modeling domain development requires using a Geographic Information System (GIS) user interface − the Automated Geospatial Watershed Assessment (AGWA: Semmens et al., 2007 ) tool for the K2 setup.    The hypothetical domains used in this study include a single hillslope (e.g., Chen et al., 2022 ), three interconnected, cascading heterogenous hillslopes, and a tilted V-catchment (Maxwell et al., 2014 ).  These domains are easy to generate and set up without external pre-processing tools. For the Lucky Hills domain, the AGWA GIS interface for K2, developed in 2002 by USDA-ARS and the US Environmental Protection Agency (Semmens et al., 2007 ; Miller et al., 2007 ), provides a preprocessing and an initial parametrization scheme. This interface offers a user-friendly platform that considers landscape information to derive spatial model inputs and visualizes model results. AGWA relies on a digital elevation model (DEM) to obtain geomorphologic and geometric parameters, surface soil data (e.g., SSURGO data), and land use data layer from NRCS, USGS, and NASA. This information contributes to developing a hierarchical structure and setting up the K2 model by facilitating the subdivision of watersheds into rectangular overland flow planes and channel elements, establishing IDs based on the hierarchical order for top-down flow routing. It extracts soil, slope, Manning’s coefficient, and land-use parameters and creates initial estimates of model parameters and the associated file format for K2. The setup process for the H1D model is conducted individually for each model element, using the unique ID numbers through the H1D graphical user interface. Here, various parameters are defined, encompassing the type of subsurface material, boundary conditions, vertical discretization, initial conditions, and time steps. H1D input requirements involve surface fluxes (evapotranspiration and rainfall). Soil properties such as field capacity, wilting point, density, and sand, silt, and clay fractions can be used to estimate soil hydraulic parameters for the van Genuchten hydraulic model (van Genuchten, 1980 ) using a neural network prediction method—specifically, the Rosetta Lite module, version 1.1 (Schaap et al., 2001 ). This method relies on pedo-transfer functions (PTFs) to estimate residual and saturated water contents, saturated hydraulic conductivity, and other soil hydraulic parameters. Evapotranspiration usually has an insignificant influence on runoff generation because of the short simulation time, and it was therefore neglected in this work, although the coupled model generally accounts for it.  2.4 Benchmark watersheds The capabilities and performance of the coupled model were evaluated based on four benchmark watersheds (Figs. 2 and 3   ), representing a diverse range of physical processes and flux components that define the expected standard simulation outcomes. In this coupling, we closely examined the properties and behavior of simulation results, comparing them with published hypothetical and observed results that allowed for a comprehensive analysis of key differences and similarities. Water balance errors and execution times for benchmark simulations were calculated and compared to literature results for equally complex modeling scenarios. 2.4.1 Hypothetical benchmark watersheds Numerical experiments are a useful tool for model intercomparison. This study explored similarities and differences between H1DK2-WS and other models using hypothetical benchmark simulations, which include H1D-K2 (Chen et al., 2022 ), HYDRUS-2D (Šimůnek et al., 2006; Šimůnek, 2015 ), and other models whose results were reported by Panday and Huyakorn (2004), Maxwell et al., (2014) , and Sulis et al. (2010) . The hypothetical benchmark watershed cases intentionally minimized the complexity in domain geometries and other features, such as topography, hydraulic and hydrogeological properties, and atmospheric forcing. However, they are complex enough to provide a thorough basis for comparing model behavior. The coupled H1DK2-WS code can simulate domains and flow conditions with varying model parameters, BCs, and initial conditions (see Table 1  ). This includes different saturated hydraulic conductivities (Ks ), initial water content distributions, initial water tables, bottom BCs (i.e., no flow and free drainage), slope ratios, and rainfall intensities and durations. The bottom BC represents the exchange flux between the vadose zone and groundwater. The no-flow BC represents an impermeable bottom layer, while the free drainage BC allows for water to drain from the bottom of the soil profile by gravity (Šimůnek et al., 2005 ). Model setups were selected in such a way as to match test scenarios that evaluate the impact of surface flow speed on infiltration and overland flow and different bottom BC types affecting the subsurface and surface flow processes. In this study, we used three hypothetical model domains (Fig. 2  and Table 1 ).1. Homogeneous Hillslope    Two types of homogenous hillslopes were examined with a 400-meter slope length, a unit width, and a subsurface thickness of 1 m (Fig. 2 a). This setup aligns with the descriptions provided by Chen et al. (2022)  and has certain similarities to the hillslope in Maxwell et al. (2014) . The domain incorporates a no-flow BC, representing an impermeable base. The subsurface was discretized into 101 elements, with mesh sizes ranging from 0.0053 m near the surface to 0.012 m at the bottom. In the K2 model, there were a total of 41 surface nodes along the hillslope's length. To initiate runoff generation, a rainfall event was applied at a rate of 3.3 × 10-4  m/s for 200 min, followed by a 100-minute recession period. For this simulation, we considered two distinct runoff generation scenarios based on the experimental setup: a. Infiltration Excess (Hortonian) Runoff . One homogeneous hillslope scenario was designed to ensure ponding on the surface of a 0.0005 slope. To achieve the Horton runoff generation, we specified a smaller Ks  (saturated hydraulic conductivity) value than the rainfall rate (3.3 × 10–4 m/min) to allow runoff generation before complete saturation of the soil column. In this scenario, we considered free drainage bottom boundary condition and three different Ks  values of 6.69 × 10-11 , 6.69 × 10-6 , and 6.69 × 10-5  m/min to change the amounts of infiltration and runoff (see Table 1  for details). The Ks  of 10-11  m/min was assumed to be comparable to an impervious surface. b. Saturation Excess (Dunn) Runoff . The second homogeneous hillslope scenario was designed to ensure ponding on a surface of a 0.0005 slope following complete saturation of the soil column. To achieve the Dunn runoff generation, we specified a larger Ks  (saturated hydraulic conductivity) value than the rainfall rate (3.3 × 10–4 m/min) to allow complete saturation of the soil column before surface ponding. In this scenario, we considered a no-flow bottom boundary condition at the bottom and specified a Ks  equal to 6.69 × 10-5  m/min. Runoff occurs after the soil profile becomes fully saturated (see Table 1  for details).    3 Heterogeneous hillslope Three hillslopes are interconnected in Fig. 2 b to illustrate the influence of variability in subsurface materials and slopes. The H1DK2-WS model domain encompasses three hillslopes and the H1D soil columns with ID numbers 1 (uphill), 2 (middle), and 3 (downhill). Each ID had distinct subsurface materials to better represent the spatial heterogeneity across the domain. The uphill and downhill H1D profiles were set with a Ks  of 6.69 × 10-6  m/s, while the middle hillslope had a Ks  of 6.69 × 10-4  m/s. The slope lengths were 150 m, 100 m, and 150 m, respectively, with corresponding water depth calculation nodes of 15, 10, and 15 in K2 simulations. Additional simulations were conducted to explore the impact of varying slopes. In this case, results from other conditions were compared to a simulation with a slope of 0.0005 and a roughness coefficient of 0.02. 3.1 A tilted V-catchment The tilted V-catchment was described in previous works by Gottardi and Venutelli (1993), Panday and Huyakorn (2004), Kollet and Maxwell (2006), Sulis et al. (2010) , and Maxwell et al. (2014) .  It is formed by joining two inclined planar rectangles to a central channel. Each of these rectangles has a width of 800 m and a length of 1000 m, and the channel has a width of 20 m (Fig. 2 c). The geometry of the tilted V-catchment is given in Table 1  and Fig. 2 c. This test case is utilized to evaluate the capability of the H1DK2-WS code to route the surface component. This scenario exclusively focuses on surface processes and excludes subsurface contributions (i.e., minimal infiltration). The saturated hydraulic conductivity value of the watershed material was set to 6.69 × 10-11  m/s to represent an impervious surface described in the Maxwell et al. (2014)  setup. The simulation scenario involves a 90-minute uniform rainfall event of 1.8 × 10-4  m/min, followed by a 90-minute drainage phase (i.e., a total simulation period of 180 min). Results are compared with other models in the literature (e.g., Maxwell et al., 2014 ). 3.1.1 Observed Experimental watershed − Lucky Hills watershed In this benchmark simulation, we considered a relatively complex headwater watershed called Lucky Hills within Arizona's Walnut Gulch Experimental Watershed (WGEW) (Goodrich et al., 2008 ). Lucky Hills is a small sub-watershed (Fig. 3 ) with an area of 0.04 km2 . The watershed has two weighing-type recording rain gauges, RG83 and RG384, with a precision of 0.25 mm and a 1-minute time step for rainfall recording. The runoff is measured with an H flume and a supercritical Santa Rita flume at two internal gauging stations (F106 and F102, respectively) and a Santa Rita flume at the outlet (F104) (Stone et al., 2008 ; Smith, 1981 ). Soils in the study watersheds are dominantly sandy loam (Ustochreptic Calciorthid) − with a desert shrub-dominated cover condition (e.g., Skirvin et al., 2008 ). The Lucky Hills watershed was discretized using 22 model elements (planes or channels) and 22 H1D profiles with 1 m depths and free drainage bottom boundary conditions. We simulated three rainfall events with runoff observations described by Meles et al. (2021) . The event data were selected from summer rainfall: July 25, 2010, July 26, 2010, and July 14, 2015, with a dry initial condition defined as a minimum of 24 h without rain with observed pre-storm moisture content values of 6–7 % VMC (volumetric water content) based the soil moisture sensors installed 5 cm below the surface in the watershed. These data are publicly available in the SWRC-DAP database (https://www.tucson.ars.ag.gov/dap ).   3.2 Model evaluation In this study, we used a comprehensive framework aimed to thoroughly evaluate the coupled model's performance. This encompassed a comparison with established results, statistical measures of predictive skills, and considerations of computational efficiency and water balance errors. 1) Comparative assessment: This evaluation involved a comparison of published results from Chen et al. (2022) , the HYDRUS-2D model (Šimůnek et al., 2006; Šimůnek, 2015 ), and an analytical solution (Gottardi and Venutelli, 1993 ) for both a single homogenous hillslope (Fig. 2 a) and the three connected heterogeneous hillslopes (Fig. 2 b). For evaluating the tilted V-catchment watershed (Fig. 2 c), the comparison was conducted through graphical inspection using published simulation results (e.g., Maxwell et al., 2014 ). Here, the graphical comparison was performed with the results associated with the OpenGeoSys (Delfs et al., 2013, 2012 ) and HydroGeoSphere (Therrien et al., 2012 ) hydrologic simulation models for which the tilted V-catchment simulations are available. Both HydroGeoSphere (HGS) and OpenGeoSys (OGS) are one of the integrated hydrological modeling systems extensively utilized for simulating watershed processes. Both HGS and OGS employ a 3D control-volume finite element groundwater model that rigorously conceptualizes interactions within groundwater and surface water systems capable of solving diffusive-wave overland and Richards equations. In addition to the flow modeling, the OGS model also simulates various physics-based processes, including thermal, mechanical, and chemical processes in porous and fractured media. The visual graphical inspection was also carried out using various simulation outputs related to the HSPF (Bicknell et al., 1993 ), HEC-1 (USACE, 1998 ), ParFlow (Kollet and Maxwell, 2006 ), and CATHY (Camporese et al., 2010 ) models. The evaluation metrics included how the simulated hydrographs and soil moisture values of the coupled H1K2-WS model tracked the time series of soil moisture redistribution, the peak flow rate, and the time to peak runoff. 2) Statistical predictive skills: This evaluation used statistical metrics to evaluate the model’s ability to simulate observed hydrographs. Goodness-of-fit statistics such as correlation coefficient, Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), Percent Bias, and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) were computed to objectively assess the model using the calibrated model outputs. In this process, we implemented a manual calibration utilizing selected parameters that were deemed to influence the two models independently. The small size of the watershed facilitated a strategic and efficient calibration process, requiring minimal time and effort despite using the manual calibration approach. It's crucial to recognize that manual calibration inherently relies on the modeler’s expertise and understanding of the model's fundamental mechanisms and interactions (Eckhardt & Arnold, 2001 ). This introduces a degree of subjectivity and provides faster calibration time. Ultimately, parameter sets yielding the best goodness of fit were selected for further analysis. Moving forward, future versions of the coupled model will include the coupling with the sensitivity analysis and automated calibration approaches. 3) Computational efficiency and water balance errors: Computational efficiency was gauged by assessing the computational time required for each analysis scenario and comparing it to available data. We also computed the total water balance errors in each simulation.   4 Results and discussion 4.1 Homogeneous Hillslope: Infiltration and saturation excess scenarios The results of the infiltration and saturation excess test cases are shown in Figure SII1, illustrating model parameters and scenarios outlined in Table 1 . The surface outflow rate and the soil moisture re-distribution with depth were plotted across the simulation period for a comparative analysis between the time series of the hillslope scale model (Chen et al., 2022 ) and HYDRUS-2D (Šimůnek et al., 2006; Šimůnek, 2015 ) model simulations. In both infiltration and saturation excess scenarios, the coupled model H1DK2-WS accurately reproduced the benchmark simulation (for details, see Supplementary Material  II ).  4.2 Heterogeneous hillslope with a uniform rainfall rate The heterogenous hillslope (Fig. 2 b) represented scenarios that capture variations in topographic and geomorphic features, geometric dimensions, surface and subsurface soil materials, and cover conditions. In this exercise, the results of the three-plane element-based H1DK2-WS model configuration accurately reproduced the simulated hydrograph of the single hillslope-based HYDRUS-2D model (Šimůnek et al., 2006 ) and the H1D-K2 hillslope model (Chen et al., 2022 ) with heterogeneous materials. Compared to both reference simulations, the coupled watershed scale model has exhibited precise tracking of water waves, except for an early arrival of the second flow wave from the upstream planes (Fig. 4  ). Compared to the HYDRUS 2D model, the second flow wave from the upstream hills, simulated using the H1DK2-WS and H1K2 models, arrives 7 min and 4 min quicker, respectively. The uphill (Plane 1) and downhill (Plane 2) planes are the low-permeability plane elements with Ks  equal to 6.94 × 10-6  m/min, resulting in immediate runoff generation. The middle hillslope, with a highly conductive material (Ks  = 6.94 × 10-4  m/min), saturates first before runoff generation starts at about 80 min, initiating the second flow wave at the outlet (at the end of the downhill plane). The hydrograph simulated by H1K2-WS shows that outflow began at 3.8 mins, increased to 6.52 × 10-4  m2 /min over 50 mins, and then gradually increased until the arrival of the second wave at about 110 mins (Fig. 4 ). The time to peak in all three models is equal at t  = 200 min. Additionally, slight disparities were observed in both the arrival time of the second flow wave and the total runoff volume between the models. These differences were 1.2 % and 2.4 % for H1D-K2 and H1DK2-WS, respectively, compared to the HYDRUS-2D runoff volume of 18.46 m3  during the simulation period. However, the peak flow, time to peak, runoff initiation time, and runoff rate (over 98 % of the simulation time) remained consistent across the HYDRUS-2D, H1D-K2, and coupled H1DK2-WS models. The minor discrepancies in runoff between the models can be attributed to differences in the model domain setup and numerical solutions. One of the factors leading to the mismatch of the hydrographs plotted in Fig. 4  and subsequent runoff figures could be the definition of kinematic wave solution that usually does not include diffusion. However, an off-centered finite difference scheme that is of the first order, as described by Ponce (1991) , introduces varying degrees of numerical diffusion depending on the size of Δx  and Δt . We compared the soil water content profiles simulated using the H1K2-WS model throughout the simulation period to the H1D-K2 and HYDRUS-2D codes in Fig. 5  . The analysis of water movement during the simulation period at various points along the hillslope − downhill (Fig. 5 a), middle (Fig. 5 b), and uphill (Fig. 5 c) − demonstrated a similar distribution pattern between the H1D-K2 and HYDRUS-2D models. Moreover, the examination across multiple plane elements indicated a broad approximation of soil profile conditions and water movement across the heterogeneous hillslope (see Figure SII2 and 5). It is important to note that the H1DK2-WS model effectively captures the general behavior of heterogeneous hillslopes similar to H1D-K2 and HYDRUS-2D, particularly in the central points of individual hillslopes. In the middle of the hillslope, the high conductive subsurface material (Ks  = 6.94 × 10-4  m/min) attained saturation throughout the columns in less than 100 min before saturation. In contrast, the uphill and downhill planes (Ks  = 6.94 × 10-6  m/min) registered water content changed only through the top 20 cm depth over the entire simulation period.  4.3 Tilted V-catchment Fig. 6   (black and gray hydrographs) shows the runoff outflow rates computed by various models for the tilted V-catchment with a rainfall intensity of 1.8 × 10-4  mm/min over 90 min. A very low hydraulic conductivity of Ks  = 6.94 × 10-11  m/min was assigned to all three elements to represent an impervious surface. Runoff outflow in m3 /s was compared visually and graphically to the results presented by Maxwell et al. (2014) , Kollet et al. (2006), and  Panday & Huyakorn (2004) . The published findings revealed significant variability between model results, underscoring the greater complexity of the domain and the diverse overland and channel routing schemes applied in each model. In this analysis, we compared simulation results from two models, OpenGeoSys (Delfs et al., 2013, 2012 ) and HydroGeoSphere (Therrien et al., 2012 ), alongside our coupled H1DK2-WS model. These simulations were conducted within the same model domain (refer to Fig. 2 b), employing identical parameter values and initial conditions (see Table 1 ). The evaluation included the similarities and differences through a graphical comparison of hydrographs (see Fig. 6 ), focusing on runoff initiation, the slope of the rising limb, steady-state flow, cessation of steady-state flow, and the slope of the recession side. The results showed that the performance of the H1DK2-WS model is well within the bounds of the OpenGeoSys and HydroGeoSphere models. Furthermore, the visual inspection of published simulated runoff rates compared to model outputs such as HSPF (Bicknell et al. 1993 ), HEC-1 (USACE, 1998 ), ParFlow (Kollet and Maxwell, 2006 ), CATHY (Camporese et al., 2010 ), and tRIBS (Ivanov et al., 2004 ), indicates that the coupled model stands closely alongside the array of model outputs noted above. This underscores the general consistency of the hydrographs produced by the coupled H1DK2-WS model with those generated by multiple other physically based integrated or coupled surface–subsurface flow models. The most significant deviations in the visual comparison occurred during the rising phase of the hydrograph rather than the recession limb phase, which is consistent with the observations in Maxwell et al. (2014) .  4.4 Lucky Hills watershed The calibrated coupled H1DK2-WS model accurately predicted the observed hydrographs at the watershed outlet and the internal gaging stations for three independent events in the Lucky Hills experimental watershed (Fig. 7  ). We implemented a manual calibration utilizing the parameters outlined and parameter spaces specified in Table 2  . In this approach, we independently calibrated model parameters for the sub-watersheds leading to each internal gauging station, encompassing both overland flow and corresponding H1D parameters. As shown in Table 3  , the model parameters are within acceptable ranges of the parameter spaces for the surface and subsurface properties of the watershed with sandy loam soil type, as detailed in Section 2.4 . The calibrated saturated water content for the three events seems to be on the higher end of the range for the soil type. The calibrated model produced simulation results with high goodness-of-fit, with a minimum Nash efficiency coefficient of 0.78 and a correlation coefficient of 0.91 for the smallest sub-watershed. The computed root mean square error (RMSE) and mean error (ME) were negligible, indicating the coupled model’s ability to simulate actual watershed processes accurately. Some of the most significant discrepancies were related to the peak flow prediction in the larger flow events. The calibrated model tends to overestimate (+ve peak runoff error) the peak flow rate, especially in large events on 07/30/2015 and 07/26/2010. The peak runoff error, computed as the difference between simulated peak runoff and observation normalized by the observed peak flow, showed less than 12 % on average, with the maximum discrepancy on the larger flow events at the watershed outlet reaching 22 %. Additionally, comparing the time to peak error, a difference between simulated time minus observation expressed in minutes, demonstrated near-perfect prediction, with differences ranging between 2 min ahead (−ve value) and 1 min behind the observed time to peak. This accuracy underscores the model's potential applicability in flood early warning prediction, highlighting its reliability in forecasting critical hydrological events. It is also encouraging that the manual calibration implemented in this study yielded predictions slightly superior to those of auto-calibrated K2 models for the three events (e.g., Meles et al., 2021 ). Previous research has underscored the importance of incorporating spatial rainfall variability in both space and time to enhance the accuracy of runoff prediction in this study area (Goodrich et al., 1995; Faures et al., 1995 ); to this end, the modeling exercise has included the two rain gauges in Luck Hills representing the rainfall variability. While acknowledging these positive outcomes, it is crucial to emphasize the potential for further enhancement in the predictive capabilities of the coupled model when applied to large watersheds. Future efforts will focus on deepening our understanding of model parameter sensitivity, identifiability, and importance across diverse scenarios and scales, requiring automatic optimization tools such as PEST (Doherty, 2004 ) or GLUE (Beven and Binley, 1992 ). Optimization algorithms and advanced sampling techniques for auto parameter identifiability and sensitivity analysis will be instrumental in improving predictive skills and increasing the implementation of the model over a broader range of scenarios. As we advance in these endeavors, the coupled model holds substantial promise for even more accurate and reliable predictions in future applications.  4.5 Water balance errors The water balance errors in the coupled systems were minimal, with a maximum of 0.31 % for the tilted V-catchment (Fig. 8  ). The water balance error in this context refers to the difference between precipitation input, outflow (runoff), a storage change in the surface and subsurface, and outflow at the bottom of the soil column, ultimately accounting for recharge.  4.6 Computational time Utilizing the common exchange time of 1 min, we compared the computational time required to simulate both a single hillslope and a series of heterogeneous hillslopes (3 connected uniform hillslopes) against the computational time of the H1D-K2 and HYDRUS-2D models (Fig. 9  ). Similar to the enhancements demonstrated by the H1D-K2 model, the coupled watershed model (H1DK2-WS) exhibited a slight improvement related to the implementation of the serialization technique (see Supplementary Material  I ). According to Chen et al. (2022) , the shortest computation time for the hillslope model (H1D-K2) with three soil profiles (refer to Section 4.2 ) was 21.36 s, followed by the HYDRUS-2D model at 32.49 s. The analogous model configured with three connected hillslopes representing heterogeneous scenarios demonstrated improvements in computation time even compared to the single hillslope H1D-K2 model. The H1DK2-WS model can easily integrate the channel routing with three hillslopes with minimal additional computational demand. This improvement also extends to a single homogeneous hillslope domain, where the coupled watershed scale model (H1DK2-WS) required a mere 17.3 s compared to 21.36 s and 32.49 s for the H1D-K2 and HYDRUS-2D models, respectively which is 14.3 % and 47 % improvement respectibely. Despite substantial improvements in computational time achieved by the coupled model, particularly for simple scenarios, parallel computing platforms present substantial opportunities for further enhancement. This would enable the model not only to explicitly couple various hydrologic components efficiently but also to create ensemble modeling techniques and conduct long-term simulations for model evaluation, assessment, and impact studies, such as those involving evaluations of climate change and management effects. Various efforts have demonstrated the utilization of distributed hydrologic models of varying capabilities on parallel computing platforms (e.g., Kollet et al., 2010; Kollet and Maxwell, 2008; Vivoni et al., 2011 ). The utilization of an external exchange strategy and hierarchical simulations across plane and channel elements is well-suited for implementing various parallel computing strategies like functional parallelism that conduct independent and simultaneous model simulations (e.g., Harada and Alba, 2020 ), as well as multifunctional parallelism (Vrugt et al., 2006; Liao et al., 2017 ).   5 Conclusion In this study, we developed the H1DK2-WS model, which couples H1D and K2 models at the watershed scale. This model is evaluated against benchmark simulations and observed watershed data. The integration encompasses a novel coupling approach with BC switching to account for surface ponding and water exchange. The benchmark simulations included a variety of test scenarios, ranging from hypothetical to real-world watershed conditions. Furthermore, we compared these benchmark simulations with models employing different structures and solution techniques, including HYDRUS-2D with an overland flow routine, OpenGeoSys, and HydroGeoSphere. The H1DK2-WS model demonstrated excellent consistency in terms of subsurface soil moisture redistribution and outflow rates at the hillslope scale for both homogeneous and heterogeneous subsurface scenarios consistent with the H1D-K2 (Chen et al., 2022 ), HYDRUS-2D (Šimůnek et al., 2006; Šimůnek, 2015 ). Despite slight differences due to numerical methods, the model provided results consistent with multi-model outputs especially in the hypothetical benchmark simulations.  Applying combined water balances and BC switching in coupling H1D and K2 has resulted in accurate model results. This approach effectively accounts for surface ponding and water exchange between the models, improving the accuracy in simulating hydrological fluxes with minimal water balance errors. The subdivision of hillslopes into a cascade of planes with varying slopes, soil characteristics, and land cover conditions allows for incorporating complex spatial heterogeneity. This approach enhances the model's ability to capture the nuances of real-world landscapes, including variability in topographic parameters (slope), roughness, land use and land cover properties, and soil and subsurface properties, thereby accurately representing hydrologic responses of domain complexities. Additionally, H1DK2-WS model demonstrates significant computational efficiency, offering faster simulation times than HYDRUS-2D. even without implementing any parallelization techniques. The findings affirm the model's accuracy in simulating hydrological dynamics across scales and underscore its potential for further development and parallel computing implementation.
1 Introduction In many parts of the world, exotic forest plantations including Eucalyptus  and Acacia mearnsii  are a major supplier of industrial roundwood, with fast growth rates and short rotations (Morris et al., 2022 ).
