Planted commercial forests only constitute 8 % of the global forest area, however, supply 46 % of industrial roundwood (Payn et al., 2015 ). A well-managed commercial forest plantation can improve soil infiltration rates (van Dijk and Keenan, 2007 ), significantly reduce soil erosion due to forest litter at the soil surface, minimise soil evaporation (Wichert et al., 2018 ) and mitigate air pollution and climate change (Ferreto et al., 2021 ). Further benefits of commercial forestry include contribution to socio-economy through employment and agricultural gross domestic product. Despite the crucial role played by Eucalyptus  and A. mearnsii  in different parts of the world (including South Africa), research have indicated that evapotranspiration (ET) by both species is significantly higher than indigenous forest stands and grasslands (Dye et al., 2001; Dye and Jarmain, 2004; Albaugh et al., 2013; Almeida et al., 2016; Reichert et al., 2017 ). In South Africa, Eucalyptus  and A. mearnsii  species are largely confined in high rainfall areas, which were previously covered by low water using grasslands and Fynbos, adjacent to catchments that are critically important sources of water for rivers (Dye, 2013 ). This has resulted in a significant reduction of streamflow, hence affecting downstream water demands by the environment, industry, agriculture and human settlements (Dye, 2013; Farley et al., 2005; Jackson et al., 2005 ). In addition, commercial forest plantations, especially the genetically improved Eucalyptus  hybrids have a deep taproot (Dye, 1996 ), providing the capability to access groundwater reserves during the dry season (van Dijk and Keenan, 2007 ). This usually results in perennial streamflow reduction and lowering of the groundwater table (Scott and Prinsloo, 2008; Lu et al., 2018 ). A study by Scott and Lesch (1997)  in the Mokobulaan experimental catchment in South Africa reported that afforestation with Eucalyptus  and pines significantly reduced the streamflow (Q) after three and four years of planting, respectively. A complete cessation of Q was observed at year nine for Eucalyptus,  and year twelve for pines, with full perennial Q returning five years after clear-felling. A study by Dye and Jarmain (2004)  on the implications of removing invading A. mearnsii  on the Q indicated that the Q increased after removal of invading A. mearnsii , attributed to high water use by this species resulting to streamflow reduction. The Two Streams research catchment (in Mistley Canema, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa) is one of the few catchments in South Africa where detailed hydrological observations have been conducted (Dye and Jarmain, 2004; Clulow et al., 2011; Everson et al., 2014 ) on A. mearnsii  for extended periods. Results indicated that A. mearnsii  ET exceeded precipitation in the first 6 years of growth by as much as 46 %, and there was sufficient evidence suggesting that trees can access deep underground water reserves using their deep taproots. In February 2018, after a 12-year rotation, the A. mearnsii  trees were harvested and E. dunnii  was planted in March 2018. The hydrological measurements resumed in September 2019. This presented a unique opportunity to quantify the catchment surface water balance for A. mearnsii  (at two different stages of growth) and E. dunnii  (in the early stages of growth) in the same study site and catchment. However, the various components of the water balance were incomplete at various times, due to research funding constraints at times as well as various equipment failures, and compiling a continuous surface water balance record was not possible. Therefore, annual measurement window periods were identified in the dataset when, 1) measurement records were complete, and 2) climatic conditions were representative of the long-term mean of Mistley Canema. The aim of this study was therefore to compare the surface water-balance for young A. mearnsii  (∼three years old), matured A. meanrsii  (∼seven years old) and young E. dunnii  (∼three years old). Since the hydrological data for measurement windows were conducted on the same study site and for similar climatic conditions, the differences in the water-balance are attributed mainly to changes in the landcover providing a unique comparison of the surface water balance for trees of different ages and species at the same site.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Description of the study site The catchment location is at Mistley Canema (29°12’19.78°S, 30°39’3.78°E) in the Seven Oaks area, northeast of Pietermaritzburg in the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa ( Fig. 1 ). The catchment is in a part of the midlands mist-belt grassland Bioregion, mostly dominated by forb-rich, tall, sour Thermeda triandra  of which few patches remain due to Aristida junciformis  invasion (Everson et al., 2014 ). The catchment size is approximately one km2  with hilly topography and rolling landscapes that dips towards the southeast, resulting in the northwest to southeast surface drainage. The study site weather classification according to Koppen-Geiger climate classification (Peel et al., 2007 ) falls within the Cwa bioclimate zone characterised by dry, cold winters and wet summer months ( Table 1 ). Acacia mearnsii  trees were planted in March 2006 (for a full rotation of 12 years) with hydrological monitoring including streamflow gauging (Q), ET, soil water content (SWC) and groundwater reserves conducted by Clulow et al. (2011)  and Everson et al. (2014) . In February 2018, the A. mearnsii  trees were harvested. The catchment was subsequently planted to E. dunnii  in March 2018. Hydrological processes measurements (Q, ET, SWC and depth to groundwater) resumed in September of 2019. A study by Clulow et al. (2011)  and Everson et al. (2014)  classified the soil profile in the catchment to be as deep as 13 m and below consists of a weathered bedrock (saprolite) and fractured basement rock under the soil profile. The soil form was classified as Hutton (Soil Classification Working Group, 1991 ). Both the A. mearnsii  and E. dunnii  crops were planted at a spacing of 2 ×3 m (1667 trees ha−1 ). Three hydrological years, referred to as measurement windows in this paper (a hydrological year starts on the 1st of October to the 30th of September in South Africa), with complete dataset of hydrological measurements including Q, ET, and weather data were identified for comparison. They were considered suitable as their annual precipitation and general climate was statistically similar over the window periods. The trees were between 2.7 and 3.7 years old in the first measurement period (October 2008 to September 2009, referred to as Amear 3  ). They were 6.7–7.7 years old (October 2012 to September 2013, referred to as Amear 7  ) in the second measurement period. After replanting E. dunnii  trees in March 2018 a final measurement window from the age of 2.6–3.6 years old (October 2020 to September 2021, referred to as Edun 3  ) was compared.  2.2 Climatic conditions An automatic weather station was installed on a flat uniform grassland area adjacent to the study site to provide supporting meteorological measurements. Measurements of air temperature (T air  ) (HMP 60, Vaisala Inc., Helsinki, Finland), relative humidity (RH) (HMP60, Vaisala Inc., Helsinki, Finland), wind speed (WS) and direction (Model 03003, R.M. Young, Traverse City, Michigan, USA), solar radiation (I s  ) (Kipp and Zonen CMP3) and gross precipitation (TE525, Texas Electronics Inc., Dallas, Tx, USA) were conducted every 30 min. The sensors were installed according to recommendations of the World Meteorological Organisation (World meteorological Organisation, 2008 ) with rain gauge orifice at 1.2 m and the remaining sensors at 2 m above the ground surface. The sensor outputs were recorded on a CR1000 datalogger (Campbell Scientific Inc., Logan, Utah, USA) at 30 min intervals. The datalogger was programmed to calculate the vapour pressure deficit (VPD) using T air   and RH measurements according to Savage et al. (1997) . The reference evaporation (ETo) was calculated using the technique described in Allen et al. (2011) . The monthly effective precipitation (P eff  ) was calculated using:(1) P  eff   = P  g   − I  l       where Pg  is the gross precipitation (mm) and I  l     is the plant canopy interception loss (mm). The negative P  eff     values were rounded off to 0 mm.  2.3 Streamflow measurements The Q was measured from a 457.2 mm 90° V-notch using a CS450 pressure transducer (Campbell Scientific Inc., Logan, Utah, USA) with data recorded in a CR200X datalogger (Campbell Scientific) for all three measurement periods. The CS450 pressure inducer sensor consists of a piezoresistive sensor housed in a water resistance stainless steel package to enhance reliability (Campbell Scientific, 2010 ). The sensor provides accurate measurements of water pressure and level that are fully temperature compensated. The water level measurements from the CS450 sensor were calibrated by directly measuring the water level from the V-notch using a measuring tape.  2.4 Evapotranspiration All data for the first two window periods were sourced from the Centre for Water Resources Research (CWRR) at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in Pietermaritzburg (details of measurement techniques and equipment used can be found in Clulow et al. (2011)  and Everson et al. (2014) . For Edun 3  , the ET was measured using an eddy covariance system (EC) to derive sensible heat flux (H), using a three-dimensional sonic anemometer (CSAT3, Campbell Scientific Inc., Logan, Utah, USA) and measurements of net radiation (Rn) and ground heat flux (G) were conducted simultaneously on the study site. The Rn was measured using a net radiometer (NRLite, Kipp and Zonen, Delft, Netherlands) attached to the lattice mast (24 m in height) on a horizontal boom 2.5 m away from the lattice mast at a height of 18.5 m. The sonic anemometer was mounted on the lattice mast at a height of 18 m. The G was measured using two HFP01-L soil heat flux plates and parallel TCAV-L averaging thermocouples (Campbell Scientific Inc., Logan, Utah, USA). The soil heat flux plates and thermocouples were buried in the middle of the compartment (approximately 2 m away from the EC system) at a depth of 0.08 m and 0.02 m below the soil surface, respectively, to estimate the heat stored in the soil. The EC is a technique based on estimation of eddy fluxes. The H used in estimation is expressed as:(2) H = ρ  a    ̅  c  p   w ′ Tair ′  ̅      where, ρ  a     is the density of dry air (kg m−3 ), c  p     is the specific heat capacity for air at constant pressure (J kg−1  K−1 ), w ′    is the vertical wind speed (m s−1 ) and T air   is the air temperature (°C). The w ′    and T air   are measured using the sonic anemometer and the primes denote fluctuation from a temporal average and the overbar represents a time average. The averaging period of the instantaneous fluctuations of w ′    and T air   should be long enough (30–60 min) to capture all the eddies that contribute to the flux and fulfil the assumption of stationarity (Meyers and Baldocchi, 2005 ). The zero plain displacement and roughness layer were determined to be at 12.0 m and 24.0 m, respectively. Therefore, the sonic anemometer height was 18 m above tree canopy. The energy balance (LE) was calculated as a residual term using the simplified energy balance equation:(3) Rn = G + H + LE     where, Rn is the net irradiance, H   is the sensible heat flux, LE   is the latent heat flux (equivalent to ET by conversion, Savage et al. (2004) ) and G   is the ground heat flux. The EC data was processed using the Eddy Pro® 7 software (Licor Inc., Lincoln, Nebraska, USA) for spikes in the data, sonic temperature corrections, co-ordinate rotation and planar fit. In addition to these processing steps, the 30-min flux data were screened using the following criteria 1) data obtained when the sensor malfunctions were removed from the analysed dataset 2) data on rainy days were excluded due to the negative impact of precipitation on turbulent fluxes as reported by Zhang et al. (2017)  3) incomplete 30-min data were removed, when the missing ratio was greater than 5 % in the 30-min raw data 4) night-time data (Rn  < 0) was removed from the analysis due to potentially large nocturnal influences at night-time (Blanken et al., 1998; Wilson et al., 2001 ).  2.5 The leaf area index The leaf area index (LAI) measurements were conducted monthly on Amear 3  , Amear 7   and Edun 3   measurement periods using a LAI-2200 Plant Canopy Analyzer (Licor Inc., Lincoln, Nebraska, USA). Measurements were conducted on a transect that was identified in the middle of the study site for each measurement window to avoid the impact of edge effect on LAI measurements (Woodgate et al., 2015 ). The transect was 250 m in length and measurements were conducted every 5 m, producing a total 50 LAI measurements, which were thereafter averaged to a single LAI measurement per month.  2.6 Canopy interception loss The Von Hoyningen-Huene is a simplistic method of modelling the interception loss (I l  ) in agricultural crops and is incorporated as part of the Agricultural Catchments Research Unit model, commonly known as ACRU model. The Von Hoyningen-Huene approach was designed for calculating precipitation interception loss (I l  ) in agricultural crops, however, Schulze (1995)  found that the approach performed very well in estimating I l   in commercial forest plantations (P. patula ). The I l   in this study was calculated using the Von Hoyningen-Huene equation (Von-Hoyningen-Huene, 1983 ):(4) I  l   = 0.30 + 0.27 P  g   + 0.13 LAI − 0.013 P  g   LAI − 0.007 LAI  2       where, Pg  is the gross precipitation (mm) measured using the automatic raingauge and the LAI is the leaf area index. The Von Hoyningen-Huene equation has been found to be only stable for Pg  daily precipitation amounts of less than 18 mm, above which it is assumed that no I l   occurs (Schulze, 1995 ). In this study, I l   was calculated monthly using Von Hoyningen-Huene equation and monthly values were summed up to annual total I l   for each measurement period. 2.6.1 Potential errors in estimating interception loss Estimating I l   using the Von Hoyningen-Huene method has been shown to be relatively accurate in commercial forest plantations, such as in Pinus patula  (Schulze, 1995 ). However, there are potential errors that may influence the accuracy of this method. One such error arises from exclusion of litter interception and evaporation loss in the I l   calculation. Forest litter has been shown to contribute a smaller, yet important role in interception losses (Bulcock and Jewitt, 2012 ). Studies (Helvey and Patric, 1986; Bulcock and Jewitt, 2012 ) have shown that litter interception is influenced mostly by water holding capacity and initial storage capacity of the litter, but also by the evaporative demand following the rainfall event. For example, a throughfall that reaches the dry litter gradually increases the water content of litter to field capacity and then to saturation. In our study, all studied crops were at canopy closure stage and the LAI was generally high (ranging from 2.45 to 4.11), suggesting that evaporative demands were very low and forest litter was relatively wet, therefore very low litter interception occurred. As a result, litter interception and litter evaporation losses in our study were deemed negligible. Another potential error was introduced by the assumption of the model that rainfall events greater than 18 mm does not cause interception losses. It was noted by Toucher et al. (2020)  that the Von Hoyningen-Huene method underestimates the I l   of Eucalyptus grandis  compared to a variable storage Gash model in 5838 quinaries. This underestimation was attributed to the Von Hoyningen-Huene model not being stable for gross precipitation greater than 18 mm. During the period of our study, majority of rainfall events were less than 18 mm, suggesting that our study results were less likely affected by this possible error.   2.7 Surface water balance The monthly catchment surface water balance for Amear 3  , Amear 7   and Edun 3   was calculated based on Pg  precipitation, ET, I l   and Q using:(5) ± Δ S = water inflow − water outflow     where, ± Δ S    is the change in the catchment water storage, water inflow   is water recharging the catchment and water outflow   is the total water loss from the catchment. Eq. 5  was further expressed using the measured variables in the surface water balance as follows:(6) ± Δ S water storage = P  g   − ET − I  l   − Q     where, P  g     is gross precipitation (mm, water inflow ), ET   is the evapotranspiration (mm, water outflow), I l   is the interception loss (mm, water outflow) and Q   is the total direct runoff (mm, water outflow which includes the baseflow). A positive value (positive surface water balance) in Δ S    indicates an increase in water availability to the soil, whereas a negative value (negative surface water balance) indicates a loss in the soil water storage. It is important to note that other components potentially contributing to the total water balance of our catchment which includes, the root uptake from groundwater, the hydraulic lift, water uptake from perched aquifer and subsurface water movement from adjacent unplanted areas were not incorporated, as they were not measured ( Fig. 2 ). Conducting such measurements is very challenging and require financial resources of which were very limited in our study.  2.8 Statistical analysis The statistical analysis was performed using the R statistical computing software (R Development Core team, 2008 ). An analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to assess the differences in hydrological parameters (Q, ET, I l   and climatic variables) between Amear 3  , Amear 7   and Edun 3  . Variables were transformed as appropriate to meet the assumption of normality. Where the overall F-statistic was significant (p  < 0.05), treatment means were compared using Fischer’s Least Significant Difference at the 5 % level of significance (LSD5 % ).   3 Results 3.1 Weather conditions The weather for three measurement periods reflected typical warm temperate climatic conditions with warm wet summers and cool dry winters ( Fig. 3 ). The daily I s   over all window periods was lowest in June (mean range: 3.1–11.7 MJ m−2  day−1 ) but more consistent, whereas December and January experienced higher and more variable I s   (reaching a peak of 30 MJ m−2  day−1 ). These conditions were consistent with clear winter days and a wetter summer season with thunderstorms at times. The maximum T air   (range: 34.1–38.2 °C) was measured in January for all measurements periods, while the lowest measured T air   was between 0 and −1 °C in June. The total measured gross annual precipitation in 2008/ 09, 2012/ 13 and 2020/ 21 was 819 mm, 862 mm and 844 mm, respectively, which mostly (70 %) occurred during summer from September to April of each measurement period. The VPD was low in the summer season and increased during the winter season with a mean of 0.59 kPa for Amear 3  , 0.62 kPa for Amear 7   and 0.72 kPa for Edun 3  . The Edun 3   period had 15 % greater annual ETo (1060 mm) compared to Amear 3   (903 mm) and Amear 7   (907 mm) (Fig. 3 ). The lowest measured daytime RH occured during berg wind conditions in September (31.8 %), December (27.5 %) and October (21 %) for Amear 3  , Amear 7   and Edun 3  , respectively. The average wind speeds were notably high in July for Edun 3   (maximum 37 m s−1 ) and in October for Amear 3   and Amear 7   (maximum 32 m s−1 ).  3.2 Effective precipitation and interception loss The monthly effective precipitation for all measurement windows was generally higher during the wet season (October to February), ranging from 57 % to 90 % for Amear 3  , 65–88 % for Amear 7   and 52–90 % for Edun 3   of gross precipitation ( Table 2 ). During the dry season (May to August), the monthly effective rainfall was low, reaching the lowest value of zero in Amear 3   and Edun 3   (May and July) while zero effective rainfall values were measured only in July for Amear 7  . The total annual effective precipitation for Amear 3   (650 mm) and Edun 3   (647 mm) were significantly (p <0.05) greater than Amear 7   (617 mm). Precipitation interception losses depended on gross precipitation and the LAI of the specific crop. The Edun 3   was found to have the highest LAI reaching a maximum of 4.11, compared to a peak LAI of 2.45 and 3.34 for Amear 3   and Amearn 7  , respectively. The summer monthly I l   ranged from 19.6–29.9 mm, 17.8–44.3 mm and 14.8–33.1 mm for Amear 3  , Amearn 7   and Edun 3   of monthly gross precipitation, respectively. The annual I l   was highest for the Amearn 7   (226 mm, 26 % of annual precipitation), followed by Edun 3   (195.2 mm, 23 % of annual precipitation) and finally Amear 3   (169.1 mm, 20 % of annual precipitation), with the Amearn 7   crop statistically (p  < 0.05) greater than the Amear 3   and statistically similar (p  > 0.05) to Edun 3  . The I l   was obviously influenced by the LAI but also by the quantity of gross precipitation received per event. For example, gross precipitation events of less than 3 mm, resulted in almost 100 % interception, while high gross precipitation events (> 10 mm) resulted to less interception loss. The I l   comparison between measurement windows indicated that Amearn 7   crop I l   was 25 % and 13.2 % greater than Amear 3   and Edun 3  , respectively, which, was as a result of a combination of higher LAI and precipitation event characteristics.  3.3 Streamflow The Q for all measurement periods was seasonal ( Fig. 4 ) and did not respond significantly to effective precipitation events of less than 10 mm, 16.9 mm and 12.2 mm for Amear 3  , Amear 7   and Edun 3   cropping periods, respectively, except after consecutive effective precipitation events where antecedent conditions played a role. During summer, (November to February) Q was generally high, reaching peaks of 18.3, 8.2 and 12.2 mm month−1  for Amear 3  , Amear 7   and Edun 3   cropping windows, respectively. The summer water yield (expressed as a ratio of total annual streamflow to total annual effective precipitation, Q/Peff*100) for Amear 7   (mean water yield: 4.4 %) was found to be statistically lower (p  < 0.05) than both the young crops (mean water yield: Amear 3   = 9.26 % and Edun 3   = 7.9 %), which were statistically similar (p  > 0.05) to each other. These results suggested that when the catchment was afforested with young trees (Amear 3   and Edun 3  ), more effective precipitation was converted to runoff, than when the catchment was planted to matured trees ( Figs. 5 a and 5 b), which was evident in annual effective rainfall for Amear 7   (617 mm) which was lower (p  < 0.05) than both Amear 3   (650 mm) and Edun 3   (647 mm). During the dry season (May to August), the Q was low at 2.1 mm month−1  for Amear 3  , 2.2 mm month−1  for Amear 7   and 1.8 mm month−1  for Edun 3  . The water yield was high in the dry season compared to the wet season, reaching a peak of 105 % for Amear 3  , 98 % for Edun 3   and 44 % for Amear 7  , which was caused by low effective precipitation in the dry season (Fig. 4 b). The total annual Q for Amear 3   (65.9 mm) and Edun 3   (59.8 mm) was statistically similar (p  = 0.30), while Amear 7   (44.7 mm) was significantly (p  < 0.05) lower than both the Amear 3   and Edun 3   crops. The differences in seasonal patterns are best illustrated using the accumulated Q, gross precipitation and effective precipitation comparison ( Fig. 6 ). The accumulated Q for the two young crop window periods (Amear 3   = 65.9 mm and Edun 3   = 59.8 mm) exceeded the matured crop Q (Amear 7   = 44.7 mm) by 32 % and 25 % for Amear 3   and Edun 3  , respectively. The accumulated ET exceeded gross precipitation for all measurement windows by 27 %, 24.5 % and 25.1 % for Amear 3  , Amear 7   and Edun 3  , respectively (Fig. 6 ).  3.4 Evapotranspiration The ET for the three measurement periods was seasonal, with the ET being higher in the wet season (November to February) and lower in the dry season (June to July). In summer (November to January), mean monthly ET for Amear 3   was statistically greater (p  < 0.05) than the Amearn 7   and Edun 3  , whereas during the dry season (May to July) both Amearn 7   and Edun 3   was statistically greater (p  < 0.05) than Amear 3  . The annual ET followed the descending order Edun 3   (1193 mm) > Amear 3   (1168 mm) > Amearn 7   (1142 mm) with no statistically significant differences (p  = 0.9).  3.5 Surface catchment water balance The monthly surface catchment water balance produced a negative result for all months in all three measurement periods, except for October 2008 in Amear 3  , October 2012 and January 2013 in Amear 7   and November and December 2020 in Edun 3   where the catchment surface water balance was positive ( Table 3 ). On an annual basis, ET for all measurement periods exceeded gross annual precipitation by 30 %, 25 % and 30 % for Amear 7  , Edun 3   and Amear 3  , respectively. The annual intercepted rainfall of 169 mm for Amear 3  , 226 mm for Amear 7   and 195 mm for Edun 3   played a significant role in inducing the negative surface water balance. As a result, the Edun 3   had a greatest deficit in the surface water balance (–603 mm) followed by the Amear 3   (–585 mm) and Amear 7   (–552 mm) (Table 3 ).   4 Discussion Studies that quantify the surface water balance of a catchment are not common, due to high implementation and maintenance costs associated with such studies as well as the complexity of the interactions of natural systems. The availability of historical hydrological data (ET, meteorological and Q) for Acacia mearnsii  at different growth stages within its rotation, followed by the exchange of genus to E. dunnii , at the same site, with ongoing hydrological measurements from the E. dunnii , provided a unique opportunity to compare the surface water balance of A. mearnsii  at two different ages and between two species at the same site. The challenge with such comparisons is that there can be differences in the water balance due to difference in weather conditions. In this study, there were differences in the weather conditions across the three window periods, but generally the weather over the long-term was comparable and unlikely to confound the comparison of the surface water balance between the three measurement periods. This implies that differences in the surface water balance were predominantly due to species differences or tree age, however, lags in the water-balance and long-term differences in soil water resources may have played a role in introducing some differences. 4.1 Catchment surface water balance The concept of water balance provides an opportunity for studying the behaviour of the catchment with an assumption that water entering the catchment is equivalent to water leaving the catchment, plus or minus any change in soil water storage (Brassington, 2006 ). Water inputs in a typical forestry catchment includes effective rainfall, groundwater uptake by roots, water access by roots in unsaturated zone or pocket of water lenses and tree hydraulic lift (Brooksbank et al., 2011; Ngubo et al., 2022 ). The roots of commercial forest plantations have been reported to penetrate as deep into the soil as possible to access the plant available soil water, unless restricted by a hard soil layer (Kimber, 1974 ). Depending on characteristics of the soil, the taproot of commercial plantations have been reported to exceed equivalent tree height in order to increase chances of water uptake (Sherry, 1971 ). In the studied catchment, the soil profile was found to be as deep as 20 m, without any impeding soil layers (Clulow et al., 2011 ). A study by Everson et al. (2014)  in the Two Streams catchment found tree roots up to a depth of 8 m during the deep drilling in October 2012, six years after planting A. mearnsii  trees. The depth to water table for the centre borehole, measured during the wet season in 2012, was ∼20.3 m (Everson et al., 2014 ), which was probably too deep for roots of all our crops to come into direct contact with ground water resources as the roots would still have been relatively shallow. As a result, groundwater resources and hydraulic lift were excluded as an input in the water balance calculation in our study and only precipitation was included. The only possible available water extraction by trees was soil water stored in the soil profile from previous wet years, water in perched aquifers, soil water that occur within the unsaturated zone or subsurface water flow from nearby unplanted areas. The challenge in such water balance studies where soils are deep and underlain by deep unspecified material down to 20 m, is that measurement of water content in these zones is challenging but possibly critical in understanding water balance deficits measured in afforested areas. 4.1.1 Evapotranspiration Evapotranspiration is one of the variables that is not commonly available in water balance studies, and it is a significant strength of this data set to have measured values of ET. In the studied catchment, ET for the three measuring periods significantly exceeded gross precipitation by 25–30 %, resulting in a negative catchment water balance, even more so if effective precipitation is considered. These results are consistent with two previous ET studies conducted on the same catchment; 1) Dye and Jarmain (2004)  used the Bowen ratio technique on four-year-old A. mearnsii  and found ET to exceed precipitation by 18 %, and 2) a study by Clulow et al. (2011)  using a large aperture scintillometer on two-year old A. mearnsii  reported 46 % greater ET than precipitation. In our study, the two young crops (Amear 3   and Edun 3  ) had a slightly higher ET than the mature crop, although not statistically different. These results were expected as literature reports that ET by commercial forestry species decreases with an increase in tree age (Roberts et al., 2001; Kostner et al., 2002; Delzon and Loustau, 2005; Soares and Almeida, 2001 ). For example, in a Brazilian study by Almeida et al. (2007) , maximum annual transpiration (> 1000 mm) was measured when E. grandis  hybrid trees were between 2.75 and 5.6 years old and a significant decrease in transpiration was observed when trees were older than 5.6 years. This age-related decline in water-use was reported to be driven by the fact that mature trees are taller and have a lower transpiration per unit leaf area than young trees (Delzon and Loustau, 2005; Scott and Prinsloo, 2008 ). In our study, the slightly lower ET in the mature trees (Amear 7  ), compared to the younger crops (Amear 3   and Edun 3  ), could be associated with lower transpiration per unit leaf area in Amear 7  . Evapotranspiration consistently exceeding precipitation at the Two Streams research catchment suggests that trees have access to water not quantified in the surface water balance such as, (1) soil water accumulated from periods when the catchment was fallow, (2) water from unplanted nearby areas moving laterally and vertically in response to gradients in soil water potential (Dye, 1996 ) or (3) water from the perched aquifer. Isotope studies are needed to determine the source of the water, although extracting isotope samples from soil and tree sap is challenging (Penna et al., 2018 ).  4.1.2 Impact of commercial forestry plantations on streamflow Several South African studies (van Lill et al., 1980; Smith and Scott, 1992; Scott and Lesch, 1997; Scott and Smith, 1997; Scott et al., 2000 ) have quantified the impact of commercial forest plantations on the Q. The study by Scott and Lesch (1997)  on the Q response to afforestation with E. grandis  and P. patula  in Mokobulaan experimental catchment in South Africa indicated that eucalypts cause a faster reduction in Q (90–100 %) compared to afforestation with pines (40–60 %). These results were verified in a study conducted by Scott et al. (2000)  where peak reductions in Q were reported between 5 and 10 years after establishing eucalypts, and between 10 and 20 years after planting pines, with the reduction driven by soil water availability. A study by Dye and Jarmain (2004)  from various catchments in South Africa indicated that a complete removal of A. mearnsii  resulted in a significant increase in Q. Results from our study indicated that the annual Q was lowest when the catchment was afforested with the mature crop (Amear 7  ) and higher when the catchment was planted with the younger crops (Amear 3   and Edun 3  ). This could be caused, in part, by annual interception loss, which was higher for the Amear 7   (226 mm) than in Amear 3   (169.1 mm) and Edun 3   (195.2 mm), resulting in a reduced effective precipitation and thereby possibly reducing the Q. These results are corroborated by other studies. For example, Ferraz et al. (2013)  reported a significantly high annual Q (384 mm) in catchments planted with young Eucalyptus  plantations (2-years-old) compared to matured plantation (5-years-old) in which annual Q was measured to be 235.1 mm. This difference was partly attributed to mature trees having high leaf area index and high forest litter, therefore intercepting water runoff to the stream. In our study, Amear 7   peak LAI was slightly higher than the Amear 3   LAI, but lower than Edun 3  , whereas the forest litter, though not measured, is considered to be higher in mature crops than in young crops. This suggests the possibility that Amear 7   trees and litter intercepted more runoff than the younger crops. In another study by Farley et al. (2005)  where 26 catchments datasets were modelled to understand the effect of afforestation on Q, results indicated 1) a runoff reduction of more than 10 % of Q in the first two to three years after catchment afforestation 2) on average, Eucalyptus  reduced runoff by 75 % as trees matured, compared with 40 % average decrease by pines.   4.2 Implications of negative catchment water balance The results from this study and those of previous studies, including the long-term paired catchment studies in South Africa, have all indicated a negative catchment water balance as a result of commercial afforestation, particularly eucalypts. Of the measured components of the catchment surface water balance, tree ET was found to be the greatest loss, while Q was found to be the least and particularly so for the mature Amear 7   window period. These results are critical in terms of planning, since most commercial forest plantations are established in high precipitation regions and are planted adjacent to catchments that provide freshwater for downstream users (Albaugh et al., 2013 ). Therefore, the management of commercial forestry plantations should consider the principles of human rights, ecosystem resilience and ecosystem services sustainability. Afforestation of commercial plantation in water-limited areas should consider water use for drinking and downstream activities, such that forest management balances wood production and water resource conservation. The previous paired catchment experiments in South Africa showed the impact of forestry on streamflow and current legislation has focussed on blue water and the impact of commercial forestry through streamflow reduction activity (SFRA). This led to forestry being declared a SFRA and a licensing system for planting was put in place. However, these studies typically didn’t have measured ET and didn’t show the immediate difference in ET with age and between species.   5 Conclusion Studies that investigate catchment surface water balances in South Africa with actual measurements of ET are few, due to time and costs associated with conducting such studies. Other confounding factors in determining the differences in ET with age and between species, include differences in site characteristics such as slope and soil type. This study provides the surface water balance by young Acacia mearnsii , mature Acacia mearnsii  and young eucalypts at the same site and with similar climatic conditions, eliminating site characteristic differences. The strategy of comparing measurement windows periods with complete records and of similar climatic conditions, due to missing water balance records at various times, worked well, but does not accommodate lags in the water balance annual cycle. Surface water balance results for all our measurement windows indicated a negative catchment surface water balance. This is similar to results from previous studies on the same catchment, suggesting that trees were accessing water from water balance components that were not measured in this study, such as water deep in the soil profile or in areas adjacent to the catchment. The evapotranspiration by trees was found to be the largest contributor to the negative catchment surface water balance relative to other terms, suggesting that adequate planning is necessary in terms of water conservation and distribution before catchment can be afforested with commercial forestry species. It was concluded that at any stage of development, both A. mearnsii  and E. dunnii  have a potential to cause a reduction in the streamflow, which may affect downstream water users who are reliant on the flow of a stream for their livelihood. Despite the challenges in using isotopes, it would be beneficial to use isotope studies to understand the source of the water used by the trees in the Two Streams research catchment. 1 Introduction Groundwater is one of the most important freshwater resources when domestic and/or industrial needs are considered. Nowadays, the amount of available water in groundwater systems significantly decreases due to unconscious and unplanned use. In this context, it is necessary to develop sustainable management strategies to use groundwater resources efficiently. Mathematical simulation models are one of the most widely used tools in developing these management strategies. These models are based on the solution of partial differential equations which require knowing the spatial structure of some hydrogeological parameters of the aquifer system (e.g. hydraulic conductivity, transmissivity, storativity, dispersivity, etc.). In this context, the identification of these parameter structures by using a limited number of hydraulic head observations based on inverse modeling is challenging. The existing literature includes numerous studies to solve the inverse parameter structure identification problems for groundwater systems. In these studies, two common parameterization approaches are mostly used to characterize the hydrogeologic parameter field: interpolation and zonation (Yeh, 1986 ). In the interpolation approach, hydrogeological parameter values, usually determined by pumping tests, are converted into continuous fields using interpolation methods. Although these approaches are very effective for most problems in practice, it is possible to obtain uncertain parameter fields when point observations cannot fully represent the true parameter field (Tung and Chou, 2004; Yeh, 1986 ). On the other hand, in the zonation approach, the aquifer domain is partitioned into a finite number of zones in which the associated parameter values are assumed to be constant within them. Although this is a very useful and applicable approach for most groundwater modeling problems, it may be difficult to determine the numbers, shapes, and parameter values of the associated zone structures. Therefore, the identification of aquifer parameters and their corresponding parameter structures by using a systematic solution approach is a crucial task for groundwater modeling studies. Integrated simulation–optimization approaches are effective tools for solving inverse groundwater parameter structure identification problems. These approaches consist of the mutual integration of simulation and optimization models in such a way that while the simulation part aims to simulate the flow and/or transport processes, the optimization part aims to determine the parameter structure together with the associated parameter values. Note that groundwater-related inverse problems usually have nonlinear, nonconvex, and discrete solution spaces (Willis and Yeh, 1987 ). For such problems, identification of the optimum parameter structure is not easy by using the deterministic optimization approaches (Sun, 1994; Tsai, 2002; Yeh, 1986 ). Considering these difficulties, the use of heuristic optimization approaches has become widespread in recent years. Heuristic optimization approaches mimic processes in nature by using some stochastic components based on random variables. In literature, there exist many different heuristic optimization approaches which are developed by considering natural processes such as genetic algorithm (GA) (Holland, 1975 ), differential evolution (DE) (Storn and Price, 1997 ), particle swarm optimization (PSO) (Kennedy and Eberhart, 1995 ), ant colony optimization (ACO) (Dorigo et al., 2006 ), artificial bee colony (ABC) (Karaboga, 2005 ), and cuckoo search (CS) (Yang and Deb, 2009 ). Note that these heuristic approaches are all population-based and do not require special initial solutions to find global or near-global optimum solutions (Abualigah, 2020; Abualigah et al., 2021; Boussaïd et al., 2013; Mirjalili, 2015 ). This is the main advantage of the heuristic approaches compared to other deterministic optimization approaches for solving the parameter structure identification problems in groundwater systems. Ant Lion Optimization (ALO) is a population-based heuristic optimization algorithm mimicking the intelligent hunting behavior of antlions. In nature, the antlions dig a cone-shaped hole in the sand and hide under the base of the cone. When an ant walks inside the pit, the antlions throw sand particles toward the ants and try to catch them. This hunting strategy of antlions was first mathematically represented by Mirjalili (2015)  and employed to the solution of various problems including feature selection (Emary et al., 2016; Emary and Zawbaa, 2019; Wang et al., 2019a; Zawbaa et al., 2016 ), data clustering (Chen et al., 2020; Majhi and Biswal, 2018; Yogarajan and Revathi, 2018 ), machine learning (Banadkooki et al., 2020; Kose, 2018; Singh et al., 2020; Yamany et al., 2016 ), and some different engineering optimization problems (Ali et al., 2017, 2016; Chandrasekaran et al., 2021; Dubey et al., 2016; Mahendru and Mehta, 2015; Samui et al., 2022; Saxena and Kothari, 2016 ). The current literature also includes some improved versions of ALO to overcome the previously reported limitations such as the requirement of high number of iterations, possibility of trapping to local optimum solutions, and premature convergence problems (Guo et al., 2020; Kilic et al., 2020; Kılıç and Yüzgeç, 2019; Li et al., 2022, 2019; Singh and Singh, 2021; Tian et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019b; Wu et al., 2017; Yue and Zhang, 2021 ). Although there are wide variety of applications of ALO and its improved variants in different fields of science, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, there is no any application to solve the inverse parameter structure identification problems in groundwater systems. Therefore, this study aims to improve the standard ALO approach and to investigate the applicability of this improved version for solving the inverse parameter structure identification problems. It should be noted that the parameter zone structure identification problem for groundwater systems is an ill-posed inverse problem that may cause unstable results due to data errors, the presence of multiple solutions, and unavailability of the sufficient field data (Ayvaz, 2007; Tsai, 2002 ). Therefore, the solution of the parameter zone structure identification problem is much more difficult than the solution of the aquifer parameter estimation problems for the known parameter zone structures. The current literature includes some studies that solve the inverse parameter structure identification problems for groundwater systems (Ayvaz, 2007; Ayvaz et al., 2007; Ayvaz and Elci, 2012; Eppstein and Dougherty, 1996; Majdalani and Ackerer, 2011; Mayer and Huang, 1999; Sun, 1994; Sun et al., 1983; Sun and Yeh, 1985; Tsai et al., 2003b, 2003a; Tsai and Yeh, 2004; Tung et al., 2003; Tung and Chou, 2004; Tung and Tan, 2005; Yeh, 2015, 1986 ). Note that the main contribution of the conducted studies above deals with solving inverse parameter structure identification problems by integrating the Voronoi Tesselation (VT) based zonation approaches to the simulation–optimization models. Note that, in VT, the first task is to calculate the Euclidean distance values between a data point and the zone center locations (basis points). Then, the corresponding data point is assigned to a zone that has the minimum Euclidean distance among all the calculated distances. Note that Euclidean distance is a special case of the Minkowski distance metric (Shahid et al., 2009 ). In literature, different derivations of the Minkowski distance metric (e.g. Manhattan distance, Euclidean distance, Chebyshev distance, etc.) which are investigated in many pattern classification studies (Battula and Ambati, 2018; Elen and Avuçlu, 2021; Nayak et al., 2022; Shahid et al., 2009 ). However, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, no study investigates the applicability of different versions of the Minkowski distance metric for determining the hydrogeologic parameter structures of groundwater systems. Therefore, this study also aims to investigate the applicability of different distance metrics to solve the inverse parameter estimation problems. The main objective of this study is to propose a simulation–optimization approach for solving the inverse parameter structure identification problems for groundwater systems. Unlike the other studies in the literature, the hydraulic conductivity parameter structure of a heterogenous and isotropic aquifer system is generated by using the general form of the VT zonation approach. Note that this is the first application of the general form of the VT in partitioning the aquifer domain into a finite number of zones. The groundwater flow process is simulated by modeling this aquifer system on MODFLOW in the simulation part. This MODFLOW-based simulation model is then integrated into an optimization model where a recently proposed Shuffled Ant Lion Optimization approach with an exponentially weighted random walk strategy (SHALO) is used (Durgut et al., 2024 ). Note that this study is the first comprehensive engineering application of SHALO which includes important modifications for the regular ALO approach. The main objective of the SHALO approach is to determine the optimum zone structure as well as the uniform hydraulic conductivity values within each zone by considering the general form of the Minkowski distance during the search process. This process is conducted by following an implicit solution procedure in such a way that the global search process is first started with the lowest number of zones and the same process is repeated by sequentially increasing the number of zones. Determination of the best number of zones is conducted by considering three criteria. Furthermore, a detailed statistical analysis is carried out by multiple executing the SHALO approach for different random number seeds. The applicability of the proposed simulation–optimization approach is evaluated by solving a hypothetical aquifer model in the literature. Identified results indicated that the proposed simulation–optimization approach produces better identification results than those of ALO, saALO, HS, and hybrid GA optimization approaches.  2 Parameter structure identification in groundwater systems As indicated previously, the domain of the aquifer system is partitioned into a finite number of homogeneous hydraulic conductivity zones utilizing the general form of the VT-based zonation approach. For this purpose, first, the problem is solved for different zone numbers, and then, the optimum hydraulic conductivity zone structure is determined by evaluating identification results using the residual error R E    , parameter uncertainty P U    , and the structural discrimination S D    , respectively. In the following sections, after presenting the main structure of the VT approach, how to calculate the measures of RE   , PU   , and SD    is described. 2.1 Voronoi Tesselation (VT) VT, first introduced by the mathematicians Dirichlet (1850) and Voronoi (1908), is a well-known pattern classification approach and widely used in hydrological studies to convert the point precipitation time series into average precipitation data over a region (well known as Thiessen polygon approach). In this study, VT is considered as a zonation approach to partition the hydraulic conductivity field into a finite number of homogeneous hydraulic conductivity zones. The mathematical structure of the VT approach can be stated as follows: Let Ω   be the domain to be partitioned into zones; n z    be the number of Voronoi zones; x ^  j  , y ^  j      be the location of the j  t h     zone’s basis point (e.g. zone center) j = 1 , 2  , 3 , ⋯ , k , ⋯ , n z     ; V x ^  k  , y ^  k       be the k  t h     Voronoi zone having the basis point location at x ^  k  , y ^  k     ; n d    be the number of data points to be partitioned; and x i  , y i      be the location of the i  t h     data point in Ω  i = 1 , 2  , 3 , ⋯ , n d     . Depending on these definitions, the data point x i  , y i      is assigned to Voronoi zone V x ^  k  , y ^  k       when the following condition is satisfied:(1) x i  , y i    ∈ V x ^  k  , y ^  k     i f  d 2 i , k   < d 2 i , j    ∀ j ≠ k      (2) d 2  i , k   = x i  - x ^  k     2  + y i  - y ^  k     2     1 / 2       (3) d 2  i , j   = x i  - x ^  j     2  + y i  - y ^  j     2     1 / 2       where d 2  i , k     is the Euclidean distance between i  t h     data point and k  t h     zone’s basis point. The mathematical equations given above state that a Voronoi zone includes a data point when the Euclidean distance between the associated basis point and the data point is minimum compared to the other basis point locations. This statement is shown on a rectangular domain consisting of 8 × 7 = 56    grid points in Fig. 1  . As can be seen, there are three Voronoi zones where the black points correspond to the locations of the basis point for each zone. According to the formulation given above, each grid point in Fig. 1  is assigned to a zone if the calculated Euclidean distance between grid point and the corresponding basis point is minimum. For instance, point 9 in Fig. 1  is assigned to the first zone since the calculated Euclidean distance d 2  9 , 1       between x 9  , y 9      and x ^  1  , y ^  1      is minimum compared to the others. It should be noted that the classical VT approach given above partitions a domain into distinct zones based on the values of Euclidean distance between data and basis points. This is an important step in data partitioning and clustering algorithms since the similarity between data points is mostly associated with the distance among them. Note that Euclidean distance is a special form of the Minkowski distance which is the generalized version of the distance metric calculations. The general form of the Minkowski distance between a data and a basis point can be described mathematically as follows:(4) d p  i , j   = x i  - x ^  j     p  + y i  - y ^  j     p     1 p       where d p  i , j     is the Minkowski distance between i  t h     data point and j  t h     zone’s basis point; and p   is the Minkowski coefficient which is used to adjust the order of measure. Note that Minkowski distance provides metric results for p ≥ 1    (Rodrigues, 2018 ). When the value of p   is set to values of 1 and 2, the Minkowski distance corresponds to the Manhattan and the Euclidean distances, respectively. Similarly, when the value of p   reaches to positive infinity, the Minkowski distance corresponds to the Chebyshev distance (Rodrigues, 2018 ). As an example, for different p   values in 1 ≤ p ≤ 2   , the calculated Minkowski distances can be seen in Fig. 2  . As can be seen, different distance paths are obtained between the data and the basis point. Among them, the path with p = 1    (Manhattan) has a maximum, and the path with p = 2    (Euclidean) has a minimum distance between the points. For the intermediate values, the length of the distance reduces as the value of p   increases from 1 to 2. Note that aquifers are heterogeneous geological structures and partitioning their hydrogeological parameter values using the Euclidean distance-based VT approach may not always represent the true parameter heterogeneity. Therefore, investigation of the partitioned parameter zone structures by considering different p   values is essential. As an example, Fig. 3   shows a hypothetical domain that is partitioned into 6 zones by considering different p   values. As can be seen, although the general patterns are similar, there are some differences in the shapes of the identified zone structures. Therefore, the general form of the VT zonation approach is considered in this work for better capturing the hydraulic conductivity field.  2.2 Determination of optimum hydraulic conductivity zone structure One of the most complicated issues of parameter structure identification in groundwater systems is to determine the optimum number of zones to represent the true hydraulic conductivity field. This is an important process since the proposed simulation–optimization approach can only solve the problem for the pre-selected number of zones. In other words, the number of zones is also unknown and needs to be determined. In this context, the optimum number of zones is determined by considering the following implicit solution procedure:(5) Ω 1  → Ω 2  → Ω 3  → ⋯ Ω k  ⋯ → Ω n z       (6) n z  ∗   = f R E , P U , S D       where n z  ∗     is the optimum zone number. As can be seen from Equation (5) , the inverse parameter structure identification process starts with the lowest number of zones, and sequentially increases the zone number until reaching the pre-selected number of zones n z     . The optimum number of zones is determined based on three criteria in Equation (6)  which are the RE   , PU   , and SD   . Among them, the RE    represents the hydraulic response of the aquifer for the generated hydraulic conductivity zone structures as follows:(7) RE  k  = ∑ m = 1  n m   ∑ t = 1  n t   h m  Ω k  , t   - h ∼  m  t      2      where RE  k    is the RE    value for the parameter zone structure Ω k   ; n m    is the number of monitoring wells on the aquifer system; n t    is the number of monitoring time steps; h m  Ω k  , t      is the simulated hydraulic head values for the parameter zone structure Ω k    at m  t h     monitoring well and t  t h     time step; and h ∼  m  t      is the measured hydraulic head values at m  t h     monitoring well and t  t h     time step. It can be seen from Equation (7)  that RE    measure corresponds to the sum of squared error between the simulated and the measured hydraulic head values and directly represents the aquifer’s hydraulic response for the generated zone structure. Theoretically, the value of RE    should decrease when the problem is solved for an increased number of zones since the heterogeneity of the hydraulic conductivity is captured better. However, for such cases, it may be possible to observe high uncertainties in the identified parameters due to the increased number of decision variables. Note that a sudden increase of the uncertainty of the identified parameters results in a problem called over-parameterization which leads to obtaining unreliable results. For such situations, the parameter structure identification process should be stopped for the corresponding zone structure and the previous zone structure should be considered as the optimum solution (Ayvaz, 2007; Tsai et al., 2003a ). Therefore, it is required to consider PU    as an additional measure since only use of the RE    is not sufficient to determine the value of n z  ∗    . Tsai et al. (2003) proposed the modified form of the covariance matrix of the identified parameters to calculate PU    for n d    computation nodes of the aquifer domain as follows:(8) Cov  k  = G k  J  T  J    - 1   n m  n t  - k   ∑ m = 1  n m   ∑ t = 1  n t   h m  Ω k  , t   - h ∼  m  t      2    G k   T      where T   is the transpose operator; G k  ∈ R  n d  × k      is the structure matrix representing the weights from i  t h     data point to j  t h     zone’s basis point j = 1 , 2  , 3 , ⋯ , k , ⋯ , n z     ; J   is the Jacobian matrix of the hydraulic heads with respect to transmissivities. Note that the value of PU    can be calculated by taking the trace or the norm of Cov  k   . When a sudden increase is observed in the value of PU   , the parameter structure identification process should be stopped at that zone structure to obtain the reliable results in terms of parameter uncertainty (Ayvaz, 2007; Tsai et al., 2003a ). The last measure to determine the optimum hydraulic conductivity zone structure is the SD    which is used to assess the difference between two identified parameter structures in terms of the model outputs. For this purpose, Tsai et al. (2003a)  proposed the SD  k    measure between the identified parameter zone structures of Ω k    and Ω k - 1     as follows:(9) SD  k  = 1 n m  n t    ∑ m = 1  n m   ∑ t = 1  n t   h m  Ω k  , t   - h m  Ω k - 1   , t      2     1 2       Equation (9)  states that if the distinction between the output of two sequentially identified parameter structures is less than a pre-defined discrimination criterion, it is not essential to discriminate into another model structure (Tsai et al., 2003a ). Depending on this definition, when SD  k  < 2 η    where η   represents the head observation error, the solution of Ω k - 1     can be represented as the best parameter zone structure to prevent over-parameterization.   3 The integrated simulation – Optimization approach The proposed simulation–optimization approach consists of the mutual integration of the independent simulation and optimization models. In the following sections, after describing the main computational structures of the simulation and optimization models, how to integrate them into an optimization framework is described. 3.1 Simulation model The simulation model aims to simulate the groundwater flow process in a confined aquifer system by numerically solving the governing equation for the given initial and boundary conditions. The governing partial differential equation of the groundwater flow process in a confined, heterogeneous, and anisotropic aquifer system for transient flow conditions can be mathematically stated as follows (Harbough, 2005 ):(10) ∂ ∂ x   K xx   ∂ h  ∂ x     + ∂ ∂ y   K yy   ∂ h  ∂ y     + ∂ ∂ z   K zz   ∂ h  ∂ z     + W = S s  ∂ h  ∂ t       where x  , y  , and z   are the Cartesian coordinates; K xx   ,   K yy     and K zz     are the hydraulic conductivity values along the x  , y  , and z   directions, which are assumed to be parallel to the major directions of hydraulic conductivity; h   is the hydraulic head; W   is the volumetric flux per unit volume representing a sink/source term; S s    is the specific storage of the aquifer media; and t   is the time. Note that hydraulic conductivity values are assumed to be isotropic for all the analyses K xx   = K yy   = K zz   = K    . The current literature includes many analytical and numerical solution methods for solving Equation (10) . Note that analytical methods can only be used for idealized conditions such as homogeneous aquifer parameters, simple solution domains, steady-state flow conditions, etc. Therefore, numerical solution methods are usually implemented to solve this equation including finite differences, finite elements, boundary elements methods, etc. In this work, the MODFLOW, a modular three-dimensional finite-difference flow model, is used in the simulation model rather than direct solving Equation (10) . Furthermore, variation of aquifer parameters in vertical dimension is assumed to be constant, and therefore, the problem is solved by considering two-dimensional flow conditions.  3.2 Optimization model The optimization model aims to determine the zone structure together with the homogeneous hydraulic conductivity values within each zone. As indicated previously, the mathematical solution space of this problem is complex, and the use of deterministic-based optimization approaches cannot be eligible to solve the problem. In this context, the problem is solved by using the SHALO approach which is the improved form of ALO. In the following sections, a brief definition of ALO and its improved version of SHALO are provided. 3.2.1 The Ant Lion optimization approach (ALO) ALO is a population-based heuristic optimization approach that mimics the hunting strategy of antlions in nature. Antlions are insects belonging to the Neuroptera family (web-winged insects) that are carnivorous in both their larval and adult stages. In the larval stage, the antlions dig a cone-shaped sand pit and hide at the bottom of the pit to hunt the ants (Fig. 4  ). When the antlion realizes that its prey (e.g. an ant) is walking in the pit, it starts throwing sand particles at the ant, trying to slide the prey towards the bottom of the pit. After catching and eating its prey, the antlion repairs the sand pit to prepare for the next hunt. Based on this hunting strategy of antlions, the solution of an optimization problem using ALO can be mathematically formulated as follows: Let T   is the maximum number of iterations ( t = 1 , 2  , 3 , ⋯ , T )   ; x   t    and x  ∼   t    be the population matrices of ants and antlions, respectively; n   be the number of ants and antlions (candidate solutions) in the population; d   be the number of decision variables of the problem; x ij  t    and x ∼  ij  t    are the elements of x   t    and x  ∼   t    for i  t h     candidate solution, j  t h     decision variable, and t  t h     is the current iteration number i = 1 , 2 , 3 , ⋯ , n ;  j = 1 , 2 , 3 , ⋯ , d ;  t = 1 , 2 , 3 , ⋯ , T    , respectively. Using these definitions, the population matrices of ants and antlions at t  t h     iteration can be given as follows:(11) x   t  = x 11  t   x 12  t   ⋯  x 1 d  t    x 21  t    x 22  t   ⋯  x 2 d  t    ⋮   ⋮  ⋱  ⋮   x n 1  t    x n 2  t   ⋯  x nd  t            (12) x ∼  t  = x ∼  11 t   x ∼  12 t   ⋯  x ∼  1 d  t    x ∼  21 t   x ∼  22 t   ⋯  x ∼  2 d  t    ⋮  ⋮  ⋱  ⋮   x ∼  n 1  t   x ∼  n 2  t   ⋯  x ∼  nd t         The elements of x   t    and x  ∼   t    are calculated randomly between the lower and upper bounds of the decision variables at the beginning of optimization ( t = 0 )    as follows:(13) x ij t = 0   = x m i n , j  t = 0   +  r a n d 0 , 1   · x m a x , j  t = 0   - x m i n , j  t = 0        where x m i n , j  t = 0     and x m a x , j  t = 0     are the lower and upper bounds of the j  t h     decision variable at initial stage, and r a n d 0 , 1       is a uniform random number in the range of 0 , 1     . After generation of x   t = 0     and x  ∼   t = 0     randomly, the corresponding fitness values are calculated as follows:(14) F t  = f x 11 t     x 12 t   ⋯  x 1 d  t      f x 21 t     x 22 t   ⋯  x 2 d  t      ⋮  ⋮  ⋱  ⋮   f x n 1  t     x n 2  t   ⋯  x nd t           (15) F ∼  t  = f x ∼  11 t     x ∼  12 t   ⋯  x ∼  1 d  t      f x ∼  21 t     x ∼  22 t   ⋯  x ∼  2 d  t      ⋮  ⋮  ⋱  ⋮   f x ∼  n 1  t     x ∼  n 2  t   ⋯  x ∼  nd t           where F t    and F ∼  t    represent the fitness vector of ants and antlions at t  t h     iteration, respectively. After calculating the fitness vector of ants and antlions, a roulette wheel (RW) approach is employed to mimic the hunting behavior of antlions. This step is important as the selection of antlions is conducted based on their calculated fitness values. The fitter antlions have a higher chance of catching the ants for consumption with the application of the RW approach (Mirjalili, 2015 ). After the selection of the antlions based on the RW approach, the sliding behavior of ants towards the bottom of the pit is simulated based on a boundary shrinking procedure in which the lower and upper bounds of the variables are adaptively reduced as follows:(16) x m i n , j  t  = x m i n , j  t  I      (17) x m a x , j  t  = x m a x , j  t  I      (18) I = 10  ω  t T      As can be seen from Equations (16) and (17) , the search space of the ants is decreased by dividing the corresponding lower and upper bounds to parameter I   given in Equation (18) . It should be noted that the value of I   is dynamically calculated depending on the ratio of t / T    and ω  . The value of ω   is used for adjusting the accuracy of exploitation and calculated by dividing the iteration domain into several segments as follows:(19) ω = 1  i f  0 < t ≤ 0.10 T   2  i f  0.10 T < t ≤ 0.50 T   3  i f  0.50 T < t ≤ 0.75 T   4  i f  0.75 T < t ≤ 0.90 T   5  i f  0.90 T < t ≤ 0.95 T   6  i f  0.95 T < t ≤ T        To simulate the entrapment process of the ants inside the pit, the lower and upper bounds of ants are updated by using the position of the antlions as follows:(20) x j , m i n  t  = x ∼  i j , RW  t  + x j , min  t   if  r a n d 0 , 1   < 0.5   x ∼  i j , RW  t  - x j , min  t   otherwise        (21) x j , m a x  t  = x ∼  ij , R W  t  + x j , m a x  t   if  r a n d 0 , 1   ≥ 0.5   x ∼  ij , R W  t  - x j , m a x  t   otherwise        where x ∼  ij , R W  t    is the position of the selected i  t h     antlion at t  t h     iteration using the RW approach. Then, the random walk process of the ants to find a forage is modeled based on the following equation:(22) X j  = 0 , X j 1  , X j 2  , ⋯ , X j t  , ⋯ , X j T       (23) X j  t  = C 2 r t   - 1       (24) r t  = 1  if  r a n d 0 , 1   > 0.5   0  otherwise        where X j    is the random walk vector for j  t h     decision variable ( j = 1 , 2  , 3 , ⋯ , d )   ; X j  t    is the t  t h     element of the X j    vector; r t      is a stochastic step function; C °      is a function which calculates the cumulative sum of the given input. Note that the elements of the random walk vector are normalized to ensure satisfying the specified lower and upper bounds of the decision variables based on the following min–max equation:(25) X j t  = x j , m i n  t  + X j t  - a j    · x j , m a x  t  - x j , m i n  t     b j  - a j       where a j  = m i n X j     and b j  = m a x X j    . Keeping the elite solution while solving the optimization problem is an important step at every phase of the search process. Thus, the best solution should be stored to guarantee the improved convergence in every iteration. In ALO, new positions of the ants are calculated using the random walk around the selected antlion with the RW approach and the elite antlion obtained from Equation (25)  as follows:(26) x ij  t  = R a  j  t  + R e  j  t   2      where R a  j  t    and R e  j  t    are the random walk around the selected (RW approach) and the elite antlions for j  t h     decision variable at t  t h     iteration, respectively. When ants get trapped at the bottom of the pit, the antlion updates its position to prepare the trap for new prey. According to the provided source code of ALO (Mirjalili, 2015 ), this process is described based on the following steps (Durgut et al., 2024 ): i)  Determine fitness vector for the recently calculated ant positions; ii)  Append the fitness vector of ants to the bottom of the fitness vector of antlions (double fitness vector); iii)  Append the position matrix of ants to the bottom of the position matrix of antlions (double position matrix); iv)  Sort double fitness vector in ascending order and determine the corresponding sort index values; v)  Re-order the double position matrix based on the sort index values; vi)  Assign new positions and fitness values of antlions from the first half of the sorted double position matrix and double fitness vector, respectively. The computational scheme described above is iterated until reaching the maximum number of iterations in the original ALO.  3.2.2 The SHuffled Ant Lion Optimization approach (SHALO) As mentioned previously, the ALO approach is employed for the solution of various optimization problems due to its interesting philosophy and simple structure. However, there are some limitations in the random walk-around antlion process of ALO. For this reason, the large part of the improved ALO approaches in literature focus on improving the solution accuracy by changing this process (Chaitanya et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022; Dinkar and Deep, 2017; El Bakrawy et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2020; Kilic et al., 2020; Kılıç and Yüzgeç, 2019; Liu et al., 2020; Rajan et al., 2017; Singh and Singh, 2021; Toz, 2019; Wu et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2019; Yao and Wang, 2017; Yao et al., 2021 ). The Shuffled Ant Lion Optimization Approach (SHALO) is one of the recently modified versions for improving the accuracy of ALO (Durgut et al., 2024 ). Like other modified versions of ALO, SHALO also focuses on modifying the random walk around antlions process with two improvements. The first modification is related to improving the boundary-shrinking procedure, which is important since the original procedure depends on a step-by-step decreasing procedure to shrink the boundary. This procedure is controlled by the parameter ω   in Equation (19)  in such a way that at some stationary iteration points the value of ω   is suddenly increases, and this change suddenly increases the value of I   according to Equation (18) . Although this procedure is useful for conducting the boundary reduction around solutions, it may reduce the random search capability due to the sudden increase of the value of I   at stationary points (Toz, 2019 ). For this purpose, a new exponentially weighted boundary-shrinking procedure is proposed in SHALO as follows:(27) I = 1  i f  k = 0   I ∼   i f  k = 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5        (28) I ∼  = I k m i n   + I  k m a x    - I k m a x   · e L k  · t - t k m i n        + λ · r a n d 0 , 1   · L k   · t - t k m i n          (29) L k  = l n I k  m i n   I k  m a x       t k  m a x   - t k  m i n         where I ∼    is the value of the proposed exponentially weighted function; I k  m i n     and I k  m a x     are the minimum and maximum I   values for k  th  region in Fig. 5  ; t k  m i n     and t k  m a x     are the minimum and maximum t   values for k  th  region in Fig. 5 ; L k    is a function whose value is calculated logarithmically based on Equation (29)  for k  th  region in Fig. 5 ; ∘    is the absolute value; and λ   is the parameter controlling the magnitude of the random deviations from the value of I ∼   . The detailed representation of the parameters used in Equations (28) and (29)  can be seen in Fig. 5 . In Fig. 5 , the iteration domain is partitioned into 6 regions k = 0 , 1  , 2 , ⋯ , 5    . In the original ALO approach, the value of I   suddenly increases at the starting points of the 1st to 5th regions while its value linearly increases inside of each region depending on the ratio of t / T    . Fig. 5  shows the variation of I   for each region in the original ALO method (black line). Note that the minimum and maximum values of I   for each region are taken as I k  m i n     and I k  m a x     in SHALO. Similarly, for each region, the minimum and maximum values of t   are considered as t k  m i n     and t k  m a x     in Equations (28) and (29) . Fig. 5  also includes the variation of the proposed exponentially weighted function of I ∼   . As can be seen, for λ = 0    (red line), the proposed exponentially weighted function does not have any stationary points where the value of I  suddenly increases. Instead, the function value exponentially increases between the same minimum and maximum values for each region. This modification increases the random search capability of the SHALO approach rather than the original ALO approach. The random search capability of the proposed exponential function can also be increased by perturbing the calculated I ∼    values with random deviations. This perturbation is also given in Fig. 5  for λ = 1    (blue line). As can be seen, although the trend of the calculated I ∼    values are the same, their values have strong local oscillations depending on the considered value of λ  . Therefore, the proper selection of the value of λ   is important since its value is used to adjust the magnitude of random deviations. The second improvement of the SHALO is related to the modification of the min–max normalization process given in Equation (25)  in the original ALO. As mentioned before, the generated random walk vector cannot be used directly to update the position of ants. Therefore, values in the vector are normalized by considering the minimum and maximum values of the random walk vector. In SHALO, the min–max normalization equation given in Equation (25)  is modified as follows:(30) X j t  = x j , m i n  t  + X j t  - a ∼  j    · x j , m a x  t  - x j , m i n  t     b ∼  j  - a ∼  j       (31) a ∼  j  = m e a n X j   - m i n X j      (32) b ∼  j  = m a x X j   - m e a n X j      where m e a n X j     is the arithmetic mean of the random walk vector for j  th  variable. As can be seen from Equation (30) , the values of a j    and b j    in Equation (25)  are replaced with a ∼  j    and b ∼  j    by including the mean of the random walk vector as an additional variable. Durgut et al. (2024)  states that this inclusion significantly increases the diversity of the random walk vector especially in early iterations since it scales and shuffles the content of the random walk vector. Note that the shuffling process occurs by considering two cases in Fig. 6  . Fig. 6  states that the cases where m e a n X j     values are lower and greater than m e d i a n X j     are called Case 1 and 2, respectively. Although the generation of Cases 1 and 2 is not important in the original ALO, it is important in SHALO to understand the nature of the shuffling process. To clarify this issue, the random walks calculated at 10th, 100th, and 800th iterations for both ALO and SHALO approaches are compared in Fig. 7  (a) to (c) in terms of trends and statistics. The comparison is conducted by using the same random number seed values for both ALO and SHALO to eliminate the influence of random numbers. As can be seen from Fig. 7 (a), the calculated random walks have the same trends although the corresponding values in SHALO are much greater than the ones in ALO. These random walks can be classified as Case 2 for both ALO and SHALO approaches since the calculated mean random walks are greater than the median values. Therefore, the influence of Equation (30)  is just observed as the scaling of the random walks compared to the original ALO. On the other hand, in Fig. 7 (b), the calculated random walks for SHALO also have greater values than those obtained in ALO. However, the values calculated in SHALO are symmetrically upside down with respect to ALO. This change is associated with the conditions in Fig. 6 ; such that ALO is classified as Case 2, while SHALO is classified as Case 1. Note that this change is not only observed as the scaling but also observed as the shuffling of the content of the random walk vector. Finally, in Fig. 7 (c), the same outcome is observed such that the random walks in SHALO are obtained as symmetrically upside down compared to ALO due to the differences of the cases in Fig. 6 . Note that the comparison of Fig. 7 (a) to (c) also indicates the decreased values of the random walks in SHALO. This modification improved the diversity especially in early iterations, by scaling and shuffling the random walks.  3.2.3 Comparison with the other improved ALO approaches In literature, there exist various modified versions of ALO which are developed to improve the solution accuracy. In a large part of these modified versions, the main aim is to improve the random walks around antlion process of the original ALO. Note that SHALO also focuses on improving the same process. Therefore, its solution performance has been compared with the standard ALO for the same initial populations, optimization parameter values, and random number seeds. Similarly, all the identified results have been compared by solving the same problem with the self-adaptive ALO (saALO) (Liu et al., 2020 ) approach for the same conditions. Note that the saALO approach also improves the boundary-shrinking procedure of the ALO by replacing the term of I   in Equation (18)  as follows:(33) s a A L O :  I = 10 ω  t T  0.5 + s i n π · t  2 T    · r a n d 0 , 1        It can be seen in Equation (33)  that the saALO approach has a similar mathematical expression to Equation (18)  where the value of I   changes linearly and dynamically depending on the ratio of t / T    and the parameter of ω  . Unlike Equation (18) , the saALO approach includes additional exponentially changed terms together with the random perturbations.   3.3 Problem formulation The problem of hydraulic conductivity parameter zone structure identification in groundwater systems can be mathematically formulated as an optimization problem. In this problem, initially, the hydraulic conductivity zone structure is randomly generated, and then, random hydraulic conductivity values are assigned to each zone. After this process, the SHALO approach determines the shape of the zone structure as well as the associated hydraulic conductivity values by minimizing the discrepancy between simulated and measured hydraulic head values at selected monitoring locations and times. Mathematically, this problem can be stated as follows:(34) min RE  k  = ∑ m = 1  n m   ∑ t = 1  n t   h m  Ω k  , t   - h ∼  m  t      2      subject to(35) ∂ ∂ x   K ^  ∂ h  ∂ x     + ∂ ∂ y   K ^  ∂ h  ∂ y     + ∂ ∂ z   K ^  ∂ h  ∂ z     + W = S s  ∂ h  ∂ t       (36) K ^  ∈ K ^  1  , K ^  2  , K ^  3  , ⋯ , K ^  k  , ⋯ , K ^  n z     ;  j = 1 , 2 , 3 , ⋯ , k , ⋯ , n z     (37) K ^  = K k   i f  d p i , k   < d p i , j    ∀ j ≠ k   ;  i = 1 , 2 , 3 , ⋯ , n d     (38) h m  Ω k  , t   ∈ h x , y , z , t       (39) Ω 1  → Ω 2  → Ω 3  → ⋯ Ω n z  ∗    ⋯ → Ω n z       (40) Ω n z  ∗    = f R E , P U , S D       where K ^    is the hydraulic conductivity values to be determined; h x , y , z , t      is the hydraulic head value at any location x , y , z     and simulation time t     on the aquifer system which is obtained from the MODFLOW solution of Equation (35) , and Ω n z  ∗      is the solution of the parameter structure identification problem with the best number of zones. As can be seen from the formulation given above, the problem is solved based on the implicit solution procedure given in Equation (5)  and the optimum number of zones is determined by evaluating the RE , P U   , and SD    measures. The decision variables of the optimization model are the locations of the basis points x ^  j  , y ^  j      for each zone; homogeneous hydraulic conductivity values K ^  j      for each zone j = 1 , 2  , 3 , ⋯ , n z     ; and the value of the Minkowski coefficient p    . In this context, the number of decision variables of the SHALO approach is 3 n  z  + 1   . The flowchart of the proposed simulation–optimization approach is given in Fig. 8  .
