As can be seen, the groundwater module (e.g. MODFLOW based simulation model) is executed for each generated hydraulic conductivity zone structure, and the result of RE    is passed through the SHALO approach. It should be noted that this flowchart is valid for a given number of zones n z     . Therefore, depending on Equation (39) , the proposed simulation–optimization approach should be executed for different zone numbers. After obtaining results for each successive solution, the best number of zones should be determined based on Equation (40) .   4 Numerical application The applicability of the proposed simulation–optimization approach is evaluated by using a hypothetical aquifer model given in the literature (Ayvaz, 2007; Tsai, 2002; Tsai et al., 2003a ). Fig. 9   shows the geometry, boundary conditions, and locations of the pumping and monitoring wells of the confined aquifer model under consideration. As can be seen from Fig. 9 , the boundary conditions of the aquifer are 100 m specified head in CD, and no-flow in the other sides. There are 5 pumping wells having pumping rates of 4000 m3 /day for W 1    to W 4    and 2000 m3 /day for W 5   . The total simulation time is 10 days, and it is assumed that all the pumping wells are continuously operated through this period. There are 7 monitoring wells where hydraulic head values are continuously recorded at the end of each day. Since transient flow conditions are considered, the specific storage coefficient is assumed to be 5 × 10  - 6     . The thickness of the aquifer system is assumed to be 40 m everywhere. The true hydraulic conductivity field of this aquifer system is given in Fig. 10   where the minimum and maximum hydraulic conductivity values are 0.66 and 14.92 m/day, respectively. The objective of the proposed approach is to determine the best parameter zone structure to capture this hydraulic conductivity field by using a total of 70 hydraulic head observations (7 monitoring wells and 10 days). Note that all the head observations are perturbed with a Gaussian noise with zero mean and 1 standard deviation to simulate the measurement errors in the field. As indicated previously, the groundwater flow process of this aquifer system is simulated by using the MODFLOW model. For this purpose, the domain of the aquifer system is discretized into 100 m ×   100 m finite difference grid blocks. MODFLOW model requires the definition of all the point and areal sources/sinks before executing the model. Since the hypothetical aquifer model just includes pumping wells, the well package of MODFLOW is activated. The generated finite difference equation set has been solved utilizing the pre-conditioned conjugate gradient (PCG2) approach in MODFLOW by considering a convergence criterion of 0.01. Note that this MODFLOW-based simulation model also includes the general form of the VT zonation approach to generate hydraulic conductivity zone structure. In this context, the generated structure as well as the associated hydraulic conductivity parameter values are included in the layer property flow (LPF) package of the MODFLOW by the simulation model. Then, this simulation model is integrated into the SHALO approach to solve the inverse parameter structure identification problem. It should be noted that the SHALO approach includes a new exponential function (Equation (28) ) for improving the boundary-shrinking procedure of the original ALO. In this function, the random search capability is increased by generating random perturbations (Fig. 5 ) where their magnitudes are controlled using the parameter of λ  . Since the selection of this parameter is important for solution accuracy, the problem is solved for 6 different λ   values λ ∈ 0 , 1 , 5 , 10 , 50 , 100       to evaluate the model performance for different magnitudes of random perturbations. Additionally, for each λ   value, the proposed approach is executed 10 times considering different random number seeds to eliminate the influence of random numbers. After determining the best λ   value, the identified results of that solution have been also compared by solving the problem using ALO and saALO approaches for the same conditions. Note that Ayvaz (2007)  and Tsai et al. (2003a)  also solved the same problem using the HS and hybrid GA-based optimization approaches, respectively. Therefore, the identified solutions have also been compared with the results of them. Note that the global search process is conducted by considering the number of antlions as n = 50    and the maximum number of iterations as T = 200    which corresponds to 10,000 objective function evaluations. The optimum hydraulic conductivity parameter zone structure has been sought by considering the parameter bounds of 0.50 ≤ K ≤ 15    m/day to obtain comparable results with Ayvaz (2007)  and Tsai et al. (2003a) . For each generated zone, the lower and upper bounds of basis point locations are taken as 1 ≤ x ^  j  , y ^  j  ≤ 32   j = 1 , 2  , 3 , ⋯ , n z      where the values of 1 and 32 correspond to the minimum and maximum column/row index values of the finite different grid blocks, respectively. Similarly, the optimum Minkowski coefficient value has been sought in the range of 1 ≤ p ≤ 2    where the values of 1 and 2 correspond to the Manhattan and Euclidian distances, respectively. Using these definitions, the proposed simulation optimization approach is executed 10 times for each different λ   value. Fig. 11   compares the mean convergence plots of 10 model executions for different parameter structures from Ω 1    to Ω 5   . As can be seen from Fig. 11 , as the number of zones increases from 1 to 5, the mean values of RE    decrease for each different λ   value. This is an expected behavior since the heterogeneity of the hydraulic conductivity parameter field can be captured better with the inclusion of additional zones. Note that, the value of RE    approaches zero, theoretically, as the value of n z    goes to infinity. However, this outcome may not be observed due to the increased value of PU    depending on the dimensions of the mathematical solution space (Tsai et al., 2003a ). After execution of SHALO for different λ   values and parameter zone structures, the best λ   value is determined by statistically evaluating the results of 10 different model executions. Fig. 12   shows Box-Whisker plots prepared for this evaluation. As can be seen from Fig. 12 , for the solution of Ω 1   , 10 different solutions resulted approximately with the same RE    for each different λ   value. This is an expected behavior since the parameter field of the aquifer system is represented by a single hydraulic conductivity zone. Note that for this solution, the optimization model just considers the homogeneous hydraulic conductivity value in a single zone as the decision variable since it is not required to use the other variables. By including an additional zone, the calculated RE    values of 10 different solutions are all decreased in Ω 2    as expected. Comparison of different solutions of Ω 2    indicates that while approximately the same model outcomes are obtained for the λ   values of 0, 1, 5, and 100, some slight differences are obtained for the solutions of λ = 10    and λ = 50   . In the solution of Ω 3   , the heterogeneity of the hydraulic conductivity field can be captured better with the inclusion of an additional zone in such a way that the calculated RE    values of 10 different solutions are significantly improved compared to the solution of Ω 2   . For this parameter structure, the solutions of λ = 5    and λ = 10    have a good performance in terms of the calculated RE    values. The same solution trend is also observed in the solutions of Ω 4    and Ω 5    such that inclusion of an additional zone improves solution accuracy compared to the previous zone structure. However, these improvements are not significant compared to Ω 2    or Ω 3   . When the outcomes of these solutions have been evaluated in detail, the solution with λ = 5    can be assumed as the best solution in terms of the minimum, maximum, mean, and median RE    values, respectively. Therefore, the final evaluation of the proposed simulation–optimization approach is conducted by considering the best solutions of λ = 5    for each parameter zone structure. The performance of the proposed simulation–optimization approach is also evaluated by solving the same problem using the standard ALO and its improved version saALO for the same conditions (10 different solutions by using the same random number seeds). Regarding these solutions, the obtained mean convergence plots are also given in Fig. 11  (dashed lines). It can be seen, although the same convergence trends are observed in Ω 1    and Ω 2   , the identified solutions of SHALO are all better than those obtained in ALO and saALO approaches according to the final RE    values for the solutions of Ω 3  - Ω 5    . The Box-Whisker plots given in Fig. 12  also includes the details of the conducted 10 different solutions of the ALO and saALO, respectively. As can be seen, although the same trends with SHALO are obtained for Ω 1    and Ω 2   , there are significant deviations in the solutions of Ω 3  - Ω 5     in terms of the calculated statistics for both ALO and saALO. For the best solutions of SHALO λ = 5    , ALO, and saALO, the calculated RE    values are compared in Table 1  . As can be seen from Table 1 , for Ω 1   , the SHALO, ALO, and saALO approaches resulted in the same RE    values of 273.79 since the hydraulic conductivity field of the aquifer system is represented by a single zone. For the other parameter zone structures Ω 2  - Ω 5     , the proposed approach resulted in better RE    values compared to ALO and saALO. It is seen that the calculated RE    values are significantly improved when the number of zones is increased from 1 to 2 and from 2 to 3. However, this improvement is not significant after the structure of Ω 3   . Table 1  also includes the results of Ayvaz (2007)  and Tsai et al. (2003a)  in terms of the final RE    values. Note that, in Ayvaz (2007)  and Tsai et al. (2003a)  the same problem was solved by using HS and hybrid GA-based optimization approaches, respectively. As can be seen, a similar trend is also observed in HS and hybrid GA solutions. Comparison of the overall RE    values in Table 1  indicates that the proposed simulation–optimization approach resulted in the best identification results compared to the other approaches. For these solutions, the identified parameter structures (with basis point locations) and hydraulic conductivity values are compared in Fig. 13  . As can be seen from Fig. 13 , very similar zone structures are obtained in SHALO, ALO, and saALO for the structure of Ω 2   . Although the identified hydraulic conductivity values in ALO and saALO are around the same, there are slight changes in their values in SHALO. When the identified zone structures are compared with those of HS and hybrid GA, it be seen that there is a difference at the intersection of both zones in Ω 2   . This difference is associated with the considered distance metric calculations. For Ω 3   , the identified zone structures of SHALO, ALO, and saALO are similar to the ones of HS and hybrid GA approaches. For the solution of Ω 4   , although the identified parameter structure of SHALO is very similar to one in HS, the shapes of the identified zone structures are different in ALO and saALO. This result can also be seen from the calculated RE    values in Table 1  in such a way that the calculated RE    of those solutions worse than the other approaches. For Ω 5   , the identified zone structure of SHALO well agrees with the one in the hybrid GA approach. For the same solution, the saALO approach determined a solution very similar to the one in HS. The overall assessment of the identified zone structures indicates that the proposed simulation–optimization approach well captures the true hydraulic conductivity field given in Fig. 10 . For SHALO, ALO, and saALO approaches, a comparison of the calculated relative error values between the true and the identified hydraulic conductivity parameter structures is given in Fig. 14  . As can be seen from Fig. 14 , for Ω 2   , the proposed parameter structure identification process mostly underestimates the true hydraulic conductivity values around the northwest part of the aquifer domain. Similarly, the identified values are overestimated around the northeast parts of the aquifer domain. This is an expected outcome since the true hydraulic conductivity field has decreased values when moving from the northwest to the northeast of the aquifer domain (Fig. 10 ). Since these regions are represented by a single zone in Ω 2   , such a result is an expected behavior. Note that the results of ALO and saALO have also the same trend for Ω 2   . In lower parts of the aquifer, it is obtained high relative error values, especially in the zone intersections around the western part of the aquifer system. These error values are greater in ALO and saALO than SHALO. With the inclusion of the additional zones, the calculated relative error values inside the zone structures are decreased in SHALO. However, the identified conductivities still have some error values around the intersections of high and low hydraulic conductivity zones, especially around the western parts of the domain. This is an expected behavior since true values in the hydraulic conductivity field significantly change when moving from northwest to southwest of the aquifer. When the identified zone structures are evaluated with each other, it is seen that the proposed SHALO approach results with lower error values than ALO and saALO approaches for each different zone structure. It should be noted that the SHALO, ALO, and saALO approaches considered the general form of the Minkowski distance as the distance metric calculations between data and basis points whereas HS and hybrid GA approaches considered the Euclidean distance. As indicated previously, the value of the Minkowski coefficient p     is also used as a decision variable together with the other variables (e.g. locations of the basis points and hydraulic conductivity values inside each zone). In this context, Table 2   compares the identified p   values for different approaches. It can be seen from Table 2 , the value of p   was taken as 2 for both HS and hybrid GA approaches since the similarity between data and basis points are determined utilizing the Euclidean distance. On the other hand, for different parameter structures in SHALO, the value p   is determined in the range of (1.127, 1.668). Similarly, ALO and saALO approaches determined the p   values in the ranges of (1.106, 1.506) and (1.049, 1.835), respectively. Depending on the results in Tables 1 and 2 , it may be concluded that the heterogeneity of the hydraulic conductivity field can be captured by using different distance metrics when p   is considered as an additional variable. As indicated previously, the best parameter zone structures to represent the true hydraulic conductivity field are determined by simultaneously evaluating the model results using RE   , PU   , and SD    measures (Equation (39) ). Among them, the value of PU    is calculated by taking the trace of the covariance matrix of the estimated parameters given in Equation (8) . Table 3   compares the calculated PU    values for the best solutions given in Table 1 . As can be seen from Table 3 , the PU    values of SHALO are obtained around the same order of magnitude. On the other hand, it is observed in ALO and saALO that there is a sudden increase in the calculated PU    values when the number of zones is increased from 4 to 5. This outcome is also observed in the results of HS and hybrid GA approaches, respectively. Note that Tsai et al. (2003a)  states that a sudden increase in the calculated PU    values corresponds to the problem of over-parameterization since the reliability of the identified parameters usually decreases. For such cases, the parameter structure identification process should be stopped, and the previous zone structure should be selected as the best structure. Depending on this definition, the solutions of Ω 4    can be the best structure for ALO and saALO. Similarly, Tsai et al. (2003a)  and Ayvaz (2007)  selected Ω 4    as the best parameter structure. Since there is not any sudden increase of the calculated PU    values, the parameter structures of Ω 4    or Ω 5    can be selected as the best parameter structure for SHALO by also considering the RE    values in Table 1 . The final evaluation of the identified results is conducted in terms of the calculated SD    values for different parameter zone structures. This is also an important analysis as it allows the determination of the hydraulic response of the aquifer system for the sequentially identified parameter structures. Depending on this definition, the calculated SD    values for different approaches are compared in Table 4  . As can be seen from the results in Table 4 , the calculated SD    values decrease as the number of zones increases for each approach. As indicated previously, if the distinction between the hydraulic responses of the aquifer system for two sequentially identified parameter structures is less than a pre-defined criterion, it is not essential to discriminate the domain into another parameter structure. Depending on this definition, for SHALO, the structures of Ω 3    or Ω 4    can be selected as the best zone structures since the distinctions between Ω 3  - Ω 4    0.131 < 2 η     and Ω 4  - Ω 5    0.080 < 2 η     satisfy the discrimination criterion η = 0.100    . These structures also satisfy the PU    condition since there is not any suddenly increased PU    values in Table 3 . For ALO, the structure of Ω 4    can be selected as the best zone structure since the discrimination criterion between Ω 4  - Ω 5    0.177 < 2 η     and the condition of PU    are satisfied with that structure. For saALO, the structures of Ω 3    or Ω 4    can be selected as the best structures in terms of the discrimination criterion between Ω 3  - Ω 4    0.181 < 2 η     and Ω 4  - Ω 5    0.099 < 2 η     and the condition of PU    are satisfied to prevent over-parameterization.  5 Discussion As can be seen from the results presented above, the proposed simulation–optimization approach can be used for solving inverse parameter structure identification problems in groundwater systems. In the following parts, the main critical points of the proposed simulation–optimization approach are discussed: Unlike the other studies in the literature, the proposed simulation–optimization approach uses the general form of the Minkowski distance for the calculation of the distance between data and basis points. In this context, all the possible zonation alternatives are investigated by adjusting the value of the Minkowski coefficient. This objective is achieved by considering the basis point locations and homogeneous hydraulic conductivity values of the zones together with the Minkowski coefficient as the decision variables of the SHALO approach. Note that this study is the first application of the SHALO by considering the general form of the Minkowski distance in the zonation approach for generating the hydraulic conductivity parameter zone structures. By doing this, the heterogeneity of the hydraulic conductivity field can be captured better using the proposed approach. The proposed SHALO approach is a modified version of the ALO by considering two improvements. The first improvement deals with eliminating stationary points in the boundary-shrinking process using an exponential function. The second improvement aims to shuffle the content of the random walk vector to increase the random search capability of the ALO approach (during this process, the SHALO approach may produce NaN decision variable values especially in early iterations and this problem can be fixed re-generating those variables randomly in the feasible search space). These two improvements and consideration of the variable Minkowski coefficient significantly improved the solution accuracy in such a way that the proposed SHALO-based approach resulted in better objective function values than those of HS and hybrid GA-based solution approaches. Furthermore , these better results have been obtained in fewer iterations in such a way that the maximum number of function evaluations in SHALO is set to 10,000 whereas the same quantity was used in HS and hybrid GA as 50,000. These results indicate the possibility of obtaining more accurate results in fewer iterations by the integration of SHALO and general VT approaches. The numerical groundwater flow process of the aquifer model in this work is simulated by the MODFLOW model. Note that, in previous works, the same problem was solved by discretizing the domain into 64 × 64 finite difference grid blocks. Since the performance of the SHALO is evaluated statistically by solving the problem many times for different random perturbations and seed values, the problem is solved in this work by considering 32 × 32 finite difference grid blocks to keep the simulation time of MODFLOW minimum. Note that all hydraulic head observations in this work are generated by executing the MODFLOW for the true hydraulic conductivity field given in Fig. 10 . After this process, all the head observations are perturbed with a Gaussian noise. Since this noise data is different from the ones in the literature, it is obtained some slight differences among the final objective function values especially for the solution of Ω 1   .  The standard ALO approach has only one solution parameter (number of populations) for solving an optimization problem. This is an important advantage compared to the other heuristic optimization approaches with more solution parameters. Note that the SHALO approach has an additional parameter of λ   which is used to adjust the contribution of random perturbations during the boundary-shrinking process. Since these random perturbations may influence the convergence behavior, the performance of the proposed approach has been evaluated for different λ   values. According to the identified results, the solution with λ = 5    provided better identification results than the other alternatives. However, this value can change depending on the problem. Therefore, it is recommended to analyze the performance of the proposed approach for different values of λ  . After determining the best λ   value of SHALO, the performance of the proposed approach is also evaluated by solving the same problem via ALO and saALO approaches for the same conditions. Furthermore, all the results are compared with the ones obtained using HS and hybrid GS-based solution approaches. All the approaches are executed from 1 to 5 zones and the best identified results are compared. This comparison indicates that the proposed SHALO-based approach provided better identification results in terms of the calculated RE    values. Similarly, the SHALO-based approach resulted in similar PU    values for each zone structure although there are sudden increases in the other approaches. This outcome indicated that the identified parameters and zone structures of SHALO have less uncertainty, especially for the zone structures of Ω 4    and Ω 5   . To evaluate the performance of the parameter structure identification process, all the identified zone structures have been compared with the true hydraulic conductivity field. For this purpose, the relative error values are calculated between the true and the calculated hydraulic conductivity values. Evaluation of these values indicates that the calculated relative errors decrease as the number of zones increases, as expected. However, there may still be observed error values around the intersections of high and low hydraulic conductivity zones. These error values around zone intersection locations may be decreased with inclusion of additional observation points around these locations. Numerical simulation of the hypothetical aquifer system is conducted by considering no uncertainty sources in the aquifer parameters, boundary conditions, etc. However, in real-world problems, the uncertainties in the related parameters should be considered during execution of the proposed approach. One of the most important limitations when solving a real-world problem is the lack of head observation data which is required for truly representing the hydraulic behavior of the aquifer system. If this data is limited, it may be possible to obtain uncertain parameter structures. A similar situation may also be observed for point source/sink terms (e.g. pumping or recharging wells). If the main characteristics (numbers, locations, pumping rates, duration of activities, etc) of these source/sink terms are missing, the identified parameter zone structures may again have uncertainties. Therefore, it is suggested to consider these limitations when solving a real-world problem using the proposed approach. As indicated previously, the groundwater flow process is simulated by using MODFLOW, a finite difference-based groundwater simulation model. Since the proposed simulation–optimization approach has a general structure, it is also possible to use different numerical modeling approaches for simulating the groundwater flow process by considering different conditions. A similar situation is also possible for the optimization model in such a way that it is possible to use a different heuristic optimization method in the proposed approach rather than SHALO. In this context, the proposed approach does not depend on the problem type and can be applicable to solve different parameter structure identification problems if the spatial distribution of the associated parameters can be represented by the zonation approach.  6 Conclusions In this study, a new simulation–optimization approach is proposed for solving the inverse groundwater parameter structure identification problems. In the proposed approach, the parameter field of the aquifer system is partitioned into a finite number of homogeneous zones utilizing the general form of the VT-based zonation approach. By using this approach, the groundwater flow process in the aquifer system is simulated using the MODFLOW in the simulation part. This MODFLOW and VT-based simulation model is then integrated into an optimization model where the recently proposed SHALO approach is used. The main objective of the SHALO-based optimization model is to determine the hydraulic conductivity zone structures by minimizing the discrepancies between the simulated and the measured hydraulic head values at monitoring well locations. The applicability of the proposed simulation–optimization approach is evaluated by solving a hypothetical aquifer model in literature for different conditions. The performance of the SHALO approach is compared with the standard ALO and its modified version of saALO approaches for the same conditions. Furthermore, all the identified results are compared with the ones obtained using HS and hybrid GA-based solution approaches in literature. Identified results indicated that the proposed simulation–optimization approach is an effective and general solution approach in the solution of inverse parameter structure identification problems in groundwater systems.
1 Introduction Accurate spatial estimation is fundamental to sustainable management of subsurface resources in hydrogeology. Complexity escalates within the confines of three-dimensional (3D) spaces owing to the inherent heterogeneity and nonstationary nature of geological media. Traditional geostatistical methods often fail to adequately capture these complex characteristics, leading to models that do not accurately represent subsurface variability and compromising the prediction of essential properties. These challenges were addressed from a geological perspective by introducing manifold embedding within a two-dimensional (2D) framework (Piao and Park, 2023; Park et al., 2024 ). However, to address the need for accurate modeling of spatial relationships in higher dimensions, we have developed a novel geostatistical approach based on manifold embedding in a four-dimensional (4D) space. This approach overcomes the limitations of existing methods by improving the accuracy of spatial estimates and offering new insights into the understanding and management of complex subsurface environments. Conventional geostatistical methods often struggle to capture the complex and nonstationary spatial correlations inherent in geological media. These methods typically assume stationarity, which can lead to an oversimplification of the intricate spatial variability present in subsurface environments. To address this limitation, we introduce a manifold embedding approach that allows for a more accurate and detailed representation of subsurface heterogeneity by incorporating an additional dimension to account for variable spatial properties. The progression to a 3D framework marks a substantial advancement from prior methodologies. Traditional geostatistical methods, which are typically not process-based (Koltermann & Gorelick, 1996 ), strive to effectively represent subsurface property distributions. The adoption of any method that can enrich this representation is deemed beneficial (e.g., Matheron, 1963; Carle & Fogg, 1996 ; Strebelle, 2002; Park, 2010; Laloy et al., 2018 ). The extension of manifold embedding to 3D space facilitates a more comprehensive depiction of the subsurface, addressing the limitations observed with 2D constraints. This advancement is pivotal for accurate modeling of hydrogeological phenomena and enhances the existing geostatistical framework by realistically accommodating the complexities of subsurface environments (Høyer et al., 2017; Zhao & Illman, 2017 ). Despite advances in geostatistical methods, traditional two-point geostatistical approaches often struggle to accurately capture the complex spatial behavior of geological properties, especially in large spatial domains characterized by pronounced directional changes and heterogeneities (Curriero, 2006; Piao & Park, 2023 ). These conventional methods, such as kriging, rely on Euclidean distances and semi-variogram models that assume stationarity and symmetry in spatial data. This assumption limits their ability to accurately model nonstationary or asymmetric spatial structures, which are common in complex geological settings. Although anisotropy plays an important role in representing geological processes, such as flow directions in aquifer environments, existing techniques have typically been constrained to the stationary cases, neglecting the dynamic and variable nature of geological media (Cressie, 2015; Chiles and Delfiner, 2012 ). Addressing the nonstationarity problem in geostatistical modeling has recently gained prominence with the adoption of approaches that utilize Riemannian manifolds and nonstationary covariance functions, allowing for effective modeling of complex spatial variations and directional changes in spatial correlations. Manifold embedding, derived from differential geometry (Feragen et al., 2015; Jayasumana et al., 2015; Pereira et al., 2022; Piao & Park, 2023 ), stands out as a particularly advanced technique. By transforming spatial coordinates according to a manifold that effectively captures geologically nuanced structures, this approach provides a sophisticated and authentic representation of geological phenomena, which is crucial for comprehensive 3D geological assessments. These developments underscore the potential of new geostatistical models to capture complex spatial variations in subsurface properties, a critical advantage in fields such as hydrogeology, where nonstationarity is a common challenge. Incorporating nonstationary estimation and simulation within this manifold embedding framework offers a diversity of interpretations unattainable using traditional methods. This advancement not only aids in capturing the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of geological processes but also enhances the geostatistical toolkit with a more adaptable and nuanced approach to subsurface modeling. In this study, we present the theoretical extension of manifold embedding to 3D spaces with an emphasis on application within geological contexts and demonstrate its capability to effectively model the intricate spatial variability of geological media. The limitations of conventional geostatistical models—particularly their inadequacy in capturing directional variability and complex spatial patterns prevalent in geological media—are addressed. The progression of the manifold embedding framework from 2D to 3D spaces, tailored for geology, enhances our understanding of the complex interplay between geological features and spatial attributes. This approach provides a pragmatic pathway for conducting sophisticated 3D subsurface analyses. Further, it effectively bridges a vital gap in spatial estimation methodologies and offers more accurate, comprehensive, and nuanced geological models, substantially contributing to the advancement of hydrogeology. While we recognize the interest in direct numerical comparisons between manifold embedding and conventional two-point geostatistical methods, such comparisons would be inherently biased due to the different capabilities and data requirements of the two approaches. Manifold embedding inherently utilizes a richer set of spatial and structural data that traditional geostatistical methods typically do not process. This disparity makes direct comparisons not only challenging but also potentially misleading, as they may underrepresent the enhanced modeling capacity and detailed insights provided by manifold embedding. Instead, our focus is to demonstrate how manifold embedding can overcome the limitations of traditional methods by effectively incorporating and exploiting complex spatial information, thereby providing a more sophisticated and nuanced understanding of geological media.  2 Importance of manifold embedding in 2D geostatistical approaches Spatial estimation in hydrogeology requires capturing the intricacies of the subsurface environment, a task with exponentially increasing complexity when advancing from 2D to 3D representations. The manifold corresponding to a 3D space extends into a 4D space, where creating a visual representation that offers intuitive understanding to the observer becomes less feasible. This increase in complexity warrants a foundational review in a more conceptually accessible 2D space. Engaging with 2D concepts provides essential clarity and builds the intuition needed to grasp more abstract higher-dimensional spaces. Therefore, this section revisits the principles of manifold embedding within the well-understood confines of 2D geostatistical modeling, laying the groundwork for the subsequent exploration of the complexities of 3D geostatistical modeling. Fig. 1   illustrates the stepwise increase in manifold complexity, marking the transition from the simplicity of Euclidean space to the complexity of a non-Euclidean manifold. The uv    plane is identified as the actual 2D spatial domain under consideration, whereas the XYZ    plane embodies the embedded 3D manifold. In this setup, the coordinates X = u    and Y = v    directly map to the uv    plane, while the Z    coordinate, defined as Z = f u , v      , introduces an additional ‘informational dimension’. This Z    dimension serves to encode structural or variable information that extends beyond the simple spatial mapping of u    and v   , offering a deeper insight into the geological properties that vary within the domain. As shown in Fig. 1 a, the Z    component is constant, reflecting the assumption of isotropic and stationary spatial correlations prevalent in conventional geostatistical models. Visually, this is represented by a green circle on the uv    plane, symbolizing the spatial correlation ellipse. It retains its shape and size when projected onto the embedded XYZ    manifold, which represents uniform spatial correlations throughout the domain, aligning with the traditional Euclidean geostatistical framework that assumes static spatial relationships. As shown in Fig. 1 b, Z = f ( u , v )    represents a linear relationship with u    and v   , signaling the emergence of static anisotropy. At this juncture, linear functions are employed to define Z = f ( u , v )   , transitioning the model toward an anisotropic paradigm. Spatial correlations are depicted as elliptical shapes, exhibiting both elongation and consistent directionality, which indicate the anisotropy of geological processes. Despite the introduction of anisotropy, these spatial behaviors remain within the modeling capabilities of traditional geostatistical methods. Established variogram models can adequately capture static anisotropic conditions; thus, manifold embedding is not necessary at this stage. As shown in Fig. 1 c, the function Z = f ( u , v )    represents a departure from simple analytical forms, indicating the presence of spatial nonstationarity. This is visually represented using notable distortions upon projection onto the uv    plane, which is an echo of the complex heterogeneity of geological media. Traditional geostatistical models that rely on affine transformations for rotation and scaling fail to capture this level of complexity. In contrast, manifold embedding provides a sophisticated framework that can characterize the nuanced spatial variability of subsurface properties. It adeptly models the dynamic nature of spatial correlations, which vary across different locations, thereby capturing the true essence of the variable characteristics of geological processes and their spatial impact. The progression depicted in Fig. 1 a–1c shows the limitations of conventional geostatistics when confronted with increasing spatial nonstationarity and manifold complexity. Affine transformations—characterized by rotation and elongation—cannot capture intricate variations in the directionality of elongation, which become more pronounced at larger spatial scales because of complex geological processes influencing spatial correlations. Manifold embedding adeptly models these spatial variabilities and associated geological complexities, surpassing the capabilities of elementary geometric transformations. This method offers a robust framework designed to capture the dynamic behavior inherent in geological nonstationarity, significantly refining geostatistical analysis in nonstationary environments. The progression illustrated in Fig. 1 a–1c encapsulates the paradigm shift required for advanced hydrogeological studies and geostatistical applications. The complex and heterogeneous nature of subsurface characteristics governs intricate flow, transport, and migration phenomena. This paradigm shift underscores the critical need for precise delineation and representation of these complex subsurface features. As methodologies evolve to encompass higher-dimensional spaces, the straightforward visual interpretation of embedded manifolds may become impractical. Nevertheless, manifold embedding remains an essential analytical tool that captures the full spectrum of spatial correlations, which is crucial for delivering accurate characterizations and predictions in subsurface modeling.  3 Theory 3.1 Intrinsic geometry and metric tensor formulation Building upon the manifold embedding principles introduced in Section 2 , where the Z    dimension was first presented as an informational dimension for 3D spaces, we now extend this concept into a more complex framework. While conventional 3D Euclidean spaces, defined by coordinates u , v , w     , often fail to capture the nonstationary and dynamic behavior of geological properties, our novel approach introduces a fourth dimension, denoted as Ω   . This fourth dimension, akin to Z    in Section 2 , serves as an informational dimension. It specifically stores comprehensive structural information critical for accurately modeling nonstationary geological fields. By integrating this fourth dimension into our manifold embedding framework, we not only enhance the precision and depth of subsurface characterization but also enable a more nuanced understanding of complex geological environments. This innovative 4D approach not only bridges the limitations inherent in traditional 3D models but also facilitates a methodological shift toward capturing the full spectrum of spatial nonstationarity encountered in advanced geostatistical analysis. In this refined theoretical construct, the coordinates u , v , w      denote conventional 3D spatial locations. The capacity of the model to encapsulate spatial property variations within the geological system is enhanced via the incorporation of the Ω    dimension, represented by the scalar field f u , v , w      . This enhancement is not explicitly represented in the standard coordinate system. By introducing a fourth dimension as an informational dimension that reflects geological structure, the embedding technique allows for more precise and intricate modeling of subsurface environments. This additional dimension effectively captures key complexities such as geological folds and stratigraphic gradient changes, which are critical in accommodating the variations characteristic of geological media. In addition, in traditional 3D modeling, the natural coordinates u , v , w      lack inherent directional information about spatial correlation. This limitation is overcome using the inclusion of f u , v , w      , which integrates essential directional aspects necessary for modeling nonstationary processes. The function f    is rendered versatile, representing any spatially variable attribute—geological or hydrogeological—and enabling the depiction of nonstationary properties that evolve with location. In geostatistical applications, manifold embedding is particularly useful for a comprehensive understanding of variables critical for subsurface characterization, such as hydraulic properties or lithology. With the adoption of the 4D framework, spatial models exhibited a marked improvement in predictive capabilities. These models can accommodate directional dependencies and nonstationary behaviors, capturing subsurface complexities that are typically beyond the reach of conventional 3D frameworks. Similar enhancements in interpretability and model efficacy through added dimensions have been demonstrated in other fields, such as in action recognition by Ji et al. (2012) , who showed that adding a temporal dimension to spatial inputs significantly boosts the accuracy of 3D convolutional neural networks. The principal innovation of this methodology lies in the integration of the fourth dimension, Ω   , which is instrumental in encapsulating the intricate spatial variation of properties. Such an advancement facilitates more refined interpretations and accurate modeling in hydrogeology for a detailed understanding of the spatial variability of subsurface properties. To develop our 4D manifold embedding approach, we interpret the X Y Z Ω    space as a Riemannian manifold (Borovitskiy et al., 2020; Pereira et al., 2022 ), formalized as an inner product space denoted by V   . Using a specific mapping function, ψ   , we relate our manifold M    to V   , enabling the computation of geodesic distances essential for modeling nonstationary spatial correlations. The mapping ψ u , v , w       is defined as follows:(1) ψ u , v , w    = X u , v , w    , Y u , v , w    , Z u , v , w    , Ω u , v , w            Where(2) X u , v , w    = u    Y u , v , w    = v    Z u , v , w    = w    Ω u , v , w    = f u , v , w             and the function f   , mapping from the product space M × M    to the real numbers R   , is a manifold that encapsulates the spatial correlation for a specific location in the space u , v , w     . Here, f u , v , w       is not merely a coordinate but a critical mathematical construct within our Riemannian framework that captures the essence of spatial variability and correlation at each point in our geological model. Upon establishing the intrinsic geometry of the manifold using the mapping function ψ    described by Eqs. (1) and (2) , we construct the metric tensor for space M   . This tensor, denoted as g   , is a fundamental entity that characterizes the geometric structure of the manifold by quantifying the infinitesimal distances between points within the space, expressed as follows:(3) g = d r  du   · d r  du     d r  du   · d r  dv     d r  du   · d r  dw      d r  dv   · d r  du     d r  dv   · d r  dv     d r  dv   · d r  dw      d r  dw   · d r  du     d r  dw   · d r  dv     d r  dw   · d r  dw                Eq. The metric tensor g    is pivotal in capturing the nuances of spatial relationships and in the quantification of non-Euclidean distances, playing a critical role in the following geostatistical analyses. This tensor reflects the intrinsic curvature of the manifold and includes the derivatives of the function f   , which encodes the spatial correlation.  3.2 Computation of geodesic distances in 4D manifold embedding In the context of manifold theory, a geodesic distance is defined as the shortest path between two points on a curved surface, similar to straight lines in Euclidean space. In Euclidean geometry, the shortest path is simply a straight line, which represents the most direct distance between two points. In contrast, on a manifold possessing intrinsic curvature, geodesic paths embody the manifold’s complex geometry. By applying the metric tensor established in Eqs. (6) and (7) , we can demonstrate that distances within the uvw    plane correspond directly to those within the X Y Z Ω    manifold. This isometry between the uvw    plane and the X Y Z Ω    manifold signifies that, despite the curvature, they retain equivalent geometric properties. This isometric relationship allows geostatistical methods to adapt to dynamic geological processes that shape subsurface media. The geodesic distance, denoted d g    , represents the shortest path between any two points on a manifold, capturing the essence of the space’s curvature. (12) , is performed using the Gauss–Legendre quadrature method to complement the intricate geometry of the manifold in question. Notably, the complexity of the manifold, such as high-frequency fluctuations, necessitates a higher number of sampling points (abscissae) to ensure precision. Consequently, an inherent balance must be attained between the precision of the results and the computational demands of the process. The efficiency of these calculations must be optimized for the scalability and utility of the geostatistical methods being developed. While the concept of a 4D manifold may seem abstract, the practical application of geostatistical analysis demonstrated in this study is grounded within our 3D reality. The methodologies described in Sections 3.1 and 3.2  effectively translate the theoretical 4D model into a manageable 3D computational problem, central to the manifold embedding technique. This translation allows for the integration of advanced theoretical concepts into practical geostatistical analyses, adeptly handling the complexities of higher-dimensional models. Calculating geodesic distances in manifold embedding introduces unique computational challenges due to the need to represent the curved geometry of the manifold accurately. Geodesic distances are calculated along the manifold’s surface, requiring numerical integration that accounts for curvature at each segment. This process is inherently more demanding than simple Euclidean distance calculations, involving multiple segmented computations that significantly increase overall computational demands. The primary scalability challenge lies in the need for numerical integration along curved paths, which is computationally intensive for two main reasons. First, each geodesic path computation is segmented, and distances within these segments are calculated and summed, linearly increasing computation time with the number of segments. Second, each segment’s calculation must account for the manifold’s curvature, necessitating gradient computations at each point (Eq. (6) , adding further computational overhead. To address these challenges, we can employ several strategies. Developing advanced algorithms tailored to the complex geometry of manifold spaces can decrease the required computations by using adaptive integration techniques, which minimize segment numbers in areas of minimal curvature. Additionally, leveraging parallel processing enables simultaneous computation of geodesic distances across different processors, considerably enhancing computational efficiency.  3.3 Implementation and efficacy of geodesic kernels in manifold-embedded spatial analysis The concept of geodesic distance inherently captures spatial affinity, which can be adeptly integrated into a multitude of spatial interpolation methods, such as nearest-neighbor algorithms, inverse distance weighting, and clustering algorithms, to refine our understanding of spatial relationships. Although geodesic distances are versatile, we used Gaussian process regression (GPR) to align with the commonly preferred methods in the field (i.e., simple kriging) and demonstrate the implementation and benefits of our manifold embedding approach. To facilitate our Gaussian process analysis for property distribution, the Gaussian and exponential kernels were employed. In general, the Gaussian kernel indicates a gradual decay of spatial similarity with incremental distance, indicating a predominant influence of proximal points. In contrast, the exponential kernel denotes a precipitous decrease in similarity as the distance increases, accentuating a distinct demarcation between proximate and remote points. The Gaussian kernel is defined as follows (Jayasumana et al., 2015; Piao and Park, 2023 ):(13) k x 1  , x 2     = exp - d g  x 1  ; x 0      2  2 ρ  2            and the exponential kernel is described as(14) k x 1  , x 2     = exp - d g  x 1  ; x 0      ρ          where ρ    is the parameter that dictates the scale of correlation on the manifold and influences the spatial reach over which data points are considered to be significantly correlated. The geodesic distance d g  x 1  ; x 0        derived from Eq. (12)  adheres to the essential metric properties: nonnegativity (d g  x 1  ; x 0     ≥ 0   ), symmetry (d g  x 1  ; x 0     = d g  x 0  ; x 1       ), and triangle inequality (d g  x 0  ; x 1     + d g  x 1  ; x 2     ≥ d g  x 0  ; x 2       ) for all points within manifold M   . This theoretical advancement in geostatistical analysis illustrates a practical application of isometric embedding. By extending traditional 3D Euclidean spaces to include a fourth dimension, Ω   , we enrich the spatial model to more accurately encapsulate critical variations. This aligns with the principles of isometric embedding reported by Curriero (2006 ), ensuring that spatial relationships are preserved. Although Feragen et al. (2015)  highlight the careful consideration required in non-Euclidean spaces, our empirical validation within a scaled-down domain supports the positive definiteness of the covariance matrix derived from the exponential kernel. The validation process provides a preliminary basis for the applicability of a kernel to larger domains. However, this extrapolation must be approached with caution. Adequate verification is essential as the domain size increases to ensure that the scalability of the model is empirically supported. This level of scrutiny is critical for maintaining the reliability and computational practicability of geostatistical models, especially when considering dynamic geological processes in subsurface media.  3.4 Practical implications of manifold embedding for geological characterization In the established manifold embedding construct, as described using Eqs. (6) and (12) , the gradients df / d u   , df / d v   , and df / d w    maintain a vital connection with the metric tensor g   . These gradients not only provide insights into the spatial orientation of geological structures at any specific point u  ′  , v  ′  , w  ′       but also align with the normal vectors to the level sets of the 4D manifold, an assertion grounded in level-set theory (Park et al., 2024 ). Within a spatially variable system guided by two-point statistics, the properties demonstrate pronounced correlations in directions orthogonal to the gradient vector d f / d u , d f / d v , d f / d w     . This orthogonal characteristic indicates that geological features naturally extend in orientations where the rate of change of a property is minimized, which is consistent with the established principles of spatial correlation within the traditional geostatistical framework and further introduces the complexity of nonstationarity. Park et al. (2024)  investigated the relationship between the orientation of spatial correlations in geological features and level-set curves as they pertain to the curvature of geological layers by focusing on the correlation with geological strike directions in 2D spatial analysis. However, they addressed only one component of the spatial characterization necessary for a complete understanding of geological structures, which are locally modeled as 3D planar surfaces characterized by both strike and dip directions. Based on these findings, this study expands the analysis into the third dimension, employing the pole-to-plane geological concept to represent the full 3D orientation of planar surfaces and provide a more robust framework for capturing the complexity of geological structures. The subsequent sections further elaborate on the adoption of pole-to-plane representations and their relationship to 3D level sets within an X Y Z Ω    manifold, extending the applicability of level-set theory to 3D subsurface characterization. In geological field surveying, pole-to-plane measurement is a fundamental empirical construct derived from strike and dip data obtained during fieldwork. The pole  refers to the point on the lower hemisphere of the projection that lies perpendicular to the plane of the geological feature being measured. In practical terms, if one were to visualize a plane extending below the surface, the pole would be the line that intersects this plane at a right angle. This line represents the true orientation of the planar surface in 3D space. The strike is the direction taken by a horizontal line on the plane, typically measured as an azimuthal angle relative to the north, whereas the dip is the angle of descent of the plane relative to the horizontal. Together, the strike and the dip define the orientation of the plane and the pole to this plane, encapsulating the full 3D spatial orientation of the geological feature. This orientation, represented by the normal vector to the plane, is analogous to the gradient vector df / d u   df / d v   df / d w         T     (or ∇ f   ) in the context of manifold embedding. It signifies the direction of the most substantial change in geological properties. Thus, the pole-to-plane model offers a pragmatic and intuitive method for representing and interpreting the 3D orientation of subsurface structures within the manifold framework. By applying the manifold embedding approach outlined in Eqs. (7) and (12) , we delve deeper into the significance of the gradients df / d u   , df / d v   , and df / d w   , which stem from the metric tensor g   . At any point u  ′  , v  ′  , w  ′       on the manifold, these gradients encapsulate the directional tendencies of subsurface structures, offering insights into both the orientation and potential magnitude of spatial variability. Using a first-order Taylor expansion based on Eqs. (1) and (2) , the immediate vicinity of point x   —corresponding to u  ′  , v  ′  , w  ′      — on the level-set surface can be expressed as follows:(15) f u , v , w    ≈ f ^  u , v , w    = f u  ′  , v  ′  , w  ′     + df  du      x  u - u  ′     + df  dv      x  v - v  ′     + df  dw      x  w - w  ′     ,      where f ^  u , v , w       defines the plane tangent to the level set at the manifold point corresponding to u  ′  , v  ′  , w  ′      . The gradient vector at x   , given by d f / d u    x   d f / d v    x   d f / d w    x         T     is orthogonal to this tangent plane, providing a geometrically accurate depiction of the orientation of geological formations within the manifold context. Field measurements such as pole-to-plane or strike-and-dip typically provide us with only the orientation of geological features, leading to a knowledge gap regarding the spatial characteristics of the manifold. This gap stems from the inability of these methods to directly measure the magnitude of spatial correlation. To address this limitation, we introduced an empirical constant tailored to directional field data, which facilitates the estimation of the magnitude of spatial correlation. This advancement improves the manifold embedding technique, marrying its theoretical potential with the practicalities of field data acquisition and enabling a more comprehensive application in geological analysis. Fig. 2   depicts a geological structure similar to a geological dome, such as a salt dome, characterized by several planar features that are suitable for pole-to-plane measurement techniques. This illustration demonstrates how complex geological boundaries and structures, derived from field observations, can be effectively modeled using the developed method. These techniques are well represented by data acquired from borehole logs or 3D seismic profiles. At any given measurement location x    on a planar geologic feature L   , the pole-to-plane vector, p   , can be described as follows:(16) p x  = - dL  du      x   - dL  dv      x   - dL  dw      x         T  ,      where the magnitude of the vector is normalized to ensure that(17) dL  du      x     2  + dL  dv      x     2  + dL  dw      x     2    = 1      The vector p    delineates the orientation of the spatial correlation at the point of investigation but fails to convey the magnitude of such correlation. Understanding the magnitude of this correlation is indispensable for accurate modeling of geological nonstationarity and nuanced interpretation of subsurface structures within geostatistical frameworks. Consequently, the development of supplementary methodologies to measure this magnitude is essential to enhance our geostatistical analysis and fully exploit the manifold embedding technique for subsurface characterization. Current methodologies fail to directly quantify the magnitude of the manifold gradient, denoted as df / d u   df / d v   df / d w         T    , from pole-to-plane measurements - d L / d u   - d L / d v   - d L / d w         T    , hindering the full characterization of spatial correlations in geological features. To bridge this gap, we assume that the correlation scale magnitude is constant and introduce a scalar factor, β   , that equates the manifold gradient vector with the pole-to-plane vector, facilitating the translation of pole-to-plane measurements into estimates of geological properties:(18) df  du    df  dv    df  dw          T  = - β ∂ L  ∂ u    ∂ L  ∂ v    ∂ L  ∂ w          T       This assumption enables us to leverage pole-to-plane measurements to infer the magnitude of spatial correlation, expanding the utility of manifold embedding in geological structure analysis.   4 Results 4.1 Incorporation of pole-to-plane information in 3D estimation In this hypothetical case, the property distributed across the 3D domain is defined as an abstract, unitless measure and estimated. By breaking down the manifold into 3D framework, we can more effectively analyze and visualize spatial data that is too complex to be handled otherwise. In the depicted scenario, Fig. 4   offers a visual representation of the regression outcomes, which resembles the plunging geological fold often observed in textbooks. Such intricate shapes cannot be estimated using conventional methods grounded in two-point statistics, highlighting the unique capabilities of the developed method. To generate these detailed visualizations, the method primarily relies on direct data (e.g., hydraulic conductivity, porosity) collected from geological surveys and borehole measurements, which provide essential spatial coordinates and subsurface properties. Additionally, indirect data, offering insights into the structural information of the subsurface domain, such as 3D seismic profiles, are integrated to enhance the model’s accuracy and depth. This fusion of direct and indirect data enables comprehensive modeling of the geological structure, ensuring an accurate representation of geological features. These visualizations are pivotal for the explication of spatial variability and offer a quantitative portrayal of the theoretical constructs applied within a geological framework. The graphical representations serve as a bridge between the abstract manifold theory developed in this study and the tangible geostatistical application when spatial nonstationarity exists in the spatial correlation structure, enhancing the interpretability of subsurface characterizations. In practice, pole-to-plane data are often discretely gathered as opposed to the idealized scenario previously discussed owing to limited field surveys or sparse sampling in 3D geophysical data (seismic profiles). This discrete nature necessitates the use of interpolation techniques to construct a continuous spatial representation throughout the 3D domain. However, the integrity of the original orientation data may be compromised if the data acquired from these measurements or samplings are not sufficiently dense. Furthermore, the interpolation process can be a computationally intensive task, introducing potential constraints on computational efficiency. These considerations underscore the importance of striking an optimal balance between the resolution of data and the computational resources required in geostatistical modeling.  4.2 Geostatistical simulations and hydraulic estimates Different from conventional two-point statistics, the developed manifold embedding method adeptly visualizes geological dome shapes, as illustrated in Fig. 5  . This technique overcomes the computational complexities associated with geodesic distance calculations and transcends the limitations of traditional search algorithms in non-Euclidean spaces. Due to the impracticality of exhaustive sequential estimations across extensive domains, the algorithm employs GPR within a sequential simulation, adopting a random path to approach unexplored locations and weaving in randomness to capture spatial uncertainty. Upon estimating an initial subset of data, the GPR-based approach performs deterministic estimations for the remaining locations, mirroring the process presented in Fig. 4 . This strategy ensures a robust representation of uncertainty while managing the computational load inherent in large spatial domains. To represent geological structures (i.e., geological dome), functions were defined for any point within the domain by coordinates u , v , w     . The figures capture the spatial nonstationarity manifested via variable orientations and elongation patterns across different areas.
