The Gaussian kernel simulation outlines a mean of − 0.042 and a standard deviation (SD) of 0.779, with property values spanning from 3.663 to 3.443 and approximating a normal distribution. Conversely, the results of the exponential kernel, depicted in Fig. 5 c and 5d, present the entire domain and a sectional view, respectively. The exponential kernel yields a more condensed distribution, evidenced by a reduced SD of 0.388, indicating a rapid decay of similarity with increasing distance. This leads to more subdued structural features across the domain with less extensive lengths and widths compared to those obtained from the Gaussian simulation. Nevertheless, the mean property value stands at 0.041, with a range from 3.029 to 3.268, showing a distribution breadth similar to that of the Gaussian kernel. To provide clarity on the computational demands associated with our manifold embedding method, we performed a detailed analysis of the processing time and computational resources required. The simulations were executed on a workstation equipped with a 2.5 GHz 28-core Intel Xeon W processor, 768 GB of 2933 MHz DDR4 memory, and leveraging MATLAB’s Parallel Computing Toolbox to fully utilize the 28 cores. For our geostatistical models, as demonstrated in Fig. 5 , the typical run time was approximately 73 s per scenario. This setup illustrates the computational intensity of our method, particularly when handling large-scale datasets with complex nonstationary variations. It also highlights the scalability challenges and the necessary efficiency optimizations for practical applications, critical for users with varying computational capabilities. Assuming the hypothetical property illustrated in Fig. 5 , which represents the log-transformed hydraulic conductivity values of a confined aquifer, we can deduce the groundwater head distribution and particle transport pathlines, as demonstrated in Fig. 6  . For this simulation, MODFLOW-2005 (Harbaugh, 2005 ) was employed, though any equivalent groundwater modeling software, including the more recent MODFLOW6 (Langevin et al., 2017 ), could also be suitable. The simulation was configured using 3D voxels measuring 100 × 100 × 10 m (Δ u × Δ v × Δ w   ) along the u   , v   , and w    directions. The transmissivity field (T   ) within the domain was calculated using the exponentiation of the property values, expressed as T = exp 2 z      , where z    represents the log-transformed transmissivity fields (Fig. 5 ). Consequently, the transmissivity range for the Gaussian kernel scenario spans from 0.0007 to 978.5 m2 /day, whereas the exponential kernel yields a range from 0.0023 to 689.5 m2 /day. In this simplified flow model, the specified head boundaries were set at 1100 m for u = 1    and u = 100   , with no-flow boundaries at v = 1    and v = 100   . In addition, a fully penetrating extraction well with a constant head of 1050 m was posited at the center of the domain at u = 50    and v = 50   . Fig. 6 a and 6c depict the drawdown distributions resulting from a centrally located constant head well modeled using the Gaussian and exponential kernels, respectively. The drawdown contours are influenced by permeability variations within the aquifer, where they either conform to low-permeability barriers or follow pathways with higher permeability. Consequently, the drawdown patterns display complex geometries that deviate from the symmetric ellipsoidal shapes typically observed in homogeneous aquifers. The complexity is particularly accentuated in Fig. 6 a, which reflects the extensive and varied property structures associated with the Gaussian kernel, as observed in Fig. 5 a and 5b. Conversely, the drawdown in Fig. 6 c, influenced by the exponential kernel, exhibits a more diffuse spread. Particle path streamlines provide a nuanced representation of subsurface heterogeneity, effectively illustrating how the flow interacts with varying permeability structures. As shown in Fig. 6 b and 6d, backward particle path streamlines emanate from the central wellbore using the specific discharge q = T / Δ w × ∇ H   , where T    is the transmissivity distribution, Δ w    is the voxel thickness along the w    direction, and ∇ H    is the gradient of the hydraulic head distribution in Fig. 6 a and 6c. In the streamline estimations, 400 particles are randomly distributed within the narrow interval of u = 50    and v = 50    along the whole thickness of the confined aquifer (from 0 to 100 along the w    axis) so that the particle starts from the central abstraction well into the domain. These streamlines converge upon the wellbore and are predominantly influenced by the dome-shaped permeability structures shown in Fig. 5 . Consequently, they highlight a zone of influence extending from the wellbore to the lower portion of the constant head boundaries, indicating that inputs from the lower regions of the boundaries considerably impact the water quality and quantity of the centrally located well. The streamline dispersion contrast between Fig. 6 a and 6c is notable: streamlines from the Gaussian kernel simulation exhibit a more eccentric pattern with a less dispersed distribution (Fig. 6 b). In comparison, those from the exponential kernel display a relatively uniform dispersion (Fig. 6 d). These disparities underscore how inherent spatial characteristics modeled using each kernel can define flow dynamics within the domain. The intricacies of 3D flow patterns must be carefully considered from an environmental management standpoint when delineating a capture zone of a well, ensuring that an improved representation of the hydraulic property distribution is incorporated, particularly when determining well locations and pumping rates. Similarly, the design of high-risk geological repositories, such as those for spent nuclear fuel or CO2  sequestration, requires a comprehensive understanding of these complex flow dynamics to prevent adverse outcomes. In these situations, the incentive of the developed method is evident among the two-point statistical approaches. Therefore, an extensive assessment that considers all potential scenarios and integrates advanced nonstationary analytical techniques, such as those presented in this study, must be conducted to complement conventional stationary geostatistical methods.   5 Discussion In the domain of subsurface characterization, the integration of manifold embedding into geostatistical models offers a significant leap forward, offering unprecedented precision in modeling the spatial variability of complex media. This method acknowledges that stationarity is merely a special case within the broader spectrum of nonstationary behaviors, thus holding transformative potential for subsurface management across a wide spectrum of applications. Manifold embedding is seamlessly integrated into various subsurface management tasks that traditionally rely on geostatistical models, such as environmental management, water resource management, oil and gas exploration, and geothermal energy development. These applications benefit from significant improvements in spatial resolution and estimation accuracy. In addition, manifold embedding can be directly integrated into numerical modeling frameworks, enhancing their spatial analysis capabilities and improving the accuracy of model predictions by providing more accurate representations of geological variability. The method also significantly enhances data assimilation processes in inverse problems, leading to more geologically plausible estimates and improving the efficiency of subsurface parameter retrieval. Although the method introduces considerable computational demands owing to the intricate calculations of geodesic distances that pose scalability challenges, it excels in scenarios laden with heterogeneity. Advanced algorithms specifically designed to handle the complex geometry of manifold spaces reduce the number of necessary computations. Parallel processing is also used, allowing each geodesic distance computation to be performed simultaneously on multiple processors, significantly reducing overall computation times. Despite the enhanced capability of the manifold embedding method to model spatial variability and subsurface heterogeneity, it encounters limitations regarding its reliance on a substantial volume of secondary information. The acquisition of in-depth geophysical data and extensive field surveys is required to accurately depict spatial correlations and heterogeneity in subsurface structures. This requirement may impose constraints on the applicability of the developed method, especially in scenarios with limited data availability or in contexts where data collection is impractical or costly. However, while manifold embedding has increased data requirements compared to traditional geostatistical methods, its flexibility in integrating diverse data types—from detailed geophysical datasets to expert geological insights—makes it a valuable tool in complex geological settings or under-characterized sites. By employing strategies to manage data requirements and adapting the method to work with limited data availability, such as incorporating qualitative insights from geological experts or leveraging sparse data like strike and dip measurements, practitioners can effectively utilize manifold embedding in various hydrogeological modeling scenarios. Unlike deep learning approaches (e.g., Zhan et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2023 ), which often require retraining or fine-tuning when applied to new sites, the manifold embedding method can be encapsulated in a software package that practitioners can use without extensive knowledge of the underlying mathematical and computational details. This transferability and ease of use make manifold embedding more accessible and practical to a wider range of users, particularly those who may not have expertise in deep learning. This is particularly valuable in hydrogeological modeling, where practitioners often need to analyze multiple sites with varying characteristics and data availability. This study calls a broader engagement of the research community to extend manifold embedding. Future research will focus on enhancing computational efficiency, improving estimation accuracy, and conducting more case application studies. Such community involvement is critical as it will drive the evolution of manifold embedding from a theoretical concept to a robust, practical tool for complex environmental modeling. Manifold embedding adeptly captures nonstationary and complex spatial correlations and excels in high-risk applications where accurate and comprehensive subsurface characterization is critical. Despite its challenges, manifold embedding can significantly improve our understanding and management of subsurface environments.  6 Conclusions We expanded the scope of geostatistical modeling by incorporating manifold embedding, thereby enriching the scenarios that can be realized through our method. This advancement allows for a more nuanced 3D characterization of subsurface environments, capturing complex geological processes that traditional methods fail to adequately model. By adding an additional dimension, our approach not only captures nonstationary properties that were previously unattainable but also aligns more closely with the intricate realities of geological media for precise modeling. The manifold embedding method represents a fundamental improvement over existing geostatistical methods, increasing the accuracy and depth of subsurface characterization across a spectrum of subsurface management tasks. This method is particularly potent in areas where an accurate representation of spatial variability is critical, such as contaminant remediation, groundwater flow characterization, and natural resource exploration. It provides a detailed and realistic representation of subsurface heterogeneity, enabling hydrogeologists to make better-informed decisions and significantly improve the understanding of subsurface environments. Our approach demands substantial computational resources and data. However, the computational and mathematical complexity introduced by manifold embedding can be effectively mitigated through strategies such as the use of high-performance computing, the development of specialized software, and the promotion of open science initiatives. These efforts make manifold embedding a more accessible and practical tool for characterizing complex subsurface environments in hydrogeology and geostatistics. Manifold embedding also excels in modeling complex geological features such as folds, faults, and unconformities that can be oversimplified by conventional geostatistical methods. This robust framework captures the intricate spatial relationships inherent in these formations, improving both the precision of geological analysis and the effectiveness of environmental management strategies. In summary, manifold embedding does not render traditional methods obsolete, but rather complements and enhances them, especially as more detailed geological information becomes available. As the field of hydrogeology and geostatistics continues to evolve, manifold embedding will play a critical role in advancing subsurface modeling and characterization. We expect that its continued development and refinement will contribute significantly to advances in our understanding of complex subsurface environments.
1 Introduction Securing water and food resources is critical for achieving the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG6 (clean water and sanitation) and SDG2 (zero hunger) (UN, 2022 ). The urban population facing water scarcity is expected to double from 930 million in 2016 to [1.7, 2.4] billion by 2050 (UN, 2023 ). Simultaneously, approximately 670 million people, equivalent around 8 % of the global population, are projected to face ongoing food shortage in 2030 (FAO et al., 2022 ). As China must feed 20 % of world’s population with only 9 % of the world's arable land and 6 % of its freshwater resources, these escalating global water and food shortage exert tremendous strain on China’s agriculture (FSC, 2019; CWRB, 2021 ). The water resources shortage and unscientific management pose significant barriers to agricultural development in irrigated areas (Gohar et al., 2015 ). Moreover, population growth and economic expansion worsen the gap between water supply and demand, posing a grave threat to food security and economic growth in these regions (Singh, 2012; Wang et al., 2022 ). Therefore, optimizing water resources allocation is crucial for meeting diverse sectoral needs, promoting harmonized development among economy, society, and environment, while also ensuring sustainable water use in irrigation areas. Water resources management in irrigated areas faces complex challenges due to conflicting interests among diverse water supply sources, distinct water-demanding regions, and various water-using sectors. In most irrigation areas, agricultural production emerges as the largest consumer of water, followed by domestic and industrial sectors (Zhang et al., 2018, 2023b ). Inevitably, human activities such as farming, livestock, manufacturing, and livelihoods, can pollute local water resources. Hence, considering economic, social, and environmental factors together has emerged as a prevailing approach for managing water resources in irrigated areas. Multi-objective programming (MOP) assumes a crucial role in balancing the conflicts between these objectives (Yin et al., 2022; Zhu and Shi, 2023 ). Conventional water resources planning optimization schemes, obtained through deterministic MOP are significantly affected by uncertainties arising from natural resources fluctuations, inaccurate statistical information, subjective perceptions, and other factors (Mirajkar and Patel, 2016; Kazemi et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2022 ). Previous studies have explored various methods to address these uncertainties, including stochastic mathematical programming (SMP), fuzzy mathematical programming (FMP), and interval parameter programming (IPP) (Fu et al., 2017; Yue et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024 ). Among these methods, SMP is widely used for exploring the tradeoffs between predefined economic targets and random water availability; nevertheless, probability distributions based on a large number of samples should be primarily determined (Wang et al., 2020 ). FMP, particularly the Fuzzy Credibility Programming (FCP) approach, is widely used to efficiently reflect the water resources managers’ subjective judgements and ambiguous information by using fuzzy sets and membership functions (Wang et al., 2022; Yue et al., 2022 ). Meanwhile, the FCP approach stands out for its self-duality and streamlined calculation process, can effectively address fuzzy uncertainty and constraint violation by prioritizing constraints fulfillment at a specific credibility level (Huang, 2006; Zhang and Huang, 2010 ). However, in most previous studies, FCP has primarily been demonstrated effective for handing fuzzy uncertainties of parameters in model constraints rather than objective functions (Li et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023a ). Some studies have explored representing fuzzy parameters in objective functions by converting them into fuzzy parameters using fuzzy sets, enabling representation with different membership degrees (Zhang and Huang, 2011a ). For example, Ren et al. (2017)  incorporated surface water amount and underground water amount as fuzzy sets in the objectives of a linear multi-objective programming model. However, they measured fuzzy parameters in the constraints by possibility measures, which are less comprehensive than credibility measure. Credibility measure, combining both possibility and necessity measures, offers a more reasonable and effective way to measure fuzzy events (Ma et al., 2020 ). Moreover, aside from some parameters that are frequently uncertain in objective functions and constraint conditions, water supply optimization is also susceptible to uncertainties stemming from the natural environment and human activities. To address such uncertainties, scenario analysis (SA) has proven to be an effective approach (Zuo et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023b ). Unfortunately, few studies have integrated fuzzy-credibility constraints and fuzzy parameters into both objectives and constraints in the multi-objective optimization of water resources scenarios in the irrigation areas. This integration is crucial for effectively tackling the various uncertainties involved in the optimal allocation of water resources and ensuring the attainment of rational and robust planning solutions. Here, to address the above problems, we proposed a systemic model (SMOFCP-WRMS), employing the scenario-based multi-objective fuzzy-credibility constrained programming (SMOFCP) model to optimize the water resource management system (WRMS) in irrigation areas under uncertainty. The SMOFCP model integrated various methodologies, including MOP, SA, and FCP. Then, the effectiveness and feasibility of the model were demonstrated through its application to the Zhaokou Yellow River Diversion Irrigation Area Phase II (ZKID-II) Project in Henan Province, China. To solve the SMOFCP-WRMS model, we initially introduced the expected value theory (EVT) to handle fuzzy parameters within the objective functions (Liu and Liu, 2002 ). Subsequently, we applied the α -cut method (Li and Huang, 2011; Ren et al., 2017 ) to transform the uncertainty model into a series of deterministic MOP models with various reliability levels. To overcome challenges in conventional multi-objective solutions, such as the subjective objective weights and difficulty in obtaining the global optimal solution (Wang et al., 2022 ), we employed the Non-Dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm III (NSGA-III) (Deb and Jain, 2014 ). This algorithm maintains population diversity through well-established dynamic reference points and exhibits enhanced convergence capabilities, ensuring a more uniform distribution of Pareto optimal solutions, especially for high-dimensional objectives (Yu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023a ). The proposed SMOFCP-WRMS framework in this study presents several noteworthy advantages, including: (a) addressing fuzzy parameters within objective functions and constraints simultaneously by incorporating fuzzy sets and various scenarios; (b) identifying optimal decision schemes effectively with compromise programming and the NSGA-III algorithm, handling complex multi-objective problems; (c) offering decision alternatives tailored to different water supply scenarios and credibility levels, aiding local water resource managers; (d) resolving conflicts among economic benefits, social water scarcity, and pollutant discharge within multi-water resource system of the ZKID-II project. The paper follows a structured format: the introduction outlines the research gap, summarizing current research and highlighting our contributions. The Methodology and application section details the SMOFCP-WRMS model, encompassing construction, solution methods, and an overview of the ZKID-II project. In the Results and discussion section, we elaborate on the water resource allocation scheme derived from the model and its efficacy. We also compare our solution method with traditional methods. Finally, the Conclusions section summarizes key findings, acknowledges limitations, and suggests future research directions.  2 Methodology and application Fig. 1   illustrates the research framework of the novel SMOFCP-WRMS model applied to the ZKID-II project in Henan Province, China. Section 1  shows the identification of the multi-water resources in the irrigation area, including an analysis of the abstraction, transportation, distribution, and discharge processes. Utilizing the input data, such as water quotas and socio-economic indicators, a table with long series of water supply and demand for ZKID-II from 1975 to 2015 was compiled. Based on empirical frequency analysis method, this paper sets three hydrological scenarios with design frequencies of P = 50 %, P = 75 %, and P = 95 % to determine the water demand of each water users and water supply from various water sources under different scenarios. In Section 2 , we introduce SMOFCP model, which effectively integrate SA and FCP to resolve fuzzy parameters and multiple uncertainties expressed as fuzzy sets and scenarios within both objectives and constraints of the water allocation models. Moreover, the incorporation of MOP adeptly handles the intricate trade-offs among multiple conflicts in the water resources management system. The resulting SMOFCP-WRMS model encompasses various objective functions associated with economic, social, and ecological dimensions, along with their corresponding constraints and solution methodology. In Section 3 , the application of SMOFCP-WRMS model is demonstrated within the context of the Zhaokou irrigation system in Henan, China. The model comprehensively considers the various water resources, encompassing local water (surface water, groundwater, and reuse water), transferring water (Yellow River), and transit water (Guo River and Huiji River). The model also considers diverse water use sectors, including domestic and livestock consumption, agricultural irrigation, secondary and tertiary industries, sanitation and greening, and landscape lake ecology. Moreover, the model extends its analysis to multiple irrigation administrative districts, namely Zhongmu County, Gulou District, Demonstration area of urban–rural integration, Xiangfu District, Tongxu County, Qi County, Taikang County, and Zhecheng County. Lastly, relying on field research, we established the principle of prioritized allocation for different irrigation, diverse water users, and distinct water sources. In Section 4 , we delve into an analysis of the optimization outcomes derived from this application, encompassing a thorough examination of water resources allocation, economic benefits, as well as pollution discharge within the designated study area. 2.1 Model formulation This section offers an in-depth exposition of the modeling procedure and the solution approach employed for the SMOFCP-WRMS model within irrigation areas. The listing of parameters and variables in the MOFCP-WRMS model is distinctly outlined in Table 1  , while Table 2   elucidates the interpretations of the abbreviations used in this study. 2.1.1 A scenario-based multi-objective fuzzy-credibility constrained programming (SMOFCP) approach Upon scrutinizing the actual water management system in irrigation area, we found that the water demand of different water users within individual administrative districts differ and pose challenges in terms of future prediction. Consequently, such fuzzy information, including water demand and available water resources, cannot be accurately represented by deterministic values. To effectively reflect the satisfaction degrees of the constraints and address constraint violations in this fuzzy context, this study adopted FCP to represent water demand and availability constraints (Li et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2020 ), this enabling the optimization of overall contentment within the MOP framework. Furthermore, certain fuzzy parameters within the objective functions, such as the costs and benefits associated with water supply, cannot be accurately represented as deterministic values (Zhang et al., 2022; He et al., 2023 ). While the amalgamation of MOP and FCP can address uncertainties expressed as fuzzy numbers on the right side of the constraints, reflecting different risk attitudes towards credibility levels, it cannot directly resolve the fuzzy parameters within the objective equation. Thus, to handle these ambiguous parameters, fuzzy sets with membership functions were utilized (Schulz et al., 1999 ). This study employed a triangular fuzzy membership function to manage fuzzy parameters in the objective functions, facilitating the quantification of essential information from fuzzy numbers into upper, lower, and most probable values (Ozgen and Gulsun, 2014; Sasikumar and Mujumdar, 2000 ). In addition, SA was employed to investigate dynamic water resources management strategies across varying water supply and demand scenarios. This approach can avoid uncertainties arising from factors like human activities and local policy, which contribute to future water demand and the availability of various water resources. Specifically, we addressed these uncertainties using the SA approach for ZKID-II projection. This includes variables, such as water resources demand, available water supply from various water sources and different water users in various administrative districts, and the Yellow River’s available water supply for different city and water users. We integrated FCP, SA, and triangular fuzzy numbers into the MOP to develop the Scenario-based MOFCP (SMOFCP) model. This model was designed to optimize the allocation of surface water, groundwater, Yellow River, Guo River, and Huiji River among different users across various irrigation administrative districts. This model aimed to achieve a balance among conflicting goals pertaining to water resources allocation, encompassing societal, economic, and ecological dimensions, all while maximizing overall benefits. These models were encoded and subsequently solved using optimization software, considering different water supply scenarios and six distinct credibility levels.  2.1.2 Model solution The SMOFCP model can address multiple uncertainties in both the objective function and the constraints within the framework of MOP. Moreover, it can provide flexible solutions and detailed analysis under various scenarios by incorporating varying credibility levels. The step-by-step solution process is outlined as follows: Step 1:  Formulate the SMOFCP model tailored for a specific study. Step 2:  Transform the triangular fuzzy numbers within the objective functions of the SMOFCP model into their respective expected values, using the fuzzy variable expectation values theory. Step 3:  Convert the constraints with fuzzy parameters of the SMOFCP model into deterministic models using FCP. For example, for the constraint C r ∑ i = 1  I  a i  x i  ⩽ ξ ∼      ⩾ λ   , ai   is the constant coefficient of the decision variable x i    , ξ ∼  = ( t ̲  , t , t  ¯   )     represents fuzzy sets of imprecise right-hand sides with credibility constraints, t ̲    , t   , and t  ¯      are the minimum, most-likely, and maximum values of ξ ∼    , λ    is the credibility level, which represents the satisfaction degree of the associated constraint and can be expressed as (Xu et al., 2017 ):(15) C r ∑ i = 1  I  a i  x i  ⩽ ξ ∼       = 1 ,   if ∑ i = 1  I  a i  x i  ⩽ t ̲      2 t - t ̲  - ∑ i = 1  I  a i  x i    2 ( t - t ̲  )   ,    if t ̲  ⩽ ∑ i = 1  I  a i  x i  ⩽ t     t  ¯   - ∑ i = 1  I  a i  x i    2 ( t - t ̲  )   ,    ift ⩽ ∑ i = 1  I  a i  x i  ⩽ t  ¯       0 ,    if ∑ i = 1  I  a i  x i  ⩾ t  ¯                 Generally, in the optimization process for management and planning, when the credibility value exceeds 0.5 (Zhang and Huang, 2011b ), the credibility constraint can be translated into a deterministic form as follows:(16) C r ∑ i = 1  I  a i  x i  ⩽ ξ ∼      = 2 t - t ̲  - ∑ i = 1  I  a i  x i   2 ( t - t ̲  )   ⩾ λ     (17) ∑ i = 1  I  a i  x i  ⩽ t + ( 1 - 2 λ )  ( t - t ̲  )       Step 4:  Solve the deterministic models using NSGA-III (Jain and Deb, 2013 ) and obtain optimal water resources allocation schemes. The algorithm was implemented in Matlab2020b software programming with PlatEMO toolbox (Tian et al., 2017 ). In addition, the same parameter settings were applied to NSGA-II for comparison in this optimization problem. Step 5:  Select the optimal solution from the Pareto frontier through compromise programming (CP) method (Abrishamchi et al., 2005; Hu et al., 2016; Karamian et al., 2023 ). The formula for measuring the proximity in CP is as follows:(18) minD ( x )  = ∑ k = 1  K  w k  × f k opt   ( x )  - f k  ( x )   f k opt   ( x )  - f k inf   ( x )        p      1 / p       Where x  is the vector of decision variables; D (x ) is the minimum proximity distance; k  is the index of the objective function; K  represents the number of objective functions;w k     is the weight of the objective function, which depends on the decision maker's measurement of the importance of the objective function;f k  ( x )     is the calculated value of the objective function;f k opt   ( x )     and f k inf   ( x )     are the maximum and minimum values of the objective function, respectively; and p  is a metric parameter that represents the maximum deviation from the ideal point, which is a real number between 1 and ∞. In this study, the weights assigned to the three objective functions, namely maximizing economic benefits (f 1 ), maximizing social benefits (f 2 ), and maximizing ecological benefits (f 3 ), were determined using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) method. Hierarchical analysis involves establishing a hierarchical structure for the indicator system. Expert determine the relative importance of the indices at each level concerning the criteria in the next higher level, using paired comparison based on their experience and knowledge (Sun et al., 2017 ). Then the judgment matrix A = ( a ij   )  n × n      will be constructed based on the results of each evaluator’s pair-wise comparisons. a ij      is the relative importance of two indices to the above level, divided into 1–9 (Table 3  ). The maximum eigenvalue and its corresponding eigenvector of the obtained judgment matrix are calculated to satisfy AX = λX   . The weight vector (W ) is then attained by normalizing the eigenvector (X ).(19) W i  = x i   ∑ i = 1  n  x i     , x i   ∑ i = 1  n  x i     , ⋯ , x n   ∑ i = 1  n  x i       = W 1  ,  W 2  ,  ⋯ W n          Given the complexity of the evaluation system and the subjective of expert choices, judgment matrices from different experts may lack consistency. Thus, the random consistency ratio (CR ) is proposed to check consistency before calculating the weight vector.(20) CR = CI  RI       (21) CI = | λ max  - n |  n - 1       where CI  is consistency indicator. RI  is average random consistency index (reference values for different n are shown in Table 4  ). n  is the number of elements compared pair-wisely based on the specified criteria. When CR  < 0.1, the judgment matrix satisfies the consistency condition; otherwise, it should be adjusted. Step 6:  Repeat steps 3 to 5 for various credibility levels of fuzzy parameters.   2.2 Case study 2.2.1 Overview of the study area The above model formulation and solution approach were applied to the ZKID-II projection in Henan Province, China. Situated in the eastern plain of Henan Province (Fig. 2  ), the ZKID-II spans an area of 2174 km2  and encompasses a population of 2.04 million, with a per capita GDP of 244.30 billion CNY. As a pivotal grain production base in China and Henan Province, the ZKID-II plays a crucial role in ensuring China's food security. It is expected to contribute to a grain production increase by 1.49 × 108  kg, accounting for 0.29 % of China's grain production target of 500 × 108  kg (EIRZKID-II, 2017 ). Notably, agriculture dominated water consumption in the ZKID-II, accounting for 76.6 % of total water consumption in 2015. The livelihoods and production activities in the ZKID-II heavily rely on the groundwater extraction and the diversion of water from Yellow River, which constituted 82.5 % and 11.4 % of the total water supply in 2015, respectively. The region exhibits not only a high-water scarcity rate of 36 % but also disorganized water resources management practices, including excessive groundwater exploitation, disorderly water distribution, and unregulated discharge of pollutants. Therefore, making a rational adjustment to the water resources becomes imperative to alleviate the water crisis and address conflicts among economic benefits, social water scarcity, and pollutant discharge of WRMS in the ZKID-II.  2.2.2 Data collection and scenario design The developed SMFCP-WRMS model relies on three types of input data: socio-economic data, water resources data, and environmental parameters. Socio-economic data.  In addition to statistical yearbooks and local standard water use quota, population, livestock numbers, economic value added, agricultural products income, and the basic water allocation quota of various water users were mainly obtained from official government planning reports, including “Preliminary Design Report of ZKID-II in Henan Province”, “Henan Province comprehensive planning of water resources”, “Zhengzhou city comprehensive planning of water resources”, “Kaifeng city comprehensive planning of water resources”, “Zhoukou city comprehensive planning of water resources”, and “Shangqiu city comprehensive planning of water resources” (ARDWQ, 2020; IUDWQ, 2020; NAPCDS, 2021 ). Water costs for various user in different regions were primarily sourced from surveys conducted by local development and reform commissions and official government websites. As an illustration, water prices of agriculture were primarily derived from WRTSHP (2018) . The water prices of the Yellow River in different departments were derived from official announcements on the National Development and Reform Commission’s website (NNDRCAWSP, 2013 ). Meanwhile, we further supplemented and validated water prices in specific districts through comprehensive surveys and interviews with local residents. Water benefits were calculated through water sharing coefficients for each user (Xiang and Gong, 2021 ). For instance, in the case of secondary and tertiary industries, water benefits were determined by multiplying the inverse of water consumption with the value added of the industries, followed by multiplication with their respective water sharing coefficients. Similarly, the water benefits of agricultural irrigation were obtained by dividing the overall agricultural product income per unit area by the irrigation quota and then multiplying it by the water sharing coefficients. Water resources data.  Water supply from various water source was mainly from documents such as the Preliminary Design Report of ZKID-II, Environmental Impact Report of ZKID-II, and Water Resources Argumentation Report of ZKID-II. Water demand was determined through water quotas allocated each water user and the socio-economic indicators from future development planning, such as population, economic value added, and irrigated area. Utilizing the aforementioned data, a table with long series of water supply and demand for ZKID-II from 1975 to 2015 was compiled. Subsequently, employing the empirical frequency analysis method (Li et al., 2023b ), the historical water demand series were ranked, resulting in the definition of three different water supply and demand scenarios for ZKID-II in 2030. These scenarios correspond to design frequencies of P = 50 %, P = 75 % and P = 95 % (Detailed data in Tables S1 and S2 ). Environmental parameters.  This mainly includes parameters such as wastewater and pollutant discharge coefficient, pollutant discharge standard, and total permitted pollutant discharge. These data were primarily sourced from the official websites of Henan Provincial Department of Ecology and Environment, as well as the Kaifeng Water Resources Bureau (WDSHRS, 2014; EIRZKID-II, 2017; WDSYRS, 2021 ).    3 Results and discussion 3.1 Selected optimal decisions In order to achieve the optimal values of the studied parameters and model validation, several iterations were performed during the algorithm process to achieve convergence and optimize the studied parameters. The optimal initial parameters were determined through trial and error based on experiences gained from various iterations. Figure S1  shows the optimization process of the three objectives solved by NSGA-III. The algorithm converged best with 200 iterations and an initial population of 100. Crossover percentage was set to 1.0 and the mutation rate was 1/N, where N is the number of decision variables (Deb et al., 2002 ). Other parameters were set to the default values of the PlatEMO toolbox. Ultimately, the algorithm generated 91 Pareto-optimal solutions with an average execution time of 56.24 s, each containing 288 non-inferior decision variables. Each point in the Pareto diagram represents a different solution within the system. The CP method was employed to identify the ideal solutions from a set of solutions considering random flow conditions. Meanwhile, the weights assigned to f 1 , f 2 , and f 3  were 0.12, 0.65 and 0.23, respectively. To justify the rationality of objectives weights, we conducted a consistency check and determined that the consistency ratio was below 0.1. Subsequently, the sequence numbers of the compromise-optimal solution under six credibility levels, corresponding to the 91 sets of non-inferior solutions from the three water supply scenarios were shown in Table S3 . Fig. 3  (a) shows the water resources allocation during the planning year of 2030 based on compromise-optimal solutions. The decisions made by decision-makers across varying credibility levels (λ) correspond to different constraints violation risks, which significantly influences the water resources allocation. As the λ increases, there was a discernible decreasing trend in the allocated water resources across all three scenarios. For instance, from λ = 0.5    to λ = 1.0   , the allocated water resources decreased by 14.95 × 106  m3  and 34.04 × 106  m3  at P = 50 % and P = 75 %, respectively. This phenomenon is mainly driven by a looser decision space in credibility constraints (Yue et al., 2022 ). Moreover, the allocated water resources showed a trend of initial decrease followed by subsequent increase as the design frequency increases. For example, the total water resources allocation under λ = 0.8    decreased from 616.27 × 106  m3  (P = 50 %) to 563.09 × 106  m3  (P = 75 %), subsequently rebounding to 588.81 × 106  m3  (P = 95 %). Remarkably, this phenomenon, contrary to the general perception, can be attributed to two main reasons as elucidated in the ZKID-II planning report: (1) The runoff of Yellow River and its arrival at the receiving area ZKID-II showed a synchronous-asynchronous encounter probability according to the historical hydrological data from 1975 to 2015. This incongruity leaded to a disparity between the change in Yellow River water diversion and that of local water source (e.g., surface water) in the ZKID-II. (2) To minimize the crop damage and ensure a reliable water supply for agricultural irrigation, the diversion of water from the Yellow River will be amplified in dry years (P = 95 %) in the scenario design. This strategic amplification meets the irrigation area’s water requirements, effectively addressing both residents’ living and production needs. In summary, more allocated water resources would be provided from Yellow River diversion under the P = 95 % scenario, resulting in a higher water supply compared to the P = 75 % scenario. Furthermore, the above results showed that the considerable variability in water availability, indicating the significance of the combined operation of diverse sources across different water supply and demand scenarios. Fig. 3 (b) presents the allocation of water resources from six different sources across various credibility levels combined with three water supply scenarios. Groundwater and the Yellow River constitute the primary water supply sources, followed by surface water and reuse water, while Huiji River and Guo River account for the smallest proportion of water resources allocation. The distribution of water resources allocation across various supply scenarios during the planning period under different credibility levels remains relatively stable with minimal fluctuations. This distribution pattern stems from the specific water resources allocation structure of the various water users in the ZKID-II. Fig. 4  (a), (c), and (e) offer a global perspective of the trade-off surface in a three-dimensional (3D) coordinate plot, where f 1 , f 2 , and f 3  are plotted on the x  ,y , and z  axes, respectively. Meanwhile, the economic benefits (f 1 ) depicted with color are added to compare the correlation between economic benefits, social water shortages, and total pollutant discharge. It is shown that the evident trade-offs exist within the multi-water resources system among economic benefits, social water shortages, and total pollutant discharge. Within the limited availability of total water resources, prioritizing the water demands of the secondary and tertiary industries increases the economic benefits (marked in red), yet concurrently leads to elevated total pollutants (i.e., COD  and NH 3 -N ) discharge. To explore the trade-off surface among above three objectives, we employed the parallel coordinates to illustrate the discrepancies among Pareto-optimal solutions (Fig. 4 (b), (d), and (f)). All Pareto-optimal solutions under P = 50 % fall within the range of 2601.5 < f 1  < 2602.5 (×106  CNY), 30.98 < f 2  < 31.09 (×106  m3 ), and 6928.3 < f 3  < 6930.0 (tonne) in Fig. 4 (b). The presence of parallel lines between f 1  and f 2 , as well as between f 2  and f 3 , indicates obvious trade-offs among three objectives. This implies a fundamental conflict between expanding irrigation for economic growth and enhancing social and ecological environment benefits in the ZKID-II. The points representing the maximum economic benefits of the water resources allocation scheme under P = 50 % are marked by red spheres in Fig. 4 (a) and represented by the dark red lines in Fig. 4 (b), respectively, which signifies relatively lower water shortage but concurrently higher total pollutant discharge. However, it is important to highlight that while maximizing economic benefits is significant, achieving synergy among all three objectives is essential for optimal water resource management. The findings underscore the importance of prioritizing compromise solutions within the non-dominated set during decision-making processes. Water resource managers can utilize these findings to prioritize schemes that achieve superior economic benefits while simultaneously minimizing adverse effects, such as water scarcity and pollutant discharge, thus ensuring sustainable and balanced water management practices in real-world applications.  3.2 Optimal decision analysis Fig. 5   shows the most optimal water allocation scheme for different water resources, water users, and administrative districts (ADs) across three water supply scenarios within the ZKID-II in 2030 under λ = 0.8   . The left, middle, and right columns mean the water allocation for different water resources, water users, and ADs, respectively. The ribbons demonstrate the interconnected relation and their intensity among water resources, users, and ADs. For instance, the allocated surface water during the planning period of 2030 would be 49.79 × 106  m3  (P = 50 %), 41.90 × 106  m3  (P = 75 %), and 36.68 × 106  m3  (P = 95 %), respectively. The trend in surface water allocation follows a continuous downward from P = 50 % to P = 95 %. Nevertheless, the water diversion from the Yellow River would decrease by 40.39 × 106  m3  from P = 50 % to P = 75 %, and then increase by 44.95 × 106  m3  to P = 95 %. These fluctuations are mainly influenced by the availability of Yellow River water resources across different water supply scenarios in the planning year 2030. Accordingly, the water allocation to AG would decrease by 47.93 × 106  m3  from P = 50 % to P = 75 %, followed by an increase of 23.83 × 106  m3  from P = 50 % to P = 75 %. Notably, AG stand as the largest water user in the ZKID-II, with allocations of 432.33 × 106  m3  (P = 50 %) and 384.40 × 106  m3  (P = 75 %), respectively. Across different scenarios, the forthcoming allocation of water resources to agricultural irrigation within irrigated areas exhibits comparatively obvious fluctuation in comparison to other water users. Therefore, to ensure the security of agricultural water use in irrigated areas, a strategic enhancement of water conservation efficiency is paramount. This entails a proactive promotion of agricultural water-saving irrigation technology and bolstering the development of agricultural water-saving initiatives specifically tailored for ZKID-II. Fig. 6   illustrates the distribution of water allocation percentages across different ADs for three water supply scenarios within the ZKID-II in 2030 under λ = 0.8   . There are significant variances in the allocated water volumes across different ADs. Among the three water supply scenarios, the proportion of water allocation across the eight ADs generally follow this order: GL < SF < ZM < ZC < TK < QX < XF < TX. Under P = 50 %, the ADs with the highest and lowest percentages are TX with 30.09 % and GL with 0.06 %, respectively. These differences primarily stem from variations in the socio-economic development scale among different ADs within the ZKID-II. Meanwhile, the proportion of water resources allocated to each AD remains relatively stable across the three water supply scenarios. For instance, the water allocation proportions for TX and QX would decrease by −0.33 % and 0.41 % from P = 50 % to P = 75 %, followed by slight decrease by 0.45 % and −0.31 % from P = 75 % to P = 95 %, respectively. This trend is largely shaped by the water consumption and supply structures within different ADs. Fig. 7   displays the optimal water allocation scheme for different ADs and users with three water supply scenarios in the ZKID-II in 2030 under λ = 0.8   . The water allocated for AG in TX would amount to 128.86 × 106  m3  (P = 50 %), 117.45 × 106  m3  (P = 75 %), and 120.66 × 106  m3  (P = 95 %) in Fig. 7 (e), respectively. Simultaneously, the water allocated to AG far surpasses that of other users, such as LI, SE, TE, SA, and LA. This trend is consistent across the entirety of ZKID-II. For example, under P = 50 %, the water allocated for AG in QX, TK, and ZC would be 93.62 × 106  m3 , 75.15 × 106  m3  and 25.75 × 106  m3 , respectively, surpassing that of other water users in the area. This phenomenon mainly arises due to the main function of the irrigation area is food production, making agriculture its predominant water user. Moreover, alterations in water allocation for AG across various ADs would exhibit relatively significant fluctuations compared to other users, spanning from P = 50 % to P = 95 %, displaying an overall trend of first increase followed by decrease. This pattern is mainly related to the availability of water resources in the irrigation area in 2030, subjected to the future local climatic and hydrological conditions, as well as the Yellow River diversion water supply policy. Fig. 8   depicts the discharges of wastewater, COD , and NH3 -N  for three water supply scenarios in 2030 under λ = 0.8   . Significant differences in the volume of discharged wastewater are evident among various (Fig. 8 (b)). For instance, under P = 50 %, TX and XF exhibit relatively high volumes of wastewater discharge: 47.93 × 106  m3  and 43.77 × 106  m3 , respectively. Conversely, GL and SF demonstrate comparably lower volumes of wastewater discharge: 0.11 × 106  m3  and 0.29 × 106  m3 , respectively. This difference is influenced by factors such as the production conditions of secondary and tertiary industries, the size of the local population, and the scale of agricultural cultivation in different ADs. Moreover, TX exhibits the highest proportion of NH 3  -N  discharge among all ADs under P = 75 % (Fig. 8 (a)). Similarly, TX exhibits the highest proportion of COD  discharge, mainly due to the extensive development of local secondary and tertiary industries and limited sewage treatment capacity. To mitigate pollutant discharge, it is essential to prioritize the construction of sewage treatment projects and enhance local sewage treatment capacity in the future, thereby promoting environmental sustainability and safeguarding water quality. Fig. 9   presents water shortages for diverse water users across three water supply scenarios in 2030 under λ = 0.8   . Different ADs would experience varying degrees of water shortage. For example, under P = 75 %, XF would face the highest water shortages volume reaching to 47.15 × 106  m3 , while GL has little water shortage. Additionally, the water shortages are mainly concentrated in AG, while SE, TE, SA, and LA experience relatively minor water shortages under all three water supply scenarios. For instance, AG would still face a significantly water shortage of 28.97 % (156.81 × 106  m3 ), while SE, TE, SA, and LA would experience water shortage of 2.62 % (1.82 × 106  m3 ), 3.91 % (0.94 × 106  m3 ), 34.07 % (4.09 × 106  m3 ), and 45.02 % (4.28 × 106  m3 ) under P = 75 %, respectively. The AG would also experience water shortage of 5.52 % under P = 50 % and 31.94 % under P = 95 %. These shortages primarily arise from the increasing design frequency, which exacerbates the contradictions between water supply and water demand.  3.3 Comparing among different solution approaches of multi-objective model Fig. 10   presents the comparison results of economic benefits (maximum economic incomes), social benefits (minimum water shortages), and ecological benefits (minimum total pollutant discharge) in 2030, obtained by solving the SMOFCP-WRMS model using five solution methods under P = 75 %, including CP method, NSGA-II, NSGA-III, combined NSGA-II with CP method, and combined NSGA-III with CP method. As depicted in Fig. 10 (a), the average economic benefits obtained by above five methods in the ZKID-II are 2527.51 × 106  CNY, [2558.46, 2568.46] × 106  CNY, [2563.13, 2570.13] × 106  CNY, 2568.45 × 106  CNY, and 2570.63 × 106  CNY. Meanwhile, the social water shortages are 180.92 × 106  m3 , [170.42, 174.35] × 106  m3 , [167.91, 169.86] × 106  m3 , 171.06 × 106  m3 , and 168.67 × 106  m3  (Fig. 10 (b)). The total pollutant discharge are 6410.70 tonne, [6751.04, 6770.07] tonne, [6775.30, 6790.01] tonne, 6769.87 tonne, and 6789.86 tonne (Fig. 10 (c)). Meanwhile, Table S4  presents the water deficient ratio under six credibility levels obtained by different methods. The results derived from solving Meta-heuristic algorithms (NSGA-II and NSGA-III) are compared with traditional methods of multi-objective programming, showing consistency with the model’s set conditions and boundary range. In addition, Table S5  shows the comparison results of three objectives between NSGA-II and NSGA-III. Results showed that combining NSGA-III with CP method outperformed the other four methods (CP method, NSGA-II, NSGA-III, and combined NSGA-II with CP method), yielding higher economic and social benefits. Specifically, compared to the traditional CP method, this combination boosted average economic benefits by 1.71 % and reduced average water deficiency by 6.77 %. Similarly, economic benefits and social benefits improved by 0.08 % and 1.39 %, respectively, compared to the combined NSGA-II and CP method. These findings are consistent with the research carried out by Zhu et al. (2023). Simultaneously, the results of compromise-optimal solutions by combined NSGA-III with CP and combined NSGA-III with CP method are included in the Pareto-optimal set of NSGA-II and NSGA-III, respectively. This is because the results of the former (in minimum CP) are selected from the Parato solution set of the latter. Furthermore, the Pareto fronts corresponding to NSGA-III are slightly better than NSGA-II (Chen et al., 2023 ). The findings also highlight a positively correlated relationship between economic and ecological benefits, indicating that increasing water allocation can boost economic benefits while potentially straining the environment. Notably, as the credibility level increases, economic and social benefits decrease (Fig. 10 (d)–(e)), while ecological benefits increase in Fig. 10 (f). The total pollutant emissions in compromise-optimal solutions obtained by the combined NSGA-III with CP method are 5.91 % and 0.30 % higher than those achieved using the CP methods and the combined NSGA-II with CP method, respectively. Consequently, in contrast to the optimization results derived from the other four methods, the combined NSGA-III with CP method in this study leans more towards maximizing economic and social benefits. Although the CP method and the combined NSGA-II with CP method excel in optimizing ecological benefits, they often overlook the broader target range and comprehensive development needs of ZKID-II. Therefore, employing the combined NSGA-III and CP method to resolve the SMOFCP-RWMS model emerges as a more reasonable approach to tackle the uncertainties associated with water resources management in irrigation areas.   4 Conclusions Here, we introduce a SMOFCP approach to effectively addresses the complex interplay among multiple objectives and uncertainties, including various scenarios and fuzzy sets. This approach adeptly handles the multiple uncertain parameters characterized by fuzzy numbers in the objective functions and constraints of the optimization model. We develop the SMOFCP-WRMS model specifically for the water management in irrigation area, along with a novel solution method that combines expected value theory and the NSGA-III algorithm. Applying this optimization model and solution method to the ZKID-II case study generates diverse water resource optimization schemes under different credibility levels. Our study reveals several important findings: (1) Tradeoffs exist among economic, social, and ecological benefits in multi-water source management, thus prioritizing a compromise solution favoring higher economic benefits and fewer negative impacts (i.e. water shortages and pollutant charge); (2) Increasing credibility levels will decrease water supply, leading to lower net economic benefits and reduced pollutant discharge; (3) Water scarcity is mainly concentrated in agriculture, with the water shortage rate increasing by 24.22 % from P = 50 % to P = 95 % under the three water supply scenarios; (4) Despite the decline in ecological benefits in compromise-optimal solutions obtained by the combined NSGA-III and CP method, there are improvements in economic benefits and social benefits compared to both the CP and the combined NSGA-II and CP method. (5) Increasing transferred water in the future can effectively alleviate water resources shortage in irrigation areas. The framework developed in this study addresses the complex challenge of water resources allocation in irrigated areas under multiple uncertainties and multi-objective conditions. By integrating uncertainties into a MOP model using fuzzy information and scenarios setting, it offers useful strategies for robust water resources management planning. Our proposed model framework and solution method can also be extended to similar areas, aiding the formulation of enhanced water resources allocation schemes and improving the water resources management effectiveness in irrigated areas. But the search capabilities of metaheuristic techniques vary depending on the type of problem being addressed. Although metaheuristic techniques (e.g. NSGA-II and NSGA-III) show satisfactory performance in conventional optimization problems, they may struggle with more complex problems characterized by intricate domains or boundaries (Mortazavi, 2022, 2024 ). Moreover, our research mainly addresses the uncertain water resources planning issues using the MOP, SA, and FCP approaches. It neglects the deep uncertainties that may yield unreliable designs owing to palpable climate change and rapid socioeconomic transformation. Thus, novel decision analytical frameworks, such as multi-objective robust decision making and dynamic adaptive policy pathways, should be further considered (Singh, 2023 ). Additionally, considering the reliance of multi-water source systems on the energy supply and maintenance, future research could explore ways to reduce carbon dioxide emissions through water resources planning and management, contributing to green and low-carbon development, particularly in the context of global warming.
1 Introduction Over the past century, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions have caused significant climate change. The Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) highlights global rapid warming, particularly evident at the land scale, with a mean air temperature increase of 0.99 °C and 1.09 °C from 2011–2020 and 2001–2020, respectively, compared to the pre-industrial period (1850–1900) (IPCC, 2021 ). The Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) reported the global mean surface air temperature exceeding 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels in June 2023 (C3S, 2023 ). Global warming intensifies the water cycle, impacts water availability, and exacerbates water-related extremes such as floods and droughts (Dai, 2013; Yang et al., 2014 ). As a climatic calamity, drought poses enduring repercussions on human civilizations, affecting agricultural yield, industrial and household water supplies, and ecological balance (Touma et al., 2015 ). Drought is a global phenomenon that exhibits regional variation; therefore, understanding its response to climate change is crucial for water resource management across diverse regions (Asadi Zarch et al., 2015; Sivakumar, 2011 ). The Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP) is pivotal role in providing essential information for comprehending the global climate system and assessing socioeconomic hazards (Eyring et al., 2016; O'Neill et al., 2016 ). Numerous studies utilizing CMIP datasets have explored socioeconomic risks and projected future changes in drought conditions at regional and global scales (Chen and Yuan, 2021; Mesbahzadeh et al., 2020; Zeng et al., 2022; Sreeparvathy and Srinivas, 2022 ). While regional studies have confirmed increased drought severity in India, China, the Mediterranean, and Southeast Asia (Leng et al., 2015; Bisht et al., 2019; Sam et al., 2019; Tramblay et al., 2020 ), global studies have identified Europe, China, Southeast Asia, and North America as experiencing increased drought severity (Cook et al., 2020; Gu et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2022 ). By assessing meteorological, hydrological, and soil droughts, both Phases 5 and Phase 6 of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP5 and CMIP6) detected an increase in the spatial extent, frequency, and duration of future droughts across regions owing to the response of drought variables (precipitation, runoff, and soil moisture) to warming temperatures (Zhao and Dai, 2015; Zhao and Dai, 2022; Wang et al., 2021 ). A study conducted in Iran indicated changes in temperature and precipitation under climate change, suggesting that drought severity and duration will intensify in the near and far future compared with historical periods (Behzadi et al., 2024 ). However, studies conducted in Southeast Asia showed a decline in future drought under the SSP2-4.5 scenario, whereas an increasing trend in drought was observed under the SSP5-8.5 scenario (Supharatid and Nafung, 2021 ). Compared with historical periods, future droughts appear to exhibit an increasing trend in most regions globally, although the aforementioned studies generally select arbitrary future periods (near future and distant future) for comparison with historical events. Despite these findings, Wu et al. (2021)  revealed a nonlinear response of drought risk changes to anthropogenic forcing, emphasizing the need for further research on regional responses under different warming levels. Compared to assessing drought over a uniform period, this study quantified the changes in future drought conditions under different emission scenarios at the same warming levels, providing a more precise quantification of the impact of global warming on future droughts. Owing to global warming and human disruptions, the stationary assumption of conventional drought indices is outdated, as hydrometeorological processes no longer maintain stationary behavior (Milly et al., 2008; Xiong and Guo, 2004 ). Some studies on future climate scenarios have recommended incorporating non-stationarity in drought assessments under global warming (Wu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022 ). By applying a dynamic approach that uses moving time windows to compute climate normals, Peres et al. (2023)  incorporated the non-stationarity of drought into their future drought projections for Italy for 2041–2070. The Generalized Additive Model in Location, Scale, and Shape (GAMLSS), the most commonly used method for non-stationary drought modeling, is considered a flexible non-stationary probabilistic model that offers a robust tool for drought assessment (Rigby and Stasinopoulos, 2005; Kang and Jiang, 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021 ). This (semi) parametric regression model characterizes non-stationarity by constructing linear or nonlinear functions between response parameters and explanatory variables (covariates) and has been studied at regional scales in countries such as China, the United States, India, and Australia in the historical period. Meteorological or anthropogenic factors, including the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), time (t), and water demand (WD), are used as explanatory variables for drought factors (precipitation and runoff) (Apurv and Cai, 2019; Das et al., 2020; Ju et al., 2021; Rashid and Beecham, 2019; Shao et al., 2022; Song et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2015 ). While a few studies have introduced non-stationarity into future drought projections (Brunner and Gilleland, 2024; Peres et al., 2023; Ploszai et al., 2022 ), most have used historical period distribution parameters to fit future drought variables based on CMIP data (stationary assumption) (Gu et al., 2020; Sofia et al., 2024; Su et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2022 ), although non-stationarity is manifested in the metro-hydrological process under global warming, with changes in mean or variance (Slater et al., 2021 ). Overall, holistic evaluations and projections of future droughts using nonstationary approaches are lacking, especially globally. Considering various elements, including precipitation, temperature, runoff, and soil moisture, and using indices such as the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), Standardized Runoff Index (SRI), and Standardized Soil Moisture Index (SSMI), comprehensive drought evaluation is essential because a single drought index only captures one aspect of the overall drought situation (McKee et al., 1993; Shukla and Wood, 2008; Beguería et al., 2014; Das et al., 2021a; Fowé et al., 2023 ). Because of its simplicity, the SPI index is extensively used to predict droughts under different climate scenarios. (Wu et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2022 ). However, as mentioned previously, global warming has intensified the hydrological cycle, increasing precipitation and temperature sensitivity (Fischer and Schär, 2009; Giorgi et al., 2001; Schär et al., 2004 ). With increasing temperature, potential evapotranspiration (PET) increases due to the increased surface vapor pressure deficits (Zhao and Dai, 2022 ). Clausius–Clapeyron (CC) is the thermodynamics relationship between atmospheric water content and temperature, and precipitation extremes follow ∼7 %°C−1  CC rate with temperature increase (John et al., 2022; Li et al., 2021 ). The impact of global warming on precipitation and temperature sensitivity has shifted the focus from precipitation to evapotranspiration as a key influencer of drought, as demonstrated by Wang et al. (2021) . The Reconnaissance Drought Index (RDI), which was proposed by Tsakiris et al. (2007) , followed the same procedure as the SPI, with the ratio of precipitation to evapotranspiration (P/PET) fitted to a lognormal distribution, thus reflecting the aggregated deficit between P and PET. Compared to the SPI, which only considers precipitation, the RDI, which emphasizes the roles of precipitation and potential evapotranspiration in drought, demonstrates a strong ability to identify droughts and addresses the limitations of the SPI in predicting droughts under climate change and increasing temperatures (Abdelmalek and Nouiri, 2020; Asadi Zarch et al., 2015; Cheng et al., 2020; Shokoohi and Morovati, 2015 ). Previous studies have demonstrated high spatial and temporal consistency between the RDI and SPEI in evaluating and predicting droughts, with a high correlation between the two indices (Adnan et al., 2018; Vergni et al., 2021 ). However, the RDI demonstrated superior performance over the SPEI in detecting severe droughts and droughts in semi-arid or arid areas (Khan et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2015 ). Simultaneously, regional non-stationary drought assessments conducted for historical and future periods have demonstrated the compatibility of the RDI with the GAMLSS model (Bazrafshan and Hejabi, 2018; Das et al., 2020; Ploszai et al., 2022 ). Consequently, RDI was chosen for future drought assessment in this study. Blöschl et al. (2019)  identified 23 major unsolved problems in hydrology (UPH) through a community initiative. In the variability of extreme hydrologic phenomena, they posed these questions: “How do flood-rich and drought-rich periods arise? Are they changing, and if so, why?” The aforementioned studies have attempted to assess the evolution of droughts under future climate simulations and changes in meteorological variables. However, assessing and comparing droughts based on stationary and non-stationary approaches under different warming levels remains lacking. This study aimed to fill gaps by investigating meteorological drought changes under 1.5–3.0 °C warming levels using both stationary and non-stationary approaches. By analyzing data from 15 GCMs in the CMIP6 dataset and two Shared Socioeconomic Pathways, we addressed three key questions: 1) What patterns and spatial distributions characterize the meteorological variables used for drought calculation under varying levels of future warming? 2) Which regions have emerged as drought response hotspots amid global warming? 3) How do non-stationary and stationary drought indices differ in the evaluation of global drought changes? Drought hotspots are identified as regions exhibiting notable increases or sustained high values of drought features (frequency, duration, severity, and spatial extent) compared to historical periods. This study fills the gap in previous studies and provides a more precise understanding of the potential impacts of climate change on global drought conditions, thus providing effective policies and planning measures for disaster prevention and mitigation.  2 Data and study area 2.1 Data Daily precipitation datasets were obtained from the Global Precipitation Climatology Center (GPCC) V.2018 at a spatial resolution of 1° × 1° (Fuchs et al., 2009 ). The observed maximum and minimum temperature datasets were obtained from the Climate Prediction Center (CPC) at a spatial resolution of 0.5° × 0.5° (https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/ ). Daily precipitation, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature simulations were derived from 15 GCMs available in the CMIP6 dataset (https://esgf-node.llnl.gov/projects/cmip6/ ). Two future scenarios were selected: Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 2-4.5 (SSP245) and Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 5-8.5 (SSP585). These scenarios incorporate greenhouse gas emissions and socioeconomic development. SSP245 represents a moderate forcing scenario with a projected stabilization of radiative forcing at approximately 4.5  W / m  - 2      by 2100 (3 °C global warming compared to pre-industrial levels), with medium land-use regulation by a partially involved management sector resulting in a declining rate of deforestation and a medium increase in land productivity, with a predominance of material-intensive consumption. SSP585 represents a high-forcing scenario with a projected stabilization of radiative forcing at approximately 8.5  W / m  - 2      by 2100 (5 °C global warming compared to pre-industrial levels), with medium land-use regulation by a completely involved management sector resulting in a declining rate of deforestation and a rapid increase in productivity, with a predominance of resource-intensive consumption (Popp et al., 2017 ). Thus, we assessed future droughts under two future development scenarios: a fossil fuel emissions limitation scenario and an uncontrolled emissions scenario. To ensure consistency in the spatial resolution, this study employed the inverse distance-weighted method to interpolate both the GCM datasets and observed data to a spatial resolution of 0.25° × 0.25°. This allowed for the seamless integration and further analysis of data obtained from various climate centers. To narrow the uncertainties of the precipitation and temperature and increase their representativeness, 15 GCMs extracted from various climate centers were chosen; further details can be obtained from Wu et al. (2022) ’s paper. This study analyzed the results based on the ensemble means of 15 GCMs.  2.2 Study area To accurately assess global drought conditions under future climate scenarios, considering the variability in meteorological and hydrological conditions across different regions worldwide is important. Hydrometeorological analyses and calculations should be performed at the sub-regional level to capture the specific characteristics of each area (Giorgi and Bi, 2005; Giorgi et al., 2001; Spinoni et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021 ). Following the approach outlined by Giorgi and Bi (2005) , we divided the world into 19 sub-regions, excluding Greenland, Antarctica, and sporadic areas. The geographic locations, latitudes, longitudes, and names of these 19 sub-regions are shown in Fig. 1   and listed in Table 1  .   3 Methodology 3.1 Definition of 1.5–3.0 °C global warming periods This study used the historical simulation data from CMIP6, covering the period from 1850 to 2014, to define the periods corresponding to global warming levels of 1.5–3.0 °C. The most recent 30 years of this historical period, specifically 1985–2014, were selected as the historical period. During this historical period, the global average surface air temperature was 0.66 °C higher than the pre-industrial periods of 1850–1900 (Ji et al., 2020; Morice et al., 2012 ). This historical period was used to determine the additional temperature increase required to reach the 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, and 3.0 °C warming levels. Specifically, these levels corresponded to global average temperature increases of 0.84 °C, 1.34 °C, 1.84 °C, and 2.34 °C above the historical period, respectively, as shown in Fig. S1 . The timeframes representing 1.5–3.0 °C warming levels for both SSPs were identified by applying a 30-year running average to the global average surface air temperature. The temperature was obtained from the mean of 15 previously referenced GCM simulations and an ensemble of multiple models. For the SSP245 scenario, the 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, and 3.0 °C warming periods were defined as S1 (2009–2038), S2 (2025–2054), S3 (2041–2070), and S4 (2062–2091) stages, respectively. Similarly, for the SSP585 scenario, the corresponding periods were defined as S1 (2008–2037), S2 (2019–2048), S3 (2029–2058), and S4 (2038–2067) stages. The historical period was identified as the S0 (1985–2014) stage.  3.2 Bias correction methods Bias-correction techniques were employed to address the challenges posed by biased model outputs in hydrologic simulations. These techniques aim to utilize information from GCMs, which often exhibit significant biases, particularly in temperature and precipitation simulations (Christensen et al., 2008 ). This study applied a bias correction method known as two-stage multivariate quantile mapping (TSQM) (Guo et al., 2019 ) to correct the GCM simulations of temperature and precipitation. The reference datasets used for the correction were obtained from the GPCC and CPC, and both the observed and GCM datasets were interpolated to a spatial resolution of 0.25° × 0.25°. The TSQM approach comprises two stages. In the first stage, the marginal distribution of each variable, including precipitation and maximum and minimum temperatures, was corrected using a univariate quantile mapping bias correction method (Chen et al., 2013 ). This method focuses on correcting the distribution of the variables. In the second stage, a distribution-free shuffle approach based on the work of Iman and Conover (1982)  was employed to reconstruct the inter-variable corrections among multiple variables. By combining these two stages, the TSQM method corrected the biases in the GCM simulations of precipitation and temperature and enhanced the accuracy and reliability of the data for further analysis in this study. This part of the calculation was performed using MATLAB software.  3.3 The reconnaissance drought index (RDI) Although the SPI is widely used in future climate risk projection analyses because of its simplicity and consideration of precipitation alone (Tramblay et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2022 ), it fails to consider that droughts can be caused by both influence of decreased precipitation and increased evaporation (Dai, 2013 ). Therefore, the incorporation of PET is crucial for drought modeling. The reconnaissance drought index (RDI) was introduced as an extension of the SPI, accounting for precipitation and PET, making it more sensitive and suitable for changing environments (Tsakiris et al., 2007 ). The RDI was calculated using the following process. First, we calculated the initial value of RDI (αk ), which represents an aggregated form at a monthly time step and is computed for each month of the hydrological year or the entire year. For the ith   year, the α k    is calculated based on a time interval of k (months) using the following equation (Eq. Second, the Standardized RDI (RDIst ), which follows a procedure similar to that of the SPI, is fitted to a lognormal distribution and then normalized (Eq. (2) ) (Tsakiris et al., 2007 ).(2) RDI  st ( k )  ( i )   = y k  ( i )   - y k   ¯    y k  ^       where y k    is ln a k  i        , y k   ¯     is the arithmetic mean of y k    and y k  ^    is the standard deviation. Among the various PET calculation methods, this study employed the Thornthwaite formula due to its low data requirements and reliance solely on temperature data. The RDI calculation process was facilitated using the SPEI package in R, which is available from the CRAN repository (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/SPEI/index.html ).  3.4 Modified Mann–Kendall trend test This study conducted trend analysis to assess the changes in the precipitation and temperature datasets obtained from the GCMs. Trend analysis employes a non-parametric method known as the Mann–Kendall (M-K) test analysis (Kendall, 1948; Mann, 1945 ), which has advantages in handling outliers (Gu et al., 2017 ). The M-K test has been widely used to detect climatic and hydrological trends (Acero et al., 2012; Da Silva, 2004 ). To handle datasets with serial autocorrelation that can affect the statistical tests' significance, a modified M-K test analysis proposed by Hamed and Rao (1998)  was applied in this study. For a specified confidence level, the null hypothesis is accepted when the Z value is less than the critical Z value (Z 1  -  p / 2    ). By applying the modified M-K test at a confidence level of 95 %, this study assessed the presence and significance of trends in precipitation and temperature datasets from the GCMs. In a changing world, the assumption that the distribution of the time series fluctuates and does not change in mean, variance, or shape is no longer applicable (Slater et al., 2021 ). In this study, we fitted the yearly P/PET ratio series to a lognormal distribution using a 30-year moving window. We then calculated the non-stationarity/stationarity of the distribution parameter (μ   and σ  , which referred to the mean and standard deviation of the P/PET series) by detecting if a trend existed in the distribution parameter’s series using the modified M-K test over the entire calculation period. The modified M-K test was performed using the ‘modifiedmk’ package in the R program (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/modifiedmk/index.html ).  3.5 The GAMLSS approach In this study, the GAMLSS model, introduced by Rigby and Stasinopoulos (2005) , was used to ascertain the correlation between the initial value of RDI (αk ) and time. GAMLSS is a unique type of univariate distributional regression model. This model allows all the parameters of the assumed response distribution to be interpreted as additive functions of the predictive variables using either linear or nonlinear functions. In the GAMLSS model, observations y i    for i = 1 , 2  , ⋯ , n   , are assumed to be independent conditional on θ  i   , with probability (density) function f y i  |  θ  i      . Here, θ  iT   = θ i 1   , θ i 2   , ⋯ , θ ip        represents a vector of p   parameters related to explanatory variables and random effects. Thus, the general GAMLSS model is defined as follows: Let y  T  = y 1  , y 2  , ⋯ , y n       be the vector of response variable observations. For k = 1 , 2  , ⋯ , p   , g k  ∙      is a known monotonic link function that relates θ k    to explanatory variables and random effects through an addictive model, given by Eq.
