(7) :(7) g k  θ k    = η k  = X k  β k  + ∑ j = 1  J k   h jk   x jk         where, θ k    and η k    are vectors of length n and X k    is a ( n X m )    matrix of explanatory variables. x jk     is the explanatory variable vector of length n for j = 1 , 2  , ⋯ , J k     and k = 1 , 2  , ⋯ , p   , and the function h jk     is the linear or nonlinear function of the explanatory variable x jk    . The first two population parameters, ϑ 1    and ϑ 2   , are typically referred to as the location and scale parameters, represented by μ   and σ  . However, due to the diverse range of distributions available in the GAMLSS family (over 80 distributions), other distribution parameters, τ   and ν  , can be utilized to fit the explanatory variables. In this study, a linear non-stationary lognormal RDI covariate was fitted using the GAMLSS framework. The parameters were estimated using the Maximum likelihood estimation method (MLE), while the location (μ  ) and scale (σ  ) parameters of lognormal distribution were fitted using the Rigby and Stasinopoulos (RS) algorithm (Rigby and Stasinopoulos, 1996 ). The RS algorithm was selected owing to its ease of implementation and successful application in fitting various distributions. All computations were performed using the GAMLSS R package available from the CRAN repository (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/gamlss/index.html ).  3.6 The non-stationary reconnaissance drought index (NRDI) The calculation procedure for the NRDI followed the same steps as the RDI construction, with the distinction that the probability distribution parameters of the lognormal distribution were non-stationary and varied over time. To fit the data of precipitation and potential evapotranspiration (α k   ) into a non-stationary model, location (μ  ) and scale (σ  ) parameters of the lognormal distribution were assumed to vary linearly with the time covariate. Unlike other studies that typically perform non-stationary fitting only for the location parameter (μ  ), this study calculated the NRDI drought index considering the changes in the location (μ  ) and scale (σ  ) parameters (Bazrafshan et al., 2018; Das et al., 2021b; Ploszai et al., 2022 ). The non-stationary index can be expressed as follows:(8) α k  t    L o g N o r m a l μ t   , σ t         (9) μ t   = a 1  + b 1  t     (10) σ t   = a 2  + b 2  t     where a 1   , b 1   , a 2   , b 2    are constants determined using the GAMLSS model described in the previous section. By establishing the time-dependent distribution function of α k   , the NRDI can be calculated as follows:(11) NRDI  st   t   = l n α k  t     - μ t    σ t          Mathematically, the RDI and NRDI follow similar calculation steps to the SPI. Consequently, the same drought classification method as the RDI was applied in this study, based on the thresholds established by McKee et al. (1993)  and Song et al. (2020) .  3.7 Drought event identification Considering that climate change impacts drought at longer time scales and previous studies have found notable differences between the NRDI and RDI for larger than 6-month scales (Bazrafshan and Hejabi, 2018; Jehanzaib et al., 2020 ), the 12-month RDI and NRDI indices were calculated in this study. An “under moderate drought” event was considered by spotting continuous spans of three months or more where the RDI/NRDI values decreased to −1 or less (Mckee et al., 1993 ), and for simplicity, the following drought events are presented as UMD. The spatial extent of the droughts was characterized by the area encompassing the number of grid points experiencing drought in each subregion at a particular moment. Drought frequency refers to the percentage of months in which drought occurred out of the total number of months calculated. The duration of a drought event was determined by enumerating the successive months during which the index remained beneath the set threshold (−1 in this study). Drought severity, on the other hand, was assessed by adding the absolute values of the drought index for a specific drought event (Yevjevich, 1967 ).   4 Results 4.1 Non-stationarity of the mean and standard deviation in drought variable series Fig. 2.1   shows the non-stationarity of the distribution parameters (μ   and σ  ) which are calculated by yearly P/PET series fitted to a lognormal distribution. In the lognormal distribution, μ   and σ   represent the mean and standard deviation of the time series, respectively. As shown in the figure, the trend of σ   shows an overall decrease in the SSP245 scenario, while ∼1/3 of the regions in the globe show a trend in μ  . Thus, we applied both RDI and NRDI indices in the whole study period and divided them into five stages representing the historical period and 1.5–3.0 °C warming levels for the evaluation of future drought conditions. In the high latitude of the north hemisphere (ALA and NAS), the northwest of China (TIB), and the Sahara (NAF) region, μ   shows an increasing trend, while in Southern North America (CAM), South America (AMZ and SSA), Southern Africa (SAF), Mediterranean region and surroundings (MED, NEU, and CAS), and Australia (AUS), μ   shows a decreasing trend. As a result, P/PET series were detected almost globally with non-stationary trends. Further, three trends of increasing, no, and decreasing in μ   and σ   were combined into nine classifications, and the percentage of different classifications in each sub-region was counted. Among various classifications, four classifications (+,−), (NO,−), (−, NO), and (−,−) dominate in most regions around the world. From the left panels in the figure, we can see that except for sub-regions which show partially no trend in both the μ   and σ  , the three classifications account for more than 90 % of all sub-regions, and the first six sub-regions, ALA, NAS, EAS, TIB, SAS, EAF, (NO,−), and (+,−) classifications dominate in these areas while in the last ten sub-regions, (NO,−), and (−,−) classifications dominate. Also, the four sub-regions AMZ, MED, AUS, and CAM have most (−,−) trends. Fig. 2.2   is the same analysis as Fig. 2.1  except applied in the SSP585 scenario. In the SSP585 scenario, the areas of decreasing trend in μ   have further expanded, while part of Australia shows an increasing trend of σ  . Thus, in the 19 sub-regions of the world, except some areas in ALA, NAS, TIB, EAF, and NAF show an increasing trend of μ  , the majority of sub-regions are dominated by decreasing trends in μ  . For the distribution parameters of the P/PET series, a decrease in μ   shows that the region might be drier in the future. Nevertheless, the decreasing trend in σ   increases uncertainty about future droughts. Thus, changes in P, PET, and drought characteristics in future periods compared to historical periods were analyzed below to identify more or less droughts and differences between the two indices in the 19 sub-regions.  4.2 Spatial distribution of drought variables changes at the 1.5–3.0 °C warming levels Fig. 3.1   shows the relative change of average annual precipitation and average annual PET in the future period (S1–S4 stages) compared to the historical period. The percentage of change for the four future stages (S1–S4 stages) compared to the historical period (S0 stage) was counted by calculating the average annual precipitation and average annual PET for each of the five stages. From the figure, we can see that each future stage has a global increase in PET compared to the historical stage, with the smallest increase in the S1 phase in the SSP245 scenario and the increase in the remaining three stages is more or less the same. Compared to the historical period, the largest increase was over 40 %, while the increase in the rest of the regions among 0 %–20 %. Inter-regional comparisons show the largest increases in PET in the Amazon (AMZ), Northern Africa (NAF), and Northwestern China (TIB). On the other hand, the results for precipitation show larger increases at high latitudes in the Northern Hemisphere (ALA and NAS), the Sahara region (NAF), and Northwestern China (TIB), with a value of more than 50 %. while decreases in the Amazon region (AMZ), Western Australia (AUS), Mediterranean region (MED), and South Africa (SAF), with a value of around 10 %. In contrast to PET, changes in precipitation manifest more and more stronger among the four future stages. The changes in both precipitation and PET lead to changes in the distribution parameters in Fig. 2.1 , due to the overall increase in the PET series, changes in the precipitation series determine the trend of the mean value (μ  ). In conjunction with the two figures, sub-regions like ALA, NAS, EAS, TIB, SAS, and EAF that are dominated by (+,−) classification, tend to have more precipitation. Sub-regions with both precipitation decrease and PET increase like AMZ, MED, AUS, CAM, and SAF are dominated by (−,−) classification. Fig. 3.2   shows the results for the SSP585 scenario, and the results remain fairly consistent in terms of spatial and temporal distribution. However, where precipitation shows a larger increase (ALA, NAS, NAF, and TIB) in the SSP245 scenario has a slight amplification of area and range in the SSP585 scenario. This amplification is also reflected in the PET results for the SSP585 scenario. This increased the μ   decreasing trend classification in each sub-region (see Fig. 2.2 ). Overall, the SSP585 scenario seems to be drier in the future compared to the SSP245 scenario. Future drought conditions manifest differently in different sub-regions at different warming levels and are further analyzed using both the RDI and NRDI index as presented below.  4.3 Spatial distribution of drought frequency changes at the 1.5–3.0 °C warming levels Fig. 4.1   presents the relative change in the frequency of UMD for future periods (S1–S4 stages) compared to the historical period (S0 stage), using the RDI and NRDI indices for the SSP245 scenario. Although there is a clear increase in drought frequency across the globe. In contrast, drought frequency in the high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere (Alaska and Northern Asia) (ALA and NAS), northwestern China (TIB), India (SAS), and North and Eastern Africa (NAF and EAF) detected a slight decrease/no trend and a decrease within onefold in the NRDI and RDI indices, respectively. This is because the RDI captured an increase in precipitation in these areas, which led to the determination that the area would become wetter. In fact, there is an increasing trend of the μ   parameter for the P/PET series in the SSP245 scenario, and using a fixed distribution parameter will lead to the underestimation of drought in a non-stationary circumstance since a lognormal distribution with a smaller μ   will overestimate the drought index by overestimating the probability. Meanwhile, drought is defined as the negative anomaly event for the drought variables and its probability always falls in the lower quartile. Thus, a decrease in the σ   parameter leads to the underestimation of droughts in the future (see Fig. 5 ). In these regions, drought conditions will be more severe than those calculated by the RDI index. The NRDI index, on the other hand, has the ability to model the non-stationary of the initial values well and is more robust under global warming. Likewise, in regions where precipitation shows an increasing trend including the Amazon region (AMZ), Western Australia, the Mediterranean region (NEU and MED), and South Africa (SAF), the RDI index overestimates the future drought conditions without considering the decreasing of the μ   parameter. The relative changes in future drought calculated by the RDI and NRDI indices are generally consistent in areas including Central North America, northwestern and southeastern Asia, and central Africa where the μ   distribution parameter does not show a trend. Relative changes in drought frequency at different warming levels suggested a higher frequency of drought in the near future at 1.5 °C and 2.0 °C warming levels (S1 and S2 stages) rather than in the far future at 2.5 °C and 3.0 °C warming levels (S3 and S4 stages). This may be explained by the continued increase in precipitation while relatively fixed PET changes among the four future stages during the SSP245 period. Among the 19 sub-regions, six sub-regions of the ENA, AMZ, MED, SAS, and EAS are defined as hotspot regions of drought due to their significant increase in drought frequency relative to historical periods in the near future period. The results in Fig. 4.2    can be validated for drought frequency changes under a higher emissions scenario (SSP585), the spatial and temporal distributions of drought frequency are very similar to the SSP245 scenario, with only minor differences. Greater drought variability in the SSP585 scenario due to changes in P and PET is found. The RDI index presents a wider range of underestimation or overestimation in the SSP585 scenario. We can come to a common conclusion that the increase in drought frequency decreased gradually from the near future (S1 and S2 stage) to the far future (S3 and S4 stage). The sub-region defined as a drought hotspot in the SSP245 scenario also shows an increase in the SSP585 scenario that exceeds that of the other sub-regions.  4.4 Changes of drought characteristics in 19 sub-regions at the 1.5–3.0 °C warming levels 4.4.1 Boxplots of drought duration and severity Fig. 6.1   presents the boxplot of the relative change in the duration of UMD for future periods (S1–S4 stages) compared to the historical period (S0 stage), using the RDI and NRDI indices for the SSP245 scenario. Broadly, there is an escalation in drought duration throughout all future stages relative to the historical period according to the two indices. On the whole, the median increase ranged from 10 % to 40 % and gradually decreased from the near future (S1 and S2 stages) to the far future (S3 and S4 stages) (Details in Table S1 ). As the warming level rises, the variability of drought duration in each region compared to the S0 stage diminishes. These findings reaffirmed that an escalation in warming levels does not translate to a linear amplification of drought duration estimated by the RDI/NRDI indices. By the S3 or S4 stage, specific sub-regions such as ALA, TIB, NAS, SAS, EAF, and EAS have detected a decrease or minor increase in median and below drought durations compared to the historical period by RDI and NRDI indices, respectively (blue or grey background). In these sub-regions, the RDI underestimates drought in all future four stages because it does not take into consideration the positive change in the distribution parameter μ  . In the remaining sub-regions, the RDI index shows more or less overestimation of the relative changes in future drought conditions compared to the NRDI index, especially in the four sub-regions in which precipitation shows a decreasing trend including CAM, AMZ, MED, and AUS (red background). Unlike drought mitigation, the difference between such stationary and non-stationary indices as above increases in global warming from the near future to the far future and is consistent with the stronger changes in precipitation series. Meanwhile, given the decline in the global distribution parameter σ   (i.e., standard deviation), we can observe in Fig. 6.1  that the upper and lower quantile changes in the box plot of the NRDI index are smaller than those of the RDI index. That means that in the future the variability of drought will decrease with the region. Fig. 6.2   shows the same analysis in drought duration applied in the SSP585 scenario. At the same warming level, the relative change in drought durations for the SSP585 scenario remains essentially the same in distribution and magnitude compared to the SSP245 scenario. That is, except for a few sub-regions (ENA, AMZ, CAM, MED, etc.) the growth is between 0 % and 40 % and relative change decreases in the near future (S1 and S2 stage) to the far future (S3 and S4 stage). With the distribution parameter μ   showing an increasing downward trend in nearly all sub-regions of the globe, sub-regions like ALA, NAS, EAS, and TIB (blue background), where the underestimation of the drought condition in the RDI index alleviates, while drought is further overestimated in sub-regions including CAS, SEA, ENA, WNA, NEU sub-regions (red background). The two indices identified a more than 50 % increase in drought durations especially in the near future periods (S1 or S2 stages) in ENA, AMZ, and CAM sub-regions under both SPP245 and SSP585 scenarios (Details in Table S2 ), and these sub-regions were defined as drought hotspots. Fig. 7.1   and Fig. 7.2   presents the boxplot of the relative change in the severity of UMD for future periods (S1–S4 stages) compared to the historical period (S0), using the RDI and NRDI indices for the SSP245 and SSP585 scenario, respectively. The relative change in drought duration and severity remains consistent across sub-regions in the future periods, with a general increase, which means more drought will occur in the future within the two emission scenarios. Nonetheless. The change in drought severity was more intense than duration, with larger multiples found in drought severity relative to the historical period and with an average change at around 40 % and a minuscule reduction than 40 % in the SSP245 and SSP585 scenarios, respectively (Details in Table S3  and Table S4 ). Similarly, drought severity shows an overall more pronounced increase in the near future (S1 and S2 stage), while little change is indicated in the far future, especially in the S4 stage. In summary, the results combining drought duration and severity show that the NRDI index detects less variability in interregional droughts in future periods due to its capability to consider non-stationarity for drought variables and change distribution parameters over time. There are regional differences in the distinction between RDI and NRDI indices, and an underestimation of the RDI index is discovered in the ALA, TIB, NAS, and EAF sub-regions (blue background).  4.4.2 Joint analysis of drought duration and severity Fig. 8.1   further substantiates the consistent change between the duration and severity mentioned above in the boxplot by comparing mean duration and mean severity across five stages and 19 sub-regions. In the figure, we present drought characteristics evaluated by both the NRDI and RDI indices using different symbols while red color represents the RDI index and blue color represents the NRDI index. The left y-axis shows the value of duration and the right y-axis shows the value of severity. For the duration, it varies from 6.0 to 9.5 among the 19 sub-regions in the S0 stage and reaches the biggest in the S1 stage with a value around 9.0–10.0 except MED and CAM sub-regions, and gradually decreases in the S2–S4 stages, although the durations are still larger compared to the S0 stage. Sub-regions with the greatest durations include EAS, TIB, SEA, SAS, SAF, and AMZ. For the severity, it ranges from around 11.0 to 12.0 in the S0 stage except for the lower value in ENA and MED, while the higher value in TIB. With global warming, the maximum severity can reach 16.0–17.0 in most of the sub-regions. Sub-regions with the most severe severity include EAS, TIB, SAS, and SAF. Compared to the historical period, the 19 sub-regions have seen an increase in average duration and severity of 20 % and 40 %, respectively. From the S0 to S4 stages, this figure indicates that future drought conditions do not follow a linear increase with continued warming. Combining the results of duration and severity, we define the six sub-regions EAS, TIB, SEA, SAS, SAF, and AMZ as the drought hotspots. Furthermore, a comparison of the NRDI and RDI results reveals three classifications, RDI overestimates drought in the historical and near future periods (S0 and S1 stage) while underestimates drought in the far future (S3 and S4 stage) compared to NRDI index in the five sub-regions of ALA, NAS, TIB, EAF, NAF (blue background). RDI and NRDI indices show minor differences in the eight sub-regions of SAS, EAS, CAS, SEA, ENA, WNA, WAF, NEU (grey background), and RDI underestimates drought in the historical and near future periods (S0 and S1 stage) while overestimates drought in the far future (S3 and S4 stage) compared to NRDI index in the six sub-regions of SAF, SSA, AMZ, MED, AUS, and CAM (red background). This is consistent with the increasing trend, no trend, and decreasing trend in the distribution parameter μ   for each sub-region shown in Fig. 2.1 . Synthesizing the previous results, due to the use of fixed distribution parameters without considering the non-stationarity of the drought variables, sub-regions where the mean P/PET shows an increase and decrease in future scenarios, the RDI would correspond to an underestimation and an overestimation of drought conditions in that area. When applying the same analytical process to the SSP585 scenario, Fig. 8.2   is shown below. As with the previous results for relative changes in drought frequency, duration, and severity, only subtle differences are found in the same warming levels (S0–S4 stages) in comparison with the two future scenarios in the magnitude of the duration and severity. The mean drought duration generally remains unchangeable between the two emission scenarios and mean severity shows an increase of less than one in most sub-regions. It’s noteworthy that except for the sub-regions in ALA, NAS, TIB, EAF, and NAF (blue background), the RDI index in the rest of the sub-regions shows an overestimation in the far future period. This can be explained by the increase in the number of μ   parameter (i.e. the mean value) with a decreasing trend in all the sub-regions (see Fig. 2.2 ) in the SSP585 scenarios. The higher emission scenario (SSP585) will intensify the non-stationarity of the drought variables thus regions like NEU, WAF, WNA, and SEA sub-regions (grey background) have manifested differences between the RDI index and the NRDI index which not found in the SSP245 scenario.  4.4.3 Spatial extent changes of droughts The above-mentioned discussed drought conditions change in frequency, duration, and severity in each grid point. Fig. 9.1   displays the spatial extent of droughts in the 19 sub-regions at the historical (S0 stage) and future periods (S1–S4) stages, as measured by the RDI and NRDI indices in the SSP245 scenario. Firstly, the number of grid points experiencing drought in each stage (S0–S4 stages) within each sub-region was counted. Following that, the spatial extent of drought within the sub-region was calculated by dividing the area corresponding to the drought occurrence grid points by the total area of the sub-region. As the figure indicates, the spatial extent of the drought within the scope of 5 %–10 % in each sub-region in the historical period (S0 stage), and swells up to 15 %–20 % in the S1 stage at 1.5 °C warming level in most sub-regions, then gradually declined to the same ranges in the historical period at 3.0 °C warming level. In the near future (S1 and S2 stage), UMD areas can be two or even three times more extended than the S0 stage, which exposes more areas to the demographic, social, and ecological threat of drought. In this part of the results, six sub-regions in EAS, TIB, SAS, ENA, and AMZ are defined as hotspots of drought with a higher magnitude and longer increase of spatial extent. In common with the drought duration, severity, and frequency, the spatial extent of drought response to global warming performs the nonlinear increase as well. Equally, the pattern of overestimation or underestimation of regional drought by the RDI index due to ignoring the non-stationarity of the distribution parameters holds true for spatial extent. The maximum increase in spatial extent in the SSP585 scenario is expressed in two stages in the near future (S1 and S2 stages), rather than in the SSP245 scenario where it occurs mainly in the S1 stage (see Fig. 9.2  ). Like drought duration and severity in the SSP585 scenario, the overestimation in the spatial extent evaluated by the RDI index tends to be displayed in more sub-regions.   4.5 Comparison between RDI and NRDI indices under different classifications of distribution parameters Although we seem to have discovered the regional patterns between trends in drought variables and differences in stationary and non-stationary drought index assessments, often multiple combinations of distribution parameters appear in the same sub-region, and it is difficult to define accurately which combination is responsible for the discrepancy. Fig. 10.1   and Fig. 10.2   statistic the differences between the RDI and NRDI indices for each classification in each sub-region under the SSP245 scenario and SSP585 scenario, respectively, with classifications accounting for less than 10 % of the total being excluded because of the limited impact on the regional average. Firstly, three classifications in (+,+), (+, NO), and (+,−) show underestimation for the RDI index in the far future period with the increasing trend of the μ   parameter. Since the drought indices were implemented across the entire study period rather than applying the distribution parameters of one stage to other stages, an underestimation of the future drought is accompanied by an overestimation of the near period. The focus of the analysis should be on trends in differences. Negative values on the y-axis mean that a drought index without considering non-stationarity will underestimate drought in the future. Therefore, the results in Fig. 10.1  and Fig. 10.2  indicate areas of increasing μ   parameter where the RDI index underestimates future drought under global warming, which mainly occurred in the sub-regions including the ALA, NAS, EAF, and TIB (blue background).. On the other hand, three classifications in (−,+), (−, NO), and (−,−) show overestimation for the RDI index in the far future period with the decreasing trend of the μ   parameter, which mainly occurred in the sub-regions including the SSA, NEU, SAF, AMZ. AUS, CAM, and MED (red background). Compared to the SSP245 scenario, SSP585 appears to have more grids where μ   parameter exhibits a downward trend (e.g. CAS, ENA, SEA, WNA, and WAF), leading to the pattern of overestimation of the drought characteristics calculated by the RDI index of these sub-regions in the previous results.. Fig. 5  explains this discrepancy, if μ   decreases in the future, the cumulative distribution curve will shift left compared to the previous curve, Using the previous curve (which refers to the stationary RDI index) will underestimate the probability of a particular value and thus overestimate the drought situation, as smaller values mean greater drought. The rest of the three classifications in (NO,+), (NO, NO), and (NO,−) show more variation, according to Fig. 5 , (NO,+) should overestimate drought conditions while (NO,−) should underestimate drought conditions in the future. Both underestimation and overestimation appear in the (NO,−) trend (e.g. ALA and ENA in the SSP245 scenario), one of the reasons might be these grid points detected a trend in the distribution parameters without significance at the 95 % confidence level.   5 Discussion The fundamental assumption that natural systems have a time-invariant probability density function with constant distribution parameters underlies the planning, construction, and management of water resource facilities. However, meteorological and hydrological variables, such as precipitation and runoff, exhibit changes in mean or variance over historical and future periods owing to the impact of climate change or anthropogenic perturbations (Li et al., 2015; Um et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2021 ). In this study, we applied nonparametric modified M-K trend tests to assess distribution parameters (μ   and σ   for mean and standard deviation, respectively) derived from a 30-year moving window for initial values P/PET values of drought indices during the study periods (1985–2091 in the SSP245 scenario and 1985–2067 in the SSP585 scenario). Results indicated that approximately 15 % and 18 % of the grid points exhibited stationary using the μ   or σ   parameter for the two scenarios. Further analysis of the relative changes in the P and PET series at the historical and four future stages revealed an overall increase in PET with global warming of 1.5–3.0 °C. A substantial 40 % increase was observed in the P series at high latitudes in the Northern Hemisphere, the Saharan region, northern India, and Northwestern China, including sub-regions in ALA, NAS, NAF, TIB, and SAS. In contrast, sub-regions, including the Amazon region (AMZ), Western Australia (AUS), Mediterranean region (MED), and South Africa (SAF), showed a decrease of 10 %. These findings are consistent with those of other studies that utilized CMIP5 or CMIP6 model data at a global or regional scale (Almazroui et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2022 ). The combined P and PET changes contributed to regional distribution parameter patterns. The combination of increasing, no, or decreasing trends in the μ   and σ   distribution parameters yielded nine classifications, revealing patterns of underestimation or overestimation of future drought conditions by the RDI index compared to the NRDI index. When μ   showed an increasing (decreasing) trend, the cumulative distribution curve for future drought shifted right (left), resulting in the underestimation (overestimation) by the RDI index. This is because the fixed distribution curve overestimated (underestimated) the drought index value, leading to miscalculation of the probability. Grid points with a trend but failing the 95 % confidence test at μ = 0    introduced uncertainty in the drought patterns, reflected globally in the far future under the SSP245 and SSP585 scenarios. Underestimation occurred in the high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere (Alaska and Northern Asia) (ALA and NAS), northwestern China (TIB), India (SAS), and North and Eastern Africa (NAF and EAF) regions. In contrast, the Amazon region (AMZ), Southern South America (SSA), Central America (CAM), Western Australia (AUS), the Mediterranean region (NEU and MED), and South Africa (SAF) observed maximum overestimation. Applying historical distribution parameters to future periods may lead to an overall overestimation or underestimation if trends in drought variables persist (Su et al., 2021 ). Alternatively, the use of percentile thresholds without distribution assumptions appears to be a more reliable choice (Ukkola et al., 2020 ). In addition to addressing the non-stationary of future drought assessments, this study highlighted drought hotspots’ responses to climate change and monitored drought performance under various warming levels and emission scenarios. In summary, there is a general upward trend in drought compared to historical periods, with Northern North America, the Amazon region, the Mediterranean region, south-central Africa, and southeastern Asia identified as hotspots due to high variability and values in drought duration, severity, frequency, and spatial extent. This is consistent with previous studies that used various drought indices, including the SPI, SRI, and PDSI (Wu et al., 2022; Zhao and Dai, 2022 ), confirming the rationality of the constructed drought indices for projecting future drought conditions. After comparing future drought performances across warming levels and emission scenarios, this study identified a nonlinear response of meteorological drought to higher warming levels in the range of 1.5–3.0 °C. Additionally, consistent relative changes, magnitudes, and spatial distributions of droughts were observed for the SSP245 and SSP585 scenarios at the same warming level. While some studies supports this nonlinear response (Gu et al., 2020 ), others disagree (Cammalleri et al., 2020 ) owing to choices in drought indices influencing the evaluations of warming levels. Therefore, different sectors such as agriculture, meteorology, and ecology, should select drought indices based on specific needs for accurate predictions of future droughts. The results from the SSP245 and SSP585 scenarios suggest that controlling emissions to delay global warming can mitigate the increase in future droughts. This study had some limitations. A potential evapotranspiration (PET) estimation method called Thornthwaite (TW), which solely considers precipitation, was used in this study. However, the TW method shows a good spatiotemporal agreement in the calculation of drought indices (RDI index) with the standard Penman–Monteith (PM) Method, which is considered as the standard by the International Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), especially for longer time scales (over six months) at the global or regional scale (Mohammed and Scholz, 2017; Ortiz-Gómez et al., 2022; Vangelis et al., 2013 ). However, the TW method leads to an overestimation in humid equatorial and tropical regions (van der Schrier et al., 2011 ) and further overestimate potential evapotranspiration under global warming due to temperature as the only input (Donohue et al., 2010 ). Incorporating additional factors (wind speed and vapor pressure) into PET calculations can yield more accurate results when data are allowed. Despite the non-stationarity shown in meteorological or hydrological variables (mean and variance) under climate change or anthropogenic influences, several studies have argued that stationarity is no longer the default assumption in water resource risk assessment (Milly et al., 2008; Peres et al., 2023 ), while others are convinced to benchmark the present climate and examine future changes (Senatore et al., 2019 ). Meanwhile, constructing non-stationary models by describing changes with deterministic equations has also been criticized (Koutsoyiannis and Montanari, 2015; Lins and Cohn, 2011; Matalas, 2012 ). In our opinion, it is necessary to recognize subregions in which existing stationary methods underestimate future drought scenarios (ALA, NAS, TIB, and EAF) and might encounter water management risks for which the current hydraulic infrastructures are unprepared. However, detecting non-stationarity in natural system variables requires careful selection of covariates and rational methods for constructing a nonstationary drought index to accurately assess future droughts amid natural variability or anthropogenic perturbations before checking the necessity of applying a non-stationarity approach. Therefore, relevant authorities (meteorological, hydrological, and agricultural departments) must choose appropriate drought indices based on specific requirements.  6 Conclusion This study employed CMIP6-simulated precipitation and temperature datasets from 15 GCMs to analyze stationary RDI and non-stationary NRDI indices. Meteorological drought characteristics, including spatial extent, frequency, duration, and severity, were assessed at warming levels of 1.5 °C, 2.0 °C, 2.5 °C, and 3.0 °C under SSP245 and SSP585 scenarios. “Hotspots,” or areas significantly responsive to future climate change, were identified, highlighting potential underestimation or overestimation of future drought risk in specific regions by conventional stationary drought indices. The key findings are as follows:1) Non-stationarity trends in the μ   and σ   distribution parameters (mean and standard deviation) of the P/PET initial values for the drought indices were detected globally. The PET exhibited an overall increase. A significant 40 % increase in P was observed at high latitudes in the Northern Hemisphere, the Sahara region, north India, and Northwestern China, whereas a 10 % decrease was noted in the Amazon region, Western Australia, and the Mediterranean regions. The combined P and PET changes resulted in regional distribution parameter patterns.  2) Three classifications in (−,−), (NO,−), and (+,−) dominated global occurrences among nine classifications obtained by combining increasing, no, or decreasing trends in the μ   and σ   distribution parameters. Owing to changes in the μ   parameter and the fixed distribution curve in the RDI index, underestimation in the high latitudes (Alaska and Northern Asia), northwestern China, India, and North and Eastern Africa, and maximum overestimation in the Amazon region, Western Australia, the Mediterranean region, and South Africa regions were found in future drought projections.  3) The results showed a maximum two- to three-fold increase in frequency and spatial extent, with maximum values of 9.0–10.0 and 16.0–17.0 for duration and severity, defining Northern North America, the Amazon region, the Mediterranean region, south-central Africa, and southeastern Asia as hotspot regions of droughts response to global warming.    The study findings revealed variations in drought performance across different warming levels for high- and low-emission scenarios. It is recommended that the relevant authorities choose appropriate drought indices based on specific requirements. Additionally, considering that future droughts will behave relatively at the same warming levels, reducing greenhouse emissions to mitigate temperature increases is an effective measure to address climate change, mitigate drought risks, and manage water resources, as lower emission scenarios imply that longer periods of warming will reach a certain level.
1 Introduction Soil is the most important and vulnerable component of terrestrial ecosystems, and soil organic carbon is one of the most active carbon reservoirs in the Earth's surface system, surpassing vegetation and the atmosphere in terms of carbon storage (Scharlemann et al., 2014; Allocca et al., 2023 ). However, soil erosion is considered to be one of the major environmental issues in the world, leading to ecosystem degradation, land degradation, and soil nutrients loss, particularly soil organic carbon (Zhu et al., 2022; Dlamini et al., 2011 ). During rainfall, an amount of soil organic carbon is lost with runoff and sediment, disrupting its natural turnover and reducing land productivity (Doetterl et al., 2012 ). Therefore, how to effectively control soil erosion and prevent the soil organic carbon loss is the most challenging task facing researchers. Vegetation restoration is considered one of the most effective and fundamental measures to prevent soil erosion (Anache et al., 2018 ). Taking the Loess Plateau as an example, with the implementation of ecological engineering, such as the “Grain for Green” project, the vegetation coverage on the Loess Plateau increased from less than 20 % in the 1980 s to 63 % in 2018, and the average annual sediment transport of the Yellow River decreased from 1.6 billion t·a-1  in 1919–1959 to 248 million t·a-1  in 2000–2018 (Hu and Zhang, 2020 ). Numerous studies have shown that various vegetation types play a significant role in intercepting runoff and sediment in gentle-slopes such as tablelands (<5°), and hillslopes of LiangMao (<25°) on the Loess Plateau (Wei et al., 2014 ). For example, when the forest and grass cover in the tablelands exceeded 50 %, runoff and sediment production were reduced by 76.35–96.73 % and 97.89–99.88 %, respectively compared to bare land (Zhu et al., 2021b ). However, there are obvious topographical differences between the hill-slopes (<25°) above the gully shoulder lines and the gully-slopes (>35°) below the gully shoulder lines, and erosion intensity in gully-slopes is obviously greater than that of the gentle-slopes (Xing et al., 2023; Niu et al., 2019 ). After the vegetation restoration, the erosion above the gully shoulder line has been basically completely controlled, but the gully-slopes below the gully shoulder line are still seriously eroded due to the steep slope and deep gully. At this point, it is particularly important to control water and soil loss in the gully-slopes. However, different vegetation types have significant differences in their effectiveness in reducing runoff and erosion (Zhu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022 ). Therefore, it is necessary to deepen research on the effects of different vegetation types on reducing runoff and erosion in gully-slopes (>35°) on the current Loess Plateau. The Loess Plateau is a high sediment-producing and low runoff-producing area in the Yellow River Basin (Dang et al., 2020 ). This region faces significant challenges, including insufficient water resources and an uncoordinated runoff-sediment relationship, which are crucial bottlenecks for the ecological protection and high-quality development of the Yellow River Basin (Dang et al., 2020 ). In recent years, the Yellow River Basin suffers from serious water resource shortage (Deng et al., 2023 ). Due to the implementation of a series of measures such as the Green for Grain Project, the annual runoff of the Yellow River has decreased (Wang and Sun, 2021 ). With the rapid economic development, the demand for water for agriculture, industry and domestic use has become larger, leading to the problem of water shortage becoming more prominent (Zhang et al., 2023 ). Therefore, in order to solve the water shortage in the Yellow River Basin, there is an urgent need to analyze the characteristics and differences of the runoff-reduction and sediment-reduction of different vegetation types in the gully-slopes on the Loess Plateau, and to explore the rational vegetation configuration measure in order to relative increase runoff and simultaneously reduce sediment into the Yellow River. Vegetation restoration can enhance soil organic carbon content. The photosynthesis of vegetation stems and leaves produces carbon input (Contreras-Cisneros et al., 2022 ). Litter can improve microhabitat conditions and provide raw materials for soil microbial mineralization (Liu et al., 2019 ). Root exudates stimulate microbial activity and soil organic matter decomposition, which can increase soil organic carbon content (Wang et al., 2023 ). Due to vegetation restoration, soil organic carbon content in semi-arid regions of China continued to increase every year with a carbon sequestration rate of 1.01 Mg·hm−2 ·y-1 , while soil inorganic carbon content continued to decrease with a loss rate of 0.16 Mg·hm−2 ·y-1  (Liu et al., 2017 ). The soil organic carbon storage in 2020 increased by 10.54 % on the loess Plateau compared with 1990 (Zhang et al., 2021 ). Soil organic carbon loss with soil erosion can be classified into dissolved organic carbon in runoff and sediment-bound organic carbon in sediment (Wang et al., 2022 ). During rainfall, raindrops impact the soil surface and disrupt soil aggregate structure, promoting the dissolution of organic carbon into runoff, forming dissolved organic carbon in runoff (Hofbauer et al., 2023 ). When runoff carrying sediment flows downward, undissolved soil organic carbon directly adheres to soil particles and is lost as sediment-bound organic carbon (Doetterl et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2022 ). Due to soil erosion, the annual total soil organic carbon loss exceeds 180 Mt C·y-1  in China (Yue et al., 2016 ). Vegetation reduces dissolved organic carbon loss and sediment-bound organic carbon loss by reducing runoff and sediment (Zhu et al., 2014; Valentin et al., 2008; Arunrat et al., 2022 ). The canopy and litterfall of vegetation can prevent direct raindrop impact on the soil surface and intercept the runoff, and vegetation roots can improve soil infiltration capacity and enhance soil corrosion resistance, which reduce the soil erosion and thus soil organic carbon loss (Feng et al., 2022 ). However, the mechanisms through which vegetation affects soil organic carbon into runoff and sediment are not clear, and the effects and differences of different vegetation types on dissolved organic carbon content and sediment-bound organic carbon content remain to be further studied. Furthermore, the main source of soil organic carbon loss coming from sediment or runoff in the gully-slopes is unclear after vegetation restoration. In conclusion, this paper has three objectives in the gully-slopes: (i) To compare the runoff- and erosion- reduction benefits of different vegetation types, and find out the vegetation matching measure that is suitable for “Relative increase runoff and reduce sediment”; (ii) To clarify the benefits of different vegetation types in reducing soil organic carbon loss; (iii) To explore whether the soil organic carbon loss mainly comes from runoff or sediment with serious soil erosion, and to build a soil organic carbon loss equation based on runoff and sediment.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Test area profile The Wangdonggou watershed (107°40′30″∼107°42′30″E, 35°12′∼35°16′N) is located in Changwu County, Shaanxi Province, Chinese Loess Plateau (Fig. 1  a). The watershed has an area of 8.3 km2 , and is 940–1220 m above sea level. It is mainly composed of tableland, slope, and valley, each accounting for one-third. The gully-slopes are very steep, generally greater than 35°. Grassland and woodland (trees and shrubs) are distributed in the whole watershed, accounting for 55.3 % and 25.78 %, while cropland is mainly concentrated in tableland, accounting for only 15 % (Zhang et al., 2023 ). The watershed is a typical continental monsoon climate area, with rainfall mainly concentrated from July to September, accounting for 58 % of the annual mean rainfall (584 mm) (Duan et al., 2016 ). The dominant soil type in watershed is Calcaric Regosols (WRB soil Classification System), and the soil texture is mainly silt loam (USDA soil texture classification) (Zhu et al., 2021a ). The main vegetation types in the watershed, especially gully-slopes, are grasses with a taproot system (Artemisia gmelinii , Medicago sativa , Taraxacum mongolicum ), and grasses with a fibrous root system (Agropyron cristatum , Cynodon dactylon , Artemisia annua ), shrubs (Amorpha fruticosa Linn , Spiraea Salicifolia , Acer Truncatum ) and trees (Sophora japonica , Robinia pseudoacacia , Pinus tabulaeformis Carr ).  2.2 Experimental design To examine the effects of different revegetation types for runoff, sediment and soil organic carbon loss, the experimental plots with a width of 2.5 m and a length of 20 m were built on one gully-slope in the Wangdonggou watershed in 2013. The slope gradient of the plots was 35°∼40°. The main soil type in plots was loess soil, with a composition dominated by silt particles. The plots were divided into four vegetation cover treatments: bare land (CK), shrub-grass community (SG), taproot grasses community (GT), and fibrous-root grasses community (GF). The SG plots were mainly composed of shrub (Amorpha fruticosa Linn ), and sparse grass (Agropyron cristatum ). The GT plots were mainly composed of Artemisia gmelinii  and Medicago sativa . The GF plots were mainly composed of Agropyron cristatum  and Cynodon dactylon . The vegetation coverage in vegetation plots was about 80 %. The mean height of Amorpha fruticosa Linn  was approximately 176 cm, and the mean height of grasses was 68–76 cm. Vegetation has been naturally restored for about 8 years. The rainfall experiments were conducted in 2021 (Fig. 1 ). The vegetation and soil properties of each plot are shown in Table 1  . On the Loess Plateau, rainfall intensity of more than 60 mm·h−1  was a typical erosive rainstorm, which can cause serious soil erosion. For example, the rainfall intensities reached 56.3 mm h−1  in Dingbian County, Shaanxi Province on the Loess Plateau, during the “7·11 rainstorm” in 2022 (Yang et al., 2023 ). Therefore, the design rainfall intensity was 60 mm·h−1 , and the time was 60 min as the rainfall duration. The simulated rainfall was repeated 3 times in each plot. A total of 12 rainfall experiments were conducted in 4 types of plots. The interval between two rainfall tests in the same plot was about 15 days. The self-made simulated rainfall device (composed of nozzles, PPR pipe, etc.) was used for rainfall. The rainfall device consisted of two rows of 18 nozzles, each positioned at a vertical height of 2 m from the ground (Guo et al., 2019 ). This rainfall device was easy to disassemble, assemble and move in the field. And chose a windless weather for the test to prevent outside interference. The error between the experiment rainfall intensity and the design rain intensity was within 5 %, and the rainfall uniformity reached more than 80 %.  2.3 Test procedure and calculation methods 2.3.1 Test procedure Before the experiment, a small number of soil samples were randomly taken from different parts of the upper, middle, and lower slopes in each experimental plot to measure the soil properties. Before the start of each rainfall experiment, a period of pre-rainfall was performed with a rainfall intensity of 10 mm·h−1 , and the rainfall was stopped when runoff appeared in the test plot. After waiting for 2 h, the formal rainfall experiment was started. To ensure consistency in initial water content, the above steps need to be repeated in different experiments on the same plot. From the beginning of runoff production, the samples of sediment-laden runoff were collected every 5 min with a 1 L capacity bottle, and the sample time was recorded to calculate the runoff rate. The collected samples were dried, and their weights were measured to determine the sediment concentration (M, kg·m−3 ). Subsequently, to determine soil organic carbon content, samples of sediment-laden runoff were collected immediately using a 10 L plastic bucket every 10 min, left to settle for 12 h. Then the upper clear liquid was preserved in a liquid bottle to determine the soil organic carbon content of the runoff. The sediment samples from the lower layer of the runoff after filtration were air-dried to analyze the sediment-bound organic carbon content.  2.3.2 Calculation methods Runoff rate (R, mm·min−1 ) was obtained as:(1) R = 60 × Q  T × A × cos θ       where Q (L) represents the runoff volume at the outlet of the experimental plot for the given time interval; A (m2 ) represents the plot area; and T (s) represents the sampling time; θ is represented the plot slope (°). The soil erosion rate (E, g·m−2 ·min−1 ) was obtained as:(2) E = 60 × M  T × A × cos θ        Using bare land plots as the reference, the effectiveness of different vegetation to runoff and sediment reduction was evaluated. The calculation formula was as follows:(3) RE = R C  - R V   R C   × 100 %     (4) SE = S C  - S V   S C   × 100 %     (5) SRE = SE  RE       where RE  (%) and SE  (%) represent the effectiveness of vegetation community in reducing runoff and soil erosion compared to the bare land plots, respectively, SRE  represents the ratio of SE  to RE . The RC   (L) and SC   (g) were used to represent the total runoff and total amount of erosion of bare plots, respectively. The RV   (L) and SV   (g) were used to represent the total runoff and total amount of erosion of vegetation plots, respectively. The sediment-bound organic carbon content (SOCC; g·kg−1 ) was determined by the external heating method of potassium dichromate, and the dissolved organic carbon content (DOCC; mg·L-1 ) in runoff was determined by the total organic carbon analyzer. The dissolved organic carbon loss rate (TOCR , mg·m−2 ·min−1 ) was obtained as:(6) TO C R  = 60 × D O C C × Q  T × A × cos θ        The sediment-bound organic carbon loss rate (TOCS , mg·m−2 ·min−1 ) was obtained as:(7) TO C S  = 60 × S O C C × M × 1 0  - 3    T × A × cos θ        The total organic carbon loss rate (TOCT , mg·m−2 ·min−1 ) was obtained as:(8) TO C T  = TOC  R  + TOC  S       Using bare plots as the reference, the effectiveness of different vegetation to dissolved organic carbon loss, sediment-bound organic carbon loss, and total organic carbon loss reduction were evaluated. The calculation formula was as follows:(9) DRE = D C  - D V   D C   × 100 %     (10) SBRE = S B C  - S B V   S B C    × 100 %     (11) TRE = T C  - T V   T C   × 100 %     where DRE  (%), SBRE  (%) and TRE  (%) are represented the effectiveness of the vegetation community in reducing dissolved organic carbon loss, sediment-bound organic carbon loss and total organic carbon loss reduction compared to the bare land, respectively. The DC   (g), SBC   (g), and TC   (g) were used to represent the dissolved organic carbon loss, sediment-bound organic carbon loss, and total organic carbon loss of bare plots, respectively. The DV   (g), SBV   (g), and TV   (g) were used to represent the dissolved organic carbon loss, sediment-bound organic carbon loss, and total organic carbon loss of vegetation plots, respectively. Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency coefficient (NSE) (Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ) was used to evaluate the performance of the model.(12) NSE = 1 - ∑ i = 1  N  ( M i  - P i  )  2   ∑ i = 1  N  ( M i  - M  ¯   )  2        where Mi  , Pi  , and M  ¯     represent the measured value, predicted value, and the mean value of the measured value, respectively. N represents the data number.    3 Results 3.1 Effects of vegetation type on runoff and soil erosion Vegetation restoration obviously changed the runoff (Fig. 2  ). The runoff rate of the bare plots (CK) increased rapidly and then tended to be stable, while the vegetation plots showed a slow rising trend. Furthermore, the mean runoff rate, runoff coefficient, and total runoff volume in the vegetation plots were both lower than CK, and SG was higher than GT and GF in vegetation plots (Fig. 2  and Fig. 4 a). The mean runoff rate in the CK was as high as 0.61 mm·min−1 , while the mean runoff rates in the SG, GT, and GF were only 0.27, 0.04, and 0.17 mm·min−1 , respectively. The runoff coefficient in the CK reached 0.59, while the runoff coefficients in the SG, GT, and GF were only 0.27, 0.05, and 0.17, respectively. The total runoff volume in the CK was up to 1777.1 L, while the total runoff volumes in the SG, GT, and GF were only 801.7 L, 139.3 L, and 502.2 L, respectively. Compared with the CK, the total runoff volume in the SG, GT, and GF decreased by 54.9 %, 92.2 %, and 71.7 %. Vegetation restoration has a significant effect on erosion (Fig. 3   ). The erosion rate in the CK increased rapidly first, and then continued to decline slowly. In the vegetation plots, the erosion rate has been in a fluctuating upward trend. Furthermore, the total soil loss, mean sediment concentration, and mean erosion rate in the vegetation plots were lower than those in the CK (Fig. 3  and Fig. 4 b). The total soil loss in the CK reached 370.62 kg, while the total soil loss in the SG, GT, and GF were only 0.13 kg, 0.69 kg, and 7.08 kg, respectively. Compared with the CK, the total soil loss of the SG, GT, and GF decreased by 99.96 %, 99.8 %, and 98.1 %. The mean value in the CK was as high as 218.94 kg·m−3 , while the mean sediment concentration in the SG, GT, and GF were only 0.17, 4.57, and 13.60 kg·m−3 , respectively. The mean erosion rate in the CK was as high as 130.34 g·m−2 ·min−1 , while the mean erosion rates in the SG, GT, and GF were only 0.045, 0.244, and 2.43 g·m−2 ·min−1 , respectively.  3.2 Effects of vegetation type on organic carbon in runoff and sediment The dissolved organic carbon content (DOCC) in runoff in vegetation types were all lower than that in the CK, but the sediment-bound organic carbon content (SOCC) in the SG and GT was higher than that in the CK (Fig. 5  a). Compared with the CK (6.15 mg·L-1 ), the DOCC in the SG, GT, and GF decreased by 14.5 %, 24.2 % and 22.6 %, respectively. Compared with the CK (4.49 g·kg−1 ), the SOCC increased by 2.42 and 1.25 times in the SG and GT but decreased by 9.3 % in the GF. Vegetation restoration obviously reduced the sediment-bound organic carbon loss rate (TOCS ) and the dissolved organic carbon loss rate (TOCR ) in runoff (Fig. 6  ). Compared with the CK (251.1 mg·m−2 ·min−1 ), the TOCS  in the SG (0.24 mg·m−2 ·min−1 ), GT (0.47 mg·m−2 ·min−1 ), and GF (2.34 mg·m−2 ·min−1 ) decreased by 99.9 %, 99.8 %, and 99.1 %, respectively. Compared with the CK, the TOCR  in the SG, GT, and GF decreased by 64.4 %, 99.4 %, and 89.6 %, respectively. Vegetation restoration obviously reduced the dissolved organic carbon in runoff and sediment-bound organic carbon in sediment. Compared with the CK (10.35 g), the dissolved organic carbon loss in the SG GT, and GF were only 0.63 g, 2.3 g, and 3.78 g. Compared with the CK (1630.6 g), the sediment-bound organic carbon loss in the SG GT, and GF were only 1.42 g, 3.16 g, and 29.58 g. The benefits of reducing the loss of sediment-bound organic carbon were > 98 %, but the benefit of vegetation in reducing the dissolved organic carbon loss was different (63.4 %, 77.8 %, and 93.9 %) compared with CK. Our experiment showed that the reduction in sediment-bound organic carbon loss far exceeded the reduction in dissolved organic carbon loss. SG had the highest benefit in reducing the sediment-bound organic carbon loss. In contrast, GT had the highest benefit in reducing the dissolved organic carbon loss compared to the bare land (Table 2  ).  3.3 Effects of vegetation type on the total organic carbon loss Vegetation restoration obviously changed the total organic carbon loss (TOCT ) (Fig. 7  ). The TOCT  in the CK rapidly increased to the peak within the first 20 min, while the rate in the SG showed an overall upward trend followed by a decrease. The TOCT  in the GF was relatively stable before 40 min, and the rate in the GT showed a low and stable trend before 30 min. Furthermore, the total organic carbon loss in the vegetation plots were both lower than CK (Table 2 ). Compared with the CK (1640.97 g), the total organic carbon loss decreased by 99.7 % in the SG (5.2 g), 99.8 % in the GT (3.79 g), and 98.1 % in the GF (31.88 g). GT had the highest benefit in reducing the total organic carbon loss among the four types of plots.   4 Discussion 4.1 Runoff- and erosion-reducing effects of different vegetation type Vegetation played an obvious role in reducing runoff, and the runoff reduction benefits of three vegetation types were different obviously. Shrub-grass arrangement (SG) (mean runoff rate: 0.27 mm·min−1 ; total runoff volume: 801.7 L), fibrous root grasses (GF) (0.17 mm·min−1 ; 502.2 L) and tap root grasses (GT) (0.04 mm·min−1 ; 139.3 L) all reduced runoff compared with bare land (CK) (0.61 mm·min−1 ; 1777.1 L). The runoff reduction benefit of vegetation was 54.9 % in SG plot, 71.7 % in GF plot, and 92.2 % in GT plot compared with the bare land (Fig. 2 ; Fig. 4 a and 4c). Liang et al. (2020)  found in field monitoring that vegetation restoration could decrease 68.0 % to 97.4 % of runoff. It is similar to the conclusion obtained by our simulation tests. The combined effect of the above-ground and underground parts of vegetation allowed a large amount of rainfall to infiltrate and intercept the runoff. The above-ground parts of vegetation (stems, leaves, and litter) intercepted rain, slowed down runoff velocity, and impeded runoff (Rosier et al., 2023 ). Furthermore, the contribution degree of the above-ground portion of vegetation to intercept runoff could reach 57 %∼72 % (Du et al., 2023 ). However, the influence of vegetation on runoff varied significantly among different vegetation types. In our experiment, the SG had abundant shrubs with a coverage of up to 94.9 % with above-ground biomass of 1695 g·m−2 , whereas the grass coverage was only 5.1 % and above-ground biomass was only 90.31 g·m−2 . On the other hand, two types of grass plots had high grass coverage of over 82 % and above-ground biomass of 226.27 g·m−2  (GT) and 302.71 g·m−2  (GF) (Table 1 ). The influence of vegetation litter on runoff and infiltration was also obvious. The more litter there was, the stronger the water storage capacity of the litter layer, which not only buffered the infiltration of rainwater into the soil but also delayed the time and volume of rainwater collection into runoff (Gong et al., 2022 ). The litter cover amount in our grasses (GT and GF) plots was 4.1–4.4 % higher than in the SG (Table 1 ). The underground root system obviously changed soil properties, such as increasing soil porosity and soil infiltration capacity (Rungee and Kim, 2017 ). Compared with CK, the soil bulk density decreased by 3.01–18.1 %, the soil porosity increased by 9.4–9.9 %, and the average soil infiltration rate increased by 1.87–2.44 times in our vegetation plots. Moreover, there were obvious differences in soil infiltration rates between the SG plot and the grasses (GT and GF) plots (Table 1 ). The average soil infiltration rate in the grass plots was 13.7–30.1 % higher than in the SG (Table 1 ). These resulted in a higher runoff rate in the SG plots than in the grass plots (Fig. 2  and Fig. 4 c). Vegetation played an obvious role in reducing soil erosion. The SG (mean erosion rate: 0.045 g·m−2 ·min−1 ; total sediment loss: 0.13 kg), GF (2.43 g·m−2 ·min−1 ; 7.08 kg) and GT plot (0.244 g·m−2 ·min−1 ; 0.69 kg) all reduced sediment compared with CK (130.34 g·m−2 ·min−1 ; 370.62 kg) (Fig. 3 ; Fig. 4 b). The total soil loss of the SG, GT, and GF decreased by 99.96 %, 99.8 %, and 98.1 % compared with the CK. Zhu et al., (2021b)  found that erosion can be reduced by 83.9 to 99.6 % when shrub and grass coverage reaches more than 50 %. Similar to the study of Zhu et al., (2021b) , the vegetation coverage in our study was > 80 %, and the sediment reduction benefits in the vegetation plots was > 98 % (Fig. 4 c). The above-ground part of the vegetation reduced soil loss by decreasing the erosive force of rainfall and runoff and by improving soil erosion resistance (Baets et al., 2007 ). Compared to the above-ground part, the vegetation root system had a more pronounced effect in reducing sediment loss. The roots form a network in the soil surface through physical processes such as entanglement, penetration, and reinforcement. This improved soil aggregate stability and enhances soil erosion resistance (Xu et al., 2024; Lou et al., 2023 ), and vegetation roots could increase the soil cohesion by 13.3–115.1 % and enhance the soil anti-erodibility by 80 % (Kono and Okuro, 2021 ). The contribution of root systems to sediment reduction can reach 66–83 % (Katuwal et al., 2013 ).  4.2 Suggestions on vegetation restoration in the current environment: Reduce sediment and relative increase runoff With vegetation restoration on the Loess Plateau, some areas have experienced excessive vegetation density and unscientific vegetation arrangement, resulting in insufficient water production and a significant decrease the runoff in the Yellow River (Cui and Jian, 2023 ). For example, despite increased precipitation, the average annual runoff from 2000 to 2016 has still decreased by more than 40 % compared to the period of 1980–1999 (Before the “Grain for Green” project) in the Yellow River (Fu et al., 2023 ). Due to the population growth and increased demand for water in industrialization and agriculture, the contradiction between supply and demand of water resources is more prominent in the lower reaches of the Yellow River (Meng et al., 2023 ), which restricts the high-quality development of Yellow River basins (Wang et al., 2023b ). In our study, the mean runoff rate in the shrub-grass arrangement was as high as 0.27 mm·min−1 , while the mean runoff rate in the tap root grasses, and fibrous root grasses were only 0.04, and 0.17 mm·min−1 , respectively. The total runoff of shrub-grass arrangement (801.7 L) was 1.6 to 5.8 times that of fibrous root grass (502.2 L) and root grass (139.3 L). There was no significant difference in sediment reduction efficiency (99.96 %, 99.8 %, and 98.1 %) among three vegetation types (Fig. 2 , Fig. 3  and Fig. 4 c). In addition, the ratio of sediment reduction benefits (99.96 %, 99.8 %, and 98.1 %) to water reduction benefits (71.7 %, 92.2 %, 54.9 %) in the GF GT SG were 1.08, 1.37, and 1.82, respectively (Fig. 4 c). This means that the sediment reduction benefits in the vegetation plots were higher than the runoff reduction benefits, and the benefit of SG was more prominent. The shrub-grass arrangement efficiently intercepts sediment while allowing large amounts of runoff to flow out (Fig. 4 ). Therefore, compared to pure grass, the shrub-grass arrangement is a more suitable vegetation combination for current water and soil conservation: reducing sediment and relatively increasing runoff on the Loess Plateau. This not only prevents sediment from entering the Yellow River but also allows more runoff water resources to flow into the Yellow River.  4.3 Vegetation restoration significantly reduced total organic carbon loss Before vegetation restoration, the exposed soil surface was vulnerable to erosion and soil organic carbon loss due to rainfall, resulting in soil impoverishment (Qiu et al., 2020 ). The improvement of soil organic carbon by vegetation was not only to increase soil organic carbon content (Zhang et al., 2022 ), but also to reduce total organic carbon loss (Table 2 ). The total organic carbon loss in three vegetation plots decreased by 98 % compared to bare plots (Table 2 ). Before vegetation restoration (bare slope), heavy rainfall increased the runoff rate and accelerated the soil erosion rate, and finally promoted the dissolved organic carbon loss rate (TOCR ) and the sediment-bound organic carbon loss rate (TOCS ); therefore, bare slope has a high rate of total organic carbon loss (Cui et al., 2018 ). After vegetation restoration, vegetation slowed down the flow velocity and runoff rate, and allowed a small amount of soluble soil organic carbon to dissolve in the runoff. Vegetation reduced soil erosion and sediment-bound content, and thus reduced sediment-bound organic carbon loss (Kumar et al., 2023 ).  4.4 Difference of soil organic carbon loss in runoff and sediment under different vegetation The difference in the soil organic carbon in runoff and sediment was obvious under different vegetation, and soil organic carbon loss mainly came from sediment compared with runoff (Table 2 ). Except for the SG plots, the sediment-bound organic carbon loss rate (TOCS ) was 4.7, 13, and 114 times higher than the dissolved organic carbon loss rate (TOCR ) in the GT, GF, and CK plots, respectively (Fig. 6 ). In addition to the SG plots, the sediment-bound organic carbon accounted for 83.4–99.4 % of the total organic carbon loss in the other three types of plots. However, the dissolved organic carbon loss in runoff only accounted for 0.6–16.6 % (Fig. 5 b). Most of the organic carbon in the soil was attached to the sediment and was lost along with the sediment (Li et al., 2019 ). In particular, the more serious the erosion (i.e., the higher the erosion intensity), the higher the proportion of the sediment-bound organic carbon loss to the total organic carbon loss. The lower the erosion intensity, the lower the proportion of organic carbon loss in sediment to total organic carbon loss. In other words, vegetation restoration obviously decreased the proportion of the sediment-bound organic carbon loss in total organic carbon loss by reducing soil erosion (Table 2  and Fig. 5 b). Soil erosion involved soil detachment, transport, and deposition of eroded sediment (Abney and Berhe, 2018 ). The transport and deposition of eroded sediment were the main causes of soil organic carbon loss (Berhe et al., 2007 ). Furthermore, vegetation protected soil from splashing and detachment and greatly controlled the transport and deposition of eroded sediment (Podwojewski et al., 2011; Prosdocimi et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2013 ), thus reducing sediment-bound organic carbon loss, and thus reducing total organic carbon loss (Table 2 ). Compared with excess sediment-bound organic carbon loss, the dissolved organic carbon loss in the runoff did not cause serious damage to soil nutrients (Kumar et al., 2023 ). The sediment-bound organic carbon loss in the CK (mean erosion rate: 130.34 g·m−2 ·min−1 ) was as high as 1630.68 g, accounting for 99.4 % of the total organic carbon loss (1640.97 g), while the dissolved organic carbon loss (10.35 g) only accounted for 0.6 %. The sediment-bound organic carbon loss (29.6 g) in the GF (mean erosion rate: 2.43 g·m−2 ·min−1 ) accounted for 92.8 % of the total loss (31.88 g), while the dissolved organic carbon loss (2.3 g) only accounted for 7.2 %. The sediment-bound organic carbon loss (3.16 g) in the GT (mean erosion rate: 0.24 g·m−2 ·min−1 ) accounted for 83.4 % of the total loss (3.79 g), while the dissolved organic carbon loss (0.6 g) only accounted for 16.6 %. However, the sediment-bound organic carbon loss (1.42 g) in the SG (mean erosion rate: 0.045 g·m−2 ·min−1 ) accounted for only 27.3 % of the total loss (5.2 g), while the dissolved organic carbon loss (3.78 g) mainly accounted for 72.7 % (Fig. 5 b). As there was almost no erosion and very low erosion rate in the SG plots, sediment-bound organic carbon loss was very small, which could be almost ignored (Fig. 4 b). This further proved indirectly that soil organic carbon loss mainly comes from sediment.  4.5 Fitting and verification of soil organic carbon loss equation Previous studies found that the soil organic carbon loss was mainly affected by runoff, sediment, DOCC and SOCC (Ding et al., 2023; Gai et al., 2023 ). The analysis of factors influencing total organic carbon loss showed that the TOCT  was significantly correlated with the runoff rate (CK plots: TOCT-ck  = 396.53 R + 30.78, R2   = 0.32, P  < 0.05; Veg plots: TOCT-Veg  = 9.11 R + 0.35, R2   = 0.82, P  < 0.01) and erosion rate (CK plots: TOCT-ck  = 1.42 E + 83.46, R2   = 0.84, P  < 0.001; Veg plots: TOCT-Veg  = 0.61 E + 1.31, R2   = 0.55, P  < 0.001), while the impact of DOCC and SOCC on soil organic carbon loss was still not significant (P  > 0.05) (Fig. 8  ). The above evidence demonstrated a significant linear correlation between the total organic carbon loss rate and both the runoff rate and erosion rate. Therefore, to evaluate the response of the soil organic carbon loss in the gully-slopes to changes in runoff and sediment, multiple linear regression analysis was used to establish the regression equation:(13) CK plots  :  TOC  T - CK   = 84.41  R   + 1.33  E   + 45.66 R  2  = 0.92 , P < 0.001 ,  N   = 21        (14) Veg plots  :  TOC  T - Veg   = 8.36  R   + 0.47  E   + 0.06 R  2  = 0.95 , P < 0.001 ,  N   = 63        where TOCT-CK  and TOCT-Veg  were the total organic carbon loss rate in the bare land and vegetation plots, R was runoff rate, and E was the erosion rate. The TOCT , R, and E in bare land plots and vegetation plots were significantly correlated (P < 0.001). Comparing the measured and predicted values of the two groups separately, it could be seen that data generally along the straight line drawing 1:1 (Fig. 9  ). There was a significant correlation between the predicted and measured values of bare land plots and vegetation plots (R2 CK   = 0.92, P  < 0.001; R2 Veg   = 0.95, P  < 0.001). In this study, the NSE values calculated using equation (12)  were 0.85 and 0.86, respectively. The above results shown that the total organic carbon loss rate predicted by equation (13)  and equation (14)  was in good agreement with the measured total organic carbon loss rate (Fig. 9 ), and both fitting equations were acceptable. Due to the large numerical difference of the factors, it was unable to equation (13)  with equation (14)  of the factor analysis and comparison. Therefore, the runoff rate and erosion rate were first normalized into dimensionless models. Then the normalized soil organic carbon loss rate (TOCT-ck1  and TOCT-Veg1 ) was obtained by multiple regression analysis as follows:(15) CK plots  :  TOC  T - CK  1   = 0.12  R  1  + 0.85  E  1  ( R  2  = 0.92 , P < 0.001 ,  N   = 21 )      (16) Veg plots  :  TOC  T - Veg1   = 0.29  R  1  + 0.69  E  1  ( R  2  = 0.95 , P < 0.001 ,  N   = 63 )      where R1 , E1  and TOCT1  were the normalized value of R, the normalized value of E, and the normalized value of TOCT . Because the constant term was small, it was ignored. In our experiment, the soil organic carbon loss rate increased with an increase in runoff rate and erosion rate. As shown in equation (15)  in the bare land plots, the slopes of the runoff factor (R1 ) and soil erosion factor (E1 ) were 0.12 and 0.85, respectively. As shown in equation (16)  in vegetation plots, the slopes of the runoff factor (R1 ) and erosion factor (E1 ) were 0.29 and 0.69, respectively. Equations (15) and (16)  indicated that soil erosion had a greater impact on soil organic carbon loss than runoff in gully-slopes. Combined with chapters 4.4 and 4.5, it was found that the soil organic carbon loss in the gully-slopes areas was mainly from sediment (more than 85 %) compared with runoff. Therefore, controlling erosion in the gully-slopes of the Loess Plateau is more effective than controlling runoff to prevent soil organic carbon loss.   5 Conclusion Our experiments investigated the effects of shrub-grass community (SG), fibrous root grasses (GF), tap root grasses (GT) on runoff, erosion, and soil organic carbon in loess gully-slopes. Shrub-grass arrangement is a more suitable vegetation combination for relatively increasing runoff and reducing amount of sediment, which prevents sediment from entering the river but more runoff water resources to flow into the river. Compared with bare land, the runoff reduction benefits of SG, GT and GF plots were 54.9 %, 71.7 %, 92.2 %. But, compared with GT and GF plots (mean runoff rate: mean: 0.04 mm·min−1  and 0.17 mm·min−1 ), the total runoff of Shrub-grass arrangement plots (0.27 mm·min−1 ) was 1.6 to 5.8 times. Compared with bare land, the sediment reduction benefits of three vegetation plots were more than 98 %. There was no significant difference in sediment reduction efficiency among the three vegetation types. Soil organic carbon loss was obviously alleviated by vegetation. Compared with bare land, nearly 98 % of soil organic carbon loss was prevented by vegetation types. A soil organic carbon loss equation based on runoff and sediment was established and validated. The R2  , P  and NSE results of the equations were 0.92–0.95, <0.001, 0.85–0.86, respectively, indicating that the fitted equations can be considered acceptable. Soil organic carbon loss mainly comes from sediment compared with runoff. More than 85 % of soil organic carbon was lost with sediment before and after vegetation restoration. Controlling erosion can prevent soil organic carbon loss more effectively than controlling runoff.
1 Introduction In the last decades, several speleogenesis models that simulate karst genesis based on a reactive transport model were proposed. Such models are relevant because of the difficulty to predict the geometry of underground karst conduit networks geometries. Some cave systems can be mapped directly in the field when they are easily accessible, however, the majority of karst geometries remain unknown. Dreybrodt (1990)  and Dreybrodt et al. (1996)  initially proposed a one-dimensional conduit model to investigate dissolution processes. Lauritzen et al. (1992)  extended the investigation into two-dimensional conduit networks with regular patterns. Groves and Howard (1994) included the effect of turbulent flow. Hanna and Rajaram, (1998)  explored the effect of initial aperture distribution. Szymczak and Ladd, 2011  worked on explaining dissolution processes in a single fracture model. All these models focused primarily on assessing insights into the physical processes of conduit development. Warren and Root, (1963)  proposed a simple sugar cube model (Lattice) to represent fractured rocks. Several karst genesis studies use this model because of its simplicity and its aptitude to reproduce the general behavior of fractured rocks. Dreybrodt et al., (2005); Dreybrodt and Gabrovšek (2018)  thus mainly studied dissolution on Lattice based fracture networks, without considering the effects of the structural properties of this initial network. However, these speleogenesis models were widely used to characterize dissolution processes and to better assess how several parameters (i.e. boundary condition, initial fracture aperture, reaction kinetics, mixing corrosion) influence the breakthrough time, aperture evolution and dissolution pattern (e.g. Gabrovšek and Dreybrodt, 2000; Romanov et al., 2003; Hubinger and Birk, 2011; Liedl et al., 2003; Kaufmann and Braun, 2000 ). Some studies are based on flow simulation in equivalent porous medium model (Gong et al., 2017), while other studies considered flow in synthetic fracture networks and neglected the matrix (Romanov and Dreybrodt, 2006 ). Also, several studies focused on two-dimensional single fracture models (Hill et al., 2001; Szymczak and Ladd, 2011; Deng et al. 2016 ) to study wormhole formation. Liu et al. (2017a,b)  developed a continuum-based model, that considers both matrix and fractures, in which they studied matrix acidizing by including fractures with different orientations, patterns, and apertures. As karstification generally initiates within fractures near inception horizons and/or faults, other studies focused on karst genesis in fracture networks (e.g. Aliouache et al., 2019; Dreybrodt and Gabrovšek, 2018 ). However, the prediction of underground Discrete Fracture Networks (DFN) geometry is rather complex which pushes most studies into using simple synthetically generated networks (i.e. lattice networks). Nevertheless, Aliouache et al. (2019)  and Wang et al. (2021)  extended the study of dissolution process in real fracture networks and investigate the effect of fracture network topology on dissolution processes. Many carbonate rocks, in which karst genesis occur, are stratified into beds and each bed is commonly composed of a bed-normal fractures set interconnected with set-normal joints (Odling et al., 1999; Josnin et al., 2002; Jourde et al., 2002a,Jourde et al., 2002b ; Jiang et al., 2022). The connectivity of fracture networks is thus particularly complex. Different configurations of fractures connectivity may cause significant flow channeling (Tsang and Neretnieks, 1998; Lei and Wang, 2016 ). Thus, the connectivity of the fracture network plays a major role in the formation of wormholes. Different authors used inversion techniques to characterize fractures and conduits networks in aquifers (e.g. Tiedeman and Barrash, 2020 ; Keplikova et al., 2020). Fischer et al. (2020)  used Discrete Network Deterministic Inversion to characterize the main flow paths based on steady state drawdown data at field site scale. More recently, Vu and Jardani (2023 ) used machine learning to predict the location of fractures based on pumping tests data. As most cave systems can not entirely be mapped, this motivates researchers to develop different techniques to predict the geometry of karst conduits network based on the minimum available information (e.g., outcrops can provide valuable information about the structural properties of underground fracture networks in the area). As a consequence, carbonate dissolution studies at fracture network scale remain of great importance. In order to quantitatively characterized karst networks geometry and topology, various authors used tools initially developed to characterize river networks (e.g., Woldenberg, 1966; Howard et al., 1970; Howard, 1971 ). As topological analysis of networks became relevant,many new metrics were proposed to characterize these networks (Boccaletti et al., 2006; Costa et al., 2007 ). Collon et al., (2017)  used metrics that are calculated based on graph theory to characterize the geometry and topology of real cave patterns. Aliouache et al.
