(2019)  developed a reactive transport model to simulate incipient karst genesis in a two-dimensional discrete fracture network. They demonstrated that the heterogeneity induced by geometrical and topological complexities can play a decisive role in the early-stage of the karstification processes in fractured carbonate rocks. Results also showed that dissolution processes in 2D fracture networks behave very differently, depending on the flow direction along or across the direction of the longest fractures set. Accordingly, there is a need to better understand the effect of structural properties and connectivity of the initial fracture network on dissolution processes. In this study, we use the term wormhole to describe one incipient karst conduit and the expression karst conduit network to describe a network of multiple wormholes. In this work, we thus focus on different objectives, which are: (i) to assess the effect of structural properties (i.e., fracture intersection types), anisotropy and connectivity of the initial fracture networks (lattice and ladder shape synthetic fracture networks with different type of intersections) on the final geometry and topology of the incipient karst conduit patterns, ii) to explore the effect of different types of boundary conditions (constant hydraulic head versus constant rate condition, directional versus concentrated recharge condition) and analyze their effect on the geometry and morphology of the developed wormholes, and (iii) to quantitatively assess these effects using different existing metrics that allow characterizing both the geometry and the topology of karstic networks (Howard et al., 1970; Collon et al., 2017; Jouves et al.,2017 ). In this study, we use five synthetically generated DFNs that have different fracture intersection type, anisotropy and connectivity: three are generated based on a lattice grid and the remaining two are generated using REZO3D, a three-dimensional model to simulate joint networks in layered rocks (; Josnin et al., 2002, Jourde et al., 2002a,Jourde et al., 2002b ). This model was developed on the basis of field observations of 3D layered fractured carbonates. For each case, we simulate incipient karst genesis in randomly generated discrete fracture networks considering either directional flow dissolution along the hydraulic gradient (constant hydraulic head boundary condition) or dissolution induced by concentrated recharge (constant flow rate boundary condition). We then present and discuss the different results as follows: Firstly, we provide a plot of the incipient karst conduit pattern for each case (DFNs with distinct structural properties and connectivity as a function of the different type of boundary condition). Secondly, we calculate different parameters (i.e., pattern intensity, anisotropy ratio and ramification degree) for the various cases. Then, we plot the evolution of the correlation dimension of flow (D2) to analyze the degree of flow channelization within the karst conduit network and the conduit diameter distribution of the final patterns. Finally, we calculate different metrics of the incipient karst conduits patterns with KARSTNET (Collon et al., 2017 ; https://github.com/karstnet/karstnet  ) and analyze the influence of fractures intersection’s type on the incipient karst conduits patterns.  2 Methodology 2.1 Reactive transport model The incipient karst generation in fracture networks is modelled as a coupled process of flow, transport of Ca2+ , and the growth of fracture aperture. The process is simulated using a finite difference technique based on a resistor network (Odling and Webman, 1991 ). The aperture of each segment is assigned independently. The local flow velocities are calculated from assigned apertures using the Poiseuille equation for laminar flow through parallel plates as follows (Zimmerman et al., 1991):(1) Q = - a  3  12 μ   ∇ p     where Q    is the flow rate, a  is the hydraulic aperture, p    is the pressure and μ    is the dynamic viscosity of the fluid. This model neglects the longitudinal diffusion as it is commonly done in the literature (e.g., Dreybrodt and Gabrovšek, 2018 ). Accordingly, dissolution is controlled by advection processes and diffusion through the fracture dead ends is not considered. The concentration is thus solved by neglecting the dispersive term using the advection reaction equation:(2) Q ∇ c = 2 R ( c )     where Q is the volumetric flow rate, c    is the concentration, R ( c )    is the reaction rate and ∇    is the gradient operator. At each grid node, the flow conservation is expressed as,(3) ∑ Q in   + ∑ Q out   = 0 ,     where Q in      and Q out      represent the rate of fluid flow into and out of the node, respectively. The reactive transport problem in the channel network is solved by assuming mass conservation at the nodes where multiple segments are connected. We assume complete mixing of solution at the nodes. In the network configuration, the concentration of the central node, c 0    , is calculated by a flux-weighted formula:(4) c 0  = c 3  + Δ c  3 - 0     Q 3 - 0   + c 4  + Δ c  4 - 0      Q 4 - 0    Q 3 - 0   + Q 4 - 0         where c 3     and c 4     are concentrations at the surrounding nodes that transfer fluids to the central node c 0    , Δ c  3 - 0      and Δ c  4 - 0      are the concentration increments of the fluid from nodes 3 and 4 to the central node 0, Q 3 - 0      and Q 4 - 0      are the corresponding flow rates along the two branches. In a sufficiently short segment, the concentration increment Δ c    can be approximated from Eq. The reaction rate R c       is expressed by (Palmer, 1991; Dreybrodt et al., 1996; Szymczak and Ladd, 2011; Dreybrodt and Gabrovšek, 2018 ):(6) R c    = k 1  c eq   - c    = k 1 + 2 . k . a  Sh . We use k = 2.5 × 10-7  m s−1 , D=6.73 × 10−10  m2  s−1 , Sh = 8 for laminar flow (Szymczak and Ladd, 2011 ) and ceq  = 2 mol m−3 . By assuming the dissolved mass is evenly distributed over a sufficiently short segment of length l , the amount of aperture growth can be calculated from:(7) δ a = 2 R ( c ) Δ t  c sol    ,     where c sol      (=2.7 × 104  mol.m−3 ) is the molar concentration of the rock phase, Δ t    is the dissolution time step. The rock phase is assumed to be pure calcite (crystallic rock). A standalone application of the reactive transport model (KARSTGEN) can be found in Github: (https://github.com/maliouache/KARSTGEN  ).  2.2 Discrete fracture networks (DFNs) This study considers five cases with distinct structural properties and connectivity of synthetically generated DFNs (Fig. 1  ):– DFN1 (Lattice)  is simply a full lattice grid. This is representative of two distinct configurations: a) the main flow paths within a single fracture or one bedding plane b) a highly fractured rock with two perpendicular sets of long fractures.  – DFN2 (Lattice – Cemented fracture segments)  is generated based on a lattice grid where some fracture segments are randomly removed (along both X and Y directions). It is representative of two distinct configurations: a) the main flow paths within a single fracture or one bedding plane with the presence of cement at random locations b) a highly fractured rock with two perpendicular sets of long fractures where random fracture segments are cemented.  – DFN3 (Lattice – Ladder like)  is generated based on a lattice grid where some fracture segments are randomly removed from one fracture set (along Y direction only), so that a ladder like fracture network is obtained. This DFN3  is representative of ladder shape fracture networks.  – DFN4 (REZO3D – Crosscut joint fractures)  is generated using the three-dimensional model REZO3D (Josnin et al., 2002 ). The fracture network is characterized by a fracture set crosscutting a longest fracture set. This fracture network is representative of joint networks commonly observed between bedding planes in layered carbonates.  – DFN5 (REZO3D – Ladder like)  is generated using the three-dimensional model REZO3D tool (Josnin et al., 2002 ). The fracture network is characterized by a fracture set (in Y direction) which does not crosscut but abut against the longest fracture set. This fracture network is representative of ladder shape networks often observed in carbonate rocks.    Whilst DFN4 and DFN5 were generated with a 3D model allowing to simulate the geometry of 3D layered fractured carbonates, DFN1, DFN2 and DFN3 were generated on the basis of a lattice grid model. Such simple models have been commonly used in former work of other speleogenesis modelers (e.g., Dreybrodt and Gabrovšek, 2018; Roded et al., 2021 ). Even though the models used in this study remain a very simplistic way of representing fracture networks, previous studies focusing on the analysis at outcrop of layered fractured limestone (e.g., Wyller, 2019; Prabhakaran et al., 2021 ) evidenced the existence of similar fracture networks with low fracture spacing (<1 m) in the form of well-defined orientation clusters (usually two perpendicular sets of fractures). These authors also highlight that Y/T shape intersections (connected to three fracture segments), in addition to I/L shape (connected to two fracture segments) and X-shape (connected to four fracture segments) intersections are dominant in such networks. Besides, they also described networks composed of primary long fractures and secondary short fractures. For each DFN case described above, 10 realizations are randomly generated. Then, the initial fracture aperture is generated using a lognormal distribution (mean aperture = 0.2 mm and standard deviation = 0.005 mm). There is no apertures’ correlation between neighboring segments. The anisotropy of a given DFN refers to a set of fractures being longer along one direction than along the other perpendicular direction. The connectivity of the fracture network is mainly controlled by the length of the fractures and the types of the fracture intersections. For instance, the longer the fractures along one direction the higher the connectivity of the network in this direction. Also, the fracture network is more connected when its abundant intersections are connected to a higher number of fracture segments. The discretization of the fractures into segments is not uniform because the distances between intersections differ. The maximum segment length is limited to 0.3 m.  2.3 Pattern intensity In order to quantitatively analyze the results of dissolution in the different DFNs, the pattern intensity of the simulated incipient karst conduits network is calculated using the following equation:(8) Pattern Intensity = cumulative length of the wormholes  surface of the domain        This parameter allows to estimate the degree of karstification in the network. In this study, a fracture segment is considered as a wormhole (i.e., incipient karst conduit) if its final aperture value is at least ten times larger than its initial value.  2.4 Anisotropy index The verticality index was introduced by Piccini (2011) to describe the vertical development compared to the horizontal development of a cavity. We here use a more general definition of this index to characterized the degree of karstification along X and Y directions (two possible fracture orientations). The anisotropy index is defined as the ratio between the cumulative length of the wormholes that developed along the X direction and the cumulative length of the wormholes that developed along the Y direction:(9) Anisotropy index = cumulative length of the wormholes in x direction  cumulative length of the wormholes in y direction        An anisotropy index    with a value greater than 1 indicates more karstification along the X direction.  2.5 Ramification degree The ramification degree is defined as the ratio between the number of nodes that have 3 branches (Y/T shape intersections) and the number of nodes that have one branch (dead end). High values of this parameter indicate highly ramified networks. Values close to 0 correspond to linear patterns.(10) R  a  m  i  f  i  c  a  t  i  o  n  D  e  g  r  e  e  = Number of nodes that have 3 branches  Number of nodes that have 1 (dead end)         2.6 Characterization of karst conduits network evolution The uneven propagation of the dissolution front within the fracture network is quantitatively characterized by the temporal evolution of the 2D correlation dimension of the flow rate, D 2 (q). The generalized correlation dimension, D i  (Cowie et al., 1995; Bonnet et al., 2001) is defined as:(11) D i  = lim L → 0   l o g ∑ k = 1  M  P k  i   log L       where i  is the fractal moment, P k     is the proportion of a measure within a grid element to the cumulative amount of the measure in the grid, L  is the dimension of the grid elements. The correlation dimension D 2  quantifies the degree of flow Channelization (Wang et al., 2017). In general, once the karstification process starts, the value of D 2 (q) drops progressively due to enhanced flow channelization caused by the enlargement of initial fracture apertures and the formation of a karstic conduits. The shape of a D 2 (q) curve can thus provide further quantitative information regarding the degree of flow channelization (and thus the competition process between different wormholes) during the course of incipient karst generation.  2.7 Karst network geometry and topology In order to calculate several metrics allowing to characterize the incipient karst conduits network geometries and topologies, we used the KARSTNET software (Collon et al., 2017 ). These different metrics are calculated based on the graph theory. On the basis of the metrics determined by Karstnet, Collon et al., (2021) characterized several real karst patterns. Parameters such as tortuosity, orientation, vertex degree, Howard’s coefficients, are thus calculated (the complete list of the calculated metrics can be found in Table 1  ) to assess geometry and topology of the simulated incipient karst conduits networks.  2.8 Boundary conditions and model dimension For each of the 5 DFN cases described above, we generated 10 realizations. The size of the domain is 50 m width and 50 m length. The three first cases (DFN 1, 2 and 3), which are lattice-based networks are characterized by a same fracture density. The last two cases (DFN 4 and 5), which are generated with the three-dimensional model REZO3D exhibit a slightly smaller fracture density. For all DFNs the connectivity is high enough so that there is only one backbone. Then, for each DFN case, incipient karst genesis is simulated as a function of three types of flow boundary conditions: a) directional flow along X direction under constant hydraulic head condition, b) directional flow along Y direction under constant hydraulic head condition and c) concentrated recharge at the top of the DFN, under constant flow rate condition. For the latter concentrated recharge boundary condition, 10 inlet points and a single outlet point are fixed for all simulations (seen Fig. 2  ). For the above-mentioned boundary conditions, we considered either (i) a fixed hydraulic gradient of 0.16 for the directional flow boundary condition along X and Y direction or (ii) a constant flow rate of 3 × 10-6  m3 .s−1  at each inlet point for the concentrated recharge boundary condition. For all the simulations, we considered the calcium concentration at equilibrium Ceq  = 2 mol.m−3 , the water dynamic viscosity µwater  = 0.001 Pa.s (20 °C), and the calcite diffusion coefficient D=6.37 × 10-10  m2 .s−1 . Note that, as the transport is advection dominated, this diffusion coefficient is used only to partly limit the reaction in case of a diffusion limited kinetics. The dissolution time step is Δt = 10 years.   3 Results and discussion For the different simulation results, we considered that a fracture segment is as a wormhole if its aperture enlargement is at least ten times its initial value; network patterns plots, extraction of the network graph, as well as the different metrics and aperture distributions are thus determined on this basis. As regards the evolution of the 2D correlation dimension D2(q), it is calculated taking into consideration the whole flow paths to be representative of the flow processes with the whole network. Results of the different simulation are presented as follows: firstly, we show one realization of the incipient karst conduit pattern for each case. Secondly, we plot the parameters corresponding to each case (i.e., pattern intensity, anisotropy ratio and ramification degree) as boxplots. Then, we calculated the correlation dimension D2 as a function of time to assess the evolution over time of flow channeling, and thus dissolution mechanism within the network. As a next step, we use KARSTNET to calculate and discuss different metrics, which are represented as boxplots for the different cases. Finally, we determined the diameter distribution of the incipient karst conduits for the different cases. 3.1 Karst conduit network pattern Fig. 2  shows a plot of normalized aperture of the incipient karst conduit (wormholes) patterns obtained for the different DFN cases and boundary conditions. The fracture segments are considered as the final pattern of incipient karst conduits if its aperture enlargement is at least ten times its initial value. For the incipient karst conduit patterns obtained considering dissolution along the X direction (constant hydraulic head boundary condition) we observe that one, relatively straight, main wormhole in the same direction of flow is obtained for DFN1, DFN4 and DFN5 cases (i.e., “Lattice”, “REZO3D-Crosscut joint fractures” and “REZO3D-Ladder like”). This result is similar to the one obtained in several former studies, which also considered a constant hydraulic head boundary condition (e.g., Dreybrodt et al., 2005; Szymczak and Ladd, 2011; Dreybrodt and Gabrovšek, 2018 ). For the DFN2 and DFN3 cases (i.e., “Lattice-Cemented fracture segments” and “Lattice-Ladder like”) exhibits a different pattern: the incipient karst conduit network is tortuous when dissolution is simulated on DFN2 case, and a higher degree of karstification (generation of several long wormholes) is obtained when dissolution is simulated on DFN3 case. Such behavior is the result of the high anisotropy ratio of the initial DFN, which affects wormholes competition processes and the characteristic spacing as also observed in Szymczak and Ladd, (2011) . Indeed, the lack of connectivity in the direction orthogonal to the flow direction limits the competition between the different wormholes, which favors the development of more than one main wormhole. Similar result was discussed in a former study, which focuses on wormholing in anisotropic media using a pore network model (Roded et al. 2021 ). Lai et al. (2016) also showed how permeability anisotropy favored a double fingering dissolution front. For the incipient karst conduit patterns obtained considering dissolution along the Y direction (constant hydraulic head boundary condition), we observe that one dominant wormhole in the same direction of flow is obtained for all cases. However, for DFN2 and DFN5 cases. (“Lattice-Ladder like” and “REZO3D-Ladder like), the incipient karst conduit networks are more tortuous. According to this result, ladder like DFNs may favor tortuous wormholes for dissolution along the Y direction (i.e., orthogonal to the longest fracture direction) and thus increase the breakthrough time (Fig. S5  in supplementary material ). For dissolution along X and Y directions under constant head boundary condition, a transition into a ramified dissolution regime is observed due to the effect of the outlet boundary. Such patterns can be observed for real karst conduits networks such as the Cent Fonts system, located on the right bank of the Hérault river that is made of three penetrable outlets (Fig. 3  .a). A dozen or so impenetrable secondary springs flowing along the river are the origin of the system's name. For all the synthetic DFNs, the incipient karst conduit networks obtained considering dissolution induced by concentrated recharge correspond to relatively similar branchwork pattern. Palmer (1991)  stated that a large percentage of known cave systems do exhibit such branchwork patterns; for example, the Mammoth cave system presented in Audra and Palmer (2013)  consists in a branchwork pattern, which is the consequence of several inlet points (dolines and sinking streams). Simulation results show that different pattern angularities and local differences in geometry can be observed for different branchwork patterns. The inlet and outlet points seem to have a considerable control on the general pattern. This can be seen in a real cave system (Fig. 3 .b) and observed in previous studies that used concentrated recharge BC to generate karst conduit networks (e.g., De Rooij and Graham, 2017 ). Also, DFN1 (Lattice) and DFN4 (REZO3D-crosscut) cases show angular patterns while the DFN2 case (Lattice-Cemented fracture segments) shows a curvilinear pattern. Accordingly, the abundance of crosscutting fractures (DFN 1 and 4) might favor angular patterns while the ladder like cases (DFN 3 and 5) seem to favor stair-like patterns. However, under the concentrated recharge boundary condition, the pattern obtained for the “Lattice-Ladder like” cases (DFN 3 and 5) do not consist in one connected wormhole as observed in the other cases (DFN 1, 2 and 4). This indicates lower dissolution rates for these cases (DFN 3 and 5) which may be the result of low connectivity in Y direction (Fig. S6  in supplementary material ). For models under constant head boundary condition and flow along the Y direction, the comparison of dissolution rates shows longer breakthrough time for anisotropic DFN cases (DFN 3 and 5). The connectivity of the DFN along the main flow direction may thus be proportional to the dissolution rate.  3.2 Pattern intensity, anisotropy index and ramification degree We did calculate the pattern intensity, anisotropy index and ramification degree for the 10 realizations of each DFN case and for all boundary condition. Fig. 4   shows a boxplot of pattern intensity, anisotropy index and ramification degree calculated for each DFN case (i.e., Lattice, Lattice-Cemented, Lattice-Ladder, REZO3D-crosscut and REZO3D-Ladder) considering different flow boundary conditions (i.e., fixed hydraulic gradient along X and Y-direction respectively, and Concentrated recharge). The red plus signs correspond to an off realization, which gives results distinct from the other realizations. For the incipient karst conduit patterns developed using a full lattice grid as initial DFN, results show a higher pattern intensity for a fixed hydraulic gradient along X and Y-direction, respectively. The high values of pattern intensity might be caused by the effect of the outlet boundary condition. For concentrated recharge boundary conditions, the pattern intensity remains similar, whatever the DFN cases. As regards the anisotropy index, it is noticeably influenced by the types of boundary conditions. For dissolution obtained considering a fixed hydraulic gradient along X direction, a higher anisotropy index is obtained for the cases where the initial DFNs were also anisotropic (i.e., “Lattice-Ladder”, “REZO3D-Crosscut” and “REZO3D-Ladder”, Fig. S6  in supplementary material ). Similar structural correlation between a mapped DFN and a subsurface mapped cave system was observed in a cave in carbonate rocks located in central Bahia, NE Brazil (Boersma et al., 2019 ). When the initial DFNs were isotropic (i.e., “Lattice” and “Lattice-Cemented fracture segments”), the anisotropy index values are close to unity. For the different anisotropic DFN cases, the main observable difference that might explain the distinct anisotropy indexes, resides in the fracture intersections. For instance, “Lattice-Ladder like” DFN has “L-shape”, “T-shape” and “X-shape” (Table 1 ) intersections (respectively connecting 2, 3 and 4 fracture segments) while “REZO3D-Crosscut” and “REZO3D-Ladder” have only “X-shape” and “T-shape” intersections connecting 4 and 3 fracture segments respectively. According to this result, outcrop data such as mapped fracture network and recharge conditions might provide valuable information about the local anisotropy of the karst conduit network underneath, which is of a great importance for flow and transport processes. The higher ramification degree is obtained for the “Lattice-Cemented”, “Lattice-Ladder” and “REZO3D-Ladder” cases, which comprise “T-shape” intersections. On the contrary, the “Lattice” and “REZO3D-Crosscut” cases, which contain mainly “X-shape” intersections, show very low ramification degree with values close to zero. According to this result, the existence of ramifications in karst conduit is partly controlled by the type of intersections in the initial fracture network. Thus, “T-shape” intersections connecting three fractures (e.g. long fractures connected with joints with no crosscuts) might increase ramification during dissolution processes.  3.3 Correlation dimension of flow D2 (q) The evolution of the 2D correlation dimension of flow (D2 ) is calculated for the ten different realizations of each DFN case, and each BC type. The plots are based on the 10 realizations; the solid line corresponds to the mean and the shaded region corresponds to the range of the results for each DFN case. Fig. 5   shows a plot of D2  as a function of a normalized time (time/final breakthrough time) for different boundary conditions: a fixed hydraulic gradient along X-direction (Fig. 5 .a) and Y-direction (Fig. 5 .b), respectively, and concentrated recharge (Fig. 5 .c). The evolution of correlation dimension of flow D2 (q) when dissolution is simulated for a hydraulic gradient along “X-direction” (Fig. 5 .a) indicates a flow initially homogeneously distributed in the fracture network (value of D2 close to 2), which then progressively channelizes within the dominant incipient karst conduits (when D2 gets closer to 1). Such result is observed for the different cases. The evolution of correlation dimension of flow D2 (q) when dissolution is simulated along “Y-direction” (Fig. 5 .b) indicates a flow initially homogeneously distributed in the fracture network (value of D2 closer to 2), which then progressively channelizes within the dominant incipient karst conduit (when D2 gets closer to 1). The flow channelization is similar for the isotropic (DFN 1 and 2) cases (i.e., “Lattice” and “Lattice – cemented”), whatever the flow direction. However, for anisotropic DFN cases (DFN 3, 4 and 5) where the main direction of flow is perpendicular to the long fractures set, less competition between wormholes was observed and a dominant wormhole emerges. Such result points out the importance of the connectivity transverse to the main direction of flow. According to this result, fractures with low connectivity transverse to the main direction of flow lead into more pronounced competition processes. For concentrated recharge BC, the evolution of the correlation dimension of flow D2 (q) indicates a sudden and important flow channeling at early stage, followed by local flow channelization (stair-like drops of D2 ), then a relatively stable flow distribution at late stage. Such behavior is different from the one observed for directional flow BC (progressive channeling through dissolution time within the domain). This result, indicates that dissolution induced by concentrated recharge induces negligible competition processes as the inlet/outlet points induce flow channelization from the beginning the dissolution processes. The sudden drop of D2 (q) at early stage is due to the concentrated inlet/outlet points. This drop is marked by a quick breakthrough of one concentrated recharge inlet point (usually the closest to the outlet point). Also, for concentrated recharge BC case, we observe a smaller range of D2 (q) decrease (from 1.6 to 1.2) than in the case of directional flow BC (from 1.9 to 1). The “stair-like” behavior of D2 (q) for this case might be explained by the wormehole’s breakthrough (wormhole connected to outlet) from different recharge inlet points at different dissolution times, which induces a small redistribution of flow. In other words, one wormhole quickly develops (wormehole’s breakthrough), then, the other wormholes related to other inlet points gradually join the main wormhole connected to the outlet.  3.4 Graph theory metrics (KARSTNET) Collon et al., 2017  proposed using the graph theory to characterize karst conduit geometry and topology. Authors also shared a tool (KARSTNET) that allows calculating different metrics which can be subcategorized. In this study, we use KARSTNET to evaluate relevant metrics to characterize the geometrical and topological properties of incipient karst conduit patterns and assess the combined effect of structural properties and connectivity of initial fracture network and flow boundary conditions on incipient karst conduit geometries.a. Number of junctions, extremities and cycles    Some simple metrics, such as the number of junctions, extremities and cycles, which are based on a simplified graph of the incipient karst conduit pattern, already give indication about the different patterns as a function of the different dissolution processes. Indeed, a high number of junctions indicates a high degree of ramification, and a high number of extremities indicates a high degree of karstification, while a high number of cycles indicates more pronounced anastomotic patterns.b. Howard coefficients    The three previous metrics (number of junction nodes, number of extremity nodes and number of cycles) allow to evaluate Howard’s coefficients. Howard’s coefficients are derived from graph theory (Garrison and Marble, 1962), and were developed to characterize braided patterns of streams (Howard et al., 1970 ). Then, these parameters were applied to quantify karst network connectivity (Howard, 1971 ). The Howard’s coefficients alpha, beta and gamma are defined as follows (Howard et al., 1970 ): The parameter α    is the ratio of the observed number of cycles to the greatest number of cycles(12) α = N cycl   2 ( N junc   + N ext   ) - 5        The parameter β    is the ratio of the number of edges to the number of seed vertices(13) β = S N junc   + N ext          The parameter γ    is the ratio of the observed number of edges to the greatest possible number of edges(14) γ = S 3 ( N junc   + N ext   - 2 )       where N cycl      corresponds to the cycles number, N junc      corresponds to the junction nodes number, N ext      corresponds to the extremity nodes number and S    corresponds to number of edges (here, the edges correspond to the enlarged fracture segments). Howard (1971)  noted that alpha, beta and gamma respective values are close to 0, 1, and 0.33 for a branch work karst; and respectively close to 0.25, 1.5 and 0.5, for a reticular one (Collon et al., 2017 ). The connectivity degree DC , expressed in percentage, can then be defined as:(15) D C  = α 0.25   + β - 1  0.5   + γ - 0.33  0.17    3       Fig. 6   represents a boxplot of Howard’s coefficient (alpha, beta and gamma) and the degree of connectivity DC  for the different initial DFN cases considering different flow boundary conditions. The high values of Howard’s coefficients are associated to anastomotic (reticular) patterns while the low values correspond to branch work patterns. Fig. 7   shows the common cave patterns according to Palmer (1991) . The highest values of these parameters are obtained for the “Lattice” DFN case and the lowest values are obtained for the three anisotropic DFN cases, whatever the boundary condition. According to this result, “Lattice” initial DFNs may favor reticular patterns while anisotropy favors branch work patterns. However, for the different cases, the calculated values of the Howard’s coefficients are closer to the typical values obtained for branch work patterns than for reticular patterns. Indeed, alpha values range from 0 to 0.12, beta values from 0.85 to 1.2, and gamma values from 0.3 to 0.4, which are very similar to the values estimated for different natural karst systems with branch work patterns (Collon et al., 2017 ). In general, the three parameters alpha, beta and gamma follow the same trend for a given flow direction. Whatever the case, the connectivity degree Dc boxplot shows a similar trend as Howard’s coefficients. Results also show that, for the concentrated recharge boundary condition, these coefficients indicate branch work patterns with a smaller variation between the different DFN cases comparing to constant head boundary condition. This result is in agreement with results from Palmer (1991)  who showed that branch work patterns are associated to concentrated recharge.c. Other graph metrics    We also calculate other relevant metrics based on the graph of the incipient karst conduit pattern (Collon et al., 2017 ). These parameters are listed as follow:– Tortuosity     Tortuosity is a common metric used to characterize karstic morphologies (Jeannin et al., 2007). Here, the tortuosity is calculated for each branch of the wormhole pattern, then, the mean is calculated and considered as the total tortuosity for the whole pattern. The tortuosity ti,j  from one seed vertex i to the following one j is the ratio between the curvilinear length li,j  along the branch and the Euclidean length di,j  between the two seed vertices:(16) t i , j   = l i , j   d i , j        – Average shortest path length ( SPL  ¯     )     For any vertex i, the shortest path length SPLi  is the average shortest path that separates i from any other vertex j of the same connected component:(17) SPL  i  = 1 N - 1   ∑ j  L ij       where N is the number of vertices in the network. We define the average shortest path length of a network as the mean of the shortest path length ratios:(18) SPL  ¯   = 1 N  ∑ i  SPL  i       The average shortest path length characterizes the efficiency of the network in terms of the distance between two given points. It is influenced by the linearity and the size of the network.– Central point dominance (CPD)     The betweenness centrality of a vertex i is calculated on the reduced graph of the network and characterizes its topology. This metric is defined as(19) B i  = ∑ jk   ξ j , k   ( i )   ξ j , k        where ξ j , k   ( i )     refers to the number of shortest paths between j and k passing through i. ξ j , k      is the total number of the shortest paths between j and k. The relative centrality is then defined as(20) B i  ∗   = B i  N  2  - 3 N + 2       where N is the number of nodes in the network. The central point dominance is defined as (Freeman, 1977)(21) CPD = 1 N - 1   ∑ i  ( B max  ∗   - B i  ∗   )      where B max  ∗      is the largest value of relative centrality. A complete graph gives a 0 CPD value while a star graph gives a 1 value.– Average vertex degree     This metric is calculated on the reduced graph of the patterns and is defined as:(22) k = 2 ( N - 1 )  N       where(23) N = 2 n 3  + 2      n3 is the number of nodes of degree 3. Values of average vertex degree superior to 2 indicate the presence of cycles; higher is the value, higher is the number of cycles in the network. Fig. 8   represents a boxplot of the different metrics (i.e. Tortuosity, Average shortest path length, Central point dominance and Average vertex degree) for the different initial DFN cases considering different flow boundary conditions. Boxplots of tortuosity show low values for all cases (highest observed values are 1.04), The low values are due to the fact that KARSTNET calculate the tortuosity on branches and not on the whole system. Nevertheless, the case “Lattice-Cemented fracture segments” show higher values of tortuosity than the other cases whatever the boundary condition. This result can also be clearly observed in the patterns shown in Fig. 2 . The lowest tortuosity values (Fig. 8 ) are obtained on the incipient karst conduits patterns exhibiting angular geometries (i.e. “Lattice” and “REZO3D-Crosscut joint fractures”) as observed for natural karst conduits patterns (Palmer, 1991 ). These DFN cases are characterized by dominant “X-shape” intersections (Fig. 10 ; Table 1 ). The average shortest path length provides an information about the linearity and size of the system (Collon et al., 2017 ). For directional flow BC along “X-direction”, results obtained for all cases (Fig. 8 ) show that the average shortest path length is relatively close to half size of the domain in X direction (25 m). It is jointly due to the direction of flow and the existence of long fractures set along this direction that favor linear wormholes from inlet to outlet. Such linear wormholes are the most common observed results in the literature (e.g., Dreybrodt and Gabrovšek, 2018; Szymczak and Ladd, 2011 ). On the other hand, for directional flow BC along “Y-direction”, results show that ladder like initial DFNs cases exhibit slightly higher values of the average SPL. The ladder like initial DFNs are characterized by a dominant “T-shape” intersections (Fig. 10 ; Table 1 ) and might explain the obtained stair-like patterns. For the incipient karst conduit patterns induced by concentrated recharge BC, the average shortest path length of all initial DFNs is higher than the values observed for directional flow BCs because of the formation of branch work patterns (Palmer, 1991 ). The central point dominance (CPD) is calculated on reduced graphs of the different networks. CPD values equal to 0 refer to a complete graph while values equal to 1 refer to a graph in a form of a star (Collon et al., 2017 ). Thus, high CPD values (closer to 1) indicate ramiform patterns while low values (closer to 0) indicate anastomotic patterns (Palmer, 1991 ). Fig. 8  show that dissolution induced by concentrated recharge BC favors the formation of a more ramiform patterns comparing to directional BCs. This is due to the location of the inlet and outlet points that highly control the pattern. Also, the radial flow that occurs near the recharge inlet points generates local star-like wormholes. The average vertex degree is calculated based on the reduced graph of the pattern and provides an information about the existence of cycles and looping in the network (values superior to 2 mean that at least one cycle exists in the network). Higher values of the average vertex degree correspond to higher number of cycles/looping in the network (Collon et al., 2021). Fig. 8  shows high average vertex degree for the “Lattice” DFN case whatever the flow BC. These high values indicate more local cycles in the pattern. Nevertheless, under concentrated recharge BC, the values of the average vertex degree for the different initial DFN cases are closer to each other. This difference in comparison with results obtained for directional BC can be explained by constant head BC near the outlet, which increases the local mazes near the outlet (Fig. 3 .a).  3.5 Conduit diameter distribution In addition to geometrical and topological metrics, the evolution of incipient karst conduit diameter during karstification is of great importance. Fig. 9   shows the distribution of incipient karst conduits diameter for the different flow BCs and the different DFN cases (“X-direction”, “Y-direction” and “Concentrated recharge”). Fig. 9 .a and .b shows that the conduit diameter distributions of the incipient karst conduit patterns obtained with directional flow along “X-direction” and “Y-direction” is unimodal. However, none of the predefined distributions provide a good fit for the distribution. as a lognormality test, we calculated R = ((<aperture2 >/<aperture>2 )3 )*(<aperture>3 /<aperture3 >) with brackets <…> representing an average. R is exactly 1 for the lognormal distribution, so R close to 1 should be a good indication of a lognormal distribution. However, R values (shown in Table S1  in the supplementary material ) range between 1.5 and 2.2. Thus, the distributions are not fully lognormal. To better characterize the conduit diameters distributions, we also plot in a log log scale the probability density of the conduits aperture/diameter. As no evident straight line is obtained (see Fig. S7  in supplementary material ), this distribution does not seem to follow a power law neither. To further analyze the diameter distribution, a “goodness to fit test” is performed for distinct distributions (lognormal, exponential, Inverse Gaussian, Weibel, Gamma). The test rejected all the distribution. The closest distributions that were identified to characterize the diameter distribution are Lognormal, Inverse Gaussian and Birnbaum Saunders (see Fig. S8  in the supplementary material ). However, the three distributions seem to have similar drawbacks as they all significantly overestimate the population for intermediate apertures and underestimate the larger apertures at the tail. Maybe the misfit is caused by the initiation of a multimodal distribution. In other words, the fracture segments with intermediate apertures evolve, by group, into fracture segments with larger apertures. On the contrary, in the case of “Concentrated recharge” boundary condition (Fig. 9 .c), bimodal distributions are observed for all cases, which is in agreement with observation made by Maqueda et al. (2023) , who showed that the evolution of conduit diameter distribution during karst genesis follow a multimodal distribution for concentrated recharge case. In this case, most of the fracture segments of the incipient conduit reach higher diameter values. The karstification process does not occur homogeneously in the catchment, but instead it proceeds in a series of multiple breakthroughs corresponding to different phases of karstification (Maqueda et al., 2023 ). In this paper, the diameter follows a bimodal distribution. The first mode corresponds to the fracture segments that have the largest diameters, which breakthrough at early stages. The second mode corresponding to the wormholes that breakthrough at later stages. We note that after a breakthrough of a wormhole, the hydraulic head at the outlet propagates into it. By having the same hydraulic head as the outlet, this wormhole thus plays a role of the outlet as well. Accordingly, the remaining developing wormholes join the closest part of the network that is already linked to the outlet.  3.6 Influence of fractures intersection on the incipient karst conduits patterns Previous studies about fracture networks highlighted the various effect of the type of fracture intersections (Fig. 10  ) on flow distribution and connectivity/DFN percolation (e.g. Lei and Wang, 2014). Here we analyze the influence of different types of fractures intersections on the incipient karst conduit patterns. Table 1 summarizes the geometrical and topological metrics of incipient karst pattern as a function of the different cases and type of fractures intersections (Fig. 10 ). Table 1  shows that the fracture dead ends seem to not correlate with any metric, which is related to the fact that our model does not account for diffusion, which is the main driver of dissolution in the dead ends. Table 1  also shows that certain geometrical and topological metrics seem to be correlated with the type of fracture intersections in the initial DFN cases. The ramification degree shows higher values when the initial DFN has dominant “T-shape” fracture intersections. This result indicates that “T-shape” fracture intersections may play an important role on ramification processes which can be explained by flow bifurcation. Secondly, the “L-shape” and “T-shape” fracture intersections increase the values of average SPL which can be explained by the increase of number of wormhole bends at these types of intersections. As mentioned before, the average SPL is also highly correlated to the type of boundary condition. The highest values of pattern intensity, mean degree (that indicates cycles) and Howard’s coefficients (that indicate tendency toward reticular patterns) are obtained for the “Lattice” DFN, which indicates anastomotic and reticular patterns. Finally, the anisotropy of the initial DFN (longer fractures along one direction than along the other perpendicular direction) induces an anisotropy of the final conduit patterns. Fig. 11   shows three real cave patterns that have some similarities with our simulated conduit patterns.– Firstly, the Crevice cave, Missouri, USA (Fig. 11 .a, b), characterized by a curvilinear branch work developed mainly along bedding planes (Palmer, 1991 ). Such pattern is obtained with “Lattice-Cemented fracture segments” initial DFNs (Fig. 11 .c). According to these observations, the abundance of cement in fractures might favor curvilinear conduit patterns.  – Secondly, the Crystal Lake cave, Iowa, USA (Fig. 11 f) shows angular patterns. Several kilometers away from the Crystal Lake cave, Panno et al., (2015)  managed to capture a map of a fracture network in crop field after a drought episode (Fig. 11 e). The mapped real DFN shows two main orthogonal fracture sets that exhibit a high number of “X-shape” fracture intersections. Similar angular conduit patterns were simulated (Fig. 11 .g) with “Lattice” and “REZO3D-Crosscut joint fractures” DFNs, which also are characterized by dominant X-type type of intersections (Fig. 11 .h). According to these results, “X-shape” fracture intersections might favor angular conduit patterns.  – Finally, the Mystery cave, Minnesota, USA (Fig. 11 .j) shows anisotropic stair-like patterns and surface outcrop shows ladder like DFNs (Fig. 11 .i). Similarly, the simulated anisotropic stair-like patterns were obtained with ladder like initial DFNs.    This study investigates the influence of the structural properties and connectivity of the fracture network on incipient karst genesis. However, the presented results remain exclusive to the considered set of flow conditions. Former studies showed how different flow conditions affect the maziness and ramifications of the developed karst network (e.g., Aliouache et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2023 ). The induced changes from different flows and boundary conditions might thus considerably affect the values of the calculated metrics obtained in this study. To further assess these effects, one way forward will be to extend this study by using other flow conditions; this will be the focus of an upcoming paper. However, to give some insights about this potential influence, we looked at the influence of two different flow conditions (change of hydraulic gradient from 0.16 to 0.32) on anisotropy, ramification degree and average Shortest Path Length. Simulations are performed in Y direction under constant head boundary condition. An increase in the hydraulic gradient induces an increase in the anisotropy index for the DFN3 case (Lattice-Ladder) and an increase of the average shortest path length for the DFN5 case (REZO3D-Ladder). It also induces an increase in the values of the ramification degree for all the different DFN cases. This test shows a flow-dependent phenomena of the several used metrics. Nevertheless, for this tested case, the comparison of one metric between the different DFN cases seems to follow the same trend for the two different hydraulic gradients. For example, for both hydraulic gradients, the anisotropy index shows a higher value for DFN3 (Lattice-Ladder) than the remaining DFN cases. Another way forward is to investigate the influence of DFN’s structural properties and connectivity on incipient karst genesis considering real discrete fracture networks.   4 Summary and conclusions In this study, a reactive transport model that simulates dissolution processes in discrete fracture networks is used to investigate the effect of DFN properties (i.e. structural properties, anisotropy and connectivity) on incipient karst conduit patterns under different boundary conditions. Five different DFNs with various types of fracture intersections (“Lattice”, “Lattice-Cemented”, “Lattice-Ladder like”, “REZO3D-Crosscut” and “REZO3D-Ladder like”) were considered to simulate dissolution and associated incipient karst conduit patterns. Results show that the structural properties and connectivity of fracture networks (i.e. anisotropy and type of intersections) have a considerable effect on the final geometry and topology of the incipient karst conduit patterns. Here are the main conclusions of this study performed on two-dimensional synthetic DFN:– Three main patterns were obtained: curvilinear, angular and stair-like patterns.  – Directional flow boundary condition induces linear incipient wormholes while concentrated recharge boundary condition leads to branch work patterns. The aperture distribution of the incipient karst conduit network seems to follow a multimodal distribution.  – Anisotropic DFNs favor the formation of anisotropic karst conduit networks. More incipient karst conduits develop in the same direction as the long fractures.  – Heterogeneity (i.e., cement, aperture) favors the formation of tortuous and curvilinear wormholes.  – The type of fractures intersection plays a major role in the final incipient karst conduit geometry and topology. Dominant “T-shape” intersections favor ramifications and stair-like conduit patterns while dominant “X-shape” intersections favor angular karst network geometries.    Finally, the confrontation of the simulations with observations made on real cave patterns shows that similar correlations between the properties of the initial fracture networks and the associated karst conduit patterns can be observed in both synthetic and real cases, which might give new insights about karst genesis in fractured carbonate rocks.
1 Introduction Floods are one of the greatest threats to the safety of human settlements and their sustainable development. It causes misery and fatalities worldwide (Mohanty et al. 2020 ). According to the International Commission on Large Dams (ICOLD), the world holds more than 57,000 large dams (dam height ≥15 m from the lowest foundation to the dam crest or a dam between 5 m and 15 m height impounding more than 3 Mm3 ) (Dhiman and Patra, 2019 ) to store river water for various purposes such as irrigation, water supply, power generation, and flood control. India ranks third with 5701 large dams after America and China (https://www.cwc.gov.in/damsafety/home  accessed on Feb 5, 2021). Majority of these dams were constructed in the previous century, with limited data and hazard assessment at that time. Previously constructed water infrastructures are becoming vulnerable due to their insufficient capacity under changing climate across the globe. The unexpected failure of such a large structure might result in substantial economic, social, and environmental losses (Heidarzadeh and Feizi, 2022 ) and even loss of life (Abdulrahman et al., 2022 ) downstream of the dam. The world witnessed more than 450 prominent dam failures post-2000, resulting in significant fatalities and monitory misfortune (ASDSO, 2020 ). In India, 36 large dam failures were recorded, of which the Machhu-II dam (Gujarat) in 1979 resulted in more than 2000 fatalities and was registered as the worst dam failure in the Guiness book of records (Dhiman and Patra, 2019 ). Such failures of dams suggest the necessity of emergency action plans (EAPs) to reduce losses in the event of dam failure (National Dam Safety, 2009; Pierce et al., 2010 ). The dam-break studies and corresponding flood inundation mapping play significant roles in preparing EAPs for quick and effective response (Álvarez et al., 2017 ). The Tiered-based dam-break flood modelling approach is suggested in the “Guidelines for Mapping Flood Risks Associated with Dams” by the Central Water Commission (CWC, 2018 ), Government of India, for the development of EAPs for all the large dams in India. Considering the risk associated with dam failure, corresponding fatalities, and financial losses, dam-break flood modelling for large dams is of utmost importance. The dam failure occurs primarily due to piping (sunny day/fair weather failure) and overtopping (rainy day/extreme weather failure) caused by internal erosion and flooding, respectively (CWC, 2018 ). The dam breach modelling comprises an estimation of the dam breach flow hydrograph and its routing in the downstream. The dam breach parameters are crucial in determining the dam breach flood hydrograph. MacDonald and Langridge-Monopolis (1984)  developed a graphical relationship for the expected values of breach parameters such as breach width, shape, and formation time. Bureau of Reclamation (1988), Froehlich (1995a,b), Wahl (1998), Froehlich (2008), Xu and Zhang (2009), Pierce et al. (2010) , and Froehlich (2016)  developed empirical equations for breach parameters while considering dam-break events in the past. Wahl (2004)  presented a quantitative analysis of uncertainties in different regression-based methods for computing breach parameters. In another study, Wahl (2014)  found breach parameters given by Xu and Zhang (2009)  offer better predictions against the observed data. However, Dhiman and Patra (2019)  concluded that the breach parameter equations proposed by Froehlich (2008)  perform better specifically for Indian dam failures than other equations. CWC (2018)  also suggested a similar equation for field engineers in India. Based on the findings of Dhiman and Patra (2019)  and the recommendation of CWC (2018) , the equation given by Froehlich (2008)  can be used to estimate dam breach parameters for Indian dams. The one-dimensional (1D) or/and two-dimensional (2D) (depth averaged) hydrodynamic (HD) models are used to obtain the dam breach flood hydrograph and subsequent flood mapping of the area. Fread (1977)  developed the first model, DAMBRK, to analyse the dam breach processes, including the computation of peak discharge through the breach, its routing, and flood inundation downstream. Further, dam-break flood studies using various numerical models such as HEC-RAS, GRASS GIS, BreZo, FLO-2D, TELEMAC-2D, MIKE 11/21 (Horritt and Bates, 2002; Yochum et al., 2008; Haltas et al., 2016; Kim and Sanders, 2016; Amini et al., 2017; Begam et al., 2018; Rashid Mohd Shah et al., 2020; Zali et al., 2021; Ge et al., 2022 ; and Abdulrahman et al., 2022 ) are reported in recent literature. Yochum et al. (2008)  suggested using high-resolution topographic data for accurate dam-break flood mapping. Kim and Sanders (2016)  highlighted investigating overtopping failure along with piping failure. Zali et al. (2021)  modelled the probable dam-break flood of AghChay Dam in Iran to obtain the flood maps for different indicators. They identified the high-hazard zones to mitigate the flood hazards and devise possible emergency plans. Abdulrahman et al. (2022)  emphasised providing dam-break flood hazard maps to risk managers for establishing EAPs. They investigated the effect of hypothetical (Khassa Chai) dam failure (piping) on people, vehicles, and structures with the application of dam breach parameter equations, a flood inundation model, and hazard mapping. Ferrari et al. (2023)  presented solutions to the shallow water equation having shock-capturing capability for the assessment of dam-failure hypothetical scenarios, which can be useful for the design of EAPs. The procedure is applied to generate hypothetical dam-break flooding scenarios for two dams in northern Italy while assuming the occurrence of failure when the water level in the reservoir equals the maximum admissible one. From the literature, it is found that dam breach modelling can be carried out with a combination of empirical dam breach equations and 1D (Zhou et al., 2015; Gaagai et al., 2022; Verma and Patra, 2022 )and 2D HD models (Azeez et al., 2020; Marangoz and Anilan, 2022; Sarchani and Koutroulis, 2022; Urzică et al., 2021 ). However, the effects of inflow with an early peak (steeper rising limb), initial reservoir level, and erosion of earthen embankment on the dam-break outflow hydrograph are not highlighted in the past literature. The dam-break flood risk maps are developed with the product of flood hazard, vulnerability, and exposure. Also, in the case of a dam-break flood disaster in densely populated areas, it is important to identify the ability of the community to resist, react, and respond to the disaster, which can be evaluated using socio-economic vulnerability. Also, exposure can define the presence of people, livelihoods, infrastructure, economic, social, cultural, and environmental assets in place that could be adversely affected during physical events and may lead to future loss or damage. With continuous change in climatic conditions and an increasing frequency of extreme (rainfall) events that can lead to heavy inflow in dams and subsequent damages therefore, exposure must be considered in the dam-break flood risk assessment, which was again missing in the past studies. In the current study, dam-break flood risk assessment is calculated by integrating the dam-break flood hazard, socio-economic vulnerability of the community, and exposure of the region, which can be used to develop the EAPs. The Ukai Dam, built on the Tapi River, is the second-largest reservoir in Gujarat, India. It has already completed 50 years since its commencement in 1972, and the gross storage capacity has been reduced over the years from 8511 Mm3  to 7414.2 Mm3 . It is an earth-fill dam, more susceptible to overtopping failure vis-à-vis other types of dams. In addition, Ukai Dam has 78 % of its live storage stored against the moving gates instead of on the static wall; in such conditions, the appropriate gate operation plays a critical role in infrastructure safety and flood control (Jibhakate et al., 2021 ). The Kakrapar Atomic Power Station (KAPS) is located on the bank of the lower Tapi River, and industries such as the National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC), the Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) of India, Reliance Industries, Larson and Toubro Ltd., etc. are situated in the floodplain of the lower Tapi River. Further, Surat city, with a population of 44,61,026 (Census, 2011 ), is located 100 km downstream of the Ukai Dam. In such a scenario, the failure of the Ukai Dam may lead to a dam-break and directly jeopardise dam safety. The city has experienced severe floods in the past. The flood of 1968, with a peak discharge of 42,450 m3 /s, was the highest recorded flood so far. The floods of the year 2006, with a peak discharge of 25,780 m3 /s released from Ukai Dam, inundated almost 80 % of the city and resulted in direct damages of 150 lives and 210 billion INR (Thakar, 2007; Patel and Srivastava, 2013, Jibhakate et al., 2023a ). Due to the severity of flooding in the Lower Tapi River, the susceptibility of the earthen dam against overtopping failure, the existence of critical infrastructure, and the high population downstream of the Ukai Dam, the Ukai Dam can be considered a high-hazard potential dam. It requires Tyre-3-type dam-break analysis (CWC, 2018 ), to avoid potential damage in the near future. In this study, several crucial aspects are addressed for the first time in dam-break analysis, aiming to yield valuable insights for mitigating future flood disasters. These include: (a) generating dam-break flood hydrographs for Ukai Dam failure under different scenarios based on the mode of failure (piping/overtopping), moment of failure (reservoir level), and erosion of the earthen embankment, utilizing empirical dam breach equations and a 1D HD hydrodynamic model. (b) simulating dam-break flood propagation using a well calibrated 2D HD model and subsequently mapping flood hazards to assess human, vehicle, and structural stability against dam-break floods. (c) computation of socio-economic vulnerability to identify the capability of the existing community and exposure at the lowest administrative level, (d) development of dam-break flood risk maps by combining the dam-break flood hazard, socio-economic vulnerability, and land use exposure. The developed inundation, hazard, and risk maps will be useful to local and disaster management authorities to develop plans for response to recovery practices, emergency action plans (EAPs) and prioritize the wards and villages during flood mitigation with scarce resources.  2 Study area and data source 2.1 Tapi Basin The Tapi River is one of the largest rivers in Western India, originates from Multai in the Betul district of Madhya Pradesh, and drains into the Arabian Sea. The total length of the Tapi River is 724 km, it passes through three different states, viz., Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Gujarat, and is spread over 65,145 km2  of area. The whole Tapi Basin is partitioned into three major sub-basins, viz., the Upper Tapi basin from origin to Hathnur Dam (29,430 km2 ), the Middle Tapi basin from Hathnur to Ukai Dam (32,097 km2 ), and the Lower Tapi basin from Ukai Dam to the Arabian Sea (3618 km2 ) (Jain et al., 2007 ), as shown in Fig. 1  . The average annual rainfall of the Tapi Basin is 815.7 mm; during 1944–2013 (Gehlot et al., 2021 ), about 90 % of the total rainfall was received during monsoon months (June–September), of which 50 % was received in July and August (Sharma et al., 2018 ). The lateral flow contribution is negligible as there is no major tributary discharge into the Lower Tapi River. The Lower Tapi River from Ukai Dam to the Arabian Sea has two existing inline structures, viz., Kakrapar weir and Singanpur weir. The Kakrapar weir (chainage 22 km) is an ogee-shaped spillway with a crest elevation of 48.78 m (above mean sea level (amsl)) and a weir coefficient of 1.881 (Subramanya, 1998 ). In comparison, the Singanpur weir (chainage 103.03 km) is a broad crested weir with a crest elevation of 6 m amsl and a weir coefficient of 1.666 (Timbadiya et al., 2015 ).  2.2 Ukai Dam and Surat city There are two major hydraulic structures across the Tapi River, viz., Hathnur Dam and Ukai Dam, to meet the water requirements in their respective command areas. The Ukai Dam is the largest multipurpose project on the Tapi River, completed in 1972, located near the Ukai village of Songadh taluka in Tapi district in Gujarat state, India. The Ukai Dam is an earthen-cum-masonry composite structure with a total length of 4927 m, including a 425 m-long principal spillway. The salient features of the Ukai reservoir are shown in Table 1  . Surat is the most prominent urban centre and densely populated city located on the bank of the Lower Tapi River and the Arabian Sea coast. Surat is the eighth-largest city, a centre for diamond cutting and polishing, the biggest textile hub in the country, and the administrative capital of Gujarat state in the western part of India. Surat is the second-fastest-growing city in India and the fourth-fastest-growing city in the world (Shahfahad et al., 2021 ). Surat city has a population of 44,61,026 (Census, 2011 ) spread over an area of 326.51 km2 . The entire city is divided into seven different administrative zones: central, north, east, southeast, south, southwest, and west (Timbadiya et al., 2014 ). Surat Urban Development Authority (SUDA) recently extended its boundary around the mainland of Surat city for the 2050 plan, as shown in Fig. 1 (e). The SUDA boundary includes the wards from Surat city and villages from the surrounding Talukas Such as Surat, Chorasi, Olpad, Mangrol, Kamrej, Chalthan, and Palsana. Surat city experienced the disastrous situation of riverine floods in the years 1994, 1998, and 2006, primarily due to heavy releases from the Ukai Dam. The warning and danger flood levels at Nehru Bridge, a gauging station in Surat city, are 8.5 m and 9.5 m, respectively (CWC, 2014 ). The detailed layout of the study area undertaken for the dam-break flood analysis considering stream gauging stations along the Lower Tapi River, viz., Kakrapar Weir, Mandavi Bridge, Ghala, and Nehru Bridge, is shown in Fig. 1 .  2.3 Data source The data required for the current study were collected from the different relevant agencies responsible for the measurement and collection of the data. The detailed description, source, and purpose of the data used in the current study are illustrated in Table 2  .   3 Methodology The detailed methodology adopted in the current study for the dam-break analysis of Ukai Dam is shown in Fig. 2   which consists of (1) the development of a 1D HD river model with a dam-break structure to obtain the dam-break flood hydrograph through a breach for piping and overtopping failure; (2) dam-break flood propagation using a well calibrated 2D HD model and hazard assessment for human, vehicle, and structural stability; (3) socio-economic vulnerability and land use exposure assessment for the SUDA administrative region. (4) flood risk assessment by combining flood hazard, socio-economic vulnerability, and land use exposure. 3.1 Development of the 1D HD model (MIKE 11) The 1D HD model to obtain the dam-break flood hydrograph was developed in MIKE 11. The model can solve the 1D hyperbolic dynamic Saint-Venant equation using an implicit six-point Abbott-Ionescu finite difference scheme (Abbott and Ionescu, 1967 ) for the staggered grid of finite-difference by double sweep algorithm (DHI, 2017a ). The 1D model comprises the channel geometry with the insertion of the dam-break structure, boundary data, and HD parameter, which are described in the succeeding paragraphs. The readers can refer to Abbott and Ionescu (1967)  and the scientific documentation of MIKE 11 for the basic one-dimensional nearly horizontal flow equations and their solutions (DHI, 2017a ). 3.1.1 Dam-break configuration in the model The 1D model domain can be created with a series of river cross-sections. The network editor in MIKE 11 enables the user to characterise the dam-break structure in the given river network. The practical approach to locating the ‘Dambreak structure’ is on a separate reservoir branch containing only three calculation points (DHI, 2017a ), as shown in Fig. 3  (a). To obtain an accurate reservoir storage characteristic, the reservoir can be modelled as a single h-point (water level point) in the model, corresponding to the upstream boundary condition where the inflow hydrograph needs to be specified (DHI, 2017a ). The additional flooded area against the reservoir water level is obtained from the capacity-elevation curve of the Ukai Dam [Fig. 3 (b)], which is used to define the reservoir storage in the model. The dam is located at the Q-point in the reservoir branch, where the momentum equation is replaced by the equation that describes the flow through the structure. The breach is selected as a failure mode, which is modelled in two different ways, i.e., failure of the crest due to overtopping and piping failure (pipe in the dam body) followed by breach failure.  3.1.2 Boundary conditions The hourly discharge hydrograph and hourly stage hydrograph are appropriate for the upstream and downstream boundary conditions, respectively, for the unsteady state simulations. In the case of the dam-break flood, the inflow hydrograph (into the reservoir) for the flood of the year 2006 is used as an upstream boundary condition, as shown in Fig. 4  (a). The flood of the year 2006 with a peak discharge of 34,110 m3 /s equals a flood of the about 95-year return period, calculated from the flood frequency analysis of the inflow data for the period of 1972 to 2016 (Supplementary Material S1 ). The tidal levels at the Arabian Sea are shown in Fig. 4 (b) and used as the downstream boundary condition for the model. The high tide at the Arabian Sea influences up to the Singanpur weir, which is located at the tail portion of the river; a critical circumstance for Surat city occurs when the spring tide coincides with the flood peak in the river.  3.1.3 HD parameters The Lower Tapi River receives the discharge from the upstream Ukai Dam and releases it into the Arabian Sea. The slope of the river is mild (Timbadiya et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2017 ); therefore, for the apparent small slopes, a high-order, fully dynamic wave equation is suitable to simulate the HD model (Chow et al., 1988 ). The values of the time step (Δt = 2 sec) and space step (Δx = 149–1700 m) were chosen such that the computation should be stable by keeping the Courant number within an optimum range. In the case of dam-break simulation, the time cantering of the gravity term (DELTA) in the momentum equation is suggested to be slightly more than the default 0.5 (DHI, 2017a ) and kept at 0.75 in the current study. In the 1D HD river model, channel roughness (Manning’s ‘n’) is the main calibration parameter. In the current study, ‘n’ = 0.03 (m-1/3s) is adopted as channel roughness, taken from past studies (CWPRS, 2000; Timbadiya et al., 2014 ) performed on the same river stretch. In a previous study by Timbadiya et al. (2014) , the 1D channel model of the Lower Tapi River was calibrated (for ‘n’ = 0.03 m-1/3s) by comparing the observed and simulated water levels at different stream gauging stations along the river.  3.1.4 Simulation of dam-break scenarios The dam-break flood hydrograph, just downstream of the Ukai Dam, is obtained for different scenarios based on the reservoir water level and erosion of the earthen embankment. In the current study, the failure moment was considered when the water level reaches the Full Reservoir Level (FRL=105.15 m), the High Flood Level (HFL=106.99 m) as piping, and 1 m overtopping (112.25 m) failure due to erosion in/of the earthen embankment (as a mode of failure). The developed model is simulated for four different inflows coming into the reservoir, viz. (a) inflow hydrograph of Ukai reservoir for the flood of 2006 with a peak discharge of 34,110 m3 /s after 40 h. (b) Inflow hydrograph with a peak discharge of 34,110 m3 /s after 1 h. (c) Probable Maximum Flood (PMF) of the Ukai Dam with a peak discharge of 59,920 m3 /s after 60 h. (d) Inflow hydrograph with a peak discharge of 59,920 m3 /s (PMF) after 1 h of inflow (worst-case scenario) as shown in Fig. 5  (a-d), respectively. Fig. 5 (b) and (d) demonstrate the hydrograph with a steep rising limb. It is considered that the reservoir is already full up to FRL and the gates are inoperative due to mechanical or human error. It resulted in a rise in water level up to the crest, which started 1 m overtopping (112.25 m) over the crest. Along with inflow, estimation of the breach parameters is critical in determining the dam-break flood hydrograph of the dam. The various empirical equations based on the failure of past events are available in the literature (MacDonald and Langridge-Monopolis, 1984; Bureau of Reclamation 1988; Wahl, 1998; Froehlich, 2008; Xu and Zhang, 2009; Froehlich, 2016 ), which have uncertainties due to the poor documentation of historical events. However, addressing the uncertainty in the breach parameters is beyond the scope of this study and can be treated as the future scope of the current study. The equation developed by Froehlich (2016)  is based on more data compared to other studies. However, the results obtained from Froehlich (2008)  are very close to Froehlich (2016) , generating the worst flood (Abdulrahman et al., 2022 ). Therefore, in the current study, equations given by Froehlich (2008)  have been adopted to determine the breach parameters for the failure of the Ukai Dam, and the results are treated as deterministic. The same equations were adopted by Kim and Sanders (2016)  for multiple dam failures in Gangneung, South Korea, and Abdulrahman et al. (2022)  for hypothetical dam failures in Kirkuk, Iraq. The typical sketch of the trapezoidal breach developed in the dam is shown in Supplementary Fig. SF2 . In cases where the failure started with piping, the flow started through the dam wall. The erosion of soil along the ‘pipe’ increases the pipe diameter and flow. Finally, the dam collapses into the void created by piping and water overtops through the breach (DHI, 2017a ). According to Froehlich (2008) , a fully developed breach reaches up to the foundation due to its erosion-resistant property compared to embankment material. Also, the presence of erosion-resistant material in the embankment and the volume of water in the reservoir at the time of failure are critical to the height of the breach. As per the digital maps of the Ukai Dam received from Ukai Civil Circle, the earthen embankment of the dam contains a layer of impervious material up to 108.81 m and a rock zone up to 85.3 m from the bottom, as shown in Fig. 6  . The 25 %, 50 % and, 75 % washout of the impervious layer in the earthen embankment, i.e., the height of breach (from the top of the dam) equals to 13.5 m, 24.6 m, and 35.7 m, are considered in the present investigation, as mentioned in Fig. 6 .   3.2 Development of the 2D HD model (MIKE 21) To find out the inundation due to the dam-break flood wave downstream of the Ukai Dam along with Surat city, the 2D HD model in MIKE 21 (having shock capturing capability) is developed using the Digital Terrain Model (DTM). The 2D model comprises bathymetry of the floodplain, boundary and HD conditions, and floodplain roughness as the main components, which are explained in detail in the succeeding paragraphs. The numerical solution of depth-averaged equations in MIKE 21 describes the conservation of mass and momentum in two horizontal dimensions to simulate the hydraulics for 2D free surface flow (DHI, 2017b ). The readers can refer to Abbott et al. (1973)  and the scientific documentation of MIKE 21 for the basic two-dimensional nearly horizontal flow equations and their solutions (DHI, 2017b ). 3.2.1 Bathymetry of the floodplain The accurate representation of topography is a fundamental and essential parameter in the 2D HD model; the bathymetry is created from DEM. The topography of the LTB consists of a narrow valley with gently sloping ground. The LTB comprises terrain variability such as hilly terrain (360 m) above mean sea level, mainly forest areas near the Ukai Dam; the middle part of the basin entails rural and agricultural fields. In contrast, the lower part of LTB (nearly 100 km downstream of the Ukai Dam) has a coastal urban floodplain where Surat-Hazira twin city is located. The lower part of LTB has flat topography, where the surface elevation ranges from −10 m to +20 m amsl. The DEM, a raster file containing pixels that describe the elevation of that point at a particular elevation, is the primary input for any hydrologic/hydraulic model. Due to terrain variability across the LTB, the DEM is developed from the contours (vector) collected from different sources, considering their respective accuracy (See Table 2 ). The contours (vector) for the LTB from different sources are combined and converted to raster by using the spatial interpolation tool ‘Topo to Raster’ in ArcGIS 10.6.1. The grid size of the raster significantly affects the computational efforts by a factor of 23  (Begnudelli et al., 2008 ), whereas a limited additional improvement has been observed in model results with a grid size finer than 50 m (Bates and De Roo, 2000 ). In the current study, 30 m × 30 m cell size bathymetry has been used for the entire LTB, and the raster file is converted into.dfs2 format by using the Grd2Mike tool in MIKE Zero (Supplementary Fig. SF3 ). To check the accuracy of the generated DEM to represent river bathymetry, the cross-sections are extracted (from DEM) at different locations along the river and compared with available surveyed data (Supplementary Fig. SF4 ), which shows reasonable accuracy.  3.2.2 Boundary conditions and HD parameters For unsteady simulations, flow hydrographs and water levels are considered as the upstream and downstream boundary conditions, respectively. Accordingly, the dam-break flood hydrograph resulting from the 1D HD model is used as the upstream boundary condition. In the 2D HD model, the upstream boundary condition was entered as a point source in the uppermost river section along the width of the river. The inflow hydrograph for each cell is computed by dividing the ordinates of flow hydrograph (Ukai release) at zero chainage of the river by 16, as a total of 16 no. of cells (30 m × 30) were identified along the river width. Along with the flow hydrograph, velocity and its direction for each cell are also needed in the upstream boundary condition for 2D floodplain modelling. The velocity at each cell is calculated by using Manning’s equation, considering the uniform flow condition. The variable tide at the Arabian Sea, synchronised with the simulation period, has been used, as a downstream boundary condition. The floodplain is considered dry in the current study, with 1 m of water depth in the channel section as an initial condition. The value of time step Δt is taken as 2 sec.  3.2.3 Floodplain roughness The classified LULC map of the study area for the year 2006 was collected from the National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), having a spatial resolution of 56 m. It has been widely used in flood simulation studies (Mohanty et al., 2018; Ghosh et al., 2021, Jibhakate et al., 2023b ). The obtained LULC map was modified to a spatial resolution of 30 m and six major land cover classes, viz., agriculture, fallow, built-up, forest, water, and wasteland (Supplementary Fig. SF5 ). The agricultural land is the dominant land class within the study area with 46.68 %. The Manning’s roughness value ‘n’ for the given land cover is given in Table 3  , adopted from past studies (Chow, 1959; Timbadiya et al., 2015; Patel et al. 2017 ). Surat city is the most prominent urban area, with a population density of 13,680 persons/km2  as per the 2011 census (SMC), and is prone to flooding due to releases from the Ukai Dam. The performance of the 2D model must be evaluated for accurately simulating the dam-break flood wave propagation in the LTB and Surat city. For the same a well-calibrated 2D HD model developed by Jibhakate et al. (2023b)  has been adopted in the present study.   3.3 Dam-break flood risk mapping Many researchers computed the flood risk as a product of hazard and vulnerability (Mohanty et al., 2020; Sahana et al., 2021; Jibhakate et al., 2023b ). However, the Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC, 2014 ) delineates exposure as a separate component of the risk. Here, we consider flood risk as product three components, i.e., hazard vulnerability, and exposure (Gusain et al., 2020; Tripathy et al., 2020 ).Risk = H a z a r d × V u ln e r a b i l i t y × E x p o s u r e      The flood risk maps can be used to identify the specific locations requiring evacuation and flood mitigation in well advance. In the current study, the flood risk maps are generated at the lowest administrative level, i.e., for the wards with Surat city and villages outside the city but within the SUDA administrative boundary, for better efficiency in decision making. 3.3.1 Dam-break flood hazard mapping Flood hazard is an indicator for identifying the possible source of threat due to flooding. Flood hazard mapping is crucial in flood risk management analysis (Mudashiru et al., 2021 ). The severity of the flood hazard depends on the flood behaviour (extent, depth, velocity, and duration) and the interaction of the flood with the topography. Smith et al. (2014)  gave the classification for dividing the flooded area into distinct hazard classes based on the combined effect of flood depth and flow velocity (D × V).
