This combined indicator specifies the hazard associated with people in different age groups, vehicles, and buildings. The D × V  thresholds linked to various susceptibility levels are given in Table 4  . The flood hazard is classified into six classes, ranging from H1, which specifies the area is safe for all, to H6, which is unsafe for all. The combined hazard curves are shown in Supplementary Fig. SF6 .  3.3.2 Socioeconomic vulnerability Vulnerability accounts for the susceptibility of the region against the upcoming hazard, indicates the inability to face or adapt the situation (Eini et al., 2020 ). The vulnerability is an internal property of the system (IPCC, 2014 ), signifying the direct (physical, social, and environmental), and indirect (socioeconomic) consequences for the region (Balica et al., 2012 ). Disaster often resulted into the loss of life, property, employment and even leads to the emotional and psychological trauma for the effected region. The socio-economic vulnerability helps to identify the resistance, reaction, and response of the belonging community or population. In the current study, the framework adopted by Sherly et al. (2015)  and Mohanty et al. (2020)  is implemented for the socio-economic vulnerability assessment of wards and villages with SUDA boundary. The detailed methodology flowchart is given in Supplementary SF7 . The methodology starts with the judicious selection of vulnerability indicators, followed by their standardization, aggregation, and ranking of the wards and villages. The total of 18 indicators representing the socio-economic status of the wards and villages are selected and further divided into sensitive (negative) and adaptive (positive) groups. The sensitive (adaptive) indicators increase (decrease) the vulnerability with higher values. The details of the indicators are given in Supplementary ST1 . To compare the indicators with different units, indicators are standardized in the range of 0 to 1 using the following (Karmakar et al., 2010 ).(1) f o r  s e n s i t i v e  ( n e g a t i v e )   i n d i c a t o r s : B j  std   = B j  - B  min    B  max   - B  min         (2) f o r  a d a p t i v e  c a p a c i t y  ( p o s i t i v e )   i n d i c a t o r s : B j  std   = B  max   - B j   B  max   - B  min         Here,B j  std     = standardised vulnerability indicator for j  th     sub-district.  B j    = vulnerability indicator for j  th     sub-district.  B  max     = maximum value of vulnerability indicator in all the sub-districts.  B  min     = minimum value of vulnerability indicator among all the sub-districts.    Various aggregation techniques for vulnerability assessment, such as simple averaging (Sherly et al., 2015 ), analytical hierarchy process (AHP; Ramkar and Yadav, 2021 ), technique for order of preference by similarity to ideal solution (TOPSIS; Sahana et al., 2021 ), data envelopment analysis (DEA; Huang et al., 2012; Mohanty et al. 2020 ), combination of AHP and entropy (Wu et al., 2015 ), combination of entropy and TOPSIS (Thakur and Mohanty, 2023 ), and cluster analysis (Kok et al., 2016 ), are available in the literature. DEA is a non-parametric technique that does not make any assumptions on the form of function (Tripathy et al., 2020 ). DEA does not require weight assignment; it reduces subjectivity with minimal possibility of rank reversal (Huang et al., 2012; Tripathy et al., 2020 ). The application of DEA is a robust technique and can be adopted for vulnerability assessment at different spatial scales (Jibhakate et al., 2023b ), and the popular Banker, Charnes, Cooper (BCC; Banker et al., 1984 ) model of DEA has been adopted in the present study. The BCC model is given as follows:(3) m i n i m i s e θ - ∊ ∑ i = 1  m  s i  -  + ∑ r = 1  s  s r  +          (4) ∑ j = 1  n  λ j  x ij   + s i  -  =  θ x ip   ,    i = 1 ,  ⋯ m   ∀ p     (5) ∑ j = 1  n  λ j  y rj   - s r  +  =  y rp   ,    r = 1 ,  ⋯ s   ∀ p     (6) ∑ j = 1  n  λ j  = 1     (7) λ j  , ∊ ≥ 0      Here, p   is the sub-district being evaluated, θ   (0 < 8θ   ≤ 1) is the technical efficiency of the sub-district, x ij     is the amount of input i  used by sub-district j, y rj     is the amount of output r  provided by the sub-district j , λ j    is the weight assigned to ward j, s i  -    and s r  +    are the slack and remnant variables, respectively, and ∊   is a non-Archimedean infinitesimal (generally taken as ∊   = 10  - 6    ). In order to use the DEA effectively, the selected indicators must have a very low correlation. The correlation among the indicators was lowered by dimensional reduction by employing principal component analysis (PCA). The PCA transforms correlated (standardized) indicators into an uncorrelated set of components called principal components (PCs). The matrix of standardise indicators, i.e., [ B i  std   ]   m × n     , where m   is the total number of DMUs (wards), and n   is the total number of indicators, has been given as input to the PCA. The PCA results into n × n    eigenvectors (termed as loadings), n × 1    eigenvalues, and variance explained by each PC. The initial principal component (PC) captures the highest available variation, and this pattern continues with the successive PCs, ensuring the retention of the maximum achievable diversity. Principal components that account for over 75 % of the total variability in the dataset are selected for inclusion in the Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) input, as proposed by Tripathy et al. in 2020 . By considering vulnerability as the state of the system prior to the occurrence of a hazard, the unity (1) (dummy) output is pre-assigned to DEA (Vittal et al., 2020 ). The DEA resulted in relative efficiency for each sub-district (DMU). Finally, the vulnerability of each sub-district is calculated by subtracting the relative efficiency from 1. The higher the efficiency of the sub-district, the lower the vulnerability.  3.3.3 Exposure The exposure component of the risk for the SUDA region is computed using the LULC of the region. The land use pattern affects the severity of the flood, as in the case of urban areas, the severity of the flood increases with the severity of the impervious region (Tripathy et al., 2020 ). The LULC of year 2023 obtained from Sentinal-2 was used, which was further reclassified into four groups (viz. open space, agriculture, urban and waterbody) over the city region. The house damage from the urban area and agricultural damage from the vegetated land were considered in the exposure. However, compared to the urban area, the agricultural area has a high tolerance to flooding with less economic damage. The urban area gets affected more with destruction to the housing, employment, and critical infrastructure such as roads, power, and water supplies. Therefore, the exposure for each village and ward is computed based on the criteria adopted Waghwala and Agnihotri (2019) , given in Eq. (8) . Here, the exposure is higher with the involvement of population and economic resources and vice versa.(8) E vw   = 10 E ur   + 0.5 E Ag   + 0 E os     A vw        Here,E vw     = exposure for the SUDA village and ward;  E ur     = represents the urban area of village and ward exposed to flooding;  E Ag     = represents the agricultural area of village and ward exposed to flooding;  E os     = open space of village and ward exposed to flooding;  E os     = total area of the village and ward.    The 10, 0.5, and 0.0 are the weights for the respective classes.    4 Results and discussion The results and discussion are divided into three sub-sections: (i) dam-break outflow hydrograph from 1D HD modelling; (ii) dam-break flood mapping across the coastal urban floodplain of Surat city; and (iii) corresponding flood risk classification for Surat city. 4.1 Dam-break outflow hydrograph from 1D HD modelling The piping and overtopping are the most common types of dam failure. The analysis of Ukai dam-break is carried out for piping and overtopping failure under 1D HD unsteady flow conditions to obtain the dam-break flood hydrograph based on the reservoir water level, inflow into the reservoir, and erosion of embankment material. A total of 36 dam-break outflow hydrographs were derived. In all cases, the reservoir filled up to FRL (105.15 m) is considered an initial condition. The maximum time required for the simulation of a dam-break outflow hydrograph using the 1D HD model (MIKE 11) is 6 min. The detailed configurations of the computational platform used in 1D HD model simulations are: Intel (R) Xeon (R) W-2155 CPU @ 3.30 GHz, 64-bit, x64-based, 32 GB RAM, and 4 TB hard disk. The same platform is also used for 2D HD simulations. 4.1.1 Dam fails when the reservoir level at FRL=105.15 m (Piping failure) The piping or internal erosion is considered a fair-weather failure; due to the element of surprise, it has a significant possibility of causing casualties (Abdulrahman et al., 2022 ). When the reservoir is at FRL (capacity = 7,414.2 Mm3 ), heavy inflow (Fig. 5 ) flows into the reservoir. The dam failed initially due to piping in the body of the earth dam, which gradually increased and collapsed, followed by flow overtopping through the breach. The breach parameters for each scenario are derived from the empirical equations provided by Froehlich (2008) , tabulated in Table 5  . Where, B avg     is average breach width (m), Vw  = volume of water in the reservoir at the time of failure (m3 ), H b    is breach height (m), B t    and B b    are the top and bottom width of the breach (m), z   = slope of the breach, K 0    = 1.0 for piping failure. For the 2006 flood as an inflow [Fig. 5 (a)] into Ukai reservoir, the dam-break simulation, using breach parameters for 75 % washout of the impervious material in the embankment, a fully developed breach resulted into a peak discharge of 1,08,488 m3 /s, shown in Fig. 7  (a). The dam breach statistics obtained from the simulation revealed that the increase in breach width is followed by an increase in breach discharge until it reaches its maximum value (1,08,488 m3 /s). After this event, breach width remains constant, and a subsequent decrease in discharge is observed. It takes 37 h for the complete development of the breach and outflow hydrograph to reach their maximum value. During the maximum discharge (velocity of 13.32 m/s), the reservoir water level is 105.36 m, which is above the FRL of the dam. It takes almost 7 days to reach a discharge of less than 5,000 m3 /s [Fig. 7  (a)]. For 25 % and 50 % washout scenarios, it resulted into peak discharge (velocity) of 21,153 m3 /s (8.45 m/s) and 55,779 m3 /s (10.95 m/s), after 78 and 42 hs, respectively. After computing the dam-break flood hydrograph, the applicability of the adopted dam breach parameters has been tested by comparing the volume of floodwater from the dam-break hydrograph with the volume of water above the corresponding breach level given in Table 6  . The difference in volume is less than 7 % in all the cases, indicating the acceptability of selected dam-break parameters. A similar analysis was carried out for the different inflow hydrographs shown in Fig. 5 . The corresponding dam breach outflow hydrographs just downstream of the Ukai Dam are shown in Fig. 7 (b-d). In piping failure at FRL, the maximum discharge (velocity) for the 25 % washout scenario is 25,906 m3 /s (8.95 m/s) against PMF as inflow at 73 h. Whereas, for the 50 % and 75 % washout scenarios, it is 60,113 m3 /s (11.21 m/s) and 1,19,758 m3 /s (13.75 m/s) after 31 and 30 h, respectively, against the inflow shown in Fig. 5 (d). In all the scenarios, the difference between the volume above the breach level and the outflow hydrograph is less than 7 %. The largest peak discharge of the Ukai dam-break flood hydrograph is 3.51 times greater than the largest observed flood at the Ukai Dam. It is worth noting that the peak discharge due to Teton dam failure (in 1976) was 20 times greater than the largest observed flood at the dam site (Chow et al., 1988 ). The investigation related to the dam fails when the reservoir level at HFL=106.99 m (started with piping) is included in Supplementary Material S2 .  4.1.2 Dam fails with 1 m overtopping (112.25 m) The overtopping failure is considered an extreme weather failure. Around 35 % of the dams around the world failed due to overtopping (Zhong et al., 2011 ). There is less possibility of casualties as the downstream community is already on alert (Abdulrahman et al., 2022 ). In the case of 1 m overtopping (112.25 m) over the crest, the embankment fails due to (erosion) breaching. The simulations are carried out for all inflows and embankment washout scenarios explained earlier. The breach parameters for the overtopping condition using Froehlich (2008)  are given in Table 7  . Here, K 0    = 1.3 for overtopping failure. The reservoir volume increased due to the rise in water level from FRL to the dam crest. For the 75 % washout scenario against the 2006 flood as an inflow [Fig. 5 (a)], based on derived breach parameters, the fully developed breach resulted into a peak discharge of 1,88,759.7 m3 /s, as shown in Fig. 8  (a). The peak discharge in the outflow hydrograph occurs after 12 h, whereas the breach takes 21 h for its complete development. The breach height of 35.6 m (Fig. 6 ) is achieved within 4 h after the overtopping starts, whereas the terminal top and bottom width of the breach are achieved after 21 h, due to this peak being observed before the complete development of the breach. During the time of peak discharge (1,88,759.7 m3 /s) the flow velocity is 14.89 m/s, and the reservoir water level is 109.5 m. It takes 4 days to attain a breach discharge of less than 5,000 m3 /s. Similar to the piping failure, the model is simulated for all inflows, and the resulting outflow hydrographs are shown in Fig. 8 . The volume of water due to the inflow hydrograph shown in Fig. 5 (d) is not sufficient to reach the water level of 112.25 m. In order to complete the simulation, the recession limb of the inflow hydrograph is modified, as shown in Fig. 8 (d). The largest peak discharge (velocity) for 25 %, 50 % and 75 % washout scenarios are 48,086 m3 /s (9.30 m/s), 1,19,756 m3 /s (12.38 m/s), and 1,93,239 m3 /s (15.10 m/s) against PMF as inflow. The volumetric comparison has been carried out and tabulated in Table 8  . It can be observed that the difference in volume is less than 6 % in all the cases. While estimating the breach parameters using the empirical equation by Froehlich (2008)  the side slope for piping failure is 0.7 whereas in overtopping failure it is 1.0. For the 2006 flood with 50 % washout of the earthen embankment, due to the rise in reservoir volume, the average breach width in the overtopping failure (658.6 m) is nearly 60 % wider than that of the piping failure (417.5 m) at FRL. While comparing the development of breach and outflow hydrograph to reach its maximum value, it takes 21 h for overtopping failure, whereas 37 h for piping failure is almost 1.76 times faster. In case of overtopping failure, the volume of water accumulated is higher in the given time period compared to piping failure. Due to this, the peak discharge and flow velocity in overtopping failure are higher than the corresponding values in piping failure. For the adopted breach parameters, the peak discharge from overtopping failure is 1.6 to 2.0 times higher than the corresponding value due to piping failure. The empirical model by Froehlich (2008)  is a function of the volume of water in the reservoir (based on reservoir level), the height of the breach, and the inflow into the reservoir. Based on the variation of these independent model parameters, a total of 36 different scenarios were generated and considered for obtaining dam-break flood hydrographs. The variation in the dam-break flood hydrographs indicates the sensitivity of the considered model breach parameters. The summary of 36 dam-break scenarios is tabulated in Supplementary Material  ST4, for better comparison of dam-break flood peak discharge and other dam breach parameters. The present safe carrying capacity of the Lower Tapi River at Surat city is 11,320 m3 /s (Jain et al., 2007 ), which is exceeded by all dam-break flood scenarios and can create flooding situations in Surat city.   4.2 Dam-break flood mapping across coastal urban floodplain of Surat city The downstream routing of dam-break flood is important for evaluating the associated flood risk and making a successful emergency management plan (Chen et al., 2020 ). Out of 36 different scenarios, the hydrograph with maximum peak discharge and minimum time for the occurrence of peak (Table 6 ; Table 8  and Supplementary ST3 ) are identified for 2D simulations. The 50 % washout scenario is selected as the breach bottom level (+86.65 m amsl) reaches up to the erosion-resisting material (rock zone) within the embankment (Fig. 6 ). In addition, the 75 % washout is considered an extreme scenario in failure at FRL, HFL, and 1 m overtopping conditions. The 2D flood simulation transforms the different magnitudes of floods into useful information, such as flood depth, flow velocity, etc., over the floodplain. The flood depth is considered a significant factor during flood loss, as the damage increases with increasing flood depth (CWC, 2018 ). Keeping in view the importance of Surat city in the study area, flood inundation maps have been developed for the dam-break flood scenarios shown in Fig. 9  . The bar graphs show the zone-wise variation of water depth across the city. The flood inundation depth has been categorised into six classes, of which 0.5 m and 1.2 m are the limiting depths for danger to children and adults in good conditions, respectively (Cox et al., 2010 ). The dam-break flood resulted from piping when the reservoir water level at FRL with 50 % washout of the embankment [Fig. 9 (a)] and almost the entire city (≈100 %) got inundated. The water depth greater than 1.2 m, which is dangerous for all healthy adults and hinders mobility as well as traffic, is observed in over 80 % of the area in five out of seven zones except the south and southeast zones, where it is found to be nearly 70 %. The north zone of Surat city is the worst affected zone, where the maximum flood depth is more than 3 m (one-story building) over 78 % of the area, which is followed by the east, central, and west zones. Nearly 15 % area of the north zone is submerged with a maximum water depth greater than 6 m (exceeding a two-story building) for 50 % washout of the embankment for piping failure at FRL, which further increases to 60 % for overtopping failure (75 % washout). The present assessment states that the south, southeast, and west (upper region) zones of Surat city are inundated with less water depth among all four scenarios considered. However, the sites with low water depth in each zone need to be identified to locate the nearby refugee place and safeguard the people from the worst-affected areas under the emergency action plan.  4.3 Dam-break flood risk assessment for Surat city 4.3.1 Flood hazard mapping Similar to flood depth, people, transport, and infrastructure are also vulnerable to the flow velocity compared to large still water depths. The combined effect of flood depth and flow velocity, i.e., the D × V  indicator, is used to address the susceptibility of people, vehicles, and buildings against the devastating dam-break flood scenarios. The hazard maps for Surat city have been developed by combining the output of the 2D HD model and GIS, as shown in Fig. 10  . The percentage of area under each hazard class is depicted in a bar chart next to the map. Due to the failure of Ukai Dam at FRL and the 50 % washout of the embankment, Surat city will be exposed to significant hazard levels (i.e., H5 and H6). Out of the total flooded area, only the 30.5 % area is safe for all (H1), however, the 30.5 % area is under significant hazard. The area under H5 and H6 (19.6 % and 10.9 %) is unsafe for all people and vehicles and can cause damage or even the failure of the buildings. For the worst-case scenario of Ukai Dam failure, i.e., 1 m overtopping and 75 % washout of the embankment [Fig. 10 (d)], the area under H5 and H6 considerably increases to 33.4 % and 44.3 % respectively. On the other hand, the area under H1 is substantially reduced to 6.8 %. The local administration should focus on the areas with high hazard during the dam-break flood event.  4.3.2 Socio-economic vulnerability In case of sustainability research, vulnerability plays an important role while integrating the human and environment connection (Turner et al., 2003 ). The socio-economic vulnerability is evaluated for the wards and villages that belong to Surat Urban Development authority (SUDA) administrative boundary. Initially, the high correlation among the selected data was removed using PCA, and the uncorrelated 2 PCs explaining more than 75 % variability (Tripathy et al., 2020; Sahana et al., 2021; Jibhakate et al., 2023b ) were further used in DEA. The socio-economic vulnerability for the wards and villages under SUDA administrative boundary is shown in Fig. 11  . Out of the total 235 wards and villages, the 102 wards and villages are under very low to low vulnerable category. This low vulnerable area is mostly spread over the villages away from the Surat city (SMC) boundary. On the other hand, the 91 wards and villages covering 30 % of SUDA area are fall under high to very high vulnerable category. It is important to note that most of the area under very-high vulnerable category is within Surat city. The high vulnerable area, which is near to the river on both banks, needs more attention in the flood mitigation strategies.  4.3.3 Exposure Exposure is calculated for the wards and villages as the sum of the product of exposure factors (weights) of the LULC type with the fraction of area covered by each type, as shown in Fig. 12  . 126 out of 235 considered wards and villages are under the very to low exposure category, which covers approximately 70 % of the SUDA administrative boundary. These low exposed areas are the villages away from the mainland city with less population and economic activities. However, 87 wards and villages are under high to very high exposure category. It is noted that, urban development, including residential and industrial areas, are grown on both sides of the Tapi River. The maximum percentage of area covered by urban land use are within the Surat city boundary. And the flood inundation in this high developed and exposed area can lead to huge monetary losses and even deaths. The exposure of critical infrastructure in Surat city to the Ukai dam-break flood hazard is also evaluated and included in Supplementary S3 .  4.3.4 Dam-break flood risk The village and ward wise relative risk maps are generated for the dam-break flood situation from the product of dam-break flood hazard, socioeconomic vulnerability, and exposure. The risk is also standardised and categorised into five classes. As the risk maps are relative, the ‘very low’ risk shown here refers to very low risk compared to the other wards and villages, however, it may be high at the absolute level. The risk maps are developed for the scenarios for which the dam-break flood hazard maps are developed and shown in Fig. 13  . The bar graphs are to represent the percentage area under different risk classes. For the dam-break flood that resulted from piping when the reservoir water level was at FRL with 50 % washout of the embankment [Fig. 13 (a)], 144 out of 235 wards and villages covering nearly 70 % of the SUDA administrative area are under low to very low risk. These wards and villages require less attention compared to other regions. On the other hand, 71 out of 235 wards and villages covering 25.2 % area is under high to very high flood risk due to Ukai dam-break event. It is worth noting that, the high-risk areas are within Surat city and adjacent to the river. For the 75 % washout scenario, the high risk increases to 90 villages and wards, covering 31.2 % area. Similar maps are generated for the piping failure at HFL (Supplementary SF10 ) and the overtopping failure of Ukai Dam [Fig, 13 (c) and (d)] The developed relative risk maps help to prioritize the wards and villages during the flood mitigation with scarce resources. It will also help to plan the response to recovery practices and evacuation strategies.    5 Conclusions The impact of the failure of a high-hazard potential dam on the downstream environment, economy, and large-scale population (loss of life) is significant. The minimization of expected losses and flood management expenses through structural and non-structural measures is the most popular economic framework in flood management. The non-structural approach is based on the modifications of human activities and societies to mitigate flood damages. Legislation, land and administrative planning, education, insurance, hydrologic forecasting, and warning are included under non-structural measures. To mitigate the risk associated with flooding, prior knowledge of flood hazard, vulnerability, and exposure is necessary. In the case of Ukai Dam, it is achieved by integrating the empirical dam breach equations and hydrodynamic modelling. In the current study, large dam failure (such as Ukai Dam) is simulated for piping as well as overtopping conditions for different scenarios associated with the effect of inflow into the reservoir, water level in the reservoir, and breach height. The observational results suggested that the highest discharge due to Ukai Dam failure at FRL, HFL and 1 m overtopping failure is 3.16, 3.41, and 5.10 times the discharge capacity of the (all 22 gates) spillway at FRL. The difference in the volume of the dam-break flood hydrograph and the total volume of floodwater above the corresponding breach level is less than 7 % for all the cases and scenarios. For all six worst possible combinations of inflow, reservoir level, and breach height considered in the 2D model simulation, the entire Surat city gets flooded. The dam-break flood resulted from piping failure when the reservoir water level at FRL with 50 % washout of the embankment, the water depth exceeding 1.2 m, dangerous for all healthy adults hinders mobility as well as traffic, observed over 80 % of the area in five out of seven zones. Due to heavy flooding, the Surat city will be exposed to a significant hazard level. For the failure of Ukai Dam at FRL and the 50 % washout of the embankment, the 30.5 % area is under significant hazard which is unsafe for all people, vehicles and can cause the damage or even the failure of the buildings. The inundation corresponding hazard is further increased for overtopping failure. The other component of the risk, socioeconomic vulnerability and land use exposure, is calculated for the wards and villages within the SUDA administrative boundary. The 91 wards and villages (out of 235) covering 30 % area are under high to very high vulnerable category. And 87 wards and villages covering 21 % area are under high to very high exposure category. Finally, the flood risk maps are developed by combining the flood hazard, vulnerability, and exposure revealed that, 71 out of 235 wards and villages covering 25.2 % area is under high to very high flood risk due to Ukai dam-break event, which is further increasing in the 75 % washout and overtopping scenario. The above-stated dam-break hazard and risk maps with potential consequences provide the disaster management authority with a framework to establish the EAP for Ukai Dam. The EAP will include specific populations and critical infrastructure considered most susceptible to the flood, particularly in areas with high hazards. Possible refuge places and evacuation routes can be planned against dam-break flooding by the local administrative agencies.  6 Limitations of the current study The present investigation of flood wave propagation due to large dam failure using the 2D HD model suffers from the following limitations based on the availability and accuracy of the data in the study area. The limitations of the current study can provide the future direction of the work.(1) The observed maximum flood depths (year 2006) used in the performance evaluation of the 2D HD model are available only within the coastal urban floodplain of Surat city. The authorities using the results should practice caution while using the observed flood depths outside the Surat city area.  (2) The local climatic conditions such as rainfall within the catchment during the event and interaction between the river water and the existing storm/sewer network, are not considered while simulating the 2D model. However, compared to the volume of the dam-break flood, the volume of the storm due to the rainfall in the city/catchment is negligible, and the coincidence is highly unlikely.  (3) The sediment transport aspect is not included in the 2D HD model. The data required for the calibration and validation of bed level variation in the river and topographic variation in the floodplain is not available.  (4) The dam breach parameters were treated as deterministic, and uncertainty in these parameters was not quantified. The quantification of uncertainty in the dam breach parameters and its corresponding effects on the flooding in the downstream of Ukai Dam can be considered as the future scope of the present study.  (5) The building collapse due to dam-break flooding was not considered and left to future work.
1 Introduction Legacy contamination in soils and sediments from historical releases remains an important environmental challenge. Monitored natural recovery, removal, and in-situ capping/treatment are common strategies for managing the contamination in sediments. In-situ capping and treatment offer a more robust approach than natural recovery, are often consistent with natural depositional processes, and are less costly than removal by dredging. Various implementation approaches have been developed to reduce contaminant migration into the overlying water and to physically isolate the contaminants from organisms in the water and the benthic organisms residing in surficial sediments. These strategies include covering the contaminated sediment with inert particulate materials, adsorbing particulate materials, and textile mats (Sharma and Reddy, 2004; Yan et al., 2019; Qiu et al., 2021 ). The cap may be constructed with multiple layers of clean sediments or sand and gravel with or without amended materials (Wang et al., 1991; Lampert and Reible, 2009; Reible et al., 2009 ). Sites with groundwater seepage or mobile contaminants may exhibit reduced effectiveness (Go et al., 2009; Himmelheber et al., 2011 ). For such sites, materials with sorptive or reactive properties are typically needed as a chemical isolation layer to be placed on the sediments or as a capping layer. This chemical isolation layer is often protected by a protective or armoring layer (Murphy et al., 2006; McDonough et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2014 ). The selection of a design approach for remediation at sites with contaminated sediment hinges on accurately modeling the long-term behavior of the contaminants. For caps or in-situ treatments, selecting the right materials to achieve remediation objectives in a cost-effective way is essential. The potential materials vary widely in their impact on contaminant fate and transport. Mathematical models predicting the fate and transport of contaminants are necessary to predict long-term performance and evaluating different design options. Contaminant fate and transport models typically describe the sediment as a one-dimensional (1-D) stratified porous media containing multiple layers of materials, including mixtures of inert material and sorbents. The vertical scale of these layers is typical cm to 10′s of cm. Horizontal spatial variations (on the scale of meters are larger) are addressed by applying the one-dimensional model separately to those areas. The model needs to include common transport processes in porous media, including diffusion, hydrodynamic dispersion, and advection, and sediment-specific transport processes such as bioturbation, hyporheic exchange, and benthic mass transfer. Benthic organisms live in the upper few centimeters below the benthic surface, giving rise to the process of bioturbation, which can mix solids and interstitial waters in this biological active zone (BAZ) (Reible et al., 1996, Thibodeaux et al., 2001, Thibodeaux and Bierman, 2003 ). Hyporheic exchange may also be significant in this BAZ, particularly when the surficial sediments are highly permeable. Also, Gilevska et al. (2019)  experimental data show that strong biodegradation of contaminants may occur in the BAZ as a result of enhanced microbial activity. Thus, the rates of diffusion and reaction may vary dramatically with depth, and the transport model must account for these variations in conditions. In addition, the transport model needs to take into the complexities of the boundary condition at the surface including the benthic boundary layer mass transfer resistances as well as bioturbation and hyporheic exchange in near surface sediments. In many sediment remedial designs, strongly sorbing materials such as activated carbon are incorporated into one or more capping layers (Zhang et al., 2016 ). Go et al. (2009)  and Reible and Lampert (2014)  took some of these factors into account in their model. However, only steady-state analytical solutions were given. Numerical models such as CapSim (Shen et al., 2018 ) have been developed to simulate contaminant fate and transport in surficial sediments. However, analytical models can often be used to advantage by providing more insight into sediment processes and contaminant behavior. Wang et al. (1991)  and Thoma et al. (1993)  found that a layer of clean sand sediment successfully reduced concentrations of the HOC 2,4,6-trichlorophenol in laboratory experiments and presented a diffusion model to describe the behavior. Chen et al. (2009)  presented an analytical solution for contaminant diffusion through a multi-layered system with a fixed concentration top boundary condition to study contaminant diffusion in a barrier system. Later, Li and Cleall (2010)  extended the work of Chen et al. (2009)  and presented an analytical solution to the sediment cap problem. Li and Cleall (2011)  proposed an analytical solution for solute transport through a finite double-layered porous medium with different boundary conditions. Shen and Reible (2015)  present an analytical solution for the one-dimensional advective–dispersive solute equation in layered porous media with an arbitrary number of layers. This study focused on the lack of consideration of hyperbolic eigenfunctions in the solutions of Li and Cleall (2011)  and Guerrero et al. (2013)  and provided an analytical solution that could be applied to modeling multi-layer sediment caps. The analytical solution proposed by Shen and Reible (2015)  can consider most factors in the design of capping systems, but the complexity of implementing their approach limits the possibility of its widespread application. The reason is that as the number of layers increases, implementing their approach involves assembling and solving a complex global matrix system to obtain the eigenvalues, and requires tedious iterations to obtain layer-dependent coefficients of the general solution (see the detailed explanation in the solution section of this paper). Thus, it is highly necessary to develop an analytical model that can consider a more comprehensive set of factors and is more practical to use. Recently, Chen et al. (2019)  developed a new solution methodology for investigating contaminant transport in a vertical barrier system. This methodology combines the variable separation method and the transfer matrix method to derive a concise analytical solution for a double-layered advection-dispersion-degradation equation. The transfer matrix method employed by Chen et al. (2019)  eliminates the need for global matrix calculations by reducing the order of the matrices to two. This approach streamlines the computational process. Additionally, the authors define layer-independent coefficients of the general solution, which eliminates the need for cumbersome iterations. These coefficients can be directly obtained through the orthogonality relationship. Although Chen et al. (2019)  limited their model to systems with only two layers, their method holds the potential to yield highly concise analytical solutions for multi-layered systems. This paper aims to apply the solution methodology of Chen et al. (2019)  to develop a new analytical model to describe the contaminant transport in a multi-layered sediment amendment system. The proposed analytical model not only will cover the transport processes in sediment amendment systems, including advection, diffusion, sorbent sorption, bioturbation, hyporheic exchange, and exchange at the sediment–water interface, but also is concise and easy to implement. The presented analytical model is verified against existing analytical and numerical solutions. The developed analytical model will be applied to analyze the impacts of selected key modeling parameters on the performance of an amendment design. This analysis will include factors such as the type of underlying contamination source (finite or infinite), the mass transfer coefficient at the benthic boundary layer, the inclusion of biodegradation in the BAZ, and the absorption capacity of the chemical isolation layer (CIL).  2 Problem formulation The schematic diagram of 1-D contaminant transport through the sediment cap system is shown in Fig. 1  . An in-situ treatment or capping layer can be typically described as being composed of up to 4 layers.– Biologically active zone (BAZ) with elevated transport of solids and interstitial water due to bioturbation and hyporheic exchange and where elevated microbial activity may be exhibited,  – Cap protection layer (CPL) which is designed to protect the sorbing amendments in a chemical isolation layer from erosion as well as separate organisms from any potential adverse consequences of exposure to the sorbents,  – Chemical isolation layer (CIL) which typically contains adsorbents and is the primary resistance to chemical release from the contaminated sediments,  – Contaminated sediments (CS)    The thickness of the four layers is given as, h BAZ , h CPL , h CIL , and h CS  for BAZ, CPL, CIL, and CS, respectively. The total thickness of the sediment cap system H  determined by adding together the thicknesses of its four constituent layers. Contaminant transport through the layered sediment cap system can be described by the governing equation (Go et al., 2009; Shen and Reible, 2015 ):(1) R  i   ∂ C  i   ( z , t )  ∂ t   = D  i   ∂  2   C  i   ( z , t )  ∂ z  2     - U ∂ C  i   ( z , t )  ∂ z   - λ  i   n  i   C  i   ( z , t )     where z  refers to the spatial variable pointing upward with its origin at the bottom ofthe CS; i  refers to the index of the layer from the bottom to the top, ranging from 1 to N , C i (z ,t ) is the contaminant concentration in i -th layer at any position z  and any time t ; n i  is the porosity; U  is the Darcy velocity; D i  is the effective diffusivity; λi   is the first-order decay rate constant; Ri   is the retardation factor. The decay rate constant can be determined by inserting the contaminant half-life into the integrated-form first-order equation λi   = ln2/t 1/2 . The retardation factor Ri   represents the ratio of total concentration versus the concentration in the porewater, can be calculated by Ri   = ni   + ρi Kdi  , where ρi   and Kdi   indicate the bulk density and the linear partition coefficient of the contaminant, respectively.
