(2019) , the analytical solution from Shen and Reible (2015) , the Generalized Integral Transform Technique (GITT) solution presented by Liu et al. (1998) , and the numerical solution provided by CapSim (Shen et al., 2018 ). The verification involves comparing the outcomes derived from the presented solution with the results documented in these papers. The parameters used for the five verification examples are summarized in Table 4  . 4.1 Comparison with the two-layer example presented by Chen et al. (2019)  Since the solution in this paper is based on the method of Chen et al. (2019) , we first use the two-layer model of Chen et al. (2019)  for verification. The thicknesses of the double-layered porous media are 0·6 and 10 m, respectively. Contaminant concentration at the inlet boundary is fixed at C 0  = 1 mg/L. A zero concentration is assumed at the outlet boundary. The initial concentration is zero in each layer. Three values of the half-life of the contaminant, i.e. t 1/2  = 10, 100, and 1000 years, are considered. The other transport parameters include the effective diffusion coefficient, porosities, Darcy velocity, and retardation factor, which are summarized in Table 4 . Fig. 2   presents the comparison of contaminant concentration profiles at t  = 100 years from the present analytical solution and Chen et al. (2019) , respectively. The results show that they agree perfectly well. This verification indicates that extending Chen et al. (2019)’s  method to multi-layered porous media is feasible.  4.2 Comparison with the three-and four-layer examples used by Shen and Reible (2015)  The three-layer and four-layer examples presented by Shen and Reible (2015)  are selected as the validation examples in this study. Both systems exhibit the same total thickness and materials loadings, with variations only in the arrangement of the adsorbate and sand layers as shown in Table 4 . The four-layer example incorporates a 1 cm adsorbate layer beneath a 10 cm sand layer serving as a filter/protective barrier, whereas the three-layer example consists of an 11 cm layer of adsorbate-sand mixture (Shen and Reible, 2015 ). The concentration profile plotted against time, illustrated in Fig. 3  , demonstrates the consistency between the analytical solution developed in this study and the solution presented by Shen and Reible (2015) .  4.3 Comparison with the five-layer example given in Liu et al. (1998)  The validity of the analytical solution is also confirmed through an example of five-layer sealed system presented by Liu et al. (1998) . The system comprises alternating layers of sand and clay, specifically arranged as sand-clay-sand-clay-sand, with detailed parameters for each layer provided in Table 4 . The system’s bottom and top boundaries are specified by mass-transfer limited and flux boundary conditions, respectively. As illustrated in Fig. 4  , the presence of thin clay layers significantly influences the solute distribution in the porous media, affecting processes such as solute diffusion into solid particles or biodegradation. The concentration profiles plotted at 2, 6, and 8 days, displayed in Fig. 4 , exhibit agreement with the results by Liu et al. (1998) , further demonstrating the accuracy of the multi-layer solution in the handling five-layer condition.  4.4 Comparison with the CapSim software by Shen et al. (2018)  This section aims to validate the accuracy of the presented model for addressing multi-layered systems with mass transfer boundary conditions. The solution of the model for a four-layer example is compared with the outcomes from the numerical software CapSim (Shen et al., 2018 ). CapSim is a numerical software developed for simulating contaminant transport through multi-layered porous media and is widely recognized for its capability to predict the remedial effectiveness in sediment environments. The specific four-layer example discussed here comprises a contaminated sediment layer of 30 cm at the base, followed by a 1 cm layer of activated carbon (AC) amendment, and topped with a 29 cm sand layer. It is assumed that biological activity is restricted to the upper 5.6 cm of the sand layer, introducing an additional mixing process near the benthic surface. The model presumes a uniform distribution of contaminants within the sediment layer, with these contaminants being transported upwards to the overlying water. The contaminant flux at the bottom of the sediment is set to zero, representing a finite source. At the sediment–water interface, an overall mass transfer coefficient of 0.1 cm/hr is applied. The detailed parameters for each layer are given in Table 4 . The concentration profiles, depicted at time points t  = 20, 50, and 100 years in Fig. 5  , are in alignment with the results obtained from CapSim.   5 Results and discussion An evolving sediment cap system with a 30 cm total cap thickness (see Fig. 1 ) is adopted in this section for analyzing the influence of several critical factors or design parameters on the behavior of the cap system. Phenanthrene is selected as the representative organic contaminant in the cap system here with an initial interstitial water concentration at 1 mg/L in the contaminated sediment. The transport properties for the cap system are collected from Go et al. (2009)  and summarized in Table 5  . The sensitivity analysis encompasses four sub-sections, examining the influence of different parameters on contaminant migration, including different bottom boundary condition types, the presence of a CIL, the involvement of biodegradation, and benthic mass transfer conditions. Within each sub-section, analyses of these parameters are conducted for both diffusion-dominated and advection-diffusion systems. 5.1 Effect of assumption on contamination source The contamination source in the sediment underlying the modeling domain is incorporated in the transport model by the bottom boundary condition. The previous studies suggested two types of bottom boundary condition by accounting for source as being finite (zero concentration below a contaminated layer) or infinite (constant concentration at bottom boundary). Thoma et al. (1993)  and Li and Cleall (2011)  assumed the contaminated layer contaminant source is limited in the sediment of a finite thickness inside the domain, and contaminant flux at the bottom of the sediment layer fixed at zero to represent the clean upwelling groundwater flow from underlying sediment. On the other hand, Go et al. (2009)  assumed a high contaminant loading in the underlying sediment that leads the concentration at the bottom of the sediment layer in the model to be fixed at a constant equal to its initial value. Both types of the contaminant source are adopted in this analytical model by selecting different boundary conditions at the bottom of the sediment layer. A sensitivity analysis on the impact of bottom boundary condition types are explored by modeling the transport of phenanthrene in a three-layer cap system (without CIL) with both finite and infinite source bottom boundary conditions. The finite source bottom boundary condition is represented by three scenarios with the finite bottom boundary conditions and the thickness of contaminated sediment layer increasing from 3 cm to 30 cm (Scenario a-c). In each scenario, the phenanthrene presents a uniform initial concentration in the contaminated sediment layers to represent the contamination level and a zero flux at the bottom to define the finite source. The infinite source bottom boundary condition is achieved by removing the contaminated sediment layer and fixing the concentration at the bottom of CPL to contamination level (Scenario d). Fig. 6   shows the contaminant concentration profiles for the four scenarios with two different bottom boundary conditions when no advection is present. The contaminant concentration profiles in the BAZ and at the sediment–water interface show moderate differences for sensitive to the choice of the bottom boundary condition or the in this particular sediment system. It can be found that when considering the diffusion in the contaminant layer rather than constant concentration, the concentration in the contaminant layer continually decreases with time. Another obvious phenomenon can also be found from Fig. 6 a, b, and c that the rate of decrease in concentration in the contaminant layer became lower with the increase of thickness of the contaminant layer. When a moderate advection presents (U =100 cm/year), there is a concentration maximum, the position of which moves from bottom to top boundary as shown in Fig. 7  a, b, and c. Therefore, the peak value of the concentration profile is not at the bottom of contaminant layer. This can be compared to the continuous decrease over time in the diffusive case, where the peak value of the concentration profile is always at the bottom. Clearly, as h CS  increases, the concentration profile within the cap layer tends to resemble the results obtained under the assumption of a constant concentration boundary. Furthermore, Fig. 8   presents the contaminant concentration curves at the interface between contaminant layer and cap system, and flux curves at top boundary considering different thickness of contaminated layer for diffusion-dominated and advection-diffusion scenario, respectively. Compared to the diffusion-dominated scenario, in the advection case, the concentration at the interface follows a pattern of initially increasing and then decreasing. As h CS  increases, the peak concentration at the interface also increases, accompanied by a corresponding time delay. From Fig. 8 b and d, it can be observed that the top flux under the assumption of a constant concentration boundary is clearly greater than that of a finite source. Taking U =100 cm/year and h CS =10 cm as an example (see Fig. 8 d), after a time period of more than 50 years, the results based on the assumption of a constant concentration boundary will significantly overestimate the actual values and thus become unreasonable.  5.2 Effect of adsorption capacity of chemical isolation layer In this section, chemical isolation layer is considered and the retardation factor of CIL is listed in Table 5 . Although adsorbent materials often have nonlinear adsorption, in this study, linear adsorption of the CIL is assumed to allow an analytical solution to the problem (Reible and Lampert, 2014; Yan et al., 2019; Qiu et al., 2021 ). Two different thickness of CIL, 1 cm and 2 cm with a sorbent layer, are adopted for analyzing the effect of sorption ability of the CIL on contaminant transport in cap system. The pore water concentration profiles of phenanthrene for the system with different thickness of CIL under diffusion-dominated and advection-diffusion scenarios are shown in Fig. 9  . For h CIL =1 cm (see Fig. 9 a) with increasing of time, the concentration on cap layer increases, and the concentration in the containment layer decrease. Comparison with Fig. 6 c shows that the adsorption layer can significantly delay the release of pollutants from the contaminated layer to the water layer. As an example, at t  = 30 years the conditions without the addition of the CIL spread 10 cm into the upper cover layer, while with the addition of the CIL the spread was only 5 cm. As h CIL  increases, the relative concentration in cap layer further decreases. For example, for adding a sorption layer thickness of 2 cm, the time required for a pollutant to spread 5 cm to the cap layer is 100 years, which delay 70 years compared to sorption layer thickness of 1 cm. By comparing Fig. 7 c, the delay effect of the sorption layer is more obvious when advection is present. Obviously, after the same time, the system with a higher h CIL  could limit more contaminants to areas closer to the containment layer. Unlike the behavior in Fig. 8 a, the concentration at the interface between CIL and cap system gradually increases and then decreases at different thickness of CIL as shown in Fig. 10  a. As the h CIL  increased, the maximum decreases from 0.27 for h CIL =1 cm to 0.18 for h CIL =2 cm. When advection is considered, the maximum concentration decreases more significantly compared to the case without an adsorption layer (Fig. 8 c). The maximum values of C/C0 decreased to 0.48 and 0.3 for sorption layer thicknesses of 1 cm and 2 cm, respectively (Fig. 10 a). A similar phenomenon can be seen in the flux curves at top cap system is shown in Fig. 10 b.  5.3 Effect of biodegradation of biologically active zone The BAZ is often in an aerobic state due to its proximity to the surface layer. According to Hyun et al. (2006) , the half-life of phenanthrene in the aerobic condition is about 30 days. The first order decay constant of phenanthrene under anaerobic conditions is an order of magnitude lower than aerobic condition. Thus, the first decay constant is assumed to 9.46 year−1  in BAZ and 0.946 year−1  in other layers. The coupling of the sorption and biodegradation was evaluated in both a diffusion-dominated scenario and advection-diffusion scenario. The mass flux versus time for sediment cap systems with four combinations of biodegradation and sorption capacity are shown in Fig. 11  a and b. For diffusion-degradation transport scenario (see Fig. 11 a), when biodegradation is considered the peak flux for without CIL scenario decreases from 2 to 0.75 mg/cm2 /year, but the time to reach the peak flux becomes earlier and is around 300 years. Similar phenomena can be observed for adding CIL scenario. With increase of the Darcy velocity, the effect of biodegradation on the flux peak for both of diffusion-dominated and advection-diffusion scenarios can also be clearly observed again in Fig. 11 b. The results indicate that degradation can play a greater role in advection-diffusion-degradation than diffusion-degradation transport scenarios. The related cumulative mass discharged versus time are shown in Fig. 11 c and d. This indicates that with considering biodegradation in the capping layer can result in decrease in total mass of pollutants released from contaminated sediment to the water layer. The reason is that the large decay rates in the capping layer are the result of higher amounts of nutrients, organic matter and electron acceptors in the layer, which results in the faster decrease of the contaminant concentration in capping layer. Hence, capping would be an attractive alternative for remediation of contaminated sediments if the biodegradation of the contaminant in the capping layer is sufficient.  5.4 Effect of benthic mass transfer condition The benthic boundary coefficient has a wide range of values and depends on many factors. Referring to Go et al. (2009)  and Yan et al. (2019) , three values of the benthic boundary layer mass transfer coefficients (0.1, 1.0, and 10 cm/hr) are adopted here for analyzing the effect of the mass transfer coefficient on contaminant transport in the sediment cap system. The presence or absence of an adsorption layer was also considered for comparative analysis. The fluxes at the cap surface versus time with different mass transfer coefficients for diffusion-dominant and advection-diffusion scenarios are shown in Fig. 12  a and b, respectively. It can be observed that, as analyzed earlier, both the convection and adsorption layers have significant impacts on the flux. However, the influence of mass transfer coefficient on the mass flux has a nearly negligible influence on flux but a substantial effect on surficial concentrations. The surface concentration versus time for diffusion-controlled and advection-diffusion sediment cap system are shown in Fig. 12 c and d. For diffusion-dominant transport scenario, with the mass transfer coefficient increasing from 0.1 to 1 cm/hr, the surface concentration decreases from 0.848 to 0.088 μg/L and from 0.415 to 0.043 μg/L for without and with CIL, respectively (see Fig. 12 c). By further increasing the mass transfer coefficient to 10 cm/hr, the surface concentration tends to approach zero. These indicate that a lower mass transfer coefficient results in a higher surface concentration. For the advection-diffusion scenario (see Fig. 12 d), the mass transfer coefficient exhibits a similar effect, but there are significant differences in the peak surface concentration. These results are also very close emphasizing that transport is largely controlled by advection in this system.   6 Conclusions An analytical model has been developed for contaminant transport in the sediment cap system, in which advection, diffusion, linear equilibrium sorption, and first-order decay processes are included. A solution methodology combining the separation of variables method and transfer matrix method is used to obtain a practical analytical solution. The analytical solutions are verified against the existing analytical and numerical solutions. Sensitivity analysis on the factors such as the type of underlying contamination source (finite or infinite), the mass transfer coefficient at the benthic boundary layer, the inclusion of biodegradation in the BAZ, and the absorption capacity of the chemical isolation layer (CIL) has been performed. Some major conclusions can be drawn from the results.(1) The flux continuously increases and reaches a stable value for the constant concentration assumption. However, after a certain period of time, there will be a decrease in the surface flux under the finite source assumption because eventually the contaminated sediment will be depleted and the constant concentration assumption will no longer be valid.  (2) The high absorption capacity of CIL can effectively isolate the release of contaminants from sediment to water. However, the effect of advection on the timing of the observed peak flux is significant. Thus, advection should be included in the prediction model as a conservative capping design.  (3) The biodegradation in the BAZ has a significant effect on the migration of the contaminant. Because biodegradation can significantly deplete contaminant, a reduction in the total mass released to the water column can be achieved.    As the number of layers increases, the advantages of the analytical solution presented in this paper become more apparent. Therefore, the present analytical solution is able to serve as a tool to investigate some new types of sediment cap systems, such as multiple amendment active sorbent layers. It is worth noting that the model presented in this paper also has certain limitations. For example, the model cannot account for nonlinear adsorption characteristics of the contaminants, especially in the CIL with strong adsorption capacity. Additionally, the model uses a relatively simple benthic mass transfer coefficient to consider the hydrodynamic influence of the surface water layer on the capping system, which is also a topic that can be further investigated in the future.
1 Introduction Land Use/Land Cover (LULC) change leads to some of the most concerning anthropogenic alterations of hydrological processes and concomitant environmental and social impacts (Foley et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2017 ). In a watershed, LULC change affects the surface water balance in many ways, including evapotranspiration (Ponette-González et al., 2014 ), surface runoff (Roa-García et al., 2011 ), infiltration (Marín et al., 2018 ), base flow, water yield (Ochoa-Tocachi et al., 2018 ), and ultimately, the watershed response via streamflow (Cepeda Arias et al., 2022; Muñoz-Villers and McDonnell, 2013; Ramírez et al., 2017 ). However, gaps persist in our understanding of the LULC change impacts on seasonal and annual streamflow (Marshall et al., 2023 ), particularly in regions like the tropical Andes (Filoso et al., 2017 ) with intense LULC changes (Bonnesoeur et al., 2019; García-Leoz et al., 2018; González-González et al., 2021; Suescún et al., 2017 ). Predicting these LULC change impacts on watershed response is critical for water management decisions in a changing environment (Montanari et al., 2013; Posada-Marín and Salazar, 2022 ). The predictions of LULC change impacts on streamflow usually rely on hydrological models (e.g., Filoso et al., 2017 ; Peña-Arancibia et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2017 ), which are generally capable of reproducing observed streamflow (Krysanova et al., 2017 ). This capability results from models being built upon physical principles, primary mass (water) conservation, as well as models having numerous parameters that can be tuned to reproduce observations (i.e., model calibration). However, the potential for making reliable predictions (e.g., for LULC scenarios) depends on the models’ ability to represent the system’s behavior for the right reasons (Kirchner, 2006 ). When the performance of hydrological models is primarily or exclusively evaluated by comparing simulated to observed streamflow (e.g., Setegn et al., 2008 ; Villamizar et al., 2019 ), there is a risk of overlooking unrealistic representations of other important water balance components, along with their drivers and associated processes (Bolaños Chavarría et al., 2022; López-Ramírez et al., 2020; Mei et al., 2023; Rajib and Merwade, 2015 ). The Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) is among the most widely used hydrological models for investigating LULC change impacts on streamflow (Marin et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2020 ). This model includes a plant growth module that represents vegetation dynamics through biomass production and Leaf Area Index (LAI). Particularly, the LAI is a key parameter for estimating evapotranspiration (including evaporation of intercepted rainfall) and precipitation partitioning (e.g., precipitation into runoff and infiltration). The original module was developed for temperate regions under the assumption that vegetation growth is controlled mainly by temperature (Neitsch et al., 2011 ), which does not hold for tropical regions where precipitation and soil moisture can exert stronger controls on vegetation (Strauch and Volk, 2013 ). Hence, the original SWAT model has a limited ability to represent the LAI seasonality of tropical vegetation (Strauch and Volk, 2013 ), affecting water balance simulation (Chen et al., 2023; Haas et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2019 ). Further, although some SWAT model variants, such as SWAT-T (Alemayehu et al., 2017 ), improve LAI simulation in tropical regions (López-Ramírez et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020 ), some limitations persist in simulating LAI seasonality, including bimodal patterns in tropical Andes watersheds (Hoyos et al., 2019 ). An additional challenge to correctly represent vegetation function in hydrological models is the uncertainty of LAI data. Remotely sensed datasets such as the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS; Myneni et al., 2015 ), the Global LAnd Surface Satellite (GLASS; Liang et al., 2021 ), the Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS; Fuster et al., 2020 ), and the MEdium Resolution Imaging Spectrometer (MERIS; Rast et al., 1999 ) have the advantage of providing almost continuous data in both time and space. However, they have a coarse spatial resolution relative to the size of small watersheds (e.g., < 10 km2 ), and their quality can be affected by multiple factors, such as cloud contamination or high aerosols concentration (Ma and Liang, 2022 ). An alternative to remotely sensed LAI data is ground-based observations. These data have the advantage of being direct observations (e.g., the area of vegetation leaves is estimated in selected plots). However, this dataset type is generally scarce and discontinuous in space and time and not generalizable to other areas due to the heterogeneity of the land surface. Additionally, satellite remote sensing products and in situ measurements generally do not coincide (Tang et al., 2019 ). Therefore, there is no practical way of determining the “true” values of LAI in a watershed over time, especially in biodiversity hotspots such as the tropical Andes (Myers et al., 2000 ), where vegetation features can vary greatly both in space and time ( Fig. 1 ; Bruijnzeel et al., 2011 ; Girardin et al., 2014 ; Ramírez et al., 2018 ; Restrepo and Vargas, 1999 ). For example, estimates of LAI for tropical mountain forests range between ∼3.00 m2 /m2  and ∼6.0 m2 /m2  depending on location, elevation, and local climatic conditions, among other factors (Supplementary Material Table S1). Further, the LAI of tropical vegetation is not necessarily constant over time but can exhibit marked unimodal or bimodal seasonal patterns (Abera et al., 2019; Alemayehu et al., 2017; Girardin et al., 2014; Hoyos et al., 2019; Huasco et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2022 ). Many studies use the original SWAT with its plant growth module (e.g., Santos et al., 2021 ; Villamizar et al., 2019 ; Yifru et al., 2021 ) or LAI data from an available global dataset or field-based observations to calibrate different SWAT model versions (Alemayehu et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2023; López-Ramírez et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020 ). Overall, these studies show that LAI-improved SWAT variants better capture not only LAI dynamics but also watershed water balance (Cai et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Haas et al., 2022 ). For example, Zhang et al. (2020)  highlighted that the original SWAT simulates lower evapotranspiration (∼11 %) and higher streamflow (∼5 %) than the SWAT-T variant for a tropical watershed in Australia. However, few studies consider the LAI uncertainty and its impacts on assessing the effects of LULC change on streamflow (e.g., Zhang et al., 2020 ), particularly in the tropical Andes. Here, we investigate the effect of different LAI representations on streamflow response to LULC change in a tropical Andean watershed. To do this, we first modify the SWAT-T variant to develop SWAT-Tb, an improved model that allows representing LAI with a bimodal seasonality. Then, we use SWAT-Tb to study streamflow response to LULC scenarios with different pasture and forest cover under constant and bimodal LAI seasonality and compare these results with the original SWAT (default LAI) and SWAT-T (unimodal LAI) simulations. Finally, we discuss the implications of LAI representation for modeling LULC change impacts on streamflow, as well as persistent model limitations and future research directions.  2 Revision of the SWAT model 2.1 The original SWAT The original SWAT (Revision 627) is a public domain, watershed-scale, process-based, hydrological model (Arnold et al., 1998; Neitsch et al., 2011 ) that can simulate the response of watersheds (e.g., streamflow) to a variety of forcing, including both climate and LULC change (Gassman et al., 2014; Tan et al., 2020 ). It is a semi-distributed model wherein a watershed is divided into sub-areas that are further divided into Hydrologic Response Units (HRUs), which are characterized by a unique soil, slope, LULC, and management attributes. Hydrological processes simulated by SWAT include evapotranspiration, surface runoff, percolation, lateral flow, groundwater flow, transmission losses, and ponds (Arnold et al., 2012 ). The model also includes parameterizations for plant growth, erosion, nutrient cycling, and pesticide degradation, among other processes (Neitsch et al., 2011 ). The classical formulation for vegetation dynamics in SWAT uses a plant growth module that simulates leaf development, light interception, and conversion of intercepted light into biomass (Neitsch et al., 2011 ). This module is based on the Environmental Policy Impact Climate (EPIC) model (Williams et al., 1989 ) that was developed for temperate regions and, therefore, is not necessarily accurate for tropical regions (Alemayehu et al., 2017 ; Strauch and Volk, 2013 ). A key reason for this is that the EPIC-based module assumes that plant growth, including leaf area development, is mainly controlled by temperature and day length variations, which are relevant for temperate environments (Mwangi et al., 2016 ). For instance, this module assumes that plant growth is reduced as day length approaches that of the shortest day of the year (winter solstice) due to dormancy (Arnold et al., 1998 ). Tropical vegetation dynamics, however, can be much less influenced by seasonal variations in temperature and day-length-driven dormancy (Ma et al., 2019 ) and much more controlled by precipitation seasonality through soil moisture availability (Yang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2006 ). Indeed, in our study watershed, LAI is more correlated to precipitation than to temperature (Section 4.1 ). Several studies have highlighted this limitation in the original SWAT and its implications for simulating streamflow or other water balance components (Haas et al., 2022; Hoyos et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2019; Marin et al., 2020; Rajib et al., 2020; Wagner et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020 ). Recognizing this limitation, previous studies have aimed to improve the representation of vegetation dynamics by using remotely sensed LAI data (e.g., Ma et al., 2019 ; Rajib et al., 2020 ) or by modifying the original plant growth module to reproduce LAI patterns of perennial vegetation in tropical regions of South America (Strauch and Volk, 2013 ) and Africa (Alemayehu et al., 2017 ). However, as discussed further below, using LAI observations or current versions such as SWAT-T still has limitations for investigating LULC change impacts on streamflow, particularly in tropical watersheds with bimodal LAI patterns.  2.2 Developing SWAT-Tb from SWAT-T Alemayehu et al. (2017)  developed SWAT-T and successfully implemented it to simulate streamflow in a tropical watershed of Kenya and Tanzania while simulating the unimodal seasonal cycle of LAI observed there through remote sensing. SWAT-T was later implemented in some watersheds of Colombia (Hoyos et al., 2019 ), Australia (Zhang et al., 2020 ), and Mexico (López-Ramírez et al., 2021 ). Building upon SWAT-T, here we introduce SWAT-Tb to represent the bimodal LAI seasonality for trees and perennial vegetation observed in some tropical (Abera et al., 2019; Hoyos et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2022 ; Supplementary Material Table S1) and non-tropical (Alhamad et al., 2007 ) regions. The SWAT-Tb executable and the associated changes with file examples (*.sub, *.mgt, and plant.dat) are available in Supplementary material S1. SWAT-T uses changes in the Soil Moisture Index (SMI, the ratio between 5-day aggregate precipitation and reference evapotranspiration) as a proxy for the dry-to-wet season transition in the tropics, which triggers the vegetation growth cycle (Alemayehu et al., 2017 ). This association assumes that the environment is water-limited, which is not true everywhere, as many tropical regions are not water- but energy-limited (Callañaupa Gutierrez et al., 2021; Gotsch et al., 2016; Ochoa-Sánchez et al., 2020 ), including the tropical Andes (Aparecido et al., 2018 ). Based on the data for our study basin (Section 4.1 ) and the assumption that the onset of the wet-dry season transition triggers plant growth (Alemayehu et al., 2017 ), SWAT-Tb uses precipitation instead of SMI as a proxy for seasonal variations in LAI. This allows linking the bimodal cycles of LAI and precipitation where appropriate. This is the case in many watersheds of the tropical Andes, where precipitation exhibits a bimodal seasonal cycle (Urrea et al., 2019 ) due to the seasonal migration of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (Espinoza et al., 2020 ), and LAI can also exhibit a bimodal seasonal cycle. In SWAT-T, the user defines an SMI threshold that triggers vegetation growth. To do this, Alemayehu et al. (2017)  introduced two parameters representing the months in which the end of the dry season (SOS1) and the beginning of the wet season (SOS2) occurs, which prevents a false start of the new growth cycle. In SWAT-Tb, we used a similar approach to initiate the vegetation growth cycle immediately after the last date of the first and second wet-dry season transition, but independent of SMI values. This is because, in some tropical regions, LAI values can be lower in the wet than in the dry season, suggesting that these ecosystems are energy-limited (Aparecido et al., 2018; Gotsch et al., 2016 ). Hence, we added three new parameters (SOS3, SOS4, and SOS5) to represent the precipitation seasonality characterized by a bimodal regime with two wet and two dry seasons. In SWAT-Tb, SOS1 and SOS2 represent the months of the beginning and end of the first wet-dry season transition, respectively. SOS3 represents the month of the end of the first dry season and the beginning of the second wet season, whereas SOS4 and SOS5 indicate the first and last month of the second wet-dry season transition, respectively. In SWAT-T, SOS1 and SOS2 parameters are estimated using the seasonal pattern of SMI based on precipitation and a reference evapotranspiration ratio (see, e.g.,  Fig. 2  in Alemayehu et al., 2017 ). The SOS(1,2,3,4,5) parameters in SWAT-Tb are user-defined using mean monthly precipitation and LAI seasonality.   3 Materials and methods 3.1 Study area This study focuses on the Chico River (CR) watershed in the tropical Andes of Colombia (Fig. 2 ). This watershed supplies water for rural communities and to a reservoir that is strategic for hydropower generation and water supply to more than 4 million people living in the Metropolitan Area around the city of Medellín (Fig. 2 c, d). The CR watershed’s area is 169 km2 , with altitudes between 2400 and 3260 m.a.s.l. (Fig. 2 e). Mean annual precipitation is 1820 mm, and mean monthly temperature varies between 12°C and 16°C with an average of 14°C. A bimodal regime characterizes precipitation seasonality with two wet seasons: March-April-May (MAM) and September-October-November (SON), and two dry seasons: December-January-February (DJF) and June-July-August (JJA). LULC in the watershed is dominated by human-established pastures (54.17 % of the area), followed by native forest (29.30 %), shrubs (11.42 %), and paramo vegetation (4.89 %) (Fig. 2 e). The CR is a representative example of mountain watersheds in the tropical Andes where a considerable fraction of native vegetation (i.e., native forest, shrubs, and paramo vegetation) has been converted into agro-pastoral uses (Berrouet et al., 2020; García-Leoz et al., 2018 ). The dominant soil type is Andic Humudepts, covering 62 % of the watershed (Fig. 2  g).  3.2 Input datasets and model parameters We obtained topography, climate, LULC, soil, and LAI from multiple data sources ( Table 1 ). We reclassified the land cover types to match with SWAT codes based on previous studies (Tapasco et al., 2015; Hoyos et al., 2019; Uribe et al., 2020 , 2018; Villamizar et al., 2019 ), adjusting the original vegetation parametrization considering the characteristics of land cover types in CR watershed (Supplementary Material Table S2). Soil map was parameterized following Machado et al. (2019)  and Uribe et al. (2020) . We divided the watershed into seven sub-basins and 659 HRUs using the SWAT2012 extension (version 1.9) within QGIS 2.6.1 (Dile et al., 2016 ). Daily hydrometeorological data (precipitation, maximum and minimum temperature, relative humidity, evapotranspiration, and streamflow) from available gauges (Fig. 2 d) were provided by the Colombian Institute of Hydrology, Meteorology and Environmental Studies (IDEAM) and the Public Utilities Company of Medellín (EPM). The SWAT’s internal WGENX weather generator (Neitsch et al., 2011 ) was used to fill missing data (less than 2 %) for daily precipitation and maximum and minimum temperature. We used the Priestly-Taylor equation (Priestley and Taylor, 1972 ) to estimate potential evapotranspiration as wind data was not available from ground-based gauges, and global datasets (e.g., reanalyses) have a limited capacity to represent wind over the complex terrain of the Andes (Posada-Marín et al., 2019 ). Finally, we obtained 8-day composites of LAI from the MCD15A2Hv006-MODIS product (Myneni et al., 2015 ) for the 2003–2016 period at 0.5 km spatial resolution. Further details on LAI data processing are given in Section S2 of the Supplementary Material.  3.3 Model calibration, validation, and uncertainty estimation We calibrated the SWAT-Tb model to simulate, first, monthly LAI, and then monthly streamflow using both manual and automated techniques. Parameters were initially selected based on a literature review (Abbaspour et al., 2015; Alemayehu et al., 2017; Strauch and Volk, 2013; Zhang et al., 2020 ) that included previous studies on Andean watersheds (Tapasco et al., 2015; Hasan and Wyseure, 2018; Hoyos et al., 2019; Villamizar et al., 2019 ; Supplementary Material Table S4). Streamflow and LAI calibration were conducted for the 2003–2016 period, while validation (only for streamflow) was performed between 1993 and 2002. Three years were added at the beginning of each simulation as a spin-up period to mitigate the influence of uncertain initial conditions, especially for soil moisture. Sensitivity and uncertainty analyses, as well as automated procedures for calibration and validation, were carried out in SWAT-CUP 2019 (version 5.2.1; Abbaspour, 2013 ) using the Sequential Uncertainty Fitting (SUFI-2) algorithm (Abbaspour et al., 2004 ). We calibrated LAI for SWAT-Tb by manually adjusting parameters (Supplementary Material Table S3) while considering land cover types separately and constant and bimodal regimes, as described below. The Breaks for Additive Seasonal and Trend (BFAST; Verbesselt et al., 2010 ) method was implemented to extract the trend and seasonality of LAI for each land cover while excluding noise from the time series, following Alemayehu et al. (2017)  and Hoyos et al. (2019) . The Pearson correlation coefficient (r), the percent bias (PBIAS), and the Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE; Gupta et al., 2009 ) were used to evaluate the agreement between simulated and observed LAI values. Streamflow calibration was focused on the dominant land cover types —pasture (RYEG) and native Andean forest (FRST) that account for approximately 80 % of the watershed (Fig. 2  f)— and on the upper soil layers that are most directly affected by vegetation change (Marín et al., 2018; Tobón et al., 2011 ). Parameters for the dominant land cover types were calibrated independently, whereas parameters for all other land cover types were grouped to reduce computational cost. Sensitive parameters were identified from a sensitivity analysis based on 500 simulations. This analysis starts with 39 parameters selected from previous studies and literature review, resulting in 21 of them as the most sensitive (p-value ≤ 0.05, Supplementary Material Table S4). We also defined an acceptable range of variability for each sensitive parameter based on performance criteria and water balance components, as described below. Subsequently, we calibrated monthly streamflow with SUFI-2 using 1000 simulations per iteration (Latin hypercube sampling) for the selected parameter ranges. The calibration goal was to obtain acceptable values for uncertainty statistics (p-value and r-value) and the performance criteria proposed by Moriasi et al. (2007; 2015). These criteria include the Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) as the objective function and other complementary statistics: PBIAS, determination coefficient, and RMSE-observations standard deviation ratio (RSR). We also looked for a reasonable representation of water balance components by considering the following metrics: fraction of total runoff as baseflow, the ratio between total evapotranspiration and total precipitation, and the ratio between surface runoff and total streamflow. Model outputs for these metrics were compared with remotely sensed evapotranspiration (the MODIS-MOD16A2v006 product; Running et al., 2017 ) and observation-based estimates for Andean watersheds (Bonnesoeur et al., 2019; García-Leoz et al., 2018; Jaramillo-Robledo, 2003; Marín et al., 2018; Suescún et al., 2017; Vásquez-Velásquez, 2016 ; Supplementary Material Figure S1 and Table S5). Since we wanted to assess the effect of different LAI representations on streamflow simulation, we also calibrated the original SWAT for monthly streamflow, and SWAT-T for both monthly streamflow and LAI using the best-fit parameters from the SWAT-Tb calibration (Supplementary Material Table S4), following a similar methodology as described for SWAT-Tb. This procedure resembles the standard practice of using SWAT without LAI calibration, included in other tropical watershed studies (e.g., Abuhay et al., 2023 ; Adhikari et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Lopes et al., 2021 ; Santos et al., 2021 ; Villamizar et al., 2019 ; Yifru et al., 2021 ). Also, as a proof-of-concept, we compared the streamflow performance of SWAT-Tb, assuming that LAI remains constant for each land cover type throughout the year. Due to the high variability of LAI in the tropical Andes (Supplementary Material Table S1), we selected two different LAI constant values for the dominant land cover types (1.3 and 1.7 m2 /m2  for pasture or RYEG, and 3.3 and 4.0 m2 /m2  for Andean forest or FRST). These values are based on a literature review and observations in the CR watershed. Below, we will refer to SWAT-Tb with bimodal LAI as “SWAT-Tb-BIM,” and with constant LAI as “SWAT-Tb-LOW” and “SWAT-Tb-HIG,” depending on the lowest or highest LAI constant values for forest and pasture.  3.4 LULC scenarios A control (CTL) scenario (LULC map for 2015, Fig. 2 f; CORANTIOQUIA and UNAL, 2015) and two extreme LULC change scenarios were simulated: full pasture (100 % pasture, PAS) and forest (100 % forest, FOR) cover. These latter scenarios are not realistic but “baseline”-type scenarios that are used to study the range of potential changes in streamflow due to LULC change in the watershed (e.g., Alvarenga et al., 2016; Peña-Arancibia et al., 2019 ). These scenarios imply changes not only in land cover parameters such as LAI but also in some soil properties that are based on land cover parameterization (e.g., SOL_K, SOL_BD, SOL_AWC from the SWAT’s list of parameters), which is important to represent forest and pasture impacts on the watershed’s water balance (e.g., García-Leoz et al., 2018 ; Marín et al., 2018 ; Tobón et al., 2011 ; Vásquez-Velásquez, 2016 ). We simulated each scenario with the different LAI representations for the period 1993–2016 (plus a 3-year spin-up) using the best-fit parameter values from the calibration and 1000 random combinations within the acceptable ranges (Table 3 ). Since everything else is equal, streamflow changes are entirely attributable to LULC changes related to the LAI representation.  3.5 Comparison of SWAT variants We compared five SWAT simulations using three model variants (SWAT, SWAT-T, and SWAT-Tb) that differ in their LAI representation: (1) SWAT default (i.e., using the EPIC-based module for plant growth; Arnold et al., 2012 ), (2) SWAT-T with an unimodal LAI seasonality, (3) SWAT-Tb with constant low LAI (SWAT-Tb-LOW), (4) SWAT-Tb with constant high LAI (SWAT-Tb-HIG) and (5) SWAT-Tb-BIM (i.e., with bimodal LAI calibrated to reproduce satellite data). Differences among scenarios and model variants were analyzed using the nonparametric Wilcoxon rank-sum, signed-rank tests (Bauer, 1972 ), and the Kruskal-Wallis Rank Sum Test (Hollander et al., 2014 ) included in the stats  R package (R Core Team, 2022 ). We assessed the significance based on the results from each of the 1000 simulations and defined statistically significant differences among LULC scenarios and SWAT variants when more than 95 % of the 1000 iterations had a p-value lower than 0.05.   4 Results 4.1 LAI calibration Both precipitation and LAI of different vegetation types exhibit a bimodal regime in the CR watershed ( Fig. 3 ). There are two wet seasons in MAM and SON and two “dry” (less rainy) seasons in DJF and JJA. The Soil Moisture Index (SMI) follows this same pattern. Relative to precipitation and SMI, LAI exhibits a bimodal pattern that can be described as mirrored to precipitation, with lower values around the peak of the wet seasons and higher values in the dry seasons. This pattern suggests that during the dry seasons, plant growth is not as limited by reduced precipitation and moisture (SMI is greater than 1 in all months but January) as it is enhanced by increased radiation due to lower cloud cover (Aparecido et al., 2018 ). These results are consistent with the role of precipitation and cloudiness on vegetation seasonality in energy-limited environments (ET peaks during the dry season(s) as shown in Supplementary Material Fig. S1), which, according to our results and previous studies (e.g., Aparecido et al., 2018 ; Gotsch et al., 2016 ), appear to dominate over the role of temperature. Further, these results evidence that the assumptions made in the EPIC model about the dominant role of temperature in plant growth (Arnold et al., 2012; Williams et al., 1989 ) is not valid everywhere, particularly in mesic tropical regions. The calibrated SWAT-Tb realistically reproduces the LAI range and seasonality for the dominant LULC types in the CR watershed ( Fig. 4 ), as indicated by the high correlation (r > 0.6) and low biases (BIAS < 10 %) between observed (MODIS) and simulated LAI values. Also, SWAT-T produces a realistic representation of LAI, but with its prescribed unimodal seasonality rather than the observed bimodal pattern. In contrast, SWAT fails to represent both the LAI range (53 % < |PBIAS| < 85 %) and seasonality (−0.59 < r < 0.0; Fig. 4 ). These results highlight that SWAT’s default vegetation module (based on the EPIC model) does not provide a realistic representation of tropical vegetation dynamics.  4.2 Streamflow calibration and validation Following the classification proposed by Moriasi et al. (2007; 2015), the SWAT-Tb (bimodal setting; i.e., SWAT-Tb-BIM) representation of monthly streamflow is “very good” and “good” for the calibration (2003–2016) and validation (1993–2002) periods, respectively ( Fig. 5  and  Table 2 ). Additionally, several simulated water balance components (baseflow, runoff, and ET/P ratios) are comparable to reference values (Supplementary Material Table S5). SWAT-T, SWAT-Tb-LOW, and SWAT-Tb-HIG also perform well (between very good and good; Table 2 ) using the best-fit parameter values from  Table 3 , suggesting a low streamflow sensitivity to LAI constant or unimodal seasonality. The performance of the original SWAT in reproducing observed streamflow varies between “very good” (for calibration) and “very good/satisfactory” (for validation), but with a higher bias in comparison with the other SWAT variants (Table 2 ), which results from its low capacity to simulate the LAI dynamics (Fig. 4  and Supplementary Material Fig. S2). On another hand, although we did not calibrate the SWAT model for ET due to limited gauge observations and missing values in MODIS-ET estimations, SWAT-Tb-BIM outperforms the original SWAT in capturing ET seasonality and magnitude (Supplementary Material Fig. S1). Indeed, SWAT produced lower annual evapotranspiration (7.47 %; 899.18 mm) and higher water yield (6.84 %; 979.44 mm) values than SWAT-Tb-BIM (966.31 mm and 912.40 mm, respectively; further details in Supplementary Material Fig. S1 and Table S5).  4.3 Effects of forest and pasture scenarios on streamflow: Comparison among SWAT variants Our results show that streamflow is more sensitive to the model variant (i.e., original SWAT vs. LAI-improved variants) than to differences in LAI representation between SWAT-T and SWAT-Tb (   Figs. 6, 7, and 8 ). Statistically significant differences between model variants emerge when comparing monthly streamflow differences between SWAT variants (i.e., SWATCTL  – SWAT-Tb-BIMCTL ; Fig. 7 ) and scenarios (i.e., FOR-CTL and PAS-CTL; Fig. 8 ). This latter comparison ensures that LULC scenarios are compared under the same parametrization setting and climate forcing (precipitation and temperature), e.g., streamflow for the PAS scenario under La Niña conditions (above-normal precipitation) is compared to the CTL scenario under the same conditions. Hence, below, we will focus on comparing the original SWAT with SWAT-Tb using the BIM case as the main reference. However, the main and supplementary figures include all the results for the LOW and HIG cases and the SWAT-T variant. Overall, the original SWAT model tends to overestimate (median±  standard deviation) monthly and annual streamflow for CTL (7.26±  4.81 % and 7.48±  3.19), FOR (3.88±  7.25 % and 4.97±  3.93), and PAS (5.59±  4.71 % and 6.36±  2.64 %) scenarios compared to SWAT-Tb-BIM simulations (Fig. 7 ). In particular, the highest differences occur from January to June and July to December in the FOR (7.72±  7.71 %) and PAS (7.31±  5.34 %) scenarios, respectively. These months correspond to periods in which the original SWAT model has the highest LAI differences (i.e., underestimation) compared to SWAT-Tb-BIM (Figs. 5 b and e). Additionally, the original SWAT model shows significant differences with SWAT-T, SWAT-Tb-LOW, and SWAT-Tb-HIGH at both monthly and annual scales. On the other hand, SWAT-T exhibits both positive (i.e., overestimation) and negative (i.e., underestimation) streamflow differences at monthly and annual streamflow relative to SWAT-Tb-BIM for CTL (0.18.12±  0.65 % and 0.18±  0.48 %), FOR (-1.15±  0.86 % and −1.15±  0.61 %), and PAS (1.12±  1.52 % and 1.22±  1.15 %) scenarios. In the case of SWAT-Tb-LOW and SWAT-Tb-HIGH, their streamflow differences compared to SWAT-Tb-BIM are smaller than 0.5 % at both monthly and annual scales. These results suggest that streamflow simulations are more sensitive to differences in LAI magnitude (i.e., SWAT vs. improved LAI model variants) than to its seasonality (i.e., constant, unimodal, or bimodal). However, despite the small differences of SWAT-T, SWAT-Tb-LOW, and SWAT-Tb-HIGH relative to SWAT-Tb-BIM (< 5 %), their outputs for CTL, FOR, and PAS scenarios show significant differences each other for some monthly and annual values, evidencing the implications of different LAI seasonality representations on streamflow simulations. The SWAT-T and SWAT-Tb results show that the potential impacts of LULC change on monthly and annual streamflow are more pronounced in the 100 % forest scenario (3.96±  7.58 % and 4.07±  4.43 %) than for the 100 % pasture (-3.69±  3.41 % and −3.81±  2.54 %) scenario (Fig. 8 ). The occurrence of 100 % forest and 100 % pasture cover in the watershed leads to increased and decreased streamflow, particularly during the dry seasons (DJF and JJA; 6.64±  6.92 % and −4.14±  3.03 %, respectively). Overall, during the wet seasons (MAM and SON), results do not show significant difference between FOR-CTL (0.88±  7.00 %) and PAS-CTL (-3.20±  3.70 %) scenarios. These streamflow changes during the dry seasons explain the annual streamflow increases and decreases for the FOR-CTL and PAS-CTL scenarios (Figs. 8 b and d), respectively. The more significant differences between model variants occur between the original SWAT and the modified versions SWAT-T and SWAT-Tb (Fig. 8 ). These differences in assessing LULC change impacts on streamflow are less pronounced between SWAT-T and SWAT-Tb. While SWAT-T and SWAT-Tb predict a streamflow increase (under the FOR scenario (relative to the CTL scenario) from December to February (3.66±  7.09 % to 5.44±  7.25 %) and June to September (6.65±  6.46 % to 8.07±  6.49 %), SWAT underestimates streamflow increase (2.52±  9.11 % and 3.71±  6.62 %, respectively; Fig. 8 a). Additionally, in most cases, SWAT overestimates the streamflow decrease in the PAS scenario throughout the year (-5.47±  3.96 %) compared to SWAT-T (-2.78±  2.95 %) and SWAT-Tb (-4.13±  3.20 % to −3.63±  3.10 %) (Fig. 8 c). At the annual time scale, SWAT-T and SWAT-Tb results indicate that annual streamflow tends to increase (2.61±  4.13 % to 4.33±  4.22 %) and decrease (-4.12±  2.46 % to −2.77 %±  2.09 %) in the FOR and PAS scenarios, respectively (Figs. 7 b and d). In contrast, SWAT output underestimates and overestimates these results for the FOR (1.09±  4.35 %) and PAS (-5.48±  2.54 %) scenarios, respectively. In this sense, the systematic streamflow overestimations in SWAT relative to SWAT-Tb-BIM (Fig. 7 ) explain why significant difference between the original SWAT model and LAI-improved variants occur only from July to November and January to March in the FOR-CTL and PAS-CTL scenarios, respectively.  4.4 Water balance components Differences in streamflow between scenarios are caused by differences in the watershed’s water balance components ( Fig. 9  and Supplementary Material Figs. S3-S6). The largest differences between the CTL and the other LULC scenarios occur in surface runoff, lateral flow, percolation, and groundwater contribution (i.e., baseflow) to streamflow (Fig. 9 b–e). The sum of these differences results in differences in water yield (Fig. 9 f). In contrast, differences in evapotranspiration are less pronounced (Fig. 9 a; note that their magnitudes never exceed ±  20 %). The effect of LAI differences on water balance components can be assessed by comparing SWAT-T and SWAT-Tb relative to SWAT outputs ( Fig. 10  and Supplementary Material Figs. S7-S9). SWAT tends to underestimate LAI for the FOR and PAS scenarios throughout the year, mainly from December to March and June to February, respectively (Fig. 10 a), which leads to mixed results in the representation of water balance components. Overall, the FOR scenario shows larger differences between SWAT and SWAT-Tb or SWAT-T than the PAS scenario (Fig. 10 b–g and Supplementary Material Figs. S7). For instance, in the FOR scenario, SWAT tends to overestimate water yield throughout the year (Fig. 10 g), with larger values (>10 %) from January to March (i.e., peak of the first dry season and transition to first wet season)This overestimation results from greater production of runoff (> 70 %, Fig. 10 c), lateral flow (>20 %, Fig. 10 d), and percolation (> 25 %, Fig. 10 e), as well as from reduced evapotranspiration (< −5 %, Fig. 10 b). In contrast, SWAT’s overestimation of water yield in the PAS scenario is marginal throughout the year (Fig. 10 g). In both scenarios, differences of evapotranspiration between models (Fig. 10 b) are low (< 10 % except for January-February and June-July), hence the effects on streamflow result mainly from variations in surface runoff and groundwater flows (i.e., lateral flow, percolation, and base flow).   5 Discussion 5.1 Contrast among SWAT model variants The original SWAT, SWAT-T, and SWAT-Tb variants do not exhibit significant differences in simulating observed monthly streamflow in the CR watershed (Fig. 5  and Table 2 ) despite their differences in reproducing vegetation dynamics through LAI (Fig. 4 ). However, the unrealistic representation of LAI can lead to significant differences in LULC change impact on streamflow (Figs. 7 and 8 ) and the underlying changes in the water balance components (Figs. 9, 10 , and Supplementary Material Figs. S3-S10) between the original SWAT model and LAI-improved variants. Our proof-of-concept illustrates how the original SWAT can be calibrated to realistically simulate streamflow despite being intrinsically unable to reproduce the observed LAI dynamics, which influences other water balance components, including evapotranspiration, surface runoff, lateral flow and baseflow (Figs. 9 and 10 ; Alemayehu et al., 2017 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Haas et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2020 ). Hence, there is a danger of getting the “right results” (e.g., the model reproduces observed streamflow) for the wrong reasons (Kirchner, 2006 ) as evidence of our results. In this sense, our results (ΔNSE=ΔR2 =0.01–0.05; ΔPBIAS=-15.40–0.9 %; ΔRSR= 0.01–0.07; Table 2 ) are consistent with Chen et al. (2023)  (ΔNSE=0.01; ΔR2 =0.0–0.01), Ma et al. (2019)  (ΔNSE=0.04–0.07; ΔR2 =0.01–0.04), and Zhang et al. (2020)  (ΔNSE=0.02; ΔR2 =0.02–0.04; ΔPBIAS=-6.4 - −5.1 %) that report minimal streamflow performance improvements between the original SWAT model and LAI-improved variants. This suggests that improving the representation of the watershed’s water balance does not necessarily lead to better model streamflow performance but points obtaining the “right” results for the “right” reasons. The unrealistic LAI representation limits the capacity of models (i.e., SWAT in the present case) to produce reliable results when used to inform environmental decisions about hydrologic responses. For example, Chen et al. (2023) , Haas et al. (2022) , and Zhang et al. (2020)  report that the original SWAT underestimates mean annual evapotranspiration between 11 % and 36 % in comparison to model variants improved to better simulate LAI, including SWAT-T (Alemayehu et al., 2017 ), for watersheds located in China, Southeast of the United States, and Australia, respectively. For these watersheds, differences in mean annual surface runoff (4 %-8 %), lateral flow (∼2 %), groundwater (∼7 %), baseflow (∼13 %), and soil moisture (<10 %) are also reported, mostly corresponding to overestimations in SWAT relative to model variants with improved LAI. These percentage differences in streamflow from previous studies are comparable to what we found between original SWAT and SWAT-Tb (|0.10|%-|8.14|%), but our differences in evapotranspiration are smaller (|∼8|%; Fig. 10 , Supplementary Material Figs. S7-S9, and Table S5) as it discussed below. These results highlight that a realistic representation of LAI is key to improve the simulation of water balance components and to assess the impacts of LULC change more reliably on water availability (streamflow). Overall, our results are robust regardless of whether LAI was simulated with a constant, unimodal, or bimodal seasonality (Figs. 7 and 8 ), which is crucial due to its uncertainties in remote-sensing estimations and limited field observations in the tropical Andes. Due to the high spatial and temporal variability of LAI (Bruijnzeel et al., 2011 ; Supplementary Table S1), as well as the uncertainty in its estimation (Tang et al., 2019 ), it is important to highlight that we obtained similar results regardless of whether LAI was constant, unimodal or bimodal (Fig. 8 ). An important implication of the differences between the original SWAT model and LAI-improved variants is that studies using the approach of calibrating and validating SWAT for streamflow but not for other water balance components that depend on LAI, which is still standard practice (e.g., Abuhay et al., 2023 ; Adhikari et al., 2020 ; Lopes et al., 2021 ; Santos et al., 2021 ; Villamizar et al., 2019 ; Yifru et al., 2021 ), may misrepresent the impacts of LULC change scenarios on streamflow (and other water balance components), especially in tropical regions where the classical LAI representation included in SWAT does not perform adequately. Indeed, our results show that, regarding LULC change impacts, the original SWAT has statistically significant differences in monthly and annual streamflow anomalies compared to SWAT-T and SWAT-Tb (Figs. 7 and 8 ). Conversely, SWAT-T and SWAT-Tb do not exhibit statistical significance differences in LULC change impacts (e.g., FOR-CTL and PAS-CTL), suggesting that the streamflow response to LULC change is more sensitive to differences in LAI magnitude than to its seasonality (e.g., constant, unimodal, bimodal). However, our results show that despite small differences between SWAT-T and SWAT-Tb, significant differences can emerge between their streamflow simulations for individual scenarios (Fig. 7 ).  5.2 LULC impact on watershed response and water availability The effects of LULC change on streamflow are highly variable in tropical regions depending on factors such as climate (Peña-Arancibia et al., 2019 ), soil types (Roa-García et al., 2011 ), original and replacement vegetation (Ochoa-Tocachi et al., 2018; Meli et al., 2024 ; Ponette-González et al., 2014 ), watershed area (Krishnaswamy et al., 2018 ), and study approach (Posada-Marín and Salazar, 2022 ). The net impact of forest cover increase or decrease generally depends on a trade-off between changes in evapotranspiration (“pump effect”) and infiltration (“sponge effect”) Krishnaswamy et al., 2018 ; Ogden et al., (2013) ; Peña-Arancibia et al., 2019 ) as described by the infiltration trade-off hypothesis for tropical regions (Bruijnzeel, 2004 ). In our SWAT-T and SWAT-Tb results, annual streamflow is slight higher in the FOR scenario (4.62±  1.39–4.69±  1.38 m3 /s) than in the PAS (4.29±  1.30–4.33±  1.29 m3 /s) scenario (Figs. 8 b and d). These results differ from many studies for small tropical watersheds (e.g., Muñoz-Villers and McDonnell, 2013 ; Ogden et al., 2017 ), which found that, in general, increased forest cover leads to decreased annual streamflow mainly due to increased evapotranspiration. However, there are contrasting ET changes caused by forest-to-pasture conversion (i.e., FOR-CTL vs. PAS-CTL scenarios) between lowlands (i.e., water-limited environments; < 1000 m.a.s.l.) and mountain (e.g., energy-limited environments; ≥ 1000 m.a.s.l.) tropical regions (Meli et al., 2024 ). Indeed, in energy-limited watersheds (such as the CR watershed, where ET peaks during the dry seasons; see Supplementary Material Fig. S1), forest and pasture cover can exhibit similar ET rates due to this is mainly driven by radiation instead by air saturation deficit associated with frequent low vapor pressure deficit (VPD) and vegetation water stress conditions (Brauman et al., 2012; Gotsch et al., 2016 ). For these reasons, forest cover increase can induce fewer reductions in streamflow due to evapotranspiration increases than in water-limited environments (Hou et al., 2023; Peña-Arancibia et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2017 ). Our results suggest that forest cover change mainly affects surface and groundwater flows (the “sponge effect”; Figs. 9 b-e) with little changes (≤ |20 %|) in monthly evapotranspiration (the “pump effect”; Fig. 9 a). For this reason, 100 % forest cover has a positive impact on dry seasons streamflow associated with higher infiltration into the soil and recharge to groundwater (Fig. 9 d) that sustains streamflow during months with lower precipitation (Figs. 9 d-9 e) consistent with the infiltration trade-off hypothesis (Bruijnzeel, 2004; Krishnaswamy et al., 2018 ). The small changes in ET (Fig. 9 a) may be explained by the climatic characteristics of the CR watershed, i.e., low evapotranspiration rates due to low atmospheric demand driven by low temperature and high relative humidity (Aparecido et al., 2018; López-Ramírez et al., 2020; Ramírez et al., 2017 ). Indeed, field observations report small to no significant differences in evapotranspiration between native Andean forest (FRST) and pasture (RYEG) at seasonal (dry and wet seasons) and annual scales in the region of the CR watershed (García-Leoz et al., 2018 ). Additionally, simulated watersheds scale, forest, and pasture evapotranspiration are comparable to values reported for tropical Andean watersheds dominated by forest and pasture covers (Crespo et al., 2011 ) and ground observation and remote-sensing estimations for the study region (Supplementary Material Figure S2 and Table S5).  5.3 Limitations and future research Our study shows that SWAT-Tb improves the representation of LAI for a tropical mountain watershed with a bimodal vegetation regime. However, some limitations of the original SWAT model persist in this variant, namely the default methods to calculate runoff and potential evapotranspiration (PET) and the inability to include additional precipitation inputs. Specifically, SWAT estimates runoff based on the widely used SCS (after the United States Soil Conservation Service) curve number (SCS-CN) method, which is controversial for certain geographic regions and land use types (Ogden et al., 2017 ). Alternative methods have been proposed (e.g., Bartlett et al., 2016 ), including adaptations for the SWAT model (Rajib and Merwade, 2015; Zhang et al., 2019 ). We used the Priestly-Taylor method to estimate ET, which has inherent limitations, such as disregarding the effect of wind (there are no reliable wind records in our study area). Rajib et al. (2020)  proposed an alternative approach by modifying the SWAT source code to assimilate remotely sensed LAI and PET, which avoids using the default scheme to simulate LAI and one of the three PET methods (i.e., Hargreaves, Penman-Monteith, or Priestly-Taylor) available in SWAT model. However, as mentioned before, this approach implies simplifying the watershed’s heterogeneity by reducing the number of HRUs. Additionally, this assimilation of observed LAI or PET does not provide data for future LULC and climate change scenarios where observations are unavailable, and simulations are required. Finally, additional precipitation sources, such as occult precipitation (e.g., via fog interception), are not simulated directly in the SWAT model and may represent an additional water input in tropical mountain watersheds. For the study area, Cárdenas et al. (2017)  estimated that this occult precipitation is lower than 10 % of the mean annual precipitation. Precipitation is treated as an input to the watershed, which may be problematic when assessing LULC change effects on streamflow in the presence of strong vegetation-mediated land-atmosphere interactions (Posada-Marín and Salazar, 2022 ). However, this is arguably relevant for large river basins while negligible for small ones such as the CR watershed (Salazar et al., 2023 ). Based on the above, we identify several lines of research for future model improvement, mainly: (1) calibration of satellite data (e.g., LAI and ET) with field measurements to better inform LAI-improved models, (2) better depiction of the precipitation, temperature, and ET spatial variability considering the complex topography of tropical mountain watersheds, (3) validating the SWAT-Tb approach in tropical watersheds with various physical and climatic settings, and (4) integration of SWAT’s improvements in different modules (e.g., plant growth, ET, and PET estimation, surface runoff, among others); thus allowing a more holistic approach for improving SWAT’s process representation.   6 Conclusions Our study of the CR watershed in the tropical Andes examines the effects of vegetation parameterizations on simulated streamflow changes under LULC scenarios. Vegetation dynamics play a key role in simulating a watershed’s hydrological response to LULC change. These dynamics are commonly represented in models such as SWAT through LAI, which can exhibit high spatial and temporal variability and uncertainty in tropical regions. Our results show that SWAT-T and SWAT-Tb variants can reproduce not only streamflow but also unimodal and bimodal LAI seasonal patterns, respectively. In contrast, the original SWAT model variants are inherently unable to reproduce some LAI seasonal patterns, although they can be calibrated to reproduce streamflow. The unrealistic LAI representation in the original SWAT model leads to significantly different results compared to SWAT-T and SWAT-Tb when assessing LULC change impacts on streamflow through multiple water balance components. Furthermore, our results highlight that LULC change impacts (i.e., FOR-CTL and PAS-CTL) on streamflow exhibit insignificant differences between constant (SWAT-Tb-LOW and -HIGH), unimodal (SWAT-T), and bimodal (SWAT-Tb) LAI representations. This suggests that the streamflow response is more sensitive to differences in LAI magnitude than to its seasonality. Regarding the effect of LULC change scenarios on streamflow, our results suggest that forest enhances water availability, increasing streamflow during the dry seasons. We found that streamflow during the dry seasons increases in the 100 % forest cover scenario while it decreases in the 100 % pasture cover scenario based on SWAT-T and SWAT-Tb results. In contrast, the original SWAT, with its default LAI representation, underestimates streamflow changes (streamflow decrease) in the FOR scenario and exaggerates decreases in the PAS scenario. These results highlight that an unrealistic LAI representation can lead to misleading results for LULC change impacts and decision-making about water security and forest conservation in the tropical Andes.
1 Introduction Coal seam water injection is a comprehensive technical method used to prevent outbursts and provide cooling (Pang et al., 2014 ), reduce dust, and mitigate disasters (Chen et al., 2021a,b ) by hydraulically wetting the coal in underground coal mines. Coal seam water injection can not only effectively prevent coal mine dust damage (Cybulski et al., 2015 ), and coal mine explosions (Cai et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020 ), but also improve gas drainage efficiency (Wang et al., 2023 ), reduce the probability of rock burst disaster (Li et al., 2019 ), and prevent gas disasters (Yue et al., 2024 ). It has significant advantages in construction technology and the prevention of gas disasters and has been widely used. In the field of hydraulic wetting of coal seams, notable scholars have made significant research advancements. A method combining laboratory experiments and simulations was utilized to assess the value of including both correct and incorrect fracture geometry and connectivity data, as well as matrix data (He et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2023 ). By successfully detecting the wetting and seepage stages of coal seam water injection by introducing a fluorescent tracer. This method provided effective detection performance for identifying the wetting range of coal seam water injection (Maldaner et al., 2018 ). The impact of water on the mechanical properties of coal samples was investigated through rock mechanics testing and numerical simulation, also explored the relationship between water and acoustic emission signals using acoustic emission count and energy statistics (Zhang et al., 2023 ). A dynamic monitoring test system for the hydraulic wetting range of coal rock under true three-dimensional stress was independently developed, conducting a comprehensive study on the influence of sample anisotropy on the seepage effect. This study was combined with acoustic wave testing to analyze the dynamic wetting range and wetting process of liquid-phase fluid under varying fluid pressures and to determine the threshold range of wave parameter changes during water contact monitoring (Chen et al., 2021a,b ). Furthermore, the Navier-Stokes equation was utilized to simulate water injection seepage in the model, finding that the seepage velocity increased with the increase of the fracture shape factor (Chen et al., 2023 ). The dynamic wetting of water in coal was found to be primarily influenced by the pore structure, as determined through the use of low-field nuclear magnetic resonance in combination with CO2 -H2 O-coal interaction experiments. This seepage process mainly disperses free gas, exhibiting characteristics of rapid attenuation (Xu et al., 2023 ). The interaction between gas and water in the process of self-priming is an important way for water to move deep into the coal seam. Self-absorption is the key to full wetting, which provides a guarantee for the water distribution in the coal seam and lays a foundation for the replacement of adsorbed gas (Yue et al., 2022 ). Directly assessed the water content within rock pores using nuclear magnetic resonance scanning and observed that as the metamorphic degree decreased, the coal sample became more prone to wetting. It contributes to the study of the relationship between pore fracture structure characteristics and water content by (Yang et al., 2022 ). As shown by (Cao et al., 2019; Guihéneuf et al., 2021; Piña et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2017 ), to investigate the flow behavior in fractured coal rock that considers the distribution of pores and fractures, as well as the influence of small pore parameters. They found that water tends to flow towards radial fractures. Pores primarily facilitate the rapid absorption and efficient transport of water. The law of water migration during the process of water injection with various pore and fracture structure types is elucidated. The significance of pores and fractures in the primary movement of water is most evident at the forefront of water migration. Based on the dissipative particle dynamics method, Static and flow simulations of fluid in typical shale fractures were conducted, closely associating the extent of contact deformation on the fracture surface with changes in the seepage field (Wu et al., 2021 ). The deformation characteristics of cracks under varying normal stresses were investigated by analyzing the contact area ratio, and the correlation between fracture surface deformation, velocity vector, and seepage pressure was analyzed (Zhang et al., 2022 ). When the geometric parameters of rock fractures are correlated, significant differences emerge between the correlation and non-correlation pore size and fracture length distributions. This highlights the scale and stress dependence of the hydraulic behavior of fractured rock (Al-Maamori et al., 2019; Baghbanan and Jing, 2008 ). The research directions of experts at home and abroad can be divided into the methods and technology of water injection, effect evaluation (Wang et al., 2022a,b ), and wetting prediction (Ibrahim, 2022 ). However, there are still some issues, such as the incomplete nature of the coal seam water injection law (Lu and Wang, 2015 ), and the lack of accuracy in determining the water injection range (Sun et al., 2018 ). When assessing the impact of coal seam water injection, significant errors may occur (Yang et al., 2023 ), Additionally, the results of water injection wetting are unsatisfactory when water injection measures are implemented (Perkins, 2018 ). Numerical simulation has enhanced research efficiency and safety in studying water injection permeation. It offers advantages such as high efficiency (Liu et al., 2022 ), repeatability (Liang et al., 2024 ), safety (Lin et al., 2023; Song et al., 2024 ), cost-effectiveness, multi-scenario simulation (Shi et al., 2019 ), data processing and analysis (Yu et al., 2021 ), and predictive capabilities. This provides crucial support for scientific decision-making. In this study, the specific wetting boundary was defined and extracted. This solved the issue of the unclear boundary of the wetting range and the challenging extraction process. Additionally, it laid the foundation for future research and processing. In summary, scholars primarily focus on coal samples under typical loads as the main research subject in the study of the hydraulic wetting effect of coal. There are limited studies on predicting the wetting range of fractured coal seams under true triaxial conditions, and most of these studies assume homogeneity under default conditions. The study of hydraulic wetting coupling of briquette specimens does not take into account the influence of the randomness of fracture distribution and its occurrence on the effect of water injection under natural conditions. In this paper, an intact model and a fractured model are established with the assistance of the finite element difference program. Additionally, a random three-dimensional DFN model is developed for the fractured model. The program's built-in fluid–solid coupling is utilized to simulate the wetting process of constant pressure water injection, offering a reference for the numerical simulation of wetting in the fractured model.  2 Research methodology The finite element difference program accurately generates the geometric shape and physical property model of the fractured model. This model allowed us to create coal sample models of equal size, taking into account the presence of numerous small random cracks. By subjecting both intact and fractured model to the same stress loading method, we were able to obtain data on pore pressure, triaxial stress–strain field, and flow rate curves. These results were then analyzed to evaluate the wetting behavior of the fractured model. 2.3.1 Model establishment Based on the authors' previous laboratory experimental research results (Wang et al., 2022a,b ), laboratory coal samples of 100 mm × 100 mm × 100 mm, identical in size to the experimental coal samples, were generated and the Mohr-Colomb constitutive model was fully employed. The model drilling hole has a total length of 50 mm and a radius of 5 mm. The sealing length measures 40 mm, and the fluid model of the sealing portion is designed with an impermeable configuration. The length of the water injection segment is 10 mm. Establish a co-directional fluid model. The remaining coal samples use the identical fluid model as the injection part. The numerical analysis employed an identical stress-loading methodology to that of the experiment. Fig. 1   illustrates the procedure for modeling and loading the coal sample. These points are used to monitor the data of the two models during the water injection and wet-ting period, focusing on stress, strain, and water injection time. Additionally, the simulation results saved at the 540 s water injection time are used to select cloud slices immediately adjacent to the inner wall of the model's injection section on both horizontal and vertical planes of the figures. Specifically, the cloud slices in the planes where they are located (x = 4.5, y = 4.5, z = 4.5) are observed for flow, triaxial stress–strain, and pore water pressure. A more accurate comparison of the hydraulic wetting range is obtained. In laboratory conditions, to enhance the control of experimental variables and accurately measure the stress–strain relationships across various directions, the simulation process is meticulously designed to better capture the predominant wetting direction during the hydraulic wetting of the intact model.   3 True triaxial wetting experiment The study examined the ultrasonic propagation characteristics of coal under true triaxial conditions and various water injection scenarios, using field experimental data from previous work. The field experiment entailed employing a press to compact a cubic specimen with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm × 100 mm. The true triaxial hydraulic fracturing-antireflection wetting experimental system of deep coal rock independently developed by the research group was used. This system consisted of three subsystems: the true triaxial loading control subsystem, the acoustic emission monitoring subsystem, and the fluid loading control subsystem. The experiment's specifics are outlined in Table 4  , with a particular emphasis on investigating the influence of various water injection and pore conditions on the propagation characteristics of the coal. The study specifically examines the subsystem responsible for controlling fluid loading and provides the specific test details in Table 4 . During the field test, the hydrostatic pressure is initially applied to the sample, gradually increasing until the experimental triaxial stress value is reached. Subsequently, a constant triaxial stress is maintained on the sample. The acoustic emission monitoring system synchronously excites and collects ultrasonic signals. Firstly, the ultrasonic transmission experiment was conducted on the sample under experimental stress, followed by the water injection experiment under various water injection conditions on the sample. After the system completes the predetermined water injection conditions, the fluid control system immediately unloads the water pressure. The field test shows that the water injection rate increases linearly with the pressure and decreases over time.
