The ultrasonic wave velocity is linearly positively correlated with pressure, exponentially positively correlated with time, and the sensitivity is weakened. The ultrasonic amplitude decreases with an increase in pressure, leading to a decrease in the attenuation coefficient. The sensitivity of both parameters to time follows a low–high-low trend. The number of rings is linearly positively correlated with pressure, exponentially positively correlated with time, and is consistent with the change in water injection (Cheng et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022a,b ). The field experiment focuses on examining the effects of different water injection and pore conditions on the ultrasonic propagation characteristics of coal under true triaxial settings. Additionally, it evaluates and examines the simulation data in comparison to the field test results. Initially, it is necessary to expose the coal samples to true triaxial stress conditions while under hydrostatic pressure. The specific loading path may be shown in Fig. 3  . The purpose of this is to incrementally achieve the desired experimental triaxial stress level. The program should be configured to keep the triaxial stress of the coal samples constant. Initiate the fluid module, sustain a consistent water pressure in the water injection section, and disengage the triaxial stress and water injection pressure after the designated water injection duration. When the water injection period is 9 min and the water injection pressure is 6 MPa, the triaxial stress–strain and water pressure behavior correspond precisely to the experimental results. Fig. 4   displays the monitoring data. The flow rates were evaluated at various injection pressures, as depicted in Fig. 5   and Fig. 6  . The fluid swiftly permeates the coal sample, dispersing outward from the injection hole as the focal point. The injection pressure is the main factor that determines the injection power. With an increase in injection pressure, the flow discharge within the coal sample exhibits a constant increase. At the same time, the hydraulic wetting range undergoes a substantial expansion. Nevertheless, with the increase in water injection duration, the flow rates of the coal experienced a significant reduction until eventually reaching a stable state. This signifies that the point of saturation has been attained at this specific water pressure. Hence, elevating the water injection pressure can effectively enhance the wetting of the coal during the wetting process. The water injection period has minimal impact on the water injection, as demonstrated in Fig. 7  . This finding is consistent with the fundamental conclusion of the true triaxial coal wetting test (Cheng et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022a,b ). Based on the sufficient test of the results shown in Fig. 4 , it can be inferred that both the simulation method and the results are valid (Wang et al., 2022a,b ).  4 Analysis of the results The stress equilibrium stage is determined by the convergence of the stress in the fissure model, which takes 420 s. The hydraulic wetting stage is defined by the 540 s water injection period, followed by an additional 500 s of unloading of the triaxial stresses after the water injection stops. The entire process takes approximately 1460 s. 4.1 Pore pressure analysis Throughout the wetting process, the pore pressure of the intact model uniformly increased in all directions, with the water injection hole positioned in the middle. Fig. 7  demonstrates that as the duration of water injection increased, the pore pressure consistently rose in all three stress orientations. The width of the ribbon in the intact model is roughly 1.3 cm, aligned with the middle principal tress and the minimum principal stress. The maximum principal stress has a circular configuration, with pore diameters that nearly correspond to the color ranges observed in the other principal stress orientations. The pore pressure within the fractured model intensifies and primarily propagates in the direction of the fracture orientation. Fracture expansion occurs as the color band widens uniformly in the direction of the intermediate principal stress and the minimum principal stress. Consequently, the horizontal plane becomes uneven as a consequence of the fracture and other pressures. Stage II (Water Injection): Upon the start of water injection, both models exhibit a gradual increase in pore pressure. As the stage progresses, the rate of increase moderates. During this stage, the intact model consistently shows a curve that exceeds that of the fractured model. This suggests that under identical injection conditions, the intact model is capable of withstanding higher pore pressure levels. Stage III (Stopped): Following the cessation of water injection, the two curves exhibit markedly distinct responses. For the intact model, the decrease in pore pressure is relatively smooth and slow, whereas for the fractured model, the pore pressure drops precipitously, almost returning to zero immediately. These trends suggest that the pore spaces within the fractured model are likely more interconnected, allowing water to escape more rapidly. This results in an abrupt reduction in pressure when the injection is stopped. Conversely, the intact model has fewer confined pore spaces, which slows down water loss and leads to a slower pressure decline. This indicates that the intact model retains pore pressure more effectively, while the fractured model exhibits weaker pressure-sustaining capability. These trends suggest that the pore spaces within the fractured model are likely more interconnected, allowing water to escape more rapidly, and thus result in the abrupt reduction in pressure upon stopping the injection. Conversely, the intact model has fewer or more confined pore spaces, which slows the water loss and results in a slower pressure decline. This indicates that the intact model retains pore pressure more effectively, while the fractured model exhibits weaker pressure sustaining capability. The pore water pressure curves demonstrate a propensity to be lower than the fluid pressure curves of the intact model. This implies that numerical simulation investigations show that models with initial fracture units have unique characteristics in the behavior of pore water pressure curves. Together with the porosity, the fractures constitute the water transport channels of the coal where the cleavage and pore space combine to create an intricate network for fluid flow. This network modifies the allocation of fluid pressure within the coal to a certain degree. Fractures facilitate the diffusion and expedite the movement of fluids within the coal. This leads to a reduced rate of variation in pore water pressure compared to the rate of variation in fluid pressure in the intact model. The pore water pressure curve generally falls below the fluid pressure curve of the intact model.  4.2 Mechanical parameters analysis 4.2.1 Triaxial stress The same stress loading method produces almost identical stress loading curves. The fracture model depicted in Fig. 8   has a convergence ratio of 1E-5 at 420 s, achieving stress balance. After the initiation of water injection, the stress is not influenced by the water injection process and remains constant. After 540 s, the water injection stops, releasing the pressure. The pressure relief stress is reduced to zero, and the disturbance is minimal.  4.2.2 Triaxial strain Fig. 9–10    demonstrates that the intact model exhibits a distinct disk-shaped band, which is centered on the water injection area and signifies a noticeable transition zone. The focal point of this region of change is located at the center of the figure. It is surrounded by a continuous expansion of the change region, with a gradual shift from the center to the outside edges. This indicates a distribution of stress that goes from being concentrated to being distributed. The color shift within the disk-shaped zone is characterized by a darker center, suggesting a significant concentration of stress, and a gradual lightening of color towards the outside edges, showing a decrease in stress concentration. The fractured model exhibits greater complexity in comparison to the entire model. The changing area exhibits an uneven shape, primarily concentrated along the direction of the fracture. The portion exhibits an elongated morphology, characterized by a very limited distribution range. The strain distribution demonstrates substantial variability in numerical magnitude, notably in the direction parallel to the fracture. The intensity and dispersion of the strain exhibit a higher level of intricacy. The complexity is also apparent in the range of color shades, where deeper hues correspond to greater strains and lighter hues correspond to lesser strains. Numerically speaking, the range of variance in the fractured model is still larger than that of the intact model. This characteristic indicates that the fracture's presence complicates and amplifies the alteration in strain following water injection. In this simulation, the model (whether intact or fractured) first undergoes a stress equilibrium stage, during which the strain remains stable. This indicates that the rock does not undergo further deformation under the initial stress because the stress level does not exceed the elastic limit of the rock. The model has been adjusted for this stress level. During the water injection phase (from 420 s to 960 s), the rock did not exhibit any significant increase in strain. This suggests that when the fluid is injected into the pores or cracks of the model, it does not induce additional stress on the outer boundary. The structure of the model is stable enough to withstand the fluid pressure without experiencing additional deformation. Finally, during the unloading stage, there is almost no difference in the decrease of strain from the chart. This suggests that even after reducing the external pressure, the model did not exhibit any recovery of deformation. This further indicates that the model did not undergo irreversible plastic deformation throughout the entire loading and unloading process.   4.3 Volumetric stress and volumetric strain Fig. 8  (d) and Fig. 10  (d) illustrate the stress-time and strain–time curves during the wetting process. Throughout the hydraulic wetting process, the injection segment remains consistently pressurized, as seen by the negative values on the curves. In post-processing, we made adjustments to the data to ensure that the stress–strain values were treated as uniform absolute values. This modification significantly enhanced the interpretability of the data. The revised curve indicates that during the hydro-wetting process, the stress in the intact model remains essentially stable at approximately 39 MPa, while the stress in the fractured model stabilizes at around 37 MPa. The strain stabilizes at about 0.003 for the intact model and approximately 0.0026 for the fractured model. As shown in Fig. 11   and Fig. 12  , the breadth of the stress–strain shadow in the intact model corresponds to the triaxial stress–strain after water injection stops, and closely resembles the water transfer contour indicated by the pore water pressure and flow rate. The vertical plane of the fractured model exhibits a considerable increase in the width of the stress data variation range, measuring 2.3 cm and 2.1 cm, respectively. This is in stark contrast to the intact model, where the measured width is only 1.3 cm. The stress shadow area in the horizontal plane is determined by the quantity of fractures, resulting in a significantly lesser effect in comparison to the vertical plane.   5 Discussion 5.1 Analysis of wetting direction The flow rate of coal water injection after wetting was depicted in Fig. 13   (a) and (b). In Fig. 13  (b), the orange oval marks the wetting range and trend that differ from the intact model due to the cracks. The intact model exhibits axial development of the flow rate path under constant injection pressure, the flow rate color bands within the fractured model displayed an irregular expansion of range, forming isolated elliptical-shaped colored regions. When fluid is injected into the fracture, the flow rate in the fracture area quickly rises, creating a new concentrated area of injection centered around the fracture location. The persistent saturation of the area surrounding the fracture leads to the creation of an elliptical shape, with the length of the fracture serving as the axis. This ultimately speeds up the process of wetting the entire area. The wetting area of coal with fractures can be approximated by representing an ellipse, where the major axis corresponds to the fracture length and the minor axis corresponds to the fracture width. As depicted in Fig. 13  (c), the flow rate experiences a rapid increase until reaching its maximum point following the injection of water. The intact model exhibits a peak flow rate of approximately 1.5e- 7L/s, whereas the intact model demonstrates a peak flow rate of approximately 3.5e-7L/s. The benefit of the fractured region for water transportation is apparent. As the injection duration increases, the flow rate of both models tends to decrease. In the initial segment of the fractured model, a rapid and fluctuating decline in the flow rate is observed. Within the first few tens of seconds, the flow rate decreases from its initial value, exhibiting minor oscillations, reaching the stability point of about 100 s. The intact model reaches a stable flow rate of 1e-7L/s, but the fractured model stabilizes at a higher flow rate of 2.8e- 7L/s. Upon cessation of water injection, an immediate decline in the water flow rate is seen. By analyzing the comparison curves, it is evident that the trend of the two models remains similar throughout the water injection process. However, the flow rate of the fractured model is consistently 2.3–2.8 times more than that of the intact model. Thus, these fractures facilitate the effective conveyance of water, allowing for fast absorption and transportation. The actual wetting range of the fractured model is larger than that of the intact model,  5.2 Relationship between hydraulic wetting paths and fracture distribution This research conducts a statistical analysis of the fractures in the fractured model in order to comprehensively explore the variations in the wetting routes of fractured model. The statistical analysis results, depicted in Fig. 14  , indicate that the majority of fractures in the fractured model occur in the northwest (NW) direction, accounting for 97 % of all fractures. The prevailing orientation is northeast (NE), representing 91.3 % of the northwest (NW)-oriented fissures. The dominant group exhibits a strike of 321°, while the dip angle is defined by a modest inclination. The data for the principal fracture orientations are as follows: The first set exhibits a fracture tendency of 51° with a dip angle of 55°, indicating that these fractures dip towards the northeast and are of a moderate inclination. The second set has a fracture tendency of 231° with a steep dip angle of 82°, suggesting that these fractures dip towards the southwest (Table 5 ) . As illustrated in Fig. 15  , the fitted curve reveals that the wetting volume of the fractured model is consistently greater than that of the intact model throughout the process. At the designated time intervals of 1, 2, and 6 min, the wetting volume discrepancies between the two models were quantified as 6.7092, 6.45, and 14.6436, respectively. The aggregate fitting of the data adheres to a quadratic function, suggestive of an augmenting divergence in wetting efficacy as a function of increased water injection duration. indicating that the difference in wetting effects increases with the extension of water injection time. These findings underscore the pronounced superiority of the fractured model in scenarios entailing prolonged water injection processes. The curve in Fig. 15  illustrates the variation in wetting volume over time. The red curve represents the wetting volume of the fracture model, while the purple curve represents the wetting volume of the intact model. The green curve represents the difference in wetting volume between the two. By observing the shape and trend of the curve, we can infer the physical meaning of the wetting process under different models. In the initial stage, the wetting volume of the fracture model increases rapidly, and the value is always larger than that of the intact model; however, the growth rate gradually slows down. The wetting volume curve of the intact model fits better, and the growth is relatively stable and continuous. This may indicate that the liquid is more evenly distributed and transmitted in the entire rock mass. The difference in wetting volume between the two gradually increases with time, reflecting the variation in permeability and storage capacity of the fracture for the liquid. These findings underscore the pronounced superiority of the fractured model in scenarios entailing prolonged water injection processes. It may be deduced that in the early phase of coal fracturing, the existence of fissures facilitates the rapid infiltration of liquid into the coal's interior, leading to a swift augmentation in the wetting volume. This occurs due to the presence of fractures, which serve as a convenient conduit for the liquid, so greatly enhancing the velocity and effectiveness of liquid infiltration. On the other hand, the intact model has a slower rate of liquid penetration into the coal. As a result, the wetness volume increases at a slower pace. To examine the variation in the hydraulic wetting range of the coal, the model's coordinates, pore water pressure, and flow rate data were imported into Tecplot for analysis. Subsequently, wetting range contours were generated using the flow rate and pore water pressure data, and three-dimensional scatter plots and envelope shading plots were produced. The visuals were created to provide a more in-depth investigation of the contours representing the range of wetness. Matlab is utilized to extract the wetting nodes from Fig. 16   and Fig. 17   above. Next, the algorithm regulates the wetting points to eliminate any irregularities in order to facilitate ellipsoid fitting and subsequent optimization. The fundamental equation of an ellipsoid is:(15) x - h     2  a 2   + y - k     2  b 2   + z - i     2  c 2   = 1      The coordinates ( h , k , i )    represent the center of the ellipsoid. The variables a   ,b   , and c    are the lengths of the semi-axes along the x, y, and z axes, respectively. The fitting results are displayed in Fig. 18  , and the semiaxis of each ellipsoid is arranged in Table 6  . The intact model is attained within a time period of 60 s, during which the three axes of the fundamental length reach an approximate measurement of 1.2 cm, showing a consistent wetting range along these axes. The maximum principal stress direction corresponds to semiaxis lengths of 1.7 cm and 2.2 cm at 120 s and 360 s, respectively. The maximum principal stress direction exhibits a greater amplitude and growth tendency compared to the other two axes. During the wetting process, it is clear that water initially distributes uniformly and then gradually stretches in a particular direction due to the maximum principal stress. This results in the formation of an ellipsoid, with the longer semiaxis aligned with the direction of the maximum principal stress. The magnitudes of the semiaxes aligned with the intermediate principal stress and the minimum principal stress are roughly equivalent. The anisotropy observed in the wetting range can be related to elements such as the length of fracture inclination, as previously stated in research. During the wetting process, water selectively permeates the fractures, resulting in the creation of an ellipsoid shape formed by the wetting range contour and the fractures as the main characteristic. A substantial quantity of fractures are observed in the x-y plane close to the injection port in the simulation. As a result, the contour undergoes rapid growth in both the x and y directions, leading to a significant rise in the length of the half-axis. Conversely, the length of the half-axis in the z-axis direction remains largely constant. The magnitude of the semi-axis in the z-direction remains relatively unchanged. Consequently, an irregular ellipsoid is formed with a long semi-axis and short semi-axis by the prevalence of fractures, and the anisotropy index formula is referenced (Zhang et al., 2024 ).(16) A I f  = f x  - f  ¯       2  + f y  - f  ¯       2  + f z  - f  ¯       2    f  ¯         The symbol f    is the anisotropy parameter of the wetting range of the coal, while f x    ,f y    , and f z     denote the axial half-lengths of the ellipsoid in the x, y, and z directions, respectively. f  ¯      is the average value of the axial half-lengths in each direction. The A I f     obtained is the anisotropy coefficient. The anisotropy coefficient fitting is illustrated in Fig. 19  . The wetting route of the intact model demonstrates enhanced stability, resulting in the anisotropy coefficient fitting curve converging towards a value near 1. The presence of fractures at different places leads to significant variations in the anisotropy coefficient of the fractured model. Nevertheless, the overall trend still aligns with that of the intact model. As the anisotropy coefficient increases, the anisotropy feature becomes more pronounced. The fractured model consistently exhibits more pronounced anisotropic properties compared to the intact model. Over time, the intact model experiences an increasing direction of the maximum main stress, while the fractured model's wetting range is influenced by the fracture location factor, which also gradually increases. The fundamental determinant of the wetting direction under true triaxial conditions, when the model is reasonably intact, is believed to be the orientation of the maximum principal stress. Nevertheless, in cases where the model exhibits evident fractures, the dominant element affecting the wetting tendency is the position of these fractures. The intact model experiences water penetration predominantly in the direction of the maximal primary stress during triaxial stress conditions. The fractured coal fracture exhibits a northwestern orientation, and the hydraulic wetting path may align with this direction. Fractures that are slanted towards the northeast make up 91.3 % of the fractures that extend in a northwest direction. Additionally, the path of hydraulic wetness gradually shifts towards the northeast as it progresses northwest. The predominant set of strikes constitutes a significant conduit or focused pathway for wetting. The dip angle is mostly determined by the mild inclination, and the hydraulic wetting channels exhibit a pretty consistent pattern. The wetting characteristics of fractures demonstrate significant stress sensitivity when subjected to true triaxial circumstances. The inclination angle has a considerable impact on the anisotropic wetting properties, with the most noticeable effect being the increase of volume. At the beginning of applying stress, the intact model experiences a rapid increase in stress and strain. This leads to the closure and compression of the coal, caused by the rise in pore pressure within the fracture due to water infiltration. Once the triaxial stress loading reached a stable state, the stress and strain of the intact model similarly reached a stable state. The residual strength of the material increases when the stress is unloaded, as a result of the fracture being there. This study employs the Mohr-Coulomb and Ubiquitous-Joint constitutive models to simulate the intact and fractured states of coal masses. However, these models may not fully capture the complex behavior of coal matter under actual geological conditions, as the real-world behavior of rock materials is typically more intricate. Additionally, our numerical simulations are predicated on the assumption of a uniform fracture distribution, whereas fractures are often irregularly dispersed in natural settings. Such irregularity could significantly impact the actual representation of wetting pathways. Despite our efforts to explore the relationship between wetting pathways and fracture distribution through statistical analysis, it must be acknowledged that this analysis does not encompass all factors that could affect fluid flow, such as the discontinuity and complexity of fractures. Therefore, while our research provides some useful preliminary insights, the universality and accuracy of our findings still require further validation under more complex and realistic geological conditions.   6 Conclusions This research uses a combination of laboratory experiments and numerical simulations to explore the fracture geometry and connectivity analysis during the hydraulic wetting process in coal. The study emphasizes the importance of accurate fracture data in evaluating the extent and effects of wetting. This research underscores the significance of fracture precision in assessing wetting impacts by integrating random fracture data. The study employs a novel methodology that integrates laboratory tests and computational simulations, introducing an anisotropy coefficient to analyze the influence of fracture data on hydraulic wetting comprehensively. However, the study has some limitations. For example, the statistical analysis may not cover all factors influencing fluid flow, such as fracture discontinuities and complexities. Additionally, differences between experimental conditions and actual geological conditions and the choice of constitutive model could affect the practical applicability of the research outcomes. The importance of integrating numerous randomly generated fractures into a three-dimensional finite difference program is emphasized for conducting accurate fluid–solid coupling analysis and exploring various visualization research methods. The proposed comprehensive experimental and simulation method opens up a new approach for assessing the hydraulic wetting effects in coal seams in future research efforts.(1) The numerical simulation of coal wetting accurately replicates the key principles observed in laboratory-scale triaxial water injection wetting studies, using a model that represents an intact and continuous coal model.  (2) In true triaxial conditions, a mere elevation in injection pressure will significantly broaden the wetting range. In contrast, a single increase in injection time will affect the pre-injection period. However, as time continues to expand, all values will eventually approach a point of inflection, resulting in no substantial additional expansion of the wetness range.  (3) The wetting range of the intact model is concentrated around the borehole and spreads evenly and symmetrically in all directions until it reaches the wetting range limit for the given injection pressure. Conversely, the intact model samples are infused with water using identical conditions, and this procedure is no longer exclusively reliant on the injection pressure. This is attributed to the existence of an inherent fluid conduit. The fluid undergoes rapid expansion towards the fracture, resulting in the creation of a wetting expansion that is centered on the fracture. This expansion can interconnect several wetting regions within the fracture. It can optimize the efficiency of water injection by increasing the process of wetting in the areas with a high concentration of fractures during operation.
1 Introduction Lakes are sentinels of the Earth and are sensitive to climate change with responses such as ice cover, water temperature, evaporation, water storage, and mixing regime (Adrian et al., 2009; Li et al., 2021; Woolway et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2024 ). Among these indicators, water temperature in lakes holds a pivotal role in the field of physical limnology (Piccolroaz et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2020 ). It provides essential insights into the intricate mechanisms governing biological, chemical, and ecological processes and is a significant determinant of water quality (Yang et al. 2018 ). Lake Balaton, as the largest freshwater lake in Central Europe, occupies a critical position in Hungary, with far-reaching implications for biodiversity, the economy, and the thriving recreation industry (G.-Tóth et al. 2011 ). Despite its significance, water temperature in Lake Balaton has often been overlooked, even as it registers a substantial increase and experiences ice-free winters in recent years. This underscores the necessity for heightened attention to this parameter, as rising temperatures can exert a profound influence on the lake's food chain structure, nutrient loads (Toffolon et al. 2014 ), and the reproduction of cyanobacteria (Kosten et al. 2012 ). Thus, conducting comprehensive monitoring and in-depth analysis of water temperature stands as a fundamental prerequisite for effective environmental monitoring and the preservation of ecological integrity. Long-term temperature data have been collected for Lake Balaton using in-situ methods. These records are valuable for continuous monitoring of the hydrological environment but are limited by their spatial coverage and temporal frequency, e.g., a limited number of points at a fortnightly frequency. Field sampling is also easily affected by windy or cold weather. Currently, the only large-scale and continuous monitoring method is spaceborne remote sensing, such as NOAA Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR), NASA Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), ESA Sentinel-3, Landsat, etc. The MODIS onboard Terra satellite (with passing at about 10:30 local time) was launched in 1999, providing a global daily land surface temperature (LST) product at 1 km resolution. Its land surface temperature measurements have an accuracy of better than 1 °C between − 10 to 50 °C (Wan et al. 2004 ), which have been validated in water bodies around the world such as lakes on Tibetan Plateau (RMSE<1 °C at night and < 2 °C in the daytime) (Lazhu et al., 2022 ), Lake Taihu (RMSE 1.2–1.8 °C) (Liu et al. 2015 ). It has also been used to generate large-scale continuous land surface water temperature products (Du et al. 2020, Yu et al. 2022 ). Although AVHRR also has a daily coverage and been used for large European lakes (Lieberherr and Wunderle 2018, Politi et al. 2012 ), it has a low spatial resolution 4 km while the average width of Lake Balaton is only 7.6 km. While Sentinel-3 temperature data has a similar resolution as MODIS and revisit time less than 2 days, it was launched in 2016, which is not ideal for decade studies. With its daily frequency, over two-decade continuous observations, and a spatial resolution 1 km, MODIS is an ideal source for analysing spatiotemporal characteristic of Lake Balaton. In addition to MODIS, Landsat offers a valuable advantage with its high 30-meter resolution, making it well-suited for localized analysis despite its nearly half-month revisit time for early images. The temperature of lake water is influenced by a multitude of factors, encompassing both human activities and natural elements. Various studies have investigated the drivers of temperature changes among different lakes, revealing that air temperature and solar radiation are primary factors, followed by surface pressure and wind speed on the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau (Yang et al. 2020, Yang et al. 2019 ). In contrast, lakes on the Tibetan Plateau are more susceptible to variations in air temperature and recharging sources such as precipitation, glacier melt, and permafrost degradation (Wan et al. 2017, Wan et al. 2018 ). A global perspective emphasizes the significance of air temperature and lake morphology in modelling and predicting water temperature (Piccolroaz et al. 2018, Toffolon et al. 2014 ), as well as long- and short-wave radiation, humidity, and wind speed (Huang et al. 2023, Tong et al. 2023 ). Concentrating on Eurasian lakes which include Lake Balaton, one study noted that shallow lakes respond more rapidly to solar and atmospheric influences than larger, deeper lakes (Du et al. 2020 ). Remarkably, despite the noticeable warming trends in Lake Balaton's temperature, there has been a dearth of dedicated research into this phenomenon, even as the local population residing in its vicinity grows increasingly concerned about the persisting absence of ice cover on the lake. Furthermore, comprehensive investigations into temperature variations across different segments of a single lake are scarce. As a substantial water body extending approximately 80 km from the southwest to the northeast, Lake Balaton exhibits a range of dynamics, including variations in water depth, localized wind speeds, distinct water inflow sources, and a complex mosaic of landcover influenced by anthropogenic activities near its coastline (Petrovszki et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2024 ). While various climate factors have been investigated for long-term analysis, the near-coast disparities in water temperature, attributed to these multifaceted impact factors, have remained largely unexplored thus far. In this study, we first estimate the efficiency of MODIS temperature products by estimating its accuracy with in-situ matchups. Then the inter- and intra-annual characteristics of water temperature in Lake Balaton are examined. Finally, the spatiotemporal variations and impact factors between different parts of the lake are investigated. The Google Earth Engine (GEE) is a planetary-scale geospatial data processing, analysis, and sharing platform (Gorelick et al. 2017 ), which provided user-friendly interface for various applications (Li et al., 2019, 2021; Murray et al., 2019; Pekel et al., 2016 ). To explore the spatiotemporal patterns of water temperature and promote public access of the data and results, GEE is used in this study as the tool for data processing, sharing, and visualization. This study can help to the understand the spatiotemporal features on the long-term trends and impact factors on variations between different parts of the lake, thereby supporting better management and conservation of this important natural resources.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area Lake Balaton is a shallow (mean depth 3 m) and large (597 km2 ) freshwater lake in Central Europe. The size of the lake is mainly due to its length (78 km), which extends over a wide variety of basement rocks and sediments (Cserny and Nagy-Bodor 2000, Kassai and Sisák 2018). Fig. 1   shows the general information of Lake Balaton, with the boundary derived with geodetic data and lake bathymetry measured by boat, both provided by the Hungarian General Directorate of Water Management. Lake Balaton is traditionally divided into 4 basins: from the westernmost, Keszhely (I), Szigliget (II), Szemes (III), to the easternmost, Siofok (IV). Stations Tihany and Balatonfüzfő are in the basin IV, which are referred to as IV-1 and IV-2 respectively. Due to the continuous northwest (NW) wind over the shallow water throughout the year, Lake Balaton is a well-mixed polymictic lake and has no stable thermal stratification during most time of the year. It was hypereutrophic as a result of heavy anthropogenic activities such as population growth, agricultural fertilization, sewage discharge, which, however, have been greatly improved due to several water management measures since the 1990 s (Hatvani et al. 2020 ). Lake Balaton is one of the main water sources for domestic use around the lake, among the karstic water, wells, and springs. The biologically treated effluents from the lakeside communities are transferred away from the catchment to the Danube. The four basins have different local hydrological characteristics. From the westernmost to the easternmost, the yearly mean Coloured dissolved organic matter (CDOM) reduced gradually from 16.6 to 3.9 mg/L, while chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) from 15.4 to 5.3 µg/L because of the main inflow of River Zala, which contributes about 50 % and 35–40 % of total water and nutrient input to the whole lake respectively (Istvánovics et al. 2007 ).Basin I is the shallowest part (about 1 m shallower than the average). Basins II and III are both nearly 1 m deeper than basin I. Basin II receives approximately 30–40 % of the lake's inflow. The deepest basin IV is 1.3 m deeper and 10 times water volume than the shallowest part (basin I). Each basin has been routinely measured fortnightly since 2001 along the centreline, which are considered to represent typical lake characteristics in these areas, indicated by red dots. The Tihany peninsula forms a ∼ 1 km narrow waterway, dividing basins III and IV. The deepest point of the lake is near this peninsula reaches a depth of −10.9 m.  2.2 In-situ, satellite, and reanalysis datasets Table 1   presents a comprehensive listing of datasets utilized in this study, encompassing in-situ samplings, satellite records, and reanalysis products, covering the study period from 2001 to 2022. In-situ measurements for water temperature are taken by boat every two weeks, mostly during ice-free periods and mild days. Six stations are visited, from the westernmost part of the lake at the outlet of the Zala River (Zala station) to IV-2 at the easternmost part of the lake (Fig. 1 ). The sampling time is between 8:30 and 11:30 in the morning, starting from the eastern stations to the westernmost stations. It should be noted that each in-situ record is the mean temperature of the whole water column, i.e., the mean water temperature from 7 different depth measurements, including 0 m (water surface), 0.5 m, 1 m, 1.5 m, 2.0 m, 2.5 m, and 3 m. To ensure unbiased intra-annual comparisons between basins, only dates for which each station has data are selected for analysis. Wind speed data for each basin was sampled on the same day by the Hungarian Water Authorities. Surface wate temperature and land cover data are derived from satellite products. With daily coverage of the entire globe since 2000, MODIS-based temperature products are an ideal data source for estimating trends and spatial variations in water temperature across the lake. To check the accuracy of the daily and 8-day satellite products, the Terra MOD11A1 V6.1 daily product (MOD-1d for short) and MOD11A2.061 8-Day Global 1 km (MOD-8d) are used. MOD-8d is the mosaic of MOD-1d to provide a cloud-free, user-ready image with eight daily images. Both datasets provide global 1 km land surface temperature (LST) with a quality flag band including quality information such as pixel quality due to cloud and other reasons (such as ocean pixel, poor input data), emissivity error, LST error, etc (Wan 1999 ). Only high-quality pixels are retained according to the quality band. For inter-annual long-term spatiotemporal trends, the MODIS-8d is used to ensure a high accuracy, while for intra-annual analysis, which requires more data for statistics, MOD-1d is used. For investigating the detailed difference caused by land cover, surface temperature derived with Landsat 8 based on GEE which has an accuracy around 1 °C is used (Ermida et al. 2020 ). Validation against in-situ data on the same day for Lake Balaton reveals a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 2.75 °C for Landsat-based water temperature (Fig. S7 ). Land cover data in 2018 is derived from multiple satellite imagery from the years 2017 and 2018 including Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8 by European Environment Agency (EEA), which include five main land cover: artificial surfaces, agriculture, forests and seminatural areas, wetlands, and water (Büttner et al. 2021 ). For monthly air temperature at 2 m above the Earth’s surface, the ERA5-Land dataset derived from ECMWF ERA5 climate reanalysis is used, which combines model data with observations from across the world into a globally complete and consistent dataset using the laws of physics (Muñoz Sabater 2023 ).  2.3 Matchups preparation Based on the GEE, the matchups between in-situ and MODIS temperature measurements on daily and 8-day scales are generated. The matchups of daily, i.e., MOD-1d, is on the same day within ± 2 h, while for 8-day, i.e., MOD-8d, is within eight days. The Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) are used to validate the relationship between the satellite water temperature and the in-situ measurements. There are two kinds of outliers, one is from mixed pixels and the other is the satellite-based temperature product. To avoid outliers from mixed pixels of the coastline which include both land and lake water due to the 1 km resolution, the MODIS-based water temperature is collected within the 1.5 km inward buffer of the lake boundary. For the same reason, the temperature of Zala station is not derived from MODIS because the Zala river is too narrow to obtain a pure water temperature value. In addition, there are outliers from the LST temperature product itself that needs to be preprocessed. Since the temperature difference values of the matchups are normally distributed, then the points with more than three standard deviations (Std) from the mean can be regarded as outliers (Pearson 2002 ). However, due to the bias in the estimation of mean and standard deviation caused by the outliers, a more robust method “3σ-Hampel identifier” (Davies and Gather 1993 ) is used in this study, where the mean is replaced by the median, and the standard deviation (Std) is calculated with:(1) Std = 1.4826 ∗ M e d i a n { | x i  - x median   | }      The temperature differences of the matchups are regarded as the array { x i  }   , while x median     is the median of the array. The 1.4826 is chosen for an unbiased estimate of the Std of the Gaussian distribution, the same as (Duan et al. 2019 ). Then once the outliers are identified based on their difference with x median     greater than the threshold 3*Std, they are replaced with x median    .  2.4 Trends and anomaly analysis The inter-annual change of water temperature is examined by linear regression for the annual minimum, mean, maximum, and seasonal mean temperatures. The change rate C m    for the month m   is calculated using Eq. (2) , where T m  k    is the monthly mean temperature for the m   th month in the k   th year, T m - 1  k    is the value for the previous month. The median is taken for each month to avoid the effect of outliers. Then the linear regression is used for the trend analysis.(2) C m  = M e d i a n { 100 ∗ T m  k  - T m - 1  k   T m - 1  k   }       Temperature anomalies are analysed from the spatial distribution of the long-term temporal anomaly. Since the daily temperature difference between different parts of the lake is very subtle and may exceed the uncertainty of the satellite data, a daily cumulative temperature anomaly relative to the mean temperature is used for each month. A temperature anomaly image in each month is calculated to show the temperature difference between different parts of the lake. The pixel-wise monthly accumulated temperature anomaly A m    for the month m  (m ∈ [1, 12]) can be calculated with Eq.3 with d   represents the total number of valid observation days for each pixel in the month, and t m , i     is the water temperature on the i th  day and Mean  m , i     is the mean water temperature of the whole lake within the 1.5 km buffered boundary. Then the number of days in one month n   is multiplied for computing monthly accumulated value in each month, here we set n  = 30 for all months for simplicity.(3) A m  = ∑ i = 1  d  ( t m , i   -  Mean  m , i   )  d  ∗ n       2.5 Multiple linear regression To understand and quantify the relationships between water temperature and the other independent variables in near- coast regions, multiple linear regression analysis is used. Water depth, crucial for littoral ecosystem health, concurrently influences water temperature. Wind speed impacts evaporation, indirectly influencing water temperature. Land cover can also exert impacts on water temperature through thermal runoff, land surface radiation, and humidity change (Luo et al. 2023, Tan et al. 2020 ). Therefore, we choose six variables as input, including wind speed, water depth, and land cover types (i.e., artificial surfaces, agriculture, forests, and wetlands). The workflow is shown in Fig. 2  . First, we generated 2456 data points at 100-meter intervals along the coastline, using the 2018 landcover dataset as a reference. Wind speed data of each coast point is derived based on a piecewise linear relationship between windspeed and longitude established according to the windspeed data. Mean water depth within the 0.2 km radius of the coast points is generated with bathymetry data. For water temperature data, we use the mean mosaic of totally cloud-free Landsat 8 images in July between 2016 and 2020, the hottest month of the year that is better for investigating temperature difference between different parts of the lake. Water areas in each image are extracted using Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI) with a threshold greater than 0. A one-pixel erosion process is then applied to the binary water image to eliminate mixed land–water pixels at the water body's edge, with visual examination ensuring their removal. Then the mean water temperature anomaly is calculated within a 0.2 km radius around the coast points. With water temperature anomaly as the dependent variable y and the others as independent variables X, the multivariate linear analysis is used for impact analysis of different factors on near-coast water temperature. To address the issue of different units of measurement among the independent variables, we standardize each variable with x i  ′  = x i  - M e a n ( x i  )   Std ( x )     , in which x i  ′    is the standardized variable of x i    and subscript i  is the index of the six independent variables. This standardization facilitates the interpretation of coefficients in terms of standard deviations, providing a common ground for comparison.  2.6 GEE for water temperature inspection This study utilizes GEE to provide an intuitive and user-friendly interface for inspecting, analyzing, and sharing water temperature data of Lake Balaton, shown in Fig. 3  . The water temperature of interest can be a user-defined point by clicking, or a region by drawing a polygon on the map. The time series plot is then automatically updated to show the change in water temperature over time, which can be downloaded as an image in png format or as a data file in csv format. The 2018 land cover and 2 m air temperature are also added to the map and left information panel respectively.   3 Results and analysis 3.1 Satellite-based temperature estimation To compare the two datasets, the annual number of samples and their coherence are shown in Fig. 4  . From Fig. 4 a, the number of in-situ data is only about 10 % of the satellite observations and may be biased since the boats usually don’t sample in winter due to cold weather or ice cover (Fig. S6 a). For the five target stations in the lake, excluding the Zala station (see Fig. 1 ) to avoid the mixed pixel effect, there are 609 same-day matchups within ± 2 h between MOD-1d and in-situ measurements, while 1195 matchups within eight days between MOD-8d and in-situ measurements. The statistics of the comparison are shown in Fig. 4 b and c respectively. Fig. 4 b shows the correlation coefficient r is 0.97, RMSE 2 °C, and MAE 1.4 °C, while Fig. 4 c shows the correlation coefficient r is 0.98, RMSE 1.6 °C, and MAE 1.3 °C, both with a very low p-value. The time series of satellite data (Fig. S1  in the supplement file ) show good agreement between the satellite measurements and the sparse in-situ data.  3.2 Inter-annual spatiotemporal variations For inter-annual trends, the statistical characteristics of temperature for the whole lake are examined using MOD-8d, as shown in Fig. 5  . In general, all indicators show an increasing trend since 2001. The annual mean temperature trend is 0.07 °C/year, while the annual minimum temperature trend exhibits a concerning warming trend of 0.21 °C/year, which is three times greater than the annual mean, both are statistically significant at the 99 % confidence level (Fig. 5 a). The 2-meter air temperature has a very similar trend 0.06 °C/year as that of MODIS. For seasonal analysis, there is a similar warming trend 0.07 °C/year for summer and autumn (Fig. 5 b). Winter shows a warming of 0.13 °C/year (at the 99 % confidence level), which is almost double that of summer and autumn. In summary, there is a general warming trend of 0.07 °C/year for the whole Lake Balaton at the beginning of the 21st century, while the low temperatures of each year are more strongly affected, with a warming rate of 0.13 °C/year in winter and 0.21 °C/year for the lowest annual temperature, which are twice and three times above the average, respectively. Basin-scale annual statistical and seasonal trends with MOD-8d (Fig. 6  and Figs. S4-S5 ) show the range of temperature changes during the study period, from minimum to maximum, as well as the seasonal specificities in each basin, helping to understand the extent of temperature fluctuations in different parts of the lake, which is important for studying the overall dynamics and thermal characteristics of Lake Balaton. Fig. 6  a shows the trends of the annual minimum, mean and maximum values of each basin. The annual minimum showed the most significant change, as the annual minimum in the westernmost basin I increased by 0.20 °C/year, while in basins II, III and IV the annual minimum changes were 0.22, 0.23 and 0.21 °C/year, respectively. The mean data showed a smaller increase, as the average annual temperature change in each basin was between 0.07 and 0.08 °C/year. The maximum values showed the least increase, as the annual change observed in each basin was 0.04 °C/year. In Fig. 6 b, the annual changes showed considerable spatial and temporal variability. In the westernmost basin I, there was a small increase in water temperature of 0.0025 °C/year during the spring season, while basins II-IV showed a slight decrease during the spring season. During the summer season, all basins showed an increase, ranging from 0.06 to 0.07 °C/year. In autumn, the outermost basins (basins I and IV) showed a greater increase than the central basins (basins II and III). During winter, all basins exhibit the highest seasonal increase, with a peak 0.15 °C/year in basin I.  3.3 Intra-annual variations between each station For intra-annual analysis, the comparison between six in-situ stations is shown in Fig. 7  . Due to very sparse sampling in winter, stations II/III are not suitable for box plots. The in-situ based temperature showed seasonal and spatial variability, with different parts of the lake showing different patterns of change. The westernmost station, Zala, has the lowest temperature in all seasons except spring. The temperature differences between Zala and the average of the other stations range from 0.9 to 1.9 °C cooler, except in spring, when it is 1.8 °C warmer than the average of the other parts of the lake. Following Zala, station I also has a 0.8 °C higher temperature in spring. Station III is 0.2–0.5 °C warmer in spring and summer than the eastern part. Correspondingly, the eastern part, i.e., the stations IV-1/2, has a ∼ 0.4 °C higher temperature in autumn and winter. The boxplot of the satellite-based temperature for the five stations of Lake Balaton (Fig. S2 ) is consistent with the in-situ data, except that autumn is 2 °C lower. This is because most of the boat samples are taken in a warmer September and October (Fig. S6  b), which leads to a 2 °C higher temperature bias for the in-situ observations in autumn. For observations in the other seasons, the satellite data shows similar quantile values as in-situ measurements within 1.0 °C, despite its substantial error (RMSE=1.6, see Fig. 4 ). To show the detailed spatial variability and statistical coherence with in-situ measurements, seasonal boxplots of water temperature along the centerline from west to east are also inspected (Fig. S3 ). There is a good statistical seasonal consistency between the two datasets. The intra-annual temperature change rate of each month compared to the previous month for each station with both in-situ and satellite data is calculated with Eq. (2)  in Section 2.4 , shown in Fig. 8  . In general, the water begins to warm rapidly from February to June, reaches a steady maximum temperature in July and August, and then undergoes a continuous and gradual cooling process until January of the following year (Fig. 8 ). The strongest warming occurs in March, with the Zala station showing the highest change rate of 179 % compared to February. In general, the western parts, including Zala and station I, warm first in February and March. Station Zala shows a slightly higher cooling rate since August. Both the in-situ and satellite measurements show the temporal asynchrony and spatial variations of water temperature in the lake.  3.4 Spatiotemporal variations of the entire lake To investigate how temperature changes among different parts of the lake over time, the spatial variations in different months and the seasonal relationship between water depth and temperature are investigated. The detailed spatial variation of the whole lake can be inspected with satellite observations. Fig. 9   shows the daily cumulative temperature anomaly distribution in each month based on Eq. (3) . The shallowest parts, Basin I and the northern parts (see the bathymetry in Fig. 1 ) have the highest cumulated temperature throughout the year except in October, November, and December. Basin III has a higher temperature than basins II and IV in July. From October to December, basins III and IV have a higher cumulative water temperature than basins I and II. The patterns have become different since January, when the shallower parts become warmer as the weather begins to warm up. It can be noted that basin II remains cooler than the other parts from May to December, even though its depth is similar as basin III and even shallower than basin IV. Throughout the year, a noticeable “cold window” is at the northern coast of basin II, which is conspicuous along the whole northern coast. Several inflows within the depicted “window” (refer to Fig. 1 ) originate from wells and springs, which have a temperature approximately 5 °C lower from June to August based on in-situ measurements. Fig. 10   shows the relationship between water depth and seasonal mean water temperature for the whole lake (Fig. 10 a) and their spatial overlay along the centerline (Fig. 10 b). The warming seasons, i.e., spring and summer, have negative relationships with water depth, while the cooling seasons, including autumn and winter, exhibit positive correlations. Notably, during the transition to warmer weather in spring, shallow water temperatures are found to be approximately 0.62 °C higher when the water depth is reduced by 1 m. Autumn shows a homogeneous temperature regardless of the water depth. During the coolest season winter, the water temperature rises by 0.11 °C for every meter of water depth increase. The seasonal mean water temperature changes along the centreline based on MOD-1d (extracted from Fig. S3 ) are overlaid with water depth, shown in Fig. 10 b. The temperature variance among the basins is limited to within 1 °C, yet it exhibits substantial fluctuations. In general, basin I, the westernmost basin, has the highest water temperature in all seasons except autumn, while basin II has a decreasing temperature from west to east, reaching a lake-wide low temperature in all seasons, followed by an increase in basin III. Basin III has a weak peak near ∼ 35 km, then a valley temperature between 40–45 km from the west for all seasons, where is also the deepest part of basins I-III. Basin IV is the deepest part of the whole lake and has a lower temperature than basins I and III, except in autumn. In particular, the valley temperature shown in basin II, which is not the deepest, shows a stable low temperature compared to the other basins, supporting the “cold window” phenomenon shown in Fig. 9 .  3.5 Impact analysis on near-coast regions Based on the multivariate linear regression introduced in Section 2.5 , the relationship between near-coast water temperature change and the driving factors are inspected with coefficients, standard deviations of the coefficients, and p-values, shown in Table 2  . The result reveals water depth, wind speed, artificial surfaces, agriculture, and wetlands are statistically significant factors on the variations of near-coast surface water temperature. Among these, wind speed has the strongest negative effect, followed by water depth, wetlands, and agriculture. Notably, artificial surface exerts the only and strong positive influence on water temperature. During summer, impermeable artificial surfaces can create urban heat island effect, which in turn affects water temperatures in their vicinity. Forest is not a statistically significant factor.   4 Discussions 4.1 Satellite insights compared to in-situ data While MODIS data for Lake Balaton may have uncertainties up to 1.6 °C, attributed to factors like sensor issues, cloud interference, atmospheric corrections, and geographical variations, Section 3  demonstrates strong agreement with in-situ measurements in terms of statistical indicators. Seasonal percentile differences remain within 1 °C. Meanwhile, MODIS data outperform in-situ measurements in terms of both spatial and temporal coverage, effectively capturing lake-wide spatial patterns that may be missed by sparse in-situ data. During the same time frame and at the same sampling locations, 364 in-situ data points were collected, whereas MODIS provides a substantial 943 records (+172 %) (Fig. S1 ). While satellite-based water temperature measurements may be less precise due to noise sources, they offer the advantage of continuous, long-term observations, resulting in a substantial data volume and robust statistical outcomes. In-situ measurements excel in precision, and the extensive satellite data compensates for accuracy limitations. Consistent, continuous observations on the same subject, leading to substantial data accumulation, still yield highly reliable statistical results. At present, there are several factors that hinder the use of satellite-derived water temperature in limnological and ecological studies. The first factor is the tradeoff between spatial resolution and temporal coverage. If a water body is too narrow or small, the satellite would have a bias because the pixel would be mixed with the land signals, which should be treated before use. The coastal pixels have greater uncertainties for the same reason. In addition, only surface water (∼5 cm) can be measured. However, it should also be noted that the in-situ temperature measurements can be biased due to different types of sensors, inconsistent methods used, such as measuring only the surface or the whole water column, and the preference for sampling during warm and good weather. Due to the sparse in-situ measurements, they should be used with caution for long-term and large-scale studies. Lack of data integrity can lead to biased estimates. For example, the observations in autumn, mainly in a warmer September and October (Fig. S6 ), would lead to an overestimation of 2 °C for the whole season, comparing the autumn temperature between Fig. 3  (in-situ) and Fig. S2  (satellite). Although there are models that can construct a seamless spatial distribution of surface water temperature based on limited field measurements or reanalysis data (Fiechter et al. 2018, Liu et al. 2020 ), the direct and objective observations from satellites are still valuable and irreplaceable. However, their seamless coverage, high temporal frequency, and long-term continuous observations over the Earth’s surface make them an ideal data source to complement labour-intensive, costly, and sparse field sampling. A continuous water temperature can be used for ecological models such as fish habitat distribution (Antonetti et al. 2023 ) or aquatic invasive species forecast (Walsh et al. 2020 ). The assimilation of satellite and in-situ measurements may be a promising way to obtain highly accurate long-term water temperature with optimal spatiotemporal resolution in the meantime and could improve the performance of the ecological models.  4.2 Impact factors on surface water temperature The water temperature of Lake Balaton has increased by 0.7 °C/decade during the 21st century, which is twice as much as a study showing an increase of 0.34 °C/decade from 1985 to 2009 for global lakes (O'Reilly et al. 2015 ). It is consistent with a study showing that European lakes have experienced an increase of 0.2 to 0.8 °C/decade from 1981 to 2016 (Lieberherr and Wunderle 2018 ), but could reach up to 1.0 °C/decade in Europe during the warm season from 1995 to 2016 (Carrea and Merchant 2019, Woolway et al. 2020 ), although these studies focused on different time periods. Long- and short-wave radiation, humidity, wind speed, and air temperature have been identified as factors contributing to the warming of the lake's water temperature (Huang et al. 2023, Tong et al. 2023 ). The highly consistent trend of a 0.6 °C/decade increase in the 2-meter air temperature further solidifies the understanding that global warming persists as the primary driver behind these inter-annual trends in Lake Balaton. The difference in temperature between the Zala station, which is on the Zala river, and the lake can be explained from the perspectives of water volume and wind force. Since the depth and width of the water is usually much smaller in the river than in the lake, the water in the river would be more easily influenced by the environment, such as sunlight. This can lead to the faster warming of the river water in the cold spring. Meanwhile, the larger volume of lake water would absorb more energy from the continuous sunlight, so the lake water would be warmer than that in the river water. In addition, the mixing of water in the lake due to strong winds in the summer also causes the whole body of water to heat up more during the season than the relatively still river water. The cumulative temperature anomalies between different parts of the lake show a significantly higher temperature over the littoral zones, mainly due to the lower water depth during spring and summer. This is consistent with previous studies showing that the shallower lakes or parts of lakes are more easily affected by the atmospheric conditions (Toffolon et al. 2014 ). The cumulative temperature difference between basins in each month can be explained both from the seasonal change in solar radiation and air temperature and from the water depth perspective. Obviously for the shallowest basin I, it has a higher temperature throughout the year, except during the cooling months from October to January, when both the solar radiation and air temperature at their lowest, it has a lower or similar temperature than the other basins. Basin IV, which is the deepest part, is cooler in the warming seasons while higher temperature from October to December spanning from autumn to winter. The only exception is Basin II, which has a lower water depth and volume, but remains cooler than Basin III and IV in summer. This may be explained by the continuous cold inflows sourced from wells and springs into the basin from the northern coast. The “cold window” in basin II along the whole northern coast further supports this assumption. Water depth exhibits a strong negative correlation with mean water temperature during spring and summer, and a positive correlation during autumn and winter. Under the assumption of homogeneity in air temperature and solar radiation across the entire lake on the same period, it becomes evident that windspeed, water depth, and artificial surfaces are the primary impact factors behind variations in near-coast water temperature among different areas of the lake. Windspeed and water depth have cooling effects by regulating the mixing regime of the lake, strengthening transpiration, and retaining heat more effectively, while the artificial surface has a warming effect due to the heat island effect caused by the impervious surfaces. The agriculture and wetlands also have a cooling effect through evapotranspiration.   5 Conclusions In this study, we explored the spatiotemporal dynamics of Lake Balaton’s water temperature and its influencing factors for near-coast water, utilizing the Google Earth Engine platform. Despite a 1.6 °C uncertainty in MODIS temperature data, daily records since 2001 facilitated a robust, long-term analysis, revealing alignment with air temperature trends. The entire lake exhibits a warming trend of 0.07 °C/year, with higher increases in annual low temperatures at 0.21 °C/year. The intra-annual analysis is based on both in-situ and satellite data at each station, unveiling spatial and temporal variations among rivers and basins. Notably, the shallower western part exhibits faster warming in spring and a slightly quicker cooling rate in autumn compared to the eastern part of the lake. The pixel-scale visualization and statistical analysis emphasize the key role of bathymetry in driving spatiotemporal water temperature fluctuations within the lake. Impact analysis shows that windspeed, water depth, and artificial surfaces play influential roles on the near-coast water temperature. We have created a user-friendly GEE interface for sharing data and visualizing temperature changes, aiding knowledge dissemination and future climate and ecological studies. Our future research will further explore the attribution of different climate factors (radiation, humidity, air temperature, etc.) to the long-term change and expand to include more water bodies across a larger area with higher spatiotemporal resolution.
1 Introduction The number of people living in cities will increase from about 55.3 % in 2018 to 68.4 % in 2050; this represents an addition to urban environments of close to 2.5 billion people (Angel et al., 2011; United Nations, 2019 ). As cities expand, large swaths of agricultural and natural land are converted to urban and suburban uses, and in some cases expansion rates of cities can be as much as twice their demographic growth (Angel et al., 2011 ). Urban, suburban, and industrial/commercial expansion (called ‘urbanisation’ or ‘urban expansion’ from here on) includes the addition of buildings, roads, sidewalks, parking lots, and other impervious surfaces to the landscape. Studies have consistently shown that imperviousness increases storm runoff and peak discharge and shortens lag time (Arnold and Gibbons, 1996; Jacobson, 2011; Sohn et al., 2020; Wagner et al., 2016 ). Urban expansion and increased imperviousness therefore have a direct impact on runoff dynamics and flood risk for a given storm. In addition to increasing runoff, building in the flood plain exposes more people and infrastructure to floods (Nguyen et al., 2021 ), so imperviousness is both a cause and a victim of floods. López-Martínez et al. (2017)  indicate that exposure to flooding increased by more than 250 % along the Spanish Mediterranean coast due to a lack of spatial planning. Similarly, Barredo et al. (2012)  attribute the increased cost of flood damage insurance claims between 1971 and 2008 in Spain to a substantial increase in exposure. Land use changes in potential flood zones is recognized as a major factor in flood risk, superior even to climate change (Winter and Karvonen, 2022 ). One method of estimating changes in imperviousness is through its direct impact on runoff (Alley and Veenhuis, 1983; Boyd et al., 1993; Ebrahimian et al., 2016 ), but remote sensing and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) techniques have become the most frequently-used approach for measuring total impervious area (Jacobson, 2011 ). These estimations, however, are not faultless as concrete or asphalt and bedrock or bare soils can be confused. In addition, shade effects from buildings and tree canopies in urban environments can mask impervious surfaces or create further confusion between categories (Myeong et al., 2001; Wu and Murray, 2003; Yang and Li, 2015 ). One way of dealing with this is by combining a GIS vector building footprint layer with very high spatial resolution (≤50 cm) aerial photographs to quantify imperviousness (Fox et al., 2019 ). The combination of urbanisation and climate change contribute to greater peak discharges (Ahiablame et al., 2017 ) and more frequent large floods in Europe (Kundzewicz et al., 2013 ) that are expected to increase flood damage in future (Feyen et al., 2012 ). The frequency of extreme events, and to a lesser degree, the magnitude of these events, is expected to increase for most regions of the world in the coming decades (Papalexiou and Montanari, 2019 ). The predicted impacts of climate change vary according to the time-step at which rainfall events are analysed, and more particularly on the presence of skewness in the distribution of extreme events, which is greater at shorter (hourly) time-steps than daily values (De Luca et al., 2024 ). As rainfall distributions evolve with climate change, historical statistics of return periods lose in accuracy (Vautard et al., 2015 ), and land use planning legislation, defined by historical events or hydraulic modeling of empirical rainfall return periods, is increasingly disconnected from actual flood risk (López-Martínez et al., 2017 ). Vautard et al. (2015)  observed a 30 % increase in daily autumn rainfall maxima in southern France since the middle of the 20th century; this corresponds to a 4 % per decade increase between 1950 and 2014. The authors attribute this trend to increasing fall temperatures that drive greater atmospheric moisture contents as September temperatures are reported to be 1.1°C warmer in 2014 than in 1950; this corresponds to a warming trend that is 50 % faster than global mean temperatures. They also note that the probability of experiencing the most extreme event of the times series (which occurred in 2014) has tripled since 1950. Others have also observed increases in mean rainfall intensity, more frequent events exceeding 200 m day−1 , and greater areas affected by high intensity rainfall events between 1961 and 2015 (Ribes et al., 2019 ). In France, municipal flood risk planning legislation was first introduced in 1982 for insurance reasons, and it incited municipal councils to integrate risk exposure maps in their planning documents. Official Risk Prevention Planning (PPR) documents became compulsory for all French municipalities starting in 1995, but it took most municipalities years to implement the new rules. A more global approach was introduced in the National Flood Risk Management Strategy (SNGRI) in 2014 which attempts to combine a regional approach with local considerations. These rules take into account both potential runoff storage applications and imperviousness thresholds. Coastal urbanization in the Mediterranean region continues to progress despite legislation to limit development (Prévost and Robert, 2016; Smiraglia et al., 2023 ). Building in the alluvial plain presents several advantages: the terrain is flat and usually well-connected to the main road network, and laying electrical lines, communication lines, and drinking and wastewater pipes is cheaper and faster in non-cohesive alluvial soils than in bedrock. The south of France has experienced unprecedented catastrophic flood events in recent decades with dozens of fatalities and billions of euros in damage. The Alpes-Maritimes department alone, located in SE France, has experienced two devastating storms in the past decade with close to 40 cumulated fatalities and hundreds of millions of euros in damage. Like elsewhere, the severity of these events is sometimes attributed to poor urban planning and sometimes to climate change. The objective of this study is to analyse the impacts of urbanisation over 3 decades (1988/90–2020) on peak discharge and on flood exposure for rainfall events of different magnitudes in SE France. The study can be broken down into 3 sub-objectives: 1) to quantify historical changes in urbanisation, 2) to model the impacts of urbanisation on peak discharge, and 3) to model the impacts of urbanisation on flooded area and buildings affected. The study uses innovate methods to measure imperviousness based on building footprint layers and to quantify exposure based on the footprint area of buildings within the flooded zones.  2 Methods The 3 study catchments are located in SE France. For each catchment, analysis was carried out in 3 steps corresponding to the sub-objectives defined above. Urbanisation rates were calculated from the building footprint layer, hydrologic modeling was performed using HEC-HMS, and hydraulic modeling was done using HEC-RAS. 2.1 Site description The study catchments (Brague, Frayère and Mourachonne) are located near the cities of Antibes and Cannes in SE France ( Fig. 1 a). The Brague river (65.5 km²) flows directly into the Mediterranean Sea whereas the Frayère and Mourachonne are tributaries of the Siagne. These two catchments (about 43 km²) are therefore located further inland and have slightly steeper slopes and higher mean altitudes in the upper reaches ( Table 1 ). For these catchments, steep slopes limit suburban expansion northwards, and potential flood plains are more restricted than for the Brague which has lower, flatter terrain near the outlet. The catchments are located in a region of high potential employment. Tourism along the Mediterranean coast is the major source of revenue in the department, and the catchments include the high-tech business park of Sophia Antipolis and an internationally recognized perfume industry centered around the city of Grasse. Finally, the region is also known for its high number of secondary residential homes, so urban pressure is high. The Brague catchment experienced a catastrophic flood in October 2015 when new rainfall intensity records were set with 2-hour maxima of about 150–175 mm; the estimated return period was greater than 100 years for the 1-hour and 2-hour rainfall intensities (Préfecture des Alpes-Maritimes, 2016 ).  2.2 Quantifying urbanization rates Urbanization was quantified using 4 indicators: number of buildings, building footprint area, built area (area within a 100 m buffer around a building), and percentage imperviousness. The vector layer with building footprint polygons for each catchment was extracted from the BD-TOPO© national database. Working backwards in time, the 2020 building layer was successively overlain on ortho-rectified aerial photographs for 2014, 1999, 1990 (Brague) and 1988 (Frayère and Mourachonne). Spatial resolution for 1988/1990 and 1999 air photos was 50 cm; for 2014 and 2020 it was 20 cm. Buildings that were not present in a given year were deleted from the layer. Buildings that were present but had been destroyed in successive time intervals were hand-digitized. Since the intervals between dates were not constant, all growth rates were normalized to decadal values. For example, the number of new buildings between 2014 and 2020 was divided by 6 and multiplied by 10. Similarly, the total interval for the Brague was 30 years, and for the Frayère and Mourachonne it was 32 years, so beginning-to-end comparisons were corrected to a 30-year equivalent time frame for the latter catchments. Absolute growth rates were also normalized for an equivalent catchment area of 50 km², an approximate intermediate surface area between Frayère/Mourachonne and Brague.  2.3 Hydrological modeling of river discharge The Hydrologic Engineering Center Hydrological Modeling System (HEC-HMS) was used to model storm discharge for theoretical 12-hr rainfall events of 3 magnitudes: 80 mm, 140 mm, and 200 mm. Rainfall magnitude, duration and distribution were defined subjectively in order to produce events that were likely to generate moderate, large and extreme floods. The theoretical rainfall events used in this study were designed with a double-triangle shaped distribution (Benabdesselam and Hammar, 2009 ) so that 60 % of the rainfall was concentred in the center third of the hyetograph and 20 % before and after, respectively. The estimated 12-hour return period for 80 mm in the Brague is about 5 years, and for the 140 mm event it is about 75 years (Cabinet Merlin Ingénieurs Conseils, 2017 ). The return period for the 200 mm event is unknown but is probably in the order of about 300–400 years. Only peak discharge (Qpeak ) at the outlet was retained for comparison between events, catchments and years as it can be most easily related to flood risk. HEC-HMS simulates a wide range of hydrologic processes. Based on a 5 m DEM obtained from the National Institute for Geographic information (IGN), the model subdivides the catchment into subbasins according to topographic divides. The number of subbasins must be selected by the user, and 4 subbasins were retained for the Mourachonne and 5 for the Frayère and Brague, respectively (Fig. 1 b). Model options for the simulations included the following: SCS-CN and Imperviousness for Loss, SCS Unit Hydrograph for Subbasin transform, Muskingum for Reach routing, Specified Hyetograph for Subbasin precipitation, a modeling timestep of 30 minutes, and baseflow. The Curve Number (CN) for normal antecedent soil moisture conditions (CN II), time of concentration, and Muskingum X and K parameters were defined after a calibration and validation step on an event in the Brague catchment. The calibration event occurred 22 Nov., 2019 and had a Qpeak  value of 135 m3  s−1 , the validation event occurred 1 Dec., 2019, with a peak of 96 m3  s−1  ( Fig. 2 ). Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) values for the calibration and validation simulations were 0.96 and 0.92, respectively, so the hydrologic model and parameter values selected below were deemed reliable. The calibrated values were applied to all catchments due to their similar characteristics. A uniform CN value was used for all catchments and years, and the impact of urbanisation on discharge was quantified through changes in imperviousness. Although CN is spatially variable, differences here were considered minor since the only land cover types present in the catchments are urban/suburban and natural with a negligible area in grassland (golf course) located in the lower part of the Brague. In addition, the only land cover change between years is increased urbanisation, so finer mapping of CN outside urban areas would have had no impact on changes in discharge since the contribution of non-urban areas to runoff was constant over time. The CN value was set at 66 after calibration/validation simulations described above. An official report of the 2015 Brague flood indicates that a CN value of between 60 and 70 provided the closest simulated Qpeak  values compared to field-estimated Qpeak  values for the event (Lebouc and Payrastre, 2018 ), so it was deemed reasonable for the catchments Temporal changes in Qpeak  were simulated by changing the imperviousness value in the Loss function of HEC-HMS. It should be noted that this method uses total imperviousness for a subbasin and is less accurate than hydraulically connected imperviousness.
