This, however, is a limitation in the model that could not be modified and will be discussed further in the Discussion. In addition to buildings, imperviousness includes sidewalks, roads, parking lots and other impervious surfaces. These are spatially associated with the presence of buildings, so buffer zones (0–10 m, 10–20 m; 20–30 m and 30–100 m) were created around building polygons and reclassed with observed imperviousness according to values in  Table 2 . Imperviousness was calculated by overlaying random points on the 2020 ortho-rectified aerial photographs and counting the number of points that fell on pervious/impervious surfaces for each buffer zone and catchment. The number of random points per category ranged from 300 for the 0–30 m buffer zones to 600 for the 30–100 m buffer zone; 750 points were used for the zone beyond 100 m from a building. The random point method was done for 2020 and the spatial relationship was considered consistent over time. For each year, the calculated imperviousness layer was inputted into HMS in the format of a 5 m raster layer, and mean total imperviousness was extracted for each subbasin. The time of concentration (Tc ) for the SCS Unit Hydrograph was estimated for each subbasin after testing several formulae during the calibration/validation step. Lag time (TL ) was considered equal to 0.6* Tc  as described in Chow et al. (1988) ; The calibration/validation step showed that the mean of the the Kirpich and Kerby methods provided the best estimate. The Muskingum X and K parameters were also defined during the initial calibration/validation step. at 0.2 and 0.6, respectively. Since the time intervals between years were not constant, the changes in Qpeak  over time were standardized to an equivalent decadal interval: for example, for changes in 1990–1999, the change in Qpeak  was divided by 9 and multiplied by 10. This enabled the direct comparison with urbanisation rates which were also standardized to the same interval. Baseflow was attributed to subbasins closest to the outlet using the Recession method and an initial discharge of 2 m3  s−1  for the Frayère and Mourachonne and of of 3 m3  s−1 , for the Brague. A recession constant of 0.3, and a discharge threshold ranging from 20 to 30 m3  s−1  depending on the subbasin, were applied. In the field, initial discharge depends on a range of factors, so the values were selected to be typical for the catchments. The values were held constant for all rainfall events and years and were small compared to peak discharge (typically less than 3 %). The recession coefficient and discharge threshold values intervene after the peak discharge, so they have no impact on Qpeak  results. In all, 36 simulations were performed: 3 catchments (Brague, Frayère, Mourachonne), 4 years (1988/90, 1999, 2014, 2020), and 3 rainfall events (80 mm, 140 mm, 200 mm / 12 hours).  2.4 Hydraulic modeling of flooding risk The Hydraulic Engineering Center River Analysis System (HEC-RAS) model was used for modeling the flooded area. No flood data were available to calibrate/validate the hydraulic modeling parameters, so reasonable values were selected from the scientific literature and HEC-RAS manual. Hydraulic modeling was carried out using a 1-m DEM obtained from the National Institute for Geographic information (IGN). A 30 m x 30 m mesh was used for most of the catchment, but this was reduced to 3 m x 3 m for channels, riverbanks, flood plains, and in regions defined as break lines (eg. roads, railways, levees…) in order to better simulate flow dynamics. Manning’s roughness coefficient values (Manning’s n) are shown in  Table 3 . Buildings were attributed an extremely high roughness to favor flow around buildings in open areas. Input hydrographs for the hydraulic modeling were obtained from the outputs of the hydrologic model described above. For the Brague, a single input point was selected on the main channel upstream of the flood plain located in the lower part of the catchment (Fig. 2 ). For the Frayère, 4 input hydrographs were selected, and for the Mourachonne, 3 input hydrographs were selected (Fig. 2 ). As for the hydrological modeling, 36 simulations were performed, and 2 outputs were retained for comparison: total area flooded and building footprint area flooded. The flooded area of a building corresponded to the entire building footprint of the impacted building, even though only a portion of the building footprint may actually have intersected with the flooded area.   3 Results The results are presented in order of the 3 sub-objectives defined above: urban expansion rates, change in peak discharge with urbanisation for rainfall events of different magnitude (hydrologic modeling), and changes in flooded area (hydraulic modeling) for each event. 3.1 Urbanisation trends Urbanisation rates are presented firstly according to changes in the number of buildings and building footprint area and secondly according to changes in built area and total imperviousness. 3.1.1 New buildings and building area In 1988/90, the Brague and Mourachonne have a similar number of buildings but the Brague has the greatest footprint area ( Table 4 ). The Frayère has the most buildings but the smallest footprint area. Therefore, the Brague catchment has the largest initial mean building size and the Frayère has the smallest mean building size. In 2020, the Brague is approaching the Frayère in the number of buildings and continues to have the greatest footprint area, so it shows rapid growth over the duration of the study interval. Mean building size in the Brague shrinks slightly from 254.7 m² in 1990–246.8 m² in 2020. Corresponding values for the Frayère and Mourachonne show increases from 132.1 m² to 141.1 m² and 208.0 m² to 216.4 m², respectively. New buildings built between 1988/90 and 2020 had mean footprint areas of 234.7 m², 171.3 m² and 243.7 m² for the Brague, Frayère and Mourachonne, respectively. Standardized growth rates for the number of buildings ( Fig. 3 ) show the fastest growth in the initial time interval with slowing over time for all catchments. Only the Brague maintains a constant rate into the second interval. Growth rates tend to be slightly greater for the Brague and lower for the Mourachonne. This corresponds to a 30-year equivalent increase of 5645, 3129, and 2455 new buildings in the Brague, Frayère and Mourachonne catchments, respectively, or increases of 64.9 %, 27.6 %, and 28.6 % in the number of buildings built between 1988/90 and 2020. Changes in footprint area ( Fig. 4 ) follow similar temporal and spatial patterns as building numbers, but building footprint area grows more slowly than the number of buildings in the Brague (59.1 % over 30 years) and more rapidly for the Frayère and Mourachonne (36.0 % and 33.6 %, respectively). As described above, this corresponds to a change in the mean building footprint where mean area decreases by 3.5 % for the Brague and increases by 6.4 % and 3.9 % for the Frayère and Mourachonne, respectively.  3.1.2 Changes in built area and imperviousness Built area is calculated from building perimeter, so we would expect trends in building footprint area and built area to be more or less identical. However, adding new buildings within the buffer zones of existing buildings (ie. infilling between existing buildings in the built area) will increase the building footprint but not change the built area; hence, building footprint would increase much faster than built area. New buildings built outside the existing built area (ie. expansion) would cause built area to increase at the same relative rate as building footprint area. Therefore, the two numbers, building footprint area and built area, say something different about urban growth and to what extent growth is by infilling or expansion: for mainly infilling, building footprint area increases much faster than total built area, for expansion outside existing built area, built area growth trends are similar to building footprint growth rate. The Brague has the greatest footprint area (Table 4 ) and built area in all years ( Table 5 ). For the Frayère and Mourachonne, building footprint (Table 4 ) and built area (Table 5 ) follow the same patterns in 1988, where building area and built area are greater in Mourachonne than in Frayère, but the order is reversed starting in 1999; from then onwards, built area is greater in Frayère than Mourachonne. This indicates that more new buildings were built outside the perimeter of exiting built area in Frayère than in Mourachonne. The trends described above are confirmed by the building footprint and built area growth rates shown in Fig. 4  and  Fig. 5 , respectively. In Fig. 4 , the Mourachonne building footprint growth rates are equal to or greater than for the Frayère in all time intervals whereas the contrary is true in Fig. 5  where built area grows faster in the Frayère than in the Mourachonne in all time intervals. Over the 30-year equivalent time interval, built area grew more slowly than footprint area at rates of 34.1 %, 14.9 % and 15.8 % for the Brague, Frayère and Mourachonne, respectively (for comparison, rates shown above for building footprint area were 59.1 %, 27.6 %, and 28.6 %), so growth is shared roughly 50/50 between infilling and expansion into previously unbuilt areas. Imperviousness is calculated from building footprint and buffer zones surrounding buildings where imperviousness decreases with distance from building perimeter as described in the Methods (Table 2 ). Changes in imperviousness therefore depend on initial imperviousness values when a new building is constructed: adding a new building next to an existing building where roads and parking lots, for example, are already present nearby increases imperviousness less than building on totally undeveloped land, sothe incremental increase in imperviousness is greater outside existing built area than within existing built area. Changes in imperviousness reflect a complex combination of changes in both new building footprint area and new built area. Temporal changes in imperviousness ( Fig. 6 ) are consistent with changes in building area (Fig. 4 ) and built area (Fig. 5 ) where growth in imperviousness is greatest for the Brague and similar for the Frayère and Mourachonne. Over the equivalent 30-year interval, imperviousness increases by 31.2 %, 20.6 % and 21.1 % for the 3 catchments, respectively.  3.1.3 Summary of urbanisation dynamics  Table 6  shows the ratios of percentage growth rates over the 30-year equivalent study interval. For example, in the Brague, the growth rate in the number of buildings over 30 years was 64.9 % while the growth rate in the building footprint area was 59.1 %: the ratio is therefore 64.9 %/59.1 %, or 1.10 as shown in Table 6 . Growth in the number of buildings in the Brague is slightly greater than growth in building footprint area thereby indicating that buildings tend to get slightly smaller over time. The contrary is true for Frayère and Mourachonne where footprint area grows faster than the number of buildings (values <1.0). The ratio of growth in building footprint to growth in built area (Table 6 ) is slowest for Brague and greatest for Frayère, indicating that of the three catchments, Brague most strongly favours infilling over expansion compared to Frayère and Mourachonne, even though absolute built area growth in ha is greatest in the Brague; hence a greater proportion of the Brague’s new building footprint is built within the perimeter of existing built area. Built area growth rate is only slightly greater than imperviousness growth rate (Table 6 ) in the Brague, and this is consistent with building in areas that are already partially impervious. For the Frayère and Mourachonne, imperviousness grows faster than built area since a greater proportion of the new buildings are built outside existing built area where the incremental increase in imperviousness with each new building is greater.   3.2 Impacts of urbanisation on peak discharge Peak discharge values shown in  Table 7  were not corrected for differences in area between catchments, but discharge ratios between catchments are very close to areal ratios: the Brague’s peak discharge is about 1.5 times the peak of the other catchments and its area is also about 1.5 times greater. Histograms for the simulations are provided in Appendix A. The Brague therefore has the greatest peak discharge every year and for all rainfall magnitudes. For all catchments and events, peak discharge increases over time, which is consistent with the urbanisation trends described above. Spatial evolutions in peak discharge ( Fig. 7 ) follow urbanisation trends: the Brague has the greatest increase in building area (Fig. 4 ), built area (Fig. 5 ) and imperviousness (Fig. 6 ) of the three catchments, and it shows the greatest increase in peak discharge. Temporal changes in peak discharge also closely resemble urbanisation patterns where peak discharge changes become smaller as urbanisation slows over time: for all catchments and rainfall events, the maximum change in peak discharge occurs in the 1988/90–1999 interval and the least change in the 2014–2020 interval. This pattern is true for all three rainfall events. The impact of urbanisation on discharge is not independent of rainfall magnitude As rainfall magnitude increases, the increase in discharge within a time interval increases for all catchments: for the 80-mm rainfall event, the 30-year equivalent increases in discharge are 9.8 m3 /s, 3.8 m3 /s and 3.3 m3 /s for the Brague, Frayère and Mourachonne, respectively. Values for the 140 mm event are 12.8 m3 /s, 4.7 m3 /s and 3.7 m3 /s, and for 200 mm, they are 13.7 m3 /s, 4.7 m3 /s and 4.4 m3 /s, so the absolute increases are systematically smallest for the 80-mm event and greatest for the 200 mm event. Although absolute discharge increases with rainfall magnitude, the relative increase in discharge is inversely proportional to the increase in rainfall magnitude.  Fig. 8  shows the percentage increase in peak discharge for each time interval. The temporal patterns within the catchments remain the same as for absolute change in peak discharge (Fig. 7 ), but the patterns when comparing rainfall magnitude are reversed: absolute change in discharge increases with rainfall magnitude while relative increase in discharge decreases with rainfall magnitude. The percentage increase in peak discharge is always greatest for 80 mm and smallest for 200 mm. For 80 mm, the percentage increase in peak discharge is about 2.2–2.6 times greater than for 140 mm, and it is about 1.3–1.6 times greater for 140 mm than for 200 mm. In addition, these ratios generally decrease over time so differences in peak discharge for the same rainfall event get smaller over time. There are therefore two distinct trends: 1- changes in discharge over time get smaller as urbanisation rates slow, and 2- as rainfall magnitude increases, the relative impact of urbanisation on peak discharge decreases. Overall, for the 80-mm rainfall event, the 30-year equivalent relative increases in discharge are 12.2 %, 6.8 % and 6.1 % for the Brague, Frayère and Mourachonne, respectively. Corresponding values for the 140 mm event are 5.6 %, 3.0 % and 2.4 %, and for 200 mm, they are 3.9 %, 1.9 % and 1.8 %. For comparison, changes in imperviousness at the catchment scale were 31.2 %, 21.6 % and 21.1 % for the Brague, Frayère and Mourachonne, respectively, as described above. Increases in peak discharge are therefore much smaller than corresponding increases in imperviousness.  3.3 Flood risk The flooded area depends on urbanisation-driven changes in Qpeak  described above, floodplain topographic characteristics specific to each catchment, and urbanisation rates within the flooded zone. 3.3.1 Spatial extent of flooded zone for different years and rainfall magnitudes The spatial extent of the flooded zone ( Table 8 ) changes with increases in discharge and local topographic conditions. Flooded area maps with building overlays are provided in Appendix B. As expected from the changes in peak discharge described above, all catchments show an increase in flooded area with increasing rainfall magnitude. The change is greatest for the Brague, which tends to have the smallest flooded area for the 80-mm event and the greatest area for the 140 and 200-mm events, where the flooded area is about 2.5–3 times greater than for the other catchments. Peak discharge values were only about 1.5 times greater for the Brague than for the other catchments, so the change in flooded area is clearly related to local topographic effects. The Brague has the lowest mean and median slope inclinations of the three catchments (Table 1 ) and, more particularly, an extensive flood plain of low slope where the flooded area expands rapidly for relatively small changes in flow depth. Flooded area trends are consistent with the impacts of urbanisation on peak discharge; within each rainfall event, the temporal increase in flooded area ( Fig. 9 ) follows the same patterns as urbanisation trends described above (Figs. 3–6 ). These changes, however, are much greater for the Brague than for the Frayère and Mourachonne. Over the equivalent 30-year study period, the Brague’s flooded area increased by 2.7 ha, 8.7 ha and 5.3 ha for the 80-mm, 140-mm and 200-mm events respectively. Corresponding values for the Frayère and Brague are all less than 1.0 ha and generally less than 0.5 ha regardless of rainfall magnitude or time interval. The relative increase in flooded area over time is shown in  Fig. 10 . Patterns within a rainfall event closely resemble urbanization trends and their impacts on Qpeak . Within each rainfall magnitude, the incremental increase in the extension of the flooded area over time diminishes with successive time intervals as urbanization rates slow. These changes vary with rainfall magnitude. The greatest relative impact is not for the 140-mm event (greatest absolute change) but for the 80-mm event, and values decrease with increasing rainfall magnitude. Since the absolute flooded area is relatively small for the 80-mm event, small changes have a greater impact on relative growth. And since the flooded area is already close to its maximum extent at 140-mm, and even more so at 200-mm, the gains in area over time due to urbanization do not translate into large relative growth rates.  3.3.2 Changes in footprint area in the flooded zone Even if the flooded area had not grown over time, more buildings would have been exposed to flooding as new buildings were added to existing flood plains. The number of new buildings impacted by floods was quantified in this study, but since the overall trends were similar to built area, we retained only the latter in order to avoid redundancy. As expected, flooded building footprint area increased with rainfall intensity within a year and over time. The Mourachonne had the greatest flooded building footprint, followed by the Brague and then the Frayère for the 80-mm event ( Table 9 ). The Brague, however, rapidly surpassed the others as rainfall magnitude increased from 80 to 140 mm and again from 140 to 200 mm. This is consistent with the change in flooded area described above. The greatest absolute change in flooded building footprint area was for the 80 mm to 140 mm transition. Flooded building footprint area ( Fig. 11 ) increased most rapidly in the first interval (1988/90–1999), particularly in the Frayère and Mourachonne. For these catchments, growth rates drop abruptly after 1999. Growth rates in building footprint area in the flood zone are at their lowest after 2014. The Mourachonne even shows a loss of area with the destruction of some large hangars for the 200-mm event in 2014–2020. The 30-year equivalent flooded zone footprint area growth rates are 76.3 %, 47.2 % and 33.4 % in the Brague for the 80-mm, 140-mm and 200-mm events, respectively. Corresponding values in the Frayère are 69.4 %, 62.3 % and 60.7 %, respectively. For the Mourachonne, they are 89.3 %, 43.0 % and 34.6 %, respectively, so growth in the Mourachonne is the greatest for the 80-mm event (buildings close to the channel). For all catchments, the relative growth in footprint area located in the flood zone diminishes with increasing rainfall magnitude. Initial building footprint area values are always lowest close to the channel (80-mm event), so the relative growth is greatest. Flooded building footprint area increases with rainfall magnitude, but the relative increases with each increment in rainfall magnitude diminishes: between 1988/90 and 2020, as rainfall magnitude increases from 80 to 140 mm, the flooded building footprint area increases on average (mean of all years) by 633.4 %, 135.1 % and 277.7 %, for the Brague, Frayère and Mourachonne, respectively. As rainfall changes from 140 mm to 200 mm, the difference is only about 28.5 %, 17.8 % and 22.0 % for the same catchments. Hence, changes in exposure due to urbanisation in the flood zone over time were much greater as rainfall increased from 80 mm to 140 mm than for the 140 mm to 200 mm increment. For comparison, the changes in flooded building footprint area outside the flooded zone are integrated in Fig. 11 . For the non-flooded zone, the values are rough estimates since some slopes are too steep for construction, but the rate of building tends to be greater within the flooded zone than in the rest of the catchment. It is worth noting that the change in flooded building footprint area between 2014 and 2020 is negligible everywhere and for all rainfall events. This will be discussed further in the Discussion.   3.4 Summary of the interactions between urbanisation, hydrology and hydraulics Urbanisation between 1988/90 and 2020 increased Qpeak  by about 6 %-12 % for the 80 mm event depending on the catchment, and the increase diminished with greater rainfall magnitudes to attain about 2 %-4 % for the 200 mm event ( Table 10 ). The change in Qpeak  increased the total area flooded for all catchments and rainfall events. Similarly to Qpeak , the percentage increase in flooded area varied according to both catchment and rainfall event: the greatest increase for all events was for the Brague and the relative increase in area decreased with increasing rainfall magnitude. Changes in peak discharge depend on infiltration/runoff dynamics addressed below in the Discussion section whereas changes in flooded area depend on both peak discharge and local topography. For the Brague catchment, the percentage increase in flooded area is close to or surpasses the corresponding percentage increase in peak discharge (Table 10 ). The gap is greatest for the 80 mm event, where flat slopes close to the river channel allow rapid spreading of flood waters. For the 200 mm event, the percentage increase in flooded area over time is slightly less than the corresponding increase in peak discharge. For the Frayère and Mourachonne, the percentage increase in flooded area is always less than the corresponding increase in peak discharge. In these catchments, altitude increases quickly with distance from the river channels, so flooded area remains more contained than in the Brague. The percentage differences between Qpeak  and flooded area highlighted just above are relatively small, but the percentage differences between total flooded area and building footprint area flooded shown in Table 10  are substantial. On average, the percentage increase in the building footprint flooded is almost 43.4 times greater than the percentage increase in total flooded area; values range from 4.0 times greater for the Brague 80 mm event to 95.1 times greater for the Mourachonne 200 mm event. Contrary to the preceding trends of Qpeak  and flooded area, the ratio of the increase in number of buildings flooded to total flooded area increases with rainfall magnitude. As rainfall depth increases from 80 mm to 200 mm in the Brague, the ratio increases from 4.0 at 80 mm (ie. 76.3/19.1) to 15.5 (ie. 33.4/2.1) at 200 mm. Corresponding increases for the Frayère and Mourachonne are 23.6–94.5 and 49.9–95.1, respectively. Hence, urbanisation rates increased everywhere, but they were slowest nearest the channel and greatest further away. As flood magnitude increases, the number of buildings affected grows disproportionately large with respect to flooded area.   4 Discussion Despite local catchment-scale differences, a number of trends identified in the study can be applied to most areas in the world undergoing rapid urbanisation. 4.1 Urbanisation and rainfall magnitude impacts on discharge Both Qpeak  and flooded area increased with urbanisation for all catchments. The increase in Qpeak  with urbanisation was always less than the corresponding increase in imperviousness. This discrepancy between changes in imperviousness and peak discharge illustrates the distinction between total and effective imperviousness. Effective imperviousness is the share of the total imperviousness that is hydraulically connected to the channel (Alley and Veenhuis, 1983; Boyd et al., 1993; Ebrahimian et al., 2016 ), so our results indicate that a substantial portion of our imperviousness runs off onto pervious surfaces, as would be expected in suburban areas. For the 80-mm event, the 30-year equivalent increase in Qpeak  was about 3 times smaller than the corresponding increase in mean catchment imperviousness, for the 140-mm and 200-mm events, the increase in Qpeak  was about 7 and 10 times smaller, respectively, than the increase in imperviousness. The relative increase in Qpeak  was greatest for the smallest rainfall event (80 mm) and diminished as rainfall magnitude increased. These results are consistent with theoretical expectations. Runoff coefficients increase with rainfall magnitude regardless of land cover type except for sealed surfaces which remain constant (Chow et al., 1988 ). As rainfall magnitude increases, spatial variations in runoff coefficients attributable to land cover type are progressively masked, so urbanisation has less impact on runoff for extreme events. This trend has been demonstrated in other cities around the globe (Braud et al., 2013; Yao et al., 2016; Zope et al., 2016 ) and confirms that the impact of urbanisation on discharge cannot be considered independently of rainfall magnitude. Theoretically, for immensely large rainfall magnitudes, Qpeak  values would converge regardless of the land cover or percentage imperviousness.  4.2 Urbanisation and exposure to flooding Urban expansion can increase exposure to flooding independently of changes in Qpeak  and flooded area since there are more buildings exposed to flooding over time. Urbanisation was generally fastest in the initial time interval of the study (1988/90–1999) and slowed afterwards. This trend is true for all catchments and it surely reflects changes in regional economic and demographic drivers. In addition, more restrictive national risk management legislation was introduced in 1995 and implemented in the years afterwards, so most of the buildings affected by a flood were already built before the legislation was implemented, and the sharp drop in construction in the flood plain between 1988/90–1999 and 1999–2014 is probably due in part to the advent of the new flood risk planning laws. Flood risk planning legislation evolves spatially and over time (Borowska-Stefańska et al., 2021 ), and local urban planning legislation is continuously being updated, so it is impossible to work back through local planning rules for each of the municipalities located in the catchments. Despite protective legislation, building continued in all potential flood zones of the study, and the flooded building results show that the increase in flood risk depends more on greater exposure than on changes in Qpeak . This, too, is consistent with observations of others in the Mediterranean basin and in other regions of the world (Barredo et al., 2012; Flores et al., 2020; López-Martínez et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2021 ), and it is probably typical of most urbanised flood-prone zones globally. There is some flexibility in how urban planning rules are interpreted and implemented locally (Borowska-Stefańska et al., 2021; Winter and Karvonen, 2022 ), and elected officials are torn between economic interests in developing new activities on the one hand and protecting citizens on the other. Urbanisation rates are slowest in the flooded area of the lowest magnitude event (80 mm) where new building growth is lower than for the rest of the catchment, and this suggests that building restrictions are historically greatest in the alluvial plain closest to the channel. Urban planning rules in France do not restrict all types of new buildings in a potential flood zone; urbanisation in areas of very high flooding risk is generally forbidden, but in areas of moderate flooding risk, some new construction is authorized. This includes buildings for activities that welcome the public during the day but not residential housing. Schools, libraries, sports facilities, concert venues, and some commercial/industrial activities, for example, can be authorized since these facilities can easily be pre-emptively closed or evacuated during the daytime in the case of extreme weather warnings. Residential buildings with no apartments on the ground floor may also be authorized in some cases. We assume that buildings built after 1999 in the 80-mm flood zone respect legislation in vigor at the time of construction and represent potential material flood damage but not necessarily greater human exposure as illustrated by the new industrial zone in the Mourachonne described above. New buildings flooded in the 140-mm and 200-mm flood zones, however, combine both greater infrastructure and human exposure. Apart from the general slowing of urbanisation rates over time, the last time interval (2014–2020) corresponds to the 2015 catastrophic flood in the Brague. After 2014, building in the flooded zone was negligible, so independently of urban legislation, the study suggests that the catastrophic flood heightened awareness of the need to reduce exposure to floods. With regards to the 2015 flood, not only were the fatalities and extensive material damage traumatising, but the mayor of the main city (Biot) located in the catchment was convicted of involuntary homicide with a one-year suspended sentence for failing to take all the preventive measures necessary to ensure the security of the population as the event unfolded. Similarly, the mayor of La Faute sur Mer in western France was recently convicted of involuntary homicide after a dyke collapsed during the Xynthia storm of 2010 (53 fatalities in all, 29 in La Faute); he was deemed responsible for authorising the construction of new housing in a high risk coastal flood zone. As the climate changes and the frequency and magnitude of extreme rainfall events increase (Ribes et al., 2019; Vautard et al., 2015 ), the greatest threat appears to be for buildings located in the flood zone defined in this study by the intermediate 140 mm rainfall event. Building restrictions will most likely always be greatest closest to the channel, so it is the zone just beyond this that will suffer most from an increase in extreme events. The 140 mm event is further and less restricted than for the 80-mm event, so the percentage increases in the buildings impacted attain their maximum values. The 200-mm event floods affect more area, but the relative growth in flooded area is more restricted as the limits of the flood plain are reached. The intermediate 80–140 mm transition therefore corresponds to the most dangerous transition in terms of the impact of urbanisation and climate change on flood risk.  4.3 Limitations and the potential for building footprint-based studies The flooded building footprint area was probably overestimated in the hydraulic modeling calculations since flood depth was not explicitly taken into account and building design may have integrated measures to elevate new buildings that are not discernible from the footprint layer. For example, the large increase in the flooded building footprint area in the Mourachonne is related to a new industrial park built right next to the river channel. From the 2020 aerial photographs, we can see that several of these buildings are storage warehouses with loading platforms that appear to be at the height of the back end of a truck, so even though the parking lot would be flooded, it is unlikely the building itself would be submerged due to building design. The hydraulic model uses a 1-m DEM where the flooded area corresponds to ground-level elevation. When a flooded depth of 20 cm is used as a criterion to evaluate the area of buildings impacted by a flood, the area retained in the Brague ranges from about 47 % of initial flooded building footprint area for the 80-mm event to 67 % for the 200 mm event. Corresponding values for the Frayère are 14–59 %, and for the Mourachonne they are 58–67 %. However, without extensive field investigation of every building, it is impossible to define local depth criteria more precisely, so values obtained here probably overestimate exposure, but the general trends remain unchanged. Over a time-interval of 3 decades, substantial flood management work took place in all 3 catchments in the form of bank stabilisation, channel widening, and the introduction of retention dams on tributary channels, for example. The impacts of these measures on flooded area were not quantified here, but their beneficial effects on bankfull capacity are not without ambiguity, since they would probably also have impacted zoning rules with regards to flood risk. It is therefore probable that building in potential flood-affected zones over time was enabled partly by these improved flood control measures, but this was impossible to verify in the context of this study. Finally, vector building layers have the potential to become the most accurate estimates of both exposure and vulnerability to floods since they can easily be crossed with several types of socio-economic data, including property values, average household income, employment rates, insurance rates… France has unique and extensive national-level GIS building footprint polygon layers and recent research has started to exploit the use of building footprint layers in flood studies (Hossain and Meng, 2020 ), including the Microsoft building footprint dataset released by Bing Maps for flood risk assessment for the Conterminous United States (Huang and Wang, 2020 ). Using building layers, the authors were able to identify weaknesses in traditional approaches (areas not previously covered, outdated data…) and a greater vulnerability of the poor to 100-yr floods. Similar databases are being developed for Europe (Florio et al., 2023; Milojevic-Dupont et al., 2023 ). The global availability of building footprint layers is therefore growing rapidly thanks to new building classification algorithms (Liu et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2023 ), so we can expect an exponential increase in the use of GIS building footprints in a range of hydrological and hydraulic approaches.   5 Conclusion Urbanisation throughout the world increases flood risk as greater imperviousness increases both runoff and exposure as new buildings are added to a potential flood zone. Peak discharge increased with urbanisation between 1988/90 and 2020 at a rate that followed temporal trends in urbanisation rates. The increase in peak discharge increased the total flooded area and the area of buildings flooded. However, the relative increase in building area flooded was more than 40 times greater than the relative increase in total flooded area, and this demonstrates that the change in flooding risk was due more to greater exposure, as new buildings were added to the flooded zone, than to greater peak discharge values. As rainfall magnitude increased from 80-mm to 200-mm, the total area and building footprint area flooded both increased. Closer to the channel, where the flooding risk is greatest, urban planning legislation provided some protection since the growth in flooded building area was lowest. As rainfall magnitude increased, less restricted areas further from the channel were exposed to flooding, and in these zones, the growth in flooding risk increased most. They were far enough from the channel to escape building restrictions, and the flatter terrain of the alluvial plain close to the main roads favoured rapid urbanisation. Hence, as rainfall magnitude increased, especially from 80 mm to 140 mm, the relative growth in buildings impacted was greatest. These intermediate zones in the alluvial plain present the greatest risk in a context of climate change where the magnitude and frequency of extreme events are expected to increase. 1 Introduction Floods are widespread and the most recurring natural disasters in terms of human and economic losses (Pradhan and Youssef, 2011 ). Millions of people every year are affected by floods due to their sudden occurrences and inadequate flood prevention measures in many countries (Mahmoud and Gan, 2018 ). A study discovered that between 2000–2015, the population that settled in flood-affected areas increased from approximately 58 to 86 million, primarily concentrated in Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. This increase represented a 10–20 % rise in the proportion of the global population exposed to floods (Tellman et al., 2021 ). India is the world’s second most flood-affected country after Bangladesh where nearly 1/8th of the geographical area is flood-prone (Bapalu and Sinha, 2005 ) and approximately 33 million people were affected between 1953–2000 (Mohapatra and Singh, 2003 ). The year 2000 stands out as the most notable flood year declared by the Government of India, because around 22.1 million people were affected by flood, and the property loss amounted to 56606.5 million (Roy et al. 2020 ). Floods occur due to complex factors associated with topography, geology, climate and human interventions (Romshoo et al., 2012 ). Nowadays, climate change and Land Use Land Cover (LULC) change are the key causes of flood events (Kanani-Sadat et al., 2019 ). Moreover, floods in arid and semi-arid areas are strongly influenced by geomorphology, geology, drainage networks and engineering structures (Bathrellos et al., 2016 ). While accomplishing zero flood risk of a river is impossible, it remains vital to diminish the consequences of floods to the highest extent possible (Mohammadifar et al. 2023 ). Therefore, understanding the hydrological behaviour, and determining the peak flow (qp  ) of a basin is important in managing natural resources and taking structural flood-controlling measures (Khaleghi et al., 2011 ). The role of basin geomorphology in understanding flood risk has been known for a long time (Swain et al., 2015 ). In this regard, basin morphometric characteristics and associated parameters have a significant impact on the hydrological responses of the basin, especially on surface runoff (Masoud, 2016 ). Linear, areal and relief parameters of the drainage network of a basin play key roles in estimating flood in ungauged basins (Bathrellos et al., 2016 ) where basins have a greater tendency to generate qp   in a short duration of time (Bhatt and Ahmed, 2014 ). Therefore, morphometric analysis and basin prioritization are essential methods for implementing various relevant basin management actions (Ahmed et al. 2023 ). Many studies showed the usefulness of various morphometric parameters for understanding the flood behaviour of basins and their prioritization using various multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM), traditional and statistical methods (Ozdemir and Bird, 2009; Youssef et al., 2011; Farhan et al., 2017; Elewa et al., 2016; Mahmood and Rahman, 2019; Amiri et al., 2019; Alam et al., 2021; Ghasemlounia and Utlu, 2021; Al-neama et al., 2022 ). Bhatt and Ahmed (2014)  studied basin characteristics from morphometric parameters to determine flood hazard potentiality using the compound factor (CF) ranking method in the upper Krishna basin, India and results showed that Krishna, Kayna and Yerla have comparatively higher and faster runoff generation potentiality and are responsible for flood in main Krishna basin. Akay and Koçyiğit (2020)  evaluated the prioritization of SBs to flash flood potential in Turkey using traditional [hazard degree (HD), CF and simple statistical method] and MCDM methods i.e., analytical hierarchical process (AHP), ANP, VIKOR, TOPSIS and ElECTRE-1. Results showed that AHP-based MCDM (AHP-VIKOR) performed well in predicting SBs with higher flood potential as compared to ANP-based MCDMs. However, morphometric parameters are not solely determinant of flash flood probability, because hydrological factors such as soil moisture, LULC properties, vegetation, and soil texture influence the potential surface runoff (Karmokar and De, 2020 ). Therefore, some studies linked the morphometric parameter-based flood hazard assessment approach with the rainfall-runoff model or parameters of the synthetic unit hydrograph (SUH) (Masoud, 2015; Singh and Singh, 2017; Karmokar and De, 2020; El–Fakharany and Mansour, 2021; Abdelkader et al., 2021; Niyazi et al., 2021 ). However, estimation of discharge in scarcely-gauged and ungauged basins by using hydrologic models and methods is tedious work due to the unavailability of stream flow data for validation purposes, and the changing behaviour of climatic and LULC patterns (Bhaskar et al., 1997; Kumar et al., 2007; Swain et al., 2015 ). Therefore, the geomorphological parameter-based rainfall-runoff model is more useful in predicting flood in ungauged and scarcely-gauged basins, because geomorphologic parameters are mostly time-invariant and have linkage with hydrologic characteristics of the basin (Bhaskar et al., 1997; Swain et al., 2015 ). For this instance, Geomorphologic Instantaneous Unit Hydrograph or GIUH (Rodríguez-Iturbe and Valdes, 1979; Gupta et al., 1980 ) can provide better insight into the hydrologic behaviour of a basin and is the most advantageous for the ungauged one (Bhaskar et al., 1997 ). Moreover, in extracting geomorphologic parameters of GIUH and morphometric parameters for water resources management studies, DEM data, GIS tools and remote sensing techniques gained widespread popularity in recent years (Kumar et al., 2007; Bhatt and Ahmed, 2014 ) that facilitated these kinds of studies. Therefore, some studies were conducted on GIUH based on Nash (1957)  and Clark (1945)  models, and very few of them related morphometric characteristics-based flood assessment with the GIUH. A very critical review of various popular SUHs from the empirical to advanced geomorphological methods was carried out by Singh et al. (2014b) , and they found that the GIUH is the most useful and interesting approach. Reddy et al. (2019)  tested the applicability of several SUHs for flood estimation at ungauged basins of Karnataka, India and found that the Nash two-parameter gamma distribution method and hybrid model satisfied the unit hydrograph (UH) criterion. Khaleghi et al. (2011)  employed a study to simulate the rainfall-runoff process over the Kasilian watershed in Iran, including Snyder, SCS, Triangular, Rosso and GIUH. The study found that the geomorphologic model had the most direct agreement for the parameters of direct runoff. Bamufleh et al. (2020)  studied GIUH using an equivalent Horton-Strahler ratio based on the Nash and Frechet Model. Results found that the Nash model performed relatively better in representing the measured hydrograph. Sahoo et al. (2006)  estimated flood discharge using GIUH based Clark and Nash model for simulating direct surface run-off (DSRO) hydrograph for the fifteen rainfall-runoff events in the Ajay River basin up to Jamtara gauging site in eastern India. The study revealed that the performance of GIUH-based Nash and Clark models-derived DSRO hydrograph is relatively accurate with observed, Clark-IUH and Nash-IUH-based DSRO hydrograph parameters. They concluded that the GIUH model has great potential to estimate peak discharge. Bhagwat et al. (2011)  employed basin management implication through morphometric characteristics and Nash-GIUH. Results showed that variations in morphometric parameters reflect the variations in GIUH properties. Sub-basins of northern transition and hilly forest zones are sensitive to generate moderate to high flood probability that is validated by semi-log plots of drainage density versus bifurcation ratio and GIUH parameters. Summarizing the above studies, it is illustrated that for the estimation of floods in ungauged basins, geomorphologic parameters play significant roles both in terms of the morphometric parameter-based and the GIUH parameter-based flood risk assessments. However, it is found that to the best of the authors' knowledge, no such studies have linked the significant morpho-hydrologic parameter-based flood hazard and prioritization models with different velocity-based Nash-GIUH models for an improved method of sub-basin prioritization. Therefore, an integrated hydro-geomorpholgic approach of sub-basin prioritization is introduced in this study. In the geomorphologic part, basin morphometric parameters are adopted to determine the flood generation potentiality (FGP) based on different ranking methods. On the other hand, in the hydrologic part, different velocity-based Nash-GIUH models have been used to approximate basin hydrologic responses such as peak flow (qp  ) to extreme events. Therefore, the application of an integrated hydro-gemorphologic approach of sub-basin prioritization in terms of morpho-hydrologic parameter-based and Nash-GIUH parameter-based flood hazard models is the main novelty of this study. In previous studies, flood or surface runoff potentiality has been estimated using a large number of morphometric parameters that are highly correlated, and prioritization of basins has been done without validating the results by hydrologic models or direct flow observation. Therefore, to bridge the research gap, in this study, only significant morphometric parameters are integrated with some important unit hydrograph (UH) parameters to strengthen the prediction capabilities of FGP models, and Nash-GIUH is used to evaluate the results of FGP models. This methodology is applied in one of the most flood-prone scarcely gauged tropical plateau fringe river basins, Shilabati in eastern India, where all of its sub-basins are ungauged. In this river, devastating floods occurred in 1888, 1913, 1922, 1942, 1956, 1959, 1968, 1973, 1978, 1984, 2000, 2007, 2013, 2017 and 2021 (I&WD, 2017; I&WD, 2021; Goswami, 2023 ). Floods in the lower part of the basin resulted from various factors, including high stream branching in its downstream, plateau fringe fan system with a very low gradient, embankments induced river siltation, short-duration high-intensity rainfall events and discharges from tributaries etc. Consequently, the lower part of the Shilabati river including Ghatal town becomes flood prone almost every year (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2015; Pal, 2014; Kar and Das, 2020; Mondal and Patel, 2023 ). Therefore, the lack of hydrologic data in this river has emerged the need for an integrated method of sub-basin prioritization, where FGP and Nash-GIUH models are used to identify high runoff and flash flood potentiality, which holds immense importance for flood mitigation purposes. The main objectives taken for this study are (a) to determine morpho-hydrologic parameter-based FGP models, (b) to develop Nash-GIUH models and to compare them with FGP models and (c) to prioritize sub-basins for flood mitigation purposes in the Master River.  2 Study area Shilabati River basin is located in the western part of the state of West Bengal which ranges between 86°64ʹ and 87°78ʹ longitude and 22°40ʹ and 23°24ʹ latitude, covering 4053.62 km2  of geographical area (Fig. 1  ). The River originates from the eastern fringe part of the Chotanagpur plateau region, Puncha block of Puruliya district and flows south-easterly direction through Bankura and west Midnapore district of West Bengal, thereafter joining the Rupnarayan River near the Ghatal town. The climate of this basin is tropical wet and dry (Aw) with a normal annual rainfall of 1357.3 mm (IMD, 2008 ) and the maximum and minimum temperatures are 43℃ and 8.3℃, respectively (IMD, 2022 ). The whole basin consists of small to medium-sized ten tributary SBs. Left bank tributary SBs are Betal (SB-3), Kubai (SB-7), Tamal (SB-8) and Parang (SB-9), Donai (SB-10) and right bank SBs are Joypanda (SB-2) and Purandar (SB-3) and other two small SBs are named SB-5, SB-6 in this study. Upper most SB of the Master River is considered as SB-1. The basin offers two distinctive geographical settings (a) the degraded plateau area and (b) the plateau fringe fan area (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2015 ). In the upper part of the SB-1 and SB-2, degraded plateau region is found where elevation ranges from 227 to 115 m and characterised by high relief, moderate slopes, undulating dissected uplands, pediplain-pediment complex, braided channels with occasional structurally controlled straight reaches, Archaean to Proterozoic gneisses formations (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2015 ) that make the region susceptible to erosion and high surface runoff (Shit et al., 2015 ). In the eastern half of the basin where the rest of the SBs are situated, a plateau fringe fan system is observed. This fan system is characterised by moderate to low elevation (4 to 115 m), buried pediments with lateritic capping, older alluvium deposits, plateau-fringe paleo-delta formations and very low channel gradient that developed a large older flood plain due to several transgression and regression of sea level during Eocene and Holocene (Mukhopadhyay, 1972; Singh et al., 1998; Bandyopadhyay et al., 2015; Mahata and Maiti, 2019 ). Besides, climatic and anthropogenic factors play a key role in flooding in the basin. Studies revealed a reduction of significant vegetation cover in this basin that possesses pronounced effects on overland flow. Moreover, intense rainfall, followed by water pooling owing to extremely flat local terrain resulted in floods in the lower part of the river and most of the time it is associated with post-monsoon tropical cyclones (Kar and Das, 2020 ) (Fig. 2  ).  3 Materials and methods 3.1 Database Shuttle radar topographic mission (SRTM) 1-arc second DEM with 30-m spatial resolution from the United States geological survey (USGS) and topographical maps from the survey of India were obtained for derivation of various physical features of the basin. In analysing FGP and GIUH, basic parameters were extracted from DEM, historical rainfall data, LULC, soil texture and Google Earth Pro. For computing LULC features, Landsat 8 satellite imagery of March 2023 was used, which was acquired from the USGS Earth Explorer data portal. For preparing the soil texture map and determining the hydrological soil group (HSG), the data from the National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use planning was used. For selecting storm rainfalls for GIUH, daily rainfall data was collected from IMD in gridded format with 25 km spatial resolution for a period of five years (2017–2021) (Pai et al., 2014 ). After selecting storm events, hourly rainfall data for selected storm events were acquired for deriving the velocity parameter of GIUH from the Indian Monsoon Data Assimilation and Analysis (IMDAA) data. IMDAA is a regional atmospheric reanalysis over the Indian subcontinent that provides high spatial (12 km) and temporal (1 hourly) resolution data over India using the 4D-Var data assimilation method (Rani et al., 2021 ). River gauge height data of gauging site Gadghat was acquired from the irrigation and waterways department of West Bengal to show historical flood events. Field visits in the most flood-prone areas of the river were conducted to understand the flood-related problems. ArcGIS, SPSS, python programming language and M.S. Excel were used for data analysis and graphical representations. A complete flow chart of the methodology is shown in Fig. 3  .  3.2 Multi-collinearity test and selection of parameters Selection of the most effective morpho-hydrologic parameters for assessing FGP is an important task as adopting insignificant parameters causes a multi-collinearity issue that deteriorates model performance. To detect multi-collinearity and remove highly correlated independent parameters, at first, Pearson’s correlation coefficients (r) are evaluated for each pair of morpho-hydrologic parameters to determine the degree of correlation. Then, the variance inflation factor (VIF) and the tolerance criteria are used (Khosravi et al., 2018 ) for the group of morphometric and hydrologic runoff conditioning parameters separately to identify multi-collinearity issues arising from their strong r values. VIF and tolerance cut-off values of > 10 and < 0.1, respectively were considered to detect the multi-collinearity problem in flood occurrence parameters (Khosravi et al., 2018; Youssef et al., 2022 ). Initially, a total of ten significant linear, areal and relief parameters (morphometric parameters) and a total of five important hydrologic parameters are taken into consideration based on literature. Afterwards, only effective morpho-hydrologic parameters are selected using multi-collinearity tests for the analysis of FGP. Morphometric parameters under linear, areal and relief aspects used in this study are bifurcation ratio (Rb  ), drainage density (Dd  ), stream frequency (Fs  ), sinuosity index (SI ), shape factor (Sf  ), circularity ratio (Rc  ), relief ratio (Rh  ), relative relief (Rr  ), Melton ruggedness number (Mrn  ), and hypsometric integral (HI ). Hydrologic parameters include basin area (A ), longest flow path length (L ), curve number (CN ), average basin slope (Y ) and time of concentration (Tc  ).  3.3 Morpho-hydrologic parameters and their relation to flood Morpho-hydrologic parameters are divided into two groups regarding their FGP. The parameters having a direct relationship with flood potentiality are assigned in group-A which comprises Rb  , Dd  , Fs  , Rc  , Rr  , Mrn , HI , Rh  , A , CN  and Y . Higher values of these parameters, the greater and faster the runoff and higher the FGP. Parameters that have an indirect relationship with FGP were allocated in group-B. These parameters are SI , Sf  , Tc   and L .  Here, the lower the value greater and faster the runoff. This relationship between FGP and its conditioning morpho-hydrologic indicators is determined from the literatures (Bhatt and Ahmed, 2014; Elewa et al., 2016; Obeidat et al., 2021; Ogarekpe et al., 2020; Ghasemlounia and Utlu, 2021; Alam et al. 2021 ). ArcGIS and Excel were used for extracting basic parameters, calculating quantitative values and analysing the morpho-hydrologic parameters. Details of all morpho-hydrologic parameters are shown in Table 1  . 3.3.1 Morphometric parameters 3.3.1.1 Linear parameters Bifurcation ratio (Rb )  It is the ratio of the number of streams of a specified order and the number of streams in the next higher order. Higher Rb   is generally found in hilly and dissected plateau areas than in the rolling plain (Horton, 1945 ). Consistent increment of Rb   in successive orders and a higher value of mean Rb   designates a strong structural control of the basin, highly dissected nature of the basin and high potentiality of flooding associated with an early peak of the hydrograph (Bhatt and Ahmed, 2014; Rai et al., 2017; Mahala, 2020 ). Drainage density (Dd )  It is defined as the ratio of the total length of channel segments to basin area (Horton, 1945 ). Low drainage density is more likely to be found in highly permeable sub-soil under dense vegetation cover with low relief, whereas high Dd   often occurs in regions where impermeable rock material, sparse vegetation and high relief are found (Biswas et al. 1999; Nag and Chakraborty, 2003 ), representing a relatively quick hydrological response to storm events and high flood peaks (Patel et al., 2012; Rai et al., 2017 ). Stream frequency (Fs)  It is defined as the ratio between the total number of streams and total basin area. High values of Fs depend on high relief, steeper slopes and underlying bedrock reflecting the finer texture of the drainage network (Horton, 1945; Bhatt and Ahmed, 2014 ). High values of Fs   also represent high surface runoff and early peak discharge in flood hydrographs (Patel et al., 2012; Romshoo et al., 2012 ). Sinuosity index (SI) . Mueller (1968)  proposed standard SI, hydraulic SI (HSI) and topographic SI (TSI) in order to identify the departure of the stream from a straight line due to either hydraulic factor or topography. Standard SI or SI is defined by the ratio of channel index to valley index (Mueller, 1968 ) (Table 1 ). The sinuous nature of the river was classified into five classes by Mueller (1968)  (for details see Ghosh and Mistri, 2012 ). SI value near 1 (<1.05) discloses a rectilinear shape or straight nature of main stream characterised by a steep slope, high relief, structural control of the area, influence of tectonics, high flood discharge and moderate to high sediment supply (Perucca and Angilieri, 2011; Sangma and Guru, 2020 ).  3.3.1.2 Areal parameters Shape factor (Sf )  The shape factor is defined as the ratio of the square of the basin length to the total area of the basin (Horton, 1945; Patel et al., 2012 ) that affects the water and sediment yield of the basin (Meraj et al., 2015 ). Low Sf   value represents relatively high relief, circular shape of the basin, short Tc  , and high surface runoff associated with early flood peaks (Farhan et al., 2017; Mahmood and Rahman, 2019; Obeidat et al., 2021 ). Circularity ratio (Rc )  Rc   is defined as a ratio of basin area to the area of a circle having the same circumference similar to the basin perimeter (Miller,1953 ). Rc   closer to 1 represents the circular shape of the basin with early flood peaks (Biswas et al. 1999; Mahmood and Rahman, 2019 ). The low Rc   corresponds to an elongated basin shape, the youth stage of geomorphic evolution with delayed flood peaks and high permeability (Farhan et al., 2017 ).  3.3.1.3 Relief parameters Relief ratio (Rh )  It is a ratio of maximum basin relief to the maximum basin length parallel to the main stream (Schumm 1956; Strahler 1964 ). The relief ratio is directly related to the slope of the streams, which affects hydrological processes (Ameri et al., 2018 ). High Rh   values correspond to shorter lag time, quick peak flow and high flash flood potentiality (Bhat et al., 2019, Obeidat et al. 2021 ). Relative relief (Rr ) . Relative relief, which is defined as the ratio of the basin relief to the length of the perimeter of the basin (Melton, 1957 ), indicates the stages of geomorphic development of a basin (Mahala, 2020 ). It is a measure of the general steepness of the basin, which has a direct relationship with flooding and denudation rate (Prabhakaran and Raj, 2018 ; Obeidat et al., 2021 ). Melton ruggedness number (Mrn )  The Mrn   is a slope index that provides a specialized description of relief ruggedness within a basin area (Melton, 1957 ). The high Mrn   indicates high roughness, erodibility and surface runoff, whereas low values parallel to low basin relief and tectonic stability (Ghasemlounia and Utlu, 2021 ). Hypsometric curve and hypsometric integral (HI)  Hypsometric analysis is a form of the relationship between the horizontal cross-sectional area of a drainage basin and relative elevation (Strahler, 1952 ), and the area below the curve forms a hypsometric integral. Lithological and structural differences and neo-tectonic activities, stages of development of a basin may account for differences in the hypsometric curve and integral (Strahler, 1952; Strahler, 1957; Schumm, 1956 ). High HI values correspond to the youth stage of geomorphic evolution, high stream power, high sediment yield capacity and high surface runoff.   3.3.2 Hydrologic parameters 3.3.2.1 Basin area (A) Basin area is a very important hydrological feature as it determines the volume of water resulting from rainfall (Patel et al. 2012; Farhan et al. 2017; Obeidat et al. 2021 ). Therefore, a large surface area can increase surface runoff and potential discharge (Islam and Deb Barman, 2020 ). However, the basin area is not linearly related to the lag time of the basin and sharp shape of the hydrograph. This is because water takes more time to travel through a large basin, and other physical factors also influence the process.  3.3.2.2 Longest flow path length (L) Longer streams indicate less infiltration and can generate high runoff volume (Strahler, 1952 ). However, Longer flow paths can increase the Tc   and lag time of the basin, which produces delayed peaks of a hydrograph. Therefore, a shorter flow path length corresponds to a high slope, faster accumulation of water to its outlet and potential for flash flooding (Meraj et al. 2015 ).  3.3.2.3 Average basin slope (Y) Slope is the most effective hydrologic factor in expressing flood peaks in a shorter period. Steeper slopes refer to the high river flow velocity and short time lag of the basin that produces relatively fast peak discharge and hazardous runoff (Romshoo et al., 2012 ; El–Fakharany and Mansour, 2019; Abdelkader et al., 2021 ).  3.3.2.4 Curve number (CN) CN is developed to estimate the runoff of a specific region characterised by a particular LULC type, HSG and precipitation depth (Halwatura and Najim, 2013 ). In uniform precipitation conditions, low CN has a heightened capacity for potential groundwater storage, whereas high CN results in maximum direct runoff in a shorter period (Rawat and Singh, 2017 ).  3.3.2.5 Time of concentration (Tc ) Tc   is defined as the travel time of runoff from the hydraulically most distant point to the basin outlet (NRCS, 2010b ). It is one of the most important parameters for calculating the peak discharge of a basin and the shape of the flood hydrograph (Alam et al., 2021; Shaikh et al., 2022 ). In uniform precipitation, basins with shorter Tc   are likely to generate early flood peaks in their outlets, resulting in high flood risk downstream (Wakode et al., 2013; El-Fakharany and Mansour, 2021 ).    3.4 Flood generation potentiality models and prioritization of sub-basins After conducting the multi-colinearity test, the selected morpho-hydrologic parameter-based five different FGP models are proposed which are based on the five most effective decision-making or ranking methods. The ranking methods used in this study are (a) traditional method that includes Compound Factor (CF) and Hazard Degree (HD), (b) statistical method that comprises Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Weighted Sum Approach (WSA), and (c) MCDM method which is AHP. The prioritization of all sub-basins is performed based on the priority scores of the best FGP model. High priority scores correspond to high FGP and high prioritization of sub-basins and vice versa. 3.4.1 Compound factor (CF) CF is one of the best approaches to comparing land surface processes in watersheds (Ameri et al., 2018 ). This approach involves assigning sequential ranks to morphometric parameters, relying on their level of contribution to the goal (Hembram and Saha, 2020 ). The average of the assigned rank of the basin indicates its relative priority in comparison to others (Bhatt and Ahmed, 2014; Patel et al., 2012 ). Parameters that are under group-A were ranked in such a way where the highest morphometric value of a sub-basin was assigned rank 10 and the second highest value was assigned rank 9 and so on. In contrast, the lowest values of parameters of group-B were assigned rank 10 and the second lowest values were assigned rank 9 and so on (Bhatt and Ahmed, 2014; Ogarekpe et al., 2020 ). Parameters having the same values were assigned equal rank. CF is expressed as Eq. (1)  where the high priority score of CF represents high FGP and vice versa.(1) F i  = ∑ i = 1  n  r ij    n a       where, Fi   represents the priority score of CF; r is the rank of the morphometric parameter; i , j  and na   refer to alternative, criterion and the total number of criteria, respectively.  3.4.2 Hazard degree The estimation of the degree of flood hazard for all parameters of 10 sub-basins was performed with a hazard scale, ranging from 1 to 5. Hazard score 1 represents a weakly hazardous sub-basin, whereas score 5 corresponds to an extremely highly hazardous sub-basin. The lowest and highest morphometric values of group-A parameters were assigned ranks 1 and 5, respectively. In contrast, the highest morphometric value of Group-B parameters was ranked 1, whereas the lowest value was assigned hazard rank 5. Prioritization using HD follows two steps. At first, HD (relative weights) values for the group A and B parameters were calculated by following Eq. (2)  and Eq. (3) . Finally, the priority score of HD was achieved by computing the average of relative weights assigned to all parameters (Eq. (4) . Higher the value of the Hazard degree, the greater will be FGP and vice versa (Mahmood and Rahman, 2019; Abdelkader et al., 2021; Al-neama et al., 2022 ).(2) w ij   = ( Y max  - Y min  )  × ( X ij   - X min  )   ( X max  - X min  )   + Y min      (3) w ij   = ( Y max  - Y min  )  × ( X ij   - X max  )   ( X min  - X max  )   + Y min      (4) R i  = ∑ i = 1  n  w ij    n      where, Ri   represents the priority score of HD; w  is the relative weight, Y max  and Y min  are the maximum and minimum rank (5 and 1); X max  and X min  are the highest and lowest morpho-hydrologic values, respectively.  3.4.3 AHP MCDA is a widely used framework for making decisions from multiple criteria against a certain goal in a complex environment. Therefore, to prioritize sub-basins based on morphometric parameters, priority scores were derived by AHP which is a semi-quantitative MCDA approach developed by Saaty (1980) . At first, a pare-wise comparison matrix was created by evaluating the relative importance of each morphometric criterion with every other criterion on a rating scale (1–9). Ratings were assigned in a pare-wise comparison matrix based on literature and some experts’ opinions in this field. In a pare-wise comparison matrix, 1 indicates equal importance of two criteria and 9 indicates that one parameter is extremely more important than the other. In the second step, the normalisation of the comparison matrix was made. In the next step, normalised eigenvectors (relative weights) of parameters were computed following Eqs. (5–6). Pair-wise comparison matrix and normalised pair-wise comparison matrix with relative weights were given in Tables S1-S2 .(5) x ij   = a ij   ∑ i = 1  m  a ij         (6) W j  = ∑ j = 1  n  x ij    n      where, x  is the normalised element value; a  represents the matrix element; W  represents relative weight. In the fourth step, the determination of consistency of the pair-wise comparison matrix was made (Table S3 ) because of inconsistency in judgement (Saaty, 1987 ). Hence, a consistency ratio of less than 0.1 is acceptable, implying that the subjective evolution of the decision goal is considered as consistent (Saaty, 1987; Ouma and Tateishi, 2014 ). It was computed using the following Eq. (7) .(7) CR = CI  RI       where, CI  is the consistency index; RI  represents the random consistency index. Finally, the priority index of all sub-basins was estimated by the linear combination method (Eq. (8) . For that task, normalisation of actual parameters’ values was performed. The equation of benefit criteria was applied for normalised group-A parameters and the cost criteria was used for normalised group-B parameters. The higher the value of priority, the greater the FGP and vice versa (Table S4 ).(8) V i  = ∑ i = 1  n  W j  f ij       where, Vi   is the priority score of AHP; W  relative weight; f  represents the normalised value.  3.4.4 Principal component analysis (PCA) Normally, morpho-hydrologic parameters have moderate to strong interrelationships between each other. This relationship results in one parameter having information involved in other parameters. Therefore, PCA was used on selected morpho-hydrologic parameters to reduce dimensionality and to find out the most significant parameters in prioritizing sub-basins. PCA was conducted in the following steps:a) After the multi-colinearity test, the selected morpho-hydrologic dataset was normalised using the Z-score normalisation method.  b) Pearson’s correlation matrix was computed.  c) Calculated the eigenvalue greater than 1 that defines the significant number of Principal components (PCs).  d) Determined the initial component matrix (un-rotated matrix).  e) A rotated first-factor loading matrix (Varimax-rotated matrix) was computed to achieve the most significant components.    The statistics of total variance explained were given in Tables S4-S5 . In the rotated matrix, the selected morpho-hydrologic parameters that are highly correlated with PCs (> ±0.9) are finally considered for the PCA-based CF approach for the prioritization of sub-basins (Farhan et al., 2017; Singh and Pandey, 2021; Kulimushi et al., 2021 ) following Eq. (1) . Higher the value of priority scores, greater will be FGP and vice versa.  3.4.5 Weighted sum analysis (WSA) WSA is a very suitable ranking approach for prioritizing small river basins (Aher et al., 2014; Arefin and Alam, 2020 ). WSA estimates the relative importance of each parameter by analysing statistical correlation among each variable and finally assigns weight to each input constraint by avoiding individual biases associated with parameters (Aher et al., 2014; Kadam et al., 2019 ). In the first step, a correlation matrix was formed to define the significance of parameters (Table S6 ). In the next step, relative weights were allocated to each parameter considering their significance. Finally, the priority score of all sub-basins was performed as follows (Eq. (9) . The Higher the value of priority scores, the greater will be the FGP and vice versa.(9) Xi = ∑ i = 1  n  w j  r ij    n      where, X  is the priority score of WSA; w  is the relative weight of WSA; r  represents morphometric rank.   3.5 GIUH-based Nash model 3.5.1 Derivation of GIUH Several researchers tried to link the response of the basin hydrology to the geomorphological characteristics of the basin (Rodríguez-Iturbe and Valdés, 1979; Gupta et al., 1980; Naden, 1992 ). However, the introduction of a geo-morphological approach to understanding the hydrological behaviour of the basin was derived by Rodríguez-Iturbe and Valdes (1979) . They developed a systematic method for incorporating the characteristics of the drainage basin composition including the Horton-Strahler ratio [Rb  , Rl   and area ratio (Ra  )] into the theoretical scheme of IUH, and thus GIUH is formed (Ros and Borga, 1997 ). GIUH may be conceptualised as the probability distribution function (PDF) of the time travel of a randomly placed water droplet at the trapping state of a hypothetical basin treated as a continuous Markovian process where the state is the order of the stream and water droplet functions from an instantaneous application of a unit volume of excess rainfall uniformly spread over the catchment at zero time (Rodríguez-Iturbe et al., 1979; Rodríguez-Iturbe and Valdés, 1979 ). Here, the value of the mode of the PDF produces the main characteristics of the GIUH, which are qp  , time to peak (tp  ) and base time (tb  ) expressed as(10) q p  = 1.31 R l 0.43   V / L Ω      (11) t p  = 0.44 ( L Ω  / V )  ( R b  / R a  )  0.55   R l - 0.38       (12) t b  = 2 / q p      where, qp   is in hr-1 , tp   is in hr, tb   is in hr, L Ω  represents the length of the highest order stream in km, and V  is the dynamic flow velocity (m/s). Rb   is given in Table 1 , while R l  and Ra   are expressed as(13) R l  = L um - 1   / L um       where, Lum   is the mean length of the stream in order u  in km, and Lum  - 1   represents the mean stream length of the previous lower order.(14) R a  = A u  / A u - 1       where Au   is the mean basin area of order u  and Au  -1  is the mean basin area of the previous lower order of order u . On multiplying Eqs. (10) and (11) , a non-dimensional term ‘IR ’ is obtained which is a geomorphologic constant to the hydrologic response structure to each sub-basin. It is the independent parameter that exhibits the computation of IUH using either parameter qp   or tp   (Rodríguez-Iturbe and Valdes, 1979 ).(15) IR = q p  t p  = 0.5764 ( R b  / R a  )  0.55   ( R l  )  0.05         3.5.2 Computation of dynamic velocity (V ) Rodríguez-Iturbe et al. (1982)  realised that in derivation of GIUH, qp   and tp   vary from storm to storm as these parameters depend on the velocity which in turn is controlled by excess rainfall intensity (Ire  ) of a given storm. Variability in the shape of GIUH occurs due to the velocity which varies from storm to storm. For that reason, various storm events were considered to get time-invariant GIUH models where Ire   was considered as constant in their respective storm durations and analytically expressed for ungauged basins as(16) V = 0.665 α Ω 0.6   I re   A Ω     0.4       where V  is in m.s−1 , Ire   is in cm.hr -1 , AΩ  is the basin area of the highest order stream (km2 ), and αΩ  is the kinematic wave parameter.(17) α Ω  = S 1 2   n r  B 2 3         where S  is the slope of the main stream (m.m−1 ), nr   represents Manning's roughness coefficient, and B  is the average width of the main stream (m). The basic parameters used to derive velocity are given in Table S7 .  3.5.3 Derivation of excess rainfall intensity (Ire  ) For the derivation of various velocities in order to get time-invariant GIUH models, derivation of Ire   is important where no river flow data is available. Ire   values of selected storm events were achieved by the SCS curve number (CN) method (USDA, 1972; Kumar et al., 2004; Sahoo et al., 2006 ). IMDAA 1-hourly gridded data (12 km spatial resolution) is used to derive hourly rainfall depths, excess rainfall depth and Ire   of the selected storms. For that task, storm spells associated with floods were selected from the daily rainfall data (IMD gridded). Then, hourly gridded rainfall data is prepared for these selected storm spells. Finally, the Thiessen polygons method is used to get average hourly rain storms for all sub-basins (Fig. S1 ). Detailed information on HSG, LULC and CN for deriving Ire   of each sub-basin is given in Table S8  and shown in Fig. S1 .  3.5.4 Selection of storm events and its relation with floods In order to select significant storm events for deriving Ire   of sub-basins, we considered those events that caused floods in the Master River. At first, daily rainfalls for the monsoon period (June-October) of the whole basin were computed by calculating Thiessen weights for IMD gridded rainfall data (25 km spatial resolution) in the GIS environment (Fig. S1 ). Thereafter, large storm spells that were associated with a rise of gauge height [above the danger level (DL) and extreme DL (EDL)] of the Master River were considered for the study following gauge data and reports of I&WD (2017) and I&WD (2021). Gauge height data was collected from the gauge station Gadghat because it is located near the outlet of the Master River.  3.5.5 Nash IUH model Nash-IUH (Nash, 1957 ) is a conceptual model in which catchment impulse response can be estimated as the outflow hydrograph obtained from the instantaneous inflow hydrograph through a cascade of n  number of linear reservoirs having an identical storage coefficient K . Though the triangular shape of GIUH would in some cases provide a satisfactory result (Rodríguez-Iturbe and Valdés, 1979 ), scale parameter (K ) and shape parameter (n ) of the Nash model is related to the Horton-Strahlar ordering scheme of the GIUH model to get its complete shape (Sahoo et al., 2006; Bhagwat et al., 2011 ). The governing equation of Nash-IUH is expressed as follows:(18) U t   = 1 K Γ ( n )   t K    n - 1   e - t / K       where U (t ) represents IUH ordinates in hr-1 , t  is the sampling interval in an hour and Γ is the gamma (γ) function. Rosso (1984)  related Nash parameters with the Horton-Strahler stream ordering scheme by equating the IR of Nash-IUH and GIUH models through a power regression (Rosso, 1984 ). This approach was successfully used in many investigations (Khaleghi et al., 2011; Grimaldi et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2019 ). The derived Nash parameters of Rosso (1984)  are expressed as follows.(19) n = 3.29 R b  / R a     0.78   R l 0.07       (20) K = 0.70 R a  / R b  R l        0.48   V - 1   L Ω        3.5.6 Initial evolution of FGP models and prioritization of sub-basins In order to find out the efficient FGP model for sub-basin prioritization, evolution and comparison of five FGP models were executed in two different stages. At the initial stage, the results of five morpho-hydrologic-based FGP models (CF, HD, AHP, PCA, and WSA) were evaluated using two statistical techniques namely, percentage of changes (Cp  ) (Eq. (21)  and intensity of changes (Ci  ) (Eq. (22)  (Ameri et al., 2018 ).(21) Δ P = N - N constant   N  × 100     (22) Δ I = ∑ i = 1  N  r i  r 2    N      where ΔP  represents Cp  , N  is the total number of sub-basins, N constant  is the number of sub-basins receiving the same rank by the two models, ΔI  is the Ci  , r 1  is the rank of the sub-basin in 1st model, r 2  depicts rank of the sub-basins in 2nd model.  3.5.7 Final evaluation of FGP models and prioritization of sub-basins The efficient FGP model from the initial evolution could be utilized to understand the effectiveness of morpho-hydrologic parameters in estimating quick peak flows. However, in the final evolution, the FGP models were validated with a hydrological model to cross-check the results obtained from the initial evolution. The qp   of Nash-GIUH based on average dynamic velocity (GIUHavg ) is used to evaluate the priority scores of FGP models using three statistical techniques i.e., correlation of determinant (R2 ), root mean square error (RMSE), Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE). Ranked values of FGP priority score and qp   of GIUHavg  were considered to assess these accuracy tests. The FGP model which has maximum similarity with the GIUHavg  model is considered as the most efficient model. Thus, the selected efficient FGP model/models from the initial and final evolution are finally used to prioritize sub-basins.    4 Results and discussions 4.1 Selection of morphometric parameters Fig. 4   shows the Pearson’s correlation coefficient of all fifteen morpho-hydrologic parameters. It is observed that the strong r values (≥0.90) of morpho-hydrologic parameters such as Y , L , A , Sf  , Rc  , Mrn  , and Rh   arise the multi-colinearity issues that may produce bias results in flood potentiality assessment. Therefore, the multi-collinearity test is performed on morphometric and hydrologic groups of parameters to select only effective runoff-generating parameters with their appropriate tolerance and VIF values in multiple linear regression (MLR) models. In the MLR model, VIF determines the degree to which the variance in morpho-hydrologic parameters is increased due to collinearity. Therefore, when the morpho-hydrologic parameters are not correlated to each other the VIF values will be low.
