Likewise, tolerance represents how much of the variance in morpho-hydrologic parameters can be explained by other parameters in the MLR model. When morpho-hydrologic parameters are highly correlated, the tolerance values tend to decrease. Therefore, using the appropriate threshold of VIF (<10) and tolerance (>0.1), a total of ten parameters that are independent of each other, are finally selected for further data analysis (Table 2  ). In the category of morphometric parameters SI , Rb  , Dd  , Fs  , Sf  , Rr   and HI  are selected as they fulfilled the criteria, whereas Y , CN  and Tc   are considered to be important maximum surface flow generating parameters in the hydrologic category.  4.2 Morphometric and hydrologic characteristics of sub-basins Fig. 5   shows the results of ten selected morpho-hydrologic parameters derived from the multi-colinearity test for all tributary sub-basins. These various morpho-hydrologic parameters have direct and indirect relationships with runoff potentiality. For the group-A parameters, higher the results, greater will be the FGP and vice versa. On the contrary, for the group-B parameters, lower the results, greater will be the FGP and vice versa. The results of the morpho-hydrologic parameters are classified into three classes i.e., high, medium and low given the natural break method. Detailed statistics of these parameters are also shown in Tables S9-S10 . 4.2.1 Morphometric parameters 4.2.1.1 Linear parameters Bifurcation ratio (Rb )  The Rb   of all sub-basins varies from 6.447 for SB-1 to 3.148 for SB-3. SB-1 followed by SB-10 and SB-4 witness the highest Rb , representing the high structural disturbances and maximum flood potentiality of that sub-basin. In contrast, the low mean Rb   values of SB-3, SB-5 and SB-7 refer to the low FGP of these sub-basins associated with delayed peak flows. Drainage Density (Dd )  The Dd   in all sub-basins ranges from 0.562 km/km2  for SB-9 to 0.784 km/km2  for SB-1. The highest Dd   value of SB-1 followed by SB-5 and SB-2 indicates the rugged topography, impermeable soil, and sparse vegetation that facilitates quick flow generation to storm events. Stream frequency (Fs)  In this study, the highest Fs   is observed 0.38 no./km2  for SB-5 followed by SB-1 and SB-3, whereas the lowest Fs   is detected for SB-10 (0.16 no./km2 ) followed by SB-9 and SB-7. Therefore, SB-1, SB-2 and SB-5 represent the high surface runoff potentiality and early qp   in flood hydrograph. On the contrary, SBs-7–10 refer to low FGP and delayed flood peaks. Sinuosity Index (SI)  Rivers of all sub-basins except SB-2 and SB-10 are straight in nature (SI <1.05). SB-2 and SB-10 are characterised by sinuous types of rivers, corresponding to gentle basin slopes and early mature stages of landform development. On the contrary, SB-5 (SI=1.019), SB-6 (SI=1.004) and SB-9 (1.017) are mainly characterised by the straight nature of channels and young stage of their basin development. TSI and HSI vary from 78.667 % and 21.333 % for SB10 to 98.864 % and 1.136 % for SB6, respectively. Therefore, the high TSI and the low HSI of SB-6 indicate the strong control of topography on stages of basin development and river dynamics (Chaubey et al., 2019 ). Statistics of SI, TSI and HIS are given in Table S11 .  4.2.1.2 Areal parameter Shape factor (Sf )  The Sf   is an important determinant of the basin shape and thereby affecting runoff generation processes. The highest value of Sf   is observed in SB-1 (Sf   = 6.137) followed by SB-2 (Sf   = 5.257) and SB-9 (Sf   = 4.955). Consequently, these sub-basins are characterised by moderate to low relief, long Tc   and delayed flood peaks. On the contrary, the low Sf   is detected in SB-3 (Sf   = 2.593), SB-5 (Sf   = 2.69), and SB-4 (Sf   = 2.792), representing circular basin shape, short lag time and sharp peak of the hydrograph.  4.2.1.3 Relief parameters Relative relief (Rr )  In the present study, Rr   varies from 0.055 for SB-8 to 0.132 for SB-4. SB-4, SB-6 and SB-5 account for high Rr   values which are 0.132, 0.124 and 0.111, respectively. Therefore, they imply high basin relief, an early mature to the young stage of geomorphic development of the basin, high surface runoff potentiality and early flood peaks (Mahala, 2020; Ghasemlounia and Utlu, 2021 ). Hypsometric curve and integral  The hypsometric curve and integral of sub-basins are shown in Fig. 6   and Table S10 . HI  ranges from 0.329 for SB-9 to 0.496 for SB-3. Moderate HI  (0.6 ≥ HI ≥0.35) and slightly convex downward and S-shaped hypsometric curves demonstrate that all sub-basins except SB-9 are in the early mature stages of landscape development. Therefore, SB-1–8 and SB-10 are characterised by moderate to high stream power, moderate to high sediment yield capacity and high surface runoff potentiality (Strahler, 1952; Soomro et al., 2022 ).   4.2.2 Hydrologic parameters 4.2.2.1 Average basin slope (Y) The average basin slope in all sub-basins varies from 0.026 m/m for SB-9 and SB-10 to 0.035 m/m for SB-1. Relatively high basin slopes (>0.030 m/m) have been observed for SBs-1–6, indicating the generation of flow in a shorter period, whereas low and gentle slopes facilitate high infiltration and high storage capacity of sub-basins (Abdelkader et al., 2021; Singh et al., 2014a ).  4.2.2.2 Curve number (CN) Weighted CN  under normal conditions (Antecedent soil moisture condition-II) is calculated from LULC and HSG for all sub-basins (Table S8  and Fig. S1 ). CN  varies across all sub-basins, ranging from 65.348 for SB-5 to 78.877 for SB-10. A high CN  value corresponds to high flood discharge, whereas a lower CN  value specifies a lower potential for surface runoff. Therefore, SB-10 has the potential to produce high discharge and an early flood peak compared to SB-5.  4.2.2.3 Time of concentration (Tc ) Tc   ranges from 10.96 hrs for SB-6 to 38.34 hrs for SB-1. Therefore, SB-6 followed by SB-3 (12.26 hrs) and SB-4 (13.33 hrs) is the most potential basin to generate early flow peaks, compared to SB-1, followed by SB-9 (34.24 hrs).    4.3 Flood generation potentiality of sub-basins After selecting the ten morpho-hydrologic parameters, five ranking methods are utilised to assess FGP according to their priority scores. A high priority score leads to a greater flood generation potentiality of a particular sub-basin and vice versa. Therefore, the priority scores of all FGP models are classified into three FGP classes from high to low given the natural break method by which prioritization of sub-basins is made (Farhan et al., 2017; Ghasemlounia and Utlu, 2021 ) (Fig. 7  ). FGP priority scores and their corresponding prioritization ranks for all sub-basins Tables S12 S16 . 4.3.1 Compound factor (CF) In the CF method, morphometric ranks of parameters and their priority scores are given in Table S12 . Table S12  and Fig. 7  show that the priority score of CF varies from 6.9 for SB-5 and SB-6 to 3.4 for SB-9. Therefore, the higher FGP is found in SB-5 and SB-6, followed by SB-4 and SB-3 (FGP>6). The lowest FGP is observed in SB-9 followed by SB-7, SB-8 and SB-10, expressing the lower FGP of these sub-basins (FGP<4.601).  4.3.2 Hazard degree (HD) The priority score of HD of all sub-basins varies from 3.719 for SB-5 to 2.084 for SB-9, representing SB-5 as the most hazardous and SB-9 as the least hazardous sub-basins (Table S13 ). Fig. 7  shows that SB-3 to SB-6 come under the high FGP class (>3.248), indicating high flood probability, whereas low FGP values (<2.563) are disclosed in SB-7-SB-10, meaning low flood mitigating measures are needed for these sub-basins.  4.3.3 Analytical hierarchy process (AHP) Following a decision goal of FGP, results show that the comparison matrix has a CR  of 0.034, indicating the decisions are consistent. Based on the AHP results, maximum relative weights are found in Tc   (0.228) followed by Y  (0.178), CN  (0.133) and Rr   (0.113). Maximum weightage on hydrological factors followed by relief and drainage network factors has also been found in some other flood hazard studies (Stefanidis and Stathis, 2013; Balasubramani et al., 2019; Costache and Bui, 2020 ). The priority scores and its corresponding prioritization ranks of all sub-basins are shown in Table S14 , which varies from 0.119 for SB-6 to 0.079 for SB-9. Therefore, the maximum priority score of SB-6 indicates the highest FGP of that sub-basin followed by SB-3 and SB-4 (Table S14  and Fig. 7 ).  4.3.4 Principal component analysis (PCA) The total variance explained by all morpho-hydrologic parameters shows that only the first three PCs had an initial eigenvalue greater than 1. These three PCs explained 86.178 % of the total variability in the original variables. In the initial component matrix, no strong correlation is found between PCs and morpho-hydrologic parameters. Therefore, to achieve very strong correlations (> ±0.9), a varimax-rotated component matrix is adopted. PC-1 illustrates a very strong positive correlation with Y  (0.956), Fs   (0.944), and Dd   (0.918). PC-2 accounts for a strong positive correlation with Tc   (0.960) and Sf   (0.952). PC-3 does not show very strong correlations with parameters, but strong or good positive correlations of PC-3 are found with SI and Rb  . Selected parameters having very strong correlations with PCs (> ±0.9) are used to determine the priority score of sub-basins. Results showed that the priority score varies from 8.6 for SB-3 to 2 for SB-9, indicating the highest and lowest FGP of these sub-basins, respectively. Details of all priority ranks and prioritization classes are shown in Table S15  and Fig. 7 , respectively.  4.3.5 Weighted sum analysis (WSA) The results of the correlation matrix reveal that the maximum relative weight is assigned to Dd   (0.23) followed by Y  (0.206) and Fs   (0.185), whereas the least relative weight is allotted to CN  (−0.104). Relative weights imply that Dd   has maximum influence on other parameters, whereas CN  is the most independent parameter in the data frame. The priority score of WSA varies from 8.177 for SB-5 to 1.992 for SB-9 (Table S16 ). Classified priority scores and sub-basin prioritization ranks are shown in Fig. 7  and Table S16 , respectively, where SB-1, SB-3 and SB-4 account for high priority scores, corresponding to high prioritization for mitigating floods.   4.4 Initial evolution of FGP models and prioritization of sub-basins Priority scores of all five FGP models are distinctive in nature, however, their ranking orders are closely similar (Tables S12-S16 ). SBs 1–6 witness moderate to high FGP, whereas SBs-7–10 show low FGP. Therefore, at the initial stage of evolution, the selection of the best FGP model as well as the sub-basin prioritization model among all five models has been made by two statistical methods, Cp   and Ci  . Results of, Cp   and Ci   are shown in Tables S17 and S18 , respectively. Results of Cp   show that AHP secured the title of the more accurate and efficient model with the highest average Cp   of 58 % after WSA (52 %) and PCA (50 %). Results of Ci   show that AHP again ranks as the top method with the highest value of Ci   of 5.792. WSA and HD secure second and third positions, respectively. Therefore, initially, it could be stated that AHP performs well to express flood potentiality in sub-basins and to prioritize them according to their ranking classes (Table S14 ).  4.5 Derivation of Nash-GIUH model 4.5.1 Extreme rainstorms and floods The monthly rainfall of 2017–2021 and daily rainfall of 2017 and 2021 along with the gauge height of Master River during monsoon (June-October) are shown in Fig. 8  . The period of June to October is considered as the season of the Indian monsoon, therefore, excess monthly rainfall in July 2017 and September 2021 caused havoc flood disasters in the lower part of the basin under the influence of the tropical cyclones (I&WD, 2017; I&WD, 2021 ). Therefore, these two months of 2017 and 2021 were considered to select storm events for deriving V  of GIUH models. In these two months, storm events of mid-July 2017 and mid-September 2021 caused massive floods in Shilabati as the gauge height crossed EDL (Fig. 8 b-c). These storm-generated flood reports were stated in the report of I&WD (2017, 2021). Therefore, IMDAA 1-hourly rainfall data of 12 km spatial resolution was utilised to determine the four most significant storm hyetographs from mid-July 2017 and mid-September 2021. In Fig. 9  , the spatial distribution of this coarse resolution storm rainfalls was depicted by preparing new raster layers (30 m spatial resolution) by interpolating coarse resolution rainfall points using the inverse distance weighted method for the mid-July 2017 and mid-September 2021 storms, representing the total storm rainfalls. Detailed statistics of storm events are given in Table S19 .  4.5.2 Derivation of excess rainfall intensity and dynamic velocity Table S19  and Fig. 10   show the distribution of Ire   of the selected storm events for all tributary sub-basins. The maximum average Ire   is found in SB-3 (3.870 mm/hr) followed by SB-5 and SB-2, representing the maximum contribution of surface runoff and FGP (Fig. 10 ). Results of derived V  from all Ire   of storms are shown in Fig. 11  . After determining all four velocities corresponding to four Ire ,  a total of five velocities with an ensemble average velocity (V avg ) are used to derive five GIUH models. Fig. 12   shows that SB-1 ranks highest with the V avg  of 0.669 m.s−1  followed by SB-3 (0.643 m.s−1 ) and SB-9, representing the probability of high runoff in these sub-basins.  4.5.3 Derivation of Nash-GIUH parameters The parameters of the Nash-GIUH models and the complete shape of the GIUH using the Nash model are shown in Table 3   and Fig. 12 , respectively. The parameter q p   of Nash-GIUH models is shown in Fig.13  . Results of all Nash-GIUH models according to each velocity are discussed below: 4.5.3.1 Dynamic velocity 1 (V 1 )  Storm-1 is used to derive V 1  and the corresponding first Nash-GIUH (GIUH1) model. The maximum and minimum qp   of GIUH1 are found in SB-6 and SB-1 which are 0.124 hr-1  and 0.020 hr-1 , respectively. The highest tp   (25.986 hr-1 ) is associated with SB-1 which makes SB-1 flattened in shape, whereas the shape of GIUH is the sharpest for SB-6 with the lowest tp   (4.041 hr-1 ), expressing ultimate hazard probability in the downstream.  4.5.3.2 Dynamic velocity 2 (V 2 )  The V 2  is derived from Storm-2 to compute 2nd Nash-GIUH (GIUH2). Parameters of GIUH2 show that the highest qp   is found 0.093 hr-1  for SB-6 followed by SB-5 (0.092 hr-1 ), whereas the lowest qp   is found 0.026 hr-1  for SB-1 followed by SB-8 (0.027 hr-1 ). The highest tp   of 19.729 hrs is observed in SB-8, whereas the lowest tp   is associated with SB-6. Therefore, SB-6 and SB-5 produce a sharp shape of GIUH and early flow peaks. On the contrary, SB-1 has a low potential to contribute to flood discharge in the Master River with its delayed qp  .  4.5.3.3 Dynamic velocity 3 (V 3 )  Third Nash-GIUH (GIUH3) is computed with the V 3  derived from the Storm-3. SB-6 is identified as the most effective flood-producing sub-basin with the highest qp   (0.117 hr-1 ) and lowest tp   (17.034 hrs) followed by SB-5 and SB-3. On the contrary, SB-8 generates flattened GIUH with the lowest qp   (hr-1 ) and most delayed tp   (89.623 hrs) followed by SB-9.  4.5.3.4 Dynamic velocity 4 (V 4 )  Fourth Nash-GIUH (GIUH4) model is prepared by the V 4  derived from storm-4. Parameter V 4  is the highest among all velocities which varies from 0.389 for SB-6 to 0.888 for SB-9. SB-3 with comparatively high velocity (0.742 m.s−1 ) and favourable geomorphological conditions generates maximum flood probability due to the sharpest shape of the GIUH4 characterised by the highest qp   of 0.105 hr-1  and lowest tp   of 5.095 hr followed by SB-5 and SB-6. In contrast, SB-1 reveals the lowest contribution in influencing flood in Master River with a flattened shape of the unit hydrograph because of the lowest qp   (0.026 hr-1 ) and highest tp   (19.477 hrs) followed by SB-10 and SB-2.  4.5.3.5 Average dynamic velocity (V avg )  It is found from the above result that SB-6 and SB-3 are the most predominant sub-basins for all Nash-GIUH models to contribute flow in the main river in a shorter period. On the other hand, SB-1 and SB-8 are discovered as the least significant sub-basins in terms of basin responses. Therefore, for making the ultimate decision, GIUHavg  is considered which is formed by V avg . In GIUHavg , the highest qp   (0.106 hr-1 ) with the shortest tp   (4.718 hrs) is found in SB-6 followed by SB-5, SB-3 and SB-4, implying that SB-6 is the most important sub-basin to generate maximum flow with shortest time resulted by relatively short L Ω , high Horton’s ratios and moderately high V avg . SB-1 followed by SB-8 and SB-9 generate a low risk of flooding, though SB-1 is characterised by high Horton’s parameters and the highest V avg . It is understood from the results that velocity is not a significant factor in influencing the shape of GIUH, because having the maximum V avg  and high Horton’s parameters, SB-1 has low flood probability. On the contrary, with moderately high V avg  and Horton’s parameters SB-3 to SB-6 have the potential to generate early flow peaks. It occurs because Hortion’s ratio parameters are less sensitive to GIUH and the shape of the GIUH is strongly controlled by L Ω  (Niyazi et al., 2021 ). Moreover, the river velocity is positively related to basin area, flow path length, number of streams and CN (El–Fakharany and Mansour, 2021 ). Moreover, we have also found moderate-strong correspondences (r > ±0.6) between some morpho-hydrologic parameters and qp   of GIUHavg . Where sub-basins are small and circular (low Sf  ), landforms are in their early mature stage of development (high HI ), the terrain is rugged and undulating (high Rr  ) and Tc   is short, the short tp   and high qp   (sharp shape of GIUHavg ) are detected (SBs 3–6). Therefore, in hydrological response analysis of sub-basins, geomorphologic and physical characteristics play an important role in tropical plateau fringe areas than the climatic factor (velocity).    4.6 Final evolution of FGP models and prioritization of sub-basins The final evolution of all sub-basins is performed by comparing the ranks of FGP priority scores and rank of qp   of GIUHavg . The qp   of GIUHavg  is classified into three classes using the natural breaking method to match the classes of FGP models. Thereafter, the ranks of all ten sub-basins are determined from the priority score of all five FGP models and qp   of GIUHavg . Results show that priority scores of AHP and qp   of GIUHavg  are aligned well after CF-GIUHavg  and PCA-GIUHavg  pairs. The high priority scores of the AHP model and the high qp   values of GIUHavg  model are both found in SB-5–6, whereas SBs-7–10 disclose the low priority scores of AHP model and low qp   values of GIUHavg . Therefore, like initial evolution, again AHP is proven to be the best model in the final evolution, that can estimate the hydrological processes related to extreme events. The lowest RMSE (1.732) and the highest R2  (0.669) and NSE (0.636) for the AHP-GUIH pair make AHP the most useful model in estimating hydrologic behaviour of ungauged sub-basins (Table 4  ). Therefore, the final flood priority of sub-basins is assigned by sub-basin-wise priority scores and their corresponding ranks from AHP model selected from both the initial and final evolutions. The highest priority for basin management and flood mitigation is assigned to SB-6 followed by SB-3 and SB-4. The group of SB-3 to SB-6 falls into high prioritized class, whereas moderate priority is assigned to SBs 1–2 and SB-10. On the contrary, SB 7–9 are allocated to the low flood priority class (Table S14  and Figs. 7, 14  ). It is well observed that in the field of hydrology, AHP gives optimum results. Fifteen morpho-hydrologic parameters that were initially selected and reduced to ten, successfully portray the role of basin geomorphologic and hydrologic characteristics to estimate the FGP of sub-basins. In the AHP model, Tc  , Y , CN , Rr   and HI  are emerged to be the important parameters for FGP analysis in which Tc   (r = -0.86), Rr   (r = 0.88) and HI  (r = 0.64) have moderate to strong correlations with qp   of GIUHavg . This means that with decreasing Tc   and increasing Rr   and HI , surface flow takes a shorter time to create its peak in the IUH. However, qp   has a negligible to weak correlation with Y  (R=0.27) and Dd   (R=0.6). Though CN is positively related to FGP, a weak negative relationship is found between CN  and qp  , because soil and LULC properties have negligible correspondences with geomorphologic parameters. Therefore, in estimating the hydrologic responses of the basin, the roles of geomorphologic parameters in terms of morpho-hydrologic parameters of Tc , Rr   and HI  are found effective which makes AHP as a strong technique in this improved hydro-geomorphologic-based basin prioritization study. Therefore, the study successfully depicts the usage of an integrated hydro-geomorphological approach in estimating FGP as well as flood prioritization model in those ungauged sub-basins which trigger floods in the lower part of the Master River. Moreover, the study suggests adaptation of either the AHP-FGP model or the GIUHavg  model for sub-basin prioritization in a data-scare environment. The study also suggests the adaptation of useful structural and non-structural measures for SB-3 to SB-6 such as weirs, small barrages, detention basins, retention ponds, channel widening, afforestation, soil and water conservation practices, flood monitoring stations etc. to mitigate high flow rate.   5 Conclusions Geomorphologic parameters have a long-established tradition in analysing the behaviour of hydrologic processes in ungauged rivers, however, the role of tributary sub-basins in triggering flood in the Master River by considering morpho-hydrologic parameter-based FGP models and geomorphologic parameter-based Nash-IUH model (Nash-GIUH) is significantly undiscovered in tropical plateau fringe ungauged river basins in Eastern India. Shilabati is one such basin where flow generated from its tributaries influences the flood phenomenon in the Master River. Therefore, the study aims to prioritize sub-basins to mitigate floods in the lower part of the Master River by this integrated hydro-geomorphologic approach and to understand the geomorphologic responses to the hydrological behaviour of sub-basins. The study reveals that a total of ten morpho-hydrologic parameters are selected for the study and among them Dd  , Fs  , Tc  , Y , Rb  , Rr   and HI  are recognised as more relevant independent parameters for FGP resulting from AHP, WSA and PCA models. Initial and final evolutions of FGP models show that AHP is the most accurate model in estimating the flood potentiality of sub-basins for their prioritization. The AHP-FGP model assigns ultimate priority to SB-6 due to its highest FGP score followed by SB-3, SB-4 and SB-5. Moderate prioritization class is assigned to SB-1, SB-2, and SB-10, whereas low prioritization class is assigned to SB-7, SB-8 and SB-9. This rank of prioritization is well-fitted with the GIUHavg  model. The highest qp   (0.106 hr-1 ) and shortest tp   (4.718 hrs) are observed in SB-6 followed by SB-5, and SB-3, whereas the lowest qp   (=0.024 hr-1 ) and longest tp   (=21.02 hrs) are observed in SB-1 followed by SB-8 and SB-9. Therefore, morpho-hydrologic parameter-based AHP-FGP model performs well in comparison with GIUH models. Hence, SB-6 followed by SB-3, SB-4 and SB-5 needs substantial structural and non-structural flood preventive measures to control their flow and to mitigate future flood situations in Master River Shilabati. In addition, the moderate to strong correlations of Tc  , HI  and Rr   with the qp   of GIUHavg  have justified the linkages of geomorphologic parameters with the hydrologic behaviour of sub-basins. Although GIUH is not utilised to derive DSRO hydrographs using excess rainfall pulses from selected storms to simulate rainfall-runoff processes, the similarities between AHP-FGP and Nash-GIUH models permit the use of either model to infer quick flow behaviour in ungauged rivers. However, for future research scopes, the study suggests that Nash-GIUH or other SUH-derived rainfall-runoff models based on design storms from observed storm events or stochastic rainfall models, can produce design flood hydrographs valuable for the design of hydraulic structures for ungauged basins (Kim and Onof, 2020 ). Besides, integrated hydrologic and hydrodynamic models can also provide insights into flood discharge and the corresponding inundated areas for basin prioritization purposes (Zhao et al., 2024 ).
1 Introduction Fluvial dikes or levees are engineered structures that confine the river flow at high discharges and provide flood protection. Several mechanisms can lead to a dike failure, such as overtopping (Rifai et al., 2017 ), slumping failure (Elalfy et al., 2018 ), piping (Vorogushyn et al., 2009 ), seepage (Onda et al., 2019 ), and the weakening of some parts of the dike caused by the actions of burrowing animals and poor maintenance (Orlandini et al., 2015 ). The failure of a fluvial dike can induce major flooding in the hinterland with detrimental consequences to local economies and potentially life losses, especially in urbanized areas. Thus, the accurate prediction of the dike breach hydrograph is of paramount importance for the estimation of flood hazard and for the determination of safe evacuation routes, especially when considering the fact that people tend to settle within flood sheltered areas (Haer et al., 2020 ). This kind of river flood risk is expected to increase in the future, as more people are exposed to floods (Tellman et al., 2021 ) and extreme precipitation is projected to increase (Madsen et al., 2014 ). The discharge partitioning in a channel with a side opening is inherently a 2D and 3D flow phenomenon (Stilmant et al., 2013; Li et al., 2021; Dewals et al., 2023 ) with flow separation, flow recirculation, and helicoidal flow near the side opening (Michelazzo et al., 2015 ). The lateral flow discharge through a side opening has been modelled successfully using 2D models (Roger et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2013; Echeverribar et al., 2019; Shustikova et al., 2020 ). Recent studies have coupled 2D hydraulic models with physically-based erosion models (Kakinuma and Shimizu, 2014; Elalfy et al., 2018; Dazzi et al., 2019 ). Also, 1D-2D hydraulic models were extended using additional computational elements, such as a physically-based description of the breach formation and evolution (Viero et al., 2013 ). Another example is the use of probabilistic frameworks for possible locations and timing of breaches along a dike with the aid of fragility curves for various failure mechanisms (Vorogushyn et al., 2010; Bomers et al., 2019; D’Oria et al., 2019; Maranzoni et al., 2022 ). Despite recent advancements (Dazzi et al., 2019; Ferrari et al., 2020 ), such models have either long computational times or large uncertainties regarding their parameterizations. This can become prohibitive for systematic analyses of the flood hazard from dike breaches since breaches at different dike locations can lead to different flood patterns. There is a need for simpler and faster modelling procedures that approximate the complex hydrodynamic processes near and through a dike breach. This is particularly relevant for sensitivity analysis (Schmitz et al., 2023a ) and for inclusion in river models, which are also subject to further simplifications (Kitsikoudis et al., 2020 ), for systematic flood risk assessment. Side weir equations provide an easy parameterization of the lateral discharge through a side opening. While side weir equations have been applied to fluvial dike breaches (Kamrath et al., 2006; Yu et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2016 ), the number of such studies is small compared to those modelling frontal dike breaches or earthen embankment breach as a frontal weir (ASCE/EWRI Task Committee, 2011; Schmocker and Hager, 2012; Wu, 2013 ). As a result, the accuracy of the side weir equations and the parameterization of the side weir discharge coefficient, C d    , for breaches in fluvial dikes have not been thoroughly evaluated yet. Mignot et al. (2020)  assessed the predictive capability of eleven semi-empirical formulations for C d    . To this end, they used laboratory experiments of flow intrusion into buildings and considered the building openings (doors, windows, and gates) as rectangular side weirs. The computed side discharge was highly dependent on the formulation of C d    . The applicability of such semi-empirical equations to fluvial dike breaches is not straightforward. Dike breaches exhibit a time-dependent complex geometry, i.e., a dynamically evolving and uneven breach profile (Rifai et al., 2017 ), that depends on the discharge in the main channel, and the dike geometry and erodibility (Schmitz et al., 2021 ). Rifai et al. (2017, 2018)  identified three stages during the development of a non-cohesive dike breach caused by overtopping (Fig. 1  ). Initially, right after overtopping occurs, the erosion rate of the dike is low because the flow depth and the velocity above the dike are also small. As the flow depth and the velocity above the dike breach increase, erosion intensifies rapidly with large water level variations near the breach (Al-Hafidh et al., 2022 ) and a downstream shift of the breach center. Finally, in the last stage, the upstream side of the breach remains almost fixed, and the breach grows more slowly in the downstream direction. Similar observations were reported by Michelazzo et al. (2018)  and Kakinuma and Shimizu (2014)  from laboratory-scale and field-scale experiments, respectively. Overall, the dike breaching process is accelerated and the final shape of the breach gets larger with increasing water level and flow discharge in the river (Yu et al., 2013; Rifai et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2018 ). The dike composition also affects the breach expansion (Yu et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2018; Rifai et al., 2021 ), so does the channel width (Schmitz et al., 2023b ) and the dike geometry, with dikes with larger volume per unit width inducing a more gradual enlargement of the breach during the rapid expansion phase (Schmitz et al., 2021 ). The breach location and its final shape govern to a large extent the flood inundation (Tadesse and Fröhle, 2020 ). The water level in the hinterland (Rifai et al., 2018 ) and the presence or not of riprap also alter the breach development (Ahadiyan et al., 2022 ). The present study investigates the suitability of different parameterizations for lateral flow through dike breaches for the incorporation of 3D flow processes into simpler and faster models. Specifically, this study assesses the performance of eleven semi-empirical side weir equations applied in two different modelling frameworks to determine the lateral outflow discharge through a breach in a dike that is parallel to the flow main direction along a straight river reach. The assessment is performed in two frameworks: by combining the side weir equations with either a spatially lumped flow model based on mass conservation or a one-dimensional flow model based on the shallow water equations. The semi-empirical side weir equations, coupled with the two models, are firstly tested with data from channels with fixed side openings and secondly with data from a channel with a dynamic evolution of a dike breach. Section 2  presents the numerical models used in this work. Section 3 briefly presents the experimental data from the literature that are used for the validation of the developed models (three experiments with a lateral outflow through a fixed geometry and one experiment with an evolving dike breach geometry). Section 4 presents how the breach discharge predicted by the semi-empirical equations compares with the experimental measurements. The performance and limitations of the models are discussed in Section 5. Finally, conclusions are drawn in Section 6.  2 Modelling of the lateral flow discharge through a dike breach 2.1 Discharge coefficient for lateral side weirs The lateral flow discharge through a breach in a dike that runs parallel to the flow direction in a straight river reach with width W    (Fig. 2  ) can be simplified as a flow over a broad-crested rectangular side weir. In such a case, the incoming flow discharge from the upstream of the channel, Q i n     , is divided at the location of the dike breach into the lateral flow discharge, Q b    , towards the hinterland and the outgoing flow discharge, Q o u t     , towards the downstream of the channel. In a straight channel, the lateral flow discharge over a rectangular side weir is expressed as:(1) Q b  = 2 3  C d  2 g h - p    3    L s      where C d     is the side weir discharge coefficient, h    is the flow depth in the main channel upstream of the side opening, p    is the crest height of the side weir, L s     is the length of the side weir, and g    is the acceleration of gravity. The discharge coefficient, C d    , is typically estimated from analytical and semi-empirical relationships based on the weir and flow characteristics. Similarly to Mignot et al. (2020) , eleven relationships from the literature for the calculation of C d     for sharp-crested weirs are used in this study (Table 1  ).  2.2 Numerical models for flow through a dike breach Two simplified models were developed using MATLAB  software to predict the lateral flow discharge, Q b    , through a side opening representing a dike breach. Section 2.2.1 presents a lumped model and Section 2.2.2 presents a one-dimensional finite volume model. Both models are coupled with Eq. (1)  and with an equation for the determination of C d     (Table 1 ). 2.2.1 Lumped model (zero-dimensional) The lumped model is based on a side weir discharge equation for the determination of Q b    (Eq. (1) ) and on the mass balance equation in a control volume, which writes:(2) dV  dt   = A xy   ( h xy   )  d h xy    dt   = Q in   - Q b  ( h xy   )  - Q out   ( h xy   )      where V    is the volume of water in the control volume, t    is the time, A xy      is the horizontal surface area of the control volume, and h xy      is the flow depth spatially averaged across the area A xy     . This numerical model estimates the spatially averaged flow depth h xy      for every timestep dt   , based on the value of h xy      in the previous timestep, the measured value of Q i n     , an experimental rating curve for Q o u t     , and the value of Q b     computed at the previous timestep with Eq. (1) . The surface area A xy      is considered as constant in each case.  2.2.2 Spatially distributed model (one-dimensional) The spatially distributed model solves numerically the one-dimensional Saint-Venant equations, i.e., the conservation of mass (Eq. (3) ) and the conservation of momentum (Eq. (4) ):(3) ∂ A  ∂ t   + ∂ Q  ∂ x   = - q b      (4) ∂ Q  ∂ t   + ∂ ∂ x   Q U + g A y    + g A S f  - S 0     = - U q b      where A    is the flow cross-sectional area, Q    is the discharge in the channel, q b     is the specific lateral discharge through the side opening, U    is the longitudinal velocity averaged over the cross-section, y    is the cross-section average of the depth, S f     is the friction slope, and S 0     is the bed slope. By considering U = Q / A   , expressing y    as a function of the cross-sectional area, y = f ( A )   , and estimating the friction slope with the Manning formula, the only remaining unknowns in Eqs. (3) and (4)  are Q    and A   . Eqs. (3) and (4)  are discretized spatially with a finite volume numerical scheme (Kerger et al., 2011 ) and in time with a two-step Runge-Kutta algorithm. q b     is computed on each spatial step, Δ x   , as a function of the local water depth and the local height of the side weir crest (h    and p    are considered constant over each cell). Δ x    was 1 cm in the experiments of Michelazzo et al. (2015)  and Mignot et al. (2020) , and 10 cm in the experiments of Roger et al. (2009)  and Rifai et al. (2017)  (see Section 3 ).   2.3 Initial and boundary conditions The initial water level in the main channel for each simulation was the same as the water level under steady flow conditions with the prescribed incoming discharge, Q i n     , of the corresponding experiment but without a dike breach. In practice, this water level was computed using our numerical models without considering any breach discharge. The equilibrium breach discharge was obtained when the flow reached a new steady state in the presence of a dike breach. The downstream boundary condition was a rating curve at the weir (Roger et al., 2009 ), sluice gate (Michelazzo et al., 2015 ), crested tailgate (Mignot et al., 2020 ), or perforated plate (Rifai et al., 2017 ) of each experiment.   3 Experimental data The accuracy of the eleven semi-empirical side discharge equations (Section 2.1 ) is evaluated by comparing the modelling results with experimental data from the literature. The considered experimental data comprise data from (a) experiments with a fixed side opening (Roger et al., 2009; Michelazzo et al., 2015; Mignot et al., 2020 ) and (b) experiments with a dynamically evolving side opening (Rifai et al., 2017 ). In all experiments, the side opening was parallel to the main flow direction and in a straight channel (Fig. 2 ), which had uniform and steady flow characteristics. The experimental setups and methods used to generate these data are briefly described in this section and summarized in Table 2  . The setup used for each test campaign is displayed in Fig. 3  . More details can be found in the referenced studies. 3.1 Experiments with fixed geometry of the side opening 3.1.1 Experiments of Roger et al. (2009)  Roger et al. (2009)  carried out laboratory experiments of a dike breach in a 1  m-wide rectangular flume. The rectangular side opening was 0.7  m long and its crest had zero height, simulating the complete failure of a dike. The lateral discharge through the side opening was propagated into a 3.5 × 4.0  m2  basin that was at the same level as the flume bottom and was made of glass. The water flowed freely off the edges of the basin, while at the downstream end of the flume the water flowed over a weir. The tested inflow discharges were equal to 0.2 m3 /s and 0.3  m3 /s and the tested undisturbed flow depths were 0.4 and 0.5  m, resulting in four experimental combinations in total.  3.1.2 Experiments of Michelazzo et al. (2015)  Michelazzo et al. (2015)  conducted laboratory experiments in a 30  cm wide recirculating flume with a slope of 0.1 % and rectangular cross section. Fine gravel was glued on the bed of the flume to provide roughness. A vertical sluice gate was placed at the downstream extremity of the flume to adjust the flow depth. A rectangular side weir with zero height diverted a portion of the flow to a lateral channel at a lower level, which conveyed water toward a storage basin through its downstream end. Ten different side weir lengths were tested and varied from 3 to 47  cm. In all cases, the incoming discharge was about 0.01  m3 /s while the sluice gate at the downstream end of the flume was always set in the same way.  3.1.3 Experiments of Mignot et al. (2020)  Mignot et al. (2020)  investigated the flow intrusion from a flooded street into buildings through openings, such as doors, gates, and windows, during urban floods. The flow through building openings, without nearby obstacles, can be considered as flow through a rectangular side weir with zero and non-zero crest height for doors/gates and windows, respectively. Alternatively, these cases can represent the total or partial collapse of a dike section. The experiments were carried out in a 0.79  m-wide flume with a smooth bed and a rectangular cross section. The slope of the flume was 0.18 % and the flow depth was regulated by a sharp crested tailgate at the downstream end of the flume. The side opening was 7.9 cm long for the cases with zero weir crest height and 15.4  cm long for the cases with non-zero weir crest height. Four and two inflow discharges were tested with zero and non-zero weir crest height, respectively. Mignot et al. (2020)  also investigated the impact of urban obstacles, such as parked cars, on the flow intrusion but these cases are not considered in this study.   3.2 Experiments of Rifai et al. (2017)  with dynamic evolution of the geometry of the side opening Rifai et al. (2017)  investigated the evolution of a breach in a sandy homogeneous trapezoidal dike due to overtopping. The experiments were conducted in a 10  m-long and 1  m-wide flume with a trapezoidal cross section. The erodible dike stretched over 3 m along the right side of the flume and separated the flume from a 4.3  m x 2.5  m area behind the dike. The bottom of this area and of the main flume was coated with impermeable whitewash to ensure a uniform bed roughness over the entire setup. A small notch was carved at the crest of the dike to initiate erosion at this specific spot. Once the dike breach began forming, its evolution was monitored with a nonintrusive laser profilometry technique (Rifai et al., 2019 ). Rifai et al. (2017)  conducted experiments for many inflow discharges and downstream boundary conditions. In this work, we focus on four experiments based on four different inflow discharges ranging from 0.02  m3 /s to 0.05  m3 /s. In all cases, a perforated plate was used at the flume downstream extremity to regulate the water level. In the experiments of Rifai et al. (2017)  the side opening evolved and grew bigger in time since the dike was made of sand that is eroded by the flow. In the cases with fixed geometry of the side opening, the lateral flow could be considered steady; however, in the experiments of Rifai et al. (2017)  the flow that goes through the side opening depends on time. For each time step, the crest height of the side weir, i.e., the breach in the dike, was determined from a scanned longitudinal line in the middle of the dike in the transverse direction. The profile of the dike breach is typically irregular; however, the models require a single crest height, either for the whole dike breach for the lumped model or for each spatial step Δ x     for the spatially distributed model. For the spatially distributed model, the crest height of each spatial step was chosen equal to the breach elevation at the center of the step, which was obtained using a linear interpolation between scanning measurements of the breach (spatial resolution of 1 cm). The side weir equations were then applied on each one-dimensional cell individually. For the lumped model, a representative crest height was chosen equal to the 15th percentile of the elevation of the scanned points along the dike crest center line that were within the dike breach.   4 Results Sections 4.1 and 4.2 present a comparison between the results obtained from the two numerical models of Section 1.1 coupled with the side weir discharge coefficients from Table 1  and the corresponding measurements from the experimental configurations with fixed and dynamic geometry of the side opening, respectively. 4.1 Side opening with fixed geometry As shown in Fig. 4  , for the four experimental cases of Roger et al. (2009) , the lumped model performed better than the spatially distributed model in estimating the lateral discharge Q  b      through the side opening for almost every C  d      formula that was tested. A notable difference is that the spatially distributed model always underestimated Q  b     , while the lumped model generated more variable results. This difference may be understood by considering that, in practice, the water level significantly drops in the vicinity of the side breach due to water acceleration. This trend is captured by the one-dimensional model. Conversely, the lumped model overestimates the water level close to the breach as it only considers an averaged value over the entire control volume. As a result, using Eq. (1)  with the average water height in the lumped model leads to larger estimations of the breach discharge. Both models, and particularly the spatially distributed model, performed better for the smaller discharge and the larger flow depth, i.e., for smaller inflow Froude number. The height of the side weir crest in the experiments of Roger et al. (2009)  was zero and as a result the C  d      formula of Bagheri et al. (2014)  was not tested because the weir crest height, p   , is used in the denominator. From the remaining discharge coefficient equations in Table 1 , the equations of Subramanya and Awasthy (1972)  and Borghei et al. (1999)  with the lumped model performed best on average, while the spatially distributed model was most successful when coupled with the equation of Nadesamoorthy and Thomson (1972) , followed by Yu-Tek (1972) . The equation of Singh et al. (1994)  performed worst with both models. However, it needs to be noted that while the discharge coefficient equations were compared with the same data, the semi-empirical equations, such as the equation of Singh et al. (1994) , were developed in different data ranges (Table 1 ). As a result, some of them were used out of their calibration range, which is the case with the Singh et al. (1994)  formulation. Roger et al. (2009)  also modelled their experiments with a 2D finite volume model and a 2D finite element model. The models underestimated the Q  b      measurements by approximately 6 % to 12 % (Fig. 4 ). The absolute deviation of the 2D models from the measurements was larger than that of the lumped model, regardless of the C  d      formula with the exception of Singh et al. (1994)  and Emiroglu et al. (2011) , and larger than most combinations of the spatially distributed model with a C  d      formula (Fig. 4 ). The experiments of Michelazzo et al. (2015)  are similar to those of Roger et al. (2009)  when considering the height of the side weir crest, which is also zero. However, in this case the length of the side weir is shorter as it varies from 3  cm to 47  cm. Contrary to the cases of Roger et al. (2009) , in the experiments of Michelazzo et al. (2015)  both the lumped model and the spatially distributed model mostly overpredicted the lateral discharge Q  b     , particularly as the length of the side weir increased (Fig. 5  ). The only consistent exception is the case where the models were coupled with the discharge coefficient equation of Singh et al. (1994) , presumably because it was used outside of the data range for which it was developed. Overall, the accuracy of both models decreased as the side weir length increased. Another difference with the experiments of Roger et al. (2009)  is that in the data of Michelazzo et al. (2015)  the spatially distributed model performed better than the lumped model, for almost every coupled discharge coefficient equation. The discharge coefficient equation of Subramanya and Awasthy (1972)  generated the best results when it was coupled with either of the two models. The rest of the discharge coefficient equations exhibited a rather erratic behavior when coupled either with the lumped model or the spatially distributed model. The formula of Bagheri et al. (2014)  was again not tested because it is not applicable to a side weir with zero crest height. With regard to the experiments of Mignot et al. (2020) , for the cases with a fixed side opening with zero crest height there was considerable underestimation of the lateral discharge through the side opening on several occasions. The C d     equations that performed best were the same as those in the data of Roger et al. (2009) , i.e., the equation of Subramanya and Awasthy (1972)  for the lumped model and the equation of Nadesamoorthy and Thomson (1972)  for the spatially distributed model. When the height of the crest of the side weir became non-zero, both models generated less accurate results compared to the zero crest height and underpredicted the experimental measurements by more than 25 % for most couplings with a discharge coefficient equation (Fig. 6  ). A notable exception was the coupling with the discharge coefficient equation of Singh et al. (1994) , where both models performed much better. Overall, the lumped model performed better than the spatially distributed model for most cases of Mignot et al. (2020) .  4.2 Side opening with dynamic evolution of its geometry As shown in Fig. 7  , for the four representative experimental cases of Rifai et al. (2017) , the lumped model followed quite well the overall evolution trend of the discharge through the gradually augmenting dike breach, although in a less smooth way. The model did not capture accurately the discharge lowering after the initial peak in Test 1. For the lower upstream flow discharge, the discharge coefficient formulations did not have a significant impact on Q  b     ; however, as the flow discharge increased the modelling results of Q  b      exhibited a considerable scatter, particularly towards the end of each experiment when the dike breach was rather stabilized. Compared to the lumped model, the spatially distributed model predicted more accurately the initial peak of Q  b      and was also able to reproduce the trend of the lateral discharge through the variable dike breach (Fig. 8  ). However, the modelled Q  b      at the stabilization phase, after approximately 100  s, mostly underpredicted the measured values and gave worst results than the lumped model for the two lowest values of Q  i  n      , i.e., 20 and 30  l/s. The different discharge coefficient formulations that were tested in the spatially distributed model did not affect Q  b      as much as they did in the lumped model, regardless of the upstream discharge that was prescribed in each experiment. The formulas of Emiroglu et al. (2011)  and Bagheri et al. (2014)  were not evaluated in this experiment because for the former there was no convergence in the numerical models and the latter is not applicable to a side weir with zero crest height. The peak breach discharge, Q b , p e a k     , was more accurately predicted by the spatially distributed model (Fig. 9  ). Indeed, the lumped model led to an average absolute error that is more than two times higher than the absolute error of the spatially distributed model. The lumped model systematically overestimated the peak breach discharge, while the spatially distributed model sometimes underpredicted the peak lateral discharge. The discharge coefficient formulations that were tested exhibited a rather erratic behavior with respect to the different tests. Overall, the results of the different formulations exhibited greater variability compared to the previous cases with fixed openings and no formulation outperformed consistently the others when coupled with either of the two models.   5 Discussion The estimation of the discharge coefficient in weir equations has typically a large empirical component that depends on the flow conditions of the laboratory experiments from which it was developed. As such, weir equations can be confidently applied in data ranges for which they have been calibrated, but their performance outside these calibration ranges is uncertain. Fig. 10   shows how the range of the experimental data used in this study relate to the data ranges in which the semi-empirical equations for the estimation of C d     were developed. It is evident that in some cases, some formulations were used outside of their development range, which may be a reason for their deteriorating performance. Ranga Raju et al. (1979)  and Singh et al. (1994)  used a 90° side channel as the side weir. The hinterland was thus confined as it corresponded to a relatively narrow perpendicular channel. In these cases, the predicted value of C d     should be underestimated compared to the case when the hinterland is not confined. This trend is very obvious for Singh et al. (1994)  when considering a fixed breach geometry and a sharp crest. This formula performs better for Rifai et al. (2017) , probably because there is a broad-crested weir in this case, which confines a bit the flow when it goes through the breach. The implementation of the different models using the data of Roger et al. (2009)  and Mignot et al. (2020)  showed that increasing the model complexity, i.e., switch from a lumped to a discretized hydraulic description, does not always improve the accuracy of the side weir equation. This is the case not only when comparing our zero-dimensional lumped model to our one-dimensional model, but also when comparing to more detailed 2D models that Roger et al. (2009)  used to simulate their experiments. A possible explanation for this result is that the flow near dike breaches has 3D features (Michelazzo et al., 2015 ) that can be more easily parameterized when modelled with a lower dimensionality model. Despite their simplicity, lumped models have exhibited a versatile and reliable behavior in a broad range of hydraulic applications, e.g., in interactions between surface flows and drainage systems (Kitsikoudis et al., 2021 ), and as such it is not surprising that such modelling tools perform relatively well when properly calibrated. The importance of proper calibration of the discharge coefficient in lumped models becomes evident from the data from the experiments of Rifai et al. (2017) , where the lumped model was outperformed by the spatially distributed model for the majority of discharge coefficient equations. The different discharge coefficient equations have been calibrated with data from laboratory experiments where the crest of the side weir was horizontal. In the experiments of Rifai et al. (2017)  the dike breach, which was considered as a broad-crested side weir, exhibited an irregular cross-section at the different time-steps due to the spatial distribution of the erosion process induced by turbulent flow. In such cases with variability of the bed level across the dike breach, the variations in flow depth will affect the discharge distribution over the dike breach (Michelazzo et al., 2018 ). In the experiments of Rifai et al. (2017) , the lumped model was used by considering a straight weir crest at the 15th percentile of the elevation of the scanned points within the dike breach. This simplification led to a considerable overestimation of the breach peak discharge by the lumped model. This inaccuracy could also be attributed to sharp variations of the breach dimensions owed to sudden breach side slope failures, which instantaneously impact the value of C d     when using the empirical formulas. These sharp variations of C d     may also be the reason why the evolution of Q b     is smoother in the experiments compared to the modelling. The spatially distributed model predicted much better the peak discharge in the dynamic dike breach (Fig. 9 ), highlighting the importance of spatial discretization in cases with large spatial variability of the side opening. For accurate hazard predictions related to fluvial dike breaching, a discretized model should be preferred. Nevertheless, the zero-dimensional model is more conservative as it tends to systematically overestimate the breach discharge (Fig. 7  and Fig. 9 ). To be on the safe side while optimizing the prediction accuracy, a trade-off consists in combining the one-dimensional model with a formulation that overestimates the breach discharge coefficient, e.g., the one proposed by Ranga Raju et al. (1979)  or Borghei et al. (1999) . It is also advised to test different formulations for the discharge coefficient to obtain an envelope curve, allowing for better uncertainty assessment.  6 Conclusions Breaches in river dikes can pose a hazard of intense flooding to nearby areas. In such cases, flood risk assessment requires not only accurate modelling of the dike breach discharge towards the hinterland, but also fast modelling tools that can be used efficiently. To satisfy these requirements, in this study the flow through a breach in a dike with its axis parallel to a straight river reach was considered similar to the flow over a side weir. Eleven semi-empirical equations from the literature were tested for the parameterization of the discharge coefficient of the side weir equation, which was coupled to either a lumped model (zero-dimensional) or a spatially distributed model (one-dimensional). These models were tested in cases with increasing complexity: from cases with a fixed side opening with zero and non-zero crest height to a dynamic dike breach that evolves over time. The performance of the different equations for the parametrization of the discharge coefficient of the side weir equation varied with the different cases, highlighting the empirical nature of most of them. The equations of Subramanya and Awasthy (1972)  and Nadesamoorthy and Thomson (1972)  performed best for a fixed opening with zero crest height while the equation of Singh et al. (1994)  performed best for a fixed opening with non-zero crest height. For the cases with the dynamic dike breach, several formulations derived good results and there was no formula that was consistently superior. Overall, the modelling results were less accurate when transitioning from the fixed opening cases of zero to non-zero crest height and to the cases with a dynamic breach. Despite its simplicity, the lumped model generated better results than the spatially distributed model for many cases with fixed openings, but the spatially distributed model was more accurate in the dynamic breach cases. This highlights the importance of spatial discretization in cases where the dike breach exhibits irregular geometry. This model type should be selected when assessing hazard related to real-world dike breaching. For the sake of safety, it should be coupled with a formulation that overestimates the breach discharge coefficient, such as the one of Ranga Raju et al. (1979)  or Borghei et al. (1999) . Uncertainty may also be considered by creating an envelope curve for the breach discharge by testing different formulations for the breach discharge.
1 Introduction Infiltration refers to the movement of a wetting fluid through a porous medium due to capillary and gravitational forces, causing it to flow within the porous material. Gravitational and capillary forces drive vertical infiltration, while capillary action alone drives horizontal infiltration (Philip, 1957; Assouline, 2013; Stewart et al., 2013 ). Infiltration is a frequently observed phenomenon that holds significant importance in various domains, including hydrogeology, engineering geology, environmental science, and agriculture. Infiltration is a key component of the water cycle, where rainfall and surface water replenish groundwater through infiltration, influencing changes in groundwater levels (Brunner et al., 2009; Bhaskar et al., 2018 ). Infiltration can result in an elevation of water content within an unsaturated soil, leading to higher pore water pressure and reduced soil cohesion. This, in turn, can lead to a decrease in the mechanical strength and stability of the soil, potentially triggering various geological hazards (Fredlund et al., 1978 ; Ng & Pang, 2000 ). During the infiltration process, contaminants in the soil are desorbed by the water medium, and the infiltrating leachate carrying these contaminants eventually enters groundwater sources, posing a threat to the safety of groundwater environments (Brusseau, 1994 ). In particular, microbes and pathogens introduced through infiltration can contaminate groundwater, giving rise to waterborne diseases (Huo et al., 2021 ). The infiltration process is crucial for agricultural irrigation. Different infiltration patterns determine the distribution of soil water within the soil matrix. Monitoring the infiltration process and determining the depth of infiltration influence, as well as selecting the optimal irrigation method based on plant and soil characteristics, facilitate the effective fulfillment of plant water needs while mitigating the risk of depleting water resources (Bethune et al., 2008 ). Since the infiltration process plays a significant role in various disciplinary domains, the monitoring of this process has become a focal point of research in academia. Various monitoring methods for soil infiltration currently exist including Time Domain Reflectometry (TDR), Electrical Resistivity Tomography (ERT), dye tracer method, and others. Among these, TDR is widely used due to its simplicity and portability in diverse monitoring applications such as plant root zone infiltration and solute migration (Mmolawa & Or, 2000), water evolution in landfill sites (Imhoff et al., 2007 ), and infiltration on volcanic ash debris slopes (Capparelli et al., 2020 ). On the basis of TDR, frequency-domain reflectometry (FDR) has also been developed. FDR offers higher monitoring precision compared to TDR technology. Feng et al. (2024)  utilized this technique for measuring unfrozen water content in frozen soils. However, the monitoring results of FDR are easily affected by soil properties. Changes in soil dry density, salt content and other conditions will lead to sensor monitoring errors. However, both two methods’ spatial monitoring range for soil water is limited to the area around the sensor probe and the method inherently involves a point-based monitoring approach. However, the infiltration process exhibits continuous changes over time and space, making point-based monitoring methods inadequate for fully capturing water content variations at different depths during infiltration. ERT offers the ability to monitor spatial water content distribution within the soil without disturbing its original structure. Nevertheless, the accuracy of ERT monitoring relies on the precision of the apparent resistivity inversion algorithm and necessitates correction for topographical conditions, thereby limiting the universality of ERT monitoring techniques (Perrone et al., 2014 ). The electrodes used in ERT monitoring are typically long-term embedded in the soil. During the evolution of the water field, these electrodes are prone to corrosion and detachment from the soil, leading to measurement errors in ERT monitoring (Xiong et al., 2023 ). Moreover, the single sampling time required by the ERT monitoring method is linked to the complexity of electrode layouts. The greater the number of electrodes and the more intricate the layout, the longer the sampling scan time, which is unfavorable for achieving continuous infiltration process monitoring (Zhou et al., 2001 ). Dye tracer methods combined with photography, X-ray scanning, and other techniques can characterize the infiltration process, determine infiltration depth, and identify preferential infiltration locations. However, this method cannot achieve quantitative monitoring of the infiltration process (Sander & Gerke, 2007 ; Filipović et al., 2020 ). Although monitoring methods for infiltration processes are continuously evolving and improving in accuracy, they are still limited by the inherent characteristics of various technologies. As a result, they are unable to fully meet the high demands for temporal and spatial continuity in infiltration process monitoring. Recent advances in the Distributed Fiber Optic Sensing (DFOS) technology offer new opportunities for various soil and rock monitoring applications, including the soil infiltration process. In the DFOS technology, the optical fiber itself serves as both a signal transmission medium and a means to acquire monitoring parameters. By installing optical fibers within rock and soil formations, and in conjunction with a demodulator, optical signals are introduced into the fibers. By analyzing the scattered and reflected light signals with a demodulator, DFOS enables obtaining physical state parameters along the optical fibers within geological materials and their spatial distribution information (Bao & Chen, 2012 ). Among DFOS technologies, Distributed Temperature Sensing (DTS) is a fully distributed fiber optic monitoring technique that, combined with the Active Heating Fiber Optics (AHFO) method, has been widely applied in soil water monitoring in recent years. Banks et al. (2022)  employed AHFO-DTS to monitor river recharge to groundwater, using the monitoring results to estimate the rate of river recharge to groundwater. Yan et al. (2015)  utilized AHFO-DTS for quantitative monitoring of slope infiltration. The on-site monitoring results reflected fluctuations in subsurface groundwater levels within the slope, successfully achieving the localization of potential sliding planes within the slope. Gamage et al. (2018)  utilized AHFO-DTS to monitor the water infiltration pattern in soil during plant drip irrigation, determining the corresponding infiltration radius and depth. While DTS has found widespread application, its current spatial resolution is limited to the decimeter-level. This level of precision is evidently insufficient to meet the demands of effective monitoring for infiltration processes primarily occurring in the shallow layers of soil. The utilization of AHFO-DTS for soil water content monitoring typically involves the use of specialized structured active-heating optical cables. Within this type of optical cable, there exists a linear heat source along with temperature-sensing fibers (Ciocca et al., 2012 ). To enhance the spatial resolution of DTS monitoring technology, some researchers have employed spiral-shaped configurations for DTS cables with active heating capabilities. By increasing the spatial distribution density of the monitoring cables, the spatial resolution of the DTS monitoring method can be improved (Sayde et al., 2010a ; Liu et al., 2013 ; Wu et al., 2020a ). However, as a heat pulse method, excessively dense cable deployment can lead to heat transfer between neighboring cables, which may affect the monitoring effectiveness (Shehata et al., 2020 ). Moreover, excessively dense spatial distribution of monitoring fibers can inevitably impact soil properties and hinder the monitoring of infiltration processes. Optical Frequency Domain Reflectometry (OFDR) is an emerging DFOS technology. When a temperature change occurs or strain is generated at a specific location along the optical fiber, it induces the optical fiber at that position to generate a Rayleigh Backscattering Spectra (RBS) shift. The accurate RBS shift amount is defined as Δν , and this parameter is a linear function of temperature and strain. The OFDR method decodes the RBS signals from various positions along the optical fiber to acquire temperature and strain field information of the surrounding rock and soil. Compared to other distributed fiber optic sensing technologies, OFDR boasts exceptionally high spatial resolution and monitoring accuracy. Specifically, OFDR can achieve a spatial resolution of 1 mm within a monitoring length of 100 m (Qu et al., 2022 ). With the use of an enhanced demodulation structure, OFDR can maintain a high spatial resolution at the centimeter level within a measurement length of 5 km (Koshikiya et al., 2007 ). When monitoring with a spatial resolution of 1 mm, the temperature measurement accuracy of this technology reaches up to ±0.1 °C, and the strain monitoring accuracy is 0.1με (Xu et al., 2022 ). OFDR's spatial resolution essentially meets the technical requirements for continuous spatial parameter monitoring, providing high-precision strain and temperature information through monitoring. This technology is extensively employed for high-precision strain monitoring, particularly in structural health monitoring of engineering structures like bridges and dams, enabling the detection of small structural defects such as cracks (Wu et al., 2020b ; Zheng et al., 2020 ). However, in the case of soil, being a porous medium, the infiltration process doesn't exert significant force on embedded optical cables, and thus, it doesn't induce notable strain in them (Chang & Hills, 1993 ). To enable spatially continuous monitoring of soil infiltration, it is essential to fully capitalize on the temperature measurement precision and spatial resolution advantages of OFDR. Thus, there is a need to develop a spatially continuous monitoring method for soil infiltration based on OFDR's temperature sensing capabilities. The primary objective of this study is to propose a new method, referred to as Active Heating Optical Frequency Domain Reflectometry (AH-OFDR), for high-resolution spatially continuous monitoring of soil infiltration employing the improved Active Heating Fiber Optics (AHFO) technique. AH-OFDR achieves continuous spatial monitoring of infiltration processes by leveraging the high spatial resolution advantages and precise temperature sensing capabilities of OFDR in combination with AHFO. This method can address the issue of spatial discontinuity in data obtained from existing infiltration monitoring technologies, providing robust technical support for the high-precision fitting of hydrological models and effective management of water resources. The paper comprehensively elaborates on the technical mechanisms of achieving spatially continuous monitoring of infiltration processes using the AH-OFDR method. By employing Infrared Thermal Imaging Technique, the study records the temperature variations of the soil within the specimen throughout the entire infiltration process. The infrared imaging results confirm the accuracy of the infiltration process recorded using AH-OFDR.  2 Technical principles and underlying mechanisms of AH-OFDR 2.1 Optical Frequency Domain Reflectometry (OFDR) OFDR is a technique that calculates the strain generated in an optical fiber and the variation in fiber temperature by demodulating the shifted amount of the RBS (Bao & Chen, 2012 ). The RBS at any position within the optical fiber is controlled by the effective refractive index (n eff ) of the fiber at that location. When there are changes in temperature or strain conditions at a certain position along the optical fiber, n eff  at that position changes, causing a shift in the RBS compared to its initial state (Ding et al., 2018 ). Fig. 1  a illustrates the typical demodulation structure for temperature and strain monitoring using OFDR. The monitoring setup commonly includes a tunable laser source (TLS) and an interferometer, consisting of an internal reference fiber path (RF) and a measurement fiber path (MF) for monitoring. The laser emitted by TLS is split into two scanning laser beams by Coupler A, which are injected into RF and MF as reference and measurement light, respectively. The reference light in RF reaches coupler B after traveling a predetermined optical distance within the instrument. When measurement light entering MF, the optical fiber's Rayleigh backscattering stimulated at locations with temperature or strain anomalies exhibits a spectral shift compared to the initial state. The anomalous Rayleigh scattering propagates back along MF and is transmitted in the reverse direction to Coupler B. The reference light transmitted by RF and the Raleigh backscattered light returned in MF undergo beat interference in Coupler B, generating a beating signal. The beating signal is then transmitted to a photodetector (PD), and subsequently sent to a data acquisition system (DAQ) and a computer (PC) for analysis. The corresponding interference localization and signal demodulation calculations are performed. The corresponding interference localization is determined by calculating the time delay between reference light in RF reaching coupler B and the return of RBS from different positions within MF back to coupler B. This process is illustrated in Fig. 1 b. The signal demodulation calculations process involves comparing the RBS information obtained by the demodulator at various points in MF with the baseline RBS information in RF, thus obtaining values at various positions in MF. This process is depicted in Fig. 1 c. The localization of OFDR monitoring information is achieved by calculating the intensity of the beat signal. The positioning calculation process of OFDR monitoring points is illustrated by Equations 1–3. The backscattered Rayleigh signal intensity propagating within the optical fiber is obtained through an OFDR demodulator, and the contained frequency information, f b , is extracted through demodulation. Since the frequency of the beat signal is a function of τ  and γ , f b  can be obtained to determine the corresponding τ , thereby establishing the distance Δz  between the reverse scattering data point and the starting point of the MF, as shown in Equation (3) . This enables the localization of the monitoring signal along the MF (Bao & Wang, 2021; Qu et al., 2022 ).(1) I ( t )  = 2 R ( τ )   E 0 2  cos 2 π f 0  τ + f b  t + 1 2  γ τ 2  + e ( t )  - e ( t - τ )              (2) f b  = γ τ     (3) z = τ c  2 n eff        where I (t ) is the intensity of the beat signal, f b  represents the frequency of the beat signal, R (τ ) is the reflectivity attenuation of MF related to the time delay τ , τ  measures the time delay between reference light reaching coupler B in RF and the return of Rayleigh scattering from different positions within MF back to coupler B, E 0  is the amplitude of the reference signal, f 0  is the initial optical frequency, e (t )-e (t -τ ) is the phase noise in the beating signal, z  is the distance between the backscatter point and the start point of MF, γ  is the optical frequency tuning rate, c  is the speed of light, n eff  is the effective refractive index of the fiber, which is associated with group index. To demodulate and acquire the RBS signal within MF, it is necessary to establish the baseline Rayleigh scattering frequency spectrum distribution for the entire MF under reference temperature and strain conditions prior to monitoring. This baseline spectrum serves as a reference value for subsequent demodulation calculations. During the monitoring process, the optical frequency domain monitoring signal captured by the photodetector is transformed into spatial domain data through the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). Using a predefined effective spatial resolution as a sliding window, the spatial domain monitoring data of MF is segmented into multiple demodulation segments. Within each demodulation segment, the RBS signal is demodulated separately. The calculation of the effective spatial resolution is provided by Equations (4) and (5) .(4) Δ X = N Δ Z     (5) Δ Z = c 2 n Δ υ       where ΔX  is the effective sensing spatial resolution. Dividing the total MF to several segments using a sliding window with a ΔX  length that contains N  data points as the spatial local Rayleigh backscattering signals. ΔX  is an adjustable demodulation parameter that can be customized based on monitoring requirements. ΔZ  represents the sampling interval between two adjacent data points within the optical fiber, which depends on the fiber's refractive index (n ) and the optical frequency modulation range (Δu ) of the incident TLS. It is an intrinsic monitoring characteristic of the fiber medium. Specifically, when monitoring soil properties, OFDR can achieve a spatial resolution of 1 mm within a monitoring length of 100 m (Qu et al., 2022 ). By improving the demodulation optical path, the OFDR method can achieve long-distance monitoring and can be applied to large scale practical engineering. By incorporating a single sideband (SSB) modulator and linewidth fiber laser (FL) into the OFDR demodulation optical path, the improved OFDR monitoring method can obtain information along a 5 km optical cable length with a spatial resolution of 5 cm (Koshikiya et al., 2007 ). In addition, there are numerous studies on improving the OFDR demodulation optical path to ensure monitoring accuracy while increasing monitoring length (Feng et al., 2020; Li et al., 2023 ). Based on the AH-OFDR technology mechanism proposed in this study, different demodulation optical path structures are adopted to meet different infiltration process monitoring needs in practice. During the demodulation of RBS signals, a cross-correlation is performed between the fundamental Rayleigh scattering spectral information of each segment within MF, which has been pre-divided based on ΔX , and the Rayleigh scattering spectral information acquired during the monitoring process. This cross-correlation analysis facilitates the comparative assessment of spectral frequency shifts observed in each segment of MF throughout the monitoring procedure. Consequently, an accurate measurement of Δν  is computed. By utilizing Δν , the temperature variations or strains experienced by MF during the monitoring process are calculated, thereby achieving the intended monitoring objective. The variation in n eff  is caused by changes in the inherent material properties of the optical fiber due to temperature fluctuations and strains, and the change in n eff  is the primary factor leading to the occurrence of RBS in the optical fiber. Therefore, when establishing formulas to represent temperature change (ΔT ) and strain based on Δν , factors that significantly impact the fiber's n eff  are chosen, such as the thermo-optic coefficient (ξ ), thermal expansion coefficient (α ), elasto-optic coefficient, and fiber Poisson's ratio (Kreger et al., 2006 ). Changes in both ΔT  and Δε  resulting in Δν  within the MF can be differentiated by integrating a linear matrix of distributed temperature and strain coefficients (Li et al., 2013 ). As the aim of this study is to utilize the high-precision temperature-sensing capability of OFDR for infiltration process monitoring, a specially designed fiber structure was used during the experimental process. The fiber deployment scheme was designed to actively eliminate the influence of strain on Δν . The Δν  resulting solely from ΔT  can be calculated using Equation (6) .(6) Δ ν = C T  Δ T  = (  α + ξ ) Δ T     where C T  is the sensitivity coefficients of the Rayleigh backscattered frequency shift to changes in fiber temperature, C T  is a sum of the thermal expansion coefficient and the thermo optic coefficient. For the silica fiber used in this experiment, the variation in α  of the monitoring fiber itself is minimal during temperature changes and is typically treated as a constant (Leng & Asundi, 2003 ). ξ  is considered the primary factor affecting the fiber's temperature sensitivity coefficient. Adamovsky et al. (2012)  discovered that when the fiber temperature is below 700 °C, ξ  does not significantly affect the fiber's effective refractive index. During the infiltration monitoring process, the fiber's temperature remains well below 700 °C, allowing us to consider a linear correlation between Δν  and ΔT .  2.2 Active-Heated fiber Optic (AHFO) AHFO is a heat-based technique for monitoring soil water content based on soil thermal characteristics. This method exploits the difference in thermal properties of soil under different water content conditions. By monitoring the temperature changes of the soil when subjected to heating through fiber optic sensors, the soil water content is determined (Sayde et al., 2010b ). According to the structural relationship between the temperature-sensing fiber and the heat source, AHFO can be divided into various methods, including the Single-Probe Heat-Pulse method (SPHP) and the Dual-Probe Heat-Pulse method (DPHP), among others.
