In the SPHP method, the temperature-sensing fiber and the linear heat source are arranged within the same optical cable structure for temperature variation monitoring. In the DPHP method, the temperature-sensing fiber is positioned at a certain distance from the linear heat source. The feasibility of monitoring soil water content using AHFO has been confirmed through various applications. However, due to spatial resolution limitations in various fiber optic monitoring techniques, AHFO is currently primarily employed for monitoring the dynamic evolution of water fields on a larger scale (Ye et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023b ). The aforementioned studies fail to meet the technical requirements for spatially continuous monitoring of soil infiltration. Therefore, based on the principles of AHFO and utilizing the high spatial resolution and precision temperature sensing capability of OFDR, this study proposes AH-OFDR as a spatially continuous and high-resolution monitoring method for infiltration processes. When monitoring based on the SPHP principle, a linear heat source within the optical cable generates heat and releases it into the soil. The temperature-sensing fiber within the optical cable monitors the temperature changes in the soil after being heated (Shehata et al., 2022 ). The SPHP method offers the advantages of simplicity in structure and minimal disturbance to the soil (Sayde et al., 2010b ). The optical cable used in this study is the NZS-DTS-C10 model developed by NanZee Sensing Technology Co., Ltd. Table 1   presents the optical cable parameters while Fig. 2   depicts different components of the optical cable. The resistive copper mesh generates heat when electrically powered. The resistive copper mesh of the entire optical cable serves as a linear heat source, while the insulating armor and waterproof jacket structures offer protection to the internal fibers. This cable employs a loose-tube structure, ensuring no contact between the internal OFDR monitoring fiber and the orange protective sheath. This design aims to eliminate Rayleigh scattering frequency shifts caused by fiber strain during the monitoring process. The SPHP technique typically relies on the spatially infinite line heat source formula for calculations, as shown in Equations (7) and (8)  (Shiozawa & Campbell, 1990; Bristow et al., 1994 ). This formula considers the influence of soil thermal properties parameters such as thermal conductivity (λ ), thermal diffusivity (K ), and volumetric heat capacity (C ) on the heat transfer within the soil. In the calculation equation for Δ1 (b, β, u ), Jn  (u ) and Y n (u ) represent the first and second-order Bessel functions of the nth  order, respectively. During the utilization of AH-OFDR for infiltration monitoring, changes in soil water content caused by water migration lead to alterations in soil thermal characteristics. This subsequently results in Δν  at certain fiber optic positions. As indicated by the result in Equation (10) , Δν  induced by infiltration is influenced by two main factors. One is the soil's thermal properties, and the other is the optical fiber's material properties and heating parameters. In the context of water content monitoring using the SPHP method, λ  represents a key parameter that determines the thermal characteristics of the soil (Ochsner et al., 2001 ). It also plays a crucial role in determining the temperature rise of the soil during the heating process (Ciocca et al., 2012 ).(10) Δ ν = Q 4 π λ   ( α + ξ )  ln 4 K  a 2  c   · t     + ( α + ξ )  Q R      In low-temperature environments, the thermal characteristics of the optical fiber (α  + ξ ) do not exhibit significant changes, and the selected heating power (Q ) remains constant. Further simplification of Equation (10)  leads to empirical Equation (11) , where parameters h  and i  can be treated as empirical coefficients during the infiltration process.(11) Δ ν = h λ  + i     where h = (α+ξ) Q  ln(4Kt /a2 c )/4π and i = (α+ ξ) QR . There are numerous models linking soil thermal conductivity (λ ) and soil water content (θ ), including theoretical and empirical models (Zhang & Wang, 2017; Cao et al., 2021 ). Based on soil properties and considering specific soil conditions, the selection of an appropriate calculation model can yield an accurate λ-θ  relationship. In conjunction with Equation (11) , a functional relationship exists between λ  and Δν  obtained from optical fiber monitoring. Therefore, when conducting soil water monitoring with AH-OFDR, it is possible to establish a computational model involving Δν-λ-θ  by employing the soil thermal conductivity as an intermediary parameter. However, the accuracy of this model is contingent upon the precision of the selected soil thermal conductivity model and the calibration accuracy of its constituent parameters. For specific monitoring soils, based on an appropriate λ-θ  calculation model, an accurate Δν-θ  calculation relationship can be established. Based on the above theory, combined with the AH-OFDR method proposed in this study, the evolution of the soil water field during the infiltration process can be accurately quantified. Most soil water content monitoring methods utilizing AHFO involve applying high power to the cable's internal resistor, rapidly generating significant heat that is released into the soil over a short period (Briggs et al., 2016; Cao et al., 2018 ). Using high-power heating allows for quickly obtaining soil water states within short time intervals, but it cannot achieve continuous monitoring of the soil infiltration process. The infiltration process of soil is characterized by temporal and spatial continuity. To achieve continuous monitoring of the infiltration process, it is necessary to continuously supply heat to the fiber optic cable and allow it to dissipate into the surrounding soil. This monitors the thermal characteristic changes of the soil around the fiber optic cable, enabling the determination of changes in soil water content. To reduce disturbance to the soil caused by high temperatures, this study employs a low-power continuous heating method in combination with the high temperature measurement accuracy of the OFDR monitoring technique. This approach enables the continuous temporal and spatial monitoring of the infiltration process while minimizing soil disturbance. Furthermore, Cao et al. (2021)  proposed a soil λ-θ  calculation model that takes into account temperature influence. Combining this model with Equation (11)  yields a Δν-λ-θ  calculation relationship considering soil temperature effects. Adopting this calculation relationship during the monitoring process can minimize the impact of temperature changes in the soil surrounding the optical fiber on the monitoring results.   3 Experimental testing program 3.1 Sample preparation for experiments Fig. 3   shows the experimental setup, including the test specimen and the monitoring equipment utilized to validate the feasibility of continuous spatial monitoring of infiltration with AH-OFDR. A sample is prepared inside an acrylic cylinder with an outer diameter of 20.0 cm, an inner diameter of 19.4 cm, and a height of 50.0 cm. The acrylic cylinder is sealed and securely affixed to an acrylic base using a hot-melt adhesive. Five installation holes for acrylic rods with a diameter of 0.8 cm and four drainage holes with a diameter of 1.0 cm are drilled on the acrylic base. One of the 1.0 cm drainage holes is positioned at the center of the acrylic base, intended for the passage of monitoring optical fibers. Five acrylic rods, each measuring 52.0 cm in length and 0.6 cm in diameter, are inserted into the mounting holes on the acrylic base and secured with hot-melt adhesive. A yellow measuring tape is affixed to the exterior of the acrylic cylinder to serve as a reference for analyzing photos of the infiltration process in subsequent stages. The monitoring optical cable is deployed within the test mold according to the scheme depicted in Fig. 4  . The fiber is securely fastened to the acrylic rods using fine wire bindings. As depicted in Fig. 2 , the NZS-DTS-C01 optical fiber used in this study contains two optical fibers, enabling simultaneous monitoring of the infiltration process with both OFDR and DTS fiber demodulators. In this study, both OFDR and DTS monitoring methods are employed simultaneously with the purpose of mutually validating the accuracy of the monitoring results obtained from each technique. However, the spatial sampling interval of DTS can only reach 20 cm. Therefore, a circular fiber optic cable deployment scheme is adopted to increase the spatial distribution density of the monitoring cables, achieving multiple DTS data sampling points within the same depth level. According to the cable layout structure shown in Fig. 4 , three layers of circular fiber optic monitoring sections and two segments of vertical fiber optic monitoring sections are arranged within the specimen. The purpose of the circular fiber optic monitoring sections is to compare the monitoring results of OFDR and DTS. The layout radius of the circular cable ring is 8.4 cm, ensuring that each layer of monitoring rings includes at least two DTS sampling points for comparison. To avoid thermal interference between the layers of cables, the vertical spacing between the circular fiber optic sections of each layer is set to 18 cm in the experiment. The vertical monitoring sections aim to utilize the high spatial resolution advantage of OFDR technology to achieve spatially continuous monitoring of the infiltration process. The length of each vertical fiber optic monitoring section is set to 10 cm. Prior to filling the mold with soil, spatial positioning of the optical cable's monitoring data is conducted to determine the height of key positions of the cable relative to the acrylic base, the corresponding spatial location of OFDR data sections, and the spatial distribution of DTS measurement points. The specific corresponding positions are indicated as shown in Fig. 4 . The determined heights of the key positions of the fiber optic cables serve as the basis for determining the infiltration depth based on the monitoring data. Simultaneously, a high-definition camera continuously captures the infiltration process within the transparent acrylic cylinder. The photographs, documenting the infiltration time and depth, can serve as a reference for validating the results obtained from the fiber optic monitoring. An infrared thermal imaging camera is employed to monitor the temperature distribution on the side of the sample during the heating and infiltration processes, providing supplementary analysis for the results obtained from both OFDR and DTS fiber optic monitoring methods. In this study, the FLIR-T620 model infrared camera is used. It operates within a wavelength range of 7.8–14.0 μm, and its calibration is completed prior to experimentation. The camera boasts a temperature sensitivity of ±0.04 °C and a temperature measurement accuracy of ±0.1 °C (Zeng et al., 2022 ). The tested soil in this work is Xiashu soil distributed widely in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River region, China. The specific soil parameters are presented in Table 2  . According to the Unified Soil Classification System (ASTMD-2487, 2017), the soil falls under the category of Lean Clay (CL), with an initial water content of 3.5 %. A layer of 2 cm of medium sand is filled at the bottom of the test mold. The Xiashu soil column has a height of 43 cm and is sampled uniformly in layers of 3 cm each, maintaining a controlled dry density of 1.3 g/cm3 . In this study, Δν  within the fiber is monitored using the OSI-S OFDR (Junno Tech Corp, Wuhan, China) fiber demodulator. The spatial resolution of this instrument can be adjusted according to monitoring requirements, with a maximum achievable spatial resolution of 1 mm. However, for the purpose of Infiltration monitoring, selecting a spatial resolution of 1 cm is sufficient to demonstrate the feasibility of this monitoring method. Furthermore, opting for a 1 cm spatial resolution can reduce the time required for each demodulation, thus enhancing the monitoring sampling frequency. The additional parameters of the OSI-S OFDR fiber demodulator instrument are presented in Table 3  . Temperature data within the same fiber optic cable is monitored using the DTS-ROTDR demodulator developed by NanZee Sensing Technology Co., Ltd. This instrument has a spatial sampling interval of 20 cm and a temperature measurement accuracy of ±0.3 °C. An adjustable DC power supply is used to supply a constant current to the active heating optical cable, ensuring uniform heating of the cable's interior through constant power dissipation across its resistance.  3.2 Monitoring process The monitoring process consists of three stages, as illustrated in Fig. 5  . The first stage involves baseline measurement and steady heating, during which the soil specimen is in its initial water state. Before introducing heat to the soil through the optical cable, the baseline OFDR-Δν  value of the sample is monitored for 25 min. Subsequently, heating is initiated at a constant power of 5 W/m and maintained for 40 min. At the end of this stage, the temperature of the soil surrounding the optical cable has reached a relatively stable phase. The selected heating power and duration are determined based on existing research findings and pre-experimental monitoring results. The adoption of this heating power and duration aims to maximize the accuracy of AH-OFDR technology in monitoring the infiltration process while also reducing the influence of active heating fiber optic cable on the soil temperature field (Cao et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2023a; Zhang et al., 2023b ). The second stage involves the infiltration monitoring phase, where the optical cable continues to be heated at a constant power of 5 W/m. A constant water head of 5 cm is applied to the top of the specimen to initiate infiltration. As the wetting front migrates downward, the soil affected by the infiltration undergoes changes in water content, causing an immediately response in the soil's thermal conductivity. Hence, the temperature of the soil surrounding the optical cable, influenced by the infiltration process, transitions from a stable phase to a rapid decrease phase. The third stage involves the cooling phase of the sample. At this stage, infiltration has been completed at various depth positions within the specimen, and water has begun to flow out from the reserved holes at the acrylic base. The optical cable ceases heating, and the cooling process of the soil surrounding the optical cable is monitored. This monitoring continues until the sample temperature returns to the state prior to cable heating, and Δν  decreases back to its initial value. Throughout the experimental monitoring process, the environmental temperature was maintained at approximately 24 °C, with fluctuations of ±0.5 °C. The temperature of the water used for infiltration was regulated using a constant-temperature water bath, also maintained at around 24 °C, and monitored by two PT100 sensors to record the actual water temperature, with fluctuations of ±0.2 °C.   4 Results and discussion During the process of increasing soil water content, the soil's thermal conductivity undergoes a transition from rapid increase to gradual increase. In dry soil, heat is primarily transmitted through contact between solid particles. In the initial stages of increasing soil water content, some of the void spaces between solid particles become filled with water, creating “liquid bridges”. Heat can quickly transfer outward through these “liquid bridges”, leading to a rapid increase in soil thermal conductivity. Once the soil water content reaches a certain threshold, the contribution of “liquid bridge” effects to heat transfer diminishes. The proportion of water filling the void spaces in the soil becomes the primary factor influencing thermal conductivity (Lu et al., 2007 ). As a result, the effectiveness of heat transfer is influenced by the ratio of water filling in the soil voids after a certain water content is reached. As the soil water content begins to increase, the soil's thermal conductivity responds immediately by rapidly increasing. The heat released by the fiber optic cable is quickly transmitted outward as the thermal conductivity increases (Cao et al., 2018 ). Thus, the moment when the cable temperature initially decreases corresponds to the moment when there is a change in the soil's thermal conductivity, marking the onset of the infiltration process. 4.1 Feasibility verification of AH-OFDR Fig. 6  a shows Δν  monitoring results of the first circular optical fiber cable section using OFDR whereas Fig. 6 b presents the ΔT  monitoring data using DTS. As shown, the cable begins to heat up and release heat into the soil at 1485 s, causing an increase in soil temperature. The Δν  detected by OFDR rapidly increases during this stage, then enters a stable phase. According to the monitoring results shown in Fig. 6 a, Δν  enters a rapid decrease phase at 4213 s and continues to decline to the minimum value. The decrease in Δν  obtained from fiber optic monitoring indicates a decrease in soil temperature around the fiber, leading to a rapid increase in soil thermal conductivity. The phenomenon of Δν  decreasing can serve as an indicator of the influence of infiltration on soil water content. The rapid decrease phase of Δν  corresponds to the rapid increase in soil thermal conductivity. When Δν  reaches its lowest value, the soil thermal conductivity enters the stable phase. At this point, the color of the soil has undergone a significant change compared to when it was dry. By comparing and analyzing the OFDR-Δν  (Fig. 6 a) and DTS-ΔT  (Fig. 6 b) monitoring data of the first circular fiber optic monitoring section, it becomes evident that both methods exhibit consistent patterns of change during the infiltration process. Both techniques respond to the soil's infiltration process at the same time instances. Therefore, these two fiber optic monitoring methods can mutually corroborate each other, demonstrating the applicability of the improved AHFO method with low-power, long-duration heating for spatially continuous monitoring of the infiltration process. Simultaneously, the well-established DTS monitoring method, which measures soil water content, exhibits the same pattern of change to OFDR fiber optic technology during the soil infiltration monitoring process. This also validates the accuracy of AH-OFDR in monitoring changes in soil water content. However, in the monitoring data depicted in Fig. 6 , it can be observed that there are certain differences even among data acquired by the same monitoring instrument at different measurement points within the same depth position. This discrepancy arises due to the unique arrangement of the optical cable. The circular monitoring cable section is connected to the vertical monitoring cable section through transition cable section, and there is an overlap between the transition cables and the circular monitoring cable section. Heat is exchanged between these overlapping sections of the cables, resulting in more heat being released into the soil at these overlapping positions. As a result, the temperature of the soil at these overlapping cable positions is higher compared to other positions along the cable. Due to the uneven distribution of soil temperature around the enveloped optical cable, variations in Δν  and ΔT  occur at different positions along the cable. However, compared to the DTS-ΔT  monitoring data, the Δν  monitoring data obtained using the OFDR method from the first circular optical fiber cable section can reflect spatial distribution differences at the centimeter level. The sampling interval of DTS is 20 cm, which reduces the spatial accuracy of the DTS-ΔT  data. Therefore, during the infiltration monitoring process, the OFDR-Δν  monitoring method demonstrates higher spatial sensitivity and monitoring accuracy compared to the DTS-ΔT  monitoring method. Addressing this thermal accumulation phenomenon, verification and analysis will be conducted using infrared thermography in Section 4.3 . The unique cable monitoring scheme leads to an uneven temperature distribution along the cable. Fig. 7   presents the monitoring results of the second circular fiber optic cable section. As shown, both OFDR-Δν  and DTS-ΔT  detect a rapid increase in soil thermal conductivity at 17,177 s. Additionally, the photographed infiltration depth reaches the location of the second circular fiber optic cable at this moment. Similar to the results from the first circular optical fiber cable section, differences in ΔT  at various positions along the cable are observed in the second circular cable section as well. These discrepancies are also attributed to cable overlap. Following validation through the first and second circular optical fiber cable sections, the improved low-power, AHFO is proven suitable for infiltration monitoring. This method ensures a continuous release of heat into the soil through the monitoring optical fiber cable during the infiltration process, allowing real-time and accurate recording of the vertical migration of soil thermal conductivity caused by infiltration. Based on the continuous heating AHFO approach, both OFDR-Δνν  and DTS-ΔT  methods exhibit distinct rapid decrease phases during the infiltration monitoring process. This clear record of thermal conductivity changes during infiltration achieves the goal of infiltration monitoring. Both OFDR-Δν  and DTS-ΔT  methods capture the same pattern of variation in the infiltration process, demonstrating the applicability of the OFDR method for monitoring changes in soil water content. However, OFDR-Δν  offers higher temperature sensitivity compared to DTS-ΔT  monitoring technology, making it more advantageous for infiltration monitoring purposes.  4.2 Validation of the spatial resolution of AH-OFDR 4.2.1 Monitoring data from the third circular optical fiber cable section Compared to the first and second circular optical fiber cable sections, which are only affected by vertical infiltration, the third circular optical fiber cable section is influenced by both lateral and vertical infiltration modes simultaneously (Fig. 8  a). Because the acrylic cylinder test mold is not fully sealed with the bottom acrylic base, a leakage point is detected near the optical cable location corresponding to the monitoring point at 5.51 m in the OFDR-Δν  monitoring data. Due to capillary action, water enters the sample from the leakage point and gradually moves away from the point of leakage along the third circular optical fiber cable section, advancing forward. This process is illustrated in Fig. 8 b. Leakage at the bottom of the specimen started at 14,999 s. According to the photographed infiltration process, vertical migration of infiltration from top to bottom has reached a height of 24.3 cm at this moment, without yet affecting the third circular optical fiber cable section. Furthermore, when the vertical infiltration reaches the depth of the third circular optical fiber cable section, the lateral infiltration has not completely covered the position of the third circular optical fiber cable section. Therefore, the third circular optical fiber cable section is simultaneously affected by both vertical and lateral infiltrations. The monitoring results of the third circular fiber optic section exhibit differences compared to the first and second circular sections. During the infiltration process, the OFDR-Δν  monitoring results of the third annular fiber optic section, as shown in Fig. 9  , clearly illustrate the influence of two kinds of infiltration processes on Δν . Because the chosen OFDR monitoring method has a spatial resolution of 1 cm, Δν  can accurately track the spatial migration process of lateral infiltration and determine the final affected area of lateral infiltration. According to the photographic records of the infiltration process, vertical infiltration reached the depth of the third circular optical fiber cable at 46,081 s, leading to a complete increase in soil thermal conductivity at that depth position to the stable phase. The corresponding section of OFDR-Δν  monitoring data for the third circular optical fiber cable ranges from 5.42 m to 5.99 m. The lateral infiltration leakage point is located at the 5.51 m position within the OFDR measurement range, as shown in Fig. 9 a. The third circular optical fiber cable can be divided into three segments based on whether they are affected by lateral infiltration: the fully affected segment, the slightly affected segment, and the unaffected segment. The positions of the optical fiber cable affected by lateral infiltration are symmetrically distributed on both sides of the leakage point. The fully affected section of the cable corresponds to the OFDR-Δν  monitoring data positions of 5.42 m-5.64 m and 5.93 m-5.99 m. These two segments of the optical fiber cable are located adjacent to the leakage point and are the first to be influenced by lateral infiltration. Before the vertical infiltration reaches the depth of the third circular optical fiber cable section, the thermal conductivity of the soil surrounding these two cable segments has increased to the stable phase, and Δν  has decreased to its lowest value, as shown in Fig. 9 c. The slightly affected section of the cable corresponds to the OFDR-Δν  monitoring data positions of 5.66 m-5.71 m and 5.83 m-5.92 m. These two segments of the cable are simultaneously influenced by both types of infiltration. Before vertical infiltration reaches the depth of the third circular optical fiber cable, lateral infiltration has already affected the soil surrounding these two cable segments, causing the soil thermal conductivity to enter the growth phase. However, due to the slightly distant location of these two cable segments from the leakage point, the capillary action results in a slower rate of water migration. As a result, the increase in soil water content occurs at a limited rate, leading to a smaller change in thermal conductivity and a reduced decrease in Δν . Eventually, primarily influenced by vertical infiltration, the thermal conductivity of the soil surrounding these two cable segments reaches a stable phase, causing Δν  to decrease to its lowest value, as illustrated in Fig. 9 d. The unaffected section of the cable corresponds to the OFDR-Δν  monitoring data positions of 5.72 m-5.82 m. This cable section is far from the leakage point, and lateral infiltration does not impact the thermal conductivity of this segment. The variation in OFDR-Δν  monitoring data for this section is solely influenced by vertical infiltration. In the OFDR-Δν  monitoring results shown in Fig. 9 c and 9d, the Δν  monitoring data exhibit a spatial sequence of abrupt decreases according to the relationship between the sampling point distance and the leakage point location. This spatial order reflects the impact of lateral infiltration on the third annular fiber optic section. According to the Equation (11) , when Δν  starts to decrease, it signifies that the respective location is being affected by the infiltration process, resulting in changes in soil water content and thermal conductivity. Hence, the spatial sequence of decreasing Δν  reflects the lateral migration process of the wetting front along the third annular fiber optic section due to lateral infiltration. In the OFDR-Δν  monitoring results shown in Fig. 10  c and Fig. 10 d, it can be observed that the fiber optic cables near the leak point are the first to enter the Δν  reduction phase. The wetting front of lateral infiltration continuously migrates forward, and the fiber optic monitoring sampling points affected by lateral infiltration gradually move away from the leak point, resulting in a spatially sequential reduction in Δν . This phenomenon demonstrates that with the high spatial resolution advantage of OFDR technology, the infiltration process monitoring method proposed in this study can achieve precise, centimeter-level dynamic monitoring of the infiltration process. During the infiltration process, the DTS-ΔT  monitoring results of the third circular fiber optic section are shown in Fig. 10 , with two DTS sampling points at 3.32 m and 3.53 m, respectively. Based on the monitoring results, the effects of lateral and vertical infiltration on the ΔT  of the third annular optical cable can be distinguished. After 14,999 s of lateral infiltration caused by leakage, the ΔT  enters the reduction phase. When vertical infiltration reaches the depth of the third circular fiber optic section after 46,135 s, the soil thermal conductivity increases rapidly, and ΔT  decreases to a stable phase. The DTS monitoring technology provides the average temperature within 20 cm sampling intervals. The 3.32 m sampling point and 3.53 m sampling point are located on either side of the leak point, with the 3.32 m point closer to the leak point. Therefore, the 3.32 m sampling point is more affected by lateral infiltration compared to the 3.53 m point, leading to an earlier entry of ΔT  into the reduction phase. Because the DTS-ΔT  monitoring data at the 3.32 m sampling point entered the reduction phase earlier, the ΔT  monitoring data at this point are consistently lower than those at the 3.53 m sampling point during the subsequent monitoring period. Comparative analysis of the OFDR-Δνν  and DTS-ΔT  monitoring results at the location of the third circular fiber optic section reveals consistent findings. Similar to the monitoring results obtained for the first and second annular cable sections, even when affected by lateral infiltration, both the OFDR-Δν  and DTS-ΔT  methods exhibit the same pattern of changes in the monitoring results at the third circular fiber optic section. However, in comparison to the infiltration process recorded by the DTS-ΔT  method, the OFDR-Δν  method achieves precise differentiation between lateral and vertical infiltration processes due to its extremely high spatial resolution and temperature sensitivity. Additionally, the OFDR-Δν  method enables dynamic monitoring of both infiltration processes. The monitoring results of the third annular optical cable provide substantial evidence of the feasibility of achieving spatially continuous monitoring of infiltration processes using the novel infiltration monitoring system proposed in this study.  4.2.2 Monitoring data from the vertical optical fiber cable section The OFDR-Δν  monitoring data for the first vertical cable monitoring section correspond to the position of 4.43 m to 4.52 m. Due to the length of the vertical cable monitoring section being only 10 cm, which is smaller than the spatial sampling interval of DTS, only the OFDR-Δν  method was used to monitor the infiltration process at the corresponding depth position of the first vertical cable section. The monitoring results are shown in Fig. 11  . When the top of the first vertical cable section is affected by vertical infiltration, Δν  starts to decrease. As the wetting front continues to migrate downward, the thermal conductivity of the soil surrounding the first vertical cable monitoring section enters a stage of increasing values in spatial sequence from top to bottom. Correspondingly, the monitoring data of Δν  exhibit a reduction in spatial order that corresponds to the migration process of the wetting front. The vertical infiltration recorded by the camera reached the depth of the top of the first vertical cable monitoring section at 5893 s. At this moment, the Δν  data at this monitoring point were undergoing a rapid decrease. Simultaneously, the camera captured the moment when vertical infiltration reached the depth position at the bottom of the first vertical cable section at 14,304 s. At this point, the Δν  data had also entered a rapid decrease phase. Therefore, for the first vertical cable monitoring section, there is a consistent correspondence between the recorded infiltration process from the camera and the changing pattern of Δν . The location of the second vertical cable monitoring section is close to the leakage point near the bottom of the specimen. Furthermore, the timing of both the vertical and lateral infiltration reaching this cable section is relatively similar. As a result, the second vertical cable monitoring section experiences the combined effects of both infiltration processes. The monitoring effectiveness of the second vertical cable section is comparatively poorer when compared to the first vertical cable monitoring section. The infiltration rate is linearly proportional to the velocity of the wetting front (Mao et al., 2016 ). Wang et al. (2018)  monitored the lateral migration process of wet fronts under constant head conditions using photographic recording and evaluated the accuracy of monitoring data using root mean square error (RMSE) and standard deviation (σ). Combining the above research, during the infiltration monitoring process, the sudden drop moments of Δν  and ΔT  correspond to the arrival time of the wet front. The depth distance between the first circular fiber optic section and the second circular fiber optic section is known. The DTS-ΔT  method recorded the average migration rate of the wet front between the depth positions of the first and second circular fiber optic sections. Meanwhile, the OFDR-Δν  method recorded the entire migration process of the wet front within the first vertical cable monitoring section with high spatial resolution, obtaining the migration rate between each measurement point. The first vertical optical fiber section is located between the first and second circular fiber optic sections. The RMSE between the migration rates recorded by the OFDR-Δν  method at various measurement points and the average migration rate of the wet front recorded by the DTS-ΔT  method within the entire depth segment is compared. Using the mature DTS-ΔT  method monitoring data as the reference, the accuracy of the wet front migration rate monitoring by the OFDR-Δν  method is evaluated. The results are presented in Fig. 12  . From the results shown in the figure, it can be observed that the difference between the OFDR-Δν  and DTS-ΔT  monitoring data is relatively small. Part of the error is attributed to the instrument sampling time intervals set by humans, which can be further reduced in the subsequent application of this technology. Based on the comparison, it can be concluded that compared to the DTS-ΔT  monitoring technology, the OFDR-Δν  monitoring technology not only ensures the accuracy of wet front localization but also possesses the continuous monitoring capability with high spatial resolution. Therefore, OFDR-Δν  exhibits more significant advantages in infiltration monitoring. The infiltration monitoring results of the third circular fiber optic section and the first vertical fiber optic monitoring section demonstrate that the newly proposed AH-OFDR infiltration monitoring method, as presented in this study, is fully capable of achieving spatially continuous monitoring of the infiltration process. Leveraging the high spatial resolution advantage and temperature sensitivity of OFDR-Δν  technology, this monitoring system can accurately capture changes in soil thermal conductivity within centimeter-scale spatial resolution. Consequently, it enables precise localization of the wetting front migration process. Based on the above results, the AH-OFDR method proposed in this study can achieve high-precision spatial continuous characterization of the infiltration process. After further calibration, this method can achieve spatially continuous quantification of the infiltration process, thereby enabling the calculation of soil infiltration rates. Spatially differentiated infiltration rate parameters play a crucial role in hydrological model fitting, surface runoff prediction, groundwater recharge estimation, and other related fields.   4.3 Verification of heat accumulation caused by fiber optic cable overlap The Infrared Thermal Imaging Technique involves the use of an infrared thermal imager to capture the thermal infrared waves radiated from the surface of an object. When the temperature of an object changes, the intensity of the thermal infrared waves emitted outward also changes. The temperature of the object can be determined based on the intensity of the radiation waves received by the thermal infrared imager (Zeng et al., 2022 ). During the infiltration process, continuous imaging monitoring of the specimen's surface using an infrared thermal imager was performed to determine the temperature variations within the soil. In the aforementioned analysis of OFDR-Δν  monitoring results, abnormal increases were observed in the Δν  monitoring values at certain cable locations. Analyzing the results from the infrared thermal imaging monitoring confirmed the accuracy of the conclusion previously proposed regarding soil heat accumulation due to overlapping cables. This validation supports the applicability of the AH-OFDR monitoring method proposed in this paper for infiltration monitoring. Analyzing two monitoring states, one where the specimen is in a dry soil state and the other where vertical infiltration surpasses the depth position of the second circular fiber optic cable, the thermal imaging camera recorded the temperature field of the specimen as shown in Fig. 13  . When the specimen is in a dry soil state, the soil temperature at the three circular fiber optic sections is notably higher than at other positions within the specimen. In the transition section where the vertical cable intersects with the annular pipe cable, the soil temperature surrounding the cable is higher than at other positions of the annular optical cable, as depicted in Fig. 13 a. As infiltration reaches the depths of the annular optical cables, the rapid increase in soil thermal conductivity causes the heat released from the cables to dissipate outward rapidly. This results in a noticeable decrease in soil temperature around the cables. This phenomenon is clearly reflected in the infrared thermal imaging monitoring results shown in Fig. 13 b. Moreover, at the various positions where infiltration was completed, due to the enhanced thermal conductivity of the soil, the thermal influence range of the optical cable expanded, resulting in an increase in soil temperature at locations relatively distant from the optical cable position. The distribution of soil temperature fields during the infiltration process, as recorded by the infrared thermal imaging method, serves to validate the accuracy of the conclusion regarding the anomalous OFDR-Δν  monitoring results due to overlapping cable positions. Furthermore, it demonstrates the exceptional temperature sensitivity and spatial resolution exhibited by the OFDR-Δν  method in monitoring the infiltration process.   5 Conclusions This study introduced a method for achieving spatially continuous and high-resolution monitoring of the soil infiltration process, referred to as Active Heating Optical Frequency Domain Reflectometry (AH-OFDR). This monitoring method is based on an improved mechanism of Active Heated Fiber Optics (AHFO) technology, combined with Optical Frequency Domain Reflectometry (OFDR) to monitor the infiltration process. We designed a feasible infiltration monitoring scheme based on the spatiotemporal continuity characteristics of the infiltration process. By extending the heating time of the optical cable and reducing its power supply, we ensured the acquisition of continuous infiltration patterns while minimizing the disturbance of monitoring activities on the soil. The feasibility of the AH-OFDR monitoring method and scheme was confirmed through experiments. The fiber optic monitoring results recorded the infiltration process at centimeter-level spatial resolution and accurately distinguished changes in soil water content caused by different infiltration directions. Two fiber optic monitoring methods were used simultaneously in the experiment, and the results obtained by the AH-OFDR method were compared with those from the widely used distributed temperature sensing (DTS) method for infiltration monitoring. This comparison confirmed not only the feasibility of the AH-OFDR method but also its high spatial resolution advantage. Additionally, infrared thermal imaging technology was used to monitor temperature changes inside the sample soil during infiltration, providing explanations for abnormal situations in the fiber optic monitoring results. It indicates that the proposed novel AH-OFDR method possesses extremely high spatial resolution, which provides robust support for achieving continuous spatial and temporal monitoring of the infiltration process in soil. The AH-OFDR method proposed in this study holds promising potential for a wide range of applications. For instance, it can be applied in the field of hydrology to achieve spatially continuous acquisition of soil water content data and corresponding infiltration parameters during the infiltration process, thereby enhancing the accuracy of hydrological model fitting. Additionally, the high spatial resolution analysis of infiltration processes serves as a basis for the development of hydrological models that account for spatial variations. In agricultural irrigation processes, this technology can be utilized to determine irrigation depths at high spatial resolutions. By selecting appropriate irrigation patterns based on crop characteristics, water resource consumption can be reduced while ensuring crop growth. The application of AH-OFDR methods enables the monitoring of shallow soil water field evolution in geological formations such as slopes under climate change conditions. By obtaining high spatial resolution information on soil water field spatial variations, critical layers prone to disasters can be identified, thereby improving the ability to prevent geological hazards. Moreover, owing to its exceptionally high spatial resolution and monitoring sensitivity, this method can also be utilized for analyzing finer-scale water migration patterns, distinguishing the effects of capillarity from gravity on water movement, and evaluating capillary barrier effectiveness, among other applications. It should be noted that this study represents an initial exploration of the AH-OFDR infiltration monitoring method and its feasibility. Further refinements are necessary in future research. For instance, it is essential to establish soil water content calculation models based on the monitored Δν  results, tailored to different cable characteristics and soil conditions. This would enable the accurate spatial and continuous acquisition of water content information at varying depths during the infiltration process. The enhanced AH-OFDR method addresses the limitations of existing infiltration monitoring methods such as time domain reflectometry sensors, dye tracer method, and electrical resistivity tomography, etc., making it an advantageous approach for monitoring shallow soil infiltration related to climate change and quantifying the evolution of soil water fields. Moreover, additional research on the AHFO technique is necessary to explore a more optimal balance between heating power and heating duration. This will minimize the impact on the soil temperature field while still meeting the technical requirements for continuous infiltration monitoring using the AH-OFDR method. The calibrated AH-OFDR method enables the acquisition of high spatial resolution soil water content information. By applying this technology to infiltration monitoring, it becomes feasible to quantitatively track the spatial migration of water within the soil continuously. Obtaining accurate and high spatial resolution information on soil water evolution is crucial for improving the precision of existing hydrological models and revealing new soil–water interaction mechanisms.
1 Introduction The Souss-Massa basin, a pivotal agricultural heartland of central Morocco, is grappling with a burgeoning crisis of water scarcity, exacerbated by a combination of climatic shifts, unsustainable agricultural practices, and the relentless demand for irrigation water. This region, responsible for over three-quarters of the nation's agricultural output, faces a daunting challenge: the balance between water supply and demand is increasingly precarious, threatening food security and livelihoods. This decline is attributed to diminished rainfall, overexploitation of groundwater resources, and an imbalanced water distribution system. Moreover, the region's groundwater resources, the linchpin of its water supply, are under severe strain (Bouchaou et al., 2011 ). Over-extraction has led to notable declines in groundwater levels, particularly in the Sebt El Guerdanne area where the water table has receded to depths of up to 250 m (Hssaisoune et al., 2017 ). This over-extraction not only jeopardizes the sustainability of groundwater reserves but also induces salinization in the phreatic aquifer due to marine intrusion, further complicating the water crisis (Bouchaou et al., 2008 ). These challenges underscore the urgent need for innovative approaches to groundwater management and conservation in the Souss-Massa basin (Attar et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, the over-exploitation of groundwater has led to the salinization of the phreatic aquifer in the downstream section of the plain due to marine intrusion, coupled with a substantial reduction in the piezometric level in the central part of the plain. Similar consequences are anticipated upstream, as all farmers have migrated to this part of the plain. This over-exploitation of the groundwater table is primarily attributed to the continuous growth in investments within the agricultural sector and an increased influx of migrants from mountainous areas to the plains in search of employment opportunities (Almulla et al., 2022 ). Mountainous areas harbour hydrogeological potential that warrants harnessing, albeit hindered by the challenge of pinpointing optimal drilling locations necessitating the application of remote sensing and geophysical prospecting techniques. As a result, water supply in these areas is severely limited, hindering economic growth and encouraging migration to the plains. Given the extant circumstances, identifying novel zones with groundwater potential holds pivotal importance for effective management, safeguarding, and optimal utilization of this invaluable resource. The mapping of groundwater potential, a validated approach for exploring and forecasting groundwater resources, hinges on diverse geo-environmental factors encompassing hydrology, geological structures, topography, geology, and climate (e.g., Oh et al., 2011 ; Echogdali et al., 2023a, 2022a ; Pham et al., 2019 ; Shao et al., 2020 ; Ikirri et al., 2023a ; Pal et al., 2024 ; Aqnouy et al., 2024 ; Kostyuchenko et al., 2022 ). Numerous methodologies, encompassing logistic regression (Nguyen et al., 2020 ), random forests (Chen et al., 2020 ), frequency ratio (Razandi et al., 2015; Saravanan et al., 2022 ), evidential belief function (Ghosh, 2021 ), genetic algorithm (Naghibi et al., 2017 ), certainty factor (Razandi et al., 2015 ), and analytic hierarchy process (Echogdali et al., 2022b; Ikirri et al., 2023a ), have been employed to restrict potential groundwater areas. In response to this pressing issue, our study seeks to harness the synergistic potential of fractal analysis and machine learning techniques, applied to gravity data, to assess and map the distribution of groundwater resources in the Souss-Massa mountainous basin (SMMB). The application of Data-Driven Multi-index Overlay (DMIO ), Geometric Average (GA ), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Logistic Regression (LR) models, in conjunction with nine key influencing factors, offers a novel approach to understanding the complex dynamics of groundwater distribution in this arid region. This study aims to answer the critical research question: How can the integration of geomatics, including GIS, GPS, and remote sensing applications, enhance the accuracy and reliability of groundwater distribution assessments in the Souss-Massa mountainous basin (SMMB)? By identifying areas with varying levels of groundwater potential and validating these findings through the calculation of each model's area under the ROC curve (AUC), we aim to provide a comprehensive, data-driven framework for groundwater assessment. This framework not only contributes to the scientific understanding of groundwater dynamics in arid regions but also offers practical insights for policymakers and stakeholders in developing sustainable groundwater management strategies. Through this research, we endeavor to address the pressing need for effective water resource management in the Souss-Massa mountainous basin (SMMB), thereby supporting the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goal 2 (Zero Hunger) by mitigating the threat of soil erosion to food security in the region. This paper advances the adoption of a machine learning approach, namely data-driven multi-index overlay (DMIO ), geometric mean (GA ), support vector machine (SVM), and logistic regression (LR), for delineating groundwater potentiality areas within the Souss-Massa mountainous basin (SMMB). The best model was chosen after comparing the results of various approaches, using the Relative Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve and geophysical data.  2 Geology and data 2.1 Study area The Souss-Massa mountainous basin (SMMB), situated in south-central Morocco between the western High Atlas (WHA) and the southern Anti-Atlas (SAA) ( Fig. 1 ), drains directly westwards into the Atlantic Ocean via the Souss and Massa rivers (Hssaisoune et al., 2012 ). The northern boundary of the plain is defined by the WHA mountain range and the South Atlas fault, which has experienced recent tectonic activity, including the Agadir earthquake of magnitude 5.9 in February 1960. This geological structure creates a distinct linear transition between the plain and the WHA relief. In contrast, the southern boundary is formed by the SAA mountain range, with no significant tectonic deformation observed since the end of the Miocene, resulting in a transition between the Souss-Massa basin and the SAA unaffected by active geological structures (e.g., Ambroggi, 1963 ; Laville and Pique, 1991 ; Teixell et al., 2003 ).  2.2 Western High Atlas range The WHA chain lithology consists of various formations: (1) Paleozoic materials in the central massif, including schists, gneiss, quartzites, granites, andesites, and rhyolites (e.g., Petit, 1976 ; Pearson et al., 1977 ; Errami et al., 2002 ) ( Fig. 2 a and Fig. 2 b); (2) Triassic materials in the Argana corridor, composed of clay-sandstone and conglomerate formations (Dutuit, 1976 ; Medina et al., 2001 ); (3) Jurassic materials in the Ida-Ou-Tanane mountains, featuring Liassic dolomitic limestones (Daoudi, 1991 ), Callovian-Rauracian-Sequanian limestone complexes, and Late Jurassic dolomitic limestones (Laville and Piqueé, 1991 ); and (4) Cretaceous and Eocene formations, primarily composed of marls and limestones (Ambroggi, 1963; Amrhar, 1995 ). The outcropping formations, such as schists, marls, and clays, present low permeability, making the WHA the primary source of surface water for the Souss Plain (Dindane et al., 2007; Boutaleb et al., 2008a ). The region’s water resources are 370 mm3 /year, with local consumption ranging from 65 to 75 mm3 /year.  2.3 Western Anti-Atlas range The general lithostratigraphic units in the “WAA” region are depicted in Fig. 2 a and Fig. 2 b. The Paleoproterozoic lithologies consist of schists and granites (Choubert, 1963 ; Choubert and Faure Muret, 1976 ; Hafid, 1992 ; Oudra et al., 2005 ) while the Neoproterozoic lithologies exhibit diverse characteristics, reflecting the various tectonic environments they were formed in Eburnian orogeny which occurred during the Paleoproterozoic and Pan-African orogeny which occurred during the Neoproterozoic. These include: (i) a complex of Cryogenian calcareous and quartzite beds (Jeannette, 1981; Hafid, 1992 ), (ii) Lower Ediacaran units comprising volcanoclastics, conglomerate interbedded with pelites and sandstones (Choubert and Faure Muret, 1973 ), and (iii) Upper Ediacaran units composed of conglomerates, sandstones, and volcanoclastic units, predominantly consisting of volcanic breccias and pelites (Choubert and Faure Muret, 1973 ) (Fig. 2 a and Fig. 2 b). The Late Proterozoic to Paleozoic units unconformably overlies the Proterozoic formations, with the Taroudant Group being the oldest among them, spanning from Neoproterozoic to Lower Cambrian times. This group is divided into the Adoudou Formation and the “Lie de Vin Series” Formation. The Adoudou Formation is further subdivided into a lower unit referred to as the Base Series (Fig. 2 a and Fig. 2 b), characterized by volcanoclastic and siliciclastic deposits, and an upper carbonate unit known as the Lower limestones (Choubert, 1963; Benssaou et al., 2017 ). The Lie-de-Vin (Taliwinian) Formation consists of purplish-red pelites interspersed with carbonate beds (Benssaou et al., 2017 ). The Tata Group comprises two formations: the Upper Dolomites Formation, characterized by massive carbonate benches interbedded with siltstone layers, and the Upper Sandstones Formation (Middle Cambrian), dominated by massive pink sandstones alternating with fine shale beds (Choubert et al., 1952 ; Álvaro et al., 2007 ).  2.4 Hydrogeology of the study area 2.4.1 WHA chain The WHA range, mainly composed of the most impermeable rock formations, is of limited importance regarding groundwater resources. However, its extensive snow cover sustains small water reserves throughout the year. These reserves are typically confined to relatively small and moderately porous areas, encompassing superficial alteration zones or fractured formations. The aquifers within the region comprise metamorphosed Cambrian limestones, Stephano-Autunian and Permo-Triassic sandstones, Upper Jurassic limestones, middle Cretaceous dolomitic limestones, Upper Cretaceous and middle Eocene limestones, and finally Neogene conglomerates. Collectively, these geological formations possess limited permeability characteristics, thereby exerting negligible control over the flow dynamics of the wadis. Occurrences of silty or clayey alteration products within these formations are infrequent. Consequently, the solid discharge within the wadis from these formations remains meager, excluding the Argana corridor, which represents an exception. Within the scope of this study, out of the total 295 identified water access points, a substantial 80 % are associated with springs characterized by low discharge rates, ranging from 1.6 l/s for the Menizla spring to 0.02 l/s for the Sidi Bounagua spring. These springs either indicate variations in the permeability of the formations or proximity to an impluvium, ultimately serving as a significant water supply source for the local settlements (referred to as “douars”). The remaining water access points are distributed, with 17 % comprising wells, predominantly tapping into alluvial deposits, and the remaining 3 % directly drawing from surface water sources through Seguias (irrigation channels).  2.4.2 WAA chain The WAA chain features a succession of magmatic intrusions and adjacent metamorphic formations, constituting the main components of this complex. Despite the diversity within the geological formations and their covers, a distinct hydrogeological uniformity is evident: all these rocks exhibit compact characteristics, and most of the tectonic faults are filled and have minimal influence on water circulation. The hydrogeological significant formations are:a. Impermeable rhyolites and andesitic formations containing an interconnected aquifer within surface fracture zones. These volcano-sedimentary zones hold notable importance in this region characterized by water scarcity. The borehole surveys conducted on these formations (approximately ten) yielded positive results with productivities ranging from 0.1 to 0.6 l/s.  b. Tectonized and fractured quartzites exhibit fissure permeability. Despite the overall steepness of their slopes, they constitute water-bearing strata. When these quartzites indicate an extensive catchment area with highly fractured beds, they act as reservoirs for water, providing relatively higher discharge rates. The borehole 633/71 case exemplifies this scenario, yielding 1.5 l/s. Other boreholes also encountered this formation; two were unproductive (587/71 and 6384/71), while the third delivered three l/s (IRE 6470/71).  c. Precambrian conglomerates exhibit hydraulic behavior analogous to that of volcano-sedimentary formations. These conglomerates, common in the Igherm area, have crack permeability connected to local tectonic events. They generally function as a drainage system for the altered zone of the Adoudounian basal shales. All twenty boreholes intersecting these formations were productive, with discharge rates ranging from 0.1 to 0.5 l/s.  d. The Adoudounian limestone and Cambrian schist-limestone series constitute a highly developed geological complex in the region, potentially acting as a reservoir. The approximately twenty reconnaissance boreholes executed in these formations are unproductive, except for five that yielded discharge rates ranging from 0 to 0.3 l/s.      2.5 Data Identifying groundwater potentiality area (GWPA) relied upon the analysis of nine key factors affecting groundwater within these rugged terrains. These factors encompassed rainfall patterns, altitudinal variations, hydraulic conductivity, incline steepness, proximity to geological lineaments, compactness of drainage networks, distance to rivers, as well as density and intersections of lineaments (Echogdali et al., 2022a; El Ayady et al., 2023; Ikirri et al., 2023a ). The DEM (Digital Elevation Model) spatial resolution 30 m was procured from the USGS (http://earthexplorer.usgs.gov/accessed  on 23 September 2023) and was employed for the derivation of intricate cartographic elements like slope, elevation, and river distributions ( Table 1 ). Distinct lineaments were extracted from the imagery of Landsat 8 OLI, captured on 05 December 2023. Meanwhile, the delineation of geological faults was achieved by digitizing information from the comprehensive 1: 100,000 scale geological maps of Morocco, Argana corridor, Taroudant, Tafraout, Ighrem, Taliwine, Agadir Melloul which are also used for the creation of the permeability map. They were generating density maps for drainage networks and contours, and their intersections employed specialized methods, namely Line Density and Euclidean distance. These techniques were applied using the spatial analysis extension in ArcGIS. Rainfall data were provided by the Souss Massa Hydraulic Basin Agency ( Fig. 3 ). Gravity data was procured through a nationwide mapping endeavor instigated by the Geology Directorate of the Moroccan Ministry of Energy and Mines during the late 1970s. The dataset employed for this study originates from a Bouguer anomaly map, computed with a correction density of 2.67 g/cm³ (Silva-Ávalos et al., 2022; Van Den Bosch, 1981 ). Gravity measurements were acquired along roadways and pathways, with sampling intervals spanning from 1 to 5 km. The Bouguer anomaly map was initially converted into a digital format from a scanned image to process and analyze the gravity dataset. Subsequently, interpolation was performed on a uniformly spaced grid to obtain data points at the nodes. Additionally, various transformation and filtering techniques were employed to facilitate data interpretation (Gérard and Griveau, 1972; Jaffal et al., 2022; Martelet et al., 2013; Miller and Singh, 1994; Ouchchen et al., 2021, 2022 ). The locations of 1156 wells were also collected from the Souss Massa Hydraulic Basin Agency and used to assess the factors and models employed. Through a random selection process, 809 (≈ 70 %) of the wells were used for training, while the remaining 347 (≈ 30 %) were reserved for validation (Naghibi et al., 2015; El Ayady et al., 2023 ). The methodology for developing and validating GWPA models is presented in Fig. 3 .   3 Methods 3.1 Generation of conditioning factors with a logistic function The spatial values of the nine factors were transformed using the logistic function, which efficiently converts raw data values into a logistic space [0,1] (Yousefi and Carranza, 2015a; Aryafar and Roshanravan, 2020 ) (Eq.1 ). Yousefi and Carranza (2015a)  demonstrated that applying the logistic function enhances and facilitates the discrimination between different data classes compared to a set of values in their original space (Micheli-Tzanakou, 1999 ). Therefore, the capabilities of each factor can be assessed to identify and eliminate factors that do not affect modeling. The Prediction-Area (P-A) plot was used (Yousefi and Carranza, 2015a, b,c ). Yousefi and Carranza (2015a)  demonstrated the ability of the P-A plot to assign reliable weights to factors and distinguish between effective and ineffective factors. The weights assigned to the factors should reflect realistic relationships between the factors and GWPA zones. Consequently, drilling site locations can be used to assess the reliability of these weights. The prediction rate (Pr ) is based on drilling site locations in the P-A plot, and the proportion of occupied area (Oa ) associated with different factor classes is plotted. Based on the intersection point parameters in the P-A plot (Mihalasky and Bonham-Carter, 2001 ), the normalized density index (Nd ) and weight of each factor (We ) can be calculated to determine the effectiveness of factors and their weights. Nd  is calculated as the prediction rate of a factor divided by its corresponding occupied area using Eq. 4  (Mihalasky and Bonham-Carter, 2001 ).(4) N  d   =  P  r    O  a           Nd , Pr , and Oa  refer to the normalized density, prediction rate, and occupied area extracted from the intersection point in the generated P-A plots for various factors. A value of Nd > 1 (We > 0) indicates a positive association with the factor in GWPA mapping, whereas a value of Nd < 1 (We < 0) indicates a negative association with the factor (Parsa et al., 2016 ). (1994)  was employed to define threshold values in a data-guided rather than arbitrary manner, aiming to obtain discretized factor maps. This method describes the relationship between the factor class and the corresponding area (Echogdali et al., 2022d; Ouchchen et al., 2021 ).  3.1.2 Integration of conditioning factors In GWPA mapping, the Data-Driven Multi-index Overlay (DMIO ), Geometric average (GA ), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Logistic Regression (LR) models were applied and their results were compared. Subsequently, the accuracy and analysis of each model were assessed using the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve and gravimetric data, respectively.   3.2 Data-driven multi-index overlay Data-driven multi-index Overlay (DMIO ) is a method in which factors are discretized into several arbitrary classes and then integrated, considering subjectively assigned weights for each factor (Bonham-Carter, 1994 ). It involves creating hyperplanes in an n-dimensional coordinate space represented by the parameters xi  of the vector x to separate points belonging to two different classes (Dixon, 2009 ; Marjanović et al., 2011 ). Consequently, it seeks the shortest distance between the closest points of each class and the hyperplane. The training points most comparable to the hyperplane are called support vectors and are essential for determining the optimal hyperplane (Yoon et al., 2011 ). However, in many cases, the data is not linearly separable, and SVMs use kernel functions to project the data into a higher-dimensional space where linear separation is possible. This technique is known as the “kernel trick” and enables the resolution of non-linear classification and regression problems (Tehrany et al., 2014 ). This means that SVMs are capable of handling data with non-linear relationships by utilizing a particular function Eq. 10  (Tehrany et al., 2014; Mojaddadi et al., 2017 ):(10) K X  i   ,  X    = φ X  i      . φ X          SVM aims to find the optimal separating hyperplane that distinguishes the two classes using the training data. If the data is linearly separable, a separating hyperplane can be defined by maximizing the separation margin between the classes using Eq. 6  (San, 2014; Anh et al., 2023 ).
