It describes the relationship between a dependent variable and several independent variables (Ohlmacher and Davis, 2003 ). The dependent variable represents the binary-coded healthy locations, with values of 1 or 0 indicating the presence or absence of a well, respectively (Park et al., 2017 ). The independent variables represent the conditioning factors of groundwater. One of the advantages of LR is that it computes the weights of each conditioning factor using the following Eqs. 12 and 13  (Xi et al., 2022 ):(12) Z =  e  − ( β  0   + β  1   X  1   + β  2   X  2   + … β  i   X  i   )        (13) P =  1  ( 1 + Z )        where, βi  is the optimal regression coefficient reflecting the contributions of each factor; β0  is the constant coefficient; Xi  is the input conditioning factors; and P is the occurrence probability of a spring.  3.6 Model validation 3.6.1 ROC curve The validation of results is an essential step in prediction modeling. Validation well data, which were not included in the training process, were fed into the models for validation purposes (Echogdali et al., 2022b ). To assess the accuracy of the four models (GA , DMIO , SVM, and LR), the relative operating characteristics (ROC) curves were plotted (Echogdali et al., 2022b; Ikirri et al., 2023a; El Ayady et al., 2023 ). This widely used method evaluates the accuracy of GWPA maps. The ROC curve represents the false positive rate on the X-axis and the actual positive rate on the Y-axis (Naghibi, 2016 ; Chen et al., 2018 ). The area under the ROC curve (AUC), ranging from 0.5 to 1, is utilized to assess the performance of the models (Kalantar et al., 2018 ). It can be classified into five categories: poor (0.5–0.6), fair (0.6–0.7), good (0.7–0.8), very good (0.8–0.9), and excellent (0.9–1) (Yesilnacar, 2005 ).  3.6.2 Processing of gravity data As the study area is situated in the mountains, groundwater will be primarily influenced by faults and hydrogeological lineaments. These need to be verified by processing and analyzing gravity data. The Bouguer anomaly map is the outcome of overlaying regional geological structures and local small-scale tectonic activities (Blakely and Simpson, 1986 ). Separating the regional component, which represents the influence of deep structures, from the Bouguer anomaly is crucial in interpreting the residual field (Zeng et al., 2007 ). The residual anomaly, arising from shallow sources, was calculated by subtracting the Bouguer anomaly from the regional field (Nzeuga et al., 2022 ). Subsequently, the horizontal gradient (HD) and Euler deconvolution methods were applied to the residual anomaly data (Belkhiria et al., 2017; Frifita et al., 2019; Nzeuga et al., 2022; Ikirri et al., 2023b ). The HD enables the identification of faults and the determination of their slopes (Khattach et al., 2006; Ikirri et al., 2023b ). A linear contact corresponds to a fault, while a circular contact corresponds to an intrusive body or diaper. HD results can confirm lineaments that often coincide with known fault locations and determine new deep faults not mapped on the surface. The HD (Cordell, 1979; Cordell and Grauch, 1985 ) can be calculated as follows in Eq. 14 :(14) HD = ( ∂ ∆ T )  2    ∂ x   + ( ∂ ∆ T )  2    ∂ y          where ΔT, x, and y are the values of the total gravimetric field, horizontal and vertical derivatives. The Euler deconvolution method is robust in quantitatively interpreting potential field data (Bencharef et al., 2022 ). In addition to locating geological structures, it allows for estimating their depth and identifying their degree of rooting (Keating and Pilkington, 2004; Cooper, 2014 ). The “structural index” choice is crucial for selecting the type of structures to highlight, and it can range from 0 to 3 (Reid et al. 1990 ). In this study, a structural index of SI=0, a window size of 10 ×10, and a tolerance level of 15 % were applied.    4 Results 4.1 Generated transformed factors 4.1.1 Slope The slope factor plays a crucial role in influencing surface water infiltration into permeable soils (Yariyan et al., 2022; El Ayady et al., 2023 ). It determines the capacity of a zone to either retain water through infiltration or promote runoff (Magesh et al., 2012 ). Areas with lower slopes exhibit reduced runoff velocities, allowing enhanced water permeation (Yariyan et al., 2022 ). The slope ranges from 0 to 70 degrees. Low slopes characterize the southeast, northwest, and northern areas of the Ait Baha locality, whereas the north, north-eastern, and southwestern slopes exhibit steep slopes ( Fig. 4 a).  4.1.2 Elevation The elevation map of the entire Souss-Massa mountainous basin (SMMB) at its mouth shows the high elevations of the High Atlas Mountain peaks, which are lower in the Anti-Atlas range. Half of the basin’s surface area is 1000 and 2000 m above sea level (Fig. 4 b).  4.1.3 Rainfall Rainfall is a primary means of replenishing subterrane and aquifers, influencing the volume of water available for infiltration (Agarwal and Garg, 2016; Masroor et al., 2023; Ishola et al., 2023 ). Examination of the rainfall distribution map demonstrates a logical correlation between the average altitude of a basin and its mean annual rainfall. Higher elevations in the upstream bas in exhibit more significant rainfall, gradually diminishing downstream (Fig. 4 c). Importantly, the High Atlas region experiences substantial rainfall above 1000 m, averaging between 400 and 650 mm annually. In contrast, the Anti-Atlas region receives notably lower rainfall due to its location within a pre-Saharan latitude zone. Regarding rainfall, the recent data in the Souss-Massa mountainous basin (SMMB) indicates an average annual rate of approximately 550 mm/year in the WHA and below 200 mm/year in the SAA (Lanari et al., 2020 ). Both the SAA and the WHA exhibit a gradual decrease in rainfall from west to east due to orographic effects (Lanari et al., 2020 ).  4.1.4 Permeability Permeability is an essential factor in describing groundwater and can affect groundwater recharge because it influences water movement through a porous material (Hong et al., 2015; Yeh et al., 2016; Mandal et al., 2016; Echogdali et al., 2022c ). The permeability was divided into five main categories: very high, high, moderate, low, and very low, based on lithological formations and degrees of their fracturation (Fig. 4 d). The areas exhibiting high permeability coincide with the Jurassico-Cretaceous carbonate formations of the northwest of the basin and the Quaternary alluvial formations in both WHA and WAA chains. Moderate permeability is observed in the Cambrian carbonate cover formations and the Precambrian granitic and volcano-detrital formations upstream of the Aoulouz region (Ait Maad Region). Widespread formations with low permeability are found in the Anti-Atlas chain, corresponding to the Adoudounian dolomitic formations and the Triassic clay formations in the Argana corridor (Boutaleb et al., 2000 ).  4.1.5 Lineaments Lineaments play a significant role in mapping groundwater potentiality as they represent linear features that function as pathways or conduits for the movement and accumulation of groundwater (Boutaleb et al., 2008b; Ishola et al., 2023 ). Analysis of satellite imagery conducted in the Souss-Massa mountainous basin (SMMB) identifies six prominent anomalies situated in the Argana corridor, Imoullass and Ait Maad regions, and the northern regions of Taliouine, Igherm, and Ait Baha in the upstream portion of the basin (Fig. 4 e). In the WHA, four major regional fracture systems, with average orientations aligned along N-S, NE-SW, E-W, and NW-SE directions, are observed. The N-S normal faults were generated as a result of extension related to the dislocation of Africa, which caused the opening of a rift basin developed mainly in the Triassic and Jurassic (Arboleya et al., 2004; Beauchamp et al., 1996; Choubert and Faure-Muret, 1962; Gomez et al., 2000; Jacobshagen et al., 1988; Laville and Pique, 1991; Mattauer et al., 1977; Teixell et al., 2003 ). This extension reactivated pre-existing NE-SW to ENE-WSW Variscan structures. An example of such a structure is the Tizi n’Test fault, which is reactivated as a left-lateral strike-slip fault (Beauchamp, 1988; Laville et al., 2004; Laville and Petit, 1984; Laville and Pique, 1991; Mattauer et al., 1977; Ouanaimi and Petit, 1992; Proust et al., 1977 ). Within the Anti-Atlas mountain range, the lineaments demonstrate well-known fault orientations, including NE-SW, NW-SE, and E-W (Boutaleb et al., 2008c ). These lineaments are associated with the Pan-African and Variscan orogenies. Notably, the largest lineaments observed stretch up to 5.2 km long, predominantly aligned along the NE-SW direction, suggesting their connection to the post-Pan-African rifting episode. These lineaments serve as conduits for groundwater flow, facilitating its movement through the subsurface. It is worth noting that these lineaments positively impact all the surrounding regions they traverse (Fig. 4 f), prompting us to consider the distance from these lineaments as a parameter influencing the availability of groundwater (Magesh et al., 2012 ).  4.1.6 Lineament intersection density The density of node intersections exhibits a positive relationship with groundwater recharge areas (Echogdali et al., 2022a, b ), and the higher the density of node intersections, the greater the water availability. Fig. 4 g illustrates that a high density of lineament intersections is observed in the northwestern, eastern, and northern parts of the Ighrem region. In contrast, a low density of lineaments dominates the southwestern and southern parts of Taliwine.  4.1.7 Drainage density Drainage density refers to the measurement of the ratio between the combined length of all streams within a specific drainage basin and the total area of that basin. The regions with higher drainage density are typically associated with reduced infiltration capacity (Masroor al., 2023 ; Echogdali et al., 2022a ; El Ayady et al., 2023 ). Consequently, areas with lower infiltration rates tend to have diminished groundwater potential. Despite the significant rainfall levels in the High Atlas compared to the Anti-Atlas range, it has a low-density hydrographic network, except in the Argana corridor (Fig. 4 h). This phenomenon appears to result from various interacting factors. A high density of linear features in this area promotes more significant rainfall infiltration and thus limits the development of an extensive drainage system (Carlston, 1963 ). This is further confirmed by the observed high drainage density in the Argana corridor, where impermeable clay formations dominate, favoring surface drainage over infiltration. The same behavior is observed in the Anti-Atlas range, where areas with high permeability and fractures exhibit low drainage density.  4.1.8 Distance to rivers The impact of distance to a river on groundwater recharge can vary depending on various factors such as geology, climate, and land use. However, in general, proximity to a river can positively influence groundwater recharge due to the potential for direct recharge through infiltration (Echogdali et al., 2023b; Ikirri et al., 2023a ). The resemblance between the map depicting distances from the hydrographic network and the actual hydrographic network itself is evident (Fig. 4 i). This can be attributed to the fact that the distance from the hydrographic network is often calculated based on the proximity to streams and rivers.  4.1.9 Recognition of the more critical factors To extract the influential factors, the locations of the wells can be used to assess the reliability of their significant spatial relationships with the GWPA map in the Souss-Massa mountainous basin (SMMB). The P-A plot method was employed to achieve this, and the normalized density index (Nd ) and weight (We ) were calculated. The transformed values of the nine factors to a [0,1] range (Fig. 4 ) were first discretized into several classes using the logistic function according to Eq. 1 . To determine threshold values for the classification of these factors, the C-A fractal model was applied ( Fig. 5 ) to obtain classified maps ( Fig. 6 ). Based on this map, the P-A plot was generated ( Fig. 7 ). The parameters of the intersection points in the P-A plots were used to select the best factors ( Table 2 ). The normalized density index (Nd ) should be greater than 1, and the weight (We ) should be greater than 0. The results show that Nd  and We  values for the nine factors' transformed values are >1 and >0, respectively. Consequently, distance to rivers and slope (Nd =1.33, We=0.28) and distance to lineament (Nd =1.27, We =0.24) are considered the most influential factors and followed by lineament density (Nd =1.22, We =0.20), drainage density (Nd =1.17, We =0.16), elevation, lineament intersection density, and rainfall (Nd =1.13, We =0.12). Permeability is the least influential factor, yielding the lowest Nd  (1.08) and We  values (0.08). Based on these results, nine selected factors are suitable for delineating the GWPA map in the study area.  4.1.10 Application of the DMIO , GA , SVM, and LR models The maps for groundwater potential areas in the Souss-Massa mountainous basin (SMMB) created using DMIO , GA , SVM, and LR models are illustrated in  Fig. 8 . After the generation of the four models, the C-A fractal model was applied to determine threshold values for classification ( Fig. 9 ). Based on these figures, the models were discretized ( Fig. 10 ). Five classes were considered as very low, low, moderate, high, and very high. The distribution of each class, relative to the applied model, is presented in  Fig. 11 .   4.2 Model validation 4.2.1 ROC curve The validation of the DMIO , GA , SVM, and LR models was assessed using the area under the curve (AUC) of ROC. For this purpose, 30 % of the validation well data were used. AUC values close to 1 represent better model prediction in GWPA (El Ayady et al., 2023 ). The area under the ROC curve (AUC) for the four models, DMIO , GA , SVM, and LR, are 0.761, 0.785, 0.815, and 0.752, respectively ( Fig. 12 ). These values are above 70 %, indicating acceptable performance of the four models. However, SVM and GA  exhibit higher accuracy than DMIO  and LR.  4.2.2 Gravity interpretation The Bouguer anomaly map displays multiple anomalies of diverse polarities, with magnitudes ranging from −95.9 to +7.7 mGal ( Fig. 13 a). A regional gradient exhibits a progressive increase from the eastern to the western parts of the Souss-Massa mountainous basin (SMMB). Two negative anomalies, situated in the basin's far northeastern and southwestern regions, respectively, correspond to the extensively fractured crystalline formations of the Siroua massif and the granitic arenas resting upon a granitic basement in the Tafraout region. Additionally, two positive anomalies in the southwestern and northwestern parts of the basin, precisely south of Ait Baha and in the Argana corridor, coincide with the shallowly situated Paleozoic schist basement. By subtracting the regional component from the Bouguer anomaly, the residual map of the Souss-Massa mountainous basin (SMMB) (Fig. 13 b) is obtained, featuring values ranging from −20.8 to +16.5 mGal. This map clearly illustrates negative and positive anomalies, allowing for a compelling correlation with the density variation of geological formations in this area. In the Tafraout region, the negative anomaly corresponds to the infilling of the Ameln valley by less dense granitic arenas, coinciding with a fault zone (ZFVA), in comparison to the outcrops of the Jbel Lkest quartzites to the north (Hassenforder, 1987 ). These faults are associated with the tectonic history of the final Pan-African phase, documented by the Tafraout pluton as NE-SW dextral rifts (Hassenforder, 1987 ). The northernmost part of the basin exhibits a substantial positive anomaly with an amplitude of +7.8 mGal. This anomaly in the Argana corridor arises from the shallow extension of the Paleozoic basement beneath a Permo-Triassic cover situated at the western boundary of the central High Atlas massif (Choubert and Marçais, 1952 ). It forms a well-defined depression between the west and central High Atlas (Choubert et al., 1952 ). Lastly, the positive anomalies respectively north of Igherm and in Taliwine regions coincide with Precambrian conglomerates and sandstone formations in the Anti-Atlas chain (Choubert and Marçais, 1952 ) (Fig. 13 b). The HD map reveals that most gravity lineaments align in east-west and northeast-southwest directions (Fig. 13 c). The Tafraout gravity lineament coincides with the ductile-brittle shear zone of the Kerdous buttonhole, exhibiting an east-west orientation (Hassenforder, 1987 ). This lineament represents a shear zone with a width of several tens of meters, situated at the boundary between the Kerdous slates to the south and the Lkest quartzites to the north (Hassenforder, 1987 ). At the upper limit of the Souss plain, the Tizi n’Test Fault Zone (ZFTT) runs parallel to the southern part of the High Atlas and traverses it obliquely in a northeast-southwest to east-west direction (Proust et al., 1977 ). The ZFTT is widely recognized as a significant fault that played a crucial role in the structural evolution of the Atlas Mountains, acting as a transcontinental break (Mattauer et al., 1972; Arthaud and Matte, 1977 ). Additionally, an east-west trending segment corresponds to the EI Menizla fault south of the Argana corridor, which represents the southernmost branch of the ZFTT. It forms an east-west fold running along the foothills of the Atlas Mountains, ultimately terminating in a Triassic fold. Euler deconvolution allows the estimation of their depth in addition to the localization of contacts in the horizontal plane (Keating, 1998; Asfirane-Haddadji and Galdeano, 2000 ). This technique confirms the lineament plots illustrated by the horizontal derivative map (Fig. 13 c). It detects their deep character (Fig. 13 d). This map enables us to delineate the geological faults that play a significant role in water drainage on the southern slopes of the High Atlas and the northern slopes of the Anti-Atlas. It demonstrates that these faults substantially impact the High Atlas water potential more than the Anti-Atlas range. Despite these faults in the basin's southern part, the lack of substantial recharge due to low rainfall (<200 mm) in this region diminishes their hydrogeological significance.    5 Discussion To varied degrees, different variables influence groundwater supply in the Souss-Massa mountainous basin (SMMB)(Pham et al., 2021 ). The distance to rivers, slope, and distance to lineaments have greater importance in GWPA mapping, followed by lineament density, drainage density, elevation, lineament intersection density, rainfall, and permeability (Table 2 ). The results of studies conducted by Kordestani et al. (2019)  and Naghibi and Pourghasemi (2015)  in Lordegan and Beheshtabad basins, respectively, confirm the impact of these factors on water availability, especially in arid-climate regions. The results of the four applied models agree that areas with high potential are located in the northeast and Imoulass region in the WHA chain, which receive abundant rainfall and is characterized by a low distance to lineaments and a moderate to low drainage density (Fig.10 ). The existence of these three parameters favors substantial infiltration of surface water. In addition, the gentle dip of the geological layers creates favorable conditions for exploiting water reservoirs in aquifers close to the hydrographic network, which facilitates the recharge of neighboring lineaments (Fig. 2 a and Fig. 2 b) (Yariyan et al., 2022 ). These results are consistent with those of Ikirri et al. (2023b)  in the nearby Ifni basin. In the Argana corridor located northwest of the SMMB, formations of very low permeability, mainly consisting of Triassic clays, limit groundwater potential in this part of the basin, except for the LR model. The WAA chain shows lower groundwater potential compared to WHA. Only superficially fissured zones resulting from rock cracking during retro-diagenesis, as well as areas of recent superficial alteration or detrital accumulation, are conducive to infiltrating rainwater and forming small aquifer reserves. However, these terrains are exceptionally water-poor due to low rainfall levels (< 200 mm/year). There are no widespread aquifers, and the scarce underground water flow occurs in recent valley fillings of varying sizes or networks of fractures within Precambrian rocks, such as shales, schists-limestones, and volcanic-sedimentary formations (andesites and conglomerates). The comparison of relative humidity derived from NASA's GEOS-FP system data between the WHA and WAA mountain ranges underscores the influence of precipitation on water infiltration at a depth of 2 m. A clear disparity is evident between the two regions: the WHA chain, benefiting from higher rainfall, naturally experiences greater infiltration of water compared to the WAA chain ( Fig. 14 ). Moreover, most geological formations exhibit significant thicknesses in the WAA, such as the Adoudounian limestones, which exceed 1000 m with a generally plunging structure. Waters infiltrated through faults and stratigraphic interfaces and thus flow deeply to feed base levels (as observed in the case of the Souss Plain aquifer). The infiltrated volumes, being relatively low compared to the rainfall rates, consequently saturate only an arrow fringe situated at considerable depths. The evaluation of the effectiveness of SVM, GA , DMIO , and LR models shows AUC values of 0.815, 0.785, 0.761, and 0.752, respectively (Fig.12 ). They classify the performance of the model application as very good to good. The high accuracy was attributed to the SVM model, chosen as the reference for comparison with the three other models. Fig. 11  depicts the underestimation of low-potential areas in terms of surface area by all three models compared to the SVM model. Conversely, the GA  model overestimates areas corresponding to shallow potential. It can also be observed that the percentages for areas categorized as “very high” and “moderate” potential are nearly identical across the four models to the SVM model. However, a significant discrepancy exists when it comes to areas classified as low or very low potential. The high-performance value of the SVM model is due to its ability to handle complex and non-linear interactions between dependent and independent variables and its robustness to noise (Yu and Kim, 2012 ). These results are consistent with those of Sajedi-Hosseini et al. (2018) , who used the Boosted Regression Trees (BRT) and multivariate Discriminant Analysis (MDA) was compared with SVM models. It is also admitted that the uncertainties of different GWPA models can be related to the gaps in input data quality (Loosvelt et al., 2012; Naghibi et al., 2016 ). The difference in performance between SVM and the other three models may be due to their structural nature and specifications errors (Rahmati et al., 2015 ). Understanding the uncertainty in the input database allows a more appropriate interpretation of the model results (Loosvelt et al., 2012 ). Additionally, the random distribution of well data used for modeling (70 %) and validation (30 %) can introduce uncertainty in GWPA mapping (Garosi et al., 2018 ). The main advantage of machine learning (SVM and LR) models is the ability to integrate different influential factors in modeling and handling missing data and address the noise content of the data (Al-Fugara et al., 2020 ). The spatial resolution of the data can also influence the model predictions (Echogdali et al., 2022b ). High-resolution satellite imagery enables more efficient extraction and detection of data (Echogdali et al., 2023a; Ikirri et al., 2023a ). The digital elevation model (DEM) and Landsat 8 OLI satellite image utilized in this study have a modest resolution of 30 × 30 m   . The high resolution of the input data can improve the generated GWPA map.  6 Conclusions GWPA maps were developed for the Souss-Massa mountainous basin (SMMB) using the Data-Driven Multi-index Overlay (DMIO ) technique, Geometric Average (GA ), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Logistic Regression (LR) with nine conditioning factors employed. The effectiveness of these factors was assessed through the Prediction-Area (P-A) plot to identify the most influential factors on GWPA. To achieve this, data from 1156 wells were partitioned into training data (809 ≈ 70 %) and validation data (347 ≈ 30 %). The results indicated that the distance to rivers, slope, and distance to lineaments exhibited the most significant influence on GWPA, while permeability had a minor significance. The generation of the four models revealed that high and very high potential areas accounted for 22.44 %, 9.80 %, 19.36 %, and 26.77 % of the study area for the DMIO , GA, SVM, and LR models, respectively. The accuracy of these models was assessed using the area Under the Curve (AUC) of the ROC curve and gravimetric data, and based on the AUC values, the DMIO , GA , SVM, and LR models had values in the order of 0.761, 0.785, 0.815, and 0.752, respectively. These results indicate that the SVM model outperforms the other models. These GWPA maps provide valuable information for decision-makers in groundwater resource management in arid and semi-arid regions. Furthermore, the methodology employed in this study can be applied in other areas with similar hydrogeological, geological, topographical, and climatic conditions. 1 Introduction In the early stages, blooms were primarily observed in lakes, reservoirs and enclosed water bodies, while they were rarely observed in rivers (Bortolini et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2019; Huo et al., 2022 ). Over the past decades, the frequency and geographical distribution of harmful blooms have significantly increased due to dam construction and climate change (Aubriot et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2021 ). Harmful algae can secrete cyanotoxins, making serious threat to nervous system (Huisman et al., 2018 ). According to the estimate, there are now around 58,000 of large dams worldwide (Mulligan et al., 2020 ). In the context of resource scarcity, it is foreseeable that more dams and reservoirs will be built in the future (Wang et al., 2024 ). Thus, algal blooms of rivers becomes a global issue. Traditional assessments of blooms relied on field experiments, utilizing limited spatial–temporal data to infer the long-term dynamics (Hunter et al., 2009 ). The limited samples could not provide representative of blooms, especially for large water bodies where blooms were distributed in patches (Hunter et al., 2010; Shi et al., 2015 ). The mechanistic models, assisted by computational approximation models such as the MIKE 21 software and environmental fluid dynamics code (EFDC), has been successfully used for simulating and predicting blooms (Elhabashy et al., 2023; Shin et al., 2023 ). However, the lack of available chlorophyll data for model validation and calibration remains a major bottleneck for their application. Additionally, compared to inorganic substances, the calibration of algae often require numerous parameters and time (Nelson et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2022 ). Retrospective assessment of blooms using remote sensing technology holds promise in providing past and current information, enabling the identification of the periodic trajectories of blooms (Cetinić et al., 2024 ). With the advancement of machine learning, quantitative inversion is no longer limited to lakes and reservoirs, nor a single chlorophyll indicator. It has been applied to rivers, providing unprecedented areal information about past dynamics (Aubriot et al., 2020; Iiames et al., 2021 ). Over years of research, the consensus has gradually emerged that river eutrophication, combined with climate change and hydrodynamic conditions, propels the development of harmful algal blooms in rivers globally (Maavara et al., 2020; Bowes et al., 2024 ). Currently, the identification of stress sources for blooms relies mainly on field experiments or mechanistic model (Nwankwegu et al., 2022 ). The MIKE and EFDC models have been widely used to assess water environmental status. However, the inherent limitations of mechanistic models, such as fixed underwater light attenuation coefficients, make the models unable to capture the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of euphotic depth. Research had indicated that underwater transparency was crucial for the growth of algae (Shiozaki et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2022 ). However, similar effects still rely on local field experiments for validation. Fortunately, the remote sensing enables the fine inversion of water quality parameters (Mamun et al., 2024 ). At the same time, the vertical stratification of EFDC can depict the stratification of water temperature, water quality, and hydrodynamics (Kwon et al., 2024 ). It's worth noting that there are discrepancies in resolution and fusion between different data sources, leading to gap of response relation between targets and variables. The complex mechanisms of blooms in the tributary bay of reservoirs still needs further explore. Environmental variables can explain the development of blooms in stable and isolated aquatic ecosystems, such as lakes and reservoirs, while the aggregation and dispersion of blooms in rivers often occur in small-scale local watersheds (Hunter et al., 2010, Rothäusler et al., 2015 ). Some perspectives suggested that the origin and development of algae were influenced by the combined effects of environmental and geographical distance (Aubriot et al., 2020, Bortolini et al., 2017 ). The statistical models, spatiotemporal models, machine learning, and hybrid models have been used to estimate the key drivers of blooms (Ajani et al., 2023 ； Lin et al., 2023, Jargal and An, 2023 ). However, most of methods focused on correlations that resolve existing deterministic relationships and did not consider the spatiotemporal autocorrelation of variables. In real environments, the relationship between variables and response variables is not constant. On the one hand, all models assume that each covariate affects chlorophyll concentration or algal density at the same spatiotemporal scale, ignoring the scale differences between different covariates. On the other hand, the process of covariates influencing environmental concentrations is spatiotemporally heterogeneous (Liu et al., 2021; Sharma and Ghuge, 2024 ). Given the current gaps in the above content and methods, the understanding of the mechanisms of blooms in rivers needs further refinement concerning geographical features and environmental variables. Three Gorges Reservoir (TGR) is the largest reservoir in China. Since 2003, a series of algal blooms have primarily occurred in the tributary bay of the Three Gorges Reservoir. However, the triggers regarding algal blooms vary depending on research. Thus, this study integrates Sentinel-2 data and EFDC model, and combines multi-scale spatiotemporal geographic weighted models to examine multiscale effects of key factors. The objectives are to analyze the spatiotemporal dynamic of blooms, explore the differences and mechanisms of influencing factors at different spatial resolution, and identify the spatiotemporal lag effect of those factors.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Study area The Daning River is a primary tributary of the Yangtze River, located 123 km upstream from the Three Gorges Dam, making it one of the important tributaries affected by the dam's operation (Zhao et al., 2016 ). The Daning River basin is located in a subtropical monsoon humid climate zone, surrounded by the hilly terrain and canyons (Fig. 1  ). Annual precipitation ranges from 700 mm to 2300 mm, and average temperature varies in the range of 17–19 °C. The water level fluctuates periodically between 145 m and 175 m each year. Based on the operational rules of the TGR, the typical year can be divided into four phases: drainage period (May to June), low water level period (July to August), impoundment period (September to October), and high water level period (November to February) (Zheng et al., 2016 ). Due to the impact of the operation, nutrients in the Daning River significantly increase and water flow slows down. Those favorable conditions trigger algae growth, leading to frequent blooms (Xiang et al., 2021 ). In order to explore the distribution pattern of blooms, spatiotemporal dynamics of blooms was conducted based on data from 2017 to 2022. The research period covered both wet and dry years. The most severe years of blooms was taken as the typical year to analyze the causes and mechanisms.  2.2 Sample collection According to the transit time of Sentinel-2, the days with clear and cloudless were selected to conduct field observations on 24 July 2022 and 15 April 2023. Due to the absence of large-scale blooms during the sampling period, high concentrations of chlorophyll from the Longchuan River next to the Daning River were selected as supplementary data  for model training. Surface water samples within 0.5 m water depth were collected and stored at low temperature in dark until transfer to the laboratory. Raw water was filtrated through Whatman GF/F (0.7 μm pore size, Φ47 mm) filters to extract algae (Xie et al., 2022 ). Then, chlorophyll-a concentration was calculated by the spectrophotometer method after acetone extraction. The Uinistrong GPS receiver was uses to record longitude and latitude during sampling. Meanwhile, transparency was measured by secchi disc. The flow chart shows the main methods involved in the research (Fig. 2  ). The purpose of Step 1   was to quantitatively invert chlorophyll and analyze its spatiotemporal dynamic patterns. For Step 2  , the EFDC model was used to generate hydrodynamic and environmental factors based on the basic data to analyze the causes of blooms. Step 3   explored the causes of blooms from different scales by introducing random forest and the multiscale geographically and temporally weighted regression model.  2.3 Retrieval algorithm of Chl-a and transparency Sentinel-2 data were collected for quantitative inversion of chlorophyll and transparency. A bulk of Sentinel-2 products (69 images) for the period of 2017–2022 were downloaded from the ESA archives (https://earthexplorer.usgs.gov/  ). 90 pairs of the in-situ Chl-a data and their concurrent satellite spectral data were used to develop the Chl-a retrieving algorithm. 23 pairs of those data were randomly selected as the model test dataset, and the rest (67 pairs) were used for training. 67 pairs of the in-situ transparency data and their concurrent satellite spectral data were used to develop the transparency retrieving algorithm. 14 pairs of those data were randomly selected as the model test dataset, and the rest (53 pairs) were used for training. The Random Forest (RF) as well as Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and Support Vector Machine (SVM) were employed to establish the Chl-a algorithm and transparency algorithm, respectively (Mahdian et al., 2023; Habib et al., 2024 ). In addition, semi-biological analysis and band ratios were also used as references for the Chl-a algorithm (Gons et al., 2005 ). The machine learning requires the selection of the proper independent variables (input parameters for an algorithm) for establishing reliable algorithms. Pearson analysis was used to examine the relationship between independent variables and chlorophyll (or transparency). Here, the normalized Rrs values were took as initial independent variables, including bands at 444 nm (B1), 497 nm (B2), 560 nm (B3), 664 nm (B4), 705 nm (B5), 740 nm (B6), 783 nm (B7), 842 nm (B8) and 865 nm (B8a) (Fig. S1 ). Previous studies have found that B2/B3, B3/B4, B5/B4, and NDCI have shown good performance in predicting chlorophyll (as shown in Fig. S1 ). B2/B3 and B3/B4 have shown good performance in predicting transparency. So they were also included in the initial independent variables. The in-situ Chl-a and transparency were selected as the dependent variable. The training dataset was applied to each machine learning model to obtain trained algorithm. All three machine learning models were implemented using PyCharm 2022. Determination coefficients (R2 ) and root mean square error (RMSE) were used to evaluate the algorithm performance (Fig. S2 and S3 ). The results show that the RF has the best performance for Chl-a retrieval, while the SVM is suitable to extract transparency.  2.4 Mechanistic modeling The Environmental Fluid Dynamics Code model (EFDC), developed by John Hamrick (1996), was utilized to simulate the hydrodynamics, water temperature and water quality in the Daning River. EFDC integrates modules for hydrodynamics, sediment transport, toxic pollutants, eutrophication and water quality (Huang et al., 2018 ). Due to fluctuation of water level within the range of 145 m to 175 m in the TGR, the contour line within 175 m was extracted as the boundary for grid subdivision and topography construction. The CVL Grid software developed by the U.S. Company DSI divided the water area into 12,912 grids (Fig. 1 ), with an average resolution of 40 m. Given that the maximum depth of the Daning River within 80 m, it was divided into 6 layers in the vertical direction in order to capture variations in vertical environmental indicators. The generalized grids were used for the hydrodynamics, water temperature, and water quality simulations in the study area. Digital Elevation Model (DEM) with 30 m resolution was utilized as input data for riverbed elevation. The boundary conditions of the model primarily included flow, water level, water temperature, water quality and meteorological data. Hydrodynamic boundaries included daily flow for the Wanzhou station in the upstream Yangtze River, as well as daily flow for the Daning River and its tributaries. The downstream boundary comprised daily water level for the Badong station. Water temperature boundaries encompassed monthly temperature data for the Wanzhou station, the Daning River and its tributaries. The downstream boundary involved monthly temperature data for the Badong station. Water quality boundaries were sourced from monthly data for Dissolved Oxygen (DO), Nitrate Nitrogen (NO3 -N), Total Nitrogen (TN) and Total Phosphorus (TP) from the Wanzhou station, as well as the Daning River and its tributaries. Data for Wanzhou and Badong stations were obtained from the Hydrology Bureau of the Changjiang Water Resources Commission. Inflow boundaries for the Daning River and its tributaries were obtained through the SWAT model, providing daily flow and monthly water quality (Chen et al., 2021 ). Water temperature data with stratification came from monthly monitoring in the Daning River. Meteorological data for the Wushan station was downloaded from the Meteorological Data Sharing Network, including atmospheric pressure, air temperature, wind speed and direction, precipitation, evaporation, relative humidity and solar radiation data. The boundary data for January was used as the initial conditions. The time step was set as a dynamic step size, ranging from 0.18 to 1.8 s, to maintain stable iterative calculations. The simulation period covered from January 1, 2018 to December 30, 2018. The hydrodynamic module was calibrated using daily water level from the Dachang and Wushan stations. The water temperature module was calibrated using stratification data at the Shuanglong, Caiziba and Peishi cross-sections to adjust the temperatures. The water quality module was calibrated using DO, NO3 -N, TN and TP data at the Shuanglong, Caiziba and Peishi cross-sections to adjust the indexes. Model performance was assessed using AE (Absolute Error), RE (Relative Error), and RMSE (Root Mean Square Error). The parameters and calibration results of the model can be found in the supplementary material s (Fig. S4-S6  and Table S1 ). The RE for all indicators were less than 10 % except for NO3 -N, indicating that the simulation results are reliable.  2.5 Multiscale geographically and temporally weighted regression model (MGTWR) Spatial non-stationarity was used to describe the characteristics of spatial relationships, indicating that the spatial relationships may vary with spatial location (Huang et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2021 ). Most studies explore deterministic models producing point-wise estimates and forecasts making no considerations for predictive uncertainty (Donnelly et al., 2024a ). In order to generate robust forecasts, it is imperative to incorporate a systematic approach for quantifying uncertainty in the forecasts, such as Monte Carlo sampling, Bayesian methods and Convolutional Neural Network (Donnelly et al., 2024b ). To measure the scale at which different processes and quantify the heterogeneity, a sensible approach was to decompose the spatiotemporal weighted matrix (Ni et al., 2023 ). Therefore, this study introduced a new Multi-Scale Geographically and Temporally Weighted Regression (MGTWR) model. This model considered the scale differences between different covariates by using specific bandwidths for each covariate (Wu et al., 2019 ). MGTWR was a powerful model for studying spatiotemporal changes and incorporating multi-scale effects into regression analysis. Currently, it was applied in various fields of research, including ecology, criminology, and health geography. The MGTWR model could examine the significant impact of covariates at each prediction point, allowing exploration of the driving role of geographic features and environmental factors on chlorophyll. The absolute values of regression coefficients indicated the extent of the influence of driving factors on chlorophyll, while the positive or negative signs of the coefficients indicated the direction of the impact. The application of MGTWR in blooms can provide new insights from both spatial perspectives (i.e., local and global scales) and temporal perspectives (i.e., long-term and short-term scales) for risk prevention. It is worth noting that bandwidth is a critical parameter in MGTWR that controls the scale of the computation. Small time and spatial bandwidths often revealed short-term patterns at the micro scale, while large time and spatial bandwidths often revealed long-term patterns at the macro scale. The core formula of MGTWR was as follows. Covariates with larger bandwidths have lower variability in their regression coefficients at larger scales (Fotheringham et al., 2017 ). The R2  for all stages were more than 0.8, indicating that the simulation results were reliable (Table S2 ).(1) y i  = ∑ j = 1  m  β bwj   ( μ i  , v i  , t i  )  x i , j   + ∊ i  = ∑ j = 1  m  f i , j   + ∊ i      (2) β j  ^  = ( X  T  W j  X )  - 1   X  T  W j  y     (3) W j  = ( 1 - D st  / b w   2  )  2   D st  ≤ b w   0  D st  > b w        where, y i    represents the dependent variable, x i , j     represents the jth    covariate at location (μ i  , v i  , t i    ), f i , j     represents the jth    additive term at location (μ i  , v i  , t i    ), and β bwj     represents the regression coefficient of the jth    feature at a specific bandwidth bwj   . D st     is the spatiotemporal distance between the regression points (μ i  , v i  , t i    ) and the other measured sample points (Huang et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2021 ).  2.6 Statistic analysis The Zonal statistics based on ArcGIS integrated the environmental factors exported by EFDC with the Chla retrieved from remote sensing to achieve the scale matching. Random Forest (RF), as a multivariate technique, was used to determine the importance of different variables in predicting Chl-a. The importance of predictors was calculated by randomly permuting variables to determine the relative increase in Mean Squared Error (MSE). The out-of-bag data error was used as an evaluation metric to measure importance (Genuer et al., 2010 ). To address multi-collinearity issues, Variable Inflation Factor (VIF) and Pearson correlation were used to assess the correlation between variables. Variables with VIF<10 and |γ|<0.7 were considered as non-collinear, and a set of non-collinear variables was selected.   3 Results 3.1 Spatial and temporal trends of Chl-a The distribution of blooms in the Daning River exhibited significant spatiotemporal heterogeneity. The mean Chl-a from 2017 to 2022 was 8.78 ug/L, 10.82 ug/L, 9.48 ug/L, 6.87 ug/L, 7.29 ug/L and 6.05 ug/L, respectively. The average Chl-a in spring, summer, autumn and winter was 10.15 ug/L, 9.55 ug/L, 6.9 ug/L and 6.44 ug/L. Specifically, the mean Chl-a from 2017 to 2022 was 2.86 ug/L, 13.70 ug/L, 9.09 ug/L, 14.26 ug/L, 7.52 ug/L and 9.27 ug/L during spring. For summer, the mean Chl-a was 11.14 ug/L, 10.73 ug/L, 12.68 ug/L, 5.21 ug/L, 10.82 ug/L and 5.09 ug/L. In autumn, the mean Chl-a was 3.19 ug/L, 9.69 ug/L, 4.66 ug/L, 7.97 ug/L and 3.34 ug/L from 2018 to 2022. Taking 10 ug/L as the threshold for blooms, it can be observed that the Daning River experienced serious blooms during 2018 and 2019, while it occurred rarely in 2020 and 2021, with the lowest risk in 2022. In term of the annual pattern, blooms were more severe during the spring and summer. The multi-year average Chl-a at the estuary, midstream and downstream was 6.96 ug/L, 10.65 ug/L and 7.84 ug/L, respectively. Specifically, average Chl-a at the estuary, midstream and downstream was 7.69 ug/L, 12.57 ug/L, and 9.78 ug/L during spring. In summer, they were 9.88 ug/L, 14.43 ug/L and 7.00 ug/L, while they were 4.47 ug/L, 8.88 ug/L and 6.65 ug/L during autumn. In winter, average Chl-a at the estuary, midstream and downstream were 5.32 ug/L, 6.13 ug/L and 6.44 ug/L. Therefore, the risk zones in spring were mainly located in the upstream and midstream sections, while risk areas were concentrated in the mid-lower reaches in summer. In addition, the midstream is a potential high-risk area every year, which deserves special attention (See Fig. 3  ).  3.2 Succession of key factors at the river scale The random forest was used to identify the important factors influencing Chl-a. The results indicated that the main influencing factors were Tem, N:P, V, Zme and LevC during the drainage period (March). During the drainage period (late May to early June), the key factors were TP, LevC, N:P, V and Zm. During the low water level period (July-August), the key factors influenced Chl-a were identified as LevC, V, Zm, Zme and Tem. Zme, RWCS, WD, Zm and V were the key factors driving Chl-a variations during the early impoundment (early September). The results showed that temperature, velocity and N: P were the key factors for the transit of risk state in the early stage of drainage. The development of state from low-risk to high-risk was mainly influenced by Zme and V. During the drainage period, nutrient played a crucial role for the transition from non-blooms to bloom. In addition, the shift from a low-risk state to a high-risk state was predominantly influenced by RWCS and V. Velocity was the key factor to transit the non blooms to blooms during low water level period. The development from low-risk to high-risk was mainly influenced by Zm and Zme during the low water level period. In the early stage of impoundment, nutrients were the key to transit non blooms to blooms (See Fig. 4  ).  3.3 Succession of key factors at the local scale (stream segment) The random forest was used to assess the importance of environmental factors in different sections of the Daning River to reveal dynamic rankings during various periods. Before the drainage period, the upper reaches were primarily influenced by TN, Zme, Zm, LevC and V. In the midstream region, the primary driving factors included N:P, Zme, V, LevC and RWCS. In the estuarine zone, the factors were ranked as N:P, RWCS, Zme, V and WD. Overall, it was dominated by nutrients and Zme, with a transition from light driven to heat driven along the upstream to the estuary. During the drainage period, Zme, V, TP, WD and LevC were the key factors in the upper reaches. In the midstream region, the primary driving factors included N:P, Zme, LevC, V and RWCS. In the estuarine zone, the factors were ranked as LevC, Zme, V, RWCS and TN. From upstream to the estuary, the driving factor of Chl-a shifted from flow velocity to the fluctuation of water level, while it was dominated by Zme. During the low water level water period, the upper reaches were affected by Zme, LevC, RWCS, Zm and WD. In the midstream region, the key factors included Zme, LevC, V, RWCS and N:P. In the estuary, V, Zm, N:P, LevC and TN played key roles. From upstream to the estuary, the driving factor of chlorophyll transited from fluctuation of water level to flow velocity. During the impoundment period, the factors driving Chl-a in upstream were Zme, Zm, TP, N:P and RWCS. In the midstream region, the primary driving factors included Zme, N:P, RWCS, LevC and V. In the estuarine zone, the factors were ranked as Zme, V, RWCS, N:P and Zm (See Fig. 5  ).  3.4 Succession of key factors at the grid scale The standard regression coefficients indicated the influence of explanatory variables on Chl-a. Based on the spatiotemporal distribution of variables, the influences of Zme, Zm and N:P were significantly higher than that of other factors during the pre-drainage period. Specifically, the average absolute value of the regression coefficient for Zme, Zm and N:P in the upper reaches was 372.80, 208.16 and 28.07, respectively. In the middle reaches, the average absolute value for Zme, LevC and Zm was 14.24, 9.10 and 6.36, respectively. In the lower reaches, the average absolute value of the regression coefficient for Zm, Zme and N:P was 152.99, 29.36 and 8.32, respectively. Zme had a positive effect on Chl-a in the upper reaches (high-risk zones). The effect of N:P showed a transition from positive impact in the upper reaches to negative impact in downstream (Fig. 6  ). The regions with positive impact were primarily located in the high-risk zones in the upper reaches. In addition, Zm had a predominantly negative effect on Chl-a. During the drainage period, the average absolute value of the regression coefficient for Zm, Zme and N:P in the upper reaches was 7.14, 5.45 and 2.52, respectively. In the middle reaches, the average absolute value for Zm, N:P and LevC was 12.98, 11.06 and 4.58, respectively. In the lower reaches, the average absolute value for Zm, N:P and Zme was 4.19, 2.98 and 2.44, respectively. The impact of LevC on Chl-a shifted from positive in the upper reaches to negative downstream, with a particularly negative impact in the lower reaches (high risk zones). V exerted negative influence on Chl-a. The impacts of Zm, N:P, V and LevC factors were significantly higher than that of other factors during the low-water period. Specifically, in the upper reaches, the average absolute value of the regression coefficient for Zm, N:P and V was 739.6, 22.42 and 7.77, respectively. In the middle reaches, the average absolute value for Zm, TN and LevC was 243.2, 16.10 and 1.64, respectively. In the lower reaches, the average absolute value for Zm, N:P and V was 85.27, 12.57, and 7.81, respectively. Zm exhibited a negative impact near the estuary. V had negative impact on areas with the high risk of blooms. During the impoundment period, the impacts of Zm, Zme and LevC were more prominent than that of other factors. Zm showed a transition from positive in the upper reaches to negative in the downstream, while Zme exhibited the opposite trend. LevC had primarily negative impact on Chl-a.   4 Discussion 4.1 The driving mechanism of blooms before the discharge period In March, the Three Gorges Dam was in the pre-drainage phase with the high water level, the slow flow and the higher temperature (Zhou et al., 2022 ). These conditions provided favorable conditions for the growth of algae. This study analyzed the triggers of blooms from three scales. The relative importance of Tem, N:P, and V at the river scale was 70.76 %, 56.17 %, and 55.34 %, respectively. At the local scale, the top three factors in the upstream (DC) were TN (53.73 %), Zme (49.97 %), and Zm (47.61 %). At the grid scale, the top three factors in the upstream (DC) were Zme, Zm, and N:P, with average absolute regression coefficients of 372.80, 208.16, and 28.07, respectively. In terms of river scale, water temperature was one of the main factors contributing to the blooms, similar to Zhou et al. (2022) , who found that temperature and water level were the major drivers of blue-green algae accumulation in early spring. Compared with the results at river scale, the heterogeneity of Tem at both local and grid scales was not prominent. Surface temperatures did not vary significantly within local river segments. Therefore, surface temperature was not a direct influencing factor of blooms, which has been identified at the local and grid scales. During the early spring, water temperature was relatively higher in estuary and upstream, but high-risk zones of blooms appeared in shallow upstream areas (Fig. S7 ). While water temperature can determine the favorable periods for blooms formation, it cannot fully explain the actual occurrence of blooms (Gao et al 2018 ). On the contrary, the importance of Zme and Zm gradually increased at local and grid scales. In the risk zone of blooms, chlorophyll was negatively correlated with Zme and Zm. Stratification of water temperature began in mid-March (Fig. S5 ). The Zme in the river was within 10, and high-risk zones appeared in shallow upstream areas (Zme < 3). The study supported the previous conclusion that when Zme was below 2.85, there was a higher risk of blooms (Yang et al, 2022 ). By the end of March, two circulation patterns formed within the Daning River. In the middle and lower reaches, the warm surface water invaded the Daning River from the Yangtze River and flowed out at the bottom. In the upper reaches, the intrusion of warm surface water from the upstream, with outflow at the bottom. The intersection point of these two circulations located around 9 km upstream (XG) from the estuary (Fig. S8 ). Due to the higher temperature of the surface layer compared to the bottom layer, vertical convection was suppressed, resulting in stable stratification structure and serious blooms (Gao et al., 2018 ). Therefore, the middle and lower reaches of the river were mainly influenced by stratification, while the upstream was primarily affected by Zme. Macro-scale analyses may overly emphasize systemic differences and overlook local micro-environmental variations. Although the causes of blooms existed scaling effect, the commonality was that nutrients were the main triggers for blooms. The nutrients were higher than the half-saturation constants for absorption of algae (TN greater than 1.4 mg/L and TP greater than 0.04 mg/L). The N:P was greater than 16, indicating phosphorus limitation (Li et al., 2022). As the intrusion position deepened, TP concentration in the Daning River increased, which relieved phosphorus limitation and exacerbated blooms. Therefore, most studies tended to nutrient regulation at the river scale, which often required a long time to show achievement. As an emergency strategy, it is more important and feasible to change the critical depth by regulating the water level.  4.2 The driving mechanism of blooms during discharge The drainage period of the Three Gorges Dam mainly occurs from May to late June. During the stage, the flow velocity increased, and the fluctuation of water level became larger. However, the blooms were more severe during the drainage period. The results indicated there were significant differences of triggers between river scale and local scale. The relative importance of TP, LevC, and N:P at the river scale was 145.87 %, 93.53 %, and 79.52 %, respectively. At the local scale, the top three factors in the upstream (DC) were Zme (92.46 %), TP (52.41 %), and N:P (51.96 %). At the grid scale, the top three factors in the upstream (DC) were Zm, N:P, and LevC, with average absolute regression coefficients of 12.98, 11.06, and 4.58, respectively. At the river scale, LevC and TP have significant impact on blooms. On the contrary, Zme and Zm were the primary triggers at local scale and grid scale. The macro analysis (river scale) emphasized the importance of water level fluctuations, while weakening the impact of Zme and Zm. In fact, the decrease of water level indirectly altered Zme and Zm, thus highlighting this triggering effect at local scales. Stockenreiter et al. (2021)  indicated the importance of the mix depth to cyanobacteria dominated phytoplankton. During the drainage period, the water level only decreased rather than fluctuated, which only affected the migration and diffusion of algae. When the local water column was stable or layered, it could still cause blooms. After May 20th, the Daning River experienced several rainfall events. Cold water masses gradually migrated downstream from the upper reaches. In early June, the surface water from the Daning River merged with the Yangtze River. Within 7 km from the estuary, the surface layer water discharged to estuary from bottom with clockwise pattern due to encountering the cold water mass. Above 8 km from the estuary, tributaries of the Daning River invaded from the bottom and discharged from upstream, forming a retention area at the XG (V<0.005 m/s), providing conditions for the growth of algae (Fig. S9 ). By mid-June, within the 7 km of estuary, the Yangtze River infiltrated into the Daning River from the surface and flowed back into the Yangtze River in the clockwise pattern from the bottom layer. Above 8 km from the estuary, the bottom layer was mainly invaded by the mainstream, while the surface water flowed from upstream to downstream. Near 7 km (BH), the encounter of upstream inflow and invading flow led to rapidly increase water age (Gao et al., 2018 ) and slowdown in flow velocity (Fig. S10 ). Due to the intensified inflow of the river at the end of June, short-term mixing occurred at all depths. However, this stratification disruption only occurred in the upstream, and its impact was significantly weakened in the middle of the river. The spatial distribution of phytoplankton was related to the longitudinal differences in hydrodynamics (Xu et al., 2021 ). Thermal stratification and water circulation patterns determine the heterogeneity of blooms. Therefore, sunny days after rain can easily trigger localized blooms, requiring early warning and emergency prevention, such as spraying medication or hydraulic dispatch.  4.3 The driving mechanism of blooms during low water level period The Daning River basin experiences its main flood season from June to August. During this period, the Three Gorges Dam maintains low water level operation to address potential flood hazards. Due to the influence of rainfall, the water level in the Daning River alternates between rising and falling, leading to pronounced the fluctuations of water level (Fig. S13 ). Comparing to the drainage period, the Chl-a concentration decreased overall during the low water level period, and the high-risk zones shrank. The relative importance of LevC and V decreased with the scale fine. On the contrary, Zme and Zm were the primary triggers at local scale and grid scale, similarly to Yang et al. (2023) . The results at river scale and local scale were similar, both emphasizing the relative importance of LevC and Zme. Kong and Song (2011)  noted that disturbances of water caused changes in the distribution of underwater light density and other physical and chemical factors, thereby influencing algae growth. Wang et al. (2011)  proposed that fluctuation of water level complicated the environmental changes in typical tributaries of the TGR and affected the selection of functional groups of phytoplankton by altering mixing depth and relative stability of water column. Regarding the flow field, the surface layer of the Daning River mainly experienced inflow from the upstream, while the bottom layer was influenced by the intrusion of the Yangtze River from mid-July to mid-August. The inflow from the upstream propelled the surface layer downstream. However, the water flow at the bottom, located in the coverage area, moved upstream under the influence of the intrusion from the Yangtze River. These two water flows generated clockwise motion throughout the Daning River (Li et al., 2021 ). On August the 20th, the Daning River basin experienced heavy rainfall. The flow in the upstream began to move downstream after August 21st, and the convergence point of the upstream inflow of Daning River and invading flow from the Yangtze River gradually migrated towards the estuary. On August the 24th, the mainstream of the Yangtze River invaded from the bottom within 10 km section upstream from the estuary, then discharged into the Yangtze River from the surface layer in counterclockwise motion. Above 10 km from the estuary, the flow drained from upstream to downstream due to the impact of rainfall. Near 10 km (XG), the encounter of upstream inflow and invading flow rapidly increased water age and slowed down flow velocity (Fig. S11 and S12 ). The concentration of Chl-a increased with the decrease of flow velocity, reaching its maximum at the convergence point. During the low water level period, the fluctuation of water level caused by rainfall altered the circulation pattern of the flow field, becoming potential trigger for blooms.  4.4 Implication of the findings Many researches have been conducted to assess the risk of blooms in rivers, while it remains questionable whether studies with a single scale can address the issue of heterogeneity (Tian et al., 2022 ). By introducing multi-source data and new analytical methods, this study explored the triggers of blooms from different scale. Based on remote sensing data (10 m*10 m) and EFDC (6 layers), transparency and mixing depth of river was obtained. Compared with single site of field experiment, the transparency and mixing depth can reflect the spatiotemporal change of key factor (Zme). Moreover, MGTWR was introduced to analyze the causes at the grid scale. This study investigated the impact of scale effect on triggers of blooms, revealing trigger-response relationships that might be obscured by traditional single scale investigations. The machine learning was utilized to capture the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of transparency. For large-scale regions, mechanistic models often lacked the capability to acquire transparency. As a result, Zme was rarely included in the factors contributing to blooms. For instance, EFDC utilized a fixed light attenuation coefficient underwater throughout the entire simulation period. The results indicated that Zme was the most important factor influencing Chl-a during the drainage period (spring), consistent with previous studies (Liu et al., 2012 ). However, there were significant differences in the importance of Zme at different river reaches. For example, fluctuation of water level has a significant impact on the estuary. Fluctuation enhanced water mixing, indirectly disrupted temperature stratification, and affected Zme (Xu et al., 2021 ). Therefore, the integrated framework of mechanism model with remote sensing helps in-depth analysis of the cause and mechanisms of blooms. The study introduced spatiotemporal non-stationarity analysis to identify the spatiotemporal scale effects of key factors by employing specific bandwidths for each covariate (Liu et al., 2021 ). The results from MGTWR indicated that the impact of factors on Chl-a varied significantly (Table S2 ). During the drainage period, V had a large bandwidth, while the spatial bandwidths of other variables were relatively smaller (ranging from 5.6 to 4). In contrast, during the low water level period, majority of the factors had larger spatial bandwidths. Because water level fluctuations were more pronounced during the low water level period, which led to increase in the neighborhood effect scale of the factors. This precise diagnosis of spatial scale relationships supports cost-effective strategies for blooms prevention. Additionally, there were differences in the temporal scale effects of the factors. During the pre-drainage period, the impact scales of RWCS was more significantly influenced by the conditions in early days. In the drainage period, the effects of factors on Chl-a were short-term and rapid. This implied that daily fluctuations in environmental factors would alter Chl-a conditions on the same day. Xia et al. (2020)  found that environmental factors within the first 10 days were optimal for predicting Chl-a in the Han River. Tian et al. (2022)  identified a lag of 1–5 days of key environmental factors on the growth of algae in the Han River from January to April 2021 through the distributed lag model. The findings of Daning River supported the conclusion that environmental conditions within 5 days were crucial for current Chl-a concentration. The diagnosis of the time scale relationship provides guidance for early warning. It is recommended to use environmental factors from the previous 5 days as input variables for predicting blooms.   5 Conclusion This study introduced RF and MGTWR to analyze the triggers of blooms at different spatial resolutions from river, local and grid scales in tributary bay of the Three Gorges reservoir. The results indicated the driving factors of blooms exhibited significant scale effects. Macro-scale analyses may overly emphasize systemic differences and overlook the micro-environmental variations of local blooms. During the flood season, the encounter between the cold flow in bottom and the subsequently warming surface flow formed stable stratification after rainfall, acting as cause of blooms. Additionally, the convergence of the clockwise and counterclockwise circulations, leading to slowdown of flow velocity at the convergence point, also triggered blooms. Compared to the drainage period, the drastic alternation of water levels during the low water level period may be the primary cause for the reduction in chlorophyll concentration. There were significant differences in the spatiotemporal bandwidth of environmental factors, while the time lag between Chl-a and environmental factors was within 5 days. This study broke the conventional approach of investigating blooms at a single scale and explored the dynamic and mechanisms of blooms from multiple scales. It provides guidance for early warning and risk management of blooms in the context of hydraulic engineering. For demonstrative purposes, the data used for analysis was limited only to 2018, which inevitably leads to difference in some years (wet year) as only a fraction of the true data is observed. The special factors for typical years could be readily identified through the extensive collecting data. Moreover, MGTWR is usually suitable for small sample analysis, and the tens of thousands of data involved in this study requires a lot of time to train. Therefore, it is necessary to introduce Cloud Computing to address barriers to time efficiency. The methodological approach outlined in this study can readily be repurposed to a variety of complex cause analysis involving scale effect. Based on the results outlined, multiscale analysis is conducive to analyzing the reasons from different perspectives and exploring the mechanisms, serving the timely prevention of blooms.
