1 Introduction Natural rivers convey water, sediments, and nutrients into the environment, being fluvial corridors for several species and the main source of fresh water for humans (Vörösmarty et al., 2010 ). The hydraulic characteristic of a river can reveal the co-evolution of the riverine system as a consequence of the interaction between climate, geology, and hydrology signature. These characteristics are usually expressed in the hydraulic geometry of cross-section, where the flow width, average depth and velocity change with discharge following at-a-station hydraulic geometry (AHG) power laws (Leopold & Maddock, 1953 ). AHG power laws have been used in the estimation of discharge by remote sensing (C. Gleason & Durand, 2020 ), nutrient flow models (Seitzinger et al., 2002 ), estimation of the hydraulic conductivity of the hyporheic zone (Stewardson et al., 2016 ), and hydraulic-biological models of habitat selection (Miguel et al., 2016 ). While there are practical applications of AHG, the physical processes behind the exponents and coefficients of different systems remain elusive (Dingman & Afshari, 2018; Mackin, 1963; Xu et al., 2021 ). The hydraulic parameters and cross-section shape are commonly discussed in relation to channel physical characteristics, but it is not clear how these properties are correlated in different environments (Closs & Lake, 1994; Zimmer & McGlynn, 2017 ). The complexity of the cross-sectional shape of natural rivers is just one of the challenges in predicting exponents (Jia et al., 2017 ). For example, the exponents and coefficients that describe the power laws of AHG are theoretically correlated with the shape, slope and roughness of the channel (Dingman, 2007 ). In triangular channels, it is expected that the variation in discharge is accommodated equally by the change in width and depth, while in parabolic or rectangular channels the width remains almost constant (Dingman, 2007 ). The slope of the channel may be the main control over the hydraulic geometry, due to the higher velocity of steeper rivers (Carrillo et al., 2021 ). On the other hand, the coefficients have been less explored in the literature especially because of the large range of values that can be found for natural rivers (Ferguson, 1986; Gleason & Smith, 2014; Stewardson, 2005 ). This is in part related to the mechanisms involving riverine characteristics, such as Manning’s coefficient, viscosity, bed shear stress, erosion and deposition rates (Dingman, 2007; Xu et al., 2021 ). Considering that the physical characteristics of a river channel is in part a consequence of the integrated process in the basin draining to a specific cross-section, it could be hypothesized that there are regional controls over AHG parameters, such as the ones that have been used to explain stream network geometry (Clubb et al., 2023; Getraer & Maloof, 2021 ). Hydroclimatic characteristics of a basin (e.g., aridity and baseflow indixes) allow quantifying aspects of the water flow response (McMillan, 2020 ) which may in turn significantly influence the geometry of the river channels. At-many-stations hydraulic geometry shows that AHG is not a local property, but it is the result of interaction throughout the river (Gleason and Smith, 2014 ). Relations between climate parameters and river width exponent suggested that regions with extreme climatic conditions (e.g., extremely dry) are more likely to have a high variability of the river width (Feng et al., 2022 ). In drier basins, for example, discharge capable of altering the shape of the channel cross-section (bankfull discharge) occurs less frequently than in wetter basins (Castro & Jackson, 2001 ). Basins with higher aridity index are usually characterized by a flatter drainage network (Chen et al., 2019 ). While the characteristics of river cross-sections are related to the local hydraulic behavior (Li et al., 2022; Singh & Zhang, 2008 ), their regionalization remains limited especially when considering the effects of hydrological signatures, channel morphology, climate change, and human activities (Berghuijs et al., 2016 ). Despite climate exercising strong control over the landscape, the extent of its influence on the hydraulic geometry of rivers is still unclear. Here, we examine 290 stream gauge sites in Brazil to comprehend how the hydroclimatic features of the basin and the shape of the cross-section influence hydraulic geometry parameters across a wide spectrum of physical attributes. We estimate AHG parameters and use spatial analysis and correlation techniques to relate them with the cross-section shape, aridity and baseflow indices. We quantify the systematic variability of AHG parameters between dry and humid basins, and how they are constrained by cross-section geometry. We include a broad analysis of the coefficients of the At-a-Station hydraulic geometry theory, which are commonly neglected in research.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Study area Brazil is a large country in South America that encompasses diverse climate configurations. Its extensive hydrographic network is extensively monitored and its data is made available by the Brazilian National Water Agency. Hydraulic geometry analyses in the region may allow the comparison of the hydraulic behavior of channels under different factors that model the morphology of rivers, such as different combinations of climate and basin physical characteristics. We selected 290 stream-gauging sites distributed throughout Brazil (Fig. 1  ). For each of the 290 gauging sites, we obtained daily streamflow and hydraulic variables (discharge, flow velocity, flow area and top-width) from the Brazilian National Water Agency. We identified and removed all sites with artificial controls at the gauging station (e.g., bridges). Measurements on days with negative or zero flow (non-perennial streams) were also discarded, as they may be caused by flow intermittency, errors in the use of instruments, and natural or artificial deviation of the current upstream of the station. Furthermore, we checked human intervention by the streamflow degree of regulation (i.e. relationship between the regularized flow and the mean flow of the basin), available in CAMELS-BR Dataset (Chagas et al., 2020 ). The degree of regulation of 90 % of the selected station is less than 10 %. Basins in the southeast and northeast regions have the highest human intervention rates in terms of reservoir regulation, with a flow degree of regulation greater than 50 % (Supplementary Figure S3 ). The catchment area of the stations analyzed varies from 51 km2  to 2.85x106 km2  (Fig. 1 a). The largest river basins monitored are located in the north of the country and decrease in size towards the south. Approximately 70 % of the gage-stations analyzed have an area between 100 and 10,000 km2  and are concentrated in the southwest region. This irregular distribution may be related to the relief and naturally the basins are smaller in this region, but there is also a greater demand for water in the Southwest due to high urbanization, which leads regulatory agencies to have a greater interest in monitoring this area. Overall, the gauge network is denser and their time series longer in the southern and southeastern region. The spatial heterogeneity of the gauging stations may bias the results in some regions, especially in spatial interpolation. Therefore, we were especially careful with the criteria to select the data set to make the study as mathematically and conceptually sound as possible. The hydrometeorological median characteristics are extracted from the CAMELS-BR Dataset (Chagas et al., 2020 ). Of the original 290 stations, only 197 had climate and hydrology data available. So, we characterize the hydraulic geometry of 290 stations, and analyze the hydroclimatic characteristics of 197.  2.2 At-a-Station hydraulic geometry Discharge, flow velocity, flow area and top-width were measured in loco . There is no protocol regarding the periodicity of these data. Generally, these measurements are performed at least once a year to validate the rating curve. Therefore, the interval between measurement dates changes between seasons and between years. We select the whole historical data available from each station. We choose consolidated data, as well as stations with the availability of at least 10 data of depth, width and flow measured per year. The longest data series has 80 years, distributed between 1926 and 2019, and 386 measurements. The shortest data series has 7 measured years, distributed between 2007 and 2019, with 42 measurements. The average number of years per gauging station is 31 while the average number of measurements per gauging station is 126 (Figure S1 ). Although the location of the measurement section defined for the station is provided in the source data, the exact location of each measurement is not detailed. Using automated methods to remove inconsistent data is difficult because there is no pattern of occurrence of this data. Therefore, we visually checked the scatterplots of width, mean velocity and depth versus flow rate for all of the available that. This step helped detect probable changes in the measurement location and possible transcription errors in field reports. In particular, the presence of groups of outliers in the scatterplots are a strong indicator of changes in the measurement section location. We carefully removed measures that were obviously inconsistent. At stations where the section changed location, we retained data from the most recent section. Sections with high dispersion in measurements and not following hydraulic geometry relationships were interpreted as unstable, and the station was excluded from the analysis. We believe that the effects of these uncertainties are small at the spatial scale we adopted, mainly due to the large availability of data. To characterize the hydraulic geometry of the cross-sections, the relationships from the Theory of Hydraulic Geometry At-a-Station were used (LEOPOLD; MADDOCK, 1953). This theory relates the change in hydraulic parameters with the variation in discharge through power laws (Equations (1)–(3) ).(1) w = a · Q  b      (2) d = c · Q  f      (3) v = k · Q  m      where Q  is the discharge (m3 /s), w  (m) and d  (m) the top-width and average depth of the wetted section, v  is the average flow velocity (m/s), a , c and k  are the coefficients and b , f  and m  are the exponents. The preliminary consistency was to plot the data and inspect them to check for errors. The values of the coefficients and exponents at each cross-section were determined empirically by ordinary least-squares regression analysis on the logarithms of values of w , h , v , and Q . The coefficients of these equations graphically represent the intersections of the adjustment lines when the flow rate is equal to a unit of measurement, while the exponents represent the slope of the curve when linearized, that is, it is the rate of change of the dependent variable with the flow rate. We test the adherence of the data to the Theory of Hydraulic Geometry as the sum of the exponents does not equal to unity in some reported cases (Dingman, 2007 ). According to the equation for continuity of an ideal fluid Q = w · d · v   , we have the relations a · c · k = 1    and b + f + m = 1   . We followed Rhodes (1977) , and we make sure that the sum of the exponents and the multiplication of the exponents were 5 % above or below one, that is, they vary between 0.95 and 1.05. We selected only the gauge stations whose performance of equations (1)–(3)  have Spearman's rank correlation coefficient greater than 0.45, and it was statistically significant (p-value  less than 0.05, Figure S2 ). It is important to highlight that we assume that the cross-section data within a river as resulting from the interaction of basin physiographic and hydro-climatological characteristics. Furthermore, hydrometry manuals recommend the installation of fluviometric stations in cross-sections with well-defined and stable banks, outside of backwaters and with a regular bed. This could reduce the heterogeneity of the sample set analyzed in this work since we use data from the national monitoring system. However, the high number of stations throughout several hydroclimatic zones in Brazil assures the representativeness of the sample data.  2.3 Geometric representation of channel shape We selected channel bathymetries that were within the same period of years as the data we used for the hydraulic geometry analyses. We visually evaluated the bathymetries one by one and discarded sections profiles that had been moved, and single sections with abrupt changes within the series. After data consistency, a total of 4498 bathymetries resulted, from 1960 to 2016. The mean of cross-section profiles available per gaging station is fifteen. Eight gauging stations only have one available or suitable bathymetry. Two hundred and twenty gauging stations have at least ten cross-section profiles available. The average interval between bathymetry dates is 18 months, with the longest interval being 20 years, and the minimum interval is less than a month. The distribution of the number of available cross-section profiles and the mean interval between bathymetry dates can be seen in Figure S4  of the Supplementary Material . To define the shape of the cross-section, it is necessary to define the total water level in the river. In river geomorphology, above a certain flow rate, the channel overflows into the floodplain, defined as a bankfull stage (Wolman & Leopold, 1957 ) or effective flow (Leopold & Maddock, 1953 ). Based on the bankfull channel stage, we limited the transversal profile, and the cross-section geometry was defined. The return period for estimating bankfull may vary between different rivers. Comparing the results of numerous studies Leopold (1994)  concluded that the bankfull stage occurs for a return period is 1.0 to 2.5 years. We adopted as bankfull stage the flow associated with a recurrence interval of 1.58 years (Q 1.58 ), whose value can be obtained from the generalized distribution of extreme values, and coincides with the peak of the probability density function from the Gumbel distribution (Dury, 1973 ). According to Dingman (2007) , assuming that the cross-section of a river is symmetrical, the curve that best fits the natural shape is estimated and is given by Equation (4) .(4) z = d fb  ∗   · 2 w fb       r  · x r  ,  to  0 ≤ x ≤ w fb   2       where z  is the height from the lowest point of the bed to the water surface, d*fb   is the maximum depth on full banks, wfb   is the top-width, r  is the shape exponent of the cross-section; and x  is the horizontal distance measured from the center of the section to the bankfull. The exponent r  of Equation (4)  represents the geometric shape that best fits the channel shape. Values of r  close to 1 indicate triangular cross-sections, r  = 2 denotes a parabolic cross-section. The higher the r  value, the closer the cross-section is to a rectangle (Dingman, 2007 ). We estimated the exponent r  for each bathymetry record available and did notfind a significant difference in the range of variation and the median value (see Supplementary Figure S5  and Table S1 ). Thus, we used the median value of shape exponent r  in the discussion, as this best represents the shape of the section along the years assuming that the geometry at a cross-section is fixed, and within-bank flows did not significantly alter the cross-section shape over the years. The theoretical relationships proposed by Leopold & Maddock (1953)  are able to predict the exponents and coefficients estimated empirically by the regression method with high reliability (Dingman & Afshari, 2018; Grison et al., 2021 ). Therefore, we evaluate the relationship between AHG parameters and the cross-section geometry (see Supplementary Table S2 ). The theoretical relationships proposed by Leopold & Maddock (1953)  are able to predict the exponents and coefficients estimated empirically by the regression method with high reliability (Dingman & Afshari, 2018; Grison et al., 2021 ). The equations are based on the premise that there are two dominant controls on AHG: the geometry of the bankfull section and the characteristics of the reach (e.g., hydraulic conductance and energy slope, Dingman, 2007 ). In this work, we discuss the controls on the cross-section shape (represented by r ) by evaluating the correlation between AHG parameters and the cross-section geometry (see Supplementary Table S2 ).  2.4 Classification of dry and humid basins Based on the hypothesis that there is a difference in the parameters of the hydraulic geometry according to the hydroclimatic characteristics, the basins were classified as dry or humid. We used the aridity index and the baseflow index available in CAMELS BR dataset, computed over streamflow timeseries between 1980 and 2018 (Chagas et al., 2020 ). The baseflow index (BI) is the ratio of long-term baseflow to long-term total streamflow, indicating the basin’s capacity to store and release water to the river (Wrede et al., 2015 ). The baseflow index was estimated from gauges that have less than 5 % of missing streamflow data (Chagas et al., 2020 ). The 96 % selected stations at this work have at least 80 % of their streamflow data checked for inconsistencies (Supplementary Figure S1 ). High values of this index indicate significant fluctuations in streamflow, which can result from either pronounced seasonality in streamflow or a rapid response to precipitation events (McMillan et al., 2017; Yokoo & Sivapalan, 2011 ). The aridity index (AI) is calculated by dividing potential evapotranspiration by mean precipitation. It represents a first control on the partitioning of precipitation into streamflow (Blöschl et al., 2013 ), and indicates the potential of a basin to lose water to the atmosphere. The CAMLES-BR does not explicitly describe the quality control measures applied to these data sources. Nevertheless, the selection of these sources is based on their high spatial resolution and comprehensive coverage of South America. This deliberate choice ensures consistency across all catchments. We adopted the same ranges as David et al. (2022)  to create six groups combining high, medium and low AI and BI (Table 1  , Fig. 1 b, c). Drier basins have a higher aridity index and lower baseflow. While humid basins have a lower aridity index and higher baseflow. Driest basins are concentrated in the Northeast region, where the aridity index is higher and the baseflow index is lower. In the North and Southeast regions are the wetter basins, which have the lowest aridity index and highest baseflow index. To test whether there is a significant difference between AHG parameters within each class, the Kruskal-Wallis non-parametric test was used. If the test has a p-value  < 0.05, we rejected the null hypothesis that the samples follow the same distribution and we used Dunn's method to find out which groups differ from the others.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Hydraulic geometry of Brazilian rivers The Hydraulic Geometry parameters are spatially coherent in Brazil with the values indicating that channels adjust the flow mainly according to the average depth and flow velocity variation and have low variation in the width (Fig. 2   and Fig. 3  ). The cross-sections with the highest exponent b  are concentrated in the Northeast region (Fig. 2 a). In contrast, the lowest values of the velocity exponents (m ) are grouped in the northeast and southeast areas, and the highest values of m  are distributed between the south and north regions (Fig. 2 c). The spatial distribution of the exponent f  is less clear (Fig. 2 b). In the Northeast, North, and South regions the lower values of f  are condensed. This spatial distribution indicates that channels in the driest basins have high adjust of the flow in the width variation, since b  is predominantly greater than m  and f  in these cross-sections. The lower values of a  are located in the southeast and southwest regions, and the larger values of a  are in the northern region (Fig. 2 d). Coefficient k  follows the same behavior as a , but the distribution is more pronounced (Fig. 2 f). As with the exponent of depth, coefficient c  has a less clear grouping when compared to the other coefficients (Fig. 2 e), with large values in the south as well as in the north region. The median of exponents b , f , and m  are 0.08, 0.41, and 0.49 respectively (Fig. 2 ). The median of f  and m  follows the same value and distribution found by Afshari et al. (2017)  and Park (1977)  in the United States of America, Li et al. (2022)  in Puerto Rico, and Dingman & Afshari (2018)  in New Zealand. The distribution of b  is strongly positively skewed and is approximately log-normal, while that of f  and m  are quite symmetrical and quasi-normal. Although the median value of b  in this work is lower than in other places, it follows the results in the literature in which the width is the one that suffers the least variation between the parameters. The adjusted values of the AHG coefficientsare highly variable also with positively pronouncing tail on the right side suchlike log-normal distribution. The median of a , c , and m  are 35.24, 0.34, and 0.10 respectively (Fig. 2 ). Most of the station (83 %) have a  less than 100. On the other hand, 91 % of coefficients of depth and all coefficients of velocity, c  and k , are less than one (Fig. 2 e and 2f).  3.2 Hydroclimatic drivers on the hydraulic geometry The exponent of width, b , is significantly related to aridity, with a significant difference between the groups with high (HAI), medium (MAI), and low (LAI) aridity (Fig. 3 b). Using Dunn's method we found out that LAI distribution significantly differs from the other groups. Humid basins, with high and medium baseflow, have the lowest median of b  (0.08 and 0.07). The basin’s classes from the baseflow index are statistically different among groups (Kruskal-Wallis test, p-value  = 0.03). The classes chosen from the baseflow index did not influence the depth exponent (Fig. 3 g) and the velocity exponent (Fig. 3 h). The relationships between climate parameters and river width exponent clustering are not as evident as they are in other environments with extreme climate conditions (e.g., extremely dry) and high river width variability, as found by Feng et al. (2022) . The ternary diagram (Fig. 3 a, e) indicates that the physical characteristics of the basin are reflected in the combination of exponents b, f  and m (Park, 1977; Rhodes, 1977 ). The cross-sections are not hydraulically differentiated according to the aridity index. The median of the three classes is very close and on the line b  + f  = m . This relationship occurs in stable channels, with little resistance to the flow, where the velocity and flow vary at the same rate, just as the velocity increases at the same rate as the section area (Simons & Richardson, 1966 ). The same behavior can be seen in the classification of basins by baseflow index. However, basins with LBI have a median closer to the relationship b = f   , which indicates sections with triangular geometry, where width and depth change in the same proportion. This visual difference in the LBI group corroborates the Kruskal-Wallis test which differentiates this group from the others. The stability of the margins is confirmed because all b  values are smaller than f  (except for two sections). The hydraulic behavior indicating more stable sections is expected for our dataset is part of the Brazilian National Water Agency systematic gauge monitoring system, and the stability of the section is one of the prerequisites in choosing the location by the responsible entities. The coefficients a , c  and k , of width, depth and velocity, do not differ between dry and humid basins. Humid basins, with high and medium baseflow and low aridity, have the greatest variation in coefficient a , but there is no significant difference between the medians (Fig. 4  a, d). Directing attention to the baseflow index, the driest basins, with LBI, have the smallest range of variation among the three classes (Fig. 4 d, e, f). The exponent c  has a small range of variation in dry basins, however there is no significant difference between the proposed classes (Fig. 4 b, e). The relationships found in this study for the spatial distribution of AHG parameters, aridity, and baseflow are valid for average values of exponents and coefficients, but cannot explain the individual value in each cross-section. It is possible that there are local singularities acting that interfere with the climate signal (e.g., McMillan, 2020 ), which could also possibly explain why the frequency distribution remains the same among studies from different locations (i.e., Ferguson, 1986 ).  3.3 Relation between coefficients and exponents To understand how the coefficients and exponents relate and restrict each other, we plot AHG variables on a semi-log graph, as proposed by Gleason and Smith (2014) . The at-many-stations hydraulic geometry phenomenon was reported in rivers in different environments (Allen et al., 2018; Feng et al., 2022; Gleason & Durand, 2020; Grison et al., 2021 ), which relates AHG of several sections along the same river through a semi-log trend. This global phenomenon can be seen when all dataset is plotted. The exponent and coefficient of velocity and depth group together on the left of the graph, while width separates into a group on the right (Fig. 5  ). The width and depth define the geometry of the section, and are correlated with the exponent of shape r  in bankfull (ρ  = 0.46). However, the exponents b  and f  have a non-significant correlation between them (p-value > 0.05). On the other hand, the velocity coefficient k  has a strong correlation with all AHG variables. The exponents f  and m  have a strong inverse correlation (ρ  = -0.92), while b  and m  have a weaker but significant inverse correlation (ρ  = -0.48). This relationship reflects the fact that the values of b  have a smaller range of variation, and, as the relationship should be understood, b + f + m = 1   , f  and m  tend to be inversely related (Dingman & Afshari, 2018 ). Adjusting the parameters of At-a-station Hydraulic Geometry necessitates data of individual cross-section sites, limiting the usefulness of AHG to gauging sites where such data has been collected (Dingman, 2007; Ferguson, 1986 ). Correlations between exponents and coefficients (Fig. 5 ) show that the relationship between hydraulic geometry exponents and the basin’s area (Fig. 8 ) contradicts the previous expectation of AHG as spatially unpredictable. On the other hand, this relationship corroborates the recent At-many-stations Hydraulic Geometry (AMHG) presented by Gleason and Smith (2014) . AMGH holds that there are temporally and spatially invariant depth, width, velocity, and discharge values that are shared by all stations of a river. AMGH is a powerful tool to predict discharge flow in ungauged catchments and understand its hydraulic behavior. However, the strength of AMHG did not correlate with any available observed hydraulic parameters (Barber & Gleason, 2018). Although we compared isolated cross-section, and AMHG compared the sections along the same river, the results show that the exponents and coefficients are related to each other for the whole dataset, which leads us to conclude that At-a-Station Hydraulic Geometry is indeed a widely prevalent natural fluvial phenomenon.  3.4 Influence of the section geometry on hydraulic geometry The characterization of the geometry of the river sections shows that there is great variation in the shape of the channels. The r  coefficient varied between 1 and 14.6, with a median of 2.6. The geometry of the sections is unevenly distributed across the study area. We did not find patterns of similar sections by region (Fig. 6  a). Basins with extreme climates have been shown to have differences in the geometry of their rivers (Feng et al., 2022 ). However, we did not find a significative difference between the cross-section shape of dry and humid basins (Fig. 6  f, g). Triangular (e.g. Fig. 6 b) and parabolic (e.g. Fig. 6 c) sections are the dominant shape. Approximately 53 % of the sections have r  less than or equal to 3. Only 52 sections had r  > 5. In these sections, the bed-width is much greater than the depth. From r  = 5, the shape exponent cannot differentiate the geometry of the section, classified as rectangular (Fig. 6 d, e). The use of climate as a predictor of channel geometry was questioned by Seybold et al. (2021) , who showed that tectonic activity has a strong influence on the concavity of the longitudinal profile cross-section of rivers. Geology has been considered an important control on change in flow velocity, as it alters bedrock stability, sediment availability, and flow resistance (Ferguson, 2007; Ferguson et al., 2019; Phillips et al., 2022 ). We analyzed the relationships of hydraulic geometry in the context of the dominant geology in the basin, using data available on CAMELS BR (Chagas et al., 2020 ). However, we did not find any significant relationships that we could use to explain the shape of the cross-sections, and the exponents and coefficients of the hydraulic geometry (results not shown). The variation in the width of the flow cross-section, represented by b , has a negative correlation with the shape of the section (Fig. 7  a). More rectangular sections, with a higher value of the exponent r , have less variation in width, as the flow is restricted to the straight walls of the channel. The coefficient a  has a positive correlation with the shape of the section (Fig. 7 b). These results are in accordance with theoretical predictions where the width/flow relationship is strongly dependent on the geometry of the section, and little influence has on the characteristics of friction and slope of the channel (Dingman, 2007 ). We also found that the width coefficient, a , has a strong correlation with the width (ρ  = 0.74) and the area (ρ  = 0.87) of the bankfull section. This same correlation was found for small nested basins in southern Brazil (Grison et al., 2021 ). We verify that it is possible to relate the coefficient a  with the area of the contribution basin (ρ  = 0.83, Fig. 8  ). This strong correlation explains the spatial distribution shown in Fig. 2 d, which may be biased by the database used in this work. The southeast region is highly populated with extensive water use which has led to a high density of monitoring stations in small basins, and where low values of the coefficient a  are concentrated. On the other hand, the Northern region has large basins and the use of this water is more distributed in space, reducing the spatial density of monitoring stations, and where large values of the coefficient a  are concentrated. Thus, the apparent spatial distribution of coefficient a  is related to the location of the measuring gauging stations because the bankfull section area versus drainage area relationship is scale-dependent (Wilkerson et al., 2014 ). While the width is controlled by the section geometry, the variation of velocity and depth with flow appears to have no direct relationship with the geometry of the bankfull section. The correlation between m  and f  is negative and very strong (ρ  = -0.92, Fig. 5 ). This result differs from the theoretical relationships proposed by Dingman (2007) , in which all exponents of hydraulic geometry are functions of the exponent r . We suppose that local factors are preponderant over the variation in velocity and average depth. However, there are a few sections with bathymetry data in the Northeast region, where the highest b  values and the highest aridity index are found. Even so, the geometry of the section does not seem to explain the patterns of this exponent, since r  does not follow a spatial pattern. According to Ferguson (1986) , it is not necessary to go beyond the hydraulics and geometry of the section to understand the hydraulic behavior of the flow. Ferguson (1986)  and Dingman (2007)  showed theoretically that the cross-sectional shape of a channel determines the rate of increase in water width with depth while flow resistance laws define the rate of increase in mean velocity with depth. However, these data are generally not available and the geometrical representation of the shape of natural rivers is always prone to associated errors. Furthermore, limiting the understanding of hydraulic geometry parameters to channel characteristics and not including regional characteristics may limit their use in other applications, such as flow forecasting. Although the k  coefficient does not have a strong correlation with the shape of the section, it has an inverse correlation with the area (ρ = -0.57) and the width of the bankfull section (ρ = -0.63). The k  coefficient has a weaker correlation than the width with the basin area (ρ = -0.56, Fig. 8 ). The k  coefficient has large values in the coastal region because the monitored basins are predominantly smaller, and its value increases in the northwest direction because the basins are larger (Fig. 2 f). However, the spatial distribution is different from that of the coefficient a  because it does not depend as strongly on the area as a . The coefficient c  does not show a significant correlation with any geometric parameter.   4 Conclusions We analyze 290 cross-sections of Brazilian rivers using the exponents and coefficients of the at-a-station hydraulic geometry (AHG). We show that the patterns of the exponents and coefficients of AHG are spatially coherent in different regions of Brazil. While these patterns do not differ significantly between dry and humid basins when classified according to the proposed aridity and baseflow classes, we find that cross-section width variability is sensitive to discharge change in arid basins with low baseflow index. Basin area and cross-section geometry play an important role in the hydraulic geometry parameters. The velocity coefficients are inversely proportional to basin area, and width coefficients are directly proportional to, with the width exponent strongly dependent on the cross-section shape. To expand our understanding of hydraulic geometry parameters, future work should consider the inclusion of geology, topographic parameters, and identification of bed material for an accurate understanding of how local factors may be interacting with the climate signal as well as testing the prediction strength of this parameters. Spatial analyses of hydraulic geometry according to basin characteristic classification is a promising tool for regionalizing flows for ungauged basins, in addition to contributing to flood management, and maintaining the natural dynamics of river channels.
1 Introduction Rocky desertification, which has been called "cancer of the earth" and has garnered widespread attention from the entire society, has emerged as the most pressing ecological and environmental problem in the southwest of China and even the entire world (Bloom, 1989; Yuan, 1997; Wang et al., 2004; Williams, 2008; Akdim, 2015 ; Jiang et al., 2014 ). The study of soil erosion processes has become a frontier in global geography due to its direct connection to the occurrence and progression of rock desertification (Sweeting, 1992 ). The international major scientific plan on "Resources and Environmental Effects of Global Karst Dynamic Systems" takes karst ecosystem and rocky desertification control as one of the main priorities as well (Luo et al., 2018 ). Since the 21st century, soil and water loss in rocky desertification areas has become one of the priorities and frontiers in the field of water and soil conservation (Febles-González et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2019; He et al., 2023 ). However, research focused on its causes and mechanisms is still in its infancy. One of the most significant features of rocky desertification areas is the mosaic distribution of the soils and the exposed bedrocks that includes exposed part (outcrops) and underlying parts (Liu et al., 2022; Canora et al., 2008 ). The rock exposure rate and rock inclination have been shown to have an impact on soil water leakage (Dai et al., 2017; Gan et al., 2020 ; Peng et al., 2022 ; Gutiérrez et al., 2014 ), but it is still unclear how the abrupt contact (lack of a transition structure because of their weak or un-weathered bedrock) between exposed bedrocks and soils affects soil and water leakage. The absence of a C layer or transition layer between soil and carbonate-matrix bedrock is the primary cause of this abrupt contact (Zhang et al., 2011 ). Cracks in the soil brought on by shrinkage and water loss are a typical natural occurrence (Davidson et al., 1985 ; Xiong et al., 2008 ; Tang et al., 2011 ), and they increase soil permeability and allow water to preferentially flow into the deeper part of the soil. Previous studies have found that cracks that are not completely closed can still provide priority channels for water transport, exhibiting clear priority flow characteristics (Greve et al., 2012 ). In addition, the development of soil shrinkage cracks can also inhibit the generation of surface runoff (Novák et al., 2000; Inoubli et al., 2016 ). Does the development of shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface occur in the rocky desertification area with frequent brief droughts and the rock soil interface with abrupt contact? Because earlier studies (Fu et al., 2016; Kulasekera and Parkin, 2017; Peng et al., 2018 ; Wang et al., 2018) used a variety of test technologies and methods to observe the runoff process in epikarst, the transition zone between soil and bedrock (Williams, 2008; Aamery et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022 ), including excavation slope sections, dye tracing, soil time domain reflectometry (Chen et al., 2009; Li et al., 2017 ), ground penetrating radar, travel time distributions of groundwater (Benettin et al., 2017; Çallı et al., 2023 ), etc., they discovered that the preferential flow on karst slopes primarily occurs at the rock soil interface (Perrin et al., 2003; Jones, 2013; Bakalowicz, 2019 ). Therefore, the key to fully comprehending the heterogeneity in hydrological flow and transport particularly the preferential flow mechanism in the epikarst is to understand the formation process of drying shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface. Current studies on the formation and evolution of soil shrinkage cracks have made significant advancements in the formation process, development mechanism and influencing factors (Karalis, 2003; An et al., 2020; Zeng et al., 2022 ). The formation of soil shrinkage cracks is a complex process that is influenced by multiple factors, such as temperature, cycles of drying and wetting, soil thickness, soil composition and boundary conditions (Tang et al., 2011; Xiong et al., 2008 ). Although most studies on the formation of soil drying shrinkage cracks regard boundary conditions (restricted shrinkage) as an external influence and have not analysed them as the focus of study (An et al., 2020 ), they have a significant impact on the formation of shrinkage cracks. The soil is more likely to produce drying shrinkage cracks when there is a boundary constraint than when there is not, which significantly affects the depth and shape of crack growth (Guo et al., 2018 ). Long-term karst processes have produced rock outcrops, discontinuous soil, and an interwoven distribution of rock and soil in the rocky desertification region of southwestern China (Sweeting, 1993; Li et al., 2014 ). Since outcrops with weakly weathered or un-weathered bedrocks and soils frequently interact at the rock soil interface in the rocky desertification region, this boundary restriction condition creates a particular environment for the growth of soil shrinkage cracks in both dry and wet conditions. However, it is still uncertain how the cracks develop under these conditions. The rock soil interface in rocky desertification areas have both internal and external conditions for developing shrinkage cracks. Firstly, the soils have the clay minerals for the development of drying shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface. It has been demonstrated that soils in various stages of rocky desertification show the same clay mineral composition, primarily montmorillonite, illite, and kaolinite, all of which are hydrophilic clay minerals (Albani et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2011 ). The composition and content of clay minerals play a significant impact on the drying shrinkage cracks of soil. Generally, the more montmorillonite content in soil, the easier it is to be developed (Mitchell, 1993 ). Additionally, there may be external environmental conditions that lead to the development of drying shrinkage fractures at the rock soil contact. Due to the developed dual hydrological system of the surface and underground, coupled with the shallow soil layer and low water-holding capacity of the soil, the limestone soils have a weak capacity to buffer against rainfall, which makes soil moisture prone to rise and fall in the rocky desertification areas. Related investigations revealed that the effective water of soils can only endure 5–10 days at most under the conditions of naturally occurring water content (Li et al., 2014 ). Despite these conditions, it is still unclear about the occurrence and development of drying shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface. The development of shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface in rocky desertification areas is crucial to understanding the leakage loss process of water and soil and the groundwater recharge. This study is an initial attempt to conduct an observation test on the development of drying shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface based on imitating the rock soil interface between rock outcrops and soils in their natural state. Therefore, the objectives of this study are to ⅰ) capture the surface dynamics in the development of shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface, ⅱ) quantify the geometric morphological characteristics of shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface and ⅲ) reveal the changes in the network of cracks and block areas cut by the network during the development of shrinkage cracks.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area and test materials Test soils were collected from karst sloping farmland located in Qingyan Town, Huaxi District, Guiyang City, Guizhou Province, China ( Fig. 1 ), which is one of the most characteristic areas in the world of the development of karst landforms. Guizhou is also the province in China with the greatest area and variety, deepest degree, and most severe of the effects of rocky desertification. The region is well investigated by previous studies (e.g. Sweeting, 1992; 1993 ). The climate in this region is a mid-subtropical humid monsoon climate. The land is characterized by its difficult terrain, steep slopes, inconsistent spatial and temporal distribution of precipitation, significant changes in water loss, and frequent regional and seasonal droughts. Winter droughts are the most frequent and intense, followed by spring, summer, and fall droughts. Dolomite and limestone are main outcrop rocks in rocky deserts. Chinese yellow soils prevail in this area. The test soils are calcareous soils that pass a 2 mm screen and are classified as Calcisols in the WRB soil classification (IUSS Working Group WRB 2022).  Fig. 2  depicts the test soils' distribution of soil particle sizes. Test limestone rocks were from the same location as the test soils and were outcrop rocks with a natural rock surface. These rocks have dimensions of 30 cm long, 30 cm high, and 15 cm wide. They all have straight surfaces that come into contact with the test soils. The test rocks and soils were placed in a square biological glass container with dimensions of 30 cm by 30 cm and varying heights (10, 20 and 30 cm). In addition, the container's bottom had drain holes for both natural drainage and water filling.  2.2 Experimental preparation and design Nine sets of soil and rock samples ( Fig. 3 ) were constructed for a natural drying water loss test to examine the development of drying shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface of outcrops. The following steps were taken to prepare the sets: the rocks were placed into the square plexiglass container whose height was chosen based on the filling soil thickness and whose bottom was covered with a layer of sand approximately 1 cm thick; the designed straight surfaces were placed in the centre of the container as the interfaces contacting the test soils, and the container was weighed; the container was filled with sieved soil material in layers based on the bulk density in the field until the surface of the soil material was flush with the surface of the container. At this point, the rocks and soils together made up approximately 50 % of the container's surface. To collect data on soil moisture content, a soil moisture sensor was also installed at a depth of 5 cm at the rock soil contact of each container. The intended soil thicknesses were 10 cm, 20 cm, and 30 cm. Every soil thickness measurement was repeated three times.  2.3 Water loss test Testing for water loss was performed from October to December 2021. It was necessary to gradually add water from the bottom of the container to completely saturate the soils prior to the soil water loss test. Then, while the containers containing the rocks and soils were being weighed, the drain valves at the bottom of the container were opened. As the timing began, this was noted as the sample’s initial state. These samples were placed in a well-ventilated chamber at a temperature of approximately 20 °C for drying and water loss. A photo of the sample's surface morphology was taken every 8 hours while it was drying using a Canon EOS 80D digital camera. The interval period was reduced to 4 hours when a crack at the rock soil contact appeared. On the exterior wall, a tape measure could be used to gauge the size of the cracks. The water loss test was deemed successful when the variations in the soil moisture content were less than 0.5 % for three consecutive days. The 81-day water loss test was conducted.  2.4 Image processing The total area, total length, average width, and other development indicators of drying shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface were extracted using digital image processing technologies. Comparing this technology to typical manual measuring, it was automatic, quick, and accurate. The following processing steps were taken: To remove the boundary influence of the container edge, the soil shrinkage area containing the shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface was first cut out as the processing object using Adobe Photoshop 2020 software, measuring approximately 26 cm in length and 15 cm in width. Next, the cut images were successively subjected to image greying, binarization, denoising, clutter removal and pixel calibration. The preprocessed image was then fed into the Particles (Pores) and Cracks Analysis System (PCAS) to detect and quantify the soil, rock, and cracks, including the total area, total length, and average width of shrinkage cracks (Tang et al., 2021 ).   3 Results 3.1 Water loss from soil samples  Fig. 4  presents the soil water loss from samples containing rocks and soils as soil temperature and time changed. Although the initial temperature and humidity environment were the same, the ranges in the increase or decrease of water loss in the three soil thicknesses were consistent with the soil temperature. However, the water loss from the three soil thicknesses exhibited a significant difference. First, during the first three days, the soil moisture contents of all three soil thicknesses fell at the highest pace throughout the whole observation period, primarily due to the removal of water via gravity from the saturated soils. During the days from the 5th to 31st, the moisture content of the soil thickness of 10 cm declined more than that of the other soil thicknesses. There were two distinct stages of water loss reduction in this case. From the 5th to the 21st days, the decrease rate of water loss was slower, and from the 22nd to the 31st days, the rate of decline was faster. Following that, the soil moisture content gradually dropped and remained essentially constant. Specifically, among these various soil thicknesses, the sample with a thickness of 10 cm maintained the lowest soil moisture content after 25 days. The drying shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface and on the soil surface caused the speed of the decrease to accelerate after the 22nd day ( Table 1 ). The water loss process of samples with soil thicknesses of 20 cm and 30 cm was relatively slower in comparison to samples with soil thickness of 10 cm, and the curves of the two soil thickness (10 cm and 20 cm) eventually intersected on the same line. The formation of drying shrinkage cracks also tended to be steady at this time, and the soil moisture content of three different soil thicknesses tended to be stable after 51 days, indicating that the water loss process was finished. Through statistical analysis of the soil moisture content and the soil temperature over the course of the test period ( Fig. 5 ), it was discovered that the soil temperature changed according to a normal distribution, while the soil moisture content presented a skewed distribution, meaning that the variation in soil moisture content was low and corresponded to the stage of water loss. The range in soil moisture content of the sample with 10 cm soil thickness was broader, and the distance between the median and the average value was the largest, while the distribution of soil moisture content of the samples with 20 cm and 30 cm soil thickness was narrower, and the distance between the median and the mean value gradually coincided. The soil thickness affects the degree and speed of soil water loss, and thin soil was more likely to lose water.  3.2 Development of shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface Real-time observations revealed that shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface (CRSI) formed and developed in a manner that was consistent across all samples containing soils and rocks. The development of the cracks was unaffected by the soil thickness, although the formation and development rate of cracks slowed down as the soil thickness increased. A rock soil interface sample with a soil thickness of 30 cm was used to illustrate the entire dynamic process of surface shrinkage crack development in  Fig. 6 . There was a drying shrinkage crack-1 at the rock soil interface formed by soil shrinkage on the border of soil when the soil moisture content declined from 44.5 % at the start of the test to 24.1 % after the 23rd day (Fig. 4  and Table 1 ), which was the first crack in the sample. In addition, there was a soil crack-2 perpendicular to the CRSI and a soil crack-3 almost parallel to the CRSI (Fig. 6 a). As time passed, three soil shrinkage cracks—two of which were parallel to soil shrinkage cracks-2 and 3, one of which was perpendicular to soil shrinkage crack-4 occurred on the 31st day, when the soil moisture content was 22.8 %. No new soil shrinkage cracks formed after the 36th day, when the soil moisture content was 22.3 %. Soil shrinkage crack-7, which was perpendicular to rock soil interface shrinkage crack-1 and soil shrinkage crack-4, appeared. No new soil shrinkage cracks appeared throughout the test procedure that followed. The following characteristics of shrinkage crack development can also be noticed in Fig. 6 . First, CRSI only formed in the contact of rock and soil. Second, all shrinkage cracks perfectly intersected one another. Regardless of when the shrinkage cracks developed, they essentially crossed in shapes of "T" or "+". Third, the CRSI and the soil cracks formed perpendicular to previous cracks, and the width increased with time.  3.3 Geometric characteristics of shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface 3.3.1 Total area of shrinkage cracks The parameters that best characterise the crack network during the formation of soil shrinkage cracks are the total area, total length, and average width of the shrinkage cracks. The links between the total area, total length, and average width of shrinkage cracks and the moisture content of the soil are shown in  Fig. 7 . Among the three soil thickness variants, a parabola with decreasing soil moisture content was present in both the total areas of the CRSI, the soil cracks perpendicular to the crack at the rock soil interface (CS perpendicular to CRSI) and the other cracks (OC). However, there were differences in the modifications of these parabolas depending on the types of fissures and soil thickness. First, for the three soil thickness variants, the total areas of the OC were often greater than those of the CRSI and the CS perpendicular to CRSI, with the CS perpendicular to CRSI being the lowest (Fig. 7 a, b and c). With regard to the thinner soil layer of 10 cm, only the total areas of the CS perpendicular to the CRSI and the CRSI presented a roughly half parabolic profile with the soil moisture content; that is, they increased initially and stabilized as the soil moisture content decreased (Fig. 7 a). Beyond that, only the total area of the CRSI had a similar pattern in the 20 cm soil thickness (Fig. 7 b). Apart from this, there was an almost full parabolic trend between the total areas of the other shrinkage cracks and the soil moisture content. That is, as the soil moisture content decreased, their total areas initially increased and subsequently decreased. Clearly, whether it was the CRSI or the CS perpendicular to CRSI and the OC, the total area of all cracks decreased to some extent the thicker the soil was. In contrast, the CRSI and the CS perpendicular to the CRSI became more stable the thinner the soil was, but the OC was less stable. In other words, the soil thickness was likely to have an impact on the total areas of the CRSI and the CS perpendicular to the CRSI.  3.3.2 Total length of shrinkage cracks The parabola fitting between the total length of shrinkage cracks and the soil moisture content was not as good as the total area of the cracks However, it is clear from the distribution of scattered points that among the three soil thicknesses, the total lengths of the OC were the greatest under various soil moisture content conditions, followed by the CRSI, and the last was the CS perpendicular to the CRSI (Fig. 7 d, e and f). Additionally, in various soil thickness variants, the total lengths of the OC consistently showed a tendency to first increase and then decrease as the soil moisture content decreased. That is, at a later stage of soil water loss, the OC would diminish to a certain level. In all soil thickness variants, with the exception of the soil thickness of 30 cm, the total lengths of the CRSI and the CS perpendicular to the CRSI increased initially before stabilizing and rapidly reached a stabilization stage as the moisture content decreased. For thicker soil (20 and 30 cm), all forms of cracks eventually closed slightly in the later stages of soil water loss. However, this phenomenon did not occur as frequently for the CRSI and the CS perpendicular to the CRSI in the shallower soil layers.  3.3.3 Average width of shrinkage cracks The average width of shrinkage cracks in the other two soil thicknesses, with the exception of the sample with 30 cm of soil thickness, was obtained by fitting a parabola, with good outcomes (Fig. 7 g, h and i). On the other hand, among these shrinkage cracks, the CRSI widened the most. The CRSI typically had the largest average width, followed by the CS perpendicular to the CRSI and then the OC. At thin soil thickness (10 cm), the average width of all the shrinkage cracks stabilized after gradually increasing with decreasing soil moisture content, whereas in the thick soil thickness (30 cm), each showed a declining trend in a later stage of soil water loss. For the intermediate soil thickness (20 cm), it was clear that only the average width of the CRSI could be stabilized after increasing, whereas the average widths of the CS perpendicular to the CRSI and the OC had a decreasing trend in the later stage of soil water loss.  3.3.4 Statistics of the geometric characteristics of shrinkage cracks Although there was only one shrinkage crack at the rock soil interface, statistics on the total area of shrinkage cracks ( Fig. 8 a) revealed that the mean area of the CRSI at various soil thicknesses and soil moisture water contents could be close to that of the OC and that the box distribution (25 %-75 %) made up of the lower and upper quartiles was more compression than that of the OC. In contrast, the mean and distribution of the area in the CS perpendicular to the CRSI were less than those in the CRSI. The CS perpendicular to the CRSI with only one crack has a significantly shorter length than the OC in both the mean and the box distribution made up of the lowest and upper quartiles (Fig. 8 b). However, it is notably higher than the CS perpendicular to the CRSI. The relatively narrow length data distribution of the CRSI and the CS perpendicular to the CRSI with fewer cracks suggests that they are more stable in length during development than the OC. In contrast, in both the mean and box distribution of width (Fig. 8 c), the CRSI was higher than the OC and even the total cracks (TC). The box distributions of the CRSI and the CS perpendicular to the CRSI were greater than the OC, in contrast to the length, showing that the width was more likely to vary significantly throughout the formation of the CRSI than the length. Despite being sparse in number and making up only approximately 40 % of the overall length and surface area of the TC, the CRSI were 1.2 times wider than all other fractures combined.   3.4 Quantitative statistics of soil blocks The surface structure of drying shrinkage cracks in the specimens consisted mainly of a network of cracks and many block areas cut by the network ( Fig. 9 ). The surface was bounded by the CRSI, and all cracks essentially intersected vertically in the form of a "T" and a "+". The CRSI split the whole specimen into a rock block area (top part of Fig. 9 a, b and c) and a soil block area. The overall soil block area was divided into smaller soil block areas by the CS perpendicular to the CRSI, and then smaller soil block areas were divided from these smaller soil block areas by the OC. As can be observed, the number of soil block zones that were split decreased as soil thickness increased. In particular, there were nine block zones for a soil thickness of 10 cm, six for 20 cm, and five for 30 cm. The general shape of each soil block zone was a quadrilateral. The geometric features of the soil block zones grew more stable or concentrated as the soil thickness increased, according to the size measurement of the soil block under the three soil thickness conditions. Both the average area and the average perimeter of the soil block areas tended to increase with increasing soil thickness, while the average length and the average width of the soil block area did not change clearly.   4 Discussions 4.1 Formation of rock soil interface shrinkage cracks It is a common phenomenon in nature that cracks are caused by soil shrinkage due to water loss (Vogel et al., 2005 ). The frequent alternation of dry and wet conditions readily results in cracking during soil drying cracking and crack closure with increasing moisture, which directly impacts soil permeability, structure and stability, especially in the context of global climate change and the urban heat island effect (Novák, 2000). Therefore, soil shrinkage crack formation and development must be understood to fully comprehend the process of soil erosion. For soil shrinkage cracks to form, evaporation is a necessary precondition (Zeng et al., 2022 ). This experiment has demonstrated that thin soil is more likely to experience evaporation. After the soil starts to lose water, it goes from being saturated to unsaturated, and when it reaches to a threshold value of soil moisture, cracking starts to happen. We discovered that drying shrinkage cracks are formed at the rock soil interface when the soil moisture content is between 24.1 % and 28.6 %, which is lower than prior findings from clay soils (Tang et al., 2011; An et al., 2020 ). Once cracks formed, the rate of decrease in the soil moisture content increased, which was confirmed by our experiment and others (Nahlawi and Kodikara, 2006 ). The formation and development of soil shrinkage cracks is an extremely complex process. According to findings from clay soils (Tang et al., 2011 ), the formation and development of the CRSI may be broken down into three parts. First, drying shrinkage cracks initially form at the rock soil interface due to the difference in the shrinkage properties between rocks and soils (Fig. 6 a). Under the guidance of the rock soil boundary, the initial crack extends and bends along the edge of the rock or soil. The CRSI divides the sample surface into two primary blocks, namely, the soil block and the rock block (Fig. 6  and Fig. 9abc). After the formation of shrinkage cracks, the number of CRSI will not increase (there is only one), but its width and depth will expand (Fig. 7 ). Second, a single shrinkage crack is randomly formed at some point in the soil block part, and this soil crack develops under the "attraction" of the CRSI and intersects it nearly vertically. This shrinkage crack forms concurrently with or after the formation of the two primary blocks of rock and soil. This crack is called the main shrinkage crack of soils, and it is perpendicular to the CRSI, that is, the CS perpendicular to the CRSI. The soil surface is divided into multiple large soil block areas by the CS perpendicular to the CRSI. In this experiment, these main shrinkage cracks are only 2–3 in number (Fig. 6  and Fig. 9abc), all of which occurred concurrently with or shortly after the CRSI and can become wider and deeper cracks as the water loss time increases. Third, at the same time as or after the formation of the CS perpendicular to the CRSI, it begins bifurcation and formation of other cracks perpendicular to these soil cracks at random points of the CS perpendicular to the CRSI. Alternatively, after the random formation of cracks in the soil block, other cracks develop that intersect the CS perpendicular to the CRS by "attraction". Meanwhile, at the same time as or after the formation of these other soil cracks, some branching cracks perpendicular to these other soil cracks are formed. The other cracks and their branch cracks, which are derived from the CS perpendicular to the CRSI, are called other soil cracks (OC). Additionally, at the same time, some CS perpendicular to the CRSI, OC and branch cracks of the OC start to appear. The width of these cracks will not be wider, however, because they often emerge at the same time as or after the formation of the OC. In contrast, the CRSI and the CS perpendicular to the CRSI, which formed earlier than the OC, are larger. Finally, after the CRSI, the CS perpendicular to the CRSI and the OC stop developing and divide the soil into several smaller blocks. No new cracks appear on the soil surface as the soil water loss time proceeds, and the blocks are no longer further divided. The cracks gradually widen until they are finally stabilized (Fig. 9abc).  4.2 Effect of rock soil interface shrinkage cracks on infiltration and runoff In the context of global warming, the urban heat island effect and increasingly frequent droughts and floods, the phenomenon of soil shrinkage cracks is becoming increasingly common through soil water loss, which directly increases soil permeability and triggers water loss in the form of preferential flow into the soil substratum. Due to the difference in geotechnical properties, shrinkage cracks developed at the rock soil interface, particularly in the karst areas where temporary droughts are frequent and the rocks and soils are in abrupt contact, may immediately lead to downwards water and soil leakage. Important factors such as soil infiltration characteristics (Bruand et al., 2001; Greve et al., 2012 ), soil water evapotranspiration (Xing et al., 2017 ), and water transport (van Dam, 2000; Inoubli et al., 2016 ) are associated with the development of drying shrinkage cracks. Our study found that after cracks are formed, the rate of decrease in the soil moisture content increases. This is because soil cracks provide a larger channel for water evaporation from soils. Similarly, such channels can also be provided for water infiltration. It was reported that the width and depth of shrinkage cracks had a considerable impact on water infiltration, and incompletely closed shrinkage cracks still offered preferential channels for water transport and clearly demonstrated preferential flow characteristics (Greve et al., 2012 ). Since the findings showed that the availability of the clay minerals is one of the major factor of the shrinkage cracks, these minerals can adsorb contaminants and might pollute the karst groundwater due to the rapid infiltration under the extreme flood events (Nerantzaki et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2020; Çelik et al., 2022 ). Soil drying shrinkage cracks also prevent the generation of surface runoff (Cao et al., 2017; Inoubli et al., 2016 ). Cracks caused by soil drying shrinkage go through two distinct processes: opening and closure. Opening unquestionably improves water infiltration and reduces runoff output, but the impact of cracks closure on these two processes is still debatable. Previous studies have concluded that drying shrinkage cracks only temporarily increase the soil infiltration rate and that as shrinkage cracks gradually close during the wetting process, the soil infiltration rate decreases and gradually returns to the uncracked soil state (Liu et al., 2004 ). However, other studies have found that even closed shrinkage cracks still provide a channel for preferential flow (Sander and Gerke, 2007 ). Rock soil structures in karst regions contain powerful seepage qualities. As a result, surface runoff is rarely generated, and runoff is mainly a subsurface process (Chen et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2018; Wilcox et al., 2007; Li et al., 2011 ). Karst fissures, pipes, holes, and caves are unquestionably crucial conduits for subsurface runoff-producing processes (Fu et al., 2016; Katsanou et al., 2015; Williams, 2008 ) and play a significant role in the high permeability and low runoff production at the surface. However, whether they are caused by the permeability characteristics of the surface soil or the special rock soil structure is still unclear. Some studies have found that preferential flow dominates the interflow on karst slopes at the rock soil interface (Peng et al., 2018; Fu et al., 2016; Sohrt et al., 2014 ). We also discovered that preferential flow at the rock soil interface, allowing water to flow to the bottom of a clay layer with poor permeability, is the primary reason for the rapid downward leakage of water in near-surface cracks in the karst rocky desertification area (Liu et al., 2022 ). This study also found that despite being sparse in number, the CRSI was 1.2 times wider than all other soil cracks. This is because the rock soil interface, where rock surfaces act as the boundary of soils, is more likely to develop shrinkage cracks in the width and depth (Guo et al., 2018 ). The main issue is that more research is needed to determine whether the occurrence of shrinkage cracks at the rock soil interface is one of the factors contributing to the development of preferential flow at the rock soil interface, how much it affects water infiltration at the surface, and whether it is a factor in the region's lack of surface runoff.  4.3 Influence of rock soil interface shrinkage cracks on soil erosion Shrinkage cracks have been proven to be able to reduce the production of surface runoff and increase the downward leakage of water, which will inevitably cause changes in the process of soil erosion on slopes. Related studies have found that shrinkage cracks were well developed in the dry season of Yuanmou in the dry and hot valley of the Jinsha River in southwestern China (He et al., 2008 ). When it rains, rainfall runoff can directly enter the interior of soils through shrinkage cracks, causing structures and blocks at the edge of soils to collapse as a result of water absorption and expansion. The soil is then quickly disseminated and washed away by water flow, accelerating the process of soil erosion. Some soil scientists have also debated whether soil crack erosion may be considered a novel type of soil erosion as a distinct source of serious soil erosion (He et al., 2008 ). Can the role of soil shrinkage cracks be used to explain the unique mechanism of surface erosion and underground leakage loss in the karst areas of southwestern China? Currently, some authors have acknowledged the idea that erosion at the rock soil interface occurs in karst environments (Sohrt et al., 2014; Vakili et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022 ). For instance, some studies have noted that the unique interface between soil and rock is an important internal cause of serious soil erosion in karst areas (Zhang and Bai, 2011 ; Zeng et al., 2024 ). This is because there is usually no layer C (transition layer) in the soil profile of karst areas; instead, there is a rock soil interface between the carbonate rock and the soil, which greatly reduces the adhesion and affinity between the rock and the soil. During rainfall, it is very easy to produce soil loss and block slip. Regional extreme weather is becoming more common due to global climate change. As a result, rock soil interface shrinkage cracks are more prone to develop, which has a special impact on the soil erosion process and may be a particular cause of soil underground leakage in this area. From the new perspective of the formation of rock soil interface cracks and the mechanism of their impact on the erosion process, the analysis of the soil erosion mechanism of rock soil structure slopes is expected to contribute to the development of soil erosion theory in karst areas.   5 Conclusions The main findings were revealed: ⅰ) Due to the drying shrinkage of soil due to water loss, drying shrinkage cracks are formed at the rock soil interface of outcrops when the soil moisture content is between 24.1 % and 28.6 %. After cracks are formed, the rate of decrease in the soil moisture content increases. The degree and rate of soil water loss is influenced by soil thickness, and shallow soil is more prone to lose water. ⅱ) The CRSI first developed along the boundary only between rocks and soils, and then soil cracks formed perpendicular to it. Under varying soil thickness conditions, every CRSI underwent a similar formation and development process that was unaffected by the soil thickness but slowed down with increasing soil thickness. ⅲ) Whether it was the CRSI or the CS perpendicular to the CRSI and the OC, the geometric parameters of shrinkage cracks increased initially before stabilizing and quickly reached a stabilization stage as the moisture content decreased. However, all eventually shrank slightly in the later stages of soil water loss in thicker soils. Of them, the CRSI were not prone to be affected by the soil thickness, followed by the CS perpendicular to the CRSI. ⅳ) In essence, every crack intersected vertically in the shapes of a "T" or a "+". The number of soil block zones separated by cracks decreased with increasing soil thickness. As soil thickness increased, the geometric dimensions of soil block zones became more stable. Despite being sparse in number and making up only approximately 40 % of the overall length and surface area of the TC, the CRSI were 1.2 times wider than all other cracks combined. Therefore, the CRSI may evolve into a key pathway for the establishment of preferential flow at the rock soil interface and a key factor in water leakage along the rock surfaces of outcrops. The main limitation of this study is the achievement of CRSI depth and the validation of CRSI acting as a key pathway for the establishment of preferential flow at the rock soil interface. Since the depth of CRSI may have a more significant impact on the water underground leakage loss in karst areas than the width and length. Meanwhile, it is crucial to reveal the influence of CRSI on the water infiltration, the surface and subsurface runoff yield, the soil erosion or underground leakage loss, and discern their contributions to establishments in the connections of the surface and underground hydrological process. It can be observed that CRSI is more likely to be triggered due to anomalous climatic changes, exhibiting more challenges for comprehending the heterogeneity in hydrological flow and transport particularly the preferential flow mechanism in the epikarst. This study is an extension and breakthrough of the current research on the types and formation of soil dry shrinkage cracks, and is a breakthrough point for a deeper understanding in the hydrological processes and soil erosion or leakage in karst areas.
