1 Introduction Drought is one of the most critical natural hazards with major impacts on ecosystems and society (Spinoni et al., 2019; Wilhite, 2000 ), aggravated in the absence of mitigation and adaptation measures (Gebrechorkos et al., 2022; Kundzewicz and Kaczmarek, 2000 ). Seasonal forecasting offers the possibility to predict drought events and thus take proactive actions (Hao et al., 2018; Rayner et al., 2005 ). However, drought predictions remain a major challenge due to the limited capabilities of dynamical models and uncertainties in observations (AghaKouchak et al., 2022; Lorenz et al., 2021; Patt and Gwata, 2002 ). In recent years, significant advances in drought seasonal forecasting have been achieved through better monitoring products and refined statistical or dynamical methods (Hao et al., 2018, 2017; Vogel et al., 2021 ). Statistical forecasting is based on empirical relationships of historical records and represents a computationally efficient alternative to dynamical models (Crochemore et al., 2017; Mo and Lyon, 2015 ). These forecasts are generally useful for providing a benchmark level of skill (Kirtman et al., 2013 ). The main drawback of these methods is that they cannot simulate unobserved drought evolution and this limitation should be cautiously taken into account in a climate change context (Pappenberger et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2012 ). On the other hand, dynamical forecasts rely on the existence of slow and predictable variations of the atmosphere, ocean, and land surface (Hao et al., 2018 ), which allows to prediction of new drought conditions, thus potentially able to adapt the model to the non-stationarity of climate (Schepen et al., 2012 ). However, seasonal dynamical models are computationally expensive and the forecast skill is low, especially regarding the seasonal forecasts for precipitation (Doblas-Reyes et al., 2013; Stockdale et al., 2010; Weisheimer and Palmer, 2014 ). From the few global assessments available, it is not clear if dynamical models provide a significant added value to climatology-based forecasts (see e.g., Dutra et al., 2014; Mo and Lyon, 2015 ). Dutra et al. (2014)  point out the significant challenges in improving long-term climatological forecasts, emphasizing that the initial conditions' memory plays a crucial role in achieving accurate forecasts. Similarly, Mo and Lyon (2015)  report that forecasts show significant accuracy across various locations and seasons, particularly for predictions up to two months ahead, primarily due to the initial conditions. They also note that the enhanced accuracy provided by dynamical models is mostly observed in areas affected by the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) teleconnections. Drought is considered a “creeping disaster” since it is usually a slow-onset phenomenon (Gillette, 1950; Schwalm et al., 2017 ), which also means that it is usually quantified with indices aggregated over several months (Wilhite, 2012 ). An indicator that is commonly used worldwide to characterize meteorological droughts on a range of time scales is the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI; McKee et al., 1993; Mishra and Singh, 2011, 2010 ). SPI is a transformation of the accumulated precipitation over several months (such as SPI–6, that is, aggregated over 6 months) into a standard Gaussian distribution with a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1. Positive values indicate surplus of rainfall, whereas negative values identify dry conditions relative to the long-term climatology. Generally, meteorological drought predictions merge observational information (for the months previous to the start month of the forecast) with seasonal predictions (Liu et al., 2012; Dutra et al., 2014; Mo and Lyon, 2015; Tang et al., 2016 ). Thus, the success of empirical or dynamical forecasts depends also on the quality of long-term observations available in near-real time. Sun et al. (2018)  examined thirty global precipitation datasets, encompassing gauge-based, satellite-derived, and reanalysis datasets. They underscore significant discrepancies in the magnitude and variability of precipitation estimates across these datasets. For instance, the annual precipitation estimates over global land vary by up to 300 mm/year among the datasets, with data ranging approximately from 600 mm/year to 900 mm/year. The study also highlights that the fidelity of precipitation datasets is primarily constrained by the density and geographical distribution of ground stations, the methodologies employed in satellite algorithms, and the models used for data assimilation. Such variability and limitations undermine the utility of these datasets in climate monitoring, attribution studies, and the validation of climatic models. Similarly, in the context of drought prediction, Mo and Lyon (2015)  indicate that there are considerable differences in observed SPI values between different datasets, especially in the tropics, and this is particularly problematic for precipitation products available in near–real time, so less time is available to retrieve and control the observations. Moreover, they suggest that, in the short term, the greatest advances in global meteorological drought prediction can be achieved through improvements in real-time precipitation observations worldwide. Within this context, Turco et al. (2020)  developed the Drought Probability dataset (DROP) that integrates all the observation-based datasets available in near-real-time and covers a period of at least 30 years, including rain gauge measurements, reanalysis data, and satellite information, to provide an accurate and up-to-date assessment of meteorological drought conditions in real- time. This tool has proven effective in drought monitoring, being successfully validated against independent data such as the soil moisture dataset from the European Space Agency (Gruber et al., 2019; Dorigo et al., 2017; Gruber et al., 2017 ), the changes in terrestrial water storage from the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE; Zhao et al., 2017 ), and the global collection of streamflow time series (GSIM; Do et al., 2018; Gudmundsson et al., 2018 ). Despite its effectiveness in monitoring, the application of DROP for forecasting seasonal droughts remains unexplored, overlooking the potential to integrate precipitation data uncertainty into the seasonal forecasting of meteorological drought. Taking all these considerations into account, this study aims to explore the SPI predictability on a global scale by combining observed climate conditions (with the near-real time DROP dataset) with precipitation forecasts based on an empirical method that is based on resampling of historical data, and the new generation seasonal forecast model developed by ECMWF (System 5; Johnson et al., 2019 ). In previous studies on seasonal drought prediction, this empirical approach was applied to Europe (Turco et al., 2017 ) and at a global scale (Hao et al., 2014 ), achieving skillful predictions of several drought indicators, and demonstrating the value of purely statistically based systems. Here we merge both the statistical and dynamical forecasts with all the datasets that constitute DROP. This allows to take into account two types of uncertainty: those related to the initial conditions and those related to the predictions. The latter encompasses model variations inherent in the differences between the SEAS5 ensemble system and the statistically driven method. Here we extend previous studies proposing a new methodology to perform and evaluate probabilistic meteorological drought predictions using multi-initial conditions.  2 Data and methods 2.1 Observed data As reference data, we use the precipitation datasets included in the DROP dataset (Turco et al., 2020 ). Initially, DROP was fed with ten global datasets operationally updated every month in near real-time: CPC (Chen et al., 2008 ), GPCC (Becker et al., 2013 ) and PREC/L (Chen et al., 2002 ) that are based exclusively on interpolated observations from meteorological stations; ERA5 (Hersbach et al., 2020 ), JRA-55 (Kobayashi et al., 2015 ), NCEP (Kanamitsu et al., 2002 ) and MERRA-2 (Gelaro et al., 2017 ), that are reanalysis data; and CAMS-OPI (Janowiak and Xie, 1999 ), CHIRPS (Funk et al., 2015 ) and GPCP (Adler et al., 2018 ) that combine satellite and rain gauge data. The latest update of DROP incorporated, as an additional member of DROP, the Multi-Source Weighted-Ensemble Precipitation MSWEP dataset (Beck et al., 2019a ), which is obtained by merging rain gauge, satellite and reanalysis estimates resulting in eleven precipitation datasets. Table S1  in the supplementary material  provides further details of these datasets. To compare the different gridded datasets, their precipitation values are remapped (first-order conservative remapping; Jones, 1999 ) from their original resolution to the coarser grid of the available datasets, defined by GPCP (2.5° × 2.5°).  2.2 Prediction methodology Fig. 1   schematically illustrates the main steps in developing the empirical and dynamical predictions. First, the drought predictions as measured by the SPI6 (i.e., the SPI index for a time scale of 6-months) merge observational information (e.g., the 2-months previous to the start month of the forecast as in the example of Fig. 1 a) with seasonal predictions for the remaining 4-months. The predictions are based on both statistical and dynamical forecasts (Fig. 1 b) and employ a leave-one-year-out methodology, as recommended by the WMO (WMO, 2010 ). The empirical method that we have applied is based on resampling of historical values and it is inspired by the ensemble streamflow prediction system (ESP; Day, 1985; Twedt et al., 1977 ; Fig. 1 c). The ESP has been broadly used for hydrological and meteorological forecasts (Turco et al., 2017; Yuan and Wood, 2013 ) and is used operationally by the National Weather Service River Forecast System (NWSRFS) and other agencies in the United States (McEnery et al., 2005 ). The ESP method is based on resampled past data to produce an ensemble of possible future climate outlooks, in which each ensemble member corresponds to a re-sampled year and preserving the observed sequence in that year. For instance, if we want to predict the SPI aggregated over the period March-August (SPI6) for the year 2021, with the forecast starting in May (thus making a prediction 4-months in advance), we already have the observations for March and April and we forecast the remaining months considering as a first member what happened in 1981, the second member what happened in 1982 and so on until the last information available that is that of the year 2020. The leave-one-year-out predictions consist of these steps: (i) we pick a test year; the whole period without the test year will be used to build the forecasts; (ii) calculate the accumulated precipitation values for the 6-months periods merging observation and resampled values (excluding the data of the test year); (iii) calculate the SPI6; (iv) repeat the steps (i) to (iii) for all the study period (1981–2020) and for the 11 databases that form DROP, resulting in an ensemble of 39 × 11 members. Finally, several types of information are extracted, such as the ensemble mean and the map of drought conditions based on different drought thresholds (Table S2 ), the drought warning (Table S3 ), and the probability of moderate drought. We name this system 4DROP (see Fig. 1 c and supplementary material  for further details). We compare 4DROP with dynamical predictions based on the ECMWF’s fifth generation seasonal forecast system (SEAS5; Johnson et al., 2019 ), operational since November 2017. SEAS5 has 51 members for the forecast system and 25 members for the hindcasts that cover the period 1981–2016 (for the years 2017 to 2020 we work only with the first 25 members). The spatial resolution is about 35x35 km and the forecast extends over 7-months. SEAS5 is based on the ECMWF’s IFS (Integrated Forecast System) atmospheric and forcing model version 43r1 (Johnson et al., 2019 ), the ocean model Nucleus for European Modelling of the Ocean (Madec et al., 2017 ) version 3.4.1 developed by the European NEMO consortium; and the Louvain-la-Neuve sea ice model version 2 (Fichefet and Maqueda, 1997 ). The land and atmosphere initial conditions are based on ERA5 reanalysis (Hersbach et al., 2020 ), and for the ocean and sea ice, the new operational ocean analysis system, OCEAN5 (Zuo et al., 2019 ), is used, which is composed of the historical ocean reanalysis (ORAS5) and the daily real-time ocean analysis (OCEAN5-RT). For more information on SEAS5 the readers are referred to Johnson et al. (2019) . The precipitation values of SEAS5 are remapped (first-order conservative remapping; Jones, 1999 ) from the original resolution of 35 × 35 km to the grid defined by GPCP (2.5° × 2.5°). Furthermore, as in the case of the statistical predictions, dynamical predictions are done in a leave-one-year-out mode merging all the observed datasets with all the forecast members, thus (i) we calculate the accumulated precipitation values. Forecast data are bias-adjusted using linear scaling, which is determined by the ratio of the long-term mean of observed to simulated data. The adjustment employs a leave-one-year-out procedure, meaning the forecast year is excluded when calculating the scaling parameters. This adjustment greatly reduced the bias of the raw data (see Figs. S1–S4 ). Further details on this procedure can be found in the supplementary materials ; (ii) calculate the SPI6; (iii) repeating the steps (i) to (ii) for all the study period (1981–2020) and for the 11 databases that form DROP, resulting in an ensemble of 25 × 11 members. We name this system S5 (see Fig. 1 c and supplementary material  for further details).  2.3 Prediction evaluation In this study, we assess the skill of SPI6 predictions for the four climatological seasons (December-January-February DJF, March-April-May MAM, June-July-August JJA, September-October-November SON) for 4- and 2-months ahead predictions. We compared the predictions against the DROP ensemble mean as well as against each of the eleven members that constitute DROP to assess how the uncertainty in the observations influences the skill assessment. We evaluate different attributes (Murphy, 1993 ) of the forecast quality: level of association between the forecast and the reference dataset with the Pearson’s r correlation coefficient; reliability through the reliability diagram (Weisheimer and Palmer, 2014 ); and resolution by the relative operating characteristic (ROC) plot (Mason and Graham, 2002 ). To estimate the uncertainties in the reliability slopes and the ROCSS score, we utilized a bootstrap resampling method. This involved drawing the prediction and observation pairs randomly with replacement 1,000 times. The confidence interval is demarcated by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of these 1,000 bootstrap replications. To ensure consistency with the spatial dependence structure of the data, the same resampling sequence is applied to all grid points within each bootstrap iteration. The accuracy of probabilistic predictions is assessed using the Brier Score (BS; Wilks, 2011 ). This score ranges from 0 to 1, with lower values denoting superior forecasting accuracy. For instance, a BS of 0 signifies that the forecast's predicted probabilities perfectly match the observed frequencies of the events. Additionally, we compute the Brier Skill Score (BSS) to measure the relative skill of our probabilistic forecast compared to a climatological reference. Further details of the verification approach that we follow are provided in Turco et al. (2017, 2020)  and in the supplementary material .   3 Results 3.1 Deterministic validation of seasonal predictions Fig. 2  a and b show the correlation of the ensemble mean of S5 and 4DROP forecasts against the ensemble mean of DROP for DJF with a 4-months forecast lead-time. Most grid points show statistically significant correlations between both S5 and 4DROP forecasts, with higher values in East Asia, Central Africa, Central America and regions of North and South America, with a few areas (Mediterranean) with correlations not significant. Slightly lower values are obtained by 4DROP, with larger areas (e.g., Southern Africa, Persian Gulf, or locally in Australia) where the correlations are not significant. As expected, and illustrated in Fig. 2 c and d, better performances are obtained with the 2-months forecasts lead-time, with statistically significant correlations in virtually all locations. Fig. 3  a and b display the correlation between the ensemble mean of S5 and 4DROP forecasts versus the ensemble mean of DROP forecasts for JJA with a 4-months lead time. In the Northern Hemisphere, most grid points exhibit non-significant correlations between S5 and 4DROP forecasts, while higher and statistically significant values are observed in the Southern Hemisphere. Slightly lower values are obtained with 4DROP. Fig. 3 c and d illustrate again better performance for the predictions with a 2-months lead time, with statistically significant correlation in nearly all regions. To summarize the results, Fig. 4   illustrates the distribution of correlation values of the predictions based on 4DROP and S5 (red boxes) for the 4 standard seasons (DJF, MAM, JJA, and SON), for 4- and 2-months lead times. In addition, we also compared the performance obtained considering the individual prediction based on a single initial condition dataset instead of considering the complete ensemble based on DROP. From this analysis, three principal conclusions can be drawn. First, the skill increases with shorter lead times of the forecast, as expected. That is, the correlation values for a 4-months lead time prediction (left panels) are generally lower than those for 2-months forecasts, (right panels), with most datasets having correlation values above 0.5 (for 4-months) and 0.7 (for 2-months). Furthermore, the interquartile range of the correlation distribution decreases from 4- to 2-months forecast lead-times. Secondly, higher skill is obtained generally in DJF (when for most of the grid points a lower percentage of the 6-months total precipitation has to be predicted; Fig. S5 ) compared to JJA. Finally, 4DROP and S5 consistently perform better than the individual forecasts. Among these, GPCC, MERRA2 and MSWEP provide good performance.  3.2 Probabilistic verification of seasonal predictions Fig. 5   provides a quick visual assessment of the reliability of probabilistic forecasts in two regions (East Asia and South Africa) for moderate drought events (i.e., SPI ≤ −0.8; Svoboda et al., 2002 ) for JJA and with a lead time of 2-months as an illustrative example. The choice of these regions illustrates the skill achieved by seasonal forecasting models when it comes to predicting the wet season (East Asia; EAS) and dry season (South Africa; SAF; See Fig. S5  that shows the seasonal mean precipitation on a global scale). Fig. 5 a compares the observed relative frequency with the predicted probability (4DROP and S5) in East Asia (EAS). A perfectly reliable system would draw a line as close as possible to the diagonal (slope equal to 1), indicating that the observed relative frequency and the predicted probability (4DROP and S5) are similar. Although the uncertainty range of the reliability line does not include a perfect line and the slope is less than 1, it is within the skillful zone (BSS > 0 and slope > 0). The ROC diagram for the same region and event type (see Fig. 5 b) indicates that both systems have some ability to discriminate drought events, in terms of identifying drought occurrence, as their curves are slightly above the identity line, where the hit rate (H) is equal to the false alarm rate (F). Fig. 5 c and d show the same analysis for the Southern African region (SAF). In this example, the scatter in the reliability plot is above the perfect reliability line (the slope is greater than 1), indicating that both systems overestimate low levels and underestimate high levels, falling within the skillful zone. Furthermore, the ROC diagram points to higher discrimination ability in this region compared to the previous case. Fig. 6   summarizes the results of the probabilistic evaluation of the forecasts (4DROP and S5) for the twenty-one regions considered (see Giorgi and Francisco, 2000 ; and Fig. S6 ), calculating the slope of the reliability plots (left panels) and the ROCSS area skill score (right panels) for DJF and JJA with a 2-months forecast lead-time and displaying them as boxplot distributions (but see Figs. S7 and S8  for other regions/seasons/lead times). Fig. 6 a and c indicate that the slopes are always positive, and in a few regions the spread of the boxplots contains the perfect reliability line (slope = 1). The slope of the majority of the regions analyzed is greater than 1, indicating that the predictions, although reliable, tend to be overconfident in those areas. Fig. 6 b and d show that the skill score of the ROC area (ROCSS) is always greater than zero, indicating skill in the predictions. Generally, the S5 predictions show better discrimination performance better than the 4DROP forecasts. To further assess the added value of considering an ensemble of observations, Fig. 7   shows the Brier score of S5 forecasts and 4DROP forecasts (Fig. 7 c left column) and of the individual predictions (right column) and subsequently averaged, for the DJF and with a lead time of 4-months. For this, moderate drought (SPI ≤ −0.8; Table S2 ) has been considered. Most of the grids show a BS of less than 0.25, demonstrating that these predictions perform better than random chance. S5 (Fig. 7 a) shows lower BS values (i.e., higher skill) in the Sahel region, India and East Asia, while in Australia, in regions close to the Persian Gulf or the Mediterranean, the BS values are lower (although with some variations for different seasons; see Figs. S9–S12 ). The averaged BS obtained from individual predictions compared to DROP (Fig. 7 b) shows slightly higher BS values (i.e., lower skill). On the other hand, there are areas where it does not change as much (e.g., Europe or the United States). For 4DROP, the BS presents very similar values to those of S5 (Fig. 7 c). However, BS values are lower in regions of Southern Africa or South America.  3.3 Case study: South America in August 2009 As an illustrative application, in Fig. 8   we compare the drought event of 2009 in South America as estimated by DROP (left panel) and as predicted by 4DROP (middle panel) and by S5 (right panel). The choice of this case study is mainly due to two reasons: (i) S5 shows particular skill in predicting the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon and the high correlation of this phenomenon with major droughts in this area is demonstrated (Wang et al., 2017 ); and (ii) Patagonia is one of the regions experiencing a sharp increase in drought frequency and severity (Spinoni et al., 2019 ). This region recorded extreme, and even exceptional, drought conditions in 2009, causing severe water supply problems, as well as decreasing crop yields by up to 40 % compared to previous years (Naumann et al., 2019 ). The SPI6 estimated by the DROP dataset is spatially similar to the 2-months predictions of 4DROP and S5 (Fig. 8 a–c, respectively). Fig. 8 d–f confirm the ability of the forecasts also in terms of capturing the drought conditions. Fig. 8 g–i, show the alert level map described in Table S3  of the supplementary material . This map allows users to focus on areas where there is greater confidence in the severity of drought conditions. The large spatial extent of this drought event is evident throughout South America with the presence of low, medium, and high drought alert levels, respectively (i.e., color from yellow to red). For example, red colors indicate high agreement among ensemble members of having SPI6 ≤ −1.3, i.e., severe drought. The “medium” warning level, on the other hand, reflects high confidence in moderate drought or low to medium confidence in severe drought. Finally, the confidence level of DROP and the probability of the 4DROP and the S5 forecasts (Fig. 8 j–l, respectively) of having a SPI6 below −0.8 is shown. The area where the values are greater than 60 % (brown colors) is generally similar. Therefore, a generally consistent and similar pattern between the DROP estimations and the forecast emerges. Finally, Fig. 8 m shows the temporal evolution of SPI6 for JJA as estimated by DROP and as predicted by 4DROP and S5 in one grid point as identified by a red arrow in Fig. 8 a. We can see how the ensembles of DROP and the predictions follow a similar pattern, which demonstrates the skill of the forecasts in this particular grid point. We can see that 2009 recorded the lowest values by DROP, that is, the most intense drought event considering the entire period of the study (1981–2020), while the predictions slightly underestimate this event.   4 Discussion and conclusions 4.1 Performances of the predictions for meteorological droughts In this study, we have proposed and evaluated a new approach for probabilistic meteorological drought predictions using multi-initial conditions. Before our work, studies by Dutra et al. (2014)  and Mo and Lyon (2015)  systematically evaluated the capabilities of forecasting seasonal droughts globally, highlighting the importance of initial conditions for forecasting skills. Our study advances previous research by integrating the Drought Probability dataset (DROP; Turco et al., 2020 ), which combines all available observation-based datasets in near-real-time. While DROP's efficacy in drought monitoring has been validated, its potential in seasonal drought forecasting was previously unexplored. By combining observed climate conditions with precipitation forecasts from both empirical methods and a dynamical model, our study demonstrates the feasibility of developing an operational forecast system, contingent on the availability of reliable observed climate variables in near-real time. Our findings indicate that using a complete ensemble of diverse monitoring datasets as initial conditions significantly improves the skill of SPI predictions across different seasons and geographical regions. This novel approach combines the best available products for generating actionable information for drought prediction and management. Specifically, this study has examined the 2- and 4-months lead times seasonal forecasts quality of meteorological drought for the four climate seasons (DJF, MAM, JJA and SON) on a global scale using the standardized precipitation index (SPI) for a time scale of 6-months. Two different seasonal forecasting systems have been contrasted: (i) statistical predictions based on the resampling of historical data to obtain 4DROP and (ii) dynamical forecasting based on the fifth ECMWF seasonal forecasting system (SEAS5; S5). Both approaches combine the DROP members (Turco et al., 2020 ) as initial conditions with the forecasts. Our assessment shows that both systems are generally able to predict drought conditions and can be useful for decision-making. Conforming to expectations, forecasts with a 2-months lead time exhibit enhanced skill (global median correlation from 0.79 to 0.91 depending on the target season) in comparison to the 4-months prediction (global median correlation from 0.51 to 0.77 depending on the target season), a logical outcome given the reduced forecasting horizon, and consistent with other studies that have focused on other forecast systems at global and regional scales (Dutra et al., 2014; Gebrechorkos et al., 2022; Torres-Vázquez et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2019 ). The dynamical forecasts perform slightly better than the naïve climatological forecasts at longer time scales and especially over tropical regions. This is due to the moderate skill of the SEAS5 precipitation forecasts for a lead of 1-month (Johnson et al., 2019 ) and for significant skill in regions influenced by the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO; Hao et al., 2018; Pozzi et al., 2013 ) for longer lead times. Indeed, the predictability of dynamical seasonal forecasts is fundamentally based on the slow yet predictable variations of environmental elements such as soil moisture, snow cover, sea ice, and ocean surface temperatures in conjunction with atmospheric interactions (Shukla and Kinter, 2006 ). At the heart of these seasonal scale forecasts is the ENSO phenomenon, which, by inducing warm sea surface temperature anomalies in the tropical Pacific, catalyzes a significant heat flux from the ocean to the atmosphere (Chang et al., 2006; van Oldenborgh et al., 2005; Balmaseda and Anderson, 2009; Weisheimer et al., 2009 ). This flux has the potential to modify the atmospheric boundary layer, reshaping the pattern of rainfall and the dynamics of latent heat release in the troposphere. Such transformations in atmospheric conditions not only influence climatic deviations in distant regions but also exemplify the intricate feedback loops within the climate system, whereby the atmospheric modifications, in turn, affect the sea surface temperatures. This interplay underscores the complex, coupled nature of our climate system, emphasizing the critical role of integrating these dynamics into seasonal forecasting models to enhance their predictive accuracy and reliability (Doblas-Reyes et al., 2013 ). These findings align with previous research (Quan et al., 2012; Yuan and Wood, 2013; Dutra et al., 2014 ) and indicate the importance of improving dynamical forecasts in mid-latitude regions beyond 1-month lead time to surpass the benchmarks set by empirical methods. Presently, 4DROP emerges as a more computationally efficient and cost-effective alternative for drought predictions in extratropical regions and holds the potential as a standard against which other models can be evaluated. These results also indicate that the skill of the SPI forecasts relies largely on the initial conditions, confirming the previous global assessments of Dutra et al. (2014)  and Mo and Lyon (2015) , but we prove for the first time that better forecasts are achieved using the proposed methodology of considering multi-initial conditions. Indeed, the main sources of predictability come from the inherent persistence of drought and thus from its cumulative nature (Schepen et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2012; Torres-Vázquez et al., 2023 ). This is also evident in the observation that predictive skill is typically greater in the winter hemisphere compared to the summer hemisphere, indicating that both systems show better results in forecasting the less rainy periods of the year. For example, the percentage of precipitation to be predicted in DJF in the northern hemisphere is usually lower than that for JJA, leading to increased forecast skill during the boreal winter. Conversely, in the southern hemisphere, there's enhanced skill during the austral winter (JJA) when a lower fraction of the total precipitation has to be predicted. These results highlight the importance of having a consistent monitoring of prior precipitation, accompanied by an accurate estimation of the seasonal cycle of climatological precipitation.  4.2 Limitations of the study and recommendations for future works Global drought monitoring and forecasting face challenges from data quality constraints (Pulwarty and Sivakumar, 2014 ), primarily due to issues with data quality, temporal data gaps, and inconsistent spatial observations (Tapiador et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2018 ). Differences in the particular observed data used to estimate the initial drought state may lead to large uncertainties in the SPI forecasts especially where the quality of observations is lower. Here we show that better forecasts are obtained by considering the full ensemble of different observed datasets as initial conditions rather than the skill obtained by merging forecasts with each individual observed product, illustrating the importance of having an ensemble of observations. The higher skill of the ensembles of 4DROP and S5 relative to their individual member (i.e., single observed product as initial condition) is an expected consequence given the larger ensemble size and likely complementary skill arising from the diversity of observations. That is, our multi-initial conditions approach can lead to higher skill since different DROP datasets may provide better estimates in different areas and the variety of information is an advantage. Therefore, this study highlights the relevance of considering observational uncertainty, and we recommend future studies not to neglect the uncertainty of the observations (Bellprat and Doblas-Reyes, 2016; Massonnet et al., 2016 ). Here we use as initial conditions the DROP datasets, that integrate station-measured, satellite, and reanalysis data (Turco et al., 2020 ). Solely station-measured datasets, while valuable, are not without limitations. These limitations include data quality issues, periods of data unavailability, and poor spatial coverage, which can significantly impact the reliability of drought assessments (Ziese et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2018 ). Conversely, gridded datasets, which serve as the primary resource for drought monitoring (see e.g., Beguería et al., 2014; Ziese et al., 2014; Hao et al., 2014 ), are subject to potential inaccuracies and errors, such as interpolation errors that escalate with decreasing network density. For instance, the Global Precipitation Climatology Centre (GPCC) uses over 85,000 stations worldwide for its precipitation products. However, spatial representativeness issues remain due to the uneven distribution and varying numbers of stations over time (Ziese et al., 2014 ). Satellites and reanalysis data provide a valuable alternative for direct observations, offering more uniform and consistent spatial coverage. However, these sources come with uncertainties such as conversion/transfer function errors, retrieval inaccuracies, biases in assimilated observations, and model limitations (AghaKouchak et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2018 ). Indeed, efforts to address these limitations include merging rain gauge and satellite data, but gridded precipitation estimates remain inherently uncertain (Herold et al., 2016 ). Reanalysis may provide consistent climate estimates but are susceptible to observation uncertainties and model limitations (Parker, 2016; Buizza et al., 2018 ). MSWEP emerges as a particularly promising dataset as corroborated by recent studies (Beck et al., 2017, 2019b; Xu et al., 2019; Turco et al., 2020 ). Its uniqueness lies in its integrated approach, merging rain gauges, satellite, and reanalysis data at a 0.1° resolution (Beck et al., 2019b ). The DROP's utility extends beyond providing initial conditions for seasonal forecasts; it also serves to evaluate these forecasts by offering (i) global coverage, which in-situ data cannot uniformly provide, and (ii) availability in near-real-time, enabling continuous assessment of their skill. Our approach balances the inherent limitations of observations and the benefits of a comprehensive, validated dataset that enhances the accuracy and operational feasibility of drought forecasting. Unfortunately, many datasets are available only at larger resolutions, such as 2.5°. In light of this, our approach was to consider this coarse grid to harmonize and use the highest number of available datasets. Also, a coarse resolution can provide a more representative average than a finer one, where the scarcity of data might lead to unreliable estimates, especially in regions where observational data might be sparse. However, we acknowledge the trade-offs involved in resolution choices. While our current approach prioritizes robustness and comparability across a diverse set of datasets, future studies could explore a different paradigm. For instance, by selecting a subset of available datasets at higher resolution, one could aim for a balance between high resolution and comprehensive dataset coverage. Our research establishes the groundwork for developing an operational global seasonal drought forecasting product. It is important to highlight that adapting our proposed methodology operationally is technically straightforward as we follow a solid, relatively simple, and transparent statistical methodology and all the data are publicly available in near-real time. For instance, to adapt our method for continuous drought forecasting throughout the year, one would need to utilize seasonal forecasts released monthly, targeting successive 3-months intervals (e.g., JFM, FMA, …, DJF). In our study, we employed a leave-one-year-out methodology to evaluate the model's predictive skill. While this provides a representation of the model's potential performance on unseen data, it is important to underline that real-time operational forecast skills might differ (Risbey et al., 2021 ). This discrepancy can be because predicting past events using the leave-one-year-out approach might not capture all challenges or influential factors that are faced when forecasting future events, leading to variations in actual skill. Moreover, with our climate experiencing rapid changes, the historical record may not always be a perfect gauge for future conditions. Hence, while our results offer promising insights, we must remain cautious in extrapolating these findings directly to real-time operational forecasting scenarios. To show the potential applicability of this system, we present a global-scale probabilistic approach to seasonal meteorological drought predictions (APP-4DROP). APP-4DROP is currently a prototype that may evolve and develop into a long-term operational prediction system, playing a significant role in drought management strategies and minimizing the impact of adverse climate conditions. The predictions from 4DROP are publicly available online up to the latest update of DROP, December 2022 (https://matv.shinyapps.io/app_4DROP/ ). Also, to ease the reproducibility of the methods and results, and to facilitate the applicability of these predictions, all codes are hosted in a GitHub repository, accessible through the following weblink https://github.com/MTAV26/4DROP  aligning with FAIR principles (Wilkinson et al., 2016 ).
1 Introduction Karst water is a precious freshwater resource (Ford and Williams, 2007 ), providing drinking water for 10 to 25 % of the world’s population (Stevanović, 2019; Goldscheider et al., 2020 ). Due to the dual or triple porosity structure characteristics (porous media, fissures, and conduits) of the karst aquifer system (KAS) (Reimann et al., 2011, Kuniansky, 2016 ), the hydrological processes of the KAS and adjacent river are more complex compared to other aquifer systems (Christensen et al., 2007 ; Mahoney et al., 2018 ). In southwestern region of China, KAS are often adjacent to rivers, with frequent and seasonal variations in precipitation. Some karst conduits or sinkholes directly connect to the surface, making accurate calculation and assessment of water resources in this area challenging. Therefore, understanding the hydrological processes of the KAS and adjacent river under the influence of precipitation infiltration recharge, especially the dynamic saturation processes of conduit and porous media, is of significant theoretical guidance for the effective development and management of karst water resources in southwestern China. Directly measuring the changes in groundwater resources caused by infiltration recharge is challenging. Currently, scholars commonly use chemical measurement methods such as tracer tests (Paylor and Currens, 2004 ), hydrochemical isotopes (Husic et al., 2019 ), physical measurement methods such as electrical conductivity (Zhang et al., 2019 ), and changes in karst spring discharge (Bittner et al., 2020; Hartmann et al., 2013 ) to indirectly quantify the infiltration recharge to groundwater and flow paths. Indirect methods observe changes in the discharge data of karst springs and river outlets, providing qualitative or localized quantitative information about the flow behavior in the infiltration recharge process. However, it is difficult to characterize the flow behavior of water in different media during infiltration recharge to groundwater using data representation (Hartmann et al., 2017 ). To broaden the understanding of groundwater flow behavior in karst aquifer during precipitation infiltration recharge process, it is first necessary to clarify the driving mechanisms of groundwater movement and the influence of infiltration recharge intensity on flow behavior. The driving mechanisms can be categorized as follows: (1) interaction of groundwater between different media driven by pressure differences or upstream flow rates (Gill et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2015; Reimann et al., 2014 ), (2) vertical movement of groundwater caused by gravity (R. Kennedy et al., 2023 ), (3) interaction of groundwater between different media caused by media exceeding their own satiration capacity. Previous studies have mainly analyzed based on driving mechanism (1). When the groundwater flow rate is low, the effect of gravity is usually not negligible; while, when the flow rate is high, some media, due to exceeding their own saturation capacity, cause groundwater to change its flow path, such as saturated groundwater saturation in conduit leading to overflow and flow towards surrounding porous media (Worthington, 1991 ). The driving intensity of precipitation infiltration recharge to groundwater can be directly influenced by recharge and groundwater flow. The hydrological processes of the KAS and adjacent river during precipitation infiltration recharge are not only affected by the internal structure and flow behavior of the KAS, but also by the hydrological paths through which water enters the system and flows to the outlet. Husic et al (2017a, 2017b)  and Al-Aamery et al (2021)  have proposed the concept of hydrological pathways for water circulation between the KAS and rivers. In these studies, karst conduits are located below the rivers, with river water infiltrating vertically into the conduits; surface water was recharged only from porous media, or can be recharged by karst springs located at lower elevations downstream. In recent years, there has been limited research on the hydrologic interactions between the KAS and adjacent river during precipitation infiltration recharge (Husic et al., 2022 ). To obtain comprehensive hydrological processes information between the KAS and the adjacent river under precipitation infiltration recharge, integration can be achieved through hydrological process curves of karst springs and river outlets. The hydrological process curves of karst springs and the adjacent rivers provide information on the recharge processes of the KAS and adjacent river due to precipitation infiltration, as well as the hydrological processes of surface water and groundwater flow (Duran et al., 2020; Mudarra & Andreo, 2011; Aquilina et al., 2006 ). Establishing an effective hydrological model becomes crucial for accurately obtaining the hydrological process curves of karst springs and rivers. The distributed karst groundwater model (Teutsch and Sauter, 1998 ) is an effective method for calculating karst water resources. This model requires discretizing the two-dimensional or three-dimensional karst systems into grids and assigning hydraulic parameters such as medium storage coefficient, hydraulic conductivity, and conduit friction coefficient to each grid (Gabrovšek et al., 2018 ). In addition, CFP allows information about the location and geometry of the conduit network to be considered by user-specific approaches or by sophisticated methods such as stochastic conduit network generators (Reimann et al., 2023 ). Groundwater flow in porous media is usually controlled by Darcy's law, while flow in conduits introduces the Darcy–Weisbach equation that better describes the characteristics of karst groundwater flow. Based on the structure division of the system, if only the estimation and prediction of karst water resources are needed, the equivalent porous medium (EPM) approach can be used. By averaging the heterogeneous characteristics caused by conduits and porous media, it is equivalent to a porous medium (Abusaada and Sauter, 2013; Rodríguez et al., 2013 ). When using this method for modeling, the average permeability coefficient and geometric characteristics of the aquifer are needed, thus unable to reflect the fast-flowing characteristics of groundwater in the KAS, especially in conduits, which limits the simulation of groundwater flow in developed KAS. Building upon this, Kordilla et al. (2012)  utilized the Double Continuum approach to represent both Darcy flow in porous media and non-Darcy flow in karst conduits through the interaction of two continua. This method establishes a linear function between different hydraulic heads of the two continua to control the exchange of groundwater between media. Therefore, the Double Continuum approach can to some extent characterize the binary nature of the KAS, but it is not only limited to the overly linear interaction between groundwater in porous media and conduits but also cannot consider the impact of conduit geometry and size on hydrological processes. To address this issue, Reimann et al. (2011)  and Shoemaker et al. (2008)  further consider the conduit continuum as discrete elements inserted into continuous porous media (MODFLOW-Conduit Flow Process), allowing the calculation of the influence of karst conduit geometry and distribution on groundwater hydrological processes in the entire KAS. This method has been widely applied to study the flow behavior and estimate water resources of karst groundwater in various regions worldwide (Chang et al., 2015; Qiu et al., 2019; Kavousi et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2020, Gao et al., 2024 ). However, to accurately obtain comprehensive hydrological process information of the KAS and adjacent river, using the Navier-Stokes equation can capture more microscopic flow characteristics (Soulaine and Tchelepi, 2016 ). In recent studies, the Navier-Stokes equation has made significant contributions to researching the interactions of various fractures and karst conduits coupled with porous media (Carrillo et al., 2020; You and Lee, 2021 ). Soulaine et al. (2021)  further expanded the Navier-Stokes equation to make it more suitable for solving multiphase flow. Lu et al. (2023)  analyzed a model of fractures and conduits as the main drainage channels distributed in porous media using the DBS equation, which combines Darcy for the solid phase region and Navier-Stokes for the fluid phase region, showing that this method could serve as an effective tool for understanding the complex flow of water in KAS. The mechanisms of the KAS and the adjacent river hydrological processes under precipitation infiltration recharge are currently unclear. Further, the existing numerical methods in research have difficulty accurately characterizing the interaction between the KAS and the stream, especially the micro-scale flow behavior of groundwater and variations in medium saturation within the karst aquifer system. Therefore, in order to further reveal the mechanisms of the KAS and the adjacent river hydrological processes during precipitation infiltration recharge, this study divides the karst conduits and the adjacent river into free-flow regions, and the soil and porous media into seepage regions. By using the Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes (DBS) equation to characterize the flow behavior of groundwater in different media of the KAS and coupling it with the free-flow processes of the adjacent river, by using the van Genuchten-Mualem and van Genuchten-modified Mualem equations to characterize the seepage processes in soil and porous media, and the dynamic changes in water saturation within the study area are captured using the Volume of Fluid (VOF) method, this study clarifies the interactions between groundwater flow behavior and medium saturation processes in the KAS under precipitation infiltration recharge and analyzes the hydrological process changes in the KAS and adjacent river during precipitation infiltration recharge. Due to the complexity of the mechanisms of the KAS and adjacent river hydrological processes, research and analysis on these require a clear understanding of how water driving modes, flow paths, and flow behaviors affect these hydrological processes. This study specifically focuses on three aspects: (1) the recharge, storage, and discharge behavior of groundwater in different media driven by the precipitation infiltration process, (2) the impact of changes in groundwater flow paths on the KAS and adjacent river hydrological processes, and (3) the influence of flow conditions on flow behavior and hydrological processes. The research results can further reveal the mechanisms of the KAS and adjacent river hydrological processes under precipitation infiltration recharge, providing a scientific basis for accurate and rational assessment of karst water resources.  2 Methods To accurately analyze the hydrological processes of precipitation infiltration recharge on the KAS and adjacent river, this study adopts the Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes (DBS) equation as the governing equation for groundwater movement in the KAS. The flow of groundwater in the media is expanded into two-phase flow to simulate the changes in water saturation in the media, thereby analyzing the variations in the storage of different media (Gao et al., 2021 ) and the impact of the saturation limits of media on the behavior of groundwater flow. This study assigns transient boundaries to the overlying soil, enabling the model to simulate natural conditions (Precipitation). Previous models rarely considered the effects of gravitational forces on water bodies, usually taking the bottom of the karst conduit as the lower boundary of the model. In this study, gravitational effects are incorporated during the simulation process, placing the karst conduits in the middle of the model to analyze the storage and bearing capacity of the lower porous media and their influence on groundwater flow. Reimann et al. (2011)  studied turbulent flow by varying the permeability of the conduit walls, and solving the turbulent flow equation using the Reynolds-averaged method (Eqs. (13)–(15) ) in the model can more accurately reflect the dissipation of turbulent flow at a global level. Building upon this foundation, the study discretizes the adjacent river and inserts it into the system in a free-flow form, constructing a hydrological model of the KAS and the adjacent river. 2.1 The volume of fluid (VOF) computational fluid dynamics method Regarding the relative permeability in unsaturated models (Mualem, 1976 ), previous models often used the Richards equation for calculations (Richards, 1931; Cueto-Felgueroso and Juanes, 2008 ). This equation can to some extent describe the changes in saturation of groundwater in shallow aquifers, but it is difficult to analyze the flow behavior of groundwater within the aquifer based solely on changes in water level. Currently, the Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) method is widely used to solve immiscible multiphase fluid flow (Zhai et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2024; Sha and Jia, 2024; Du et al., 2024 ), and has been applied to solve the relative permeability of fractured media at the mixed pore scale (Lanetc et al., 2024 ). To describe the seepage of porous media and the free flow process of conduits and adjacent river, the two-phase flow of non-miscible and incompressible fluids in porous media is described using the Darcy-Brinkman-Stokes (DBS) equation (Nillama et al., 2022; Carrillo et al., 2020; Lu et al. 2023 ).
