This study focuses on the impact of precipitation infiltration recharge on the interaction between the KAS and adjacent river as a single process. Therefore, it is assumed that precipitation does not significantly affect the water level of the adjacent river, and the recharge from the river to the KAS can be neglected, with the recharge to the KAS only coming from precipitation infiltration. Fig. 1 b describes the boundary conditions for the precipitation response, I ( t p  )   , where the red dashed box represents the discrete region of the model. The porous medium is surrounded by a no-flow boundary, with the karst outlet and adjacent river serving as discharge boundaries. The “discharge boundary” is a mixed boundary condition, which is a zero-gradient condition when the water flows out of the boundary, and a fixed value when the boundary reverses the inflow. A fixed value 0 was set in this study to prevent backflow. As shown in Fig. 1 , “spring” refers to the outlet of karst conduit discharging into the river. “Conduit outlet” refers to the interaction boundary where the karst conduit in the computational domain interfaces with the internal aquifer. The “Conduit outlet” boundary is the Neumam boundary condition, which allows the water to interact with the external. “River inlet” is the Dirichlet boundary. h r  x , t      is the change in water level of the adjacent water during model calculations. Since the entire aquifer is replenished by precipitation, the water level rise on the outer and inner sides of the porous medium at the left boundary of the computational domain is consistent. Therefore, the subtle interactive flow of the porous medium on the left is ignored on the x-y plane, and the boundary condition is set as no-flow. The yellow region represents a continuum of fractured matrix with “multistage permeability and porosity” variations, which envelopes the sinkhole and conduit, and exhibits a gradual decrease in permeability and porosity towards the porous medium area. The permeability and porosity of the riverbank also decrease progressively. The two-phase (air–water) flow can be described by the control Eqs. (1)–(3) . Eqs. (5)–(7)  couple the porous medium region with the conduit and adjacent river region, and all three sharing a set of momentum equations where the source terms differ in different flow regions. The water retention properties of porous medium are described by Eqs. (8)–(12) . The turbulent flow process throughout the aquifer is described by the unsteady Reynolds-average equation. The conduit, adjacent river and the surrounding porous medium exchange fluids through the pressure differences, with the conduit exhibiting free-flow conditions at low saturation levels, and becoming pressurized flow when still receiving recharge after saturation.  2.3 Simulation parameters The following equation was used for the precipitation infiltration recharge boundary condition in this study (Chang et al., 2015 ):(17) I t R    = b 2 π σ  2     e  - t R  - μ  a     2  2 σ  2              where t R    is the precipitation duration, I t R       is the cumulative precipitation, μ  , σ  2   , and a   are constants set to 90, 1.5, and 20, respectively (Chang et al., 2015 ). In precipitation infiltration recharge, the variation of precipitation intensity is achieved by changing the dimensionless parameter b  . A higher value of b   indicates higher precipitation intensity. In a precipitation event, a portion of the precipitation directly recharges the river, while the remaining precipitation infiltrates and recharges the KAS. The groundwater that recharges the karst conduit drains into the adjacent river through the conduit, while the groundwater that is not captured by the conduit vertically recharges the porous medium II and then laterally seeps into the porous medium III. During this process, water flows through the lower wall of the karst conduit and infiltrates into the porous medium III, finally discharging into the adjacent river laterally after passing through a low permeability layer (Fig. 1 a).  2.4 Model settings In previous studies, karst conduits were typically positioned at the bottom of the models and fixed within the grid (Kavousi et al., 2020; Pardo-Igúzquiza et al., 2018; Li et al., 2023 ). After determining the position of the riverbed and river width, the adjacent river is defined in the model in the same manner, with the right boundary of the river being a symmetry boundary. Based on this, the grids outside the adjacent river and conduit are defined as porous media. As shown in Figs. 1 b and 2  a, the porous media is vertically divided into layers I, II, and III to more effectively simulate and analyze the flow behavior of groundwater under different conditions. Since the free flow in the conduit requires fine grid resolution to capture water levels and interface fluctuations, local mesh refinement of the conduit grid is necessary. Groundwater flows in the porous media through seepage, and the farther away from the discharge end, the slower the flow of groundwater in the porous media (forming a drawdown funnel shape). Therefore, the grids between pairs of porous media are sequentially expanded, with the outermost grids near the conduit being twice the length of the grids nearby. This discretization method provides relatively uniform representation, capturing more accurate flow near the discharge end and reducing more computational resources at the far end of drainage. Fig. 2 b shows the variation in saturation of the KAS and the flow behavior occurring between the conduit and porous media under different precipitation infiltration intensities. The range of parameter settings in the model is shown in Table 1  . The sinkhole has a radius of 1 m, a permeability of 10–6 m2  and a porosity of 0.65. The conduit has a radius of 1 m and operates under free-flow conditions without setting permeability. The sinkhole is vertically connected to the conduit. Surrounding the sinkhole and the conduit is a multilayer fissured matrix continuum with radial ranges from the inside out being (1–3 m, 3–10 m) for the sinkhole and (1–1.1 m, 1.1–1.2 m) for the conduit. The multilayer fissured matrix continuum exhibits permeability values that decrease from the innermost layer at 10−7  m2  to the outer layer at 10−8  m2 . The outermost layer of this porous medium has a permeability of 10−9  m2 .   3 Results 3.1 Influence of flow behavior and changes in medium saturation on hydrological processes Fig. 3  a and b shows the hydrological process curve of the adjacent river and karst outlet under different precipitation intensities and the changes in conduit saturation when the karst conduit has a height of 3 m and a radius of 1 m. As the precipitation intensity increases, the peak of the hydrological process curve of the adjacent river gradually increases, and the recession time advances. When the precipitation intensity rises to b = 8   , the recession process of the adjacent river hydrological process curve is characterized by rapid drainage mainly driven by the conduit initially, causing a rapid drop in the curve, followed by a gradual decline dominated by base flow. Fig. 3 b shows that the peak of the hydrological process curve for the karst conduit increases with the increase in precipitation intensity, and the recession time gradually advances. By comparing Fig. 3 b and c, it can be obtained that the variations in precipitation intensity can affect both the peak of the hydrological process curve and the onset of recession. Additionally, a “step-like” behavior emergers during the mid-stage of the recession process in the karst conduit. This occurs because at the beginning of the recession, the karst conduit rapidly discharges groundwater. Concurrently, groundwater also flows from porous media I to the karst conduit. As the saturation of the conduit continues to decrease, the pressure in the conduit gradually decreases, and the water level continuous to drop, allowing the conduit to accommodate more groundwater inflow from the surrounding porous media. This increases the recharge from the porous medium to the karst conduit, thereby sustaining the high-intensity recession of the conduit. The discharge at the outlet of the adjacent river is composed of two parts: that from the karst conduit and the lateral recharge from porous media to the river. Fig. 4   illustrates the proportion of discharge from the karst conduit in the total lateral recharge, to analyze the time period when the karst conduit plays a dominates role in discharge. As shown in Fig. 4 a and b, when the precipitation intensity is low, the proportion of discharge from the karst conduit increases with increasing precipitation intensity. From the variation in conduit saturation at different precipitation intensities (Fig. 3 c), it can be inferred that under low precipitation intensity, the conduit flow is minimal, allowing groundwater to be rapidly discharged to the adjacent river through the conduit. On the other hand, under this precipitation intensity condition, groundwater is mainly discharged to the adjacent river through porous media, hence, there is no dominance rapid drainage during the recession process. As the precipitation intensity continues to increase, the proportion of discharge from the karst conduit in the lateral recharge gradually increases (Fig. 4 c), the dominance of rapid drainage has occurred. If the precipitation intensity continues to increase, the proportion of groundwater discharge through porous media in lateral recharge will also increase (Fig. 4 d). It can be observed from the changes in the saturation level of the karst conduit under different precipitation intensities (Fig. 3 c), when the conduit reaches saturation, precipitation infiltration still contributes to the KAS, and at this stage, but there is no significant increase in conduit discharge during this stage. This indicates that after exceeding the capacity of the conduit, the excess flow will pass through the conduit wall into the porous media, causing overflow phenomena (Worthington, 1991 ). Therefore, in conditions of high precipitation intensity, the proportion of lateral recharge from porous media in the discharge is lower. The “step-like” recession behavior is delayed in time due to the lagging decrease in conduit saturation with increasing precipitation intensity. Based on Fig. 3 c, it is found that when the conduit saturation declines to around 40 %, the quantity of water from porous media I to the karst conduit is insufficient to maintain rapid discharge to the adjacent river. However, under low precipitation intensity conditions (b = 3   ), the groundwater from porous media I can still be discharged to the river through the karst conduit. When the precipitation intensity further increases (3 < b ≤ 8   ), the karst conduit remains capable of accommodating the supply from porous media I. When the precipitation intensity continues to increase (8 < b ≤ 12   ), the conduit reaches a higher saturation level due to greater recharge. In the early stage of recession, a large amount of groundwater is recharged to the conduit through porous media to maintain fast drainage. As the storage of porous media decreases, the recharge to the conduit also reduces, resulting in a decrease in discharge through the conduit, leading to slow recession. At this stage, precipitation infiltration is unable to maintain a high storage level in porous media I, and the recharge to the conduit relies solely on its own storage. When the recharge further increases (b > 12   ), the contribution of the karst conduit is reversed, and the proportion of conduit discharge decreases with increasing precipitation intensity. This is because when the conduit reaches saturation, the excess groundwater cannot be discharged through the conduit in a timely manner due to its limited capacity, causing this portion of groundwater to be discharged to the adjacent river through the porous media. In summary, in Fig. 4 , the proportion of discharge from porous media initially decreases with increasing precipitation. When the conduit capacity exceeds its limit, the proportion of discharge from porous media increases with increasing precipitation intensity. The hydrological process curve of the adjacent river is composed of the discharge from the karst conduit, porous media I, porous media II, and porous media III. Because the discharge of groundwater through porous media II to the adjacent river is small, it mainly serves as a medium for groundwater exchange between the media. Therefore, the discharge proportion of groundwater through porous media I and porous media III to the adjacent river is mainly analyzed. Fig. 5  a indicates that under low precipitation intensity (b = 3   ), the contribution of late-stage drainage to the adjacent river mainly comes from porous media I and porous media III. A part of groundwater in porous media I is captured by the karst conduit and discharged to the adjacent river, while another part of the groundwater vertically moves into porous media II due to gravity. Both the conduit and the groundwater in porous medium II recharge porous medium III under the influence of gravity. Therefore, when the precipitation intensity is low, gravity plays a dominant role, causing groundwater in the media to flow towards porous media III, reaching the weakly impermeable layer at the bottom and eventually laterally discharge to the river. Fig. 5 b shows that with the increase of precipitation intensity, the discharge proportion of groundwater through porous media I and porous media III increases to some extent, but the proportion of discharge from porous media III gradually increases. This indicates that since porous medium III is still capable of accommodating external recharge, it has not yet reached saturation. Therefore, the infiltration recharge brought by higher-intensity precipitation will preferentially recharge the lower porous medium (porous medium III). Concurrently, as the precipitation intensity increases, the external recharge increases, and after the groundwater is captured by the conduit, due to the faster flow rate of the groundwater in the conduit and weaker influence of gravity, a proportion of the groundwater is directly discharged to the adjacent river through the conduit. Fig. 5 c–e demonstrate that as the precipitation intensity increases (8 < b ≤ 12   ), the proportion of discharge to the adjacent river from Porous Media I during its early and middle stages gradually approaches that of Porous Media III. A “contribution mutation” occurs in porous medium III at 8,000 s, and at this time, porous medium I also experiences a sharp reduction in discharge to the adjacent river. This behavior is observed to occur when the saturation of the karst conduit (②) is below 40 %, as shown in Fig. 3 c, indicating that the groundwater in the conduit is undergoing a rapid “step-like” recession. At this point, the karst conduit and the upper porous medium are no longer able to provide significant recharge to porous medium Ⅲ. Therefore, during this stage (corresponding to the baseflow recession stage in Fig. 3 a), most of the groundwater is discharged to the adjacent river through porous medium III. The “contribution mutation” is further delayed compared to the situations in Fig. 5 c–e. This is because, with the increase in precipitation intensity, the time for the saturation of the karst conduit to 40 % is further delayed (Fig. 3 c), and correspondingly, the point at which the conduit stops recharging the porous medium III is also postponed. Fig. 5 f illustrates that with the increase in precipitation intensity (b = 15   ), the proportion of discharge to the adjacent river from porous medium I during its early and middle stages surpasses that of porous medium III. During this phase, since porous medium III is unable to rapidly brought the external recharge, the medium gradually becomes saturated. Consequently, the infiltration recharge brought by the higher-intensity precipitation is discharged through the upper porous media (porous medium I and porous medium II) and via conduit overflow. Therefore, in Fig. 5 , when precipitation intensity is lower, gravity plays a dominant role in the groundwater flow process, resulting in a higher proportion of groundwater discharge through porous media III. As the precipitation intensity increases and porous media III reaches its capacity, the proportion of groundwater discharge through porous media I increases. When overflow occurs, porous media I becomes the main medium for discharge to the adjacent river. The “contribution mutation” occurs synchronously with the timing of groundwater depletion in the karst conduit, further reflecting the timing of river baseflow recession.  3.2 Impact of changes in flow regime on hydrological processes Through Fig. 6  , it can be observed that when the precipitation intensity is relatively higher, the recession process of the adjacent river consists of multiple stages of recession behavior. In order to further analyze the controlled factors of this behavior, this study considers the impact of groundwater flow in karst conduit under laminar and turbulent conditions on the hydrological process of the adjacent river when the precipitation intensity b  = 8   . Fig. 6  illustrates the flow of groundwater in karst conduit as laminar and turbulent states, affecting the hydrological process curve of the adjacent river, the discharge from the karst conduit to the adjacent river, and the saturation of the karst conduit. As shown in Fig. 6 a, during the early to middle stages of recession, when the flow in the conduit is in a laminar state, the discharge to the adjacent river is higher. The modelling results show that the saturation of the conduit decreases more under laminar flow conditions (Fig. 6 d). The conduit will have more dry space to receive recharge from the porous medium than under turbulent flow conditions, and the excess recharge will be discharged through the conduit into the adjacent river (Fig. 6 b). When the precipitation intensity is b = 8   , the conduit can maintain high saturation for a long time and rapidly discharge water, therefore, the main focus here is on analyzing the flow behavior of groundwater in the conduit (Fig. 6 b). When the flow in the conduit is in a laminar state, except for a brief period close to the turbulent flow conditions at the beginning of the pre-precipitation stage, the discharge of groundwater through the conduit is higher than in the turbulent state for the remaining stages. As shown in Fig. 6 c, except in the early stage, the hydrological process curve of the KAS tends to flow towards the adjacent river due to the faster groundwater flow velocity under laminar flow conditions and lower water levels in the direction of the adjacent river. Consequently, the discharge rates are smaller than those under turbulent conditions. Fig. 6 b suggests that more water is allocated to the adjacent river under laminar flow conditions. As shown in Fig. 6 d, due to the faster groundwater flow rate in the laminar state, the groundwater discharge rate to the adjacent river is faster through the conduit, so the saturation of the conduit is lower, allowing the storage of medium I in the porous medium to recharge groundwater to the conduit to maintain its rapid drainage. As the supply of groundwater through the porous medium to the conduit increases, the storage in the porous medium I also decreases rapidly. Therefore, in the recession process under laminar flow, there is a stage where the laminar discharge briefly approaches the turbulent discharge state. Since the saturation of the conduit is relatively low, the groundwater head in the conduit is lower than that of the surrounding porous medium II. After the groundwater in the conduit is quickly discharged, the conduit starts to capture the storage in the porous medium II. Due to the smaller storage in the porous medium II, after a brief replenishment to the conduit, the groundwater in the porous medium II is drained completely.  3.3 Variation process line of average flow velocity and interfacial flow velocity under different simulation methods Fig. 7  a illustrates the variation process of the average flow velocity at the river outlet when the precipitation intensity is b = 8   , using the DBS method (Eqs. (1)–(3) ) and the N-S simulation (based on the multiphase flow in the renowned fluid dynamics software Ansys Fluent) under the grid of this study. Since the flow curves are directly related to the flow velocity, we used the software Ansys Fluent to verify the mean flow velocity change at the outlet of the adjacent river and to compare the difference in flow velocity between the two methods in the interior of the karst aquifer. Because the N-S simulation scheme dose not consider the water retention characteristics of the porous medium, while the relative permeability of the water–air two-phase in the DBS method changes, there is a certain discrepancy between the simulation results of the DBS method and the N-S method. Fig. 7 b shows the tangential flow velocity between points (48, 55, 3) and (50, 55, 3) in the porous medium and the conduit at a precipitation intensity of 8 and a simulation time of 5600 s. Morad and Khalili (2009)  indicates that there is a transition layer between the interface and the stable Darcy seepage in the porous medium area, and that the seepage velocity in this transition layer will be greater than the Darcy velocity. Therefore, the seepage velocity in the transition layer of the porous medium using the DBS method will be greater than the seepage using the Darcy's law (N-S simulation method), and this velocity will gradually decay to uniform seepage.   4 Discussion 4.1 Effect of different water retention equations on the discharge of the KAS to adjacent river and the process of medium saturation Fig. 8   demonstrates the variations in water retention curve, discharge from the karst conduit to the adjacent river, and saturation of the karst conduit when applying the VGM model (Eqs. (9) and (10) ) and the VGMM model (Eqs. (11) and (12) ). As shown in Fig. 8 a, for the same infiltration time, the VGM model computes a higher water content compared to the VGMM model, but the VGMM model predicts groundwater travel distances farther than the VGM model. As depicted in Fig. 8 b, in the early stage of simulation results by the VGMM model, groundwater discharges to the adjacent river later than in the VGM model, but the discharge volume is slightly higher in the mid-to-late period. In Fig. 8 c, during the initial stages of simulation results by the VGMM model, the increase in medium saturation lags behind compared to the VGM model, while during the recession process, the saturation predicted by the VGMM model remains higher than that by the VGM model. To further analyze the reasons for these differences, this study utilized different water retention models to derive hydrographs for the porous medium I and porous medium III. In the early stages of the hydrological process, the VGM model yielded slightly higher results, but the VGMM model gradually exceeded the VGM model results as the recharge continued (Fig. 9  a). Based on the results from Figs. 9 b and 8 b, the discharge of groundwater through the conduit is larger in the VGMM model, resulting in a consistently lower hydrograph curve for porous medium III in Fig. 9 b compared to the VGM model. Although different water retention equations have little difference in overall discharge impact, they can cause lag and peak variations in the inter-medium discharge process, as well as differences in the degree of fluid redistribution between the karst conduit and porous media under precipitation recharge. Therefore, it is particularly important to select different water retention equations based on soil characteristics.   5 Conclusions This study established a numerical model of karst aquifer coupled with the adjacent river by considering the relative permeability coupling different water retention equations through the DBS equation. The VOF phase change method was applied to investigate the effects of precipitation infiltration on the groundwater flow behavior, saturation process variations, as well as the influence of laminar and turbulent flows on the karst aquifer system (KAS) and hydrological processes of the adjacent river. The results indicate that the saturation degrees of each medium, which are indirectly controlled by the recharge intensity, directly influence the flow behavior and flow paths of the medium and surrounding media. Throughout the process, the conduit initially experiences free-flow conditions when it is being recharged, transitions to pressurized flow during the peak of precipitation, and then returns to free-flow conditions during the recession phase. The transition between these flow states is accompanied by corresponding changes in the flow behavior of the surrounding porous medium. Under low precipitation intensities, the main groundwater flow path is through porous medium III, while under moderate precipitation intensities, the main groundwater flow path is through the karst conduit. During high-intensity precipitation, due to the limited carrying capacity of the karst conduit, it is unable to accommodate a large amount of groundwater supply from porous medium I. As a result, a portion of the groundwater flow path shifts from the original drainage through the karst conduit to drainage through the porous medium. The impacts of laminar and turbulent flows on the groundwater flow status in the karst aquifer system and hydrological processes of the adjacent river vary. These differences are reflected in the changes in conduit saturation. In the case of drainage through the conduit under laminar flow conditions, the saturation decreases rapidly, making it easier for the porous medium to supply the conduit and discharge towards the adjacent river. The contribution of the adjacent river to the KAS can be neglected, and the recharge of the KAS only comes from precipitation infiltration. However, under seasonal variations, the precipitation intensity changes frequently, causing alternating changes in the water levels of the adjacent river and the KAS, resulting in a more complex interaction process. Future studies could focus on the interaction process between the KAS and the adjacent river under seasonal variations.
1 Introduction Geothermal energy contained in hot dry rocks (HDR) buried at depths of 3–10 km is an important strategic resource for many countries due to its abundant reserves, wide distribution, cleanliness and renewability (Sun et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024a ). In the natural state, HDR reservoirs are of high density with extremely low porosity and permeability (less than 0.001mD). Reservoir fracturing, a technique initially used for extracting oil and gas resources, has been adapted for extracting deep geothermal resources, creating the enhanced geothermal system (EGS) (Lu, 2018; Guo et al., 2019 ). Complex fracture networks are artificially generated in HDR reservoirs to form fluid flow channels, and fluid continuously absorbs heat from the high-temperature fractured rocks during the flow process. The extraction of HDR geothermal energy depends largely on the fluid flow and heat transfer processes in natural and hydraulic fractures. Therefore, it is essential to understand the flow and heat transfer processes in high-temperature fractured rocks to improve the efficiency of geothermal energy extraction (Hu et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2023 ). Traditional studies on fluid flow behavior in fractures have assumed that the variation in fracture apertures is negligible compared to their length and width, and the corresponding fluid flow follows classical cubic law (Zhao et al., 2017; Shu et al., 2023 ). However, rough natural and hydraulic fractures have substantially different convection heat transfer behaviors than smooth ones. Many scholars have conducted experimental studies on convection heat transfer behavior in single rough fractures using the Brazilian splitting method or three-dimensional (3D) printing technology to prepare fractured rock (Bai et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2019 ). By conducting a series of convection heat transfer experiments on granite samples with artificial rough and smooth fractures, Li et al. (2017)  found that the fracture surface roughness significantly improved the overall heat transfer intensity, and the samples’ external temperature showed strong nonlinear characteristics. Similarly, the experimental results of Ma et al. (2018)  indicated that the water temperature distribution in rough fractures did not increase linearly along the flow direction, and the surface roughness significantly impacted the heat transfer characteristics of rough fractures. Limited by the immaturity of experimental equipment at high temperature and internal monitoring technology for fractures, it is difficult to conduct heat transfer experiments on high-temperature HDR. Furthermore, the fluid flow and heat transfer behaviors cannot be accurately characterized, which significantly restricts the study of HDR (Osgouei and Akin, 2021; Shu et al., 2022 ). Numerical simulations, which are widely used for studying the heat transfer characteristics of rock fractures, can be used to characterize the local heat exchange in rough fractures. He et al. (2018)  established a two-dimensional (2D) single rough fracture that considers various thermophysical properties, and showed that the local heat transfer coefficient decreased with the increasing rock temperature and increased with a decrease in the fracture opening. Zhan et al. (2022)  found that the average heat transfer coefficient increased with increasing fracture surface roughness, and the local heat transfer coefficient was closely related to the undulating and fluctuating degree of fracture surface. After defining the contribution of wall roughness to the overall flow, Wang et al. (2021a)  quantitatively identified the primary and secondary wall roughness of 2D rough fractures. The secondary roughness caused larger and more irregular eddies, which promoted local heat exchange between the higher-temperature fracture walls and the lower-temperature fluid. However, 2D numerical models of fractured rocks are a simplification of real 3D fractures. They only reflect the flow and heat transfer characteristics along the flow direction but cannot accurately describes the complexity of fracture void structures (Liu et al. 2021 ). Chen and Zhao (2020)  found that the variations in fracture voids increased the heterogeneities of the water temperature distributions in the artificial fracture. The simulation results of He et al. (2020)  revealed that the inner surface temperature perpendicular to the flow direction followed a parabolic distribution. Influenced by the surface roughness of rock fractures, the fluid flow presents strong heterogeneity which directly affects the heat transfer processes between the flowing fluid and fractured rocks (Zhang et al., 2019; Rong et al., 2020 ). However, the aperture fields of natural and hydraulic fractures are not completely connected, and the contact characteristics between two fracture surfaces have been demonstrated to affect fluid flow behavior (Chen et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2022 ). Xiong et al. (2018)  analyzed the fluid flow behavior in single rough fractures with different contact ratios. The results showed that the nonlinear flow behavior was affected by the Re  number and the complex void structures, and the surface contact can generate eddies which complicate the flow field. Wang et al. (2021b)  studied the effect of surface contact on fluid flow and solute transport processes in fractures. The void structure became increasingly complex as the surface contacts increased, which greatly enhanced the heterogeneous flow. Wang et al. (2023)  changed the fracture surface contact by applying shear displacement and stronger flow channeling in fracture voids was observed. The widely distributed small contact spots resulted in more tortuous flow paths. However, most studies included the contact properties of fracture surfaces only for analyzing fluid flow and solute transport behaviors. Researchers investigating the heat transfer characteristics of fractured HDR still assumed that the fractures had no/little contact areas or used statistical approaches, such as self-affine, to generate fracture voids (He et al., 2019; He et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024b ). A comprehensive and accurate analysis of fluid flow and heat transfer processes in realistic rock fractures with complex void structures under different surface contacts is lacking. This is hampering a clear understanding of flow channeling and heterogeneous heat transfer in fractured rocks. This study aims to analyze the influence of realistic void structures (distinct from planar plate-shaped fractures with little or no surface contact) on flow channeling and heterogeneous heat transfer in fractured rocks. The aperture field of a realistic granite rock fracture is directly applied various normal displacements, and 3D numerical models with a single fracture at different contact ratios are generated to simulate the fluid flow and heat transfer processes in rock fractures. The effects of complex void structures on fluid flow and heat transfer behaviors in a single fracture are analyzed, and low-flow regions are identified. An empirical model is proposed to describe the relationship between heat transfer coefficient and complex void structures. The heterogeneity of fluid flow and heat transfer under different initial rock temperatures and flow directions is further discussed. The findings may further deepen the understanding of flow and heat transfer behaviors in fractured HDR with real complex voids.  2 Material and methods 2.1 3D fracture of granite In this study, the granite from the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area was selected as the experimental object. Standard cylindrical specimens with a dimension of Φ 50mm × h 100mm were used to prepare tensile fractures through Brazilian splitting, as shown in Fig. 1  (a) and (b). 3D fracture models were generated from the topographic data obtained by 3D laser scanner with a scanning accuracy of 0.2 mm. The contact was defined as the set of points with eI   < 0.01 mm (where e I  = Z I u  - Z I b     is the aperture of the fracture at grid point I, and Z I u    and Z I b    are the elevations of the upper and lower surfaces of the fracture at grid point I, respectively), and the points with eI   > 0.01 mm were regarded as the fracture voids. Besides, isolated voids surrounded by contact areas were not be considered in the numerical simulation (Thorn and Fransson, 2015 ). The distribution of the fracture aperture is presented in Fig. 1 (c). Similar to Xiong et al. (2018)  and Kling et al. (2018) , the fractures with different contact ratios (F 0.0 、F 0.3 、F 0.6 、F 0.9 , where F 0.0  is the original fracture) were generated by directly applying normal displacements of 0.3, 0.6, and 0.9 mm to the upper surface, respectively. The associated aperture distributions are shown in Fig. 1 (d), and the detailed information of four tested fracture are listed in Table 1  . The fracture was gradually compacted with the increase of normal displacement (surface contacts), and the aperture distributions tended to smaller apertures due to the increase of contact areas.  2.2 Governing equations In this study, the permeability of the rock matrix is neglected and only fracture flow is considered. The flow behavior of steady-state, incompressible fluid in rock fractures follows the Navier-Stokes equation (Zimmerman and Bodvarsson, 1996 ), which can be expressed as:(1) ρ f  ( u  · ∇ )  u  + ∇ P = μ ∇ 2  u     ρ f  ∇ · u  = 0         where ρf   (kg/m3 ) is the fluid density, u   (m/s) is the velocity vector, P  (Pa) is the reduced pressure, and μ  (Pa∙s) is the fluid dynamic viscosity. Considering the fluid flow is generally slow through deep rock fractures and the operation period of EGS when fluid flow and heat transfer are under a steady state, the steady state process of fluid flow and heat transfer through rock fractures is assumed in this study. (Liu et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021a ). The heat transfer in the granite matrix with low permeability is considered to be governed only by heat conduction, and thus the energy conservation equation for the rock matrix at steady-state can be expressed by:(2) ∇ · ( - λ r  ∇ T r  ) = 0     where λr   (W/m/K) and T r  (°C) are the heat conduction coefficient and temperature of the rock matrix, respectively. For fracture flow, the heat transfer at steady-state is governed by both heat convection and conduction. Therefore, the energy conservation equation of fluid can be defined by (Chen and Zhao, 2020 ):(3) ρ f  C p , f   u · ∇ T f  + ∇ · ( - λ f  ∇ T f  )  = 0     where Cp,f   (J/kg/°C) is the specific heat capacity of the fluid under constant pressure, λf   and Tf   are the heat conduction coefficient and temperature of the fluid, respectively.  2.3 Simulation setup The commercial finite element software COMSOL® was used to solve the relevant governing equations in Section 2.2 . The temperature-dependent properties of fluid (water in this study) were set using the default material settings in COMSOL®. The density of the granite selected in the simulations was constant (2580 kg/m3  at room temperature). The temperature-dependent properties of the thermal conductivity and the constant pressure heat capacity (Cp ,r  ) of granite were determined based on the experimental results of Zhang et al. (2017) . The temperature-dependent properties of the water and granite are shown in the forms below:(4) ρ f  = 838.47 + 1.40 T f  - 0.003 T f 2  + 3.72 × 10 - 7   T f 3      (5) μ = 1.38 - 0.02 T f  + 1.36 × 10 - 4   T f 2  - 4.64 × 10 - 7   T f 3     + 8.90 × 10 - 10   T f 4  - 9.08 × 10 - 13   T f 5  + 3.85 × 10 - 16   T f 6          (6) C p , f   = 12010.15 - 80.41 T f  + 0.31 T f 2  - 5.38 × 10 - 4   T f 3  + 3.62 × 10 - 7   T f 4      (7) λ f  = - 0.87 + 0.009 T f  - 1.58 × 10 - 5   T f 2  + 7.98 × 10 - 9   T f 3      (8) C p , r   = 448.30 + 1.26 T r      (9) λ r  = 2.75 - 9.06 × 10 - 4   T r       Initial and boundary conditions were applied to the 3D fracture models (see Fig. 2  ). For the fracture flow, the inflow boundary was set as constant volume flowrates q , and the outflow boundary was set as atmospheric pressure. The volume flowrates were gradually increased, corresponding to Reynolds number (Re = ρf  q/μw , where w  is the fracture width) from 0.01 to 10. The fracture walls were set as no-flow and no-slip boundaries. The initial temperature of the fracture-matrix system was 100 °C, and water flowed into the inlet at an injection temperature of 25 °C. A temperature boundary was set for the side of the cylindrical model, with a constant temperature of 100 °C, and an adiabatic boundary was set for the two bottom surfaces. In the numerical simulation, the fracture and rock matrix were meshed with different mesh densities. The fracture with complex void structures had much finer mesh to adapt the irregular geometries. The boundary layer mesh was utilized for the fracture walls to ensure the accuracy of the computed results (see Fig. 3  ) (Liu et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2021 ). The specific mesh numbers for the different numerical models were determined by performing a sensitivity analysis to ensure that the computed results were independent of mesh size (Huang et al., 2019 ), and the detailed results are listed in Table 2  .   3 Results and analysis 3.1 Flow behaviors in fractures with complex void structures 3.1.1 Channeling flow due to the increasing surface contacts The velocity streamlines in four fracture voids for different contact areas are shown in Fig. 4  , where U  (m/s) is the velocity magnitude. The figure shows a significant decrease in the ability of the fracture to transmit flow, with stronger flow channeling observed in the fracture voids with increasing surface contacts. For the fractures with little contact, the fracture voids are highly connected and the velocity streamlines spread through most of the fracture voids, as shown for F 0.0  in Fig. 4 (a) and Fig. 4 (b). However, the fluid flow is blocked in the complex voids with increasing surface contacts. More flow is concentrated in limited and highly conducive areas, the stronger channeling flow constituted the dominant flow channels which play a major contribution to the overall flow within fracture voids (Huang et al., 2017; Zou and Cvetkovic, 2020; Naets et al., 2022 ), as illustrated in Fig. 4 (c) and Fig. 4 (d). There are two reasons for flow channeling. The first one is the aperture field heterogeneity in well-connected fractures. The complex geometric structure of fracture voids leads to the redistribution of flow paths, where the local flow contribution is directly controlled by the local aperture (Zou and Cvetkovic, 2020 ). Comparing the flow field of F 0.0  in Fig. 4 (a) with the aperture field of F 0.0  in Fig. 1 (a) shows that the high-flow regions in fractures with well-connected aperture fields usually have high apertures. The second reason is the weak connectivity between fracture apertures. The flowing fluid is concentrated in the well-connected fracture voids, resulting in flow channeling. For the part of the void regions with large aperture and volume, it was difficult for fluid to flow into these regions from the main flow channels because of its weak connectivity to the main connected regions, as presented in the areas marked by the red dotted circle in Fig. 4 (c) and Fig. 4 (d). Fluid flow in these fracture voids is almost negligible. The normalized velocity magnitude UN   (UN   = U /Umean  , where Umean   is the mean of the velocity magnitude) was defined to evaluate the difference in velocity distributions in different flow fields. Fig. 5   displays the distribution of UN   for different inlet flow rates and contact areas. As Re  increased, the frequency distribution of UN   approached 1 and the peak value decreased (see in Fig. 5 (a) and (b)), indicating a more uniform flow velocity distribution in the fracture voids. However, the distribution range of UN   widened as the surface contact increased, as indicated by the increase in the maximum value of UN   from 3.33 for F 0.0  to 30.94 for F 0.9  at Re =  1, which shows that the distributions of flow velocity in fracture voids became more nonuniform (see Fig. 5 (c) and (d)). The increasing complexity of the fracture voids caused by the surface contact led to large differences between the flow velocity near the contact areas and that in the flow channels, as shown in Fig. 4 .  3.1.2 Effect of removing low-flow regions on flow behavior The contribution of each flow path to the overall flow was determined by extracting the flow velocity at each point in the fracture voids to quantify the effect of low-flow regions. The threshold was set at 1 % of the average flow velocity to identify and then remove the flow paths that contribute negligibly to the overall flow (low-flow regions). The flow and heat transfer simulations were conducted for the reconstructed fractures with low-flow regions removed. The simulation results indicate that the velocity streamline patterns of the reconstructed fractures in Fig. 6   are essentially the same as that of the original fractures in Fig. 4 . Removing the low-flow regions had a negligible influence on flow channeling in the fracture voids. Normalized transmissivity T /T0   (where T  is the apparent transmissivity calculated by T  = μq /wp  in the process of flow, and T0   is the intrinsic transmissivity in Darcy’s flow state) was used to reflect the ability of the fracture to allow fluid flow and the T  at Re  = 0.01 was taken as T 0  (Zimmerman et al., 2004 ). The normalized transmissivity of the reconstructed fractures closely matched with their original ones, showing less than a 2 % discrepancy in the normalized transmissivity for all fracture pairs (see Fig. 7  ). The most contacted fracture F 0.9  removed the largest amount of low-flow region, accounting for 24.66 % of the entire void areas. However, the overall flow in F 0.9  was not significantly affected by removing the large amount of fracture voids. This indicates that the internal aperture field connectivity plays a crucial role in the hydraulic properties of fractures with surface contact. For rock fractures that have increasingly complex fracture voids due to surface contact, it is crucial to carefully consider the flow contributions in local regions to accurately describe the flow behavior in realistic rock fractures. Moreover, the increase in contact areas is more likely to induce the transition from linear to nonlinear flow (Xiong et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2023 ). This indicates that the nonlinear flow behavior in rock fractures is primarily determined by the Reynolds number and the characteristics of fracture surface contact (Zhou et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2019 ). The normalized fracture resistance RN   (RN   = R /RCL  , where R  and RCL   = 12 μl /we m 3    are the fracture resistance obtained from the numerical simulation and cubic law, respectively) and the normalized maximum velocity VN   (VN   = Umax  /Umean  , where Umax   is the maximum velocity magnitude) were calculated for the reconstructed fractures to analyze the effect of surface contact and Re  on fluid flow behavior (Wang et al., 2021b ). The detailed results are listed in Table 3  . The RN   increases with increasing Re , and higher flow velocities result in larger friction loss. Moreover, the RN   increases abruptly from 1.75 (F 0.0 ) to 29.84 (F 0.9 ) at Re  = 1, indicating that the failure of classical cubic law to describe the heterogeneous flow behavior induced by surface contact. Increasing Re  promoted the uniform distribution of flow velocity and a decrease of VN  . However, VN   increases with the increasing surface contacts, such as where the VN   of F 0.9  at Re  = 1 is 29.82, which is much higher than that of the remaining three reconstructed fractures. The fluid is highly concentrated in the dominant flow channels caused by surface contact, and the flow velocity is considerably higher in the dominant flow channels than that in the other regions (see Fig. 6 ), resulting in nonuniform distributions of the flow velocity.   3.2 Heterogeneous heat transfer in fractures with complex void structures 3.2.1 Heterogeneous heat transfer in fractures induced by increasing surface contacts The water temperature distributions of the four tested fractures (without removing the low-flow regions) at Re  = 1 are shown in Fig. 8  . Stronger heterogeneous heat transfer in the fracture voids can be observed with increasing surface contacts. For fractures with no or little surface contact (such as F 0.0  with a contact ration of 0.37 %), the water temperature formed an almost symmetrical distribution from the fracture’s center to the periphery (Ma et al., 2018; He et al., 2019 ), as shown in Fig. 8 (a). As the surface contacts increases, the heat exchange between the hot walls and flowing fluid is more adequate in the fracture voids with large apertures and well connectivity, as shown in Fig. 8 (b) to (d). The heat lost by the hot walls due to convection heat transfer is much higher than the heat recharged to the fracture walls by heat conduction from the rock matrix, resulting in the heat cannot be recharged in time. The fluid temperature is lower in these fracture voids than that in the other voids after the temperature of the fracture-matrix system has stabilized, showing a stronger heterogeneity of heat transfer in the entire fracture voids, as clearly illustrated in Fig. 8 (d). The flow behaviors directly control heat transfer in rock fractures. Complex geometric structures formed by surface contact encourage the formation of channeling flow, promoting the local heat exchange between the flowing fluid and hot walls (Chen and Zhao, 2020; Gao et al., 2022 ). This clearly demonstrates that heterogeneous heat transfer largely depends on the geometric structures of fracture voids. Fig. 8  shows that the water temperatures in the low-flow regions are significantly higher than those in the other regions, contributing little to the overall heat exchange. Fig. 9   displays the water temperature distributions of four reconstructed fractures at different Re . The water temperature distributions in Fig. 9  at Re  = 1 are generally identical to that of the original fractures in Fig. 8 . Removing the low-flow regions has little influence on the local heat transfer behavior between the flowing fluid and the hot walls in the reconstructed fractures, which indicates that the stronger flow channeling induced by the complex void structures is the primary reason for the heterogeneous heat transfer. Moreover, increasing the Re  further encourages local heat exchange between the flowing fluid and hot walls, and temperature fronts move more quickly, as shown in Fig. 9  at Re  = 10.  3.2.2 Comparison of temperature distributions after removing low-flow regions The local heat transfer process at the microscopic scale can be manifested at the macroscopic scale by its effect on the water temperature distributions in rock fractures. The water temperature along the flow direction (y -axis) for the reconstructed and original fractures at Re  = 1 and Re  = 10 are plotted in Fig. 10  . The trend of water temperature variations in the reconstructed fractures are generally identical to that in the original fractures, and the water temperature increases nonlinearly along the flow direction. However, the water temperature in the reconstructed fractures along the flow direction is lower than that in the original fractures because of removing the low-flow regions with higher temperatures. Few fluctuations are observed in the water temperature of F 0.0  at Re  = 1 in Fig. 10 (a), but it fluctuates with increasing surface contacts. The water temperature of F 0.9  has high fluctuation along the flow direction, which indicates that the larger surface contact enhances the heterogeneous heat transfer, resulting in nonuniform distributions of the water temperature. In contrast, the water temperature distributions of the reconstructed and original fractures are more nonuniform along the flow direction at Re  = 10 in Fig. 10 (b), the amplitude and frequency of the fluctuation increases with surface contacts. This phenomenon is primarily attributed to the generation of eddies induced by surface contacts. The flowing fluid shows stronger nonlinear flow characteristics in the complex voids of the fracture at high Re . These eddy zones near the contact areas are separated from the main flow channels and become higher-temperature stagnation zones (Tan et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021a; Guo et al., 2022 ). The water temperature near the contact areas is significantly higher than that in the fractures’ central areas, as shown in Fig. 8 . Therefore, despite the general increase in water temperature along the flow direction, the water temperature distributions fluctuate due to local reduction caused by the different sizes of eddy zones formed at various flow regions (Tan et al., 2021 ). Removing the low-flow regions reduces the influence of eddy zones, and the water temperature distributions of the reconstructed fractures are more uniformly spread than that in the original fractures along the flow direction. Fig. 11   shows the fracture surface temperature in the radial direction (y  = 20, 40, 60 and 80 mm) along the flow direction at Re  = 1. The fracture surface temperature increases from the fractures’ central area to both sides. However, the fracture surface temperature (y  = 20 mm) shows nonlinear characteristics along the radial direction for the fractures with no or little surface contacts, as shown in Fig. 11 (a). This phenomenon is closely related to the aperture field heterogeneity in fractures with surface roughness. Fracture voids with large apertures are generally of high flow velocity, resulting in the significant changes in local temperature and a non-parabolic distributions of fracture surface temperature along the radial direction (Huang et al., 2019; He et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2021 ). The distributions of fracture surface temperature along the radial direction become more complicated with increasing surface contacts, which also indicates that surface contact is more likely to induce the heterogeneous heat transfer in fracture voids, as depicted in Fig. 11 (b) to (d). Increasing the Re  exacerbated the complexity of the fracture surface temperature variation along the radial direction, as shown in Fig. 12  . The heat exchange in the part of the fracture regions affected by heterogeneous heat transfer is more adequate than that in the other fracture regions at high Re , and more obvious nonlinear characteristics of the fracture surface temperature are observed due to the increasing temperature difference between these regions.  3.2.3 Effect of surface contacts on heat transfer coefficients The heat extraction rate Q  from a fracture can be calculated by the following equation (Zhang et al., 2017 ):(10) Q = H out   M - H in   M     where Hout   and Hin   are the water enthalpy at the fracture inlet and outlet, respectively. M  is the mass flow rate. The heat transfer coefficient is an important parameter that measures the heat transfer capacity of fractured rocks. The overall heat transfer coefficient h  can be calculated as follows (Li et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2021 ):(11) h = q w  T w  - T f        where qw   is the average heat flux of the fracture wall, and Tw   are Tf   are the mean temperatures of the fracture wall and fluid, respectively. The h  of all fractures increases gradually with the increase in Re , as shown in Fig. 13  (a). The h  shows a slight increase at low Re  (Re  < 1) and a more significant increase at high Re  (Re  > 1). The eddies induced by the complex geometric structures enhance the mixing of the higher-temperature flow near the contact areas with the lower-temperature flow in the fractures’ central areas. The further generation and expansion of irregular eddies at high Re  promote local heat exchange between the flowing fluid and the hot walls, and more heat is extracted at the same initial rock temperature (Zou et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021a ). However, the h  of the reconstructed fractures is larger than that of the original fractures, and this difference becomes more pronounced as the contact areas increases. The difference between the water temperature and the fracture surface temperature decreases because the low-flow regions removed. Therefore, the h  is larger than that of the original fractures, which contain the higher-temperature stagnation zones (see Fig. 8 ). In addition, removing the low-flow regions where there was still a small amount of heat exchange between the flowing fluid and the hot walls causes the Q  of the reconstructed fractures to be slightly lower than that of the original fractures, as shown in Fig. 13 (b). The Q  shows a significant downward trend with the increasing surface contacts. This phenomenon may be associated with the highly contacted fractures has smaller heat transfer areas and narrower voids, and the heterogeneous heat transfer prevents the flowing fluid from exchanging sufficient heat with the hot walls in the entire fracture voids. In general, the highly contacted fractures have a higher h  and a lower Q , such as the h  of reconstructed fractures (at Re  = 1) increases by 4.67 %, 55.09 % and 119.22 % with increasing contact ratio, but the Q  decreases by 3.19 %, 8.97 % and 15.07 %, respectively. The heat exchange between the hot walls and flowing fluid was enhanced by complex void structures, but the enhanced heterogeneous heat transfer and reduced heat transfer areas (the heat transfer area of F0.9   is 54.36 % smaller than that of F0.0  ) weaken the heat extraction.    4 Discussions 4.1 Heat transfer coefficient models of fractures with increasing surface contacts The heat transfer coefficient in rough rock fractures is closely related to the complex void structures and flow velocity (see Fig. 13 (a)) (Zhao, 2014 ). When water flows through rock fractures, the complexity of heat transfer mainly comes from the aperture field heterogeneity in fractures caused by surface contacts. Therefore, the hydraulic aperture (eh  ) can be used to determine the heat transfer coefficient (Chen and Zhao 2020 ). Many previous studies have demonstrated that the hydraulic aperture is highly sensitive to the aperture distribution (Walsh, 1981 ; Tan et al., 2020 ). For fractures with the same contact ratio may have different hydraulic aperture due to the aperture field heterogeneity. Considering the surface contact and aperture distribution, an improved equation is proposed by introducing aperture correction term and contact correction term (Xiong et al., 2011 ; Zhu et al., 2023 ).(12) e h  e m     3  = ( 1 - σ e m   )  ( 1 - 1 C max   C r  )      where Cmax   is the maximum contact ratio. Here Cmax   is determined by the stress-contact model proposed by Kling et al. (2018) . Based on the fractures with four contact ratios in Section 2.1 , three new numerical fracture models (with normal displacements of 0.15, 0.45, and 0.75 mm) were established. Fig. 14   indicates a good agreement between the theoretical eh   calculated by Eq. (12)  and the simulated eh   obtained from numerical simulation (Zhou et al. 2015 ). In this study, a logarithmic expression to describe the relationship between the overall heat transfer coefficient (h ) and hydraulic aperture (eh  ) is proposed as follows (Liu et al. 2021 ):(13) h = a ln ( e h  ) + b     where a  and b  two empirical/fitting parameters. The relationship between h  and eh   is well described by Eq. (13)  with R2   ≥ 0.9142 (see Fig. 15  ), where eh   was calculated by Eq.
