1 Introduction Precipitation serves as a key factor linking atmospheric and terrestrial hydrological processes, exerting a significant influence on runoff and nutrient transport at the watershed scale (Alnahit et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2017; Miralha et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2012 ). Rainfall, marked by its pronounced heterogeneity with significant temporal and spatial variations, presents a fundamental challenge in hydrological modeling (Miao et al., 2015; Sirisena et al., 2018 ). Precise and dependable precipitation data hold significant implications for simulating terrestrial water cycle processes, regulating water resources, and forecasting sudden events such as floods and pollution (Liu et al., 2017; Tan et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2022 ). Different techniques, such as Tyson polygon, inverse distance interpolation, Kriging interpolation, and water vapor transport-inverse distance interpolation (Cheng et al., 2017a,b ), have been employed to enhance the spatial and temporal resolution of precipitation data, aiming to address spatial variability. In regions with limited of meteorological stations, interpolation methods often lead to the smoothing out of local differences in precipitation, posing challenges in accurately depicting the spatial and temporal heterogeneity of precipitation within small watersheds (Falck et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2020 ). Moreover, these methods fail to consider the substantial impact of topographic elevation on the spatial distribution of precipitation, especially in mountainous watersheds (Basist et al., 1994; Um et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2024 ). The advancement of 3S (Remote Sensing, Geography Information Systems, and Global Positioning Systems) information technology has facilitated development of high-resolution precipitation products, including radar, satellite-based remote sensing, and reanalysis of precipitation data, which are increasingly adopted for their improved representation of regional spatial heterogeneity (Ge et al., 2023; Le, 2022; Li et al., 2018; Sirisena et al., 2018 ). In order to explore modeling uncertainties and identify suitable precipitation datasets for hydrologic simulations, some researchers have assessed hydrologic modeling outcomes (particularly runoff) driven by different precipitation products. Wang et al.(2020)  assessed two satellite precipitation products (TRMM and CDR) and two reanalysis-based precipitation products (CMADS and CFSR) using the SWAT model for hydrological simulations. They found that satellite-based products exhibited superior compared to reanalysis-based ones. In the wet season, TRMM precipitation demonstrated the best performance, whereas CDR precipitation showed superior performance in the dry season. Musie et al. (2019)  evaluated the impact of gridded precipitation from the CFSR reanalysis and three satellite-based precipitation datasets (CHIRPS, PERSIANN-CDR, and TRMM-3B 42V7) on runoff using the SWAT model. The study revealed that all satellite-based precipitation products exhibited a stronger correlation and lower error values compared to CFSR, although CFSR performed better in mountainous catchments. Previous studies have recognized the capability of satellite-based remote sensing and reanalysis-based meteorological data to address the limitations posed by sparse meteorological station data (Andrade et al., 2024; Awange et al., 2019; Lemma et al., 2019; Li et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2017; Musie et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020 ). Nevertheless, there exists a significant need for higher-resolution (<0.1°) input data to improve the accuracy of simulating localized hydrological responses, especially for small mountain rivers (Noorduijn et al., 2021 ). To tackle the challenge of coarser spatial resolution in satellite and reanalysis precipitation datasets, downscaling techniques are frequently utilized. As an example, the Weather Research and Forecasting model (WRF) employ dynamic downscaling algorithms to refine coarser-resolution regional reanalysis data, satellite data, meteorological station records, and radiosonde observations into finer-resolution gridded data. Utilizing numerical weather prediction models to obtain meteorological data such as precipitation and temperature has become a promising approach to enhancing hydrological simulation performance. Among the numerous mesoscale numerical weather prediction models, the WRF model is distinguished by its capacity to capture the intricate atmospheric-land surface interactions over complex terrain in localized areas, and to generate higher spatial and temporal resolution meteorological elements. Furthermore, it offers a diverse array of physical schemes that enhances the accurate prediction of meteorological variables, making it one of the most popular and advanced atmospheric models (Liu et al., 2020a,b; Patel et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2021 ). In recent years, the integration of high-resolution numerical weather prediction models with hydrological models to improve runoff simulation studies has become a common practice. This method has been extensively employed in nutrient loss assessment (Yuan et al., 2018 ), non-point source pollution (Zhang et al., 2022a,b ), and flood forecasting (Charoensuk et al., 2024; Jam-Jalloh et al., 2024 ). However, many of these approaches fail to account for the inherent limitation of hydrological models when establishing the coupling system. For example, in the construction of the WRF-SWAT coupling model, the deficiencies in the rainfall distribution mechanism were not adequately addressed. The Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT), a widely used distributed hydrological model for simulating runoff and pollutant load, typically selects the rain gauge closest to the centroid of the sub-basin in its rainfall allocation subroutine. Subsequently, it assigns the same precipitation data to all Hydrological Response Units (HRUs) within a sub-basin, neglecting the spatial heterogeneity of HRUs. Furthermore, the simulated surface runoff from all of the HRUs within a sub-basin were integrated to give the corresponding results for each sub-basin. This oversight presents challenges in accurately modeling water quantity and the associated high-pollution nutrient loads, particularly in mountainous watersheds. In areas with few rainfalls monitoring stations, multiple sub-basins may rely on the same rain gauge for rainfall input, resulting in both underestimation and overestimation of basin rainfall, amplifying the uncertainty in runoff predictions (Liu et al., 2020a,b; Shen et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2021 ). Therefore, when establishing a coupled atmosphere-hydrology model, it is of paramount importance to direct attention not only to the precision of the spatial resolution of the precipitation data, but also to the modification of the precipitation allocation mechanism during the initial HRU homogenization process. This study aims to fill this gap by proposing the utilisation of the area-weighted method to derive HRU-specific precipitation data based on the Weather Research and Forecast (WRF) model for the first time, and further improving the precipitation allocation mechanism of the SWAT model subroutine, to enhance the accuracy of the hydrological model in simulating rainfall runoff. In deriving HRU-specific precipitation data, the WRF model of the study area was constructed using the ERA-Interim reanalysis dataset and meteorological station data to generate high-resolution (3 km × 3 km) gridded precipitation data. Subsequently, the gridded precipitation data was associated with the HRUs using an area-weighted approach to obtain precipitation data that accounts for variations in soil, land use, and slope characteristics. In the precipitation allocation process, the precipitation allocation subroutine (pmeas.m) in the SWAT model was modified, replacing the previous method that solely relied on sub-basin precipitation to determine the precipitation data for the HRUs. To validate the effectiveness of the modified SWAT model, it was tested to simulate runoff from the Pengxi River basin in China. The major objectives of our study are to: (i) obtain the HRU precipitation data utilizing the WRF model and area-weighted mothed; (ii) improve the rationalization of the hydrologic processes of the SWAT model by modifying the precipitation allocation subroutine (pmeas.f); (iii) apply and test the improved coupled model to simulate the rainfall-runoff process in a typical mountainous basin within the Yangtze River basin, contrasting it with the original SWAT runoff simulation driven by meteorological stations precipitation data; and (iv) discuss the implications of neglecting the spatial heterogeneity in precipitation on runoff simulation.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The Pengxi River (PXR), with coordinates spanning from 107°56′ E to 108°54′ E and 30°50′ N to 31°42′ N, is the most prominent mountainous river along the northern shore of the Three Gorges Reservoir, covering Yunyang and Kaizhou counties in Chongqing (Fig. 1  ). Spanning a mainstream length of 182 km, the area exhibits elevations ranging from 148 m to 2549 m. The basin encompasses an area of 5172 km2  and incorporates the East River, the South River, and the Puli River. The upper reaches are characterized by rugged mountainous terrain, while low hills and flatland with gentle slopes predominantly characterize the lower reaches. Land cover is mainly classified into cropland-dominated and forest-dominated areas, collectively constituting over 85 % of the basin area. Land cover types exhibit distinct spatial heterogeneity within the basin. Forests prevail in the upper reaches of the Dong River, while croplands and grasslands are predominant along the Nan River and Puli River (Fig. 2  c and d). A subtropical continental monsoon climate chiefly influences the precipitation regime in this watershed. The long-term mean annual precipitation in the area varies from 1000 mm to 1500 mm, with the primary rainy season typically spanning from May to September, contributing around 80 % of the total annual precipitation (Shi et al., 2017 ). The average annual maximum temperature reaches 23.75℃, while the annual average temperature fluctuates within the range of 13.60 °C to 19.71 °C. Additionally, the region encounters an average annual maximum wind speed of 10.2 m/s.  2.2 Datasets 2.2.1 Digital elevation model (DEM), land use, and soil data DEM is essential for the models to extract slop, river networks and automatically identify basin boundaries (Bai et al., 2015; Du et al., 2017 ). In this study, a 30 m × 30 m resolution DEM was downloaded from the Resource and Environmental Science Data Center of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (https://www.resdc.cn/ ), for delineating the watershed and river network (Fig. 2 b). Slop characteristics, land use and soil attributes are the primary datasets needed to define hydrological response units (HRUs) in SWAT model. The classification of topographic slope follows the slope class definitions outlined by Zhang et al.(2022): undulating land (0 ∼ 20 % slope), hilly areas (20 ∼ 40 % slope), and mountainous areas (>40 % slope). Land use information with a spatial resolution of 30 m × 30 m and soil spatial data with a resolution of 1 km × 1 km spatial resolution was obtained from the National Earth System Science Data Center (https://www.geodata.cn/data/ ). The predominant land use in the watershed is Cropland, covering 52.49 % of the area. Forests account for approximately 34.11 % of the watershed area. The distribution of 13 soil types was elaborated upon displayed in the prior study conducted by Shi et al.(2017) . These datasets were clipped to the generate the SWAT model within the study area, utilizing the watershed polygons previously delineated in ArcGIS 10.2.  2.2.2 Observed meteorological, runoff, water quality, and pollution source data The study area includes 14 in-situ meteorological gauge stations: Hexing, Yujia, Qiaoting, Wushan, Nanmen, Xinghua, Nanya, Linjiang, Zhonghe, Zhengba, Wenquan, Dajin, Yanshui, and Guanmian. Daily meteorological data from 2009 to 2013 was acquired from the National Meteorological Information Centre (https://data.cma.cn/ ). The daily runoff data from the Wenquan hydrological gauge station, covering the period between 2010 and 2013, was acquired from the Hydrological Bureau of the Yangtze River Water Resources Commission and the Chongqing Municipal Institute of Environmental Sciences. Pollution source data were considered based on the first national census of pollution sources and are consistent with the literature (Shi et al., 2017 ).  2.2.3 WRF model gridded precipitation data The WRF model, jointly developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and the National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP), is a high-resolution, mesoscale numerical weather model. In the horizontal direction, the WRF model utilizes the Arakawa-C grid while employing a terrain-following coordinate system in the vertical direction. Additionally, the WRF model employs a Runge-Kutta time integration scheme to solve the non-hydrostatic Euler equations. According to Gao et al. (2017) , the WRF model exhibits exception a performance in simulating and forecasting mesoscale weather phenomena. The spatial resolution of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ERA-Interim reanalysis dataset is also taken into account. ERA-Interim data with a spatial resolution of 0.5° × 0.5° and a temporal resolution of 24 h served as the initial field and boundary conditions for the WRF model. The Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) utilized its data assimilation system to acquire ERA-Interim data, encompassing three-dimensional variables like temperature, wind patterns, geographical altitude, and relative humidity. Studies by Massari et al. (2017)  attest to the dataset’s superior performance in the Northern Hemisphere. Furthermore, it provides two-dimensional variables, including surface pressure, mean sea level pressure, surface temperature, 2 m dew point temperature, 2 m relative humidity, 10 m wind patterns, soil temperature, soil moisture, soil layer depth, snow coverage, and sea ice status. The study employed the WRF model, operating in a two-way interactive mode and employing a two-domain spatial setup (D01: 9 km × 9 km; D02: 3 km × 3 km). The inner domains, spanning the entire research area and measuring 3 km in width, as shown in Fig. 2 (a), yield a daily simulated dataset. Gridded precipitation accuracy was assessed using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and Pearson Correlation Coefficient (CC). CC indicates the degree of linear association between simulated and observed precipitation data at meteorological stations, with an optimal value being 1. Meanwhile, it quantifies the extent of discrepancies between simulated and observed precipitation data gathered at these stations, with the optimal value for RMSE being 0. The validation of the WRF simulation rainfall has been thoroughly described in a previous study (Zhang et al., 2022a,b ).   2.3 Overview of the SWAT model 2.3.1 Hydrology module SWAT is a semi-distributed hydrological watershed model developed by USDA-ARS (Arnold et al., 1998). It has found applications in diverse research areas, such as surface runoff forecasting, evapotranspiration, agricultural non-point pollution, water resource assessment, and climate change studies (Chen et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2022a,b ). The hydrology module acts as the foundational component in the SWAT model, impacting soil erosion, nutrient dynamics, and other modules. The HRU represents the smallest computational spatial unit, simulating runoff generation. This runoff is then directed to sub-basins and eventually connected through a river network to transport both runoff and nutrients to the river channel (Arnold et al., 2012; Neitsch et al., 2011 ). Precipitation stands the foremost input variable shaping the simulation of the hydrological cycle within river basins. The precision of the output is significantly dependent upon the quality of the precipitation data employed (Fu et al., 2011; Sirisena et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2023 ). The simulation of the hydrological cycle in the SWAT model relies on the water balance equation, primarily encompassing four hydrologic variables: surface runoff, evapotranspiration, soil water, and groundwater. These hydrological variables are forecasted individually for each HRU. The cumulative runoff volume of the watershed is then determined through routing (Eq. (1) ).(1) S W t  = S W 0  + ∑ i = 1  t  R day   - Q surf   - E a  - w seep   - Q gw           where SWt   represents the final soil water content (mm), SW0   denotes the initial soil water content (mm), t  signifies the time (days), Rday   stands for the amount of precipitation on the day i  (mm), Qsurf   indicates the amount of surface runoff on the day i  (mm), Ea   represents the amount of evapotranspiration on the day i  (mm), wseep   reflects the amount of percolation and bypass flow exiting the soil profile bottom on the day i  (mm), and Qgw   denotes the amount of return flow on the day i  (mm). Surface runoff arises when the rate of water application to the ground surface surpasses the rate of infiltration. This runoff is estimated utilising either the SCS-CN method or the Green & Ampt infiltration method. Among these, the SCS-CN method necessitates solely daily precipitation and temperature data to simulate daily runoff. This method is employed in various versions of SWAT to compute streamflow. In contrast to the SCS-CN method, the Green & Ampt infiltration method simulates runoff using hourly meteorological data. However, its application is constrained by the scarcity of input data, particularly at large catchment scales. Therefore, the SCS-CN method was selected for used in this study. Surface runoff is calculated as follows (Eq. (2) ).(2) Q suf   = ( R day   - 0.2 · S )  2  R day   + 0.8 · S       where S  represents the retention parameter (mm), which varies spatially due to alterations in soils, land use, management, and slope and temporally due to changes in soil water content. The theory discussed above introduces inherent uncertainties in simulating the runoff process. Primarily, the distribution of meteorological data depends solely on the distance between the sub-basin centroid and meteorological points, neglecting the substantial impact of complex terrain on catchment meteorological conditions. Precisely determining meteorological data for a sub-basin often requires a weighted integration of data from multiple surrounding meteorological stations. The current SWAT methodology overlooks variations in meteorological conditions, particularly precipitation and temperature, at different altitudes within the same latitude. Secondly, assuming all HRUs within a sub-basin share identical precipitation data overlooks the significant spatial heterogeneity of precipitation, as highlighted by previous research (Zhao et al., 2022 ). Certain areas may experience sunny conditions, while others may encounter rainfall, leading to notable disparities in local precipitation patterns. As a result, significant uncertainty exists in simulating runoff.  2.3.2 Modification of the precipitation module Given the limitations indicated earlier, simulating surface runoff requires high-resolution, and high-density meteorological data. This includes precise and detailed precipitation information rather than relying exclusively on existing allocation methods. Consequently, modifications were made to the program governing the precipitation inputs into the SWAT model. Furthermore, other meteorological variables like temperature, wind speed, relative humidity, and solar radiation were collected from the original SWAT model. This enabled the reading and distribution of precipitation data to the relevant sub-watershed subroutine when implementing the modified model. In the following sections, detailed method and enhancements related to the acquisition of high-precision, high-density precipitation data, along with the model refinements, were elucidated. 2.3.2.1 Mapping grid precipitation into HRUs The precipitation data obtained from the WRF model features a spatial resolution of 3 km × 3 km. Enhancing the model, requires the provision of precise precipitation data to each HRU by establishing a correlation between the grid precipitation from the WRF model and HRU. This is crucial as HRU serves as the smallest computational spatial unit for hydrological simulation. Precipitation for each HRU was estimated by applying a weighted factor derived from the overlapping area between the grid precipitation data and the irregular polygons defining the HRUs in the SWAT model (Fig. 3  ). To enhance the accuracyof this estimation, the area size was considered. The calculation for HRU precipitation was conducted as follows (Eq. (3) ):(3) PR E  hru   = ∑  i = 1  n    ( P R E  g r i d _ i   × A  o v e r l a p _ i   )   A  hru         where PREhru   represents the daily precipitation of the HRU (mm); PREgrid_i   denotes the precipitation of the grid where the i -th subblock of the HRU is located (mm); Aoverlap_i   stands for the area of the region occupied by the i -th subblock of the HRU (m2 ); and n  represents the number of subblocks defined by the HRU.  2.3.2.2 Modification of the precipitation module in the SWAT model In this study, modifications were made to the source code of the precipitation data assignment module (pmeas.f) in the SWAT model. Rather than relying on the originally assigned precipitation data to determine the precipitation for all HRUs, it now directly calculates the simulation of subsequent hydrological processes using the PREhru   rainfall data estimated in section 2.3.2.1. The technical approach of this modified coupled model is illustrated in Fig. 4  .   2.3.3 Calibration and validation of modified model In this study, a stepwise calibration procedure was adopted for the simulated runoff in the modified model. Calibration of runoff was conducted for 2010–2011, and validation was performed for 2012–2013. The time series utilized to calibrate and validate of the modified model remained consistent with those of the original model, which relied on precipitation data from in-situ meteorological stations, thereby guaranteeing the comparability of the results. The modified SWAT model was calibrated based on our previous studies (Chen et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2017a,b; Shi et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022a,b ), keeping calibration parameters consistent with earlier investigations to minimize discrepancies in model performance resulting from calibration variations. Ten hydrological parameters were identified for initial calibration based on the SWAT-CUP manual and previous studies (Chen et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2017a,b; Shi et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022a,b ). The range of values for each parameter was defined to be within the acceptable range of the truthfulness and reliability during the rate validation process. In this study, streamflow prediction calibration and validation analysis were conducted using the Sufi-2 algorithm (Abbaspour et al., 2015 ). The model's performance was evaluated using the Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), Coefficient of Determination (R2 ), and percent bias (PBIAS) as indicated in Eqs. The R2  value falls between 0 and 1, with lower values indicating more significant errors, and R2  values exceeding 0.5 are considered acceptable. NSE  can range from −∞ to 1, with values closer to 1 indicating a more reliable agreement between simulated and observed data. PBIAS  quantifies the percentage bias of simulated values relative to observed ones, with a perfect match at 0. These interpretations are based on earlier reported studies (Abbaspour et al., 2015; Arnold et al., 2012; Moriasi et al., 2015; Narsimlu et al., 2015 ). After completing the initial parameterization, we ran the SWAT model with observed rainfall data, and then calibrated the runoff result against measured runoff to acquire optimized parameters for the modified model. For detailed calibration and validation of the original model using precipitation data from in-situ meteorological stations, please refer to Chen et al. (2019)  and Shi et al. (2017) .    3 Results 3.1 Evaluation of PREhru   products To mitigate potential errors originating from the disparity in the difference between PREhru   precipitation data and rainfall station data during the quantitative assessment of the PREhru   precipitation products (Miao et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2016 ), we employed the inverse distance weighting method (IDW). This method facilitated the interpolation of the PREhru   rainfall data derived from the WRF simulation results to the rainfall stations. This allowed us to evaluate the quality of PREhru   products across two-time scales, daily and monthly, in the PXR basin spanning from 2009 to 2013. The data of four rainfall stations (Guanmian, Wenquan, Linjiang and Yujia) were selected from the 14 rainfall stations, following the principle of ensuring coverage across the entire basin. These stations were selected to compare the two rainfall products, PREhru   and PREsta   (based on meteorological gauge stations), in terms of their temporal and spatial dimensions within the PXR basin, as depicted in Figs. 5 and 6   . Fig. 5  illustrated that the trends of the two precipitation products remained consistent on a daily scale, with an R2  ranging from 0.63 to 0.92 for the PREhru   and PREsta   data. The maximum daily precipitation recorded was 151.7 mm for PREhru   and 165.0 mm for the PREsta  , respectively. To better visualize the differences in monthly rainfall intensity and pattern between the two precipitation products, we divided the monthly precipitation data into two hydrological periods and then evaluated the rainfall dataset for each hydrological period. In the PXR Basin, the high flow period spans from May to September, whereas the low flow period extends from October to April of the following year. The comparison of the monthly precipitation simulation results (Fig. 6 ) highlights substantial seasonal variation in rainfall. Precipitation levels from May to September considerably surpass those from April to December, reaching a peak in July with an average precipitation of approximately 265.01 mm. The estimated precipitation of PREhru   products differs from that of PREsta  , across different hydrological periods. This variance primarily arises from the fact that the precipitation data from the WRF grid captures spatial differences, which become more pronounced when correlated with HRUs. Furthermore, we conducted a spatial comparison between PREhru   and PREsta   rainfall, focusing on mean annual rainfall, as shown in Fig. 7  . The mean annual surface rainfall centers and the distribution zones of rainfall magnitude in PREhru   closely resemble those of PREsta   rainfall. Their spatial distribution generally exhibits a decreasing trend from northeast to southwest, with areas of higher precipitation primarily situated in the northeast and along the southern edge of the basin. The annual average rainfall for PREhru   and PREsta   was recorded at 1329.98 mm and 1211.96 mm, respectively. Notably, the average precipitation order across the three major tributary areas is East River > South River > PuLi River. The spatial heterogeneity of precipitation can be attributed to several factors. One significant factor is the northeastern and southern edges of the watersheds, which primarily consist of forested and grasslands at higher elevations. These features act as barriers to moist airflow, causing it to ascend. As the air rises, it cools down, leading to condensation and ultimately precipitation formation. This phenomenon highlights the influence of high elevation on altering the local microclimate (Arx et al., 2012 ). Moreover, it is noted that the spatial heterogeneity of PREhru   significantly surpasses that of PREsta  . This suggests that the PREhru   was more adept at capturing the spatial variations in precipitation within mountainous watersheds, as emphasized by (Chen et al., 2015 ).  3.2 Evaluation of simulated runoff To address the issue of discrepancies in simulation results arising from inconsistent parameters, the runoff simulation parameters of the SWAT model remained unchanged before and after the improvement. However, it was observed that the sensitivity of runoff of these parameters varied to some extent after the modification of the SWAT, as indicated in Table 1  . Despite these changes, the best fitting parameters fall within an acceptable range when the objective function values of the improved SWAT model attain their optimal values. The runoff curves simulated using PREhru   and PREsta   precipitation data generally exhibit consistency with the observed runoff curves on a daily scale (Fig. 8  ). This suggests that the modified SWAT model is capable of reasonably replicating the observed runoff patterns. During both calibration and validation periods, the R2   values for the SWAT simulated runoff were 0.62 and 0.70, respectively. Additionally, the NSE  values were 0.60 and 0.63 for the calibration and validation periods, respectively. The R2   values of the modified SWAT gradually increased to 0.88 and 0.93, while the NSE  values rose to 0.86 and 0.90, respectively. Referring to the performance measures (PMs) and corresponding performance evaluation criteria (PEC) outlined by Moriasi et al.(2015) , the high R2  values (0.75 < R2  ≤ 0.85) and high NSE values (0.70 ≤ R2  ≤ 0.80) indicate a “good” correlation between daily observed and simulated flows on a watershed scale (Moriasi et al., 2015; Paul and Negahban-Azar, 2018 ). The objective function results, including R2  and NSE, indicated that the performance of the modified SWAT model was deemed good, Moreover, it surpasses the original SWAT model in its capacity to simulate runoff during both calibration and validation periods. Compared to the original SWAT model, the improved model depicts a more gradual runoff change process during the non-rainy season, avoiding abrupt rises and falls. Additionally, it has exhibited improved performance in capturing the peak runoff events during the flood season. This improvement can be attributed to the utilisation of the PREhru   data derived from high-resolution grid precipitation, which enables a better representation of spatial and temporal precipitation heterogeneity. Moreover, the modified model helps mitigate the overestimation or underestimation of rainfall within individual hydrological response units (Liu et al., 2017 ).  3.3 Changes in runoff across various hydrological periods Combined with the statistical chart and percentage bias of multi-year monthly average runoff during the study period (Fig. 9  ) The mean value of simulated runoff from PREhru   closely aligns with the measured value from the hydrological station. During the dry season spanning from October to April of the subsequent year, the simulated runoff values produced by PREhru   exhibited significant discrepancies when compared to the actual measured runoff values, either underestimating or overestimating the true values. During the wet season from May to September, the discrepancy between the simulated runoff values of PREhru   and the measured flow values was significantly smaller compared to the disparity between the simulated runoff values and the measured runoff values obtained from precipitation data collected at rainfall gauge stations. Additionally, the flow simulated by PREsta   was notably underestimated, with a PBIAS ranging from 21.47 % to 34.46 %. This underestimation can be attributed to the limited number of rainfall stations, which hinders the accurate representation of spatial variations in precipitation. Furthermore, the original model exhibits shortcomings in its precipitation allocation mechanism, including issues with rainfall equalization and multi-purpose allocation of one station (Shen et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2021 ). The PBIAS of the flow value simulated by PREhru   ranges from −19.20 % to −5.28 %, Compared with the runoff simulation results of PREsta  , the precipitation data from PREhru   demonstrated remarkable performance in simulating mountain rivers, particularly in regions characterized by sparse rainfall stations and mountainous terrain.   4 Discussion 4.1 Changes in precipitation within the watershed This study generated higher spatial distribution characteristics of precipitation data (PREhru  ) in the PXR Basin, as depicted in Fig. 7 . The results revealed a spatial distribution pattern of precipitation characterized by “higher mountains, more rain”, which is typical in mountainous regions of southwest China (Zhang et al., 2024 ). Precipitation in the northeast alpine region of the PXR Basin exhibited higher levels compared to the southwest low-altitude area. The spatial patterns of the two precipitation products varied during different periods, with consistent trends observed, albeit to varying degrees. Furthermore, HRU-based precipitation can capture precipitation differences between the left and right banks at the sub-basin scale, thereby offering a more precise depiction of precipitation within the basin. The spatial distribution and variation characteristics of precipitation were found to be closely associated with regional topography and climate zones (Bai et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024 ). In the simulation of runoff on the basin scale, particularly in mountainous watersheds, relying completely on sparse meteorological stations for meteorological data input may fail to capture the spatial variation of precipitation adequately. Therefore, enhancing the quality of precipitation data, which directly impacts the accuracy of simulating the entire hydrological cycle, is crucial for reducing simulation errors and uncertainty associated with runoff.  4.2 Advantages of the modified over the original SWAT model The advantage of the modified SWAT model lies in its capacity to replicate hydrological processes precisely at the basin scale. Utilising the high-resolution precipitation data from the WRF model, the modified SWAT model can more closely replicate processes such as rainfall infiltration and runoff generation. This integration comprehensively takes into account the influence of meteorological factors on hydrological processes, thereby improving the accuracy and reliability of hydrological simulations. The HRUs serve as the smallest spatial computing unit for modeling hydrological cycle processes. Ensuring precise precipitation record for each HRU by correlating fine resolution and high-density precipitation data with individual HRU is essential for improving model accuracy. Moreover, the modified model also lightly improved the accuracy of runoff simulation. While both the modified and the original SWAT models achieved “good” runoff simulation performance, they employ two different set of model parameters in the runoff determination process. Indeed, one of the drawbacks of inverse modeling is the occurrence of “same parameter, different effect” and “different parameter, same effect” scenarios (Ruddell et al., 2019 ). Various studies have investigated the hydrological evaluation of gridded precipitation estimation at high spatial resolutions across different watersheds (Musie et al., 2019; Tong et al., 2014; Tuo et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2018 ). Nevertheless, few studies comprehensively assess both the statistical and hydrological performance of gridded precipitation datasets concurrently. In mountainous watersheds characterized by intricate topography, employing high-resolution precipitation products to drive land-surface hydrological models can effectively capture localized microclimatic variations and enhance the accuracy of hydrological simulations (Ward et al., 2011 ).  4.3 Limitations and outlook In this study, despite the significant enhancement in SWAT model performance through coupling with the WRF-based meteorological dataset, two limitations warrant attention. Firstly, the precipitation data from the WRF model are generated at a daily output step, while research suggests that hourly rainfall data outperforms daily rainfall data in simulating peak flow using the SWAT model (Li et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020 ). Given that mountain flood events are often sudden and short, relying exclusively on daily precipitation data presents challenges in accurately capturing the regional precipitation patterns. Secondly, the coupled model has not yet been applied in plains watersheds and other mountainous regions due to the lack of pollution sources data, rainfall, and hydrologic validation data. We highlight the significance of precipitation data that accurately represent terrestrial topography and spatial heterogeneity of HRU for hydrological models, particularly in predicting runoff output in regions with complex terrain and during short-duration extreme precipitation events. Future research endeavors should aim to enhance both the spatiotemporal resolution of precipitation data and the output step size of hydrological models. This improvement will facilitate the investigation of sediment load and nutrient pollution transfer and transformation processes in large-scale watersheds under varied rainfall runoff conditions (Terink et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2020 ), offering promising directions for future investigations. Finally, applying he modified coupled model to other mountain watersheds is an important next step. Additionally, extending the application of the coupled model to other mountain watersheds represents an essential next phase.   5 Conclusion In this study, the precipitation of each HRU was estimated by calculating the overlapping region’s size using the high spatial resolution precipitation from the Weather Research and Forecast (WRF) model. Additionally, the precipitation distribution subroutine of the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) model was modified to accommodate this approach. Comparing the modified SWAT model with the original version in the Pengxi River (PXR) basin revealed significant improvements in simulating runoff. Notably, the modified coupled model outperformed its predecessor by providing more accurate representations of runoff dynamics. Additionally, this study revealed that the original SWAT model consistently underestimated precipitation levels across various regions when contrasted with the modified coupled version, highlighting the latter’s ability to capture a broader range of precipitation patterns. An analysis of the relationship between precipitation and simulated runoff by both models revealed shortcomings in the original model’s representation of intermediate hydrological cycle process variables. This shortcoming highlights the importance of refining process-based hydrological models to accurately capture the complex interactions between precipitation, runoff, and other hydrological processes. Moving forward, the configuration of such models should prioritize the reliability of precipitation simulations to mitigate the need for excessive calibration parameters and minimize the risk of over-parameterization, which may compromise the accuracy of runoff simulations at the expense of other hydrological processes. Furthermore, the precipitation module and integration algorithms developed to incorporate WRF data into HRUs offer broader applicability beyond the PXR basin. These advancements can be adapted to support water resources planning and management in various watersheds, offering enhanced predictive capabilities and facilitating informed decision-making processes.
1 Introduction Mass diffusion is an important transport mechanism involved in various processes, either natural or industrial. In natural environments, the diffusion of contaminants to and from low-permeability zones is a key issue for safety and remediation operations. In the case of underground nuclear waste storage, diffusion is a key mechanism to help reducing the migration of radionuclides and toxic chemicals around the geological repository (Delay et al., 2007 ). For CO2  geological storage, diffusion may play a significant role too: the injected CO2  flows through the preferential flow-paths of high hydraulic conductivity, in contact with the host rock matrix of lower permeability offering a large volume for storing dissolved CO2 . Diffusion is then an important process in surrounding geological levels especially in the low permeability like as the non-conductive porosity and the cap rock. This transport mechanism could be encountered in soils that are also characterized by variable chemical and high concentration gradients and hydraulic heterogeneities due to the presence of roots, microorganisms, interactions with the soil surface (Staunton, 2008 ). Industrial applications are also concerned by diffusion processes for separation purposes like filtration, sieving, or selective extraction operations. In the particular case of CO2  storage in deep saline aquifers, understanding Fickian mass diffusion of electrolytic aqueous solutions requires a detailed description of the physicochemical and electrochemical solute–solute and solute-water interactions with charged phase interfaces. The concentration-driven mass transfer rate of salt mixtures is described by the specific diffusion coefficients of the different species. Additionally, these coefficients depend on the thermodynamic conditions (temperature, pressure, composition of the mixtures). Due to the conservation of the neutrality of the electric charge, the species associate and the diffusive behavior resembles that of molecules. As a result, the experimental measurements of the diffusion coefficients of salts provide an effective or apparent value, equivalent to that of a neutral molecule. The link with the diffusion coefficients of species, depending on thermodynamic conditions, is not trivial. This motivated us to perform tentative original measurements of the diffusion coefficients of a limited number of salts in order to get a better understanding of the link between apparent measurements and species diffusion coefficients. The comparison between the two has been obtained by computing the species diffusion coefficients by numerical simulations by means of the PHREEQ-C solver, on one side, and, on the other side, by experimentally measuring the effective mass diffusion coefficients by means of the optical technique of shadowgraphy. PHREEQC is a geochemical software commonly used for speciation, batch-reaction, one-dimensional transport, and inverse geochemical calculations (Appelo, 2017; Muniruzzaman and Rolle, 2019; Parkhurst and Appelo, 2013 ). For the experiments we used dynamic shadowgraphy, a light scattering technique in the near field which allows us to study the non-equilibrium density fluctuations during free-diffusion experiments, thus measuring the mass diffusion coefficients of the salts, as done in a number of previous studies (Bataller et al., 2016; Croccolo et al., 2013, 2012; Giraudet et al., 2014; Lizarraga et al., 2017, 2016; Ndjaka et al., 2022 ). In section 2 , we provide the theoretical bases of the diffusion of ionic species in a solution. We introduce PHREEQC and carry out free-diffusion simulations of the main salts present in deep aquifers, sodium chloride NaCl   , calcium chloride Ca Cl  2     and sodium sulfate Na  2  SO  4    . The values of the concentration profiles simulated before allow us to develop an improved method for analyzing the shadowgraph data. In section 3  we describe the experimental procedure. In section 4  we discuss the results. Finally, in section 5  we provide concluding remarks and some perspectives.  2 Theoretical framework 2.1 Modelling of multicomponent ionic transport in water In aqueous electrolyte systems, charge‐induced ion‐ion interactions lead to the electrostatic coupling of ionic fluxes that results in a coordinated movement of charged species to maintain local charge balance. The relevance of these Coulomb effects has been explored in details under diffusion-dominated and macroscopic advection-dominated conservative and reactive transport conditions, which led to the development of multicomponent diffusion theories and the concept of multicomponent ionic dispersion (Appelo and Wersin, 2007; Muniruzzaman and Rolle, 2019 ). Similar consideration would apply to the diffusion of Ca Cl  2    .  2.2 PHREEQC software PHREEQC is a geochemical software for speciation, batch-reaction, one-dimensional transport, and inverse geochemical calculations (Appelo, 2017; Muniruzzaman and Rolle, 2019; Parkhurst and Appelo, 2013 ). Based on the numerical resolution of the full Nernst-Planck equation, it allows to include external electric fields effects, the medium porosity as well as temperature and concentration dependencies on species diffusion coefficients. The latter are correction factors for aqueous concentrations to account for the non-ideal behaviour of solutes in real solutions. PHREEQC uses specific databases of thermodynamic and physicochemical properties of solutes, minerals and gases. These databases include, in particular, information about the activity coefficient model used consistently with the tabulated thermodynamic data of the chemical compounds. Thus, their domain of validity is limited by that of the associated activity coefficient model. These databases were established according to either ion-association equations (Davies, B-dot, Debye-Hückel (Debye and Hückel, 1923 ), extended Debye-Hückel equations) or specific ion-interaction equations (Pitzer equations (Pitzer, 1991 )). More specifically, the diffusion coefficient concentration-dependence is calculated with Kohlrausch's law, according to the formulation proposed by Appelo (Appelo, 2017 ):(10) D aq , i   = D aq , T , i  0  e x p - a 1 i   A z i    I s    1 + κ a          Where D aq , T , i  0    is the diffusion coefficient at infinite dilution at temperature T  , a 1 i     is a coefficient, A   is the Debye-Hückel parameter (0.51 ( m o l / dm  3  )  - 0.5      at 25 °  C   ), I s    is the ionic strength and κ a    is(11) κ a = κ I s   a 2 i   1 + I s  0.75          With a 2 i     a second coefficient and κ is the Debye length, defined by: κ = 1 F  ε w  R T  2000 I s       , where ε w    is the dielectric permittivity of water (6.94·1010 F/m at 25 °C). The exponential term dampens the temperature dependence of the diffusion coefficient, which is smaller than the variation of viscosity with temperature. Note that no physical meaning was given by the author to the a 1 , i    , a 2 , i     and d i    coefficients. The coefficients a 1 i    , a 2 i     and d i    were optimized by Appelo to cover a wide range of applications (Appelo, 2017 ). Note that when the derivative term of the activity coefficients is negligible, equations (14)  reduce to the Nernst equation in the case of homogeneous diffusion. From Eqs. (10) to (12)  it is possible to calculate the species diffusion coefficients at any concentration and temperature. Given the high concentrations of solutes, up to 6 mol·kg−1 , the activity coefficients are calculated according to the Pitzer equations (Pitzer, 1991 ) associated with reliable sets of specific interaction parameters, namely (Lach et al., 2017 ) for NaCl   , (Lach et al., 2016 ) for Na  2  SO  4    , and (Lassin and André, 2023 ) for Ca Cl  2    . In Fig. 1   we report the apparent diffusion coefficient calculations and the measured values from the literature for the three salts as a function of the concentration at 25 °C and atmospheric pressure. For NaCl    (Fig. 1 a), the measurements of Vitagliano and Lyons date from the 1950 s and were carried out by Gouy interferometry (Hall et al., 1953; Lyons and Riley, 1954 ). The measurements of Rard and Miller were made in the late 1970s by Rayleigh interferometry (Rard and Miller, 1979a ). The measurement of Guo et al. has been performed in the late 1990s by phase shifting interferometer (Guo et al., 1999 ). These three series of measurements are in very good agreement and show a non-ideal behaviour of the diffusion coefficient of NaCl    in water as a function of concentration. More recently, Torres et al. (Torres et al., 2012 ) and Nimdeo et al. (Nimdeo et al., 2014 ) have made measurements that confirm the non-ideal behaviour, but disagree with the initial measurements, mainly at higher concentrations. The dashed black line in Fig. 1 a represents the calculations of the apparent diffusion coefficient obtained with PHREEQC’s Appelo’s values for the ionic strength-dependence coefficients. The obtained values describe well the steep decrease of the diffusion coefficient at very low concentrations less than 0.1 mol·L-1 , but not at medium and high concentrations. They also do not describe the second extremum, even qualitatively. To improve the fit between experimental data and calculated values, the coefficients a 1 , Na  +     , a 2 , Na  +     , a 1 , Cl  -      and a 2 , Cl  -      have been optimized by minimizing the cost function based on the deviations between the experimental and the calculated diffusion coefficients at every concentration. However, it was found that the a 1 , i     and a 2 , i     coefficients influence the diffusion coefficient computed from the combination of Eqs (10) , (11)  and (14a)  mostly at high concentrations (above c.a. 1 mol·L-1 ). Therefore, in the optimization process, the weight set to diffusion coefficient data was greater at the highest concentrations than at lower concentrations. As a result, a set of a 1 , i     and a 2 , i     coefficients was obtained (Table 1 ) that significantly improves the calculated diffusion coefficients of NaCl    over the whole range of concentration, and more specifically above the concentration of 2 mol·L-1 . These calculations are represented by the solid red line in Fig. 1 a. For CaC l 2    , optical measurements of the mass diffusion coefficient (Fig. 1 b) were made first by Gouy interferometry (Hall et al., 1953; Lyons and Riley, 1954 ). They were confirmed by Rayleigh interferometry in the late 1970s by Rard and Miller (1979a) . Again, the dashed black line in Fig. 1 b represents the apparent diffusion of CaC l 2     calculated using the a 1    and a 2    coefficients for C a  2 +      and C l  -     proposed by (Appelo, 2017 ). Clearly, the calculations based on these values rapidly deviate dramatically from the experimental data, above 0.5 mol·kg−1 , which made it necessary optimizing new a 1 , Ca  2 +       and a 2 , Ca  2 +       coefficients while keeping the a 1 , Cl  -      and a 2 , Cl  -      coefficient previously optimized, for consistency. The same optimization procedure as described above was applied. The results are represented by the red full line in Fig. 1 b, illustrating the improvement obtained. Note that experimental data above 4 mol·kg−1  of CaC l 2     where not considered because of the appearance of the CaC l  +     aqueous species (Lassin and André, 2023 ), what makes Eq. (14c)  inapplicable above this concentration. The N a 2  S O 4     diffusion coefficient was measured by Rayleigh interferometry (Rard and Miller, 1979b ) in the entire concentration range (Fig. 1 c). More recent measurements at high (Annunziata et al., 2000; Fu et al., 2001 ) and low concentrations (Rard, 2021 ) have confirmed the first measurements. The most recent measurements have benefited from computerized image acquisition and processing means. As above, the dashed black line in Fig. 1 c represents the apparent diffusion of N a 2  S O 4     calculated using the a 1    and a 2    coefficients for N a  +     and S O 4  2 -      proposed by (Appelo, 2017 ). The decreasing trend of the apparent diffusion coefficient is correctly described, but the match with experimental data could be improved by optimizing the a 1    and a 2    coefficients for S O 4  2 -     , while keeping fixed the values of the a 1    and a 2    coefficients for N a  +     obtained for NaCl   . The red full line in Fig. 1 c represents the results of this new optimization. In summary, the theoretical framework developed by (Appelo, 2017 ) for considering multicomponent diffusion in water, and implemented in the PHREEQC geochemical software, can help describing aqueous electrolyte diffusion measurements in concentrated simple brines, up to several mol·kg−1 . However, Appelo (Appelo, 2017 ) optimized the initial values of the coefficients that describe the ionic strength-dependence of the species self-diffusion coefficient on an aqueous solutions specific conductance database. These values had to be corrected in the present work to reproduce the apparent diffusion coefficients reference experimental data. They are given in Table 1 . In summary, the values were decreased for cations and increased for anions, compared to the values proposed by Appelo. However, our optimized values do not degrade significantly the description of the specific conductance, as shown in the appendix . Besides, when aqueous complexation reactions occur, interpreting the diffusion processes based on a single apparent diffusion coefficient may not be relevant anymore since it is necessary to integrate explicitly the additional charged species (aqueous complex).  2.4 Numerical simulations A typical free-diffusion experiment consists in the superposition of two horizontal layers of two different and miscible mixtures stable in the gravity field (Fig. 2  ). Here, we focus on the free-diffusion of two mixtures of the same salt solution, but at two different concentrations (Fig. 2 ). The two superimposed layers are thus ideally separated by an initially sharp, horizontal interface. As soon as the fluids are put in contact, a diffusive flow begins to transport mass across the interface so that the concentration close to the boundary begins to change. As time goes by, the thickness of the diffusing region grows progressively. For experiments performed in the gravity field, the densest layer is usually placed at the bottom of the diffusion cell in order to avoid any initial convective instability. Mass flux can be considered unidirectional in the vertical direction (z). For binary mixtures (a solute or molecule in a solvent) the free-diffusion process is well understood, nowadays (Vailati and Giglio, 1998 ). The concentration at the top (z = h   ) and the bottom (z = 0   ) of the sample is assumed to remain constant for a long time (Dirichlet condition). This assumption is true in the case of unbounded diffusion, where two infinitely thick layers of binary fluids are allowed to diffuse into each other. In practice the assumption is valid only during a given time interval after the beginning of the diffusion process. This time is called characteristic diffusive time τ d    and depends on the vertical size of the vessel and on the value of the mixture mass diffusion coefficient. As soon as the concentration at the boundaries begins to change, the features of the macroscopic diffusion process cease to depend on the diffusion coefficient only, and are influenced by the height of the vessel, too. To obtain quantitative information about the concentration profile c ( z , t )    of the solute and the gradient ∂ c / ∂ z z , t      we need to formalise the problem using the one-dimensional continuity equation for concentration since, due to the symmetry of the problem, ∂ / ∂ x = 0    and ∂ / ∂ y = 0   :(15) ∂ c  ∂ t   = - ∂ J z   ∂ z       In a 1D transport simulation with PHREEQC, the percolation column is discretized in a number of cells, which are considered at each time step as perfect homogeneous batch reactors. With such a principle, each cell is considered as a closed system, so that the mass is conserved, the aqueous solutions are electrically neutral and the chemical reactions and the solutions are systematically at thermodynamic equilibrium. These assumptions are considered for applying the mass action law and calculate the activity-concentration relationship over space and time for all chemical species involved in a specified cell (in PHREEQC the resolution is done by considering each independent species and their mutual influence). Then flow and transport of species are performed by transferring part of the aqueous solution of one cell to the next according to mixing factors that are defined by the flow and/or the diffusion rates of the system. To solve the transport process through mesh cells, the initial and boundary conditions must be defined. In our case studies sketched in Fig. 2 , initial concentrations are defined by a vertical step function:(16) c z , t 0    = c bottom    z ∈ ( 0 , a )    c top     z ∈ ( a , h )            where t 0  = 0    is the initial time, a   is the vertical position of the initial boundary between the two layers and h   is the total thickness of the two superimposed layers (Fig. 2 ). To match our experimental setup (see section 3 ) we took a = h / 2    and h = 10 m m   . The liquid column, composed of the two layers, was divided into 100 cells, the thickness of each being therefore Δ z = 0.1 m m   . The time step between two elementary calculation loops has been fixed to δ t = Δ z  2  / 3 D a     with D a    calculated at infinite dilution. To complete the equation setting, the boundary conditions must be specified. In our experimental setup, the walls of the vessel are impermeable to mass, which results in the condition:(17) ∂ c  ∂ z   = 0   z = 0 , z = h      The characteristic diffusive times were estimated with the formula τ d  = a  2  / D a    , which gives an estimation of the time to diffuse through half of the column taking D a    equal to the literature value at the mean concentration of the experiment. The maximum time for a simulation has been fixed to τ max   = 4 τ  d    , which gives an estimation of the time to diffuse through the entire column. The number of calculated time steps is thus set to N = τ max   / δ t   . In Table 2   we report the configurations that we have studied in this work, both experimentally and numerically. c   is the mean of the molar concentration of the salt of the two layers, which corresponds to the equilibrium concentration at the end of the diffusion process. Δ c    is the difference of the molar concentration of the two initial layers. The temperature of the isothermal column was set at T = 25 °  C   . Experiments (see section 3 ) and simulations were performed at atmospheric pressure. In Fig. 3   we show the time evolution of the simulated concentration profiles plotted as a function of the vertical position in the cell for the experiment #1. For experiments #2 and 4 the results obtained are given in Fig. B  of the appendix. For the three salts, we can see in Fig. 3 , Ba and Bb  (the latter two in the Appendix) that the anions (triangles) evolve as fast as the cations (circles). This result had already been anticipated at the end of paragraph 2.1. and we retrieve the fact that the diffusive behavior of salts is equivalent to that of a neutral molecular species with an apparent diffusion coefficient given by Eq. (14) . Knowing the vertical concentration profile as a function of time allows us to calculate the value of the concentration gradient at any point along the fluid column at any time. As we will see later, the value of the concentration gradient represents a fundamental quantity for the analysis of experimental data.  2.5 Concentration non-equilibrium fluctuations In a binary mixture at equilibrium, there are spontaneous local temperature fluctuations δ T    and concentration fluctuations δ c    that represent small perturbations of the macroscopic spatial distribution of the temperature and concentration macroscopic fields. If the equilibrium state is perturbed by applying e.g. a concentration gradient, the fluctuations intensity will be modified significantly. These non-equilibrium fluctuations (NEFs) are orders of magnitude more intense than those occurring at equilibrium and they have been described theoretically and observed experimentally (Brogioli and Vailati, 2000; Croccolo et al., 2016; Vailati and Giglio, 1998 ). Such concentration NEFs (c-NEFs) originate from stochastic fluctuations in the velocity field that delocalise fluid volumes into layers of different concentration. The intensity enhancement is then induced by the coupling between the velocity fluctuations and the existing concentration gradient. The c-NEFs can provide an interpretation of the mass flow associated with the mass diffusion process (Brogioli and Vailati, 2000, 2017 ). It has been observed experimentally and predicted theoretically that gravity strongly influences NEFs, damping them beyond a certain characteristic scale (Croccolo et al., 2006a; Vailati and Giglio, 1997 ). For even larger spatial scales other phenomena can be observed by the analysis of NEFS, like confinement effects and coupling between different modes (Croccolo et al., 2019b; García-Fernández et al., 2019; Ortiz de Zárate et al., 2020 ) generating propagating oscillations in the system at the Brunt–Väisälä frequency (Carpineti et al., 2021 ). c-NEFs during the free-diffusion process have been extensively studied in the literature (Castellini et al., 2023; Croccolo et al., 2019a, 2007, 2006a, 2006b; Ndjaka et al., 2022 ), where it is common to use the dynamic structure factor S ∼  ( q →  , t , Δ t )     to obtain valuable information about the statistical properties of δ c   :(18) S ∼  q →  , t , Δ t   = 〈 δ c q →  , t   ∙ δ c q →  , t + Δ t    ∗   〉      where q →    is the 2D-spatial wave vector. We identify two different times scales Δ t    and t  , the first is the fast one in which the c-NEFs take place, while the second is the slow one in which the evolution of the macroscopic state takes place, i.e. the time scale of the free-diffusion process. The brackets indicate the correlation operation. Following first an original work (Vailati and Giglio, 1998 ), we assume having an infinitesimal layer of a solute in a solvent characterised by a concentration c   which defines a diffusion coefficient D ( c )    and a kinematic viscosity ν ( c )   .
