In the absence of propagating modes, the decay time of NEFs varies as a function of q   according to a well-known scaling law (Croccolo et al., 2007; Segrè et al., 1993; Segrè and Sengers, 1993 ) in which both the influence of mass diffusion (dominant at high q  ) and gravity (dominant at low q  ) appear, due to their impact on the fluctuations:(23) ξ q , t   = D a  ( c )  q  2  1 + q ro   q     4          2.6 Dynamic shadowgraphy Light scattering methods allow to measure transport coefficients in fluid mixtures, thanks to their ability to analyse density fluctuations when a sample is irradiated (Berne and Pecora, 1976 ). The optical technique used in this work is Dynamic Shadowgraphy (Ndjaka et al., 2022 ), based on the analysis of differences between successive shadowgraph images to probe the system dynamics. The obtained result (more details will be given later) is the images structure function (SF   ) given by:(24) SF ( q , t , Δ t )  = 2 T ∼  q   S ∼  q , t   1 - g ∼  q , t , Δ t     + B ( q , t , Δ t )        where B ( q , Δ t )    is the image background, S ∼  q , t      is the static structure factor and g ∼  q , Δ t      is the normalized correlation function, all having already been discussed in the previous section. The term T ∼  q      is the optical transfer function of the shadowgraph. We assume that T ∼  q      and S ∼  q , t      can be considered simultaneously as a single property, A q , t   = T ∼  q   S ∼  q , t     , called the amplitude term. Thus, the expression for the structure function becomes:(25a) SF ( q , t , Δ t )  = 2 A q , t   1 - g ∼  q , t , Δ t     + B ( q , t , Δ t )        Background term includes different contributions like electronic noise due to the camera and all the acquisition chain. For transient processes, it is customary to introduce a quadratic dependence as a function of the correlation time. This term is actually related to the imperfect planarity of the experimental cell, as recently reported (Castellini et al., 2024 ). Even if our cell is checked for planarity before each experiment, small misalignments can produce this image drift effect. The corresponding classical structure function for a simple exponential decay is then:(25b) SF ( q , t , Δ t )  ≈ 2 A q , t   1 - e  - ξ ( q , t ) Δ t     + C q , t   + E q t   ∙ Δ t  2          2.7 Thickness effect During a Shadowgraph measurement, the signal is actually the superposition of signals coming from all the layers crossed by the detecting light beam through the fluid sample. The sample thickness can be in some cases not negligible, like it is the case in this work (h = 10 m m )   . Following recent developments (Castellini et al., 2023; Zapf et al., 2022 ), the structure factor is therefore the integral of the structure factor of the infinitesimal layers (Eq. (21)  over the entire thickness of the sample:(26) S q , t , Δ t   = 1 h  ∫ 0  h  S ∼  q , t   ∙ g ∼  q , t , Δ t   ∙ d z     Then, we introduce the distribution of reciprocal decay times G ξ , q , t     , so that one can write:(27) g q , t , Δ t   = ∫ ξ m   ξ M   G ξ , q , t   ∙ e  - ξ ( q , t ) Δ t   ∙ d ξ     where ξ m    et ξ M    correspond to the minimum and maximum values of the inverse decay times, respectively. Therefore, the structure function can be written as:(28) S q , t , Δ t   = S q , t   ∙ g q , t , Δ t       The problem is then shifted to the description of the distribution function G ξ , t , q     . Different approaches have been proposed in the literature (Castellini et al., 2023 ). Here we propose a different strategy considering the following points:1- With the concentration profile c t , z      obtained by the PHREEQC simulations described in the previous section, one can compute the concentration gradient profile within the sample ∇ →  c ( t , z )    .  2- By means of Eq. (20) , one can compute the roll-off wave number q ro   ( t , z )    , therefore also the inverse decay time ξ q , t , z      through Eq. (23) .  3- By means of Eq. (19b) , one can then compute the static structure factor S ∼  q , t , z      in any layer of the sample cell.  4- With the precedent results, one can then obtain the average static structure factor of the sample:   (29) S q , t   = 1 h  ∫ 0  h  S ∼  q , t   ∙ d z     5- By means of Eq. (22) , one can compute the correlation function g ∼  q , t , Δ t , z      at any layer of the sample cell.  6- By means of Eq. (26) , one can compute the overall dynamic structure factor S q , t , Δ t     .  7- By means of Eq. (28) , one can compute the overall correlation function g q , t , Δ t     .  8- After Eq. (27) , the distribution of reciprocal decay times can be calculated by inverse Laplacian transform (ILT) of the overall correlation function g q , t , Δ t     . This can be achieved, for example, by means of CONTIN analysis (Liénard et al., 2022; Scotti et al., 2015 ).    In Fig. 4   we report the results for g q , t , Δ t      in log-lin scale and the corresponding G ξ , q , t      in lin-log scale for the experiment #1. In Fig. 4 a we report the correlation functions g q , t , Δ t      as a function of the correlation time Δ t    at different times t   during the free-diffusion process for wave vector q = 100 cm  - 1      and in Fig. 4 c for q = 400 cm  - 1     . In Fig. 4 b and 4 d we report the corresponding distributions of the inverse decay times G ξ , q , t      after performing a CONTIN decomposition of the correlation functions. In order to characterize the width of the distributions we performed Gaussian fits, as indicated by solid red lines in Fig. 4 b and 4d, corresponding to the classical equation:(30) G ξ   = a e  - ξ - ξ  ¯      2  2 σ  2          with ξ  ¯     the mean value of the distribution and σ   its standard deviation. We introduce here a polydispersity index defined as p = σ / ξ  ¯   × 100 %   . In Fig. 5   we report the obtained values as a function of the reduced time t / τ d     for different wave numbers. As can be seen from Fig. 4 , the distribution of the inverse decay times has a Gaussian shape, i.e. it is spread around an average value ξ  ¯     with a certain variance σ  . For large wave numbers q > 200 cm  - 1     , the average value does not change with the macroscopic evolution of the free-diffusion process, as the decay times in the diffusive regime are always determined by the 1 / ( D a  q  2  )    dependence and the mass diffusion coefficient does not vary along the process. The dispersion due to the concentration profile is a simple Gaussian with a constant dispersion of about 15 % for sample #1. For smaller wave numbers q < 200 cm  - 1     , the average value ξ  ¯     changes along with the evolution of the free-diffusion process. In fact, the effect of gravity on fluctuations depends on the intensity of the concentration gradient that slowly decreases with time. The variation of the fluid properties is more important at small times and it affects more the smaller wave numbers because they correspond to larger spatial scales that are, consequently, more influenced by macroscopic variations within the sample. As visible in Fig. 4 a, the departure from exponential behaviour is visible only for small times and for small wave number, similar to what previously reported in (Croccolo et al., 2007 ) where a more important density gradient was present in the fluid under investigation. This is visible also in Fig. 5 , where the dispersion at larger wave number decreases significantly with time, while it is almost constant at small wave number. When the polydispersity index of the distribution of the reciprocal decay times is small (p < 20 % )   , the cumulant method allows to develop the expression of the correlation function around the average value (Frisken, 2001; Liénard et al., 2022 ):g q , t , Δ t   ≈ e  - ξ  ¯   ( q ) Δ t   1 + σ  2  2  Δ t  2        A simple replacement in Eq. 25a or 25b yields the following SF    expression, assumed to be valid for a free-diffusion process in thick samples with limited polydispersity:(31) SF ( q , t , Δ t )  ≈ 2 A q , t   1 - e  - ξ  ¯   ( q , t ) Δ t   1 + σ  2  2  Δ t  2      + C q , t   + E q t   ∙ Δ t  2  )        For small wave numbers this approximation is not valid (Fig. 5 ). For intermediate wave numbers is only valid for times larger than 50 % of the characteristic diffusive time τ d   . For large wave numbers it can be assumed valid at any time.   3 Experimental procedure 3.1 Materials and solution preparation NaCl (Sigma-Aldrich, 746398-500G, anhydrous, ACS reagent, purity 99 %), CaCl2.  (Labkem, Cach-A0P-1 k0, anhydrous, purity ≥ 94 %) and Na2 SO4  (Sigma-Aldrich, 239313-500G, anhydrous, ACS reagent, purity 99 %) were used without further purification. De-ionized water (with resistivity of about 18.5 M Ω c m   ) retrieved from a Millipore Milli-Q filtration station, was degassed and used to prepare a volume of 100 m L    for every saline solution to the required concentration in mol · L  - 1     . The salt masses required to prepare the solutions were weighted using an analytical balance (Sartorius TE313S, with resolution of 10  - 2   g / 200 g   ).  3.2 Set-up To determine the diffusion coefficient of a binary mixture, two layers of the same mixture but at different concentrations must be superimposed in a cell, with the denser one at the cell bottom. In this work we used a cell developed for the study of free-diffusion of a molecular binary mixture (Ndjaka et al., 2022 ). The experimental details and the procedure for analysing the c-NEFs to obtain the mass diffusion coefficient are similar to those used in our previous study. For a brief reminder of the filling procedure of the cell and of the experimental procedure, the diffusion cell is first filled with the less dense solution and subsequently, the denser solution is introduced from the bottom of the cell and, at the same time, the less dense solution is introduced from the top until both of them fill half of the cell. At this time, the valves are closed and the free-diffusion process starts. The difference of concentration Δ c    between the bottom and the top layers is an important parameter of the experiments. The experimental shadowgraph setup used in the present work operates on exactly the same principle as described in (Ndjaka et al., 2022 ). The only difference is in the camera sensor used, a CCD Allied Vision Technologies camera (PIKE-F421B), whose detection plane is positioned at a distance of z = ( 10.0 ± 0.5 ) c m    from the sample central plane. The camera attributes were adjusted with National Instruments Measurement & Automation Explorer acquisition software NI-MAX. This camera allows acquiring a series of raw images at a constant framerate by means of a custom ‘LabView’ software. The camera is capable of acquiring images at a maximum frame rate of 15 H z    at full frame resolution of 2048 × 2048    square pixels with a pixel side of l pix   = 7.32 μ m   . Like in our precedent study, series of N = 2500    images of 1024 × 1024 pix  2     have been recorded at frequency f = 7.8 H z   , every 5 min (after closing the valves) over the first 20 min of each experiment, and then every 10 min until the equilibrium state.  3.3 Image processing The images acquired in the near field consist of an intensity map I ( x →  , t )  , generated by the interference on the camera plane between the portion of the incident beam that has passed undisturbed through the sample and the beams scattered by the refractive index fluctuations occurring within the sample. Here, x →    and t  stand for the position in the image plane and the time lapsed during the acquisition, respectively.  Thanks to the interference of different beams, the fluctuations in the fluid density, that are proportional to the fluctuations of the fluid refractive index, are transformed into fluctuations of the light intensity at the detector plane. Therefore, in order to study the dynamics of the density fluctuations in our samples, we calculate the SF    of the light intensity, i.e. of the acquired images, by means of an already proven Differential Dynamic Algorithm (DDA) (Cerchiari et al., 2012; Norouzisadeh et al., 2021 ). The DDA algorithm consists of the following main steps: first, each recorded image I ( x →  , t )    is Fourier transformed in the 2D spatial space of the detector plane to obtain I q →  , t   = F I ( x →  , t )    , then the Fourier transform (FT) is normalized by dividing it by the zero spatial frequency i q →  , t   = I q →  , t   / I 0 →  , t      in order to remove the source intensity fluctuations. Then, the differences between normalized FTs at a given time difference Δ t    (the correlation time) Δ i q →  , t , Δ t   = i q →  , t   - i q →  , t + Δ t      are calculated. These Δ t   ’s  are, of course, multiples of the time delay dt  min     of the recording process, and cannot be larger than the acquisition duration. Finally, the 2D correlation functions are calculated by determining the square moduli Δ i q →  , t , Δ t      2    of the FT differences, and the individual spatial Fourier transforms of the image differences are averaged, first over all times t  and second over the modulus of the wave vector q →   . The result 〈 Δ i q , Δ t      2  〉  q , t     is the SF    of the recorded intensity fluctuations. In order to reduce the computational time to calculate the structure function out of the image series, we make use of a graphic card taking advantage of the massive parallelization on the Graphic Processing Unit (GPU) and in-house developed software (Cerchiari et al., 2012; Norouzisadeh et al., 2021 ). Examples of SF    obtained 30 min after closing the valves in experiment #1 are shown in Fig. 6  a, as a function of q   for different Δ t   , and in Fig. 6 b as a function of Δ t    for different q  . The oscillatory behaviour shown in Fig. 6 a is due to the optical transfer function (Eq. 24 , 25 , and 31 ) of the shadowgraph. For wave numbers q > 300 cm  - 1      the signal intensity becomes comparable to the background noise. According to the number of images and acquisition rate, the maximum correlation time is 320 s    in this study. However, in order to minimize the impact of the transient effect and not consider noisy experimental points (related to a weak statistic at long correlation times) the fitting of the SF    with Eq. (31)  is performed up to Δ t = 32 s    for all the measurements. We found that the latter was enough to capture the “plateau” of the investigated wave numbers (see Fig. 6 b as example). A q , t   , ξ  ¯   q , t   , σ q , t   , C q , t      and E q , t      are the fitting parameters at each wave number. The fitting is performed through MatLab and an implemented Levenberg-Marquardt non-linear least-square fitting routine. At the end of the fitting, we proceed to the analysis of the dynamics of the fluctuations through the reciprocal decay times ξ  ¯   q , t     .   4 Results and discussion In Table 2  we provided the experimental configurations studied in this work. In Fig. 7   we report the obtained SFs    as a function of the correlation time Δ t    for different wave numbers q   (left panel) for images acquired 30 min after closing the valves in experiment #1 together with the fitting obtained through Eq. (25b) and (31)  and (right panel) the corresponding relative error. In Fig. 7 b we report the corresponding relative errors between the fitting and the experimental points, in dashed curves with Eq. (25b)  and in circles with Eq. (31) . Colors correspond to the wave number colors of Fig. 7 a. For the three wave numbers, the relative error is slightly smaller with Eq. (31) . At large wave numbers the residuals remain well below 1 % and randomly distributed around zero over the entire range of correlation times analysed. However, at small wave vectors the residuals are more important, but do not exceed 2 % with Eq. (31) . This can be explained because, as already anticipated at the end of paragraph 2.7, Eq. (25b)  does not consider coupling effects particularly affecting the signal at small wave vectors, and moreover Eq. (31)  is not valid for too high polydispersity of reciprocal decay times. The quantity A q , t   / C q , t      provides a useful indication of the signal-to-noise ratio of the measurements. In Fig. 8  a, the signal-to-noise ratio is shown for experiment #1 at different times after closing the valves. In Fig. 8 b signal-to-noise ratio is shown for experiments #1, #2 and #3, at 11 min after closing the valves. In Fig. 8 c, a comparison of the signal-to-noise ratio at 11 min after closing the valves is shown for the three concentrations (average and difference) of Na2 SO4 . All those reported results have been obtained with Eq. (31)  for the analysis of the SFs   . One can note that the positions of the maxima and minima in Fig. 8 a, 8b and 8c remain the same, being related to the optical transfer function of the shadowgraph setup that is the same for all the experiments. From Fig. 8 a one can appreciate that the signal-to-noise ratio decreases with time as the experiment runs, witnessing the decrease of the overall concentration gradient within the system. From Fig. 8 b one can detect that the overall signal-to-noise ratio is comparable for all the salt mixtures presented, even though the q ro     are different from one experiment to another. For example, for Na2 SO4 , the second peak is remarkably more intense, showing that the q ro     should be larger. On the contrary, the first peak is more intense for NaCl, showing that the intensity limit at small q   should be larger for this mixture couple. From Fig. 8 c, one can note that the intensity of NEFs is much larger for the molar concentration of 0.5 mol/L than in the other two cases. From the fitting of the SFs   , we obtained also the reciprocal decay times ξ q , t   = 1 τ c  ( q , t )       as a function of q   for different times after closing the valves. In Fig. 9   we report the decay times as a function of q   and for different times after closing the valves for the experiment #1. Only points for which the SN ( q ) > 1    and 0.128 s < τ c  q   < 3 s    are reported. As can be seen in Fig. 9 , the log–log plot of τ c  q      vs. q   shows the classical bell-shape curve at each time. The time decays are slightly different depending on the used SF    model adjustment. By considering the data points of Fig. 9 , the fitting of the c-NEFs decay times as a function of q   was performed with Eq. (23) . The fit to the data turns out to be better with Eq. (31) , particularly visible in Fig. 9 b at the smallest wave vectors. This fitting provides the values of the mass diffusion coefficient D a    as well as the cut-off wave number q ro    , which corresponds to the q   value of the maximum of the bell-shape curve. As already reported in a number of publications (Croccolo et al., 2012, 2006a ), for wave numbers larger than q ro     the system exhibits a diffusive behaviour for c-NEFs so that the mass diffusion coefficient D a    is obtained from the fitting of the experimental data points through Eq. (23)  in this wave vector range. In Fig. 9 , one can note that all the curves collapse onto a single one for large wave numbers, meaning that the mean mass diffusion coefficient remains constant during the free-diffusion process. This is consistent with the fact that the peak of the distribution of inverse time decays shown in Fig. 4 d does not move in time, as already mentioned above. Additionally, as time goes by, the cut-off wave number decreases with time, therefore, the decay time curves move towards larger decay times. This reflects the decrease of the concentration gradient with time due to the diffusion process. The standard deviation of the distribution of reciprocal decay times shown in Fig. 10   shows an opposite behaviour with respect to the decay time. For small wave vectors, the standard deviation is proportional to q  - 2    , while for large wave vectors it is proportional to q  2   . Like the decay time, the standard deviation collapses in the diffusive regime. As the diffusive process evolves, standard deviation for small wave numbers decreases, which is, again, a mark of the smoothing of the concentration gradient, i.e. of the decreasing stratification of the layers in terms of fluid properties. The dashed line corresponds to the standard deviations calculated from the simulated concentration profile 30 min after the start of the free diffusion experiment. The calculations confirm the parabolic trend. The adjustment with the data coming from the fit is remarkably good at medium and large wave vectors. In Fig. 11  , we plot the mass diffusion coefficient D a    as a function of the normalised time (i.e. t/τd  ) for the three binary mixtures obtained from analysis of the decay times after fitting the SFs    with Eq. (31) . The circles are for the experiment #1, squares for #2 and triangles for #3. Historical literature values (Rard and Miller, 1979b , 1979c) are represented by the horizontal dashed lines for each binary mixture of interest. The modeling of SFs    with Eq. (31)  gives constant values over time and in good agreement with these literature values. According to the experimental procedure, the recording of images started 5 min after introducing the fluids into the cell and closing the valves. We can see in Fig. 11  that from the beginning of the experiment we obtain the correct estimation of the value of the diffusion coefficient. We do not have to wait for the end of the diffusion process in order to evaluate the diffusion coefficient, which is a major advantage compared to techniques which exploit the kinetic evolutions of concentration profiles. Slightly different results are obtained after fitting the SFs with Eq. (25b) . The values are also constant over time, but they are systematically underestimated respect to the reference values. In Fig. 1  we reported with red points the average apparent diffusion coefficient values and associated uncertainties on the point series obtained from the modelling of SFs    with Eq. (31) . Those mean values are given in the Table A1  of the appendix.  5 Conclusions Following the Nernst-Planck formalism we have developed the equations of the diffusive fluxes of the ionic species of salts dissolved in water at high concentrations. As expected, due to the conservation of the neutrality of the electric charge (electro-neutrality principle), the species associate and the diffusive behavior resembles that of molecules. We obtained expressions for the apparent diffusion coefficients of NaCl   , Ca Cl  2     and Na  2  SO  4    , depending on the diffusion coefficients of corresponding species and the activity coefficients of the dissolved salts. Using the PHREEQC geochemical software we calculated the species diffusion coefficients and the activity coefficients thanks to the Pitzer formalism. A comparison with experimental literature reference measurements shows that the calculations of apparent diffusion coefficient, carried out with default species ionic strength-dependence coefficients, well describe the steep decrease of the diffusion coefficient at very low concentrations but not at medium and high concentrations. By modifying the values of the ionic strength-dependence coefficients it is possible to find the values of the apparent diffusion coefficients at small and high concentrations, these values were optimized for the four ionic species involved in the three salts studied in this work. The theoretical framework for considering multicomponent diffusion in water implemented in the PHREEQC can help describing aqueous electrolyte diffusion measurements in concentrated simple brines, up to several mol·kg-1 . When aqueous complexation reactions occur, interpreting the diffusion processes based on a single apparent diffusion coefficient may not be relevant anymore, as we saw with Ca Cl  2    . Then we simulated with PHREEQC free-diffusion experiments with the three salts, at different average concentrations and for different concentration differences between the two layers of superimposed saline solutions. Knowing the vertical concentration profile as a function of time allows us to calculate the value of the concentration gradient at any point along the fluid column and at any time. The value of the concentration gradient proved to be a fundamental quantity for the analysis of experimental data. We carried out experimentally the free-diffusion experiments previously simulated. Unlike classical optical techniques, which measure horizontally the vertical concentration profile, we have studied by shadowgraphy in the vertical direction the dynamics of c-NEFs in the horizontal plane during the diffusion process. Given the thickness of the system, the profile of the concentration gradients leads to a polydispersity of the c-NEFs decay times. Since the shadowgraph measured signal is an integration of all the signals coming from all the layers crossed by the detecting light beam through the fluid sample, we have integrated the decay times polydispersity into the autocorrelation function of the c-NEFs, as reported in recent literature. Starting from the concentration gradient profiles we found that the distribution of the reciprocal decay times can be assumed to be Gaussian. When the polydispersity index is low (valid all the time at large wave numbers and for times greater than 50 % of the characteristic diffusive time at intermediate wave numbers), the cumulants method allows to develop the autocorrelation function around the mean value of the distribution and to introduce the standard deviation of the distribution. We have therefore proposed an equation for fitting the image SFs and integrating the thickness of the sample. Based on an adapted measurement protocol, the analysis of the SFs allowed us to measure and from the earliest stages of the diffusion process the diffusion coefficients for the three salts studied. They are in very good agreement with literature reference measurements. This therefore validates the technique and method of analysis of c-NEFs during the free-diffusion of salts with high initial concentration gradient at 25 °C and atmospheric pressure. The diffusion cell used in this work is designed to operate at pressure up to 500 bars and, with the help of the Peltier elements which finely regulate the temperature of the cell, it is possible to heat up to 70 °C. Moreover, the diffusion cell can be used with other aqueous electrolyte combinations. This allows for studies of salt diffusion in more realistic reservoir conditions.
1 Introduction Floods are the most frequent type of natural disasters, accounting for 44% of all natural disasters between 2000 and 2019 (CRED and UNDRR, 2020 ). Particularly in urban settlements, the intensity and frequency of the urban flood events are increasing due to the increasing anthropization of the watersheds and to increasing frequency and intensity of the extreme rain events caused by climate change (Sörensen et al., 2016 ). High water volumes from heavy rains fall onto the cities or enter the cities due to river overflows and/or the incomplete rural infiltration. Large volumes then overflows from the saturated sewers to the streets (MacDonald, 2011 ) and runoff on the impermeable surfaces of the urban area (Pazwash, 2016 ). Urban flood waters generate a high level of risk for inhabitants, buildings and urban furniture (Smith et al., 2014 ). A recent review on urban floods by Mignot and Dewals (2022)  states that significant recent advancements have generated valuable insights for assessing these urban flood risks. Nevertheless, the risk associated to the water quality during urban flooding has received much less attention by the scientific community. Pollutions related to urban flooding encompass various forms, ranging from waste to micro-pollutants (Genouel et al., 2024 ). Addison-Atkinson et al. (2022)  recently reviewed the available research works dedicated to the microbial pollution risk to citizens caused by urban floods, gathering around ten studies. The main approach for characterizing such a pollution consists in collecting and analyzing samples of water that overflows from the sewers to the street surface through manholes. ten Veldhuis et al. (2010)  reported high concentrations of faecal contaminants, i.e. Escherichia coli (from 8 . 7 × 1 0  3      to 1 . 0 × 1 0  5      cfu 100 ml−1 ), Campylobacter and intestinal enterococci (from 5 . 0 × 1 0  4      to 3 . 7 × 1 0  5      cfu 100 ml−1 ), during the 16 July 2007 urban flood in the Hague, the Netherlands. de Man et al. (2014)  also reported high concentrations of Campylobacter and noroviruses that present a great risk of exposure for children due to hand-mouth contact. Chemical hazards were also collected in urban flood waters. Raith et al. (2017)  and Miller and Hutchins (2017)  reported pollution caused by fuel leakage or transported goods from damaged vehicles due to traffic accidents or from drifted vehicles during urban floods. Other studies exhibited the presence of hydrocarbons (Flipo et al., 2018 ) or mine tailings (Wilcox et al., 2016 ) in sediments deposited during the flood, with populations then surrounded by strong hydrocarbon odors and oil slicks. These pollutants expose humans to infections or diseases, causing gastroenteritis, bloody diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting (Rodrigues and Cunha, 2017 ) as the pollution hazard is linked to the nature of the pathogen (de Man et al., 2014 ) or chemical (Miller and Hutchins, 2017 ) and to the routes of exposure (oral, dermal, and inhalation). Several authors such as Pathirana et al. (2011), Mark et al. (2018), Sämann et al. (2019), Fernández-Pato and García-Navarro (2021), Fang et al. (2022)  and Sämann et al. (2022)  attempted to simulate pollutions overflowing from the sewer system and transported in a street network by using two-dimensional (2D) shallow water equations models coupled with the 2D advection–diffusion equations. A recent review by Mignot et al. (2023)  showed that 2D numerical models used to compute mixing in shallow flows, and in particular the expression and the values of the diffusivity tensor, are usually not validated based on experimental (field or laboratory) data-set. Among the 28 studies discussed by the authors, eight formulations of this diffusivity tensor could be identified, such as the use of an isotropic or non-isotropic tensor, coefficients with dimensional diffusivity values, normalized coefficients by the Elder approach or based on a Schmidt number. There is currently no agreement on the most efficient coefficient formulation or values to be used. High-quality data-sets of pollutant concentration are therefore required in urban flood configurations, to test and compare the various diffusivity tensor formulations. In an open-channel flow, a pollutant is subject to three main mechanisms of transport, namely the advection in the two horizontal directions, the dispersion within the cross-section and the turbulent diffusion. The advection in the horizontal plane by the time and depth-averaged flow is the main mode of pollutant transport, while the pollutant mixing in the cross-sections is governed by turbulent diffusion due to turbulent eddies and by the dispersion caused by the non-uniform distribution of velocity over the water depth, including the secondary currents. The pollutant transport in a flooded street network is then expected to depend on the urban geometry, the pollutant release location, the release duration, as well as the complex flow patterns. The basic configurations of a street network mainly consist in the combination of the bifurcations, junctions, and intersections of four streets meeting orthogonally, denoted as crossroads, considered as superposition of bifurcations and junctions (Rivière et al., 2011 ). Arrault et al. (2016), Smith et al. (2014), Finaud-Guyot et al. (2019), Mejía-Morales et al. (2021)  and Li et al. (2022)  measured the flow patterns and discharges in small-scale street networks. They reported recirculation flow zones and contracted flow zones in the streets downstream of the intersections. In addition, significant secondary currents with a streamwise axis and turbulent eddies occur just downstream of junctions and bifurcations in the vicinity of the recirculation zones (Neary et al., 1999; Weber et al., 2001 ) and the contracted zones (Ramamurthy et al., 2007 ). All these 3D flow structures are expected to govern the pollution transport in a street network. The first objective of the present study is to investigate the hydrodynamic processes that drive the transport of pollutant in a flooded street network comprising several intersections (crossroads and bifurcations). The second objective is to assess the sensitivity of the pollutant distribution to the location of the pollutant release. The last objective is to propose a simplified 2D model of the pollutant transport in such a configuration. To address these issues, our study relies on experiments on a highly-simplified street network with a central impervious city block surrounded by four streets, as presented by Mejía-Morales et al. (2021) , under steady flow conditions, with a continuous, punctual and vertically uniform pollutant release. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2  describes the experimental set-up, the pollutant release system, and the techniques used for measuring the pollutant concentration across the streets and at the streets outlets. Additionally, it outlines the procedure to compute the pollutant discharge across a street section based on the concentration and velocity distributions. Section 3  highlights the main hydrodynamic patterns measured in the street network. Section 4  provides pollutant concentration maps, and assesses the mixing efficiency for one reference release location centered in an inlet street. Section 5  highlights the influence of the pollutant release location on the pollutant transport in the street network. Section 6  finally provides a simplified 2D model of the pollutant behavior in the street network and predicts its distribution towards intersection outlet branches.  2 Experiments 2.1 Urban model The experiments were performed on a physical model, named M.U.R.I (‘Modèle Urbain pour l’étude du Risque d’Inondation’, i.e Urban Model for the study of Flood Risk), located in the HHLab (Hydraulics and Hydro-morphology Laboratory) of INRAE, Villeurbanne, France (Fig. 1 a). The 1:50 scale model in the horizontal plane, previously used by Mejía-Morales et al. (2021), Chibane et al. (2021)  and Mejía-Morales et al. (2023) , is a 5.4 m long and 3.8 m wide platform that can be tilted in the longitudinal direction (slope S  X     along X  -axis) and in the transverse direction (slope S  Y     along Y  -axis). In the present study, the flow along X  -axis is favored by S  X    =   0.12%. As a transverse flow is induced by a flow depth gradient (see end of Section 2.1 ), no additional transverse bed slope is used, i.e., S  Y    =   0%. The block side-walls, made of PETG, and the platform bottom made of smooth PVC plates, are hydraulically smooth. All the street cross-sections are rectangular (of width b  =   15 cm, and height of 15 cm, Fig. 1 b). In the present study, the working area is reduced to the area centered on one impervious city block surrounded by four streets with two inflows and four outflows (Fig. 1 c). This geometrical configuration was denoted as C00-00 by Mejía-Morales et al. (2021) . The reader is invited to refer to this paper for more details. The street network is composed of two bifurcations (three-branch intersections) denoted as b  1     and b  2    , and two crossroads (four-branch intersections) denoted as c  1     and c  2    .  Two steady inflow discharges Q  i 1    =   4.5 l/s and Q  i 2    =   2.0 l/s are injected at inlets 1 and 2, respectively (Fig. 1 c). These discharges are monitored with valves and flowmeters (OPTIFLUX 2000 by KROHNE) with a measurement discharge error of 3% (Mejía-Morales et al., 2021 ). A honeycomb is placed at each street entrance (Fig. 1 d). At the downstream end of each street, a vertical weir permits to adjust the water depth (weir crest height ω  =   4 cm at outlet 1 and ω  =   3 cm at the three other outlets, Fig. 1 c). The water then falls in a recovery tank and each outflow discharge (Q  o i     with i  =   1 to 4) is measured with a flowmeter before the water returns to the main tank. The larger inflow discharges Q  i 1     than Q  i 2     along with the higher weir height at outlet 1 (ω  =   4 cm) than at the three other outlets maintains a higher water depth in the Right street which favors a transverse flow towards the parallel street: the Left street.  2.2 Flow measurement The techniques for measuring the hydraulic parameters were presented in details by Mejía-Morales et al. (2021) , and are only briefly summarized here. First, an ultrasonic distance-measuring sensor (BAUMER UNDK, 20I6914/S35A) is used to measure the water depths h  . The accuracy and reproducibility are better than 0.3 mm and 0.5 mm, respectively. The measurement duration is 50 s at a rate of 50 Hz. Second, an Acoustic Doppler Velocimeter (ADV) with a side-looking probe (NORTEK Vectrino +) is used to measure the three instantaneous velocity components with a duration of 300 s at a rate of 100 Hz, with an accuracy of 0.5% of the measured value. A possible misalignment between the probe and the streamwise direction is also accounted for (Peltier et al., 2013 ). Third, the surface velocity field is measured in each intersection (c  1    , b  1    , c  2     and b  2    ) using the Large Scale Particle Image Velocimetry (LSPIV) technique with a video camera (Panasonic, HC-V770) fixed 1.40 m above an intersection. The resolution is set to 1920 px ×   1080 px and wood chips are used as floating tracers (with a diameter between 1 and 4 mm). The video recording duration is set to 70 s with 25 frames per second. The images are processed with the Fudaa-LSPIV software co-developed by EDF and INRAE (Le Coz et al., 2014 ). To estimate the flow discharge across a street, the time-averaged streamwise velocity is measured along 13 vertical profiles, 11 of them with a transverse interval of 1.3 cm, and two additional vertical profiles 0.3 cm away from each side-wall. Along each vertical profile, the velocity is measured at nine elevations in the water column with a vertical interval of 0.7 cm between two measuring points. The explored area thus covers approximately z / h ∈ [ 0 . 12 ; 0 . 96 ]     and y / b ∈ [ 0 . 02 ; 0 . 98 ]    . The velocities in the blind zones close to the side-walls and bottom are extrapolated using a power function reaching zero at the walls. In the near-surface layer, the velocity is considered constant between the upper most measuring point and the water surface (Le Coz et al., 2012 ). The flow discharge through each measuring cross-section S  i     (Fig. 2 a), denoted as Q  S  i      , is then obtained by integrating the time-averaged streamwise velocity across the section using the trapezoidal method (see Appendix B  for the accuracy on the flow discharge measurement). The local bulk velocity is finally defined as U  b  S  i       = Q  S  i     / ( b × h )    .  2.3 Pollutant release and concentration measurement 2.3.1 Pollutant release characteristics A punctual source of pollutant is modeled here, by using a steady release of tracer uniformly distributed over the water depth at a given position (X  , Y  ) of the street network. The release system built with a 3D printer (Fig. 2 b and c) is a profiled narrow vertical tube (to minimize flow disturbance) with holes along the downstream face, and spanning the whole water column. The soluble tracer used to mimic the pollutant is a solution of sodium bicarbonate (conforms to EN 898), water and alcohol (Ethanol 96°UN 1170). The alcohol constitutes 10% of the solution volume to maintain the solution density close to that of the water. The solution density (d  =   1.025) is verified with a density meter (DMA 35, accuracy 0.001 g/cm3 ). The solution concentration is set to C  i n j    =   60 g/l. The release discharges are defined in Section 2.3.3  as they depend on the type of measurement method. Throughout the article, the term ‘pollutant’ refers to this sodium bicarbonate solution.  2.3.2 Releasing locations Nineteen release locations are considered, throughout the street network (Fig. 2 a reports the X  -and Y  -positions of the release locations). Nine releases are performed in the upstream branch of the Right street, either close to the inlet boundary (denoted as u   for upstream), close to the first bifurcation (d   for downstream), or in-between (m   for middle). For each streamwise position, three transverse locations are considered, near each street side-wall (l   for left and r   for right) and in the center (c  ) of the street. In addition, three releases are considered near the entrance of the Left street (l u  ′     , c u  ′     , r u  ′     ) and five in the crossroad c  1     (c r 1   , c r 2   , c r 3   , c r 4   , c r 5   ). Finally, additional releases are performed at the bottom of the inlet tanks of the Right street (i u   ) and Left street (i u  ′     ) to ensure a concentration fully mixed as the flow enters the inlet street, before reaching the first intersections (b  1     or c  1    ).    2.3.3 Local measurement of pollutant concentration Conductivity probes (4-electrode digital probes CLS82D from Endress Hauser) are used to measure the water conductivity σ   (μ  S/cm). A probe located in the upstream tank measures the background water conductivity (σ  u p    ) that slowly increases in our closed-loop experiment. A mobile probe, fixed to the automated carriage, moves in the flow along the X  -, Y  - and Z  -axes. Finally, downstream probes are located in the recovery tanks inside smaller mixing tanks where the concentration is perfectly mixed to measure the outflow concentration. The calibration curve of each probe is performed with a linear relationship σ  = A  ×  c  +  B   , where A   and B   are two coefficients that must be adjusted. The instantaneous concentration c  i     in the street network is measured by the probe n°i   with c  i   ( t )  = ( σ  i   ( t )  − B  i   )  / A  i   − ( σ  u p   ( t )  − B  u p   )  / A  u p      where t   is time and σ  u p    , B  u p    , A  u p     are the corresponding parameters of the upstream probe. c  i     can be seen as the concentration gain with respect to the inflow concentration measured by the upstream probe. A minimum duration of five minutes is required for the flow stabilization before the initiation of the pollutant release. The concentration measurements then begin after at least an additional five-minute duration, thus at least ten minutes after switching on the experimental device. Two types of concentration measurements are carried out in the street network: measurements across a street and measurements at a street outlet. To optimize the signal-to-noise ratio, two release discharges of the pollutant (provided by a peristaltic pump) are defined : Q  i n j    =   26.5 l/h for a measurement at a street outlet or Q  i n j    =   10.4 l/h for measurements across a street. The time-averaged concentration measured across a street is then normalized by the theoretical perfectly mixed concentration, denoted as C  m   = ( C  i n j   × Q  i n j   )  / ( Q  i 1   + Q  i 2   + Q  i n j   )    . The concentration measurement duration is set to 100 s in the streets and 400 s at street outlets, at a rate of 10 Hz, ensuring a concentration uncertainty lower than 1.5%. These durations are based on time-convergence tests of the concentration signal detailed in Appendix A .  2.3.4 Pollutant discharge measurements The measurements across a street are carried out at sections S  1    , S  2    , S  3    , S  4    , S  5     and S  6     (Fig. 2 a). The estimate of pollutant discharge Q m  S  i        through S  i     requires to measure the cross-sectional distributions of time-averaged streamwise velocity U ( y , z )     and concentration C ( y , z )     (see Section 2.2 ), where (y  , z  ) are the transverse and vertical directions associated with the local reference frame in each cross-section (see Fig. 2 ). In the blind zones, the concentration is extrapolated by assuming a constant (or “zero-gradient”) concentration in the directions perpendicular to the boundaries (side-walls and water surface) (Kader and Yaglom, 1972 ). Based on preliminary measurements, it was found that the time-averaged turbulent flux u  ′   c  ′    ¯    through each cross-section is a thousand times lower than the time-averaged flux U C    (see Appendix B ). Consequently, the time-averaged pollutant flux through the cross-section S  i     reads : (1) Q m  S  i     = ∫  y = 0  y = b   ∫  z = 0  z = h   C ( y , z )  × U ( y , z )   d z  d y      Besides, the normalized standard deviation of concentration distribution in a cross-section, denoted as E  m     (Eq. (2) ), permits to quantify the homogeneity of concentration distribution (Pouchoulin et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023 ). The concentration is homogeneous across the section as E  m   ≈ 0   . (2) E  m   = 1  C  m e a n     1  N   ∑  j = 1  j = N   ( C  j   − C  m e a n   )   2         where N  =   99 (11 points in the transverse direction, 9 points in the vertical direction), C  m e a n   = 1  N   ∑  j = 1  j = N   C  j      is the time and spatial average concentration over the cross-section and C  j     is the local concentration. Besides, measuring the time-averaged concentration C  o i     in the recovery tank of a street outlet n°i   permits to compute the pollutant outflow discharge as Q m  o i   = C  o i   × Q  o i     . Under steady flow conditions, the mass conservation requires Q  i n j   × C  i n j   = ∑  i = 1  i = 4   Q m  o i   = ∑  i = 1  i = 4   Q  o i   × C  o i     . Finally, the normalized pollutant outflow discharge is defined as Q m  o i    ̂   = Q m  o i   / ( C  i n j   × Q  i n j   )    , which is the percentage of the injected pollutant recovered at the street outlet n°i  . The error on the pollutant mass conservation for each injection location ranges from −3.7% to 4.5%.    3 Hydrodynamics in streets and intersections Mejía-Morales et al. (2021)  previously proposed a large view of the surface velocity field in the street network (see their figure 9). Herein, we focused on the hydrodynamics at intersections b  1    , b  2    , c  1     and c  2     using the same LSPIV technique. In addition, we repeated velocity measurements over the water column in some selected street cross-sections. 3.1 Time-averaged surface velocities in the bifurcations and crossroads Fig. 3  depicts the spatial distribution of time-averaged surface velocity magnitude, U  s    2   + V  s    2      , and the corresponding streamlines in each intersection. The well-documented recirculating and contracted flow zones are retrieved in the downstream branches of the crossroads in Fig. 3 a and b (Nania et al., 2011; Rivière et al., 2011 ) and in the lateral branches of bifurcations in Fig. 3 c and d (Neary et al., 1999; Ramamurthy et al., 2007 ) with an additional recirculation zone at the outer wall of the Right street downstream from b  2     (Mignot et al., 2013 ). Besides, transverse shear layers appear at the interface between the contracted and the recirculation flow zones and also at the interface between the inflows in the crossroads. Last, the continuous lines in Fig. 3  depict the dividing streamlines that start at the upstream corner (yellow lines) or end at the downstream corner (red lines) of each intersection. The distance d  1     between the side-wall and the red line upstream from the intersection can be then assessed. These dividing streamlines play an important role in the pollutant transport throughout the street network, and quantifying d  1     will allow us to assess the amount of pollutant distributed towards each outlet street in the simplified model that will be presented in Section 6.3 .    3.2 Time-averaged velocities over the water column The time-averaged streamwise velocity distributions in the cross-sections S  1    , S  2    , S  3    , S  4     and S  5     (Fig. 4 a) exhibit complex flow patterns and substantial differences from one cross-section to another, both in terms of velocity magnitude and spatial distribution. In S  1    , U ( y , z )     is typical of a narrow quasi-uniform flow (Bonakdari et al., 2008; Nezu, 2005 ) with e.g. a peak velocity at z / h ≈ 0 . 8   . In S  3     and S  4    , located in the lateral branches of bifurcations, the transverse velocity gradients highlight the persistent influence of the recirculating/contracted flow zones between y / b   =   0.2 and 0.6. Particularly in S  3    , the isocontours of streamwise velocity are vertical. In S  5     (located just downstream from a crossroad), U ( y , z )     is maximum on the left-hand side and minimum on the right-hand side of the cross-section, corresponding, respectively, to the downstream imprint of the contracted and recirculating flow zones in the downstream branch of crossroad c  1     (Rivière et al., 2014; Nania et al., 2011 ). The cross-sectional distribution of time-averaged streamwise velocity in S  2     is similar to that measured by Mejía-Morales et al. (2021) . Similarly, the relative differences of percentage flow discharge across S  2     and S  5    , and at the four outlets do not exceed 4.7%. The time-averaged transverse and vertical velocity vectors, normalized by the bulk velocity U  b  S  i        , are plotted in Fig. 4 b at sections S  3    , S  4     and S  5     (no data are available for S  1     and S  2     where the transverse velocity magnitudes are too low to be accurately measured with the ADV probe). Helical secondary currents with a streamwise axis are observed on the left-hand side of S  4     (with counter-clockwise orientation) and S  3     (with clockwise orientation), with V / U  b  S  i          reaching 13% for S  3     and 25% for S  4    . These secondary currents may arise from combined effects of (i) clockwise skew-induced secondary motion (Prandtl’s first kind) in the transverse outflows of the bifurcation (b  1    , b  2    ) (Neary et al., 1999 ), (ii) the turbulence anisotropy originating from the shear layer at the separation zone interface (Mignot et al., 2014; Blanckaert and de Vriend, 2010 ) and (iii) the depth-averaged transverse motion typically encountered upstream from a crossroad (Rivière et al., 2011 ). Moreover, S  5     exhibits high time-averaged transverse velocities towards the right bank, reaching 45% of the bulk velocity due to the recirculation zone tail formed in the downstream branch of crossroad c  1     (Nania et al., 2011 ).    3.3 Transverse exchange of streamwise momentum across the streets The time- and depth-averaged transverse exchange of streamwise momentum reads ρ ( u v )   d    ¯  = ρ u  ′   v  ′    ¯   d   + ρ ( U ( V − V  d   )  )   d   + ρ U  d   V  d      (Proust et al., 2013 ), where d   subscript refers to depth-averaging, (  ̄    ) and capital letters denote time-averaging, ρ   is the fluid density, u   and v   are the instantaneous streamwise and transverse velocities and u  ′     and v  ′     the corresponding fluctuations. The first term of the right-hand-side ρ u  ′   v  ′    ¯   d      is the depth-averaged transverse Reynolds shear stress, the second term ρ ( U ( V − V  d   )  )   d      represents the advective transport of momentum by the dispersive term of the time-averaged transverse velocity V   over the depth (due, for example, to helical secondary currents reported in Fig. 4 b). The last term ρ U  d   V  d      depicts the advective transport of streamwise momentum by the transverse depth-averaged flow. Fig. 5  compares the transverse profiles of these three terms in sections S  3    , S  4    , and S  5    . The relative contribution of each momentum exchange term greatly varies from one cross-section to another. In S  3    , the Reynolds stress ρ u  ′   v  ′    ¯   d      is a high contribution to the momentum exchange between y / b   =   0.2 and 0.5. This is consistent with the high transverse gradients of streamwise velocity (vertical isocontours of time-averaged streamwise velocities in Fig. 4 a). In S  5    , the term ρ U  d   V  d      dominates for y / b  ∈  [ 0 . 3 ; 0 . 7 ]    , in accordance with the findings in Fig. 4 b, where the transverse velocities towards the right bank reach up to 45% of the bulk velocity. In S  4    , the three momentum fluxes are of the same order of magnitude, indicating that secondary currents (or dispersion), turbulent diffusion and depth-averaged transverse flow all contribute to the transverse momentum exchange. As these three physical processes participate to the transport of momentum, we may assume that they also contribute to the transport of pollutant within the streets.     4 Pollutant transport for the reference release location 4.1 Pollutant discharges For the reference injection location c u    (Fig. 2 a), the normalized pollutant discharge Q m  S  i      ̂   = Q m  S  i     / ( C  i n j   × Q  i n j   )     through each section S  i     (Eq. (1) ) and the normalized outflow pollutant discharge Q m  o i    ̂   = Q m  o i   / ( C  i n j   × Q  i n j   )     through each outlet n°i   (Section 2.3.4 ) are reported in Fig. 6 . In bifurcation b  1    , the pollutant plume splits between the Right street (97.1%) and the Upstream street (5.3%), with an error in mass balance of 2.3%. All the pollutant from Upstream street turns to the Left street downstream of crossroad c  1    , so that Q m  o 4    ̂    =   0%. In b  2    , the pollutant discharge distribution towards the Downstream street (51.3%) slightly exceeds that towards outlet 1 (47.0%). This ratio is very similar to that of water discharge. This similar water and pollutant distribution at b  2     can be explained by the quite symmetrical pollutant concentration with respect to the center of the street, reaching b  2     as measured at section S  2     (Fig. 7 b). Last, the pollutant from the Left and Downstream streets merge in crossroad c  2     and a large amount reaches outlet 2 (38.0%) while a lower amount reaches outlet 3 (17.0%). Most of the highly polluted Downstream street flow turns right towards outlet 2 while outlet 3 receives the low polluted flow from the Left street and only a limited portion from the Downstream street.    4.2 Concentration distributions and mixing efficiencies Fig. 7  shows significant differences in the cross-sectional distribution of concentration in sections S  1     to S  5    , as also reflected by the normalized standard deviation of concentration distribution E  m     (Eq. (2) ). As expected, the inhomogeneity in concentration (measured by E  m    ) decreases from upstream (S  1    ) towards downstream (S  3     and S  4    ), except for S  5    , as discussed below. Upstream from the first bifurcation b  1     (in S  1    ), the concentration distribution (Fig. 7 a) is characteristic of a purely transverse mixing for a pollutant release at the center of a 1D flow (Fig. 4 a) (Rutherford, 1994 ). The concentration is maximum (C / C m   =   3.35) approximately at the center of the street and decreases when approaching the sidewalls. E  m    =   0.63 in S  1     confirms this inhomogeneity with the highest E  m     value among the five tested sections. In S  2     (Fig. 7 b), the pollutant then continues to mix transversely downstream (E  m    =   0.25 ) with a shift of the maximum values towards the left sidewall, due to the transverse motions in b  1     and b  2     towards the Upstream and Downstream streets. In S  3     (Fig. 7 c) and S  4     (Fig. 7 e), fairly homogeneous concentration distributions are observed, indicating an effective pollutant mixing (with E  m    =   0.12 and 0.19, respectively). As shown in Fig. 4 b, the secondary currents in S  3     and S  4     highly contribute to the mixing of the pollutant across these Upstream and Downstream streets (Zhu et al., 2022 ). In addition, the high level of turbulent diffusion (Fig. 5 ) across S  3     contributes to a strong local pollutant mixing. In S  5     (Fig. 7 d), the time-averaged concentration distribution is more heterogeneous than in S  4     even if located further downstream: E  m     increases from 0.19 to 0.38. This heterogeneity is due to the Left street inflow (Inlet 2) of clear water reaching the crossroad c  1     and partially ending up near the left sidewall of S  5     (Fig. 3 a).     5 Sensitivity of the pollutant distribution to the release location To assess the sensitivity of the pollutant distribution to the release location, nineteen locations of the pollution release were considered (Fig. 2 a), including the reference location c u    discussed in Section 4 . 5.1 Release location in the inlet streets The normalized pollutant outflow discharges in the streets (leaving the studied domain) are highly sensitive to the location where the pollutant is released across an inlet street (Fig. 8 ). For example, changing the injection location in the Right street from l u    to c u    and from c u    to r u    increases the pollutant discharge Q m  o 1    ̂     at outlet 1 from 12% to 75% but decreases Q m  o 3    ̂     at outlet 3 from 52% to 8% and Q m  o 2    ̂     at outlet 2 from 40% to 22%. This high sensitivity is due to the interaction of the pollutant plume with the dividing streamline of bifurcation b  1     (shown in Fig. 3 c). As depicted in Fig. 9 a, the amount of pollutant located on the left-hand side of this streamline mainly reaches the lateral branch of the bifurcation (Upstream street), while the rest remains in the main branch (Right street). The same sensitivity is observed at crossroad c  1     where changing the injection location in the Left street from l u  ′      to c u  ′      and from c u  ′      to r u  ′      increases Q m  o 3    ̂     by 7% and 40% and decreases Q m  o 4    ̂     by 90% and 56%, respectively. In contrast, a longitudinal change in the release location in the Right street has a weak influence on the pollutant outflow discharges. The curves corresponding to the ‘upstream’ (l u   , c u   , r u    in blue), ‘middle’ (l m   , c m   , r m    in green) and ‘downstream’ (l d   , c d   , r d    in brown) injections in the Right street deviate from each other by no more than 5% (Fig. 8 ).  5.2 Release location in the crossroads The pollutant distribution through the street network is also sensitive to the release location in crossroad c  1     with respect to the local dividing streamlines (Fig. 3 a). Injections c r 1   , c r 4    and c r 5    are located on the right-hand side of the downstream corner dividing streamline of c  1     (Fig. 3 a). This behavior is confirmed by the low pollutant discharge measured at outlet 4 (Q m  o 4    ̂    ≤   6% in Table 1 ). If neglecting the effect of the turbulent diffusion and secondary currents at the two incoming flows interface, the whole pollutant amount reaches the Left street and ends up in outlet 3 after crossing c  2     (Fig. 3 b). Oppositely, locations c r 2    and c r 3    are located on the left-hand side of the dividing streamline (Fig. 3 a). For c r 3   , all the pollutant reaches outlet 4 (Q m  o 4    ̂    ≈   100%). For c r 2   , the pollutant plume overlaps the dividing streamline and the amount of pollutant is divided into two parts among both outlets of c  2    . 86.1% ends up in outlet 4 and 16.4% reaches the Left street and ends up in outlet 3 (Table 1 ).       6 Simplified 2D model for pollutant transport in a street network This section proposes a descriptive model (Squazzoni et al., 2020 ) of different scenarios of pollutant transport for a single subcritical and steady flow configuration in the present simplified street network with only 90° intersections. The required inputs are (i) the flow discharge in each street (measured or computed by solving the 2D shallow water equations), (ii) the exact location of the pollutant release for the estimation of the pollutant distribution in the upstream intersections and (iii) the measured concentration distribution at the entrance of the intersections located further downstream. 6.1 Pollutant transport in the inlet street For a vertically homogeneous local release in a street, where the flow is considered as 1D (such as the upstream reaches of the Right and Left streets), the plume follows a purely transverse mixing. The transverse concentration profiles exhibit Gaussian distributions and the mirror method assumes that the concentration is fully reflected by the sidewalls (Rutherford, 1994 ). The transverse profile of depth-averaged concentration is then predicted using an analytical solution proposed by Rutherford (1994)  where the normalized transverse mixing coefficient E  y   / ( h u  ∗   )    , calibrated in Fig. 9 b and c equals 0.079, identical to the coefficient calibrated in the unique street, see Appendix C . A fair agreement between the analytical solutions and the measurements is obtained at S  1     (Fig. 9 b) for releases in r u   , c u   , and l u   , and at S  6     (Fig. 9 c) for release c u  ′     .  6.2 Pollutant behavior in the intersections As a pollutant plume reaches an intersection, six configurations can be considered (Fig. 10 ). (i) First, as an inhomogeneous polluted inflow enters a bifurcation, it splits into two parts from either side of the dividing streamline and remains inhomogeneous in the two downstream branches (case 1). This corresponds to the local releases in the Right street when passing through b  1    . (ii) As a homogeneously polluted inflow reaches a bifurcation, it remains homogeneous in both downstream branches (case 2). This corresponds to the release location i u    when reaching b  1    . As an inhomogeneous (iii) or a homogeneous (iv) polluted main inflow enters a crossroad, it splits into two parts from either side of the dividing streamline, mainly ends up in the lateral downstream branch where it remains, respectively, inhomogeneous (case 3) or homogeneous (case 4). The rest merges with the secondary inflow and ends up inhomogeneous in the main downstream branch. The case 3 corresponds to the release locations in the Left street (c u  ′     , l u  ′      or r u  ′     ) when reaching c  1    . The case 4 corresponds to the release locations c u    or i u  ′      when entering c  2     or c  1    , respectively. As an inhomogeneous (v) or a homogeneous (vi) polluted inflow reaches a junction, it simply merges with the other inflow (case 5 and case 6, respectively) and ends up inhomogeneous in the downstream branch (Mosley, 1976; Webel and Schatzmann, 1984; Yuan et al., 2016 ). In all cases, the pollutant distribution in the square intersections is governed by the 2D time-averaged horizontal advection flow (Soulhac et al., 2009 ) where the polluted inflows either merge or split by following the dividing streamlines. The turbulent diffusion and dispersion processes do not affect this distribution due to the short length of the mixing zone. The pollutant then strongly mixes in all downstream intersection branches both vertically and transversely before reaching the next intersection.    6.3 Pollutant distribution towards outlet branches at intersections Assessing the pollutant distribution in a square intersection requires to estimate the distance d   (Fig. 10 ) between the downstream corner dividing streamline and the side-wall of the inlet branch. The LSPIV data already permitted to estimate d  1     (Fig. 3 ) and two alternative estimations d  2     and d  3     can be computed based on the mass flow conservation presented in Table 2 , assuming that the streamwise velocity remains constant along the transverse and vertical axes. This assumption seems to be valid in the inlet streets, e.g. across S  1     and S  6    , as well as S  2    , where the standard deviation of the time-averaged streamwise velocity does not exceed 15% of the bulk velocity. However, it is less valid across S  3    , S  4    , and S  5    , where this standard deviation ranges from 47% to 87% of the bulk velocity. The final distance is then averaged as d = ( d  1   + d  2   + d  3   )  / 3    with a standard deviation, denoted as δ d    (Table 2 ). The final step consists in integrating the predicted (in b  1     and c  1    ) or measured (in b  2     and c  2    ) transverse profile of depth-averaged concentration entering the intersection by using the trapezoidal method over the transverse axis delimited by d   and the side-wall (see Fig. 9 a e.g. for b  1    ). The predicted normalized pollutant discharges in the lateral branches of the intersections, denoted as P  S  i       across S  i     or P  o i     in outlet i, follow Eqs. The second objective focused on the sensitivity of the pollutant distribution to release locations. In addition, a simplified 2D model to describe the pollutant transport at intersections is proposed. The following conclusions can be outlined: – For a pollutant release located far downstream from an intersection, the pollutant transport is mainly governed by transverse mixing due to dispersion and turbulent diffusion. – The pollutant strongly mixes in the street sections located between two consecutive intersections due to helical secondary currents and turbulent diffusion generated by the juxtaposition of a recirculation flow and a contraction zone. Nevertheless, the contribution of these processes to the pollutant mixing greatly varies from one street to another, depending on the type of intersection and the magnitude of the transverse gradients of the streamwise velocities. – The transport of the pollutant in the square intersections is mainly governed by the 2D advection in the horizontal plane, despite intersections having shear zones and 3D flows. The pollutant plume either merges or splits by following quite fairly the intersection dividing streamlines. – The pollutant transport is highly sensitive to the transverse release location in the streets with a variation in pollutant outflow discharges from 10% to 75%. In contrast, this variation does not exceed 5% for a change in the longitudinal locations as tested herein. The exact location within a crossroad also affects the pollutant transport. This high sensitivity is due to the interaction of the pollutant plume with the dividing streamlines in the intersections and highlights the significance of considering the precise release location for urban flood management strategies when assessing health risk due to a pollution transport. – An analytical model was proposed to predict the pollutant distribution at the intersections. The accuracy of the model appears to strongly depend on the capacity to precisely locate the dividing streamlines. Given the complexity of the problem, imposing a steady state for the flow and pollutant release serves as a first step in understanding pollutant transport in urban flooding. The experimental configuration composed of three-branch and four-branch intersections is quite representative of all street networks. Under steady and subcritical flow regime, it is expected that the pollutant transport processes reported above can be generalized to other street networks. The numerical models when validated against the present data-set under our simplified conditions, could be used to investigate the pollutant transport in more complex and realistic (e.g. unsteady) urban flood conditions.
1 Introduction Groundwater, the world's largest storage of freshwater, plays a vital role in agriculture, industry, and domestic water use. It is replenished by recharge from surface water (runoff, snowmelt, rivers, streams, and lakes) and exhibits lower susceptibility to short-term climatic variations and multi-year fluctuations than surface water reservoirs (Taylor et al., 2013a,b; Pokhrel et al., 2013 ). However, in many arid and semi-arid regions with low rainfall and high evapotranspiration rates (Döll and Fiedler, 2008; Wada, 2016 ), groundwater replenishment rates remain exceedingly minimal. Concerns over the long-term sustainability of groundwater have emerged due to the ever-increasing freshwater demand and the sustained global overexploitation spanning several decades (Shah et al., 2001; Wada et al., 2010; Dillon et al., 2019 ). The history of groundwater overexploitation can be traced back to the mid-20th century, coinciding with technological advances that made extracting water from aquifers easier (e.g., Teatini et al., 2006 ). This led to a rapid increase in the number of wells and the volume of water extracted, resulting in an estimated depletion rate of 283 (±40) km3  per year (Wada et al., 2010 ) globally. The state of California has experienced overexploitation of groundwater starting in the early 1900 s when the scarcity and high price of water clashed with the abundance of land and incentivized further depletion of limited underground water sources (Leahy, 2016). For example, approximately 41 % of water for irrigated agriculture in California comes from groundwater during normal years, but this percentage can increase to over 58 % during drought periods (California Department of Water Resources, 2020 ). Extensive studies have thoroughly examined the impacts of droughts and excessive groundwater pumping, shedding light on a range of alarming consequences. Notably, these include substantial declines in water tables, slow rate of groundwater recovery, and the occurrence of land subsidence (Dillon et al., 2019; Gale and Dillon, 2005; Schreiner-McGraw and Ajami, 2021 ). The unregulated extraction of groundwater has also triggered a series of detrimental outcomes, such as seawater intrusion, dried-up wells, degradation of water quality, reduction in base flow to streams and rivers, among others (Lees et al., 2022a,b; Dillon et al., 2019; Tularam and Krishna, 2009; Changming et al., 2001 ). Despite the well-documented risks associated with groundwater over-exploitation, the global demand for this resource continues to escalate (Wada and Heinrich, 2013 ). Consequently, over-exploitation remains a pressing issue in various regions across the globe. Decline in the groundwater table has resulted in increased pumping costs and compelled the abandonment of numerous water supply and irrigation wells (Kinzelbach et al., 2003; Tularam and Krishna, 2009 ). Collectively, these adverse effects underscore the urgent need for sustainable groundwater management and heightened awareness regarding its long-term implications. Groundwater depletion has become a critical issue in several major aquifers worldwide, including the Ogallala and California Central Valley aquifers in the western USA, the Arabian aquifer spanning several countries in the Middle East, the Indus Basin in India and Pakistan, the Canning basin in Australia, and the Murzuk-Djado in North Africa, among others (Famiglietti et al., 2011; Faunt, 2009; Famiglietti, 2014; Wada and Heinrich, 2013; Aeschbach-Hertig and Gleeson, 2012; Liu et al., 2022 ). These studies underscore the urgent need for practical and sustainable groundwater management to halt further depletion. Failing to address this escalating trend could have severe ramifications for agricultural production and economies, from local communities to the global stage. Neglecting this issue threatens agricultural livelihoods and poses a significant risk to the broader economy. Furthermore, detrimental effects of this trend are expected to worsen with the looming threat of climate change and population growth (Liu et al., 2022 ). Global and regional water security requires sustainable groundwater management, which demands significant investment and legislative frameworks. Preserving the diverse range of ecosystem services and ensuring a healthy environment for the global population hinges on the availability of sustainable groundwater resources. Paradoxically, despite its critical importance to global water supplies, groundwater frequently receives less management attention than surface water sources like rivers and reservoirs that are more visible (Calow et al., 2010 ). Moreover, sustainable groundwater management continues to be challenging because of the imbalance in water supply and demand, and poor monitoring systems and oversight, especially in the developing world. In response to the state of groundwater depletion, modeling a broad array of managed aquifer recharge (MAR) scenarios and effects of various water conservation practices in aquifer replenishment have been evaluated (e.g., Kourakos et al., 2019 ). MAR intentionally diverts water into aquifers faster than natural processes (Bouwer, 2002; Kocis and Dahlke, 2017 ; Scanlon et al., 2016). As described by Zhang et al. (2020) , MAR techniques are generally classified into five major categories based on the recharge and storage technique used: 1) spreading methods, 2) in-channel modifications, 3) recharge by well or shaft and boreholes, 4) induced bank filtration, and 5) runoff harvesting. Most MAR research to date has focused on the use of these technologies on valley floors (flat terrain) owing to the presence of existing infrastructure and favorable topographical conditions for water conveyance. One of the most promising avenues for increasing groundwater sustainability is winter recharge projects that employ surplus runoff water to restore depleted aquifers. Viable and scalable approaches toward sustainable water supply solutions include infiltrating excess off-season surface water supplies. In particular, stormwater has commonly been captured, stored, and infiltrated on floodplains (Flood-MAR), farmlands (Ag-MAR) (Ulibarri et al. al., 2021; Alam et al., 2021), and infiltration basins (Dillon and Arshad, 2016; Voisin et al., 2018 ). Aquifer storage and recovery wells (ASR) and drywells also have shown considerable potential for MAR (Maliva, and Maliva, 2020; Missimer et al., 2015 ). ASR wells release water directly into aquifers and can rapidly impact the water quantity and quality of aquifers. Costly pretreatments are therefore required for ASR operations to ensure groundwater quality is not adversely impacted (Lin et al., 2006; Page et al., 2011 ). In contrast, drywells and infiltration galleries release water into the vadose zone, and infiltrating water undergoes natural filtration and contaminant attenuation process before reaching the water table (Edwards et al., 2016 ). Both ASR and drywells can bypass low permeability soil layers and therefore have shorter recharge times than surface MAR approaches (Sasidharan et al., 2021 ; Mermillod-Blondin et al., 2015). However, clogging is a reoccurring problem for all MAR approaches, especially for ASR and drywells (Holländer et al., 2009 ). The localized nature of MAR projects and their reliance on runoff availability during specific periods raise questions about their effectiveness in achieving sustainable water use. In addition, MAR approaches operate under several uncertainties affecting the timeframe from infiltration to groundwater replenishment, including subsurface heterogeneity, the depth to the water table, and subsurface connectivity (de Barros et al., 2016; Engel et al., 2021; Eykholt et al., 1999; Maples et al., 2019; Perzan et al., 2023a,b ). These uncertainties also encompass the accessibility of stored water for future use (Bloetscher et al., 2020 ), the potential leaching of contaminants (Bachand et al., 2014 ; Waterhouse et al., 2020), and changes in reaction, transformation, and transport due to ponding water (Zheng et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2021 ; Steffen et al., 2015). Additionally, further knowledge is needed on the quality of the source water for recharge, particularly in the case of recycled water, and the magnitude/volume of recharge in relation to the level of depletion. Several studies have employed geophysical tools to identify high permeability porous media for faster infiltration and to optimize the hydrogeologic setting for recharge (Shishaye and Abdi, 2016; Goebel and Knight, 2021; Knight et al., 2022; Pepin et al., 2022 ). However, relatively little research has focused on the effectiveness of MAR techniques and the differences between the techniques and conveyance systems, especially in comparison to hillslopes. In modeling groundwater, a no-flow boundary condition at the interface of valley floors, hillslopes, and mountains and a flow input via streamflow infiltration at the mountain front or with injection wells are commonly employed to simulate mountain recharge (Faunt et al., 2009 ). Yet, the limited attention given to hillslope dynamics restricts the applicability of groundwater models in analyzing MAR strategies beyond valley floor regions. A recent review suggests that hillslopes and mountains can contribute significantly to recharge in valley floors, ranging from 5 to 50 % (Markovich et al., 2019 ). Furthermore, surface MAR approaches on valley floors primarily impact recharge at the top of unconfined aquifers, whereas hillslope and mountain recharge have been reported to also influence water levels in deeper aquifers (Wilson and Guan, 2004; Manning and Solomon, 2005; Aishlin and McNamara, 2011 ). This underscores the necessity for more comprehensive investigations into methods for expanding recharge beyond flat terrains and assessing their advantages and limitations. This paper aims to assess current efforts in replenishing groundwater and explore the potential for expanding recharge methods from valley floors to hillslopes and mountains. The goal is to identify any potential gaps, uncertainties, and limitations associated with commonly used MAR techniques that could hinder the ability to achieve effective and sustainable groundwater management. We will also explore innovative strategies that could improve the ability of countries, states, or water management districts to increase recharge and reliability of aquifer systems. This will involve considering alternative MAR techniques, water sources, potential locations, and their integration with surface collection and storage systems to promote enhanced recharge.  2 Managed aquifer recharge initiatives 2.1 Sustainable groundwater management The issue of groundwater depletion and ecosystem degradation have received global attention, prompting the inclusion of groundwater sustainability as a policy instrument in various water codes and management directives worldwide (Elshall et al., 2020 ). Despite periodic investments and legislative frameworks aimed at promoting sustainable water management, many countries, states, and water management districts continue to struggle with imbalances in water supply and demand. To address these challenges, the concept of sustainable groundwater management has been applied across several priority aquifer systems. This approach integrates sustainable development principles to achieve a balance between economic, social, and environmental needs such that “development meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs” (Brundtland, 1987 ). In recent decades, several countries have embraced sustainable water policies and legislation Rohde et al., 2017 .
