For instance, the European Union implemented the Water Framework Directive (European Commission, 2000 )), Australia introduced the National Water Initiative (Council of Australian Governments, 2004), South Africa established the National Water Act (Republic of South Africa. 1998 ), and Brazil adopted the National Water Resources Policy and National Groundwater Management Plan (National Water Act, 1997 ). These institutional initiatives reflect the commitment to sustainable groundwater management at the national level. Among these institutions and legislations, the recent Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA) in California, USA, stands out as a leading example of a comprehensive framework focusing on avoiding undesirable outcomes (i.e., lowering of groundwater levels, reduction of groundwater storage, seawater intrusion, land subsidence, water quality degradation, and depletions of interconnected surface water) in all California groundwater basins. SGMA encompasses policy coverage, technical assistance, and financial support at all levels, making it a model for effective groundwater management. Notably, the Central Valley aquifer system, particularly in the southern two-thirds, has experienced the second largest groundwater overdraft in the US (Faunt et al., 2009 ), accelerating the timeline to achieve sustainable groundwater management (California Department of Water Resources, 2020 ). Regions and countries that have implemented sustainable water policies and legislation have aimed at addressing the challenges associated with groundwater depletion and ecosystem degradation, paving the way for a more sustainable and balanced approach to groundwater management. Achieving sustainability necessitates well-designed policies, robust legislative frameworks, strong financial support, and sound science capable of capturing the dynamics and complexities of hydrogeology and its interdependencies with ecological and human systems. Integrated transdisciplinary groundwater management approaches that closely integrate science technology and policy (or vice versa) are vital, as are case studies addressing the effective development and implementation of a wide range of solutions to alleviate the depletion of groundwater. These combined efforts will contribute to a more resilient and sustainable groundwater future, addressing pressing issues surrounding groundwater depletion and ecosystem degradation.  2.2 MAR technologies MAR techniques for valley floors have been reviewed and summarized previously (Ajjur and Baalousha, 2021; Braune and Israel, 2021; Gale and Dillon, 2005; Sherif et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020 ), including Flood-MAR, Ag-MAR, infiltration basin, drywells, and ASR wells. Only a brief description of these methods and their advantages are presented in Section 2.2. Flood-MAR methods are strategies that utilize excess flood flows during wet seasons to replenish aquifers, primarily through seasonal flooding of working lands (California Department of Water Resources, 2019; Sprenger et al., 2017 ). These methods aim to manage water resources through the voluntary storage of floodwater resulting from rainfall or snowmelt events in landscapes such as refuges, floodplains, and flood bypasses (Ghasemizade et al., 2019; Imig et al., 2022 ). By harnessing these floodwaters, Flood-MAR offers several potential advantages, yet the implementations are less quantified and understood in terms of where and when the water can be recovered. In addition to recharging aquifer systems connected to flood plains, Flood-MAR can also help reduce the risks associated with peak floods and mitigate flood-related hazards. However, there is a significant gap in understanding the extent and benefits of flood risk reduction associated with floodplain. This includes may also the challenge of incorporating climate prediction in implementation of reservoir release for rechange in anticipation of flooding storms months before its occurrence. Secondary benefits of Flood-MAR also include restoring and maintaining natural wetland habitats and riparian areas for migratory birds and other wildlife (Ulibarri et al., 2021 ). Flood-MAR also provides increased baseflows (Alam et al., 2020) that supports spawning fish species (Kirk et al., 2020 ), but rapid groundwater-surface water interactions limit its delivery for long term use when there is high hydraulic connectivity between the aquifer and river. The increased connectivity between surface water and aquifers due to the implementation of Flood-MAR, on the other hand, could also improve groundwater dependent ecosystems and enhance in-stream and downstream ecological functions (Nevill, 2009). In general, Flood-MAR is a proactive, integrated approach to managing water resources by utilizing and storing large volumes of floodwater in a controlled manner. However, its success depends on the availability of stored water for later use which requires systematic data collection, a thorough understanding of flow paths and storage of the infiltrated flood water. Agricultural land is primarily used for crop production, but Ag-MAR is an innovative approach that capitalizes on existing agricultural practices to promote aquifer recharge as a secondary objective. Ag-MAR is also known as agricultural groundwater banking or on-farm recharge (Levintal et al., 2022; Bachand et al., 2014 ). Ag-MAR involves the deliberate application of irrigation water, treated water, runoff, or large volumes of flood water onto expansive agricultural areas and redirects it towards replenishing aquifers instead of allowing it to discharge from available water systems. Even in farmlands with lower recharge rates, Ag-MAR enables the capture of significant water volumes over short periods. This is particularly beneficial in areas experiencing significant climate variations with infrequent but intense rainfall events. It allows large capture that would otherwise overwhelm other localized MAR technologies like wells or infiltration basins (Kourakos et al., 2019 ). Moreover, Ag-MAR utilizes existing agricultural infrastructure and land, resulting in relatively lower implementation costs in regions utilizing pre-existing channel systems compared to areas necessitating the construction of new conveyance and boundary structures. Successful Ag-MAR implementation relies on the willingness of landowners to incorporate this strategy into their practices. Infiltration basins (ponds, tanks) are a commonly used MAR method (Levintal et al., 2023a,b ) that uses land designed and solely dedicated for infiltration and recharge. The distinction between Ag-MAR and infiltration basins has significant implications for designing, implementing, and managing these MAR systems (Ghasemizade et al., 2019; Levintal et al., 2023a,b ). Examples of dedicated infiltration basins include Gilbert ponds (Williams and McLain, 2012 ) and long-term storage credits (LTSCs) through aquifer recharge with the Colorado River water (Bernat et al., 2020 ). Infiltration basins involve continuous operation (e.g., pumps, canal systems) to recharge large volumes of water depending on the availability of source water and the size of storage ponds. It also involves periodic maintenance to manage clogging and enhance infiltration rates. Periodic wetting and drying of infiltration basins are needed to manage clogging from sediment buildup and the algae and microbial growths. This alternating wetting and drying allow alternating redox conditions, enhancing nutrient and pathogen biodegradation (Abel et al., 2012; Williams and McLain, 2012 ). Mechanical agitation of the basin surface (e.g., raking, dredging) also helps to mitigate clogging and enhance recharge rates. Drywells are a stormwater management system consisting of a vertical borehole in the vadose zone lined with a geotextile membrane and filled with gravel and crushed stone. Drywells, vadose zone injection wells, and infiltration galleries are designed to bypass the root zone and low permeability layers that inhibit downward migration from spreading techniques (Zhang et al., 2020 ) so that infiltrating water is released into more permeable soil layers of the vadose zone. Apart from reducing stormwater runoff, drywells can also increase groundwater recharge, eliminate losses by evapotranspiration, require minimal space, and allow continued operation of land (Sasidharan et al., 2021 ). Furthermore, infiltration and recharge from drywells are concentrated over a relatively small area, and water is released deeper in the vadose zone (10–40 m below the surface) than in surface MAR approaches (Flood-MAR, Ag-MAR, and infiltration basins). This produces faster rates of infiltration and recharge and less vadose zone storage (LACDPW, 2014, Sasidharan et al., 2018, Sasidharan et al., 2019, Sasidharan et al., 2020 ). Drywells are often combined with low-impact development practices to minimize the negative impact of traditional stormwater management methods, such as detention basin, riparian buffers, flood plains, etc., on the aquatic ecosystem. Similar to drywells, ASR is a technique used to replenish depleted aquifers that utilize wells to inject treated water directly into the saturated zone (Bloetscher et al., 2014; Zuurbier et al., 2014 ) during times of surplus. However, unlike drywells, ASR involves speedy recharge and storage in the aquifer in areas where surface infiltration is impractical (Khan et al., 2008 ). These wells are equipped with pumps and monitoring systems to regulate the injection and recovery processes, ensuring the water quality and quantity meet specific requirements (https://www.epa.gov/uic/aquifer-recharge-and-aquifer-storage-and-recovery ). ASR requires a high-level of treatment before it is injected because the water is released directly into an aquifer (Sheng, 2005; Maliva et al., 2020 ). Regulatory constraints, as seen in California, may limit ASR locations and increase expenses. The stored water can then be retrieved from the same well or nearby extraction wells during periods of high-water demand or drought. Recovered water may require another level of treatment before use. The treatment and pumping of the water to and from the ASR facility make this approach more energy intensive than other water supply options. The various MAR technologies have been shown to effectively contribute to sustainable groundwater management and play a complementary role in broader objectives related to environmental water conservation and societal benefits. Flood-MAR, Ag-MAR, infiltration basins, drywells, ASR, and other methods have been globally employed to restore depleted aquifers, fostering economic and societal sustainability. Although selection of these MAR methods depends on factors such as water source, hydrogeology, costs, expertise, and aquifer depletion levels, these technologies have predominantly been applied in flat terrain regions. Furthermore, these methods may have significant limitations, uncertainties, and hurdles that hinder their effectiveness and even raise concerns about potential unintended consequences.   3 Unknowns and limitations in MAR In the following sections, we will explore the unknowns, significant limitations, and uncertainties that potentially hinder seamless integration of MAR technologies, dominantly implemented in flat terrain settings, into groundwater management. The unknowns and limitations inherent in various MAR approaches include critical factors like timing, availability, and quantity of water for recharge; proximity of available water for recharge and recharge locations; identifying suitable recharge locations (hydrogeological characteristics); recovery after recharging; issues of clogging; and uncertainties in biogeochemical reactions, landowner participation, and associated costs. 3.1 Limited recharging space and time (flood plains and winter flood periods) Water availability for augmented recharge is typically highest during winter and rainy seasons (November – April) when the irrigation demands are lowest. However, many existing groundwater recharge projects, such as Ag-MAR or Flood-MAR, and other basin spreading methods, face spatial and temporal limitations (Levintal et al., 2022). Recharge technologies often contend with constrained storage capacity for recharge water, a challenge evident in ASR and drywells. These methods rely on short-lived excess flows, which may not align with suitable recharge sites. Furthermore, the volume of available water during excess flows poses difficulties in moving it away from stream channels, thereby limiting available area to apply water for recharge. Higher intensity and shorter duration runoff may reduce recharge because recharge is slow relative to streamflow. Available storage capacity is quickly filled, and excess flows are lost downstream if additional water storage infrastructure is not developed. The effectiveness of recharge techniques is also being impacted by climate change, particularly by reducing the duration of surplus runoff that can be used for recharge purposes. In certain regions, studies have revealed a rising trend in runoff caused by climate change. California, for instance, is experiencing an increase in runoff; however, this occurs within a limited timeframe, thereby diminishing the capacity for diffuse groundwater recharge. Huang et al. (2020) observed a 25 % reduction in snowfall and a 50 % increase in runoff due to more frequent and intense rainfall events and decreases in snow to rain ratio. Furthermore, recharge seasons are becoming shorter due to decreases in the duration of the winter season due to climate change (Makoto et al., 2014; Woolway et al., 2022 ). The timing of available runoff aligns with periods of higher water availability which is usually very short in groundwater-depleted regions such as California, the Middle East, the Mediterranean, etc., and becoming shorter due to climate change (e.g., Trenberth, 2011; Pfister et al., 2004 ). It is also essential to indicate in mountainous areas typically characterized by fractured hard-rock formations and/or karst aquifers featuring preferential conduits and fractures, the augmented runoff from intense rainfall events may enhance recharge (e.g., Hartmann et al., 2017a,b; Messerschmid et al., 2018; Letz et al., 2021; Bresinsky et al., 2023 ). Projects that rely on a continuous water supply, such as those using recycled water (e.g., Bouwer, 1991; Donaldson, 1997; Williams and McLain, 2012 ; Mendoza-Espinosa et al., 2004), have a more consistent recharge potential. The use of floodplains as recharge space is constrained by their location, i.e., the proximity to the river that controls the groundwater-river interaction. Floodplains and paleo-glacial outwash deposits may not be over the most overexploited aquifers. Even though Flood-MAR increases baseflow (Alam et al., 2020; Kirk et al., 2020 ), the enhanced stream-aquifer connection creates generally rapid groundwater-surface water interactions limiting its delivery for long-term use. The dual purpose of Ag-MAR introduces potential conflicts with other land uses that limit its application for recharge and scalability. In Ag-MAR, which involves farmland-based field-flooding with surplus water (Kocis and Dahlke, 2017 ), its expansion requires the farmers’ acceptance of potential risks associated with unknown effects on crop production. The impacts of Ag-MAR on crop production depend on crop tolerance to flooding as it limits the aeration of the soil (Ganot and Dahlke, 2021 ), which may negatively affect the overall agricultural yields (Levintal et al., 2022). The ponded water would also produce greenhouse gas emissions (Malyan et al., 2022 ). Other potential impacts of Ag-MAR include reduced oxygen levels in the subsurface that can damage crop health, leach and mobilization of legacy contaminants, such as nitrate, pesticides, etc., from the root zone with infiltrating water, which were otherwise attached to the soil (Levintal et al., 2022; Dahlke et al., 2018; Grinshpan et al., 2021 ). The excess water introduced into fields can mobilize and transport contaminants in the source water and soil into underlying groundwater or adjacent water bodies, posing environmental and human health risks. Successful implementation of Ag-MAR and infiltration basin systems requires consideration of factors such as land availability, community acceptance/willingness, types of crops, and the effect of ponded water over a long time on crop health and productivity. These challenges must be carefully addressed to expand Ag-MAR for large-scale groundwater replenishment applications. Therefore, regular monitoring and appropriate management of in-situ contaminants are essential steps for maintaining a healthy and productive crop environment within Ag-MAR systems.  3.2 Hydrogeological characteristics and potential impacts on groundwater flow and storage Hydrogeology plays a critical role in determining the feasibility of the project and selecting the appropriate location and structure (Zhang et al., 2020 ). In addition to site-specific aquifer characteristics, the success of MAR projects often relies on assessing surface and subsurface connectivity and the time for infiltrated water to reach the groundwater table. Hydrogeological factors should be considered when assessing the feasibility of MAR including but are not limited to geological and hydraulic boundaries, aquifer spatial extent and hydraulic characteristics (i.e., hydraulic conductivity and transmissivity, storage capacity, and porosity), inflows and outflows (i.e., water balance component), and natural recharge and discharge areas (Gruetzmacher and Kumar, 2012; Maples et al., 2019 ). Perzan et al., (2023a,b)  also underscored the significance of the initial saturation state of the vadose zone, especially the clays, in influencing recharge effectiveness. Additionally, understanding the complex heterogeneity of the vadose zone and aquifer is essential. Subsurface heterogeneity refers to spatial variations in physical properties of subsurface materials. These variations can result in preferential flow paths for water, causing it to bypass or accumulate in certain areas of the aquifer (Casillas-Trasvina et al., 2022; Maples et al., 2019 ). In some cases, subsurface heterogeneity can be beneficial for MAR projects, as it can enhance storage capacity and improve water quality by promoting mixing and filtration. However, heterogeneity can also pose challenges to MAR by affecting the distribution and movement of water within the aquifer (de Barros et al., 2016; Engel et al., 2021; Eykholt et al., 1999; Perzan et al., 2023a,b ). The impeding clay layers might prevent the recharged water from reaching the targeted depleted aquifers, forming perched water tables above the main aquifer system. Therefore, understanding subsurface heterogeneity is critical for designing effective MAR systems. MAR implementation benefits from our ability to map subsurface materials, including the location and the thickness of impeding layers, and thus identify sites with the potential for maximum impact. This involves site characterization through geological, geophysical, and hydrological studies, as well as hydrogeological modeling to simulate and optimize recharge performance under different subsurface conditions (Hartmann et al., 2017a,b; Uhlemann et al., 2022; Pepin et al., 2022 ). These methods make use of geological maps that rely on the interpretation of surficial geology, borehole lithology, and geophysical methods to offer insights into the type and composition of the subsurface. Furthermore, advances in geophysical imaging methods such as airborne electromagnetics (AEM: Goebel et al., 2019; Knight et al., 2018; Kang et al., 2021 ) and towed transient electromagnetics (tTEM: Behroozmand et al., 2019 ; Auken et al., 2018), have revolutionized our ability to image the subsurface to great depth with high lateral resolution. This capability is exemplified by regional mapping campaigns such as the California Department of Water Resources statewide AEM mapping campaign to image the state’s critical groundwater resources (https://water.ca.gov/programs/sgma/aem  , accessed 1June, 2023). Electromagnetic methods can image resistivity models of the subsurface, a parameter that can be linked to sediment texture (Knight et al., 2021 ). However, resistivity is also controlled by the subsurface saturation state and pore water chemistry (Binley and Slater, 2020 ). By linking resistivity models to adjacent or co-located borehole lithology logs, rock physics transforms can be used to translate the resistivity model to an estimated geological model (Foged et al., 2014; Knight et al., 2018 ). Proper use of geophysical models can provide an excellent starting point for selecting optimal recharge locations (Pepin et al., 2022; Knight et al., 2022 ). Fig. 1   shows examples from two geophysical surveys at proposed Ag-MAR sites from California separated by approximately 18 km. Towed time domain electromagnetics (tTEM) resistivity cross sections through the two sites are given in Fig. 1 a and b, while Fig. 1 c–e show the 1D resistivity profile, cone penetrometer sediment texture log, and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) water content log, respectively, at the dashed black line in Fig. 1 a. In the top example, the subsurface is dominated by laterally extensive, low resistivity features associated with silt and clay-rich sediments, which likely represent poor recharge targets. The bottom example, by contrast, shows a thick region of high resistivity overlying a very low resistivity layer. This likely represents a sand-rich zone overlying a thick clay layer. If this interpretation is correct, getting infiltrating water below this clay layer to the deeper water table would be very difficult, but it may be possible to instead create a perched aquifer overlying the clay layer. These examples highlight how understanding subsurface heterogeneity can inform the assessment and implementation of recharge strategies. Furthermore, integrating these cutting-edge geophysics tools presents an opportunity to refine effective recharge strategies and periodic monitoring of the recharge process as the water makes its way to the target aquifer (Uhlemann et al., 2022 ). The recharge water path also involves various processes like transformation, degradation, retention, mobilization, and transport of contaminants to groundwater. It also acts as an attenuation zone, reducing pollutant concentration through natural processes. Biogeochemical alterations occur in the source water (e.g., BOD, COD, pathogens, organic matter), root zone content (fertilizers, pesticides), and vadose zone (containing oxyanions) along the recharge water flow path. Challenges such as clogging (due to microbial activities, chemical precipitates, suspended solids, sediment, and debris in source water), costs of different recharge technologies, infrastructure development, land acquisition, and landownership identification are discussed in Supplementary Material  I. These limitations underscore the challenges of MAR applications in flat terrain regions and emphasize the need to consider geological, hydrological, social, and economic complexities during implementation.   4 Expanding MAR capacity and effectiveness Implementing MAR technologies in flat valley regions through spreading raises significant concerns about leaching of contaminants to groundwater, especially in areas that have been extensively farmed. The presence of substantial clay and silt layers overlying deep aquifers further complicates MAR efforts, by potentially forming perched aquifers that add weight on clay layers and exacerbate land subsidence in certain regions (Smith and Knight, 2019; Lees et al., 2022a,b ). Furthermore, it is uncertain when and where the recharged water from deeper aquifers will be recoverable, given that deep vadose zone recharge can occur in the order of decades or even centuries. In shallow groundwater regions, especially in areas close to flood plains and riparian areas, MAR applications often improve hydraulic connectivity of groundwater with the surface water and thereby facilitates drainage of recharged water to streams. This process impedes the primary objective of MAR to store water in the aquifer for later use. Although several pilot MAR projects have been initiated in flat terrain regions, MAR has been described as the “moon shot” for replenishing depleted aquifers (Maven’s Notebook, Nov. 19, 2020) and attaining sustainability. Despite the limitations of MAR, global implementation of MAR can reduce groundwater depletion problems (Wada and Heinrich, 2013 ). However, the reliance on flat terrain regions may inadvertently overlook the unique challenges and opportunities present in other topographical settings. As mountainous regions receive higher precipitation than valley aquifers, there's a growing recognition that MAR strategies may need to be adapted for mountainous and hilly terrains. The foundation for implementing MAR in these areas lies in understanding of recharge processes in the mountain aquifer unit and how mountain systems recharge aquifers in valley floors. In general, mountains contribute to two key recharge pathways in the valley floor. These pathways include Mountain Front Recharge (MFR) as a result infiltration of perennial and ephemeral mountain-fed streams in the piedmont zone (Wilson and Guan, 2004 ), and Mountain Block Recharge (MBR) due to subsurface flow from mountain aquifers to valley fill aquifers (Wilson and Guan, 2004; Markovich et al., 2019; Schreiner-McGraw and Ajami, 2022 ). The source of MBR is precipitation that infiltrates through mountain bedrock, thereby contributing to the regional groundwater recharge (Markovich et al., 2019; Wilson and Guan, 2004 ). MBR is controlled by precipitation patterns, lithology, discrete permeable geological features within the mountain block such as steeply dipping fault zones, and fracture density. These features can significantly impact groundwater recharge by creating preferential pathways for groundwater flow (Welch et al., 2012), or creating barriers for groundwater movement (Medici et al., 2020). MFR, on the other hand, is influenced by various factors such as topography, soil characteristics, vegetation cover, and precipitation patterns. This classification accounts for the complexity of groundwater flow in mountainous regions and emphasizes the distinction between recharge pathways within the mountain block and mountain front. Capturing the front-slope flow to enhance MFR or diffuse recharge across the valley is paramount for the future of groundwater as these regions are typically covered by highly permeable sediments. Numerical experiments have shown that extreme events (>25 mm/d) contribute to 50 % of focused recharge in drylands (Schreiner-McGraw et al., 2019 ). The in-place recharge estimates for the Sierra Nevada mountains using the Basin Characterization Model (BCM: Flint et al., 2021 ) indicate significant recharge potential in the mountainous regions (Fig. 2  a), along with substantial in-place runoff directed towards the Central Valley (Fig. 2 b). While the BCM accurately predicts recharge and runoff within individual cells, it lacks consideration of the potential transformation of runoff into recharge in neighboring cells, nor does it address how recharge in one cell may contribute to baseflow in another. This highlights the distinct opportunity presented by mountain regions for exploring and tailoring MAR techniques. However, any recharge enhancement project in the mountain block requires understanding of geological structures such as faults, joints, and fractures (Katsura et al., 2009; Welch and Allen, 2014), and other related lineament (O’Leary et al., 1976), the state of bedrock weathering (Worthington et al., 2016), and groundwater circulation depth (Frisbee et al., 2017 ; Manning et al., 2020). Active circulation depth within the mountain block influences groundwater residence times, and recharge rates to valley aquifers (Goldscheider et al., 2008; Markovich et al., 2019 ; Schaller and Fan, 2009). However, such information is often not available in mountain watersheds given the complexity of recharge processes in high relief terrains and limited availability of observations (Ajami et al., 2011 ; Katsuyama et al., 2005; Tetzlaff and Soulsby, 2008). Under the existing rate of groundwater utilization for consumptive use and chronic groundwater depletion that has been accumulated over several decades, in addition to exploring strategies for efficiently managing water demand and conservation through technologies such as precision agriculture (Bwambale et al., 2022 ), exploring additional ways to purposefully add water to the groundwater seems crucial. The first involves implementing MAR technologies situated along the hillslope/mountain utilizing water collected from hillslope contributing areas or transported from other sources. The second approach focuses on roadside collection and conveyance systems. Fig. 3   provides schematic representations of Hillslope-MAR and Road-MAR. 4.1 Hillslope/mountain flow system Hillslope/mountain recharge initiatives should consider the entire mountain block and foothills regions to manage and enhance recharge. However, this requires understanding of the complex interactions between bedrock hydrogeology and weathering, groundwater circulation depth, and the degree of connectivity between the mountain block and valley fill aquifer. Hence, characterizing hillslope recharge processes will require identifying suitable locations and technologies to enhance hillslope/mountain recharge at a field scale and understanding the sensitivity and contribution of recharge techniques on aquifer replenishment, and its impact on sustainable management strategies. If we take the example of California, hillslopes are the predominant landform units, where the mountain ranges account for 60–70 % of the total landscape contributing flow to the Central Valley aquifer system. Expanding recharge potential beyond the regions in the Central Valley will be an essential addition to the initiatives aiming to successfully replenish the severely depleted groundwater. Enhancing mountain front contributions to increase baseflow in headwater rivers, while perhaps modest in its impact on regional groundwater, can serve as a strategy to alleviate pressure on deep aquifer exploitation during the crop growing season using the increased baseflow. Another important approach involves redirecting runoff and excess water from the mountain front to mountain block regions, which play a significant role in deep aquifer recharge, despite their lesser area compared to the 60–70 % hillslopes landscape contributing to the Central Valley. Inter-annual groundwater level fluctuations in the Central Valley indicate that deep groundwater is hydraulically connected to the neighboring mountain ranges, which raises the possibility of developing MAR techniques to promote upland recharge in the foothills and mountain regions surrounding the Central Valley. Hillslope-driven MAR activities require slope modification that affects surface flow connectivity and flow velocity beyond what is naturally occurring. Moreover, using hillslope for MAR implementation also requires the development of sound site selection procedures that consider the hydrologic significance of these landforms. These include factors such as the amount of precipitation received at higher elevations (including rainfall and snowpack), the size of contributing area, slope length, and presence of lineaments, faults, fractures, and their connectivity. Geology of the hillslopes and mountain fronts covers the early Paleozoic to late Jurassic metamorphic belt in the foothills and dominantly Cretaceous granitic batholite in the upper portion of the Sierra Nevada with fragments of ophiolites, which are dominant formation in the Klamath mountains (Koirala and Hayashi, 2010 ). Mapping the upland areas that are potentially connected and flow contributing to the basin-fill aquifers in the Central Valley would provide the necessary insight into the extent of the hillslope influence in groundwater replenishment. Despite their importance in maintaining groundwater supplies, the process of groundwater recharge on hillslopes is poorly understood, with limited research into the amount and conditions involving topography, climate, vegetation, and geology. Recharge in hillslopes vary depending on the geological setting, the extent of the unsaturated zone, slope, and land cover conditions. In some hillslopes, recharge has been observed at rates of 56 % of those typically observed in flat areas (Tao et al., 2021 ). For instance, Gabrielli and McDonnell (2018)  used isotopic signatures, noble gas temperatures, and an empirical recharge model in the Maimai watershed, revealing the importance of understanding geological controls, such as the extent of secondary porosity (faults or fractures), where 90 % recharge only occurred from 55 % of the annual precipitation. Other studies have demonstrated that hillslope recharge depends on the precipitation intensity, magnitude, and frequency (Allen et al., 2010; Owor et al., 2009; Taylor et al., 2013b ) and may be altered due to climate changes drivers (Taylor et al., 2013a,b ; Scanlon, et al., 2013). Under existing conditions, hillslope/mountain recharge conditions represent a naturally occurring recharge process. In addition to understanding recharge processes in hillslopes and how this process connects to the underlying aquifer, one may ask: What are the possible landscape modifications that can enhance recharge condition while also weighing the feasibility of such modifications? The feasibility of landscape modifications includes legal (changes in the natural scenery of the hillslopes), environmental (unknown effects of the modification), and economical (high cost and long-term commitment are required) implications and monitoring to quantify the impacts over time. For instance, trenching, though it may not be feasible in all locations, has been shown to increase the amount of recharge (Somers et al., 2018 ). Several hillslope modification techniques are available to enhance water infiltration and percolation into the aquifer. Table 1   provides a comprehensive summary of major techniques applicable in the hillslope/mountain domains. An individual or a combination of the techniques may include: constructing runoff collection structures to capture runoff from hillslopes/mountains before it exits the potential recharge zones in the mountain front, construction of diversion structures (weirs and channels) to redirect runoff water and snowmelt in the perennial streams to designated recharge sites in the mountain front, and implementation of various flow regulation mechanisms that include physical and biological systems that regulates the flow of water and enhance infiltration. The implementation of the recharge enhancement techniques requires identifying permeable sediments in the colluvium/channel overlying aquifer streams, paleo-glacial outwash deposits at the mountain front in addition to locating lineaments, fracture systems, faults, and fold systems that facilitate substantial recharge. Additionally, hillslopes play an essential role in the travel time distribution within the subsurface, ultimately affecting the extent of connectivity to streamflow in the valley floors (Allison et al., 1994 ). Improving recharge using these techniques may also lead to an increase in streamflow, and understanding the drawbacks of any of the landscape modifications and assessing their feasibility and impact on the local environment is essential. Hillslope recharge studies are complex and require properly designed monitoring systems. Studies of hillslope processes with respect to water budget and partitioning have relied on studies related to apparent water ages and isotope compositions (Ajami et al., 2011 ; Ma et al., 2009; Eastoe and Long, 2004) and computation of recharge ratio through monitoring of the vadose zone soil moisture dynamics (plant water use patterns) and groundwater table on headwater watershed (Dralle et al., 2023 ). There is a need to assess the potential zoning for groundwater recharge, their connectivity to streams and the deeper aquifer, and the impact and distribution of geo-morphological structures such as lineaments (faults and folds). To evaluate the effectiveness of various techniques, modeling experiments, and field observations are required. Lineaments are geological structures, such as faults, cleavages, fractures, and various discontinuous surfaces, arranged in a straight line or a slight curve (O’Leary et al., 1976). In areas with igneous and metamorphic rocks with poor primary porosity (Sander, 2007 ), such as the Sierra Mountains east of the Central Valley, joints and faulted terrains play an important role in subsurface water flow. A high lineament-length density infers high secondary porosity in the crystalline aquifer, which indicates a zone with high groundwater occurrence, flow, and recharge (Yeh et al., 2009 ). The rule of thumb is that the higher the lineament density, the more likely high recharge will occur. A lineament density of 0–0.6 km/km2  indicates poor groundwater recharge potential, while a density of 8–10 km/km2  indicates a very high potential (Mussa et al., 2020 ). In addition to slope modifications and placement of recharge systems in areas with increased secondary porosity, foothills with paleo glacial outwash deposits at the base of the Sierra Mountain (Bennett et al., 2006 ) play an important role in groundwater recharge. These deposits consist of sand, gravel, and other sediment deposited by melting glaciers, allowing water to seep through. Placement of the recharge structures on the outwash deposits on the hillslopes/foothills act as the attenuation zone (i.e., a natural filter) for removing impurities and contaminants from water as it passes through the porous sediment. The impacts of recharge enhancement or hillslope modification systems require a wide range of understanding beyond the technical, economic, and environmental appropriateness and feasibility. The legality and acceptability of engineered systems on hillslopes must be explored.  4.2 Roadside collection and conveyance system Substantial runoff can be generated in locations with a high concentration of roads running through hillslopes and mountain fronts. The magnitudes of runoff and recharge (see Fig. 2 ) shows the significance of the mountain landscape for enhancing recharge activities. The primary focus of road system design is the structural integrity of the road and associated hydraulic structures, with the goal of preventing damage from large amounts of runoff that often flow through the road system network. Roadside drainage systems are also usually discussed in connection with water conservation and reduction of the amount and erosive forces of generated runoff. This is normally discussed within the context of green road initiatives (Mulmi, 2009; Woldearegay et al., 2015; Djalante, and Oneyama, 2020 ) such as EPA’s Green infrastructure design (Foster et al., 2011 ; Beauchamp, and Adamowsk, 2013) and urban sustainable drainage system (Lentini et al., 2022; Charlesworth et al., 2003 ). This review emphasizes the significance of utilizing the abundant water resources collected in roadside channel systems by repurposing the drainage systems to serve both transportation functions (safely and quickly removing runoff from the area to prevent flooding and erosion of the surrounding) and water conservation (as a new source of water for recharge) and the position and distribution of lineaments and other geological structures (fractures, faults, etc.) (see Fig. 4  ). It is important to note that repurposing road systems for water conservation and recharge may require complex design and regulatory considerations. Highway and road design standards for water conservation aim to minimize or eliminate adverse impacts on natural resources while considering environmental values and public services (e.g., California Department of Water Resources, 2020 ). However, one approach will not fit all design needs. Engineers must be aware of and sensitive to the land use and community context, including design objectives related to community benefits associated with water resources. One such objective in existing design standards is the use of exfiltration (recharging trench) in road systems. This would promote recharge, reduce peak flow by allowing more water to infiltrate, and improve water resource sustainability. An exfiltration trench is an underground drainage system consisting of a perforated pipe surrounded by natural or artificial aggregate that stores and infiltrates runoff. Exfiltration trenches comprise an inlet and elevation control between the outlets and a catch basin (retention space) connected to a perforated pipe (trench) segment, which collects stormwater runoff (Fig. 5  ). The stormwater is then transported through the pipe perforations and delivered into the surrounding coarse aggregate covered by external filter fabric. Exfiltration trenches are usually recommended in areas where the available water management facilities are limited and high right-of-way acquisition costs are anticipated. Moreover, the success of exfiltration trenches relies on hydrogeological conditions suitable for runoff infiltration (i.e., permeable soils where hydraulic conductivity exceeds 3.05 x 10-6  cum/m2  per foot of head) (Chin and Jones, 2017 ). The exfiltration design considers stormwater as a resource, whereas other road system designs frequently consider stormwater as a liability that needs to be removed for the safety of structures and drivers. To fully integrate recharge functionality into road infrastructure, the effectiveness of existing exfiltration systems still must be assessed to determine their potential role in groundwater replenishment. This information could be used to optimize the management and number of exfiltration structures to increase their recharge capacity. Furthermore, issues related to clogging require additional costs for future maintenance and/or replacement in planning these systems.  4.3 Road system based MAR The road system-based MAR initiative includes the implementation of exfiltration trenches along the road infrastructure (e.g., culverts, roadside channels, etc.) and the design and implementation of independent recharge structure (e.g., recharge basin, drywells, etc.) that uses water captured by the roadside channels as the main source. The application of drainage systems that favor stormwater reuse, infiltration, and peak flow reduction within the built environment has been previously introduced as a concept. These technologies are also called sustainable urban drainage systems, low-impact development practices, or stormwater structural best management practices (Sansalone and Teng, 2004 ). The recharge water source for these systems is the stormwater runoff collected from the built/impervious surfaces. Unless treated, this runoff can contain higher concentrations of heavy metals such as zinc, copper, cadmium, chromium, iron, and nickel (Charters et al., 2021; Grantano et al., 2003; Hvitved-Jacobson and Yenisei, 1991 ) than the runoff water from surrounding hillslopes. In addition to the water quality issues, implementing exfiltration trenches or other sustainable urban drainage systems can be costly due to the need for new construction and major retrofitting. The exfiltration system's performance depends on the size of the trench and the contributing area of the runoff. For instance, some designs have shown significant recharge capacity, such as the 2.5 km exfiltration system in Etobicoke, Toronto, that completely captured a long-duration rainfall event, ≤28 mm over 22.5 h overflowing to the storm sewer (Li et al., 2015 ). In non-urbanized systems such as roads outside cities and townships, the availability and less right-of-way acquisition costs increase the viability of implementing such technologies on a scale required to address water deficits. Retrofitting and rebuilding exfiltration systems in existing roadside drainage systems and their environmental impact required a case-by-case evaluation of the system with their contributing area. One advantage of roadside drainage systems in MAR is that they can be scaled up to the level required to address water deficits. The dominant recharge water source of stormwater in roadside systems is from the contributing area rather than the paved surface of the road, resulting in smaller quantities of particulate, aqueous, and complex constituents in the roadside channels. There is significant literature on the design, performance, and limitations of exfiltration trenches. However, expanding and redesigning these systems to the scale required to mitigate groundwater depletion requires a high level of coordination and planning. The implementation of roadside MAR relies heavily on the collaboration and integration among different departments such as transportation, water resources, county and state-level administrators, and farmers, which entails addressing a complex set of issues, including financing, design, construction, and understanding the hydrologic and geologic conditions of road segments. Roads connecting states and cities typically traverse non-urbanized landscapes, drainage networks, and hillslopes, requiring less right-of-way acquisition costs than urbanized systems. Roadside drainage systems play a crucial role in collecting and discharging runoff water into surrounding water bodies or natural drainage systems, which helps to dilute contaminant concentrations from impervious and traffic systems. They are designed to quickly remove stormwater (Brown and Farrelly, 2009; Novotny et al., 2010 ), control water amount to prevent flooding (Novotny et al., 2010 ), and to protect the structures' functions and integrity. These are typically paved channels with steep longitudinal slopes to attain safe and efficient drainage to prevent flooding and erosion. If directed to a right-of-way site with properly designed retention, exfiltration, and flow modification systems, the collected water can be an important source for MAR. Another aspect of roadside drains on mountainsides and hillslopes is that they pass through areas with a high density of faults with potential connectivity to the deep aquifer that may facilitate a faster recharge. Diverting large volumes of water in roadside channels and transporting it to lineaments, fracture systems, faults, and fold zones and other highly permeable sediments in the colluvium and incised channel fills may be an important way to achieve groundwater sustainability. Lineaments and related geological structures can act as vertical downwards water conduits from faulted or fractured zones to the aquifer overlaid by unconsolidated material. In addition to the fractures, faults, and related lineaments, diverting runoff water towards the alluvial fan and permeable sediment deposits that are connected to the deeper aquifer systems (Guo, 2024 ) results in more recharge in the mountain front. The mapping of lineament features on various types of maps or remotely sensed data is key for groundwater exploration (Sander, 2007; Kellgren, 2002; Kellgren and Sander, 1997 ), especially in areas with igneous and metamorphic rocks with low primary porosity, commonly referred to as hard rock terrain. Usually, it is measured as a lineament density per unit length or area. For example, the Sierra Nevada Mountains east of the Central Valley are highly faulted, with lineaments dissecting the landscapes mainly on the water divide or the foothills. However, the presence of lineaments does not always indicate connectivity to the regional aquifers, and compressional stress perpendicular to the lineament may negatively affect its transmissive properties (Banks and Robins, 2002). Combinations of high lineament and drainage density in a given area may also imply groundwater movement away from the desired site rather than to the areas suitable for groundwater exploration (e.g., Sander, 2007 ).   5 Future perspectives and research directions This paper questions the extent of existing groundwater replenishment strategies and the associated issues affecting sustainability. As water demand continues to rise for agricultural, municipal, and domestic use, the path to sustainability becomes increasingly intricate. Acknowledging the need for customizing different MAR technologies to suit each site's unique conditions and ensuring optimal benefits while minimizing potential risks is essential. It's also important to acknowledge that a one-size-fits-all solution may not be feasible due to varying geographical factors, aquifer types, and temporal dynamics. Consequently, there's a growing need to explore novel approaches to groundwater replenishment and gain a more comprehensive understanding of the strengths and limitations of existing methods to ensure sustainability. In certain regions, like those reliant on paleo groundwater reservoirs such as sections of the Ogallala aquifer, recharge technologies may not offer a viable solution due to unique hydrogeological conditions and a history of long-term depletion. In such cases, it becomes essential to consider alternative strategies for managing water demand and enhancing water conservation, such as implementing precision agriculture (Bwambale et al., 2022 ) and improving overall water use efficiency to extend the usable lifespan of these aquifers. Achieving sustainability in other aquifers requires answering key questions such as the amount of water added through current MAR initiatives, how this compares to a region's deficit level, and whether existing experiences are guiding us towards sustainability. Additionally, we need to understand and develop new potential recharge capabilities that can be maximized to reverse present deficits and ensure a sustainable groundwater supply to support the economy. The highly folded and faulted geology of hillslopes and mountains has important implications for groundwater recharge strategies. Designing and implementing these strategies requires careful consideration of those lineaments in the bedrock and their connection to the aquifer. Although locating and identifying these lineaments in complex geological areas can be challenging, there are regional resources like the California geologic database (https://maps.conservation.ca. gov/geology/ , accessed on 1 July 2023) containing information on faults, folds, and joints and understanding various aspects such as their orientation, aperture, depth, and properties of the surrounding rock formation (e.g., Singhal, 2008; Henriksen and Braathen, 2006 ) can improve the effectiveness of recharge projects. However, saturating unconsolidated earth material during groundwater recharge projects carries risks. Saturation can alter the pressure and shear stresses in the slope and underlying bedrock and lead to instability (e.g., Huggel et al., 2012; Lanni et al., 2013 ). Before expanding recharge projects to hillslopes and mountain fronts, a landslide susceptibility assessment is necessary, considering factors such as lithology, elevation, slope angle and aspect, curvature of the relief, and soil depth (Duan and Grant, 2000; Schmidt et al., 2001; Minder et al., 2009; Bednarik et al., 2012 ; Hofierka, 2003; Krcho, 1990, 1999; Irigaray and Chacón 1996; Pauditš 2005; Lee and Touch 2006). Slopes with angles greater than 25 degrees facing south and southwest, convergent and convex slopes are more susceptible to landslides due to water and material accumulation at the base of the slope or tension cracks forming at the crest. To make the most of the lineaments and fracture/faults distribution in mountain fronts and foothills, carefully considering site-specific factors when designing and implementing groundwater recharge strategies is crucial. It is critical to identify faults, fractures, and joints in the bedrock and their connection to the deeper aquifer. For example, databases of California faults, folds, and joints are available and collected using various techniques such as aerial photography, remote sensing, geophysical surveys, and drilling (Kellett et al., 2004 ′ Kresic, 1995; Sander, 2007 ). Understanding the connectivity of lineaments would benefit from using the recent development of high-resolution geophysics scanning technologies imaging system technologies described in Section 3.5. These also include other techniques, such as other geophysical techniques and tracer tests by injecting a known quantity of a tracer substance (e.g., Goldscheider et al., 2008 ), pumping tests that allow determining the permeability and hydraulic conductivity (Maréchal et al., 2004 ), and hydrogeochemical analysis, including isotopic and chemical signatures of the water (Cochand et al., 2020 ). Moreover, passive methods can be used to show how groundwater levels respond to natural perturbations such as atmospheric pressure fluctuations and Earth tides (He et al., 2023; Toll and Rasmussen, 2007 ). This can provide information on hydraulic properties and connectivity of a fault-damage zone within crystalline rock. Accurate estimation of recharge in mountain areas and understanding hillslope processes are contingent upon appropriately representing topography in numerical models, which significantly influence moisture redistribution. Furthermore, the limited availability of weather stations in the mountainous watershed and uncertainties in gridded precipitation and temperature products further influence the accurate estimation of water available for recharge. Recent studies by Schreiner-McGraw and Ajami (2020  and 2022) underscore the substantial impact of precipitation and temperature data uncertainty on simulated groundwater recharge from mountainous watersheds. The process of implementing and evaluating hillslope recharge, or Hillslope-MAR, benefits from numerical modeling-based analysis of various landscape modification scenarios. This entails utilizing hydrologic models to assess the efficacy of different slope modification technologies listed in Table 1  while accurately representing the topographic features and comparing them to naturally occurring recharge while monitoring fluxes. To achieve these goals, several types of models are employed in the modeling investigation. One example is the coupled Hydrus 1D and KINEROS2 model developed by Chen et al. (2022) , which can be used to analyze the impact of microtopographic changes such as berms for slope modification and changes in roughness associated with grass strips, among other factors. Additionally, models that use the Saint Venant formulation of surface flow, such as FullSWOF developed (Delestre et al., 2014; Crompton et al., 2023 ), can also be applied for this purpose. Physics-based distributed models such as MIKE SHE (Refshaard and Storm, 1995 ), HydroGeosphere (Brunner and Simmons, 2012 ), and ParFlow (Maxwell et al., 2011 ) are particularly useful in assessing the impact of recharge enhancement on hillslopes as they can be used to connect scales from hillslope runoff to recharge. These models use high-resolution digital elevation information and other datasets that are not typically collected in traditional modeling exercises, such as roughness, surface and near-surface layer conductivities, and depth of impeding layers, among others, to parameterize land surface and subsurface hydrologic characteristics. These models either couple or fully integrate the 2D overland flow equation with the 3D Richard’s equation to solve variably saturated subsurface flow. Given the high computational demand of most physics-based integrated hydrologic models, it is important to develop and implement models that are computationally efficient and capable of accurately simulating diverse flow processes. Moreover, the application of downslope travel distance concept in hillslopes with impervious or leaky impeding layers (Jackson et al., 2014; Meles Bitew et al., 2020 ), provides important insight into the extent and amount of recharge enhancement activities in complex landscapes. Here are some of the main questions (See Supplementary Material  II for possible research questions) related to investigating hillslope-based recharge potentials to understand controlling processes, evaluation of impacts, and to assist decision-making.1) What are the most effective hillslope modification activities for maximizing groundwater recharge on mountain landscapes?  2) How can roadside infrastructure, such as road channels and exfiltration structures, be designed and implemented to enhance groundwater recharge potential?  3) What are the long-term performance, maintenance requirements, and potential environmental impacts associated with utilizing stormwater runoff from roadside channels for groundwater recharge?  4) What are the optimal design practices and cost-effective approaches such as right-of-way acquisition costs, maintenance needs, and potential environmental implications for implementing MAR using water captured from hillslopes and/or roadside channels?    The modeling considerations requirements are suggested but not limited to specialized models that incorporate functionalities to evaluate slope modifications. With the objective of investigating mechanisms and processes controlling groundwater rechange and the ability to conceptualize the slope modification techniques (trenches and dikes along the hillslope contours, grass strips, construction of berms, micro basins) in order to fully understand the processes and predict the necessary fluxes.  6 Summary and discussion As global freshwater demand continues to increase, the need for sustainable and efficient water management practices becomes more critical. MAR has emerged as a potential solution for enhancing water security and meeting the growing water demands. The global MAR interest is expected to grow significantly in the next few decades due to the increasing demand for water and the need to address issues such as groundwater depletion, seawater intrusion, and climate change. The Flood-MAR methods, particularly Ag-MAR, have shown promising impact regarding the quantity of water recharged towards storing water in threatened aquifers. However, implementation of these methods for recharging runoff water is limited to certain conditions, i.e., specific time (during winter and the rainy season), limited space (in the flood plains with low depth to groundwater table), and farmlands with suitable subsurface systems for MAR and cooperative landowners. When problems of flooding and over-drafted groundwater coexist, an integrated approach towards maximizing infiltration before water reaches flood plains is preferred. In areas where water is abundant for only a short period (such as a season), expanding the area for MAR beyond limited spaces that are allocated for surface infiltration is necessary. Methods that combine common sense floodwater management- such as having too much water; and not having enough water, as evidenced by critically over-drafted groundwater basins (e.g., Jacobson, 2019), require looking into MAR techniques that best fit the site and community needs. This paper recommends using mountain/hillslope managed aquifer recharge (Hillslope -MAR) and water captured by the roadside channel networks as a potential new water source and setting for MAR applications. It suggests comparing Mountain/Hillslope MAR to currently employed Ag-MAR and Flood-MAR approaches while highlighting potential limitations such as costs, access, and hillslope stability. The paper raises questions such as whether faults/fractures are required for mountain/hillslope recharge and how the mineralogy/rock type/geology of the bedrock impacts water quality and recharge. It also suggests a road system-based managed aquifer recharge (Road-MAR) initiative that involves implementing exfiltration trenches, which utilize water captured by the roadside channels as a source. Another significant aspect of roadside drains on mountainsides and hillslopes is their potential to pass through areas with a high concentration of lineaments, which could enhance connectivity to deep aquifers and facilitate faster recharge. In conclusion, this paper emphasizes the importance of exploring new ways of groundwater recharge and understanding the strengths and limitations of existing strategies, particularly implementation of hillslope modification to maximize recharge. The impacts of recharge enhancement or hillslope modification systems also require a wide range of understanding beyond the technical, economic, and environmental appropriateness and feasibility. The legality and acceptability of engineered systems on hillslopes must be explored well. Further research is needed to evaluate the potential benefits and limitations of mountain/hillslope MAR compared to currently employed Ag-MAR and Flood-MAR approaches in valley floors.
1 Introduction Direct field measurement of soil hydraulic properties poses significant challenges. As a result, these properties are often obtained in the laboratory using small, undisturbed soil samples or indirectly estimated through pedotransfer functions (PTFs) based on the readily available basic properties of the soil. Equilibrium methods, such as pressure plate extractors and sandbox apparatus, are traditionally employed in the laboratory to acquire water retention data. These methods involve establishing hydrostatic equilibrium between a soil sample and a porous medium at a certain pressure head. The HYPROP system (Hydraulic Property Analyzer, Meter Group Inc., Pullman, WA, USA) is an automated evaporation-based benchtop laboratory system (Schindler et al., 2010b, 2010a ) that is increasingly becoming the standard approach for measuring soil hydraulic properties in the laboratory (Haghverdi et al., 2018; Schindler et al., 2016 ). It has several advantages over traditional equilibrium methods, such as pressure plate extractors and sandbox apparatus, including the rapid measurement of high-resolution soil water retention and hydraulic conductivity data in wet and intermediate ranges, with minimal variability between replicates (Schelle et al., 2013b ). The HYPROP measurements can be complemented with dry-end data from the WP4C Dew Point PotentioMeter instrument (METER Group, Inc., Pullman, WA, USA) to capture the entire soil water retention curve (SWRC). The parametric and pseudo-continuous PTFs (PC-PTFs) can be used to estimate the SWRC (Haghverdi et al., 2012; Patil and Singh, 2016; Singh et al., 2020 ). The PC-PTF is a strategy for developing PTFs for continuous soil water retention estimation, employing machine learning approaches like artificial neural networks (PCNN -PTF) and support vector machines (Haghverdi et al., 2014 ). This approach learns the shape of the SWRC directly from the actual measured water retention data, making high-resolution measured data crucial for adequate model training (Haghverdi et al., 2018 ). Haghverdi et al. (2018)  developed the first HYPROP-based water retention PCNN -PTFs models using a Turkish data set and reported promising results. Then, the first international evaporation/HYPROP-based water retention and hydraulic conductivity PCNN -PTFs were developed by Singh et al. (2021, 2020) , utilizing the international dataset published by Schindler and Müller (2017) . The outstanding performance of these PTFs (RMSE of water retention = 0.043 cm3  cm−3 , RMSE of hydraulic conductivity (Log K(h)) = 0.52) positions them among the most accurate international PTFs available for estimating soil hydraulic properties. The reliability of PTFs developed using laboratory data should be examined when applied to new soils outside their training bounds and under field conditions. Laboratory measurements using small soil samples may not accurately represent actual field conditions due to scale mismatch and field variability (Hopmans et al., 2002 ). While some studies have compared in-situ to laboratory-measured SWRCs (e.g., Campbell et al., 2018; Ishimwe et al., 2018 ) and evaluated laboratory-based PTFs against field data (e.g., Wassar et al., 2016 , and Gribb et al., 2009 ), there is a notable gap in research comparing HYPROP-WP4C data and HYPROP-based PTFs with in-situ soil water retention measurements. Inverse modeling (IM) serves as an alternative method for estimating hydraulic model parameters using in situ data collected through transient water flow experiments (Hopmans et al., 2002; Šimůnek et al., 1998a, 1998b ). IM allows for the simultaneous estimation of water retention and hydraulic conductivity functions, eliminating the need for achieving hydrostatic equilibrium (Hopmans et al., 2002; Šimůnek et al., 1998a, 1998b ). Inverse methods operate by minimizing an objective function that gauges the deviations between measured and predicted variables, such as water retention data. Several studies have utilized the IM technique to estimate hydraulic parameters with the HYDRUS model (da Silva et al., 2020; Ket et al., 2018; le Bourgeois et al., 2016; Naseri et al., 2022; Pinheiro et al., 2019; Rashid et al., 2015; Šimůnek et al., 1999 ). To achieve a unique solution, input data with a broad range of water content, soil pressure head, and additional retention curve data obtained through simultaneous measurement of pressure head and water content in the soil profile is necessary (Šimůnek et al., 1999 ). Recent advancements in soil sensing technologies offer scientists a tool for rapid and accurate measurement of water content and tension. Wang et al. (1998)  employed simultaneous measurements of soil water content and tension from TDR probes and tensiometers, respectively, to develop and test infiltration models through IM. Schelle et al. (2013a)  proposed that instrumentation of weighable lysimeters equipped with soil moisture and tension sensors can significantly enhance parameter estimation through the inverse solution. In their IM experiments, Rezaei et al. (2016)  utilized tension disc infiltration measurements along with TDR-derived soil moisture content to compare in-situ and laboratory soil hydraulic properties. However, with some exceptions, there is a shortage of IM studies employing simultaneous in-situ measurements of soil tension and water content for estimating the SWRC. The main objective of this study was to assess soil water retention data obtained from the HYPROP-WP4C system and the HYPROP-based PCNN -PTF approach, utilizing in situ soil moisture sensor measurements from irrigated turfgrass research plots in inland southern California. Additional objectives included (I) evaluating the performance of HYPROP-based PCNN -PTFs against the Rosetta model (Schaap et al., 2001 ), one of the most widely used parametric PTFs, and (II) comparing the parametrization of the van Genuchten model (van Genuchten, 1980 ) using HYPROP-WP4C data with those calculated by IM using the HYDRUS-1D model and in-situ soil moisture and tension data.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Study area and irrigation trial The study site was located at the University of California Riverside Agricultural Experiment Station (33◦57′47.0″N 117◦20′13.4″W) in Riverside, California, with a well-drained low-runoff Hanford coarse sandy loam soil (websoilsurvey.sc.egov.usda.gov ). The study area consisted of 12 hybrid bermudagrass irrigation research plots (3.7 m × 3.7 m), each receiving a different irrigation treatment via a Weathermatic Smartline 4800 controller (Telsco Industries, Inc., Garland, TX, USA). Irrigation levels varied from 39 % to 66 % reference evapotranspiration (ETo ). Irrigation frequency for half the plots was set to 3 days per week, while the remaining plots were under an “on-demand” irrigation scenario where the smart controller autonomously regulated the frequency based on the evaporative demand. The soil characteristics of the research plots are shown in Table 1  . One plot was excluded from this study due to sensor malfunction issues. Readers are referred to (Haghverdi et al., 2021 ) for more information about the irrigation trial.  2.2 In situ measurements Near-surface soil moisture data were collected from all 11 plots between May and September 2019. Each plot was instrumented with a pair of SDI-12 Digital Time Domain Transmissometer (TDT) soil water content (Acclima Inc., Meridian, ID, USA) and MPS6 (METER Group, Inc., Pullman, WA, USA) soil tension sensors placed side-by-side at approximately 10 cm of depth. The DataSnap (Acclima Inc., Meridian, ID, USA) and EM50 (METER Group, Inc., Pullman, WA, USA) loggers were used to collect soil moisture data every 30 min. The TDT sensor has a measurement range of 0 to 100 % volumetric water content (VWC) with a 0.06 % resolution and accuracy of ± 2 %. The MPS6 sensor has a measurement range of 9 to 100,000 kPa with a 0.1 kPa resolution and accuracy of ± (10 % of reading + 2 kPa) from 9 to 100 kPa, according to the manufacturer. The MPS6 determines the water potential of its porous ceramic disc, which comes into hydraulic equilibrium with its surrounding soil. The raw data were filtered for obvious measurement errors outside the physically possible ranges. If either of the two measurements (i.e., soil moisture tension and TDT readings) did not contain meaningful readings, data corresponding to that timestamp was disregarded. Two soil cores (250 cm3  stainless-steel cylinders – inside diameter: 8 cm, height: 5 cm) from each plot were collected from areas surrounding the soil moisture sensors in early 2020. Initially, all the plots were irrigated to refill the shallow layer to saturation. Soil coring started after a few days when the plots reached their field capacity, with two plots sampled weekly. Sampling continued for approximately one month. Soil moisture sensor readings from all plots were recorded just before soil sampling to develop site-specific linear calibration equations, assuming no sensor-to-sensor variability. No irrigation was applied during the sampling period, leading to a gradual decline in soil moisture due to transpiration and deep percolation. The composite dataset was assumed to represent the wet-to-dry SWRC. For the TDT sensors, the factory-calibrated raw measurements (VWCsensor  ) were plotted against the measured volumetric water content data (VWCcalibrated  ) to develop the following linear calibration equation:(1) VW C calibrated   = 0.6909 × V W C sensor   + 0.0568 ; R  2  = 0.69      For the MPS6 sensors, the measured volumetric water content data were converted to equivalent soil tension values using the VG equation with parameters obtained from HYPROP measurements. Then, the MPS6 soil tension data (Tensionsensor  ) were plotted against the back-calculated soil tension (Tensioncalibrated  ) values to develop the following linear calibration equation.(2) Tensio n calibrated   = 0.8667 × T e n s i o n sensor   + 11.706 ; R  2  = 0.92       2.3 Laboratory measurements The laboratory SWRCs were determined for the soil cores using the HYPROP-WP4C system. All samples were saturated. Subsequently, two vertically aligned tensiometers were installed in two holes created with a small auger, positioning the tips of the tensiometers 1.25 cm below and above the center of the cylinder (2.5 cm). Throughout the HYPROP measurement campaigns, the soil tensions at the two tensiometers were automatically monitored using HYPROP-VIEW software, while the weight of each sample was continuously recorded. The measurement campaign spanned 5 to 7 days for each soil sample. Following the completion of HYPROP measurements, the WP4C was employed to measure dry-end (∼pF>4) soil water retention data. A total of 4–5 subsamples (each ∼ 7 cm3 ) were collected from the top, middle, and bottom of the original undisturbed sample with varying water contents. These subsamples were sliced off the original sample and stored in capped small sample cups (15 cm3  capacity). The soil tension of each subsample was measured using the WP4C, and the weight of the sample was immediately recorded. Finally, oven-dry weight was obtained for the subsamples and the remaining soil material from HYPROP, which was used to determine the dry bulk density (BD) of the soil (Blake and Hartge, 2018 ). The soil hydraulic parameters obtained by fitting the VG model (Eq. (3) ) for each soil sample during the evaporation experiment were inputted from the HYPROP-FIT software. HYPROP-FIT works based on a revised version of SHYPFIT2.0 (Peters and Wolfgang, 2015 ) to estimate the best parameter combination.(3) θ h    = θ r  + θ s  - θ r   1 + α h    n     m       (4) m = 1 - 1 / n     where θ    is volumetric moisture content [cm3  cm−3 ] at matric potential h  [cm]; θ r     [cm3  cm−3 ]; and θ s     [cm3  cm−3 ] are residual and saturated moisture contents, respectively; α    [cm−1 ] and n  are curve-shaped parameters. Large values of n  result in a steeper curve and lower values of α  indicate a larger air-entry value.  2.4 Pedotransfer functions The laboratory measured data via the HYPROP-WP4C system and field data collected via soil moisture sensors were used to evaluate the performance of PCNN -PTF (Singh et al., 2020 ) and Rosetta (Schaap et al., 2001 ). Fig. 1   shows the textural distribution of the soil cores collected from the hybrid bermudagrass irrigation plots. The PCNN -PTF (a three-layer feed-forward perceptron NN model) was trained using a combination of the international dataset published by (Schindler and Müller, 2017 ) and a Turkish dataset by (Haghverdi et al., 2018 ). Soil texture (SSC), BD and soil tension were used as inputs to the model, and the output was VWC. The hydraulic properties of the soils in both datasets were measured using the evaporation experiments and the HYPROP system. Readers are referred to (Singh et al., 2020 ) for more information about the development of the international HYPROP-based PCNN -PTF used in this study. SWRC estimations using the parametric model Rosetta were also made with SSC and BD as inputs. Rosetta is an ANN-based PTF that uses a hierarchical approach to suit specific cases of input data available to estimate water retention VG parameters, saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ks ), and unsaturated hydraulic conductivity. Rosetta was used for estimating the VG parameters of the SWRC utilizing the nonlinear least-squares optimization program RETC (van Genuchten, 1991 ):  2.5 Inverse modeling using HYDRUS-1D In this study, the HYDRUS-1D (Rassam et al., 2018; Šimůnek et al., 1998a, 1998b ) model was utilized to estimate the in-situ soil water dynamics at the burial depth of the sensors (10 cm). HYDRUS-1D is a computer program that applies the Richards equation (Richards, 1931 ) for unsaturated, non-steady flow in the soils.(5) ∂ θ  ∂ t   = ∂ ∂ z   K h    ∂ h  ∂ z   + 1           where t  is time [T], z  is the vertical distance [L], h  is the soil moisture tension [L], and K  is the hydraulic conductivity [L/T] which is a function of h . Soil water flow simulation using HYDRUS-1D requires knowledge of the hydraulic parameters, head and flow boundaries, atmospheric boundary conditions, and time-dependent inputs. Simulations were performed at a daily timestep to better highlight the changes in soil moisture dynamics due to variations of meteorological conditions such as rainfall and evapotranspiration fluxes. The free/zero-gradient drainage boundary condition is suitable for water flow simulation of unsaturated soil in which the soil domain of interest is not affected by groundwater. Therefore, a free drainage boundary condition was assigned to the bottom of the flow domain, and an atmospheric boundary condition was assigned to the soil surface. The atmospheric boundary condition at the surface was described using ETo  measurements taken from the nearest California Irrigation Management Information System (CIMIS) station #44, located about 260 m from the site. The time-dependent inputs are the combined irrigation and precipitation rate [LT−1 ] (sum of the values for input into the model), evaporation rate [LT−1 ], and transpiration rate [LT−1 ]. The evaporation (E) and transpiration (T) rates must be input as separate values, which was achieved as follows (Belmans et al., 1983 ):(6) E = E T . e - k . L A I       (7) T = E T - E     where k  is the extinction coefficient for solar radiation and LAI is the plant’s leaf area index [L2/L-2 (−|-)]. A k  value of 0.39 was used for HYDRUS-1D simulations. The LAI of hybrid bermudagrass was reported to be low (around 2), especially in the late summer months (Fontanier and Steinke, 2017 ). Thus, our study assumed LAI to be 2 from May to September. The observation nodes were set at 10 cm following the location of the TDT and MPS6 sensors. At the beginning of the simulation in the soil profile domain, the soil moisture was set to the initial observation from TDT sensors. HYDRUS-1D estimates root water uptake via the model proposed by (Feddes et al., 1978 ), where root water uptake rates are assigned according to the soil tension at the point of interest. The root distribution was assumed to be 1.0 (maximum number of roots possible) between the soil surface and a 10 cm depth and to decrease linearly from 1.0 to 0.0 (no roots) from a 10 cm depth to a 50 cm depth. Inverse solutions to flow problems can be solved where measured data is used to estimate soil hydraulic parameters. For the inverse modeling utilizing HYDRUS-1D, the objective function was minimized using the Levenberg-Marquardt nonlinear minimization (Marquardt, 1963 ). For the optimization of the initial VG parameters (Table 2  ), a combination of three sets of data, i.e., the water content in daily time steps θ(t) from the TDT sensors, soil water tension in daily time steps h(t) from the MPS6 sensors, retention pairs θ(h) from simultaneous measurements of TDT and MPS-6 were used. Raw sensor data were averaged to obtain mean daily values. All parameters of the VG equation (Eq. (3) ) for the SWRC were optimized. Ks data were obtained from the HYPROP-FIT.  2.6 Performance assessment To evaluate the performance of the SWRCs estimated by PCNN -PTF and Rosetta PTF, the root mean square error (RMSE , Eq.
