The texture and water retention data are shown in Fig. 1 . Samples belonged to loamy sand (n = 1) and sandy loam (n = 10) soil textures. The BD values ranged from 1.49 to 1.90 g cm−3  with an average of 1.72 g cm−3 . The slight variability in soil texture and BD among samples shows that spatial heterogeneity exists even in relatively small areas. The bermudagrass plots were under deficit irrigation treatments, with the highest irrigation treatment being 66 % ETo . This allowed us to have a high range of the in-situ soil moisture tension observed in the field, especially from the lowest deficit irrigation treatments, therefore providing retention data ranging from pF (the logarithmic transformation of soil tension in cm of water) equal to 2 up to roughly 4.2 (permanent wilting point) for most of the plots. The laboratory-obtained SWRCs covered the entire curve range from saturation to air-dry tension, with HYPROP data covering the wet and intermediate ranges and WP4C data covering the dry end. Fig. 2   depicts a time series of soil moisture and tension data measured in the field at 30-minute intervals. Fig. 3   shows the measured and estimated SWRCs in this study. An abrupt steepening of the slope close to the saturation indicates a distinct air-entry value, the tension at which moisture begins to drain from the soil pores. The lab-obtained SWRCs had a similar shape, indicating comparable air entry and the sudden reduction in soil moisture as tension increased. The MP6 sensors had an upper limit of −9 kPa (pF = ∼2), which is the air entry value of the sensor, thus resulting in a lack of in-situ water retention points close to saturation (Campbell et al., 2018 ). There were only a few moisture retention data points in the wet range for the in-situ data because most of the data were greater than the pF value of 2. For instance, only ∼ 1.5 % of retention points were in the wet region for the data collected at the 30-minute interval for 2019, ∼70 % of data lies in the intermediate range, and ∼ 28 % in the dry region. There were no retention points in the wet region for the daily average of data collected during the summer of 2019. Previous studies have shown that differences between laboratory and field measurements of soil hydraulic properties are attributed to several factors, including hysteresis and entrapped air (Bordoni et al., 2017; Pirone et al., 2014; Schuh et al., 1988 ), inadequate representation of large pores in the laboratory (Field et al., 1984 ), spatial variability, sample disturbance (Field et al., 1984; Ishimwe et al., 2018; Schuh et al., 1988 ), and sample size-related scale effects (Pachepsky et al., 2001; Schuh et al., 1988 ). The in-situ SWRCs demonstrated good agreement with the lab SWRCs for most samples, particularly within the pF 2 up to approximately 3.5 range. Beyond this point, a more gradual decline in soil moisture was observed as tension increased. This finding aligns with a study conducted by Campbell et al. (2018)  on similar soil textures, where they reported strong agreement between lab and in-situ data for pF ranging from around 2 to 3.7 for sandy loam and loamy sand. Notably, Campbell et al. (2018)  also employed HYPROP and MPS6, contributing to the observed similarities between the findings of the two studies. However, our field data exhibited more scatter, primarily because Campbell et al. (2018)  only used drying in situ data, excluding wetting data that could reveal distinct patterns and deviations from drying data due to hysteresis. In contrast, Iiyama’s in-situ SWRCs showed approximately 10 % smaller VWC than the lab SWRCs (Iiyama, 2016 ). This difference was attributed to the natural conditions of hysteresis, causing the wetting process to consistently yield smaller moisture values than the drying process for a given soil tension. We did not observe the same pattern in all our plots. This is partly attributed to different instruments and sensors used in the two studies for laboratory and field measurements. Iiyama (2016)  utilized the hanging-water-column and pressure-plate methods for lab SWRC measurement, employing capacitance-type soil moisture sensors and tensiometers in the field. While tensiometers generally offer high accuracy in the wet range, capacitance-type soil moisture sensors typically exhibit low accuracy (Evett et al., 2012 ). Table 2  shows the VG parameters from HYPROP-FIT, Rosetta and IM. Since IM was based on the in-situ soil moisture and tension observations, variations in the values of VG parameters obtained from IM and HYPROP-FIT allowed us to identify the differences between laboratory and in-situ SWRCs. The VG parameters α  and n  affect the steepness of the SWRC, where α  relates to the inverse of air-entry value and n  indicates the steepness of the slope. The parameter α  ranged from 0.006 to 0.53 with an average of 0.019 for the lab SWRCs and from 0.001 to 0.038 with an average of 0.013 for the in-situ VG parameters obtained through IM. The parameter n  ranged from 1.24 to 1.52 with an average of 1.33 for the lab SWRCs and from 1.11 to 1.46 with an average of 1.27 for the in-situ SWRCs. This is also evident in Fig. 3 , as the air-entry value is lower, and the steepness of the SWRC is higher for the lab-obtained curves than the in-situ curves.  3.2 Performance of the models 3.2.1 In-situ SWRCs Table 3   summarizes the performance statistics of the PCNN -PTF and Rosetta for laboratory and in-situ water retention measurements. PCNN -PTF showed RMSE of 0.048 cm3  cm−3  for the in-situ data collected at intervals of 30 min during the year 2019, and MBE of −0.012 cm3  cm−3  was observed. SWRCs estimated using parameters obtained from Rosetta performed worse than the PCNN -PTF with RMSE=0.082 cm3  cm−3 . Rosetta showed a tendency to underestimate VWC, indicated by MBE of −0.079 cm3  cm−3  for in-situ data, also evident in Fig. 4  . Correlation coefficients (R) of 0.91 and 0.90 were observed for PCNN -PTF and Rosetta, respectively. The PCNN -PTF performed better than Rosetta in estimating the in-situ SWRCs. Hysteresis refers to the changes in the SWRC due to wetting and drying of the soil in the field. In-situ soil moisture can also be affected by physical processes such as hysteresis, somewhat evident in 30-min soil moisture data of plots under 62 % ETo -3d wk−1 , 62 % ETo -on-demand, 66 % ETo -3d wk−1 , and 66 % ETo -on-demand irrigation treatments. Hysteresis measurement can be challenging both in the laboratory and field due to the lack of enough data to quantify the wetting and drying cycles. Because of the complexities, only the drying hydraulic path is generally considered in laboratory measurements, although drying and wetting alternate in the field. Numerous efforts continue to address the effects of hysteresis on SWRC measurements (Bordoni et al., 2017; Hedayati et al., 2020; Iiyama, 2016; Pirone et al., 2014 ). It is worth mentioning that the current implementation of the PCNN -PTF ignores the effect of hysteresis since the lab measurements using HYPROP are made on the drying hydraulic path. We separately calculated the error terms for drying and wetting cycles to determine if PCNN -PTF performed better for drying than wetting data. However, we observed no difference between the two (data not shown here). This suggests that lab-based PTFs developed based on drying data do not necessarily work better for drying than wetting cycles in field conditions. Furthermore, Iiyama (2016)  suggested that soil moisture hysteresis can be ignored in the field under dry conditions as numerous repetitions of wetting and drying cycles may have occurred while soil moisture remains within the routinely observed range. The same could be said for our study since the plots were maintained under deficit irrigation for extended periods (Haghverdi et al., 2021 ).  3.2.2 Laboratory SWRCs For the lab measurements using the HYPROP-WP4C system, PCNN -PTF (RMSE=0.034 cm3  cm−3 ) performed better than Rosetta (RMSE=0.063 cm3  cm−3 ). A tendency to overestimate the VWC was observed for the PCNN -PTF (MBE=0.022 cm3  cm−3 ). A more pronounced underestimation was observed for Rosetta (MBE = −0.056 cm3  cm−3 ), indicated by a high magnitude of negative bias. The correlation coefficient was greater than 0.90 for both models, showing an overall good agreement between the measured and the estimated VWC (Table 3 ). Larger and more complete databases with soil hydraulic properties measured with a standardized technique and uniform distribution of samples among soil classes should increase the predictive capability of a PTF (Vereecken et al., 2010 ). Since PCNN -PTF is a machine learning approach, its performance is expected to improve as more soil hydraulic data measured with HYPROP experiments becomes publicly available for training the model. The SWRCs estimated using the VG parameters obtained from the IM in HYDRUS-1D also showed reasonable accuracy with RMSE of 0.043 cm3  cm−3 , indicating comparable performance to Rosetta. A slight underestimation of the estimated VWC was observed (MBE = −0.007 cm3  cm−3 ), which is also shown in Fig. 4 . The agreement between the measured and estimated VWC was high (R=0.85) but lower than what was observed for the PCNN -PTF and Rosetta models (Table 3 ). In our study, all parameters of the VG model for SWRC were optimized using IM. Better results may be expected if parameters such as θs  and θr  are constrained within practical limits (Šimůnek et al., 1998a, 1998b ). Nonetheless, results from our study indicate that in-situ SWRCs can serve as a reliable source for obtaining soil moisture information if lab-obtained SWRCs are not available.   3.3 Performance of PTFs at wet, intermediate, and dry tension regions of the SWRC 3.3.1 In-Situ SWRCs Table 4   shows the performance of PCNN -PTF and Rosetta for lab and in-situ measurements in three regions of the SWRC. In the wet range of the SWRC, PCNN -PTF (RMSE=0.008 cm3  cm−3 ) performed better than Rosetta (RMSE=0.076 cm3  cm−3 ) for the in-situ data. No considerable over or underestimation of the VWC was observed in the wet region by PCNN -PTF, whereas Rosetta underestimated at all the retention points (MBE = −0.76 cm3  cm−3 ). Similarly, PCNN -PTF performed better in the intermediate region (RMSE=0.023 cm3  cm−3 ) than Rosetta (RMSE=0.080 cm3  cm−3 ). A slight tendency for overestimation of VWC was observed for the PCNN -PTF (MBE=0.012 cm3  cm−3 ), whereas underestimation was observed for Rosetta (MBE = −0.076 cm3  cm−3 ) in the intermediate region. Both models showed comparable performance in the dry region of the SWRC, with PCNN -PTF performing slightly better (RMSE=0.083 cm3  cm−3 ) than Rosetta (RMSE=0.087 cm3 cm−3 ). Both models underestimated the VWC in the dry region with MBE = −0.073 and −0.085 cm3  cm−3  for PCNN -PTF and Rosetta, respectively. R ranged from 0.55 in the dry region to 0.76 in the intermediate region for PCNN -PTF and from 0.24 in the wet region to 0.65 in the intermediate region for Rosetta.  3.3.2 Laboratory SWRCs For the lab-obtained SWRCs, the lowest performance for the PCNN -PTF was observed in the wet region of SWRC (RMSE=0.038 cm3  cm−3 ), where the model showed a tendency to overestimate the VWC for most of the soils (MBE=0.028 cm3  cm−3 ) as also indicated in Fig. 4 . The best performance was observed in the dry region (RMSE=0.026 cm3  cm−3 ) followed by the intermediate region (RMSE=0.030 cm3  cm−3 ). No substantial over or underestimation was observed in the dry range (MBE = −0.005 cm3  cm−3 ), whereas a slight overestimation of VWC was evident in the intermediate range (MBE=0.017 cm3  cm−3 ). The R value was 0.68, 0.81, and 0.70 in the wet, intermediate, and dry regions of the SWRC, respectively. The better performance of PCNN -PTF in the intermediate and dry region of SWRC compared to the wet region can be attributed to the lack of measured retention points at soil saturation (θs ) in the training dataset (Singh et al., 2020 ) and strong nonlinearity in the measured data close to saturation. Although laboratory-measured θs  is underestimated compared to the in-situ values because of incomplete saturation and air entrapment of the soil (Verbist et al., 2009; Wassar et al., 2016 ), overestimation in lab methods is also possible (Abbasi et al., 2003 ). The lack of measured data in the wet and dry regions of the SWRC can be addressed by including arbitrary data points to each soil sample of the training dataset as adopted by Haghverdi et al. (2018)  by adding retention pair at oven-dry point (i.e., pF=6.8 and VWC=0 cm3  cm−3 ). These arbitrary points, such as θs  and θr  estimated from other PTFs, can further enhance the performance of PCNN -PTF when training data sets are limited. For Rosetta, the lowest performance was observed in the intermediate region of SWRC (RMSE=0.070 cm3  cm−3 ), where the model tended to underestimate soil moisture (MBE = −0.065 cm3  cm−3 ). The best performance was observed in the dry region (RMSE=0.027 cm3  cm−3 ) followed by the wet range (RMSE=0.061 cm3  cm−3 ). Underestimation was observed in both the dry (MBE = −0.014 cm3  cm−3 ) and wet (MBE = −0.056 cm3  cm−3 ) regions but was less pronounced compared to the intermediate region. The best agreement between the observed and estimated VWC was in the dry region, reflected by R value of 0.93, followed by the intermediate and wet regions with R values of 0.77 and 0.75, respectively (Table 4 ). As per the SWRCs obtained from the IM (Table 5  ), the lowest performance was observed in the dry region (RMSE=0.071 cm3  cm−3 ), followed by the wet region (RMSE=0.042 cm3  cm−3 ). The best performance was observed in the intermediate region (RMSE=0.036 cm3  cm−3 ) and with slight overestimation, as indicated by MBE of 0.014 cm3  cm−3 . Underestimation of the VWC was observed in the wet region (MBE = −0.031 cm3  cm−3 ), whereas overestimation was observed in the dry region (MBE=0.063 cm3  cm−3 ), as reflected in Fig. 4 , where most of the data points are above the 1:1 line at lower VWC and below the line at the higher values of VWC.   3.4 Novelty and limitations of this study and directions for future research The novelty of this work was threefold. Firstly, we addressed a research gap by comparing in-situ soil water retention measurements with HYPROP-WP4C measurements and HYPROP-based PCNN -PTF estimations of the SWRC. Secondly, we utilized calibrated sensor measurements to create a comprehensive field-based soil tension and water content dataset for inverse modeling of the SWRC using HYDRUS-1D. Thirdly, we developed the first web application for estimating the SWRC using the PCNN -PTF approach. This study only focused on measuring and estimating SWRC. We recommend further studies to investigate the differences between soil hydraulic conductivity curves obtained in the lab versus field measurements and evaluate the performance of hydraulic conductivity PTFs such as the PCNN -PTF developed by Singh et al. (2021)  for new soils and under field conditions. The HYPROP-WP4C system, similar to other standard laboratory techniques, only measured the main drying SWRC, while sensor pairing in the field captures both drying and wetting branches of the SWRC. We showed that the HYPROP-based PCNN -PTF can provide a reasonable estimation of soil water retention under field conditions, albeit at lower accuracy than laboratory data. Cautions should be made, however, for future field applications since PCNN -PTF only estimates the main drying curve, while field data encompass wetting and drying cycles. Therefore, we recommend that future lab-based PTFs be developed to estimate both main drying and wetting curves (as the upper and lower bounds) to better capture soil moisture dynamics under natural field conditions. In addition, we leave it to future research to determine if new sets of PTFs could be developed based on field data and sensor pairing techniques. A limitation of the MPS6 sensor is its requirement for equilibrium to provide soil tension measurements, which may not correspond to instantaneous TDT-based soil moisture measurements. This may impact sensor pairing data when soil moisture changes in short timestamps, such as during irrigation events. Additionally, MPS6 sensors did not capture the very wet soil condition close to saturation since it is outside the sensor’s measurement range. We did not consider hysteresis during inverse modeling and leave it to future research to determine whether that could enhance the performance of the inverse modeling approach using HYDRUS-1D.   4 Conclusion In this study, the PCNN -PTF approach was employed to estimate the complete soil water retention curve (SWRC) using soil texture (SSC) and bulk density (BD). The PCNN -PTF was trained using a combination of previously published international and Turkish datasets, all measured through evaporation experiments and HYPROP. The HYPROP system offers the advantage of providing a quasi-continuous description of the retention function within the tensiometric moisture range (up to pF 3), with dry-end (pF>4) measurements obtained using the WP4C Dew Point PotentioMeter. Our PCNN -PTF demonstrated superior performance compared to Rosetta in estimating soil water content data in both laboratory settings and field conditions. Particularly for in-situ soil moisture measurements, PCNN -PTF provided a more accurate estimation of SWRC than Rosetta in the intermediate region, although caution is advised in the wet region. Inverse modeling of VG parameters from in-situ soil moisture data reasonably estimated VWC in the intermediate region. Unlike the HYPROP-WP4C system, the in-situ SWRCs created in this study did not cover the entire soil moisture range from saturation to dryness, mainly due to limitations in the measurement range of soil moisture sensors. Field data also exhibited more scattering, primarily attributed to hysteresis induced by wetting and drying cycles. Nevertheless, field sensors are increasingly used due to advancements in irrigation technology, generating substantial data. Therefore, it is crucial to explore the utility of directly using field-collected data for soil hydrological estimations. Our results indicate that PCNN -PTF could serve as an essential tool for future research in this direction.
1 Introduction Internal erosion in porous media refers to the detachment and transport of fine particles from the solid skeleton due to the liquid flow through the pore space. This process will affect the particle size distribution of the porous system and potentially alter the force chain of the internal structure, leading to the change of hydraulic and mechanical properties, which may eventually result in the instability of the porous material. Internal erosion is recognised as one of the main factors responsible for the instabilities of water-retaining structures such as dams, embankments, and dikes (Foster et al., 2000 ). The resulting failure is highly destructive and poses severe threats to human life and properties. The process of internal erosion involves interacting multi-physical processes and multi-phase flow. Multiple challenges are present in the development of a mathematical model for internal erosion, including the complexity of multi-physics, phase interaction/transition, hydraulic/mechanical boundary conditions, and large deformations of the mixture at the post-failure stage. Conventionally, two types of numerical method can be considered to simulate the internal erosion process. The first type is based on discrete mechanics in which the solid particles are treated as individual elements and the interparticle interaction is defined. A typical example includes the discrete element method (DEM). In DEM, the erosion process is simulated either by direct removal of fine particles (e.g., Muir Wood et al., 2010; Scholtès et al., 2010; Shire and O'Sullivan, 2013 ) or by the coupling with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to consider the effect of pore fluid flow (e.g., Hosn et al., 2018; Kawano et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2019 ). The advantage of this numerical scheme is that it enables the micro-properties to be measured and the kinetics of fines removal can be tracked, but the application of DEM to give a full representation of the prototype scale problem is a formidable task due to the involvement of huge numbers of particles and demanding computational costs. These features make DEM suitable for the study of micro-scale mechanism but less attractive for large-scale problems. The second type is based on the continuum mechanics where a set of coupled particle differential equations (PDEs) is established for the description of the mass balance, momentum transfer of each phase involved in internal erosion, and different numerical techniques (mesh-based or meshfree) were employed to solve these governing equations. This method can be conveniently applied to engineering-scale problems thanks to the continuum assumption. Pioneering work by Vardoulakis et al. (1996)  initiated the use of a multi-phase continuum model to study the internal erosion phenomenon for the application to sand production. In their formulation, the whole system comprised three phases: the solid skeleton, the fluidized particles and the fluid, the phase transfer between solid phase and fluidized particles phase was considered to describe the internal erosion. However, in their method, the evolution of the fines content in the solid phase was not resolved, and the deformation in the solid phase was also neglected. Later, Schaufler et al. (2013)  proposed a four-phase model in which the erodible fines attached to the solid skeleton were considered as one phase, and the evolution of fines content in the solid phase was resolved. However, the deformation of the solid phase was still not taken into account in their application. To address this limitation, Yang et al. (2019b)  improved upon the model by Schaufler et al. (2013)  by incorporating an elastic model to predict solid phase deformation. The improved model was then further enhanced to incorporate a fine-dependent constitutive model for strength weakening due to erosion (Yang et al., 2019a ), and extend the study to three dimensions for the simulation of sinkhole formation (Yang et al., 2020b ). The development of the aforementioned continuum models was based on mesh-based methods, such as the finite difference method (FDM), and the finite element method (FEM), which suffer from mesh distortion issues when dealing with large deformations. This hinders the application of these methods to the analysis of the entire failure process triggered by internal erosion. In recent years, mesh-free methods have been successfully applied to study internal erosion, enabling analysis from pre-failure small deformations to post-failure large deformations. Maeda and Kondo (2014)  made the first attempt to use the meshless method smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) to study progressive seepage failure and ground depression with internal erosion. Two sets of particles were adopted to represent the solid phase and liquid phase, respectively (i.e., multi-layer multi-phase approach). Each set of particles was overlapped and moved according to their own governing equations. The erosion process was simulated by the mass transfer between the solid particles and the liquid particles. In contrast, Yerro et al. (2017)  applied a single set of particles to solve the multi-phase problem in MPM (i.e., single-layer multi-phase approach). The governing equations for both the soil phase and the water phase were solved within a single particle, while the internal erosion was described by the mass exchange between the solid and liquid phase. However, for the above two models, the details of the model development were not provided, and no validations were conducted. Lei et al. (2020)  employed the generalized interpolation material point (GIMP) method with a single-layer approach to study the rainfall-induced erosion and slope failure. Their method addressed the full coupling of seepage-deformation-erosion, and validations were provided. However, the influence of erosion on the material strength was not considered in their study. More recently, Ma et al. (2022)  adopted the single-layer framework to describe the internal erosion process in porous materials in SPH. A simple fine-dependent constitutive model was formulated to capture the strength reduction of materials caused by internal erosion. The zeroth-order Shepard filter was introduced to filter out the numerical noise, and the viscous damping term was applied to the elastic porous material to stabilise the solution and to remove undesirable fluctuations. Results showed that their method captured the entire seepage-induced internal erosion and subsequent failure process. It is worth mentioning that SPH has also been successfully applied to the analysis of rapidly-varied flows of liquid-sediment mixture involving sediment erosion and bed load transport (e.g., Fourtakas and Rogers 2016, Manenti et al. 2019, Chang et al. 2024 ). It can be seen that the state-of-the-art meshfree methods have achieved some success for the modelling of internal erosion phenomena, and the recent development in SPH has captured the coupling of seepage, deformation, and erosion as well as the influence of erosion on the mechanical behaviour of the material. However, there are still some remaining computational challenges that need to be addressed. For example, although the constitutive model by Ma et al. (2022)  has effectively captured the weakening of material strength due to internal erosion, the assumption of a linear relationship between fines content and material strength may limit the applicability of the method to porous materials that are either highly or less vulnerable to the erosion of fine particles. Furthermore, the stability of the numerical scheme has not been well studied and addressed. While the use of viscous damping in SPH to stabilise the simulation is effective for elastic materials, its use in materials undergoing plastic deformation is less clear. Nevertheless, the absence of a necessary dissipation term in the simulation for elastic–plastic material can still lead to instability due to the full dynamics in each phase and the lack of intrinsic dissipation in SPH. Moreover, the use of the Shepard filter to mitigate numerical errors introduces empiricism in selecting the applied frequency and the potential for over-filtering in long-duration simulations. In this study, a new three-phase five-component SPH model in the u -w -p  formulation is proposed to describe the unsaturated/saturated condition as well as the seepage-induced erosion, transport, and deposition within the erodible porous material. The fine-dependent constitutive model by Ma et al. (2022)  is modified to account for the nonlinear relationship between fines content and material strength. The boundary treatment and diffusion algorithm developed by Feng et al. (2024)  for hydro-mechanical coupling are extended to adapt to the erosion-transportation of fine particles for the coupled seepage-erosion-deformation processes. A new viscous dissipation term is proposed to further stabilise the numerical simulation. The validity of the proposed computational framework is assessed through a series of benchmark tests. The remaining part of this paper is organised as follows: Section 2 presents the basic definition of the computational model, governing equations for the multi-phase erodible porous mixture and the constitutive models for hydraulic, mechanical, and erosive behaviour of the porous material. The SPH implementation of the governing equations, as well as the treatment of boundary conditions and the development of the stabilization technique, are presented in Section 3. Section 4 examines the validity of the proposed methodology through a series of benchmark tests. Finally, conclusions are summarized in Section 5.  2 Governing equations of unsaturated erodible porous material 2.1 Basic definitions The physical domain of concern is a partially saturated porous material that contains solid grains, liquid, and air. When subjected to certain hydro-mechanical conditions and gradation conditions, the solid grains that comprises both coarse and fine particles, allow for the erosion of the fines fraction by liquid flow. The eroded fines particles are then transported away, along with the flowing liquid, resulting in the change of hydraulic and mechanical properties of the porous medium. To describe the process, the porous material is treated as a multi-phase multi-component continuum. As shown in Fig. 1  , the multi-phase porous system is generally composed of solid phase S , liquid phase L , and air phase A,  and can be further separated into five components (e.g., Lei et al. 2020 ): S  = {ss , se }; L  = {le , w}; and A  ={a }, in which the solid grains S  consists of the non-erodible solid skeleton (ss ) and solid erodible fines (se ); the liquid mixture L  is represented by liquidised eroded fines (le ), and pore water (w ); and the air phase A  is assumed to contain only dry pure air a . Each phase/component has its own physical quantities and interacts with each other with mass or momentum exchange due to the presence of different physics (such as seepage forces, internal erosion) for different coupling behaviour. The fines detachment is reproduced by the phase transfer from solid erodible fines se  to liquidised eroded fines le , while the fines transport is described by considering the liquidised fines as a part of the liquid flow. It is also possible to consider the clogging or deposition of fluidised fines by phase transfer from le  to se . The continuum mixture theory is applied to establish the mathematical model of the erodible porous material. Given a representative elementary volume (REV) of the three-phase porous material that has a volume V , five different components are involved with the assumption of homogeneity and continuity. Each phase/component can be treated as a continuum and occupies an individual volume. The sum of individual volume equals to the total volume V . The concept of the volume fraction is then introduced for the purpose of quantifying the mass and momentum contribution of each phase/component to the whole mixture. The volume fraction nα   of a phase/component {α } is defined as the ratio of the volume occupied by this phase/component Vα   to the total volume V , and the following relation is established,(1) n S  + n L  + n A  = n ss  + n se  + n w  + n le  + n a  = 1     It is noted that for the three-phase five-component problem, four variables are needed to describe the volume occupancy of each phase and component. For the volume fraction of solid phase S  and liquid phase L , taking the term commonly used in soil mechanics, the porosity and degree of saturation is applied. The porosity is defined as the volume fraction of pore spaces, i.e., ϕ = nL  + nA  , and the relative volume fraction of liquid mixture to the pore spaces is referred as the degree of saturation SL   = nL   / ϕ . In addition, to give better insights into the fines detachment and transport, the erodible fraction of the solid phase is represented by the fines content f c  = nse   / nS  , and the concentration of liquidised eroded fines is defined as the Cle   = nle   / nL  . Therefore, the volume fraction of the solid phase and its components can be defined as ns   = 1 – ϕ , nse   = f c (1 − ϕ ), and nss   = (1 − f c )(1 − ϕ ). For the liquid phase, the volume fractions are nL   = SL  ϕ , nle   = Cle SL  ϕ , and nw  =(1 − Cle  ) SL  ϕ , while the volume fraction of air phase can be expressed as n a  = (1 – SL  )ϕ . Upon determining the volume fraction, the partial (or apparent) physical quantities, i.e., partial density ρ  ¯   α    and partial stress σ  ¯    α   , can be evaluated from their intrinsic density ρ α    and intrinsic stress σ  α   , respectively, using the following relationship,(2a) ρ  ¯   α  = n α  ρ α      (2b) σ  ¯    α  = n α  σ  α       Accordingly, the total density and total stress applied to the whole mixture can be calculated as,(3a) ρ m  = ∑ α  ρ  ¯   α  = 1 - ϕ    ρ S  + S L  ϕ ρ L  + 1 - S L     ϕ ρ A      (3b) σ  = ∑ α  σ  ¯    α  = 1 - ϕ    σ  S  + S L  ϕ σ  L  + 1 - S L     ϕ σ  A      (3c) ρ L  = 1 - C le      ρ w  + C le   ρ S       To describe numerically the multi-phase porous mixture, the single-layer multi-phase formulation is adopted in this study due to its efficiency in computation as well as boundary treatment. The geometry of the physical domain is defined as the solid skeleton and discretised by a single set of particles that carries all the information of each phase and moves according to the deformation of solid skeleton, and the movement of other phases is described with respect to the solid skeleton. In the following section, the governing equations of the porous mixture will be discussed.  2.2 Governing equations The coupled formulation for the erodible porous mixture is obtained based on the mass conservation and momentum conservation of each phase. Some general assumptions are adopted in the model development as follows:(1) The modelled process is isothermal;  (2) The solid grain is assumed to be incompressible and the intrinsic densities of all components in the solid phase and the liquidised fine particle are the same (i.e., ρS   = ρss   = ρse   = ρle   = constant). The pore water is considered as weakly compressible (i.e., ρw   is variable);  (3) The solid skeleton is compressible and can be described as an elasto-plastic material with Bishop’s effective stress being applicable;  (4) The flow of liquid mixture follows the generalised Darcy’s law;  (5) All components within the solid phase share the same velocity v  S   = v  se   = v  ss  , while this also applies to the liquid phase v  L   = v  le   = v  w  ;  (6) The components within the liquid phase share the same intrinsic pressure σ L   = σ w   = σ le   = pw  I  ;  (7) The air density is assumed to be negligible, and the air pressure is assumed to be zero σ A   = pA  I   = 0 (Lei et al., 2020, Lian et al., 2022, Ceccato et al., 2021 );  (8) The relative acceleration of the liquid phase with respect to the solid phase is assumed to be negligible.    Additionally, in the derivation, the material derivative is assumed to be attached to the solid skeleton ss , given by,(4) d ss   ·    dt   = ∂ ·    ∂ t   + v  ss   ∇ ·   = ∂ ·    ∂ t   + v  S  ∇ ·        The sign convention is as follows: (1) the compressive stress and strains for the solid phase are considered as negative; (2) positive pore water pressures are assumed for compression in the water phase; and (3) inflow is regarded as positive for the flow discharge q . The detailed derivations of the three-phase five-component formulation for erodible porous materials are provided in Appendix A. Given the assumption of constant air density and air pressure, the governing equations for the air phase can be disregarded. Consequently, the mass balance equations and momentum equations for the erodible porous mixture in the present study are presented as follows: (1) mass balance equations. In this paper, the total stress tensor is calculated using the Bishop’s effective stress concept with the effective stress parameter taken as the degree of saturation, according to,(9) σ  = σ ′   - S L  p w  I       The proposed formulation presents several distinctions from existing formulations for erodible porous material, such as Lei et al. (2020) , and Ma et al. (2022) . A notable difference is the approach adopted for the porosity calculation. Unlike other numerical schemes for internal erosion, which utilize Eq. (A9) that integrates the effects of both deformation and erosion to compute porosity, this study employs Eq. (8) for porosity evaluation. The use of Eq. (8) leads to separate calculations of the volumetric deformation for ρ  ¯   ss     and the erosion term fc  . This approach facilitates the need for SPH particle density (which will be discussed later in section 3.1), and possesses the benefit of avoiding possible precision loss using Eq. (A9). The latter point arises from the fact that the contribution of volumetric solid deformation to porosity may be significantly larger than the mass exchange term, potentially leading to the loss of precision for the erosion term in the computation. The resulting discrepancy due to the precision loss of the erosion term could be particularly noteworthy for low erosion rates over long durations. In addition, it is noted that, for the hydro-mechanical components, the proposed methods adopt the u -w -p  formulation (u  represents the solid displacement, w  is the relative velocity of liquid, and p  denotes pore water pressure), while in other existing formulation for internal erosion, the u -v  formulation (e.g., Lei et al., 2020 ), and u - hhyd   (or u -p ) formulation (e.g., Ma et al., 2022 ) are used, where v  stands for the liquid velocity, hhyd   denotes the hydraulic head. u -w -p  form (e.g., Bandara et al., 2016, Morikawa and Asai, 2022, Feng et al., 2022, 2024 ), u -v  form (e.g.,Yerro et al., 2015, Wang et al., 2018, Ceccato et al., 2021 ), and u -p  form (e.g., Zhang et al., 2009, Zheng et al., 2013, Xu et al., 2017 ) are three main categories of formulations for the hydro-mechanical coupling in the literature. The u -p  formulation provides a simple and efficient way to describe the coupling while the u -v  formulation represents the full dynamics of each phase. The advantages of using the u -w -p  formulation in the current application is to mitigate the pressure instability problem that may arise when using the u -p  formulation with an explicit numerical framework (Song et al., 2017, Lei et al., 2020 ), to avoids the requirement of second derivative calculation in the u -p  formulation as well as the issues associated with the Laplacian operator in SPH (Asai et al., 2023 ) and to simplify the implementation of the flow flux boundary condition such as infiltration boundary and impermeable boundary. Another difference of the governing equations comparing to existing erosion formulation pertains to the computation of the pressure in the liquid phase. In the proposed formulation, the pore water pressure is solved, whereas other formulations typically solve for pore pressure of the liquid mixture. The adoption of pore water pressure instead of pore liquid pressure is because the constitutive behaviour of the liquid mixture consisting of water and varying liquidised fines remains unclear in theory, particularly in terms of the relations of liquid pressure with the density variation of liquid mixture, and the relations of the concentration of liquidised fines with the bulk modulus for the liquid mixture. In contrast, the pore water pressure can be straightforwardly evaluated from the water density by a constant water stiffness in accordance with the theory of weakly compressible flows. In the proposed formulations, the primary variables include: (1) volume fraction: ϕ , f c , Cle  , SL  , n ̂  ex    , (2) density: ρ  ¯   ss    , ρw  , (3) kinematic variable: q L  , v  S  , and (4) mechanics variable: pw  , σ  ʹ. There are 7 governing equations with 11 unknown variables in the formulation, thus additional constitutive relations are required to close the governing equations, and to achieve the coupling of seepage-erosion, and erosion-deformation.  2.3 Constitutive relations 2.3.1 Erosion/deposition laws To describe the internal erosion induced by seepage, this study addresses two primary mechanisms: the erosion of erodible solid fines and the deposition of liquified eroded fines. The estimation of the mass exchange term n ̂  ex     can be expressed as,(10) n ̂  ex   = n ̂  e  - n ̂  d      where n ̂  e    and n ̂  d    are the erosion and deposition rates, respectively. The negative sign before the deposition term denotes that it is a mass gain concerning the solid phase, in contrast to the erosion term that represents a mass loss. A number of empirical relations have been proposed in the literature to reproduce the erosion process by linking the rate of erosion to flow properties such as specific discharge or hydraulic gradient. In this study, the erosion term by Cividini and Gioda (2004), Cividini et al. In this study, the effective stress is calculated from the strain of the solid skeleton based on the elastic–plastic analysis, while the pore water pressure is estimated from the water density variation due to the weakly compressible assumptions (e.g., Monaghan, 1994 ). It is noted that the use of a constitutive model is independent of the proposed SPH formulation. Other advanced constitutive models can be easily implemented in this framework to capture different material behaviour. By employing the elastic–plastic theory and considering the Jaumann stress rate of Cauchy stress for the objectivity of stress under rigid body rotation, the rate of effective stress σ ′  ̇     is computed as,(14) σ ′  ̇   = D   ep   : ε ̇   - ω ̇   · σ ′   + σ ′   · ω ̇       where D   ep     is the elastic–plastic stiffness matrix, the operator (:) denotes the double dot product, ε ̇     is the strain rate tensor, and ω ̇     is the spin rate tensor, in which ε ̇     and ω ̇     are calculated by,(15a) ε ̇   = 1 2  ∇ v  + ∇ v     T         (15b) ω ̇   = 1 2  ∇ v  - ∇ v     T          The solution of Eq. (14) for stress updating depends on the adopted constitutive relations. In the present analysis, the general elasto-plastic constitutive model is adopted with the Drucker-Prager yield criteria and non-associated plastic flow. The yield function f 0  and the plastic potential function g 0  are calculated as,(16a) f 0  = α φ  I 1  + J 2   - k c      (16b) g 0  = α ψ  I 1  + J 2       where I 1  and J 2  are respectively the first principal stress invariant and the second deviatoric stress invariant; αφ   and kc   are model constants that are linked to Coulomb’s material constants c  (cohesion) and φ  (friction angle) according to,(17a) α φ  = tan φ  9 + 12 tan 2  φ    ,     (17b) k c  = 3 c  9 + 12 tan 2  φ    ,     and, αψ   is a dilatancy factor. Its value is related to the dilation angle ψ  in a similar manner to that between αφ   and friction angle φ . In this work, three mechanisms are considered to evaluate the strength parameters (i.e., cohesion and friction angle) of the erodible porous material under saturated/unsaturated condition, including the strain-softening, the hardening due to the suction pressure, and the dependence of material strength on the fines content. The strength parameters are considered to consist of two components: an effective part and a suction-dependent part. Accordingly, the cohesion and friction angle are calculated as follows (Lian et al. 2022, Ma et al. 2022 , and Feng et al. 2024 ),(18a) c = c r ′  + c p ′  - c r ′     e - η c  κ   + c s      (18b) φ = φ r ′  + φ p ′  - φ r ′     e - η φ  κ   + φ s      where c ′p   and c ′r   denote the peak and residual effective cohesion, φ ′p   and φ ′r   stand for the peak and residual effective friction angle, respectively. ηc   and ηφ   are the softening coefficients that control the degradation rate of cohesion and friction angle, respectively. κ  is the equivalent deviatoric plastic strain. cs   and φs   represent the additional cohesion and friction angle acquired due to suction, calculated as follows,(19a) c s  = c sp   1 - e - B s  p c  p atm               (19b) φ s  = A s  p c  p atm          where csp   represents the maximum cohesion gain due to suction. As   and Bs   are the rates at which the friction angle and cohesion change with respect to suction, respectively, patm   denotes the atmosphere pressure with a typical value of 101 kPa. In addition, to take into account the erosion-triggered deformation, the fines-dependent constitutive model by Ma et al. (2022)  is modified to further incorporate the nonlinearity between fines content and material strength. Based on reported experimental findings regarding the influence of internal erosion on soil mechanical behaviour (Chen et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2015 ), this study assumes that the peak shear strength is influenced by the erosion, and that the peak strength parameters decrease nonlinearly with the increase of erosion until they reach their residual values. Accordingly, the peak strength can be written as,(20a) c p ′  = c r ′  + c p 0  ′  - c r ′     1 - f c 0   - f c   f c 0   - c ∞  f c 0       η e          (20b) φ p ′  = φ r ′  + φ p 0  ′  - φ r ′     1 - f c 0   - f c   f c 0   - c ∞  f c 0       η e          where ηe   is the coefficient that controls the rate of strength degradation due to the loss of fines content. While seepage-induced internal erosion, such as suffusion, mostly occurs in cohesionless soils, the reduction of cohesion due to seepage-induced erosion is also considered in Eq. (20). This is based on experimental observations of suffusion occurrence in cohesive soils under high hydraulic gradients (e.g., Sato and Kuwano, 2015, 2018 ). The relationship between the normalised peak strength N φp  (the same as N cp ), defined as N φp  = (φ ′p   – φ ′r  )/ (φ ′p  0  − φ ′r  ), and the degree of erosion De  , defined as De   = (fc  0  − fc  )/fc  0 ., by the proposed formulation with different value of η e  is plotted in Fig. 2  . The value of N φp  ranges from 0 to 1, in which N φp  = 1 represents the undisturbed material strength while N φp  = 0 indicates the total loss of peak strength. The value of De   ranges from no erosion (De   = 0) to full erosion (De   = 1 − c ∞ ). Note that De   cannot reach a value of 1 in practice, as there will always be some residual fines content remaining within the porous material that cannot be eroded. As shown in Fig. 2 , the present formulation enables the description of a wide range of nonlinear relations between f c  and c /φ  by varying ηe  , and it reduces to the formulation by Ma et al. (2022)  if ηe   = 1. Another modification made is the use of c ∞ f c0  instead of f c∞  in the denominator to describe the rate of degradation due to the loss of fine particles. It avoids the singularity (i.e., f c0  − f c∞  = 0) when ih   = 0 and f c  = f c0  = f c∞  by using Eq. (12). It also prevents the situation when f c  is less than f c∞ , with f c  − f c∞ <0 and (f c0  − f c )/(f c0  − f c∞ ) > 1, since the value of f c∞  may increase with the decrease in the hydraulic gradient, leading to unphysical increase of material strengths. For the solution of the above-mentioned constitutive relations to update the effective stress, either the explicit stress updating algorithm by calculating the elastic–plastic stiffness or the semi-implicit stress updating algorithm, such as the one presented in Ma et al. (2022) , can be used. In present analysis, the semi-implicit iterative stress updating algorithm by Feng et al. (2024)  is adopted. The additional fines-dependent strength can be straightforwardly incorporated into their algorithm by adjusting the yield function. The adopted fines-dependent constitutive model in this study provides a simple way to capture the strength reduction due to internal erosion. However, other influencing factors such as relative density and stress state on the behaviour of erodible soils are not taken into account in this model. For such complex responses, more advanced constitutive models (e.g., Yin et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020a ) are required. These constitutive models can be readily incorporated into the proposed SPH framework. However, they often involve a large number of constitutive parameters, leading to challenges in calibrating some of these parameters.  2.3.3 Constitutive model for the water For the pore water pressure, taking the idea from the weakly compressible SPH for fluid dynamics, the equation of state by Morris et al. In SPH, the physical domain is discretised into a set of particles carrying field variables, and the governing equations are discretised to evolve those field variables. The SPH approximations of the gradient of a scalar f  and the divergence of a vector f  are calculated as,(26a) ∇ f    i  = ∑ j = 1  N  m j  ρ j   f j  + f i     ∇ i  W ij        (26b) ∇ · f     i  = ∑ j = 1  N  m j  ρ j   f  j  - f  i     · ∇ i  W ij        where 〈…〉 denotes the SPH interpolated quantities; the subscripts i  and j  represent the interpolating particle and its neighbours, respectively; ∇i Wij   = ∇i W (x i  -x j  , h ) and fj   = f (x j  ) are respectively the gradient of the kernel function W  with respect to the coordinate of particle i  and the value of function f  for the particle j  at the position x j ,  in which h  is the smoothing length of the kernel function, N  is the number of neighbour particle j  within the interpolating radius of particle i , mj   and ρj   are the mass and density of the particle j . In the present analysis, the material derivative is attached to the solid skeleton and the movement of particle represents the deformation of solid skeleton, thus the density and mass of the SPH particles are taken as the partial density of the solid skeleton ρ  ¯   ss     and its corresponding mass. Since there is no mass variation in the solid skeleton phase, the mass of the SPH particles is conserved and can be kept as a constant throughout the calculation. In the following, indicial notation and Einstein convention are applied to present the equations, in which α , β  and γ  denote Cartesian coordinates. For general applications, two types of boundary conditions are adopted, namely the solid wall boundary condition and the free-surface boundary condition. The boundary treatment by Feng et al. (2024)  is adopted for the complex hydro-mechanical case scenarios, such as infiltration boundary, potential seepage face boundary, hydraulic head boundary, impermeable boundary, and stress boundary, but extension of this boundary treatment is required to resolve the concentration of liquidised fine particles near the boundary. 3.2.1 Solid wall boundary condition In this study, the solid wall boundary is represented by several layers of fixed boundary particle. For each boundary particles, b , a ghost node, g , is projected into the domain in a direction perpendicular to the boundary surface to interpolate field variables from surrounding domain particles, j , with the first-order consistent SPH interpolant by Liu and Liu (2006) . The detailed enforcement of v  S  , σ ʹ , q  L  , and ρw   for different types of boundary conditions can be found in Feng et al. (2022, 2024)  and is not repeated here. In the following, the boundary treatment for the concentration of liquidised fines particle Cle   is discussed. In general, two types of numerical boundary condition, i.e., natural boundary condition and essential boundary, may be adopted for various applications. For example, if there are outflows at the boundary, the concentration is unknown and is part of solution, but for inflow boundaries, a given value of concentration is needed. The values and gradients of Cle   at the ghost node, represented by Cle.g   and ∂α Cle.g  , are evaluated in the first from neighbour domain particle j  with corrected interpolation according to,(33) C le . g     ∂ x  C le . g       ∂ y  C le . g           = N  gj  - 1   · ∑ j  C j  W gj    V j     ∑ j  C j  ∂ x  W gj   V j      ∑ j  C j  ∂ y  W gj   V j               For the natural boundary condition, the value of Cle   at boundary is not required to be prescribed but is extrapolated from the physical domain. Despite various free surface searching algorithms in the literature, the simple one based on the estimation of particle divergence is adopted (Lee et al., 2008 ). For the case with complex topological change, a more advanced searching algorithm can be conveniently implemented in the present framework. This free-surface searching algorithm is simple but effective, and it has been successfully adopted to identify free-surface particles for particle shifting algorithm (Lind et al., 2012 ), free-surface incompressible flows (Chen et al., 2013 ). For the 2-D problem, this threshold is set to be FST = 1.7 in the present analysis (Feng et al. 2024 ). Commonly, the artificial viscosity by Monaghan (1992)  is included in the momentum equation to suppress the numerical oscillations and to stabilise the simulation, but in some cases, the sole use of artificial viscosity may not be able to efficiently mitigate the numerical oscillations, resulting in numerical instabilities and the need of a relatively large artificial viscosity that may cause unphysical over- dissipation. This situation can be especially pronounced for the fully coupled problem because the oscillations in the solid acceleration could also affect the liquid phase, making the simulation prone to instability. One possible reason could be that the artificial viscosity term is mainly for the dissipation of the bulk deformation and only activated when particles are approaching to each other (i.e., v  ij  ⋅x  ij   < 0). For the region with a relatively small bulk deformation (or a small v  ij  ⋅x  ij  ) but with the presence of shear deformation, the solution could be of under-dissipation, leading to the development of numerical oscillations. Therefore, a new viscous dissipation term is investigated to enable the option of the dissipation of the shear momentum and to further stabilise the numerical analysis. The artificial dissipation term Π ij  α β     in the present analysis involves the artificial viscosity term and a new viscous dissipation term. The artificial viscosity acts mainly on the bulk deformation while the viscous dissipation term is designed to dissipate the shear component. The momentum equation (Eq. (27e) is rewritten as,(38) d v α   dt     i  = 1 ρ m . i    ∑ j = 1  N  m j  ρ j   σ i α β   + σ j α β      ∂ W ij    ∂ x i β     + α μ  c s 0   h ∑ j = 1  N  m j  ρ  ¯   ij    μ ij   ∂ W ij    ∂ x i α     + α π  c s 0   h ∑ j = 1  N  m j  ρ  ¯   ij    π ij  α β   ∂ W ij    ∂ x i β     + g i α      where αμ   and απ   are respectively the viscous coefficient and the dissipation coefficient controlling the magnitude of artificial viscosity and viscous dissipation. The value of αμ   is normally taken as 0.1 (e.g., Antuono et al. 2012, Bui and Nguyen, 2021 ), while απ   for viscous dissipation takes the value of 0.0 ∼ 1.0 according to numerical experiments. Tuning of απ   may be needed to achieve stable simulations. c s0  is the numerical speed of sound for solid material, defined as c s 0   = E / ρ S      , ρ  ¯   ij     is the mean particle density, defined as ρ  ¯   ij   = ρ i  + ρ j     / 2    . The viscous term μ ij     and dissipation term π ij  α β     are calculated as,(39a) μ ij   = v ij  β  x ij  β   x ij  β    2  + η 2     v ij  β  x ij  β  < 0    0   v ij  β  x ij  β  > 0            (39b) π ij  α β   = v ij  α  x ij  β   x ij  β    2  + η 2        in which η  = 0.1 h  is the numerical parameter introduced to avoid numerical singularity. It can be noted that viscous term μ ij     is the finite difference form of the velocity divergence while the dissipation term π ij  α β     approximates the finite difference form of the velocity gradient. As analysed in Appendix B, the combination of artificial viscosity and the new viscous dissipation term could produce a dissipation equivalent to the viscous damping term by Feng et al. (2024)  (e.g., α μ  = α π ), but the current method provides a general way for the artificial dissipation in momentum equation. This new term approximates the Laplacian of velocity, which is analogous to shear viscosity in fluid dynamics and dissipates shear momentum. The advantage of using viscous damping term by Feng et al. (2024)  is that it replaces the artificial viscosity term that is commonly used in soil momentum equation with improved stability and the number of dissipation parameters in the system remain unchanged. However, in some cases this term may include excessive numerical dissipation into the simulation since it operates on both the bulk and shear components of the momentum. By contrast, the new viscous dissipation term only acts on the shear component of the momentum, while leaving the bulk component unchanged. The combination of artificial viscosity and the new viscous dissipation term introduces an extra tuning parameter into the formulation but offers the ability in controlling the numerical dissipation.  3.3.2 Particle shifting Another challenge in applying SPH for solid mechanics is the occurrence of tensile instability, which manifests as particle clustering and the generation of numerical fracture or cavitation. In addition, it is observed that when the failure of material is triggered and the shear deformation develops along the boundary, there may be severe particle disorder and penetration of particles into the boundary (Feng et al. 2024 ). Tensile instability is found to be triggered by the negative pressure in the calculation, and thus it would be more prevalent in the application to the partially saturated porous material due to the presence of the suction pressure. To avoid these issues, the particle shifting technique is applied to regularise anisotropically disordered particles (e.g., Xu et al. 2009, Lind et al. 2012 ). The shifting method involves displacing each particle by a certain distance at the end of each time step based on the particle concentration. This allows particles located in denser regions to move towards areas with lower particle concentration, promoting better particle distribution and reducing clustering effects. The shifting algorithm used herein this study is based on the work of Feng et al. (2024) , which is a modified version of the optimized particle scheme (OPS) proposed by Khayyer et al. (2017) . The formulation of the shifting technique is not presented here to avoid repetition. For details and the implementation of the shifting algorithm, readers are referred to the work by Feng et al. (2024) .  3.3.3 Diffusion algorithm Although the solution can be much improved with appropriate momentum dissipation terms and regularised particle distributions (e.g., Rastelli et al. 2022, Feng et al. 2024 ), numerical noise can still present in the prediction of physical variables, due to the collated nature of SPH and lack of consistency for the SPH approximation. In this study, the diffusion algorithm is adopted to smooth out the numerical noise (e.g., Antuono et al. 2010, Feng et al. 2024 ). The primary variables that require the use of diffusion algorithm in the present formulation include Cle  , and ρw  . The diffusion term is incorporated into their respective governing equations, leading to(40a) d ρ w   dt     i  = - 1 C ri    ρ wi   ∂ q L α   ∂ x α      i R  + S Li   ε ̇  v . i   + n ̂  ρ w . i      + δ L  h c l 0   ∑ j = 1  N  m j  ρ j   ψ ρ w . i j  α   ∂ W ij    ∂ x i α           (40b) d C le    dt     i  = 1 S Li   ϕ i    q Li  α  ∑ j = 1  N  m j  ρ j   C le . i   - C le . j       ∂ W ij    ∂ x i α    + n ̂  C . i      + δ L  h c l 0   ∑ j = 1  N  m j  ρ j   ψ C . i j  α   ∂ W ij    ∂ x i α        where Cr   is the storage term can be expressed as,(41) C r  = ϕ S L  - K w  ∂ S L   ∂ p c           cl  0  is the characteristic speed of specific discharge, which is estimated as ten times the possible maximum discharge velocity. δL   is the dimensionless diffusion coefficient, whose value is normally taken as 0.1 (Antuono et al. 2012, Feng et al. 2024 ). The diffusion operators ψ ρ w . i j  α   , and ψ C . i j  α    are formulated according to the structure by Antuono et al. (2010) , as follows,(42a) ψ ρ w . i j  α  = 2 ρ w . i   - ρ w . j      x ij  α  x ij  β    2  + η 2    - ∂ ρ w  / ∂ x α     j L  + ∂ ρ w  / ∂ x α     i L         (42b) ψ C . i j  α  = 2 C le . i   - C le . j      x ij  α  x ij  β    2  + η 2    - ∂ C le   / ∂ x α     j L  + ∂ C le   / ∂ x α     i L          It will be demonstrated in the following sections that the diffusion algorithm enables stable numerical simulations. It is worth mentioning that apart from differences in governing equations and constitutive models as described in section 2.2 and section 2.3, the proposed SPH model exhibits several distinctions compared to the existing SPH model for internal erosion (e.g., Ma et al., 2022 ), particularly in terms of boundary conditions and stabilisation techniques. In Ma et al. (2022) , the boundary treatment by Bui et al. (2008)  is adopted, while the present work applied the boundary treatment by Feng et al. (2021)  and extended it for the boundary condition for fluidised fines concentrations. Generally, the boundary method adopted in Ma et al. (2022)  is easy to implement and requires less computational costs but may result in numerical fluctuation issues near the boundary due to the lack of consistency. The boundary method used in this study slightly increases the computational costs in order to evaluate the properties of boundary particles but offers better accuracy with first-order consistency. A comparison of these two different boundary conditions has been presented in Feng et al. (2021) . In addition, Ma et al. (2022)  adopted the combination of the artificial stress method to mitigate the tensile instability issue, the Shepard filter to smooth out the numerical noise, and the damping term by Bui and Fukagawa (2013)  to remove undesirable numerical oscillations. These techniques are also convenient to implement and have demonstrated the capability to improve the stability of the simulation. However, these techniques are known to have certain limitations (Antuono et al. 2012 , Bui and Nguyen, 2021 , Feng et al. 2024 ). For example, the artificial stress method requires case-dependent tuning of two parameters and its extension to 3-D is challenging. The Shepard filter is zeroth order accurate in space, which could filter out high-order information and may affect the overall accuracy of the SPH solution. The filter is commonly applied every certain number of time steps to mitigate the issue of over-filtering, and thus the applied frequency is empirical and may require tuning through trial numerical tests for different test cases. The artificial damping term by Bui and Fukagawa (2013)  operates on the total momentum. The magnitude of the damping coefficient is inversely proportional to the particle spacing. As a result, a large dissipation could be introduced for a small particle spacing. By contrast, in this study, the combination of the shifting algorithm by Feng et al. (2024) , the newly extended diffusion term, and the new viscous dissipation term is employed to address the aforementioned numerical issues and to overcome the limitations of existing techniques. The shifting algorithm adopts a fixed parameter settings and its 3D extension is straightforward. This method has demonstrated efficiency in improving numerical clumping and voids, providing enhanced accuracy as shown in Feng et al. (2024) . The diffusion term is formulated to approximate the Laplacian of the quantity being smoothed. Therefore, it is second order in spatial discretisation, which has minimal effect on the SPH discretisation scheme that is up to second order accuracy. A fixed coefficient is used for the diffusion term, which eliminates case-specific tuning. The new viscous dissipation term is convergent with the refinement of particle spacing and is constructed to operate on the shear component of the momentum. Its combination with artificial viscosity offers flexibility in controlling the artificial dissipation added into the system.   3.4 Time integration scheme In the present work the temporal integration of the governing equations is achieved using the explicit second-order Symplectic Position Verlet scheme (Domínguez et al., 2021 ). The variable time step is adopted in the analysis and its value for the two-phase coupled hydro-mechanical problem is computed according to (Feng et al., 2022 ),(43a) Δ t f  = min i  h / f i α            (43b) Δ t cv   = min i  h c s 0   + max j  h v ij  α  x ij  α   x ij  α  x ij  α  + η 2            (43c) Δ t sp   = min i  γ w  K w   h 2  c v   2 K          (43d) Δ t = C 0  min Δ t cv   , Δ t f  , Δ t sp          where C 0  is the Courant number, and its value is taken as 0.2 in present analysis. The coefficient cv   is computed as,(44) c v  = ϕ S L  - K w  ∂ S L   ∂ p c              4 Validation cases The proposed multi-phase fully-coupled SPH model for internal erosion is implemented in the CPU branch of open-source SPH code DualSPHysics (Domínguez et al., 2021 ). Fig. 3   illustrates the detailed computational flow of the proposed multi-phase SPH model. Several benchmark tests, including an element shear test, 1-D infiltration/evaporation test, 1-D consolidation test, Sterpi’s erosion test, 1-D erosion-transport-deposition test, and erosion triggered embankment failure experiment are adopted to test the validity of the proposed numerical scheme. The infiltration/evaporation test, Sterpi’s erosion test, and fines transport test are adopted to validate the unsaturated/saturated seepage framework, the coupling of seepage flow and fines erosion, and the solution of the combined process of fines erosion, migration, and clogging, respectively. In these test, only liquid flow with the movement of fines is evolved, the mechanical deformation is assumed to be negligible to make the numerical test comparable to analytical solutions and experiment conditions. The particles are fixed in space as a rigid body and the dependence of permeability on the porosity, i.e., Eq. (25), is not considered to facilitate the comparison against reference data. The element shear test validates the implementation of the constitutive model for the mechanical behaviour of eroded soils, and the liquid flow is not considered in the analysis. The coupling of solid deformation and liquid flow is tested by the consolidation test, while the full consideration of the coupling of seepage-erosion-deformation is studied in the embankment failure experiment triggered by erosion. 4.1 Element shear test The capability of the modified constitutive model in capturing the erosion-induced strength reduction and its implementation in SPH is verified by conducting a series of simple shear test on eroded specimens. The element shear test is a widely used benchmark test for evaluating constitutive relations. It involves simulating the pure shear of a square specimen subjected to a given confining stress. The simulation measures the shear stress and shear strain of the specimen, and the numerical results are compared to the single-element solutions. The details of numerical implementation of the simple shear test can be referred to Feng et al. (2021) . In the present analysis, the simulation domain is a square with a length of 0.1 m. The initial particle spacing dp  is set to be 0.01 m, resulting in a total of 100 particles. The particles representing the solid material are positioned at the centre of the domain, which are surrounded by the boundary particles. The hydrostatic components of stress for all particles are initialized as σxx  = σyy  = σzz   = 100 kPa to enforce an initial confining stress. The velocity of all the boundary particles is restricted to a given value of vx   = 0.01z , and vz   = 0 for a constant shear rate, while the central solid particle is allowed to move freely. The simulation is carried out under the condition of no gravity. The mechanical properties of the porous column and adopted numerical parameters are listed in Table 1  . Three specimens with different degree of erosion De   = 0, 0.5, and 1.0 are tested. Fig. 4   compares the predicted stress–strain relationship by SPH with the single-element solution. Clearly, the strain-softening behaviour and peak strength degradation due to internal erosion are captured with the present constitutive model, and the SPH results agree well with the reference solutions. The reduction in peak strength due to internal erosion from De   = 0 to De   = 0.5 shows a lesser extent than the strength degradation caused by the erosion from De   = 0.5 to De   = 1.0.  4.2 1-D infiltration/evaporation test To validate the proposed framework in describing the transient seepage in unsaturated porous material, the simulation of 1-D infiltration/evaporation test is conducted. This case simulates the pressure evolution of an initially unsaturated porous column due to the water infiltration and evaporation. The finite element solutions present by Gardner (1958)  serves as the reference solution for comparison and the same numerical configurations and material parameters are applied in the present analysis. Fig. 5  (a) shows the geometry and applied boundary conditions. The porous column is 3 m in height and is discretised using SPH particles with an initial particle spacing set to 0.02 m. The unsaturated solid column is initially in a hydrostatic condition with the pore water pressure equals to pw   = − ρL gz . The numerical parameters and hydraulic properties are listed in Table 2  . The following SWCC model and HCC model are adopted,(45a) S L  = 0.23 + 1.0 - 0.23    exp - 2 P e   ρ L 0   g          (45b) K = K sat   exp - 2 p c   ρ L 0   g           The one-dimensional water flow is modelled by applying periodic boundary conditions to the lateral side of the domain. A prescribed specific discharge is applied to the top free-surface particles with qL  .z  = 0.1 m/day for the infiltration test and qL  .z  = -0.002 m/day for the evaporation test, while the bottom is set to the impermeable boundary using boundary particles. Fig. 5 (b) shows the evolution of pore water pressure profile of the unsaturated porous column due to the water infiltration and evaporation. The applied infiltration/evaporation water flux at the top gradually decreases/increases the suction pressure in the porous medium. It can be found that the use of the proposed numerical framework results in a clear wetting/drying process with a noise-free pressure profile. The calculated pore water pressure profiles against the finite element solutions at different time instants is plotted in Fig. 6  . Clearly, satisfactory agreement between the SPH results and the reference solution is achieved, demonstrating the ability of the proposed method to solve the transient seepage problem in unsaturated porous medium.  4.3 1-D consolidation test This case refers to the classical one-dimensional consolidation test, which is adopted to verify the coupling of seepage flow and soil deformation in the proposed scheme. Stabilization techniques, including the diffusion term and the artificial dissipation term, are implemented to assess their ability in mitigating issues such as unphysical oscillations and numerical noise. The one-dimensional consolidation test is the process of gradual vertical compressions of a saturated soil element due to the expulsion of pore water under a vertical constant surcharge. Analytical solutions are available for the consolidation problem for the comparison (e.g. Verruijt 2016 ). Fig. 7   illustrates the geometry and the initial/boundary condition of the 1-D consolidation test. The height of the porous column is 1 m. Three sets of particle resolutions of dp  = 0.1, 0.05 and, 0.02 m are considered. The porous column is initially fully saturated, with both pore water pressure and effective stress initialised as 0 kPa. Similar to the 1-D infiltration test, periodic boundary conditions are applied to both sides to reproduce the one-dimensional water flow and soil deformation. The bottom boundary is set to be impermeable and no-slip, using wall boundary particles. For the top boundary, two consecutive stages are considered. In the first stage, a constant stress is applied to the top, together with the undrained condition for the liquid phase. The stress is applied gradually in a ramp function according to,(46) q = q 0  t t L     t ⩽ t L     q 0    t > t L             where the surface surcharge q 0  is set as 50 kPa, and the loading period tL   is taken as 0.01 s. At the end of the loading stage, excess pore water pressure is built up, with the value of pore water pressure equal to almost pw  0  = 50 kPa, while the effective stress remains nearly at its initial value. Then, the stress boundary is maintained at q 0  = 50 kPa, while the hydraulic boundary is changed to the drainage boundary, which is a prescribed pressure boundary with pw   = 0 kPa. The drainage boundary allows the excess pore water pressure to be dissipated, resulting in the consolidation of the saturated porous medium. The simulation is conducted in the absence of the gravity. The linear elastic model is adopted for the constitutive relations of the solid. Table 3   presents the hydro-mechanical properties of the porous column and numerical parameters adopted in the simulation. Fig. 8   reports the isochrone of excess pore pressure obtained from SPH in comparison with the analytical solutions. It is evident that the calculated pore water pressure profile by SPH matches well the analytical solution. The L 2  norm error calculated for the three resolutions at initial transient stage t  = 0.05 s indicates an order of convergence of 1.44, which is typical for an SPH scheme with kernel gradient correction (Khayyer et al., 2008 ). In addition, the evolution of the effective stress at three different heights predicted by SPH is plotted in Fig. 9  , along with the corresponding analytical solutions. Again, agreement between the SPH results and analytical solutions is achieved. The same conclusion can be also made for the surface settlement as shown in Fig. 9 . The results demonstrate that the proposed scheme can capture well the hydro-mechanical coupling in the porous material. Furthermore, simulations of the 1-D consolidation test with lower permeabilities, i.e., K  = 10-6  m/s, and K  = 10-7  m/s, are also conducted, and the results are plotted in Fig. 10  . Simulations with such low permeabilities pose computational challenges due to the increased susceptibility to numerical fluctuations. Consequently, a higher dissipation coefficient is employed in such scenarios for the simulations utilizing only artificial viscosity or simulations combining the artificial viscosity with a viscous dissipation term. Clearly, as can be seen in Fig. 10 , a highly fluctuating pressure profile can be found in the case that solely employs artificial viscosity without additional stabilization terms, as shown in Fig. 10 (a) and Fig. 10 (c), even when employing a very large viscous coefficient αП   = 5.0. This issue can be attributed to the reason that the use of artificial viscosity only cannot effectively mitigate the stress fluctuation in the solid phase. These fluctuations further influence the liquid phase and cannot be adequately dissipated due to the presence of low permeability. With the use of the proposed stabilisation technique, the numerical fluctuations are notably reduced as shown in Fig. 10 (c) and 10(d), resulting in a more accurate and stable prediction. The results also demonstrated the applicability of the proposed SPH scheme to materials with very low permeability such as silt, clay.  4.4 Sterpi’s erosion test In this case, the internal erosion test conducted by Sterpi (2003)  is simulated to test the performance of the new method to describe the coupling of seepage flow and erosion. The erosion test simulated the upward seepage within a sand-silt mixture. Two hydraulic-head controlled water reservoirs were connected to the top and bottom of the soil specimen to maintain a constant hydraulic gradient during the test. The experiments were conducted at five different hydraulic gradients, and the eroded mass collected from the outflow was dried and measured, which can be used as reference data for comparisons. The boundary setup and geometries of the erosion test are shown in Fig. 11  . The soil column is H  = 14 cm in height, and it is discretised using a particle resolution equal to dp  = 0.005 m. The soil column is initially fully saturated with an initial pressure profile corresponding to the hydraulic gradients measured in the experiment, which are 0.18, 0.39, 0.55, 0.60, and 0.75. This initial condition enables a steady-state seepage condition from the beginning of the simulation. Prescribed discharge boundary conditions are applied to the top and bottom boundaries, with the steady-state discharge velocity, to maintain the steady-state seepage during the simulation. The lateral boundaries are set as periodic boundaries to generate one-dimension uniform flow condition. Material properties of the porous column and numerical parameters adopted in the simulation are listed in Table 4  . The critical hydraulic gradient is assumed to be lower than 0.18, and thus the erosion is triggered under the hydraulic condition for all the tests. A fixed time step is adopted for the simulation with a physical time of 50 h. Fig. 12   presents the comparison between the eroded fines content obtained from SPH results and experimental measurements. The eroded fines content gradually increases with time under the applied hydraulic gradient, while the rate of erosion decreases during this process. Eventually, the erosion rate becomes insignificant once the fines content reaches its ultimate value. It is observed that the ultimate amount of eroded fines content increases with the rise in the applied hydraulic gradient, indicating higher erodibility under stronger hydraulic gradients. The SPH model reproduces the experimental observations and effectively captures the mass loss due to internal erosion. The slight discrepancies can be attributed to the limitations of the adopted erosion law.  4.5 1-D erosion-transport-deposition test In this case, the validity of the transport of liquidised fine particle, and its coupling with erosion and deposition processes are assessed. The performance of the extended diffusion term and the extended boundary treatment for the solution of concentrations of liquidised fines Cle   are also tested. The fines transport is governed by Eq. (5c), which is in a form of the advection equation with a source term. Conventionally, the solution of the advection problem presents non-physical spatial oscillations (also referred as numerical wiggles). The diffusion term for the concentration is applied to mitigate this issue. In this test, two case scenarios are considered, the first case simulates the 1-D steady-state seepage flow with an initial given profile of liquidised fine distribution but without internal erosion. Driven by the seepage flow, the liquidised fine particle will be transported along with the direction of the flow, resulting in the evolution of the concentration. The problem is thus simplified as a 1-D pure advection problem, and there are analytical solutions available for comparisons. For an initial concentration profile Cle  0  = Cle  (z , 0) and a constant 1-D specific discharge qL.z  , the analytical solution of the concentration profile at time t  is Cle  (z, t ) = Cle  0 (z  − qL.z t /(SL ϕ )). For the second case, the same initial profile is adopted but internal erosion is considered, thus the combined process of fine detachment, mitigation, and clogging is simulated. The problem of concern becomes the 1-D advection with a source term. As there is no analytical solution for this type of numerical problem, the finite difference solution is adopted as the reference solutions. In this case, the dependency of permeability on the porosity is not considered, thus the specific discharge is maintained throughout the simulation.
