A soil column of 1 m height is considered in present analysis and is discretised using SPH particles with the initial particle spacing of 0.02, 0.01, and 0.005 m, respectively. The initial concentration profile is given as,(47) C l e 0   = 0.25 sin 4 π z - 0.125       + 1      z > 0    0   z ⩽ 0             Periodic boundary conditions are applied to both the lateral side of the soil column to achieve one-dimensional water flow. A constant hydraulic gradient of ih   = 0.8 is imposed on the porous column for a steady state seepage. For the boundary with inflow, that is the top boundary with higher pressure, the value of Cle   at the boundary is prescribed as 0 using boundary particles, while Cle   is not prescribed for the boundary with outflow. The same material properties as in the erosion test are considered in this case, but with a higher erosion coefficient for a noticeable erosion of fines. The parameters adopted in the simulation are listed in Table 5  . The simulation is conducted for 1 hour of physical time. The contour plot of the concentration profile at different time instants is shown in Fig. 13  . The influence of internal erosion is evident, as the case involving the combined processes of erosion, transport, and deposition exhibits a significantly higher concentration of liquidised fines compared to the case involving pure transport. In Fig. 13 (c), the simulation without the diffusion term presents notable numerical wiggles during the transport. However, the use of diffusion term in Eq. (40b) effectively mitigates this issue, as demonstrated in Fig. 13 (b), where a clear transport process of the liquidised fines is observed without numerical fluctuations. Fig. 14   plots the SPH results from dp  = 0.005 m for the evolution of the concentration in the direction of water flow, compared to the analytical solutions. Apparently, the calculated results match well with the analytical solutions. The use of the diffusion term results in a smooth and accurate concentration profile. Moreover, the introduction of the new diffusion term does not appear to affect the accuracy of the results. The convergence behaviour of the concentration shown in Fig. 15   also indicates that the solution is converged with the order of convergence of approximately 1.71. In addition, for the second case scenario that the internal erosion is considered, the comparison of the time evolution of concentration between SPH and finite difference solution is shown in Fig. 16  . Again, a close agreement with the reference solution has been achieved, as can be seen in Fig. 16 . The concentration of liquidised fines along the length of the porous column increases with time, which can be attributed to the transfer of solid fine particle to liquidised fine particle due to the internal erosion. In addition, by comparing the case with and without the consideration of deposition, it is observed that particle clogging leads to a reduction in concentration profile. This effect becomes particularly pronounced over a longer duration and near the outflow side. Furthermore, the SPH prediction of the temporal evolution of the eroded fines content and porosity is plotted against the reference solutions in Fig. 17  . Clearly, the SPH predictions match well with the reference solutions. Internal erosion results in an increase of the mass loss of the solid skeleton and enlarges its porosity, while the deposition reduces this process, especially in the region with high concentration and on the downstream side of the seepage flow. The results presented in this section demonstrate that the proposed model can effectively capture the essential physical behaviours associated with internal erosion, including the combined process of fine detachment, migration, and deposition, and the variations in the porosity.  4.6 Erosion triggered embankment failure experiment The final case studies an embankment failure experiment triggered by internal erosion, devoted to examining the ability of the proposed method in capturing the coupling of seepage flow, internal erosion, and soil deformation, as well as the effectiveness of the proposed stabilisation technique in enhancing the stability and accuracy of the simulation. The experiment conducted by Fox et al. (2007)  is simulated in this case. The geometry and experimental configuration are shown in Fig. 18  . In the experiment, a small-scale embankment was built with a water tank constructed at one side. A constant water head was imposed and maintained throughout the experiment to allow the water inflow and a steady state seepage. Internal erosion was observed at the downstream toe of the embankment due to the seepage, and finally resulted in the failure of the embankment at the time t  = 726 s. The simulation is conducted in two-dimensional plane-strain condition. As shown in Fig. 18 , the model embankment has a height of 30 cm and a length of 90 cm, with a slope inclined at 60°. It is discretised using SPH particles with an initial particle spacing dp  = 0.0125 m. The embankment is initially saturated with a suction pressure pc   = 6 kPa. The initial stress profile is obtained through gravitational loading under the given initial pressure profile. The proposed solid wall boundary treatment in Section 3.2.1, utilizing boundary particles, is adopted to simulate the constant water head at the upstream side and to enforce an impermeable condition along the bottom boundary. The potential seepage face boundary condition is applied to the remaining free-surface particles. The hydro-mechanical properties of the test soil are taken from Ma et al. (2022) . The numerical parameters as well as material properties used in the simulation are present in Table 6  . The critical hydraulic gradient to initiate the internal erosion is set to be ich   = 0.35. Fig. 19   shows the evolution of the degree of saturation obtained from the proposed SPH method, which characterises the migration of the wetting front. The saturation front starts at the upstream side due to the presence of a constant water level. It then propagates towards the downstream slope, forming a seepage exit zone along the slope, which eventually leads to a steady seepage. It can be found that the use of the proposed method provides a smooth transition from the transient seepage flow to the steady-state flow in absence of numerical issues. The formation and evolution of the failure surface predicted by the SPH method, characterised by the deviatoric plastic strain profile, are shown in Fig. 20  , alongside experimental results for comparison. Clearly, seepage-driven internal erosion results in a progressive failure of the embankment. Failure first initiates locally at the embankment toe, which is found to have the largest specific discharge and the most pronounced erosion, and then the failure zone is further enlarged due to the combined action of seepage and erosion, resulting in a complete sliding surface at the end. The results obtained from the proposed SPH model generally reproduce the failure mechanism observed in the experiment, indicating that the proposed method can qualitatively capture the erosion-triggered failure process. However, the formation of tension cracks and overhanging failure mechanism observed in the experiment is not well captured with the proposed SPH model. The underlying reasons for these discrepancies could be manifold, such as differences in material properties between numerical analysis and experiment, or heterogeneity of the test soil in experiment. This may also suggest that an advanced constitutive model is required, and this will be investigated in future work. The evolution of fines content of solid phase and the concentration of liquidised fines predicted by the proposed SPH model are shown in Figs. 21 and 22   , respectively. Initially, in the early stage of wetting front migration, only a few eroded fine particles are observed. As the seepage exit zone is formed and the specific discharge increases within this zone, erosion becomes more significant at t  = 300 s. Subsequently, the erosion propagates backward, showing a trend of backward erosion and eventually results in the failure. On the other hand, the concentration of liquefied particles follows the liquid flow, with the largest intensity of liquefied fines concentrating at the toe of the wetting front. The fines concentration grows with time during the transport as more fine particles are eroded. The concentration profile starts to decrease when the wetting front reaches the downstream slope, as the formation of the seepage exit zone allows the fines to flow out of the embankment. In addition, it is noted that the use of diffusion algorithm improves the spatial oscillations in the calculation, resulting in a noise-free profile. Fig. 23   reports the calculated pore water pressure at different time instants. Conventionally, numerical noise may be present during large deformations, both for the solid and liquid phases. This issue has been notably improved with the proposed diffusion algorithm, resulting in a smooth and stable profile. To assess the new dissipation term in Eq. (38), Fig. 24  (a) shows the results of the calculated specific discharge magnitude and eroded fines content profile at t  = 1 s with the sole use of artificial viscosity using αμ   = 0.1. It is found that numerical instability is triggered during the initial water infiltration when a small artificial viscosity αμ   = 0.1 is applied, resulting in unphysical large discharge velocity and unphysical erosion of fines content. Consequently, embankment failure is observed at this stage due to the erosion-induced weakening of material strength. However, it is noted that this observed failure is solely attributed to numerical instability rather than physical instability. The use of a relatively large viscous coefficient αμ   = 0.8 can improve this issue and provide a stable result during the wetting front propagation, as shown in Fig. 25  (a), but instabilities reoccur when the wetting front reaches the downstream slope before the establishment of steady-state seepage conditions. A stable result from the wetting front mitigation to the steady-state seepage can be achieved by further increasing the viscous coefficient to αμ   = 1.0, as shown in Fig. 26  (a), but again it fails to maintain the stability in the post-failure stage. The underlying reason for these instabilities could be that artificial viscosity mainly operates on bulk deformations and does not provide sufficient dissipation for shear deformations. As a result, oscillations in the velocity profile occur. When solid acceleration is factored into the calculation of specific discharge using Eq. (7b). The oscillations in solid velocity cause the oscillation in specific discharge, and these instabilities grow further in both phases and may eventually cause the simulation to crash. By contrast, as shown in Fig. 24 (b), 25(b) and 26(b), the inclusion of the new viscous dissipation significantly mitigates the instability, providing a noise-free stable result throughout the entire seepage process from initial water infiltration, propagation and steady state. Finally, additional numerical experiments are conducted using the same test configuration but the softening coefficient for erosion ηe   increases from 1.0 to 2.0. Fig. 27   displays the resulted evolution of deviatoric plastic strain with ηe   = 1.0 and 2.0. It is observed that the simulation with ηe   = 2.0 remain stable at t  = 400 s , while the local failure has been initiated in the simulation with ηe   = 1.0. The onset of local failure of the test using ηe   = 2.0 occurs at t  = 570 s , and no subsequent sliding surface is observed thereafter. The material with a large softening coefficient indicates that the strength of the material is very sensitive to the erosion of fine particles, while a lower softening coefficient describes a material that has a high tolerance for internal erosion. It is evident that the new modified constitutive model enables a widely applicable description of the fine-dependent behaviour of porous materials.   5 Conclusions In this paper, a new multi-phase SPH framework is formulated for the coupled seepage-erosion-deformation process in porous materials. The framework includes several key components: a new multi-phase single-layer SPH formulation for erodible porous material, a new modified fine-dependent constitutive model that captures the nonlinear relationship between fines content and material strength, new extensions of a first-order consistent boundary treatment and diffusion algorithm for seepage-deformation to adapt to the erosion-transport process, and an investigation into a new artificial dissipation term to mitigate numerical instability in hydro-mechanical coupling. The proposed approach performs well in benchmark tests, showing satisfactory agreement with available analytical and numerical solutions, as well as reasonable match with experimental data. The new viscous dissipation term introduces a tuning parameter but demonstrates the ability to significantly improve the stability of the numerical solution, which is particularly crucial in hydro-mechanical coupling. The extended diffusion algorithm enhances the accuracy and robustness of the numerical framework. The modified constitutive model enables a nonlinear description of the material response to the loss of fine particles caused by internal erosion. It is shown that the new multi-phase SPH model successfully captures the entire coupling process of seepage-erosion-deformation, from the development of transient-steady state seepage to the onset of instability triggered by erosion and subsequent motion of the sliding mass. The proposed method can be further enhanced by incorporating a more sophisticated constitutive model for erodible porous materials. Such a model would allow for the consideration of the influence of relative density, stress state, and gradation. The development and validation of a rigorous constitutive model will be considered as a future investigation. Additionally, the present analysis adopts a simple erosion/deposition law based on empirical correlation between the fine content and specific discharge. While this approach captures the basic characteristics of internal erosion, it may fail to capture other important factors reported in the literature, such as the influence of gradation and stress state. Future work can be developed to implement a more rigorous erosion law.
1 Introduction Earthquakes can trigger a variety of hydrogeological phenomena, such as changes in stream flows, groundwater levels, and soil liquefaction (Wang and Manga, 2021 ). Coseismic groundwater response can occur over large distances (hundreds of kilometers), which cannot be achieved by common hydraulic activities such as pumping and injection. Monitoring changes of well water levels is the most convenient and direct way for studying the interaction between earthquakes and groundwater. Coseismic well water-level responses mainly include step-like, gradually-sustained and oscillatory changes (Wang and Manga, 2021 ). In the far field, water-level oscillations and triggered seismicity caused by earthquakes are the two principal phenomena resulting from seismic waves propagating over long distances (Manga et al., 2012, Brodsky and van der Elst, 2014 ). This suggests a potential coupling between hydrogeological processes and the triggered seismicity (Manga and Wang, 2007 ). Therefore, the mechanism of water-level response to seismic waves provides a probe to understand how seismic waves trigger earthquakes through pore-pressure changes. The observation of coseismic well water-level response, even for small earthquakes, is crucial to improving our understanding of the generic behavior of water-level response to seismic waves. With the rapid increase in water-level observations at high sampling rates, it has become difficult to manually pick all the water-level signals for a comprehensive study, and there is a need for effective and automated techniques specifically designed to detect coseismic water-level oscillations. In this study, we develop an automatic algorithm for the detection of coseismic water-level oscillations. We also apply our algorithm to a 10-year worth of water-level data recorded at the Plate Boundary Observatory (PBO) station B078 near Parkfield, California, to investigate the predominant factors controlling the water-level response to seismic waves. Furthermore, we update the empirical relation with the seismic energy density, the hypocentral distance and the moment magnitude. The predicted seismic energies using this new empirical relation are generally consistent with the observed seismic energy to within two orders of magnitude.  2 Data We use the pore-pressure record at the PBO station B078 (120.35°W, 35.84°N) near Parkfield from 2008 to 2017 (downloaded from http://pore.unavco.org/pore/goldhl078bcs2006 ) which has a high sampling rate of 1 Hz (traditional sampling interval is minutes) and a resolution in the hundredths of hPa (Gottlieb et al., 2017 ). The well has a depth of ∼ 182 m with an open interval between 158.5 m and 170.7 m. The well water level h   can be converted from recorded borehole pore pressure p   using the relation h = p / ρ g   , where ρ   is the water density (103  kg/m3 ), and g   is the gravitational acceleration (9.8 m/s2 ). Since we focus on the oscillations of water level caused by seismic waves, we bandpass filter the data to the period band of 3–300 s. At the same time, we use seismic record to verify the detection of water-level oscillations and estimate the energy of the seismic waves responsible for the water-level oscillations. Although there are downhole seismometer and strainmeter co-located at B078, the seismometer is a short-period sensor and does not provide the long-period information that is important to the generation of water-level oscillations, whereas the strainmeter only record the dynamic strain in the horizontal direction (Barbour, 2015 ). Therefore, we employ the seismic record from the nearest broadband station PKD (120.54°W, 35.95°N) which is about 20 km from station B078 (BDSN, 2014 ). Fig. 1   shows the locations of the stations. PKD provides a high-quality continuous record with a 40 Hz sampling rate over the same observation period. We filter the recorded vertical ground velocities to the frequency band of 0.01–5 Hz, given the corner frequency of the seismometer at PKD of 0.01 Hz.  3 Methods We combine the time-domain short-term average/long-term average (STA/LTA) method and the frequency-domain spectral analysis to detect the coseismic water-level oscillations. 3.1 Detection of earthquakes and water-level responses by the STA/LTA algorithm Oscillations of well water level caused by seismic waves have similar waveforms to the seismic waves. This means that methods used to detect seismic signals can also be used to identify water-level oscillations. A well-established and most popular approach in seismic arrival detection is the STA/LTA method, which tracks the ratio of energies in a short-term window and a long-term window (Allen, 1978 ), and is effective for detecting arrivals with amplitudes larger than the background noise (Trnkoczy, 2009 ). Even though there are more sophisticated detection methods developed in seismic detection, such as PhaseNet (e.g., Zhu and Beroza, 2019 ) and template matching detection (e.g., Shelly et al., 2007 ), the STA/LTA is still efficient for recognizing water level oscillations due to the fact that seismic events which can cause the water-level oscillations cannot be too small. Given that the peak of the water-level oscillation is more prominent than the background noise in most cases, the STA/LTA method is a reasonable choice to detect water-level oscillations effectively. The basic principle of the STA/LTA method is that an event is identified when the ratio of the average energy in the short-term window to the average energy in the long-term window exceeds a pre-set threshold (Allen, 1978 ). The algorithm can be expressed as:(1) S T A i   = 1 N STA    ∑ j = i - N STA   + 1  i  C F j   ,         (2) L T A i   = 1 N LTA    ∑ j = i - N STA   - N LTA   + 1  i - N STA     C F j   ,         (3) STA / L T A i  = S T A i   L T A i    ≥ λ o n     o r  STA / L T A i  = S T A i   L T A i    ≤ λ off  ,       where S T A i      and L T A i      are the average energy in the short-term and long-term window prior to point i   for the given time point i  , respectively, N STA     and N LTA     are the numbers of points in the short-term and long-term windows, respectively, λ o n     and λ o f f     are the pre-set ‘on’ and ‘off’ thresholds, respectively, and CF  stands for the characteristic function. Here, we use C F i   = x  2  ( i )    , where x ( i )    represents the input signal at time point i  . The STA detects the event signal, whereas the LTA measures the background noise level. When the ratio of STA/LTA exceeds the threshold λ o n    , an event is ‘declared’, whereas when the ratio is below the threshold λ o f f    , the event ends. Usually, λ o n     is larger than λ o f f    , which can reduce the likelihood of incorrectly determining event termination due to minor fluctuations in the STA/LTA value. Good recognition of ending time can help determine the timing of stopping the frozen operation, as mentioned later. The thresholds for identifying water level oscillations are set to capture the oscillations as many as possible, while the values for determining earthquakes are set on the premise that most of the detected earthquakes should be able to cause water level oscillations. Through extensive testing, we reached the values of 13 and 8 for λ o n     and λ o f f    , respectively, for well water level response detection, and 33 and 15, respectively, for seismic event detection. We set the lengths of the STA window at 5 s, the minimum duration of typical coseismic water oscillations; and the LTA window at 6000 s, longer than the maximum duration of an event signal. The STA/LTA method calculates the average values of the characteristic function in two consecutive moving-time windows. Therefore, events with large or long-time oscillations can raise the value of LTA, potentially resulting in the missing detection of a following small event. To improve the detection of small events that follow larger ones, we adopt a ‘frozen-in’ operation. Specifically, when the ratio of STA/LTA is larger than the pre-set threshold λ o f f    , the LTA value is kept fixed at the current value until the LTA window no longer contains the signal of events (Fig. 2  a). This frozen-in operation is also commonly used in the detection of seismic events (Trnkoczy, 2009 ).  3.2 Detection of water-level responses by spectral analysis The STA/LTA ratio is more sensitive to oscillations with significant amplitude changes, but less so for small amplitude changes or significant changes in frequency (Fig. 2 b). To overcome this limitation, we adopt the spectral analysis to further enhance the detection capability. The spectral analysis is invoked only when an earthquake is detected with no corresponding water-level response detection by STA/LTA. For spectral analysis, we cut the water-level data from 8000 s before the seismically detected arrival to 8000 s after the end of the detected seismic event, which is long enough to account for the background noise. We calculate the spectrogram of the water-level data using a 1200-s long moving time window, and use the total power spectral density (PSD) in the 0.02 − 0.075 Hz frequency band to track the change in the low-frequency signal. To detect a significant change in the signal, we adopt the z-score, defined as z = x - μ  σ    , where x   is the raw data of the point, μ   is the mean value of all points and σ   is the standard deviation. Z score is a statistical measurement that describes how many standard deviations a given value is from the mean of a group of values (Altman, 1968 ). A water-level oscillation event is ‘declared’ when the z-score reaches 3, as illustrated in Fig. 2 (b). Since the calculation of the water-level spectrogram over time is time-consuming, we only apply the spectral analysis to water-level data when there is a detected seismic event but no water oscillations detected by STA/LTA. In summary, we first apply the STA/LTA algorithm with frozen-in operation to detect water-level oscillations and seismic events. All detected water oscillations with no corresponding seismic detections are discarded. Secondly, we apply spectral analysis to the water-level data if a seismic event is identified but no associated water-level oscillation is detected by STA/LTA. Finally, all the detected water-level oscillations contain pickings in both the time and frequency domains. The workflow is shown in Fig. 2 (c).   4 Results and discussions 4.1 Detected water-level oscillations We apply our detection algorithm to the pore-pressure data at PBO station B078 and the seismic records at station PKD from 2008 to 2017. Initially, a total of 867 water-level responses are detected, of which 648 events are detected by STA/LTA and 219 events are detected by frequency-domain spectral analysis. Afterward, we check the detected events, discarding the ones with problematic pore-pressure data (see examples in Fig. S1 ). Upon this review, we retain 853 reliable events, with 634 detected by STA/LTA and 219 by spectral analysis.  4.2 Evaluation of the detection of water-level oscillations To validate the performance of our detection algorithm, we manually pick the water-level oscillations caused by seismic waves during 2016–2017 (a total of 130) as the ground truth catalog. The performance of our algorithm is evaluated by PRECISION and RECALL defined as (Powers, 2011 ):(4) PRECISION : P = T p  T p  + F p    × 100 % = T p  P p   × 100 % ,         (5) RECALL : R = T p  T p  + F n    × 100 % = T p  R p   × 100 % ,         where T p    and F p    are the numbers of true and false positives, respectively, i.e., T p    is the number of automatically detected water-level oscillations that are indeed triggered by seismic waves, whereas F p    is the number of automatically detected water-level oscillations that are not due to seismic waves; F n    is the number of false negatives, or water-level oscillations that are not detected by the automatic program; P p    and R p    are the numbers of predicted and real positives, respectively, i.e., P p    is the number of automatically detected response events, and R p    is the number of manually picked events considered to be real. PRECISION represents the proportion of the automatic detection that is truly caused by seismic waves, and RECALL measures the proportion of the real water-level oscillations that are successfully detected by the algorithm. Based on our ground truth catalog, the PRECISION and RECALL of our algorithm are 92.8 % and 89.2 %, respectively (Table 1  ), which demonstrates that our algorithm can be effective in the detection of water-level oscillations caused by seismic waves. When there is no nearby seismic station, our automatic detection algorithm can still be applied to water-level data only, but the recall and precision of detection might be less than those of using seismic events as a cross-check. The data set to which we apply our detection algorithm is recorded in 1 s sample rate, which is not the traditional minute-based water level recordings. Lower sample rate measurements of water level can only capture the waves that last longer than the sample interval and contain energy in the frequency band below the Nyquist frequency. For instance, if the sample rate is 1 min, only the waves with energy in the frequency band of 0–0.0083 Hz can be recorded, which might mean only the large distant earthquakes can meet the requirement. This indicates that minute-based sampling limits the number of observable coseismic water-level oscillations. However, even with water oscillations recorded at a sample rate of minutes, our detection algorithm still works well to identify the signals (see Text S1 , Fig. S2  in Supporting Information ).  4.3 Relation between observed seismic energy and well water-level oscillation In order to investigate the relationship between seismic wave energy and water-level oscillations, we identify the seismic events that correspond to the detected water-level oscillations from the earthquake catalog. To do this, we compare the start times of the detected water-level oscillations with the arrival times of P- and S-waves estimated in the PREM model (Dziewonski and Anderson, 1981 ) from both global earthquakes in the USGS catalog (https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/search/ ) and local events in the NCSN catalog (https://ncedc.org/ncedc/catalog-search.html ). In the end, a total of 726 events are found to be associated with known earthquakes, including 559 detected by STA/LTA and 167 by spectral analysis. We will focus on these events in the subsequent analysis. We use the observed peak ground velocity (PGV) observed at seismic station PKD to measure the seismic energy at PBO station B078. Since PKD is ∼ 20 km from B078, we corrected the PGV at PKD to that at B078 using the attenuation equation of Kanamori et al. (1993) :(6) log 10  V 2    = log 10  V 1    + 1.2178 × log 10  D 1  D 2     + 0.002302 × D 1  - D 2     ,         where V 1    and V 2    are the recorded and corrected velocities at the recording and target sites, respectively, D 1    and D 2    are the corresponding epicentral distances in km. After the correction for site location difference, we estimate the seismic energy density at the target site by:(7) e ≈ ρ V  2  ,         where V   is the PGV and ρ   is the density of the ground rock, which we use 2.7 ×   103  kg/m3  in the current study (Barbot et al., 2009 ). To investigate how the seismic energy affects the well oscillation, we compare the peak amplitude of water-level oscillations with the seismic energy density. The water-level response detected in the frequency domain tends to be small and is often overwhelmed by background noise at a relatively high frequency band (Fig. S3  in Supporting Information ), so we re-filter the water-level data only detected in the frequency domain to the frequency band of 0.02 – 0.075 Hz, which is the same as that in the spectral analysis. The water-level oscillation exhibits an evident linear relationship with logarithmic seismic energy: the larger the logarithm of the observed seismic energy density, the larger the peak amplitude of water-level oscillation (Fig. 3  a), irrespective of whether the water-level oscillations are detected by STA/LTA or spectral analysis. Seismic energy density is therefore a major factor controlling coseismic water level oscillations. Besides the good linear relationship, there are some deviation responses (Fig. 3 a). The response of water level to seismic waves varies with the frequency of seismic waves due to the well-bore construction, aquifer properties, and the dilatation of seismic waves (Cooper et al., 1965 ), so the frequency of the strongest water level response might not be the same as that of the seismic waves with the maximum energy. This mismatch could cause a deviation in coseismic water level oscillations. Seismic energy density is a well applicable metric in earthquake hydrology (Wang, 2007 ). The different energy thresholds of various coseismic hydrologic responses indicate variable sensitivities to physical processes and are helpful to distinguish different mechanisms (Wang and Manga, 2021 ). Our frequency-domain detection results indicate that the threshold of seismic energy density for causing well water-level response is about 5 ×   10−9  J/m3  (Fig. 3 a). This is notably lower than the threshold of 10−6  J/m3  for initiating coseismic water-level response at Davils Hole, a location known for its extreme sensitivity to earthquakes (Weingarten and Ge, 2014 ). Conversely, the energy threshold of the global hydrogeological responses to earthquakes, estimated based on the empirical relation of Wang (2007) , is 10−6  J/m3  (Wang and Manga, 2021 ), which is 3 orders of magnitude larger than what our result indicates. The smallest dynamic strain for triggering earthquakes is 2 ×   10−9 , whose corresponding PGV is ∼ 7 ×   10−6  m/s based on a seismic wave velocity of 3.5 km/s (van der Elst and Brodsky, 2010 , Miyazawa et al., 2021 ). Our detected PGV threshold causing water-level oscillation is ∼ 1 ×   10−6  m/s, which is several factors smaller than the threshold of dynamic earthquake triggering. Our new automatic algorithm improves the detectability of the water-level responses to earthquakes. In addition to seismic density, we find frequency of the waves is also important to cause coseismic water level oscillation. We found several examples of seismic waves with energy densities above the threshold but that do not cause water-level oscillations (Fig. S4 ) and they are basically high-frequency waves and lack of signal at 0.01–0.1 Hz (Fig. 4  ). Our detected earthquakes caused water-level oscillations with seismic energy densities just above the threshold but less than 2.7 ×   10−8  J/m3  (approximately the smallest energy density of the time-domain detected earthquake) are all far-field earthquakes, whose seismic waves energy are predominantly in the low-frequency of 0.01–0.1 Hz (Fig. S5 , and Fig. 4 ). We suspect this phenomenon is due to the well-bore storage effect and the amplification of water level to the strain of surface waves. The well-bore storage effect makes the response of the well water level more sensitive to the pressure head fluctuations caused by seismic waves at lower frequencies (Cooper et al., 1965 ). In addition, the amplification of pore pressure to surface wave can result in a larger amplification compared to other phases (see details in Text S2 , Fig. S6  in Supporting Information ). Determining which factor plays a more important role in causing earthquake-induced water-level oscillations requires further investigation in the future.  4.4 Comparison between observed and predicted seismic energy densities Wang (2007)  proposed the empirical attenuation equation by combining the ground motion attenuation equation in Southern California (Cua, 2005 ) and the relation between earthquake energy and magnitude (Båth, 1966 ):(8) log  10  e r   = - 3 log  10  r + 1.44 M - 4.38 ,         where e ( r )    is the seismic energy density in J/m3 , r   is the hypocentral distance in km, and M   is the magnitude of the earthquake. The empirical relation has been commonly used to predict the seismic energy density at sites where coseismic hydrogeological processes occur. Note that the constant in the equation in Wang and Manga (2021)  was mistaken. Details of the derivation are provided in Supporting Information  (Text S3 ). Fig. 3 (b) shows the relationship between water-level oscillations detected at B078 and seismic energy predicted by Eq. (8) . The result still shows a linear relation between water-level oscillation and seismic energy predicted by the empirical relation, but with a larger deviation than that in Fig. 3 (a) with seismic energy obtained from the observed PGV. Even after applying the magnitude conversion in the empirical function mentioned later, the linear relation is still more scattering than that of the energy approximated by ρ V  2     (Fig. S11 ). This suggests that ρ V  2     provides a better estimation for the seismic energy density than the empirical relation in Eq. (8) . To quantify the difference between the observed seismic energy density using PGV and the predicted seismic density using the empirical function, we compare the predicted and observed seismic energy densities at the B078 station. The comparison in Fig. 5   reveals that the predicted seismic energy densities are systematically greater than the observed ones for earthquakes with M ≤ 6.2    (Fig. 5 a, 5b). We find that the systematic discrepancy is due to the types of earthquake magnitudes used in the empirical relation in Eq. (8) . The relationship between seismic energy and earthquake magnitude (Båth, 1966 ) is based on surface-wave magnitude M S   , so the magnitude used in Eq. (8)  must also be M S   . Consequently, differences between M S    and other types of magnitude can result in a systematic discrepancy. When the magnitude is smaller than 6.2, the other types of magnitude correspond to a smaller surface wave magnitude (see Fig. S7  in Supporting Information ). After converting all magnitudes to M S    (see Text S4  in Supporting Information ), the discrepancy between the observed and predicted seismic energy density is reduced (Fig. 5 c, 5d). Even so, there is still a slight systematic difference between the observed and predicted energy densities when M ≤ 6.2   . It should be noted that the difference between the observed and predicted energy densities using m b   , even after converted to M S   , can still exceed two orders of magnitude (Fig. 5 d). To explore whether the systematic shift between the observed and predicted seismic energy when M ≤ 6.2    is a generous phenomenon, we compare the predicted and observed seismic energy at the station BAR (116.67°W, 32.68°N) in Southern California and the station MAJO (138.20°E, 36.55°N) in Japan from 2022 to 2023, and find both show a similar discrepancy when M ≤ 6.2    (see Text S5 , Fig. S8  in Supporting Information ). This indicates that the systematic discrepancy when M ≤ 6.2    is due to the type of magnitude rather than the site effects. Overall, the discrepancy between the observed seismic energy densities and predictions using the empirical relation is mainly within two orders of magnitude, and the observed seismic energy is systematically smaller than the predicted ones when M ≤ 6.2    without converting to surface wave magnitude. We further examine the azimuthal distribution and focal mechanisms of the events whose observed seismic energy densities deviate from the predicted values by more than one order of magnitude from the mean deviation (0.357). The pattern in Fig. 6   does not suggest any clear relationship between the energy discrepancies and either azimuth or focal mechanism. The discrepancies may be due to the complexity of wave propagation, which is caused by the earth’s lateral heterogeneity and site effect. In addition, the effects of source dimension and rupture directivity might also be important, which are ignored in the point-source approximation in deriving the empirical relationship (Wang and Manga, 2021 ). However, our observation does not have enough near-field data to identify this effect.  4.5 An updated empirical relation using M W    The most robustly determined magnitude nowadays is the moment magnitude M W    proposed in Kanamori (1977) . To ensure the compatibility with modern earthquake catalog and facilitate the application of the empirical relation, we develop an updated empirical relation in terms of M W    following the argument in Wang (2007) . We replace the energy-magnitude relation of Båth (1966)  used in Wang (2007)  by the Gutenberg-Richter relation (Gutenberg and Richter, 1956 ), which is expressed as:(9) logE = 1.5 M s  + 4.8 ,         where E   is the seismic energy given in J. The relation in Eq. (9)  agrees closely with that of Båth (1966) , with a logarithmic difference of less than 0.3 orders of magnitude (Fig. S9  in Supporting Information ). Following Kanamori (1977) , M S    and M W    can be used interchangeably in this equation. According to Wang and Manga (2021) , at a given site the seismic energy density from an earthquake can be expressed as(10) e r   = 3 E  4 π     r  - 3   ,         where e   is the seismic energy density and r   is the epicentral distance (in m). Combining Eq. (9)  with Eq. (10)  and changing the unit of r   to km, we have the updated empirical attenuation relation(11) log  10  e = - 3 log  10  r + 1.5 M S  - 4.82 .         Based on the regression relation between M S    and M W   , the distinction between the two types of magnitude is pronounced only when M W  ≤ 6.2   . Therefore, we can establish the following empirical relations based on Eq. (11)  for moment magnitude M W   :(12) log 10  e = - 3 log 10  r + 2.24 M W  - 9.57 ,  for  M  W  ≤ 6.2 ,   - 3 log 10  r + 1.5 M W  - 4.82 ,  for  M  W  > 6.2 ,        where for events with M W    ≤ 6.2, we convert M S    to M W    using the equation from Das et al. (2011)  (refer to Eq. S6 in Supporting Information Text S4 ). It should be pointed out that we simplify the magnitude conversion by ignoring the case of hypocentral depth exceeding 70 km and the lower magnitude bound (Das et al., 2011 ). These simplifications do not result in a seismic energy density prediction difference from the observed values by more than two orders of magnitude based on our results. The difference between the seismic energy densities predicted by the relation of Wang (2007)  in Eq. (8)  and our updated relation in Eq. (12)  is within a factor of 2.5, indicating that our updated empirical function is applicable to other places as the old empirical function (Fig. S10  in Supporting Information ). The comparison in Fig. 6 (a) also shows a good agreement between the observed energy densities and those predicted by the updated empirical relation. It is worth noting that the above relations are based on the attenuation relation for Southern California. The energy prediction equations of other regions having different seismic attenuation properties might have different sets of parameters in the relationships.   5 Conclusions Our automatic detection program of coseismic well water-level oscillations combining time domain recognition (STA/LTA) and frequency domain recognition (using PSD) has a precision of 92.8 % and a recall of 89.2 %, which can pick up the coseismic well water-level oscillations efficiently and effectively. Application of the algorithm to a decades’ worth of data from the PBO station B078 near Parkfield clearly demonstrates that the well water-level responses are mainly controlled by seismic energy. The enhanced frequency-domain sensitivity enables us to detect previously undetected coseismic responses, and we find that the seismic energy density threshold for groundwater responses to earthquakes is about 5 ×    10−9  J/m3 , three orders of magnitude smaller than our current understanding. However, not every earthquake with a seismic energy density above the threshold can cause water-level oscillations. The seismic events whose energy at lower frequency (<0.1 Hz) above the threshold are more likely to cause coseismic water-level oscillations. Comparing the relation between water-level response with the predicted and observed seismic energy density, the approximation of the seismic energy density estimated by the square of peak ground velocity is better than that using the empirical relation. In addition, we find that the type of magnitude in the empirical relation in Wang (2007)  should be surface-wave magnitude. The impact of the types of magnitude is significant for earthquakes with M < 6.2   , but negligible for earthquakes with M > 6.2   . Given that modern earthquake catalogs predominantly utilize moment magnitude M W   , we derive an updated empirical relation between seismic energy, epicentral distance, and moment magnitude, which facilitates a more straightforward estimation of the predicted seismic energy density based on M W   . The discrepancy between the predicted and observed seismic energy is generally within two orders of magnitude. Notably, this discrepancy is independent of the focal mechanisms and azimuths.
1 Introduction Under the background of global climate change and strong human activities, the uncertainty of extreme hydrological events increases (Walsh et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2006 ), drought and flood events occur more frequently in multiple spatial and temporal dimensions, and the risk of drought and flood increases among sub-basins. The drought and flood encounters in the basin have a profound impact on local and downstream water security, ecological security and sustainable socio-economic development (Su et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2022 ). It is urgent to conduct in-depth research on the law of drought and flood encounters and spatial cascade effects in the source region-upper-middle-lower reaches of the basin. The drought and flood encounters in different sub-regions of the basin are essentially a multi-regional combination problem of meteorological and hydrological variables (Zhang et al., 2023a,b; Wang et al., 2024 ), as shown in Fig. 1  . On the one hand, once the meteorological drought and flood events occur, it may affect the deficiency and abundance of soil water and runoff through the process of water cycle, thus affecting the safety of water resources in the basin. On the other hand, there are many interactive processes in the process of drought and flood propagation in different spatial domains. Human activities such as agricultural irrigation, dam and reservoir regulation and water diversion projects in the middle and lower reaches have a significant impact on the process of drought and flood propagation (Fang et al., 2020 ). At the same time, land–atmosphere interaction, water-heat balance and climate change will also aggravate the uncertainty of the spread of drought and flood events (Jehanzaib et al., 2020 ), resulting in a complex relationship of mutual influence and time-delay transmission of drought and flood events in the source-upper-middle-downstream spatial domain (Lopez et al., 2013). Multi-scale factor activities such as regional climate, geography, hydrological conditions and human activities jointly control the spatial and temporal process of drought and flood propagation. There are not only many driving factors, but also the driving contribution is time-varying, so that the effects of the same drought and flood and flood-drought scenarios are also different. Therefore, it is very important to understand the encounter rules of different types of droughts and floods in different regions of the basin, clarify the response relationship and potential transmission mechanism among different systems, and improve the ability of disaster warning, risk control and water resources allocation in the basin. The drought-flood encounter in the basin is a multi-dimensional complex process including frequency domain, time domain and spatial domain (Ding and Wei, 2022; Zhou et al., 2023 ). The construction and calculation of drought and flood index is an important basis for the quantitative study of regional drought and flood, and a variety of different types of drought and flood index have been proposed for different classification and application objects. Among them, the standardized precipitation/runoff index (SPI/SRI), which characterizes meteorological/hydrological droughts and floods, is often widely used in areas with detailed measured precipitation data (Spinoni et al., 2019 ). According to SPI/SRI simulation, it was found that the SRI of the Yangtze River Basin from 1980 to 2018 was mainly characterized by a non-significant wetting trend. The trend of meteorological drought was mainly concentrated in the upper reaches of the Jialing River Basin, the upper reaches of the Hanjiang River and the Jinsha River, while the middle and lower reaches showed a wetting trend (Sun et al., 2019 ). From 1961 to 2020, the frequency of drought in the Yellow River Basin was greater than that of floods, and severe drought events occurred about once every 10 years (Wang et al., 2020 ), but the overall trend was wetting. Focusing on the quantification of drought and flood propagation characteristics and process description, many scholars have found that there are significant differences in the lag time of meteorological-hydrological drought and flood in different climatic regions by using correlation analysis. In recent years, non-correlation methods such as joint probability distribution function (Guo et al., 2020 ), multiple regression (Wang et al., 2019a,b ), Bayesian probability theory (Shin et al., 2020 ) and cross wavelet transform (Yao et al., 2020 ) have been gradually introduced into the study. The propagation process of drought and flood is controlled by many factors. Due to different climate and water system characteristics, the propagation time of meteorological-agricultural drought in the Yangtze River Basin is longer than that in the Yellow River Basin (Zhang et al., 2021 ).Huang et al. (2021)  pointed out that the lag time of meteorological-hydrological drought and flood propagation in the Yellow River Basin was 1–2 months by using the sliding window Copula entropy method and the lag time grey correlation method. Ding et al. (2021)  used wavelet analysis to study the propagation of meteorological-hydrological droughts and floods in eight sub-regions of China, indicating that climatic conditions are important factors affecting drought propagation. The drought propagation relationship in humid climate regions (such as warm temperate climate regions) is stronger, while the drought propagation relationship in arid climate regions is weaker. In different seasons, the response relationship of drought propagation is also different. The propagation relationship in summer and autumn is stronger than that in spring and winter, which may be related to the seasonal distribution of precipitation and snow melting. In addition, a multi-dimensional joint distribution simulation method of meteorological and hydrological variables represented by Copula function (Zhu et al., 2021 ) is formed on the analysis of drought and flood encounter characteristics in different spatial domains. Studies have shown that the transfer between different time scales of runoff in the lower reaches of the Yangtze River is relatively stable, with a probability of 6.26 % −16.76 %, which provides a theoretical basis for river basin water resources planning and management (Xu et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2020). Some achievements have been made in the study of drought and flood in the basin, which has laid a solid foundation for the follow-up study, but there are still some points to be supplemented: Previous studies mostly focused on the whole basin as the research object, especially in the division of river basin zoning for the ' China Water Tower ' river source area is not taken into account. In addition, the drought-flood encounter problem involves multiple partitions (source region-upper-middle-downstream) and multiple levels (meteorological-hydrological drought and flood). Most studies focus on determining the propagation law between different types of droughts and floods. The identification of the law of meteorological-hydrological drought and flood encounters in the basin and the spatial cascade effect, and the quantitative evaluation of the superimposed effects of drought and flood under different scenarios need to be further studied. The Yangtze River and the Yellow River Basin span multiple climatic zones, and the terrain and climate spatial heterogeneity of different sub-regions is obvious. Affected by the complex underlying surface and geographical environment, the drought and flood events are regionally significant and the hydrological situation is more complex (Omer et al., 2021 ). In view of this, the main objectives of this study include: (1) Analyze the evolution law of extreme drought and wetness events in the source region-upper-middle-lower reaches of the two major basins; (2) Correlation analysis and transfer function analysis were used to explore the response relationship and lag effect of hydrological drought and wetness in different sub-regions of the basin to meteorological drought and wetness. (3) The Copula function method is used to quantitatively analyze the joint probability of drought and flood encounters of 9 combined events, and the effects of drought and wetness superposition and drought mitigation under different drought and wetness encounter scenarios are deeply analyzed.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The Yangtze River originates from the Tanggula Mountains in Qinghai Province and eventually flows into the East China Sea. It is about 6300 km long. The total area of the basin is 1.8 million square kilometers, and the water resources are abundant. The average water resources for many years are 995.9 billion m3, accounting for about 36 % of the total water resources in the country (Zhang et al., 2022a,b ). The Yellow River is the second longest river in China, second only to the Yangtze River. It originates from the northern foot of the Bayan Har Mountains on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. It flows eastward into the Bohai Sea with a total length of 5464 km and a total area of 795,000 square kilometers. The geographical location is shown in Fig. 2  (a). The Yangtze River and the Yellow River Basin are also important strategic water resources in China. They are mainly recharged by precipitation, with a small amount of glacier meltwater, seasonal snowmelt, and groundwater recharge. The two basins span multiple climatic zones. Under the influence of climate diversity and topographic complexity, the temporal and spatial distribution of precipitation is uneven. In recent years, heavy droughts and floods in the Yangtze River and Yellow River Basin have occurred frequently, such as the 7.20 Henan heavy rainstorm disaster, which caused a total of 14.786 million people to be affected, and the direct economic loss was 120.06 billion yuan. From August 18 to November 15,2022, a serious drought occurred in the Yangtze River Basin. During the peak period of drought in late August, the drought area of crops in the Yangtze River Basin reached 66.32 million acre, with 810,000 people and 920,000 large livestock having temporary difficulty in drinking water due to drought. Affected by the same drought in the whole region, the drought in the lower reaches increased, and the water level of Poyang Lake and Dongting Lake reached a record low. Under the background of climate change driven by natural and human activities, the transformation relationship between water cycle factors in the two major basins will be more complex, which will make the drought and flood risk in this area full of complexity and uncertainty (Yang et al., 2020 ).  2.2 Materials In this paper, the hydrological data used include the monthly runoff data of 8 typical hydrological stations in the main stream of the Yangtze River and the Yellow River from 1956 to 2020, which is derived from the ' Hydrological Yearbook '. Tangnaihai, Toudaoguai, Huayuankou and Lijin stations are selected as the source-upper-middle-downstream control stations in the Yellow River Basin, as shown in Fig. 2 (b). Zhimenda, Yichang, Hukou and Datong stations are selected in the Yangtze River Basin, as shown in Fig. 2 (c). The monthly precipitation data of 422 meteorological stations in the two basins from 1956 to 2020 are shown in Fig. 2 , which is derived from the National Meteorological Information Center of China Meteorological Administration (https://data.cma.cn/ ).  2.3 Methods According to the framework of ' evolution characteristics-propagation process-drought and flood encounter ', the key content and technical route of this study are put forward. Firstly, based on the SPI representing meteorological drought and wet and the SRI representing hydrological drought and wet, the evolution law of extreme drought and wetness events in the source region-upper-middle-lower reaches of the two basins is analyzed. Secondly, the correlation analysis and transfer function analysis are used to explore the response relationship and lag effect between the two in different partitions. Finally, a two-dimensional joint distribution model is constructed by Copula function to quantitatively analyze the joint probability of drought and wetness encounters of 9 combined events, and the influence of different encounter scenarios of drought and wetness is deeply analyzed. Among them, the meteorological-hydrological drought and wetness, drought and wetness encounters in different sub-regions can be divided into two categories: synchronous (wet-wet, drought-drought, normal-normal) and asynchronous (wet-drought, wet-normal, normal-drought, normal-wet, drought-wet, drought-normal). The occurrence of drought and wetness scenarios usually aggravates the impact of local disasters, resulting in a deterioration of the scale and severity of disasters. When the wetness-drought scenario occurs, it can play a role in mitigating drought to a certain extent, making the degree of drought lighter or normal. Therefore, the adverse scenarios of wet-wet and drought-drought, and the favorable scenarios of wet-drought are selected to deeply analyze the superposition of drought and wetness and the mitigation effect of drought under different scenarios of drought and wetness. The technical route is shown in Fig. 3  . 2.3.1 Calculation of drought and flood index In recent years, the continuous development of multi-source data fusion technology has rapidly supplemented the observation data of regional meteorological and hydrological elements, and the continuous improvement of extreme value evaluation indicators has better described the evolution characteristics of drought and flood. From the perspective of the impact of drought and flood evolution at home and abroad, different types of drought and flood indexes are proposed (Mukherjee et al., 2018 ). This study mainly focuses on meteorological and hydrological drought and flood (Table 1  ). The drought-flood cascade refers to the phenomenon of shifting from one type (spatial) drought-flood to another type (spatial) drought-flood (Tian et al., 2022 ). There is a close relationship between different types of drought and flood. It is well known that the main source of surface river runoff is atmospheric precipitation. The amount of precipitation is the starting point of other types of drought and flood, and has a strong correlation with various types of drought and flood (Yang et al., 2023 ). Therefore, in this study, SPI and SRI indexes with precipitation and runoff as input factors were used to explore meteorological and hydrological drought and flood respectively. The two indices are widely used in the study. The SPI index based on Gamma distribution can better fit the precipitation time series. SRI uses the same principle as SPI to evaluate hydrological drought and flood, which has the characteristics of simple calculation and clear significance (Wang et al., 2022a,b ). And studies have shown that it has strong applicability in the identification of drought and flood in the source area (Sadhwani and Eldho, 2024 ). According to the national meteorological grade standard, the specific drought and wetness classification is shown in Table 2  :  2.3.2 Transfer function analysis (TFA) The TFA method uses fast Fourier transform to sample the time-domain signal into a frequency-domain signal, and then uses auto-spectrum and cross-spectrum to obtain the estimation of coherence function, amplitude (gain) and phase frequency response (Claassen et al., 2016). The transfer function of an unknown system consists of three parameters: coherence, gain and phase (Fig. 4  ). Coherence (θ(f )) is used to measure whether there is a response between two signals. The gain (|H (f )|) measures the strength of the response system. The phase (Φ(f )) lag can be converted into a time lag in the time domain. The negative phase lag represents that the change of SRI lags behind SPI or the SRI of the next partition lags behind the SRI of the previous partition, and the positive phase is the opposite. In the frequency domain analysis, the Nyquist frequency of SPI and SRI sequences is 190nHz, and the fastest oscillation period observed is about 60 days. According to the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem (Zhou et al., 2021 ), there is more noise on the scale less than 60 days.  2.3.3 Copula function According to Sklar 's theorem, Copula theory refers to the decomposition of any n-dimensional joint cumulative distribution function into n marginal cumulative distributions and a Copula function (Zavareh et al., 2023 ). The marginal distribution functions are F (x ) and F (y ), respectively. F  (x , y ) is the joint distribution of random variables x and y. If F (x ) and F (y ) are continuous, then there exists a unique Copula function C(F (x ), F (y )) such that.(1) F x , y     = C F 1  x    , F 2  y             The common univariate fitting distribution functions (lognormal distribution, generalized extreme value distribution, Weber distribution) are used to fit the two characteristic variables of SPI and SRI respectively, and the optimal marginal distribution function is selected. Based on Copula function theory, the AIC criterion method and OLS criterion method are used to evaluate the goodness of fit of three joint distribution function parameters of Gumbel-Copula, Clayton-Copula and Frank-Copula. The smaller the values of AIC and OLS, the better the fitting degree of Copula function (Fan et al., 2022 ). Set two sets of data SPI, SRI are x ,y  respectively. x1  、x2  、y1  、y2   are the threshold values of SPI and SRI (SPI/SRI > 0.5 is wetness, SPI/SRI < − 0.5 is drought), and their corresponding marginal distributions are F1  (x1  )、F1  (x2  )、F2  (y1  )、F2  (y2  ), respectively. F  (xi  , yi  ) is the Copula function of x  and y . P is the probability of drought and wetness encounter in different scenarios. Drought and wetness encounter refer to the combination of drought, normal and wetness changes that may occur in the region during the same period. The probability of wet and drought evolution is calculated according to the Copula function, and the calculation formula is shown in Table 3  . The drought and wetness encounters can be divided into synchronous and asynchronous types, and the combination of the same drought and wetness in the two sub-regions is defined as an unfavorable scenario. Wet-drought, wet-normal, normal-drought are defined as favorable scenarios; normal-flood, drought-wet, drought-normal, normal-normal are other scenarios.  2.3.4 Impact analysis of drought and flood encounters In the analysis of the impact of drought and wetness, firstly, based on the identification results of SPI and SRI, the meteorological, hydrological drought and wetness events are sorted in chronological order. Taking the meteorological drought-hydrological drought combination scenario as an example, assuming that there are m meteorological wetness events and n hydrological drought events, a matrix X of m × n can be formed. Each element Xmn  in the matrix represents a pair of meteorological-hydrological drought events to be detected. The matching methods of the other 21 drought-flood combination scenarios (Table 4  ) are also shown above. Combined with the obtained lag time results, the affected original sequence is one-to-one corresponding to the lagged sequence and subtracted. For the wet- wet scenario, if it is greater than 0, it indicates that the wetness is aggravated; drought-drought scenario less than 0 indicates that the drought is aggravated; for wet-drought scenarios, greater than 0 indicates drought relief.    3 Results 3.1 Spatial and temporal evolution characteristics of drought and flood in the Yangtze River and Yellow River basins 3.1.1 Multi-scale temporal variation of meteorological drought and flood events in the whole basin Fig. 5  (a)–(d) and (e)–(h) reflect the variation trend of SPI at different scales in the Yellow River and the Yangtze River Basin, respectively. SPI-1 and SPI-3 have frequent alternation of drought and wetness. Before 1990, the Yellow River Basin was prone to spring drought and summer wet, and the Yangtze River Basin was prone to spring drought. After 2004, winter drought and summer wet are prone to occur. With the increase of time scale, the changes of SPI-6 and SPI-12 are stable and the fluctuation period is long. The drought and wet grades in the same period show a trend of gradual relief. The duration of drought and wet in the same period is also different, and the start and end time is delayed accordingly. For example, the maximum values of SPI-1 and SPI-3 in the Yellow River Basin in 2020 are 1.44 and 1.69, respectively, showing heavy wet, and the wet duration is 8 months and 6 months, respectively, while SPI-12 is 1.06, showing light wet in 12 months. On the whole, the two major basins showed a trend from drought to wet. The SPI-12 in the Yellow River Basin was between-1.57 and 1.32, and that in the Yangtze River Basin was between-1.24 and 1.11. The severity of drought and wet in the Yellow River Basin was higher than that in the Yangtze River Basin.  3.1.2 Spatio-temporal evolution of SPI and SRI in different regions Fig. 6  (a) shows the spatial distribution of the annual average SPI index in the Yellow River Basin, which shows the west of the upstream and the south of the middle reaches are wet, and the source area, the middle and lower reaches are dry. According to statistics, wetness in the Yellow River Basin mainly occurred before the 1980 s. The frequency of wetness in the lower reaches of the 1960 s and 1970 s was the highest, reaching 91 times and 37 times respectively, and the frequency of wetness in the upper reaches of the 1980 s was the highest, reaching 70 times. After the 1990 s, the frequency of wetness in the basin decreased, all of which were concentrated in the source area, with 76 occurrences in the past 30 years. On the contrary, drought events are mainly concentrated after the 1990 s, with higher frequency in the middle and lower reaches (Fig. 6 (f)–(g)).Fig. 6 (b)–(e) show the monthly distribution of SPI and SRI in the source region, upper, middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River Basin, respectively. The overall trend of the two is similar, both of which are characterized by drought mitigation, but the precipitation and runoff in different regions are still quite different in each period. The SPI in the upstream was dominated by drought before 1980, while the SRI was alternated between drought and wet. After 1993, the SPI in the middle and lower reaches was alternated between drought and wet, while the SRI showed drought. Fig. 7   is the spatial distribution map of the annual average SPI index in the Yangtze River Basin. In the Yangtze River Basin, the north of the middle and lower reaches is humid, and the source area and upstream is dry. Drought events were mainly concentrated in the 1970 s, and 51 times occurred in the source region and the upper reaches. The frequency of drought and wetness in other decades was similar. The SPI and SRI in the source area, upper, middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River Basin showed an upward trend, indicating a significant wetting trend in recent years. Compared with the Yellow River Basin, the trend of meteorological drought and wet in the Yangtze River Basin is more similar to that of hydrological drought and flood, but there is also a certain lag effect.   3.2 The dynamic response relationship of meteorological-hydrological drought and flood in different regions 3.2.1 Correlation between meteorological-hydrological drought and wetness in different regions Fig. 8   is the correlation analysis diagram of SPI and SRI in the source area-upper-middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River and the Yangtze River Basin at different time scales. The correlation degree of the Yellow River Basin is higher than that of the Yangtze River Basin, and the hydrological drought and wetness events in the upper reaches of the Yangtze River have a weak impact on the middle reaches.  3.2.2 Response relationship of meteorological-hydrological drought and wetness based on transfer function analysis Fig. 9  (a)–(d) shows the coherence, gain and phase spectrum of SPI-SRI in different regions of the Yellow River Basin.
