The drought and wet events identified by SPI/SRI in this study are very consistent with the typical drought and wet years in the history of the two major river basins. The typical drought and wet events such as the drought in the Yellow River Basin in 1965 and 1997, the flood in the Yellow River Basin in 2013, the summer drought in the Yangtze River Basin in 2006, and the rainstorm and flood in July 2012 were accurately identified, indicating that the index has good applicability in the two major river basins. In terms of time, some studies have pointed out that the runoff in the source area and upstream of the Yellow River has decreased significantly since the 1990 s, which has seriously affected the runoff in the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River, resulting in the closure of the lower reaches of the Yellow River in the 1990 s and seriously affecting the water resources in North China (Wang et al., 2019a,b ), which is consistent with the results of this study. The spatial difference of drought and wet distribution in the Yangtze River Basin is closely related to the water vapor transport of the East Asian monsoon (Liu et al., 2022 ). The large interannual fluctuation of water vapor divergence in the lower reaches will increase the probability of extreme precipitation events in the lower reaches, which will have an important impact on flood control in the lower reaches. In recent years, both basins have developed in the direction of wets, and the frequency of wets in the source area is the highest. This is mainly due to the combined effects of high-altitude topography, monsoon influence, terrain and slope changes, geographical location, and snowmelt water supply (Zhou et al., 2021 ). Meteorological droughts and wets are the external driving force of hydrological droughts and wets. Although the evolution mechanism of the two is different, there is a certain response relationship between the internal water cycle (Um et al., 2022 ). A number of studies have also shown that the change trend of SPI and SRI in the basin has a high similarity (Haile et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2020 ). Wang et al. explored the relationship between meteorology and hydrological drought in the Hanjiang River Basin, and obtained the strongest correlation between the two on the annual scale, which is consistent with the results of the correlation between meteorological and hydrological drought and wetness in the two basins in this paper. The response relationship of the same type of drought and wetness in different regions is also different due to different climate and underlying surface conditions. In the source areas of the two basins, there is a phenomenon that the SPI is dry, while the SRI is alternating between drought and wetness. This is due to the complex mechanism of hydrological drought and wet in the source area. In addition to the influence of precipitation, it may also be affected by the complex multiphase water cycle such as glacier snow melting water and soil freezing and thawing (Wang et al., 2022a,b ); After 1993, the SPI in the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River Basin alternated between drought and wet, but the SRI showed a dry state. In addition to the decrease of precipitation, it may also be related to the operation of Xiaolangdi Reservoir. construction has changed the spatial pattern of drought in the middle and lower reaches, resulting in longer duration and stronger intensity of drought in the lower reaches (Chen et al., 2022 ). Similar situations have occurred in the Yangtze River Basin. In recent years, with the operation of hydropower stations and the further refinement of reservoir operation and the implementation of a series of wet control and disaster reduction measures, flood disasters have decreased significantly.  4.2 The propagation law of drought and wetness in the Yangtze River and Yellow River Basin The basin water resources system is affected by high-dimensional systems such as meteorology, society and ecology, and there is a complex relationship of time-delay transmission between different systems. For the two major basins of the Yangtze River and the Yellow River, the climate environment and basin characteristics are different, and the corresponding drought and wetness response and propagation characteristics are different. On the one hand, the correlation degree of meteorological-hydrological drought and wet in the Yangtze River Basin is significantly higher than that in the Yellow River Basin. This is due to the greater impact of precipitation on runoff in the Yangtze River Basin, and the causal relationship between precipitation and runoff is the key to understanding the spread of meteorological to hydrological drought. Ding et al. (2021)  divided China into eight sub-regions according to the climatic zone, and studied the meteorological and hydrological droughts from 1902 to 2014. The results showed that the arid environment had a weaker propagation relationship than the humid environment, which further confirmed the results of this study. On the other hand, for the drought and wet propagation between the source region-upper-middle-lower reaches of the basin, the correlation degree of the Yellow River Basin is higher than that of the Yangtze River Basin. Among them, the hydrological drought in the upper reaches of the Yangtze River has a weak impact on the middle reaches. This is due to the fact that China 's reservoirs are mainly concentrated in the southern region. According to statistics, as of 2021, more than 50,000 reservoirs of various types have been built in the Yangtze River Basin, with the largest distribution in Hunan Province, reaching 14,047. The regulation and storage of the middle reaches of the Yangtze River, especially the Three Gorges Reservoir, interferes with the hydrological cycle process of the basin, making the hydrological drought and wet response between the upper and middle reaches less sensitive (Xu et al., 2021 ). From the perspective of the lag time of drought and flood propagation in the two basins, the lag time of hydrological drought and wetness propagation between different spatial domains is longer than that of meteorological-hydrological drought and wetness propagation. Because the hydrological drought and flood propagation process is more susceptible to a variety of factors, such as human activities, watershed characteristics, climate types, land use characteristics, etc., the uncertainty of propagation is increased. For the propagation of hydrological drought and wet, the propagation time of the upper-middle and middle-lower reaches of the Yangtze River Basin is longer than that of the Yellow River Basin. This may be due to the fact that the vegetation coverage in the Yangtze River Basin is better than that in the Yellow River Basin, and its widely distributed coniferous forest, hardwood forest and shrub forest, as well as the large watershed area may prolong the drought and wet response (Gu et al., 2020 ). For the spread of meteorological-hydrological droughts and wets, the lag time in the source area and the middle reaches is short. Wu et al. (2018)  found that the area with large forest coverage has a long time of drought propagation, and the drought propagation time of grassland is short. More than 76 % of the source area is dominated by grassland, coupled with the less interference of human activities in the source area, the anti-interference ability of the regional natural environment is strong, and the degree of response between drought and wet will be reduced accordingly. In addition, most studies have found that human activities will slow down the spread of hydrological drought, and the downstream of the basin is strongly affected by human activities, and the corresponding lag period is also longer. At the same time, the construction of artificial canals and reservoirs has also increased hydrological variability. There are more reservoirs in the upper reaches of the Yangtze River and the Yellow River Basin, which also explains the long lag time of meteorological-hydrological drought and wetness propagation in the upper reaches. Through quantitative analysis, Huang et al. (2021)  found that the propagation time of meteorological drought to hydrological drought in the Yangtze River Basin was prolonged after the implementation of the Three Gorges Project, which further verified this conclusion. Droughts and wets are transmitted through the water cycle and are also controlled and affected by climate change. Studies have pointed out that since the 1980 s, the Yellow River Basin has less precipitation, higher temperature, and a corresponding increase in evapotranspiration, resulting in a larger water deficit (Shi et al., 2021 ), which may lead to more frequent and more severe hydrological drought events. The results are consistent with the results of this study, and the hydrological drought in the middle and lower reaches is particularly prominent. In addition, from the perspective of the lag time of drought and wetness propagation, the propagation of meteorological-hydrological drought and wetness shows significant seasonal characteristics. For example, Apurv et al. (2017)  found that climatic characteristics such as seasonality, dry period and rainfall duration are the main reasons for the transmission mechanism of drought and flood, among which rainfall duration has the greatest impact. Drought and wet events are closely related to atmospheric circulation anomalies. The influence of atmospheric circulation on the spread of drought and wet is mainly achieved by affecting precipitation and evapotranspiration (Huang et al., 2017 ).Ma et al. (2022)  found that teleconnection factors have a great influence on the autumn drought propagation in the Weihe River, a tributary of the Yellow River Basin.Among them, the Arctic Oscillation, El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Pacific Decadal Oscillation indirectly change the drought propagation process in the Weihe River Basin by affecting variables such as precipitation and soil moisture. Many researchers have found that the propagation characteristics of drought and wet are different under different climate types. Haslinger et al. (2014)  found that there is a stronger correlation between meteorological drought and hydrological drought during low-flow hydrological drought in summer, and the correlation between the two is stronger in humid climates than in arid climates. The results of this study also show that the correlation between meteorological-hydrological drought and wet in the Yangtze River Basin is significantly higher than that in the Yellow River Basin. Climate change will accelerate the spread of drought and flood (Jehanzaib et al., 2020 ). As climate change intensifies, the process of drought and wetness transmission will present greater uncertainty, and drought and wet events are expected to be more frequent and more extreme in the future.  4.3 The impact of drought and wetness in the Yangtze River and Yellow River Basin The consistency of drought and wet events in the two basins is strong, and the probability of occurrence of the same drought and wet scenario is high. Overall, it is not conducive to the spatial aggregation response to drought and wet events. The frequency of the same drought in the source area-upper-middle-lower reaches of the Yellow River Basin is greater than that of the same wet, and the overall water shortage risk is greater. In the Yangtze River Basin, the same wet is greater than the same drought. Attention should be paid to preventing flood risks and considering how to make full use of incoming water to improve water use efficiency. In the favorable scenario, the probability of wet-normal and normal-wet occurrence in the two basins is relatively large. The advantage is that the flood resources during the flood period can be effectively utilized through engineering measures to supplement the ecological water use in the normal water year area. In this case, the groundwater between the two regions can recuperate each other and conserve water sources (Zhang et al., 2022a,b ); The probability of wet-drought occurrence is small. Once such a scenario occurs, it can be used to replenish water resources for possible drought-drought or drought-normal periods in the future, so as to realize water resources adjustment, multi-source complementarity, and surface water and groundwater replacement in the two regions. When the wet-wet scenario occurs, the degree of wet in most areas is aggravated, but the middle reaches of the Yangtze River are less affected by upstream wets. This is because the water conservancy projects built from the upper reaches to the middle reaches of the Yangtze River effectively regulate and store upstream wets (Sun et al., 2023 ). In the drought-drought scenario, the upstream is less affected than the middle and lower reaches. This is because the main recharge source of upstream runoff includes glacier snow melting in addition to precipitation. When the temperature regulation of runoff is higher than that of precipitation, the impact of drought stress will be relatively small (Yang et al., 2022 ). There are few wet-drought scenarios in both basins. It should be pointed out that when such scenarios occur, most of the wetness in the previous catchment can play a role in alleviating the drought in the next catchment to a certain extent, making the drought degree lighter or normal. However, if heavy wetness occurs in the previous catchment area, it may also cause the next catchment area to change from drought to wetness. As shown in Fig. 15 (f), when wetness occurs in the upper reaches of the Yangtze River and drought occurs in the lower reaches, there are two event pairs that change from light drought to moderate wet. Therefore, there is still a problem of determining the propagation threshold, that is, what degree of wet in the previous catchment will cause the next catchment to change from drought to wet. On the whole, the wet-drought scenario is a favorable scenario, which can effectively alleviate the degree of downstream drought. The Yellow River Basin has more favorable scenarios than the Yangtze River Basin, especially in the source-upstream and upstream-midstream sections, while the Yangtze River Basin has few, even none in the midstream-downstream section.  4.4 Uncertainty analysis and prospect of indicators and methods First of all, the drought and flood index are uncertain. Under the background of environmental change, drought and flood are affected by many factors. In order to overcome the limitations of univariate indicators, many scholars have proposed multivariate drought index (Eslamian and Parvizi, 2023 ). This study only considers the quantitative indicators related to precipitation and runoff, and there may be some factors that cannot be directly quantified, such as human activities. How to select the most suitable drought and flood indexes from many drought and flood indexes and how to further improve the quantitative indicators are still the difficulties in carrying out drought and flood research. In addition, since the propagation of drought and flood involves complex atmospheric and hydrological interaction processes and dynamic changes of surface variables, it is impossible to fully explain the mechanism of the propagation process only by mathematical equations. In order to improve the ability to explain the mechanism of drought and flood propagation process, many scholars use meteorological and hydrological physical models to model the drought propagation process. This kind of hydrological model usually considers the interaction of precipitation, runoff, evapotranspiration, soil moisture and watershed topography during the propagation process, and can simulate the propagation process from daily scale to annual scale (Apurv and Cai, 2020 ). The meteorological and hydrological physical model can supplement the physical mechanism explanation and constraint of drought and flood propagation process for mathematical statistical methods. At the same time, the mathematical statistical analysis method can provide a simple calculation process for the parameter calibration of the meteorological and hydrological physical model. Therefore, how to couple the mathematical statistical analysis method and the meteorological hydrological physical model to quantitatively model the drought and flood propagation process is also a key research direction. Secondly, based on different research methods, the conclusions and viewpoints are uncertain. Many scholars have developed models such as joint probability distribution function, multiple regression, Bayesian probability theory, cross wavelet transform and heuristic segmentation (Zhang et al., 2023a,b ), which are mainly used to determine the probability and threshold of drought and flood propagation. In this study, the Copula function was used to calculate the probability of drought and flood encounters between meteorological-hydrological and different catchment areas in the two basins. However, in the study of drought and flood propagation, another key question (Liu et al., 2023 ) is: what degree of meteorological drought and flood can lead to what degree of hydrological drought? What degree of drought and flood in the previous catchment will spread to the next catchment? In recent years, Bayesian networks have been gradually applied to the modeling of drought and flood propagation processes. The nodes in the directed acyclic graph of Bayesian network represent random variables, and the causal variable pairs are connected by arrows, which are mainly used to describe the conditional dependence between random variables. Based on Bayesian probability theory, Shin et al. (2020)  developed a hydrological drought prediction model considering the relationship between drought prediction and drought propagation. The research shows that the model can well predict hydrological drought and effectively capture the propagation information between meteorological drought and hydrological drought. By integrating the law of drought and flood propagation into Bayesian network for drought and flood prediction, the network can perform better in long-term drought and flood prediction. Huang et al. (2021)  constructed a meteorological-hydrological drought characteristic propagation model for each sub-basin of the Yangtze River Basin, which can predict the duration or intensity of hydrological drought after propagation. In addition to Bayesian networks, complex network theory has also begun to be introduced into the study of drought and flood propagation in recent years, and new breakthroughs have been made in the identification of three-dimensional spatial–temporal structures and propagation sources (Konapala et al., 2022 ). Therefore, in the future, Bayesian and complex climate network methods should be combined to further understand the problem of drought and flood propagation and carry out in-depth research.   5 Conclusions In this study, the Yangtze River and the Yellow River basins were taken as the research objects. Based on the SPI index representing meteorological drought and flood and the SRI index representing hydrological drought and flood, the evolution law of extreme drought and wet events in the source region-upper-middle-lower reaches of the two basins was analyzed. On this basis, the correlation analysis and transfer function analysis are used to explore the response relationship and lag effect between the two in different partitions. A two-dimensional joint distribution model is constructed by Copula function to quantitatively analyze the joint probability of drought and wet encounters of 9 combined events, and to deeply analyze the impact of drought and wet encounters. The results of the study are as follows: (1) The severity of drought and wet in the Yellow River Basin is generally higher than that in the Yangtze River Basin. In recent years, the two major basins have shown a trend from drought to wet. Spatially, the Yellow River Basin is humid in the source area, the western part of the upper reaches and the southern part of the middle reaches, and dry in the middle and lower reaches. The Yangtze River Basin is characterized by the source area, the northern part of the middle and lower reaches is wet, and the upper reaches is dry. The change trend of SPI and SRI has a high similarity, and the outbreak period of hydrological-meteorological drought and wetness has a consistent synchronization. Compared with the Yellow River Basin, the change trend of meteorological drought and wet and hydrological drought and wet in the Yangtze River Basin is more similar. (2) The correlation degree of meteorological-hydrological drought and wet in the Yangtze River Basin is significantly higher than that in the Yellow River Basin; For the spread of drought and wet in the spatial domain of the basin, the correlation degree of the Yellow River Basin is higher than that of the Yangtze River Basin; From the perspective of the lag time of drought and wet propagation in the two basins, the lag time of hydrological drought and wet propagation in the two basins is longer than that of meteorological-hydrological drought and wet propagation, and the lag time of meteorological-hydrological drought and wet propagation in the source area and middle reaches is shorter. The lag period of hydrological drought and wet propagation in the upper-middle and middle-lower reaches of the Yangtze River Basin is longer than that in the Yellow River Basin. (3) The drought and wet events in the two basins have good consistency, and the probability of occurrence of the same drought and wet scenarios is high, which is not conducive to the spatial aggregation response of drought and wet events as a whole. In the drought-drought and wet-wet scenarios, except for the spread of hydrological drought and wet in the upper and middle reaches of the Yangtze River, most of the disasters are aggravated. The wet-drought scenario can play a role in mitigating drought to a certain extent, making the drought degree lighter or turning into normal and light wet. More than 52 % of the events have obvious drought mitigation effects, and such favorable scenarios in the Yellow River Basin are more than those in the Yangtze River Basin.

1 Introduction Worldwide, floods rank as the predominant natural disasters responsible for the most significant amount of property damage, as quantified by the extent of material harm attributed to this event (Jacinto et al., 2015 ). As a result of the ongoing climatic changes that have intensified over the past few decades, it has become evident that floods have become more frequent and severe (Peng-cheng et al., 2016; Yue et al., 2021 ). High-resolution flood susceptibility modeling with high model performance allows for the identification of areas with varying levels of flood risk (Zhou et al., 2023a) . As the quality of freely available spatial data for flood hazard modeling and management improves, flood hazard modelers have greater opportunities to boost model performance. This can be achieved through several strategies (MarkovML, 2024 ): (i) data-related approaches, (ii) model-related techniques, (iii) training and optimization tactics, and (iv) evaluation and validation methods. To improve machine learning model performance, data-related strategies involve data quality and cleaning to remove errors and inconsistencies, feature engineering to create impactful features, data augmentation to diversify datasets, and dataset balancing to address class imbalances through resampling or synthetic generation (Zhou et al., 2023b ). Model-related strategies include model selection through various algorithms and frameworks, hyperparameter tuning with methods like grid search, regularization techniques to prevent overfitting, ensemble learning to combine multiple models, and transfer learning by fine-tuning pre-trained models (Gu et al., 2024 ). Training and optimization strategies encompass early stopping to avoid overfitting, dynamic learning rate scheduling to prevent convergence issues, batch normalization and data shuffling for stable training, and cross-validation to ensure robustness (Wei et al., 2023 ). Evaluation and validation strategies involve using comprehensive metrics like accuracy and F1 score, conducting out-of-sample validation to gauge generalization, and performing error analysis to identify and correct patterns or biases in incorrect predictions (Yin et al., 2023a ). Romania ranks second behind France in terms of the economic damage caused by floods at an EU level. Romania must, like all countries in Europe, ensure that its flood risk management program is in compliance with the Directive 2007/60/EC (Afriyanie et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, the evaluation of flood vulnerability is likewise one of the most critical non-structural measures implemented in order to reduce material losses and lives that result from natural disasters such as flooding (Arora et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023 ). The use of GIS and Remote Sensing methods allows the very fast identification of vulnerable surfaces (Saha et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2021 ). It is clear that the efficiency of any GIS process will be determined, in a considerable measure, by the accuracy of its input data, as well as by the combination of GIS models with statistical and machine learning algorithms (Hu et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2021 ). A growing number of studies that have used GIS techniques in combination with some models specific to machine learning and bivariate statistics to identify and map flood-exposed zones, have been published in recent years (Ahmadlou et al., 2021; Costache et al., 2021a; Wu et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2021 ). Among the machine learning methods used to detect those surfaces showing flood prone characteristics, the most commonly used ones are: decision trees algorithms, adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference systems, support vector machines and artificial neural networks (Alizadeh et al., 2018; Khosravi et al., 2018; Xiong et al., 2019 ). Also, in the literature there can be noticed the use of some new methods like averaged neural networks (avNNet), proposed by Choubin et al. (2023)  for deriving the flood maps for different return periods in Iran. Another interesting approach was proposed by Taromideh et al. (2022)  who analyzed the flood risk in an urban environment with the help of 6 machine learning algorithms. One of the key advantages characteristics for machine learning models resides in the high automation that they provide (Costache et al., 2020a; Zhang et al., 2022 ). The main input data in these machine learning models is represented by the flood locations and flood predictors which are the geographical factors (Costache, 2014 ). Many researchers who assess the potential for flooding in a specific region typically take into consideration a range of geographical factors that impact the characteristics and severity of this natural disaster (Costache et al., 2015 ). These commonly included flood predictors consist of lithology, plan curvature, precipitation, soil types, proximity to rivers, slope angles, and land use (Chowdhuri et al., 2020 ). By overlaying the flood data in GIS software and evaluating their respective influences, one can calculate the susceptibility to floods. The flood susceptibility can be determined by a straightforward overlay of flood data in GIS software and an examination of their effects. Advance models that allow the weighting of these factors are also able to determine flood susceptibility (Bui et al., 2020 ). As a general rule, flood conditioning factors are weighted according to their spatial relationships with historical flood occurrences (Azareh et al., 2019 ). A notable research gap in the scientific literature related to flood susceptibility assessment in Romania is the limited utilization of optimization methods in machine learning models. This deficiency is addressed in the current study, where we employ the Particle Swarm Optimization method. Given these considerations, the primary objective of this research is to delineate areas prone to flooding within the hilly and mountainous basins of the Prahova River using four distinct models. Specifically, we utilize the Deep Learning Neural Network (DLNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and two optimized models incorporating Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to estimate flood susceptibility. As part of the model training process, we consider ten flood predictors along with historical records of 158 flood events. To evaluate the accuracy of the findings, we assess the results through the computation of various statistical parameters, generate ROC curves, and calculate the area under the curve.  2 Study area For optimization of the selected model development, the flood data inventory from the upper and middle sections of the Prahova River basin (PRB), Romania was collected during the extensive field visits( Fig. 1 ). The PRB covers approximately 2600 square kilometers and exhibits an elevation range from 128 to 2505 m. During the period of the year, the distribution of rainfall on the surface of the river catchments has a great influence on the hydrological regime of the rivers. During the summer season, there is a variable amount of rainfall in the area, which frequently causes flash floods and flooding. Approximately 12.43° is the mean value of slope angle, one of the most powerful factors that influence flooding processes. It is also important to note that the areas covered by soil groups C and D, which are also present in the mountainous as well as hilly regions of the PRB, favor the occurrence of floods as well. Using hydrometric information from the research zone, Costache (2019b)  has synthesized a review of the recent flood events.  3 Data 3.1 Flood inventory The inventory was carried out to gain a better understanding of how geographic factors contribute to flooding by examining 158 flood-prone locations in Romania, using data from the archive of General Inspectorate for the Situations of Emergencies (GIES) of Romania. GIES provided the flood-prone locations using the name of the localities and the rivers where the phenomena occurred, or through the other elements like roads, bridges or coordinates. There are several types of floods like: flash-floods, river floods and coastal floods. It should be noted that for the present research the river floods were taken into account in the susceptibility modelling. To ensure a balanced comparison, an equal number of non-flooding locations were randomly chosen and located within the areas surfaces where flood events were not reported before, following guidance from Chowdhuri et al. (2020)  and Khosravi et al. (2018) . In order to ensure the analysis objectivity, the non-flood points were automatically derived using ArcGIS 10.8 Create fishnet  tool. More specifically, the non-flood points were randomly selected from the points generated in the center of each fishnet cell. Based on Tehrany et al., (2017) , these locations were then randomly divided into training (70 %) and validation (30 %) datasets, using the Subset tool in ArcGIS 10.8 software. The same partitioning of training and validation dataset helped in the previous research works on the same are to obtain high accurate results (Costache, 2019b; Costache et al., 2023 ). The training set comprised 110 flood-prone locations and 110 non-flooding locations, while the validation set included 48 flood-prone locations and 48 non-flooding locations. To refine the training process, the original training set was further subdivided into a new training dataset (77 flooded locations and 77 non-flooded locations) and a testing dataset (33 flooded locations and 33 non-flooded locations).  3.2 Flood predictors To better estimate flood susceptibility, it's crucial to identify the key geographical factors that drive flooding (Dahri and Abida, 2017 ). In studies that assess flood susceptibility in specific areas, choosing the right flood conditioning factors is a vital step. To understand flood susceptibility in the Prahova river catchment, researchers selected ten conditioning factors based on a comprehensive review of existing studies and the specific conditions in the catchment (Al-Juaidi, 2023; Wang et al., 2023 ). These factors include slope angle, topographic wetness index (TWI), elevation, convergence index, and plan curvature, all derived from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) Digital Elevation Model (30 m database). Each contributes uniquely to surface runoff. Other factors, obtained from different geoprocessing databases, include land use from the Corine Land Cover 2012 database, lithology from the Geological Map of Romania (1:200,000), and rainfall interpolation based on data from meteorological and hydrometrical stations to create a spatial model of average annual rainfall from 1980 to 2015 (Costache and Bui, 2019 ). Distances from rivers were calculated using the Euclidean distance from locations to the nearest river network. Slope angles are critical in influencing runoff, with most flood events occurring on slopes less than three degrees (Zhou et al., 2023c ). About 40 % of the study area has slopes between seven and fifteen degrees ( Fig. 2 a) (Bui et al., 2019 ). Elevation plays a role, as lower zones tend to collect water (Wu et al., 2024 ); eight classes of elevation were identified, with 70 % of flood locations falling between 200 m and 600 m (Fig. 2 d) (Kanani-Sadat et al., 2019 ). Regarding distances from rivers, 40 % of flooding events occur within the first 50 m from the river network (Fig. 2 c) (Chapi et al., 2017 ). The Corine Land Cover (2018) European database was used to identify land use, revealing ten categories, with forests making up 50 % of the area and built-up areas containing most of the remaining pixels constitute 50 % of the flood pixels (Fig. 2 e). Hydrological soil groups are also important, with hydrological group C having the most floods (68 %) ( Fig. 3 d). Lithology affects water infiltration, with 12 categories (Fig. 2 f), and 80 % of flood pixels occur in clay and sandstone areas (Yang et al., 2022b, 2022a ). Rainfall is a direct contributor to flooding (Qiu et al., 2024 ). The Inverse Distance Weighted (IDW) interpolation method was used to derive rainfall data from 21 hydrometric and nine meteorological stations (1980–2017), showing a range from 531 mm/year to 1250 mm/year across seven rainfall classes (Fig. 3 a). TWI values were calculated by dividing a specific basin area by its slope, with five intervals (Fig. 3 b). The middle class, with a range from 8.5 to 12, has the most spatial extension and the greatest percentage of flood pixels (33 %). Convergence index is another morphometric variable with five groups, with all flood events occurring within negative convergence index areas (Fig. 2 b). Finally, plan curvature, divided into three classes, identified as11.8 – 0, 0.1 – 0.5, 0.6 – 8.5 (Fig. 3 c), shows that 75 % of flood incidents occur in the middle class, which has the highest percentage of total area. These insights are critical for understanding flood susceptibility and developing effective mitigation strategies.   4 Methods 4.1 Deep learning neural network (DLNN) Deep learning is a rapidly growing area of research in machine learning based on artificial neural networks, and is able to detect and classify patterns of data using multidimensional representations (Li, 2022; Ngo et al., 2021 ; Jiao et al., 2024 ). In a data transformation, the maximum number of layers (depth of network) can be extracted in order to give the best hierarchical representation of the data (Cheng and Fu, 2022; Liu et al., 2016 ). It should also be noted that in addition to the many hidden layers, two neurons in the output layer will represent flood and non-flood points, which will capture the effects of flooding. As the assessment of flood susceptibility is really a binary classification process, flooding locations would be assigned the value of 1, while non-flooding locations would be assigned zero (Costache et al., 2021b ). The sigmoid function E(Y=i/x) is implied in the training process of DLNN. More details regarding the Deep Learning characteristics and equations can be found in the research work done by Costache et al. (2021).  4.2 Support vector machine (SVM) The aim of the SVM algorithm is to determine a hyper-plane that divides the training data in an optimal manner (Kavzoglu et al., 2014; Li et al., 2022 ). The support vectors, which represent the closest data elements to the hyperplane, are considered to be the most essential elements in training data (Pham et al., 2016; Saha et al., 2024 ). An equation that describes a linear hyperplane that should be used to classify new data can be written as follows (Tehrany et al., 2019 ):(1) f x    = sign ∑ i = 1  n   y  i   α  i    x  i   , + b        where α i   are Lagrange multipliers, x  is the independent variable, y  is the dependent variable, while b  represents the hyper plane offset determined from the origin. However, in practice the non-linear hyperplane is mainly involved. The nonlinear kernel function from Eq. (1)  is rewritten using the form shown here:(2) f x    = ∑ i = 1  n   α  i   − α  i  *      K  x  i   , x    + b     where αi  and αi  * are Lagrange multipliers (αi  ≥ 0, αi  * ≤ C) and K (x i  , x j  ) is the kernel function. In  Fig. 4 a is represented the linear hyper-plane, while in Fig. 4 b is represented the non-linear hyperplane. In the present research the Radial Basis Function (RBF) was particularly used in order to apply the SVM models. The RBF was selected to be used for the present, because it has multiple advantages compared to other kernel function. Thus, here it can be mentioned the BRF ability to process high-dimensional data, a faster testing and training process duration, and its ability for the approximation of continuous functions with unrestricted accuracy (Mahato et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2011 ). Also, the determination of parameters C and γ  is crucial for the precision of SVM models. The cross validation is the most common method used to estimate the C and γ  optimally values.  4.3 Particle swarm optimization Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithm was developed as a way to simulate a complex adaptive system (CAS) (Li et al., 2019 ). Each optimization problem in PSO is solved by one of the particles (Jain et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2023 ), which is called a "bird" in the search space (Cao et al., 2020; Sachdeva et al., 2017 ). In a PSO, random particles are used to initialize the system and it is used to search for the ideal solution by iterative evolution (Alqadhi et al., 2022; Javidi and Mansoury, 2017 ). The particles are able to update themselves automatically during each iteration by tracking the extreme values of velocity and position (Bui et al., 2017 ). The dynamics of the above-mentioned particles was mathematically highlighted in the research work done by Jain et al. (2018) . The optimal position of the population in PSO algorithm is reached according the scheme presented in  Fig. 5 . It should be noted that the following initial parameters of PSO will be determined and analyzed in the present research: Swarm size, acceleration constants C 1   and C 2   and also for different values of inertia weight. The determination of these parameters will be based on a trial-and-error procedure. Thus, will be selected those initial parameters that corresponds to the lowest RMSE value. Among all the optimization algorithms, PSO was chosen for the present study because it has several advantages such as (Rahman et al., 2016 ): i) it is easy to implement due to the fact that only few parameters are required; ii) it requires less computing work being more efficient; iii) has a higher degree of flexibility and is able to maintain a balance between local and global searches within its space search; iv) it is not sensitive to the scaling process of the design variables. The PSO will be involved in the training process of Support Vector Machine in order to optimize the C and γ  parameter, a procedure intended to increase the precision of SVM model. Also, in terms of DLNN model the PSO algorithm will help in order to determine optimal number of hidden layers and hidden neurons which are associated with the lowest error. The Mealpy (Xie et al., 2022 ) Python library was used in order to apply the SVM, DLNN and also the PSO for both algorithms.  4.4 Statistical index (SI) Statistical Index (SI) is a widely used method in natural hazards estimation domain (Bui et al., 2011 ). The calculation of SI coefficients can be performed using the next equation (Regmi et al., 2014 ):(3) SI  ij   = ln f  ij    f      = ln Npix S  i       Npix N  i         ∑  Npix S  i        ∑  Npix ( N  i               where: SI ij   – is the coefficient provided for a specific category/class i  of parameter j ; f ij  -  represents the density of flood pixels in the class i  of parameter j , f  – represents the density of flood pixels in the entire study area, Npix(Si)  represents the number of flood pixels in class i, while Npix(Ni)  represents the total number of pixels in the same parameter class. The main benefit of using the SI method is given by the fact that the user who executes the analysis is able to determine and verify the combinations of the conditioning factors which are used in the evaluation (Pourghasemi et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016 ). Another benefit of using the SI method is represented by the possibility of bringing the values of all flood conditioning factors into a common gap, which in the case of the present study falls between −3 and 1. This regulation of the factors allowed the efficient development of the training process of the models because the SI values of the factor classes/categories will be used as input data in flood susceptibility models.  4.5 ROC curve and statistical metrics ROC graphs are designed to represent relationships between sensitivity on the X axis and 1-specificity on the Y axis (Bradley, 1997; Zhong et al., 2022 ). As the most significant statistic indicator in the field of statistics, AUC represents the area under the ROC curve that indicates the critical information regarding the performance of the model (Bhuyan et al., 2024 ). The Area Under ROC Curve can be calculated using the following relation (Costache, 2019b ):(4) AUC = ( ∑  TP +  ∑  TN   )  ( P + N )       where P is equal to the flood points number, N is equal to the non-flood points number, TP (true positive), TN (true negative) the points belonging to floods and non-floods that are the correctly classified. According to this study, statistical indices are considered significant if they can provide empirical evidence for a spatial correlation between the location of observed floods and non-floods and the areas that are estimated to be highly susceptible to flooding (Costache and Bui, 2019 ). The next formulas are used to compute the statistical metrics represented by Specificity, Kappa Index, Sensitivity and Accuracy (Yin et al., 2023b ):(5) Sensitivity = TP  TP + FN       (6) Specificity = TN  FP + TN       (7) Accuracy = TP + TN  TP + FP + TN + FN       (8) k = p  o   − p  e    1 − p  e          FP (false positive) – flood pixels that are classified in an erroneously manner, FN (false negative) – non-flood pixels that are classified in an erroneously manner, k  – kappa coefficient, p o   – observed flood pixels, and p e   – locations that are susceptible to flood (Yin et al., 2023c ). The six main steps applied for this research are represented in  Fig. 6    5 Results 5.1 Multicollinearity assessment and feature selection In terms of multicollinearity assessment, the Tolerance and Variance Inflation (VIF) indices were used. The lowest value of Tolerance was of 0.301 and was assigned to slope predictor, while the highest one was equal to 0.878 and was attributed to Plan curvature. Instead, the VIF maximum value was assigned to slope (3.035), meanwhile the minimum VIF belongs to Plan curvature (1.14) ( Table 1 ). According to the results of modelling, there is no serious multicollinearity detected among the flood predictors. The next values were achieved using the Gain Ratio (GR) method for feature selection ( Fig. 7 ): Slope (0.966), Lithology (0.402), Distance from river (0.379), Land use (0.361), Topographic Wetness Index (0.215), Plan curvature (0.206), Elevation (0.197), Hydrological Soil Group (0.135), Convergence index (0.12), Rainfall (0.083). Since all the GR values are higher than 0, all the predictors will be taken into account for the susceptibility modelling.  5.2 Results of statistical index (SI) It should be remarked that a number of 19 flood predictors classes or categories do not contain any flood locations. Since the lowest SI coefficient of a class/category that contains at least 1 flood events was −2.71, it was took the decision that, for those classes/categories which not contain nor flood events, to assign, in a conventional way, the value of −3 (Table 1 ). For example, slope values higher than 7° received the value −3 because the accumulation of water on such surfaces, which would further lead to the phenomenon of flooding, is almost impossible. At the same time, the same SI value was assigned for Plan Curvature values above 0.6. It must be said that such high values of Plan curvature favor the rapid drainage of the surface to the detriment of water accumulation. Reduced values of SI, of −2.71, were assigned, for example, to areas located at most 1000 m from the hydrographic network. This is explained by the fact that water courses are the main sources that determine the phenomenon of flooding and, obviously, the more distant the areas, the lower the probability of flooding. The maximum SI value was 0.69, and it was achieved by a number of 8 flood predictor classes/categories. Slopes below 3° obtained the maximum value of SI, this being due to the almost flat surfaces in which water can easily accumulate. At the same time, the high values of TWI, over 15.1 and which characterize the valley areas, received an SI coefficient of 0.69. Built areas characterized by a high degree of impermeability obtained a high SI value of 0.66. Further the computed SI coefficients were used as input data in the machine learning models.( Table 2 )  5.3 Computation of FFSI maps 5.3.1 DLNN-SI and PSO-DLNN-SI The models accuracy and the degree in which the target data managed the output, following the training procedure of both DLNN-SI and PSO-DLNN-SI hybrid models, are highlighted in  Fig. 8 . According to Fig. 8 , for targets and outputs of training data a number of 250 samples were used, meanwhile for testing data a number of 100 samples were used for both DLNN-SI and PSO-DLNN-SI ( Fig. 9 a and b). In Fig. 8 c and i are represented the error values across the 250 training samples, while in Fig. 8 e and k the same parameter is represented in correlation with the number of 100 samples that is assigned to the testing sample. It should be remarked that the RMSE value in the case of DLLN-SI for training sample (0.223) is higher than RMSE value in the case of PSO-DLNN-SI also for training sample (0.137). Further, it should be noted that in terms of testing sample the RMSE of DLNN-SI (0.239) is also higher than the value of the same parameter in the case of PSO-DLNN-SI (0.2127). Therefore, it can be stated that the optimization of DLNN-SI with the help of PSO algorithm managed to reduce the error of the model. The time needed for the models running ranged between 46, in the case of DLNN-SI and 122 seconds, in the case of PSO-DLNN-SI. It can be also observed that the errors for DLNN-SI model are concentrated especially between −0.5 and 0 (Fig. 8 d,f). The same situation is highlighted by Fig. 8 j,i for PSO-DLNN-SI. In order to supplementary estimate the PSO-DLNN-SI model performance, RMSE si R2  values were analyzed for several variables like: Swarm size, acceleration constants C 1   and C 2   and also for different values of inertia weight. Thus, according to  Table 3 , in terms of training sample, the highest R2  value was equal to 0.988 and was achieved with a swarm size of 200. The same Swarm size managed to achieve the lowest value of RMSE which was equal to 0.033. The use of testing sample revealed that the highest R2  (0.988) was provided by a Swarm size of 1000. Using the same Swarm size, the lowest RMSE (0.035) was obtained. According to  Table 4 , both acceleration constants (C 1   and C 2  ) that were equal to 1.42 (assigned to Model number 8) provided the highest R2  of 0.909. The use of the same combination of acceleration constants lead to the achievement of the lowest RMSE equal to 0.033. In terms of testing sample, the model number 3, characterized by C 1   = 2.59 and C 2   = 1.26, achieved the highest R2  = 0.904 and also the lowest RMSE = 0.04. The inertia weight parameter of 0.8 leads to the achievement of the highest R2  and the lowest RMSE for both training (R2  = 0.976, RMSE = 0.022) and testing (R2  = 0.975, RMSE = 0.024) samples ( Table 5 ). The ranking of R2  and RMSE were included also in Tables 3, 4 and 5 . Also, it should be noted that the DLNN-SI model achieved the lowest error using an architecture containing 3 hidden layers and 100 hidden neurons in each hidden layer (Fig. 9 a), while PSO-DLNN-SI achieved the lowest accuracy with an optimal architecture with 3 hidden layers and 83 hidden neurons in each hidden layer (Fig. 9 b). The training process allow the user to determine the importance of flood predictors. Thus, in the case of DLNN-SI hybrid model the highest importance was assigned to Slope predictor (0.315), followed by Lithology (0.131), Distance from river (0.124), Land use (0.118), Topographic Wetness Index (0.070), Plan curvature (0.067), Elevation (0.064), Hydrological Soil Group (0.044), Convergence index (0.039) and Rainfall (0.027). The PSO-DLNN-SI hybrid model revealed also that Slope predictor achieved the highest importance (0.269) followed by Distance from river (0.129), Land use (0.123), Topographic Wetness Index (0.113), Lithology (0.110), Convergence index (0.082), Hydrological Soil Group (0.072), Elevation (0.067), Rainfall (0.028) and Plan curvature (0.006) ( Fig. 10 ). Using the importance of flood predictors, the Flood Susceptibility Index (FSI) was computed for each of the 4 hybrid models. Thus, the FSI DLNN-SI has values between −0.9 and 0.59 which were classified into 5 intervals with the help of Natural Breaks classification method. The very low class of values are spread on 24.7 % of the middle and upper Prahova River basin. In these regions, the possibility of flooding is very low because there are slopes of over 15°, superimposed on areas with permeable soils that favor water infiltration. Also, such areas are at a considerable distance from the river network, being at the same time close to the interfluvial line. The low susceptibility covers 27.36 % of the study zone ( Fig. 11 a) and is characterized by properties very close to those associated with areas with a very low potential for producing floods. In general, the population in these areas is little exposed to floods. The surfaces with moderate flood susceptibility can be found on around 23.39 % of the territory, while the high and very high flood susceptibility manage to account approximately 24.55 % of the study area. The high and very high values of flood susceptibility appear in the valley areas characterized by low slopes of less than 3°, which appear especially in the areas where there are built and impervious surface. In the present case, there are important localities such as the touristic ones in the Prahova Valley area that can be affected by floods with a high probability. In terms of FSI PSO-DLNN-SI its values range from −0.97–0.62 (Fig. 11 b) and were also split into 5 classes with the same Natural Breaks method. The very low susceptibility has a total surface equal to 21.45 % of the study zone, while the low susceptibility is present on 30.12 % of the middle and upper zone of Prahova River basin. Moderate flood susceptibility has a percentage of 24.67 %, while, together, high and very high flood susceptibility span on 23.76 % of the entire study zone.  5.3.2 SVM-SI and PSO-SVM-SI The matching between targets and outputs for both training and testing samples, after the application of SVM-SI and PSO-SVM-SI hybrid models, is shown in  Fig. 12 . Similarly, to DLNN-SI and PSO-DLNN-SI, the same number of samples for training and testing procedure were used in the case of SVM-SI and PSO-SVM-SI (Fig. 12 ). Moreover, there is represented also the RMSE that is lower in the case of optimized PSO-SVM-SI hybrid model (0.147) comparing to SVM-SI (0.252) for training sample. Additionally, the errors associated to SVM-SI model that are highlighted in Fig. 12 d and f are mainly concentrated below to 0. The same situation can be observed for the errors estimated for PSO-SVM-SI in terms of training procedure, while the testing procedure shows an equilibrium between the positive and negative values of errors. The time needed for the models running ranged between 34, in the case of SVM-SI and 67, seconds in the case of PSO-SVM-SI. The three parameters (Swarm size, acceleration constants (C 1   and C 2  ) and inertia weight) were also used in the case of PSO-SVM-SI performance evaluation. For training sample, the swarm size of 200 lead to the highest R2  (0.992), while the lowest RMSE (0.035) was achieved using a swarm size of 100. In terms of testing sample, the highest R2  (0.992) was associated to a swarm size of 1000, while the lowest RMSE (0.037) was assigned for the swarm size of 400. According to Table 4 , both acceleration constants (C 1   and C 2  ) that were equal to 1.38 (assigned to Model number 8) provided the highest R2  of 0.911. The use of the combination C 1   = 2.52 and C 2   = 1.19 constants lead to the achievement of the lowest RMSE equal to 0.035. Moreover, the same case occurs in terms of testing sample. Thus, the R2  for C 1   = 1.38 and C 2   = 1.38, was equal to 0.904 and also the lowest RMSE = 0.04 was assigned to the combination of C 1   = 2.52 and C 2   = 1.19. The inertia weight parameter of 0.8 leads also in this case, to the achievement of the highest R2  and the lowest RMSE for both training (R2  = 0.974, RMSE = 0.02) and testing (R2  = 0.973, RMSE = 0.022) samples (Table 5 ). Like in the case of DLNN-based hybrid model, also for SVM-based hybrid model models were derived the importance for each flood predictor. Thus, in terms of SVM-SI model, the highest importance was obtained by Slope (0.287), followed by Lithology (0.120), Distance from river (0.113), Land use (0.107), Elevation (0.088), Hydrological Soil Group (0.070), Convergence index (0.065), Topographic Wetness Index (0.064), Plan curvature (0.061) and Rainfall (0.025). For the PSO-SVM-SI model, the following hierarchy was revealed: Slope (0.283), Land use (0.151), Elevation (0.103), Hydrological Soil Group (0.1), Lithology (0.099), Distance from river (0.091), Convergence index (0.064), Topographic Wetness Index (0.044), Plan curvature (0.039) and Rainfall (0.027). The calculated importance of each flood predictor was used to estimate the flood susceptibility across the study area. Thus, for FSI SVM-SI the values are situated between −0.92 and 0.59 and, like in the previous 2 cases, were grouped into 5 classes using the Natural Breaks method (Fig. 11 c). It should be noted that the FSI value of −0.92 represents the lowest flood susceptibility, the occurrence of this hazard within the areas associated to this value is almost impossible. The first class, which is assigned to very low values, has a total percentage of 23.54 % of the study zone, while the low susceptibility is found on 28.2 % of the entire middle and upper zone of Prahova River basin. The moderate values quantify approximately 23.39 % of the study area, while the high and very high flood susceptibility is spread on 24.87 % of the research zone. The FSI PSO-SVM-SI values range from −0.83–0.59. According to the Natural Breaks classification method, the very low-class values cover around 24.04 % of the research perimeter, while the low flood susceptibility accounts for 28.49 % of the same surface. Around 22.1 % of the research area is attributed to moderate flood susceptibility, while the high and very high values appear on a percentage of 25.37 %.   5.4 Results validation The ROC Curve represents the first method used to validate the flood susceptibility results. Thus, the Success Rate built with training data sample, shows that the best model was PSO-DLNN-SI having an AUC of 0.952. In terms of AUC, this model is followed by PSO-SVM-SI (AUC = 0.944), DLNN-SI (AUC = 0.93) and SVM-SI (AUC = 0.928) ( Fig. 13 a). The Prediction Rate, constructed using the validation sample, highlights also that the best model was PSO-SVM-SI (AUC = 0.926), followed by PSO-SVM-SI (AUC = 0.921), DLNN-SI (AUC = 0.904) and SVM-SI (AUC = 0.858). According to the Table 3 , the statistical metrics calculated for each flood susceptibility model show very good performances of this algorithms. Thus, using the training sample the accuracy values is characterized by the following hierarchy: PSO-DLNN-SI (0.959), PSO-SVM-SI (0.955), DLNN-SI (0.931) and SVM-SI (0.919). The same sample highlights the next ranking of K-index values: PSO-DLNN-SI (0.919), PSO-SVM-SI (0.911), DLNN-SI (0.861) and SVM-SI (0.837). In terms of validating sample, the most accurate model was also PSO-DLNN-SI (0.954), followed by PSO-SVM-SI (0.935), DLNN-SI (0.907) and SVM-SI (0.889). The K-index, with the validating sample, has the next values: PSO-DLNN-SI (0.907), followed by PSO-SVM-SI (0.870), DLNN-SI (0.833) and SVM-SI (0.778).( Table 6 )   6 Discussions It will never be possible to prevent all natural disasters, including complex natural hazards like floods (Bui et al., 2019 ). For this reason, it is exceptionally important so that flood prediction methods and flood mitigation tactics are improved in order to minimize the risk of loss of lives and the socio-economic effects of floods; this will enable us to minimize the long-term impacts of flooding (Dodangeh et al., 2020 ). An important part of flood modeling and risk assessment is the process of mapping flood susceptibility in for a specific region. Through flood susceptibility maps it can be identified where floods are increasingly likely to occur within a given area, and also can be determined the best way to prevent flood damages using non-structural and structural measures that can enhance the flood resilience (Hong et al., 2018; Mahato et al., 2021 ). The present research work is an attempt to apply and compare the results of four machine learning state-of-art models (DLNN-SI, PSO-DLNN-SI, SVM-SI and PSO-SVM-SI) in order to estimate the flood susceptibility degree in the middle and upper part of Prahova River basin from Romania. It should be noted that frequently, flood susceptibility mapping focuses on identifying the most vulnerable areas by considering a variety of factors that affect flooding (Kanani-Sadat et al., 2019 ). The severity of floods is mainly determined by several geographical variable like hydrological parameters (Costache, 2019a ), geological features, meteorological conditions, morphological and topographical characteristics of a specific study region (Chowdhuri et al., 2020 ). Additionally, only specific flood predictors have an impact on flood susceptibility models; and thus, the choice of the right factors can affect the flood risk estimation. In the current study, a practical method of selecting features (Gain Ratio) for flood susceptibility estimation was applied and allowed the selection of an adequate set of input flood predictors through which the flood susceptibility models were trained. According to the results of the Gain Ratio method, slope angle has the highest predictive ability in terms of flooding phenomena, while hydrological soil group, convergence index and rainfall were the least important predictors. These results are in agreement with many studies that were carried out before (Costache et al., 2020b; Dano et al., 2019; Hosseini et al., 2021; Khosravi et al., 2019 ). It is true that rainfall is the primary cause of flooding, but the effect of rainfall on flooding is not always linear (Khosravi et al., 2019 ). In terms of elevation, there is a general agreement that the higher altitudes are less prone to flooding than the lower ones (Sahana and Patel, 2019 ). The construction of ROC curves as well as the computation of a several statiscal metrices facilitated the validation of the model's performance. According to the results of the validation phase, both hybrid models DLNN-SI and SVM-SI were significantly improved by using Particle Swarm Optimization. Overall, the PSO-DLNN-SI outperformed the other models by achieveing an AUC-ROC Curve of 0.952 comparing with PSO-SVM-SI whose AUC was 0.944. It should be noted that there is almost a generall agreement among the results of the four models according to which a quarter of study area have a high and very high flood susceptibility. Also, it is evident that these high and very high potential affected zones are located in the extremely southern part of the study zone, but also along the main rivers and depressions of the study area. Another study focused on the present research area and whose central theme was the assessment of flood susceptibility was carried out by Costache (2019b) . In that study, the following 4 models were used: Statistical Index stand-alone, Certainty Factor, Fuzzy-Support Vector Machine and Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System. It should be noted that the maximum accuracy offered by the 4 models used in the mentioned study was 0.921. Thus, unlike this value, in the present study it was possible to achieve a maximum accuracy of 0.959 associated with the PSO-DLNN-SI model. Thus, it can be said that an improvement was made for the study area in terms of the precision with which the areas exposed to floods can be identified. Researchers or maybe the persons in charge with flood hazard management may find the outputs of this research study very useful in selecting the most appropriate method for the simulation of flood susceptibility. This type of studies has also a main limitation which refers to the impossibility to calculate the flow velocity or depth. Moreover, there can be mentioned other limitations elements like: i) Uncertainty in data - flood susceptibility models rely on various data inputs such as topography, land use/land cover, precipitation, and hydrological data. However, these data may have inaccuracies, errors, or uncertainties, which can affect the accuracy and reliability of flood susceptibility assessments. The climate changes, due to the modification in the rainfall regime, can also induced in the next years some uncertainties in the present flood susceptibility assessment. The same influence can be mentioned also for land use changes process; ii) Lack of historical data - flood susceptibility models often rely on historical flood events to calibrate and validate their accuracy. However, historical flood data may be limited, incomplete, or not available for certain areas, which can impact the reliability of flood susceptibility assessments, especially in regions with low flood frequency; iii) complex and dynamic nature of floods which are complex events influenced by various factors such as rainfall intensity, soil saturation, antecedent conditions, and human interventions (Zhu et al., 2022 ). Flood susceptibility models often simplify these complex interactions, and may not fully capture the dynamic nature of floods, resulting in potential inaccuracies. However, the importance of such studies for policy makers is indisputable. Policy makers play a critical role in managing and mitigating flood susceptibility through the development and implementation of policies and regulations aimed at reducing the impacts of flooding. Policy makers can implement land use planning policies that guide development away from flood-prone areas, such as floodplains, coastal zones, and other vulnerable areas (Islam et al., 2021 ). This can include zoning regulations, building codes, and restrictions on development in high-risk areas. Policy makers can establish floodplain management policies that focus on measures such as floodplain mapping, floodplain zoning, and land acquisition or relocation of properties in flood-prone areas. This can help to prevent or reduce development in areas that are susceptible to flooding (Mudashiru et al., 2021 ). Policy makers can develop policies related to infrastructure and engineering, such as construction standards for buildings and infrastructure in flood-prone areas. This may include requirements for flood-resistant design and construction techniques, as well as the development of adequate stormwater management systems to reduce flood risk (Dahri et al., 2022 ). Policy makers can also implement early warning systems that use advanced technology and communication networks to provide timely and accurate information about impending floods (Hou et al., 2023 ). This can enable communities to take proactive measures, such as evacuations, to reduce the impacts of flooding (Malik et al., 2020 ). Including the influence of climate change in flood susceptibility assessment studies represents also a new approach adopted by researchers today (Avand et al., 2021; Chakrabortty et al., 2021; Li et al., 2020 ). These studies can provide valuable details on how flood susceptibility will evolve under future climate scenarios. Thus, in the future studies the authors will incorporate the climate changes characteristics in order to evaluate the flood susceptibility on Prahova River basin from Romania. Moreover, if we refer strictly to the study area on which this paper is focused, we mention the fact that in the future it is considered to collect additional data on the locations affected by floods in the past, so as to allow the application of new procedures such as those of cross-validation necessary to the assessment if the models generalization. Additionally, in the future studies it is mandatory to conduct an n-fold cross-validation procedure in order to better examine the robustness of the applied models.  7 Conclusions In the present research paper, a bivariate statistical method (SI), two machine learning models (DLNN and SVM) and the Particle Swarm Optimization method were combined in order to create four hybrid models able to estimate the flood susceptibility in Prahova River basin from Romania. The four models were trained using a number of 10 geographical predictors along with 158 flood locations identified based on governmental sources. A first selection of predictors was carried out with the help of Gain Ratio method, this algorithm showing that all 10 predictors should be considered for the analysis. Also, through VIF and Tolerance indices was determined that among the flood predictors there is no serious multicollinearity. The use of ROC Curve and statistical metrics highlights that all the four models (DLNN-SI, PSO-DLNN-SI, SVM-SI, PSO-SVM-SI) achieved very good performances confirmed by AUC ROC Curve higher than 0.85. In addition to the very high accuracy of the results obtained in the present study, which recommends the use of the models applied in other regions as well, of great local and regional importance is also the effective identification of the areas that have a high and very high exposure to the phenomenon of flooding. Given the area's history of severe floods in the years 1970, 1975, 2005 and 2010, highlighting these areas as accurately as possible is mandatory for adequate flood risk management in the study area. Thus, measures can be taken to reduce the potential damage caused by floods and at the same time detailed studies can be done using hydraulic modeling in areas that have proven to have a high and very high flood potential. Moreover, in order to increase the sustainability and durability of measures to reduce the potential negative effects of floods, future studies will also take into account climate change scenarios as well as land use changes. 1 Introduction In recent years, the world has witnessed an increase in urban flood disasters. These incidents have severely impacted the smooth functioning of cities. Urban flood usually causes traffic jams, ecological destruction, and could even result in human casualties and property damage. Accurate assessment of urban flood risk is imperative for effective disaster relief decision-making (Qian et al., 2022; Rafiei-Sardooi et al., 2021 ). Despite the rapid advancement in microwave remote sensing, its application in identifying floodwater bodies and comparing pre-disaster and post-disaster flood areas still faces challenges, including low spatial and temporal resolution, limited accuracy, and often compounded by tree occlusion (DeVries et al., 2020 ). Additionally, this technology lacks the ability to determining the depth of flood (Liang and Liu, 2020 ). Moreover, although electronic and radar water level gauges have been deployed at critical urban points to enable real-time monitoring of urban flood depth, these systems are costly to establish and do not support high spatial coverage (Nam and Lee, 2015; Paul et al., 2020 ). Consequently, there is still an urgent need for an intelligent, cost-effective system for the high-resolution urban flood level monitoring. With the advent of 5G and the widespread deployment of surveillance cameras in cities, flooded image, sourced from surveillance or social media networks, has emerged as a novel and widely distributed medium in urban systems, thus showing great potential for urban flood monitoring (Iqbal et al., 2021 ). In the meanwhile, there have been significant advancements in computer vision technologies, notably in the use of convolution neural network (Voulodimos et al., 2018 ). These developments present an opportunity to integrate the rich image data in urban systems with cutting-edge analytical techniques. Previous research has used a number of reference objects such as bridges (Disse et al., 2019 ), pavement fence (Jiang et al., 2019 ), traffic signs (Alizadeh Kharazi and Behzadan, 2021 ), traffic bucket (Jiang et al., 2020 ), bicycles (Chaudhary et al., 2020 ), and water markers (Jafari et al., 2021 ) to determine urban flood levels. While these studies have achieved promising outcomes with specific references objects, the limited appearance of such reference objects limits their widespread applicability in urban settings. Pedestrians are more commonly present in urban systems, making them frequently utilized as reference for flood depth estimation (Quan et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2020; Li et al., 2023; Meng et al., 2019; Nair and Rao, 2017; Bin et al., 2019 ). However, challenges such as the low resolution of pedestrian in images often prevent accurate flood depth recognition, and the scarcity of pedestrians in severely flooded areas further reduces the practicality of using pedestrians as reference object for estimating deep flood level. Vehicles, as critical components of urban mobility, are more frequently present during flood events and exhibit resilience in severely flooded conditions, making them ideal reference objects for urban flood level identification. The employment of vehicles as reference objects for urban flood depth identification has been explored in the literature. For example, Park et al. (2021)  employed Mask R-CNN (He et al., 2017 ) to detect flooded vehicles and subsequently used VGGNet (Simonyan and Zisserman (2015) ) to match these detections with 3D rendered vehicle feature images for flood depth estimation. Similarly, Huang et al. (2020)  used Mask R-CNN to detect flood levels by identifying the inundation status of vehicle tires, and then employed the height difference method or the collinear theorem to calculate the depth of flood. The YOLO (You Only Look Once) (Redmon et al., 2016 ) series, regarded for its speed and accuracy in real-time object detection, has gain popularity in urban flood detection, with various studies employing YOLOv3 (Redmon and Farhadi, 2018 ), YOLOv4 (Bochkovskiy et al., 2020 ) and YOLOv5 (Puliti and Astrup, 2022 ) for flood level detection and flood risk assessment (Hao, 2022; Wang, 2022; Zhong et al., 2023 ). Despite the successful application of utilizing vehicles as reference objects for urban flood detection, current studies remain constrained by small sample size, insufficient classification of submerged states, dependence on fully visible and intact vehicles, and reliance on outdated versions of the YOLO algorithm. In response to these deficiencies, this study will compile a more comprehensive dataset using images from social media, and divide the inundation state of flood vehicles into more categories adhering to safety standards and reflecting changes in vehicle height. Scenarios where vehicles are partially visible or occluded by other objects will also be included in the constructed dataset, thereby significantly enhancing the dataset's diversity. YOLOv8 (Glenn, 2023 ), the latest version of the YOLO algorithm, has demonstrated high accuracy and fast detection speed on standard COCO dataset (Lin et al., 2014 ), will be extensively explored using the newly constructed dataset to identify the urban flood level. This study aims to enhance urban flood level detection through advanced image recognition techniques using a comprehensive dataset, addressing limitations in current urban flood monitoring dataset and methods. More specific, our aims are as follows:1) A more comprehensive flooded vehicle dataset is constructed and the correlation between flood vehicle and urban flood level is clarified. The newly constructed dataset is available online, supporting public research on urban flood level identification.  2) The performance of four YOLOv8 configurations in urban flood level detection is evaluated through K-fold cross-validation training, varying sample size and label accuracy experiments, as well as complex scenarios detection.  3) Clear guidelines on selecting the appropriate YOLOv8 configuration for specific environmental conditions and computational resources are provided, which will help in optimizing the deployment of these models in diverse urban settings.    The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2  describes the dataset, experimental design and model evaluation metrics employed in this study. Section 3  presents the experimental results and provides a detailed analysis of these findings. Section 4  discusses the broader implications of the results and YOLOv8 configuration recommendation. Finally, Section 5  summarizes the main conclusions and outlines directions for further work.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Construction of dataset In this study, a comprehensive flooded vehicle dataset with a total of 2000 images is compiled, which includes vehicles with various states of submergence. The images in the newly constructed dataset are varying in resolution and size. These flooded vehicles are obtained from Microsoft Bing, Google and Baidu searching with the keywords “urban flooding” and “urban flood”. During the process of flooded vehicles selection, complex and challenging scenarios are also included, such as nighttime, muddy water, and scenes with water splashing caused by vehicle movement, which is designed to ensure our dataset is more robust and capable of handling diverse flood situations. There are a diverse range of vehicle types in the 2000 images selected. However, our analysis specifically focuses on Sedans, SUVs, and Vans, which were selected due to their similar height features such as tire and window heights, and the similarity risk levels exposed to the floods. Consequently, five flood levels have been established, and the details of vehicle instances and flood risk levels are presented in Table 1  . LabelImg (Lin,2015 ) was utilized to annotate the 2,000 images within the flooded vehicle dataset, identifying 6,300 vehicle instances. The distribution of these instances across the defined flood levels are detailed in Table 1 . Besides, we assigned three graduate students to double check the accuracy of the bounding boxes and the flood risk level annotations. The labeling results are stored in YOLO format (Redmon et al., 2016 ), including the coordinates of the vehicle bounding boxes as well as the vehicle flooding level labels. The dataset is available at https://github.com/ywszxdd/original_dataset .  2.2 Target detection model 2.2.1 Outlook of YOLOV8 The YOLO model is distinguished by its optimal balance between speed and accuracy, making it highly effective for rapid and precise target identification across various domains. The latest iteration, YOLOv8, represents the most advanced version of the YOLO series and shows superior performance attributes. The architectural design of YOLOv8 is depicted in Fig. 1  . The YOLOv8 model comprises three primary components: Backbone, Neck, and Head. The Backbone section includes an input module, several Conv modules, C2f modules and a Spatial Pyramid Pooling-Fast module at the tail. The Neck part processes the features extracted from the backbone network. The Head section employs a decoupled head structure that separates the tasks of detection and classification, which solves the problem of different focuses of classification and localization concerns and adopts the Anchor-Free target detection to accelerate the detection process. For a comprehensive understanding of the implementation principles and computational details of YOLOv8, readers are referred to Glenn (2023) . There are four YOLOv8 configurations, YOLOv8n, YOLOv8s, YOLOv8m, YOLOv8l, each are designed with different depth and width of the network to satisfying different demands. These variants differ in size and number of parameters, and each demonstrates distinct performance metrics when trained on the COCO dataset (Lin et al., 2014 ). The key features for the four YOLOv8 configurations models are presented in Table 2  .  2.2.2 YOLOv8 settings In this study, we implemented transfer learning to enhance the training process of the YOLOv8 models across various experiments. This approach used pre-trained weights from models that were initially trained on the COCO dataset, available for download from Glenn (2023) . By using these pre-trained weights, we significantly improve the training efficiency and reduced the time required to achieve convergence. All experiments were executed on a Windows server equipped with an Intel i7 CPU, 32 GB RAM, and an NVIDIA GTX 3090 TI GPU. Some more details about the hyper parameters are as follow: learning rate of 0.001, momentum of 0.8, and epochs 100 were set for stochastic gradient descent algorithm.   2.3 Design of experiments The original flooded vehicle dataset was systematically segmented to meet diverse experimental needs, including the K-fold cross-validation experiment, varying sample size experiment, varying labeling accuracy experiment. In additional, complex scenes prediction experiment was also designed to evaluate the performance of four YOLOv8 configurations in detecting complex urban flooding scenarios. 2.3.1 K-fold cross-validation experiment K-fold cross-validation is a method widely utilized in data mining and machine learning to evaluate the generalization of a model (Wong and Yeh, 2020 ).
