The dataset is evenly split into K separate folds. Each fold acts as a validation set during one round of training while the remaining K-1 folds are combined and used as the training set. In this experiment, we set K = 10, and the dataset was divided into 10 equal subsets of 200 images each. This division allowed us to form 10 non-overlapping groups, where each group contained a training set of 1,800 images and a validation set of 200 images. These groups are labeled as DS_K_Fold (K from 1 to 10). For example, DS_4_Fold means that the 4th fold is used as validation set, while the remaining 9 folds are combined and used as the training set. The 10-fold cross-validation process is shown in Fig. 2  .  2.3.2 Varying sample size experiment In this experiment, 6 subsets randomly selected from the DS_4_Fold training, using the first 300, 600, 900, 1200, 1500, and 1800 images from the 1800 training images respectively, are constructed for this purpose. These subsets are labeled as DS_300, DS_600, DS_900, DS_1200, DS_1500, and DS_1800.  2.3.3 Varying labeling accuracy experiment In this experiment, the labels of the first 0, 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 samples from the 1800 training images in DS_4_Fold group were deliberately mislabeled for this purpose, forming 6 new training sets. These sets are labeled as DS_LE_0, DS_LE_20, DS_LE_40, DS_LE_60, DS_LE_80, and DS_LE_100. These datasets are available at https://github.com/ywszxdd/error_label_dataset .  2.3.4 Complex scenes prediction experiment In this experiment, we selected two particularly challenging scenes to evaluate the performance of four optimal YOLOv8 configurations in detecting complex urban flooding scenarios, as depicted in Fig. 3  . Fig. 3  (A) shows a multi-scale mixed partial occurrence scene, featuring vehicles at varying scales and partial visibility due to changes in camera angles and distances. Fig. 3  (B) illustrates how the complexity of urban flooding scenarios intensifies during nighttime or rainy conditions, which can significantly degrade image quality and complicate the detection process.   2.4 Evaluation metrics We employ the mean average precision (mAP), a widely recognized metric in target detection model assessment, to evaluate the performance of various YOLOv8 configurations in detecting submerged vehicle status. mAP is calculated as the sum of the average precision for all labels, divided by the total number of categories. A higher mAP value indicates greater average accuracy across the model, reflecting better overall detection performance. The calculation of mAP is shown in Equation (1) :(1) mAP = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  A P i  = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  ∫ 0 1  P i  ( R i  ) d R  i     where n is the number of categories, Precision (P) is used to measure the false detection rate of the model and Recall (R) is used to measure the true detection rate, the formulas for P and R are shown in Equations (2) and (3) :(2) P = TP  TP + F P       (3) R = TP  TP + F N       where TP denotes a true positive case, FN denotes a false negative case and FP denotes a false positive case. The metrics mAP50 and mAP50:95 are employed to evaluated the performance of YOLOv8 configurations. Intersection over Union (IoU) quantifies the degree of overlap between the true bounding box (labeled using annotation software) and the predicted bounding box (produced by the algorithm), with values ranging from 0 to 1. A higher IoU value indicates greater accuracy of the prediction, indicating a larger overlap between the true and the predicted boxes. Specifically, mAP50 refers to the mean average precision using IoU threshold of 0.5, meaning the prediction is considered correct if the IoU is 0.5 or higher. mAP50:95 calculates the average of the mAP values from IoU thresholds of 0.5 to 0.95, increasing in steps of 0.05. These metrics, mAP50 and mAP50:95, allow for a comprehensive and objective assessment of model prediction accuracy and are widely utilized in the field of target detection.   3 Results 3.1 10-fold cross-validation results In this section, we present a comparative analysis of the results obtained from the four YOLOv8 configurations, each was trained and validated on the 10 datasets presented in section 2.3.1 . Fig. 4   illustrates the distribution and variation of the 10-fold cross-validation output results for the evaluation metrics associated with these four configurations. Table 3   presents the mean and median values of the mAP50 and mAP50:95, as well as the training time derived from the 10-fold cross-validation for each YOLOv8 configurations. It shows in Fig. 4  (A) that the mAP50 results for YOLOv8n and YOLOv8s tend to cluster more tightly, indicating more consistent performance, whereas the outcomes for YOLOv8m and YOLOv8l show larger dispersion, suggesting variability in their effectiveness across different training folds. Additionally, We could observe that as the network width and depth increase, there is a corresponding upward trend in median values of mAP50. Combined with Table 3 , we can find that YOLOv8n records the lowest mAP50 median value of 66.4 %, while YOLOv8l achieves the highest value of 70.0 %. YOLOv8s is 0.7 % more accurate than YOLOv8n, and YOLOv8m is 1.5 % more accurate than YOLOv8s. YOLOv8l is 1.4% more accurate when compared to YOLOv8m. Similarly, we can also see that for the mean of the mAP50, YOLOv8s is 1.5 % more accurate than YOLOv8n, and YOLOv8m is 1.4 % more accurate than YOLOv8s. YOLOv8l is only marginally more accurate by 0.3 % when compared to YOLOv8m, but with an extra 997s of training time. From Fig. 4  (B) we could find that the mAP50:95 results for YOLOv8 models show greater dispersion than mAP50, suggesting more variability in their effectiveness across different training folds. However, as the network width and depth increase, there is also a corresponding upward trend in median value of mAP50:95. Combined with Table 3 , it shows that YOLOv8n still records the lowest median value of 49.5 %, and YOLOv8l achieves the highest median value of 53.4 %. YOLOv8s demonstrates a noticeable improvement over YOLOv8n, with increment of 1.2 %. YOLOv8m shows an improvement of 1.3 % when compared with YOLOv8s. YOLOv8l, when compared to YOLOv8m, shows an improvement of 1.4 %. In addition, for the mean value of the mAP50:95, YOLOv8n records the lowest mean value of 49.7 %, and YOLOv8l achieves the highest value of 53.6 %. YOLOv8s demonstrates the improvement over YOLOv8n, with increment of 1.8 %. Similarly, YOLOv8m shows improvement of 1.3 % compared to YOLOv8s. YOLOv8l, when compared to YOLOv8m, exhibits only marginal gains of 0.8 %.  3.2 Varying sample size results In this section, we present a comparative analysis of the results obtained from the four YOLOv8 configurations, each was trained and validated on the 6 datasets presented in section 2.3.2 . Fig. 5   shows that for YOLOv8s, YOLOv8m and YOLOv8l, both mAP50 and mAP50:95 metrics improve consistently as the sample size increases. But for YOLOv8n, with the sample size increased from 300 to 900, mAP50 and mAP50:95 increase, while sample size increased from 1200 to 1500, mAP50 and mAP50:95 decrease. Notably, YOLOv8l shows a larger enhancement in algorithm performance when compared to the other three configurations. More specifically, when the sample size is less than 1800, YOLOv8l's performance does not surpass that of YOLOv8m or YOLOv8s; however, at the maximum sample size of 1800, YOLOv8l outperforms both. Conversely, YOLOv8n generally shows the weakest performance, while YOLOv8m generally exhibits better performance as sample sizes increase.  3.3 Varying labeling accuracy results In this section, we present a comparative analysis of the results obtained from the four YOLOv8 configurations, each was trained and validated on the 6 datasets presented in section 2.3.3 . It is clear from Fig. 6   that as the number of mislabeled samples increases, there is a significant decline in the mAP50 and mAP50:95 metrics across all trained models. Specifically, Fig. 6  (A) shows that for the mAP50, both YOLOv8n and YOLOv8s show a continuous decrease in performance as the mislabel count rises. In contrast, YOLOv8m initially shows a decrease with the mislabeled samples increase from 0 to 20, then an unexpected increase with the mislabeled samples increase from 20 to 60, before declining again. While YOLOv8l shows a significant decrease as the sample goes from 0 to 40, followed by a steady increase as the mislabeled sample increases. Furthermore, YOLOv8n consistently underperforms the other three configurations throughout the tests. YOLOv8l demonstrates the best performance when the number of mislabeled samples is fewer than 20; however, as mislabeling increases beyond this point, YOLOv8m emerges as the most robust configuration. In addition, it can be seen from Fig. 6  (B) that as the number of mislabel sample increases, the mAP50:95 of all trained models shows a decreasing trend as well. More specifically, YOLOv8l is continuing to decrease, with a significant drop in the number of mislabeled samples from 0 to 40 and a smooth region after 40. YOLOv8m and YOLOv8n initially show a decrease with the mislabeled samples increase from 0 to 20, then an increase with the mislabeled samples increase from 20 to 40, before declining again. YOLOv8s initially shows a decrement with the mislabeled sample increased from 0 to 40, then an unexpected increase with the mislabeled samples increased from 40 to 60, before declining again. In conclusion, YOLOv8n consistently underperforms the other three models throughout the tests. YOLOv8l demonstrates the best performance when the number of mislabeled samples is fewer than 20; however, as mislabeling increases beyond this point, YOLOv8m emerges as the most robust model, handling increasing inaccuracies more effectively than its counterparts.  3.4 Complex scenes prediction results In this section, we present a comparative analysis of the results obtained from the four optimal YOLOv8 configurations, each determined through 10-fold cross-validation in Section 3.1 . These configurations were specifically tested on complex urban flooding scenes to assess their robustness and effectiveness in challenging conditions. It is clear from Fig. 7   that all the four optimal  YOLOv8 configurations can correctly detect the submerged state of three vehicles at the upper-left edge of the image. YOLOv8m, while managing to segment the submerged state of the three vehicles on the left, exhibits overlap in the bounding box generation. In contrast, YOLOv8s and YOLOv8l demonstrate more precise segmentation detection of the submerged state for these three vehicles, with YOLOv8s displaying higher overall confidence in the submerged state detection compared to YOLOv8l. Besides, for the vehicles at the upper-middle and upper-right edge of the image, YOLOv8s and YOLOv8l did not detect any one, although YOLOv8n and YOLOv8m detect one vehicle, but fail to correctly determine its submerged level. Furthermore, YOLOv8n incorrectly identify the closest largest gray car as Level 2, the other three models correctly identify it as Level 3. Moreover, Fig. 8   presents the detection results for the image blurring and corruption scenario. It shows that YOLOv8m is not able to detect the submerged vehicle positioned at the upper-right edge of the image. The other three configurations can successfully detect these two vehicle, and accurately identify the submerged state level. Besides, YOLOv8s incorrectly identifies the vehicle's windshield and the background environment as a submerged state of Level 1. YOLOv8l not only localizes the vehicle on the left side but also accurately identifies the complete bounding box of the vehicle on the left side and its submerged state level.   4 Discussion 4.1 Impact of sample size Sample size is a crucial factor that significantly affect the performance of YOLOv8 configurations. The experiment results presented in section 3.2  shows a clear trend that as the number of samples increases, there is a corresponding improvement in both mAP50 and mAP50:95 across all YOLOv8 models. This improvement is attributed to the enhanced learning and generalization capabilities of the models. The increased sampling size not only allows for a more comprehensive understanding of the key features of the detection targets but also provides a broader range of annotated instances from which the models can learn. Therefore, this extensive learning from varied scenarios enhances the YOLv8′s capability during the validation process. The impact of sample size varies among the different YOLOv8 configurations. YOLOv8l, which has the largest model parameters, is particularly sensitive to the size of the dataset. When provided with a sufficiently large dataset, such like DS_1800, YOLOv8l exhibits the best performance among all configurations. However, its sensitivity also makes it more prone to performance fluctuations when the available sample size is limited. On the other hand, YOLOv8n, which has the least model parameters, exhibits the smallest gains in performance as the sample size increases. Although the performance improvement with YOLOv8n is less pronounced, it tends to be more stable across different sample size experiments.  4.2 Impact of labeling accuracy Mislabeling is an inevitable during sample annotation, and even a single erroneous label can have an unpredictable impact on both training and validation results. It is, therefore, essential for algorithms to demonstrate robustness in the face of such inaccuracies. Our findings in section 3.3  reveal that all four YOLOv8 configurations exhibit significant decline in performance metrics when samples containing incorrect annotations. Among the YOLOv8 configurations, YOLOv8n and YOLOv8s are particularly sensitive to mislabeling, showing a rapid drop in performance with the introduction of erroneous samples. YOLOv8l initially performs the best, its performance rapidly declines and crosses below YOLOv8m when there are more than 20 erroneous labels. This crossover indicates that while YOLOv8l is more robust against fewer mislabels, YOLOv8m is more effectively to higher levels of erroneous labels, becoming the most suitable configuration for scenarios with substantial erroneous labels. The robust performance of YOLOv8l and YOLOv8m in the presence of erroneous labels can be attributed to their large neural networks. These deep networks are capable at capturing a wide range of features from diverse inputs and provide a buffer against mislabeling. This ability to generalize effectively from flawed datasets makes them particularly effective in scenarios where label accuracy is compromised. This phenomenon aligns well with the findings presented by Zhang et al. (2021)  which explained why large neural networks generalize well in practice.  4.3 YOLOv8 configuration recommendation Given the unique characteristics of each YOLOv8 configuration across varied experiments, it is necessary to carefully select optimal configuration under different urban flood environment. YOLOv8l is the top performer in terms of accuracy and overall performance, particularly when ample correctly annotated samples are available. This configuration is ideal recommended for complex scenes given substantial computational resources. YOLOv8m is highly effective in environments with limited sample sizes, making it an excellent choice for achieving good performance with fewer data inputs. YOLOv8m performs well not only in environments with ample data samples but also shows resilience in the presence of labeling inaccuracies. This good behavior makes it a highly recommended choice for practical urban flood environment where data quality and quantity may vary. Although YOLOv8s and YOLOv8n underperform relative to the above two YOLOv8 configurations, they require fewer computational resources. This makes them ideal choices for scenarios constrained by limited computational capabilities.   5 Conclusions This study addresses the critical challenge of urban flood risk management by investigating the performance of four YOLOv8 configurations in the automatic detection of urban flood levels. A comprehensive dataset consisting of 2000 images was compiled first, which includes flooded vehicles in various states of submergence. By annotating the vehicle flooding status into 5 levels, we end up with identifying 6,300 vehicle instances. This study then explored the performance of four YOLOv8 model configurations under various experimental conditions, yielding the following empirical findings:1) YOLOv8l and YOLOv8m provided the best results in terms of accuracy and robustness for flood level detection. In contrast, YOLOv8s and YOLOv8n show less reliability while require generally fewer computational resources.  2) YOLOv8m are more effectively to higher levels of erroneous labels, becoming the most suitable configuration for scenarios with substantial erroneous labels.  3) The study provided clear guidelines on selecting the appropriate YOLOv8 configuration based on specific environmental conditions and computational resources. These guidelines help in optimizing the deployment of these models in diverse urban settings.    This study successfully demonstrates the effectiveness of our methodology in urban flood identification using the YOLOv8 model. While effective, it struggles with detecting vehicles that are completely submerged or fall outside the visible water range, posing significant challenges in comprehensive flood scenario analysis. Additionally, our current framework lacks the capability to provide quantitative measurements of flood depth, which are essential for a detailed and actionable flood risk assessment. Future work will focus on developing numerical quantification methods for flood depths to improve assessment accuracy.
1 Introduction The frequency, intensity, and spatial extent of extreme events are increasing with global warming (Zhang et al., 2022 ). The extreme high temperature events are particularly severe in urban areas and densely populated areas (Zhang et al., 2023 ). Extreme weather events directly and indirectly impact ecological society (Liu et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2021 ). Global and regional extreme events have received great attention and have become important indicators for monitoring and studying climate change (Donat et al., 2013; IPCC, 2021; Kim et al., 2016; Ren et al., 2015; Ren & Ren, 2011; Zhang et al., 2023 ). According to previous studies, global warming will alter the intrinsic characteristics of temperature, precipitation, and other climate phenomena, increasing the risks of extreme weather (Seneviratne et al., 2012; Zhou & Liu, 2018 ). Furthermore, it should be noted that global warming has also resulted in longer persistence, longer traveling distances, and slower propagation heatwaves. It will pose a serious threat to human health and the environment (Luo et al., 2024 ). It has been reported that compound extremes would amplify the damage of individual events in time and space, resulting in more significant or persistent destructive impacts than any of these hazards alone (Cai et al., 2020; Gu et al., 2022; Hao, 2022; Ren et al., 2023 ). Global Climate Models (GCMs) are important tools to simulate climate changes during historical and future periods (Cheng et al., 2017; Mehrotra & Sharma, 2010; Sun et al., 2015 ). Due to the coarse resolution of GCM, the downscaling approaches should be employed before conducting local investigations (Cannon, 2018; Piani et al., 2010; Wood et al., 2004; Yue et al., 2021 ). The statistical downscaling has been applied for a long time (Wilby & Wigley, 1997 ). The statistical downscaling develops relationships between large-scale atmospheric circulation variables and in-situ climate data (Gangopadhyay et al., 2005 ). The projections of atmospheric variables can be translated into forecasts of local climate variables by utilizing these observed relationships (Gangopadhyay et al., 2005 ). Therefore, the statistical downscaling is used to downscale raw GCMs in this study. Previous research has applied various statistical downscaling methods to simulate climate changes in different areas. For instance, Mahmood and Babel (2014)  simulated the future variations in extreme temperature events in the Jhelum River Basin by Statistical Downscaling Model (SDSM). Ren et al. (2021)  projected the changes in heatwaves by the Stepwise Cluster Downscaling (SCD) model over Guangdong Province. The Bias Correction Spatial Disaggregation (BCSD) was proposed by Wood et al. (2004) . The BCSD is a powerful tool for downscaling GCM from a large spatial scale to a specific spatial scale (Duan, Huang, Zhou, et al., 2021; Ren et al., 2023 ). Recently, the BCSD has been coupled with the quantile mapping (QM) in the bias correction step (Xu & Wang, 2019 ). However, the QM could not effectively preserve the observed trends in precipitation (Kim et al., 2021 ). The cause of this issue may lie in the fact that the QM have been shown to modify the trends in simulating precipitation (Cannon et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2021 ). The bias correction algorithms should not only correct systematic errors relative to historical observations but also make efforts to preserve the relative changes (Cannon et al., 2015 ). It is difficult for traditional BCSD to maintain the observed trends and relative changes in precipitation (Kim et al., 2021 ). Thus, the BCSD model needs to be improved in simulating precipitation. Over the past decades, many studies have focused on investigating the spatiotemporal characteristics (e.g., the occurrence frequency, duration and intensity) of compound extreme events at different spatial scales. Ren et al. (2023)  projected the occurrence frequency, average duration, total intensity and maximum duration of compound heatwaves and heavy precipitation events in Guangdong province. Wu et al. (2019)  primarily investigated the variations in frequency and spatial extent of compound extreme precipitation and temperature events (including dry/warm, dry/cold, wet/warm and wet/cold combinations) in the summer and winter over China. However, these studies pay less attention to considering the compound extremes with the teleconnection factors (e.g., ENSO) or the underlying mechanisms. On the other hand, some studies focus on the historical and future relationships between individual extreme events and teleconnection factors. For example, Wang et al. (2023)  applied the station observations and global reanalysis datasets to investigate the relationships between leading modes of winter cold days and teleconnection metrics. Sun et al. (2021)  investigated the changed relationships between precipitation and ENSO in eastern China. However, these studies need more exploration of compound extremes. However, compound extreme events will lead to a significant impact on society. And it will result in environmental hazards and economic losses (Bevacqua et al., 2021 ). Hence, it is necessary to explore the influence of compound extremes and their inherent mechanisms over China under global warming. Therefore, the characteristics and underlying mechanisms of compound extreme events would be investigated based on developed statistical downscaling methods in this study. Therefore, the objective of this study is to investigate compound dry-warm (CDDW) and wet-warm (CDWW) extreme events based on the proposed QDMSD method. The objective includes: (i) The QDMSD will be proposed to analyze the spatiotemporal characteristics in CDDW and CDWW as well as their future mechanisms over China. The performance of QDMSD will be evaluated by comparing observations in the period of 1985 to 2014. (ii) The Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF ) analysis was employed to investigate the spatiotemporal characteristics and the relationships between compound extremes and teleconnection factors in the historical period (1961–2020). (iii) Five CMIP6 GCMs for temperature and precipitation would be statistically downscaled by the QDMSD under two Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) scenarios (i.e., SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5). It aims to investigate the frequencies of CDDW and CDWW in the future. The future period (2030–2099) will be divided into two 35-year periods, that is, the 2050s (i.e., 2030–2064) and the 2080s (2065–2099). (iv) The mechanisms governing the projected changes in compound extremes are revealed through the analyses of the potentially influenced factors and their regressions with CDDW and CDWW. The developed QDMSD has significant improvements in simulating precipitation. The results could provide valuable references for future simulations in compound extremes over China.  2 Data and methodology 2.1 Data In this study, the daily mean temperature (Tmean ) at the resolution of 0.25˚ × 0.25˚ could be obtained from the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) Reanalysis in the fifth generation (ERA5). The ERA5 provided datasets of precipitation and Tmean  with temporal coverage from 1950 to now (Hersbach et al., 2020 ). The ERA5 reanalysis was widely used to investigate climate changes in recent studies (Johnson et al., 2023; Ren et al., 2023; Tan et al., 2023 ). In this study, the roles of ERA5 were shown as follows: (i) The ERA5 reanalysis in the training period (1985 to 1999) was used to train the QDMSD model, and the ERA5 in the evaluation period (2000 to 2014) was utilized to evaluate the performance of QDMSD in simulating Tmean . (ii) The ERA5 in the period of 1980 to 2014 was used to downscale Tmean  in the future period (2030–2099). (iii) The ERA5 was also employed to calculate the frequencies of CDDW and CDWW in the historical period (1981–2020). (iv) The ERA5 was applied to investigate the potential relationships between climate factors and dominant modes of CDWW and CDDW in the historical period. The daily precipitation at the resolution of 0.5˚ × 0.5˚ could be acquired from the Climate Prediction Center (CPC) of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) in the period from 1980 to 2020 (Silva et al., 2007 ). It was proven that CPC could provide stable estimated values at temporal and spatial scales (Jiang et al., 2023 ). The roles of CPC were listed as follows: (i) The CPC dataset in the training period was employed to train the QDMSD model and the CPC in the evaluation period (2000 to 2014) was utilized to evaluate the performance of QDMSD in simulating precipitation. (ii) The CPC in the period of 1980 to 2014 was used to downscale precipitation in the future period. (iii) The CPC was also used to calculate the frequencies of CDDW and CDWW in the historical period. (iv) The CPC was applied to investigate the potential relationships between climate factors and primary patterns of CDWW and CDDW in the historical period. Due to the different resolutions of ERA5 and CPC reanalysis, the ERA5 was bilinearly interpolated to the resolution of 0.5˚ × 0.5˚ to retain the same resolution of CPC reanalysis. The monthly mean sea surface temperature (SST) in the historical period could be obtained from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Extended Reconstructed SST dataset version 5 (ERSST V5), with a resolution of 2.5° × 2.5° (Huang et al., 2017 ). It aims to investigate SST anomalies (SSTA) and influenced factors linked with compound extremes in the historical period. In addition, the outputs from phase 6 of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6) Global Climate Models (GCM) were used to investigate the characteristics of compound extremes and their inherent mechanisms in the future. The CMIP6 GCMs were also employed to investigate driving factors of projected changes in compound extremes in the future period (2030–2099). The number of five GCMs has been shown to be reasonable for simulating temperature and precipitation in China (Duan, Huang, Li, et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2021 ). In addition, the GCMs selected in this study have been proven to simulate temperature and precipitation well (Lei et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2024 ). The selected CMIP6 GCMs include monthly SST, geopotential height (GHT), horizontal wind speed (UWIND), vertical wind speed (VWIND), precipitation (PRE) and Tmean  (Eyring et al., 2016 ). The detailed GCMs’ information is shown in Table 1  . Two large-scale circulation metrics were also utilized to explore their potential impacts on compound extremes. The monthly AMO and Niño 3 metrics could be respectively obtained from https://climatedataguide.ucar.edu/sites/default/files/2022-03/amo_monthly.txt  and https://psl.noaa.gov/gcos_wgsp/Timeseries/Data/nino3.long.data . These large-scale circulation patterns have been shown to affect the climate of China (or Asia) and will be used to explore the relationship between large-scale changes and the spatial characteristics of compound extremes.  2.2 Methodology In this study, a QDMSD method was developed and then used to statistically downscale Tmean  and precipitation over China. The detailed processes of the QDMSD method were elaborated in the Supplementary Material  (Text S1). The QDMSD method improves the simulation performance of precipitation relative to the BCSD model. The detailed comparisons could be found in the Supplementary Material  (Table S1 ). The QDMSD could effectively maintain the variability of precipitation. The QDMSD has better performance than BCSD in simulating precipitation. Based on previous research (Peng et al., 2023; Ren et al., 2023 ), selecting the period from 1985 to 1999 as the training period is sufficient to train the QDMSD method. Choosing the period from 2000 to 2014 as the validation period helps evaluate the ability of the QDMSD model. In this study, the period of 1985 to 1999 will be selected as the training period. The period of 2000 to 2014 will be selected as the evaluation period. The raw GCMs (in the evaluation period) were downscaled by reanalysis datasets (ERA5 and CPC; in the training period) and then downscaled GCMs were validated to reanalysis datasets in the evaluation period. The evaluation metrics of R 2 , root mean square error (RMSE) and Pearson’s r  are used to assess the performance of QDMSD downscaling. The evaluation results represented by the Taylor diagram (Taylor, 2001 ) show that QDMSD-downscaled GCMs could reproduce Tmean  and precipitation at a seasonal scale (Figure S1 ). Therefore, the QDMSD-downscaled GCMs (including Tmean  and precipitation) are able to maintain the interannual variability of ERA5 reanalysis (Figure S2 ). Since the high-temperature and precipitation extremes mainly occur from June to August in China (Zhou & Liu, 2018 ). Therefore, the frequencies of CDWW and CDDW in summer (June − August, JJA) are investigated. Specifically, following previous research (Beniston, 2009; Hao et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2019; Zhou & Liu, 2018 ), the 75th  and 25th  quantiles were calculated as daily precipitation thresholds in JJA. As for temperature, the 75th  quantile was computed as a daily temperature threshold because the warm extremes were mainly concerned in summer. By the employment of the peak-over-threshold method (Ren et al., 2023 ), the frequencies of CDWW and CDDW were tracked based on gridded daily Tmean  and precipitation. Consequently, the CDWW occurred when strong precipitation events coincided with warm extremes. Similarly, the CDDW occurred when dry events coincided with warm extremes. To conveniently investigate mechanisms of CDWW and CDDW events in the historical period over China, the empirical orthogonal function (EOF ) analysis was applied to extract the leading modes and their corresponding principal component (PC ) in the historical period. The results obtained from EOF  analysis follow the North’s rule (North et al., 1982 ). In addition, other methods include linear correlation and linear regression. The detailed flowchart of this study is shown in Fig. 1  .   3 Temporal and spatial characteristics of CDDW and CDWW events during the historical period In this research, the extremes of temperature and precipitation were independently identified by using individual metrics, and the co-occurrence of two extreme events is identified as a compound extreme event. The frequencies of two compound extremes in the period of 1981 to 2020 are shown in Fig. 2  . The compound extreme wet-warm (CDWW) events are widely distributed in Northeast China and the Tibetan Plateau area in summer (June to August, JJA), as shown in Fig. 2 (a). The compound extreme dry-warm (CDDW) events are widely distributed in northwestern and southeastern China in JJA, as shown in Fig. 2 (b), which is consistent with previous research results (Wu et al., 2019 ). On the contrary, the frequencies of CDDW are lower in Northeast China and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau region. Previous studies have indicated that the correlation between temperature and precipitation will influence the spatial extent of summertime compound extremes (Wu et al., 2019; Zhou & Liu, 2018 ). For instance, if a negative correlation exists between precipitation and temperature, the projected CDDW will be predominant (Zhou & Liu, 2018 ). Conversely, if there is a positive correlation between precipitation and temperature, the likelihood of CDWW is projected to be higher (Zhou & Liu, 2018 ). Therefore, the occurrence of CDDW in southern and northwestern China is attributed to a significantly negative correlation between precipitation and temperature, while the higher occurrence of CDWW in Northeast China and the Qinghai-Tibet region is due to a positive correlation between precipitation and temperature. In addition, we also investigated the annual frequency of the historical CDWW and CDDW in JJA, as shown in Fig. 2 (c). We found that the increasing ratio of CDWW was 0.26 day/decade. The increasing rate of CDDW was 0.69 day/decade in the historical period. The first modes of CDWW and CDDW have been extracted by EOF  in JJA, as shown in Fig. 3  . According to North's test (North et al., 1982 ), the two modes are clearly distinguishable. The EOF 1 CDWW   is distributed in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and the northeastern region of China, explaining 37 % of the total variance (Fig. 3 a). It indicated that the variations of CDWW are mainly located in these regions. The pattern of EOF 1 CDWW   is similar to the climatology of CDWW (Fig. 2 a). The EOF 1 CDWW   illustrates the CDWW events in Qinghai-Tibet Plateau were mainly affected by the combined influence of the westerlies and the Asian summer monsoon (Li & Ma, 2018; Qian et al., 2009; You et al., 2021 ). Previous studies have also shown that the transition from warm-dry to warm-wet patterns in northwest China occurred after the 1980s (Shi et al., 2003; Zhu et al., 2019 ). This change has been accompanied by precipitation, glacier melting, and increased vegetation (Shi et al., 2003; Zhu et al., 2019 ). The moisture is transported by westerly in northwestern China. It has caused moisture convergence and increased rainfall. In addition, the westerlies anomalies play a critical part in contributing to the formation of summer floods in eastern China (Qian et al., 2009 ). A stronger summer monsoon can bring southerly flow to northern and northeastern China, while a weaker summer monsoon prevails in the Yangtze River Basin (Qian et al., 2009 ). The southerly flow enhances moisture convergence and facilitates to form precipitation in these areas. Therefore, these factors will contribute to the frequent precipitation extremes and CDWW events in northern, northeastern and eastern China. The corresponding PC 1 CDWW   shows weaker interannual oscillations in the period from 1981 to 2001 (Fig. 3 c), but exhibits stronger interannual variability in the period from 2001 to 2020. The gaps between the two adjacent peaks are approximately 3 to 5 years. The EOF 1 CDDW   is mainly located in northwest China (Fig. 3 b), explaining 32 % of the total variance. It illustrates that the changes of CDDW are mainly distributed in the northwestern China. The pattern of EOF 1 CDDW   is similar to the climatology of CDDW (Fig. 2 a). The possible reason is that northwest China is far from the ocean, and the warm-humid air flows are hard to reach this region. It will lead to a lack of precipitation. Additionally, the northwest China is relatively arid and lacks precipitation due to the westerlies (You et al., 2021 ). On the other hand, the topography in northwest China blocks the flow of moisture to the central region, resulting in the formation of huge desert basins (Li & Ma, 2018 ). These factors have led to frequent drought events. Therefore, it favors the occurrence of CDDW in the northwestern China. The corresponding PC 1 CDDW   shows stronger interannual variability in the period from 1990 to 1995 and exhibits stronger interannual oscillations in the period from 2001 to 2020. The gaps between the two adjacent peaks are also 3 to 5 years. Therefore, it suggests that CDDW and CDWW in the period from 2001 to 2020 are likely to be further influenced by large-scale patterns such as ENSO. The SST anomalies (SSTA) could be respectively obtained by subtracting the corresponding multi-year averaged SST from annual SST in two historical periods (i.e., 1981–2000 and 2001–2020). The SSTA is respectively regressed onto PC 1 s   in two historical periods for investigating the potential impacts of SSTA on the primary patterns of compound extremes, as shown in Fig. 4  . In the period of 1981 to 2000, the PC 1 CDWW   was negatively correlated with the SSTA over the northwestern Pacific, as shown in Fig. 4 (a). Therefore, the SSTA may be a potential factor in the increment of CDWW in the period from 1981 to 2000. The PC 1 CDDW   is positively correlated to the SSTA in the period of 1981 to 2000 over the northwest Pacific, as depicted in Fig. 4 (c). It indicated that SSTA could influence the occurrence of CDDW from 1981 to 2000 through positive feedback at a significance level of 0.1. In the period of 2001 to 2020, the extents with strong feedback to SSTA exhibit an obvious decrease over the western Pacific, as shown in Fig. 4 (a) and 4(b). The PC 1 CDWW   is negatively correlated with SSTA at a significance level of 0.1, as shown in Fig. 4 (b). The PC 1 CDDW   is positively correlated with SSTA near 35 ˚N area, as shown in Fig. 4 (d). Therefore, the SSTA near the 35 °N area may play a role in modulating the two compound extreme events. Previous studies have found that warm SSTA associated with El Niño may have stronger intensity and longer duration after 2001–2020, and the strong warming of the Southwest Indian Ocean triggers a series of ocean-atmosphere interactions (Chen & Li, 2022 ). It will lead to stronger anomalous anticyclones over the Northwest Pacific (Chen & Li, 2022 ). Therefore, abnormal anticyclones will transport abundant water vapor to China and lead to an increase in precipitation. In addition, the atmosphere is usually more sensitive to SSTA according to the Clausius-Clapeyron relationship (Held & Soden, 2006; Hu et al., 2021; Seager et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2022 ). The saturation vapor pressure increases exponentially with increasing SST (Held & Soden, 2006; Hu et al., 2021; Seager et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2022 ). The increase in saturated vapor pressure enhances atmospheric moisture content (Breshears et al., 2013 ). It causes moisture convergence and strengthens the upward motion of warm-humid air flow over China (Wang et al., 2015 ), thereby facilitating the formation of clouds and precipitation from 2001 to 2020. Therefore, these factors will favor the occurrence of CDWW events. The interannual variations of PC 1 CDWW   would increase from 2001 to 2020 (Fig. 3 c). In contrast, the warming of SST related to El Niño was relatively weaker in the period of 1981 to 2000. It will result in weak climate interactions between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific, and therefore have few impacts on precipitation over China. Table 2   displays the relationships between the PC 1 s   (i.e., PC 1 CDWW   and PC 1 CDWW  ) and large-scale metrics (i.e., AMO and Niño 3) in two historical periods (i.e., 1981 to 2000 and 2001 to 2020). In the period of 1981 to 2000, the PC 1 CDWW   showed a positive correlation with the Niño 3 metrics. The PC 1 CDWW   showed a significantly negative correlation with AMO (Pearson’s r  = -0.45). In the period of 2001 to 2020, the PC 1 CDDW   showed a significantly negative correlation with Niño 3 (Pearson’s r  = -0.39). Moreover, the PC 1 CDWW   showed a positive correlation with the Niño 3 and a negative correlation with AMO. Therefore, it is necessary to investigate the historical modulation of the negative large-scale metrics (i.e., AMO and Niño 3) in ocean-atmospheric physical processes over China. Fig. 5   illustrates the correlation between SSTA and teleconnection metrics (i.e., AMO and Niño 3) in two periods. From 1981 to 2000, it was found that the SSTA had positive feedback to AMO. This relationship mainly occurred between 15 ˚S and 45 ˚N, as shown in Fig. 5 (a). From 2001 to 2020, the negatively correlated relationship between Niño 3 and SSTA was mainly distributed in the region of 15 ˚S to 45 ˚N and 130 ˚E to 160 ˚E. Therefore, the teleconnection metrics (i.e., AMO and Niño 3) could affect the spatial distributions of correlated areas over the West Pacific during different time periods. Based on these factors, the SSTA will influence compound extremes. Specifically, the SSTA exhibits a negative correlation with AMO in the period of 1981 to 2000, as shown in Fig. 5 (a). Meanwhile, PC 1 CDWW   shows a decreasing trend response to SSTA, as depicted in Fig. 4 (a). The Niño 3 may affect the variability of PC 1 CDDW   over China in the period from 2001 to 2020. The SSTA had negative feedback to Niño 3 over the western Pacific from 2001 to 2020 (Fig. 5 b). Additionally, PC 1 CDDW   displays a positive response to SSTA (Fig. 4 d). Therefore, the Niño 3 could be the driving factor of changes in PC 1 CDDW   in the period from 2001 to 2020.  4 Projections of CDDW and CDWW Fig. 6   shows the annual trends of CDWW and CDDW in the future period (2030–2099) under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. Overall, all projections showed increasing trends under two emission scenarios. It should be noted that the frequencies of compound extremes under the SSP2-4.5 are higher than those under the SSP5-8.5 before 2080. The frequency of CDWW under SSP5-8.5 exceeds that under SSP2-4.5 around 2080 (Fig. 6 a), while the frequency of CDDW under SSP5-8.5 exceeds that under SSP2-4.5 around 2070 (Fig. 6 b). During the period of 2030 to 2099, the growth ratio under SSP5-8.5 is greater than that under SSP2-4.5. This is because of the greater amount of greenhouse gas emissions from human activities under SSP5-8.5. It will lead to generally higher levels of projected temperature and precipitation under SSP5-8.5, leading to an increase in the frequencies of extreme high-temperature events and extreme precipitation events. Therefore, the increasing rate of compound extremes under SSP5-8.5 is higher than that under SSP2-4.5. Fig. 7   shows the spatial distributions of CDWW and CDDW under two scenarios (i.e., SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5) in the future period (2030–2099). It is evident that the frequency of CDDW is higher in northwestern and southwestern China under both scenarios (Fig. 7 a and 7c), indicating that this region is vulnerable to extreme hot and drought disasters. In northeastern China and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, the frequency of CDWW is higher under both scenarios (Fig. 7 b and 7d), indicating that northeastern China is susceptible to disasters caused by high temperatures and floods. Additionally, the CDWW events would be frequent on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau in the future period whether under SSP2-4.5 or SSP5-8.5. It indicates that this region is prone to disasters caused by extreme hot and wet conditions.  5 Analysis of potential mechanism Fig. 8   displays the regression patterns of winds and geopotential height (GHT) onto compound extremes under SSP2-4.5 at two pressure levels (i.e., 500 hPa and 850 hPa). The future period is divided into two 35-year periods: 2030–2064 (2050s) and 2065–2099 (2080s). At 500 hPa, the positive GHT anomalies accompanied by an anticyclone anomaly will weaken from the 2050s to 2080s (Fig. 8 b). The changes in circulation will strengthen the moisture convergence (Ma & Xie, 2013; Seager et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2018 ). It will promote the rising motion of warm-humid air from 2050s to 2080s (Tan et al., 2017 ). Therefore, the more frequent precipitation extremes will occur in extratropical regions (Betts, 1998; He, 2015; Held & Soden, 2006; Wang et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2018 ). It will eventually favor the formation of precipitation and CDWW in Northeast China, North China, and East China. Similarly, the weakening of high-pressure systems will elevate warm-humid airflow over central and northern China. These changes in circulation could affect moisture convergence. It will potentially cause precipitation extremes and frequent CDWW events. During the 2050s to the 2080s, a weakened Asian low-pressure system over India will weaken southerly winds (Fig. 8 c and 8d). It will reduce warm-humid airflow in the Qinghai Tibet Plateau region and lead to decreased precipitation. The reduction in southern Tibet (Fig. 7 b) may be a response to this situation. At 850 hPa, two positive GHT anomalies occur over Siberia and the Aleutians (Fig. 8 e and 8g), while negative anomalies could be found in the western Pacific near 20 °N (Fig. 8 e and 8g). Positive GHT anomalies over Siberia and the Aleutians are projected to weaken from the 2050s to the 2080s (Fig. 8 f and 8h). The negative GHT anomalies will also weaken over the western Pacific near 20 °N (Fig. 8 e and 8f). Weakening positive GHT anomalies will elevate warm-humid air in Northeast, East, and North China (Tan et al., 2017 ). It will promote CDWW events, resulting in more frequent precipitation extremes. Additionally, northward-moving warm-humid airflow encounters fewer dry-cold air masses (Fig. 8 h). It is difficult to form precipitation further favoring CDDW events in northwest and central China (Li et al., 2022 ). Fig. 9   presents the regression of winds and GHT onto compound extremes in two future periods under SSP5-8.5. At 500 hPa, the anticyclonic and positive GHT anomalies will be greater than that under the SSP2-4.5 scenario (Fig. 9 c). These variations in circulation will strengthen the moisture divergence. It will hinder the rising motion of warm-humid airflow in northern and eastern China (Tan et al., 2017 ). Consequently, it is difficult to form precipitation in these regions, and the distribution of CDDW is more widespread (Fig. 7 c). Similarly, the weakening of the positive GHT anomalies will enhance the rise of warm-humid airflow in central China. It may lead to precipitation and frequent CDWW events. At 850 hPa, the two positive GHT anomalies will occur in Siberia and the Aleutians (Fig. 9 e and 9g), while negative GHT anomalies could be found in the western Pacific near the 20 °N area (Fig. 9 e and 9g). The positive GHT anomalies over Siberia and the Aleutians would be projected to weaken from the 2050s to the 2080s (Fig. 9 f and 9h). The negative GHT anomalies will weaken at low latitudes (Fig. 9 f and 9h). The weakened positive GHT anomalies will promote the rising motion of warm-humid air (Wang et al., 2015 ). It will promote precipitation and CDWW events in northeastern, eastern and northern China. Due to the limited weakening of the negative GHT anomalies, the water vapor could be transported from the Bay of Bengal (Fig. 9 h). It will lead to more precipitation in southern China in the future, thereby resulting in the frequent occurrence of CDWW events in southern China. Fig. 10   presents the Pearson correlation coefficients between standardized time series of compound extremes and SST. A significant correlation could be found between compound extremes and SST in the Northwest Pacific at a significance level of 0.01. Particularly, a significantly positive correlation is found in the area near 20 ˚N. This suggests that variations in SST around 20 ˚N latitude may have a substantial impact on compound extremes. Under the SSP2-4.5 scenario, the SST with a significant positive correlation in affecting CDWW exhibits a noticeable decrease from the 2050s to 2080s (Fig. 10 a and 10b). Similarly, a significant positive correlation between CDDW and SST could be found in the Northwest Pacific (Fig. 10 c and 10d). The SST anomalies associated with La Niña tended to expand near 20 ˚N area in the western Pacific from the 2050s to the 2080s, as shown in Fig. 10 (d). This suggests strong positive feedback between CDDW and La Niña-pattern SST in the 2080s. Consequently, the compound extremes have closer relationships with SST in the Northwest Pacific. Additionally, both compound extremes exhibit stronger negative feedback to the SST in the part of the Indian Ocean (70 ˚E to 130 ˚E) in the 2080s (Fig. 10 b and 10d). It indicates that the SST in the Indian Ocean has a negative impact on the compound extremes over China. Under the SSP5-8.5 scenario, the SST with a significantly positive correlation in governing compound extremes exhibits a more considerable expansion relative to that under SSP2-4.5 (Fig. 10 e to 10h). It indicates a closer relationship between compound extremes and SST in the Northwest Pacific under SSP5-8.5. Additionally, during the 2080s, the negative correlation is insignificant between compound extremes and SST during the 2080s in areas of 70 ˚E to 130 ˚E (Fig. 10 f and 10h). This could be attributed to greater temporal and spatial uncertainty under the higher emission scenario. Fig. 11   shows the regression at 850 hpa of GHT and winds onto the area-averaged SSTA (SSTAAA  ) for the region (−10 °N to 30 °N and 45 °E to 75 °E) in the Indian Ocean under two SSP scenarios. The GHT and winds will have responses to SSTAAA   in the western Pacific under SSP2-4.5, with an anticyclonic anomaly and positive SSTA near 15 °N at a significance level of 0.1 (Fig. 11 a). This anticyclonic anomaly will indirectly result in a southwest wind anomaly over South China. Therefore, the warm-humid airflow could be brought to Southern China. The negative GHT would exist with cyclonic anomalies over the Aleutian Islands under both scenarios, as shown in Fig. 11 (a) and Fig. 11 (b). Additionally, the SSTAAA   lead to a cyclonic anomalies with a negative GHT over Siberia, causing northerly winds anomalies over Northeast China and North China Plains (Fig. 11 a). Accordingly, these factors will favor the invasion of cold air from high latitudes into inland China. The southward-moving cold air encounters the northward-moving airflow with warm-humid vapor over the Yangtze River Basin. These two situations will lead to precipitation, as shown in Fig. 11 (a). Therefore, it will favor the occurrence of CDWW in Central China. Furthermore, it will prevail westerly winds from low to high latitudes in Xinjiang and Tibet of China, as shown in Fig. 11 (a). This hinders precipitation in the Turpan Basin and therefore favors the occurrence of CDDW. However, precipitation is likely to increase due to the temperature decrease caused by the ascent of warm-moist air masses over the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. And it will promote the CDWW in some regions of the plateau, as shown in Fig. 11 (a). Under the SSP5-8.5 scenario, the anticyclonic anomalies would be weakened by the modulation of SSTAAA   over the low-latitude northwest Pacific. The anticyclonic anomalies will be closer to China's southeastern coast, as shown in Fig. 11 (b). Consequently, the southwest winds will be weakened over South China. Moreover, the cyclonic anomalies modulated by the SSTAAA   will be weakened over Siberia. The SSTAAA   will be an influencing factor for the weakening cyclonic anomalies over the Aleutian Islands, as shown in Fig. 11 (b). These factors are not conducive to the southward movement of cold air from high latitudes. However, these factors will favor the northward shift of southwestern wind anomalies over South China. This situation will reduce the occurrence of CDWW in the Yangtze River Basin, promoting the future expansion of CDDW in China at a large scale under SSP5-8.5. In conclusion, the SSTAAA   has a modulating effect on anticyclonic anomalies over the low-latitude western Pacific, cyclonic anomalies over the Aleutians, and cyclonic anomalies over Siberia. Additionally, the westerly wind anomalies will also be regulated by the SSTAAA   over Xinjiang and Tibet provinces in China. And it will induce the increasing temperature and precipitation in those regions. Under the SSP5-8.5 scenario, the anticyclonic anomalies over the Pacific will weaken and move westward due to the modulation from SSTAAA  . Furthermore, the SSTAAA   leads to a weakening of cyclonic anomalies over Siberia and the Aleutian Islands. Thus, the SSTAAA   will modulate CDWW in the future by regulating circulation anomalies at high latitudes. Consequently, these factors ultimately lead to a reduction in CDWW and an increase in CDDW within China under SSP5-8.5.  6 Conclusions In this study, the projected changes in summertime compound extremes (i.e., CDDW and CDWW) were investigated by the developed QDMSD model and their underlying mechanisms were explored in China. The performance of QDMSD was first evaluated by reanalysis datasets (i.e., CPC and ERA5) in simulating seasonal and monthly climate variables (e.g., precipitation and mean temperature) for the period of 2000 to 2014. The QDMSD was also compared to traditional BCSD in reproducing monthly mean temperature (Tmean ) and precipitation. Moreover, the dominant modes of compound extremes were extracted and used to investigate their relationships with potential climate factors (e.g., teleconnection metrics and SSTA). Subsequently, the summertime characteristics of CDWW and CDDW were analyzed based on the QDMSD-downscaled results in two future periods (e.g., 2030–2064 and 2065–2090). It aims to investigate how compound extremes respond to global warming under different anthropogenic factors. Furthermore, the underlying mechanisms governing the projected changes in compound extremes were discussed through correlation and regression analysis. The validated results indicated that the simulations obtained from QDMSD could reproduce the Tmean  and precipitation over China relative to ERA5 reanalysis. However, we found that the performance in simulating precipitation and Tmean  in summer and winter was worse than that in spring and autumn. Additionally, the QDMSD could capture the peaks of Tmean  and precipitation in June. Furthermore, the QDMSD could reproduce the monthly Tmean  and precipitation relative to the traditional BCSD model. In particular, the QDMSD had better performance in reproducing precipitation. The projected changes in compound extremes implied that CDWW and CDDW will keep increasing in the future whether under SSP2-4.5 or SSP5-8.5. In terms of the spatial distribution, the projected CDDW would increase from northeast to southwest. The projected CDWW would increase from south to north. Therefore, more attention should be paid to preventing compound extreme warm and wet disasters in northern China. Meanwhile, the policy-makers should focus on the impact of compound warm and drought extremes. The driving factors of projected changes in compound extremes were investigated in the historical period (1981–2020). The results indicate that the patterns of AMO and Niño 3 alternately modulated SSTA and thereby resulted in the changes in compound extremes over China during the historical period. In the period of 1981 to 2000, the AMO triggered positive SSTA in the Northwest Pacific. The AMO also triggered abnormal circulation and descent over the North Pacific in the summer (Lin et al., 2023 ). These circulation changes can alter regional wind patterns, leading to increased subsidence and reduced upward motion (Svendsen et al., 2002 ). These factors have enhanced abnormal moisture divergence over China (Gimeno et al., 2016 ), leading to a decrease in precipitation and frequent occurrence of drought extremes. Therefore, the CDDW events occurred frequently. In the period from 2001 to 2020, the Niño 3 promoted a significantly negative SSTA in the Northwest Pacific. Therefore, the SSTA would favor the CDWW in China through a series of ocean-atmosphere interactions (Chen & Li, 2022 ). The mechanisms governing projected changes in compound extremes were analyzed in two future periods under two SSPs through an investigation of climate factors (e.g., GHT, winds and SST). The anticyclonic and positive GHT anomalies over Siberia will occur under the SSP2-4.5 scenario. The intensity of negative GHT and cyclonic anomalies would be weakened. These factors will facilitate the moisture divergence (Tan et al., 2017 ). Additionally, the rising motion of warm-humid air would be hindered in northwestern China. The precipitation might be difficult to form and the drought extremes will occur frequently. Therefore, it will lead to a widespread distribution of CDDW in the future. Under the SSP5-8.5 scenario, the negative GHT anomalies could occur in the Northwest Pacific near the 20 ˚N area because of the warming SST. Additionally, the projected positive GHT anomalies will weaken over Siberia. These factors may strengthen the moisture convergence and upward motion of warm-humid air. Therefore, it will favor the occurrence of precipitation and flood extremes. Finally, it promotes the occurrence of CDWW in northeastern, eastern, and northern China. The QDMSD is a statistical-based approach. It does not address the potential local details or variability in climate response, such as the potential changes in temperature or precipitation trends with elevation (Schnorbus et al., 2014 ). Furthermore, QDMSD is similar to the BCSD method in computational costs. The computation of QDMSD strictly relies on the grid scale. The computational cost of QDMSD will also exponentially increase with the spatial resolution of the dataset, similar to the BCSD (Shen et al., 2021 ). Future research can be focused on these two aspects to reduce the error of precipitation simulation over China by introducing better statistical methods. In addition, the summer compound extreme events may also be modulated by other climate factors (e.g., relative humidity, relative vorticity, etc.) in China. Future research can discuss the response of compound extreme events to these climate factors.
1 Introduction Soil water is a key variable that connects climate, vegetation, and hydrological processes and is also an important factor in regulating the land water cycle and ecosystems (Amundson et al., 2015; McColl et al., 2017; Vereecken et al., 2022 ). Under the trend of climate change, increasingly frequent global droughts may lead to soil water depletion, which threatens to limit vegetation growth (Schwalm et al., 2017; Reich et al., 2018; Satoh et al., 2022; Qing et al., 2022 ). Due to factors such as terrain, climate, soil, and vegetation, the soil moisture content (SMC) exhibits high spatial and temporal variability. In particular, for hillslopes, predicting the spatial distribution pattern of SMCs is challenging, hindering the restoration of mountain vegetation and the ecological balance. Therefore, understanding the spatiotemporal dynamics of soil hydrology on hillslopes remains an important prerequisite for simulating hydrological processes on hillslopes. Generally, SMC is controlled by mainly static factors (land use, terrain, and soil properties) and dynamic factors (meteorological conditions and vegetation growth) (Penna et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2016; Dymond et al., 2021 ). A mountain slope is a fundamental hydrological unit of a watershed and is also the area with the greatest spatial heterogeneity of soil water. In terms of static factors, the soil water on hillslopes is strongly controlled by soil properties and steep terrain (Zhang et al., 2022 ). Soil physical and hydraulic properties change with slope position (Morbidelli et al., 2018 ), leading to an increase in SMC in the downhill direction under the influence of gravity (Canton et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2019; de Queiroz et al., 2020; Dymond et al., 2021 ). In terms of dynamic factors, SMC exhibits significant seasonal variations with vegetation growth, root development, and evapotranspiration rate (Tokumoto et al., 2014; Dymond et al., 2021 ). Vegetation affects the dynamic changes in SMC by altering the processes of rainfall interception, infiltration, water absorption, and evapotranspiration. Moreover, plants reduce SMC during the growing season, and a low SMC limits evapotranspiration (Liu et al., 2023 ). Therefore, land-use types and vegetation types have significant impacts on soil hydrological processes (Zhao et al., 2017; Jensen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019, 2022; Zhou et al., 2022 ). Vachaud et al. (1985)  proposed the theoretical concept of temporal stability, which is defined as “the time-invariant association between spatial location and classical statistical parameters of a given soil property”, which means that SMC dynamics are synchronized and similar in spatial location. Therefore, within a certain range, SMC may exhibit both spatial variability and temporal stability. Since then, temporal stability analysis has been widely applied to SMC assessments in different climate zones and land-use types. By reviewing and summarizing relevant literature in recent years, it has been found that the temporal stability of SMCs is influenced by various factors, such as terrain attributes, soil properties, vegetation characteristics, climate conditions, and regional scales (Duan et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017,2019; Liu et al., 2017; He et al., 2019 ; Lee et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2023 ). In general, SMC exhibits temporal stability under different terrain conditions and vegetation types. Due to its relatively stable retention effect, deep SMC has stronger temporal stability than shallow SMC (Duan et al., 2017; He et al., 2019; Dymond et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2023 ). However, although the temporal stability of SMC has received widespread attention and recognition, there are still some controversial issues that need to be clarified. For example, Wang et al., (2016b)  observed SMCs on hillslopes and reported that the temporal stability during wet periods was greater than that during dry periods. Liu et al. (2022)  argued that the temporal stability in the dry season was greater than that in the rainy season. The above two differences may be related to differences in climatic regions and changes in dry-wet conditions. In addition, phenology affects the temporal stability of SMC, and an increase in vegetation coverage during the growing season often weakens temporal stability (Penna et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2015 ). Moreover, rainfall after long-term drought or drought after continuous rainfall may lead to temporal instability of SMC (Dari et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2020 ). Therefore, when the interaction of control factors changes, the spatiotemporal pattern of SMC may become unstable. However, currently, the occurrence frequency and potential conditions of temporal instability are unclear. Traditional linear correlation analysis (Spearman rank correlation analysis and Pearson correlation analysis) can determine whether SMC has temporal stability (Li et al., 2017 ) and this analysis has been widely used in the identification of overall similarity at the measurement scale. However, such analysis cannot reveal the scale correlation between soil water and control factors. At different scales, the factors controlling soil water are different and cannot be identified by traditional correlation analysis (Biswas and Si, 2011 ; Li et al. 2023). The influence of the sampling period and scale on the temporal stability and similarity of SMCs is highly important, and a factor may exhibit inconsistent correlations at different scales. The wavelet coherence based on the wavelet transform can assess the correlation between two series at different locations or times, distinguish the variability in data in temporal or spatial sequences, and thus determine the spatiotemporal similarity of SMCs at different scales (Biswas and Si, 2011 ). This approach even has reference value for understanding the mechanisms of temporal instability. Therefore, it is widely used to study the similarity of SMC patterns at different scales based on soil properties, terrain location, climate and meteorology, vegetation type, and soil profile depth (Li et al., 2017, 2019; Liu et al., 2017; Lee and Kim, 2019; Li et al., 2023a; Liu et al., 2023 ). Unlike in other regions, karst slopes have thin soil layers, poor soil continuity, and bedrock with high water permeability (Hartmann et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2017 ). These special surface environmental characteristics lead to poor soil hydrological regulation and storage functions, frequent droughts, and even the formation of rocky desertification landscapes with exposed bedrock. Therefore, most plants growing on karst slopes are drought-resistant shallow-rooted plants (Cai et al., 2023 ). By reviewing the literature in the field of SMC in karst slopes, these studies have evaluated the effects of seasons, vegetation types, terrain, and microgeomorphic conditions on the distribution patterns and spatial heterogeneity of SMC (Tokumotoet al., 2014; Canton et al., 2016 ; Wang et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016, 2019 ; Zhao et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2022 ) and found that soil water exhibits rapid dry-wet alternations and high heterogeneity. To date, the spatiotemporal similarity of SMCs among different land-use types and profile depths in karst depressions has been demonstrated (Li et al., 2017 , 2019). It is nearly indisputable that deep soil water has temporal stability, and spatial variability mainly occurs in shallow soil (Potts et al., 2010; Traff et al., 2015 ). In the complex underlying environment of karst areas, especially on hillslopes, the spatial distribution patterns and dynamic changes in shallow SMCs are particularly complex, making it difficult to predict temporal and spatial patterns and dynamic processes. In summary, previous reports have lacked observations of SMC dynamics and evaluations of spatiotemporal similarity in shallow soil environments on slopes, which may have limited our true understanding of soil hydrological processes on karst slopes and in shallow soil landscapes in other regions. In addition, whether there is spatiotemporal similarity in shallow SMCs under different vegetation types and slope positions remains an unanswered question. The answer to this question is not only an important supplement to the knowledge system of soil hydrology on hillslopes but also highly important for improving the prediction accuracy of soil hydrological processes in karst areas and vegetation restoration. To address this knowledge gap, we used control experiments to observe and evaluate shallow SMC dynamics and their spatiotemporal similarities under different vegetation types on karst slopes. The main aims of this study were to (1) analyse the dynamic characteristics of shallow SMCs, (2) determine whether there is spatiotemporal similarity in shallow SMCs under different vegetation types and slope positions, and (3) reveal the effects of vegetation type, slope position, and meteorological conditions on shallow SMCs.  2 Methods 2.1 Study area We conducted soil hydrological observations at the Guanling Karst Ecosystem Observation and Research Station, Guizhou Province, Southwest China. (Fig. 1  ). This area features typical karst landforms, such as plateau gorges, which are dominated by a mid-subtropical climate. The lithology is Middle Triassic dolomitic limestone, and the soil is classified as calcareous soil or yellow soil. Due to extensive human destruction and agricultural activities throughout history, hillslopes have suffered severe soil erosion, resulting in a fragile ecological environment with severe surface water scarcity and thin soil. In addition, due to long-term water erosion and karstification, microgeomorphological features, such as karrens, fissures and karst stony teeth, are widely distributed. Since 1996, natural restoration measures for returning farmland to forests have been implemented in the area. At present, the land-use types are mainly farmland, abandoned land and forestland, which are mainly planted with drought-tolerant economic crops (Li et al., 2022 ).  2.2 Experimental setting and data collection We selected a hillside as the observation site in the study area in 2016, with an average slope of 15°. To avoid interference from other factors, three experimental plots for slope hydrological observation with a length of 12 m and a width of 3 m were constructed on the slope using cement and bricks (Fig. 1 ). Based on the main land-use and vegetation types in the study area, two experimental plots were planted with peanut (PN) and Zanthoxylum bungeanum  (ZB) and cultivated for 3 years; the other plot did not contain any vegetation and served as a control plot for the abandoned land (AL). The average soil thickness in the three plots was 25 ± 7 cm, and the average pH was 7.80 ± 0.06. Table 1   shows the soil properties of the three plots. In 2019, we installed 5 soil moisture sensors (ECH2 O-5TE, Meter Group, Inc., USA) at a distance of 2 m from the upper slope to the bottom slope of each plot at a soil depth of 20 cm. The soil volume moisture content and soil temperature (ST) were recorded on a data logger (EM50, Meter Group, Inc., USA) every 30 min. The bottom slope to the upper slope were lined with Sensors 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 (Fig. 1 ). During the observation period, we avoided tillage and irrigation. In addition, two meteorological stations (ATMOS, Meter Group, Inc., USA), four soil evaporation systems (DJ-300, Dianjiang Group, Inc., CHN) and a cosmic-ray soil moisture observing system (CRS-1000B, Hydroinnova Group, Inc., USA) were established near the three experimental plots; these systems also synchronized the recording of meteorological and hydrological data at 30 min intervals. All the data were collected from June 9, 2019, to November 9, 2021 (1250 days), with 60,000 measurements taken by each sensor.  2.3 Data analyses 2.3.1 Wavelet coherence analysis The wavelet coherence analysis localizes the correlation coefficients of two time series in the time and frequency domains. Wavelet coherence can identify the similarity of spatial patterns between two spatial series. In this study, the wavelet coherence of two time series is defined as follows (Torrence and Compo, 1998; Grinsted et al., 2004 ):(1) Coherence = S ( s  - 1   W n  XY   ( s )  )    2  S ( s  - 1   W n  X  ( s )     2  )  · S ( s  - 1   W n  Y  ( s )     2  )        where X  and Y  are two time series, W n  XY   ( s )     is the interactive wavelet power of the time series X  and Y , W n  X  ( s )     and W n  Y  ( s )     are wavelet transforms of the time series X  and Y,  respectively, and S  is a smoothing operator. The wavelet coherence value is 0–1, which represents the local information of the linear relationship between two processes. A detailed introduction to the theory and application of wavelet coherency can be found in previous studies (Si and Zeleke, 2005; Biswas and Si, 2011; Li et al., 2017, 2019; Liu et al., 2017 ). In this study, we use the Morlet wavelet transform (ω = 6) and wavelet coherence toolbox provided by Grinsted et al. (2004) , and the code is available at http://noc.ac.uk/using-science/crosswavelet-wavelet-coherence . In the significance testing for wavelet coherency, the significance of the wavelet power spectrum was tested at the 95 % level using the red noise of the soil moisture as the background spectrum.  2.3.2 Statistical analysis In this study, one-way analysis of variance was used to examine the significant differences in SMC and ST among the different plots and slope positions. Before analysis, the distribution normality and homogeneity of the variance in all the data were checked. IMB SPSS Statistics 22 (IBM, Inc., USA) was used to analyse the mean, standard deviation, and coefficient of variation (CV, which measures the variability of a series of numbers and is a normalized measure of the degree of dispersion of a probability distribution, defined as the ratio of standard deviation to the mean) of parameters, and one-way analysis of variance and a Spearman rank correlation test were performed. The figures were drawn with Origin 2021 (OriginLab, Inc., USA). The wavelet coherence analysis was implemented with MATLAB R2016a (MathWorks, Inc., USA).    3 Results 3.1 Meteorological and hydrological statistics During the observation period, the total precipitation was 3282.9 mm, and the rainy season accounted for 79.0 % of the annual rainfall (Table S1 ). The average air temperature, relative humidity, atmospheric pressure and photosynthetically active radiation were 21.2 ℃, 73.8 %, 92.9 kPa and 235.8 μmol m−2  s−1 , respectively. Rainfall events mainly occurred between May and October, and the atmospheric pressure pattern was greater in the dry season and lower in the rainy season, which was opposite to the trend of air temperature and photosynthetically active radiation (Fig. 2  ); the average cosmic-ray SMC was 22.4 %. The trend of the SMC variations corresponded to that of precipitation (Fig. 2 ). The daily average soil evaporation was 2.1 mm, which was slightly lower than the daily average rainfall. Overall, the soil evaporation during the rainy season was greater than that during the dry season.  3.2 Temporal-spatial dynamics of soil moisture and soil temperature During the observation period, the average SMCs in the three plots were ranked as follows: ZB (25.8 %) > PN (23.1 %) > AL (21.4 %). Similarly, the average STs were ranked as follows: AL (21.4 °C) > PN (21.3 °C) > ZB (20.9 °C). As shown in Fig. 3  , the SMC exhibited significant differences (p < 0.01) among the different slope positions in the three plots. The average SMC of the five slope positions in PN was ranked as follows: PN4 (26.8 %) > PN2 (24.0 %) > PN8 (22.7 %) > PN10 (21.8 %) > PN6 (20.1 %), with a CV of 10.1 ∼ 17.9 %; ZB was ranked as ZB2 (28.9 %) > ZB4 (27.3 %) > ZB10 (25.9 %) > ZB8 (25.1 %) > ZB6 (22.6 %), with a CV range of 8.5 ∼ 13.6 %; and AL was ranked as AL2 (24.7 %) > AL6 (24.0 %) > AL4 (22.6 %) > AL8 (21.9 %) > AL10 (18.1 %), with a CV range of 11.3 ∼ 21.8 %. Among the three plots, the CV of SMC in the AL treatment was the highest, while that in the ZB treatment was the smallest. The middle and upper parts of the slopes (6 ∼ 10 m) were the areas where soil water variations were most common. Compared with that of the SMC, the variation amplitude of the ST at each slope position was relatively large, with a CV range of 25.1 ∼ 29.2 %. Moreover, there was no significant difference in ST among the different slope positions. Fig. 4   shows the spatiotemporal dynamics of the shallow SMC at the different slope positions in the three plots. The shallow soil water exhibited a significant alternation between dry and wet periods during the rainy and dry seasons, indicating the strong influence of the external environment (temperature and rainfall). Especially in the rainy season, the variation in shallow soil water on slopes alternated repeatedly with rainfall events and high temperatures. In most cases, the SMC at the bottom of the plots was significantly greater than that at the top, and the duration (retention) of the SMC was relatively long. In most cases, the shallow SMC on the bottom slope was significantly greater than that on the upper slope in the plots, and the duration (retention) was relatively long. However, there were differences in the spatiotemporal dynamics of the SMC among the three plots. By comparison, the dry-wet alternation phenomenon in the AL treatment was more significant than that in the other treatments, with a faster decrease in SMC after rainfall events. The SMC in the AL treatment was relatively low during the dry season, especially during the dry season at the upper position (Fig. 4 c). The variation in SMC in the ZB treatment was relatively stable (Fig. 4 b). Compared with that in the AL treatment, the shallow SMC at the bottom slope of the ZB treatment (2–4 m) was relatively high during the rainy season (Fig. 4 a). The dynamics of ST among the three plots were nearly consistent, and all slope positions tended to be greater in the rainy season and lower in the dry season (Fig. 4 d-f). To analyse the dynamic differences in SMC and ST among the different slope positions, we compared the dynamic coefficients of variation in SMC and ST among the five slope positions in each plot (Fig. 5  ). Overall, the CV of the ST was relatively high during the dry season but relatively low during the rainy season. The CV of SMC was mainly affected by the alternation of dry-wet conditions, with a smaller CV occurring during rainfall, while drought intervals could lead to an increase in the CV. Comparatively, the CV between SMC and ST was the highest among the different slope positions in the AL treatment.  3.3 Spatiotemporal similarity based on wavelet coherence Spearman's rank correlation analysis revealed a significant positive correlation (R  > 0.50, P  < 0.01) in the SMC among the different slope positions of the three plots (Fig. 6  ). The similarity in SMC dynamics among different slope positions indicates the temporal stability of the SMC. Based on the above results, to reveal the similarities and differences in the dynamics of shallow SMC on slopes, we used wavelet coherence to analyse the correlation of SMC between different slope positions in each plot in the time series (Fig. 7  ), as well as the correlation of SMC between different plots in the same slope position in the time series (Fig. 8  ). In most cases, SMC between different slope positions and between different plots had similarity in time series, with significant areas reaching over 75 %. By comparison, the farther the adjacent slope positions in the same plot were, the lower the significant area for SMC between two slope positions. The frequency distribution of coherence (Fig. S1 ) shows that frequencies of > 0.9 had the highest proportion, but the farther the adjacent slope positions in the same plot were, the lower their frequency. Comparatively, the significant area for SMCs between the different slope positions of PN was the highest, reaching more than 96.6 %. Similarly, the significant area for SMCs between the different slope positions of the ZB treatment was relatively low, and the significant area between ZB10 and ZB2 was only 76.1 % (Fig. 7 ). In addition, the significant areas for SMC between the same slope positions in the three plots were mainly found at 6 m on the middle slope, while the relatively small significant areas were mainly found at 2 m on the bottom slope (Fig. 8 ), and the coherent frequency of > 0.9 was relatively low (Fig. S2 ). According to Fig. 6 , except for atmospheric pressure, the other meteorological parameters exhibited a significant positive correlation (P  < 0.01) with the SMC at all slope positions. Moreover, there was a significant positive correlation (P  < 0.01) between SMC and ST (Fig. 9  ), indicating that meteorological factors had a controlling effect on SMC.
