1 Introduction The extensive applications of petroleum and organic products often lead to significant subsurface contamination of light non-aqueous phase liquids (LNAPLs), posing severe threats to ecological and human health (Cavelan et al., 2022; Mineo, 2023 ). Migration and distribution of LNAPLs is important to assess and regulate soil and groundwater pollution. Petroleum exploration areas mainly located in seasonal frozen regions (Iwakun et al., 2010; Li et al., 2021b; Muir and Galarneau, 2021 ). Freeze-thaw cycles (FTCs) can significantly alter soil conditions (Li et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021a; Potapowicz et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021b ), presenting significant challenges in predicting the migration and distribution of LNAPLs in FTCs (McDonald and Knox, 2014 ). In recent years, subsurface contamination of petroleum with dynamic four-phase systems (water-ice-air-oil) affected by FTCs in cold regions have been widely investigated (Ji et al., 2019; Lundberg et al., 2016; Wagner and Barker, 2019; Zhao et al., 2014 ). Laboratory quantitative identification of the distribution of LNAPLs is challenging to achieve rapid, undisturbed, and accurate analysis, particularly in conditions involving repeated and seasonal FTCs. Gamma ray method (Tuck et al., 1998 ), nuclear magnetic resonance (Chen et al., 2023; Dou et al., 2022 ), two-dimensional (2-D) slot glass beads model method (Niven and Singh, 2008 ), X-ray micro-computerized tomography method (Costanza-Robinson et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2011; Tidwell and Glass, 1994 ), fluorescein tracer method (Arenson and Sego, 2006 ), and electrical conductivity probes method (Kamon et al., 2003 ), have been widely used. The non-destructive light transmission visualization (LTV) technique has been proven to be more effective in determining the NAPL distribution using a 2-D flow chamber compared to traditional methods. This technique allows for the simultaneous analysis of NAPL distribution and migration under freeze–thaw conditions (Alazaiza et al., 2020; Alazaiza et al., 2017; Ye et al., 2009; Zheng et al., 2015 ). The concept of representative elementary volume (REV) can be used to analyze the unit scale of LNAPL saturation (Sn ). The REV is defined as the volume within which the characteristic parameters of the medium remain unchanged regardless of the observation scale (Costanza-Robinson et al., 2011; Singh, 2017; Müller et al., 2010 ). At the scales smaller than the REV, the material properties dramatically change with observation scales. In the classical Darcy hydrogeological and geological site sizes, which are larger than the REV, the material properties exhibit fluctuations (Kim and Mohanty, 2016; Teruel and Rizwan, 2010; Singh, 2017 ). On the REV scale, a porous medium can be considered a continuum (Brown et al., 2000; Kang et al., 2003 ). In-situ sampling and model simulation are crucial for identifying, evaluating, and remediating groundwater petroleum pollution. Determining the REV of Sn  (Sn -REV) is essential for accurate sampling and simulations. Currently, most studies on REV focus on dense non-aqueous phase liquids (DNAPLs) at normal temperature. However, few studies have been conducted on the REV of LNAPL saturation under freeze–thaw conditions. Research was conducted on the variations in the REV of DNAPL (tetrachloroethene, PCE) during its migration under normal temperature conditions, considering multiple factors. The natural factors affecting the medium, such as the reduced permeability, decreased porosity, and increased heterogeneity, can decrease the REV of DNAPL saturation (Wu et al., 2017a, 2017b, 2017c, 2020a, 2020b ). The environmental factors, such as the introduction of the surface activator and the increase in the background solute concentration (e.g., NaCl), also led to the decrease in the REV of DNAPL saturation (Wu et al., 2018, 2019 ). Additionally, the range of REV distribution and REV value is more extensive under a low water table than that under a higher water table (He et al., 2022 ). Moreover, the impacts of various factors on the REV of DNAPL saturation are interconnected. In low-permeability media, the ionic strength of the solute in the medium background contributed to a decreasing trend in terms of the mean REV of DNAPL saturation. Whereas in high-permeability conditions, the mean REV decreased by an insignificant amount (Wu et al., 2019 ). In addition, heterogeneity exhibited a more significant effect on the mean REV of DNAPL saturation than that of the background solute concentration. At low and high solute concentrations, the mean REV decreased by 13.5 % and 28.9 %, respectively, owing to heterogeneity (Wu et al., 2020b ). Therefore, changes in the medium structure, solute background, and ambient temperature can affect the REV of DNAPL saturation. However, does freeze–thaw affect the REV of LNAPL saturation (Sn -REV)? If the Sn -REV changes under FTCs and the analysis unit scale at normal temperature is still used in freeze–thaw conditions, the distribution of LNAPL will be erroneously associated with both micro- and macro-scales. This inaccuracy can lead to either an exaggerated or underestimated evaluation of LNAPL saturation, which may cause inaccurate assessments of LNAPL distribution. In addition, the comprehension and application of scale effects and simulation studies related to petroleum contamination are limited to normal temperature conditions, which fail to accurately capture the migration and distribution of petroleum contamination in seasonal frozen-ground regions. Therefore, the dynamic characteristics of the REV of Sn  (Sn -REV) and its influencing mechanism under freeze–thaw conditions are necessary to be studied. Based on the above considerations, this study aimed to conduct a 2-D directional freeze–thaw simulation experiment and adopt modified light transmission technology for the accurate identification of LNAPL. The objectives of this study are to (1) identify the dynamic variation mechanism of Sn -REV in the process of FTCs and (2) determine the empirical value interval of Sn -REV that is suitable for LNAPL migration and simulation in homogeneous sandy vadose zones under FTCs. This study provides a robust foundation for studying the migration of LNAPL in a four-phase system (water-ice-air-oil) during FTCs.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Experimental device The experimental device consisted of a temperature-controlled system (Fig. 1  b) and an LTV system (Fig. 1 a). The LTV system, consisting of a camera connected to a computer, a 2-D flow chamber, and a light source panel, was placed in a temperature-controlled cabinet that was able to control and adjust the ambient temperature. The 2-D flow chamber served as a site for unidirectional freeze–thaw and LNAPL migration. The top of the chamber was equipped with a removable thermostatic top plate, where the temperature was controlled by a refrigerated circulator (Fig. 1 b). And the bottom was linked to a CO2  tank and a Markov bottle filled with water. Eight temperature probes connected to a computer were placed along the side of the 2-D flow chamber. When the light was emitted from the light source panel, it traversed through the 2-D flow chamber and was captured by the camera to generate 2-D light intensity data. The data were converted into 2-D LNAPL saturation distribution data after being calculated using the improved LTV method (Wang et al., 2021a ). 2.1.1 2-D flow chamber The 2-D flow chamber (Fig. 1 a) was filled with a porous medium. Measuring 30 cm in width, 45 cm in height, and 2 cm in thickness, the interior space of the flow chamber was enclosed by glass panels at the front and back, steel plates at the sides and bottom, and a removable thermostatic plate at the top. It was uniformly filled with 20/40 mesh semitransparent silica sand (>99.8 %, SiO2 ), which was dried at 45℃ for 48 h after being washed repeatedly with distilled water until the light absorption coefficients of the cleaning solution remained consistent. A higher temperature or longer desiccating time can cause silica sand to discolor. The dodecane (C12 H26 , Sigma-Aldrich, USA) with low water solubility (3.7 µg/L in water), low volatility (boiling point: 214 − 216℃), and low freezing point (−12℃) (Niven and Singh, 2008 ) was selected as LNAPL. Organic soluble Oil-red-O dye (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) at a concentration of 0.1 g/L was used for staining to enhance the accuracy of the LTV method (Oostrom et al., 2007 ). The low enough dye (0.4 mg) ensured that it could not precipitate from LNAPL at low temperatures (the lowest is −10℃).  2.1.2 LTV system The LTV system (Fig. 1 a) was based on a 2-D flow chamber and consisted of a Canon EOS M2 digital camera (Canon, China) positioned in front of the flow chamber and a light source panel equipped with 48 LED lights (Panasonic, Japan) situated behind the flow chamber. Two shades were placed on the sides to ensure that only light passing through the flow chamber could be captured by the camera. When the LED lights were activated, the uniform light from the light source plate passed through the flow chamber, where it was transmitted and absorbed before being captured by the digital camera positioned 20 cm in front of the flow chamber. The camera recorded the RGB information for each pixel in the flow chamber, creating a 2-D image. The images had a resolution of 720 × 480 pixels, which resulted in a spatial resolution of 0.21 mm2  per pixel. All images were captured using two 10 nm bandpass filters with central wavelengths of 515 nm and 575 nm, which were mounted on 52 mm lenses (Nikon 18–55 mm f/3.5–5.6G). In our experiments, the 515 nm bandpass filter was used to quantify dyed dodecane, as the absorption measurements indicated its peak absorption near this wavelength. The high absorption coefficient of dyed dodecane at 575 nm, in contrast to the low absorption coefficient at 515 nm, enhanced the accuracy of the calculated LNAPL saturation. All images were taken with a fixed aperture of F-5.6 as well as an exposure time of 1/20 of a second.  2.1.3 Temperature control system The temperature control system (Fig. 1 b) consisted of a temperature-controlled cabinet (Xutemp, Inc., Hangzhou, China) and refrigerated circulator. The temperature-controlled cabinet, with an interior volume of 60 cm (width) × 60 cm (depth) × 70 cm (height), had a fast response time, enabling stable control of the temperature gradient (±0.5℃) within the interior space. A thermostatic top plate connected to a refrigerated circulator (Fig. 1 b) controls the porous media in the flow chamber for unidirectional (downward) freezing/thawing. Eight temperature probes (Fig. 1 a) were positioned along the side of the flow chamber to monitor temperature changes in the medium. In the initial experimental stage, both devices were set to room temperature (approximately 25℃). In the second stage, FTCs were carried. The temperature-controlled cabinet was set to −5℃, while the thermostatic top plate was set to −20℃ during the freezing periods. Conversely, during the thawing periods, the temperature-controlled cabinet was set to 5℃ and the thermostatic top plate was set to 20℃.   2.2 Methods 2.2.1 Experimental procedures Flow chambers offer the advantage of directly illustrating the migration of pollutants (Xie et al., 2018; Zaheer et al., 2017 ). The 2-D flow chamber was filled with dry silica sand every 2 cm. After each layer was filled, the top layer was stirred, and a new layer was filled and compacted. In this way, the layered structure of the porous media can be minimized. Subsequently, an initial image (Ia ) capturing the dry sand (air-saturated) state was recorded, followed by CO2  gas with the volume ten times as the pore volume blowing slowly through the flow chamber to remove air bubbles in the flow chamber (Niven and Singh, 2008 ). A peristaltic pump was used to saturate the porous medium in the flow chamber by slowly infusing distilled water from the bottom at a rate of 150 mL/min. After soaking the porous medium for 4 h, an image (water-saturated) (Iw ) was generated. Subsequently, another 12 h of drainage was performed (Schroth et al., 1998 ) to establish an upper unsaturated and lower saturated zone within the flow chamber (Alazaiza et al., 2018, 2019 ), and images were taken to obtain an incomplete saturation image (Id ). Following the described procedures, a 4 mL LNAPL injection was performed using an injection needle connected to the XMSP-C injection pump (Ximai Nanotech, China) at a rate of 0.5 mL per minute. The injection was conducted at a depth of 7 cm along the axis of the flow chamber. The experimental process was divided into two stages. The first stage was conducted at a room temperature of approximately 25℃, such that LNAPL could fully migrate to a stable state in the flow chamber. During this stage, images were captured at 2-hour intervals to assess the attainment of a stable state by the LNAPL within the flow chamber. In the second stage, 10 FTCs were performed, and images were obtained after every FTC. During the freezing period of each FTC, the temperature-controlled cabinet was set to −5℃ while the thermostatic top plate was set to −20℃ for 10 h. During the thawing period of each FTC, the temperature-controlled cabinet was set at 5℃ and the thermostatic top plate was set at 20℃ for 10 h. These setups resulted in a downward freezing-thawing direction in the flow chamber.  2.2.2 Modified LTV technique Prior to the analysis of the graphed images, a correction for distortion resulting from the utilization of a wide-angle lens was conducted using the Capture NX 2 software. Image Pro Plus software was used to crop the post-orthodontic photos and convert the images from the red, green, and blue (RGB) system to grayscale. The grayscale, regarded as the light intensity when the reflectivity is zero, was analyzed using MS Excel software in the same area of interest (AOI) by using the improved LTV technique to calculate Sn . The per-pixel LNAPL saturation and bulk volume in the flow chamber 1 h after each injection were calculated using the modified LTV technique. The α n  j  - α n  i       value was adjusted to ensure correct mass balance with the image injected with 1 mL LNAPL, presenting a value of −4.12 cm−1 , which was then used for LNAPL saturation calculation in subsequent images cumulatively injected with 2.0 to 4.0 mL LNAPL. Subsequently, an AOI (range of LNAPL distribution image in Fig. 6 ) was delineated with an AOI size of 25.0 cm × 18.1 cm. The total volume of LNAPL Vc  in the 2-D flow chamber calculated by image analysis was calculated using the following equation:(10) V c  = ∑ i = 1  x  S n   i  ∙ A ∙ d ∙ n     where A    is the actual area of the pixel, S n   i     is the LNAPL saturation of the i   -th pixel, x    is the total number of pixels. A plot of the added volume of LNAPL against the volume calculated from image analysis at room temperature was presented in Fig. 3  . A strong correlation (R2  = 0.997) was observed between the added and calculated amounts of LNAPL. To further assess calculation errors in Sn , Wang et al. (2021a)  plotted the histograms exhibiting the distribution of false LNAPL saturation in AOI unaffected by LNAPL for 1 and 3 mL LNAPL images. The symmetry and goodness of the normal distribution fit of the data in the histograms (R2  = 0.9919 and 0.9178) are depicted in Fig. 4  , indicating that measurement errors in light intensity were primarily due to unavoidable camera noise and are acceptable. After confirming the acceptability of instrument errors in the error analysis, the issue of calculation errors caused by the LNAPL itself during freeze–thaw cycles, primarily the change in the absorption coefficient of dyed LNAPL, was required to be addressed. FTCs can elevate the absorption coefficient of the dyed dodecane in the NIR band of the optical spectrum. This increase was attributed to the enhanced molecular cross-linking with each FTC, leading to increased light scattering and, consequently, a higher absorption coefficient. Arabul et al. observed a similar effect in polyvinyl alcohol gels after multiple FTCs (Arabul et al., 2014 ). This alteration can result in the deviation in LNAPL saturation calculated according to Eq. (9)  using the absorption coefficient measured at normal temperature. Therefore, it is crucial to consider the effect of temperature when using the LTV method. To achieve this purpose, we adjusted the absorption coefficients in each experimental period based on the known actual total LNAPL rather than measuring them with spectrophotometers. The actual total LNAPL in the 2D flow chamber remained fixed at 4 mL with no loss after all injections. Therefore, we adjusted the absorption coefficients in each experimental period until the calculated total of LNAPL also accurately equaled 4 mL (error less than 0.01 mL, i.e., 0.25 %), consistent with the actual total. The absorption coefficient obtained through this method increased in absolute value with an increase in FTCs, which was consistent with the aforementioned observations. These highly accurate absorption coefficients ensured that the LNAPL calculation for each pixel using the modified LTV method was unaffected by freezing and thawing. The distribution area of the LNAPL could be determined by multiplying the pixels occupied by the LNAPL by the pixel area. The space matrix method was used to calculate the vertical centroid of the pollution body, thereby providing a quantitative description of the impact of FTCs on LNAPL migration.  2.2.4 REV value calculation Following the utilization of the modified LTV method to calculate 2-D Sn  data within the flow chamber, the concept of REV (Fig. 5  b) was applied to obtain the range of the observation scale, in which the mean Sn  represented a slight fluctuation with an increase in the observation scale (Al-Raoush and Papadopoulos, 2010; Al-Raoush and Willson, 2005; Brown et al., 2000 ). The starting point of this range is REVmin , which can be regarded as the REV value. As the flow chamber in this study had a 2-D structure, the core cuboid model (Costanza-Robinson et al., 2011 ) was applicable (Fig. 5 a). The thickness of the core cuboid and square observation window in the front view corresponded to the thickness and a portion of the surface area of the 2-D flow chamber, respectively. In this model, the length (L   ) of the observation window was defined as the edge length of the square cross-section, and the cuboids with an equal difference in side length were formed as the observation scale expanded. In our experiment, the thickness of these cuboids was equal to that of the flow chamber (i.e. 2 cm), and the sectional area of the cuboids matched the area occupied by the pixels. The REV value can be determined through the criteria of the three points relative gradient error (ε g  i    ) method (TPM) (Costanza-Robinson et al., 2011 ):(11) ε g  i  = φ  i + 1   - φ  i - 1    φ  i + 1   + φ  i - 1        1 Δ L   ≦ 0.2     where φ  i     denotes the average of Sn  at the i  t h      observation scale; Δ L    represents the length increment of system volume; and ε g  i     is the relative gradient error value of average of Sn  between the (i - 1 )  th      and (i + 1 )  th      observation scale. Furthermore, the five-point-line method (FPM) was used based on the TPM, averaging five ε g     at contiguous scales to mitigate the adverse impact of drastic fluctuation in the relative gradient error curve (RGEC) (Marchand and Marmet, 1983; Matsumoto and Komatsu, 2015; Xu, 2015 ):(12) ε  ¯   g  i  = ε g  i - 2   + ε g  i - 1   + ε g  i  + ε g  i + 1   + ε g  i + 2    5  ≦ 0.2      After the relative gradient error of the mean Sn  in each region of each image was calculated using the above two methods, a threshold value of 0.2 was used to determine the Sn -REV. In the ideal scenario, Sn  can fluctuate sharply outside the REV range and weakly within the REV range. This characteristic generates an obvious “valley” in the RGEC within the REV range (Fig. 5 b). The starting point of “valley” on the left-hand side corresponded to REVmin , namely Sn -REV. Therefore, the “valley” of the RGEC can play very important role in the determination of Sn -REV, and the number and occurrence time of “valley” are closely related to the sensitivity of the RGEC to Sn . Both TPM and FPM were used to process the Sn  of OC 5 in Row II with intense remigration of LNAPL during the second FTC. It was observed that the RGEC of the TPM can be more sensitive to the fluctuation of Sn  and prone to multiple short “valleys” (Fig. 5 c). Three obvious “valleys” appearing in this RGEC greatly interfered with the selection of “REV” range. However, although the RGEC calculated by the FPM avoided the interference of multiple “valleys”, it was insensitive to the fluctuation of Sn , which delayed the observation of LNAPL entering a stable fluctuation stage below the threshold value. Therefore, in this experiment, the center-periphery combined method (CPM), derived to combine the TPM and FPM, aimed to optimize the RGECs calculated by TPM and FPM for achieving the balanced RGECs sensitive enough to Sn , thereby avoiding the occurrence of the multiple “valleys” (Fig. 5 c). By applying this approach, the observation length, namely the Sn -REV value, can align extremely close to the true value, where the relative gradient error value falls below the threshold of 0.2 (Costanza-Robinson et al., 2011 ).(13) ε cp  i  = ( ε g  i  + ε  ¯   g  i  )  / 2 ≦ 0.2     where ε g  i     denotes the relative gradient error value of average saturation of LNAPL between the (i - 1 )  th      and (i + 1 )  th      observation scale in TPM; ε  ¯   g  i     denotes the average value of ε g  i     within the (i - 2 )  th      and (i + 2 )  th      observation scale in FPM; ε cp  i     represents the center-periphery relative gradient error value of average saturation of LNAPL within the (i - 1 )  th      and (i + 1 )  th      observation scale in CPM. The vertical and lateral migration of LNAPL occurred in the flow chamber at room temperature, resulting in stable distribution after 40 h (Fig. 6  a–c). The main distribution area of LNAPL was evenly categorized into nine lateral strips from top to bottom, labeled Rows I–IX (Fig. 6 c). Furthermore, 32 OCs covering the LNAPL distribution area were selected within the nine rows (Fig. 6 d). Vertically, Rows I–IX and the corresponding OCs were positioned at distances of −12.5 mm, 0.0 mm, 15.3 mm, 30.6 mm, 49.1 mm, 68.5 mm, 83.3 mm, 99.1 mm, and 118.0 mm from the injection site, respectively. The side length of the OCs was determined as 15 mm based on previous studies of the REV (Wu et al., 2017a, 2017b, 2017c ).    3 Results and discussion 3.1 Migration of LNAPL during FTCs During freezing, the LNAPL migrated downward, accompanied by a significant expansion of its distribution area (Fig. 6 e–g). The vertical centroid of the LNAPL gradually migrated downward by 10.18 mm, while the distribution area expanded by 25.46 cm2  (Fig. 7  a). In contrast, during thawing, the vertical centroid of LNAPL migrated upward by 4.17 mm, and the distribution area notably reduced by 14.32 cm2  (Fig. 7 a), which was smaller than that caused by freezing. The downward migration and distribution expansion of LNAPL during freezing exceeded the upward migration and distribution contraction during thawing (Fig. 7 a). Consequently, with successive FTCs, LNAPL gradually migrated downward and expanded until reaching stability (Fig. 7 b). And large quantities of LNAPL were stored both above and below the water level (Fig. 6 e–g). During the FTCs process, the number of highly LNAPL-saturated pixels gradually decreased (Fig. 6 h–p). In addition, the median saturation gradually decreased from 0.064 to 0.055. Each FTC induced a significant migration of the vertical centroid of LNAPL to greater depths, accompanied by an expansion of the distribution area (Fig. 7 b). However, after the sixth FTC, the amplitude of the vertical centroid and distribution area began to decrease, indicating that the redistribution of LNAPL under the impact of FTCs gradually reached stability (Fig. 7 b). After 10 FTCs, the vertical centroid of LNAPL migrated downward by 19.91 mm, accounting for 12.7 % of the vertical distribution range of LNAPL at room temperature. The distribution area increased by 35.13 cm2 , which was 33.65 % of the steady-state distribution area at normal temperature.  3.2 Variation law of Sn -REV with FTCs The CPM was used to characterize the RGECs of the 32 OCs distributed in Rows I–IX. Most of the RGECs of OC 4–6 in Row II (Fig. 8  ) demonstrated a single “valley” pattern, proving that the CPM is conducive to determining Sn -REV. During the freezing, the mean Sn  in Row II decreased by 26.6 %, accompanied by a forward movement of the “valley” of RGECs, representing a gradual increase in the mean Sn -REV (2.16 mm in total) (Fig. 8 b–e). During the thawing, the mean Sn  increased by 14.0 % and the “valley ” moved backward, representing a gradual decrease in Sn -REV value (1.97 mm in total) (Fig. 8 f). After 10 FTCs, the Sn  in Row II gradually decreased by 51.8 %. And the “valley” of RGECs moved forward and the Sn -REV value gradually increased by 66.2 % (Fig. 8 f). Therefore, the increase or decrease in Sn  can be closely related to the increase or decrease in Sn -REV. Furthermore, the dynamic changes in the mean Sn -REV (32 OCs) calculated using TPM, FPM, and CPM during FTCs were analyzed (Fig. 9  ). The mean Sn -REV increased during freezing, and gradually decreased during thawing. However, the extent of the decrease in Sn -REV during thawing was less than that during freezing. Therefore, with the process of FTCs, the mean Sn -REV exhibited an overall trend of gradual increase. Moreover, in the first six FTCs, the mean Sn -REV increased significantly (Fig. 9 b). The mean Sn -REV calculated using the TPM, FPM, and CPM methods increased by 23.7 %, 38.6 %, and 30.5 %, respectively. After the rapid upward period, the Sn -REV reached a stable level. Meanwhile, LNAPL gradually reached a new stable distribution without obvious migration with the subsequent FTCs (Fig. 6 l–p). To explore the impact of FTCs on Sn -REV, the mean Sn -REV of 32 OCs in various periods within the FTCs was statistically analyzed. Certain parameters, including the distribution frequency, cumulative frequency curve, and fitted Gaussian curve of Sn -REV in each period, were determined (Fig. 10  ). The Gaussian curve provides insights into the discreteness and fitting mean value of the Sn -REV value (Wu et al., 2019 ). Meanwhile, according to the Sn -REV (2.88 mm and 3.80 mm) of the cumulative frequency of 33.3 % and 66.6 %, all the Sn -REV (352 in total) of the 10 FTCs were sorted into (1 mm, 3 mm), (3 mm, 4 mm), and (4 mm, 10 mm) as low, medium, and high Sn -REV intervals. During the freezing of the second FTC, an increase of 6.3 % was observed in the proportion of OCs in the high Sn -REV interval, accompanied by decreases of 3.2 % and 3.1 % in the proportion of OCs in the medium and low Sn -REV intervals, respectively (Fig. 10 b–e). The movements of OCs indicated an increase in the mean Sn -REV within these OCs. This movement during freezing was depicted in the Gaussian curve by the advancement and elevation of the peak (Fig. 10 b–e). The advancement signified an increase in the mean Sn -REV, and the elevation indicated an aggregation of Sn -REV in OCs due to a decrease in the number of OCs with low Sn -REV. However, during the thawing of the second FTC, some of the OCs returned to the low and medium Sn -REV intervals (Fig. 10 e–f). The proportion of OCs in the high Sn -REV interval decreased by 15.6 %, whereas the proportion of OCs in the medium Sn -REV interval increased by 6.3 %. The movements of OCs indicated a decrease in the mean Sn -REV within these OCs. This trend caused the peak of the Gaussian curve to regress and decline (Fig. 10 e–f). The regression also represented a decrease in the mean Sn -REV, and the decline signified a disaggregation of Sn -REV in OCs due to an increase in the number of OCs with low Sn -REV. These trends during thawing were opposite to those during freezing, but to a lesser extent, indicating that only some of the OCs moved back to the low Sn -REV interval (Fig. 10 b–f). Therefore, the thawing weakened the increase in mean Sn -REV in the 32 OCs during freezing, but to a lesser extent, resulting in an increasing trend of mean Sn -REV during the second FTC. When FTC = 0, the frequency distribution of Sn -REV was similar to a relatively standard Gaussian curve with a low mean value, indicating that the OCs were aggregated in the low and medium Sn -REV intervals (Fig. 10 a). With the process of FTCs (Fig. 10 g–n), the peak of the fitted Gaussian curve gradually advanced and increased, indicating that OCs continuously moved from lower Sn -REV intervals to higher Sn -REV intervals. Ultimately, the Gaussian curve maintained a relatively towery shape (Fig. 10 n). In this process, the peak of the curves continued to move forward, representing that the fitting mean value increased gradually from 3.27 mm to 4.08 mm.  3.3 Mechanism of Sn -REV variation with FTCs FTCs strongly changed the structure of the medium and the distribution of water and LNAPL. Following the “supercooling period”, water continued to absorb negative temperatures, resulting in continuous freezing of the remaining unfrozen water (Zhou et al., 2020 ). During the freezing process in this experiment, the temperatures at all depths of the LNAPL distribution area rapidly dropped below the freezing point and reached a constant temperature stage (Fig. 11  a), indicating that the water was fully frozen. With the FTCs, the water underwent a repeated cycle of thawing and refreezing, contributing to an increase in the volume occupied by both water and ice. Singh and Niven (2013)  proposed that two-phase (water-oil) and three-phase (water-oil-gas) systems exhibited various degrees of volume expansion after freezing (Fig. 11 b). In the water-oil two-phase system (Fig. 11 b1), the incompressible LNAPL cannot provide redundant space for the volumetric expansion of frozen water (ΔVw ), resulting in freezing-induced pressure. However, in the water-oil-gas three-phase system (Fig. 11 b2), the freezing-induced pressure relied on water saturation and LNAPL saturation. At extremely low LNAPL saturation, sufficient freezing-induced pressure cannot be generated and LNAPL does not migrate (Chuvilin and Miklyaeva, 2003; Chuvilin et al., 2001 ). According to the mechanism of freezing-induced expulsion (Singh et al., 2011 ), LNAPL is subjected to a high local pressure at the exterior of its upgradient pore throat, while with a normal (unfrozen) pressure outside its downgradient throat(s), it is pushed through the downgradient throat. Meanwhile, during freezing, the water in the unfrozen zone migrated upward, and the decrease in the water content in the pores led to an increase in the pore size. The decrease in the capillary pressure of LNAPL destroys the capillary pressure balance and promotes the downward migration of LNAPL (Wang et al., 2021a ). Therefore, the freeze-induced pressure and reconstruction of the capillary force balance induced by water freezing resulted in LNAPL remigration and expansion of the distribution area of LNAPL. In this experiment, the distribution area of LNAPL expanded by 33.65 % after 10 FTCs. When LNAPL migrated because of freeze-induced pressure, the pore-scale distribution pattern of LNAPL was also altered. According to the freezing-induced cutoff mechanism, the LNAPL ganglia were cut off and segmented owing to unbalanced pressure in various directions. As a result, most multi-pore ganglia were divided into numerous single- and sub-pore ganglia, indicating that LNAPL tended to be distributed in a discrete pattern from the form of agglomeration (Singh et al., 2011 ) (Fig. 11 c2). This phenomenon was intensified by the multiphase flow. During freezing, LNAPL migrated in the freezing direction, whereas water migrated against the freezing direction. The movement of water along the soil particles and ice divided the LNAPL (Xu et al., 2017 ), forming a fragmented residual LNAPL (Fig. 11 c2). In contrast to the freezing process, single- and sub-pore ganglia partially reassembled into multi-pore ganglia during the thawing process (Niven and Singh, 2008 ) (Fig. 11 c3). Moreover, the thawing of ice leads to the release of pressure, resulting in the migration of LNAPL in the direction opposite to freezing. This migration provided conditions for the reassociation of the LNAPL ganglia and partial shrinkage of the LNAPL distribution area. The reassociation of LNAPL ganglia during thawing was weaker than the fragmentation caused by freezing. Therefore, with FTCs, the fragmentation of LNAPL continued to increase until LNAPL reached a new stable distribution. At room temperature, LNAPL was relatively aggregated, making it easier to obtain weak fluctuations in Sn  at small observation scales. With the process of FTCs, the continuous increase in the distribution area of LNAPL leads to more discrete LNAPL and more fragmented ganglia (Fig. 11 c4), ultimately resulting in a decrease in the mean and median of Sn  (Fig. 11 d). Numerous LNAPL in the form of single- and sub-pore ganglia were not connected to each other and were distributed discretely, requiring larger scales to obtain weak fluctuation of Sn . Therefore, the mean Sn -REV increased with FTCs. To verify the mechanism of Sn -REV with FTCs, the mean Sn  and Sn -REV in all LNAPL distribution areas were statistically analyzed (Fig. 11 e). In FTCs, the decrease in mean Sn  can be attributed to the segmentation of multi-pore ganglia into numerous small single- and sub-pore ganglia with a more discrete distribution of LNAPL. In contrast, the increase in mean Sn  corresponded to the reverse process. During freezing, the mean Sn  decreased by 19.1 % and increased by 9.7 % to a lesser extent during thawing. This cyclical trend resulted in a tatol decrease in Sn  of 33.5 % after 10 FTCs. The mean Sn -REV showed an opposite trend to that of the mean Sn , which increased by 17.0 % during freezing and decreased by 10.7 % to a lesser extent during thawing. This cyclical trend resulted in a total decrease in Sn -REV by 24.8 % after 10 FTCs. The decrease and increase in Sn  corresponded to the increase and decrease in Sn -REV, respectively. A correlation analysis was conducted between the mean Sn  and mean Sn -REV in the FTCs (Fig. 12  ). A negative correlation was observed between mean Sn  and mean Sn -REV (R2  = 0.868).  3.4 Determination of the empirical interval of Sn -REV Considering the influence of OC position and density on Sn -REV statistics, Gaussian confidence intervals can be used to predict the true range of REV (Wu et al., 2019 ). In statistics, a Gaussian confidence interval defines the interval range that determines the true value of an estimate of a random variable with a specified degree of confidence. In this experiment, the confidence intervals of Sn -REV were obtained with a significance level of α = 5 % (confidence level = 95 %) (Fig. 13  ). With the process of FTCs, the fitted mean Sn -REV exhibited an overall upward trend (Fig. 13 ). However, owing to the fluctuation of the standard deviation, the confidence interval increased slightly in the former FTCs, but contracted and fluctuated sharply between the third and seventh FTC, and finally stabilized to a smaller interval after the seventh FTC. The confidence intervals of Sn -REV during FTCs were overlapped by a light blue range from 2.18 mm to 5.92 mm (Fig. 13 ). This range represents the empirical interval of Sn -REV under the influence of multiple FTCs. This empirical interval represents the Sn -REV selection interval as the minimum analysis unit for field experiments and the model simulation of LNAPL in a homogeneous sandy vadose zone under FTCs. The confidence intervals in the second FTC continued to increase and expand during freezing, followed by sinking and contraction after thawing (Fig. 13 a). The dynamic confidence intervals during the second FTC also covered the empirical interval of Sn -REV, demonstrating that the empirical interval derived from FTCs is applicable to Sn -REV selection in a single freezing or thawing process. This empirical interval can be used for studying the scale effect of LNAPL and can be further applied in site pollution control, pollution tracing and prediction simulations, sample size selection for laboratory tests, and other related purposes.   4 Conclusions An LNAPL migration experiment was conducted in a two-dimensional homogeneous sandy vadose zone under unidirectional FTCs to investigate the dynamic characteristics and mechanism of Sn -REV under FTCs. The modified LTV method was used to monitor the two-dimensional distribution of LNAPL. Furthermore, the TPM and the FPM were combined as the CPM to quantify the Sn  fluctuations under FTCs and calculate the Sn -REV. The results indicated that LNAPL migrated downward and expanded during the freezing, whereas the opposite occurred to a lesser extent during thawing. Therefore, the mean Sn  decreased during freezing and increased during thawing, resulting in a total decrease of 33.5 % after 10 FTCs. A strong negative correlation (R2  = 0.868) was observed between the mean Sn  and Sn -REV during the FTCs. Specifically, during the second FTC, Sn -REV increased by 17.0 % during freezing, decreased by 10.7 % during thawing, and ultimately increased by 24.8 % after 10 FTCs. Furthermore, based on the confidence interval of Sn -REV, the empirical interval of Sn -REV in the homogeneous sandy vadose zone under freeze–thaw conditions was determined to range from 2.18 mm to 5.92 mm. This study could provide an accurate analysis of scale effects for LNAPL contamination remediation under freeze–thaw conditions, offering important insights for understanding and remediating LNAPLs in seasonally frozen soil regions.
1 Introduction Terrestrial ecosystems play a pivotal role in the global carbon cycle by absorbing, fixing, and transferring atmospheric CO2  into biomass through photosynthesis, thus serving as essential carbon sinks (Battin et al., 2009; Cole et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2022 ). However, a significant portion of the net ecosystem production in terrestrial ecosystems, estimated at approximately 3.2 Pg C year−1  (Battin et al., 2023 ), leaks into rivers. This leakage constitutes the main carbon input to rivers, affecting carbon biogeochemical processes (Marx et al., 2017; Wehrli, 2013 ) and aquatic metabolism (Bernhardt et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2023 ) within river ecosystems. Moreover, this process has consequential impacts on river water quality (Brett et al., 2017; Lapierre et al., 2013; Stanley et al., 2012 ) and overall ecosystem health (Battin et al., 2023; Bernhardt et al., 2018 ). Given the substantial carbon exchange fluxes between terrestrial and riverine ecosystems, accurately estimating terrestrial carbon inputs into rivers is of paramount importance for understanding global carbon budget and its implications for climate change. Yet, the unknown spatiotemporal variations of terrestrial carbon inputs introduce considerable uncertainty (Battin et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2022 ). Therefore, to address this gap, it is imperative to delineate the pathways and quantify the spatiotemporal variability of terrestrial carbon inputs into rivers. Groundwater discharge is a key hydrological driving force for transporting terrestrial carbon into streams and rivers. Recent studies using high-resolution monitoring have shown that groundwater carries high concentrations of terrestrially derived carbon into these aquatic systems (Lupon et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2023 ). It is important to note that groundwater discharge involves different flow pathways that integrate various catchment processes over space and time. Local groundwater discharge originates from shallow riparian soils and follows short, shallow pathways before entering streams from the sides. This makes local groundwater discharge more vulnerable to changes in the riparian zone (Duvert et al., 2018; Leith et al., 2015; Öquist et al., 2009 ). On the other hand, regional groundwater discharge follows longer, deeper pathways and enters streams vertically, providing greater stability against hydrologic fluctuations (Evans & Davies, 1998; Gardner et al., 2011 ). While previous studies have recognized the importance of groundwater discharge in transporting terrestrial carbon into rivers, they often overlook the complexity associated with different groundwater flow pathways and fail to differentiate between various sources or components of groundwater (Duvert et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2023 ). This limitation hinders the development of comprehensive conceptual models and our ability to predict changes in terrestrial carbon inputs under the influence of climate change and human activities (van Hoek et al., 2021 ). Seasonal fluctuations in groundwater discharge are well-known in the field of hydrology, and these fluctuations can determine the dynamics of groundwater carbon inputs (Birkel et al., 2020; Duvert et al., 2018 ). For example, Atkins et al. (2017)  found that during rainy seasons, increased groundwater discharge significantly contributes to groundwater CO2  input into a coastal floodplain creek. Additionally, Öquist et al. (2009)  and Leith et al. (2015)  emphasized that spring stands out as the main season for groundwater dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and CO2  inputs into boreal headwater streams due to the pronounced lateral groundwater discharge from the shallow soil layer at this time. Floods have also been found to flush groundwater dissolved organic carbon (DOC) into forest-dominated streams (Laudon et al., 2011 ). In addition to the natural seasonal drivers related to climate and hydrology, human activities are exerting increasing influence on the seasonality of water and carbon exchange between terrestrial and riverine ecosystems (Battin et al., 2023; Rocher-Ros et al., 2023 ). However, there remains a scarcity of research concerning the seasonal evaluation of groundwater discharge and concurrent groundwater carbon inputs into rivers. Agricultural rivers, in particular, are expected to show great seasonal variations due to both natural and human influences. Notably, agricultural landscapes cover about 40 % of the world’s continental area (Foley et al., 2005; Ramankutty et al., 2008 ), emphasizing the need to investigate seasonal variations in groundwater discharge and groundwater carbon inputs within the context of agricultural land use. Here, we conducted a comprehensive investigation of an agricultural headwater river across four distinct seasons. Each season was characterized by different levels of disturbance from seasonal climate fluctuations and agricultural activities. Our hypothesis is that vertical groundwater discharge (VGD) emanating from riverbeds and lateral groundwater discharge (LGD) originating from riparian zones exert distinct influences on groundwater carbon inputs. To quantify VGD, we used an advection–dispersion model to simulate vertical profiles of 222 Rn and Cl−  collected from the riverbeds. We then combined the constrained VGD with differential flow gauging measurements to determine LGD. By integrating groundwater discharge rates with measured groundwater carbon concentrations from both the riverbeds and shallow riparian zone, we estimated and compared groundwater CO2 , CH4 , DIC, and DOC inputs through VGD and LGD. We aim at quantifying seasonal variations in groundwater discharge and groundwater carbon inputs, and identifying the main drivers behind these seasonal patterns.  2 Methods 2.1 Study site description Our study area, the Hailiutu River catchment, is located in Yulin City, Shaanxi Province, in northwest China (Fig. 1  a). This catchment has a semi-arid continental climate, with a relatively low annual mean precipitation (∼340 mm yr−1 ) and a high annual mean potential evapotranspiration (∼2184 mm yr−1 ) (Yang et al., 2012 ). Most of the precipitation occurs from June to September. However, it is often sporadic and of low intensity, which hinders effective aquifer recharge and subsequent groundwater discharge (Ma et al., 2017 ). The land surface is predominantly covered by xeric shrubland (∼88 %), while crop land and wind-breaking trees represent only 3 % of the total surface area and are primarily concentrated along the river valley. The regional aquifer consists of the Holocene Maowusu sand dunes, with a thickness ranging from 0 to 30 m, underlain by the upper Pleistocene Shalawusu sandstone with a thickness of 5 to 90 m. The Hailiutu River and its tributary, the Bulang River, are the two primary rivers in the studied catchment (Fig. 1 a). Both rivers are perennial and sustained by groundwater discharge (Wang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021 ). The riparian zone and riverbed mainly consist of homogeneous unconsolidated sand, with sparse vegetation and some cropland in the riparian zone. Over recent decades, human activities, such as land use changes and river diversions for agricultural irrigation, have increasingly influenced the flow pattern of the Hailiutu River (Yang et al., 2012 ). This impact is particularly notable in the middle reach of the Hailiutu River, where the expansion of cropland has led to the construction of dams and channels to allocate river water for irrigation purposes. During the growing season (April to October, mainly in summer and autumn), these dams are closed to divert river water into irrigation channels (Fig. 1 d), resulting in reduced river levels and discharges compared with the non-growing seasons. This catchment serves as a representative site affected by agricultural activities and is well-suited for investigating seasonal variations in groundwater discharge and groundwater carbon inputs.  2.2 Field sampling and laboratory measurements To examine the seasonal changes in groundwater discharge and groundwater carbon inputs, our study focused on the middle reach of the Hailiutu River, which is known for its intense agricultural activities. We conducted investigations during four distinct seasons: autumn (September 2020), winter (December 2020), spring (March 2021), and summer (June 2021). For each season, we collected samples from six designated sites (H08-H14, see Fig. 1 d), encompassing river water, riverbed groundwater at various depths, and riparian groundwater. The summer and autumn investigations coincided with the growing seasons, while the winter and spring investigations represented the non-growing seasons (referred to as such hereafter). In the field, we used manual differential flow gauging techniques with a flowmeter, as described in Wang et al. (2021) , to measure streamflow rates at the six designated sites. For river water samples, we directly collected water from the middle of the river. Regarding riparian groundwater sampling, we excavated pits situated alongside the river within the bank channels. These pits were approximately 0.5 m wide and 0.4–0.6 m deep, designed to capture the most representative samples of shallow and lateral groundwater flows, while minimizing the disruptions associated with extensive pumping (mixing). After excavation, we used plastic buckets to empty the pits and allowed time for groundwater replenishment before collecting samples. Taking into account the significant hydraulic gradient towards the river (∼0.1), the replenished water primarily originates from the upstream segment of the shallow aquifer without contamination from river water. Sampling riverbed groundwater involved using a drivepoint (Solinst, Canada, see Fig. 1 c) with a 5 cm screen length and 1 cm internal diameter. We collected samples at different depths to capture hydrochemical variations in the hyporheic zone and ensure access to deep groundwater in the riverbeds, thereby allowing us to better characterize the vertical groundwater flow. The default sampling depths were set at 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, and 1.6 m below the riverbeds. In cases where the default depth was inaccessible due to potential clay clogging, we sampled at the deepest reachable point in the field. After installing the drivepoint at the specific depth, we used a pump with a flow rate of 1.5–2 L min−1  to continuously extract riverbed groundwater into a flow-through unit for sampling. We started the collection of riverbed groundwater after purging residual water in the tubes and ensuring stable electrical conductivity and temperature readings. Our measurements included temperature, pH, electrical conductivity, and dissolved O2 , which were obtained using Hach HQ40d multiparameter probes (Hach Company, USA). On-site measurements of 222 Rn activities were conducted using RAD7 detectors coupled with the RAD H2 O accessory (Durridge Company, USA). Before each measurement, we purged the RAD7 for a minimum of 15 min to eliminate residual radon gas and prevent contamination from previous measurements. Additionally, we allowed an equilibrium time of approximately one hour for each 222 Rn measurement to ensure that radon equilibrium was achieved. Concentrations of CO2  and CH4  were determined through the headspace equilibrium method (see Johnson et al., 1990 ). Initially, we used the sampled water to rinse a 500 ml gas-tight syringe, then collected 200 ml of bubble-free water in the syringe. Next, we introduced 100 ml of high-purity N2  into the syringe to create a headspace. Gas equilibrium was achieved by vigorously shaking the syringe for at least 2 min. The equilibrated headspace gas was then injected into a pre-evacuated 500 ml aluminum foil airbag (Cali5 Bond, Calibration, USA). This process was repeated twice for each water sample to obtain a total of 200 ml of equilibrated gas for CO2  and CH4  partial pressure measurements. These partial pressures were quantified by a Picarro 2131-i  instrument (Picarro Company, USA), and then converted to dissolved CO2  and CH4  concentrations using Henry’s Law, following the calculation method described in Johnson et al. (1990) . In the field, we collected water samples for laboratory analysis. These samples were used to measure cation, anion, DIC, DOC, δ13 CDIC , 2 H, and 18 O. The collected water samples were filtered through 0.22 μm membrane filters and stored in a fridge at 4 ℃ until laboratory analysis. Samples designated for cation and DOC analysis were acidified with HCl. The cation analysis was performed using an ICP-OES (iCAP 6300 DUO, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), while anion concentrations were determined via ion chromatography (Dionex ICS-1100, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). DIC and DOC concentrations were quantified using a TOC analyzer (SHIMADZU TOC-L, Japan). For δ13 CDIC  measurement, we used a Gasbench and MAT 252 instrument (accuracy: ≤0.1 ‰, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). The δ13 CDIC  values were reported relative to the Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite (VPDB) carbonate standard. All measurements were conducted at the Key Laboratory of Surficial Geochemistry of the Ministry of Education and the State Key Laboratory for Mineral Deposits Research at Nanjing University. The δ18 O and δ2 H were measured on a Laser Spectroscopic Liquid-water stable isotope analyzer (Los Gatos Research, accuracy = ±0.1 ‰ for δ18 O and ±0.3 ‰ for δ2 H), at the CSHL, Nanjing Hydraulic Research Institute. The δ18 O and δ2 H values were reported relative to Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water (VSMOW). Additionally, the 0.22 μm filtered membranes were collected for 16S rDNA analysis at LC-Bio Technology Co. Ltd. in Hangzhou, China. The samples were initially stored in a dry ice container at around −20 ℃ environment and subsequently transferred to a laboratory refrigerator at −80 ℃ before analysis. The 16S rDNA results provided information about the microbial communities existing in the river and groundwater at our research site.  2.3 Quantification of groundwater discharge into the river Vertical hydrochemical profiles obtained from riverbeds provide valuable information about river-groundwater exchange rates, as demonstrated in previous studies (Buenavista et al., 2023; Cranswick et al., 2014 ). In this study, we used detailed 222 Rn and Cl−  data collected at different depths (0.1–1.6 m) in the riverbeds to quantify vertical groundwater discharge (VGD) rates, following the methodology described in Buenavista et al. (2023) . We employed a one-dimensional advection–dispersion equation, which accounts for decay and production processes, to fit the vertical profiles of 222 Rn and Cl−  within the riverbeds (detailed description available in Supporting Information  (SI) Text S1). The calibration of the model parameters was accomplished using the DiffeRential Evolution Adaptive Metropolis Scheme (DREAM algorithm, see Vrugt et al. (2009) ). Specific calibration parameters are provided in SI Table S1 . In addition, an evolutionary Markon chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach was applied to improve the efficiency of the DREAM algorithm. The resulting VGD rates at the six designated sites (H08-H14) were subsequently used to calculate cumulative VGD at the reach scale by multiplying the riverbed area and the average rates upstream and downstream at each reach. Besides estimating VGD, we used differential flow gauging techniques to determine the total groundwater discharge at the reach scale. The disparity between the total groundwater discharge and the VGD was attributed to lateral groundwater discharge (LGD) from the riparian zone.  2.4 Quantification of groundwater carbon inputs into the river Based on the reach-scale evaluation of VGD and LGD, we estimated the groundwater CO2 , CH4 , DIC, and DOC inputs into the river. We assumed that the carbon concentrations beneath the hyporheic zone reflected the carbon contribution from VGD, whereas the carbon concentrations in the riparian shallow groundwater revealed LGD’s carbon contribution. To determine the groundwater carbon inputs, we multiplied the cumulative groundwater discharge by the average groundwater carbon concentrations upstream and downstream of each reach.   3 Results 3.1 Spatiotemporal variations in streamflow rates We measured streamflow rates in the studied section during four different seasons and presented the results in Fig. 2  . The streamflow rates consistently increased from the beginning of the section (H08) to the most downstream point (H14), with the exception of H09-H10 reach, which was affected by a river diversion (Fig. 1 d). In non-growing seasons, the streamflow rates increased from 1.57 m3  s−1  at H08 to 2.75 m3  s−1  at H14 in spring, and from 1.35 m3  s−1  at H08 to 2.46 m3  s−1  at H14 in winter. In comparison, during the growing seasons, the streamflow rates initially decreased after the river diversion and then increased downstream (Fig. 2 ). Specifically, the streamflow rates varied from 1.10 m3  s−1  at H08 to 1.00 m3  s−1  at H14 in summer and from 1.09 m3  s−1  at H08 to 1.28 m3  s−1  at H14 in autumn. The river diversion outflow rates were 1.08 and 1.39 m3  s−1  in summer and autumn, respectively, which were very close to the streamflow rates at the closest upstream site. Clearly, the river diversion for agricultural irrigation, is the main factor driving the seasonal variations in streamflow, posing a significant threat to the continuous flow of the river. The river diversion resulted in noticeably lower river levels and streamflow rates during the growing seasons compared with the non-growing seasons. This pronounced seasonal variability in the hydrological regime is expected to directly affect the water and carbon exchanges between groundwater and the river.  3.2 Seasonal variability of groundwater discharge into the river In this study, we constrained VGD at the six sites by fitting the profiles of 222 Rn and Cl−  concentrations collected from the riverbeds. The 222 Rn activities increased with depth and eventually reached equilibrium at deeper riverbeds (see Fig. 3  ). The modeling results for 222 Rn are generally reasonable, although there are some deviations between the modeled trends and the observed values, such as in spring and autumn at H08, autumn at H09, and summer at H13 (see Fig. 3 a). These deviations may be caused by sediment mineralogy heterogeneity or regional groundwater discharge (Cranswick et al., 2014 ). On the other hand, the modeled Cl−  concentrations show good agreement with the measured values (Fig. 3 b). Since Cl−  is a conservative tracer, its concentration was expected to remain constant at depths below the hyporheic zone, which was clearly observed at all six sites. The constrained VGD rates at the six sites ranged from 0.04 to 0.84 m d−1  (see SI Fig. S1 ), which aligns with the findings (0–0.8 m d−1 ) from seepage meter measurements in a similar sandy streambed study area in the Upper Middle Loup watershed in the US (Humphrey et al., 2022 ). The increasing streamflow rates indicate a gaining condition in this river, aligning with a previous evaluation by Wang et al. (2021) . Excluding the inflow of the Bulang River and outflow of river diversion, the increases in streamflow rates equal the total groundwater discharge rates for the studied reaches. In this study, we assumed that the difference between the total groundwater discharge and the VGD was due to LGD. The total groundwater discharge rates for the studied reach (H08-H14) were 0.96 and 0.86 m3  s−1  during spring and winter, respectively. In comparison, the total groundwater discharge rates were 0.97 and 1.57 m3  s−1  during summer and autumn, respectively. Therefore, the total groundwater discharge rates were noticeably higher during growing seasons than during the non-growing seasons. Moreover, the average groundwater discharge rates per unit of river length were also higher during the growing seasons (summer: 4.97 m2  d−1  and autumn: 8.04 m2  d−1 ) compared with the non-growing seasons (spring: 4.92 m2  d−1  and winter: 4.4 m2  d−1 ). The comparison of reach-scale groundwater discharge is shown in Fig. 4  . Importantly, both VGD and LGD were significant contributors to river flow, with each playing a dominant role during specific seasons. VGD had a more significant contribution during the non-growing seasons (spring and winter), especially in winter, while LGD had a greater impact during the growing seasons (summer and autumn).  3.3 Distinct groundwater endmembers To understand the mixing patterns between groundwater and the river, we compared carbon concentrations and isotopic values of river water, riverbed groundwater, and riparian groundwater (see Fig. 5  ). The results showed that riverbed groundwater and riparian groundwater were distinct endmembers, with significant differences in hydrochemical and isotope characteristics. Riverbed groundwater emerged as a more concentrated and stable endmember, whereas riparian groundwater exhibited considerable spatiotemporal variations. This finding emphasizes the importance of distinguishing the individual contributions of these sources to groundwater carbon inputs into the river. Riparian groundwater had significantly higher CO2  concentrations than river water, which is consistent with previous studies (Boodoo et al., 2019; Duvert et al., 2018; Rasilo et al., 2017 ), while riverbed groundwater had only slightly higher CO2  concentrations than the river water (Fig. 5 a). CH4  concentrations in riverbed groundwater were consistently lower than those in river water. However, CH4  concentrations in riparian groundwater varied greatly, and in certain localized hotspots, they were several orders of magnitude higher than in the river water. DIC and DOC concentrations were highest in riparian groundwater, followed by river water, and lowest in riverbed groundwater. Particularly high DOC concentrations were observed in both riparian groundwater and river water, especially in the spring. Stable water isotopes revealed that riparian groundwater had higher values of 2 H and 18 O compared with riverbed groundwater, which was due to the evaporation effect in the shallow riparian groundwater (with an unsaturated zone of less than 1 m at the riverbank). Furthermore, the 2 H and 18 O values in the river water were positioned along the mixing line between riparian groundwater and riverbed groundwater, strongly indicating that the river water was a mixture of riparian groundwater and riverbed groundwater. In terms of δ13 CDIC , riparian groundwater emerged as the most variable and negative endmember. The river water displayed similar δ13 CDIC  values but significantly higher DIC concentrations than riverbed groundwater. Additionally, the 16s rDNA data revealed clear differences among the microbial communities in river water, riparian groundwater, and riverbed groundwater. Notably, riparian groundwater and deep riverbed groundwater generally had more diverse microbial communities and higher microbial abundances (see Fig. 6  ). In contrast, river water and shallow riverbed groundwater contained less diverse microbial communities with lower abundances.  3.4 Seasonal variability of groundwater carbon inputs into the river Our reach-scale evaluation showed seasonal fluctuations in VGD and LGD. Furthermore, we also observed notable differences in carbon concentrations between the riverbed and riparian groundwater. This led us to anticipate seasonal variations in the contributions of VGD and LGD to groundwater carbon inputs into the river. To calculate VGD’s contribution, we considered carbon concentrations at a depth below the hyporheic zone (i.e., 0.8 m) in the riverbed. Groundwater carbon inputs encompass various forms, such as CO2 , CH4 , DIC, and DOC. In our study, groundwater DIC input (2.2–4.3 mol m−2  d−1 ) emerged as the dominant form, with fluxes nearly one order of magnitude higher than groundwater DOC (0.15–0.56 mol m−2  d−1 ) and CO2  inputs (0.10–0.43 mol m−2  d−1 , see Fig. 7  ). Groundwater DIC input was also several orders of magnitude greater than groundwater CH4  input (9 × 10−5 –9 × 10−3  mol m−2  d−1 ). Seasonal variations were observed in groundwater carbon inputs. For instance, groundwater CO2 , CH4 , and DIC inputs into the river peaked during autumn when both the total groundwater discharge and LGD contributions were highest (Fig. 4 ), indicating the influence of hydrology on groundwater carbon inputs. On the other hand, groundwater DOC input reached its maximum during spring, coinciding with the peak DOC concentration in the riparian groundwater. Notably, groundwater carbon inputs were lowest during winter, including groundwater CO2 , CH4 , DIC, and DOC inputs. We also observed significant differences in groundwater carbon inputs between non-growing and growing seasons (see SI Fig. S2 ). Specifically, growing seasons experienced several times higher groundwater CO2  and DIC inputs, and even several orders of magnitude greater groundwater CH4  input compared with non-growing seasons (see Fig. 7 ). Groundwater DOC inputs during growing seasons were higher than in one of the non-growing seasons (winter) but lower than another one (spring).   4 Discussion 4.1 Seasonal contributions of lateral and vertical groundwater discharge Groundwater discharge involves complex flow pathways originating from different depths. Shallow groundwater from the riparian zone enters the river laterally, while deeper groundwater from hillslopes feeds the river vertically through the riverbeds (Duvert et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2023 ). The differentiation between VGD and LGD aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the actual pathways of groundwater flow and explore their respective impacts on carbon transport. To estimate VGD rates at designated sites, we modeled 222 Rn and Cl−  profiles within the riverbeds and extrapolated these rates to the reach-scale to assess the cumulative effect of groundwater discharge. It is essential to acknowledge that the reach-scale results do not account for spatial heterogeneity at smaller scales and should be interpreted as average estimates (Cook, 2013 ). Seasonal variations in groundwater discharge were clearly observed in the river. Our results indicate that during the growing seasons, not only the total groundwater discharge increased, but the contribution of LGD to the total groundwater discharge also rose (see Fig. 4 ). This highlights the amplified impact of LGD during these periods. This shift in seasonality is primarily caused by river diversion, which considerably reduces streamflow rates and water levels during the growing seasons. As a result, the hydraulic gradient towards the river intensifies, leading to greater groundwater discharge compared with the non-growing seasons (Gribovszki et al., 2010 ). Furthermore, our findings suggest that LGD is more susceptible to disturbances in riparian areas, as it mainly represents shallow groundwater flow pathways, while VGD remains relatively stable throughout the seasons. Additionally, our study revealed that VGD and LGD play different roles depending on the season, with VGD dominating in non-growing seasons, particularly in winter, while LGD has a more significant contribution during the growing seasons. The seasonality of groundwater discharge is expected to affect the seasonal dynamics of groundwater carbon inputs.  4.2 Significant increase in lateral groundwater carbon inputs during the growing seasons Seasonal variations in groundwater discharge have a direct impact on groundwater carbon inputs into the river, with VGD and LGD being distinct sources characterized by different carbon concentrations and water exchange fluxes. Interestingly, riparian groundwater showed significantly higher levels of CO2 , DIC, and DOC concentrations than riverbed groundwater (see Fig. 5 ). Additionally, CH4  concentrations in riparian groundwater varied greatly, with some areas exhibiting concentrations several orders of magnitude higher than the river water and riverbed groundwater, indicating that shallow riparian groundwater is a hotspot for CH4  production and leakage into the river. Despite differences in water exchange fluxes between VGD and LGD, the elevated carbon concentrations in riparian groundwater led to larger groundwater carbon contribution from LGD compared to VGD (see Fig. 7 ). LGD contributed disproportionately more groundwater CO2  (up to 92 %) and CH4  (up to 99 %) to the river, particularly during the growing seasons. While both VGD and LGD play important roles in groundwater DIC and DOC inputs, LGD has a stronger impact during the growing seasons, while VGD exhibits relatively higher contributions during non-growing seasons. During the growing seasons, riparian grasses and plants enter their active growth phase, leading to increased soil respiration in the riparian zone, as evidenced by more negative δ13 CDIC  (SI Fig. S3 ). This increased soil respiration enhances the potential for carbon sources to leach downward into the groundwater and eventually reach the river (Leith et al., 2015; Öquist et al., 2009 ). The combination of higher groundwater carbon concentrations and increased groundwater discharge during the growing seasons, compared with the non-growing seasons, results in a significant increase in groundwater carbon inputs into the river (see Fig. 7 ). Our study highlights that the growing seasons represent hot moments for groundwater carbon inputs into the river.  4.3 Implications Accurate quantification of groundwater carbon inputs into rivers is vital for constructing reliable carbon budgets for both terrestrial and riverine ecosystems (Battin et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2022 ). However, this endeavor faces significant challenges owing to the heterogeneous characteristic of groundwater flow paths and carbon concentrations, as demonstrated in our study. To deepen our comprehension, it is imperative to pinpoint groundwater discharge pathways and locate hotspots for carbon production and leakage into rivers. Furthermore, the marked heterogeneity of carbon exchange and transport across the terrestrial-riverine interface reinforces the significance and necessity of conducting high-resolution investigations in space and time. Of the various methods, naturally dissolved gases emerge as one of the most promising environmental tracers to track carbon’s physical exchange and biogeochemical reactions, as exemplified by Wang et al. (2023) . Additionally, the injection of dissolved gases provides a straightforward and robust technique for lighting up invisible gas transport process across groundwater-stream and stream-atmosphere interfaces (Blanc et al., 2024; Brennwald et al., 2022 ). Looking ahead, future studies should also integrate high-resolution spatial and temporal data and develop physically based models to unravel the mechanisms governing carbon transport and transformation across the terrestrial-riverine continuum, as indicated by previous studies (Boodoo et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Wen et al., 2022 ). A process-oriented understanding holds the potential to offer invaluable insights into carbon cycling across the terrestrial-riverine continuum, especially in the context of climate and land use changes (van Hoek et al., 2021 ). This study revealed pronounced seasonality in groundwater discharge and current carbon inputs within agricultural rivers, predominantly driven by the fluctuating contributions of LGD, as illustrated in Fig. 7 . During the growing seasons, groundwater carbon inputs originating from LGD nearly double compared with non-growing seasons. This marked increase in LGD-derived carbon inputs profoundly shapes the observed seasonal fluctuations in groundwater carbon inputs. Notably, LGD exerts an even more substantial influence in humid regions, where increased precipitation infiltration and soil preferential flows act to expel a greater volume of terrestrial-derived carbon into rivers (Li et al., 2022 ). In conclusion, the growing season emerges as a hot moment for groundwater carbon inputs into agricultural rivers, a factor that should be carefully considered when estimating the annual carbon exchange and budgets between terrestrial and riverine ecosystems (Cole et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2022 ). Recognizing and incorporating these seasonal dynamics is essential for achieving a precise understanding of the global carbon balance and for informing effective strategies to mitigate climate change impacts. Groundwater carbon inputs also have a significant impact on river water quality and ecosystem health. CO2  and CH4  from terrestrial sources are known to contribute to greenhouse gas oversaturation and emissions in rivers. These gases accumulate in terrestrial environments through processes like soil and root respiration, as well as carbonate weathering (Crawford & Stanley, 2016; Hotchkiss et al., 2015; Marx et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2023 ). In addition, groundwater DIC inputs play a role in influencing carbonate buffering systems within river ecosystems (Duvert et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021 ). An in-depth analysis by Lapierre et al. (2013)  on boreal freshwaters highlights the stimulation of organic carbon processing in rivers within an increase in terrestrially derived carbon. It is important to note that excessive amounts of groundwater organic carbon can negatively impact river water quality (Brett et al., 2017; Stanley et al., 2012 ). Furthermore, the mixing of high-quality DOC from terrestrial ecosystems with low-quality DOC in river water creates specific hotspots where organic carbon degradation accelerates. This can cause ecological processes to shift from stochastic to deterministic status and elevate abundances of microbial taxa (Caverly et al., 2013; Stegen et al., 2016; Stegen et al., 2018 ). Therefore, understanding the seasonal variability of groundwater carbon inputs is crucial, as it influences the dynamics of carbon cycling and its implications for both water quality and ecosystem functioning.   5 Conclusion We examined seasonal variations in groundwater discharge and groundwater carbon inputs into an agricultural headwater river. VGD was quantified through an advection–dispersion simulation of vertical 222 Rn and Cl−  profiles collected from the riverbeds, while LGD was determined based on differential flow gauging and VGD estimation. We found that river diversion for agricultural irrigation during growing seasons significantly reduced river levels, thereby enhancing groundwater discharge into the river, particularly LGD. LGD contributed more water during the growing seasons, whereas VGD was more critical during the non-growing seasons. LGD and VGD represented shallow and deep groundwater inflow pathways, respectively, and exhibited distinct carbon concentrations. The higher carbon concentrations and more diverse microbial communities in the shallow riparian groundwater than in the riverbed groundwater determined the major role of LGD in contributing carbon to the river, especially for CO2  and CH4 . Enhanced groundwater discharge in the growing seasons increased groundwater carbon inputs into the river. This study highlights that the growing season is a hot moment for groundwater discharge and groundwater carbon inputs into agricultural rivers and riparian shallow groundwater serves as a hotspot for the production and leakage of groundwater carbon into these rivers.
1 Introduction Accurate estimation of flood inundation maps of specific annual exceedance probability (e.g., 100-year return period) is crucial for effective water resources management, infrastructure design, and risk mitigation. In the United States, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) is responsible for developing flood insurance rate maps, where the 100-year flood map is a standard measure for establishing zoning regulations and building standards, striking a balance between public protection and the imposition of stringent regulations (Holmes and Dinicola, 2010 ). These maps represent areas with a 1% annual risk of flooding, or 26% likelihood of experiencing flooding at least once over a 30-year span (FEMA, 2022 ). Estimation of flood maps typically involves a two-stage approach: initially, the 100-year peak flow is estimated through Flood Frequency Analysis (FFA) methods, followed by the use of a hydraulic model to calculate the inundation extent for the identified peak flow (Cea et al., 2022 ). Although various methodologies have been proposed for FFA (Hamed and Rao, 2019; England et al., 2014; Wright et al., 2014; Dawdy et al., 2012 ), they primarily rely on two approaches: (1) statistical analysis of stream gauge observations, or (2) “design storm” methods. The former fits annual peak flow data to parametric probability distributions (Stedinger and Griffis, 2008 ). The latter involves generating a synthetic storm based on Intensity Duration Frequency (IDF) curves to force a hydrological model to estimate the flood hydrograph. Both methods, however, face challenges either by data constraints and model assumptions. For instance, statistical stream gauge analysis is limited to gauged sites and influenced by observational record length, outliers, and typically relies on the assumption of stationarity (England et al., 2019 ). The “design storm” method, while versatile in application and capable of incorporating climate and land-use changes, assumes a 1:1 return period equivalence between rainfall and modeled peak flow (Watt and Marsalek, 2013; Harvey and Connor, 2017; Rogger et al., 2012 ), implying that the watershed initial conditions such as soil moisture and snowpack cannot modulate the transformation of rainfall quantiles into peak flow quantiles (Yu et al., 2019 ). This oversight fails to capture the spatial–temporal variability inherent in hydrological processes that drive flood events (Wright et al., 2014 ). Recent studies have highlighted the potential of using Stochastic Storm Transposition (SST) methods to generate a large number of realistic storm events to force process-based hydrological models and conduct FFA. Hereafter, the use of SST to conduct FFA through process-based hydrological modeling is referred to as FFA-SST. The core principle behind FFA-SST is recreating joint distributions of flood-producing meteorological and hydrological processes that are resolved with process-based hydrological models (Wright et al., 2020 ). FFA-SST can be implemented with any process-based hydrological model that takes rainfall as input and produces streamflow as output. The first implementation of FFA-SST used a lumped hydrological model (Franchini et al., 1996 ). Advances in distributed process-based hydrological modeling provided ways to explore the interactions between rainfall, runoff production, and channel processes across various scales, something not achievable with lumped models. These advancements paved the way for the first applications of FFA-SST using distributed hydrological models (Wright et al., 2014; England et al., 2014 ). These studies proved that FFA-SST, when used alongside distributed hydrological models, can provide robust estimates of peak flow quantiles. Since then, several studies have emerged using FFA-SST to analyze the effect of flood-producing meteorological and hydrological processes in peak flow quantiles, including, the spatial–temporal resolution of rainfall fields (Zhu et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2021 ), climate-driven changes regarding snowmelt and soil moisture seasonality (Yu et al., 2021, 2019 ), future climate projections (Yu et al., 2020 ), variations in storm trajectories (Perez et al., 2021 ), and the effect of small dams in flow reduction (Post et al., 2024 ). Furthermore, the FFA-SST framework has also been applied to evaluate the performance of alternative methods to estimate peak flow quantiles such as regional regression models (Perez et al., 2019b ) and machine learning techniques (Gurbuz et al., 2023 ). Each of the following distributed models have been used on FFA-SST applications: the Two-Dimensional Runoff, Erosion, and Export (TREX) model (Velleux et al., 2011 ), the Gridded Surface Subsurface Hydrologic Analysis (GSSHA) (Downer et al., 2006 ), the Hillslope-Link Model (HLM) (Mantilla et al., 2022 ), the Watershed Modeling Framework (WMF) (Velásquez et al., 2023 ), the Weather Research and Forecasting Hydrological (WRF-Hydro) (Gochis et al., 2018 ), and the Hydrologic Modeling System (HEC-HMS) (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE), 2018 ). These distributed process-based hydrological models vary in complexity and model conceptualization, but in principle, they represent the same fundamental hydrological processes, including evapotranspiration, infiltration, percolation, runoff, and, in some cases, groundwater storage. Overall, these models decompose the landscape in analysis units (e.g., hillslopes, rectilinear grids, or unstructured mesh elements) and resolve some form of 2D overland flow and/or 1D channel routing over a prescribed river network. Where subsurface flow dynamics are included, these models commonly extend 2–3 m into the soil column to capture vertical infiltration and may exclude “deeper” groundwater storage or rely on a lumped approach. Departing from these previous hydrological models, a different class of models known as Integrated Surface-Subsurface Hydrological Models (ISSHMs) offers a more intricate representation of the hydrological system (Maxwell et al., 2014; Le et al., 2015 ).
