ISSHMs differ from the previously mentioned distributed hydrological models in two key aspects: First, ISSHMs use the 3D Richards’ equations to capture subsurface flows, allowing for a more detailed representation of complex geological formations and soil properties at depths ranging from tens to hundreds of meters, which is essential for accurately modeling spatial patterns in the water table and realistic soil moisture content. Second, ISSHMs are topography-resolving models that use the 2D shallow water equations for overland and channel routing. This approach naturally leads to the emergence of rivers and flooded areas in the landscape without the prescription of a river network, enabling the potential for analyzing flood extent dynamics. Despite the comprehensive nature of ISSHMs, the high computational demands and the need for detailed soil and geological data have historically limited ISSHM applications mainly to idealized hillslopes and smaller catchments (Sebben et al., 2013; Gutiérrez-Jurado et al., 2019; Partington et al., 2013 ). However, the growing availability of extensive hydrological datasets describing watershed properties (e.g., soil type, soil cover, and depth to bedrock, among others), combined with increased access to high-performance computing resources, have broadened the application of ISSHMs for large spatial scale applications. Recent examples have showcased their use for large watersheds and even at continental scales (Keune et al., 2016, 2018; Maxwell et al., 2015; Kollet et al., 2018; Condon and Maxwell, 2019; Condon et al., 2020; O’Neill et al., 2021; Politano et al., 2023; Mascaro et al., 2015; Piras et al., 2014 ). Importantly, recent studies have shown that ISSHMs reduce the need for extensive calibration (Bhanja et al., 2023; Tijerina et al., 2021 ) by relying more on prior information and spatially distributed datasets that describe soil and geological properties. This last aspect makes ISSHMs attractive to model hydrological systems affected by natural and anthropogenic perturbances while avoiding equifinality issues (Khatami et al., 2019 ). Previous efforts by FFA-SST have successfully estimated peak flow quantiles throughout river networks but fell short of producing flood inundation maps, which ultimately are the main resource for assessing flood hazard and population flood exposure. Since ISSHMs are topography-resolved models, they have the potential to provide flood depths and, as a result, flood inundation maps. However, the reliability of these flood inundation maps is contingent upon accurately representing both channel and floodplain topography in the ISSHM. This suggests the need for high-resolution (< 100  m   ) surface mesh elements, significantly increasing computational demands and challenging the feasibility of generating inundation maps directly from ISSHMs. Overcoming this challenge to enable the estimation of flood extent maps through ISSHM runs, eliminating the necessity for a separate use of a hydraulic model, would represent a significant leap forward for FFA-SST. This study introduces the first-of-its-kind application of an ISSHM in FFA-SST to estimate and analyze flood extents. Our research aims to achieve three main objectives. First, we aim to evaluate the ability of an ISSHM, using only prior information for model setup, to simulate hydrological fluxes and reproduce flood hydrographs. Second, we showcase the integration of an ISSHM within the FFA-SST framework by analyzing the resulting peak flows and flood extents up to a 500-year return period. Third, we demonstrate how the resulting flood extents can be used to quantify flood hazard and population flood exposure at the basin scale. Based on these objectives, we will show, for the first time, using physical-based hydrological simulations, the complex relationship between annual recurrence intervals of peak flow, basin inundation fraction, and flood exposure. This insight will be crucial for developing more accurate flood risk management and mitigation strategies. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 , we describe the FFA-SST framework and provide details on the SST and ISSHM models that are used in the case study. Following this, Section 3  outlines the selected basin and the datasets used to demonstrate the FFA-SST implementation using an ISSHM. Section 4.1  focuses on evaluating the ISSHM performance through both long-term hydrological outputs (e.g. evapotranspiration, soil moisture content, groundwater storage, and streamflow) and extreme flood events (e.g. peak flow and flood extent). Section 4.2  analyzes the outputs from the FFA-SST, with a primary focus on peak flows, basin inundation fractions, and number of people exposed to flooding for annual recurrence intervals up to a 500-year return period. Finally, Section 5  addresses the limitations and potential future applications of FFA-SST using ISSHMs, and Section 6  summarizes our key findings and contributions.  2 Methods The FFA-SST framework is widely reported in several studies (Wright et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2021, 2023; Perez et al., 2021 ). Here, we expand it by incorporating an ISSHM as the process-based hydrological model, which enables us to extend the analysis from peak flows to flood extents and then quantify population flood exposure (Fig. 1 ). In particular, we start by describing how to conduct FFA-SST regardless of the type of models used for SST and ISSHM. Then, we describe the SST and ISSHM models used in the case study presented in this paper. At its core, FFA-SST provides annual peak flow quantile estimates at any point within a watershed under analysis. This is done by simulating, with a process-based hydrological model, flood responses from a large number of synthetic extreme storm events generated through SST. For a given watershed, the following are the detailed steps to conduct FFA-SST with an ISSHM with the objective of performing flood hazard and flood exposure analyses: Step 1.  Delineation of the transposition domain:  The user must define this domain by identifying a region that shares similar meteorological conditions with relatively homogeneous patterns in rainfall statistics in relation to the watershed where storm events are intended to be transposed. The main assumption is that any observed storm within this domain is equally likely to occur at any other location within the domain.  Step 2.  Detection of parent storms:  Parent storms are storm events within the transposition domain that are detected from gridded rainfall datasets. The selection of these parent storms depends on diverse parameters defined by the user on the SST scheme, mainly depending on the maximum rainfall accumulation during a prescribed storm duration and the spatial extent of the storm event.  Step 3.  Resampling and transposition of parent storms : Synthetic storms for the watershed of interest are generated by randomly sampling parent storms and then randomly transposing them into the watershed of interest. To do this, a random number of storms k   is generated by modeling the annual “arrival process” of storms over the domain. This storm arrival process is usually prescribed by a parametric distribution (e.g., Poisson distribution). This sampling and transposing process can generate any given user-controlled number of synthetic years (e.g., 500 years) of storm data, with each year containing k   synthetic storm events (e.g., 20 storms per year). Since SST is used for annual flood frequency analysis, only the largest storm events for every synthetic year are retained for later use in the hydrological simulations. Previous FFA-SST implementations have retained between 1 to 5 storm events per year based on the total basin rainfall accumulation (Wright et al., 2020 ).  Step 4.  Definition of ISSHM parameters:  Recent studies (Bhanja et al., 2023; Tijerina et al., 2021 ) have demonstrated that ISSHMs can diminish the reliance on extensive site-specific calibration processes by leveraging prior information and extensive spatial datasets detailing soil and geological characteristics for the definition of model parameters. Given this advantage, the definition of model parameters in ISSHMs should prioritize using prior information alongside extensive, spatially distributed datasets when feasible. In cases where such information is not available, unknown hydrological model parameters must be set through standard automated calibration procedures, such as genetic algorithm or the Shuffled Complex Evolution approach. Ideally, such calibration must be focused on a multi-objective calibration procedure, where multiple variables (e.g., streamflow, peak flows, evapotranspiration) are used during the calibration process.  Step 5.  Evaluation of the ISSHM:  Evaluating the ISSHM is crucial to ensure its reliability in capturing the complex, non-linear dynamics that govern flood processes. This evaluation must be focused on a multi-objective procedure where model outputs must be able to capture long-term observations, on variables such as streamflow, evapotranspiration, soil moisture content, and groundwater storage. Furthermore, the evaluation process must include comparing peak flow responses and flood inundation maps produced by the ISSHMs against benchmark maps derived from historical flood events.  Step 6.  Rainfall-Runoff simulations:  Flood hydrographs and flood depths for all storm events generated in Step 3 are computed using the ISSHM. The rainfall-runoff simulations must be initialized with hydrological states that resemble realistic initial conditions. To this end, initial conditions are sampled from long-term historical hydrological simulations (Step 5), in which, for each rainfall-runoff simulation, the selected initial condition must match the seasonality of the date of the parent storm used to generate the synthetic storm event (Yu et al., 2021 ).  Step 7.  Estimation of peak flow for annual recurrence intervals:  Peak flow outputs computed in Step 6, for a given river network location, are used to create a series of annual peak flows by retaining the maximum simulated peak flow recorded for each synthetic year. Then, peak flows for different annual recurrence intervals are estimated using a non-parametric distribution by calculating the exceedance probability p   for each annual peak flow as p = j / ( T  m a x   + 1 )     where j   is the rank of the peak flow in the annual series and T  m a x     the number of synthetic years.  Step 8.  Estimation of basin inundation fraction for annual recurrence intervals:  Basin inundation fractions, the ratio of the inundated area to the total basin area, from the outputs of Step 6 are used to create an annual series of basin inundation fractions by retaining the highest inundation fraction recorded for each synthetic year. In particular, for a given rainfall-runoff event, the basin inundation fraction is calculated from the maximum flood depth experienced at each location (mesh element) in the watershed during the rainfall-runoff event. Since the degree of flood hazard changes as a function of flood depth magnitude, basin inundation fractions are computed for different thresholds of flood depth. Then, similar to Step 7, the basin inundation fraction for different annual recurrence intervals is computed using a non-parametric distribution.  Step 9.  Estimation of population flood exposure for annual recurrence intervals:  The number of people impacted by flooding across the entire basin for each rainfall-runoff event in Step 6 is computed by overlaying the resulting flood inundation map, associated with a specific flood depth, onto spatial census data. An annual series of people affected by flooding is obtained by retaining the highest number of people impacted by flooding for each synthetic year. Then, similar to peak flows (Step 7) and basin inundation fractions (Step 8), a non-parametric distribution is used to compute the number of people affected by flooding for different annual recurrence intervals.  Step 10.  Estimation of SST uncertainty:  Uncertainty bounds are computed for different annual recurrence intervals in the estimation of peak flows (Step 7), basin inundation fractions (Step 8), and population flood exposure (Step 9). This is achieved by performing new sets of rainfall-runoff simulations (Step 6) with new storm realizations generated in Step 3. In other words, Steps 6 to 9 are repeated for N   realizations of Step 3, from which the uncertainty bounds of the outputs of the N   realizations are derived. These bounds represent the uncertainty caused by the resampling and transposition of parent storms (Step 3).     Steps 8 and 9 denote the specific contributions within the FFA-SST framework presented in this study. Importantly, one of the most appealing features of the FFA-SST framework is to avoid using the assumption of 1:1 return period equivalence between rainfall and modeled peak flow such as the one presented in the “design storm” method. Instead, it allows the watershed initial conditions to modulate the transformation of rainfall quantiles into peak flow quantiles (Wright et al., 2017 ). This same rationale extends to the frequency analysis of basin inundation fractions (flood hazard) and the number of people exposed to flooding (flood exposure), which are explored for the first time in this study. In other words, a 100-year peak flow does not necessarily produce the 100-year basin inundation fraction. Similarly, the 100-year basin inundation fraction does not need to produce the 100-year flood exposure. This flexibility is possible because the FFA-SST framework calculates the annual frequency distributions directly from a sampled population of each variable of interest. These differences among the mapping and modulation of annual recurrence intervals among peak flow, basin inundation fraction, and flood exposure, and their implication to flood risk management are further explained in the discussion section. 2.1 Stochastic storm transposition We used the open-source Python package RainyDay (Wright et al., 2017 ) to conduct SST in our case study. RainyDay is designed to perform SST with gridded rainfall data, facilitating flood frequency analysis (Perez et al., 2019b, 2021; Yu et al., 2023, 2020; Wright et al., 2020 ). RainyDay’s SST methodology incorporates the steps described in the previous section and includes the following key components: (i) Compilation of a storm catalog, comprising the m   largest temporally non-overlapping storms within a transposition domain, using an n  -year gridded rainfall dataset. These storms have the same rainfall accumulation, duration, and share the size, shape, and orientation of the targeted watershed to transpose events. (ii) Random generation of an annual storm count, denoted as k  , following a Poisson distribution. (iii) Random selection of k   storms from the storm catalog. (iv) Random transposition of the associated rainfall fields for each selected storm in east–west and north–south directions. (v) The transposed storms are saved and associated with a synthetic year. Steps (ii) to (v) are repeated a user-specified number of times, denoted as T  m a x    , to provide the desired number of synthetic years. For more details of RainyDay’s capabilities and limitations, see Wright et al. (2013) .  2.2 Integrated surface-subsurface hydrological model We used Amanzi–ATS (Coon et al., 2020, 2019 ) model as an ISSHM for our case study. ATS is a parallel, spatially resolved hydrological model for integrated surface-subsurface flow and transport processes. It includes multiple physical processes and can operate at high spatial (meter scale) and temporal (sub-daily) resolutions. ATS is a spatially-resolved model where the watershed surface is represented by an unstructured mesh that allows for variable spatial resolution, thereby concentrating computational resources on hydrologically critical areas such as the river channel and floodplains. Leveraging this capability, ATS represents the river corridor topography using elongated quadrilateral cells along river centerlines, while triangles are used in the rest of the domain. This approach yields model performance similar to highly refined meshes but with significantly reduced computational cost (Rathore et al., 2024 ). Regarding physics, ATS accounts for water fluxes and storage changes within a 3D domain, covering surface, subsurface, canopy, and snowpack interactions. Subsurface flow is modeled with the 3D Richards equation, while overland flow is modeled using the diffusive wave equation for solving the 2D St. Venant equations. The model ensures continuity of both pressure and flux between the surface and subsurface. Additionally, it represents snow and canopy water dynamics at each surface grid cell through simple differential equation-based models. The modeling of water fluxes includes mechanisms for snow interception, accumulation, sublimation, and melt, as well as canopy interception and transpiration, and bare-ground evaporation. ATS uses a modified Priestley–Taylor model for potential evaporation and a single-layer radiation balance for evapotranspiration modeling. Detailed descriptions and mathematical formulations in ATS are available in Bhanja et al. (2023)  and Li et al. (2023) . Overall, ATS’s performance in community benchmarks has consistently affirmed its reliability among different ISSHMs (Kollet et al., 2017 ). Importantly, ATS has been proved to capture hydrological processes, including evapotranspiration and streamflow, without the need for model calibration, but instead relying on prior information and spatially distributed datasets encompassing vegetation, land cover, topography, and soil properties (Bhanja et al., 2023 ).     3 Case study We selected the Village Creek basin in Southeast Texas, US, with the USGS streamflow gauge 08041500 at the basin outlet and drainage area of 2227 km  2    , as our testbed (Fig. 2 a). The domain population is 20,739 based on data from the Texas Water Development Board (Texas Water Development Board, 2023 ), which uses LandScan population estimates (Weber et al., 2022 ) to provide building datasets with population counts (Fig. 2 b). The main populated areas within the basin include Woodville, Wildwood, Warren, and Ivanhoe. This basin has a topographic gradient from 4.5 m at the basin outlet to 147 m at the most upstream location (Fig. 2 c). According to the National Land Cover Dataset (NLCD) (Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium, 2021 ), the land cover varies, with 49% Evergreen Forest, 15% Woody Wetlands, 9% Grassland/Herbaceous, 9% Mixed forest, and 18% developed and other land covers (Fig. 2 d). Subsurface characteristics from the Soil Survey Geographic Database (SSURGO) (United States Department of Agriculture, Natural Resources Conservation Service, 2021 ), reveal porosity values ranging from 0.3 to 0.5 in the topsoil (Fig. 2 e), while the Global Hydrogeology Maps (GLHYMPS) (Gleeson, 2018 ) indicate porosity values between 0.05 and 0.25. Data on soil depth extracted from Pelletier et al. (2016)  shows variations from 5 m to 50 m (see supplemental material). 3.1 Model setup and model performance evaluation This section describes the details for implementing the FFA-SST framework in our case study using the ATS and RainyDay models. This implementation follows the steps established in Section 2 . Our SST analysis uses the Stage-IV hourly rainfall data (Du, 2011 ) with 4 × 4 km spatial resolution covering the period from 2002 to 2021. The transposition domain (Step 1, Section 2 ) is delineated as a geographical polygon bounded by longitudes 85.15°W to 96.34°W and latitude 31.55°N, extending to the Gulf of Mexico’s coastline (Fig. 2 a). This domain was chosen based on its meteorological homogeneity, as evidenced by a consistent topographical gradient and the spatial distribution of extreme storm events’ statistical parameters (mean and standard deviation) from 2002 to 2021 (see supplemental material). From the Stage-IV dataset, we initially selected 400 parent storm events (Step 2, Section 2 ) spanning three days each. These events were subjected to a detailed visual examination to identify and exclude any data anomalies, such as radar blockages or leakages, leading to the removal of 12 storms and resulting in 388 parent storms. We then generated 500 synthetic years of storm data (Step 3, Section 2 ), applying a Poisson distribution in RainyDay with an expected number of 20 storms per year. For each synthetic year, only the storm with the highest total precipitation was retained, yielding a dataset representing 500 synthetic years, with one storm per year. This process was replicated 10 times to assess uncertainty (Step 10, Section 2 ), producing a dataset of 5000 storms or 10 realizations of 500 synthetic years. The decision to focus solely on the most severe storm event per year aimed to optimize the computational demands of hydrological simulations within ATS. This choice is elaborated upon in the discussion section. To construct the ATS model for Village Creek, we used the Watershed Workflow Python package (Coon and Shuai, 2022 ) to create a mixed-polygonal surface mesh, incorporating channel elements as elongated quadrilateral and polygonal elements with triangles away from the channel (Rathore et al., 2024 ). The resulting model domain encompasses 109,817 surface elements and is uniformly extruded to form 17 subsurface layers, with depths ranging from 5 cm at the top to 10 m at the bottom, for a total of 1.9 million cells. This setup resulted in an average surface element size of 138 m, varying from 7 to 222 m. This resolution aims to balance computational efficiency with a reasonable depiction of flood mapping at the basin scale. The impact of ATS mesh resolution on the analysis of flood inundation areas is discussed further in Section 5 . ATS parameters (Step 4, Section 2 ) were established based on a priori  information and extensive spatial datasets, which include soil properties from the SSURGO and GLYHMPS datasets, following the approach of Bhanja et al. (2023) . Unlike Bhanja et al. (2023) , we incorporate spatially variable roughness coefficients (Manning’s coefficient) dependent on land cover, based on values found in U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (2023) . For Manning’s coefficient in river channels, we used the values reported by Zheng et al. (2022) , which uses Manning’s coefficients as a function of stream order and were estimated for the southeast Texas region, which encompasses our testbed, Village Creek. The Supplemental material provides an exhaustive description of the model parameters used in this case study. Long-term hydrological simulations spanning from 2001 to 2021 were conducted for model evaluation (Step 5, Section 2 ), using meteorological data sourced from DayMet. DayMet provides data with a 1 km spatial resolution and a daily temporal resolution, encompassing variables such as rainfall, relative humidity, air temperature, surface temperature, and incident shortwave radiation. The evaluation focused on a multi-objective approach including streamflow, evapotranspiration, soil moisture content, and changes in water storage. Modeled streamflow at the basin outlet is compared to measurements at USGS gauge 08041500. Modeled evapotranspiration is compared to data spanning from 2010 to 2020 from the SSEbop model (Senay et al., 2013 ) extracted from Climate Engine (Huntington et al., 2017 ), which leverages remotely sensed observations to form a mixed model-observation product. Soil moisture content in the top soil was evaluated by using the NASA SPoRT-LiS product (Kumar et al., 2006 ), with data available for the period from October 2015 to March 2016. Finally, changes in water storage from 2003 to 2021 within the watershed were compared to data from NASA’s GRACE-FO products (Landerer and Swenson, 2012 ), including the product versions from the processing centers Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) and the Center for Space Research (CSR) at the University of Texas, Austin. A second focus of our multi-objective evaluation process centered on ATS’s performance in capturing flood events, both peak flows and flood extents. Specifically, we evaluate the ATS performance in capturing the top 40 extreme rainfall-runoff events from 2002 to 2021. These events were selected based on the peak flow from the hourly USGS streamflow observations, where a 10-day time window was used to avoid overlapping events. In addition, since the long-term simulations were conducted using DayMet, which has a daily resolution, we conducted a separate set of ATS hydrological simulations with a Stage-IV dataset with an hourly rainfall resolution to quantify the impact of temporal rainfall resolution in flood hydrographs. The rainfall-runoff simulations using Stage-IV were initialized with initial conditions extracted from the long-term simulations of daily rainfall from DayMet. We remark that for this process, Stage-IV data was used only for conducting rainfall-runoff simulations of the top 40 rainfall-runoff events. The decision to use Stage IV solely for these 40 events, rather than for the entire 20-year period, is based on two critical considerations. First, while Stage-IV offers a finer temporal resolution, its data is susceptible to radar beam attenuation and blockage issues, limiting its utility to specific events where data integrity can be ensured. Second, the computational burden of processing two decades of hourly rainfall data in ATS simulations is substantial; simulating only the top 40 events is a more practical approach. To evaluate the ability of ATS to capture flood inundation maps, we used the flood inundation map from Hurricane Harvey in 2017, provided by Wang et al. (2023) , as a benchmark. This map was generated with the Python package GeoFlood (Zheng et al., 2018 ), using the Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) method (Nobre et al., 2011 ) and flow depths computed from synthetic rating curves based on the maximum flow rates from the National Water Model (NWM). The spatial and temporal resolutions of all the datasets used in the multi-objective evaluation process are detailed in Table 1 . For the simulations of the 5000 rainfall-runoff events (Step 6, Section 2 ), the initial conditions for each rainfall-runoff simulation were randomly paired with season-like conditions drawn from historical long-term simulations. Following this, as outlined in Steps 7 through 9 in Section 2 , the outputs from these simulations were used to calculate frequency curves up to a 500-year return period for peak flows, basin inundation fractions, and population flood exposure. In terms of computational resources, ATS hydrological runs were conducted using the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center’s (NERSC) high-performance computer Perlmutter, equipped with CPU nodes (AMD EPYC 7763), each containing 128 cores. Based on the Village Creek mesh configuration, we have determined that the optimal efficiency for hydrological runs is achieved using 7 nodes (896 cores), which allows for an average estimation of 70 h for 20 years of long-term hydrological simulations and an average of 6 min for a seven-day rainfall-runoff simulation.      4 Results 4.1 Model evaluation ATS’s ability to capture hydrological processes is evidenced by its strong agreement with observed streamflow data (Fig. 3 a), as well as by the accurate representation of spatially integrated evapotranspiration (Fig. 3 d), soil moisture content (Fig. 3 e), and changes in water storage (Fig. 3 f) against reference datasets. The hourly streamflow outputs at the basin outlet demonstrated a relatively good match with the observed streamflow, achieving a modified-Kling–Gupta Efficiency (mKGE) of 0.77. A mKGE of 1 denotes a perfect match with observations, while a score of 0 suggests accuracy no better than using the mean of the observed data. In comparison, streamflow estimates from the calibrated NWM Version 2 (Cosgrove et al., 2024 ) recorded a mKGE of 0.66 at this gauge. The monthly evapotranspiration signal reported by SSEBop closely matches the observed ATS output with an mKGE of 0.98, with monthly evapotranspiration ranging from 25 to 180 mm/month. The soil moisture content in the top 2 m from August 2015 to March 2016 closely mirrors the reference dataset from NASA’s SPoRT-LiS with an mKGE of 0.68, with ATS’s relative soil moisture values ranging from 20% to 70%. Although the time span for evaluating soil moisture content in the top 2 m is quite limited (only 7 months), it provides an important reference that bolsters confidence in the ATS’s robustness in representing soil moisture conditions. ATS closely matches the reference GRACE-FO dataset for water storage with an mKGE of 0.79 for GRACE-FO JPL and 0.85 for GRACE-FO CSR, with ATS fluctuations ranging from −0.5 to 0.2 m, with the primary discrepancy, observed mainly in 2011 and 2012, likely due to the extreme dynamics caused by the extraordinary Texas drought during that period (Nielsen-Gammon, 2012 ). The reference dataset GRACE-FO offers a significantly coarser spatial resolution (rectangular pixel area of 90,000 km  2    ) compared to the area of the Village Creek basin (2227 km  2    ); we presume that the close agreement with GRACE products for Village Creek likely stems from the homogeneity of water storage changes across the Southeast Texas region. Regarding ATS’s effectiveness in simulating extreme flood events, we found that for the analyzed top 40 rainfall-runoff events during 2002–2021, the resulting flood hydrographs are better captured using Stage-IV rainfall in comparison to DayMet data, with a median mKGE of 0.67 for Stage-IV and 0.57 for DayMet (Fig. 4 a). The results from the NWM exhibited an average mKGE of 0.51. When we focused on the peak flow magnitude of these 40 events, the simulations with Stage-IV again showed superior performance, exhibiting a percentage bias of 7.47%, compared to 22.32% for DayMet and 31.13% for the NWM (Fig. 4 b). This comparison underscores the importance of using hourly rainfall data (Stage-IV) inputs for modeling extreme flood events at Village Creek.   To assess the ability of ATS to represent flooded areas during Hurricane Harvey in August 2017, we set a flood depth threshold of 0.5 m to generate flood inundation extents from both ATS and GeoFlood (Fig. 5 ). We found that the ATS model achieved a True Positive (TP, area where both the predicted and reference maps classify the pixel as flooded) area of 173 km  2     and a True Negative (TN, area where both maps classify the pixel as not flooded) area of 1930 km  2    . However, it also produced a False Positive (FP, area where the predicted map classifies the pixel as flooded, but the reference map classifies it as not flooded) area of 47 km  2     and a False Negative (FN, the predicted map classifies the pixel as not flooded, but the reference map classifies it as flooded) area of 82 km  2    , resulting in a positive predictive value ((TP)/(TP+  FP)) of 79%. In terms of basin inundation fraction, we found that using a flood threshold of 0.5 m resulted in similar basin inundation fractions during Hurricane Harvey for both ATS and GeoFlood, with 13.7% for ATS and 14.1% for GeoFlood. However, the population flood exposure derived from these maps shows that GeoFlood identifies 452 people within flooded areas, while ATS identifies 980 people. Because Hurricane Harvey is an extraordinary event, this is not necessarily representative of the distribution of flood extents caused by all the storm events simulated in our FFA-SST implementation; however, at least this serves as an indicator of the error induced due to the coarser mesh resolution. The implications of mesh resolution in flood hazard and population flood exposure are further explained in the discussion section.     4.2 Frequency analysis: Peak flows, basin inundation fractions, and flood exposure The peak flow quantiles at the basin outlet, estimated using the FFA-SST framework, are shown in Fig. 6 a. For comparative purposes, we also present peak flow quantiles derived from an 86-year period (1924 to 2022, with 13 years of missing data) of annual peak flow records. These records were analyzed using two distinct data-driven approaches: the parametric approach of Bulletin 17C, which uses the Log-Pearson Type 3 distribution, and the non-parametric empirical probability distribution method. Bulletin 17C integrates advanced statistical techniques, including enhanced outlier detection and the Expected Moments Algorithm for a more accurate estimation of statistical moments (England et al., 2019 ). In contrast, the empirical probability distribution uses the Weibull plotting position formula. Additionally, we reported peak flow estimates using the regional regression equation developed by the USGS for undeveloped watersheds in Texas (Asquith and Roussel, 2009 ). Notably, all peak flow estimates closely align for return periods up to 20 years. Beyond this threshold, discrepancies begin to emerge, with Bulletin 17C and the empirical methods indicating higher peak flow values than those estimated from FFA-SST. Conversely, the regional equation presents lower estimates compared to FFA-SST. For analyzing the annual recurrence intervals of flood inundation maps, we calculated the frequency curve of basin inundation fractions up to a 500-year return period for various flood depth thresholds (Fig. 7 a). It is important to note that approximately 1% of the total drainage area is comprised of water bodies, including rivers and lakes, which provides a baseline for assessing the extent of basin inundation fractions. Looking at the results for the 0.5 m threshold, we observed that the basin inundation fraction increases from 7.5% for a 10-year return period to 12.5% for a 100-year return period, and further to 16% for a 500-year return period. Our analysis revealed that the Basin Inundation Fraction (BIF) exhibits a power-law increase relative to the logarithm of the return period, T r   , as B I F = a × log ( T r )   b     , where b  , the scaling exponent, varies from 0.44 at a flood depth threshold of 0.1 m to 0.64 for thresholds of 1 m. Frequency curves for population flood exposure (Fig. 8 a) offer a basin-scale perspective, quantifying the expected number of people affected during a flood event across the entire basin. In specific, for a flood depth threshold of 0.5 m, we observed that the expected number of people affected by flooding increased from 800 individuals for a 10-year return period to 1100 for a 100-year period and further to 1400 for a 500-year return period. Similar to the frequency curves of basin inundation fraction, these curves exhibit a scaling relationship with the logarithm of the return period. In particular, the scaling exponent increases from 0.6 for a flood depth of 0.1 m to 1.03 for a flood depth of 1 m.     5 Discussion The evaluation of ATS for various hydrological variables, including streamflow, evapotranspiration, soil moisture content, changes in water storage, peak flows, and flood inundation extent, provides confidence in its robust, process-based representation of hydrological processes. This comprehensive evaluation underlines the ATS capability to simulate the complex interplay of flood-driving processes adequately, thereby enhancing our predictive capabilities regarding flood behavior. The differences in peak flow quantile estimates from FFA-SST compared to data-driven approaches such as Bulletin 17C, empirical distribution, and regional regression can be attributed to the fundamental nature of each approach. Data-driven approaches rely on the assumption of stationarity and depend on the availability of a long period of peak flow observations, dating back to 1924 for our case study. Notably, the annual peak flow records include the extraordinary flood from Hurricane Harvey, shown in Fig. 6  as the maximum value in the empirical distribution. This extraordinary flood event, being 2.5 times larger than the second-highest peak flow on record, is expected to heavily influence quantile estimates from non-parametric and parametric distributions (Heidarpour et al., 2017 ). For example, based on the empirical distribution, the peak flow during Hurricane Harvey has an estimated return period of approximately 90 years. However, this estimate is limited by the length of available observations, as this method cannot determine return periods beyond this range. In contrast, FFA-SST estimates do not require the assumption of stationarity, as the peak flow outputs reflect the meteorological conditions observed over the 20 years of rainfall data used in SST. Despite FFA-SST can offer significant advantages in capturing flood dynamics, it is crucial to acknowledge its limitations. Its applicability is restricted to watersheds with clearly definable transposition domains, a task that becomes challenging in areas characterized by complex topographies and variable rainfall patterns (Zhou et al., 2019 ). Also, the variability of storm events generated from SST is limited by the observed variability of precipitation inputs used within the transposition domain Wright et al. (2020) . Furthermore, hydrological interpretations derived from FFA-SST are subject to uncertainties inherent in the hydrological modeling process. Nonetheless, these uncertainties can be significantly mitigated through the deployment of exhaustive model evaluation strategies, such as the multi-objective model evaluation employed in this study. The extension of FFA-SST from peak flows to basin inundation fraction and population flood exposure opens the doors to studying flood risk in a more comprehensive view. In particular, studying the frequency curves of basin inundation fractions and population flood hazards can provide new insights into understanding flood risk at the regional scale. This holistic perspective is crucial as it enables the development of flood mitigation strategies on a regional level, transcending the focus from individual areas to a broader outlook. For instance, understanding these curves and the resulting spatial distribution of population flood hazard could inform strategic planning for resource allocation and aid distribution, ensuring that resources are directed towards the most critical regions across the domain. In terms of specific studies on these frequency curves, future analysis on what controls the power-law scaling of the frequency curves of basin inundation fractions and population flood hazards will be critical to understanding the interplay between the previously reported scaling characteristics on watersheds (e.g. river networks Rinaldo et al., 1998; Rodriguez-Iturbe and Rinaldo, 1997 , topography Le and Kumar, 2014; Dodds and Rothman, 2000 , peak flows Perez et al., 2018a,b, 2019a ) and human planning decisions (e.g., territorial development plans for urban areas) for managing flood risk effectively at both the regional and basin scales. In terms of flooding realism, the topography-resolving nature of ATS allows rivers and flooded areas to emerge from the mesh, allowing to represent pluvial flooding, backwater effects, and intermittently active channels (e.g., stormwater drainage, ephemeral streams, etc.), whereas they are typically not represented in network-based models or rainfall-runoff models. A key aspect of the potential use of an ISSHM, such as ATS, for flood inundation mapping lies in balancing the need for high mesh resolution to resolve inundation versus computational cost accurately. Recent studies that integrate both hydrologic and hydraulic dynamics at high-resolution scales have illustrated this challenge for large-scale applications of flood mapping (Cea et al., 2022; Xia et al., 2019; Dey et al., 2022 ). For our case study, despite the ATS surface mesh being coarser, with an average surface element size of 138 m (ranging from 7 to 222 m), compared to the 3-m resolution inundation map produced by GeoFlood, the positive predictive value in flood extent in ATS of 79% demonstrates that overall flood patterns are reasonably represented, and they may offer a valuable first-order approximation for understanding the broad dynamics of flood extent at the basin scale. However, when it comes to assessing flood exposure for populations, even minor inaccuracies in these maps can drastically change the estimated impact on residential areas and the broader population. This discrepancy is evident in the differing numbers of individuals identified within flood zones during Hurricane Harvey by GeoFlood (452 people) and ATS (980 people). Future research that uses high-resolution, topography-informed downscaling or interpolation methods, akin to those used in the HAND approach for generating flood inundation maps, could enhance the accuracy of predictions beyond the current mesh resolution’s capabilities. A key advantage of the FFA-SST framework is its ability to avoid assuming a direct one-to-one annual recurrence interval relationship among precipitation, peak flows, flood impact, and flood exposure. This means that a 100-year storm event does not necessarily result in a 100-year peak flow event, allowing the initial soil moisture condition and the spatial structure of rainfall fields to influence the rainfall-runoff translation. Similarly, a 100-year peak flow event does not automatically lead to a 100-year basin inundation fraction, and a 100-year basin inundation fraction does not necessarily result in the 100-year number of people affected by flooding. This flexibility is made possible because the FFA-SST framework calculates the annual frequency distributions directly from a sampled population (5000 rainfall-runoff simulations) of each variable of interest. In other words, the mapping between probability distributions is a non-injective transformation where there is no one-to-one correspondence between the recurrence intervals of precipitation, peak flows, flood impacts, and flood exposure (Fig. 9 ). This result is unique as it demonstrates for the first time, based on physical-based hydrological simulations, the complex relationship between these variables. A critical aspect that needs further exploration is a comprehensive understanding of what controls the modulation from rainfall to peak flows, then to flooding, and finally to flood exposure. For instance, antecedent soil moisture is considered a first-order control in modulating the transition from rainfall to peak flows. Regarding the modulation between peak flows and inundation areas, backwater effects, pluvial flooding in poorly drained areas, and intermittently active channels are likely to play a significant role. In terms of population exposure, socio-economical decisions on settlements and urban planning will play a critical role in the intersection of flooded areas with population centers and residential zones. Overall, future studies dissecting these relationships would be key for developing more accurate flood risk management and mitigation strategies.  The observation that the 100-year basin inundation fraction does not always equate to the 100-year population flood exposure highlights how two flood events with the same basin inundation fraction can yield very different internal flood patterns, affecting varying numbers of people. To demonstrate this concept, we compare the basin inundation fraction and population flood exposure resulting from two distinct storm events (Storm 1 and Storm 2), which generate approximately the same 100-year peak flow at the basin outlet (Fig. 10 ). Both events were selected from the 5000 rainfall-runoff events conducted in FFA-SST. Despite both storms producing a similar peak flow magnitude at the basin outlet, their respective impacts and flood exposure differ markedly at the regional scale (right panels of Fig. 10 ). In particular, Storm 1 is characterized by a peak flow of 2525 m  3   / s    with a 100-year return period, a total three-day precipitation of 386 mm (100-year return period), a basin inundation fraction of 11% (40-year return period) for a 0.5-m flood depth threshold, and a population flood exposure of 1002 people (50-year return period). In contrast, Storm 2 has a similar peak flow at the outlet (2529 m  3   / s   , 100-year return period) but results from a significantly higher total three-day precipitation of 480 mm (250-year return period). This leads to a higher basin inundation fraction of 14% (180-year return period) and a larger population flood exposure of 1189 people (100-year return period). Overall, the detailed breakdown of these metrics underlines the strength of the FFA-SST framework in offering more precise and differentiated insights into flood risks, which are critical for stakeholders engaged in flood mitigation planning. It is important to note, as outlined in Section 2  describing the FFA-SST steps, that more than one storm event can be included in a synthetic year to expand the catalog of extreme storm events. In our approach, we simulate only the most extreme storm event per synthetic year to maintain the feasibility of numerically simulating 5000 flood events, a process that is highly computationally demanding. Nonetheless, future studies should consider simulating additional storm events per synthetic year to assess their impact on flood hazard and exposure more comprehensively.    6 Conclusions This study presented a novel application of process-based Flood Frequency Analysis using Stochastic Storm Transposition (FFA-SST) with an Integrated Surface-Subsurface Hydrological Model (ISSHM) to compute flood hazard and flood exposure up to a 500-year return period for a watershed of 2227 km  2     drainage area in Texas, US. This was achieved through the use of the ISSHM Amanzi–ATS, which was used to simulate the flood response of 5000 synthetic storm events created from the SST model, RainyDay. The key contributions of our research to the FFA-SST framework are outlined in the following three points: 1. The ATS hydrological model, which does not require calibration and relies on prior information and extensive spatial datasets for parameter definition, was used in FFA-SST. This approach was supported by multi-objective model evaluation in streamflow, evapotranspiration, soil moisture content, water storage change, flood hydrographs, peak flows, and flood inundation mapping.  2. Flood hazard was analyzed by calculating frequency curves of basin inundation fractions up to a 500-year return period. This was made possible since ATS is a topography-resolving model that uses the 2D shallow water equation, leading naturally to the emergence of rivers and flooded areas in the landscape.  3. Population flood exposure at the basin scale up to a 500-year return period was assessed by overlaying ATS generated flood inundation maps with spatial census data.    By integrating the FFA-SST framework with an ISSHM like ATS, we provide a holistic method for modeling flood dynamics across entire basins through a detailed, physics-based understanding of hydrological processes. This approach is particularly compelling because the ATS operates without the need for calibration, relying solely on prior information and extensive spatial data. This is crucial for modeling hydrological systems influenced by both natural and human perturbations while avoiding equifinality issues. This aspect is highly relevant for future studies aimed at predicting flood estimates that incorporate changes in land use. Overall, our vision is that the key end-user metrics derived from the FFA-SST framework with an ISSHM, such as the frequency curves of basin inundation fractions and the number of people affected by flooding at the basin scale, can revolutionize regional-scale flood impact analysis. These metrics can serve as a powerful resource for stakeholders, guiding the planning of flood mitigation strategies at a regional scale. Future research should focus on leveraging ISSHMs to enhance the granularity and accuracy of flood impact analyses. This includes incorporating key flood properties such as the duration of flood events and their flow velocity. Such a nuanced approach will allow for a detailed understanding of flood events and associated risks, thereby providing a more comprehensive view of the potential impacts on infrastructure, ecosystems, and communities. We acknowledge that the accuracy of flood extents derived from our application of the ATS in this case study represents a coarse approximation of the actual flood extent. This limitation highlights the need for further research. Our frequency curves for flood hazard and population flood exposure should be viewed as preliminary approximations, showcasing the potential of integrating FFA-SST with an ISSHM. Future studies should aim to enhance mesh resolution to finer scales, while carefully balancing the trade-off between the need for detailed resolution and the significant computational resources required by ISSHMs.
1 Introduction Floods, triggered by intense rainfall and unfavorable geography, rank among the most impactful natural disasters (Chen, 2022; IPCC, 2023; Khosravi et al., 2018; Pham et al., 2021 ). From 1970 to 2019, they comprised 44% of global disasters, causing 31% of economic losses (IPCC, 2023 ). China, heavily impacted, averaged 149 million affected individuals annually, with 2165 fatalities and $340 billion in losses from 1990 to 2017 (Du et al., 2019 ). With climate change and human interference, future floods are expected to worsen (Didovets et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2021 ). Despite societal and technological advances, effective flood mitigation remains limited, especially in vulnerable regions lacking comprehensive risk analysis. Given the complexity of floods, tailored risk assessments are crucial for formulating suitable management plans and implementing effective mitigation measures (Costache et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2021; Ogie et al., 2018 ). Due to the complexity of floods, the strategies for addressing them vary depending on the circumstances in different flood-prone regions. Therefore, flood risk assessment plays a crucial role in devising appropriate flood management plans and implementing effective flood prevention measures (Costache et al., 2023; Deroliya et al., 2022 ). Flood risk assessment, an extension of natural disaster risk evaluation, aligns with the fundamental theory of disaster risk systems. Risk arises from the interaction of natural and societal factors, defined as the likelihood of adverse outcomes due to climate change (Smith, 2013 ). This probability involves intricate interactions among hazard, exposure, and vulnerability, theoretically expressed as the probability of hazard events or trends occurring and their impact product (Bin et al., 2023; IPCC, 2021; Kron, 2005 ). Flood hazard is defined as the potential risk of floods causing harm or damage to individuals, properties, or other entities, emphasizing the inherent natural attributes of flood disasters (Mudashiru et al., 2021 ). The characteristics of flood exposure involve the sensitivity of individuals, livelihoods, species, ecosystems, tangible assets, services, and resources to flood impact (Rentschler et al., 2022 ). Vulnerability manifests as the combined socio-economic sensitivity, population adaptive capacity, and societal responses in a region (De Brito et al., 2018 ). This study necessitates simultaneous consideration of three key subsystems in flood risk assessment: hazards, exposure, and vulnerability. Despite comprehensive past research analyzing these elements, their interactions have been overlooked (Bin et al., 2023; Chang and Huang, 2015 ). These interrelationships influence the occurrence and evolution of disasters, resulting in complex and variable characteristics. Recognizing these interactions among subsystems is crucial for understanding the potential impact of flood risk in assessments, an aspect often insufficiently explored in comprehensive flood risk studies (Kai et al., 2017 ). Creating fundamental flood risk maps is crucial for precise risk management in flood risk assessment (Cunha et al., 2017 ). Scholars have proposed various mapping methods, including statistical analysis (Arabameri et al., 2019; Collet et al., 2018 ), hydrological and hydraulic models (Grimaldi et al., 2016; Jane et al., 2018 ), multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) (Daksiya et al., 2021; De Brito et al., 2019 ), and machine learning (Bui et al., 2023; Saravanan et al., 2023 ). Statistical analysis and machine learning require extensive historical flood data (Saha et al., 2022; Siahkamari et al., 2018 ), while hydrological and hydraulic models necessitate precise data and substantial resources (Deroliya et al., 2022 ). In contrast, the MCDA methods do not rely on historical flood data and exhibit significant flexibility and adaptability. These methods allow stakeholders to participate in the decision-making process and can be tailored to specific needs of the study area to provide flood risk management strategies that better meet community needs (Ali et al., 2020; Kanani-Sadat et al., 2019 ). However, MCDA methods often require parameter setting, and the subjective judgment of experts in parameter setting may affect the objectivity of the assessment (Deroliya et al., 2022; Sherly et al., 2015 ). In recent years, FlowSort, an algorithm tailored for multi-criteria sorting problems, has garnered attention for its effective application in risk assessment, socio-economic analyses, and other domains (Emamat et al., 2022; Lolli et al., 2015; Tu et al., 2023a ). FlowSort is recognized for its reduced demand for parameters, the ability to independently allocate, and fully sort alternative options (Pelissari et al., 2019 ). Nevertheless, there are still certain subjective issues in the setting of the reference profile in FlowSort. To address this issue, this study introduces a novel flood risk grading evaluation method, the DBSCAN-FlowSort method, which combines clustering technology with sorting algorithms. Additionally, determining the weights of input indicators is essential in implementing this method. Previous flood risk assessment studies commonly relied on methods like the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) (Bhuyan et al., 2023 ) and the Entropy Weight Method (EWM) (Tu et al., 2023b ) for weight calculation. While AHP is favored for its simplicity, its inherent subjectivity has sparked debate in the academic community. Conversely, although EWM offers objective weights based on data, it may struggle with decision-makers’ expertise. This study employs the Decision-Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL) method to incorporate expert considerations of the interplay between indicators. Concurrently, the Probabilistic Linguistic Term Set (PLTS) is introduced to quantify the uncertainty of expert information. The PLTS-DEMATEL method combines the expressive power of probabilistic linguistic sets with the structural analysis capabilities of the DEMATEL approach, offering a flexible and in-depth solution for multi-criteria decision-making (Du and Zhang, 2022 ). Furthermore, this study integrates the EWM to strike a balance between subjectivity and objectivity. The hybrid approach of combining subjective and objective weights is expected to enhance the utility and accuracy of the decision-making process. In summary, this study proposes a novel method for the grading assessment of flood risk, taking the county-level regions of Anhui Province as the subject of research to verify the effectiveness of the method. The specific research objectives and innovations include: (1) To establish a set of flood risk assessment indicators and utilize a novel indicator weighting synthesis method—the PLTS-DEMATEL & EWM method.  (2) To conduct a grading assessment of flood hazard in county-level regions of Anhui Province utilizing the DBSCAN-FlowSort method, a novel multi-criteria sorting approach, and compare it with the traditional FlowSort method.  (3) To analyze flood risk grading assessment results by considering and not considering the interactions between different subsystems, aiming to examine the impact of these interactions on the accuracy and comprehensiveness of the flood risk evaluation.    Based on these research objectives and innovations, this study aims to provide a more scientific and systematic methodology for flood risk assessment and management, thereby offering more effective theoretical support for flood resource allocation in flood risk management. The paper’s structure is outlined as follows: Section 2  details the study region and data sources and the methodological process. Section 3  presents research results and discussions. Section 4  summarizes key findings and proposes future research directions.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study region Anhui Province, situated in central-eastern China between approximately 114°  54 ′    E to 119°  37 ′    E longitude and 29°  41 ′    N to 34°  38 ′    N latitude, spans an area of around 140,000 square kilometers (see Fig. 1 ). It comprises 16 prefecture-level cities and 104 county-level regions, with a permanent population of 61.13 million people as of the end of 2021. The topography is diverse, featuring higher elevations in the southwest and lower elevations in the northeast, characterized by plains, hills, and low mountains. Anhui Province covers the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River, with a complex network of inland waterways.  The climate transitions from north to south, with an average annual precipitation ranging from 700 to 1700 mm. Precipitation is higher in the southern part and lower in the northern part, with mountainous regions receiving more rainfall than plains and hilly regions. Throughout history, the province has grappled with recurring flood-related challenges. About 50% of arable land, 60% of the population, and 70% of the GDP face imminent flood threats. Recent years have witnessed an increase in extreme flood disasters due to global climate change, necessitating urgent comprehensive flood risk management in Anhui Province.  2.2 Data sources Building upon previous research in the field of flood risk assessment and considering the availability of data for this study, we have identified key indicators that influence flood risk from the three subsystems of hazard, exposure, and vulnerability. The indicators utilized in this study are primarily sourced from two channels: one is textual data from the statistical websites of county-level governments in Anhui Province, which includes Crop Sown Area (CSA), Resident Population (RP), Gross Regional Product (GRP), Expenditure on Disaster Prevention and Emergency Management (DPEM), and Healthcare Staff Count (HSC); the other is derived from various geospatial data resource websites, typically in raster or vector format, and processed using ArcGIS 10.8 software. Furthermore, all indicators are categorized into two types: risk indicators and protective indicators. For risk indicators, a higher value signifies a greater flood risk, whereas for protective indicators, the opposite is true. Additionally, this study specifically selected the flood warning data jointly issued by the Department of Water Resources of Anhui Province and the Anhui Meteorological Bureau from July 2021 to June 2022, based on which a historical flood dataset was constructed. This dataset, taking the county-level administrative division as the fundamental unit, provides detailed geographical and hydrological information for flood warning research. Within the scope of this study, areas that have never received flood warning information are clearly demarcated as non-flood areas, while all other regions are defined as flood areas. This categorization aims to streamline the model validation process and facilitate subsequent analytical work. The period for the indicator data used in this study is primarily based on the year 2021, and due to varying degrees of difficulty in data acquisition, some indicators have been substituted with the average values of data from adjacent years, as referenced from past research. A detailed description of the indicators will be presented in the subsequent sections and Table 1 .  (1) Hazard indicators In flood hazard assessment, we have selected a set of key indicators, considering that floods are often associated with multiple factors. The following indicators are included. • Annual Precipitation (AP)  is a pivotal indicator in gauging the susceptibility to flood hazards, as it mirrors the volume of rainfall that may precipitate the occurrence and severity of floods (Ma et al., 2021 ).  • Maximum Monthly Precipitation (MMP)  is an indicator for assessing extreme rainfall events (Liu et al., 2021 ).  • Drainage Network Density (DND)  is the ratio of the total length of rivers within a given area to the total area of that area (Khosravi et al., 2018 ).  • Elevation (EL)  is a significant factor in triggering floods. Areas with lower elevations are more prone to flooding due to water flowing down from higher elevations (Tehrany et al., 2015 ).  • Slope (SL)  is another critical factor influencing flood hazards. Areas with lower slopes are more susceptible to water accumulation, making them more prone to flooding (Tehrany et al., 2013 ).  • Soil Moisture (SM)  is the amount of water in the soil, and high soil moisture means more surface runoff (Ma et al., 2021 ).  • Natural Runoff (NR)  is the natural flow of water from precipitation and snowmelt towards bodies of water, occurring without human intervention. The quantity of natural runoff directly impacts the scale and extent of floods (Suriya and Mudgal, 2012 ).    (2) Exposure indicators A set of indicators to measure the degree of exposure to flooding was selected for the flood exposure assessment, as shown below. • Crop Sown Area (CSA)  serves as an indicator of agricultural vulnerability to flooding, with a larger CSA indicating a higher potential impact on agricultural productivity during flood events (Sun et al., 2020 ).  • Resident Population (RP)  is a crucial indicator of exposure, reflecting the number of people at risk in human settlements. A larger population typically means a greater potential for loss of life and property during floods (Trigila et al., 2015 ).  • Nighttime Artificial Lighting Intensity (NALI)  is a vital indicator for flood exposure assessment. Higher NALI suggests increased urban development and infrastructure, indicating a higher exposure to flood-related risks in these regions (Peng and Zhang, 2022 ).    (3) Vulnerability indicators Vulnerability indicators contribute to a comprehensive assessment of the study region’s susceptibility to and recovery capacity from flood disasters, which can be seen below. • Gross Regional Product (GRP)  reflects the economic size and vitality of an area, serving as an indicator for assessing its resilience to flood shocks (Amadio et al., 2019 ).  • Fractional Vegetation Cover (FVC)  indicates the vulnerability of natural vegetation to floods, with lower values suggesting reduced protective cover and increased susceptibility to related flood risks (Tang et al., 2021 ).  • Road Density (RD)  is linked to impermeable surfaces; higher road density increases impermeable surface area, leading to heightened surface runoff and a significant rise in flood risk (Pham et al., 2021 ).  • Expenditure on Disaster Prevention and Emergency Management (DPEM)  signifies a region’s dedication to readiness and resilience. Increased DPEM indicates a proactive stance in mitigating flood impact, reducing vulnerability (Tu et al., 2023b ).  • Healthcare Staff Count (HSC)  quantifies the level of rescue operations concerning flood disasters (Pham et al., 2021 ).    The spatial distribution of the indicators is shown in Fig. 2  respectively.    2.3 Methodology This study proposes a novel MCDA framework for achieving flood risk grading assessment. The core structure of this framework is based on the FlowSort method within the realm of MCDA. Other methodologies, including the Probability Language Term Set (PLTS) - Decision Experiments and Evaluations Laboratory (DEMATEL), the Entropy Weight Method (EWM), as well as the Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN), are employed to improve the performance of FlowSort. The specific procedure is illustrated in Fig. 3 .   2.3.1 Multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) MCDA is a general term referring to a range of methods that employ structured frameworks to assist decision-makers in considering multiple factors in flood risk assessment and making informed decisions based on comprehensive evaluations (De Brito and Evers, 2016 ). This study adopts an advanced MCDA method—FlowSort. This method is a multi-criteria sorting method based on the PROMETHEE method, distinguished by its ability to flexibly handle both independent assignments and fully ordered categories (Nemery and Lamboray, 2008; Pelissari et al., 2019 ). In flood risk assessment, independent assignments imply that, for each assessment indicator, while the reference profiles remain fixed, the flow rates for the same reference profiles may vary across different regions due to geographical differences. Furthermore, the characteristic of complete sorting in FlowSort facilitates better resource allocation and policy formulation by decision-makers to address potential flood risks (Tu et al., 2023a ). However, considering that FlowSort relies on expert-defined indicator weights, thresholds, and reference profiles, this study improves upon its performance. Firstly, an enhancement is made to the method of calculating indicator weights, utilizing the PLTS-DEMATEL method to account for interdependencies among indicators to obtain subjective weights and the EWM to obtain objective weights, which are then combined as the final indicator weights. Secondly, an improvement is made to the method of extracting reference profiles (Yin et al., 2024 ), where this study utilizes DBSCAN to cluster indicator data and subsequently sets reference profiles based on the clustering results.  2.3.2 The PLTS-DEMATEL & EWM method The DEMATEL method, developed by the Battelle Memorial Institute in the 1970s, is a graph theory tool for analyzing structural models with elements as vertices and causal relationships as edges (Ocampo and Yamagishi, 2020 ). It considers interdependencies between indicators, analyzes causal relationships, and calculates weights for these relationships. While DEMATEL effectively assesses dependencies, it cannot accurately represent expert judgments and preferences as precise numbers (Kanani-Sadat et al., 2019 ). This study proposes an enhanced DEMATEL method, incorporating PLTS and the Dempster–Shafer Evidence Theory (DST), which is applied to address potential ignorance or partial credibility in expert-provided evaluations. This integrated approach mitigates subjective bias in flood risk assessment (Du and Zhang, 2022; Ji and Wang, 2023; Li et al., 2022 ). The procedure is as follows: Step 1.  Input the system elements. System elements are identified in Section 2.2 . Step 2.  Construct the direct-relation matrix through PLTS. (1) According to the PLTS method (for a detailed description of PLTS, please refer to the “A1” section of Supplementary Material S1), experts established a LTS (S = { s  i   | i = − τ , … , − 1 , 0 , 1 , … , τ }    ) to evaluate the degree of interaction between indicators. The LTS used in this study to measure the degree of impact is defined as: τ = − 2   : negligible importance; τ = − 1   : low importance; τ = 0   : moderate importance; τ = 1   : high importance; and τ = 2   : critical importance. Experts use PLTSs to evaluate the interaction between indicators. For example, the u  th expert evaluates the degree of influence of the i  th indicator on the j  th indicator, which can be expressed as L  i j u  ( k )    ( p )  = { L  i j u  ( k )    ( p  ( k )    )  | k = 1 , 2 , … , # L  i j u   ( p )  }    , where u   denotes the number of corresponding experts in which u = 1 , 2 , … , N   . (2) For N   experts, there are a total of N   linguistic term sets L  i j u    ( u = 1 , 2 , … , N )     of the influence of the i  th indicator on the j  th indicator. Here, the DST method (for a detailed introduction to DST, please refer to the “A2” section of Supplementary Material S1) is used to fuse L  i j u     into L  i j    . (3) Since L  i j     is a set linguistic term set, in order to more conveniently combine it with DEMATEL, it needs to be converted into clear numbers, and the expected value of L  i j     can just solve this problem (Wu et al., 2018 ). Step 3.  Normalize the initial direct-relation matrix G = ( g  i j   )   n × n      to G  ̃   = ( g  ̃    i j   )   n × n      by Eq. (1) . As a machine learning clustering method, DBSCAN is recognized for its adaptability to diverse cluster shapes and its proven efficacy in managing potential noise in geographical spatial data (Alsmadi and Alhami, 2015; Hahsler et al., 2019 ). This study innovatively incorporates DBSCAN with FlowSort, which enhances the objectivity of the reference profiles in the FlowSort method, traditionally reliant on expert input. The DBSCAN-FlowSort method is applied to flood risk assessment in this study. The specific steps are as follows: Step 1.  Define the MCDA problem. Let A = { A  1   , A  2   , … , A  m   }     represent the set of m alternatives to be sorted, each of which is evaluated on a set of I = { I  1   , I  2   , … , I  n   }    . The objective of FlowSort is to allocate alternatives of A   to k   predetermined ordered categories, denoted as C  1   , C  2   , … , C  k     . In this study, A   comprises 104 county-level regions awaiting assessment in Anhui, I   represents 15 flood risk indicators, and the definition of categories is provided in Table 2 .  Step 2.  Generate reference profiles. The set R  , consisting of reference profiles r  1   , r  2   , … , r  k + 1     , is obtained through DBSCAN and is used to generate categories. The FlowSort method assumes that the performance of alternatives in set A   falls between the worst reference profile r  k + 1     and the best reference profile r  1    . As categories are completely ordered, each reference profile is considered superior to its subsequent ones (Pelissari et al., 2019 ). This implies that the condition stated afterward is a prerequisite. (7) Condition:   r  1   ≻ r  2   ≻ … ≻ r  k   ≻ r  k + 1        To apply DBSCAN for generating appropriate reference profiles, configuring the neighborhood radius (ɛ  ) and density threshold (min P t s   ) is crucial. In this study, ɛ   is determined based on the change curve of k  -nearest neighbor distances. min P t s    is set based on the data distribution structure and continually adjusted. It is important to note that each indicator’s data is treated independently, requiring separate configuration of parameters “ɛ  ” and “min P t s   ” (for details, refer to the “A4” section of Supplementary Material S1). DBSCAN-generated clusters define their data range by identifying minimum and maximum values within each cluster. Reference profiles are then established by segregating indicator data values according to these cluster-specific ranges. Step 3.  Compute the preference strength. The preference strength, denoted by π ( x , y )    , which quantifies the degree of preference of alternative x   over alternative y   based on the decision maker’s preferences, can be computed for all pairs of alternative ( x , y )    within the set R  i    . It quantifies how much alternative x   outperforms alternative y   with respect to indicator j  . The weight w  j     is computed using Eq.
