Moreover, it is closely linked to the local production and life of the people. Based on the calculations and analyses of the three social impact evaluation indicators, the social impact comprehensive evaluation coefficient of the Luhun Reservoir was taken as 1 in this study after consulting the local people and experts with certain knowledge of the project and combining it with the actual local situation.   3.2 Evaluation results of dam economic life Based on the calculation results of the relative importance of the evaluation indicators, the comprehensive costs and benefits of the operation of the Luhun Reservoir dam were calculated using Eq (16) and (17) . Considering the effect of inflation, the costs and benefits after the 1990 s were discounted to 1990 s levels at the prevailing social discount rate. Table 8   presents the results of the study. Based on the above data, the relationship between comprehensive cost and benefit over time was fitted to obtain a “cost-benefit” relationship curve over time for the Luhun Reservoir. The tipping point was identified as, t* =2031(when potential dam breach losses were not considered, t* =2103). The comprehensive cost change curve was B  (t ) = 1.444t 3  + 323.1t 2 -11420 t  + 33340000 and the comprehensive benefit change curve was C  (t ) = -28.26t 3  + 4238t 2 -232700 t  + 39420000, as shown in Fig. 11  . Based on the tipping point t* , the social impact comprehensive evaluation coefficient for the Luhun Reservoir must be further analyzed to determine its final economic life, as shown in Eq (22) .(22) T = T 0  + t *  - t 0     1 + φ ∑ k = 1  n  W k        = 25 + ( 2031 - 1990 )  1 + 1 × 0.199    = 74.16          According to the above analysis and calculations, the Luhun Reservoir currently operates within its life span and can be maintained in smooth operation while satisfying the safety and economic conditions. Based on the ‘cost-benefit’ relationship, the economic life of the Luhun Reservoir was calculated to be 74.16 years. It is expected to move beyond its economic life span into the non-economic operating range by 2039 s.   4 Discussion The quantified results of the cost-benefit indicators during the operation of the Luhun Reservoir indicated that the loss of potential dam breaches and flood control benefits each accounted for more than 50 % of the comprehensive operating costs and benefits, which have a significant impact on the results of the dam economic life evaluation. In general, reservoirs with greater flood control benefits cause greater losses in the event of dam breaches. Therefore, in the case of large reservoirs wherein flood control is the primary objective, the most effective means of improving their economic life involves reducing the possibility of dam breaches by implementing reasonable control measures in a timely manner from a safety perspective. In addition, the irrigation benefits of the Leuven Reservoir accounted for 20 % of its comprehensive operating benefits. The reservoir's irrigation infrastructure was completed and opened to water in 1974. Therefore, the maintenance of irrigation facilities and reasonable increases in the amount of water supplied by reservoirs for downstream agricultural irrigation could also be effective in increasing the economic life of reservoirs. According to Fig. 11 , the Luhun Reservoir is expected to reach its tipping point by 2031 s. At this time, the comprehensive operation costs of the dam are going to equal to its comprehensive operation benefits. In engineering communities, it is generally accepted that dams have a design life of 50 to 100 years. In this study, the economic life span of the Luhun Reservoir was calculated to be 74 years by comprehensively considering the economics of the reservoir's operation and its positive social impact on local production and life. The reservoir is expected to operate into the non– economic life interval until the 2039 s. According to the analysis in Fig. 11 , reservoir dredging measures can increase the reservoir storage capacity in combination with the actual engineering situation of Luhun Reservoir. However, as the benefits of power generation at Luhun Reservoir are a relatively small part of the total benefits, it is not obvious that the operational life of dams can be improved through improvements in the power generation conditions. With increased water storage in reservoir dams, measures to enhance irrigation benefits can also be undertaken. However, the primary factor limiting irrigation benefits is the level of irrigation facilities when the amount of water used for irrigation is certain. Therefore, we must focus on the maintenance of irrigation facilities while increasing the reservoir storage capacity to effectively extend the economic life of Luhun Reservoir. Compared to existing methods for analyzing the economic life of dams, this study considered the loss of potential dam breaches under conditions of sustained social and economic development, and quantified the 'cost-benefit' relationship under the impact of uncertainty. In this study, a comprehensive social impact evaluation coefficient was introduced to comprehensively analyze the social impact of dams on local production and life, making the final evaluation results more comprehensive and scientific. In addition, an operational economic evaluation and economic life calculation method were proposed for dams rehabilitated with various rehabilitation measures, thus improving the usefulness and completeness of the model. The evaluation model aimed to improve the risk management system for reservoir dams and provide new ideas for the operation and management of reservoir dams. However, owing to the differences in the social situation of each country, the evaluation indicators and certain parameters must be adjusted according to the laws, regulations, and standards of each country in the process of applying the model. And the establishment of a system of indicators and a model for evaluating the economic life of reservoir dams must satisfy the needs of the country's own strategy. In this study, the accuracy of the economic life evaluation was strongly affected by the results of the quantification of the comprehensive costs and benefits of the operation. In this case, the loss of potential dam breaches depends on whether a dam breach occurs and also on the year in which the breach occurs and the economic situation of the inundated area, which is highly uncertain. To ensure the accuracy of the assessment results, the effects of the structural nature of the dam and changes in the surrounding environment over time on the quantitative results should be considered. In addition, owing to the paucity of academic research on dam economic life spans, there is no uniformity in the analysis of the social impacts on economic life spans.  5 Conclusion Based on the analysis of the impact factors on a dam’s economic life, an economic life evaluation indicator system was established in this study considering the impact of potential losses caused by dam breaches. A quantitative method for three types of evaluation indicators, such as cost, benefit, and social impact was proposed. A comprehensive social impact evaluation factor was introduced to consider the social impact of dams on local production and life. Based on cost-benefit theory and economics, the changes characteristic of “cost-benefit” for dams over time were analyzed. A dam economic life evaluation model was constructed. The model was applied to the Luhun Reservoir in Henan Province and was calculated to have an economic life of 74 years based on the quantification of the combined costs and benefits of the Luhun Reservoir and a comprehensive analysis of its social impact factors. According to the calculation analysis, we can extend the economic life of the Luhun Reservoir by maintaining the dam structure or rehabilitating irrigation engineering facilities. However, the accuracy of the model's evaluation results was largely affected by the quantitative results of operating costs and operating benefits, which will be further improved and enhanced in future research and practice.
1 Introduction Essentially, ecosystem services are all the direct and indirect benefits that nature provides to people, which offer a practical guarantee of human production and survival and are closely associated with sustainable development and human welfare (Jia et al., 2014; Immerzeel et al., 2023 ). The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment classifies ecosystem services into four functional categories: regulating, provisioning, supporting, and cultural (Sterling et al., 2013 ). The water retention function refers to the process and ability of an ecosystem to retain water by intercepting, infiltrating, and storing precipitation over a certain space and time period through the forest canopy, litter, soil, lakes, reservoirs, etc. (Shi et al., 2021; Novotny et al., 2023 ); this function is a key component of the attributes and processes that produce water-related ecosystem provisioning services (Li et al., 2021a ). As a branch of Water retention, soil water retention (SWR) is also crucial for maintaining soil water quality, resolving droughts, consolidating soils, improving soil drainage, and conserving water (Qiao et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2022 ). Obtaining quantitative information on the impact of climate and underlying conditions on the water retention of soil and vegetation systems in alpine-cold areas is crucial for ensuring primary water supply productivity and conserving and rationally allocating soil and water resources; it is also crucial for ensuring ecosystem health and sustainable eco-social development (Ma et al., 2022 ; Wojkowsk et al. 2022). Natural processes and conditions play a significant role in providing water-related services (Caro et al., 2020 ). Water retention is affected mainly by the processes of supply, interception, and infiltration, which depend on the climate and hydrological conditions, the structure of the land surface and its exploitation as well as the physical properties of the soil (Pham et al., 2019 ). Previous studies have shown that the factors affecting water retention can be divided into two main categories: climate and underlying surface (Bai et al., 2019; Oliveira et al., 2021 ). As found by Wang et al. (2022)  in their simulation of SWR in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, precipitation and vegetation cover were identified as the primary factors influencing SWR increase in the region, with correlation coefficients of 0.87 and 0.67, respectively. Climate can affect water retention through changes in meteorological variables such as precipitation and temperature (Prodanovic et al., 2019 ). Vegetation cover affects ecosystem water retention through its impact on precipitation and evapotranspiration (Fang et al., 2022 ). Furthermore, topographic features such as elevation and slope affect water production and infiltration, which in turn impact water retention (Yang et al., 2018 ). At the same time, land use and cover (LUC) patterns, as the most obvious consequence of human activities on the ecosystem (Xu et al., 2019 ), affect the water retention of ecosystems by mainly influencing surface evaporation and runoff formation processes, soil infiltration capacity, and groundwater recharge and discharge. (Chen et al., 2022a; Wojkowski et al., 2022 ). An investigation of the influence of the abovementioned climatic and basic condition-related specific elements on regional water retention is of great importance not only for clarifying ecosystem water retention mechanisms but also for rational planning and protecting water resources and maintaining a healthy land surface ecology (Xiao et al., 2020 ). In general, previous studies have evaluated ecosystem water retention by examining small watersheds, with case examples that include measures of soil water storage of precipitation, annual runoff discharge, groundwater recharging, and comprehensive water storage capacity (Butsic et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2019 ). With the advancement of fundamental theories and technological tools, methods of water retention in ecosystems have been continuously enhanced (Schibalski et al., 2022 ). Models that can simulate complex ecohydrological processes are playing an increasingly important role in the evaluation of water-related ecosystem services, which are more extensively evaluated on larger scales (Sharma et al., 2022 ). Included among these models are the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT), the Artificial Intelligence for Ecosystem Services (ARIES), the water balance model (WAB), and the Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Tradeoffs (InVEST) (Wei et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2022 ). Among them, the InVEST model includes a water yield module that facilitates large spatiotemporal scale modeling based on the water balance principle (Dashtbozorgi et al., 2023 ). Ecosystem SWR can be modified by introducing factors that reflect the effects of topography and soil (Li et al., 2021b ). Compared to other models, the InVEST model operates in the gridded map at an average annual time step, which is conducive to long-term and continuous estimation with an expression of spatial heterogeneity, particularly the incorporation of ArcGIS in the last few decades (Benra et al., 2021 ). By a wide margin, the InVEST model has been utilized in the evaluation of numerous ecosystem services, and it has accomplished significant and trustworthy studies (Hu et al., 2020 ). From the ecohydrological point of view, when the water storage method is used to evaluate the water conservation capacity of ecosystems, soil water storage capacity is considered to be one of the most important evaluation indicators (Gao et al., 2023; Ng and Peprah-Manu, 2023 ), that is, the SWR determined using the InVEST model, which makes the assessment of ecosystem water conservation more concrete (Rafiei-Sardooi et al., 2022; Wang and Xu, 2022 ). Although the InVEST model combining the hydraulic, topographic, and soil element modeling of SWR has been widely used by numerous researchers to assess the regional SWR, comprehensive quantification of the effects of climate and underlying surface variability on regional SWR is rare (Daneshi et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022; Zou et al., 2022 ). More specifically, this study aims to fill a gap in assessing the relative contribution of climate, vegetation, topography and LUC to SWR on long time and vast spatial scales, especially in alpine-cold river source areas (Qiao et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022 ). Proper resolution of the above scientific issues provides policy-makers with theoretical guidance to mitigate interregional water conflicts, which is essential for the protection of delicate alpine ecosystems and regional water balance (Gao et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023 ). The SGP stands as a quintessential example of the alpine-cold river source areas, characterized by abundant precipitation and diverse LUCs. The significant disparities in climate and underlying surface underscore the evident regional spatial heterogeneity, rendering simulations with the InVEST model more effective and realistic (Yang et al., 2022 ). Simultaneously, the spatial and temporal continuity of the model outputs facilitate the exploration of the impact of multi-factor integrated contribution calculation methods on SWR (Guo et al., 2023 ). Based on the aforementioned, the main objectives of the present study are (1) to localize InVEST model; (2) to determine the spatiotemporal characteristics of SWR in the SGP; (3) to quantitatively assess the comprehensive effect of climate and underlying surface influential factors and their interactions on SWR over a specific spatio-temporal span.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The southern Gansu Plateau (SGP) administratively includes the entire Gannan Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture and Linxia Hui Autonomous Prefecture in Gansu Province of China, geographically located between 33°06′N ∼ 36°12′N and 100°46′E ∼ 104°45′E. It is an important water source area in the northeastern part of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (Fig. 1  a) and a crucial water conservation and regulation zone in the upper reaches of the Yellow River and Yangtze River (Fig. 1 b). The total area is 44,900 km2 , where forestland and grassland are widely distributed, accounting for 82.84 % (Fig. 1 c), and the elevation ranges from 1159 ∼ 4866 m a.s.l. Loamy soil is distributed the widest in the SGP region, with an area percentage of 76.65 %. Sandy soil is predominantly found at higher elevations, with a relatively small percentage of 20.46 %. The regionally averaged annual temperature is 2.68 ℃, and the annual total precipitation is 606 mm concentrated in the rainy season from June to September. The relatively lower temperature and abundant precipitation, typical of a dependent continental plateau climate (Cui et al., 2012 ), cause the SGP to naturally develop many tributary systems of the Yellow River (e.g., the Daxia River, the Tao River, etc.) and Yangtze River (e.g., the Bailong River), making it remarkable in terms of water retention. In the past several decades, the unstable development of ecosystems under the influence of climate change and human activities has seriously affected the protection of regional water resources and the security of the ecosystem. For the scientific management of water and soil resources in the SGP, the spatial and temporal distribution and variation in SWR, as well as the analysis of its influence by climate and underlying surface factors, are crucial (Wang et al., 2016 ).  2.2 Data The daily meteorological dataset (1951–2019) came from the China National Meteorological Administration (http://data.cma.cn ), and the national gauge station-based series were interpolated by using the thin plate spline method (Zhang et al., 2018 ). Where daily precipitation, maximum, and minimum temperatures were extracted for the SGP. Surface net solar radiation data were released by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) (https://www.ecmwf.int ), with a spatial resolution of 0.25° and a temporal resolution of 3 h and a period from 1979 to 2022. The normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) data were published by the National Earth System Science Data Center, National Science & Technology Infrastructure of China (https://www.geodata.cn ), with a spatial resolution of 5 km and a longer time span from 1982 to 2020. The aforementioned NDVI datasets were extensively employed for evaluating the regional vegetation cover status over extended periods (Sun et al., 2022 ). LUC data were published by the Resource and Environmental Science and Data Center (https://www.resdc.cn ), with a spatial resolution of 1 km and a period from 1980 to 2020, once every five years. Soil data (e.g., soil texture) were obtained from the same website as the NDVI, with a spatial resolution of 1 km. Surface soil moisture data were from the study of Chen et al. (2021) , with a spatial resolution of 0.1° and a period from 2003 to 2018. We used the topographic data derived from the 30 m accuracy digital elevation model (DEM) from the Chinese Academy of Sciences Geospatial Data Cloud (http://www.gscloud.cn ). Actual measured monthly sequences of river channel discharges from the Zheqiao and Hongqi observational stations downstream of the Daxia and Tao River basins were collected. To reduce systematic errors in raster overlay analysis with different spatial resolutions of multisource data, all data were resampled and interpolated using the inverse distance weighting method to unify the spatial resolution to 1 km. The time scope for all the aforementioned series has been unified to 1990–2019. Due to the similarity of their water sediment retention functions, a small proportion of other forestland was merged into open forestland using reclassify method. Table 1   is a listing of the LUCs after their reclassification.  2.3 Methods 2.3.1 Determination of SWR (1) Water yield The water yield module based on the InVEST model is an estimation method based on the hydrothermal coupling equilibrium hypothesis of Budyko (Wei et al., 2022 ). The method entails constructing new series based on sequence variation across various time periods; the medians of the series were used to determine the magnitude of variation. The Mann–Kendall method (M–K) is a nonparametric test approach used to determine the statistical significance of a trend analysis (Mann, 1945; Kendall, 1995 ). (2) Mutation diagnosis. The M–K method was used to construct a new ordinal list Sk   to represent the sequential curve of UF  and the inverted curve of UB . The part of UF  that exceeds the critical level of significance corresponding to an upward or downward trend, the intersection of the two curves, is defined as the mutation time of the series (Mann, 1945; Kendall, 1995 ). In this study, we used the M–K method to test the mutation points of SWR time series. (3) Transfer matrix. The transfer matrix is derived from system analysis and is used to quantitatively describe the original and transfer states of the system (Xu and Zhao, 1993 ). In this study, a transfer matrix was utilized to examine the transformation of SWR at various grades.  2.3.3 Attribution analysis (1) Redundancy analysis (RDA) Multivariate RDA represents a direct gradient analysis technique used to statistically analyze the relationship between two sets of variables (Rahman et al., 2022 ). RDA can accurately assign the contribution rate of each environmental variable to the response variables, and it can conduct statistical tests on multiple explanatory variables. In RDA, the angle between the vectors (α ) represents the signal of the correlation between the environmental and response variables, and the approximated correlation is positive when the angle is acute and negative when obtuse (Zhou et al., 2022 ). Using RDA, we analyzed the effects and contributions of key environmental variables on SWR in diverse ecosystems. (2) Geodetector Geodetector is a novel spatial statistical method based on four modules (factor detector, interaction detector, ecological detector, and risk detector) that examines the spatially stratified heterogeneity of target factors and their drivers (Wang et al., 2010 ). The principal of the method is to divide a region into smaller regions; a region is heterogeneous if the sum of the variances of these smaller regions is less than the variance of the region. In addition, Geodetector can quantify how possible interactions between these factors influence the response variable (Chen et al., 2022 ). In this study, the effects of environmental factors and their interactions on SWR were primarily analyzed using factor detector and interaction detector modules. The degree of explanation of SWR by environmental factors is measured by the q -statistic of the factor detector.(12) q = 1 - ∑ h = 1  L  N h  σ h 2    N σ 2         where q  is the value of the explanatory power of the independent variable on SWR; h  is the number of classifications of the influencing factor; N  represents the total number of spatial units across the overall study area; and σh  2  and σ2  are the variances in the layer and the whole region, respectively. The q  value ranges from 0 to 1, and the larger the value of q is , the greater the explanatory power of the dependent variable. An interaction detector was used to determine whether the interaction of any two influences would increase or decrease the explanatory power of SWR. Wang et al. (2010)  provides a further explanation of the interaction detector.    3 Results 3.1 Evaluation and verification 3.1.1 Evaluation of InVEST The determination of the empirical constant Z  value is crucial to the evaluation of the InVEST model (Zhao et al., 2019 ). Z , also known as the “seasonal parameter”, depicts the local precipitation pattern and hydrogeological characteristics and is approximated roughly by the Formula Z  = 0.2 × N , where N  represents the annual precipitation frequency (Donohue et al., 2012 ). In the present study, statistics revealed that the Daxia and Tao River basins, both of which are located in the northwestern part and overlap the study area by 95 % and 80 %, respectively, and feature a cold and semihumid climate as well as a warm and semiarid climate, could represent the eco-geographical situation of the SGP as a whole (Fig. 1 c). The parameter Z  of the InVEST model was determined taking into account the entire catchment area of the two basins. Given the unpredictability of the annual precipitation periods and sensitivity of parameter Z  to the InVEST model, the bisection method was used to determine the precise value of Z.  In this method, the water yields from InVEST’s output and gauge streamflow data across the Daxia River Basin and the Tao River Basin between 1990 and 2019 were compared based on the above formula estimates, thus accurately and efficiently determining Z . The results of the two series comparison were plotted as a Taylor diagram and are shown in Fig. 2  . After parameter calibration, the parameter Z  applicable to SGP was determined to be 8.00, and the correlation between the two series was the most significant, while the values of root mean square deviation (RMSD) and standard deviation were the smallest.  3.1.2 Verification of soil saturated hydraulic conductivity Soil saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ksat  ) is one of the important parameters used to characterize soil infiltration capacity and plays an important role in calculating the SWR (Albalasmeh et al., 2022 ). In the present study, 21 sampling sites were chosen from the SGP to collect soil samples (Fig. 1 c) according to different underlying surface conditions (e.g., LUC and soil properties). After laboratory determination of the relevant physical quantities, the experimental Ksat   Eq. (8)  was obtained by the constant pressure head and infiltration method. At the same time, Ksat   calculated based on Eq. (7)  was compared with Ksat   measured in the laboratory (Fig. 3  ). The determination coefficient of the two series was assessed as 0.67 (P < 0.05), and most of the data points fell within the 95 % confidence interval. The results of the scatter fit indicated that the calculated Ksat   had a good fit with the experimental Ksat  , and Eq. (7)  could be used to estimate regional Ksat   with reasonable accuracy.  3.1.3 Verification of SWR On the basis of the InVEST model and Ksat   validation, we further evaluated the simulated SWR from the spatiotemporal scale; the results are shown in Fig. 4  . Annual runoff depths in the Daxia and Tao River basins were used as a comparison with annual SWR values to verify the accuracy of the modeling results on the time scale (Fig. 4 a). The results showed that the annual SWR calculated based on the InVEST model fit well with the annual runoff depths in the two watersheds, with a high correlation coefficient of 0.87 (P < 0.01). Meanwhile, the interannual variation in SWR was generally similar to that of annual runoff depth. Furthermore, according to the validation of SWR by Xu et al. (2022) , we used satellite-derived surface soil moisture to assess the SWR spatially. Spatial contrasts were determined by a 15 km raster scale calibration. The results indicated that the multiyear mean surface soil moisture for the period of 2003–2018 and simulated SWR had a good scatter match overall, with a correlation coefficient of 0.63 (P < 0.01, Fig. 4 b). Therefore, our simulation results for SWR are reliable.   3.2 Spatiotemporal distribution and variation in SWR 3.2.1 Temporal variation The precipitation, reference evapotranspiration, water yield, and SWR in the SGP from 1990 to 2019 are shown in Fig. 6 . The multiyear averaged precipitation in the SGP was 591.16 mm, and the overall interannual variation trend of precipitation showed an increasing trend, fluctuating at a rate of 4.44 mm/a (P < 0.01, Fig. 5  a). The minimum precipitation appeared in 2002 (459.27 mm), and the maximum precipitation appeared in 2016 (880.58 mm). The multiyear averaged reference evapotranspiration was 812.80 mm and showed an overall slightly increasing trend in the past 30 years at a rate of 0.93 mm/a (P < 0.05). The minimum reference evapotranspiration appeared in 1992 (743.08 mm), and the maximum reference evapotranspiration appeared in 2006 (871.22 mm). In the context of climate element changes, the SGP had a multiyear average water yield of 161.70 mm and fluctuated with an overall increasing trend at a rate of 3.14 mm/a (P < 0.01). Similar to the interannual variation characteristics of water yield, the multiyear averaged value was 18.67 mm across the SGP, with an overall increasing trend at a rate of 0.46 mm/a (P < 0.01). A comparison of the interannual dynamics of each element in Fig. 6  a revealed that the years with high SWR values in the SGP corresponded to years of high precipitation, and the variation trend was largely consistent. The M–K method-tested mutation was found in 2010 (Fig. 5 b). Prior to 2010, the annual SWR decreased at a rate of 0.01 mm/a (P < 0.05) and averaged 10.83 mm, whereas it increased at a rate of 0.93 mm/a (P < 0.1) and averaged 15.72 mm afterward.  3.2.2 Spatial distribution and variation The policy “Technical Guidelines for The Delineation of Ecological Protection Red Line” was used in conjunction with the natural breaks method (Jenks) in ArcGIS (Wang et al., 2022 ) to categorize the multi-year average SWR for six Grades (Li et al., 2021c ). The results showed that SWR displayed different spatial patterns in the SGP. High SWR values were primarily found in areas near the mountain divides with abundant precipitation, while low SWR values were prevalent in loess areas in the north, farming land in the central, and valley areas featuring lower altitudes. For example, in northwestern Maqu, which is located in the southwest of the SGP with high altitude where precipitation is abundant, SWR can exceed 22.78 mm; however, where the mainstream of the Yellow River develops in the southeast, SWR was less than 10 mm (Fig. 5 a). Statistically, the areal percentage of SWR between 0 ∼ 16.12 mm was 69.83 % (Fig. 5 e). During the statistical period, SWR increased in the majority of the area, with a range of −1.52 ∼ 2.08 mm/a, and the area percentage was 84.18 %, where SWR changed at variable rates of 0 ∼ 0.50 mm/a (Fig. 5 b and f). In the majority of the SGP, the variation in SWR was significant at P ≤ 0.01, particularly in the northern and southwestern regions. Before the mutation, the increased part of SWR only 42.41 % (Fig. 6  c and g), and after the mutation it reached more than 90 % (Fig. 6  d and h). Furthermore, the SWR in the low altitude zone varied from decreasing to increasing after the mutation, which might be related to the warming of the climate.   3.3 Spatial division of SWR importance 3.3.1 Spatial characteristics The spatial alterations in SWR before and after the mutation were examined based on the classification depicted above (Fig. 7  ). According to the Technical Guidelines for The Delineation of Ecological Protection Red Line, areas of Grade V and VI are ecological function zones of the utmost importance that must be vigorously protected. After the mutation, most of the northern loess zone was converted from Grade I to Grade II (Fig. 7 a and b). Furthermore, the areas of SWR Grades IV and V expanded substantially across the SGP, especially in the south-central region of the SGP, such as the Maqu areas in the southwest, due to the increase in precipitation following the mutation (Fig. 5 ).  3.3.2 Magnitudes of intensity transitions The areas of different grades of SWR before and after mutation, together with the transitioned changes, were measured through pixel statistics of the two raster maps (Fig. 7 a and b). The areal percentage remaining nontransition comprised 56.33 %, 23.68 %, 9.68 %, 11.28 %, 31.54 %, and 99.68 %, corresponding to the six grades from Grade I to Grade VI (Table 2  ). Grade VI was the most stable, indicating that areas with a high SWR were less affected by climate and human activities and would be easier to protect. However, Grade I to Grade V had a greater potential to transfer; for example, 80.33 % of Grade IV transformed into Grade V, and none transferred in the opposite direction. In particular, the transition from the lower grade to the higher grade accounted for larger proportions. For example, the total areal percentage of grades I ∼ III was 76.19 % before the mutation and 55.96 % after the mutation. Correspondingly, the total areal percentage of grades IV and V was 21.71 % before the mutation and 35.58 % after the mutation. Note that grade-skipping transitions between grades were uncommon, indicating that the development of SWR was sustained in the context of climate change and human activities, which was beneficial to the conservation of the ecosystem in the SGP.   3.4 Responses of SWR to LUC LUC is affected by the comprehensive impact of climate change and human activities, and researching the influence of LUC changes on water resources in more detail is an essential step for sustainable water resource management (Masum et al., 2017 ). The SWR values for the corresponding years were extracted from six periods of the LUC raster data, and then the average values were calculated for the entire study period. The statistical results showed that the average SWR of the diverse LUCs was different (Fig. 8  a) across the SGP during the period of 1990–2019. Overall, the average SWR of GMC was the largest, with values of 23.15 mm, which was mainly caused by differences in vegetation structure than others, though precipitation had an effect. For LUCs influenced more by human regulations (e.g., frequent tillage and hardening of roads), the CPD and BUP exhibited lower average SWRs. The average SWR of CFD and OFD in the forestland ecosystem (FLD, i.e., CFD, SHD, and OFD; Areal PCT is 27.41 %) was lower than that of SHD, except for the influence of precipitation, possibly because the actual evapotranspiration of the vegetation canopy of CFD was large, and the water conductivity of the bare surface of the OFD was inadequate. In particular, the average SWR of the grassland ecosystem (GLD, i.e., GHC, GMC, and GLC; areal PCT is 55.43 %) was higher overall. The higher SWR value of the USD might be due to the widespread distribution of alpine tundra with abundant precipitation (Fig. 5 a). In the case of increased precipitation, the average SWR of WAR was lower than it was prior to mutation, indicating in part the difficulty of quantifying the water conservation function of WAR. The SWR variations in diverse LUCs were measured using Sen’s slope method, as shown in Fig. 8 b. In addition to WAR and WTD, the SWR of various LUCs had an overall increase throughout the study period. The increase rate of SHD was the largest, and the CPD was the smallest, with rates of 0.39 mm/a and 0.09 mm/a, respectively. The possible reason was that SHD is more vulnerable to climate change. The above results indicated that the maintenance of SHD in the forestland ecosystem was essential for SWR variation. WAR had a negative Sen's slope value, which might be related to higher evaporation from the surface layer as the climate warmed. After the mutation, the SWR of forestland and grassland systems increased dramatically, with both systems exceeding 0.68 mm/a, indicating that the potential for SWR in these systems was enormous.  3.5 Attribution analysis 3.5.1 Contribution of time-varying factors to SWR We selected the main climatic factors (annual maximum and minimum temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, and reference evapotranspiration) and vegetation factor (NDVI) as the time-varying factors to analyze their contribution to the SWR of different LUCs. CPD, FLD, and GLD accounted for 91.76 % of the total area of the SGP. The WTD is a landscape vegetation type of the study area and is susceptible to climate and human activity influences. According to the response analysis of SWR to LUC, the SWR and its variability in the FLD and GLD interior were generally consistent. To avoid the interference of LUCs with similar attributes on the attribution analysis results, this study conducted only time-scale attribution analysis for the four ecosystems mentioned above. The RDA results for each time-varying factor and diverse LUCs are shown in Fig. 9  . Generally, selected environmental factors explained 90.51 % of the SWR of various LUCs (Fig. 9 a). For the entire time period, the SWR of each LUC correlated most strongly with precipitation, up to 77.30 %, and the ordering of the different LUCs was GLD > FLD > CPD > WTD. SWR was then followed by reference evapotranspiration, which amounted to −11.70 % and was most significant in the WTD. The NDVI was positively correlated with the SWR of each LUC, particularly the WTD, indicating that the vegetation cover of the WTD had a greater effect on its SWR. Solar radiation had the least effect on the SWR of different LUCs. Compared with that before mutation, the interpretation of SWR environmental factors after mutation was enhanced in diverse LUCs (Fig. 9 b and c), and the effect of precipitation on SWR was more pronounced, especially for FLD and GLD, while the effect of reference evapotranspiration was diminished. The third key factors that changed before and after the mutation, namely, annual minimum temperature and NDVI, indicated that vegetation cover was the primary factor affecting the SWR of different LUCs after mutation, excluding precipitation and reference evapotranspiration. Notably, both before and after the mutation, the annual minimum temperature exhibited an unfavorable effect on SWR.  3.5.2 Spatial interactions In this study, in addition to the time-varying factors mentioned in subsection 3.5.1, the spatial impacts of topographic factors (elevation and slope) and LUC on SWR were analyzed using Geodetector (Fig. 10  ). The q  value indicates that one factor explains 100 × q % of SWR. When considering the action of a single factor, reference evapotranspiration had the greatest spatial effect on SWR during the entire study period, while slope had the smallest (Fig. 10 a). After mutation, the effect of each factor on SWR was diminished except for slope and LUC, with the annual minimum temperature being the most pronounced (Fig. 10 b and c). The interactive effects of all pairwise factors on SWR were calculated employing the interaction detector. If the q  statistics for factor interactions are greater than the maximum of both x 1  and x 2  but less than their sum, then the two factors are mutually enhanced (e.g., LUC and annual maximum temperature). If the q  statistics for factor interactions exceed the sum of x 1  and x 2 , then the two factors are nonlinearly enhanced (e.g., slope and precipitation). The finding results showed quite clearly that the interactive q  statistic of the pairwise factors was greater than that of the corresponding individual factors (Fig. 10 a), suggesting that the explanatory power of an individual factor might be enhanced when interacting with other factors. LUC and other contributing factors demonstrated the most substantial interactive effects on SWR, surpassing the impact of LUC in isolation. Moreover, these interactive effects exhibited stronger correlations with climate elements, underscoring the dominant influence of climate on SWR. For example, the interaction between LUC and precipitation was the most significant. Compared with those before mutation, the interaction between most of the factors was weakly reduced. While the interactions of LUC and various factors after mutation had enhanced effects on SWR, especially the coeffect of LUC and reference evapotranspiration (Fig. 10 b and c). According to the exhaustive analysis, precipitation, reference evapotranspiration, annual maximum and minimum temperature, elevation, and LUC influenced the spatial heterogeneity of SWR. Statistically significant differences between precipitation and annual minimum temperature, as well as reference evapotranspiration, support the aforementioned conclusion.    4 Discussion 4.1 Dominance of the Z  value The InVEST model has widespread application in the study of ecological and hydrological processes on a regional scale (Caro et al., 2020 ). The accuracy and effectiveness of the InVEST model largely depend on the value of parameter Z , which represents the local precipitation model and hydrogeological characteristics. However, the selection of parameter Z , as an empirical constant, is uncertain (Sharp et al., 2018 ). For the model simulation results to be more reliable, the Z  value must be determined rationally. On the one hand, there are numerous studies that determine Z  by calculating the empirical value ω  (Xu et al., 2013 ); on the other hand, Z  can be calculated using the annual precipitation number N  (Donohue et al., 2012 ). Nevertheless, the accuracy of the Z  value calculated by the two approaches described above is not close enough (Liang and Liu, 2014 ). Based on a rough estimate of Z  using the value of N , simulations were validated by comparison with gauge observations at outlets of the Daxia and Tao River basins and the water yield results of the InVEST model in the present study, which helped to enhance the accuracy of this model. Furthermore, we introduced the bisection method to enhance computing efficiency, since studies by Daneshi et al. (2021)  showed that when the difference between the two sequences above was minimal, the related Z  value spanned a greater range. In conclusion, the value of 8.00 was found to be appropriate for the parameter Z  of the SGP; thus, the water yield module under the Z  value can be applied to regions with close geographical locations or other similar climatic backgrounds.  4.2 Main drivers of the regional SWR SWR is one of the most important regulation services provided by the ecosystem; it functionally represents the ability of the soil to retain water under certain conditions (Qiao et al. 2020), and it plays critical roles in improving flood control, drought resistance, soil consolidation, and water conservation (Shi et al., 2021 ). Numerous studies have analyzed the impact factors of SWR differently, though the main influencing factors can be classified into four categories, e.g., climate, LUC, vegetation, and topography, which is consistent with the results of this study (Berghuijs et al., 2017; Gong et al., 2017 ). Based on the analysis of the spatial and temporal distribution and variation in SWR, we summarized the dominant factors affecting regional SWR. The positive effect of precipitation on ecosystem maintenance cannot be overstated (Kim et al., 2022 ). According to the changing characteristics of precipitation and SWR in the SGP from 1990 to 2019 (Fig. 6 a) as well as the RDA and Geodetector analysis (Fig. 10 ), precipitation was the dominant driver factor affecting the SWR, which was consistent with many other studies that emphasize the significance of precipitation inputs for the InVEST model (Boithias et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2019 ). The majority of the SGP is characterized by high elevations, frigid climates, and abundant precipitation. Consequently, reference evapotranspiration and temperature had a substantial impact on SWR by influencing vegetation growth (Kayet et al., 2018 ). More specifically, reference evapotranspiration affected the actual evapotranspiration, and temperature is a prerequisite for vegetation in alpine regions to recover from thermal stress; these factors ultimately influence regional SWR (Or and Lehmann, 2019 ). The above results were consistent with the study of Xiao and Ouyang (2019)  and also supported by the large influence of reference evapotranspiration and temperature interaction with LUC on SWR in the present study (Fig. 10 ). In the context of a warming climate, the vegetation in the alpine-clod river source area is being dynamically enhanced (Yang et al., 2014). Meanwhile, the improvement of vegetation in the SGP promoted the increase in SWR (Liu et al., 2021 ), of which the positive effect of NDVI on SWR in this study was substantially evident. Topography influences climate by affecting regional hydrothermal conditions, which in turn affects vegetation structure, debris accumulation, and the physical and chemical properties of soils and ultimately determines the regional SWR (Xu et al., 2022 ). Our study showed that the effect of elevation on SWR was not negligible, which was consistent with the findings of Ma et al. (2022) . In addition, LUC has an effect, from an ecohydrological point of view, on surface runoff and the confluence of water, which in turn had an effect on the amount of water lost from the topsoil-vegetation system (Masum et al., 2017 ). Our results indicated that FLD and GLD had a greater impact on SWR, especially GMC and SHD; this finding should be considered in the ecological restoration of SGP in the future. In accordance with the conclusion of Xue et al. (2022) , the results also demonstrated that LUC interacted most significantly with other factors, highlighting the significance of LUC for regional SWR.  4.3 Implications for water resource protection The SWR of diverse LUCs has increased significantly since 2010, indicating that the ecological restoration process of the SGP is beginning to bear fruit. The specific quantification of SWR by each influencing factor in this study is necessary to provide decision-makers with a scientific basis for better ecological protection and water conservation (Oliveira et al., 2021 ). Our study revealed a spatiotemporal pattern of a “general increase” in SWR across the SGP. In this context, more attention should be given to balancing the water demand of the environment, society, and economic development in this region. Sustainable ecological restoration should be maintained at high elevations in the western high-altitude zone of the SGP, which has abundant precipitation and strong soil water storage capacity (Ali et al., 2020 ). With less precipitation and higher temperature, the fragile ecosystems in the northern part, where CPD and GLC are widely distributed, necessitate conservation tillage and grassland fencing, which facilitate the infiltration of precipitation and thus promote a beneficial increase in SWR (Li et al., 2020 ). At the same time, these measures facilitate runoff regulation while also augmenting the volume of water available for both production and domestic purposes in this part. In the southwestern and southeastern alpine tundra areas (USD), although abundant precipitation allows for high SWR simulations, the Special physical properties of soil forces us to make anthropogenic interventions to retain SWR for longer periods, such as the pragmatic introduction of cold-tolerant grass species, as a way to achieve healthy ecosystem recovery (Wang et al., 2021 ). Notably, according to the Technical Guidelines for The Delineation of Ecological Protection Red Line, SGP areas with Grades V and VI before and after mutation deserve public attention and priority protection (Li et al., 2021c ).  4.4 Limitations and improvements Even though the coordinate system and spatial resolution of all data were unified, errors were inevitable in multisource data fusions and station-based interpolations (Novotny et al., 2023 ). The InVEST model disregards certain hydrological processes, such as the interaction between surface water and groundwater, the dynamic changes in lakes and wetlands, and the impact of other human activities, such as artificial water extraction (Wang et al., 2022; Ali et al., 2020 ), which may be the reason for the small, simulated values of SWR in WAR and WTD (Long et al., 2022 ). Thus, in the present study, we discuss the response of the main drivers to SWR, whereas research on the specific mechanisms of each factor on SWR is insufficient. Although some uncertainties were present, the InVEST model served its annual water yield well in this study (Butsic et al., 2017 ). Based on this finding, we calculated the regional soil water storage capacity by integrating parameters such as the coefficient flow rate, the topographic index, and the soil saturated hydraulic conductivity, with the primary aim of assessing the impacts of climate and underlying surface changes on annual SWR and informing policy and decision-makers of expected future impacts on regional water security (Gong et al., 2017 ). Overall, the results of our study are reliable, and they are comparable to the findings of other studies that used InVEST (Xiao and Ouyang, 2019 ). However, future research must gain a better understanding of the important underlying dynamic ecohydrological processes that influence stream flows, pay attention to the localization correction of the SWR calculation formula, and improve the observation of hydrological processes in wetlands (Zhao et al., 2019 ); these factors can help optimize model input data and parameters and can be embedded in external modules (Wu et al., 2023 ). For instance, a growing corpus of research emphasizes the significance of including precipitation inputs in rainfall-runoff models, especially the InVEST model (Benra et al., 2021 ). Incorporating snowfall and ice (or snowmelt) as a default InVEST element allows for more accurate model estimates. Given the existing coarse size at which the Budyko framework is being applied, the scale of analysis should also be rethought in this particular scenario (Hu et al., 2020 ). On the time scale, we should improve the model so that water yield is an output at the monthly scale; comparing water yield in various months can not only predict flood events during the rainy season but also achieve a rational allocation of water resources throughout the year (Yang et al., 2019 ). Spatially, meteorological observation stations can be added to capture the relevant hydrological processes and the heterogeneous precipitation and evapotranspiration patterns in greater detail (Rafiei-Sardooi et al., 2022 ).   5 Conclusion In this study, the regional SWR function of the SGP was quantified over the past 30 years by introducing key modification factors. The spatiotemporal distribution and variation in SWR were determined, and the effects of different factors on SWR were analyzed and quantified in depth. The results showed that the SWR function in the region has improved, and the change in SWR is the result of the comprehensive effects of climate and the underlying surface. The southwest of the SGP is an important water resource protection area in this study area, which needs sufficient attention and priority protection. Precipitation and reference evapotranspiration temporally promote and inhibit the increase in SWR, respectively. In addition to precipitation and reference evapotranspiration, the spatial influence of temperature and elevation on SWR should not be underestimated. Additionally, both factor interactions were greater than the effects of individual interactions on SWR, with the most significant interaction between LUC and each factor. The InVEST model with localized parameters can be applied to other regions with similar climatic and hydrogeological backgrounds. Moreover, methods such as RDA and Geodetector might be used as a case example for quantitatively analyzing the contribution of influencing factors and their interactions to SWR in other alpine-cold river source area. The cognitive analysis of ecological conservation and water resource management, informed by the aforementioned findings, proves to be highly insightful. However, due to the limitations of data collection and model mechanisms, the influence of some hydrological processes on SWR and the study of the specific mechanisms of each factor on SWR were neglected. Surveys on engineering measures regarding the above uncertainties and optimization of model input data and parameters will be the focus of our future studies.
1 Introduction Drylands (hyper-arid, arid, semi-arid, and dry sub-humid environments) cover about 45 % of the Earth’s land surface and support more than 38 % of the world’s population (Prăvălie, 2016; Schimel, 2010 ). With infrequent precipitation and high potential evapotranspiration rates, these regions face severe water scarcity, limiting crucial ecosystem services, such as water and climate regulation, biodiversity support, nutrient cycling, and productivity (MEA, 2005 ). According to the IPCC (2013) , drylands will receive less rainfall and experience higher temperatures, more severe droughts, and extreme events in the future. This will exacerbate land degradation risk in these already vulnerable ecosystems (Huang et al., 2017 ). Therefore, maintaining the stability and functionality of drylands becomes imperative in the face of ongoing and projected environmental changes. Understanding biotic interactions and the interplay between biotic and abiotic factors in drylands provides insights into ecosystem functioning and dynamics. Due to water scarcity and soil nutrient limitations, vascular plants in drylands are typically sparse with patchy coverage and dominated by specific drought-tolerant shrubs and grasses (Deblauwe et al., 2008 ). A significant expanse of exposed soil creates an ideal niche for the colonization of biological soil crusts (biocrusts), which is a cohesive layer in the uppermost millimeters of soil, consisting of photoautotrophic organisms including cyanobacteria, lichens, and mosses, as well as heterotrophic organisms, such as bacteria, fungi, and archaea (Weber et al., 2022 ). Biocrusts typically exhibit remarkable tolerance and resilience in harsh environments, allowing them to widely inhabit drylands. Biocrusts cover about 30 % of the global dryland surface (Rodriguez-Caballero et al., 2018a; Rodriguez-Caballero et al., 2018b ) and account for 13.9 % of drylands in China (Qiu et al., 2023a ). Biocrusts act as ecosystem engineers in drylands and can modify various soil surface properties (e.g., texture, roughness, porosity, cohesion and stability, micro-topography, and nutrient levels) and impact associated hydrological, biogeochemical, and ecological processes (Belnap, 2006; Bowker et al., 2018; Eldridge et al., 2020; Kidron et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2024a; Xiao et al., 2019 ). In addition, it has been found that biocrusts affect local and global climate through the modification of surface reflectance (Rodríguez-Caballero et al., 2015) and reduction of atmospheric dust emissions (Rodriguez-Caballero et al., 2022 ). Nevertheless, in comparison to the broader attention given to vascular plants in drylands, investigations about the ecohydrological function of biocrusts are limited, and findings have remained controversial (Eldridge et al., 2020; Kidron et al., 2022 ). In some arid and semi-arid regions, vascular plants e.g., grasses and shrubs coexist with biocrusts, forming mosaic patterns at local scales (Maestre et al., 2010 ). However, in terms of the hydrological impacts of biocrusts on vascular plants, previous studies reported both positive (Chamizo et al., 2016 ) and negative influences (Kidron, 2014 ). On one hand, an extensive cover of biocrusts developed in interplant patches typically acts as runoff sources, benefiting vascular plants by increasing the availability of runoff water (Rodriguez-Caballero et al., 2018a; Rodriguez-Caballero et al., 2018b ). On the other hand, the impediment of biocrusts on soil infiltration may result in water availability decrease for the growth of perennial plants in areas covered by biocrusts (She et al., 2022 ). Therefore, our knowledge of potential effects of biocrusts on plants is still limited. Further investigations are accordignly required to experimentally address the hydrological roles of biocrusts beneath vascular plants and their potential effects on these plants. Evapotranspiration (evaporation and transpiration) is critical to the water cycle in the Soil-Plant-Atmosphere Continuum (SPAC) (Fisher et al., 2017; Novák, 2012 ). Around 60 % of the precipitation on Earth’s surface is returned to the atmosphere through evapotranspiration, and this percentage can reach 90 % in arid regions (Novák, 2012 ). The rate of evapotranspiration primarily depends on atmospheric demand, solar radiation intensity, and water availability in soil (Verstraeten et al., 2008 ). Although it is widely accepted that biocrusts significantly impact soil evaporation (Sun et al., 2024b ), most studies in the literature are comparative experiments between biocrusts and bare soil and do not consider vascular plants. Until now, the impact of biocrusts on grassland evapotranspiration has remained unknown. Given the possible effect of global warming on dryland ecosystems, it is urgent to clarify how grassland evapotranspiration responds to biocrust cover. Even only considering soil evaporation, the role of biocrusts is far from conclusive. Specifically, there are several distinct perspectives on the impact of biocrusts on soil evaporation, which include increasing (Kidron and Tal, 2012; Li et al., 2022 ), decreasing (Chamizo et al., 2016; Eldridge et al., 2020 ), or relying on specific conditions, such as soil texture (Xiao et al., 2010 ), seasonality (Cantón et al., 2004; Xiao et al., 2016 ), rainfall (Li et al., 2010 ), and the moisture content of biocrusts and soil (Jiang et al., 2018; Guan et al., 2020 ). Such controversial results possibly indicate the key role of temporal and spatial heterogeneities. Moreover, differences in measurement devices and their accuracies may also contribute to variations in results (Kidron et al., 2022 ). Most importantly, current biocrust evaporation characteristics are primarily derived from simulated experiments (from wet to dry) conducted over several days, which may not fully capture the natural evaporation process due to short time scales considered. As suggested in the recent review by Kidron et al. (2022) , the consideration of the evaporation stage is necessary, highlighting the need for a longer time scales and period of in-situ field measurements. In this study, we hypothesized that the presence of biocrusts would deeply influence evapotranspiration including surface soil evaporation and vegetation transpiration in drylands. Based on this hypothesis, we used micro-lysimeters to continually monitor evapotranspiration processes of bare soil, cyanobacterial-moss mixed biocrusts, gramineous and leguminous grasses with and without biocrusts over two months on the northern Chinese Loess Plateau. The primary objectives of this study were to: (i) quantify the impact of biocrusts on soil evaporation and grassland evapotranspiration, and (ii) analyze mechanisms through which biocrusts influence evaporation and evapotranspiration. Our study contributes valuable insights into the ecohydrological functions of biocrusts and their influences on vascular plants in dryland ecosystems.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area This field experiment was conducted in the Liudaogou watershed (38°46′–38°51′ N, 110°21′–110°23′ E) on the northern Loess Plateau of China (Fig. 1  A), with an elevation ranging from 1,081 to 1,274 m covering approximately 6.9 km2 . The region features a typical semiarid continental monsoon climate with an annual precipitation of 454 mm (around 80 % in summer), potential evaporation of 1,337 mm, and an average wind speed of 2.2 m/s. The average annual temperature is 8.4 ℃ with monthly variations from − 9.7 ℃ in winter (December–February) to 23.7 ℃ in summer (June–August). The watershed is situated in the Wind-Water Erosion Crisscross Region, characterized by a topography of rolling hills and deep gullies (Huo et al., 2008 ). According to the USDA soil taxonomy, the soil in the area is categorized as Entisols, specifically an aeolian sandy soil with a prevailing texture of loamy sand (Xiao et al., 2016 ). In the past two decades, the “Grain for Green” program has been implemented to address soil erosion and aid in the rehabilitation of this ecologically fragile area. The predominant vegetation consists mainly of perennial herbaceous species, such as Bothriochloa ischaemum  (Linn.) Keng, Medicago sativa  Linn., Artemisia ordosica  Krasch., Achnatherum splendens  (Trin.) Nevski and Lespedeza davurica  (Laxm.) Schindl, as well as shrub species, such as Caragana korshinskii  Kom. and Robinia pseudoacacia  Linn. (Gao et al., 2017 ). Biocrusts develop extensively on the stabilized soil surface, with ground cover ranging from 20 % to 30 %, occasionally reaching as high as 70 % to 80 % (Xiao et al., 2010 ). The biocrusts in the area comprise cyanobacterial, cyanobacteria-moss mixed, and moss biocrusts. Dominant moss species include Didymodon vinealis  (Brid.) Zander, Bryum argenteum  Hedw., and Barbula vinealis  Brid., while the dominant cyanobacterial species consist of Lyngbya allorgei , Oscillatoria granulata , and Microcolus paludosus  (Wang et al., 2023 ).  2.2 Experimental design In this study, all measurements were conducted on the same flat ground with a slope less than 5 degrees and an area of ∼ 1000 m2  (Fig. 1 B). Three pairs of treatments with five replicates were conducted: (i) bare soil (BS; soil without any cover; Fig. 1 C) and biocrusts (BC; soil with both ∼ 50 % of cyanobacterial and moss cover; Fig. 1 D); (ii) gramineous grass (GG; Fig. 1 E) and gramineous grass with biocrusts (GG + BC; soil with both ∼ 50 % of cyanobacterial and moss cover; Fig. 1 F); (iii) leguminous grass (LG; Fig. 1 G) and leguminous grass with biocrusts (LG + BC; soil with both ∼ 50 % of cyanobacterial and moss cover; Fig. 1 H). Two species, i.e., A. splendens  and L. davurica  were selected to represent gramineous grass and leguminous grass. There was no significant difference in plant characteristics (i.e., plant height, root length, aboveground biomass, belowground biomass, and total biomass) within the pair of GG vs.  GG + BC or LG vs.  LG + BC (Table 1  ). The belowground biomass of LG was significantly higher than GG, but the aboveground biomass showed no significant difference between LG and GG (Table 1 ). More specifically, the mean values for the plant height and root length were 24.3 and 25.9 cm for the GG greater than 23.0 and 24.1 cm for the LG. For aboveground, belowground, and total biomass the mean values were respectively 4.7, 5.5, and 10.3 g for the GG, while 3.6, 17.7, and 21.3 g for the LG (Table 1 ). For three pairs of treatments, we conducted two in-situ experiments over two months (from August 19 to October 20, 2023). One measurement was daily evapotranspiration for the bare soil, biocrusts, gramineous and leguminous grasses with and without biocrusts under natural field conditions. Notably, the evapotranspiration of the bare soil and biocrusts exclusively involves evaporation. Another set of measurements was volumetric soil moisture (θ , in cm3  cm−3 ) and temperature (T s , in °C) at the depth 10 cm as well as climatic factors including daily rainfall (in mm), air temperature (T air , in ℃) and relative humidity (RH, in %).  2.3 Measurements of evapotranspiration The in-situ evapotranspiration measurements were conducted by weighing cylindrical PVC micro-lysimeters (20.0 cm in inner diameter and 32.0 cm in height), with five PVC micro-lysimeters employed for each treatment as replicates. During sampling the bare soil and biocrusts, the micro-lysimeter was inserted vertically into the soil to collect intact soil cores from 0–30 cm depth. During sampling the grasses with and without biocrusts, we first cleared surface litter around the selected grasses (each plant’s size is similar) and then carefully passed the micro-lysimeter through the aboveground part of the grass. Subsequently, we excavated the soil surrounding the micro-lysimeter using a shovel and then slowly inserted it into the soil to obtain a complete intact sample from the 0–30 cm depth. The bottom of all micro-lysimeters was covered using a 300-mesh nylon net to ensure free drainage and prevent ponding during rainfall. Each micro-lysimeter was installed within a larger PVC cylinder (25.0 cm in inner diameter and 32.0 cm in height) and subsequently placed vertically into a soil pit to avoid direct sunlight exposure on the side of the micro-lysimeter faced outward. The soil surface inside the micro-lysimeter was level with the outside ground. Finally, we filled the interspace between the micro-lysimeter and the larger PVC cylinder with 5 cm thick polystyrene to reduce potential thermal convection (Fig. 1 C–H). To ensure soil stabilization and plant survival, all micro-lysimeters were installed two weeks prior to the measurements. During this period, no withering or mortality of grasses inside the micro-lysimeters was observed. We conducted the measurements on clear days (49 out of 63 days) and suspended them on rainy days. The micro-lysimeters were manually weighed with an electronic balance (±0.1 g) every morning (7:00 am) and every sunset (19:00 pm) to monitor their daily mass changes (m , in g). Daily evapotranspiration rate (ET , in mm d–1 ) and cumulative evapotranspiration amount (ET c , in mm) were calculated through Eqs. (1) and (2) , respectively:(1) ET = 10 m  ρ π r 2        (2) E T c  = ∑ i = 1  n  E i  ( E T i  )      where ρ  is the density of water (=1.0 g cm−3 ); r  is the inner radius of the micro-lysimeter (=10.0 cm); and n  is the number of experimental days (=49 days). It should be noted that for bare soil and biocrusts, the “ET ” refers to merely evaporation, as there is no transpiration component. The effect of biocrusts on the evapotranspiration was determined by calculating the difference in the daily evapotranspiration rate (ΔET , in mm d−1 ) between the biocrusts and bare soil as well as between the grass with biocrusts and grass without biocrusts, as defined as follows:(3) Δ E T = E T BC  - E T BS     E T GG + BC   - E T GG     E T LG + BC   - E T LG             where ET BC , ET BS , ET GG , ET GG+BC , ET LG , ET LG+BC  are the daily evapotranspiration rates of the biocrusts, bare soil, gramineous grass, gramineous grass with biocrusts, leguminous grass, and leguminous grass with biocrusts, respectively. The contribution of ET BC  to ET GG+BC  and ET LG+BC  was calculated from ΔET /(ET GG+BC ) and ΔET /(ET LG+BC ), respectively. The change of ET  induced by the biocrusts was calculated from ΔET /ET GG  and ΔET /ET LG .  2.4 Measurements of soil moisture, temperature, and climatic factors The θ  and T s  were continuously measured at the 10  cm depth in situ using ECH2O 5TE sensors (METER Group, Inc. USA; ±0.02 cm3  cm−3  for θ  and ± 0.1 ℃ for T s ) for different treatments. These sensors were horizontally installed into the soil within six other micro-lysimeters to prevent interference with the weighing (Fig. 1 I). At a nearby location (∼50 m apart), the T air  and RH at 2.0 m were monitored using an HMP155 probe (Vaisala in Finland). Rainfall was measured with a TE525MM (Texas Electronics, Inc. USA) and an automatic recording rain gauge. All the probes were connected to a CR3000 micrologger (Campbell Scientific, Inc. USA), which recorded measurements every 10 s and stored them in 10-minute and daily tables throughout the experimental period.  2.5 Measurements of soil properties and traits of biocrusts and grasses In the field, we demarcated five plots, ∼1 m2  each spaced ∼ 20 m apart, for each treatment. After removing aboveground plants within the plots, we photographed the soil surface. Using the ENVI 5.3 software, we determined the biocrust coverages (total, moss, and cyanobacterial) from the digital photographs. The biocrust samples and underlying soil (0–2 cm depth) were collected using Petri dishes (9.0 cm in diameter and 2.0 cm in height) the for biocrust trait measurements (n  = 5). Additionally, soil cores (5 cm in height and 100 cm3  in volume) were used to collect the upper 0–5 cm of intact soil for the measurement of soil properties (n  = 5). In the laboratory, the biocrust thickness was measured using digital Vernier calipers. The moss biomass was determined by separating the mosses from subsoil through a 2-mm screen and subsequently drying at 65℃ for 24 h. The Chlorophyll a  content of biocrusts was extracted using ethanol and measured at 663 nm and 645 nm using a UV–VIS spectrophotometer (TU-1818, Persee Instruments, Beijing) (Zhang et al., 2018 ). The soil bulk density was determined via the oven-drying method, and soil total porosity was calculated from the measured bulk density by assuming the value of 2.65 g cm−3  for the soil particle density (Hillel, 2003 ). Field capacity was determined using the Wilcox method (Hanks et al., 1954 ), and saturated hydraulic conductivity was measured using the constant-head method (Carter and Gregorich, 2006 ). The soil particle size distribution was analyzed using a laser diffraction method (Mastersizer 2000, Malvern Instruments Ltd in UK). The soil organic matter content was measured via the dichromate redox titration method (Carter and Gregorich, 2006 ). After the evapotranspiration experiment, we removed grasses from the micro-lysimeters and measured their traits. Their fresh grass with stubble not longer than 0.5 cm was collected from the ground, and the remaining part was placed in a 0.5 mm mesh gauze bag and washed to obtain the roots (Ding et al., 2022 ). The fresh above- and below-ground parts were oven-dried at 65 °C for 48 h, and their masses were measured and recorded separately. The aboveground and belowground biomasses were summed to calculate the total biomass.  2.6 Data analysis The normality of the data was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test, and the homogeneity of variances with Levene’s test. Subsequently, we examined the differences in the biocrust and plant traits as well as soil properties among different treatments using the one-way ANOVA (α  = 0.05) followed by Tukey’s HSD post hoc test. Considering that the ET , θ  and T s  were obtained from repetitive measurements on the same samples, we employed the repeated-measure ANOVA (α  = 0.05) to test their differences among all treatments. The Pearson correlation was used to analyze the correlation between ET  and other parameters T air , RH, θ , and T s  for each treatment. Furthermore, a partial least squares path modelling (PLS-PM) approach was applied to test the hypothetical causal relationships among the ET , soil cover type, T air , RH, θ , and T s . The model was evaluated using the goodness of fit statistic. All statistical analyses were performed using the R software (version 4.0.3).   3 Results 3.1 Biocrust traits and their effects on soil properties As listed in Table 2  , the cyanobacterial-moss mixed biocrusts was 11.28–12.10 mm thick with 0.13–0.14 g cm−2  moss biomass and 0.99–1.05 mg g−1  chlorophyll a  content. Moreover, the biocrusts underneath grasses generally developed well showed greater thickness, moss biomass, and chlorophyll a  content compared to those outside grasses. However, these differences were not statistically significant (P  > 0.05, Table 2 ). Whether outside or underneath grasses, the presence of biocrusts reduced the bulk density and saturated hydraulic conductivity, while increased the organic matter, clay and silt content, total porosity, and field capacity at the 0–5 cm depth (Table 2 ). Specifically, the biocrusts significantly deceased the bulk density by 8.1–14.1 % and increased the total porosity by 10.3–22.6 % (P  < 0.05). Moreover, in comparison to the soil without biocrusts, the biocrusts had up to 50.7–70.2 % higher content of fine particles (clay and silt), while the sand content in the biocrusts decreased by 3.5–4.3 % (P  < 0.05). They caused the field capacity to increase by 57.9–70.6 % but the saturated hydraulic conductivity to reduce by 22.2–26.3 % (P  < 0.05). In addition, the biocrusts remarkably increased the soil organic matter content, reaching 2.9- to 3.4-fold greater than that of the soil without biocrusts (P  < 0.05, Table 2 ).  3.2 Biocrust effects on soil evaporation and grassland evapotranspiration Fig. 2   shows the measured ET  against the time for each two treatments. As can be seen, through the entire period of experiments, the trends of ET  for each two treatments were similar. Their daily ET  values, however, exhibited differences up to some extent (Fig. 2 A–C). Generally, the ET  for the biocrusts (BC), gramineous grass with biocrusts (GG + BC), and leguminous grass with biocrusts (LG + BC) treatments was greater than that for the bare soil, gramineous grass (GG), and leguminous grass (LG) treatments, respectively (Fig. 2 D). The ANOVA results showed that the average ET  from the bare soil, 1.10 mm d−1 , was statistically different than that from the biocrusts, 1.33 mm d−1  (F  = 5.86, P  < 0.001). Similar results were observed by comparing the average ET  from the GG and GG + BC (F  = 4.48, P  = 0.035), with values of 1.85 and 2.14 mm d−1 , respectively (Fig. 3  A). However, the average ET  from the GG (1.60 mm d−1 ) and GG + BC (1.76 mm d−1 ) were not significantly different (F  = 1.98, P  = 0.160). As shown in Fig. 3 B, there was a significant difference in the average ΔETs  among three pairs of treatments (F  = 3.81, P  = 0.043). Specifically, the ΔET  for the LG vs . LG + BC (0.27 mm d−1 ) was significantly higher than that for the GG vs . GG + BC (0.17 mm d−1 ). Taking the first 5 days after four typical rainfall events with rainfall amounts of 0.9 mm (October 7), 11.9 mm (September 8), 19.0 mm (September 2), and 47.4 mm (August 25 to 27) as examples, the daily ET  of all treatments exhibited an initial rapid increase, followed by a subsequent decrease (Fig. 4  ). Overall, with increasing rainfall, the differences in the ET  within each pair of treatments became more pronounced. The largest difference in the ET  between treatments within each pair occurred on the second day following a 47.4 mm rainfall, ranging from 21.8 % to 27.2 % (Fig. 4 D). Compared to the bare soil, the biocrusts caused a significant increase, by 20.9 %, in the average ET  from the soil (Fig. 3 B). The average ET  of GG and LG was increased by 9.4 % and 13.4 % due to the presence of the biocrusts (Fig. 5  A). In addition, for the GG + BC and LG + BC, the ET  of biocrusts contributed 8.1 % and 10.6 % to the total ET  (Fig. 5 B). Similar to the ET , statistically differences in ET c  were observed between the bare soil and biocrusts, as well as LG and LG + BC (Fig. S1 ). The presence of biocrusts led to an increase in the ET c  for the GG and LG by 7.01 and 13.16 mm, corresponding to 8.9 % and 14.4 %, respectively (Fig. S2 A). Moreover, for the GG + BC and LG + BC, the contribution of biocrusts to ET c  was 8.2 % and 12.6 %, respectively (Fig. S2 B).  3.3 Facilitating effects of soil and climatic conditions on evapotranspiration During the 63-day experimental period (with 14 days experiencing rainfall of ≥ 0.1 mm), the value of total rainfall amount, T air , and RH was 126.7 mm, 15.4 ℃ and 72.3 %, respectively (Fig. 6  A). The mean θ  of the biocrusts (0.09 cm cm−3 ) was 12.5 % greater than that of the bare soil (0.08 cm cm−3 ), while the mean θ  of the GG + BC (0.09 cm cm−3 ) and LG + BC (0.08 cm cm−3 ) were 10.0 % and 20.0 % lower than those of the GG (0.10 cm cm−3 ) and LG (0.10 cm cm−3 ), respectively (P  > 0.05, Fig. 6 B–D). The mean T s  of the biocrusts (17.1 ℃) was 3.4 % lower than that of the bare soil (17.7 ℃), while the mean T s  values of the GG + BC (16.6 ℃) and LG + BC (14.0 ℃) were 9.9 % and 2.9 % higher than those of the GG (15.1 ℃) and LG (13.6 ℃), respectively (P  > 0.05, Fig. 6 B–D). As shown in Fig. 7  , the Pearson correlation coefficients indicated that the ET  of all treatments exhibited a significant and positive correlation with θ , T s , T air , and RH (R  ≥ 0.34, P  ≤ 0.05), except for the correlation between RH and ET  of grasses with or without biocrusts. Among the soil and climatic factors, the θ  showed the strongest correlation with the ET  for the bare soil (R  = 0.59, P  ≤ 0.01) and biocrusts (R  = 0.71, P  ≤ 0.01), while the T air  exhibited the strongest correlation with the ET  of GG, GG + BC, LG, and LG + BC (R  ≥ 0.71, P  ≤ 0.01). The constructed PLS-PM model could explain the 60 % (R 2  = 0.60) of the variation in the ET . Among the soil and climatic factors, the θ  (r  = 0.43, P  < 0.01), T air  (r  = 0.86, P  < 0.01), and soil cover type (r  = 0.15, P  < 0.05) had significant direct effects on the ET . Moreover, it was found that the soil cover type exerted a greater indirect effect on the ET  by influencing the θ  and T s  (r  = 0.29) than a direct effect. The total effects of these environmental factors on the ET  ranked as T air  (r  = 0.93) > θ  (r  = 0.44) = soil cover type (r  = 0.44) > T s  (r  = 0.12) > RH (r  = 0.07) (Fig. 8  ).   4 Discussion 4.1 How does biocrust affect soil evaporation process? As expected, our results indicated that the evaporation from the biocrusts was significantly (P  < 0.01; Figs. 2–3 ) higher than that from the bare soil. Biocrusts can alter most soil properties, despite their thickness ranges only from a few millimeters to several centimeters. A comparison with the bare soil revealed higher content of soil fine particles (clay and silt) and organic matter in biocrust-covered soils, which further enhanced the total porosity and field capacity (Table 1 ). This fine-enriched layer improves water retention of biocrusts and prolongs their near-saturated conditions due to the small pore spaces in fine particles (Chamizo et al., 2013; Kidron et al., 2022 ). Biocrusts also increase soil organic matter through photosynthesis, extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) production, and debris decomposition (Drahorad et al., 2013 ), leading to greater water absorption (Kidron, 2021; Nishanth et al., 2021 ). These changes in soil properties ultimately influence the process of evaporation. Besides enhancing water retention, biocrusts often have higher microrelief or surface roughness and darker color, reducing albedo, potentially increasing evaporation (Chamizo et al., 2013; Kidron et al., 2022 ). Our results showed a significant increase in the θ  at 10 cm depth attributed to the presence of biocrusts, consistent with previous studies highlighted the enhanced water retention capacity of biocrusts in surface layers (George et al., 2003; Qiu et al., 2023b; Xiao et al., 2019 ). Change in θ  could subsequently impact evaporation dynamics. Usually, the evaporation process can be categorized into three distinct stages (i.e., Stages I, II, and III). In Stage I (lasts only 1–2 days after rainfall events), soil surface is nearly saturated and experiences high evaporation, which is primarily controlled by weather conditions and also determine the available energy for vaporizing soil water (Tugwell-Wootton et al., 2020 ). While a biocrust layer could potentially increase evaporation at high θ  conditions, it may also temporarily clog soil pores due to the swelling of EPS (especially in cyanobacterial biocrusts), leading to a decrease in evaporation (George et al., 2003; Kakeh et al., 2021 ). Thus, while the evaporation from the biocrusts was generally higher than that from the bare soil after rainfall, their difference was not significant on the first day (Fig. 4 ). Additionally, Kidron et al. (2022)  indicated that biocrusts may prolong the duration of Stage I by impeding drainage through wet layer or providing water to the surface via capillarity. The evaporation during Stage II, which typically lasts 1–3 weeks after Stage I, is influenced by water availability and progressively decreases below the potential evaporation rate (Li et al., 2022 ).
