During this stage, biocrusts conserves more water at surface compared to bare soil, which can promote water loss. Liu et al. (2007)  found that the higher water retention of biocrusts impeded the formation of a dry sand layer, ultimately increased evaporation rate. During Stage III, evaporation is minor and controlled by soil adsorbing characteristics (Davarzani et al., 2014 ), constituting only 1/10 of Stage I and typically < 5 % of the total evaporation (Qiu and Ben-Asher, 2010 ). Our results showed that, although the θ  of the biocrusts was higher than that of the bare soil in Stage III, the evaporation from the biocrusts and bare soil were nearly identical and not significantly different. Nevertheless, Li et al. (2022)  found that the evaporation of moss-dominated biocrusts during Stage III surpassed that of bare soil, indicating that the type of biocrusts perhaps play a significant role in influencing evaporation. In addition to the θ , the T s  is another important factor that regulates evaporation. In our study, the biocrusts under grasses increased the T s  at 10 cm depth (Fig. 6 C–D), consistent with prior studies showed that biocrust-covered surfaces reduced albedo and led to higher T s  and increase in evaporation potential (Kidron and Tal, 2012 ). In our study, however, the biocrusts slightly decreased the T s  at 10 cm depth compared to the bare soil (Fig. 6 B). This was mainly due to the following reasons. First, the substantial organic matter in the biocrust layer limited the heat flow into the subsurface. Second, the biocrusts prevented the formation of a dry layer at the surface facilitated greater heat removal through evaporation (Li et al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2019 ). The effects of biocrust on evaporation may vary from one type and region to another, leading to diverse outcomes (Li et al., 2022 ). Nevertheless, it can be affirmed that compared to the bare soil, the variations in the θ  and T s  for the biocrust-covered soil will markedly influence soil evaporation potential. Climatic variations play a significant role in driving evaporation, potentially amplifying the impact of biocrusts on soil evaporation.  4.2 How does biocrust affect grassland evapotranspiration process? ET  is a pivotal process in the hydrological cycle and plays a critical role in various biogeochemical processes, such as carbon and nutrient cycles (Eamus et al., 2013 ). In water-limited drylands, understanding ET  dynamics is essential to unravel an ecosystem functionality and to predict its response to ongoing global environmental changes (Maestre et al., 2012 ). Despite the fact that biocrusts and grasses are two key biotic components of semi-arid grassland ecosystems globally, impacts of biocrust-grass coexistence on ET  process have been inadequately explored (Kidron et al., 2022; Li and Xiao, 2022 ). Our findings indicated that the combined effect of biocrusts and grasses on the ET  surpass that of either one alone (Figs. 2–3 ), which means that the presence of biocrusts underneath grasses leads to an increase in the ET . We observed a 9.4 % increase in the average ET  for the GG and a 13.4 % increase for the LG in the presence of the biocrusts, as illustrated in Fig. 5 A. In drylands, vegetation patches and open areas exhibit contrasting hydrological behavior with higher infiltration rates and lower water losses through run-off and evaporation beneath vegetation (Bhark and Small, 2003 ). On the other hand, the θ  within vegetation patches can be consumed by the transpiration of plants, and the available soil water in the profile may be depleted through root water uptake when there is an insufficient supply from precipitation (Wang et al., 2019 ). Thus, it is expected that biocrusts underneath grasses affect the overall ET  possibly by influencing both soil evaporation and plant transpiration processes. As discussed in section 4.1 , biocrusts can significantly intensify evaporation by reshaping soil properties and increasing surface soil water retention. In our study, we observed no significant difference in the biocrust traits between those beneath grasses and those in open areas. However, our results suggested that the biocrusts developed at different locations had different effects on the θ . Under grasses, the presence of the biocrusts led to some reduction in the θ  at 10 cm depth. This is not in accord with our other finding i.e., compared to the bare soil the θ  was higher in the 0–10 cm layer of biocrust-covered soil. A possible mechanism contributing to the reduced θ  under the GG + BC and LG + BC may be attributed to the impediment of biocrusts on infiltration. The extensive root systems of grasses are expected to create a network of fine channels in soils, facilitating both horizontal and vertical water movement (Germann et al., 2012 ). This network, coupled with improvements in soil physical properties (e.g., soil porosity, bulk density, and microstructure) induced by grass root distribution (Guo et al., 2019 ), collectively enhances water infiltration. However, biocrusts may impede infiltration by obstructing water flow through grass root tunnels and macropores, leading to increased water content in the surface layer (<10 cm depth) and reduced soil moisture at depths of 10 cm or below, which potentially intensifies surface evaporation potential. There exists evidence that soil drying results in the gradual closure of stomata and, subsequently, a decrease in transpiration rate (Comstock, 2002; Sinclair et al., 2005 ). Thus, one should expect the shallow distribution of θ , caused by biocrusts, to reduce water availability in deeper layers and, consequently, to weaken transpiration. Based our results of the effects of biocrusts on the ET  and θ , we conclude that the biocrusts beneath grasses promoted the soil evaporation more than they impeded the plant transpiration, thereby enhancing the total ET .  4.3 The hydrological effects of biocrusts and their impact on vascular plants As the prevalent interface between soil and atmosphere in drylands, biocrusts play crucial roles in water dynamics, including soil moisture, infiltrability, infiltration-runoff partitioning, evaporation, and non-rainfall water (e.g., fog, dew, and water vapor sorption) (Eldridge et al., 2020; Weber et al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2022 ). On one hand, most studies argued that these living ground covers effectively regulate water fluxes and moderate surface hydrology, which contribute to water balance within ecosystems. On the other hand, some studies reported that biocrusts may have an overall negative effect on soil water balance in drylands by regulating evaporation outputs and non-rainfall water or infiltration inputs (Li et al., 2022 ). The effects of biocrusts on various hydrological processes may accumulate or partially offset each other, leading to complexity in their overall impacts on soil water regimes. Additionally, biocrust characteristics, such as type, cover, and surface morphology, as well as external factors including climate regimes, soil type, topography, and vegetation distribution patterns, play crucial roles in regulating the hydrological behaviors of biocrusts. By modulating hydrological processes, biocrusts influence water availability for vascular plants, as illustrated in Fig. 9  . In some arid areas, although soil water content in biocrusts increased after wetting events, it subsequently decreased rapidly due to strong evaporation, resulted in low water availability. This may explain the observed low above-ground biomass and fecundity in plants from biocrust-covered surfaces in the Gurbantunggut (Zhuang et al., 2015 ), Negev (Kidron, 2019 ) and Australian (Grigg et al., 2008 ) deserts. However, in semi-arid regions, the retention of more available water in biocrusts would extend the bioactive time for organisms (e.g., microbes, seedlings, and surrounding plants) residing in the surface layer. In other words, biocrusts can benefit shallow-rooted annual plants reliant on surface water. Within vegetation patches, biocrusts are expected to reduce available water in deeper layers, disadvantaging deep-rooted shrubs (Xiao and Hu, 2017 ). Additionally, biocrusts developed in open areas (particular on upslopes) usually act as runoff sources, potentially enhancing water availability to dryland vegetation by intensifying horizontal water redistribution (Baldauf et al., 2023; Rodriguez-Caballero et al., 2018a; Rodriguez-Caballero et al., 2018b ). Therefore, it is necessary to further assess the comprehensive role of biocrusts in dryland hydrology and their ecological consequences, which will help inform ecological conservation and vegetation restoration efforts to maintain dryland ecosystem functioning and services in the face of global changes.  4.4 Limitations and uncertainties Although this study provided insights into the impacts of biocrusts on grassland ET , we should note that there exist limitations and uncertainties that may affect results interpretation and their generalization. For instance, our study was conducted during the middle and late stages of the plant growth season, and grasses experienced wilting due to frost towards the end of the experiment. This potentially resulted in a significant weakening of plant transpiration. In this case, the influence of biocrusts on plant transpiration is extremely weak and almost negligible. Consequently, the grass condition during the experiment period may affect the overall results. Due to the finite size of the micro-lysimeters, there is a chance that water might have flowed outside the micro-lysimeters along branches and leaves. There might be errors in the micro-lysimeter-based ET  measurements for grasses with or without biocrusts. Before the experiment began, we measured the horizontal distribution range of the selected plant roots, which was about 20–25 cm. Therefore, the micro-lysimeters that we used may have limited the horizontal growth of the plant roots during the experiment. In some studies conducted in arid environments (annual precipitation < 220 mm), micro-lysimeters were uauslly placed almost level with the soil surface to simulate natural conditions (Feigenwinter et al., 2020; Uclés et al., 2013 ). However, the upper end of our micro-lysimeters was positioned 2 cm above the soil surface. We believe this design can, to some degree, prevent splashing and runoff generation due to more frequent rainfall events (annual precipitation = 454 mm). Although we believe that inferring reduced plant transpiration from decreased soil moisture is reasonable, the lack of direct measurements of plant transpiration rates may reduce the credibility of the results. Lastly, the varied combinations of biocrusts with grasses were not fully considered. Generalizing results to broader regions should be carried out with caution and careful considerations of the specific conditions in each ecosystem.   5 Conclusions The cyanobacterial-moss mixed biocrusts significantly increased the soil evaporation rate by 20.9 % compared to the bare soil. Under gramineous and leguminous grasses, the presence of biocrusts led to a 9.4 % and 13.4 % increase in the evapotranspiration rate, respectively, contributed 8.1 % and 10.6 % to the average evapotranspiration rate. The increased soil evaporation induced by the biocrusts was largely due to their enhanced water retention in the surface layer. Notably, beneath grasses, the biocrusts decreased the soil moisture at depth 10 cm, attributed to their strong impediment of rainfall infiltration into the deeper layers. The plant transpiration would potentially be limited due to low water availability in the root zone. Thus, we concluded that biocrusts beneath grasses promoted the soil evaporation more than they impeded the plant transpiration. However, the higher surface water content under the biocrusts indicated that they may not reduce the surface water availability through increased evaporation, thus avoiding water stress for shallow-rooted annual plants. For species with relatively deep roots, biocrusts could potentially exacerbate water scarcity, increasing the risks of their mortality and further land degradation during drought years. These findings contribute to a better understanding of the effects of biocrusts on dryland water balance and the survival of vascular plants, which has profound implications on the stability of the dryland ecosystems worldwide.
1 Introduction The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) categorizes weather and climate events relevant to extremes (Seneviratne et al., 2021 ) into three areas: weather and climate variables (e.g., temperature, precipitation, wind), phenomena related to weather and climate (e.g., monsoons, El Niño and other modes of variability, tropical and extratropical cyclones) and the impacts on the natural physical environment (droughts, floods, extreme sea levels, waves, and coastal impacts). There is clearly a strong connection between these three categories. For instance, extreme precipitation relates to phenomena such as cyclones (hurricanes) with severe impacts such as sea level rise, coastal erosion, property loss and fatalities. There has been a clear positive trend in the long-term records of major hurricanes, especially in the North Atlantic (Kossin et al., 2020; Walsh et al., 2016 ). It has been reported that global warming due to the rise in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions will cause the average intensity of global tropical cyclones to increase and shift towards stronger storms (Knutson et al., 2010 ). Landsea et al. (1999)  explored the relationships between various environmental factors (Caribbean Sea level pressures and 200-MB zonal winds, the stratospheric Quasi-Biennial Oscillation, the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, etc.) and Atlantic hurricanes. The authors concluded that there are significant and concurrent relationships between these factors and the frequency, intensity, and duration of Atlantic hurricanes. Specifically for the North Atlantic region, “the tropical cyclone power dissipation is highly correlated with tropical sea surface temperature during hurricane season on time scales of a few years and longer”  (Emanuel, 2008 ). In other words, this statement indicates we should be expecting more destructive cyclones in the coming years. The timely dissemination of disaster risk information is important to alleviating damage such as casualties and property destruction resulting from hurricanes. This enables all stakeholders such as vulnerable and exposed populations, national or provincial authorities, and emergency workers to prepare for and prevent human loss and associated economic damage. Reliance on observation from land-based weather stations is limited since challenges include a lack of presence on the oceans and operations being disabled due to intense winds or extreme precipitation. In addition, the number of stations available is limited. Radar is a good option to use to address this issue, but radar’s spatial coverage is limited because of the cost involved in radar installation and operation. A good alternative is satellite-based rainfall estimations. Rainfall observations from satellite sensors cover a large spatial extent with high temporal resolutions. They are also high-resolution precipitation products (HRPPs) that can be used to resolve small-scale precipitation processes (Turk et al., 2008 ). The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) established the integrated multi-satellite retrievals for GPM (IMERG; Huffman et al., 2019a, b , c) in 2014 as a GPM successor to the experimental Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) Multi-satellite Precipitation Analysis (TMPA) (Huffman, 1997; Huffman et al., 2007; Huffman et al., 2010 ). The IMERG algorithm provides seamless precipitation estimates globally through interpolation of all the passive microwave and microwave-calibrated infrared satellite estimates from the constellation of satellites by NASA and the Japan Aerospace and Exploration Agency’s (JAXA) other international partners (NASA, 2023 ). The accuracy of IMERG has been reported in various studies (Yuan et al., 2018; Silva Lelis et al., 2018; Rozante et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2017, Zhang et al., 2018; Boluwade, 2020a; Boluwade, 2020b ); however, none have focused on hurricanes Dorian and Fiona in the North Atlantic. In addition to these satellite rainfall estimates, there are other reanalysis-based products that can be used for hydroclimatic extremes. A good example is the Canadian Precipitation Analysis (hereafter: CaPA). This product provides rainfall gridded data in real time through the optimal interpolation (data assimilation) of three main products: the first guess/trial field forecast from a regional climate model (Regional Deterministic Prediction System (RDPS)), gauged precipitation and radar estimates (Fortin et al., 2015 ). The verification of precipitation forecasts, satellite-based estimates, etc. can be done using various metrics. These metrics can be from conventional (i.e., continuous, categorical) or spatial-based perspectives (Ebert, 2008 ). Continuous approaches involve methods such as root mean square error (RSME) and MAE. Categorical techniques involve probability of detection (POD), Critical Score Index (CSI), success ratio (SR), etc. The two afore-mentioned techniques are based on point-to-point, point-to-grid, or pixel-to-pixel correspondence; in other words, the spatial attributes of the extreme precipitation processes may be missed, may not be fully captured, or may not predict the exact (precipitation) values with the gauged observation, especially at high spatial resolutions (Ebert, 2008 ). Gilleland et al. (2009)  provided a comprehensive review of the intercomparison of spatial forecast verification methods. Spatial verification methods are based on fuzzy or neighborhood conceptualization (e.g., Fractional Skill Score (FSS)) (Ebert, 2009; Gilleland et al., 2010 ). This is when an area (neighbor) around each grid point is searched through a convolution kernel smoother for fractional estimates or coverage and mean values that are greater than or equal to certain thresholds (i.e., intensity) in both gauge observation and verifying images (i.e., satellite estimates). Methods such as true metrics (Zhu et al., 2011 ) based on the spatial alignment summary concept involve using a simple scalar number to measure the amount of overlap between two verifying fields. Other methods such as the Intensity Scale (IS) are based on assessment of the precipitation rate intensity and spatial scale of the error in both verifying fields (Casati et al., 2004 ; Casati, 2008; Casati, 2010 ). These methods provide added advantages to both continuous and categorical verification. For instance, spatial verification techniques overcome the “double penalty” problems in both categorical and continuous metrics in that the estimate “of a precipitation feature that is correct in terms of intensity, size, and timing, but incorrect concerning location, results in very poor categorical error scores (many misses and false alarms), and large RMSE ” (Ludwig-Maximilians-University (LMU), 2023; Keil and Craig, 2009 ). In other words, RMSE will exhibit a “double penalty” issue when used on two HRPPs, whereas the error in the verifying field (i.e., IMERG products) may just be a positional shift or locational misalignment (Zhu et al., 2011 ). Therefore, in this study we combine the strengths of all the verification methods from continuous, categorical, and spatial perspectives. Furthermore, Gilleland et al. (2009)  provided various scenarios and questions that may be of interest in verification purposes and associated verification techniques that can be applied in such situations. Their recommendations are not restricted to spatial verification methods alone, as continuous and categorical methods were also suggested. For instance, conventional methods can be used to quantify intensity errors and distributions of a satellite-based precipitation field. The primary objective of this study is to quantify the reliability of CaPA and IMERG products in capturing and correctly reproducing hydroclimatic extremes in the North Atlantic. This study will focus on two recent hurricanes (i.e., Dorian and Fiona) that impacted the northeastern coast of the North Atlantic, causing significant damage and power outages. This study will answer important research questions by employing a mixture of continuous, categorical, and spatial verification methods to provide useful information about the reliability of these two precipitation products. These questions include (1) How did the three IMERG products perform throughout the duration of the hydroclimatic extremes? (2) What was the timing error of the three IMERG products on each date of the two extreme events? (3) Did the three IMERG products provide the right climatology (distribution) of the events over the course of the hydroclimatic event duration? And (iv) how do the average IMERG products improve with increasing scale?  2 Materials & methods 2.1 Study area The total area used for this study is approximately 2,829,761.308 km2  (Fig. 1  ), covering United States regions such as Maine (ME), New Hampshire (NH), and part of Vermont (VT). In Canada, the study area covers the provinces of Nova Scotia (NS), Prince Edward Island (PE), Newfoundland & Labrador (NL), Quebec (QC) and New Brunswick (NB). The North Atlantic has recorded 917 total hurricanes between 1851 and 2018. Within this same period, the number of major North Atlantic hurricanes was around 315 (NOAA, 2023a ). For 2019 alone, there were 20 Atlantic cyclones (3 major) with a total accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) of 132.2 (Colorado State University (CSU), 2023 ). For 2022, there were 14 total recorded storms (2 major) with an ACE of 95.1 (Colorado State University (CSU), 2023 ). This study focused on the major hurricanes that had the most impacts on the northeastern coast of the North Atlantic in 2019 and 2022, which are Hurricane Dorian and Hurricane Fiona. The hurricane tracks shown in Fig. 2   indicate that both extremes follow different paths with variations in their associated precipitation intensities. 2.1.1 Hurricane Dorian Dorian started (19 August 2019) in the Atlantic Ocean with a trajectory towards the Windward Islands, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and the Bahamas (Bruijn et al., 2022; Avila et al., 2020 ). The track of the tropical cyclone’s path is shown in Fig. 2  with the associated precipitation intensities. Dorian was a Category 5 hurricane and is considered the most damaging and strongest tropical cyclone of the 2019 season (Avila et al., 2020 ). It was a post-tropical cyclone when it reached Atlantic Canada with sustained tropical force winds covering most of NS and leading over 400,000 people to go without power in NS (Associated Press, 2019 ). Heavy rainfall amounts were recorded at various locations along the track of the hurricane. For instance, storm-total rainfall of up to 580 mm, 386 mm and 152.4 mm was recorded at Hope Town in the Bahamas, Pawleys Island in South Carolina and across several areas of NS, respectively. The highest storm surge was measured at Shediac, NB. The tide gauge at this location was 6.50 ft above normal (Avila et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, a storm surge of 4.66 ft above normal was also recorded in Halifax, NS. Storm surges above normal were also recorded at Charlottetown, PE; Port-aux-Basques, NL; and Magdalen Islands, QC. There was also flooding due to the impacts of storm surges along the coastline of Atlantic Canada plus other areas such as the Northumberland Strait and shores of the Gulf of St. Lawrence (Avila et al., 2020 ). From both an insured damages and resulting casualties standpoint, more than 200 people lost their lives in the Bahamas with associated damages of $3.4 billion. In the United States, more than 160,000 buildings had power outages. The total estimated damages from Dorian in the USA were around $1.6 billion. Finally, in Canada over $105 million in insured damage was reported. This amount is distributed according to each province as PE (∼$17.5 million), NB ($22.5 million), NL ($2.5 million), NS ($62.2 million), and QC ($300,000).  2.1.2 Hurricane Fiona Fiona was one of the strongest storms in Canadian history. Fiona’s total duration was between September 14 and 27, 2022; however, only September 22–25, 2022 will be considered in this study. Fiona has been referred to as the “deepest cyclone by minimum pressure on record for Canada”  (Pasch et al., 2023 ). Fiona started as a tropical wave from Africa’s coast on 7 September 2022. The storm track is shown in Fig. 2 . By September 24, Fiona had made landfall in the southeastern part of NS (Pasch et al., 2023 ). A peak wind gust of 111 mph (179 km/h) was recorded in Arisaig, NS. Fiona’s wind speed was reduced with its movement northward over eastern NS (Pasch et al., 2023 ) on the latter part of 24 September 2022. Fiona’s lingering process or movement may be responsible for the destruction and damages seen in many parts of the Maritime provinces. Fiona caused an initial $660 million CAD in insured damage (IBC-BAC, 2022 ). On 25 September 2022, the wind speed reduced to 50 kt over QC and NL. Due to the heavy precipitation events during Fiona, areas such as Puerto Rico recorded between 203 and 405 mm in both southern and eastern areas (Pasch et al., 2023 ). Also, up to 210 mm, 127.5 mm, and 118.6 mm were recorded at Cape Breton (NS), Souris (PE), and Crowe Brook (NB), respectively. In terms of storm surges, large areas of southwestern NL, NS, PE and NB experienced destructive storm surges. For instance, the tide gauge in Shediac (NB), Escuminac (NB), and Port aux Basques (NL) was 3.9 ft, 3.7 ft, and 2.3 ft above high-water large tide, respectively. In terms of casualties, Fiona was directly responsible for two deaths in Canada. Also, Fiona left more than 500,000 customers without power, including 80 % of all NS customers and 95 % of PEI customers (Globe and Mail (GM), 2022; Greg and Salmaan, 2022 ).   2.2 Datasets descriptions The datasets used for this research are described below and were obtained from the sources shown in Table 1  .i. Gauged Observation     The gauged observation (hereafter: OBSERVED) was extracted from the Global Historical Climatology Network daily (GHCNd). This repository is composed of daily climate records acquired from different sources, and they have passed through common quality control measures (NOAA, 2023b ). These sources include more than 180 countries and territories that have contributed to more than 100,000 stations. Durre et al. (2010)  describe the protocol involved in the quality control used in the GHCNd. The FedData  package in R statistical software (Bocinsky, 2022 ) was used to extract the OBSERVED with relevant dates (For Dorian (September 6–9, 2019) and Fiona (September 22–25, 2022)). Concerning the time of observation, the GHCNd's day (i.e. 24-hr precipitation accumulation) is defined according to the time zone of the region where the weather station is located (NOAA, 2024). There was no specific uniform global time zone mentioned in the documentation for the GHCNd. Furthermore, in the referenced NOAA documentation above, “Time of Observation is the (2-digit hour, 2-digit minute) 24-hour clock time of the observation given as the local time at the station of record ”. Furthermore, weather stations contributed by the United States network (one of the world’s most consistent and reliable) concluded that the “time of observation varies by location ” (Menne et al., 2012 ).ii. GPM IMERG Products     GPM, which is co-led by NASA and JAXA, contains two core sensors (dual-frequency precipitation radar (DPR) and the GPM Microwave Imager (GMI). The DPR has both 13.8 (Ku) and 35.5 (Ka) GHz channels, while the GMI is composed of a 13-channel passive microwave radiometer (NASA, 2023 ). In addition, the GMI has four more high-frequency millimeter-wave channels in addition to those on the TRMM’s microwave imager (Huffman et al., 2019 a , b &c). All IMERG product’s time of observation is at 00 UTC.a. IMERG-E : This is the earliest and accelerated version of the daily GPM IMERG, which is the daily accumulation of the valid retrieved precipitation obtained from the half-hourly version of the GPM (GPM_3IMERGHHE). According to Huffman et al., (2019a) , the latency of this product should be around four hours after observation time, and it uses only forward propagation (morphing). The IMERG algorithm is based on the 2017 version of the Goddard Profiling Algorithm (GPROF2017), which is gridded, inter-calibrated and then combined into half-hour GPM fields at a spatial resolution of approximately 10 km (Huffman et al., 2019a ). The GPM IMERG Early Precipitation version 6 (L3 1 day 0.1° x 0.1° GPM_3IMERGDE) was used in this study. It was obtained from the NASA geoportal (https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/GPM_3IMERGDE_06/summary ).  b. IMERG-L:  This dataset is also the daily accumulation of the half-hourly GPM_3IMERGHHL produced by the NASA Goddard Earth Sciences (GES) Data and Information Services Center (DISC) (Huffman et al., 2019b ). The daily dataset has a latency of 14 h after observation. This additional 10-hour lag in this IMERG version makes it possible to allow data transmissions that were not available during the early-run version (Huffman et al., 2019b ). Also, this version has both forward and backward propagation (morphing). The GPM IMERG Late Precipitation version 6 (L3 1 day 0.1° x 0.1° GPM_3IMERGDL) was used in this study. It was obtained from the NASA geoportal (https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/GPM_3IMERGDL_06/summary ).  c. IMERG-F:  This dataset is also the daily accumulation produced by the GES & DISC organizations by summing the half-hourly GPM_3IMERGHH. The dataset has a latency of ∼ 3.5 months using forward and backward propagation as well as monthly gauge analyses (Huffman et al., 2019 ). While both IMERG-Early and IMERG-Late have no “concluding calibration”, IMERG-Final has a month-to-month adjustment with a recommendation to use the “best” products for any research activities. The GPM IMERG Final Precipitation version 6 (L3 1 day 0.1° x 0.1° GPM_3IMERGDF) was used in this study. It was obtained from the NASA geoportal (https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/GPM_3IMERGDF_06/summary). Notably , IMERG-F is not available for Fiona due to the suspension of V06 IMERG production by NASA.  iv. Canadian Precipitation Analysis     CaPA was developed by the Canadian Centre for Weather and Environment Prediction (CCWEP), Environment and Climate Change Canada. CaPA is a seamless precipitation analysis field produced (four analyses per day on 6-hour amounts and two analyses per day on 24-hour amounts) at various spatial (2.5 km for all of Canada, 10 km for the whole of North America) and temporal resolutions (6 hr. and 24 hr. accumulated rates). Three precipitation-based inputs are assimilated into CaPA. They are gauge precipitation from weather stations, weather radar (Fortin et al., 2015 ) and forecasts from the RDPS. The CaPA data product is “run at four analyses per day on 6-hour precipitation amounts valid at synoptic hours (UTC run time [00, 06, 12, 18]) and two analyses on 24-hour amounts valid at 06 and 12 UTC ( Canada, 2019 )”— the 24-hr. analysis version valid at 12 UTC is used in this study. More information about CaPA can be found in Lespinas et al. (2015), Fortin et al. (2015), Friesen et al. (2017), Boluwade et al. (2018) , etc. Table 1  shows where the version used in this study was downloaded from. In addition, the original dataset is in the Stereographic reference system. A “gdal_translate”  utility in the Geospatial Data Abstraction Library program was used to translate from this reference system (Polar Stereographic global reference system) to the geographic system (using latitude and longitude for coordinates) so that both CaPA and all the IMERG products can be in the same reference system. The original IMERG products were also re-gridded to have the same spatial extent and resolution as CaPA. The observation time varies slightly for CaPA and all the IMERG products (00 UTC). For instance, CaPA's daily 24-hour precipitation generated at 12 UTC used in this analysis and valid on September 24th, 2022 means the precipitation data would encompass the period from September 23rd, 2022 at 12 UTC to September 24th, 2022 at 12 UTC (Canada, 2019 ). This allows the assimilation of “a large number of 24-hour precipitation reports that are only available at 12 UTC ” (Fortin et al., 2015 ).  2.3 Verification methodology The verification methods used in this study are based on both traditional and spatial verification scores. The traditional verification metric is applied because the original gauged observation is point-set based, and it would be helpful to assess the performance of the IMERG products and CaPA at this scale. The spatial verification technique was applied (with CaPA as reference) since traditional verification scores often suffer from poor performance due to small-scale variability and “double penalty” problems. In practice, the extent of extreme events is always assessed spatially. A number of techniques were applied to answer various questions about the performance of the IMERG products for Hurricanes Fiona and Dorian. The SpatialVx R statistical package developed by Gilleland (2020) was employed to assess the reliability. The flowchart and sequential process used in this study is presented in Fig. 3  . 2.3.1 Continuous and categorical verification indices This type of verification is used to assess how the values of the satellite observations ( P )    differ from OBSERVED ( O )   . The verification methods compute the average amount by which OBSERVED is greater than IMERG products (BIAS), mean absolute errors or difference (MAE) and root mean square error (RMSE) (Table 3 ). The optimal values of these indices are defined in Table 2   . For the categorical verification, both IMERG products, CaPA and OBSERVED were converted into a dichotomous protocol where the possible outcomes are “yes, an event with a certain threshold did occur” or “no, the event did not occur” (WCRP, 2015; Boluwade, 2020a ). Table 3  provides a summary of the joint distribution called the contingency table, which states that:a :    signifies that the satellite products estimated rain would occur, and it did occur (“Hit”);  b :    signifies that the satellite products estimated rain would occur, but it did not occur (“False Alarm”); and  c :    signifies that the satellite products estimated rain would not occur, but it did occur (“Miss”).  d :    signifies that the satellite products estimated rain would not occur and it did not occur (“Correct Negatives”).    Categorical metrics (and their optimal values) such as probability of detection (POD), false alarm ratio (FAR), bias score (frequency bias), and Critical Success Index (CSI) are derived using the various relationships shown in both Tables 2 & 3 . A performance diagram developed by Roebber (2009)  displays all these metrics on the same page. Furthermore, an R statistical software package (verification) in Gilleland (2015)  can be used to compute and plot the metrics.  2.3.2 Spatial verification indices i. Fractions Skill Score (FSS)  : This verification method is based on the work of Roberts and Lean (2008) . FSS compares the fractional coverage of hydroclimatic extremes in a moving window surrounding both OBSERVED and satellite products (Ebert, 2008 ). A moving window is defined as the filter or grid/cell size group used to evaluate how the spatial structure of precipitation products (in this case IMERG & CaPA) evolves and compares with the gauged observation. FSS provides the metrics to assess if the frequency of an event in the satellite products is similar to the events in the OBSERVED. In other words, the decision model for this method is: “A forecast is useful if the frequency of forecast (i.e., satellite estimates) events is similar to the frequency of observed events” (Ebert, 2008 ). This metric will be used to quantify the fraction of grid points exceeding a chosen threshold within the satellite product and CaPA neighborhood. FSS (with the best match as 1 and complete mismatch as 0) is computed as spatial fractions of CaPA (Z o  )     and IMERG products ( Z p  )    for a given neighborhood size, N  , and scale, s   (in both x and y directions) (Ebert, 2008 ):   (1) FSS = 1 - FBS  1 N  ∑ N  Z O    s 2  - ∑ N  Z P    s 2             Where FBS (Fraction Brier Score) is calculated as:(2) FBS = 1 N  ∑ N  Z O    s  - Z P    s      2       FSS will be calculated at various thresholds and scales. The resulted plots for each day will be an intensity-scale matrix plot where the thresholds (i.e., intensity) will vary along the x- axis and the scale will vary along the y-axis (Ebert, 2008 ). The window-sizes for the intensity-scale plot are odd dimensions and could be truncated when at least half of the domain size is reached (Ebert, 2008; Gilleland,et al., 2009 ). The SpatialVx package (Gilleland, 2022 ) in R Statistical software was used for the computation.ii. Metric Verification (metrV)  : This is a binary location metric method proposed by Zhu et al. (2011)  with the aim of measuring how far away a forecast product’s intensity is from the gauge observation. This method is a linear combination of two important measures: the total amount of overlap (dist  op   )     between two HRPPs and the mean error distance (dist  ob   )     as described by Peli and Malah (1982) . A lower value of the verification metric signifies a better IMERG product since this low value means this satellite product is less distant from the observation (in this case, CaPA) (Zhu et al., 2011 ). Intensity-Scale Technique (IS)  : This method is a spatial verification technique that applies various statistics to both observation (i.e., CaPA) and satellite-based rainfall products (i.e., IMERG products) (in wavelet space) of “a discrete wavelet decomposition (DWT) of the binary error fields for a verification set” (Gilleland, 2022 ). In other words, “for each threshold, the forecast and observation fields are transformed into binary fields: where the grid point precipitation value exceeds the threshold, it is assigned 1; where the threshold is not exceeded, it is assigned 0” (Casati, 2010 ). It is important to evaluate the bias between CaPA and IMERG products at different scales and to compare their scale structures, where Energy (hereafter: Energy) and its percentages (hereafter: Energy %) are computed on binary fields. Therefore, the mean Energy   , (i.e., the average of the field gridpoint, p & 0    squared values) per cell of both gridded satellite-based rainfall products, P   and observed, O   are defined as (Casati, 2010 ):   (5) E ( P )  = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  p i 2  ; E ( O )  = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  o i 2       The Energy Relative Difference (hereafter: ERD) is computed as (Casati, 2010 ):(6) E n e r g y Re l a t i v e D i f f e r e n c e = [ E ( P ) - E ( O ) ]  [ E ( P ) + E ( O ) ]        The plots of Energy, Energy (%) and ERD against scale can be extracted from the IS method, which would be applicable in quantifying the performance of the average satellite-based rainfall products distribution (i.e., climatology). Notably, scale (level) is defined as “the neighborhood lengths over which the levels^2 nearest neighbors are averaged for each point”  (Gilleland, 2022 ).    3 Results & discussion To investigate the possible benefits of using CaPA and IMERG satellite estimation in reproducing the hydroclimatic extremes of hurricanes Dorian and Fiona, the following questions were addressed. The answers to these questions, the aid of the various metrics mentioned in section 2.4 will help in quantifying the usefulness of all the IMERG products:a) How did the three IMERG products and CaPA perform throughout the duration of the hydroclimatic extremes?  b) What was the timing error of the three IMERG products on each date of the two extreme events?  c) Did the three IMERG products provide the right climatology (distribution) of the events over the course of the hydroclimatic event duration or how do the average IMERG products improve with increasing scale?    3.1 How did the three IMERG products and CaPA perform throughout the duration of the hydroclimatic extremes for both hurricanes Dorian and Fiona? The spatial distributions of Dorian from September 6–9, 2019 are shown in Fig. 4  . The first, second, third and fourth columns represent CaPA, IMERG-E, IMERG-L, and IMERG-F, respectively. The colored legend is mm/day. Across all the products, the plots on September 6 (1st row) show that precipitation has a consistent spatial pattern. This is at the onset of Dorian’s landfall in the northeastern coast of North Atlantic. The intensity on this day was up to 50 mm, and all the products captured this intensity. Although it might appear from the precipitation pattern that there is a landfall on this date, the storm eyewall is yet to arrive. On September 7, there is an eyewall of up to 450 mm seen on the ocean, but it is only captured by IMERG-E and IMERG-L. CaPA and IMERG-F have already been gauge-adjusted, but this intensity did not seem to be captured. Gauging stations are not installed on the ocean, which may be the main reason why both CaPA and IMERG-F failed to reproduce this storm. On September 8, 2022, all the products reproduced the intensity of more than 150 mm centred on NB and part of QC. This similar pattern is also seen on September 9, when the storm is weakened, power is dissipated, and the hurricane has died down. The evolution of Fiona from September 22–25, 2022 is shown in Fig. 5  . The first, second and third columns represent CaPA, IMERG-E and IMERG-L, respectively. There is a consistent spatial pattern of extreme precipitation across all the products on September 22, except for a higher value seen in areas close to ME, which was only captured by the IMERG products. There is an intensity of up to 250 mm on September 23. Only the IMERG products reflected this event. However, there seems to be a consistent pattern across all the products on September 24. A storm eyewall of more than 200 mm was captured by all the products at areas close to NS. Also, on September 25 all the products show a similar pattern, and the storm is now weakened with patches of rainfall, mostly in NL. In general, these spatial patterns and distribution show agreement and consistency between CaPA and all the IMERG products, except on certain days when IMERG-E and IMERG-L overestimated CaPA estimates. Comparing these two plots (Figs. 4 and 5 ), it seems that Fiona lingers longer, having almost 48 hrs of residence time on the North Atlantic coast. This is likely one of the reasons why the associated insurance damage for Fiona was more than $800 million (Pangilinan, 2023 ) compared to the $75 million reported for Dorian, despite Dorian being a Category 5 hurricane. Table 4   shows the descriptive statistics of OBSERVED, CaPA and satellite-based precipitation estimates (IMERG-F, IMERG-E, and IMERG-L) for Hurricane Dorian (September 6–9, 2019) and Fiona (September 22–25, 2022). For Dorian, the average extreme precipitation for OBSERVED, CaPA, IMERG-E, IMERG-L, and IMERG-F is 6.13 mm/day, 6.90 mm/day, 8.72 mm/day, 9.36 mm/day and 8.47 mm/day, respectively. This shows that, on average, OBSERVED is almost the same as CaPA; however, all the IMERG products overestimated the gauge precipitation. The maximum intensity for OBSERVED, CaPA IMERG-E, IMERG-L, and IMERG-F is 161 mm/day, 134.51 mm/day, 188.53 mm/day, 153.07 mm/day and 164.26 mm/day, respectively. CaPA underestimated the reported maximum extreme from the gauging station; however, IMERG-F (bias corrected) captured this daily maximum. The coefficient of variation (CV) for OBSERVED, CaPA, IMERG-E, IMERG-L, and IMERG-F is 320 %, 296.67 %, 286.70 %, 277.45 % and 270.56 %, respectively. The variabilities within all the products are very close compared to the gauged precipitation. All the products are gridded and may have the effect of smoothening where large values are underestimated, and low values are overestimated. For Fiona, the mean intensity for OBSERVED, CaPA, IMERG-E, and IMERG-L is 10.03 mm/day, 11.67 mm/day, 16.07 mm/day and 18.15 mm/day, respectively. Again, the OBSERVED and CaPA average extreme precipitation intensity values are very close, whereas IMERG-E and IMERG-L overestimated the gauge precipitation. In addition, the maximum precipitation rate for OBSERVED, CaPA, IMERG-E, and IMERG-L is 127.80 mm/day, 131 mm/day, 201.78 mm/day and 197.70 mm/day, respectively. This also shows that both OBSERVED and CaPA almost agree, whereas all the IMERG products overestimated the maximum precipitation rate. The CV pattern seen in Dorian is also replicated in Fiona. Table 5   shows the RMSE, ME and BIAS (continuous metric) values for both hurricanes. For Dorian, the RMSE for CaPA, IMERG-E, IMERG-L, and IMERG-F is 18.1 mm, 28.75 mm, 29.01 mm and 26.78 mm, respectively. The lower values for CaPA demonstrate its superiority. The MAE for CaPA, IMERG-E, IMERG-L, and IMERG-F is 5.58 mm/day, 10.97 mm/day, 11.15 mm/day and 10.37 mm/day, respectively. This result also shows that all the IMERG products have ME values that are almost twice that of CaPA. This further confirms the superiority of CaPA over other products. The BIAS for CaPA was also smaller than all the IMERG products. For Fiona, the RMSE for CaPA, IMERG-E, and IMERG-L is 23.2 mm/day, 29.51 mm/day and 32.73 mm/day, respectively. Further, the MAE for CaPA, IMERG-E, and IMERG-L is 12.54 mm/day, 17.8 mm/day and 19.72 mm/day, respectively. Similarly, for BIAS, CaPA, IMERG-E, and IMERG-L have values of −1.64, −6.04 and −8.12, respectively. When using these three continuous verifications for Dorian and Fiona, CaPA outperforms all the satellite products. This confirms the effect of gauge precipitation integration into CaPA. In other words, all these metrics demonstrate that CaPA can be used as a proxy for gauged precipitation, especially during hydroclimatic extremes. The categorical performance of CaPA (black), IMERG-E (blue), IMERG-L (green) and IMERG-F (red) at thresholds of 5 mm, 10 mm, 30 mm, 50 mm, and 150 mm for Dorian (left panel) and Fiona (right panel) (Fig. 6  ). All the categorical verification metrics such as SR, POD, BIAS and CSI are displayed on this plot. The BIAS (categorical based) is shown as the dashed lines that have extended labels on the upper (2nd) of both the x and y axes. Also, the contour lines in solid format indicate the CSI values. Considering Dorian, the POD (∼0.75) for all precipitation thresholds was consistent for CaPA (except at 150 mm), whereas other IMERG products show a consistent reduction from low to high precipitation thresholds. Furthermore, the SR for all thresholds (except 150 mm) for CaPA was consistent at around 0.6. This is the ratio of the number of hits divided by the total of both hits and false alarms, meaning that CaPA consistently correctly predicted the hits (agreement with gauge observation) for all thresholds. This is in contrast with IMERG products where there were consistent reductions in the SR values at all thresholds. In terms of BIAS, all the IMERG products overestimated the OBSERVED at all precipitation thresholds. For CSI, there is evidence of consistent reductions from low to high thresholds for all the IMERG products. For CaPA, the CSI for all thresholds (except at 150 mm) was around 0.45. Fig. 6  (right panel) shows the categorical performance during Fiona. All the products consistently overestimated the OBSERVED at all thresholds. In terms of detection, CaPA has the highest POD (∼0.6) at 5 mm. There is a consistent reduction in POD throughout the thresholds. This performance is also noticed in SR at all thresholds. The implications of this are that both CaPA and IMERG products had challenges in reproducing the intensity of Fiona at high thresholds, especially at intensities above 5 mm. Notably, this categorical test is a point-to-grid approach whose performance may not directly reflect the similarities among the products seen in the spatial distributions and patterns discussed above.  3.2 Spatial verification of satellite production quantifying the timing and spatial alignment errors of IMERG products Accurate timing is very important, especially for high extremes. A slight or significant spatial misalignment or error in timing can be catastrophic, especially from an early warning effort standpoint. It can significantly impact relocation efforts, especially for vulnerable populations. It is also important to understand the lead or lag time of these satellite products for better calibration and improvement in their underlying algorithms. This section equally performed the verifications of the satellite products on a daily temporal scale for both Dorian and Fiona. Considering Dorian, Fig. 7   shows the FSS between CaPA and satellite-based rainfall products (IMERG-E (left panel); IMERG-L (middle panel) and IMERG-F (right panel)) from September 6–9, 2019. FSS captured the similarities of the CaPA and IMERG product probabilities within the increasing neighborhoods. The white areas or regions in the matrix plot (1st row, 3rd column) show where the intensity-scale combination could not be resolved (Ebert, 2008 ). On 6 September 2019 (onset of Dorian in the northeastern coast of North Atlantic), all the products show a consistent FSS increase (up to 0.7) for both the 10-mm and 20-mm thresholds with increasing scales. These thresholds show that with a neighborhood distance of 65 (i.e., 650 km), there are more similarities of the IMERG products. It is also clear that on this day (September 6, 2019), all the IMERG products could not reproduce high rain thresholds. On 7 September 2019, all the products performed poorly with an FSS of 0.3 throughout the IMERG products. Looking through the spatial distribution and pattern shown above (Fig. 4 ), it seems there are significant areas of no-overlap on this day. This might be due to a lack of CaPA capturing the intensities. CaPA contains gauged precipitation from weather stations, which may have a problem capturing this event. September 8, 2019, seems to be the day where the similarity of CaPA and IMERG product event probabilities has the highest value. There is a consistent increase in FSS for all the thresholds and scale from 1 (10 km) to 65 (650 km). This shows that the IMERG products captured most of the intensities on this date. For the same defined intensities on September 9, 2019, all the IMERG products did not have any overlap with CaPA. This shows that once over land with more than 24 hrs. after hitting the mainland, Dorian was cut off from its heat and moisture sources (Hurricane, 2023 ) and finally died down; its power had dissipated, but there were still patches of rainfall across the North Atlantic. Fig. 8   shows the FSS score between CaPA and satellite-based rainfall products (IMERG-E (left panel) and IMERG-L (right panel)) from September 22–25, 2022. Again, the white areas or regions in the matrix plot (4th row) show where the intensity-scale combination could not be resolved (Ebert, 2008 ). FSS scores on September 22, 2022, show an increase for both the 10-mm and 20-mm thresholds for all scales and for both IMERG products. On September 23, 2022, the FSS score increased up to 0.8 at 650 km for the 10-mm threshold. Also, there is an additional increase of up to 0.7 for IMERG products from the 20-mm threshold. The similarities seen in both IMERG products on this date may be due to their spatial distribution and pattern similarities on this date discussed above (Fig. 5 ). The IMERG products’ performance on September 24, 2022, seems the best. There is a complete agreement and similarities between CaPA and IMERG products from a probability comparison framework perspective. FSS increased from 0.8 (10-km scale) to a perfect 1 (650-km scale) through the 10–30-mm thresholds. This is consistent with the almost perfect overlap of the high intensity seen between CaPA and both IMERG products discussed above (Fig. 5 ). Again, the satellite products could not reproduce these thresholds at all scales on September 25, 2022. Although this section did not consider smaller thresholds (i.e., 3 mm or less), it is likely that both IMERG products would still be useful (Boluwade et al., 2017). The next section, which deals with the average spatial distribution of the extreme events, will consider lower thresholds. In general, for both hurricane events, the FSS values for both IMERG products are greater for light 10-mm, 20-mm and 30-mm thresholds and larger scales. The most useful FSS skill is displayed at spatial scales of around 650 km. The IMERG products have challenges in reproducing the heaviest rainfall intensities (>50 mm/day). It should be noted that these products are compared with CaPA, whose accuracy is tied to the assimilated gauge precipitation from weather stations. The IMERG products captured some events located on the ocean, and these events are missing in CaPA. Importantly, there is no striking difference in the spatial verification performance of both IMERG products, meaning that IMERG-E (high latency) will be useful for many hydroclimatic applications. Interestingly, there has been a discussion about assimilating IMERG as additional observation in CaPA (Boluwade et al., 2017). Therefore, this study further establishes the accuracy and reliability of IMERG-L as a candidate for assimilation in CaPA. Table 6   shows the spatial alignment verification summary for Dorian and Fiona between CaPA and IMERG-E, IMERG-L, and IMERG-F satellite-based rainfall products. These scalar metrics (in pixels) measure the spatial alignment or displacement of a chosen threshold between CaPA and the IMERG products. When Dorian is considered on September 6, 2019, the metrV values at the 20-mm thresholds for IMERG-E, IMERG-L and IMERG-F are 16.93, 12.41 and 16.05, respectively. This shows that IMERG-L has the lowest displacement from CaPA at this threshold. For September 7, 2019, the metrV values (at 200 mm) for IMERG-E, IMERG-L and IMERG-F were 8.68, 7.93 and 5.87, respectively. Again, at this threshold IMERG-F is less distant from CaPA. This is reasonable since both products have gauge precipitation. On September 8th at the 30-mm thresholds, the metrV values for IMERG-E, IMERG-L and IMERG-F were 23.06, 22.17 and 22.90, respectively. A similar systematic performance pattern was also seen on September 9, 2022 (IMERG-E (18.50), IMERG-L (28.90) and IMERG-F (48.77)). For Fiona, the metrV values for IMERG-E and IMERG-L on September 22, 2012 (50-mm threshold) was 15.56 and 14.52, respectively. This shows that IMERG-L has the lower displacement from CaPA at this threshold. On 23 September 2022, the metrV values for IMERG-E and IMERG-L (50-mm threshold) were 22.30 and 21.20, respectively. For September 24, 2022, the metrV values (at the 200-mm threshold) for IMERG-E and IMERG-L were 7.39 and 8.95, respectively. This shows that IMERG-E’s displacement at the 200-mm threshold is closer to CaPA. On September 25, 2022, the metrV values (at the 10-mm threshold) for IMERG-E and IMERG-L were 21.98 and 22.57, respectively. Finally, in terms of timing error and spatial alignment, these products responded according to CaPA on each day of both Dorian and Fiona. In other words, some areas where noticeable differences in the spatial distribution and pattern should be expected, though there is significant agreement on the day-to-day evolution of the hydroclimatic events. This shows that the IMERG products at various thresholds and latencies can be used in monitoring hurricanes in the northeastern coast of North Atlantic.  3.3 Spatial verification of average climatology (distribution) of the Dorian and Fiona hurricane events This section evaluates if the right climatology (distribution) of the event over the course of the hurricane duration, the average of each IMERG product and CaPA were used in answering this question. The energy, energy (%) and ERD are used also in answering this question. Fig. 9   shows the averaged spatial distribution of the hurricanes throughout the duration of Dorian and Fiona. Interestingly, in Fig. 9 a, there are strong similarities between CaPA (1st Column) and the IMERG products. For Dorian, there are similarities (Fig. 10  ) between the Energy for CaPA and IMERG-E up to the 30-mm threshold. The grey color shown in the plots are regions where there are no values. The ERD shows that, at lower thresholds, there is a difference between CaPA and IMERG-E’s Energy per cell at 2 mm, 10 mm, 20 mm and up to the 70-km scale distance. Similar performances were also seen in IMERG-L (see Supplementary (S2) ) and IMERG-F (Supplementary (S3) ). The similarities could also be that the study area includes large oceanic areas (and land areas with very sparse gauges), so the GPCC gauge analysis lacks information and therefore, IMERG-L and IMERG-F look similar. The implication of this verification is that the energy per cell at various thresholds and scale (sampled discreetly) can provide information about the climatology. Considering Fiona, the spatial distribution of the averaged IMERG-products is shown in Fig. 9 b. It is clear that there are similarities in the spatial pattern and distribution of these two products. The Energy, Energy (%) and ERD (Supplementary (S4) ) for IMERG-E show that there are similarities in energy per cell with CaPA up to the 30-mm threshold and 70-km scale. Again, the grey color shown in the plots are regions where there are no values. Similar performances were also seen in IMERG-L (see Supplementary (S5) ). However, it seems that IMERG-L performed better when the ERD is considered. The implication of this is that IMERG-E and IMERG-L captured the spatial extent and distribution magnitude of Fiona from a climatology perspective based on CaPA as a proxy for gauged observed precipitation.  3.4 Implications of satellite-based rainfall estimation for hydroclimatic studies in the North Atlantic The IPCC Synthesis Report for the Sixth Assessment Report (IPCC, 2023 ) stated that climatic extremes due to heavy precipitation are likely owing to increasing GHGs, meaning that we will likely continue to be exposed to the impacts of climatic extremes. Monitoring and early-warning systems are crucial in this regard. Satellite-based rainfall monitoring has a strong role in filling this gap and providing timely information that can be used for decision-making. This study has been able to quantify the reliability and usefulness of these satellite products using different verification methods focusing on important questions. This study shows the importance of gauge observation and how it can be used in the bias adjustment of satellite information. Therefore, the continuous installation of more weather stations or radar is important to achieving this objective. The conventional verification paradigm has shown that IMERG-E & IMERG-L datasets are poor to moderate in performance; however, verification based on FSS, metrV and IS provide an argument in support of IMERG-E and IMERG-L and their usefulness in assessing hydroclimatic extremes. This study used CaPA as the reference field for the spatial verification study. Using various spatial-based verification techniques, this study reveals that an IMERG product (i.e., IMERG-E) could be used to provide additional observation data in CaPA. In other words, this study shows that there is no striking difference between IMERG-E and IMERG-L considering all the verification methods. IMERG-E is without any adjustment and has high latency; therefore, it should be a candidate in the CaPA assimilation process as advocated in Boluwade et al. (2017).   4 Conclusion & recommendations This study quantified the reliability of reanalysis and satellite-based rainfall packages/products in capturing the magnitude, timing, and structural scale of hydroclimatic extremes. Hurricane Dorian and Fiona impacted the North Atlantic from September 6–9, 2019 and September 22–25, 2022, respectively. This study applied continuous, categorical, and spatial verification techniques to answer pertinent questions. In the spatial verification (using CaPA as a reference), the IMERG products correctly reproduced the various distributed intensities of both Dorian and Fiona. Based on the results of this study, the following concluding remarks were drawn:1) Both CaPA and IMERG products were able to capture the low-to-medium-range intensities using conventional verification methods. The superiority of CaPA for various thresholds of the products was demonstrated throughout the durations of both Dorian and Fiona. Gauge observation and radar inputs were assimilated into CaPA. These results were in agreement with previous studies that established that CaPA can be used as a proxy for gauged observed precipitation.  2) Based on the spatial verification technique using FSS, CaPA was used as the benchmark to quantify the timing error and spatial alignments of the IMERG products to quantify if the CaPA features occur in a nearby location or not. Results revealed a moderate spatial closeness (alignment) between both products up to the 200-mm thresholds. Results indicated that the that IMERG products were consistent in reproducing the spatial extent and distributions of both Dorian and Fiona. Notably, there were instances where CaPA failed to capture some high intensity storms, but they were reproduced in the IMERG products.  3) Results from the climatology perspective indicated the strong similarities between averaged spatially distributed CaPA and IMERG products for both Dorian and Fiona. The energy, energy (%) and ERD showed similar values with that of CaPA up to the 30-mm threshold. The results showed no significant statistical differences between all the IMERG satellite-based products.    This study will be useful for atmospheric scientists involved in studying climatic extremes involving hurricanes or cyclones. Moreover, this study can provide the basis for the development of accurate early warning systems for decision makers who will be engaged in planning to tackle these extreme events. The Canadian Precipitation Analysis data are available at: https://eccc-msc.github.io/open-data/msc-data/nwp_rdpa/readme_rdpa-datamart_en/#file-name-nomenclature .
