1 Introduction Since the Industrial Revolution human activities have caused unprecedented and unsustainable changes to Earth. The growing global population, economic expansion, and demographic and lifestyle changes, led to an intensifying demand for natural resources, making these progressively insufficient to meet demand, posing an urgent global challenge and a crucial security threat in the 21st century, by fuelling conflicts over limited resources, triggering food and economic crises, encouraging migration, and contributing to political instability, that demands urgent attention (D. Gu et al., 2020 ). Simultaneously, severe natural disasters and consequences related to Global Climate Change (GCC) and weather patterns’ alterations have become increasingly frequent. Scientists believe these are mainly caused by human activities including the burning of fossil fuels, deforestation, increasing livestock farming, and the use of fertilizers, all of which are causing Global Warming. The unprecedented intensity of human activities is profoundly changing the state of natural water systems (J. Gu et al., 2021 ), increasing hydrographic pressure. Tangible evidence of that is drought, an extended dry period with a lack of precipitation, that leads to water scarcity, that can be measured by rainfall shortage (that may lead to drought and, simultaneously, is an explanation for it) and/or by people’s perceptions of drought in their residential area, a very efficient and impartial method to gauge socioeconomic drought (Edwards et al., 2015 ). Drought already indirectly affects 40 % of the world’s population (World Health Organization (WHO), n.d. ) and directly affects approximately 55 million people annually (Tsegai et al., 2022 ). In many regions this hazard together with water stress is becoming more frequent as is the uncertainty surrounding water supply. Water scarcity affects over 2.3 billion people, where 160 million children are endangered by severe and prolonged droughts (Tsegai et al., 2022 ). 1.42 billion people reside in areas of high or extremely high vulnerability (UNICEF, 2021 ), and roughly two-thirds of the global population experience acute water shortage in at least one month annually (Mekonnen & Hoekstra, 2016 ). Droughts, considered to be one of the costliest natural disasters, impacting a variety of sectors (Esfahanian et al., 2017 ), are expected to become common by 2050. While drought consequences may sometimes be hard to perceive as an individual, due to their gradual onset, their invisible effects, and the complex nature of ecosystems, these have a strong impact on certain locations and involve several physical and social aspects, affecting society’s well-being and economic stability (Edwards et al., 2019 ). As stated by Cook et al. (2016) , the extent of drought risks is not evenly distributed, economically or geographically. Economically, drought consequences are typically more severe in developing nations, as they heavily rely on natural resources and have limited capacity to manage climatic variations. Geographically, regions such as Southern Africa, the Mediterranean basin, Central Asia, and Central North America are experiencing a risk of up to five times higher than the rest of the world (Tabari et al., 2021 ), increasing the vulnerability of its population as the warming trend occurs side by side with population growth, rising migration movements, and even greater water demand (Linares et al., 2020 ). The Mediterranean Basin, where Portugal is included, currently faces extremely hot summers, increasingly frequent and severe heat waves, and changes in the precipitation pattern. It is a hotspot due to its geographic location and one of the regions more vulnerable to the impact of GCC. That is why the country is already facing severe changes in its hydrological resources, given that 60.4 % of the territory is in severe drought and 39.6 % in extreme drought (IPMA, 2022 ). In line with WWF (2021) , Portugal has a high level of Water Physical Risk, which considers both naturally occurring and human-induced conditions within river basins. It comprises four categories: Water Scarcity (high risk), Flooding (medium risk), Water Quality (high risk), and Ecosystem Services Status (almost high risk). The categories mentioned − Water Scarcity, Flooding, Water Quality, and Ecosystem Services Status − correspond to the levels of risk assigned to Portugal within its river basins, as outlined by WWF (2021) . Portugal ranks a concerning 198th place in Basin Physical Risk (amongst 251 countries, where the territories with the least risk are on the top of the chart). The lack of academic literature on this topic results in a substantial research gap, especially if we specify the Portuguese population. Given the significant impact of GCC on extreme droughts worldwide, a research question (RQ) was formulated to explore the potential direct role and influence of individuals in this phenomenon.▪ To what extent both the impact of extreme drought and awareness of water scarcity influence consumer behaviour?    The study seeks to understand the psychological impact of Portugal’s drought on consumer behaviour and explore how proximity to the problem influences perception and potential actions to promote a positive impact. It also examines factors affecting water consumption and best practices for sustainable water use, such as affect, social factors, perceived consequences, habits, intention, water-saving consumption behaviour, the impact of extreme drought, and awareness of water scarcity, providing insights for improving Portugal’s hydrographic situation and developing strategies for sustainable water consumption. Water resources, essential for agriculture, sustainability, and environmental systems (Akhtar et al., 2021 ), are affected by factors like GCC, agricultural practices, and urban waste (Nagaraju et al., 2016 ). Behaviour inefficiencies (influenced by socioeconomic, institutional, and environmental factors) (Callejas Moncaleano et al., 2021 ), and psychological factors (e.g. risk perception, norms, or attitudes), have not been properly assessed in their influence on water use, leading to risks in water quality, availability, and biological characteristics, posing risks to both human health and biodiversity (AghaKouchak et al., 2016; Akhtar et al., 2021; Bell et al., 2018 ). In short, the direct and indirect effects of this phenomenon will include reduced quality of life, health issues, unemployment, and increased financial pressure, potentially leading to migration, hunger, and poverty (Hallegatte et al., 2017 ). Those depending on water for economic livelihood (e.g. in agriculture) will be especially affected (Evans, 2019 ). However, the consequences extend beyond specific sectors, causing economic strain with service loss and job cuts (Edwards et al., 2019 ). Over the next decade, ensuring that the landscape is less susceptible to drought is a top priority (De Jager et al., 2022 ), as well as taking urgent action to reverse worsening of drought trends aggravated by climate and detrimental land use practices. The Environmental Footprint (EF) associated with resource consumption is used as a KPI (Key Performance Indicator) for environmental management, demonstrating companies’ commitment to social responsibility and suggesting a sustainable maximum to the consumption of a resource, simultaneously measuring its availability and what is already consumed. According to Hoekstra & Wiedmann (2014) , the EF is currently unsustainable, and it is expected to rise, due to the worsening of climate conditions and the overall impact of human activities on the environment that is exceeding Earth's capacity to support these demands in the long term. The Water Footprint (WF), a component of the EF, focuses on individual water consumption, promoting awareness, responsible behaviour, enabling sustainable management and educational programs (Gómez-Llanos et al., 2020 ). Managing a growing WF, like other EFs, may involve compromises, as reducing one footprint can increase another. Collaboration among stakeholders is crucial to positively impact all economic sectors, emphasizing the need for international cooperation and creation or reinforcement of water management policies (Hoekstra & Wiedmann, 2014 ). Although GCC is global, in developed countries people often overlook their WF, neglect water conservation, and disregard consumption due to the reliable and seemingly unlimited water supply. Despite water scarcity, easy access creates a misleading perception of abundance (Koop et al., 2019 ), leading to inefficient water use, which will then have societal, economic, environmental and health effects (Callejas Moncaleano et al., 2021 ). Consumers contradicting the previous pattern have a minimal effect in consumption reduction (Kelly et al., 2015 ). Habitual behaviour, driven by this misperception and selective attention we previously mentioned, will also reinforce people’s choices and attitudes, contributing to the persistence of certain behaviours even in the face of water scarcity (Steg & Vlek, 2009 ). Despite the possible existence of intention-behaviour gap, which is falling short of the intention to engage in a behaviour (El Haffar et al., 2020), namely in an habitual water-saving consumption behaviour that may lessen the intention toward it since individuals already have developed a routine and even if that implies saving water, habit outweighs intention (Gardner et al., 2020 ). The truth is that these habitual pro-environmental behaviours have become integral predictors of eco-friendly actions (Laroche et al., 2001 ), such as purchasing and consumption choices. Emotional dimensions, particularly affective connections to nature and anticipated emotions, play a crucial role in pro-environmental behaviour. Several studies emphasize the impact of emotions like worry, hope, joy, and anticipated guilt and pride in influencing individuals' intentions to engage in environmentally friendly actions (Carrus et al., 2008; Gifford, 2014; Ojala, 2008 ). As water scarcity poses an extraordinarily strong and growing challenge, water-saving measures and conservation are important when managing water resources. People’s perception will also increase when experiencing hot and dry days and their concerns with GCC, revealing the role of personal experience with elevated temperatures, extreme heat, droughts, and global warming (Marlon et al., 2021 ). Sometimes people’s insufficient awareness of the severity of water scarcity emphasizes the importance of understanding individuals’ backgrounds, experiences, perceptions, attitudes, and values to address the problem and promote behavioural changes (Abbott & Wilson, 2012; Kelly et al., 2015 ). Steg (2023)  emphasizes the importance of making consumers aware of their impact on the climate. Proving this point, Gilg & Barr (2006)  questioned 1600 UK households and found that if people consider themselves in danger, they will be more likely to save resources. So, a clear reduction in consumption numbers (in the domestic sphere and agriculture) is seen when experiencing drought and water scarcity but having an environmental attitude alone may not be sufficient to achieve adequate results. Strategies such as media campaigns, a mix of water use limitations, price incentives, and education can be effective in increasing water saving during drought periods (Kneebone et al., 2018 ). Providing water use feedback in real-time or promptly after an action can also be successful, but its effectiveness may depend on the context and location (Fielding et al., 2013; Tiefenbeck et al., 2016 ). While normative messages may increase concern and intention to act, they may have weak effects on households already affected by drought (Schultz et al., 2016 ). Understanding decision-making is complex, but behavioural economic and psychological theories help provide insight. Our research confirms that behaviour strongly influences people’s decisions, and even with measures in place, attitudes, emotions, and habits play a crucial role in maintaining a pro-environmental and sustainable lifestyle. Studying theories that explain pro-environmental behaviours promotes their adoption, as highlighted by Pronello and Gaborieau (2018) , supports decision-makers, researchers, and scientists in their drought-related decisions and studies (Cravens et al., 2021 ). Various theories are applied when addressing drought and water scarcity, including the theory of planned behaviour (TPB) (Ajzen, 1991; Schrieks et al., 2021 ), that primarily centres around individual attitudes, subjective norms, and intentions, perhaps not capturing the interpersonal interactions and aspects of behaviour that contribute to sustainable water-related decisions; Social identity theory (SIT) (Turner & Tajfel, 1986; Wright et al., 2020 ), that while provides valuable insights regarding the influence of social identity and group dynamics on behavioural intentions, it cannot capture as well interpersonal aspects of behaviour, including personal relationships, habit formation, facilitating conditions and the emotional dimensions that shape water-related decisions within households; and protection motivation theory (PMT) (Rogers, 1975 ), although valuable for understanding threat and risk perception and motivation to protect oneself and the community, diverges from our focus since our study extends beyond threats and focus more in the exploration interpersonal interactions, personal relationships, and habitual patterns that shape sustainable water behaviours. The Theory of Interpersonal Behaviour (TIB) is crucial to our research due to its insights into decision-making complexities. TIB posits that behaviour is influenced by intention, habit strength, and facilitating conditions (Mumtaz et al., 2022 ), aligning with our focus on multifaceted dynamics in water-saving behaviour. TIB recognizes the impact of personal emotions (Webb et al., 2013 ) and habits, providing valuable insights into the influences on sustainable water management (Heydarian et al., 2020; Taghikhah et al., 2021 ). This emphasis on personal and social factors is reinforced by Dissanayake et al. (2022) , highlighting the importance of these in influencing intentions for behavioural change. Additionally, TIB suggests that behavioural intentions are shaped by rational, affective beliefs, and social factors, such as norms, roles, and self-concept (H. C. Triandis, 1977 ), highlighting the complex interplay in attitudes toward effective water management (Kelly et al., 2015 ). In summary, TIB offers a comprehensive framework that aligns with the intricacies of decision-making in the context of water-related behaviours, making it a fitting theoretical lens for our research. This research intends to deepen our understanding of the determinants impacting extreme drought and water scarcity. To accomplish this objective, a conceptual framework was constructed drawing from TIB (H. C. Triandis, 1977 ) comprising eight key constructs: affect, social factors, perceived consequences, habits, intention, water-saving consumption behaviour, the impact of extreme drought, and awareness of water scarcity.  2 Research model The research model depicted in Fig. 1   is founded on TIB and exhibits eight constructs, namely affect, social factors, perceived consequences, habits, intention, water-saving consumption behaviour, extreme drought, and water scarcity. Sociodemographic control variables such as gender, age, and education were included in the research model, as is standard in studies on user behaviour (Bernerth & Aguinis, 2016 ). The connection between the constructs will be hypothesized to enhance the explanatory power of the model. 2.1 Water saving consumption behaviour Behaviour, according to TIB, is the actual physical act of doing a specific action and is characterized by its duration, intensity, frequency, and possibility of occurrence. It is affected, partly and directly, by factors like intention and habit (Triandis, 1977 ). TIB emphasizes the relationship between intention, habit, and eventual behaviour (Bamberg et al., 2003; Triandis, 1977 ). When someone has the intention and the habit of performing an action, this action takes place (Bamberg & Schmidt, 2003 ). It is important to distinguish this from habit, which involves unconscious processes, such as automatic and repetitive behaviour (Larose et al., 1998 ). Even with this emphasized difference, Fishbein (1967)  underscores that behaviour is linked to intentions, as individuals typically act based on their intentions.  2.2 Affect Affect toward a certain behaviour refers to someone’s emotions when experiencing it. It is either the positive or negative, the stronger or weaker emotions that the behaviour provokes (Gagnon et al., 2003 ). Triandis (1977)  highlighted the feelings of happiness, euphoria, enjoyment, sadness, aversion, dissatisfaction, and animosity. TIB also shows a significant connection between a person’s affect regarding behaviour and the subsequent intention to carry it out (Limayem et al., 2004 ). We propose the following: H1:  Affect has a positive effect on people’s intentions to perform a water-saving consumption behaviour.  2.3 Social factors In TIB, social factors embrace an individual’s assessment of the cultural and subjective beliefs within their reference group, as well as the agreements they make with others in particular social situations (Woon and Pee, 2004 ). These factors play a role in behavioural intention (Jackson et al., 2005 ) since social pressure may influence the likelihood of performing a behaviour. Therefore, social factors influence behavioural intentions (Limayem et al., 2004 ). Based on that, we hypothesize: H2:  Social factors have a positive influence on people’s intentions to perform water-saving consumption behaviour.  2.4 Perceived consequences According to TIB, perceived consequences refers to the probability of certain events occurring following a specific behaviour, producing outcomes that are either positive or negative in value for the individual (Woon and Pee, 2004 ). People attach value to consequences, which is why these refer to how well or how bad they would feel if the anticipated consequences happened (Limayem et al., 2004 ). The connection to intention might be that, according to Triandis (1977) , potential and perceived consequences influence someone’s intention to perform a certain behaviour. Thus, we posit: H3:  Perceived consequences have a positive influence on people’s intentions to perform a water-saving consumption behaviour.  2.5 Habits In TIB, habit is described as an automatic and routine behaviour, triggered by the environment, and done without self-instruction and deliberation. A behaviour becomes habitual when performing it is the actual goal and there is no reasoning in what the best thing to do is (Larose et al., 1998 ). Habit, just like intention, predicts future behaviour effectively (Orbell et al., 2016 ). When intentions are consistently formed, these will most likely cause a repetition of the behaviour. In this way habit becomes a more accurate predictor of behaviour than intention, as repeated behaviour becomes controlled by habit (Triandis, 1977 ). Hence, the subsequent hypotheses are put forth: H4a:  Habits have a positive influence on people’s intentions to perform a water-saving consumption behaviour. H4b:  Habits have a positive influence on water-saving consumption behaviour.  2.6 Intention Intention, as TIB states, is an individual’s self-directed plan or instruction to engage in a behaviour (Triandis, 1977 ). It is the behavioural intention to perform a specific behaviour and illustrates the willingness and effort required to carry out a specific action. Normally, it is linked to behaviour since it is usually its precise predictor and its antecedent (Cook et al., 2016; Limayem et al., 2004 ). A person's behaviour is a function of the intentions, of habitual responses, and of the circumstances surrounding the situation, according to Triandis (1977) . Intentions, in turn, are influenced by various factors, including social, affective, and rational ones. Therefore, if a user has a specific purpose to engage in a behaviour, such as water-saving, it may significantly impact whether or not the behaviour is carried out. Accordingly, we postulate: H5:  Intention has a positive influence on water-saving consumption behaviour.  2.7 Impact of extreme drought There are several definitions of extreme drought, but the broader and most used one refers to an extended period with the normal levels of precipitation being lower than expected, provoking a hydrological imbalance. Normally the duration considered is one season or more resulting in a water deficiency (Extreme Drought Definition | Law Insider, n.d. ), so one brief period of water shortage may lead to an extended period of water shortage, aggravating the situation. Thus, we hypothesize: H6:  The impact of extreme drought has a positive influence on people’s intention to perform a water-saving consumption behaviour.  2.8 Awareness of water scarcity Water scarcity is a relative concept indicating an insufficient amount of freshwater that can be accessed physically, due to increased demand, lack of or inadequate infrastructures, or limited water supply, to meet the peoples’ and environmental necessities. It is a growing problem around the world that affects developing communities the most (Britannica, n.d.; FAO, 2012; UN-Water, n.d. ). So, the awareness of water scarcity is when people are conscious of the current difficult situation. Therefore, we postulate: H7:  The awareness of water scarcity has a positive influence on people’s intention to perform a water-saving consumption behaviour. As discussed just above, both constructs, “extreme drought” and “water scarcity”, pose significant challenges, prompting a pressing need for action. Therefore, these might have a connection to intention,influencing people to act and address these problems. Even with such concerns, positive attitudes and intentions toward the environment do not always translate into actual behaviour, due to low facilitating conditions and external events that interfere (Echegaray & Hansstein, 2017; Gonçalves et al., 2020 ). Intention is influenced by attitudes and context, particularly in long-term water conservation. Environmental concern plays a role in this intention, driving people to act when allowed to reduce water waste and prevent extreme drought and water scarcity (Ambaum et al., 2023; Moldovan et al., 2022 ). However, according to Sheeran and Abraham (2003) , stable intentions usually lead to action, and the stronger the motivation the more likely it is that it translates into action (Ajzen, 1991 ), especially if these are relevant to someone’s identity (Sheeran & Webb, 2016 ).   3 Methodology 3.1 Measurement The survey questions were formulated based on the conceptual model’s constructs (Fig. 1 ) and adapted from several studies considering the concerned construct (see Appendix A ). The question items were Likert Scale questions measured on a seven-point scale (between (1) − strongly disagree to (7) − strongly agree), in the original scale, with a few exceptions to adapt them to best fit the study’s context. These were only administered in Portuguese since the instrument was directed to Portuguese people or people residing in Portugal. The data were collected through a survey – the study’s instrument – using the platform Qualtrics (https://www.qualtrics.com ). The questionnaire was available online and shared on social media (Instagram, Facebook) and chat channels such as WhatsApp. The sample for this study was drawn through word of mouth (WOM), reaching out to friends and co-workers without specific expertise or experience criteria, who in turn, invited others to participate in the survey. This approach allowed us to include individuals without regard to their background, experience, or qualifications.  3.2 Data To assess the instrument, a pilot test was conducted with 49 respondents, which were excluded from the final sample. With this, we could assess if questions were easily understandable or if we had any issues that needed to be addressed It also allowed us to make an initial observation of the instrument’s reliability and validity. There were slight adaptations following this initial examination and some of the question items were refined since they might not be well interpreted. The final survey was active for two weeks between the end of February and beginning of March 2023. 374 people started to respond but only 244 finished, comprising the final sample used for analysis. The common method bias was examined using Harman’s one factor test (Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). Eigenvalues of the correlation matrix represent variance explained by principal components/factors. The first eigenvalue (the larger one) accounts for only 36 % of the total variance of the items, and is thus well below the threshold of 50 %, indicating no common method bias in our dataset. As an additional test for common method bias the marker variable technique was employed, and the calculated variance is 0.030276, which is considered low (Johnson et al., 2011; Lindell & Whitney, 2001 ). Therefore, no significant common method bias was found in the data set. According to the respondents’ characteristics (Table 1  ), the gender distribution in our sample, with 71 % females and 29 % males, reflects the outcome of the recruitment process rather than a deliberate selection bias. Our data collection method relied on snowball sampling using social networks, which may have led to an overrepresentation of female participants due to the nature of the key informants and their subsequent network connections. While we acknowledge the gender disparity in our sample, it was not intentional, but rather a result of the recruitment strategy's dynamics. The two main age gaps are above 44 years old (40 %) and between 25 and 34 years old (32 %). Regarding the respondents’ education, it is seen that only 17 % have lower than a bachelor’s degree, and more than a third have a master’s degree or higher. Concerning their occupation, most respondents, 75 %, are employed, 10 % are self-employed, and the remaining 15 % are either student, unemployed, retired, or other.   4 Data analysis and results We used partial least squares (PLS), a type of structural equation modelling (SEM) approach, to test our research model and analyse the data, more specifically SmartPLS 4.0.9.0. SEM is a complete research approach that combines multiple parts of the research process. It merges descriptive and explanatory techniques, which allows for the modelling of both imperceptible constructs and cause-effect relationships between them. The measurement model component of SEM controls for measurement errors in the indicators used to measure each construct. This is important when measuring unobservable dimensions. The structural model allows for the simultaneous modelling of multiple independent and dependent variables. There are two main methods of conducting SEM, one of which is PLS. The PLS method was chosen because it is specifically designed for predictive purposes, none of the variables under consideration requires a normal distribution, and lastly, the research model is perceived as complex (Henseler et al., 2009 ), making it an appropriate selection. It also requires fewer assumptions about sample sizes and variables than other covariance-based techniques, which makes it a viable choice for small sample sizes (Chin, 1998 ), which is the case in the present study. The evaluation of the hypotheses developed in SEM involves a two-stage pre-analysis process, which includes examining both the measurement model and subsequently the structural model. 4.1 Measurement model The measurement model is evaluated based on internal consistency, convergent validity, and discriminant validity (Hair et al., 2021 ). Internal consistency is assessed through composite reliability (CR) and Cronbach’s alfa (CA), which must be above 0.70, as suggested by Hair et al. (2021) . Table 2   shows CR and CA, and only the construct extreme drought fails to meet this condition, since it has a value of 0.615. Nevertheless, van Griethuijsen et al., (2015)  refer to 0.7 or 0.6 as reference values considered acceptable, also seen in other studies such as the one conducted by Šprajc et al. (2019) . Convergent validity was assessed using the average variance extracted (AVE), meeting the Fornell and Larcker (1981)  criterion, which is the AVE being above 0.50, so that the latent variables can possess significant explanatory capacity, as they account for over 50 % of the variance in their indicators. Since all of them are above 0.70, they are statistically significant and, therefore, indicate convergent validity (Götz et al., 2010 ), as shown in Table 2 . Finally, to confirm the discriminant validity of the relationship of loadings and cross-loadings, the square root of the AVE (also known as the Fornell-Larcker (Fornell & Larcker, 1981 )), and the Heterotrait-monotrait (HTMT) ratio of correlations, were examined (Matsuno et al., 2005 ). First examined was the cross-loading criterion, whereby the loadings of each indicator should be higher than cross-loadings (Götz et al., 2010; Grégoire and Fisher, 2006 ). As seen in Table 3  , the criterion is met. Constructs AFF1, ED1, ED3, WSCB4, WSCB5, and WSCB6 were excluded as they did not meet the criterion. Secondly, the Fornell-Larcker (Fornell & Larcker, 1981 ) emphasizes that the square root of AVEs (Table 2  – bold values displayed in the diagonal) should be higher than the correlation between all the other constructs (constructs in the off-diagonal line). This criterion is also met. Thirdly, the Heterotrait-Monotrait ratio of correlations (Table 4  ) is below 0.90 (Henseler et al., 2009 ), providing evidence of discriminant validity.  4.2 Structural model and hypothesis The path coefficients and t-statistics of the model testing values were extracted from R  2     bootstrapping, which was based on 5,000 resamples, providing support for six of the eight hypotheses. The variance inflation factor (VIF) ranged between 1.418 e 2.350, indicating that no collinearity issues are present, as the interval is lower than 5 (Hair et al., 2017; Hair et al., 2013 ). Our research model (Fig. 2  ) explained 60.7 %, of the variation of intention, supported by affect (H1; β ^     = 0.117, p < 0.05), perceived consequences (H3; β ^     = 0.357, p < 0.001), habit (H4a; β ^     = 0.226, p < 0.001), and water scarcity (H7a; β ^     = 0.163, p < 0.05). Social factors (H2) and extreme drought (H6), contrary to our expectations, did not support intention. The research model also explained 54.2 % of the variation of water-saving consumption behaviour, which was supported by both habit (H4b; β ^     = 0.508, p < 0.001) and intention (H5; β ^     = 0.217, p < 0.05). None of the control variables had a significant effect: age (β ^     = -0.005, p > 0.10); education (β ^     = 0.018, p > 0.10); and gender (β ^     = -0.149, p > 0.10).   5 Discussion This study sought to shed light on what influences consumer behaviour when participants are under conditions of extreme drought and water scarcity. To accomplish this and draw upon the results of the literature review, eight constructs were developed, and eight hypotheses were formulated. Only two of these failed to receive support, and it can be seen that most of the selected hypotheses were validated based on the findings. 5.1 Theoretical implications Prior research approaches, in which TPB is used, differ considerably from the one we employed. Our methodology differed substantially, since one single model, based on TIB, was adapted to the research and into it two constructs were integrated – impact of extreme drought and awareness of water scarcity. Findings align with those of earlier research, establishing the validity of most of the hypotheses explored in our investigation regarding the factors that influence our study’s main topic. Intention is explained by affect, perceived consequences, and habit, which aligns with previous research considering that affect can, in fact, positively influence pro-environmental intention, since environmentally friendly behaviour tends to associate with positive emotions, which in turn can motivate people to choose such behaviour (Onwezen, 2015 ). Perceived consequences play a significant role in predicting intentions, agreeing with Monteiro et al. (2012) , who found that these are strong predictors of intentions that lead to behaviour. Habit, according to the literature, has contrasting opinions on whether it has an impact on intention or not. Boazar et al. (2019)  declared that it was not a predictor of intention. Their conclusions contrast with those of Boots and Treloar (2000)  and Heydarian et al. (2020)  stated that habit was a strong predictor of intention when applying TIB. In technology use, as experience increases, habit also becomes a stronger predictor of use than intention (Azman Ong et al., 2023; de Blanes Sebastián et al., 2023; Rifqi Hidayat et al., 2023; Venkatesh et al., 2023 ) so once habit is settled, behaviour is more likely to be influenced by it than by intention (Gardner, 2009 ). Unlike affect and perceived consequences, social factors did not have a positive impact on intention, which was surprising since many other studies have mentioned this construct as having a strong positive influence: either in the adoption intention of HEMS (Home Energy Management System) (Chen et al., 2020 ), CAVIE (consumer’s intentions of electric vehicle adoption) (Singh et al., 2020 ), adoption of climate change-related behaviours (Cialdini & Jacobson, 2021 ), or even in green products’ consumer purchase intention (Zhuang et al., 2021 ). Therefore, both affect (emotions) and perceived consequences have more impact on intention, showing a limited social influence. Individuals might perceive water-saving consumption behaviour as a personal responsibility rather than as a social norm, as every person should do their part and if they do not, it could result in negative consequences, individually and collectively, thereby contributing to the loss of the commons as it lacks the importance it deserves as a social norm. Like social factors, the impact of extreme drought did not have a positive impact on intention. Individuals might consider extreme drought more of a long-term problem (and thus “far away”), unlike water scarcity, which is more immediately alarming and had a positive impact on intention, due to that urgency to prevent water shortages (Jury & Vaux, 2007 ). Additionally, water scarcity might seem more manageable through individual actions, unlike extreme drought which usually requires collective action and systemic change.  5.2 Practical implications Hydrological changes and increasing drought frequency require water conservation and management policies that will protect and save water and meet future water issues. Nevertheless, this is not enough, since prompt intervention has a limited impact (Cravens et al., 2021; Wang & Chermak, 2021 ) and maintaining individual water conservation behaviours, even when water scarcity is no longer that predominant, is a challenge (Moglia et al., 2018 ). A multitude of responses such as research and investment in policies and programs, effective and improved legislation, awareness, and collective action must be implemented to reverse the current situation (Bamberg et al., 2018 ). Without changes from individuals, any efforts will be incomplete. It is therefore of growing importance to involve society, encourage water literacy, an individual's understanding of water-related issues, including water conservation, management, and environmental impact, such as personal water consumption, knowledge of sustainable water practices, and an understanding of the broader ecological implications of water use. Greater and more widespread water literacy in the population will make it easier to begin truly meaningful discussions such as the present one (Dean et al., 2016 ). This will allow cross-sectoral development (McCarroll & Hamann, 2020 ) and reach sustainable solutions (Bell et al., 2018 ). It might also be helpful to adopt other water-saving measures starting with small efforts such as water-saving appliances, which are accessible in the Portuguese market and complemented by government programs at a municipal level that offer low-cost water-saving appliance kits, and progressing to social feedback comparison (helpful for heavy water users but counterproductive for light water users), incentives (which are not many when it comes to water saving), and residential water tariffs and pricing that aim to strike a balance between water conservation and affordability by increasing prices based on consumption levels or simple water saving attitudes like repairing dripping taps or reusing bathwater (Kelly et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2019 ). Priorities should be well defined and there should exist transversal cooperation between the environment, economy, and society, to achieve sustainable economic, environmental, industrial, and human development (McCarroll & Hamann, 2020; Wright et al., 2020 ), because climate change is going to change human adaptability, and all efforts are needed (Evans, 2019 ).  5.3 Limitations & recommendations for future works Regarding the limitations of the present study, it is important to note that data are cross-sectional, which means they were collected for only a certain period. So, as a recommendation, it could be beneficial to do longitudinal research, to gather and study people's perceptions at several points of time or apply the Q method, a mixed method approach, for an exploration of how subjective thought and perceptions influence human behaviour. In addition to that, data were collected from only a specific public, the Portuguese population. Additionally, this study could be expanded to explore potential societal and cultural norms that may influence the values associated with water and therefore water use behaviours in Portuguese society (Haddad, 2015; Otte et al., 2021 ). The sample for this study was drawn through word of mouth (WOM), reaching out to friends and co-workers without specific expertise or experience criteria, who in turn invited others to participate in the survey through social media and chat channels. This approach allowed us to include individuals without regard to their background, experience, or qualifications. However, this method did not involve key informants, which is a limitation of our study. Future researchers should consider employing a qualitative approach with key informants to enhance the validity and depth of the findings. While our research adopts Theory of Interpersonal Behaviour (TIB) to explore the interaction of personal and social factors in household water management, several other constructs or other theories connected to environmental psychology could be applied. RANAS model (Mosler, 2012 ) specifically, holds promise as a valuable theory for studying water conservation behaviours since it incorporates factors such as risk perception, attitude formation, norm, ability, and self-regulation. It provides a robust foundation for analysing, designing, and implementing behaviour-change interventions, particularly in the realm of pro-environmental behaviours. It can capture a wide array of influences on decision-making, making it a valuable tool for understanding water-related behaviours, also providing a deeper understanding into multifaceted nature of household water conservation. Additionally, it is possible that some of the questions asked in the questionnaire regarding reducing water scarcity have a more limited scope for the user level. A more comprehensive question would be more relevant and broader. Moreover, we also recommend the exploration of the influence of family structure on water conservation behaviours to provide a more comprehensive understanding of factors affecting decision-making processes and their implications on water conservation behaviours. For future studies, it could also be useful to consider in-person distribution since it may enhance the method, allowing for researcher guidance, clarification of participant queries, and potential observation of non-verbal cues during the sorting process. Finally, the exclusion of certain items from the study was based on statistical indicator criteria, overlooking potential inclusion with justifiable explanations. However, their incorporation could introduce bias into the interpretation of study results. Future studies could explore these same questions in different geographies and test for differences.   6 Conclusions The human brain is influenced by a multitude of events and can trigger so many different behaviours, that its exploration in previous studies remains substantially unexplored. This study seeks to understand how people use water and their behaviour impacts consumption during droughts. In many ways, people are influenced by others (Franks, 2010 ) and this research demonstrates that social psychology will serve as a predominant guiding principle for understanding human behaviour. We introduced a paradigm shift in research methodology by breaking from conventional research and embracing the theory of interpersonal behaviour (TIB) to integrate extreme drought and water scarcity into understanding consumer behaviour. The theoretical contribution arises from the also surprising fact that intention was independent of social factors (H6 was not supported). It is also interesting to note that the TIB (main) hypothesis, suggesting the influence of social factors on intention was not supported, which may happen when individuals might perceive water-saving consumption behaviour as a personal responsibility rather than as a social norm. Notably, the impact of extreme drought is not having the expected influence on intention contrasting with water scarcity's prompting of urgency and personal responsibility, positively impacting intention towards water-saving behaviour. So, our findings align with prior research since most hypotheses are validated, yet unveiling insights: while affect, perceived consequences, and habits strongly influence intention, social factors surprisingly exhibit limited impact. Besides that, the study underscores the crucial role of extreme drought and water scarcity in elevating awareness about limited water resources, emphasizing the need for comprehensive strategies spanning policies, legislation, societal engagement, and water literacy efforts to achieve sustainable solutions and sustainable development through cooperation in the environment, economy, and society. It is crucial to start developing a strong body of evidence about household water consumption today so that it can be used to shape water conservation policies when needed in the future. From theoretical development, the results highlight the need for researchers to develop both tailor-made research models and not simply test theories that already exists. It is challenging to fully embrace a single model across a variety of possible situations. The integration of TIB with outer dimensions that complement each other, means that their combination is useful for understanding how behaviour impacts consumption. Future research may draw on other theories to explore the effects of other factors. We encourage researchers to conduct replication studies to confirm (or possibly challenge) this study’s findings, in different regions or countries. 1 Introduction Inadequate water management is recognized as a primary instigator of water scarcity, among other factors such as population growth, rapid industrialization, economic growth, and environmental pollution, to name a few (Dolan et al., 2021 ). Water scarcity is projected to increase even further in the future due to climate change effects (UN, 2018 ). There is also increasing evidence that these effects do not impact all sections of society in the same manner, with marginalized and poor communities being disproportionately affected by water scarcity (Organization et al., 2019; He et al., 2021 ). Therefore, adequate management approaches that effectively deal with water shortages are not only critical for supporting resource conservation efforts but also for protecting vulnerable segments of society and upholding social justice and equity in the consuming population. Reducing water demand through an increase in consumption efficiency is often seen as an appealing solution to deal with water shortages (Hatfield and Dold, 2019; Ward and Pulido-Velazquez, 2008 ). Agriculture, being the largest consumer of freshwater has been the primary target of such interventions. These interventions however are observed to fall victim to various externalities and rebound effects, whereby water demand adjusts in a manner that offsets the original decrease in consumption (Grafton et al., 2018 ). Moreover, efficient consumption technologies alone are also inadequate in compensating for supply fluctuations driven by climate change-induced environmental shocks. Since these technologies remain largely inaccessible to vulnerable segments of society, especially in developing countries (Deichmann et al., 2016 ), the disparity in climate risk exposure becomes even more pronounced. Therefore, despite remarkable progress in water-use efficiency, there is a distinct need to devise specific approaches to promote a fair sharing of such risks among the consuming population. Among such approaches, water allocation mechanisms may ensure a fair distribution of risk by implementing systematic procedures that prioritize equitable access to water resources among different users (Hassan et al., 2023 ). In this paper, we explore the performance limits of allocation mechanisms in achieving both equitable water access and other system-level targets of interest. Water allocation mechanisms form an integral part of agricultural activity, and are often designed to support key economic objectives (Liang et al., 2020 ). These objectives may include maximization of agricultural yield, resource conservation, satisfaction of demand, and cost minimization (Dinar et al., 1997; Speed et al., 2013 ). Many allocation mechanisms prioritize consumers in accordance with these objectives and allocate water to them in order of their priority (Li et al., 2020; Hassan et al., 2021 ). In some other systems, these priorities may be fixed beforehand on the basis of seniority, birthright, or other historical claims (Ali Shah et al., 2022 ). Many allocation schemes currently practiced in large-scale irrigation systems, prioritize users according to these, or related criteria (we discuss some representative systems in the following sections). However, multiple studies report instances where allocation systems designed for maximizing economic performance fail to ensure fairness and equity in water distribution (Bell et al., 2015; Muhammad et al., 2016 ). This failure arises from the fact that while optimizing their prescribed objectives, these systems inadvertently neglect the distributional impacts on marginalized or disadvantaged segments of society. In such systems, the very criteria that enhance productivity and economic output undermine considerations of social justice and fairness. Hence, even within allocation mechanisms, tension persists between the objectives of maximizing productivity and promoting social justice (Hu et al., 2016 ). While legacy allocation mechanisms from the age of the Industrial Revolution (such as those practiced in many large-scale irrigation systems), are designed for equity, they are dominantly supply-based, without the flexibility to adjust allocation during run-time to enhance the productivity of water that is already scarce to begin with Basharat (2019)  and Anwar et al. (2016) . Therefore, there is a need to explicitly incorporate equity-based design within priority-based allocation frameworks to balance productivity and equity goals. Hybrid allocation schemes like these are currently operational in various real-world irrigation systems, and specific examples are elaborated upon in the subsequent sections. In this paper, we concern ourselves with the limits of equity that can be achieved across an extensive spectrum of water allocation schemes. As mentioned previously, these limits are sensitive to the availability of water at each particular time. In practice, various methods of assessing equity are employed such as the coefficient of variation (Siddiqi et al., 2018; Molden and Gates, 1990 ), the Gini coefficient (Anwar and Ul Haq, 2013 ), and other statistical measures that report the variation of a distribution. However, less thought is given to the limits of performance that can be obtained w.r.t. these statistical metrics and the entire range of the metrics is often assumed to be in play. Here, we assert that the performance space of any allocation mechanism is fundamentally constrained by limits inherent to the mechanism itself. These limits, if understood correctly, can provide valuable insights into the potential of the individual mechanisms to achieve equitable distribution and perform well w.r.t. measures related to fair resource allocation. Furthermore, if the sensitivity of these performance limits to variability in the resource supply is quantified beforehand, it can help predict the performance of the allocation mechanism when subjected to climate shocks and other perturbations to prevailing environmental conditions. Thus, the evaluation of any allocation mechanism should not be restricted to single measures of equity alone, but must also be coupled with measures of reliability in supply. While we have taken equity as a representative metric for fairness or justice among users, it is essential to acknowledge that there also exist multiple other notions of fairness (Francez, 2012 ). For example, Benthamite Utilitarianism theory of fairness maximizes the overall welfare of all users (Mulgan, 2014; Viner, 1949 ), and Rawlsian theory of fairness suggests providing maximum benefit to the neglected part of the society (Kittay, 2018; Sen, 1976 ). In this particular study, we have used the Egalitarian principle of fairness, which states that all users are equal (Cohen, 2021; Woodburn, 1982 ), and we have used the coefficient of variation to assess equity (Siddiqi et al., 2018; Molden and Gates, 1990 ). It is important to note we do not advocate for a singular definition of justice. Instead, we quantify parameters that can be adjusted to enhance the performance of the water allocation mechanism. This parameter tuning can be guided by principles of fairness, irrespective of the specific notion of justice being considered. Nonetheless, one can view this work as a blueprint for other fairness notions as well. Even with the above understanding of there not being any universal definition of fairness, we also wish to highlight that the coefficient of variation is only one measure of equity among multiple others that exist. Indeed many researchers in the irrigation sector assert that the coefficient of variation can be used as a primary summary statistic to measure equity (Siddiqi et al., 2018; Molden and Gates, 1990 ). In many other studies however, researchers employ the Gini coefficient to measure equity (Anwar and Ul Haq, 2013 ), and this coefficient is also widely applied in the irrigation system of Pakistan (Shah et al., 2016 ) and the distribution of other economic resources (Bell et al., 2016 ). For many practical cases, the coefficient of variation and Gini coefficient are positively correlated, implying that the general conclusions of our analysis should remain the same for either indicator. However, it has been observed that for quantities that are relatively precise (such as the adequacy of irrigation water) the coefficient of variation is more sensitive to individuals in the right tail of the frequency distribution (also called outliers). Therefore, the coefficient of variation may often be recommended over the Gini coefficient if a measure of relative precision is selected to assess inequality (Bendel et al., 1989 ). In what follows, we conduct a novel analysis of the performance limits of water allocation mechanisms in a coupled equity–reliability space. We begin by introducing a typology of canonical water allocation mechanisms that categorize all possible mechanisms w.r.t. the resulting distribution of demand fulfillment among individual consumers. Uniform distribution, resulting from equity-inspired allocation schemes lies at one end of the spectrum, whereas prioritized distribution, resulting from efficiency-inspired allocation schemes lies at the other end. Hybrid mechanisms that combine aspects of both uniform and priority-based mechanisms lie in between. After defining system-level metrics of supply reliability, and distribution equity, we rigorously derive the theoretical performance limits of all canonical allocation mechanisms w.r.t. these metrics. We discuss the equity–reliability space in detail and comment on feasible operating regions within this space. We see that for the entire range of supply reliability, the best performance w.r.t. equity is obtained when allocation is purely uniform, whereas the worst performance is obtained when allocation is purely priority-based. Any operating point in-between may be realized by varying the proportion of initial entitlements in a hybrid allocation scheme. Our analysis also underlines the limitations of both uniform and priority-based allocation methods in accommodating the diverse needs of end-users and local contexts as these do not give freedom to improve performance by simply tuning some parameters during the allocation process. Our findings suggest that a hybrid allocation mechanism is capable of addressing the heterogeneity among users and local conditions. The theoretical results are complemented by numerical simulations of a selected agricultural district in the Central Punjab region of Pakistan. In the end, we speculate about the application of this study to large-scale irrigation systems of hierarchical structure where satisfactory performance must be obtained at multiple levels within the hierarchy. We conclude with a discussion of limitations and directions for future research.  2 Water allocation mechanisms Here, we characterize allocation mechanisms based on the adequacy distribution of individual users. Adequacy is the widely used metric for performance evaluation of irrigation water allocations (Kharrou et al., 2013; Molden and Gates, 1990 ). It is defined as the fraction of water demand that is fulfilled. We categorize the widely used water allocation mechanisms into three canonical types: priority-based allocation, uniform allocation, and hybrid allocation. Priority-based and uniform allocation can be viewed as special cases of hybrid allocation. The canonical types of water allocation mechanisms, their adequacy distributions, and real-world examples of countries where these canonical allocation mechanisms are applied at different locations and sectors are described in Table 1 . It is important to note that these canonical allocation types do not consider the temporal dynamics of water allocation schemes and also do not cover the entire range of possible allocation mechanisms. Therefore, we separately define the arbitrary allocation mechanism with any possible adequacy distribution. Below, we describe the types of water allocation mechanisms in detail.   2.1 Priority-based allocation In such type of allocation mechanisms, some users are prioritized over others. In priority-based allocation, some users receive water exactly equal to their demand, one user’s demand is partially fulfilled and remaining users receive no water at all. The water allocation principle of “first in time, first in right” used in Western United States is one example of the priority-based allocation (Savenije and Van der Zaag, 2000 ). Many demand-based allocation mechanisms fall into the category of priority-based allocation. These demand-based allocation mechanisms prioritize users according to their water demand. For example, in a demand-based allocation mechanism described by Hassan et al. (2021) , users bid for water by providing information of water demand and willingness to pay the water authority. Next, the water authority arranges the competing users’ bids so that users with the highest bid receive water with the first preference and so on. The scale of such allocation mechanisms remains low due to lack of demand information availability (Nakasone and Torero, 2016 ). Various regions in different other countries use priority-based allocation mechanisms to fulfill demand of users e.g., Kazakhstan (Karatayev et al., 2017 ), Iran (RazaviToosi and Samani, 2019 ), and Australia (Gómez-Limón et al., 2020 ).  2.2 Uniform allocation In this type of allocation, adequacy level of all users is same. One example of uniform allocation is supply-based allocation. Supply-based allocation mechanisms do not take into account the actual water demand of the users. Water delivered in excess of the demand is usually wasted in the form of run-off. Similarly, any deficit in supply is borne by the crop as water stress. Suppose the irrigation delivery schedule determined by the authority does not align with a farmer’s crop water requirements. In that case, the farmer either has to invest in an expensive alternative such as pumped groundwater or face a low yield. For example, in Indus basin irrigation system, water is allocated at the farm level using a supply-based fixed rotational schedule scheme, known as warabandi , institutionalized under British colonial rule (Anwar and Ahmad, 2020 ). Under this supply-based scheme, during a rotation cycle, each user receives a fixed amount of water in fixed turns depending upon her farm land size (Ireson, 2019 ). This is in contrast to demand-based water allocation schemes, where the water received by farmers depends upon their demand (Xiao et al., 2016 ). Various regions and countries in the world use supply side water allocation mechanisms to ensure equitable supply of water among users, e.g., Pakistan, Mexico, India, Netherlands, Europe, Chile, and Australia (Hassan et al., 2021; Khepar et al., 2000; Delorit et al., 2019; Gleick, 2003; Van Rijswick et al., 2012; Van Rijswick, 2015 ).  2.3 Hybrid allocation In such type of distributions, all users receive a base amount of water equivalent to their entitlement or water right, and some users receive additional water depending on their demand using priority-based allocation approach. For example, in water markets, water entitlements or initial water rights provide a base amount of water to users and users with high water demand buy additional water (Bajaj et al., 2022 ). Hybrid allocation mechanisms are commonly implemented in two ways. In one case, all users first receive their entitled water then additional water is allocated to certain priority users. The prioritized users are defined based on their socio-economic vulnerability or other similar factors. In second case, demand fulfillment of prioritized users is ensured first. The remaining water is then distributed equally among the other users (Wheeler, 2014 ). Hybrid allocations have recently gained popularity in many regions of the world, e.g., California, United States (Arellano-Gonzalez et al., 2021 ), Australia (Ann Wheeler and Garrick, 2020 ), and Chile (Donoso et al., 2021 ).  2.4 Arbitrary allocation In arbitrary allocation, we consider the possibility that the canonical allocation mechanisms may not represent all real-world allocation mechanisms. Therefore, we separately study mechanisms in which adequacy distributions may take any form and call them arbitrary allocation mechanisms. These cover the canonical allocation mechanisms and any other allocation mechanism. The statistics for the allocation distribution arising from the canonical allocation mechanisms are more easily analyzed than arbitrary allocation mechanisms. Thus, in this paper we first assess the adequacy, reliability and equity of the canonical allocation mechanisms. The analysis is then extended towards arbitrary allocation mechanisms.   3 Metrics for performance assessment The performance of an allocation scheme can be gauged by how well adequate and reliable water supply is provided equitably to users (Fan et al., 2018; Molden and Gates, 1990 ). In an irrigation system, if farms do not receive adequate water, crops may go under stress. Furthermore, the reliable water supply gives farmers the ability to predict and plan to obtain maximum agricultural yield. Moreover, a successful irrigation system requires fairness among water users (De Loë and Bjornlund, 2008 ). Thus, measuring the current performance of allocation mechanisms is necessary, so actions can be taken to improve the performance of the allocation mechanism. Performance assessment is regarded as an effective method to reduce the gap between the actual and projected performance of allocation schemes (Kazbekov et al., 2009 ). For performance assessment, different performance measures are used to analyze water allocation schemes. Performance assessment of the water allocation schemes is performed for various reasons, such as comparing the performance of one allocation mechanism with another (Molden et al., 2007; Cordery et al., 2009 ), evaluating trends of the water users (Moreno-Pérez and Roldán-Cañas, 2013 ), and diagnostic evaluation (Shakir et al., 2010 ). The performance assessment measures of allocation schemes are classified into internal and external assessment measures. Most allocation schemes’ performance evaluation research focuses on external assessment indicators, mainly water-use efficiency, economic efficiency, environmental footprints, and agricultural yield (Xu et al., 2011; Hollanders et al., 2005 ). Although there is also substantial literature evaluating internal performance indicators of water allocation schemes, such as adequacy, reliability, and equity, less thought has been given to the performance limits that can be obtained w.r.t., these measures. The performance measures of adequacy, reliability, and equity are considered when assessing allocation mechanisms from the water supply and demand management perspective. Adequacy is a measure of supply to demand, one of the main targets of an allocation system. Adequacy is used to calculate reliability and equity. Reliability is defined as the temporal stability of the water supply; it is the degree to which the allocation mechanism satisfies the expectations of the users. Equity is the notion of fairness among users. Equity and reliability depend on water supply, water management policies, legal structure, regulations, and infrastructure for water deliveries (Klümper et al., 2017 ). The definition of sustainable water availability for water users also has an embedded notion of reliability, and equity (Siddiqi et al., 2018 ). Reliability and equity vary depending on the adequacy distribution encountered as a result of the selected allocation mechanism. Thus, in this research, we use adequacy, reliability, and equity to gauge the performance of different allocation mechanisms. Equity and reliability depend on a number of factors that include surface water supply, water entitlements, allocation policy, access and management of infrastructure and regulations for water supply (Klümper et al., 2017 ). Equity in surface water allocation is achieved when the amount of water provided to each user is proportional to her water demand. Reliability represents consistency in surface water supply to users. The reliability of surface water supply is very crucial for users like farmers, as it enables them to optimally use and predict water availability that can help improve crop production. We suppose there are N   users in the water allocation and distribution network. A single user is denoted by n ∈ { 1 , 2 , 3 , … , N }    . A complete cropping season consists of a total of K   allocation cycles. The k  th allocation cycle is ( ( k − 1 )  T , k T ]   , where k ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 , … , K }     and the fixed time interval T   denotes the duration between successive water allocation decisions. 3.1 Adequacy We define the adequacy α  n   ( k )     as a ratio of amount of water received to the water demand. The ratio α  n   ( k )     for the user n   in the k  th decision cycle is as follows (1) α  n   ( k )  = min 1 , water  received  water  demand     .      The above ratio is such that α  n   ( k )  = 0    when no water is received by a user, 0 < α  n   ( k )  < 1    when water received by a user is less than her demand, and α  n   ( k )  = 1    when water delivered is equivalent to the water demand. If a user receives water greater than her water demand, the extra water received is of no use. Therefore, we assume that the maximum adequacy value is 1. An adequacy distribution α ( k )     for an allocation cycle is a vector of adequacy values for each user in that allocation cycle interval, i.e., α ( k )  = [ α  1   ( k )  , α  2   ( k )  , α  3   ( k )  , … , α  N   ( k )  ]    .  3.2 Interval reliability Interval reliability r ( k )     is the average water received by all users in the k  th decision cycle. This metric measures the range in which water demands are met for all users during the k  th decision cycle. If the water demand of all N   users is fully met during the k  th decision cycle of a cropping season, then r ( k )  = 1   . Interval reliability is calculated as follows: (2) r ( k )  = ∑  n = 1  N   α  n   ( k )   N   .      The maximum value for interval reliability is attained when all users receive water equal to their demand, i.e., α  1   ( k )  = α  2   ( k )  = α  3   ( k )  = ⋯ = α  N   ( k )  = 1   . Now, replacing these α  n   ( k )     values in (2)  gives us the value 1 for the interval reliability. It implies that interval reliability cannot get value more than 1   when water is being distributed using any allocation scheme. The minimum value of the interval reliability is achieved when no one receives water, i.e., α  n   ( k )  = 0   ∀  n   . In this case interval reliability would be zero. So, the interval reliability always remains in the interval [ 0 , 1 ]   . It implies that the interval reliability cannot get value less than zero or greater than 1.  3.3 Interval equity Interval equity e ( k )     is the coefficient of variation (Brown, 1998 ) of adequacy (α  n   ( k )    ) across the users in a water allocation network during the k  th allocation decision cycle. This concept is derived from the idea that geographical variation in performance can be used to assess equity (Molden and Gates, 1990; Kaghazchi et al., 2021 ). When the variation across users in a k  th decision cycle is low, then interval equity e ( k )     is low. Water allocation is absolutely equitable when e ( k )  = 0   . Interval equity quantifies the variation in water allocation across different users, and it evaluates whether different users in a water allocation and distribution network are getting equal water supply or not. For example, if the water received by all users is 90% of their water demand in a k  th decision cycle, then perfect interval equity is achieved. In contrast, the interval equity value is higher if half users are receiving 40% of their water demand while the rest are receiving 80% of their demand. The maximum value for interval equity e ( k )     is attained when N − 1    users have α  n   ( k )  = 0    and only one user has non-zero α   value, i.e., α  N   ( k )  = a   , where 0 < a ≤ 1   , Cox (2010) . Now, replacing these α  n   ( k )     values in (3)  give us a maximum interval equity value of N    . It shows that interval equity cannot get value more than N     when water is being distributed using the priority based allocation. The minimum value of the interval equity is achieved when all users receive same amount of water, i.e., α  n   ( k )  = a   ∀  n   . In this case μ ( α  n   ( k )  )  = a    and σ ( α  n   ( k )  )  = 0   ∀  n   , therefore interval equity would be zero. Therefore, the interval equity always remains in the interval [ 0 , N   ]   , where N   is the total number of users. It implies that interval equity cannot get a value less than zero and greater than N    .  3.4 Reliability Reliability R   is define as the mean of interval reliability r ( k )     across all allocation cycles. Reliability is calculated as follows: (5) R = ∑  k = 1  K   r ( k )   K   .      The reliability range is same as the interval reliability range [ 0 , 1 ]   , since reliability is simply the mean of the interval reliability.  3.5 Equity Equity E   is defined as the mean of interval equity e ( k )     across all allocation cycles. Equity is calculated as follows: (6) E = μ ( e ( k )  )  = ∑  k = 1  K   e ( k )   K   .      The equity range is same as interval equity range [ 0 , N   ]    since equity is simply the mean of interval equity.  3.6 The equity–reliability triangle In previous subsections, ranges of the performance metrics are given in general when water is allocated to users through any water allocation mechanism. In reality, these metrics are related to each other, i.e., they influence each others ranges. Intuitively, this also makes sense, because reliability and equity depend on the same adequacy distributions, therefore there exists some co-relation between these two quantities. In next sections, we will prove that the equity–reliability space is as shown in Fig. 1  when water is allocated using any allocation mechanism. The shaded region in Fig. 1  shows the range of equity values for each reliability value that is achievable when water is allocated through any mechanism. In case of water abundance, when all users receive water equal to their demand, the perfect equity–reliability point is achieved in the equity–reliability space, i.e., R = 1    and E = 0   , as shown in Fig. 1 . Ideally, one wants to operate an allocation mechanism at perfect equity–reliability point. However, under scarcity the worst-case performance degrades as shown in Fig. 1 . In case of scarcity, the reliability decreases which can be distributed among users in many ways. The best case occurs if scarcity is distributed among users equally and the reliability–equity point occurs on reliability axis. The worst case occurs when scarcity is distributed disproportionately towards only few users. It is important to note that since the reliability is average of interval reliability across multiple allocation cycles, therefore it is possible to perform even worse than that of a single allocation cycle. The given equity–reliability space uncovers counterintuitive insights, particularly regarding the worst-case performance of water allocation schemes. Take, for example, a situation where water is scarce, yet we notice that the performance of the water allocation mechanism used is better compared to the worst-case performance in equity–reliability space. This reveals that our current performance is relatively satisfactory given the scarcity. Without the performance limits provided by our analysis, there is a risk of misinterpreting the performance of the allocation scheme as worse performing under scarcity.     4 Performance limits In this section, we first derive the performance limits for equity and reliability of each canonical allocation mechanism. The performance limits define the range between the maximum and minimum attainable values of equity and reliability. We present the detailed mathematical calculations, discuss the placement of each mechanism in the equity–reliability space, and identify how allocation policy can be tuned to traverse this space. In the end, we show that the bounds are valid for adequacy distributions arising from any possible allocation mechanism, not just the three canonical mechanisms for which the bounds are calculated. 4.1 Priority-based allocation In priority-based allocation, the water authority makes a priority list and allocates water to the first user in the priority list. Next, if there is still water left, a user with second priority gets water, and so on. Therefore, when water is allocated through a priority-based allocation mechanism, some users’ demand gets fulfilled, one user’s demand gets partially fulfilled and the remaining users get no water. Hence, in a network of N   users, fulfilled population count is i  , one user’s demand is partially fulfilled, and unfulfilled population count is N − i − 1   . For priority-based allocation, we assume that first i   users’ in the set { 1 , 2 , 3 … N }    are the users with fulfilled demand, the i + 1   th user in the set is the user with partially fulfilled demand and N − i − 1    users with unfulfilled demand are the users from i + 2    to N   user in the same set { 1 , 2 , 3 … N }   . The adequacy level of the i   users with fulfilled demand, the one user with partially fulfilled demand, and the N − i    users with unfulfilled demand is one, 0 ≤ b ( k )  < 1   , and zero, respectively. Graphical demonstration of the priority-based allocation is shown in Fig. 4 a. Next, to find reliability and equity performance limits, we first need interval reliability and interval equity when i   users’ demand is fulfilled. 4.1.1 Relationship between interval equity and interval reliability We first calculate the interval reliability when water is allocated through priority-based allocation. Therefore, the interval reliability for uniform allocation is equal to the adequacy level of an allocation cycle because the interval reliability is the simple mean of the adequacy of all users in an allocation cycle. If adequacy level for all users in an allocation cycle is equal to a ( k )    , the interval reliability is calculated by placing α  1   ( k )  = α  2   ( k )  = ⋯ = α  N − 1   = α  N   = a ( k )     in (2) , which give us interval reliability equal to the adequacy level a ( k )    . The graphical demonstration of the uniform allocation is shown in Fig. 4 b. In this case, the interval equity value would be zero. To find the reliability and equity, we use the above calculated interval reliability and interval equity values for uniform allocation. The reliability is simply the mean of the interval reliability a(k), i.e., R = ∑  k = 1  K   a ( k )   K   = a ( k )    . Thus, for uniform allocation, the equity always remains zero because the interval equity is zero during all allocation cycles.  4.3 Hybrid allocation In hybrid allocation, a user is either receiving water equal to their demand or a minimum base amount of water equal to their entitlement. Therefore, when water is allocated through hybrid allocation, a user is either part of the population count i   with fulfilled demand or population count N − i    with partially fulfilled demand. For hybrid allocation, we assume that first i   users in the set { 1 , 2 , 3 , … , N }    are the users with fulfilled demand, and remaining N − i    users in the set are the users with partially fulfilled demand. The adequacy level of the i   users with fulfilled demand and N − i    users with partially fulfilled demand is one and c   respectively, where 0 ≤ c ≤ 1    is called minimum adequacy level. The graphical demonstration of the hybrid allocation is shown in Fig. 4 c. The minimum adequacy level c   is decided at the beginning of the season and remains constant throughout the season because initial water rights or entitlements are same once decided. The setup is constructed from data gathered from a real-world irrigation district in Central Punjab in Pakistan. Then we present simulations for arbitrary allocation. We develop Monte-Carlo simulations to analyze equity and reliability over the realistic range of model parameters for priority-based, hybrid, and arbitrary allocation. 5.1 Simulation setup The selected study area is located in the Moza Joyia area in the Okara district of the Punjab province, Pakistan. The 91 093/L watercourse irrigates the case study area. There are 24 farmers who own a portion of the land in the case study region, i.e., N = 24   . Data collected at the case study site is from July 2018 to October 2018. We use data for a khareef cropping season, from July 2018 to October 2018, which is 17 weeks, that is, K = 17   . We carry out Monte-Carlo simulations by changing the parameter values over a range that mimics the real-world context. We need data on water demand and water supply in the study area to carry out the simulations. We assume that the study area watercourse design capacity is equivalent to the design capacity of the watercourse adjacent to our study area as the area irrigated by both watercourses is approximately equal. The design capacity of the adjacent watercourse is 1 . 6 × 1 0  6      cusec/week (On Farm Water Management, 2017 ). Hence, the Surface water supply range is [ 0 , 1 . 6 × 1 0  6   ]    cusec. The water demand of a farm is calculated using deep percolation constant, reference evapotranspiration, crop coefficient, precipitation, soil moisture level, maximum moisture level threshold, and minimum moisture level threshold. Details about measuring ranges of these parameters in the study region are provided by Hassan et al. (2021) . The maximum and minimum moisture level threshold depends upon the soil type. Our study area is so small that the soil type is same throughout the area. Therefore, we assume constant maximum and minimum moisture level thresholds. The values of maximum and minimum moisture level thresholds are 0.25 and 0.10 respectively for all farms. For each farm, the initial soil moisture level is selected from an interval [ 10 % , 25 % ]    using a uniform distribution. The design capacity of the study area watercourse is not available. The dimensionless deep percolation constant range is [ 0 . 5 × 1 0  − 4   , 2 × 1 0  − 4   ]   . The reference evapotranspiration and crop coefficient are randomly chosen from the range provided by Ullah et al. (2001)  for the study region. The precipitation data set for the study region is taken from the NASA data portal (NASA, 2021 ). We have used data with daily temporal resolution and its spatial resolution is 4 km ×   4 km. We have taken the rain data of 21 years from 2001 to 2021, and the given 21 samples are used to randomly select daily precipitation for the study region.  5.2 Priority-based allocation We validate the reliability and equity performance limits derived in Section 4.1  of priority-based allocation by presenting Monte-Carlo simulations for a particular priority-based allocation mechanism describe in details by Hassan et al. (2021) . In this priority-based allocation mechanism, each user is interested in securing a shared resource, i.e., surface water. The shared resource is managed by a central planner. The complete season is divided into time interval of fixed duration. At the beginning of each time interval, the central planner asks for bids from the users. Users’ bids consist of information on water demand and their valuation of water. Then, based on the demand, valuation, and availability of the shared resource, the central planner sorts the bids in descending order and starts fulfilling the demand from the top. Details of this mechanism are provided in Hassan et al. (2021) .
