This mechanism of resource allocation falls under the category of priority-based allocation, as some users are receiving water equal to their demand and remaining users do not receive water. Fig. 8 a represents the equity vs. reliability relationship for Monte-Carlo simulations when water is allocated using the demand-based allocation mechanism described above. We have reiterated the simulations for 1 × 1 0  4      time instances. There are 24 users in the network, i.e., N = 24   . equity for the range of reliability should remain within the upper and lower bounds of the priority-based allocation. For the Monte-Carlo simulations, all the equity and reliability values stay within these limits as shown in Fig. 8 a, which validates the upper and lower bounds derived earlier.    5.3 Hybrid allocation Next, we validate the reliability and equity performance limits of hybrid allocation by presenting Monte-Carlo simulations for a particular hybrid allocation mechanism. This hybrid allocation consists of two steps: surface water allocation based on initial water rights and demand-based surface water reallocation and distribution based on a priority-based mechanism. First, the central planner allocates water based on initial water rights. We call the initial water rights the minimum adequacy level. Next, the central planner distributes the remaining water using the priority-based allocation mechanism described in Section 5.2 . This mechanism of allocating resources falls under the category of hybrid allocation, as some users receive resources equal to their demand and remaining users receive resources equal to the minimum adequacy level. Details of this mechanism are provided in Hassan et al. (2023) . Fig. 8 b represents the equity vs. reliability relationship for Monte-Carlo simulations when water is allocated using a particular hybrid allocation mechanism described above. We have reiterated the simulations for 1 × 1 0  4      times. For hybrid allocation, when there are 24 users in a network, i.e., N = 24   , and minimum adequacy level is 2%, i.e., c = 0 . 20   . Then, the equity for the range of reliability should remain below the upper bound of the hybrid allocation. In this case, the lower bound on equity is zero for the complete range of reliability. For the Monte-Carlo simulations, all the equity and reliability values remain within the upper and lower bounds. Hence, the simulations validate the performance limits of the hybrid allocation derived previously.  5.4 Arbitrary allocation We validate the reliability and equity performance limits of arbitrary allocation mechanism by presenting Monte-Carlo simulations. Fig. 8 c represents the equity vs. reliability relationship for Monte-Carlo simulations when water is allocated using arbitrary allocation. In Monte-Carlo simulations, we assume there are 24 users, i.e., N = 24    in the network, and the season consists of 17 allocation cycles, i.e., K = 17   . We have repeated the simulations for 0 . 206 × 1 0  6      times. The adequacy level for each user during each allocation cycle is generated using the beta distribution with a mean value between 0 and 1. Fig. 8 c shows that the equity and reliability value for each simulated point remains within the upper and lower limit of the equity and reliability, which implies that these bounds are valid for any allocation mechanisms. In Fig. 8 , there are some regions with zero point count and some regions with multiple point count. This is mainly because of the selected scarcity range for each simulation.   6 Towards large-scale irrigation systems In this paper, we have conducted a comprehensive analysis of the performance limits for water allocation mechanisms w.r.t. a coupled equity–reliability space. The analysis conducted applies to the allocation of water at a single level, i.e., a single allocation scheme that directly receives water from the supply and distributes it to the farmers without the action of any intermediary decision-making bodies. While our study encompasses all allocation systems of this kind, it is essential to recognize that the assumption of a single-level hierarchy being valid in practical systems holds true only up to a certain scale. This assumption is rarely applicable to large-scale irrigation systems. Fig. 9  illustrates the hierarchical structure of large-scale irrigation systems, featuring representative irrigation districts in Pakistan and China.1  1 These systems are depicted here as representative examples. Such large-scale hierarchical irrigation systems exist in many other parts of the world as well (Plusquellec, 2009 ).   The process of resource allocation in these system is complex and consists of multiple spatial and temporal scales. For example, in the Indus Basin Irrigation System (IBIS) in Pakistan (Shah et al., 2016 ), primary canals draw water from large reservoirs or headworks located on main rivers. The water drawn in these canals is subject to the decision of a national-level authority that is responsible for determining the water share of each province. Each province is further subdivided into administrative units referred to as circles, also known as zones. The provincial-level authorities are responsible for managing water allocation among these circles. These circles are then divided into smaller divisions, with secondary canals serving as conduits for water distribution among these divisions. A circle-level authority assumes the responsibility of allocating water resources among the various divisions. Subsequently, divisions are further segmented into irrigation districts. At this level, divisional authorities make decisions regarding the allocation of water among these districts. Within each district, decisions pertaining to water distribution are made by the district irrigation authority, and the actual distribution of water is facilitated through tertiary canals. On farms, water is accessed directly from these tertiary canals by utilizing watercourses. At the farm level, the agriculture department assumes responsibility for the equitable distribution of water among individual farmers. A similar hierarchical structure is commonly observed in other large-scale irrigation systems worldwide.   The analysis of our paper is concerned with only a single level of hierarchy. In order to apply the analysis to a large-scale hierarchical irrigation system, the framework will need to be extended. In such an application, the individual decision-making blocks are situated in a cascaded manner, so that the decisions made at each stage are propagated down to the subsequent stage until the farm-level decisions are implemented. Since the allocation decisions themselves are made in accordance with the water demand, information on the demand travels in a feedback manner from the farm level in a stage-wise sequence up to the highest decision-making level. While the performance analysis presented in this paper can be applied in isolation to each level, the framework will need to be extended so that feedback from each individual level is effectively incorporated in order to evaluate the performance of the entire irrigation system as a whole. Fig. 10  depicts our vision of the application of our performance evaluation framework to a large-scale hierarchical irrigation system. The figure shows the cascaded decision-making levels and the propagation of demands as feedback in the hierarchy. Under the scope of this study, we have considered the evaluation of allocations made over the entire season as a batch process. Since the decisions are typically made over smaller intervals2  2 For instance in the IBIS, the allocations at the farm level are made according to a weekly schedule.   an opportunity is lost to compensate for any degradation in performance due to unforeseen circumstances at run time such as climate shocks and other associated disturbances. If the performance evaluation can be reformulated as an iterative process, the allocations can be adjusted according to the current performance of the system in order to salvage some of the potential performance of the system over the duration of the entire season. This presents a compelling avenue for future research.  7 Discussion and conclusion Although equity and reliability values are widely used to inform policymakers, their performance limits and the relation between these assessment indicators are not commonly used in practice, to the best of our knowledge. The performance limits calculated in this paper can enable policy makers and irrigation system planners to gauge the overall performance of any selected allocation mechanism. To assess an allocation mechanism’s performance, the irrigation planners can measure the equity and see where these values fall on the equity–reliability triangle. If the equity vs. reliability point is close to the zero equity axis in the equity–reliability triangle in Fig. 1 , the allocation mechanism is working well. However, if the equity vs. reliability point is located towards the worst performance bound, then the irrigation planners may seek to modify the allocation scheme. Theoretically, as per the analysis in this paper, the best way to allocate water is through uniform allocation since the equity value is zero for all reliability values in this case. Practically however, uniform allocation is difficult to implement since the irrigation planner needs to devise policy to achieve multiple objectives in water allocation, from ensuring water rights and environmental flows to attaining tough economic goals. To meet these economic, environmental, and social objectives, policymakers allocate water using priority-based allocation in many parts of the world. But the worst-case performance of the priority-based allocation is low compared to the hybrid allocation. As shown in Fig. 6 , the upper bound of equity for priority-based allocation is represented by the c = 0    line. As the policymaker adjusts the value of c   the worst-case performance of the hybrid allocation improves compared to the priority-based allocation. Thus, using hybrid allocation, policymakers may tune the parameter c   to meet the different economic, environmental, and social objectives while simultaneously performing well in terms of equity. In the past, researchers have conducted case studies and developed allocation mechanisms to improve performance by using hybrid allocation mechanism approach, i.e., by adjusting the minimum adequacy level c  . For example Hipel et al. (2013)  and Wang et al. (2003)  presented an allocation mechanism which in first step allocate water entitlements and in second step reallocate and distribute water for social welfare maximization. In the context of our framework, the allocation mechanism presented by Hipel et al. (2013)  and Wang et al. (2003)  adjust minimum adequacy level c   to improve fairness among farmers. Fig. 1  shows the equity. vs. reliability space when water is allocated using any water allocation mechanism. Policymakers may seek to improve the performance of their allocation mechanism when the operating point is not close to the perfect equity vs. reliability point. Priority-based allocation cannot guarantee any desired equity because the irrigation planner has to prioritize some users over others. This is also true for uniform allocation because irrigation planner is already allocating water equitably and there is no degree of freedom to move the operating point in the equity–reliability space. Therefore, priority-based and uniform allocation mechanisms fail to consider the heterogeneity among users and the specific local contexts of water distribution, as they lack the flexibility to enhance performance through parameter tuning during allocation. However, hybrid allocation mechanisms are capable of addressing the heterogeneity among users and local conditions. Since in hybrid allocation, the irrigation planners may control the minimum adequacy level c  . As we can see in Fig. 6 , as the value of c   increases, the worst-case performance improves. Hence, policymakers can tune the parameter c   to improve performance if their operating point is not close to the perfect equity–reliability point to better align with the specific needs of end-users and local conditions. To know performance of an irrigation system over time, we need equity–reliability as a phase space over which trajectories are analyzed. Although we have not looked at irrigation systems that evolve over seasons, the framework is perfect to look at how a system would evolve over time, whether it has stalled in performance, improving or deteriorating. This type of information can be really useful for practitioners and policymakers. Finally, the scope of the proposed framework is not only limited to water allocation mechanisms. The framework applies to any resource allocation problem. Far example, in COVID-19 pandemic allocation of resource in health care (Silva et al., 2020 ), resource allocation in cloud computing (Abid et al., 2020 ), power allocation in communication technologies (Jayakumar et al., 2021 ), and scheduling in smart grids (Nair et al., 2018 ). We have presented this framework as a guideline for equitable allocation of resources in practice, with the hope that it will stimulate further research to add economic, social, and environmental dimensions to the physical distribution of water.  8 Open research The data on which this article is based are available in Hassan et al. (2021, 2023) .
1 Introduction Ecosystem water use efficiency (WUE ), usually defined as the ratio of gross primary production (GPP ) to evapotranspiration (ET ), measures the strength of coupling between carbon and water cycles (Beer et al., 2009 ). Ecosystem WUE  has been widely used to examine ecosystem responses to elevated atmospheric CO2  concentration and climate change (Hu et al., 2008; Li et al., 2023a ). Although dryland (i.e., semiarid and arid areas) ecosystems are usually characterized by low GPP  and ET , they account for over 40% of the global land surface (Wang et al., 2022 ). Therefore, dryland ecosystems have been shown to play a critical role in driving the trend and interannual variations in global carbon budget and hydrological cycle (Ahlström et al., 2015; Lian et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022 ). However, the temporal dynamics and driving factors of the coupled carbon–water cycle remain under-examined for dryland ecosystems due to a lack of long-term in situ  measurements, which are readily available for many mesic forests and grasslands around the world (Scott et al., 2023 ). Both environmental factors (e.g., air temperature, solar radiation, soil moisture, and atmospheric humidity) and biological factors (e.g., leaf area index, stomatal conductance, and plant functional type) affect the temporal dynamics of WUE  (Ma et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2023 ). However, the relative contribution of these biophysical factors to variations in WUE  vary among ecosystem types (Ma et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2021 ). For example, the temporal dynamics of WUE  in boreal forests and alpine grasslands were shown to be regulated by air temperature (Brümmer et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2021 ). Higher temperatures could extend the growing season length, promoting photosynthetic carbon assimilation over transpirational water consumption (Brümmer et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2016 ). Water availability has been shown to influence the temporal variations in both GPP  and ET  in water-limited ecosystems (Jia et al., 2016a; Biederman et al., 2017, 2018; Scott et al., 2023 ). However, it is yet uncertain as to whether GPP  and ET  respond differentially to changes in factors related to water availability or plant water stresses (e.g., precipitation, soil moisture, and vapor pressure deficit, VPD ). Many studies have attributed seasonal and interannual variations in ecosystem WUE  in water-limited grasslands, croplands, and shrublands to changes in leaf area index (LAI ) or vegetation greenness arising from plant phenology and human activities (Hu et al., 2008; Scott et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019 ). Increased LAI  or vegetation greenness has been shown to promote the transpiration fraction (i.e., T /ET , where T  represents plant transpiration), which in turn led to higher ecosystem WUE  [WUE  = GPP /ET  = (GPP /T ) (T /ET )] (Hu et al., 2008; Scott et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2019 ). Recent studies based on measurements at local to regional scales highlighted the importance of hydrometeorological factors (e.g., soil moisture, precipitation frequency, and aridity) in regulating WUE  dynamics (Liu et al., 2020a; Dong et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021 ). The importance of these factors was explained by the fact that soil evaporation usually accounts for a non-negligible fraction of ET  in sparsely vegetated semiarid and arid areas, leading to more dynamic responses of ET  than GPP  to fluctuations in water availability (Wang et al., 2021 ). These inconsistent patterns among ecosystems may partially be ascribed to the timescale of analysis, as ecosystem processes (e.g., photosynthesis, evaporation, and T ) have been shown to respond differently to slow- vs . fast-varying biophysical factors (Hu et al., 2008; Biederman et al., 2016 ). It remains to be elucidated how vegetation and hydrometeorological factors act in concert to regulate the temporal dynamics of WUE  in dryland ecosystems. Ecosystem carbon and water exchange has been suggested to be constrained by low soil water content (SWC ) and/or high VPD  (Novick et al., 2016; Hao et al., 2023; Xi and Yuan, 2023 ). The effects of low SWC  and high VPD  on carbon and water exchange are determined primarily by the differential responses of abiotic processes (e.g., evaporation) and biotic processes (e.g., plant stomatal behavior, photosynthesis, and T ) to environmental conditions (Kimm et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020b; Roby et al., 2020 ). Soil water deficiency not only limits abiotic evaporation at soil or canopy surface, but also restricts biotic (plant) carbon assimilation and T , thereby potentially influencing WUE  in multiple ways (Novick et al., 2016; Kimm et al., 2020 ). Increases in VPD  can promote both evaporation and T  under conditions of abundant soil water supply, leading to increases in ET  (Sulman et al., 2016 ). However, high VPD  has also been suggested to trigger stomatal closure when soil water supply is limiting, thereby down-regulating canopy conductance, GPP , and ET  at the ecosystem scale (Novick et al., 2016; Sulman et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2022 ). Ecosystem WUE  is expected to be modified by atmospheric dryness if GPP  and ET  exhibit different sensitivities to VPD . Soil water scarcity has been extensively reported to constrain ecosystem WUE  in dryland ecosystems (Eamus et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2012; Dong et al., 2021 ). However, VPD  has been recently proposed as the dominant constraint over SWC  on plant stomatal behavior (Kimm et al., 2020 ) and carbon and water fluxes (Novick et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2022; Hao et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023a ) at local to global scales. Furthermore, a recent assessment on semiarid ecosystems (Roby et al., 2020 ) and a global analysis based on eddy-covariance (EC) measurements (Li et al., 2023a ) revealed decreases in ecosystem WUE  in response to increases in VPD . A recent study based on satellite data found that the relative effects of SWC  and VPD  on WUE  varied among regions (Xi and Yuan, 2023 ). Therefore, further studies are needed to resolve the relative importance of SWC  and VPD  in regulating WUE  in different types of ecosystems. Ongoing climate warming and a more variable future precipitation regime are expected to further decouple SWC  and VPD , and thus promote their independent effects on GPP  and ET  in water-limited ecosystems (Novick et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2023 ). This context highlights the need to disentangle the relative importance of SWC  and VPD  in regulating WUE  in semiarid shrublands. The southern fringe of the Mu Us Desert is situated in a critical ecotone between semiarid and arid areas, where ecosystems are susceptible to anthropogenic disturbances and extreme climatic events such as droughts and heatwaves (Jia et al., 2016a ). During the second half of the 20th century, this region experienced severe vegetation degradation due to overgrazing and unsustainable agricultural activities (Jia et al., 2016a ). Regional rehabilitation efforts, such as fencing, grazing prohibition, and revegetation, have been implemented in the last two decades to prevent desertification and aid in vegetation recovery. The recovered vegetation consists primarily of xerophytic shrub species including Artemisia ordosica  and Corethrodendron fruticosum  var. mongolicum . Based on EC measurements, we have reported that the seasonal pattern of precipitation, drought events, and vegetation greenness were responsible for the seasonal and interannual variations in carbon balance and ET  in a representative shrubland ecosystem in the Mu Us Desert (Jia et al., 2014; Jia et al., 2016a; Mu et al., 2022; Hao et al., 2023 ). As a follow-up study, the present work quantified the temporal dynamics of ecosystem WUE  during 2012–2016, and examined the influence of vegetation and hydrometeorological factors (precipitation, VPD , and SWC ) on WUE . We hypothesized that (1) higher vegetation greenness, which has been reported to promote T /ET , would enhance canopy photosynthesis more than ET , and thus lead to higher WUE ; (2) high VPD , which is known to induce partial stomatal closure and constrain photosynthetic carbon assimilation more than ET , would dominate over low SWC  in constraining ecosystem WUE . Results of this study can help understand and predict how temperate semiarid shrublands will respond to ongoing climate change, and may provide insights into optimizing water resource use in ecosystem rehabilitation efforts.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study site This study was conducted at the Yanchi Research Station (37°42′31″N, 107°13′37″E, 1530 m a.s.l.), which was founded by Beijing Forestry University in 2006. The study site is situated on the southern fringe of the Mu Us Desert, where a mid-temperate semiarid continental monsoon climate prevails. The mean annual air temperature (Ta  ) during 1954–2022 was 8.4 °C, and the mean monthly Ta   varied from –13.8 °C in December to 25.2 °C in July (meteorological data for 1954–2011 were obtained from the Yanchi Meteorological Station, which is about 20 km from the study site). The cold winter usually causes soils to freeze from December to March. The mean annual precipitation was 292 mm during 1954–2022, ranging 145–587 mm across years. The annual potential ET  averaged about 1300 mm for 2012–2020, with little interannual variations (Mu et al., 2022 ). Although about 80% of the annual precipitation fell during the growing season (April–October), drought periods with little rainfall and rapid soil water depletion were common in spring and summer (Jia et al., 2016a, 2020 ). Growing-season droughts have been observed to result in leaf coloring, defoliation, and even plant mortality. Snowfall accounts for a minor fraction of annual precipitation due to the usually dry winters in the study area. The soil is of sandy texture, characterized by a bulk density of about 1.54 ± 0.08 g cm−3  (mean ± standard deviation, SD) and a field capacity of 20.31 ± 3.33% (g g−1  × 100) in the 0–20 cm soil layer (Jia et al., 2018; Hao et al., 2023 ). The vegetation cover is about 70%, and the shrub canopy reaches a height of about 1.5 m. Typical plant communities comprise semi-shrub or shrub species (60% cover) such as A. ordosica , C. fruticosum  var. mongolicum , and Salix psammophila , and herbaceous plants (10% cover) such as Leymus secalinus , Pennisetum flaccidum , Stipa caucasica  subsp. glareosa , Incarvillea sinensis , and Vincetoxicum mongolicum . All semi-shrub or shrub species are deciduous, and thus do not contribute any productivity in winter. The roots of dominant species are mainly distributed in the 30–70 cm layer of the soil profile. Precipitation represents the only water source for plants, as ground water table is too low (>8.0 m) to be accessible to plant roots.  2.2 Eddy-covariance and auxiliary measurements The CO2  and water vapor fluxes were measured continuously using an EC system during the study period. The EC system was mounted on a scaffold tower at a height of 6.2 m above the ground, and consisted of a three-dimensional sonic anemometer (CSAT3, CSI, Logan, UT, USA) and a closed-path infrared gas analyzer (IRGA, LI-7200, LICOR, Lincoln, NE, USA). Raw signals from both the sonic anemometer and the IRGA were recorded at a frequency of 10 Hz with an analyzer interface unit (LI-7550, LICOR, Lincoln, NE, USA). The flux tower is located on a flat terrain, where a uniform fetch extended over 500 m of the tower in all directions. The 90% cumulative flux footprint extended to about 220 m upwind of the tower. Routine on-site instrument check, maintenance, and data downloading were performed on a weekly basis. Upon each site visit, sensor calibrations, filter replacement, and cleaning of the optical path were performed if considered necessary according to our site management protocol. Downloaded raw signals were post-processed to obtain half-hourly CO2  and water vapor fluxes (see Section 2.3). Half-hourly supporting variables were measured simultaneously, including Ta   and relative humidity (RH ) (HMP155A, Vaisala, Helsinki, Finland), wind speed (u ) and direction (034B, Met-One Instruments, USA), global solar radiation (Rg  ) (CMP3, Kipp & Zonen, Delft, The Netherlands), net radiation (Rn  , CNR-4, Kipp and Zonen, The Netherlands) and its components (incident and reflected shortwave and longwave radiation), and incident and reflected photosynthetically-active radiation (PAR , PAR-LITE, Kipp and Zonen, the Netherlands). All these sensors were mounted on the EC tower at a height of 6.0 m. VPD  was calculated from Ta   and RH  following Coopman et al. (2021) . The normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI ) was calculated from downwelling and upwelling PAR  and shortwave measurements using a tower-based approach (Huemmrich et al., 1999; Wilson and Meyers, 2007; Jia et al., 2016a ). SWC  and soil temperature (Ts  ) were measured at four depths (10, 30, 70, and 120 cm) below the soil surface using three sets of four ECH2O-5TE probes (METER Environment, Pullman, Washington State, USA) installed at three locations within 20 m of the EC tower. Rainfall was measured with three tipping-bucket rain gauges (TR-525 M, Texas Electronics, Dallas, TX, USA) installed at three locations about 50 m from the tower. Soil heat flux (G ) was estimated as the sum of heat flux at 10-cm depth (G 10 ) and the heat storage term (Sb  ) for the 0–10 cm soil layer. Five soil heat flux transducers (HFP01, Hukseflux Thermal Sensors, The Netherlands) were used to measure G 10  within 20 m of the tower. Values for Sb   were estimated from Ts  , SWC , and soil bulk density measured at 10-cm depth following Ochsner et al. (2007) . Detailed descriptions on field measurements can be found in our previous studies (Jia et al., 2014; 2016a; Mu et al., 2022; Hao et al., 2023 ).  2.3 Data post-processing Half-hourly water vapor (mmol m−2  s−1 ) and CO2  (μmol m−2  s−1 ) fluxes were calculated from 10 Hz records using the EddyPro 7.0.2 software (LI-7200, LICOR, Lincoln, NE, USA). The post-processing procedure mainly included the following steps: spike removal, double coordinate rotation, frequency-loss correction, time-delay correction, detrending (with the block-averaging method), and flux computation (Burba, 2013; Jia et al., 2014, 2020; Mu et al., 2022 ). The Webb-Pearman-Leuning (WPL) correction was not included in the post-processing procedure as the closed-path IRGA we used enables outputting mixing ratios (Burba, 2013 ). A half-hourly flux value was considered unreliable and thus was discarded if missing 10 Hz records exceeded 10% of the total records for any variable used in calculating that flux value (Jia et al., 2016a ). Spikes in half-hourly fluxes were detected and screened following the “median of absolute deviation about the median” (MAD) criterion described in Papale et al. (2006) . Power failures, instrument maintenance, and data quality control procedures together resulted in 9–22% and 3–19% missing water vapor flux values for daytime and nighttime hours, respectively, on an annual basis. Missing daytime and nighttime CO2  flux values accounted for 9–20% and 66–71% of annual total records, respectively. Gaps in water vapor fluxes were estimated following Amiro et al. (2006) . Nighttime missing values were assumed to be zero. For daytime missing values, the regression relationship between water vapor fluxes and the available energy (i.e., Rn   – G ) was estimated for a moving window of 240 quality-controlled data points. The data window moved at a step of 48 points. At each step the regression relationship was reevaluated to estimate missing water fluxes. In cases where Rn   or G  was also missing, the gaps were filled by applying the mean diurnal variation (MDV) method to consecutive 15-day data blocks (Falge et al., 2001 ). The extent of energy balance closure, measured as the slope of the regression relationship between daily turbulent energy (i.e., sum of latent and sensible heat fluxes) and available energy, was 0.75 over the study period. The R package “REddyProc” (version 1.3.2) was used to screen nighttime CO2  fluxes, fill gaps in CO2  flux values, and partition daytime CO2  fluxes into GPP  and ecosystem respiration (Reco ). Friction velocity (u *) was used to evaluate whether a CO2  flux was measured under low-turbulence nighttime (i.e., Rg   < 10 W m−2 ) periods. The u * threshold (0.22–0.32 m s−1 ) was estimated for each year using the “moving point” method (Papale et al., 2006; Wutzler et al., 2018 ). CO2  fluxes were screened for periods when u * was lower than the threshold. All CO2  fluxes that passed the quality-control procedure were considered approximates of net ecosystem exchange (NEE ). The marginal distribution sampling (MDS) algorithm (Reichstein et al., 2005; Wutzler et al., 2018 ) was used to fill gaps in NEE  timeseries. The nighttime-based method was used to partition NEE  into GPP  and Reco  (Wutzler et al., 2018; Jia et al., 2020 ). Missing values in auxiliary variables (e.g., Ta  , Ts  , VPD , and u ) were estimated with replicate measurements at the site. The MDV method was used instead when replicate measurements were unavailable. The flux and auxiliary datasets used in this study have been made publicly available (Han et al., 2023 ) and are freely downloadable from Science Data Bank (https://doi.org/10.57760/sciencedb.ecodb.00094) . Daily ecosystem WUE  was calculated as the ratio of daily total GPP  to concurrent total ET  during the growing season (April–October). Negative daily WUE  values, which resulted largely from random measurement errors and flux-partitioning uncertainties, were excluded from analysis based on daily values. Monthly (annual) WUE  values were calculated as the ratio of monthly (annual) GPP  to monthly (annual) ET , while growing-season WUE  was calculated as the ratio of growing-season GPP  to growing-season ET . In order to investigate the biophysical controls on GPP , ET , and WUE , we calculated half-hourly bulk surface conductance (gs  , mm s−1 ) by inverting the Penman-Monteith equation (Monteith, 1965 ):(1) g s  = γ λ E T g a   Δ ( R n  - G )  + ρ C p  V P D g a  - λ E T ( Δ + γ )        where ET  and VPD  are in units of g m−2  s−1  and kPa, respectively; Δ  denotes the rate of change of saturation vapor pressure with T a  (kPa K−1 ), ρ  the air density (kg m−3 ), Cp   the specific heat capacity of air (J kg−1  K−1 ), γ  the psychrometric constant (kPa K−1 ), λ  the latent heat of vaporization (J kg−1 ), Rn   the net radiation (W m−2 ), G  the soil heat flux (W m−2 ), and ga   the aerodynamic conductance (mm s−1 ). Aerodynamic conductance was calculated following Monteith and Unsworth (1990) :(2) g a  = u u ∗ 2    + 6.2 u ∗ - 0.67       - 1       where u  and u * are in units of m s−1 . We only calculated gs   for half-hours when incident shortwave radiation exceeded 100 W m−2  (i.e., midday hours) to avoid spurious gs   values due to low solar elevation (Jia et al., 2016a ). Following our previous studies (Jia et al., 2016a; Mu et al., 2022; Hao et al., 2023 ), data recorded on rainy days or on rainy days plus the following one or two days were excluded from analysis to ensure that gs   represents the conductance for water vapor under dry canopy conditions. Surface conductance under dry-canopy conditions aggregates water vapor transport from both the dry canopy (i.e., T ) and the wet soil surface (i.e., soil evaporation). We assumed that growing-season gs   reasonably reflects the dynamics of canopy-integrated stomatal conductance (Jia et al., 2016a, b ). This assumption is partially supported by the dominance of growing-season ET  by T  (T /ET  being about = 60%) (Hao et al., 2023 ).  2.4 Statistical analysis Regression analysis was used to examine the relationships between WUE  and biophysical factors at seasonal and interannual timescales. We focused mainly on the effects of vegetation-related variables (i.e., NDVI  and gs  ) and hydrometeorological factors (rainfall, VPD , SWC , and PAR ) on WUE . The variance inflation factor (VIF ) was calculated to assess the multicollinearity among these explanatory factors. The VIF  values ranged 1.44−2.08 for daily variables and 2.06−5.77 for monthly ones, being lower than the rule-of-thumb threshold for detecting strong multicollinearity (i.e., 10). Such moderate levels of multicollinearity are considered unlikely to have significant impacts on bivariate regressions (Miles, 2005 ). Soil water content at 10, 30, and 70-cm depth was used in analysis because shrub roots are mainly distributed in the 30–70 cm soil layer, and SWC  at rooting depths can effectively represent the soil water available for plant photosynthesis and T  (Jia et al., 2014, 2016a, 2020; Mu et al., 2022; Hao et al., 2023 ). We also binned daily WUE  values into a series of bins of explanatory variables, and then used bin-averaged values to investigate how WUE  responded to vegetation and hydrometeorological factors. The bin-averaged relationship between WUE  and PAR  was evaluated for both high and low groups of VPD  (>1 vs . ≤1 kPa) and SWC  (>0.1 vs . ≤0.1 m3  m−3 ). These cutoff points were selected to facilitate inter-group comparison in the clearest way, and to ensure sufficient data points in each group (Jia et al., 2014; Mu et al., 2022 ). Data binning by taking averages within each bin has been suggested to effectively offset random measurement errors from a statistical perspective (Falge et al., 2001 ). Furthermore, data binning can help alleviate multicollinearity among variables, thereby reducing confounding effects and increasing robustness in regression analysis (Falge et al., 2001 ). In order to investigate the relative importance of VPD  and SWC  in constraining WUE , we also binned daily WUE  values into two-dimensional grids defined by the deciles of VPD  and SWC . This data binning technique allows for the examination of how WUE  varies with one factor when the other is near-fixed. We also used a machine-learning model based on random forest and the extreme gradient boosting (xgboost) algorithm to assess the relative importance of vegetation and hydrometeorological factors in regulating the WUE  dynamics. The xgboost algorithm was run using the “caret” R package (version 6.0–94). Sixty percent of the daily dataset was randomly sampled to train the model, which was then tested against the remaining 40% data. The relative importance of the examined factors was evaluated in terms of their respective “gain factors” calculated. Gain quantifies the extent to which each feature’s split point enhances the model’s performance, thereby reflecting the individual contribution of each feature (Chen et al., 2020 ). The final score for feature importance was determined by averaging gain values across splits, i.e., dividing the total gain over all trees by the total number of splits. Only growing-season (April–October) data were used in regression and xgboost analyses, as the canopy remains dormant and leafless during the non-growing season. In order to compare our results with previous studies, we synthesized EC-based annual or growing-season values of GPP , ET , WUE , and precipitation reported for semiarid and arid ecosystems around the world. The synthesized dataset comprises a total of 47 sites (9 forests, 4 croplands, 21 grasslands, and 13 shrublands); and includes 73, 74, and 105 records for GPP , ET , and WUE , respectively (see Table S1 in Supplementary Online Material  #1 for site information). One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed on the synthesized dataset (including data from this study) to compare ecosystem WUE  and its two components among ecosystem types, and regression analysis was used to examine precipitation effects on GPP , ET , and WUE  across all sites and for individual ecosystem types. Croplands were not included in ANOVA when comparing GPP  and ET , as only one or two records were available (i.e., insufficient degrees of freedom). Gross primary production and WUE  were log-transformed prior to ANOVA to improve normality and homoscedasticity, which were examined with the Shapiro-Wilk and Levene’s test, respectively. Tukey’s Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) test was used for pairwise comparisons. All statistical analyses were performed using the R software (version 4.3.3, The R Development Core Team).   3 Results 3.1 Seasonal and interannual variations in biophysical factors Daily mean Ta   and VPD  showed both prominent seasonal variations and repeated annual cycles (Table 1  ; Fig. 1  a, b). Daily mean Ta   ranged from about −10.0 °C in winter to over 25.0 °C in summer (Fig. 1 a). Annual mean Ta   averaged 9.4 °C over the study period, varying from 8.7 °C in 2012 to 9.8 °C in 2013. Daily mean VPD  was generally lower than 0.5 kPa in winter, and reached high values of about 3.0 kPa in June or July (Fig. 1 b). Annual mean VPD  averaged 0.73 kPa, varying from 0.67 kPa in 2012 to 0.78 kPa in 2013. Daily total PAR  showed low values of <20 mol photon m−2  d−1  in winter and high values of 50−60 mol photon m−2  d−1  in mid-summer (Fig. 1 c). Annual total PAR  averaged 10.63 kmol photon m−2  yr−1  over the five years, varying from 9.97 kmol photon m−2  yr−1  in 2015 to 11.54 kmol photon m−2  yr−1  in 2012. Variations in SWC  during the growing season followed the seasonal pattern of rainfall events, showing pulsed increases in response to water input and rapid depletion during inter-storm periods (Fig. 1 d). Daily mean SWC  at 10, 30, and 70-cm depths (SWC 10 , SWC 30 , and SWC 70 , respectively) ranged 0.04−0.13 m3  m−3 , 0.05–0.17 m3  m−3 , and 0.06–0.17 m3  m−3 , respectively. SWC 10  was lower than SWC 30  and SWC 70  most of the time, but showed more dynamic fluctuations than SWC 30  and SWC 70  in response to day-to-day variations in rainfall events. SWC 70  showed little response to rain events smaller than 20 mm d−1 , which did trigger strong fluctuations in SWC 10  and SWC 30 . SWC 120  remained inert to most rain events, and only showed large fluctuations in the spring of 2012 and 2016 as a result of soil thawing, and in the summer of 2013 as a result of large or frequent rain events. Rainfall amount varied greatly across seasons and years (Fig. 1 e). Although more than 85% of annual rainfall was concentrated in the growing season, inter-event depletions in SWC  were obvious for all years (Fig. 1 d, e). Annual rainfall averaged 321 mm over the study period, varying from 278 mm in 2013 to 342 mm in 2014 with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 8.82% across years (Table 1 ) Surface conductance and NDVI  showed clear seasonal and interannual variations (Fig. 1 f). NDVI  increased rapidly from late-spring to early-summer, reaching its peak values in late-summer, followed by gradual declines in autumn. Seasonal maximum NDVI  varied from 0.24 in 2015 to 0.33 in 2013, with a CV of 13.13% (Table 1 ). Daily mean midday gs   was generally lower than 2 mm s−1  during the non-growing season and showed high values of 4–8 mm s−1  in late-spring or summer (Fig. 1 f). Annual mean gs   varied from 1.21 mm s−1  in 2014 to 1.96 mm s−1  in 2012 (Table 1 ).  3.2 Seasonal and interannual variations in GPP , ET , and WUE  GPP  and ET  showed similar seasonal patterns (Fig. 2  a, b). They both increased from late-spring to early-summer, plateaued in late-summer, and gradually decreased towards the non-growing season (Fig. 2 a, b; Fig. S1 a, b in Supplementary Online Material  #2). Seasonal maximum GPP  varied from 3.44 g C m−2  d−1  in 2014 to 7.69 g C m−2  d−1  in 2012. Daily ET  dropped to near-zero values in winter, and annual maximum daily ET  varied from 2.48 mm d−1  in 2014 to 3.61 mm d−1  in 2013 (Fig. 2 b). Daily WUE  was smaller than 1.5 g C kg−1  H2 O in early-spring and late-autumn, and reached 2.0–7.0 g C kg−1  H2 O during summer months (June–August) (Fig. 2 c, S1 c). Seasonal maximum daily WUE  varied from 6.0 g C kg−1  H2 O in 2012 to 7.4 g C kg−1  H2 O in 2016. Annual (January–December) GPP  was highest in 2012 (503 g C m−2  yr−1 ) and lowest in 2014 (277 g C m−2  yr−1 ), with a CV of 22.5% across years (Table 1 ). Annual ET  was highest in 2016 (296 mm yr−1 ) and lowest in 2014 (194 mm yr−1 ), with a CV of 18.7%. Annual WUE  varied from 1.43 g C kg−1  H2 O in 2014 to 1.78 g C kg−1  H2 O in 2012, with a mean annual value of 1.64 g C kg−1  H2 O during the study period (Table 1 ). Growing-season WUE  averaged 1.78 g C kg−1  H2 O across years, varying from 1.57 g C kg−1  H2 O in 2014 to 1.94 g C kg−1  H2 O in 2016.  3.3 Vegetation and hydrometeorological controls on GPP , ET , and WUE  Monthly GPP , ET , and WUE  increased lineally with monthly mean gs   and NDVI , and also increased asymptotically with monthly rainfall during the growing season (Fig. 3  ). The three factors explained 68%, 51%, and 30% of the variability in monthly GPP , 63%, 38%, and 25% of the variability in monthly ET , and 34%, 39%, and 27% of the variability in monthly WUE , respectively. Responses of monthly GPP , ET , and WUE  to rainfall tended to level off when monthly rainfall exceeded 60 mm mon−1  (Fig. 3 c, f, i). Both monthly GPP  (R 2  = 0.27, P  < 0.01) and ET  (R 2  = 0.37, P  < 0.01) increased lineally with monthly PAR  (Fig. S2 ), while monthly WUE  was not correlated with PAR  (R 2  < 0.01, P  = 0.58). Monthly mean midday gs   also increased linearly with monthly mean NDVI  (Fig. 4  a) and asymptotically with monthly rainfall (Fig. 4 b). Monthly WUE  also increased linearly with increasing monthly T /ET  (Fig. S3 a), which in turn was promoted by increases in NDVI  (Fig. S3 b). Neither monthly mean VPD  nor SWC  showed significant correlations with GPP , WUE , or gs   (results not shown). Monthly ET  was positively correlated with monthly mean VPD  (R 2  = 0.22, P  < 0.01), but not with SWC  (results not shown). Bin-averaged daily WUE  increased linearly with NDVI  and SWC 30  (Table S2 ; Fig. 5  a, c), decreased with increasing VPD  (Table S2 ; Fig. 5 b), but was independent of SWC 10  (R 2  = 0.05, P  = 0.50) and SWC 70  (R 2  = 0.17, P  = 0.18) (Table S2 ; Fig. 5 c). Bin-averaged daily mean values of midday gs   increased with NDVI  (Fig. 5 d) and SWC 10  (Table S2 ; Fig. 5 f), decreased with increasing VPD  (Table S2 ; Fig. 5 e), but was unaffected by SWC 30  (R 2  = 0.06, P  = 0.44) or SWC 70  (R 2  = 0.15, P  = 0.24) (Table S2 ; Fig. 5 f). The correlation between gs   and SWC 10  became non-significant after data on rainy days plus the following two days were excluded (Fig. S4 ). When binned into two-dimensional grids defined by the deciles of SWC  and VPD , WUE  showed no clear pattern in response to changes in SWC  across VPD  deciles (Fig. 6  a–c), but showed consistent decreasing trends in response to increasing VPD  across SWC  deciles (Fig. 6 d–f). Bin-averaged daily WUE  decreased linearly with increasing PAR  under both low SWC  and high VPD  conditions (Fig. S5 ). The machine-learning model based on random forest and the xgboost algorithm revealed that VPD  and NDVI  contributed the most to the dynamics of daily WUE , followed by SWC 10 , SWC 70 , gs  , SWC 30 , and PAR  (Fig. 7  a). Surface conductance contributed the most to variations in monthly WUE , followed by VPD , NDVI , SWC 30 , PAR , SWC 10 , and SWC 70  (Fig. 7 b). Both annual and growing-season WUE  were independent of examined vegetation and hydrometeorological factors (Table S3 ).  3.4 Ecosystem WUE  and its two components across semiarid and arid ecosystems Synthesized data from semiarid and arid areas showed that annual or growing-season ecosystem WUE  as well as its two components all differed significantly among ecosystem types (Fig. 8  ). Specifically, forests had significantly higher GPP , ET , and WUE  than other ecosystem types (Fig. 8 a, c, e). Grasslands and shrublands showed similar GPP  and ET , and non-forest ecosystems showed similar WUE . Annual or growing-season GPP , ET , and WUE  increased linearly with precipitation across all semiarid and arid sites (Fig. 8 b, d, f). For a given ecosystem type, positive precipitation effects were observed for annual GPP  at forest and grassland sites, for annual ET  at grassland and shrubland sites, and for annual WUE  at forest sites.   4 Discussion 4.1 Comparison of WUE  among semiarid and arid ecosystems Ecosystem WUE  has been found to vary greatly among ecosystem types (Xiao et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2021 ). Annual GPP  values (277−503 g C m−2  yr−1 ) reported here fell within the range reported for global semiarid and arid shrubland ecosystems (Fig. 8 a), while our annual ET  values (194−296 mm yr−1 ) fell within the lower end of the previously reported range (Fig. 8 c). Consequently, our annual WUE  values, influenced by lower ET , are larger than most values reported for shrublands (Fig. 8 e). These comparisons suggest that shrub species at our site are more water-efficient in CO2  assimilation than those in other shrub-dominated dryland ecosystems. One of our previous studies measured leaf traits for the dominant shrub species A. ordosica  at the site, and compared our measurements with those reported for other semiarid and arid areas dominated by different species. That study revealed high foliage nitrogen content (2.21−3.59 g m−2 ) and photosynthetic capacity (116.6−226.0 μmol m−2  s−1 ) for A. ordosica  (Xu et al., 2022 ). These plant traits are expected to enhance WUE  at the ecosystem level. Annual or growing-season GPP  and ET  tended to increase with precipitation across ecosystem types (Fig. 8 b, d). In addition, GPP  was more sensitive to precipitation than ET , resulting in a positive relationship between WUE  and precipitation (Fig. 8 f). The positive precipitation dependence of annual WUE  is in line with many previous studies on semiarid and arid ecosystems, indicating water limitation to WUE  (Xiao et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2021 ). In contrast, Xiao et al. (2013)  reported saturated responses of ecosystem WUE  to high precipitation (e.g., >1000 mm) across biomes. Ecosystem WUE  is expected to plateau at wet sites (e.g., evergreen forests and wetlands), where a large proportion of annual precipitation may be lost to runoff and drainage rather than through ET.   4.2 Vegetation and hydrometeorological controls on WUE  We observed stronger effects of NDVI  than other factors on WUE  dynamics (Fig. 3 ). In addition, our results support our first hypothesis that high vegetation greening would lead to increases in canopy photosynthesis over ET  (i.e., enhanced WUE ) by promoting T /ET  (Fig. S3 ). A stronger sensitivity of GPP  than ET  to NDVI  (Fig. 3 b, e, h) has also been reported previously, indicating that carbon assimilation, rather than water loss, dominated vegetation effects on WUE  (Hu et al., 2008; Jiang et al., 2020 ). The strong phenological dependence of WUE  indicated here is consistent with findings of previous studies in temperate croplands, shrublands, and grasslands (Hu et al., 2008; Scott et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017; Dong et al., 2021 ). Elevated WUE  was observed at our site during the mid-growing season (Fig. 2 c), indicating that GPP  increased faster than ET  in response to rising NDVI  in early-growing season. This is likely because higher vegetation greenness both enhances light use efficiency and reduces soil evaporation (Beer et al., 2009 ). Increases in NDVI  not only enhance the transpiring area and the amount of light intercepted by the canopy, but also reduce the evaporating area at soil surface (Yang et al., 2011; Scott et al., 2015; Hao et al., 2023 ). Reduced soil evaporation potentially leads to more water available for use by plant T  and photosynthesis. At our site, periods of highest vegetation cover coincide with thermal and hydrometeorological conditions favorable to plant photosynthesis and ecosystem ET  (Figs. 1, 2 , S1 ; Jia et al., 2016b; Mu et al., 2022; Hao et al., 2023 ). Therefore, further increases in vegetation cover or LAI  in the studied area as a result of continued restoration efforts are expected to enhance ecosystem WUE , and may lead to stronger vegetation controls on WUE  dynamics. Water availability is usually considered the dominant factor controlling seasonal variations in GPP , ET , and ecosystem WUE  in water-limited ecosystems (Scott et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2021 ). We found saturated response of monthly WUE  to rainfall during the growing season (Fig. 3 i), indicating that water supply might have exceeded vegetation water demand during wet periods (Hao et al., 2023 ). Alternatively, part of water input during wet seasons may have lost through subsurface runoff and/or deep drainage (i.e., hydrological losses, see Biederman et al., 2016; Jia et al., 2016a; Mu et al., 2022 ). Additionally, our results revealed strong VPD  and SWC  controls on daily WUE  (Fig. 5 b, c), but much weaker VPD  and SWC  controls on WUE  when monthly data were evaluated (results not shown). These results indicate that hydrometeorological factors regulated ecosystem WUE  over short timescales (e.g., daily), while vegetation factors played a more important role in regulating WUE  over longer timescales (e.g., seasonal). The reductions in WUE  under high VPD  and low SWC  conditions were probably mediated by drought-induced down-regulation of gs   (Fig. 5 b, c, e, f), which reasonably reflects the dynamics of canopy-integrated stomatal conductance.  This finding highlights the role of land–atmosphere interactions in regulating ecosystem carbon and water exchange (Kimm et al., 2020 ). Ecosystem WUE  seemed to show stronger correlations with root-zone SWC  (30−70 cm) than with surface SWC  (10 cm) (Table S2 , Figs. 5, 7 ). This provides support for the link between water availability to plant roots and the regulation of ecosystem WUE  by vegetation factors such as gs   and NDVI . Our previous studies at the site have shown that growing-season droughts suppressed GPP  more than ET  (Hao et al., 2023; Mu et al., 2024 ). Although data-binning and xgboost analysis showed varying importance of SWC  at different depths in regulating ecosystem WUE  (Fig. 5 c, 7, S4 ), our results, consistent with previous findings (Scott et al., 2015; Dong et al., 2021 ), revealed SWC  controls on ecosystem WUE  and the linkage between above- and belowground moisture constraints on eco-physiological processes. The inconsistent importance of SWC  at different depths shown by different analyses may be related to the variable importance of surface and root-zone SWC  in regulating physical (e.g., evaporation) and physiological (e.g., T  and photosynthesis) processes. Alternatively, different temporal resolutions of the data used (Fig. 7 ) and different analytical methods used may also have contributed to inconsistent results. Our main conclusion highlights the role of vegetation factors and atmospheric dryness in regulating ecosystem WUE , despite uncertainties regarding soil moisture effects on WUE . Neither annual nor growing-season WUE  showed significant correlation with biophysical factors (Table S3 ), probably as a result of the limited length of measurements (2012–2016). Moreover, annually-aggregated values of biophysical factors do not always serve as adequate predictors of the interannual variation in coupled carbon and water fluxes (Pilegaard et al., 2011 ). Firstly, WUE  dynamics are determined by both GPP  and ET  responses to biophysical factors. Therefore, WUE  may be relatively invariant if GPP  and ET  show similar sensitivities to biophysical factors (Tong et al., 2014; Li et al., 2023b ). Secondly, our previous studies at the site revealed that inter-seasonal soil moisture carryover and wet-season hydrological losses (i.e., to runoff and deep drainage) decoupled annual rainfall and ecosystem fluxes (Jia et al., 2016a; Mu et al., 2022 ). We also found that interannual variations in T /ET  were strongly affected by the seasonal pattern of rainfall, with a high frequency of large rain events promoting growing-season T /ET  (Hao et al., 2023 ). Therefore, future studies using longer data records (e.g., decadal or multidecadal datasets) are needed for re-evaluating the preliminary results reported in the present study, and for testing the effects of precipitation seasonality, climate legacies, and hydrological losses on the interannual variations in WUE .  4.3 Effects of atmospheric vs . soil dryness on WUE  Atmospheric and soil dryness, which are usually coupled across spatiotemporal scales, have been proposed to regulate ecosystem carbon and water fluxes (Novick et al., 2016; Kimm et al., 2020; Fu et al., 2022; Roby et al., 2020 ). However, their relative importance has been shown to vary across studies. Previous studies have highlighted the role of water availability in regulating WUE  in semiarid grasslands and shrublands (Scott et al., 2015; Biederman et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2021 ). Our results revealed stronger controls of VPD  than SWC  on the dynamics of daily ecosystem WUE  (Fig. 5 b, c, 6  and 7 ). This finding supports our second hypothesis that high VPD  is more important than low SWC  in constraining WUE , and is in agreement with previous analyses based on EC and satellite data showing dominant VPD  effects on ecosystem WUE  (Roby et al., 2020; Xi and Yuan, 2023 ). The negative effects of VPD  on WUE  may be ascribed to the greater declines in GPP  than ET  in response to increasing atmospheric dryness. On the one hand, high VPD  directly induces partial stomatal closure to prevent excessive water loss through T . Previous studies have shown greater effects of stomatal conductance on leaf CO2  uptake and assimilation than on ET  (Medlyn et al., 2011 ). Reductions in stomatal conductance induced by high VPD  can draw down intercellular CO2  concentration, which constrains CO2  assimilation while promotes photorespiration (Dai et al., 1992; Sulman et al., 2016 ). Such VPD -induced GPP  reductions can even occur under high soil moisture conditions (Sulman et al., 2016 ). On the other hand, declines in WUE  under high VPD  conditions may partially result from elevated atmospheric evaporative demand and thus stimulated evaporation from soil and canopy surfaces (Roby et al., 2020 ). The lower sensitivity of WUE  to SWC  than VPD  may occur when drying soil surface limits evaporation while persisting root-zone moisture continues to support plant T  and photosynthesis (Roby et al., 2020 ). SWC  has been shown to inhibit plant physiological processes only when it is below species-specific stress thresholds (e.g., root-zone soil moisture stress) (Fu et al., 2022 ), making SWC  less important in constraining WUE  under a wide range of hydrometeorological conditions (Kimm et al., 2020 ). Our results suggest that warming-induced increases in VPD  and more frequent drought events under climate change may make ecosystem production less water efficient in temperate semiarid shrublands in the future.   5 Conclusions We examined the temporal dynamics of WUE  during 2012–2016 using EC measurements in a temperate semiarid shrubland in northern China. Vegetation factors such as gs   and NDVI  played a primary role in promoting monthly WUE  during the warm and moist growing-season (April–October), while high VPD  and low root-zone SWC  were key hydrometeorological factors that imposed constraints on daily WUE . Our analyses using a machine-learning model (based on random forest and the xgboost algorithm) and a data-binning approach identified NDVI  and VPD  as the most important factors regulating WUE  dynamics. Atmospheric dryness dominated over soil dryness in regulating the seasonal variations in WUE . Anticipated warming and increasingly frequent extreme events (e.g., droughts and heatwaves) under climate change are expected to accentuate the role of atmospheric dryness in constraining ecosystem WUE  and the carbon sequestration potential in temperate semiarid drylands. In addition, increasing vegetation cover in the Mu Us Desert as a result of continued restoration efforts is expected to enhance ecosystem WUE , and may lead to stronger vegetation controls on WUE  dynamics.
1 Introduction and motivation Runoff estimation is vital for a broad range of objectives such as irrigation planning (Ben-Asher and Berliner, 1994 ), agriculture production estimation (Barrow, 2014 ), commercial and domestic water consumption (Bouwer et al., 2006 ), and water resources policy development (Wester et al., 2018; Izzi et al., 2021 ). Runoff is also a critical variable that is used to track the impact of climate change at local and regional scales (Koch et al., 2011 ). The recent (August 2022 to September 2022) catastrophic floods in South Asia highlight the importance of runoff estimation in regions threatened by climate change, such as South Asia. Runoff is also an important component of the terrestrial water budget as it controls the changes in water storage within a system (Savenije, 1996; Wolock and McCabe, 1999; Oki et al., 1995; Ghajarnia et al., 2020 ). Previous studies established a positive correlation between soil moisture and runoff (Scipal et al., 2005; Penna et al., 2011; Crow et al., 2018 ). Soil moisture controls the partitioning of incident rainfall into surface runoff and water that undergoes infiltration (Kirkham, 2014 ). Soil moisture influences runoff by controlling soil infiltration capacity (Mayor et al., 2009 ). Saturation level of soils is determined by their water storage capacity. Saturated soils that have a limited capacity of further water storage, and thus low infiltration, render the incident rainfall to flow laterally (Kirkham, 2014 ) thereby resulting in increased surface runoff. Conversely, dry soils have relatively high infiltration capacities, and therefore, yield lower surface runoff for the same precipitation event as compared to wetter soils. Model representation of the soil moisture and runoff connectivity controls the impact of changes in antecedent soil moisture on total runoff generated (Crow et al., 2018 ). A varied range of approaches have been implemented for runoff estimation. Oki et al. (1995)  leveraged atmospheric vapor flux convergence for estimation of the water balance in a river basin. The difference between precipitation and evaporation was compared with observed discharge data and showed differences in magnitude but corresponded well in terms of seasonality. Their experiments also showed that a conventional hydrological water balance yielded higher global runoff estimates than an atmospheric water balance method. Similarly, Sebastian et al. (2016)  used the difference between precipitation and evaporation based on reanalysis datasets to reduce uncertainty in the estimation of available water. However, their results suggested better performance of estimated water availability when using the atmospheric budget rather than the individual estimates of precipitation and evaporation. Estimation approaches based on assimilating satellite-observed data into hydrologic models to improve runoff estimation have also been explored. Brocca et al. (2010)  assimilated the Advanced Scatterometer (ASCAT, Bartalis et al. (2007) ) soil wetness index (SWI) product into a rainfall-runoff model to improve runoff prediction. They concluded that the SWI can be leveraged to improve runoff prediction, especially if information about the initial soil wetness condition is unavailable. Aubert et al. (2003)  implemented sequential assimilation to improve streamflow estimation. Measurements of soil moisture and streamflow were assimilated into a lumped, conceptual rainfall-runoff model. It was observed that the assimilation of soil moisture was most useful during flood events while low flows benefited from streamflow assimilation. Analogously, data assimilation experiments were performed for catchments of varying sizes across Europe to investigate the influence of European Space Agency Climate Change Initiative (CCI) soil moisture assimilation on streamflow simulations (De Santis et al., 2021 ). Improvements were more pronounced in catchments where the model was not accurately representing the regional land-atmosphere processes as quantified by evaluation metrics or where precipitation estimates were inaccurate. The assimilated dataset accuracy was identified as the prominent contributor to assimilation efficiency. Estimation degradation was observed across humid catchments and areas where the antecedent soil moisture conditions had relatively limited influence on streamflow. Baguis et al. (2022)  assimilated ASCAT backscatter observations into a hydrological model using a calibrated water cloud model as the observation operator. They observed marginal improvements in streamflow via backscatter data assimilation but noted that the performance statistics depended on the analysis period. Bechtold et al. (2023)  assimilated Sentinel-1 backscatter into a land surface model across two catchments in Belgium for streamflow estimation at a fine spatial scale (0.01°  ). They showed that Sentinel-1 backscatter assimilation improved streamflow estimation in the catchment where the connectivity between soil moisture and runoff was strong. Based on results from different studies, it seems that study area characteristics and model physics, i.e. , precipitation and soil moisture connectivity primarily influence data assimilated estimates. In this study, a land surface model is used to estimate runoff and streamflow across South Asia and the influence of assimilation on these two geophysical variables is analyzed. Previous attempts at runoff estimation across South Asia vary in their methodologies based on the study objectives. Hopson and Webster (2010)  implemented conditional postprocessing to calibrate probabilistic estimates of river discharge driven by satellite precipitation for two major rivers in South Asia. The utility of correlated, satellite-derived flow to track the downstream propagation of river flood waves was shown to have potential across some major rivers in South Asia (Hirpa et al., 2013 ). Sikder et al. (2019)  evaluated the skill of various global runoff datasets using a river model and concluded that the selection of land surface model coupled with the prescribed meteorological inputs affect discharge simulation the most. Although these studies have advanced the current understanding of spatiotemporal patterns in runoff across South Asia, there is no consistent dataset publicly available that provides daily runoff estimates at finer spatial scales (< 0 . 25 °   ) for South Asian river basins. This gap in information serves as the motivation for the present study in which streamflow is estimated at a relatively fine grid resolution of 0.05°. The main objectives of this study are to analyze: (a) the impact of assimilating coarse scaled soil moisture estimates on fine scaled runoff estimation and (b) the utility of satellite-based soil moisture assimilation across river basins that are heavily irrigated. The presented study estimates runoff and streamflow at a fine resolution (relative to contemporary land surface models) and investigates the influence of surface soil moisture assimilation on estimated runoff and streamflow. Furthermore, this study aims to explore the impact of changes in antecedent soil moisture on surface flow and baseflow via land surface modeling and data assimilation. The Noah-MP land surface model (details provided in Section 3.1 ) was used to model the hydrologic cycle across the three main river basins in South Asia, which is a largely unguaged region. Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) soil moisture retrievals (O’Neill et al., 2021 ) were assimilated into the land surface model to analyze the influence on subsequent runoff and streamflow estimation. Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) brightness temperature and soil moisture retrievals have been used in several studies for runoff estimation (Jadidoleslam et al., 2019; Crow et al., 2019; Akbar et al., 2019 ). Sujud and Jaafar (2022)  developed an online application to estimate dynamic runoff by calculating global curve numbers at high resolution from satellite-based precipitation and SMAP soil moisture. In this study, runoff is categorized as the flow computed at each grid cell by the land surface model, while streamflow is the volumetric flow (discharge) estimated by hydraulically routing the runoff at each grid cell through a river network (further details in Section 3.2 ). The term volumetric flow rate (i.e. , L 3     T−1 ) is used for streamflow to differentiate from modeled runoff, which has dimensions of length per time for each grid cell. Streamflow has dimensions of volume per time and represents discharge, whereas soil moisture has dimensions of volume of water per volume of soil matrix. This study not only explores the impact of assimilation on runoff estimation, but also analyzes the limitations in our current modeling frameworks and highlights the key advancements needed to improve future streamflow estimation across irrigated areas. The study domain is described in Section 2 ; Section 3  details the implemented methodology; Sections 4.2 and 4.3  present the results of the assimilation experiment; and Section 5  highlights the main conclusions of the study.  2 Study domain In this study, we focused on three large river basins and the adjoining areas within South Asia: (1) Indus, (2) Ganges, and (3) Brahmaputra, see Fig. 1 a. All three of these rivers originate in the Hindukush-Karakoram-Himalayan (HKH) mountain range and eventually flow southwards towards lower elevation areas. These rivers contribute significantly to the maintenance of regional ecosystems and socioeconomic sustenance of the local populace (Wester et al., 2018 ).  Fig. 1 b presents the spatial extent and location of the landcover types across the study domain based on the NCEP/MODIS-based International Geosphere–Biosphere Programme (Friedl et al., 2002 ) classification. The prominent landcover types present within the study domain are barren (25.3%), croplands (21.7%), and shrublands (20.2%). The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) provides a global map of area fraction per grid cell that is equipped with irrigation as part of the Global Map of Irrigation Areas (GMIA) product (Siebert et al., 2005 ) (see Fig. 4 g). Grid cells categorized as croplands are consistent with grid cells having high percentages of total irrigated areas. The high percentages of per pixel irrigated areas highlight the presence of an extensive irrigation network in South Asia. The study region includes a range of different climatologies. As a result, precipitation patterns across the study domain are spatially heterogeneous. Malik et al. (2010)  used the Asian Precipitation Highly Resolved Observational Data Integration Towards the Evaluation of Water Resources (APHRODITE) precipitation dataset and highlighted the occurrence of greater mean monsoonal rainfall across the eastern part of South Asia – Ganges and Brahmaputra river basins – compared to the western region, where the Indus basin is located. Magnitudes ranged from ∼  300 to > 2400    mm per season across the Ganges and Brahmaputra river basins while the Indus river basin had magnitudes ranging from 0 to ∼  1200 mm per season. Maina et al. (2022)  concluded that precipitation is one of the main drivers of greening in mid and low elevation areas that are covered by evergreen and mixed forests, whereas irrigation enhances greening in croplands. Location of the HKH mountains renders snowmelt and glacier melt a prominent contributor to the total freshwater flow through these three river systems. Several studies (Immerzeel et al., 2009; Bookhagen and Burbank, 2010; Armstrong et al., 2018 ) attempted to calculate the individual contributions of snowmelt, glacier-melt, and precipitation to runoff. The percentage of contribution estimated by each of the studies varies, however, all conclude a relatively higher contribution of snowmelt and glacier melt to the Indus River. These studies underlined the importance of each individual contributor towards accurate runoff estimation in South Asia.  3 Methods and datasets 3.1 Noah-MP land surface model The Noah-Multiparametrization version 4.0.1 (Noah-MP) land surface model (Niu et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2011 ) was used to simulate the land surface processes across the study domain. Noah-MP includes a multilayer soil profile, explicit modeling of frozen soil, a multilayer snowpack, and coupled water and carbon cycles (Niu and Yang, 2006 ). Surface runoff and baseflow are both parameterized as exponential functions of the depth to water table (Niu et al., 2007, 2011 ). Soil moisture updates would affect the depth to water table, and thereby, subsequently influence the surface runoff and baseflow. Surface runoff is modeled using the saturation-excess runoff technique (a.k.a Dunne runoff). In other words, the water (computed as the sum of rainfall, dew, and snowmelt) incident on the fractional saturated area of a model grid cell is categorized as surface runoff. The fractional saturated area, F  s a t    , is then parameterized as: (1) F  s a t   = F  m a x   e  − 0 . 5 f ( z  ∇   − z  ′   )        where f  is the runoff decay factor. The value of f  = 6 was used, which was based on calibration with global runoff data (Niu et al., 2007 ). F  m a x     is the maximum surface saturated fraction and is set equal to 0.38, which is the global mean value (Niu et al., 2011 ). z  ′     is the total depth of the soil profile and is set equal to 2 m. The rate of baseflow, R  s b    , (also known as subsurface runoff) is parameterized as: (2) R  s b   = ( 1 − F C R  m a x   )  R  s b , m a x   e  − Λ − f ( z  ∇   − z  ′   )        where R  s b , m a x     is the maximum baseflow and is taken equal to 5.0 × 10−4  mm/s. Niu et al. (2007)  selected this value after calibration using global runoff data. Λ   is the mean wetness index and is set equal to a global mean of 10.46. F C R  m a x      is the maximum impermeable fraction of grid cell due to frozen soil. Table 1  contains the Noah-MP configuration implemented in this study. It is important to note that irrigation is not explicitly modeled within the Noah-MP modeling system. However, Noah-MP does include a simple representation of glacier mass balance physics which is important for water cycle modeling in South Asia since glacier meltwater is a predominant source of freshwater in the region. Noah-MP was run within the NASA Land Information System (LIS, version 7.4) framework. LIS is a software platform that includes a suite of land surface modeling and data assimilation methods (Kumar et al., 2006; Peters-Lidard et al., 2007 ).    3.2 Hydrological Modeling and Analysis Platform (HyMAP) Hydrological Modeling and Analysis Platform (HyMAP) is a flow routing module that routes horizontal water fluxes estimated by a land surface model through a prescribed river network (Getirana et al., 2012 ). HyMAP estimates water level, discharge, and storage in rivers and floodplains using four modules that represent: (i) the time delays in surface runoff and groundwater baseflow, (ii) the interface between the river and the floodplain, (iii) the routing of flow through river channels and floodplains, and (iv) evaporation from open water surfaces. HyMAP is included within the LIS framework and was used here for runoff routing. HyMAP takes the runoff estimated by the land surface model (at each grid cell) as input and simulates the streamflow in a prescribed river network. HyMAP was run at a 15-minute timestep using a kinematic wave equation. HyMAP parameters were derived from the Multi-Error-Removed Improved-Terrain (MERIT) DEM at a 3 arcsec spatial resolution (Yamazaki et al., 2017 ). Over South Asia, the MERIT DEM is based on the NASA Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM; Farr et al. (2007) ) processed with successive correction of absolute bias, stripe noise, speckle noise, and tree height bias using multiple satellite datasets and filtering techniques. As a result, the MERIT DEM provides a more reliable representation of floodplains and wetlands than the original SRTM DEM.  3.3 Experimental framework Three separate Noah-MP simulation runs were implemented: (1) spin-up, (2) open loop (OL), and (3) data assimilation (DA). A single replicate spin-up was first run to provide the initial conditions for the OL and DA simulations. The spin-up consisted of Noah-MP being propagated in time using a single replicate from 1 January 2005 to 31 December 2014. These dates were selected to provide the model ∼  10 years to spin-up prior to the introduction of SMAP soil moisture retrievals. 3.3.1 Open loop The OL consisted of the propagation of Noah-MP+HyMAP (land surface model and runoff routing model) in time in ensemble mode using 20 replicates, see Fig. 2 . The OL was initialized using the restart file yielded by the spin-up simulation and was run from 1 January 2015 to 30 September 2020. The study period spans over five water years starting in 2015 when the SMAP soil moisture retrievals became available. The OL provided reference estimates that represented model-only behavior, i.e. , the estimation capabilities of Noah-MP and HyMAP modeling routines in the absence of assimilated observations.    3.3.2 Data assimilation The DA run consisted of Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) soil moisture retrievals (O’Neill et al., 2014 ) assimilated into the Noah-MP land surface model as it is propagated in time in ensemble mode, see Fig. 2 . Noah-MP runoff estimates obtained post-assimilation were then routed using HyMAP to obtain the DA streamflow estimates. A 1D Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) technique was applied to assimilate the SMAP retrievals into Noah-MP. The two main steps in EnKF are the propagation and update steps. The state vector (y  t    ) is propagated in time using the forward model (Noah-MP is this case). The posterior state estimate is computed in the update step using Eq. (3) : (3) y  t  +   ( x )  = y  t  −   ( x )  + K  t   ( x )   ( z  t   ( x )  + v  t   − H ( y  t  −   ( x )  )  )      (4) where  K  t   ( x )  = C  y  t   z  t     ( x )  [ C  z  t   z  t     ( x )  + C  v v   ]   − 1       where y  t  +   ( x )     is the posterior state estimate, y  t  −   ( x )     is the prior state estimate, K  t   ( x )     represents the Kalman gain matrix, z  t   ( x )     is the observed value (i.e. , SMAP retrievals), v  t     is the observation error where v ∼ N ( 0 , σ  v  2   )    , H  (.) is the observation operator, C  y  t   z  t     ( x )     represents the cross-covariance between the state and predicted observation errors, C  z  t   z  t     ( x )     is the predicted observation error covariance, C  v v     represents the observation error covariance, x   represents a point in space, and t   is time.  3.3.3 Simulation framework Meteorological boundary condition perturbations were applied to force and propagate the state ensemble. Precipitation was estimated with the IMERG dataset while near surface air temperature and radiation forcings were approximated using MERRA2 (see Table 1 ). IMERG is provided at a temporal resolution of 30 min at 0.1° × 0.1°, while MERRA2 is available at 3-hour intervals on a 0.5° ×   0.625° grid. Multiplicative perturbations based on Gaussian distributions with a mean of one and standard deviations equal to 0.5 and 0.3, respectively, were used for precipitation and shortwave radiation. Additive perturbations based on Gaussian distributions with a mean of zero and standard deviations equal to 50 Wm 2     and 1 K, respectively, were applied to longwave radiation and near-surface air temperature. These values are based on contemporary literature (Kwon et al., 2019 ) and test simulations that were conducted to better optimize (tune) the data assimilation routine. Observation error was assumed to be Gaussian with an error standard deviation (σ  v     in Eq. (3) ) equal to 0.04 m 3    /m 3    . A series of test simulations was conducted to select the observation error (results not included). The observation error standard deviation was increased from 0.02 to 0.1 m 3    /m 3     and the corresponding DA estimated soil moisture accuracy was computed by comparing with ground observations. It was seen that the best agreement was obtained by using an observation error standard deviation equal to 0.04 m 3    /m 3    . SMAP data availability starts from 31 March 2015. Therefore, the DA run was initialized using the restart file output from the OL for 31 March 2015. No pre-processing was applied to the observations prior to assimilation. In a study presented in Ahmad et al. (2022) , results from assimilating CDF-matched versus no-preprocessing based observations were extensively analyzed. It was seen that the best performance was achieved by assimilating no-preprocessing based observations across the study area. The results from assimilating CDF-matched observations showed that the difference between model-only and data assimilation estimated soil moisture and runoff was minimal. The inherent bias in the model-only estimates is due to a lack of irrigation information in the model physics. Modeling irrigation in this region is quite a complex task since irrigation is not governed by clear systematic rules. At present, an accurate and robust parameterization of anthropogenic irrigation (based on actual ground data) in South Asia does not exist. Hence, we present a framework that can implicitly help improve modeled runoff estimates. It must be noted though that, in general, it would be best to have an observation bias correction scheme prior to assimilation. For study regions where the model climatology is inherently biased, any pre-processing of satellite observations should be based on regionally representative observations rather than model estimates. However, therein lies the main challenge for South Asia, i.e. , the currently available information about regional water management practices is insufficient as there is limited recorded data about irrigation water usage and local storage reservoir operation.
