Until this information becomes readily available, assimilation frameworks (such as the one described in this study) provide a useful method of improving the model estimation accuracy. In accordance with standard procedure, it is advisable to process the observations prior to assimilation using unbiased state variable climatology. The modeled state values were spatially aggregated to the SMAP observation grid resolution using the observation operator, H   in Eq. (3) . SMAP retrievals were assimilated at the time they were collected by the satellite. Since these experiments are reanalysis simulations, therefore, assimilation occurs when the model reaches the time at which the observations were collected by the SMAP satellite. Only SMAP retrievals that passed the quality checks were assimilated. Quality checks are based on the rating provided with the SMAP datasets. If the quality of the retrieved soil moisture is poor, as flagged by the data development team, then such values were not assimilated. The DA run extended from 1 April 2015 to 30 September 2020 (end of the 2020 water year). All Noah-MP simulations (spin-up, OL, and DA) were run at a 15-minute timestep and at a spatial resolution of 0.05°   × 0.05°  . Further details about the assimilation framework, and the ensuing soil moisture estimates, are included in Ahmad et al. (2022) . Please refer to Ahmad et al. (2022)  for a detailed analysis of OL and DA soil moisture estimates and their evaluation using in-situ measurements. In this manuscript, runoff and streamflow estimates are analyzed.   3.4 Datasets 3.4.1 SMAP level-3 soil moisture for assimilation Level-3 surface soil moisture retrievals (O’Neill et al., 2021 ) from the Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) satellite mission were assimilated into the Noah-MP land surface model. The passive microwave-based surface (∼  5 cm depth) retrievals were used during assimilation as they provided data for a longer time period (from 31 March 2015 onward). The L3SMP Level-3 soil moisture product provides global soil moisture observations as retrieved by the L-band radiometer (O’Neill et al., 2021 ). The dataset is provided on a cylindrical 36 km Equal-Area Scalable Earth Grid, Version 2.0 (Brodzik et al., 2012 ). A comparative study was performed by Stillman and Zeng (2018)  who concluded that the SMAP soil moisture retrievals had greater accuracy across various land cover types compared to other soil moisture retrievals. Therefore, SMAP soil moisture retrievals were selected for assimilation. However, it is worth noting here that there are data gaps associated with frozen soils and overlying snow.  3.4.2 In-situ streamflow measurements for evaluation In-situ measurements obtained from five regional organizations were used during evaluation of the HyMAP derived streamflow (Section 4.3 ). Table 2  summarizes the individual station network information. Fig. 1 a illustrates the location of the stations. These stations span a wide range of flow magnitudes and provide a unique opportunity to evaluate Noah-MP+HyMAP performance across a range of flow conditions.  The four upstream stations located in the Indus basin- Kabul, Tarbela, Marala, and Mangla- are more representative of natural river flow as there are no large storage reservoirs upstream from these stations. However, these stations are located directly adjacent and upstream of hydroelectric dams and are, therefore, influenced by dam heights. It is expected that the modeled streamflow will be underestimated as the restriction in water flow due to the presence of dams is not included in the model physics used in this study. The three downstream stations- Sukkur, Guddu, and Kotri- are significantly influenced by the upstream reservoir activity as well as the surface water withdrawals via links/canals for irrigation. Hence, it is expected that the HyMAP streamflow might be higher in magnitude compared to station measurements at the downstream stations since the upstream water reservoir operations are not included in the routing model. The stations located within the eastern Indus Basin (Kashmir), Ganges, and Brahmaputra are assumed to be less impacted by surface water impoundments and withdrawals considering their upstream locations. One station, Bhairab, is located outside the Brahmaputra basin boundary, however, due to its close proximity to the river basins of interest it is added in the station evaluation dataset.  3.4.3 Global Land Data Assimilation System Datasets Four suitable datasets from the Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) catalog were selected for evaluation with the Noah-MP OL and DA estimated runoff (Section 4.2.3 ). Data products GLDAS_ NOAH025_3H, Beaudoing and Rodell (2020a) , GLDAS_CLSM10_3H (Li et al., 2020a ), GLDAS_VIC10_3H (Beaudoing and Rodell, 2020b ), and GLDAS_CLSM025_DA1_D (Li et al., 2020b ) were used for comparison with both the surface runoff and baseflow as estimated by the OL and DA runs. Details about these four different datasets selected for comparison are included in Table 3 . It is important to note that irrigation information is not included in the modeling frameworks of the GLDAS datasets discussed here. Comparison of OL and DA estimates with the GLDAS datasets provides insights into multi-model differences in estimated runoff across South Asia.      4 Results and discussion 4.1 Changes in soil moisture Assimilating SMAP retrievals into Noah-MP impacted soil moisture estimated by the DA run. Fig. 3  shows the soil moisture estimated by the OL and DA run and the difference between the two simulations for water year (WY) 2017. Subplots (a) and (b) show the average soil moisture in the top ∼  5 cm for the winter months as modeled by the OL and DA simulations, respectively. Similarly, subplots (d) and (e) present average soil moisture for the summer months as modeled by the OL and DA simulations, respectively. Subplot (c) and (f) highlight the difference between DA and OL estimated soil moisture for the winter and summer months, respectively. Comparing these results with Fig. 4  (included below), it can be seen that the spatial patterns in subplots (c) and (f) from Fig. 3  and Fig. 4  are similar, i.e. , the positive differences in DA minus OL soil moisture (represented by red color in Fig. 3 ) coincide with the positive differences in DA minus OL total runoff (represented by red color in Fig. 4 ). Differences in soil moisture and total runoff are seen across areas that are collocated with pixels with a higher percentage of irrigation-equipped area (Fig. 4 g). The differences in soil moisture and total runoff are primarily apparent across irrigated areas, indicating that the systematic differences between SMAP and model soil moisture are limited.   Further details about the impact of assimilation on soil moisture are discussed in Ahmad et al. (2022) . In order to reduce duplicity in published results, we have not included soil moisture analysis in this paper. Instead, specific references to Ahmad et al. (2022)  are included in relevant sections.  4.2 Runoff analysis The Noah-MP land surface model provides surface runoff and baseflow outputs at each grid cell. The sum of these two components is total runoff. The following analyses focus first on the total runoff and then its constituent components, i.e. , surface runoff and baseflow. Results included in this section are based on water year 2017, starting in October 2016 and ending in September 2017. Similar results were observed for water years 2016 to 2020. 4.2.1 Total runoff Fig. 4  highlights the OL versus DA estimated total runoff during the winter and summer seasons for water year 2017. Subplots (a) and (b) present the OL and DA estimated total runoff averaged over the winter months while (c) highlights the difference between the two maps. Subplots (d), (e) and (f) show the same maps averaged during the summer months. The FAO GMIA dataset is used here to represent irrigation equipped areas (subplot h). The GMIA dataset is provided at a 5-arc minute (0.0833°  ) spatial resolution. Comparing Figs. 3 and 4 , it is noted that there are larger differences between OL and DA estimated soil moisture than total runoff during the winter months (relative to the summer months), when the irrigation signal driven by surface water redistribution is captured. During the summer monsoon months, the soil moisture is generally large in magnitude for both the OL and DA, and therefore the difference between them is relatively smaller. While the DA and OL soil moisture differences are relatively lower in summer, the total runoff differences are large in summer. It seems that even a small difference in soil moisture during high precipitation months leads to large (nonlinear) differences in total runoff. Surface soil moisture and runoff are not directly correlated in this framework, rather there is an indirect relationship between these two hydrologic variables. Thus, model representation of the soil moisture and runoff connectivity controls the impact of changes in antecedent soil moisture on total runoff generated. In Fig. 4 , the location of positive occurrences of DA minus OL total runoff values are consistent with the location of grid cells having high percentages of irrigation-equipped areas (subplots c, f, and g). It is apparent that the soil moisture assimilation is implicitly accounting for the water contributed by irrigation. For example, in the Indus basin, the OL estimated total runoff does not explicitly account for the redistribution of water via irrigation (subplots a and d). In contrast, the DA estimated total runoff is more spatially representative of the irrigated conditions as the runoff through the Indus river and the adjoining areas (subplots b and e) is more consistent with the location of the river and the irrigated areas (subplot g). The DA estimated total runoff is relatively higher than the OL estimated total runoff across irrigated areas. Since most of the surface water irrigation channels branch off from the main river, most of the croplands lie adjacent or near the river bed. Therefore, it is expected that the total runoff would be higher if we effectively include the influence of irrigation via data assimilation. The DA minus OL total runoff values observed during the winter and summer months are predominantly positive and indicate higher total runoff estimates yielded by the DA simulation, particularly within irrigated areas. During the summer months there are negative DA minus OL values visible across western India. However, the magnitude of total runoff estimated at these locations by both the OL and DA runs is relatively high. It is worth noting that during the summer months, high magnitudes of DA minus OL total runoff values are generally collocated with precipitation events and are predicated by wetter antecedent soil moisture conditions in the DA relative to the OL. Subplot 4 h shows the monthly-averaged DA minus OL total runoff for grid cells with greater than 30% grid cell area equipped with irrigation for WY 2017. There are two main crop seasons per year in South Asia: (1) the summer crop (Kharif), and (2) the winter crop (Rabi) (Biemans et al., 2016 ). Subplot 4 h exhibits a bi-modal pattern with peak DA minus OL differences observed in both February and July. Considering double crop cultivation in South Asia, the bi-modal temporal pattern in DA minus OL total runoff seems to originate due to missing irrigation information in the OL (i.e. , missing model physics). Irrigation would increase the soil moisture conditions which would then affect soil infiltration capacity and subsequent runoff generation. The selection of irrigation method and type of crop for cultivation varies within and between the three river basins. Areas with higher average precipitation in summer may have rice as the main crop (such as in Bangladesh), whereas cotton or sugar cane could be preferred in areas with lower probability of standing rainwater (such as Punjab, Pakistan).  4.2.2 Surface runoff and baseflow Fig. 5  presents the decomposition of the total runoff into its constituent components, i.e. , surface runoff and baseflow. Subplots 5 a–d highlight the spatial patterns in the precipitation boundary conditions (IMERG) along with the DA versus OL estimated runoff for the winter months. The similarity in the spatial patterns visible in subplots 5 (b) and 5 (d) suggests that baseflow is the dominant contributor to the difference between DA and OL estimated total runoff during the winter months. In comparison, the magnitudes for surface runoff are much lower than baseflow and indicate that the OL and DA estimated surface runoff magnitudes are quite similar. Considering the relatively low precipitation magnitudes during the winter months, it is expected that the OL and DA estimated surface runoff would be similar.  For the summer months, the contribution of surface runoff to the difference between DA and OL increased (relative to the winter months) as shown in Fig. 5 g. However, the dominant contribution still originates from baseflow. The main difference between the two seasonal results is due to the average precipitation intensities. During the summer, higher precipitation was observed in the major river basins. The precipitation events resulted in larger surface runoff and baseflows. Due to differences in the antecedent soil moisture conditions in the DA and OL simulations, the runoff generated was correspondingly modulated. Therefore, positive differences are observed in the DA minus OL maps during summer in both Figs. 4 and 5 . Comparing Fig. 5  with Fig. 4 g, it can be seen that the grid cells having positive DA minus OL baseflow are, in general, collocated with highly irrigated areas.  4.2.3 Comparison with GLDAS2 simulations The OL and DA estimates of surface runoff and baseflow were compared against four different GLDAS products (details in Section 3.4.3 ) to highlight the differences between OL/DA estimates and conventional land surface model-based datasets. For temporal consistency between the different datasets, the 3-hourly GLDAS datasets were aggregated in time to yield daily-averaged values. Surface flow. Figs. 6  and 7  compare the spatial patterns in surface runoff as estimated by the Noah-MP (4.0.1) OL and DA runs along with those of GLDAS products. Fig. 6  shows similarities between surface runoff estimates in the high mountain regions. However, the GLDAS VIC and CLSM products exhibited larger surface runoff magnitudes relative to the other products. Fig. 7  shows larger magnitudes for all datasets in the lower Brahmaputra basin. Similar to Fig. 6 , VIC exhibits the highest magnitudes in Fig. 7 . Interesting to note is the minimal amount of gridded surface runoff within the Indus Basin in all the products in Fig. 7  apart from the soil moisture DA estimates. This suggests the influence of adjusted antecedent soil moisture conditions on subsequent surface runoff (Ahmad et al., 2022 ).  Baseflow.   Figs. 8  and 9  compare the spatial patterns in baseflow as estimated by the Noah-MP (4.0.1) OL and DA runs relative to the GLDAS products. Baseflow in these estimated products can be quite different in terms of spatial patterns as well as in terms of magnitude. In Fig. 8 , the OL and DA estimates exhibit similar spatial patterns (apart from the Indus Basin and the lower Brahmaputra basin). CLSM datasets (subplots 8 e and 8 f) exhibit relatively low baseflow values. This behavior is also noted in Figs. 9 e and 9 f for the summer months. In contrast to the winter months, the summer baseflow estimates for Noah 3.6 and VIC datasets (subplots 9 c and 9 d) exhibit better spatial consistency with respect to the OL and DA across the Brahmaputra basin and western India.   These results corroborate the findings of Crow et al. (2018)  as a stronger coupling between baseflow (dominant runoff generation process in Noah-MP) and root-zone soil moisture manifests in the higher impact of assimilation on baseflow as compared to surface runoff. Other land surface models can have a stronger coupling between surface runoff and surface/root-zone soil moisture, which could lead to a potentially higher impact of assimilation for other models. Potential underestimation of storm runoff and soil moisture coupling in Noah-MP, as suggested by Crow et al. (2018) , means that there could be a higher impact of assimilation on streamflow estimation for high-flow tributaries in truth.  Modified correlation coefficients. Figs. 6  through 9  presented the seasonally-averaged, spatial distribution of surface runoff and baseflow as estimated by different models. In order to better understand the temporal consistency between various datasets, modified correlation coefficients were computed. The modified correlation coefficient, R  m     (see appendix Eq. (5) ), is a useful statistic as it takes into account the individual standard deviations of each timeseries (McCuen and Snyder, 1975 ). It is of hydrologic importance as it takes the size of the two hydrographs into consideration as well. R  m     values range from −1 (high negative correlation) to 1 (high positive correlation). R  m     was calculated separately for each grid cell. Datasets with finer resolution were up-scaled to the coarser grid size for spatially-consistent comparisons between datasets of different resolution. For datasets with the same resolution, no spatial up-scaling was necessary. Tables 4 and 5  present the spatially-averaged R  m     values between each pair of datasets for surface runoff and baseflow, respectively. Apart from the OL and DA, all pairs of datasets have R  m    <  0.3, which can be classified as poor correlation. OL and DA have higher correlation in terms of surface runoff (R  m    = 0.87) compared to baseflow (R  m    = 0.71). The highest R  m     magnitude for the GLDAS surface runoff estimates is computed between VIC and CLSM surface runoff (R  m     = 0.28) which had the same temporal and spatial resolution as well as used the same precipitation boundary conditions. Sikder et al. (2019)  investigated the influence of the land surface model used, applied boundary conditions, and spatiotemporal resolution on the estimated runoff for South Asia. They used a suite of GLDAS products and concluded that the meteorological boundary conditions and land surface model together had the highest influence while the spatiotemporal resolution had the least influence on the simulated discharge. Conjoining these findings with the R  m     values included in Table 4 , the importance of adequate numerical representation of physical processes in land surface models and boundary conditions is highlighted. Products that had the same meteorological boundary conditions (Noah 3.6, VIC, and CLSM) have higher correlation (R  m     = 0.18 and 0.28). However, it must be noted that all the correlation magnitudes in Table 4  (apart from OL or DA) are low and indicate differences between the surface runoff estimated by the individual datasets. In Table 5 , the modified correlation values for baseflow are also quite low. Apart from the OL or DA, the highest R  m     magnitude is computed for Noah 3.6 and VIC (R  m     = 0.21). Similar to surface flow, the correlation in baseflow estimated by the various datasets is quite low.   The spatial patterns in surface runoff and baseflow (Figs. 6 and 9 ) suggest better consistency between the OL, DA, and GLDAS products than the modified correlation values show. These results highlight the importance of statistical evaluation in cases where time-averaged spatial results can seem consistent. Considering the low R  m     values observed for the GLDAS datasets, it is recommended that runoff datasets should be thoroughly investigated against in-situ data prior to utilization for runoff trend analysis or flood analysis.    4.3 Streamflow analysis Streamflow estimates obtained for the OL and DA runs are evaluated with respect to in-situ streamflow measurements from the three main river basins in South Asia. Fig. 1  shows the location of the in-situ stations. Unfortunately, there are several data gaps in the station timeseries due to access limitations and restricted public data availability. The relative influence of soil moisture assimilation on streamflow across the three river basins is discussed in Section 4.3.2 . 4.3.1 Evaluation using in-situ station data Timeseries analysis. Multi-year timeseries for a station in the upper Indus Basin is shown in Fig. 10 . The station is located upstream near the Karakorum mountains where SMAP soil moisture retrievals are not available. Please see Figure 6f in Ahmad et al. (2022)  for a spatial representation of percentage of days that SMAP observations were available at each location. SMAP retrievals are not provided in regions of complex terrain or where partially or completely frozen surface soil conditions exist. Therefore, it is expected that the OL and DA streamflow estimates at this station will be quite similar. That is, the influence of soil moisture assimilation is expected to be more pronounced at downstream stations where the SMAP retrievals are more prevalent, and hence, the impact of soil moisture assimilation on the corresponding station drainage is higher.  The seasonal variation in the OL and DA estimated streamflow shows similarity with the measured data. As discussed previously in Section 3.4.2 , this station is located upstream of a reservoir. The dams and reservoirs are not explicitly modeled in the OL and DA setup. Since the influence of restricted water flow and anthropogenic water management is not explicitly accounted for within the routing module, it is expected that the OL and DA streamflow would be systematically biased. Fig. 10  clearly displays this bias in the modeled estimates. Fig. 11  shows the timeseries for two stations in the eastern part of the domain. The Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) values for OL and DA are the same at these two stations. Subplots (a) and (b) depict a time-lag in the OL and DA streamflow estimates, however, the streamflow magnitudes are similar in range to the station data. Considering the similarity in the OL and DA results, it does not seem that the soil moisture assimilation is impacting the streamflow at these stations to any considerable extent.  Statistical analysis.  The statistics presented in Table 6  are computed using publicly-available data, which in some cases was restricted just to the monsoon months (July–October), see Table 2 . Also, measurements are not provided daily for some stations. Therefore, it is acknowledged beforehand that these statistics may not adequately represent the ground conditions in some cases. Due to limited data for the study years (2015–2020), there are several gaps in the station timeseries. Therefore, the evaluation of the OL and DA results is more detailed at some stations (i.e. , those with complete multiyear timeseries) compared to stations with fewer measurements available (Table 2 ). All the statistical formulas are provided in the appendix.  If the temporal mean is used to represent the streamflow during the whole water year then the KGE value would be equal to 0. For strongly seasonal flows, the annual mean is not a representative value (Knoben et al., 2019 ). In general, it is desirable that the modeled estimates yield KGE >   0. Considering that the streamflows in these basins have strong seasonal regimes, KGE >   0 indicates the superiority of modeled estimates relative to the climatological mean. For the OL, three stations yielded a negative KGE value while for the DA experiment, negative KGE values were computed for two stations only. After assimilation (DA), the KGE value increased at 8 out of 18 stations, at 4 out of 18 stations the value decreased while it remained unchanged at 6 stations. However, the maximum difference in KGE values computed for the OL versus DA streamflow is only 0.1. This is a relatively small amount of change. In terms of modified correlation (R  m    ), assimilation improved the correlation at 7 stations, degraded the correlation at 6 stations, and did not induce any change at 5 of the total 18 comparative stations. However, all the modified correlation values have positive signs. For RMSE, the normalized information content, NIC (see appendix for Eq. (5) ), values are quite low (e.g. , highest NIC R M S E     = 0.05). Positive and negative NIC values were computed for 13 of 18 and 5 of 18 stations, respectively. Comparable NIC values were computed in terms of bias for most of the stations. Most of the stations have positive NIC values, which suggests that soil moisture assimilation is adding beneficial information content to the modeled streamflow. However, the extent of the added information is limited (i.e. , computed NIC R M S E     magnitudes are between − 0 . 05    to 0.05). Based on the results in Table 6 , it can be stated that, in general, assimilation moved the estimates in the right direction at the station locations. However, the magnitude of change at these particular locations was too small to be considered significant and was not corrective at all locations.  Annual average hydrographs. Fig. 12  includes average annual hydrographs for stations along the Indus river where streamflow data for multiple years was available. For subplots (a), (b), (g) and (h), the OL and DA estimates are quite similar. Considering the scarcity of soil moisture retrievals across complex terrain with completely or partially frozen soils, it is anticipated that the influence of soil moisture at upstream locations would be minimal. Additionally, both the OL and DA streamflow values underestimate the station streamflow as is expected due to the presence of reservoirs, discussion in Section 3.4.2 .  Figs. 12 e and 12 f show upstream stations with relatively low mean flows. The OL and DA streamflow estimates show consistency in terms of general seasonality with respect to the station measurements, apart from the spike in September. Considering the low flow magnitudes, any small discrepancy in model precipitation could introduce large differences with respect to the station measurements. The highest impact of soil moisture assimilation is seen at the most downstream stations, subplots 12 c and 12 d. This highlights the accumulation of OL and DA streamflow differences within the contributing tributaries. In Fig. 4 , the OL and DA runoff shows larger differences across the croplands which are located in the areas adjoining the Indus river and its floodplain. Subsequently, these differences are effectively integrated as seen in the streamflow at the downstream stations. Interesting to note is that the OL and DA streamflow estimates show similar magnitudes of differences throughout the entire year with larger magnitudes during the peak monsoon months of July and August.   4.3.2 Relative change in streamflow Comparison of the OL and DA estimated streamflow with station measurements did not indicate any considerable impact of soil moisture assimilation on streamflow estimated at those station locations. However, the station data used in Section 4.3.1  are quite limited in time (gaps present in timeseries) and space (data from only 18 stations was available). Therefore, the influence of SMAP soil moisture assimilation on streamflow simulation is examined in a spatially distributed manner in Fig. 13 .  Figs. 13 a and 13 c show the general increase in DA minus OL values as the total drainage area contributing to the streamflow within the corresponding grid cell increased. A majority of the values have a positive sign indicating a general presence of higher streamflow magnitudes after assimilation. Also, the magnitudes of negative DA minus OL values are quite small compared to the positive values. This feature is apparent during both seasons; however, the magnitude of DA minus OL is greater during the summer monsoon months compared to the winter months. The higher summer magnitudes are explained by the increase in precipitation during the summer months. The change in soil moisture via assimilation influences the partitioning of incident precipitation into surface runoff and infiltration, thereby generally yielding greater DA streamflow. In Figs. 13 b and 13 d, the relative change in streamflow for grid cells that are collocated with the main river tributaries (Figs. 1 and 12 ) is quite low compared to the surrounding areas. This highlights the variation in the influence of assimilation across different grid cells. The magnitude of streamflow for the main river tributaries (Fig. 10  and Fig. 11 ) is quite large and is on the order of 10 4     m 3    /s. A majority of the DA minus OL values are <  250 m 3    /s (Figs. 13 a and 13 c). Comparing the station streamflow magnitudes with the DA minus OL magnitudes, it is apparent that the relative influence of soil moisture assimilation at high streamflow (> 1000    m 3   / s   ) locations is limited. This explains the small differences between the OL and DA statistical metrics presented in Table 6 . All the stations used to calculate the metrics are either located on the main river tributaries or in upland, high elevation areas where the availability of SMAP retrievals is limited. As a result, the relative change after assimilation is quite low at these station locations. This limits evaluation with respect to station data of the OL and DA estimated streamflow across areas where the actual impact of assimilation occurs such as the lower Indus basin. The spatial patterns in Figs. 13 b and 13 d are quite similar to the spatial patterns in DA minus OL runoff shown in Fig. 5 . This suggests that the differences in the OL versus DA gridded runoff are manifested in the OL versus DA streamflows. Considerable relative change (> 0 . 7   ) in streamflow after assimilation is noted across the lower Indus basin, which is highly irrigated, as well as near the downstream conjunction of the Ganges and Brahmaputra basins where high precipitation magnitudes occur. Therefore, it can be stated that the soil moisture assimilation yielded greater streamflow relative to OL across irrigated areas within the Indus basin and high precipitation locations at the downstream confluence of the Ganges and Brahmaputra basins. In Fig. 14 , an increase in the DA minus OL interquartile values is observed as the percentage of irrigation equipped area per grid cell increases from 0 to 40%. A generally increasing linear relationship is noted between seasonally mean DA minus OL streamflow and percentage of irrigation equipped area per grid cell (until 30%). The values remain predominantly positive as the percentage of irrigation equipped area per grid cell increases beyond 40%. However, there is a decreasing trend noted in seasonal mean values beyond 30%. A number of factors contribute to this pattern. There exists a non-linear relationship between the increase in DA estimated streamflow (as compared to OL) and the percentage of area equipped with irrigation. Streamflow at a grid cell is dependent on the streamflow contributed by the total drainage area. Therefore, DA minus OL value will be large at a location that has a drainage area which includes grid cells that are impacted by assimilation (see Fig. 12 ). For a location which may have higher percentage of grid cell area that is equipped with irrigation, the average DA minus OL value could be small if the drainage area contributing to that location comprises grid cells that lie in either non-irrigated regions or where the general impact of assimilation is limited.  The mean of the seasonally averaged DA minus OL streamflow values for highly irrigated grid cells (i.e. , percentage of irrigation greater than 80%) are lower than less irrigated areas, as seen in Fig. 14 . From Fig. 4 , we know that highly irrigated areas are located in regions that are adjacent to the main rivers and are irrigated via surface water (often through naturally sloping channels). These regions inherently have high soil moisture conditions and often have very high flows that are due to extreme precipitation resulting in similar OL and DA streamflow values. Therefore, the impact of assimilation is limited in such areas as exhibited by the low DA minus OL values in Fig. 14  and relative change subplots 13 b and 13 d. Additionally, DA minus OL streamflow is not only influenced by the percentage of irrigation equipped area per grid cell but also by the amount of precipitation that falls on the soil. A higher streamflow could be generated at a location that has higher precipitation as compared to a low precipitation area for the same soil moisture value. Therefore, it cannot be concluded that highly irrigated areas would always yield higher DA-OL values. The presented study shows that the relative impact  of DA is higher across irrigated areas (as compared to OL estimated streamflow). However, it does not necessarily mean that a linearly increasing relationship exists between the percentage of irrigation and impact of DA.    5 Conclusion The goal of this study was to determine and characterize the influence of soil moisture assimilation on estimated runoff and streamflow across three main river basins in South Asia using the NASA Land Information System (LIS). SMAP soil moisture retrievals were assimilated into the Noah-MP land surface model. The land surface model estimated runoff at each grid cell in dimensions of depth per time. The HyMAP runoff routing model was utilized to hydraulically route the gridded runoff into streamflow values in units of volume per time for a defined river network. Analysis of the open loop (OL, model-only) and data assimilated (DA, soil moisture retrieval assimilation) Noah-MP runoff estimates highlighted the increase in estimated runoff across irrigated areas. The updates in soil moisture translated into increased runoff (per grid cell) across the irrigated areas. The average contribution of baseflow to the differences between OL versus DA estimated runoff was higher than for the surface flow. Soil moisture assimilation modulated baseflow more relative to the surface flow. Comparison of the OL and DA estimates with several GLDAS products showed poor correlation in terms of runoff between the individual datasets, apart from the OL and DA. It highlighted the importance of thorough evaluation of runoff products with respect to in-situ data prior to their usage for flood analysis or other hydrologic studies. The HyMAP routed streamflow was evaluated with respect to in-situ measurements from stations across South Asia. The OL and DA generally underestimated the streamflow at upstream stations and overestimated the streamflow at downstream stations within the Indus basin largely due to missing physics associated with reservoir management. In this study, the natural flow of the river was modeled whereas the ground observations represent the volumetric streamflow observed at manually operated reservoirs. Surface water is one of the main sources of irrigation in the Indus basin and a network of channels takes water out from the main river and distributes it across the adjacent fields. It is expected that the OL and DA modeled streamflow will be higher than the observed values since the observations account for the surface water that has already been taken out for irrigation. However, the framework presented here models the natural flow of the river. The lateral distribution of surface water is another challenge that must be accounted for when modeling irrigation (and flow of surface water) in this region. For stations located in the Ganges–Brahmaputra basins, the OL and DA estimation performance varied (highest KGE magnitude = 0.5 while lowest KGE magnitude = 0 for a station with only seasonal measurements available). Across these two basins, DA improved the KGE values compared to the OL. However, the average improvements were minimal in magnitude. Data sparsity limited the extent of evaluation with respect to in-situ measurements as several stations had only seasonal measurements available. In general, the differences between the DA versus OL estimated streamflow increased as the total drainage area contributing to the corresponding grid cell increased. Analysis of the relative change in streamflow due to soil moisture assimilation showed that DA yielded greater streamflow relative to OL across irrigated areas within the Indus basin, similar to the spatial patterns observed in the OL versus DA runoff. There is a lack of publicly available streamflow measurements from most of the study domain, in particular within non-irrigated areas. It is important to consider that any improvement (however incremental) is useful in this ungauged area. Since it cannot be ascertained whether the updates (irrespective of their magnitude) are correct or incorrect in non-irrigated areas, therefore, it would be inadvisable to make a conclusion based on the limitations in evaluation data across non-irrigated areas. In order to adequately evaluate the utility of soil moisture assimilation across non-irrigated areas, reliable ground measurements of streamflow are needed. It can be summarized that the assimilation of SMAP soil moisture retrievals improved gridded runoff and volumetric streamflow across irrigated areas. However, it had a limited impact on volumetric streamflow along high-flow river tributaries and across high elevation regions containing completely or partially-frozen areas such that SMAP soil moisture retrievals were not available. These conclusions are similar to the results presented by De Santis et al. (2021) . Significant improvement in modeled estimates across the South Asian river basin could potentially be brought about by incorporating reservoir storage information into the routing model routine, thereby improving the modeling systems representativeness of ground conditions. Multi-variate assimilation of soil moisture and snow mass could also potentially further improve the magnitude of streamflow for these snow-dominated river basins.
1 Introduction Nearshore areas and some basins of the lower Laurentian Great Lakes (Lakes Erie and Ontario) are currently undergoing a process of re-eutrophication. Eutrophication, which is associated with increases in the extent and duration of harmful algal blooms, oxygen depletion, ecosystem disruption, and contaminated drinking water (Environment and Climate Change Canada and Ontario Ministry of the Environment and Climate Change, 2018; Schindler, 2006 ), is usually attributed primarily to excess inputs of phosphorus (P; Schindler et al., 2016 ). The Great Lakes experienced severe eutrophication in the mid-20th century, which was mitigated largely by reducing point source P inputs from municipal and industrial sources (De Pinto et al., 1986 ). However, since the 1990s, symptoms of eutrophication have returned to the lower Great Lakes (Michalak et al., 2013; Scavia et al., 2014 ). To curb ongoing eutrophication and achieve nutrient loading targets established in bi-national agreements between Canada and the United States (GLWQA 2012), focus has shifted from managing point sources of P to managing non-point sources of P, particularly agricultural sources (International Joint Commission, 2014; Maccoux et al., 2016; Scavia et al., 2017 ). To reduce non-point sources of P loading to the Great Lakes, it is important to understand relationships between agricultural land management and P transport to the Great Lakes at the watershed scale in any effort to reduce non-point sources of P. Recent reviews have established a need for a better understanding of the details between land management and downstream nutrient loading at a regional scale (Mohamed et al., 2019 ). One key toolset to investigate links between land management and nutrient transport consists of process-based watershed water quality models (Fu et al., 2019; Wellen et al., 2015 ). These models simulate natural and anthropogenic watershed processes by computing the flow of water and other substances from precipitation, through the landscape, and to receiving water bodies (Lindström et al., 2010 ). Water quality models have been widely applied to better understand catchment processes (Cheng et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2020 ), to assess the impacts of climate and/or land use on nutrient loads (Mehdi et al., 2015; Michalak et al., 2013 ), and to evaluate best management practices (BMPs) for environmental decision making (Liu et al., 2016; Martin et al., 2021; Scavia et al., 2017 ). While extensive work using process-based models to simulate water quality has been conducted in the United States' portion of the Great Lakes basin (Martin et al., 2021; Scavia et al., 2017 ), work in the Canadian portion of the basin has focused on single river systems such as the Grand River (Hanief and Laursen, 2017; Liu et al., 2016 ) or the St Clair-Detroit River system (Dagnew et al., 2019 ). Water quality models require accurate and appropriate input, boundary condition, and calibration data, including field observations of water quality. It is common to use monthly grab sample measurements of water quality constituents to calibrate water quality models as higher frequency data are not always available (Jiang et al., 2020; Piniewski et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2016 ). Previous work has attempted to quantify the influence of calibration data sample frequency on model performance with mixed results. Several studies have found that model calibration using high frequency data can improve model performance and accuracy for a range of water quality constituents such as total suspended solids, nitrate, total nitrogen, and total phosphorus (Piniewski et al., 2019; Ullrich and Volk, 2010 ). However, other studies found little loss in model performance when water quality models are calibrated with lower frequency data. For example, Woodward et al. (2017)  found that nitrate observations were reproduced well whether high (daily) or low (monthly) frequency data were used. In addition, Jiang et al. (2019)  found that prediction uncertainty was only marginally improved by using higher frequency data. In southern Ontario, the most widely available source of water quality data is the Provincial (Stream) Water Quality Monitoring Network (PWQMN; Ontario Ministry of the Environment Conservation and Parks, 2021 ). The PWQMN collects data for a number of water quality constituents in streams and rivers across the province of Ontario on an approximately monthly basis during ice-free conditions. PWQMN data are often used to calibrate or develop water quality models in the region (e.g. Dagnew et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016; Van Meter et al., 2021 ). In addition, a number of place-specific studies have sought to supplement the PWQMN with event samples collected throughout the year (e.g. Long et al., 2015, 2014 ). Recent efforts involving more intense water quality monitoring include the Multi-Watershed Nutrient Study (MWNS). The MWNS was led by the Ontario Ministry of the Environment Conservation, and Parks (MECP) and collected baseflow, event flow, and snow melt water quality data at higher frequency (e.g. hundreds of samples per year) from 11 headwater agricultural watersheds in southern Ontario (Nelligan et al., 2021; Rosamond et al., 2018 ). Data generated from the MWNS have been used in several recent studies (Biagi et al., 2022; Ross et al., 2022 ), and these works have collectively highlighted that nutrient transport preferentially occurs during relatively large hydrological flow events, though inter-event downstream transport of nutrients is also significant in these watersheds (Ross et al., 2022 ). Due to its robust sampling (Biagi et al., 2022; Nelligan et al., 2021; Ross et al., 2022 ) and strategic selection of 11 watersheds representing the agricultural headwaters of the Lower Great Lakes (Rosamond et al., 2018 ), the MWNS provides an excellent opportunity to compare performance of a distributed water quality model when calibrated with PWQMN and MWNS data. Since it is not clear how calibrating a watershed water quality model using PWQMN vs. MWNS data will affect model performance, we used these datasets to calibrate and validate an application of Hydrological Predictions for the Environment (HYPE; Lindström et al., 2010 ), a process-based watershed water quality model, for southern Ontario. The purpose of this study was to (i) develop an application of the HYPE model for southern Ontario, which has not previously been done; (ii) assess the effects of using water quality data from distinct monitoring programs with divergent observation frequencies and goals to calibrate and validate the HYPE model; and (iii) determine which landscape factors may contribute to the variability in model performance of discharge, total phosphorus (TP), and soluble reactive phosphorus (SP) loads. This study differs from previous work assessing the effect of calibration dataset characteristics on process-based watershed water quality model performance by using water quality data from two distinct sampling regimes rather than sub-sampling a high-resolution dataset.  2 Methods 2.1 Study area The study area is southern Ontario, except for the watersheds draining the major population centre of the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (Fig. 1  ). The Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area was excluded as these areas are heavily urbanized, and this study focuses on modelling relationships between agricultural land management and nutrient loss. The resultant study area is approximately 86,000 km2  and is composed of predominantly agricultural land (52.13 %), followed by forest cover (23.70 %), wetland (12.06 %), urban (7.38 %), water bodies (0.69 %), and bare land and open vegetation (0.03 %). The study area drains primarily into the Great Lakes (Lake Ontario, Lake Erie, and Lake Huron and Georgian Bay), but also into the St Lawrence and Ottawa Rivers, and roughly corresponds to the Lower Great Lakes Watershed Priority Area as outlined by Fisheries and Oceans Canada (https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/species-especes/sara-lep/cnfasar-fnceap/priority-priorite/profiles/great-grands-eng.html ). The Mixedwood Plains ecozone of Southern Ontario and a small part of the Ontario Shield ecozone (Crins et al., 2009) cover the study region. The Mixedwood Plains ecozone has one of the mildest climates in Canada, with cool winters and warm summers. Mean annual temperatures in the Mixed Plains ecozone range from 4.9 to 7.8 °C and mean annual precipitation ranges from 720 to 1000 mm (Crins et al., 2009). Temperatures are slightly lower in the Ontario Shield section of the study area, with mean annual temperature range 2.8 to 6.2 °C (Crins et al., 2009). The bedrock of Southern Ontario is predominantly limestone and much of the region is covered by thick glacial deposits including till (Barnett et al., 1991; Crins et al., 2009), which can necessitate the use of tile drains for agriculture in large parts of the region (Van Meter et al., 2021 ).  2.2 HYPE model HYPE is a semi-distributed process-based watershed model developed by the Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute (SMHI) that simulates hydrology and nutrient transport at a daily time step (Lindström et al., 2010 ). HYPE domains are spatially divided into sub-basins (SMHI, 2022 ), which are in turn divided into Soil and Land use Classes (SLCs). SLCs are not tied to a geographic location but are defined as fractions of sub-basin area. Each SLC is divided into a maximum of three soil layers, and within each layer processes related to hydrology and nutrient transformation are computed. HYPE simulates the movement and transformation of water and nutrients from rainfall, through soil pools, to rivers, and lakes. For example, in soils, some of the processes modeled include adsorption and desorption of P with soil particles, the decay of humus to the pool of immobile organic P in the soil, and decay of immobile organic P to dissolved particulate P. HYPE simulates particulate P, soil organic P, soluble reactive P, and total P as input/output values. Detailed descriptions of the HYPE model are available in Lindström et al. (2010)  and the HYPE reference manual (SMHI, 2022 ).  2.3 Basic model setup data To set up a model domain, HYPE requires detailed information on sub-basin boundaries, climate, hydrology, dams, wastewater discharge, soil, land use/land cover (LULC), and management data (Lindström et al., 2010 ). Details on this data are provided below and in Table 1  . Much of this information related to LULC, soil, or management is assumed to be time-invariant in a HYPE run. For this study, HYPE sub-basins were delineated using a 30 m resolution hydrologically-enforced digital elevation model (DEM) from the Ontario Integrated Hydrology Database (Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources and Forestry, 2019a ) and the ArcHydro toolbox in ArcGIS. Climate data (daily precipitation and daily average, maximum and minimum temperature) were derived from ERA-Interim reanalysis data (10 km resolution) produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (Dee et al., 2011 ) and spatially interpolated using inverse distance weighting (Mandal and Simonovic, 2017 ). The ERA-Interim uses a global physical model that assimilates meteorological observations at the surface, aloft, from ground based radar, and from satellites to estimate a continuous, physically consistent grid of various meteorological properties, including precipitation. Precipitation stations from all over the world, including the study area, are used to constrain the weather model. This approach was used due to the significant uncertainties involved in interpolating precipitation fields from point data. The use of re-analysis products to drive models is a standard approach in regional hydrological modelling, see e.g. Mai et al., 2022 . Data on dam operation were obtained from the Ontario Dam Inventory, which contains information on medium and large dams throughout Ontario (Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources and Forestry, 2020 ). Data for monthly average TP concentration in wastewater was retrieved from provincial databases for municipal (MECP, 2019a ) and industrial (MECP, 2019b ) sources. Soil data were obtained from Ontario Soil Survey Complex data produced by the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs (OMAFRA, 2019a ). Soils were aggregated into 24 textural classes and treated as such throughout the model application (e.g. all silt loam soils were treated the same regardless of location). Detailed soil properties were averaged across all the individual soils in the textural class. LULC data were obtained from the Ontario Land Cover Compilation v.2.0 (Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources and Forestry, 2019b ). 42 LULC classes (36 crop rotation and 6 other land types) were derived by aggregating the Ontario Land Cover Compilation v.2.0 (Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources and Forestry, 2019b ) with crop rotation classes provided by Agriculture and Agri-food Canada (Agriculture and Agri-food Canada, 2023 ). Management data required by HYPE include crop rotation data, tillage practices, tile drainage information, and fertilizer and manure application rates and placement. Crop rotation data were derived from Agriculture and Agri-food Canada’s Crop Rotations in Canada dataset (Agriculture and Agri-food Canada, 2023 ). Information on tile drainage presence was obtained from the OMAFRA Tile Drainage Area dataset (OMAFRA, 2019b ), and depth was assumed to be 750 mm as per regional surveys done by Dagnew et al. (2019) . Tillage data at the county level were obtained from the Canadian Census of Agriculture product, Tillage and Seeding practices, 2011 and 2016 (Statistics Canada, 2017 ). Specifically, the proportions of crop area with the majority of residue tilled, the majority left on the surface, and not tilled at all were summarized to the county level. It was assumed that these three tillage levels were uniformly distributed within each county, and summarized to each watershed with area-weighted overlays. We used the estimates of fertilizer and manure application rate data from Reid and Schneider (2019) . Briefly, Reid and Schneider (2019)  used manure production coefficients and Census of Agriculture estimates of animal populations to estimate the amount of P generated by the animals raised in each county. It was assumed that all the manure generated in each county was applied to farmland uniformly in that county. Reid and Schneider (2019)  then disaggregated the Ontario fertilizer sales statistics by assuming application to each county based on crop needs while accounting for the manure applied and the soil test P levels as estimated from the running P mass balance that began in 1960. Reid and Schneider (2019)  also pro-rated the application rates of fertilizer P to ensure that the sums of P fertilizer applied did equal the actual sales. We then allocated the total fertilizer P to each crop type uniformly in each county. We also did the same with the manure P. We assumed that pasture received no phosphorus inputs.  2.4 Water quality and streamflow data Two distinct water quality datasets were used in this study: one derived from PWQMN data (MECP, 2021) and one derived from MWNS data (Ross, et al., 2022; Ross et al., 2022; Nelligan et al., 2021; Rosamond et al., 2018 ). PWQMN has been in operation since 1964, and 400 sites are currently monitored across Ontario for various water quality constituents on an approximately monthly basis during the ice-free season (8–10 times per year per site). Sampling for the PWQMN is conducted by local conservation authorities, who decide when sampling at individual monitoring stations will be conducted. We selected a subset of PWQMN monitoring sites based on the following criteria: (i) the availability of total phosphorus (TP) and soluble reactive phosphorus (SP; note we use SP to denote soluble reactive phosphorus for consistency with HYPE documentation; SMHI, 2022 ) data for the years 2005–2018; (ii) the availability of daily discharge data at or very near each water quality monitoring station for the same time period (the greatest distance to a flow monitoring station was 975 m, but 30 of the 32 chosen sites were within 100 m of flow monitoring stations); and (iii) the available TP and SP observations covered up to at least the 80th percentile of discharge at the corresponding gauging location. These selection criteria resulted in a dataset of 32 PWQMN sites. Daily stream discharge data for the selected PWQMN sites were obtained from the Water Survey of Canada (WSC) National Water Data Archive (WSC, 2022 ). The MWNS was led by the Ontario MECP, in part to better understand relationships between nutrient export, landscape, and agricultural land use/land management in southern Ontario’s Great Lakes basin (Rosamond et al., 2018 ). To that end, 11 watersheds in the Lake Huron, Erie, and Ontario basin were intensively monitored beginning in 2015 and ending in 2020, including relatively frequent sampling for a wide range of water quality constituents. Sampling for water quality analysis was conducted periodically during baseflow conditions and with increased frequency (∼4–8 h) during high flow, snow melt, and storm events using an autosampler, resulting in good sampling coverage of the variable flow conditions at each site (Biagi et al., 2022; Nelligan et al., 2021 ). These samples were analyzed for a variety of analytes, including concentrations of TP. While MWNS samples were analyzed for total dissolved P concentration as well, only TP was used for MWNS sites as HYPE simulates SP rather than total dissolved P (SMHI, 2022 ). Daily flow weighted mean TP concentrations were calculated from the MWNS data, resulting in a dataset with an average of ∼ 5 daily TP concentration records per month. For MWNS sites, we calculated daily streamflow from 15-min WSC discharge data from each MWNS watershed. We quantified the differences between various aspects of the watersheds in each dataset and their averages for each dataset. We conducted Mann-Whitney U tests on the median streamflows and concentrations at the MWNS sites, in comparison with the PWQMN sites. We found that the MWNS sites had a significantly lower discharge median and a significantly higher concentration median (p < 0.05). We also note that the median watershed size, number of observations, proportion of months with TP measured, and median discharge were all significantly different between the two datasets (p < 0.05). We present boxplots of these differences as Fig. SI2 . We also present a table summarizing the differences between the two datasets as Table 2  . We provide a detailed list of all water quality sites used in Tables S1 and S2 .  2.5 Calibration and validation To compare the influence of calibration dataset characteristics like frequency and corresponding flow conditions on model performance, we performed two rounds of calibration and validation, detailed in Table 3  . For the first round (denoted calval1), calibration data were daily average discharge and TP and SP loads for the PWQMN sub-watersheds and validation data were daily average discharge and TP load for the MWNS sub-watersheds. TP and SP loads were calculated internally by HYPE from the concentration and discharge input data (see Section 2.4 ) The spin-up period (period where the model is run to equilibrate and initialize pools e.g. lake volumes; SMHI, 2022 ) for calval1 was 2005–2010, the calibration period was 2011–2018, and the validation period was 2016–2018. For the second calibration and validation (denoted calval2), calibration data was daily average discharge and TP load for MWNS sub-watersheds and validation data was daily average discharge and TP and SP load for PWQMN sub-watersheds. Both rounds were independent of one another. The spin-up period for calval2 was 2010–2015, the calibration period was 2016–2018, and the validation period was 2011–2018. The validation conduct in this way is a spatial validation, meaning that different locations were used for calibration and validation (e.g. Mai et al., 2022 ). This is a fairly stringent form of validation. The same data were never used for calibration and validation. Calibration involved global calibration, meaning that parameters were the same everywhere. HYPE and other similar models are often calibrated using a step-wise approach, but we chose to use a simultaneous multi-objective approach as there is evidence that calibrating parameters relating to hydrology and water quality together is not only more efficient, but more appropriate as hydrology and water quality are related (Yin et al., 2016 ). Both rounds of calibrations were performed automatically using Differential Evolution Markov Chain (DEMC) with 250 generations and 50 populations (Ter Braak, 2006 ). DEMC is a simplified Markov chain Monte Carlo method in which new parameters are proposed and then either accepted or rejected. In addition to inheriting traits from other members, the new generated parameters have a random number added to them. The advantage of DEMC is that it can quickly converge on an optimum parameter value while also giving a probability based uncertainty estimate of the optimum (Ter Braak, 2006 ). The number of populations was chosen to be close to the number of parameters, while the number of generations was chosen based on computational cost. A multivariate objective function was used for calibration, comprising of the Nash Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE; 90 % weight) and percent bias (PBIAS; 10 % weight). We gave equal weight to each station and equal weight to discharge, TP, and SP concentrations. Specifically, the objective function was:Obj = 0.9*NSE_Q + 0.1*PBIAS_Q + 0.9*NSE_TP + 0.1*PBIAS_TP + 0.9*NSE_SP + 0.1*PBIAS_SP,   where the NSE and PBIAS were the average values for all stations. Thus both temporal and spatial variability is represented in the objective function. The convergence of each calibration was confirmed through visual inspection of plots showing the relationship between the objective function and the simulation number (Fig. S3 ). Of the hundreds of adjustable parameters in HYPE, we chose to calibrate parameters related to processes that were identified as sensitive in previous work (Jiang et al., 2020; Stadnyk et al., 2020; Yin et al., 2016 ) and HYPE’s correction parameters that are specifically designed to be calibrated (SMHI, 2022 ). Correction parameters (or super-parameters) can either simultaneously adjust several processes at once or correct input data. The list of calibration parameters used is included in Table 4  . To aid the reader in understanding how to interpret correction parameters, we offer this explanation using the phoscorr parameter as an example. The function of the phoscorr parameter is to adjust all of the initial P levels in the soil (the PartP0, HumusP0, FastP0) as well as the erodibility of each soil. The adjusted values of all of these parameters is AdjustedPar = InputPar*(1 + phoscorr). This approach of adjusting input parameter values en masse rather than individually calibrating all of them is common in hydrological modelling (e.g. Jiang et al., 2020 ). The remaining non-calibration parameter values were derived from previous applications of the HYPE model in different domains (Donnelly et al., 2016; Pers et al., 2016 ). After calibration was complete, we simulated the annual downstream TP loads for each major drainage basin (Lake Erie, Lake Ontario, Lake Huron, Georgian Bay, Ottawa River, St Lawrence River) for HYPE calibrated with PWQMN and MWNS. We also assessed similarities between calibration and validation phases by computing the correlation (Spearman's rank correlation coefficient) matrices between performance metrics (NSE and PBIAS) for PWQMN and MWNS watersheds when used in calibration or validation.  2.6 Exploring explanatory factors for model performance To investigate potential reasons for differences in model performance between PWQMN and MWNS sites, we calculated the Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient (ρ ) and its significance between site NSE and characteristics of the site’s contributing sub-basin. The investigated characteristics were the number of observations, HYPE sub-basin size, mean annual temperature, and number of frost days. In addition, we used the Mann-Whitney U  test to determine if there was a difference in the population of NSE values for sites with and without dams in their sub-basin. These factors were chosen because of either their documented effect on hydrology and/or P transport (Donnelly et al., 2016; Kao et al., 2022; Maavara et al., 2015 ), potential effect on error metrics (Clark et al., 2021 ), or strength of effect on parameters in regionalization approach (Hundecha et al., 2016 ).   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Comparison of calibration and validation with PWQMN and MWNS data Results show that there is not a large difference in HYPE model performance when calibrated with data from the PWQMN or the higher-frequency MWNS data. Both the regionally aggregated and median model performance as measured by NSE and PBIAS were similar for the different calibration and validation stages (Table 5  ). We tested the median NSE and PBIAS between the calibration and validation of the same sites in calval 1 and calval2 using a Mann-Whitney U  test (e.g. between MWNS sites in calval1 and calval2). We found no significant differences in the NSE (p > 0.05) for any sites or constituents but did find significant differences between the PBIAS for both the PWQMN sites and the MWNS sites between calval1 and calval2. For the PWQMN sites, this difference was fairly trivial (median PBIAS of 15.8 vs −18.1). For the MWNS sites, the difference was not trivial, with the MWNS sites having a more negative bias during the calibration. The reason for this difference is not obvious. The regionally aggregated NSE value for TP at PWMQN sites was 0.15 whether HYPE was calibrated on MWNS or PWQMN data. For MWNS sites, when HYPE was calibrated with MWNS data, model performance at these headwater sites was slightly improved compared to when HYPE was calibrated with PWQMN data. For instance, the median NSE for TP at MWNS sites was 0.36 when calibrated with PWQMN and 0.49 when calibrated with MWNS. Therefore, there was a slight loss of skill in predicting TP when HYPE was calibrated on PWQMN vs. MWNS data, but this loss was small. When comparing our results to other application of HYPE, our fits are somewhat lower, though not dramatically so. Donnelly et al. (2016)  show that across Europe, more than a third of stations had NSE values for daily flow less than 0, with a median NSE of just under 0.4. Mai et al. (2022)  report a median NSE for daily flow in the Great Lakes region of 0.41. While our flow fits are lower than these, our TP fits are comparable, suggesting that the flow may be a limiting factor in our TP calibration. Another indication there was little difference in HYPE model performance when calibrated with PWQMN data or MWNS data is the positive and mostly strong correlations between performance metrics for sites used in calibration or validation for individual constituents (Tables S3–S6 ). For PWQMN, the Spearman ρ  values between calibration and validation NSE were 0.84, 0.99, and 0.99 for flow, TP, and SP, while ρ  values for PBIAS were 1.0, 0.99, and 0.98 again for flow, TP, and SP. Correlations for MWNS sites were lower but still positive, with ρ  value between calibration and validation NSE of 0.44 and 0.30 for flow and TP and ρ  values of 0.98 and 0.96 for PBIAS.  These high correlation metrics show that the sites well calibrated in calval1 were the same sites well calibrated in calval2. There was a wide range of NSE and PBIAS values for both calval1 and calval2 (Figs. 2, 3   ); some sites had good agreement between observed and simulated values, while others had poor agreement between observed and simulated values. However, the spread of NSE and PBIAS values for the different constituents and calibration and validation phases did tend to be wider for the PWQMN sub-watersheds, in particular for SP (Fig. 4  ). Furthermore, visual inspection of the observed and simulated time series (Figs. S3–S12 ) showed variations in the quality of temporal pattern replication; in particular, HYPE appears to have difficulty replicating very high TP load observations at PWQMN sites (Fig. S4, S11 ). Notably though, when calibrated with higher quality MWNS data, replication of very high TP load observations at PWQMN sites does not improve. An explanation of the relatively modest fit statistics is in order. While section 3.2  explores why the model fits better in some areas than in others, and indeed some excellent fits were achieved at some sites, overall the fit was modest to poor. A number of factors likely explain this, and they are related to the data used to drive and parameterize the models. Mai et al. (2022) , in a model intercomparison project focusing on flow in the Great Lakes, highlight that models with global parameters values tended to do poorer than those with local parameter values. Our global approach to model parameterization may handicap the model somewhat. Further, it is also possible that the weather reanalysis product we used was not ideal for all sites. Future work could compare a number of weather products to evaluate comparative performance, similarly to what was done by Daggupati et al. (2018) , who found that the choice of weather data did make a difference in model performance. While they did not test the re-analysis product used in this model, they found that the climate forecast system reanalysis product they did test fared poorly compared to interpolated measurements. It is possible that the weather data we use were not optimal for our sites. Finally, many sites are regulated by reservoirs, which are notoriously difficult to include in a watershed model (Tefs et al., 2021 ). However, our results in Section 3.2  did show that performance was not worse in regulated vs unregulated catchments. The PWQMN and MWNS water quality datasets are different in several ways including sampling frequency and strategy. Considered in the context of sampling frequency and strategy alone, it is surprising that HYPE model performance was similar when calibrated with these two datasets because: (i) P loss tends to be driven by extreme events (Ross et al., 2022 ), which are less likely to be captured in low frequency sampling regimes like PWQMN (Long et al., 2015; Piniewski et al., 2019 ), although we did select PWMQN sites with water quality sampling that covered at least the 80th percentile of discharge; and (ii) statistical models for TP constructed with PWQMN data have been found to be less accurate than statistical models constructed with event-based data (Long et al., 2015 ). In particular, PWQMN data have been found to be lacking in event samples, which tend to have the highest concentrations of TP (Long et al., 2015 ). Previous work comparing high and low frequency sampled TP datasets for model calibration has found There are a number of potential reasons for the similarity in model performance despite differences in dataset sampling frequency and strategy, which we discuss below. These include the importance of error sources other than calibration error, the sensitivity of chosen calibration parameters, the built-in information in process-based models, and other differences in the PWQMN and MWNS datasets. First, one potential reason why model performance was similar when HYPE was calibrated with PWQMN and MWNS is that other sources of error are larger than error associated with calibration. Jiang et al. (2019)  compared HYPE model performance and prediction accuracy when calibrated with daily vs. fortnightly nitrate data. While they found that HYPE better reproduced observations when calibrated with daily vs. fortnightly nitrate data, they also found only modest improvements in prediction uncertainty when high frequency calibration data was used. Jiang et al. (2019)  suggest that increasing sampling frequency may not always improve model performance or uncertainty. The authors note that model structural error, measurement error, and input data error dominate the uncertainty of HYPE predictions. And, because calibration will not affect these sources of error, improving calibration data will not necessarily affect model performance. Examples of model structural error include how HYPE represents certain processes. Previous work comparing high and low frequency TP data had found that high frequency data actually led to poorer model results (Lannergård et al., 2024 ). However, that study also used proxies to infer the high frequency TP data, and the strength of the proxies was a factor the authors highlighted as an important reason for poorer performance. This study did not use proxies but had a very high frequency sampling protocol. In the present study, several assumptions and generalizations were necessarily made about model setup data such as fertilizer and manure inputs. It is possible that improvements to these input data would improve HYPE predictions more so than improvements to calibration data. Second, another potential explanation for the similarity in model performance is that the chosen calibration parameters were not sensitive. For most of the parameters calibrated in this study, there is no obvious optimum value during calibration (Figs. S13–S20 ), which could indeed indicate that parameters are not sensitive. To more fully explore this hypothesis, a much more in depth calibration exercise would be necessary that includes more parameters than is typical in watershed model calibration. For reference, we had a total of 117 parameters, when accounting for the land use and soil dependencies. It is also possible that the parameter bounds were set to a region of the parameter space that constrained the model solution, and that a much wider exploration of the parameter space would reveal that there were some differences when calibrating to the two datasets, though we emphasize our parameter bounds were similar to past studies (e.g. Yin et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2020 ). We again suggest a more computationally expensive calibration exercise to address this question. A third reason for model performance similarity is that process-based models contain much more internal information via process representation than statistical models. Therefore, process-based model such as HYPE may be able to overcome the data limitations of lower frequency datasets because of the rigid nature of process-based models. And, process-based models may have an advantage over statistical models for low frequency water quality sampling regimes. While nitrate behavior differs from phosphorus, Woodward et al. (2017)  found that nitrate observations were well reproduced by the StreamGEM model when calibrated with both daily and monthly nitrate concentrations. They suggest that because process-based models are highly effective at modelling catchment processes, monthly nitrate data contains sufficient information to calibrate these models. A fourth possibility exists. The MWNS sites were carefully chosen to represent the full spectrum of variability of the PWQMN sites, as detailed in Rosmond et al. (2018). This spectrum of variability included both structural and functional characteristics. Structural characteristics included land cover, soil particle size, and slope (structural), while functional characteristics included runoff generation and phosphorus mass balance estimates. It is possible that the MWNS sites serve as an effective proxy for the PWQMN sites because they have been successfully chosen for this purpose. The results in Table 2  corroborate this hypothesis. The coefficient of variation (CV) of the median TP concentrations in space was quite similar between the PWQMN and the MWNS sites, indicating a similar ‘spread’ around their respective median concentrations. We also note that the CV of total phosphorus concentrations at each site was not that different on average between the PWQMN and MWNS sites, indicating the data had a similar spread even if the means were different from one another. This may be due to the careful subsetting of the PWQMN sites to select those with 12 month sampling and sampling up to the 80th percentile of flows. We emphasize that other cases where the event sampling sites or ambient monitoring sites are chosen more opportunistically may not have the same results. Several studies have assessed the effect of calibration data temporal resolution on water quality model performance. The water quality sampling frequency needs for calibration have been found to vary with nutrient studied, the model employed, and it is likely that other site-specific dynamics come into play. In contrast to our results, some studies have found that using higher frequency water quality data leads to improved model performance. For example, Piniewski et al. (2019)  found that increasing sampling frequency from 12 to 26 samples per year led to a marked improvement in model performance for total suspended solids and TP loading in the Soil & Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) model. Interestingly though, Piniewski et al. (2019)  also found that evidence for the effect of flow-proportional vs. regular sampling on model performance was weak. Jackson-Blake and Starrfelt (2015)  also found that using daily rather than fortnightly data resulted in a reduced risk of obtaining unrealistic results for the INtegrated CAtchment model of Phosphorus dynamics (INCA-P) model, although they did find that peaks in total dissolved P concentration were as well simulated using fortnightly data. Notably, both Piniewski et al. (2019)  and Jackson-Blake and Starrfelt (2015)  used far fewer sites in their analyses (four each) than used in our analyses. On the other hand, in agreement with our results, there are also several studies that show little difference in model performance for models calibrated using data from water quality monitoring data at typically low and high frequency. For example, while nitrate export behavior differs from phosphorus, Woodward et al. (2017)  found that flow and nitrate observations were well reproduced by the StreamGEM model when calibrated with both daily and monthly nitrate concentrations.  3.2 Exploring reasons for performance differences within model domains We explored the possibility of relationships between site model performance as measured by NSE and various explanatory factors: number of observations, watershed size, mean annual temperature, number of frost days, and presence of dams (Table 6  ). There did not appear to be a strong effect of number of observations, watershed size, or dams on model performance, despite the influence of these factors on performance metrics, P transport and/or hydrology (Clark et al., 2021; Donnelly et al., 2016; Kao et al., 2022; Van Cappellen and Maavara, 2016 ). For the number of observations, a significant correlation (Spearman's rank correlation coefficient) was only found between NSE and number of observations for flow during the MWNS validation in calval1, where number of observations was negatively correlated with model performance. For watershed size, no significant correlations were found. For the presence of dams, Mann-Whitney U  test indicated no significant difference in NSE values for watersheds with and without dams. On the other hand, temperatures do appear to have an effect of model performance. For mean annual temperature and frost days, there were significant correlations with NSE for flow and SP in PWQMN calibration and validation. The correlation was positive between NSE and MAT and negative between NSE and number of frost days, indicating that performance is lower for colder sub-watersheds. This could be because of poor representation of freezing and frost processes in the HYPE model; many catchment-scale water quality models, including HYPE, do not adequately represent cold-region processes such as the effects of freeze–thaw cycles on nutrient release (Costa et al., 2020 ). We do however stress the minor nature of the north–south temperature gradient in our study area, and that cooler, northern areas in our study area also correspond to more forested conditions. In contrast, in a European implementation of HYPE for flow that focused on developing a regionalization approach, model performance was linked to soil, upstream area, and elevation (Hundecha et al., 2016 ). Donnelley et al. (2016)  did not show a poor HYPE model fit across colder areas in Europe. The correlation between temperature and model performance in our study area may well be due to confounding factors as well as model structural inadequacies.  3.3 Annual load simulations The total downstream mean annual TP loads for each major drainage basin simulated for different calibration datasets are shown in Fig. 5  . For each major basin, the TP load simulated by PWQMN-calibrated HYPE is slightly larger than TP load simulated by MWNS-calibrated HYPE. However, these differences were relatively small; the percent difference in TP load predictions for the different major basins were between 7 and 26 %. Notably, for the Lake Erie basin, when calibrated with PWQMN data, HYPE predicted an annual average TP contribution of 936 tonnes (544 to 1648 tonnes per year). Whereas when calibrated with MWNS data, HYPE predicted an annual average TP contribution of 816 tonnes (446 to 1566 tonnes per year), which is only 13 % lower.
