Other estimates of annual mean TP loads for Lake Erie tend to be higher than either of our simulated annual mean values, but, when given, are not outside the range of estimated loads for individual years (Table S7 ). Notably, it is difficult to directly compare estimates for other Great Lakes basins as the entire drainage areas are not included in our study area, whereas for Lake Erie our study area includes the entire Canadian side of the Lake Erie catchment. For example, Robertson et al. (2019)  estimated a much higher annual average watershed load to Lake Erie from the Canadian side of 1710 tonnes using the SPAtially Referenced Regression On Watershed attributes (SPARROW) model. Similarly, Maccoux et al. (2016)  estimated that for 2003–2013, the annual average TP load to Lake Erie from Canadian rivers was 1358 tonnes. However, during that time period, the annual TP load ranged from 507 to 2653 tonnes, so our TP load values do fit within the envelope of these estimates for individual years. Likewise, using similar methods to Maccoux et al. (2016), Environment and Climate Change Canada (2021)  (Environment and Climate Change Canada, 2021 ) estimated a wide range of annual TP loads (559 to 2320 tonnes) for 2008 to 2020, and while their annual average estimate (1486 tonnes) is higher than both of our estimates, our values are close to the lower estimates of the annual TP load.  3.4 Future work An important finding of the current study is that the HYPE model performance was similar when calibrated with data from either PWQMN (baseflow biased samples) or MWNS (event flow samples supplemented with baseflow), despite significant difference in data set characteristics. The two data sets differ based on temporal and spatial characteristics. These temporal characteristics include the sample temporal resolution, the total number of samples over the monitoring period, the data set duration, and the flow conditions for which chemistry samples are available. In terms of spatial differences, PWQMN watersheds are highly variable in terms of land use and total drainage area, while the MWNS watersheds are all relatively small headwater agricultural watersheds, albeit carefully selected to cover a range of physiography (Rosamond et al., 2018 ). Our results suggest that the significant amount of modelling work that has been done in Southern Ontario, much of it to inform the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement and assess nutrient loads to the Great Lakes (e.g. Mohamed et al., 2019; Robertson et al., 2019; Dagnew et al., 2019 ), is actually well supported by the existing regional data, should the models use PWQMN sites that fulfill the same criteria we used here. We do emphasize that the result that ambient sampling is sufficient to constrain a process based model may be specific to the conditions in the study region. Specifically, the MWNS sites were not opportunistically chosen but were carefully chosen to mirror the characteristics of the PWQMN sites (Rosamond et al., 2018 ). Further, it is possible that at the scale of individual catchments there is simply not enough information in an ambient sampling dataset to constrain a model, whereas with 32 ambient sites there is significantly more information. Further, we carefully chose the ambient monitoring sites to sample up to a fairly high flow threshold (80th percentile). If ambient monitoring sites are not chosen so carefully this same result may not hold. Finally, in regions with fairly different mechanisms of TP transport, especially where TP transport is much more episodic, it is possible that ambient sampling is totally unable to constrain mechanistic models. Therefore more work in other regions with both ambient and event sampling networks is needed to confirm this result. A small number of studies have assessed the influence of data characteristics on estimates of nutrient loads from different watersheds, with most attention afforded to sampling frequency (Johnes, 2007; Williams et al., 2015 , see also references in Section 3.1 ). Such exercises have been performed for rating curve and interpolation models (Johnes, 2007; Williams et al., 2015 ), but less commonly for process-based models like HYPE. Isolating the influence of factors such as sampling frequency on modeled results is challenging, given the necessary computational requirements and our current data set limitations (e.g., overall duration). However, doing so would help lead to guidelines that could be used globally for calibrating process based models such as HYPE, SWAT, INCA, and others that have been applied globally to support critical environmental policy and management (Wellen et al., 2015 ), yet the event sampling typically needed to empirically calculate loads is not particularly common. We provide several suggestions for future work related to the interaction between spatiotemporal features of calibration data sets and other aspects of model application. These suggestions will be directly pertinent to other modeling exercises using PWQMN and MWNS data in Ontario, and other efforts using process based water quality models around the world. It would be beneficial for future work to assess the influence of calibration data set temporal characteristics in a more systematic way to isolate the effects of 1) temporal resolution, 2) corresponding sample flow conditions, and 3) temporal aggregation to the daily time step. Regarding temporal resolution, a higher-frequency (i.e., daily) calibration data set could be used and subsequent calibration attempts could be made with uniformly thinned calibration data. This could be insightful for understanding system variability and as a cost-benefit analysis where cost is related to sample acquisition and the benefit is model skill. In contrast, a calibration data set like the MWNS could be scrutinized to determine the corresponding flow conditions of each water chemistry sample. Based on the site-specific flow exceedance probability curves, samples could be removed or aggregated from the calibration set to emphasize specific segments of the exceedance curve or to ensure equal representation across flow conditions. In this way, the effects of potentially superfluous samples on predictions could be assessed. If model predictions are relatively stationary regardless of thinning, then such an approach could be used to mitigate future monitoring costs and to implement more parsimonious calibration procedures. Finally, it would be informative to assess the influence of sample concentration aggregation on HYPE predictions. For example, since programs like the MWNS focus on event hydrologic responses, there are days in the data set with multiple discrete water quality samples. In this study, we calculated a flow weighted average of such samples to obtain a mean daily concentration (as required by HYPE) and as a result, it remains unclear how predictions might differ if a single random sample was selected for each day or if some other averaging approach was taken. By averaging multiple samples to the daily time step, we have ignored sub-daily variability in concentration – information that is characteristic of the MWNS data set. These types of exercises would be highly informative and would help clarify the type of monitoring programs that are needed for different goals (e.g., understanding sub-daily concentration dynamics versus annual solute loading). Outcomes of such exercises are likely to be affected by local context and the degree of temporal variability within the modeled system. Regardless of these factors, performing these tests would be highly informative for future model implementations and at the very least could provide insights for the development of new calibration data sets. We also have suggestions for future work related to calibration data set spatial components. We note that in the literature we presented in Section 3.1 , few studies examined the effect on station location and numbers of stations on water quality models. The headwater agricultural MWNS watersheds were explicitly selected for regional representativeness using a data-driven, statistical approach (Rosamond et al., 2018 ). It is unclear if using data from a subset of the MWNS watersheds would influence the calibrated results, or if specific individual MWNS watersheds exerted disparate leverage on the regional-scale predictions. These hypotheses could be assessed by comparing our results with implementations calibrated using sparser MWNS data (i.e. fewer sites). Since PWQMN watersheds cover a different set of physiographic features than the MWNS watersheds, it would also be informative to assess predictions using a random subset of PWQMN watersheds. It is possible that since more PWQMN sites were used than MWNS sites in this study, that broader spatial representation in the PWQMN calibration data compensated for the relatively lower temporal resolution. Finally, it is possible that other factors such as the modelling package or the selection of the calibration parameters interact with the calibration dataset used in important ways. It is possible that other modelling packages (e.g. INCA, SWAT) are more sensitive to the calibration datasets used. It is also possible that different sets of parameters or parameter ranges would have resulted in a greater sensitivity to datasets. We suggest that a model intercomparison project amongst watershed water quality models to ascertain the interacting influences of datasets, parameters, and algorithms would be of great interest (e.g. Mai et al., 2022 ). Notably, these suggestions for different calibration exercises are not exhaustive, and demonstrate the wide range of data manipulations that could be performed to advance process-based model calibration.   4 Conclusion Our results indicate that low frequency sampling (e.g. roughly monthly) water quality data may be adequate to calibrate the HYPE model for phosphorus species in Southern Ontario, should the low frequency monitoring sites be carefully chosen to include winter sampling and relatively high flows (up to the 80th percentile). Two datasets with different sampling strategies were used to calibrate the HYPE model: one with approximately monthly (ice-free) frequency and one with more frequent (year-round) sampling where the strategy was to sample periodically during baseflow and every ∼ 4–8 h during flow. We found that first, median and regionally-aggregated performance metrics were similar for the different datasets. Second, performance metrics were positively and mostly strongly correlated between calibration and validation phases. And third, annual mean simulated loads for different major drainage basins in the study region are similar; importantly estimates for Lake Erie have only 13 % difference between modelling scenarios. In addition, model performance for each constituent across calibration and validation varied widely by site but were spatially similar between the two approaches. We found evidence that this range in performance could be due to poor representation of freezing processes in the HYPE model as sites with higher MAT and fewer freezing days had better model performance. The fact that model performance and simulated TP loads are similar for both high and low frequency calibration datasets is an important result for future modelling efforts in Southern Ontario as well as other regions. Efforts are underway to reduce P loading to the Great Lakes to mitigate eutrophication, particularly for Lake Erie; using watershed water quality models to test the effects of different management scenarios on P loading is an important part of that effort. Our results indicate that the lower frequency water quality datasets available throughout the province of Ontario and indeed much of the American Great Lakes basin (e.g., Dagnew et al., 2019 ) can play a role in those modelling efforts as they are sufficient to calibrate the HYPE model should the sites be chosen according to the criteria described herein. In addition to southern Ontario, many other regions lack high frequency water quality datasets. Our results also point to the feasibility of using lower frequency water quality data to constrain water quality models in other regions as well.
1 Introduction Concerns about the increasing frequency of flooding events in urban areas have led to examination of their causes. A primary reason is recognized as the intensification of heavy precipitation events as the planet warms, and this intensification spans from sub-daily to seasonal time scales, demonstrated through improved physical understanding, extensive modeling, and increasing observational corroboration (Douville et al., 2021 ). On a global scale, the increase in heavy precipitation corresponds to a rate of nearly 7 % per degree Celsius of warming in the near-surface atmosphere, subject to regional variations and influences of complex dynamic factors (Formayer & Fritz, 2017;Zhang et al., 2019 ). Considering these findings, to ensure that the urban drainage system continues to provide effective flood protection for both the site and downstream areas, infrastructure should be resilient and adaptable, and/or have sufficient capacity to cope with the increased rainfall due to climate change (Ballard et al., 2015; Berg et al., 2019 ). As awareness of the hydrological and environmental impacts of catchment urbanization has grown, the focus of urban drainage design has shifted towards nature-based solutions, which mimic the pre-development hydrological processes like infiltration and evapotranspiration (Dietz, 2007). Grass swales are one of these solutions; they convey and reduce stormwater runoff flows and thereby reduce flood risk (Davis et al., 2012 ), and can also provide improved water quality benefits (Gavrić et al., 2019 ). Moreover, grass swales are widely recognized as cost-effective stormwater management solutions (Rujner, et al., 2018 ). Although their sizing is usually constrained by site-specific factors, including topography and available space (Yu et al., 2001 ), their long-term function depends on maintaining sufficient saturated hydraulic conductivity (ksat ) values (Yang et al., 2024 ). Presently, urban drainage and stormwater management solutions, including grass swales, are designed not only to manage urban flooding during rainfall events, but also to achieve many additional objectives (Sage et al., 2015 ). For instance, the design of grass swales may aim to fully retain the runoff from the 90th percentile storm (Ekka et al., 2021 ), or provide temporary runoff storage and gradual release of water to avoid increases in downstream flood risks (e.g., limiting outlet flows to 1 to 2 L/s/ha) (Kellagher, 2002 ). Current guidelines acknowledge the multifunctional role of grass swales, integrating various design criteria, such as ensuring adequate storage capacity for a specified return period, the safe conveyance of extreme flows, and resilience even during successive rainfall events by achieving half-empty status within 24 h (Ballard et al., 2015 ). The spatial and temporal changes in precipitation patterns necessitate adaptive design modifications of stormwater control measures to effectively manage shifting runoff regimes (Rosenberger et al., 2021 ). Several modified swale designs have been proposed to increase runoff volume reduction, including infiltration swales with check dams, wetland swales, and grass swales with underlying perforated pipes (Abida & Sabourin, 2006;Hunt et al., 2015;Eliea et al., 2008 ). The use of check dams is often proposed in stormwater design manuals, aimed at controlling flow velocity, increasing hydraulic retention times, and encouraging enhanced infiltration (NCDEQ, 2017 ). Winston et al (2019)  compared the hydrologic performance of grass swales before and after retrofitting with two rockfill check dams, resulting in an increment in swale retention capacity from 22 % to 53 %, respectively, for small and moderate events. Furthermore, the introduction of check dams resulted in a 40 % increase in the wetted area, providing additional surface storage of 14 m3 . However, this retrofit also had unexpected negative consequences, arising from “blinding” of rockfill check dams by runoff solids, with the first check dam losing permeability within the first six months of operation. For mitigating these consequences, the authors suggested “quarterly” maintenance (Winston et al., 2019 ). Davis et al. (2012)  found that the inclusion of check dams improved grass swales hydrological performance, in terms of total volume reduction and flow attenuation, with a negligible effect for large rainfall events (greater than 37 mm). However, this study did not directly compare the differences with and without check dams in order to isolate the influence of this type of retrofits. Similarly, Yu et al, (2001)  found that the inclusion of check dams in a grass swale increased hydraulic retention times and temporarily decreased flow velocities leading to improvements in pollutant removal. Moreover, there has not been a study regarding design variations, and its effect on swale hydrological functionalities (Powell & Hunt, 2015 ). Retrofitting grass swales with check dams has shown some limitations, primarily due to clogging and intensive maintenance requirements. These issues have resulted in an impermeable surface caused by sediment trapped between stone barriers, loss of vegetation, and prolonged inundation upstream of the check dams, limiting the grass swale's storage capacity for subsequent events (Winston et al., 2019 ). Clogged check dams negatively impact the vegetation health in the swale, consequently undermining the swale's ability for sedimentation and filtration, and potentially creating a sediment source (Winston et al., 2012 ). Additionally, there has not been an in-depth study including the presence of systematic uncertainties during measurements, and how these uncertainties can influence the estimation of the hydrological effect of the implementation of swale retrofits. Other effects of check dams in swales would be increased sedimentation in the space between the check dams, increased overall hydraulic roughness of the swale, and potential for mosquito breeding in shallow water between the dams. To enhance the resilience of stormwater control measures, the focus should be on versatile and practical modifications that can adapt to a broad range of potential climatic conditions, even those that deviate from historically observed conditions (Tirpak et al., 2021 ). To reduce the likelihood of flooding caused by urban development and climate change, grass swale design should focus on three primary objectives: 1) controlling the runoff volume and peak outflow discharged from the site, 2) gradually releasing outflows at suitable gradients, and 3) providing flexibility and adaptability to cope with conditions that deviate from their initial design (Ballard et al., 2015 ). The integration of dynamic storage capacity into swale design allows for a continuous flow of water through the system, thus creating space for subsequent events to be stored, rather than merely increasing water ponding caused by the complete obstruction of surface runoff. This approach might increase the effective grass swale surface area, promoting infiltration across various larger swale sections and at greater depths. The general objective of this study is to investigate whether swale outflow controls can improve the functionality of existing swales in terms of conveyed runoff volume reduction and peak flow attenuation for various targeted inflow rates. This study aims to provide scientific evidence of how a swale outlet control weir (SOCW) enhances detention storage and infiltration in existing drainage swales, thereby potentially reducing hydraulic loads on downstream urban drainage systems.  2 Methods 2.1 Site description A 30-meter section of a grass roadside swale, located in the City of Luleå, in Northern Sweden, was selected as the study site (65°34′42.92″N, 22°15′16.89″E). The swale was designed to manage drainage flows from an asphalt bus lane and specifically constructed to receive lateral runoff originating on the roadway. The swale has a triangular-trapezoidal cross-section, with the bottom width varying from 0.2 to 0.7 m, relatively steep side slopes (1:2 to 1:2.5), and a depth of 1.4 m (refer to Fig. 1  ). The top 50 cm of native soil is predominantly loamy sand, consisting of clay (0.3–3.1 %), silt (6.6–32.4 %), and sand (60.8–93.1 %) fractions (Rujner et al., 2018 ). The infiltration capacity of the swale was previously evaluated through a series of point infiltration measurements (in triplicates) using the Modified Philip-Dunne (MDP) infiltrometer (Ahmed et al., 2014 ). The measured hydraulic conductivity (ksat ) values ranged from 22 to 1382 mm/hr, with a geometric mean of 81 mm/hr. The highest ksat  values were observed on the swale's right shoulder, while the lowest were recorded on the swale bottom. This variation could be attributed to the deposition of sediments on the swale bottom, spatial variation in soil properties and the degree of compaction (Mantilla et al., 2023 ).  2.2 Hydrological measurements The swale was outfitted with five water content reflectometers installed every 5 m along the swale bottom to monitor volumetric water content (VWC) and soil temperature (ST). Additionally, a 50-cm soil-profile probe was used to measure VWC, ST, soil permittivity (P) and electrical conductivity (EC) at different depths (5, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 cm) (see Fig. 1 ). The analysis excluded readings from depths of 5 cm and 10 cm, as ponding conditions were detected to cause inconsistencies in the VWC measurements at these levels. A pressure sensor installed on the bottom of the swale was used to measure the water level from which the weir head was calculated. A variable-frequency drive connected to a submergible pump was used to control the pumping rate, and an in-line electromagnetic flowmeter was installed in the system to measure the inflow rates for different irrigation scenarios. The pump was submerged within a storage container of 7 m3 , and the swale outflow was continuously recirculated throughout the experiments. Readings were logged at a 60-second interval (Table 1  ). A V-notch weir was installed at the downstream end of the swale (with either a 30° or 120° angle), and water levels in the swale were continuously measured with a pressure transducer sensor. Outflow rates were calculated according to the Kindsvater-Carter formula (Kindsvater & Carter, 1957 ) (Eq. (1) ):(1) Q = ( C  d  · 8 15  · t a n  ( θ / 2 )   ( 2 g )  0.5   · H  2.5   ) ∗ 1000      where Q  is the flow rate (L/s), Cd   a non-dimensional discharge coefficient, θ the angle of the V-notch, g  the gravitational acceleration, and H  the head over the weir. Discharge coefficients were applied as taken from (International Standard Organization, 2017 ), with values of 0.585 for the 30° (SOCW scenario) and 0.595 for the 120° (WO scenario). Ground level was lowered downstream of the weir to maintain free flow conditions and prevent backwater effects during irrigation-driven runoff experiments.  2.3 Field irrigation experiments Field irrigation experiments were conducted during the summer and early autumn seasons (between August and October) of 2022. A controlled irrigation system was designed to simulate runoff flows from a roadway adjacent to the grassed swale and from upstream areas (see Fig. 2  ). By using a submersible pump, stored water was continuously supplied through a longitudinal inflow at the upstream end of the swale and along a 20-meter distributed lateral inflow at the road shoulder, which represented approximately 30 % of the total irrigation inflow (or a ratio of 0.3). This ratio was selected based on the proportion of the catchment area that is impermeable. At the lateral inflow, orifices were perforated at 30-centimeter intervals, facilitating irrigation at the right-side slope adjacent to the road. A second submersible pump at the downstream end returned water to the storage container, enabling the recirculation of all outflows during the experiments. Outflow control was achieved using a stainless-steel weir plate with a 30-degree V-notch, while a 120-degree V-notch was employed for the baseline scenario with minimal outflow restriction. Both weir structures were also used to measure outflow rates (refer to Section 2.2 ). The weir plates were securely mounted on a sturdy wooden base to withstand the water pressure exerted on them. The target inflow rates were determined based on a constant rainfall intensity over a 30-minute duration for selected return periods. The adoption of constant intensity represents peak conditions, providing a safety factor for evaluating the influence of swale outflow controls. Water volumes, which were supplied uniformly, corresponded to individual return periods and are presented in Table 2  . The choice of rainfall duration was based on design considerations for drainage systems in Sweden, including historical rainfall time-series (Hernebring et al., 2018 ). The estimation of design storms (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 years) was derived from the cloud-physics theory in the form of a general national equation used to estimate rainfall intensities (refer to Eq. (2) ) (Dahlström, 2010 ):(2) i ( T , t r  )  = 190 T 3  ln ( t r  )  t r  0.98    + 2     where i  denotes the rainfall intensity (L/(s-ha)), T  denotes the return period (months), and t r     is the rainfall duration (30 min for the studied cases). Target inflow rates were then calculated using the rational method (Eq. (3) ):(3) Q = A · φ · i ( T , t r  )  ·  k f      where A  denotes runoff contributing area, φ    the runoff coefficient (dimensionless), and k f     the climate factor. A  was assumed to be 0.055 ha based on the site characteristics (the existing drainage flow patterns routes and topography), and ϕ  was assumed to be 0.8.The factor kf   represents the increase of rainfall intensity due to climate change and was set to 1 for inflow rates representing the current climate and to 1.25 for inflow rates representing future climate conditions, as recommended by Swedish Water (Svenskt Vatten (SV), 2011 ). The adoption of a climate change factor of 1.25 agrees with projected mean daily rainfall increment according to Olsson et al, (2017)  and was done here for the sole purpose of testing SOWC for more intensive rainfalls. The values for the catchment area and runoff coefficients were determined based on the delineation of the adjacent roadway, representing relatively impervious surfaces consisting of concrete or asphalt. Mean inflow values ranged from 2.5 L/s to 8.7 L/s, which correspond to 1- and 50-year return periods, respectively (refer to Table 2 ). Several replicas (n)  were made of six targeted inflow rates (i.e. chosen return periods under current climate without a climate change factor), and two scenarios: 1) SOCW, representing a swale with an outflow control weir, and 2) WO, representing the same swale but without the weir (baseline scenario).To test the swale with outlet control resilience, additional experiments were done for four return periods (from 1- to 10-year) in a future climate characterized by a climate factor of 1.25, for both SOCW and WO scenarios. The analysis excluded scenarios involving 20-year and 50-year rainfall intensities with a 1.25 climate factor, due to limitations in the irrigation system. These limitations include inadequate storage capacity, reduced pump efficiency at high flow rates, and inconsistent performance (specifically in the case of 20-year events). Hence, a total of 43 field irrigation-driven runoff experiments were conducted. The pump's manual operation and limitations in the irrigation system led to unsteady inflow rates, resulting in standard deviations (SD) that ranged from 0.09 L/s to 0.54 L/s for 1- and 50-year return period (refer to Table 2 ). Consequently, mean inflow volumes ranged between 4.4 m3  to 15.7 m3 , for 1- and 50-year return period, respectively. The measured inflow rates for each individual replica and their variations throughout the experiment are detailed in Table S1 a (supplementary material ). To reduce uncertainties caused by naturally varying initial soil moisture (Rujner et al., 2018 ), an attempt was made to control the initial volumetric water content (VWC) at the swale surface. This was achieved by pre-wetting the swale with about 1 m3  of water. Consequently, the experimental conditions represent a worst-case scenario, and for rainfall-runoff events with drier initial conditions, swale outflows are expected to be smaller than reported in this study. The highest initial VWC was observed in section 1, with a mean value of 0.46 m3 /m3 . The lowest VWC was recorded at the 20 cm soil depth, with a mean value of 0.28 m3 /m3 . VWC measurements at various soil depths, ranging from 20 to 50 cm, were conducted exclusively 15 m upstream of the swale outlet. High VWC values on the swale bottom significantly influence the swale's response during field irrigation-driven runoff experiments. This effect is attributed to limited pore space availability, which in turn reduces the swale's infiltration rates. Soil characteristics at this site reported by Rujner, et al. (2018)  included porosity values of 0.45 ± 0.08 (for sandy loam textures). This value aligns with observed VWC values at different swale sections, indicating soil saturation conditions or variability of soil textures. Furthermore, VWC values at the deeper soil layers of 20 and 40 cm demonstrated higher variability and lower water content levels, with values oscillating between 0.28 and 0.44 m3 /m3 , as detailed in Table 2 . Pre-wetted conditions were intentionally established to maintain high VWC throughout all irrigation experiments, which is demonstrated by relatively small variations in VWC values across the different return periods.  2.4 Data analysis 2.4.1 Performance indicators for individual runs The initial step of data analysis involved selecting valid field-driven irrigation replicas based on three primary criteria: a) desired inflow duration, b) deviation between measured and theoretical inflow volumes, and c) inflow variability. Simulations that met the predefined criteria, including the inflow duration in the range from 29 to 31 min, were considered satisfactory. Inflow volume and variability were quantified based on their respective percentage deviation and coefficient of variation, with an established maximum tolerable limit of 10 %. The uniformity of both the ascending and descending limbs of the outflow hydrographs was assessed for physical consistencies The final selection yielded 23 replicas for the SOCW scenario and 20 replicas for the WO scenario. The estimation of performance indicators for all replicas corresponding to SOCW and WO scenario are presented in Table S1 a. The data analysis focused on runoff volume reduction (Vred ) and peak flow attenuation (Qred ). The evaluation of performance metrics was carried out at three distinct levels: 1) individually for each of the 43 field irrigation-driven runoff experiments (refer to Table S1 a in supplementary material ), 2) as a mean for each set of replicas, i.e. for each combination of return period and SOCW/WO scenarios (refer to Table 4   ) and, 3) pairwise, comparing the scenario with outflow controls (SOCW) to the baseline scenario (WO) to quantify the effect of adding the SOCW (refer to Table 5  ). The runoff volume reduction (Vred ) was calculated according to Eq. (4) :(4) V red    =  V inflow   - V outflow    V inflow       ∗ 100 %     where Vinflow  and Voutflow  correspond to total inflow and outflow volumes. The peak flow reduction (Qred ) was calculated as the difference of median inflow and maximum outflows as a percentage of the median inflow (Eq. (5) ).(5) Q red    =  ( Q  medianinflow   ) - ( Q  maxoutflow   )   ( Q  medianinflow   )       ∗ 100 %     where Qmedian inflow   and Q max outflow   indicate the median inflow and maximum outflow rates, respectively. For each set of replicas, the mean across all replicas was then calculated for each of the metrics described above, denoted as Vred-mean  and Qred-mean .  2.4.2 Comparison between outflow control (SOCW) and baseline (WO) scenarios For both Vred-mean  and Qred-mean , the differences represented as ΔVred  and ΔQred  between SOCW and WO were determined by calculating the percentage point difference between the mean values of each replica set (Eqs. The sources of uncertainty that were included in the analysis, and their corresponding sampling distributions are detailed in Table 3 . Inflow rates were omitted from the analysis due to the precision (±0.5 %) and consistency of the instrumentation across a broad range of flow conditions. Following the identification of MCM variables, a sample size of 106  was applied to the calculation procedure described in section 2.4  (for estimating Vred  and Qred  metrics). The resulting distributions for all performance metrics are presented here using the central 95 % confidence interval (CI) and visually using boxplots.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Swale performance indicators The comparative analysis between the scenarios with outflow controls (SOCW) and the baseline (WO) revealed significant differences in swale performance, as well as differences in the factors influencing performance. In the SOCW scenario, the mean volumetric performances showed a declining trend with increasing rainfall intensities, ranging from 54 % for lower-intensity (2-year) to 29 % for higher-intensity (50-year) return periods (refer to Table 4 ). This pattern aligns with expectations. Despite this trend, the swale with outflow controls effectively managed runoff volumes for a wide range of intensities, achieving a Vred  of over 29 % even during the less frequent 20- to 50-year return periods. These findings highlight the swale's retention capacities, demonstrating its effectiveness beyond serving as a runoff conveyance element. However, complete runoff capture was not achieved, even during low-intensity periods corresponding to 1- and 2-year return periods. From a water balance perspective, differences in initial abstractions due to variations in initial conditions had a lower impact on swale responses with outflow controls compared to the baseline scenario. This was indicated by the high consistency in Vred  performance across individual replicas, as shown in Table S1 a (supplementary material ). However, notable performance variations were observed within the 5-year return period among replicas, which can be largely attributed to different initial conditions. Specifically, the second replica began with pronounced ponding, showing an initial water level of 4.3 cm, significantly higher than the 0.1 cm and 0.9 cm levels in the other replicas. Differences in initial water levels between replicas might indicate a lack of complete control of initial conditions for the irrigation experiments. These deviations were observed to be more pronounced when consecutive irrigation experiments were conducted, with replicas at the end of the day tending to have higher initial water levels. Such variations resulted in increased performance disparity among replicas, as detailed in Fig. 3  b. In the WO scenario, Vred  estimation did not exhibit a consistent trend across various return periods. Volumetric performance fluctuated between 32 % for 1-year and 21 % for 5-year events, without a clear link between higher performance and lower rainfall intensities. While maximum Vred  was noted at lower intensities, the values for 20- and 50-year periods (32 % and 29 %, respectively) exceeded those of intermediate return periods (2- to 10-year) (refer to Table 4 ). Moreover, mean volumetric performances did not surpass 35 %. In addition, the absence of outflow controls resulted in channelized surface flow at the swale's bottom and a diminished wetted surface area, where lower infiltration rates were previously observed (Mantilla et al., 2023 ). This led to underutilization of the swale's cross-sectional area, subsequently diminishing its capacity to handle runoff volumes. The variability of Vred  values among individual replicas within identical return periods for the WO scenario, suggest a heightened sensitivity and more variability in the experimental conditions. This was evidenced by lower reproducibility of results across replicas, leading to increased uncertainties (refer to Fig. 3 b). For instance, the second replica of the 2-year and the first replica of the 5-year scenarios, with relatively high initial water levels of 2.9 cm and 3.3 cm respectively, exhibited lower abstractions and diminished performance (refer to Table S1 a). A similar trend was seen in the first replica of the 20-year period, which started with a water level of 3.1 cm and recorded a lower Vred  of 25 %. These variations are likely influenced by the swale's irregular bottom topography. (Rujner, et al. 2018 ) observed that this topography includes a depression storage capacity of about 0.61 m3 , affecting initial abstractions and the overall swale response. While higher initial water levels may explain lower retention capacities, additional factors such as inflow distribution and spatial variability in infiltration rates may also influence retention capacity. VWC values across the swale sections exhibited minimal differences between initial and final states in each replica, with variations below 0.01 m3 /m3  (refer to Table S1 a). These slight changes in VWC did not demonstrate a correlation with swale volume reduction in any scenario. Furthermore, pre-wetted conditions were intentionally established to maintain high VWC throughout all irrigation experiments, which is demonstrated by relatively small variations in initial and final VWC. Empirical outcomes presented in this study (with outflow controls) show volume reductions comparable to those of a previous study using check dams under moderate rainfall intensities, with mean Vred  values ranging from 27 % to 63 % (Davis et al., 2012 ). Additional research on grass swales also aligns with the runoff volume reduction observed in both scenarios (with and without outflow controls), reporting values between 30 % and 46 % (Deletic, 2001; Rushton, 2001 ). The high performance obtained in the present study under extreme events (20- and 50-year) can be largely attributed to the high infiltration rates on the right shoulder of the swale, which had an average ksat  of 480 mm/hr (Mantilla et al., 2023 ). Furthermore, the design of our irrigation system, which simulated lateral swale inflows, favored infiltration on the swale's side slope. The estimation of peak flow attenuation for the SOCW scenario, showed better performance for lower-intensity events, with mean values ranging between 48 % for 2-year to 23 % for 50-year return periods (refer to Table 4 ). There was a distinct trend of decreasing peak flow attenuation with increasing rainfall intensities. Overall, Qred  values showed more similarity across return periods for low to moderate rainfall intensities. For example, mean Qred  values for 1- and 2-year, ranged narrowly between 47 % to 48 %, and for 5- and 10-year, between 38 % to 40 %, respectively. However, a more pronounced difference in performance was evident in higher intensity return periods, with a wider spread in performance, ranging from 32 % for the 20-year period down to 23 % for the 50-year period (refer to Fig. 3 c). Similarly, the influence of initial abstraction on the reduction of peak flow (Qred ) values proved to be significant, as can be seen from the variations in performance among individual replicas within the same return period. For instance, in the first replica of the 5-year return period, the absence of ponding, indicated by a zero initial water level, led to a 45 % peak flow attenuation. In contrast, the second replica of the same return period, which began with a water level of 4.3 cm, achieved a lower peak flow attenuation of only 29 %. A similar pattern was observed in the 2-year return period, where the second replica showed the least effective performance at 42 %, a difference attributed to its higher initial water level (3.9 cm) compared to other replicas within the same return period. Results from the WO scenario showed a maximum mean peak flow attenuation of 28 %, corresponding to 20-year return period. In contrast, the minimum Qred  was observed for the 5-year, with a value of 16 %. There was no clear pattern associating higher peak flow attenuations with lower rainfall intensities across the return periods. This inconsistency might be partly due to differences in initial water levels among individual replicas and the sensitivity of results to experimental conditions like ponding in surface depression storage. For instance, considering the results for individual replicas (refer to Table S1 A), the lowest Qred  values, 9 % for the 2-year and 12 % for the 50-year periods, occurred in replicas with ponding conditions. These two replicas were marked by initial water levels of 2.9 and 2.5 cm, respectively. This highlights the significant impact of initial water levels, which lead to lower initial abstractions and subsequently a decreased peak outflow attenuation. In a similar study, Davis et al. (2012)  reported a negligible peak flow reduction (around 1 %) for high-intensity return periods, suggesting that the swale’s ability to attenuate peak flows will cease once the grass height is overtopped (thereby reducing roughness), and the soil infiltration is exceeded. The outcomes achieved in our study in terms of peak flow attenuation above 20 %—even for high-intensity events—were due not only to the throttling effect of outflow controls. Results in reduction of peak outflows were also likely influenced by the incorporation of lateral inflows into the design of the irrigation system, where higher infiltration rates were estimated.  3.2 Analyzing uncertainties in swale performance Lower uncertainties were found under the SOCW scenario, an effect attributed to the higher accuracy of the instrumentation used to measure outflow rates, employing a 30-degree V-notch weir, compared to the use of a 120-degree V-notch weir in the WO scenario. Additionally, the narrower span in 95 % CIs for mean Vred  values, resulting from the integration of volumes over a 30-minute period, contributed to lower uncertainties (refer to Table 4 ). In contrast, Qred  estimation is sensitive to the precise timing of maximum outflow measurements and can vary significantly with a small change in flow conditions. For instance, peak flows could be influenced by the manual pump operation and thereby the variability of inflows, incidental outflow measurement errors or backwater effects at the swale outlet. The more stable nature of total runoff volumes over time, as opposed to the variability of peak flow rates, accounts for the lower uncertainties observed in Vred  estimations. Similarities in Vred  were noted between the SOCW and WO scenarios, as can be seen from the overlapping 95 % CIs for high-intensity return periods. For instance, the observed overlap under the 50-year return period does not allow for differentiating the performance of the two scenarios (refer to Fig. 3 ). This finding suggests that outflow controls may no longer be effective in enhancing retention capacities under high intensities. Moreover, the consistency of Vred  values for the SOCW scenario under both 20- and 50-year return periods, may indicate a lack of significant differences in performance for such return periods. These similarities are due to a limited surface storage, above rainfall intensities equivalent to a 20-year return period, leading to similar swale responses. In general, the results suggest a noticeable divergence in performance at lower and moderate rainfall intensities (between 1- to 10-year return periods), but they provide less definitive conclusions about runoff reduction during higher return periods (20- and 50-year). On the other hand, estimations of mean peak flow reductions showed notable consistency in performance across all consecutive return periods for the WO scenario. This is evidenced by 95 % CI overlap of Qred  values across all return periods (refer to Fig. 3 ). These results are attributed to similarities in maximum peak flows between subsequent return periods, influenced by a limited wetted surface area at the swale bottom. When comparing the SOCW and WO scenarios, results indicate a divergence in peak flow attenuation for return periods between 1- to 5-years. Furthermore, for high-intensity return periods, the similarity in performance precludes drawing definitive conclusions about peak flow attenuations. While multiple irrigation replicas were performed to ensure the reliability of results, inconsistencies were noted in the patterns for certain return periods. These irregularities could arise from factors not accounted for in the study, such as variations in grass height, vegetation cover during the tests, differences in infiltration rates, or the distribution pattern of the irrigation system. Notably, as highlighted by Kirby et al. (2005) , the hydraulic resistance posed by vegetation can significantly influence surface flows in grass swales, as depicted through flow retardation curves based on grass height.  3.3 Swale hydrograph response The hydrodynamic response of the grass swale to different return periods was assessed by examining individual outflow hydrographs. For the SOCW scenario, the narrower shaded bands for return periods between 1 and 20 years indicate a higher confidence in the reliability of the results. For the specific case of the 50-year return period, the wide span of the shaded band signifies higher uncertainty, with a more pronounced effect on the peak of the outflow (refer to Fig. 4  a). In contrast, for the WO scenario, a wider range in the confidence intervals, represented by the shadow bands, makes it difficult to distinguish the swale's response to different rainfall intensities. The wider spread of shadow bands represents the variability in outflows obtained from each replica within the same return period. This uncertainty is exacerbated by the hydrograph shape compared to the SOCW scenario, where hydrographs show a longer duration of higher outflows at their peak. In addition, the hydrographs shown in Fig. 4  illustrate a less pronounced steepness in outflows under the SOCW scenario. This trend indicates a detention and gradual outflow, which can increase the response time downstream, and a real time control system approach could be used to manage downstream flood risk in an efficient manner. Additionally, the extended timeframe provided enables ecosystems to adapt to changes in water quality, fostering a healthier environment (Sohn et al., 2020 ). On the other hand, the outflow hydrograph in the WO scenario for the 1–20-year return period resulted in high flows over a more extended duration during the experiment. This behavior is indicated by the flat shape of the hydrograph once the maximum outflow is reached. In contrast, the outflow rates for the 50-year return period showcased a distinct pattern, with a prominently defined peak outflow. Such a pattern may lead to challenges in managing downstream runoff flows, with an increased flood risk, especially if downstream drainage systems and water bodies cannot accommodate the persistent high flow (Berggren et al., 2018 ).  3.4 Hydrological impact of swale retrofits The comparison of the SOCW and WO scenarios, detailed in Table 5 , reveals an improved swale performance with outflow controls in place, resulting in reduced runoff volumes and peak flows. An increase in volume reductions (ΔVred ) was observed across all return periods, with values varying from 1 to 32 percentage points which correspond to 50- and 2-year return periods, respectively. The results indicate that swale retrofits have a more significant impact on flows generated by lower to moderate rain intensities, which include return periods ranging from 1 to 10 years. An additional mean runoff volume reduction (ΔVred ) of 18 percentage points was achieved by incorporating outflow controls across all return periods under the current rainfall intensities. Additionally, a considerable degree of uncertainty was observed for lower to moderate intensities, as reflected in the 95 % confidence intervals (refer to Table 5 ). Alternatively, the effect of outflow controls with respect to attenuating peak flows, showed a positive effect for all the return periods, with values of ΔQred  (additional peak flow attenuation) that ranged between 4 and 32 percentage points, corresponding to the 50- and 2-year return period, respectively. In general, an increment in ΔQred  of 18 percentage points was achieved by retrofitting the swale. The 95 % confidence intervals revealed a significant uncertainty in estimating ΔQred  for all return periods (higher compared to ΔVred  values) with a span in the confidence intervals of more than 24 percentage points. This uncertainty may be attributed to inherent uncertainties in flow measurements (the use of a 120-degree V-notch weir in the WO scenario), and the distinct characteristics of outflow hydrograph shapes (e.g., prolonged duration in maximum peak outflows for the WO scenario).  3.5 Practical implications From a decision-making perspective, the high level of certainty associated with swale outflow controls offers a robust, evidence-based strategy for mitigating flood risks in urban areas. The demonstrated effectiveness in managing lower to moderate rainfall intensities is especially significant, given the frequency of such conditions and their cumulative effect on urban drainage systems. Previous research on grass swales focused on various design modifications, encompassing alterations in geometry and adaptation of swale features (West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection (WVDEP), 2012 ). These adaptations aimed to promote sedimentation, filtration through the soil matrix, evapotranspiration, and infiltration into the underlying natural soil. Two primary design considerations supporting effective stormwater management include: (1) a system with sufficient flexibility and adaptability to accommodate future increases in rainfall intensities, and (2) a flow control structure with the capability to efficiently drain the site, while providing dynamic water storage for future storm events. Such a structure, in the shape of a vertical short-pipe riser (see Fig. 5  ), would be placed over the drop inlet manhole of the storm sewer system receiving swale outflow. As described below, the riser would have three outflow openings: (a) the top edge, serving as a flow bypass weir (when the capacities of the other two openings are exceeded), (b) a weir opening in the riser wall, holding an exchangeable weir plate serving for adjusting the degree of flow control (i.e., by varying flow capacities), and (c) a small opening at the riser bottom providing positive drainage between events. Two other details of the riser are suggested below:(a) A vertical slot would be added at the riser's top, equipped with grooves to hold a weir plate. This allows adjustment of the overflow opening and outflow rates by inserting weir plates of various shapes and flow capacities. The slot would be on the riser's downstream face to reduce the risk of clogging by floating debris.  (b) Below the flow control weir, a small opening at the riser's bottom is located and provides positive drainage between events.    Additional considerations in the design of swales needed to ensure desirable performance, and reflecting experience from various countries, with or without SOCW, include: (a) the groundwater aquifer should have inflow dissipation capacity to counteract the effect of seasonal water tables and prevent groundwater mounding, with minimum infiltration rates of 1 cm/hr (Abida & Sabourin, 2006 ); (b) the swale should have conveyance capacity corresponding to the drainage area and generated runoff volume (i.e., the ratio of the swale footprint area to the runoff contributing impervious area should range from 5:1 to 10:1) (Credit Valley Conservation (CVC), (2010) ); and (c) the swale should be designed with a sufficient cross-sectional area to provide higher conveyance capacity (trapezoidal geometry) (Ekka et al., 2021 ). Moreover, when considering the volume of water introduced, there is a potential for a localized rise in the groundwater table, possibly resulting in groundwater mounding. This can diminish the infiltration capacities due to increased capillary forces and a shallow unsaturated zone beneath the swale bottom (Roldin et al., 2013 ).  3.6 Study limitations and future work The study demonstrates the successful implementation of a modified swale design as a viable contribution to stormwater management and adaptation to increased hydraulic loading, in comparable ambient conditions. However, continuation of further longer-term field and/or modeling studies is recommended to assess grass swale with outflow control performance over longer periods, under varying seasonal conditions and different levels of soil moisture content, which would provide a better understanding of the proposed systems' efficacy and applicability. Therefore, the results presented herein should be considered with caution, recognizing that they cannot be transferred elsewhere by linear scaling of design parameters from one location to another (Mantilla et al., 2022 ). Five main assumptions were considered, which may not be fully applicable elsewhere: (1) Selection of a climate change factor to represent an increment in rainfall intensities of 25 %, (2) Design storms of uniform rainfall intensity and duration of 30 min, for rain intensities corresponding to return periods ranging from 2 to 50 years, (3) Estimation of inflow rates (to a 30-m swale section) corresponding to a catchment area of 550 m2 , and 30 % of swale lateral inflow from the right-side slope, (4) Swale channel storage capacity corresponding to the study site in Luleå (Sweden), and (5) No influence of sediment load carried by the swale flow (based on field experience with swales in the Luleå area). Further comments follow. Although increments (25 %) of rainfall intensity were applied in the study to account for climate change, as recommended by the Swedish Water (Svenskt Vatten (SV), 2016 ), further research is clearly needed to determine the appropriate factors to represent future rainfall intensities (Arnbjerg-Nielsen et al., 2013 ). This might involve the use of regional climate models, and the selection of a downscaling technique to obtain outputs at finer temporal and spatial resolutions (Berg et al., 2019 ). Moreover, Lind & Kjellström (2008)  projected greater changes during the winter season and in northern Sweden in terms of precipitation intensity, with a mean increment around 25 %. While climate predictions inherently have a degree of uncertainty (Douville et al., 2021 ), it was observed that the introduction of a climate change factor reduced the swale retention and detention capacity given by outflow controls. This effect will be expected to remain if a greater increment in precipitation intensity were considered, given by the finite storage offered by the swale outlet control weir. In addition, the adoption of uniform rainfall intensity during the experiments represents a consistent peak, providing a safety margin in the evaluation of the effects of outflow controls. This approach might represent a simplification of the hyetograph of a real rainfall event. For instance, Olsson (2019)  found that a rainstorm with an intermediate peak intensity (produced by a Chicago Design Storm) generally results in greater peak discharge compared to observed empirical hyetographs. Similarly, hyetographs with delayed intensity peaks have been found to generate higher hydrograph flow peaks than those produced by an advanced (early) peak hyetograph (Watt & Marsalek, 2013 ). Further research should evaluate the swale's response under rainfall events with varying hyetographs (instead of uniform rainfall intensity), which include bursts with advanced, intermediate, or delayed intensity peaks, as well as those with high peakedness. In addition, this study assumed a catchment area of 550 m2 , which was used in the estimation of runoff volumes for different return periods and assumed 30 % ratio of lateral to longitudinal inflow. Since the effect of the right-side slope of the swale was found to positively influence retention capacity due to significant infiltration at this location, the overall water balance might change depending on the percentage of lateral inflow. García-Serrana et al. (2017)  found that the percentage of water infiltrating the side slope is considerably greater than that infiltrating the swale bottom. The same study concluded that the side slope of a roadside swale is the main component contributing to the loss of runoff by infiltration, and the swale bottom primarily conveys the water that runs off the side slope. In addition, while changes in grass height were observed across the irrigation experiments but not accounted in this study, this effect might influence the hydraulic roughness and thereby the peak flow attenuation. Fiener & Auerswald (2005)  found that the hydraulic roughness in a grass swale drops drastically in case of grass submergence, affecting the runoff characteristics. It is important to highlight that the influence of the swale outlet control weir on detention capacity will depend on the specific design features of the weir. A different crest height will result in greater water retention, which could enhance the swale’s capacity to reduce runoff volumes. This effect will also increase the grass swale's storage capacity, enabling it to hold more water, which can be beneficial for managing larger, more intense rainfall events. Additional factors influencing the effectiveness of outflow controls include the facility-catchment area ratio, the percentage of lateral inflow with respect to total inflow, and ksat  values varying between 14 and 1384 mm/hr. Consequently, the findings of this study might potentially underestimate outcomes for actual storms with lower initial soil moisture levels, larger contributing areas, and groundwater interception. Moreover, our findings correspond to a hypothetical catchment area, which may contribute to an underestimation of inflows if a larger catchment area were to be considered. Thus, the definitions of low and high-intensity events used here are specifically tailored to the context of this study and may not fully align with other scenarios or studies.   4 Conclusions This study evaluated the performance of swale outlet control weir (SOCW) in comparison to an existing facility (WO scenario) for a 30-meter-long irrigated grass swale. The findings revealed an improvement in the swale's ability to reduce runoff volumes (ΔVred ), with mean increments spanning from 1 to 32 percentage points, for design events (30 min. duration, uniform rain intensity) of 50- and 2-year return periods, respectively. This indicates an additional runoff volume reduction facilitated by swale retrofits under the current rainfall intensities and hyetographs. The implementation of outflow controls also enhanced the swale's peak flow attenuation, with ΔQred  values ranging from 4 percentage points to 32 percentage points for 50- and 2-year return periods, respectively. This effect was consistent with the estimation of ΔVred  values, demonstrating a correlation between higher performance and low rainfall intensities. Additionally, a less pronounced steepness in outflow hydrographs under the SOCW scenario indicates a detention potential with a more gradual release of water. In contrast, the outflow hydrograph in the WO scenario reveals peak flows persisting over a more extended duration along the irrigation run. The continuous high flow rate could increase downstream flood risk. It emphasizes the importance of carefully balancing outflow rates to ensure both efficient drainage and the stability of downstream areas.
1 Introduction The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) anticipates a 50 % increase in global irrigated food production by 2050. However, this growth is constrained to a 10 % rise in agricultural water withdrawal, relying on advancements in irrigation methods and increased yields (FAO, 2017 ). This underscores the importance of enhanced water productivity, aiming for higher crop output per unit of water. Rice cultivation covers over 30 % of the world's irrigated land, crucial in global food security as a staple food for over half the global population. Traditional water-intensive practices in rice-paddy cultivation, such as flooding and puddling, are becoming less sustainable due to water scarcity and environmental concerns. Global rice water productivity currently stands at 0.6–1.6 kg m−3  (0.2–1.2 kg m−3  in India), comparatively lower than other crops (Surendran et al., 2021 ). Efforts are shifting towards improving irrigation efficiency through optimizing fertilizer application, selecting suitable rice varieties and planting schedules, and addressing field-specific issues like salinity. Additional measures include deficit irrigation, managing unproductive water losses (evaporation, runoff, and deep percolation), and maximizing rainfall utilization. These strategies aim to reduce water usage while maintaining productivity (Surendran et al., 2021 ). Implementing structural measures in fields of low adoption regions, where farming communities are less accepting or resistant to sudden changes in traditional practices, is challenging. In such situations, incorporating short-to-medium-range weather forecasts has proven valuable for enhancing real-time irrigation planning. Numerous studies have explored using weather forecasts in irrigation scheduling (Cai et al., 2009; Cai et al., 2011; Hejazi et al., 2014; Perera et al., 2014; Lorite et al., 2015; Linker and Sylaios, 2016; Jamal et al., 2019; Roy et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024 ). Initially, the investigations focused on deriving reference crop evapotranspiration (ETo) from weather forecasts for irrigation guidance (Cai et al., 2009; Cruz-Blanco et al., 2014; Perera et al., 2014; Lorite et al., 2015 ). However, these studies predominantly focused on arid to semi-arid regions, neglecting the importance of incorporating rainfall forecasts. Several studies have demonstrated a combination of rainfall forecasts with ETo forecasts to estimate irrigation requirements and inform decision-making. Most of these studies emphasized rule-based irrigation scheduling (Wang and Cai, 2009; Mishra et al., 2013; Anupoju et al., 2021; Gedam et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024 ). Some efforts also explored simulation–optimization methods to optimize irrigation schedules (Cai et al., 2011; Hejazi et al., 2014; Linker and Sylaios, 2016; Jamal et al., 2019; Roy et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2023 ). However, establishing an objective function for the optimization of irrigation applications is found to be challenging, especially in developing countries where there is no pricing structure for irrigation water (Mishra et al., 2013; Cao et al., 2019; Gedam et al., 2023 ). In irrigation scheduling studies, researchers have attempted to generate weather forecasts using stochastic weather generators due to the simplicity of the procedure. These generators are conditioned based on historical weather records of the region (Wang and Cai, 2009; Mishra et al., 2013; Anupoju et al., 2021; Gedam et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024 ). However, studies have shown that the ongoing shifts in climatic conditions have led to observable alterations in the seasonal patterns of weather (Mishra et al., 2013; Linker and Sylaios, 2016; Gedam et al., 2023 ). In response, researchers are exploring using outputs from process-based Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models to understand the changing rainfall patterns (Delgoda et al., 2016; Perera et al., 2016 ). Studies emphasize the value of adopting high-resolution regional scale models to reduce weather uncertainties, particularly in predicting rainfall at the farm level (Hejazi et al., 2014; Vanella et al., 2020 ). Rainfall integration into real-time crop irrigation scheduling aims to reduce excessive water through effective irrigation. Rainfall and its variability in space and time are considered the most challenging meteorological variables to forecast (Sangha et al., 2023 ). Rainfall forecasts introduce uncertainties that impact the efficacy of the irrigation decision framework (Hejazi et al., 2014; Perera et al., 2016 ). Past studies emphasized deterministic rainfall forecasts, but current research has expanded to include probabilistic/ensemble rainfall forecasts in irrigation planning to capture rainfall forecast uncertainty (Hejazi et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2024 ). The need exists to integrate absolute Quantitative Precipitation Forecast (QPF) values derived from probability forecasts into simulation models for precise real-time irrigation scheduling (Delgoda et al., 2016; Muller et al., 2021; Sangha et al., 2023 ). The time-extent (short, medium, or long term) of the decision horizon is crucial in designing the framework for irrigation decisions (Anupoju et al., 2021; Ajaz et al., 2023 ). While season-long forecasts or multi-week lead times offer other benefits, such as for crop planning, their utility for real-time irrigation scheduling is limited (Hejazi et al., 2014; Jamal et al., 2019; Sangha et al., 2023 ). Shorter intervals (3–7 days) prove advantageous in dry years, while slightly longer horizons (bi-weekly) offer greater benefits in normal and wet years (Wang and Cai, 2009 ). Moreover, forecast reliability may reduce after a lead time of 2–3 days, contingent upon weather variability (Wang and Cai, 2009; Kelly et al., 2023 ). Additionally, field-specific constraints, such as water availability to farmers, resource availability, and farmers' behavior, are noted to impact the optimal time window for making irrigation decisions (Mishra et al., 2013; Gedam et al., 2023 ). Although weather forecasts are expected to enhance irrigation water productivity, uncertainties may arise at various stages of the integration process. Factors such as the quality of weather forecasts, the length of the forecast time horizon, the availability of historical weather data, model input uncertainties related to site-specific crop inputs and soil characteristics, irrigation practices, real-time soil moisture representations, farmers' behavior, and uncertainties in irrigation supply can significantly impact the simulation results from crop growth model (Chen et al., 2020; Kelly et al., 2021 ). Therefore, the practical advantages obtained from integrating weather forecasts across various typologies, remain uncertain (Bergez and Garcia, 2010; Cao et al., 2019 ). The study incorporates ensemble rainfall forecasts (with a 3-day lead time) into a regionally calibrated gridded crop model, aiming to represent real field conditions in a rice-paddy intensive system closely. The ensemble weather forecasts from prevalent and publicly available global climate model datasets, such as the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) and National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) with a 3-day lead time, are utilized in the study. A high-resolution (4 km x 4 km) WRF multi-physics ensemble model, calibrated for diverse seasons and regions within southern peninsular India, is also employed (Kirthiga et al., 2021 ). A Quasi-Farmer Behavior Routine is proposed to mimic local farmers' decision-making practices. The derived irrigation decision is integrated into a calibrated rice-crop growth model to estimate irrigation and crop yield. The major objectives of the study are: 1) Quantify precipitation forecast uncertainty across different models and climatic regimes. Evaluate the added value of high-resolution convective-scale ensembles from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model 2) Develop a rule-based weather-crop simulation framework (Quasi-Farmer Behavior Routine) emulating local rice farmers' behavior. Consider uncertainties in ensemble weather forecasts when making irrigation decisions, and 3) Assess the impact of perfect and imperfect weather forecasts on irrigation water productivity through a methodically designed set of 800 simulation experiments representing diverse hydro-climatic conditions. The present study is designed to assess the practical impact of incorporating weather forecasts into irrigation decision-making, considering the constraints posed by input and model uncertainties.  2 Methodology The proposed framework incorporates short-term probabilistic weather forecasts into a physical crop growth model (ORYZA), representing rice-paddy's growth dynamics. A decision-making framework that emulates local farmers' preferences and behavior (Quasi-farmer behavior irrigation decision routine in the manuscript) is proposed for real-time irrigation decisions. For assessing the practical applicability, the crop model is implemented across the Tamirabharani basin (referred as gridded crop model in the manuscript), representing a range of realistic field conditions. The analysis also encompasses a range of rainfall forecast sources, incorporating different strategies for deriving Quantitative Precipitation Forecasts (QPFs) from the ensemble forecasts. The methodology is subjected to testing in both dry and wet years to comprehensively assess the efficacy and associated risks under varying climatic conditions. Accordingly, the methodology section is organized into seven key components. These encompass the description of the crop growth model, working procedure of the farmer behavior routine, characteristics of the study region, details of the field monitoring sites, the gridded crop model framework, sources and pre-processing of ensemble weather forecasts, and an elaboration of the various scenarios used to measure the impact of the methodology. 2.1 Crop growth model The ORYZA model, a dynamic eco-physiological model, is designed to simulate rice (Oryza sativa L.) growth under potential production and limited water availability conditions. It covers various rice ecosystems such as lowland, upland, and aerobic environments. The model simulates daily rates of photosynthesis, respiration, and senescence processes. The physiological age of rice is determined by its developmental stage (DVS), derived from the integral of phenological development rate using daily average surface temperature and photoperiod. Dry matter generated daily is allocated to plant organs and grain-filling using partitioning factors linked to the developmental stage. Inputs include daily weather data, crop sowing date, soil information, crop density, genotype data, and management details. For this study, Oryza (v3) (Li et al., 2017 ) is parameterized for lowland rice ecosystems under potential production and water-limited scenarios.  2.2 Quasi-farmer behavior irrigation decision routine The Quasi-Farmer Behavior Routine is developed with the objective of emulating the decision-making actions of a farmer upon receiving quantitative guidance derived from short-term weather forecasts. This routine, as depicted in Fig. 1  , comprises two modules (Module I and Module II) encompassing three consecutive checkpoints (represented by orange diamond-boxes in Fig. 1 ). Checkpoint 1) Based on rainfall forecasts for the next 3-days (Module I). Checkpoint 2) Based on the antecedent water level (Module II). Checkpoint 3) Based on the forecasted crop evapotranspiration (Module II). These checkpoints translate the weather forecasts and their associated uncertainties into binary choices for daily irrigation scheduling during the simulation period. The crop growth model is incorporated into the routine throughout the growing season, facilitating the implementation of checkpoints 2 and 3. The details of the operational methodology of this quasi-farmer behavior routine and the significance of critical parameters are discussed in the following sections. 2.2.1 Module I – Rainfall forecast check: Irrigation decision based on forecasted rainfall Following an analysis of rainfall forecast performance over an extended time period (elaborated in section 3.2 ), the rainfall forecast values are grouped into three classes according to the context of irrigation and crop water requirements viz.: 1) High Irrigation Possibility (HIP), 2) Moderate Irrigation Possibility (MIP), and 3) Low Irrigation Possibility (LIP) (details are in section 3.3 ). The “no rain (<2.5 mm/day)” category is classified as HIP, the categories of light and moderate rain (2.5–35.5 mm/day) are grouped as MIP, and the rather heavy to very heavy rains (>35.6 mm/day) are classified as LIP (the definition of daily rainfall intensities from India Meteorological Department (IMD) nomenclature). For a selected forecast model, each irrigation likelihood category is linked to a predetermined value known as the Rainfall Confidence Quotient (RCQ), determined by the reliability of precipitation forecasts (Fig. 1 ). These RCQ values, denoted as RCQ1, RCQ2, and RCQ3, correspond to lead times of 1-day, 2-day, and 3-day, respectively. The values of the RCQs are standardized within a range of 0 to 1. A higher RCQ value (RCQ1/ RCQ2/ RCQ3), closer to 1, signifies a more reliable rainfall forecast with agricultural significance, suggesting a reduced likelihood of irrigation. The reliability of rainfall forecasts depends on the skill of the selected forecast model for the region of interest. Based on the extended period analysis conducted in this study (not shown here for brevity), it was observed that the performance skill of forecast models varied across different rainfall thresholds and lead times. Consequently, optimizing individual RCQ values for each forecast model, lead-time and irrigation likelihood classes is essential. Considering the significance of the next 3-day forecasts in irrigation scheduling, the cumulative sum of the 3-day RCQs holds considerable importance. Additionally, determining the optimal value above which this sum ΣRCQ, should activate the no-irrigation switch (NO-IRR) is crucial. Hence, the task evolves into a multi-stage optimization problem comprising two stages: optimizing individual RCQ values and optimizing the threshold value for ΣRCQ (Fig. 1 ). As a first stage, individual RCQ values are optimized utilizing 1000 samples of threshold values randomly sampled from the range of 0 to 3. Lower and upper limits of the ΣRCQ are established based on the minimum and maximum summation values derived from the individual RCQs. The optimization employs a genetic algorithm (GA) to maximize the kappa coefficient (Sim and Wright, 2005 ). The inputs to the genetic algorithm (GA) model include classification into irrigation (IRR) or no-irrigation (NO-IRR) based on actual observed weather data. Additionally, feasible value ranges (0 to 1) of individual RCQs (a total of 9 RCQ variables i.e. RCQ1, RCQ2 and RCQ3 for 3 irrigation likelihood classes) are considered for each lead time and irrigation likelihood class. A fixed population size of 100, mutation probability at 20 %, one elite individual retained in the population, crossover probability set to 50 %, 30 % allowable portion included from the previous generation, and a 'two-point' crossover type is used for one selected threshold value for ΣRCQ. Likewise, 1000 iterations across all the threshold value samples are performed. The output of the GA model is optimized individual RCQ values aimed at maximizing the classification accuracy (kappa coefficient). The classification accuracy is calculated for distinguishing between irrigation and no-irrigation occurrences predicted by forecast models compared to actual weather data. Training data encompass forecasts from October to March of the 2015–16 crop year, while testing data comprises forecasts from the subsequent crop year, 2016–17. Consequently, a look-up table for RCQ values is derived from the one-time analysis for each forecast model, irrigation likelihood class, and lead-time. In the subsequent step, the designated RCQ values are used for calculating ΣRCQ and the appropriate threshold value is optimized with the same objective function to maximize the kappa coefficient of the classification. Fixing value of ΣRCQ value directly for each irrigation likelihood class, as demonstrated by Cao et al. (2019) , may seem straightforward. However, previous studies have highlighted performance differences across forecast lead times, indicating better performance during shorter lead times (Kirthiga et al., 2021; Gedam et al., 2023 ). Hence, to construct a robust model and capitalize on the varying skill across lead times, a two-stage sequential GA procedure is implemented. Simultaneously, an appropriate threshold value for ΣRCQ is determined for each forecast model that does not change across years. When crop model is executed on a daily basis, the QPFs from a forecast source are obtained for each day in the 3-day horizon, the corresponding RCQ values are extracted from the pre-defined look-up table. If the sum of these RCQs exceeds the apriori set threshold value, the system transitions to module II, activating the NO-IRR switch. Conversely, if the sum does not exceed the threshold, the system proceeds with the IRR switch, bypassing module II and resulting in the final decision (Fig. 1 ). The primary objective of the concept of RCQs is similar to a bias correction procedure, but instead of adjusting actual rainfall quantities, it assigns new RCQ values for selected irrigation likelihood classes that can be used in rule-based approach to take irrigation decisions. This helps eliminate the uncertainty associated with using actual rainfall quantities. In addition, it takes into consideration the consecutive 3-day forecasts. This process is conducted as a one-time exercise specific to a given study region, aimed at mitigating the systematic bias in predicting specific rainfall intensities by each forecast model. Once established, these optimized RCQ values are consistently employed in subsequent analyses without requiring re-optimization, thereby ensuring stability across different forecast models within the same study region. It is crucial to underscore that the key goal of designing the concept of RCQs is to effectively reduce false alarms in irrigation advisories. Assigning a constant RCQ value across the upcoming 3 days could potentially overlook the varying risks associated with different lead times. This rational approach, adopted with the specific intention of minimizing the potential risks associated with crop damage, is more conservative from the farmers' perspective to avoid risk. It ultimately enhances the reliability of the NO-IRR decisions made based on the forecasts by avoiding predicted false alarms. Although the effects of missed rainfall forecasts are not fully addressed, they are accounted for in subsequent forecast runs by updating them with concurrent observations.  2.2.2 Module II – Crop water requirement check based on crop model Simulation: Irrigation decision based on forecasted crop water requirements Module II consists of two consecutive checkpoints: Checkpoint 2 and Checkpoint 3, based on the outputs from previous time-step of the crop model.
