If the Module I verification process triggers the NO-IRR switch, the antecedent water level obtained from the previous time-step run of the crop model is assessed to determine if it falls below critical levels. The critical water levels, detailed in Table 1  , are predetermined through field assessments and recommendations from the state agricultural university, aligning with crucial crop growth stages. When the check indicates an adequate water depth to skip irrigation, Checkpoint 3 is activated. Checkpoint 3 compares the next 3-day evapotranspiration (from model run – previous time-step) and the 3-day rainfall forecast accumulation (current forecast). This process utilizes the 3-day cumulative actual evapotranspiration forecasts, obtained by running the model with forecasted surface weather variables (ensemble mean value of each variable). The absolute rainfall quantities derived from the ensemble rainfall forecasts are also considered. If the outcome of this comparison suggests that the forecasted evapotranspiration is less than the forecasted rainfall, a NO-IRR switch is passed which is irrigation is not applied on the current day. If an IRR switch is activated, the irrigation is applied for the current day. The irrigation amount applied during each irrigation application is determined based on the values provided in the “total irrigation water requirement during the given crop phase” column in Table 1 . The irrigation amount of each irrigation is adjusted according to the number of irrigation cycles within a given crop growth phase to ensure that the total irrigation amount does not exceed the prescribed limit specified in the table. The significant advantage of the routine lies in its sequential consideration of the three checkpoints, with greater emphasis placed on the cumulative RCQs rather than the individual forecast values of different lead times. The algorithm undergoes validation through multiple scenarios outlined in Section 2.7 . Subsequently, it is applied across various evaluation sites, as detailed in Section 2.5 . Following the specified scenario, the crop model is executed daily throughout the season, incrementing by one day at a time. During the simulation, the quasi-farmer decision routine is triggered when there is a need to irrigate (based on the selected irrigation strategy, section 2.7 ). The results obtained from this routine are then incorporated back into the crop model for the subsequent run. As the simulation progresses through the timeline of the crop season, the weather data in the crop model is updated with actual weather information as it becomes available. The weather within the forecast time horizon is sourced from forecast models, while historical averages are utilized for the remaining time period until the end of the season. This cyclic process continues throughout the entire season, deriving irrigation schedules based on the evolving conditions and inputs.   2.3 Hydro-climatic characteristics of the study area – Tamirabarani basin Located in southern Tamil Nadu, India, the perennial River Tamirabarani meanders through two districts—Tirunelveli (encompassing 70 % of the river basin area) and Thoothukudi (covering 21 % of the river basin area), spanning a length of 22 km. The total basin covers about 5717.08 square kilometers and comprises seven main sub-basins. For better analysis and visualization of spatial disparities based on hydro-climatic conditions, we have organized and grouped these sub-basins into six major zones viz. Z1- Upper Tamirabarani; Z2 – Gadananadhi; Z3 – Chittar; Z4 – Uppodai; Z5 – Lower Tamirabarani; Z6 – Coastal Tamirabarani (Fig. 2  a). The majority of the climatology with the river basin in general belong to Tropical savanna climate or tropical wet and dry climate (Aw) under the Köppen climate classification (KCC). However, parts of the basin (Z1) come under the Humid subtropical climate (Cfa), and some parts, including Z3 and Z4, belong to the Hot semi-arid climate (BSh) classification. The Z2 belongs to the rain shadow region with most parts belonging to the BSh classification, and Z6 represents the impacts of coastal dry humid climatology. Taking advantage of rainfall from both the South-West (SWM) and North-East (NEM) monsoons, farmers in the Tamirabarani basin typically adopt a double and / or triple cropping pattern, except in cases of monsoon failure. Paddy rice cultivation holds the largest share, accounting for about 77 % of the cropped area. The rice cultivation calendar features two primary seasons: 'Pishanam'  (from November to February, primarily during NEM) and 'Kar'  (from June to September, coinciding with SWM). The Pishanam  season is the primary season, contributing to 75 % of rice production and acreage within the basin. The soil type is predominantly alluvial and sandy loam in areas covered by the Tamirabharani river drainage (encompassing Z1, Z2, and Z5). Parts of Z2 belong to the red loamy soil category; Z3 and Z4 consist mainly of black loamy or clay soil (unfertile soils); and Z6 is characterized by sandy soil (Table 2  ). The cropping pattern of the Pishanam  season exhibits significant spatial variability across different Taluks. The general sowing period for Pishanam  is based on reservoir releases and typically falls between late October to early December across the basin. The upstream zones (Z1 and Z2) experience earlier sowing and harvesting dates than the downstream zones (Z5 and Z6). In general, the rice varieties ASD 16, ASD 36, and ASD 18 are cultivated in the basin with a growth duration of 110–115 days. The average Pishanam  rice yield for the basin ranges from 3260 to 5800 kg/ha, with the fertile river-fed upper zones (Z1 and Z2) yielding more compared to the lower basins (Z5 and Z6) and the semi-arid low fertile zones (Z3 and Z4). The net cultivated area spans 175,108 ha, with approximately 66.3 % having access to irrigation. Irrigation sources primarily stem from canals (in Z1, Z2, and Z5), supplemented by irrigation tanks (shallow manmade traditional/ancient water bodies) (in Z3) and groundwater sources like well-pump sets (in Z4 and Z5). During the Pishanam  rice cultivation period, water consumption ranges from 8,700 to 14,000 cubic meters per hectare, resulting in a water productivity of 0.4–0.9 kg m−3  (Senthilkumar et al., 2008 ). In comparison, the global water productivity of rice stands at 0.6–1.6 kg m−3  and 0.2–1.2 kg m−3  in India. Hence, addressing the need for enhanced irrigation water productivity in Tamirabharani river basin is imperative, given its relatively low levels compared to national and global averages. Considering the provision of free water across the irrigation sources, individual farmers have minimal motivation to curtail their water consumption. The timing of canal water release for irrigation is generally beyond the control of individual farmers, leading them to utilize maximum water during their allotted access periods (Senthilkumar et al., 2008 ).  2.4 Field monitoring sites To understand the local practices and preferences of the farmers in the basin, agricultural field conditions are obtained from seven designated farmer fields (location shown in Fig. 2 b) for the Pishanam  season of 2015–16. Farmers manually enter the information, which is then monitored and collected by the field in-charge. A subject expert digitizes the data and cross-validates it with nearby fields is conducted. Additionally, the recorded irrigation application data undergoes cross-validation with water level data in the same field to ensure consistency. Field monitoring encompasses a range of information, such as the sowing and transplanting dates of crops, irrigation schedules including the timing and quantity applied throughout the season, daily water levels gauged through simple tube instrumentation that factored in evapotranspiration and percolation, yield outcomes at the end of the season, crop height measurements during various growth stages, and qualitative assessments of field conditions. The paddy plots followed a continuous flooding irrigation regime, where a layer of standing water is consistently maintained between 10 mm and 50 mm throughout the entire crop growth period. The farmers customized their irrigation quantities according to different crop growth stages, considering guidelines provided by the agricultural department and their traditional knowledge base (Table 1 ). The vegetative and reproductive phases are critical, necessitating increased irrigation during these periods to attain a satisfactory yield. Daily rainfall data from 2015 to 2017 is collected from a network of 25 rain gauges distributed across the zones (Fig. 2 a), maintained by the state Water Resources Department (WRD).  2.5 Gridded crop growth model implementation for assessing irrigation water requirement across a large heterogenous command area on a river basin scale Establishing a crop growth model for impact assessments, such as irrigation scheduling, has proven challenging due to its data-intensive nature (Solgi et al., 2022; Kelly et al., 2023 ). As a result, previous studies have predominantly focused on studying and reporting improvements in irrigation water productivity within controlled and data-rich field conditions. Earlier studies acknowledge that conclusions drawn from such single-site investigations could significantly diverge when confronted with uncertainties introduced by heterogeneous climate regimes, soil types, crop variations, and distinct crop and water management practices. For practical application and operational reliability, there is a compelling need to comprehend the impact of weather forecast uncertainty on irrigation decisions across spatial and temporal dimensions (Cao et al., 2019; Kelly et al., 2023 ). The study proposes employing a gridded version of the ORYZA crop model, wherein the model is parameterized to represent clusters of rice-paddy cultivation within Tamirabharani basin (supplementary material Fig. S1 ). These clusters are identified based on their spatial coverage and uniformity in crop and management practices. Evaluating the effectiveness of the model framework as a real-time decision support tool involves determining irrigation schedules and water quantities. This is achieved by employing the Quasi-farmer behavior irrigation decision routine in conjunction with the pre-calibrated gridded crop model. The resultant irrigation decisions are then analyzed to derive crucial insights into crop-water productivity, encompassing factors such as crop yield, irrigation timing, quantity, and runoff across the larger river basin (supplementary material Fig. S1 ). 2.5.1 Data and methods to setup gridded crop model Earlier basin-wide studies were primarily focused on forecasting reference crop evapotranspiration for assessing crop water requirements (Perera et al., 2014; Lorite et al., 2015; Medina et al., 2018 ), and a few studies focused on actual evapotranspiration for crop water requirements (Perera et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018 ). Cao et al. (2019)  attempted a comprehensive analysis covering six diverse rice-cropping regions with varying cropping patterns and climatic conditions. They examined the effects of utilizing 3-day weather forecasts for irrigation decision-making. However, their analysis assumed uniform irrigation management practices and crop coefficients across all six regions, ignoring their spatial and temporal variability. The study aims to fill the gap in irrigation decision analysis under diverse climate and soil conditions by utilizing remote sensing satellite data and globally available spatial inputs. The ORYZA model is implemented in a gridded mode (supplementary material Fig. S1 ), where the crop model is configured for different stations across the basin (Fig. 2 a). The field data gathered from the seven sites (Fig. 2 b) is utilized to establish a field understanding and extend this to other spatial points within the basin for setting up the ORYZA model. Fig. 3    provides a schema of the gridded ORYZA model configuration utilized in this study to assess various weather forecast scenarios across 25 station sites. Rainfall data is obtained from 25 rain gauge locations within the state Water Resources Department. Daily weather variables including solar radiation, relative humidity, minimum temperature, maximum temperature, and wind speed, are prepared from the India Meteorological Department (IMD) reanalysis data (IMDAA). This data, with a resolution of 0.12°x0.12°, is accessed from https://rds.ncmrwf.gov.in/dashboard/download  (Rani et al., 2021 ). The variables comprises surface downward short-wave radiation flux [W/m2 ], Relative Humidity at 2 m [%], Maximum Temperature at 2 m [K], Minimum Temperature at 2 m [K], and Wind Speed at 10 m [m/s]. The hourly data are accumulated into daily data and interpolated at station locations using the nearest-neighbor method for setting up the ORYZA model. Remote sensing products are used to derive the crop-related parameters. A multi-sensor image classification process is employed to categorize the significant irrigated rice clusters within the basin. The classification procedure involved the use of Sentinel 2 (optical sensor) and Sentinel 1 (microwave sensor) products in conjunction with vegetative index products from Landsat-8 (Dari et al., 2021 ). Based on this, the dynamic rice crop map of the Pishanam  season rice cluster for 2015–16 and 2016–17 was obtained and observed to record an overall classification accuracy of 92 % and 87 %, respectively (district wise reported rice-paddy crop acreage statistics is used for validation). These rice grids are clustered into parcels each greater than 100 ha (centroids of the clusters shown as    in Fig. 2 a) and each of the parcels are associated with the nearest weather station / IMDAA grids for gridded crop model configuration. Leaf Area Index (LAI) datasets from Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Terra and Aqua sensors (Myneni et al., 2015 ) are utilized to acquire 4-day LAI products (referred to as MODIS-LAI in the manuscript) at 500 m resolution for each crop season. To prevent the selection of non-representative (non-rice, which could occur due to the heterogeneous nature of crop management practices in the study area) LAI profiles, a neighborhood search is conducted for the time-series data. The pixel corresponding to the closest representation of the rice-paddy phenology is selected for each evaluation site. Sowing dates are extracted through smoothening and curve-fitting algorithm applied to the LAI time-series (Cai et al., 2017; Jeba et al., 2018 ). The crop pattern classification derived from LAI products for the two seasons is outlined in Table 2  and aligned well with reservoir releases and district-level reported dates for sowing and harvesting. Soil profile properties are derived from the ICAR-National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (NBSS & LUP) soil map at a scale of 1:250,000 (https://nbsslup.icar.gov.in/ ). Soil textural properties, hydraulic conductivity, available water capacity, and organic carbon content are directly obtained from the datasets, while field capacity and wilting point values are derived based on pedo-transfer functions (Saxton et al., 1986 ). Table 2  provides the broad textural classes of soils for different station locations. The observed irrigation schedule recorded from the field monitoring sites exhibited notable variation in irrigation water availability and usage throughout the season. The vegetative phase (typically from late November to the end of December) experienced fewer irrigation cycles but with higher applied irrigation quantities. Conversely, the reproductive phase (typically from early January to the end of January) featured more frequent irrigation cycles but with lesser applied irrigation water depths. NRSC soil moisture data, obtained using passive microwave data at a 25 km resolution, was downloaded from the Bhuvan website (https://bhuvan.nrsc.gov.in/ ). After preprocessing with rainfall data, representative pixels are processed to extract irrigation timings from the soil moisture data. Studies have indicated challenges in employing passive microwave data derived soil moisture observations in lowland paddy-cultivated areas, where the land remains completely submerged for over two weeks before sowing and often stays inundated for several weeks after paddy sowing (Singh et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2021 ). Singh et al. (2019)  demonstrated that the soil moisture product exhibited an underestimation bias compared to actual rice-paddy field conditions (ponded/saturated), particularly during the peak growing phase. Consequently, relying on the absolute soil moisture value is less suitable and may introduce errors. This study utilizes temporal profiles of soil moisture pattern changes, focusing on relative change rather than absolute values, to determine irrigation timings. These timings closely match the observed field data (collected from monitoring sites −section 2.4  and refer to supplementary material Fig. S2  for the agreement) and the canal/sluice releases. Despite the coarser resolution, the pixel centroids aligned well with the different irrigation regimes represented by the zones (Fig. 2 ). The irrigation amount applied during each irrigation application is determined based on the values provided in the “total irrigation water requirement during the given crop phase” column in Table 1 . The irrigation amount of each irrigation is adjusted according to the number of irrigation cycles within a given crop growth phase to ensure that the total irrigation amount does not exceed the prescribed limit specified in the table. These crop, soil, and weather inputs collectively contribute to implementing a robust gridded crop model across the basin. Further, this model configuration is tested to assess the performance of various scenarios elaborated in section 2.7 .  2.5.2 Calibration and validation of crop model The peak vegetative phase and crop duration (start of season and end of season) derived from MODIS LAI data are utilized to adjust the leaf area growth parameters. Among the developmental parameters of ORYZA, the Development Rate in Juvenile Phase (DVRJ) and Reproductive Phase (DVRR) were identified as the most sensitive from the sensitivity analysis. The simulated LAI peaks exhibited a slight over-prediction. Hence, adjusting the Maximum Relative Growth Rate of Leaf Area (RGRLMX) parameter helped in reducing the deviation. MODIS Evapo-Transpiration (ET) products (Running et al., 2017 ) are employed to calibrate the soil parameters. These products are used to spatially adjust the soil parameters such as volumetric water content at field capacity and wilting point. The irrigation schedules (mainly the applied irrigation amount) are also fine-tuned independently according to the MODIS ET data for both crop seasons, i.e., 2015–16 and 2016–17. Initially, irrigation timings are mainly determined using NRSC soil moisture data. Subsequently, irrigation amounts are adapted according to the recommended values outlined in Table 1 , aligning with the general practices of the farmers for each growth stage. However, the accuracy of these prescribed amounts might vary, as individual farmers often have different preferences. Hence, adjustments based on MODIS ET are primarily made to the irrigation water applied for each irrigation cycle. Calibration locations from among the 25 stations are strategically chosen to represent the hydro-climatic diversity and cropping patterns within the basin (marked with * in Table 2 ). The correlation coefficient between simulated LAI and MODIS LAI during training was recorded as 0.60, while during validation, it averaged around 0.45 across crop seasons. Similarly, for ET season totals, the correlation coefficient stood at 0.65 for the training set and 0.52 for the validation set. The calibrated model simulated crop yield strongly agreed with the recorded crop yield at the field level and the average crop yield across the districts. Specifically, the district-wide simulated average yield for 2015–16 was 5135 kg/ha, closely aligning with the observed yield of 4800 kg/ha. Similarly, for 2016–17, the simulated average yield was 3250 kg/ha, which closely matched the observed yield of 3400 kg/ha.   2.6 Short-term ensemble weather forecasts 2.6.1 Forecast sources The authors in their earlier works, including Kirthiga et al. (2021) , as well as in another manuscript currently under consideration for publication and accessible at https://dx.https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4237456 , investigated the sensitivity of the WRF model and methodically configured a 4-km model to generate a 7-member multi-physics ensemble. The model is tested during critical monsoon seasons within the region of interest. The simulated rainfall forecasts display reasonable accuracy in capturing the spatial and temporal variations of rainfall intensities. The High-Performance Computing System at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), Pune, the AADITYA supercomputer was utilized. To execute 1080 simulations (spanning 6 months X 2 cropping years X 7 ensembles X 3 days lead-time) for the entire basin at a 4-km resolution, it took 45 days of runtime for the simulation period covering October-March of two crop years, 2015–16 and 2016–17 for the selected model domain. The outputs of the WRF model are used to compute daily forecasts of surface rainfall, solar radiation, minimum temperature (at 2 m), maximum temperature (at 2 m), relative humidity (at 2 m), and wind speed (at 10 m) for the next 3-days. In order to understand and quantify the significance gained from the computationally intensive procedure of generating high-resolution weather forecasts, a comparative analysis is conducted against publicly available global forecasts at coarser resolution from TIGGE (The Observing System Research and Predictability Experiment (THORPEX) Interactive Grand Global Ensemble) (Bougeault et al., 2010 ). TIGGE accommodates both single-model and multi-model ensembles, and data is made publicly available at a resolution of 50 km through https://tigge.ecmwf.int/ . For this study, daily rainfall forecasts from two sources are utilized: the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) with a 50-member ensemble (referred to as ECM in the manuscript) and the National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) global forecast system with a 20-member ensemble (referred to as GEFS in the manuscript). The other surface variables like solar radiation (Surface net short-wave radiation), minimum temperature (at 2 m), maximum temperature (at 2 m), relative humidity (at 2 m) (derived from 2 m air temperature and 2 m dewpoint temperature), and wind speed (at 10 m) (derived from 10 m U wind component and 10 m V wind component) are also processed for each model and used in the study.  2.6.2 Ensemble rainfall forecasts This section elaborates on how the study represents the ensemble spread of rainfall forecasts. It is essential to emphasize that the decision routine (as outlined in Section 2.1 ) places greater importance on precipitation forecasts. Consequently, the study includes an evaluation of the ensemble nature of rainfall. Conversely, for weather variables other than rainfall, the ensemble mean of the members is utilized in the proposed framework. Earlier studies have reported that the ensemble rainfall forecasts can tend to be under-dispersive, i.e., the ensembles do not capture the range of variability observed in the actual rainfall (Clark, 2019 ). Therefore, looking into ways to increase the spread or number of ensemble members without adding too much to the computational resources, cost, and time is important. The concept of neighborhood ensembles has emerged as an effective post-processing technique to enhance the number of ensemble members and achieve a smoother probability distribution. The fundamental concept involves generating a new probability value for each grid by averaging the probabilities or values of the neighboring points for each ensemble member. The size of the neighborhood is predetermined, typically based on the spatial accuracy of forecast models, and is maintained within a specified influence distance or square window. This approach is particularly relevant for convective-scale ensemble forecasts to reduce errors from the under-dispersive nature of limited ensemble members. Nevertheless, the applicability of this idea extends to forecasts at coarser resolutions, addressing spatial shift errors (Schwartz and Sobash, 2017; Roberts et al., 2023 ). Sensitivity tests were conducted using the WRF model for distances ranging from 5 km to 120 km to determine the optimal neighborhood influence. Similarly, for GEFS and ECM, distances between 50 km and 150 km were considered, given their coarse resolution. The reduction in mean squared error, compared to IMDAA reanalysis data, exhibited stabilization after 12 km for WRF and 50 km for ECM and GEFS forecasts. The reduction in mean squared error (in comparison to IMDAA reanalysis data) was observed to stabilize after 12 km for WRF and 50 km for ECM and GEFS forecasts. Therefore, a 3x3 window is utilized for the WRF neighborhood ensemble, yielding a total of 63 ensemble members at convective permitting scales in conjunction with 7 multi-physics ensembles. Similarly, ECM employs a 4-neighbor approach with 50 original ensemble members, resulting in 200 ensemble members, while GEFS produces 80 members (4 neighbors × 20 original ensemble members). Converting probabilistic rainfall forecasts into quantitative values suitable for a crop model poses challenges. Previous studies attempted to assess forecasts based on the probability of occurrence (Cao et al., 2019 ), but the low dispersiveness of rainfall forecasts from numerical weather models might result in a low probability of agriculturally significant rainfall (Clark, 2019 ). Utilizing the ensemble mean directly may also result in a smoothed rainfall value, potentially underestimating the occurrence of a moderate to extreme rainfall event. Efforts have been made to run the crop model for each ensemble member to derive irrigation decisions, as explored in earlier studies (Guo et al., 2023 ). The irrigation decisions are made multiple times during the crop season, requiring daily runs of the crop model throughout the entire season for each decision. However, running the model for every ensemble member is not a viable solution due to the extended run-time and the complexity of the results. The study introduces the concept of percentiles, which is widely used in impact-based applications like agriculture water management and flood forecasting (Cafaro et al., 2021; Muller et al., 2021; Roberts et al., 2023 ). Percentiles, such as P25, P50, P75, and P90, are derived from the ensemble rainfall forecasts along with the ensemble mean. They represent specific points in the distribution, aiding in understanding the likelihood of an event occurring below a specific value. The probability of an event (e.g., rainfall amount) falling below a certain percentile is proportional to the percentile value. The 50th percentile (represents the median), and the probability of an event falling below the median is 50 %. Therefore, rainfall quantity can be estimated by considering the distribution characteristics of the ensemble members rather than relying on the specific value of any individual ensemble member. Incorporating these percentiles into the quasi-farmer routine and crop model enables irrigation decisions based on the ensemble spread rather than individual member values.  2.6.3 Verification of weather forecasts The simulated QPFs are verified against the daily rain gauge data for 25 stations sourced from the state Water Resources Department (section 2.6 ). Furthermore, microclimatic and surface variables, such as minimum temperature, maximum temperature, relative humidity, and wind speed, are compared to the IMDAA reanalysis data (elaborated in section 2.7 ) following a resampling procedure. Standard statistical metrics, including Root-Mean Squared Error (RMSE) and mean bias, are employed to quantify the performance of the weather forecasts. In particular, the normalized RMSE, normalized standard deviation, and correlation coefficients are calculated to compare the performance among variables and illustrate it through a Taylor diagram. For general assessment, the ensemble mean values of each weather variable are used for verification. For assessing the accuracy of Quantitative Precipitation Forecasts (QPFs), a classification system based on the India Meteorological Department (IMD) for daily rainfall is used. This classification is compared to observed data from the rain gauges to validate the predicted rainfall amounts. The IMD classification encompassed seven primary categories: No-Rain/Very Light Rain (NR) (<2.5 mm/day), Light-Rain (LR) (2.5 – 7.5 mm/day), Moderate-Rain (MR) (7.6 – 35.5 mm/day), Rather Heavy Rain (RHR) (35.6 – 64.4 mm/day), Heavy Rain (HR) (64.5 – 124.4 mm/day), Very Heavy Rain (VHR), and Extremely Heavy Rain (>124.5 mm/day). The Critical Success Index (CSI) or Threat Score is utilized to quantify and highlight the performance of the models under each rainfall category. CSI evaluates the ratio of true positives (hits, where the event is correctly predicted in both observations and forecasts for a specific rainfall threshold) to the sum of hits, false alarms (false positives), and misses (false negatives), i.e., (hits) / (hits + false alarms + misses). Its value ranges from 0 to 1, with 1 indicating a perfect forecast. Additionally, the Probability of Detection (POD) (hits/(hits + misses)) and False Alarm Ratio (FAR) (false alarms/(hits + false alarms)) are also employed.   2.7 Evaluating irrigation water productivity The study evaluates the effectiveness of weather forecast-based irrigation decisions across a spectrum of variables, resulting in realistic (near-field practices and conditions) to ideal (hypothetical but optimal) scenarios. As explained in the introduction, the variability in water savings is influenced by changes in climatology, irrigation strategy, and the quality of forecast data. Therefore, it is crucial to quantify the performance of each scenario to gain a comprehensive understanding of the implications of the proposed procedure. The following evaluation scenarios are considered (supplementary material Fig. S1 ):• No Forecast (NF): Represents farming practices without relying on forecast information, serving as a benchmark  scenario. The scenario is designed to emulate real-world practices by incorporating field-collected data (refer to section 2.4 ), reservoir and canal releases, satellite observations, coarser district-scale compiled data, and a calibrated crop model that captures the spatio-temporal variability of the rice-paddy in the region. In this scenario, a fundamental assumption, which aligns with real-world conditions, is that farmers have limited awareness of upcoming weather conditions. Even if they possess awareness, their lack of confidence in weather forecasts leads them to not consider these forecasts when scheduling irrigation. Therefore, this scenario facilitates an evaluation of the potential impact of improved forecasts and their effective communication on encouraging farmers to incorporate them into real-time decision-making.  • Perfect Forecast (PF): Symbolizes a theoretical scenario with perfectly accurate weather forecasts, representing the highest forecast reliability for achieving maximum water savings. In this case, perfect forecast values are obtained directly from observed values, assuming a 100 % confidence level in predicting rainfall for all three days. Although this scenario is hypothetical, it establishes an upper limit for potential improvements with the proposed procedure. (Scenario class – weather forecast source )  • WRF, ECM, GEFS based forecasts (Imperfect forecasts): Imperfect forecast cases using different sources of weather forecasts. (Scenario class – weather forecast source )  • Realistic Irrigation (RI): In realistic irrigation (RI), water availability follows a rotational schedule, where water for irrigation is available only at defined intervals. Whenever, the irrigation water becomes available, the irrigation decision routine is called. This scenario is particularly designed to align with real field conditions and canal water releases in the Tamirabharani basin. (Scenario class − irrigation strategy )  • Auto Triggered condition (AT): In the alternative irrigation method auto-triggered (AT) strategy, the irrigation decision routine is activated when the standing water depth falls below predefined thresholds (Table 1 ). This scenario assumes an ideal case where farmers have continuous access to water whenever the model signals a need for irrigation. (Scenario class − irrigation strategy )  • Ensemble Mean as QPF: The QPF value used in the Quasi-farmer behavior algorithm is derived from ensemble mean of the probabilistic forecasts. (Scenario class − ensemble nature of the rainfall forecasts)   • P90 as QPF: The QPF value used in the Quasi-farmer behavior algorithm is derived from the 90th percentile of the forecast probability distribution of the probabilistic forecasts. (Scenario class − ensemble nature of the rainfall forecasts)     Three major categories of scenarios, based on forecast source, irrigation strategy, and QPF derivation method from ensemble forecasts, are considered along with one benchmark scenario (NF). The cross-mapping of the scenarios is done as elaborated in Table 3   to understand the combination effects of each scenario. The No-Forecast (NF) case, i.e. the benchmark scenario is executed only once for a given crop season, specifically for the RI scenario, as the auto-triggered scenario condition does not align with the farmers' behavior in the basin. Additionally, ensemble rainfall forecast methods are irrelevant for this run, as it solely involves farmers' irrigation planning based on their past experiences and canal releases. The Perfect Forecast (PF) scenario is specifically conducted for RI and AT strategies, as EM and P90 are not applicable in the case of a perfect forecast as they would yield the same results. The Realistic Irrigation (RI) scenario produces apriori irrigation schedules for the entire season by combining 1) observed data on the past irrigation patterns followed by the farmers, 2) current reservoir releases, and 3) satellite-based soil moisture estimates (as detailed in section 2.5.1 ). On each irrigation application day identified from historical records (typically the day when water becomes available), the quasi-farmer behavior routine (Fig. 1 ) is triggered, updating the “irrigation decision switch” based on the outcome of the routine. As the routine incorporates most of the constraints considered critical by farmers, the assumption is that the farmer would promptly accept the irrigation decision from the routine. The revised irrigation decision obtained from the routine is updated in the framework, and the subsequent trigger for an irrigation decision occurs only when irrigation water becomes available again. As a result, the risk of losing irrigation is high in this scenario, as the field must endure until the next instance when water becomes available, in the event of a failure in the forecasted rainfall. In the context of this study (essentially a retrospective analysis), the effectiveness of the proposed method is evaluated by implementing the RI scenario with the derived irrigation schedules (from field observed data and satellite soil moisture data, section 2.5.1 ). In real-time scheduling (when the routine is utilized for real-time decisions), this would parallel to a situation where the farmer checks the decision tool for getting short-term advisory on irrigation application while having access to water from the canal system. The auto-triggered (AT) irrigation strategy is designed as an alternative method, assuming the availability of irrigation water sources whenever the farmer needs it. In this approach, the crop growth model identifies the requirement for irrigation based on auto-trigger conditions. The condition used in the study is that whenever standing water depth falls below a predefined threshold, as outlined in Table 1 , the irrigation call will be sent to the routine (Fig. 1 ). As the crop growth model already checks the threshold depth, checkpoint 2 is skipped for this strategy (red dotted lines in Fig. 1 ). Hence, the AT scenario is executed only with two checkpoints, namely checkpoint 1 and checkpoint 3 (Fig. 1 ). The irrigation water depth applied will be determined according to the specific crop growth stages. For instance, during the transplanting or vegetative phase, an irrigation water depth of 50 mm is utilized, while during the reproductive phase, a depth of 30 mm is specified. Finally, during the ripening stage, a depth of 15 mm is applied. These depths are predetermined based on the common practices prescribed by local agricultural university. However, in any case the total irrigation applied for a given crop stage will not exceed the irrigation amounts mentioned in table 1 (column 3). Earlier studies predominantly focused on ideal irrigation strategies like AT for simulation, but significant deviations from reality were observed (Wang and Cai, 2009; Mishra et al., 2013; Roy et al., 2022; Gedam et al., 2023 ). By considering the two primary irrigation strategies, RI and AT, this study highlights the uncertainty arising mainly from irrigation representation and constraints related to irrigation water source availability within the weather forecast-based irrigation advisory framework. In section 2.6.2 , irrigation decisions rely on Quantitative Precipitation Forecasts (QPFs) calculated through various methods, covering the ensemble mean, P25, P50, P75, and P90. Notably, the most significant findings concerning simulated irrigation decisions and water conservation emerge from runs based on the ensemble mean (EM) and the P90 amongst the other methods. Thus, this manuscript includes results from scenarios involving only EM and P90 QPFs for brevity and clarity. The considered scenarios are executed for two major crop seasons to include varying rainfall characteristics in the discussions. The years 2015–16 and 2016–17 represent a rainfall excess year and a rainfall deficit year (declared as a drought) (refer to Table 2 ). In summary, a total of 800 simulation experiments (16 combinational scenarios X 2 crop seasons X 25 evaluation stations). These experiments aim to comprehensively evaluate diverse conditions using key metrics, including irrigation water productivity (IWP), calculated by dividing total productivity by the volume of irrigation water applied (kg/m3 ). Additional metrics like the frequency of irrigation cycles and the amount of water reduced through runoff are also computed for a comprehensive analysis across scenarios.   3 Results 3.1 Assessment of surface weather variables forecasted from WRF Accurate surface weather forecasts are crucial for determining crop water needs within the forecast lead-time. Analyzing surface variables (using ensemble mean on the raw forecasts) across crop growing seasons (2015–16 and 2016–17) and various forecast models and lead times showed a slightly higher bias for ECM and GEFS, particularly for temperature and windspeed forecasts (Table 4  ). Interestingly, ECM and GEFS exhibited lower RMSE than WRF for longer lead times (2-day and 3-day), attributed to a narrower ensemble spread (explained in Section 3.2  and Fig. 5  ). With common spatio-temporal bias patterns among models, the discussion primarily concentrates on WRF forecasts due to the high-resolution outputs and relevance for a detailed presentation. WRF performed relatively well in predicting daily maximum temperature and windspeeds, displaying lower NRMSE and a stronger correlation with values derived from IMDAA reanalysis datasets (Fig. 3 ). Notably, there was a deviation in daily minimum temperature and rainfall values from the reference data, especially with an increasing forecast lead time. The model generally underpredicted minimum (RMSE: 1.48℃; Mean Bias: −1.05℃) and maximum (RMSE: 1.3℃; Mean Bias: −0.38℃) temperatures. Overall, there was a slight overestimation of relative humidity by approximately 4.9 % − 5.8 %. Windspeeds were slightly underestimated, with an average RMSE value of 2.3 m/s. Errors in surface variables led to an overestimation of rainfall in model simulations. Rainfall values exhibited higher standard deviations compared to the observed values, with a lower correlation coefficient, particularly for a lead time of 3 days. Regarding the spatial distribution of surface variables, a cold bias (∼-3mm/day) in rainfall and a warm bias (∼0.5 ℃) in temperature forecasts were observed in the upper catchment zones (Z1 and Z2, forested areas). The Pishanam season (Nov-March) encompasses three distinct climatic patterns: The Northeast Monsoon (NEM) in November and December, the Winter season in January and February, and the Summer season in March. The evaluation revealed that WRF simulated surface variable characteristics, such as the diurnal temperature and rainfall variability, exhibited better performance during the Winter and NEM seasons. In contrast, the Summer season was characterized by an increased cold bias in temperatures, with increased error growth as the lead time increased. Additionally, it is important to highlight findings from the study by Linker et al. (2018) , where similar assessments were made for maximum temperature, minimum temperature, reference ET, and rainfall in the context of irrigation forecasting. The weather forecasts were derived from deterministic high-resolution weather model which is locally tuned with a 4-day lead time and a horizontal resolution of 1 km by 1 km. The RMSE (correlation coefficient) values for maximum temperature were 1.5-2℃ (0.7–0.8), minimum temperature was 2-3℃ (0.9–0.95), and rainfall was reported to be 1––1.5 mm/day (0.1–0.3) at one station in Greece. Notably, the average observed rainfall in the crop season (10 May 2015–22 October 2015) reported for the Greece station was 1.05 mm/day (158 mm/season). The RMSE values obtained from the current study are comparable or slightly better than those reported by Linker et al. (2018)  and a higher correlation coefficient for all variables. This is to be attributed to the local calibration methods used in Kirthiga et al. (2021)  and the ensemble nature of the forecasts at the convective scale.  3.2 Detailed assessment of rainfall forecasts by different models A comprehensive evaluation of rainfall forecasts was conducted at 25 rain gauge stations across different forecast models to measure the level of uncertainty. The analysis resulted in an overall root mean square errors (RMSE) of 11 mm/day, 9 mm/day, and 8.9 mm/day, based on the ensemble mean derived QPFs (after application of neighborhood ensemble method) from the WRF, ECM, and GEFS models, respectively. However, a detailed examination of the rainfall distribution revealed that the WRF model outperformed the other forecast models (ECM and GEFS) in simulating the rather heavy rainfall category (RHR) (35.6 to 64.4 mm/day), as shown in Table 5  . Specifically, the WRF model ensembles exhibited good skill in forecasting the heavy rainfall (HR) and very heavy rainfall (VHR) categories (>64.4 mm/day) even up to a 3-day lead time (supplementary material Fig. S3 (d)). In contrast, the ECM and GEFS ensembles showed minimal skill in day 2 and day 3 forecasts for these categories. It was evident that the ECM and GEFS forecasts consistently underestimated higher rainfall values and failed to capture rainfall above 35.5 mm/day for 2-day and 3-day lead times (supplementary material Fig. S3 (b-c)), as indicated by the Probability of Detection (POD) values in Table 5 . For the 3-day forecast lead time (supplementary material Fig. S3 (c)), the WRF model slightly overestimated rainfall exceeding 30 mm/day. This pattern in bias was observed consistently across the 25 stations, with larger discrepancies in the upper catchment zones of Z1 and Z2. Interestingly, the ECM forecasts consistently performed well for the moderate rain (MR) category across various lead times, with the highest values of POD and False Alarm Ratio (FAR) (Table 5 ). However, all the models exhibited poor performance in capturing the low rain category (i.e., 2.5–7.6 mm/day), with higher number of false alarms and a lower POD in this range (Table 5 ). The analysis indicated that the QPFs derived using the 90th percentile (P90) behaved as an upper limit for potential water savings based on the given forecasts and are presented in the manuscript along with the conventional ensemble mean (EM) approach. There is an increase in the false alarm ratios by about 10 % when the QPFs were derived from P90 instead of EM (Table 5 ). Nevertheless, the probability of detecting heavy rainfall events increased by about 30 %, which could be beneficial from a water-saving perspective. The ensemble mean-derived QPFs of ECM and GEFS models were unable to capture rainfall events exceeding 35.5 mm/day. However, with the P90 derived QPFs, the Critical Success Index (CSI) of these forecast models also improved (Table 5 ).  3.3 Assigning irrigation likelihood classes based on forecast rainfall categories The assessment of rainfall forecasts revealed that the reliability in predicting the likely rainfall category of the event was much higher than the accuracy in terms of absolute magnitude of Quantitative Precipitation Forecasts (QPFs) across the forecast models. Accordingly, to streamline the evaluation process, the QPFs were classified into broader classes representing irrigation likelihood classes, viz.: 1) High Irrigation Possibility (HIP), 2) Moderate Irrigation Possibility (MIP), and 3) Low Irrigation Possibility (LIP). The “no rain (<2.5 mm/day)” category was classified as HIP, the categories of light and moderate rain (2.5–35.5 mm/day) were grouped as MIP, and the rather heavy to very heavy rains (>35.6 mm/day) were classified as LIP (elaborated in section 2.2.1 ). Fig. 6   elucidates the probability of observed rain levels corresponding to the forecasted irrigation likelihood classes. The highest confidence was observed when HIP was forecasted, indicating a minimal chance of missing a rainfall event with the proposed framework (Fig. 4 ) (similar to results from Linker et al., 2018 ). However, when MIP was forecasted, there was a 55–60 % probability that it would be a HIP event. Similarly, LIP had a 6–14 % probability of falling into the HIP category. The mixing of MIP with LIP was prominent, but from an irrigation decision perspective, this became critical only if the forecasted rainfall quantity fell below the next three days' water usage for the crops and/or critical water depth levels needed to be maintained for rice-paddy cultivation. It is important to note that the WRF model exhibited higher confidence in predicting rainfall events, with the highest probability of detection (POD) and low false alarm ratio (FAR) across all three irrigation possibility levels (Fig. 4 a and Table 5 ). As mentioned earlier, the ECM model performed slightly better in simulating MIP events (Fig. 4 b and Table 5 ).  3.4 Optimization of rainfall confidence quotients The Rainfall Confidence Quotients (RCQs) for each lead day (RCQs – RCQ1, RCQ2, RCQ3) were determined using a one-time Genetic Algorithm (GA) procedure for each forecast model (explained in section 2.2.1 ). Initially, assuming a broader range of 0–1 for each RCQ led to longer convergence times and occasional failures. The search space was narrowed to refine the optimization procedure based on the initial runs and insights gained from rainfall forecast verification. The High Irrigation Possibility (HIP), which exhibited high predictability across all models (95–99 %, Fig. 4 ), was excluded from further optimization by assigning an RCQ value of 0 to this category. The Low Irrigation Possibility (LIP) class, predicted with higher confidence (combined probability of detection 83–94 %, Fig. 4 ), had its search space reduced from [0 to 1] to [0.5 to 1] after few iterations. Final values for MIP and LIP classes at different stations, forecast models, and lead times were determined through the Genetic Algorithm (GA) and the results are presented in the supplementary material Fig. S4 . The 2nd day (RCQ ∼ 0.2–0.7) and 3rd day (RCQ ∼ 0.3–0.7) of the forecast resulted in a broader range of values for the MIP category due to the inherent uncertainty associated with predicting this class. Similarly, the LIP in the day-3 forecast had a broader range (0.6–1), reflecting the increased fuzziness in predicting events as lead-time increases. The RCQ values were found to vary across forecast sources (representative of the systematic bias of the forecast model), but the variability remained consistent across the stations. Thus, an averaged value (across stations in the study region) of RCQ for each forecast model, lead time and irrigation likelihood category were used in the study (Table S2 ). Following multiple iterations, a threshold value of 0.7 was resultant from the optimization procedure. This threshold value exhibited minimal variation among different forecast models and was used uniformly within the framework. Whenever the cumulative ΣRCQs exceeds this threshold value (0.7), then a no-irrigation (NO-IRR) switch was passed (Fig. 1 ).  3.5 Assessment of derived irrigation decisions The zone-wise performance of the irrigation decision algorithm is detailed in Table S3 . The CSI values were computed by comparing the irrigation and no-irrigation classifications generated by the forecast models with those derived from actual weather data. Among the forecast models and zones, the decision to trigger irrigation (IRR switch) demonstrated the highest level of certainty (Table S3 ). To keep it concise and prioritize the primary objective of increasing the usage of effective rainfall in irrigation scheduling, this section emphasizes the performance specific to the ‘No-Irrigation (NO-IRR) switch’ (Table 6  ). The Probability of Detection (POD) and False Alarm Ratio (FAR) were specifically computed for the no-irrigation class to assess the performance of different forecast models across years. These metrics provide insights into the reliability of the proposed method when making no-irrigation decisions, which is considered risky. The QPF from P90 outperformed the QPF from EM, particularly in zones Z1 and Z2 (Table S3 ) and during the rainfall deficit season of 2016–17 (Table 6 ). Zones Z1 and Z2 are situated in the upstream region of the basin, which receives heavy rains during the season. The P90 based QPF captured the extreme rainfall occurrences in the forecast model, which were smoothed out and lost in the ensemble mean based QPF. The irrigation decisions derived from the WRF model showed higher POD and lower FAR, like the performance of the rainfall forecast categories (Table 6 ). Interestingly, the P90 QPF derived NO-IRR decision for ECM ensembles exhibited slightly superior performance with this methodology. The use of the 90th percentile captured the skewed nature of the ECM ensembles and represented some heavy rain events that were missed in the ensemble mean of ECM, thus improving the overall performance of the irrigation decisions. However, the GEFS recorded lower performance values compared to the other models and benefited less from the P90 based QPF due to the lesser spread among the ensemble members. During the Pishanam  season of 2016–17, the overall performance was poor due to the rainfall characteristics of the NEM season. The stations recorded low rainfall totals with fewer rainy days (Table 2 ). As discussed earlier, the low to moderate rains were poorly represented in the forecast models, resulting in low POD and higher FAR (Table 6 ) for the simulated irrigation decision in this period. Zones Z3 and Z4 also exhibited lower performance among the forecast models, as most of the rainfall in these regions fell into the moderate rainfall category (Table S3 ). The analysis conducted during the drought year, 2016–17 played a pivotal role in the development of the 3-checkpoint algorithm. It was observed that the cumulative evapo-transpiration checkpoint (Checkpoint 3) had minimal advantages during the wet year of 2015–16. However, in 2016–17, the inclusion of the third checkpoint became imperative to reduce the adverse effects of wrong forecasts on crop yield resulting from an increased number of crop water stress days. Significantly, the incorporation of the three-level decision checks in the proposed methodology led to a reduction in FAR for the predicted 'NO-IRR' decision, effectively minimizing the propagation of uncertainty in rainfall forecasts to irrigation decision, thus reducing the risk due to making a NO-IRR decision.  3.6 Improvements in crop water productivity 3.6.1 Scenario class − irrigation strategy Fig. 5 a and b display the enhancement in irrigation water productivity (IWP) compared to the no-forecast scenario, under two distinct conditions: realistic irrigation (RI) and auto-triggered (AT) settings during the Pishanam  season of 2015–16. During RI conditions (Fig. 5 a), the improvement was highest (20–40 %) across most forecast models. Conversely, the use of AT irrigation strategy (Fig. 5 b) resulted in only a minimal increase (0–10 %) in water productivity. Notably, the realistic irrigation approach led to a significant reduction in the frequency of irrigation. In contrast, the AT scenario (Fig. 5 a) involved a slight delay in triggering the irrigation between different forecast sources (no forecast vs perfect vs imperfect forecasts), but the frequency and quantity of irrigation remained largely unchanged due to the assumption of unrestricted availability of water at any time during the different crop growth stages. However, with AT irrigation strategy, when the critical water depth value was reduced for auto irrigation, there was an increase in irrigation water productivity, accompanied by a reduction in irrigation frequency (not shown here for brevity). Therefore, in scenarios where water availability is not limited, the integration of weather forecasts with advanced water-saving techniques such as alternative wetting and drying (AWD) or the System of Rice Intensification method (SRI) becomes crucial to expand the scope of water savings. The RI-based scenarios provided a more accurate representation of the irrigation water availability (rotational irrigation) in the study area. As this scenario aligns with the primary focus of this study and effectively demonstrated the significant impact of utilizing weather forecasts, the subsequent discussions are predominantly centered around the RI strategy.  3.6.2 Scenario classes – Weather forecast sources and ensemble nature of the rainfall forecasts The differences in the resulting crop water productivity between the different forecast models and the perfect forecast (observed weather data) was minimal in the realistic irrigation scenario. This clearly demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed methodology in handling uncertain forecasts. Particularly, the uncertainty of the moderate rainfall intensities, which are critical for irrigation decisions, was well handled by the robust methodology proposed for irrigation decision checks. However, GEFS-based forecasts exhibited lower performance compared to WRF and ECM-based forecasts (Fig. 5 a). As described in the methods Section 2.7 , the ensemble mean (EM) and 90th percentile (P90) were utilized to determine the QPF value used in irrigation decision-making. Fig. 5 a illustrates the improvement in IWP when P90 was employed. The simulations with QPF from P90 enhanced the usability of weather forecasts, performing on par with perfect forecast cases. In some instances, imperfect weather forecasts resulted in better water savings than perfect forecast cases (observed weather data), primarily due to the efficiency of the proposed methodology in using the uncertainty in rainfall prediction by the ensemble forecasts. The methodology employed in this study addresses the false alarms by ensuring that in case of highly uncertain forecasted rainfall event, irrigation is skipped only when the soil moisture levels are higher than the specified critical levels. The conservative model algorithm was able to utilize soil moisture buffer to accommodate uncertain forecasts, thus lesser irrigation frequency in anticipation of falsely forecasted rainfall. The irrigation decisions derived from EM tend to smoothen the extremes, yielding slightly lower performance when compared to perfect forecast cases. The ECM-based forecasts exhibited similarity in the simulated IWP values to that from WRF while using QPFs from P90, mainly attributed to the higher number of ensembles and the skewed nature of the ECM ensemble members. Consequently, due to this characteristic, WRF simulations demonstrated more significant improvements in Irrigation Water Productivity (IWP) than ECM in simulations involving EM. In both cases (EM and P90), the GEFS-based ensembles produced similar results, as the spread between the ensemble members was the least among the three weather forecast models. The most significant differences in water savings performance between the ensemble mean and P90 methods were observed in zones Z1, Z2, Z3, and Z4. The P90 method notably exhibited superior performance in enhancing IWP, reducing runoff, and lowering irrigation frequency. In zones Z1 and Z2, improvements were observed due to better simulation of moderate to heavy rains, while in Z3 and Z4, the P90 method effectively represented low to moderate rainfall events.  3.6.3 Performance during different crop years The impact and implications of the methodology were demonstrated during two Pishanam  seasons: one characterized by rainfall deficit (2016–17) and the other by rainfall excess (2015–16). These two years showed significant variations in the number of rainy days, rainfall intensity, and cumulative rainfall for the season. In 2016–17, the observed rainfall mainly fell within the low-moderate category (<35.5 mm/day), with an average of around 20 rainy days. Some stations received rainfall for only 4–10 days (Table 2 ), making predictability for these moderate events crucial during the 2016–17 Pishanam  season. The perfect forecasts (Fig. 5 c), with lower uncertainty, yielded the highest improvement in irrigation water productivity. Spatial plots and graphs in Fig. S5  further illustrated that the perfect forecast scenario resulted in higher IWP, reduced runoff, and decreased irrigation frequency compared to imperfect forecast cases for 2016–17. Variability between the source forecast models was more pronounced during the year 2016–17, particularly in zones Z3 and Z4, due to uncertainty in forecasted rainfall in those regions (Section 3.4 ). The simulations with QPF from P90 demonstrated better performance in improving water savings (Fig. 5 d). On the other hand, EM failed to improve IWP during the Pishanam  season of 2016–17. The proposed method was strictly constrained using a 3-checkpoint algorithm and assignment of variable RCQs to the 3-day forecasts with the primary aim of minimizing the risk of crop water stress. As a result, the improvement in IWP was not as prominent when the QPFs from EM were used. In contrast, P90 effectively utilized forecast uncertainty and represented certain events smoothed out in the ensemble mean.   3.7 Spatial variability in the performance of IWP, runoff reduction, and irrigation frequency Building upon the findings presented in section 3.5  and considering the recommendations from study by Muller et al. (2021) , we strategically utilized the 90th percentile (P90) of the forecasted rainfall quantities during the vegetative and ripening stages of the crop season. In contrast, we employed the ensemble mean (EM) from the QPFs during the transplanting and reproductive stages (most critical phases). Instead of uniformly applying either P90 or EM throughout the entire season, the QPF was strategically calculated to utilize uncertainty in weather forecasts, particularly during less critical phases of crop development. From analyzing the zone-wise distribution of the improvement in IWP (Fig. 6 ), it was evident that perfect forecasts (observed weather data) outperformed weather forecast models in most zones. Nevertheless, perfect forecasts showed a higher spread (25th percentile – 75th percentile boxes) in zones Z3 (green) and Z4 (blue). Particularly, the 25th percentile range of IWP improvement was considerably lower in perfect forecasts compared to WRF and ECM-based forecasts. This suggested that for certain sites, WRF and ECM-based forecasts yielded higher improvements due to the advantage of the proposed methodology. As explained earlier, the conservative methodology successfully capitalized on forecast uncertainties with only minimal impact on crop yield (without undue crop water stress that may affect the yield). Water wastage in the form of runoff from rainfall was notably reduced in zones Z3, Z4, Z5, and Z6, with similar reductions observed across perfect, WRF-based, and ECM-based simulations (Fig. 6 b). It is instructive to highlight that the usage of WRF and ECM forecasts led to a reduction in irrigation frequency comparable to that achieved with perfect forecasts. In some sites (Z3 and Z6), the irrigation frequency was even lower than that of perfect forecasts (not shown here for brevity). As irrigation scheduling effectively utilized the forecasts in the proposed method, the IWP became more correlated with rainfall (Fig. S6 ). The correlation is higher as the quantity of rainfall increased, resulting in higher variability between forecast sources. Among the weather forecast models, the IWP based on WRF forecast-based irrigation schedules showed the highest correlation (0.54) with rainfall totals. Notably, the most significant improvements were observed for perfect forecasts, closely followed by WRF forecasts, particularly when seasonal rainfall exceeded 250 mm. In some instances, WRF outperformed perfect forecasts due to reduced irrigation frequency in anticipation of rainfall in specific zones. This was due to the slightly over-predicting behavior of WRF-P90 forecasts used in the methodology. For moderate seasonal rainfall totals (100–250 mm), ECM forecasts were on par or slightly better than the other forecast models. The superiority of the ECM model in predicting moderate daily rainfall contributed to generating reliable irrigation decisions specifically in this rainfall category. Nevertheless, in cases of low rainfall scenarios (less than 50 mm/season), no enhancements in IWP were evident when compared to situations without forecasts, even when perfect forecasts were employed. This outcome can be attributed primarily to the robust 3-step decision check algorithm, which prioritized minimal risk from a crop water stress standpoint.  3.8 Discussion A detailed analysis of day-wise simulations at representative sites is presented in Fig. 7  . In Fig. 7 a, the accumulated rainfall forecasts for a 3-day window are compared to observed rainfall in the top panel, with simulated irrigation signals from the decision algorithm in the middle panel and simulated water levels at the “Gadana Dam” (ID No 6 from Fig. 2 ) site during the Pishanam  season of 2015–16 in the bottom panel. The field-collected data at the “Gadana Dam” site allowed us to assess the performance using ground-realized irrigation schedules. During the major rainfall period from 22 Nov 2015 till 15 Dec 2015, the forecast models accurately represented the rainfall, leading to significantly reduced irrigation application. The water levels remained near the bund height of 70 mm throughout this period, even without irrigation, indicating effective water conservation. In the actual field-applied irrigation schedules more water was lost in runoff during this period due to the unanticipated rainfall with existing irrigation practices (NF). The proposed methodology saved approximately 190–230 mm of irrigation water and reduced irrigation frequency by 4–6 times within the season. The water savings from WRF and ECM was comparable to the perfect forecasts. However, during one moderate rainfall event (<30 mm/3 days – 25 Dec 2015 – 29 Dec 2015), the imperfect forecasts (WRF and ECM) missed the opportunity for water saving due to the strict 3-check procedure employed in the proposed methodology that minimizes the crop water stress due to an uncertain forecast. Fig. 7 b shows that all the rainfall recorded at the “Gadana Dam” site during the Pishanam  2016–17 season fell within the range of < 50 mm/3-days. There were three opportunities to save water during this season, but imperfect forecasts (WRF and ECM) were only able to capitalize on one event due to the strict constraints applied in the 3-step decision check algorithm. Even though rainfall was simulated in the last week of December 2016 and the third week of January 2017, irrigation application was not stopped due to the next 3-day cumulative evapotranspiration exceeding the expected rainfall amount. The simulations from the “Palayamkottai” (ID No 16 from Fig. 2 ) site during Pishanam  2015–16 (Fig. 7 c) showed that the water savings from imperfect forecast scenarios were slightly higher than that of the perfect forecast scenario. In the perfect forecast scenario, the event that occurred in mid-December 2016 was not considered as its magnitude was lower than the consumptive water use of the crop. However, the forecasts from WRF and ECM exhibited a slight overestimation of this event, indicating an early initiation of the rainfall event, which allowed them to take advantage of the false anticipation of its early occurrence. However, such false anticipation could result in increased errors and the unnecessary skipping of irrigation when rainfall is not actually expected. The proposed methodology was developed to address this limitation by ensuring that uncertain rainfall forecasts are considered in the decision-making process only when the crop growth stage was not critical and antecedent water levels are significantly above critical levels. Fig. 7 d reveals that imperfect forecasts highly overestimated the rainfall for the “Kalampatti” (ID No 10 from Fig. 2 ) site from 28th October 2016 to 10th November 2016 in the Pishanam  2016–17 season. However, these overestimations did not lead to a NO-IRR switch because the water levels dropped significantly, reaching critical levels during the algorithm's reproductive phase. The WRF-based irrigation decisions were able to save slightly more water than ECM and GEFS due to better simulation of rainfall quantity and timing on 15th November 2016. It is vital to highlight that in most crop sites, more significant water savings were achieved whenever rains were forecasted during the vegetative phase. This favorable outcome was due to the overlap of this phase with the peak North-East Monsoon season, during which forecasts from different model sources exhibited reasonable certainty. Furthermore, the water depth limit for the vegetative phase was set lower based on guidelines from previous studies (Luo et al., 2022; Gedam et al., 2023 ), allowing the model to accept the decision of no irrigation even with lower standing water depths. The zones categorized as early and mid-rice (Z1, Z2, Z3, and Z4) most used these rainfall occurrences. During the Pishanam  season of 2016–17, moderate spells were observed in January 2017, which the rainfall forecasting models also captured. However, the uncertainty surrounding these events was high, resulting in more false alarms. Given the critical importance of the reproductive phase (which coincided with January), a higher standing water depth threshold was adopted to avoid potential water stress and its adverse impact on crop productivity during this stage. As a result, most rainfall occurrences during this period did not trigger a NO-IRR decision. Significant spatial variations were observed within the Tamirabharani basin, primarily attributed to the distinct climate regimes and soil types. Regions with higher levels of rainfall (e.g., Z1, Z2) demonstrated improvements in IWP, with 30 % improvement across forecast models for 2015–16 and 10 % for 2016–17 in Z1, and 37 % improvement for 2015–16 and 12 % for 2016–17 in Z2. In contrast, semi-arid areas and low fertile soil types, like Z4 (23 % for 2015–16; 2 % for 2016–17) and Z5 (18 % for 2015–16; 2 % for 2016–17), experienced a lesser enhancement in IWP. With the proposed methodology, regions with clay and silt soil types (Z3 and Z4) exhibited a pronounced reduction in runoff. Furthermore, the choice of cropping pattern was found to play a crucial role in the derived benefits from weather forecasts. The proposed method proved advantageous in regions with early sowing dates, allowing crops to maximize benefits from regional rainfall patterns. Overall, using model and neighborhood ensembles increased the reliability of the rainfall forecasts. After implementing the neighborhood ensemble approach, the differences between the forecast sources were reduced significantly. The improvements in IWP for ECM ranged between 3–35 % which is similar to WRF based implementation. However, the regional scale model ensemble from the WRF configuration significantly improved the predictability of heavy rainfall events, the accuracy of simulated rainfall quantities, and the timing of occurrences. Despite a slight decrease in rainfall performance with increasing lead times across forecast models, the non-uniform RCQ helped reduce uncertainty in utilizing these forecasts in irrigation decision-making. The proposed 3-checkpoint algorithm was designed to minimize crop water stress, and in the 800 simulations conducted, crop yield reduction was nearly non-existent. The methodology positively utilized highly uncertain rainfall forecasts in numerous instances when the risk of crop water stress was minimal. This was particularly evident during conditions with higher standing water depths and lower 3-day cumulative evapotranspiration, influenced by factors such as overcast conditions or the crop's phenological stage. Table 7   demonstrates that, for the WRF forecasts, the CSI (Critical Success Index) for predicting a “No Irrigation Switch” (NO-IRR) was higher than the CSI for forecasting a rain event across most zones and crop years. The 3-checkpoint algorithm reduced the risk from a crop water stress perspective, leading to an overall increase in CSI values of the resulting No-IRR switch classification. However, it is to be noted that the irrigation interval in the study region was relatively short (<10 days), so the implications of false alarms might be more significant in regions with longer intervals between irrigation applications. The methodology allows for modifying water level and consumptive water use thresholds based on the averaged interval between irrigation expected in the region of interest. The proposed approach demonstrated reasonable water savings even in zones with longer intervals between irrigation cycles (Zones Z3 and Z4). Moreover, during the monsoon failure year of Pishanam  2016–17, the methodology effectively utilized the available opportunities to save water without causing crop water stress. The proposed methodology demonstrated its potential utility across diverse hydro-climatic conditions, including arid-like climatology and regions with limited irrigation water access, through 800 experiments conducted in various scenarios within the context of regional agricultural practices.   4 Conclusions The study focused on incorporating ensemble rainfall forecasts (with a 3-day lead time) into a regionally calibrated gridded crop model, aimed to closely represent real field conditions in a rice-paddy intensive system. The ensemble weather forecasts from prevalent and publicly available global climate model datasets, such as the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) and National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) with a 3-day lead time, were utilized in the study. A high resolution (4 km × 4 km), WRF multi-physics ensemble model, calibrated for diverse seasons and regions within southern peninsular India, was also employed. The study introduced a novel quasi-farmer behavior decision routine featuring a unique 3-checkpoint algorithm that combines probabilistic weather forecasts with a crop model to make irrigation decisions. The validity and usefulness of the methodology have been rigorously tested across a range of scenarios, each representing unique climate regimes, soil types, cropping seasons, and management practices, encompassing approximately 800 simulation experiments. The key insights from the study are as follows:• The study recommended employing a neighborhood ensemble approach to address spatial biases observed across different forecast models. This technique significantly enhanced the accuracy of publicly available, coarser resolution ECM forecasts (50 km; 50 ensembles) to a level comparable with locally configured, computationally intensive WRF forecasts (4 km; 7 ensembles). The proposed method helped in utilizing the increased number of ensembles and their characteristics, allowing information extraction from ECM (increased to 200 ensemble members) that equaled the performance of the WRF model (increased to 63 ensemble members). This outcome underscores the importance of robust methodologies for integrating weather forecasts into irrigation decision-making rather than solely focusing on forecast accuracy improvements (Mishra et al., 2013; Gedam et al., 2023 ). In 2016–17, characterized by a lower frequency of moderate-intensity rain events, WRF forecasts outperformed other models due to their improved precision in event timing and quantity. Additionally, WRF demonstrated superior performance for stations experiencing heavy rainfall.  • Methodical incorporation of QPFs calculated by the ensemble mean, and the 90th percentile from the ensemble members of each model into the crop modeling framework helped reduce the risk due to uncertain forecasts while utilizing the uncertainty range positively. The upper threshold, represented by the 90th percentile, was adopted during less risky crop phenological stages, such as vegetative and ripening. Conversely, the ensemble mean was employed during high-risk crop growth stages like transplanting and reproduction. This novel strategy reduced the computational time needed for running the model with each ensemble member and effectively utilized the ensemble forecasts' probabilistic nature.  • The study introduced an innovative strategy by suggesting the inclusion of Rain Confidence Quotients, a normalized value assigned based on the likelihood of occurrence of a rainfall category that would be relevant for irrigation decisions. The RCQs vary based on the rainfall category, forecast model, and forecast lead time. The value of RCQs was also optimized based on the classification accuracy of the resultant binary (yes/no) irrigation decisions. This approach proved particularly beneficial for making an irrigation decision based on the rainfall category rather than specific rainfall quantities from uncertain weather forecast models. The irrigation decisions derived from the high-resolution locally tuned WRF model showed higher POD (0.81) and lower FAR (0.29) in most zones, similar to the performance of the rainfall forecasts.  • The examination of the performance during drought crop season, Pishanam  2016–17, played a crucial role in developing a 3-checkpoint algorithm. This algorithm encompassed forecasts of crop water requirements as one of the checkpoints. In the year 2015–16, this checkpoint showed limited benefits. However, during the Pishanam  season of 2016–17, the implementation of rainfall-based and water level-based checkpoints (checkpoints 1 and 2) alone led to a reduction in yield followed by a subsequent increase in irrigation frequency compared to the conventional irrigation scenario. This increase in irrigation frequency resulted from increased crop stress due to skipped irrigation at critical time from decisions based on uncertain weather forecasts, as observed in Cao et al. (2019) . Depending solely on two checkpoints overlooked the significance of cumulative evapotranspiration (crop water requirement), a critical factor, particularly in the arid-like conditions witnessed in 2016–17. This additional crop water requirement checkpoint (checkpoint 3) overcame this limitation.  • The enhanced methodology increased the irrigation water productivity (IWP), averaging around 20–30 % across spatial locations and various forecast model sources during the Pishanam  rice season 2015–16, in contrast to the conventional irrigation approach (NF scenario). In the Pishanam  season of 2016–17, the improvement in IWP ranged between 2–10 %. These improvements were accompanied by a noteworthy reduction of 20–33 % in surface runoff from rainfall during 2015–16 and a 6–23 % reduction in surface runoff during 2016–17, which was effectively used to meet the crop water requirement. Additionally, an average reduction of 3–4 % in irrigation frequency was observed in 2015–16, while a 1–2 % reduction was noted in 2016–17. On an average, 200–500 mm of water savings were recorded in the Pishanam  season of 2015–16, while 100–300 mm of water savings were achieved during the Pishanam  season of 2016–17.  • In 2015–16, there was no significant difference between the results from perfect and imperfect forecasts, encompassing WRF, ECM, and GEFS. Given the wet year conditions, differences were minimal with the proposed methodology. In several cases, using the QPFs from P90 of WRF and ECM exhibited equivalent performance to perfect forecasts in enhancing IWP. In the Pishanam  season of 2016–17, a significant difference was noticed between the usage of perfect and imperfect forecasts. Limited rainfall events underscored the importance of accurate timing and quantity of rainfall for IWP enhancement. While stations with perfect forecasts recorded increased IWP by 20–35 %, imperfect forecasts yielded a more modest 3–20 % improvement. The WRF-based irrigation decision methodology yielded higher IWP (10–60 % during 2015–16; 0–30 % during 2016–17) than publicly available forecast models such as ECM and GEFS.    The study emphasizes quantifying the utility of ensemble weather forecasts in irrigation decision-making, utilizing fixed water depths for simulation. Future research could explore optimization with variable water depths (more dynamically varying across space and time) and alternative wetting and drying methods, accounting for practical challenges in developing nations without water pricing structures (Mishra et al., 2013; Cao et al., 2019; Gedam et al., 2023 ). While the binary irrigation decision approach suits evaluation, transitioning to a spectrum of risk levels for real-time application, as suggested by Guo et al. (2023)  and Chen et al. (2024) , offers independent decision-making opportunities for the farmers. The irrigation intervals in the study was not exceeding 10 days.
