However, for regions or years when the irrigation is available in longer intervals, adaptive adjustments to decision window duration within a given season could be more relevant (Wang and Cai, 2009; Kelly et al., 2023 ). The seamless integration emphasized in our study and the detailed gridded model setup can fuel the use of weather forecasts across diverse sectors, particularly in aiding decision-making for various agricultural management practices. Importantly, our proposed methodology avoids the complexity of relying heavily on observed weather data or field water measurements. Instead, it connects this knowledge to implement effective strategies, utilizing readily available global weather model forecasts and remote sensing techniques. Establishing such a framework, supported by comprehensive field-scale data collection efforts, can significantly contribute to instilling trust and reliability among farmers. Furthermore, integrating these robust field-scale models into basin-scale hydrological models allows for examining their impact on water allocations and formulating guidelines responsive to evolving climatic conditions (Jiang et al., 2021 ).
1 Introduction Soil salinization stands as a significant process contributing to global land degradation and soil desertification (Peng et al., 2019; Jia et al., 2022 ). Approximately 11.74 million hectares of land worldwide are salt-affected, especially in arid and semi-arid as well as coastal regions, with 60.8 % situated in Asia (Hassani et al., 2020 ). Countries such as Kazakhstan, Russia, China, Iran, India, and Indonesia in Asia grapple with severe soil salinization (Vargas et al., 2018 ), leading to decreasing crop yield, agricultural productivity and posing a significant threat to local food security and ecosystem health (Hamdy and Aly, 2014 ). Therefore, understanding the distribution of salt-affected soils and their driving factors is critical for sustainable agriculture and development. Traditional soil monitoring relies on a combination of field sampling and laboratory analysis, which provides accurate discrete data for each sampling site (Guo et al., 2021 ). However, this method is time-consuming, labor-intensive and expensive, making it impractical for large-scale applications (Zeng et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2021 ). Discrete data are usually converted into spatial continuous data using predictive methods of spatial distribution. Currently, spatial interpolation methods are extensively utilized in soil sciences to characterize soil properties due to their solid theoretical foundation and easy implementation such as inverse distance weighting (Shukla et al., 2020 ), global polynomial interpolation (Antal et al., 2021 ), splines (Wu et al., 2013 ), radial basis function (Bhunia et al., 2016 ) and ordinary kriging (Abdulmanov et al., 2021 ). However, the accuracy of these interpolation methods hinges on intensive samples, rendering them less effective with sparse samples, primarily applicable at field or small basin scales (Long et al., 2018; Zhao and Wang, 2020 ). In the coastal field of Miyandoroud in Iran, Emadi and Baghernejad (2014)  characterized the spatial distributions of soil pH and electrical conductivity (ECe) using three interpolation techniques. In the Sangong River watershed in arid northwest China, Wang et al. (2018)  identified the spatial patterns of soil salt content using geostatistical methods. While some efforts have been made to upscale these techniques to larger scales, such as national levels, challenges persist due to uncontrollable accuracy. For instance, Eldeiry and García (2011)  observed unacceptable predictions for soil salinity when using the geostatistical interpolation technique with sampling spacing larger than 1,500 m. Therefore, studying the spatial characteristics of soil salinity or sodicity at the national or global scale remains a considerable challenge (El hafyani et al., 2019 ). Prediction models based on remote sensing (RS) data and multiple spatial data have emerged as alternatives to overcome limitations associated with spatial interpolation techniques. These models facilitate spatial prediction without necessitating intensive sampling and laboratory analysis, proving crucial for monitoring environmental indicators like soil salinization, atmospheric pollution, and natural hazard assessment (Bozdağ et al., 2020; Pourghasemi et al., 2020; Taghizadeh-Mehrjardi et al., 2021 ). Notably, researchers have employed such models to predict soil salinity from field to regional scales (Ochieng et al., 2013; Hassani et al., 2020; Ivushkin et al., 2019 ;). For instance, Cui et al. (2023)  demonstrated the utility of multi-spectral remote sensing data combined with machine learning models for quickly monitoring farmland soil salt content. Wang et al. (2019)  employed a multi-algorithm approach and environmental covariates to determine the spatial distribution of soil salinity in three distinct areas in Xinjiang Province, China. Mandal et al. (2009)  mapped the salt-affected soils in India, while Ivushkin et al. (2019)  enhanced the global understanding of soil salinity by generating a classification map using random forest classification with soil properties maps. Furthermore, Hassani et al. (2020)  integrated machine-learning (ML) techniques with a comprehensive set of climatic, topographic, soil, and remote sensing data to predict the spatiotemporal distribution of soil salinity and sodicity on a global scale from 1980 to 2018. Although the prediction models based on RS data can achieve results from field to global scales, quantifying their uncertainty is crucial for evaluating the credibility of prediction results. However, current studies only provided the definite prediction value at a specific point, ignoring the prediction uncertainty analysis (Baroni et al., 2017 ). Therefore, combining predictive models and uncertainty analysis is imperative for more accurate estimations of target variables. In the researches aforementioned, environmental covariates data typically derive from RS data, terrain attributes, climatic variables, and the derivatives of soil maps (Baltensweiler et al., 2021 ). These data sources are easily accessed and offer comprehensive coverage of factors influencing soil formation (Omuto et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020 ). For instance, RS data provide multiple levels of information reflecting crucial elements such as soils, organisms, and parent material (Ivushkin et al., 2019 ). Topography plays a significant role in soil salt distribution and redistribution (Taghizadeh-Mehrjardi et al., 2014 ), while climate significantly impacts the formation of salt-affected soils in arid and semi-arid regions (Qadir et al., 2008 ). ECe represents the degree of soil salinity, while ESP indicates the degree of soil sodicity (Richards, 1954; Isbell, 1995 ). Soil pH is another crucial indicator for diagnosing saline soils, as alkaline conditions can exacerbate the accumulation and mobility of salts in the soil (Datta et al., 2019 ). Therefore, the USDA classification scheme for salt-affected soils recommends using at least these three indicators-ECe, ESP, and pH, to accurately assess and classify salt-affected soils (Omuto et al., 2020 ), which has been widely adopted in the field of soil salinization assessment (Chhabra, 2005 ; Abbas et al., 2013; Li et al., 2022 ). However, existing regional studies mainly concentrate on soil salinity (measured by ECe), while few address soil sodicity (represented by ESP), leading to an incomplete understanding of soil salinization dynamics. For instance, Ivushkin et al. (2019)  predicted global soil salinization by generating a classification map that primarily emphasized soil salinity and did not consider soil sodicity. However, the classification of soil sodicity is also important, as the chemical properties and treatment of sodic soils differ significantly from those of saline soils (Qadir et al., 2007; Choudhary and Kharche, 2018; Litalien and Zeeb, 2020 ; Daba and Qureshi, 2021). This underscores the need for a more comprehensive approach to studying soil salinization that includes both soil salinity and soil sodicity. The mathematical relationship between target soil variables and their predictors can be elucidated from traditional regression models to sophisticated ML models (Omuto et al., 2020 ). While multiple regression models are straightforward to build and understand, they tend to be less accurate in complex environments. In contrast, ML models can better fit complex nonlinear relationships, although the model performance varies across different datasets. For example, Peng et al. (2019)  used Cubist to achieve good results with a coefficient of determination (r 2 ) of 0.92 in predicting soil salinity in a desert-oasis ecotone of the Aksu River Basin in China. Conversely, the soil salinity prediction accuracy (r 2 ) of Taghizadeh-Mehrjardi et al. (2014)  was only 0.11 in the Ardakan region, central Iran. No single algorithm suits soil salinity prediction in all scenarios (Abedi et al., 2021 ). Therefore, a comparison of various algorithms is recommended to obtain the optimal predictive model (Wang et al., 2020 ). Cubist, random forest (RF), quantile regression forest (QRF), and quantile regression neural network (QRNN) generally perform well in soil properties mapping, with QRF demonstrating remarkable success in regional soil mapping, globally (Baltensweiler et al., 2021; Helfenstein et al., 2022 ). Asia spans an extensive area of 44.58 million km2 , which is threatened by serious soil salinization with the largest area of salt-affected soil (Mandal et al., 2018; Hassani et al., 2020; Negacz et al., 2022 ). The region encompasses diverse climate zones, including cold, temperate, and thermal regions, characterized by complex climate patterns such as monsoons and continental climates. The terrain is highly undulating, with elevated central areas surrounded by lower terrain. The latest FAO’s Global Map of Salt-Affected Soils (GSASmap) covers 118 countries (FAO, 2021 ), while the results are not available for half of Asian countries, such as Kazakhstan, China, Iran and Indonesia. The large-scale area and complex environmental conditions make it particularly challenging and necessary to understand its spatial distribution, characteristics and underlying driving factors for the sustainable development of saline agriculture in this region. To address these issues, we carried out the study to take both soil salinity and sodicity into account to produce maps of salt-affected soils with uncertainty assessment in Asia by using and comparing 5 machine learning methods, and the soil salinization driving factors in this region were then analyzed. The overall objectives of this study are to (1) distinguish the best prediction model from 5 ML models, including Cubist, RF, QRF, QRNN and a simple model for comparison, MLR; (2) generate the spatial distribution of soil salinization indicators, namely ECe, pH, and ESP, as well as salt-affected soils at the continental scale to fill the gap in Asia; (3) evaluate the uncertainty of the optimal model for each prediction indicator; (4) identify the main driving factors of soil salinity and sodicity at two depths (0–30 cm and 30–100 cm). The results aim to deepen our understanding of soil salinization and provide a comprehensive method for predicting the spatial pattern of soil attributes with significant variability at a large scale.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The study area is mainly located in Asia and Russia, which crosses both Asia and Europe as shown in Fig. 1  , situated between longitude 25°39′ E ∼ 137°03′ E and latitudes 05°55′N ∼ 55°26′N. The topography is complex and varied, comprising five major terrains: mountains, hills, basins, plateaus and plains, with elevation ranges from a maximum of 8,660 m to a minimum of −412 m (Werner, 2001 ). Various land use patterns are evident in the region predominantly featuring farmland, towns, forests and water bodies. Overall, the temperature demonstrates a decreasing trend from south to north across the region, with a maximum annual average temperature of 31.71 °C and a minimum annual average temperature of −20.94 °C (Fick and Hijmans, 2017 ).  2.2 Soil salinization data The three predictive variables used were ECe, pH and ESP. Observed data of these three variables were obtained from various databases and literature, including the World Soil Information Service (WoSIS) (Batjes et al., 2020 ), Soil and Topographic Database (SOTER) (van Engelen and Ting-tiang, 2013 ), ISRIC-Wise database version 3.1 (WISE3) (Batjes, 2009 ), Land Resources of Russia (Stolbovoi and McCallum, 2002 ), and Saline Soils in China (Wang et al., 1993 ). The number and depth of samples for each soil profile were different. To ensure consistency, the three soil salinity variables (ECe, pH, ESP) were harmonized by weighted averages at two standardized soil depth intervals (0–30 cm and 30–100 cm). The locations and summary statistics of the final data used are shown in Fig. 2  . The total non-zero data for ECe numbered 22,803, distributed across 4,066 soil profiles. Non-zero pH data totaled 30,821, spanning in 6,146 soil profiles. Non-zero data of ESP numbered 12,961, spanning in 2,692 soil profiles. Across all samples, the ranges of ECe, pH, and ESP varied from 0.001 to 96.74 dS/m, 4.00 to 9.19, and 0.11 to 74.56 %, respectively. The mean values of ECe, pH, and ESP were 2.19 dS/m, 6.85, and 5.85 % for topsoil (0–30 cm), and 1.89 dS/m, 6.64, and 6.75 % for subsoil (30–100 cm). Moreover, ECe and ESP exhibited strongly variability with a coefficient of variation (C.V.) ≥ 119.52 %, while pH exhibited moderately variability with C.V. ≤ 20.66 %.  2.3 Predictors In this study, the predictors chosen to predict the target soil variables (ECe, pH, ESP) were based on the five main environmental factors, including soil, climate, organism, relief and parent material (McBratney et al., 2003 ). A total of 24 predictors were used, categorized into three types: 15 remote sensing (RS) image derivatives, 6 digital elevation model (DEM) derivatives, and 3 climatic derivatives as shown in Table 1  . RS image derivatives served as predictors representing soil, organisms and parent materials for predicting salt-affected soils (Taghizadeh-Mehrjardi et al., 2021 ). DEM derivatives represented relief (Peng et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019 ), while climate emerged as an important driving factors of soil salinization, particularly in arid and semi-arid areas (Schaetzl and Anderson, 2005 ). All the predictors were normalized using a Z-score method to ensure that all variables had the same scale and range, and all variables were resampled to a joint spatial resolution of 1000 m. 2.3.1 RS image derivatives Average annual RS images with cloud coverage of < 10 % for the period of 2013–2021 were acquired from Landsat-8 Tier 1 SR (surface reflectance) via the Google Earth Engine (GEE) Platform (Gorelick et al., 2017 ). 14 image indices were used in this study as shown in Table 1 , such as NSI , SI 1, SI 2, SI 3, SI 4, SI 5, SI 6, SAVI , VSSI , NDSI , NDVI , SR , CRSI , and BI , which were obtained from six Landsat-8 image bands (B2 (Blue, 450–520 nm), B3 (Green, 520–600 nm), B4 (Red, 630–690 nm), B5 (Infrared, 770–900 nm), B6 (Shortwave Infrared, 1550–1750 nm) and B7 (Shortwave Infrared, 2090–2350 nm)). It is worth noting that original images from B2-B7 with a spatial resolution of 30 m were resampled to 1000 m in GEE. The 14 image indices calculated are presented in Fig. 3  . The correlation coefficients between the 14 image indices are shown in Fig. S1 (a). The values greater than 0.80, implied a higher probability of multicollinearity problem in the RS image derivatives. Consequently, the multicollinearity was removed by reducing the data bulk using the principal component analysis (a commonly used method for dimensionality reduction and multicollinearity elimination of data). According to the principal component presented in Fig. S1 (b), the first 5 principal components (PCs), which accounted for over 98 % of the explained variation, were deemed sufficient to represent the 14 image indices effectively. Additionally, the land cover/use was represented by a single variable lcover  as shown in Table 1  and Fig. 3 (o). It is a data product of RS image derivatives representing the comprehensive result of surface landscapes influenced by natural conditions and human activities, providing vital information for soil salinity modeling. This data was produced by the European Space Agency (ESA) Climate Change Initiative (CCI) (https://www.esa-landcover-cci.org/ ). The initial spatial resolution of the land cover image is 300 m and resampled to 1000 m in this study.  2.3.2 DEM derivatives Five topographic variables including DEM , slope , loncurve , ls , cnbl  and valley  (Table 1  and Fig. 4  ), were calculated as input variables using SRTM DEM (Shuttle Radar Topography Mission) (Werner, 2001 ) and the System for Automated Geoscientific Analyses-Geographic Information System (SAGA–GIS) software (Olaya and Conrad, 2009 ). SRTM DEM data was collected in 2000 with a spatial resolution of 30 m, which can be downloaded using the Google Earth Engine (GEE) platform (https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/USGS_SRTMGL1_003 ).  2.3.3 Climatic derivatives Three climatic covariates, rain , tmax , and wind  (Table 1  and Fig. 5  ) used in this study, were obtained from the WorldClim version 2.1 dataset (https://www.worldclim.org/ ) with a spatial resolution of 1000 m (Fick and Hijmans, 2017 ). All input covariates exhibited a variance inflation factor (VIF) of less than 10, indicating no significant multicollinearity among the predictors (Kroll and Song, 2013; Phan et al., 2024 ).   2.4 Methods for spatial modeling of indicators of salt-affected soils The three indicators (ECe, pH, ESP) used to classify the salt-affected soil levels were modeled employing 5 different ML methods, from which the most effective was selected for prediction. Subsequently, the uncertainty of these indicators was assessed. Finally, the main drivers of soil salinity and sodicity at two depths (0–30 cm and 30–100 cm) were identified using feature importance (FI) and local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME) methods. The methodological framework of the study is shown in Fig. 6  . 2.4.1 Machine learning methods used to predict the three indicators The mathematical relationships between the indicators of salt-affected soils (ECe, pH, ESP) and predictors were established by ML models. Specifically, the most suitable model was selected from 4 different types of ML models, including Cubist, Random Forest (RF), Quantile Regression Forests (QRF) and Quantile Regression Neural Network (QRNN). To provide a comprehensive assessment of these ML models, a simple mathematical model, Multiple Linear Regression (MLR), was also used in this study. Cubist is a rule-based ML model and popular in predicting soil salinity (Peng et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020 ). As each rule contains an MLR model for predicting a target variable, Cubist is also considered a piecewise linear tree model (Ma et al., 2017 ). Cubist generally provides superior predictions than results from simple models and is also easier to understand compared to neural networks. RF is a bagging-based ensemble learning technique, and its basic unit is classification and regression trees (CARTs) formed by bootstrap sampling (Breiman, 2001 ). As the final prediction is produced by voting among the trees or averaging all the trees (Yuan et al., 2017 ), RF is more accurate and robust to overfitting and noise than single CART, which can be expressed as:(1) μ ̂  x    = ∑ i = 1  n  w i  x    Y i      where, wi  (x ) is the weight vector; Yi   is observations; n  is the number of observations; μ ^  x       can be viewed as the approximation of the conditional mean of Y  given covariate X   = x . QRF, an extension of RF, specifically estimates conditional quantiles (Meinshausen, 2006 ), retaining the value of all observations in that leaf. Consequently, QRF is particularly well suited for high-dimensional data and is more competitive than linear and tree-based methods (Baltensweiler et al., 2021 ). In detail, RF only provides the approximation of the conditional mean E (Y  | X   = x ) by a weighted mean over the observations of Y  (Eq. (1) ), while QRF also estimates the cumulative distribution function (c.d.f.) F (y  | X   = x ), namely(2) F ( y | X = x )  = P ( Y ⩽ y | X = x )  = E 1 { Y ⩽ y }   | X = x          (3) F ̂  ( y | X = x )  = ∑ i = 1  n  w i  ( x )  1 Y ⩽ y           where, F y | X = x       is the cumulative distribution function of Y  given a covariate X ; F ^  y | X = x       is the estimation of E (1{ Y  ≤ y  }  | X   = x ) by the weighted mean over the observations of 1{ Y  ≤ y  } ; wi  (x ) is the same weight vector as for RF. Similar to QRF, QRNN is an extension of multi-layer perceptron neural networks (MLPNN), which is a flexible nonlinear form of quintile regression. It was first proposed by Taylor (2000) . QRNN consists of multiple layers: an input layer, at least one hidden layer, and an output layer. The model error is propagated backward through the network, and the loss function is then minimized by adjusting the weights and biases of the network during training. QRNN characterizes the conditional quantiles of the response variable Y  compared to MLPNN. Therefore, QRNN enhances the robustness and precision of model fitting and forecasting by furnishing more comprehensive information (Cao et al., 2018).  2.4.2 Model accuracy evaluation The entire dataset was randomly split into a training set (75 %) for model building and a test set (25 %) for the validation of model performance. The performance of the five models was evaluated using the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE ), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE ), Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE ), and coefficient of determination (r 2 ), which are calculated as follows,(4) MAPE = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n   y 0  - y m   y 0      × 1 00 %     (5) RMSE = ∑ i = 1  n  ( y 0  - y m  )   2  n        (6) NSE = 1 - ∑ i = 1  n  y 0  - y m      2   ∑ i = 1  n  y 0  - y  ¯   0      2        (7) r 2  = ∑ i = 1  n  ( y 0  - y  ¯   0  )  ( y m  - y  ¯   m  )    ∑ i = 1  n  ( y 0  - y  ¯   0  )  2  ∑ i = 1  n  ( y m  - y  ¯   m  )  2       2      where n  is the number of sample points; y0   and ym   are the actual and predicted values, respectively. y  ¯   0    0  andy  ¯   m     are the means of actual and predicted values, respectively. The algorithm with NSE  values closer to 1, r 2  closer to 1, and smaller MAPE  and RMSE  was selected as the optimal model. Subsequently, the optimal model was used to predict the spatial distribution of ECe, pH and ESP at 0–30 cm and 30–100 cm in the whole region.  2.4.3 Model uncertainty assessment Uncertainty assessment involves calculating the prediction interval width (PIW ) at a 95 % confidence level using the bootstrap method. The nonparametric bootstrap method is effectively and commonly employed to estimate PIW  (Huang et al., 2021 ). PIW  was used as a measure of model uncertainty. Generally, a narrower PIW  indicates lower model uncertainty and higher reliability of the predictions. PIW  per 1 km pixel at each predicted depth was categorized into four grades: AAA, AA, A, and “None” according to the thresholds of 0.3 mean units, 0.6 mean units, and 1 mean unit. These accuracy thresholds are specified by Global Soil Map (GSM) Tier 4 products and have been successfully used in the digital soil mapping uncertainty assessment (Helfenstein et al., 2022 ). The model uncertainty gradually decreases as the PIW  goes from “None” to AAA, indicating that the users can be highly certain about predictions at AAA locations while least confident about predictions at “none” locations. Specifically, the PIW  is less than 0.3 times its mean unit for an AAA pixel and less than 1 times its mean unit for an A pixel. The spatially explicit PIW  at the significance level α  was obtained at every 1 km pixel as a measure of prediction uncertainty as follows:(8) PIW = P I U  - P I L  = 2 z 1 - α / 2   σ y 2        where PIU   and PIL   are the upper and lower bounds of prediction intervals, respectively; z 1- α  /2  is (1 − α /2) quantile. σ y  2     is the variance of the model, which is calculated as,(9) σ y 2  = 1 B - 1   ∑ i = 1  B  ( y i   - y  ¯   )      where B  is the resample times; yi   is the prediction of the i -th regression model; y  ¯      is the average of prediction outputs of B -regression models. The bootstrap obtains the times of subsample dataset (B ) by uniformly resampling with replacement from the original sample set shown in Fig. S2 .  2.4.4 Driving factor analysis method Two interpretation techniques, feature importance (FI) and local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME), were used to quantify the importance of environmental variables on salt-affected soils at the global and local scales, respectively. FI assessed variables contribute to the prediction accuracy of the model at the global scale. Specifically, the importance of the input variable is determined by the rise in the model prediction error when the corresponding covariate is permuted (Xu et al., 2022 ). The feature importance of each input variable is calculated as follows:(10) F I featur e j      = s - 1 K  ∑ k = 1  K  s k , j       where s  represents the model reference score on the original dataset, such as the R 2  value; K  denotes the total number of random permutations performed; sk,j   is the model score on the k- th dataset, which has been permutated for the j -th feature. LIME, a locally interpretable model, was used to estimate the relative importance of environmental variables for individual predictions. Its fundamental principle involves learning an interpretable model g  locally around the prediction, approximating the original complex model f  (e.g., ML models). Subsequently, g  interprets the prediction f (x ) at the specific observation x  instead of relying on complex ML models. The explanation produced by LIME is calculated as follows:(11) ξ ( x )  = argmin  g ∈ G   L f , g , π x      + Ω ( g )      where Ω(g ) is the complexity measures of g ; πx   is the neighborhood proximity around x ; and L    is the fidelity function, which measures the loss of g  in approximating f  in the locality defined by πx  . In this paper, we employed FI and LIME to comprehensively analyze the drivers of soil salinization at different scales, facilitating an understanding of the complex relationship between environmental variables and soil salinity. FI and LIME were calculated in the R 3.5.6 software environment using the dismo  and lime  packages, respectively.  2.4.5 Block prediction technology The necessity for extensive data in large-scale modeling poses several challenges. Firstly, the substantial data amount required consumes significant disk space, rendering storage impractical. Secondly, transmitting such a substantial volume of data takes considerable time. Thirdly, predicting an extensive dataset as a whole demands time and effort. To address these challenges and enhance efficiency, block prediction becomes essential. However, the uneven distribution of soil salinization data introduces challenges to block prediction, including lower prediction accuracy in some blocks due to fewer data, and an inconsistent prediction at block boundaries. This study adopted overall model training and block prediction to mitigate these challenges. This hybrid technique strikes a balance, addressing disk space constraints and transmission time issues associated with extensive datasets while ensuring a more accurate and efficient prediction process.    3 Results 3.1 Model performance The model training and validation performance of five models, including RF, Cubist, QRF, QRNN and MLR for ECe, pH and ESP at different depths in Asia is shown in Table 2  . Notable differences in prediction accuracy were observed among these ML models as MAPE  values ranged from 22.39 ∼ 146.14 %, 0.51 ∼ 13.15 % and 6.78 ∼ 120.58 %, RMSE  values from 1.53 ∼ 4.71 dS/m, 0.10 ∼ 1.01 and 3.03 ∼ 9.54 %, r 2  values from 0.26 ∼ 0.86, 0.36 ∼ 0.98 and 0.22 ∼ 0.90, NSE  values from 0.09 ∼ 0.84, 0.38 ∼ 0.98 and 0.17 ∼ 0.89 across all models for ECe, pH and ESP in the calibration; MAPE  values ranged from 47.44 ∼ 158.37 %, 2.54 ∼ 13.35 % and 26.66 ∼ 108.42 %, RMSE  values from 3.06 ∼ 4.94 dS/m, 0.38 ∼ 1.02, 7.17 ∼ 10.68 %, r 2  values from 0.02 ∼ 0.75, 0.38 ∼ 0.74 and 0.14 ∼ 0.70, NSE  values from 0.04 ∼ 0.61, 0.38 ∼ 0.72 and 0.10 ∼ 0.55 in the validation. It is important to note that while MAPE  is a valuable indicator, it could exaggerate prediction errors, especially in scenarios involving small actual values.  Comparatively, RF, Cubist, QRF, and QRNN significantly outperformed MLR in predicting ECe, pH, and ESP, and their performance in predicting soil indicators at the same depth indicated the following ranking: QRF > RF > Cubist > QRNN. Hence, QRF was the optimal model for predicting ECe, pH, and ESP in both the 0–30 cm and 30–100 cm soil layers, which was then used to map the spatial distribution of ECe, pH, and ESP at different depths across Asia in this study.  3.2 Spatial prediction of soil indicators and salt-affected soils The spatial distributions of ECe, pH and ESP at two depths across Asia are illustrated in Fig. 7  , while the distributions of salt-affected soils derived from these three soil indicators are shown in Fig. 8  . Traditionally, ECe, pH and ESP serve as indicators for categorizing salt-affected soils into saline (ECe > 0.75 dS/m, pH < 8.5 and ESP < 6 %), sodic (ECe < 0.75 dS/m, pH > 8.5 and ESP > 6 %) and saline-sodic soils (ECe > 0.75 dS/m, pH < 8.5 and ESP > 6 %). Soils with ECe levels of < 0.75, 0.75 ∼ 2, 2 ∼ 4, 4 ∼ 8, 8 ∼ 15, and > 15 dS/m are categorized as none, slight, moderate, strong, very strong, and extreme salinity, respectively. Soils with ESP values of < 6, 6 ∼ 10,10 ∼ 15, 15 ∼ 25, > 25 % are considered as none, slight, moderate, strong sodicity, and very strong sodicity, respectively. The areas of salt-affected soils for depths of 0–30 cm and 30–100 cm in Asia derived from the developed model were 466.4 million ha and 377.7 million ha, respectively. Specifically, the areas dedicated to saline, saline-sodic, and sodic soils were 444.1, 10.0, and 12.3 million ha, respectively. Additionally, the areas of slight, moderate, and strong-extreme saline soils were 365.2, 58.7, and 20.2 million ha, respectively, and the areas of slight and moderate sodic soils were 11.6 and 0.7 million ha, respectively. Moreover, the areas of salt-affected soils for each country in the study region were calculated using the ArcGIS “Zonal Statistics” tool and compared with results from other studies, shown in Table S1 . The results illustrated that salt-affected soils were mainly distributed in Russia, China, Iran, India and Pakistan. While only a few countries in Asia provided detailed spatial distribution data of soil salinization, e.g., Russia (Afonin et al., 2008 ), India (Mandal et al., 2011 ) and Bangladesh (Nguyen and Tran, 2020 ). The estimated extents of salt-affected soils by the developed model were 119.78 and 92.74, 26.54 and 16.71, 1.33 and 1.15 million ha for depths of 0–30 cm and 30–100 cm in these countries, respectively. These estimates and their spatial patterns were in accordance with the existing studies. In countries lacking spatial distribution data or relevant information, the developed model succeeded in making reasonable predictions, providing valuable data support for these regions. For example, 44.33 million ha of topsoil (0–30 cm) and 32.84 million ha of subsoil (30–100 cm) were estimated to be salt-affected in China. They were mainly distributed in the arid and semi-arid regions and coastal areas, such as Xinjiang, Gansu, Inner Mongolia, Ningxia, Qinghai, and coastal wetlands, which was close to the results obtained by the National Soil Census Office (1996) . Similarly, the estimated areas of salt-affected soils in other countries also aligned with published results or fall within their given range, as detailed in Table S1 . These results indicated that the assessment of salt-affected soil areas was reasonable. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the areas with high values of ECe (with an average value > 0.99 dS/m) in two soil layers were mainly in the arid regions, such as northwestern China, the desert zone in central and eastern Iran, northwestern India, and Kazakhstan. These regions are characterized by high temperatures (with annual average value > 31.2℃), intense evaporation, and limited rainfall (with annual precipitation value < 297 mm), which contribute to the accumulation of soil salts. Additionally, it was also observed that coastal areas, including those in China, India, and Pakistan, as well as regions surrounding the Caspian Sea and southwest Pacific, exhibited higher ESP values (with an average value > 13.0 %). This phenomenon can be attributed to salts in seawater, which have the potential to seep into the soil and result in sodium salt accumulation. Conversely, upland and mountainous areas usually have lower ECe and ESP values. Examples include regions in South, East, and Southwest China, as well as inland areas of Southeast Asian countries like Indonesia, Philippines, Malaysia, and Vietnam, and South Asian countries such as Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and Nepal. These areas are characterized by abundant rainfall and rapid water movement, which facilitate the leaching of salts from the soil. As a result, these regions generally have relatively lower ECe (with an average value < 0.62 dS/m) and ESP (with an average value < 5.22 %) levels. Soil pH is an indicator of diagnosing salt-affected soils. Acidic or neutral soils are usually less prone to salinization, while alkaline soils are more prone to salinization, especially in arid areas, e.g., the average ECe and ESP value of alkaline soils are 0.80 dS/m and 6.81 %, respectively, which are significantly higher than the average results of 0.54 dS/m and 4.10 % for acidic or neutral soils. This is because acidity reduces the dissolution of salts in soils, while alkalinity promotes the dissolution of salts in soils. These findings provide valuable insights for soil management practices and agricultural planning to ensure the health and sustainability of soils in the region.  3.3 Model uncertainty assessment The uncertainty for predictive indicators was evaluated using the bootstrap method. The PIW  of ECe, pH, and ESP at a 95 % confidence level is illustrated in Fig. 9  (A1) ∼ (F1), with corresponding uncertainty grades shown in Fig. 9  (A2) ∼ (F2). The distribution of areas across different PIW  grades for ECe, pH and ESP at two depths is presented in Fig. 9  (A3) ∼ (F3). At the depth of 0–30 cm, the majority of areas exhibited AAA PIW  grades, encompassing 78.3 % for ECe, 99.8 % for pH and 60.4 % for ESP. The percentage of areas with PIW  grades worse than AA (i.e., A and “None”) for the three indicators were 10.7 %, 0.1 %, and 13.2 %, respectively. Similar trends were observed for the results at the depth of 30–100 cm, where AAA PIW  grades covered 71.9 %, 98.2 % and 68.5 % of the areas for ECe, pH, and ESP, respectively. And the percentage of areas with PIW  grades worse than AA (i.e., A and “None”) for the three indicators were 12.9 %, 0.4 %, and 11.0 %, respectively. From “None” to AAA, PIW  is increasingly narrow, indicating increasing certainty in model predictions. Helfenstein et al. (2022)  considered a percentage less than 39.5 % for “None” as an acceptable model accuracy for soil pH. Naturally, a higher proportion of AAA areas is desirable for enhanced spatial support. Overall, the small PIW  values of ECe, pH, and ESP at the depths of 0–30 cm and 30–100 cm indicate the minimal uncertainty and the highly plausible spatial predictions of these indicators.  3.4 Identification of driving factors of soil salinization 3.4.1 The global analysis The relative importance of the predictive variables for the soil indicators of salt-affected soils was evaluated, and Pearson’s correlation coefficients between soil indicators of salt-affected soils and important predictive variables at different depths were calculated, as shown in Fig. 10  . The relative importance of different factors for ECe, pH and ESP varied. For ECe, the top three variables were DEM derivative, slope , and climatic derivatives like maximum temperature(tmax ) and the annual precipitation (rain ), with relative importance of 19.0 %, 15.6 % and 13.9 % at the depth of 0–30 cm, and 14.8 %, 14.3 % and 13.5 % at the depth of 30–100 cm. The most important variable for pH was the RS derivative (e.g., salinity index V (SI 5)), with relative importance exceeding 39 % and 50 % at depths of 0–30 cm and 30–100 cm, respectively, followed by rain  and tmax , each with approximately 10 % relative importance. DEM  is the most important variable for ESP at 0–30 cm depth, with relative importance exceeding 28 %, followed by two climatic derivatives, i.e., tmax  and rain , with relative importance of 14.8 % and 11.0 %, respectively. For ESP at 30–100 cm depth, climatic derivatives (i.e., tmax  and rain ), were the top two variables, followed by DEM derivative slope , with the relative importance of 29.5 %, 13.9 % and 11.6 %, respectively. Pearson’s correlation coefficients shown in Fig. 10 (g) corroborated these findings. All these environmental variables, except for valley , exhibited significant correlations (p  < 0.05 or p  < 0.01) with ECe, with slope  demonstrating the highest correlation (p  < 0.05), followed by rain  (p  < 0.05). SI 5 showed the strongest correlation with pH at both depths (p  < 0.05), followed by rain  (p  < 0.05) and DEM  (p  < 0.01). slope  was the most strongly correlated variable for ESP at depths of 0–30 cm and 30–100 cm (p  < 0.01). In summary, remote sensing derivative SI 5, climatic derivatives rain  and tmax , DEM , and its derivative slope  were the most important environmental variables for predicting soil indicators of salt-affected soils in Asia.  3.4.2 The local analysis The driving factors of soil salinization were analyzed for 5 countries using LIME, including Russia, China, Pakistan, India, and Indonesia. These countries face significant challenges related to soil salinization alongside extensive agricultural activities, necessitating a comprehensive investigation for sustainable agriculture development. The average percentage of predictive variables ranked from first (1st) to fifth (5th) in importance for ECe, pH and ESP at different depths in each country is shown in Fig. 11  . The relative importance of the driving factors for ECe, pH and ESP at different depths revealed significant differences. Climatic derivative rain  was the most important driving factor for ECe at 0–30 cm depth of across all countries, while DEM  was the most important for ECe at 30–100 cm depth. This highlights that topsoil salinity was more susceptible to the direct influence of climatic factors, while subsoil salinity was more influenced by topography. rain  consistently ranked first for pH at depths of 0–30 cm and 30–100 cm in the five countries, indicating the foremost driving factor for pH. Variables affecting pH at both depths, ranked second, third, and fifth remained consistent, e.g., tmax , SI 5 and BI , while the fourth variable varied. Variable valley  ranked fourth for pH at 0–30 cm, while DEM  held this position for pH at 30–100 cm. In different countries, the most significant driving factor for ESP was either rain  or tmax . For instance, in Russia, India and Pakistan, the importance of tmax  was higher than that of rain  and ranked first. However, rain  ranked first for ESP in China and Indonesia. Furthermore, DEM  and slope  exhibited contrasting importance for ESP at depths of 0–30 cm and 30–100 cm. DEM  was more influential than slope  for ESP at 0–30 cm but less so for ESP at 30–100 cm. These findings underscore the spatial differences in the factors affecting the parameters of salt-affected soils. Overall, tmax , rain  and DEM  are the primary factors affecting soil salinization.    4 Discussion 4.1 Model selection The model performance of the 5 ML models (Cubist, RF, QRF, QRNN and MLR) is summarized in Table 2 , with QRF demonstrating superior performance, followed by RF, Cubist, QRNN and MLR. This may stem from the inherent characteristics of the algorithms. QRF and RF are nonparametric integrated learning methods, which are more flexible in capturing complex nonlinear relationships and handling multiple sources of data compared to Cubist. QRNN requires substantial data support for optimal performance due to its inherent complexity (Ryu et al., 2022 ). Similar observations were found by Schmidinger and Heuvelink (2023) , which compared QRF, RF, and QRNN in the spatial prediction of soil pH and soil organic carbon, reporting favorable performance of QRF and RF over QRNN. Chappell (2022)  also underscored the superiority of QRF for soil organic carbon prediction compared to Cubist. These results indicate that QRF is a promising model for digital soil properties mapping (Helfenstein et al., 2022 ). However, it is worth noting that model performance varied across different datasets. For example, Jahandideh Mahjenabadi et al. (2022)  reported a higher accuracy of RF in predicting wheat grain yield compared to Cubist, while Raath (2023)  reached the opposite conclusion. Wang et al. (2020)  emphasized that no single algorithm can perform optimally across all datasets, highlighting the importance of evaluating algorithm performance specific to the dataset under consideration. Additionally, we observed that the prediction accuracy decreases with increasing soil depth, which is consistent with Helfenstein et al. (2022)  and Wang et al. (2020) .  4.2 Salt-affected soil areas The salt-affected soils in Asia mapped in this study mainly occurred in arid regions, such as Indo-Gangetic Plains in India, Iran, Kazakhstan and northwestern China, as well as coastal areas bordering the Caspian Sea and southwest Pacific. This distribution pattern aligns closely with that of the FAO/UNESCO soil salinization map of the world. Moreover, the areas of salt-affected soils in Asia derived from the developed model were 466.4 million ha of topsoil (0–30 cm) and 377.7 million ha of subsoil (30–100 cm), which was close to the FAO/UNESCO estimation of 443.7 million ha in Asia (FAO/UNESCO, 1970–1980. ) and slightly exceeded the approximation of 332 million ha by Wicke et al. (2011) . A previous global study estimated the area of salt-affected soils in Asia (excluding Russia) to be 714 million ha (Hassani et al., 2020 ), which seemed to be highly overestimated. In contrast, the results of this study were significantly lower and more reasonable. Moreover, the area of salt-affected soils in China estimated by this study was 44.33 million ha of topsoil (0–30 cm) and 32.84 million ha of subsoil (30–100 cm), owning a significant deviation from the 211.75 million ha by Hassani et al. (2020) , and is closer to the 36 million ha documented by the National Soil Census Office (1996) . Additionally, our results for the area of salt-affected soil in other Asian countries were also close to the published values, as shown in Table S1 . Several factors contribute to the more reasonable results of this study. Firstly, a more extensive dataset on soil salinization in Asia was employed for modeling. Secondly, the influence of pH on soil salinization was considered. These considerations likely enhanced the accuracy and reliability of our findings.  4.3 Driving factors The results of this study showed that the remote sensing derivative SI 5, the climatic derivatives rain  and tmax , DEM  and its derivative slope  were the main driving factors for soil salinization in Asia. The climate is a key driving factor in the formation of salt-affected soils, especially in arid and semi-arid regions (Hassani et al., 2020; Omuto et al., 2020 ), characterized by high temperature, intense evaporation and low precipitation. These conditions contribute to salt accumulation in the soil over time. Terrain exerts a direct or indirect influence on soil salinization processes (Chaaou et al., 2022; Triki Fourati et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2015 ). Similar results were found in Hassani et al. (2021) , where rain  was the most important predictor in soil salinity modeling at the global scale with relative importance of 14 %, and DEM  as well as slope  also had the significant importance on soil salinity, with relative importance over 7 %. However, DEM  and slope  were not identified as drivers of soil salinity in Taghizadeh-Mehrjardi et al. (2021) . This discrepancy underscores the multifaceted nature of soil salinization, which is affected by a confluence of soil, climate, topography and biology operating at different scales, resulting in diverse drivers across different study areas. RS derivatives have shown effectiveness in predicting soil salinity, although the wide variety of RS covariates can yield inconsistent study outcomes. For instance, Wang et al. (2020)  identified Canopy Response Salinity Index (CRSI ) as the most important covariate, while another study found Extended Enhanced Vegetation Index (EEVI ) to be more important than CRSI  (Wang et al., 2019 ). Additionally, RS image derivatives like SI 5, which combine blue and red bands, have demonstrated sensitivity to saline soils and have been identified as optimal RS indices for mapping salt-affected soils (Wang et al., 2013). Therefore, acquiring RS variables closely associated with soil salinity is crucial for accurate prediction and mapping efforts.   5 Conclusions To cope with the challenges associated with spatial prediction of soil salinization at large scales, we developed a prediction model based on ML models and a comprehensive dataset comprising climatic, topographic, soil, and remote sensing data. This enables to predict the distribution of salt-affected soils at intercontinental scales. The uncertainty of the prediction map was quantified by employing the bootstrap technique. Furthermore, the driving factors of soil salinization in Asia were comprehensively and quantitatively assessed using FI and LIME. This study represents a significant advancement in predicting the spatial pattern of soil attributes characterized by strong variability at a large scale. The main conclusions are as follows:(1) The model performance of the five ML models in recognizing salt-affected soils in Asia ranked as QRF > RF > Cubist > QRNN > MLR. QRF was a promising model for digital mapping of soil properties especially on large scales.  (2) The model exhibited minimal uncertainty, with over 60.4 % of the region showing a PIW  of AAA quality across both depths of ECe, pH, and ESP, indicating small uncertainty and highly plausible spatial predictions of these indicators.  (3) The salt-affected areas at depths of 0–30 cm and 30–100 cm in Asia were estimated at 466.36 million ha and 377.68 million ha, respectively, which align closely with FAO estimates. Furthermore, the salt-affected soils in each country also exhibited reasonable assessment.  (4) Spatial differences were observed in the factors influencing parameters of salt-affected soils. Overall, the climatic derivatives rain  and tmax , DEM  and its derivative slope , and the remote sensing derivative SI 5 significantly influenced the spatial distribution of soil indicators and were the main driving factors of soil salinization in the region.
1 Introduction Hydrological models are crucial for modeling and predicting hydrological processes, and they have significant applications in areas such as water resources management, monitoring and forecasting of extreme events such as drought and flood, and optimizing reservoir operations (Kittel et al., 2020; Mei et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2019 ). As one of the critical factors influencing the reliability of simulation results, model parameters are usually calibrated using observed streamflow data. However, streamflow gauges are sparsely distributed worldwide, and in many catchments of interest, they are even unavailable (Qi et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2020 ). Such catchments are referred to as “ungauged catchements” (de Lavenne et al., 2023 ). Therefore, the traditional streamflow-based parameter calibration method does not apply to ungauged catchments, which presents a significant challenge in the estimation of hydrological parameters for these regions (Kunnath-Poovakka et al., 2016; Mizukami et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2022 ). Regionalization, a method commonly used for parameter estimation in ungauged catchments, involves transferring calibrated parameters from gauged to ungauged catchments (Beck et al., 2016; Kittel et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020 ). Numerous studies on regionalization have made significant advancements. However, challenges still exist, including insufficient simulation results and limited prediction accuracy, especially in large-scale or remote regions due to the sparse streamflow gauges (Guo et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2020; Song et al., 2022 ). In such situations, remote sensing (RS)-based products have been increasingly utilized for model parameter calibration in ungauged catchments benefits from their large-scale coverage and easy access (Demirel et al., 2018; Herman et al., 2018; Hulsman et al., 2021; Lopez et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020 ). RS-based data offers several advantages in model parameter calibration. Firstly, it provides spatially distributed information that allows for parameter calibration at each grid cell, facilitating a more accurate representation of the internal hydrological processes within the catchment (Huang et al., 2020 ). Secondly, the wide coverage and improving spatiotemporal resolution of RS data make it a valuable tool for parameter calibration in remote or ungauged regions (Liu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2021 ). As the most critical component of the water cycle, evapotranspiration (ET) plays an important role in water and energy balance, and RS-based ET data has become the most widely used resource for parameter calibration in ungauged catchments. Previous studies have demonstrated the feasibility of calibrating model parameters solely against RS-based ET data (Guo et al., 2022; Herman et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020 ). However, it is important to acknowledge that ET is not directly measurable by satellites but estimated indirectly, leading to potential quality issues with RS-based ET data. This uncertainty poses challenges for its applicability in parameter calibration (Huang et al., 2020; Hulsman et al., 2021 ). Furthermore, the performance of RS-based ET data in parameter calibration can vary significantly across different climate regions (Dembele et al., 2020a; Kunnath-Poovakka et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020 ). Several studies have highlighted the need for a bias correction procedure to reduce potential biases in RS-based ET data before utilizing it for parameter calibration (Huang et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2022 ). Indeed, evaluating or directly correcting RS-based ET data at a large scale is a challenging task due to the limited availability of in-situ ET data (Dembele et al., 2020a ). This limitation highlights the necessity of introducing innovative approaches that can reduce the uncertainty of RS-based ET data without relying on gauged observations. The triple collocation (TC) technique, originally proposed by Stoffelen (1998) , is a valuable method for estimating the error variance of the input datasets without the need for ground truth data. To advance the methodology, Yilmaz et al. (2012)  introduced the TC-based least square merging technique. This approach leverages the estimated error variance obtained from the TC technique to merge multiple input parent products and generate a new improved product. Recently, several studies have attempted to merge multiple ET datasets by utilizing the TC technique. These studies have demonstrated that the TC-based merging method is feasible and effective for enhancing the accuracy of ET data (Li et al., 2023b; Park et al., 2023 ). However, the extent to which streamflow simulation reliability improves through parameter calibration in ungauged catchments using ET estimates from the TC-based merging method remains understudied. More comprehensive research is necessary to quantify the impact of incorporating merged ET data on streamflow simulation accuracy in these catchments. Such evaluations would shed valuable light on the effectiveness and applicability of the TC-based merging approach in enhancing streamflow simulation reliability. In addition to directly reducing the uncertainty of RS-based ET data through bias correction or data merging, researchers have also explored the simultaneous calibration of hydrological parameters using ET data along with other variables to mitigate the potential uncertainties arising from inaccuracies in RS ET data (Dembele et al., 2020b; Lopez et al., 2017; Mei et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2021 ). Generally, the multi-variable calibration based on RS ET and other hydrological variables can be categorized into two types. The first type involves calibrating model parameters using RS ET in combination with observed streamflow. For example, Zhang et al. (2021)  proposed a parallel computing-based and spatially stepwise strategy for parameter calibration using observed streamflow and RS ET data. Multivariate calibration based on observed streamflow and RS ET data can improve the overall representation and modeling of various hydrological processes (Yeste et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2021 ). However, the inclusion of observed streamflow data in the calibration process restricts its applicability to gauged catchments, making it less suitable for ungauged catchments. The second type of multi-variable calibration involves the calibration of model parameters using RS ET in combination with other RS-based variables, primarily soil moisture and/or terrestrial water storage (Dembele et al., 2020a; Hulsman et al., 2021; Kunnath-Poovakka et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2022; Lopez et al., 2017 ). This type of parameter calibration offers feasibility for ungauged catchments. However, it is important to acknowledge the limitations associated with this approach. Firstly, the relatively coarse spatial resolution of variables like soil moisture and terrestrial water storage restricts the resolution at which parameter calibration can be performed. This limitation hampers the ability to capture the spatial variability of internal hydrological processes within the catchment accurately, especially in regions with heterogeneous hydrological conditions (Kunnath-Poovakka et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2021 ). Moreover, this type of calibration does not directly incorporate streamflow-related variables. As a result, improvements in streamflow simulation accuracy may not be as significant (Zhang et al., 2021 ). To overcome these limitations, further research should incorporate streamflow-related variables into the parameter calibration processes. The streamflow features, such as the runoff coefficient (RC) and baseflow index (BFI), provide valuable information for understanding the runoff behavior in hydrological systems and are suitable for parameter calibration in ungauged regions (Yang et al., 2019 ). Beck et al. (2015)  developed a global dataset of streamflow features at a 0.05° spatial resolution using a data-driven approach based on streamflow observations from thousands of catchments worldwide, which offers a rare opportunity for fine-scale hydrological model parameter calibrations across the entire land surface. However, the comprehensive evaluation of the combined benefits of using ET and streamflow features for model parameter calibration in ungauged catchments is still lacking. Conducting such assessments would be valuable in advancing our understanding of the synergistic advantages and potential challenges involved in integrating these data sources for improved parameter calibration. In summary, RS ET data provides valuable information for model parameter calibration in ungauged catchments. However, improving the reliability of calibrated parameters solely against raw RS ET data remains a challenging task. The key to applying the RS ET data in parameter calibration is to identify and employ a suitable method that can effectively reduce the uncertainty associated with raw RS-based ET data. In this study, we conducted a comparison of two methods aimed at reducing the influence of uncertainty associated with raw RS ET data on parameter calibration. The first method involved using merged ET data obtained through TC technology for parameter calibration. The second method utilized both ET and streamflow features as calibration targets. Specifically, the main objective of this study was to answer the following three questions: (i) Does the merged ET data, obtained through the TC technology, outperform the three raw RS-based ET datasets in terms of model parameter calibration? (ii) What is the relative performance of the multi-variable calibration scheme, which incorporates both ET and streamflow features as calibration targets, compared to the single-variable calibration scheme based solely on ET data? (iii) How does the improvement in simulated streamflow vary under different climate conditions when comparing the merged ET-based calibration scheme (multi-variable calibration scheme) with the raw RS ET-based calibration scheme (single-variable calibration scheme)? The performance of these calibration schemes is evaluated and compared by applying the variable infiltration capacity (VIC) model (Liang et al., 1994; Liang et al., 1996 ) to 49 catchments in China.  2 Study area and data sets 2.1 Study area In this study, a total of 49 catchments were selected to assess the efficacy of our proposed parameter calibration schemes. The primary focus of the selection of these catchments was to ensure that each catchment had a minimum of 10 years of daily streamflow data. The selected catchments exhibited a wide range of drainage areas, spanning from 1080 to 81638 km2 , with an average drainage area of 9470.2 km2 . Additional information about the 49 hydrological stations corresponding to the selected catchments is presented in supplementary material s (Table S1 ). The selected 49 catchments were strategically situated in regions characterized by Humid, Dry sub-humid, and Semi-Arid climate classes, as depicted in Fig. 1  . This deliberate selection allowed us to comprehensively evaluate the efficacy of our proposed parameter calibration schemes under diverse climatic conditions. The classification of climate classes was determined based on the Aridity Index (AI) values, which represent the ratio of annual mean precipitation to potential evapotranspiration. These AI values were derived from the study conducted by Zomer et al. (2022) . A higher AI represents more humid conditions, while a lower AI corresponds to higher aridity. The climate classes in Fig. 1  are determined by the AI values as follows: AI <0.03 corresponds to Hyper Arid, 0.03 – 0.2 indicates Arid, 0.2 – 0.5 represents Semi-Arid, 0.5 – 0.65 denotes Dry Sub-Humid, and AI >0.65 is categorized as Humid. A commonly used AI threshold of 0.65 is employed to classify regions into arid or humid categories (Zomer et al., 2022 ).  2.2 Data sets The meteorological data used to drive the hydrological model, including precipitation, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature, were obtained from the National Meteorological Science Data Center (https://data.cma.cn ). In this study, all parameter calibration schemes were conducted at a spatial resolution of 0.05° × 0.05°. The meteorological data were interpolated using the inverse distance method. Three evapotranspiration products, namely surface energy balance based global land evapotranspiration (EBET, https://data.tpdc.ac.cn/home ), global land evaporation amsterdam model (GLEAM, https://www.gleam.eu/ ), and evapotranspiration product from the version 2 of the Penman-Monteith-Leuning model (China) (PML-V2 (China), hereafter referred to as PML, https://data.tpdc.ac.cn/home ), were considered. The EBET data is primarily generated using the latest revised surface energy balance system algorithm proposed by Chen et al. (2019) . The dataset has a spatial resolution of 0.05° and a temporal resolution of daily. GLEAM is a set of algorithms that estimate the different components of land evaporation separately. It has undergone continuous revisions and updates since its development in 2011. In this study, GLEAM version 3.6a with a spatial resolution of 0.25° and daily temporal resolution was used (Martens et al., 2017; Miralles et al., 2011 ). The PML dataset has a daily temporal resolution and a spatial resolution of 500 m. It covers the period from February 26, 2000, to December 31, 2020. Compared with its global version, the accuracy of the PML product has been greatly improved (He et al., 2022 ). The GLEAM data was resampled to a spatial resolution of 0.05° using the bilinear interpolation method. The PML data were spatially aggregated to a resolution of 0.05° using a simple arithmetic average. The Global Streamflow Characteristics Dataset (GSCD, https://www.gloh2o.org/gscd/ ) is a collection of global maps that provide information on 17 streamflow characteristics. These characteristics offer valuable insights into the behavior of runoff across the entire land surface, including regions where streamflow measurements are not available (Beck et al., 2015; Beck et al., 2013 ). For this study, the latest version of the GSCD (version 2.0) with a spatial resolution of 0.05° was utilized. The BFI and the RC play a significant role in understanding the hydrological behavior of specific regions and were selected as the primary calibration targets. The observed streamflow data used for validating our proposed parameter calibration schemes were obtained from the Hydrological Yearbook. This reliable source provided accurate records of streamflow measurements for the selected catchments, which ensured the credibility of our parameter calibration schemes validation. In situ daily soil moisture data from 174 soil moisture stations (Fig. 1 ), obtained from the Information Center (Hydrological Monitor and Forecast Center), Ministry of Water Resources, P.R. China, were selected to validate the simulated soil moisture of different calibration schemes. The length of soil moisture observations varied across stations, ranging from 103 to 2803, with an average of 1107 values for each station over the period from January 2008 to November 2020. Soil moisture measurements were taken at three different depths (10, 20, and 40 cm). To facilitate comparison with simulated soil moisture, observed values at the three depths were integrated to 0–40 cm. The data quality of this dataset was reliable and has been used utilized in several previous studies to validate simulated soil moisture (Wu et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2022 ). We employed six catchment characteristics, including mean annual precipitation (Pre), mean annual temperature (Tem), mean annual potential evapotranspiration (Pet), AI, mean elevation (Ele), and the mean annual normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), to investigate the variations in the model performance of different calibration schemes across diverse range of climatic and geographical conditions. Pre and Tem were calculated based on the above-mentioned meteorological data. Pet and AI data from Zomer et al. (2022)  were employed to obtain basin-averaged Pet and AI in each basin. The Ele was determined using the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) elevation data (https://earthexplorer.usgs.gov ). Basin-averaged NDVI was obtained using NDVI data from the National Earth System Science Data Center, National Science & Technology Infrastructure of China (https://www.geodata.cn ).   3 Methodology 3.1 The VIC hydrological model The VIC model is a commonly employed hydrological model that simulates the water and energy fluxes at the land surface (Liang et al., 1994; Liang et al., 1996 ). It is specifically designed to capture the intricate processes involved in water movement, storage, and redistribution within a grid-based framework. The VIC model is equipped with the capability to simulate various hydrological components, including evapotranspiration, runoff, soil moisture, and other related variables. The VIC model incorporates essential factors, including precipitation, temperature, soil properties, vegetation characteristics, and land cover, to accurately depict the diverse hydrological processes occurring on the land surface. The parameters of the VIC model can be categorized into climate-geographic, vegetation, soil, and hydrological parameters. The climate-geographic parameters were mainly determined based on meteorological forcing data and the SRTM elevation data. The leaf area index and vegetation types for each grid cell are determined using Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) data (https://modis.gsfc.nasa.gov/data/ ). A China dataset of soil hydraulic parameters pedotransfer functions for land surface modeling was used to determine soil parameters (Dai et al., 2013 ). The VIC model includes eight hydrological parameters. Among these parameters, the exponent used in the baseflow curve (C, typically set to 2) and the thickness of the first soil moisture layer (d1, typically set to 0.10 m) do not require calibration. The remaining six hydrological parameters cannot be directly determined and require calibration using observed data. These parameters are as follows: variable infiltration curve parameter (infilt), maximum velocity of the baseflow (Dsmax), fraction of Dsmax where nonlinear baseflow begins (Ds), fraction of maximum soil moisture where nonlinear baseflow occurs (Ws), the thickness of the second soil moisture layer (d2) and the third soil moisture layer (d3). There are two primary reasons for using the VIC model. Firstly, the VIC model has gained extensive usage worldwide for simulating runoff (Addor and Melsen, 2019; Yeste et al., 2023 ). Secondly, the model requires calibration for only six hydrological parameters. Furthermore, it has been observed that variations in these parameters have diverse impacts on simulated ET (Xu et al., 2022 ), which justifies the possibility of calibrating these parameters using ET data. To assess the effectiveness of various parameter calibration schemes in replicating observed streamflow, the VIC model simulated grid-based runoff and baseflow are routed to the basin outlet using the large-scale routing model developed by Lu et al. (2015) . For all calibration schemes, a calibration period spanning from 2001 to 2010 was selected, the validation period varied among catchments based on the length of the available observed streamflow data (Table S1 ). To initialize the model state, both the VIC and routing models were pre-run for two years before the calibration and validation periods.  3.2 Triple collocation-based merging of evapotranspiration In this study, TC technology is employed to estimate the errors of PML, EBET, and GLEAM datasets in the absence of known true values. In the TC technology, the relationship between the estimated and the true values can be expressed as:(1) X 1  = α 1  + β 1  X t  + ε 1     X 2  = α 2  + β 2  X t  + ε 2      X 3  = α 3  + β 3  X t  + ε 3              where X1  , X2  , X3   represent the estimated value of ET from PML, EBET, and GLEAM datasets, respectively; Xt   represents the unknown true values of ET; ε1  , ε2  , and ε3   represent zero-mean random error associated with the PML, EBET, and GLEAM datasets, respectively; α1  , α2  , α3   represent the systematic additive biases for the PML, EBET, and GLEAM datasets, respectively; β1  , β2  , β3   represent the systematic multiplicative biases for the PML, EBET, and GLEAM datasets, respectively. For rescaling, one product is arbitrarily chosen as the referenced dataset (PML in this study). The other two datasets are then rescaled to this reference dataset (Li et al., 2023b ), which are calculated as:(2) X 2 ∗  = β 2 ∗  X 2  - X 2         + X 1        X 3 ∗  = β 3 ∗  X 3  - X 3         + X 1                where β 2  ∗  = β 1  / β 2     and β 3  ∗  = β 1  / β 3     represent scaling factors for the EBET and GLEAM, and ·      represents the temporal average. The scaling factors can be estimated in the following way:(3) β 2 ∗  = X 1  - X 1        X 3  - X 3             X 2  - X 2        X 3  - X 3                 β 3 ∗  = X 1  - X 1        X 2  - X 2             X 3  - X 3        X 2  - X 2                          Assuming the errors of the three data sets are independent from the truth, the error variances of rescaled ET anomalies can be calculated by averaging the cross-multiplied dataset differences as follows:(4) σ ε 1 ∗    2  = X 1 ∗   - X 2 ∗       T  X 1 ∗   - X 3 ∗              σ ε 2 ∗    2  = X 2 ∗   - X 1 ∗       T  X 2 ∗   - X 3 ∗               σ ε 3 ∗    2  = X 3 ∗   - X 1 ∗       T  X 3 ∗   - X 2 ∗                       where σ ε 1 ∗    2    , σ ε 2 ∗    2    , σ ε 3 ∗    2     represent the error variances of rescaled ET anomalies for the PML, EBET, and GLEAM datasets, respectively. In a least-squares merging framework, the ET merging weights can be determined using the error variances of the rescaled ET anomalies as follows:(5) w 1  = σ ε 2 ∗    2  σ ε 3 ∗    2   σ ε 1 ∗    2  σ ε 2 ∗    2  + σ ε 1 ∗    2  σ ε 3 ∗    2  + σ ε 2 ∗    2  σ ε 3 ∗    2       w 2  = σ ε 1 ∗    2  σ ε 3 ∗    2   σ ε 1 ∗    2  σ ε 2 ∗    2  + σ ε 1 ∗    2  σ ε 3 ∗    2  + σ ε 2 ∗    2  σ ε 3 ∗    2       w 3  = σ ε 1 ∗    2  σ ε 2 ∗    2   σ ε 1 ∗    2  σ ε 2 ∗    2  + σ ε 1 ∗    2  σ ε 3 ∗    2  + σ ε 2 ∗    2  σ ε 3 ∗    2               where w 1    , w 2    , w 3     represent the weight coefficients of rescaled ET anomalies for the PML, EBET, and GLEAM datasets, respectively. The least-square-based optimal merging of the ET anomalies (E T M ∗    ) can be expressed as:(6) E T M ∗  = w 1  E T 1 ∗   + w 2  E T 2 ∗   + w 3  E T 3 ∗        The E T M ∗     can be converted back into their original scale, i.e., the multi-source merged ET data, using the climatology variability derived from the reference ET dataset.  3.3 Parameters calibration and validation methods In this study, a total of eleven parameter calibration schemes were considered (Table 1  ). Among these calibration schemes, Schemes 1 to 5 were single-variable calibration schemes that utilized either ET or GSCD as the calibration target. Schemes 6 to 9 were multi-variable calibration schemes that used both ET and GSCD as the calibration targets. Scheme 10 was the “Regression scheme”, where the parameter values for each grid were determined using the regression relations between model parameters and catchment characteristics as proposed by Wu et al. (2007) , to evaluate the contribution of the model calibration. The results of the Regression scheme are only presented in Section 4.1 . Scheme 11 employs equal-weighted ET, wherein the weights for the EBET, GLEAM, and PML datasets were uniformly set to 1/3 (EW scheme), as the calibrated target. Scheme 11 was primarily used to validate the applicability of the TC method and was discussed in the Section 5 . For the schemes that use ET as the calibration target (Schemes 1 to 4 and Scheme 11), the model parameters are adjusted to minimize the difference between the model-simulated ET and the observed ET (merged ET and three raw RS-based ET data). The Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) (Gupta et al., 2009 ) defined in Eq. (7)  is utilized as the objective function for Schemes 1 to 4 and Scheme 11.(7) F 1  = 1 - r - 1     2  + α - 1     2  + β - 1     2        where r represents the Pearson correlation coefficient, α is the ratio between the variance of the modeled ET and the variance of the observed ET data, and β is the ratio between the mean of the modeled ET and the mean of the observed ET data. The KGE ranges from −∞ to 1.0, with an ideal value of 1.0. In Scheme 5, the RC and BFI from GSCD dataset are used as the calibration targets. It should be pointed out that although Scheme 5 involved the use of two variables during the calibration process, both of these variables were related to streamflow. Therefore, this study categorizes Scheme 5 as a single-variable calibration scheme. The objective function for each grid cell can be expressed as follows:(8) F 2  = 1 - R C sim    R C ref     - 1     2  + BF I sim    BF I ref     - 1     2        where RCsim   and RCref   represent modeled RC and reference RC from the GSCD dataset, and BFIsim   and BFIref   represent modeled BFI and reference BFI from the GSCD dataset. Schemes 6 to 9 aim to calibrate parameters using both ET data and streamflow characteristics simultaneously. The objective function for Schemes 6 to 9 is defined as:(9) F 3  = F 1  + F 2       By considering different calibration schemes with varying calibration targets, the objective of this study is to investigate whether the merged ET-based parameter calibration scheme outperforms three raw RS ET-based parameter calibration schemes. Additionally, it aims to assess whether the multi-variable calibration schemes provide better results compared to the single-variable calibration schemes. The six hydrological parameters of the VIC model for each grid cell are calibrated using the Rosenbrock algorithm (Rosenbrock, 1960 ) by the aforementioned parameter calibration schemes. The performance of different parameter calibration schemes was compared and validated using observed streamflow and soil moisture data. The evaluation of the simulated daily and monthly streamflow was conducted using two performance metrics: the KGE and the Nash-Sutcliffe coefficient of efficiency (NSE). The NSE can be calculated using the following formula:(10) NSE = 1 - ∑ t = 1  n  Si m t  - O b s t      2   / ∑ t = 1  n  Ob s t  - Obs   ¯       2        where Simt   and Obst   represent the simulated and observed values at time t, respectively. Obs   ¯      is the mean value of the observed values, and n represents the number of samples. The NSE value ranges from −∞ to 1.0, and the closer the NSE is to 1.0, the more reliable the modeled streamflow becomes. The simulated soil moisture was evaluated using the correlation coefficient (CC) and root mean square error (RMSE), calculated using the following formulas:(11) CC = ∑ t = 1  n  Si m t  - Sim   ¯      Ob s t  - Obs   ¯         ∑ t = 1  n  Si m t  - Sim   ¯       2  ∑ t = 1  n  Ob s t  - Obs   ¯       2          (12) RMSE = 1 n  ∑ t = 1  n  Si m t  - O b s t      2        where Sim   ¯      is the mean value of the simulated values.   4 Results 4.1 Overall performance evaluation of different calibration schemes Fig. 2   illustrates the box plots depicting the NSE and KGE metrics for the simulated streamflow obtained through the implementation of different parameter calibration schemes. Table 2   presents the mean values of the two evaluation metrics for the simulated streamflow obtained from different parameter calibration schemes. The accuracy of monthly streamflow simulations was consistently higher than that of daily streamflow simulations across all schemes. Among the three raw RS ET-based calibration schemes, the GLEAM scheme displayed superior performance compared to the PML scheme, while the EBET scheme exhibited the worst performance. These findings are consistent with the evaluation of ET products using the TC method and water balance method (Fig. S1 ). The TC scheme exhibited the overall best performance in streamflow simulation compared to the three raw RS ET-based calibration schemes. However, the TC scheme exhibited poorer performance in streamflow simulation compared to the GSCD scheme. Compared to the five single-variable calibration schemes, the four multi-variable calibration schemes demonstrated a significant improvement in the NSE of streamflow simulation. However, when considering KGE, the multi-variable calibration schemes outperformed those schemes based on ET data. Yet, their superiority was less pronounced when compared to the GSCD scheme, except for the monthly streamflow simulated by the GSCD_TC scheme. The Regression scheme outperforms the EBET scheme but is inferior to other calibration schemes. This result indicates that the proposed streamflow-free calibration schemes have great potentional for simulating streamflow in ungauged catchments. To investigate whether the performance of various calibration schemes is influenced by catchment characteristics, we conducted additional analysis by examining the relationships between the NSE/KGE metrics and six catchment characteristics. Taking daily streamflow as an example, Fig. 3   (Fig. S2 ) illustrates relationships between NSE (KGE) metrics of different calibrated schemes and the corresponding catchment characteristics. The background of each subplot represents the significance of the correlation coefficient between two target variables. Among the nine parameter calibration schemes, the NSE/KGE metrics of the PML scheme exhibit significant relationships with all the six catchment characteristics. Notably, three catchment characteristics, namely Pre, AI, and NDVI, demonstrate significant positive relationships with NSE/KGE in the majority of single-variable calibration cases. These results indicate that streamflow simulation tends to be less accurate in relatively dry catchments compared to relatively humid catchments. These findings are consistent with previous studies conducted by researchers such as Liu et al. (2022), Xu et al. (2022) , and Zhang et al. (2020) . The inherent challenge of hydrological simulations in relatively dry catchments, as compared to relatively humid catchments, may offer a plausible explanation for these outcomes (Liu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2020 ). However, most characteristics exhibit no significant relationships with the NSE/KGE metrics of GSCD and the four multi-variable calibration schemes (p > 0.10), except for NDVI, which exhibits a significant relationship with the NSE values. These findings suggest that incorporating streamflow characteristics into the calibration process may help mitigate the regional discrepancies observed in the streamflow simulation performance with ET-based single-variable calibration schemes. In situ soil moisture data were employed for a more comprehensive evaluation of various parameter calibration schemes. As depicted in Fig. 4  (a), both the GLEAM and PML schemes demonstrated superior performance in capturing the temporal variation of soil moisture compared to the EBET scheme. Among the four ET-based single-variable calibration schemes, the TC scheme achieved the overall best model performance in reproducing temporal variations in soil moisture. However, the performance of the GSCD scheme was inferior to that of the ET-based single-variable calibration schemes (except for the EBET scheme), which may be attributed to the loss of information in the time series when using streamflow characteristics as calibrated targets (Yang et al., 2019 ). Furthermore, the performance of the multi-variable calibration schemes was worse than their corresponding ET-based single-variable calibration schemes (except for the EBET scheme), which is inconsistent with the results of the streamflow simulation.
