1 Introduction Hydrologic partitioning, which is the partitioning of precipitation into runoff, evaporation, and storage change, reflects the complex interactions of climate, soil, vegetation, and geology (Troch et al., 2013; Trancoso et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020a ). The accurate quantification of hydrological partitioning is crucial for sustainable water resource management (Shao et al., 2012; Mo et al., 2023 ). Consequently, for decades, many attempts have been made to quantify hydrologic partitioning and further develop hydrological models to conceptualize catchment hydrologic processes at different time scales (Liang et al., 1994; Zhang et al., 2008; Xing et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020a ). Among the models of different time scales, the development of monthly hydrological models has garnered significant interest due to their simple structure and good performance (Nasseri et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2020; Fathi et al., 2023 ). The partitioning principles proposed thus far primarily include the Budyko and proportionality hypotheses. Budyko (1974)  proposed a semi-empirical expression for the long-term water-energy balance, known as the Budyko hypothesis, which provides a first-order explanation for the partitioning of precipitation into runoff and evaporation. According to the Budyko hypothesis, the ratio of actual evapotranspiration (E ) to precipitation (P ) is a function of the ratio of potential evapotranspiration (Ep  ) to P  and is expressed as(1) E / P = F E p  / P        Over time, changes to the original Budyko model have been observed (Choudhury, 1999; Zhang et al., 2004; Potter et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2007; Donohue et al., 2010; Williams et al., 2012 ). Various Budyko analytical functions with one or more parameters have been developed and widely applied over the last two decades because they can effectively capture catchment characteristics (Bagrov, 1953; Milly, 1994; Zhang et al., 2004; Moriasi et al., 2007; Gerrits et al., 2009 ). The parametric Budyko equations have the following forms (Yang et al., 2008b ):(2) E / P = F E p  / P , c        where c  is a catchment characteristic parameter taken as a lumped variable representing the combined effects of climate and the underlying surface system (Cheng et al., 2023 ). Two typical analytical solutions are proposed for Eq. (2)  with a single parameter. Fu (1981)  derived an equation through dimensional analysis and mathematical reasoning, known as the Fu’s equation, which was subsequently revised by Zhang et al. (2004) . The other was analytically presented by Yang et al. (2008b)  as the coupled water-energy balance equation-Yang (CWEB-Yang). The CWEB-Yang gained both theoretical validation and widespread application in subsequent studies (Xin et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020b; Xu et al., 2022 ). Additionally, the proportionality hypothesis (PH) exists among the behaviours of hydrological partitioning at various temporal scales and is regarded as a signature of the co-evolution of natural ecosystems (Wang and Tang, 2014; Wang et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2016 ). The PH was initially derived from the Soil Conservation Service (SCS) curve number method and then generalised by Poncea and Shetty (1995)  to express the hydrological principle that the ratios of various hydrological variables to their potential values should be equal. Further studies have revealed that the maximum entropy principle serves as the theoretical foundation for the PH (Wang et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2016 ), whereas an analytical solution of the Richards' equation provides a physical basis (Hooshyar and Wang, 2016 ). In fact, the Budyko hypothesis and PH are the main approaches used in hydrological partitioning. Both methods were initially proposed based on empirical evidence and later validated with a theoretical foundation, however, they differed only in their formulations. It would be meaningful to find out if the two differing hypotheses are related. In the previous work, Wang and Tang (2014)  developed a Budyko-form equation based on PH and believed that the equation could be transformed into the Fu’s equation when specific parameters were considered, thereby linking PH with the Budyko theory (Wang and Tang, 2014 ). The CWEB-Yang is another representative Budyko-form equation with a theoretical basis. Exploring the theoretical connection between CWEB-Yang and PH can further establish the connection between the Budyko hypothesis and PH and provide new insights into the hydrological partitioning, which is the first objective of this paper. Despite the aforementioned advancements in understanding the water balance control factors, developing models that can be used for quantitative hydrological predictions at the catchment scale is still challenging (Zhang et al., 2008 ). Monthly hydrological models are commonly used to simulate the monthly hydrological processes in catchments. These models are based on the water balance equation and use a variety of empirical formulas to generalise the relationships between hydrological variables (Cheng et al., 2020 ). Owing to its simple structure and strong practicality, it plays an important role in water resource management, regional water resource assessments, and runoff simulations for ungauged catchments (Wang et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2020c; Deng and Wang, 2021 ). The first monthly water balance model was originally proposed in the 1940s by Thornthwaite (1948) , and subsequently revised by Thornthwaite and Mather (1955) . Various monthly hydrological models with different structures have been proposed thereafter. Thomas (1981)  proposed a monthly water balance model with four parameters (ABCD model), which demonstrated excellent model performance. In 1999, Xiong and Guo (1999)  presented a two-parameter monthly water balance model (TWBM) with a very simple structure. Since it provides good simulation accuracy with only two parameters, TWBM has been one of the most popular models in monthly runoff modeling. Mouelhi et al. (2006)  built a monthly model by using a stepwise approach, called GR2M. Yang et al. (2008a)  extended the mean annual coupled water-energy balance equation and developed a monthly model with a single parameter that considers the effect of soil moisture. They found that this parameter was related to leaf area index. More recently, several monthly water balance models based on the PH have been proposed, such as TSPM (Deng and Wang, 2021 ), PWBM (Zhang et al., 2020a ) and TMPH (Zou et al., 2023 ), which provide strong evidence regarding the applicability of the PH on monthly hydrologic partitioning. After decades of development, in order to meet different application purposes and achieve more physical soundness, various monthly hydrological models were proposed from simple to complex, with an increasing number of parameters (Deng and Wang, 2021 ). Most of these models can achieve runoff simulation using 2–5 parameters, whereas several use more than 10 parameters (Pitman, 1973; Hughes, 2013 ). However, increasing the number of model parameters does not significantly improve its accuracy; in contrast, it can make the model more uncertain (Deng and Wang, 2021 ). Additionally, the fact that most models are empirical and lack a theoretical basis also limits their applicability. Hence, another motivation for this study was to explore the possibility of developing a new hydrological model with a strong theoretical foundation that can achieve a balance between model performance and complexity. Therefore, the objectives of this study were (i) to establish potential linkages between two different hydrologic partitioning theories, namely CWEB-Yang and PH, and (ii) to develop a new monthly model for monthly runoff simulation with a strong theoretical basis and fewer parameters. The model developed for objective (ii) was evaluated using the CAMELS dataset from the United States and applied to the Hanjiang River Basin in China as a case study. Moreover, it was compared with the widely used ABCD and TWBM models to verify its applicability. Our work contributes to the understanding of hydrological partitioning and further reveals its underlying mechanisms. The rest of the paper is organised as follows: in Sections 2 , the methodology is introduced in detail; Section 3  describes the study area and data sources; and Section 4  presents the results of model applications; finally, the discussions and conclusions are summarised in Section 5  and Section 6 .  2 Methodology 2.1 Relationship between PH and CWEB-Yang 2.1.1 Proportionality hypothesis equation The PH presented by Poncea and Shetty (1995)  expresses the principle of hydrological partitioning. Without considering the initial abstraction, it can be written as(3) X a  X P   = Y a  Y p   = Acutualvalue  Potentialvalue       where Xa   and Ya   represent the elements involved in hydrological partitioning, Xp   and Yp   represent the potential value of Xa   and Ya  , respectively. In other words, when the initial abstraction of the basin is not considered, the ratios of the different hydrological variables to their potential values should be equal. Taking the mean annual scale as an example, where the change in water storage content was negligible, precipitation was partitioned into evaporation and runoff. Following the PH, the partitioning of precipitation in a catchment can be expressed as follows: The ratio of evaporation to its potential value should be equal to the ratio of runoff to water availability.(4) E t  E p   = Q t  P t       where Pt   stands for the precipitation; and Q t    denotes the runoff.  2.1.2 Coupled water-energy balance equation-Yang The Budyko hypothesis states that the mean annual evaporation is determined by precipitation and potential evaporation, and this relationship can be expressed through a specific mathematical function. Based on this hypothesis, Yang et al. (2008b)  proposed a partial differential equation to describe the long-term coupled water-energy balance in a catchment and provided an analytical solution for the above equation, that is, the CWEB-Yang equation, which can be shown as follows:(5) E t  = E p  P t   P t n  + E p n     1 / n        where n  is a catchment-specific parameter, representing the underlying basin surface characteristic.  2.1.3 Theoretical connection Taking the mean annual scale as an example, the PH and CWEB-Yang equations can be expressed through a simple transformation, as follows:(6) E t  P t   + E t  E p   = 1     (7) E t  P t     n  + E t  E p     n  = 1      The two equations have similar forms, as evidenced by the fact that they both consist of two key elements, the water supply (E t  / P t    ) and energy supply ratios (E t  / E p    ), both of which describe the complementary relationship between water and energy. The PH equation (Eq. (6)  can be considered as a special case of the CWEB-Yang equation (Eq. (7)  for n  = 1. In fact, parameter n  of the CWEB-Yang equation was selected as the underlying basin surface characteristic parameter, which can effectively capture the characteristic differences among different basins. Thus, n  is important in reflecting the water-energy balance in a specific catchment. In this way, we can define a water-energy complementary relationship at the mean annual scale, which can be expressed as the sum of the nth power of the ratio of evaporation to water availability and that of the ratio of evaporation to potential energy being equal to unity. For a deeper understanding of Eq. (7) , E t  / P t     n    can be interpreted as the partial elasticity of E t    with respect to P t   , whereas E t  / E p     n    can be explained by the partial elasticity of E t    with respect to E p   , as follows:(8) ∂ E t  / E t   ∂ P t  / P t    = 1 1 + P t  / E p     n     1 + 1 / n     P t  E t   = 1 1 + P t  / E p     n    = E t  P t     n     ∂ E t  / E t   ∂ E p  / E p    = 1 1 + E p  / P t     n     1 + 1 / n     E p  E t   = 1 1 + E p  / P t     n    = E t  E p     n           In this case, the partial elasticities with respect to P t    and E p    indicate the sensitivities of evaporation to water and energy, respectively. Thus, the complementary relationship can be used to quantify the relative impact of changes in P t    and E p    on evapotranspiration and runoff to evaluate the contribution of water P t    and energy E p   . In fact, this complementary relationship is consistent with the findings in Zhou et al. (Zhou et al., 2015 ); that is, for any Budko function, the partial elasticities of E t    with respect to P t    and that with respect to E p    add to unity, as follows:(9) ∂ E t  / E t   ∂ P t  / P t    + ∂ E t  / E t   ∂ E p  / E p    = 1        2.2 Developed model based on water-energy complementary equation 2.2.1 Water-energy complementary equation Over the long term, precipitation is partitioned into evaporation and runoff when changes in water storage are negligible compared with other fluxes (Potter and Zhang, 2009; Wang et al., 2015 ):(10) P t  = E t  + Q t       In this case, the partitioning of precipitation into evaporation and runoff can be explained by the water-energy complementary relationship, as shown in Eq. (7) . In fact, basin water storage changes should not be neglected for monthly or even annual water balance partitioning (Han et al., 2020 ), which can be expressed as follows:(11) P t  + S t - 1    ⏟  W t   = Q t  + E t  + S t      where St  −1  and S t    represent water storage in the basin at the beginning and end of time t , respectively. Here, the sum of Pt   and St  −1  was defined as the total available water, W t   . The available water was partitioned into three components: evaporation, runoff, and final basin water storage. Thus, monthly water balance partitioning is determined based on the water and energy supplies, where evaporation Et   is controlled by both available water, W t  - S t    , and available energy, i.e., potential evaporation Ep  , and the final basin water storage is controlled by available water, W t  - E t    , and available energy, i.e., water storage capacity Sp  .  Based on the water-energy complementary concept, this partitioning is quantified by the following water-energy complementary equations:(12) E t  S t - 1   + P t  - S t      n  + E t  E p     n  = 1    S t  S t - 1   + P t  - E t      n  + S t  S p     n  = 1            This set of equations can be interpreted as the sum of the nth power of the water ratio (the ratio of hydrological elements to water supply) and that of the energy ratio (i.e. the ratio of the element to energy availability) to unity. Specifically, the sum of the nth power of the ratio of evaporation to water availability and that of the ratio of evaporation to its potential value is equal to unity, and the sum of the nth power of the ratio of water storage to water availability and that of the ratio of water storage to its potential value is equal to unity. These equations describe the complementary relationship between water and energy in the hydrological cycle, providing a theoretical basis for understanding the water-energy balance in catchments. Here, parameter n  is set as a constant that reflects the characteristics of the underlying basin surface. According to Roderick and Farquhar (2011) , n  may vary seasonally. In the absence of better information, we assume that n  remains constant over time. The first equation in Eq. (12)  is a Budyko form equation. Through a mathematical transformation, it can be expressed as a conventional Budyko model as follows:(13) E t  = E p  ( S t - 1   + P t  - S t  )   E p n  + ( S t - 1   + P t  - S t  )  n     1 / n         Note that this equation has a similar structure as Eq. (5) , but differs in that the Pt   used to represent the available water in Eq. (5)  is replaced with S t - 1   + P t  - S t    , thus taking into account the effect of basin water storage on evapotranspiration on a monthly scale. In addition, it is worth mentioning that the available water here is also different from the available water P t  + S t - 1      in the coupled water-energy balance equation at an arbitrary time scale derived by Yang et al. (2008a) . The present model suggests that the available water that can be used for hydrologic partitioning should be calculated as the precipitation minus the change in basin water storage, i.e., P t  - Δ S t    , and the precipitation is prioritized to replenish basin water shortage before being allocated for hydrologic partitioning. To validate the water-energy complementary equation, Eq. (12)  was used for hydrological modelling to assess the monthly water balance. In general, there are two ways to estimate Ep  : one is to use empirical formulas such as the Penman formulation (Penman, 1948 ) or the Hamon formula (Hamon, 1961 ), and the other is to estimate based on actual pan evaporation data. In practice, the selection of an appropriate method depends on the availability of relevant data. In this study, Ep   was estimated using two methods, one using the Harmon formula as follows (Hamon, 1961 ):(14) E p  = K × 0.615 × 216.7 × N × e s  T + 273.3         where the K  is proportionality coefficient, N   represents the daytime length (x / 12    hours), T  represents the average monthly temperature (°C), and e s    is the saturation vapour pressure (mb), which can be calculated by the following formula:(15) e s  = 6.108 e 17.27 T  T + 237.3           The other can be found by multiplying the pan evaporation by a correction factor, as follows:(16) E p  = k × E pan       where E pan     represents the pan evaporation and k  is a correction factor for evaporation. A dichotomous method was used to solve Eq. (12)  to find E t    and S t   . Finally, the monthly runoff, Q t   , was obtained using the water balance equation.(17) Q t  = S t - 1   + P t  - E t  - S t        2.2.2 Model calibration Three parameters needed to be calibrated in the developed model: the evaporation parameter, K(k)  (dimensionless), the characteristic parameters of the underlying basin surface, n  (dimensionless), and the water storage capacity of the basin, Sp   (mm). Table 1   lists the definitions and ranges of the parameters. To ensure the validity of the simulation results, the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) was selected as the objective function for parameter calibration, which will be introduced in detail in Section 2.3 . Moreover, the shuffled complex evolution (SCE-UA) algorithm was applied to optimise the objective function. SCE-UA is a global optimisation algorithm proposed by Duan et al. (1993)  and is widely used in rainfall-runoff models. It is particularly adept at solving common problems, such as discontinuity, nonlinearity, and multiple extrema (Zhang and Shi, 2011 ). More details concerning the SCE-UA can be seen in Duan et al. (Duan et al., 1994 ).   2.3 Evaluation index In this study, the NSE coefficient (Nash and Sutcliffe, 1970 ) was primarily used to evaluate the applicability of the model in the study area. NSE is the most commonly used index for evaluating the performance of hydrological models. Its value ranges from - ∞    to 1. The closer the value is to 1, the better the simulation is. In general, the model performance can be considered satisfactory if NSE > 0.50 (Moriasi et al., 2007 ). NSE is defined as follows:(18) NSE = 1 - ∑ i = 1  n  ( Q sim , i   - Q obs , i   )  2   ∑ i = 1  n  ( Q obs , i   - Q obs    ¯   )  2        where Q sim , i     and Q obs , i     are the simulated and observed runoff at time step i , respectively, Q obs    ¯     represents the average of all observations, and n  is the number of months for the simulation. Furthermore, two indices, the Kling-Gupta efficiency coefficient (KGE) (Gupta et al., 2009 ) and volume error (VE) (Gupta et al., 1999 ), were considered to assist in the judgment. KGE is highly sensitive to variance and high flow, and its value ranges from - ∞    (poor fit) to 1 (poor fit). In general, a KGE value greater than 0.5 indicates that the model has good performance (Gupta et al., 2009 ). The KGE function consists of three basic indicators: Pearson’s linear correlation coefficient (r ), the ratio of the standard deviations of the simulation and observation (α ), and the ratio of the mean values of the simulation and observation (β ).(19) KGE = 1 - ( r - 1 )  2  + ( α - 1 )  2  + ( β - 1 )  2         VE was used to measure the relative error between the simulated and observed runoff volumes. A VE value of zero means a perfect simulation of the total runoff volume. VE is calculated as follows:(20) VE = ∑ i = 1  n  ( Q obs , i   - Q sim , i   )   ∑ i = 1  n  Q obs , i       × 100 %       2.4 Benchmark models In addition, we compared the performance of WECM with that of two widely used monthly water balance models: the TWBM and ABCD models. The TWBM has a simple structure with only two parameters and shows strong applicability in China and other regions. This has been widely validated and compared since it was first reported (Xiong et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2019 ). Therefore, it is frequently used as the evaluation standard, and the data chosen in this study are the same as those in the TWBM study. Moreover, the ABCD model achieved a high score for model performance among conceptual monthly models and was difficult to surpass (Deng and Wang, 2021 ). Therefore, it is often used as an evaluation standard. The parameters of benchmark models are given in Appendix B . 2.4.1 TWBM model TWBM was developed by Xiong and Guo (1999)  using only two parameters. Two major modules are involved in the TWBM: the estimation of actual evapotranspiration (Eq. (21) ) and the runoff solution (Eq. (22) ).(21) E t  = C × E P t  × tanh P t  / E P t          (22) Q t  = S t  × tanh S t  / S C         Expanding this further, we have:(23) Q t  = S t - 1   + P t  - E t     × tanh S t - 1   + P t  - E t     / S C        where EPt   is the pan evaporation value, C  represents the evaporation coefficient, and SC  represents the catchment’s field capacity.  2.4.2 ABCD model The ABCD model is a simple and efficient four-parameter conceptual hydrological model that was proposed by Thomas (1981) . The ABCD model conceptualises a catchment as a system consisting of two storage systems: soil water and groundwater. This can be expressed as follows:(24) W t  = S t - 1   + P t  ,  Y t  = S t  + E t      (25) Y t  = W t  + b  2 a   - W t  + b  2 a     2  - b W t   a        (26) S t  = Y t  e - E p  / b       (27) D R t  = ( 1 - c )  ( W t  - Y t  )      (28) G t  = G R t  + G t - 1    1 + d   ,  G D t  = d G t      (29) Q t  = D R t  + G D t      where Wt   and Yt   are two state variables representing the available water and evapotranspiration opportunity, respectively, Gt   is groundwater storage, DRt   is direct runoff, and GDt   is baseflow. Parameter a  describes the propensity for runoff to occur before the soil is completely saturated, parameter b  represents the upper soil zone water holding capacity, parameter c  signifies the ratio of groundwater recharge to surface runoff, and parameter d  is the groundwater discharge rate.    3 Study area and data To accurately evaluate the versatility and reliability of the proposed hydrological model, a large sample dataset encompassing a diverse range of climates and hydrological conditions was required. Consequently, the model was assessed using the CAMELS dataset. Furthermore, to analyze the spatial distribution of parameters, the model was subsequently applied to the Hanjiang River Basin in China as a case study. This study area was chosen to maintain consistency with the TWBM model study conducted by Xiong and Guo (1999) . 3.1 CAMELS dataset To comprehensively evaluate the performance of the proposed model under large-sample conditions, the CAMELS dataset was used for comparison. This dataset consists of daily meteorological time series and runoff data for 671 small and medium-sized catchments across the contiguous United States with limited human disturbance (Newman et al., 2015; Addor et al., 2017 ). To disregard the impact of snowmelt, 222 basins in HUC regions 3, 6, 8, 11, 12, 13, 15, 17, and 18 were selected and defined as rainfall-dominated basins because they were located in the U.S. sunshine belt or the West Coast with long summers and mild and short winters (Mazrooei and Sankarasubramanian, 2019 ). The 222 selected basins included various climatic conditions, and the spatial distribution of the aridity index (AI) is shown in Fig. 1  . The data cover the period from 1980 to 2013, with the first 20 years (1980–1999) used for calibration and the remaining 14 years (2000–2013) for model validation. The daily time series of variables included precipitation, potential evapotranspiration, and runoff observations. The potential evapotranspiration was calculated using the Hamon formula (Hamon, 1961 ). Daily data, converted to a monthly scale, were used for hydrological modelling.  3.2 Hanjiang River basin The Hanjiang River is the largest tributary of the Yangtze River, covering a basin area of 159,000 km2  and is an important water source for the middle route of the South-to-North Water Diversion Project. The basin is characterised by a complex topography, and the general terrain elevation is low in the southeast and high in the northwest ranging from −4 to 3334 m. Because of the effect of the subtropical monsoon climate, the annual average temperature ranges from 15 to 17 °C, and the annual average precipitation is approximately 897 mm with 80 % of the total rainfall occurring from May to October. The basin has abundant water resources, its distribution is uneven, and the interannual change is significant. This study considered the Hanjiang River Basin as the study area and selected 37 subbasins to test and verify the proposed model. A schematic of the Hanjiang River Basin is shown in the Fig. 2  . The data in this study include monthly rainfall, pan evaporation, and runoff of 37 subbasins in the Hanjiang River Basin. The main characteristics of these subbasins are shown in Appendix A . The data series used spans from the 1960s to the 1980s, effectively avoiding the influence of human activities (Xiong and Guo, 1999 ).   4 Results 4.1 Model performance evaluation under large sample conditions The proposed WECM model and the benchmark ABCD and TWBM models were evaluated using the CAMELS dataset. Fig. 3   illustrates the spatial distribution of the NSE values of the WECM, which assesses the simulation performance of the proposed model during both the calibration and validation periods. Visually, the proposed model demonstrates strong performance in terms of NSE, with values exceeding 0.6 for most of the basins. Basins exhibiting lower NSE values were primarily located in arid regions of the central United States. Fig. 4   shows the NSE, KGE, and VE values for the 222 selected basins. As shown in Fig. 4 , the model proposed in this paper performs better than the TWBM model and is comparable to the ABCD model. Table 2   presents the average values of the hydrological indicators for the selected basins. The results highlight that the WECM outperforms the TWBM and slightly surpasses the ABCD model across diverse indicators, indicating superior simulation accuracy. The outstanding performance of WECM during the validation period is particularly noteworthy, achieving an NSE of 0.645, a KGE of 0.684, and a VE of 16.881 %, surpassing both ABCD and TWBM. To further study the performance of the model under different climatic conditions, the 222 basins were categorised into arid, sub-humid, and humid regions based on their AI values. The AI is defined as the ratio of mean annual values of potential evaporation and precipitation, and the classification principle states that areas are categorised as arid if the AI value is greater than 2, sub-humid if the AI value is between 1 and 2, and humid if the AI value is less than 1 (Budyko, 1974; Deng and Wang, 2021 ). Fig. 5   shows the performance of the three models under different climatic conditions. The different climatic conditions have significant impacts on the models. All models achieved the best performance in humid regions, followed by sub-humid regions, and performed the worst in arid regions. In general, the model performance decreased as the AI value increased, which may have been due to the heterogeneity of the hydrological processes in the arid basin (Bai et al., 2015 ). Overall, the WECM and ABCD models demonstrated comparable performances under different climatic conditions, and the TWBM also achieved satisfactory results in humid basins. However, its performance in semi-humid and arid basins was significantly lower than that of the ABCD and WECM models, particularly in arid regions where the average NSE and KGE values were negative. The results, validated with large datasets, highlight the applicability and robustness of WECM in hydrological modelling. Subsequently, we applied it to the Hanjiang River Basin for further analysis.  4.2 Application results in Hanjiang River basin 4.2.1 Parameters calibration results analysis Three parameters—k , n , and Sp  —were determined when applying the proposed model. The calibration results for the model parameters are listed in Table 3  . Parameter n , representing the underlying basin surface characteristics, ranges from 1.0 to 2.0. Nearby basins exhibited similar n  values. The value of Sp   was primarily concentrated between 100 and 300 mm, except in Jiangwan, which had the highest Sp   value of 726.3 mm. One possible reason for this is its proximity to the Danjiangkou Reservoir, which has a significant water storage capacity. Parameter k  represents the evaporation correction parameter, and its values are close to 1. Fig. 6   shows the spatial distributions of the model parameters. The values of Sp   were higher in the central part of the Hanjiang River Basin and gradually decreased in all directions; the highest Sp   value occurred near the Danjiangkou Reservoir, which is abundant in water resources and has a large water storage capacity. Model parameters n  and k  also exhibited a strong regional distribution pattern, which may be related to geographical characteristics and climate. The value of parameter n  varied with latitude, with higher latitudes resulting in a larger n  value, indicating that n  may be greatly affected by climate. This conclusion agrees with the study conducted by Roderick and Farquhar (2011) . The value of parameter k  is higher downstream and varies with latitude, indicating that k  may be influenced by both geographical characteristics and climate.  4.2.2 Model performance evaluation For each basin, the dataset was divided into two parts: calibration (70 % of the dataset) and validation (30 % of the dataset). The results show that the proposed model performs well in the 37 subbasins, with average NSE values of 0.883 and 0.863 for the calibration and validation periods, average KGE values of 0.900 and 0.868, and mean VE values of 4.352 % and 7.469 %, respectively. Fig. 7   and Fig. 8   present the spatial distribution of the NSE values for the WECM during the calibration and validation periods, respectively. There were 15 subbasins with NSE > 0.9 during the calibration period and 13 during the validation period, representing approximately 41 % and 35 % of the total basin count, respectively. Additionally, there were 35 subbasins with NSE > 0.8 during the calibration period, and 32 during the validation period, accounting for 95 % and 86 % of the total basin count, respectively. Furthermore, based on model performance throughout the study basin, higher NSE values were obtained in the western region of the Hanjiang River Basin. For a clearer demonstration of the simulation ability of the model, Fig. 9   shows the observed and simulated monthly runoff in the four subbasins of Zhulinguan, Tiesuoguan, Lianghekou, and Chaiping during the validation period. Most of the points fall within a narrow range of the function y = x   . The runoff process graphs show that the WECM model can effectively capture the changes in runoff processes in these basins.  4.2.3 Comparative analysis The proposed model was compared with the widely used four-parameter ABCD and TWBM models. The NSE, KGE, and VE values for the 37 subbasins of the Hanjiang River are shown in Fig. 10  . All three models performed satisfactorily, with WECM demonstrating the best performance, particularly during the validation period. This is evidenced by the highest NSE and KGE values as well as the lowest VE values at different percentiles. A detailed comparison of the evaluation indices for all basins is given in Table 4  , which demonstrate that the WECM performs well and is better than the TWBM and ABCD models in the 37 subbasins of the Hanjiang River Basin. Specifically, during the calibration period, the average NSE values increased by 2.2 % and 1.7 % compared to those of the TWBM and ABCD model, and the average KGE values increased by 0.3 % and 2.3 %, respectively. During the validation period, the average NSE values increased by 3.3 % and 2.3 %, and the average KGE values increased by 4.8 % and 4 %, respectively. Regarding the VE value, the ABCD model demonstrated the best performance throughout the calibration period, with a mean value of only 2.448 %. This was followed by TWBM and WECM, with mean values of 3.602 % and 4.352 %, respectively. During the validation period, the WECM demonstrated the best performance, achieving a mean VE value of 7.469 %. In contrast, both the ABCD and TWBM models exhibited VE values above 10 % (10.038 % and 11.243 %, respectively). Furthermore, the exceedance probabilities of the NSE and KGE values, as well as the non-exceedance probabilities of the VE values during the validation period, are shown in Fig. 11  . The exceedance probability of NSE (KGE) = 0.9 is 16 % (22 %) for TWBM, 24 % (19 %) for ABCD, and 35 % (43 %) for WECM. Moreover, the exceedance probability corresponding to the NSE (KGE) value of 0.8 is 73 % (73 %) for TWBM, 68 % (73 %) for ABCD, and 86 % (89 %) for WECM. For the VE values, the non-exceedance probability of VE = 10 % are 62 % for both TWBM and ABCD, with the highest probability being 78 % for WECM, whereas the probability of VE ≤ 20 % are 81 % for TWBM, 89 % for ABCD, and 95 % for WECM. The results showed that the performance of the WECM model was better than that of the TWBM and ABCD models.    5 Discussion This paper has developed a water-energy complementary model for simulating monthly runoff. In this section, the model development and improvement, model parameters and model structure complexity are discussed. In the WECM, two major modules need to be focused on: the evapotranspiration module and the basin water storage module, which are expressed using the water-energy complementary relationship. It is worth mentioning that the equation describing evapotranspiration is essentially a Budyko-form equation. It has the same structure as the mean annual coupled water-energy balance equation derived by Yang et al. (2008b) ; meanwhile, it is distinguished from the coupled water-energy balance equation at an arbitrary time scale derived by Yang et al. (2008a) . Specifically, the water-energy complementary equation in this study considers basin water storage change as a part of available water, rather than the current basin water storage suggested by Yang et al. (2008a) . This adjustment may be one of the reasons for the increased accuracy of the simulation. On the other hand, the paper has successfully extended such complementary relationship to basin water storage, which is a novel exploration and provides a new insight into the behavior of hydrologic partitioning. As to whether the relationship can also be generalized to other hydrological variables, such as infiltration, further exploration is still needed. The use of only three model parameters in the WECM ensures its simplicity and practicability. The parameters include the evaporation parameter (k ), the basin’s underlying surface characteristic parameter (n ), and the water storage capacity parameter (Sp  ). These three parameters have a clear physical meaning and represent the combined effects of geographic characteristics and climatic characteristics that influence catchment hydrological partitioning. Parameter Sp   is related to the maximum storage capacity of the basin, and the optimized values of Sp   exhibit a strong regional distribution pattern (Xiong and Guo, 1999 ). Parameter n  reflects the characteristics of the underlying surface of the basin, which is consistent with the parameter in the coupled water-energy balance equation of the Budyko-type model. The spatial distribution diagram of the parameter n  shows that its values change with latitude, indicating a close relationship with climate. In fact, according to Roderick and Farquhar (2011) , n  may vary seasonally. In the absence of better information, we assume that n  remains constant over time in this study. Its seasonality has not yet been expressed, so further exploration is necessary in future studies. The value of the parameter k  fluctuates around 1, which may be affected by both geographical and climatic characteristics. In addition, parameter uncertainty in conceptual hydrological models have been widely studied. In the actual calibration process, the WECM model demonstrates strong stability and robustness, attributed to the simplicity of its parameters. It is one of the advantages of this model compared to a multi-parameter model. Actually, it is important to simplify the parameters of the monthly hydrological models. Several studies have focused on the relationship between model structural complexity and model performance (Jakeman and Hornberger, 1993; Perrin et al., 2003 ), and concluded that increasing the number of model parameters can result in over-parameterisation and ill-conditioned problems during the optimisation process (Kokkonen and Jakeman, 2001; Perrin et al., 2001 ). In the case of achieving the same level of accuracy, it is advisable to select a model with a simpler structure to minimize model uncertainty. Despite its simple structure, the WECM model achieves high simulation accuracy, even surpassing the ABCD model, which has been highly evaluated in the field of hydrological simulation. The WECM model effectively captures the characteristics of hydrologic partitioning in arid areas. It confirms that a reduced model is sufficient to simulate basin hydrological behaviour, as suggested by Kokkonen and Jakeman (2002) . Finally, it is worth mentioning that this paper successfully extended the complementary relationship to basin water storage. However, the theoretical basis behind it still needs further exploration in future work.  6 Conclusion In this study, we investigated the link between the PH and the CWEB-Yang equations and derived a water-energy complementary equation to evaluate the water-energy balance. More importantly, the water-energy complementary equation was successfully applied for hydrological modelling of the monthly water balance (WECM). The use of only three model parameters in the WECM guarantees its simplicity and practicality. Moreover, the proposed WECM model was evaluated using large catchment samples, that is, the CAMELS dataset from the United States. Previous studies have confirmed the significance of large catchment samples in hydrological modelling, and a large test sample is thought to be the only way to ensure significant improvement (Andersson, 1992; Perrin et al., 2003 ). Using large test samples, we ensured the versatility and robustness of WECM under different climatic conditions. Moreover, we applied the WECM to 37 subbasins of the Hanjiang River Basin in China and compared it with the widely used ABCD and TWBM models. In addition, we conducted a model parameter analysis. The major conclusions are as follows:(1) Without considering the initial abstraction, the PH equation can be considered a special case of the CWEB-Yang equation for n = 1   . Based on this finding, we defined the water-energy complementary relationship as the sum of the nth power of the water supply ratio and that of the energy supply ratio to unity.  (2) For large catchment samples, WECM achieves an NSE of 0.645, a KGE of 0.684, and a VE of 16.881 % in validation period, surpassing both ABCD and TWBM. Under different climatic conditions, the WECM model showed a performance comparable to that of the ABCD model and significantly outperformed the TWBM in sub-humid and arid regions.  (3) WECM performed well in the Hanjiang River Basin with the average values of NSE are 0.883 and 0.863 for the calibration and validation, respectively. In terms of NSE, KGE, and VE, the WECM performed slightly better than the ABCD and TWBM models, particularly during the validation period, yielding the highest NSE and KGE values and the lowest VE values at different percentiles. Moreover, the model parameters exhibited a strong regional distribution pattern, which enhanced their physical interpretations.    In conclusion, the WECM demonstrated strong applicability and clear advantages in monthly runoff simulations, providing technical support for water resource planning and rational allocation.
1 Introduction Flooding is one of the most common and destructive natural disasters, resulting in significant damage and severe property loss, threatening human life (Jiang and Yu, 2022 ). Flooding disasters are gaining widespread attention since they are characterized by strong outbreaks, significant peak values and wide damage areas (Bajabaa et al., 2014; Salvadore et al., 2015 ). Hydrologic and hydrodynamic models are critical for predicting flooding processes to help prevent or mitigate the damaging effects of floods on people and communities. A hydrologic model is used to simulate runoff generation and routing to save modeling and computing costs when the spatiotemporal distribution of the flood information is not the focus (Hunter et al., 2007 ), while a hydrodynamic model is used to simulate the inundation processes in one-dimensional (1D) rivers and two-dimensional (2D) floodplains, where the spatiotemporal distributions of flow velocity, flow discharge and water depth are important for flood management (Liu et al., 2019 ). Coupled hydrologic-hydrodynamic models are widely used to translate the amount of rainfall obtained from weather forecasting models or rain gauge observations into surface inundation (Xia et al., 2019 ). Coupled hydrologic-hydrodynamic models, which are extensively employed, are typically classified into three distinct categories. The first coupling type involves the coupled hydrologic and 1D hydrodynamic models. In this configuration, the 1D hydrodynamic model is used to simulate flood evolution in 1D rivers, while the hydrologic model is used to simulate the rainfall-runoff across the entire watershed. Examples of such coupled models include Routing-Enhanced Detailed Urban Stormwater model (REDUS) (Pan et al., 2012 ), and coupled Mike SHE and Mike 11 (Thompson, 2004). This coupling type has high computational efficiency, but it is difficult to accurately simulate the inundation process using the 1D hydrodynamic model, especially in areas with significantly changing terrain, such as the flows near hydraulic structures. The second coupling type simulates the surface runoff using a 2D hydrodynamic model in the whole regions (HM2D) (Kuiry et al., 2010; Timbadiya et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2021 ). The subtraction of infiltration from rainfall serves as the source term in the hydrodynamic model. This coupling type has satisfactory and acceptable numerical accuracy and has been widely used. However, as the 2D hydrodynamic model is solved on finer grids across the entire domain, it can be computationally expensive and unsuitable for large-scale watershed flood simulation. Besides, its numerical stability needs to be paid more attention, especially in shallow water regions (Kim et al., 2012 ). The third coupling type is the indirect coupling of hydrologic and 2D hydrodynamic models (ICM2D). The hydrologic model is used to simulate the overland flow, while the 1D hydrodynamic model is used to simulate the water flow within the 1D rivers. When the water surpasses the drainage capacity of the 1D rivers, a portion of it overflows onto the 2D surface, creating inundation regions. In these regions, the 2D hydrodynamic model is applied. Compared with the coupled hydrologic and 1D hydrodynamic models, the ICM2D has satisfactory numerical accuracy. It also costs less computation time and resources in comparison with HM2D. Therefore, the ICM2D has been widely applied (Hus et al., 2000; Seyoum et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2017 and 2018; Li et al., 2019; Sindhu et al. 2021; Nandi and Reddy, 2022 ). However, the ICM2D assumes that the rainfall runoff first enters the 1D rivers, and then discharges into 2D inundation regions (see Fig. 1  (a)). The hydrologic model is not directly coupled with the 2D hydrodynamic models. In the natural rainfall process, runoff can flow into both the 1D and 2D inundation regions simultaneously. In this case, it is necessary to directly couple the hydrologic, 1D and 2D hydrodynamic models (see Fig. 1 (b)). There are deviations between the indirectly coupled hydrologic-2D hydrodynamic model and flood propagation process in the coupling mechanism. The direct coupling of hydrologic, 1D and 2D hydrodynamic models can reflect the flooding process more truly, which deserves more attention (Brewer et al., 2018 ). To address the limitations of existing coupled models, the authors proposed a dynamic bidirectional coupled distributed hydrologic-2D hydrodynamic model (DBCM), in which the hydrologic and 2D hydrodynamic models are directly coupled in a two-way manner (Jiang et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2021 ). The hydrologic model simulated overland flow, while the 2D hydrodynamic model simulated the runoff process in 1D rivers and 2D inundation regions. The governing equations of these two models were reformulated and synchronously solved in a unified codebase. The hydrologic and 2D hydrodynamic models were coupled bidirectionally, with a time-dependent coupling interface. The DBCM automatically simulates the evolution of surface flow, fully accounting for flow states involving both mass and momentum transfer. The DBCM employs a more realistic coupling mechanism than the ICM2D because runoff can flow into both 1D rivers and 2D inundation regions simultaneously, which better reflects the flooding evolution process. The DBCM reduces computational time and complexity compared to the HM2D by applying the 2D hydrodynamic model only to relatively small local regions. However, the DBCM does not distinguish between 1D rivers and 2D inundation regions, which can lead to errors if the 2D hydrodynamic model is applied to both regions. On the one hand, rivers in watersheds are typically narrow and embanked, with widths often measuring only a few dozen meters or less. Finer grids are used to divide watersheds to reflect the flow process in rivers. It is well-known that finer grids mean a high computational burden and resources. Besides, using 2D grid cells to discretize 1D rivers results in zigzagged river channels, making it difficult to accurately represent their spatial location and changes in water surface width. This is due to the fact that the width of the river surface varies with the water level during the simulation. Addressing the shortcomings of the DBCM lacking a 1D hydrodynamic module, this study develops a direct dynamic bidirectional coupling of distributed hydrologic, 1D hydrodynamic, and 2D hydrodynamic models (DCM2D). It includes three coupling strategies: the coupled hydrologic-1D hydrodynamic module (HH1D), coupled 1D-2D hydrodynamic module (HH2D) and coupled hydrologic-2D hydrodynamic module (DBCM). Such a new coupling type is more in line with the flood propagation mechanism and thus efficiently simulates the flooding process. Four examples were used to assess the performance of the DCM2D.  2 Methods Fig. 2   illustrates the DCM2D framework, consisting of three components and three coupling strategies. For the model setup, it is first required to design the mesh. The computational domain is discretized into non-inundation regions, inundation regions, and 1D rivers using uniform structure grids. These three regions are interconnected, allowing for the exchange of runoff. The 1D hydrodynamic model simulated the flood evolution in 1D rivers. The hydrologic model simulated the runoff generation and surface flow on the hillslopes, while the 2D hydrodynamic model simulated the flow in 2D inundation areas. The hydrologic model was coupled bidirectionally with the 1D hydrodynamic model, and the improved river links (RLs) was proposed to represent the flow direction in 1D rivers. The hydrologic and 2D hydrodynamic models were dynamically and bidirectionally coupled through a Coupling Moving Interface (CMI). The 1D hydrodynamic model was also dynamically coupled with 2D hydrodynamic model. The DCM2D's advantages in representing the flood evolution mechanism are readily apparent. In ICM2D, such as the Mike series, surface runoff must first enter 1D rivers and then flow into 2D low-lying regions from the 1D rivers. This is inconsistent with the natural flood evolution path. The DCM2D addresses this problem by directly coupling the hydrologic model with both 1D and 2D hydrodynamic models bidirectionally. 2.1 Governing equations 2.1.1 Hydrologic model Referring to the runoff calculation in SWMM, where a 1D nonlinear reservoir (NLR) model, including water balance and 1D Manning equations, was used to simulate rainfall runoff (Rossman, 2015 ), a fully distributed model (i.e., 2D NLR) was proposed to simulate the 2D surface runoff routing (Shen and Jiang, 2023 ). The locations of inundation regions changed in response to accumulated rainfall, leading to subsequent changes in inflow interfaces, flow paths, and discharge. Runoff in both inundation and non-inundation regions mutually influences each other. However, in most current coupled hydrologic-2D hydrodynamic models, the hydrographs on the boundary obtained from the hydrologic model are used as the input of the 2D hydrodynamic model, with only mass being calculated at the coupling boundary. Since flow information is transferred in a one-way manner from the hydrologic to 2D hydrodynamic models, existing coupling schemes cannot capture the mutual interaction between runoff production and flood inundation. In this study, a dynamic bidirectional coupled hydrologic and 2D hydrodynamic model was applied. The hydrologic and 2D hydrodynamic models were bidirectionally coupled through a CMI, allowing for a two-way exchange of information. Both mass momentum conservation was ensured. The couplings were detailed in Jiang et al. (2021)  and Shen et al. (2021) .  2.2.2 Coupled hydrologic-1D hydrodynamic module The coupled hydrologic-1D hydrodynamic module (HH1D) was divided into the following two steps. Step-1: Determine the river flow direction The River Links (RLs) were used to couple the hydrologic and 1D hydrodynamic models. The RLs were automatically determined by the coordinates of 1D rivers, and discharge exchange occurred at prescribed points along the RLs (Thompson et al., 2004 ). The coupled Mike SHE and Mike 11 simplified flow directions in 1D rivers to only two directions (x  and y ), as shown in Fig. 3  (a). This simplification significantly differed from the natural flow directions in rivers. The 1D rivers must be evenly divided into sections with equal lengths between adjacent nodes of RLs, corresponding to the grid size of the 2D cells. Besides, Mike SHE and Mike 11 are two independent components coupled through an application programming interface (API). This coupling involves storing and transmitting calculation data between the two models at each time step, increasing computational resource requirements. It is considered as an external coupling model. In this study, the hydrologic and 1D hydrodynamic models were reformulated and synchronously solved in a single code base. The RLs were improved to couple these two models. Unlike the coupled Mike SHE and Mike 11, the improved RLs allowed for four flow directions: 0°, 45°, 90°, and 135° (see Fig. 3 (b)). This better aligns with the natural flow directions in rivers. Therefore, the length between two adjacent nodes of RLs was not necessarily equal. The 2D surface cells covered the entire domain, where the fully distributed hydrologic model was applied. The 1D hydrodynamic model was used to simulate the flooding process in the RLs. Discharge was exchanged between the RLs and the 2D surface grid cells. Step-2: Calculate the exchange discharge between 1D rivers and 2D regions Existing coupling modules (e.g., Mike SHE and Mike 11) assumed the presence of a weir between 1D rivers and 2D regions. The weir flow equations were employed to compute the exchange flow between these domains (Dutta et al., 2007 ). Flow discontinuity occurred at the weir, transitioning from subcritical to supercritical regimes. The application of the weir flow equation is appropriate when a substantial water level difference exists between the 2D regions and 1D rivers. However, when water levels in 1D rivers closely approximate those in the 2D regions, flow remains continuous without any significant transition. Employing the weir flow equations to calculate the exchange discharge may introduce substantial errors under these conditions, potentially compromising the simulation accuracy of the coupling models. A new coupling scheme of hydrologic and 1D hydrodynamic models was proposed in this study, where the role of dikes was also considered. RLs were the interfaces that connect 1D rivers and 2D regions. In sections with embankments, the RLs positions coincided with the embankment positions. However, in sections without embankments, the RLs positions varied according to the river's water depth. Depending on the relationship between the water levels of the 1D rivers and 2D regions and the weir elevation, three cases were proposed to calculate the exchange discharge, as summarized in Table 1  . In all the cases, if there was a dike, then z weir   > z 2 d     , as shown in Fig. 4  ; conversely, if there was no dike present, then z weir   = z 2 d     . In case 1, the water levels in both 1D rivers and 2D regions were below the weir elevation (refer to Fig. 4 (a) and 4(b)). No exchange discharge occurred. In case 2, the water level in either 2D regions or 1D rivers exceeds the weir elevation, resulting in a discontinuous water flow between these regions. The transition from subcritical to supercritical flows was observed, and the weir flow equations were employed to calculate the exchange discharge. If the water level in the 2D regions exceeded that in the 1D rivers, as shown in Fig. 4 (c), the exchange discharge was determined using Eq. (10); conversely, if the water level in the 2D regions was lower than that in the 1D rivers, as shown in Fig. 4 (d), the exchange discharge was calculated using Eq. (11). In case 3, the water level in both the 2D regions and 1D rivers exceeded the weir elevation. Flow remains continuous without any significant transition (see Fig. 4 (e) and 4(f)). The exchange discharge was identical to that calculated by the hydrologic model in the previous time step (see Eqs.(12) and (13)). If the water level in the 2D regions exceeded that in the 1D rivers, water flowed from the 2D regions to 1D rivers; while conversely, water flowed from the 1D rivers to 2D regions. The exchange discharge was considered as the source term for both hydrologic and 1D hydrodynamic models, as listed in Eqs.(14) and (15).(14) ∂ A  ∂ t   + ∂ Q  ∂ s   = q L      (15) V i n + 1   - V i n   Δ t   = Q x     ini   - Q x     outi   + Q y     ini   - Q y     outi   + A i  q ri  n  + Q L      where Q L     is the exchange discharges between the 1D rivers and 2D surface cells (m3 /s), which is calculated by Eq. The river bed slopes on the left and right sides are −0.05 and 0.05, respectively. The bottom slope of the channel in the x  direction is 0, but 0.02 in the y  direction. The Manning coefficients on the hillslope and main channel are 0.015 and 0.15, respectively. The detailed dimension and related information of the V-shaped catchment was shown in Fig. 5  . The rainfall duration was 5400 s and the rainfall intensity was 10.8 mm/h. At the initial time, the water depth and flow rate throughout the entire region are negligible. The simulation time was 10800 s. The proposed HH1D was used to simulate the rainfall runoff, with the main channel simulated using the 1D hydrodynamic model and the rainfall runoff on the 2D hillslopes simulated using a hydrologic model. The 2D hillslopes were discretized into cells with a resolution of 10 m × 10 m. The DBCM, full 2D hydrodynamic model (HM2D) and coupled Mike SHE and Mike 11 were also used to simulate the rainfall runoff. In DBCM, structured grids with a cell size of 10 m × 10 m were used to divide the computational domain. All boundaries were set as reflective, except for the main river boundary. In the HM2D, the 2D hydrodynamic model was used to simulate the rainfall runoff in this watershed. In the coupled Mike SHE and Mike 11, Mike 11 was used to simulate the runoff in 1D rivers, while Mike SHE was used to simulate the rainfall runoff in the 2D hillslopes. The discharge hydrographs obtained from different models are shown in Fig. 6  . The hydrographs obtained from DBCM were well aligned with the measured data, indicating that the dynamic bidirectional coupling scheme of the hydrologic and 2D hydrodynamic models could reliably reproduce the flood wave propagation and thus obtained satisfactory accuracy. However, there were slight differences in the rising limb of the DBCM and HM2D, which may be caused by the different flow calculation schemes. Initially, the water depth in the computational domain was shallow, and the hydrologic model was used to simulate the runoff in the DBCM. As the accumulated rainfall increased, the water depth increased, and the DBCM transitioned from using the hydrologic model to simulate runoff to using the 2D hydrodynamic model. In contrast, the 2D hydrodynamic model was consistently used to simulate rainfall-runoff in the HM2D. Consequently, the hydrograph obtained from the DBCM and HM2D exhibited differences. The hydrograph obtained from the proposed HH1D is closer to the analytical solutions compared with that obtained from coupled Mike SHE and Mike 11. This indicates that the proposed coupling schemes of hydrologic and 1D hydrodynamic models has satisfactory accuracy. The coupled Mike SHE and Mike 11 assume the existence of a weir between the 1D rivers and 2D hillslopes, resulting in discontinuous water flow at the weir. This discontinuity leads to a transition from subcritical to supercritical flow regimes. However, the V-shaped catchment exhibits continuous water flow between the 2D hillslopes and 1D main channel, with no noticeable flow transition. Therefore, it is inappropriate to employ weir flow equations to simulate the continuous water flow observed in the V-shaped catchment. In the proposed HH1D, the exchange flow was calculated by the hydrologic model in the last time step and considered as the source term in the calculation of the 1D hydrodynamic model. This coupling scheme is more in line with the real conditions and exhibits satisfactory accuracy. The Nash Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) of different models were calculated to further evaluate the performance of the proposed HH1D quantitatively, as shown in Table 2  . The NSEs of all the models are close to 1, indicating that the proposed DBCM and HH1D has satisfactory accuracy. The NSE of HH1D is higher than that of the coupled Mike SHE and Mike 11. This further supports the notion that the coupling methods proposed in this study are more robust and reliable.  3.2 Case Ⅱ: Validate the coupled 1D-2D hydrodynamic module Referring to Liang et al. (2007) , a case to evaluate the coupled 1D-2D hydrodynamic module was developed, as shown in Fig. 7  . The computational domain is composed of a 1D river and 2D floodplain. The river is 200 m long and 4 m wide, whereas the 2D floodplain measuring 200 m × 200 m is designed. The river is evenly divided into 10 sections. The Manning coefficients of the 1D river and 2D floodplain are 0.02 and 0.05, respectively. The 1D river is connected in series to the 2D floodplain at the downstream end of the river. Both the bed elevation of 1D and 2D regions were 0. Within both the 1D river network and 2D floodplain, the water was assumed to be quiescent, with a constant water level of 0.5 m. The upstream inflow of the 1D rivers increased from 0 to 4 m3 /s over the first 10 s of the simulation and remained constant thereafter. The 1D hydrodynamic model was applied to the 1D rivers, whereas the 2D hydrodynamic model was used to simulate the flood process in the 2D regions. The total simulation time was 1800 s. The HM2D was also used to simulate the runoff in the whole domain without distinguishing 1D rivers and 2D regions to evaluate the performance of the HH2D. The water level obtained from different coupling schemes at t  = 1800 s is shown in Fig. 8  . It was steady at the end of simulation time. The water level in the 1D river network gradually decreased in the downstream direction. The water level simulated by the HH2D exhibited a consistent trend with the results reported by Liang et al. (2007)  and Yu and Huang (2015) , indicating the suitability and effectiveness of the proposed coupling strategies. The upstream water level obtained from HM2D was lower than that obtained from the HH2D, while the downstream water level was higher than that simulated by the HH2D. The water level slope in HM2D was also lower than that in the HH2D. To simulate the flood process in 1D rivers, the 2D SWEs were used in HM2D, while the 1D hydrodynamic model was employed in HH2D. In HM2D, transmissive boundary conditions were applied to all boundaries, implying a zero water level gradient at the river boundary. Under these conditions, only frictional forces acting on the riverbed were considered. In natural flood processes, however, both the riverbed and the river banks offer resistance to water flow. The 1D hydrodynamic model incorporated frictional forces acting on both the riverbed and banks. Consequently, the water level decreased more rapidly in the HH2D simulation compared to the HM2D simulation. Alternatively, if reflective boundary conditions were employed in HM2D, the flow velocity at the river boundary was set to zero. The flow velocity of 2D cells adjacent to the river banks was also zero. This, in turn, led to changes in the river shape. To accurately exhibit the river shape, it is necessary to develop finer grids near the river banks. Mesh refinement is not only laborious but also increases computational time. Therefore, compared with 2D hydrodynamic model, 1D hydrodynamic model is more suitable for simulating flood processes in 1D rivers, especially in narrow rivers.  3.3 Case Ⅲ: Compare the performance of DCM2D and ICM2D In ICM2D, the runoff first enters the 1D rivers and subsequently flows into the 2D low-lying regions through these rivers. These coupling methods are inconsistent with the actual flood evolution process, especially when the 2D low-lying regions are situated along the river banks. The computational error arising from the irrational coupling mechanism of ICM2D has not been discussed in any prior research paper. In this case, a computational domain composed of 2D regions and 1D rivers (see Fig. 9  ) was designed to compare the performance of the DCM2D and ICM2D. The 2D regions have a length of 20 m and a width of 10 m. The terrain gradually decreases from left to right, with a slope of 0.0016. There is a low-lying region on the right side, near the 1D rivers (see Fig. 9 ). The roughness of the 2D regions is 0.025 s/m1/3 . On the right side of the 2D region, there is a 1D river with a length of 10 m and width of 4 m. The roughness of the 1D rivers is 0.015 s/m1/3 . The rainfall intensity is 10.8 mm/h for duration of 200 s. A uniform grid is used to divide the 2D regions, with a grid size of Δx  = Δy  = 0.1 m. Initially, the flow is steady with a uniform water surface slope in the 1D river, while the 2D regions are assumed to be dry. The 2D hydrodynamic model was used to simulate the inundation process in the 2D low-lying regions, the 1D hydrodynamic model was used to simulate the runoff in the 1D rivers, and the hydrologic model was applied to the remaining regions. The results obtained from the DCM2D was compared with that obtained from the ICM2D. Since the HM2D was solved by the finite volume method in Godunov-type format with second-order accuracy in time and space, it has high computational accuracy. Therefore, the HM2D was used to simulate the rainfall runoff in the entire regions, and the simulation results obtained from HM2D were compared with those obtained from DCM2D and ICM2D to evaluate their performance. The discharge hydrograph at the outlet and water depth in the inundation regions obtained from different models are shown in Fig. 10  . It was observed that the discharge obtained from DCM2D matched well with that obtained from HM2D, especially in the peak discharge and rising limb. The hydrograph obtained from ICM2D is significantly lower than that obtained from the HM2D, especially the peak flow and the receding limb. This indicates that ICM2D leads to non-conservation of mass. In ICM2D, the non-inundation and inundation regions are two separate spaces that do not affect each other. Runoff in the 2D regions entered the 1D rivers first, and then flowed into the low-lying inundation regions, where a 2D hydrodynamic model was used to simulate the inundation process. When simulating the inundation process in 2D inundation regions, the discharge hydrograph and water depth at the current time step were determined based on the outputs from the 1D hydrodynamic model at the current time step and 2D hydrodynamic model at the previous time step. These results are independent of the calculations obtained from the hydrologic model at the current time step. However, in real-world runoff process, the upstream runoff can enter both the 2D inundation regions and 1D rivers, while the flow within the 1D rivers can also discharge into the inundation regions. The simulation results in the inundation regions at the current time step are determined based on the outputs obtained from the hydrologic, 1D hydrodynamic, and 2D hydrodynamic models. In the proposed DCM2D, the upstream runoff can flow into both the inundation regions and 1D rivers. The hydrologic model is directly coupled with the 2D and 1D hydrodynamic models, which is more in line with the real flood process. Consequently, the discharge hydrograph and water depth (see Fig. 11  (b)) obtained from DCM2D are closer to those obtained from HM2D. Fig. 11  shows the flow direction obtained from HM2D, DCM2D and ICM2D at different times, respectively. Initially, the water depth in 2D regions is lower than that in 1D rivers, resulting in a flow of water from the 1D rivers to 2D rivers. The results obtained from various models exhibit minimal variation, as shown in Fig. 11 (a). As the accumulated rainfall increases, the water depth in 2D region gradually increases. When the water depth in 2D regions exceeds that in 1D rivers, it flows from the 2D regions back into the 1D rivers. The flow direction obtained from DCM2D is similar to that obtained from HM2D. The runoff from the upstream non-inundation regions discharges into the 2D inundation regions and 1D rivers simultaneously, as shown in Fig. 11 (b1) and (b2), which is more consistent with the actual flood process. However, as depicted in Fig. 11 (b3), the observed flow direction in inundation regions runs counter to that of the upstream non-inundation regions, which clearly deviates from the expected behavior during a real flood process. In ICM2D, the non-inundation and inundation regions are two independent spaces that do not affect each other. The runoff from non-inundation regions upstream flows into the 1D rivers initially, and then enters the 2D regions from 1D rivers. Therefore, the flow direction at the interface between the non-inundation and inundation regions is opposite. The flow direction obtained from ICM2D is inconsistent with the real-life flood process, especially in the presence of inundation regions surrounding the 1D rivers. To demonstrate the runoff paths in DCM2D and ICM2D, a particle tracking method was used to express the runoff path. In this method, particles are transported with the runoff. From Fig. 12  (a), at t  = 100 s, in ICM2D, the particle count is 0 in the inundation regions, whereas there were already particles in DCM2D. In ICM2D, particles were transported into 1D rivers first with the runoff, and subsequently moved into 2D regions. In contrast, in DCM2D, particles originating from non-inundation regions upstream were discharged into both the 2D inundation regions and 1D rivers. Therefore, Fig. 12 (a2) clearly illustrates the presence of particles in DCM2D. As the simulation progressed, water from the 1D rivers discharged into the 2D inundation regions, leading to the transport of particles into the 2D inundation regions. Fig. 12 (b1) indicates the presence of particles in the 2D inundation regions at t  = 300 s in ICM2D. Once particles were present in the inundation regions, they were transported to the surrounding areas via runoff. Due to the opposite flow direction at the interface between the inundation and non-inundation regions, particles presented in the non-inundation regions cannot be transported to the inundation regions, and vice versa. Consequently, a significant accumulation of particles occurs at the interface between the inundation and non-inundation regions. In DCM2D, particles from upstream regions were transported into the inundation regions and 1D rivers through rainfall runoff, resulting in a transport process that better reflects reality.   4 Application of the DCM2D to real-world watersheds 4.1 Case study and available data The Yanqi River Basin, encompassing the Yanqi River and Yanqi Lake, drains an area of 128.7 km2  in Yanqi Town, Huairou District, which is located in the northern part of Beijing, as illustrated in Fig. 13  . The overall terrain gradually decreases from northwest to southeast, which is consistent with the trend of the main channel, and the elevation ranges from 50 to 1500 m. This basin experiences more rainfall in summer and less rainfall in winter, with an average annual precipitation of 655 mm. This watershed is prone to flooding in the summer, which can also lead to water pollution. The DCM2D was used to simulate the flooding process in this watershed. The 1D hydrodynamic model was used to simulate the water flow in rivers. The 2D hydrodynamic model were used to simulate the flooding process in the Yanqi Lake, while the hydrologic model was used to simulate the overland rainfall runoff. The cells with sizes of 35 m × 35 m were used to divide the watershed, and the watershed was divided into 134,960 cells. The model input data included rainfall, DEM, land use and soil types. Rainfall data was acquired from two stations (see Fig. 13 ), and the inverse distance interpolation method was employed to estimate precipitation data across the entire watershed. The DEM was obtained from the GDEMV2 database with a spatial resolution of 12.5 m. The land use was divided into cultivated, forest, grassland, water, and residential areas. Manning's roughness coefficient varies across different land use types. There were three soil types: brown, moisture and cinnamon. Infiltration rates vary across different soil types.  4.2 Calibration and validation of model parameters The model parameters were calibrated. The rainfall occurred in July 18–20, 2015 (see Fig. A1  in Appendix ) was simulated to calibrate model parameters. The simulation results were illustrated in Fig. A2  in Appendix . From this figure, the simulated water level and flow rate were coincided well with the measured values. The NSE of the simulated flow and water level were 0.812 and 0.797, respectively, indicating satisfactory agreement between the simulated and observed values. The errors were within the acceptable range. The calibrated parameters were listed in Table A1 to A3  in Appendix .  4.3 Results The rainfall occurred in July 19 to 23, 2016 (see Fig. 14  ) was simulated to evaluate the performance of the DCM2D. Fig. 15   shows the simulated discharge and water level hydrographs at the Baiyachang station, along with the measured data and results obtained from other models for comparison. It shows that the hydrographs obtained from DCM2D are consistent with the measured data, indicating the reasonableness of the DCM2D. Slight deviations were observed between the hydrographs obtained from DCM2D and DBCM, which could be attributed to the different computation schemes employed by these two models. In DBCM, the 2D hydrodynamic model was applied to both Yanqi River and Yanqi Lake. Compared with 2D hydrodynamic model, the 1D hydrodynamic model is more suitable for simulating flood process in 1D rivers, especially in narrow rivers. It is also observed that the hydrographs obtained from DCM2D exhibited a higher degree of agreement with the measured data compared to those obtained from ICM2D. ICM2D assumes that the runoff first enters the 1D rivers and then discharges into 2D inundation regions. The hydrologic model is not directly coupled with the 2D hydrodynamic models, which is inconsistent with the physical flood process. In contrast, the hydrologic, 1D hydrodynamic, and 2D hydrodynamic models can be directly coupled in DCM2D, which has demonstrated superior performance. The NSEs of different models are listed in Table 3  . All the NSEs were close to 1, and the minimum NSE is 0.896. The NSEs of DCM2D were higher than that of DBCM and ICM2D. This quantitative comparison indicates that the DCM2D has superior performance and can reliably reproduce the rainfall-runoff process.   5 Discussions and conclusions 5.1 Discussions The proposed DCM2D is characterized by the following features: (1) Reasonable coupling mechanism. The fully distributed hydrologic model, 2D NLR, was used to simulate the rainfall routing in the slope, the 2D hydrodynamic model was used to simulate the flood process in the 2D low-lying inundation regions, and the 1D hydrodynamic model applied to the 1D rivers. The DCM2D bidirectionally couples the hydrologic, 1D hydrodynamic, and 2D hydrodynamic models. It demonstrates superior physical representation of the flood process compared to the widely used model, ICM2D, particularly in scenarios where inundation occurs around the 1D rivers. This model achieves a satisfactory level of simulation accuracy. The flow directions obtained from ICM2D are inconsistent with the actual flood process, leading to non-conservative mass. The non-inundation and inundation regions are two separate spaces that do not affect each other. Runoff in the 2D regions first entered the 1D rivers and subsequently flowed into the low-lying inundation regions, where a 2D hydrodynamic model was used to simulate the inundation process. When simulating the inundation process in the 2D inundation regions, the discharge hydrograph and water depth at the current time step were determined based on the outputs from the 1D hydrodynamic model at the current time step and 2D hydrodynamic model at the previous time step. These results are independent of the calculations obtained from the hydrologic model at the current time step. In the proposed DCM2D, the upstream runoff can flow into both the inundation regions and the1D rivers, and the hydrologic model is directly coupled with the 2D and 1D hydrodynamic models, which is more in line with the real flood process. (2) Complete function The DCM2D is fully functional and has advantages over other coupling types. It includes the functions of existing coupling models; conversely, the existing coupling types do not have the functions of DCM2D. By altering input parameters, the DCM2D can be transformed into other models. For example, if both the 1D rivers and 2D inundation regions are calculated by 2D hydrodynamic model, the DCM2D can be converted to the DBCM. If DBCM disregards the impacts of the hydrodynamic models on hydrologic model, it can be converted to a one-way coupling model. Conversely, one-way coupling models lack the capabilities of the DBCM because they employ two distinct models and incorporate fixed boundary nodes. If the hydrologic model was applied to both the non-inundation and inundation regions, the DCM2D can be converted to the HH1D, which can improve computational efficiency. If the 2D hydrodynamic model is used to simulate surface flow over the entire watershed, the DCM2D can be converted to HM2D. However, the HM2D cannot be converted back to the DCM2D because the hydrodynamic model does not calculate hydrologic runoff routing. (3) High computational efficiency. Within the DCM2D framework, the hydrologic, 1D hydrodynamic, and 2D hydrodynamic models are coded in one software and operated synchronously in time, which avoids cumbersome module invocation as seen in coupled models like Mike SHE and Mike 11. Only the local 2D inundation regions were simulated by 2D hydrodynamic model, the DCM2D can save more computational time and resources compared to HM2D. Future research will explore the application of multi-grids to subdivide the watershed, with the aim of enhancing computational efficiency and resource utilization. This approach has the potential to broaden the applicability of the proposed DCM2D.  5.2 Conclusions A two-way coupling of the fully distributed hydrologic, 1D hydrodynamic, and 2D hydrodynamic models (DCM2D) was proposed, including three coupling modules: the coupled hydrologic-1D hydrodynamic module (HH1D), coupled hydrologic-2D hydrodynamic module (DBCM) and coupled 1D-2D hydrodynamic module (HH2D). The hydrologic and 1D hydrodynamic models were coupled using the improved RLs. If there is a discontinuation of water flow and flow transitions occur, the exchange discharge is calculated using weir flow equations. Conversely, the exchange discharge is calculated using the hydrologic model. The exchange discharge is treated as the mass source term of the hydrologic and 1D hydrodynamic models. The hydrologic and 2D hydrodynamic models were dynamic bidirectional coupled through a CMI. The 1D and 2D hydrodynamic models were dynamically coupled through the discharge conservation and water level conditions at the coupling interface. Four cases were developed to evaluate the performance of the proposed DCM2D. The NSE of HH1D is 0.986, which is superior to that of the coupled Mike SHE and Mike 11 (0.925), indicating the reasonability of the proposed coupling schemes for hydrologic and 1D hydrodynamic models. This holds true particularly in scenarios without evident flow transitions. The NSEs for DCM2D (discharge: 0.937, water level: 0.947) were higher than those for DBCM (discharge: 0.925, water level: 0.897) and ICM2D (discharge: 0.919, water level: 0.896). The DCM2D demonstrates superior physical representation of the flood process compared to the ICM2D, particularly in scenarios where inundation occurs around the 1D rivers. The flow directions obtained from ICM2D is not consistent with the actual flood process.
