What’s more, the DCM2D is more suitable for simulating the flood process in 1D rivers, particularly in the narrow rivers, as compared to DBCM, where the 2D hydrodynamic model was utilized for both the 1D rivers and 2D inundation regions. The hydrologic model considers only surface runoff, which is appropriate for the intense rainfall-induced flood events examined in this study. However, a complete hydrologic model should include surface flow, interflow, and underground runoff. In future works, the interflow and underground runoff could be calculated in the hydrologic model. In addition, applying multi-grids to divide the watershed could further enhance computational efficiency and resource utilization, thereby expanding the potential applications of the proposed DCM2D.
1 Introduction The Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) highlighted that global warming is progressively intensifying, climate change is manifesting in diverse forms across all regions of the world, and the global water cycle is amplifying, resulting in more frequent occurrences of extreme events (Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021 ). The study of extreme climate events has become a prominent topic in the fields of global and domestic climate change and meteorological disasters (Fouillet et al., 2006; Zheng et al., 2022 ). The detrimental consequences of drought cannot be disregarded, as its frequency, prolonged duration, and extensive impact make it one of the most devastating natural disasters (Ciais et al., 2005; Choat et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2023 ). Previous studies have extensively investigated drought from various aspects such as propagation patterns, threshold identification, vulnerability assessment, and the development of composite indices (Li et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023a ; Han et al., 2022; Upadhyay & Sherly, 2023 ). In order to provide theoretical understanding on drought resistance, it is essential to investigate the evolutionary patterns of drought and reveal its underlying mechanisms. There exist various types of droughts, primarily classified as meteorological, agricultural, hydrological, socio-economic, and vegetation droughts. Interconnections among these different forms of drought are evident (Raposo et al., 2023 ). Relevant studies have examined individual extreme climate events and their corresponding impacts (Alexander et al., 2006; Guo et al., 2023 ). It is noteworthy that multiple concurrent extreme weather events often manifest (Hao et al., 2013; Mazdiyasni & Aghakouchak, 2015; Zhang et al., 2015 ). Currently, the simultaneous occurrence of extreme climate events has garnered significant attention from both the academic community and the public (Aghakouchak et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2017 ). Heatwaves frequently coincide with droughts, and their simultaneous occurrence engenders a mutually reinforcing positive feedback, resulting in adverse impacts that typically surpass those of individual extreme events or the cumulative effects of two separate events (Feng et al., 2020; Alizadeh et al., 2020 ). Several studies indicate an escalating likelihood of complex dry heat events in the context of global warming (Hao et al., 2018a; Wu et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019a ). Recurrent dry-heat events, induced by elevated temperatures and droughts, are likely to exert amplified detrimental effects on water resources, energy security, food security, and ecosystems (Wang et al., 2021; Min et al., 2023; Jha et al., 2023 ). Most studies on temperature and drought focus on complex dry-heat events (Wang et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2019; Kang et al., 2022 ). Several studies have focused on assessing the impacts of complex dry-heat events on vegetation, carbon fluxes, and the carbon cycle (Hao et al., 2019c; Wu et al., 2020; Wu & Jiang, 2022 ). Wu et al. (2022)  proposed a novel dry-heat composite index. Hao et al. (2019a,b)  developed a comprehensive monitoring and forecasting system for complex dry and heat events. The investigation of the relationship between droughts and its response can furnish a scientific foundation for early warning systems regarding drought (Huang et al., 2015; Cao et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2023 ). Previous studies have primarily focused on the lag time of drought propagation, propagation threshold and the characteristics of drought (Guo et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022; Li et al., 2021a ), while overlooking the investigation of temperature response to droughts. The influence of temperature on evaporation may impact the response between droughts. The determination of whether temperature on agricultural drought responding to meteorological drought is promotive or inhibitory, as well as the identification of temperature threshold values, represents a pressing issue that requires attention. Agricultural drought refers to a certain extent of soil moisture deficiency (Guo et al., 2023 ). Temperature and precipitation are the primary factors influencing changes in soil moisture (Guo et al., 2023 ). Increasing temperature will produce higher vapor pressure deficit and evaporation demand, resulting in increased evapotranspiration and decreased soil moisture (Hao et al., 2019c ). However, the relationship between soil moisture and air temperature may vary across different regions, and the impact of changes in air temperature on the response of soil moisture to meteorological drought remains unclear. Temperature may either enhance the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought or hinder the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought. For instance, in regions characterized by abundant glaciers, the escalation of temperatures and subsequent glacial melting can mitigate agricultural drought conditions (Liu et al., 2014 ), elevated temperatures will impede the occurrence of agricultural drought. However, for some areas, the temperature increases, evaporation increases, soil moisture decreases, and high temperature promotes agricultural drought (Guo et al., 2023 ). The impact of climate warming on warm and dry regions poses a significant challenge to both the ecological environment and human survival. Therefore, effective management strategies and rational water usage programs are imperative in mitigating the adverse effects of local aridification. It is imperative to analyze the temperature threshold and influence mechanism from suppressing to promoting agricultural drought. The investigation of temperature thresholds can provide a scientific basis for implementing effective measures to mitigate agricultural drought, thereby facilitating the optimal utilization of resources and enhancing our ability to adapt to climate change. The primary objectives of this study are twofold: firstly, to investigate the impact of temperature on agricultural drought responding to meteorological drought; and secondly, to determine the temperature threshold from suppressing to promoting agricultural drought under meteorological drought. To achieve these objectives, the present study developed a method to quantitatively assess the sensitivity of temperature on agricultural drought responding to meteorological drought and to determine the temperature threshold. The standardized temperature index (STI), standardized precipitation index (SPI), and standardized soil moisture index (SSI) were employed to characterize the temperature, precipitation, and soil moisture respectively. The copula function was widely employed as an indispensable method for characterizing the interdependence among random variables (Nabaei et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2015 ). Drawing upon previous research, the utilization of vine copula presents significant merits in constructing the joint distribution of drought indexes (Bevacqua et al., 2017 ). It overcomes the limitations of traditional multivariate copulas in describing the dependence among multivariate variables, which are limited by few alternative types and dependent parameters. Therefore, the vine copula method was employed in this study to establish the joint distribution of SPI, SSI, and STI. The bivariate conditional probability of agricultural drought was calculated under meteorological drought, while the trivariate conditional probability of agricultural drought was calculated under both meteorological drought and temperature stress. When the state of STI changes, the trivariate conditional probability also changes accordingly. The corresponding STI state can be identified as the temperature threshold when the trivariate conditional probability is equal to the bivariate conditional probability. The innovative aspect of this study lies in the framework of the proposed method, which offers a simple and data-efficient approach to calculate the degree of temperature's influence on agricultural drought responding to meteorological as well as determine the temperature threshold. Geographic detector is a spatial analysis method used to detect spatial differentiation and reveal the driving force, which is widely employed in driving force analysis (Wang et al., 2010 ). Geographic detectors possess distinct physical significance, devoid of linear assumptions, and enable objective detection of the extent to which independent variables interpret dependent variables (Wang et al., 2016; Wang & Xu, 2017 ). The geographical detector method is employed to analyze the dominant factors influencing the spatial distribution of sensitivity and temperature threshold. Understanding the complex dry-heat events impact on agricultural drought and the driving force is crucial for formulating disaster risk management strategies in response to global warming. In conclusion, scholars have conducted extensive research on compound drought and hot events and achieved significant results (Baldwin et al., 2019 ; Gebremeskel Haile et al., 2019; Naumann et al., 2018 ). However, there are still research gaps to be explored, particularly in the field of temperature thresholds. Firstly, previous studies on compound drought and hot events have focused on the characteristics, driving factors, and dynamics. There has been a lack of research on the temperature regulation in agricultural drought response to meteorological drought. Determining whether temperature promotes or inhibits the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought is an urgent concern. Furthermore, previous studies on drought threshold primarily relied on the binary Copula function and considered only two variables. Enhancing the calculation method for the drought threshold remains a pressing scientific challenge. Therefore, the objective of this study is to develop a model that quantifies the impact of temperature on agricultural drought response to meteorological drought. The sensitivity of agricultural drought responding to meteorological drought on STI and temperature threshold can be calculated based on this model framework. The investigation of temperature thresholds can provide a scientific foundation for the implementation of effective agricultural drought resistance measures, thereby facilitating optimal utilization of water resources and enhancing human capacity to adapt to climate change.  2 Study area and data 2.1 The study area China is situated in the eastern part of Asia and along the western coast of the Pacific Ocean, with geographical coordinates ranging from 73°33′ to 135°05′ east longitude and 3°51′ to 53°33′ north latitude (Ali et al., 2021 ). The topography of mainland China exhibits a ladder-like distribution with significant spatial variation in elevation, characterized by high terrain in the west and low terrain in the east (Wei et al., 2020 ). It is predominantly influenced by monsoon climate, which displays strong spatial heterogeneity of solar radiation due to its wide north–south cross-latitude (Ayantobo et al., 2017 ). Precipitation gradually decreases from southeast to northwest because of differential thermal properties between land and sea (Wang et al., 2023b ). Over the past half century, mainland China has experienced a significant intensification of extreme weather events, including high temperatures and heavy precipitation. This increase in extreme weather has led to more frequent droughts, resulting in substantial economic and environmental losses (Sun et al., 2019; Sippel et al., 2018 ). This study focuses on mainland China, specifically examining its nine river basins: the Songliao River basin, Haihe River basin, Huaihe River basin, Yellow River basin, Yangtze River basin, Pearl River basin, Southeast River basin, Southwest River basin and Inland River basin (Fig. 1  ).  2.2 Data The drought index calculation utilized precipitation (P), soil moisture (SM), and temperature (T) data from 1982 to 2018. The monthly precipitation data and monthly temperature data were obtained from the National Meteorological Information Center of China. The dataset was generated by the National Meteorological Information Center using observation data from 2,472 ground stations in China for precipitation and temperature (Zhang et al., 2022a ). Spatial interpolation was performed using the thin disk spline method combined with three-dimensional geospatial information (Zhong et al., 2020 ). The original observation data has been thoroughly examined by the National Meteorological Information Center, ensuring high data quality (Zhang et al., 2022a ). Additionally, numerous reports and studies have confirmed that the grid dataset exhibits a strong correlation with the fundamental observation data values, accurately reflecting the changing characteristics of precipitation and temperature (Wei et al., 2024 ). The soil moisture data is obtained from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset provided by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which is generated through modified land-surface hydrological models and is widely used in several studies (Guo et al., 2023 ). The underlying surface data utilized encompass slope, slope aspect, elevation (DEM), leaf area index (LAI), soil type, and land use information. Meteorological factors data include actual evapotranspiration (E) and potential evapotranspiration (EP). Human activity data incorporated in this study comprise gross domestic product (GDP) and night light intensity. The atmospheric circulation data considered are North Atlantic oscillation (NAO), Arctic Oscillation (AO), Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), Southern Oscillation Index (SOI), El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO). Detailed sources of all the datasets can be found in Table 1  . The temporal range of all time series spans from 1982 to 2018. All datasets were resampled to achieve a consistent spatial resolution of 0.5 degrees.   3 Methodology 3.1 Standardized drought index The standardized drought index effectively mitigates the confounding effects of seasonality and regional variations, thereby providing a more accurate representation of the deviation exhibited by each grid data point from the overall average state throughout the entire period. Therefore, this study uses Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), Standardized Temperature Index (STI) and Standardized Soil Moisture Index (SSI) (Mishra & Singh, 2010; Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010 ) to characterize meteorological drought, temperature state and agricultural drought (Li et al., 2021b; Guo et al., 2023 ). In the construction of standardized indices, priority is generally given to the parametric method. In cases where certain grid points cannot be constructed using the parametric method, the non-parametric method is employed. The drought index in this study is constructed using a non-parametric method. Taking the calculation of SPI as an illustration, the precipitation series is firstly arranged in ascending order to obtain a new sequence y i   . This sequence is then evenly divided within the interval [1/2n , 1–1/2n ]. The single-variable Gringorten method is employed to calculate p i   (Li et al., 2021b; Gringorten, 1963 ).(1) p i  = i - 0.44  n + 0.12   ( i = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n )      where n  is the length of the sequence y i   , and i  is the order of the sequence y i   . The SPI value is obtained by normalizing p i    in an inverse manner.(2) SP I j  = Φ - 1   ( p i  )  ( i = 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n )       The calculation methods for SSI are identical to that of SPI. The definition of STI in this study is consistent with previous studies (Hao et al., 2018b; Muthuve & Mahesha, 2021 ). In the case of temperature STI > 0 (or 0.5, 1) denotes abnormally hot conditions while STI < 0 represents the cooler conditions. The drought index employed in this study is based on a seasonal scale, with the three-month drought index for August representing the summer drought conditions (Wei et al., 2022 ).  3.2 Copula Sklar (1959)  introduced the copula function as a convenient method for solving joint distributions and studying complex dependence relationships between variables. Different from the traditional linear correlation coefficient, copula function has many advantages such as flexible application and excellent properties. Let F x 1  , x 2  , ⋯ , x n        be the joint distribution function of n random variables X 1  , X 2  , ⋯ , X n    , with marginal distribution functions F 1  x 1    , F 2  x 2    , ⋯ , F n  x n      . In this case, there exists an n-element copula function C 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n     that satisfies the following equation.(3) F x 1  , x 2  , ⋯ , x n     = C 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n   F 1  x 1    , F 2  x 2    , ⋯ , F n  x n            If F 1  x 1    , F 2  x 2    , ⋯ , F n  x n       are continuous variables, then the n-element copula function C 1 , 2 , ⋯ , n     is uniquely determined. Bedford & Cooke (2001)  propose a “vine” graphical tool that decomposes a multivariate copula into a sequence of binary pair copulas, providing an effective means for modeling complex dependence structures. The Vine copula model, based on Sklar's theorem and incorporating the decomposition method of pair copulas, effectively addresses the limitations of traditional multivariate copulas in capturing the dependence relationships among multiple variables (Aas et al., 2009; Czado et al., 2013; Hobæk Haff et al., 2010 ). The commonly used vine structures, namely C-vine and D-vine, visually represent the interdependence among multiple variables through graphical illustrations (Czado. 2010; Stober et al., 2013 ). Consequently, the vine copula model has gained extensive application in hydrology and water resources research (Vernieuwe et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2021 ). The relevant results are obtained by utilizing the vine copula package in the R programming language. This study applies five types of bivariate copula functions, namely the Normal copula, T-copula, Clayton-copula, Gumbel-copula, and Frank copula. Among these, Normal Copula and T-Copula are members of the Ellipse copula family; while Clayton-Copula, Gumbel-Copula, and Frank Copula belong to the Archimedes copula family (Grimaldi et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2017 ).  3.3 A methodology for quantifying the impact of temperature on the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought Calculate the probability P1 of agricultural drought under the condition of meteorological drought. When scenario 1 is set: the drought states of agricultural drought and meteorological drought are both below light droughts, the probability value P1 is calculated as follows.(4) P 1 = F SS I t  | S P  I t    = P ( S S I t  ≤ - 0.5 | S P I t  ≤ - 0.5 )      where, SPI  and SSI  are meteorological drought and agricultural drought respectively, t  is the time scale. In this study, t was three months. In the condition of more severe than light meteorological drought, and a specific temperature condition, the probability of agricultural drought occurring as light drought or below can be calculated.(5) P1  '   = F  S S I  t   | S P  I  t   , S T I  t       = P S S I  t   ≤ - 0 . 5 | S P I  t   ≤ - 0 . 5 , S T I  t   ≤ s t i         where, STI is the temperature state, sti  is the given temperature state. The STI value exhibits a range of −4 to 4 with an increment of 0.05, the multiple P1′ values are computed. Let STI be represented on the x-axis and P1′ on the y-axis (Fig. 2  ). There are two conditions: firstly, high temperature promotes the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought (Fig. 2 (A)); secondly, high temperature inhibits the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought (Fig. 2 (B)). The curves are fitted using linear regression method to obtain P1′=aSTI + b (Fig. 2 ), where a represents the degree of influence of temperature on the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought. Meanwhile, a can also be denoted as the sensitivity of agricultural drought to temperature under specific meteorological drought scenarios. When the sensitivity value a is greater than 0, it corresponds to the orange curve which represents the region where high temperature promotes the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought. When the sensitivity value a is less than 0, it corresponds to the blue curve, which represents the region where high temperature inhibits the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought. The greater the absolute value of sensitivity, the stronger the influence of temperature state on the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought. According to Fig. 2 , when meteorological drought occurs, for the orange curve, high temperature promotes agricultural drought, while low temperature inhibits agricultural drought. For the blue curve, low temperature promotes agricultural drought, and high temperature inhibits agricultural drought. On the premise of meteorological drought, the transition threshold of temperature on agricultural drought from inhibition to promotion was calculated. When P 1 ′  = P 1   , the corresponding STI  value is the temperature threshold. As shown in Fig. 2 , the temperature threshold is STI = 1.6 for the orange curve and STI = −0.3 for the blue curve. The method can be employed to investigate the transition threshold of STI on agricultural drought responding to meteorological drought from inhibition to promotion under diverse drought conditions.  3.4 Geographical detector The geographical detector is a statistical method developed by Jinfeng Wang and his team at the Chinese Academy of Sciences (Wang et al., 2010 ), aimed at investigating spatial heterogeneity and identifying driving forces within geographical layers (Song et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2022 ). This approach enables the assessment of the explanatory power of a specific factor on the dependent variable Y, quantified using q values ranging from 0 to 1. A higher q value indicates a stronger influence of the factor on Y. The calculation formula for this measure is as follows.(6) SSW = ∑  h = 1  L  N h  σ h 2      (7) SST = N σ 2      (8) q = 1 - ∑  h = 1  L  N h  σ h 2   N σ 2    = 1 - SSW  SST       where, N  represents the total number of units encompassing the entire area; σ2  denotes the variance of Y values across the entire area; h  signifies the classification of influencing factors, with h ranging from 1 to L ; Nh   corresponds to the number of units in layer h ; σ h 2    indicates the variance of Y values within layer h ; SSW  and SST  respectively denote the sum of variances within layers and total variances across the entire area.  3.5 Correlation and partial correlation The Pearson correlation coefficient is employed to ascertain the correlation between two variables, and its formula can be expressed as follows:(9) r SPI , S S I   = ( S P I - SPI   ¯   ) · ( S S I - SSI   ¯   )  σ SPI   · σ SSI         where SPI   ¯     and σ SPI     are the arithmetic mean and standard deviation of SPI , while SSI   ¯     and σ SSI     are the arithmetic mean and standard deviation of SSI . The accurate description of the mutual relationship between nonlinear and non-stationary variables is challenging when using the Pearson correlation coefficient. In the analysis of multiple time series correlations, the association between two time series can be influenced by their relationships with other time series (Lin et al., 2023 ). Therefore, this study also employs partial correlation analysis as a research method. To mitigate the impact of variable STI  on the cross-correlation between SPI  and SSI , we calculate the first-order partial correlation coefficient as follows.(10) r SPI , S S I · S T I   = r SPI , S S I   - r SPI , S T I   · r SSI , S T I    1 - r SPI , S T I  2     · 1 - r SSI , S T I  2               4 Results and discussion 4.1 Correlation analysis of meteorological drought and agricultural drought Pearson correlation coefficients were computed for SPI and SSI. From a spatial distribution perspective, a positive correlation between SPI and SSI is observed in most regions of mainland China during the summer (Fig. 3  (A)). The positive correlation is strong in the Songliao River basin, Yellow River basin, Huaihe River basin, and Yunnan Province. The partial correlation coefficients of SPI and SSI with controlling for STI were lower than the Pearson coefficients during the summer season (Fig. 3 (B)). Specifically, the statistical correlation coefficient indicates a 90.63 % positive correlation between SPI and SSI in the summer. However, when adjusting for STI, this positive correlation decreases to 83.88 %. In summary, controlling for the variable of STI reveals a significant change in the correlation between SPI and SSI, indicating a complex interplay between temperature, meteorological drought, and agricultural drought. After controlling for STI, the partial correlation coefficients of SPI and SSI showed a significant decrease in the Southeast River basin, middle and eastern Yangtze River basin, central and eastern Pearl River basin, southwest Songliao basin, and southern Haihe River basin. This conclusion can be explained by the negative correlation between soil moisture and temperature. Zhang et al. (2022b)  demonstrated a significant negative correlation between temperature and soil moisture in most parts of eastern China during summer, particularly in the Southeast River basin, the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River Basin, and the Haihe River Basin. High temperatures accelerate evaporation and decrease soil moisture (Miralles et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2020 ).  4.2 The sensitivity of agricultural drought responding to meteorological drought on STI According to the proposed methodology in this study for quantifying the impact of temperature on agricultural drought responding to meteorological drought, we calculated the sensitivity of agricultural drought responding to meteorological drought on STI during summer in mainland China under the following situations (Table 2  ). Scenario 1 represents the temperature threshold corresponding to SSI below −0.5 when SPI is also less than −0.5; Scenario 2 indicates a temperature threshold associated with SSI below −1 when SPI is less than −1; Scenario 3 indicates a temperature threshold associated with SSI below −1.5 when SPI is less than −1.5; Scenario 4 indicates a temperature threshold associated with SSI below −2 when SPI is less than −2. The results demonstrate an overall positive sensitivity, with only a few regions in northwest mainland China exhibiting negative values (Fig. 4  ). The indexes of sensitivity, namely sensitivity_1, sensitivity_2, sensitivity_3, and sensitivity_4, exhibited values greater than 0 in percentages of 89.9 %, 89.7 %, 89.3 %, and 88.8 % respectively. Under the condition of meteorological drought, as STI increases from low to high, the probability of agricultural drought occurrence increases. This indicates that high temperatures have a promoting effect on the occurrence of agricultural drought under meteorological drought conditions. In regions characterized by sensitivity values below 0, agricultural drought responding to meteorological drought is more likely to be induced by low temperatures. According to Fig. 4 , it was observed that eastern mainland China exhibited greater sensitivity compared to western mainland China. Furthermore, there were significant variations in the sensitivity of STI across different basins. The sensitivity of several areas within the Inland River basin exhibits a negative value, with the Inland River basin demonstrating relatively lower sensitivity compared to the other eight basins. The sensitivity was compared under different drought scenarios. The sensitivity is high in the Songliao basin, Huaihe River basin, Haihe River basin, Yellow River basin, Yangtze River basin, and Southeast basin. The sensitivity of Inland River basin and Southwest River basin is low in summer. Under the conditions of meteorological and agricultural drought intensification, the sensitivity was observed to decrease. The sensitivity of nine River basins is shown with box-plots under four different drought combination scenarios (Fig. 5  ). The mean sensitivity of agricultural drought to temperature is found to be the lowest in Inland River basin, followed by Southwest River basin, in the case of meteorological drought. The mean sensitivity of agricultural drought to temperature is found to be high in Songliao River basin, Southeast River basin, Haihe River basin, Pearl River basin, Yangtze River basin, Yellow River basin. The weak drought combination scenario exhibits a significant variance in the sensitivity coefficient within the inland river basin and the southwest basin, indicating a strong spatial heterogeneity of the sensitivity coefficient in these regions. As drought intensifies, however, there is a decrease in the variance of the sensitivity coefficient within both basins. The sensitivity exhibits low variance across the Songliao basin, Haihe River basin, Southeast River basin, and Pearl River basin, with a spatial distribution that is predominantly uniform except for isolated outliers. The impact of temperature on soil moisture primarily occurs through the process of evaporation (Fan et al., 2022 ). As temperatures increase, evaporation rates escalate, leading to a subsequent decline in soil moisture (Yang et al., 2020 ). As the combination of drought scenarios intensifies, the available water for soil evaporation decreases with increasing severity of meteorological drought. Consequently, the regulatory effect of temperature on agricultural drought response to meteorological drought weakens with the aggravation of drought conditions. The negative correlation between temperature and soil moisture supports the conclusion that sensitivity is positive. Zhang et al. (2015)  demonstrated a significant negative relationship between temperature and soil moisture across the majority of eastern China. In general, elevated temperatures and increased atmospheric demand contribute to the enhanced evaporation, consequently leading to a decline in soil moisture (Brunner et al., 2021; Miralles et al., 2019 ). Numerous studies have found that high temperature anomalies exert an adverse impact on agricultural drought (Ault. 2020; Dai et al., 2018 ; Hao et al., 2018b ). However, elevated temperatures are not only contributing to agricultural drought. In areas with negative sensitivity, high temperatures inhibit the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought. Several studies have confirmed that in glacial regions, elevated temperatures can augment the melting of water as a compensatory mechanism for insufficient precipitation (Slosson et al., 2021; Van Tiel et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024 ). The southern region of the Inland River basin is situated within the Tibet Plateau, characterized by abundant glaciers (Zhang et al., 2021a ). Owing to its distinctive geographical features, the elevated summer temperatures have the potential to induce glacial melting, thereby exerting a mitigating effect on agricultural drought (Wu and Hu. 2023 ). The upper reaches of the Yangtze River basin, the upper reaches of the Yellow River basin, and the northwest region of the Southwest River basin are characterized by higher elevations, resulting in a comparatively lower level of sensitivity within these areas. Kong et al. (2020)  revealed that the negative correlation between temperature and precipitation is weaker in high-altitude regions compared to low-altitude areas.  4.3 The threshold of temperature on agricultural drought responding to meteorological drought The transition threshold of temperature state, from inhibiting to promoting agricultural drought response to meteorological drought, was calculated under the four corresponding drought combination scenarios in Table 2 . The region with a sensitivity coefficient greater than 0 facilitates the transfer of meteorological drought to agricultural drought when the temperature exceeds the threshold, but inhibits this transfer when the temperature is below the threshold. Conversely, when the sensitivity coefficient is less than 0, the transfer from meteorological drought to agricultural drought is promoted when the temperature is below the threshold, and inhibited when it exceeds the threshold. According to the spatial distribution of thresholds, the spatial distribution of temperature thresholds in mainland China in summer is not uniform (Fig. 6  ). The value of threshold_1 is small in the Southeast River basin, the lower reaches of the Yangtze River basin, the Pearl River basin, the southern Songliao River basin, and the Haihe River basin. The value of threshold_1 is high in the Yellow River basin, the western part of the Yangtze River basin, the southern part of the Inland River basin and Yunnan Province. The threshold values under four drought combination scenarios were compared. The results indicate that the thresholds decrease as meteorological drought and agricultural drought intensify in regions with a low threshold_1. However, for the region with a higher threshold_1, the threshold increases as meteorological drought and agricultural drought intensify. The mean thresholds in the Songliao River basin, Yellow River basin, and Huaihe River basin are relatively higher compared to other basins (Fig. 7  ). Additionally, the spatial distribution of these thresholds appears to be uniform within these basins. The southeast River basin has the lowest mean threshold value, and the distribution of threshold values is uniform throughout. The median thresholds of the Yangtze River basin, Southwest River basin, Inland River basin, and Haihe River basin are higher than the mean thresholds. The sensitivity is negative in the southern of the Inland River basin, where the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought is suppressed when the temperature exceeds the temperature threshold. Given that the southern region of the Inland River basin is characterized by glacial terrain, the rise in temperatures leading to glacier melt can effectively mitigate agricultural drought (Wu and Hu. 2023 ). This phenomenon elucidates the higher temperature threshold observed in the southern region of Inland River basin. In most areas of mainland China, the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought is enhanced when the temperature exceeds the threshold. The temperature threshold is low in the Southeast River basin, the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River basin, the middle and lower reaches of the Pearl River basin, the southern of the Haihe River basin, and the southwestern of the Songliao River basin. Furthermore, as can be seen from Fig. 3 , upon controlling for the STI variable, the partial correlation coefficients of SPI and SSI exhibit a significant reduction in these regions. This observation suggests that the influence of STI on agricultural drought response to meteorological drought is more pronounced in these regions. Consequently, the small temperature thresholds in certain regions can be elucidated through the findings of partial correlation analysis. The smaller the temperature threshold of the region, the higher the risk of compound drought and hot events. Kong et al. (2020)  found that there were more compound drought and hot events in the central and eastern Yangtze River basin, the eastern and central Pearl River basin, the Southeastern River basin, the Haihe River basin and the southwestern Songliao River Basin. The study period is divided into two periods: period 1 spans from 1982 to 1999, while period 2 encompasses the years from 2000 to 2018. Subsequently, dynamic changes in sensitivity and temperature threshold for scenario 1 are computed. The difference in sensitivity between period 2 and period 1 is presented in Fig. 8  (A). The sensitivity is increasing in most areas of mainland China, while it is decreasing in the Inland River basin and Southwest River basin. Similarly, the difference between the temperature thresholds of period 2 and period 1 is calculated and presented in Fig. 8 (B). The temperature threshold primarily decreases in southern mainland China, the northern region of Songliao River basin, and the southern of the Inland River basin. Conversely, it predominantly increases in the northern and eastern of the Inland River basin, as well as in the northern of Yellow River basin and Haihe River basin. In summary, in the context of global warming, the combined risk of drought and hot events in mainland China is predominantly exacerbated.   5 Discussion To investigate the driving mechanism behind sensitivity and temperature threshold, we utilized the geographical detector method to calculate the degree of influence from various factors. Several studies have confirmed that the occurrence of compound drought and hot events is influenced by a multitude of factors, encompassing meteorological, terrestrial, and atmospheric circulation factors (Zhang et al., 2021b; Zscheischler et al., 2020 ). In addition to the individual factor, coupling factors also exert an influence on compound drought and hot events (Mukherjee et al., 2020; Hao et al., 2022 ). Several studies suggested that the coupling of soil moisture with precipitation, as well as the coupling of soil moisture with temperature, can effectively delineate land–atmosphere interaction (Diro et al., 2014 ; Orlowsky & Seneviratne, 2010; Zhou et al., 2019b ). Guo et al. (2023)  studied the dominant factors of agricultural drought evolution through the coupling of ocean circulation and meteorological factors. Hao (2022)  confirmed that land-atmospheric feedback and ocean circulation are the main drviers leading to the negative correlation between drought and extreme high temperature. Hao et al. (2022)  discovered that the complex interactions among the atmosphere, land, and ocean in the context of global warming have resulted in the occurrence of compound drought and hot events. Table 3   lists the influence factors that may affect the temperature threshold. The influence factors can be divided into single factor and coupling factor. The coupling factor is the Pearson correlation coefficient between the two factors. The impact factors can be subdivided into five categories, including meteorological, underlying surface, human activity, land–atmosphere interaction, and ocean–atmosphere interaction factors. The geographical detector method was used to screen the dominant influencing factors that affect the sensitivity and temperature threshold. The q-value is calculated to determine the extent to which influencing factors interpret the sensitivity and temperature threshold. Due to the consistent dominant factors across all four scenarios, only the factors for sensitivity and threshold in scenario 1 are presented. A larger q-value indicates a higher degree of interpretation by the independent variable of the dependent variable. The primary determinant of the sensitivity in the nine basins lies in the interplay between temperature and soil moisture (Fig. 9  ). The coupling of temperature and soil moisture in land-air coupling factors reflects the correlation between temperature and soil moisture, which has a significant impact on the sensitivity of agricultural drought responding to meteorological drought on STI. Numerous studies have confirmed that the feedback between soil moisture and temperature plays a dominant role in compound drought and hot events (Zhang et al., 2022b; Zscheischler et al., 2020; Hao et al., 2022 ). Zhang et al., (2021b)  confirmed that there was a significant negative correlation between summer temperature and soil moisture in eastern China, and the occurrence of compound drought and hot events was influenced by the correlation between soil moisture and temperature. The dominant factors influencing the sensitivity in the Yangtze River basin and Yellow River basin are intricate. The primary influential factors in the Yangtze River basin encompass the interplay between temperature and soil moisture, elevation, temperature, GDP, SOI and temperature coupling, as well as potential evaporation. Kong et al. (2022) found that elevation exerts a significant influence on the probability of occurrence of compound drought and hot events. The primary influential factors in the Yellow River basin encompass the interplay between temperature and soil moisture, actual evaporation, GDP, soil moisture, PDO and temperature coupling. The Yellow River basin is a water-limited region characterized by limited water resources, where evaporation significantly influences soil moisture (Zhao et al., 2023; Nie et al., 2024 ). GDP serves as a reflection of human activities, and the anthropogenic emissions of greenhouse gases and aerosols contribute to climate change (Hu and Sun. 2021 ), which subsequently has the potential to modify the sensitivity of agricultural drought responding to meteorological drought on temperature. The primary influential factors in the Inland River basin encompass the interplay between temperature and soil moisture, elevation, and soil type. The area with negative sensitivity in the Inland River basin is characterized by high elevation and abundant glacier soil. Elevated temperatures can induce glacial melting and increased soil moisture, thereby impeding the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought (Slosson et al., 2021 ). The temperature threshold is mainly affected by the coupling of precipitation and soil moisture in Yellow River basin, Southeast River basin, Yangtze River basin, Inland River basin, Songliao River basin, Southeast River basin, Southwest River basin and Pearl River basin (Fig. 10  ). Considering the calculation process of the threshold value in this study, the response degree of agricultural drought to meteorological drought greatly affects the threshold value. Therefore, the transition threshold of temperature on agricultural drought responding to meteorological drought shifting from promotion to suppression is primarily influenced by the coupling relationship between precipitation and soil moisture within the land–atmosphere interaction. The temperature threshold, to a certain extent, serves as an indicator of the regional land–atmosphere coupling condition. The land–atmosphere coupling correlation (Corr (P, SM)) is the primary influencing factor of temperature threshold, thereby substantiating the rationality and reliability of the threshold results. Furthermore, the spatial distribution results of partial correlation between SPI and SSI can also verify the temperature threshold. The temperature threshold in the Yangtze River basin is influenced by several key factors, including the interplay between precipitation and soil moisture, temperature, potential evapotranspiration, and elevation. The dominant factor influencing the temperature threshold in the Huaihe River basin is the coupling of temperature with circulation factors arising from interactions between oceanic and atmospheric processes. This is specifically characterized by correlations between El Niño and temperature, the Southern Oscillation Index and temperature, as well as the Pacific Decadal Oscillation and temperature. The key determinants of the temperature threshold in the Haihe River basin encompass temperature, elevation, and night light. The temperature threshold in this study can determine whether temperature exerts an inhibitory or promoting effect on the transmission of meteorological drought to agricultural drought. Due to the lack of research on temperature thresholds, the verification of temperature thresholds can also be elucidated by the influencing factors and risks associated with compound drought and hot events. Several studies have shown that the interaction between soil moisture and atmosphere has a significant impact on the distribution of latent heat and sensible heat flux, which is a crucial factor influencing the relationship between droughts and hot events (Kong et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2011 ).  6 Summary and conclusions In this study, a copula-based coupling model is developed to integrate agricultural drought, meteorological drought, and temperature state. This model calculates the sensitivity of temperature on agricultural drought in response to meteorological drought and also determines the temperature threshold that shifts the response from suppression to promotion. The method is employed to assess the sensitivity and temperature thresholds in mainland China under multiple drought combination scenarios. Furthermore, the dominant factors influencing the spatial distribution of sensitivity and threshold were examined using a geographical detector methodology. The results are as follows.(1) The sensitivity of agricultural drought to temperature is predominantly positive across most regions of mainland China under meteorological drought conditions, particularly in the eastern region. These regions are characterized by high temperature promote the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought. However, some areas in northwest China showed negative sensitivity, indicating that low temperatures promote the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought in this region.  (2) The thresholds are lower in the Southeast basin, the lower reaches of the Yangtze River basin, the Pearl River basin, the southern Songliao River basin, and the Haihe River basin. The thresholds are higher in the Yellow River basin, the western part of the Yangtze River basin, the southern part of the Inland River basin and Yunnan Province.  (3) The sensitivity is primarily influenced by the interaction between temperature and soil moisture, while the threshold is mainly determined by the coupling of precipitation and soil moisture. In other words, the land–atmosphere coupling plays a crucial role in determining both sensitivity and threshold levels.    This study introduces a novel perspective in exploring the response of agricultural drought to compound drought and heat events using the vine copula approach. However, it is essential to recognize the limitations and uncertainties inherent in this research. The focus is primarily on the impacts of compound drought and heat events on agricultural drought. Vegetation plays a vital role in the land–atmosphere coupling process (Hao et al., 2021 ), and future investigations will concentrate on exploring the influence of vegetation on compound drought and hot events and determining temperature thresholds for vegetation vulnerability.
1 Introduction Groundwater is a valuable natural resource for maintaining sustainable economic development and healthy ecosystems (Morris et al., 2003 ). Groundwater resources provide drinking water for more than 2 billion people (Morris et al., 2003 ) and account for approximately 43 % of the world’s irrigation water (Alley et al., 2002; Siebert et al., 2010 ). The global reliance on groundwater to meet water demand has increased due to natural influences (e.g., droughts) (Scanlon et al., 2012; Castle et al., 2014; Thomas et al., 2017 ) and anthropogenic interventions (e.g., increasing population, agricultural activities) (Gleick, 2000; Morris et al., 2003; Scanlon et al., 2007 ). Groundwater observations are limited in many parts of the world (Giordano, 2009; Sophocleous, 2010; Scanlon et al., 2012 ), and even when groundwater records do exist, interpretation can be difficult due to data availability, effective quality control, and sparse metadata (Rodell et al., 2007; Famiglietti et al., 2011 ). Increased global reliance combined with limited and inaccurate storage surveillance render groundwater resources in many parts of the world to be exploited (Famiglietti, 2014 ), a phenomenon observed at regional (e.g., Rodell et al., 2009; Scanlon et al., 2012; Thomas and Famiglietti, 2015 ) to global scales (e.g., Gleeson et al., 2012; Taylor et al., 2013; Döll et al., 2014; Richey et al., 2015a, 2015b ). Remote sensing has produced robust datasets to augment groundwater surveillance, providing vital information to quantify changes in groundwater storage. The Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) mission, launched in March 2002, stands alone in its ability to measure variations in the gravity field due to redistribution of mass in the Earth system (Tapley et al., 2004 ). Gravity variations observed by GRACE are interpreted as changes in terrestrial water storage anomalies (GRACE-TWSA) after removal of signals from tides, atmosphere, oceans, and solid earth (Tapley et al., 2004; Bettadpur, 2007; Syed et al., 2008 ). GRACE-TWSA represents monthly estimates of vertically integrated terrestrial water storage, which includes snow water equivalent anomalies (SWEA), soil moisture storage anomalies (SMA), surface water storage anomalies (SWA), and groundwater storage anomalies (GRACE-GWA) (Syed et al., 2008 ). Individual water budget components (SWEA, SMA, and SWA) are utilized to isolate GRACE-GWA from GRACE-TWSA across sufficiently large basins (≥∼100,000 km2 ; Scanlon et al., 2016 ). The water budget equation, also known as the mass balance equation, is consistently employed to isolate GRACE-GWA from GRACE-TWSA assuming that removal of signals attributed to other terrestrial water stores (i.e., SWEA, SMA, and SWA) would leave a signal representative of groundwater storage (e.g., Rodell and Famiglietti, 2002 ). In this approach, GRACE-GWA is isolated from GRACE-TWSA using the equation:(1) GRACE ‐ GWA  t   = G R A C E ‐ TWSA  t   - ( SWEA  t   + SMA  t   + SWA  t   )      where the subscript (t ) accounts for time (Rodell and Famiglietti, 1999 ). Robust estimation of GRACE-GWA relies on accurate accounting of water budget components in equation (1) , a challenging task due to the lack of direct observations of water budget components over space and time. To overcome this challenge, researchers have commonly turned to auxiliary datasets, such as outputs from land surface models (LSM), hydrological models, in-situ measurements, reanalysis products, or remotely sensed observations, to estimate water budget components (Rodell et al., 2007, 2009; Xavier et al., 2010; Frappart et al., 2011; Shamsudduha et al., 2012; Feng et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2014; Richey et al., 2015b; Thomas and Famiglietti, 2019; Shamsudduha and Taylor, 2020; Li and Wang, 2022 ). Different models employ different algorithms, assumptions, and parameterizations to partition water within the terrestrial environment which result in variable estimates of storage components (Saxe et al., 2021 ). Differential water partitioning within the modelled terrestrial environment is referred to here as model structural bias, terminology that deviates from previous works (Clark et al., 2008; Ruddell et al., 2019; Konapala et al., 2020 ). An approach applied to mitigate the influence of model selection in the estimation of water budget components is to average multiple model outputs, which further is used to generate GRACE-GWA error (Rodell et al., 2009; Shamsudduha et al., 2012; Voss et al., 2013; Feng et al., 2013; Castle et al., 2014; Nanteza et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016 ). Accounting for variance of the sum in this fashion requires that the data are independent, an assumption that is violated given that many Land Data Assimilation System (LDAS) models assign identical forcing data (Rodell et al., 2004; Mitchell et al., 2004; McNally et al. 2017 ). Further, averaging water budget components masks the transfer of bias that may impede a robust assessment of groundwater storage change. The question of model structural bias in relation to GRACE applications is not new, where studies documented discrepancies between simulated water storage against GRACE-TWSA (Ahmed et al., 2016; Scanlon et al., 2019; Müller Schmied et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2021; Ju et al., 2023 ). However, open questions remain regarding the use of model output and different sets of data in combination with GRACE-TWSA to estimate variability in groundwater storage. Previous work has called attention to accounting inefficiencies of the water budget framework, highlighting their impact on GRACE-GWA (Rodell et al., 2007, 2009; Moore and Fisher, 2012; Jin and Feng, 2013; Chen et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2018; Bonsor et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2020; Saxe et al., 2021; Li and Wang, 2022; Li et al., 2023 ). Xiao et al. (2015)  revealed noteworthy distinctions in groundwater storage changes when comparing combinations from GRACE-TWSA and LSMs included in the NASA Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) data with in-situ groundwater measurements in the Mid-Atlantic region, with the most substantial differences observed in correlation (0.50) and standard deviation (3.00 cm). Śliwińska et al. (2019)  conducted a study comparing groundwater storage changes across two Polish river basins using combinations of GRACE data and 10 LSMs included in GLDAS and the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5), alongside in-situ groundwater data. They noted correlation coefficients varying from −0.67 to 0.74 and root mean square error (RMSE) values between 8.52 and 13.29 cm for the Odra basin, and between −0.64 and 0.80 and 5.37 to 10.89 cm for the Vistula basin. In a study across Tasmania, Australia, Yin et al. (2020)  assessed the accuracy of groundwater storage anomaly estimations using GRACE-TWSA with GLDAS and the WaterGAP Global Hydrology Model (WGHM), comparing results with in-situ groundwater data. Notably, over study period 2003 to 2015, significant differences were observed in Pearson correlation, RMSE, and Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) with maximum deviations of −58.8 %, –32 %, and −126 %, respectively. The observed variability in GRACE-GWA underscores irregularity in groundwater assessments, emanating from inefficiencies in water budget components. However, these studies often employed a restricted number of auxiliary datasets, lacked comprehensive comparisons with in-situ groundwater data, or centered their attention on regional-scale basins characterized by similar intricate hydrological dynamics (Xiao et al., 2015; Śliwińska et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2020 ). A comprehensive and systematic framework is necessary to assess GRACE-GWA variability due to selection of water budget components, and rather than apply an averaging approach to account for model structural bias, we argue that multi-model combinations can bring about new insights about groundwater behaviors. No study to date has approached the question of inefficiency by systematically collecting water budget components to assess the practicality of GRACE-GWA estimation. The goal of this study is to address this research gap by systematically assessing distortions in GRACE-GWA, with a specific emphasis on the consequences of water storage component data selection. The study framework incorporates a comprehensive comparative analysis, specifically focus on three hydrologically similar basins with significant snow and surface water storage components that possess in-situ groundwater data. In our comparative analysis, basin-scale in-situ groundwater observations are deemed “truth” to compare GRACE-GWA estimates extracted using assorted water budget components. This detailed comparative analysis integrates five GRACE-TWSA solutions, eight SWEA solutions, six SMA solutions, and three approaches for SWA, resulting in a total of 720 GRACE-GWA realizations across each study basin. This extensive dataset, sourced from existing literature, allows scrutiny of variability in GRACE-GWA estimates while capturing heterogeneity, offering insights into the intricate dynamics influenced by the selection of different water budget components. By utilizing a diverse set of GRACE-TWSA solutions and water budget components, our aim is to provide a nuanced understanding of how these choices impact GRACE-GWA outcomes. Moreover, our systematic analysis was extended to encompass 12 additional basins, each distinguished by unique hydrologic features and varying levels of aridity. This multifaceted approach highlights inconsistencies in accounting for water budget components within equation (1)  to regulate estimation of GRACE-GWA (e.g., Rodell et al., 2007; Famiglietti et al., 2011; Castle et al., 2014 ). The importance of this study arises from the ubiquitous application of GRACE to assess changes in groundwater storage (e.g., Chen et al., 2016 : Frappart and Ramillien, 2018 ). At question is the reliability in retrieving signals representative of groundwater changes from GRACE-TWSA using the water budget framework. Do the predictions of GRACE groundwater storage change capture “true” groundwater changes? What inconsistencies in GRACE-GWA occur simply due to selection of water budget components? Rather than offer a recipe for extraction of GRACE-GWA, we highlight the importance of robust multi-model output and exhaustive accounting of water budget components to enhance assessment of GRACE-GWA variability that may be obscured by averaging model output. Further, we restrict our accounting of water budget components to readily available datasets and apply our analysis to the GRACE (i.e., not GRACE-FO) hydrology datasets.  2 Data and methods 2.1 Study basins   Our comparative study required basins with adequate in-situ groundwater observations over the GRACE record, a suitable mix of water budget components (i.e., prominent lakes, seasonal snowpack), and be of large-enough size (i.e., ≥∼100,000 km2 ). This led us to select three basins: (1) Saskatchewan, (2) Red-Saskatchewan, and (3) Ottawa, located in Canada and the contiguous United States (Fig. 1 ), which offer a wide range of constructive attributes. We further expanded our systematic analysis to encompass an additional 12 basins, each characterized by diverse hydrologic features and aridity (Fig. 1 , Table S1  in the Supporting Information ). The incorporation of these additional basins significantly strengthens our capacity to assess disaggregating GRACE-TWSA based on the selection of water budget components within equation (1) .  2.2 GRACE terrestrial water storage anomalies (GRACE-TWSA) Five GRACE-TWSA solutions were employed in our framework, including spherical harmonics (SH) (Landerer and Swenson 2012 ) and mass concentration (mascon) solutions (M) (Watkins et al., 2015; Wiese et al., 2016 ). The utilization of multiple GRACE-TWSA solutions, each with its own distinct characteristics (Scanlon et al., 2016 ), was applied given that solutions can yield varying estimates of GRACE-TWSA. TWSA-SH were processed from the latest release RL-06 V04 with 1˚ × 1˚ global grids by three data processing centers: the Center for Space Research (CSR-SH), Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL-SH), and GeoForschungsZentrum (GFZ-SH) (https://grace.jpl.nasa.gov/ ). TWSA-M were provided by CSR (CSR-M) from RL-06 V02 with 0.25˚ × 0.25˚ global grids (https://www2.csr.utexas.edu/grace/ ) and by JPL (JPL-M) from RL-06 V02 with 0.5˚ × 0.5˚ global grids (https://grace.jpl . nasa.gov/ ). In this study, the adoption of scale factors derived from the Community Land Model (CLM) hydrology model to recover smoothed-out signals was not employed. These scale factors serve the purpose of redistributing and effectively reducing mass to smaller sub-mascon spatial scales, with the primary aim of minimizing leakage errors (i.e., signal distortion) when precise averaging kernels are used to calculate mass flux within specific hydrological basin boundaries (Wiese et al., 2016 ). Unlike harmonic-based grids, these scale factors typically have much smaller magnitudes, often approaching unity (Wiese et al., 2016 ). The decision to not use provided scale factors is derived from the recognition of CLM limitations to accurately simulate snow processes, a dominant factor in the majority of basins examined in this study (Wiese et al., 2016 ). GRACE-TWSA solutions (CSR-M, JPL-M, CSR-SH, JPL-SH, GFZ-SH), which are anomalies relative to the baseline average (January 2004 to December 2009), were compared over the study period March 2003 to December 2016. Gridded GRACE-TWSA datasets were clipped by basin boundaries while retaining their original spatial resolution. Uncertainty in TWSA-SH encompasses both measurement and leakage errors. Measurement errors are derived from GRACE-TWSA residuals, excluding the long-term trend and annual/interannual signals (Wahr et al., 2006 ). Leakage errors are assessed through the root mean square (RMS) difference between unfiltered and filtered monthly mean TWSA estimates from the GLDAS-NOAH, which are then scaled by the ratio of RMS variability between the filtered GRACE-TWSA and GLDAS-NOAH time series (Landerer and Swenson, 2012 ). Due to spatial correlation of grid cell errors, actual basin scale uncertainties were calculated following Landerer and Swenson (2012 ; calculation code is available at: https://grace.jpl.nasa.gov/ ). CSR-M uncertainty includes the measurements errors, which were estimated from GRACE-TWSA residuals after removing long-term trends and interannual, annual, and semi-annual amplitudes (Wahr et al., 2006; Scanlon et al., 2016 ). The RMS of the residual approximates the measurement uncertainty in CSR-M. Uncertainty in JPL-M was derived by considering measurement errors provided by JPL (https://grace.jpl.nasa.gov/ ). Given grid resolution of CSR-M and JPL-M, leakage errors were assumed to be negligible through this study (Scanlon et al., 2016 ).  2.3 Auxiliary water budget datasets 2.3.1 Soil moisture Monthly soil moisture anomalies (SMA) were extracted from the NASA Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) (Rodell et al., 2004 ), the Famine Early Warning System Network (FEWS NET) Land Data Assimilation System (FLDAS) (McNally et al. 2017 ), the WaterGAP Global Hydrology Model (WGHM) (Müller Schmied et al., 2014 ), and ERA5-Land (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021 ). Four land surface models were used to calculate SMA, namely: NOAH at 1◦  × 1◦ , and 0.10◦  × 0.10◦  (McNally et al. 2017; Koren et al., 1999 ), Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) at 1◦  × 1◦  (Liang et al., 1996 ), and Catchment Land Surface Model (CLSM) at 1◦  × 1◦  (Li et al., 2019a ). Land surface models (i.e., NOAH, VIC and CLSM) simulate soil moisture through a constant-thickness multi-layer soil profile using different model parameterization (Rodell and Famiglietti, 2001; Thomas et al., 2017 ). In this study, 0–1 m depth soil moisture was considered, as the lowest layers have the potential to become fully saturated (Thomas et al., 2017 ). WGHM simulates monthly soil moisture within the effective root zone (Müller Schmied et al., 2021 ) at a resolution of 0.5◦  × 0.5◦  (Döll et al., 2003; Müller Schmied et al., 2016 ). WGHM utilizes a one-layer soil water storage compartment, considering land-cover, soil-specific maximum storage capacity, and soil texture. ERA5-Land stands as a reanalysis dataset that offers a consistent view of changes in land-related variables, enriched by a higher resolution of 0.10˚ × 0.10˚. Within ERA5-Land, volumetric soil water is represented across a constant thickness of four soil layers, with considerations for soil texture, soil depth, and the underlying groundwater level (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021 ). For our analysis, we exclusively considered soil moisture within the 0–1 m depth from ERA5-Land. Soil moisture products were converted to anomalies by removing the time series mean for January 2004-December 2009 to be consistent with GRACE-TWSA processing. Gridded soil moisture datasets were clipped by basin boundaries while retaining their original spatial resolution.  2.3.2 Snow water This study encompassed a diverse set of 15 basins, each residing within a range of distinct climate conditions. Notably, the initial 11 basins, numerically designated as 1 to 11 (Fig. 1 ), exhibit seasonal snowpack. The remaining basins, situated across Africa and numbered 12 to 15 in Fig. 1 , typically do not experience notable seasonal snowpack. The derivation of SWEA involved the integration of multiple distinct datasets. These datasets encompass NOAH at 1◦  × 1◦ , and 0.10◦  × 0.10◦  (McNally et al. 2017; Koren et al., 1999 ), VIC at 1◦  × 1◦  (Liang et al., 1996 ), CLSM at 1◦  × 1◦  (Li et al., 2019a ), WGHM at 0.5◦  × 0.5◦  (Döll et al., 2003; Müller Schmied et al., 2016 ), along with remote sensing/observation based datasets, such as GlobSnow at 0.25◦  × 0.25◦  (Luojus et al., 2021 ). Additionally, reanalysis data from ERA5-Land (Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021 ) were incorporated into our analysis. Furthermore, we included the Historical Gridded Snow Water Equivalent and snow water fraction over Canada (HGSWE) at 0.25◦  × 0.25◦  (Mudryk et al., 2015 ). It is important to note that the inclusion of HGSWE datasets was spatially limited to the first three basins, specifically the Saskatchewan, Red-Saskatchewan, and Ottawa basins. Similar to SMA, the time series mean for January 2004-December 2009 was removed from the snow water products, to ensure consistency with the processing of GRACE-TWSA. Additionally, we ensured that the gridded snow water datasets were clipped by basin boundaries while preserving their original spatial resolution.  2.3.3 Surface water storage Lake water-level observations for the initial three basins, namely Saskatchewan, Red-Saskatchewan, and Ottawa basins (as shown in Table 1   and Fig. 1 ), were obtained from the Canadian Water Office (https://wateroffice.ec.gc.ca/ ). Meanwhile, for the remaining study basins (as listed in Table S2  in the Supporting Information ), lake water-level observations were sourced from the Global Reservoirs and Lakes Monitor (G-REALM; https://ipad.fas.usda.gov/cropexplorer/global_reservoir/ ). Lake water-level observations were combined with lake area from the global lakes bathymetry datasets (GLOBathy) to calculate monthly average lake water storage anomalies, a function of lake area and water height (Refer to Figs. 2 and 3    for the initial three basins and Fig. S1  in the Supporting Information  for the remaining basins; Khazaei et al., 2022 ). The calculations considered the variations in lake-surface area due to fluctuations in lake water-level. Monthly average lake water storages were converted to anomalies by removing the time series mean for January 2004-December 2009 to align with the processing of GRACE-TWSA. After estimation of lake storage anomalies, the resulting anomalies must be spatially distributed to estimate water equivalent depth anomalies. In this study, two simple approaches were examined: the basin average approach (SWAav. ) and the grid approach (SWAgrid ). The basin average approach applies uniform mass-change distribution across the basin as a water equivalent thickness. For each basin, individual lake storage anomalies were summed and scaled by basin area. The grid approach projected lake water height anomalies to GRACE grid resolutions. This required subjecting lake water height anomalies to processing steps mirroring those applied to GRACE data. Notably, the grid approach was implemented differently for SH versus mascon solutions, reflecting the distinct processing steps employed in each approach. For SH solutions (SWAgrid 1° ), lake water height anomalies were projected to GRACE grids and underwent similar processing steps, including truncation at harmonic degree 60, destriping using a decorrelation filter following Swenson and Wahr (2006) , and smoothing with a 300 km radius Gaussian filter. The grid approach for mascon solutions (SWAgrid 0.25°  for CSR-M and SWAgrid 0.5° for JPL-M) assumed that potential leakage across GRACE grids is minimized during processing, and thus lake water height anomalies were directly removed from respective GRACE-TWSA grids prior to averaging to the basin scale.   2.4 Extraction of GRACE-GWA Groundwater storage anomalies (GRACE-GWA) were extracted by removing water budget components from GRACE-TWSA using the water budget equation (Eq. (1) ) (Rodell and Famiglietti, 1999 ). The application of the water budget equation varied across study basins to account for the unique water budget components present in each basin. For basins 1–11 (Fig. 1  and Table S1  in the Supporting Information ), which include seasonal snowpack, the calculation of GRACE-GWA from GRACE-TWSA involved incorporating SWEA into equation (1) . For basins 12–15 (Fig. 1  and Table S1  in the Supporting Information ), SWEA was assumed to be zero in equation (1)  due to no significant seasonal snowpack. The combinations of five GRACE-TWSA solutions (CSR-SH, JPL-SH, GFZ-SH, CSR-M, JPL-M), eight SWEA datasets (SWEANOAH 1° , SWEANOAH 0.1° , SWEAVIC 1° , SWEACLSM 1° , SWEAWGHM 0.5° , SWEAGlobSnow 0.25° , SWEAHGSWE 0.25° , SWEAERA5-Land 0.1° ), six SMA datasets (SMANOAH 1° , SMANOAH 0.1° , SMAVIC 1° , SMACLSM 1° , SMAWGHM 0.5°,  SMA ERA5-Land 0.1° ), and three SWA datasets (no-SWA (i.e., assuming SWA = 0), SWAav.,  SWAgrid ) produced 720 realizations of GRACE-GWA across Saskatchewan, Red-Saskatchewan, Ottawa basins (numbered 1 to 3 in Fig. 1 ). For the other snow basins (numbered 4 to 11 in Fig. 1 ), where the spatial coverage of SWEAHGSWE 0.25  was limited, 630 realizations of GRACE-GWA were generated. Finally, for the basins without a snowpack signal (numbered 12 to 15 in Fig. 1 ), the exclusion of the SWEA component from equation (1)  resulted in 90 realizations of GRACE-GWA for each basin. Whereas previous GRACE-GWA studies used combinations (i.e., averages) of water budget component datasets which allowed for estimation of uncertainty following Rodell and Famiglietti (2002) , our approach applied a single estimate for each component (i.e., SWEA, SWA, SMA) to account for water storage heterogeneity and thus we have not estimated uncertainty in GRACE-GWA realizations.  2.5 Basin-scale in-situ groundwater observations In-situ groundwater observations were accessible specifically for the Saskatchewan, Red-Saskatchewan, and Ottawa basins. These observations were provided by the Groundwater Information Network (GIN) (https://gin.gw-info.net/service/api_ngwds:gin2/en/gin.html  ) and the National Groundwater Network (NGWMN) (https://cida.usgs.gov/ngwmn/index.jsp ). A total of 608, 866, and 524 observation wells data were extracted across Saskatchewan, Red-Saskatchewan, and Ottawa basins, respectively, many with irregular temporal observations. A well selection algorithm was applied to isolate suitable observation well data with no more than one missing seasonal measurements through each calendar year, identifying 95, 317, and 21 quality-controlled observation wells across Saskatchewan, Red-Saskatchewan, and Ottawa basins, respectively (Fig. 1 ). Interpolation to monthly in-situ groundwater storage changes applied geospatial and temporal gap filling approaches (Zeng and Levy, 1995 ) given as:(2) gw est  = ∑ k =1  n  w k  gw k   ∑ k =1  n  w k        (3) w k  = 2- ( x k  -  x o  )  2  + ( y k  -  y o  )  2   D  2   + ( t k  -  t o  )  2  T  2       2+  ( x k  -  x o  )  2  + ( y k  -  y o  )  2   D  2   + ( t k  -  t o  )  2  T  2            The interpolator utilizes both temporal and spatial information to estimate missing values, taking advantage of conditions where spatial information is substituted for temporal information if it is missing, and vice versa (Zeng and Levy, 1995 ). Equations (2) and (3)  were applied with a 1-month time step (T), and an arbitrary 100 km spatial range (D). The selected spatial range was set high to capture numerous water level observations, while recognizing that near well data exerts a larger influence on missing observations as the weight diminishes with the distance. The variables x k    , y k    , and t k     represent the location and time of the non-missing groundwater observation gw k     within the distance D and time range T. Similarly, x o    , y o    , and t o     represent the location and time of the missing groundwater observation gw est     within the same distance D and time range T. The weight assigned to each non-missing monthly value, w k    , is based on its temporal and spatial gap from the missing monthly groundwater observation, meaning that higher weights are given to close wells with concurrent groundwater observations. Previous studies successfully applied the interpolator to rectify irregular in-situ groundwater records for comparisons with GRACE-GWA (Nanteza et al., 2016; Thomas et al., 2017 ). Spatial bias, whereby observation wells are not uniformly distributed across a basin, is commonly encountered in hydrogeology studies (Rodell et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2016; Li and Wang, 2022 ). To evade spatial bias concerns in development of a basin average time series, Rodell et al. (2007)  constructed an average groundwater time series using Thiessen Polygon (TP) interpolation. Chen et al. (2016)  upscaled in-situ observations to 1◦ x1◦  grids, later using grids to obtain a groundwater level time series for the study region. In this study, in-situ groundwater observations were spatially interpolated using TP interpolation (Brassel and Reif, 1979 ) to produce a basin-scale groundwater observation time series (Fig. S5  in the Supporting Information ). The TP interpolation method is applied given the simplicity and rapid replication of the approach. Bootstrapping interpolations were conducted to validate our approach, whereby different numbers of wells were removed from spatial averaging methods to assess variability in the resulting basin-scale groundwater observation time series. Results documented an unremarkable influence of missing observations on the basin-scale groundwater observation time series (Figs. S2–S4  in the Supporting Information ). The basin-scale groundwater observation time series was transformed to an in-situ anomaly time series by removing the time series mean for January 2004-December 2009. Converting an in-situ anomaly time series to groundwater storage anomalies requires information on the aquifer storativity (i.e., Sy for unconfined aquifers). Rodell et al. (2007)  heralded the importance of applying representative storage coefficients despite the recognized challenges of estimating Sy (Sun et al., 2010; Thomas et al., 2017 ). As no Sy data was readily available for our study basins, the in-situ anomaly time series was normalized to facilitate meaningful comparisons with GRACE-GWA. For consistency, we refer to the normalized time series as the normalized in-situ groundwater anomaly.  2.6 Metrics of comparison Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient (ρ) and an amplitude ratio were applied to conduct comparisons between various time series. Spearman’s ρ was utilized to measure the strength of the monotonic relationship between variables and is applied here for consistency with previous GRACE studies (Sun, 2013; Nanteza et al., 2016; Ouatiki et al., 2022; Han et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021; Amiri et al., 2023 ). The amplitude ratio was utilized to assess the degree of variability or difference between two time series (Müller Schmied et al., 2021 ). The annual amplitude of time series was calculated using cosinor  R-package (Sachs, 2015 ; https://github.com/sachsmc/cosinor ). The outcome of time series (Y) with time variable (t) and fixed period (D) is of interest to fit periodic model given as:(4) Y t    = α + A ∗  cos 2 ∗ π ∗  t D  -  β 1   +  ε      where α    is the intercept, A is the amplitude of the time series, β1  is the acrophase, and ε    is an error term with mean 0. The amplitude ratio between two time series A1,2  was calculated as(5) A 1 , 2   = A 1  / A 2      An amplitude ratio of one implies identical amplitudes (e.g., A1  = A2 ), while any deviation from one signifies differences in the amplitudes.   3 Results 3.1 Comparisons of GRACE-Terrestrial Water Storage Anomalies (GRACE-TWSA) Our goal is to assess variability in GRACE-GWA resulting from water budget component selection. However, it is crucial to recognize that the choice of GRACE-TWSA solutions can also impact the extraction of GRACE-GWA. Thus, our analysis commences with a comparison of various GRACE-TWSA solutions, focusing on three basins: Saskatchewan, Red-Saskatchewan, and Ottawa. Agreement in GRACE-TWSA amplitudes were visibly noted during the anomaly calculation period 2004–2009 (pink boxes in Fig. 4  ) as compared to the remainder of the study period. A correlation matrix using Spearman’s ρ was applied to depict the relationship between GRACE-TWSA solutions (Fig. S6  in the Supporting Information ). High correlations were noted for Saskatchewan, Red-Saskatchewan, and Ottawa basins, with correlation magnitudes ranging from 0.93 to 0.98, 0.94 to 0.98, and 0.91 to 0.98, respectively, documenting GRACE-TWSA solutions similitude across study basins. While accounting for GRACE-TWSA uncertainty relative to SH solutions and mascon solutions, GRACE-TWSA solutions were found to be within estimated uncertainty (Fig. 4 ). The consistency observed among GRACE-TWSA solutions serves as an important validation of the approach involving the clipping of gridded GRACE-TWSA datasets based on basin boundaries while preserving their original spatial resolution.  3.2 Quantifying variability in water budget components 3.2.1 SMA and SWEA products   SWEA and SMA water budget components are often applied as the primary water budget components in extraction of GRACE-GWA, with some studies estimating GRACE-GWA assuming effectively no signal contribution from SWA (Rodell et al. 2007, 2009; Chen et al. 2014; Hachborn et al., 2017; Meghwal et al., 2019 ). Combinations of SWEA + SMA datasets exhibit variable seasonality and amplitudes (Figs. S7–S9  in the Supporting Information ), factors that can influence the timing and amplitude of GRACE-GWA. Correlation matrix depicting Spearman’s ρ between combinations of SWEA and SMA are shown in Fig. 5  . Correlation coefficients ranged from 0.48 to 1.00, 0.49 to 1.00, and 0.76 to 1.00 for Saskatchewan, Red-Saskatchewan, and Ottawa basins, respectively. Correlation amongst SWEA + SMA combinations was lower when VIC, CLSM, and WGHM were used to account for SMA as compared to combinations from NOAH and ERA5-Land. The lowest correlation among the combinations was found when comparing VIC combinations to those that applied ERA5-Land across Saskatchewan and Red-Saskatchewan basins, and to those that applied CLSM across Ottawa basin. Notably, it is important to recognize that these widespread Spearman’s ρ magnitudes occur between datasets assumed to represent the same combination of water budget components (i.e., SWEA + SMA). Amplitude ratios similarly captured distinct differences in combined SMA and SWEA from the various datasets (Fig. 6  ). Amplitude ratios ranged from 0.12 to 2.66, 0.08 to 2.56, and 0.08 to 4.26 for Saskatchewan, Red-Saskatchewan, and Ottawa basins, respectively (Fig. 6 ).
