Differences in correlation and amplitude across unique combinations reflect limitations between reanalysis products, simulating snow processes (Singh et al., 2015 ) and model structure for soil moisture (Clark et al., 2015 ). Amplitude ratios were clearly influenced by select model budget accounting, where large ratios were attributed to VIC in Saskatchewan and Red-Saskatchewan and NOAH 0.10◦  for Ottawa. Bias was applied to provide a measure of the differences between various combinations of SWEA and SMA. Bias of SWEA and SMA combinations were measured relative to average SWEA and SMA from 1-degree GLDAS output (NOAH, VIC, CLM) to provide a measure of comparison with previous GRACE studies (e.g., Rodell et al., 2007, 2009; Famiglietti et al., 2011; Shamsudduha et al., 2012; Voss et al., 2013; Feng et al., 2013; Castle et al., 2014; Richey et al., 2015b; Nanteza et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016, Xu et al., 2021; Ali et al., 2022 ; Fig. 7  ). Wide inconsistencies were noted (Fig. 7 ) with bias exceeding −100 % when applying the GlobSnow product to account for SWEA. The varying degrees of bias suggest significant inconsistency between GRACE-GWA time series that result due to model data selection.  3.2.2 SWA accounting The current state of GRACE-GWA studies in basins with surface water stores reveals a lack of a well-defined framework for converting lake storage data to SWA within equation (1) . We explored the influence of assumptions on SWA using the basin average approach (SWAav. ) and the grid approach (SWAgrid 1° , SWAgrid 0.5° , SWAgrid 0.25° ) (Fig. 8  ). Notable differences in amplitude values were observed among applied approaches (Fig. 9  ). Amplitude ratios ranged from 0.29 to 3.50, 0. 51 to 1.98, and 0. 33 to 3.01 for Saskatchewan, Red-Saskatchewan, and Ottawa basins, respectively (Fig. 9 ). Notable differences in time series amplitude are attributed to repercussions of spherical harmonic solutions including mass leakage (Longuevergne et al., 2013 ) and truncation (Longuevergne et al., 2010 ) influenced by the location of lake storage mass change within the basin (Fig. 1 ). For example, the sole lake in the Saskatchewan basin was located at the edge of the basin, while in the Red-Saskatchewan basin, lakes are concentrated toward the centre of the basin (Fig. 1 ). The location of the lake storage mass change within the basin impacts lake mass leakage (Longuevergne et al., 2013 ), whereby significant mass was lost for the Saskatchewan basin as compared to the Red-Saskatchewan basin.   3.3 Comparison of GRACE-GWA estimates with normalized in-situ groundwater anomaly A total of 720 realizations of GRACE-GWA were extracted for our three comparative basins, namely, Saskatchewan (1), Red-Saskatchewan (2), and Ottawa (3) basins, from unique combinations of water budget components (Fig. 10  ). Correlation magnitudes ranged from 0.51 to 0.76 across Saskatchewan basin, 0.60 to 0.87 across Red-Saskatchewan basin and 0.33 to 0.77 across Ottawa basin (Fig. 11  ). The wide range of correlation magnitudes highlights the influence of seasonality and temporal offsets known to effect dynamic change (i.e., timing) in GRACE-GWA (Akhtar et al., 2022; Li and Wang, 2022; Thomas et al., 2017 ). Accounting for SWA within the water budget equation resulted in incremental improvements in the correlation between GRACE-GWA and normalized in-situ groundwater anomalies (Fig. 11 ). Correlation increases ranging from 0 to 0.02, 0 to 0.10, and 0 to 0.20 were observed across Saskatchewan, Red-Saskatchewan, and Ottawa basins, respectively, when accounting for SWA (Fig. 11 ). However, the application of different SWA accounting approaches (SWAav. , SWAgrid ) demonstrated a differential impact on the correlation between GRACE-GWA estimates and basin-scale in-situ observations (Fig. 11 ). For mascon solutions, SWAgrid  demonstrated incremental improvements in the correlation compared to SWAav. , while for SH solutions, SWAav.  exhibited incremental improvements in the correlation compared to SWAgrid  (Fig. 11 ). In general, correlation results revealed variable outcomes when comparing GRACE-GWA estimates with normalized in-situ groundwater anomalies. However, in all cases, correlations were statistically significant, and thus we are unable to make rigorous statements about a change in correlation significance with and without SWA. Increases in correlation magnitudes of up to 0.20 are notable, especially given that the Spearman’s ρ is a bounded metric (i.e., [-1,1]). Thus, although the results cannot be supported by statistical measures, a clear benefit is observed as measured by incremental improvements in correlation magnitude.  3.4 Variability in GRACE-GWA estimates across the additional basins We broadened our study framework to incorporate an additional 12 basins (4 to 15 in Fig. 1 ) to highlight the disparities in GRACE-GWA estimates across basins with variable water budget components and aridity, thereby augmenting the global relevance of our study. Our water budget framework facilitated the generation of 630 GRACE-GWA estimates for basins numbered 4 to 11. These combinations applied 5 GRACE-TWSA solutions, 7 SWEA datasets, 6 SMA datasets, and 3 SWA scenarios, as detailed in Table S3  and Figs. S10–S17  in the Supporting Information . In parallel, we derived 90 GRACE-GWA estimates for basins numbered 12 to 15 (Table S4  and Figs. S18–S21  in the Supporting Information ), where the absence of snowpack led to the exclusion of the SWEA component from the water budget equation (Eq. (1) ). Since in-situ groundwater data was unavailable for these basins, no comparisons were conducted between GRACE-GWA estimates and basin-scale in-situ groundwater observations. Instead, we employed a cross-correlation matrix between GRACE-GWA estimates, which allowed us to reveal variability existing among these estimates (Figs. S22–S33  in the Supporting information ). Box and whisker plots depicting results of the cross-correlation analysis reveal wide correlation magnitudes among GRACE-GWA estimates (Fig. 12  ). In cases where there is SWA is ignored, the absence of SWEA signal in the African basins (numbered 12 to 15 in Fig. 1 ), or the presence of low SWEA amplitudes in basins numbered 10 and 11, mitigated the effect of model structural bias. As a result, a decrease in the variability among GRACE-GWA estimates is noted when compared to the remaining basins (Fig. 12 ). Inclusion of SWA in the water budget equation expanded the range of correlation magnitudes among GRACE-GWA estimates. The application of different SWA accounting approaches (SWAav. , SWAgrid ) demonstrated varying impacts on the correlation magnitudes between GRACE-GWA estimates (Fig. 12 ). The location of lake storage mass change within the basin played a crucial role in defining the distinctions between SWAav.  and SWAgrid  when linking lake storage to SWA in equation (1)  (as described in section 3.2.2). Noteworthy, the most substantial effect of incorporating SWA within the water budget equation was observed in basin 12 (Victoria basin), driven by significant volume variations in Lake Victoria. Conversely, the smallest influence of SWA on GRACE-GWA estimates was noticed in basin 6, primarily due to its minimal lake volume variations. Our findings document that integration of SWA into the water budget equation may increase the range of variability among GRACE-GWA estimates (Fig. 12 ).   4 Discussion GRACE has been heralded as a key tool to characterize large-scale changes in groundwater storage (Famiglietti, 2014 ). In the clamor to use GRACE to assess groundwater storage changes, it is sometimes overlooked that extraction of GRACE-GWA from GRACE-TWSA is troublesome despite validation studies (Yeh et al., 2006; Rodell et al., 2007; Scanlon et al., 2012; Feng et al., 2013; Castle et al., 2014 ). Early GRACE studies applied large-scale (1-deg) GLDAS output to account for water budget components to extract GRACE-GWA, employing an averaging approach to level out recognized inconsistencies in model representations of water budget components (e.g., Rodell et al., 2009; Shamsudduha et al., 2012; Voss et al., 2013; Feng et al., 2013; Castle et al., 2014; Nanteza et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016 ). Although the averaging approach provides a method to estimate uncertainty by calculating the variance of water budget sums, in this study we followed an experimental design whereby individual model output was applied to account for a water budget component, thus allowing for numerous realizations of GRACE-GWA using Equation (1) . Results document the influence of model water partitioning differences and model structural bias to isolate GRACE-GWA (Figs. 5 and 6 ). Comparison of GRACE-GWA and normalized in-situ groundwater anomalies clearly document a range of correlation magnitudes, suggesting that the use of Eq. (1)  conflicts both the timing of groundwater dynamics and the seasonal variabilities in groundwater storage. Notably, combinations of water budget components were found to exhibit a pronounced inability to faithfully capture observed groundwater changes (Fig. 11 ). Various combinations of SWEA and SMA produced a range of bias as compared to 1-deg GLDAS LSM output (Fig. 7 ). In the extreme case, a bias of −135 % was documented, meaning that comparative differences due only to water budget data selection can equate to alarmingly high unreliability. Amplitude ratios exhibited similar patterns. Although not quantified here, amplitude disagreements in water budgets influence the magnitude of storage change assessments, particularly with respect to trend estimation (Scanlon et al, 2016 ). GRACE users adhere to the message that the lack of global data requires using output from hydrologic models and LSMs to account for water budget variables, and although users are aware of structural bias in how models partition water (Clark et al., 2008; Ruddell et al., 2019; Konapala et al., 2020 ), there is a general devotion to using a select few model outputs. Recent studies have used various model output to assess groundwater storage trends (Rateb et al, 2020; Scanlon et al., 2021 ) but have ignored the monthly storage variations that may capture short-term changes driven by climate and anthropogenic use (Thomas and Famiglietti, 2019; Thomas and Nanteza, 2023 ). Additionally, by considering the range of outcomes in extraction of GRACE-GWA from different combinations of water budget components, we capture the heterogeneity in the outcomes, each of captures legitimate adherence to equation (1) . In this analysis, comparison between various GRACE-GWA time series have applied nonparametric correlation, and thus informs of ranked correlation but fails to capture seasonal differences and amplitudes. By applying the amplitude ratio, we can further resolve the influence of water budget components to assess the efficacy of applying equation (1) . Comparisons for the Ottawa basin (Fig. 6 (3)) highlight extreme amplitudes magnitudes, with seasonal variability between SWEA + SMA resulting in amplitude ratios of up to 4, meaning that combinations of SWEA + SMA result in amplitude differences of 4x that of other combinations. A comprehensive analysis comparing 720 GRACE-GWA estimates spanning three basins, namely, Saskatchewan, Red Saskatchewan, and Ottawa, documented a considerable range of groundwater changes (Figs. 10 and 11 ). Differences in seasonality and amplitudes in water budget components from assorted auxiliary datasets were found to affect dynamic change in GRACE-GWA, corroborating previous studies (Akhtar et al., 2022; Li and Wang, 2022; Thomas et al., 2017 ). The wide-ranging variability underscored the disparities in the capability of GRACE-GWA estimates to accurately capture the true behavior of groundwater resources, with certain estimates falling short in adequately depicting observed dynamic behavior. The lack of a clear framework to account for SWA in equation (1)  has resulted in a wide range of assumptions and methods to convert surface water (i.e., lakes and reservoir) storage to SWA (Shamsudduha et al., 2012; Sultan et al., 2014; Nanteza et al., 2016; Agutu et al., 2019; Ramjeawon et al., 2022 ). Assuming reduced importance of SWA in equation (1)  has led researchers to frequently omit or inaccurately account for this factor in the water budget equation. This is despite the acknowledged influence of SWA on GRACE-GWA estimates (Kim et al., 2009; Han et al., 2009; Shamsudduha et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2016; Getirana et al., 2017 ). Theoretically, this results in estimating available water (AW; Castle et al., 2014; Thomas and Nanteza, 2023 ), i.e., a time series representing groundwater and surface water storage, instead of solely groundwater. The strict adherence to equation (1)  means that ignoring SWA leads to inappropriate groundwater interpretations. Global datasets providing lake bathymetry and surface water elevation changes provide new ways to account for SWA (Yigzaw et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019b; Khazaei et al., 2022; Busker et al., 2019; Tortini et al., 2020; Hou et al., 2022 ). Although explicit statements regarding statistical significance change while accounting for surface water storage change cannot be made, inclusion of surface water storage to account for SWA incrementally increased correlation for most cases considered. Results document that the ideal estimate of GRACE-GWA should thus account for lake and reservoir change, even if only incremental improvements in correlation were noted in this study. These incremental improvements demonstrate an enhanced capacity of GRACE-GWA in accurately capturing observed groundwater dynamics. The findings add to the numerous studies documenting the importance of surface water accounting to isolate a groundwater signal (Scanlon et al., 2012; Shamsudduha et al., 2012; Longuevergne et al., 2013; Nanteza et al., 2016 ). A systematic analysis of an additional 12 basins, each showcasing a diverse range of hydrological characteristics and aridity, underscored the inconsistency in GRACE-GWA retrievals. Cross-correlation results for GRACE-GWA revealed considerable variability among the realizations (Fig. 12 ). Notably, the incorporation of SWA within the water balance equation (Eq. (1) ) resulted in reduced cross-correlation values, signifying that time series integrating SWA increase precision in GRACE-GWA realizations. The application of our comparative study was restrained by limitations. As if often the case, a lack of storativity data limited estimation of observed groundwater storage anomalies for direct comparison to GRACE-GWA. Instead, the in-situ groundwater time series was normalized to capture seasonal changes. Further study to address model output uncertainty within a multi-model approach to extract GRACE-GWA is warranted, as our approach focused on single model output contributions to water budget components. Spearman’s ρ simply measures the strength of the monotonic relationship between two variables, and thus fails to account for important GRACE-GWA signals including seasonal amplitudes. By applying an amplitude metric, the amplitude ratio (Equation (5) ), we show how combinations of water budget components can result in inaccurate or misleading groundwater storage loss, potentially resulting in misleading decisions about groundwater use and conservation.  5 Conclusion The successful achievement of groundwater sustainability is contingent upon the implementation of effective surveillance of groundwater resources (Morris et al., 2003; Giordano, 2009; Gleeson et al., 2020 ). Through effective surveillance, stakeholders can track changes in groundwater levels, identify potential threats to groundwater resources, and make informed decisions about the use of these resources. Model structural bias pertaining to how hydrologic models and land surface models vertically partition water regulated estimation of GRACE-GWA, while simple accounting methods to account for surface water were found to consistently increase correlations with respect to basin in-situ groundwater time series (Fig. 11 ). The wide range of variability observed in GRACE-GWA underscores the uncertainty in the current state of knowledge within groundwater resources (Figs. 10, 11, and 12 ). These findings underscore the paramount importance of relying on accurate multi-model output. This precision is not only a nicety but a necessity in elevating the reliability and robustness of GRACE-GWA estimates, thereby advancing our understanding of groundwater dynamics with unparalleled accuracy. This study not only contributes substantially to a comprehensive understanding of the challenges inherent in isolating GRACE-GWA from GRACE-TWSA using the water balance equation (Eq. (1) ) but also advocates for a comprehensive appraisal of water budget components in GRACE groundwater studies. Such a holistic approach promises to yield reliable and trustworthy estimates of GRACE-GWA, providing a solid foundation for future assessments. Additionally, our research serves as a catalyst for revisiting and advancing critical GRACE-GWA studies, particularly those focused on basins experiencing groundwater depletion. This re-examination aims a nuanced assessment of groundwater storage dynamics, crucial for effectively mitigating challenges associated with this vital resource. Data Availability Statement . 1 Introduction Water-rock interaction is prevalent in subsurface environment (Ahmat et al., 2022 ), and the resulting dissolution/precipitation of minerals alters the pore structure of porous media, subsequently impacting their hydrogeological and mechanical properties (Fan et al., 2023; Tan et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024 ). Consequently, this phenomenon inevitably influences the operational efficiency and safety of various subsurface projects such as the exploitation of underground resources and energy sources (e.g., groundwater extraction and geothermal energy development), and waste geological disposal (e.g., CO2  and nuclear waste). This process is thought to be accelerated and intensified through the involvement of CO2 , as it dissolves in water and leads to acidification, thereby augmenting the reactivity of water towards various carbonate and silicate minerals (An et al., 2021 ). The CO2 -water–rock interactions, as exemplified by the natural formation of karst caves in the limestone formations, are anticipated to be enhanced during CO2  geological storage (CGS) due to elevated levels of CO2  content and partial pressure (Chen et al., 2023 ). CGS, considered as one of the most promising techniques for mitigating greenhouse gas emissions and addressing climate change (Castelletto et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2005 ), is being demonstrated through various projects worldwide. Representative demonstration projects includes Sleipner project in Norway (Furre et al., 2016 ), Salah project in Algeria (Deflandre et al., 2010 ) and Weyburn project in Canada (Srivastava et al., 2000 ). The injection efficiency and sequestration safety, which are heavily influenced by the hydrogeological parameters (e.g., porosity and permeability) and mechanical properties (e.g., bulk and shear moduli) of rocks, are of paramount concern to the industry when injecting significant amounts of CO2  into subsurface reservoirs. Therefore, it is imperative to gain a more profound comprehension of the influence mechanism of CO2 -water–rock interactions on these parameters (Ye et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2016; Zhong et al., 2022 ). While numerous macro-scale studies have been conducted to investigate the impact of CO2 -water–rock interaction on permeability evolution and mechanical response, the prevailing approach for characterizing these parameters primarily relies on their correlation with porosity (Alonso et al., 2012; Gan et al., 2021; Kang et al., 2014; Tian et al., 2014; Tian et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2015 ). However, it should be noted that alterations in hydrogeological and mechanical properties of rock fundamentally arise from variations in microscopic pore structure, and the underlying mechanism driving these changes still remains elusive. For instance, variations in mineral species and their spatial distribution, along with intricate storage conditions (such as temperature and flow conditions), can lead to disparities in mineral reaction characteristics and pore structure evolution. Consequently, even at the identical porosity levels, permeability may exhibit dissimilarities (Miller et al., 2017 ). Not to mention the mechanical properties of rocks, which are not solely determined by pore structure, but also depend on the type, content and spatial distribution of minerals (Li et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2020 ). Therefore, to comprehend the mechanism of mineral dissolution/precipitation induced by CO2 -water–rock interaction on rock permeability and mechanical properties, it is imperative to concentrate on the evolution of pore structure and types and spatial distribution of minerals at the pore scale. X-ray microtomography (micro-CT) technique is a highly effective method for observing the dynamic changes in pore morphology during mineral reactions. By analyzing pre- and post-reaction scanning images, the evolution of pore structure and characteristics of mineral dissolution or precipitation can be determined (Al-Khulaifi et al., 2017; Gouze and Luquot, 2011; Menke et al., 2015 ). According to the fluid flow rate and pressure difference between the inlet and outlet of the sample, the permeability of the rock sample before and after reaction can be calculated using Darcy’s law. However, it is challenging to accurately measure the mechanical properties of the same sample before and after the reaction, as mechanical testing often causes damage to rock samples. The trend of changes in mechanical properties can only be determined by increasing the number of test samples (some samples undergo mechanical testing without undergoing water–rock reactions, while others undergo water–rock reactions prior to mechanical testing) (Li et al., 2018 ). However, inherent variations in mechanical properties in rock samples prior to reaction can introduce ambiguity into the interpretation of mechanical test results, representing a significant limitation of this approach. Pore-scale numerical simulations represent another effective approach to address the aforementioned issues with high accuracy and reliability. The Lattice Boltzmann method (LBM), as a mesoscopic approach, is increasingly utilized to simulate reactive transport processes associated with the CGS. Kang et al. (2006); Kang et al. (2007)  developed an LBM reaction model that can simulate reactive transport with multiple aqueous components. The model was then used to simulate CO2  induced carbonate mineral dissolution and precipitation in 2D porous media (Kang et al., 2010 ). Because their concentration boundary is immovable, Chen et al. (2013)  proposed a general LBM concentration boundary that can handle reactive and moving solids. Tian et al. (2016)  simulated calcite reaction at fractured reservoirs and considered that each ion can penetrate the interior of the rock. Due to the lack of research on geometric heterogeneity and mineral diversity, Gao et al. (2017)  conducted a long-term calcite dissolution simulation in 3D real digital cores and verified by their experiments. In addition, Fazeli et al. (2019)  and An et al. (2021)  built a GPU parallelization reaction model that coupled Volumetric LBM and PhreeqcRM to predict the dissolution progresses of caprock in large scale. Recently, the pore-scale LBM multiphase flow and reactive transport modeling have been comprehensively reviewed by Chen et al. (2022)  and Wang et al. (2023) . In general, there is a considerable body of research on CO2 -water–rock interaction at the pore scale, encompassing both experimental and numerical simulation studies. However, to the best of our knowledge, most existing LBM simulation studies have primarily focused on the mechanism of mineral dissolution or precipitation and model development (Chen et al., 2018; Hao and Xu, 2023; Zhang et al., 2012 ). Few studies have incorporated permeability calculation (Fazeli et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2023; Yoon et al., 2017 ), and even fewer permeability assessments have been conducted based on real 3D samples (Jiang and Tsuji, 2014; Tsuji et al., 2019 ). Besides, the subsequent simulations addressing mechanical properties evolution remain scarce, because the principles of LBM dictate that it is not highly applicable for mechanical simulation. Therefore, it necessitates integration with other methodologies to achieve a comprehensive multi-field simulation encompassing fluid flow, mass transfer, geochemical reactions, pore structure alteration, and evolution of rock permeability and mechanical properties. For instance, the finite element method (FEM) is extensively employed for calculating the mechanical properties of materials containing composite inclusions (Arns et al., 2002; Garboczi and Berryman, 2001; Meille and Garboczi, 2001; Roberts and Garboczi, 2002 ). In this study, the coupled LBM-FEM model is proposed to quantitatively investigate the hydrogeological and mechanical properties evolution of rock invaded by saturated CO2  solution. The fractal parameters are introduced to more effectively evaluate alterations in pore structure caused by CO2 -water–rock interaction. First, the methodology involved is presented, encompassing the fundamental governing equations and coupling approach of lattice Boltzmann and finite element models, as well as fractal theory. Then, the model setup process is introduced, including the simulated sample, initial and boundary conditions of the model. The subsequent section gives the primary simulation findings. Finally, an insightful discussion is made and the main conclusions are expounded.  2 Methods 2.1 Reactive transport modeling and pore structure updating 2.1.1 Fluid flow and solute transport The LBM is an efficient numerical method for simulating fluid flow and mass transfer with complicated boundary conditions (Xin et al., 2021 ). The three-dimensional LBM simulation technique used in this work is based on the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK) method (Wang et al., 2022; Weinmiller et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2021 ). As a result of CO2  dissolution, carbonic acid is formed and can further dissociate to form hydrogen ions and bicarbonates:(11) CO  2  + H 2  O ⇌ H 2  CO  3  ⇌ H  +  + HCO  3  -       The acidification of brine disrupts the initial equilibrium between water and rock, thereby initiating new reactions. In this study, only the reaction involving calcite is considered due to its widespread occurrence in both sandstone reservoirs and mudstone caps, as well as its significantly higher reaction rate compared to feldspar and clay minerals. Consequently, it often serves as the primary reactant with CO2  and water (Xu et al., 2011 ). Previous studies have demonstrated that, in addition to hydrogen ions, carbonic acid can also undergo direct reaction with calcite, resulting in the dissolution of calcite (Gray et al., 2018; 2021 ).Therefore, the dissolution of calcite induced by CO2  can be described as:(12) H  +  + C a C O 3  ⇌ Ca  2 +   + HCO  3  -      (13) H 2  CO  3  + C a C O 3  ⇌ Ca  2 +   + 2 H C O  3  -       Given the small time-step utilized in the LBM model, in order to accurately quantify the reaction rate and obtain reliable results, it is imperative to incorporate the kinetics of calcite dissolution. In contrast, the dissociation rate of H2 CO3  into H+  and HCO3 −  is significantly higher than that of mineral precipitation or dissolution, thus it is commonly regarded as an equilibrium reaction. Based on the aforementioned reactions governing calcite dissolution, the reaction rate can be expressed as (Gray et al., 2021 ):(14) R = - h 1  a H  +   ( 1 - Q 1  / K e q 1   )  - h 2  a H 2  CO  3    ( 1 - Q 2  / K e q 2   )      where R    is the calcite dissolution rate, h 1     and h 2     represent the reaction rate constants for H+  and H2 CO3 , respectively. a H  +     , a H 2  CO  3       are the activities of H+  and H2 CO3 , respectively. Keq   is the equilibrium constant, Q i , i = 1 , 2      are the ion’s activity products which can be expressed as: Q 1  = a Ca  2 +    a HCO  3  -   / a H  +     , Q 2  = a Ca  2 +    a H C O 3  -   2  / a H 2  CO  3      . For simplicity, all dissolved CO2  in brine is assumed to produce H2 CO3 . Thus, the species in the solution include g 1  ( H  +  )    , g 2  ( Ca  2 +   )    , g 3  ( HCO  3  -  )    , and g 4  ( H 2  CO  3  )    . For heterogeneous mineral reactions at the fluid–solid interface, we extend the concentration boundary condition proposed by Chen et al. (2013)  to three dimensions. For more details about this method, please refer to Zhang et al. (2021b) .  2.1.3 Porosity and permeability updating The variation of porosity of rock sample can be easily determined based on the extent of mineral dissolution/precipitation. In terms of permeability, it can be calculated using the Darcy’s law:(18) k = L v ρ Q  A 2  Δ P       where Q  is the flow rate through the cross sectional of the rock sample, A 2     is the cross sectional area,ΔP  is the pressure difference between the inlet and outlet, v    and ρ    are the fluid viscosity and density, respectively, and L  is the sample length.   2.2 Rock mechanical properties evolution modeling The numerical simulations commonly employed geotechnical engineering methods, including the finite difference method (FDM), finite element method (FEM), boundary element method (BEM), and semi-analytical method. Among these techniques, the FEM stands out as the most mature and widely utilized approach (Barros et al., 2023 ). Its advantages encompass: 1) Convenient and accurate representation of complex constitutive relationships pertaining to rock and soil materials; 2) Robust capability to handle intricate boundaries; 3) Availability of well-established methodologies and computational procedures. In this study, ELAS3D (Lee et al., 2024; Tao et al., 2023 ), an open-source program specifically designed for the calculation of elastic properties based on digital images of random materials, was employed to determine the pre- and post-CO2 -water–rock interaction elastic properties of rock. The fundamental principle of the program involves imposing strain boundary conditions on the digital rock surface, computing the initial elastic energy, and subsequently solving for the stress–strain state corresponding to the minimum elastic energy using the conjugate gradient method. This is followed by calculating average strain and stress tensors in order to determine the average bulk and shear moduli of the digital rock. The elastic potential energy of an elastomer is determined by its elastic modulus and strain (Garboczi and Berryman, 2001 ):(19) E n  = 1 2  ∫ ε α  C α β   ε β  d V , ( α ,  β = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ ,  6 )       where ε α     and ε β     represent the strain of the tiny unit inside the elastomer, and C α β      represents elastic modulus tensor. If the pixel is taken as the element, the elastic energy of the element can be expressed as (Garboczi, 1998 ):(20) E n  = 1 2  ∫ a   T  M  a  d V     where a    represents the element node displacement vector, M    is the stiffness matrix of element. Using the Simpson’s rule to perform the integration, the elastic energy can be expressed as (Garboczi, 1998 ):(21) E n  = 1 2  ∑ e  a   T  M  xyz   a      where M  xyz      is the stiffness matrix of the integration point. Considering the application of periodic boundary conditions, the elastic energy of a boundary element can be given by (Roberts and Garboczi, 2002 ):(22) E n  = 1 2  ∑ e  a   T  M  xyz   a  + 2 δ   T  M  xyz   a  + δ   T  M  xyz   δ         where the components of 8-vector δ    are related to the location of the node. The total energy of the digital rock is obtained by summing over all elements/pixels (Garboczi, 1998 ):(23) E n  = 1 2  U   T  A  U  + C  U  + d     where U    is the displacement vector of all nodes, A    is assembled by the element stiffness matrix M    according to the position of the node, C    is assembled by δ   T  M    , and d    is a constant. According to the variational principle, the elastic energy in equilibrium tends towards its minimum value under specified boundary conditions, and the gradient of the energy will then be (Arns et al., 2002 ):(24) ∂ E  ∂ U   = A  U  + C  = 0      After calculating the average stress and strain tensors of digital rock, its average bulk and shear moduli can be determined (Arrowsmith et al., 2012 ):(25) K  ¯   = 1 3  × σ 11   ¯   + σ 22   ¯   + σ 33   ¯    ε 11   ¯   + ε 22   ¯   + ε 33   ¯         (26) G  ¯   = 1 3  × σ 23   ¯   ε 23   ¯    + σ 31   ¯   ε 31   ¯    + σ 12   ¯   ε 12   ¯           where σ ij    ¯      and ε ij    ¯      are the components of average stress and strain tensors, respectively.  2.3 LBM-FEM coupling scheme As illustrated in Fig. 1  , the Hydraulic-Chemical-Mechanical (HCM) coupled simulation of CO2 -water–rock interaction is achieved by employing a sequential coupling method. Firstly, the fluid's flow velocity is determined by solving the flow equation in D 3  Q 19     model. Subsequently, this information is transmitted to the solute transport equation in D 3  Q 7     model for calculating ion concentration in the solution. Once these steps are completed, chemical reaction simulation is conducted to determine mineral dissolution or precipitation quantities, and the rock skeleton is subsequently updated accordingly. In other words, the coupling between fluid flow and chemical reactions occurs through the exchange of information such as flow rate and solute concentration, while the interaction between chemical reactions and mechanical property evolution is facilitated by updating the grid to the incorporate skeleton evolution information.  2.4 Model validation Given the thorough validation and widespread adoption of the opening source program ELAS3D for mechanical simulation (Ikeda et al., 2017; Ikeda et al., 2021 ), we will solely focus on validating the newly developed LBM model in this study. The accuracy of the LBM reactive transport model is validated by comparing the simulation results with those obtained from the experiment conducted by Gray et al. (2021) . The experimental material comprises a pure calcite specimen with a centrally drilled cylindrical channel measuring 1 mm in diameter across its cross section. The sample is 18.2 mm in length and has a non-reactive steel on the left side, which includes a 3 mm circular aperture for injecting the reaction solution. The injected fluid is a CO2  solution with a concentration of 0.93 mol/L. During the experiment, the injection rate of CO2  solution was maintained at a constant rate of 1.07 mm3 /s, while the ambient temperature was precisely regulated to 50 °C. The above experiment was replicated through LBM simulation, and the simulated dissolution of calcite was compared to experimental values. It is worth noting that two schemes were considered in the simulation: one involving direct reaction between carbonic acid and calcite (i.e., Eq. (13) ), and another excluding this reaction. As present in Fig. 2  , the amount of dissolved calcite obtained from the scheme incorporating Eq. (13)  closely matches the experimentally measured value, with a maximum relative error of 3 %. However, if we neglect the reaction between calcite and carbonic acid and consider only its reaction with hydrogen ions (i.e., Eq. (12) ), the simulated solution amount of calcite will be approximately one order of magnitude lower. This emphasizes the necessity of incorporating Eq. (13)  into the model.  2.5 Fractal theory The pore structure of the medium is inevitably altered by mineral dissolution/precipitation, and porosity alone cannot fully capture this transformation. Therefore, fractal theory was employed in this study to characterize changes in pore structure during the mineral reaction using two crucial parameters − fractal dimension (D F    ) and succolarity (β   ). Fractal dimension is useful for characterizing the physical properties of scale-invariants, and box counting is the most common and efficient method of calculation (Xia et al., 2019 ). In this algorithm, boxes of different scales r    are used to cover the samples, and the number of boxes that cover the pores is recorded as N r    . According to N r   r    relationship, the fractal dimension can be obtained by (Lim et al., 2023; Milicic, 2018 ):(27) D F  = lim r → 0   lg N r   lg ( 1 r  )        In addition to fractal dimension, succolarity is also a crucial parameter in fractal geometry theory. Compared to fractal dimension, succolarity is more effective in capturing the directional information of pore structure. According to different box scales r   , the calculation of succolarity necessitates the determination of the total virtual pressure over the whole sample, as well as the total virtual pressure of the boxes containing pores (de Melo and Conci, 2013 ). In order to make the succolarity dimensionless, its value can be characterized as the pressure occupation equation (de Melo and Conci, 2013; Devi and Vidivelli, 2022 ):(28) β ( B S ( k )  , r )  = ∑ k = 1  n  OP ( B S ( k )  × P R ( B S ( k )  , p c )    ∑ k = 1  n  OP ( B S ( k )  × m a x P R ( B S ( k )  , p c )            3 Model setup 3.1 Sample and discretization The mineralogically heterogeneous Berea sandstone was selected as the simulation material for this study, and the mineral segmented data (mixed-wet sample) developed by Garfi et al. (2020)  were employed (it is available at http://www.digitalrocksportal.org/projects/265 ).  As a typical porous media sample, the Berea sandstone was widely used in many other pore-scale studies for CO2  geological sequestration (Dawson et al., 2015; Iglauer et al., 2014 ). As depicted in Fig. 3  a, the image is segmented into six phases including clay minerals, quartz-feldspar minerals, calcite, other highly X-ray attenuating minerals, brine phase and oil phase. The region encompassed by the brine and oil phases is designated as pore space. The initial size of the digital rock is 1200  3     voxels, which greatly surpasses the computational capacity. Thus, images from (400 to 800 voxels), (200 to 600 voxels), and (0 to 400 voxels) along the x, y, z directions (with the actual size of 0.8 ×    0.8 ×    0.8 mm) were randomly selected as the volume of interest (VOI). The selected images were then scaled 43  times to 1003  size to further reduce the computational load (i.e., the simulation domain is evenly discretized into 100 grids along the x, y and z directions). The finite element simulation and lattice Boltzmann simulation employ an identical mesh structure, consisting of a series of cubes with six faces and eight nodes. The number of meshes remains constant throughout the simulation. However, in regions where mineral dissolution occurs, the mesh structure transitions from a rock skeleton to pore space, and vice versa. Fig. 3 b illustrates the spatial distribution of each mineral and phase in the simulated domain. Quartz and feldspar are the most abundant minerals in simulated sample, accounting for 72.6 % in terms of volume fraction, followed by calcite with a volume fraction of 3.7 %. The initial porosity of the simulated domain is 20.84 %. The spatial morphology of calcite and its vertical distribution in terms of volume fraction are depicted in Fig. 3 c and 3d, respectively. The uneven distribution of calcite within the simulated domain is evident, with a significantly higher content observed on the right side. According to the initial connected pore structure and streamline distribution (as shown in Fig. 3 e), the region exhibiting favorable permeability is predominantly situated towards the middle and left sections of the sample, whereas the area enriched with calcite (located on the right side of the sample) demonstrates inferior permeability. Details of model size, grid discretization and mineral content are given in Table 1  .  3.2 Initial and boundary conditions The sandstone is initially saturated with brine having a pH of 7.85, which is in equilibrium with calcite under the conditions of 20 MPa and 60 °C (i.e., pressure and temperature conditions commonly encountered in a CGS reservoir at a depth of approximately 2000 m). Subsequently, a CO2 -saturated solution is injected into the sandstone through the top inlet. The concentration gradient of all solutes at the bottom outlet is set to zero, while the remaining four lateral boundaries and non-reactive mineral surfaces adhere to the bounce-back rule to simulate no-slip and no-flux boundary conditions. The parameters used in LBM simulations are dimensionless, thus requiring conversion from physical units to lattice units. The conversion parameters mainly include characteristic length (L0   = Ll /Lu  ), time step (t0  = tl /tu  ) and characteristic density (ρ0   = ρl/ ρu  ), where subscript l  and u  represent the lattice unit and the physical unit, respectively. The remaining parameters all can be converted based on the three parameters mentioned above. In general, the physical and lattice units of the parameters used in this study are given in Table 2  . In the finite element simulation, different bulk modulus and shear modulus are assigned based on distinct mineral types (as shown in Table 3  ). It is important to note that due to the similarity in grayscale mapping obtained by CT scan, distinguishing between quartz and feldspar becomes challenging. Therefore, they are usually collectively referred to as quartz-feldspar group minerals (Garfi et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, the mechanical properties of feldspar closely resemble those of quartz (Li et al., 2024 ), with a bulk modulus of approximately 40 GPa (slightly higher than that of 37 GPa of quartz) and a shear modulus of around 30 GPa (slightly lower than that of 44 GPa of quartz). Consequently, it is feasible to assign the mechanical properties of quartz to the quartz-feldspar mixture. As for the “other” minerals, as depicted in Fig. 3 a, primarily pertain to minute solid particles suspended within brine or oil. Since these minerals do not directly interact with the solid framework, their influence on the overall mechanical properties of the rock is negligible and can be disregarded. Strain boundary conditions were imposed on the digital rock in order to obtain the initial elastic potential energy. The strain boundary applied in this study is ε xx   = ε yy     =ε zz      = 0.1, ε xz     =0.05, ε yz     =0.1, ε xy     =0.15 (Garboczi, 1998 ).  3.3 Simulation scenarios In order to investigate the dissolution characteristics of calcite and its subsequent impact on rock permeability and mechanical properties under varying hydrodynamic conditions, the injection velocities (Darcy velocity) of saturated CO2  solution at the inlet end were set at 1500 m/year, 150 m/year, and 15 m/year. According to previous studies, the injection velocities mentioned above can represent the flow conditions in proximity, intermediate distance, and far from the injection well, respectively (Al-Abri et al., 2009; Kang et al., 2010 ). Furthermore, it is anticipated that varying injection rates of CO2  saturated solution will induce distinct flow conditions within the digital sample, leading to disparate dissolution quantities and locations of calcite. This presents a remarkable opportunity to investigate the mechanism underlying the influence of mineral dissolution amounts and spatial distributions on rock permeability and mechanical properties.   4 Results 4.1 Calcite dissolution and pore structure evolution The simulation results demonstrate a positive correlation between the dissolution rate of calcite and the injection rate of saturated CO2  solution. As depicted in Fig. 4  , after a reaction time of 20 min, the proportions of calcite dissolution (Δ V C a l c i t e     ) were found to be 31.7 %, 10.4 %, and 9.1 % in the schemes with injection rates of 1500 m/year, 150 m/year, and 15 m/year respectively. In the scheme with an injection rate of 1500 m/year, the dissolution amount of calcite reached 74.8 % after 120 min of reaction. Subsequently, the dissolution of calcite in the rock sample became challenging because part of the calcite is located in regions characterized by inadequate pore connectivity, i.e., areas with underdeveloped streamlines (as shown in Fig. 3 e), where fluid ingress becomes difficult. In contrast, in the scheme employing a fluid injection rate of 150 m/year, the dissolution amount of calcite only attained 73.5 % after a reaction time of 360 min; whereas for the scheme utilizing an injection rate of 15 m/year, it was merely at a level as low as 58.1 % after 360 min. Based on the variation of calcite content in the sample along the direction of fluid injection, as illustrated in Fig. 5  , it is evident that the dissimilarities observed in calcite dissolution under varying fluid injection rates can be attributed to a pronounced inhibition of calcite dissolution in both middle and downstream regions when the fluid injection rate decreases. Taking the scheme with the lowest injection rate (i.e., 15 m/year) as an example, after 360 min of reaction, the calcite in the lower part of the sample hardly dissolves. In general, the limited dissolution of calcite in the middle and downstream regions can be attributed to two factors. Firstly, there is an insufficient supply of reactants, and secondly, the high concentration of product inhibits the continuation of the reaction. As depicted in Fig. 6  a, the solution pH is consistently below 4.5 after 60 min, irrespective of the injection rate of the reactive fluid. This indicates that there exists a relatively high concentration of H+  in the solution, and the limited dissolution of calcite cannot be attributed to an inadequate supply of reactants. The concentration distribution of reaction products, i.e., calcium ion (Fig. 6 b) and bicarbonate (Fig. 6 c), reveals that despite the smaller amount of calcite dissolution in the two schemes with lower fluid injection rates compared to the scheme with an injection rate of 1500 m/year, they exhibit nearly double concentrations of calcium ion and bicarbonate (approximately 0.015 mol/L and 0.03 mol/L, respectively) in the middle and downstream regions. This observation indicates that the reduction in fluid injection rate hinders product discharge, thus impeding the dissolution of calcite. As mentioned above, the strong correlation between fluid flow, solute transport, and chemical reaction results in varying dissolution rates and sites of calcite when different injection rates of CO2  solution are applied. It can be envisioned that even with consistent rock porosity after calcite dissolution (i.e., equal amounts of calcite dissolved), the pore structure may significantly differ under different injection rates. Fig. 7   illustrates this phenomenon by showing that at the same dissolution ratio of 33.8 % of calcite (indicating a consistent rock porosity of 0.221), the morphology of dissolved calcite varies across these schemes with distinct injection rate, as evidenced by more dispersed areas of calcite dissolution observed under higher injection rate. Therefore, relying solely on porosity is insufficient for accurately characterizing the changes in pore structure caused by calcite dissolution. To address this issue, two fractal parameters, namely fractal dimension and succolarity, are introduced. Fig. 8   illustrates the relationship between these two parameters and porosity under different fluid injection schemes. It can be observed that the fractal dimension of rock pores after calcite dissolution exhibits a subtle increasing trend with an increase in injection rate (Fig. 8 a). For instance, the fractal dimensions of the rock are 2.067, 2.071, and 2.073 when the porosity is 0.221, under fluid injection rates of 15 m/year, 150 m/year, and 1500 m/year respectively. In contrast, the trend of the succolarity shows a much more pronounced increase with higher injection rates (Fig. 8 b). Specifically, the succolarities of the rock are 0.212, 0.214, and 0.217 respectively at a porosity of 0.221, under fluid injection rates of 15 m/year, 150 m/year, and 1500 m/year. The comparison of the accuracy in characterizing the evolution of permeability and mechanical properties caused by calcite dissolution through porosity, fractal dimension and succolarity will be conducted in the following sections.  4.2 Evolution of permeability The dissolution of calcite inevitably modifies the permeability of the rock. As depicted in Fig. 9  a, the dissolution of calcite leads to an increase in porosity (horizontal axis) and a significant enhancement in permeability (vertical axis). Specifically, when the porosity rises from 0.2084 prior to the reaction to approximately 0.236, there is a corresponding increase in permeability from the initial value of 640 mD to around 800 mD. It is noteworthy that varying injection rates of reactive fluids result in different growth amplitudes of rock permeability at identical porosities, with higher injection rates yielding greater increases in permeability. Particularly during the early stage of the reaction, characterized by minimal changes in porosity, notable discrepancies exist among various schemes regarding permeability. As shown in Fig. 10  , the permeability of the sample under different fluid injection schemes is 745 mD (1500 m/year), 736 mD (150 m/year), and 729 mD (15 m/year), respectively, when the porosity is 0.221 (i.e., Δ V C a l c i t e     =33.8 %). As previously mentioned, a decrease in the flow rate of the injected fluid leads to a reduction in the amount of calcite dissolved in the middle and downstream regions along the injection direction. Therefore, given equal porosity conditions, the low injection rate scheme results in a more concentrated calcite dissolution near the inlet end, less corrosion and poorer pore connectivity (as depicted in Fig. 10  by sparser streamlines) in the middle and downstream sections. Consequently, the increase in rock permeability is comparatively smaller in the scheme with lower injection rate of reactive fluid. With the further increase of dissolved calcite, its spatial morphological differences in different schemes gradually diminish, as well as the rock permeability. Due to the non-uniform dissolution of calcite, there may be inaccuracies in predicting permeability changes resulted from calcite dissolution using porosity-based approaches. As depicted in Fig. 9 b, when employing the classical power function form for permeability prediction, the best-fitted curve (n = 2.25) exhibits a correlation coefficient (R2 ) of 0.934. However, within regions characterized by relatively low levels of calcite dissolution (enclosed by the pink line frame), the R2  drops to merely 0.742, indicating suboptimal fitting performance. In contrast, if an exponential expression is employed, higher accuracy can be achieved with an overall R2  of 0.968 and an increased R2  of 0.867 within areas exhibiting lower degrees of calcite dissolution. The utilization of porosity as a predictor for permeability changes induced by calcite dissolution does not yield highly satisfactory outcomes primarily due to the inability of porosity to characterize the spatial structural characteristics of pores. In order to address this limitation, we introduce two fractal parameters, namely fractal dimension and succolarity, for predicting the evolution of permeability. As depicted in Fig. 9 c, when employing fractal dimension as a predictor, an exponential expression was still utilized, resulting in an overall R2  of 0.978 and an R2  of 0.904 for regions with relatively minimal calcite dissolution. Encouragingly, if the succolarity is employed for prediction purposes, the overall R2  can reach an impressive 0.986. Even in regions where calcite dissolution is relatively insignificant, the R2  can attain a remarkable 0.945 (as shown in Fig. 9 d). The findings suggest that the fractal dimension, particularly the succolarity, provides a more precise characterization of permeability changes resulted from calcite dissolution compared to porosity. Even in cases where the dissolution amount of calcite is limited, i.e., significant dissimilarities in dissolution sites arise due to different fluid injection schemes, the parameter of succolarity can still accurately depict the evolution of rock permeability under various modes of calcite dissolution.  4.3 Evolution of mechanical properties The evolution of rock mechanical properties, i.e., the bulk modulus and shear modulus, resulted from calcite dissolution under varying injection rates is depicted in Fig. 11  . It is evident that as calcite dissolves and rock porosity increases, there is a significant decrease observed in both the bulk modulus and shear modulus of the rock. Specifically, when porosity reaches 0.236, the bulk modulus decreases from an initial value of 22.2 GPa to 19.9 GPa (Fig. 11 a), while the shear modulus decreases from an initial value of 22.3 GPa to 20.4 GPa (Fig. 11 b), representing reductions of approximately 10.3 % and 8.5 %, respectively. Considering that dissolved calcite only constitutes a volume fraction accounting for merely 2.8 % of the total rock volume, it becomes apparent that calcite dissolution exerts a substantial influence on both the bulk modulus and shear modulus. Similar to permeability, the magnitude of changes in rock mechanical properties under the same porosity varies with different fluid injection rates. Overall, an increase in fluid injection rate tends to result in a higher attenuation amplitude of elastic modulus, particularly shear modulus, at a specific porosity. On the other hand, unlike the phenomenon where differences in permeability under varying injection rates primarily occur in regions with low calcite dissolution, disparities in mechanical properties predominantly manifest in areas with moderate calcite dissolution (as depicted in Fig. 12  a and 12b). The relationship between porosity and mechanical parameters is described by a linear fitting curve. As illustrated in Fig. 12 a, the overall R2  for the correlation between values of bulk modulus obtained by linear fitting formula and the simulation results is 0.996. In regions with moderate calcite dissolution, R2  drops to 0.949. However, the predictive capability of porosity on shear modulus is considerably weaker (with the overall R2  of 0.989), particularly within areas featuring moderate calcite dissolution, where R2  stands at only 0.852 (as shown in Fig. 12 b). The utilization of fractal dimension for predicting the bulk modulus and shear modulus yields overall R2  values of 0.998 and 0.992, respectively. Moreover, in the regions of moderate calcite dissolution, these R2  values are further enhanced to 0.975 and 0.901, respectively (as shown in Fig. 12 c and 12d). In contrast, utilizing the succolarity for predicting the alterations in bulk modulus and shear modulus due to calcite dissolution exhibits inferior performance compared to fractal dimension and even falls short of porosity; yielding overall R2  values of only 0.965 and 0.967, respectively (as depicted in Fig. 12 e and 12f).   5 Discussion The LBM-FEM coupled model is proposed in this study to quantitatively investigate the impact of CO2 -water–rock interaction on rock permeability and mechanical properties. It is observed that the injection rate of reactive fluid (i.e., saturated CO2  solution) significantly influences both the quantity and spatial morphology of dissolved calcite. As the rate of fluid injection increases, the dissolution range of calcite expands, which aligns with previous experimental findings (Gao et al., 2023; Garcia-Rios et al., 2015 ). The dissimilar dissolution sites of calcite inevitably impact rock permeability. Our simulation results demonstrate that an increase in fluid injection rate leads to higher permeability in rock with the same porosity. This phenomenon has also been observed in previous studies (Menke et al., 2016; Xie et al., 2023 ). Our simulation provides an explanation for this occurrence: the inconsistency in calcite dissolution range causes variations in permeability. Furthermore, in order to address the limitation of porosity in accurately describing evolution of pore structure induced by calcite dissolution, fractal parameters (i.e., fractal dimension and succolarity) were introduced to characterize the post-reaction pore space. Remarkably, it was observed that the evolution of rock permeability induced by calcite dissolution could be effectively elucidated by employing succolarity as the independent variable. The finite element simulation results demonstrate a robust correlation between the evolution of rock mechanical properties and the extent of calcite dissolution, which diminishes as the dissolution amount increases and exhibits a more pronounced decline with higher fluid injection velocities. Our study reveals that when utilizing porosity as a means to characterize the evolution of rock mechanical properties under distinct dissolution modes of calcite, there may be certain inaccuracies (particularly in terms of shear modulus) observed during moderate levels of calcite dissolution. By contrast, fractal dimension demonstrates better predictive performance. The coupled LBM and FEM pore scale simulation model proposed offers a quantitative analysis tool for investigating the permeability and mechanical property evolution of rocks under CO2 -water–rock interactions. It resolves the ambiguous depiction of mineral dissolution and its spatial morphology in experiments, as well as addresses the influence of rock damage on results in mechanical property testing. Based on the simulation results, a detailed analysis is conducted to investigate the impact mechanism of calcite dissolution on rock permeability and mechanical properties. This study is expected to provide a theoretical foundation for developing corresponding constitutive models that accurately capture the evolution of permeability and mechanical parameters. Although the current research solely focuses on the dissolution of a single mineral, calcite, we are confident that this study can enhance comprehension of the associated processes and demonstrate the viability of the newly proposed simulation method. In future investigations, we aim to incorporate multi-mineral reactions into our models. Moreover, the successive inversion techniques and geostatistical methods appear to possess the capability of characterizing the evolution of rock properties (Zhuang et al., 2023; Zhuang et al., 2024 ), thereby offering a substantial amount of inversion data for model validation.  6 Conclusions A hybrid LBM-FEM model is proposed in this work to simulate the evolution of rock permeability and mechanical properties caused by CO2 -water–rock interaction. To investigate the effect of hydrodynamic conditions on calcite dissolution characteristics, three different injection rates, i.e., 1500 m/year, 150 m/year and 15 m/year, are set in the simulation. Furthermore, fractal dimension and succolarity are introduced to predict the subsequent evolution of rock permeability and mechanical properties induced by calcite dissolution. According to numerical simulation results and analyses, the main conclusions are as follows:(1) The reduction in the injection velocity of the reactive fluid, i.e., the saturated CO2  solution, hinders timely discharge of reaction products, thereby impeding further progress of the reaction and resulting in a decline in calcite dissolution rate. Therefore, as the fluid injection rate decreases, preferential calcite dissolution primarily occurs close to the inlet, while the dissolution of calcite in the middle and lower reaches is significantly constrained.  (2) The dissolution of calcite exerts a significant influence on permeability. For instance, when the dissolution of calcite leads to an increase in porosity from the initial value of 20.84 % to 23.6 %, the corresponding permeability rises from its original level of 640 mD to approximately 800 mD. However, due to distinct modes of calcite dissolution, the relationship between rock permeability and porosity varies at different rates of fluid injection. Particularly during the early stages of reaction, there may be substantial disparities in predicting permeability solely based on porosity. In contrast, succolarity exhibits exceptional predictive capability for assessing changes in permeability.  (3) The dissolution of calcite also significantly influences the mechanical properties of rock. For instance, when the dissolved calcite constitutes 2.8 % of the rock volume, there is a reduction in both the volume modulus and shear modulus by 10.3 % and 8.5 %, respectively (in the scheme with fluid injection rate of 1500 m/year). Furthermore, distinct modes of calcite dissolution result in varying evolution rules of mechanical properties. Unlike permeability, when predicting changes in rock bulk modulus and shear modulus using porosity, errors primarily occur within regions exhibiting moderate calcite dissolution. Encouragingly, employing fractal dimension effectively enhances the accuracy of predicting these two mechanical parameters.
1 Introduction Over the past century, global water demand has risen by 600 % owing to population growth, economic development, expansion of cultivated croplands, and shifting water usage and dietary habits, among others (Boretti and Rosa, 2019; Ma et al., 2020 ). Concurrently, climate change has led to a reduction in global runoff, spotlighting groundwater, especially in arid and semi-arid regions, a significant resource in satisfying water demand. This situation is compounded by increased variability in precipitation and longer dry summer seasons, which further intensify the pressure on groundwater resources (Konapala et al., 2020; Salehi, 2022; Taylor et al., 2013 ). Consequently, the unrestrained consumption of water resources has led to a global reduction in water quantity and quality, with far-reaching consequences for human life and ecosystems (Hartmann et al., 2021; Jasechko and Perrone, 2021 ). Aquatic ecosystems in lakes and rivers are particularly affected, undergoing alterations in biological diversity and treatability (Grizzetti et al., 2019 ). Similarly, terrestrial ecosystems, especially in semi-arid regions, are experiencing increased stress due to changes in soil water balance and groundwater recharge, leading to shifts in vegetation patterns and ecosystem functions (Li et al., 2022; Yaraghi et al., 2019 ). Additionally, the over-exploitation of groundwater resources, predominantly due to irrigation practices, is adversely impacting the habitat suitability for groundwater-dependent species in various regions (Hare et al., 2021; Jasechko and Perrone, 2021; Wu et al., 2020 ). This complex scenario of increasing water demand and environmental stress underscores the challenge of achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal of ensuring access to enough freshwater. As pollution in surface and groundwater persists worldwide, the task becomes even more alarming (Damania et al., 2019; United Nations, 2015 ). Agricultural practices, particularly the widespread use of chemical fertilizers and organic soil amendments such as manure, are the primary contributors to nitrogen pollution, pushing the levels beyond the planetary boundaries (Bijay-Singh and Craswell, 2021; Campbell et al., 2017; Nikolenko et al., 2018; Rockström et al., 2009 ). Moreover, with significant portions of industrial and urban wastewater, approximately 80 % of which is untreated, infiltrating groundwater systems, the challenge of maintaining clean water supplies is further exacerbated (Kookana et al., 2020; Pratap et al., 2023 ). Increased NO3 – -N pollution levels in aquifers disrupt aquatic ecosystems, leading to eutrophication and other detrimental effects. If such nutrient-containing groundwater reaches surface water bodies, it can cause toxic algal blooms, hypoxia and adversely affect aquatic life, including their growth, reproductive function, incidence of genetic defects, and survival (Camargo et al., 2005; Friedrich et al., 2014; Gomez Isaza et al., 2020; Le Moal et al., 2019; Schindler, 2012; Singh et al., 2022 ). Additionally, NO3 – -N pollution also negatively impacts human health, increasing the risk of methemoglobinemia, diabetes, bladder cancer, ovarian cancer, and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma if groundwater is used for drinking water purposes (Picetti et al., 2022; Singh et al., 2022; Ward et al., 2018 ). According to the available research (Tyagi et al., 2018 ), NO3 –  contamination in groundwater impacts more than 80 million people across the world. These widespread and severe impacts of NO3 – -N pollution necessitate effective and urgent action. Given the complexities in remediating contaminated groundwater, preventive strategies are critical for maintaining water quality (Huno et al., 2018 ). A key step in this process is identifying the NO3 – -N pollution sources, which is fundamental for developing effective mitigation strategies and ensuring the long-term viability of water resources (Gutiérrez et al., 2018 ). Particularly in arid and semiarid areas where additional hydrological and hydrogeological methods − developed in temperate regions − have failed for contaminant source identification, hydrochemical indicators have become more widespread (Linhoff, 2022; Qi et al., 2022; Qu et al., 2022 ). However, biogeochemical processes such as denitrification alter the NO3 – -N concentration, making it difficult to identify the pollution sources correctly. This urgency to address NO3 – -N pollution leads us to explore advanced methodologies capable of providing detailed examination into pollution sources and dynamics. The Positive Matrix Factorization (PMF) model is a valuable tool for analyzing data with non-negativity constraints (Paatero and Tapper, 1994 ). PMF has been widely applied in various fields such as computational biology, environmental monitoring, geology, and more recently, for tracing pollution sources in groundwater (Mao et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2023; Zanotti et al., 2019 ). This model has significant potential for quantifying the source apportionment of chemical ions and elucidating natural and anthropogenic factors that influence the physicochemical properties of groundwater. Complementing PMF, nitrate stable isotopes (δ15 NNO3  and δ18 ONO3 ) have been widely used in recent decades, providing a comprehensive analysis into NO3 – -N sources (Matiatos et al., 2021; Re et al., 2021 ) and associating biogeochemical processes, including denitrification, nitrification, and ammonia volatilization (Gutiérrez et al., 2018; Nikolenko et al., 2018 ). To enhance the accuracy of this approach, it has been integrated with other techniques, including the use of GIS techniques to derive land-use patterns (Pastén-Zapata et al., 2014; Torres-Martínez et al., 2021 ), hydrochemical índices (Linhoff, 2022; Qu et al., 2023; Torres-Martínez et al., 2021 ), multivariate statistics (Torres-Martínez et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2019 ), multiple isotopes (δ34 S, δ11 B, δ13 C, 3 H) (Biddau et al., 2023; Carrey et al., 2021; Harris et al., 2022; Kaown et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023 ), contaminants of emerging concern (Halder et al., 2022; Linhoff, 2022 ), microbial tracers (Carrey et al., 2021; Kaown et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2019 ), and Bayesian isotope mixing models (BIMM) (Kaown et al., 2023; Linhoff, 2022; Qu et al., 2023; Torres-Martínez et al., 2021 ). Building upon these advancements, the dual isotope fingerprinting method, particularly the pairing of δ11 B with δ15 N values, stands out as a promising technique to differentiate nitrate sources in groundwater more accurately. This dual approach significantly improves the distinction between agricultural and urban nitrate sources, including differentiating between animal (manure) and human (sewage) waste contributions. Its effectiveness in tracing contaminants has been demonstrated in diverse geographical contexts, including Djibouti (Awaleh et al., 2018 ), Morocco (Re and Sacchi, 2017 ) and Tunisia (Boumaiza et al., 2023; Re et al., 2021 ) in Africa, Korea (Koh et al., 2023 ) in Asia, the USA (Seiler, 2005; Tamborski et al., 2020 ) and Canada (Kruk et al., 2020 ) in America, and France (Briand et al., 2017; Erostate et al., 2018; Widory et al., 2005 ), Belgium (Christiaens et al., 2023 ), Spain (Carrey et al., 2021; Puig et al., 2017 ), Italy (Biddau et al., 2023, 2019; Lasagna and De Luca, 2019; Martinelli et al., 2018 ), and Portugal (Fernandes et al., 2019 ) in Europe. Furthermore, the recent integration of this isotope pairing into BIMM methodologies, especially in humid environments, underscores its potential in enhancing our understanding of groundwater contamination sources (Boumaiza et al., 2023; Kaown et al., 2023 ). As such, applying these globally recognized methods to the Meoqui-Delicias aquifer (MDA) in Northern Mexico could provide essential knowledge in NO3 – -N pollution sources. This aquifer has the highest NO3 – -N concentrations in the Chihuahua State, largely due to the excessive use of nitrogen and phosphate compounds as organic and chemical fertilizers, such as NH3 , CH₄N₂O, and (NH4 )3 PO4  (Espino et al., 2007; Gutiérrez et al., 2021; Villalobos Gutiérrez, 2021 ). In 2010, Espino-Valdés (2010)  evaluated the δ15 NNO3  values in groundwater from 19 wells, suggesting that NO3 – -N pollution is derived from a mixture of chemical fertilizers and human/animal waste. However, the use of single isotope ratios was not a conclusive tool for evaluating source apportionment; consequently, the origin of NO3 – -N in groundwater has not yet been accurately confirmed in this important aquifer. We hypothesize that comparing δ15 NNO3  vs. δ11 B in the BIMM method will provide a detailed and precise assessment of the origin of nitrate pollution in the semiarid MDA system. The formulation of this concept arises from a critical evaluation of the limitations associated with traditional isotopic pairings, notably δ15 NNO3  vs. δ18 ONO3 , in effectively distinguishing between manure and sewage NO3 -N pollution sources. The aim of this study extends beyond the qualitative and quantitative differentiation of NO3 – -N pollution sources and biogeochemical transformations that occur in the MDA system in a semiarid region of Mexico. Instead, the endeavor serves as an archetype, presenting an innovative methodology that challenges the conventional dual-isotope techniques (δ15 NNO3  vs. δ18 ONO3 ) by introducing the alternative isotopic pairing: δ15 NNO3  vs. δ11 B applied to a BIMM. This innovative approach addresses a gap in the existing literature on the application of BIMM in semiarid regions. The specific objectives of this study are as follows: (1) to identify the potential NO3 – -N pollution sources in groundwater, with an emphasis on differentiating between pollution originating from manure and sewage; (2) to establish the different biogeochemical processes occurring within the system (e.g., nitrification or denitrification); (3) to quantify the proportional contributions of pollution sources using two different BIMM’s (comparing the isotopic signatures of δ15 NNO3  vs. δ18 ONO3 , and δ15 NNO3  vs. δ11 B); and (4) to perform a comparative analysis between the two proposed BIMM’s and the PMF model.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Description of the study area The MDA, covering an area of 4,380 km2 , is located in the Mexican state of Chihuahua, and supports a population of approximately 265,000 inhabitants (Fig. 1  a ). This water resource system serves several municipalities, including Meoqui, Delicias, Saucillo, La Cruz, San Francisco de Conchos, and Camargo. Notably, there are three major cities: Delicias, Meoqui, and Saucillo (Fig. 1 b ), with populations of 150,000, 45,000, and 30,000 inhabitants, respectively (INEGI, 2020 ). A recent national census conducted by the National Association of Water and Sanitation Utilities (ANEAS, 2023 ) identified six wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) within this area, all operating with lagoon-based systems. These facilities have a combined treatment capacity of ∼ 260 l/s. In terms of distribution, the municipalities of Rosales, Saucillo, and Camargo each have one WWTP, while Meoqui is equipped with three facilities, and Delicias has no WWTPs (JCAS and IMTA, 2018 ). Following treatment, the effluent from these plants is either discharged directly into the San Pedro River or used in agricultural distribution channels. Given this disposal method, there is a growing concern about the vulnerability of the MDA to pollution, particularly from inadequately treated wastewater. The potential for contaminants to infiltrate the aquifer is significant, highlighting the need for a thorough assessment of treatment efficacy, as well as enhanced treatment technologies. This concern is particularly pressing in light of the MDA’s role in supporting one of northern Mexico's most important irrigation systems, the Delicias irrigation district, which supports a robust agricultural economy (∼84,300 ha) (SIAP, 2021a ). Approximately 83 % of the water required for this operation comes from two reservoirs (La Boquilla and Francisco I. Madero, Fig. 1 b ), whereas the remaining 17 % is supplied by groundwater extraction from over 1,000 production wells in the MDA. The dominant crops in the area, including alfalfa, peanuts, maize, cotton, jalapeno pepper, and onions, constituted 97 % of the cultivated land in 2021 (detailed information in Table S1  ). In recent decades, there has been a significant shift in cropping patterns, with approximately 65,000 ha now dedicated to water-intensive crops like alfalfa and pecans, accounting for half of the water used in the study area (Villalobos-Cano et al., 2019 ). Additionally, Chihuahua is Mexico's most significant cattle export region, making livestock the second-most important economic sector in the study area. The latest report from the National Agri-food Information System (SIAP, 2021b ) indicates that, in 2021, there were more than 90,000 dairy and meat cows in the region (detailed information in Table S2  ), a substantial number of which are housed in concentrated animal feeding operations (Rivas-Lucero et al., 2008 ). This concentration of livestock poses additional demands and impacts on water quality in the MDA. The intensive agricultural activities, especially those related to livestock, contribute to the increased nutrient load in the aquifer. The hydrogeological characteristics of the MDA play an important role in how these agricultural practices impact the aquifer. The MDA comprises two hydrogeological units (see details in Fig. S1  ) and the basement. The geological base of this region is formed by Paleozoic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous rocks characterized by low permeability, consisting of calcareous shales, sandstones, and limestone horizons interspersed with evaporites (SRH, 1973 ). This unit is overlain by Tertiary volcanic rocks, primarily tuffs and rhyolites. Despite its volcanic origin, this layer exhibits an elevated permeability caused by matrix fractures and forms recharge zones to the east of the study area, being the currently exploited aquifer (SRH, 1973 ). The uppermost unit, composed of highly permeable Tertiary and Quaternary alluvium, covers most of the valley (Fig. S1  ). This unit functions as an unconfined aquifer and is the main exploited layer, reaching thicknesses of up to 500 m (SRH, 1973 ). The dynamics between these hydrogeological units and surface activities, notably livestock farming, play a crucial role in influencing the aquifer’s water quality and availability. The climatic conditions of the region, BWh climate related to a hot desert climate (CONAGUA, 2020 ) typical of northern Mexico, further exacerbate the challenges faced by the MDA. Characterized by an arid climate with an average annual temperature of 19 °C, total annual precipitation of 284 mm, and an average annual potential evaporation of 345 mm (CONAGUA, 2020 ), the area’s scarce precipitation means groundwater recharge primarily occurs over alluvium. This recharge is mainly driven by the infiltration of surface water from the San Pedro and Conchos rivers, along with leaks from irrigation distribution channels, and return flows from irrigation. Regional groundwater flow is originated in the southern region near the La Venada mountain range (CONAGUA, 2020 ) (Fig. 1 c ) and in the western region of the MDA aquifer in the Sierra Alta mountain range (Saucedo, 1995 ). Natural groundwater flow typically moves from south to north, following the paths of the San Pedro and Conchos rivers (CNA, 1999 ). Currently, the MDA is facing a myriad of environmental challenges. The National Water Commission (Comisión Nacional del Agua − CONAGUA) has identified significant overexploitation of the aquifer, reporting an annual water deficit of 165 Mm3  (CONAGUA, 2020 ). Groundwater table levels vary considerably within the region, with depths ranging from 10 to 20 m in areas close to the rivers, while the remaining areas experience levels between 30 and 60 m (Rodriguez Lozano, 2022 ). Since 2005, a noticeable and rapid decline in groundwater levels has been observed, particularly affecting areas near Rosales (0.87 m/year), La Cruz (0.37 m/year), Meoqui (0.81 m/year), and Delicias (0.25 m/year) (Rodriguez Lozano, 2022 ). This downward trend has led to the formation of depression cones, which have significantly altered the natural groundwater flow direction. Such changes pose further challenges to the sustainability of this critical water resource (Rawling, 2022 ).  2.2 Sample collection Given the prevailing climatic conditions characterized by a hot desert climate in the region, it is reasonable to assume that seasonal variations in groundwater quality are negligible (CONAGUA, 2020 ). According to the International Groundwater Resources Assessment Centre (IGRAC, 2008 ) it is recommended a minimum of one monitoring well per 25 to 100 km2 . Consequently, a single monitoring campaign was conducted in November 2021, wherein 38 groundwater samples were collected from production wells strategically located throughout the primarily groundwater exploited region of the MDA (Fig. 1 c ). This area, including cropland and built-up land, covers approximately 1,300 km2 . The sampling strategy was designed with a density of one sample per 34 km2  to ensure representative coverage of the study area. The samples were collected from private wells in the irrigation district, tapping into alluvium geology at depths ranging from 60 to 200 m. To ensure the accuracy of the samples, stagnant water was avoided by circulating the water column until both the pH and electrical conductivity (EC) stabilized. This step was crucial for obtaining representative groundwater samples. In-situ measurements of multiple field parameters (pH, temperature, dissolved oxygen (DO), and EC) were conducted using a calibrated YSI Professional Plus multiparameter meter. Additionally, alkalinity was determined on-site through an acid titration procedure using 0.02 N H2 SO4  until a pH of 4.3 was reached.
