For laboratory analysis, anions, cations, NO3 – -N, B, and water isotope samples were filtered using membranes of 0.45 μm pore-size and stored in high-density polyethylene (HDPE) bottles, which were previously rinsed three times. To preserve the integrity of the cation samples and prevent precipitation or adsorption of major elements, they were acidified to pH 2 with ultrapure HCl. All samples for cations, anions, B, and water isotope analysis were stored at 4 °C prior to analysis. In contrast, samples collected for NO3 – -N isotope analysis were frozen at −20 °C to minimize any biologically induced alteration.  2.3 Laboratory analyses The laboratory analysis of the major ion samples was conducted at Activation Laboratories Ltd., Canada. Concentrations of cations, including Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Na+ , and K+ , were measured using an Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometer (ICP-MS, Perkin Elmer Sciex ELAN 9000). Anions such as Cl− , F− , SO4 2− , and NO3 – -N were analyzed through Ion Chromatography (IC, DIONEX DX-120). Boron concentration measurements were carried out at the Isotope Science Laboratory of the University of Calgary, Canada, using a Thermo Scientific iCAP-Quadrapole Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometer (Q-ICP-MS). The accuracy of these results was validated by estimating the charge balance error, with a maximum acceptable deviation set at 10 %. Water-stable isotope analyses (δ2 HH2O  and δ18 OH2O ) were performed at Tecnologico de Monterrey, Mexico. The method used was off-axis integrated cavity output spectroscopy (OA-ICOS, LGR-DLT-100), following the procedure outlined by Mello et al. (2020) . The analytical accuracies achieved for δ2 HH2O  and δ18 OH2O  were ± 0.8 ‰ and ± 0.2 ‰, respectively. The nitrate isotopes (δ15 NNO3  and δ18 ONO3 ) were analyzed at the Environmental Isotope Laboratory at the University of Waterloo, Canada. This analysis followed the methodology described by McIlvin and Altabet (2005) , utilizing a trace-gas isotope ratio mass spectrometer (TG-IRMS; GVI IsoPrime) using a cadmium catalyst. The accuracies of δ15 NNO3  and δ18 ONO3  were ± 0.3 ‰ and ± 0.8 ‰, respectively. Additionally, B isotopes (δ11 B) were measured at the Isotope Science Laboratory at the University of Calgary using a Neptune Multi-Collector Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometer (MC-ICP-MS), as per the method of Guerrot et al. (2011) , with an accuracy of ± 0.4 ‰. Delta values (δ), denoting variations in the per mil (‰) notation with respect to international standards (Eq. (1)  ), were used to report all stable isotope ratios for H2 O, NO3 – -N, and B:(1) δ  sample   ‰    = R  sample   - R  standard    R  standard     ∗ 1000     where, Rsample/standard   is the sample-to-standard abundance ratio (2 H/1 H, 15 N/14 N, 11 B/10 B, or 18 O/16 O). Hydrogen and oxygen isotope ratios were reported based on the Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water (VSMOW), whereas the nitrogen reference was atmospheric N2 , and the B notation was relative to untreated boric acid (NIST SRM 951).  2.4 Data analyses 2.4.1 Statistical analysis The use of multivariate statistical methods, such as sample clustering, in groundwater chemistry has multiple critical objectives (Cloutier et al., 2008; Reghunath, 2002 ). Primarily, it facilitates the demarcation of clusters within groundwater samples based on their similar hydrogeochemical characteristics (Cloutier et al., 2008; Reghunath, 2002 ). This analytical approach yields invaluable insights into the fundamental mechanisms and origins responsible for variations in groundwater chemistry (Cloutier et al., 2008; Narvaez-Montoya et al., 2023; Reghunath, 2002 ). However, significant considerations arise when the data are expressed as a fraction of a whole (e.g., mg/L or meq/L in water chemistry), and such data are considered compositional (or close) (Buccianti et al., 2014 ). Accordingly, the centered log-ratio (clr) transformation technique (Eq. (2)  ), proposed by Aitchison (Aitchison, 1982 ), was applied using CoDa pack software (Thió-Henestrosa and Martín-Fernández, 2005 ). This methodological choice was dictated by the compositional nature of the data and the typical non-normal distribution of chemical parameters. Major cations (Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Na+ , and K+ ) and anions (Cl− , F− , SO4 2− , HCO3 –  and NO3 – -N) were subjected to this transformation.(2) c l r x    = l n x 1  g ( x  )   , l n x 2  g ( x  )   , ⋯ , l n x n  g ( x  )          where g(x ) = [x1 *x2 *…*xD ]1/D  is the geometric mean of the composition x.  Following data transformation, Self-Organizing maps (SOM) (Kohonen, 1982 ) were used to classify water samples (Narvaez-Montoya et al., 2023 ). For this classification, the Kohonen R-package (Wehrens and Buydens, 2007 ) was used by applying the heuristic rule of w = 5 m     , where w  is the number of output layer neurons, and m  is the number of samples. Hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA) was applied to the training weight vector using Ward's method and the Euclidean distance, providing a more solid interpretation of the results. After establishing the groups, the Shapiro–Wilk test was conducted to determine the normality of each group, and an analysis of variance (ANOVA) test (p > 0.05 ) was used to compare the variables between the groups. The non-parametric Kruskal–Wallis test was used if the normality assumption was rejected.  2.4.2 MixSIAR model The proportional contributions of different NO3 – -N pollution sources to the groundwater samples were determined using a Bayesian isotope mixing model (BIMM) incorporating the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) technique within a Bayesian framework. The models were implemented using MixSIAR R-package (Stock et al.,2018 ). Several studies have effectively utilized the dual isotope technique to determine the primary sources of nitrate pollution, including chemical fertilizers, soil nitrogen, manure, sewage, and NO3 – -N in precipitation (e.g., Fenech et al., 2012 ). The mathematical representation of the mixing model for a group of N  mixture measurements, using j  isotopes and k  sources, can be expressed by the following equations:(3) X ij   = ∑ k = 1  k  p k  S jk   + C jk      + ε ij       (4) S jk    N ( μ jk   , ω jk  2  )      (5) C jk    N ( λ jk   , τ jk  2  )      (6) ε ij    N ( 0 , σ j  2  )      where Xij   represents the isotope value j  of mixture i , i  ranges from 1 to N , and j  ranges from 1 to J . The source value k  of isotope j , denoted as Sjk  , follows a normal distribution with mean μjk   and standard deviation ωjk  . The proportional contribution of source k , pk  , is estimated using the MixSIAR model. The isotope fractionation factor of isotope j  on source k  is described by Cjk  , which also follows a normal distribution with mean λjk   and standard deviation τjk  . Additionally, εij   represents the residual error that accounts for unquantified variation between individual mixtures. εij   follows a normal distribution with mean zero and standard deviation σj  . In this study, the potential contribution of NO3 – -N derived from precipitation was excluded a priori because of the arid climate prevalent in the study area, characterized by sparse precipitation events. Furthermore, it is imperative to note that in the context of δ15 NNO3  vs. δ18 ONO3  values, manure and sewage are treated as indistinguishable due to intrinsic constraints in isolating their respective isotopic signatures (Nikolenko et al., 2018 ). Notably, this limitation was overcome by employing δ11 B values, which allowed for more nuanced source differentiation (Puig et al., 2017 ). The isotopic signatures of the chosen potential pollution sources used in the models (Table 1  ) were obtained from the literature (Chalk, 2020; Nikolenko et al., 2018; Torres-Martínez et al., 2020; Wang and Zhang, 2019; Widory et al., 2005; Xue et al., 2009 ). Even though the dual-isotope biplot technique (δ15 NNO3  vs. δ18 ONO3  and δ15 NNO3  vs. δ11 B) provided useful qualitative information about the various NO3 – -N pollution sources, quantifying the contribution of each source remained a challenge. To address this, two BIMMs were developed in this study, implementing a robust statistical approach. This led us to employ the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method, carefully setting parameters to ensure reliable results. Each MCMC simulation consisted of 300,000 iterations, with the initial 200,000 iterations serving as the 'burn-in' period, and thus excluded from the final analysis. A thinning interval of 100 was implemented to manage data size and reduce autocorrelation, retaining every 100th iteration post-burned period. Further enhancing the reliability of our models, three independent MCMC chains were run, with their convergence towards similar results crucial for bolstering confidence in the model’s accuracy and stability (Khadam and Kaluarachchi, 2006 ). To ensure the stability and convergence of the MCMC model, a suite of statistical diagnostics was employed. The Gelman-Rubin test was vital for assessing convergence across multiple MCMC chains by comparing the variance within each chain to the variance between chains. A ratio close to 1 would indicate successful convergence to the same distribution, affirming the model's stability (Brooks and Gelman, 1998 ). The Heidelberg-Welch test was implemented to check for stationarity and convergence within each chain, utilizing a combination of stationarity testing and half-width comparisons (Heidelberger and Welch, 1983 ). Additionally, Geweke's diagnostic compared the means of the early and latter segments of the Markov chain with similar means, indicating that equilibrium had been reached (Geweke, 1991 ). These tests – Gelman-Rubin, Heidelberg-Welch, and Geweke's – were integral to our validation process, instilling confidence that our MCMC model had adequately converged and the results were stable and reliable (Du et al., 2022; Roy, 2020 ). Transitioning from the statistical rigor of our MCMC methods, we also recognized that isotope ratios are naturally susceptible to different isotopic fractionations that usually generate products that enrich light isotopes (Xue et al., 2009 ). To accurately reflect the isotopic fractionation occurring through different transformations within the groundwater flow, it was applied the Rayleigh equation (Eq. (7)  ) (Van Breukelen, 2007 ). This equation was used in conjunction with δ15 NNO3  and δ18 ONO3  measurements, considering the specific points along the groundwater flow path (Table S3  ).(7) δ S  t  = δ S  0  + ε l n ( S t  / S 0  )      where δS0  and δSt  are the isotopic compositions of the substrate at time 0 and t, respectively, and S0  and St  are the concentrations at time 0 and t, respectively; t and 0 were determined by sampling at neighboring locations along the groundwater flow path.  2.4.3 Sensitivity analysis In implementing the MixSIAR model, which employs arithmetic means and standard deviations of isotopic signatures (δ15 NNO3 , δ18 ONO3 , and δ11 B) from different pollution sources, conducting a sensitive analysis was essential. The primary objective of this analysis was intended to account for the variability in isotopic signatures from literature and to identify which isotope compositions significantly influence the model's predictions. This involves not only understanding the individual impact of each marker but also examining potential interactions and cross-correlations among them. To achieve this, the sensitivity analysis was meticulously carried out by systematically varying the values of each isotope signature. This involved adjusting the mean values of δ15 NNO3 , δ18 ONO3 , and δ11 B for different pollution sources, applying increments and decrements of 10 % and 20 %, as well as considering a baseline case with no change. This structured approach was crucial in evaluating the impact of changes in each isotopic marker on the model's output. By observing and documenting the outcomes of these parameter adjustments, we were able to determine the relative sensitivity of each tracer. This process provided key insights into the interdependencies among the isotope values and significantly enhanced our understanding of the MixSIAR model's ability to respond to variations in these crucial input parameters. Consequently, this sensitivity analysis was instrumental in assessing the robustness and predictive accuracy of the model.  2.4.4 PMF model The Positive Matrix Factorization (PMF) model is a sophisticated multivariate technique proficient in discerning individual sources in a mixture while concurrently ascertaining their contributions to specific chemical species (Paatero and Tapper, 1994 ). Functioning as a specialized tool in multivariate factor analysis, the PMF model deconstructs a high-dimensional data matrix into two discrete matrices, G  and F , representing the factor contributors and factor profiles, respectively. The primary aim of this receptor model is to solve the chemical mass balance, thereby correlating the observed species concentrations with their corresponding source profiles (Eq. (8)  ). Moreover, the PMF model employs a weighted least squares optimization technique to minimize the objective function Q  for a predetermined number of factors denoted as p . The objective function Q  measures the model's goodness-of-fit and is strategically designed to quantify the deviation between the observed and estimated values, weighted by their respective uncertainties (Eq. (9)  ).(8) X ij   = ∑ k = i  p  g ik   f kj   + e ij       (9) Q = ∑ i = 1  n  ∑ j = 1  m  X ij   - ∑ k = 1  p  g ik   f kj    u ij       2      In this mathematical formulation, Xij   denotes the observed value for the ith   sample and jth   hydrochemical parameter. gik   represents the contribution of the kth   source to the ith   sample, whereas fkj   represents the concentration of the jth   hydrochemical parameter in the kth   source. eij   represents the residual error associated with the observed and estimated values. Lastly, uij   is the uncertainty of the jth   chemical component of the ith   sample. For values Xij   falling below the detection limit (DL), the implemented imputation strategy involved setting Xij   to 0.5 DL. Simultaneously, the corresponding uncertainty, uij  , was determined to be 5/6 DL. Conversely, in the cases where Xij  ≤ 3DL, u ij   = DL  3  + 0.2 f kj     .  For values of Xij  > 3DL,  the uncertainty was computed as u ij   = DL  3  + 0.1 f kj      (Ju et al., 2023 ).    3 Results and discussion 3.1 Sampling groups and hydrochemical characteristics Based on the Meoqui-Delicias database, 30 neurons (w = 5 38     ) and 15,000 iterations were used for the SOM training. Cluster analysis using SOM and HCA was employed to categorize the groundwater samples. The results of the SOM analysis revealed that, initially, groundwater chemistry could be grouped into three clusters based on their similarities and geographical proximity. However, subsequent in-depth analysis, including ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis tests, showed that there was no significant statistical difference between two of these groups. This insight led to the combination of two groups, refining the assessment to a two cluster analysis (Fig. S2  ). Table 2   provides a statistical summary of the two groups regarding field parameters, major ions, and isotopic ratios of the groundwater samples collected (the complete dataset is shown in Table S3  ). Results showed that the pH from Group (2)  (7.3 ± 0.2) was significantly lower (p < 0.01 ) than Group (1)  (7.8 ± 0.4). There were no significant differences (p > 0.05 ) in temperature, EC, and total dissolved solids (TDS) between Group (1)  (Temp: 25.5 °C; EC: 1253.4 μS/cm; TDS: 811 mg/L) and Group (2)  (Temp: 24.4 °C; EC: 1403.3 μS/cm; TDS: 924.2 mg/L). DO concentrations in Group (2)  (5.7 ± 2.7 mg/L) were significantly higher (p < 0.05 ) than in Group (1)  (3.9 ± 3.0 mg/L). Except for Cl– , the average concentrations of the major ions were significantly higher (p < 0.01 ) in Group (2) . Both groups followed the cation concentration order of Na+ >Ca2+ >Mg2+ >K+ , whereas anions showed for Group (1)  the order of HCO3 – >SO4 2 – >Cl– >F– >NO3 – -N; for Group (2) , the order was SO4 2 – >HCO3 – > Cl– >NO3 – -N > F– .  3.2 Groundwater isotopic composition The isotopic compositions of H2 O, NO3 – -N, and B in groundwater were determined to trace the origin (anthropogenic or natural) and transformations of these ions within the aquifer system. The water-stable isotopic compositions exhibited δ18 OH2O  values ranging from −8.3 to −5.2 ‰ and δ2 HH2O  values ranging from −56.9 to −37.2 ‰. There were no statistically significant differences between the two groups (p > 0.05 ) (Table 2 ). The δ15 NNO3  and δ18 ONO3  values ranged from 3.5 ‰ to 12.6 ‰ and from −0.1 ‰ to 9.3 ‰, respectively. No statistically significant differences were detected between groups (p > 0.05) for both isotopic signatures. Boron concentrations in the groundwater varied from 0.10 to 0.94 mg/L, while δ11 B values ranged from −10.4 ‰ to 35.9 ‰. The B concentration and isotope signatures were not significantly different between the groups (p > 0.05 ). The nitrate and boron isotope compositions did not match any single pollution source but rather indicated a mixture of sources, including chemical fertilizers, soil, manure, and sewage.  3.3 Groundwater origin and recharge Stable water isotope results suggest that groundwater was of meteoric origin, as samples fall close to the Global Meteoric Water Line (GMWL, δ2 HH2O  = 8.2δ18 OH2O  + 11.2) (Rozanski et al., 2013 ) and the Local Meteoric Water Line (LMWL, δ2 HH2O  = 7.4δ18 OH2O  + 4.3) (Mahlknecht et al., 2008 ) (Fig. 2  a ). Group (1)  showed a linear trend defined as δ2 HH2O  = 5.3δ18 OH2O  − 11.7 (Fig. 2 a ), close to the slope range between 2 and 5, indicating that samples underwent an evaporation process during groundwater recharge (Fig. 2 b, c ), which is common in semiarid regions (Jasechko, 2019; Mayr et al., 2007 ). Moreover, this pattern indicates evaporation during irrigation return flows and infiltration from surface water (Fig. 2 c ), typical in agricultural fields in semiarid regions (Jia et al., 2020; Sethy et al., 2022 ), as in our study area. Meanwhile, Group (2)  (δ2 HH2O  = 6.9δ18 OH2O  − 1.9) showed a higher slope, between 5 and 8, which is very close to the LMWL and might be attributed to groundwater recharge caused by rainwater infiltration (Fig. 2 a, c ). In general, the post-condensation evaporation of precipitation under low relative humidity conditions results in low d-excess values (Müller et al., 2017; Wassenaar et al., 2009 ). Most d-excess values of groundwater samples from MDA fall between 0 ‰ and 10 ‰ (Fig. 2 b ), which confirms the occurrence of this process. Typically, d-excess values from groundwater of Northern Mexico range from 3 ‰ to 6 ‰ (Roy et al., 2022; Wassenaar et al., 2009 ).  3.4 Hydrogeochemical processes Multiple approaches can be used to evaluate the diverse factors that control groundwater chemistry. For MDA, a Piper diagram (Fig. 3  a ) was used to depict the chemical differences between the two groups. The Piper diagram’s rhomboid generally differentiates the groups, indicating distinctive geochemical processes. In Group (1) , 60 % of the samples were associated with the Na-HCO3  type, suggesting that a cation exchange process was the dominant mechanism (Fig. 3 d ). This inference is further corroborated by the presence of Phaeozems soils within the study area (Fig. S4  ), which are characterized by their rich organic matter content (Blake et al., 2008 ). Such soils facilitate cation exchange processes (Zhang et al., 2020 ), enhancing the mobilization of Na+  from the soil matrix into the groundwater system. The remaining 40 % of the samples were of the Na-SO4  type, which might be attributed to dissolution of evaporites or oxidation of sulfides and cation exchange. In contrast, the samples from Group (2)  exhibited different chemical profiles. In this group, 60 % of the samples were of the Na-SO4  type, 9 % were classified as the Ca-HCO3  type, which is typical of recharge areas (Fig. 3 d ), and 22 % were of the Ca-SO4  type, which typically indicates the dissolution of evaporites such as anhydrite and gypsum (Fig. 3 d ). Gibbs (1970)  categorized the natural processes of hydrochemical components in surface water as rock weathering, evaporation, and precipitation. By re-examining the Gibbs diagram in conjunction with groundwater chemical analysis, Marandi and Shand (2018)  concluded that Na/(Na + Ca) and Cl/(Cl + HCO3 ) values below or close to 0.5 and TDS values varying between 100 and 1000 mg/L are considered to be the primary dominant processes in the water–rock interaction. Groundwater samples from the MDA fell within the range of rock dominance (Fig. 3 b and 3c ), and silicates and evaporites were the dominant rock-forming minerals (Fig. 3 f ). However, as shown in Fig. 3 c , the samples belonging to Group (1)  surpassed the zone identified by Marandi and Shand (2018) , suggesting that another groundwater chemical process was also active, that could include cation exchange, evaporation, or anthropogenic inputs (Marandi and Shand, 2018 ). As observed from the linear trend for both groups, with a negative slope of 1 in Fig. 3 e,  cation exchange seems to be a highly relevant process. Furthermore, the increase in HCO3 –  could be consistent with a denitrification process caused by the anoxic biodegradation of organic materials, such as manure (Gilabert-Alarcón et al., 2018; Rivett et al., 2008 ) (Eq. (10)  ).(10) 5CH2 O + 4NO3 -  → 2 N2  + 4HCO3 -  + CO2  + 3H2 O     3.5 Nitrate pollution sources and biogeochemical transformations 82 % of the groundwater samples from the MDA exceeded the NO3 – -N natural background level (3 mg/L as N) (Kim et al., 2015 ), while almost all of the samples (except for sample A04, which had a NO3 – -N concentration of 17.7 mg/L) did not exceed the World Health Organization (WHO) drinking water threshold of 10 mg/L as N. Therefore, the increasing NO3 – -N concentration can be attributed to anthropogenic processes, which should be properly identified to develop effective mitigation strategies. Hydrochemical tracers and isotopic fingerprints are typically used to identify NO3 – -N sources. Chloride is commonly viewed as a conservative tracer because it is typically not involved in biological or chemical reactions in aqueous systems. The NO3 – /Cl–  ratio versus Cl–  concentration was employed to determine the different natural and anthropogenic contributors to NO3 – -N pollution in groundwater. This hydrochemical tool helps track natural and anthropogenic sources, such as pristine waters, mineral dissolution, fertilizers, animal waste, and wastewater. For instance, the NO3 – /Cl–  ratio in chemical fertilizers is very high, whereas sewage waste has a high concentration of Cl–  but a low NO3 – /Cl–  ratio. As is shown in Fig. 4  a , Group (1)  exhibits an average NO3 – /Cl–  ratio of 0.36 ± 0.36 with a Cl–  concentration of 1349 ± 996 μmol/L, suggesting that NO3 – -N pollution is derived from different pollution sources, probably manure and sewage (Liu et al., 2006; Widory et al., 2005 ). The low NO3 – /Cl–  ratio is partly caused by the fact that the N in these sources is NH4 , which has not yet been transformed to NO3 –  (Chen et al., 2009 ). Additionally, the low ratio may also be influenced by Dissimilatory Nitrate Reduction to Ammonium (DNRA), a process more prevalent in ecosystems with high organic matter content, such as agricultural soils (Putz et al., 2018; Rütting et al., 2011 ). In contrast, Group (2)  exhibits a slightly elevated NO3 – /Cl–  ratio (0.53 ± 0.31) and slightly lower Cl–  values (1103 ± 806 μmol/L) compared to Group (1) , which could be indicative of Group (2)  to be also affected by chemical fertilizers (Liu et al., 2006 ). Furthermore, there was no significant correlation between NO3 –  and Cl–  (p > 0.05 ) in either group, and they did not match any particular potential NO3 – -N input. This confirms that the origin of NO3 – -N pollution is not derived from a single source (Liu et al., 2006 ). Furthermore, Fig. 4 b  confirms that there was more than one NO3 – -N input, suggesting an influence from agricultural and sewage inputs. Another common approach for identifying NO3 – -N pollution sources is the use of dual-isotope fingerprints. Nitrate sources can be inferred using NO3 – -N isotope compositions (δ15 NNO3  and δ18 ONO3 ) in conjunction with groundwater chemistry (Kendall and Aravena, 2000 ). Based on an examination of potential pollution sources in the literature (Chalk et al., 2019; Fenech et al., 2012; Jung et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2018 ), δ15 NNO3  values of groundwater samples in this study fell between the overlapping zones of synthetic fertilizers (−6‰ to 6 ‰), soil organic nitrogen (3 ‰ to 8 ‰), and manure/sewage source (4 ‰ to 35 ‰) (Fig. 4 c ). Similarly, δ18 ONO3  values extended across the range of these end-members (+0.5 ‰ to 5 ‰) and the theoretical value of NO3 − -N produced during microbial nitrification (+10 ‰). The isotopic fingerprint of nitrate in groundwater samples did not match the atmospheric deposition range (δ18 ONO3 : +25 ‰ to 75 ‰). Therefore, it was not considered in the source apportionment mixing models. Boron isotope ratios provide an alternative method for differentiating groundwater pollution sources. A notable advantage of using boron isotopes is that they are not subjected to denitrification-induced isotope fractionation. Accordingly, a comparative analysis between the NO3 – /Cl–  ratio against δ11 B was done, trying to differentiate the groundwater pollution sources (Fig. 5  a ). This analysis revealed that the samples from Group (1)  were located within the overlapping region of sewage and soil, whereas most of the samples from Group (2)  were closely aligned with a manure source. Some samples were situated at the intersection of manure, sewage, and fertilizer sources, suggesting a mixture of nutrient sources. Moreover, using the δ11 B vs. 1/B scatterplot (Fig. 5 b ), a similar tendency was identified with samples from Group (1)  mainly falling in the soil source region. In contrast, the samples from Group (2)  exhibited an increasing trend, suggesting a manure source. Similarly, pairing δ15 NNO3  and δ11 B can help to qualitatively elucidate the potential NO3 – -N pollution sources. Fig. 4 d  shows that δ11 B fell between the ranges of fertilizer (−8‰ to 24 ‰), soil (−7.9 ‰ to 9.7 ‰), manure (10.9 ‰ to 42.4 ‰), and sewage (−4.8 ‰ to 12.9 ‰). Samples that did not fall within a specific source range were inferred to have been affected by mixing between two or more sources, as evidenced previously by different approaches. Remarkably, there was a minimum overlap between the manure and sewage ranges. Typical NO3 – -N biogeochemical processes inherent to shallow aquifers include nitrification, denitrification, and volatilization at elevated pH values. Groundwater samples of the MDA did not exhibit a clear correlation between the concentrations of NO3 – -N and δ15 NNO3  or δ18 ONO3  in both groups (r2  = 0.098 and r2  = 0.099, respectively). This suggests that different mixing sources and biogeochemical transformations were involved in affecting the NO3 –  concentrations. The environmental conditions that could promote nitrification or denitrification were evaluated with the aid of Fig. S3 a . According to the scientific literature, denitrification occurs at water pH values between 5.5 and 8 with low DO concentrations (<4 mg/L) (Nikolenko et al., 2018 ), resulting in a decrease of NO3 – -N concentrations and enrichment of 18 O and 15 N in the remaining nitrate with a typical δ18 ONO3 /δ15 NNO3  ratio between 1:1.13 and 1:2.1 (Böttcher et al., 1990; Fukada et al., 2003 ) (Fig. 4 c ). In contrast, nitrification requires pH values between 6.5 and 8 with DO concentrations of > 4 mg/L (Nikolenko et al., 2018 ). This process increases NO3 – -N concentration and decreases δ18 ONO3  and δ15 NNO3  values (Kendall and Aravena, 2000 ). Fig. S3 a  shows that both nitrification and denitrification occurred between the groups. In addition, employing the δ18 OH2O  fingerprint allows for estimating the δ18 ONO3  produced by microbial nitrification. Literature-derived data indicate a wide range for the predicted δ18 ONO3  (−10 ‰ to 10 ‰) (Xue et al., 2009 ). Nevertheless, it is possible to conduct a local approximation of the δ18 ONO3  derived from nitrification for the MDA using Eq. (11)   (Andersson and Hooper, 1983 ).(11) δ18 ONO3  = 2/3 δ18 OH2O  + 1/3 δ18 OO2     where δ18 OH2O  represents the isotopic values measured in the groundwater samples, and δ18 OO2  represents the oxygen isotopic composition of atmospheric O2  (∼+23.5 ‰) (Kroopnick and Craig, 1972 ). The isotopic analysis of MDA reveals that microbial nitrification has an important role in the system's nitrogen cycle, as evidenced by δ18 ONO3  values ranging from 2.3 ‰ and 4.4 ‰. The soil pH within the MDA, which ranges from 8.0 to 8.4 (Fig. S5  ), is ideally suited for nitrification, further supporting this process (Li et al., 2020 ). Moreover, the prevalence of nitrification is also corroborated by our findings, which indicate that a significant proportion of samples (60 % of Group 1 and 56 % of Group (2)  exhibited clear isotopic evidence of undergoing nitrification. The remaining samples had higher theoretical δ18 ONO3  values, suggesting a shifting in the isotopic composition, indicative of a denitrification process (Fig. S3 b ). These observations are consistent with the previously discussed environmental conditions for the MDA. Moreover, the average oxidation–reduction potential of the system was 175 mV, indicating an environment favorable for denitrification. Finally, the low levels of N2 O (<0.5 mg/L as N) suggest that denitrification is occurring but may not progress towards completion. Therefore, there is an opportunity to explore potential strategies to enhance this natural attenuation pathway for the removal of dissolved nitrate from groundwater. Excessive use of manure on agricultural land produces a significant amount of urea (Eq. (12)  ). This promotes the nitrification of NH4 +  (Eq. (13)   and Eq. ( 14 ) ) in receiving soils (Norton and Ouyang, 2019 ). The application of organic fertilizers using doses from 100 to 270 kg/ha is a common practice in the study area (Gutiérrez et al., 2021; INEGI, 1999 ).(12) CO(NH2 )2  → NH3  ↔ NH4 +  → NO3 –    (13) 2NH4 +  + 3O2  → 2NO2 –  + 2H2 0 + 4H+    (14) 2NO2 –  +O2  → 2NO3 –     In contrast, denitrification occurs predominantly in zones adjacent to rivers. Riparian zones are recognized as “hot spots” for this biogeochemical process because of favorable conditions such as the presence of a slope, suitable sediment texture, and direct hydraulic connection between the river and aquifer (Lutz et al., 2020; Popp et al., 2020; Vidon and Hill, 2004 ). These factors facilitate permanent N removal through N2  and N2 O gas emissions.  3.6 Source apportionment models according to δ15 NNO3  vs. δ18 ONO3 , δ15 NNO3  vs. δ11 B, and PMF 3.6.1 BIMM’s models The MixSIAR model results, considering δ15 NNO3  vs. δ18 ONO3 , reveal critical insights into NO3 – -N pollution sources in the MDA. In Group (1) , the most important contributors to NO3 – -N pollution were manure and sewage, accounting for 67.3 ± 20.2 % of the total nitrate input. This indicates that improper waste management practices from livestock and/or human activities affect water quality. The second major source is soil, contributing 20.4 ± 18.5 %, and could be attributed to organic matter decomposition. Finally, fertilizers derived from agricultural practices apport the remaining 12.3 ± 13.6 % (Fig. 6  a ). In Group (2) , the order of contribution is similar: manure and sewage (64.0 ± 20.2 %) dominate as the primary source of NO3 – -N pollution, followed by soil (22.5 ± 18.9 %) and chemical fertilizers (13.5 ± 14.1 %) (Fig. 6 b ). Overall, taking into consideration the entire MDA system, the most critical pollution source was manure and sewage (65.3 ± 20.2 %), followed by soil (21.7 ± 18.7 %), and the lowest contributor was chemical fertilizers (13.0 ± 13.9 %) (Fig. 6 c ). Despite the inclusion of isotope fractionation resulting from biogeochemical transformations into the model and the fact that narrow isotopic ranges for the various sources of NO3 – -N pollution, the δ15 NNO3  vs. δ18 ONO3  Bayesian model can not distinguish between the contributions of manure and sewage. To address this issue, a BIMM that contrasts δ15 NNO3  with δ11 B was proposed, considering that manure pollution can be distinguished from sewage pollution and that there is minimal overlap between the probable pollution sources. The BIMM results showed no difference in the probable NO3 – -N pollution sources between Groups (1)  (Fig. 6 d ) and 2 (Fig. 6 e ). Therefore, based on the findings, the δ15 NNO3  vs. δ11 B Bayesian model obtained lower contributions considering the sum of manure and sewage (57.1 %) as the δ15 NNO3  vs. δ18 ONO3  Bayesian model (65.3 %). Thus, based on this distinction, it is possible to conclude that manure (52.4 ± 12.4 %) is the most significant anthropogenic source of NO3 – -N pollution in the MDA system (Fig. 6 f ). It represents, on average, a contribution of 3.5 mg/L of NO3 – -N to groundwater (Table S4  ). This is in line with what was expected given the elevated manure production (∼1,760 tons/day, Table S2  ) brought on by intensive livestock activity, which is more cost-effective than chemical fertilizers and encourages their widespread use throughout the study area. Although MDA is indeed an intensive agricultural region, the contribution from chemical fertilizers to groundwater nitrate pollution is relatively low (5.5 ± 7.9 %). Nevertheless, this result may be hidden if excessive fertilizer is applied (more than the crop requirements). This is because fertilizers applied to the soil are easily volatilized to NH3  and then nitrified to NO3 – -N in less than two weeks, thus directly threatening groundwater quality (Bijay-Singh and Craswell, 2021; Lu et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2016 ). Therefore, it is more accurate to describe agricultural soils as anthropogenically influenced sources of NO3 – -N contamination in groundwater, which contribute substantially (37.4 ± 14.4 %). This significant soil contribution to NO3 – -N levels in groundwater is, to a large extent, a reflection of the incorporation of synthetic fertilizers and manure, highlighting the impact of human-induced nitrogen inputs on soil and water quality. Finally, sewage pollution was expected to be high because Delicias, the largest city in the MDA, has no wastewater treatment facilities. Instead, sewage flows straight into the irrigation channels (Ramírez-Marfil et al., 2021 ). Nevertheless, comparable to chemical fertilizers, sewage represents a negligible share of pollution sources (4.7 ± 6.8 %).  3.6.2 Sensitivity analysis The integrity of the MixSIAR model is intrinsically linked to the isotopic compositions assigned to the end-member pollution sources. A sensitivity analysis was conducted to rigorously assess the impact of these isotopic signatures on the model outputs. This analysis scrutinized the repercussions of varying input parameters on isotopic compositions in subsequent source apportionment. As delineated in Fig. S4   for the δ15 NNO3  vs. δ18 ONO3  model, marginal deviations were observed in relation to the base scenario (0 % change). Specifically, the standard deviations for the end-members were quantified as follows: for fertilizers, the standard deviation ranged between 0.6 % and 1.4 %; for soil, it varied from 1.1 % to 2.2 %; and for manure and sewage, the standard deviation fluctuated between 1.4 % and 3.1 %. Similarly, Fig. S5   displays the sensitivity analysis executed using the δ15 NNO3  vs. δ11 B isotopic framework. Notably, this model demonstrates lower variability in its outcomes than its δ15 NNO3  vs. δ18 ONO3  counterpart. Specifically, the standard deviations for fertilizers ranged from 0.18 % to 0.27 %, soil from 0.32 % to 0.94 %, manure from 0.13 % to 3.13 %, and sewage from 0.10 % to 0.45 %. This empirical observation provides evidence supporting the idea that a robust model can be developed using isotopic values from the existing literature, which frequently includes a wide range of samples representing different end-members. It is pertinent to mention the sensitivity analysis conducted by Ji et al. (2022)  using a BIMM for δ15 NNO3  vs. δ18 ONO3 , which employed a more constrained set of local end-member samples (15 for precipitation, 10 for fertilizer, 32 for soil, and 7 for sewage). Despite the limited sample size, significant variations were observed in the sensitivity analysis, particularly for sewage-related inputs. This accentuates the argument that while collecting local end-members holds intrinsic value, using isotope values derived from the literature does not necessarily restrict the application of BIMMs as long as the database is sufficiently comprehensive to generate precise models.  3.6.3 PMF Groundwater pollution sources in the MDA were rigorously investigated using the EPA-PMF modeling approach. The model was parameterized using an array of nine chemical constituents: Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Na+ , K+ , Cl- , F- , SO4 2- , HCO3 –,  and NO3 – -N. These selected parameters demonstrated signal-to-noise (S/N) ratios within the range of 8.4 to 9.0, attesting to the high quality of the groundwater data utilized. The optimal number of factors to be incorporated into the model was determined through a series of computational tests involving 3 to 5 factors. Each scenario was subjected to 100 base runs with a stochastic initialization of seed numbers. The objective was to minimize the discrepancies between the objective function Qtrue  and Qrobust . Based on these empirical analyses, four factors were identified as most appropriate for inclusion in the model. This selection was based on multiple criteria: (1) the majority of the sample residuals were observed to fall within the numerical bounds of −3 to 3, (2) robust theoretical Q values were obtained (evidenced by the lowest Q value), and (3) a high degree of correlation was noted between scatterplot data of predicted and observed values, with correlation coefficients ranging from 0.63 to 0.87. The PMF model elucidated four dominant factors responsible for groundwater pollution In the MDA: water–rock interactions, manure & sewage, fertilizers, and soil pollution (Fig. 7  ). These factors were quantitatively and qualitatively evaluated for their respective contributions to the overall chemical profile of groundwater. Factor 1 predominantly emanated from manure and sewage pollution, accounting for 60.2 % of the NO3 – -N concentrations variance. This factor has also been identified as a significant contributor to the SO4 2- , Cl- , Na+ , and K+  (Hao and Chang, 2003; Martín Del Campo et al., 2014 ). This result is consistent with previous BIMM estimations using δ15 NNO3  vs. δ18 ONO3  (65.3 %) and δ15 NNO3  vs. δ11 B Bayesian models (57.1 %). Factor 2 indicates a water–rock interaction mechanism that contributes zero percent to nitrate pollution. Nevertheless, it significantly influences contributions to HCO3 – , SO4 2- , F- , Cl- , Na+ , Ca2+,  and K+ . Factor 3 was implicated in soil contamination, accounting for 21.9 % of the total NO3 –  variance. This factor is particularly associated with elevated HCO3 – , Na+ , Cl- , and F- concentrations. Finally, Factor 4 was principally attributed to chemical fertilizer use, explaining 17.9 % of the variance in NO3 – -N concentrations. SO4 2- , Mg2+ , and K+  are the key contributors to this factor (Bijay-Singh and Craswell, 2021). The primary advantage of the PMF model is that the required chemical information of groundwater samples is more economically accessible than stable isotope ratio data, resulting in a promising tool for identifying groundwater pollution (Mao et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023 ); nevertheless, it is not without its challenges. The appropriate model application requires in-depth knowledge of the study area and the potential pollution sources to correctly interpret the contributing factors. This differs from the Bayesian models, which are easier to understand and interpret.   3.7 Nitrate management strategies Given previously reported findings, nitrification is one of the most influential biogeochemical processes in the MDA system, leading to increased NO3 – -N concentrations in groundwater and consequently reducing its water quality. The BIMMs results suggest that the extensive use of organic and inorganic fertilizers was primarily responsible for nitrification. As agriculture is the principal economic sector of the region, reducing the use of fertilizers might not be straightforward. However, it may be possible to implement measures to reduce the NO3 – -N leaching process, as has been done in other regions. For instance, in China, the adoption of controlled-release N fertilizers, nitrification, and urease inhibitors, higher frequency of split fertilizer application, and optimization of the N rate based on soil N test results have all been shown to reduce NO3 – -N leaching into groundwater (Xia et al., 2017 ). Furthermore, crop rotation techniques can help preserve microbial diversity and soil health, and reduce N residues (McDaniel et al., 2014; Orr et al., 2011 ). Manure management practices should be simultaneously improved, beginning with collection, storage, processing, and applications at appropriate times. As an alternative to applying manure to farmland, biogas digesters can utilize manure for various purposes (Niles et al., 2019 ). Although sewage was not deemed an essential source in the analysis, upgrading the sewage system by building wastewater treatment facilities is vital to limit the potential human health and ecological impacts of dumping sewage directly into the rivers.   4 Conclusions This study offers a comprehensive assessment of NO3 – -N pollution sources in the groundwater of the Meoqui-Delicias aquifer system. The pollution sources were differentiated using hydrochemical data and isotope ratios. Multiple biogeochemical transformations that regulate the system were identified, and the contribution of each source was quantified using contrasting Bayesian isotope mixing models involving NO3 – -N and B isotope ratios. The results are compared with those of a positive matrix factorization model. Although the research area can experience pollution caused by extensive agriculture, animal operations, and poorly treated wastewater, the results show that NO3 – -N levels exceed the natural background; however, in most cases, they are below the drinking water limit (11 mg/L as N). To create effective NO3 – -N management strategies and preserve the water quality, it is essential to correctly identify the sources of the preceding pollution. Notwithstanding, hydrochemistry and the multi-isotopic approach (δ18 OH2O , δ2 HH2O , δ15 NNO3 , δ18 ONO3 , and δ11 B) suggested that the mixing of nutrients and contaminants from various sources contributed to the water quality deterioration: soil, chemical fertilizers, manure, and sewage. Leaks in manure storage and the intensive use of organic fertilizers in croplands have also favored nitrification, which is the most significant biogeochemical process. Conversely, denitrification controls NO3 – -N pollution in groundwater and occurs in isolated areas adjacent to the MDA riparian zones. A Bayesian model comparing δ15 NNO3  vs. δ18 ONO3  suggests that manure and sewage (65.3 %), soil (21.7 %), and chemical fertilizers (13.0 %) all contribute in different proportions to NO3 – -N contamination in groundwater. The overlapping of isotopic signatures of various sources was overcome with the use of a δ15 NNO3  vs. δ11 B Bayesian model, which assisted in the differentiation, revealing that manure (52.4 %) was the most important pollution source, followed by soil (37.4 %), fertilizers (5.5 %), and sewage (4.7 %). It is crucial to note that chemical fertilizers likely contribute more, but because of nitrification, they are rapidly transferred to the soil N pool, making differentiation impossible using this method. Finally, the PMF model results validate the δ15 NNO3  vs. δ11 B Bayesian model by indicating that 60.2 % of NO3 –  pollution could be associated with manure and sewage, which is in line with the previously obtained values (65.3 % and 57.1 %), despite taking into account a higher contribution of fertilizers (17.9 %) that the Bayesian model did not identify. This discrepancy likely arises because some of the chemical fertilizers are reflected in the soil contribution, making them challenging to distinguish. Consequently, it becomes apparent that chemical fertilizers, often difficult to isolate in BIMMs due to their assimilation into soil profiles, are more clearly delineated in the PMF results. Therefore, the PMF data make a significant contribution by providing a more realistic and detailed breakdown of NO3 –  pollution sources, particularly in highlighting the often-overlooked role of chemical fertilizers. These models could assist local authorities in developing appropriate solutions for nitrate contamination, effectively controlling pollution from manure, which has not been achieved in prior studies, and mitigating NO3 – -N groundwater contamination. To improve these models, monitoring isotopic values from local pollution sources to minimize uncertainty is essential. While the immediate application of this study pertains to the Meoqui-Delicias aquifer system, its implications are far-reaching and can be employed globally. This study lays the groundwork for future research and extends innovative methodologies to aquifer systems worldwide, which have great potential for shaping the future direction of international research in this field. The insights from this study provide an evidence base to significantly impact policy-making and guide decisions regarding agricultural and livestock facility regulations to best protect drinking water quality. Therefore, this study exemplifies innovative scientific exploration and contributes substantially to public health and environmental sustainability, both locally and globally.
1 Introduction Deltaic channels are crucial part of estuaries connecting rivers and the sea, which have significant role in delivering water, sediment and nutrients, and for sustaining diverse ecosystems and human activities like ports and shipping (Costanza et al., 1997; Stark et al., 2017 ). However, most deltaic channels have undergone great filling or serious erosion in response to the change of riverine water and sediment input as well as the alteration of local estuarine topography and hydrodynamic regime induced by human modifications (Avoine et al., 1981; Syvitski et al., 2005; Dai et al., 2016; Ralston et al., 2019 ). It is necessary to understand morphodynamic processes of deltaic channels under the dual stresses of the nature and intense anthropogenic intervention, which is also pivotal for comprehension of entire estuarine development, management of estuaries and relevant policy-making (Giosan et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2021 ). Deltaic channels have experienced distinct morphological change with human interferences in recent decades years (Syvitski and Saito, 2007; Dai, 2021 ). Owing to sediment starvation induced by dam construction in the upstream, most estuaries and delta worldwide are facing the danger of channel erosion and tidal flat recession (Syvitski et al., 2009; Blum and Roberts, 2009 ), like the Mississippi Delta, the Mekong River delta and the Danube delta (Blum and Roberts, 2009; Giosan et al., 2013; Anthony et al., 2015 ). Meanwhile, massive estuarine dredging, diking and reclamation, can also dramatically alter the hydrodynamics, sediment transport and morphology of deltaic channels (Scorpio and Rosskopf, 2016 ). In the Mersey estuary, dredging work helped maintain the water depth and training wall could stable the channel and guide the water, the ebb tidal flow was concentrated in the main-channel region under the combine effects of these works (Blott et al., 2006 ). Land reclamation within the Ems Estuary would increase suspended sediment concentrations by reducing accommodation space for fine-grained sediments (Van Maren et al., 2016 ). Liu et al. (2019)  found that deltaic channels in the Pearl River Delta were substantially deepened because of large-scale sand excavation. Despite intensive artificial interferences, the fluctuation of fluvial water discharge may account for seasonal and multi-year cycles in morphological evolution, which can be seen in the Gironde Estuary and Qiantang Estuary (Billy et al., 2012; Wei et al., 2016; Xie et al., 2018 ). The river discharge that varies dramatically from dry season to wet season could modify erosion and deposition pattern of deltaic channels, which further greatly influenced the channel capacity and morphology (Azhikodan and Yokoyama, 2019 ). Furtherly, the response of deltaic channels where Estuarine Turbidity Maximum (ETM) exist, may lag to the reduction of sediment upstream (Kim et al., 2006; Jiang et al., 2013; Vinh et al., 2014 ). ETM is a region where sediment concentration is several times or even tens of times higher than that of the upstream and downstream. Severe deposition could occur within ETM because sediment from river and sea is trapped in this region, which can be seen in many estuaries all around the world (Pontee et al., 2004; Asp et al., 2016; Hesse et al., 2019 ). Furtherly, deltaic channels deepened by dredging works owns greater navigation depth, being capable of carrying more vessels and playing an important shipping value. However, significant deepening by dredging can greatly reduce the bottom friction and turbulent mixing, which often results in an increase in tidal amplitude, estuarine circulation and tidal asymmetry (Winterwerp and Wang, 2013; Ralston et al., 2019 ). Such variations can enhance the up-estuary sediment transport and suspended sediment concentrations, which induces deposition in channel, increasing the maintenance dredging needs and disposal (Hossain et al., 2004; Van Maren et al., 2015; Martelo et al., 2019 ). Thereafter, understanding of the morphodynamic processes in dredged channels is conducive to taking appropriate measures to alleviate accretion in channels. Especially, under multiple effects from both nature and human interventions, the morphodynamic evolution of a deltaic channel over the many large rivers all around the world is complicated with requirement of comprehensive understanding, such as the Mega-Changjiang delta. The Changjiang River is the longest river in China, which originates from the Qinghai Tibetan and flows eastward for a distance of 6300 km to the East China Sea, with a catchment area of 1.8 × 106  km2  (Chen et al., 2001 ; Fig. 1  a). Due to the plentiful sediment transport from upstream, the Changjiang Delta has advanced seaward more than 200 km since the mid-Holocene and gave rise to the contemporary configuration, which is sequentially bifurcated by four islands and forms four deltaic channels (Hori et al., 2001; Dai et al., 2015; Dai, 2021 ; Fig. 1 b). The Changjiang Delta is a fluvial-tidal delta, where the tidal regime is irregular and semi-diurnal with average tidal range of 2.67 m (Dai et al., 2013 ). In the past decades, the Changjiang Delta has been affected by large-scale and intense human modifications from both upstream catchment and within the delta itself (Mei et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2019 ). Over 50,000 dams and reservoirs have been built along the Changjiang River basin, which led to a drastic decrease of sediment load delivered to the Changjiang Delta (Yang et al., 2011 ). In particular, after the construction of Three Gorges Dam (TGD) in 2003, the sediment transported to the delta has decreased by 70 % (Dai et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2015 ). Meanwhile, estuarine engineering like land reclamation, dam construction and navigational projects, has also altered the evolution of the deltaic system (Wei et al., 2016; Lou et al., 2020 ). North Passage (NP) is one of the four deltaic channels of the Changjiang Delta, located between Hengsha Shoal and Jiuduansha Shoal (Fig. 1 c). It is not only one of the main waterways of the Changjiang estuary for transporting water and sediment but also an important navigation channel for vessels (Dai et al., 2013 ). However, there is a huge mouth bar system within NP and the shallowest water depth is only about 6.5 m, which seriously hinder the development of maritime trade (Li et al., 2016 ). In order to improve the navigation conditions, Deep Waterway Project (DWP) was conducted in NP during 1998–2010, which was carried out in three phases, including five main works, namely, 49.20 km long south dike and 48.08 km north dike, diversion submerged dikes, 19 groins with a total length of about 30 km, and dredging works of 92.2 km long and 350–400 m wide (Dai, 2021 ; Table 1  ). Some studies have been conducted with mainly focus on the hydrodynamics and sediment transport mechanism of NP (Shi, 2004; Hu and Ding, 2009; Jiang et al., 2012; Li et al., 2016; Pu et al., 2016; Hua et al., 2019 ). E.g., Shi (2004)  found that the formation of the turbidity maximum of the NP closed to tidal asymmetry, near-bed periodic tidal resuspension and turbulence suppression by suspension/salinity stratification. Pu et al. (2016)  demonstrated that tidal stirring, longitudinal and lateral depth-mean strainings play dominant roles in the neap–spring tidal variability of mixing and stratification within the main channel of NP. However, little information involves holistic understanding of the morphodynamics of entire NP at the time scale of the excavation and maintenance dredging of 12.5 m navigation channel. In this study, high-resolution bathymetric data of NP during 1997–2020 and a series of the measured hydrological and sediment data were used to discern the morphodynamic evolution of NP. The main purposes of this paper were to (1) explore the variations of NP in recent decades; (2) distinguish the erosional and depositional patterns of NP; (3) diagnose the possible driven factors of NP evolution. The present work can provide an important reference point for the response of NP and similar deltaic channels worldwide to natural effects and integrated artificial interferences.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Data and materials Four groups of data were collected in this study. The first group consists of 70 high-precision bathymetric charts covering NP from 1979 to 2020, including depth data in 1979 and 1990 obtained from nautical chart, 68 contiguous surveys during 1997–2020 which was measured by the Changjiang Estuary Waterway Administration Bureau (CJWAB, https://www.cjkhd.com/ ). Dual-frequency echo sounders with a vertical error of 0.1 m and GPS positioning were used to measure the water depth once every quarter every year, mostly in February, May, August and November. The data was scaled on 1:10,000 or 1:25,000 which ensures 8–40 surveyed data points are contained every square kilometer (Dai et al., 2014 ). The second set of data, including monthly runoff and suspended sediment concentration (SSC) during 1979–2020 at Datong station which is the most downstream hydrologic station of the Changjiang River as well as the tidal limit of the Changjiang Estuary, was acquired from the Bulletin of China River Sediment (BCRS, http://www.cjh.com.cn/ ). It was used to detect the impact of riverine dynamics on the morphodynamic variations of NP. The third group of data is the ebb flow ratio which is in the interface between North Passage and South Passage. The collected data was from the Changjiang Water Resources Commission (http://www.cjw.gov.cn/ ). Moreover, the fourth set of data is the measured flow data within a 25-hour tidal cycle at gauge stations in the NP (Fig. 1 c), which was also surveyed by the Changjiang Estuary Waterway Administration Bureau. The measured data was used to diagnose the effect of the alteration of hydrodynamics on the morphology variations of NP.  2.2 Methods The bathymetric data was digitized and analyzed by using ArcGIS 10.6 platform. The original data was converted to the elevation relative to the coordinates of Beijing-1954 and corrected to the theoretical datum. Subsequently, the bathymetric data was gridded to Digital Elevation Model (DEM) with 100 m × 100 m cell unit using Kriging interpolation method. The erosion and deposition in different periods were explored, which can represent the water depth changes in adjacent periods. Meanwhile, the volume below 0 m is regarded as the river channel capacity, the volume between 0 m and 5 m represent the shoal zone, while the volume below 8 m is on behalf of the deep channel (Dai et al, 2013; Lou et al., 2020 ). In order to recognize the morphological changes of NP, four transverse sections named sequentially as NPC1, NPC2, NPC3, and NPC4 that represent the entrance, upper, middle, lower sections evolution of NP, as well as water depth of the thalweg were extracted from the DEM (Fig. 1 c). In addition, the region that is enclosed by the groins and the dikes is called groin region, and other region which is enveloped by the heads of groins is named as main-channel region (Fig. 1 c).  2.3 Empirical orthogonal function analysis Empirical orthogonal function (EOF) analysis was invented by Pearson (Pearson, 1901 ), its main goal is to recognize and extract physical and dynamically independent modes from the original dataset (Kim and Wu, 1999 ). Mathematically, EOF analysis decompose a dataset into a series of uncorrelated components called principal components, where any two components orthogonal to each other (Zhang et al., 2009 ). These components are ordered according to their representations of data variance and the first few leading components can always account for the most of total variance, effectively reducing the data set while preserve majority of the variability in the data (Wang et al., 2017 ). Therefore, this method has been widely used in different disciplines (Yoo and Kim, 2004; Dai et al., 2013; Mei et al., 2018 ). Specifically, assume the original dataset Y   is the matrix of N × M   , where N   represents the number of locations and M   represents observations at each location. Then Y i j   = Y x i  , t j       represents the value at the location x i    and at time t j   , i = 1 , 2  , ⋯ , n    and j = 1 , 2  , ⋯ , m   . Then EOFs could be found by calculating the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C Y   , which is(1) C Y  = 1 M - 1   Y Y  T       C Y    is a positive semidefinite real matrix with N   rows and N   columns, therefore, it can be diagonalized by the orthogonal matrix of its eigenvector, there is,(2) C Y  = E D E  T       E   is a matrix whose columns are the orthogonal eigenvectors of C Y   , i.e., EOFs, D   is a diagonal matrix whose elements are the eigenvalues of C Y   . Each EOF’s time series, i.e., PCs, can be computed by P = Y  T  E   . The eigenvalues explain the variances of the original data for the corresponding eigenvector. Then the eigenvectors are reorder in descending order according to eigenvalues, so the first eigenvector explains the largest variance of the original data, the second eigenvector explains the largest remaining variance and so forth. When the cumulative variances of the first k   (k ≪ n )    eigenvectors account for a large proportion of the total variances of the data, it is considered that these k eigenvectors can well explain the changes of the data, thus simplifying the analysis of the original data to a large extent. In this study, Y   is the bathymetric data which was removed the time average value.  2.4 Wavelet analysis Wavelet analysis was originated in the 1980s and firstly used to analyze seismic signals (Morlet et al., 1982 ). With the further development of wavelet theory in mathematics, it was also obtained a series of applications in other fields like rainfall, seafloor bathymetry, and ocean wind waves (Kumar and Foufoula-Georgiou, 1997 ). Wavelet analysis is very useful for studying the local variation characteristics of time series. By transforming a time series into time–frequency space, we are able to determine the dominant modes and how these modes change with time (Torrence and Compo, 1998 ). Assume f t      is a time series, i.e., NP's channel capacity variations between surveys in this study, then the continuous wavelet transforms of f t      is(3) W f s , t   = ∫ - ∞  ∞  f u   ψ  ¯   s , t   u   d u s > 0     where ψ s , t   u      represent a series of functions called wavelet, ψ  ¯   s , t   u      is the complex conjugate of ψ s , t   u     . Common wavelets include Mexican hat and Morlet wavelet. In this study, we choose the Morlet wavelet, which is given as(4) ψ t   = π  - 1 4    e  - i ω 0  t   e  - t  2  2    ω 0  ≥ 5     where s   is scale parameter. Difference values of s   correspond different time scales of behaviors of f t     . From the above formula, we can see that when s   increases the wavelet functions are stretched and takes only long-time behavior of f t      into account and vice versa. Therefore, the wavelet transform is similar to a microscope, with a magnification of 1 / λ   , and different wavelets are similar to different optical devices.   3 Results 3.1 vol changes of North Passage Between 1979 and 2020, NP capacity had a net loss of 1.91 × 108  m3  with average rate of 4.63 × 106  m3 /yr (Fig. 2  ). Furtherly, NP capacity presented stage variations, which can be divided into four stages according to DWP engineering phases. Before the construction of DWP (1979.09–1997.12), NP capacity show a net increase of 2.81 × 107  m3  with slow rate of 1.54 × 106  m3 /yr (Fig. 2 ). In the second stage (1997.12–2002.02), NP capacity was in a state of quick fluctuation and showed a slight increase of 8.51 × 107  m3  in comparison with that in 1997.12 (Fig. 2 ). However, during the subsequent stage (2002.02–2007.08), NP capacity indicated a significant decrease trend with a mean rate of 7.87 × 107  m3 /yr (Fig. 2 ). Meanwhile, the capacity of main-channel region and groin region emerged remarkable increase and decreased trend, respectively (Fig. 3  a). During the third stage (2007.08–2020.11), NP capacity displayed a slow rising trend, experiencing a minor net increase of 1.29 × 108  m3  with an average speed of 9.77 × 106  m3 /yr, where the capacity of main-channel region and groin region maintained inverse changing trend (Fig. 3 ). Moreover, it can be found that relative remarkable fluctuations exist in NP capacity between 1997 and 2020 (Fig. 4  ). Based on wavelet analysis method, there are two significant peaks in the variance coefficient curve, which exceeds the 95 % confidence level (Fig. 4 a, b). The time scales corresponding to the two peaks are 13 months and 25 months respectively, indicating that annual and biennial fluctuations exist in the evolution of NP. The magnitude of 25 months fluctuation is almost an order larger than that of 13 months, showing main role of 25 months in fluctuation components and time series of real coefficients are depicted for better demonstration.  3.2 Variations of shoal and deep channel The volume between 0 m and 5 m, regarded as the shoal zone, experienced considerable decrease with an average speed of 1.18 × 107  m3 /yr during 1979–2020 (Fig. 5  a), meaning serious deposition continuously occurred in the shoal zone in the last 23 years. Meanwhile, the volume changes of the shoal zone can be separated into three stages. In the first stage (1979–2001), the shoal zone was showed a slight decrease with net volume reduction of 2.17 × 107  m3 . The subsequent stage (2001–2017) was fast-descend period for the shoal zone, which decreased from 1.60 × 109  m3  in 2001 to 1.15 × 109  m3  in 2017 with a mean rate of 2.71 × 107  m3 /yr. In the third stage (2017–2020), the shoal zone was converted into steady state, which basically maintained in the volume of 1.15 × 109  m3  that was in the end of the second stage. Inversely, the volume below 8 m, named as deep channel, showed significant growth trend during 1979–2020, rising at a rate of 6.83 × 106  m3 /yr (Fig. 5 a), indicating deep channel was constantly in erosion. Compared with the volume change of the shoal zone, the variation of deep channel can be divided into two stages. Between 1979 and 2008, it exhibited slow increase with an average rate of 2.77 × 106  m3 /yr. However, in the next stage (2008–2020), the deep channel volume turned into rapid growth state, increasing from 1.41 × 108  m3  in 2008 to 3.41 × 108  m3  in 2020 with an average speed of 1.67 × 107  m3 /yr. Briefly, during 1979–2020, the shoal zone experienced slow accretion, rapid sedimentation, basically stable period, while deep channel underwent slow scouring and quick erosion stage. The two displayed a distinct inverse relationship (Fig. 5 b), which largely indicated that lateral sediment transport may exist between the shoal zone and deep channel, due to the vertical and horizontal exchange of water in the shoal zone and deep channel.  3.3 Configuration alteration of cross sections The shape of the entrance section was converted from “L” shape to “U” shape during 1979–2020 (Fig. 6  a), where the deep channel moved southward and its width was decreased by about 0.6 km. Both two side experienced significant accretion and the maximum siltation could reach up to about 8.00 m. The middle part exhibited erosion during 1979–1997, but it was turned into successive deposition during 1997–2006, and then it was switched to erosion during the later period. Meanwhile, the shape of the upper section was transformed from flat shape with average water depth of 4.56 m to “V” shape whose maximum water depth was around 12.81 m (Fig. 6 b). From the horizonal direction, the river channel width was narrowed to 3.69 km but deep channel width was increased to 2.29 km. In the vertical direction, the groin region was in continuous deposition with mean accumulation depth of 4.83 m, however, the main-channel region was dominated by lasting erosion (Fig. 6 b). Moreover, the middle section was converted from flat shape with mean water depth of 6.16 m to “V” shape between 1979 and 2020 (Fig. 6 c). The river channel width was reduced from 7.23 km to 6.05 km while deep channel was expanded to 2.28 km wide. The groin region was controlled by accretion, where the average accumulation depths for north and south were 3.03 m and 6.44 m respectively. The main-channel region showed spatial variability where its southern part was in deposition and its northern part was dominated by erosion (Fig. 6 c). Furtherly, the shape of the lower section was changed from flat shape with average water depth of 6.56 m to “U” shape during 1979–2020 (Fig. 6 d). The groin region was mainly in deposition, where the average siltation depths for two sides were 1.71 m and 2.85 m respectively. In addition, the main-channel region displayed spatial differences where its southern part was in accretion and its northern part was in erosion. The deep channel width was increased from 0 km to 2.69 km (Fig. 6 d). In briefly, four transects share analogous evolutionary mode, which can be shown as “deposition over the two sides, and erosion occurred in the middle channel” between 1979 and 2020.  3.4 Erosion and accretion process of North Passage According to DWP engineering phases, the erosion and accretion of NP can be divided into four stages. Before the construction of DWP (1979–1990 and 1990–1997.12), erosion patches and siltation patches were alternately distributed in NP, where the mean erosion strength and the average sedimentation intensity about around 1.00 m (Fig. 8   a, b). NP roughly showed a state of deposition–erosion balance during these periods (Fig. 9  a). Meanwhile, the channel thalweg presented a shape of two crests, and its average depth grew from 7.61 m in 1979 to 8.24 m in 1997.12 (Fig. 7 ). During the first phase of DWP (1997.12–2001.05), strong siltation occurred in the north side of the entrance section, groin region, main-channel region of the middle section, where the siltation intensity mainly focused on 1–3 m (Fig. 8 b). Intense erosion appeared in the main-channel region of the upper section and the north side of the middle section, in which the mean erosion strength was about 1.5 m (Fig. 8 b). As a result, the crest of the channel thalweg in the upper section was cut off, and the average depth of the channel thalweg increased to 9.16 m (Fig. 7 ). On the intermission period (2001.05–2002.05), the majority part of NP had experienced siltation especially the south side of the middle section while the scoured zone scattered in the NP (Fig. 8 c), where the net accretion rate was 2.43 × 107  m3 /yr (Fig. 9 a). During the second phase of DWP (2002.05–2005.02), strong deposition occurred in the groin region and the entrance section of NP, where the mean siltation thickness was about 1.30 m (Fig. 8 d). Due to the serious accumulation in the entrance section, the channel thalweg was turned to a flat shape, with mean depth rise from 9.16 m to 10.05 m (Fig. 7 ). The main-channel region was in the state of erosion with an average erosion intensity of about 0.86 m (Fig. 8 d). However, accretion also occurred in the main-channel region, which distributed in strips with deposition rate of 9.82 × 106  m3 /yr (Fig. 9 b). In the intermission period of DWP (2005.02–2006.08), the groin region was in serious siltation (Fig. 8 e), where the siltation rates for north and south were 4.45 × 107  m3 /yr and 3.47 × 107  m3 /yr respectively (Fig. 9 c, d). Strong erosion appeared in the main-channel region of the lower section but intense deposition occurred in the main-channel region of the upper and middle section. During the third phase of DWP (2006.08–2010.02), the main-channel region was mainly in scour state with mean erosion intensity of around 1.2 m (Fig. 8 f). As a consequence, the channel thalweg was further deepened, increasing its average depth from 10.05 m to 12.27 m (Fig. 7 ). The groin region was still in siltation, with an average thickness of 0.80 m. In addition, a slender siltation zone was located in the south side of the main-channel region of the middle and lower section. During the period after the completion of DWP (2010.02–2020.11), the erosion and accretion of NP was similar to the pattern of the third phase of DWP (Fig. 8 g). Meanwhile, the slender siltation zone expanded northward and moved downstream.   4 Discussion 4.1 Impacts of runoff and suspended sediment discharge Riverine water and sediment delivered to the ocean has been strongly affected by human activities (Syvitski et al., 2005 ). In recent decades, because of the increasing anthropogenic intervention such as dams and reservoirs especially the operation of TGD in upstream area, Suspended Sediment Discharge (SSD) represented notable decrease trend between 1979 and 2020 reducing by about 80 %, but the runoff did not show apparent increase or decrease trend which oscillates around 9.00 × 1011  m3 /yr (Fig. 10  a). However, it seems that the response of NP to the changes of sediment delivered into the Changjiang Delta was insensitive (Dai et al., 2014 ). NP capacity manifested stage variations and it continuously reduced during 2002–2007 instead (Fig. 2 ), which disagreed with the knowledge that reduction of sediment supply should induce erosion and further cause an increase of the channel capacity (Dai et al., 2015 ). Meanwhile, both runoff and sediment flux presented no statistically significant correlations with NP capacity (Fig. 10 b), where the Pearson correlation coefficients are 0.124 and 0.393 respectively, indicating runoff and SSD may have minor effect on the development of NP likely due to proximal and local factors. Although the runoff and SSD may play a secondary role on the morphodynamcs of NP, they could be probably one of important factors controlling periodic characteristic of the changes of NP capacity which indicate cyclical fluctuations of 13 months and 25 months (Fig. 4 b). NP capacity change tended to lag 3 months and 10 months after the alteration of runoff, while it preferred to delay 7 months and 1 months after the variations of sediment flux (Fig. 11  ). Similarly, runoff may affect the oscillation of erosion and sedimentation in estuarine channels, which can also be found in South Passage in Changjiang Estuary (Wei et al., 2016 ), the Qiantang Estuary (Xie et al., 2018 ).  4.2 Impacts of estuarine turbidity maximum ETM is the typical feature in estuaries, which is defined as the zone where sediment concentrations are higher than those found seaward and landward (Dyer, 1988; Davis, 2012 ). ETM has a close relationship with the distribution and transportation of suspended sediment, which plays an important role in the formation, development, and evolution of deltaic channels. Here, ETM experienced alterations during the construction of DWP, where the center of ETM located was shifted upstream for a certain distance. Specifically, the center of ETM was in ng9 gauge station (about 40 km away from the ng1 gauge station) in 2002 and it moved 5 km upstream to ng8 gauge station (about 30 km away from the ng1 gauge station) in 2007 (Fig. 12  a, b). In 2011, the location of the center of ETM remained basically unchanged but the limits of ETM extended to the upper section of NP (Fig. 12 c). However, as morphodynamic adjustment of NP after the construction of DWP, the center of ETM moved downstream for around 10 km, which was shifted back from ng8 gauge station to ng9 gauge station, while the range of ETM extended to the lower section of NP (Fig. 12 d, f). Accordingly, the siltation zone in the main-channel region of NP was mainly in the upper section and middle section of NP during 2002–2005 and 2005–2006 (Fig. 8 c, d), while it concentrated on the middle section and lower section of NP during 2006–2010 and 2010–2020 (Fig. 8 e, f). Obviously, the location of ETM and siltation zone were consistent with each other to a certain extent, meaning that sedimentation induced by mixing of runoff and tidal currents may be one of important factors causing the formation of the siltation zone in the main-channel region of NP (Shi, 2004; Liu et al., 2011; Shen et al., 2020 ). Furtherly, the location of dredging works of the navigation channel was basically in this region, and large-scale routine maintenance of the navigation channel is required every year (Liu et al., 2011; Shen et al., 2020 ). This is different from the dredging in Southwest Pass of the Mississippi delta which is fluvial-dominated, where sediment is controlled by riverine dispersal processes and ETM rarely exist (Coleman et al., 1998; Corbett et al., 2006; Maloney et al., 2018 ). Nevertheless, the Yangtze River delta is mixed fluvial-tidal dominated delta, which suggests tidal currents continuously reciprocate in the NP, as a consequence, ETM has always existed within NP and long-term dredging works need to be carried out.  4.3 Impacts of estuarine engineering The construction of diversion works, double dikes and groins during DWP had changed the regional flow pattern and caused water blocking effect. The flow diversion of the NP has come down since 1999, with the ebb flow ratio decreased from 61.4 % to 42.2 % (Fig. 13  a). The decline of sediment carrying capacity of the flow in the inlet of NP, contributing to continuous siltation in the entrance section and hence reduced NP capacity (Jiang et al., 2012 ; Fig. 8 ). It could be noted that the ebb flow is positively correlated with NP capacity (R = 0.85, p < 0.001) (Fig. 13 b), indicating the descend of the ebb flow corresponds with the decrease of NP capacity (i.e., accretion). Meanwhile, the flow velocity was reduced and small eddies were produced in the groin region, which led to serious deposition in the groin region (Luan et al., 2016; Jiao et al., 2020 ; Figs. 8 and 9 ). Furtherly, the construction of double dikes and groins converged the flow into in the main-channel region. The flow pattern along the main-channel region was converted from rotary current to alternating current and the flow velocity within the main-channel region was intensified (Hu and Ding, 2009; Ge et al., 2010; Pan et al., 2012 ). The scouring ability was enhanced, which was conductive to the erosion of the main-channel region (Fig. 8 ). Moreover, dredging works during and after DWP significantly changed the water depth of the navigation channel of NP. The navigation channel had been continually dredged by using trailing-suction hopper dredgers during DWP (Wu et al., 2016 ). The total dredging volume was 1.10 × 109  m3  during 1999–2020 with average rates of 5.00 × 107  m3 /yr. (Fig. 14  a). Such a huge dredging volume was an important factor leading to the navigation channel, where the channel thalweg was converted into a flat shape and its average water depth was increased to 12.27 m (Fig. 7 b). Meanwhile, significant positive correlation was found between the average water depth of the channel thalweg and dredging volume (R = 0.85, p < 0.001) (Fig. 14 b), implying the increase of the dredging volume was conductive to the deepen of the navigation channel.  4.4 Impact from proximal sediment sources The decrease of fluvial sediment entering into the sea may have minor impact on the morphological changes of NP (Fig. 10 ), and ETM perhaps was responsible for local accretion in the navigation channel (Fig. 12 ). Meanwhile, continuous large-scale dredging work need to be conducted within the entire navigation channel, meaning that proximal sediment sources may be exist. Proximal sediment source also had important influence on the morphological evolution of deltaic channels (Jia et al., 2013; Lou et al., 2020 ). Previous work indicated that the high-turbidity water from Hengsha East Shoal could move southeastward along the north dike and spill over the north dike during the spring ebb tides and be brought into NP by tidal current on the following flood tides (Song and Wang, 2013 ). Meanwhile, the high sediment flux from Jiuduansha shoal could overtop the south dike and flow into NP when the water level is higher than the south dike during high tide or extreme event (Shen et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2020 ). Therefore, the water and sediment exchange between NP and two shoal could still occur in specific conditions although two dikes were built.. In particular, both Hengsha East Shoal and Jiuduansha shoal experienced great expansion and rapid vertical accretion as a result of reclamation projects (Wei et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2018 ), further weakening the sediment blocking ability of double dikes. Therefore, the high turbidity water from Jiuduansha shoal and Hengsha shoal could be converged and settled down in the NP, leading to accretion in the middle and lower section of NP (Fig. 8 ). Meanwhile, because of the construction of the Qingcaosha Reservoir project and Changxing Submerged Dike project, Hengsha Passage was suffered from severe erosion during 2002–2013 (Wu et al., 2016 ).
