A large amount of eroded sediment from Hengsha Passage could be trapped in the upstream of NP with the changes of hydrodynamic conditions, causing serious accretion occur in the north side the entrance section of NP during this period (Fig. 8 ).  4.5 Evolution mode of North Passage While evolution of NP is complicated with interlaced temporal and spatial information, the structured patterns of NP’s development can be identified by EOF analysis. As shown in Fig. 15  , the first two modes explain 84 % of the correlation of the spatial and temporal variation of water depth, which is adequate to represent the evolution of NP. The characteristics of the first two EOF were described below to explain the evolution characteristics of the NP. The first mode, explains 77 % of the correlation, in which the contour map shows positive zone and negative zone are located in the groin region and the main-channel region of NP separately (Fig. 15 a). The spatial pattern is consistent with the layout of engineering works. Combine the first mode eigen weightings curve which shows a rising trend (Fig. 15 b), it can be indicated that between 1979 and 2020, the main-channel region was continuously deepened especially in the navigation channel, and the groin region and shoals were constantly in serious accretion, which corresponds to volume changes and geomorphic variations of NP (Figs. 2, 5–7 ). Meanwhile, the first mode eigen weightings curve increased rapidly during the DWP and keep relatively stable before and after the project, which has a good negative and positive linear correlation with the volume of the shoal zone and deep channel respectively (Fig. 16  a, b). Therefore, the first mode mainly reflects the impact of human engineering on NP especially the DWP. This is consistent with previous work (Dai et al., 2013 ), meaning that although it has been 10 years since the DWP was completed, the NP’s change pattern is basically unchanged. The second mode accounts for the 8 % of the correlation (Fig. 15 c). The contour map reveals that a huge positive zone extends from the entrance section to the main-channel region of upper section and middle section, indicating extensive mouth bar system exists in the NP (Fig. 15 c). Meanwhile, the eigen-weightings curve of the second mode can be divided into four stages which is basically consistent with DWP: decrease from 1979 to 1997, rise during 1997–2005, stable between 2005 and 2008, and down from 2008 to 2020 (Fig. 15 d). This means state transition existed in the evolution process of NP, where mouth bar system moved upstream during DWP, but moved seaward accompanied by decrease in its extent after DWP. In addition, the curve has a good negative and positive linear correlation with the deep channel of the entrance section and the shoal zone of main-channel region respectively (Fig. 16 c, d). Therefore, the second mode may represent the transition of the erosion/deposition state of mouth bar system within NP under the impact of human engineering, ETM, proximal sediment sources, local sediment exchange. Briefly, under the impact of dredging works and the construction of groins (Fig. 17  a), NP mainly exhibited that long-term continuous erosion dominated the main-channel region and persistent deposition controlled the groins region (Fig. 17 a). Meanwhile, Hengsha experienced great accretion after the reclamation projects (Fig. 17 b). However, although the mouth bar was cut off by dredging works (Fig. 17 b), serious accretion could still occur in main-channel and navigation channel due to the existence of ETM (Fig. 17 b). The formation of ETM closely relates to fine sediment carried by river discharge, marine sediment brought by tidal current, and overtopping flow from Jiuduansha and Hengsha during high tide level (Fig. 17 ). In order to maintain the navigation water depth, periodic dredging is needed in the present and foreseeable future, which would consume lots of effort, time and money.   5 Conclusion Morphodynamics of deltaic channels has received widely concern in recent decades years due to intensive human interventions. In this study, the NP changes and relevant driving factors were explored through long-term morphological and hydrological data. The main findings are as follows:(1) During 1979–2020, NP capacity presented stage changes: gentle increase stage, fluctuation stage, fast-descend stage, slow growth stage, and periodic signals of 13 and 25 months can be detected in NP capacity. Meanwhile, the shoal zone and the deep channel showed long-term decrease and increase trend respectively, making NP turn into a narrow and deep deltaic channel. Severe accumulation occurred in the entrance section and groin region, and slender siltation zone could appear in the main-channel region especially the middle section of NP. Intense scouring zone focused on the main-channel region with stage spatial changes, which shifted from the upper section to lower section of NP and finally ran through the entire navigation channel.  (2) NP presented two main morphodynamics modes. The first mode reflects long-term continuous erosion dominated the main-channel region and persistent deposition controlled the groins region. The second mode illustrates the transition of the erosion/deposition state of NP, where mouth bar system moved upstream during DWP and shifted downstream to the lower section of NP accompanied by a reduction of its extent after DWP.  (3) Although riverine water and sediment delivered to the ocean may have minor impact on NP, their periodic changes possibly contributed the oscillation of NP capacity changes. The construction of engineering structures and long-term dredging works resulted in constant deposition in the groin area and continuous erosion in main-channel region. The presence of ETM was conductive to the accretion in the main-channel region, meaning routine dredging maintenance is required every year.    Moreover, this study investigated the morphodynamic evolution of the human-controlled NP with different interferences, revealing that accumulation could still occur in the main-channel region of NP due to the existence of the mouth bar. However, NP is about 55 km with high-spatial variation of morphology, sediment accretion caused by the coupling of fluvial-tidal forces and morphology is complex. Meanwhile, when large-scale accumulation occurs in NP, dredging works would be conducted in the siltation zone, which further increases the difficulty of studying the morphodynamic pattern of the NP. Considering that dredging works would be carried out every month after the third phase of DWP, it is possible to explore the trajectory of dredging works and link it to the siltation zone caused by the coupling of fluvial-tidal forces, especially the location of ETM. Machine learning could be used to quantify the position and amount of siltation in the NP.
1 Introduction In some arid and semi-arid regions with limited rainfall, water resources can be conserved by using saline groundwater for irrigation (Pereira et al., 2002 ). Moreover, the quality of irrigation water is of critical importance in such regions (Muyen et al., 2011 ). Because poor irrigation water quality, inadequate leaching, and high evaporation rates worsen secondary soil salinization, impacting the delicate balance between agricultural sustainability and water resources (Karimzadeh et al., 2024 ). Soil salinization is a severe and irreversible form of soil degradation, leading to increased soil salinity and sodicity (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2021, Stavi et al., 2021 ). Salinity induces osmotic stress, impairing leaf expansion and disrupting nutrient uptake and ionic balance. Toxic ion accumulation can mimic drought conditions, adversely affecting plant biomass and physiological functions (Hussain et al., 2017 ). High sodium (Na+ ) content can lead to dispersion, where clay particles swell and separate when wet. Upon drying, the soil becomes dense and loses its structure. This dense layer can hinder water infiltration and root growth. Exposing sodic subsoil due to topsoil erosion increases erodibility, negatively affecting plant growth (Muyen et al., 2011, Adeyemo et al., 2022 ). Therefore, it is necessary to implement appropriate management practices for irrigating with saline water. In this regard, the assessment of soil permeability under irrigation with saline water is typically conducted based on its salinity (Electrical conductivity, EC) and sodicity (Sodium adsorption ratio, SAR). It classifies saline water into several types according to the degree of impact on infiltration performance (Ayers and Westcot, 1985 ). The water quality assessment method has limitations regarding the impact of high saturation Na+  levels and saline concentration on soil infiltration rate. High saturation Na+  level and saline concentration indeed determine clay particle dispersion, leading to clogged soil pores and reduced hydraulic conductivity in water channels (Tedeschi and Dell’aquila, 2005 ). However, the forces that bind clay particles together are disrupted when too many Na+  come between them at the same time. Weak aggregate stability increases the susceptibility of soil surface layers to crack formation (Mohammadzadeh-Habili et al., 2018 ), creating preferential flow that reduces irrigation efficiency and increases groundwater contamination risk (Li et al., 2023 ). Preferential flow is common in natural unsaturated soils (Hardie et al., 2011 ), where water moves along specific paths through the soil profile, bypassing the soil matrix and accelerating infiltration (Qi et al., 2020 ). As water transport paths shorten, soil drying greatly increases permeability, reducing the effectiveness of clay as a liquid barrier (Yesiller et al., 2000 ). Due to the heightened risk of soil cracking caused by climate change-induced dry periods (Luo et al., 2023, Cui and Zhong, 2024 ), it is essential to integrate soil cracking and its associated preferential flow concerns into the existing water quality assessment standards. The addition of soil cracking to the water quality assessment standard raises a new question of whether EC and SAR alone can sufficiently characterize crack formation accurately. Na+  is the primary ion responsible for soil structure deterioration (Bennett et al., 2016 ), particularly impacting the dispersion of clay particles. This is attributed to Na+  occupying a significant proportion of cation exchange sites and its small ionic radius combined with a large hydration radius. Consequently, the adsorption of Na+  onto soil colloid surfaces results in increased particle spacing and heightened dispersion (Yz et al., 2019 ). In ionic interactions, the combined effect of Na+  and other ions may be greater than that of Na+  alone. Zhu et al. (2019)  found that Mg2+  itself has no direct effect on dispersion, but it can exacerbate the negative effects of Na+ . Thus, when Na+  and Mg2+  are the dominant cations in the soil solution, bridging forces between soil clay particles and aggregates are weakened (Qadir and Schubert, 2002, Dontsova and Norton, 2002 ). This, in turn, can make soil particles with low cohesion more vulnerable to external disturbances like wetting and drying cycles, ultimately leading to soil cracking (Awedat et al., 2021, Pulido-Moncada et al., 2022 ). Our previous researches also confirmed through experiments that Mg2+  does indeed have a special effect on soil cracking (Yan et al., 2024a, 2024b, 2024c ). However, SAR assumes that Mg2+  promotes soil flocculation just as Ca2+ , which limits its ability to accurately describe the characteristics of soil crack formation (Ayers and Westcot, 1985 ). Hence, a comprehensive evaluation of the impact of saline water quality on soil infiltration requires the implementation of a novel index that considers the relationship between Mg2+  and Na+ , combined with EC and SAR. Notably, many arid irrigated areas, such as Yinbei Irrigation District, Hetao Irrigation District and Xinjiang Salinization Regions in northwest China, are characterized by dominant cations Na+  and Mg2+  (Wang et al., 2001, Lin et al., 2007, Guo et al., 2011 ). The same is expected elsewhere of the world. Therefore, it is necessary to analyze soil cracks linked to Mg2+  and Na+  for managing saline water irrigation in arid regions. In sum, to refine the current water quality assessment standard, it's vital to integrate crack and crack-related assessment indicators into the existing framework. We selected the soil of the Hetao Irrigation District, a typical arid salt-affected irrigation region in China, as the research object. The specific objectives of this study were to (1) investigate the complex relationships between EC, SAR, water-salt movement and cracks; (2) identify factors beyond EC and SAR that contribute to crack formation and propose potential indicators for assessing soil quality; (3) refine the existing water quality assessment standard. This study aims to establish a more precise and reliable standard for assessing water quality and contribute to the improvement of water quality management and protection efforts.  2 Material and method 2.1 Soil and water samples Soil samples were collected from a 0–15.0 cm field soil layer at the Shuguang Experimental Station (40°46′N, 107°24′E, 1039 m) in the Hetao Irrigation District, Bayannur city of Inner Mongolia, Northwest China. The study area is arid with a temperate monsoon climate, characterized by an average annual temperature of 6.9 °C, precipitation of approximately 142.1 mm, evaporation of 2306.5 mm, and around 3200.0 annual sunshine hours. Groundwater depth in the area is around 2.5 m. Soil particle size distribution was determined using the Laser Mastersizer 2000 (Malvern Instruments, Malvern, UK) and classified according to international standards for soil texture (Table 1  ). Soil bulk density was measured with the soil core method, while water content was determined through gravimetric analysis. The electrical conductivity of saturated extract (ECe ) and pH of saturated extract were measured using a DDS-307 conductivity meter and PHS-3C pH meter, respectively. A total of 35 treatments were set up with 5 EC levels (3.0, 4.0, 5.0, 6.0 and 7.0 dS m−1 ) (Table 2  ). In the Hetao Irrigation District, Na+  is the dominant monovalent cation in both soil solution and groundwater (Guo et al., 2011, Cheng et al., 2023 ). Therefore, when preparing saline water, we only considered Na+ , Ca2+  and Mg2+ , and did not take K+  into account. Each treatment had three replications. In order to better reflect the action of Mg2+ , the coefficient of Mg2+  in SAR was corrected according to the equation of CROSS (Cation ratio of soil structural stability) (Rengasamy and Marchuk, 2011 ). Based on the differential flocculation powers of Ca2+  and Mg2+ , Mg2+  coefficient was changed to 0.6, and the revised SAR (SARr) equation was:(1) S A R r = N a +   ( ( C a 2 +   + 0.6 M g 2 +   )  / 2 )  0.5        where the chemical element symbols represent charge concentrations in mmolc  L-1 . Turbidity of soil suspensions, crack formation, and water-salt transport indicators were analyzed concerning EC and the SARr.  2.2 Experimental scheme and apparatus Each cylinder was 11.0 cm in outer diameter (side walls were 0.3 cm thick) and 20 cm in height, and each column was filled with 15.0 cm soil. Soil samples were air-dried and ground to pass through a 2.0 mm sieve. The soil column had six drainage holes, each with a diameter of 0.5 cm. A 5.0 cm layer of quartz sand was used as a filter at the bottom of the column. The soil was filled in 5 cm sections with a bulk density of 1.5 g cm−3 . Alternate leaching was implemented, with the initial irrigation designed to fill the soil pores, corresponding to approximately 1.2 L. It was calculated as follows (Xu and Huang, 2010 ):(2) V p  = V s  · T P     (3) TP = ds - B D  ds       where V p  is pore volume (cm3 ), V s  is volume of filled soil (cm3 ), TP  is soil total porosity (%), ds  is soil particle density (2.65 g cm−3 ), and BD  is bulk density (g cm−3 ). After the initial irrigation, each treatment leached approximately 0.15 ± 0.01 L of leachate. To maintain soil saturation, each subsequent irrigation was backfilled with 0.15 L. The experiment involved 12 irrigation events at 7-day intervals over a span of 3 months.  2.3 Measurements Surface cracking in the soil was observed to initiate first and was most prominent. Therefore, only cracks in the soil surface were analyzed in this study, and the analysis for parameters such as K sat, ECe , salt accumulation capacity (Sac ) and turbidity focused solely on the surface soils (0–5.0 cm). Soil columns were scanned using X-ray CT (uMI 780, United Imaging; Shanghai, China). The scan thickness of each slice was 0.05 cm, and the pixel size was 0.068 cm × 0.068 cm. Crack area and width were measured using the Imagej software (National Institutes of Health, USA). Following the completion of the CT scan, the surface soil was sampled using a ring knife. The soil core's bottom was covered with cheesecloth and then saturated in tubs with water for at least 24 h before measuring K sat (Çerçioğlu et al., 2019 ). And the saturated hydraulic conductivity was calculated as follows (Sahin et al., 2011 ):(4) K sat =   V l  · H  A · t · H + h           where V l  is leachate volume (cm3 ), H  is the length of filled soil (cm), A  is the surface area of soil column (cm2 ), t  is leaching time of measurement (min), h  is the height of constant water head (cm). Soil salinity is determined by measuring the electrical conductivity of saturated extract (ECe ) using a DDS-307 conductivity meter. Salt accumulation capacity (Sac ) was calculated as follows:(5) S ac = m e  / m p      where m e  represents end-of-experiment soil salinity, while mp  represents pre-experiment soil salinity. Soil spontaneous dispersion was measured at 25 °C using a turbidimeter (WZS-186, Shanghai, China) to quantify the amount of particles < 2.0 μm dispersed. The method used was modified from Rengasamy et al. (2002) . In this method, 20 g of air-dried and sieved soil (2.0 mm) was placed into a 0.25 L measuring cylinder, followed by the slow addition of 0.2 L distilled water. After approximately 5 h, the soil particles were gently stirred into suspension and allowed to settle for another 2 h. Next, a 0.010 L sample of the soil suspension was collected from a 10 cm depth and measured for turbidity in Nephelometric Turbidity Units (NTU).  2.4 Statistical analysis Statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS 22.0 software. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was applied, and the least significant difference (LSD) test was used at a significance level of P < 0.05. All figures were generated using Origin 2024 software.   3 Results 3.1 Turbidity of soil suspensions Turbidity of soil suspensions was not linearly correlated with SARr under the same EC (Fig. 1  ). For saline water with an EC ranging from 3.0 to 5.0 dS m−1 , turbidity exhibited an initial rise followed by a subsequent decline as the SARr value increased. Notably, the SARr value associated with the peak turbidity level fell within a comparable range.  3.2 Ece  and salt accumulation capacity There existed a positive correlation between salt accumulation capacity (Sac) and EC of saline water (Fig. 2  ). When considering the same SARr value, higher saline water EC levels were associated with greater ECe  and Sac values. Additionally, there was an inverse correlation observed between Sac and SARr. For saline water with equivalent EC levels, higher SARr values were linked to reduced Sac.  3.3 Crack formation Crack area and width showed a consistent trend with variations in EC and SARr (Fig. 3  ). EC and SARr jointly affected crack formation. For the EC = 3.0 dS m−1  treatments, at SARr around 4.0 (mmolc  L-1 )0.5 , cracks were abundantly generated, surpassing other treatments. Conversely, at EC = 7.0 dS m−1  treatments and SARr around 20.0 (mmolc  L-1 )0.5 , the soils did not show notable crack formation, exhibiting the least cracks among all treatments.  3.4 Correlation between EC, cation concentration and other characteristics EC and Na+  concentrations were the key factors impacting crack formation with similar effects (Fig. 4  ). EC and Na+  concentrations were significantly and negatively correlated with crack width, area and saturated hydraulic conductivity. Their effects were higher than those of Ca2+  and Mg2+ . Ca2+  widened the cracks, while Mg2+  had minimal impact on crack formation but affected soil salt accumulation capacity. Increasing the Mg2+ /Na+  ratio reduced soil suspension turbidity and enhanced cracks generation, and thus reduced saturated hydraulic conductivity.  3.5 Sarr thresholds for cracks affecting K sat For EC = 3.0 dS m−1  and SARr < 4.0 (mmolc  L-1 )0.5  treatments, it was observed that higher Mg2+ /Na+  ratios led to lower K sat values (Fig. 5  ). When SARr exceeded 4.0 (mmolc  L-1 )0.5 , Mg2+ /Na+  ratio positively influenced K sat. For EC = 4.0 dS m−1 , the impact of Mg2+ /Na+  on K sat was found to be more significant (P < 0.05) for SARr > 9.0 (mmolc  L-1 )0.5  compared to SARr < 9.0 (mmolc  L-1 )0.5 . Similarly, for EC = 5.0 dS m−1 , it was observed that under SARr < 11.0 (mmolc  L-1 )0.5 , higher Mg2+ /Na+  ratios were associated with lower K sat values. However, when SARr exceeded 11.0 (mmolc  L-1 )0.5 , increasing Mg2+ /Na+  did not significantly (P > 0.05) decrease K sat. For EC = 6.0 dS m−1 , it was found that as SARr exceeded 16.0 (mmolc  L-1 )0.5 , increasing the Mg2+ /Na+  ratio led to higher K sat values. Under EC = 7.0 dS m−1 , for SARr < 21.5 (mmolc  L-1 )0.5 , higher Mg2+ /Na+  ratios were associated with lower K sat values. Conversely, when SARr exceeded 21.5 (mmolc  L-1 )0.5 , higher Mg2+ /Na+  ratios resulted in increased K sat values.   4 Discussion 4.1 Interaction between water, salt and cracks In general, higher SARr values indicate lower K sat when irrigating with saline water of the same EC. Because high SARr maximized soil dispersion, clogging pores with small particles and reducing effective porosity, inhibiting water infiltration (Liu et al., 2022 ). However, for EC between 3.0–5.0 dS m−1 , SARr between about 10.0–15.0 (mmolc  L-1 )0.5  resulted in an abrupt increase in turbidity followed by a gradual decrease with increasing SARr (Fig. 1 ). This might be due to that the breakdown of bonds between soil particles caused by Na+  (Bardhan et al., 2016 ). Moderate SARr narrowed hydraulic conductivity pores, reducing saturated hydraulic conductivity (Yz et al., 2019 ). More severe inputs caused the bond breakdown, leading to irreversible dispersal of clay particles and long-term destruction of soil aggregates (Kramer and Mau, 2023 ). When SARr reached the threshold, aggregate stability decreased, soil pore system tends to become simplified (Yan et al., 2024a ). Increasing SARr transformed the soil solution into a clay suspension flow, with leached clay increasing soil pore volume and reducing dispersion (Keren and Singer, 1988 ). Soil particles essentially changed soil density and particle dispersion washing away excess salt (Xie and Sun, 2023 ). For EC between 5.0–7.0 dS m−1 , the higher solute concentration compared to EC levels of 3.0–5.0 dS m−1  was found sufficient in preventing the observed changes in K sat through this mechanism. Because increased soluble salt concentrations lead to soil flocculation, thus counteracting the effects of soil sodicity (Shainberg, 1984 ). Soils treated with an EC of 5.0–7.0 dS m−1  saline water exhibited a negative correlation between salt accumulation capacity and SARr (Fig. 2 ). Increased Na+  concentration destabilized and simplified the soil pore structure (Taghizadehghasab et al., 2021 ), reducing the interaction between soil solutes and particles and mitigating salt accumulation. Taghizadehghasab et al. (2021)  also found the same results, it was attributed to the soil structural damage caused by clay dispersion and aggregate destabilization. Under field conditions, although salt accumulation in soil was reduced, there was an elevated concentration of dissolved salts in groundwater. This led to challenges such as rising water-table depth and heightened salinity (Wang et al., 2023 ). In arid and semi-arid regions with limited irrigation and high evaporation, these factors could intensify secondary soil salinization (Zhang et al., 2024 ). The accompanying issues of degraded water quality and soil salinization posed challenges to sustaining and restoring vulnerable terrestrial ecosystems (Khosravi et al., 2018 ). And in the case of low EC, a lower SARr led to increased crack formation, which was in contrast to the relationship between SARr and turbidity (Figs. 1 and 3 ). Denser soils with high SARr had higher water content, both water infiltration and evaporation were slower compared to lost pore space (Dexter and Kroesbergen, 1985 ). This likely counteracted the destructive forces of soil dryness and wetness, reducing the formation of microcracks (Taghizadehghasab et al., 2021 ). In addition, soils with low SARr consistently generated a higher volume of aggregates than soils with high SARr (Rengasamy and Marchuk, 2011 ). As a result, they were more susceptible to fracturing at lower tensile stresses (Hewage et al., 2023 ). Low EC favored the generation of surface cracks over high EC (Fig. 3 ). High electrolyte concentrations effectively counteracted SARr's negative effects, and higher EC values increased soil stability for soils with the same SARr (Qadir et al., 2021 ). However, it is important to note that high EC in irrigation water could still pose significant hazards, resulting in an elevated osmotic potential (Karimzadeh et al., 2024 ). The presence of excessive salts in the soil solution created competition with plants for water, and certain salts could be toxic, leading to damage to plant roots and leaves (Porter and Marek, 1992 ). The effects of EC and SARr on soil water-salt-cracks behavior (Figs. 1-3 ), varied due to differences in cationic composition among various treatments (Table 2 ). The presence of Ca2+  and Mg2+  could moderately inhibit the negative impacts of Na+ . Ca2+  and Mg2+  have separate impacts, with Ca2+  affected crack width and Mg2+  influenced salt accumulation capacity (Fig. 4 ). Soluble Ca2+  added could promote soil aggregation and Na+  leaching, followed by reduced EC and SARr. When both EC and SARr decreased, it might not accurately reflect changes in turbidity and salt accumulation capacity, but it could indicate the formation of cracks directly (Figs. 1-4 ). Among all treatments, those with low EC and SARr had the highest potential for crack formation (Fig. 4 ). However, Ca2+  was only significantly (P < 0.05) correlated with crack width and not with crack area (Fig. 4 ). It was likely due to that soil cracking occurred in two stages: initial extension along one or multiple directions, followed by subsequent crack widening (Zeng et al., 2020 ). Soils with low EC and low SARr exhibited greater susceptibility to cracking and accelerated crack initiation and propagation compared to other treatments, entering the second stage of increased crack width earlier (Bordoloi et al., 2020 ). In this study, only surface cracks at the end of the experiment were analyzed, as most treatments had already entered the second stage, with notable variations primarily observed in crack width. Notably, Mg2+  did not show a correlation with crack width or crack area (Fig. 4 ). Instead, crack formation was influenced by the Mg2+ /Na+  ratio. It is worth noting that Mg2+  played two roles: a direct effect on soil aggregate stability and an indirect effect through its interaction with Na+  (Zhang and Norton, 2002 ). However, the direct impact of Mg2+  was not well-defined and depended on the clay type and soil's ability to release electrolytes (Alperovitch et al., 1981 ). Moreover, Mg2+  could disrupt soil structure by exacerbating the negative effects of Na+ . Compounding the clay dispersion caused by Na+ , Mg2+  could cause soil disaggregation (Oster et al., 2016, Qadir et al., 2018 ). On the one hand, the breakup of soil aggregates exposed more dispersed surfaces to contact with water flow, which promoted dispersion even more; on the other hand, the dispersion of clays was accelerated by the lack of cementation agent (Alperovitch et al., 1981 ). This exacerbating process contributed to increased crack formation. In the Hetao irrigation area, as irrigation time increased, the Mg2+  concentration in the drainage water decreased by about 1/3 compared to the irrigation water, while the Na+  levels remained consistent (Liu et al., 2011 ). This suggested that more Mg2+  was retained in the soil, resulting in a gradual increase in Mg2+ /Na+  values in soil solutions. The potential soil structure destruction caused by high Mg2+ /Na+  values is a significant concern.  4.2 Revised saline water assessment method Increased crack width and area significantly enhanced K sat (Fig. 4 ). Despite the reduced hydraulic conductivity of the soil matrix as affected by soil salinity and alkalinity, cracks provided more rapid water flow pathways that would accelerate water flow (Tang et al., 2021 ). Mg2+ /Na+  ratio appeared to be an effective indicator to characterize this effect (Fig. 4 ). Mg2+ /Na+  effect on K sat at EC 3.0–7.0 dS m−1  was SARr-dependent, with a threshold (Fig. 5 ). Below the threshold, Mg2+ /Na+  negatively correlated with K sat, while above it, Mg2+ /Na+  positively correlated with K sat (Fig. 5 ). Below the threshold, hydraulic conductivity decreased due to cation-induced soil pore occlusion. However, as relative fraction of Na+  in the exchange complex increased, the bonds between soil particles began to break down. This weakened cementation allowed Mg2+ -induced soil disaggregation and cracking, ultimately facilitating water infiltration. Thus, the influence of saline water on soil infiltration properties, evaluated by EC and SARr, might not increase linearly with increasing SARr. Rather, a threshold linked to EC exists (Fig. 6  ). Data on both sides of each SARr threshold in Fig. 5  were selected for linear regression analysis to determine the SARr thresholds within the EC range of 3.0–7.0 dS m−1 . Treatments with EC = 6.0 dS m−1  were excluded due to having only one data point to the left of the threshold. Under field conditions, except cations in soil solution, factors affecting crack formation include transpiration-induced soil suction, root reinforcement, plant root exudates altering soil aggregation, tree spacing and plantation practices, and plant traits (Bordoloi et al., 2020 ). Soil particle size composition and mineral types can also impact the thresholds (Li et al., 2023, Yudina and Kuzyakov, 2023 ). For example, in clay soils, higher salt concentration can cause soil clay dispersion, hindering soil water infiltration; in contrast, in loam or loamy sand type soils, increased salinity can enhance soil water infiltration rate by raising the soil water suction potential (Henry et al., 2018 ). Therefore, the threshold range and the dominant factor identified in this study (Mg2+ /Na+ ) may not be universally applicable to soils in other regions. Additionally, the EC of the saline water in this study ranged from 3.0 to 7.0 dS m−1 . Further investigation is required to assess the applicability of the findings to saline water with EC values outside of this range. However, the SARr thresholds in this study could be fine-tuned to achieve more accurate classification thresholds for complex conditions.   5 Conclusion EC, SARr, Crack and K sat interactions were evaluated by observing soil water-salt transport and surface cracking under saline water irrigation with varying EC and SARr. The results are summarized below: In general, EC, SARr, soil cracks and K sat had a complex interaction. Under certain SARr thresholds, high SARr levels resulted in increased dispersion of soil clay particles, leading to reduced rates of soil water infiltration, which was unfavorable for soil salt leaching. High EC could mitigate SARr's negative effect. Various EC levels in saline water irrigation had a different SARr threshold. Beyond this threshold, soil was more vulnerable to external disturbances and was at risk of cracking. Cracks might facilitate preferential flow in the soil and hinder the decrease in infiltration rates caused by clay particle dispersion. The Mg2+ /Na+  ratio could effectively characterize this destructiveness, and it should be included in the saline water assessment methodology. In summary, according to the revised standard for assessing the quality of saline water, it could be categorized into two types: one primarily influenced by EC and SAR, and the other additionally influenced by the Mg2+ /Na+  ratio. It is important to note that these findings may not apply to soils in other regions due to factors like particle size, mineral type and plant characteristics. More studies are needed to refine SARr thresholds for accurate classification under different conditions.

1 Introduction Rainfall nowcast which predicts the rainfall for a short range of time ahead (normally 0 ∼ 2 h, and even 0 ∼ 6 h) is playing a key role in the prevention of damages due to natural hazards including storms and floods to societies (Ayzel et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020 ). Timely and valuable alerts of weather hazards to societies can be issued by the meteorological authorities based on nowcasts to avoid casualties and losses of properties even lives in affected regions, especially urban areas, during emergency events (Liu et al., 2016; Miao et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Casellas et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022 ). Notably, the spatiotemporal resolution requirement for nowcasts is much higher than those of the normal daily to weekly rainfall forecasts. Nowcasting challenges aiming for rational predictions of rainfall with high spatiotemporal resolutions are intrinsically difficult due to the limit of forecasting lead time, namely the lead time between prediction and occurrence of an event, and the rapidly changing atmospheric conditions of the convective weather systems. Severe convective weather including thunderstorms, tornadoes, and hail, which can occur and vanish very suddenly, normally results in intense precipitation (Shi et al., 2018; Sideris et al., 2020; Tu et al., 2022; Turner et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023a ). Traditional Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models consider the whole atmospheric condition on a synoptic scale (over 1000 km) and produce forecasts over large areas with a spatial resolution, for example less than 4 km of a pixel. It also requires a spin up period where initial and boundary conditions of the atmosphere are fed into the model to initiate the simulation by solving computationally expensive differential equations (Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2023 ). For a city-scale precipitation forecast, it normally requires the spin up period to be 6 to 12 h (He et al., 2013 ). Since it is time-consuming to run NWP models, they are not suitable for rainfall nowcast for a lead time of a few hours (Bi et al., 2023 ). Moreover, those weather models normally cannot provide reliable rainfall predictions for a specific location with a resolution of 5–10 km2  in the next 1–3 h in the case of emergency (Sun et al., 2014; Trebing et al., 2021; De Luca and Capparelli, 2022; Feng and Chen, 2023 ). Existing methods to provide precipitation predictions for a specific location, optical flow method for example, are based mostly on the extrapolation of radar echo maps of reflectivity (Pulkkinen et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020 ). Then, those existing nowcasting methods cannot predict the formation or decay of the weather system or the regional change in strength within the system (Bonnet et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2023 ). With the development of deep learning methods and advances in the design of neural networks, attempts have been made to perform rainfall nowcast with different algorithms through using radar images of clouds (Hernández et al., 2016; Lebedev et al., 2019; Ravuri et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2022 ). Radar echo maps of past observations and future predictions can be viewed as a spatiotemporal sequence with changes in both time and space scales from the deep learning perspective (Agrawal et al., 2019; Chapman et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023 ). Applied deep learning algorithms are required to capture the spatiotemporal features of the change in radar echo intensity from the observations to make predictions of future radar echo intensity for rainfall nowcast. However, nowcasting results from the deep learning algorithms tend to lose prediction accuracy significantly with a longer lead time (Pan et al., 2019; Yen et al., 2019; Song et al., 2020; Czibula et al., 2021; Fang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022; Pirone et al., 2023 ). Moreover, the features of different deep learning algorithms are considerably different, and then suitability of those algorithms should be clarified. To enrich our understanding of AI-based methods for improving rainfall nowcast capability, this paper adopts three state-of-the-art deep learning algorithms for nowcasting rainstorm clouds, and then the nowcasting results obtained through using several rainfall cases are evaluated by several performance metrics for prediction accuracy.  2 Backgrounds Previous research attempted to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the extrapolation of radar echo maps for rainfall nowcast through using deep learning algorithms and treating radar echo maps as a sequence of varying images (Sato et al., 2018 ). Current recorded images from the weather radars are used as observations to predict future frames in real time in the form of video frame prediction (see Fig. 1  ). Several neural networks previously used for video frame prediction are applied in nowcasting rainfalls, producing higher accuracy than the existing conventional methods which include the optical flow method, the cross-correlation method and the particle filter method (Xu et al., 2018; Ayzel et al., 2020; Han et al., 2021; Senocak et al., 2023 ). Early research of neural networks applied the simple feed-forward algorithm to rainfall prediction through using infrared temperature obtained from satellite imagery (Rivolta et al., 2006 ). Recently, there are mainly two types of deep learning structures used for nowcasting rainfalls, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) (Fig. 2  a-b). They have different basic units, convolutional units and recurrent units, respectively. Convolutional units extract feature maps from the input observations by convolutional calculation while down-sampling. It can be viewed as zooming in on a small area with representative features in the whole observation. On the other hand, recurrent units feed the down-sampled feature map back to the input. It can be then viewed as connecting the observations from the last time step and the next time step and finding their common features. Thus, CNNs are more accurate in analyzing spatial data while RNNs are better in dealing with temporal sequences (LeCun et al., 2015 ). Therefore, some novel explorations combine both structures for the spatiotemporal learning of radar map sequences (Kumar et al., 2020 ). Optical flow calculation originates from Horn and Schunck (1981) where the pattern of the brightness of an image is defined as a field. The motion of pixels, known as the optical flow, in the image at the next time step follows the change in the pattern of brightness or the optical flow field. The field is then derived through solving the optical flow constraint and minimizing the cost function J  (see the equation below):(1) J = ∬ [ ∂ I  ∂ t   + u ∂ I  ∂ x   + v ∂ I  ∂ y   ]  2  d x d y     where I  is the brightness of the pixel. With the optical flow field of the radar echo map of the current time step, the radar echo map of the next time step can be extrapolated for every pixel moving along the field. The whole cloud cluster shown in the radar echo map is then extrapolated without considering any change in shape or intensity or any formation of a new cloud cluster that is not presented currently (Bowler et al., 2004 ). Shi et al. (2015)  proposed the Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory network (ConvLSTM) for the weather nowcasting task, which combines the CNN and the RNN in the learning framework of a multi-layer neural network through replacing the previously fully connected inner structure of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) with convolutional counterpart (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997; Li et al., 2023 ). Multiple ConvLSTM layers are stacked in both the encoding network and the forecasting network to store and unfold the spatiotemporal features captured (Sønderby et al., 2020 ). Raw radar echo maps of rain events (Fig. 1 ) are fed into the model for preprocessing, predicting, and postprocessing automatically without manually altering the echo intensity. The output radar echo map can be used directly for rainfall nowcast analysis by weather forecasters. ConvLSTM is more suitable for spatiotemporal data than the original LSTM because of the convolutional structure added for image analysis. The model shows better nowcasting accuracy than the previous optical flow-based algorithm used by the Hong Kong Observatory (HKO) (Woo and Wong, 2017 ). Further, the recurrent networks through adopting Convolutional Gated Recurrent Unit (ConvGRU) evidenced a slight advancement in nowcasting accuracy. Both Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) and LSTM are RNNs with recurrent learning structures. Compared with LSTM, GRU uses fewer gates and then fewer parameters in the inner structure (Chung et al., 2014 ). Therefore, GRU requires less computational capacity and training time than LSTM but achieves similar prediction accuracy which could make a timelier rainfall nowcast with the same data input (Oliu et al., 2017 ). This convolutional variant of the GRU model is tested with a real-time dataset of radar echo maps of rain events in Guangdong, China in 2019, and it is evidenced that the GRU model results in a more accurate nowcast than previous extrapolation techniques (Chen et al., 2021 ). Furthermore, Shi et al. (2017)  improved the previous ConvLSTM and ConvGRU through forming a new network structure named Trajectory GRU (TrajGRU) which is also a model combining the CNN and the RNN to better capture the spatiotemporal features. The new network includes a sub-network to dynamically determine the recurrent relationships in the GRU (Shi et al., 2017 ). Firstly, the GRU structure is adopted over the LSTM due to the faster computation speed shown by previous works (Cho et al., 2014 ). The training time is greatly reduced due to fewer parameters used in the network. Moreover, the convolutional structure is modified to better suit the spatiotemporal data. The connection and weights for input are the same for all locations and lack the ability to learn the feature change in space. With the new trajectory RNN, the recurrent connection is dynamically determined with a local neighborhood set at each location and each time step generated from the input and the state of the network. It shows that the TrajGRU is superior to the ConvGRU and the ConvLSTM through using the HKO-7 dataset collected by the HKO between 2009 and 2015 (Adewoyin et al., 2020 ). Ayzel et al. (2019)  introduced an all-convolutional neural network model called DozdyaNet which represents a systematic attempt using the CNN approach instead of the RNN. All-convolutional neural networks replace the pooling layer with a convolutional layer without introducing extra loss in the image recognition task (Springenberg et al., 2014 ). The model shows the great advantage of the deep learning approaches that growth and decay of the rainfall intensity in the rainfall events can be predicted with observed radar images compared with the traditional optical flow method. Lebedev et al. (2019)  adopted the U-Net architecture that is previously used for semantic segmentation in image-to-pixel processing (Ronneberger et al., 2015 ). The model is based on a series of convolutional blocks from the CNN. The encoder operates the input image with basic convolutional computation and down-samples the data iteratively with the convolutional block. The decoder first applies basic convolutional blocks and then up-samples the encoded image to produce the final output (Agrawal et al., 2019 ). The advantage of the U-Net structure is the accurate learning of image features with the convolution block. To cover more areas for prediction, geostationary satellite images of 3 km per pixel resolution from the Meteosat-8 satellite operated by EUMETSAT are integrated with the radar echo maps from the Russian ground-based radar network by interpolations (Aminou, 2002 ). The model can perform rainfall nowcast based on rainfall rate classification to regions previously uncovered by radars with similar quality. Wang et al., (2023b)  constructed a Predictive Recurrent Neural Network (PredRNN) based on Spatiotemporal LSTM (ST-LSTM) units. It keeps the LSTM structure rather than the GRU structure due to its higher accuracy when trained with a larger dataset, sacrificing the training speed (Byeon et al., 2017 ). The spatial features and temporal variations are stored in the same memory pool in the network becoming a new spatiotemporal memory. The special spatiotemporal memory would react with the LSTM. It delivers the high-level memory state from the top layer to the bottom one and gives spatiotemporal predictive learning. Multiple ST-LSTM units are stacked as the ConvLSTM in the overall structure with memory zigzagging across layers. This novel network shows better 60-minute lead time prediction accuracy than both ConvLSTM and TrajGRU with consecutive observations from the radar echo map dataset recorded in Guangzhou, China (Wang et al., 2023b ). Although the prediction accuracy has been significantly increased, rainfall nowcasts are still with the issues of low accuracy for longer lead time and loss of information for the output nowcasts. Most importantly, deep learning algorithms work as ‘black boxes’ without clear explanations of their suitability and effectivity. To enhance our knowledge and capability in using AI-based methods for nowcasting rainfall, the goal of this paper is to analyze the use of deep learning algorithms in rainfall nowcasting by comparing existing algorithms with a new dataset. Moreover, the paper carries out experiments on the nature of deep learning algorithms to improve the interpretability and the explainability of nowcasting rainfall from the perspective of real-world application for higher accuracy and longer lead time.  3 Methods and implementation 3.1 Algorithms According to the current available state-of-art deep learning algorithms combining CNN and RNN, this paper adopted three algorithms, ConvLSTM (Shi et al., 2015 ), TrajGRU (Shi et al., 2017 ) and PredRNN (Wang et al., 2023b ), for comparison, together with the benchmark of the optical flow method. All three algorithms are in operational use by the weather authorities in Guangdong Province and Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, respectively. ConvLSTM, as the ground-breaking method in AI-based rainfall nowcast, relies on the spatiotemporal prediction ability of its stacked basic structural unit (see Fig. 3  a). The original LSTM unit is fully connected and recurrent, passing the information in a loop (see Fig. 2 ). This kind of structure builds up a connection in the time series, allowing the full information from the last time step to be passed to the next. However, the addition of convolution structure in ConvLSTM unit brings in the spatial feature extraction ability to better suit the nature of the spatiotemporal radar echo sequence. Similarly, for TrajGRU basic unit, it also brings in a convolution structure together with a trajectory variant to the recurrent GRU to enhance the spatiotemporal prediction ability (see Fig. 3 b). These actively-learned trajectories allow the recurrent structure to be more location-flexible. In other words, spatial information is better passed in the temporal structure for learning. These two algorithms are well-established and show that a combination of CNN and RNN can give high accuracy spatiotemporal prediction. Then, PredRNN, which also combines CNN and RNN, shows a new way of spatiotemporal learning in terms of memory flow (see Fig. 3 c). Such spatiotemporal memory connects the two adjacent time steps by passing the most concentrated spatial information after convolution from the upper top level to the bottom down level. It is therefore chosen in this paper to compare against the two previously well-known algorithms to test the rainfall nowcasting ability of deep learning algorithms in general.  3.2 Preprocessing As the usual procedure of application of deep learning algorithms, the raw data are preprocessed to better suit the purpose of training. The quantity and quality of data have a great impact on the accuracy of the prediction. Due to a normal limitation about the number of available rain gauges for monitoring weather, the resolution of rainfall gauge is one per 5–10 km2  which is not enough for high accuracy nowcasting (Leathers et al., 2020; Treppiedi et al., 2023 ). To overcome the limitation, observed radar echo intensity data are used instead; notably, the radar map resolution can reach 1 km2  and the radar echo intensity values can be converted into rainfall intensity values with an empirical formula (Marshall and Palmer, 1948 ). Therefore, currently, the dataset applied in rainfall nowcasting is the sequence of radar echo maps and mostly a mosaic of radar echo maps from several radars to cover a larger area. Consequently, the quality of the images might not be consistent. Moreover, missing data from a specific radar results in empty or incomplete radar echo maps. Selected high-quality sequences of radar echo maps of rain events are fed into the algorithm to learn the spatiotemporal features of a severe convective weather system, mainly resulting in heavy rainfalls. As part of the preprocessing, the dataset is divided into a training set, a validation set and a testing set to avoid underfitting or overfitting for any numerical models (Hastie et al., 2009 ). In order to explore the deep learning capability in rainfall nowcast, this paper adopts a new dataset, named as the Shenzhen dataset hereafter, which is a subset of the radar echo mosaic images of rain events collected between 2010 and 2020 by the Meteorological Bureau of Shenzhen Municipality using dual polarization radars. The areas of the Shenzhen dataset cover the whole Guangdong Province of China, including Guangzhou (see Fig. 4  ) which is the area of the previous study using PredRNN (Wang et al., 2023b ). Each radar echo map covers an area of 256 km × 256 km with a spatial resolution of 0.01°×0.01° (each pixel represents about 1 km × 1 km area), and each radar echo map sequence lasts at least 120 min with a 6-minute time interval. Therefore, each sampled sequence includes 20 (=120/6) frames long, 10-frame radar echo maps as input data to those nowcasting models and 10 as the ground truth for evaluating 1-hour (=10 × 6) model nowcasting results. Moreover, in this study, there are 2000 independent sequences in total; 1400 sequences of radar echo maps are used to train those nowcasting models, and 600 are used to test and validate those model performances.  3.3 Training Training of a neural network in a deep learning algorithm plays a key role in the task of rainfall nowcast. Before the training process, some parameters, namely hyperparameters, should be determined, and they are the number of maximum iterations, batch size, learning rate, number of layers and kernels. Hyperparameters in the study for the three algorithms are set to be the same following the prediction procedure of PredRNN. The maximum iteration is set to be 80,000 to allow enough time for the networks to learn and a 10-4  learning rate is used (Wang et al., 2023b ). Fig. 3  shows the structures of the three algorithms. For the ConvLSTM (Fig. 3 a), after several trials, the algorithm consists of 2 layers of ConvLSTM units with 64 hidden states in each layer and 3 × 3 kernels (Shi et al., 2015 ). For the TrajGRU (Fig. 3 b), there are both 3 layers of TrajGRU units in the encoder and the forecaster with convolutional computation, down-sampling (for the encoder) and up-sampling (for the forecaster) between them. The TrajGRU layers also have 3 × 3 kernels as ConvLSTM for comparison (Shi et al., 2017 ). For the PredRNN (Fig. 3 c), 4 layers of ST-LSTM unit are included in the network, with convolutional kernels of size 5 × 5. The main difference between the algorithms is the inner unit of the network (LSTM, GRU or ST-LSTM) instead of the number of layers. The unit affects how the neural network learns and predicts while the hyperparameters facilitate the algorithms to achieve the best efficiency and accuracy.  3.4 Postprocessing Some postprocessing steps for analyzing the data should be done before the final evaluation to better compare the performance among the different algorithms from the perspective of real-world application. Also, the grey scale raw radar echo maps are colored according to the echo intensity pixel by pixel (see Fig. 1 ) to highlight those regions with different echo intensities. For example, if a specific pixel (1 km × 1 km area) has a corresponding echo intensity value between 35 dBZ and 40 dBZ, that pixel will be colored yellow. Notably, the higher the echo intensity, the redder the region, the higher the intensity of the precipitation triggered. The lower the echo intensity, the bluer the region, the lower the intensity of the precipitation triggered.  3.5 Performance metrics To evaluate the predictions from the deep learning algorithms, this study adopts confusion matrices that consist of true positive (TP, hit), false positive (FP, false alarm) and false negative (FN, miss) through using the actual echo intensity from the radar echo maps. Each output pixel is evaluated through using the binary classification represented by the confusion matrix. Notably, the confusion matrix itself does not contain values from the predictions but shows two groups of classification. True and false just indicate if the prediction matches the observation of that pixel while positive and negative just show if the prediction indicates the presence of a certain condition (radar echoes). In our study, a true positive is obtained when the prediction of echo matches the actual radar echo map. A false positive is obtained when there is a prediction that does not appear on the record. Finally, a false negative means there is an echo shown in the map that has not been predicted and a true negative means both the observation and the prediction show no presence of radar echoes. The confusion matrix can be extended with a threshold value, k , on radar echo intensity level instead of the presence (see Table 1  ). True positive can be defined as the case where the predicted echo intensity for the specific pixel and the actual echo intensity both pass the threshold value, k . False positive means the predicted intensity is stronger than the threshold while the actual intensity is weaker. False negative means the predicted intensity is less than the threshold value while the actual record shows stronger. For each radar echo map, every pixel is evaluated and classified into one of the four categories of the confusion matrix: TP, TN, FP and FN. Each category is then counted and a proportion can be calculated.(2) CSI =  TP  TP + F P + F N       (3) FAR =  FP  TP + F P       (4) POD =  TP  TP + F N        With the confusion matrix, several performance metrics can be derived, such as Critical Success Index (CSI) (equation (2) ), False Alarm Ratio (FAR) (equation (3) ), and Probability of Detection (POD) (equation (4) ), and each is in the range between 0 and 1. CSI and POD show the proportion of TPs (correct predictions) so the higher both metrics, the better the performance of the algorithm. On the contrary, FAR shows the proportion of FPs (false alarms) so a lower FAR gives a better performance of the algorithm (Jolliffe and Stephenson, 2012 ). Mean Square Error (MSE) (equation (5) ) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) (equation (6) ) are also used. Equations (5) and (6)  are given below:(5) MSE =  1 N  ∑ n = 1  N  ( x n  - x n  ^  )  2      (6) MAE =  1 N  ∑ n = 1  N  x n  - x n  ^         where x n     is the predicted radar echo intensity at the nth  frame, x n  ^     is the observed echo intensity at the nth  frame, and N  is the total number of frames. Therefore, MSE  and MAE  show the difference between predictions and observations. The lower both metrics, the better the performance.   4 Results 4.1 Performance of algorithms The performance of the three chosen deep learning algorithms is compared against the prediction using the traditional extrapolation method based on the optical flow calculation by the ROVER (Real-time Optical flow by Variational methods for Echoes of Radar ) algorithm (Woo and Wong, 2017 ). Performance metrics adopted for comparison are CSI , POD , MSE  and MAE  (see section 3.5 ). With consideration of rainfall occurrences and related intensities in association with different radar echo intensities (see Table 2  ), the threshold values of k  for radar echo maps are chosen to be 20 dBZ, 30 dBZ and 40 dBZ. Therefore, the performance metrics of each k  threshold value are represented by Metric-k (hereafter in the paper), e.g., CSI-20 represents CSI of 20 dBZ threshold. The Shenzhen dataset records the rain events of different intensity levels between 2010 and 2020 that occurred in Guangdong province in South China. It is mainly dominated by a sub-tropical climate, and constantly affected by tropical cyclones where rainfall varies greatly in intensity from one event to another due to the moisture from the sea. Table 2  shows the distribution of different radar echo intensities in the dataset. 40 dBZ radar echo intensity, which corresponds to around 20 mm/h rainfall intensity, is considered to trigger severe rainfalls. Notably, from the table, we can observe that the frequencies of different radar echo intensities are highly imbalanced since there are less strong rainfall events in the Shenzhen dataset. The whole test dataset with 600 sequences of radar echo maps is used to make 1-hour lead time nowcasting using all four methods, the traditional optical flow-based method, namely ROVER, and three deep-learning algorithms, producing 10 future frames of radar echo maps. Therefore, a total of 6,000 (=600 × 10) frames are generated by each method and every frame is evaluated pixel by pixel (totally, there are 65,536 (=256 × 256) pixels per frame) using the performance metrics listed above. All the obtained values from every pixel of every predicted frame are averaged for each performance metric to indicate the overall capability of the four methods. Notably, totally, there are 393,216,000 (=6,000 × 65,536) values. Table 3   lists the average performances of the four methods. From the table, we can observe that for the lowest 20 dBZ threshold, ConvLSTM and TrajGRU have a marginal advantage over the ROVER algorithm, and PredRNN improves the performance by 29 % from 0.466 to 0.601 in terms of CSI-20. It is also true for CSI-30 where PredRNN improves the performance by 49 % from 0.246 to 0.366. Notably, PredRNN boosts the CSI-40 metric by 51 % from 0.095 to 0.143 since the accuracy on the high echo intensity threshold is relatively low for the previous methods which will be discussed in the next section using three representative examples of different intensities from the test dataset. Overall, in terms of all performance metrics, the deep learning algorithms (namely ConvLSTM, TrajGRU and PredRNN) perform better than the traditional extrapolation method (namely ROVER) does. Moreover, it is clear that PredRNN has the best performance among the four methods through using the Shenzhen dataset.  4.2 Prediction examples Apart from the average performance metrics, nowcast capability can be discussed and explained with representative rainfall events from the test dataset. Three specific rainfall cases with different radar echo intensities (strong, medium and weak) are selected from the Shenzhen dataset to reveal the nowcast capability of the algorithms with a 60-minute lead time. These three cases are selected because each represents one level of radar echo intensity based on both the highest echo intensity and the average echo intensity recorded in the case which evaluates the robustness of the algorithms for nowcasting. The strong intensity case represents a severe weather event with a maximum echo intensity over 40 dBZ and spreads over 50 % of the radar echo map, averaging echo intensity over 25 dBZ. The medium intensity case also represents a medium weather event with a maximum echo intensity over 40 dBZ but spreads less than 50 % of the radar echo map, averaging echo intensity over 20 dBZ with a smaller affected region. The weak intensity case represents a weak weather event with a maximum echo intensity below 40 dBZ and an average echo intensity around 20 dBZ. The first case (Fig. 5  a) selected from the Shenzhen dataset is of strong echo intensity recorded at 17:15 on May 16th, 2011, Zhongshan, Guangdong. This strong rainstorm resulted in a 6-hour accumulated rainfall of 85.8 mm. During the event, the radar echo with high intensity (over 30 dBZ) almost covers the whole observed area. The region with the highest radar echo intensity (over 50 dBZ) is at the bottom quarter of the image, especially the bottom left corner for the lead time of 12 min (indicated by the red boxes in Fig. 5 a), resulting in the strongest precipitation with dense clouds. Notably, the overall echo intensity distribution can be well predicted by all three deep learning algorithms. However, the nowcast results from ConvLSTM and TrajGRU lost much of the information on the edge of the cloud clusters, mixing different regions of similar radar echo intensity. PredRNN is still able to provide the boundaries between the areas with some unwanted grey areas (0–5 dBZ) as noise. Notably, more noises for predictions of longer lead time appear while the accuracy of the model drops. The performance of PredRNN drops with both a longer lead time and a higher threshold value (see Fig. 6  ). For example, CSI-20 maintains over 0.6 before 24 min but drops below 0.5 after 54 min. POD-20 stays above 0.7 before 24 min. The longer lead time makes the prediction more difficult due to the changing conditions of the convective weather systems. Average POD drops from 0.658 for threshold 20 to 0.077 for threshold 40 while average FAR rises from 0.153 to 0.244 and 0.445 for higher thresholds. The training dataset includes fewer high radar echo intensity events than media and low radar echo intensity events; therefore, the algorithm tends to predict a decline in the overall intensity and affects the prediction accuracy for the pixels with corresponding higher radar intensity. Such a drop in predicted echo intensity greatly affects the prediction accuracy after 54 min. The second case (Fig. 5 b) is of medium radar echo intensity recorded at 15:40 on June 11th, 2016, Maoming, Guangdong. This long rainstorm with 6-hour accumulated rainfall of 38.9 mm and 24-hour accumulated rainfall of 73.5 mm only resulted in the radar echo over the top half of the map but medium to strong echo intensity (over 25 dBZ) for the area affected. The region with the highest echo intensity (over 40 dBZ) is in the top right corner which is also successfully predicted by the three algorithms (indicated by the red boxes in Fig. 5 b). It is worth noting that the dissipation of the strong echo region at the top is also successfully predicted by PredRNN. The general trend in terms of performance metrics is the same for the medium and strong cases (Fig. 5 a and 5b). Accuracy of the PredRNN model (Fig. 6 ) drops for both longer lead time and higher threshold value with the results better than that of the strong case due to the lower radar echo intensity overall (0.825 average POD-20 compared to 0.658 for the strong case). Medium radar echo intensity is easier for the model to predict with a longer lead time with the most training data in the Shenzhen dataset (both CSI-30 and POD-30 remain at a high level around 0.4 for both CSI-30 and POD-30 after 60 min). This extensive training enables the algorithm to predict precipitation for a longer lead time for timely alerts. The third case (Fig. 5 c) is of low radar echo intensity recorded at 15:40, May 26th, 2015, Heyuan, Guangdong. The rain event only showed the radar echo in the middle of the map with lower echo intensity (mainly around 20 dBZ, indicated by the red boxes in Fig. 5 c). The weakening of the echo intensity is predicted but not as accurate as in previous cases especially for longer lead time because the average intensity is low for this case, affected by the decline in the predicted intensities. The performance metrics (right column Fig. 6 ) are very low especially for threshold 40 dBZ in this case because there is barely any location with echo intensity over 40 dBZ. As for 20 dBZ and 30 dBZ thresholds, performance still worsens along with lead time increase, but at a faster rate which makes the predictions at 60 min very undesirable compared to the ground truth (also can be seen in Fig. 5 c). Overall, the prediction results of consistent quality through all cases show that deep learning algorithms are able to handle different rainstorm scenarios at different echo intensities from strong to weak. The algorithm can provide more skilful nowcasting for medium and strong rainfall cases than for weak ones. Performance for lower echo intensity threshold is better than the higher intensity counterpart due to the imbalance distribution of data. Algorithms cannot be trained well with limited data. Although the performance for weaker echo is not as good as the performance for stronger echo, the algorithm manages to give detailed output that would be useful to weather forecasters. These prediction examples show the value of deep learning algorithms, especially PredRNN. It keeps as much information as possible in the output compared to the other two deep learning algorithms. The boundary of the predicted echo intensity cluster is very clear thus the shape of the cloud can be better inferred. ConvLSTM and TrajGRU also give the change in the shape of clouds but the information is lost on the boundary of clusters. This shows that deep learning algorithms perform better in rainfall nowcasting not only in terms of the performance metrics but also from the real-life application point of view for weather forecasters.  4.3 Effect of different data sources for training and testing on model performance The effectiveness and robustness of deep learning algorithms in rainfall nowcast can be further explained from another multi-source experiment using the PredRNN algorithm. In the previous experiments, the deep learning algorithms are always trained and tested with the dataset of the same source. For example, in the last section, PredRNN is trained and tested using the Shenzhen dataset obtained from the Meteorological Bureau of Shenzhen Municipality. Both the training dataset and the testing dataset cover the same area of Guangdong Province. The rain events are under the exactly same climate conditions. With that source of data, PredRNN shows high accuracy for nowcasting rainfall with a lead time of 60 min. To test if it is equally effective when there is a different source of datasets, two new testing subsets are constructed, each consisting of 200 sequences of radar echo maps for rain events with the same duration of 120 min. The first subset comes from the Shenzhen dataset, and the second subset comes from the HKO-7 dataset collected by the HKO. The complete HKO-7 dataset only covers the area of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Regions of China to the south of Guangdong Province (see in Fig. 4 ). The underlying climate conditions are similar for Guangdong Province and Hong Kong. The PredRNN algorithm previously trained with the Shenzhen dataset is tested through using the two new datasets and Table 4   lists the average results of every predicted pixel. From Table 4 , it can be seen that nowcast accuracies from both testing datasets are very consistent and the experiments using the same data sources result in better performances. Although the deep learning algorithm is trained using the training set from the Shenzhen dataset, it reaches high CSI and POD for the Hong Kong testing dataset and the difference between the results from two testing datasets can be as low as 0.2 % (POD-30). Low intensity prediction accuracy in regards to CSI-20, CSI-30, and POD-20 is similar with a difference less than 5 % due to the frequent presence of low intensity regions in the training set. Performance discrepancy on higher intensity level (over 40 dBZ) is slightly larger since the algorithm cannot achieve consistent accurate prediction for high intensity regions in both datasets. With limited high intensity training data, the nowcasting accuracy and consistency are affected. This multi-source experiment shows that the training dataset and the testing dataset are not limited to a single source. The algorithm is able to capture similar spatiotemporal features from different data sources. This will be especially beneficial when the data from a specific region is limited and will help the building of a rainfall dataset through introducing data from nearby regions influenced by the same climate.  4.4 Effect of the number of iterations The number of iterations plays an important role in the prediction efficiency for the training process of deep learning algorithms in order to provide rainfall nowcasts. More iterations make the training time longer and will affect the real-time online setting if the prediction accuracy cannot be improved by the larger number of iterations. This study tests the effect of the number of iterations through comparing the performance of the PredRNN. Table 5   lists the evaluation result using different iterations in terms of radar echo intensity, and different thresholds are set on the confusion matrix (30 dBZ and 40 dBZ are selected). MAE in the table here is of the whole testing sequence due to the smaller difference. From the perspective of lead time, prediction accuracy drops significantly from 6 min to 60 min for this dataset. There are more grey regions in the radar echo map (see Fig. 7  ) representing low echo intensity noise (0–5 dBZ) that does not appear in the ground truth. In the ground truth image, the echo intensity distribution of the rainstorm cloud is more uniform. However, the cloud clusters still have a decreasing echo intensity from the center to the margins. When the lead time gets longer, the algorithm’s ability to predict high echo intensity area drops and shows an overall decrease in the predicted intensity. When the predicted intensity falls, the central area with higher intensity will be predicted with a medium level intensity while the margins with lower intensity will be predicted as low level to even zero intensity and appear as grey noise in the colored echo map. The predicted cloud echo images are then surrounded by grey areas of noises and this loss of accuracy on the margins requires a better deep learning algorithm for a longer lead time in future research. From the perspective of the number of training iterations, a larger number of iterations does not improve the performance but instead results in overfitting the training set. In terms of the performance metrics of CSI, POD and FAR, 40,000 to 50,000 times of training iterations result in the best overall prediction accuracy. Although there is less grey area (low intensity noise) in the predictions after 80,000 times of training, the accuracy is actually lower and the marginal areas have lower echo intensity than the central areas. Compared with the 80,000 times of iteration set for the PredRNN training procedure, less iteration is required due to the nature of the Guangzhou dataset and the Shenzhen dataset. For the Guangzhou dataset (adopted by Wang et al., 2023b ), it consists of 10,000 consecutive frames of radar echo maps and the sequences are obtained with a moving window. Adjacent sequences have overlapping frames and great similarity. For the Shenzhen dataset, radar echo maps of independent rain events are adopted and the similarity between sequences is smaller. A larger training iteration number would bring overfitting and lower prediction accuracy. The results show that although increasing the number of iterations could improve some performance metrics, stopping at 40,000 to 50,000 times of iterations saves training time and gives overall better nowcasting results for the PredRNN algorithm for real-world application with a dataset that consists of mostly independent events. Such a dataset would also be desirable for further training and testing.   5 Discussion Interpretability and explainability play an important role in understanding the capability of a deep learning algorithm and they represent two different aspects of the deep learning algorithm. Interpretability refers to human’s ability to interpret the structure of an algorithm and understand its inner connection. In this study, it means to interpret the functionality of the convolution structure, recurrent structure and their combination used in the algorithms. On the other hand, explainability refers to human’s ability to explain the results provided by the algorithm and find a suitable way to improve the results. In this study, it means to explain the performance difference for different lead times and intensity levels. Notably, those deep learning algorithms in this study all combine the CNN and the RNN features (see in Fig. 2 c) to improve the prediction accuracy. Since the input data, radar echo map sequence, are varying both in space and time, the algorithm should be able to capture both the spatial and the temporal features of the input. Learning the spatiotemporal features of the training data, the algorithm can predict the future frames of new sequences. To interpret the convolution structure, its calculation essentially uses a small matrix (convolution kernel, obtained from extensive training) to multiply the larger matrix (radar echo map, which is stored in the form of a matrix of echo intensity) to obtain a new matrix. Such calculation is repeated by sliding the kernel on the echo map to cover the whole image and multiple matrices are obtained. Such matrices, with the same dimension as the kernel, contain a correlation between the central element and its surroundings from the radar echo map. That is the spatial information required in nowcasting. Meanwhile, a recurrent structure passes information along the timeline by feeding the output from the previous time step back to the input of the next time step. The 6-minute interval radar echo maps contain the evolution of rainstorms. By predicting how the clouds would evolve, rainfall nowcast can be obtained with the estimate of echo-rainfall conversion. The recurrent structure is able to capture the temporal dynamics of the sequence and improve the nowcasting. It is therefore reasonable and necessary to apply both convolutional functions and recurrent functions and such a combination proves effective for all three algorithms, namely ConvLSTM, TrajGRU, and PredRNN. On top of that, PredRNN adopts the unique zigzagging spatiotemporal memory to deliver the information of different layers (see in Fig. 3 c). Unlike the memory flow in ConvLSTM and TrajGRU which only travels directly within the same recurrent layer i.e., no spatial information, the novel memory method zigzags between the top layer and the bottom layer, delivering extra spatial correlation for prediction. This special feature facilitates the network to reduce the dependency on the quality of the input sequence and improves learning performance. Meanwhile, the deep learning algorithms that achieve more accurate predictions with Hong Kong and Guangzhou experiments (Shi et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2023b ) also show high accuracy when trained and tested through using the Shenzhen dataset of 10-year time span with similar climate and rainfall records. Patterns in the echo intensity from radar echo maps and the change of the intensity are similar amongst those cities during the 10-year time span therefore the algorithms can capture the spatiotemporal features in a different dataset with higher accuracy. It is also true when there are multiple data sources for training and testing. The datasets are different both in space (cities) and time (time periods) yet consistent results are obtained. It can also be seen that more training iterations do not result in higher accuracy after an optimal point is reached for the independent rain events with the radar echo mosaic images. This promotes the building of high-quality rainfall event dataset for deep learning algorithms as more data from the area are available when there is no restriction in time and space, with a possibility of data fusion between different cities of different time periods. A well-developed algorithm should be able to provide nowcasts in any city in the area while trained with data from any cities in the same area in recent years. Deep learning algorithms can be applied to places with limited access to weather data with a pre-trained deep learning algorithm, and, therefore, deep learning algorithms can be used extensively and effectively in rainfall nowcast. The main source of errors comes from the nature of the radar echo map data. The subset is relatively small compared to the previous ones. The network would not be able to learn enough features from the training set to make accurate nowcasts. It becomes obvious for performance metrics with a threshold of 40 dBZ of echo intensity. It is very rare for echo intensity to be larger than 40 dBZ so the network does not get enough training samples to predict high radar echo intensity events. Also, the radar echo maps are mosaic images from different radars which affect the consistency in the quality of samples. There are potentially missing areas and general background noises, and the training of networks would be more difficult. Meanwhile, due to the limitation of the Shenzhen dataset, some valuable aspects of the deep learning algorithms cannot be stressed in this paper. The Shenzhen dataset is a 10-year radar echo mosaic image dataset of rain events. It is highly selective and imbalanced in time scale that does not take into consideration of the varying seasons or climates within that period. The focus of our study is the rainfall nowcast ability on independent weather events. The algorithm’s robustness against climate change in one location or its suitability for multiple locations with different climates cannot be explored in this paper. A comparison of the ConvLSTM model, the TrajGRU model and the PredRNN model revealed that with a similar combination of CNNs and RNNs, prediction accuracy can vary but they all outperform the traditional optical flow method.
