Convolution manipulation is able to extract the spatial links in a nearby area of close radar intensity while recurrent gates make temporal change in intensity clearer. There is still room for improvement for the current top performers because they all fail in maintaining the high intensity prediction in a longer lead time. The algorithm is trained with data where lower intensity regions are more common. It is then hard for it to identify the high intensity region. For future work, in terms of improvement, there are two possible aspects, the fundamental neural network and the entire deep learning algorithm. Improving the basic neural network means that to extend the effective lead time of the algorithm with an algorithm with stronger spatiotemporal prediction ability especially in high echo intensity areas. Algorithms such as the attention mechanism can be added to the existing algorithm to focus on the high-intensity observation for nowcasting heavy rainfalls. Such fusion can utilize algorithms with different architectural designs. Meanwhile, the sole use of neural networks in predicting radar echo intensity and then rainfall intensity still lacks a physics foundation. In the absence of atmospheric conditions used by traditional NWP models, the algorithm’s performance is limited by mathematical calculation. It treats input sequences only as numbers in a mathematical way, trying to find patterns, while the real-world atmosphere, although volatile it is, is still constrained by laws of nature. Incorporation of meteorological factors could be of great help to transform the entire nowcasting procedure for higher accuracy.  6 Conclusions From the evaluation results, PredRNN shows the best performance among all four methods using the new Shenzhen dataset. It has better accuracy in every metric compared with ConvLSTM, TrajGRU and especially ROVER for the optical flow method. Specifically, the CSI scores are significantly improved for the thresholds of 20, 30 and 40 dBZ. The ST-LSTM units successfully capture the spatiotemporal features in the radar echo maps and make predictions that are useful for real-world applications. The overall moving trend of the cluster of clouds can be modelled and predicted, and then rainfall intensity can be nowcasted. The formation of new systems and decay of the existing systems can also be projected with the deep learning algorithm. Overall, rainfall nowcast by modelling the evolution of rainstorm clouds using deep learning algorithms shows better results compared to conventional methods in terms of both performance metrics and practical applications. The Shenzhen dataset used in this paper covers 10 years of radar echo maps in the Guangdong Province, China. Compared to the performance of the Guangzhou dataset of Wang et al. (2023), the results presented in this study show that deep learning algorithms are capable of handling radar data from the same region with a similar climate. Deep learning has a promising future for rainfall nowcast when trained with historical data. It also indicates a possibility of the fusion of data from different cities in the region as the algorithms show similar accuracy when trained with a different dataset and even tested with a different dataset from the trained one. However, nowcasting output is still not good enough for practical applications as the network requires a high-quality training set and a longer lead time (e.g., more than 2 h) for forecasting and warning. Current application of the algorithms is restricted within the 1-hour lead time due to the general decrease in accuracy along with the time. Performance worsens significantly with a longer lead time for all cases with different radar echo intensities. Research for a better network structure to accurately capture spatiotemporal features with longer lead time is a further focused task and such a network should be evaluated with more attention on the real world to produce serviceable rainfall nowcasts. This study on rainfall nowcasting focuses on the video frame prediction problem using the radar echo maps from the AI-based deep learning point of view. However, there is a huge potential in improving the current methods by integrating numerical meteorological models on rainfall into the neural networks to achieve higher efficiency and accuracy. An improved nowcasting framework that combines deep learning and numerical weather models is desired for both performance and interpretability.
1 Introduction Groundwater flow models are used to forecast the spatial and temporal distribution of hydraulic heads, including water table elevations, from the local to the regional scales. By simulating flow in regional hydrological systems, groundwater models can also help in developing resilient and sustainable groundwater management strategies (Jakeman et al., 2016 ). When applying groundwater flow models to regional groundwater systems, it is of interest to include surface water - groundwater (SW-GW) interactions, as they play a critical role in the water balance of catchments (Brunner et al., 2017 ). Several approaches exist to represent SW-GW interactions in a groundwater model. However, the choice of a specific approach is often guided by the availability of data or computing resources. The impact of the approach taken on the simulation of hydraulic heads and, by extension water table elevations, is seldom identified. The most widely applied approach to account for SW-GW interactions consists in a weak coupling , or loose coupling, of groundwater and surface water flow (Maxwell et al., 2014; Barthel & Banzhaf, 2016 ). For this type of coupling, SW flow is simulated independently to generate internal head or flux boundary conditions for a groundwater flow model. Alternatively, precipitation and evapotranspiration can be computed externally with climate data to generate net precipitation, which is assumed equal to groundwater recharge and is assigned as the boundary condition for the groundwater model. It is a one-way coupling because groundwater flow is then simulated asynchronously with respect to the surface water flow simulation, without feedback of the groundwater flow solution to surface flow. To allow for SW-GW feedback, a strong coupling  approach has been proposed where a SW flow model and a GW flow model are coupled to simulate, for example, surface water flow routing and/or unsaturated flow (Maxwell et al., 2014 ). The SW and GW flow models are run sequentially and the output of one model is used as input to the other model, typically in the form of a boundary condition at the interface between the two models. The models can be run once for every simulation time or an iterative loop can be added (e.g., Flipo et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2012 ). Barthel (2014)  present extensive discussions of existing models based on a strong coupling. Finally, a fully-coupled or globally implicit  approach has been developed, where SW and GW flow are represented by a single system of nonlinear equations that are solved simultaneously (Simmons et al., 2020; Maxwell et al., 2014 ). Compared to the previous approaches, the fully-coupled approach only requires using a single computer code and does not require pairing different codes (Furman, 2008; Kampf and Burges, 2007 ). Because fully-coupled models must solve systems of nonlinear equations, they often require significant computational resources, which can make their application challenging for regional flow simulations. In comparison, models based on a weak coupling require less computational power but the impact of neglecting feedback between SW and GW, which is inherent to the weak coupling approach, has not been systematically investigated, especially at the regional scale. The study of Guay et al. (2013)  is one of the few examples that formally assessed the potential impact of neglecting feedback between SW and GW by comparing two different model setups at the hillslope scale. The authors showed that the explicit consideration of SW-GW feedback might produce larger groundwater recharge rates. Analyses of the potential effects of neglecting SW-GW feedback for regional simulations of the water table are also non-existent (Bresciani et al., 2016; Barthel & Banzhaf, 2016 ). This despite the fact that the water table elevation is of primary interest to water resources managers since it provides an indication of the amount of water stored in unconfined aquifers. The temporal variation of the water table is also commonly used to monitor and assess the state of a groundwater body. The water table furthermore plays a key role for the interactions between groundwater, surface water, vegetation, the land surface and the atmosphere, by either directly or indirectly controlling other important hydrological variables like soil saturation, evapotranspiration, or base flow, to name a few. A comparison of weak and full coupling should thus be of great interest to water resources managers interested in knowing the impact of the modelling approach for regional simulations of water table elevations. Such a comparison should ideally require that two or more groundwater flow models, each based on a different coupling approach, be compared for the same aquifer or hydrogeological system. However, the significant time and effort required to set up, calibrate and validate even a single regional scale model very often prevents the simultaneous development of multiple models (Hrachowitz & Clark, 2017; Doherty & Simmons, 2013 ). Even when models based on different coupling approaches are applied to the same system, a direct comparison is often not straightforward unless the models are built within a single computer code. If different computer codes are used, differences between simulated results may also arise from various aspects not related to the representation of SW-GW interactions such as variable grid geometries (Karan et al., 2021 ), different numerical formulations (Maxwell et al., 2014; Kollet et al., 2017; Sulis et al., 2010 ), or different governing equations, parameters or boundary conditions (Habets et al., 2010 ). It is therefore difficult to isolate and quantify the impact of a model on the representation of SW-GW interactions. The motivation for this study is to identify the impact of SW-GW feedback on regional scale flow simulations by comparing two models for the simulation of water table elevations for a regional-scale aquifer system that covers 36,900 km2  in Southern Quebec, Canada (Fig. 1  a). The two models are developed with the same computer code. The only difference between them is the representation of SW-GW interactions, with one model simulating two-way feedback between SW and GW, while the second model does not. The model that simulates two-way feedback between SW and GW has already been described in Delottier et al. (2021) , where a hybrid approach for an explicit simulation of baseflows was introduced. In contrast, the present study focuses on the comparison of the impact of the coupling scheme on the simulated water table elevation and its sensitivity to the hydraulic conductivity of the different hydrogeological units. The simulations are run for a representative one-year period that covers a full seasonal cycle. In the following, Section 2  provides a description of the regional study area and the fully coupled regional scale SW-GW flow model that served as the basis for this work. The one-way regional scale groundwater flow model variant is then described in Section 3 . The parameter-sensitivity analysis is presented in Section 4 . The outcomes of the competing models are compared in Section 5 . In Section 6 , the results are discussed. Conclusions are drawn in the last section.  2 Study area and base hydrological model setup 2.1 Study area Southern Quebec is a 36,900 km2  region located south of the St. Lawrence River, between Montreal and Quebec City, in Canada (Fig. 1 a). The region is characterized by a temperate continental climate with warm and humid summers and cold and dry winters. It is divided into a relatively flat area along the St. Lawrence River in the north and a more mountainous area in the south. The main rivers flow in a north-westerly direction and discharge into the St. Lawrence River, which forms the entire north-western border of the region. The regional hydrogeological system consists of a regional bedrock aquifer overlain by a thin sequence of Quaternary sediments that are laterally and vertically discontinuous. The bedrock is the only continuous water-bearing unit in the region and effectively controls the regional water table elevation. The permeability of the Quaternary sediments is highly variable but the more permeable sediments, such as sands, can represent local aquifers. The water table in the region is relatively shallow, with water table depths ranging from 0 to a maximum of 15 m at higher elevations in the Appalachians. Spatially variable weathering rates have resulted in significant regional variations in bedrock hydraulic conductivity (K ), which also decreases significantly with depth (Snowdon et al., 2021 ). Delottier et al. (2021)  present a more detailed hydrogeological description of the study area.  2.2 The fully-coupled model A regional surface water and groundwater flow model was developed for the region by Delottier et al. (2021)  with the HydroGeoSphere (HGS) code. HGS is an integrated, fully-coupled, spatially distributed physics-based numerical surface water and groundwater model (Aquanty Inc, 2022; Brunner & Simmons, 2012 ). In HGS, variably saturated groundwater flow is simulated, which is the most realistic and theoretically rigorous way to simulate the water table. HGS can simulate a wide range of different hydrogeological systems (see for example Gilfedder et al., 2019; Schilling et al., 2019b; Ameli & Creed, 2017; Partington et al., 2013 ), from local to regional scales (Cochand et al., 2019; Hwang et al., 2018; Schilling et al., 2017a,b ). HGS monothically solves the governing partial differential equations for surface water and groundwater, corresponding to a globally implicit  coupling, with two-way interactions between the surface and the subsurface. Surface water flow is represented by the 2D diffusion-wave equation, while subsurface flow is represented by the 3D variably-saturated Richards’ equation. The equations are coupled with a first-order exchange term that incorporates the volumetric fluid exchange rate between the surface and subsurface domains and a coupling length (Liggett et al., 2012 ). The coupling term is formulated as:(1)  d o   Γ o   =  k r    K v   l exch     ( h  -  h o  )      where do  is the surface water depth [L], Γo is the volumetric fluid exchange rate [L3  L−3  T−1 ] between the subsurface and surface domains, lexch  is the coupling length [L], K v  [L T−1 ] is the vertical saturated hydraulic conductivity of the underlying porous medium, h [L] is the hydraulic head in the subsurface and h0  [L] is the hydraulic head in the overland flow domain. The relative permeability kr  [-] is that of the underlying porous medium when water flows from subsurface to surface. When water flows from surface to subsurface, the relative permeability is instead determined by the ratio of the surface water depth to the total obstruction height at the surface. More details on the governing equations solved by HGS are provided in Aquanty Inc (2022) . The model presented by Delottier et al. (2021)  discretizes the entire Southern Quebec region with a 2D unstructured triangular mesh with lateral node spacings ranging from 500 to 1000 m (Fig. 1 b). The model extends vertically from the surface down to a depth of 200 m, which is deemed sufficient for the modelling objectives. A total number of 20 finite element layers of variable thicknesses is used to discretize the model vertically. The resulting 3D mesh has a total of 1.8 million nodes and 3.4 million elements. A critical depth boundary condition is assigned at the surface of the model along the St. Lawrence River to allow surface water to freely exit the model domain. In the subsurface, no-flow conditions are applied to the bottom and lateral boundaries. A coupling length of 1 m was used for the entire domain. The model simulates two-way dynamic feedback between SW and GW as it explicitly simulates fully coupled, variably-saturated SW and GW flow, allowing surface water infiltration and groundwater exfiltration (Fig. 2  a). In the more general case of a HGS model application, precipitation such as rain or snowfall is applied to the top of the surface domain. Evapotranspiration is then calculated internally in HGS to generate net precipitation that can either enter the subsurface or become surface runoff. HGS can further account for snow accumulation and snowmelt. However, computing evapotranspiration and accounting for snow accumulation and snowmelt can significantly increase simulation times. Considering the large size of the region and the large number of nodes in the model, Delottier et al. (2021)  chose to assign temporally variable potential infiltration rates as a specified flux boundary condition at the top layer of the subsurface instead of precipitation at the surface layer to reduce simulation times. Potential infiltration rates are pre-computed at the start of every simulation time, prior to solving the coupled SW and GW flow equations, by subtracting evapotranspiration and direct runoff from precipitation. Snowfall, snow accumulation and snowmelt are accounted for to compute the potential infiltration rate. These potential infiltration rates are computed with a Surface Water Mass Balance module (SWMB), which was described in Delottier et al. (2021)  and has been reused in this study.  2.3 Regional scale forcing Daily precipitation and minimum and maximum temperatures, at a spatial resolution of 1 km2  and ranging from September 2011 to August 2015, were downloaded from the Daymet (version 3) database, a North America gridded data product (Thornton et al., 2022 ). From the native database's spatial resolution, the data were spatially aggregated over a uniform 25 km2  rectangular forcing grid, which corresponded to the resolution for computing the potential infiltration rates with SWMB. To reduce the computational time for the transient model simulations, instead of simulating the full September 2011 to August 2015 period Delottier et al. (2021)  developed and used a representative monthly annual cycle for the potential infiltration rate as input for HGS. The cycle was generated by first running the SWMB module daily from September 2011 to August 2015. The daily transient potential infiltration rates were then aggregated to 4-year monthly averages based on the 4 years of available data. A monthly annual cycle was constructed based on the 2011–2015 period, allowing the representation of the main seasonal and hydrometeorological variations in the region, which are primarily snow accumulation and snowmelt. The representative monthly values of potential infiltration rates were then assigned at the top of the HGS model for a one-year transient simulation, from September to August. As the study area is strongly affected by winter snowfall and snowmelt, a snowpack reservoir has been added to the SWMB module, where snow accumulation and melt is calculated via the enhanced temperature-index model with radiation developed by Massmann (2019) . For each cell in the forcing grid, direct liquid precipitation, or the equivalent liquid precipitation resulting from snowmelt, is partitioned into actual evapotranspiration, direct runoff and infiltration using a lumped parameter approach that considers minimum and mean soil water capacity (DCRT  and CRT , respectively) as well as the maximum infiltration capacity of the soil (FN ) (Fig. 1 b). While larger values for CRT  and DCRT  result in more evapotranspiration, smaller values generate more runoff and/or infiltration. Following this first partitioning, the potential infiltration rate is calculated according to the concept of Horton (1941) , whereby the infiltration capacity of the soil acts as a direct control on partitioning between runoff and infiltration, with small values of FN  limiting infiltration. The values of DCRT , CRT , and FN  were taken from the reference database of Monteil (2011)  according to the types of soil and land use (Table 1  ). Readers are referred to Delottier et al. (2021)  for further information on the SWMB-based precipitation partitioning. Simulations of coupled SW and GW flow require a model spin-up to generate initial hydraulic heads and surface water depths that are coherent with the boundary conditions (Ajami et al., 2014 ). For the model spin-up, the one-year period from September to August was simulated repeatedly 9 times using the potential infiltration rates computed with SWMB. The initial hydraulic heads and surface water depths for a given one-year simulation are the simulated heads and depths at the end of the previous simulation. The heads and depths simulated at the end of the 9th repetition were then taken as initial values for the simulation. The 9 spin-up runs plus the one-year transient simulation took about a week of runtime for completion. Snapshots of the spatial distribution of assigned potential infiltration are shown in Appendix 1. For the global sensitivity analysis, a single average value for the entire year was used, therefore representing average hydrodynamic conditions. To ensure an adequate flow solution, the convergence criteria of the transient solver were set low enough to guarantee simulations within an error of about 1 % in the water balance, which was considered sufficient according to the measurement error in regional forcing data.  2.4 Model calibration The model was calibrated by Delottier et al. (2021)  using the representative average annual cycle computed from September 2011 to August 2015. The hydraulic conductivity of the regional bedrock (K ) was therein estimated via pilot point inversion (Doherty, 2003; Schilling et al., 2022 ) using the Levenberg-Marquardt form of the Iterative Ensemble Smoother (IES) (Chen & Oliver, 2013 ) as implemented in the software PEST++ (PEST++ Development Team., 2022 ). To account for the observed vertical decrease in K  with depth, an exponential relationship proposed by Janos et al. (2018)  was applied, thus partially accommodating the regional anisotropy of K  for the regional bedrock. The IES-based calibration resulted in an ensemble of 187 parameter realizations. For the present study, the ensemble mean was used as a single set of optimal hydrodynamic parameters. The assigned heterogeneous bedrock maximum hydraulic conductivity distribution (over the pilot points) had a mean value of 6.45·10-4  m.s−1  with a standard deviation of 0.80 (log space), while the homogeneous mean bedrock porosity was 0.05 (Table 2  ). Readers are referred to Delottier et al. (2021)  for a comprehensive list of all the input model parameters.   3 One-way coupling In the second model configuration (Fig. 2 b), developed specifically for this study, HGS was used as a one-way groundwater model, neglecting SW-GW feedback for the simulation of regional hydraulic heads and regional water table elevations. This configuration corresponds to a weak coupling. Both models used the same mesh, simulation parameters, material properties, solvers, and convergence criteria. Furthermore, the same monthly mean potential infiltration rates were applied to the top of both models. The only difference is that, although a surface flow domain was also specified for the one-way model, surface water flow was not simulated. Instead, a specified head boundary condition was assigned to all nodes on the surface domain, with the specified head equal to the node elevation. The location of these surface nodes coincided with the location of the top nodes of the subsurface domain and the first-order exchange term between surface and subsurface allowed for groundwater exfiltration but not surface water infiltration (Aquanty Inc, 2022 ). This is because the head boundary condition was applied to the overland flow domain and was therefore treated as “water depth”. When the prescribed head was larger than a surface node's elevation, the respective node behaved like a sink and removed all water until the actual water table was equal to the surface node's elevation. If the water table was already equal or below a surface node's elevation, that surface node neither behaved like a sink nor a source. As a result, surface nodes could only act as sinks for groundwater exfiltration but not as sources of additional infiltration from the surface, thereby eliminating exfiltrating water from the global water balance. Although HGS’s default setting allows for a two-way feedback between SW and GW, because of the absence of surface flow routing and accumulation of water depth in the overland flow domain, HGS in this configuration mimicked the behavior of a one-way groundwater model configuration where backflow of previously exfiltrated groundwater to the subsurface is not possible. This corresponds to what Barthel and Banzhaf (2016)  and Maxwell et al (2014)  referred to as weak coupling.  4 Sensitivity analysis As part of the model comparison, an analysis to qualitatively assess the consequences of neglecting SW-GW feedback with respect to the sensitivity of the simulated water table elevation to the hydraulic conductivity of the bedrock was carried out. For coupled models, a sensitivity analysis is often performed using simulated streamflow but, because the one-way groundwater model did not simulate surface water flow routing, streamflow was not considered here. The following two paragraphs describe the methodology as well as the development of a synthetic dataset for the parameter sensitivity analysis. 4.1 Methodology To minimize the effects of local interactions between the parameters, which are more likely to influence the outcome of a sensitivity analysis with non-linear models compared to simpler linear models, a sensitivity analysis based on Morris multi-start perturbation method was conducted (Morris, 1991; Pianosi et al., 2016 ). The Morris method is a computationally efficient global sensitivity analysis that is suited for regional scale applications such as the one conducted herein. The sensitivity analysis was performed using PEST++ (PEST++ Development Team., 2022 ) and focused on the potential impact of model parameters on the model objective function, defined here as the least square residuals between model simulations and observations. The bedrock hydraulic conductivity was chosen because the bedrock is a continuous regional aquifer throughout the entire region. Bedrock hydraulic conductivity is therefore a controlling parameter for the regional water table. As the regional bedrock aquifer is parameterized with pilot points, the sensitivity, expressed as the absolute change in hydraulic heads, was calculated individually for the 360 pilot points. For each pilot point, the absolute change in hydraulic heads was evaluated using four different parameter perturbations, leading to the execution of 1440 individual model runs to complete the sensitivity analysis. To reduce computational burden for the sensitivity analysis, only the average hydrodynamic conditions were considered, which means that a single average value for the entire representative annual cycle was taken. Because of the pseudo-steady state assumption involved in the parameter sensitivity analysis, storage parameters were not included.  4.2 Generation of a synthetic dataset The number of available observed water table elevations measurements from the study region is relatively small and their locations are unevenly distributed, which does not represent ideal conditions for the sensitivity analysis. Hence, instead of directly using the observations, a representative synthetic water table elevation dataset was generated for the global sensitivity analysis. The synthetic water table elevations were generated for 130 virtual observation wells that are evenly distributed over the domain (Fig. 1 a). For that purpose, the two-way integrated model was forced with yearly mean effective precipitation rather than the mean potential infiltration flux described previously. The effective precipitation was obtained by subtracting from the liquid precipitation the evapotranspiration computed with the SWMB module. The two-way integrated model was then run in transient mode with constant forcing until a pseudo-steady state was reached. This simulated pseudo-steady state water table elevation was then extracted at each of the 130 virtual observation wells. Before integrating these synthetic water elevations into the parameter sensitivity analysis, measurement noise was added to each observation using a random probability density distribution with a mean of 0.0 m and a standard deviation of 0.05 m.   5 Results The one-year representative cycles simulated with both models are compared in the following, with results illustrated in Fig. 3  . For the comparison, the water table elevation simulated by the one-way groundwater model was subtracted from the water table elevation simulated by the two-way integrated model. HGS does not directly simulate the water table elevation but it outputs the depth to the water table, which can be used to compute the water table elevation. The depth to the water table is obtained at the x-y location of each node at the top of the simulation domain by scanning the hydraulic head at the underlying nodes at the same x-y location and interpolating the depth where the pressure head is equal to zero. For each node, the differences in water table elevations were computed for each of the 12 months, and the computed differences for each node are provided in Fig. 3 a-b in a Cartesian projection. Only the differences in the regional water table elevations for the months of February and April are shown, as these are the two most representative months for low and high water table elevations, respectively (see Appendix 2 for the full 12 months). Fig. 3 c shows the water balance (exfiltration/infiltration) calculated for the two competing models over the simulated 12 months. Fig. 3 a-b shows that the differences between the models are mostly positive, revealing that simulations with a one-way groundwater model result in an overall deeper water table compared to a two-way integrated model. This result does not come as a surprise, since a one-way groundwater model neglects two-way SW-GW interactions and permanently removes exfiltrating groundwater from the system, thereby blocking any re-infiltration of exfiltrated water further downstream and reducing the overall amount of water available for infiltration. The differences observed in the regional water table elevations between the two competing models are therefore a direct result of the coupling between SW and GW. The water balance, as illustrated in Fig. 3 c, shows more exfiltration for the two-way integrated model, which is a result of the water table being closer to the surface, and this, in turn, is a result of more water being available overall. In this context, it is of particular interests to look at the spatial distribution of exchange fluxes (i.e., the spatial infiltration and exfiltration patterns) across the whole domain. As for the water table elevations, the infiltration and exfiltration fluxes are illustrated for the two critical months of February and April in Fig. 4  a and b, respectively. As can be seen in Fig. 4 , the two-way integrated model not only produces more exchange flux overall, but also more complex spatial patterns, while the one-way groundwater model generates only exfiltration fluxes. Omitting SW-GW feedback for regional water table simulations thus clearly removes an important part of catchment hydrology and a catchment's water balance, and is prone to significantly overestimate the depth to groundwater, which may, in turn, lead to critically wrong decisions in water resources planning. While an overall deeper water table in a one-way groundwater model is a somewhat expected result, the mismatches between the two models are not uniform across the entire modeled region. The two models produce similar results, that is smaller differences in the water table elevation, in the upland areas (Appalachians) in the south of the region, where the water table is deeper and therefore not directly hydraulically connected to the surface water flow domain. In the Appalachians, it thus becomes evident that adding SW-GW feedback does not significantly modify the simulated water table elevation, and that the primary interaction pathway is the one-way percolation of infiltrated water down to the water table. Much larger differences, on the order of 10 to 100 cm, are located in valleys and in the predominantly flat areas in the northern part of the region (Fig. 3 a-b). In those areas, the water table is closer to the ground surface and shallow groundwater systems are more likely to be hydraulically connected to the surface. Groundwater exfiltration and potential re-infiltration further downstream is more likely to occur. Consequently, neglecting the simulation of SW-GW feedback in these flatter areas has a greater influence on the simulated water table elevation. This is also evident in the distribution of exchange fluxes, which are more common and larger at lower elevations, matching the increased occurrence of hydraulically connected environmental features such as streams and lakes in lowland areas (Fig. 4 a-b). Of interest are also the seasonal variations of the water table and exchange flux differences. The most pronounced variations are illustrated in Fig. 3 a-b, where the low-flow dominated month of February is compared to the high-flow dominated month of April. Results show that, in February, the presence of a snowpack significantly reduces infiltration rates (see Appendix 1), such that the potential re-infiltration of groundwater that has exfiltrated in connected upstream areas becomes more relevant in simulating the regional water table. In April, snowmelt maximizes the amount of water available at the surface, and thus for potential infiltration, which greatly reduces the importance of the re-infiltration of previously exfiltrated groundwater for the simulation of the regional water table. Under low-flow conditions, exchange fluxes are significantly less developed when feedback is omitted, indicating that the one-way groundwater model is likely hydraulically disconnected from the overland flow domain (Fig. 4 a). For the two-way integrated model, re-infiltration fluxes maintain high water table elevations, facilitating exchange fluxes between surface water and groundwater during low flow conditions. During high-flow conditions, the modeled domain is mostly characterized by high potential infiltration fluxes (see Appendix 1) and the water table is higher and more strongly connected to surface water flow features, thereby facilitating groundwater exfiltration into the overland flow domain (Fig. 4 b). As a result, re-infiltration, which is neglected in the one-way model, is proportionally less important under high flow conditions and has less impact on simulated regional water table elevations. The simulation of the regional water table is therefore much less sensitive to the representation of SW-GW interactions during high-flow periods, while considering two-way SW-GW feedback is crucial for the simulation of the water table during low-flow periods. For comparison purposes, the mean sensitivities of the simulated water table elevation to the bedrock hydraulic conductivity K  with the one-way groundwater model are subtracted from the mean sensitivities computed with the two-way integrated model. Results of the sensitivity analysis for all individual pilot points and both models are thus presented in a combined fashion in Fig. 3 d. Fig. 3 d shows that most differences in sensitivities are negative, revealing that the simulations are in average more sensitive to bedrock K  in the one-way groundwater model. From the perspective of model calibration, including SW-GW feedback reduces the sensitivity of water table elevation observations to estimate K . Note that the results of the sensitivity analysis show no significant differences between lowland and upland areas (see Appendix 3). Thus, topography does not appear to affect the sensitivity of water table elevation observations to bedrock K .  6 Discussion The purpose of this study is to assess the impact of the representation of SW-GW feedback for the simulation of regional water table elevations. To this end, two competing models, a two-way integrated model that includes SW-GW feedback and a one-way groundwater model that does not account for SW-GW feedback are compared. The same numerical code is used for both models and they are applied to the same regional hydrological system. This study clearly shows that neglecting SW-GW feedback is highly likely to result in the simulation of overly deep (disconnected) water tables in shallow regional aquifer systems, where groundwater and surface water are typically hydraulically connected. This observation is in agreement with Guay et al. (2013) , who found that a two-way integrated model developed at the hillslope scale might result in more recharge, leading to potentially higher water table elevations. It is also clear that low-elevation watersheds are more likely to experience dynamic SW-GW interactions, highlighting the importance of two-way feedback for the simulation of water table elevations in such regions (Rahimi et al., 2015 ). However, in regions where groundwater is not hydraulically connected to surface water bodies, the competing models produced similar water table elevations, thus revealing that simplified approaches are more suited for regions with deeper water tables. The differences between the competing models also depend on the hydraulic regime simulated over a representative seasonal cycle, with a larger importance of considering two-way feedback when simulating low-flow periods compared to high-flow periods. This observation is reasonable, since accounting for SW-GW interactions generally enhances the simulation of low flows (Rassam et al., 2013 ). Although the interpretation of a model parameter sensitivity analysis is influenced by the chosen model parameterization (e.g., piecewise spatial uniformity; pilot points) and the choice of observations, some generally valid interpretations can nevertheless be formulated based on the results obtained in this study. As such, it became evident that the inclusion of two-way SW-GW feedback reduces the importance of hydraulic conductivity in controlling the simulation of the water table elevation, which, if turned around, indicates that in a one-way groundwater model, (bedrock) K  likely compensates for the absence of SW-GW feedback. The results of this study also demonstrate that the inclusion of SW-GW feedback may reduce the potential of water table elevation observations to constrain hydraulic conductivity during model calibration. Therefore, increasing model complexity with respect to SW-GW interactions calls for complementary data types such as stream flow data, hydrologically relevant satellite observations and/or tracer information when regional hydraulic conductivity values have to be estimated through history matching/model calibration (Schilling et al., 2019a ). Although including SW-GW feedback also allows (and is encouraged) for complementary type of observations to be considered, it also requires the definition of additional parameters. In the end, the capability of a regional model to be calibrated is always case-specific. A comprehensive investigation of the capability of history matching to constrain unknown model parameters lies beyond the scope of this article, but interested readers should refer to, for example, Zhou et al., (2014), Rajabi et al., (2018), Doherty and Moore (2020) , or Schilling et al., (2019a) . The two competing models compared here can be considered as two end-members in the representation of SW-GW feedback, from the most simplified one-way representation to the most representative, fully-coupled two-way representation. Models that use hybrid forms of coupling between the GW and SW flow systems, which lie somewhere between the two end-members, are also used for regional scale hydrological simulations (see, for instance, Ntona et al., (2022)  for a review of SW-GW model configurations). One can expect that these hybrid models would generate results that lie somewhere between the results obtained in this study. The results presented here can therefore be considered as guidance in choosing a suitable model configuration and process representation regarding SW-GW interactions on the regional scale. For systems where re-infiltration of exfiltrated groundwater is assumed to be important and where the water table is assumed to be relatively close to the surface, choosing a one-way groundwater model will likely significantly overestimate the depth to groundwater and a fully-coupled or hybrid form should be chosen. Unless there is convincing evidence of unidirectional flow between SW and GW to be dominant in a given region, a two-way feedback is generally better suited to ensure consistent characterization of SW-GW interactions (Quichimbo et al., 2020; Elrashidy et al., 2023; Uhl et al., 2022 ). The transferability of the conclusions to other hydrogeological systems will likely depend on how much the climatic, geologic and hydraulic conditions differ from those for the region considered. However, owing to the very large regional scale that is considered (36,900 km2 ), anything from local influences typically found in both small catchments and/or hillslopes to larger scale influences controlling regional groundwater flow paths and processes have been considered. Hence, meaningful conclusions can be drawn for many temperate and alpine regions. For instance, in temperate regions where shallow regional unconfined aquifer systems dominate and dynamically interact with surface water flow systems, such as some hydrogeological systems found in the Canadian Shield, the results of our model comparison are particularly representative and therefore relevant. For more arid regions or in regional multilayered confined aquifer systems, the regional aquifer system considered in our study is not representative. However, in such arid or regional multilayered confined aquifer systems, water tables are also generally deep and not directly connected to surface water bodies, such that our conclusion that regional water table simulations with weak coupling  should be as reliable as simulations with two-way coupling also generally applies.  7 Conclusions We presented a numerical experiment that identified the impact of SW-GW feedback on the simulation of regional scale water table elevations. A finding of particular interest is the fact that neglecting SW-GW feedback may lead to overly deep (disconnected) simulated water tables in shallow regional aquifer systems. The importance of accounting for SW-GW feedback for region-wide simulations of water tables potentially decreases with increasing depth to groundwater. Meanwhile, the consideration of two-way SW-GW interactions proved to be the most relevant for the simulation of low-flow periods. However, the inclusion of SW-GW feedback into the numerical model may reduce the sensitivities of the simulated water table elevations to hydraulic properties, highlighting the need for additional and complementary types of observations when hydraulic properties need to be estimated.
1 Introduction The phenomenon of fluid flow in porous media pervades both the natural world and human industrial activities, with significant implications for a multitude of sectors. These include the exploitation of oil and gas resources, flow of engineering water in dam foundations and tunnel surrounding rocks, groundwater conservation, and nuclear waste management, all of which place considerable emphasis on the study of fluid flow in porous media, prompting extensive research efforts (Yun et al. 2009, McCartney et al. 2016, Zhou et al. 2020 ). The efficient development of oil and gas resources, integral to national economy and security, hinges on understanding the flow patterns of oil and gas in subterranean reservoirs, rendering this a research area of paramount importance. The Darcy's law, proposed by French engineer Darcy in 1856, established the foundation of fluid mechanics in porous media. The subsequent development of the theory of fluid mechanics in porous media, based on the assumptions of continuous media and the Darcy equation, greatly enhanced the understanding of multiphase flow in porous media. This advancement has played a significant role in the exploration and development of oil and gas resource (Yao et al. 2023 ). The governing equations, continuity equations, and auxiliary equations are generally solved by numerical methods to obtain macro parameters, but it is difficult to describe the flow mechanism at the micro scale. The pore network model, continuous medium model, and lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) based on digital rock technology provide methodological support for exploring the flow law at the micro-nano scale, promoting the understanding of the flow law of oil and gas at the micro scale (Liu et al. 2020, Wang et al., 2023 ). The pore network model simplifies the pores of the reservoir, approximates the irregular pore space as a ball-stick model (Zhao et al., 2023 ), and carries out flow simulation based on this, it has a simple model and high computational efficiency, and the simulation results are in good agreement with the experiment. The continuous medium model solves the N-S equation of fluid in porous media to obtain the pressure field and velocity field of the fluid. This method is easy to obtain the macro characteristics of the fluid, but the calculation cost is high, especially the unconventional oil and gas generally develops micro-nano pores, the fundamental assumption of fluid flow is conflict to the continuous medium model. The LBM, predicated on microscopic scale models and the kinetic theory of Boltzmann gas molecules, exhibits mesoscopic model characteristics that bridge the gap between microscopic molecular dynamics models and macroscopic continuum models. This method offers several advantages, including a straightforward description of fluid interactions, ease of setting complex boundaries, suitability for parallel computation, and ease of program implementation (Yang et al. 2016 ). Nowadays, the research direction of global oil and gas resource development has shifted towards unconventional reservoirs. The complex pore structure and micro nano effects of unconventional reservoirs pose new challenges to LBM simulation (Zou et al. 2019 ). The solution of the Navier-Stokes (N-S) equation and LBM involves significant computational complexity and time consumption, as the size and dimension of the model increase, the complexity and computational cost of the model and program also increase. In recent years, the rapid development of artificial intelligence algorithms has provided new methods for permeability calculations in porous media, improving computational efficiency (Wang et al. 2021a ). One common approach is to use rock images as inputs to deep learning models, enabling data-driven prediction of physical parameters of the rock. Alqahtani et al. (2020)  trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) model to predict porosity, specific surface area, and average pore size of 2D core slices. Additionally, they employed ResNet and ResNext networks to learn the geometric shapes and conductivity of pore spaces in porous media, enabling the prediction of permeability (Alqahtani et al. 2021 ). Rabbani et al. (2020)  constructed a CNN model called DeePore, which predicts various physical properties of rock based on images. These properties include the Leverett J function, which reflects fluid flow characteristics, as well as wet-phase/non-wet-phase relative permeability. To capture the flow field distribution characteristics in porous media, traditional CNN network structures may not suffice. The Unet network, with its characteristic of having the same input and output size, has been used to predict flow field distribution characteristics in porous media. Wang and Zai (Wang and Zai 2023 ) demonstrated that using Unet for velocity field computation in rock images can reduce computation time by 98.59 % compared to the LBM. Hennigh (2017)  constructed the LAT-NET network to predict velocity and electromagnetic fields, and further improvements were made to the LAT-NET network through active learning techniques (Hennigh and Chertkov 2018 ). Santos et al. (2020)  improved the ResUnet network structure and established the PoreFlow-Net network, which enables fast and accurate fluid velocity field predictions. Wang et al. (2021b)  introduced a gated convolution after the initial convolution in each block of the Unet network and incorporated a network-in-network layer before skip connections, resulting in a modified Unet network called the Gated U-Net CNN, this network was used to predict the velocity field distribution within the rock. Zhou et al. (2022)  enhanced the generalization capability of the model by incorporating coarse-grid velocity fields as additional input data to the Unet network. The LAT-NET, PoreFlow-Net, and Gated U-Net CNN architectures have indeed modified the loss function of the model. However, it is important to note that these modifications are primarily based on numerical errors and do not explicitly consider the constraints imposed by the N-S equations and LBM equations themselves. In recent years, the utilization of deep learning techniques for direct solution of complex partial differential equations has emerged as a prominent research focus in the field of computational fluid dynamics. The physics-informed neural network (PINN), proposed by the Karniadakis team (Raissi et al. 2017, Raissi et al. 2019, Raissi et al. 2020 ), presents a deep learning algorithm framework that builds upon the traditional artificial neural network approach for solving ordinary and partial differential equations. PINN has been extensively employed for solving the N-S equations, which describe fluid flow in the form of partial differential equations. Initially, the model was constructed using a deep neural network (DNN), and Cheng and Zhang (Cheng and Zhang 2021 ) further enhanced the predictive accuracy of the PINN model by embedding the N-S equations into a ResNet network. Numerous studies have been conducted on the application of PINN networks for solving the N-S equations, and for a comprehensive review, please refer to the review article by the Karniadakis team (Cai et al. 2021 ). In the context of subsurface fluid flow problems, the research team led by Dongxiao Zhang (Wang et al. 2020, Xu et al. 2021 ) has employed the principles of PINN to propose a theoretical-guided DNN called TgNN for solving subsurface fluid flow equations. Subsequently, they introduced the TgCNN network, which replaces the DNN network with a U-Net architecture, enabling the solution of pressure and saturation fields in subsurface fluid flow (Wang et al. 2022 ). Shan et al. (2023)  used PINN to solve the Buckley Leverett partial differential equation for two-phase flow in porous media. He et al. (2020)  constructed a multi-physics parameter PINN network incorporating the Darcy equation and convection–diffusion equation to compute permeability, hydraulic head, and concentration in subsurface fluid flow processes. Almajid and Abu-Al-Saud (2022)  utilized the PINN model to simulate drainage in water-saturated porous media and found that the PINN model exhibited better extrapolation performance when trained solely on early saturation profiles compared to an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) model. While the aforementioned models provide methods for simulating flow at the reservoir scale, they are not suitable for investigating fluid microscale flow mechanisms at the core scale. Kamrava et al. (2021)  introduced mass conservation and the N-S equations as constraints into a CycleGAN-based network, resulting in the PIRED network, which enables the simulation of pressure and velocity fields in porous media at different time steps. The understanding of microscale flow behavior in rock cores is of significant importance for the effective development of oil and gas resources. Compared to traditional numerical simulation methods, deep learning algorithms offer increased efficiency. However, there has been limited research on the application of PINN networks in simulating porous media flow at the microscale, particularly using the LBM. Lou et al. (2021)  proposed the PINN-BGK model, which utilizes the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK) equation to constrain the neural network. This model adopts DNN networks as neural network for solving the distribution function of LBM theory, and the boundary conditions of the testing are simple. Because the boundary conditions of porous media are complex, and the DNN network is very difficult to deal with the complex spatial structure of porous media, the boundary conditions are not convenient added in DNN network, so the PINN-BGK model proposed by Lou et al. (2021)  cannot be directly applied to porous media with complex structures, and there is currently a lack of research in this area. In this study, the aim is to improve the PINN-BGK model by introducing the Unet network and transform neural network, enabling it to simulating the flow behavior in complex structured porous media. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. The Section 2  introduces the LBM-BGK theory, the principle of PINN-BGK model and the principle of Unet network. Based on this, the PI-Unet-BGK network is built. The Section 3  verifies the PINN-BGK model built in this work by the Taylor-green flow. The Section 4  compares the effects of the PI-Unet-BGK network proposed in this work and the Unet network in predicting the steady-state flow field, and further uses the PI-Unet-BGK network to simulate the dynamic flow process of single-phase fluid in porous media.  2 Model and theory 2.1 Lattice Boltzmann method The LBM possesses a lucid physical foundation, being established upon the principles of molecular kinetic theory and statistical mechanics. Consequently, it enables the microscopic description of macroscopic motion patterns. The LBM equations originate from the Boltzmann equation, which is discretized to yield the fundamental equations of the LBM. For an isolated system devoid of external forces, the Boltzmann equation can be expressed as follows:(1) ∂ f  ∂ t   + c · ∇ f = Ω     where f  represents the particle distribution function, t  denotes the time, c  represents the particle velocity, and Ω   is the collision operator, which is a function of f . Therefore, Eq. (1)  is a challenging integro-differential equation to solve. In 1954, Bhatnagar, Gross, and Krook proposed the LBM with the BGK model, which replaces the collision term in the Boltzmann equation with a simple operator, this greatly simplifies the difficulty of solving the Boltzmann equation, and the form of the LBM-BGK model is as follows:(2) ∂ f i   ∂ t   + c i  · ∇ f i  = - 1 τ  f i  - f i eq         f i neq   = f i  - f i eq           where f i eq     represents the equilibrium distribution function, f i neq     represents the nonequilibrium distribution function, i  represents the discrete velocity direction.(3) f i eq  = ω i  ρ 1 + c i  · u  c s 2   + c i  · u   2  2 c s 4    - u 2  2 c s 2         where ω   and c  are related to the discrete velocity model. In this context, considering the case of two-dimensional flow, and therefore, the D2Q9 discrete velocity model is employed. c s    represents the lattice speed of sound, c s  = 1 / 3     . ρ  is the density and u  is the velocity. The formulas for calculating the macroscopic physical quantities, ρ  and u , are as follows:(4) ρ = ∑ i = 0  n  f i  = ∑ i = 0  n  f i eq       (5) u = 1 ρ  ∑ i = 0  n  c i  f i  = 1 ρ  ∑ i = 0  n  c i  f i eq     The macroscopic pressure is obtained through the equation of state:(6) p = ρ c s 2        2.2 PINN-BGK network The PINN utilizes the excellent fitting capability of neural networks to approximate unknown functions. By incorporating the physical equations as constraint terms, the performance of the neural network is enhanced. The key lies in designing the loss function for the neural network. In the PINN-BGK network proposed by Lou et al. (2021) , the loss function consists of three terms, the network structure is shown in Fig. 1  . In this work, the loss function is defined as L = L M  + L Eq   + L IC   + L BC     , where L M    represents the numerical loss of the macroscopic physical quantities, L Eq     represents the loss of the LBM-BGK equation, which takes into account the velocity discretization model. L IC     represents the error in the initial conditions, and L BC     represents the error in the boundary conditions. The formula for calculating the numerical loss of the macroscopic physical quantities L M    is as follows:(7) L M  = MSE ρ , u   *  , ρ , u   p       where MSE represents the mean squared error, the superscript * denotes the true value, and p  represents the predicted value, MSE A , B    = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  A i  - B i     2    . (8) , f i eq     can be calculated by Eq. (3) . Considering the significant differences between f i eq     and f i neq    , Lou et al.(2021)  designed two separate DNN networks to compute f i eq     and f i neq    . One of the deep neural networks (NNfeq ) is utilized for the computation of macroscopic physical quantities ρ  and u , while the other deep neural network (NNfneq ) performs the calculation of nonequilibrium distribution function f i neq    , and the distribution function f i  = f i eq   + f i neq     . The distribution function f i    consists of the equilibrium part (f i eq    ) and the non-equilibrium part (f i neq    ), and f i  = f i eq   + f i neq     , the magnitudes of f i eq     and f i neq     can be very different. f i eq     can be more than 100 times larger than the f i neq     in continuous flows. Due to the dominance of f i eq     and f i neq     cannot be solved accurately if approximate f i    by one deep neural network directly. However, f i neq     has a strong influence on the convergence of the governing equation in Eq. (2) , therefore apply two DNNs to approximate f i eq     and f i neq    , respectively. (Ronneberger et al. 2015 ), primarily applied in medical image segmentation. This model excels in classifying images at the pixel level and demonstrates exceptional performance, hence, both Unet and its advanced variants have been employed in digital rock image segmentation tasks (Karimpouli and Tahmasebi 2019, Ar Rushood et al. 2020, Alqahtani et al. 2022 ). The Unet network can be delineated into two distinct components: the encoder and the decoder. The encoder undertakes the extraction of semantic features from the input data via a series of convolutional layers. On the other hand, the decoder deciphers the encoded semantic features by means of multiple upsampling operations. Notably, a concatenation technique is employed to amalgamate the convolutional and upsampled feature maps at the corresponding scale. This operation allows the Unet network to effectively incorporate both deep and shallow layers of semantic information, thereby enabling accurate prediction of the flow field at the pixel level. To facilitate the prediction of flow field distribution within the porous medium, it becomes imperative to adapt the original Unet network's loss function. In this work, the MSE loss function is utilized:(14) L = MSE Y *  , Y ′         where Y *    represents the label data and Y ′    represents the Unet network prediction data.  2.4 Physical-informed Unet network for BGK equation Porous medium has an intricate structure, which leads to a very complex fluid flow law, it becomes imperative to account for the structure characteristics of the porous medium in the context of PINN. Training a Unet network for the purpose of predicting the distribution of velocity fields in porous medium has been substantiated as a highly effective approach. Consequently, this work adopts the Unet network instead of the conventional DNN and employs the geometric structure of the porous medium as an input parameter to construct the PI-Unet-BGK model. By doing so, the PINN-BGK theory becomes more aptly suited for addressing the flow quandary encountered within the porous medium. Based on the principles outlined in Section 2.2  , the PI-Unet-BGK network consists of two sub-networks, both of which are Unet networks. The fundamental structural parameters remain identical to those of the Unet network discussed in Section 2.3  , with adjustments required for the number of input and output channels, as depicted in Fig. 2  . The Unet-1 network accepts inputs of time (t ), position (x , y ), binary rock images (G ), and outputs corresponding to macroscopic parameters ρ , u , and v . Consequently, Unet-1 requires 4 input channels and yields 3 output channels. On the other hand, the Unet-2 network receives inputs of time (t ), position (x , y ), binary rock images (G ), its output is the non-equilibrium distribution f i neq    . Therefore, the number of input channels for Unet-2 is 4, and the number of output channels is 9 because the D2Q9 model is adopted. Given the substantial disparity in magnitude between the network output and the non-equilibrium distribution function, particular attention must be paid during the computation of the particle distribution function. The loss function for the PI-Unet-BGK network is computed in the same manner as the loss function for the PINN-BGK network outlined in Section 2.2  . In practical implementation, the time (t ) and position (x , y ) data exhibit relatively monotonic characteristics. Consequently, directly inputting these variables into the PI-Unet-BGK network for learning may not output optimal results. To address this, a neural network is employed to extract additional valuable information and enhance accuracy by processing the time (t ) and position (x , y ) data. This additional neural network is depicted in Fig. 2 . When training the PI-UNET-BGK network, all training data will be input into the network epoch by epoch. The position (x , y ) data and image at t  = 0 are input in the Unet-1 network and Unet-2 network to predict the initial flow field, and then the initial condition error (Eq. (11) ) is calculated. The boundary condition (time t , position (x , y ) data and image) are input in the Unet-1 network and Unet-2 network to predict the flow field at the same time, and then the boundary condition loss (Eq. (10) ) is calculated.   3 PINN-BGK model training and validation Taylor-Green flow is a kind of unstable flow attenuation of eddy current, it exists the exact solutions in two-dimensional periodic boundary conditions:(12) u x , y , t    = - cos x   sin y   e - 2 t ν      v x , y , t    = sin x   cos y   e - 2 t ν      p x , y , t    = - 1 4  cos 2 x    + cos 2 y       e - 4 t ν            In this case, the viscosity of fluid ν   is 0.01, x ∈ - π , π      , y ∈ - π , π      , t ∈ 0 , 10      , and the computational domain is meshed in 200 × 200 grids, the time domain has 20 sampling points with a total of 800,000 data.
