In each iteration, 8000 sets of data are randomly selected in all samples to calculate the numerical loss L M    and LBM-BGK equation loss L Eq    , and 300 points were randomly selected to calculate the boundary condition loss L BC     and initial condition loss L IC    . The Epoch is set to 300 for training, the loss function decreases by 4 orders of magnitude and becomes stable at 30000th iteration, as shown in Fig. 4  . However, the error fluctuates in the later stage of training, possibly due to the large value of the learning rate. As shown in Fig. 5  , the predicted values of PINN-BGK are in good agreement with the analytical values, and the RMSE values are all at 10−3  (Table 1  ). The error is very small, indicating that the PINN-BGK model constructed in this work is effective.  4 Single phase flow simulation based on PI-Unet-BGK network 4.1 PI-Unet-BGK network structure The structural configuration of the Unet network is illustrated in Fig. 6  . In this research paper, the Unet network architecture incorporates four successive downsampling and upsampling procedures. The input data is initially sized at 66 × 66 pixels, while the output flow field data have the same size, Table 2   is specified its corresponding parameters. Each downsampling operation within the encoder consists of two convolutional layers, utilizing a 3 × 3 convolution kernel with a stride size of 1. The maximum pooling layer is configured with a window size of 2 × 2, a stride size of 2, and zero padding. A batch standardization layer follows each convolutional layer, enabling normalization of the output feature map from the convolutional layer. This normalization process ensures that the data does not lead to network performance instability due to excessively large values during nonlinear transformations. The nonlinear activation function employed is the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) function. Each upsampling process within the decoder comprises an upsampling layer, which utilizes bicubic interpolation with a multiplicative factor of 2, and two subsequent convolutional layers. The convolutional layers employ a 3 × 3 convolution kernel with a stride size of 1.  4.2 Steady flow simulation by PI-Unet-BGK 4.2.1 Training datasets and model training The rock data utilized in this study is derived from Berea sandstone, as depicted in Fig. 7  . The Watershed module of ImageJ is used to increase connectivity of the original images, then the Erode module is used to increase the width of the channel. Due to computational limitations, the images are cropped into samples of size 64 × 64 × 1445. For the calculation of velocity and density fields within the two-dimensional rock pores under stable conditions, the LBM is employed. The discrete velocity model utilizes the D2Q9 model. The boundary conditions encompass the utilization of Zou-He pressure boundary conditions for the lateral boundaries and standard bounce-back boundary conditions for the upper and lower boundaries. To apply the boundary conditions, a lattice unit space is added surrounding the computational domain of the core image. The pressure gradient is set at 3.94 × 10−6 , while the fluid viscosity is 0.2 and the fluid density is 1. The relaxation time factor of 1.1 is employed. It should be noted that the computational time required for the 1445 two-dimensional slices exceeds 24 h, each image is simulated with 10,000 time step. The dataset comprising the 1445 sets of data is divided into 1000 sets for training purposes and 445 sets for testing. A total of 1000 rock images, along with the corresponding velocity and density fields are employed for training the Unet network. The image data is normalized to the range 0 and 1, while the velocity field and density field data are standardized. The training process involves 150 epochs, with a batch size of 5. The Adam optimization method is utilized to optimize the network parameters, with a learning rate of 0.00001, β 1  =  0.5, β 2  =  0.95. Fig.8   illustrates the MSE loss during the training process. After 100 epochs, the MSE loss experiences a reduction of two orders of magnitude. The training of the Unet network requires approximately 1.86 min, its calculation time is approximately 1/777 that of LBM simulation. To trainng the PI-Unet-BGK network, the position (x , y ) coordinates need to be transformed into a 3D tensor and subsequently flattened for a neural network transition. Since the PI-Unet-BGK network is utilized for simulating stable single-phase flow, the time variable remains invariant, and considering that the relaxation time in this part, f i , N N f n e q  neq   = 10 × f i neq     . The training process for the PI-Unet-BGK network involves 150 epochs with a batch size of 5. The Adam optimization method is utilized to optimize the network parameters, with a learning rate of 0.00001, β 1  set to 0.5, and β 2  set to 0.95. Fig. 8  shows the loss during the training process. After 100 epochs, the loss experiences a reduction of one orders of magnitude. The loss function of the PI-Unet-BGK network takes into account the f i neq     error, boundary condition error and initial condition error, which is three more than the Unet network, so the loss value is larger than Unet network. The training of the PI-Unet-BGK network requires approximately 2.17 h. Comparatively, the Unet network exhibits a lower loss compared to the PI-Unet-BGK network and a more stable training process with less time consumption. In comparison to LBM simulation, the PI-Unet-BGK network indeed exhibits significantly shorter calculation time when predict the flow field (200 ms for 445 images), amounting to less than one-133th of the time required by LBM for a new image. This highlights the computational efficiency advantage of the PI-Unet-BGK network over the LBM simulation. But LBM simulation uses 8.7G CPU memory, PI-UNET-BGK uses 19.5G GPU memory, 20G CPU memory.  4.2.2 Model validation and analysis Randomly select a rock image from the test datasets and input it into the Unet network for the computation of its velocity and density. The computed values are then compared with the real velocity field, as depicted in Fig. 9  (a) . The real velocity field, obtained through LBM calculations, reveals higher velocities in the throats and lower velocities in the larger pores. Notably, the Unet network's predictions also exhibit this phenomenon. However, a discernible disparity is observed in the velocity residual image between the Unet network's predictions and the LBM calculations. The velocity field predicted by the Unet network exhibits irregularities and significant fluctuations, resulting in MSR of 4.44 × 10−4 m/s. The PI-Unet-BGK network's predictions demonstrate better agreement with the LBM calculations, yielding smaller MSE (Fig. 9 (b) ), with an MSE of 1.63 × 10−4 , indicating enhanced accuracy compared to the velocity measurements obtained from the Unet network. Remarkably, the PI-Unet-BGK network exhibits superior performance in regions characterized by rapid changes in throat and pore geometry. Fig. 10   presents a comparison of the velocity distribution at the inlet, outlet, and middle positions in both the X and Y directions. It is evident that the velocity errors are more pronounced in the large pores than in the small pores, for both the Unet and PI-Unet-BGK networks. Both networks exhibit non-smooth fluid transport, characterized by significant fluctuations in the velocity field. The Unet's predicted velocity is notably more unstable when compared to the predictions made by the PI-Unet-BGK network. The velocity field and density field predicted by the Unet and PI-Unet-BGK networks for the test datasets are utilized to calculate the permeability of the rock slices. Fig. 11   illustrates the comparison between the LBM simulation permeability and the permeability calculated by the Unet and PI-Unet-BGK networks. Both networks yield permeability distributions that are more concentrated compared to the permeability distribution of the real rock. The RMSE between the permeability distributions calculated by Unet and the real permeability is 0.8631 whereas for the PI-Unet-BGK network, it is 0.7894. This indicates that the PI-Unet-BGK network exhibits higher accuracy in permeability estimation. Additionally, the R2  for Unet is 0.2127, whereas for the PI-Unet-BGK network, it is 0.2788, indicating better performance and robustness for the PI-Unet-BGK network, the R2  has increased by 0.06. Because the training data in this manuscript is based on sandstone rock, for verifying the applicability of the PI-Unet-BGK network, the trained PI-Unet-BGK network is applied to predict the flow field of steady single-phase flow in both carbonate rock and shale image. The original samples are displayed in Fig. 12  , and they have been preprocessed using the watershed algorithm. The results, as presented in Fig. 13  , demonstrate that the predicted velocities closely align with the real data. The velocity residuals for carbonate and shale are −1.37 × 10−4 m/s and −1.30 × 10−4 m/s, respectively. Moreover, the permeabilities calculated for both carbonate and shale samples are closed to the real values, as indicated in Table 3  , the larger relative error is due to the smaller real permeability value. This demonstrates the promising potential of the PI-Unet-BGK network for accurately computing velocity and density fields for various rock samples, it is reliable that extend its applicability to a wide range of scientific and industrial purposes.   4.3 Dynamic flow simulation by PI-Unet-BGK 4.3.1 Training datasets and model training The previous sections focused on steady flow simulations, where the velocity fields were time-independent. However, single-phase flow in porous media is a more intricate and dynamic process that involves time-dependent behavior. This section aims to validate the capability of the PI-Unet-BGK network in simulating single-phase flow in porous media, considering the complex and sequential nature of such phenomena. Select a rock slice image from the Berea sandstone dataset and use the LBM method to calculate the fluid flow process for the first 2000-time steps. The simulation parameters are consistent with before, it is sampled every 2-time in first 1500-time steps step for training, while the others are used for prediction. The PI-Unet-BGK network settings parameters remain the same as before. It consumed 21.02 h for training, the training process is shown in Fig. 14  , the rate of loss reduction slows down after 120 epochs.  4.3.2 Model validation and analysis The predicted density field of the Berea sandstone at different times are displayed in Fig. 16   (a) . As the time steps progress, the predicted density field gradually transports from the entrance to the middle of the pores. Although the initial error is relatively large, it decreases significantly when it reaches 200 steps. A similar phenomenon is observed in Fig. 15 , which illustrates the residual of density and velocity of the Berea sandstone, carbonate, and shale samples between the simulation results obtained by LBM and the predictions by the PI-Unet-BGK network. The trained PI-Unet-BGK network is also applied to predict single-phase flow in the carbonate and shale samples, as depicted in Fig. 16 (b)  and (c) . This demonstrates the network's capability to learn and predict fluid flow behavior across different porous media, exhibiting its versatility and potential for diverse applications. The prediction of carbonate rock and shale in the early stage exhibits considerable deviations from the true values, leading to inaccurate density distribution predictions. However, as time progresses, the PI-Unet-BGK network shows a density transport phenomenon, and the prediction error gradually reduces. The errors of carbonate rock and shale sample originate from the weak ability transfer learning of the PI-Unet-BGK network that trained based on Berea sandstone only. Adding more different sample data will have a foreseeable improvement for the PI-Unet-BGK network to simulate flow in different samples. In Fig. 15 , both the velocity and density residuals gradually decrease with increasing time steps and stabilize after 200-time steps. The error between carbonate rocks and shale is significantly larger than that of Berea sandstone, because the training data is from Berea sandstone. These observations provide valuable indication into the network's limitations and potential areas where to enhance its predictive capabilities in handling dynamic fluid flow simulation. The average error of density and velocity are mostly less than 10−3 . Although the PI-Unet-BGK model can predict the dynamic flow processes of fluids to a certain extent, it exhibits notable inaccuracies during the initial stage and in regions with rapid variations in pore size. These discrepancies can be attributed to two potential reasons: (1) The scarcity of data pertaining to significant changes in fluid flow at specific times hampers the training process. (2) Despite incorporating a neural network to convert time (t ) and spatial coordinates (x , y ) prior to feeding them into the Unet network, the transformed data still poses challenges for comprehension by the PI-Unet-BGK model, leading to amplified fluctuations in damage assessment compared to Unet. Consequently, this model can be further enhanced in the following facets: (1) Augmenting the volume of training data, particularly data captured during crucial moments in different porous medium; (2) Elevating the network's depth and bolstering its capacity to learn temporal (t ) and spatial (x , y ) information; (3) Enhancing computing device performance and enlarging the batch size for more efficient processing.    5 Conclusion In this work, a physical-informed Unet network (PI-Unet-BGK) is established based on LBM-BGK method to simulate single-phase flow in complex porous medium with introducing Unet and transform neural network. Berea sandstone, carbonate rock and shale samples were used to verify the accuracy of PI-Unet-BGK network in calculating steady and dynamic velocity fields and density fields. The research shows that the PI-Unet-BGK network constructed in this article predicts steady-state velocity and density fields better than the Unet network, and has a wider range of applications. The model proposed in this article also can simulate the dynamic flow process in the same sample, but the effect is not good on different rock samples with significant errors at initial stage. For its calculation time is much shorter than LBM simulation and the accuracy is higher than Unet, it has broad application prospects. In addition, due to limitations in computing devices, the PI Unet BGK model established in this article is only applicable to two-dimensional situations.
1 Introduction In the middle reaches of arid inland river basins, the desert ecosystems (such as sandy desert and gravel desert) coexist with the oases, and are an indispensable component of hydrological and biogeochemical cycles. Water is the dominant factor controlling biological processes in the desert ecosystems, where limited precipitation is the primary water source and precipitation patterns play a critical role in water utilization by plants (Touchette et al., 2012 ). Soil water movement determines the flux and amount of drainage to groundwater, and whether plants can use water from capillary rise in the groundwater-soil-plant-atmosphere continuum (GSPAC ) in the deserts. Soil water availability limits plant growth and productivity, whereas plant root distribution affects the soil water content (SWC ), and biomass accumulation reflects the relationship between water availability and carbon storage (Zhu et al., 2019; Mao et al., 2021 ). Identifying hydrological processes within GSPAC  and quantifying water utilization are critical for determining the sustainability of the desert ecosystems and water resource management of arid inland river basins. Accurately partitioning evapotranspiration (ET ) is essential for determining hydrological flux and water allocation to carbon sequestration under changing climate conditions. It is also critical for developing process-based models and coupling the hydrologic and biogeochemical cycles in earth surface models (Sun et al., 2019 ). A few studies have reviewed ET  partitioning. For example, Schlesinger and Jasechko (2014)  found that the ratio of transpiration (T ) to ET  (T/ET ) was 51±15 % from 81 studies in semiarid ecosystems. The studies have showed the controlling influence of meteorological factors, climate change, and vegetation dynamics on ET  partitioning in dryland environments (Xu et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2021 ). Plant type and architecture affect T  proportion via fraction of canopy-shaded surface, biomass allocation, root water uptake rate, and water availability in the desert ecosystems (Moran et al., 2009 ). Accurately quantifying ET  and its components in the desert ecosystems is essential but challenging due to sparse observation networks and complex surface conditions. Methods of measuring ET  and its components include eddy covariance systems, sap flow meters, lysimeters, stable isotope composition measurements, gas-exchange chambers, etc (Sun et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021 ). All of these types of measurements are time- and labor-consuming, and have a confined spatial extent with high accuracy. In contrast, modelling using monitored meteorological data, soil properties and vegetation characteristics may be preferable. The Penman-Monteith equation has been successfully used for ET  estimation of various crops at station, local, regional, and global scales (Bodner et al., 2007; Naghedifar et al., 2018; Li and Wang, 2021 ), but its application in the desert ecosystems has been rare due to parameter uncertainties and difficulty in determining certain parameters. Mata-Gonzalez et al. (2005)  argued that applying crop coefficients to natural vegetation would overestimate plant water use in arid regions experiencing severe water stress. However, Liu et al. (2010)  reported the feasibility of the Penman-Monteith equation with dual crop coefficients for ET  estimation in the Otindag Sandy Land of China. Complex surface conditions and lack of observation on shrub features (such as canopy shape, shaded fraction, leaf resistance, and root system phenotype) have limited the availability of reliable crop coefficients and the application of the Penman-Monteith equation in the desert ecosystems. Monitoring and modelling of the hydrological cycle in the desert ecosystems are needed to clarify the interactions among soil water, plants and groundwater. For example, previous studies have shown the role of deep soil water and groundwater in sustaining phreatophyte and desert vegetation in arid and semiarid regions (Miller et al., 2010; Dai et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2018 ). Li et al. (2020a)  quantified soil water exchange with groundwater, and separated the contribution of rainfall to plant growth from that of groundwater in the margin of the Badain Jaran Desert after measuring the 0–300 cm SWC  and groundwater level (GL ) over three years. Models such as the Root Zone Water Quality Model (Hanson et al., 1998 ), the Soil-Water-Atmosphere-Plant model (Crescimanno and Garofalo, 2005 ), the Landscape Hydrology model (Hyndman et al., 2007 ), and the HYDRUS model (Šimůnek et al., 2018 ) are promising for simulating hydrological processes in ecosystems. Vertical water movement dominates the hydrological cycle of GSPAC  in arid ecosystems, and monitoring data with the inverse solution of the Richards’ equation can properly depict water flow dynamics (Liu et al., 2018 ). The HYDRUS-1D program based on the Richards’ equation is suitable for modelling variability-saturated water flow in the vertical domain. It has been successively used in simulating the reuse of saline drainage water by alfalfa (Medicago sativa  L.) (Shouse et al., 2011 ), the soil water balance for varying coverage of natural vegetation in Israel and Gaza (Dafny and Šimůnek, 2016 ), heat and water transfer in mulched and bare soils (Kader et al., 2019 ), irrigation schedule optimization in inland river basins of China (Ren et al., 2016; Li, 2020 ), etc. The flat topography of the gravel desert and its relatively uniform distribution of SWC  result in primarily vertical water flow in the soil, and indicate the feasibility of the HYDRUS-1D model in simulating the hydrological cycle in this region. Hydrological cycle of the deserts is driven by climatic factors, mediated by vegetation and soil features, and constrained by water availability (Liu et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2018 ). Factors such as precipitation (Raz-Yaseef et al., 2012 ), soil properties (Duniway et al., 2018 ), ET  (Xu et al., 2020 ), and irrigation in the adjacent oases (de Graaf et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2021 ) affect water processes of GSPAC  in the desert ecosystems.  The Heihe River is the second largest arid inland river basin in China, and oases coexist with sandy desert and the gravel desert in the middle reaches where water exchanges between river, soil, and groundwater are significant. Precipitation scarcity and development of irrigated agriculture alter hydrological processes, making hydrological regimes of oasis-desert systems relatively complex. The change in water availability impacts the survival and succession of natural vegetation in the desert ecosystems, which are sensitive to the hydrological processes in the vadose zone. Previous studies have mainly focused on the redistribution and utilization of rainfall (Liu et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2022 ), ET  estimation (Zhao et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2017, 2020 ), water cycle, water consumption, and water exchange of cropland, shelterbelts and sandy desert (Zhao et al., 2010, 2017; Yi et al., 2014 ), and irrigation schedule optimization (Li, 2020; Li and Wang, 2021 ) in the desert-oasis ecotone. The gravel desert has experienced very little human disturbance and can provide an excellent location to generate insights into the hydrological processes of GSPAC  and to understand how hydrological cycles respond to the development of irrigated agriculture. Few studies have focused on the gravel desert. Zhang (2014)  analyzed SWC  and organic carbon content in the 0–200 cm soil layer and plant diversity in the gravel desert over two years. Zhou et al. (2017)  identified the water source for Nitraria sibirica  and its response to growing season rainfall in the gravel desert in 2015. Groundwater is known to be a critical source of water for natural vegetation in the ecotone (Liu et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020a ), but its influence on water movement in the vadose zone of the gravel desert remains unclear. Temporal series of SWC  and GL  can provide large amounts of water flow information, but short-term measurements can only provide limited information. The flexible structure of the HYDRUS-1D model enables it to capture the underlying hydrological processes of GSPAC  from monitoring data under long-term varying conditions. Therefore, simulation using the HYDRUS-1D model based on long-term monitoring of SWC , meteorological factors and GL  is essential for depicting water movement processes and for clarifying the interactions between groundwater and plants in the gravel desert. The objectives of this study were: 1) to partition ET  and depict the movement and fluxes of water in GSPAC , and 2) to clarify how plants respond to and utilize precipitation and capillary rise of groundwater under varying conditions, using the HYDRUS-1D simulation with twelve-years of measured data from the gravel desert in the middle reaches of the Heihe River in northwestern China.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area and field monitoring The study area (39.41°N, 100.12°E, 1389 m a.s.l.) was about 1 ha in the gravel desert, located in the southern margin of the Badain Jaran Desert ( Fig. 1 ), and was about 6 km north of the Linze Inland River Basin Research Station (39.35°N, 100.13°E, hereafter referred to as “Linze station”). The region has a continental arid temperate climate, with annual mean air temperature of 7.6 °C. The highest and lowest air temperatures are 38.6 °C in July and −26.2 °C in January, respectively. Mean annual precipitation is about 117 mm, with rainfall from June to September occupying 80 % of the annual precipitation. Annual mean gale days and dust storm days are 15 and 11, respectively. Zonal soil type is sand with small gravel covering the surface, and parent material is diluvial-alluvial deposits formed in the Quaternary period. The dominant vegetation species are Nitraria sphaerocarpa  and Reaumuria songarica . Nitraria sphaerocarpa  is in the form of small nabkha, and Reaumuria songarica  is low and relatively dense. Rainfall can penetrate up to 130 cm in the gravel desert (Yu et al., 2012 ), and the maximum rooting depth of the shrubs is about 160 cm (Xu et al., 2017 ). Volumetric SWC  was monitored at 10–cm depth intervals in the 0–150 cm soil profile using a neutron probe by three aluminum access tubes located about 30 m apart from the south to the north (Fig. 1 ). The SWC  measurements were generally made every 10 days during the growing season (April to October, beginning in 2005), with additional measurements made within two days after each rainfall event. Gravimetric SWC  at the same depth intervals near the tubes was measured by the oven drying method in May, July, and September each year to calibrate the neutron probe. Three soil profiles of 0–150 cm were dug in 2005 and 2011 to determine bulk density, saturated hydraulic conductivity (K s  , cm day−1 , constant water head method) and particle size distribution (laser diffraction, Mastersizer 2000 analyzer). Daily meteorological observations of precipitation (P ), solar radiation, maximum and minimum air temperature, wind speed, relative humidity and vapor pressure were monitored by a standard automated weather station at the Linze station, and were available beginning in September 2004. Groundwater level was manually monitored via a groundwater well every 10 days from January 2004. Measured data analyzed in this study were from January 2005 to December 2016 ( Fig. 2 ). The number of measurement events ranged from 19 to 30 for volumetric SWC  and averaged 36 for GL  in each year. The region was enclosed to prevent grazing, and phenological observations of the shrubs were recorded to classify growth stages (Table S1 ). Vegetation surveys were done in six, 10 and 10 quadrats (5×5 m) in August of 2005, 2010 and 2015, respectively. Height, coverage, and biomass of leaves, branches and litter of the shrubs were recorded. Belowground biomass of each quadrat was estimated by excavating roots in soil of 1×1×1 m (length × width × depth), 0.5×0.5×1 m and 0.5×0.5×0.5 m for the large, medium and small individual shrubs, respectively ( Table 1 ). All measured data were from the Data Submission and Sharing Infrastructure of the Linze Inland River Basin Research Station (lzstation@yeah.net).  2.2 Determination of evapotranspiration The FAO Penman-Monteith equation with the dual crop coefficient approach is suitable for frequent wettings of soil by sporadic rainfall events, and was calculated as (Allen et al., 1998 ):(1) E T  0   = 0.408 Δ ( R  n   − G ) + γ ( 900 / ( t + 273 ) ) u  2   ( e  s   − e  a   )  Δ + γ ( 1 + 0.34 u  2   )     E T  p   = ( K  e   + K  c b   ) E T  0         where ET 0   is reference evapotranspiration (mm day−1 ), Δ   is the slope of the saturation vapor pressure-temperature curve (kPa °C−1 ), R n   and G  are net radiation at the canopy surface and soil heat flux density, respectively (MJ m−2  day−1 ), γ  is the psychrometric constant (kPa °C−1 ), t  and u 2   are mean daily air temperature (°C) and wind speed (m s−1 ) at 2 m height, respectively, e s   and e a   are saturation vapor pressure and actual vapor pressure (kPa), respectively, ET p   is potential evapotranspiration (mm day−1 ), and K cb   and K e   are basal crop coefficient (dimensionless) and evaporation coefficient (dimensionless), respectively. The Richards’ equation was used as the governing equation:(9) ∂ θ  ∂ t   = ∂ ∂ x   [ K ( ∂ h  ∂ x   + 1  )   ]  − S ( h )      where θ  is volumetric water content (cm3  cm−3 ), t  is time (day), x  is a spatial coordinate (cm) (positive upward), K  is unsaturated hydraulic conductivity (cm day−1 ), h  is water pressure head (cm water), and S(h)  is the volume of water removed from a unit volume of soil per unit time due to root water uptake (cm3  cm−3  day−1 ). Soil hydraulic properties were specified by the van Genuchten-Mualem constitutive relationship (van Genuchten, 1980 ). For a non-uniform distribution of potential water uptake rate over a root zone of arbitrary shape, S(h)  was calculated as (Feddes et al., 1978 ):(10) S ( h )  = α ( h )  b ( x )  T  p          where α(h)  is water stress response function (dimensionless), b(x)  is the normalized water uptake distribution (cm−1 ), and T p   is potential transpiration rate (cm day−1 ). An atmospheric boundary condition with the surface layer and a variable pressure head were selected as the upper and lower boundary conditions, respectively. Daily P , E  and T  values and linearly-interpolated daily GL  data were input as time variable boundary conditions. The simulation was conducted for the 0–13 m vertical soil profile during the growing seasons from 2005 to 2016. The soil profile was discretized into 260 equidistant nodes with 5-cm thickness interval. Initial SWC  values were the measured data, averaging the measured data from the soil surface to the node located 100 cm (N 100  ) above GL , linearly increasing to saturation (θ s  , cm3  cm−3 ), and keeping θ s   for the 0–150 cm, from 160 cm to N 100  , from N 100   to GL , and from GL  until the bottom, respectively. The soil profile was divided into three material layers: 0–20 cm, 20–60 cm, and 60–1300 cm considering lateral root allocation and the difference in particle size distribution. Parameters θ s  , residual water content (θ r  , cm3  cm−3 ), inverse of air-entry pressure (α , cm−1 ) and pore size distribution index (n , dimensionless) of the van Genuchten model (van Genuchten, 1980 ) fitted by the Rosetta program were used as initial values during the inverse solution. Soil hydraulic parameters below 150 cm were generally assumed to be the same as those in the 140–150 cm layer due to the similarity in particle size distribution. Values of θ s  , n  and K s   of the three soil material layers were inversely estimated, and θ r   and α  values were fixed, taking into account the number of optimizing parameters and model uniqueness ( Table 2 ). Parameterization was assessed by diagnostic information of model fit and inverse algorithm convergence. The measured 0–150 cm SWC  data in 2008, 2009, and 2014 were used to calibrate the model, while data from the remaining nine years were used to validate the model. Comparisons of SWC  between the measured and simulated data were specified for the 0–20 cm, 20–60 cm, 60–90 cm, 90–120 cm and 120–150 cm layer to facilitate visual inspection. Model performance for the calibration and validation data sets was assessed with the coefficient of determination (R 2  ), root mean square error (RMSE ), and Willmott’s index of agreement (d , Willmott, 1982 ). The vadose zone was classified into three layers: 0–20 cm for topsoil SWC  fluctuations, 0–160 cm for rooting depth, and 0–10 m for capillary rise of groundwater. Daily drainage below a specified layer was calculated as:(11) P  i   + V  i − 1   − E  i   − T  i   − D P  i   − V  i   − R  i   = 0     where P i   is rainfall (mm), E i   is soil evaporation (mm), T i   is transpiration (mm), V i-1   and V i   are depth-equivalent water (mm) in the layer on the (i-1) th   day and i th   day, respectively, R i   is runoff, and DP i   is drainage (mm) with positive values indicating percolation out of the layer and negative values indicating water risen from deeper layers.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Soil water content dynamics in the root zone The SWC  dynamics were satisfactorily simulated by the model, and the simulations matched well with the measurements. The d  and RMSE  values for the calibration dataset ranged from 0.7147 to 0.9967 and from 0.0012 cm3  cm−3  to 0.0057 cm3  cm−3 , respectively, among the soil layers ( Fig. 3 ). Pooling the SWC  data from all soil layers in each year, RMSE  values were close to 0, and the values of d , and slope a  and R 2   of the fitted linear regression approximately equaled 1 (Table S2 ). Good agreement between the simulated and measured SWC  values verified the robustness of the model parameterization. This result concurs with the report that the inverse optimization algorithm of the HYDRUS-1D model provided unbiased and reliable soil hydraulic parameters (Wang et al., 2016; Dettmann et al., 2019; Li, 2020 ). The RMSE, d , a , and R 2   values for the validation dataset varied from 0.0034 cm3  cm−3  to 0.0064 cm3  cm−3 , from 0.9086 to 0.9828, from 0.9838 to 1.0211, and from 0.6601 to 0.9338, respectively (Table S2 ). The calibrated model was thus reasonable and accurate in simulating SWC  and its dynamics. Fluctuation in SWC  mainly occurred in the upper 60 cm, especially the 0–20 cm topsoil. The changes in SWC  were closely related to surface soil features and precipitation patterns. Gravel scattered on the soil surface limited rainfall infiltration and prevented E  from the topsoil. Precipitation of <5 mm, 5–10 mm, 10–20 mm and 20–30 mm occupied 83.8 %, 10.7 %, 4.5 % and 0.6 % of the precipitation events and 39.1 %, 27.1 %, 22.8 % and 5.4 % of the precipitation amounts over the twelve years, respectively. Frequent small rainfalls (<5 mm) wetted only the topsoil and water was lost soon after rain. The occurrence of consecutive rainfall events of greater than 5 mm was followed by an increase in SWC , which was remarkably apparent in the 0–20 cm soil layer (Fig. 3 ,  Fig. 4 ). Dewfall formation by water vapor adsorption may also contribute to high SWC  of topsoil (Zhuang and Zhao, 2017 ). The time series of SWC  below 60 cm (about 0.05 cm3  cm−3 ) suggested that rainfall events hardly affected deep soil during the growing seasons (Fig. 3 , Fig. 4 ). Relatively higher SWC  at the start of each growing season might be due to an early-spring thaw of frozen water in soil (Fig. 3 , Fig. 4 ). Soils in the gravel desert froze in early December, reached a maximum frozen depth (about 100 cm) at the following February, and thawed totally by mid-April. Thawing of frozen water in soil acted as a rainfall pulse and filled soil pores (Yi et al., 2014 ).  3.2 Evapotranspiration partition and its dynamics The approach of combining crop coefficients with ET 0   was suitable for ET  component estimation. Maximum K e   values ranged from 0.81 to 1.20, and maximum K cb   values generally increased from 0.25 to 0.48 with the increasing vegetation coverage (Table 1 ). The K cb   values ranged from 0.15 to 0.48 in the twelve years and kept pace with those of desert plants. The K cb   values ranged from 0.02 to 0.50 for a temperate desert steppe in Inner Mongolia (Yang and Zhou, 2011 ), from 0.20 to 0.40 for sand dunes and from 0.16 to 0.46 for Reaumuria songarica  in the Horqin Sandy Land (Li et al., 2020b ), and from 0.12 to 0.40 for plants in the southern Guerbantonggute Desert (Yin et al., 2021 ). These results showed that the dual crop coefficient approach provided a feasible way of partitioning ET  of shrub community in the gravel desert. Atmospheric evaporative demand was well met, and scarce and sporadic rainfall was primarily consumed by E  in the gravel desert. Daily actual E  (E a  ) values closely matched daily potential E  during the twelve growing seasons, with the slopes of the linear regression and R 2   values both approximating to 1 ( Fig. 5 ). Evaporation was mainly controlled by SWC  in the early and late growth stages, and by soil water exceeding field capacity in the middle growth stage (Bao et al., 2021 ). Maximum daily E a   occurred within three days after rainfall events and ranged from 3.10 mm in 2005 to 5.69 mm in 2008, with a mean value of 4.69±0.78 mm (mean ± one standard deviation) ( Table 3 ). For example, E a   of 4.40 mm and 5.00 mm occurred on the first and second days after a rainfall of 14.40 mm on 16 April 2007. Soil evaporation increased from 2.10 mm on the day prior to 30.60 mm of rain (July 14, 2013) to 5.09 mm on the second day following the rain. Total E a   during the growing season varied from 46.58 mm in 2016 to 116.32 mm in 2007, averaging 75.56±18.38 mm. Growing-season rainfall (P 1  ) accounted for 88.0 %–99.3 % of P , and about 55.1 %–83.7 % of P 1   (averaging 72.3 %±8.6 %) was consumed by E a   in the gravel desert. These results confirmed previous reports that E a   totaled 81±10 mm and contributed significantly to the water budget in the desert-oasis ecotone (Zhao et al., 2016 ), and about 79 % of rainfall was nonbiologically consumed in the sandy deserts without available groundwater in northwestern China (Liu et al., 2017 ). Individual morphology and physiological activity of plants in the gravel desert were impacted by precipitation pattern. Early spring thawing of frozen water in soil or snowfall provided timely water for seed germination of ephemeral herbs and the increasing seedling survival of shrubs. The synchronization of high T  values with the occurrence of large rainfall events in the late developing stage and middle stage indicated that summer rainfall offered a preferential water source (Fig. 2 ,  Fig. 6 ). Branches of Nitraria sphaerocarpa  were fine and low, with most branches positioned near to soil surface, facilitating the occurrence of throughfall. The Reaumuria songarica  and Nitraria sphaerocarpa  community responded after the occurrence of a large rainfall event or a series of small pulses. Daily actual T  (T a  ) increased from 0.18 mm to 0.33 mm under consecutive rainfall events of 2.80 mm, 4.00 mm, and 30.60 mm from July 12 to July 14, and then peaked at 0.99 mm on July 16 in 2013. This result suggests that large and infrequent precipitation events increased root water uptake and significantly affected T a  . This result was similar to previous reports. For example, shrubs transpired at peak rates after the occurrence of large rainfall events in the Chihuahuan Desert (Scott and Biederman, 2017 ). Water uptake of Nitraria tangutorum  from the 0–50 cm soil increased from 6.7 % to 36.5 % after a 22.40-mm rainfall in the desert-oasis ecotone (Zhou et al., 2017 ). Both Nitraria sphaerocarpa  and Reaumuria songarica  responded significantly to rainfall >10 mm during the growing season in the gravel desert (Wang et al., 2019a ). Roots extracted water harder from soil in dry years than in normal and wet years. About 110 mm of rainfall was needed to sustain the physiological activity of Nitraria sphaerocarpa , and significant growth occurred only when mean rainfall was greater than 140 mm in two consecutive years in the gravel desert (Li et al., 2004 ). The P 1   averaged to 105.72 mm in the twelve years, and P 1   in 2007, 2013 and 2016 was 155.70 mm, 105.60 mm and 60.60 mm, representing wet, normal and dry years, respectively. Maximum root water uptake (sink) values were 0.0137, 0.0229, and 0.0241 cm3  cm−3  day−1  in 2007, 2013 and 2016, respectively (Table 3 ). Under severe arid conditions, activation of the regulatory genes of Reaumuria songarica  will reduce both the photosynthesis and the functions of carbon assimilation and metabolism. Cell dehydration under persistent drought induces the increases in osmotic substances in cells and the activity of antioxidation enzymes (Wei, 2021 ). This mechanism protected Reaumuria songarica  from damage due to water stress. Daily T a   values in the developing stage and middle stage in wet and normal years were higher than those in the dry year, and T a   peaks in the dry year were delayed (Fig. 6 ). This agrees with the observation that biological indicators and biomass of desert vegetation depended mainly on the frequency and intensity of rainfall of rainy season in Kuwait (Abdullah et al., 2021 ). Root water uptake occurred in the 150 cm soil profile within the first 30 days of the growing season and then from the 0–60 cm soil in the gravel desert. Maximum sink values occurred in the 0–20 cm topsoil at the end of the developing stage, and generally increased from 0.0115 to 0.0245 cm3  cm−3  day−1 , averaging 0.0184±0.004 cm3  cm−3  day−1  over the twelve years ( Fig. 7 , Table 3 ). Root water uptake pattern of the shrubs was related to the phenotype or architecture of the rooting systems. The abundant root mass of Nitraria sphaerocarpa  was distributed in the top 50 cm soil in the Ulanbuh Desert (Li, 2014 ). Reaumuria songarica  had a rich lateral rooting system of both adventitious roots and fine initial roots, and its lateral and tap roots extended 119.0 cm horizontally and 62.30 cm vertically in the southwestern Alxa Plateau (Ma and Wang, 2020; Zhang et al., 2021 ). Nitraria sphaerocarpa  nabkhas in the gravel desert were small and in the late stage, and large amounts of adventitious roots were on the buried stems (Luo and Zhao, 2019 ). Allocating more biomass to lateral roots is a unique strategy of Nitraria sphaerocarpa  and Reaumuria songarica  to capture more water in order to withstand drought in the gravel desert. Yu et al. (2012)  showed that both Nitraria sphaerocarpa  and Reaumuria songarica  relied on soil water below 185 cm in the gravel desert. Stable isotope analysis is useful for identifying the source of water for plants (Chimner and Cooper, 2004; Li, 2014 ). However, simulation by the HYDRUS model using twelve years of measurements seems to be more robust in reflecting water flow than the isotope analysis of Yu et al. (2012)  derived from a few samplings in one month. This result agreed with previous findings. Canopy T a   was controlled by SWC  in the lateral root zone (10–20 cm) (Raz-Yaseef et al., 2012 ), and water uptake of Nitraria sphaerocarpa  in the rainy season relied on lateral roots in the 10–30 cm soil layer in the Ulanbuh Desert (Li, 2014 ). Nitraria sphaerocarpa  relied on shallow soil water and showed shorter duration of quick physiological response to rainfall >10 mm, while Reaumuria songarica  maintained physiological activity for a longer period of time due to more water from deeper soils (Liu and Zhao, 2009; Wang et al., 2019a; Ma and Wang, 2020 ). Divergent water use strategies constitute a vital trait reflecting better self-regulation and adjustment capacity by Reaumuria songarica  and Nitraria sphaerocarpa , guaranteeing sufficient utilization of soil water in the gravel desert. The T a   values ranged from 32.71 mm in 2006 to 64.95 mm in 2010, averaging 47.39±12.17 mm in the twelve years ( Fig. 8 ). The mean T a   value was remarkably smaller than that of 166 mm observed for the Calligonum mongolicum  community in the desert-oasis ecotone (Zhao et al., 2016 ). Maximum daily T a   values varied from 0.47 mm in 2005 to 0.99 mm in 2013, averaging 0.80±0.18 mm (Table 3 ). The values were 32.6 %–60.7 % of those (1.44–1.63 mm) for Nitraria tangutorum  and Calligonum mongolicum  in the desert-oasis ecotone (Xu et al., 2017 ). Low daily T a   may be ascribed to strong E  from exposed soil surface and water lost via excessive infiltration runoffs generated from neighboring mountains under infrequent large rainfall events in the gravel desert. Actual ET  (ET a  ) ranged from 79.90 mm in 2016 to 170.89 mm in 2007, with a mean value of 122.95±22.70 mm. Mean annual ET a   value was lower than those observed for a temperate desert steppe in Inner Mongolia (150.9 mm, Yang and Zhou, 2011 ), and for the Calligonum mongolicum  community in the desert-oasis ecotone (251 mm, Zhao et al., 2016 ), but within the range of 190 mm and 50 mm in the midstream and downstream deserts of the Heihe River (Xu et al., 2020 ). Canopy interception evaporation (I p  ) would range from 2.88 to 8.58 mm, averaging 5.58±1.71 mm according to the method of Shachnovich et al. (2008) . These values were lower than those of 9.00 mm and 9.54 mm reported for Calligonum mongolicum  and Nitraria sphaerocarpa , respectively, in the desert-oasis ecotone (Zhao et al., 2016, 2022 ). Negligible I p   values were mainly due to small plant size and sparse distribution of Reaumuria songarica  and Nitraria sphaerocarpa  in the gravel desert. Higher ET a   than P 1   confirmed the importance of rainfall in meeting atmospheric and vegetative demands for water. These results demonstrated that ET  consumed almost all of the rainfall in the desert-oasis ecotone (Zhao et al., 2010, 2016 ) and 95 % of rainfall in dry ecosystems (Raz-Yaseef et al., 2012; Stoy et al., 2019 ).  3.3 Water stress and water use efficiency assessment Water use efficiency (WUE ) is an important physiological indicator affected by water stress and is used to assess the interactions between carbon and water cycles. Water stress was reflected by the ratios of T a   to potential T  (T p1  ), ET a   to potential ET  (ET p1  ), and T a  /ET a   during the growing season, and WUE  was calculated as the ratio of aboveground net primary productivity (ANPP ) to ET a   in this study. The water demand of Reaumuria songarica  and Nitraria sphaerocarpa  was partially satisfied in the gravel desert. Daily T a   coincided with T p1   within the first 20 days of the growing season, and then remained lower than T p1   until the end of growing season (Fig. 6 ). The T a  /T p1   values decreased sharply within the first 40 days from more than 90 % to about 20 %, thereafter increasing slightly and exhibiting bimodality during the latter half of the developing stage and the entire middle stage (Fig. 6 ). T a   accounted for 13.5 %–44.0 % of T P1  , averaging 26.9 %±9.4 % over the twelve years (Fig. 8 ), indicating that the shrubs were suffering from severe water stress. This coincided with that the shrubs regulated T  under long-term strong evaporative demand (Schmidt-Walter et al., 2014 ). A reduction in shrub height and biomass in the gravel desert was a positive response to water stress (Table 1 ). Annual ET a   accounted for 27.0 %–64.4 % of ET p1  , and E a   and T a   were 46.1 %–73.0 % and 27.0 %–53.9 % of ET a  , respectively (Fig. 8 ). Annual mean E a   and T a   accounted for 61.3 %±8.1 % and 38.7 %±8.1 % of ET a  , respectively, suggesting that less than 40 % of water consumption was used for plant growth. A major fraction of E a   sustained previous reports that E /ET  fell within 61 %–84 % in the mobile sand dune of Horqin Sandy Land (Bao et al., 2021 ), annual range of 40 %–70 % among ecosystems (Moran et al., 2009; Staudt et al., 2011 ), and global range of 50 %–76 % (Schlesinger and Jasechko, 2014; Wei et al., 2017 ). The ANPP  in 2005, 2010 and 2015 was estimated by multiplying aboveground biomass by 1.6933 reported in the study region (Zhao et al., 2010 ). The ANPP  values varied among quadrats, and averaged 17.15, 16.87, and 37.43 g C m−2  in 2005, 2010, and 2015, respectively. The WUE  ranged from 0.10 g C m−2  mm−1  to 0.28 g C m−2  mm−1  in 2005, from 0.05 g C m−2  mm−1  to 0.21 g C m−2  mm−1  in 2010, and from 0.07 g C m−2  mm−1  to 0.76 g C m−2  mm−1  in 2015. Mean WUE  values were 0.15, 0.11, and 0.34 g C m−2  mm−1 , respectively. These values were lower than those of 0.68 g C m−2  mm−1  for Tamarix chinensis  community in central Asia (Liu et al., 2019 ) and 0.7 g C m−2  mm−1  for desert ecosystems in northwestern China (Wang et al., 2021 ). Difference in WUE  of the studies may be attributed to the changes in water availability, vegetation features and types of desert ecosystem. The WUE  values observed in 2005 and 2010 agreed with that of 0.16 g C m−2  mm−1  for the shrubs in the desert-oasis ecotone (Li et al., 2020a ), and WUE  in 2015 was near to rainfall use efficiency (0.26 g C m−2  mm−1 ) reported for the sandy deserts without available groundwater in northwestern China (Liu et al., 2017 ). Water availability controls the spatiotemporal patterns of WUE  in the desert ecosystems. Rainfalls of 10.80 mm and 14.40 mm occurred on May 15 and May 25 in 2010, and E a   within the following three days amounted to 8.71 mm and 12.39 mm, respectively. Ineffective water consumption after rainfall during the developing stage led to less leaf and litter and lower aboveground biomass in 2010 (Table 1 ). This may explain the lower WUE  in 2010 than in 2005 and 2015. Additionally, accurate quantification of plant dynamics was difficult, which may explain the inconsistency between coverage and biomass of the shrubs in 2010 (Table 1 ). The P 1   and ET a   values in 2015 were lower than those in 2005, but mean aboveground biomass of the quadrats in 2015 was about twice the amount observed in 2005 (Table 1 ). In summary, WUE  increased by 1.3 times from 2005 to 2015, and P 1   was more efficiently utilized for biomass production in dry years.  3.4 Water flux dynamics Drainage from the 0–20 cm soil layer (DP 20  ) occurred after a single rainfall >5 mm or consecutive rainfall events, and the peak values and the end of drainage were delayed one to two days. For example, rainfall of 12.00, 1.40, 6.20, 18.00, 0.20, 12.40, and 0.20 mm on the 125th, 126th, 129th, 134–137th days during the growing season in 2005 resulted into continuous drainage of 0.03–3.07 mm from the 125th to the 140th day. Maximum daily DP 20   values of 0.71 mm and 3.07 mm occurred on the first day and the second day after the rainfalls of 12.00 mm and 18.00 mm, respectively ( Fig. 9 ). Upward rise into the 0–20 cm layer (UR 20  ) mainly occurred in the initial and late stages when there was little rainfall (Fig. 9 ). The DP 20   and UR 20   values during the growing period ranged from 2.76 mm to 40.43 mm and from −44.81 mm to −17.49 mm in the twelve years, respectively (Table 3 ). The least amount of drainage occurred in 2016, and the maximum DP 20   and UR 20   values occurred in 2010. The difference between DP 20   and UR 20   varied from −31.90 mm to −4.14 mm, averaging −16.63 mm. Water movement in the topsoil of the gravel desert was significantly affected by rainfall pattern and dominated by moisture rise from lower soil depths. Daily values of drainage from the 0–160 cm soil layer (DP 160  ) and water risen into the layer (UR 160  ) were negligible (Fig. 9 ). The DP 160   and UR 160   values during the growing season varied from 0.29 mm to 6.02 mm and from −9.83 mm to −0.66 mm over the twelve years, respectively, averaging 2.77 mm and −4.85 mm, respectively (Table 3 ). Summation of the two values ranged from −8.08 mm to 1.99 mm and averaged −2.08 mm. The amounts of water that drained out of the 0–160 cm soil and of that entered up into the same layer were small. This result indicates that rainfall did not affect soils below 160 cm while deep soil water or groundwater was barely able to recharge the root zone. Drainage from the 0–10 m soil profile (DP 1000  ) and soil water risen into this layer from lower layers (UR 1000  ) occurred alternatively (Fig. 9 ). The DP 1000   and UR 1000   values during the growing season varied from 26.67 mm to 78.67 mm and from −89.78 mm to −43.49 mm, respectively, averaging 49.02 mm and −71.27 mm, respectively (Fig. 8 ). Net UR 1000   varied from −55.92 mm to −5.02 mm with a mean value of −22.25 mm over the twelve years. The DP 1000   generally decreased and UR 1000   increased from 2005 to 2016 (Fig. 8 ). Water exchange of above 10 m soil was dominated by risen of water from deeper layers, and its dynamics were in response to GL  fluctuations. Variations in the capillary fringe height (CF ) and SWC  near to GL  reflected capillary rise dynamics. The CF  varied from 101.50 cm to 267.40 cm, averaging 204.86 cm, within the growing seasons of the twelve years ( Fig. 10 , Table 3 ). This result agreed with that capillary water will not rise higher than 200 cm in most soils (Liu et al., 2018 ). Soil materials between CF  and GL  were wetted to varying degrees, and distinct variations in simulated SWC  were observed below CF  (Fig. 4 ). The lowest capillary water rise occurred at the start of the growing season, and the capillary force stimulated CF  to be higher than 100 cm over time (Fig. 10 ). Variations of CF  could be described by power functions with R 2   values greater than 0.95 (except in 2014, Fig. 10 ). The highest CF  occurred in the late stage, but not necessarily at the end of growing period. For example, the largest CF  values occurred in mid-October 2014 and mid-November 2015 (Fig. 10 ). Sand and fine particle fractions were 96.3 % and 3.7 % in the 260–300 cm soil layer in the desert-oasis ecotone, respectively, and those in the 250–300 cm soil of the gravel desert were 77.0 % and 20.4 %, respectively (Zhang, 2014; Li et al., 2020a ). The greater amounts of fine particles in the gravel desert soil resulted in more small pores and favored higher capillary water rise.  3.5 Groundwater level fluctuation Groundwater dynamic has been altered by the development of irrigated agriculture in the oases. Fluctuation of GL  in the gravel desert responded to irrigation of cropland in the adjacent Pingchuan oasis that relies mainly on groundwater pumping (Li and Wang., 2021 ). The GL  deepened during the growing season, became shallower after crop harvest, slightly decreased during winter irrigation from late November to early December, and recovered and remained stable until the next March. The GL  increased linearly from 12.25 m to 10.95 m from 2005 to 2016, with a rising rate of 11.82 cm year−1  (Fig. 2 ). Water resource allocation of the Heihe River Basin and the application of water-saving irrigation techniques in adjacent irrigation districts have limited water consumption by agriculture, and groundwater aquifer of the gravel desert has been recharged. However, the rising groundwater was still far beyond the reach of Nitraria sphaerocarpa  and Reaumuria songarica  roots. This result supports the fact that phreatophytes preferentially use surface soil water from rainfall instead of groundwater in the rainy season (Meglioli et al., 2021 ), and Nitraria sphaerocarpa  cannot use groundwater in the gravel desert (Zhou et al., 2017 ). Liu et al. (2017)  pointed out that vegetation was able to use more rainfall with GL  shallower than 6.3 m in arid northwestern China. Future studies using the HYDRUS and MODFLOW simulations based on continuous monitoring in the next decades will be required to evaluate potential relationships between groundwater and WUE  of the shrubs in the gravel desert. In addition to sparse rainfall, deserts are characterized by obvious daily and seasonal differences in temperature. Heat and water transfer are complex and highly coupled via water vapor transport in topsoil (Zeng et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2017 ). Driven and controlled by temperature gradient, vapor transfer contributes to fog or dew formation, and may be a critical form and supply of water for natural vegetation that could improve productivity and maintain ecological functions (Kaseke et al., 2017; Qiao et al., 2020 ). For example, annual mean fog of 132.79 mm was 5.4 times mean rainfall, and fog droplets and dew formation supplied rich moisture to topsoil in the Namib Desert (Wang et al., 2019b; Adhikari and Wang, 2020 ). Dewfall supplied water for topsoil and increased seed germination and photosynthesis of annual plants in the desert-oasis ecotone (Zhuang and Zhao, 2017 ). Deep soil water vaporized in the dry sand layer on the surface of mobile dunes, and evaporated into the atmosphere by vapor diffusion during the dry season in the Horqin Sandy Land (Bao et al., 2021 ). Ignoring vapor transfer in the gravel desert soil may underestimate water flux. However, lack of measurements of soil water and temperature in the first few centimeters of soil limited the simulation of vapor transport by the HYDRUS-1D model in this study. Increased monitoring of soil temperature and SWC  in the topsoil and of the dewfall formation process will be necessary to improve our understanding of vapor transfer and its effect on water supply for plants in the gravel desert.   4 Conclusions This study simulated the hydrological processes of GSPAC  and assessed WUE  of the shrub community based on twelve-years observations of meteorological factors, phenological signals, SWC , and GL  in a gravel desert of the middle reaches of the Heihe River, northwestern China. The Penman-Monteith equation with the dual crop coefficient approach was adopted to partition the ET  of the shrubs, and the HYDURS-1D model was developed to perform the simulation. The results showed that soil evaporation amounted to 75.56±18.38 mm and consumed 72 % of growing-season rainfall. The Reaumuria songarica  and Nitraria sphaerocarpa  community responded to a single large rainfall event or a series of small rainfall events. Shrubs obtained water from shallow soil, and water demand was fully satisfied only in the first 40 days of the growing season. Roots extracted soil water harder in dry years, and T a   ranged from 32.71 mm in a dry year to 64.95 mm in a wet year, averaging 47.39±12.17 mm in the twelve years. Annual ET a   ranged from 79.90 mm in a dry year to 170.89 mm in a wet year, with a mean of 122.95±22.70 mm, and only 39 % of ET a   was used for shrub growth. Utilization of growing-season rainfall for biomass production was more efficient in a dry year. Mean WUE  values were 0.11 g C m−2  mm−1 , 0.15 g C m−2  mm−1  and 0.34 g C m−2  mm−1  in wet, normal, and dry years, respectively. Rainfall >5 mm remarkably increased the 0–20 cm SWC  during the growing season, but did not affect soil below 60 cm. Water exchange in the 0–10 m soil was dominated by rise of water from deeper layers. The capillary fringe height ranged from 101.50 cm to 267.40 cm, averaging 204.86 cm during the twelve years. The GL  increased linearly at a rate of 11.82 cm year−1  from 2005 to 2016, but was still far below the rooting depth of Nitraria sphaerocarpa  and Reaumuria songarica . These findings indicate that available soil water is efficiently used by the shrubs, and the hydrological cycle of the gravel desert was affected by the irrigated agriculture and is slowly recovering. The rising groundwater seems to be promising for the shrubs’ utilization in the grave desert in future. Increased monitoring of soil temperature and SWC  in the topsoil, the dewfall formation process, and GL  fluctuations, and simulations by the HYDRUS and MODFLOW models will be necessary in the next decades to understand the effects of vapor transfer and groundwater evaporation on water supply for the shrubs in the desert. This study properly determined the crop coefficients and partitioned the ET  of the shrub community, successively simulated the water movement of the GSPAC, and identified the water source of the shrub community in the gravel desert in twelve years. The findings of this study provided a hydrological basis for simulating the response of the desert ecosystems to the development of irrigated agriculture under climate change in the middle reaches of the Heihe River or other similar arid inland river basins in future.
1 Introduction Groundwater is the largest freshwater resource in the world and a crucial component of freshwater supplies for human life, ecosystems, agricultural production and other uses (de Graaf et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022; Scanlon et al., 2023 ). However, Rapid economic and social growth has led to a gradual increase in the demand for groundwater, resulting in increasing adverse consequences of over-exploitation of groundwater (Aeschbach-Hertig and Gleeson, 2012 ). The continuous decline in groundwater level will not only lead to the loss of groundwater reserves but also to a series of environmental geological problems, such as ground subsidence and seawater intrusion (Li et al., 2018 ). Strictly limiting mining or recharging groundwater through managed aquifer recharge (MAR) system is the most effective means of restoring groundwater reserves (Qi et al., 2021; Wada et al., 2014; Xie et al., 2020 ). Moreover, groundwater recharge reduces the negative impacts of rainstorms and floods (Masetti et al., 2015; Rathay et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019 ). However, stormwater or other recharge water sources often contains fine solid particles, artificial groundwater recharge is often accompanied by the migration of fine solid particles. These solid particles can be captured by porous media grains and accumulate in the pore spaces, causing clogging within geological formations and reducing the permeability of porous media (Han and Kwon, 2023; Russell et al., 2021 ). Clogging problems are a serious constraint to the widespread use of artificial groundwater recharge (Wang et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2020 ). Aquifer clogging mechanisms are usually classified as physical, biological or chemical clogging, depending on the cause. Physical clogging, the most common type, is caused by suspended particles (Du et al., 2018 ; Wang et al., 2020 ). Solid particles in aquifers and recharge sources are extremely polydisperse (Bradford and Leij, 2018; Zou et al., 2023 ) and have a size range from nanometres to millimetres under natural and engineered conditions (Zamani and Maini, 2009 ). Particles and porous media in aquifers are usually negatively charged, an unfavourable condition for attachment (Bradford et al., 2011; Wan and Tokunaga, 2002 ). Particle clogging reduces the porous media permeability, not only limiting the application of MAR, but also potentially leading to structural damage to earth dams and levees, preventing the operation of the ground source heat pump system (Han and Kwon, 2023; Wang et al., 2023 ). In addition, particle clogging in porous media is also involved in the application of water treatment filters as well as channel clogging of engineered nanoparticles during transportation (Rasmuson et al., 2019 ). The clogging mechanism of polydisperse particles in porous media has primarily been studied through physical experiments (Wang et al., 2021; Ahfir et al., 2017 ). These experiments have typically involved using sand columns and tanks to simulate the transport and deposition of particles in porous media under various conditions. The development of clogging has been quantitatively assessed by calculating hydraulic conductivity using Darcy's law. These experiments have focused on understanding the interactions among water flow, polydisperse particles, and the physicochemical properties of porous media. Specific factors include the hydrodynamic properties of water flow (Ahfir et al., 2017; Alem et al., 2013; Bennacer et al., 2022; Zou et al., 2019 ), recharge water ionic strength (Bennacer et al., 2017 ), solid particle concentration (Du et al., 2018 ), particle size (Ahfir et al., 2017; Bennacer et al., 2022 ), shape of the aquifer media and many other factors (Wang et al., 2021 ). However, it has been demonstrated in current research that the ratio of suspended particle size to porous media grain size is the dominant factor affecting the location of physical clogging occurrence (Du et al., 2018 ). As this ratio increases, heavier clogging is more likely to occur. The mechanism of macroscopic clogging is the particle deposition on the surface of the porous media grain at the microscopic scale. Gravity and interception are the main effects of transport for particles larger than 10 µm, whereas transport of smaller particles (<1 µm) is mainly controlled by Brownian motion, and all of the above forces and mechanisms can contribute to the transport and capture process for particles with sizes in between 1 and 10 µm (Kermani et al., 2020; Zou et al., 2023 ). The causes of particle deposition at the microscopic scale are Van der Waals and double electric layer forces between the particles and the surface of the media grains, as well as other mechanical external forces that impede the motion of the particles. However, the relationship between the deposition of particles of different sizes at the pore scale and clogging phenomena observed at the macroscopic experimental scale still lacks a detailed description. Establishing a link between the pore-scale particle capture probability η and the macroscale particle deposition coefficient k is the most important approach to resolving the relationship between the two scales (Johnson and Hilpert., 2013 ). The surface morphology of the media grain and the particle size of the polydisperse particles are important factors affecting the particle capture probability. However, the current colloid filtration theory (CFT) and upscaling approach only applies to the assumption that the media grains are ideal spheres and the suspended particles are of a uniform size (Molnar et al., 2015 ), and the mechanism of scale transition and deposition of polydisperse particles beyond the assumption is not clear yet. Evaluating the effect of media grain surface morphology on particle deposition is necessary to accurately predict the fate and transport of particles in porous media. The deposition mechanism of polydisperse particles in response to the surface morphology of media grains has not been clarified (Li et al., 2022 ). Macrophysical experiments can monitor the main parameters of clogging development, but they cannot detect particle deposition within porous media. Microscopic observation methods are typically employed to address this issue. These methods include the direct observation of particle deposition using SEM (Li et al., 2022 ), obtaining the pore media structure through CT scanning during particle transport in porous media (Han and Kwon, 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021 ), and using a high-resolution camera-equipped microscope to directly observe the micro-modelling experimental process (Nishad et al., 2021 ). Overall, these methods aim to obtain more accurate spatial information on particle deposition. The overarching objective of this study was to determine the clogging mechanism of polydisperse particles in saturated porous media at irregularly shape. Three median particle sizes (dp50  = 0.66, 4.05, 11.83 μm) of polydisperse particles were used as the solid particles in the recharge water in the experiments. The specific objectives were to (1) explore the effect of particle size on the transport and deposition of polydisperse particles in porous media using laboratory sand column experiments, (2) determine the particle clogging patterns during groundwater recharge, and (3) characterize particle deposition in porous media at pore scale using SEM. The study investigated in detail the deposition of particles in porous media and clogging development patterns under groundwater recharge conditions. The findings of this study analysed the effect of particle size on the pattern of particle clogging development. The results of the study analysed the effect of particle size on the pattern of particle clogging development. Valuable insights are provided for the effective control of particle clogging in MAR applications and the mechanism of particle deposition at the micro-scale. It also contributes to the development of more generalizable numerical models that can simulate actual recharge conditions.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Laboratory column experiments Quartz sand was used in this study to simulate porous media. The size distribution of quartz sand ranged from 0.31 to 0.86 mm, with an average diameter (dg50 ) of 0.525 mm (Fig. 1  ). The average porosity of porous media is 0.46. Before filling the sand columns, in order to ensure uniform experiment conditions, the quartz sand should be fully cleaned through the same steps. The sand was soaked in dilute hydrochloric acid at a concentration of 0.01 M for 24 h to remove metallic impurities from quartz sand surface (Bennacer et al., 2017 ). In addition, through SEM observation, it was found that low concentration of dilute hydrochloric acid basically does not affect the surface morphology of quartz sand. To ensure that the experiment has neutral environment, the sand was then rinsed with purified water and immersed in NaOH at a concentration of 0.1 M for 6 h. Afterwards, the sand was washed repeatedly with deionized water until the conductivity of the sand washing solution was less than 1 µs/cm and the pH was 6.8 ± 0.2. Finally, the sand was dried in a baking oven at 105 °C. The particles used in the experiments were polydisperse SiO2  spherical particles. The dp50  of the SiO2  particles was 0.66, 4.05, and 11.83 µm. More than 75 % of the particles in Scheme 1 being smaller than 1 μm, more than 98 % of the particles in Scheme 2 being between 1 and 10 μm, and over 60 % of the particles in Scheme 3 being larger than 10 μm. The particle size distribution is shown in Fig. 2  . This experimental device consists of a recharge system (water storage barrel, blender, peristaltic pump), a porous media system (plexiglas column, quartz sand), and an observation system (pressure sensor, paperless recorder). The experimental device is shown in Fig. 3  . The sand columns were filled with quartz sand to a height of 51 cm, and the sand was packed wet using deionized water and manually compacted at 3 cm intervals to minimize potential stratification and air trapping in the columns. The quartz sand at the top of the column was covered with 4 cm of glass beads with a diameter of 5 mm to buffer the water flow and prevent the quartz sand from being dispersed. This experiment system was a constant-head recharge system based on the artificial groundwater recharge condition, and thus the water level at the top of the sand column was kept constant. An overflow outlet was provided 5 cm from the glass beads, and overflow occurred when the water surface exceeded the overflow outlet. The recharge efficiency was quantitatively assessed based on outlet flow rate. There were 8 pressure sensors placed from top to bottom of the column, and the distribution of pressure transducers was not uniform; the sensors were 10, 13.3, 16.6, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 cm from the overflow opening, which could finely portray the variation in hydraulic conductivity in the upper part of the sand column. The quartz sand portion of the sand column was divided into 8 sections based on the location of the pressure transducers (Fig. 3 ). During the experiment, the blender in the storage barrel was agitated at 300 r/min to prevent particle from settlement and flocculation, and the particulate suspension was pumped through a peristaltic pump to the upper part of the sand column for uninterrupted constant-head recharge. To ensure that recharge is carried out at the usual temperatures in the natural environment, the laboratory temperature was maintained at around 20 °C during the preparation stage and experiment. Unfavourable attachment conditions in the natural environment are prevalent, as most particles and media grain surfaces are negatively charged in the prevailing pH environment (Bradford et al., 2011; Wan and Tokunaga, 2002 ). The recharged water during the experiment was a NaCl solution with a concentration of 0.01 M, and the ionic strength (IS) of the recharge water was measured to be 0.01 M. The surface potentials of quartz sand and particles under these conditions were measured using a Zetasizer (Nano ZS90, Malvern Instruments Ltd, Southborough, Massachusetts), and the average zeta potential values were -13.9 mV and -23.5 mV, respectively. The electrical properties of the sand surface and recharged particles were both negatively charged and satisfied unfavourable deposition conditions. The concentration of supplied particles was set at 20 mg/L. The only variable in the experiments was the particle size distribution of the SiO2  particles, and the specific experimental scheme is provided in Table 1  . A stable chemical environment was obtained after 18 h of deionized water recharge, followed by 6 h of electrolyte solution (0.01 M NaCl solution). After completing a total of 24 h of nonparticle recharge, the polydisperse particles were placed in the recharge system. The experiment was stopped when clogging developed to the point that an unsaturated phenomenon occurred in the sand column. When the pressure sensors record abnormal variations or it is clear that local unsaturation is observed in the sand column, the point of unsaturation is reached, and the experiment should be stopped at this time. For each experiment, the effluent flow and the effluent particle concentration were measured. Particle concentrations in the effluent were determined using a priori correlations between measured particle concentrations and values in NTUs given by the turbidimeter. At the end of the experiment, the sand column was divided from top to bottom into 8 sections, as shown in Fig. 3 . Each section was dried separately in oven and the weight of each section after drying was measured with a high precision electronic scale. The suspended particles deposited on the porous media were rinsed using deionized water and dried again and weighed, and the mass of the depositional particles (M dep1    ) was the difference in mass of the media particles before and after cleaning, thereby determining the spatial distribution of the retained suspended particles in the sand column.  2.2 SEM observation experiment To analyse the deposition characteristics of particles on the media surface during recharge, the outflow valve at the bottom of the sand column was closed at the end of the sand column experiment, followed by disassembling the sand column and randomly collecting sand samples at different sections, with minimal human-induced shaking during sampling. The removed quartz sand particles were placed in a beaker and dried at 80 °C. Observation samples were prepared, and the sand samples were observed using SEM (Zeiss supra55, Carl Zeiss AG, Germany). In addition, sand samples from the sand columns of Schemes 2 and 3 were randomly selected and the number of attached particles was counted at 10 randomly selected observation positions. The SEM images were quantitatively analysed using ImageJ 1.54d software.  2.3 Data analysis 2.3.1 Darcy’s law The change in hydraulic conductivity (K ) over time (m d−1 ) in different sections in the sand column is calculated using Darcy's law (Equation (1) :(1) K = Q × l  Δ H × π r 2        where Q  is the flow rate (m3 ·d−1 ), l  is the length (m) between any two sensors, ΔH  is the water head difference (m) for distance l , and r  is the radius (m) of the sand column.  2.3.2 Calculation of deposition particle mass According to the mass conservation of particles, the total mass of deposited particles M d e p 2      in the whole sand column can be obtained by calculating the difference between the mass of particles input into the sand column and the mass of particles out of the sand column.
