The predicted values of the model are initialized as a constant, typically the average of the target values, while simultaneously computing the first-order gradients and second-order gradients of the target values. This process occurs during the iterative training phase. Each decision tree is constructed based on the predictions of the previous tree. In each iteration, the current model's predicted values and residuals are calculated and used to train the next tree. The calculation formula is as follows:(1) y ^  i  = ∑ k = 1  K  f k  ( x i  )      where k represents the number of trees, y ^  i     denotes the predicted value of the i-th sample, and f k  ( x i  )     represents the predicted value of the k-th tree for sample x i    . The optimization is then performed by minimizing the loss of the objective function to determine the optimal splitting points for each tree. The loss term of the objective function is computed as follows:(2) X Obj   = ∑ i = 1  N  l ( y i  , y ^  i  )  + ∑ k = 1  K  Ω ( f k  )      where y i     represents the true value of the i-th sample, ∑ i = 1  N  l ( y i  , y ^  i  )     denotes the difference between the predicted value and the true value, and ∑ k = 1  K  Ω ( f k  )     represents the regularization term. The introduction of the regularization term is aimed at controlling the complexity of the model and preventing overfitting. It comprises the complexity of the trees and the scores of the leaf nodes. The regularization term of the objective function is calculated as follows:(3) Ω f k     = γ T + 1 2  λ ∑ j = 1  T  w j  2      where T represents the number of leaves, w j     represents the weight of leaf node j, γ and λ are the regularization parameters.  2.3 Interpretable method As the computational capacity and complexity of machine learning models continue to advance, it often becomes challenging to comprehend the internal workings of these models and how they arrive at decisions. Several studies have confirmed that while models perform well during training, their performance can deteriorate significantly in real-world applications (Fong and Vedaldi, 2017; Rudin, 2019 ). The high predictive accuracy of a model is insufficient to guarantee its reliability. Enhancing the interpretability of “black-box” models enables individuals to grasp their predictions, thereby augmenting the generalizability and credibility of machine learning algorithm applications. SHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanation) is a machine learning interpretability technique inspired by cooperative game theory (CGT) (Štrumbelj and Kononenko, 2014 ). Its primary objective is to reveal the extent of influence that each input feature has on individual predictions. The theoretical foundation of this method draws from cooperative game theory, where individual features are regarded as “contributors.” Within the context of SHAP analysis, the prediction values for each sample are viewed as a game, and each feature is associated with a corresponding SHAP value, which represents the contribution of that feature to the prediction. Positive SHAP values indicate a positive impact of the feature on the prediction outcome, while negative SHAP values indicate a negative impact. Summing up the SHAP values of all features allows for the explanation of the difference between the prediction result and a reference value (Stojic et al., 2019; Aas et al., 2021 ). In comparison to conventional feature importance analyses, SHAP holds an advantage by not only presenting the importance of features but also explicitly elucidating the specific influence of each feature on individual predictions (Li et al., 2022 ). This aids in understanding the predictive process and decision rationale of complex “black-box” models. The SHAP values is calculated as:(4) ϕ i  ( f , x )  = ∑ S ⊆ N \ { i }   | S | ! ( | N | - | S | - 1 ) !  | N | !   [ f ( x S  ∪ { x i  }  )  - f ( x S  )  ]       where ϕ i  ( f , x )     represents the SHAP value of feature x i    , f denotes the predictive function of the model, N and S are the sets encompassing all features and the set excluding x i     respectively. x S     signifies the input under the given feature set S, and | N |    and | S |    correspond to the sample count of sets N and S respectively. In this work, we describe an interpretable machine learning approach for hydrological simulation in ungauged basins on large-sample hydrology datasets, can be represented by Fig. 1  . The hydrometeorological time series dataset from the Caravan, comprising a large number of basins, is used to calibrate the hydrological models for each basin. The SCE-UA algorithm is employed for iterative optimization to obtain the optimal parameter combinations for the hydrological models. The static attributes, such as hydrological, meteorological, and land use properties, along with the optimal parameter combinations for each basin, are utilized by XGBoost to establish complex nonlinear relationships and uncover underlying patterns, resulting in well-trained local models. In this process, the hydrological patterns inherent in TOPMODEL, derived from the large-sample dataset, are utilized as prior knowledge for XGBoost to learn from. Additionally, we introduce the interpretable method SHAP to elucidate how the parameter predictions generated by machine learning respond to the basin attributes. For ungauged basins, we employ the pre-trained XGBoost model for simulation, transferring the experience gained from previous missions on the large-sample dataset to support the hydrological model parameterization and generate hydrological simulations in the new mission.   3 Data In this research, we utilized the Caravan dataset, which encompasses a comprehensive set of data, including basin meteorological forcings, streamflow data, and static basin attributes (such as geophysical, sociological, and climatological data), derived from the latest large-scale studies (Kratzert et al., 2023 ). The Caravan dataset comprises over 6,830 basins, spanning 482 basins from Camels (US), 376 basins from Camels-BR, 150 basins from Camels-AUS, 314 basins from Camels-CL, 408 basins from CAMELS-GB, 4621 basins from HYSETS and 479 basins from LamaH-CE (Addor et al., 2017; Alvarez-Garreton et al., 2018; Arsenault et al., 2020; Chagas et al., 2020; Coxon et al., 2020; Fowler et al., 2021; Klingler et al., 2021 ). These basins were selected based on their minimal human activity impact and suitability for model calibration. Additionally, the basin attributes in Caravan are sourced from ERA5-Land time series, enabling global coverage (Linke et al., 2019; Muñoz-Sabater et al., 2021 ). The attributes of these basins can be represented by Table 2  . Furthermore, our method relies on the Caravan dataset, which provides daily hydro-meteorological time series data for most of the time period spanning from 1980 to 2020. The attributes of these basins can be represented by Table 2 . To ensure parameter transfer occurs within similar climatic regions, all acquired basins were partitioned into five climatic zones (Tropical, Arid, Temperate, Cold, and Polar) based on 1-km Köppen-Geiger climate classification maps (Beck et al., 2023 ). The geographical locations and climatic zone delineation results are depicted in Fig. 2  .  4 Experiments 4.1 Model setting and parameterization We utilize the SCE-UA algorithm to optimize reliable parameter values for the TOPMODEL. Daily precipitation, evaporation, and runoff data from the Caravan dataset are employed for calibrating the TOPMODEL. To mitigate the impact of randomly initialized parameter settings on state variables, we incorporate model run warm-up periods of one year during the calibration phase and three months during the validation phase, respectively. The control parameters of the SCE-UA algorithm were configured with a composite quantity of 4 and a maximum iteration count of 10,000. The objective function selected was the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) of the simulation results, and computations were conducted in parallel across all basins. The aforementioned experiments yielded the optimal parameter combinations' performance for the hydrological model in each basin. Due to the extensibility of these attributes at a global scale, the opportunity arises to transfer hydrological patterns captured by machine learning to ungauged basins worldwide. We established correspondences between basin attributes and hydrological parameters within each of the five climatic zones. In this process, hydrological parameters T0,  Szm , SRmax , Td , SR0  and K are used to transfer between basins. Prior to feeding this dataset into the XGBoost model, data transformation was necessary to convert it into samples and labels recognizable by the model. Machine learning algorithms employ gradient-based optimization, which can be sensitive to the scale of input data and typically requires normalization for convergence. Additionally, we integrated a reverse scaling process to reconvert the network's output, yielding the final parameter predictions. Furthermore, to mitigate the effects of uneven data distribution and isolated basin areas, 10-fold cross-validation was applied to the XGBoost models within each climatic zone. The parameters obtained from cross-validation, along with the corresponding evaluation metrics of simulated flow processes, were used to assess the framework's performance (Fig. 3  ). The configuration of XGBoost is determined by various parameters such as the number of generated trees, the maximum depth of trees, the criteria for minimum leaf node sample weight, and the learning rate (Xia et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2021 ). Among these parameters, the estimators value dictates the quantity of classifiers, reflecting the model's learning capacity. The maximum depth of the trees and the specification of the minimum leaf node sample weight are parameters that describe the tree structure, used to control overfitting tendencies. A higher learning rate accelerates the pace of iterations, although convergence to the true optimum might not be guaranteed. Conversely, a smaller learning rate enhances the potential to locate a more precise optimal value. It allocates more room for subsequently constructed trees, albeit at the expense of slower iteration speeds. For fairer comparisons in the training of each hydrological parameter, we conducted an automated optimization of these control parameters through random search on a subset of the 10-fold cross-validation, ensuring that each model achieves optimal performance in predicting different hydrological parameters. The parameter ranges included: the number of trees ranging from 100 to 1000, the maximum depth of each tree ranging from 3 to 10, the minimum leaf node sample weight ranging from 1 to 10, and the learning rate ranging from 0.001 to 0.1. We employ several benchmarks to validate the proposed framework, including transfer learning models based on LSTM and Transformer (TL-LSTM and TL-Transformer). These models are pre-trained using existing observational data in data-rich basins to develop well-trained local models. In this process, hydrological principles are provided as prior knowledge for LSTM and Transformer to learn. For ungauged catchments, we deploy these local models for simulation, where the experience from previous tasks is transferred to support new tasks. Due to their strong capability in feature extraction from large datasets, deep learning models have recently been utilized to support hydrological simulations in data-scarce basins on a large scale. Therefore, they are employed as the benchmarks in this study.  4.2 Performance evaluation criteria For performance evaluation of different models, we employ the following statistical error measures: Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), bias and low-flow bias. The mathematical expressions of these metrics can be described as follows:(5) NSE = 1 - ∑ i = 1  n  Q 0  - Q c     2   ∑ i = 1  n  Q 0  - Q c   ¯      2         Where Q 0     (m3 /s) and Q c     (m3 /s) represent the discharge of the observed and simulated hydrographs, respectively; Q 0   ¯      is the mean value of the observed discharge, and n  is the data points number. NSE measures the ability of the model to predict variables different from the mean, gives the proportion of the initial variance accounted for by the model, and ranges from 1 (perfect fit) to −∞. Values closer to 1 provide more accurate predictions.(6) RMSE = ∑ i = 1  n  Q 0  - Q c     2  n         The RMSE is sensitive to the maximum and minimum errors, enabling it to effectively reflect the accuracy of the prediction results. RMSE values closer to 0 provide more accurate predictions.(7) bias = ∑ i = 1  n  ( Q 0  - Q c  )   ∑ i = 1  n  ( Q 0  )         The bias can evaluate the overall accuracy of the simulation results. Additionally, flow rates below 25 % are used to calculate the bias under low-flow conditions, which reflects the predictive accuracy of hydrological processes in such scenarios. These values range from −100 % to 100 %, with values close to 0 indicating more accurate predictions.   5 Results and discussion 5.1 Performance of TOPMODEL in Caravan basins We conducted daily rainfall-runoff simulations in 5,764 basins using the TOPMODEL model with a global parameter optimization method based on SCE-UA. The overall performance of the hydrological model in these basins was evaluated, and Fig. 4   illustrates the NSE (Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency) values calculated for all basins. The results show that majority of basins achieved satisfactory simulations when the optimal parameter combination was obtained for TOPMODEL. Among all basins, 4,600 (80 %) basins had an NSE exceeding 0.6, with higher overall NSE values observed in the UK and Chile regions, where almost all basins remained above 0.7. However, there were some basins that did not perform as well, such as those in the central United States and southern Austria. These observed patterns align with prior daily-scale runoff simulation results within the same regions (Mizukami et al., 2017; Pool et al., 2021 ). In comparison, we achieved more favorable results in a larger number of basins, which can be attributed to data quality control and parameter benefits brought by the global optimization algorithm.  5.2 Evaluation of parametric regionalization alternatives generated from machine learning The aforementioned study obtained a dataset of optimal parameter values for TOPMODEL simulations in 5764 basins, which includes 6 parameters * 5764 basins = 34,584 features. To explore the power of machine learning in reconstructing the complex relationships between basin attributes and hydrological model parameters, we partitioned the training and validation sets within each climate region following a 10-fold cross-validation principle. The static attribute data for each basin, totaling 11 attributes * 5,764 basins = 63,404 features, were added as inputs to XGBoost, while the aforementioned parameter values were used as outputs to train the machine learning model for parameter estimation. We examined the parameter fields generated by XGBoost through cross-validation and compared them with the default TOPMODEL parameter fields. Fig. 4  shows the scatter and density distributions of the predicted and actual values of each parameter on the validation set. The predictions for all parameters exhibit favorable performance in most basins, with high-density scatter points often distributed near the 45-degree line. Significant disparities in parameter simulation are evident across different climatic zones. Parameters SRmax , Td , and K tend to concentrate towards lower values within their respective ranges, while T0  and Szm  exhibit more scattered distributions. Among them, parameters T0 , SRmax , and K shows a smaller overall bias, particularly within the Temperate and Tropical zones. Compared to other climatic zones, SRmax  in Arid regions demonstrates a broader distribution. SR0  tends to concentrate between 0.4 and 0.6, with simulated values in the high-density positions being closer to the actual values, particularly evident in Arid, Temperate, and Cold zones. However, the estimation of Szm  demonstrates overestimation in high-density regions, with unsatisfactory simulation results at high-value positions, which is more pronounced within the Cold zone.  5.3 Comparison of the proposed framework and other benchmarks in ungauged basins We conducted hydrological modeling on all basins based on estimated parameters obtained through XGBoost cross-validation. The same experimental conditions were applied to set up TL-LSTM and TL-Transformer. The training set from the 10-fold cross-validation served as the source basins for pre-training in deep transfer learning, while the validation set was used for estimation in ungauged basins. The Fig. 5   illustrates the model performance using NSE, RMSE, bias, and low-flow bias. Both the hydrological model based on XGBoost and the deep learning algorithms demonstrated a certain capability for streamflow estimation in ungauged basins, but the former showed more stable performance and smaller accuracy loss overall. In data-rich conditions, both LSTM and Transformer achieved satisfactory simulation results, with LSTM performing better, having 75 % of basins with NSEs exceeding 0.7 and 0.6, respectively. Compared to physical hydrological models, deep learning supported by ample data exhibited a better capability to capture rainfall-runoff characteristics. However, when addressing the simulation tasks of ungauged basins, the advantage of deep learning was somewhat reversed. The hydrological model supported by XGBoost achieves an NSE exceeding 0 in 75 % of the basins, with an RMSE below 7.5, and absolute values of bias and low-flow bias below 0.5 and 2, respectively. Some basins, such as those within Polar, exhibit a certain degree of error in simulated streamflow supported by XGBoost. This systematic bias may have been caused by overestimation or underestimation of precipitation forcing, inaccurate rainfall-runoff records, and the inherent adaptability of the hydrological model. While deep learning algorithms could reflect flow processes in a few basins, they exhibited a wider range of bias and generally poorer performance, indicating that this method is not entirely reliable. Due to their black-box nature, deep learning models often struggle to respond to new hydrological datasets, especially those not included in the pre-training scope, which frequently occurs in hydrological simulation tasks for ungauged basins. In contrast, hydrological models with physical constraints do not suffer as much performance loss in the same tasks.  5.4 Understanding hydrologic parameter responses to basin attributes through SHAP In order to investigate the fundamental patterns and interpretability of XGBoost in the regionalization of hydrological parameters, we quantified the response of TOPMODEL hydrological parameters within each climatic zone to various basin characteristics using SHAP values. Fig. 6   illustrates the feature importance within each climatic zone. In descending order of importance, the average evapotranspiration or precipitation-related features predominantly influence basin characteristics for hydrological parameters such as Szm , SRmax , and SR0 . It is noteworthy that the additional computation and inclusion of topographic index significantly affect the prediction of T0 , aligning with the physical mechanism whereby the hydraulic gradient of saturated groundwater is represented by local surface slope. In most cases, the aridity and moisture index rank lower, indicating their relatively minor impact on XGBoost predictions, possibly due to the physical constraints of the hydrological model limiting their explanatory power in large datasets. Across different climatic zones, parameters in Tropical, Arid, and Temperate regions are more influenced by precipitation, with parameters in the Tropical region being closely associated with terrain. Parameters in Cold and Polar regions exhibit greater sensitivity to snowfall. We calculated the SHAP value distribution of the features most significantly impacted by each parameter within each climate zone to reveal the response mechanism of the parameters to the features, as illustrated in Fig. 7  . The x-axis represents SHAP values, where positive SHAP values indicate a positive impact on the parameter, and negative SHAP values indicate the opposite. Each point represents a basin, with colors ranging from red to blue, indicating increasing feature values. For the parameter T0 , the red points of TI mostly have SHAP values greater than 0, indicating that higher topographic index values lead to greater saturated hydraulic conductivity, which aligns with the physical meaning. Low values of precipitation duration and moisture index positively impact the estimation of the maximum water deficit depth in the unsaturated zone (Szm ). Snowfall is positively correlated with the gravitational drainage lag time parameter (Td ), indicating that in basins with larger snowfall, the rate of vertical water movement from the unsaturated zone to the saturated groundwater zone is relatively slow. These results demonstrate that the nonlinear relationships between basin characteristics and hydrological parameters captured by interpretable machine learning correspond to hydrological physical processes, thereby enhancing the understanding of hydrological features. A hydrological model serves as a pivotal physical tool for comprehending the patterns of rainfall-runoff processes within a basin in academic research (Goetzinger and Bardossy, 2007 ). The calibration of hydrological parameters with extended sequences of hydrological data is requisite to achieve a relatively optimal fit of the flow hydrograph. However, in basins where observational data are scarce, the application of this approach for accurate flow estimation becomes challenging (Sellami et al., 2014 ). Consequently, we propose an approach wherein the a priori knowledge obtained from well-calibrated hydrological models on a large dataset is imparted to interpretable machine learning techniques to enhance predictive capabilities. The performance of the proposed method is explored through comparison with deep learning algorithms, revealing the response of hydrological parameters to basin characteristics on large samples. In this study, we have developed an interpretable hydrological parameter regionalization scheme based on XGBoost and SHAP. The purpose is to predict parameters for ungauged basins within climate zones, building upon the validation of hydrological models across a large sample of basins and leveraging the enriched basin attributes from ERA5. Experimental results indicate that hydrological model parameters estimated by XGBoost can support hydrological simulations in these ungauged basins, yielding benefits even in the absence of sufficient calibrated runoff data. Notably, some predictive efficacy is observed for certain hydrological characteristics parameters, potentially due to the more comprehensive representation of underlying factors such as terrain and vegetation in the existing data. Optimal hydrological model parameters, serving as key indicators of basin runoff characteristics, can be captured by machine learning methods in their nonlinear relationships with basin topography, climate, and other attributes, especially within a large dataset. Previous research on estimating hydrological parameters for ungauged basins has primarily relied on traditional regression, even linear regression. Recent advancements in deep transfer learning have enabled the transfer of pre-trained hydrological knowledge to ungauged basins. Although ideal transfer effects have been observed in some basins, the inability to effectively respond to relationships in new datasets limits overall reliability. In contrast, our XGBoost-supported hydrological model demonstrates a more stable capability in predicting cross-regional rainfall-runoff processes. The process of prediction achieved through machine learning needs to be elucidated and contributes to the enrichment of hydrological knowledge. By computing SHAP values for parameters representing distinct physical meanings within each hydrological model, the response patterns of these parameters to basin attributes on a large scale can be visualized within the context of XGBoost. The transfer of hydrological model parameters occurs within the same climatic zones. They exhibit different responses to basin attributes across various climatic zones, as evidenced by the hydrological significance represented by the parameters. Previous research often focused solely on how to achieve accurate hydrological simulations in data-scarce regions using artificial intelligence methods, lacking explanations for fitting the nonlinear rainfall-runoff relationships under unknown conditions. Combining the physical mechanisms in hydrological models with interpretable machine learning for parameter transfer is more reliable, as it makes decisions in accordance with natural physical laws. Simultaneously, a substantial volume of samples and advanced machine learning algorithms serve as prerequisites for realizing this endeavor. In comparison to the studies of Lebecherel et al. (2016), Rojas-Serna et al. (2016)  and Feigl et al. (2022) , we have chosen a greater number of basin samples and incorporated a more extensive set of attribute values, thereby unveiling more extensive and diverse latent relationships. This approach potentially enhancing the prospects of identifying hydrologically similar donor basins and mitigating the risk associated with isolated basin areas. Interpretable methods provide a pathway to gain insights into how machine learning works, separating relationships between attributes or variables and enabling people to comprehend them. This is a data-driven approach to reverse derivation to generate new understandings of hydrological signatures.   6 Conclusions We proposed a cross-regional transfer learning approach based on interpretable machine learning to address the limitations of hydrological simulation in data-scarce regions. This method leverages abundant hydro-meteorological and feature information from large samples to overcome the challenges of hydrological modeling in regions without available data. This transfer learning strategy offers tangible benefits by enabling the accurate modeling of complex nonlinear relationships between basin attributes and hydrological parameters. The main conclusions obtained are as follows:(1) The TOPMODEL hydrological model, optimized using the SCE-UA algorithm, accurately estimates flow processes in large samples, with 80 % of the basins achieving an NSE above 0.6, which is a prerequisite for implementing this transfer framework.  (2) The introduced XGBoost model is utilized to fit basin attributes and obtain optimal parameters within each climatic zone, subjected to 10-fold cross-validation. The model exhibits relatively accurate parameter estimation, aiding hydrological simulations in data-scarce basins.  (3) Algorithms based on deep transfer learning, TL-LSTM, and TL-Transformer, are used for comparison. In contrast, the proposed method with physical constraints exhibits more stable and generally higher accuracy for the same task. While deep learning performs excellently in data-rich basins, its simulations in ungauged basins show a larger range of deviations. Due to their black-box nature, deep learning models often struggle to respond to new datasets, especially those catchments not included in the pre-training scope.  (4) Interpretable methods are utilized to visualize the internal prediction processes of machine learning models. Precipitation or evaporation in basins emerges as the primary influencing factor. The response of the hydrological parameters learned by XGBoost to the basin characteristics is explained by the hydrological physical process. This data-driven reverse inference process underscores the potential benefits of incorporating prior knowledge of basin hydrological attributes into machine learning.    Despite these advancements, areas for improvement persist. For instance, future research could consider incorporating more basin attributes into the extensive dataset or drawing from hydrologists' experiential knowledge of basin runoff characteristics. Additionally, the framework's applicability could be extended to validate other data-scarce basins and regions, potentially yielding broader impacts at regional or even global scales.
1 Introduction River water surface slope (WSS) is one of the key hydrological parameters for calculating river discharge and velocity (Scherer et al., 2023 ). It shows great significance in analysis of river flow dynamics (Desrochers et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023a ), sediment and bedload transport (Meirovich et al., 1998 ). Being defined as the average changing rate of water surface elevation along a river reach, calculation of WSS helps assimilating water levels obtained from multiple measuring approaches. For instance, water levels obtained by satellite virtual stations and ground gauging stations usually have different locations and sometimes have systematic bias. In most cases it remains challenging to compare gauged water level data directly with satellite altimetry data, while water level can be assimilated into hydrodynamic modeling by transforming into WSS in advance (Revel et al., 2023 ). Availability of water level data is the prerequisite for calculating water surface slope. Ground observation approaches, such as gauging stations and field surveys, usually provides water surface elevation data with the best quality (Scherer et al., 2023 ). However, availability of ground-observed water levels can be negatively affected by a variety of factors, such as limited ground monitoring conditions (Hrachowitz, et al., 2013 ), restricted data-sharing mechanism among transboundary countries (Rahaman and Varis, 2009; Bhattarai, 2009; Lyu et al., 2023 ), and uneven in situ network distribution along the river (Huang et al., 2020; Biancamaria et al., 2011 ). This data-deficient or even ungauged situation happens especially in small river reaches (Allam et al., 2020 ), including those located in mountainous regions of river basins where there is few or even no gauging station (P.C. and Sawazaki, 2021 ), calling for the necessity of remote sensing in water level measurement for WSS calculation. Satellite altimetry was developed initially for sea surface measurement (Łyszkowicz and Bernatowicz, 2017 ). As the altimeter is working, short pulses of microwave radiation or laser beam would be transmitted toward the sea surface (Chelton et al., 2001, Neumann et al., 2023 ), with reflection distance calculated based on travel time of radiation or photons. The altitude of water surface can then be obtained by taking out the reflection distance from satellite altitude (GGOS, 2023). For inland rivers, water level data of satellite altimetry is available at the intersection points between satellite orbits and river water surfaces, namely the virtual stations. Temporal resolution of satellite altimetry data depends on the repeat periods of satellites, which ranges from approximately 10 to 91 days (Hulsman et al., 2020; Schwatke et al., 2015, Neumann et al., 2023 ). A previous case study in Indonesia (Sulistioadi et al., 2015 ) demonstrates the ability of satellite radar altimeters in measuring water level of medium-sized (200–800 m in width) rivers with high accuracy and the potential observability of small river with 40–200 m width. Satellite-based WSS data product has been developed within global range (Scherer et al., 2023 ) supported by the ICESat-2 ATL13 water surface height measurements (Jasinski et al., 2023 ) with the SWOT Mission River Database (SWORD) that providing river width and centerline (Altenau et al., 2021 ). River width included in this global dataset ranges from less than 100 m to larger than 10 km. Coding package based on R language was created for extracting ICESat-2 ATL13 virtual stations and calculating both along-track (satellite ground track) and across-track WSS along the rivers (Christoffersen et al., 2023 ). However, quality of the satellite-based WSS in global range is not fully compatible with small rivers, with fewer numbers of valid estimation exist over the SWORD river nodes. A certain amount of the small rivers is also omitted by the global-range river morphology dataset. Although the ICESat-2 altimeter has a initial along-track sampling distance of 0.7 m, the ATL13 dataset that is officially filtered based on water body dataset such as GLWD (Lehner and Döll, 2004 ), HydroLAKES (Messager et al., 2016 ) and GRWL (Allen and Pavelsky, 2018 ) for inland water bodies still fails to identify the narrow water surface of small river reaches such as the mountainous section of Yongding River from Guanting to Lugouqiao. One of the main solutions for high-resolution satellite water surface observation is to use the ICESat-2 ATL03 photon height dataset which reserves the initial 0.7 m along-track resolution and manually identify the river water surface via statistical approaches such as histogram-based analysis (Xie et al., 2023a ), Gaussian kernel distribution (Coppo Frias et al., 2023 ) and density-based classification (Xie et al., 2023b ). Instead of locating water bodies with water mask that based on water boundaries or satellite images that has been commonly used in large river and reservoir monitoring (Wang et al., 2023 ). These water surface identification and denoising methods focusing on the statistical characteristics of satellite photon heights. They have been used in sea surface determination, underwater terrain identification (Xie et al., 2023a ) and inland river research such as hydraulic modeling in Yellow River basin in China (Coppo Frias et al., 2023 ), providing reliable selection of photons corresponding to water surface. In our study on satellite-based WSS estimation, we calculated the WSS based on the ICESat-2 ATL03 photon height over 11 pairs of cross-sections along the mountainous section of Yongding River flowing from Guanting to Lugouqiao. With minimum river width less than 50 m, the Yongding River is not included in open-source river morphology dataset like SWORD or the river WSS dataset developed by Scherer et al., 2023 . The Yongding river is also the focus during the extreme storm and mountain flood happened in July 2023 in Beijing. The key motivation of our study is to verify the feasibility of satellite-based WSS estimation over a small mountain river supported by high-resolution data from satellite altimetry. We are aiming at seeking for appropriate water surface identification approaches for the challenging situation in the Yongding River with less discharge and narrower cross-section than most of the previous studies. Performance of satellite-based WSS estimation over the Yongding River would also be discussed in terms of the selection of buffer area and the natural terrain of river channel. In the following parts of the article, section 2  provides information about the study area of this research. Section 3  introduces the methodology and materials that have been used in WSS estimation over the Yongding River based on satellite altimetry. Section 4  presents the main results and performance of WSS calculation compared to those obtained by gauged data. Section 5  further discusses the uncertainties brought by buffer width alongside the river and the relationship between WSS estimation performance and terrain of river channel. Section 6  finally summarizes the conclusions achieved in this study.  2 Study area Located in northern China, the mountainous section of Yongding River starts from the downstream of Guanting Reservoir, flowing across Hebei Province and Beijing City, and finally reaches to Lugouqiao (Fig. 1  ). Water surface elevation of the Yongding River declines from approx. 440 m at Guanting station to around 61 m at Lugouqiao station with a total length of 122 km. As a tributary of the Haihe River, the Yongding River from Guanting to Lugouqiao can be recognized as a small river of which the water surface width ranges from less than 50 m in mountainous area to more than 500 m in downstream before the weir of Lugouqiao. During the extreme rainfall from 28th July to 1st August in 2023 (Mahmut et al., 2024 ), the flood peak at Lugouqiao station reached up to the second highest in history with sharp rising speed of water level and discharge (Liu et al., 2023b ), which is the main characteristic of mountain river flood process.  3 Methodology and materials 3.1 Virtual stations and across-track WSS estimation Due to the narrow width of the Yongding River in the mountainous area from Guanting to Lugouqiao, it was determined that across-track estimation of WSS (Scherer et al., 2023 ) is a more suitable method for measuring small river channels in this region. The point where a satellite's ground track intersects with a river channel is defined as a satellite virtual station. The method for calculating the WSS between two virtual stations is represented by the following equation:(3.1) WSS = h Up   - h Down    L      In equation (3.1) h Up      and h Down      are water surface elevations, namely water levels, at the two satellite virtual stations located in upstream and downstream of a river reach. Each pair of water levels for WSS estimation should be measured at the same time or at least have the closest time of measurement. L    is the distance between the two virtual stations along the river. The WSS calculated show the average changing rate of water surface elevation between the two virtual stations. Typically, different satellites traverse the river channel at distinct time points. It is challenging to locate virtual stations of various satellites that sharing the same time of measurement. In this study the multiple laser beams of each ICESat-2 satellite (McGill et al., 2013 ) makes it possible to obtain pairs of virtual stations with same observation time. The ICESat-2 satellite measures the elevation of the earth’s surface via three pairs of laser beams (namely “ground tracks”). Vertical distance between the two neighboring pairs of ground tracks is 3 km. Each pair of ground tracks consists of a strong beam and a weak beam (Zhu et al., 2020 ) with a 90 m distance in between. Under this condition each single ICESat-2 satellite can provide a group of virtual stations for WSS estimating at the same time. In this research the strong and weak beams of ICESat-2 were not distinguished between each other as long as valid measurements of water levels can be obtained.  3.2 Identification of river water surface and denoising Fig. 2   shows the process of obtaining satellite water levels at virtual stations, calculating water surface slopes and validate them. When the ICESat-2 satellite flying across the river channel, the lidar altimeter produces photon cloud at the river cross-section. Correct identification of river water surface is the precondition of accurate extraction of water levels and further estimation of WSS. Since the mountainous section of the Yongding River have minimum width of water surface less than 20 m, open-source satellite images, of which the resolutions are usually not higher than 10 m, were not able to effectively identify the water surface in the narrow mountainous river channel. Statistical methods become the first choice in filtering and denoising the ICESat-2 ATL03 photon cloud for correctly picking up the photon height on river water surface. This is because the water surface is flatter than other types of ground surface, making the photon height on water usually concentrates within a small interval, forming a peak in frequency distribution. Before applying the histogram-based statistical approach for water surface identification, a preliminary screening of photon cloud over river cross-section was carried out by selecting the photons located within the buffer area alongside the river centerline. Since there is no valid permanent water surface mask available over the mountainous section of the Yongding River for direct determination of buffer width, buffer areas alongside the river centerline which are 20 m, 50 m, 100 m and 200 m in width on each side of the river centerline were created and used in photon selection respectively. Impacts of buffer width on WSS estimation accuracy would be discussed in section 5 , and the results with highest precision were finally reserved. After the preliminary screening of photon cloud at river cross-sections, a simple histogram-based approach was used to identify the correct photon height that is able to represent the water surface elevation. For each cloud of photons, a histogram was created with bin width of 1 m, and the median photon height within the highest bin were selected on behalf of the water level at the river cross-section. Position of the photon at which the elevation is closest to the selected median photon height was treated as the location of satellite virtual station at the river cross-section. For nine of the eleven cases in this study, WSS calculated by equation (3.1)  were validated by the WSS calculated with gauged water levels. Since the position of satellite virtual stations and gauging stations are different from each other under most circumstance, closest river sections were chosen for validation. There were two special cases of WSS that requires different ways of validation. The first special case is the WSS estimated between satellite virtual stations on 20190516, with gauging stations not yet constructed at that time. Average gauged water levels during the 2022 flood season were used as WSS reference for validating the satellite-based WSS during this ungauged period of time. Another special case is the WSS estimated near ZW gauging station. Since the two virtual stations were located in upstream and near downstream of ZW station respectively, we chose to validate the satellite-based WSS using another WSS value between ZW and the downstream virtual station as the WSS reference. The main reason for preserving these two special cases is that they belong to the four groups of results which are located within a relatively steeper section of the Yongding River, reflecting the impact of terrain on WSS estimation performance. Different performance of satellite-based WSS estimation influenced by terrain condition will be further discussed in section 5 .  3.3 Data 3.3.1 River morphology In this study, river centerline was used to create buffer area alongside the Yongding River for preliminary selection of photon cloud over the river cross-section. As Yongding River is not included in open-source river morphology dataset such as the SWORD (Altenau et al., 2021 ) and the GRWL database (Allen and Pavelsky, 2018 ), a combination of satellite imagery with data from the official water conservancy survey carried out by the Ministry of Water Resources and the National Bureau of Statistics of People’s Republic of China and provided by the Beijing Water Authority was applied in building river centerline from Guanting to Lugouqiao station. River centerline obtained via water conservancy survey starts from Laohugang to Lugouqiao, while the part from Guanting to Laohugang section was created based on the 10 m-resolution true color image of Sentinel 2A (ESA, 2021 ).  3.3.2 Ground observations Before the year 2022 there were only five gauging stations constructed along the mainstream of the Yongding River’s mountainous section, including Guanting (GT), Yanchi (YC), Longjiazhuang (LJZ), Sanjiadian (SJD) and Lugouqiao (LGQ). Since 2022 another five automatic gauging stations, i.e., Laohugang (LHG), Xiangyangkou (XYK), Zhuwo (ZW), Anjiazhuang (AJZ) and Dongwangping (DWP) were put into service for water level and discharge measurement. In the research, we used observed water surface elevations provided by the Beijing Water Authority at gauging stations for validating the WSS estimated by satellite virtual stations in corresponding river reaches. Riverbed elevations (RBE) at gauging stations were also involved in discussion on terrain’s effect on satellite-based WSS estimation quality. Gauged data along the mainstream of Yongding River from Guanting to Lugouqiao is available mostly in the year 2023.  3.3.3 Satellite altimetry For effectively capturing narrow water surface of the Yongding River flowing across mountain area, ICESat-2 ATL03 photon data (Neumann et al., 2023 ) becomes the only option for accurate estimation of WSS along the river. The ICESat-2 ATL03 data obtained via the NASA Earth Data Search website provides lidar photon cloud with minimum along-track sampling distance of 0.7 m. Three variables of the ICESat-2 ATL03 data were used in this study, including “h-ph” that is the photon WGS84 height in meter, and “lat-ph” together with “lon-ph” which gives the coordinates of each received photon. Due to the 91-day long repeat period of ICESat-2, together with the requirement that we need to focus on the time points at which both satellite and gauged water levels are available, WSS estimations at 11 discrete time points were finally obtained for validation instead of considering continuous temporal dynamics of WSS.    4 Results 4.1 Virtual station and water surface identification As described in section 3 , the ICESat-2 ATL03 photons were first screened by buffer areas on both sides of the river centerline to locate the general position of the target cross-sections. Then the histogram-based method was used to select and determine the satellite water level of the target cross-section together with the position of the satellite virtual station. In this section, six of the eleven groups of the results in three river reaches with 100 m buffer areas were presented here respectively for upstream, midstream and downstream of the Yongding River mainstream from Guanting to Lugouqiao. WSS estimation stability with varying buffer width will be further analyzed in the discussion section, together with the final results of WSS for all groups of satellite virtual stations. 4.1.1 Upstream, GT to LHG For the river reach from GT to LHG station, two groups of satellite virtual stations were applied in WSS estimation. As displayed in Figs. 3a and 3b   , water surface of the Yongding River with minimum width of less than 50 m were correctly identified using the histogram-based denoising method, with 100 m-wide buffer area on both sides of the river centerline. Distribution of gauging stations along the Yongding River has relatively low density especially within the upstream section that start from the GT station. The two groups of virtual stations with almost the same location cover about 1/3 of the total length of the river reach between GT to LHG.  4.1.2 Midstream, ZW to YC Located in midstream of the mountainous section of Yongding River, three satellite virtual stations participated in estimation of WSS along the river mainstream from the ZW to YC station (Fig. 4a  ). The histogram-based denoising method also show reliable performance in picking up photons on river water surface from the photon cloud within the 100 m buffer area (Fig. 4b  ). The three virtual stations were arranged into two groups for WSS estimation over the river reach between ZW and YC. The first combination is VSUP, gt3l  and VSUP, gt1l  which is more similar to distribution of gauging stations, and the other group of WSS estimation was made between VSUP, gt2l  and VSUP, gt1l  which covers the 1/3 mid-part of this river reach.  4.1.3 Downstream, LJZ to SJD Figs. 5a and 5b    shows another case on downstream river reach between LJZ and SJD station on 20220906. In this case of water surface identification, a small pond exists beside one of the cross-sections of satellite virtual stations (Fig. 5a ), which requires correct distinguishment of water surface between multiple water bodies. As shown in Fig. 5b , the histogram-based denoising method performs effectively in identifying the ICESat-2 ATL03 photons on water surface in the Yongding River channel. In the top-left plot of Fig. 5b  (cross-section of VSUP,gt3l ), the histogram-based approach correctly distinguished the river water surface from another water surface of a small pond located on the south of the river mainstream with 100 m buffer area. This can be further verified by using the smallest 20 m buffer area as shown in the smaller figure beside. Since the satellite ground track has a relatively large crossing angle with river centerline at VSUP,gt3l , width of the blue water surface shown in the top-left plot of Fig. 5b  is closer to the real water width at this cross-section, which is no larger than 50 m. This also demonstrates the possibility of water level measurement in very small mountain river using high resolution satellite altimetry data represented by the ICESat-2 ATL03. For another virtual station VSUP,gt3r  on the upstream of the river reach from LJZ to SJD, the satellite passes through the river centerline with a relatively small crossing angle which results in an intersecting line of approximately 300 m, however it was still not sufficient for estimating along-track WSS since there was no significant change in photon height along the blue line of water surface.   4.2 WSS estimation Across-track WSS has been calculated for each of the eleven groups of satellite virtual stations in this research, showing an overall correlation coefficient of 0.98 with relative error ranging from 0.13 % to 9.02 %. WSS estimated with six of the eleven pairs of satellite virtual stations, located in three river reaches of upstream, midstream and downstream of the Yongding River respectively, using 100 m buffer are on both sides of the river centerline for water surface identification, were displayed in this section. Impact of buffer width on WSS estimates, together with the final results for all eleven pairs of virtual stations, will be further discussed and presented in section 5 . 4.2.1 Upstream, GT to LHG, 100 m buffer Located in the very upstream of the Yongding River after the Guanting Reservoir, the river reach between the two virtual stations in Fig. 6   accounts for about 1/3 of the middle part of the river reach from GT to LHG. WSS estimation between GT and LHG stations by the ICESat-2 ATL03 data shows a relative error (RE) of 0.35 %, despite the small river width of no more than 50 m and the difference between distribution of gauging and virtual stations. In this case of WSS estimation, satellite water levels of the two virtual stations locate right on the line between the GT and LHG stations. Since there are no other observations of water levels apart from the gauging stations and satellites, with the assumption that water level changes linearly at river-reach scale, results in Fig. 6  also indicates good consistency between gauged and satellite water levels with almost no systematic bias.  4.2.2 Midstream, ZW to YC, 100 m buffer River section from ZW to YC station have the highest slope of water surface along the Yongding River from Guanting to Lugouqiao. WSS estimation with RE of 3.7 % to 6.2 % has been obtained under the analysis scenario with 100 m buffer area (Fig. 7  ). Water level at the virtual station of satellite ground track 3L (gt3l) have high consistency with the observed water level at the ZW station located nearby. For the other two virtual stations gt2l and gt1l, satellite-observed water levels are slightly lower then the line between gauged water levels at the ZW and YC station, without significantly affecting of quality of WSS estimation.  4.2.3 Downstream: LJZ to SJD, 100 m buffer An example of WSS estimation in downstream of the mountainous section of the Yongding River is shown in Fig. 8   between LJZ and SJD on 20220906. Upstream water level measurement of the ICESat-2 ATL03 data show high consistency compared to gauged water level especially at the virtual station of gt3r which locate right on the water surface line of gauging stations. With small underestimate of water level at the downstream, WSS estimation of these two groups of virtual stations show RE of 3.59 % and 4.13 % respectively.    5 Discussion 5.1 Impact of buffer width on WSS estimation With open-source data lacked on river morphology of the Yongding River, buffer zone was established on both sides of the river centerline. The buffer zone was used to conduct a preliminary screening of lidar photons at the locations of the satellite virtual stations. Width of the Yongding River water surface at virtual stations varies between less than 50 m and greater than 500 m from the GT to LGQ station. The size of the buffer area used for preliminary screening of the water surface can potentially affect the quality of satellite-based water surface elevation and WSS estimates. For clarifying the real influence of buffer width on satellite-based WSS in a small mountain river like Yongding River, this study employed buffer areas which are 20, 50, 100 and 200 m in width on both sides of the river centerline in preliminary screening of water surface before applying the histogram-based denoising method. We looked into the pattern of relative errors (RE) (%) in WSS estimation with different buffer width applied, which are given in the Table 1   with Fig. 9  . WSS estimated with the ICESat-2 ATL03 data appears stability in most of the cases in this research. For river reach 5.1 and 6.2, relative error of the satellite-based WSS increases significantly from less than 5 % to higher than 10 % or even 20 % when buffer width reaches to 200 m that is no longer suitable for correctly identifying the photon heights on the river water surface. On the other hand, it is not necessary that narrower buffer area bring better estimation of WSS, as the relative error decreases with smaller buffer width in only five of the eleven river reaches (river reach no.2, 4.1, 4.2, 6.1 and 6.2). Buffer width which is no larger than 100 m on both sides of the river centerline can be seen as a relatively safe option over the Yongding River from Guanting to Lugouqiao as all the values of relative errors would stay in their lowest intervals.  5.2 Impact of terrain on WSS estimation The Yongding River’s mountainous section descends from the GT station, where the riverbed is situated at an elevation of roughly 438 m, to the LGQ station, where the riverbed stands at approximately 59 m in height. The influence of terrain on the calculation of WSS has also been confirmed by examining the distribution of reference and estimated WSS values in Fig. 10  . As river water surfaces was identified with 4 levels of buffer width in WSS estimation, results with the lowest relative errors were selected as the final outcome of satellite-based WSS calculation and participated in comparison with riverbed slopes (RBS) as shown in Table 2  . As shown in Fig. 10 , WSS estimation over the steeper section of the Yongding River, especially the XYK-YC river reach including case no. 2, 3, 4.1 and 4.2 with RBS larger than 3 m/km, has higher correlation coefficient (0.95) between estimated and reference values of WSS. WSS estimation at other cross-sections have a relatively lower correlation coefficient of 0.73. There is a slight and systematic overestimate of WSS within the XYK-YC river reach compared to the other results, with two possible reasons: (1) Due to data availability, distance between gauging stations is usually larger than that between satellite virtual stations. In this situation, virtual stations may catch the steeper slopes within the interval of two gauging stations. (2) Variation of satellite data quality can also bring slight underestimation of water level at downstream virtual stations, which lead to overestimation of WSS, such as the case in Fig. 7 . The overall correlation coefficient of 0.98 verifies the feasibility and effectiveness of WSS estimations within the mountainous section of the Yongding River with small water surface.   6 Conclusion This study aims to assess the water surface slope (WSS) in a mountainous section of the Yongding River using the ICESat-2 ATL03 lidar photon data. The objective is to evaluate the suitability and efficiency of satellite altimetry for monitoring water levels and WSS in small mountain rivers. These rivers are typically challenging to be observed on the ground and are often overlooked in global-scale open-source datasets related to river morphology or water slope. By using a straightforward and inexpensive approach, the satellite-based WSS estimation across 11 groups of virtual stations demonstrated a strong overall correlation coefficient of up to 0.98 when compared to the reference values of WSS throughout the validation process. The histogram-based water surface identification and WSS estimation methodology show generally stable performance with different widths of buffer area along river centerline, providing qualified WSS estimates in mountainous areas of the Yongding River with varying terrain conditions. The ICESat-2 satellites have a remarkable 0.7-meter along-track sample resolution, which enables the monitoring of water surfaces in narrow mountain rivers like the Yongding River from Guanting to Lugouqiao. However, the ICESat-2 satellite data, due to its limited temporal resolution, cannot offer continuous water level monitoring for the rivers it traverses. The current investigation is limited by the fact that it is not possible to achieve both high spatial and high temporal resolution with a single satellite altimetry data product. This issue could be addressed by the advancement of high-resolution satellite data products or by utilizing a combination of satellite and aerial observation methods when ground observation is restricted in a river basin. In summary, this paper provides a technical verification of satellite-based water surface elevation measurement and WSS estimation in a small mountain river in northern China with relatively narrow river channel and water surface. The Yongding River, including others of the same type, usually have limited ground observation conditions, and are often overlooked by open-source datasets that primarily focus on larger rivers. The result of this study has demonstrated the feasibility of using low-cost methods to derive accurate estimates of WSS in a small mountain river using satellite data, which has important implications for using satellite observations to monitor river water surface in date-deficient or ungauged regions in the absence of ground observations.
1 Introduction Nitrogen cycling in the agricultural soil-groundwater system is a crucial process in the global nitrogen cycle, attracting considerable attention (Galloway et al., 2008 ). In order to achieve optimal crop yields, intensive agricultural regions often rely on excessive nitrogen inputs, which enhance the natural nitrogen cycling processes in the soil-groundwater system (Sutton et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2018 ). However, inefficient utilization leads to significant nitrogen losses into the environment, resulting in adverse ecological consequences and health implications such as water body eutrophication, soil acidification, and intensified greenhouse effect (Gu et al., 2023; Buss et al., 2004; Yoshikawa et al., 2015 ). A substantial amount of the lost nitrogen may accumulate in the soil-groundwater system, posing a potential risk of secondary pollution to both soil and water environments. Unfortunately, the lack of flux monitoring information at the water-soil interface in most intensive agriculture areas makes it difficult to determine the legacy nitrogen content and nitrogen transport and transformation fluxes. However, by utilizing flux modeling, it becomes possible to quantitatively assess the nitrogen cycling process and provide a reference for optimizing nitrogen management measures in farmland. The Integrated Nitrogen Catchment Model (INCA-N) is a semi-distributed dynamic model based on physical processes that employs a mass balance approach to track fluxes and nitrogen transport pathways in both the terrestrial phase and river channel, enabling simulation of nitrogen fluxes and evaluation of key processes within the catchment (Whitehead et al., 1998; Wade et al., 2002; Lu et al., 2017 ). The INCA-N model has gained widespread global adoption due to its ability to minimize data requirements and simplify the complexity of model structure (Pathak et al., 2018 ; Jin et al., 2016 ; Ervinia et al., 2020 ). Li (2016) employed INCA-N to investigate the River Avon in Hampshire, establishing a connection between upstream processes and downstream water quality, while examining the impact of riverbed geology and macrophyte cover on nitrogen dynamics at the catchment scale. Pathak (2018)  conducted an analysis on the water quality characteristics of the Ramganga River, a significant tributary of the Ganges. Monthly data from 1991 to 2009 was utilized in this study, and the INCA-N model was applied to assess watershed dynamics, successfully simulating seasonal changes in nutrient fluxes and large-scale spatial variability within the Ramganga River basin. Ervinia (2020)  employed the INCA-N model to discern the origins and mechanisms governing nitrogen (N) discharge from rivers in the Jiulong River Basin along the Chinese coast, while simulating prospective riverine N export under diverse climate and land use change scenarios. Cremona (2022)  employed the INCA-N model to forecast cyanobacterial biomass and nitrate concentrations in a vast shallow eutrophic lake located in Estonia. In a general context, the INCA-N model exhibits a high level of proficiency in simulating the majority of critical nitrogen transformation processes occurring within the soil-groundwater system. However, currently, the model is predominantly employed for investigating nitrogen fluxes and dynamics in watersheds, with limited application to the examination of nitrogen cycling in intensive agricultural areas. Furthermore, the absence of stable isotope data input capability in INCA-N poses challenges in validating results indicated by isotopic analysis. Commonly employed models for simulating nitrogen transport and transformation processes in soil and water environments also encompass SWAT (Glavan and Pintar, 2012 ; Francesconi et al., 2016 ), and HSPF (Duda et al., 2012 ). However, the SWAT model does not account for ammonia leaching-induced pollution to underground aquifers, while the HSPF model overlooks the role of plant growth in nitrate nitrogen uptake. The INCA-N model is capable of simulating the leaching flux of nitrogen from the surface to the aquifer, as well as most of the key processes involved in nitrogen transport and transformation within the soil–water environment. Therefore, considering the available data in the study area, we have chosen to employ the INCA-N model for evaluating the nitrogen cycle between soil and groundwater. In addition to numerical modeling methods, stable isotope analysis, water chemistry assessment, microbial community characterization, mathematical statistics, and other techniques have been extensively employed for the analysis of nitrogen fate (Menció et al., 2016; Kazakis et al., 2020; Cao et al., 2022 ). Due to the distinct isotopic signatures originating from different sources, the combined utilization of multiple stable isotope tracer methods along with water chemistry techniques and statistical models (e.g., SIAR, MixSIAR model) has gained significant traction in recent years (Ryu et al., 2021; He et al., 2022; Ren et al., 2022 ). However, water chemistry methods, although straightforward and user-friendly, can only provide qualitative insights into the nitrogen transport transformation process. Stable isotope analysis and Bayesian hybrid modeling techniques can offer semi-quantitative assessments of N pollution sources but cannot yield specific flux measurements for each source. Therefore, integrating INCA-N with hydrochemical and stable isotope approaches can complement one another's strengths and mutually validate findings, thereby furnishing more valuable information for analyzing the soil-groundwater nitrogen cycle. The Songhua River Basin in the Sanjiang Plain (SRB) is a large-scale irrigation area where rice cultivation dominates, serving as one of China's key grain production bases. Despite the substantial annual application of nitrogen fertilizers in this watershed region, the extent of nitrogen transformation losses to the soil-groundwater system remains unknown, and there is limited research on both the origin and conversion processes of nitrogen within aquifers. The present study was conducted in the SRB as the study area, aiming to achieve the following objectives: (1) utilize the INCA-N model to evaluate the annual nitrogen fluxes within the soil-groundwater system of the watershed; (2) identify the sources and transformation processes of nitrogen pollution in groundwater; (3) verify the consistency between the results obtained from INCA-N model and MixSIAR model, and comprehensively evaluate the nitrogen cycling process in soil-groundwater system within the basin. This study will contribute to the optimization of nitrogen management practices in agricultural fields, thereby providing valuable insights for water conservation strategies in agricultural areas.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area The SRB is situated in the southeastern region of Heilongjiang Province, China. The mainstem of the Songhua River traverses a low-lying plain characterized by level topography, abundant wetlands, expansive channels, numerous tributaries, and substantial channel storage capacity. Prominent tributaries encompass the Wutong River, Heli River, Dulu River, and Anbang River (Fig. 1  ). The catchment area spans approximately 528,277 km2 , while the annual runoff amounts to about 985.6 × 108  m3 . The climatic characteristics of the study area are primarily distinguished by substantial inter-annual variations in precipitation and highly disparate intra-annual distribution. The average multi-year precipitation in the district ranges from 440 mm to 650 mm. Precipitation is predominantly observed during the period of June to September, constituting approximately 70 % of the annual precipitation. Over the years, the average evaporation rate ranges between 550 mm and 840 mm. The major land use types in the study area comprise paddy fields, dry fields, grasslands, woodlands, residential lands and wetlands. The Quaternary strata in the study area primarily consist of Pleistocene and Holocene deposits. Based on the S-S' section depicted in Fig. 1 , it is evident that the stratigraphy within the study area comprises Qp1 s, Qp2 n, Qp3 1-2 x, Qp3 3 b, Qp3 3  and Qh  units arranged from oldest to youngest. The lithology of the mountainous stratigraphy predominantly consists of Neoproterozoic Mudstone formations, while groundwater characteristics are characterized by clastic rock type pore and fissure water. The shallow groundwater in the plains primarily occurs within the sand and gravel pore aquifers of the Quaternary and Tertiary systems. Pore water within river valley floodplains is predominantly distributed along these floodplains, with minimal clayey soil coverage on the ground surface. Groundwater runoff is slow on account of the gently sloping terrain. The groundwater flow in the northwestern part of the study area is predominantly southeasterly, as depicted in Figure S4 . Additionally, in the eastern part of FuJin City, the direction of groundwater flow is northeasterly. The primary sources of groundwater recharge include infiltration from atmospheric precipitation, surface water irrigation leakage recharge, well irrigation return recharge, and lateral recharge during flood season from surface water. Artificial mining and submersible evaporation are the principal methods for discharging groundwater.  2.2 Sample collection and analysis The data utilized in this study encompassed INCA-N modeling data alongside groundwater quality data. The literature on surface water and the corresponding water quality data for the Jiamusi and Baoquanling stations were collected from 2011 to 2020 for modeling purposes. Additionally, agricultural nitrogen fertilizer application data from 2011 to 2020 were also gathered. All the data utilized in the INCA-N modeling are specified in Table 1  . A total of 110 shallow groundwater quality samples were collected in July and October 2018, out of which nitrogen–oxygen isotopes were tested for 20 samples, while deuterium–oxygen isotopes were analyzed for 52 samples. The collection of field groundwater samples was conducted with the aim of encompassing diverse land use types, and adhered strictly to the Technical Specification for Groundwater Environmental Monitoring (China, HJ/T 164–2004) in terms of sampling and preservation procedures. The water analysis test items encompass total dissolved solids (TDS) and various cations, including K＋ , Na＋ , Ca2+ , Mg2+ , NH4 + , Fe, Mn, as well as anions such as Cl- , HCO3 – , CO3 – , SO4 2- , F- , NO2 – , NO3 – . After being washed with distilled water, the water sample bottles underwent three rinses with environmental samples. Subsequently, the water samples were sealed on site using Parafilm film and labeled to indicate the items for analysis. The samples for metal ion analysis were preserved on site by acidification with HNO3  to achieve a pH value below 2. After the samples were collected, they were kept under refrigeration at below 4 °C and immediately sent to the Key Laboratory of Groundwater Resources and Environment, Ministry of Education, Jilin University for water quality testing. All water samples were filtered through 0.45 μm and 0.2 μm filters before analysis. Ammonia nitrogen was determined by indophenol blue colorimetric method, and nitrate nitrogen was determined by ultraviolet spectrophotometric method. The reliability of the data was checked by calculating the charge balance error (CBE), and data with CBE greater than 10 % were excluded. Deuterium-oxygen isotopes were analyzed using a laser absorption water vapor isotope analyzer (Picarro-i2120, CA, USA). Nitrogen and oxygen isotope values in dissolved NO3 –  samples were determined by the AgNO3  method. The international standard for nitrogen isotopes was atmospheric nitrogen and for deuterium oxygen isotopes was Vienna Standard Mean Seawater. The analytical error for δ15 N and δ18 O in nitrate was ± 0.5 ‰, while the analytical errors for δ18 O and δ2 H in water were ± 0.1 ‰ and ± 1 ‰, respectively. 2.2.1 Meteorological and hydrological aspects The meteorological data required for the INCA model consist of daily time series, encompassing precipitation, air temperature, soil moisture deficit, and hydrologically effective precipitation. The datasets for daily precipitation and air temperature were obtained from the Meteorological Data Centre, while those for daily soil moisture deficit and hydrologically effective precipitation were derived using the PERSiST model. The PERSiST model is a catchment-scale rainfall runoff model with a semi-distributed structure, specifically designed to generate an input series for the INCA family of models. Both models share the same conceptual framework regarding water storage (Futter et al., 2014 ). The PERSiST model is a bucket-based framework that incorporates a user-defined number of linear reservoirs, enabling the representation of various hydrological processes encompassing snowmelt, direct runoff generation, soil storage, aquifer storage, and stream network flow. For this study, three distinct containers were specifically designed to capture and analyze runoff, soil water, and groundwater.  2.2.2 Land use The land use data in the study area were obtained from the Resource and Environment Science Data Centre of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Subsequently, these data were reclassified into distinct categories including paddy fields, dry fields, forest lands, grasslands, wetlands, and residential areas. A comprehensive representation of the land use types and their respective proportions can be found in Figure S1  and Table 2  .  2.2.3 Input of nitrogen (1) Fertilisation of agriculture. Data on nitrogen application and arable land area of relevant municipalities and the Bureau of Reclamation from 2011 to 2018 were obtained from the Heilongjiang Statistical Yearbook and the Heilongjiang Provincial Yearbook of Reclamation. Nitrogen application intensity was standardized based on the proportion of arable land area, using a city-based approach. Due to the administrative sector reform in Heilongjiang Province, the Heilongjiang Statistical Yearbook for 2019–2020 incorporates data on agricultural reclamation. Consequently, nitrogen application intensity was calculated based on statistics from the Heilongjiang Statistical Yearbook regarding nitrogen application amounts and arable land areas in relevant municipalities during 2019–2020 (Table S1 ). The allocation of nitrogen fertiliser to the study area was calculated on a monthly basis, taking into account the proportion of fertiliser applied during each application period. Considering that nitrogen fertilisers are typically applied in the study area from the middle to the end of each month, we utilized the discounted nitrogen amount applied during a given month as the surface input for the subsequent month in our model. This quantity was evenly distributed across each day. Detailed calculations can be found in Table S2  (for 2020). (2) Domestic pollution A significant proportion of villages and towns in the study area lack proper sewage treatment systems, resulting in surface pollution being attributed to domestic sources. The nitrogen intensity of domestic pollution sources can be determined by combining the manual of production and discharge coefficients for domestic pollution sources published by the Department of Ecology and Environment (Table S3 ) with population data.   2.3 Methods 2.3.1 INCA-N model The INCA model contains two main modules: Hydrology submodule and Nitrogen mass balance calculation module. Fig. 2   shows the structure of the land component of the INCA model, which takes into account the key nitrogen cycle processes and includes both the saturated and unsaturated zones. The soil reactive zone is assumed to leach water to the deeper groundwater zone and the river. The Hydrological Model provides information on flow through the soil zone, the groundwater zone and the river system. Simultaneously whilst solving the flow equations it is necessary to solve the mass balance differential equations for nitrate-N and ammonium-N in both the soil and groundwater zones. (1) Hydrology submodule. The hydrological processes within the catchment were simulated using a simplified two-box approach, with modeling focused on the soil response zone and the deeper groundwater zone. The primary factors influencing water flow in these zones include the dominant residence time and the rate of flow through both soil and groundwater. The transport of complex nitrogen transformation products in the soil reaction zone to streams can occur through lateral flow, vertical movement on the soil surface, and groundwater pathways. The corresponding water flow models are presented in Equations (1) and (2) , while river flow models are provided in Eqs. 3, 4, and 5 of the Supplementary data . The INCA-N hydrology sub-module requires daily hydrologically effective rainfall (HER), soil moisture deficit (SMD), actual precipitation, and air temperature as input data. HER is a key input that drives soil water and groundwater storages, which in turn regulate streamflow. HER and SMD are the key variables controlling runoff generation for nitrogen transport and are estimated by the PERSiST hydrological model. The conceptual hydrological model of PERSiST borrows heavily from the HBV model and the INCA model, requiring only temperature and precipitation as the main inputs.For a description of the PERSiST hydrological model, see Futter et al. (2014) . Soil zone:(1) d x 1   dt   = 1 T 1   U 1  - x 1          Groundwater zone:(2) d x 2   dt   = 1 T 2   U 8  x 1   - x  2          In the equation: x 1    is the output flow rate of the soil (m3 / s)；x 2    is the output flow of groundwater (m3 / s)；U 1  is the effective rainfall for hydrology(mm)；T 1  and T 2  is a time constant (lag time)；U 8  is the base flow index (ø). (2) Nitrogen mass balance calculation module. The nitrogen mass balance can be calculated for three components: the soil layer, the underground aquifer, and the river. The module assumes that key nitrogen transformations occurring in the soil include ammonia nitrification, nitrate denitrification, nitrogen fixation, plant uptake, nitrogen mineralization, etc. Microbiological processes do not occur in the groundwater saturated zone, whereas the predominant nitrogen transformation processes in riverine systems primarily involve nitrification and denitrification within the river channel. Equations (6) , 7, and 8 present mathematical models for nitrate nitrogen associated with various processes in the soil zone, groundwater, and river, respectively. Mathematical models for ammonia nitrogen are depicted in equations (9) , 10, and 11 of the Supplementary data . Nitrogen transformation processes occurring in soils under different land use types include ammonia nitrification, nitrate denitrification, nitrogen fixation, plant uptake, mineralization. These processes are represented by a set of six equations and the flow equations are solved along with the mass balance equations for these processes. The numerical method for solving the equations is the fourth-order Runge-Kutta technique. The estimated parameters include nitrate uptake rate, denitrification rate, nitrification rate, nitrogen fixation rate, ammonia uptake rate, ammonia fixation rate, mineralisation rate, river denitrification rates, river nitrification rate. The range values of the parameter estimates are listed below with the initial values of the model parameters (Table 3  ).  3.1.2 Hydrology submodule Due to the limited availability of monitoring data in the study area, we have selected Jiamusi Station, Baoquanling Station, and Tongjiang Station as our model flow observation sites. The parameter testing period spans from 1 January 2011 to 31 December 2015, while the validation period covers the timeframe from 1 January 2016 to 31 December 2020. The nitrogen observation sites utilized in the model are the Hinnon Drainage and Irrigation Station. The testing period spans from 1 May 2017 to 31 December 2018, while the validation period extends from 1 January 2019 to 31 December 2020. The utilization of the Monte-Carlo method for a global sensitivity analysis enables a reduction in calibration efforts and enhances simulation accuracy by evaluating the impact of parameter sets on the objective function. The sensitivity parameters analyzed in this study included the rainfall coefficient, evapotranspiration, runoff time constant, flow a, flow b, and channel rainfall coefficient. These sensitivity parameters were further optimized using the Lmfit optimizer. The results of the flow simulation are presented in Fig. 4   and Table 4  . The observed and modelled flows exhibited strong agreement at all stations, with R2  values ranging from 0.61 to 0.87 and Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) values ranging from 0.6 to 0.86.
