For the solute transport analysis, the generated breakthrough curves (BTCs) through integration and normalization of measured EC data for finite pulse input were fitted to the solute forward model (SFM) in Eq. (4) . In the results, the solute front velocities (v fit  s    ) and solute dispersion coefficients (D fit  s    ) were estimated. During the fitting process, the diffusion coefficient of sodium chloride in free water was applied based on the reference value provided by Vitagliano and Lyons (1956) . In the case of the heat transport analysis, however, thermal diffusivity values depend on the porous medium in use. For this reason, the thermal properties of sand were firstly estimated by fitting the temperature time-series data obtained from heat transport experiments under no flow condition to the CPS model in Eq. (6) . After that, analogous to the solute transport analysis, heat transport experiments conducted at various flow velocities were interpreted by the MCPS model in Eq. (7)  by matching the model to the obtained experimental data based on the estimated bulk thermal properties determined previously. As mentioned in Section 2.1 , the velocity and dispersion coefficient related to the solute and heat transport for Sand #4 (coarser with d50   = 0.76 mm) were estimated in the previous study (Baek et al., 2022 ) and they were re-used for this study. To compare those parameters to the parameters of Sand #5, the experimental data of Sand #5 (finer with d50   = 0.52 mm) were analyzed in the same manner, by fitting the analytical solution to the data (Baek et al., 2022 ). In the current study, parameter estimation was carried out by nonlinear least-squares curve fitting between the measurements and analytical models. The fitting quality was quantitatively evaluated by the root mean square error (RMSE   ). The fitting procedure resulted in an estimation of the thermal front velocities (v fit  t    ) and thermal dispersion coefficients (D fit  t    ).  2.3 Hydrodynamic dispersion in porous media For both solute and heat, the dispersion coefficient in a longitudinal direction D L     [m2 /s] consists of diffusion and hydromechanical dispersion terms as follows (de Marsily, 1986; Rau et al., 2012 ):(9) D  L  s , t   = D  0  s , t   + α  L  s , t   · ( v  s , t   )  m       where α L      is the longitudinal dispersivity of solute or heat; v    is the tracer front velocity of solute or heat [m/s]; superscript s  and t  mean the solute and heat, respectively. The exponent m    represents the relationship between the velocity and dispersion coefficient and is equal to 1 for solute transport assuming a linear relationship (de Marsily, 1986 ). However, it is usually nonlinear for heat transport because this occurs under a different transport regime at the same flow velocity based on the fact that thermal diffusion is much faster than solute diffusion (Rau et al., 2012 ). In this study, the molecular diffusion coefficient of sodium chloride in free water D 0  s     was set as 1.47 × 10−9  m2 /s (Vitagliano and Lyons, 1956 ). For heat, the thermal diffusion coefficient is composed of the bulk thermal conductivity λ    [W/m·K] and the bulk volumetric heat capacity ρ c    [J/m3 ·K] that was estimated by fitting Eq. (6)  to the temperature time series obtained from the heat tracer tests under no flow condition. For heat transport, Prandtl number (Pr   ) is defined as (Coulson and Richardson, 2001 )(17) Pr = μ ρ D 0  t          2.4 Collecting literature datasets Solute dispersivity has been shown to be a function of the porous media particle size (Xu and Eckstein, 1997 ). However, a potential dependency of thermal dispersivity on particle size has yet to be examined to the authors’ best knowledge. Heat transport occurs in different transport regimes compared to solute transport for the same flow velocities. This affects the exponent of the power law for which different values have been suggested in previous studies (e.g., Green et al., 1964; Lu et al., 2019; Metzger et al., 2004; Rau et al., 2012 ). In order to compare our experiments and to elucidate the dependency of thermal dispersivity and its exponent on particle sizes, heat and solute tracer experimental datasets were collected from previous studies available in the scientific literature.   3 Results 3.1 Solute and heat transport in sand #5 Fig. 2   shows the results of fitting analytical solutions to experimental data to determine the velocity and dispersion parameters of solute and heat transport through Sand #5. Fig. 2a  provides a comparison between the measured data and the fitted analytical model (Eq. (4) ) at a Darcy flux of 14.35 m/d as an example. It's worth noting that all fitting results demonstrated the analytical model's effectiveness in explaining the normalized concentration curves, with an RMSE    of less than 0.020 in all cases. In contrast to solute transport experiments, heat transport experiments were conducted in two distinct phases: (1) a no-flow scenario was employed to specifically investigate thermal diffusion; followed by (2) a series of flow scenarios aimed at exploring hydrodynamic dispersion (See Table 2  for details). When fitting the CPS model using Eq. (6) , which characterizes temperature changes in a no-flow scenario dominated by thermal diffusion, the highest RMSE observed was 0.070 K. The derived bulk thermal conductivity (λ   ) was 4.13 ± 0.56 W/m·K, and the bulk volumetric heat capacity (ρ c   ) was estimated to be 1.78 ± 0.020 MJ/m3 ·K. These estimates exhibited errors well below the sensor accuracy threshold of 0.1 K affirming their reliability. Moreover, the thermal properties of the sand, specifically concerning diffusion (thermal conductivity and volumetric heat capacity), were observed to align with the anticipated range for dry sand (Stauffer et al., 2013 ). Notably, Sand #5 exhibited higher thermal conductivity and lower volumetric heat capacity when compared to Sand #4 which had a thermal conductivity of 3.85 ± 0.25 W/m·K and a volumetric heat capacity of 1.94 ± 0.056 MJ/m3 ·K (Park, 2019 ). Fig. 2b  provides an example of the fitting results of the MCPS model (Eq. (7) ) used to explain temperature propagation under various flow conditions. The quality of the fitting was also assessed using the RMSE    and consistently fell below 0.029 K affirming that the selected analytical solution effectively replicated the experimental results. Fig. 3   offers valuable insights into the results obtained from experiments that investigated solute and heat tracers, with a particular emphasis on front velocities and dispersion coefficients. In Fig. 3a , it is evident that the estimated solute front velocities and solute dispersion coefficients across all experiments fell within the range of 16.14 to 46.80 m/d and 4.74 × 10−7  to 1.86 × 10−6  m2 /s, respectively. Hereafter, we did not distinguish the experimental data according to the monitoring locations since an influence of the distance to the source, also known as a scale effect, was not distinctly evident in Sand #5 for both solute and thermal dispersion (See Figs. S1  and S2 ). The most accurate description of solute front velocities and dispersion coefficients was achieved when setting m    =  1.03 in Eq. (9) , indicating only a small deviation from the linear relationship. This resulted in a calculated longitudinal solute dispersivity (αL s  ) of 0.0043, determined through regression analysis with an R  2     = 0.927. On the other hand, thermal front velocities and thermal dispersion coefficients, as shown in Fig. 3b , exhibited estimates ranging from 11.10 to 34.36 m/d and 6.07 × 10−7  to 1.51 × 10−6  m2 /s, respectively. In contrast to solute transport, these thermal parameters displayed a nonlinear relationship with an exponent m    of 2.78 and R  2     = 0.719. Notably, the longitudinal thermal dispersivity α L  t     = 1331 which is higher than expected.  3.2 Comparing solute and heat transport results in Sand #4 and Sand #5 The relationship between the normalized dispersion coefficient (D norm     ) and the Péclet number (Pe   ) is described by Eq. (11)  for both solute and thermal dispersion. However, Eq. (11)  involves two unknown parameters (exponent m    and coefficient A   ) within a single equation, making it impossible to find a unique solution that fully describes how D norm      behaves with respect to Pe   . In this study, we addressed this challenge by employing the least square method to estimate the coefficient A    for each m    value. The range considered for m  was 0.8–1.5 for solute transport and 0.5–3 for heat transport. To enable a physically meaningful comparison of dispersivity across different sands, we needed to select a consistent m    due to dimensional constraints. The most representative combination of m    and A    for the various sands was determined by maximizing the sum of the R  2     values, as depicted graphically in Figs. 4a and 4d  . The results for m    and A    for solute and heat transport are presented in Figs. 4b and 4e . It is noteworthy that in the context of solute transport, A    displayed a declining pattern as m    increased, whereas in the realm of heat transport, A    demonstrated an inverse trend, rising as m    increased. This discrepancy can be attributed to the different transport regimes for solute and heat tracers expressed by the Péclet number when the flow velocities are similar. In this study, it is important to note that all P e  s     exceeded 1, with values spanning from 66 to 501. This observation implies that, as the parameter m    increased, A    had to decrease in order to effectively account for the same phenomena. Conversely, most P e  t     values were below 1 (ranging from 0.04 to 1.1), resulting in A    showing an opposite variation compared to solute transport. The most representative m    values determined for solute and heat transport were 1.10 and 2.61, respectively. Using these m    values, we calculated the longitudinal dispersivity for solute and heat (α L  s     and α L  t    , respectively) using Eq. (12) . The results, as shown in Figs. 4c and 4f , revealed that Sand #5 exhibited a larger α L  s     value (1.60 × 10-4  m0.9 ·s0.1 ) compared to Sand #4 (1.05 × 10-4  m0.9 ·s0.1 ), while α L  t     was larger in Sand #4 at 680 s1.61 /m0.61  compared to Sand #5 at 341 s1.61 /m0.61 . Note that in the nonlinear relationship between velocity and dispersion, the unit of dispersivity is not meters.  3.3 Categorization of collected experimental data As stated in Section 2.4 , to investigate the impacts of particle size and transport regime on the relationship between the velocity and dispersion coefficients, experimental data (Péclet numbers, and respective normalized dispersion coefficients) reported from previous studies (Bandai et al., 2017; Guedes de Carvalho and Delgado, 2003; Gossler et al., 2019; Levec and Carbonell, 1985; Metzger et al., 2004; Rau et al., 2012 ) were gathered. These experimental results help to strengthen our understanding of transport behavior within porous medium. Nonetheless, given that these experiments were carried out using distinct porous materials and varied experimental conditions such as flow velocity, background temperature, and heat source, it became imperative to categorize the collected data in order to facilitate a trustworthy comparison of the experimental results with one another. To streamline the analysis, the data was initially segregated into two primary categories: “ideal” (Category I) and “natural porous material” (Category N). Furthermore, within the subset of heat tracer experiments, a secondary division was introduced, separating experiments into those employing a resistor as a heat source (Subcategory R) and those involving the injection of hot water (Subcategory H). Collectively, this classification scheme resulted in four distinct categories, effectively facilitating the explanation of how particle size influences dispersion. Detailed information about each experiment is presented in Table 3  . Subsequent to categorization, Section 4  will provide a comprehensive discussion of the relationship between velocity and dispersion with particle size, with a focus on potential influences from experimental conditions, such as fluid properties, porous material type, and heat injection method.   4 Discussion Particle size, its distribution, and pore-scale heterogeneity, along with the violation of the Local Thermal Equilibrium (LTE) assumption for heat transport, could potentially impact thermal dispersion estimation. Recent studies have highlighted that violating LTE (also known as Local Thermal Non-Equilibrium, LTNE) may be incorporated into dispersion estimates under the LTE assumption (hereafter referred to as LTE-based dispersion), resulting in overestimation of thermal dispersion (Baek et al., 2022 ; Gossler et al., 2020). However, it is important to note that LTNE is interconnected with other influencing factors, such as particle size, thermal properties of porous materials, and heterogeneity (Baek et al., 2022; Bandai et al., 2023 ; Gossler et al., 2020 ; Kaviany, 2012 ). Nonetheless, the connection between LTNE and other factors influencing thermal dispersion has not been sufficiently explored. This makes it challenging to differentiate LTNE from other factors solely using LTE-based dispersion. Therefore, we focused on analyzing and interpreting LTE-based dispersion estimates, prioritizing factors relevant to our research goals for practicality. 4.1 Reviewing experimental data to explore the potential influences for dispersion The higher the velocity, the stronger the mechanical dispersion. As explained in Section 2.3 , mechanical dispersion is usually described by a power-law relationship with velocity. In this study, both the exponent and proportional coefficient of the power-law equation were estimated for solute and heat transport to reveal the influence of the particle size. Dispersion at the pore scale can be influenced by factors beyond particle size, including particle shape and non-uniformities within the porous media, which may amplify pore-scale dispersion (Guedes de Carvalho and Delgado, 2003 ). Hence, this section delves into an examination of potentially influential factors, such as experimental conditions and the uniformity of the porous media, before assessing the effects of particle size on the correlation between flow velocity and dispersion coefficients. First, the P e L    , as defined in Eqs. (14)  and (15) , was plotted against the Péclet number for solute and heat transport to visualize how fluid properties impact dispersion estimates (Fig. 5  ). As shown in Fig. 5a , the majority of P e L     values for solute transport displayed the constant ratio of velocity and dispersion coefficients. In other words, mechanical dispersion dominantly occurs during solute transport. In the case of ideal porous media, the same Sc    yielded a similar P e L     value. However, for natural porous media, the similar Sc    resulted in a noticeable difference in P e L    . This indicates that the grain size distribution and particle shape also contribute to dispersion. According to Guedes de Carvalho and Delgado (2003) , porous media consisting of non-spherical particles can increase the longitudinal dispersion coefficient, thereby leading to lower P e L     values. In fact, natural porous media exhibited lower P e L     values for similar Sc    values compared to ideal porous media. In the case of the thermal dispersion (Fig. 5b ), most data points closely align with the 1:1 line for P e  t     and P e L     indicating that the longitudinal dispersion coefficient matches with the diffusion coefficient i.e., diffusion-dominant transport occurs. As P e  t     increased, the data points shifted below the 1:1 line, suggesting an escalation in dispersive transport. An intriguing observation was that, despite the potential enhancement of dispersive transport due to heterogeneity, in the I–H (Ideal porous media – Hot water injection) category, most cases exhibited lower P e L     at lower P e  t     when compared to the N–R (Natural porous media – Resistance heating) category. This phenomenon can be attributed to the overestimation of dispersion coefficients resulting from heat exchange at the thermal front during hot water injection, as discussed by Bandai et al. (2017) . As illustrated in Fig. 5b , the overestimation of dispersion was more pronounced at lower P e  t    , particularly for smaller particle sizes (d50   = 0.41 and 1.10 mm within the I-H category). This is primarily because the interfacial (or specific) surface area increases with decreasing particle size, consequently leading to heightened heat exchange between the solid and fluid phases at the thermal front (Bandai et al., 2017 ). In the context of thermal dispersion, unlike solute dispersion, the P e L     for ideal porous materials increases with particle size, even when fluid properties are comparable (d50   = 0.41, 1.10, and 4.94 mm; Pr  = 2.95, 3.01, and 2.84, respectively), whereas it remains comparable for similar particle sizes but different fluid properties (d50   = 4.94 and 5.5 mm; Pr  = 2.84 and 0.91, respectively). This implies that, unlike solute transport, heat transport is predominantly affected by particle size rather than fluid properties. This seems to be closely related to the fact that heat propagates in both the solid and fluid phases, unlike solute transport, which only occurs through the fluid (Rau et al., 2012 ). Next, to explore the influence of heterogeneity in particle size and shape on the correlation between velocity and dispersion, we applied the procedures outlined in Fig. 4  to the experimental data obtained by Bandai et al. (2017) . Their study encompassed similar laboratory experiments utilizing ideal porous media, characterized by spherical particles, thereby minimizing potential impacts stemming from non-ideal particle shapes. Bandai et al. (2017)  carried out laboratory experiments with three distinct glass bead diameters (4.94, 1.10, and 0.41 mm) using heat and solute tracers to investigate how particle size affects dispersion estimates. Fig. 6   presents the results and a comparison of the dispersivity of the exponent m    between our study and Bandai et al. (2017) . As shown in Fig. 6b , natural sand exhibits higher dispersivity compared to ideal glass beads of similar mean particle sizes. According to Xu and Eckstein (1997) , porosity and uniformity are the primary influencers of dispersivity. Despite the negligible difference in porosity between the two media (refer to Table 3 ), the variation in dispersivity is attributed to differences in grain and void size and shape heterogeneity. These results align with previous findings indicating a correlation between dispersivity and uniformity coefficient (Xu and Eckstein, 1997 ), and the potential for non-spherical particle shapes to increase longitudinal disperision (Guedes de Carvalho and Delgado, 2003 ). Section 4.2  provides a detailed discussion on how particle size impacts dispersivity, encompassing 11 different media types. In the study conducted by Bandai et al. (2017) , it is worth noting that the optimal m    value for heat transport was lower than that for solute transport, and notably, it was even less than 1, specifically at 0.9 (Fig. 6d ). This can be elucidated by the tendency to overestimate dispersion at lower Pe   , resulting in a more gradual increase in the gradient. In simpler terms, the substantial dispersion observed at low flow velocities primarily stems from water injection, which introduces an increase in dispersion due to experimental factors rather than being a direct consequence of the fundamental physical processes.  4.2 Velocity-dispersion relationship depending on the particle size As delineated in Eq. (9) , the dispersion coefficient is influenced by two key factors: (1) dispersivity and (2) the exponent. Initially, to examine the effects of particle size on dispersivity estimates, longitudinal dispersivity was computed by setting m    to 1, and the results were juxtaposed with the empirical relationship proposed by Xu and Eckstein (1997) , as follows. As depicted in Fig. 7a  , the estimated dispersivity values exhibited a rise as particle sizes increased, both for solute and heat transport. Remarkably, thermal dispersivity displayed a similar positive correlation with particle sizes, mirroring the behavior of solute dispersivity. Furthermore, both solute and thermal dispersivities fell within a comparable range, in accordance with the theoretical predictions of Xu and Eckstein (1997) . Thermal dispersivities closely aligned with the predicted line for a uniformity of 1, whereas solute dispersivities fell between the predicted lines for uniformities of 1 and 1.68. This result complies with the understanding of heat transport being less sensitive to structural heterogeneity than solute transport, as the latter can only move through pores. However, it is notable that estimated thermal dispersivity values are similar regardless of particle size for mean grain sizes smaller than 2 mm. No clear discernible patterns emerge when categorizing the compiled dispersivity estimates based on the porous media type (ideal or natural) and the tracer injection method (resistance heating or hot water injection). In order to assess the influence of particle size on the exponent in the power law relationship between velocity and dispersion coefficients, the procedures outlined in Fig. 4  were applied to the entire dataset. In the results, the optimal combination of m    and A    in Eq. (11)  was determined by selecting the values that yielded the lowest RMSE . As illustrated in Fig. 7b , the optimal m    values were predominantly proximate to 1. Notably, a substantial portion of the exponents related to solute transport fell within a 20 % deviation from 1, indicative of linearity, irrespective of particle size. An exponent value of 1 signifies a linear relationship between velocity and dispersion coefficient, which was predominantly observed in solute transport experiments, representing a dispersion-dominant transport regime where dispersion increases linearly with velocity. In contrast, for heat tracer experiments, the exponents displayed variations across different particle sizes. Unlike dispersivity estimates, the exponent estimates were clearly distinguished by categories. Non-linearity in the relationship between velocities and dispersion coefficients, as indicated by m    values greater than 1, was only evident in the context of thermal dispersion during resistance heating scenarios (N–R and I–R). As previously discussed in Section 4.1 , the lower m    values observed with hot water injection scenarios can be attributed to experimental effects.  4.3 Velocity-dispersion correlation based on transport regime Based on the premise that solute and heat transport exhibit distinct behavior within different transport regimes at identical flow velocities, we estimated the most representative m    values and plotted them alongside the corresponding Péclet numbers. These Péclet numbers serve as indicators of the transport regime and account for both particle sizes and flow velocities. Before confirming the optimal m    values relative to the Péclet number, we examined the reliability of the linear relationship (m    = 1) for all experimental data. The results, as depicted in Fig. 8a  , revealed a clear trend with respect to the transport regime. In the case of the primary mechanical dispersion-dominant regime, where dispersive transport assumes significance, the R2   values for the linear relationship exceeded 0.9. However, in the transition regime, where dispersive and diffusive transport exerts comparable influence, the linear relationship proved insufficient for elucidating the connection between velocity and dispersion. While the exponent values for both solute and heat transport could not be solely explained by particle size, as demonstrated in Fig. 7b , these values were clearly differentiated by the transition regimes as defined by the Péclet number (Pe   ). Specifically, for Pe    values exceeding 5, where dispersion supersedes diffusion dominance (de Marsily, 1986; Bons et al., 2013 ), the estimated m    values were closely approximated 1. Nonetheless, in the transition regime, there was an observable escalation in the disparity between m    and 1, particularly evident with decreasing Pe    for natural porous media. This phenomenon can be attributed to the intricate small-scale heterogeneity within the pore space and flow paths, which likely contributes to larger dispersion estimates, as previously noted by Perkins and Johnston (1963) . Given that the pore space in natural porous media tends to be more heterogeneous compared to ideal porous media, and heterogeneity amplifies dispersion, we posit that the increasing heterogeneity in natural porous media fosters a heightened level of nonlinearity in the relationship between velocity and dispersion (refer to Fig. 9  ). By comparing experimental data from studies conducted by Rau et al. (2012) , which employed sand (a natural porous material) with resistance heating as the heat source, and Metzger et al. (2004) , who utilized glass beads (an ideal porous material), it becomes evident that increased dispersion coefficients manifest within the transition regime. This contributes to the augmentation of non-linearity between velocity and dispersion during this transitional phase. After the transition regime (Pe    > 5), the normalized dispersion coefficients exhibited a linear increase relative to Pe   . Furthermore, Van Deemter et al. (1956)  observed an upsurge in dispersion coefficients with diminishing particle sizes for sands (d 50     < 0.595 – 0.841 mm). They attributed this trend to the growing irregularities in microscale packing and particle shape as particle size decreased. In our study, we also noted the prevalence of larger dispersion coefficients in smaller particle sizes, as depicted in Figs. 4c and 4f . Notably, the disparities were more pronounced for solute dispersion compared to thermal dispersion. This is primarily because heterogeneity tends to exert a more pronounced impact on solute transport than on heat transport, given that solute can only migrate within pores. While it holds true that small-scale heterogeneity contributes to increased dispersion coefficients, we observed that within the pure mechanical dispersion regime, the linearity between velocity and mechanical dispersion remained unaltered. However, as we transitioned into the intermediate regime, a non-linear increase in dispersion concerning velocity emerged, and this nonlinearity can be attributed to the influence of small-scale heterogeneity in the pore distribution within natural porous materials. In this study, we validated the nonlinear increase of thermal dispersion with velocity in the transition regime using laboratory experimental data with sand of mean grain sizes 0.52, 0.76, and 2 mm. While sand particles typically range from 0.062 to 2 mm (Friedman and Sanders, 1978 ), our study focused on a narrower range. Conducting additional experiments with a wider variation in particle size could further enhance the understanding of the nonlinear dynamics of thermal dispersion related to velocity in natural porous materials.  4.4 Implications for thermal dispersion modeling Thermal dispersion plays a crucial role in assessing and predicting heat transport in many real-world applications, such as ground source heat pump systems (Lo Russo and Civita, 2009; Park et al., 2018; Pophillat et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2023 ) and using heat as a tracer to quantify water flow (Rau et al., 2014; Ren et al., 2018 ). Nonetheless, in the majority of heat transport models, thermal dispersion is conventionally depicted through a linear relationship with flow velocity, much like the representation of solute dispersion. As depicted in Fig. 8 , solute transport predominantly occurs within the dispersion-dominant regime under natural flow conditions. Consequently, it's evident that solute dispersion exhibits a linear increase with velocity, regardless of the medium involved (as shown in Fig. 7 ). However, when it comes to heat transport, this linear correlation doesn't consistently hold. Given that thermal diffusion is approximately two orders of magnitude larger than solute diffusion (de Marsily, 1986; Domenico and Schwartz, 1998 ), heat transport primarily takes place in the transition regime under natural groundwater flow conditions (as indicated in Fig. 8 ). Due to the limited availability of experimental data on thermal dispersion (as noted by Piga et al., 2017 , and Park and Lee, 2021 ), it has been common practice to estimate it based on solute dispersion. The findings of this study underscore the importance of exercising caution when employing such estimates in practical applications. In essence, within the dispersion-dominant regime, solute and thermal dispersion may be of comparable magnitude, whereas in the transition regime, thermal dispersion should be represented using a power-law relationship. Moreover, we demonstrate that such nonlinear relationships in the transition regime can be further influenced by the average grain size and heterogeneity of the porous medium (as shown in Figs. 8b and 9 ). For practical use, dispersivity serves as the site-specific parameter for describing dispersive transport. Fig. 10   illustrates empirical dispersivity plotted against mean grain size using fixed exponent of 1 (linear) and 2 (nonlinear). Only the natural porous material and resister tests showed a nonlinear relationship, with the thermal dispersivity values ranging from 0.1 to 10 s. It is important to note that dispersivity is an empirical concept aimed at capturing increased dispersion with higher flow velocity. Its unit lacks physical significance and should be adaptable to best represent the velocity-dispersion relationship. We note that actual field conditions are significantly more intricate than controlled laboratory experiments and tend to exhibit heightened heterogeneity. Consequently, the effects stemming from non-linear relationships may be even more pronounced in real-world applications. This is especially true for natural porous materials which consist of grain size distributions that show considerable heterogeneity. Further research is required to elucidate thermal dispersion under such conditions.   5 Conclusions We conducted extensive heat and solute tracer experiments using two distinct natural sands to explore the connection between flow velocity and dispersion. These findings were meticulously compared with experimental results obtained from the existing body of literature encompassing different flow and transport conditions. Our experiments exhibit an exceptional alignment with analytical solutions, with R 2  values exceeding 0.9, affirming the validity and accuracy of these solutions. For all collected data (including our experiments), a linear relationship between velocity and dispersion can be suitably applied beyond the transition regime (Pe    > 5). When assuming this linearity between velocity and dispersion, the dispersivity of both solute and heat falls within the expected theoretical range, at least within a laboratory-scale context. Nevertheless, non-linearity between velocity and dispersion becomes more pronounced as particle sizes decrease within the transition regime (Pe    < 5), except in the case of hot water injection experiments. We posited that this increased non-linearity may be attributed to small-scale heterogeneity of the pore space, a factor likely to be even more influential in real-world field conditions with increased natural heterogeneity in the grain size distribution. Our study underscores the potential necessity for employing non-linear thermal dispersion modeling, particularly when dealing with smaller particle sizes within the transition regime. Further research is required to elucidate the influence of grain size distributions and quantitatively assess the applicability of non-linear thermal dispersion modeling for predicting thermal plumes.
1 Introduction Groundwater has been a major factor in India's socio-economic development as it is the primary source of potable and irrigational water. The increasing population and climate change have impacted the availability of this vital resource, resulting in a decreasing trend of groundwater storage (GWS) (Tiwari et al., 2009 ). The decreasing trend of groundwater has resulted in a decreased river aquifer exchange in the major rivers (Das et al., 2021a, 2021c; Mukherjee et al., 2018 ), affecting the riverine ecosystem (Malard et al., 2002 ) and water quality (Yang et al., 2020 ). It is critical to obtain information on the geographical and temporal availability of water resources for comprehensive surface water and groundwater management planning (Tao et al., 2023 ). Water resource management requires an accurate volumetric assessment of water in each storage (hydrological variables) throughout the hydrological cycle, which includes the spatial and temporal quantification of surface water and groundwater storages (Rainfall, Evapotranspiration, Soil Moisture, Runoff to streams, Groundwater recharge, groundwater storage, groundwater pumping and groundwater leakage to streams) (Ahi and Cekim, 2021; Yihdego and Khalil, 2017 ). Estimating all these parameters is complicated due to the economic (the cost of installation, observation and maintenance) and topographical (inaccessibility and spatial heterogeneity) reasons, especially when high temporal and spatial resolution is required. Remote sensing has been the most economical and effective solution for observing hydrological variables per unit area coverage (Hakeem et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022 ). It has provided a more significant opportunity for water resource monitoring and data assimilation over a large inaccessible area at regular intervals (Tao et al., 2023 ). The Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) satellite mission in 2002 revolutionized the quantification of Groundwater storage anomalies (GWSA), which was mainly calculated as the residual of observed water fluxes or by combining the observed and the modelled fluxes (Humphrey et al., 2023 ). Earlier methodologies required highly accurate observed hydrological fluxes and hydrological models (Hirschi and Seneviratne, 2017 ). The GRACE provided the first direct observation of Terrestrial Water Storage Anomalies (TWSA). GRACE-TWSA provides monthly anomalies relative to the short-term TWS baseline (2004–2009) for a grid size 30  × 30  at each location. This resolution is too coarse to conduct hydrological analysis at the basin scale. Several methods have been developed to downscale the GRACE-TWSA to finer-resolution data products, including data assimilation and model-based downscaling (Pascal et al., 2022a ). The data assimilation technique requires high-resolution ancillary data such as NDVI (normalized difference vegetation index) and MODIS-ET (MODIS observed evapotranspiration) to fit a regression model to predict the GRACE-TWSA to the fine-resolution (Ahi and Cekim, 2021; Arshad et al., 2022 ). The simulated hydrological parameters of physically based land surface models such as GLDAS (Global Land Data Assimilation System) are used as predictors to train regression (Chen et al., 2023; Pulla et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023 ) or Machine learning models (Sabzehee et al., 2023; Tao et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2022a, 2022b; Zhong et al., 2021 ) to obtain TWSA at a higher resolution. The observed GRACE-TWSA has been assimilated with Global Land Surface Model outputs to derive Groundwater Storage (GWS) and its anomalies for large-scale studies (Srivastava and Dikshit, 2022; Sun, 2013; Vishwakarma, 2020 ). The simulated hydrological variables from GLDAS (such as Soil Moisture (SMS), Canopy water storage (CWS), Snow Water Equivalent (SWE), and Surface Runoff (Qs)) are used to calculate the GWS trends from the GRACE-TWSA (Jing et al., 2020; Pascal et al., 2022b; Srivastava and Dikshit, 2022 ). Finer-scale simulated hydrometeorological variables from the Famine early warning systems network Land Data Assimilation System (FLDAS) have shown a significant correlation with GRACE-derived TWSA (GRACE-TWSA) in the downscaling of GRACE-TWSA to 1 km resolution (Khorrami et al., 2023 ). The finer-scale local hydrological models retain the most significant correlation to the observed precipitation in an area while highly correlated with GRACE-TWSA (Kalu et al., 2024 ). The precipitation is a primary driver of TWSA and has been used as an in-situ parameter for validation in the downscaling of TWSA in tropical regions (Kalu et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2022a ). Precipitation is also the primary driver for simulating hydrological variables in a model (Neitsch et al., 2011 ). Apart from the global scale hydrological model, a local watershed model, such as the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) (Arnold et al., 2012 ), has never been used for downscaling GRACE data. SWAT has been developed to provide accurate watershed-level hydrological variables and stream flow simulation with high parameterization and multivariate calibration (Du et al., 2013 ; Rajat and P., 2021 ; Yang et al., 2008 ). The SWAT has been widely used to simulate overland processes along with stream flow routing, integrated with overland and stream nutrient transport. The integration of SWAT with different models such as MODFLOW for integrated surface water and groundwater modelling (Preetha et al., 2021; Tewari et al., 2024 ), with global climate models output for prediction of hydrological fluxes (Gaur et al., 2023 ) and along with GRACE data to calculate the canal operations (Arshad et al., 2022 ), has shown improved estimation of the hydrological variables. Integrating SWAT with groundwater flow models is still a very complex task, although required for holistic water resource management. The additional parameters impart uncertainty in the integrated model, which requires additional observation data for the calibration. The global hydrological model, such as GLDAS, provides the temporal TWS and other variables, which cannot be directly used for quantifying hydrological parameters at the basin scale due to biases. The GRACE-TWSA has been used to remove the bias in the TWS by optimizing the residual between GRACE-TWSA and TWSA calculated with GLDAS-TWS (Kalu et al., 2024; Khorrami et al., 2023 ). The GWS has been calculated from the corrected TWS, which has been further used to budget groundwater to determine the water-stressed regions. Artificial neural networks (ANN) have been used in many research with good accuracy related to the field of groundwater potential zonation (Sameen et al., 2019; Tamiru and Wagari, 2022 ), groundwater simulation–optimization (Bahrami et al., 2016 ), Downscaling of GRACE-TWSA (Seyoum and Milewski, 2017 ) and Climate Model outputs (Nourani et al., 2018 ), and prediction of climate variables (Abhishek et al., 2012 ). The ability to capture intricate patterns and nonlinear relationships in the training data during downscaling allows ML models to generate detailed estimates at a localized level (Rogers and Dowla, 1994 ). However, the downscaling accuracy heavily depends on the quality and representativeness of the training data (Kumar et al., 2021 ) and the chosen network architecture. The training data quality is associated with data management, including selecting the independent variables (predictors) having a high correlation with the dependent variable (the downscaled variable). The network architecture must be modified with optimal hyperparameters to achieve a robust and accurate model for a given dataset (Vulpe-Grigorasi and Grigore, 2021 ). The ANN has been used with the SWAT model for hydrological simulations with improved accuracy and downscaling of climate model data (Ghaith and Li, 2020; Pradhan et al., 2020 ), but it has never been used for the downscaling of GRACE data with SWAT HRU variables as independent variables. A holistic methodology for integrated water resource management using the SWAT model outputs and GWS has been presented. The GWS has been calculated through downscaling and bias correction of GLDAS-TWS using an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) model with GRACE-TWSA. This ANN model was trained with GRACE-TWSA, ensuring a refined and more accurate estimation of Groundwater Storage. The calculated GWS has been downscaled to the HRU level by another ANN model, utilizing the simulated hydrological variables of the SWAT model of the Lower Middle Ganga Basin (LMGB). The main objectives covered in this research work are as follows.I. Determination of GWS using GRACE-TWSA  II. Downscaling of GWS to HRU level with ANN  III. Determination of groundwater level with downscaled GWS  IV. Determination of specific yield for the HRUs  V. Surface water and Groundwater budgeting at the block (district subdivision) level     2 Study area The lower middle Ganga basin from Prayagraj to Varanasi has been taken as the study area (Fig. 1  ). It ranges from 80.46° E to 83.12° E and 24.12°N to 25.66°N, covering an area of 25,668 Km2 . Apart from the Ganga, the area is covered by two major tributaries- Tons and Varuna River. Tons has the most significant watershed area, around 17,535 Km2,  while the Varuna River covers 3346 Km2  of the basin area. The area is covered by a high density of low-order streams, providing adequate drainage to the Ganga River during storm events. The primary land use is agriculture, which covers 68.5 % of the study area. The Vindhyan rock is underlain by fertile alluvium. The forest covers 12.6 % of the land, mainly limited to the hilly areas in Mirzapur, Satna and Rewa districts. 8.9 % of the area is either bare soil or barren land. The geology of the study area can be broadly divided into Alluvium and Vindhyan groups. The north part of the area (Varanasi, Jaunpur, Sant Ravidas Nagar, northern part of Mirzapur and Prayagraj) contains quaternary alluvium consisting of older and younger alluvium, deposited on the weathered bedrock of Vindhyan supergroup. The newer alluvium mainly consists of clayey sand with Kankar, while the older alluvium is fairly consolidated clay with Kankar and fine to medium sand with some gravel. As we move towards the Southwest, the outcrops of upper Vindhyan become visible, covering the Mirzapur, Rewa, and Satna districts. The Vindhyan group in Mirzapur is represented by fine to medium-grained Kaimur sandstone or quartzite and is highly jointed. In the Satna and Rewa districts, the Vindhyan is overlain by shale. Groundwater occurs within the primary porosity of alluvial sediments; here, the aquifer materials are medium to coarse-grained sand. Shallow aquifers exist in unconfined conditions, whereas deeper aquifers exist in semi-confined and confined conditions. Groundwater in the widely covered Vindhyan Plateau region occurs primarily unconfined within the formation's secondary porosity. However, exploration data suggest that Kaimur sandstone has sufficient groundwater potential at depths. After the leaching of cementing material, these sandstones disintegrate and reduce to silica sand, which acts as a promising groundwater repository. The area covered by shale is found to have reasonable secondary porosity development and a moderate prospect of groundwater occurrence. In the northern and eastern parts of the Vindhyan region, the aquifers are mainly of an alluvium nature. The groundwater development practices are mainly limited to the first unconfined and second semi-confined aquifer layers. The study area can be divided into two parts based on the elevation and climatic conditions: the Vindhyan region and the Gangetic plain. The high-elevated area of Vindhyan, combining parts of Mirzapur, Rewa and Satna, has high annual average rainfall and temperature compared to the low-elevated Gangetic plain. The average annual rainfall observed from 2001 to 2014 in the lower Vindhyan region was 1016 mm, while in the Gangetic plain, it was 829 mm.  3 Datasets We used different data streams, including satellite observations, model outputs, and ground-based observational data, to downscale GRACE-derived GWS to HRU-GWS. Details of data used in the current study are provided below and summarised in Table 1  . 3.1 GRACE-TWSA Terrestrial water storage (TWS) is a term used to represent the summation of all surface and subsurface water. It integrates soil moisture, groundwater, root zone soil moisture, snow/ice, river water, lake water, and vegetation storage (Girotto and Rodell, 2019 ). Given that GWS represents groundwater storage, SWE is snow water equivalent, LIS represents land ice, CWS is canopy water, SMS is water as soil moisture, and Qs is water available as surface water, the TWS is expressed as(3.1) TWS = G W S + S W E + L I S + C W S + S M S + Q s     The TWS varies due to an imbalance in the major hydrological fluxes, such as rainfall, evapotranspiration, groundwater extraction, glacier melt, etc. TWS fluctuation occurs throughout a broad spectrum of natural climatic variability and human activities. These include droughts and floods as transitory extreme occurrences and seasonal, decadal, and inter-annual changes caused by high groundwater extraction and glacial mass loss. Because it combines variations in all water fluxes and responds to feedback from atmospheric and oceanic variability, TWS is an essential long-term memory variable for the water cycle and the Earth system. Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) has been monitoring the TWS Anomalies (TWSA) since 2002 by measuring the time-varying anomalies in the earth's gravity (Humphrey et al., 2023 ). After the GRACE ended its science mission in October 2017, the GRACE Follow-on (GRACE-FO) has been collecting the TWSA. GRACE-TWSA provide vertical estimates of monthly anomalies relative to the short-term (Jan 2004- Dec 2009) TWS baseline at each location, with a spatial resolution of 330Km × 330Km. The monthly JPL-mascon (Mass concentration blocks) TWSA product is provided with 0.50  × 0.50  resolution (≈55Km), although the effective resolution is 30  × 30 . The product has been corrected for GIA (Glacial Isostatic Adjustment) and ocean/land leakage, so it does not require additional filtering or signal leakage correction (Save et al., 2016; Vishwakarma, 2020 ). The JPL-mascon data has shown less residual in the long-term trends for the Ganga River Basin than CSR-mascon data compared to the CSR Tellus gridded spherical harmonics rescaled data (Scanlon et al., 2016 ). Although the CSR-mascon data is of higher resolution than JPL-mascon, it under estimates the decreasing trends of TWSA in the Ganga River Basin, and hence, we used the JPL-mascon data in this study.  3.2 GLDAS outputs The GLDAS aims to create optimal fields of land surface states and fluxes by ingesting satellite and ground-based observational data products using sophisticated land surface modelling and data assimilation techniques (Rodell et al., 2004 ). The unrealistic model states are curbed by data assimilation with satellite-based observation on the Land Surface Model (LSM) developed with ground-based measurements of forcing data. The general water balance components related to surface and subsurface (SMS, CWS, Qs) have been used in the study for downscaling and calculating GWS.  3.3 Environmental variables The independent environmental variables are used as predictors for the ANN model. For downscaling the GRACE TWSA to 0.25° spatial resolution, soil moisture (SMS), plant canopy surface water (CWS), and Storm surface runoff (Qs) from the GLDAS outputs have been used, as the Pearson's correlation coefficient for these parameters were most significant. For further downscaling the GWS to HRUs scale, the nine outputs of the SWAT model with a correlation greater than 0.5 have been used as predictors. Table 2   summarises the relationships and equations used to simulate these HRU variables in SWAT. These variables are directly correlated to the groundwater storage as source (PRECIPmm, PERCmm, DA_RCHmm ) or sink (PETmm, REVAPmm, SURQ_CNTmm, GW_Qmm, WYLD_Qmm ). The spatial resolution of HRUs varies from 0.75 Km2  to 480 Km2 .  3.4 Ground-based measurements Pre- and post-monsoon groundwater level data has been collected from the Uttar Pradesh Water Resource Department and Madhya Pradesh Water Resource Department for 257 monitoring wells (measured corresponding to pre- or post-monsoon season from 2001 to 2012). As GRACE-derived GWSA cannot be directly compared with the water level fluctuations, we calculated the groundwater level anomalies with respect to the short-term baseline (mean GWL for the years 2004 to 2009), similar to the GWSA.(3.2) GWL A i  = G W L i  - GWL  ¯       Where GWLA  is the groundwater level anomalies at time step 'i ' and GWL  ¯     is the short-term average (2004–2009). The anomaly in the downscaled GWS with respect to the baseline has been compared to the GWLA to assess their correlation. The GWLA has also been utilized to calculate the Specific yield (Sy  ) by robust optimization. River discharge data from two gauging stations (Prayagraj and Varanasi) has been collected from the Central Water Commission. The data has been utilized for the inlet discharge data for the upstream watershed and calibration of the SWAT model.  3.5 Ancillary data The land use data has been derived from the Landsat 8 multi-spectral images using the random forest classification algorithm. The area has been classified into major land use classes (water body, Agricultural area, vegetation, barren land and built-up area) for SWAT simulation. The FAO Soil database was used as the soil parameters in the SWAT model. Apart from the measured river flow, the MODIS 8 days cumulative evapotranspiration and the observed reservoir dynamic storage volume have been used as calibration datasets. The five subbasins have been selected across the study area, and the mean monthly evapotranspiration has been downloaded from “AppEEARS” (Table 1 ).   4 Methods The downscaling of GWS to HRU-scale has been presented in two stages (Fig. 2  ). The first stage incorporates the ANN model to correct the bias in the GLDAS-TWS (resolution 0.250 ) using GRACE-TWSA (resolution 0.50 ). The TWSA from GLDAS (GLDAS-TWSA) has been calculated by isolating the baseline TWS (mean from 2004 to 2009). The calculated GLDAS-TWSA has been aggregated to the GRACE-TWSA to train the ANN model, and the trained model was used to determine the TWSA at 0.250  resolution by disaggregation. The baseline TWS has been added to the predicted TWSA to determine the corrected TWS. The GWS has been calculated by subtracting the Qs and SMS from the corrected TWS. In the second stage, the GWS is downscaled to the HRU scale by another ANN model, which has been trained with HRU variables as predictors aggregated to the 0.250  resolution. Further, the application of downscaled GWS has been discussed for (a) the determination of the groundwater levels (GWL) at a finer scale, (b)the determination of Specific Yield (Sy ) by robust optimization and (c) the holistic budgeting of surface water and groundwater by assimilating the observation, downscaled and simulated data. 4.1 Surface water model The hydrological parameters for downscaling the GWS to the HRU scale have been simulated in the SWAT model (Arnold, J. et al., 2012). The SWAT is a physically based, distributed hydrological model used to analyze watersheds at the basin scale. It uses physical relationships to simulate various hydrological processes within a river basin, such as rainfall-runoff, sediment transport, and nutrient cycle. The water balance is the main driving force in SWAT for simulating every process (sediment and nutrient transport). The hydrological simulation of the watershed has been carried out in two phases. The first was the land phase of the hydrologic cycle, and the second was the routing phase, which defines the movement of water, sediments, and nutrients in the stream network. The land phase of the hydrologic cycle is based on the water balance equation:(4.1) SW  t  = SW  0  + ∑ i = 1  t  R day   - Q surf   - E a  - w seep   - Q gw         Where SWt   is the final soil water content (mm), SW0   is the initial soil water content (mm), t  is the time (days), Rday   is the amount of precipitation on the day i  (mm), Qsurf   is the amount of surface runoff on the day i  (mm), Ea   is the amount of evapotranspiration on the day i  (mm), wseep   is the amount of percolation and bypass flow exiting the soil profile bottom, on the day i  (mm), and Qgw   is the amount of return flow on the day i  (mm). All the units are represented in the equivalent water depth in mm. SWAT modelling simulates two aquifers within each subbasin: an unconfined, shallow aquifer that contributes to the subbasin's main channel flow and a confined deep aquifer which is assumed to affect streamflow beyond the watershed boundaries (Neitsch et al., 2011 ). An aquifer percolation coefficient routes a fraction of the shallow recharge to the deep aquifer in each time step. A revap coefficient partitions the water in shallow aquifers to move in the plant root zone in response to groundwater deficiency. The overall budget of the groundwater module of SWAT is given as (Neitsch et al., 2011 ).(4.2) a q sh , i   = a q sh , i - 1   + ( 1 - β deep   ) w  rchg   - Q gw   - w revap   - w pump       Where aqsh,i   is the amount of water stored in the shallow aquifer on day i  (mm), aqsh,i-1   is the amount of water stored in the shallow aquifer on day i-1  (mm), β deep     is the deep aquifer percolation coefficient, wrchrg   is the amount of recharge on day i  (mm), Qgw   is the base flow on day i  (mm), wrevap   is the amount of water moving into the soil zone in response to water deficiencies on day i  (mm), and wpump   is the amount of water removed from the shallow aquifer by pumping for irrigation on day i  (mm). 4.1.1 Model setup The SWAT Model for the 247 km Lower Middle Ganga Basin stretch from the City of Prayagraj to Varanasi has been prepared using the ArcSWAT interface. The one arc-second (∼30-meter resolution) SRTM DEM has been used to delineate the watershed and the streams. A threshold value of 5000 ha has been used to define the flow accumulation, delineating 293 watersheds in the basin. The land use, soil, and slope data have been reclassified in accordance with the determination of their unique combination for HRU delineation (Fig. 3  ). Multiple HRUs (1741) have been defined based on dominant features (land use, soil, or slope). Weather inputs (daily rainfall and temperature) have been processed within the weather generator module with IMD 2D gridded data from 1998 to 2014. The PET has been calculated with Hargreaves's method (Hargreaves and Samani, 1985 ), as it has shown better simulation results in previous studies with available temperature data (Itenfisu et al., 2003 ). The inlet discharge at the Prayagraj has been defined to account for the discharge from the watershed upstream of the selected reach of the Ganga River (Fig. 3 ). The six major reservoirs have been defined in the model, and their corresponding properties have been updated in the input files (Table 3  ). Before automatic calibration, the seepage co-efficient has been manually calibrated to match the stream flow and reservoir volume. The detailed modelling approach of reservoirs can be found in the theoretical documentation of SWAT (Neitsch et al., 2011 ). The irrigation requirement is the major cause of groundwater draft in the area (CGWB, 2017 ). The majority of the irrigation is dependent on groundwater in the study area (Khan and Singh, 2017 ). The irrigation has been modelled with auto irrigation in SWAT management operations. Irrigation in an HRU is applied automatically when plant water stress exceeds a specified threshold value. The deep aquifer has been selected as the source of irrigation in each HRU. The model has been set up for the monthly simulation with a 3-year warmup period.  4.1.2 Calibration The SWAT model has been calibrated with multiple datasets (monthly river discharge, monthly reservoir volume, and evapotranspiration). The river discharge at Varanasi gauge station has been taken as the target variable for cumulative flow. The monthly reservoir volume was available for the Jirgo dam and has been used as calibration data. The monthly evapotranspiration has been derived from the 8-day cumulative evapotranspiration product (MOD16), for the five sample subbasins (Fig. 1 ) are used as calibration targets (Koltsida and Kallioras, 2022 ). The Sequential Uncertainty Fitting (SUFI-2) algorithm in SWAT-CUP (Abbaspour, 2019 ) has been used to calibrate the model with Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) as the objective function. A total 21 of the most sensitive parameters have been calibrated. The parameter ranks, based on sensitivity, have been presented in Table 4  . The uncertainties resulting from simplified models, processes not included in the model, and processes the modeller is unaware of make the calibration process difficult (Abbaspour et al., 2007 ). The modelling of the given study area has uncertainties due to (1) the accuracy of input data, (2) groundwater pumping for irrigation and domestic use, (3) biases in observed data and (4) unknown processes such as river water abstraction. The calibration using a single variable can introduce bias in other hydrological fluxes (Abbaspour, 2019 ). The multiple variables (River flow, evapotranspiration, and reservoir volume) were used during the calibration, and the performance was evaluated using NSE and R2 . The overall performance of the fitted parameters is satisfactory, as presented in Fig. 4  .   4.2 Calculation of GWS TWS is a function of other water cycle components (Eq.3.1), which can be used to calculate other components when observed data is available (Rodell et al., 2009 ). Groundwater Storage (GWS) is a major component of TWS , representing the aquifers' available groundwater. The model architecture and hyperparameters for both stages have been selected differently based on the dataset involved. To avoid confusion, the ANN model used for first stage is termed ANN1 and for the second stage, ANN2. In both stages, the individual model has been trained for each large-scale grid (22 ANN1 models for the first stage and 65 ANN2 models for the second stage). In the first stage, the ANN1 has been used to downscale the GRACE-TWSA to the GLDAS scale to calculate GWS (Eq (4.5)  . The predictors from GLDAS have been aggregated (by taking the mean of the GLDAS grids overlain by GRACE) to the 0.50  resolution to train the ANN model (ANN1 in Fig. 2 ). All the hyperparameters have been fixed for each grid, except for the number of neurons, which has been adjusted for best accuracy (Table 5  ). In the second stage, the GWS was downscaled to the HRUs. The predictors from HRUs have been aggregated to the GLDAS grid by calculating the area-weighted average (Eq. (4.7) .(4.7) va r HRU , i   = 1 ∑ j  N  A j    ∑ j  N  V j , i   A j      Where va r HRU , i      is the value of the HRU predictor at time step i  (Table 2 ), N is the number of HRU under the GWS grid (0.250  × 0.250 ), Aj   is the area of the jth  HRU which intersects the GLDAS grid, and Vj,i   is the predictor value of jth  HRU at time step i.  The HRU area intersected by GLDAS grid boundaries has been determined in GIS with the intersect tool. After this, the aggregated predictor HRU variables were prepared and used for model training. Each ANN2 model was trained with the aggregated values as the independent variable and GWS as the dependent variable. The model's hyperparameters have been tuned for best accuracy (Fig. 5  ). The Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) and coefficient of determination (R2 ) were used to assess the model's accuracy during training and testing. After testing the model, the GWS has been predicted for each HRU within the GLDAS grid. The GWS for HRUs on the boundary of adjacent GLDAS grids (which has been separated during the training) has been combined by taking area-weighted mean (i.e. The multiple predicted values of common HRUs due to prediction at each grid have been aggregated by area-weighted average).  4.4 Determination of Sy  with regularized robust optimization According to (Fetter, 2001 ), the GWS change (in terms of equivalent water thickness) can be related to the mean hydraulic head change (Δ h   ) as(4.8) Δ G W S = 1 C  ∑ j  M  S j  C j  Δ h j  , C = ∑ j  M  C j      Where M  is the number of subareas of the aquifer, Cj   is the size of subareas j , and Sj   is the Specific Yield (Sy  ) of subarea j . There are M  number of observation wells in an HRU. The area of the HRU has been divided by the Thiessen polygon method corresponding to each observation well. Eq. (4.8)  can be rewritten for downscaled GWSA as a linear system with Sy   as spatially distributed unknowns for an unconfined aquifer system (Sun et al., 2010 )(4.9) GWSA ≈ 1 C  ∑ j  M  S j  C j  GWLA  j      Or equivalently(4.10) A  x  ≈ b      Where rows of A  correspond to the average GWLA (area-weighted) for the i-th  timestep, and the columns correspond to the HRU. The x  represents the unknown Sy   for the HRU, and rows of b represent the GWSA for the i-th  timestep for the corresponding HRU (column). The solution of the Eq (4.10)  is often given by least square regression. Here, A and b are both uncertain due to measurement errors, and the distribution of the errors is not necessarily Gaussian. To overcome this problem, Sun et al., 2010  proposed a robust optimization method to minimize the worst-case bounds based on user-defined uncertainty. The robust optimization approach is less sensitive to outliers than the standard least square regression (Massart et al., 1986 ). We formulated a robust optimization problem in which the robust solution to Eq (4.10)  is obtained within the constraints of possible realization based on data uncertainty (Sun et al., 2010 ). The Huber loss function compromises the squared loss (least square regression) for small residuals and the absolute loss for large residuals. To constrain the spatial uniformity of the solutions, the Tikhonov regularization (Ridge regularisation)(Hilt et al., 1977 ) has been added to the objective function to improve the stability further. The objective function for robust optimization with Huber loss and Tikhonov regularisation is given as(4.11) O b j e c t i v e x , A , b , δ , λ   = m i n ∑ i = 1  N  L δ  y i  - y ^  i    + λ ∑ j = 1  M  x j  2        Where λ   is the regularisation parameter; y i  a n d y ^  i     are observed and predicted GWSA; δ   is the Huber loss parameter, and the Huber loss function (L δ   ) is given as(4.12) L δ  = 1 2  r 2   f o r r  ≤ δ   δ r  - 1 2  δ    f o r r  > δ        Where r  is the residual between observed and predicted GWSA. The Eq (4.11)  has been solved in Python with the scipy library.  4.5 Error metrices NSE  and R2   have been used to measure the model's accuracy. The NSE was used as the objective function during the calibration and validation of the SWAT Model. The ANN Models were assessed for their prediction accuracy with NSE  and R2  . The bias in the TWS of the GLDAS outputs has been corrected with GRACE-TWSA, and GWS was calculated at GLDAS resolution. The GWS was further downscaled to HRUs using the SWAT hydrological variables as predictors. The downscaled resolution is dependent on the scale of SWAT model development. Even finer resolutions of up to 900 m2  can be achieved by taking the lower threshold for HRU delineation. The finest resolution corresponds to the least resolution data (DEM, land use, and soil) used for the HRU delineation. The threshold number of cells required for flow generation can be adjusted to generate smaller HRUs. However, a step-wise process is recommended such that a second SWAT model for smaller areas is developed, and the GWS is further downscaled to the smaller model to reduce the computational requirements. 5.1.1 HRU variables and their correlation with GWS The predictor variables were selected based on their correlation with the GWS. The Pearson correlation of all the HRU variables has been checked with GWS and among themselves. The variables with the highest correlation with GWS have been selected. Since most of the variables are highly correlated with each other, only one variable from each correlated set has been selected. A total of nine well-correlated hydrological parameters of SWAT output have been selected as the predictor variable in the second stage of downscaling. Seven parameters were positively correlated with GWS, with a correlation coefficient ranging from 0.26 to 0.77. The deep aquifer storage (DA_STmm) has the highest correlation, followed by the deep aquifer recharge (DA_RCHGmm) (co-efficient 0.57). The other two parameters have shown a negative correlation, with the highest (−0.58) shown by the potential evapotranspiration (PETmm) and minimum of −0.28 by the “revap” value (water in the shallow aquifer returning to the root zone in response to a moisture deficit (REVAPmm)). The soil water estimates from SWAT are calculated using the water balance approach, incorporating all the significant hydrological variables (Eq.4.1), which resulted in a good correlation with GWS (Fig. 6  ). The main contributor to the fluctuations in aquifer storage is groundwater recharge prompted by precipitation (Scanlon et al., 2012 ). The area with high groundwater recharge is susceptible to significant long-term anomalies in the GWS. The long-term anomalies in the GWS are mainly affected by relative inter-annual variability in the unsaturated zone in response to hydrologic variability and climatic events (Frappart et al., 2019; Swenson et al., 2008 ). The climate variables and groundwater development are the primary drivers of hydrologic changes. The short-term variation can be attributed to the excessive groundwater pumping and flooding. The SWAT can simulate groundwater pumping for irrigation requirements but does not consider the domestic demands (Neitsch et al., 2011 ). The SWAT outputs are spatially heterogeneous following skewed normal, multi-gaussian or even no distribution, making the downscaling problem suitable for machine learning. The advantage of ML algorithms in mapping the non-linearity in the dataset makes it perfect for prediction based on SWAT outputs since most parameters have complex nonlinear relationships with hydrological factors (Table 2 ). Precipitation is one of the main drivers of the GWSA, followed by ET and groundwater extraction in the area. Average precipitation in the area varied from 604 mm to 1085 mm during 2001–2014. The rainfall is high in the Vindhyan region. The simulated potential evapotranspiration (PET) is also high in the Vindhyan region due to the yearly average temperature (Fig. 7  ).  5.1.2 GWS downscaled to HRUs The training accuracy for the first stage of downscaling with ANN1 was in the range of NSE: 0.74 to 0.94 and R2 : 0.79 to 0.96. The model was validated, and the accuracy was well within the satisfactory range (NSE: 0.81 to 0.95 and R2 : 0.80 to 0.95) (Fig. 8  . A1-A4). After the downscaling of TWSA to the GLDAS scale, the GWS was calculated. The GWS has been downscaled to HRUs by the ANN2 model trained with the HRU predictors. The training accuracy was in the NSE range of 0.81 to 0.98 and R2 : 0.82 to 0.99, while the testing accuracy was found in the NSE range of 0.70 to 0.91 and R2 : 0.72 to 0.89 (Fig. 8 . B1-B4). The Mann-Kendall test at 95 % confidence for GWS at the GLDAS level shows no significant trend for most of the grids inside the study area. Only five grids (two at the eastern and the southern boundary) have shown significant increasing trends of 4.8 mm/year. The maximum decreasing trend of 7 mm/year and maximum increasing trend of 4.8 mm/year have been observed for the grids inside the study area. The overall mean GWS has shown a downward trend of 2.29 mm/year in the study area from 2001 to 2014. The GWS trend at the 95 % confidence level for the downscaled data at the HRU scale was insignificant for 645 HRUs. These HRUs manifest a yearly trend of −1.8 mm/year to 2.4 mm/year. A total of 786 HRUs show an increasing trend in the range of 1.0 mm/year to 6.6 mm/year. The remaining 310 HRUs show a decreasing trend in the range of −1.4 mm/year to −6.9 mm/year. The spatial pattern of GWS has been normalized for comparison, and the GWS trend for the GLDAS and HRU scales is presented in Fig. 9  . The Gangetic plain residing on the northern side of the Ganga River has shown a decreasing trend in GWS in the range of −1.4 mm/year to −6.9 mm/year, while the plain between the foothills of the Vindhyan range and Ganga River has shown mixed trends. The western part of the alluvial plain between the foothills of the Vindhyan range and the Ganga River has shown an increasing trend of up to 6.6 mm/year, while the eastern part manifested a decreasing trend of −1.3 mm/year. Most of the Vindhyan area (50 %) has manifested an increasing trend from 0.9 mm/year to 6.1 mm/year. About 38 % of the Vindhyan area has no significant trend. The remaining 12 % of the Vindhyan area has shown a decreasing trend in the range of −1.3 mm/year to −3.9 mm/year (Fig. 9 .B3). The correlation between downscaled GWS and observed GW level from the year 2001 to 2014 has been calculated using the Pearson correlation coefficient (ρ) to validate the downscaling accuracy. Out of 1741 HRUs, the 257 monitoring wells covered only 181 HRUs. The Pearson correlation coefficient for these 181 HRUs was found to be in the range of 0.12 to 0.91, with a mean of 0.6. A total of 124 HRUs have shown a good correlation (ρ > 0.5), while 34 HRUs have shown a satisfactory correlation (ρ > 0.3). The correlation analysis represents a satisfactory accuracy since 81.3 % of HRUs have shown a good correlation with observed GWL. The GWS variation of four wells (two in Gangetic Plain and two in the Vindhyan region) has been plotted with respect to the observed GWL (Fig. 10  ). The average monthly precipitation corresponding to the wells in the Gangetic and Vindhyan regions has also been plotted. A similar trend has been observed for the GWL, downscaled GWS and Precipitation in the study area.   5.2 Determination of groundwater level in the HRUs Determination of the groundwater level (GWL) is a crucial task in groundwater management due to costly measurements and inadequate piezometer distribution, often supplemented by simulated heads from groundwater models (Omar et al., 2020 ). The GRACE-derived GWS provides a state-of-the-art solution to this problem. The GWL is directly proportional to groundwater storage (Eq (4.8) . The GWS and GWL should ideally have a linear correlation; however, poor model fitting may result from observational uncertainty and the temporal mismatch between the time of satellite data acquisition and observation. The poor model fit can also arise due to the scarcity of time series data (Kumar et al., 2021 ). Decision tree-based machine learning models are best suited for prediction with scarce datasets (Kumar et al., 2021 ). Here, we utilized the downscaled GWS data and the observed GWL to predict the groundwater depths over the study area. As the groundwater is highly influenced by topography (Condon and Maxwell, 2015 ), GWS, latitude, longitude, and elevation were also selected as the independent variables. Multiple machine learning models (Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), random forest regressor (RFR)(Breiman, 2001 ), support vector regressor (SVR), K-nearest neighbour (KNN), and Cat boost regressor (CBR)(Dorogush et al., 2017 )) have been tested for the prediction accuracy with RMSE  and R2  . The R2   is sensitive to the data range and can provide false accuracy. Since the standard deviation of the observed GWL is in the range of 0.54 mbgl to 8.3 mbgl (average 2.58 mbgl), which is less when compared to the groundwater heads (in the range of 60.42 masl to 226.5 masl), the groundwater depths have been predicted instead of the heads to avoid overestimation of R2 . The decision tree-based models (RFR and CBR) have performed better with RMSE of 2.24 (R2 :0.76) and 2.16 (R2 :0.77), respectively, compared to ANN (RMSE 4.00: R2  0.23), SVR (RMSE 4.51: R2  0.12), and KNN (RMSE 4.2: R2  0.15). The CBR model has been selected for predictions, and its hyperparameters have been tuned to optimum values using grid search. The final RMSE and R2  achieved was 2.06 and 0.8 respectively, with optimal hyperparameters as 'depth’= 6, 'iterations’=1500, 'l2_leaf_reg’= 5 and 'learning_rate’= 0.1. The overall groundwater shows a decreasing trend during the pre-monsoon season from 0.04 cm to 8.6 cm per year for 71 % of the total area, with a significant contribution from the Vindhyan region, where the trend is high. However, groundwater replenishment is high in the Vindhyan region compared to the water-stressed Gangetic plain, resulting in an overall increasing trend of groundwater. The Varanasi, Sant Ravidas Nagar, and Mirzapur districts in the Gangetic Plain have shown a decreasing pre-monsoon groundwater trend varying from 2.2 cm to 4.6 cm per year. The rest of the study area has shown an increase in water level ranging from 0.01 cm to 4.7 cm per year. The area faced approximately 60 % of the expected average rainfall from 2004 to 2010. The effect of decreased rainfall can be observed in the groundwater level in the pre-monsoon (month of May) GWL up to 2011 (Fig. 11  ).  5.3 Determination of Specific yield Transient groundwater flow simulations and water resource planning rely heavily on aquifer storage parameters. Obtaining representative Sy  values using traditional approaches (e.g., core analysis, pumping test) is more complicated, particularly at the regional scale (Sun et al., 2010 ). The localized conditions (such as a well in a highly transmissive aquifer) during pumping tests can introduce errors in regional groundwater modelling (Liu et al., 2022 ). In some models, where the data is limited, Sy   is also taken as a calibration parameter, which increases the uncertainty of the model results. Sun et al. (2010)  have presented a robust optimization methodology to determine the Sy   based on Eq. (4.9) , utilizing the GRACE-derived GWS and observed groundwater level data. Compared to least square regression, robust optimization was unaffected by the uncertainty in the data. The data uncertainty of the GWL measurements and GWS downscaling method results in the erroneous calculation of Sy   with least square regression. We calculated the Sy   with a regularised robust optimization method. Several realizations have been sought within the uncertainty range of the parameter based on the previous literature in the study area to find the optimum estimate of Sy  with the temporal variation of GLWA and GWSA. The study conducted for the hydrological typologies by (Bonsor et al., 2017 ) in the Ganga River Basin has reported the Sy  in the range of 0.05 – 0.15. We started with the mean value of 0.1, and the model estimates were optimized using the Huber loss function. The overfitting of the model was controlled with Tikhonov regularisation. The regularisation ensures that the model does not fit any unrealistically high or low value of Sy  . The Sy   of the target HRU has been calculated using the best-fitted model. The groundwater level for the HRUs containing multiple wells has been calculated using the area-weighted average method. Out of 1741 HRUs in the area, 1560 have no wells inside or near their boundaries (buffer of 1.0 Km). Further, out of 181 HRUs, 57 have not shown a good correlation (correlation > 0.5) with GWS; therefore, only 124 HRUs with sufficient observation wells have been used for Sy   calculation. The Sy   for the rest of the HRUs has not been calculated and is represented as blank spaces in the plot (Fig. 12  C ). To overcome the scarcity of GWL observations, one can first predict or interpolate the groundwater level for the entire area. The groundwater variation can then be utilized to calculate the Sy  . However, this method can reduce accuracy due to uncertainty in the interpolation or prediction method. The calculated Sy   in the study area varies from 0.012 to 0.115, with a mean of 0.053. Most areas of the Vindhyan region have a specific yield ranging from 0.012 to 0.083, with a mean of 0.05. The alluvial plain has shown a specific yield ranging from 0.02 to 0.115 with a mean of 0.058. The area under the Vindhyan region comprises both types of aquifers (i.e., Vindhyan supergroup and alluvium in the northern and eastern parts). It manifests in the considerable variation in the histogram of Sy   (Fig. 12 B ). The calculated Sy   values are well within the values reported by Bonsor et al. (2017)  and the specified range of 0.04 to 0.12 for alluvium and 0.01 to 0.04 for Vindhyan range as recommended by the Ground Water Resource Estimation Committee 2015 (CGWB, 2017 ).  5.4 Integrated surface and groundwater budgeting with SWAT and GRACE data Budgeting water volume within various reservoirs of the hydrologic cycle and its spatiotemporal distribution is crucial for the stakeholders to take suitable interventions. It is vital to assess the long-term effect of constraining discharge and recharge for sustainable groundwater development (Wiebe et al., 2015; Yihdego and Khalil, 2017 ). Hydrological models such as SWAT do not parameterize groundwater reservoir storage and extraction for domestic and industrial water uses, which requires integrating groundwater flow models (Maxwell et al., 2014 ). The groundwater models come with uncertainties in the estimation due to the lack of data on natural variability (Mustafa et al., 2018 ). The downscaled observed GWS data can aid the water budget estimations to account for groundwater reservoirs. If the groundwater storage variation (ΔGWS) is caused by the aquifer recharge and discharge (base flow to streams, groundwater development (GWD)), the water budget within a zone can be given as −(5.1) Δ G W S i  = ∑ R i  - ( E T i  + Q surf , i   + Q lateral   + G W _ Q  i  + R e v a p i  )    - ∑ G W D i  + B L i        Where Ri   is rainfall, BLi   is the boundary leakage through the assessment zone, ETi   is evapotranspiration, Qsurf,i   is surface runoff to the streams, Qlateral   is the lateral and return flow to the streams, GWDi   is the groundwater pumping for irrigation, domestic and industrial use, GW_Qi   is the base flow to the streams and Revapi  is the amount of groundwater reaching to vadose zone for transpiration. Data assimilation based on SWAT outputs and downscaled GWS to equation (5.1)  has been utilized to determine the unknown hydrological fluxes in the study area. The hydrological variables (ET, Qsurf , Qlateral , GW_Q,  and Revap ) have been taken from the calibrated SWAT model outputs. Further, the groundwater extraction (GWD ) for irrigation, industries, and domestic use has been curated from the NAQUIM Reports (Central Groundwater Board) of all the districts in the study area. The methodology for calculating GWD  in the NAQUIM Reports cuts through various aspects of observed groundwater demand from domestic, cattle, irrigation and recreational purposes (CGWB, 2017 ). The ΔGWS was calculated using the downscaled GRACE data. The block-wise annual average surface water and groundwater budget estimates have been calculated for 75 blocks from 14 districts in the study area (Fig. 13  ).
