The area-weighted average of SWAT variables was calculated at the block boundary. The unknown boundary leakage from each block has been calculated by rearranging Eq (5.1)  as(5.2) ∑     B L i  = Δ G W S i  - ∑ R i  - E T i  + Q surf , i   + Q lateral  + G W _ Q  i  + R e v a p i      + ∑ G W D i       The net annual groundwater extraction per unit recharge area is high for the blocks in the Gangetic Plain due to heavy dependency on groundwater (87.5 %) (Khan and Singh, 2017 ). Almost all the subbasins are losing their groundwater reserves in the Gangetic Plain during the assessment period. Out of 33 blocks in the Gangetic alluvium, 12 were on the verge of being groundwater-scarce regions, while the rest were in the critical stage. Boundary leakage is also high for the regional aquifer system. The negative value of boundary leakage represents gaining conditions such that these subbasins are fulfilling their overdraft from the upstream aquifers, as the regional flow of groundwater is towards the Ganges River from the northwest direction. The blocks in the Vindhyan region have less groundwater development, and most of the area is still groundwater-sufficient. The river Ganga separates the two regions based on groundwater deficiency. The lower part of the Vindhyan region fulfils the overdraft demand of the lower alluvial plain and further drains into the river Ganges as base flow (Das et al., 2021b ).   6 Conclusion The HRU scale downscaling of GRACE-TWSA has been presented to determine the fine-scale GWS values. The GRACE-TWSA downscaled to GLDAS with ANN1 has been used to correct the biases in the GLDAS-TWS, and the GWS has been calculated. Further, the GWS at the GLDAS scale has been downscaled to the HRU scale, with ANN2 utilizing the nine highly correlated HRU variables as predictors. The groundwater head was determined using the downscaled GWS, and the groundwater level was observed using a decision tree-based Cat boost regression model. The HRU scale calculation of the Specific Yield was presented using downscaled GWS and observed groundwater levels. The volumetric budget of the major surface water and groundwater parameters has been calculated, and the groundwater deficiency for each block in the study area has been determined. The accuracy of the ANN model in the downscaling process has been satisfactory, with HRU variables as predictors. The HRU variables have shown a high correlation with GWS. The high correlation of observed groundwater levels to the downscaled GWS has accurately determined specific yield. The distributed groundwater levels for all the subbasins have also been accurately determined using GWS as the predictor variable. The Gangetic plain in the study area has shown a decreasing trend of −1.4 mm to −6.9 mm per year in groundwater storage from 2001 to 2014. The specific yield for the Gangetic plain has shown high heterogeneity, representing spatially variable aquifer characteristics in the alluvium. The water budgeting in the area suggests that most of the blocks in the Gangetic Plain are water-stressed and require interventions to increase natural recharge. This study uses GRACE data to propose a novel subbasin scale surface water and groundwater management method. The study has the potential to replace groundwater modelling for calculating dynamic groundwater head and budgeting, which is time-consuming in integrated water resource management. Data assimilation using downscaled GWS and SWAT outputs can lead to more accurate calculation of basin-wise hydrological parameters.
1 Introduction Karst areas cover 7–12 % of the Earth's continental surface (Hartmann et al., 2014 ), and provide drinking water for approximately 25 % of the world's population (Ford and Williams, 2007 ). Karst is more widespread in China, with approximately 33 % of its land area covered by carbonate rocks and approximately 25 % of the country's groundwater sources of karst origin (Yuan, 1994 ). Carbonate aquifers are important freshwater resource in many regions worldwide, particularly in arid and semi-arid areas (Rusjan et al., 2019 ). In recent decades, the combined effects of extreme climates and intense human activity have induced groundwater depletion and degradation (de Graaf et al., 2019 ). Karst aquifers contamination has been detected in multiple countries and regions worldwide such as the United States (Musgrove et al., 2016 ), Brazil (Galvão et al., 2017 ), Italy (Balestra and Bellopede, 2023 ) and China (Huo et al., 2015 ). Frequent contamination of karst waters poses an immediate threat to karst resources (Lall et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2022 ). Protecting, managing, and sustainably utilizing karst water resources has become a challenging for residents and governments. Given the importance of maintaining the sustainability of karst water resources, it is important to trace the contaminates from their eventual fate back to their origin. This remains a challenge because of the inherent heterogeneity of karst landscapes. Karst is widely known as the most vulnerable areas with variable hydrological connectivity, high transmissivity and poor self-purification (Einsiedl and Mayer, 2006 ). In porous media, there are highly diverse pathways by which its associated contaminants travel from recharge to discharge. It was found that contaminants can easily affect karst water by continuous leakage from the surface (Abdelmohsen et al., 2020 ), indirect infiltration by leaching (Rogers et al., 2023 ) and even direct injection due to the presence of temporary/occasional sinkholes (Lorette et al., 2022 ). Worse still, the variability in permeability and transmissivity within the karst aquifers results in an uneven distribution of contaminants (Torres et al., 2018 ), exacerbating difficulties in tracing contamination sources and migration pathways (Liu et al., 2023 ). Diverse catchment characteristics give rise to a multitude of contamination pathways (Jutebring Sterte et al., 2021 ), highlighting the variable interconnections between water flow and contamination in karst systems. Karst can be classified as exposed karst, covered karst or buried karst depending on its exposure to the land surface (Veress, 2016 ). Exposed karst aquifers, owing to their direct relationship between surface morphology and subsurface hydrology (Gutiérrez et al., 2014 ), are particularly vulnerable to the contaminant infiltration. Within covered karst and buried karst aquifers, layers of sediment or bedrock act as barriers, hindering the direct influx of contaminants but making it difficult to pinpoint the exact location of contaminant entry (Laskow et al., 2011 ). In subsurface karst regions, dissolution-generated sinking streams, caves, and fracture networks provide low-resistance pathways for water and contaminants, thus posing an environmental risk to karst water quality (Husic et al., 2020; Morales et al., 2017; Zheng and Yang, 2022 ). Although numerous investigations on karst contamination have been undertaken, they have largely focused on uncovered systems with frequent water exchanges (Fang et al., 2021 ). Deeply buried groundwater systems constitute important freshwater reservoirs. Groundwater buried at depths > 150 m was found to contain fresh and usable groundwater in certain areas, with 88 % exhibiting total dissolved solids (TDS) concentrations of < 1000 mg/L (Kang et al., 2019 ). However, to date, little research has been conducted on the contamination sources and specific migration pathways. Over the past decades, over-pumping of karst groundwater and mining activities have intensively developed. Increasing withdrawals to meet growing human needs have led to an 80 % reduction in the spring flow in northern China (Liang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2023 ). The mining depth of coal mines can reach approximately 600 m in karst mining areas, and extend to a dep with a speed of 12 m/a (Qiao et al., 2014 ). Whether these activities cause buried karst groundwater pollution and migration pathways remains unclear. With the increase in the depth of groundwater extraction, the contamination process of buried karst systems deserves more attention. Isotopic investigation of contamination sources in groundwater is crucial for properly assessing anthropogenic impacts on groundwater quality, particularly for hidden, buried groundwater (Guo et al., 2016 ). Stable isotopic compositions of water have been used to constrain water dynamics, interactions of surface water and groundwater, and flow lines in aquifers (Joshi et al., 2018; Li et al., 2021; Windler et al., 2021 ). The δ34 S value of dissolved sulfate is a sensitive tracer identifying the sources of sulfates and related mixing processes, the analysis and interpretation of which can help to understand mixing between different sources, whether natural or anthropogenic (Ren et al., 2021; Rogers et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2017 ). Previous studies demonstrated that the contamination processes within hydrological systems can produce distinct carbon isotopic compositions of dissolved inorganic carbon (Pinzone et al., 2019 ). The 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio is also a useful indicator for determining the type of geology that interacts with groundwater (Glok-Galli et al., 2022 ). The joint application of chemical data analysis and environmental isotopes will allow the evaluation of the contamination sources and the migration pathways of contaminants. Considering the intricate hydrological connectivity of buried karst systems, contaminants in buried carbonate aquifers can originate from any karst water recharge location. Our study aimed to uncover the multiple sources and specific migration pathways of contaminants in complex buried karst systems. Taking Jinci Spring as an example, we analyzed its hydrochemical characteristics to identify the occurrence of karst water contamination under the cover layer. Multiple isotopes (δ2 H, δ18 O, δ34 S, δ13 C and 87 Sr/86 Sr) combined with the buried condition of karst aquifers were employed to further determine the sources of pollution and trace the migration pathways of contamination. This study enriches our understanding of groundwater contamination in buried karst areas, and lays the foundation for the protection of karst water resources.  2 Study area The Jinci Spring region is located in the western mountains of Tai Yuan, central of Shanxi Province, China (Fig. 1  ). The total area is 2731.9 km2  and exposed soluble rock accounts for 34.9 %. The climate is a temperate semi-arid continental monsoon type, with annual average. The study area is characterized by a middle-low mountainous area (1,300–1,500 m in elevation) in the west and a plain area (780–850 m) in the east (Fig. S1 ). The Fenhe River and its tributaries constitute the primary surface water system of this region. The climate is a temperate semi-arid continental monsoon type, with annual average evaporation and precipitation of 1872 mm and 467 mm, respectively, and the wet season is from July to September. The land cover patterns of the study area are detailed in Fig. S2 . The study area is inhabited by > 4 million people, primarily concentrated along the Fenhe River and in the basin. The basin and adjoining areas of the river are covered with croplands. Karst aquifers in Jinci are greatly impacted by intensive domestic, industrial and agricultural activities. The main stratigraphic units in the study area comprise Early Paleozoic and Mesozoic formations (Fig. 1 (a)). Being the main karst aquifers in the Jinci catchment, the middle Ordovician limestone strata contains interlayers of thin lenses of gypsum. Jinci Spring is divided into two parts by the Gujiao section of the Fenhe River. In the north, well-developed karst crevasses are distributed in the bare limestone mountain area, and karst water exists in the form of unconfined water. However, the southern mountainous area is overlain by the Permian mudstone and shale, with karst water converted to a confined state (Fig. 1 (c)). In this case, contaminants generally have difficulty in entering karst water aquifers. There are abundant coal resources in the area. The most distinctive geologic feature of coal-bearing strata overlying carbonate rocks renders karst aquifers highly vulnerable to irreversible influences through coal mining activities. Giant thick-laminated Quaternary sediments were deposited in the southeastern part of the study area, where the basin directly contacts the mountains by a large drop this contact zone is considered to be the basin-mountain coupling belt. Under the influence of the NNE-trending fault, karst in the Ordovician limestone developed and a strong groundwater runoff zone formed. The primary recharge source for the spring area is rainfall, which infitrates the widely exposed Ordovician limestone in the northern and western parts. The riverbed strata of the Fenhe and Fenhe Ⅱ reservoirs are mostly composed of soluble carbonate rocks, among which Middle Ordovician limestone strata with developed karst are the most widely distributed. In addition, with the uplift of the faults, the carbonatites were exposed at the bottom of the riverbed and superimposed on the influence of reservoir construction, and a karst seepage section of nearly 44 km extended from the Fenhe River reservoir to the boundary of the spring area. The well-developed Gujiao fault zones, extending in the NEE-SWW direction, are hydraulically permeable with a steep inclination and pass through the Fenhe River (Li et al., 2021 ). Surface water is input into the groundwater via these faulting structures and/or river channel leakage. Karst water flows from the northern and western mountainous areas to the southeastern part of the study area and eventually drains into the basin-mountain coupling belt. The discharge of karst water includes the natural excretion of Spring (Jinci and Ping Spring), lateral recharge to the basin and artificial exploitation.  3 Materials and methods In total 101 samples were collected from the Jinci Spring area. Groundwater samples were collected in April and supplemented with surface water samples collected from the gullies in September. Forty-three karst water samples were collected to comprehensively cover the groundwater flow paths. Dense sampling was conducted in areas with intensive karst water extraction (Fig. 1 (b)). To investigate the hydrochemical characteristics of the waters occurring in different aquifers, 24 pore and 14 fissure water samples were obtained from the drilled and observed wells. Karst water samples encompass both artesian spring water and groundwater sourced from carbonate rock aquifers. Pore water is mainly sourced from groundwater within the Quaternary aquifer, whereas fissure water comprises water aggregated from fractures by the weathering of Permian sandstone. Goaf, surface, and precipitation samples were collected for comparison. A portable device (HQ40d, HACH, USA) was used to determine unstable parameters, such as pH, temperature, oxidation–reduction potential (ORP) and dissolved oxygen (DO). All water samples in the field were filtered with a 0.45 μm filter membrane then collected in polyethylene bottles which had been thoroughly cleaned. Alkalinity was measured on-site using the acid titration method with 0.025 mol/L HCl on the day of sampling. The samples were analyzed at the State Key Laboratory of Biogeology and Environmental Geology, China University of Geosciences. Samples for cation and trace element analyses were treated with 63 % nitric acid at pH < 2 to prevent precipitation. The cation (Na+ , K+ , Ca2+  and Mg2+ ) and anion (Cl- , SO4 2-  and NO3 – ) concentrations were determined using ion chromatography (Dionex ICS-2100, USA) with a measurement accuracy of 2 %. Trace elements were measured using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (Agilent 7500a, Japan) with a relative standard deviation of ＜3%. Analytical quality was controlled using standard reference materials, replicates and blanks. The quality of the chemical analysis was verified by calculating the charge balance-errors, which were generally within 10 %. Isotopic characterization included δ2 H and δ18 O of water, δ34 S of dissolved sulfate, δ13 C of dissolved inorganic carbon, and 87 Sr/86 Sr of dissolved Sr. The isotope ratios (2 H/1 H and 18 O/16 O) of water samples were reported in per mil (‰) relative to Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water with an analytical accuracy of ± 1 ‰ for δ2 H and ± 0.1 ‰ for δ18 O. The δ2 H and δ18 O values of water samples were determined using a liquid water isotope analyzer (LGR IWA-35EP, USA). To determine δ34 S, the dissolved SO4 2−  was precipitated as BaSO4  by adding BaCl2 ·2H2 O after acidification with concentrated nitric acid and the sulfur isotopic composition was analyzed using an elemental analyzer coupled to isotope ratio mass spectrometers (SerCon Integra2, UK). The Canyon Diablo Troilite was used as the reference for δ34 S values and the analytical error was ± 0.2 ‰. The δ13 C values were analyzed using a GasBench-II headspace autosampler in line with an isotopic mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientifics Delta V Advantage, Germany). The laboratory standards were calibrated against Vienna Peedee Belemnite. The analytical error was ± 0.2 ‰. The isotopic composition of dissolved Sr (87 Sr/86 Sr) was measured in duplicate using a multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer (Nu Instruments Plasma II, UK). The Sr isotope standard was NIST SRM 987 (87 Sr/86 Sr 0.71034 ± 0.00026). The analytical error was ± 0.01 %.  4 Results and discussion 4.1 Karst water chemistry and pollutants . The median, range, and standard deviation (SD) of the physicochemical variables (pH, ORP, and DO), major ions (Ca2+ , Mg2+ , Na+ , K+ , Cl- , NO3 – , HCO3 – , and SO4 2- ) and trace elements (B and Sr2+ ) for the different types of water samples in Jinci spring area are summarized in Table 1  . For all analyzed water samples, pH values ranged from 6.93 to 9.24, with the majority falling within the neutral to slightly alkaline range. Most samples exhibited positive ORP values, signifying an oxidizing environment, whereas samples 2, 10 and 12 possessed negative ORP values and low DO content, suggesting a reducing environment. The boron concentrations varied among the different aquifers, with means of 0.13 mg/L and 0.12 mg/L identified in the fissure and surface waters, respectively. A mean of 0.05 mg/L was observed in the karst water. Boron in groundwater originates naturally from the weathering of igneous rocks or artificially from pesticides and sewage effluents (Voutsa et al., 2009 ). Boron in the fissure water may naturally come from the weathering of igneous rocks, whereas the high boron concentration in the surface water, without the complex water–rock interaction, is inferred to be the result of sewage drainage. The mean of Sr2+  concentration in karst water was 1.43 mg/L, with ranges from 0.44 to 9.58 mg/L in pore water and 0.98 to 8.14 mg/L in fissure water. The relatively high levels in the pore and fissure water can be attributed to the weathering of Sr-bearing clastic rocks. The box plot visually represents the presence of outliers or skewness in regards to TDS and major ions in surface water, groundwater, mining wastewater and atmospheric precipitation (Fig. 2  ). The median concentration of TDS in the water samples generally exhibited high values, in the mining wastewater, with a median of 3595 mg/L (Fig. 2 (a)). Notably, the karst water has several outliers with TDS values > 2000 mg/L, exceeding the quality standard for groundwater (1000 mg/L; China), indicating the occurrence of severe contamination. The cations in the karst water were dominated by Ca2+  and Mg2+ , followed by Na+  and K+  (Fig. 2 (b, c, d and e)). As shown in (Fig. 2 (f, g, h and i)), the major anions in the karst water are HCO3 –  and SO4 2- . The high Ca2+  and HCO3 –  levels and concentration variability in the karst water can be attributed to the varying degrees of carbonate dissolution. The mean Na+  concentration was 29.3 mg/L in karst water, demonstrating a relatively lower level in comparison to other water samples (mean: 54.0 mg/L, 71.4 mg/L and 119.3 mg/L in fissure, pore and surface waters, respectively). The direct discharge of domestic sewage into rivers may be an important reason for the high Cl-  concentrations in surface water. However, several anomalies were observed, with values reaching 303 mg/L (Fig. 2 (d)). Notably, these outliers in karst water with high Na+  generally coincide with elevated Cl- . Na+  in groundwater is naturally derived from Na-bearing minerals in igneous and metamorphic rocks (Xing et al., 2022 ). Thus, the exceptionally high Na+  and Cl-  concentrations in karst waters were inferred to be influenced by anthropogenic inputs (Li et al., 2022). Heavily involved in the formation of water-insoluble secondary minerals (water mica, montmorillonite, and sericite) and readily adsorbed by plants, K+  is commonly low in groundwater, in Fig. 2 (e). Wide ranges and high SDs in the NO3 –  concentrations were observed in the pore and fissure waters. In contrast, the range of NO3 –  concentrations in the karst waters displayed a narrow variation. However, there were several outliers, the high NO3 –  concentration in karst waters may be related to biological nitrification or potential contamination from frequent agricultural activities. Karst waters have relatively high SO4 2-  concentrations, ranging from 11.2 to 1738 mg/L, with a median of 402 mg/L. The relatively high sulfate content may be due to the natural dissolution of gypsum along the flow direction or contamination.  5 4.2 spatial distribution of concerned pollutants The spatial distribution of the chemicals allows the identification of areas with higher concentrations and possible sources. A bubble diagram representing the ion concentration is shown in Fig. 3  , where significant spatial heterogeneity in the TDS and the concentration of contaminated ions among the samples is observed. The minimum karst water TDS values occurred in the northern recharge area (Fig. 3 (a)). This could be ascribed to the direct infiltration of atmospheric precipitation. Elevated TDS values were observed in samples from the basin-mountain coupling belt, primarily because of mineral dissolution along the direction of groundwater flow. As illustrated in Fig. 3 (b), Na-rich karst samples were sporadically scattered in the leakage section and the basin-mountain coupling belt. Spatially, karst waters with high Cl-  concentrations were extensively distributed in the leakage section, with surface waters also displaying high Cl-  concentrations (Fig. 3 (c)). The presence of unusually high Na+  and Cl-  levels suggests the contamination of the leakage section. Urbanization and associated sewage discharge are commonly responsible for the accumulation of Na+  and Cl-  in surface and groundwater. It can be inferred that domestic sewage was the primary source of contamination in this case. Additionally, elevated Cl-  concentrations were detected in the pore and karst waters near the basin-mountain coupling belt, which may be attributed to the use of fertilizers and pesticides in agricultural activities. These findings illustrate the diversity and prevalence of chlorine sources in the study area. In Fig. 3 (d), NO3 −  concentrations are not homogeneously distributed, large differences being observed among samples located close to each other. The nitrate concentration was relatively high in fissure and pore waters, particularly in the basin-mountain coupling belt. Nitrate also displayed high concentrations in some karst waters. Based on site investigations, thick Quaternary deposites exist in the southeastern part of the study area, where agricultural activities are intensive and fertilizer application is frequent. This could serve as a good reference for nitrate-contaminated water that receives nitrates from agricultural activities. The SO4 2-  distribution map (Fig. 3 (e)) displays a wide range of SO4 2-  concentrations. The area having high sulfate concentrations was examined in detail, as shown in Fig. 3 (f), and the SO4 2-  concentration in the karst water was several times higher than that in the recharge area. Gypsum weathering can naturally provide substantial amounts of sulfate. However, natural water–rock interactions could not account for the extremely high sulfate content here, thus, adjacent coal mine activities may be responsible for an additional source. Additionally, acidic coal mine drainage with relatively lower pH values are more prone to dissolving Na-bearing minerals, and water affected by discharge and/or leaking recharge of coal mining drainage display high Na+  contents (Li et al., 2021 ). This provides a reasonable explanation for the elevated Na+  levels shown in Fig. 3 (b). Focusing on the concentration of dissolved ions, karst water contamination is characterized by the presence of ion outliers, particularly for Cl- , SO4 2- , and NO3 – . The pronounced elevation of these ions signifies the presence of contaminants and provides evidence of their origin and dispersion. They are regarded as the characteristic contaminants of karst water and can distinguish contaminated karst water from other types of water samples.  6 4.3 sources and pathways of karst water contamination 6.1 4.3.1 contamination sources Ca2+  in karst waters originates solely from the dissolution of calcite and gypsum, which is accompanied by a significant increase in Ca2+  and sulfate concentrations. Thus, the high molar ratio of SO4 2- /Ca2+  serves as an indicator, highlighting the potential contribution of mining activities. Coal mining wastewater, displaying the highest molar ratio of SO4 2- /Ca2+  up to 2.84, can serve as an end member in mining activities (Fig. 4  (a)). Apparently, the high molar ratio of SO4 2- /Ca2+  (0.15–1.42) in Fig. 4  (a) reveals the impact of mining activities. Agricultural activities generate the elevated molar ratio of NO3 – /Ca2+ . Karst water samples tended to vary in two directions, indicating that mining and agricultural activities impact karst water. The plot of NO3 – /Cl-  ratios versus Cl-  in Fig. 4 (b) is used to preliminary distinguish whether NO3 –  is derived from agricultural, soil nitrogen, or sewage inputs (He et al., 2022 ). As evidenced by the high Cl-  concentrations and low molar ratios of NO3 – /Cl- , the concentration of chloride ions in surface waters appears to be controlled by domestic sewage. The high molar ratios of NO3 – /Cl-  observed in the pore and fissure waters can be attributed to the dominant influence of agricultural activities, which is further reinforced by the high molar ratios of SO4 2- /Ca2+  (Fig. 4 (b)). The scattered variations in Cl-  with the molar ratio of NO3 – /Cl-  among most karst waters in the study area tended to show mixing processes, highlighting the contribution of multiple sources of NO3 –  and Cl-  in the composition of karst waters.   7 4.3.2 vertical leakage of contaminated river water The H and O isotopes in water (δ2 H and δ18 O) provide insight into the origins, hydrologic cycle and mixing of H2 O in groundwater (Bowen et al., 2019 ). Fig. 5  (a) displays the δ18 O versus δ2 H values. For surface water and groundwater, samples plotted below the global (GMWL: δ2 H = 8δ18 O + 10; Craig, 1961 ) and local meteoric water lines (LMWL: δ2 H = 6.42δ18 O-4.66; Jia et al., 2015 ), revealing a meteoric origin of water. The distribution in surface waters tend to be enriched in heavy isotopes, with a linear evaporation trend in the dataset (δ2 H = 5.31δ18 O-17.73). The slope of δ2 H and δ18 O fit for the surface water was lower than that of the LMWL, reflecting a relatively intense evaporation process (Torres-Martínez et al., 2021a ). Plotting the δ18 O data versus Cl-  concentration reveals three distinct trends (Fig. 5 (b)): (Ⅰ) Large variations in δ18 O values with small changes in the Cl-  content of groundwater samples. (Ⅱ) A simultaneous increase in δ18 O values with increasing Cl-  content in pore and karst waters. (Ⅲ) A strong increase in Cl-  content without significant changes in δ18 O values. Trend Ⅰ may suggest that the groundwater shares a common origin but has undergone varying levels of evaporation; pore and fissure waters with shallow buried depths are enriched in heavy isotopes due to more intense evaporation. The mean δ18 O values for the karst and surface waters were −9.4 ‰ and −8.4 ‰, respectively. The δ18 O value and Cl-  concentration were elevated in the surface water. The consistency of δ18 O values with increasing Cl-  content observed in karst water for trend Ⅲ reflects the influence of surface water intrusion. The correlation between Cl-  concentration and δ18 O values for trend Ⅱ may be due to the combine effect of evaporation and surface water leakage. The water isotopic compositions were employed to further ascertain the conversion relationship between the identified chlorine-enriched hotspots in surface water and groundwater (Fig. 5 (c)). The H and O isotopic composition of the karst water were close to the meteoric water line (Fig. 5 (c)), indicating the direct replenishment of rainwater on the exposed karst surface. The karst waters in the recharge area exhibited lower δ2 H and δ18 O values, whereas the δ2 H and δ18 O values showed an increasing trend along the flow direction of karst water. Notably, certain karst samples (7, 8, and 10) deviated from the other samples, being located near the surface water end members, with significantly elevated δ2 H and δ18 O values. The isotopic similarity between karst and surface waters suggests the influence of surface water seepage on karst waters. The application of B-bearing compounds, particularly Na perborate, as bleaching agents in detergents leads to the enrichment of B in groundwater (Vengosh et al., 2005 ). Consequently, the elevated B content in groundwater can often be used as a basis to determine whether groundwater is affected by domestic sewage and surface water leakage (Carrey et al., 2021 ). The presence of elevated levels of B and chlorine levels in river water serves as a clear indicator of the impact of sewage discharge on surface water (Fig. 5 (d)). Samples 7 and 8 were characterized by higher B and Cl-  concentrations, further supporting the notion that the downward penetration of river water contaminated by domestic sewage affects karst water. Further analysis suggested that the leakage contamination was likely associated with high-angle faults and joint structures along the Fenhe River. The faults provide a channel for surface water leakage and they elevate the carbonate rock stratum, resulting in the exposure of the karst aquifer at the bottom of the riverbed. In the recharge area, bare karst efficiently captured atmospheric precipitation and converted it into pure karst water. In the leakage sections, despite the presence of unconsolidated Quaternary sediments, structural fractures and interbedded dissolution fissures in Ordovician aquifers served as preferential pathways for the vertical migration of contaminated river water. The construction of the Fenhe and Fenhe Ⅱ Reservoirs in the study area increased the surface water level and facilitated the infiltration of surface water, consequently impacting the quality of karst water. The direct discharge of domestic sewage leads to surface water pollution and has a significant impact on the quality of groundwater.  8 4.3.3 leaking recharge by coal mining wastewater Distinct increases in sulfate and TDS were observed along the groundwater flow direction (Fig. 6  (a)). However, the samples with higher SO4 2- (＞1000 mg/L) and TDS(＞2000 mg/L) display a pronounced deviation compared to the other samples in proximity to the mining wastewater end-member. This observation suggests a close hydraulic connection between these samples and the mining wastewater. A sequence of environmental studies has adopted sulfate and δ34 SSO4  to recognize geogenic and anthropogenic pollution pathways (Colombani et al., 2019; Hosono et al., 2011 ). Sulfate dissolved in groundwaters can originate from various sources including atmospheric deposition, evaporite dissolution, and authropogenic activity (Torres-Martínez et al., 2021b ). Of the different hydrogeochemical processes that may influence the isotopic composition, the dissolution of evaporite results in the enrichment in heavy isotopes, ranging from + 25 ‰ to + 30 ‰ (Krouse and Mayer, 2000 ). An increase of δ34 S value of dissolved sulfate may result from microbial sulfate reduction, which is typical of anoxic groundwater and sediment pore water (Szynkiewicz et al., 2008 ). However, the high DO (3.88–8.79 mg/L) and positive in ORP (70.2–188.4 mV) confirm that the karst water in the discharge area is in an oxidizing environment, not considered the sulfate reduction. The δ34 S values ranged from 0 to + 6 ‰ for sulfate in atmospheric deposition (Moore et al., 2006 ), whereas SO4 2−  generated by coal mining activities had lower δ34 S values, with typical values ranging from −35 ‰ to + 5 ‰ (Zhou et al., 2018 ). On the basis of water isotopic composition of karst water, most karst water originates from atmospheric precipitation. Karst waters display a consistent increase in δ34 S values and sulfate concentrations along the runoff direction, peaking in the discharge area, which is a consequence of the addition of gypsum dissolution. In comparison to the other samples, the mining wastewater exhibited notably high SO4 2-  concentration (mean 2858 mg/L) and negative δ34 S values (mean −6.9 ‰), primarily as a result of pyrite oxidation from the mining activities. Certain karst samples close to mining wastewater (20, 28 and 41) had similar characteristics to mining wastewater. The sulfur geochemistry in these karst waters is best interpreted as a result of mixing with mining wastewater from the overlying aquifers. Although aquitards of certain thicknesses exist between coal strata, coal mine tunnels, goafs and karst aquifers, the presence of primary geological defects facilitates the hydraulic connectivity between mining wastewater and karst water. The coal seam floor is susceptible to damage throughout the coal mining process, allowing the direct infiltration of mining wastewater and its subsequent impact on karst aquifers through intricate crevices. Abandoned wells can also serve as migration pathways for mine water (Chapman et al., 2013 ). The lingering mining waste water within abandoned mine voids and shafts infiltrates and replenishes karst water through the leakage from abandoned wells, culminating in its contribution to the degradation of the karst water environment. Moreover, surface and fissure waters are also significantly influenced by mining wastewater, which may also indirectly impact karst aquifers.  9 4.3.4 reverse recharge from deep quarternary aquifers Nitrate pollution occurs mainly in the basin-mountain coupling belt. According to the hydrological characteristics based on previous research and our field investigations, the pore groundwater system can be divided into two unconsolidated aquifers: shallow (0–41 m，Q3 and locally Q4) and mid-deep (41–500 m, Q1 and Q2) types. Denitrification may occur in deep anoxic aquifers, leading to the attenuation of nitrate pollution in the groundwater flow, whereas nitrification under conditions of sufficient oxygen induces an increase in NO3 – . Given the differences in the depths of biogeochemical transformations, pore waters at different burial depths were distinguished to better analyze the interaction. Nitrate concentrations in the shallow pore water displayed a range of 7.17–45.9 mg/L, with a mean of 21.2 mg/L. Conversely, the middle- and deep-pore waters demonstrated a wider range of nitrate concentrations, varying from 5.39 to 202 mg/L, with a mean of 58.0 mg/L. The pronounced disparity in nitrate concentrations between the deep and shallow layers indicated distinct contamination levels. The nitrate concentration in the nitrate-contaminated karst water within the basin-mountain coupling zone varied from 15.0 to 50.8 mg/L. It is evident that the abundant nitrates in the karst water were due to the input of soil nitrogen and agricultural activities (Fig. 4 (b)). The carbon isotopes of DIC and the molar ratio of nitrate to bicarbonate further reveals the process in the target region (Fig. 7  (a)), under the assumption that: 1) the δ13 C value is close to 0 ‰ for carbonate minerals (Clark and Fritz, 1997 ); 2) the δ13 C value of DIC generated by organic matter degradation in soils falls in the range of −25.0 to –23.0 ‰ (Glok-Galli et al., 2022 ). Distinct variations can be observed in samples, karst water has an overall smaller molar ratio of nitrate to bicarbonate (0–0.17) and a higher δ13 C value (from −10.8 ‰ to −5.4 ‰), showing a dominance of carbonate weathering. The δ13 C value in shallow pore water varied between −16.6 ‰ and −11.3 ‰, whereas in deeper samples the value was significantly higher, ranging from −12.5 ‰ to −9.5 ‰. The carbon isotope fingerprints in shallow pore water indicated the dominance of biogenic soil CO2.  If denitrification occurs, a decrease in δ13 C and NO3 –  may be identified (Ren et al., 2022 ). Therefore, denitrification was not a prominent process in deep aquifers. High molar ratios of nitrate to DIC (0.43) and having δ13 C values of −12.5 ‰, sample 67 was identified as an end member of nitrogen fertilizer input (Li et al., 2010 ). However, samples 16, 20 and 28 differed from the others in that they appeared to be nitrate-enriched, similar to the nearby deep pore water, indicating that the karst water was obviously laterally recharged by pore water. Groundwater draining from a silicate terrain typically exhibits an 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio > 0.7200, whereas groundwater draining from a carbonate terrain shows an 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio variation between 0.7070 and 0.7110 (Han and Liu, 2004 ). A small range of 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios, with a completely different distribution range in the karst and pore water samples is displayed in Fig. 7 (c). Samples along the flow direction were characterized by an increase in the Sr concentration released by the dissolution of minerals in the aquifer. The Sr isotopic values were not modified by many near-surface processes (Zieliński et al., 2021 ). Thus, the Sr isotopic composition of the water reflects the mixing of Sr from its predominant sources (Christensen et al., 2018 ). Broad variations were observed in the 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios between shallow and deep pore water. The deep pore water has a mean 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio of 0.7124, whereas the shallow pore waters has a lower mean of 0.7099, which is related to the shallow pore water receiving karst water recharge. This process is illustrated in detail in Fig. 7 (c), where the shallow circulating karst water recharges the shallow pore water in the form of undercurrents. In addition, the karst water that emerged in the form of a spring penetrated vertically again and recharged the shallow pore water, resulting in similar Sr isotope fingerprints between the shallow pore and karst waters. Conversely, significantly elevated 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios were observed in karst samples 16, 20, and 28 compared with the other samples, indicating the influence of deep pore water. Of interest is that the affected karst samples are in the area of artificial exploitation and water drainage for coal mine (Fig.S3 ), hence the process is related to karst water over-exploitation (Li et al., 2024 ). As shown in Fig. 7 (c), the increased demand for domestic and irrigation water has led to the over-exploitation of groundwater (Fig.S4 ), and the groundwater level drops to form a cone of depression, where pore water laterally resupplies the karst water.  10 4.4 Conceptual model Evidence from hydro-geochemistry and isotopic fingerprinting reveals the contamination characteristics and specific contaminant migration processes of Jinci Spring. Hydrogeological conditions, geochemical characteristics and spatial distribution of pollution sources combine to influence buried karst groundwater contamination pathways. A typical contamination model incorporating three pollution pathways for karst is summarized in Fig. 8  . In the seepage section of Fenhe river, the direct discharge of domestic sewage leads to a deterioration in the quality of surface water. The contaminated karst water, characterized by the presence of elevated chloride levels with a mean of 79.4 mg/L, coupled with high mean values of −64.5 ‰ in δ2 H and −8.8 ‰ in δ18 O, respectively, confirms that surface water contaminated by domestic sewage further affects karst water through vertical seepage from the river. In covered karst areas, river water can infiltrate vertically into the karst aquifer through primary fractures. In addition, the impacts of large-scale hydraulic projects, such as reservoirs, also contribute to the leakage of surface water (Gutiérrez et al., 2015 ). Therefore, vertical leakage of river water needs to be recognized as a significant pathway for contamination within the covered karst area. Groundwater resources are highly susceptible to mining activities. To our knowledge, the overlying layers of the karst aquifer play a crucial role in impeding the surface infiltration of contaminates (Vilhar et al., 2022 ). However, coal mining activities has an impact on the hydrogeochemical properties of the underlying karst aquifer. The karst aquifer may be contaminated by the seepage layer of mine drainage through the hydraulic connection channel driven by the groundwater head difference. This is evident in the elevated levels of sulfate (mean 1454 mg/L) and depleted low δ34 S values(mean −1.6 ‰) of the contaminated karst water. Additionally, mine drainage may spill over the surface, it infiltrates through water-conducting fractures, thereby contaminating the surface water and fissure water. Consequently, treatment should be conducted to address the concerns. The interaction between karst water and pore water is observed in the basin-mountain coupling belt. Partial pore water has been contaminated by intensive agricultural activities and chemical fertilizer application. The high intensity of karst water extraction activities has led to a decline in water levels. Consequently, localized cones of depression have formed, introducing deep pore water into the karst water. The most prominent effects of excessive extraction of deep groundwater include changes in aquifer structure, groundwater resources and flow field (Lv et al., 2020 ). Deeply buried karst is generally difficult to access, yet the covert nitrate contamination with a mean concentration of 27.1 mg/L in karst aquifer strongly attests to the detrimental impact of excessive groundwater exploitation on water quality. Therefore, it is vital important to formulate water resources management programs and develop groundwater resources reasonably and sustainably for water resources protection.  11 4.5 environmental and human implications Groundwater, the Earth’s largest and most accessible freshwater stock, is a global sustainability concern (Lall et al., 2020 ). In recent decades, due to the contamination of shallow groundwater, deep confined groundwater is being extensively extracted and utilized. However, deep groundwater contamination is becoming increasingly recognized (Kang and Jackson, 2016 ). This is more pronounced in karst aquifers, which are fragile and susceptible to degradation. Our results uncover that the intensification of human activities further contributes to an excess of concerned chemicals (Cl- , SO4 2- , NO3 – ) in buried karst aquifers, resulting in the ecological water shortage and health hazards. Targeted measures should be implemented to prevent the deterioration of buried karst aquifer according to the migration pathways of contaminants. The vertical leakage of river is regarded as an important way to recharge groundwater, whereas untreated domestic sewage contaminates groundwater in the same way. It’s required to establish management practices and standards to avoid the direct discharge of untreated sewage. The leaking recharge of mining waste water is facilitated by the abandoned mine without proper treatment. It is urgent to improve the environmental awareness of mining enterprises, strengthen environmental supervision, and standardize the waste disposal in the mining process. Long-term leaching of fertilizers and over-exploitation contribute to the contamination in deep groundwater, thus deep groundwater monitoring and rational resources management are imperative.  12 Conclusions Jinci Spring, a typical large-scale karst water system in northern China with multiple burial types, is threatened by severe karst groundwater contamination. A combination of hydrogeochemisty and isotope fingerprinting is applied to elucidate the sources and migration pathways of the contaminants. The conclusive remarks are summarized as follows:Contaminants from anthropogenic activities in surface water leak vertically into the buried karst water, with a remarkably high Cl-  and B contents and heavier water isotopic signatures (δ18 O: mean −64.5 ‰, δ2 H: mean −8.8 ‰). Domestic sewage discharges directly contaminate the surface water and leak into the lower karst aquifers through river channels.  The low δ34 S values(mean −1.6 ‰) and high sulfate concentration (mean 1454 mg/L) in certain karst waters allow for a better understanding of the process that mine drainage leaking recharge karst water. Coal mining activities pose an imminent threat to the groundwater environment. Abandoned mines and geological defects formed during the mining process provide favorable conditions for the leakage of mining wastewater.  Over-pumping may induce changes in the water exchange processes, leading to contamination. The elevated nitrate concentration (mean 27.1 mg/L) and a high 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio (mean 0.7124) in deep buried karst aquifers is a consequence of reverse recharge by neighboring confined pore water.    This study highlights the importance in combining hydrogeochemical and isotopic tools as contamination tracers. The conclusions shed a comprehensive light on karst contamination in Jinci Spring and can be easily extrapolated to other deeply buried karst systems.
1 Introduction Droughts are a common and recurring phenomenon with significant impacts on hydrology (Hasan et al., 2019 ) and crop production (Kuwayama et al., 2019 ), therefore altering virtual water trade (VWT) (Marston and Konar, 2017 ). The VWT is the flow of water embodied in the production process of food and other commodities traded between and within countries (Allan, 1998 ). Despite the well-documented adverse effects of droughts on water resources and crop production, studies have less concentrated on the impacts of droughts on VWT. Moreover, the majority of research has primarily focused on the immediate consequences of specific types of droughts (Li et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020; Khalili et al., 2023 ), with little emphasis on the long-term effects of prolonged droughts on the development of other types of droughts or the underlying physical processes causing them. For instance, climate anomalies, which are the root cause of meteorological droughts, can persist over extended periods, ultimately affecting other natural processes and leading to various types of droughts, such as hydrological, agricultural, or groundwater droughts (He et al., 2018 ; Masud et al., 2015 ; Apurv and Cai, 2020 ; Pathak and Dodamani, 2021 ). Due to the time it takes for droughts to transition between different forms (e.g., from meteorological to hydrological droughts) and the lag in the response of hydrological systems (Huang et al., 2024 ), the recovery of hydrological processes may be delayed even after the end of a specific drought type that occurs earlier in the cycle (e.g., meteorological or agricultural droughts) (Huang et al., 2024 ). In addition, the hydrologic system behavior may change following a given drought. For instance, the precipitation following an agricultural drought may not contribute to runoff in the same way as during a pre-drought condition. Similarly, evapotranspiration rates (ET, also known as green water flow following Falkenmark and Rockström (2006) ) may change following agricultural drought conditions (Deb et al., 2019; Saft et al., 2015 ). Such changes in the hydrological processes can cause hydrological droughts to persist for a more extended period after the termination of the initial agricultural droughts. Sustained agricultural droughts (so-called “droughts” hereafter) can lead to significant and prolonged reductions in water yield (WYLD- the net volume of freshwater, including surface runoff, lateral flow, and groundwater generated in a catchment) despite their termination (Yang et al., 2017 ). The persistent reduction in WYLD following agricultural droughts (so-called “post-droughts” hereafter) is often attributed to factors such as increases in ET and shifts in the annual rainfall-runoff relationship (Saft et al., 2016 ). It can also be related to changes in the seasonality of rainfall (Pepler et al., 2021 ), reductions in pre-drought precipitation (Wasko et al., 2020 ), increased soil moisture depletion (Filipović et al., 2018 ), and reductions in heavy rainfall frequency (Elliott et al., 2015 ). Furthermore, changes in soil physical properties (e.g., soil hydraulic conductivity, bulk density, available water capacity) due to droughts (Van Loon and Van Lanen, 2013 ), and soil conservation techniques, during and after the droughts can also contribute to reduced WYLD, which can exacerbate the adverse effects of post-droughts on hydrology (Cornish et al., 2020 ). In addition, plain regions with minimal slope and slight topographic relief can generate less runoff as compared to highlands (Khalili et al., 2023 ) due to greater rates of infiltration and ET. This can exacerbate the adverse effects of agricultural droughts on runoff generation after their termination. Increases in atmospheric evaporative demand following a drought and the changes in vegetation growth patterns and water use can also impact runoff generation and streamflow (Mastrotheodoros et al., 2020 ). Moreover, reduced recharge to groundwater during a prolonged drought can also contribute to the decline in groundwater levels and further exacerbate the streamflow reduction after the drought is termination (Khalili et al., 2023; Fowler et al., 2020 ). Therefore, the post-drought persistence of WYLD decline and streamflow reduction are complex processes influenced by a wide range of factors. After a prolonged drought, the altered terrestrial and atmospheric processes create a diverse range of variations in hydrological water components and environmental conditions. However, most studies have focused on the short-term direct impact of a given type of drought (e.g., agricultural droughts) (Li et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020; Khalili et al., 2023 ), while the examination of long-term (multi-year) changes in hydrological processes due to progression into the hydrologic system at a watershed scale in a post-drought period is limited. The changes in hydrological processes following a prolonged drought event can impact crop yield (Y, tonne/ha) and the time it takes for crops to recover from a given drought (Iqbal et al., 2020; Lesk et al., 2016 ). Understanding the effects of post-drought conditions on Y and its linkages with watershed hydrology (e.g., green water and WYLD) can inform sustainable water and food management strategies (Hamal et al., 2020 ; Krishnamurthy et al., 2022 ; Srivastav et al., 2021 ). However, there is currently a limited understanding of the post-drought effects on Y due to the complexity of post-drought processes, lack of long-term data on spatiotemporal variability in recovery of hydrological regime and Y after a drought event, and difficulty in controlling for other factors such as changes in land use and management practices. Field-based research studies have demonstrated that the recovery of Y from drought can be quicker than that of the watershed hydrology, leading to further stress on the hydrological balance (Orth and Destouni, 2018 ). This is attributed to the increased infiltration rate after a drought, when the soil is dry, demanding a greater proportion of precipitation to infiltrate the soil instead of contributing to surface runoff (Qiu et al., 2023 ). However, the infiltrated water can primarily replenish the topsoil moisture for crop use, leaving limited soil water for groundwater recharge, which can result in a continuous reduction of groundwater levels (Khalili et al., 2023 ). The reduced groundwater level can ultimately lead to reduced soil moisture for crop ET, which otherwise could be accessible from a high groundwater table through capillary fringe for root water uptake (Karamouz et al., 2011 ). The reduced groundwater levels can also decrease subsurface water contribution to streamflow, decreasing the return flow or base flow to the streams (Wossenyeleh et al., 2020 ), potentially impacting irrigated Y (OECD, 2016 ). As a result, the recovery of Y under post-drought conditions is highly related to the hydrological processes driving soil water and the feedback between crop growth and soil moisture availability. The virtual water content, VWC (m3 /tonne), associated with the trade of crops is quantified based on the ratio of crop ET (mm) to Y (tonne/ha) (Hoekstra, 2003 ), which can be variable depending on the geospatial, hydrological, and climatological characteristics, as well as agricultural management practices where crops are produced. The VWC also depends on the water source used in the production process of the crops, including blue (i.e., WYLD in this study) and green (i.e., actual evapotranspiration based on rain) water resources. Given that all these factors can be considerably impacted by droughts, the VWC and the pattern of the trade of crop products can also be affected by droughts. VWT is based on the combined effects of traded commodities and their water content (VWC). Despite the wide range of studies on VWT, a comprehensive assessment of the impacts of droughts and post-drought conditions on VWT is limited. Previous research on VWT has primarily concentrated on the role of VWT on water resource management, water savings, and socioeconomic drivers of VWT and the VWT networks (Chapagain et al., 2006; Mekonnen and Hoekstra, 2020; Oki et al., 2017; Qu et al., 2018; Faramarzi et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2016; Zhuo et al., 2016 ; Konar et al., 2011 ). However, these studies have largely overlooked the role of natural factors such as droughts and post-drought conditions in local hydrological processes driving VWT. Additionally, these studies have primarily focused on historical observations (Hoekstra and Mekonnen, 2016; Mekonnen and Hoekstra, 2020 ) and have not adequately addressed the changes under future extreme event conditions such as droughts and post-drought periods under global warming scenarios. The most recent studies focusing on the effects of climate change on VWT (Graham et al., 2020 ) provided detailed insights into the potential impacts on food production and trade under projected average future climate conditions. Overall, the ensemble mean model projections show a promising future with increases in precipitation, heat units, and Y for mid-to-high latitude regions (He et al., 2018; Khalili et al., 2021 ; IPCC, 2022 ; Masud et al., 2019 ). However, these studies lack assessment of the impacts of extreme dry events, such as drought and post-drought conditions, on hydrological processes and blue-green water interchange, which are critical drivers of crop growth and VWT (Khalili et al., 2023; Marston and Konar, 2017 ). Therefore, to fully understand the combined and long-lasting impacts of droughts on hydrology, Y, and VWT, it is imperative to conduct a comprehensive analysis that considers the complex interactions and relationships among these factors in the same analytical framework. Such a study can help inform and guide sustainable water management and food production strategies in the face of global warming scenarios. More specifically, the agricultural watersheds of mid-to-high latitude regions, such as Canadian Prairies, are prone to frequent droughts, while they are also important breadbaskets of the world (Khalili et al., 2021; Rubin and Hurst, 2017 ). Given the potential adverse effects of post-droughts on water availability and crop production, it is crucial to assess the effects of droughts and post-droughts on potential VWT from these regions and the impacts on global food security. Therefore, the primary goal of this study is to examine the impacts of droughts and post-droughts (i.e., agricultural droughts) on not only crop yields and production potentials at a regional scale but also the progression and the impacts on hydrological processes (e.g., WYLD) and their linkages through assessment of VWT under global warming scenarios. To achieve this goal, the objectives of this study are to: (1) analyze the past and projected changes in WYLD under average, drought, and post-drought conditions using Nelson River Basin (NRB) as a study region, which is the largest agricultural watershed (1.2 million km2 ) in Canadian Prairies, covering various ecohydrological conditions; (2) assess the past and projected changes in Y, under average, drought, and post-drought conditions in NRB; (3) evaluate the impacts of drought and post-drought conditions on VWT under historical and future scenarios in the NRB which is one of the important breadbaskets of the world and exports crops to over 170 countries around the world. The findings of this study are applicable to other large river basins in mid-to-high latitude regions, which often play a crucial role in socioeconomic development, food export, and global food security.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study region and data collection 2.1.1 Study region The Nelson River Basin (NRB) is the largest agricultural watershed in western Canada, and it supplies wheat crops and other agricultural commodities to over 170 countries worldwide (Statistics Canada, 2022 ). While located in Canada and a small part of the northern US, known as one of the most water-abundant regions in the world (World Bank, 2021 ), crop production in NRB is highly reliant on variable hydrological processes (Masud et al., 2018 ) (Fig. 1  ). Commencing in the Rocky Mountains at an altitude of 3,227 m in the west, the basin extends from South Dakota, USA, in the south to central areas in Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba, Canada, in its northern borders to near Lake Superior in the eastern region. Covering an area of approximately 1.2 million square kilometers, the basin discharges about 2370 m3 /s into Hudson Bay, which is the most extensive inland sea globally (Fig. 1A, 1B ). With over 40 % agricultural land, the NRB is recognized for its fertile soils and ideal conditions for crop production. Wheat is one of the most extensively grown crops, with the prairie provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba producing about 25 million tonnes per year and contributing to over 85 % of Canada's total wheat production in NRB (Fig. 1 C) (Statistics Canada, 2022 ). Although irrigation is practiced in some regions of the Prairies to supplement precipitation and sustain crop growth, rainfed crop production is the primary approach in most areas (Government of Canada, 2021 ). In addition to wheat, the area is also a major producer of canola (Fig. 1 D), with over 19 million tonnes of canola production per year, accounting for over 90 % of the country's canola production (Statistics Canada, 2022 ). The NRB exports an average of 17 million tonnes of wheat and 10 million tonnes of canola to various countries worldwide, which accounts for over 60 % and 55 % of Canada’s wheat and canola exports, respectively (Statistics Canada, 2022 ). This level of crop export scores the Canada at the 3rd rank after the European Union and Russia, being the top-most exporters of wheat globally; and making Canada the leading region with 70 % contribution to the global canola production and export (International Grains Council, 2021 ; Canola Council of Canada, 2021 ; Statistics Canada, 2022 ). The mean temperature range for the growing season (i.e., May to September) across croplands of NRB is between 15 °C and 25 °C, with some areas experiencing higher temperatures. The average annual precipitation for the growing season in the agricultural region of NRB ranges from 200 mm to 500 mm, with some areas experiencing higher amounts of rainfall (Khalili et al., 2023 ). For detailed spatial distribution, refer to Fig. S1 . It is important to note that the prairies in the southern regions of the basin, such as south Alberta and Saskatchewan, tend to be hotter and drier than the northern and eastern regions of the basin, such as north Manitoba. Additionally, the eastern Prairies in the basin, near Lake Superior, tend to receive a larger amount of precipitation than the western regions.  2.1.2 Input data To achieve the objectives of this study, we used the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT, see section 2.2 ). This agro-hydrological model was previously calibrated and validated for hydrological simulation (Khalili et al., 2023 ). The specific parameters calibrated for hydrology and crop yield are detailed in Table S1 and S2 . This agro-hydrological model of NRB (see section 2.2 ) was developed utilizing a diverse range of geospatial maps and time series data, including Digital Elevation Models (DEM) (Jarvis et al., 2008 ), a detailed land use-land cover map (Government of Canada, 2021 ), and a processed soil map (Cordeiro et al., 2018 ; FAO, 2015 ). For model setup and calibration, the WATCH Forcing Data ERA-Interim (WFDEI) historical climate dataset (Weedon et al., 2014 ), measured streamflow data from hydrometric stations, and daily operation data of 44 large reservoirs/dams were incorporated (Khalili et al., 2023 ). The WFDEI data included daily precipitation, maximum and minimum temperatures, solar radiation, wind speed, and relative humidity. This climate data product has produced superior results for Canadian studies (Wong et al., 2017 ) and successfully reproduced the historical trends and fluctuations of streamflow and crop yields at the NRB (Khalili et al., 2023 ). Hence, we used WFDEI for this study, ensuring consistency and reliability in our modelling efforts. The simulation period (including calibration and validation) for this study was from 1987 to 2016. Additional information regarding the model development can be found in Khalili et al. (2023) . In order to simulate rainfed crops in our hydrological model, an extensive amount of agricultural management data was collected, including planting and harvesting dates, volume and rate of fertilizer application, and crop-specific information such as plant growth parameters, phenological development stages, and potential heat units for spring wheat and canola (see Table S3 ). Crop-specific fertilizer application rates (represented as N:P:K ratios), maximum annual fertilizer application (measured in kg/ha per year), and the potential heat units required for crops (degree days) were obtained from various sources such as Statistics Canada (2022)  and the United States Department of Agriculture (2021)  and earlier studies (Faramarzi et al., 2017; Masud et al., 2019, 2018 ). For calibration purposes, the yearly Y time series for rainfed spring wheat and canola was acquired at the CAR level from Statistics Canada (2022)  and Alberta Financial Service Cooperation (AFSC), as presented in Fig. 1 . The entire agricultural lands in the NRB encompass 37 Canadian census agricultural regions (CARs) and seven agricultural regions in the United States (collectively referred to as CARs, hereafter) (Fig. 1 B). Planting and harvesting dates were obtained from the literature (Faramarzi et al., 2017; Mezbahuddin et al., 2020 ) and other available sources (see Alberta Agricultural and Rural Development, 2004 ; Government of Saskatchewan, 2020; Government of Manitoba, 2020), and they were further modified through the calibration process. The future climate data were incorporated from an ensemble of six Global Climate Models (GCMs) of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) for future projections of the hydrological processes and crop growth (see Table S4 ). The future climate data are based on two contrasting Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP126 and SSP585) representing the lowest and highest radiative forcing levels projected for the year 2100. For future hydrology and crop simulations in the study, the concentration of CO2  was set to 350, 450, and 850 ppm for the historical, SSP126, and SSP585 future periods, respectively (Eyring et al., 2016 ). Most CMIP6 projected climate projections indicate more critical global warming effects near the end of the 21st century, albeit subject to a greater spread of prediction uncertainty. Therefore, the analyses were performed for the 2070 to 2099 period using the two most extreme SSP scenarios. In an earlier study (Masud et al., 2021 ), the future climate data were statistically downscaled based on historical daily gridded climate data using multiple techniques, including Climate Imprint, Quantile Delta Mapping, Constructed Analogues, and Bias Correction/Constructed Analogues with Quantile mapping reordering. This study used downscaled climate data for future periods to force the agro-hydrologic model. More detailed information can be found in Khalili et al. (2023)  and Masud et al. (2021) .   2.2 Model configuration and evaluation metrics SWAT is a process-based semi-distributed model that simulates various hydrological, plant growth, sediment, and nutrient cycling-related processes (Neitsch et al., 2011 ). The model has been used to simulate the impacts of climate change and management operations on hydrology, crop growth, sediment and nutrient transport, and their fate from catchment to large watersheds and continental scales (Haney et al., 2018; Karamouz et al., 2021; Loiselle et al., 2020 ). It partitions a basin into sub-basins and Hydrological Response Units (HRUs) based on a topographic map, soil, land use-land cover, and slope parameters. Within each HRU, the processes are simulated based on the user-provided soil, vegetation, climate, and management data and then aggregated to sub-basin and basin levels. More specifically, the model is capable of simulating a wide range of processes, including actual ET (AET) and potential ET (PET), surface runoff, snow accumulation and melt, groundwater recharge, subsurface flows, crop growth and crop water consumption, soil temperature, soil nutrient cycling, nutrient loads and transport, and erosion and sediment loads and transport among others (Neitsch et al., 2011 ). In this study, we utilized a calibrated hydrological model of the NRB (Khalili et al., 2023 ) to develop a crop growth model using the ArcSWAT 2012. The calibrated hydrological model of the NRB delineated the region into a total of 1988 sub-basins based on the DEM map (Khalili et al., 2023 ). Following the calibration of hydrological processes, the wheat growth simulation module underwent calibration and validation using wheat Y time series data in the study by Khalili et al. (2023) , as explained in section 2.1.2  (Table S1 and S2 ). In our current study, we utilized their calibrated hydrologic model and further calibrated and validated the rainfed canola yield for the 1987–2016 period. Given the close relationships between hydrological processes, Y, and AET (Faramarzi et al., 2010, 2017 ), the calibration of our model against streamflow and Y ensured the reliability of AET simulations. It is worth noting that while assimilation of remote sensing (RS) data for the assessment of Y and ET is suggested (Ma et al., 2022 ), we chose to rely on CAR data because of the specific objectives of this study which required understanding of various agro-hydrological processes such as WYLD and NVWE in addition to Y and AET under both historical and future climate change scenarios where RS data are not available. In addition, all RS data require careful validation, which is beyond the scope of our current study (Ma et al., 2022 ). The effectiveness of SWAT in simulating crop growth, especially under varying climatic conditions, has been well-documented in the literature, illustrating its robustness in capturing the complexities associated with crop production at a regional scale (Chen et al., 2019; Haney et al., 2018; Khalili et al., 2021; Zare et al., 2023 ). The calibrated model was then used to project hydrology and Y for the 2070–2099 period. Overall, the two Y models for the simulation of rainfed wheat and canola growth were built upon a hydrology model developed and calibrated in an earlier study by Khalili et al. (2023) , which provided the foundation for the crop growth simulation. The hydrology model and the calibration and validation of the spring wheat crop are discussed in greater detail in Khalili et al. (2023) . In the present study, we constructed a canola yield simulation model. The heat unit requirements were optimized in the model through a calibration procedure to represent different varieties of crops planted across the watershed, differing in their growing degree-days. The total fertilizer application per year in different sub-basins and the application rate were defined from the available data. Still, fertilizer application frequency and timing were set to the auto fertilizer option of the SWAT model, which was controlled by the nutrient stress factor and plant-water-stress threshold simulated in the model (Neitsch et al., 2011 ). For future projections in this study, the agricultural and soil management practices were kept consistent with the historical patterns, focusing primarily on assessing the impact of climate drivers. Prior to conducting the calibration process, we performed a sensitivity analysis (SA) for model parameter selection using a methodology similar to Faramarzi et al. (2017) . The SA can determine critical parameters that affect hydrology and crop growth in various regions. The selected parameters were scaled to simulate regional variations in geospatial, hydro-climatic, and ecological conditions (Faramarzi et al., 2017 ). We identified 26 and 27 scaled parameters for six major hydrological watersheds (Fig. 1 A) and 44 CARs (Fig. 1 B), respectively (Khalili et al., 2023 ). To calibrate and evaluate the efficacy of our model, we followed an iterative procedure that involved the publicly available Sequential Uncertainty Fitting program (SUFI-2) (Abbaspour, 2015 ) and a parallel processing program scheme to utilize a 200-core advanced computer for parallel processing of the simulations (Khalili et al., 2023 ). The first iteration starts by assigning the largest physically meaningful range for each sensitive parameter, and they are sampled using Latin Hypercube Sampling to create 1000 sample parameter sets. Then, parameters are updated, and the model is forced based on each of the 1000 sample sets, for which 1000 sets of output variables, i.e., streamflow and Y, are generated and compared to the measured data. If the comparison results are unsuccessful, a new iteration is performed by revising the initial parameter ranges until satisfactory results are obtained. The calibrated model against streamflow (Khalili et al., 2023 ) used several objective functions to assess model performance for each of the 1000 streamflow simulations. These objective functions included the coefficient of determination (R2 ), the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), the percent bias (PBIAS), and the Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE). In this study, to evaluate the agreement between the simulated and observed Y, we used the mean square error (MSE). The simulated data at the sub-basin level were aggregated to the CAR level to maintain a consistent spatial resolution with the observed yield data. Given the large spatial extent of the study region and various sources of uncertainty in the modelling (Khalili et al., 2021 ), two significant measures were employed to evaluate the model calibration and uncertainty performance of a given iteration. The p-factor , which represents the percentage of data bracketed within the 95 % prediction uncertainty (95PPU) band, and the r-factor , which measures the average width of the band relative to the standard deviation of the corresponding measured variable. At the scale of this study, the model is forced to capture the majority of the measured data within the simulated 95PPU band, indicating a high level of model accuracy (i.e., p-factor  close to 1), and to result in a narrow uncertainty band, i.e., r-factor  of 3–5 is an acceptable range for Y simulations (Faramarzi et al., 2017, 2010 ). Additional information regarding the model calibration, validation, and uncertainty analysis can be found in Khalili et al., (2023) .  2.3 Drought severity index calculation To predict drought conditions, we used the widely-used Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) approach (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010 ). The SPEI is a multi-scalar drought index that considers both precipitation and PET to evaluate the onset, duration, and severity of agricultural drought conditions. The calculation of the SPEI involves the analysis of precipitation (P) and PET times series data for a given time period (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010 ). For instance, using a monthly time series, a climatic water balance (WB) is first calculated as the difference between P and PET for each month. To determine whether the WB amount is in deficit or surplus for a specific period, we accumulate the monthly WB data over the period of interest, ranging from 1 month to 12 months (i.e., 1-month, 2-month, …, 12-month accumulated data). For example, to construct a 9-month time series data set for WB, we first accumulate data from the initial 9 months. Subsequently, we employ a rolling-and-moving window of one month to create successive 9-month cumulative data until the entire study period is covered. The accumulation period is any period of interest that quantifies the standardized surplus or deficit of WB (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2010 ). In this study, we constructed 9-month SPEI indices to consider the legacy soil moisture from previous months that could affect soil water availability for crop production during the growing season in our study region. To construct the SPEI for NRB, we used our model-simulated PET and the precipitation data described in section 2.1.2 . Note that a modified Penman-Monteith equation is used in our SWAT model to simulate PET (Neitsch et al., 2011 ). The selection of 9-month SPEI was verified by performing a correlation analysis between SPEI of different accumulation times (ranging from 1 to 12 months) and observed Y anomaly data (i.e., Y differences from the long-term average Y) for the 1987 to 2016 period. The highest correlation with Y anomaly was related to the 9-month time series in most regions (Fig. S2 ). Overall, the SPEI approach quantifies WB as a standardized departure from a selected probability distribution function that models the raw data (i.e., 9-month WB data in this study). The raw data are typically fitted to a best-performing probability function distribution and then transformed to a normal distribution to generate the SPEI indices. The constructed indices can then be interpreted as the number of standard deviations by which the observed anomaly deviates from the long-term mean (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2014 ). In this approach, negative index values indicate drought events and positive values indicate wet events. The resulting SPEI indices are then employed to quantify drought severity using a drought classification system, such as the one detailed by Svoboda et al. (2004)  and employed by the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM) (Svoboda et al., 2002 ). This classification approach interprets SPEI values to their corresponding degree of varying drought and wetness conditions and lists them from D0 (abnormal) to D4 (exceptional) droughts and from normal to extreme wet conditions. Table S5  summarizes all drought and wet events with their corresponding SPEI values and their ecological implications (Svoboda et al., 2004 ). Considering that precipitation and PET data typically exhibit right-skewness due to the nature of rainfall patterns, a gamma distribution has been recommended as the most suitable fit (Wang et al., 2019 ), a methodology consistent with previous findings (Khalili et al., 2023 ). As such, we fitted a gamma distribution to the constructed 9-month WB times series for each sub-basin. Using the gamma distribution, we further calculated the cumulative probability function (F(x)) for each WB value (x). Next, we constructed the standardized indices (SPEI) using the inverse of the standard normal distribution function (Φ-1 ) as follows:(1) SPEI = Φ - 1   F x             Finally, we aggregated the sub-basin level SPEI time series to the NRB level to analyze the effects of regional droughts on Y, WYLD, and VWT (section 2.4 ).  2.4 WYLD, Y, and VWT accounting 2.4.1 WYLD and Y calculation In the SWAT model, the WYLD in each day and for a given sub-basin is calculated as follows:(2) Q WYLD   = Q Surf   + Q Lat   + Q GW   - Q TLoss        Where Q WYLD      is WYLD (mm), Q Surf      is surface runoff (mm) generated in the sub-basin, Q Lat      is lateral flow, which is the volume of water that moves laterally within the soil profile and enters the main channel in each sub-basin (mm), Q GW      is the water from the shallow aquifer that enters the main channel when the groundwater level is high (mm), Q TLoss      is water loss in each sub-basin due to transmission through the streambed (mm). Y is also determined by various factors, such as leaf area development (simulated in the model), light interception, and conversion of intercepted light into biomass, using a plant species-specific radiation use efficiency at a daily time step. The model simulates above-ground and below-ground biomass using 40 crop-specific phonological parameters (such as potential heat units, base temperature, optimum temperature, maximum leaf area index, radiation use efficiency, etc.), and agricultural management data (such as crop planting areas, planting and harvesting dates, fertilizer and pesticide application, irrigation, tillage, and harvest and kill operations). First, optimal biomass and potential yields are simulated under ideal growing conditions, which include adequate water and nutrient supply and a favorable climate, such as optimum temperature. Then, actual yields are simulated based on constraints induced by deficiency or surpluses in soil water availability, soil nutrient availability, and temperature stresses, which are simulated on daily time steps across different soil layers in each sub-basin. Biomass development begins when the temperature exceeds the plant-specific base temperature from planting to harvest date or until it reaches the crop-specific maximum heat units. Actual water uptake by the crop is simulated based on PET, biomass development (above-ground and below-ground), and water availability in the soil layers on a daily basis (Neitsch et al., 2011 ). 2.4.1.1 Virtual water content (VWC) and VWT accounting The virtual water content (VWC) is a measure of the amount of water required for crop production, expressed as the volume of water per unit of mass-produced (Hoekstra, 2003 ).
