The VWC (m3 /tonne) in our study was calculated as follows:(3) VWC = AET  Y  × 10      Where, AET is the simulated crop water consumption (mm) of rainfed wheat and canola during the crop growing period, Y is the simulated Y (tonne/ha) specific to these crops. To convert the simulated AET (mm) into m3 /ha, a factor of 10 is used in the calculation. A higher VWC indicates a greater amount of water used per tonne of crop production, resulting in a lower water use efficiency. The VWC of wheat and canola were calculated for historical (1987–2016) and future (2070–2099) periods for each sub-basin using simulated Y and AET data. We further calculated the net virtual water trade, i.e., net virtual water export (NVWE, m3 ) from the NRB to assess the effects of drought and post-drought on regional water resources in relation to crop productions and their potential exports. The NVWE is the volume of water that is associated with the export of crops (Hoekstra and Chapagain, 2007; Mekonnen and Hoekstra, 2011 ). As the total volume of crop exports is not known for future scenarios, we assumed the crop surplus that is not consumed domestically would be potentially available for export. As such, we excluded the water embedded in the production of crops that are consumed domestically in the NRB. Therefore, we estimated both the domestic crop consumption (P r    , tonne) and the total crop production (P a    , tonne) in the NRB. We calculated domestic crop consumption using the approach proposed by Ercin and Hoekstra (2014)  as follows:(4) P  r   = 1.2 × p e r  c a p i t a  c r o p  c o n s u m p t i o n × T o t a l  p o p u l a t i o n      For the purpose of this study, the per capita consumption rates of wheat and canola were obtained from the FAOSTAT Commodity Balance Sheets (FAOSTAT, 2021 ). The per capita crop consumption was assumed to be constant for both past and future scenarios. This assumption was based on the relatively stable trends observed in crop consumption patterns in the historical data. For future scenarios, the total population was estimated based on the historical growth rate observed over the last 30 years, data sourced from the U.S. Census Bureau and Statistics Canada. This projection assumes that the historical growth rate will remain consistent over the years. However, given potential future changes in fertility, mortality, and migration trends, this carries inherent uncertainty. Then, total crop production in the region was calculated as follows:(5) P a  = Y × A     Where, Y is simulated crop yield (tonne/ha), A is the area under cultivation (ha) for each crop type, derived from crop inventory maps (Government of Canada, 2021 ). The crop inventory maps have a grid resolution of 30 m × 30 m, and provide annual area under cultivation for various crops. It is important to note that not all grid cells have a 100 % cultivated area for a given crop. In our analyses, we considered any grid cells with the cultivated area of ≥ 10 %. Finally, we summed the product of P a     for all crop types (rainfed spring wheat and canola in this study) to obtain the total crop production in the NRB. The VWT (m3 ) for the future period was calculated as follows:(6) VWT = Σ ( ( P  a  -  P r   )   c  × ( V W C  c  ) )      ( P  a  -  P r   )   c     is the surplus of a given crop that is not consumed domestically and potentially available for export (tonne), (VWC)c  is the virtual water content of a given crop (m3 /tonne). Overall, the positive VWT in Eq. (6)  indicates net virtual water that flows outside the region (NVWE), and the negative values indicate otherwise. It is worth noting that, in the current state of affairs, a substantial portion of crop surplus in the NRB is indirectly exported through the production and export of meat, live animals, dairy products, and beverages (AAFC, 2021 ). However, this study did not explicitly determine the VWC and NVWE associated with these commodities. Instead, we assumed that all crop surplus could be directly exported as grain without further processing.    2.5 Drought and post-drought analysis of WYLD, Y, and VWT Using the regional SPEI times series explained in section 2.3 , we computed all drought events with an intensity of less than −0.5 and selected the most severe droughts for the impact assessment in this study. Again, in this study, we opted to simulate the effects of agricultural droughts during and after their termination (referred to as droughts and post-droughts) on hydrological processes (i.e., WYLD) as well as Y and NVWE. Note that the −0.5 threshold delineates D0 or worse drought events, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor categories (see Table S5 ). Next, using the regional SPEI times series, we calculated the regional drought duration for the NRB based on the successive number of months experiencing a drought intensity of less than −0.5. For our impact assessment, we selected the drought events that lasted the longest. We further performed impact analysis for the longest duration and the most severe drought events (LMDs). It is noteworthy that the use of regional SPEI times series for regional drought assessment may result in non-drought conditions for some sub-basins in the region. To address the post-drought effects of Y, WYLD, and NVWE, establishing a clear definition of the end of a given drought event is crucial. The definition of the end of a drought can vary depending on the index employed and the research objectives. In this study, based on the USDA drought classification approach, we generally defined the end of a drought as the time when the SPEI index is greater than −0.5. Theoretically, an SPEI value greater than −0.5 indicates a reduced deficit between precipitation and PET, which implies improvement of the agro-hydrological conditions to a state of relative normalcy (Nam et al., 2015 ). To assess the response of Y, WYLD, and NVWE to post-drought conditions, we analyzed the data for the five years following the cessation of the longest and most severe droughts (LMD) at a regional scale, as predicted by each of the six GCMs. We selected a five-year post-drought period based on our observation that the impacts of the drought were undetectable beyond this period at the regional scale. Our results are reported as the ensemble mean values for the five-year post-drought periods. The LMD for each GCM and each SSP scenario was calculated based on the lowest SPEI values from the regional averaged time series (see section 2.3 ), as the lower values indicate greater severity droughts. The longest drought was determined by the highest count of consecutive months where the regional SPEI value was less than −0.5, indicating sustained periods of at least D0 event or worse. For the years after the selected LMDs, we simulated Y, WYLD, and NVWE using our calibrated model (named D  Scenario, hereafter), and we compared the results with a ‘theoretical scenario’ where we assumed there was no LMD in our model (ND  scenario). To simulate ND  scenario, we modified the model input climate data (e.g., daily precipitation, maximum and minimum temperature, solar radiation, wind speed, and relative humidity of the air). Specifically, we replaced climate data from the years identified as non-drought years. With this approach, we ensured the sequence of years in the ND  scenario reflected continuous and uninterrupted time series data of non-drought conditions. Since the Y model was calibrated based on CAR-based observed yield data, we aggregated our simulated results from sub-basin to CAR and presented them at CAR spatial resolution (section 3 ). Next, we evaluated the differences between the D  and ND  scenarios to explore the post-drought recovery of the Y, WYLD, and VWT in different eco-hydrological regions and under different SSP scenarios in the future.   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Model performance evaluation metrics The calibration and validation processes were conducted across 44 CARs, encompassing both canola and spring wheat crops. For the sake of conciseness, we present the results of our analysis at the average watershed level for both crops in Table 1  . Detailed information on the crop model calibration and validation results can be found in Table S6 and S7 . The model successfully reproduced observed annual rainfed canola yields for the calibration period (1992–2016). The average p-factor  for the calibration period exceeded 87 %, indicating that the observed yield data was adequately captured within the simulated 95PPU. The average r-factor  values were 2.05 and 2.41 for wheat (Khalili et al., 2023 ) and canola, respectively (Table 1 ). The average mean squared error (MSE) values across the study region for wheat and canola yields were 0.16 and 0.10, respectively. A similar performance was observed during the validation period (Table 1 ). The minimum and maximum statistics for all CARs demonstrated overall satisfactory performance for both rainfed crops for the calibration and validation periods. It should be noted that improvements in p-factor  were occasionally achieved at the cost of increased r-factor  and higher MSE values in certain regions. Consequently, the calibration process must establish a reasonable balance between the p-factor and r-factor. Large-scale models present inherent uncertainties due to errors in input data, process simplification, and variations in historical management practices. Nevertheless, the model performance was deemed satisfactory for most regions and time periods within the study area.  3.2 Historical and future variation of WYLD, Y, and VWT under long-term average conditions for the growing season 3.2.1 Precipitation patterns and WYLD The analysis of historical data and future projections for the growing season (May-September) under the SSP126 and SSP585 scenarios revealed noteworthy changes in precipitation (Fig. 2  a). Across the study area, monthly precipitation during the growing season varies considerably, ranging from 45 mm/month in the agricultural watersheds of southern Alberta and Saskatchewan to 100 mm/month in the southeastern region of NRB, which covers parts of both the Canadian and U.S. agricultural lands. The ensemble mean precipitation data from the six downscaled future climate data for the 2070–2099 period indicated that the majority of the study area will likely experience a precipitation increase of 6 % and 10 % per month for the growing season under SSP126 and SSP585 scenarios, respectively. Furthermore, the projected future scenarios demonstrated an increase in WYLD compared to the historical period. In particular, the monthly WYLD projections during the growing season showed an increase of 30 % (i.e., 1.5 mm) under SSP126 and more than 200 % (i.e., 10 mm) under SSP585 relative to the historical period (Fig. 2 b).  3.2.2 Rainfed wheat and canola yields The simulated results for the historical period indicated that the average spring wheat yield (2.3 tonne/ha) was higher than that of canola (1.4 tonne/ha) (Fig. 3  ). For the historical period, simulated Y for both crops was higher in the eastern and western sub-basins of the study area, ranging between 2–5 tonne/ha for spring wheat and 1–3 tonne/ha for canola. Lower yields were observed in the central regions, with approximately 0.5–3 tonne/ha for spring wheat and 0–2 tonne/ha for canola. The long-term average projected data showed that Y will likely increase under both SSP scenarios (SSP126 and SSP585). On average, the projected ensemble mean data showed that wheat and canola yields are likely to increase by 9 % (reaching 2.3–2.6 tonne/ha) and 8 % (reaching 1.3–1.5 tonne/ha) under SSP126 and by 26 % (up to 2.9 tonne/ha) and 29 % (up to 1.7 tonne/ha) under SSP585, respectively.  3.2.3 VWC and VWT Our simulated VWC for the rainfed wheat and canola crops during the historical period indicated that, on average, canola exhibits higher VWC (1000–2000 m3 /tonne) than spring wheat (700–1700 m3 /tonne), suggesting a greater water requirement for producing a tonne of canola compared to spring wheat (Fig. 4  a and 4c). VWC analysis of the western and eastern regions revealed that these regions are characterized by higher precipitation, greater AET, and lower VWC compared to the central regions of the study area. It is important to note that while the western and eastern regions exhibit higher AET, they also demonstrate significantly higher crop yields than the central regions. This disproportional increase in yields relative to AET results in lower VWC values. Despite increased AET, the higher yields in the western and eastern regions indicate a more optimal conversion of AET to crop yields. In contrast, the central areas experiencing higher water stress, as discussed by Khalili et al. (2023) , have less efficient water use, leading to higher VWC despite their lower AET. Future VWC projections displayed a reduction of VWC from the SSP126 to SSP585 scenarios. The reduced VWC is attributed to the lower projected AET under the SSP585 scenario, where elevated CO2  concentrations result in reduced stomatal opening in crops, decreasing plant transpiration as compared to SSP126 (Deryng et al., 2016; Masud et al., 2019 ). The analysis of modelled historical data indicated that, of the total net virtual water export (NVWE), spring wheat accounts for an average of 66 %, while canola constitutes the remaining 33 %. This means that spring wheat contributes two-thirds of the total NVWE, with canola contributing one-third. The results revealed that the average annual NVWE for the historical period is 41.4 billion m3  and 20.9 billion m3  for spring wheat and canola, respectively, totalling 62.3 billion m3  per year for the historical period. This is associated with the potential export of surplus crop grains that are not consumed domestically. However, a considerable share of surplus crops is consumed in the food industry and indirectly exported from the NRB. Some examples are the export of meat (e.g., beef), live animals (e.g., cattle, calves), dairy products, and beverages (Statistics Canada, 2022 ). While this study did not explicitly calculate the VWC and VWT of these commodities, we assumed that all crop surplus could be directly exported in the form of grain. Future export potential of wheat and canola crops under the SSP126 scenario indicated likely export of 41.1 billion m3  and 20.1 billion m3  per year of virtual water, respectively, representing a relatively similar volume of NVWE to their historical volumes. This amount decreased to 38.5 billion m3  and 19.5 billion m3  under the SSP585 scenario. It is important to note that we assumed future cropping areas remain the same as historical coverage. Overall, using the simulated Y for the future period and based on historical crop area inventory maps, the projected annual export potential for wheat and canola is likely to increase from 35.1 and 12.6 million tonnes during the historical period to 37.9 and 13.2 million tonnes under SSP126, respectively, with further increases up to 42.1 and 13.7 million tonnes under SSP585. However, as discussed in the following sections, the volume of crop production and export potentials and their associated NVWE can differ under drought and post-drought events.   3.3 Impacts of drought and post-drought conditions on WYLD, Y, and VWT 3.3.1 WYLD, Y, and VWC response to droughts The ensemble mean simulated SPEI, representing different severity levels of agricultural droughts, was 1.1 (representing D1 drought) for the historical period, 1.7 (representing D3 drought) for the SSP126 scenario, and 1.5 (representing D2 drought) for the SSP585 scenario. Consequently, the mean projected duration of the LMDs for the historical period was 11 months, while it was 18.5 months for the SSP126 scenario and 16.8 months for the SSP585 scenario. Unlike the long-term average conditions, under the projected LMD events, the ensemble mean precipitation decreased in all scenarios (historical and future) for most of the NRB (Fig. 5  a). During the historical LMD period, a reduction of up to 17 % in precipitation compared to the historical average condition was observed (Fig. 5 a). The projected precipitation during future LMDs indicated a reduction of up to 27 % under the SSP126 and up to 35 % under the SSP585 compared to the historical average condition (Fig. 5 a). This suggests a likely drier LMDs for the region in the future than in the historical period. Unlike the long-term average projections, which indicate a wetter overall future (Bush and Lemmen, 2019 ), with the SSP585 as the wettest scenario (Fig. 2 a), the projections suggest that droughts will be drier in the future. Despite the lower magnitude of precipitation occurring during the LMD events of the SSP585 scenario as compared to SSP126 and the historical period (Fig. 5 a), Fig. 5 b shows the WYLD increased by up to 80 % in some areas under the projected LMD events of the SSP585 compared to the average historical period. However, the 80 % anomaly is particularly evident in the regions where WYLD is not substantial (e.g., of 0–5 mm) under the historical average conditions (Fig. 5 b), resulting in a meagre amount of WYLD generated under the SSP585 scenario in the future. The 80 % increase under the SSP585 scenario is also related to the elevated atmospheric CO2  concentration, which reduces crop water use, resulting in greater precipitation contributing to water yield. In contrast, under LMD conditions of the SSP126 and historical years, we observed up to 55 % and 50 % reductions in water yield compared to the average historical period (Fig. 5 ). This also highlights the complex interplay between precipitation, CO2  concentration, and water yield under various climate change scenarios, particularly during extreme hydrological conditions (Khalili et al., 2021 ). The analysis of the spring wheat yields indicated a 32 % reduction during historical LMD years compared to the historical average condition (Fig. 5 c, Figure S3 ). However, under the SSP126 scenario, there was a 10 % improvement with only a 22 % reduction during LMD years and almost no change or improvements during LMD years of the SSP585 scenario compared to the historical average condition (Fig. 5 c, Fig. S3 ). In contrast, canola yield showed only a 9 % reduction during historical LMD years (Fig. 5 d), while SSP126 and SSP585 scenarios displayed up to a 29 % and 6 % decline, respectively, compared to the historical average condition (Fig. 5 d). The lower percentage reduction of canola than wheat during historical droughts can be attributed to the fact that most precipitation decline occurs in the southeastern regions (Fig. 5 a), where canola is not extensively cultivated (Fig. 1 ). The analysis of VWC indicated an increase of 0–50 % across the NRB under the LMD years of the historical and SSP 126 scenarios compared to the historical average condition (Fig. 5 g and 5 h, and Fig. S3 ). This suggests a likely decrease in water use efficiency by crops, indicating a greater consumption of water to produce a tonne of wheat or canola during LMD events under both historical and SSP126 scenarios compared to average conditions. In some areas, the increase of VWC is attributed to either reduced Y (Fig. 5 c and 5d, and Fig. S3 ), necessitating more water to produce a tonne of the crop, or droughts are often accompanied by high temperatures and low humidity, both of which can increase soil water evaporation and AET (Trenberth et al., 2013 ; see Eq.3). Moreover, considering that VWC is a fraction term, where AET constitutes the numerator and Y forms the denominator, our findings in some areas indicate that during historical LMDs, both the numerator and denominator decreased. This is logical because reduced precipitation and diminished soil water availability can lower total AET in the numerator and reduce Y in the denominator. However, we observed that the relative decrease of Y in the denominator exceeded the reductions in AET, leading to a higher VWC than the average historical conditions (Fig. 5 ). The SSP585 scenario showed an improvement of up to 30 % in VWC under future LMDs (i.e., reduction in VWC) as compared to historical average conditions (Fig. 5 g and 5 h, and Fig. S3 ), but yet in most areas where historical VWC was relatively low. The simulated results showed a reduced NVWE of wheat and canola crops for historical and future LMDs. Regardless of their corresponding scenarios, the reduced NVWE of both crop types is related to a more significant decline in Y (Fig. 5 b) than changes in VWC under the LMD conditions (Fig. 5 g,h).  3.3.2 Post-drought recovery of WYLD and Y and variations among regions Analysis of data for the post-drought period (D scenario, see Section 2.5 ), revealed variable recovery times for WYLD, Y, and VWT across different agricultural and eco-hydrological regions as compared to non-drought conditions (ND scenario, see Section 2.5 ) (Fig. 6   and Fig. 7  ). Under SSP 126, in some CARs (e.g., MA1, Fig. 6 d), it appears that even after five years following the agricultural drought, the WYLD does not fully recover. This is evident as the red line (representing the D scenario) consistently remains far from the blue line (representing the ND scenario). Conversely, some other CARs, such as AB10 (Fig. 6 a), exhibit a rapid recovery, approximately after a year in the post-drought condition. This is partially attributed to the topographical characteristics and steeper land gradients found in some regions, which can reduce the infiltration time of water. In such areas, a larger proportion of precipitation contributes to surface runoff, leading to a faster recovery of WYLD after LMD events. As shown in Fig. 6 , in most of the CARs, the WYLD is not recovered immediately or after a few years from the termination of the LMD events (i.e., shown by red and blue lines remaining in distant proximity over the first few years). In most CARs, the two lines ultimately overlap after the first few years elapse, indicating that it takes approximately 3–5 years for the WYLD to recover from the LMD. It is worth noting that this recovery pattern is also evident within each CAR, which includes various sub-basins (shown as circles in each scatterplot in Fig. 6 ) with different precipitation ranges (on the x-axis of the plots). In contrast to WYLD results, no significant differences were found for Y under D and ND scenarios, especially for spring wheat (Fig. 6 , S4 and S5 ). This resilience of Y, despite the elapsed LMD, can be attributed to several factors. Primarily, the sustained Y during post-drought periods is related to the availability of soil moisture. After a drought, soil moisture is replenished by post-drought precipitation, making the soil water available for crop use and evapotranspiration (ET) rather than generating excess saturation for surface runoff and WYLD. This is reflected in the WYLD results during post-drought periods, where recovery is not achieved shortly after the drought events (Fig. 6 ). This suggests that while future wheat yields may increase or remain stable after the agricultural droughts, they will likely occur at the expense of reduced WYLD, affecting hydrological droughts in these regions. While several studies project improved Y for mid-to-high latitude areas in the future and following drought events (Challinor et al., 2014; He et al., 2018; Masud et al., 2018 ), these projections should be treated cautiously. Our results illustrate that hydrological and water balance processes are closely connected with vegetation growth and crop types, emphasizing the need for a multi-disciplinary approach to the management of agricultural cropping patterns, such as the selection of optimum crop types during and after extreme droughts, to ensure the security of food production and watershed hydrology. Another reason for Y resilience during a post-drought period is attributed to the potential accumulation of soil nutrients during drought years. During an LMD event, under rainfed conditions, Y decline (Fig. 5 c and 5d) implies that less nutrients are extracted from the soil (Rattalino Edreira et al., 2017 ). This can result in soil nutrient accumulation, which can be carried over to post-drought years, creating a short-term positive 'legacy' effect for crops, increasing their yields (Siebert et al., 2019; Bista et al., 2018 ). Fig. S6  presents nitrogen (N) stress days for historical period comparing D and ND scenarios. As shown, the N stress days for wheat crop are significantly reduced during the D period (2000–2002), which is related to the N accumulation in the soil due to the reduced uptake of N by wheat. Following the drought, nitrogen stress days gradually increase, indicating enhanced nutrient uptake that contributes to the rapid recovery of wheat yield. This process is more pronounced under future scenarios (i.e., SSP126 and SSP585) because with increasing atmospheric CO2  concentrations, the water use efficiency and VWC can improve (Fig. 4 a and 4c), resulting in improvement of Y under reduced soil water conditions (Deryng et al., 2016; Khalili et al., 2021; Masud et al., 2019 ). However, the availability and deficiency of nutrients in the soil can be a controlling factor because elevated CO2  concentrations can enhance potential crop growth, thereby increasing the nutrient demand and consumption from the soil, as discussed by Khalili et al. (2021). It is noteworthy that similar to SSP126, wheat Y showed speedy recovery after the LMD events under the SSP585 and historical periods (Figs. S4 and S5 ). Overall, the regional average decrease of wheat Y immediately after the LMD (year 1) was only 0.9 tonne/ha for the historical period (Fig. S4 ), which was relatively similar for the SSP126 (i.e., 0.9 tonne/ha, Fig. 7 ) and SSP585 (i.e., 1.2 tonne/ha, Fig. S5 ). The reduced Y rapidly recovered in the following years until no difference was observed between the D and ND scenarios (i.e., Fig. S4 j). 3.3.2.1 VWT recovery and differences under future scenarios The analysis of our modelled data under SSP126 scenario indicated that the NVWE associated with the potential export of surplus wheat (presented as an example dominant crop) would likely decrease by up to 4.7 % (corresponding to 12.8 km3 ) under the D as compared to the ND scenario in the first year after the LMD termination (Fig. 7 , Year 1). The reduction in NVWE in the first year after LMD was 2.4 % (corresponding to 5.4 km3 ) and 3.4 % (corresponding to 8.5 km3 ) under the historical (Fig. S7 ) and SSP585 (Fig. S8 ) scenarios, respectively. As shown in the figures, the reduction of NVWE in all scenarios is greater immediately after the LMD termination (i.e., positive anomalies in the y-axis), and it diminishes by time reaching near zero decline (i.e., a full recovery from drought, illustrated with zero anomalies in the y-axis) during the later years (e.g., year 5). The SSP585 demonstrates the fastest recovery (Fig. S8 ), followed by SSP126 (Fig. 7 ), and then the historical scenario (Fig. S7 ). As shown in Fig. S8 , two years after the drought (i.e., in year 2) in the SSP585 scenario, the NVWE under the D scenario exceeds that of the ND scenario, which is a different trend compared to historical and SSP126 scenarios. This is because, during the post-drought period, soil water is replenished more rapidly under SSP585 than under other scenarios (Fig. 2 b and 5b), which can aid the dissolution of remaining soil nutrients from drought years (Bista et al., 2018 ), making them readily available for plant use. The availability of water and nutrients in the soil under the D scenario drives plant growth, increasing the total volume of plant transpiration and AET (Liu et al. 2017). The increased volume of AET results in a greater NVWE under the D scenario compared to the ND scenario.     4 Global and regional implications The results of this study have compelling implications for the agricultural watersheds of mid-to-high latitude or similar regions, particularly concerning VWT for drought and post-drought periods. As one of the major global agricultural exporters in the mid-to-high latitude regions, the Nelson River Basin, covering most of the Canadian Prairies, plays a crucial role in global food security (Bajracharya et al., 2020 ). Unlike the long-term average projections from the global-scale studies, which often suggest a wetter overall future (Bush and Lemmen, 2019; Collins et al., 2013 ; IPCC, 2022 ) in the mid-to-high latitude regions, our study projections highlight that droughts will be drier in the future. While agricultural watersheds of the mid-to-high latitude areas, especially the Canadian Prairies, are susceptible to extreme drought conditions, often resulting in a significant yield loss (Lesk et al., 2016 ), the results of this and other studies demonstrated that the long-term Y will likely improve in the future depending on the crop types, geographical locations, and global warming scenarios (Rosenzweig et al., 2014 ). However, our results revealed that the improvement of Y under extreme droughts will likely be compounded with increases in their VWC, meaning that crops will consume more water to produce a tonne of the same crop compared to the historical conditions. This will likely cause a substantial depletion of the net annual freshwater generated in hydrologic catchments, reducing water yields. The reduced water yield may have implications for economic sectors and ecosystems (Vörösmarty et al., 2010 ), including also the irrigated crop production and export potentials during extreme drought conditions in these regions (Deryng et al., 2014 ). During post-droughts, our results indicated a decrease in NVWE, with a stable rainfed Y following drought events in the future. However, the reduced NVWE and sustained yields following drought events are associated with a substantial decline in water yield in both historical and future scenarios. The continued decline of water yield during and after agricultural droughts, as shown in this study, can exacerbate the impacts of droughts on various economic sectors (Rosa et al., 2020 ) and the environment (Gleeson et al., 2020 ). The aquatic environment, for instance, is highly sensitive to the concentration of nutrients and organic material (Moe et al., 2016 ). The decline of water yield during and after severe droughts, as shown in this study, can reduce streamflow, especially in upstream tributaries and during low-flow seasons, which can then increase the concentration of chemicals and nutrients, triggering adverse impacts on aquatic health. Therefore, an integrated assessment and management of agricultural Y, virtual water export associated with the potential export of crops, and the linkages with hydrological water balance (e.g., WYLD) are crucial for sustainable water and food management and adaptation to climate change extremes. Our study showed considerable differences in Y, VWC, and WYLD between wheat and canola crops during drought periods. For instance, the wheat crop exhibited lower VWC during drought events than the canola crop. Therefore, changes in cropping patterns, e.g., selection of optimum crop types during and after extreme droughts, can be a promising strategy for improved WYLD and integrated management of water and food under extreme climate conditions in the agricultural watersheds of mid-to-high latitude regions. However, more crops (e.g., drought-tolerant crop varieties) should be examined using the approach and the framework we have developed in this study. Another approach to conserve WYLD while maintaining Y during and after agricultural droughts could be implementing soil conservation practices and enhancing water retention capacity, such as conservation tillage, cover cropping, and mulching (Powlson et al., 2016 ). These practices help maintain adequate soil moisture for rainfed crops during and after droughts, which can help conserve WYLD and hydrologic water balance (Zhang et al., 2020). However, the tradeoffs and the effects of such practices should be systematically examined in a modelling framework similar to this study. Our study indicated that NVWE of wheat is different from that of canola under extreme drought conditions. Given that the VWC of the crops varies spatiotemporally and among crops, optimization in NVWE could be another strategy to improve soil water and, therefore, WYLD under extreme droughts in the future. Optimizing cropping patterns corresponding to the virtual water trade strategy has been suggested in a limited number of studies (Antonelli and Sartori, 2015; Faramarzi et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2023 ) and more in the context of water-scarce countries. However, a modelling framework similar to this study provides the basis for examining how an optimum cropping pattern strategy and NVWE can conserve WYLD under future extreme droughts while maintaining regional crop production levels crucial for global food security in the crop-exporting watersheds of global breadbaskets in mid-to-high latitude regions. Overall, this study underscores the importance of addressing global and regional implications of drought and post-drought periods in crop-exporting regions, such as the Canadian Prairies. The projected reduced NVWE, with stable or increased rainfed Y, and reduced WYLD observed in our study present both challenges and opportunities for the region. The adaptation strategies that enhance crop Y while conserving WYLD and reducing NVWE can foster a more sustainable and resilient economy, environment, and agricultural system. Developing interdisciplinary research studies is vital for examining and incorporating these factors into regional and global agricultural policies and water management strategies for adaptation in global food systems, especially under extreme climate conditions.  5 Conclusions This research provides insights into the linkages between WYLD and crop Y, and it elaborates on NVWE as a measure to investigate the production and export potentials under future climate change scenarios. The study elucidates the impacts of future agricultural drought and post-drought conditions on hydrological variables and the reliability of global breadbaskets by modelling WYLD, Y, and NVWE in the Nelson River Basin, a large agricultural watershed in western Canada that supplies food to over 170 countries globally. Under mean climate conditions, the study results reveal a wetter overall future with larger precipitation, greater WYLD, and improved crop Y under SSP126 and SSP585 scenarios compared to the historical period. However, the simulated impacts under the projected future droughts present significantly contrasting results, suggesting more extreme droughts in the future than in the historical period. In both SSP scenarios, the long-term average data illustrates a net regional benefit achieved by decreasing NVWE, coupled with an enhanced export potential of more rainfed wheat and canola production from the NRB compared to the historical average period. However, the results of future projections indicate a substantial reduction in precipitation, Y (rainfed wheat and canola in this study), and WYLD under agricultural droughts. Under SSP126, the reduction of precipitation, WYLD, Y, and NVWE during future droughts remains the same or is more severe than historical droughts, specifically in the central regions, which are prominent for grain production in the NRB. In contrast, SSP585 demonstrates slight improvements in agro-hydrological variables during future droughts, mainly due to the CO2  effects on plant photosynthesis. However, the improvement of Y is not uniform across the region and crop types, with canola Y demonstrating less improvement than wheat Y, leading to greater VWC of canola than wheat under future agricultural droughts. The larger VWC of canola in central areas suggests larger crop water consumption in producing a tonne of crop, resulting in a considerable reduction of WYLD compared to wheat crops and relative to the other regions across NRB. Overall, the regional scale WYLD, Y, and VWC show improvement during SSP585 droughts compared to SSP126; however, they remain considerably lower than during historical droughts, regardless of crop type and geographic location. There will be variable recovery times for WYLD, Y, and NVWE after the termination of agricultural droughts in the future, with the WYLD demonstrating slower recovery times than Y. The study results show a decrease in NVWE during post-drought years, with a stable or slightly increased rainfed crop Y in the years after the drought termination in the future. However, the reduced NVWE and sustained Y following the agricultural drought events in the future are associated with a substantial decline in WYLD. Losses in WYLD during the post-drought years can significantly affect not only the environment ecosystem and several economic sectors but also the irrigated crop production and export potential from these regions. This finding highlights the connections between local hydrology and global trade systems. Future adaptation measures can be considered to preserve water yields in agricultural watersheds during extreme droughts to promote integrated water and food security. Considering these findings, it is essential to acknowledge the limitations of this study. The export potentials, pivotal in VWT and NVWE within this research, are predicted assuming all surplus grains are exported from the region. However, trade dynamics in this and most breadbaskets of the world depend on various local-to-global socioeconomic factors demanding integration with economic and trade models. Additionally, future research could benefit from incorporating future agricultural management practices through socioeconomic modelling. Such modelling integration would offer a more comprehensive understanding of how local hydrological changes due to droughts can interact with and influence global trade patterns, particularly regarding VWT. Moreover, examining more detailed process-based agricultural models such DSSAT (Qian et al., 2019 ) or similar models can help identify various crop species and assess adaptable cropping patterns corresponding to improved NVWE-WYLD in the future. This is because these models incorporate a more detailed representation of the crop growth processes at plant genetic levels and, therefore, have the potential for examination of a wide range of crop genotypes under various management conditions.
1 Introduction Feedback between silicate weathering and atmospheric CO2  is thought to be essential for maintaining Earth’s habitability over geological time scales (Walker et al., 1981 ). This is of great importance to understanding variability and its controlling parameters in chemical weathering (e.g., Brantley et al., 2023; Maher and Chamberlain, 2014; West et al., 2005 ). Stable isotopes (e.g., Mg, Li, Ca, Si, Ge, etc.) are sensitive tracers of chemical weathering and they can provide insights into the sources and processes of river chemical flux (e.g., Baronas et al., 2018; Brenot et al., 2008; Gaspard et al., 2021; Gou et al., 2019, 2023; Li et al., 2023; Millot et al., 2010a,b; Négrel et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2019, 2022a,b, 2024 ). Utilizing these isotopes is thought to identify and quantify weathering processes from multiple perspectives (Baronas et al., 2018; Pogge von Strandmann et al., 2012; Tipper et al., 2012 ), because different elements and their isotopes have different sources and natural properties. Consequently, they transport and transform in different ways. Despite their potential, it should be noted that these isotopes may as well present challenges for data interpretation (e.g., Tipper et al., 2012 ). Lithium and magnesium are thought to be coupled in their chemical behavior during weathering (Huh et al., 1998 ) due to their similar mineralogical origins in silicate minerals (such as biotite, hornblende, and pyroxene). Li+  tends to substitute for Mg2+  in crystal structures due to similar ionic radii. Both lithium and magnesium isotopes have been highlighted as potential tracers for characterizing various weathering processes in previous studies (e.g., Brenot et al., 2008; Henchiri et al., 2016; Wimpenny et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2022a,b ). The light Li isotope is preferentially incorporated into secondary solid weathering products like clays and Fe hydroxides (Dellinger et al., 2015; Gou et al., 2019 ). As a result, river water is isotopically heavier than parent rock. The foremost control factors of lithium isotope fractionation between solid and solution are the type of solid Li formed or adsorbed and the amount of Li incorporated or adsorbed in the solid phase (Wang et al., 2015 ). Mg isotopes not only fractionate during silicate weathering but also through organism’s uptake (e.g., plant) and secondary carbonate formation (Bolou-Bi et al., 2010; Pogge von Strandmann et al., 2012, 2019; Wimpenny et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2019 ). Current studies at the basin scale have shown that biological processes have a limited effect on δ26 Mg in large river waters (Bolou-Bi et al., 2010; Fries et al., 2019 ), except for Siberian permafrost rivers (Mavromatis et al., 2014 ). Carbonate mineral formation affecting river δ26 Mg was reported in the arid region (Zhao et al., 2019 ) and near the caldera (Pogge von Strandmann et al., 2019 ). Though about half of riverine Mg is derived from carbonate weathering (Meybeck, 1987 ), river δ26 Mg variations could still be significantly affected by silicate weathering, as suggested by the covariation between Li and Mg isotopes in the Mackenzie River (Tipper et al., 2012 ). Therefore, the Li and Mg isotopes may be suited for tracing the silicate weathering process as a combination. While basic knowledge of Li and Mg isotope behavior in surface processes has been acquired through spatial investigations in river systems (Gou et al., 2019; Pogge von Strandmann et al., 2012; Tipper et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2022a,b, 2024 ), controlling factors (or processes) of temporal variation in the Li and Mg isotopic composition of river water, which may provide useful information to understand the response of chemical weathering to climate change, are controversial. Gou et al. (2019)  suggested that temporal variation of riverine δ7 Li was dominantly controlled by temperature in the Yellow River. Yet, Liu et al. (2015)  found that the hydrological cycle-controlled residence time dominates the δ7 Li variation of river water and that there was no direct correlation between climate factors and dissolved δ7 Li. In a highly weathered watershed of Luquillo, the exported δ26 Mg is dominated by bedrock dissolution delivering Mg to the stream through a deeper weathering zone (Chapela Lara et al., 2017 ), with δ26 Mg in streams showing an obvious hydrological control. On the other hand, Fries et al. (2019)  suggested that most of the Mg in the river was supplied by throughfall, and seasonal δ26 Mg values showed little change during hydrological events at a similar highly weathered catchment in Guadeloupe. Additionally, recent studies on seasonal variation of river δ26 Mg and its mechanisms have focused on small tropical catchments with high weathering intensity (e.g., Chapela Lara et al., 2017; Fries et al., 2019 ). Studies on large river basins at the intermediate weathering stage are needed to obtain a comprehensive understanding. In this study, we investigated the Li and Mg isotopes of year-long time-series water samples in the lower reaches of the Nujiang River, southeast Tibetan Plateau. The Nujiang is the only natural large river without large dams in China, meaning that the influence of artificial intervention on river chemistry is negligible. This study aims to assess the seasonal change of δ7 Li and δ26 Mg in a large river originating from the Tibetan Plateau, and to reveal which process dominantly controls the seasonal variation of isotopic compositions and how Li and Mg isotopic compositions respond to climate and hydrology change.  2 Study area The Nujiang (Fig. 1  ) originates at Jirepaige in the Southern Tanggula Mountains on the Tibetan Plateau. The drainage basin area and the total length of the main flow within China are 1.38 × 105  km2  and 2013 km, respectively. The climate, vegetation cover, and soil types vary significantly from the upper to the lower Nujiang. The upper reaches (upstream in Jiayuqiang) are characterized by plateau semi-arid to semi-humid climate with annual precipitation of 300–800 mm. Contrastingly, the lower reaches typically experience a subtropical monsoon climate with annual precipitation of 1000–3500 mm. Seasonal climate variations are pronounced due to the Southwest Monsoon and East Summer Monsoon, with ∼ 90 % of precipitation occurring from May to October. Vegetation cover varies from alpine meadow, brushwood, coniferous forest, to evergreen broad-leaf forest along the river’s course. Inceptisols are widely distributed in the upper reaches, while the dominant soil type along the river channel is Alfisols. The lower reach areas are covered by Alfisols and Ultisols, which are both acidic soils with pH values of 4–7 (National Soil Census Office, 1998 ). The clay mineral composition of Alfisols is predominantly composed of illite, vermiculite, and chlorite, with a slight amount of montmorillonite and kaolinite. Ultisols in this basin are rich in kaolinite. The runoff in the upstream basin ranges 150 mm to 400 mm, while it exceeds 500 mm in the downstream basin. The main water sources of the river are rainfall and groundwater. In the upstream region, groundwater contributes approximately 40 % of the annual river water volume (Yang et al., 2021 ). The average annual sediment flux of the Nujiang is 41.5 million tons and shows an increasing trend from upstream to downstream. Sediment flux from June to August accounts for 84 % of the annual sediment flux (Chinese Water Conservancy, 1985 ). The topography of this basin is characterized by high relief. Once the river enters the Hengduan mountain area, it flows in a large canyon with depths ranging from 1000 m to 1500 m, stretching for 780 km downstream. The Bangong-Nujiang suture zone traverses the Nujiang River basin, leading to the development of geothermal springs (Fig. 1 ). Geologically, the Nujiang River basin is mainly covered by granitoid rocks and Triassic, Carboniferous and Devonian clastic rocks (mainly sandstone, siltstone, limestone, shale, and volcaniclastic rock). Some metamorphic rocks, such as sand slate, gneiss, and marble, can be found in the source area.  3 Methods Water samples were collected at monthly intervals at the Daojieba Hydrological Station (Fig. 1 ) from September 2013 to August 2014. The water pH was measured in the field using a portable EC/pH meter (with an uncertainty of ±0.05). The water samples were filtered in the field through 0.22 μm filters. Suspended particulate material (SPM) content was determined by filtering a certain volume of river water. The HCO3 −  was determined using a titration method. Samples for analyzing the δ13 C of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) were sealed in glass bottles with HgCl2  added to prevent biological activity. Samples for major cations, trace elements, strontium ratio, lithium isotope, and magnesium isotope measurements were acidified with concentrated HNO3  and stored in polyethylene plastic bottles. The elemental and isotopic composition data analysis was conducted at the Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (IGGCAS). The cations and trace elements (Sr, Li, and Ge) were analyzed by a PerkinElmer  DRC-E Inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometer (ICP-MS) with a ±5 % precision (Wang et al., 2022 ). Major anions were measured by Dionex  ICS-1500 ion chromatography with a precision of ±10 % based on repeated analyses. Aqueous silica concentrations were determined by the molybdate blue spectrophotometric method. The δ13 C of DIC was measured by a Finnigan  MAT 252 gas mass spectrometer. The CO2  was extracted from water samples by 85 % phosphoric acid, purified after cryogenic removal of H2 O, and preserved cryogenically for measurements. Carbon isotopes are expressed as δ13 C relative to the Vienna PDB standard. The precision based on an internal laboratory standard for repeated measurements with samples was better than 0.1 ‰ for δ13 C. 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio, Li isotope, and Mg isotope were measured by Neptune plus  Multi-Collector Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometer (MC-ICP-MS). Samples containing 2 μg Sr were purified by ion chromatography using the AG50-X8 (200–400 mesh) resin. The reproducibility was verified by determinations of the NBS 987 standard. The average 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio of this standard for determinations was 0.710249 ± 0.000018 (2SD, n = 12). Lithium was separated from the sample matrix by ion-exchange chromatography employing the chemical separation method from Wang et al. (2015) . Water sample containing 1 μg Li was loaded on a homemade quartz column with AG-50 W X8 resin, and 0.15 N HCl was used to elute Li. The recovery of Li after the separation was higher than 99 %, and the blank of the total procedure was less than 2 ng Li. The Li concentration of the sample and standard solution was adjusted to 100 μg/L, which yielded a beam intensity of 5–7 V for 7 Li (low-resolution mode). A “wet” system with a quartz spray chamber and a 50 ul/min PFA nebulizer was used to introduce samples and standards to Ar plasma. Li isotope ratios were measured using the standard-sample bracketing method to correct instrumental mass fractionation. Data of Li isotopes are presented as delta notation relative to the L-SVEC standard. The measured δ7 Li values of the reference rocks BHVO-2 and AGV-2 were 4.8 ± 0.3 ‰ (n = 4) and 7.4 ± 0.2 ‰ (n = 3), respectively. A detailed description of the chemical purification of Mg and measurements of Mg isotopes are given in An et al. (2014) . The resin was conditioned with 5 ml 1 N HNO3 . About 20 μg Mg was loaded on 2 ml AG50-X12 (200–400 mesh) resin and eluted by 1 N HNO3 . The total blank and the recovery of this procedure were less than 10 ng and more than 98 %, respectively. The Mg concentration of the samples and standard solutions was adjusted to 2 mg/L, which typically yielded a beam intensity of 8–10 V for 24 Mg (medium-resolution mode). A “wet” system with a quartz spray chamber and a 50 ul/min PFA nebulizer was also used. Mg isotope ratios were measured by MC-ICP-MS using the standard-sample bracketing method. The standard-sample sequences were repeated at least 4 times for each sample to ensure reproducibility. All data are reported in delta notation relative to DSM-3. Long-term external reproducibility for δ26 Mg was better than ±0.05 ‰ (2SD) (An et al., 2014 ). BHVO-2 was processed identically to the samples, giving δ26 Mg values of −0.22 ± 0.03 (n = 5), which is in good agreement with the reported values (Liu and Han, 2021 ).  4 Results Table 1   and Table 2   report elemental and isotopic data of river waters. The monthly average flow and day flow vary significantly at the Daojieba station, from 470 m3 /s to 4353 m3 /s and 434 m3 /s to 5292 m3 /s, respectively (Fig. 2  ). The sample-collecting day flow in Jun and August is much higher than the monthly average, indicating rain events over the basin. Total dissolved solids (TDS) vary by a factor of two, from 84 to 164 mg/L, with the highest in November and the lowest in August. Major cation and anion abundances of the river water follow the order Ca2+  (45–50 %) > Mg2+  (25–31 %) > Na+  (23–25 %) > K+  (1–2 %) and HCO3 −  (79–81 %) > SO4 2−  (9–11 %) > Cl−  (8–9 %) > NO3 −  (1–3 %). The concentrations of various elements decrease by a factor of ∼2 during high-flow seasons compared to an increase in water discharge by about 10 times, and this refers to as the “chemostatic behavior” (Godsey et al., 2009 ). The seasonal variation in δ13 CDIC , 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios, and δ7 Li and δ26 Mg values are shown in Fig. 3  . The δ13 CDIC  varies from −11.4 ‰ to −2.5 ‰, with the most negative value occurring in August. The 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios, δ7 Li and δ26 Mg values range from 0.71360 to 0.71522, 3.8 ‰ to 17.7 ‰ and −1.01 ‰ to −0.77 ‰ respectively. Their variation pattern is quite similar, with high values generally occurring during high-flow seasons (Fig. 3 ). Samples in June and August show the highest values of δ7 Li and 87 Sr/86 Sr, while there is a slight decrease in δ26 Mg value.  5 Discussion 5.1 Variations of 87 Sr/86 Sr: increased silicate weathering contribution during high-flow seasons 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio has been widely used as a conservative tracer. The discharge-dependent 87 Sr/86 Sr variation in river water and its implication for chemical weathering processes have been reported in many studies (e.g., Tipper et al., 2006; Tripathy et al., 2010; Wei et al., 2013 ). In general, silicate weathering solution has a higher 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio than that of carbonate. From this, an increasing contribution of river solute from silicate weathering during high-flow seasons in the Nujiang at the Daojieba Hydrological Station (Fig. 3 ) can be inferred from the high 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios. The validity of this assertion is further confirmed by the positive correlation between 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio, Si/Ca molar ratio, and δ13 CDIC  (Fig. 4  a, b), as Si/Ca molar ratio and δ13 CDIC  are also used as indicators to distinguish the sources of weathering materials between silicate and carbonate (Galy and France-Lanord, 1999 ). Moreover, considering that high runoff generally results in more lateral flow, the 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio during high-flow period could be affected by soil weathering and leaching. The Nujiang River basin is covered by vast Alfisols and Ultisols (such as burozem and laterite, National Soil Census Office, 1998 ), both are acid soils characterized by low pH values and high 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios (Henchiri et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2018 ). As shown in Fig. 3  and Fig. 4 c, water pH variation is inversely related to 87 Sr/86 Sr, which indicates the enhanced contribution of weathering of silicate materials in soil during high-flow seasons. Interestingly, the time series observations in the Nujiang are consistent with those in upper reaches of the Salween, while they are contrary to analogous studies in southern Himalayan rivers (such as Ganga and Brahmaputra, Rai and Singh, 2007; Tipper et al., 2006 ). These contrasting studies documented lower 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios during high-flow seasons than those during low-flow seasons, which is attributed to the quick weathering kinetics of carbonate relative to silicate (Rai and Singh, 2007 ). The explanation of such differences will be described by δ7 Li variation in Section 5.2.1 .  5.2 Seasonal variations of river δ7 Li and δ26 Mg 5.2.1 Lithium isotope: secondary mineral formation-related fractionation and congruent weathering Dissolved Li in the Nujiang River water at the Daojieba Hydrological Station is mainly (>90 %) derived from silicate weathering (Table S1 ). However, δ7 Li values of river water (3.8 ‰ to 17.7 ‰) are significantly different from those of silicate rocks in this area (−1‰ to 6.6 ‰, Tian et al., 2018; Weynell et al., 2017 ). This offset results from the preferential incorporation or adsorption of 6 Li in/onto secondary minerals, leading to the enrichment of 7 Li in river water. As shown in Fig. 5  a, river waters in which Li is depleted (relative to Na) show higher δ7 Li values. Especially during high-flow seasons, δ7 Li data clearly points to weathering conditions that favored Rayleigh-type secondary mineral formation. During these seasons, water discharge increased ten times while Li concentration decreased only four times, despite plenty of Li (usually >50 % Li released by rock weathering) having been incorporated into secondary minerals (Dellinger et al., 2015; Henchiri et al., 2016 ). These observations suggest plausible mechanisms that induce chemostatic behavior of Li, such as an increased contribution of Li from soil solution and silicate mineral weathering (Clow and Mast, 2010 ). Previous studies have suggested that dissolved δ7 Li is correlated with surface weathering intensity (e.g., Dellinger et al., 2015 ), and rivers draining highly weathered river basins show relatively high δ7 Li values, such as the Congo River (15–25 ‰, Henchiri et al., 2016 ), Reunion (21–30 ‰), Java in Indonesia (20–45 ‰) (Henchiri et al., 2014 ), and the lowland of Amazon River (δ7 Li of 12–16 ‰, Dellinger et al., 2015 ). In this context, soil can be regarded as a reservoir of retaining high δ7 Li solution due to the incorporation of Li in secondary minerals. As shown in Fig. 5 b and 5c, samples with high discharge and SPM content are close to the rivers draining laterite soils with high values of δ7 Li and 87 Sr/86 Sr. Flushing of solutes from soil micropores and macropores could be accentuated under high-flow conditions (Clow and Drever, 1996 ), thereby elevating river δ7 Li. On the other hand, δ7 Li values of river water from the low-flow seasons (November to April, 3.8 ‰ to 6.8 ‰) are close to those of local silicate rocks (∼3‰), reflecting a more congruent silicate weathering signal. The widespread presence of geothermal waters in the river basins of the southeastern Tibetan Plateau (Nujiang, Lancangjiang, and Jinshajiang) has been documented (Han et al., 2015 ). Due to high-temperature water–rock interactions, geothermal waters could present low δ7 Li values (e.g., 1 ‰–5.7 ‰ in Sao Miguel, Henchiri et al., 2014 ; 1.6 ‰–7.1 ‰ in Guadeloupe, Millot et al., 2010a; Rad et al., 2013 ). In the Tibetan Plateau region, most of the reported δ7 Li of geothermal waters ranges from −1.7 ‰ to 6.2 ‰ (Weynell et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022 ). The geothermal waters transport vertically and laterally along with the fractures and crevices and mix with subsurface groundwater, which becomes the main recharge of river water during low-flow seasons. It is reported that for the Naqu River, upper reaches of the Nujiang, groundwater contributes 40 % of river discharge annually (Yang et al., 2021 ), and for the adjacent upper reaches of Lancangjiang and Yarlung Zangbo River, the proportions of groundwater are more than 40 % (Li et al., 2000; Shi et al., 2021 ). The increased contribution of geothermal water results in a more carbonate influence on river 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios (Fig. 5 b), thus leading to lower 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios during low-flow seasons than those during high-flow seasons, despite the quick weathering kinetics of carbonate during high-flow seasons. Additionally, the impact of geothermal water on the seasonal variation of the water chemistry of the Nujiang River could also be observed by Ge/Si molar ratios of river water (Fig. 3 ). Generally, in the silicate weathering-controlled river system, high river Ge/Si occurs during high-flow periods, because the dissolution of clay minerals (with a relative high Ge/Si ratio, 3–6, compared with parent silicate rock, 1.5–2.5) is more evident (Han et al., 2015; Lugolobi et al., 2010 ). Yet, in rivers affected by geothermal inputs, a low Ge/Si ratio of river water is observed during high-flow periods (Fig. 3 b), because geothermal water usually exhibits an extremely higher Ge/Si ratio (133–308, Wang et al., 2022 ), so the decreased proportion of geothermal water during high-flow seasons could lower the riverine Ge/Si ratio. The temporal variation pattern of Li isotopic composition in the Nujiang River suggests δ7 Li and discharge are positively related (Fig. 5 c). This is similar to the Tibetan Plateau rivers like Yarlung Tsangpo River and Jinshajiang River (Ma et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022 ), while it is different from most rivers in the world as there is a globally negative correlation between δ7 Li and annual runoff covering small to large rivers (Zhang et al., 2022 ). Such unique annual variation in Tibetan Plateau rivers highlights the significant impact of geothermal water on river δ7 Li, which is also associated with the varying hydrology at the basin scale. These inconsistent trends may bring uncertainties in interpreting the global feedback between river δ7 Li and runoff.  5.2.2 Magnesium isotope: source control and differential weathering The dissolved δ26 Mg in the Nujiang at Daojieba Hydrological Station also reveals a temporal response. River δ26 Mg (−1.01 ‰ to −0.77 ‰) falls between those of carbonate (−5‰ to −1‰, Galy et al., 2002; Higgins and Schrag, 2012 ) and silicate rocks (−0.7 ‰ to +0.9 ‰, Li et al., 2010; Telus et al., 2012 ), a fact that is supposed to be suggestive of a mixture of silicate and carbonate weathering. The δ26 Mg values of −0.89 ‰ to −0.77 ‰ during high-flow seasons (May to October) are higher than those during low-flow seasons (Fig. 3 ), suggesting an increased contribution of silicate weathering during the high-flow periods, this is consistent with the inference from 87 Sr/86 Sr ratio. However, unlike closely related 1/Sr and 87 Sr/86 Sr (not shown, R2  = 0.5), 1/Mg does not show two binary mixing trends with δ26 Mg (not shown, R2  = 0.06). Besides conservative mixing, other processes such as the incorporation of Mg into clay (Wimpenny et al., 2014 ), ion exchange processes (Xu et al., 2023 ), and prior weathering of isotopically distinct minerals (Hindshaw et al., 2019 ) which could affect the riverine δ26 Mg are also considered. Clays have an affinity for 26 Mg, affecting riverine δ26 Mg (Wimpenny et al., 2011, 2014 ). In the Nujiang, there is a positive relationship between the Mg/Na molar ratio and δ26 Mg of river water in the Nujiang (Fig. 6  a). In the high-flow seasons during which secondary mineral formation more affects river isotope signal (suggested by δ7 Li), river water should have evolved to a low Mg/Na ratio and low δ26 Mg value direction. However, this observation does not fit Mg isotope data. Recently, Xu et al. (2023)  proposed that in the Nujiang River channels, Mg-Na ion exchange between river water and suspended load could result in an elevated river δ26 Mg due to the preferential absorption of light Mg isotope in suspended clays. However, we did not observe significant isotope fractionation of ion exchange process at the lower reaches of the Nujiang, as the δ26 Mg of river water remained consistent despite a threefold difference in suspended particulate matter (SPM) content between samples in June and October. Here, the preferred weathering of Mg-rich silicate minerals with isotopically heavy Mg (e.g., illite and chlorite) could be the most plausible explanation for a synergistic variation between Mg/Na ratios and δ26 Mg values in the river water, especially since illite and chlorite, the most abundant clays in the Nujiang sediment (Fig. S1 ), are rich in Mg and have high δ26 Mg value (illite: 0.18 ‰, Wimpenny et al., 2014 , clinochlore: −0.27 ‰ to 0.4 ‰, Beinlich et al., 2014; Chapela Lara et al., 2017 ). A data set containing 3584 soils and river sediments in lower reaches of the Nujiang shows that MgO and Na2 O content ranges from 0.26 to 11.22 wt% and 0.15 to 3.25 wt%, respectively, with a high mean Mg/Na molar ratio of ∼4 (Zhang et al., 2020 ). The weathering of Mg-bearing minerals (such as chlorite) and its impact on river δ26 Mg value have also been observed both in a highly weathered catchment (Chapela Lara et al., 2017 ) and in a glacier catchment (Hindshaw et al., 2019 ). Overall, differential weathering of Mg-rich minerals could be an important mechanism for the elevated δ26 Mg value during high-flow seasons. However, due to the presence of a interflow and overland flow path during high-flow seasons, which leaves a short time for weathering reactions, it is speculated that differential mineral weathering may not only directly release high Mg/Na ratio solution into the river, but also widely affect the Mg/Na ratio and δ26 Mg value of soil solution (and soil labile complex), thus influencing the river water in this period.   5.3 Hydrology-driven seasonal cycles of weathering process and Li and Mg isotopic compositions in the Nujiang The variation of riverine δ7 Li and δ26 Mg reflects that weathering process shifts as the discharge varies at the Daojieba station. Samples in June and August present the highest δ7 Li, while the Mg/Na ratio and δ26 Mg values slightly decrease compared with samples in adjoining months (Figs. 3 and 6 ), which suggests that Li and Mg is lost due to incorporation into secondary minerals. The daily flows of these two samples are significantly high because of rainstorm events in the basin (Fig. 2 ), which could lead to a great contribution of surface soil solution due to the overland flow path, thus resulting in an abnormal drop of δ26 Mg and a dramatical increase of δ7 Li. Just as previous studies have suggested, surface soil solutions show a large different Li and Mg isotopic composition compared to bedrock and deep soil solution, due to the combined effect of atmospheric input and preferential incorporation of 26 Mg and 6 Li into secondary minerals (Chapela Lara et al., 2017; Fries et al., 2019 ). As shown in Fig. 7  a,b, changes in water discharge can have an obvious impact on δ7 Li and δ26 Mg values by changing the hydrological flow path in which the dominant reaction of mineral dissolution and secondary mineral formation vary over the Nujiang River basin. Studies have reported that seasonal variations in riverine δ7 Li are dominantly controlled by temperature, with a fractionation gradient of −0.18 ‰/°C in the lower reaches of the Yellow River (Gou et al., 2019 ). However, the temperature-controlled δ7 Li change is not observed here. The Nujiang River basin has a significant topographic gradient. The impact of runoff on river isotope signal which is strongly related to deep/surface weathering contribution, is more obvious than temperature, at least at a short-term scale. This discordance reflects a different controlling mechanism of monsoon climate on weathering processes, especially in high-relief river basins (Ma et al., 2023 ).  5.4 The positive correlation between δ7 Li and δ26 Mg in rivers and its implication for chemical weathering Lithium and magnesium isotopes in a river system are both controlled by mineral dissolution and secondary mineral formation yet to a different extent. Mg has a weaker affinity for clay minerals than Li (Verney-Carron et al., 2011 ) and riverine Mg could be strongly affected by carbonate weathering. Therefore, there will appear to be more significant source control on river δ26 Mg (Brenot et al., 2008; Hindshaw et al., 2019 ). However, unexpectedly, there is a positive correlation between δ7 Li and δ26 Mg in the Nujiang River water at the Daojieba station (Fig. 6 b, R2 = 0.84, except for June and August). Such a relationship between δ7 Li and δ26 Mg is not unique. Tipper et al. (2012)  first reported such a correlation in the Mackenzie River at the high-latitude region (Fig. 8  a). Similar to the Nujiang, there remains a positive relationship between the Mg/Na ratio and δ26 Mg value of river water in the Mackenzie River (R2  = 0.43, Fig. 8 b). Considering that the dominant minerals in the soil over the Mackenzie River basin are chlorite and mica (Kodama et al., 1993 ), the weathering of Mg-rich minerals may appear to be responsible for δ26 Mg and Mg/Na variation in the river water. Compiling the world river's literature data, including the Orinoco and Amazon with high weathering intensity, δ7 Li and δ26 Mg values of river water fit the trend (Fig. 8 a, Tipper et al., 2012 ), while these rivers exhibit relatively high δ26 Mg values and low Mg/Na ratios compared with the Mackenzie River, and δ26 Mg and Mg/Na ratio did not show a positive correlation (Fig. 8 b). Among the world's large rivers, the proportion of Mg derived from carbonate weathering has a significant influence on Mg isotopic composition of river water. For instance, tropical rivers (e.g., Orinoco and Amazon) present a lower proportion of solute from carbonate weathering than rivers in temperate and subarctic regions (e.g., Yenisei, Lena, and Mackenzie, Gaillardet et al., 1999 ), while showing higher δ26 Mg values. As proposed by Zhao et al. (2022b) , there is a strong negative correlation between river δ26 Mg and the solute proportion from carbonate weathering among the world’s large rivers. Hence, the correlation between δ7 Li and δ26 Mg of large rivers worldwide in Fig. 8 a reflects that with the increase of weathering intensity (increased river δ7 Li), the proportion of dissolved Mg from carbonate weathering decreases (increased river δ26 Mg).   6 Conclusions We determined a year-long time series of Sr, Li, and Mg concentrations and their isotopic compositions at the Daojieba Hydrological Station in lower mainstream of the Nujiang River. The Sr, Li, and Mg isotopic compositions exhibit obvious temporal variations, following the pattern of higher values occurring during high-flow seasons, which is closely linked to seasonal changes in chemical weathering across the drainage basin. The fluctuation in river 87 Sr/86 Sr ratios indicates an increased contribution from silicate weathering during high-flow periods. Combining this with tracers such as Si/Ca molar ratio, δ13 CDIC , and river pH, we infer an enhanced weathering of silicate materials in soil during high-flow periods. Interestingly, river δ7 Li displays an atypical seasonal pattern compared to many other rivers, attributed to a complex interplay of processes including the contribution of Li from the soil solution and silicate mineral weathering, influenced by mineral dissolution and clay formation during high-flow seasons, and geothermal input influenced by congruent weathering during low-flow periods. Additionally, the relationship between Mg/Na molar ratio and δ26 Mg in the Nujiang suggests the weathering of Mg-rich silicate minerals. The anomalous drop of Mg/Na and δ26 Mg in June and August, coupled with a significant increase in δ7 Li value and water discharge, shows a greater contribution from surface soil solution (a more isotope fractionated source). These findings underscore the hydrological control on seasonal cycles of weathering process and Li and Mg isotopic compositions in the river water. Finally, we explored the positive correlation between Li and Mg isotopic composition of river water, which not only reflects the isotope fractionation during silicate weathering, but also the potential link between silicate weathering intensity and carbonate weathering contribution in rivers.
1 Introduction Large bodies of standing water, reservoirs and lakes serve a variety of purposes, including irrigation, hydropower, drinking water storage, and leisure. Because chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) is present in all photosynthesizing organisms, it is a common environmental metric of algae, or phytoplankton, biomass development as well as the eutrophication process in oceans, lakes, and reservoirs (Latif et al., 2003 ). Chlorophyll is a group of green compounds (forms a, b, c, d, e, and f) encountered in cyanobacteria cells and in all other living forms, including plants and various algae species, that have chloroplasts or tylocoidal membranes (Wetzel, 2001; Schinck et al., 2020 ). Chl-a, a molecule encountered in all photosynthesizing organisms, is the primary player in photosynthesis, the process by which plants and algae convert sunlight into energy. Because the range of green wavelengths that each type of chlorophyll reflects varies slightly, its well-known optical characteristics permit that the phytoplankton is easily quantified and therefore the chlorophyll. In fact, a straightforward and precise technique for determining the concentration of phytoplankton, or microscopic algae, and, by extension, the biological activity, is the optical measure of chlorophyll concentration. Thus, measuring the amount of chlorophyll allows one to directly monitor the growth of phytoplankton and, consequently, the processes leading to eutrophication in lakes and reservoirs. Physico-chemical and biological processes in reservoirs may be significantly impacted by algae outbreak. As is well known, algal blooms degrade the water quality of reservoirs and lakes and potentially poses a health risk. High Chl-a levels and the proliferation of toxic algal blooms are linked to harmful algal blooms (Pip and Bowman, 2014; Yuan et al., 2014; Vilán Vilán et al., 2013; Schinck et al., 2020 ) which produce cyanotoxins that endanger recreational and drinking water supplies (Watzin et al., 2006, Kalaji et al., 2016 ). In light of this, it is possible to consider the Chl-a concentration as a surrogate for the presence of cyanobacteria in a reservoir and, in circumstances where the cyanotoxin concentration is not available, it serves as an estimation of dangerous blooms of cyanobacteria (HABs) (McQuaid et al., 2011; Vilán Vilán et al., 2013; Schinck et al., 2020 ). Thus, in order to prevent further contamination and reduce any health risks, forecasting the concentration of Chl-a is crucial to managing water quality (Wheeler et al., 2012; Schinck et al., 2020 ). Furthermore, the Water Framework Directive of the European Commission (Directive 2000 /60/EC) and other European directives mandated phytoplankton biomass, and the metric chosen to represent this biomass is called Chl-a. However, Chl-a prediction has not always worked out in lakes and reservoirs (Di Toro et al., 1971; Brown et al., 2000; Tufford and McKeller, 1999; Reynolds, 2006 ). Water quality assessed by Laplacian mathematical models require a lot of data that is nearly impossible to obtain or unavailable because they rely on the internal physico-chemical processes that take place in reservoirs or lakes. They also present a challenging computer implementation and require a significant amount of computational time. To estimate the concentration of Chl-a in the El Val reservoir (in the northeastern Spanish region of Aragón), a novel regressive model that uses the Support Vector Regression (SVR) technique is successfully implemented in this study (see Fig. 1  a-e). In aquatic environments such as the El Val reservoir, abnormal proliferation of algae can pose a significant environmental threat. The central region of Aragón receives its drinking water from this reservoir. Therefore, it is important to prevent serious hazards like toxic algal blooms by employing the concentration of Chl-a as a forewarning indication. Because of this, the novel method that combines the Support Vector regression (SVR) approximation (Vapnik, 1998; Cristianini and Shawe–Taylor, 2000; Schölkopf et al., 2000; Hastie et al., 2003; Hansen and Wang, 2005; Li et al., 2008; Steinwart and Christmann, 2008 ) with the optimization algorithm Grid search  (GS) (Eberhart et al., 2001; Bergstra and Bengio, 2012; Chong and Zak, 2013; Aggarwal, 2020; Agrawal, 2020 ) to forecast the Chl-a levels could be a compelling method since, as far as the we are aware, very few prior studies of water quality in lakes and reservoirs have addressed the Chl-a concentration. Furthermore, statistics developed the SVR technique, a statistical learning methodology that can handle nonlinearities, including variable interactions (Rasmussen, 2003; Dym and McKean, 2008; Ebden, 2015). With the purpose of estimating the Chl-a concentration output variable for comparative analysis, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) (Hassoun, 1995; Shepherd, 1997; Haykin, 1999; Fine, 1999; Van-Mata, 2020 ) with GS optimizer, multivariate linear regression (MLR) and M5 model tree models were additionally fitted to the observed dataset. Regression problems can be solved using the SVM approach (Vapnik, 1998; Cristianini and Shawe–Taylor, 2000; Schölkopf et al., 2000; Hastie et al., 2003; Hansen and Wang, 2005; Li et al., 2008; Steinwart and Christmann, 2008 ), a supervised learning approximation that has great robustness and the capacity to handle nonlinearities. SVMs have been shown to be useful in a variety of fields, encompassing solar energy (De Leone et al., 2015 ), hydro-climatic factors (Shrestla and Shukla, 2015 ) and solar radiation (Chen et al., 2013 ), according to earlier research. Specifically, we can cite two important previous investigations in the field of hydrology using SVMs technique: the first research work was applied to the surface quality data to optimize the monitoring program (Singh et al., 2011 ) with success; and the second research work is a review of different practical applications of SVMs to the various hydrological problems (Raghavendra N and Chandra Deka, 2014 ). Certainly, the following are some arguments supporting the utility of the suggested SVM approximation (Vapnik, 1998; Cristianini and Shawe–Taylor, 2000; Schölkopf et al., 2000; Hastie et al., 2003; Hansen and Wang, 2005; Li et al., 2008; Steinwart and Christmann, 2008 ): (1) since the cost function that builds the model only uses the training data, the SVM approach only needs a portion of the training data; (2) support vectors, a subset of the decision function's training points, are used by the SVM model to improve its accuracy and memory efficiency in high-dimensional spaces; (3) SVM technique offers the kernel trick  inside the algorithm itself so that the regression of nonlinear data has become easier and any complex problem can be solved; and (4) SVM approach is robust to outliers when hyperparameter tuning is done correctly. As it is less influenced by outliers, the precision of the results is high. Using support vector regression (SVR) and the GS optimizer, the prediction of Chl-a levels in El Val reservoir from the remaining variables, measured periodically, mandated by the Water Framework Directive (Directive 2000 /60/EC) in all water bodies was the aim of the current study. This model builds a new algorithm to measure the concentration of Chl-a (Chen, 1970; Smith, 2006; Riegl et al., 2014 ) in lakes and reservoirs and analyze phytoplankton density in them. Actually, the amount of Chl-a present in a reservoir or lake can be thought of as a basic indicator of the presence of surplus nutrients, including nitrogen and total phosphorus (Fields, 2004 ), which ultimately signals the beginning of eutrophication in these water bodies. This article is structured as follows: Section 2  describes the SVR, M5 model tree, MLP, and MLR, as well as the experimental setup and all study variables. In Section 3 , the relevance rankings of the variables, the observed values, and the SVR results are combined to provide a summary of the outcomes achieved with this innovative method. Finally, Section 4  wraps up the research by listing the main findings of the inquiry.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study area This work centers on the El Val reservoir situated along the Val River in the province of Zaragoza, Aragon region, north-eastern Spain. Geological analysis reveals the presence of robust conglomerate formations, indicative of ancient alluvial fan deposits, interspersed with layers of clay, silt, and sandstone. The reservoir's morphology, characterized by elongated geometry and tributary ravines, reflects its location within a steep valley (Castiella, 1975 ). Fed by the Val and Queiles rivers, the reservoir boasts a capacity of 25 hm3 , the flooded area is 112.23 ha, the surface of the basin is 179 km and serves irrigation, although originally it was also for population supply. The dam, completing in 2001 and standing at 94.4 m, features dual outlets, including one feeding the Magallón irrigation canal. This study sheds light on the reservoir's geological context and hydrological significance, highlighting its role as a vital water resource in the region.
