The type to which this body of water belongs is 7, which corresponds to a monomictic reservoir, calcareous in humid areas, with an average annual temperature of less than 15 °C, belonging to headwater rivers and upper reaches. Monomictic is a rating that it is applied to masses of water that are stratified once a year, due to variations of temperature. Labelled in the last reservoir reports, years 2020, 2021 and 2022, by the Ebro River Basin Authority as eutrophic (Ebro Hydrographic Confederation, 2023 ), ranking among the most polluted in the basin. The excessive nutrient buildup in the reservoir, largely stemming from discharges from the wastewater treatment plant (EDAR) and local industries, as well as runoff from agricultural activities, contributes significantly to its heightened eutrophication levels. Boating is permitted on this reservoir (no restrictions for rowing and sailing, and not motorable).  2.2 Experimental dataset The GS/SVM methodology's numerical results were acquired over a five-year period (from 2018 to 2022). There is no data for April 2020 and the samples start on 20th of January of 2018. Using sampling protocols for reservoirs and lakes that are in line with those approved by the European Union and created by the Spanish Ministry for the Ecological Transition and Demographic Challenge, data collection takes place approximately every five minutes (Smith et al., 2008; World Health Organization, 1998 ). We have 240,765 samples. We compute the daily average of every variable and our final dataset contains data for 1,624 days. The samples were taken with a self-positioning multiparameter probe that automatically, autonomously and at different depths measures the values of parameters representative of water quality. The multiparameter probe measures temperature, pH, conductivity, redox, dissolved oxygen, turbidity and chlorophyll, and incorporated a Secchi disk (Willame et al., 2005 ). It has also a manual operating mode. These depths were calculated from the Secchi depth, defined as the depth at which the pattern on a Secchi disk (see Fig. 2  ) becomes invisible due to water turbidity. Within the euphotic zone—the region with enough light for photosynthesis—they were selected at equal intervals. The other experimental data in this investigation were the standard physico-chemical variables from limnological studies (Brönmark and Hansson, 2005; Negro et al., 2000; Reynolds, 2006 ).  2.3 Variables of the model The main object of this research was to find a way to predict the Chl-a amount (µg/L) in El Val reservoir. Chl-a is a commonly used biomarker of eutrophication in lakes and reservoirs because it indicates the biomass of algae in the water (Latif et al. 2003 ). High chlorophyll content typically denotes the presence of algal blooms (USEPA, 2014 ) and, consequently, a decline in the quality of the waters in reservoirs and lakes. Given that it absorbs the light energy used for photosynthetic processes, chlorophyll is without a doubt a crucial pigment in green organisms. The existence of these green organisms, phytoplankton, is linked to chlorophyll (American Public Health Association, 2005 ). The Chlorophyll levels are also recognized as an alternate indicator of the existence of cyanobacteria, which can produce cyanotoxins and endanger the population (Wheeler et al., 2012; Schinck et al., 2020 ). In the SVR model, the same chemical and physico-chemical variables are employed as estimators (see Table 1  ). Physico-chemical variables are as follows:• Photic layer depth (m): Measured using a depth profiler equipped with appropriate sensors to detect the depth at which photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) reaches 1 % of its surface value. This parameter reflects the penetration of light into the water column, influencing primary production and Chlorophyll distribution.  • pH: Determined using a calibrated pH meter at the water surface. pH serves as an indicator of water acidity or alkalinity, affecting nutrient availability and biological processes.  • Water temperature (°C): Recorded using a calibrated thermometer or temperature sensor placed at the water surface or at specific depths. Water temperature influences the metabolic rates of aquatic organisms and nutrient cycling dynamics.  • Conductivity (μS/m): Measured using a conductivity meter to quantify the capacity of the water to conduct an electrical current, indicative of dissolved ion concentrations. Conductivity is correlated with salinity and nutrient levels in freshwater systems.  • Redox potential (V): Assessed using a redox potential meter to gauge the oxidation–reduction potential of the water column. Redox potential impacts the availability of electron acceptors and determines the prevailing biogeochemical processes.  • Reservoir elevation (or height) ( masl) : Obtained from topographic surveys or satellite-based altimetry to account for variations in water level within the reservoir. Elevation influences hydrodynamics, residence time, and nutrient retention within the reservoir.  • Dissolved o xygen (mg/L): obtained measuring the amount of dissolved oxygen in the water with oxygen probes or sensors. Dissolved oxygen is vital for aerobic respiration and functions as a gauge of ecosystem health and water quality.  • Turbidity (NTU): Evaluated using a turbidity meter to quantify the degree of light scattering caused by suspended particles in the water column. Turbidity affects light availability, phytoplankton growth, and sediment transport processes.    The continuous measurement probe (Aquadam) provided the data set that was used in this investigation, which records these parameters throughout the water column up to 573 m above sea level, to be exact, in the reservoir; profiles are conducted every 6 h throughout the year. As an initial data analysis, a correlation matrix is calculated for all the variables that take part in the process. Fig. 3   shows graphically how close the two variables are to having a linear relationship with each other. Each variable in the Table 1  is correlated with each of the other variables.  2.4 Support vector machines (SVMs) Support vector machines (SVMs) were developed to address binary classification issues. Due to the circumstances, it was quickly realised that the essential principles supporting them could be used to deal with a different type of challenge, like regression issues (Vapnik, 1998; Cristianini and Shawe–Taylor, 2000; Schölkopf et al., 2000; Hastie et al., 2003; Hansen and Wang, 2005; Li et al., 2008; Steinwart and Christmann, 2008 ). Next, let's take a dataset as an example where the training set consists of the values of the continuous dependent variable y i  ∈ R ,   ∀ i = 1 , 2 , . . . , m    and the covariates x  i  ∈ R p  ,   i = 1 , 2 , . . . , m   . As a result, the support vector regression  (SVR) technique creates a function f x    = w   T  x  + b    where w  is the hyperplane's perpendicular vector, also termed the director vector , and b / w       denotes the perpendicular distance between the origin of the coordinates and the hyperplane. Additionally, for all x  i    training cases, this approximation must give place to a maximum deviation from the true value y i    of ε   and at the same time must also be as flat as possible. The flatness is obtained by minimizing the Euclidean norm w    2    and the model is modified penalizing the total of deviations greater than ε  . In fact, the SVR approach aims to resolve the following problem of optimization:(1) min w  , b , ξ   +  , ξ   -    1 2  w    2  + C ∑ i = 1  m  ξ i +  + ξ i -         subject to various inequality constraints:(2) y i  - w   T  x  i  + b    ⩾ ε + ξ i +      i = 1 , . . . , m    w   T  x  i  + b    - y i  ⩾ ε + ξ i -       i = 1 , . . . , m    ξ i +  , ξ i -  ⩾ 0      i = 1 , . . . , m           so that C  is the regularization constant and ξ   +  , ξ   -  ∈ R m     are called slack variables. The regularization constant C  in Eq. (1)  limits the penalty applied to observations outside of the interval ε  , taking a positive numeric value, which helps to prevent overfitting. This number establishes the trade-off between the reduced complexity of the model and the horizontality of the objective function (Li et al., 2008; Steinwart and Christmann, 2008 ). Every training vector has slack variables, which allow deviations greater than ε   but penalize those deviations in the objective function. The area that y i  ± ε ,    ∀ i    encloses is called an ε -    insensitive tube (see Fig. 4  ). We will employ the kernelization method to address problems like this one that are highly nonlinear. The foundation of this approach is the mapping of the initial dataset to a higher-dimensional space H  known as the feature space . A kernel function K x  i  , x  j        is used to carry out the application, and it finds an inner product in H . To solve the primal optimization problem given by Eq. (1) , we will formulate it in this manner, using its dual form. When the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions are met, the optimization problem is dual-formulated  (Cristianini and Shawe–Taylor, 2000; Schölkopf et al., 2000; Hastie et al., 2003; Steinwart and Christmann, 2008; García-Nieto et al., 2022 ):(3) max α   +  , α   -      ∑ i = 1  m  y i  α i +  - α i -      - ε ∑ i = 1  m  α i +  + α i -     - 1 2  ∑ i , j = 1  m  α i +  - α i -     α j +  - α j -     K x  i  , x  j          with the constraints of equality and inequality:(4) ∑ i = 1  m  α i +  - α i -     = 0 ,        0 ⩽ α i +  ⩽ C ,      i = 1 , . . . , m    0 ⩽ α i -  ⩽ C ,      i = 1 , . . . , m           The function f x       given below can be used to calculate the regression estimation for a new sample x :(5) f x    = ∑ i = 1  m  α i +  - α i -     K x  , x  i      + b     The technical bibliography uses a variety of common functions as kernels expressed as (Cristianini and Shawe–Taylor, 2000; Schölkopf et al., 2000; Hastie et al., 2003; Li et al., 2008; Steinwart and Christmann, 2008; García-Nieto et al., 2022 ):• Pearson VII Universal Kernel (PUK):   (6) K x  i  , x  j     = 1 1 + 2 x  i  - x  j     2 ( 1 / ω )   - 1    σ    2     ω       • RBF (radial basis function) type kernel:   (7) K x  i  , x  j     = e - σ x  i  - x  j     2        • Polynomial kernel:   (8) K x  i  , x  j     = x  i  · x  j  + 1    p      • Sigmoid kernel:   (9) K x  i  , x  j     = tanh σ x  i  · x  j  + a        so that the kernel's typology is determined by the p , a , σ   and ω   parameters. In conclusion, in order to map nonlinearly separable data in a feature space (or higher-dimensional space) and solve the regression problem using the support vector machine (SVM) approach, it is convenient to choose a suitable type of kernel and its ideal hyperparameters. Moreover, representative parameters of the SVR technique can be summarised as (Cristianini and Shawe–Taylor, 2000; Schölkopf et al., 2000; Hastie et al., 2003; Li et al., 2008; Steinwart and Christmann, 2008 ):• Regularization constant (C ): Another name for it is cost function . The trade-off (or balance) between the slack variables and the margin is represented by this constant. It is one of the SVR hyperparameters that requires pre-tuning.  • ε   parameter: This number sets a maximum width for the permitted margin of error. The insensitive loss function, which highlights that it takes errors less than ε  (that is, at a distance ε   from the real value) into account, is used to calculate the empirical error , which is the objective function’s second term (see Eq. (3) ) that was reliant on the ε   factor.  • p , a , σ   and ω  : these parameters specify how the various kernels in the final model are expressed mathematically.    Therefore, it is practical to use a mathematical method that accurately determines the aforementioned hyperparameters. The grid search (GS) method, which is described below, worked well in this investigation.  2.5 Multilayer perceptron-type artificial neural network (MLP) It was demonstrated by Minsky and Papert (Haykin, 1999; Van-Mata, 2020 ) that nonlinear problems (such as XOR) could not be resolved by the adaptive linear element (ADALINE) or the simple perceptron (Fine, 1999; Haykin, 1999; Van-Mata, 2020 ). Some nonlinear problems could be solved by combining a few straightforward perceptrons, but there was no automatic system in place to adjust the hidden layer's weights. Rumelhart and colleagues first proposed the Generalized Delta Rule  (GDL) in 1986 (Van-Mata, 2020 ). This rule permits weight adjustments by sending errors toward the lower hidden layers or backwards. This allows for the possibility of working featuring nonlinear activation functions and several layers. This multilayer perceptron (MLP) can be demonstrated to be a universal approximator (Hassoun, 1995; Shepherd, 1997; Fine, 1999; Haykin, 1999; Van-Mata, 2020 ). To ascertain a nonlinear relationship between independent and dependent variables, a multilayer perceptron can be employed. One of the most popular architectures is now this ANN. A specific kind of multiple-layer artificial neural network (ANN) called an MLP is capable of solving issues that are not amenable to linear solutions (Hassoun, 1995; Shepherd, 1997; Fine, 1999; Haykin, 1999; Van-Mata, 2020 ). This problem is the main constraint on the simple perceptron. On the other hand, MLP can be fully or locally networked. For a layer to be fully linked, each neuron in that layer must be connected to every other layer's neuron. An MPL with a local connection does not fulfill this prerequisite. Three types of layers can be found in an MLP (see Fig. 5  ) (Hassoun, 1995; Shepherd, 1997; Fine, 1999; Haykin, 1999; Van-Mata, 2020 ):• Input layer: this layer only receives information about the independent variables; there is not a procedure involved.  • Output layer: this is where the link to the dependent variables is made.  • Hidden layers: these are layers that sit between the input and output layers and are responsible for processing and transferring data between them.    These neural networks are trained using the mathematical concept of backpropagation, also termed the generalized delta rule or error backpropagation (Hassoun, 1995; Shepherd, 1997; Fine, 1999; Haykin, 1999; Van-Mata, 2020 ). An MLP is also known as a Backpropagation Artificial Neural Network. An additional crucial component of these ANNs is that the processing units, or neurons, have derivable transfer functions. The multilayer perceptron (MLP), which adjusts the connection weights depending on the differences between the predicted and observed output values, applies this type of learning. Backpropagation, an extension of the linear perceptron's lowest mean square (LMS), is utilised to implement this improvement. The error at node j  for data point n  is e j  n   = d j  n   - y j  n     , where d  is the actual value and y  is the value that the multilayer perceptron predicted. The overall error to be corrected is (Hassoun, 1995; Shepherd, 1997; Fine, 1999; Haykin, 1999; Van-Mata, 2020 ):(10) ε n   = 1 2  ∑ j  e j 2  n        By applying the gradient descent method , we find that these variables influence the weight changes (Hassoun, 1995; Shepherd, 1997; Fine, 1999; Haykin, 1999; Van-Mata, 2020 ):(11) Δ w ji   n   = - η ∂ ε n    ∂ v j  n     y i  n       where:• η   is termed the learning rate.  It needs to be chosen carefully because a large value could prevent the optimization from convergent, and a small value could cause the optimization to converge very slowly. The acceptable value range is 0.1 to 0.8.  • The output of the neuron's activity in the preceding layer is y i   .  • The localized induced field is denoted by v j   . It can be proven that, with regard to a particular output node:   (12) - ∂ ε n    ∂ v j  n     = e j  n   · ϕ ′  v j  n          so that ϕ ′    the activation function's derivative. The following factors determine how the weights for the hidden layer's nodes vary:(13) - ∂ ε n    ∂ v j  n     = ϕ ′  v j  n      ∑ k  - ∂ ε n    ∂ v k  n     w kj   n        The nodes from the output layer, whose subscript is k , influence the hidden layer's weight changes. Beginning with the output layer's weights and accounting for the activation function's derivative, the method backpropagates to adjust the weights of the preceding layers.  2.6 M5 model tree Quinlan initially presented the M5 Model Tree (M5 Tree), which focuses on a binary decision tree (Quinlan, 1992; Mitchell, 1997; Kisi, 2015 ). At the terminal (leaf) nodes, this type of statistical learning method produces linear regression functions that elaborate a relationship between the independent and dependent variables (Quinlan, 1992; Hastie et al., 2003; Kisi, 2015 ). The M5 model tree building thus necessitates two distinct phases (Solomatine and Xue, 2004; Rahimikhoob et al., 2013; Kisi, 2015 ). A decision tree is constructed and data are divided into subsets in the first step. The splitting criterion is based on handling the class values' standard deviation and computing the anticipated decrease in this error as a result of testing each attribute at that node. One way to obtain the standard deviation reduction (SDR) is (Pal and Deswal, 2009; Behnood et al., 2015; Kisi, 2015; Khorrami et al., 2020 ):(14) SDR = s d ( T )  - ∑ T i    T    s d T i         In this way, sd  is the standard deviation, T i    is a subset of examples that have the i th outcome of the potential set, and T  is a set of examples that arrive at the node (Rahimikhoob et al., 2013; Kisi, 2015; Seghier et al., 2018 ). The data in secondary nodes are purer than the data in main nodes because of the splitting process, which results in lower standard deviation. Then, M5Tree chooses the one that maximizes the predicted error reduction. This division may lead to a subpar generalization and often gives place to a massive tree-like structure. The overgrown tree is pruned in order to solve this issue, and in the second stage, linear regression functions are used in place of these sub-trees. The parameter space is extended into regions, or subspaces, using statistical learning, and a linear regression model is made for each one. The division process results in data that is purer from the secondary nodes (children) because their standard deviation is lower than that of the principal nodes (parents). The M5 model tree looks at every possible division in detail and selects the option that optimizes the required error reduction. This splitting can lead to poor generalization and frequently creates a large tree-like scheme. The overgrown tree is pruned in the second phase in order to overcome this problem, and these subtrees are substituted with linear regression functions. By creating zones, also known as subspaces, out of the parameter space, this approximation creates a linear regression function for each of these areas (Pal, 2006 ). In Fig. 6  , a basic M5 model tree illustration is presented.  2.7 Multivariate linear regression (MLR) To depict the relationship of dependence between an output variable Y , m  input variables X i    (with m ∈ Z +    ), and a random term ε   (stochastic error), a mathematical model called multivariate linear regression  (MLR) is used (Weisberg, 2013; Fox, 2015; Roback and Legler, 2020; Montgomery et al., 2021; Stone, 2022 ).
