A hyperparameter is a value that is used to regulate how algorithms learn; tuning  or selecting the optimal parameters  is the process of choosing hyperparameters obtained by means of an optimization process that minimizes a specified loss function. Cross-validation is routinely used to assess the effectiveness of these considered approximations (Steinwart and Christmann, 2008; Bergstra and Bengio, 2012; Aggarwal, 2020; Agrawal, 2020 ). The Grid Search  (GS) is the most popular algorithm for selecting the ideal parameters (Eberhart et al., 2001; Steinwart and Christmann, 2008; Bergstra and Bengio, 2012; Chong and Zak, 2013; Aggarwal, 2020; Agrawal, 2020 ). The GS optimizer is a detailed manual search over a predetermined searching set of a learning algorithm's hyperparameter space. It chooses the best parameters from a list for the optimization problem. Although this optimizer can be applied to a wide range of optimization problems, machine learning techniques are the ones that use it most frequently to identify the best efficiency strategy and optimal parameters. Therefore, Grid Search optimizer is used to find the optimal hyperparameters of a machine learning model which results in the most accurate predictions.  2.9 Preciseness of the approximation Using the eight predictive input variables that were previously discussed in subsection 2.3 above, a novel GS/SVR–based technique was created. The estimated variable is the Chl-a concentration. The model that most closely matches the actual dataset is chosen to forecast Chl-a from the eight remaining input variables with accuracy and reliability. The coefficient of determination R 2    was the primary rule used in this investigation (Knafl and Ding, 2016; McClave and Sincich, 2016 ). We will compare the values estimated by the model y i    with the observed values t i   . The following sums of squares, provided by, can now be defined: (Wasserman, 2003; Bishop, 2006; Freedman et al., 2007; McClave and Sincich, 2016 ):• S S reg   = ∑ i = 1  n  y i  - t  ¯      2    : is the sum of squares explained.  • S S tot   = ∑ i = 1  n  t i  - t  ¯      2    : this summation has a direct correlation with the sample variance.  • S S err   = ∑ i = 1  n  t i  - y i     2    : we refer to it as the residual sum of squares.    where t  ¯     is the average value of the experimental data as indicated by:(24) t  ¯   = 1 n  ∑ i = 1  n  t i      Next, we have the coefficient of determination (Wasserman, 2003; Freedman et al., 2007 ):(25) R 2  ≡ 1 - S S err    S S tot         The closer the R 2  statistic gets to 1.0, the less difference there is between the experimental and predicted data. The adjusted coefficient of determination R adj  2   , also called corrected coefficient of determination, measures the goodness of fit of a regression model taking into account the number of explanatory variables included in the model. The formula to calculate the adjusted coefficient of determination is as follows:(26) R adj  2  ≡ 1 - n - 1  n - k - 1   1 - R 2         where:• R 2  is the ordinary coefficient of determination given by the Eq. (25) ;  • n  is the sample size; and  • k  is the number of explanatory variables in the regression model.    Thus, the adjusted coefficient of determination measures the percentage explained by the regression model, penalizing for each explanatory variable introduced in the model. In general, the more variables a regression model has, the better it explains the data sample, but the more complicated the model will be. Two additional criteria considered in this study were the root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) (Hastie et al., 2003; Wasserman, 2003 ). These statistics are also used frequently to evaluate the forecasting capability of a mathematical model. Indeed, the root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) are given by the expressions (Freedman et al., 2007; Wasserman, 2003 ):(27) RMSE = ∑ i = 1  n  t i  - y i     2   n       (28) MAE =   ∑ i = 1  n  t i  - y i      n      If the root mean square error (RMSE) has a value of zero, it means that there is no difference between the predicted and observed data. Mean Absolute Error (MAE) is the average vertical distance between each point and the identity line. MAE is also the average horizontal distance between each point and the identity line. MAE has a clear interpretation as the average absolute difference between t i    and y i   . Various approaches have been developed, including the SVM–based approximation, MLP–type approach, multivariate linear regression (MLR) and M5 model tree model, to successfully determine a precise Chl-a estimation employing the coefficient of determination R 2 . Furthermore, as was already mentioned, the regularization constant C , the width of the allowable margin of error (ε   parameter), and the final values of p , a , σ   and ω  , which define the unique kernels' mathematical expression, are all crucial factors in the SVM approximation. Additionally, the common methodology used in this work to find the best parameters for SVM and MLP models is Grid Search (GS), also referred to as parameter sweeping  (Eberhart et al., 2001; Steinwart and Christmann, 2008; Bergstra and Bengio, 2012; Chong and Zak, 2013; Aggarwal, 2020; Agrawal, 2020 ). It is just a comprehensive manual search using that statistical machine learning algorithm across a preset subset of the parameter space. There are two sets within the dataset: the training set utilizes 80 % of the data and the testing set utilizes the remaining 20 %. In this manner, the GS/SVM model is built employing the training collection. The GS algorithm is used to calibrate the hyperparameters of the SVM model through a 10–fold cross-validation method (Efron and Tibshirani, 1997; Picard and Cook, 1984 ). Once the best parameters were identified, the model was built using the entire training dataset. The next step involves applying this model to estimate the elements of the testing set. We compare these forecasts to the actual values and calculate the goodness–of–fit of the approximation. Fig. 8   now shows the process diagram for the GS/SVM employed in this study. Furthermore, to determine the true coefficient of determination (R 2 ) in this situation, cross-validation is widely employed (Wasserman, 2003; Freedman et al., 2007 ). Clearly, a total 10–fold cross-validation approach was used in this study to assess the GS/SVM-relied approximation's predictive ability (Efron and Tibshirani, 1997; Picard and Cook, 1984 ). In order to do this, the open-source machine learning program WEKA  has been used to implement regression modeling using the SVM approximation (Hall et al., 2009; Witten et al., 2016 ). The intervals for the hyperparameters used in this work are shown in Table 2  . The GS optimizer is suitable for optimizing the SVM parameters. The analysis of differences of the cross-validation error in each iteration allows the GS to identify the optimal C , ε, p, a,  σ and ω   parameters. The variation space is multidimensional, meaning that there is one dimension for every parameter. In this work, the GS/MLP approach has been applied for research purposes. Similarly, we are aware that MLP depends on the subsequent factors (Hassoun, 1995; Shepherd, 1997; Fine, 1999; Haykin, 1999 ):• Learning rate (LR ): This parameter is utilized to make sure the weights converge to an oscillation-free response as soon as possible.  • Momentum (m ): It is a version of the stochastic gradient descent  in neural networks.  • Number of hidden layer neurons (h ): Generally speaking, the hidden layer has between 70 % and 90 % (or roughly 2/3) as many neurons as the input layer.    For this parameter tuning, an optimizer based on Grid Search (GS) was used (Eberhart et al., 2001; Steinwart and Christmann, 2008; Bergstra and Bengio, 2012; Chong and Zak, 2013; Aggarwal, 2020; Agrawal, 2020 ). Fig. 9   displays the diagram of the process flow for this GS/MLP model. Similarly, the 10-fold cross-validation method yielded the coefficient of determination (R 2 ) (Efron and Tibshirani, 1997; Picard and Cook, 1984 ). The Grid Search optimizer and open-source machine learning program WEKA  were also used to model the multilayer perceptron (MLP) (Hall et al., 2009; Witten et al., 2016 ). The GS/MLP parameters' initial intervals are displayed in Table 3  .   3 Results and discussion Table 1  above displays all eight of the input independent variables, or eight physico-chemical variables. 240,765 samples in total were used in this investigation, meaning that in accordance with the European Water Quality Directive (Directive 2000 /60/EC), 240,765 experimental samplings were obtained and processed in El Val reservoir. A daily average for every variable was computed and we were left with data for 1,624 days (see Appendix A). In order to tackle this intricate problem, the entire data set must be divided into two parts: a training set that consists of 80 % of the data, and the remaining data, 20 % is used as testing set. The main concept is to use training data to create an SVR–relied model, then use the GS optimizer to find the model's ideal parameters and use it to create predictions by applying it to test data. Table 4   lists the ideal parameters of the best-fit SVR–relied approach that the GS optimizer encountered, in accordance with this methodology. Moreover, Table 5   presents the ideal GS/MLP parameters that were discovered. In light of the completed calculations, the GS/SVR–relied approach has made it possible to build a model with large tolerances for determining the Chl-a levels using the test data. Undoubtedly, the dependent Chl-a variable had a correlation coefficient r  of 0.9499 and a value of R 2  of 0.8989 for the best SVR approach. The outcomes are displayed in Table 6  . For comparative purposes, we have also built models using other cutting edge techniques like Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Multivariate linear regression (MLR), and M5 model tree. In every instance, the GS/SVR–PUK produces superior results. Table 6  displays the outcomes. A computer with a CPU Intel Core i7-4770 @ 3.40 GHz with eight cores and 15.5 GB RAM memory was used, taking 11 min to optimise the parameters of the model and < 1 s to obtain the final Chl-a concentration values. The first and second order terms that come together to form the excellent SVR–relied approach with PUK kernel for the Chl-a concentration are shown in Fig. 10   below as a pictorial graph. 3.1 Relevance of variables Another significant finding of this study is the significance of the input variables in predicting the Chl-a levels for this complex nonlinear models (see Tables 7 and 8   , and Fig. 11  ). The best model is GS/SVR-relied model with PUK kernel function. The following approach was used to assess the significance of the input variables: the training set was employed to build the model, and its goodness– of– fit was examined to gauge the input variables' significance. Then we take out one variable and measure it again. We do this with all the independent variables. Table 7  below displays the results: An indicator of the importance of a variable is given by the loss in goodness–of–fit: when a variable is eliminated from the model, the error increases proportionately to its significance. We have used the increase of RMSE to rank the importance of the variables as it is indicated in Table 8  below. Thus, in the El Val reservoir's Chl-a prediction, the Photic layer depth (m) is the most significant input variable based on the GS/SVR approach with PUK kernel function. Next, pH is the second important input variable followed by Water Temperature, Conductivity, Redox Potential, Height, Dissolved Oxygen, and Turbidity. Photic layer depth emerged as the most influential factor affecting chlorophyll concentrations. This result aligns with previous research highlighting the crucial role of light availability in regulating primary productivity and, consequently, chlorophyll production in aquatic environments. Deeper photic layers restrict light penetration, diminishing the energy available for photosynthesis and thereby limiting chlorophyll synthesis. Removal of this variable led to a notable decrease in the goodness-of-fit (r = 0.92507   ), highlighting its indispensable role in capturing the influence of light availability on chlorophyll synthesis. Following photic layer depth, pH exhibited significant influence on chlorophyll concentrations. pH serves as a fundamental indicator of water quality, impacting various biochemical processes, including nutrient availability and phytoplankton growth. Optimal pH levels facilitate enzymatic activity and nutrient uptake, promoting chlorophyll synthesis. Deviations from optimal pH can disrupt these processes, leading to fluctuations in chlorophyll abundance. Its removal resulted in a considerable decrease in goodness-of-fit (r = 0.9284   ), emphasizing the role of water chemistry in shaping phytoplankton communities and chlorophyll dynamics. Water temperature ranked third in importance among the predictor variables. Temperature profoundly influences biochemical reactions and metabolic rates in aquatic organisms, including phytoplankton. Elevated temperatures accelerate metabolic processes, potentially enhancing chlorophyll production through increased photosynthetic activity. Conversely, extreme temperatures can induce thermal stress, impairing physiological functions and suppressing chlorophyll synthesis. Its exclusion led to a notable decrease in goodness-of-fit (r = 0.9346   ), emphasizing the role of temperature in regulating metabolic processes and phytoplankton growth rates. Conductivity, reflecting the water's ion concentration, emerged as the fourth most influential variable. Ionic composition affects nutrient availability and osmoregulation in aquatic organisms, thereby influencing chlorophyll synthesis indirectly. Higher conductivity levels may indicate elevated nutrient concentrations, promoting phytoplankton growth and chlorophyll production. Its removal led to a decrease in goodness-of-fit (r = 0.9383   ), underscoring its importance in capturing the physicochemical conditions of the aquatic environment. Redox potential, indicative of the water's oxidative-reductive balance, ranked fifth in importance. Redox conditions influence nutrient availability, microbial activity, and organic matter decomposition, all of which impact chlorophyll dynamics. Oxygen-rich environments support aerobic respiration and nutrient cycling, fostering phytoplankton growth and chlorophyll accumulation. Its exclusion resulted in a decrease in goodness-of-fit (r = 0.9414   ), highlighting its role in shaping chlorophyll dynamics through its influence on biogeochemical processes. Reservoir elevation, representing the water body's altitude above sea level, exhibited moderate influence on chlorophyll concentrations. Elevation influences temperature gradients, hydrological dynamics, and nutrient inputs, which collectively shape chlorophyll dynamics in aquatic ecosystems. Higher elevations may experience cooler temperatures and lower nutrient inputs, potentially limiting chlorophyll production compared to lower elevations. Its removal led to a decrease in goodness-of-fit (r = 0.9442   ), indicating its contribution to capturing spatial variations in chlorophyll concentrations. Dissolved oxygen content, a critical parameter reflecting oxygen availability in aquatic systems, ranked seventh in importance. Adequate oxygen levels are essential for aerobic metabolism and respiratory processes in phytoplankton. Oxygen deficiency can suppress chlorophyll synthesis and promote anaerobic conditions, altering community composition and chlorophyll dynamics. Its exclusion resulted in a decrease in goodness-of-fit (r = 0.9452   ), highlighting its role in shaping phytoplankton metabolism and chlorophyll production. Turbidity, representing water clarity or suspended particle concentration, emerged as the least influential variable in our model. While turbidity indirectly affects light availability and nutrient dynamics, its impact on chlorophyll concentrations is relatively minor compared to other factors. High turbidity levels may reduce light penetration, limiting photosynthesis and chlorophyll production, particularly in shallow water bodies. Its removal resulted in a decrease in goodness-of-fit (r = 0.9513   ), indicating its limited contribution to capturing chlorophyll variability compared to other predictors. Overall, our study underscores the multifaceted nature of chlorophyll regulation in aquatic ecosystems, elucidating the hierarchical importance of various environmental variables. By quantifying the relative relevance of each variable and assessing their individual contributions to model accuracy, we provide valuable insights for understanding and managing chlorophyll dynamics. These findings have implications for ecosystem monitoring, water quality management, and the development of targeted mitigation strategies to address excessive chlorophyll levels and associated ecological consequences. Further research incorporating temporal and spatial variability will enhance our understanding of these complex interactions and facilitate more effective management strategies for maintaining water quality and ecosystem health. Without a doubt, Fig. 12   compares the predicted and experimental Chl-a concentration’s values employing the MLR model (Fig. 12 (a)), GS/MLP model (Fig. 12 (b)), M5 model tree (Fig. 12 (c)), and GS/SVM–relied approximation (PUK kernel) (Fig. 12 (d)). As a result, employing a SVM approach is crucial to getting the most excellent approach possible for the regression issue at hand. These findings clearly show that the GS/SVM–relied approach (PUK kernel) offers the most excellent fit and uphold the vital statistical goodness–of–fit criterion (R 2 ). Therefore, combining the SVR methodology (PUK kernel) with the GS optimizer is essential to solving this problem. Additionally, Figs. 13–16      indicate the comparison between the experimental and predicted Chl-a concentration values employing the eight kinds of models for the testing dataset. Consequently, to solve this nonlinear regression problem, it was fundamental to bring together the GS/SVR–model with PUK kernel to produce an original hybrid strategy that was significantly more reliable and efficient than the other seven regression methods.   4 Conclusions Based on the previous findings, the principal conclusions of this investigation can be inferred and highlighted:• First of all, it is noteworthy that the existing analytical models, which predict the Chl-a concentration based on observed values, are insufficiently precise due to their significant simplification of a highly complex and nonlinear problem. As a result, the innovative hybrid GS/SVR–relied approach with PUK kernel used in this study, which leverages machine learning techniques, has proven to be the most effective method for accurately estimating the concentration of Chl-a.  • Secondly, El Val reservoir, classified as eutrophic one, serves as further validation of the assumption that the Chl-a concentration can be accurately obtained employing a hybrid GS/SVR–based approximation with PUK kernel in water bodies such as reservoirs and lakes.  • Thirdly, using SVR, the experimental dataset related to the Chl-a concentration yielded a good coefficient of determination and correlation coefficient, with values of 0.8989 and 0.9499, respectively.  • In fourth place, the abiotic input variables involved in estimating the Chl-a levels were ranked, or classified for importance. One of the main conclusions of this research is this. When forecasting Chl-a concentration, depth in particular needs to be considered as the most significant factor. Regarding this, it is also important to stress how crucial it is to consider the pH, water temperature, conductivity, redox potential, height, dissolved oxygen, and turbidity in that order with the purpose of obtaining the desired Chl-a concentration result.  • Conclusively, the main contribution of precisely determining the hyperparameters in the SVR–relied methodology to the Chl-a concentration regression performance is established. Here, the Grid Search (GS) optimizer proved to be effective in calculating these ideal hyperparameters.    In conclusion, this process could be effectively utilized to foretell the amount of Chl-a in various reservoir types. Nonetheless, it is typically required to take unique features into account for every reservoir and experiment. Therefore, the GS/SVR–relied method with PUK kernel can be considered a reliable and practical solution to the nonlinear challenge of calculating the Chl-a concentration using experimental samplings in lakes and reservoirs.
1 Introduction In mountain watersheds, precipitation and snowmelt are transmitted from terrestrial to aquatic ecosystems as saturation- or infiltration excess overland flow (McGlynn and McDonnell, 2003 ), shallow groundwater drainage along low permeability geologic contacts (Tromp-van Meerveld and McDonnell, 2006 ), and via permeable bedrock features (O’Sullivan et al., 2020 ). Gaining headwater stream sections have strong hydrologic connectivity to the local landscape, yet parsing the volumetric contributions to streamflow from various hillslope runoff and other routing mechanisms is challenging because these contribution processes are often transient in nature and vary spatially across watersheds (e.g., Covino, 2017; Rey et al., 2019; Conant Jr, et al., 2019; Lewandowski et al., 2020; Stewart et al., 2022 ). During periods of lower precipitation and/or higher energy availability, hydrologic routing can shift from terrestrial hillslopes to more resilient baseflow sources as shallow soil reservoirs are depleted. Systematic shifts in hillslope water sources influence stream ecosystem function by changing important energy and material fluxes, such as organic carbon, inorganic nutrients, and water temperature (Snyder et al., 2015; Larsen et al., 2018; Zimmer and McGlynn, 2018; Radke et al., 2019; Saiers et al., 2021; Stewart et al., 2022 ). Stream corridors with pronounced groundwater discharge from deep hillslope or regional flowpaths can buffer stream networks from climate-induced shifts in streamflow volume (Tague et al., 2008; Hughes et al., 2012; Safeeq et al., 2014, Warix et al., 2021 ), and reduce coupling with air temperature at the lowest flows, buffering stream temperatures during hot and cold seasonal extremes (Briggs et al., 2018 ). Conversely, in streams where base flow is predominantly sourced by shallow hillslope groundwater, the thermal buffering effect of groundwater inflow is reduced, and baseflow regimes are less resilient to droughts and larger climate trends (Kurylyk et al., 2015; Hare et al., 2021 ). Although some headwater catchments are dominated by specific hillslope reservoirs (e.g., shallow groundwater), substantial variability has been documented in stream-riparian-hillslope hydrologic connectivity over space, seasons, and between years (Payn et al., 2009; Jencso et al., 2010; Johnson et al., 2017; Warix et al., 2023 ). Using repeat solute tracer injections, Payn et al (2009)  documented seasonal shifts in hillslope water contribution to streams driven by localized valley structure and geology. By installing riparian and hillslope piezometers across a nearby mountain catchment to measure water level and electrical conductivity, Jencso et al (2010)  mapped shifts in summer hillslope water dominance as snowmelt-recharged hillslopes dried, in many places to the shallow bedrock contact. Jencso et al (2010)  suggested that hillslope hydrologic connectivity was related to landscape structure, including the relative size of the riparian area compared to adjacent hillslopes. Simulations of headwater stream expansion, contraction, and longitudinal channel connectivity (i.e., patchy stream drying) in the Western Cascade Mountains, Oregon, USA, have highlighted the importance of hillslope contributing area vs. valley subsurface flow capacity in controlling stream base flow and drying patterns (Ward et al., 2020 ). These recent model-based inferences have been further supported by empirical data collected across catchments in the Blue Ridge Mountains, Virginia, USA where Briggs et al. (2022)  demonstrated that localized changes in bedrock depth can drive streamwater gains and losses, peak summer stream temperatures, and the relative dominance of hillslope runoff vs. groundwater sources. Efficient methods for characterizing temporal patterns in stream-hillslope connectivity remain elusive, in part because shifts in hillslope water sources tend to be non-linear and threshold-based (McDonnell, 2003 ). As a result, there is a paucity of data from headwater streams because the complexity in hydrologic partitioning, vegetation distribution, and orographic impacts on climatic conditions defy interpretation across spatial and temporal scales. The difficulty in parsing streamflow sources has led to divergent stream temperature forecasts in existing literature that also lack needed resolution to capture spatial ‘patchiness’ (e.g., Leach and Moore, 2019; Isaak and Luce, 2023 ). At seasonal to annual timescales, recent methodological advances in paired air–water temperature signal analysis have led to inferences into the general characteristics of stream-groundwater exchange at kilometer-scale spatial resolutions (Snyder et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2017; Briggs et al., 2018 ), including post wildfire stream-hillslope connectivity (Rey et al., 2023 ), where streams with deep groundwater influence may be the most resilient to changes in thermal regime (Rey et al., 2023; Beyene and Leibowitz, 2024 ). Hare et al. (2021)  paired annual temperature signal analysis with baseflow separation at hundreds of sites to show streams with less local groundwater influence had streamflow regimes that were generally more dominated by runoff processes, although runoff influence was not parsed by season. More recently, McGill et al. (2024)  used cluster analysis of linear paired air–water temperature sensitivity metrics to show how stream thermal sensitivities shifted by season as a function of environmental variables such as geology and snowmelt. Annual air:water temperature signal analysis has also been used in recent attempts to improve spatially explicit process-guided deep learning models of stream temperature in the Delaware River Basin (USA) (Barclay et al., 2023 ). However, to our knowledge, no studies have used diel temperature signals to assess sub-seasonal streamflow generation dynamics. Stream temperature and the health of aquatic ecosystems are inextricably linked as water temperatures exert a primary control on biogeochemical and physical processes that drive habitat suitability for aquatic species (Rasmussen et al., 2011; Fellman et al., 2014; Brewitt et al., 2017; Ouellet et al., 2020; Hitt et al., 2023; Hare et al., 2023 ). Opportunities to harness stream temperature records for hydrological analysis are rapidly expanding, as stream temperature is now monitored at nested scales across headwater stream catchments (e.g., Briggs et al 2022). Increasingly ubiquitous observations enable analysis of stream temperature at daily timescales to investigate rainfall-runoff responses and larger changes in watershed hillslope connectivity. For example, Miralha et al. (2023)  found characteristic stream temperature hysteresis patterns during spring and summer storm events in two headwater catchments. Yet, hysteretic behavior was significantly correlated to physiographic characteristics in one headwater catchment and meteorological metrics in another, indicating differing physical controls on streamflow generation. Here we explore the utility of paired air and stream water diel temperature analysis to efficiently map local variations in hillslope-stream connectivity at high spatial resolution (i.e., longitudinal kilometer (km) scale) across glaciated and unglaciated mountain headwater systems. Using diel air–water temperature sinusoid characteristics (amplitude ratio, phase lag, mean ratio) that quantitatively describe aspects of signal coupling as tracers of streamflow generation process, we present new methods for mapping spatiotemporal patterns in stream-hillslope connectivity. We fit simple polynomial regression models to capture nonlinear seasonal patterns in calculated diel air–water temperature metrics and compare diel temperature signal analysis to more commonly used metrics of stream water sensitivity and baseflow contribution to stream discharge. Further, we utilize conceptual stream heat budget models to develop mechanistic insight into the controls on observed trends in diel air–water temperature signal relations. We conclude that diel air–water signal analysis can identify areas of pronounced local stream-hillslope connectivity, helping to elucidate periods of groundwater dominance and providing insight into how headwater streams drain landscapes across seasons and the prevalence of cold-water stream habitats.  2 Study sites Our primary field site was the glaciated, forested Neversink River watershed upstream from Neversink Reservoir (hereafter Neversink Reservoir watershed) in the Catskill Mountains of New York, USA (Fig. 1  a; Briggs et al 2022 ). The catchment drains 172.5 km2  of generally steep terrain, with prevalent thin, rocky soil cover (or exposed bedrock) at higher elevations and with low permeability glacial till along hillslopes into which most streams are incised (Fig. 1 c; Odom and Doctor, 2023 ). The larger lower elevation streams (Fig. 1 e) consist of the east and west branch Neversink River that confluence 10 km upstream from Neversink Reservoir. Tributaries of East Branch and West Branch Neversink River (Fig. 1 d) show similar sediment thicknesses although sediment thickness is greatest under the west branch stream channels, ranging greater than 20 m to bedrock (Fig. 1 c; Odom and Doctor, 2023 ). Stream base flow is generated from a range of groundwater sources, from bedrock fracture flow through sandstone, siltstone, and conglomerate layers to shallow hillslope colluvium flowpaths, with documented localized spatial transitions of shallow to deep groundwater discharge (Burns et al., 1998 ). Summer storm events have been shown to generate substantial shallow soil ‘quickflow,’ causing flashy streamflow response (Brown et al., 1999 ). Recently, the catchment has been used as a groundwater/surface water ‘technology testbed’ for the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Next Generation Water Observing System Program, as detailed by Briggs et al., (2022a) , focused on multiscale monitoring of groundwater discharge processes. Six active streamgages are in the greater watershed (Fig. 1 c), and meteorological data are collected locally at two sites along the West Branch Neversink River. Many streams of the unglaciated, forested Shenandoah National Park, Virginia, USA (Fig. 1 a, b) have been extensively characterized for groundwater connectivity using a combination of paired air–water temperature analysis, ambient and introduced tracers, statistical modeling, geophysical mapping, and baseflow separation analysis (Plummer et al., 2001; Snyder et al., 2015 ; Briggs et al., 2018 b; Johnson et al., 2017 ; Briggs et al., 2018 a, 2022b). Located in the Blue Ridge Range, subwatersheds are typically steep and narrow, with valley slope generally > 15° and width < 60 m. Two sub-watersheds were determined to be end-members of high and low groundwater influence, Staunton River and Paine Run, respectively (Johnson et al., 2017; Briggs et al., 2022b ). Staunton River had the deepest average depth to bedrock (3.4 m) of eight sub-watersheds extensively surveyed with passive seismic methods, creating a more resilient shallow reservoir of soil moisture for baseflow generation than Paine Run, where bedrock averaged 2.2 m depth. Annual air–water temperature signal analysis indicated persistent signatures of deeper groundwater influence at Staunton River compared to other Shenandoah River tributaries, which was confirmed by summer baseflow analysis (1993–2020) that averaged 0.62, compared to 0.46 for Paine Run (Briggs et al., 2022b ).  3 Methods This study used co-located air (streambank) and stream water temperature observations from 46 fixed sites within the Neversink Reservoir watershed over the 2021 and 2022 water years. Shenandoah National Park stream and local air temperature data from 10 sites collected over periods from 2012 to 2016 (Snyder et al., 2015 ) that were previously analyzed for weekly to seasonal patterns, were repurposed here for analysis of diel temperature signals for comparison to the Neversink Reservoir watershed. Neversink temperature observations were collected with Tidbit model V2 and MX 2203 water temperature loggers (Onset, Massachusetts, USA) at continuous 15-minute intervals. At each station, a stream temperature logger was housed within a short, slotted polyvinyl chloride (PVC) pipe and affixed to a boulder in small pool locations that were expected to stay submerged at the lowest flows. Air temperature loggers were housed in a sunlight shield and affixed to the north side of large riparian trees; additional instrument deployment details are provided by Terry et al. (2023) . Given the inherent decoupling of air and water temperatures near freezing (Letcher et al., 2016 ), all pairs of air and water temperature observations were removed for timeframes when water temperatures dropped below 1 °C, similar to Hare et al (2021) . Summer stream temperature at these headwater sites generally were < 25 °C, so air–water signal decoupling that can occur at high temperatures (not related to groundwater inflow) was not expected, and no warm season data were culled. In addition to the paired air–water temperature monitoring stations, several discrete hillslope spring emergence locations along the upper West Branch Neversink River were instrumented from May to October 2022 with single iButton 1922L model temperature loggers embedded in steel pipes and inserted into respective spring origination points. Because daily temperature data are generally sinusoidal (Fig. 2  ), stream and air temperature signals can be expressed as a linear combination of sine and cosine functions with separate coefficients and a constant that accounts for the offset of the signal mean (similar to the extraction of annual temperature signals by Briggs et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2020; Hare et al., 2021; Rey et al., 2023; Hare et al., 2023 ). To extract diel signals from air and water data, hourly mean temperature (centered in time) was first computed from raw 15-minute observations (Fig. 2 a). Best fit diel sinusoidal parameters (mean, amplitude, phase) were estimated by minimizing the root mean squared error between the daily signal fit and the hourly observed data (Fig. 2 b). Diel air–water temperature signal metrics were determined as the water:air signal amplitude ratio (Amplitude Ratio, AR_d ), the lag in the air to water signal timing or phase (Phase Lag, PL_d ), and the ratio of the water:air signal means (Mean Ratio, MR_d ) (Fig. 2 c). Only days where the regressed diel sinusoid explained > 70 % (error values less than two standard deviations from the mean) of the observed variance in air or water temperature were used, so poor signal fits stemming from short-term hydroclimatic variability were dropped from the hydrological analysis (i.e., ∼6.5 % of data across all sites). Preliminary analysis indicated many stream sites showed non-linear temporal trends in daily Ar_d  and PL_d  metrics. Seasonal non-linearity in AR_d  and PL_d  metrics showed time series with repeatable concave up or concave down patterns, where AR_d  and PL_d  often showed inverse relationships. To quantify non-linear seasonal patterns, we fit second-order polynomials (i.e., ax2  + bx + c) to combined 2020 and 2021 AR_d  and PL_d  data that were smoothed with using a rolling 7-day mean across each water year (average r2  = 0.62). Best fit polynomials optimized through least squares regression were developed for AR_d  and PL_d  metrics at each site and used for this study (Fig. 2 d). The sign and magnitude of leading coefficients for regressed polynomials signifies the direction and rate of change for the regression equation. Consequently, the leading coefficient was used to broadly signify differences in non-linear temporal trends between paired air–water temperature metric time-series at different sites from early season high flows to later-season low flows (Fig. 2 d). This helped us to distinguish sites that showed either reduced or increased air–water temperature signal coupling during warmer, drier periods, as expressed by the AR_d  and PL_d  metrics, and differentiate from sites that showed no distinct seasonal pattern. Seasonal streamflow records have been widely used to estimate the relative fractions of runoff-quickflow vs. groundwater discharge contributing to streamflow through graphical and chemical separation of base flow (e.g., Eckhardt, 2008; Ladson et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2015 ). We used daily mean streamflow retrieved from two streamgages (01434017 on East Branch Neversink River (hereafter East Branch), and 01,434,498 on West Branch Neversink River (hereafter West Branch), Fig. 1 c) from the USGS National Water Information System (NWIS; USGS, 2022 ) for periods that overlapped our paired air and water temperature records. For each Neversink River streamgage, the Baseflow Index (BFI) Algorithm (Wahl and Wahl, 1988 ) was used to graphically separate the baseflow component of streamflow. This baseflow separation algorithm is categorized as a smoothed minima approach and has been widely adopted, used, and compared to numerous other chemical and graphical baseflow separation methods (e.g., Miller et al., 2015, Lott and Stewart, 2016 ). Once base flow was separated from daily streamflow values, daily cumulative baseflow values were calculated, as was the BFI, which was computed as the ratio of cumulative volume of base flow by the cumulative volume of discharge for each time-period of interest (e.g., day, water-year). Baseflow characteristics had previously been derived from streamflow records for the Shenandoah National Park sites (e.g., Briggs et al 2022 ). To assess the effects of groundwater inflow, shading, seasonality, and downstream distance on local diel air and stream water temperature metrics, total stream heat budget model scenarios were developed using the numerical Matlab code HFLUX (Glose et al., 2017 ), modified to allow time-variable temperature of groundwater inflow (Briggs et al., 2018 , Johnson et al., 2024 ). Details of model construction and parameterization are explained in the data release Hare and Briggs, (2024) . Briefly, 5-km linear model domains were specified with 0.5-m linear spatial resolution for 10 repetitive days. Two days were chosen when baseflow separation results from the West Branch Neversink River streamgage (01434498) indicated a lack of recent event-driven runoff: April 24 and August 15, 2022 (USGS, 2022). Streamflow at the West Branch Neversink River on those days averaged 1864 L/s and 440 L/s, respectively. Those streamflow rates were assigned to the upper boundary of the April and August Base-Case model scenarios, which is represented as 0 % discrete groundwater inflow (Table 1  ). Channel dimensions were estimated based on a target stream velocity of 0.5 m/s at the upper model boundary, with a constant channel width of 3 m for all scenarios based on visual field observations. Air temperature for those days was specified as a best fit sinusoid fit to observed data from the Biscuit Brook streamgage (01434025; USGS, 2022), a headwater stream site in the upper West Branch Neversink River watershed. Upper boundary stream temperature was scaled using an AR_d  of 0.4 to those idealized air temperature signals using air–water temperature signal metrics, except for the August ‘Spring Run’ scenarios (Table 1 ). For the latter, streamflow was assumed to emerge entirely from a discrete spring at constant 9 °C in August, generally based on observed riparian spring temperatures recorded at the West Branch streamgage by instrumentation deployed by the USGS Next Generation Water Observing System Program (Briggs et al., 2022). A Spring Run scenario was not developed for April conditions due to the observed prevalence of large hillslope runoff contributions to the tributary streamflow during that period. Incoming solar radiation (above the canopy, no clouds) was estimated as the global horizontal irradiance calculated from the Ineichen and Perez model (e.g., Perez et al., 2002; Stein et al., 2012 ) implemented with the Python pvlib (v0.10.1) package (Holmgren et al., 2018 ). For the Base-Case scenarios, shading for the forested setting was estimated at 0.95, but reduced to 0.5 for a range of scenarios to represent downstream sections with less riparian tree cover and infer the relative importance of shading versus groundwater inflow in controlling diel air–water temperature signal relations. Groundwater was added to the simulated stream reach at 4000–4020 m from the upstream channel boundary, and models with a range of parameters were used to test the effects of large discrete inflows on diel air–water temperature relations. Specifically, scenarios for groundwater increasing streamflow volume by 10, 25, 35, and 50 % were simulated. Groundwater temperature was specified as a constant 6 °C for April and 9 °C for August, similar to the Spring Run scenarios. Two additional discrete 50 % groundwater inflow scenarios for April and August were developed based on a hillslope spring monitored in 2022 that showed (muted) diel temperature variability, with derived mean diel air–water metrics of AR_d  = 0.05 and PL_d  = 5.5 hr.  4 Results 4.1 Stream thermal heat-budget model results The conceptual stream heat budget models showed paired reductions in AR_d  and MR_d  as a function of groundwater influence (fraction of total streamflow) in April and August model runs (Fig. 3  a,c; Table 1 ), agreeing with long-held ecological theory regarding groundwater dependent habitat being buffered and cooled in summer at diel timescales (e.g., Arrigoni et al., 2008 ). April and August MR_d  decreased from ∼ 1 to 0.85 as groundwater inflow percentage increased from 0 to 50 % by volume (Fig. 3 a). In contrast, AR_d  showed slight seasonal differences as April values declined from ∼ 1.0 to 0.7 and August AR_d  values decreased from ∼ 0.4 to 0.2 as the fraction of groundwater inflow increased from 0 to 50 % (Fig. 3 c). Unlike the influence of groundwater inflow on AR_d  and MR_d , negligible changes were observed in PL_d  as a function of higher groundwater contributions (Fig. 3 b). Thermal perturbations via local groundwater inflows are attenuated downstream as heat serves as a non-conservative tracer and stream water temperature moves toward an equilibrium condition with other dominant channel water heat fluxes. This is apparent in model runs where the top of the reach was sourced exclusively from groundwater inflow (i.e., a groundwater spring), and no additional groundwater inputs were provided downstream. Across these model runs, AR_d  and MR_d  increased non-linearly downstream in the absence of additional groundwater inputs (Fig. 3 d), and AR_d  were attenuated more rapidly in stream segments with less shading (i.e., 50 % vs. 95 %). However, for all stream heat budget simulations, groundwater inflow had a more dominant effect on AR_d , MR_d , and PL_d  metrics than varying shading (Fig. 3 a-c), as shading primarily affected downstream signal attenuation.  4.2 Water and air temperature observations and trends Observed trends in AR_d  and PL_d  were non-linear and diverged between early season high flows and later season low flows (Fig. 4  ). These non-linear trends manifested as either a concave or convex regression fit, as captured by the sign of the leading coefficient fit (a negative ‘a’ coefficient indicates convexity and a positive ‘a’ coefficient indicates concavity). Over our observational period, all parabola minima or maxima occurred during warmer months (e.g., Fig. 4 ), ranging from day 150 (i.e., late May) to day 240 (late August) with a mean of day 190 (i.e., July). Despite the lack of sensitivity of PL_d  to additional groundwater inflow in stream heat budget models, observed PL_d  trends showed characteristic behavior that was often inversely related to AR_d  trends (Fig. 4 ). Sites that exhibited the largest seasonal changes in AR_d  and PL_d  metrics were associated with larger magnitude (positive or negative) ‘a’ coefficient values, as the leading regression coefficient indicates the width of regressed polynomials (Fig. 5  ). Trends in AR_d  (as captured by coefficients of the regression model) were indicated by conceptual stream heat budget models to be sensitive to local groundwater influence and were therefore compared to a widely used and well understood metric for assessing air–water coupling. Stream thermal sensitivity (Fig. 5 , x-axis) generally represents the slope of the linear best-fit line when air and stream temperatures are compared, with a slope of 1 indicating that water temperatures rise and fall the same amount as air temperatures. Stream thermal sensitivities have commonly been used to assess air:water coupling in regions where more stable groundwater temperatures buffer stream temperature from changes in ambient air temperature. Paired air–water temperature stations whose AR_d  reached their minimum during warmer drier periods (i.e., indicative of increased groundwater influence) had the lowest thermal sensitivities to rising air temperatures, as can be seen in the inverse correlation (p < 0.01) between stream temperature response and AR_d  regression coefficients for Neversink River and Shenandoah National Park sites (Fig. 5 ). Conversely, sites whose AR_d  trends maximized during warmer drier periods (enhanced summer diel air–water signal coupling) tended to have the highest stream thermal sensitivities throughout the watershed per degree of air temperature rise (stream temperature response; Fig. 5  x-axis). The relationship between AR_d  trends over the observational period and stream thermal sensitivity was comparable for both Shenandoah and Neversink sites because the range in magnitude of the regression slopes were similar. However, Shenandoah sites displayed a more muted stream temperature response to rising air temperatures. This is evidenced by lower AR_d  values at Shenandoah for their respective connectivity type (i.e., high vs. minimal groundwater influence) when compared to similar Neversink locations (Fig. 4 ) and by lower smaller stream thermal sensitivities (Fig. 5 , x-axis). Within the Shenandoah observations, sites previously characterized as having high groundwater influence showed a more significant decrease in AR_d  over the observational period, reaching their minima during warmer drier periods (i.e., represented by large positive leading regression coefficients). Conversely, Shenandoah sites previously demonstrated to have minimal groundwater influence generally had a contrasting response, with AR_d  trends that reached their maxima between June and August, suggesting a higher degree of coupling between water and air temperatures during summer months (Fig. 4 ). Trends in calculated paired air and stream water temperature metrics clustered by watershed position across our analyses. Specifically, tributary sites demonstrated lower thermal sensitivities when compared to valley sites (Fig. 5 ) and experienced decreasing trends in AR_d  that generally reached their minima between June and August (Fig. 4 , Fig. 6  a). Tributary sites also tended to show small increases in PL_d  (i.e., larger circles, Fig. 6 a), indicating a larger temporal offset between peak stream and air temperature over summer months. Valley stream sites generally showed air–water coupling patterns opposite those observed in tributary settings, as sites along the West Branch, East Branch, and main stem of the Neversink River had AR_d  trends that maximized between June and August (i.e., reddish circles, less local groundwater influence during warmer drier months; Fig. 6 ), and PL_d  trends that minimized over the over the same period (i.e., smaller circles, less temporal offset between peak air and stream temperatures; Fig. 6 ). Unlike the non-linear trends observed in AR_d  and PL_d  metrics, MR_d  exhibited linear behavior from spring to fall that reset over the winter and into the start of spring (Fig. 7  b-c). Specifically, MR_d  slowly increased throughout the observational period for all sites, with high variance during the spring months when daily mean water and air temperatures were similar (Fig. 7 a-b). We interpret these linear trends as seasonal warming of shallow soils and groundwater due to heat accumulation in hillslopes during sustained periods of higher net radiation. Tributary sites consistently demonstrated lower MR_d  values across the year but had the highest rates of increase in MR_d  trends representing a larger gap between diel water and air temperature signal means early in the season that decreases throughout the year despite similar trends in daily mean air temperatures (Fig. 7 c-e). Higher rates of warming at tributary sites likely reflect a larger fraction of shallow groundwater contributing to their streamflow when compared to main-stem valley settings. Daily mean streamflow time-series from selected streamgages reflect differences in hydroclimatic conditions between the two water years considered (Fig. 8  b, c). Specifically, a wet summer in water year 2021 (Fig. 8 b) and a dry summer in water year 2022 (Fig. 8 c). Hydrographs as well as separated base flow and calculated BFI values binned by month (Fig. 8 a) capture general precipitation discharge relationships across the Neversink River watershed. Specifically, spring snowmelt leads to a relatively drier period, followed by an increase in precipitation driven by midlatitude storms and tropical moisture in the late summer and fall (Fig. 8 a–c; Towey et al., 2018 ). Over the summer months, statistically significant differences were observed between tributary and main-stem sites for AR_d , PL_d , and MR_d  metrics (Fig. 7 d, e). Kruskal-Wallis tests produced significant (p < 0.01) test statistics indicating non-equal sample medians for daily metrics binned by month of the year. Statistically significant differences were primarily identified from May through September, further supporting observed relationships between derived regression coefficients and stream thermal sensitivities (Fig. 5 , Fig. 8 d–e). AR_d  at tributary and main-stem sites tended to be most similar during spring months, before diverging both in value and variance (Fig. 8 d). Similar to calculated AR_d , MR_d  showed similar sample medians during the spring snowmelt period that became significantly different during periods of higher net radiation, as MR_d  at tributary sites remained low indicating daily mean water temperature signal amplitudes that differed significantly from those of ambient air. During the spring, variance in MR_d  was high across both tributary and main-stem sample populations, which decreased from May through October. Across all metrics, significant differences in sample medians between May and September coincides with results from AR_d  and PL_d  metric regressions used to describe seasonal non-linearity, where respective minima and maxima were generally reached during summer months (Fig. 4 , Fig. 6 ). Spearman's correlation tests were run for all sites comparing AR_d  and daily separated BFI and daily mean discharge (Fig. 8 f-g) because AR_d  values were shown in conceptual heat budget models and comparisons to traditional stream thermal sensitivities to be sensitive to groundwater induced air–water decoupling. At tributary sites, BFI was inversely correlated (p < 0.01) with AR_d  and positively correlated with daily mean streamflow (Fig. 8 f), as lower AR_d  values indicate increased groundwater influence (22 of 28 sites). Conversely, at valley stream locations, few significant correlations were found between AR_d  and BFI (Fig. 8 g). However, changes in AR_d  were inversely correlated with daily mean streamflow, indicating stronger diel air–water signal coupling at the lowest flows, as would be expected in the absence of substantial local groundwater inflow (Fig. 8 g). Results from Spearman's correlation tests for main-stem sites show that higher AR_d  values occur at times of lower streamflow in non-tributary settings. This is consistent with the conceptual understanding of stream thermal regimes typically being more coupled to air temperature during periods of high solar forcings and lower streamflow volume, in the absence of local groundwater inflows.   5 Discussion Although air temperature is not the primary driver of stream temperature (e.g., Sinokrot and Stefan, 1993; Webb and Nobilis, 1997 ), observations of local streambank air temperature can provide a useful benchmark for assessing stream response to radiative forcing across headwater networks (Johnson, 2003; Arismendi et al., 2014 ). Coupling between air and water temperature is influenced in part by stream connectivity to runoff and subsurface hillslope flowpaths that vary across space and time (e.g., Shanley and Peters, 1988; Kobayashi et al., 1999 ; Covino et al., 2017). Localized groundwater connectivity affects a range of critical stream ecological processes from low-flow persistence and channel connectivity to daily temperature regimes during cold and warm periods (Briggs et al., 2022b ). This renders easy to collect local stream and air temperature time-series data valuable for characterizing sections throughout headwater stream networks that are more and less hydrologically connected to the landscape. Normalizing stream water temperature signals by local air temperature signals enables comparisons of diel signal metrics across altitude, shading influence, and even ecoregion (e.g., Hare et al., 2021 ). In this study, we demonstrate the utility of pairing diel air–water temperature signals for tracking dynamic changes in how terrestrial hillslopes contribute to low-order streamflow generation. We identify seasonal shifts in stream-hillslope connectivity, specifically stream segments lower in the network with daily heating and cooling cycles that appear dominated by stream water volume (i.e., thermal inertia), as would be expected in the absence of prominent lateral hillslope inflows comprising a substantial fraction of stream discharge. Here we show that the diel air–water temperature metrics developed in this study (AR_d , PL_d , and MR_d ) translate directly to long-known and important niche thermal habitat characteristics such as buffered, lagged, and cooled/warmed. Consequently, this novel study demonstrates both the utility of diel metrics for identifying high-resolution spatiotemporal patterns in stream-hillslope connectivity, and provides immediately transferrable metrics for the characterization of heterogeneous cold-water stream habitat patches at management-relevant scales (e.g., Sullivan et al., 2021; Mejia et al., 2023 ). Decoupling of air and water temperature sinusoids have been used to quantify in-stream groundwater influence on annual timescales (Briggs et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2020; Hare et al., 2021; Hare et al., 2023 ); however, the sensitivity of diel temperature signals to transient contributions from hillslope inflows has remained unexplored. Previous headwater stream temperature research has indicated daily mean air and stream temperatures are most synchronized over the summer season (Letcher et al., 2016 ). However, mean daily stream temperatures mask subdaily dynamics that are important to a wide range of biotic stream processes and the viability of niche cold water habitats. Our investigation of diel air–water signals metrics showed clear divergent behavior as lower valley sites had the greatest coupling in summer, yet tributary sites were most coupled in spring and later fall and least coupled during summer low flows when baseflow dominates streamflow generation (i.e. Fig. 8  f-g). Our interpretation of observed trends in diel air–water signal relations were partially informed by numerical stream heat budget models that demonstrated the sensitivity of diel air–water temperature metrics to groundwater inflow fraction, open and closed tree canopy, and thermal equilibration with distance in the absence of additional groundwater contributions. The conceptual model results show that based on daily mean water:air temperature ratios (i.e., MR_d ), and the amplitude of daily water temperature fluctuations relative to air (i.e., AR_d ), air and stream temperature signals become increasingly decoupled in predictable trajectories as the fraction of modeled groundwater inflow increases (Fig. 3 a,c). Specifically, increasing groundwater inflow fraction (from 0 to 50 % total streamflow increase) notably reduces both MR_d  and AR_d  under spring and summer conditions at the 1-km reach scale, confirming the expected sensitivity of the observed diel air–water temperature data to local groundwater connectivity. Important to the development of diel air–water temperature metrics as tracers of hydrologic processes, changes in average reach shading from 95 % (heavy canopy) to 55 % (partial canopy) imposed minimal additional change on MR_d  and AR_d  at the 1-km downstream transport scale. The large effect of lateral advection via groundwater inflows versus canopy shading indicate that groundwater contribution to streamflow is a dominant control on our observed air–water coupling patterns. However, the ‘Spring Run’ models scenarios show that MR_d  and AR_d  begin to rapidly equilibrate (within a few kilometers) with ambient air during downstream transport and that this signal attenuation is strongly impacted by riparian shading, even when starting with a pure groundwater temperature signal at the stream origination point (Fig. 3 d-e). These simulated results suggest that observed spatial changes in air–water metrics throughout the Neversink Reservoir watershed are likely driven by shifts in local (few kilometers) hillslope groundwater connectivity. The thermal impact of local connectivity is further supported by significant positive correlations with base flow in tributary streams, and inverse correlations with valley streams (Fig. 8 f). Specifically, in the absence of local connectivity, conceptual model scenarios show that MR_d  and AR_d  trend toward strong coupling with air in August (i.e., ratios at or near 1) as streamflow is low during the summer months and solar input to the stream corridor is maximized. At our mountain watershed study sites across the Neversink Reservoir watershed and Shenandoah National Park, observed seasonal patterns in daily air–water decoupling (i.e., AR_d , PL_d ) were nonlinear, indicating a shift in hillslope source water dominance (Fig. 4 , Fig. 5 , Fig. 6 a-b). Specifically, sites whose AR_d  decreased (i.e., greater decoupling between air–water temperature amplitudes) from higher springtime values to low summertime values were interpreted to have a high fraction of local groundwater inflow contributing to total stream volume. This indicates that when AR_d  values are low, we are seeing the enhanced  net influence of local groundwater connectivity on small stream thermodynamics despite this period having the lowest flows and highest radiative forcing. While net radiation is widely recognized as one of the prominent drivers of stream thermal budgets (Beschta, 1997; Rutherford et al., 2004; Isaak et al., 2020 ), the dominance of cold advective inputs from groundwater contributions has also been widely observed in similar low-order mountain catchments (e.g., Lisi et al., 2015; Isaak et al., 2018; Cline et al., 2020; Roesky and Hayashi, 2022 ), driving unexpected stream temperature dynamics at the reach scale during the lowest flows (e.g., Moore et al., 2023 ). In the absence of advective local groundwater discharge, even heavily forested tributaries would be expected to have water temperature patterns dominated by net radiation during summer months (e.g., Wondzell et al., 2019 ), as the presence of dense forest canopy should limit nighttime longwave radiative losses back to the atmosphere while simultaneously depressing turbulent fluxes (Dugdale et al., 2018; Swartz et al., 2020; Leach and Moore, 2019 ). Local stream network sections of air–water decoupling (using metrics other than diel signals) have been widely observed in spatially distributed studies of stream temperature (e.g. Hilderbrand et al., 2014; Lisi et al., 2015; Wissler et al., 2022; Leathers et al., 2023 ), and have been attributed to a suite of physical and ecological drivers in riparian areas, including focused groundwater discharge (e.g., Kelleher et al., 2012; Luce et al., 2014; Isaak et al., 2016; Hitt et al., 2023 ). Decoupling driven by local groundwater discharge dynamics is important to identify across space and time, as it has been cited as a source of uncertainty in low-order headwater streams for spatially explicit stream temperature models that rely on empirical relationships between air and water temperature (Luce et al., 2014; Isaak et al., 2017; Leach and Moore, 2019 ). Recent efforts to reconcile the impacts of groundwater in spatially explicit stream temperature models have leveraged paired air–water temperature methods on annual timescales, attempting to reduce error in groundwater dominated reaches (Barclay et al., 2023 ). Diel air–water temperature signal decoupling characteristics observed in tributary settings were not reflected in temperature signals at valley sites lower in the same network. Valley sites had AR_d  values maximize during summer months (i.e., non-linear increase, concave down pattern), and minimize during higher spring and late fall streamflows (i.e., non-linear increase, concave down patterns). This supported our inference that the stream thermal dynamics at valley stream sites are dominated by thermal inertia (channel water volume) and the lack of local, pronounced hillslope groundwater connectivity. Conclusions surrounding our physical interpretation of observed non-linearity in AR_d  were supported by: (a) modeled responses of diel air–water temperature metrics as a function of groundwater inflow (Fig. 4 a-c), (b) significant (p < 0.01) correlations with BFI values derived from streamflow that confirm network-scale transitions from runoff/quickflow to baseflow dominance (Fig. 8 a,f,g), (c) comparisons to linear stream thermal sensitivity metrics that have been extensively used to indicate areas of strong groundwater influence (Fig. 5 ; Kelleher et al., 2012; Lisi et al., 2015; Hitt et al., 2023 ), and (d) concurrent observed patterns in two well characterized Shenandoah National Park streams that represent runoff/quickflow versus groundwater dominance end-members across that park (Fig. 5 ; Johnson et al., 2017; Briggs et al., 2022b ). Seasonality in stream-hillslope connectivity that we suggest is driving our two general classes of non-linear trends in AR_d  has been routinely documented in previous studies of headwater streamflow generation. Specifically, previous work has documented shifts towards deeper hillslope contributions to streamflow, or even complete hydrologic disconnection between hillslopes and streams during periods of higher energy and lower water availability (Jencso et al., 2010; Pacific et al., 2010; Blume and van Meerveld, 2015; Covino, 2017 ). While AR_d  provided a direct measure of air–water decoupling induced by local groundwater contributions to streamflow, interpretations of PL_d  trends are less clear. Specifically, conceptual heat budget scenarios showed that adding groundwater at a constant temperature to modeled stream reaches had minimal impacts on PL_d , failing to produce > 1 hr offsets in daily sinusoid phases that were observed across numerous stream sites. (Fig. 3 b, Fig. 4 , Fig. 6 ). Since these model results were produced using constant temperature groundwater inflows, observed signal phase lags may be driven by lagged diel signals in shallow groundwater that are transferred to tributary stream sites via strong local groundwater connectivity, a phenomenon not captured by model scenarios. On annual timescales, phase lags provide a characteristic signal indicative of shallow groundwater contributions, as heating of hillslope aquifers creates shallow groundwater temperatures that are shifted forward in time and are ultimately conveyed to streams with increased contributions from shallow groundwater flowpaths (Briggs et al., 2018; Hare et al., 2021 ). The presence of shifts in phase within shallow hillslope aquifers on daily timescales, and whether these signals are translated to streams in areas of local groundwater inflows, remains unclear. In this study we lacked a meaningful number of temperature observations from groundwater hillslope seeps, having data from only one location showing measurable diel signals. Although the diel signal phase at that seep was lagged several hours from local air in summer, the signal amplitude was highly muted. When these diel signals phases were used in model boundary conditions for groundwater inflow temperatures, the net effect on modeled stream diel temperature signals was not profound, though modeled phase lags were enhanced compared to those of the constant temperature groundwater inflow models ('diel’ case Fig. 3 b). Larger diel groundwater temperature variations would likely need to be included in the heat budget models to recreate the nonlinear trends observed in PL_d  metrics, and more widespread monitoring of shallow hillslope groundwater in coarse colluvium is a target of ongoing field data collection. Whatever the controlling mechanism, we did observe characteristic patterns in PL_d  trends across both tributary and valley stream sites that were related to network position, with PL_d  often showing non-linear seasonal trends that were inversely related to AR_d  values (Fig. 4 ). Seasonal patterns in PL_d  at valley sites minimized in summer, agreeing with our physical interpretation of AR_d , in that the thermodynamics of daily stream signals in valley stream settings are dominated by water volume (thermal inertia) as higher AR_d  and lower PL_d  in summer indicate stronger air–water coupling (Fig. 4 ; Fig. 6 ). Additionally, tributary sites had increases in PL_d  during warmer drier months when AR_d  values minimize (Fig. 4 ; Fig. 6 ), which may be indicative of higher contributions from shallow groundwater flowpaths, as we speculate that diel signals exist in shallow hillslope aquifers given the presence of steep rocky hilllslopes (i.e., talus and moraine) with high thermal conductivity. However, demonstrating the sensitivity of observed in-stream trends in PL_d  to diel fluctuations in shallow hillslope aquifers would require more ubiquitous monitoring of temperature at emergent groundwater seepage locations, which is currently beyond the scope of this initial study. On annual timescales, the ratio between mean air and water temperature signals generally offer little insight into local groundwater dominance as the cooling of stream water during summer months is often offset by winter (Briggs et. al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2020 ) unless impacted by geothermal activity or anthropogenic manipulation via dam operation and power plant discharges. As a result, both streams primarily driven by atmospheric coupling and those dominated by advective groundwater inflows often have mean ratios close to 1 on annual timescales (i.e., similar annual air and water temperature sinusoid means), and deeper vs. shallow groundwater influence cannot be distinguished. However, results from this study indicate that on daily timescales, MR_d  values indicate runoff/quickflow vs. local groundwater influence, with higher, more stable values lower in the stream network where hillslope drainage is reduced compared to total channel water volume. Like AR_d  values, MR_d  values were most similar across sites during periods of high surface water inputs (Fig. 8 e). However, higher MR_d  values were indicative of main-stem sites that lacked local advective cooling during summer periods when solar inputs were high and discharge was low (e.g., low thermal thermal inertia). Outside of periods with high MR_d  variation likely driven by the dominance of runoff and very shallow near-surface flowpaths, MR_d  were persistently lower at sites whose thermal regimes were dominated by groundwater inflow from local hillslopes (tributary sites; Fig. 7 ; Fig. 8 e). However, a gradual rise in MR_d  was observed at all sites throughout the year for both tributary and valley streams (Fig. 7 c), with the rates of increase being slightly higher in tributary stream sites (Fig. 7 d-e). This gradual rise in MR_d  may be indicative of throughflow warming as a result of heat accumulation in terrestrial hillslopes and suggests local groundwater discharge zones may be sourced from groundwater flowpaths that are shallow enough to be sensitive to warming on seasonal timescales, as also indicated by analysis of annual temperature signals from these same sites (Briggs et al., 2022a ). The ability of shallow groundwater warming to affect stream temperature in local regions of high groundwater discharge has been discussed in physical stream heat budget models (Kurylyk et al., 2014; Leach and Moore, 2019 ), used to explain trends in stream temperature observations (Cline et al., 2020; Hare et al., 2021 ), addressed in proposed analytical solutions (Kurylyk et al., 2015; Gruszczyński et al., 2023 ), and considered in predicting long term ‘climate refugia’ (Briggs et al., 2018 ). Benz et al. (2024)  present evidence for shallow groundwater water warming at accelerated rates globally; however, warming effects on daily to seasonal timescales remain limited, particularly in stream temperature data (Cline et al., 2020 ; Gruszczyński et al., 2023 ). Additionally, the warming of shallow groundwater has also been thought to only be captured by process-based models of stream heat budgets, and has been suggested as a reason why empirical stream temperature relationships might underpredict stream temperature warming in mountain watersheds under a changing climate (Leach and Moore, 2019 ). Consequently, gradual warming trends observed in MR_d  might provide a way to qualitatively distinguish source flowpath depth using diel air–water signal relations and improve cold water habitat forecasts. By utilizing coupled diel air–water signals, we were able to identify areas of local groundwater influence at the network scale and discern periods when these stream segments were dominated by runoff/quickflow as opposed to more sustained hillslope groundwater contributions (Fig. 9  ). Specifically, homogeneous air–water coupling across the network observed in spring and fall coincides with periods of higher precipitation and lower BFI due to spring snowmelt and mid-latitude storm patterns that peak between late-August and October (Fig. 8 a-b; Fig. 9 ; Thaler, 1996; Towey et al., 2018 ). Several years of seasonal field work in the Neversink Reservoir watershed by the authors of this study have yielded consistent observations of generally saturated hillslope conditions in early spring generating saturation overland flow and numerous seeps that dry substantially by early summer (Terry et al., 2023 ). Recent enhancements to the West Branch (01434498) and main-stem (01435000) streamgages have provided several years of shallow hillslope and riparian zone piezometer data designed to monitor local groundwater discharge exchange dynamics as described by Briggs et al., (2022a) . Time-series modeling of seasonal shallow groundwater seepage rates at the West Branch sites (McAliley et al., 2022 ) showed a clear transition from circumneutral seepage in summer to enhanced seepage starting in the fall when wet weather returned and transpiration decreased upslope where flowpaths are constrained by very shallow bedrock (<1 m depth). These observations support our hydrologic interpretation of a transition to deeper hillslope flowpaths contributing to streamflow generation during warmer drier periods. Specifically, drier periods with high fractional groundwater contributions to streamflow (i.e., higher BFI) elucidated stream reaches where local groundwater contributions were focused and sustained. This was in direct contrast to observations lower in the network (valley streams) distal to preferential groundwater inflows, as these locations had increased air–water coupling despite valley streamflow being comprised of network cumulated groundwater (Fig. 9 ). In contrast, tributary stream settings that were closer to groundwater discharge origination points had thermal regimes dominated by advective contributions from local hillslopes, driving non-intuitive decoupling of air–water temperature signals in summer.  6 Conclusion Here we demonstrate that diel air–water temperature signal metrics contain a wealth of information related to localized stream-hillslope connectivity as expressed through clear spatiotemporal dynamics that diverge between smaller tributaries and large valley streams in the same watershed. Analysis of diel air–water signal coupling enables the efficient identification of stream reaches with significant local runoff vs groundwater influence, and the ability to track the net influence of groundwater contribution to stream thermal regimes on daily to seasonal timescales. We utilized high-resolution observations of locally paired air–water temperature data whose interpretation was partially informed by site-based numerical models to extend previous air–water temperature metric methodology from annual to daily temperature sinusoids. This novel approach highlighted spatiotemporal differences in hillslope flowpath contributions to low-order streamflow generation across the main channels and tributaries of a headwater stream network. In-stream thermal responses to dynamic changes in stream hillslope connectivity, such as those observed here, may help provide metrics sensitive to groundwater discharge. Stream temperature metrics sensitive to groundwater discharge are often missing as covariates for statistical models of critical stream ecological processes such as empirical air and stream water temperature regressions. Consequently, spatially explicit models of stream temperature often lack the requisite spatial patchiness or finer scale temporal dynamics required for predicting the response of headwater stream thermal refugia to a changing climate. The utilization of local air temperature signals to standardize water temperature observations will allow for this type of diel temperature signal comparison across a range of settings and scales. Consequently, the collection of local stream and air temperature time-series data may provide a relatively easy way to qualitatively assess spatiotemporal trends in landscape hydrologic connectivity throughout headwater stream networks, where a paucity of data has led to divergent conclusions on what drives energy and material fluxes in these settings.

1 Introduction Accurate streamflow prediction plays a crucial role in sustainable water resource management, flood early warning, and decision-making in irrigated agriculture, among others (Tang et al., 2023 ). However, according to World Bank statistics, river monitoring networks in 78 % of low- and middle-income countries and 86 % of least developed countries fall short of meeting current needs (Tang et al., 2023 ). Moreover, policy restrictions prevent the public availability of streamflow observations in certain areas (Feng et al., 2021 ), posing a significant challenge to achieving accurate prediction of streamflow in ungauged catchments. Thus, in 2003, the International Association of Hydrological Sciences initiated the prediction in ungauged basin (PUB) 10-year program (Sivapalan et al., 2003 ). Despite the progress achieved in this program and after the PUB Decade, the prediction of streamflow in ungauged catchments continues to be an elusive challenge in the field of hydrologic science and engineering (Guo et al., 2021; Hrachowitz et al., 2013; Prieto et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2023 ). Meeting this challenge largely depends on the ability to successfully extrapolate hydrological information from gauged to ungauged catchments, a process often referred to as “regionalization” in hydrologic literature (Kratzert et al., 2019b; Prieto et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2023 ). Traditional regionalization studies commonly use physical or conceptual models based on hydrological processes. The main methods for regionalization include spatial proximity-based, physical similarity-based, and regression-based methods (Yang et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2021; Xu, 2021; Qi et al., 2022 ). Nevertheless, spatial proximity-based approaches are not suitable for regions characterized by intricate spatial variations (Ali et al., 2012; Reichl et al., 2009 ). On the other hand, physical similarity-based techniques heavily depend on the precision of similarity metrics (Oudin et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2021 ), while regression-based methodologies run the risk of disregarding the correlation between model parameters and encountering multicollinearity issues (Kokkonen et al., 2003; Kuczera and Mroczkowski, 1998; McIntyre et al., 2005 ). Recently, Cluster-based regionalization methods have gained attention due to their ability to consider hydrological similarity and the challenges in classifying catchments without detailed analysis (Agarwal et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2021; Papageorgaki and Nalbantis, 2016 ). In recent years, there has been a widespread utilization of deep learning (machine learning)-based data-driven models in hydrological runoff prediction studies (Mohammadi, 2021 ). Among them, the long short-term memory neural network (LSTM) model usually has higher prediction accuracy compared to traditional hydrological models and artificial neural network models (Gao et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020 ). Kratzert et al. (2018, 2019a, 2019b)  were pioneers in applying the LSTM to regionalized modeling and substantiated its efficacy in achieving performance levels close to individually calibrated LSTM models, which have opened up new avenues and directions through use of data-driven models for runoff prediction in ungauged catchments. Subsequently, an increasing number of scholars have embarked on studying regionalized modeling based on deep learning methodologies. Data-driven models such as LSTM (Arsenault et al., 2023; Choi et al., 2022; Feng et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023 ; Nogueira et al., 2022; Rasheed et al., 2022; Won et al., 2023 ), LSTM-Variants (Tang et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022 ), and Transformer (Yin et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2023 ), etc., have been employed in these studies. Despite the differences in methodologies, regions, and ideas among these studies, the final results consistently indicate that deep learning-based regionalization modeling methods (LSTM, LSTM-Variants, and Transformer, etc.), outperform traditional hydrological models, and exhibit significant potential in predicting streamflow in ungauged catchments.
