Noticeably, considering that the WWI  is defined based on the relationship between the evaporative energy and water amount of the certain climate type which the TP belongs to, the WWI  now is applicable for the TP and other regions with same climate type.  2.3 Wet and dry zones Governed by large terrain structure and complex atmospheric circulation, different combinations of heat and moisture conditions are formed over the TP. According to annual aridity index and annual precipitation, various climate subregions are defined over the TP to better study climate change in different climate environments (Zheng, 1996 ). Considering the humid/semi-humid region is the transition region, so we merge it into the humid region and here adopt four subregions (arid region, semi-arid region, semi-humid region, and humid region) in this study (Fig. 1 ). By the way, the threshold indicators of wet and dry regions over the TP have been given as well (Table 1  ).  2.4 Linear regression In this study, trend characteristics of temperature, precipitation, and WWI are evaluated by one-dimensional linear regression equation, which is a robust trend estimator used widely:(6) y i  = a + b x i       where i  is the time step while a  and b  are regression constant and linear regression coefficient. During the calculation process, x  is the annual time series (1961–2020) and y  is the specific climate variable such as temperature and precipitation, further, the significance is determined by a T -test (Student, 1908 ). To explore distributions of different climate variables as independent data to WWI as an examined dependent variable, multiple linear regression model is used in the study, which can be expressed as:(7) y = β 0  + β 1  x 1  + β 2  x 2  + ⋯ + β k  x k  + ε      where y  is the dependent variable, x 1   , x 2   , …, x k    are the independent variables such as temperature and precipitation, β 1   , β 2   , …, β k    are regression coefficient estimated by least-squares methods, ε     represents the error term. Further, several statistical parameters such as the lowest mean square error root (RMSE) and the goodness of fit (R2 ) of the regression line are applied to evaluate the accuracy and reliability of multiple linear regression model. According to the assumptions of the regression model, the multiple regression equation in the study is shown as follow:(8) E W W I   = β 0  + β 1  ∗ T + β 2  ∗ P + β 3  ∗ L H + β 4  ∗ S H        3 Results 3.1 Temperature, precipitation, and surface heat flux changes over the TP We observed an evident northwest-southeast gradient in annual mean temperature, increasing from nearly –8°C in the northwestern part to approximately 10°C in the southeast of the TP (Fig. 2  a ). The annual average precipitation varies from 100 to 800 mm in most regions, with relatively high values in the southeastern part of the TP (Fig. 2 b ). In other words, the heat and moisture conditions decrease sequentially from the humid region to the arid region. In recent decades, corresponding to the context of global warming, the annual mean temperature over the TP has shown significantly increasing trends throughout the whole region at rates of 0.2–0.5 °C per decade during 1961–2020, especially in the arid region and semi-arid region (Fig. 2 c ). Qaidam Basin, for instance, has shown a warming rate of nearly 0.53°C per decade at average during 1961–2010, which is revealed by previous study (Wang et al., 2014 ). By comparison, the variations of annual mean precipitation are more complex with a maximum increasing trend of about 10 % per decade in the eastern semi-arid region and decreasing trends in the humid region (Fig. 2 d ). Due to the huge span, upward and downward trends are both detected in the arid region and semi-arid region. Nevertheless, semi-humid region has obviously experienced increase of precipitation and humid region has already significantly dried out. Given the above, the warming trends are overall observed among four subregions, however, the wetting trends are varied from regions to regions. Noticeably, the northeastern TP belonging to the arid region and semi-arid region has become the key zone of wetting. Further, as the primary source of the thermal forcing, the distribution and variation of surface LH and SH over the TP during 1961–2020 have been investigated in this study. In recent years, station observations, reanalysis data, satellite remote sensing data, and other sources have been widely used to study the thermal fluxes over the TP. However, there are significant variations in the quality of different data sources (Wang et al., 2012; Duan et al., 2014 ). Therefore, the applicability of thermal fluxes from ERA5 have been evaluated before calculating the long-term trends. Since the observations are station-based, we first spatially interpolated ERA5 to obtain the LH and SH at each corresponding station based on bilinear interpolation. Spatially, ERA5 shows high correlations with observations, especially LH with mean correlation of 0.52 (Fig. 3  a ). Noticeably, although the mean correlation coefficient of SH is only 0.22, ERA5 still performs better compared to other reanalysis data such as JRA55 (Mean correlation: 0.15), NCEP2 (Mean correlation: 0.14), and MERRY2 (Mean correlation: 0.27) (Figures abbreviate). Temporally, LH derived from ERA5 exhibits a significantly high correlation with observations over the TP, with the annual mean correlation of 0.87, indicates that ERA5 can effectively capture the interannual variations of LH over the TP. Regarding SH, with annual mean correlation coefficients of 0.50, ERA5 also performs well, especially during summer (Fig. 3 b ). Finally, ERA5 can generally capture the annual cycle of LH and SH over the TP as well. The discrepancy between ERA5 and observations for LH and SH is within 12.5 to 29.9 and -21.9 to -10.5 W·m-2  (Fig. 3 c ). After the above three comparisons, we can conclude that ERA5 can accurately present the annual variation characteristics and spatio-temporal change of SH and LH over the TP. Therefore, we use ERA5 data to analyze the spatio-temporal characteristics of SH and LH over the TP and calculate the defined WWI during 1961-2020 in subsequent study. Similar to the pattern of temperature and precipitation (Fig. 2 a, b ), an increasing northwest-southeast gradient of LH has been revealed, showing its importance to climate change (Fig. 2 e ). Statistically, the annual LH of the semi-arid region, semi-humid region, and humid region exceed 25 W·m-2 , and the highest values are recorded for the Hengduan Mountains and the Yarlung Tsangpo River Basin. However, greater regional diversity of SH over the TP is shown based on the analysis. With higher elevation, the southwestern part of the semi-arid region exhibits values of SH of more than 50 W·m-2 , but values of the semi-humid region and humid region are generally less than 20 W·m-2  (Fig. 2 f ). Corresponding to rapidly changing climate over the TP, we then detect the linear trends and significance of LH and SH from 1961 to 2020. LH has shown a significantly increasing trend in the humid region with a rate of more than 1 W·m-2  per decade but has decreased in other areas, especially in the semi-arid region (Fig. 2 g ). On the contrary, a significantly increasing trend in SH has been detected in the semi-arid region, while other regions have experienced a weak decline in SH (Fig. 2 h ), which is basically consistent with previous study (Wang et al., 2022 ). Despite some uncertainties, the above trends can be explained by the changing wind speed and ground-air temperature difference (Han et al., 2017 ). Temporally, the overall region of the TP has experienced significant warming-wetting during the period 1961–2020 (Fig. 4  ). The regional trends for annual mean surface temperature and precipitation are 0.34°C per decade (significant at the 99% level) and 0.7% per decade (significant at the 90% level), respectively. Despite large spatial heterogeneity mentioned previously, both LH and SH have overall increased from 1961 to 2020 with rates of 0.08 and 0.19 W·m-2  per decade (significant at the 95% level). However, apart from temperature, pronounced fluctuations can be found in the series of other climate variables. From the perspective of different regions, it is worth noting that the arid region has shown warming-wetting trends but the humid region has exhibited a warming-drying trend (Table 2  ), reflecting the internal regulation of “Asian water tower”. In addition, semi-arid region and semi-humid region both have experienced increase of annual temperature and precipitation, which is consistent with the overall changes of the TP. Correspondingly, the upward trends of LH and SH have been detected in most of regions. In general, the alpine climate of the TP is expected to change partly, causing a better ecological environment (Shen et al., 2015; Xia et al., 2021 ).  3.2 Comprehensive WWI changes over the TP Combining annual temperature, precipitation, and surface heat flux, WWI shows a similar northwest-southeast gradient (Fig. S1  ), which reveals the spatial pattern of moisture and heat conditions over the TP and reflects the rationality of the index. Correspondingly, the net primary production and species abundance of ecosystem over the TP increase from northwest to southeast (Liu et al., 2018 ). To better understand the variations of WWI during the study period, the trends at different decadal levels are presented in the following as well (Table 3  ). Persistent increase of WWI can be discovered over the entire TP from 1970s to 1980s with the rates of 1.49 and 2.13 per decade, especially over the humid region and semi-humid region (Fig. S1 a-c ). In the following two decades, arid region has experienced noticeable increase of WWI while humid region has experienced persistent decrease, although the whole TP has become warmer and wetter (Fig. S1 d, e ). Noticeably, in the latest decade, WWI over the TP has decreased with the rate of 0.81 per decade (Table 3 ), corresponding to the decrease of precipitation over the TP during 2010s (Fig. 4 b ). To summarize, despite the significant interdecadal variations, the humid region of the TP, with relatively high annual temperature and precipitation in climatology, has shown a significantly downward trend of WWI during 1961–2020. Conversely, the WWI in the semi-humid and eastern semi-arid region have increased significantly, which is almost consistent with the trend of precipitation. As a whole, considering the context of the TP warming, the increasing trend of WWI is more dependent on the enhancement of precipitation. For better visualization of changes, the regional annual anomalies series for WWI during the period in different climate zones are given (Fig. 5  ). Temporally, based on the 5-year moving average method, the variations of WWI over four subregions of the TP all show interdecadal fluctuation, indicating non-consistent changes of climate conditions over the TP during 1961–2020. Interestingly, the humid region with large precipitation has experienced decrease in WWI, with a significant rate of -0.21 per decade (Fig. 5 ). Conversely, arid region (0.30 per decade), semi-arid region (0.29 per decade), and semi-humid region (0.99 per decade), which possess relatively poor moisture conditions, have witnessed a significant upward WWI. In summary, the so-called “warming-wetting trends” is most pronounced in the relatively drier regions, and the “warming-drying trends” is true in the relatively wetter regions, which is similar to Northwest China (Zhang et al., 2021 ). Further, considering the obvious asymmetry of temperature and precipitation in different seasons which leads to closer association between phenology and season (Zhu & Yang, 2020 ), annual and seasonal changes of WWI are demonstrated to better understand the climate change over the TP (Fig. 6  ). Significant increasing trends have been shown in four seasons during the period, especially winter with a rate of 3.47 per decade. Moreover, with a significant increasing trend of 1.11 per decade during 1961–2020, spring has experienced significant warming-wetting as well. In contrast, the upward trends are relatively gently with rates of 0.41 and 0.64 per decade in summer and autumn. In addition, seasonal trends of different regions are provided as well (Table 4  ). The entire TP including four subregions has become warmer and wetter during spring and the increasing rate of the humid region even exceeds the arid region and semi-arid region (Fig. S2  ). However, when it comes to summer, the warming-wetting trends of the entire TP has weakened, and even declined in the humid region with a rate of -0.36 per decade of WWI (Fig. 7  ). Although precipitation over the TP is concentrated in summer, the increase of WWI in summer is the least significant. Similar to summer, the changing trends during autumn are relatively mild (Fig. S3  ). By comparison, winter has made a great contribution (Fig. 8  ). The increasing rates of the arid region, semi-arid region, and semi-humid region have reached 5.55, 3.25, and 8.78 per decade, which even exceed the total of the other three seasons. Despite the significantly increasing trends over other regions, humid region still has experienced a decline in WWI. In general, the WWI over the humid region has constantly decreased except in spring. Considering all these facts, we may reasonably conclude that winter, on the whole, is the most significant season for warming and wetting over the TP while summer is the least significant season. Correspondingly, due to a commonly accepted notion that little biological activity during winter, which is widely known as the “dormant season”, ecological research over the TP is consequently lack of attention (Campbell et al., 2005 ). However, recent research has proved that winter is would be a key period for ecological processes, highlighting the importance of focusing on ecological changes during winter over the TP, particularly under the background of warming and wetting. Finally, we explore the contributions of temperature, precipitation, and surface heat flux to WWI under various climate conditions based on multiple linear regression methods (Table 5  ). From the perspective of the entire TP, the regression coefficient of precipitation reaches 0.76, while the coefficients of temperature, latent heat flux, and sensible heat flux are 0.43, 0.40, and 0.45, respectively. Therefore, during the process of warming and wetting over the TP, the increase in precipitation contributes the most, while the contributions of other climate variables are relatively small and the difference between them is not significant. Interestingly, the increase in temperature is more important in the relatively dry regions but almost ineffective in the relatively wet regions, where the regression coefficients are only 0.16 and 0.14. Despite the indisputable importance in the four subregions, precipitation do contribute more in the arid region and semi-arid region with the regression coefficients of 0.65 and 0.89, which decrease in the semi-humid region and humid region. This difference also applies to SH. Nevertheless, the contributions of LH are similar in the different regions. In a word, the “warming-wetting trends” in the arid region and the “warming and drying trends” in the humid region over the TP is proposed (Fig. 9  ), which is mostly accounted by the variation in precipitation. Temperature can contribute a lot in the arid region but less in the humid region, while surface heat flux plays an important role in the humid region.   4 Discussion According to the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, the saturation water vapor pressure in the atmosphere is a function of air temperature and increases at a rate of 6–7% per degree of surface warming. Based on this, Held and Soden (2006)  proposed a theory of “dry gets drier, wet gets wetter” assuming that the lower-tropospheric relative humidity is unchanged and that the flow is unchanged. Compared to more uncertainty over land (Greve et al., 2014 ), this paradigm better describes the pattern of precipitation changes over the oceans (Allan et al., 2010 ). Notably, the paradigm is also conditioned by choice of different metrics and datasets used (Xiong et al., 2022 ). In general, however, this paradigm has been a widely accepted consequence of the hydrological cycle over land (Hu et al., 2019 ). In contrast, with the interesting “warming-wetting trends”, the TP has shown an opposite pattern in recent decades, which has become a complex scientific matter in the field of climate change. From the perspective of the driving mechanisms, the accelerated regional water circulation and increased water vapor transport are the main reasons for the wetting TP (Tang et al., 2020 ). On the one hand, the climate warming leads to an increase in evapotranspiration and atmospheric water storage over the TP. The precipitation recirculation rate increases with temperature, and the contribution of evapotranspiration to precipitation within the TP increases, providing more water vapor for the TP (Guo & Wang, 2014 ). On the other hand, with the enhancement of the South Asian monsoon circulation, the westerlies shows signs of northward movement, enhancing the transportation of water vapor to the interior of the TP by the southerly flow, and increasing the control range of monsoon precipitation, which is conducive to the increase of precipitation over the TP (Gao et al., 2014 ). It can be seen that the increase of water vapor contribution from the South Asian monsoon control area and the TP locally account for the opposite pattern of “dry gets wetter”. In addition, it has been pointed out that the TP will further become wetter along with the reduction of anthropogenic aerosol emissions in the future (Jiang et al., 2023 ). Noticeably, hydrological processes such as precipitation, evaporation, and runoff, as well as the ecological processes of energy and matter exchange between surface and atmosphere need to be taken seriously over diverse underlying surfaces. In general, the current understanding of the mechanisms behind the warming-wetting trends over the TP is in its infancy, and further research on the climate system is needed to comprehensively reveal the mechanisms from the perspective of multi-disciplinary interactions such as atmosphere, hydrology and ecology. In fact, located in high-latitude and high-altitude area, the warming trend over the TP is at a relatively high level compared to the global, Northern Hemisphere and the same latitude regions means (Fig. S4 a ). Similarly, despite poor moisture conditions due to the vast distance from the sea, the TP has experienced significant wetting trend in recent decades compared to other regions around the world (Fig. S4 b ), which is consistent with the results of the literature (Jin et al., 2020; You et al., 2021a ). Considering the vulnerable ecological environment which is sensitive to global climate change, the local climate-land surface feedback caused by warming amplification may lead to more severe regional climate change in the future over the TP during the sustained warming process. Indeed, current climate change has already affected the phenology of the TP (Shen et al., 2015 ). The increase in nighttime temperature and the decrease in diurnal temperature range will affect the regional vegetation dynamics and even the ecosystem, as has been confirmed in studies on the effect of temperature change on vegetation in the Yellow River Basin (Yuan et al., 2020 ) and Northwest China (Du et al., 2019 ). As a sensitive area of global climate change, the observation and analysis of the regional climate system of the TP should be strengthened to better play its role as an indicator of climate change. In this study, the proposed WWI enables the integration of both heat and moisture conditions and thus is expected to aid the quantitative evaluation of the warming-wetting trends over the TP. However, some limitations of the index still exist, which may induce uncertainties. Firstly, the proposed WWI is mainly developed based on a warming-wetting TP, the temperature conversion to an equilibrium energy level of precipitation is not defined as a universe criterion globally. Instead, the relationship between the evaporative energy and water amount is defined according to the climate feature for certain types. That is, the index is not completely applicable for other regions. In addition, the quantification of degree of wetness mainly depends on the precipitation and heat flux parts in the proposed WWI, however, soil moisture is also an important factor to consider, which exerts a more directive effect on ecosystems, land use and management (Zeng et al., 2015 ). Considering that there are already a number of excellent indicators to evaluate climate change over the TP, the extension and enhancement of the proposed WWI will be addressed in our future work to provide an alternative way to characterize the warming-wetting trends. Despite the overall warming-wetting trends over the TP, the imbalance and inhomogeneous changes in dry and wet conditions pose challenges and opportunities to the ecological environment of the TP. On the one hand, with higher temperature and precipitation in most regions, the ecosystem over the TP has experienced great changes in the structure and function under the warming-wetting trends, which is generally beneficial to the improvement of vegetation conditions. For instance, spring vegetation phenology over the TP has advanced significantly and the tree line has also shifted upward with various amplitudes (Piao et al., 2019 ), which is also beneficial for agricultural production over the TP. In addition, it is revealed that the surface runoffs in most regions with the warming-wetting trends have shown a significant increasing trend in recent decades (Zhang et al., 2019a ), making the title of “Asian Water Tower” more authentic. However, it is worth mentioning that rapid lake and runoff expansions have improved water resources over the TP but also have exerted pronounced influences human living environment. In fact, with considerable expansion trends of lakes and runoffs, substantial numbers of settlements and road in eastern TP will be submerged within the next 20 years, and the flooding risk triggered by lake expansion will increase as well (Cheng et al., 2021 ). On the other hand, it is also confirmed that some regions over the TP have dried out in recent decades. Due to drought enhancement, vegetation degradation can be found in part of southern TP (Wang et al., 2021 ). At the same time, the water security of this region will face new problems and challenges. As a result, more attention should be paid to the TP due to the imbalance climate changes over different climate zones (Najafi & Alizadeh, 2023 ). Thus, effective measures are bound to be taken to grasp the opportunities of climate change in order to better play the important role of the TP as an ecological security barrier for China and even Asia based on the current understanding level of the warming-wetting trends over the TP. Further, timely adjusting and optimizing the layout of local agricultural industrial structure and improving the early warning and resilience to extreme weather and climate events are necessary, which can provide scientific decision-making basis for disaster prevention and enhance the ability to prevent ecological, human living and water resources security risks. Finally, due to accelerated transformation of ice and snow into liquid water, the Asia water tower is facing imbalance, while global warming will amplify this imbalance in further (Yao et al., 2022 ). Considering the importance of the TP to Asia and even the world, accurate future projection of the warming-wetting trends is essential to climate change research over the TP. However, the overall simulation ability of current climate models for climate over the TP is still insufficient, and there is a certain degree of cold bias in simulating temperature, while a significant overestimation in simulating precipitation (Zhu & Yang, 2020 ). The terrain and terrain of the TP are complex, with diverse underlying surfaces. In future research, regional climate models can compensate for the lack of accurate information on precipitation and temperature over the TP due to the scarcity of monitoring stations (Fu et al., 2021 ). In addition, due to inconsistent selection of baseline climate periods, there will be significant differences in the response to different warming thresholds of the TP. Therefore, considering the uncertainty caused by various factors such as data, models, scenarios, and methods in projection research, timely verification and correction of the results are essential. Despite the large uncertainty of the future of the Asia water tower, more work are needed to improve our understanding of future climate change over the TP under the background of intense climate change and water resource instabilities.  5 Conclusion With the aid of a set of descriptive indices, observed changes in heat and moisture conditions over the TP under global warming during 1961–2020 have been further explored. The main conclusions are as follows: From the perspective of trends, eastern arid region, eastern semi-arid region, and semi-humid region have experienced significantly increasing precipitation but western arid region, western semi-arid region, and humid region have become dry, while upward trends of temperature can be detected throughout the TP. Therefore, integrating temperature and precipitation, western semi-arid region and semi-humid region are regions with the most significant warming and wetting. On the other hand, as the primary source of the thermal forcing, LH and SH have experienced noticeable variations during the period, which show great spatial heterogeneity but overall increase with the rates of 0.08 and 0.19 W·m-2  per decade during the study period. In addition, revealed by comparative analysis of data during the period, the whole TP has experienced statistically significant warming since the 1960s with the linear rate of 0.34°C per decade in annual mean surface temperature, which is obviously higher than those in the region of the same latitude (0.24°C per decade), Northern Hemisphere (0.29°C per decade) and the global (0.23°C per decade). In addition, the linear rate of 0.7% per decade in annual precipitation has also exceeded region of the same latitude (-0.49% per decade), Northern Hemisphere (0.26% per decade) and the global (0.13% per decade) (Fig. S4  ). Defined mainly by the above variables, WWI has shown a persistent increase over the entire TP from 1960s to 1980s, then the variations have become relatively mild in the following two decades, finally forming a spatial pattern of significant increase in the eastern semi-arid region and semi-humid region and significant decrease in the whole humid region. In general, arid region, semi-arid region, and semi-humid region have experienced significant increase of WWI with the rates of 0.30, 0.29, and 0.99 per decade, however, humid region has experienced decrease with the rate of -0.21 per decade. That is, the warming-wetting trends is most pronounced in the relatively drier regions, which is different from the common point that dry regions get drier. Further, from the perspective of seasons, winter has overall experienced the most significant warming-wetting in spite of the smallest values in the climatology of temperature and precipitation. By comparison, with highest temperature and most of annual precipitation, the increasing trend of WWI in summer is very little. In addition, the moisture and heat conditions in spring and autumn have experienced various degrees of growth. From the perspective of four subregions, the WWI over the humid region has constantly decreased except in spring. The order of amplitude of warming -wetting in other regions is winter, spring, autumn, and summer. Considering the synergistic impacts of westerlies and monsoon (Chen et al., 2021; Song et al., 2022 ), much work is needed to better understand the driving mechanisms of seasonal differences. Finally, during the process of changing WWI, precipitation contributes universally the most in different subregions, while temperature contributes a lot in the relatively dry regions but less in the relatively wet regions. By comparison, although the regression coefficients of surface heat flux are less prominent, SH and LH still play vital roles, especially in the semi-humid region and humid region. For the entire TP, the increase of precipitation is most important for the warming-wetting trends, while the increase of temperature and surface heat flux also make a difference.
1 Introduction Since the Industrial Revolution, the increasing concentration of greenhouse gases has contributed to increasingly severe global warming (Walker et al., 2021; Yoro and Daramola, 2020 ). Soil, as an important constituent of terrestrial ecosystems, plays a vital role in regulating carbon emissions (IPCC, 2014; Smith, 2008 ). Global warming could accelerate the decomposition of soil organic carbon (SOC). With every 1 °C increase in temperature, soils are predicted to emit 11–34 Pg of CO2 , further exacerbating global warming (Batjes, 2014 ). It is estimated that releasing 1 ton of SOC is equivalent to emitting 3.67 tons of CO2  into the atmosphere (Baldock, 2007; Yang et al., 2022 ). Obviously, even a small variation in soil carbon (C) pools can have a profound impact on atmospheric CO2  levels and the terrestrial C cycle (Guo et al., 2024; Johnston et al., 2004; Lin et al., 2022a ). Therefore, it is highly important to enhance carbon-sequestration and emission-reduction to mitigate greenhouse effects and achieve carbon neutrality (Lal, 2004; Terrer et al., 2021 ). Soil erosion, especially hydraulic erosion, is responsible for land degradation and soil loss (Doetterl et al., 2016; Ji et al., 2024; Quijano et al., 2020 ). This natural phenomenon promotes the migration of soil materials and influences the SOC dynamics, in turn affecting the biogeochemical cycling of SOC (Lal, 2005; Polyakov and Lal, 2008 ). However, the role of erosion as a net sink or source has been highly controversial (Lal and Pimentel, 2008 ). Thus, probing the dynamics of SOC stocks during erosion and deposition processes is beneficial for obtaining a deeper understanding of the regional C budget and balance. Soil aggregates, the basic soil structural unit, mediate numerous physical, chemical, and biological properties of soils (Gupta and Germida, 2015; Six et al., 2000b; Trivedi et al., 2015 ). Their composition and stability serve as crucial indicators for assessing soil fertility, quality, and erodibility (Bronick and Lal, 2005 ). Previous studies have demonstrated that the stability of soil aggregates is intimately associated with various drivers, such as climate, pedogenic parent material, soil microorganisms, vegetation, and other nutrients (Angst et al., 2021; Bissonnais et al., 2002; De Gryze et al., 2006; Dimoyiannis, 2012; Nciizah and Wakindiki, 2014; Zhong et al., 2021 ). However, the binding materials that promote the formation of soil aggregates are pivotal agents influencing the composition and stability of soil aggregates (Six et al., 2004 ). Zheng et al. (2019)  suggested that soil organic matter (SOM) and iron-aluminum (Fe and Al) oxides act as the most important cementing substances in the processes of formation, stabilization, and breakdown of soil aggregates. Their components and morphology vary with the soil aggregates, and an increase in the contents of SOM fractions and Fe-Al oxides could effectively enhance the aggregation capacity (Lin et al., 2022b; Tisdall and Oades, 1982 ). Accordingly, clarifying the distribution characteristics of SOM fractions and Fe/Al oxides in soil aggregates, along with their relationships with aggregate stability, is of paramount importance for understanding the underlying mechanisms governing aggregate stabilization. Numerous studies have shown that water erosion is considered a major factor in the fragmentation of soil aggregates, exerting a significant impact on their distribution and stability (Barthès and Roose, 2002; Parsakhoo et al., 2014 ). Generally, soil aggregates are mainly formed by the bonding of various organic (SOM fractions) and inorganic (Fe-Al oxides) cementing substances with mineral particles, where these binding agents in soils act as the cornerstone of aggregate stabilization (Ghosh et al., 2019; Xue et al., 2019a ). Tisdall and Oades (1982)  reported that SOM determines the formation of water-stable aggregates, and different SOM components have varying colloidal effects on the aggregates, which in turn also has different influences on the stability of soil aggregates. Fe-Al oxides, as crucial inorganic binding materials, can often be adsorbed on the surface of clay particles to produce Fe/Al plaques owing to their strong surface activity, thereby promoting the formation of stable aggregates (Kögel-Knabner et al., 2008; Six et al., 2004 ). Based on the hierarchical theory of soil aggregation, these cementitious materials may be unevenly distributed in different-sized aggregates, thus playing distinct roles in soil aggregation (Tisdall and Oades, 1982 ). In addition, differences in the crystallinity, specific surface area, and surface charge of different forms of Fe-Al oxides may result in variations in their abilities to bind humus and clay minerals and in aggregation (Barthès et al., 2008; Duiker et al., 2003; Eusterhues et al., 2005; Wagai and Mayer, 2007 ), because these materials often interact (Li et al., 2023 ). To date, there is no consensus on the mechanisms through which the different forms of Fe-Al oxides and SOM influence the aggregation process. Undoubtedly, water erosion not only affects the contents of organic cementing materials, but also influences microbial activities, alters the soil microenvironment, and affects the morphology and content of Fe-Al oxides, thereby impacting the stability of soil aggregates (Chen et al., 2020; Nciizah and Wakindiki, 2015; Zeng et al., 2024 ). However, it remains unclear how the binding materials in soil aggregates will change under erosion and deposition conditions, especially in the hilly red soil region of southern China (HRSR), where water erosion is severe. The HRSR is a tropical and subtropical zone characterized by extremely abundant Fe-Al oxides with highly active redox potentials, making it sensitive to natural disturbances (Huang and Zhao, 2014; Huang et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2016 ). Intensified weathering, leaching, and biogeochemical cycles determine the vulnerability and instability of the ecosystem in the red soil region (Zhang et al., 2023 ). Owing to its unique climate, relatively plentiful hydrothermal resources promote desilicification and allitization in red soil (Huang and Zhao, 2014 ), resulting in significant differences in the contents of SOM components and Fe-Al oxides, which in turn impacts the formation and stability of aggregates (Xue et al., 2019b ). Consequently, elucidating the underlying mechanisms controlling the formation and destruction of red soil aggregates under erosion–deposition conditions is central for combating soil erosion. Therefore, this study was conducted on a typical eroded slope in the HRSR to determine the composition and stability of soil aggregates at different eroding sites. We also measured the contents of organic and inorganic binding materials, including SOM components and Fe-Al oxides, in bulk soils and different-sized aggregates. The specific objectives of this study were as follows: (i) to explore the effects of erosion and deposition on the composition and stability of soil aggregates; (ii) to investigate the influence of erosion and deposition on the contents of organic and inorganic binding materials in aggregates of different particle sizes; and (iii) to quantify the contribution rate of each cementing substance to soil aggregation and reveal the central predictors of aggregate stability under erosion–deposition conditions. Our findings provide a theoretical basis for a thorough understanding of the theory of soil stabilization and dynamic management of SOC pools.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 Experimental site and soil samples The research site is located in the Xitang watershed (26°38′-27°10′N, 114°56′-115°30′E; Fig. 1  ) in the Qingyuan District, Ji’an city, Jiangxi Province, southern China. The region has a subtropical monsoon climate with four distinct seasons, and an annual average temperature of 18 °C (Guo et al., 2024 ). The annual precipitation is 1487 mm,  >80 % of which falls from April to June. The mean annual light and frost-free periods in this area are 1814 h and 277 d, respectively. This region is characterized by a low hilly mountainous terrain with an elevation of approximately 300 ∼ 320 m above sea level. The soil, categorized as red soil in the Chinese soil classification or as a typical Ultisol  in the USDA classification, is composed of Quaternary parent materials or coarsely crystalline granite. The dominant tree species are Cunninghamia lanceolata (Lamb.) Hook , Dicranopteris linearis (Burm.) Underw  and Cinnamomum camphora (Linn) Presl . The understory vegetation is sparse. Due to the abundant rainfall and hydrothermal resources, the red soil in this region is easily eroded by rainfall and suffers severe water erosion. Thus, it is an ideal place for us to conduct erosion-related studies in this area. We selected a typical eroded slope in this watershed as the experimental site with average length and width values of ∼80 m and 40 m, respectively. The slope gradient ranges from 0° to 33.41°. First, three representative transects perpendicular to the contour lines were chosen on this slope. Along the eroding Ultisol  landscape, each transect was divided into four different landscape positions (i.e., the top-slope, up-slope, mid-slope, and toe-slope) from top to bottom (Fig. 1 ). According to the 137 Cs tracing and field erosion needle results, we identified the different erosion and deposition characteristics of these sites (Table 1  ). This slope underwent severe erosion, and more detailed information has been described in Guo et al. (2024) . Briefly, the up-slope, mid-slope, and toe-slope were referred to as erosional sites, and the flat top-slope was considered a depositional site. Subsequently, in April 2020, we established three sampling quadrats (2 m × 2 m) at each site, and five sampling points were established in each quadrat. The samples collected in this study included undisturbed soil and topsoil (0–20 cm). Notably, during the process of sample collection, the bulk soil samples were collected and stored in hard plastic boxes to maintain their original state for aggregate analysis. Moreover, five individual samples from each quadrat were mixed to obtain one composite sample, for a total of 36 samples (3 transects × 4 sites × 3 quadrats).  2.2 Soil water-stable aggregates Soil water-stable aggregates were determined by the wet-sieving method (Cambardella and Elliott, 1993; Elliott, 1986 ). Briefly, 50 g of air-dried undisturbed soil was placed on top of a set of sieves with 2-, 0.25-, and 0.053-mm mesh sizes from top to bottom, installed on a wet-sieving shaker, and submerged in distilled water for 10 min. Then, after shaking the sieves up and down with an amplitude of 3 cm and a frequency of 40 r min−1  for 30 min, the remaining materials on each sieve were rinsed and transferred into a glass beaker, and finally dried at 60 °C and weighed to obtain four fractions. The mean weight diameter (MWD ), geometric mean diameter (GMD ), percentage of >0.25 mm water-stable aggregates (WR>0.25  ), and fractal dimension (FD ) were used to evaluate the effects of erosion on the stability of the soil aggregates (de Melo et al., 2018; Kemper and Rosenau, 1986; Tyler and Wheatcraft, 1992 ).(1) MWD = ∑ i = 1  n  x i  × w i       (2) GMD = e x p ∑ i = 1  n  w i  × ln x i           (3) lg w δ < x i       w     = 3 - F D     lg x i  x max          where xi   denotes the average diameter of each size class i  (mm); wi   represents the mass of the aggregates in size class i ; n  is the number of sieves; w (δ  < xi  )/w  represents the quality fraction smaller than size class i ; and xmax   represents the maximum diameter of the aggregates. Generally, higher MWD  and GMD  values indicate stronger aggregation of the soil aggregates. Additionally, FD  commonly serves as a sensitive indicator for assessing soil structure composition. The smaller the FD  value is, the better the soil structural stabilization, and the stronger the soil erosion resistance.  2.3 Soil humus matter components in bulk soils and aggregates Humus (HF) in the bulk soil or in each size class of the soil aggregates was extracted following the method proposed by Nelson and Sommers (1996) . Specifically,  ∼5 g of air-dried sample was placed into a 250 mL plastic bottle, and 50 mL of a sodium pyrophosphate-sodium hydroxide solution (0.1 mol/L) was added. The mixture was shaken for 30 min in a thermostatic shaker (25 °C) and then left to stand for 14–16 h. Approximately 5 ∼ 15 mL of the extract was transferred to a rigid test tube and neutralized with 0.5 mol/L sulfuric acid (H2 SO4 ), which was determined by the color depth. Each tube was heated in a thermostatic water bath at 80 ∼ 90 °C until the solution was evaporated to dryness. Finally, the total C content of HF was measured by dichromate oxidization with an external heating method. Additionally, 20 ∼ 50 mL of the extract was added to a 100 mL beaker, and the pH was adjusted to ∼1.5 by adding H2 SO4 . The solution was held at 80 °C for 30 min and left overnight to fully separate the C of humic acid (HA) from that of fulvic acid (FA). After filtering the solution through filter paper, the precipitate on the filter paper was washed several times with 0.025 mol L−1  H2 SO4  until the filtrate was colorless. In addition, 0.05 mol L−1  NaOH was used to dissolve the precipitate at 40 ∼ 50 °C. Thereafter, 10 ∼ 20 mL of solution was transferred to a rigid test tube and neutralized with H2 SO4  (0.5 mol L−1 ), after which the solution was evaporated to dryness. Eventually, the C content of HA was determined following the same procedures as those described above. The C content of FA was calculated by the difference between the HF and HA values (Swift, 1996 ).  2.4 Free-form, amorphous and complexed iron aluminum oxides Selective dissolution procedures were applied to quantitatively analyze the mineralogy of the Fe-Al oxides (Wen et al., 2019 ). The free-form Fe-Al oxides (Fed  and Ald ) were extracted with 0.1 mol/L dithionite-citrate-bicarbonate (DCB) solution (Lalonde et al., 2012 ). The amorphous Fe-Al oxides (Feo  and Alo ) were extracted via the acidic ammonium oxalate method at pH 3.2, shaking at 250 r min−1  and 25 °C for 2.5 h in the dark (McKeague and Day, 1966 ). The complexed Fe-Al oxides (Fep  and Alp ) were determined after the extraction with 0.1 mol L−1  sodium-pyrophosphate and shaking at 180 r min−1  for 16 h at pH 8.5 (McKeague, 1967 ). After centrifugation of these extractions at 4000 rpm for 8 min, the contents of Fe and Al in the supernatants were measured by absorbance on a spectrometer (UV-2700, Shimadzu, Japan).  2.5 Statistical analysis One-way ANOVA and least significant difference (LSD ) multiple comparison tests were applied to examine significant differences in the particle size distributions and stability indices of the soil aggregates and organic and inorganic cementing materials among the different erosion sites at the 95 % confidence level. Before the statistical analysis, all datasets were tested for normality (using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test ) and homogeneity of variance (using Levene's test ). Logarithmical transformation was performed on data that did not meet the assumption of normality of variance. In addition, all the corresponding figures were plotted using Origin 2023b software. Statistical analysis of all experimentally measured data (means ± standard errors, n > 3) in this study was performed in Excel 2016 and SPSS software (SPSS 22.0 for Windows, SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). The boosted regression tree (BRT) is a machine learning method that integrates regression trees and boosting statistical models (Elith et al., 2008 ) and has been widely applied in ecological and environmental research (Han et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022 ). Compared with statistical methods, multiple regression trees can improve model performance. First, BRT models can capture complicated nonlinear relationships by combining a congression algorithm that eliminates interactions among predictive factors using recursive binary splitting (Carslaw and Taylor, 2009 ). In addition, massive ensembles of small regression trees can be constructed to express nonlinear relationships (Elith et al., 2008 ). Besides, BRT models have a powerful learning capacity and flexibility in managing complex data, and the interaction or correlation of independent variables does not need to be considered (Elith et al., 2008; Han et al., 2022 ). Additionally, the importance and marginal effects of the independent variables can be captured (Elith et al., 2008; Leathwick et al., 2006 ). The former has the ability to quantify the contribution of each independent variable, while the latter indicates the potential effects of the independent variables as their magnitudes change (Hu et al., 2020 ). In this study, we performed the BRT algorithm to evaluate the effects of various cementing substances on the stability of soil aggregates in RStudio (version 1.4.1106). The cementing materials (organic and inorganic) and aggregate stability indices (indicated by the MWD) were used as the independent and dependent variables, respectively. Prior to applying the BRT model, we used the variance inflation factor (VIF) test to assess collinearity among the independent variables (Han et al., 2022 ). The results showed that the VIF values of all independent variable were lower than 5, demonstrating the absence of severe multicollinearity among these agents. Consequently, these variables could be used for further analysis. Finally, the BRT model was employed to investigate the contribution of each variable. The specific parameter settings for our BRT model included tree complexity, learning rate, and bagging fraction, which were 5, 0.005, and 0.50, respectively. Notably, 50 % of the data were available for training, and 10-fold cross validation (CV) was utilized to select the superior model (Hu et al., 2020; Van and Hans, 2001 ).   3 Results 3.1 Soil physicochemical properties among different landscape positions Significant differences in basic soil physicochemical properties such as bulk density, pH, SOC, TN, AN, C/N and soil texture were observed among the different eroding sites, as shown in Table 2   (P < 0.05). The soil BD and pH values at the eroding sites were markedly greater than those at the depositional sites (P < 0.05), while at the eroding sites, there were no obvious differences among the various landscape positions along the slope. In contrast, the SOC and TN contents in the depositional areas were 1.34 and 1.18 times greater than those in the eroding areas, respectively. The soil texture differed significantly between the eroding site and depositional site (P < 0.05), while no marked differences were detected among the various positions of the eroding sites.  3.2 Particle size distribution and stability of the soil aggregates Changes in the proportion of soil aggregates varied widely among the different landscape positions (Fig. 2  ). The weight percentages of >2 mm large macroaggregates were significantly greater at the top-slope than at the other sites (P < 0.05), being 1.68, 2.31 and 1.30 times greater than those of the up-slope, mid-slope, and toe-slope, respectively. However, the small macroaggregate fractions (2–0.25 mm) showed no significant differences among all the positions, with a range of 18.17 ∼ 31.66 %. In contrast, the proportion of 0.25–0.053 mm microaggregates was remarkably greater in the eroding zones than in the depositional zones. Besides, the silt + clay fractions (<0.053 mm) exhibited a similar pattern, roughly showing a significant increasing trend from the top-slope to the toe-slope. These results indicate that water erosion resulted in a pronounced decrease in macroaggregates (>0.25 mm), whereas the opposite trend was observed for microaggregates (<0.25 mm), especially for the silt + clay fraction aggregates (<0.053 mm). In other words, the soil aggregate structure is dominated by macroaggregates in the depositional area, and by microaggregates in the eroding area. The aggregate stability indices were significantly different at varying landscape positions (Fig. 3  ). The mean MWD and GMD values followed the order of top-slope > toe-slope > up-slope ≈ mid-slope. The top-slope had the highest MWD and GWD values (1.42 and 0.56, respectively), followed by the toe-slope, and the up-slope and toe-slope had the lowest. The differences in MWD and GMD values were significant between the top-slope and the other sites (P < 0.05). However, except for the top-slope, there were no significant differences in the MWD or GMD values among the other sites. In addition, erosion also dramatically affected the fractal dimension (FD) of the soil aggregates, with the FD values varying from 1.83 to 2.65. It is worth noting that the changing pattern of FD was less consistent. There were significant differences in the FD values among the different sites (P < 0.05). Its values increased along the slope except for the mid-slope. The toe-slope had the largest FD (2.52), and the top-slope had a lower FD value (2.25), which was 6.22 % and 12 % lower than those of the up-slope and toe-slope, respectively. Overall, erosion exerted a greater impact on the stability of soil aggregates, leading to a reduction in MWD and GMD values and an increase in FD values in the eroding areas, and vice versa.  3.3 SOM components in different aggregates and bulk soils Fig. 4   shows that significant differences existed in the contents of the SOM fractions in the different-sized aggregates and bulk soils among the different sites (P < 0.05), especially between the eroding sites and the depositional sites. The HF and FA contents in bulk soils and varying aggregates were substantially reduced by erosion, primarily with higher values in the depositional zones than in the eroding zones (Fig. 4 a and c). There were significant differences in the contents of HF in the <0.25 mm aggregates and FA in the <0.053 mm aggregates among the different sites. Similarly, the HF, HA, and FA contents in the aggregates of other size classes exhibited noticeable differences between the erosional sites and the depositional sites, with no significant differences among different positions other than the top-slope. Notably, the HA content in the bulk soils displayed the same pattern as the other components at various sites, with an overall decreasing trend. However, the opposite trends were observed for the >0.25 mm aggregates, with the highest HA (0.39 g kg−1 ) occurring at the toe-slope, but the HA contents in the macroaggregates were not significantly different among the various sites (Fig. 4 b). Furthermore, Fig. 4 d clearly suggests that the HA/FA ratio changed from 17 % to 65 %. Consistent with the HA and FA results, the HA/FA values in the bulk soils were remarkably greater at the top-slope than at the other sites, indicating that erosion was not conducive to soil humification. Among the various landscape positions, the HA/FA ratios of the different-sized aggregates also varied. The maximum HA/FA values for the top-slope and mid-slope soils were observed for the <0.053 mm soil aggregates, and those for the up-slope and toe-slope soils were found for the 2–0.25 mm particle sizes.  3.4 Inorganic cementing materials in bulk soils and different aggregates As shown in Fig. 5  , the distributions of inorganic cementing materials in the aggregates, i.e., free-form Fe-Al (Fed , Ald ), amorphous Fe-Al (Feo , Alo ), and complexed-form Fe-Al (Fep , Alp ), differed at various positions on the eroded slope. The contents of Fed  and Ald  ranged from 2.07 to 5.76 g kg−1  and 0.55 to 2.53 g kg−1 , respectively (Fig. 5 a and b), with overall trends of lower Fed  and Ald  in aggregates of various size fractions at the top-slope than at other sites. Compared to the top-slope, the Fed  content in the >2 mm particle sizes at the toe-slope significantly increased by 91.61 % (P < 0.05), while it displayed no significant difference in the other size classes among the various positions. Similarly, the Ald  content was significantly greater in the <0.053 mm size fraction at the toe-slope than at the other sites, with no significant differences among the other particle sizes. Interestingly, both Fed  and Ald  contents were higher in microaggregates (<0.25 mm) at the toe-slope. The Fep  and Alp  contents at each erosion site ranged from 0.12 to 0.52 g kg−1  and from 0.12 to 0.52 g kg−1 , respectively (Fig. 5 c and d). There were no significant differences in the Fep  content in the bulk soil among the various sites. Both the Fep  and Alp  contents in the <0.25 mm aggregates decreased along the slope, exhibiting a pattern of toe-slope > up-slope > mid-slope > top-slope in the >2 mm particle size aggregates. The Fep  contents in <0.25 mm microaggregates were greater, with the maximum values observed at the top-slope. Moreover, the Alp  contents in the bulk soils and >0.25 mm macroaggregates were statistically significantly lower at the up-slope than at the other sites (P < 0.05), while similar patterns of significant differences were not observed for the Alp  contents in <0.25 mm microaggregates among the different sites. The amorphous Fe-Al oxides displayed uniform distributions (Fig. 5 e-f). Specifically, in both bulk soils and in the aggregates of different particle fractions, the Feo  and Alo  contents were the highest at the toe-slope and were significantly greater than those at the top-slope (P < 0.05). Their contents ranged from 0.65 to 1.73 g kg−1  and 0.27 to 0.85 g kg−1 , respectively. Additionally, the amorphous Fe-Al oxides all exhibited higher contents in <0.25 mm microaggregates. Overall, erosion significantly affected the Fe-Al oxide contents, which did not have a consistent change pattern along the eroded slope. Fed , Ald , Fep , Feo , and Alo  primarily existed in microaggregates, while Alp  was predominantly found in macroaggregates.  3.5 Effects of cementing materials on the stability of soil aggregates The final BRT model explained 11.50 % of the deviance using CV, with a correlation coefficient of 0.70 for the training data. The CV correlation between the training and test data was 0.38. Fig. 6  a ranked the RI scores for each variable derived from the BRT. The results indicate that the three most crucial cementitious substances contributing to the aggregate stability index (indicated by the MWD) on the eroded slope were FA (36.70 %), Feo  (19.00 %), and Ald  (12.71 %), followed by Alo  (7.55 %). The cumulative RI value for these variables was 75.96 %. The RI scores for the other predictors (Alp , Fed , Fep  and HF) were lower than or equal to the median RI score (HA, 6.97 %), which was considered to indicate low importance. Furthermore, the partial dependence plots (PDPs) explicitly illustrate that the MWD sharply increased with FA moving from ∼0.78 ∼1.01 g kg−1 , following which it decreased and then mostly stabilized thereafter. Fed , Ald , and Fep  had positive correlations with the MWD in the ranges of 3.20–3.50 g kg−1 , 0.30–1.10 g kg−1  and 0.25–0.30 g kg−1 , respectively (Fig. 6 b). Feo , Alo  and Alp  were negatively correlated with the MWD within the ranges of 0.60–1.25 g kg−1 , 0.30–0.58 g kg−1 , and 0.55–0.90 g kg−1 , respectively. However, the relationship between HA and the MWD is not evident.   4 Discussion 4.1 Effects of erosion and deposition on the stability of soil aggregates We found that, in this study, the proportion of macroaggregates at the depositional sites was greater than those at eroding sites (Fig. 2 ), indicating that the soil aggregates at the depositional sites were highly aggregated and stable. This may be related to the different external erosive forces on the soil aggregates and the selective migration of fine particles (Doetterl et al., 2015; Nie et al., 2018 ). Compared to those in the eroding zones, the soil aggregates in the depositional zones were disrupted to a lesser extent; thus, they had larger particle sizes (Sadeghian et al., 2021; Van Hemelryck et al., 2011 ). Furthermore, the input and accumulation of massive amounts of labile organic matter and large-sized particles migrated from the eroding site to the depositional site, which facilitated an increase in particle size (Xiao et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2023b ). The transport of soil aggregates during soil erosion is influenced by two main factors (Shi et al., 2012 ). On the one hand, the degree to which the soil structure is broken increases with the increasing rainfall intensity since the impact of raindrops on the exposed soil increases, causing macroaggregates (>0.25 mm) to be disrupted into fine-sized aggregates (Wang et al., 2023; Wuddivira et al., 2009 ). The wetting effects of rainfall also promotes the rapid disintegration of large aggregates into small aggregates (Almajmaie et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2016 ). In addition, slaking by fast wetting due to raindrop impact effects is one of the primary mechanisms for aggregate disintegration (Le Bissonnais, 1996; Li et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2018 ). On the other hand, the runoff transport capacity is enhanced, so surface runoff could migrate the eroded sediments to low-lying areas (Doetterl et al., 2016; Stallard, 1998 ). Consequently, water erosion tends to disrupt soil water stable macroaggregates and correspondingly increase the content of microaggregates. Furthermore, we observed that the stability of the soil aggregates was greater in the depositional zone, as indicated by the highest MWD and GMD, and lowest FD (Fig. 3 ). This is mainly attributed to the fact that surface runoff carries a portion of large-sized soil aggregates during erosion, and soil erosion is more intense in different topographical landforms (Chen et al., 2018; Doetterl et al., 2016 ). Therefore, the proportions of soil macroaggregates at the depositional sites increased. Additionally, the input of large amounts of active SOM as well as the transport and deposition of lighter soil materials, along with a higher clay content (Table 2 ), contributed to the binding of soil particles with OM. These favorable conditions could foster soil aggregation (Totsche et al., 2018; van Hall et al., 2017 ). Based on the widely used aggregate hierarchical theory (Tisdall and Oades, 1982 ), labile SOM and plant debris can decompose into binding agents (such as OM, and polysaccharides), facilitating the entanglement of hyphae and microaggregates to form macroaggregates, which in turn improves the stability of soil aggregates (Wei et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2017 ). Simultaneously, erosion undermines the structure of soil particles and increases soil aeration, leading to poorer protection of soil particles and looser soil structure, exacerbating the degree of aggregate disintegration (Nsabimana et al., 2020; Totsche et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2021 ). Therefore, erosion induces a decrease in the stability of the soil aggregates.  4.2 Effects of erosion and deposition on organic cementitious substances Our results revealed that the HF and FA contents were significantly lower in the erosion zone than in the deposition zone (Fig. 4 a and c). This may be attributable to the fact that the effects of slaking and mechanical dispersion during water erosion resulted in the breakdown of water-stable aggregates, releasing the occulated particulate OM that was originally protected within macroaggregates (Six et al., 2000a ). Therefore, this might be why the OM content significantly decreased and varied among the different-sized classes. Besides, macroaggregates are formed by the cementation of microaggregates and OM and contain many initially unstable freshly produced OM fractions (i.e., particulate C, light fraction C, and microbial biomass C) (Kögel-Knabner et al., 2008; Wagai and Mayer, 2007 ). Owing to water erosion, these labile materials were easily transported to low-lying regions, resulting in a higher content of OM components at the depositional areas than at the eroding areas (Guo et al., 2024 ). The substantial enrichment of SOM at the deposition sites is conducive to the formation of water-stable aggregates, which to a certain extent isolates microorganisms from OM and strengthens physical protection (Cui et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2016 ). Thus, the formation of soil aggregates can effectively improve the OM stability in the soil and reduce the risk of mineralization. The FA contents were dramatically greater than those of HA, with an HA/FA ratio < 1 (Fig. 4 ), which was in accordance with the results reported by Guggenberger and Zech (1994) . They demonstrated that the humic acid content was generally low in forest soils and that cementation was primarily dominated by fulvic acid during aggregate formation. This may be a result of unique conditions, such as relatively high temperature, humidity, and vegetation cover, as well as strong microbial degradation in southern China (Zhao et al., 2017 ). Additionally, we observed that the FA contents in each aggregate particle size group exhibited patterns of depositional sites > eroding sites, which may be associated with their lower molecular weight and greater hydrophilicity (Bai et al., 2022; Kou et al., 2022 ). Owing to its simple structure, FA was first destroyed by combining with water during rainfall erosion. Subsequently, runoff erosion also occurred, and FA components migrated and were lost along with the runoff and sediments, resulting in a significant reduction in FA in all size classes. Importantly, in the present study, except for the <0.053 mm particle size, there was no significant difference in the HF content among the various sites. A possible explanation may be the hierarchical saturation of C in eroded sediments from small to large particles. According to the carbon saturation theory proposed by Stewart et al. (2007) , C is preferentially stabilized in clay and silt particles because their capacity is limited, and C remains available for rapid mineralization after it reaches saturation. Moreover, for the macroaggregates, the HA contents displayed the highest values at the toe-slope. The reason for this discrepancy may be that the toe-slope is located at the watershed outlet, where severe splash and scouring erosion has a negative impact on soil microbial diversity and functionality (Hou et al., 2014 ), soil moisture is maintained at a relatively high level during this erosion process, and anaerobic conditions reduce the relative microbial abundance and activity of the soil, which is not beneficial for the mineralization of carbon in macroaggregates.  4.3 Effects of erosion and deposition on inorganic cementitious substances We found that the Fed  content at the eroding zones was much greater than that in the depositional zones, which was linked to the unique topography and soil pH. Generally, compared to the eroding site, the stronger microbial activity at the depositional sites promoted the weathering of silicate minerals in soils, which in turn increased the amount of Fed . However, due to the special topography of this eroded slope, the newly-developed Fed  at the top-site could have migrated downward along with runoff and sediments. Second, pH plays an important role in the morphology of Fe-Al oxides. The higher pH values at the eroding sites are more favorable for the formation of well-crystallized metal oxides (i.e., hematite) (Cudennec and Lecerf, 2006 ). Furthermore, except for amorphous Fe-Al oxides, the contents of other oxides at the eroding sites were lower, which might be linked to the SOM quality and the soil texture. Le Bissonnais (1996)  reported that lower OM is inimical to the production and transformation of iron and aluminum oxides. Additionally, the lower content of clay particles constrained the adsorption capacity of Fe-Al oxides at the eroding sites (Table 2 ). In this study, the Fe-Al oxides significantly varied depending on the particle size and were mainly present in microaggregates (Fig. 5 a-e). This is in accordance with previous results (Xue et al., 2019a; Zhao et al., 2017 ). The primary reason for this may be the greater cation exchange capacity and higher surface charge in microaggregates, where mineral surfaces are dominated by multilayer adsorption for better adsorption of clay particles, which facilitates the enrichment of Fe-Al oxides (Li et al., 2023 ). Nonetheless, we observed that Alp  mainly existed in macroaggregates, except at the toe-slope (Fig. 5 f), which may be related to the erosion degree and the SOM content. It was suggested that the complexed oxides were negatively correlated with soil erodibility and positively correlated with the index of soil erosion resistance. The continuous scouring and influx of rainfall and runoff from the top to the bottom caused severe erosion at the toe-slope (Cui et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2024 ). Microaggregates tend to easily migrate downward with rainfall runoff, and some microaggregates are deposited at the toe-slope, resulting in a significantly lower percentage of microaggregates at the upper sites than at the toe-slope (Fig. 3 ). Consequently, Alp  mainly influences macroaggregates to maintain stabilization. Notably, Feo  and Alo  exhibited maximum contents at the toe-slope and were largely concentrated in microaggregates, which may be related to the weaker stability of the soil aggregates (Fig. 3 ). One possible explanation is that large quantities of microaggregates from the upper layer converge at the toe-slope, and then amorphous Fe-Al oxides can bond with the microaggregates (Chen et al., 2020 ), thereby resulting in higher Feo  and Alo  values within the microaggregates. Hence, this contributed to the formation of macroaggregates, which aptly explains the greater percentage of >0.25 mm aggregates at the toe-slope than those of the up-slope and mid-slope (Fig. 2 ).  4.4 Interactions between cementitious substances and aggregate stability Different cementitious substances play varying roles in the stability of soil aggregates (Zhu et al., 2016 ). Previous studies have shown that the distribution of SOM fractions in aggregates, the contents and morphologies of Fe-Al oxides, and the presence of organo-mineral complexes are the basis for the formation of aggregates and play an instrumental role in aggregate stability (Goldberg and Glaubig, 1987 ). Erosion not only alters the in situ SOM and nutrients (Table 2 ), microbial activities, and soil microenvironment (Berhe et al., 2007; Doetterl et al., 2016 ), but also changes the content and nature of the binding materials (Zeng et al., 2024 ), which in turn profoundly impacts the stability of soil aggregates (Regelink et al., 2015 ). Our BRT results demonstrated that the three crucial binding materials controlling aggregate stability were FA, Feo , and Ald  (Fig. 5 a and b), indicating that both organic and inorganic binding materials jointly promote aggregate stabilization. This is in line with the findings of Zhao et al. (2017) , who reported that SOC and free-form Fe-Al oxides played dominant roles in aggregate stability. We also observed that the contribution of FA was greater than that of HA, suggesting that the colloidal effect of humus may be dominated by FA in the formation of aggregates, which is consistent with the results of Zhao et al. (2017)  and Lin et al. (2022) . Given the relatively high proportion of FA in the red soil region of southern China, even a minor change in the FA content can significantly affect aggregate stability. Furthermore, Igwe et al. (2009)  found a better correlation between amorphous Fe-Al oxides and aggregate stability, which supports our BRT results. This may be because erosion-induced soil redistribution alters the soil pH, and the contents and morphologies of Fe-Al oxides in soils, which further affects aggregate stability. Zhu et al. (2016)  also revealed that SOM and Fe-Al oxides were the primary drivers influencing the stability of aggregates. This may be attributed to the large surface area of Feo , which is a major contributor of active hydroxyl groups, resulting in a stronger aggregating effect and thus playing a significant role in aggregate stabilization (Goldberg and Glaubig, 1987; Lin et al., 2022; Regelink et al., 2015 ). We found that water erosion markedly decreased the Fed  and Ald  contents, but the contribution rate of Ald  to aggregate stability was greater (12.71 %). This is probably attributable to the fact that the Ald  was tightly bound to the clay particles and was not easily dispersed, which is conducive to the formation of stable aggregates. Generally, compared to ferric iron ions (Fe3+ ), trivalent aluminum ions (Al3+ ) have a greater charge density and higher adsorption capacity (Schulten and Leinweber, 2000 ). Thus, the effect of Ald  on aggregate stability was stronger than that of Fed . Additionally, the tested soil was acidic, and the surfaces of the aluminum oxides carried more positive charges, making them more susceptible to binding with negatively charged clay minerals and enhancing soil aggregation (Schulten and Leinweber, 2000 ). Moreover, Alp , Fed , Fep , and HF were less important predictors (Fig. 6 a), which is not consistent with several results that showed a better correlation between the complexed Fe-Al oxides and aggregate stability (Igwe et al., 2009 ). This may arise from the differences in the contents and morphologies of Fe-Al oxides under complex erosion and deposition processes, where the roles of different forms of oxides are distinct. Erosion dramatically reduced the Alp  and Fep  contents, weakening their adsorption capacities, and at this point, soil particles rely more on other forces to promote aggregation.   5 Conclusions and prospects This study investigated the effects of water erosion on aggregate stability, based on the particle size distribution, soil organic matter fractions, and Fe-Al oxides of different-sized aggregates at various eroding sites in the hilly red soil region of southern China. The results suggest that water erosion altered the soil properties and the particle size distributions of the aggregates at the different sites, thus affecting the stability of the soil aggregates. With the exception of the complexed Fe-Al oxides, erosion significantly reduced the contents of the humus fractions and Fe-Al oxides in the bulk soils and aggregates. Free-form and amorphous Fe-Al oxides, together with complexed Fe oxide, primarily exist in microaggregates, while the complexed Al oxide was found in macroaggregates. The results of the BRT analysis revealed that the three most important predictors of soil aggregate stability on the eroded slope were FA (36.70 %), Feo  (19.00 %), and Ald  (12.71 %), respectively. These findings confirm that under the impact of erosion and deposition, the organic and inorganic cementing materials of the aggregates jointly contribute to the stability of the soil aggregates in the red soil region of southern China. The results of this study contribute to our in-depth understanding of the underlying mechanisms of erosion- and deposition-driven changes in binding materials on aggregate stabilization, providing theoretical knowledge for regional carbon cycling. Our work investigated the primary binding materials (organic and inorganic) in soil aggregates and identified the crucial factors influencing aggregate stability in southern China. However, this study has several potential limitations. First, the effects of organo-mineral complexes, such as Fe/Al-bound OC and calcium-bound OC, on aggregate stability cannot be overlooked and should be considered in future studies. Second, we failed to reveal the mechanism of aggregate stabilization from a more microscopic perspective. Future studies further clarifying the underlying mechanism using advanced techniques, such as SEM and X-rays, should be conducted. Third, given that the soil is a complicated ecosystem, a result of the interactions of various physical, chemical, and biological processes, the stabilization of soil aggregates is affected by multiple factors; therefore, more attention should be given to this aspect. Future studies should integrate regional and global-scale data, and apply meta -analysis to establish specialized models coupled with additional influencing factors to better reveal the mechanisms of aggregate formation and stability.
1 Introduction In light of the increasing expansion of drylands due to climate change (Huang et al., 2016 ), the balance between ecosystem productivity and water consumption has recently garnered increased attention (Gentine et al., 2019; Tian et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2023 ). Water use efficiency (WUE) is a key indicator of the coupling of carbon and water cycles (Guerrieri et al., 2016 ), as it reflects the relationship between vegetation carbon assimilation and water consumption (Beer et al., 2009; Huang et al., 2015 ). In alpine ecosystems, with their unique environmental features—such as low temperatures, dryness, and low nutrient content—the contradiction between water consumption and carbon sequestration is exacerbated (Li et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2020 ). Moreover, alpine ecosystems are relatively fragile and sensitive to climate change, leading to prolonged and severe aridity in these ecosystems (Ding et al., 2018 ). Therefore, it is necessary to quantify the changes in WUE in alpine ecosystems under arid conditions to deepen our understanding of how alpine ecosystems respond to aridity. Aridity directly or indirectly affects ecosystem carbon sinks through water stress (Li et al., 2019; Malone et al., 2016 ), but the relationship between aridity and WUE remains controversial. Gross primary productivity (GPP), which constitutes the largest carbon flux between terrestrial ecosystems and the atmosphere (Beer et al., 2010 ), directly reflects the photosynthetic capacity of plants (Liu et al., 2021 ). Water stress caused by drought leads to a decrease in the GPP of vegetation to levels less than evapotranspiration (ET), leading to increased carbon fixation with reduced water consumption, and therefore, a higher WUE (Campos et al., 2013; Malone et al., 2016 ). However, the results of other studies suggest that drought could lead to a decrease in WUE (Yang et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2017 ). The response of WUE to water conditions varies in ecosystems with different degrees of aridity; for example, WUE is negative in arid areas but can be either positive or negative in humid areas (Huang et al., 2017 ) and decreases with an increasing aridity index (AI) in arid regions (Xu et al., 2019 ). Thus, it is evident that the response of WUE to aridity varies by region. Under arid conditions, the potential of the atmosphere to extract water from the soil and plants increases, exerting greater hydrological pressure on alpine vegetation (Wu et al., 2019 ). Aridity significantly reduces GPP in alpine ecosystems (Xu et al., 2021 ). Water stress may decrease WUE in fragile alpine ecosystems because of a decline in the carbon sequestration capacity (Malone et al., 2016 ). Considering these findings, it is important to explore the responses of alpine ecosystems to different degrees of aridity. Temperature and precipitation are the main factors causing aridity as well as the main climate drivers of WUE (Umair et al., 2020 ), especially in fragile alpine ecosystems (Zhang et al., 2018 ). Annual temperature is one of the main drivers (Guerrieri et al., 2016 ). The results of other studies have indicated that water availability is more important than temperature in driving WUE in alpine ecosystems, and that ecosystem WUE is enhanced with increasing annual precipitation (Bernacchi and VanLoocke, 2015; Zhang et al., 2018 ). Vapor pressure deficit (VPD) is related to relative humidity and air temperature and influences the closure of plant stomata (Hsu et al., 2021 ), which controls physiological processes, such as transpiration and photosynthesis, and has a significant impact on evapotranspiration and WUE. In contrast with the research in alpine grasslands, studies of WUE in alpine ecosystems have been conducted using data from eddy covariance (EC) sites (Wang et al., 2020 ), and there is a lack of regional studies on shrub ecosystems. The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau has experienced significant warming in recent decades (Piao et al., 2011 ), leading to shrubland expansion. Knowledge of the long-term WUE response to aridity in alpine shrubs remains limited; our understanding of how WUE is driven by climatic factors at a regional scale remains incomplete, and there may be potential differences in the response of WUE to changes in precipitation and temperature. The aim of this study was to investigate the spatiotemporal variations in WUE in alpine shrub ecosystems across different aridity zones and their meteorological driving factors. The eco-physiological parameters of alpine shrubs were calibrated using parameter estimation (PEST) based on the observed EC flux data from the Haibei station. A calibrated Biome-BGC model was employed to quantify the spatiotemporal distribution of shrub GPP, ET, and WUE in Qinghai Province, China, in five climatic regions from 1980 to 2019, and the relationships between climatic factors, AI, and WUE were analyzed. The hypotheses tested in this study were: (1) the WUE of shrub ecosystems increases in different regions with an increase in aridity and (2) the WUE of shrub ecosystems is potentially driven by mean annual precipitation (MAP), mean annual temperature (MAT), and VDP.  2 Material and methods 2.1 Study area and climatic divisions The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, known as the “roof of the world,” is the highest plateau in the world and a typical alpine ecosystem sensitive to climate change. Qinghai Province, in the northeastern part of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, spans from 31°36′ to 39°19′N and from 89°35′ to 103°04′E, with an area of approximately 696,500 km2  (Fig. 1  ). It has a continental plateau climate with long winters, short summers, and low annual precipitation. The annual average temperature is between −5.1 and 9.0 degrees Celsius (°C), with large diurnal differences. The average annual precipitation ranges from 250 to 550 mm and generally decreases from southeast to northwest. Qinghai Province is an ecologically fragile region sensitive to climate change (Piao et al., 2011 ). The main shrub species native to Qinghai include Rhododendron  L., Dasiphora fruticosa , Hippophae rhamnoides , and Salix oritrepha , which are mainly distributed in the southeastern region. The annual precipitation and temperature patterns of Qinghai shrubs (Fig. S1 ) for 1980–2019 are shown in Fig. S1 ; as can be seen in the figure, the annual temperature showed an upward trend in the study period.
