1 Introduction Cropland inundation is one of the most disastrous phenomena that occurs in mountain dominated agricultural environments. For example, South China is characterized by mountains, hills, plains, river valleys, and intermountain basins staggered in distribution. Because of the dense population and intensive land utilization, numerous small-scale cropland have been established and are widely dispersed across those narrow flat areas. Steep slopes and connected morphology mean these systems are often able to respond quickly to intense rainfall with little or no warning of flooding (Zhao et al. 2018 ). The inundation of crops can result in crop damage, the proliferation of crop pests and diseases, contamination of soil and water sources, and destruction of agricultural infrastructure (Samuele et al. 2022 ). The success in the assessment of the impact of inundation on cropland requires both accurate cropland and water extent maps (Bofana et al. 2022 ). Field surveys or hydrological models may pose challenges when rapidly making these maps. Remote sensing offers a solution by providing a method to acquire large-scale information simultaneously. Typically, two types of remote sensing data: optical imagery and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery are useful in this task. Optical imagery is well-suited for mapping land cover (LC) i.e. cropland due to its superior signal-to-noise ratio compared to SAR imagery. Currently, several global LC datasets have been developed and available for public access. These datasets encompass: 1) WorldCover from European Space Agency (ESA) (Zanaga et al. 2021 ), 2) Land cover v2 from the Environmental Systems Research Institute (ESRI) (Karra et al. 2021 ), 3) Finer Resolution Observation and Monitoring of global land cover from Tsinghua University (FROM) (Gong et al., 2019 ), 4) Global land-cover product with Fine Classification System 2020 from Aerospace Information Innovation Institute, Chinese Academy of Sciences (FCS30) (Zhang et al. 2021b ), and 5) Globeland30-2020 from National Geomatics Center of China (GL30) (Jun et al. 2014 ). These LC datasets are all generated based on Sentinel or Landsat data using machine learning methods. However, optical data availability is often hindered by cloudy weather conditions, while SAR data are unaffected by cloud cover and can operate day and night (McCormack et al. 2022 ), making them ideal for mapping water extent. The distinction in backscatter response forms the basis for identifying inundation areas against the background in SAR images. Common SAR data utilized for flood monitoring include Envisat ASAR (Schlaffer et al. 2015 ), Radarsat (Giustarini et al. 2016 ), Sentinel-1 (Guan et al. 2023; McCormack et al. 2022; Singha et al. 2020 ), and GF-3 (Zhang and Xia 2022 ). Consequently, researchers have introduced several image segmentation algorithms (Hossain and Chen 2019 ) to waterbody or flood mapping including thresholding (DeVries et al. 2020; Grimaldi et al. 2020; McCormack et al. 2022; Samuele et al. 2022; Singha et al. 2020 ), supervised/unsupervised classification (Amitrano et al. 2018; Martinis et al. 2022; Zhang et al. 2021a ), region-based segmentation (Tong et al. 2018 ), edge-based segmentation (Ku et al., 2022 ), and deep learning based semantic segmentation (Bonafilia et al. 2020; Li et al. 2019; Li and Demir 2023 ). Yet, the method described above for utilizing SAR images to delineate cropland inundation is commonly employed in areas with relatively flat topography. When these methods applied to South China, where predominantly mountainous with extensive land use, it will result in a significant number of false alarms (FP). These are FPs triggered by radar shadows, smooth surfaces such as concrete pavement, highways, industrial areas, and parking lots, as well as permanent water bodies and floodplains. This poses two challenges to precise cropland inundation mapping: First, existing public cropland data often lack the precision required to effectively filter out FP associated with inundated croplands. The diverse agro-climatic conditions in mountain dominated region, along with variations in agricultural practices and the complexity of crop fields, contribute to the challenges in cropland mapping. In response, researchers have explored multiple area-of-interest (AOI) filters to compensate for the imperfections in cropland data. One of the representative research (McCormack et al. 2022 ) implemented six AOI filters: 1) a snow test to identify areas susceptible to snow cover, 2) an orbit direction filter to remove suspected radar shadow, 3) a consecutive images filter to remove short duration temporary waterbodies (Clement et al. 2018; Li et al. 2018 ), 4) a topographic filter to remove unlikely floods at high slope areas (DeVries et al. 2020; McCormack et al. 2022; Schlaffer et al. 2015 ), 5) a land-use filter to remove airports, motorways, golf courses and entire urban areas (Grimaldi et al. 2020; McCormack et al. 2022 ), and 6) a coastal filter to eliminate sea water floods (Martinis et al. 2022 ). However, the FPs cannot be completely eliminated by automated methods, since the public AOI data contain many errors (McCormack et al. 2022 ). A better alternative is to design a single high-precision cropland data, rather than integrating multiple AOI data. Recently, some studies successfully extracted high-precision cropland information from very high resolution (VHR) imagery by convolutional neural networks (CNN) based semantic segmentations i.e. PSPNet (Zhang et al. 2020 ) or Deeplab V3+ (Wang et al. 2022 ). However, this data-driven method is intensively sample demanding, as it requires pixel-level labeling. The transfer learning models Segformer (Xie et al. 2021 ) was firstly pre-trained on a large open sample set and then fine-tuned on the local datasets. In contrast, traditional CNN based models were trained directly on local datasets. It demonstrated that the Segformer achieved state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with better accuracy using fewer training samples. Second, an excessive number of FP may adversely impact the effectiveness of the local-adaptive flood identification algorithm (Jiang et al. 2021 ). The flood segmentation algorithm can be applied either to the entire region or to each clipped tiles individually. The Otsu thresholding (Bofana et al. 2022; Samuele et al. 2021 )(Liang and Liu 2020; McCormack et al. 2022 ) relies on histogram statistics allows for adaptation to local scenarios. However, challenges arise when local scenario undergo significant changes. For instance, in areas characterized by rugged terrain, where radar shadows outnumber flooded areas significantly, the ideal bimodal pattern of the histogram may be disrupted, posing challenges in identifying the optimal threshold. Hence, for flood area identification in mountain dominated regions, an algorithm with adaptive capabilities for various scenarios is essential. Additionally, it should also ensure result consistency across different scenarios, especially during significant scenario changes. To address these two challenges, a two-stage method is proposed. Firstly, an active learning-based semantic segmentation approach is applied to Google Very-High-Resolution (VHR) imagery to extract a high-precision cropland mask, referred as GSC. Secondly, a potential flood area is extracted using marker-controlled watershed segmentation (MCW) on Sentinel-1 SAR imagery, and then filtered by GSC to obtain the final cropland inundation area. Additionally, we assessed the performance of various algorithms including the active contour by Chan-Vese (CV) algorithm (Chan and Vese 2001; Tong et al. 2018 ), the Single Global Thresholding (SGT) algorithm, and the local-adaptive Otsu thresholding algorithm as references, evaluating their accuracy and parameter tuning difficulty. Finally, the framework was applied to estimate cropland inundation areas in Guangdong during the monsoon season for each year from 2017 to 2022.  2 Study area and data 2.1 Study area Guangdong Province, situated in the southernmost of mainland China, encompasses an area of 179,700 km2 (Fig. 1  ). The terrain is complex and diverse, including mountains, hills, terraces and plains, which account for 49.78 %, 17.62 %, 12.82 % and 19.78 % of the province's total land area respectively (https://dfz.gd.gov.cn/sqyl/jbsq/content/post_4093243.html ). As a result, this topographical composition has engendered a fragmented agricultural landscape. The average crop field area is only about 0.1-0.3 ha. The major crops include paddy rice, peanut, sugarcane, potatoes, and vegetables. The climate of Guangdong Province falls within the subtropical monsoon climate zone with an annual rainfall of approximately 1787 mm (https://slt.gd.gov.cn/zhyw/content/post_4193427.html ). Especially the continuous and large-scale precipitation concentrated from May to July in recent years. The flood disaster in June 2022 caused great losses to crop production.  2.2 Data 2.2.1 Sentinel-1 data and preprocessing The flood area extraction was based on Sentinel-1A Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data from European Space Agency. For this study, we used the Level-1 Ground Range Detected (GRD) data product with Interferometric Wide Swath (IW) mode and VH/VV polarization. The spatial resolution is 10 m. A total of 833 scenes covering in Guangdong from May to July each year from 2017 to 2022, were freely downloaded via API sentinels from Copernicus Open Access Hub. A standard workflow was applied to preprocess the Sentinel-1 GRD data (Filipponi 2019 ). It was created by using the official Sentinel application platform version 8.0. The workflow is: 1) Apply orbit file; 2) Thermal noise removal; 3) Border noise removal; 4) Calibration; 5) Speckle filtering using Refined Lee filter; 6) Terrain correction with SRTM DEM in 30 m resolution; 7) Conversion to dB.  2.2.2 Very high resolution remote sensing imagery The high resolution cropland and waterbody was extracted from Google Earth and Mapbox VHR imagery. The imagery dataset is continually updated from multiple sources including commercial providers, NASA, and USGS. The satellite data is generally updated every 1–3 years. The scale of the dataset used is at 18-level, with approximately 0.6 m/pixel spatial resolution, which is adequate for displaying the geometry and structure of cropland and waterbody. According to Google (https://mts0.googleapis.com ) and Mapbox (https://api.mapbox.com/v4/mapbox.satellite/ ) Satellite service, the global VHR satellite imagery is organized as RGB color patches with size of 256 × 256 pixels, and access through WMS service API. The data accessing period was from August to November in 2022. The patches are mosaicked into image tiles with a size of 0.05°×0.05° and a resolution of 0.000005°/pixel in WGS 1984 geographic coordinates. We first collected 6,675 Google Earth image tiles covering Guangdong province. Among them, 6,408 (96 %) were valid data, while the other 267 (4 %) were of poor quality due to no data, cloud pollution, inconsistent illumination, etc. We manually identified these tiles and replaced them with cloud-free Mapbox image tiles (Fig. 2  ).  2.2.3 Global land cover data To evaluate the performance of the proposed method and the public cropland datasets in identifying cropland inundation in mountain regions, this study involves five global land cover (LC) datasets including 1) ESA (Zanaga et al. 2021 ), 2) ESRI (Karra et al. 2021 ), 3) FROM (Gong et al., 2019 ), 4) FCS30 (Zhang et al. 2021b ), and 5) GL30 (Jun et al. 2014 ). The five LC data are all produced based on Sentinel or Landsat data, human-interpreted samples and machine learning methods. The summary of the five global LC datasets is shown in Table 1  . Except for the representative period of FROM data is 2017, the representative period of the other four LC data is 2020. Although there is a three-year gap, the differences may not be obvious in provincial cropland changes. The declared accuracy of the five data are all above 72 %.  2.2.4 DEM data Referring to Fabio’s study (Cian et al. 2018 ), the lands suitable for cropping naming SLOPE is extracted by thresholding pixels with a slope ≤ 5° (Fig. 3  ). Slopes are computed using Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) DEM, which is a 30 m resolution product with void-filled using elevation data from various sources.  2.2.5 Precipitation data In this study, the precipitation data is applied to identify cropland inundation caused by intense rainfall. The data are radar Quantitative Precipitation Estimation (QPE) products provided by the Guangdong Meteorological Bureau. The data was derived from an S-band dual-polarization weather radar network over southern China, with a spatial resolution of 1 km and a temporal resolution of one day.  2.2.6 Ground truth data The cropland and waterbody samples were manually labeled from very high-resolution (VHR) imagery into shapefile format utilizing the QGIS software. The acquisition of these samples occurs gradually rather than simultaneously, guided by the active learning strategy (Mittal et al. 2023 ). Fig. 3  visually represents the spatial distribution of all collected samples, with Roman numerals indicating the chronological order of sample production in this study. Further details regarding the sampling methodology are provided in Section 3.1.1 . Lastly, examples of cropland and waterbody samples are illustrated in Fig. 4  . The cropland sample consists of 41,707 polygons, with each polygon delineating a unique cropland area. Specifically, there are 37,623 cropland polygons situated in plain areas and 4,084 in mountainous areas. In order to enhance the model's robustness, the cropland samples encompass a wide array of cropping practices and crop types. These include, but are not limited to, paddy, irrigated cropland, dry cropland, terraces, fallow land, and cropland with scattered trees. The waterbody samples consist of 9,238 polygons, encompassing various water bodies such as rivers, oceans, reservoirs, lakes, ponds, and other types..  2.2.7 Statistical cropland area The Department of Agriculture and Rural Affairs of Guangdong Province reported (https://dara.gd.gov.cn/zwgk2278/bmdt/content/post_4014819.html ) the official cropland area to be 18,987 km2  in 2020. This statistical data serves as a benchmark for validating the accuracy of our extracted cropland data GSC, alongside existing cropland datasets such as ESA, ESRI, FCS30, FROM, GL30, and SLOPE.    3 Methods We proposed a framework for mapping cropland inundation areas in mountain dominated regions using Sentinel-1 and VHR imagery (Fig. 5  ). The framework comprises two stages. Firstly, we extract high-precision AOI data at the provincial scale from VHR imagery using semantic segmentation performed via active learning of the Segformer model. The extracted cropland and waterbody were denoted as GSC and GSW, respectively. Secondly, a parameter tuning method is developed based on histogram analysis of small water bodies in VH, VV, and GSW data, allowing for determination of the optimal parameter for waterbody identification. Subsequently, a waterbody extraction method is constructed via MCW on Sentinel-1 SAR imagery. The cropland inundation is then obtained by filtering the extracted waterbody with GSC. Finally, the cropland inundation caused by intense rainfall is generated using QPE data. 3.1 Stage 1: Cropland extraction with semantic segmentation The two AOI layers GSC and GSW were extracted by proposed method. Among them, the GSC has two purposes: 1) serve as a benchmark to assess the 6 existing cropland AOIs data; 2) to construct the cropland inundation mapping algorithm, by combining cropland filter with potential flood identification. The GSW also has two purposes: 1) serve as a benchmark to assess how many permanent waterbodies were incorrectly included in the cropland AOI data; 2) to test the optimal parameters of MCW and active contour by CV segmentations suitable for provincial-scale application. 3.1.1 Sampling by active learning strategy The active learning strategy starts by labelling some image tiles and training the Segformer model by this initial sample set. The model is then used to predict croplands across the entire study area. Predicted labels are reviewed and fully corrected on tiles containing significant commission or omission errors. Corrected samples are added to the initial sample set, and the process is iterated. The iteration continues until no major artifacts or misidentifications are observed, serving as the criterion for stopping. This correction-based labeling approach significantly reduces time compared to hand-labeling all samples. In our implementation, cropland labeling commenced with tiles from the Nansha District in Guangzhou City. The active learning cycles were repeated a total of 9 times (Fig. 3 ). Similarly, the identification of waterbodies followed a similar approach but required fewer samples and was repeated 6 times.  3.1.2 Segformer model The SegFormer semantic segmentation model consists of two main modules: 1) a hierarchical Transformer encoder, which generates high-resolution coarse features and low-resolution fine features; and 2) a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) decoder, which is to fuse these multi-level features to produce the final semantic segmentation AOI (Xie et al. 2021 ). The framework of SegFormer is shown in Fig. 6  . The encoder of SegFormer has four Transformer blocks, while each block can be divided into three main parts, including the Efficient Self-Attention layer, Mix-FFN layer, and Overlap Patch Merging layer. The structure and improvements of each part are briefly depicted as follows. 1) Efficient Self-Attention layer. This layer is the main computation bottleneck of the encoders. In the original multi-head self-attention process, each of the heads Q , K , V    have the same dimensions N × C   , where N = H × W    is the length of the sequence, and C is the channel number. The self-attention is expressed as following:(1) A t t e n t i o n Q , K , V   = S o f t m a x Q K  T   d head            where d head     is the dimension of the head. The computational complexity of this process is O N  2      . To reduce it, a reduction ratio R is introduced to reduce the length of the sequence. It is first reshaped into N / R × C Â · R      and then simplified by a fully connected layer. Therefore, the new K has dimensions N / R × C   . As a result, the complexity of the self-attention mechanism is reduced to O N  2  / R     . 2) Mix-FFN layer. ViT uses positional encoding (PE) to express the location information. It influences the test accuracy when the image resolution is not the same as in the training because the positional code needs to be interpolated. To alleviate this, Mix-FFN considers the effect of zero padding to leak location information, and a 3 × 3 convolution is used in the feed-forward network (FFN). Mix-FFN can be formulated as following:(2) X out   = M L P G E L U Conv  3 × 3   M L P X in           + X in        where X in     is the feature from the self-attention module. Mix-FFN mixes a 3 × 3 convolution and an MLP into each FFN. The Gaussian error linear unit (GELU) is an activation function. X out     is the output of the Mix-FFN. 3) Overlap Patch Merging layer. This is a simple but useful improvement. The patch merging in ViT is designed to combine non-overlapping image or feature patches; thus it in fails to preserve the local continuity around those patches. Instead, this layer use an overlapping patch merging strategy. The decoder of SegFormer consists of only MLP layers. This avoids the handcrafted and computationally demanding components typically used in other methods. The All-MLP decoder consists of four main steps: 1) Multi-level features from the encoder go through an MLP layer to unify the channel dimension. 2) Features are upsampled to 1/4th and concatenated together. 3) An MLP layer is adopted to fuse the concatenated features. 4) Another MLP layer use the fused feature to predict the segmentation AOI.  3.1.3 Data augmentation Appropriately augmenting the training samples can reduce the model's dependence on certain features, thereby improving the generalization ability of the model. Since VHR images are composed of multi-source satellite data, the data of each region differs in resolution and rendered colors. To simulate these situations, this study conducted three types of data augmentations, including flip, sharpness adjustment, and Hue-Saturation-Value (HSV) color adjustment. The parameter settings are shown in Table 2  . At last, the total sample size was 12 times the original size (Fig. 7  .).  3.1.4 Experimental setting The experiments were conducted on AMD EPYC 7452 32-Core CPU, with 512 GB RAM, and two NVIDIA GeForce GTX 3090 GPU. The Segformer implementation was based on MMsegmentation (https://github  com/open-mmlab/mmsegmentation) by PyTorch (Paszke et al. 2019 ). MMSegmentation provided several parameter settings that apply to different data sets. We use default training setting that configured for Cityscapes dataset. Among them, the loss function is the cross-entropy loss, the learning rate value is 10–6 , the number of iterations is 160,000, the weights using MiT-b2 were pre-trained based on ImageNet-1 K dataset. Before model training, the VHR image tiles (size of 0.05° × 0.05°) and corresponding labels was clipped into image patches with size of 1024 × 1024 pixels. In this process, we refer to a pair of image patches and labels as a sample. Since Google and Mapbox images are composed of multi-source satellite data, the data of each region differs in resolution and rendered colors. There are a total of 94,632 and 26,400 augmented samples for cropland and waterbody respectively. In addition, the total sample set is split into 3 subsets including training, validation, and testing, the proportions of which account for 70 %, 15 % and 15 % respectively. In order to compare the performance of seven AOI datasets, we unified the resolution of the each AOI to 10 m. Among them, the GSC was is upscaled from 0.6 m to 10 m resolution, FCS30, GL30, and SLOPE were downscaled from 30 m to 10 m resolution.   3.2 Stage 2: Potential floods identification and AOI filtering Following pre-processing, the Sentinel-1A images were clipped into tiles of uniform size, each measuring 2000 × 2000 pixels, resulting in 956 tiles covering the study area. The potential flood area was then generated by applying marker-controlled watershed (MCW) segmentation to each tile. Finally, the cropland inundation map was derived by filtering the potential flood area using the GSC layer. Details of the MCW algorithm, along with a brief overview of other comparison algorithms, and the parameter tuning methods for all algorithms, will be introduced subsequently. 3.2.1 MCW segmentation The watershed algorithm is a classical method for image segmentation, renowned for its clear principles, precise boundary positioning, and rapid execution. In the context of extracting water bodies from SAR backscatter images using MCW, the process typically involves three steps: 1) Identifying markers: Marking areas in the image that are relatively confirmed to be water bodies or non-water regions. 2) Calculating image gradient: The Sobel operator is utilized to convolve the image and compute its gradient. 3) Performing MCW segmentation: The MCW segmentation algorithm iteratively expands the markers corresponding to water bodies or non-water regions and determines optimal boundaries based on the gradient between these markers. This process continues until the remaining unlabeled pixels are classified as either water bodies or non-water regions. In this study, a simple thresholding method with two parameters is applied to identifying the markers:w a t e r b o d i e s i f ρ ≤ T w     n o n w a t e r i f ρ > T nw             where Tw  and Tnw  are thresholds to identify waterbody/non-water with higher credibility in image ρ  .  3.2.2 Alternative segmentation algorithms for comparative analysis In addition to MCW segmentation, this study also evaluated the performance of Otsu, SGT, and CV segmentation for comparison. The Otsu thresholding automatically segment an image into two classes, typically waterbody and non-water, by minimizing the intra-class variance. It is considered a local adaptive method since it operates using tile-based statistics, where the optimal threshold varies for each tile. In contrast, the SGT is considered a global method, as its segmentation utilizes a uniform threshold across all tiles to differentiate between water bodies and non-water areas. However, this method underestimates the mixed pixels at the edge of the waterbody (Jiang et al. 2014 ). In comparison, both MCW and CV methods use the SGT method to generate the initial mask of waterbody, and then optimize the initial mask through certain rules. Among them, MCW adopts edge-based strategy and the CV adopts region-based strategy.  3.2.3 Parameters tuning To successfully apply MCW segmentation, it is important to choose the optimal parameters of Tw  and Tnw . We tested the backscatter coefficients in different AOIs using histogram analysis. Among them, The AOIs are divided into three categories including large waterbody, small waterbody, and cropland according to the GSC and GSW. The large and small waterbodies are distinguished by identify whether the area of a waterbody is larger than 25 ha, which corresponds to a 5 × 5 pixels. Both the VH and VV polarizations are tested and the observation period is in November 2021, which is the month with the least average precipitation between July 2021 and June 2022. Then, we observe the curves corresponding to each category of the histogram, and use the most representative curve characteristics as the basis for parameter selection (Fig. 8  ). Finally, using the GSW data as a reference, we test the highest accuracy that the algorithm can achieve in the entire area by exhaustive test all of the parameters within a certain range. This helps us to verify whether the proposed parameter tuning method is effective. In the potential flood identification algorithm, there are 3 modules that are replaceable, and we tested different options. Among them, the first module was between 2 options that whether AOI filtering was adopted. The second was between 3 image segmentation algorithms i.e. MCW, SGT, and CV. The last was between two polarizations, i.e. VH and VV. By combining different module options, we obtain 12 test scenarios. In addition, each scenario was performed on several parameters (Table 3  ). To make the accuracy of different algorithms comparable, the parameter T w    in three algorithms i.e. SGT, MCW, and CV were tested in the same value range. Note that the parameters λw  and λnw  in CV algorithm were set as a whole since they were related.   3.3 Validation approach The of image segmentation consists of 4 basic metrics: Precision, Recall, F1-score, and IoU.Precision = TP  TP + F P       Recall = TP  TP + F N       F - s c o r e = 2 ∗ P r e c i s i o n · R e c a l l  Precision + R e c a l l       IoU = TP  TP + F P + F N        where TP are true positive and TN are true negative, both of which are correct. FP is false positive that wrong identifications, and FN false negative that miss identifications. F1-score is the harmonic mean that balancing the importance of Precision and Recall. IoU refers to the consistency of the identified AOI with the in-situ AOI. Among them, the IoU is applied to assess the accuracy of GSC and GSW layer. In addition to consistency of GSC with 6 existing cropland layers. The Precision, Recall, and F-Score is applied to assess the accuracy of waterbody extracted by Sentinel-1 imagery. It should be noted that we set an evaluation criterion: the result F-score are worth considering only if the corresponding precision and recall are both greater than 0.8 (PRG80). The Segformer model was trained and evaluated for 9 iterations using incrementally labelled samples. At last iteration, the number of total samples is reach to 94,632. In each iteration, if verified by the test samples in the current iteration, the accuracy of the model is above 89 %. However, when we verify the model using the final sample set, we find that the accuracy of the model varies greatly. Among them, the highest IoU reached to 89.65 % at last iteration, while the lowest IoU achieved is only 38.54 % at first iteration. In addition, the most significant improvement in IoU is in third iteration, which reached to 83.69 % comparing with 42.14 % in the second iteration. The most notable characteristic of this area is that it has rich diversity of cropland, gardens, plantation land and bare land. These are the most confusing categories, since the appearance of cropland may change with crop types, seasons, and management. The highest IoU of waterbody was achieved to 96.46 %. The reason is that, compared with croplands, waterbodies are easier to identify in image and is almost no need to consider seasonal influences.  4.2 Comparison of the seven cropland data We validated 7 existing cropland layers including ESA, ESRI FCS30, FROM, GL30, SLOPE, and GSC (Fig. 9   a-g) using statistical area and GSW layer. Then we assessed consistency of 6 existing cropland AOIs data wtih GSC. (1) Proportion of cropland AOI area to statistical area (PCS): compare the overall area of cropland AOI data with the statistical area. Among the 7 AOIs (Table 5  ), the areas of GSC, ESA and ESRI are reasonable estimated, accounting for 88.0 % to 96.13 % of the official reported cropland area. However, the areas of FCS30, FROM, GL30, and SLOPE are significantly over estimated, since their area is equivalent to 2 to 3 times of official statistics. (2) Proportion of the permanent waterbodies to croplands (PWC): analyzed the proportion of permanent waterbodies in the 7 cropland layers (Table 6  ). The GSC achieved the lowest PWC of 1.54 %. There were few permanent waterbodies contained in GSC. The error mainly came from misclassification of paddy fields and fish ponds. Then, the PWC of ESRI is relatively low which accounts for 5.31 %. Then follow by FROM and ESA, which is 11.88 % and 16.03 %, respectively. We found that a large number of errors came from areas where fish ponds are densely distributed. For GL30 and FCS30, the PWC is up to 26.25 % to 38.35 %. This show that the image with a resolution of 30 m is incapable to identify the small ponds. From above analysis, the 4 cropland AOI data FCS30, FROM, GL30 and SLOPE are not suitable for the mapping of cropland inundation, thus they are excluded and only GSC, ESA and ESRI are considered in subsequent analysis. (3) Consistency: cross calculate the IoU of GSC, ESA, and ESRI to evaluate their consistency, the results were shown in Fig. 10  . In plain regions, taking GSC as the benchmark, the IoU achieved by ESRI (52.07 %) and ESA (48.31 %) is relatively high. However, the IoU of ESA and ESRI is only 40.71 %. The major difference between ESA and ESRI is that ESA contains more permanent waterbodies in plain regions. In mountainous regions, the IoU of GSC and other AOIs are overall lower than that in plain regions. Especially, the IoU related with ESRI is smaller than 19 %. This is mainly due to ESRI underestimation (Fig. 11  ) and misclassification of croplands in mountainous regions. To sum up, the GSC has three main advantages including high accuracy, mostly excluded the permanent waterbodies, and the area is close to the statistical value, in contrast to other 6 existing cropland data. Thus, it is a reasonable choice to use GSC to build algorithm of cropland inundation mapping in following section.  4.3 Performance of potential flood identification algorithms The maximum F-score (Fig. 12  ) obtained for each test was chosen as accuracy evaluation metric. It should be noted that when the SGT method was applied to the VV data, the results could not meet the criteria of PRG80. But for the completeness of Fig. 12 , we choose the F-score that most closely satisfies PRG80 criterion as an alternative. (1) Visual Comparison of Module Performance in Waterbody Extraction Methods. The results of waterbody extraction within the study area using VH data with four segmentation algorithms, with and without AOI filtering, were illustrated in Fig. 13  . Note that the VV data yields similar results across the entire region, and thus is not shown for simplicity. It is evident that regardless of the segmentation algorithm utilized, AOI filtering is crucial as it effectively eliminates a substantial number of predominantly induced by radar shadows. Notably, Otsu segmentation demonstrates the poorest performance, exhibiting the most pronounced over-estimation when AOI filtering is not applied (Fig. 13 a). Additionally, discontinuous artifacts are noticeable in the results across different tiles, which persist with or without AOI filtering (Fig. 13 a and b). The differences among the other three algorithms are less apparent, a more detailed examination is as follows. (2) Metrics Comparison of Module Performance in Waterbody Extraction Methods. Results show that, among the three modules, the AOI filtering plays a significant impact on the F-score. The F-score derived by with AOI filtering were ranging from 0.712 to 0.837, while methods without AOI filtering were ranging from 0.593 to 0.685. In contrast, the differences between each polarization data used were smaller. For segmentation algorithms, except for Otsu, the differences between other three algorithms were small. We were still able to find out, regardless of other module chosen, the F-score derived from VH band were all higher than those from VV band. Among the four algorithms, while AOI filtering incorporated, the order of accuracy is CV, MCW, SGT, and Otsu. The reason are discussed in Section 5.2 . (3) Parameter tuning difficulty. We further analyzed the variation in accuracy with parameters changing of three algorithms i.e. CV, MCW, and SGT. The Otsu is not including in this analysis since it is a nonparametric method. The derived F-score were listed in two matrices (Fig. 14  a and b), which corresponding to VH and VV bands. Each matrix contains the F-score derived from three algorithm with AOI filtering. In Fig. 14 , the parameter T w    of the three methods were set as x-axis, while other parameters, which were T nw     in MCW method and λw  with λnw  in CV method, were represented as y-axis. The results shown that: In all tests with the parameters in Table 3 , the F-score derived by VH band is higher than derived by VV band, regardless the algorithms used. In terms of highest F-score obtained, the three algorithms rank from high to low are CV, MCW, and SGT. However, once the T w    parameter of CV corresponding to the highest F-score is increased or decreased by 0.5, the obtained F-score will not satisfy the PRG80 criterion. This indicates that the CV algorithm is quite sensitive to the T w    parameter. Consider the R P R G 80     of SGT, MCW, and CV algorithms. For VH data, they were 0.111, 0.185, and 0.037, respectively. For VV data, they were 0, 0.024, and 0.019, respectively. Compared with CV, the MCW has greater flexibility with respect to parameter tuning. Therefore, in the subsequent monthly cropland inundation area analysis, we all adopted the VH data, as well as the MCW method with the optimal parameters e.g. T w    and T nw     were set as –22.0 and −14.0 (Fig. 8 ). (4) Computing time. We evaluated the computational time of Otsu, SGT, CV, and MCW over the study region using the parameters corresponding to the highest F-score obtained in the VH band. Table 7   illustrates significant differences in the computational time of the four methods. Specifically, the Otsu, MCW and CV method took 3, 57 and 1625 times longer as the SGT method, respectively.  4.4 Spatiotemporal pattern of cropland inundation caused by intense rainfall The spatial and temporal progress of rainfall floods was observed from the monthly maps of cropland inundation caused by intense rainfall (CIIR), as shown in Fig. 15  . The monthly CIIR map is obtained by combining all single cropland inundation map within each month, and then filtered by mask where monthly cumulative precipitation of QPE data is greater than 400 mm. The analysis of monthly CIIR maps showed that the flooded croplands was generally occurred in large regions and scattered in small fragmented areas. The monthly CIIR area varied approximately ranging from 6.6 km2  to 436.1 km2  in Guangdong during monsoon season (May to July) of 2017–2022. During the peak flooding stage, the monthly CIIR area covers approximately 2.6 % of Guangdong. Within the study period, the maximum three monthly CIIR area were occurred in July 2022, May and June 2022, respectively. The minimum three monthly CIIR area were occurred in July 2020, May 2017, and May 2020. The monthly CIIR area of 21 cities in Guangdong were shown in Fig. 16  . Sorted by the sum of monthly CIIR area in 18 months, the cities mostly vulnerable to cropland inundation disasters are Jiangmen, Yangjiang, Qingyuan, Zhanjiang, Shanwei, Maoming, and Shaoguan. Among these cities, the distribution of monthly CIIR in Zhanjiang City is relatively concentrated. This is because the proportion of mountainous areas in Zhanjiang is only 9 % and has the largest croplands area in Guangdong. Although the intense rainfall is small, the area of croplands affected is relatively large. In contrast, the distribution of monthly CIIR in other 6 cities are relatively scattered (Fig. 16 ), since the proportion of mountainous areas in other 6 cities are all exceeds 50 %.   5 Discussion 5.1 Evaluation of various cropland map Accurate cropland maps play a crucial role in assessing crop flood disasters in mountain dominated agricultural environments. However, existing public cropland data often lack the required accuracy, particularly in South China, which is characterized by rugged terrain and fragmented agricultural landscape. Therefore, the primary goal of this research is to develop an automated procedure for producing high-precision cropland maps suitable for our study areas. The results demonstrated that the resolution of the data source plays a decisive role in the accuracy of cropland data. Although the declared global accuracy of the five data ESRI, ESA FCS30, FROM, and GL30 are as high as 72 % to 86.0 % (Table 1 ). These accuracies are only valid for samples with the same resolutions (10–30 m). If the data is verified with samples of higher resolution, the accuracy will be greatly reduced. The lowest accuracy were obtained by four 30 m level cropland layers including FCS30, FROM, GL30, and SLOPE. The areas of four layers are significantly over estimated to 2 to 3 times of official statistics. Subsequently, the 10 m level ESRI and ESA were superior to the four layers. The areas of ESA and ESRI are close to official statistics, but there are still some defects. Typically, the ESA contained 16.04 % of false positives that comprised instances of permanent waterbodies (Fig. 17  b) and the ESRI is seriously underestimated in mountainous region that its IoU with GSC is smaller than 18 % (Fig. 17 g and k). Besides, there are many linear false positives including roads and ridges in plain area on ESA and ESRI data (Fig. 17 n and o). These errors can significantly impact the accuracy of cropland inundation mapping. Ultimately, the GSC data at the 0.6-meter level exhibit superiority in three key aspects: high accuracy, exclusion of fishery ponds, and proximity to the statistical area, when compared with six publicly available cropland datasets. It's worth mentioning that the lack of timely updates in Google Earth and Mapbox images can pose challenges, particularly when it comes to detecting changes like the conversion of cropland into other artificial surfaces or the construction of new cropland. However, this issue isn't a significant concern for Guangdong. Statistical data provided by the Guangdong Department of Natural Resources reveals that the largest variation in cropland area over the four-year period from 2019 to 2022 amounts to just 0.40 % of the total cropland area in 2022.  5.2 Uncertainty analysis in potential flood identification The second objective of this study is to explain why proposed method is more suitable for flood identification under mountainous region. Among the three modules in proposed method including polarization, segmentation algorithm, and AOI filtering: The most significant and important improvements is achieved by using AOI filtering, the F-score of the potential flood identification using VH data and MCW with AOI filtering was increased from 0.685 to 0.828. In contrast, the different options in other two modules result in less improvements. The VH data outperforms VV data, irrespective of the algorithms chosen. This can be explained by, the VV data is more sensitive to surface roughness than VH data. Thus VV data usually result in less FP on smooth surfaces but more false negatives of waterbody than the VH data (Twele et al. 2016 ). Among the four waterbody segmentation algorithms, Otsu segmentation demonstrates the poorest performance, particularly it will produce discontinuous artifacts in the results across adjacent tiles. This is consistent with our assumption that a simple local-adaptive algorithm is not suitable for areas with complex scenes and frequent changes. For other three algorithms MCW, CV, and SGT. Although CV achieve the highest accuracy. When the optimal parameters are slightly changed, the accuracy decreases immediately and cannot meet the PRG80 principle. In contrast, the results of MCW are stable. The advantage is that the parameters are easy to obtain. Combined with histogram analysis (Fig. 8 ), we can now conclude that the two parameters Tw  and Tnw  of MCW are highly correlated with the value range of small waterbodies. In practice, the values of two parameter ​​can be roughly estimated only by knowing the high and low values ​​of small waterbodies, which makes it easy for the MCW method to determine the parameters. Through the above discussion, we think that that accurately eliminate a large number of FPs is crucial to accuracy of potential flood identification where excessive FP exists. In comparison, the choice of polarization method and segmentation algorithm has less impact on the accuracy. It should be emphasized that the abrupt and gradual changes of floods may impact mapping accuracy. Satellite-based SAR technology detects inundation areas through scattering mechanisms. Typically, an abrupt changing water may increase the roughness of water surface, leading to higher backscatter coefficients. This potentially affects the accuracy of threshold-based water identification algorithms.  5.3 Challenges and implications Assessing crop damage following extreme rainfall typically involves a comprehensive evaluation that considers both local agricultural conditions, including crop practices and soil characteristics, and the hydraulic conditions of the event, such as duration, velocity, intensity, and the quantity of material transported (Samuele et al. 2022 ). While the proposed method can provide a rough estimation of cropland inundation area at a large scale, achieving a comprehensive assessment of crop damage requires additional information: 1) Water persistence: The water persistence significantly influences the extent of crop damage. Continuous monitoring of water persistence is essential for effective assessment. However, open accessible SAR data is not as prevalent, with Sentinel being the most widely accessible option. However, with the inoperability of Sentinel-1B since December 23, 2021, the observation interval is limited to 12 days using Sentinel-1A alone. Except for areas between adjacent satellite orbits, allowing for two observations to be obtained (Fig. 18  ). To ensure timely and comprehensive flood monitoring, it is imperative to complement Sentinel-1 data with other SAR imagery sources, such as the Chinese GF-3 satellite. 2) Inundation type: During extreme rainy events, inundation areas can be attributed to either floods or soil saturation. In soil-saturated areas, stagnant water appears clearer due to fewer sediments, primarily caused by rainfall. This water can be absorbed by soil or flowed away, resulting in a minor damage. In contrast, flooded areas are characterized by water influenced by river dynamics, containing numerous sediments and debris. Additionally, the high laminar force of water flowing across fields can lead to crop lodging. Classifying the type of inundation requires multiple datasets, including topography, soil type, drainage infrastructure, and proximity to rivers or water bodies, as detailed in the work by (Samuele et al. 2022 ). 3) Crop parcels: In this study, the extracted cropland was not subdivided into individual parcels. However, achieving this level of granularity (plot level) would better describe damages within the agronomic context. To overcome this limitation, we are investigating the use of instance segmentation techniques. 4) Crop Type and Phenology: Floods can enhance crop condition by depositing nutrients or water during the early phenological stages; however, during late stages, they may compromise yield. Hence, accurately identifying crop type and phenological stage is crucial. Typically, crop identification relies on analyzing time series observation curves throughout the complete phenological period of the crop. Exploring methods to obtain crop type information through remote sensing during the early stages of planting is a promising avenue for future research.   6 Conclusion In this paper, a robust framework of cropland inundation mapping for mountainous region based on multi-resolution imageries is proposed. A high-precision cropland is extracted based on Google/Mapbox VHR imagery with Segformer model, which is built using samples collected iteratively via active learning strategy. Then, the cropland inundation area is obtained using MCW segmentation on Sentinel-1 SAR imagery with AOI filtering. Results indicated that the IoU of extracted cropland and ground truth achieved to 89.65 %, while other 6 public cropland data products have shortcomings including over-estimating area, misidentifying ponds, or omitting mountain croplands. In addition, with AOI filtering, the F-score of the potential flood identification using MCW was increased from 0.685 to 0.828. At last, the monthly cropland inundation caused by intense rainfall varied approximately from 6.6 km2  to 436.1 km2  during monsoon season of 2017–2022 in Guangdong. The estimated cropland inundation area is helpful to the government for food security evaluations. This study also illustrates the necessity of high-precision cropland data for cropland disaster monitoring. Future study will be dedicated to developing methods for identifying detailed information on damage levels for different crop types.
1 Introduction The years 2015–2022 were recorded as the eight warmest on record, with 2022 recorded as the fifth warmest since 1880 (WMO, 2022). The global mean temperature in 2022 was 1.15 °C [1.02–1.28] above the 1880–1900 average (WMO, 2022). In addition to large-scale warming, 2022 will be remembered for its unprecedented hot summers (Lu et al., 2022 ). The Eurasian continent and North America suffered from extraordinarily long-lasting extreme heat events. In 2022, China experienced the most extreme and longest drought since records began in 1961, which spread across central, eastern, and southern China (Lin et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2022 ). Droughts in Sichuan Province and the Yangtze River Basin led to water resource and power shortages and caused adverse effects on the lives and productivity of local people (Hao et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2022; Zhang 2022). Severe droughts caused water levels to drop considerably in Poyang Lake, which is the largest freshwater lake in China. However, in contrast to the high temperatures and droughts in eastern China, flooding occurred in the arid regions of northwest China. In August 2022, unprecedented floods occurred in the Tarim River Basin (TRB), the driest region of arid Central Asia and the longest endorheic river in China. From mid-June to early September, flooding spread across almost all of the alpine headwaters and the main stream of the TRB, with the longest running and largest runoff volumes since records began in 1957. In addition, flooding lasted for 80 d along the main stream of the TRB. Unprecedented heat waves and droughts in large parts of the Northern Hemisphere (NH) were responsible for the extraordinary atmospheric circulation in the summer of 2022 (Lu et al., 2022 ). The El Niño–Southern Oscillation is the most important driver of weather and climatic events worldwide. However, La Niña conditions emerged in mid-2020 and continued until late 2022, marking a third consecutive year (WMO, 2022). The Indian Ocean Dipole contributes to major weather and climatic events worldwide. In addition, the western North Pacific subtropical high (WPSH), plays a major role in Asian weather and climatic events and global atmospheric circulation (Lu and Dong, 2001; Zhou et al., 2009; He et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2015; Wu and Wang, 2015 ; Liu et al., 2019), which extended farther westward in the summer of 2022. At the mid-latitudes, unusual westerly winds swept across the globe and brought additional rainfall to northern China. However, the reason for the extraordinary atmospheric circulation in the summer of 2022 is an interesting scientific issue. Many high-impact events occurred worldwide in 2022. In addition to high temperatures and droughts, extreme rainfall was another high-impact event that occurred throughout the year. In conjunction with these factors, it led to other high-impact events such as devastating flooding. Floods were particularly severe in Pakistan, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Southern Africa, and the arid regions of China during the summer of 2022 (WMO, 2022). The factors driving floods varied across locations and primarily included heavy rainfall and snow/glacial melt. In alpine glacierized catchments, floods were affected by high temperatures in addition to heavy rainfall, and the flood magnitude was dependent on the rainfall and snow/glacier melt contributions to discharge (Fang et al., 2018 , 2022). The lengthy and persistent heat waves during the summer of 2022 caused global cryospheric changes, leading to massive glacial losses. For example, in the European Alps, glacial mass loss broke records in 2022 (WMO, 2022). The western Third Pole area, including Tian Shan, the Pamir Plateau, Karakoram, and adjacent mountains, is the most glacierized (>50 % of the area) and snow-concentrated region (Su et al., 2022 ). Glacial meltwater plays an important role in sustaining water supplies downstream from river basins (Biemans et al., 2019; Pritchard, 2019 ), particularly in the Syr Darya, Arm Darya, and Tarim Rivers, which rely heavily on mountain meltwater from glaciers (Duethmann et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2018 ). The Tarim River is located in the alpine region of Central Asia and originates in the Tianshan, Pamir, Karakorum, and Kunlun Mountains (Fang et al., 2022). Mountain-sourced water plays an important role in the hydrological processes and water supply downstream of the TRB (Fang et al., 2018 ). These alpine waters are recharged by rainfall and snow/glacier melt, which are highly dependent on the glacierization of alpine tributaries. Increasing temperatures and related increases in glacial meltwater dominate streamflow trends in the Aksu River, which is a glacial melt-dominated catchment of the Tarim River (Duethmann et al., 2015 ). Flood patterns are primarily influenced by catchment characteristics and weather conditions. TRB floods mostly begin in the upper mountains, and the downstream river flood is formed by floods upstream of the mountainous area. TRB flood patterns are dominated by heavy rainfall, high temperatures, and mixed floods (Zhang Q, et al., 2015; Mao et al., 2016). Previous investigations focused on TRB flooding changes and the contributions of climatic factors to these changes but ignored the hydro-meteorological drivers and the large-scale circulation driving mechanism of extreme flooding. Summer floods along the Tarim River in 2022 were the most extensive since 1957, raising major concerns regarding their socioeconomic impact. In this study, we investigated the hydro-climatological drivers of extreme floods in August 2022 along the Tarim River, Central Asia.  2 Study area, data and methods 2.1 TRB The TRB is located in southern Xinjiang, China (Fig. 1  ). It is the largest arid inland river basin in China with an area of 1.02 million km2 . The TRB is surrounded by high mountains, including Tianshan in the north, Eastern Pamir and Karakorum in the west, and Kunlun in the south (Fang et al., 2022). The Tarim River is China's longest inland river and is now mostly recharged by four major headwaters: the Yarkant, Aksu, Hotan, and Kaidu Rivers. The basin is characterized by low precipitation and high evaporation (Zhang et al., 2015 ). The mean annual precipitation in the mountainous regions is > 300 mm, with > 54 % of the annual precipitation occurring between June and August (Tao et al., 2011 ). The Tarim River is fed by snowmelt, glacier melt and precipitation in headwaters in the mountains, which drain into the TRB, and peak flow months are July, August and September (Tao et al., 2011 ). In this study, five typical river water systems were selected for flood analysis according to their geographical locations: the Aksu, Yarkant, Hotan, and Kaidu River systems (Table 1   and Fig. 1 ).  2.2 Diagnosis of the August 2022 event We examined the state of the climate in the TRB during the summer of 2022 and the extreme flood events. We obtained the observed daily precipitation and maximum temperatures (TEM_Max) at more than 1000 automated meteorological stations in the TRB from the China Meteorology Administration (CMA) during the summer of 2022. These observed datasets capture rainfall variability due to orography along the river from 1000 to 5500 m, which is an essential feature of the TRB. For the same period, the daily and maximum discharges were obtained from the Xinjiang Tarim River Basin Management Bureau. These stations are associated with different tributaries of the Tarim River, including the Aksu and Kaidu Rivers located on the southern slope of the Tianshan Mountains, and the Yarkand, Hotian, and Cherchen Rivers located on the northern slope of the Kunlun Mountains. We used the daily maximum discharge to investigate TRB floods and their driving factors. The flooding recession was rapid and shows a steep curve, whereas the base flow recession was gradual and gentle because of the different flow processes causing the flow. Thus, we used inspection of the flow curves to examine the flood flow periods (Ng et al., 2007 ). Monthly anomalies in cumulative precipitation, mean temperature, and TEM_Max in the TRB were calculated for 34 climate stations based on the 1991–2020 monthly mean. We also used daily gridded meteorological data for precipitation, TEM_Max, and incoming shortwave radiation at the surface from the ERA 5 dataset.  2.3 Definition of flood driving mechanisms In this study, we focused on processes that drive flooding (rainfall, or snowmelt). According to Berghuijs et al. (2016), three major mechanisms may lead to flooding: rainfall, excess soil moisture, and snowmelt. The TRB is an arid region that experienced high temperatures and drought processes during the previous period; thus, we assumed that floods were only caused by heavy rainfall or snowmelt water, which individually or jointly stimulated flood events (Sivapalan et al., 2005; Pall et al., 2011 ; Berghuijs et al., 2016, 2019; Zhang et al., 2016; Blöschl et al., 2017 ). Extreme precipitation:  In extreme precipitation floods, flood occurrence and extreme precipitation should fall into the same period of the year (Fang et al., 2022). Snowmelt:  In snowmelt floods, the peak flow is caused by (and thus occurs during the same time of the year as) the largest daily snowmelt of the same period of the year. The daily melt was calculated based on an empirical degree–day model (Shangguan et al., 2017 ):(1) M = max T a v g   , 0    ∙ D D F      where M  (mm water equivalent) is the daily melt, max represents the maximum of the two values, Tavg   (°C) is the daily average air temperature, and DDF  (mm °C−1  d-1 ) is a degree–day factor for snow and ice in glaciers, established at 2 mm per day per °C (Berghuijs et al., 2019 ).  2.4 Large-scale atmospheric drivers of August 2022 extreme floods The near-surface atmospheric drivers of extreme floods were investigated using the ERA 5 dataset and CMA-observed products. Based on the CMA automated meteorological observation network, we analyzed the distribution patterns of TEM_Max and precipitation at different altitudes in the TRB during August 2022 according to a 500-m altitude gradient. We also selected six representative observation stations with different elevation gradients in each watershed to reveal the relationship between TEM_Max (or precipitation) and flood evolution. Daily large-scale atmospheric conditions were examined using data from the National Center for Atmospheric Prediction/National Center for Environmental Prediction (NCAR/NCEP) Reanalysis 1 project (Kalnay et al., 1996 ), which is globally available at a spatial resolution of 2.5°(https://psl.noaa.gov/data/composites/day/  ). For the summer analysis, we used the WPSH and Iran Subtropical High (ISH) to describe the atmospheric circulation in the lower- and mid-troposphere in summer. The WPSH and ISH variabilities were measured using 500 hPa geopotential height fields. According to the method of Liu et al. (2019), the WPSH intensity index was defined by the sum of the cumulative area encircled by the 5880 gpm isobar within the region bounded by 110°E–180°E and 10°N–70°N, and the difference between the grid point heights exceeding 5880 and 5870 gpm, respectively. The westernmost point of the WPSH was defined by the longitude of the westernmost 5880 gpm isolines within the ranges of 90°E–180°N and 10°N–70°N. If this lies west of 90°E, it is uniformly denoted as 90°E. The definition of the ISH intensity index was similar to that of the WPSH intensity, except for the ranges of 20°W–60°E and 10°N–60°N. The daily WPSH intensities and location features were downloaded from the National Climate Center (NCC/CMA, http://cmdp.ncc-cma.net/download/precipitation/diagnosis/wpshdaily/wpsh_idx_daily.txt  ) based on the NCAR/NCEP database (Liu et al., 2019), and the mean August values were calculated for the 1991–2020 period. The daily ISH intensity index was downloaded from the NCC/CMA (http://cmdp.ncc-cma.net/Monitoring/cn_index_130.php  ). We used the 500 hPa geopotential height data (HGT 500) averaged temporally over the three periods used for the analysis: early August (1–10), mid-August (11–20), and late August (21–31).   3 Results 3.1 Record floods From May–September 2022, unprecedented floods spread across almost all the alpine headwaters and the main stream of the extensive endorheic TRB in Central Asia. The TRB alpine headwater runoff volume during this period was 1.5 times higher than that during a similar period during the year, which broke the record observed in the TRB since 1957. Twenty-five rivers, including the main stream of the TRB and its alpine headwaters, the Yarkand, Hotian, and Aksu Rivers, experienced excessive flood discharge warnings. Moreover, seven rivers, including the Yurungkash, Kalakash, and Kashgar Rivers, and the main stream of the TRB exceeded the guaranteed discharge floods. The flood events lasted for 80 d in the main stream of the TRB. The floods in the summer of 2022 occurred earlier and lasted longer in almost all the tributaries. For example, the Tuoshigan and Aksu Rivers flooded 42 and 27 d earlier, respectively, than the previous year. The duration of the excessive discharge warning in the main stream of the TRB was significantly prolonged, which also broke the historical record. Many types of floods occurred during this period across the TRB alpine headwaters, such as rainstorm, snowmelt, and glacial outburst floods, which appeared to compound floods events. During the summer of 2022, extensive flooding in the TRB occurred from August 10–22, and the peak flood discharge gradually decreased after August 22. During this TRB flood process, the maximum daily flood peak discharges and occurrence dates showed significant differences between the main stream of the TRB and those of its alpine headwaters (Table 2  ). In the headwaters of the Aksu River and the main stream of the Tarim River, the maximum flood peak discharge occurred on August 10–11, and the average discharge increased from 868 m3 /s to 1072 m3 /s on August 10. The maximum flood peak discharge of the rivers on Kunlun Mountains occurred on August 14–18, and the flooding process was significantly different between the eastern and western regions. As typical rivers in the eastern Kunlun Mountains, the Cherchen and Yurungkash rivers have similar flood processes, with longer durations of excessive flood discharge warnings. For example, flooding at the Tongguziluok station on the Yurungkash River lasted for 11 d, with the maximum flood peak discharge occurring much earlier (August 14). In the western Kunlun Mountains on the Yarkant and Kalakash Rivers, flooding was consistent, and flood levels increased dramatically over time. The above-mentioned rivers experienced maximum floods on August 17; the maximum flood discharge at the Kakun station on the Yarkand River was twice the average discharge of the previous period (August 3–11), and that of the Tuoman station on the Kalakash River was 2.7 times that of the previous period. Flooding of the Kaidu River, which originates in the Tianshan Mountains, stabilized, and the maximum flood discharge at the Dashankou station (August 19) was 1.97 times that of the average during the previous period (August 3–11). Thus, there were significant differences in the flood processes of rivers originating from different TRB regions. Fig. 2   also shows the differences in flooding times in different basins. Specifically, flooding in the northern Kunlun Mountains (in the Yarkand and Hotian Rivers) occurred later than that in the Tianshan Mountains (in the Aksu River), and the floods in the latter receded quickly. Flood recession is dominated by the driving factors that caused the flood. Generally, recession of flooding caused by extreme rainfall is rapid and exhibits a steep curve, whereas recession of flooding caused by high temperature is gradual and gentle because of the meltwater processes that caused the flood. Thus, we further hypothesized that the Aksu River flood was dominated by extreme rainfall and the Chelchen and Yurungkash River floods were dominated by high temperatures.  3.2 Climate state and extremes during summer 2022 3.2.1 TRB climate state during summer 2022 Unprecedented heat waves scorched many regions of the global surface during the summer of 2022. The average summer air temperature across continental China in 2022 broke records established in 1961, at an observed 1.1 °C above normal (1991–2020) levels (CMA, 2022). From June 13 to August 30, 2022, several regions in China experienced record-breaking high-temperature events, with the longest-running, most extensive area recording > 40 ℃; the most intense since observed records began in 1961, according to monitoring by the CMA. In addition, there was a lack of rain across China during the summer of 2022. The Yangtze River Basin in southern China experienced the worst drought on record, combined with high temperatures and little rain. The average summer temperature in the TRB in 2022 was recorded as the warmest since 1961 and was 0.9℃ higher than that of the average summer temperature of 1991–2020 (Fig. 3  a). High-temperature days (defined as daily TEM_Max reaching or exceeding 35 °C) in summer exceeded 30 d in the TRB and increased by 7.6 d over the normal levels. The increase in the number of high-temperature days in the summer of 2022 was the greatest in the observational record in the TRB, and the Yarkand River Basin had the greatest number of high-temperature days. Daily TEM_Max broke records in seven counties in the TRB, including Yuepuhu, Alar, and Maigati. In addition, six counties in the TRB (including Bachu, Yingjisha, and Tashkurgan) ranked second in the historical records. Thus, the TRB experienced record-breaking high-temperature processes and high-temperature days during the summer of 2022. The 2022 summer precipitation in the TRB was 32.3 mm, which was 11 % less than the 1991–2020 average (Fig. 3 b). Spatially, regions with additional precipitation anomalies were in the western TRB and on the northern slopes of the Kunlun Mountains. Summer precipitation in the upper reaches of the Aksu and Yarkand River Basins was more than double the average during summer. The summer precipitation in the upper reaches of the Aksu River and Yarkand River Basin was more than double the average summer precipitation. Precipitation was primarily distributed in August and was 105 % above the average August precipitation for 1991–2020, whereas precipitation during June and July was 50 % less than the normal levels. The frequency of short-term severe convective weather was high, and local extreme heavy precipitation occurred frequently in the TRB, with a total of three extreme heavy precipitation events during August 2022.  3.2.2 TRB high temperatures and extreme rainfall during the August 2022 extreme floods The TRB experienced significantly high temperatures and precipitation in the mountainous regions in August 2022. The TRB had a significant daily TEM_Max temperature lapse rate (TLR) during August 2022. The daily TEM_Max TLR below 3000 m was higher, whereas the TLR above 3000 m was more stable (Fig. 4  ). In terms of the 500 m altitude gradient, the average TEM_Max decreased from 32.4℃ below 1000 m to 19.5℃ in the 2500–3000 m gradient, with little change evident in the 2500–3000 and 3500–4000 m gradients, decreasing from 19.5℃ to 17.7℃. The TEM_Max in the gradient above 4000 m was more stable, and that in the 5000–5500 m gradient was 13.4℃, reflecting continuous high-temperature stability during August in the TRB alpine headwaters. The median daily precipitation for each elevation gradient in August was < 5 mm. Heavy rainfall primarily occurred in the central mountainous region between 1000–3000 m, whereas there was no obvious heavy rainfall in the area above 3000 m (Fig. 4 ). According to the accumulated precipitation distribution in August (Fig. 5  a), the TRB precipitation anomalies primarily occurred in the central mountain belt regions on the southern slopes of Tianshan Mountain and the northern slopes of Kunlun Mountain. The Yarkant, Aksu, and Kaidu River Basins were the most anomalous, with precipitation 1–4.3 times greater than the normal level. On August 16, an extremely heavy rainfall occurred over most of the TRB, primarily in the Yarkant River Basin (Fig. 5 b), with a maximum daily precipitation of 37.3 mm and 16 stations breaking the historical daily precipitation record for August.   3.3 Large-scale drivers of August 2022 extreme floods 3.3.1 Relationship between TRB floods and high temperatures, and extreme rainfall Based on high-density automated stations and ERA5 reanalysis data, Fig. 6   shows the spatial distribution of the 5-d average TEM_Max, accumulated precipitation, and incoming shortwave radiation at the surface for August 2022. The TEM_Max and precipitation spatial distributions shown by the two datasets were relatively consistent, however, the ERA5 data underestimated TEM_Max and accumulated precipitation compared to that obtained from the station observations. In the pre-flood period (August 1–5), the TRB was blanketed by high temperatures, including the alpine headwaters with temperatures > 20 ℃ and high shortwave radiation, with local heavy precipitation along the Yurungkash River only, however, no flooding occurred in the TRB. During the second period (August 6–10), the area and intensity of the high temperatures expanded further, and the shortwave radiation was stronger. Heavy rainfall occurred in the Aksu River headwaters, leading to flooding in the Tuoshigan and Kumalike Rivers (the Aksu River headwaters), on August 10, with the maximum flood discharges reaching 661 and 1070 m3 /s, respectively. The main stream of the Aksu River reached maximum flood discharge on August 11. From the meteorological gradient observations of the Aksu River, the TEM_Max remained stable at approximately 20 °C until August 20, after which the TEM_Max decreased by 10 °C, which was inconsistent with the flooding process (Fig. 6 a). Heavy rainfall occurred over the entire basin on August 10, increasing with elevation, and a daily rainfall of 38.6 mm was observed at 2695 m. This extreme precipitation in the Aksu River was consistent with the flooding process. Similarly, heavy rainfall was observed below 2500 m on August 2, however, there was no precipitation in the high-altitude region, and the river was at average discharge, indicating that high-altitude precipitation plays a key role in flooding along the Aksu River. Therefore, heavy precipitation at high altitudes against a background of high temperatures was the dominant factor driving the Aksu River floods on August 10–11. The high temperature area expanded, high temperatures and shortwave radiation intensities were enhanced during August 11–15, and heavy rainfall occurred primarily in the Yurungkash and Yarkand River headwaters. The maximum flood peaks were observed at Heishan and Tongguziluok stations on the Yurungkash River on August 14 with discharges of 927 and 1077 m3 /s, respectively, and at the Heiliyazi station of the Yarkand River headwaters on August 15 at 93.4 m3 /s. The high temperature and shortwave radiation areas and intensities in the TRB reached a maximum during August 16–20, with heavy rainfall occurring in both the Hotan and Yarkant Rivers. The Yarkant River Basin experienced extremely heavy rainfall on August 16, and the most severely affected areas were Yecheng and Shache Counties, which received daily rainfall of > 37 mm. The maximum flood peak occurred in the Yarkant River on August 17, with maximum discharges of 1470 and 1720 m3/ s at the Kulukalangan and Kaqun stations, respectively, and a maximum discharge of 1095 m3 /s at the Tuoman station on the Kalakash River. With continuous high temperatures and rainfall, the Yarkant River discharge increased slowly during the early period, and floods were caused by heavy precipitation (primarily at 2000–2600 m) during August 16–17, followed by rapid recession of the flood. For the Kalakash River, extremely heavy precipitation occurred in the alpine headwaters (>4000 m) with a maximum accumulated precipitation of 60 mm, resulting in maximum flood discharge on August 16–18, whereas no rainfall fell below 4000 m, indicating that the Kalakash River flooding was closely correlated with heavy precipitation in the alpine headwaters. In addition, the sharp rise in TEM_Max (increasing 8–10 °C) before August 11 caused an increase in river discharge, suggesting that the temperature rise during the pre-flood period prompted the snowmelt flooding of the Kalakash River. The Yurungkash River exhibited two flood processes, the first of which occurred on August 8, with a peak discharge of 904 m3 /s. This flood was primarily driven by high temperatures without precipitation. Subsequently, continuous rainfall from August 10–14 caused the second flood peak (1077 m3 /s on August 14), and the high temperature weakened during precipitation, after which the flood subsided. This indicates that floods in the Yurungkash River are primarily driven by high temperatures. Notably, the high temperatures remained stable in August, and the high temperatures below 4000 m decreased significantly after August 22. However, high temperatures were maintained above 4000 m. This indicates the persistent influence of high temperatures in the alpine headwaters of the TRB on flooding events. The lack of precipitation and rising high temperatures in the Cherchen River in August caused an increase in flood discharge. The TEM_Max observed at 4343 m increased from 16.3 °C on August 8 to 20.1 °C on August 11, with a consequent discharge increase from 30.3 to 99.7 m3 /s. High temperatures were maintained at high levels, which led to flooding on August 17, with a maximum discharge of 173 m3 /s. As high temperatures decreased, flooding decreased on August 18. Thus, flooding of the Cherchen River was dominated by high temperatures in the alpine headwaters. The Kaidu River experienced a rainfall event from August 9–12, with river discharge increasing from 222 m3 /s on August 9 to 394 m3 /s on August 12. Temperatures then increased rapidly, with the TEM_Max observed at 2408 m increasing from 12.1 °C on August 12 to 24.6 °C on August 15, which caused the flooding (the maximum discharge was 418 m3 /s) on August 19. As the high temperatures decreased, the flooding decreased on August 20. As a result, heavy rainfall events in the Kaidu River cause flooding, reaching a maximum flood peak under high temperature conditions.  3.3.2 Large-scale drivers of August 2022 extreme floods The above analysis suggests that the TRB flooding was directly influenced by record-breaking persistently high temperatures during the summer of 2022. The subtropical high-pressure system was the immediate driver of the high temperatures, and changes in the WPSH that affected its stable maintenance was a key factor that led to the record-breaking persistently high temperatures. Liu et al. (2019) found that WPSH changes were closely correlated with the distribution of floods and droughts over China during summer. The WPSH has increased in area and intensity and experienced a significant westward extension since the 21st century (Fig. 8   a–b). The WPSH hovers above the central and lower reaches of the Yangtze River Basin during a typical August (Liu et al, 2019). However, the WPSH intensity index during August 2022 was more than double the standard deviation of the normal value, breaking the observational record. In particular, the westernmost point was located more westerly than normal in August 2022, and the abnormal westward movement of the WPSH reached the headwaters of the TRB. In addition, the WPSH ridge line in August 2022 moved further northward and southward, and the WPSH area index broke the observational record. The Iranian high pressure had the most pronounced influence on summer high temperatures over the TRB region. The Iranian High jumped eastward and hovered above the TRB region during the summer of 2015, leading to high temperatures and floods (Mao et al., 2016). The intensity of the Iranian high has significantly increased since the beginning of the 21st century, however, the intensity index for August 2022 was weaker than that over the last 10 years (Fig. 8 c). Therefore, the Iranian High was not a direct driver of the TRB high temperatures in August 2022. Fig. 9   shows the distribution of the geopotential height and its anomalies at 500 hPa (Z500) from early to late August 2022. Positive Z500 anomalous centers were observed over the Iranian Plateau and north China in late July 2022, subsequently moving westward with the increasing strength of the WPSH in early August, reaching maximum intensity in mid-August (Fig. 9 a–c). During a typical summer, the Iranian high and WPSH are typically broken up by high mountains such as the Himalayas. However, multiple high-pressure systems were connected to encircle the globe at a certain latitude in August 2022, which could explain the high temperatures in the TRB region and China. We also discussed the planetary-scale circulation system changes for this TRB flood process. The South Asian High (SAH) is one of the most pronounced planetary-scale circulation systems in the NH during boreal summer (Mason and Anderson, 1963), and covers large parts of southern Asia and the Middle East (Nützel et al., 2016). Changes in the intensity, location, and movement of the SAH at 100 hPa can have a significant impact on climatic anomalies around the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau and China. Recent studies have demonstrated that movement of the SAH is related to high-temperature anomalies in the TRB region (Mao et al., 2016). Fig. 10  (a) compares the climatological mean position of the SAH during summer for 1991–2020 and 2022 and indicates that the location and intensity of the SAH during the summer of 2022 was greater than the climate status. This indicates that the intensity of the SAH center in the summer of 2022 was the strongest since 1981, and that its intensity gradually strengthened in late June and reached historical strength during August (Fig. 10 b). The location of the SAH center was observed over the Tibetan Plateau in early August and subsequently moved eastward with increasing strength in mid-August (Fig. 11  a–c). Therefore, the anomalous strength of the SAH in the upper troposphere was a planetary-scale system that triggered the persistence of high temperatures and floods in the TRB. The daily changes in the intensity, westernmost point of the WPSH, and SAH intensity during the summer of 2022 are shown in Fig. 12  . The WPSH intensity strengthened significantly from July to early August, with the westernmost point of the WPSH extending westward to 90°E, and the SAH intensity also increased significantly. The WPSH and SAH intensities peaked in mid-August and gradually decreased in late August. The SAH intensification and westward extension of the WPSH were consistent with the high temperatures and flood evolution of the TRB, reflecting the direct influence of the large-scale circulation drive.    4 Discussions As one of the most severe climate-related disasters, floods are affected by climate change, and their intensity and frequency are altered worldwide (Milly et al., 2002; Hirabayashi et al., 2013; Dottori et al., 2018; IPCC, 2021 ). In addition, as one of the most dangerous disasters, flooding has caused tens of billions of US dollars in losses and thousands of deaths each year during the previous decade; thus, it has long been a popular research topic (Maskey & Samuels, 2021 ; Fang et al., 2022). A few studies have suggested that global warming increases the flood risk in mountainous areas (Haeberli et al., 2007; Allamano et al., 2009 ; Slater et al., 2016). In alpine glacierized catchments, rivers are exposed to a higher flood risk because they are affected by extreme meteorological factors, changes in melt rates, and associated processes (Veh et al., 2020 ). Flood-generating mechanisms vary across locations and are influenced primarily by river recharge and catchment characteristics. The Tarim River is recharged by rainfall, glaciers, and snowmelt, which has increased flood magnitudes and frequencies over the past few decades (Fang et al., 2022). In August 2022, unprecedented floods spread across almost all the alpine headwaters and the main stream of the large endorheic TRB. In this study, we investigated the mechanisms of extreme floods in 2022 and found that the TRB extreme floods were caused by unprecedented high temperatures in all regions and anomalous extreme precipitation during August 2022.
