Driving factors attributed to flood events vary among catchments at different altitudes and glacier coverages (Fang et al., 2022). Our results showed that the Aksu River flood was dominated by extreme rainfall, the Chelchen and Yurungkash River floods were dominated by high temperatures, and the others were dominated by both. The high temperatures promoted the snow/glacial melt rate, which enhanced the flood peaks because it was jointly influenced by heavy precipitation. This result is generally consistent with the conclusion proposed by Fang et al. (2022) based on the random forest approach, who concluded that rainfall was the dominant factor for increased flooding in most catchments of the Tianshan Mountains and that temperature played a greater role in the northern Kunlun Mountains. Keilholz et al. (2015)  suggested that increasingly unstable Tarim floods will occur in the future due to warming. At higher temperatures, glacial melting in alpine areas will increase leading to increased flooding in the summer. In addition, the probability of the occurrence of floods similar to those of the TRB floods during August 2022 will significantly increase in the future. However, when glacial melting reaches a critical point, flooding decreases (Glazirin et al. 2010; Sorg et al., 2012 ). In this study, our results suggest that extremely high temperatures were the leading drivers of the TRB extreme floods in August 2022 and that the high temperature anomalies were caused by the direct effect of the anomalously strong and westward extension of the WPSH. Factors affecting WPSH anomalies, in addition to being related to global warming (Yang et al., 2022), are also related to thermal anomalies during La Niña and tropical SST anomalies on a seasonal scale (Xiang et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017 ). La Niña conditions emerged in mid-2020, lasted for two winters, and continued to develop during the summer of 2022, with cold SSTs in the equatorial Central–East Pacific, particularly in the Central Pacific (Niño 4 region). This is likely to continue as an unusual triple-dip La Niña event (WMO, 2022). The anomalous cooling in the Central Pacific (CP) suppresses local convection (Yang et al., 2022), strengthening the WPSH by generating a westward propagated atmospheric Rossby wave (Wang et al., 2013; Xiang et al., 2013; Stuecker et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017 ). The anomalous warming of the SST and enhanced convection on the Maritime Continent associated with La Niña also strengthens the WPSH by modulating local Hadley circulation with an increased anticyclonic circulation in the northwestern Pacific (Sui et al., 2007; Chung et al., 2011 ). Positive SST anomalies in the tropical North Atlantic drive positive WPSH anomalies by inducing anomalous cooling of the CP and suppressing convection (Ham et al., 2013; Hong et al., 2015; Zuo et al., 2019 ). Focusing on the Indian Ocean, the anomalous warming triggers warm Kelvin waves emanating into the tropical western Pacific, inducing an anomalous anticyclone at the low troposphere of the northwest Pacific (Yang et al., 2007; Xie et al., 2009 ). Yang et al (2022) also suggested that both the cool SST anomalies in the Niño 4 region of a La Niña event and warm SST anomalies in the Indian and/or tropical Atlantic Ocean strengthen the WPSH by promoting anticyclonic anomalies over the northwestern Pacific region. An anomalous strengthening of the westward extension of the WPSH and connection with the Iranian High formed a stronger pressure system, which prevented moisture transport from the Indian Ocean to the TRB, causing extreme high-temperature events in the NH region. In addition, Eurasian–Atlantic telecorrelation in early summer can be induced by the persistence of the SST three-pole structure in the North Atlantic, which affects atmospheric circulation in the mid- and low-latitudes of East Asia (Li et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2022). An anomalous change in atmospheric circulation in August at mid- and high latitudes, showing the “+-+” atmospheric wave train with the Ural Mountains high-pressure, Siberian low-pressure, and North Pacific high-pressure anomalies (Fig. 7 ), is an important process causing the persistence of high temperatures. Sun et al. (2022) suggested that mid- and high-latitude atmospheric circulation anomalies are closely related to the unusual behavior of mid-latitude westerly winds and Arctic climate anomalies. The westerly anomalies brought rain to northern China, including the TRB region, during August 2022 but mostly bypassed southern China. In addition, the Central Asian Trough is the primary weather system that causes extreme rainfall in the TRB region (Yang et al., 2018 ). The large-scale circulation anomalies for the TRB floods in August 2022 are summarized in a schematic diagram (Fig. 10 ). In the summer of 2022, floods flowing through the Taklamakan Desert in the lower reaches of the TRB created a rare desert lake landscape that attracted widespread public attention. These floods caused less damage to downstream habitats and properties, whereas flood events played a key role in the formation of the Tugai forests (Thevs et al., 2008 ), which had the highest impact on groundwater recharge (Tang et al., 2007; Keilholz et al., 2015 ). Thus, the Tarim floods have critical ecological significance for desert ecosystems, desert riparian forests, and floodplains. The local government and the water management department have taken measures such as flood diversion and ecological water transfer to use the flood water for agricultural irrigation, ecological replenishment of the Populus euphratica  forest, and strengthening floodwater resource utilization. The area of the Populus euphratica  forest along the flooded river in the summer of 2022 increased by 1.335 million acres, which is 50 % greater than the mean level, and increased the floodwater resources by 3.193 × 108 m3 , with a floodwater resource utilization rate of 80 %. Therefore, there is a need to strengthen research on the resource utilization of floodwater in desert areas.  5 Conclusions In this study, we investigated the hydro-climatological drivers of the August 2022 extreme floods along the Tarim River, China, based on the observed gradients of high-density automated meteorological and hydrological data. The conclusions are as follows:1. The TRB experienced a record-breaking high-temperature process and high-temperature days in the summer of 2022. In August 2022, the TRB precipitation was 105 % higher than the August average, and it experienced three heavy rainfall events, primarily distributed in the central mountainous zone (1000–3000 m). An unprecedented flood occurred in the TRB in August 2022. Twenty-five rivers in the TRB were flooded above the warning flow, and the mainstem flood process duration was 80 d.  2. The record-breaking persistently high temperatures over the entire TRB and extreme precipitation in the mountains were the dominant factors in the unprecedented TRB flooding in August 2022. The dominant factors attributed to flooding vary among catchments with different hydro-climatological drivers. Heavy rainfall was the dominant factor leading to flooding in the Aksu River, whereas high temperatures played a greater role in the Chechen River. The Yarkand, Hotan, and Kaidu River floods were influenced by both high temperatures and heavy rainfall.  3. In August 2022, the westward shift of the record-breaking WPSH merged with the ISH forming a subtropical high zone, which was a driver of the unprecedented high temperatures controlling TRB regional conditions. South Asian high-pressure intensification and westward extension of the WPSH were consistent with the high temperatures and flood evolution in the TRB, reflecting the direct influence of the large-scale circulation drive on TRB flood evolution.
1 Introduction Over 6000 climate reconstruction studies that rely on high-resolution proxy data, such as tree rings, historical documents, ice cores, and speleothems, have been conducted worldwide, spanning from hundreds to thousands of years. Temperature and precipitation are the two main reconstruction targets, accounting for 40 % and 37 % of these studies, respectively (Hua et al., 2021 ). The spatial density of proxies for precipitation and temperature reconstruction is similar (Burgdorf, 2022; Consortium, 2017; He et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022 ), while the spatial variation of precipitation regimes (characteristics of the monthly distribution of precipitation at a particular location) is more significant than that of temperature (Bombardi et al., 2019 ). Moreover, the correlation of precipitation time series between different locations decreases more rapidly with distance compared to temperature (Cook et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2018 ). As a result, the skill (measured by cross-validation statistics) of regional or gridded precipitation reconstruction at the continental scale is weaker than that of temperature reconstruction for most locations in Europe (Guiot, 2012; Luterbacher et al., 2004; Pauling et al., 2005 ), North America (Stahle et al., 2020; Trouet et al., 2013 ), and Monsoon Asia (Cook et al., 2012; Feng et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2015, 2018 ). It is worth noting that the skill of precipitation reconstruction over the past several hundred years in East Central China is significantly better than in other regions, which is largely due to the unique Dryness/Wetness Index (DWI) proxy data available for this area. The DWI is a five-point scale annual index for 120 sites in China dating back to 1470. The first version of this dataset was published in 1981, covering the period from 1470 to 1979. The source data comprised more than 2200 Chinese local gazetteers and various historical documents. A normal distribution is assumed to convert key descriptors of the onset, duration, areal extent, and severity of each drought or flood disaster in each location into five ordinal grades, i.e., 1 for very wet (10 %), 2 for wet (25 %), 3 for normal (30 %), 4 for dry (25 %), and 5 for very dry (10 %) (CAMS, 1981 ). Later, this dataset was extended through the year 2000 (Zhang et al., 2003; Zhang and Liu, 1993 ). The compilation of the DWI dataset is a milestone in international past global change research (Nash et al., 2021 ). Since its publication, it has been extensively used in a large number of studies, including gridded precipitation dataset reconstruction (Feng et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2017, 2018 ), spatial patterns of precipitation in China over the last half millennium (Gong et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2016 ), multi-scale association characteristics of precipitation changes and climate oscillations (Chen et al., 2021; Kang et al., 2023 ), as well as the impact of climate change on socio-economic sectors (Cui et al., 2017a; Sun et al., 2023 ). Additionally, in reconstructing local or regional hydroclimate changes by tree rings and speleothems, or in simulating hydroclimate variations in climate models, the DWI series within the study area is often used as the "ground truth" for comparison (Deng et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2019; Peng, 2021; Xu et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2015, 2022a ). However, the updated DWI data (1980–2000) were entirely derived from the classification of precipitation anomalies from June to August (or May to September) (Zhang et al., 2003; Zhang and Liu, 1993 ), deviating from the method used in the earlier period (1470–1979) which relied on descriptions of drought and flood disasters (CAMS, 1981 ). Although the updated data ensured a consistent probability distribution of the five grades, the main methodological approaches used to derive indices had changed, reducing the homogeneity of the data across periods. To avoid terminological confusion, the following part of this paper text will refer to the 1470–1979 DWI as the “original DWI”, which primarily depends upon historical records of drought and flood disasters, and the 1980–2000 DWI as the “precipitation-based DWI”, which is entirely calculated from instrumental precipitation measurements. Therefore, precipitation reconstruction using the combined DWI data (original DWI and precipitation-based DWI) to calibrate and validate against instrumental precipitation data from the latter half of the 20th century, may overestimate the reconstruction skill to some extent. Shi et al. (2018)  pointed out this issue, but thus far, no study has provided a quantitative assessment of it. Moreover, studies have found significant regional differences in the representativeness (the most sensitive climate variable and seasonal window) of the same proxy indicator (e.g., tree-ring width) (George, 2014 ). Up to now, there has been no research on the regional differences in the representativeness of the original DWI. To address the above two issues, this study first utilizes province-level data of crop failure due to drought and flood disasters in China to establish the 1978–2008 DWI series (hereafter referred to as “disaster-based DWI”) using the same method as for the original DWI. We then calculate the optimum seasonal window for disaster-based DWI to reflect precipitation and soil water in multiple layers, respectively, and analyze the regional differences in the hydroclimate representativeness of the disaster-based DWI proxy data. Finally, we use the precipitation-based DWI and disaster-based DWI series to reconstruct the summer precipitation changes in China, quantitatively evaluating the differences between their reconstruction skills, in other words, the overestimation of reconstructed variance from precipitation-based DWI. The results of this study contribute to a deeper understanding of the climate information preserved within China's DWI proxy data and will assist scholars in the palaeoclimatological community to better utilize precipitation reconstruction datasets derived from DWI.  2 Materials and methods 2.1 The original DWI dataset and its characteristics  Fig. 1  shows the 120 sites of the original DWI, of which over 80 sites in East Central China (105–125°E, 25–42°N) have better data completeness during the historical period (usually having less than 15 % missing values) and are most widely used in precipitation reconstruction (Feng et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2023, 2022; Shi et al., 2017, 2018 ). The original DWI primarily covers the Ming (1368–1644) and Qing (1644–1912) Dynasties of Chinese history, during which the national administrative divisions were structured into three levels: province, prefecture, and county. The number of administrative regions fluctuated during the Ming and Qing periods, with about 20 provinces, 200–360 prefectures, and 1100–1500 counties (Zhao et al., 2022b ). The "province-prefecture-county" structure roughly corresponds to the current "province-city-county" administrative divisions in China, which, as of 2022, includes 34 provinces, 333 cities, and 2843 counties. Each original DWI site corresponds to 1–2 prefectures (equivalent to 1–2 cities today), and their primary sources containing drought and flood disaster descriptions come from the documents of each prefecture and its subordinate counties (CAMS, 1981 ). The climate information recorded in historical documents was later supplemented and compiled into the “Compendium of Chinese Meteorological Records of the Last 3000 Years” (Zhang, 2013 ), with data from the early to mid-Qing Dynasty already digitized and categorized into an electronic database (REACHES) (Wang et al., 2018 ). Fig. 1  also shows the locations of county-level sites recorded in REACHES. Historical documents contain nearly 20 types of climate-related records ( Fig. 2 ), among which the records used to distinguish the five grades mainly include direct descriptions of the amount of precipitation, descriptions of the duration and severity of drought or flood disasters, descriptions of crop yield reductions due to drought/flood disasters (the unit commonly used in ancient China to express changes in quantities is “cheng”, equivalent to 10 %), and descriptions of human injuries caused by drought/flood disasters. Fig. 2  presents a network of about 50,000 records in REACHES, where the layout uses attractive forces between adjacent nodes and repulsive forces between distant nodes (Fruchterman and Reingold, 1991 ). The results show that crop yield (“Crops” marker in Fig. 2 ) has the largest number of records and occupies a central position in the network of various record types, closely linked to precipitation and drought/flood disaster events. Therefore, descriptions of crop yield conditions should be the most frequently used record type for calibrating drought/flood grades in historical times. This paper will construct the DWI from 1978 to 2008 using crop yield data (i.e., disaster-based DWI), to ensure maximum homogeneity with the original DWI.  2.2 Construction of the drought/flood disaster-based DWI in 1978–2008 According to the Chinese agricultural statistical survey system, each administrative region annually compiles data on the cultivation of major crops and the occurrence of flood and drought disasters. The statistical indicators closest to the narrative evidence for the original DWI classification from historical documents are the crop area covered by flood (drought) disasters, crop area affected by flood (drought) disasters, and crop area of total loss by flood (drought) disasters, corresponding to the area of crop yields reduced by at least 10 %, 30 %, and 80 % due to flood (drought) disasters, respectively (MEM, 2020 ). However, many county and city-level public statistical materials do not provide such data. The currently available data includes the crop area covered by flood (drought) disasters and crop area affected by flood (drought) disasters in 31 provincial-level administrative regions, sourced from the “China Compendium of Agriculture Statistics 1949–2008” (MOA, 2009 ). The data from 1978 to 2008 are complete and are used to generate the disaster-based DWI in this paper. Moreover, since the total sown area of crops varies from year to year, we calculate the ratio of crop area with flood/drought disasters to the total sown area in each year. It is important to note that identifying the grade in a region is relatively straightforward when only drought or flood occurs over a period. However, in many provinces of China, both droughts and floods coexist or rapidly alternate within the same year. In such cases, determining the grade level requires a further comparison of the extent of these disasters. Studies have shown that the provinces of Hubei, Anhui, and Sichuan in the Yangtze River basin, as well as Fujian, Guangdong, and Guangxi in Southeast China, frequently experience abrupt alterations between drought and flood disasters (Bi et al., 2023; Meng et al., 2024 ). Consequently, this paper selects Hubei Province as an example to introduce the method for establishing a disaster-based DWI series below (more examples for other provinces are shown in Fig. S1-S5 ).  Fig. 3 a shows the proportions of crop areas covered and affected by flood (drought) disasters relative to the total sown area in Hubei Province during 1978–2008. Beginning with this data, there are three main steps. Step 1: Generate the Dryness Index (DI ) and Wetness Index (WI ) using crop area covered and affected by corresponding disasters, respectively. To reflect the spatial extent and severity of drought or flood disasters, DI  and WI  are calculated by weighting the crop area covered and affected by corresponding disasters according to the amount of crop yield reduction:(1) DI  = (S D1  +3S D2  )/S C     (2) WI  = –(S W1  +3S W2  )/S C     where S D1   and S D2   are crop areas covered and affected by drought disasters, S W1   and S W2   are crop areas covered and affected by flood disasters, and S C   is the total sown area of crops. To match the grade order of the original DWI (grades 1 and 2 for floods, grade 3 for normal, and grades 4 and 5 for droughts), WI  is multiplied by a factor of −1 to be represented by negative values. DI  and WI  for Hubei Province are shown in Fig. 3 b. Step 2: Calculate the preliminary Dryness/Wetness Index (DWI 0 ) from DI  and WI . Fig. 3 a-b illustrates that both drought and flood disasters can occur simultaneously, a scenario that is also common in historical drought/flood disaster records. The original DWI data addresses this by prioritizing the condition prevalent in the majority of the sub-regions within a given site when both drought and flood conditions are present (CAMS, 1981 ). Therefore, to ensure methodological consistency with the original DWI, this study compares the absolute values of DI  and WI  each year and takes the larger one as the DWI 0  value, with its time series shown in Fig. 3 b. The formula for calculating DWI 0  is:(3) DWI 0  = max(|DI |,|WI |) × sgn(|DI |–|WI |)   where max is the function to find the maximum value, and sgn is the sign function. Step 3: Establish the five-grade disaster-based DWI considering the probability distribution of DWI 0 . Specifically, all DWI 0  values are divided into 5 intervals according to 10 %, 35 %, 65 % and 90 % percentiles. This method ensures that the disaster-based DWI and the original DWI have similar frequency distributions, namely, 10 % for grades 1 and 5, 25 % for grades 2 and 4, and 30 % for grade 3. Finally, Fig. 3 c illustrates the disaster-based DWI in Hubei Province.  2.3 Method to analyze the hydroclimatic representativeness This paper examines the hydroclimatic representativeness of China's disaster-based DWI, focusing on hydroclimate variables including precipitation and soil water in five layers. The monthly precipitation data are from the China Meteorological Data Service Center (Version 2.0), with a spatial resolution of 0.5° (Zhao et al., 2014 ).1  1 The precipitation data is currently unavailable from the China Meteorological Data Service Center. The same data at daily resolution can be downloaded from https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/mz8hjgwn7z/1 .   The monthly soil water data in five layers come from ERA5 reanalysis data (Hersbach et al., 2020 ), including skin reservoir content (SRC), the volumetric soil water in layer 1 (0–7 cm, SWL1), layer 2 (7–28 cm, SWL2), layer 3 (28–100 cm, SWL3), and layer 4 (100–289 cm, SWL4). The spatial resolution of soil water data is 0.1°, which is then rescaled to 0.5° resolution using the box-shaped kernel method. Although the disaster-based DWI calculated in this study is provincial data, the distribution of cropland across provinces is highly uneven. Therefore, when evaluating the hydroclimatic representativeness, it is essential to consider the impact of cropland spatial heterogeneity on provincial-scale precipitation and soil water. We employ the latest remote sensing-based dataset of cropland change in China (Yu et al., 2021 ) to spatially weight the hydroclimate variables. The cropland data is resolved annually in time and its spatial resolution is 5 km, utilizing the Albers Equal Area projection. Initially, cropland maps are unprojected to unevenly spaced geographic coordinates using the Mapping Toolbox from Matlab. Subsequently, they are interpolated onto a 0.05° regularly spaced latitudinal and longitudinal grid through a linear function. Finally, they are upscaled to a 0.5° resolution using the spatial interpolation function with a box-shaped kernel from the climate toolbox (Greene et al., 2019 ), which also employs sparse linear algebra and partial differential equation discretizations to prevent missing data along boundaries.  Fig. 4  shows the distribution and change of cropland in China between 1978 and 2008. During this period, the cropland area in most provinces showed a declining trend, with only a few provinces in Northeastern China and Xinjiang showing an increasing trend. Since the temporal resolution of the cropland data is annual, the distribution of cropland is presumed to remain consistent across the 12 months of the year when it is used as a weighted mask to calculate monthly-resolved province mean precipitation and soil water. The method for analyzing the representativeness of the disaster-based DWI involves two steps. The first step is calculating the annual-resolved time series of each hydroclimate variable by averaging monthly values over different seasonal windows. These are then correlated with the disaster-based DWI series to select the variable and window with the optimal significance level. The test range for window length is 3–12 months, and the sliding range for the window is from the prior December to the current December (referring to the end month of the window). For example, a window length of five with an end month in August means calculating the correlation coefficient between April-August mean hydroclimate variable (e.g., precipitation) and the disaster-based DWI during 1978–2008.  2.4 Method for precipitation reconstruction To evaluate the differences in the predictive skill of reconstructing summer precipitation in China between precipitation-based DWI and disaster-based DWI series, this study adopts the state-of-the-art best subset regression method recently used for gridded precipitation reconstruction in Asia (Liu et al., 2022 ). Since the precipitation-based DWI is city-level data and the disaster-based DWI is provincial-level data, their reconstruction methods differ slightly. For the disaster-based DWI, the model is constructed with the target province's precipitation as the response variable and the disaster-based DWI of that province and its neighboring provinces as predictors. For the precipitation-based DWI, the model similarly uses the target province's precipitation as the response variable but the predictors are the precipitation-based DWI from stations within the province and nearby stations from adjacent provinces. Given that most provinces in China have 3–6 neighboring provinces, we select 6 candidate stations from these adjacent provinces for further calibration. Calibration models are established by province with summer (June-August) precipitation as the target. The overlap interval of precipitation-based DWI and disaster-based DWI is from 1980 to 2000, which is chosen as the calibration period. Best subset regression constructs multiple linear regression models by fitting the response variable using all possible combinations of predictor variables. The criterion for model selection is the maximization of the variance of observations explained by the model’s predicted values from the cross-validation procedure (predicted R-Squared), thus avoiding the introduction of redundant multi-collinear predictors that would inflate the R-Squared during the modeling phase (Liu et al., 2022 ). Cross-validation is conducted using a state-of-the-art rolling window division of the dataset into training and prediction sets (Nguyen et al., 2020 ). Note that we withhold a contiguous 20 % segment of the data points for validation and train the model on the remaining 80 % in each cross-validation run. We leave a slightly smaller proportion (1/5) of data in the validation fold compared to 1/4 by Nguyen et al. (2020)  because the number of observations in our case is 21, and we need enough data to calibrate the model. Moreover, to prevent potential overfitting, the maximum number of predictors in the best subset model is set at three (given the calibration sample size of 21 in this study), adhering to the statistical regression principle that the sample size should be substantially larger (preferably 10 times) than the number of predictors (Sekaran, 2003 ). It is important to note that during the calibration period of this study, there was an adjustment in China's provincial administrative divisions. In 1997, the original Sichuan province was divided into Sichuan and Chongqing. The provincial-level agricultural drought and flood disaster data for Chongqing also began from 1997. Given that the precipitation-based DWI data only extend to 2000, and the overlap period with Chongqing's agricultural drought and flood disaster data is only four years, the sample size is insufficient for model calibration. Therefore, this study continues to treat Sichuan and Chongqing as one province after 1997 to calculate the representativeness of disaster-based DWI and to conduct precipitation reconstruction.  2.5 Method to identify the relationship between the representativeness of disaster-based DWI and other factors The regional difference in the representativeness of disaster-based DWI may be influenced by multiple factors including climatic types, climate variability, topography, and agricultural technology. This study selects the mean precipitation and mean temperature from 1978 to 2008 to demonstrate climatic types, and uses the standard deviations of precipitation and temperature changes during this period to demonstrate climate variability, with data sourced from the China Meteorological Data Service Center (http://data.cma.cn/ ). The topographic factor is indicated by the average elevation of cropland within each province, with data obtained from the Joint Institute for the Study of the Atmosphere and Ocean (http://research.jisao.washington.edu/data_sets/elevation/ ). Agricultural technology is represented by the ratio of the effective irrigation area to the total sown area, with data derived from the "China Compendium of Agriculture Statistics 1949–2008" (MOA, 2009 ). The effective irrigation area is primarily determined by the availability of hydraulic facilities such as reservoirs, canal systems, and pumping wells, thereby providing a reliable indicator of the level of agricultural technology. Partial correlation is used to describe the relationship between the representativeness of disaster-based DWI and a test variable while taking away other variables. The representation is visualized in a polar coordinate system, in which a colored sector indicates the seasonal window with the best proxy-target correlation. The circle is divided into 12 equal parts, starting from 90° with every 30° representing a month in a clockwise direction. The central angle of the sector corresponds to the window length, and the positions of two radii correspond to the start and end of the window. The color of the sector represents the correlation coefficient. The disaster-based DWI shows the strongest correlation with precipitation primarily in Northeast and East Central China, with most correlation coefficients ranging between − 0.88 and − 0.65 (p  < 0.0001). Shanghai is an exception, exhibiting a relatively weaker correlation coefficient of − 0.54, which is still significant at the p  = 0.005 level. In Northeast China, specifically in Heilongjiang and Liaoning, the disaster-based DWI correlates with April-August precipitation, whereas in Jilin, it correlates with June-September precipitation. For the majority of provinces in East Central China, including Tianjin, Shandong, Henan, Anhui, and Shanxi, the disaster-based DWI also correlates with April-August precipitation. Additionally, for Hubei and Jiangxi, the most sensitive seasonal window to precipitation is March-July, while for Beijing and Shanghai, it is May-August. In the case of Hebei and Hunan, the window is May-July, and for Zhejiang and Jiangsu, it is June-September. The correlation coefficients of the disaster-based DWI with precipitation in the Southern, Central, and Western provinces of China lie between − 0.71 and − 0.49. Although these are lower than those in Northeast and East Central China, they are all significant at the p  = 0.005 level. In Southern China, Fujian and Guangdong (in east Southern China) demonstrate the most sensitive window to precipitation during February-July and February-June, respectively. For Guizhou and Guangxi (in west Southern China), the most sensitive periods are July-September and June-September, while for Hainan (the southernmost province), it is from the prior October to the current March. Shaanxi and Sichuan (including Chongqing) show precipitation representativeness in June-September and April-August, respectively, presenting similar seasonal windows but relatively weaker correlations compared to the adjacent provinces in East Central China. In contrast, Central to Western China exhibits different sensitive periods: February-June and March-May for Inner Mongolia and Ningxia (in North Central China); February-July for Qinghai, Gansu, and Yunnan (along 100°E); and March-June for Xinjiang and Tibet (the westernmost provinces). Overall, the disaster-based DWI in Northeastern and East Central provinces reflects precipitation from April to September, with a window length of 3–5 months. In contrast, the most sensitive seasonal windows for precipitation in the Southern, Central, and Western provinces are primarily distributed from February to July, with a window length of 4–6 months. These windows commence 1–2 months earlier and extend 1–2 months longer than those in the Northeastern and East Central regions. This spatial variation in precipitation representativeness is largely attributed to climatic and agricultural factors. The Northeastern and East Central China experience a semi-humid to humid climate with the rainy season spanning from May to September and the main crop growing season from April to September (Cui et al., 2017b; Liu et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2022 ). Consequently, the disaster-based DWI records the strongest precipitation signal from April to September. Southern China, being warmer with more rainfall and a longer crop growing season, leads to extended precipitation-sensitive windows for the disaster-based DWI. The Central to Western provinces, located in semi-arid to arid zones with less rainfall, depend more on meltwater from snow and glacier ice, as well as groundwater for irrigation (Chen et al., 2014 ), resulting in a relatively weaker correlation between the disaster-based DWI and precipitation compared to the East. Moreover, the wet season in these regions begins earlier than in the East (Bombardi et al., 2019 ), explaining the earlier precipitation-sensitive window for the disaster-based DWI. The correlation coefficients of the disaster-based DWI with precipitation in China's 30 provinces vary between − 0.88 and − 0.49. For a more detailed analysis of the disaster-based DWI's performance in capturing precipitation extremes, four representative provinces were selected ( Fig. 6 ): Shandong (r  = − 0.860), Hubei (r  = − 0.781), Shaanxi (r  = − 0.587), and Xinjiang (r  = − 0.494). In Shandong province, the result accurately captures all precipitation extremes (e.g., high precipitation in 1990 and 1998, and low precipitation in 1989, 1992, and 2002), with deviations in other years not surpassing one grade. Hubei's disaster-based DWI similarly reflects most precipitation extremes effectively (e.g., high precipitation in 1980, 1983, 1996, 1998, and 2002, and low precipitation in 1978, 1981, 1988, 2000, and 2001), with deviations in most years not exceeding one grade and only one year recording a two-grade deviation (2005). In Shaanxi, the disaster-based DWI captures most precipitation extremes (e.g., high precipitation in 1981, 1984, and 1988, and low precipitation in 1991 and 1997), with most years showing deviations within one grade and one year each recording a two-grade (2003) and a three-grade (1993) deviation. Despite its lower correlation coefficient, Xinjiang's disaster-based DWI still identifies approximately half of the rainfall extremes (e.g., high precipitation in 1987 and 1988, and low precipitation in 1989 and 2001), with eight years exhibiting two-grade deviations, constituting about 25 % of the entire series. This comparison substantiates that, even though not directly derived from instrumental precipitation data, the disaster-based DWI is still an effective indicator of precipitation changes.  3.2 Soil water representativeness Using the same visualization method as in Fig. 5 ,  Fig. 7  illustrates the soil water representativeness of the disaster-based DWI across five layers. For SRC (Fig. 7 a), the correlation coefficients span from − 0.78 to − 0.33, with the weakest correlations observed in Shanghai (-0.33) and Qinghai (-0.42), significant only at the p  = 0.1 and p  = 0.05 levels, respectively. The remaining provinces exhibit correlation coefficients that are significant at least at the p  = 0.01 level, with the strongest correlations found in Northeastern China and the North China Plain. Here, the disaster-based DWI for most provinces reflects the SRC signal predominantly from April to August. In the southernmost provinces, the disaster-based DWI's correlation with SRC is also notably stronger, reaching − 0.70 in Guangdong, Hainan, and Yunnan, although with remarkable differences in seasonal windows (February-June, prior October-current February, and May-July, respectively). The most sensitive seasonal windows to SRC in Western and Central China are observed in spring to summer, typically spanning three months, i.e., April-June in Xinjiang, March-May in Ningxia and Gansu, May-July in Hubei and Jiangxi, and June-August in Hunan and Guizhou, though the correlations are comparatively weaker. For SWL1 (Fig. 7 b), the correlation coefficients span between − 0.84 and − 0.28. Shanghai exhibits the weakest correlation (-0.28), which is not significant at the p  = 0.1 level. In other provinces, all coefficients are below − 0.49, each significant at least at the p  = 0.01 level. Over 40 % of the provinces have a three-month window. Specifically, for five provinces in Northern China (Tianjin, Hebei, Shanxi, Shaanxi, and Henan) and Jilin in Northeastern China, the most sensitive seasonal window to SWL1 is July-September; for Inner Mongolia, Hunan, and Jiangxi, it is May-July; for Guizhou, it is June-August; for Zhejiang, August-October; and for Xinjiang, April-June. The disaster-based DWI in Hainan Island indicates SWL1 from the prior October to the current March, mirroring its precipitation pattern. Meanwhile, other provinces' seasonal windows are primarily distributed between March and September, lasting 4–5 months. For SWL2 (Fig. 7 c), the correlation coefficients range between − 0.84 and − 0.31, with Shanghai again showing the weakest correlation (-0.31, p  < 0.1). The coefficients in other provinces are all below − 0.44 (p  < 0.05). The disaster-based DWI's representativeness for SWL2 in 23 provinces is consistent with SWL1, with only seven provinces showing differences. Except for Ningxia, which shifts from May-August for SWL1 to April-June for SWL2, the window in other provinces only experiences minimal changes (not exceeding one month). For SWL3 (Fig. 7 d), the range of correlation coefficients is also between − 0.84 and − 0.31, with Shanghai again demonstrating the weakest correlation (-0.31, p  < 0.1). The coefficients in other provinces are all below − 0.39 (p  < 0.05). Over 50 % of provinces' disaster-based DWI indicates SWL3 over a three-month window, occurring in summer to early autumn, mainly in Northern China. In contrast, most southern provinces feature window lengths of 3–5 months, distributed from May to October. For SWL4 (Fig. 7 e), the correlation coefficients vary between − 0.70 and − 0.11. Only Shandong, Henan, Jiangsu, Anhui, Jiangxi, Guangdong, Fujian, and Guizhou display stronger correlations, with windows either from June to August or August to October. Other provinces, despite having similar representativeness (July-September or August-October), show significantly weaker correlations compared to SWL1-SWL3. Collectively, the disaster-based DWI demonstrates strong representativeness for SRC and the soil water in the upper three layers (0–7 cm, 7–28 cm, and 28–100 cm), but exhibits a weaker correlation with the soil water in the deepest layer (100–289 cm). This pattern is attributed to the fact that most crops have 50 % of their root systems concentrated in the top 20 cm of soil, with 95 % of roots located within 1 m of the surface (Fan et al., 2016 ). Consequently, the disaster-based DWI's correlation with SWL4 is notably weaker. Furthermore, the findings of this study indicate that as soil depth increases, the seasonal window tends to occur later in the year, aligning with the tendency of crop roots to absorb more water from deeper layers as the growing season progresses (Yang et al., 2018 ).  3.3 Optimal hydroclimatic representativeness Upon assessing the representativeness of the disaster-based DWI for both precipitation and soil water at various depths, the most sensitive variable for each province is identified and its seasonal windows are depicted in  Fig. 8 . The results reveal that the disaster-based DWI predominantly reflects precipitation in East Central China. In most of these provinces, a five-month window is observed, specifically, April-August for Tianjin, Shanxi, Shandong, Henan, and Anhui, and March-July for Hubei and Jiangxi. Provinces with a shorter, four-month window include Shaanxi and Zhejiang, from June to September, and Shanghai, from May to August. Hebei and Hunan, featuring a three-month window, exhibit precipitation sensitivity from May to July. Notably, Jiangsu and Beijing's most sensitive variable is SRC rather than precipitation, yet the correlation of SRC with the disaster-based DWI is only marginally stronger than that for precipitation (at comparable significance levels). The disaster-based DWI prominently reflects soil water characteristics in Northeastern, Southern coastal, Southwestern, and Northwestern regions. In the Northeastern region, it shows a robust correlation with SWL2 from April to August in Heilongjiang and SWL3 from June to August in Liaoning. Along the Southern coast region, it is aligned with July-September SWL4 for Fujian, February-June SRC for Guangdong, and prior October-current February SRC for Hainan. In the Southwestern region, it is linked to May-August SWL1 for Sichuan (including Chongqing), May to August SWL3 for Guizhou, and May to July SWL2 for Yunnan. In the Northwestern region, it indicates May-August SWL1 for Ningxia, March-August SWL1 for Qinghai, and April-June SWL1 for Xinjiang. Overall, the disaster-based DWI in provinces west of 100°E primarily reflects soil water. In the arid regions of the Northwest, it indicates soil water in shallow layers, while in the humid regions of the Southwest, it signifies soil water in deeper layers. Conversely, in provinces east of 100°E, it shows a greater sensitivity to precipitation, especially in most areas of East Central China. However, in the Southeastern provinces (Fujian, Guangdong, and Hainan), which experience abundant precipitation (>1800 mm per year), it demonstrates a heightened sensitivity to soil water.  3.4 Overestimation of reconstructed variance from precipitation-based DWI This section discusses the differences in the skills of reconstructing summer precipitation in China using precipitation-based DWI and disaster-based DWI.  Fig. 9 a presents the cross-validation statistics for the reconstruction by disaster-based DWI, with predicted R-Squared values ranging between 14.7 % and 76.8 % (p  < 0.1). Applying stricter thresholds, results fail to pass the p  = 0.05 and p  = 0.01 levels for two provinces (Yunnan, Qinghai) and four provinces (Henan, Shanghai, Gansu, Tibet). The predicted R-Squared for the remaining provinces all surpass at least the p  = 0.01 level, with Jiangxi, Hubei, and Inner Mongolia exhibiting the highest skills (>60 %), and Beijing, Jilin, Anhui, Shandong, Ningxia, and Xinjiang showing significant skills (>50 %). The count of provinces with predicted R-Squared values above 60 %, 50 %, 40 %, and 30 % are 3, 9, 16, and 24, respectively. The average predicted R-Squared value is 43.0 %, with eastern regions demonstrating superior performance compared to the west. Fig. 9 b displays the cross-validation statistics for the reconstruction using precipitation-based DWI, where predicted R-Squared values span from 14.9 % to 84.3 % (p  < 0.1). Under stricter criteria, results fail to pass the p  = 0.05 and p  = 0.01 levels for only one province (Tibet) and three provinces (Xinjiang, Qinghai, Hainan). The predicted R-Squared for the other provinces all surpass at least the p  = 0.005 level, with Beijing, Tianjin, Liaoning, and Henan leading in skill (>70 %), followed by Hebei, Jilin, Anhui, Shandong, Hubei, Guangdong, Guizhou, and Yunnan (>60 %). The number of provinces with predicted R-Squared higher than 60 %, 50 %, 40 %, and 30 % are 12, 20, 25, and 27, respectively. The average predicted R-Squared value stands at 53.6 %, also indicating better performance in the eastern regions compared to the west. Fig. 9 c illustrates the disparity in reconstruction skills between the two types of DWI. A total of 23 provinces demonstrate superior predicted R-Squared values with precipitation-based DWI, with the most notable improvements (>40 %) occurring in Tianjin, Henan, and Yunnan. Other provinces such as Liaoning, Shanghai, Guangdong, Guizhou, and Gansu experience enhancements in the range of 20 %-30 %. Conversely, seven provinces yield better predicted R-Squared values with disaster-based DWI. Notably, Inner Mongolia, Heilongjiang, Xinjiang, and Tibet, situated in the northernmost and westernmost parts of China, have larger areas but fewer precipitation-based DWI sites, leading to less effective reconstruction. Similarly, Hainan, with only one proxy data site, and distant from sites in Guangdong and Guangxi, also shows reduced skill in reconstruction compared to the eastern provinces on the mainland. Jiangxi and Zhejiang, despite a slight decrease in predicted R-Squared using precipitation-based DWI compared to disaster-based DWI, maintain nearly equivalent levels of statistical significance. Although comparison results are available for 30 provinces, the absence of original DWI data in Western, Southern, and Northeastern China before 1950 results in only 70–100 original DWI sites in East Central provinces (indicated by a black border in Fig. 9 ) being commonly utilized for gridded precipitation reconstruction datasets. Fig. 9 d further displays the violin distributions of the predicted R-Squared values for the reconstructions from precipitation-based DWI and disaster-based DWI in these provinces. The mean for precipitation-based DWI reconstruction stands at 58.6 %, with a median of 56.8 %, and a 25 %-75 % percentile range from 47.2 % to 66.2 %. These values align with validation results from multiple studies using this data to reconstruct precipitation in Eastern China (Feng et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2023, 2022; Shi et al., 2018 ). On the other hand, the mean for disaster-based DWI reconstruction is 45.0 %, with a median of 44.2 %, and a 25 %-75 % percentile range from 36.4 % to 52.6 %. The mean and corresponding percentiles demonstrate a reduction ranging between 11 % and 14 %, which essentially represents the overestimation of the predicted R-Squared when using precipitation-based DWI for calibration. Despite this inflated R-Squared, the disaster-based DWI remains a highly reliable source for historical precipitation reconstruction.  3.5 The relationship between the representativeness of disaster-based DWI and other factors Based on the preceding analysis of the representativeness of disaster-based DWI for precipitation and soil water in multiple layers, it is evident that, except for Hainan Island, which is entirely located in the tropics, the seasonal windows for other provinces are distributed across spring and summer. Consequently, we employ partial correlation analysis to calculate the relationship between the hydroclimatic representativeness of the DWI and six variables, including March-August precipitation amount and its standard deviation, March-August mean air temperature and its standard deviation, mean elevation of cropland, and the percentage of effectively irrigated area ( Table 1 ). The results indicate that while there are differences in significance levels, precipitation amount, standard deviation of temperature, elevation, and effectively irrigated area all have a negative correlation with the representativeness of disaster-based DWI for precipitation and soil water in multiple layers. Conversely, the standard deviation of precipitation shows a significant positive correlation with the representativeness of disaster-based DWI for precipitation and SWL4. The impact of mean air temperature is the weakest among all the variables tested, with absolute partial correlation coefficients below 0.15, not reaching the significance level of p  = 0.1. The results of partial correlation analysis can somewhat elucidate the spatial variations in the optimal representativeness of disaster-based DWI. In the northwestern provinces of China with arid climates, which are generally characterized by high altitudes and low precipitation, the effective irrigation area emerges as the predominant factor determining the optimal representativeness. Gansu and Shaanxi, with lower effective irrigation areas (averaging 26.6 %), indicate better precipitation representativeness similar to that of the eastern regions. Conversely, higher effective irrigation areas are observed in Xinjiang, Qinghai, and Ningxia (averaging 51.8 %), which have a significant negative effect on the representativeness of disaster-based DWI for precipitation while their impact on soil water representativeness is weak (Table 1 ), making the disaster-based DWI a better indicator of SWL1 in these provinces. In the provinces from the upper to the middle reaches of the Yangtze River, where precipitation amount and effective irrigation areas are comparable and the altitude's impact on the representativeness of disaster-based DWI with precipitation and soil water is consistent, the standard deviation of precipitation becomes the key factor determining the optimal representativeness. The upper reaches, including Yunnan, Guizhou, and Sichuan, exhibit a lower standard deviation in precipitation (averaging 94 mm), whereas the middle reaches (Hubei, Hunan, and Jiangxi), display a higher standard deviation (averaging 174 mm). According to Table 1 , an increase in the standard deviation of precipitation enhances the representativeness of disaster-based DWI for precipitation, with negligible effects on SWL1 and SWL2; thus, the disaster-based DWI demonstrates better representativeness for precipitation in the middle reaches and for SWL1 and SWL2 in the upper reaches. In the southern coastal provinces (Guangxi, Guangdong, and Fujian), Guangxi, with the least precipitation and lowest effective irrigation area, shows the best representativeness for precipitation. In contrast, disaster-based DWI better indicates soil water in Guangdong and Fujian. Moreover, the significantly higher altitude of Fujian compared to Guangdong and Guangxi facilitates the indication of deeper soil water. In the North China Plain, disaster-based DWI primarily indicates precipitation, but in Jiangsu and Beijing, it indicates soil water, albeit influenced by different factors. Jiangsu, with a notably higher effective irrigation area (45.9 %) compared to adjacent Anhui, Henan, Shandong, and Zhejiang (averaging 36.8 %), exhibits subdued effectiveness in indicating precipitation. The effective irrigation area is 59.2 % in Beijing, substantially higher than Hebei (45.6 %) but similar to Tianjin (63.3 %). This suggests that the lower representativeness for precipitation in Beijing might also be relate to other factors, such as water resource management policies (Li and Fu, 2015 ). To further explore the contribution of seasonal climate variability to the disaster-based DWI, we extract the first principal component of hydroclimate change from precipitation and soil water in five layers during the spring (March-May) and summer (June-August) for each province. Subsequently, multivariate regression is employed to calculate the standardized regression coefficients and significance of the two season’s principal components on disaster-based DWI, as illustrated in  Fig. 10 . When the p -value of the spring (summer) variability regression coefficient reaches at least 0.1 level and is less than one-tenth of the p -value for the summer (spring) variability regression coefficient, spring (summer) variability is considered the dominant factor for the disaster-based DWI. If both spring and summer regression coefficients' p -values reach 0.1 level without a tenfold difference between them, both seasons’ variabilities are considered joint dominant factors influencing the disaster-based DWI. The results indicate that only in northwestern China (Xinjiang, Ningxia, and Gansu), the disaster-based DWI is dominated by spring variability. In contrast, both spring and summer variabilities are significant in the western and southern regions including Tibet, Qinghai, Yunnan, and Guangdong, whereas summer variability predominates in eastern China. This pattern may be associated with the precipitation regime (Bombardi et al., 2019 ) and sources of moisture (Nieto et al., 2019 ). Future research should focus on exploring the underlying mechanistic linkages. Agricultural technology is a crucial factor influencing the representativeness of disaster-based DWI, varying not only across regions but also progressing over time. We divided the disaster-based DWI series into two periods (1978–1993 and 1994–2008) to study its association with changing agricultural technology. Compared to the earlier period, the later period witnesses an average increase of 14.6 % in effective irrigation area, yet there is a decline in the representativeness of disaster-based DWI for precipitation and soil water in five layers, with average decreases of 1.24 %, 4.57 %, 3.09 %, 6.04 %, 10.48 %, and 12.83 %, respectively ( Fig. 11 ). In the historical period, when agricultural technologies were more rudimentary and effective irrigation areas were lower, the correlations between disaster-based DWI and hydroclimate variables are likely to have been stronger in the more distant past. Moreover, future studies could utilize the historical changes in the correlation between DWI and variables such as precipitation to retroactively infer the characteristics of changes in agricultural technology.  3.6 Correlations between disaster-based DWI and tree-ring width The DWI and tree-ring width series are primary proxy data utilized in reconstructing high-resolution climate changes over the past several centuries in China and East Asia (Chen et al., 2023, 2024; Cook et al., 2010; Hou et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2017, 2018; Zhao et al., 2023 ). This paper further analyzes the correlation between them, utilizing tree-ring width data from the International Tree-Ring Data Bank (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/paleoclimatology/tree-ring ) and the above-mentioned studies.  Fig. 12  illustrates the correlation coefficients and significance levels between each tree-ring width chronology and the corresponding provincial disaster-based DWI series from 1978 to 2008. Given the varying lengths of tree-ring chronologies, the correlations shown in Fig. 12  are adjusted to a degree of freedom of 29 for comparison. Out of 154 tree-ring width chronologies tested across China, 24 show significant correlations with the disaster-based DWI series, predominantly positive, and are primarily located in the Tianshan Mountains in Xinjiang with a continental climate. Although there are fewer tree-ring sampling sites in eastern China, existing tree-ring series in eastern Shaanxi, western Henan, Beijing, southern Heilongjiang, and the border area between Anhui and Zhejiang also exhibit high correlations with disaster-based DWI. The Tibetan Plateau and its surrounding areas, where tree-ring sampling is most abundant in China, show relatively poor correlations with disaster-based DWI. Comparing Fig. 12  and Fig. 4 , the correlation between tree-ring width and disaster-based DWI is weaker when the sampling sites are far from cropland areas (as in Qinghai Province), whereas sites within or near cropland areas (such as the northern slopes of the Tianshan Mountains in Xinjiang) show higher correlations. This suggests that disaster-based DWI and tree-ring width chronologies in adjacent regions contain consistent hydroclimate signals. Furthermore, we noticed that the regional tree-ring chronology, synthesized from multiple individual tree-ring series (Chen et al., 2023, 2024; Hou et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2023 ), exhibited a stronger correlation with the disaster-based DWI compared to a single-point tree-ring chronology. Therefore, attention should be paid to spatial scale matching when corroborating reconstructions by multiple climate proxies.   4 Conclusion This study establishes a disaster-based DWI series for 30 provinces in China covering the period 1978–2008, which is derived from statistical data on crop yield reductions due to droughts and floods, thus ensuring homogeneity with the methodology of the original DWI from 1470 to 1979. Furthermore, we explore the hydroclimatic representativeness of the disaster-based DWI and its accuracy compared to the precipitation-based DWI in reconstructing summer precipitation in eastern China. The key conclusions are:(1) The disaster-based DWI primarily indicates precipitation in most areas of East Central China, with the season window distributed between April and September, generally lasting for five months. However, it shows a greater sensitivity to soil water in the Western, Northeastern and Southeastern regions of China. The most sensitive layer is shallow in the arid regions of the Northwest but deep in the humid regions of the Southwest and Northeast.  (2) The average predicted R-Squared values for summer precipitation reconstruction in 30 provinces in central and eastern China using precipitation-based DWI and disaster-based DWI are 58.6 % and 45.0 %, respectively, with medians of 56.8 % and 44.2 %. The overestimated skill using precipitation-based DWI for calibration is about 13 %. Excluding this inflated R-Squared, using disaster-based DWI for reconstructing historical precipitation changes still maintains at least the p  = 0.05 level, making it a reliable proxy for precipitation reconstruction.    Europe is the earliest region to develop documentary-based climate indices. In recent years, the potential of documentary sources as climate proxies has also been explored in Asia (India), the Americas (Mexico and Argentina), and Africa (Malawi and Namibia) (Nash et al., 2021 ). However, these series typically do not extend into the late 20th century, and it is common practice to connect them with instrumental data series, resulting in heterogeneity issues. This study presents a case study on extending the DWI series in China, which may be helpful in homogenizing similar proxies in other regions. However, constrained by the availability of agricultural drought and flood data, the disaster-based DWI presented in this paper is at the provincial level. Given the vast area of some Chinese provinces (such as Xinjiang and Inner Mongolia), which encompass multiple climatic types, the representativeness of these provincial DWI series may not be as pronounced as in smaller provinces. Future research could utilize multi-source data, such as municipal and county-level socio-economic statistics on agricultural droughts and floods, as well as gridded hydrological disaster data monitored via remote sensing, to establish municipal-level disaster-based DWI series and extend the original DWI dataset station by station.
