1 Introduction Tipping-bucket rain gauges (TBRGs) are very widely used worldwide for the recording of rainfall depths over a range of accumulation durations (minutes, hours, daily, etc.), and are in fact the most widely-deployed type of gauge (Molini et al., 2005; Muñoz et al., 2016 ). The operation and calibration of TBRGs has been extensively researched (Fankhauser, 1998; Overgaard et al., 1998; Habib et al., 2001; La Barbera et al., 2002; Ciach, 2003; Gorman, 2003; Hodgkinson et al., 2004; Gorman, 2011; Santana et al., 2018; Kochendorfer et al., 2017; Segovia-Cardozo et al., 2021, 2023 ). Studies of calibration requirements include both the 'static' calibration (essentially, establishing the volume of water needed to tip the bucket mechanism when water is added at a slow, controlled rate) and the 'dynamic' calibration (assessing the volume actually passing through a bucket as it tips, at various inflow rates: Niemczynowicz, 1986; Jørgensen et al., 1998; Gorman, 2003; Shin et al., 2005; Kvicera and Grabner 2006; Liao et al., 2021 ). The bucket tipping time and behaviour have been investigated using various methods, including high-speed photographic and video imaging (Duchon et al., 2014; Liao et al., 2020 ). These studies have shown that, among other factors, the tipping time is affected by the mass of the bucket mechanism. In addition to needing periodic recalibration as metal and other surfaces age, oxidise, or weather, TBRGs are known to be vulnerable to a multitude of potential error sources, including the effect of wind and turbulence around the gauge on the gauge catch (Pollock et al., 2018; Colli et al., 2018; Cauteruccio et al., 2021b ), especially if gauges are mounted above ground level (Goormans and Willems 2008 ). Significant dynamic biases arise from the continued inflow from the collecting funnel during the brief bucket tipping process, as quantified during dynamic gauge calibration (Marsalek, 1981 ). One outcome of this is that in sufficiently intense rain, a TBRG designed to tip after, say, 0.2 mm of rain will actually under-record the true rainfall depth, owing to additional water (beyond the notional 0.2 mm) that enters a bucket as it tips. This dynamic error becomes worse at higher rain rates, but can partially be corrected by dynamic calibration (Niemczynowicz, 1986; Humphrey et al., 1997; Santana et al., 2018; Sypka, 2019 ). Luyckx and Berlamont (2012)  for instance reported errors of ∼−20 % at 200 mm h−1 . If a gauge underestimates rainfall amounts, then it also under-estimates the associated mean rainfall rate in the tallying period involved. Though it is not frequently explicitly noted, the dynamic error means that TBRGs will typically yield less biased data on rainfall amounts and intensities in locations that experience low-intensity rain than at places where high-intensity convective storms occur. Given the high erosivity of intense rainfall, these are just the environments where reliable intensity data are perhaps most needed. The dynamic error also means that TBRGs are not reliably able to record short-term intensity bursts in any rainfall climate, and will tend therefore to under-estimate the peak intensities that occur during a rainfall event. These can have significance for environmental processes such as soil erosion (Dunkerley, 2019 ) and urban flash-flooding. In urban hydrologic contexts, Burckhardt-Gammeter and Fankhauser (1998)  stressed the importance of 1-minute intensity data. Some post-processing methods for deriving intensity from TBRGs (discussed below) further reduce the representation of short-interval intensities. This includes methods for estimating 1 min intensities or intensities calculated over longer integration times. In order to reduce the variation of dynamic bias with rainfall rate just referred to, many TBRGs are supplied by the manufacturer equipped with a syphon, typically a simple bell syphon (Garrett, 1991, Maksimović et al., 1991 ) fitted between the collecting funnel and the tipping buckets, and designed to regulate the rate at which water enters the buckets (Kimball et al., 2010 ). Rain gauges with no syphon are commonly referred to as “straight-through” designs. The goal of a syphon is to keep the rate of flow into the buckets as nearly constant as can be managed, rather than permitting very high inflow rates in rain of high intensity. The bell syphon has a small reservoir, able to hold a volume of water which is typically less than the amount needed to fill one tipping-bucket. TBRG syphons have two ranges of behaviour. For inflow rates below a threshold related to the syphon geometry and dimensions, the syphon fills and empties in a cyclic manner, such that during the filling stage, which may have a duration of many minutes, no water at all is released to the tipping buckets. The syphon then moves to the emptying stage, drains quickly in as little as 2 s or less, and the cycle then repeats. At high inflow rates, the syphon no longer cycles, but instead releases an uninterrupted stream of water to the tipping buckets. In the first state, the syphon discharge cycle is triggered by the water level rising beyond the outlet tube (Fig. 1  ). The rainfall intensity at which bell syphons in TBRGs cease to cycle is typically ∼150–175 mm h−1 . As will be shown below, in rain exceeding these intensities, dynamic calibration corrections may remain necessary, and this makes additional post-processing of TBRG data necessary if rainfall data of high quality (amount or intensity) are required, regardless of the presence of a syphon. It is emphasised here that the purpose of the syphon is to optimise the ability of a TBRG to record rainfall amounts (depths) during some nominated time interval. However, the effect of syphons on the efficacy of TBRGs in estimating short-term rainfall intensities has not been thoroughly documented. Addressing this knowledge gap is the focal point of the current research. The methodology for determining the optimal design volume and draining time of TBRG syphons remains unclear. The TBRG tested here is described in detail below, and as an example, it is equipped with a syphon whose volumetric capacity is 4.2 mL, whilst the buckets nominally have an operating volume of 6.47 mL. Overgaard et al. (1998)  performed a series of laboratory performance tests on a TBRG, and recommended that the syphon volume should ideally be less than half the capacity of the associated tipping-bucket. However, these nominal, static volumes are not directly applicable to the performance of a syphon during rainfall, owing to the effects of continued inflow to the syphon during its emptying phase. This ensures that even if the syphon has a nominal design capacity of, say, 4.2 mL, or perhaps simply half of the bucket volume, that it will deliver more than this during the emptying cycle if inflow from the rain gauge funnel continues. That is, the syphon behaves as though its volume was larger. Under these conditions, the emptying cycle would also require more time to complete. Thus, even if a syphon had been designed to have a capacity bearing a certain relationship to the bucket volume, it will deliver more than this during rainfall, and the excess will be larger at higher intensities. From the foregoing, it would appear that syphons are of benefit to the improved recording of rainfall depths mainly through a restricted range of intensities, from moderate to high rainfall rates. Whilst this is helpful for the accurate recording of rainfall amounts, the influence of the syphon on the estimation of rainfall intensity over short periods may well be detrimental to data quality. Interestingly, it has been reported that whilst TBRGs may tend to under-record rainfall amounts at high intensities, they can over-estimate rainfall amounts at low intensities. The cause of this has not become clear, though Vasvári (2005)  suggested that it arose from incomplete bucket emptying, and reported over-estimation by up to 22 % under intensities of up to 30 mm h−1 . Other suggestions include surface tension effects and ripples in the ponded water caused by drop arrivals or sudden syphon cycling. Experiments reported below provided the opportunity to explore whether the syphon had an influence on this phenomenon. The objectives of a series of experiments reported here was to explore TBRG operation, using a high-quality gauge equipped with a syphon, and in matched tests with the syphon removed. The experiments sought to address the following issues:a) how the presence of the syphon, with its variable filling and emptying rates, affects the variability of bucket inter-tip times from which rainfall intensity might be judged;  b) how the results in a) vary with the intensity of rain (equivalent to the water inflow rate to the syphon); in other words, does the syphon affect intensity data more at low or at high intensities?  c) to document the way in which syphon emptying time varies with the rate at which water is delivered to it from the rain gauge collecting funnel;  d) to offer comment on what the results of a)−c) above suggest for the reliability of rainfall intensity data derived from TBRG inter-tip times (ITTs) in syphon-equipped TBRGs.  e) to explore the possible influence of the syphon on over-estimation of rainfall amounts at low rainfall intensities.    We turn first to a brief review of the use of TBRG data to estimate rainfall rates and intensities, as necessary background to research questions a)−c) and to the experimental work reported later. Experimental methods are then described. 1.1 The estimation of rainfall intensities from TBRG inter-tip times Short-term intensities, over periods of minutes, are important in various fields. These range from the triggering of urban flash-floods, the attenuation of radio transmissions, and problems of soil erosion on agricultural fields or in post-wildfire landscapes (International Telecommunications Union and Sector, 2017; Dunkerley, 2019; Kilsdonk et al., 2022; Peleg et al., 2023 ). There is currently also evidence for increasing intensity of short-duration rainfalls over intervals as brief as 10 min (Ayat et al., 2022 ), and reliable intensity data are needed to document this. The sequence of inter-tip times (ITTs), representing the times taken for successive bucket filling and tipping events, can readily be calculated if the time of each tip event is logged. This is straightforward using readily-available event data loggers. In some studies, the times of the individual tip events are not recorded, but rather only the total rainfall amount in 1 min, 5 min, or some other interval is logged, or else this is calculated later from the individual tip times (Mandeep and Hassan, 2008; Wang et al., 2008; Song et al., 2017 ). These approaches lose some of the intensity information that a TBRG can potentially provide. It has been widely argued the sequence of tip events and ITTs derived from them represent the highest temporal resolution of rainfall arrival that is possible with a TBRG (Sadler and Busscher, 1989; Cauteruccio et al., 2021a ). In an early application in which a computer was linked directly to a TBRG, Williams and Erdman (1987)  recorded individual tip events in laboratory trials, calculating intensity from successive ITTs. They speculated what the maximum intensity of natural rainfall might be, if judged in this way, from successive tip events. For a typical TBRG, the ITTs can be brief. For instance, using a TBRG having 0.2 mm sensitivity and a 200 mm diameter collecting funnel, the ITT at 100 mm h−1  is 7.2 s, and this declines to 4.8 s at 150 mm h−1 . Consequently, at these intensities, even logging the accumulated rainfall depth every minute loses the information contained in 8–12 individual tip events and the associated varying ITTs. Aggregating data over 5 min intervals thus potentially pools more than 60 tip events and sacrifices the intensity data they contain. Muñoz et al. (2016)  calculated intensities from ITT data, a procedure which they referred to as the 'tip counting method'. Other researchers have summed the tip events occurring in successive clock minutes, calculating the 1-minute rainfall (Mandeep and Hassan, 2008 ). Wang et al. (2008)  tallied the rainfall recorded in minutes during which one or more tip events occurred ('tip minutes'), although much of the rain responsible for a tip event might well have occurred the previous minute or minutes. Methods exist in which the water responsible for a tip event is divided among the minutes whose clock-time boundaries subdivide the ITT (Song et al., 2017; Rachmawati et al., 2022 ). One of several problematic issues with estimating intensities from successive ITTs is that the intensity is never zero, though it becomes increasingly small for longer ITTs. In ITT data derived from TBRGs, it therefore becomes necessary to adopt an arbitrary 'no-rain' criterion as indicating the cessation of rainfall for the purpose of identifying separate rainfall 'events', or for identifying the presence of intermittency in rainfall arrival. Wang et al. (2008)  adopted various intervals for the event separation criterion, ranging from 10 min to 1 h. Interestingly, neither Mandeep and Hassan (2008)  nor Wang et al. (2008)  reported whether their TBRGs were equipped with syphons. Intensity data can be smoothed by fitting cubic splines in post-processing the data. This is associated with further problems, including the generation of some negative intensities, and inability to detect short 'no-rain' periods in the data (Song et al., 2017 ). Overall, then, there seem to be good reasons to wish to retain the intensity information potentially obtainable from sequences of ITTs, but if the TBRG concerned includes a syphon, then further examination of possible syphon artefacts in the data becomes necessary. Artefacts from the operation of the syphon constitute an additional problem to be faced in interpreting intensity from ITTs, and have been documented previously. Parkin et al. (1982) presented an analysis of what they termed the “double-tipping” phenomenon that can arise from the syphon rapidly discharging more water than can be accommodated in a single tipping-bucket. This perturbation was analysed by Maksimović, et al. (1991)  and also noted as “annoying” by Harremoës and Mikkelsen (1995) . As will be shown by the experiments reported below, at higher intensities, the syphon-induced artefacts can become more complex than just the creation of a “double-tip” ITT sequence, though the additional patterns of perturbation appear not to have been documented previously. The laboratory and experimental methods used are described in the following section, prior to reporting the results relating to syphon artefacts in ITT sequences.   2 Methods The influence of the syphon on the dynamics of the tipping-bucket mechanism, including the sequence of ITTs, was investigated by analysing the performance of the TBRG bucket mechanism with a syphon installed, and with it removed. The operation of the syphon itself was explored separately. The TBRG examined was a high-quality RIMCO model 8020 gauge produced by McVan Instruments, Melbourne, Australia (gauges of this pattern are now distributed by the Observator group: https://observator.com/ ). This gauge has gold-coated brass buckets, presumably to resist corrosion or oxidation. Gold plating is hydrophilic, having a contact angle with water of ∼62° (Somlyai-Sipos and Baumli 2022 ), and a more strongly hydrophobic surface might be preferable. The gauge was equipped with a machined brass syphon (Figs. 1 and 2  ). When tests were made with the syphon removed, the outlet tube (Fig. 1 ) was replaced with a similar length of hard PVC tubing having the same inside diameter. This tube is necessary to ensure that the water draining from the funnel discharges directly above the pivot point of the tipping-bucket mechanism. Details of the RIMCO gauge are provided in Table 1  . During testing, limited comparisons were also made with a moulded plastic syphon from a TB4 TBRG, Manufactured by Hydrological Services Ltd., Sydney, Australia. These gauges are now distributed by Kisters AG (https://www.kisters.eu/ ). Some of the experiments described below employed a peristaltic pump (Masterflex L/S) to supply fixed inflow rates to the test TBRG. These pumps are distributed by VWR (https://www.vwr.com/) under the name 'Avantor'. The performance and calibration accuracy of the pump was checked at several fixed pump flow rates, to represent a wide range of rainfall rates. The nominal flow rates were calibrated by delivering flows at five rates (8, 10, 30, 54, and 81 mL min−1 ) for 5 min and catching and weighing the water actually delivered on a laboratory balance (resolution 0.01 g) to determine the calibrated volume delivered by the pump. The actual flow rates (Qmeas  ) were found to be ∼ 10 % above the nominal flow rates (Qnom  ), and the following relation established:(1) Q meas   = 1.11 Q nom   - 0.51     where Qmeas   and Qnom   are both expressed in mL min−1  and for which r2  = 0.999. Calibration of the TBRG was then evaluated by sustaining the constant pumped inflow at each fixed rate until 100 tips had occurred, the count being displayed on a digital electronic counter that had been wired to the second of two reed switches in the RIMCO gauge. The water passing through the tipping-bucket mechanism was caught in a tray beneath the gauge and its volume recorded at the conclusion of each test using appropriate calibrated measuring cylinders of 250 mL, 500 mL, and 1000 mL capacity. This then permitted the actual flow rate, and equivalent rainfall intensity to be confirmed. These tests were conducted with the syphon installed in the TBRG, and repeated with the syphon removed. To address research objective (c) (above), the dynamic performance of the syphon, removed from the TBRG, was also measured at various fixed, pumped inflow rates, by timing the duration of its emptying cycle (the time interval during which water is discharged to the tipping-buckets) by direct visual observation. Mounted in a laboratory clamp, the syphon was fed with water using the peristaltic pump until 5 discharge cycles had occurred. The volume discharged per cycle was determined by weighing the water caught in a small container mounted beneath the syphon, and taking the mean. Additionally, the emptying time of the syphon initially filled with water and then allowed to discharge was also recorded. As this time is brief (<2 s), this was done using video recordings of the syphon, which was carefully filled with water at a slow rate using a wash bottle. A very high-resolution stopwatch with digital display (Laurel Electronics, California, USA (https://www.laurels.com/ ); time resolution set to 1 ms) was placed in the camera field of view during recording. The slow-motion video frame rate of the smart phone used was 240 frames per second, which limited the video time resolution to ∼6 ms. From the video recording, the moment at which the syphon began to empty, and when it ceased to empty, could be recorded with high temporal resolution by stepping through individual frames of the video recording. Hand timing with an ordinary digital stopwatch proved inadequate, in light of the brief emptying time of ∼2 s and the significant human reaction time (∼0.25 s). The emptying time indicates the maximum emptying rate, and hence the maximum rainfall intensity at which the syphon can operate. At intensities that exceed this value, the syphon would be overtopped, filling more rapidly than it could empty, and thus ceasing to cycle. The syphon would then simply release a continuous stream of water to the tipping buckets. Research objectives (a) and (b) (above) were addressed by supplying the test TBRG with a number of fixed pumped water flow rates. Each test was performed with the syphon installed and repeated with no syphon. Each test at a fixed flow rate was maintained for a period of 15 min, with nominal inflow rates (set using the pump control panel) from 10 mL min−1  to 150 mL min−1 . For the RIMCO gauge, these nominal flow rates correspond to rainfall rates of 18.5 mm h−1  to 278 mm h−1 . The time of each tip event was logged using a HOBO® event data logger, to the nearest 1 s. The variation in inter-tip times (ITTs) was then analysed, all tip event data logged in the Gregorian calendar first being converted to Modified Julian days. These date and time conversions were made using software routines from the International Astronomical Union “Standards of fundamental astronomy” subroutine library (http://www.iausofa.org/ ). The nominal calibrations of the pump flow rate supplied by the manufacturer were once again not relied upon, and instead all water passing through the TBRG mechanism was caught in a tray and measured volumetrically at the end of each 15-minute test. The actual pumped flow rate was then determined. The lowest flow rate deliverable by the peristaltic pump was 8 mL min−1 , the equivalent of ∼15 mm h−1  rainfall intensity. Because typical rainfall intensities at many locations are considerably lower, supplementary tests were carried out using a constant-head reservoir mounted above the TBRG to achieve lower constant inflow rates. Flow rates were adjusted using a small inline gate valve, and could readily be set to <1 mL min−1 . Such low flow rates consist of a sequence of drips at intervals of a few seconds. For the test TBRG, an inflow rate of 1 mL min−1  is the equivalent of 2 mm h−1  intensity. In order to log a meaningful number of tip events and ITTs, tests at such low flow rates were continued for at least 1 h. Tip events were logged using the HOBO® event data logger, and the commencement times of syphon emptying cycles were noted by direct visual observation of the water level in the syphon, observed from just above the rainfall collecting funnel (the debris mesh filter having been removed), and the time recorded according using a stopwatch. In data processing, imposed flow rates were converted to equivalent rainfall rates using the relations set out in Eqs. (2) and (3) . The collecting area of the gauge funnel is 323.65 cm2 . Thus, 1 mL applied over this area corresponds to 0.0309 mm rainfall depth, and thus a pumped flow rate of 1 mL per minute is equivalent to (60 × 0.031) or ∼1.854 mm h−1 . Thus, measured pumped flow rates Q  (mL min−1 ) can be converted to equivalent rainfall rates RR  (mm h−1 ) according to the relation(2) RR = 1.854 Q     Equivalently, rainfall rates can be converted to pumped flow rates using the relation(3) Q = R R / 1.854       3 Results 3.1 Behaviour of the syphon-equipped TRBG at low inflow rates A first test was made by supplying the syphon-equipped TBRG with a constant, low inflow rate of 0.91 mL min−1 , the equivalent of an intensity of 1.7 mm h−1 . This low intensity ensures that there is negligible inflow to the syphon during its brief emptying cycle (documented next), such that the volume discharged from the syphon when it reached the level that triggers an emptying event could be documented. The test was run for 83 min, and during this time 75.6 mL of water was discharged. There were 12 TBRG tip events and 18 syphon emptying cycles during the 83 min (Fig. 3  ). This reveals that the mean tip volume of the buckets was 6.3 mL (just less than the nominal 6.47 mL), and the mean volume of the syphon emptying was 4.2 mL. These volumes are not equal, such that a single syphon cycle would be insufficient to fill a bucket and result in a tip event. Two emptying cycles would consequently be required, but this would deliver more than the capacity of one bucket, the excess partially filling the second bucket after the tip with a volume of (2 × 4.2) − 6.3 = 2.1 mL. A further syphon cycle would fill this bucket (2.1 mL + 4.2 mL = 6.3 mL) and trigger a tip, leaving the next bucket empty; the cycle would then repeat. The test thus consisted of syphon cycles uniformly distributed in time (every 4.5 min, approx.) owing to the uniform pumped inflow rate. However, the bucket tip events were unevenly spaced − the ITTs being alternately ∼9 min (two syphon cycles) and ∼4.4 min (one syphon cycle) (Fig. 3 ). Thus, the ITTs corresponded to a rainfall intensity of either ∼1.3 mm h−1  or ∼2.6 mm h−1 . The actual mean intensity through the entire 83 min test at constant flow rate was ∼1.7 mm h−1 . The pattern of ITTs, of T and 2T, where T is the time for the syphon to cycle, was reasonably, but not completely, regular. However, this regularity cannot persist at higher rainfall intensities (inflow rates) because the volume of water entering the syphon as it drains becomes larger, and correspondingly the syphon emptying times become longer (documented below). Thus, at higher intensities, the syphon would not discharge the 4.2 mL just documented, but up to several additional mL contributed by the inflow during emptying. Correspondingly, the regular ITT pattern of T and 2T is unlikely to occur at all rainfall intensities. Additionally, during rainfall of fluctuating intensity, the variation of ITTs resulting from the syphon operation would be compounded with the fluctuating inflows. The implications of this are considered in the Discussion section.  3.2 Emptying times of the syphon at eight fixed inflow rates Emptying times with no inflow rate were determined by slow-motion photography, the syphon being filled carefully using a wash bottle, with filling suspended instantly the syphon began to discharge. This resulted in a mean emptying time of 1.8 s. For the RIMCO gauge, with a syphon volume of 4.2 mL, this amounts to a discharge flow rate of ((60/1.8)  ×  4.2) mL min−1 , or ∼140 mL min−1 . In turn, this is equivalent to a rainfall intensity of ∼260 mm h−1 . When varying continuous inflow rates were fed to the syphon, the emptying time became significantly longer, as the inflow offset part of the outflow, delaying the fall of the water level below the syphon trigger. Tests were made at fixed inflow rates of 20, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, and 90 mL min−1 , and the syphon emptying time for 10 cycles was recorded. As the emptying times increased to almost 10 s at an inflow of 90 mL min−1 , the cycles were recorded using a digital stopwatch reading to 0.01 s. The data (Fig. 4  ) can be described by an exponential regression model of the form(4) S et   = 1.85  exp  0.008 R R     where Set   is the syphon time (s) to empty, and RR  is the rainfall rate in mm h−1 . For this relationship r2  = 0.96. These tests were only performed up to inflow rates of 90 mL min−1  (equivalent to ∼167 mm h−1 ) because above this intensity, the RIMCO syphon was unable to cycle, instead delivering a continuous stream of water to the tipping buckets. Supplementary video 1  shows a syphon cycle recorded in slow-motion with the milli-second stopwatch display in the camera field of view. The larger syphon discharge volume at higher rainfall intensities means that the regular T, 2T sequence of ITTs described above at negligible inflow rate (1.7 mm h−1 ) cannot occur. This is documented further in Section 3.4  below.  3.3 Depth measurement accuracy of the TBRG at various flow rates with and without a fitted syphon (for 100 tips) The need for dynamic calibration of TBRGs is well-known, because at high inflow rates unmeasured water continues to enter the emptying bucket as it tips. Syphons are intended to reduce the magnitude of this unmeasured component of the rainfall depth. This was explored by recording the volume discharged by the TBRG mechanism in 100 tips, for varying inflow rates from 0.9 to 150 mL min−1 . The results are summarised in Fig. 5  (A). This shows that with a syphon installed, the RIMCO gauge is very close to its nominal bucket capacity of 6.5 mL up to an intensity of ∼225 mm h−1 , equivalent to the inflow rate of ∼100 mL min−1  reported previously as the point at which the syphon can no longer operate. Above an intensity of 225 mm h−1 , the RIMCO gauge shows increasing volume per tip, which would go unmeasured if only the number of tips was known, as is normally the case in logged data. Here, the true volume passing through the buckets was known because the water was caught in a tray beneath the TBRG, and measured volumetrically. Contrasting behaviour was found with no syphon fitted (Fig. 5 (B)). In this case, the RIMCO gauge discharged less than the nominal 6.5 mL per tip up to an intensity of ∼225 mm h−1  (that is, it over-estimated the rainfall amount) and above this intensity, discharged more than the nominal bucket capacity (i.e., it under-estimated the rainfall amount). However, the performance with and without the syphon was essentially the same − an under-estimate of the true rainfall amount. Interestingly, the mean of the estimates of mL/tip with no syphon fitted was 6.49, very close to the manufacturer's design specification of 6.47 mL/tip, and the mean with a syphon installed was very similar, at 6.60 mL/tip. Both results are very close to the calibration value, as would be expected of a high-quality TBRG such as the RIMCO device. This would not be the case in persistently low-intensity rain, when the absence of a syphon resulted in over-estimation of the rain depth (that is, tipping with a smaller volume of water than the expected, calibrated value), or in persistently high-intensity rain, when both configurations under-estimate the rain depth. The aggregate error in recorded rainfall depth in any real rainfall event of fluctuating intensity cannot readily be determined, and the specifications of accuracy for TBRGs provided by manufacturers presumably arise from laboratory calibrations at constant inflow rates.  3.4 Judging intensity from TBRG ITTs with and without a fitted syphon, for 15 min fixed-flow-rate tests The foregoing results have focussed on the buckets and syphons, and their capacities and operation at various constant inflow rates. These results primarily bear on the question of how well the TBRG records rainfall amounts with and without an installed syphon. In rainfall having an intensity up to ∼225 mm h−1 , the syphon-equipped gauge performed very well, but in this intensity range without a syphon the buckets appear to tip when filled with less than the nominal volume required according to the calibration (Fig. 5 ). Under-estimation of rainfall amount, generally cited as the reason for dynamic calibration of TBRGs, does not appear to be a problem for the RIMCO gauge except at intensities >225 mm h−1 . At these higher intensities, the syphon does not cycle, and both with and without a syphon, the gauge tends to under-record the volume of rainfall (that is, the data show a larger effective tip volume than the nominal calibrated value that would ordinarily be relied upon to work out the rainfall depth in some monitoring period). We now turn to the possible influence of the syphon on the estimation of moment-to-moment intensities, using the ITTs. This was noted in the Introduction to be widely-considered the highest resolution source of intensity data that can be derived from TBRG records. The influence of the syphon is explored using the logged bucket tip times during 15 min tests at constant inflow rates, with and without the fitted syphon. Thus, what has been referred to as the “double tip” effect (Parkin et al., 1982; Maksimović et al., 1991 ) arises, with a first ITT being relatively long (∼9 min as described in Section 3.1  above), followed by two tips much closer together in time (∼4 min as described above). This is well-illustrated in data from a fixed flow rate of 56.7 mL min−1  (equivalent to an intensity of 105 mm h−1 ) with the syphon installed (Fig. 6  ). In this test, the mean ITT was 6.44 s, but this reflected both the long (mean = 7.3 s) and the intervening two short (mean = 2.8 s) ITTs. The rainfall intensity range among the ITTs was 60 mm h−1  to 360 mm h−1 , whilst the true mean intensity through this 15 min test at constant inflow rate was 105 mm h−1 . The range of possible outcomes from this phenomenon at various intensities (inflow rates) is further illustrated by plotted snapshots from the experimental data in Fig. 7  . This figure compares the time-sequence of tip events with and without a syphon, at various fixed inflow rates. The very regular 'staircase-like' tip sequence that results when there is no syphon (Fig. 7 (A)) contrasts strikingly with the irregular, long ITT−short ITT patterns that result from the syphon operation. Fig. 7 (B) shows 5–6 short ITTs between each longer ITT. Fig. 7 (C) shows a more complex ITT sequence in which two relatively long ITTs separated by 1–3 shorter ITTs alternates with long ITTs separated by up to six shorter ITts. Finally, Fig. 7 (D) shows relatively long ITTs separated by 4 and 5 shorter ITTs. It is evident that even under a single constant pumped inflow rate, the syphon cycling is not completely regular. The syphon is small, and contains spaces that are bridged by surface tension menisci. Even the outlet tube, immediately above the tipping buckets, can be seen upon examination to have a bulging surface tension meniscus that eventually breaks up to allow the syphon emptying cycle to commence. (This can be seen in Supplementary video 1 ). A small volume of water retained in the lowermost syphon outlet tube, as well as below the syphon bell chamber, was documented by Cai et al. (2020)  using dyed water and a transparent plastic syphon. The effect of syphon cycling on the sequence of ITTs depends on the rainfall intensity (the inflow rate to the syphon during its emptying cycle). It was shown above that the syphon influence is clearly evident even at intensities <2 mm h−1 . The variability of ITTs in the TBRG with and without the installed syphon, for various inflow rates, is shown in Table 2  . Both ITTs in seconds, and the corresponding nominal rainfall intensity (assuming for the moment that the nominal calibration of 0.2 mm per tip is valid) and the actual imposed intensity based on the volume of water caught during each test, are shown. The absolute values of the ITTs of course vary with the intensity, with mean ITTs of >6 min at 2 mm h−1 , declining to ∼2.25 s at 168 mm h−1 . To contrast the outcome with and without the syphon, several measures can be used. First, it is notable that the ratio of the longest ITT to the shortest ITT averages 3.12 with a syphon, but only 1.44 without a syphon. The same ratios apply to the ratios of the intensity corresponding to the longest and shortest ITTs. Another parameter that provides a useful summary of the syphon/no syphon results is the coefficient of variation, defined as CV  = σ /μ  where σ  is the standard deviation of the ITTs, and μ  is the mean ITT for each test at a fixed intensity. Table 2  shows that the average coefficient of variation is 0.3 (maximum 0.4) for the syphon tests, but only 0.1 (maximum 0.19) for the no-syphon tests. It is thus evident that whilst all of the tests reported in Table 2  were carried out at fixed pumped flow rates, the presence of the syphon has resulted in a considerably larger variation in ITTs, and hence in estimates of intensity that might be made using the ITTs. Suppose for example that owing to continued inflow, the syphon discharges 4.9 mL per emptying cycle rather than the 4.2 mL mentioned in section 3.1  above. Assume that the buckets still require 6.3 mL to tip. Then the first syphon cycle fails to fill the bucket, and no tip results. The second cycle fills and tips that bucket, using 1.4 mL of its discharge, and thus partly fills the second bucket with 3.5 mL. The third cycle fills and tips the second bucket, using 2.8 mL, and delivers the remaining 2.1 mL to the first bucket. The fourth cycle fills and tips bucket 1 using 4.1 mL, adding 0.7 mL to bucket 2. The fifth cycle would fill bucket 2–5.6 mL, and no tip would result. The sixth cycle however would result in a rapid tip, since only an additional 0.7 mL would tip bucket 2, and the remaining 4.2 mL would partly fill bucket 1 again. A seventh cycle would rapidly fill bucket 1 to tipping point, using only 2.1 mL. At intervals, the two cycles needed to fill a bucket and result in a tip would result in an anomalously long ITT, which follows several prior shorter syphon cycles. This occurs despite the inflow rate being constant. Under natural rain of varying intensity, more complex sequences of ITTs must be expected. It is appropriate to consider the errors in rainfall intensity estimated from individual ITTs, for both syphon-equipped and straight-through gauges. For each Table 3   shows, for each pumped inflow rate, the ITT (in s) expected for a bucket of 6.4 mL capacity, together with the measured average ITT. Also shown are the intensity that would be estimated from the minimum and maximum recorded ITTs. These results show that when using the minimum observed ITT, the syphon-equipped gauge data yield an intensity estimate that averages 105 % too high (reaching a maximum of >240 % too high), and when using the maximum observed ITT, yields an intensity estimate that is on average 34.2 % too low. These figures compare with an average of 33 % and 12 % for the straight-though gauge. In other words, the errors in the syphon-equipped gauge are on average about three times greater than those from a straight-though gauge. Errors for particular flow rates are higher than these average values. In summary, the constant inflow rate experiments demonstrated that syphon artefacts arise in the sequence of ITTs at all intensities tested, from ∼2 mm h−1  to >300 mm h−1 . No single pattern of perturbed ITTs is apparent, and instead patterns differ among applied intensities. However, as Table 2  illustrates, the coefficient of variation of ITTs is always larger for the syphon-equipped TBRG than when the syphon had been removed. Residual variation in ITTs in that case is likely to reflect occasional perturbations by surface tension, air entrapment with the syphon, or other effects of this kind. These, and temperature-related viscosity effects on syphon cycling remain to be investigated.   4 Discussion The test results presented here document some aspects of syphon-equipped TBRG performance. Syphon cycling during increasingly intense rainfall discharges a larger volume of water, and takes a longer time (in some cases, exceeding 10 s) to complete the draining cycle. Thus, during natural rainfall (rather than constant flow rate experiments) there can be no pre-defined volumetric relation between syphon and bucket, because inflow during syphon emptying can mean that more than the static syphon volume (4.2 mL in the case of the tested RIMCO TBRG) is discharged to the tipping buckets. At low intensities, the syphon normally discharges about 65 % of one bucket volume. However, at moderate and high intensities, the syphon can in fact discharge more than one bucket volume, comprised of the static syphon volume plus the inflow during the emptying time. The excess outflow may be sufficient to cause multiple tip events in rapid succession, so falsely indicating rain of higher intensity than may actually have been the case during syphon filling time, given that it empties at a rate equivalent to ∼260 mm h−1  (Section 3.2 ). Under these circumstances, it is not clear what can really be understood from the static capacity of the syphon specified by some manufacturers of TBRGs. It therefore is important that published findings based on TBRG data, if they involve the analysis of intensity from ITT sequences, should make it clear whether the gauge was syphon-equipped or a 'straight-through' design. Many published studies of TBRG performance and calibration do not mention the role of the syphon, nor point to the current situation in which some TBRGs on the market are syphon-equipped, whilst others are not. Lanza and Stagi (2008) for instance, in their review of rainfall data accuracy standards, do not mention TBRG syphons. Colli et al. (2018)  determined intensity from ITT sequences, but employed as Casella TBRG which was probably of 'straight-through' design, although this was not stated. In their discussion of intensity assessed from ITT sequences, Wang et al. (2008)  did not mention what form of TBRG was used. Mandeep and Hassan (2008), Fiser and Wilfert (2009), Muñoz et al. (2016)  and others have also failed to comment on the form of gauge that they used for ITT analysis of rainfall intensities. It is widely appreciated that TBRGs are not ideal devices for the recording of short-term rainfall intensities, primarily as a result of the time needed for bucket-filling and tipping, but with multiple additional attendant problems (Dunkerley, 2023a ). However, the situation is made more complex by the addition of a syphon. The resulting irregular sequence of ITTs, demonstrated here as occurring even in strictly constant inflow, leaves this “highest resolution source of intensity data obtainable from a TBRG” (Cautericcio et al., 2021) badly degraded if syphon-equipped TBRGs are used (Table 2 ). The various patterns and irregularities in sequences of ITTs (Fig. 7 ) cannot entirely be the result of a notional mismatch between syphon and bucket capacities. Especially at low intensities, surface tension influences syphon filling and draining, as evidence for instance by the progressively bulging meniscus at the outlet of the syphon drain pipe during syphon filling (see Supplementary movie 1 ). The syphon is a small device, with the water having to move through narrow gaps of just a few mm. Indeed, in the RIMCO gauge the gap under the bell, though which the water enters and rises within the bell, is just 2.5 mm wide. Moreover, just as oxidation, corrosion and adhering particles can influence the filling and emptying of tipping-buckets, so too they seem likely to influence syphon operation. Possible perturbations of syphon operation owing to air bubbles has been suggested (Overgaard et al., 1998 ), perhaps more likely in rain of high intensity. These effects, and a proper evaluation of surface tension and viscosity influences on syphon operations, remain to be fully explored. During the field data collection for this paper, an infra-red non-contact thermometer was used to record the temperature of the TBRG copper collecting funnel heated by the sun, immediately prior to the arrival of afternoon thunderstorm rain. The surface temperature was >61 °C, and as a consequence quite warm water, with abnormally low viscosity, would, initially at least, have drained to the syphon and the tipping-buckets. In relation to research objective (e), the present study confirmed that a straight-through TBRG can over-estimate rainfall amounts at low- to moderate-intensities (Fig. 5 ). In this study, over-estimation occurred from ∼2 mm h−1 , the lowest intensity tested, to ∼75 mm h−1 . This means that the bucket mechanism tips before the bucket fills to its nominal, calibrated volume. The cause of this effect is unclear, but seems likely to relate to processes such as ripples on the pool of water in a bucket, or splash effects, both of which could displace the centre of mass. The use of a wettable bucket material such as gold-coated brass might act to exacerbate such influences, but further testing is needed. Overgaard et al. (1998)  tested syphons of various sizes in several TBRGs. They concluded that a syphon with a volume of less than half the volume of a tipping bucket would best reduce syphon artefacts in the ITT sequence. However, it is arguable that a preferable path would be to remove the syphon altogether. Then, with proper calibration, the unaggregated sequence of individual ITTs could each be separately calibrated according to laboratory testing under various rainfall intensities. Such a procedure involves no complex calculations, and would maintain ITTs as the highest-resolution source of intensity data obtainable from a TBRG. Commercially-available TBRGs that operate on this principle are available. An example is the Xylem H-3401-SDI gauge, manufactured by YSI (https://www.ysi.com/rain-gauge ). This is a straight-through gauge, in which intensity (and hence rainfall amount) are derived from individual ITTs, corrected by an on-board processor according to prior calculation of the increasing volume of water represented by ITTs of varying duration. There are also devices that can be interposed between a TBRG and a data logger, and designed to correct the recorded data. An example is the High Sierra 'tip rate compensator' (https://hsierra.com/product/tip-rate-compensator-model-2400-50/ ). It is worth emphasising here that other approaches to rainfall recording, including acoustic methods (Dunkerley, 2020, 2023b ), have the capacity to record intensity from moment to moment with much higher temporal resolution than a TBRG, even when individual ITTs are recorded. Such methods may avoid many of the complications that arise with TBRGs.  5 Conclusions The work reported above has demonstrated that whilst the inclusion of a syphon in a TRBG can improve the quality of recorded rainfall depths over a wide range of intensities, it degrades the usefulness of intensity data derived from the inter-tip times at all intensities. The sequence of ITTs has often been regarded as the source of the highest-resolution intensity data available from a TBRG, but this is difficult to defend in the presence of syphon cycling artefacts. For the case of constant intensities as tested here, TBRG data aggregated over time intervals of 5–10 min duration or longer yield the same mean intensity (actually better referred to as a “rainfall rate”) whether or not the TBRG contains a syphon. However, these findings cannot readily be transferred to natural rainfall in which the intensity may fluctuate widely from moment-to-moment. In that case, the emptying time of a syphon may reflect not the intensity at a particular moment, but rather the sequence of intensities over an unknown antecedent period. A syphon may respond rapidly to a small increase in intensity, if it is already largely full, or more slowly, if the intensity has been low since it last emptied. The sequence of ITTs was shown above to be perturbed by syphon operation, which can result in somewhat erratic and unpredictable changes in ITT even under constant inflow. In the case of a completely unknown actual inflow in the field application of a TBRG exposed to natural rainfall, when intensity may fluctuate from moment-to-moment, it would be virtually impossible to derive reliable intensity data from individual logged ITTs. It is in the estimation of short-term peak intensities that the perturbations caused by a syphon are perhaps most severe, and this is problematic for studies where short-term intensities are important, such as soil erosion or in documenting the effects of climate variability on short-duration rainfall intensities. Short-interval rainfall rates, such as 1-minute, 5-minute, or 10-minute data, are important in various fields. As mentioned earlier, this includes the analysis and prediction of urban runoff and flash-flooding, and detection of changes in short-interval rainfall intensities linked to climate change. As argued above, syphon-equipped tipping bucket gauges perturb short-period intensity data derived from inter-tip times. Given the near-impossibility of disentangling actual intensity fluctuations from syphon artefacts, the results reported here suggest that intensities judged from the ITTs of a syphon-equipped gauge are likely to be reliable only if they are processed from accumulation durations no shorter than about 10 min. Therefore, in studies where hourly data are sufficient, syphon-equipped gauges do not pose any difficulty. However, in the kinds of fields just mentioned, where resolution of minutes is needed, syphon-induced artefacts are problematic. Syphon artefacts would also be problematic in the application of syphon-equipped gauges for ground-truth evaluation of intensity data derived from other methods, including radar-based methods, acoustic methods, and others. Furthermore, given that the detection of the start and end of rainfall can be affected by time-lags related to syphon filling time, studies of sub-hourly intermittency will also potentially suffer degraded data quality if syphon-equipped gauges are used. If intermittency cannot be reliably detected, then apparent hourly intensities will be misleading. It therefore appears that for routine climatological and related studies in which only hourly or daily rainfall data are required, syphon-induced artefacts cause no difficulties, and indeed, the benefits of the syphon in minimising dynamic errors are significant in this kind of application. This supports the wide adoption of syphon-equipped gauges in such work. In contrast, studies of short-interval intensities are likely to be degraded if syphon-equipped gauges are employed. Thus, gauge data quality issues in relation to the objectives of rainfall monitoring need to be considered carefully. In consequence, some studies may be best to adopt syphon-equipped gauges, whilst others may require straight-through gauges. Importantly, the nature of tipping-bucket gauges used particularly in studies of short-interval intensities must be clearly reported, together with the data themselves. There seems little doubt that the collection of high-resolution intensity data should preferably be done with a TBRG having no syphon installed. In such a case, there is no perturbation of the sequence of ITTs beyond that caused by external rainfall intensity fluctuations. Dynamic calibration could then be performed and the logged data corrected for dynamic bias at the level of individual ITTs, raising the possibility of obtaining both accurate rainfall depth data and, at the same time, reliable short-term intensity data.
1 Introduction Water resource management is crucial for sustainable development, ensuring reliable water supplies, flood control, and hydropower generation, with reservoirs playing a pivotal role (Yang et al., 2022 ). Reservoirs are characterized by complex nonlinear objectives and operational constraints, such as the mass balance equation, release boundaries, and storage limits (Solomatine and Ostfeld, 2008 ). Therefore, robust reservoir simulation models are vital in estimating the reservoir features that allow policymakers to foresee the reservoir reaction (Liu et al., 2022 ). Data Science Techniques (DST) are popular models that can autonomously learn and simulate reservoir operations from hydrological data alone (Yang et al., 2022 ). DSTs are artificial intelligence models that extract insights and knowledge from structured and unstructured data (Mahmoud et al., 2023 ). Among DSTs, ANNs are widely employed to simulate reservoir operations. Compared to classic techniques, ANNs have shown superiority in forecasting optimal reservoir outflow to maximize hydropower generation (Chen et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2019 ). A recent study reported that ANN could offer optimal reservoir outflows with a 17.5 % higher sustainability index than the Conventional Reservoir Operation method (Moeini and Hadiyan, 2022 ). Zhang et al. (2018)  compared the performance of ANN, SVR, and LSTM in simulating the reservoir outflow and reported its superiority when the training dataset is limited. However, due to their opaque internal calculations, ANNs functioning as black boxes raise concerns about their alignment with the underlying theories governing reservoir operations. The alignment of DSTs, in general, and ANNs, in particular, with underlying theories governing hydrological problems could be enhanced by incorporating prior knowledge regarding those theories into their loss function as supplementary constraints. This approach is known as the theory-guided data science technique (TGDS) (Herath et al., 2021 ). The initial integration of prior knowledge into the ANN's framework occurred in 2005 when, in a groundbreaking move, Hu et al. (2005)  underscored the potential of this approach to refine the accuracy of ANN in runoff prediction. They embedded the linear increment of runoff concerning the watershed's antecedent precipitation index (API) as constraints in the model's architecture and achieved higher accuracy than traditional approaches. Recently, Hoedt et al. (2021)  embedded mass conservation into the LSTM's architecture as additional constraints to ensure cumulative streamflow predictions do not exceed precipitation inputs. Their TGDS was found to be a more accurate predictor than standard LSTM. Herath et al. (2021)  proposed the Machine Learning Rainfall-Runoff Model Induction (ML-RR-MI), a TGDS that is hydrologically informed. ML-RR-MI incorporates the existing body of hydrological knowledge as a constraint in the training process of genetic programming to maintain consistency. They have found ML-RR-MI as a flexible Rainfall-Runoff modeling framework for predicting accurate and physically consistent runoff in different watersheds. Considering the field of reservoir operation, there is only one study that exclusively proposed a TGDS approach. Zheng et al. (2022)  developed a Physical-Guided LSTM (i.e., PG-LSTM) to simulate a reservoir system by incorporating the water balance principle, the monotonic relationship between inflow and outflow, and outflow boundaries as constraints in the optimization scheme of LSTM. They found that PG-LSTM outperforms classic LSTM and Gradian Boosting Regression Tree. Nearing et al. (2021)  stressed the importance of research into TGDS approaches for reservoir operation, pointing out a lack of detailed analysis of the pros and cons of TGDS in existing studies. Although Zheng et al. (2022)  confirmed the effectiveness of TGDS in reservoir simulation, they did not detail the conditions under which inconsistencies may arise or how incorporating specific constraints mitigates them. Elucidating these issues enables scholars to anticipate such discrepancies and, by applying relevant principles, enhance the adaptability of models while avoiding the unnecessary incorporation of constraints. The mass balance constraint is the most crucial principle in reservoir simulation models, surpassing other important operational principles such as release boundaries and storage volume limits (Wang et al., 2010 ). While evaluating consistency with release boundaries and storage limits is relatively straightforward, accurately assessing a model's adherence to the mass balance principle demands simultaneous estimation of all its components, including reservoir storage volume, release flow, and losses. Xu et al. (2020)  emphasized the complexity of this task due to the limitations and interconnections of these components. Notably, most studies (Chen et al., 2022; Moeini and Hadiyan, 2022; Niu et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018 ) often sidestepped these challenges by overlooking reservoir losses and primarily focusing on estimating reservoir outflows. Therefore, there is a pressing need to develop a robust multi-output DST that simultaneously estimates these elements while adhering to the principles governing them. Moreover, despite the widespread application of ANNs in reservoir simulation, no TGDS based on this framework have been developed. Given the inherent simplicity and reduced computational demands of ANNs, a TGDS that utilizes this model could offer a fast, straightforward, adaptable, and robust method for addressing complex reservoir management challenges. This study aims to identify the conditions under which principal inconsistencies arise and elucidate how integrating operational principles mitigates these inconsistencies. In doing so, it introduces a theory-guided multi-output model in which fundamental operational principles, such as release boundaries, storage volume limits, and the mass balance principle, are included as supplementary constraints in the model's training process. We define eight scenarios, ranging from an unconstrained setup to a fully guided scenario incorporating all three principles. By evaluating these scenarios under various hydrological conditions, we assess the frequency of each type of inconsistency and clarify how integrating the corresponding principle helps to mitigate it. Moreover, this study aims to present the advantages and disadvantages of incorporating each principle concerning the reservoir operation mechanism. Our model, the Theory-Guided Multi-Objective Artificial Neural Network (TG-MO-ANN), is developed based on ANN to address the gap created by neglecting this framework. To enable simultaneous estimation of all mass balance components, our model introduces a novel parallel framework for ANNs. This framework facilitates the independent yet concurrent estimation of all mass balance equation components while maintaining a unified training process that integrates operational principles. Unlike previous studies, our approach incorporates a multi-objective optimization algorithm for training to ensure independent estimation of each target, specifically the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm III (NSGA-III). Meanwhile, we employ the Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to the Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) to autonomously select the optimal solution from the Pareto front generated by NSGA-III, ensuring the most effective model performance. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2  summarizes the fundamental concepts used in this study and describes the methodology of TG-MO-ANN for reservoir simulation. Details on the selected case study are described in Section 3 , followed by the comparative results in Section 4 , where the frequency of principal inconsistencies and the influence of incorporating different principles are explored. Section 5  discusses the beneficial and detrimental impacts of incorporating each principle and highlights the research significance, implications, and limitations. Eventually, conclusions are drawn in Section 6 .  2 Methodology 2.1 Artificial Neural network ANNs, modeled after the human brain, consist of networks of neurons that transmit information via signals (Moayedi et al., 2019 ). A standard ANN includes input, hidden, and output layers. In fully connected ANNs, inputs are sent to all neurons in the hidden layer through synaptic weights. These inputs are then weighted, combined with a bias, and processed through an activation function within each neuron. This procedure is repeated between the hidden and output layers to produce the network's final outputs. Typically, ANNs use non-decreasing activation functions such as sigmoid or hyperbolic tangent for neurons in the hidden layers, while the output neurons use sigmoid or linear functions. The mathematical mechanism of an ANN with one hidden layer and two outputs can be expressed as follows:(1) Y 1  = φ  out   b out - 1   + ∑ j = 1  m  w j - 1   φ j  b j  + ∑ i = 1  n  w i - j   × x i            (2) Y 2  = φ  out   b out - 2   + ∑ j = 1  m  w j - 2   φ j  b j  + ∑ i = 1  n  w i - j   × x i            ANNs are trained by adjusting the synaptic weights and biases to minimize the difference between the network's outputs and predefined targets (i.e., the network's error), typically represented by the Mean Square Error between the output and target vectors. In the case of multi-output ANNs, each output has its error, and the entire network's error is the normal or weighted average of these errors. However, when one of the outputs has a deficient error while the other has a higher error, the average value may not precisely represent the network's error, potentially jeopardizing the training process. Moreover, according to equations (1) and (2) , the product of neurons in the hidden layer, expressed by the term φ j  b j  + ∑ i = 1  n  w i - j   × x i      , is analogous for both outputs. Therefore, only the synaptic weights and biases of neurons in the output layer (i.e., wj-1 , wj-2 , bout-1,  and bout-2 ) can cause different outcomes at each output neuron. These issues are the main reasons for the shortcomings of classic multi-output ANNs (Moayedi et al., 2019 ).  2.2 New structure for multi-output artificial neural networks To overcome the shortages described in multi-output ANNs, scholars often employ multiple independent ANNs to predict different outputs (Haykin, 2009 ). However, in particular problems, like reservoir simulation, mathematical relationships such as the mass balance principle exist between different outputs. Due to the inevitable aleatoric uncertainties in the training process of each independent ANN, the predicted outputs may not adhere to these relationships. Consequently, inconsistencies with the principal theories result in systematic errors in the estimations. To tackle this issue, we propose a new architecture featuring multiple parallel sub-networks, each tailored to a specific output. These sub-networks are not fully connected, enabling dedicated neurons for each output in the hidden and output layers. The network uses a unified training process through a multi-objective optimization algorithm to minimize the error for each output individually. Following the previous studies in which scholars have utilized DSTs to simulate the reservoir operation (Aboutalebi et al., 2015; Moeini and Hadiyan, 2022; Niu et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2010 ), the most influential operation data, including the current time step (t), current inflow (It ), the previous release with one-moment lag (Rt-1 ), the previous storage volume with one-moment lag (St-1 ) and the previous losses with one-moment lag (Lt-1 ) are considered as inputs. Three parameters, including the current storage volume (St ), current release flow (Rt ), and current losses (Lt ), are considered as outputs. Accordingly, the proposed model in our study offers a one-step prediction of the reservoir features. This choice is motivated by the operational nature of reservoir management, which often necessitates immediate responses to current conditions. One-step predictions suffice for making prompt adjustments based on real-time data, such as sudden changes in weather or water demand (Pulido-Calvo and Portela, 2007 ). Moreover, extending the prediction horizon decreases forecast accuracy, especially given the uncertainties in input variables. Consequently, inaccuracies may lead to unpredictability in the model. Conversely, one-step predictions typically yield more reliable and accurate outputs, crucial for operational decision-making. The storage capacity can be calculated as a function of the water level in the reservoir. Difft  is the difference between predicted and expected storage volumes; w is the dynamic weight. Due to the heuristic nature of the algorithm that trains the TG-MO-ANN, its solutions in the initial iterations are not optimal and exhibit high constraint violations, significantly affecting the algorithm's convergence. A dynamic weight (w) is employed in the CV1  calculations to address this issue. Throughout iterations, w changes from 1 to 0. Thus, the algorithm initially focuses on minimizing objectives and then gradually prioritizes the mass balance constraint. When w is set to 0, the constraint will be deemed satisfied only when Difft  equals zero. The defined constraint for release flow in equation (15)  has two boundaries and thus needs two constraint violation values as follows:(20) CV  2  = ∑ t = 1  T  R t  +   T                  R t  +  = R t  ANN   - R max  t   i f R t  ANN   > R max  t      0 i f R t  ANN   ≤ R max  t              (21) CV  3  = ∑ t = 1  T  R t  -   T                 R t  -  = R min  t   - R t  ANN   i f R t  ANN   < R min  t      0 i f R t  ANN   ≥ R min  t              where R t  +    and R t  -    represent the violation of predicted release from the upper and lower release boundaries at time t, respectively. The storage constraint is also defined with two constraint violation values as follows:(22) CV  4  = ∑ t = 1  T  S t  +   T                  S t  +  = S t  ANN   - S max  t   i f S t  ANN   > S max  t      0 i f S t  ANN   ≤ S max  t              (23) CV  5  = ∑ t = 1  T  S t  -   T                   S t  -  = S min  t   - S t  ANN   i f S t  ANN   < S min  t      0 i f S t  ANN   ≥ S min  t              where S t  +    and S t  -    are the violations of predicted storage from the upper and lower storage limit at time t, respectively.  2.6 The training process of TG-MO-ANN TG-MO-ANN is trained by minimizing the defined loss function in equations (11)-(16). In this process, the weights and biases in equations (3)-(5) constitute the decision variables vector. In contrast to classic training algorithms like backpropagation, where various objectives and constraints are converted into a single weighted loss function, meta -heuristic multi-objective algorithms can minimize each objective independently. The codes in this study are developed in the MATLAB environment, and the optimizations are carried out using PlatEmo (Tian et al., 2017 ). Among the 162 available algorithms in PlatEmo 3.0, 27 are explicitly designed for solving constrained problems. However, our computational experiments show that genetic-based algorithms, with their mutation and crossover operators, have superior exploration capabilities compared to other methods. This finding aligns with a recent study in which a meta -heuristic theory-guided ANN was developed (Mahmoud et al., 2023 ). Consequently, several variations of the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm were examined, and due to its shorter computational time and better performance, NSGA-III, one of the most commonly used algorithms, was chosen for training TG-MO-ANN. A thorough explanation of constrained and unconstrained optimization using NSGA-III is detailed in (Deb and Jain, 2014; Jain and Deb, 2014 ). 2.6.1 Ɛ-dominance method Ɛ-dominance (Laumanns et al., 2002 ) is a constraint-handling method that eliminates the need for extra hyperparameters to incorporate constraints as additional terms in the objective function. Applied to two decision variable vectors, x1  and x2 , it can be stated that for a Ɛ > 0, fi (x1 ) Ɛ-dominance fi (x2 ) if and only if ∀ i = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ ,  m     f i  x 1    - ε ≤ f i  x 2      . Recalling the constraint violations in equations (17)-(23), the total Constraint Violation (CVT ) of an individual decision variable vector like x can be expressed as (Cuate et al., 2020 ):(24) CV  T  x   = ∑ j = 1  5  max 0 , CV  j  x         Accordingly, x1  Ɛ-dominance x2 , if and only if one of the following conditions is satisfied:1. CVT (x1 ) = 0 and CVT (x2 ) > 0  2. CVT (x2 ) > CVT (x1 ) > 0  3. CVT (x2 ) = CVT (x1 ) = 0 for each objective i, f i  x 1    - ε ≤ f i  x 2       is satisfied     2.6.2 Technique for order of preference by similarity to the ideal solution Multi-objective optimization algorithms yield a set of optimal solutions known as the Pareto optimal set. However, only one optimal solution can be used for training TG-MO-ANN. Therefore, TOPSIS autonomously selects the most suitable solution from the Pareto optimal set. Given an array of solutions evaluated based on multiple criteria, TOPSIS ranks each solution according to the shortest and longest Euclidean distance from the Positive Ideal Solution (PIS) and Negative Ideal Solution (NIS) (Hwang and Yoon, 1981 ). In this study, the non-dominated solutions within the Pareto optimal set are considered an array of n solutions evaluated based on eight criteria, comprising three objectives and five constraint violation values. The following matrix demonstrates the array of solutions:(25) X n × 11   = Obj  1    X 1     X 2     ⋮   X n            Obj  2    O b j  3    C V  1     C V  3   ⋯    C V  5    x 1 - 1    x 1 - 2         x 1 - 3    x 1 - 4    x 1 - 5    ⋯  x 1 - 8     x 2 - 1    x 2 - 2         x 2 - 3    x 2 - 7    x 2 - 8    ⋯  x 2 - 8     ⋮   x n - 1         ⋮   x n - 2              ⋮   x n - 3         ⋮   x n - 7         ⋮   x n - 8         ⋮   ⋯       ⋮   x n - 8                   TOPSIS ranks the solution in five steps (Mahmoud et al., 2021 ). In the first step, TOPSIS normalizes the solutions by the following equation:(26) r i - j   = x i - j   ∑ i = 1  n  x i - j  2           i = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ ,  n ;    j = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ , 11      In Step 2, a weight vector is applied to the normalized solutions as follows:(27) V i - j   = r i - j   × W j            i = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ ,  n ;    j = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ ,  11      Since the loss function of TG-MO-ANN has a minimization goal, Step 3 determines PIS and NIS by the following equations:(28) PIS =  min  j   V i - j       i = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ ,  n   = V 1  +  , V 2  +  , ⋯ , V 10  +  , V 11  +        (29) NIS = max  j   V i - j      i = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ ,  n   = V 1  -  , V 2  -  , ⋯ , V 10  -  , V 11  -         In Step 4, TOPSIS computes the Euclidian distance of each solution from PIS and NIS as follows:(30) d i  +  = ∑ j = 1  11  V i - j   - V j  +     2               i = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ ,  n     (31) d i  -  = ∑ j = 1  11  V i - j   - V j  -     2               i = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ ,  n      Eventually, Step 5 computes the relative closeness (CC) to the ideal solution for each solution as follows:(32) CC  i  = d i  -  d i  -  + d i  +               i = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ ,  n      The CCi  is a value between zero and one. Solution i is closer to the PIS when the value of CCi  is close to 1. Consequently, the solution with the highest CCi  gets the first rank, and so on. It should be noted that the decision-maker usually defines the weight vector in Step 2. Nevertheless, in the present study, this vector is calculated using the Entropy Weight Method (EWM) proposed by Burillo and Bustince (1996) . Considering the matrix in equation (25) , EWM calculates the weight vector in equation (27)  as follows:(33) p i - j   = x i - j   ∑ i = 1  n  x i - j                                        i = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ ,  n ;    j = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ ,  11     (34) E j  = - ∑ i = 1  n  p i - j   × ln P i - j      ln n                     i = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ ,  n ;    j = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ , 11     (35) W j  = 1 - E j   ∑ j = 1  11  ( 1 - E j  )                               i = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ ,  n ;    j = 1 ,  2 ,  ⋯ ,  11     Here, Pi-j  represents the standardized value, and Ej  denotes the entropy of the jth  objective, which ranges from 0 to 1. Higher entropy for an objective (or criterion) indicates that the solutions within this objective have a greater degree of differentiation. Thus, a lower entropy value signifies less disorder within the system. Therefore, according to equation (35) , objectives with higher entropy are assigned greater weight. The pseudo-code of the TG-MO-ANN training process is provided in Algorithm 1. This algorithm briefly explains the essential functions developed for training TG-MO-ANN with a meta -heuristic algorithm. Normalization is performed using the Min-Max scaling approach (Zhang et al., 2018 ). Here, particular attention should be attributed to the constraint violation of the mass balance principle (i.e., CV1 ). Equations (18) and (19)  provide reliable outcomes only through the original values of the source data. Hence, within the CV1  calculations,  the data needs to be denormalized. This issue does not arise in other constraint violation values since the maximum and minimum values of storage volume and release can be represented as 0 and 1 in the normalized data. To assess the impact of incorporating each constraint, as detailed in Table 1  , eight distinct scenarios have been defined, each incorporating a different set of constraints. To clarify the subsequent discussion, scenario S1, which does not consider any constraints, is denoted as MO-ANN, and scenario S8, which considers all constraints and is fully guided, is denoted as TG-MO-ANN. The training algorithm, NSGA-III, is run for 2000 iterations with a population size of 40 in all scenarios, and both mutation and crossover rates are set to 0.5. TG-MO-ANN has one hidden layer with 15 neurons in all scenarios (i.e., five neurons for each sub-network), all utilizing a tangent sigmoid activation function. The neurons in the output layer have a pure line activation function. Note that the hyperparameters mentioned above are determined through test and error trials.  2.8 Evaluation metrics 2.8.1 Simulation accuracy metrics The NSE (Arya Azar et al., 2021 ) and MAE are utilized to investigate the simulation accuracy of estimations. A newly proposed approach is adopted to decompose MAE into three sub-measures to investigate the source of error in the estimations made under each scenario (Robeson and Willmott, 2023 ). In doing so, MAE is decomposed into MAEb , MAEp,  and MAEu .(36) NSE = 1 - ∑ i = 1  N  ( T i  - O i  )  2   ∑ i = 1  N  ( T i  - T  ¯   )  2        (37) MAE = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  T i  - O i        (38) MAE  b  = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  b b + p i  + u i    × T i  - O i        (39) MAE  p  = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  P i  b + p i  + u i    × T i  - O i        (40) MAE  u  = 1 N  ∑ i = 1  N  u i  b + p i  + u i    × T i  - O i        (41) b =  T  ¯   -  O  ¯         (42) p ^  ′  i  = p ^  i  - ( T  ¯   -  O  ¯   )      (43) p i  =  p ^  ′  i  - T i         (44) u i  = p ^  ′  i  - p ^  i        wherein Ti  and Oi  denote the ith target and output values, respectively. T  ¯     and O  ¯     are the average value of the target and output values, respectively. b is the absolute mean bias error; p ^  i    is the distance of Oi  from the linear regression line between targets and outputs. Accordingly, p ^  ′  i    is the unbiased predicted regression value, which denotes the distance of unbiased Oi  from the linear regression line between unbiased targets and outputs; pi  is the weight for the relative importance of proportionality error for each output. ui  denotes the weights for the relative importance of each prediction's unsystematic error. According to this decomposition, the total MAE in equation (37)  is equivalent to the sum of MAEb , MAEp,  and MAEu . These sub-measures are illustrated in Fig. 2  , and their detailed explanation can be found in (Robeson and Willmott, 2023 ). The bias error in Fig. 2 (a) represents a systematic error caused by incorrect estimation of the target mean and can originate from various sources, such as the training data and framework of the estimator. As illustrated in Fig. 2 (b), by removing the bias error from outputs, the proportionality error represents a systematic error that arises when the trendline slope between output and target data deviates from unity. Fig. 2 (b) also illustrates the unsystematic error, which for a specific output is the distance from its scattered place on the correlation plot to its corresponding place on the unbiased trendline. In addition to the employed statistical criteria, the Mann-Whitney test is used to investigate the statistically significant differences between the outcomes of different scenarios and the target dataset. The null hypothesis of this test is that there is no significant difference between the two datasets, and they come from the same population in terms of their distribution.  2.8.2 Principal inconsistency metrics Five metrics are introduced to evaluate the inconsistency of the estimations with the reservoir operation principles. The POMBV in equation (45)  indicates the percentage of estimations that violate the mass balance principle. It should be noted that the constraint violations of the mass balance principle (i.e., CV1 ) were never precisely equivalent to zero. Thus, regardless of the negligible differences between the expected and estimated storage volumes in equation (45) , the actual POMBV values were extraordinarily high and were not useful for the comparisons. Therefore, the POMBV values are calculated using the ± 0.5 % difference between the expected and estimated storage volumes as the acceptable tolerance to rectify this issue. The POLF and POEF indicate the percentage of estimated release flows that are lower and higher than release boundaries, respectively. Similarly, the POLS and POES are the percentages of estimated storage volumes that are lower and higher than the storage limits, respectively.(45) POMBV = ∑ t = 1  T  VS  t   T  × 100          VS  t  = 1 i f S t  ANN   - S t  Exp     > 5 1000  × S t  Exp      0 i f S t  ANN   - S t  Exp     ≤ 5 1000  × S t  Exp              (46) POLF = ∑ t = 1  T  VR  t  -   T  × 100                                  VR  t  -  = 1 i f R t  ANN   < R min      0 i f R t  ANN   ≥ R min              (47) POEF = ∑ t = 1  T  VR  t  +   T  × 100                                 VR  t  +  = 1 i f R t  A N N   > R max      0 i f R t  A N N   ≤ R max              (48) P O L S = ∑ t = 1  T  V S  t  -   T  × 100                                    V S  t  -  = 1 i f S t  A N N   < S min      0 i f S t  A N N   ≥ S min              (49) P O E S = ∑ t = 1  T  V S  t  +   T  × 100                                   V S  t  +  = 1 i f S t  A N N   > S max      0 i f S t  A N N   ≤ S max              where V S  t   , V S  t  -    and V S  t  +    denote whether the predicted storage volumes violated the mass balance equation, minimum and maximum storage limits, respectively. Likewise, V R  t  -    and V R  t  +    denote whether the predicted releases violated the lower and upper release boundaries.    3 Case study This paper utilizes the Three Gorges Reservoir (TGR) as a case study, a multi-purpose facility that supports a variety of objectives, including hydropower generation, flood control, water supply, and navigation. Each objective is governed by a distinct operational pattern characterized by long-term and short-term temporal variabilities. The inclusion of TGR in our study allows for a comprehensive assessment of the robustness of our proposed model within a complex and dynamic operational framework. This rigorous testing under diverse and challenging conditions not only confirms the model's effectiveness but also underscores its potential applicability to other regions dealing with similar multi-objective water resource management challenges. As depicted in Fig. 3  (a), TGR is situated upstream of the Yangtze River, China's longest river, with a length of 6418 km, a catchment area of 1.96 × 1016  km2 , and an annual water discharge of 98 billion m3  (Hu et al., 2020 ). TGR features a dam height of 185 m and NWL of 175 m, offering a storage capacity of 39.33 billion m3 . It generates 22500 MW of power from 34 stand-alone turbines, making it the world's largest hydropower plant (Hu et al., 2014 ). The primary objective of TGR, with a flood storage capacity of 22.15 billion m3 , is to effectively mitigate flood risk in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River, which constitutes China's most populous and economically developed plain (Wang et al., 2020 ). Fig. 3 (b) illustrates the established reservoir operation rule curves of TGR in which months are plotted as the abscissa, and the reservoir water level is plotted as the ordinate (Hu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2011; Rheinheimer et al., 2016; Zheng, 2016 ). These curves are established based on objectives related to flood control, hydropower generation, navigation, water supply, environmental protection, and other regulatory goals, which divide the entire operational chart of TGR into four zones, denoted as A-D in Fig. 3 (b). Zone A, the flood control zone, takes precedence over other operations, where the water level must be maintained at the FLWL of 145 m during the flood season, spanning from June to the end of September. Within zone A, the TGR release rate should not exceed 55,000 m3 .s−1  to ensure downstream safety; however, if the reservoir inflow surpasses 55,000 m3 .s−1 , TGR retains the floodwaters.
