Once the flood event subsides, the surplus water is released to maintain a water head of 145 m (Lai and Wang, 2017; Zheng, 2016 ). During the impoundment period, which extends from early September to the beginning of October, the TGR operates in zone B. The goal is gradually raising the water level from 145 m to 175 m. Although the water release is reduced in this zone, it cannot fall below 6,000 m3 .s−1  to meet the downstream environmental and navigation requirements while ensuring minimum hydropower generation (Zheng, 2016 ). From October to the end of April of the following year, the TGR operates in Zones C (firm hydropower output zones) and D (decreased hydropower output zones). In these zones, the TGR strives to keep the water level as high as possible to maximize hydropower generation, but it cannot exceed the NWL. Furthermore, similar to the flood season, the release rate cannot exceed 55,000 m3 .s−1 . From the beginning of May, the TGR shifts to zone B and starts its drawdown to gradually decrease the water level to 145 m, preparing the reservoir for a new flood season (Hu et al., 2020 ). Due to the dynamic nature of demands, such as hydropower generation, domestic, irrigation, and industrial supplies, the established operational rules are modified consistently. Therefore, in practice, each zone's starting and ending times may vary in different years. To assess the capability of TG-MO-ANN in deriving rule curves and examine the principal consistency of its estimations, the training dataset must strictly adhere to the reservoir operation principles. The actual operational data are significantly influenced by operator decisions and often exhibit diverse unregulated patterns. Consequently, simulations based solely on actual data may violate those principles and fail to offer a comprehensive perspective for policymakers. Therefore, studies concerning reservoir simulations and the derivation of reservoir operational policies commonly rely on Deterministic Optimization Method (DOM) or Conventional Reservoir Operation (CRO) results (Aboutalebi et al., 2015; Moeini and Hadiyan, 2022; Niu et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2010 ). Given that the TGR must fulfill multiple objectives, relying on a DOM to satisfy all objectives may present challenges. This approach not only represents a sophisticated methodology but may also result in outcomes that partially violate operational constraints. Alternatively, employing the established operational chart through CRO represents a straightforward approach with a proven track record. This method ensures principal consistency, reduces computational efforts, and incorporates a margin of safety to account for uncertainties. Furthermore, the established operational charts are continually optimized based on site data, resulting in more realistic outcomes. Therefore, a CRO model, designed based on the rule curves in Fig. 3 (b), the aforementioned operational principles, and the latest update from China Three Gorges Corporation, is established to provide the training dataset. The daily inflow data is sourced from the China Three Gorges Corporation (https://www.ctg.com.cn/  ) to feed the CRO. The collected dataset covers sixteen years, from 1 January 2006 to 31 December 2021, accounting for 5,478 daily data. It is worth noting that reservoir losses primarily include spilled water, evaporation, and seepage. However, due to data availability, this study considers evaporation as the primary loss factor. Monthly evaporation rates for the same period are obtained from the Global Reservoir Evaporation Dataset (Tian et al., 2022 ). Subsequently, the collected data, including historical inflow and evaporations, are incorporated into the CRO model, and the remaining operational information for the TGR, including daily releases and storage volumes, is derived. Since the present study aims to enhance generalizability in the proposed models, we have intentionally reduced the size of the training dataset to a level where underfitting does not occur. Accordingly, through trial-and-error experiments, 66.66 % of the data are selected for training, while the remaining 33.33 % are reserved for testing. The targets are structured as time series data. Therefore, daily data obtained from CRO between 1 January 2006 and the end of 2015 are utilized for training and validation to mitigate look-ahead bias and ensure that future data is not used to predict past events. Consequently, the remaining data from 1 January 2016 to the end of 2021 are reserved for testing. Table 2   provides statistical information on the training and testing datasets. The training dataset is extensively shuffled to avoid any temporal bias, and 10 % of it (365 data points) are randomly selected for validation. The validation data is employed during training to prevent overfitting using the early-stopping approach (Vilares Ferro et al., 2023 ). This approach halts the training process if the validation loss increases despite a reduction in the training loss and fails to exhibit a descending trend after a specific number of iterations.  4 Results Fig. 4.   illustrates the training curves of MO-ANN (i.e., baseline scenario S1) and TG-MO-ANN (i.e., target scenario S8), showcasing the RMSE between normalized targets and output over the training process. The figures show that the MO-ANN training trend is smoother than TG-MO-ANN, which displays more fluctuations in its training curves. This is due to additional constraints in the TG-MO-ANN's loss function that complicate the search space. However, with sufficient epochs, NSGA-III effectively explores this space, eventually identifying feasible non-dominated solutions and notably reducing the RMSE for all objectives. The validation mechanism terminates the training process of MO-ANN after 1342 epochs, while TG-MO-ANN continues until 1757 epochs. This more extended training period suggests that although MO-ANN trains more smoothly, it may be more susceptible to overfitting than TG-MO-ANN, which benefits from the regulatory effect of its additional constraints. 4.1 Comparison of simulation accuracy between MO-ANN and TG-MO-ANN Table 3   compares MO-ANN (or scenario S1) and TG-MO-ANN (or scenario S8) in terms of NSE and MAE during the training, validation, and testing stages. The comparison of training and testing results for both approaches reveals that they both achieve NSE values above 0.92, indicating acceptable performance across the board. Mann-Whitney tests conducted on the outcomes during the testing phase show no statistically significant difference between the estimations by both methods and CRO results at a 90 % significance level. However, TG-MO-ANN shows higher p-values than MO-ANN, suggesting less evidence to reject the null hypothesis, which indicates a closer alignment with CRO outcomes. During the validation stage, TG-MO-ANN displays higher accuracy than MO-ANN, potentially due to the inclusion of principal constraints that mitigate overfitting in the training process. Overall, the results in Table 3  demonstrate that the proposed parallel structure enables the ANN to estimate multiple targets simultaneously. The negligible difference between the NSE of MO-ANN and TG-MO-ANN during the training and testing stages implies that both approaches exhibit acceptable generalization performance in terms of simulation accuracy. Notably, the reported MAE values indicate meaningful differences between MO-ANN and TG-MO-ANN. Therefore, through equations (38) , (39), and (40), the MAE of the estimated release flows and storage volumes during the testing period is decomposed into three components (Robeson and Willmott, 2023 ), allowing for a more detailed analysis of the error sources in the most prominent targets. Fig. 5   highlights the variability in unsystematic and proportionality errors across all comparative scenarios, including MO-ANN (i.e., S1) and TG-MO-ANN (i.e., S8), primarily due to their specific constraints. Despite varied constraints, all scenarios display similar MAE biases, contributing about 10 % to 20 % of the total MAE. This consistency across scenarios is expected as they share the same structure, training data, and training algorithm. The minor role of bias error suggests that the model adequately estimates average flows and storage volumes. Fig. 5 (a) shows that scenarios S3, S5, S7, and S8, which incorporate storage constraints, have reduced proportionality errors in storage volume estimations, indicating that storage constraints effectively minimize these errors. Similarly, Fig. 5 (b) reveals that scenarios S2, S6, S7, and S8, which apply release constraints, submitted lower proportionality errors in release estimations, affirming the benefits of release constraints on this metric. Furthermore, scenarios S4, S5, S6, and S8, which include the mass balance constraint, demonstrate lower unsystematic errors in estimating both targets. The subsequent discussion will explore these results in depth, clarifying the effects of release and storage constraints on proportionality errors and the impact of the mass balance constraint on unsystematic errors.  4.2 Comparison of principal inconsistency between MO-ANN and TG-MO-ANN Table 4   summarizes the principal inconsistencies under MO-ANN and TG-MO-ANN. The results demonstrate that TG-MO-ANN exhibits significantly lower principal inconsistencies than MO-ANN, with 9 % and 14.48 % lower average principal inconsistencies in the training and testing stages, respectively. Table 4  also implies a considerable disparity in MO-ANN's principal consistency between the training and testing stages. Despite MO-ANN's acceptable generalization performance in simulation accuracy, it exhibits weak generalization in principal consistency. In contrast, TG-MO-ANN significantly enhances generalization performance in this aspect. TG-MO-ANN ensures the consistency of estimations with release and storage principles in both the training and testing stages, while there is only a 0.36 % difference between the consistency with the water balance principle in the training and testing stages in this approach. To gain deeper insights into the frequency of principal inconsistencies in MO-ANN and TG-MO-ANN across varying conditions, a focus was placed on 2017 and 2020, representing the driest and wettest periods within the test duration. Fig. 6  (a)-6(B) present the time series of one-step predictions of release flows and storage volumes during these years. Additionally, bubbles in Fig. 6 (a) and 6(A) depict the average principal inconsistencies for MO-ANN (i.e., S1) and TG-MO-ANN (i.e., S8) on a monthly basis. These monthly averages are derived from all principal metrics. These inconsistencies are further dissected and visualized in Fig. 6 (c)-6(D). Fig. 6 (a) confirms the similarity between the estimated storage volumes by MO-ANN and TG-MO-ANN compared to the CRO results. However, MO-ANN exhibits lower storage volumes than CRO and TG-MO-ANN from July to the end of September. Likewise, after the flood season, during October and November, MO-ANN exhibits higher storage volumes than CRO and TG-MO-ANN. These deviations are most pronounced during the flood season in a dry year, with MO-ANN reaching a peak principal inconsistency of 38.7 % in August when TGR is operated in zone A. Before and after the flood season, when TGR operates in zone C, the MO-ANN still exhibits noticeable inconsistencies, though these are less severe than during the flood season. Fig. 6 (A) demonstrates a similar pattern for MO-ANN during the wet year, with maximum average principal inconsistencies at 20.6 % in August. Generally, the magnitude of principal inconsistencies in the wet year is smaller than in the dry year. Notably, except during the flood season, TG-MO-ANN reduces principal inconsistencies to zero in other periods. Even during the flood season, its values are significantly smaller than MO-ANN's. Fig. 6 (b) and 6(B) reveal a striking similarity between the estimated release flows by TG-MO-ANN and MO-ANN. However, clear discrepancies arise during January and February, when TGR is operated in zone C, in both dry and wet years. During these periods, a substantial portion of the estimated release flows by MO-ANN falls below 6,000 m3 .s−1 , potentially posing risks to navigation and environmental requirements. Moreover, Fig. 6 (B) implies that during the flood season of the wet year, MO-ANN's release flows exceed 55,000 m3 .s−1  on three days, presenting a potential downstream flood risk. In contrast, the estimated release flows by TG-MO-ANN consistently adhere to the release flow boundaries. Fig. 6 (c) and 6(C) show that MO-ANN produces unfeasibly high storage volumes above NWL during the non-flood season, particularly noted from October to December, with a 17.42 % higher likelihood in wet years compared to dry years. This period corresponds to zone C operation, where the reservoir is at its capacity, with these issues more pronounced during wet years due to higher inflow rates. MO-ANN also produces unreasonable storage volumes below the FLWL, primarily during the flood season, with a 21.55 % higher frequency in dry years. Exploring the POLF values in Fig. 6 (c) and 6(C) show that release flows less than 6000 m3 .s−1  in MO-ANN are primarily observed during January and February when TGR operates in zone C, with a 20.52 % higher likelihood in dry years. POEF values show that release flows beyond 55000 m3 .s−1  are absent in dry years, and they are only encountered during the flood season of wet years. It is crucial to emphasize that the occurrence of flows beyond 55000 m3 .s−1  under MO-ANN during this period could have catastrophic consequences. Upon investigating the occurrence of water imbalances in MO-ANN, it becomes evident that they are the most common inconsistencies observed, occurring frequently during flood and non-flood seasons. A comparison between POMBV values in Fig. 6 (c) and Fig. 6 (C) indicates that water volume imbalances are 46.43 % more likely during dry than wet years. However, water imbalances occur infrequently in November, December, January, and February. During this period, TGR operated in zone C, and as there was no flood, the reservoir mainly remained stable. Similar observations can be made for May when TGR is operated in zone B before the flood season, and the reservoir maintains a stable state. Fig. 6 (d) and 6(D) show that TG-MO-ANN maintains consistency with release and storage principles. The reported inconsistencies by TG-MO-ANN are mainly attributed to the water imbalance. Nevertheless, incorporating principal theories into TG-MO-ANN leads to significant improvements in water balance, both in dry and wet years, with minimal violations compared to MO-ANN. For instance, the maximum POMBV value in MO-ANN occurred in August 2017, resulting in violations of the mass balance principle on 30 days that month. In contrast, TG-MO-ANN reduced this value to zero, and its highest POMBV value was observed in July 2017, amounting to only 12.9 % (occurring on just 4 days out of 31). Overall, principal inconsistencies are primarily observed in zones A and C, with a 6.49 % higher frequency during dry years. Incorporating principal theories into TG-MO-ANN allows it to eradicate principal inconsistencies in zones B, C, and D, and its principal inconsistencies in zone A are solely related to water imbalances. The average frequency of water imbalance in MO-ANN in zone A during both dry and wet years was 47.87 %, while TG-MO-ANN reduced this value to a mere percentage of 6.11 %.  4.3 Impact of incorporating different constraints Pairwise comparisons between comparative scenarios are carried out to assess the influence of each constraint on the principal consistency and simulation accuracy of estimations. 4.3.1 Storage volume constraints Fig. 7  (a) highlights the impact of implementing storage volume constraints in scenario S3 compared to the baseline scenario S1. The blue arrows show that the sole inclusion of storage volume constraints effectively eliminates unreasonable storage volumes below the FLWL or above the NWL. However, as shown by the red arrow, this leads to an increase in the occurrence of unfeasible flows below 6,000 m3 .s−1  from 5.75 % to 14.34 %. Although the sole inclusion of storage volume constraints slightly reduces the occurrence of water imbalance, it does not significantly improve this factor, as the POMBV remains higher than 17 %. Fig. 7 (b) reveals that including both release and storage constraints in S7 eliminates flows and storage volumes beyond their specified limits, while S2, with the sole inclusion of release constraints, can only eliminate unfeasible flows. However, as marked by the red arrow, adding storage constraints in S7 increases the probability of water imbalance by 7.5 %. Fig. 7 (c) demonstrates that incorporating both storage and mass balance constraints in S5 eliminates unreasonable storage volumes and reduces the occurrence of observing flows less than 6000 m3 .s−1  by 6.74 % compared to S4, which solely includes the mass balance constraint. However, as shown by the red arrow, the addition of storage constraints in S5 results in a 3.18 % higher probability of water imbalance. As shown in Fig. 7 (d), our fully guided scenario, S8 and scenario S6, which include release and mass balance constraints, can eliminate unfeasible flows. However, blue arrows indicate that adding storage constraints in S8 eliminates unreasonable storage volumes. Even though both S6 and S8 consider mass balance constraints, including storage constraints in S8 increases the occurrence of water imbalance by 2.63 % compared to S6. Fig. 5 (a) indicated that including the storage volume constraints led to a lower proportionality error in the estimated storage volumes. To investigate the impact of storage constraints, the unbiased estimations made by scenarios S6 and S8 have been plotted against the target values (CRO results) in Fig. 7 (e), and data points contributing to proportionality errors are distinguished. Both scenarios S6 and S8 incorporate the mass balance and release constraints, with the distinction being the inclusion of storage constraints in S8. Therefore, comparing these two scenarios elucidates the influence of including storage constraints on proportionality error. S6 tends to overestimate and underestimate storage volumes when the reservoir approaches NWL and FLWL, respectively. Red circles in Fig. 7 (e) indicate these discrepancies, while the exact estimations under S8 are marked with blue circles. Implementing storage constraints in S8 prevents unreasonable estimations of storage volumes below FLWL and above NWL. Consequently, the trendline of S8 approaches the unity line, resulting in its lower proportionality error compared to S6. Overall, incorporating the storage constraint independently or with other constraints eliminates unreasonable storage volumes below FLWL or above NWL. This, in turn, prevents overestimating and underestimating storage volumes and decreases the proportionality error. However, it does not significantly influence the consistency with the release principle. The red arrows in Fig. 7 (b), 7(c), and 7(d) show that the combination of storage constraint with release or mass balance constraint increases the inconsistencies with the mass balance principle.  4.3.2 Release boundary constraints The comparison of S1 and S2 in Fig. 8  (a) reveals that including the release constraints mitigates unfeasible flows and reduces water imbalances from 25.78 % to 4.05 %. However, this constraint does not eliminate unreasonable storage volumes. As shown in Fig. 8 (b), applying storage constraints in both S3 and S7 eliminates unreasonable storage volumes, while the addition of release constraints in S7 enables it to eliminate unfeasible flows, reducing POLF and POEF to zero from initial levels of 14.34 % and 0.27 % in S3. Notably, including the release constraints in S7 also reduces the water volume imbalance by 5.74 % compared to S3. Fig. 8 (c) shows that including release constraints and water balance in S6 eliminates unfeasible flows while reducing water volume imbalances by 1.82 % compared to S4. However, this leads to an increase in unreasonable storage volumes lower than FLWL and higher than NWL by 5.96 % and 0.93 %, respectively. Fig. 8 (d) demonstrates that considering both mass balance and storage constraints in scenarios S5 and S8 eliminates unreasonable storage volumes. The addition of release constraints in S8 not only eliminates unfeasible flows but also reduces the occurrences of water imbalance from 5.8 % in S3 to 2.85 % in S8. Fig. 5 (b) implied that including release constraints results in lower proportionality error in estimating release flows. Both scenarios, S5 and S8, incorporate storage and mass balance constraints, with the only difference being the imposition of release constraints in S8. Hence, comparing the unbiased values of estimated release flows by these scenarios in Fig. 8 (e) elucidates the influence of release constraints on proportionality error. This figure illustrates that as release flows approach the upper and lower boundaries, scenario S5 generates numerous infeasible solutions beyond the release boundaries. However, including release constraints in scenario S8 mitigates these infeasible solutions, bringing them back within the feasible range and alleviating the overestimation and underestimation of flows. Consequently, this action reduces the deviation of the trendline from the unity line in S8 and minimizes the proportionality error compared to S5. In summary, as shown by the blue arrows corresponding to POLF and POEF in Fig. 8 , the application of the release constraints, either alone or combined with storage volume and water balance constraints, eliminates the unfeasible flows. Consequently, preventing the overestimation and underestimation of release flow reduces the proportionality error. Moreover, as the blue arrows corresponding to POMBV in Fig. 8  indicate, the sole inclusion of release constraints or its combination with any other constraint reduces the probability of water volume imbalance. However, the small blue arrows corresponding to POES and POLS in Fig. 8 (a) show that the sole inclusion of release constraints does not significantly improve the consistency with the storage limit principles. Furthermore, the red arrows in Fig. 8 (c) show that the joint inclusion of release and mass balance constraints increases the inconsistency with the storage limit principle.  4.3.3 Mass balance constraint The blue arrows in Fig. 9  (a) show that the sole imposition of the mass balance constraint in S4 improves the overall consistency with the reservoir operation principles compared to the baseline scenario S1, but it does not guarantee full adherence to the principles. Compared to S1, water imbalances, unfeasible flows beyond 55000 m3 .s−1 , and unreasonable storage volumes below the NWL in S4 are reduced by 23.16 %, 22.12 %, and 13.3 %, respectively. However, the occurrence of flows less than 6000 m3 .s−1  in S4 is 3.12 % higher than in S1. Fig. 9 (b) demonstrates that the imposition of release constraints in S6 and S2 eliminates unfeasible flows; however, including the mass balance constraint in S6 results in a significantly minor POMBV value close to zero (i.e., 0.8 %). Furthermore, including mass balance constraints in S6 reduces the occurrence of unfeasible storage volume above NWL by 16.69 % compared to S2, although it does not affect the occurrence of unreasonable storage volume below FLWL when POLS remains at 13.79 % in S6 (i.e., 0.49 % smaller than S2). As depicted in Fig. 9 (c), considering storage constraints in both S3 and S5 eliminates unreasonable storage volumes. The addition of the mass balance constraint in S5 not only reduces the probability of water imbalance by 11.49 % but also decreases the occurrence of flows less than 6000 m3 .s−1  from 14.34 % in S3 to 2.13 % in S5. Fig. 9 (d) suggests that the simultaneous inclusion of release and storage constraints in both S7 and S8 ensures consistency with the corresponding principles, while by adding the mass balance constraint, the probability of water imbalance in S8 was reduced by 8.7 % compared to S7. Fig. 5  indicates that including the mass balance constraint led to a lower unsystematic error in estimating release flow and storage volume. Inspecting the efficacy of mass balance constraints throughout the entire testing period introduces ambiguity into the exploration. Therefore, the flood season of dry years, during which mass balance inconsistencies are more prevalent, is chosen for a more precise investigation. Fig. 9 (e) and 9(f) show the unbiased values of estimated storage volumes, and release flows by S7 and S8 during the 2017 flood season versus the target values. Fig. 9 (e) illustrates the lower unsystematic error of S8 in estimating storage volume compared to S7 when there are 35 outlier solutions in S7, which are scattered far from its trendline. In contrast, only six outliers correspond to S8 and are notably closer to its trendline than those of S7. Fig. 9 (f) also reveals a similar pattern, demonstrating lower unsystematic errors of S8 in estimating release flows when there are precisely 35 outliers in S7 and 6 in S8. To understand the impact of the mass balance constraint, the outlier solutions in Fig. 9 (e) and 9(f), which are the major contributors to the unsystematic error, should be thoroughly investigated. In doing so, Fig. 10   displays the estimated storage volumes in scenarios S7 and S8 during the same period. In addition, days when the mass balance principle is violated are marked. Furthermore, the magnitudes of violations are represented using bubbles in each figure. The constraint for the mass balance principle in equation (19)  is designed to minimize the discrepancy between expected and estimated storage volumes (i.e., left and right sides of the mass balance equation). Thus, correlation plots between expected and estimated storage volumes are also presented to analyze the effectiveness of the mass balance constraint. According to Fig. 10 (a), S7 violates the mass balance principle on 35 days, with the maximum violation of 0.59 billion m3 . Fig. 10 (b) demonstrates that S8 violates the mass balance principle in only six days, with a maximum violation of 0.24 billion m3 . Hence, including the mass balance constraint not only reduces the occurrence of water imbalance but also reduces the magnitude of mass balance violation. The correlation plot within Fig. 10 (a) reveals a weak correlation between expected and estimated storage volumes when 35 data points correspond to days in which the mass balance principle is violated distant from the unity line. On the contrary, the correlation plot in Fig. 10 (b) illustrates that by incorporating the mass balance constraints, S8 significantly improved the correlation between the expected and estimated storage volumes, achieving an NSE of 0.918. Remarkably, most data points fall within the 90 % confidence line, with the six outlier solutions representing instances where water imbalances were observed. The mass balance principle implies that the release flow should decrease when storage volume increases and vice versa. When the mass balance principle is violated, the right side of the mass balance equation (i.e., S t - 1   + I t  - R t  - L t    ) deviates from its left side (i.e., St ), indicating that the model is not following the mass balance principle. Thus, either both storage volume and release flow increase and decrease concurrently, or their increment or decrement does not comply with the mass balance equation. The proposed results in Fig. 10  reveal that the outlier solutions in Fig. 9 (e) and 9(f), contributing to the unsystematic error, align with the same days the mass balance principle is violated. Consequently, it can be inferred that the explicit inclusion of the mass balance constraint establishes a clear relationship between storage volume and release flows. This informs the model to decrease the release when the storage volume increases and vice versa. As a result, the model's ability to discern the underlying process of reservoir operation is enhanced, reducing unsystematic error. In summary, the sole inclusion of the mass balance constraint improves estimation consistency with the mass balance and release principles, but it cannot guarantee complete adherence. Moreover, as indicated by the red arrow in Fig. 9 (a), the sole imposition of the mass balance constraint increases the inconsistency with the storage principle. The blue arrows corresponding to POES in Fig. 9 (b) and POLF in Fig. 9 (c) indicate that including the mass balance and another constraint can partially improve consistency with the not incorporated principle. However, this does not guarantee complete adherence to the unincorporated principle. The mass balance constraint guides the model in adjusting the release flow and storage volume per mass balance principle. This adjustment aids the model in finding more reasonable and accurate solutions, ultimately leading to a reduction in unsystematic error.   4.4 Selecting the best scenario Fig. 11   summarizes the impact of incorporating different constraints on principal consistency. Fig. 11  demonstrates that the highest level of principal consistency is achieved by simultaneously incorporating all three constraints. Additionally, the figure indicates that by incorporating two constraints, the consistency with the corresponding principle is either maintained or improved. However, the consistency with the unincorporated principle either worsens or remains unchanged. Considering all constraints, TG-MO-ANN (or S8) provides balanced solutions, ensuring no single principle is neglected. On the other hand, considering all constraints reduces both proportionality and unsystematic errors in estimations, collectively yielding an accurate, consistent, and robust estimation of the system.   5 Discussion Fig. 12   simplifies the discussion by depicting the schematic of TGR and its operational parameters. It shows changes in the storage volume upon receiving an inflow at time t (It ), which affects the storage water level. The red dashed lines mark the storage volume limits, corresponding to NWL and FLWL. The figure also consolidates the two primary releases (i.e., spilled water and hydropower release) into a single current outflow at time t (Rt ), which must stay within the set release boundaries (Rmax  and Rmin ). At the bottom of the figure, it is illustrated that storage volume variations adhere to the mass balance equation, assuming a monotonic relationship between release flow and storage volume. The study highlights improvements in principle consistency through integrating constraints related to release boundaries, storage limits, and mass balance. However, discussing the advantages and disadvantages of incorporating each is essential, facilitating the diagnosis of errors arising from incorporating each constraint. 5.1 Pros and Cons of storage constraints Pros: (1) The model's training process compels it to estimate higher storage volumes and lower release flows in the firm hydropower output zone (C). It also compels it to estimate lower volumes and higher flows in the flood control zone (A). Storage constraints are primarily effective when storage volume approaches NLW in zone C and FLWL in zone A. Considering Fig. 12 , during the non-flood season, when the reservoir encounters peak inflows, It  unusually increases, which leads to a higher St . The imposition of storage constraints in this situation eliminates the overestimation of St  and prevents the reservoir from impounding excess water beyond NWL. During the flood season, the imposition of storage constraints eliminates the underestimation of St  and safeguards against water levels falling below the FLWL. Accordingly, the imposition of storage constraints curtails the model from producing unreasonable storage volumes when it receives abnormal inflows, enhancing its generalizability.    Cons: (1) Fig. 11  showed that the sole inclusion of storage constraints (S1 to S3 transition) increases inconsistencies with the release principle. Fig. 6  indicates that inconsistencies with the release principle are more prevalent in zone C when, in the non-flood season, TGR encounters unusually low It . In this situation, the model maintains the St  at its maximum, even though the imposition of storage constraints has already curtailed the reservoir's ability to store additional water. Given the absence of surplus water for augmentation of the It  and the subsequent increase in Rt , the model consistently releases the same amount of inflow (Rt  = It ), which could be less than 6000 m3 .s−1 . This behavior results in heightened inconsistencies with the release principle.  (2) As indicated in Fig. 11 , adding storage constraints to the release constraints (transition from S2 to S7) increases the inconsistency with the mass balance principle. Fig. 6  indicates that inconsistencies with the mass balance principle are prevalent during the flood season. In this period, TGR impounds the floodwater and releases the excess water to maintain the water level at the FLWL after the flood passes. Rt  is expected to increase during this event, while the imposition of release constraints in S7 allows the model to freely estimate any Rt  as long as it is less than Rmax . Considering the monotonic relationship between Rt  and St , as Rt  increases, the St  is expected to decrease. At the same time, the imposition of storage constraints in S7 compels the model to maintain St  above the FLWL, preventing the model from reducing St  proportionally to the increment of Rt . This situation leads to an imbalance between the left and right sides of the mass balance equation in Fig. 12  and increases the occurrence of water imbalance in S7.  (3) Fig. 11  implies that including storage constraints alongside the mass balance constraint (transition from S4 to S5) aggravates consistency with the mass balance principle. Due to the limited flexibility of the model in estimating St  imposed by the storage constraints, satisfying the mass balance principles in S5 necessitates adjusting Rt . However, considering that the magnitude of St  surpasses that of Rt  by nearly tenfold, this adjustment can lead to estimations of Rt  that deviate from accuracy, conflicting with the model's training objectives. Consequently, the system reaches an equilibrium solution, striving to estimate more accurate Rt  and satisfy the constraints simultaneously. This equilibrium solution may not precisely adhere to the mass balance equation, increasing the occurrence of water imbalance.     5.2 Pros and Cons of the release constraints Pros: (1) Considering Fig. 12 , the release constraints are intended to maintain Rt  within the bounds of Rmax  and Rmin . The imposition of release constraints prevents Rt  from exceeding Rmax  during the flood season of wet years and avoids underestimation of Rt  when the reservoir experiences unusually low It  in the firm hydropower output zone (C). In this way, the imposition of release constraints enhances the model's generalizability by preventing unreasonable estimation of release flows when the reservoir receives abnormal inflows.  (2) Considering the transition from S4 to S6 in Fig. 11 , incorporating release constraints alongside the mass balance constraint improves the consistency with the mass balance principle. As indicated in Fig. 8 (d), the imposition of release constraints reduces the proportionality error and leads to a more accurate estimation of Rt . As storage constraints are not incorporated in S6, the model tends to satisfy mass balance constraints by adjusting St . Simultaneously, accurate estimation of Rt  within the defined boundaries allows the mass balance constraint to provide precise values for St . The accurate estimation of Rt  and St  not only enhances consistency with the mass balance principle but also reduces the occurrence of storage volumes below FLWL as was observed by the comparison of the POES between S6 and S4 in Fig. 8 (c).    Cons: (1) Scenario S6 exhibits an amplified inconsistency with the storage principle. During the flood seasons, Rt  rarely exceeds Rmax , allowing S6 to estimate higher values of Rt  while they remain below Rmax . In this period, TGR tends to impound floodwater and increase St  when encountering high amounts of It . After the flood passed, TGR releases excess water to maintain St  close to the FLWL. According to the monotonic relationship between Rt  and St , S6 freely reduces the St  and increases Rt  to satisfy the mass balance constraint. While this behavior amplifies consistency with the mass balance principle, it results in numerous unreasonable St  below the FLWL, aggravating the consistency with the storage principle.     5.3 Pros and Cons of the mass balance constraint Pros: (1) The release and storage constraints have specific impacts in zones C and A, particularly when their respective targets approach their limits. In contrast, the influence of the mass balance constraint is more widespread, not confined to a specific zone. The mass balance constraint seeks to minimize the deviation between the left and right sides of the mass balance equation in Fig. 12 . Consequently, it instructs the model to adhere to the monotonic relationship between Rt  and St . According to Fig. 6 , inconsistencies with the mass balance principle are more pronounced during the flood season. Fig. 10 (a) and 10(b) depict that when TGR encounters flood peaks and receives higher It , it strives to impound them, leading to an increase in St . Correspondingly, Rt  needs to decrease while the model has learned to increase the Rt  during the flood season. This discrepancy results in a deviation between the left and right sides of the mass balance equation, increasing inconsistency with the mass balance principle. As reservoir operation is a continuous process, this deviation affects the estimations in subsequent days, resulting in more days where the mass balance principle is violated. Notably, the inclusion of mass balance constraints mitigates this issue by adjusting the amount of Rt  with respect to St . This represents a clear exhibition of improved generalizability due to the inclusion of the mass balance constraint. When faced with abnormal inputs, the model can provide reasonable solutions.    Cons: (1) Fig. 11  demonstrates that, among all evaluated constraints, the mass balance constraint exhibits the least adverse impact on inconsistency with other operational principles. However, the exclusive inclusion of the mass balance constraint and the transition from S1 to S4 led to a worsened inconsistency with the release principle when the estimated Rt  is less than Rmin . This issue predominantly arises in zone C, where the model tends to increase St  and decrease Rt  during this period. When the reservoir encounters unusually low It , the imposition of the mass balance constraint compels the model to decrease Rt  for having St  close to NWL, and given the higher magnitude of St  compared to Rt , adjusting Rt  regardless of its boundary results in having Rt  less than Rmin , which amplifies inconsistency with the release principle in S4.     5.4 Research significance, limitations, and implications Previous studies on reservoir simulation using DSTs have primarily focused on predicting a single target, predominantly reservoir outflow, as evidenced in studies by Aboutalebi et al. (2015), Cancelliere et al. (2002), Moeini and Hadiyan (2022), Niu et al. (2019), Wang et al. (2010)  and Zheng et al. (2022) . The models proposed in our study predict three distinct targets and consider the alignment with reservoir operational principles, a critical component not addressed in earlier studies. Consequently, the performance of our models cannot be directly compared with those from previous studies, as they fundamentally differ in both the number of targets and evaluated aspects. This distinction underscores the innovative aspects of our approach, which accurately predicts all components of the mass balance equation through the proposed parallel framework of ANN. Although recently Zheng et al. (2022)  integrated several reservoir operation principles into their LSTM framework and developed the PG-LSTM, their study focused on a cascade reservoir system, which differs significantly from our study's emphasis on a single, multi-purpose reservoir. Consequently, a direct comparison of our models' performance with the PG-LSTM is not feasible due to the differing contexts and objectives of the reservoir systems studied. However, while Zheng et al. (2022)  incorporated mass balance and release boundaries in their PG-LSTM model, their study did not explicitly address the circumstances under which principal inconsistencies might arise, nor did it discuss their prevalence during different operation periods. Furthermore, it remained unclear how including operational principles within their model mitigated principal inconsistencies. Conversely, this study delves into the frequency of principal inconsistencies under specific conditions, pinpointing the potential for various types of inconsistencies across different operating zones during wet and dry years. We explored how integrating each operational principle affects the principal consistency of predictions and highlighted the constrictive and detrimental impacts of incorporating each principle. These findings not only enhance the predictive capabilities of the simulation model but also provide a clearer understanding of the decision-making processes. One of the most pressing challenges in water resource management is the effective allocation of available water supplies to meet immediate needs while ensuring long-term sustainability, especially during prolonged drought periods (Sun et al., 2023 ). This task demands a careful balance between strict adherence to water level management protocols and the advantages of drought mitigation efforts. Our research provides policymakers with valuable insights, enabling them to tailor the simulation model to either strictly adhere to water level protocols by integrating all constraints or to relax some constraints to enhance drought mitigation. Additionally, our study illuminates the potential errors that may arise from incorporating each constraint, thereby offering a more comprehensive understanding of the trade-offs involved in the decision-making processes. Another pertinent implication involves the trade-offs between flood control and hydropower generation (Niu et al., 2019 ). By applying different constraints and recognizing their impacts, policymakers can simulate scenarios to either maximize hydropower generation or enhance flood control. Such simulations are crucial for optimizing reservoir management, ensuring that while one objective might be prioritized, the other is not significantly compromised. It is also essential to acknowledge the limitations of this study. Due to data availability constraints, the evaporated water from the reservoir is considered the sole contributor to total loss, exhibiting a notably lower magnitude than other targets such as reservoir volume and release flow. Consequently, this minimizes the influence of losses on the mass balance principle in this study. However, in a real-world scenario, total loss encompasses various factors, including seepage, spilled water, and evaporation, collectively yielding a magnitude comparable to the release flow. Since the loss is incorporated into the model's framework, our methodology can segregate spilled water from the total release flow and augment it with evaporation to have more significant losses. It is worth noting that this study does not address other crucial objectives of reservoir operation, such as flood control and hydropower generation, although these objectives significantly influence the operational mechanism. Hence, incorporating them into the model framework will enhance the reliability of the outcomes. Incorporating reservoir operation principles enhances the model's generalizability in response to abnormal inputs, such as sudden inflow variations. This improvement is through minor, specific adjustments that bring the estimations within the feasible area and enhance their reasonableness based on their interconnection. We have found that these subtle adjustments are not efficiently measured by standard metrics like NSE and MAE or diagnostic tests like Mann-Whitney. The research advises scholars not to rely solely on standard statistical criteria for model evaluation. Instead, it suggests using new metrics introduced in the study or adopting error decomposition methods, which are better suited for assessing the reliability of reservoir simulation models, particularly in terms of principal consistency. Our results advocate using TG-MO-ANN (under scenario S8) to derive reservoir operation rules since this model can precisely replicate the optimal values of the deterministic optimization methods, guaranteeing the outcomes' feasibility. This improved reservoir simulation approach could also be used in reservoir optimization studies by providing a more accurate and consistent system simulation, improving the reliability of the optimal values. Furthermore, scholars can use the proposed insight regarding the frequency of principal inconsistencies and the influence of incorporating each principle to anticipate inconsistency types and apply the relevant principles for mitigation. Future enhancements to the proposed model include incorporating factors like the annual hydropower generation, the average remaining capacity for flood control, and the rate of flood risk as additional training objectives within the TG-MO-ANN framework, which enhance the model's practicality. Furthermore, by segregating spilled water from hydropower release, hydropower capacity, and its associated criteria can be integrated as additional constraints. This expansion would further bolster the versatility and applicability of TG-MO-ANN to a broader spectrum of real-world challenges.   6 Conclusion This study introduced the Theory-Guided Multi-Objective Artificial Neural Network (TG-MO-ANN) to explore principal inconsistencies in reservoir simulation and elucidate how integrating operational principles mitigates these inconsistencies. Compared to the existing models, TG-MO-ANN simultaneously estimates all components of the mass balance equation while maintaining compliance with fundamental operational theories governing them. It employs a novel parallel structure to estimate the reservoir’s storage volumes, release flows, and losses, facilitating a comprehensive evaluation of consistency with the mass balance, the most critical operational principle. Our model's performance showed that although integrating all principles into the TG-MO-ANN did not substantially enhance the goodness-of-fit, it notably reduced the average rate of principal inconsistencies from 15.05 % in the MO-ANN to just 0.57 %. Assessment of the baseline scenario with no constraints during wet and dry years showed frequent inconsistencies with the storage principle from July to December, especially as water levels approach the FLWL or NWL. Instances of unreasonable storage volumes below the FLWL are prevalent during the flood season, with a 21.55 % higher likelihood in dry years. Conversely, unfeasible storage volumes above NWL are more frequent in the non-flood season, with a 17.42 % higher likelihood in wet years. Incorporating the storage principle eliminated unreasonable estimations by preventing underestimating and overestimating storage volumes in flood control and firm hydropower output zones. This adjustment brought estimations within the feasible area, reduced the proportionality error in estimating storage volume, and decreased the violation of storage limits from 5.96 % in MO-ANN to zero. However, including only the storage constraint increases inconsistencies with the release principle. Further, combined with the release constraint, it exacerbates inconsistencies with the mass balance principle. Additionally, pairing the storage constraint with the mass balance constraint increases inconsistencies with the mass balance principle. Inadequate release flows predominantly occur in January and February when TGR is operated in the firm hydropower zone, with a 20.52 % higher likelihood during dry years. Flows beyond the release boundary were confined to the flood season of wet years. Incorporating the release constraint prevented underestimation and overestimation of release flows, reducing the model's proportionality error in estimating this target. As a result, violations of release boundaries were reduced from 43.5 % in MO-ANN to zero. However, simultaneously incorporating the release and mass balance constraints increases inconsistencies with storage limit principles. Water imbalances are the most common inconsistencies occurring year-round, with a 46.43 % higher likelihood during the flood season of dry years. Including the mass balance constraint enhances the logical relationship between estimated targets by enforcing the monotonic relationship between storage volume and release flow. Consequently, this adjustment helped the model produce more reasonable solutions, reducing the model's unsystematic errors. However, the exclusive inclusion of the mass balance constraint worsens inconsistency with the release principle. It was found that including all three constraints simultaneously is necessary to achieve the highest level of consistency. It reduces both proportionality and unsystematic errors in the estimations, yielding a comprehensive approach that offers an accurate, consistent, and robust reservoir simulation model. Our fully guided TG-MO-ANN (i.e., scenario S8) ensured consistency with the release and storage principles while significantly reducing inconsistencies with the mass balance principle from 25.8 % in the baseline scenario (MO-ANN) to just 2.8 %. In contrast to previous studies, our research determines the frequency of each principal inconsistency, demonstrates how integrating operational principles can mitigate these inconsistencies, and details the constructive and detrimental impacts of incorporating each principle. However, limitations exist, such as considering only evaporated water as the sole contributor to total loss, which minimizes the influence of losses on the mass balance principle. Our findings enhance decision-making processes in water resource management, especially under challenging conditions like prolonged droughts. It allows policymakers to adjust simulations for balancing water level management and drought mitigation and offers insights into the consequences of applying or relaxing specific constraints. Additionally, the study supports using the TG-MO-ANN for deriving reservoir operation rules in regions facing erratic hydrological conditions, as it replicates optimal values and ensures outcome feasibility, thereby improving the reliability of the derived policies. Thus, practitioners are recommended to consider the TG-MO-ANN model in their operational strategies, while researchers should continue refining these models using emerging technologies in artificial intelligence to handle reservoir management complexities.
1 Introduction Deep geothermal energy possesses huge potential for clean energy utilization. Unlike other renewable energy sources such as solar, wind, and biomass energy, the utilization of deep geothermal energy is not largely dependent on external environmental conditions. Furthermore, geothermal energy offers a relatively stable and consistent source of power. One common type of deep geothermal energy is known as hot dry rock (HDR). The HDR heat at the depth of 3–10 km underground is abundant (about 2 . 52 × 1 0  25      J in China) (Tester et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2013 ). Deep geothermal energy has a good utilization prospect. Enhanced geothermal system (EGS) is an effective technology for harnessing the potential of deep geothermal energy. The concept was first introduced in the Fenton Hill project (Lu, 2018 ). Many researchers have done a large number of studies about EGS. Many EGS engineering projects are established around the world, including Soultz EGS in France (Genter et al., 2010 ), Rosemanowes EGS in the UK (Richards et al., 1994 ), and Cooper Basin EGS in Australia (Meixner et al., 2014 ). EGS extracts deep geothermal energy through heat exchange between cold fluid and fractured reservoirs (Liu et al., 2021 ). The fracture network plays a key role in the heat extraction process, which can provide heat exchange channels. Therefore, constructing a good-connective fractured reservoir is very necessary. There are many kinds of fracturing technologies to construct artificial fractured reservoirs, including thermal fracturing (Turcotte and Schubert, 2002, England; Wang et al., 2015 ), hydraulic fracturing (Ma et al., 2020c; Yu et al., 2020 ), CO2  fracturing, N2  fracturing (Hu et al., 2018; Brown, 2000 ), chemical stimulation (Li et al., 2018 ), and so on. In order to keep a long-term fracture network conductivity during the production process, as shown in Fig. 1 , proppant is always injected into fractured reservoirs with fracturing fluid to promote fracture initiation and prevent fracture closure (Hu et al., 2021 ). In addition, how the well-connective fractured reservoirs affect EGS performance is also worth studying. In the simulation research of EGS, both analytical and numerical methods have been widely utilized. In solving the heat extraction process of EGS using analytical methods, Akdas and Onur (2022)  introduced innovative analytical methods for forecasting and enhancing energy extraction from an idealized HDR via a multistage hydraulically fractured horizontal well doublet. The findings show that these analytical approaches offer potential efficiency in predicting, designing, and optimizing EGS systems. In addition, Laplace transformation is also an efficient method for solving such equations, particularly in scenarios involving the injection of hot water into an oil-bearing layer (Lauwerier, 1955 ). The transformation is applied to both distance and time variables for comprehensive analysis. Gringarten et al. (1975)  also presented a theory of heat extraction from fractured HDR, and the study provided a more efficient mechanism for heat extraction in EGS. Onay (2020)  introduced innovative analytical models to forecast temperature and heat recovery in four varied hydraulically fractured well configurations. The impact of temperature gradients and fracture porosity on production performance has been well explored. However, the heat extraction process in EGS is highly complex, given the intricate environment within the fractured reservoir. Complex issues are often challenging to solve analytically, with some requiring specific conditions for analytical solutions, which may not always be feasible in practical scenarios. Additionally, certain problems may lack analytical solutions altogether. Given this context, numerical solution methods are widely applicable. Fracture network is a key part of EGS, which often determines the success of EGS engineering. The heat extraction process in fractured reservoir is very complex, and numerical methods have been widely utilized in simulating heat extraction process. The discrete fracture network model is often used to describe fluid flow in fracture network realistically (Li et al., 2019; Yao et al., 2018 ). It is difficult to detect fracture distribution in artificial reservoirs (Tang et al., 2019; Mustanen et al., 2017 ). Therefore, fracture network is regarded as random distribution (Chen et al., 2018b; Fox et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2017; Qu et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018a; Wang et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019b ). Different characteristic parameters are studied. Results show that the output mass flow rate increases with the increase in fracture network density (Xie et al., 2021 ). Shi et al. (2019a, b)  studied the effects of fracture network geometries on multilateral-well EGS, showing that fracture position and quantity have obvious effects on the multilateral-well EGS efficiency. Uneven distribution of natural fractures and CO2  is researched. Results show that unconnected natural fractures lead to a small heat extraction rate (Shi et al., 2018, 2019c ). Ma et al. (2020a)  studied the impact of fracture aperture, quantity, and length on the thermal performance of EGS using a 2D fracture network model. The findings reveal that a greater fracture aperture heightens the risk of short circuits and thermal breakthroughs. Shi et al. (2023)  examined how fracture morphology and the quantity of fracture blocks impact heat extraction in reservoirs. Their findings reveal that EGS exhibits elevated production temperatures with increased fracture block numbers. Ma et al. (2020d)  assessed heat production performance based on a fractured reservoir with two intersecting fractures. Results reveal a more uniform distribution of fractures within the reservoir corresponds to a faster heat extraction rate of flowing water from the surrounding reservoir. Guo et al. (2019)  investigated the influence of dominant flow fractures and natural fractures on EGS productivity. The findings indicate that the heat extraction rate diminishes with escalating fracture aperture and permeability. Wang et al. (2022)  analyzed the quantitative rankings of the effecting parameters (running parameters and reservoir properties) on EGS performance. They found that fracture permeability is the secondary dominating factors affecting heat extraction performance. In addition, the application of proppant has received a lot of attention. Chen et al. (2020)  studied EGS performance in fracture network embedded with proppant. Found that high proppant distribution density increases the net heat-extraction rate and reduces the thermal breakthrough time. Hu et al. (2021)  studied the effects of proppant pumping schedule on EGS heat extraction performance based on proppant transport model. Showing that the EGS heat extraction with propped fractures is higher than that of non-propped fractures. The distance for fluid transport within the fracture increases as the injection velocity of proppant increases, and decreases as the diameter of the proppant increases. However, previous scholars often studied the impact of fracture networks and permeability on heat extraction performance from a macroscopic perspective, often overlooking the connectivity variations within fracture networks due to geological conditions and proppant concentration. In engineering applications, the most direct manifestation in fractured reservoirs is the distribution variation of reservoir permeability. Different permeability distributions can result in significant fluid losses and short-circuiting within fracture reservoirs. For instance, the Hijiori EGS project in Japan encountered a severe short-circuit effect in fractured reservoirs (Yamaguchi et al., 2000 ), ultimately halting circulation tests. Additionally, significant fluid loss contributes to unsuccessful EGS attempts, as observed in the Fenton Hill EGS project (Whetten et al., 1987 ), where a vast portion of fractured areas remain disconnected, resulting in substantial fluid loss. In the Soultz project in France (Genter et al., 2010; Valley et al., 2007 ), unidentified fault blockages hinder the enhancement of fractured reservoir connectivity between GPK2 and GPK3. These real-world EGS projects show the flow complexity of fractured reservoirs. Hence, it is imperative to investigate the detailed influence of permeability distribution differences on heat extraction performance. In this study, we established a 3D thermal-hydrologic (TH) coupling model to thoroughly study the influences of permeability distribution on heat extraction rate, heat extraction ratio, flow impedance, temperature field and pressure distribution. The steps of the study are described as follows: First, a mathematical model is established and validated. Second, based on the Qiabuqia geothermal field, the geometric model is constructed along with the setting of initial conditions. Third, characteristic parameters are set to characterize the heat extraction performance of fractured reservoirs. Fourth, the systematic effects of permeability variations in the same layer are investigated. Finally, the impact of permeability differences in different layers on heat extraction performance is studied. This study could provide useful suggestions for practical EGS proppant pumping scheme.    2 Mathematical model This section introduces the TH coupling model in detail. Firstly, we made some assumptions about the heat exchange process in fractured reservoirs. Then, some governing equations of the TH coupling model are introduced. Lastly, a single fracture model and a fractured reservoir model are used to verify the TH coupling model. 2.1 Model assumptions In practical EGS engineering, the fluid heat exchange is very complicated. The fractured reservoir includes cold fluid, fracture, rock, injection well, production well and measuring points. To simulate the fluid interchange process in fractured reservoirs, some basic assumptions should be made to establish the mathematical model: (1) HDR is viewed as homogeneous and isotropic. (2) The fractured reservoir only considers hydraulic fractures with proppant. Fractures often include many proppants, and therefore fractures in fractured reservoirs could be regarded as porous media (Chen et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2019 ). In addition, permeability affects fluid flow in fractures more than other parameters. The other fracture parameters are assumed to be uniformly distributed spatially (Xie et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022 ). (3) Fourier’s law is used to describe the heat exchange process in fractured reservoirs. Joule-Thomson effects and energy dissipation effects are not considered. (4) Darcy’s law is used to express the fluid flow process in fractured reservoirs. (5) Fluid is seen as single phase in fractured reservoirs. (6) The fracture hydraulic aperture in this study is high enough that the effects of surface roughness on heat exchange are very small (He et al., 2021; Chen and Zhao, 2020; Li et al., 2024 ). Therefore, the effects of surface roughness are not considered.  2.2 Governing equations Based on the above assumptions, the thermal-hydrological coupling model in a fractured reservoir is characterized by the following governing equations. The fluid flow within the rock matrix is represented by the mass conservation equation (Shi et al., 2019a; Li et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2020b; Lv et al., 2022 ): (1) S ∂ ( p )   ∂ t   + ▽ ⋅ ( q )  = Q  m       where S   is the specific storage of the rock matrix (1/Pa). p   is the hydraulic pressure. t   denotes time (s). Q  m     is the external mass/fluid source and sink term in the rock matrix (1/s). q   denotes Darcy velocity in rock matrix (m/s), and it can be expressed as (2) q = − k  u  f     ( ▿ p + ρ  f   g ▽ z )      where u  f     represents the dynamic viscosity of fluid (Pa s). ρ  f     represents fluid density (kg/m3 ). k   is the rock matrix permeability (m2 ). g   represent the gravitational acceleration (m/s2 ). ▽   is the spatial gradient operator (/m). z   is a unit vector in the direction over which the gravity acts. ρ  f   g ▽ z    is the gravity term. The fluid flow in discrete fractures can be written as follows: (3) d  f r   S  f r   ∂ ( p )   ∂ t   + ▽  τ   ⋅ ( d  f r   q  f   )  = Q  f       where d  f r     represents fracture aperture. S  f r     is the specific storage of the rock matrix (1/Pa) The item q  f     represents the Darcy velocity in fracture (m/s), which is expressed as (4) q  f   = − k  f r    u  f     ( ▿  τ   p + ρ  f   g ▿  τ   z )      where k  f r     denotes the fracture permeability (m2 ). ▿  τ     denotes the gradient operator restricted to the fracture’s tangential plane; and Q  f     is the source and sink term on the fracture plane, (m/s). Under the circumstances without an external source and sink, Q  m    =   0 and Q  f    =   0. In our EGS modeling, there are no external source or sink terms throughout the fractured rock mass domain. However, due to the substantial discrepancy in permeability characteristics between rock matrix and fractures, the flow velocity in fractures surpasses that within the rock matrix. Seepage processes in the rock matrix and fractures are governed by distinct equations, with mass flux exchange occurring at the interface between rock matrix and fracture. Thus, Q  m     denotes the mass exchange from the fracture penetrating into the rock matrix, while Q  f     represents the mass exchange from the rock matrix penetrating into the fracture. The relationship between Q  m     and Q  f     is expressed as Q  f    =  − d  f r   Q  m     . Additionally, Q  f     can be formulated as (Chen et al., 2013; Yao et al., 2020 ) (5) Q  f   = − k  f r    u  f     ∂ p  ∂ n       where n   is the normal direction of the fracture surface. The energy equation, including both the solid phases and fluid, is expressed as (6) ρ C  p      e f f   ∂ T  ∂ t   + ρ  f   C  f   q ⋅ ▿ T − ▿ ⋅ λ  e f f   ▿ T = ϕ  m       where T   denotes the reservoir temperature(K). ρ C  p      e f f     is the effective volumetric capacity, which is written as ρ C  p      e f f   = φ ρ  f   C  f   + 1 − φ   ρ  s   C  s     , where ρ  s     is the solid density (kg/m3 ). C  f     and C  s     are the heat capacity (J/kg k) of fluid and solid, respectively. λ  e f f     is the effective thermal conductivity, which is written as λ  e f f   = φ × λ  f   + 1 − φ   × λ  s     , where λ  f     and λ  s     represent the thermal conductivity (W/ (m K)) of fluid and solid, respectively. The energy conservation equation in fractures can be written as (7) d  f r   ρ C  p      e f f   ∂ T  ∂ t   + d  f r   ρ  f   C  f   q  f   ⋅ ▿  τ   T − ▿  τ   ⋅ λ  e f f   d  f r   ▿  τ   T = ϕ  f        ϕ  m     represents the heat source term and indicates the heat exchange from the fracture plane penetrating to the rock matrix (W/m3 ). ϕ  f     represents the heat exchange from the rock matrix penetrating to the fracture plane (W/m2 ). Similar to the aforementioned fluid flow theory, ϕ  m     and ϕ  f     show the relationship of ϕ  f    =  − d  f r   ϕ  m     ; and ϕ  f     is governed by Refs. Ma et al. (2020b), Chen et al. (2013), Yao et al. (2020)  and Gong et al. (2020) . (8) ϕ  f   = ρ  f   C  f   ( − k  f r    u  f     ∂ p  ∂ n   )  T − λ  e f f   ∂ T  ∂ n        The above equations are subject to appropriate initial condition (9) p ∣  t = 0   = p  0   ( x , y , z )      (10) T ∣  t = 0   = T  0   ( x , y , z )      boundary conditions (First type) (11) p ∣  Γ  1     = p  1       (12) T ∣  Γ  1     = T  1       boundary conditions (Second type) (13) − k  u  f     ∂ p  ∂ n  b     ∣  Γ  2     = q  v       (14) − λ ∂ T  ∂ n  b     ∣  Γ  2     = f     where n  b     denotes the external normal direction to the boundary; p  1     and T  1     denote specified pressure and temperature at the first type boundary Γ  1    . q  v     is the flow rate and f   is the heat exchange in the second boundary Γ  2    . Setting q  =   0 and f  =   0 indicates impervious and insulated boundaries, respectively.  2.3 Validation of numerical model 2.3.1 Validation of a single fracture model In order to verify the feasibility of the TH model in simulating the flow heat exchange process in a fractured reservoir, simulation results and analytical solutions in a fracture model are compared. The TH model is established using the commercial software COMSOL Multiphysics. The analytical solutions are derived by Lauwerier (1955), Cheng et al. (2001), Li et al. (2022) , and it has been seen as a good verification in EGS simulation. A lot of simulation work (Hu et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2020; Song et al., 2018 ) in fractured reservoirs is verified based on the single fracture model’s analytical solution. The single fracture model’s analytical solution (Lauwerier, 1955 ) is expressed as (15) T = T  0   + ( T  i n   − T  0   )  e r f c λ  s   x + q  f   d  f   ρ  f   C  f   | y |   2 ρ  f   C  f   d  f     ρ  s   C  s    q  f   λ  s   ( q  f   t − x )        U ( t − x  q  f     )      where e r f c    is the complementary error function. U   denotes the unit step function.  The single fracture model is a 100 m ×   100 m rock matrix with a fracture (Fig. 2 ). The fracture aperture is 1 mm, and the fracture is at the center of rock matrix. Fluid (water) is injected into the fracture from the left side, and injection temperature and injection velocity are 30 °C and 0.01 m/s, respectively. Rock’s initial temperature is set at 80 °C. The boundary conditions around rock matrix are regarded as impermeability and insulation conditions. Rock matrix is seen as isotropic and homogeneous. The total simulation time is set at 3000 d (days). Table 1  shows the properties of rock matrix and water. Fig. 3 (a) shows the comparative results in the temperature distribution of rock at 2700 d. This can prove that the TH model is feasible in space distribution simulation. In addition, Fig. 3 (b) shows the temperature variation at different points. It is clear that simulation results and analytical results have good consistency. This can prove the proposed TH model has good application in simulating EGS work.     2.3.2 Validation of 3D fractured reservoir model To verify the applicability of the proposed TH coupling model, we applied the model to simulate EGS production. The geothermal reservoir used in the simulation is a cube measuring 1000 m ×   1000 m ×   200 m. It contains two fractures. The distance between the injection well and the production well is 350 m, with a wellbore length of 50 m. The top temperature is 473 K, and the temperature gradient in the depth direction is 0.05 K/m. The initial pressure of the reservoir is 30 MPa, while the production well pressure remains fixed at 20 MPa. The injection mass rate and temperature are set at 10 kg/s and 293 K, respectively. The rock permeability is assumed to be 5 × 1 0  − 15      m2 , and the fracture porosity is 0.4. We compared the production temperature obtained from our model with the results from a validated thermal-hydraulic-mechanical (THM) model, as shown in Fig. 4 . The comparison demonstrates a high level of consistency between our production results and the THM results reported by Guo et al. (2019) . This indicates that our proposed model is capable of accurately simulating EGS performance.      3 Calculation model In this section, suitable reservoir parameters are set based on the Qiabuqia geothermal field. In addition, the heat extraction rate, flow impedance, heat extraction ratio, pressure field and temperature field are used to comprehensively analyze heat extraction performance. 3.1 Geometrical conditions The geometrical model includes HDR, fracture network, injection well, and production well. Fig. 5 (a) shows the calculation area with the size of 1000 m ×   1000 m ×   150 m at the depth of 3550–3700 m. The calculation area includes three layers, and the height of every layer is 50 m. The fractured reservoir is the middle layer of the calculation area. The well control for the injection well is a specified injection rate, while the well control for the production well is a specified bottomhole pressure (BHP). The injection rate is set at 25 kg/s. The injection fluid temperature is 293 K. The BHP in production well is fixed at 30 MPa. The length of injection and production wells is 50 m, and the distance between injection and production wells is 500 m. The discrete fracture network is embedded into the middle layer. In addition, the fracture network is divided into five sections toward the production well. There is a predominant fracture area between the injection well and the production well. To detect pressure changes from injection well to production well. There are 7 measuring points along the predominant fracture area (Fig. 5 (b)). The distance between Point 1 and Point 2 is 50 m, which is the same as the distance between Point 6 and Point 7. The distance between the other points is 100 m. Referring to the Qiabuqia geological field, the rock matrix is monzonitic granite (Zhang et al., 2019, 2018; Yan, 2015; Chen et al., 2019a ). Table 2  shows the main properties of rock matrix and fracture.     3.2 Initial and boundary conditions (1) Seepage field. The injection fluid is water. The bottom initial pressure of the calculation area is 34.8 MPa, and the pressure gradient is set at 9529 Pa/m. The external boundaries of the calculation area are considered impermeable. (2) Temperature field. The bottom temperature of the calculation area is set at 508 K. Temperature gradient in the entire fractured reservoir is 0.0473 K/m. The reservoir’s external boundaries are set for thermal insulation.  3.3 Simulation mesh We utilized the COMSOL finite element solver to address the fluid flow and heat transfer partial differential equations in mathematical model. Fig. 6 (a) shows the meshing scheme for the geothermal reservoir, employing the swept mesh method. Triangular elements are generated on the middle fractured reservoir surface, and then swept vertically (z direction) to create prismatic elements on the top and bottom surfaces. The fracture network meshes are refined to ensure simulation accuracy, given that fluid flow and heat transfer primarily occur in the fractured reservoir. Details of the mesh refining scheme are shown in Fig. 6 (a). In order to ensure independence of simulation results from the finite mesh number, average production temperatures over 30 years are calculated under various mesh numbers, as depicted in Fig. 6 (b). It is evident that the average production temperature stabilizes when the mesh number exceeds 247 000. However, computational time increases as the mesh number rises. Considering computational time and precision, a mesh number of approximately 584 112 is utilized in subsequent simulation studies. Additionally, we used a fully coupled method to solve the partial differential equations in COMSOL. We studied a total heat extraction period of 30 years, using a time step of 1 year and setting the tolerance factor to 0.1 as the convergence criteria for numerical solutions.    3.4 Characteristic parameter definition In this study, three characteristic parameters are used to evaluate EGS heat extraction performance, including heat extraction rate (W), flow impedance (Z  R    ) and heat extraction ratio (η  ).
