To enable the ELA metrics to be calculated for the error surfaces resulting from the 420 CRR models with the different combinations of attributes tested (i.e. 4 CRR models × 5 catchments × 3 error metrics × 7 calibration data sets), Latin Hypercube sampling is used to generate 1000 samples from the parameter space for each of the 420 error surfaces based on the findings of Zhu et al. (2022a, b)  (Fig. 1 ). The generated samples are used to calculate values of three ELA metrics (Fig. 1 ). These metrics relate to three features that have been shown to have an impact on CRR model calibration problems (see Duan et al., 1992; Kavetski et al., 2007; Kavetski and Kuczera, 2007; Maier et al., 2019; Guillaume et al., 2019 ), including roughness (fine-scale, non-smooth surface features), flatness (the distribution of error surface values) and optima dispersion (the extent of clustering of the local optima). All three metrics have been shown to be effective in identifying the above fitness landscape features for a number of benchmark functions (Mersmann et al., 2010; Munoz et al., 2015; Munoz and Smith-Miles, 2017 ). Furthermore, the selected metrics have been found to have low dependence on problem dimensionality and sample size (Zhu et al., 2022a ), enabling them to be applied to real-world problems, as demonstrated by Zhu et al. (2022b) . To enable the impact of the different attributes on the features of the error surfaces to be assessed in an easy-to-understand fashion for the large number of combinations of attributes considered, the values of the three ELA metrics for each of the 420 error surfaces are represented as five categorical values, with 1 corresponding to the most desirable value of each of the error surface features (e.g. very low roughness, very low flatness, very low optima dispersion) and 5 corresponding to the least desirable value of each of the error surface features (e.g. very high roughness, very high flatness, very high optima dispersion). This was done as the raw values of the metrics span different ranges that do not have an intrinsic meaning (see Appendix C ). Consequently, the use of categorical values enables the relative values of the different metrics to be compared in a manner that is intuitive and easy to interpret (i.e. same scale, interpretable scale where higher values are less desirable). As shown in Fig. 1 , the categorisation of the raw values of the metrics was achieved by applying K -means clustering to values of each individual metric separately, where the value of K  was set to 5 (i.e. the number of desired categories). The numerical study was conducted using the University of Adelaide’s supercomputing facilities, which consist of 48 Skylake nodes, with 80 CPUs and 377 GB of memory per node. The R package Hydromad (Andrews et al., 2011 ) was used for model simulation, Latin Hypercube Sampling (generated using the lhs package in R) was used for sample generation and the R package FLACCO (Kerschke and Trautmann, 2016 ) was used for the calculation of the three ELA metrics. Details of the CRR models, catchments, error metrics and ELA metrics used are given in Sections 2.2 . 2.3. 2.4 and 2.5, respectively.  2.2 CRR models  All of the four models (AWBM, GR4J, IHACRES and Sacramento) are based on Unit Hydrograph theory (Andrew et al., 2011), and consist of a two-component structure including a soil-moisture accounting (SMA) module and a routing hydrograph module (Shown in Fig. 2  ). These models require a daily time series of rainfall and potential evapotranspiration (PET) as inputs and predict daily streamflow as an output. The differences between the models considered in this paper include variations in the SMA and routing models. The first model, AWBM, contains three production stores (S 1  , S 2     and S 3   ) with different capacities (see Appendix A ). On each day, precipitation P   is added to each store, and effective rainfall P r    is produced when the storage exceeds the corresponding store capacity. To reduce the parameter size for the storages in AWBM from three to one, Boughton (2004)  proposed an average capacity parameter to define the capacities of all three stores, at no loss of model performance. In addition to the single storage parameter, a parameter related to the multiplier of input PET is also considered. As a result, two parameters require calibration in the AWBM model, making it the simplest model considered in this study. The second model, GR4J, contains two stores (production store and routing store) where the store water exchange in the production store is related to the degree of catchment wetness (see Appendix A ). On wet days, a net precipitation P n    is produced, and a portion of P n   , denoted as P s   , fills the production store. On dry days, on the other hand, a net evaporation En   is produced, and a portion of En  , denoted as Es  , is extracted from the production store. The remaining component, P r    , is produced based on the updated water level in the production store, and undergoes a further routing process based on quick flow and slow flow components. In addition to the surface water, groundwater exchange is also considered in each component, where the final streamflow is the sum of each component. A total of four parameters require calibration in the GR4J model. In IHACRES, the level of storage is represented by the catchment moisture deficit (CMD), which is the difference between the store capacity and the current water level (see Appendix A ). The CMD is used to define whether the day is dry or wet, which is related to the proportion of PET transferring to AET. In addition, CMD is also a function of the production of effective rainfall P r    from the store. The produced P r    is subjected to a routing process, which splits P r    into quick and slow flows with two different unit hydrographs with different time base. The final streamflow of IHACRES is equal to the sum of the quick and slow flows. In total, IHACRES has six parameters that require calibration. The structure of the Sacramento model can be split into three zones, including the surface, upper and lower zones (see Appendix A ). The surface zone is split into permeable, additional impermeable and impermeable areas. The net precipitation in the permeable area drains to the upper zone, while that in the impermeable area generates direct flow. The additional impermeable area generates direct flow when the catchment tension water requirements in the upper zone are met, otherwise the net precipitation also drains to the upper zone. The upper zone consists of tension and free water. Inflow exceeding the tension water store drains as surface flow. A proportion of free water percolates to the lower zones, which also consists of tension and free water. A proportion of free water in the lower zone can also produce baseflow. As a result, the total flow at each time step produced by the Sacramento model is the sum of the flows produced in the three zones. The Sacramento model is the most complex of the models considered in this paper, with 13 parameters that require calibration.  2.3 Catchments Fig. 3   shows the names and locations of the five catchments considered. As can be seen, the catchments are located in climatologically different regions in Australia, as defined in the Australian Köppen climate classifications of Stern et al. (2000) . The historical data required for CRR model calibration are average daily rainfall, PET and runoff at each location. Daily rainfall data were obtained from a single rain gauge within each of the Scott Creek, Black River, Elizabeth River, and Adelong Creek catchments, while the rainfall data for the Huge River catchment were obtained by spatially averaging values from three rainfall gauges using the Thiessen polygon method. Daily runoff data were obtained from gauging stations at the outlet of each catchment. PET data were calculated using the Penman-Monteith model, which requires data on temperature, relative humidity, solar radiation and wind speed (Guo et al., 2017 ). These data were obtained from weather stations near each catchment. Table 1   summarises the climate characteristics of the five catchments. As can be seen, the catchments were categorised into wet, med and dry catchments based on their annual rainfall, PET and runoff. The data for each catchment consists of a 10-year period from 01/01/1995 to 31/12/2004. As mentioned previously, in order to assess the impact of data length on the features of the error surface, three groups of 1-year and 5-year data (with different start and end dates) are used as inputs, in addition to the entire 10-year period.  2.4 Error metrics As mentioned above, the NS coefficients of flows and log-transformed flows were used as two of the three error metrics. The equations of NS and LOGNS are given as:(1) NS = 1 - ∑ t = 1  T  ( Q s t  - Q o t  )  2   ∑ t = 1  T  ( Q o t  - Q o   ¯   )  2        (2) LOGNS = 1 - ∑ t = 1  T  ( ln Q s t  + 1 ) - ln Q o t  + 1     2    ∑ t = 1  T  ( ln Q o t  + 1 ) - ln Q o  ¯  + 1     2        where Q s  t    and Q o  t    are the simulated and observed flow at time step t ; Q o   ¯     is the average observed flow, T  is the total number of time steps, and ln(·) is the natural logarithm, and the constant one is added to each log-transformed flow to avoid the negatively infinite values caused by zero flows. Both error metrics have a range from negative infinity to 1, where 1 indicates a perfect fit. It can be seen that the only difference between NS and LOGNS is the log-transformation of the flows. The impact of this log-transformation is to increase the influence of low flows on the metric value. For example, Shin et al. (2013)  demonstrated that the parameter related to the time constant for the slow flow store (τs ) of IHACRES became insensitive when using NS. In contrast, the parameter related to the time base of the unit hydrograph in GR4J (x4  ) became more sensitive with NS, but less sensitive with LOGNS, as the time base of the unit hydrograph is more sensitive to capturing high flows. As parameter sensitivity is highly related to features of the error surface, it is very likely that features of the error surface change when the error metric is changed. In addition to NS and LOGNS, WLS is also included as an error metric due to its differences in the treatment of heteroscedasticity in model errors. Unlike NS error metrics, WLS considers the heteroscedasticity of flow errors, by using two additional parameters to estimate the variance of errors, which depend on the flow volume in each time step. The WLS metric assumes errors between predicted and observed flows are normally distributed as(3) ε t  ∼ N ( 0 , a + b ·  Q o t  )    where ε t    is the error between observed and simulated flow at time step t ; Q o  t    is the observed flow at time step t ; a and b are constant parameters to describe the linear relationship between the variance of ε t    and Q o  t   . The likelihood function is the product of the likelihood of ε t    at each time step, and is given by:(4) p ( ε )  = ∏ t = 1  T  f ( ε t  | a , b , Q o t  )      where f (x |y  ) is the error likelihood of x  given parameters y  ; T  is the total number of time steps; and p ε       is the joint likelihood of the time-series of errors. It can be seen from Eq (3)  that higher flows have a bigger error variance, while the variance is smaller for lower flows. As a result of this heteroscedasticity, the error surfaces of models using WLS as an error metric are likely to be significantly different in comparison to those using NS. The LOGNS function also treats the errors as heteroscedastic (see McInerney et al., 2018 ), however, there are differences in the strategy used to treat heteroscedasticity − WLS uses a direct conditioning approach with a linear increase of error variance with flow while LOGNS uses a transformational approach, which induces a non-linear increase in error variation with flow – with differences becoming more prevalent for higher flows/higher errors (see McInerney et al., 2017 ). These differences between WLS and LOGNS will likely result in different CRR model parameter estimates and hence different exploratory landscape metrics. For the interested reader, a detailed discussion of differences between WLS and LOGNS in particular, and likelihoods and objective functions (termed as error metrics in this paper), in general, is provided in McInerney et al. (2017, 2018) .  2.5 Fitness landscape metrics As mentioned above, three typical features are considered relevant in CRR model calibration problems, including roughness, flatness and optima dispersion (see Duan et al., 1992; Kavetski et al., 2007; Kavetski and Kuczera, 2007; Maier et al., 2019; Guillaume et al., 2019 ). An illustration of the relative impact of these features on the error surface of CRR models is shown in Fig. 4  . As can be seen, eight different conceptual error surfaces based on different combinations of the relative values of the features are shown. The calibration efficiency of the error surfaces on the right side of Fig. 4  ((e) to (h)) is considered to be less than that for the error surfaces on the left side of Fig. 4 ((a) to (d)). This is generally due to the increased relative roughness of the error surfaces on the right side, which may lead to a greater number of evaluations required to converge to the global optimum, or even to a failure to identify the global optimum due to pre-mature convergence. This problem can be severe even for flat error surfaces, such as those in Fig. 4  (f) and (h), as there is lack of information to guide the search out of the rough areas. In contrast, the calibration efficiency of error surfaces on the left side is considered relatively greater, as there is no roughness to slow down or mislead the search. Consequently, even though the error surfaces in Fig. 4  (b) and (d) are relatively flat, their calibration efficiency is still likely to be greater, unless they are completely flat, in which case there would be no gradient information to guide the search at all. The error surfaces in Fig. 4 (c), (d), (g) and (h) are expected to have parameter uniqueness problems, regardless of whether calibration efficiency is hindered due to the roughness of the error surface or not. This is because these error surfaces contain multiple local basins or regions of attraction with a wide distance between them, indicating that parameter non-uniqueness is a structural problem, rather than a problem of roughness. This is illustrated by the error surfaces in Fig. 4  (c) and (d), which are smooth and therefore have a high calibration efficiency. However, they still have a problem with parameter uniqueness, as two different parameter sets have the same error metric value. To enable the above features (i.e. roughness, flatness and optima dispersion) to be quantified for the error surfaces of models with different attributes (Fig. 1 ), three ELA metrics are utilised in this paper. These metrics have been used in previous studies for classifying the features of benchmark problems (Mersmann et al., 2010; Munoz et al., 2015; Munoz and Smith-Miles, 2017 ), have been shown to have low dependence on sample size and problem dimensionality (Zhu et al., 2022a ) and have been shown to provide useful information on the features of the error surfaces of multi-layer perceptron artificial neural network used for modelling a range of hydrological variables (Zhu et al., 2022b ). Details of these three metrics are presented in the following subsections.  2.6 Maximum entropy of information content (Degree of Roughness) The maximum entropy of information content  metric (Hmax  ) (Munoz et al., 2015 ) is used to measure the multimodality of the error surface. Feature multimodality (Mersmann et al., 2010 ) refers to the number of local optima on the error surface, which is highly correlated to the roughness of the error surface. Error surfaces with higher degrees of multimodality have a higher density of local optima, which manifest themselves as rough surfaces. In contrast, error surfaces with lower multimodality have a lower density of local optima, which are manifest as smooth surfaces. The Hmax   metric builds a ternary sequence based on the fitness values of a sequence of samples, where values of “1″, “-1” and “0” are used in the sequence to refer to fitness values of a sample that is bigger, smaller and equal to that of the following sample. The sequence of a rough surface will involve frequent changes in number. In contrast, a smooth surface will have a relatively consistent sequence. The maximum entropy of the sequence is calculated to characterise the frequency of change in the sequences. The theoretical range of this metric is [0, 1].  2.7 Epsilon of information content (Degree of Flatness) The epsilon of information content  metric (Munoz et al., 2015 ) characterises the plateaus (Mersmann et al., 2010 ) of error surfaces, which refer to regions of flatness. Error surfaces with more plateaus are generally flatter, and can cause parameter identification problems and slow down the calibration process. In contrast, error surfaces with fewer plateaus have a better shape, which corresponds to more sensitive and identifiable parameters. The epsilon of information content  metric utilises the same sample sequence as Hmax  . A tolerance value (ε ) is assigned for comparison of whether the fitness values of two neighbouring samples are to be considered as equal. The corresponding ternary sequence is generated as for Hmax  , but where the strict equality for label “0” is replaced by the ε  interval about the given sample value. The epsilon of information content metric value is the value of ε  that returns a sequence completely of the label “0”. A relatively flat surface will return a very small ε  value, whereas a highly variable surface will return a large ε  value. The logarithm of the ε  values is used for result presentation. The theoretical range of this metric is [−∞, ∞].  2.8 Median basin centroidal distance (Degree of Optima Dispersion) The median basin centroidal distance  is a metric that assesses the distribution of local basins (Mersmann et al., 2010 ). A local basin is defined as a region on the error surface that contains multiple local optima that are located within a very short distance of each other. This local basin conception is similar to multiple optima and regions of attraction as defined by Kavetski and Kuczera (2007)  and Duan et al., (1992) , respectively, for error surfaces of CRR models. The metric finds a large pre-specified number of local optima using a gradient algorithm, and uses hierarchical clustering to collate local optima within a very small distance in the same local basin. It calculates the pairwise distance between the identified local basins and uses the median to summarise the average distance. Therefore, a long distance represents local basins or regions of attraction that are dispersed on the error surface, so that values of model parameters are more difficult to identify. In contrast, a short distance means that local basins or regions of attraction are contained within a small region on the error surface, making the parameter identification process less difficult. The theoretical range of this metric is [0, ∞].   3 Results and discussion 3.1 Overview The heatmaps in Fig. 5   indicate the relative influence of the four attributes investigated (i.e. model structure and complexity, catchment climate condition, error metric and calibration data length) on the three error surface metrics considered (i.e. roughness, flatness and optima dispersion). It should be noted that the results for the different combinations of calibration data for data lengths of 1 and 3 years have been combined, resulting in a comparison of the features of 180 (4 models × 5 catchments × 3 error metrics × 3 data lengths) error surfaces. The colour of the heatmaps indicates the relative desirability of the error surface characteristics based on the five categorical values for each fitness landscape metric (see Appendix B ), with lighter colours (i.e. white) indicating more desirable characteristics (i.e. a lower value) and darker colours (i.e. dark blue) indicating less desirable characteristics (i.e. a higher value) (see Section 2.1 ). There are some cells of optima dispersion of the Sacramento model that are shown as “NAN”, which indicates a failure to identify local optima for these cases. This is most probably due to the broadly acknowledged complex and poorly-behaved structure of the Sacramento model, which potentially contains numerical errors that are overwhelmed by uncertainties in the data and governing equations (Clark and Kavetski, 2010 ). The numbers in the cells of the heatmap are the calculated ELA metric values for the given features (see Section 2.5 ). It should be noted that lower values of the epsilon of information content  indicates a higher level of relative flatness (which is opposite to Hmax   and the median basin centroidal distance , where larger values represent higher levels of relative roughness and optima dispersion, respectively) so that larger values of each of the three metrics correspond to less desirable fitness landscape features. It should also be noted that these results only refer to the features of the error surfaces, and not calibration performance in terms of absolute values of the error metrics. For example, a problem with higher calibration difficulty could contain lower absolute error values and vice versa. As can be seen from a visual inspection of Fig. 5 , based on the results of the experiments presented here, model structure and complexity appear to have the largest influence on the metrics, with an increase in relative roughness and optima dispersion as model complexity is increased (i.e. from AWBM to Sacramento). Catchment climate condition also appears to have an influence on relative roughness and optima dispersion, with wetter catchments (i.e. catchments at Burnie and Darwin) resulting in rougher, less dispersed error surfaces. In contrast, the impact of different error metrics on the error surface characteristics appears to be confined to particular ELA metrics, model structures and catchment climate condition. The most pronounced influence of error metrics is associated with the application of the WLS metric to simpler models, especially for wetter catchments (see Rows 3 and 6 in all of the three heatmaps in Fig. 5  for catchments at Burnie and Darwin). As can be seen from Fig. 5 , error surface roughness appears to increase when the WLS metric is used for models with a small number of parameters, such as AWBM (see Row 3, Column 1 to 3 in Fig. 5 (a)), as use of this metric results in a significant relative increase in the number of parameters (see Section 2.4 ). In contrast, use of the WLS metric appears to reduce error surface flatness and optima dispersion for simpler models, especially for wetter catchments, resulting in more well-defined regions of attraction in the parameter space (see Row 3 and 6, Column 1 to 6 in Fig. 5 (b) and Fig. 5 (c)). The results in Fig. 5  (by comparing the 1-, 5- and 10-year results for each catchment location and model) also indicate that there appears to be no pronounced impact of calibration data length on error surface characteristics for the experiments conducted. Given that model structure and complexity, and catchment climate condition, appear to have the biggest impact on the error surface metrics considered, these are discussed in detail in the subsequent sections.  3.2 Impact of model structure complexity The impact of model structure (i.e. error surface dimensionality and how inputs are transformed to outputs) on the relative roughness, flatness and optima dispersion of the error surfaces is shown in Fig. 6  , where boxplots of the percentage of the categorical values (i.e. 1 to 5) for each model and each of the metrics is presented. As can be seen, there is a general increase in the relative roughness in the error surface as model complexity increases (Fig. 6 (a)), with AWBM (2 parameters) clearly the smoothest and Sacramento (13 parameters) clearly the roughest. The roughness of GR4J (4 parameters) and IHACRES (6 parameters) is very similar and clearly in-between the roughness of AWBM and Sacramento. The rate in relative increase in roughness tends to decrease for more complex models, most likely because the underlying roughness of more complex models is already very high. These trends can also be observed in the raw values of the metrics (Appendix C ). The increase in the relative degree of optima dispersion with an increase in model complexity is even more pronounced than that for relative roughness, with a clear increase in the degree of dispersion of optima across the error surface as the number of model parameters increases (Fig. 6 (c), Appendix C ). However, based on the results obtained, there appears to be no clear relationship between model complexity and the relative flatness of the error surface (Fig. 6 (b)). Instead, this seems to be more affected by particular model structures. For example, for the experiments conducted, the relative flatness of the error surface of GR4J is much higher than that of the other models. The fact that, based on the results of the experiments conducted, more complex models have rougher error surfaces (i.e. Fig. 7  ) suggests that, by inference, they should have decreased optimisation efficiency (i.e. they should require a larger number of function evaluations to find the globally optimal solution in the error surface). This is because all optimisation algorithms search the error surface in an iterative fashion, generally starting at random locations and using various mechanisms (e.g. gradient information, evolutionary operators) to move the search to regions with lower errors in subsequent iterations based on information derived from the error surface (Maier et al., 2019 ). If the error surface is rougher, the information about the error surface used to guide optimisation algorithms is “noisier” and potentially misleading at times, thereby slowing down the optimisation process. The above inferences align with the findings of a number of previous studies (see Fig. 7 ). For example, Garcia-Romero et al. (2019) calibrated 3 CRR models of different complexity (GR4J [4 parameters], HBV [10 parameters], Sacramento [16 parameters, with the three extra parameters associated with surface vegetation area and groundwater transferring]) on 9 catchments using the SCE-UA algorithm and found that the simplest model (i.e. GR4J) only required around 1,000 iterations for convergence, whereas the most complex model (i.e. Sacramento) required around 6,000. While Sorooshian et al. (1993)  did not vary model complexity, they found that when calibrating the complex Sacramento model (13 parameters) over a number of trials using the Multistart Simplex algorithm, a very large number of function evaluations (an average of 45,887) was required for convergence, indicating low optimisation efficiency for this complex model. By inference, the results in Fig. 6  also suggest that optimisation difficulty (i.e. how difficult it is to find the global minimum in the error surface as part of the optimisation process) is likely to increase with increasing model complexity as a result of a corresponding increase in the dispersion of the optima over the error surface (Fig. 7 ). This is because the global minimum in the error surface is more difficult to find if there are multiple regions of attraction at greater distances from one another (i.e. disparate regions with low errors), as the feedback from the error surface is equally likely to direct the search to locally optimal solutions than the globally optimum solution. However, the degree to which this is the case is also likely to be affected by the explorative capability of the optimisation algorithm used (Maier et al., 2019 ). If this degree is low, as is the case for gradient methods, whether a local or the global optimum in the error surface is identified is generally highly dependent on the starting position of the search, as such algorithms are unable to escape local optima (Maier et al., 2019 ). However, if the exploratory capability of the algorithm is increased (e.g. by using multi-starts or evolutionary algorithms), a wider area of the error surface is explored, including the different regions of attraction, making it more likely that the globally optimal solution is identified. The finding that the optima of more complex models are likely to be dispersed over a greater region of the error surface also implies that the parameters of more complex models identified as part of the optimisation process should be less unique (Fig. 7 ). This is because if optima are distributed over a smaller region of the error surface, the calibrated parameter values that are likely to be identified as part of the optimisation process are likely to be concentrated in a smaller region of the parameter space. As a result, even if there are different local optima, the resulting parameters values are similar to each other, ensuring that the values of the calibrated parameters are more well-defined. The above inferences align with the findings of a number of previous studies (see Fig. 7 ). For example, McIntyre and Al-Qurashi (2009)  found that when they calibrated IHACRES models with 3, 4 and 5 parameters, respectively, the model with 5 parameters performed worst, even though it had the greatest number of degrees of freedom, suggesting that it was more difficult to find the global optimum in the error surface as model complexity increased. García-Romero et al. (2019)  found that while the calibrated parameters of the simpler GR4J models (4 parameters) generally had unique values, this was not the case for the more complex Sacramento model (16 parameters), where calibrated values for 10 of the 16 parameters corresponded to a large range of values. Each of these was found approximately the same number of times as part of the calibration trials conducted, suggesting the existence of optima that are more widely distributed over the error surface, increasing the difficulty of the optimisation problem and decreasing the uniqueness of the parameter values identified. Andréassian et al. (2001)  and Shin et al. (2015)  had similar findings, where unique sets of parameter values were able to be obtained for simpler models, but not for more complex ones. In the case of Andréassian et al. (2001) , the parameter values obtained for a GR3J model (an earlier 3 parameter version of GR4J) were unique, while those obtained for TOPMOD (6 parameters) and IHACRES (6 parameters) were not. In the case of Shin et al. (2015) , unique parameter sets were able to be identified for both GR4J (4 parameters) and IHACRES (4 parameters), whereas this was not the case for SIMHYD (9 parameters) and Sacramento (13 parameters). It is interesting to note that Andreassian et al. (2001) were not able to identify unique parameter sets for IHACRES, while Shin et al. (2015)  were. One potential reason for this is that the former used a gradient method for calibration, which has limited exploratory capability, whereas the latter used 5 different global search algorithms (SCE, NSGA2, DREAM, DE, CMA-ES), which have greater exploratory ability and are therefore more likely to find global minima in error surfaces that have more widely distributed optima, as discussed above. It should be noted that the ability to identify unique sets of calibrated parameters by finding the global minimum in the error surface as part of an optimisation process is related to the well-known issue of parameter identifiability (Guillaume et al., 2019 ). However, parameter identifiability is also related to the quality of the calibration data (e.g. how well the calibration data represent the underlying physical processes being modelled). If the quality of the calibration data is low, the global minimum in the error surface found with the aid of the optimisation algorithm is not necessarily the “true” optimum (Maier et al., 2019 ). This was demonstrated by Andréassian et al. (2001)  and Shin et al. (2015) , who found that parameter uniqueness could be improved by improving the quality of the calibration data. This highlights (i) the potential futility of treating model calibration solely as an optimisation problem, as there is no point in attempting to identify the global optimum of an error surface that is not representative of “true” model performance, and (ii) the importance of resolving any model-data discrepancies (Vilas et al., 2023 ). Similar issues could also arise when assumptions underpinning the calculation of error metrics (e.g. the shape of the distribution, autocorrelation or heteroscedasticity of the residuals) are violated.  3.3 Impact of catchment climate condition The impact of using input and output data from catchments with different climatic conditions on the relative roughness, flatness and optima dispersion of the error surfaces is shown in Fig. 8  , which shows a column chart with the primary category as the model type, and the secondary category as the error metric. The change of relative metric results is calculated as follows: for a given model structure and error function, the averaged value of the raw results for the dry catchments and the wet catchments are calculated separately, and the raw results for the dry and wet catchments are used to find the corresponding relative scores based on the categorisation and scores defined in Section 2.1 ; then the change of the relative metric values is calculated as the difference between these two scores. For example, in Fig. 8 (b), it is seen that for AWBM, the relative flatness is higher for wet catchments when using the LOGNS error function (a changed value of 1), but it is lower when using the WLS error function (a changed value of −1). As can be seen, there is a general increase in the relative roughness of the error surface as catchment wetness increases (Fig. 8 (a)). In contrast, increasing catchment wetness generally results in a decrease in the relative degree of optima dispersion (Fig. 8 (c)) for simpler models (i.e. AWBM and GR4J). As was the case for the influence of model complexity, there appear to be no clear trends for the impact of catchment climate condition on the relative flatness of the error surface (Fig. 8 (b)), with increases in flatness for some models and error metrics, and decreases for the three simplest models when the WLS error metric is used. Based on inference, the above results suggest that optimisation efficiency is likely to decrease with increasing catchment wetness (Fig. 9  ). This is in agreement with Thyer et al. (1999) , who found that the number of function evaluations required for an SCE-UA algorithm to converge when calibrating a modified SFB model for the wetter Allyn River catchment was 7,000, while this number was only 4,000 for the dryer Scott Creek catchment. As the results in Fig. 8 (c) indicate that, for the experiments conducted, optima dispersion decreases for wetter catchments, it can be inferred that parameter uniqueness should increase accordingly (Fig. 9 ), which agrees with the findings of a number of previous studies. For example, Lidén and Harlin (2000)  found that for dry catchments, it was not possible to identify unique values of parameters related to baseflow, but that unique parameter values could be identified for a wet catchment. When calibrating a modified SFB model for twenty-five Australian catchments with different climates, Sumner et al. (1997)  found that unique parameters sets could be identified for wet catchments. However, this was not the case for semi-arid catchments. When examining plots of the error surface for wet and dry catchments for the same CRR model, Thyer et al. (1999)  found that the error surface for the dry catchment had multiple local optima, thereby providing an explanation for the difficulty in finding unique parameter values for such catchments. Similar results were found by Xiong and O'Connor (2000) , who visualised error surfaces for catchments in a humid region in Japan and a semi-arid region in Tanzania, where the error surfaces for the semi-arid catchment had more optima that were more widely dispersed. The reason why so many studies have similar findings (i.e. that catchment wetness results in an increase in parameter uniqueness) is likely because many commonly-used rainfall-runoff models demonstrate a trade-off between fitting high and low flows (i.e. there is insufficient flexibility in the model structure to achieve both), resulting in some parameter sets better at reproducing high flows, while other parameters sets better reproduced low flows. In a dry catchment, there are fewer high flow events than in wet catchments and the ability to model behaviour associated with low flows becomes more important than in wet catchments. Hence different parameter sets associated with better fitting to either low flows or high flows becomes a key component of the error landscape in drier catchments. It should be noted that while the above analysis was conducted for catchments in different climatic zones (e.g. dry, wet), similar analyses could also be conducted under different conditions experienced in a particular catchment at different times. For example, the application of ELAs could be used to determine if the characteristics of the error surface change (i) at different times of the year (e.g. different seasons) by only using data from those time periods for the analysis or (ii) under expected changes in future conditions as a result of climate or environmental change (e.g. Partington et al., 2022 ) using climate perturbed data (Culley et al., 2019; 2021; McInerney et al., 2023 ), for example.  3.4 Implications and next steps As shown by this analysis, ELA metrics are able to summarise properties of the fitness landscape across combinations of model structures, datasets, and error metrics. Visualisations such as heatmaps (Fig. 5 ) and boxplots (Fig. 6 ) enable graphical inferences that are consistent with existing CRR modeller experience and literature, validating the ELA metrics recommended in Zhu et al. (2022a) . We appreciate that the analysis presented in this paper provides a “proof of concept” of what the potential capabilities of the proposed approach are. Additional analyses are required to better understand the true utility of using ELA metrics for error surface analysis by investigating how the calibration efficiency, difficulty and parameter uniqueness of conceptual rainfall runoff models change under (i) a wider range of error metrics (e.g. sum of squared errors, maximum likelihood, information criteria, relative volume error (see Sorooshian, 1981; Sefe and Boughton, 1982; Young, 1989; Jie et al., 2016 )); (ii) a broader range of model types (e.g. more parsimonious models, such as data-based mechanistic (DBM) models (Young and Beven, 1994; Young, 2003 ), which should have more well-defined parameters); and (iii) under a broader range of conditions (e.g. under changing catchment conditions (see Partington et al., 2022 )). In addition, given the general applicability of the proposed approach, its potential benefits could be assessed for the calibration of other types of models, irrespective of model structure, data and objective function, and other types of optimisation problems, in addition to model calibration (Maier et al., 2014; 2019 ). In order to further strengthen our findings, statistical analysis would be a natural next step but may be limited by issues of transferability of results. In the domain of large sample hydrology (Gupta et al. 2014 ), there is potential to calculate ELA metrics on a larger number of catchments and apply techniques to identify general trends and patterns. Similarly, virtual labs could be used to identify patterns for future conditions (Partington et al., 2022; Thyer et al., 2024 ). The applicability of patterns to individual cases could be handled by developing predictive models that use ELA metrics as dependent variables to predict optimisation efficiency (He et al., 2007; Miranda et al., 2017; Saleem and Gallagher, 2022 ) or other relevant emergent properties of fitness landscapes. New theory would likely be needed, drawing particularly on work on structural identifiability (Guillaume et al. 2019 ). Similar to the case of prediction in ungauged basins where dependent variables are often broadened to include catchment characteristics or data from other basins (Gibbs et al., 2012; Hrachowitz et al. 2013 ), one would expect that predicting optimisation efficiency could make use of additional dependent variables including model performance metrics (Bennett et al. 2013 ), hydrological signatures (Gupta et al. 2008 ), and information about optimisation performance under comparable benchmarks (Maier et al., 2014 ). As mentioned previously, knowledge of the characteristics of the error surface and predictions of optimisation efficiency or other relevant properties of the error surface opens the door to being able to select the most appropriate optimisation algorithm for the calibration problem being considered. As discussed in Maier et al. (2014) , this provides the opportunity to apply optimisation methods more judiciously, rather than “blindly” trying different algorithms to see which works best in a given situation, as has been demonstrated in a number of previous studies (e.g. Gibbs et al., 2015 ). The above approaches could also be extended to multi-objective optimisation problems (Cheng et al., 2002; Madsen, 2000; Jie et al., 2016 ). As discussed in Maier et al. (2019) , different objectives in multi-objective problems have their own error functions. As many multi-objective problems have competing objectives, the global optima in the different error surface are not coincident, resulting in the well-known Pareto front of optimal solutions (rather than a single optimal solution). While this paper includes some hypotheses for possible causes of observed fitness landscape properties, effective diagnosis to address any specific case is likely to require more than just predictive models. In general, structural non-identifiability can be addressed by changing model structure or data, and practical non-identifiability can also be addressed by changing error metrics and optimisation algorithms (Guillaume et al. 2019 ). Currently, we often take brute force approaches or informed guesses about what changes might obtain the desired result. Being able to diagnose the cause of fitness landscape characteristics and identifiability problems would enable a paradigm shift in modelling practice. Ultimately, the hope is that these and other new ELA metrics could support model development and new modelling techniques (Thyer et al., 2024 ). Calculation of ELA metrics on different parameter subspaces has the potential to provide more information than just the location of optima and their uncertainty. Measurement of landscape characteristics has the potential to support new forms of regularisation or model complexity controls. In the context of the method of multiple working hypotheses (Clark et al. 2011 ), identification of specific model structure-data mismatches that result in fitness landscape anomalies has the potential to result in more targeted data collection and model structure development. While ELA metrics are far from a magic bullet, this analysis has shown that they are a promising new tool for our hydrological modelling arsenal.   4 Summary and conclusions The calibration of conceptual rainfall-runoff (CRR) models has been the subject of a large number of research papers. While the impact of attributes such as model structure and complexity, catchment climate conditions, error metrics and calibration data length (and properties), as well as the optimisation method used, has received significant attention in these studies, there has been a lack of focus on systematic approaches to quantifying how the features of the error surface are affected by these attributes. This makes it difficult to provide a transparent, objective and repeatable assessment of the impact model structures, catchment climate conditions, error metrics and calibration data properties have on calibration efficiency, difficulty and parameter uniqueness. In order to address this shortcoming, three exploratory landscape analysis (ELA) metrics are proposed in this paper as a way to quantify key features of the error surfaces of CRR models. The metrics were applied to 420 error surfaces of CRR models consisting of different combinations of model structures of varying complexity, catchments with different climate conditions, a range of error metrics, and calibration data sets of different lengths. Results show that, in the experiments conducted, there are clear differences in error surface roughness and optima dispersion between different models and catchments with different levels of wetness. More complex models are shown to have higher roughness and optima dispersion, while wetter catchments have higher roughness but lower optima dispersion. However, the generality of these findings needs to be tested using a wider range of combinations of models and conditions. The primary contribution of this paper is the presentation of an alternative approach to identify useful information to support decisions that have to be made during the development of CRR models, such as the selection of an appropriate model structure, the selection of an appropriate optimisation algorithm and the selection of appropriate values that control the searching behaviour of the selected optimisation algorithm (e.g. relative degree of exploration and exploitation). The results for the experiments conducted also provide valuable insight into how optimisation efficiency, optimisation difficulty and parameter uniqueness can be affected by different models and the degree of catchment wetness (Fig. 10  ). For the experiments conducted, the results suggested that more complex models applied to wet catchments have lower optimisation efficiency, medium optimisation difficulty and medium parameter uniqueness. However, when such models were applied to dry catchments, there was an increase in optimisation efficiency and an increase in optimisation difficulty. Irrespective of whether catchments were wet or dry, the results indicated that reducing model complexity for the models used in this study resulted in an improvement in all three performance measures. However, as mentioned above, the generality of these results needs to be tested using a larger number of experiments, considering a larger number of combinations of factors that contribute to the characteristics of error surfaces. The fact that the three ELA metrics proposed in this paper are able to identify key features of the error surfaces of CRR models, including relative roughness, relative flatness and relative optima dispersion, provides support for the findings of Zhu et al. (2022a, b) . This creates opportunities for determining and comparing the features of the error surfaces of a broad range of CRR models under a wide range of conditions in an effective and efficient manner, providing insight into how these features change in response to different attributes. Consequently, as mentioned above, future studies should apply the approach introduced in this paper to a larger number of combinations of CRR models, catchments and error metrics in order to test the generality of the findings of this study and to potentially provide high-level guidance on the selection of CRR models and optimisation approaches for different types of catchments. It could also guide the development of novel CRR models that can be calibrated more easily and efficiently and have more well-defined parameters.
1 Introduction A property is termed anisotropic if its values depend on the space direction along which it is measured (Hristopulos, 2020 ). Various applications have shown that when the direction and magnitude of anisotropy are well understood, they can significantly improve modeling quality in geostatistical methods such as ordinary and universal kriging (Boisvert and Deutsch, 2011; Goovaerts, 1997; Li et al., 2018 ), collocated cokriging (Doyen et al., 1996; Xu et al., 1992 ), Bayesian kriging (Al-Mudhafar, 2019 ), and stochastic simulations (Al-Mudhafar, 2021; Alabert and Massonnat, 1990; Journel, 1990; Journel and Alabert, 1990; Pirrone et al., 2016 ). Geoscientific objects and processes, such as river systems, fluvial landforms, folds and so on, often exhibit features of locally varying anisotropy (LVA) (Boisvert et al., 2009; Fouedjio and Seguret, 2016; Stroet and Snepvangers, 2005 ). However, the typical assumption of second-order stationarity in classical geostatistics, does not hold in such situations, thus the corresponding geostatistical modeling results are usually inaccurate or biased. Therefore, a crucial goal of modern geostatistics is to reveal complex spatial continuity characteristics by taking advantage of all available information. Methods such as multiple-point statistics (Chen et al., 2018; Lam et al., 2020; Mariethoz and Caers, 2014; Strebelle, 2002; Vannametee et al., 2014 ), high-order statistics (Dimitrakopoulos et al., 2010; Mustapha et al., 2011; Yao et al., 2018 ), and the integration of LVA in traditional geostatistics (Boisvert and Deutsch, 2009; Boisvert et al., 2009; Fouedjio and Seguret, 2016; Stroet and Snepvangers, 2005 ), have been developed to address this issue. For classical geostatistics with LVA, one possible solution is using moving windows. The methods based on moving windows handle the issue by assuming that second-order stationarity exists within the local search neighborhood associated with each location being estimated or simulated (Deutsch and Lewis, 1992; Machuca-Mory and Deutsch, 2013; Stroet and Snepvangers, 2005; Xu, 1996 ). However, it can be challenging for complicated geological settings to determine an appropriate neighborhood that guarantees a reasonable number of local samples while maintaining local stationarity. Additionally, samples that belong to the intersection of two search windows might be assigned to two entirely different, or even divergent, spatial dependence structures. An exaggerated example of such limitations is shown by Boisvert and Deutsch (2011) . Another typical method that can deal with the LVA integration problem in geoscience is space deformation (Fouedjio, 2016; Fouedjio et al., 2015; Sampson and Guttorp, 1992 ), which usually transforms the originally nonstationary space into a different dimension such that the stationarity assumption is satisfied. A well-known variant of this method uses non-Euclidean distances (Almendral et al., 2008; Boisvert and Deutsch, 2008; Boisvert and Deutsch, 2011; Boisvert et al., 2009; Greenberg et al., 2011 ) to account for realistically nonlinear features in geostatistical modeling. This approach follows the basic idea of two-point or variogram-based geostatistics (Al-Mudhafar, 2021; Goovaerts, 1997; Hristopulos, 2020; Huijbregts and Journel, 1978; Isaaks and Srivastava, 1989; Li and Heap, 2014 ) and has been richly developed in many aspects. These include inference of the LVA fields (Fouedjio et al., 2016; Fouedjio and Seguret, 2016; Lillah and Boisvert, 2015 ), calculation and application of the optimum distance among the LVA field (Boisvert et al., 2009 ), and associated variogram modeling, geostatistical estimation, and simulation (Boisvert and Deutsch, 2011; Boisvert et al., 2009; Fouedjio et al., 2016 ). Moreover, corresponding programs are readily available to the public (Boisvert and Deutsch, 2011 ). However, to guarantee positive definiteness of kriging system of equations, the non-Euclidean distances associated with real geological characteristics cannot be applied straightforwardly, and often must be transformed to generate corresponding straight-line distances in a high-dimensional Euclidean space before geostatistical modeling. This process of distance transformation can be accomplished by classical multidimensional scaling (MDS) (Kruskal, 1964 ) or its variant L-ISOMAP (Boisvert and Deutsch, 2011; Tenenbaum et al., 2000 ), which can significantly reduce computational requirements in the case of numerous estimated or simulated points. Based on such mapped distances in a higher-dimensional Euclidean space, a limited number of standard covariance functions are positive definite, thus the kriging and sequential simulation can be executed favorably. Accordingly, the mainstream geostatistical modeling with LVA is performed in a high-dimensional Euclidean space instead of using non-Euclidean distances, which can be consistent with realistic geological features. However, this replacement by approximation may not always be appropriate (Boisvert, 2010 ), especially when the estimation grid is significantly large or complex. Moreover, only a few commonly used variogram models can be safely applied to yield a valid solution to kriging system. Additionally, introducing high-dimensional space makes it challenging to visually illustrate and analyze the calculation process. In this study, we introduce a new method called direct kriging (DK), offering an alternative to classical geostatistics for addressing LVA. Its main flowchart is shown in Fig. 1  . Unlike classical kriging, this approach directly integrates shortest path distance data into estimation without relying on a system of equations. Instead, it formulates estimation error variance minimization as a direct optimization model. An objective function is designed to minimize error variance while ensuring the validity of error variance and estimated values, thereby validating the model and accommodating SPD. The method is implemented using a genetic algorithm and evaluated with two datasets from a fluvial channel system: a delta deposit and a meandering channel. Our findings demonstrate that this method outperforms classical solutions, providing a more explicit representation of curvilinear structures and enhancing interpolation accuracy, as indicated by normalized mean absolute error and normalized root mean square error measurements.  2 Methods 2.1 Classical kriging Kriging, widely used in geosciences, provides best linear unbiased estimations and some nonlinear types of estimation (Goovaerts, 1997; Hristopulos, 2020; Huijbregts and Journel, 1978 ). Classic kriging estimators like simple kriging (SK) and ordinary kriging (OK) use the least squares method for optimization, yielding equations known as the kriging system (Huijbregts and Journel, 1978 ). For instance, the SK system is as follows:(1) K λ x   = k     where K    is the matrix of sample-to-sample covariances, k    is the vector of sample-to-unknown covariances, and λ x      is the vector of SK weights at the unknown location x   . Note that the system in Eq. (1)  has a unique solution if, and only if, the covariance matrix K    is strictly positive definite and thus has a strictly positive determinant (Huijbregts and Journel, 1978 ). Furthermore, the covariance function must be “positive definite” to ensure that the variance of any finite linear combination of the random variables with any weights, is non-negative. Therefore, the validity of the following two variances should be guaranteed:(2) Var Z  ∗   x   - Z x      = σ  E  2   x   ≥ 0   Var Z  ∗   x      ≥ 0                          where Z x       and Z  ∗   x       represent the random variables for the true and estimated values, respectively. Expression (2   ) satisfies the condition for obtaining a stable and unique solution to the kriging system, which explains why only a limited number of covariance or variogram models are allowed in Euclidian space. As a result, most non-Euclidian distance-based solutions to address the LVA problem cannot be directly achieved within the classical kriging paradigm.  2.2 Direct kriging Considering the limitations of the classical kriging paradigm in the presence of LVA, this paper proposes a method to approach the minimum error variance directly instead of calculating the accurate minimum value by solving the kriging system. Based on this, the estimation weights are obtained by directly searching for the minimum error variance, which is regarded as a general optimization problem given by:(3) λ x    ∗   = arg  min  λ x   ∈ D   σ  E  2   x          where D ⊂ R  n x         and D    is the definition domain of λ x      . Note that using the matrices K    and k    in Eq. (1) , the error variance in Eq. (3)  can be calculated by:(4) σ  E  2   x   = C 0   - 2 λ x    T   k + λ x    T   K λ x        Consequently, constraints in Eq. (2)  can be rewritten as the following:(5) Var Z  ∗   x   - Z x      = C 0   - 2 λ x    T   k + λ x    T   K λ x   ≥ 0   Var Z  ∗   x      = λ x    T   K λ x   ≥ 0                                  In summary, the complete optimization process can be summarized as:(6) λ x    ∗   = arg  min  λ x   ∈ D   C 0   - 2 λ x    T   k + λ x    T   K λ x        s . t . C 0   - 2 λ x    T   k + λ x    T   K λ x   ≥ 0   λ x    T   K λ x   ≥ 0               As shown in Eq. (6) , the primary form of this framework contains one optimization objective with two primary constraints. With the resulting weights, the corresponding estimate and error variance can be calculated straightforwardly. It is important to note that the proposed framework in Eq. (6)  only involves the most fundamental elements in terms of traditional kriging; it can be viewed as another form of SK in this respect. However, this framework is flexible enough to accommodate most intrinsic constraints in conventional kriging. For instance, in the case of OK, the sum of weights should equal 1. Additionally, practical restrictions, such as the valid value range of estimates, can be incorporated into this framework if needed. Moreover, the requirement for the covariance matrix to be strictly positive definite is greatly weakened within this framework. The validity of most coefficients related to the estimation can be constructed as a constraint and guaranteed during the optimization process. As a result, as long as valid estimation weights exist in the definition domain D    in Eq. (3) , our proposed kriging framework would work. Also, the limitations of the proposed method should be acknowledged. Given the optimization model in Eq. (6) , a stochastic optimization algorithm is the most straightforward approach selected to find its appropriate solution. However, unlike classical kriging, this selection is challenging because the stochastic algorithm cannot theoretically guarantee an exact solution. Despite this, empirical evidence suggests that this issue has minimal impact on modeling results. It is crucial not to terminate the stochastic algorithm prematurely, as this may hinder achieving an acceptable solution. Therefore, we recommend setting stricter termination conditions to ensure a comprehensive evaluation of the search space. Another potential challenge when using a stochastic algorithm for optimization is ensuring that the spatial interpolation acts as an “exact” interpolator. This requirement dictates that estimates at sampled locations match the sampled values precisely. To address this, the optimization algorithm can incorporate various initial solutions, including special initialized solutions like 1, 0, 0…, effectively resolving the issue. By doing so, the algorithm can swiftly identify the optimal solution while maintaining the exactness requirement. In this context, a population-based stochastic optimization algorithm is preferable. Hence, we select the genetic algorithm to implement this model, as it is a typical population based stochastic algorithm that will be elaborated on below.  2.3 Genetic algorithm The genetic algorithm (GA) is a typical meta -heuristic and evolutionary algorithm proposed by John Holland and his colleagues in 1960 s (Goldberg, 1989; Holland, 1975 ). GAs have been widely applied in many areas of science and engineering due to their ability to mimic the evolution process of natural populations (Clarke, 2017; Jafari-Marandi and Smith, 2017 ). Genetic operators such as selection, crossover, and mutation are employed to generate new populations in the evolution. Fig. 2   illustrates a typical procedure of using a GA to search for a solution. The following elements should be considered when using GAs to solve optimization problems: objective functions, chromosome representation, genetic operations, termination criterion, and so on. More detailed descriptions of GAs can be found in the literature, e.g. (Goldberg, 1989 ).  2.4 GA-based direct kriging Many population stochastic optimization methods, such as differential evolution, particle swarm optimization, and GA, can be employed to solve the typical optimization problem expressed in Eq. (6)  for direct kriging. Among the frequently employed optimization methods is the GA selected in this study. Besides its indisputable contributions to a large number of fields in science and engineering (Konak et al., 2006 ), another reason for this selection is that the authors' experiences and domain knowledge indicate that GAs could produce favorable results for complex mathematical modeling and optimization problems with robustness and computational efficiency (Clarke, 2017; Li et al., 2018 ). Once the evolution process of GA stops, the optimized kriging weights corresponding to the best individual can be used to yield an estimate and its accompanying error variance.  2.5 Algorithm implementation This section illustrates an alternative implementation of a GA-based ordinary kriging model within the proposed framework (GOK), with a detailed description of its key GA operations and algorithm. 2.5.1 Objective function Considering its well-known applicability, the paradigm of ordinary kriging is adopted in this implementation. A new constraint is added to Eq. (6) , requiring that the sum of the estimation weights is equal to 1.0, resulting in the following objective function:(7) λ x    ∗   = arg  min  λ x   ∈ D   C 0   - 2 λ x    T   k + λ x    T   K λ x        s . t . C 0   - 2 λ x    T   k + λ x    T   K λ x   ≥ 0   λ x    T   K λ x   ≥ 0                                       ∑  i = 1  n x     λ  i   x   = 1.0                                                   where n x       is the number of neighborhood data closest to  x   .  2.5.2 Chromosome representation There are two main types of chromosome representations in GAs: binary strings and real (floating point) numbers (Akopov et al., 2019; Goldberg, 1989; Herrera et al., 1998 ). In this research, real coding is adopted because it is more natural and preferable when dealing with a continuous search space (Herrera et al., 2003 ). Using this coding scheme, the series of candidate estimation weights in Eq. (7)  can be directly applied in the GA evolution process without requiring conventional encoding and decoding operations in a binary representation (Goldberg, 1989 ).  2.5.3 Initial population Each chromosome gene in the initial population is assigned a random number within the valid range. In addition to this random initialization, traditional kriging weights can also be added as an individual of the initial population, thus improving the convergence velocity of the algorithm.  2.5.4 Genetic operators Selection, crossover, and mutation are essential for the GAs to evolve a population of search space solutions. Various options are available for each of these components, including ranking or tournament selection, simple or two-point crossover, and random or non-uniform mutation. In this implementation, we employ the blend crossover operator (BLX-a) (Abido, 2009; Herrera et al., 2003 ) and Gaussian mutation (Hinterding, 1995; Xing et al., 2021 ) on the chromosomes resulting from roulette wheel selection. The basic idea of BLX-a    operator (Abido, 2009 ) is to randomly choose a number from the interval x i  - α y i  - x i       , y i  + α y i  - x i         , where x i     and y i     are the i -th parameter values of the parent solutions and x i  < y i    . The undetermined coefficient α    controls the balance between interpolation and extrapolation of the search space and is often set to 0.5. In Gaussian mutation (Xing et al., 2021 ), the original gene value is perturbed using a zero-mean normal distribution. The new value of the mutated gene is calculated using the expression x i  + N 0 , σ        , where σ    stands for the standard variance of the Gaussion distribution, and is set to 1.0 in this study. It is worth noting that in most applications, the gene value generated from either a crossover or mutation is limited within a certain value range. However, this limitation is abandoned in this study because the estimation weights λ x       in Eq. (7)  do not have any constraints.  2.5.5 Termination methods The algorithm is terminated either when it reaches the maximum number of generations, or when no improvement to the objective function could be made from a generation.  2.5.6 Implementation flow Following the methods and procedures illustrated above, the implementation details of GOK estimation are presented in Algorithm 1. It is evident that the overall structure of GOK is similar to that of traditional kriging, and hence most traditional kriging programs can be readily adapted to implement this algorithm with minimal modifications required.
