As depicted in Fig. 1 , a complete application of this method involves six basic steps: (1) obtaining sample data at measured points and generating the estimation grid, (2) generating the LVA field associated with nonlinear features, (3) calculating the corresponding OSPD data, (4) computing the OSPD-based variogram, (5) utilizing the proposed method to estimate each point of the estimation grid, and (6) outputting the estimated results upon completion of estimation for all locations. The key aspects of Steps (2)-(5) are elaborated below. The generation of the LVA field can be viewed as the construction of a series of local variograms across the study area. Fig. 1 b illustrates the local continuity directions in an LVA field corresponding to a saddle surface, with the main characteristics observed in Fig. 1 f. Typical data used to generate an LVA field include exhaustive secondary data, discrete point measurements of orientation, and so on (Lillah and Boisvert, 2015 ). Generally, the accuracy and reliability of an LVA field significantly affect the modeling results. To mitigate this effect, the LVA field in each case study is generated from an exhaustive dataset (assumed as the true dataset), ensuring accuracy and reliability. Additionally, the same LVA field is used for all evaluated methods. The calculation of SPD is based on the generated LVA field (Boisvert and Deutsch, 2011 ). Unlike the relatively simple anisotropic distance when only one global variogram model is used, in an LVA field, the anisotropic distance between two points can have many possible values because the path between them is not unique. Among all possible paths, only the shortest anisotropic path is needed, known as the SPD. Commonly used shortest-path algorithms, such as Dijkstra's algorithm, address this concern effectively. Fig. 1 c shows the SPD of a given point (to be estimated) between other grid nodes, demonstrating consistency with the LVA field. During variogram modeling, a global variogram is calculated using the original SPD. Due to the use of anisotropic distance, we derive an isotropic variogram model, eliminating the need to calculate variograms in different directions. It is worth noting that calculating variograms in diverse directions is not straightforward due to the non-Euclidean space being considered. In the core estimation procedures, we initially compute the point-to-point and point-to-unknown OSPD for each estimated point. These distances are then fed into the modeled covariance kernels. Subsequently, a genetic algorithm-based optimization model is employed to minimize error variance and derive corresponding estimates. Fig. 1 e presents an example of the searched neighborhood samples measured by point-to-unknown SPD, with curves connecting the estimated point and sample locations representing the corresponding search path guided by the OSPD. These curves align with the LVA field, implying satisfactory estimates.   3 Case studies In the following case studies, two exhaustive datasets with different LVA characteristics are generated and employed to assess the estimation performance of GOK and traditional OK (TOK). The first dataset (e_dataset_1 ) is a delta deposit, while the second one (e_dataset_2 ) is a synthetic meandering channel. To enable distance mapping, L-ISOMAP (Almendral et al., 2008; Boisvert and Deutsch, 2011 ) is applied to generate the mapped SPD (MSPD) from original SPD (OSPD) for TOK and GOK, respectively. To demonstrate the capability of the proposed method in incorporating different variogram models, three commonly used variogram models (the exponential, spherical, and Gaussian) are imposed on GOK. However, only the exponential model is applied to TOK, as the positive definiteness of the other two models is not warranted in high-dimensional Euclidean space. Thus, there are four test estimators in the following applications: MSPD-based TOK with an exponential model and OSPD-based GOK sequentially with an exponential, spherical, and Gaussian model. For convenience, the four methods are abbreviated as TOK-EXP, GOK-EXP, GOK-SPH, and GOK-GAU. In addition to the correlation coefficient (CC) and mean error (ME), the primary error metrics used in this research are the normalized mean absolute error (NMAE) and normalized root mean square error (NRMSE), which are calculated using the following formulas (Li et al., 2018 ):(8) N M A E = 1 σ  N   ∑ i  = 1  N  z   ∗   x i      - z  x i             (9) N R M S E = 1 σ   1 N  ∑ i  = 1  N  z   ∗   x i      - z  x i         2        where z  ∗   x i        and z x i        are, respectively, the estimated value and the measured value for the i -th location; N    is the number of estimated points; and σ    is the standard variance of the measured values. The basic experimental procedure described below contains the following steps: (1) preparing an exhaustive dataset; (2) calculating or assuming the related estimation parameters, such as the used LVA field and variogram models; (3) generating a randomly sampled dataset, i.e., a random subset of the exhaustive dataset, to estimate the 'unsampled' locations; (4) evaluating and analyzing the estimates from the test methods; and (5) reconfirming the corresponding results in the case of different sampling strategies. Essentially, the accuracy assessment method employed in both case studies is a form of cross-validation through random subsampling (Al-Mudhafar, 2016 ). Additionally, we conduct an extended evaluation using k-fold cross-validation (with k = 16) (Al-Mudhafar, 2016; Wang et al., 2014 ), where we randomly select 16 sample datasets from the exhaustive dataset, each consisting of 300 random locations. The corresponding results are depicted in Figs. 3-6S  in the Supporting Information . The key characteristics revealed in these figures align with those presented in the main text. 3.1 Case study 1 3.1.1 Experimental data: A delta deposit The test utilizes two datasets, e_dataset_1  and s_dataset_1 , to evaluate the prediction accuracy of the tested methods. e_dataset_1  is a ground truth dataset, constructed as a 150 × 200 regular grid from the delta deposits (layer 3) of the Stanford VI-E dataset, a well-known prograding fluvial channel system dataset (Lee and Mukerji, 2012 ). Meanwhile, s_dataset_1  consists of 300 randomly selected locations extracted from e_dataset_1 . Fig. 3   displays the exhaustive dataset, its corresponding LVA field, and the sample locations, while Table 1   shows the basic statistics.  3.1.2 Estimation parameters The OSPD and MSPD of the dataset e_dataset_1  are presented in Fig. 4  , revealing that MSPD is a compressed version of OSPD. However, MSPD data is not a favorable representative of OSPD since much valuable information is lost regarding the 45-degree line (y = x). Thus, estimates produced by TOK based on MSPD may not be highly accurate. The experimental variograms calculated from MSPD and OSPD are automatically modeled (Li et al., 2018 ) and illustrated in Fig. 5  , showing that the range of the MSPD based variogram model is shorter than that of the OSPD based variogram model, in accordance with the distance reduction observed in Fig. 4 . Note that both MSPD and OSPD represent anisotropic distances. This implies that experimental variograms based on MSPD and OSPD are considered isotropic models. This scenario is akin to using a constant anisotropic distance model. Consequently, conventional variogram interpretation and modeling (Gringarten and Deutsch, 2001 ) are simplified in this context, where only the omnidirectional experimental variogram is calculated and modeled. Other estimation parameters, including GA parameters and search neighborhood, are listed in Table 2-4    . Fig. 7 S in the Supporting Information  reveals the evolution processes of estimation weights and error variance corresponding to the first three estimated points. It is worth noting that altering these coefficients in a reasonable way does not significantly affect estimation results, and the conclusions of this study remain valid.  3.1.3 Estimation results and analyses Estimation results and analyses are presented in Figs. 6-8    , which show the estimates from TOK-EXP, GOK-EXP, GOK-SPH, and GOK-GAU, along with the corresponding comparisons to actual values. The results suggest that GOK estimates exhibit more realistic curvilinear features than those from TOK, and all three GOK methods yield more accurate estimates than TOK-EXP. Moreover, the superiority of GOK over TOK appears to be relatively stable and not explicitly dependent on variogram. In addition to these qualitative exhibitions, Table 4  quantifies the estimation errors from the four methods. GOK demonstrates more favourable characteristics than TOK across all four error metrics: ME, CC, NMAE, and NRMSE. While GOK-GAU provides the most accurate results, the differences among the three GOK estimates are negligible. Overall, all GOK estimates indicate a higher accuracy than TOK estimates. To further evaluate the stability of the prediction performance of GOK and TOK, ten sample datasets (named D1, D2, …, D10, corresponding to an increasing sampling number of 100, 200, …, 1000, respectively) are randomly sampled from e_dataset_1  and used to execute TOK and GOK estimations at other 'un-sampled' locations. The sampling details and the associated TOK and GOK estimation results are demonstrated in Fig. 1 S in the Supporting Information . Fig. 9   shows the NMAEs and NRMSEs of the estimates, confirming that GOK is more likely to produce accurate estimates than TOK. Furthermore, the estimates of GOK are relatively stable in the context of varying sampling densities, whereas TOK is sensitive to this context. Therefore, all GOK estimates reasonably exhibit the delta deposit associated with the underlying LVA field, and maintain the high accurate estimates.   3.2 Case study 2 3.2.1 Experimental data: A fluvial channel Two datasets, a sample dataset and an exhaustive dataset, are prepared to compare the performance of GOK and TOK, as in the previous section. The exhaustive dataset (e_dataset_2 ) consists of 30,000 porosity points on a 150 × 200 rectangular grid and is generated from the meandering channels (layer 2) of the Stanford VI-E dataset, which corresponds to a fluvial channel system prograding into a basin (Lee and Mukerji, 2012 ). The sample dataset (s_dataset_2 ) contains 300 locations randomly drawn from e_dataset_2 . Both datasets are depicted in Fig. 10  , with the corresponding summary statistics shown in Table 5  .  3.2.2 Estimation parameters Fig. 11   depicts the OSPD and MSPD data associated with e_dataset_2 , showing the discrepancy between OSPD and MSPD and leading to a marked difference between the MSPD and OSPD-based variograms (in Fig. 12  ). Other estimation parameters, such as GA parameters and search neighborhood, are the same as those used in the first case study (shown in Table 2-4 ). The evolution processes of the main parameters for the first three estimated points are illustrated in Fig. 8 S in the Supporting Information .  3.2.3 Estimation results and analyses Figs. 13 and 14    show the estimates from the four test methods and their comparisons to the true values. Qualitative and quantitative analyses of the estimation errors are also presented in Fig. 15   and Table 6  . It can be observed that TOK omits many significant characteristics of the meandering channel, such as those highlighted by the white circles in Fig. 13 , while GOK estimates preserve most of these features and produce more realistic and accurate results. The comparisons of GOK and TOK demonstrated here are similar to those shown in the first application above. GOK produces more realistic and accurate estimates than TOK, regardless of the variogram type used. To test the stability of the methods under different sampling strategies, ten sample datasets named D1, D2, …, and D10 are prepared, each containing an increasing number of randomly selected samples, ranging from 100 and 1 000, to carry out the estimations on the unsampled locations of e_dataset_2 . A detailed description of the sampling locations and their corresponding estimates can be found in Fig. 2 S in the Supporting Information . Fig. 16   illustrates the interpolation errors of TOK and GOK estimates using the ten sample datasets. GOK is superior to TOK regardless of the dataset used. Moreover, it is noticeable that as the sample data size increases, GOK's superiority over TOK becomes less pronounced. This phenomenon is reasonable since LVA modeling will probably not be necessary when a substantial amount of sampling data is available. Therefore, GOK would be more helpful when the sample data size is relatively small.    4 Discussion and conclusions Numerous earth system structures, such as braided rivers and meandering channels, pose a challenge in adequately characterizing and expressing their continuity in different directions. Obtaining the realistic SPD associated with nonlinear features becomes crucial in such cases. However, because the SPD is not always linear, it cannot be directly incorporated into classical kriging methods. To overcome this issue, a commonly used solution is replacing the original SPD with a scaled or mapped distance, compromising distance accuracy. Therefore, making full use of the SPD in geostatistics remains a challenge. This study proposes a generalized kriging framework termed direct kriging (DK), which offers a more reliable and flexible solution for LVA modeling. Unlike traditional geostatistical methods, DK searches for optimized weights that minimize error variance directly, rather than using kriging equations to determine estimation weights. This results in several key benefits, such as the ability to directly incorporate OSPD data in the presence of LVA, the applicability of commonly used variogram models, and the flexibility to add additional constraints on estimation weights, estimates, and error variances. The method proposed in this study was implemented using a genetic algorithm and then applied to two datasets corresponding to a fluvial channel system: a delta deposit and a meandering channel. In addition to visually comparing the modeling results with the ground truth, two typical cross-validation methods, random subsampling and k-fold cross-validation, are adopted to ensure the accuracy of the modeling results. Our results show that the proposed method outperforms classical solutions, providing a more explicit representation of curvilinear structures and improving interpolation accuracy, as measured by classical error metrics such as NMAEs and NRSMEs. It should be noted that DK is an open framework that can be applied beyond geostatistical modeling with LVA. For instance, since positive definiteness is not strictly required, DK can use a wider range of mathematical functions that accurately fit experimental variograms, which is generally impossible with traditional kriging methods. Moreover, the employed GA may not be the most appropriate. On a regular laptop (equipped with an Intel Core i7 CPU, 2.60 GHz) using a C++ based implementation, the estimation time for a 150 × 300 grid takes about 7 min, indicating the need for improving computational efficiency through advanced optimization methods and computational models (Gutiérrez de Ravé et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018 ). Furthermore, other potential approaches exist for addressing LVA modeling. For example, emerging deep learning methods and more advanced geostatistical frameworks, such as deep generative models and the stochastic local interaction model (Hristopulos and Agou, 2020; Hristopulos et al., 2021 ), present promising avenues. These areas will be the focus of future research.
1 Introduction In a changing climate, snow water resources in mountains are becoming increasingly important. Almost everywhere, there is a dominance of negative over positive trends in snow cover characteristics whilst global air temperature is increasing (Hansen et al., 2010 ). Therefore, the trends documented even in the short term can have serious consequences for the study area, including, for example, lower annual groundwater recharge or surface runoff (Hammond et al., 2018 ). In mountain catchments, melting snow typically accounts for a significant proportion of total runoff (Barnett et al., 2005; Hock et al., 2006 ). Therefore, spatio-temporal snow monitoring is crucial for studying mountain water resources and predicting surface runoff. A good spatio-temporal estimate of Snow Water Equivalent (SWE) changes is crucial for many economic and scientific fields. SWE is relevant for: water cycle modelling, freshwater management, hydrology and operational meteorology, drought and flood risk assessment, calibration of numerical remote sensing models (Rohrer and Braun, 1994; Barnett et al., 2005; Clark et al., 2011; Viviroli et al., 2011; Freudiger et al., 2014; Dozier et al., 2016; Fayad et al., 2017; Stigter et al., 2017; Dong, 2018; Stuefer et al., 2020; Winkler et al., 2021; Beaudoin-Galaise and Jutras, 2022 ), avalanche forecasting (Lehning et al., 2002; Hatchett et al., 2017 ), in hydropower operation planning (Barnett et al., 2005; Skaugen et al., 2012 ), or in ecological studies (Huss et al., 2017 ). It is also commonly used in long-term climatological and hydrological studies (Marty et al., 2017; Helmert et al., 2018; Winkler et al., 2021; Colombo et al., 2022 ). Recent IPCC reports (2013, 2021) and other works (e.g. Hall et al., 2014 ) suggest that the flood risk from spring snowmelt may increase in mountainous regions. This also applies to the Elbe and Oder river basins (Mudelsee et al., 2003 ), which include the Western Sudetes, where a reduction in the frequency of solid precipitation has also been confirmed (Urban et al., 2023 ). In regions with a temperate climate, an increase in SWE towards the end of winter can compensate for the smaller snow depth and thereby prolong its duration on the ground. Hence, even when snow duration decreases, higher SWE values, combined with faster melting, may increase the risk of more rapid spring runoff (Metcalfe et al., 2018 ). Monitoring and modelling snow cover and melting in mountain catchments is difficult, especially due to the high spatial variability of snow characteristics and the limited availability of measurement data (Hlavčová et al., 2015 ). SWE is particularly difficult to measure on a regular basis and is labour-intensive. Thus, there are few long-term studies based on direct measurements of SWE in the mountains. Usually, the estimation of SWE (SWEi), at different temporal and spatial scales, is done indirectly using satellites, remote sensing, drones, etc. (Stähli et al., 2004; Gutmann et al., 2012; Kinar and Pomeroy, 2015; Koch et al., 2019; Niedzielski et al., 2019 ), or point measurements of snow cover duration and depth (Lapin and Faško, 2005; Jonas et al., 2009 ). Recent studies indicate that SWE can be accurately estimated using a semi-empirical model based on daily snow depth measurements (Winkler et al., 2021; Colombo et al., 2022 ). Despite the existence of many remote methods to measure snow density and SWE, their classic manual measurements (using a snow core sampler and scale) are still very important. Due to the ease and speed of snow measurements (at least for relatively small depths), snow core samplers are still the most commonly used devices for measuring SWE (Pirazzini et al., 2018; López-Moreno et al., 2020 ). Some of the more interesting works that use direct SWE measurements in their analyses, taking into account altitude, slope exposure and land cover, include studies in the Swiss Alps (Rohrer et al., 1994 ) and in Japan (Tanaka and Suzuki, 2008 ). Comprehensive analyses of SWE changes based on measurements including seasons, air temperature and precipitation, for the entire Alpine area, indicate a successive decrease in this snow characteristic, especially in spring (Marty et al., 2017 ). Previously, the significant influence of orographic exposure/screening and macro-exposure of slopes on the snowiness and thermal severity of winters (Urban et al., 2018 ), as well as changes in the snow cover persistence index (Urban et al., 2019 ) in the Western Sudetes, was shown. The decreasing trends in the index of thermal severity and snowiness of winters and the increasing frequency of mild and low-snow winters in the area were noted (Urban et al., 2018, 2019 ). It has been shown that a long-term increase in air temperature, changes in precipitation and its structure (a decrease in the proportion of solid precipitation), an increase in sunshine and changes in atmospheric circulation - modified on the orographic barrier formed by the Sudetes, cause a reduction in the thickness and duration of snow cover. In addition, the shortening of snow cover duration in the Western Sudetes is more influenced by changes in its end dates than in its start dates (Urban et al., 2023 ). With reference to the results from the author's aforementioned publication on snow cover in the Western Sudetes, it was decided to estimate SWE values (to distinguish from the measured value, the estimated value is denoted SWEi) and to investigate its long-term changes in the area. The research hypotheses were: 1) the demonstrated decreasing trends in the duration and depth of snow cover (Urban et al., 2023 ) result in a consequent decrease in the water resources contributed by the snow cover, 2) in warmer climates the maximum SWEi values are lower and occur earlier. For the Western Sudetes, no climatological SWE studies based on actual manual measurements have been carried out so far. Patrol SWE measurements were only usually used for operational purposes by regional Hydrological Forecasting Offices. It should be mentioned that adjacent areas in river basins with source areas in the Western Sudetes (e.g. Elbe, Bóbr, Łomnica, Kamienna) are often threatened by snowmelt surges (Kasprzak, 2010; Niedzielski et al., 2019 ). In addition, efforts are being made in many countries, including Poland and the Czech Republic, to reduce the costs of surveying and maintaining full-time and contract/freelance observers. Hence, estimating, inter alia, SWE and its changes based on a simple method seems to be very necessary.  2 Source data, study area and methods This paper is a continuation of the author's series of articles on snow cover in the Western Sudetes (Urban et al., 2018, 2019, 2023 ). Thus, the basic period of analysis (1961/62–2020/21) and the reasons for choosing the study area (Western Sudetes) refer to the cited publications. The distribution and characteristics of the measurement stations are shown below ( Fig. 1 ,  Table 1 ). SWE measurements are made irregularly and are conditioned by various guidelines and premises. According to the current Instructions for Polish Meteorological Stations of the Institute of Meteorology and Water Management - National Research Institute (acronym IMGW-PIB), SWE is measured after observation at 06:00 UTC when the thickness of the cover is at least 5 cm (Janiszewski, 1988; Różdżyński et al., 2014 ). These measurements should be made on the following days and dates:– on the 5th, 10th, 15th, 20th, 25th and last day of the month,  – each day if the air temperature on the previous day was above 0°C,  – regardless of the day and time - immediately after heavy snowfall and blizzards,  – by special order of the IMGW-PIB.    According to the instructions, SWE measurements are performed by meteorological stations with full-time observers (Śnieżka, Jelenia Góra). Unfortunately, at lower-level stations (climatological and precipitation stations), with contractors, the above-mentioned recommendations were not always followed. Hence, the frequency of measurements at these stations is lower than at meteorological stations. Measurements were carried out with the Chomicz and WS-43, with spring scale, snow samplers, followed by the WS-43 and WMD 03, with digital scale. The snow samplers consisted of a metal tube for snow sampling, a scale and a cutter. The principle of operation and measurement methodology was the same throughout the years of the study. The difference between the snow gauges was the type of scale used, manual or electronic. At the University of Wrocław (UWr) Observatory on Szrenica, the SWE measurement methodology was similar to that of the IMGW-PIB station network. However, at the Czech Hydrological and Meteorological Institute (CHMI), SWE measurement is carried out according to the Observers' Manual (Lipina and Židek, 2014, 2022 ). The regular date for SWE measurement is Monday 06:00. On other days of the week, SWE measurements are not normally performed. If a measurement takes place on a day of the week other than Monday, this is known as an exceptional SWE measurement. Exceptional SWE measurements are organised during the occurrence of exceptional and dangerous hydrometeorological phenomena or situations. Observers take measurements when there is a snow cover of at least 4 cm at the station at the time of observation. However, an observer may make measurements even when the snow cover is less than 4 cm and the snow cover on the ground is continuous (e.g. selected stations for hydrological forecasts). Measurements were initially made with a METRA scale snow sampler (equivalent to the Polish Chomicz and WS-43 snow samplers). Subsequently, the SM DOLFI 100–50 and 150–50 scale snow samplers were used, in the shape of a graduated tube ending in serrated notches to facilitate sampling, made of glass laminate. The cross-sectional area of both snow samplers is 50 cm2 . The tube lengths of the SM DOLFI instrument are 100 or 150 cm. It uses the HDB 10K10 digital hook scale from the German company Kern and Sohn. Recently, this snow sampler has also been implemented at IMGW-PIB. The operating principles of the snow samplers used at IMGW-PIB and CHMI are the same. In general, the number of SWE measurements depends directly on the location of the station in question. The higher the altitude, the better the snow conditions (snow remains longer and deeper), which should in principle result in a higher number of measurements. At the analyzed stations, measurements of snow depth (HS) have been and continue to be carried out in accordance with the applicable Instructions for meteorological stations in Poland (Janiszewski, 1988; Różdżyński et al., 2014 ) and in the Czech Republic (Lipina and Židek, 2014, 2022 ). Previous instructions regarding the methodology of measuring snow depth and its water equivalent did not differ from the currently applicable ones. According to the aforementioned instructions, HS measurements are conducted daily at 6:00 UTC when the snow depth on the ground is not less than 1 cm and covers a minimum of 50 % of the terrain surface. Snow depth measurement is performed using a snow gauge with a centimeter scale, with an accuracy of 1 cm. All instructions are based on guidelines for the location of meteorological stations and the methodology for measuring snow depth and other meteorological elements issued by the World Meteorological Organization (e.g., WMO, 2008 ). Precipitation measurements under mountain conditions are subject to error, especially during high winds and snowfall (Green and Helliwell, 1972; Wolff et al., 2015; Pollock et al., 2018 ). The largest measurement errors occur in the summit surface zone. Hence, in the present study, precipitation totals from Śnieżka or Szrenica should be considered as measured rather than actual. In contrast, the number of days with precipitation and the type of precipitation are reliable (Urban et al., 2023 ). Field measurements of SWE are labour-intensive and therefore their temporal resolution is lower than that of snow depth measurements. In this situation, various methods of determining SWE from snow depth measurements can be an alternative (Jonas et al., 2009; Sturm et al., 2010; Luks, 2012; Schöber et al., 2015 ). The estimation of SWE can be made using a simple general relationship between snow depth and water equivalent, provided that the area is forest-covered and characterised by a relatively mild climate (Tanaka and Suzuki, 2008 ). The Western Sudetes is an area with such characteristics. Thus, an estimation of SWE in the Western Sudetes was made based on the mentioned relationship using simple regression equations. The Pearson correlation and coefficient can be used in estimating SWE from snow depth measurements (Rovansek et al., 1993; Elder et al., 1998; Schöber et al., 2015 ). It should be mentioned that regression equations are a commonly used method to interpolate data (Schöber et al., 2015; Ben Aissia et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2018; Podani et al., 2021 ). Simple empirical methods to estimate SWE, based on the relationship between snow depth and SWE (Jonas et al., 2009; Sturm et al., 2010; López-Moreno et al., 2013 ), are still  effective (Schöber et al., 2015 ). The results obtained from them are not inferior to others with advanced measurement techniques, also applied in the mountain catchments of the Western Sudetes (Niedzielski et al., 2019 ). Given the complex topography, land cover and frequent snow redistribution in the mountains, SWE is usually characterised by strong spatial variability even within a small area (Bray, 1973; Liston and Sturm, 2002 ). Hence, the establishment of representative SWE values for a given location seems necessary based on at least a few measurements (Watson et al., 2006 ). The estimation of SWE values (SWEi) was based on a strong correlation between measured snow depth (HS) and measured SWE values. The analysis was performed for each station and each winter season, which was taken as the period November–April. For example, the 1981 winter season starts on 1 November 1981 and ends on 30 April 1982. The direction and rate of change of SWEi were also determined. The statistical significance of the determined trends and correlation coefficient values (R) was checked using the Student's t-test. The longest 60-year sequences of HS measurement data were used to analyse SWEi trends. Trends from shorter periods, where cited, are only supplementary information. They are not analysed or compared since they are determined for different periods. The standard error of estimation was used as a measure of the fit of the regression model to the actual SWE values. However, to evaluate the model's predictions, the "Leave One Out Cross Validation" (LOOCV) method was used. In this method, "m" models for SWE are constructed by creating subsets of the original data, each formed by sequentially removing one element at a time. The evaluation was based on the values of the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) as the primary diagnostic measure, and the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE).  3 Results and discussion 3.1 Evaluation of SWE estimation error SWE is shown not to be correlated with snow density at all stations, but it is strongly and positively correlated with snow depth ( Fig. 2 ,  Table 2 ; see also e.g. Jonas et al., 2009 ; Sturm et al., 2010 ; Valt et al., 2018 ). The correlations for individual months are stronger than those shown graphically for the whole season, and the correlation coefficients (except for November and April at the Karpacz_2 station, due to the small sample size) are statistically significant (Table 2 , Fig. 2 ). The standard error of estimate of SWE was greater at higher altitude stations due to generally greater snow accumulation. However, the greatest standard error of estimate usually occurred in February or March, the months with the highest snow cover (Table 2 ). The actual HS versus SWE relationships are approximately rectilinear, so Pearson's correlation coefficient was used in the analyses. The study used simple regression equations, which were determined for each month of the winter season and each station. The equations were determined on the basis of all actual HS and SWE measurements from the period 01.01.1961–31.12.2022 at a given station, while only for the station Karpacz_1 the study period was different and resulted from the operation of the station (Tables 1 and 2 ). It should be noted that the temporal range of SWE measurements was often much shorter than snow depth, as measurements of this parameter started later than HS (e.g. Jakuszyce, Desná-Souš, Harrachov, Horní Maršov, Vysoké nad Jizerou). Thus, as in previous studies, factors directly influencing snow density and SWE were taken into account: month/season, snow depth, station location - height above sea level and exposure (Fig. 2 , Table 1 ; see also Mizukami and Perica, 2008 ; Jonas et al., 2009 ). For the estimation of SWE values, only days with a snow cover of at least 5 cm were taken. This assumption was due to the fact of different criteria in IMGW-PIB and CHMI for SWE measurements (see chap. 2), which have now been unified, and to the values of the determined "b" coefficients in the simple regression equations, which in some cases, at low HS, generated illogical (e.g. negative) data. For example, in April at the Horní Maršov station, for a daily HS of 4 cm, the value of SWEi calculated from the regression equation (y=0.3993x-2.8836) would be −1.3 cm. A similar situation with negative SWEi would occur in February at Szrenica, with a daily snow cover less than 19 cm (Table 2 ). Such cases were rare during the study period and were excluded from the analysis. A similar approach, due to the increase in measurement uncertainty at low HS, was used in SWE studies in the Alps, where days with HS below 10 cm were discarded from the analysis (Marty et al., 2017 ). Possible errors in SWE measurements due to the influence of current meteorological conditions (e.g. wind rocking the scale), physical characteristics of the snow, differences in the design of the measurement equipment or the observer's accuracy in sampling, were considered impossible to determine and were omitted from the considerations. Differences between SWE measurements, or between repetitions for a given snow sampler at a given location, are mainly due to instrumental differences (when different types of snow samplers are used at the same time and location), or observer-induced differences, or natural variability of snow cover on a small spatial scale (López-Moreno et al., 2020 ). Regardless of the models used to estimate SWE, the largest differences occur at low snow depths (López-Moreno et al., 2020 ). This is because shallow snow cover can evolve from fresh, fluffy, low-density snow in autumn to dense slush in spring. A seasonal evolution of both depth, snow density and SWE can therefore be expected. This is confirmed by the following graph presenting, among other things, the long-term average values of snow depth, snow density, and SWE in the winter season for selected stations ( Fig. 3 ). The stations represent different elevations above sea level, terrain forms, and climatic zones, from summit-ridge areas (Szrenica), through slope areas (Bedřichov, Świeradów Zdrój) to the lowest-lying areas (Hejnice, Jelenia Góra) (Table 1 ). The average snow depth and its SWE gradually increase during the season until reaching maximum values in February or March, after which they decrease significantly. Snow density, on the other hand, reaches an average maximum in April, except at the lowest stations, where the thin and usually ephemeral snow cover is not able to give sufficiently high SWE values (Fig. 3 ). This effect has been described in many previous studies (Elder et al., 1991; Rohrer et al., 1994; Sturm and Holmgren, 1998; Anderton et al., 2004; Mizukami and Perica, 2008 ) and corresponds to an increase in snow density caused initially by subsidence and later also by other processes in the shaped snow cover, e.g. ablation. The spread of the standard deviations of the differences as well as the magnitude of the mean differences between SWEi and SWE is considerable. The magnitude of the mean difference ranges from about 3 % at the highest to more than 20 % at the lower locations ( Fig. 4 ). This is because the model does not take into account previous meteorological conditions that influence the development of the retrieved snow profile for SWE determination (Onuchin and Burenina, 1996; Sturm and Holmgren, 1998; Meloysund et al., 2007 ). This fact is particularly relevant at lower locations (Rohrer et al., 1994 ). However, this conclusion was not fully confirmed at the location in question. This may be due to the abundance of data at individual stations, as well as the accuracy of some measurements or the natural variability of SWE on a small spatial scale. The relatively high value of the mean difference (29 %) at the Benecko_2 station may be due to the fact that the percentage of the largest differences (>150 %) there accounts for more than 7 % of all differences. The situation is similar at the Horni Marsov station (Fig. 4 ). This may also indicate possible irregularities when taking measurements at these locations. The overall mean difference (from all 16 stations) was 16.8 % (Fig. 4 ). The analogous mean difference for the Italian Alps was 15.6 % (Guyennon et al., 2019 ). Both values are also comparable to the magnitude of the difference within a location, estimated at 13–30 % in the Swiss Alps (Jonas et al., 2009 ). Furthermore, the results obtained are also comparable to the differences in SWE estimation using more advanced techniques (using unmanned aerial vehicles) in the catchments of the Western Sudetes, where the average error reached 18.9 % (Niedzielski et al., 2019 ). This result supports the finding that the quality of the results for SWEi, obtained from more sophisticated methods for estimating snow volume density, is no better than those obtained from relatively simple methods (Schöber et al., 2015 ). In principle, regression models give the best SWEi results for high locations and at higher snow depths (Schöber et al., 2015 ). Hence, due to the lower absolute altitudes and thinner HS in the Western Sudetes than in the Alps, the expected mean differences in SWEi should be larger. The results obtained for the Western Sudetes can therefore be considered satisfactory. The weakest relationship between SWE and SWEi tends to occur at the beginning and/or end of the winter season ( Table 3 ). However, SWEi values show a high correlation with SWE. The seasonal correlations between SWE and SWEi values are strong and positive. The correlation coefficients R range from about 0.8 at the lowest stations to more than 0.9 at the stations with the highest locations ( Fig. 5 , Table 3 ). These coefficients for individual months tend to be high, ranging from 0.50 to 0.99. The R-value is also influenced by the number of cases analysed, which tends to be lowest in the months beginning and/or end of the season ( Tables 3 and 4 ). The greatest correlation of SWEi to SWE tends to occur at higher locations. There, snow cover has greater depth and stability and ablation occurs less frequently (Urban et al., 2019 ). In contrast, at lower altitudes, melting can occur throughout the season, resulting in greater variability in HS parameters and consequently SWE. Analogous results have been obtained in previous studies (Jonas et al., 2009; Schöber et al., 2015; Marty et al., 2017 ). In addition, the relatively high correlation coefficients between SWE and SWEi in the Western Sudetes, usually higher at the end of winter than at its beginning (Table 3 ), make the method used useful for applications in the study of snow hydrology and the wider water management of the area. The magnitude of the differences was influenced by the frequency of cases with large positive differences between SWE and SWEi ( Fig. 6 ). Most of the largest differences (>150 %) occurred during the early or late winter season ( Table 5 ). Errors calculated using cross-validation (RMSE and MAE) and simple regression methods (RMSE_reg and MAE_reg) are highest at stations with the best snow conditions (Śnieżka, Szrenica, Jakuszyce, Bedřichov, Desná-Souš) and lowest at stations located at the lowest elevations with the least snow cover (Jelenia Góra, Hejnice). The magnitude of the errors obtained is due to the average snow depth at the analyzed stations during the winter season. Correlation coefficients (R) between SWE and SWEi are high for each location, ranging from 0.80 to 0.96. These values are very similar to the correlation coefficients (R_reg) obtained from the simple regression equations ( Table 6 ).  3.2 Spatial and temporal characteristics of SWEi At the summit surface locations (Śnieżka, Szrenica), the highest HS and SWEi averages occur in March. In the others, the highest HS average falls in February (10 stations) or March (4 stations). In contrast, the highest SWEi averages fall almost everywhere in March, except for stations Benecko_1 and Benecko_2, where SWEi occurs in February ( Fig. 7 ), which is related to changes in snow density. The spatial distribution of mean seasonal SWEi in the Western Sudetes ranges from about 1.5 cm at the lowest locations (Jelenia Góra, Hejnice) to about 24–30 cm at the highest locations. High average values of SWEi are characteristic for stations with southern macro-exposure, located in the 750–900 m altitude zone in the Jizera Mountains, e.g. Jakuszyce, Desná-Souš. The greatest contrast between stations located at similar altitudes (e.g. Harrachov and Szklarska Poręba, Horní Maršov and Karpacz_2), but with opposite macro-exposures, occurs in the 500–900 m zone (  Figs. 8 and 9 ). Significantly higher (around 35–50 %) values of SWEi are found at stations with southern macro-exposure than at stations at analogous altitudes with northern macro-exposure (Fig. 9 ). The strong differentiation of snow cover parameters in this area is a result of many factors, including the altitude of the stations, the diversity of relief and, above all, the macro-exposure of the slopes and the orographic deformation of the air mass flow field shaping precipitation and air temperature (more strongly in the N-S than E-W direction). The intensity of processes forming and ablating snow cover depends on the overall atmospheric circulation, including local phenomena such as foehn winds. The influence of circulation on snow cover in the Western Sudetes (local scale) is associated, among other factors, with the foehn wind effect. This, in turn, is conditioned by the arrangement of baric centers over Europe, causing the inflow of air from the south-western/southern direction, perpendicular to the main axis of the Sudetes (WSW-ENE). Wind frequency from these directions predominates in the cold season, favoring the occurrence of foehn winds (Kwiatkowski, 1972, 1975, 1979; Kwiatkowski and Hołdys, 1985; Głowicki, 1995; Ustrnul, 1992; Łapińska and Badnorz, 2013 ). The location of the main ridge of the Karkonosze Mountains (in the WNW–ESE axis) is, besides atmospheric circulation, a secondary factor influencing the distribution of air temperature and atmospheric precipitation in winter in the Karkonosze. Therefore, slopes with a north-facing macro-exposure are more often influenced by foehn winds than those with a south-facing macro-exposure. Foehn, as a warm, dry, and gusty wind descending, contributes to the faster disappearance of snow cover on the leeward side of the mountains. The greater the elevation difference between the mountain ridge and the foothills, the stronger the influence of foehn on the disappearance of snow cover in the lower parts of the slopes. The spatial distribution of SWEi values is analogous to the distribution of other snow cover parameters and indices (e.g. its maximum and average thickness, number of days with snow cover, index of severity and snowiness of winters) in the Western Sudetes conditioned by the mentioned factors (Urban et al., 2018, 2019, 2023 ). Seasonal SWEi values increase with altitude. In contrast to the higher growth rate of snow cover parameters with altitude (e.g. thickness, number of days) on slopes with a northern macro-exposure than a southern one (Urban et al., 2023 ), no clear differences in the rate of increase with elevation above sea level between macro-exposures are found for SWEi (Fig. 9 ). Temporal distribution of relative SWEi (which is the quotient of SWEi value in a given season by the average seasonal value of SWEi in the examined multi-year period expressed in percentage) indicates that seasons in which the snow cover in the predominant area of the Western Sudetes was abundant in water were: 1962, 1964–1967, 1969, 1986–1987, 1998–1999, 2001 and especially 2004–2005, locally 2011. Water-poor seasons included: 1970–1972, 1988–1990, 2006–2007 and especially the period 2013–2020. On a decadal basis, the snow cover rich season included 1961–1970, while the water-poor season included 2011–2020 ( Table 7 ). The last decade analysed was the warmest among those analysed globally (IPCC, 2021 ) as well as in the study area (Urban et al., 2023 ). It was also marked in the Western Sudetes by the highest frequency of mild and low-snow winters (Urban et al., 2018 ) and winters with snow cover instability (Urban et al., 2019 ). The obtained results also confirm earlier findings from studies on snow cover in low mountains in Germany, indicating that from 1961 to 2016, SWE exhibited a linear decline and exceptionally snowy and extremely cold winters completely disappeared by the end of the 1980s (Dong and Menzel, 2020 ).  3.3 Seasonal patterns of SWEi and their trends of change The course of seasonal values of SWEi shows clear changes from year to year ( Fig. 10 ). The highest SWEi values occurred in the 1986/87 and 2005/06 seasons, with 4 cases each. The lowest were in the last decade, in particular the 2019/20 and 2013/14 seasons, at 5 and 4 stations respectively. The winter seasons of the decade 2011–2020 proved to be the least abundant in terms of water contribution to the environment through snow cover over the entire study period (Fig. 10 ). This is due to the successive warming of the lower and middle troposphere, both in terms of annual and decadal temperature values over Poland (Urban et al., 2021 ). The decade 2011–2020 was the warmest among those analysed (IPCC, 2021 ). The increase in tropospheric thermals translates, among other things, into a gradual decrease in snowfall, thickness and duration of snow cover in many areas of the globe (IPCC, 2021 ), including the Western Sudetes (Urban et al., 2023 ), resulting in a decrease in snow water resources. The seasonal SWEi at all locations show decreasing trends from about 0.1–0.2 cm/decade at the lowest stations to about 1 cm/decade at the middle parts of the slopes ( Table 8 ;  Fig. 11 ). In the vast majority of cases, these trends are statistically significant. The same is also true for the individual months of the winter season (Table 8 ). It is noteworthy that the rate of decrease in SWEi is significantly faster and statistically significant in the months at the end of the season (during the phase of spring snow cover disappearance) than at its beginning ( Fig. 12 ; Table 8 ). This is related to the demonstrated shortening of snow cover duration and thickness in the Western Sudetes, conditioned by a higher rate of change in snow cover end dates, an increasing trend of spring sunshine and an increase in anticyclonic weather types (Urban et al., 2023 ). Declining trends in SWE have also been found in other mountain areas of Europe. For example, an analysis of simulated SWE in Slovakia over the last five decades shows a decrease in its value and duration of snow cover in every altitude zone and in all months of the winter season. Similar decreasing trends in mean SWE, comparable to those obtained in this study, were observed in the years 1965–2014 in the elevation zone of 700–1000 m above sea level in five mountainous areas of the Czech Republic (0.4–0.6 cm/decade). The strongest declines were observed in the research catchments in the Western Sudetes and the Bohemian Forest, with sporadic occurrences in the Eastern Sudetes. During the period 1990–2014, a decrease in mean SWE values was observed at all elevations, particularly evident in several Czech catchments in the Western Sudetes at approximately 800 m above sea level, reaching 1.6–2.0 cm/decade (Nedelcev and Jenicek, 2021 ). Clear decreasing trends were found in December, January and February, especially in the highest altitude zone (Hlavčová et al., 2015 ). SWE in the Alps has also been decreasing over at least the last six decades at all altitudes (Marty et al., 2017 ). The observed decreases in SWE are clearly greater in spring (April) than in winter (February). In April, most alpine stations show significant decreasing trends in SWE. In absolute values, they range from about 0.1 cm/decade at the lowest stations to about 2 cm/decade at the highest stations. In relative terms, April losses are 80 % and 10 % respectively. For example, a spring SWE loss of 100 mm over 5 decades would correspond to an earlier snow cover loss of 4 days assuming a snow loss of 5 cm/day (Marty et al., 2017 ). This is consistent with the observed earlier date of snow cover loss at two high-alpine stations (Marty and Meister, 2012 ). Particularly low SWE values in the last 2–3 decades have been observed not only in the Alps but also in other low- and high-mountain areas worldwide. In the former, negative trends have been identified in southwestern Germany (Dong and Menzel, 2020 ) and in the Czech Republic (Nedelcev and Jenicek, 2021 ). In high-mountain areas, including the western United States (Mote et al., 2018 ) and Asia (Kraaijenbrink et al., 2021 ), similar trends have been observed. Similarly, decreasing trends are found for maximum (MSWEi) and mean maximum values (MMSWEi) ( Fig. 13 ,  Table 9 ). In most cases, the trends in MMSWEi are statistically significant. In contrast, MSWEi are statistically significant at only two stations: Bedřichov and Desná–Souš (Table 9 ). The average date of MSWEi occurrence in the summit-ridge zone falls at the beginning of the second decade of March, in slope areas during the first and second decades of February, and in the lowest locations at the end of January. In most stations, it is characterized by a non-significant decreasing trend, not exceeding 2.5 days per decade. The negative trend indicates that the maximum MSWEi appears earlier. On Śnieżka, the increasing trend in the timing of MSWEi occurrence (2.7 days per decade) is most likely caused by strong winds (average annual speed over 12 m/s), which promote snow metamorphism (Table 9 ). In the years 1965–2014, decreasing trends in maximum SWE values reached 2–4 cm per decade in several Czech catchments in the Western Sudetes at approximately 800 m above sea level (Nedelcev and Jenicek, 2021 ). Similarly, all alpine stations showed a decreasing trend of maximum SWE over the period 1968–2012, but no prior occurrence of maximum SWE was observed (Marty et al., 2017 ). This result is consistent with the decrease in annual maximum snow depth observed in the Swiss Alps (Klein et al., 2016; Marty and Blanchet, 2012 ) and with the decrease in SWE at around 2500 m a.s.l. on 1 May, which corresponds to the timing of the SWE maximum at this altitude. The stronger decrease in spring SWE compared to winter SWE is consistent with greater spring warming (Rebetez and Reinhard, 2008 ), as well as a stronger spring decrease in snow cover thickness (Marty and Meister, 2012 ). Increasing air temperature results in a decreasing snowfall-to-rainfall ratio and more intensive melting of snow cover (Serquet et al., 2013 ), especially in spring at lower locations (Marty et al., 2017 ). Similar results were obtained for the Western Sudetes (Urban et al., 2023 ). If the observed trends continue, it is expected that spring peak runoffs will occur earlier and the contribution of snowmelt to river runoff will decrease due to less snow accumulation and earlier melting. In a warmer climate, snowmelt runoff and snow water resources, both in large and small catchments, are thought to decrease (Ruiz-Villanueva et al., 2014 ). Climate change projections for the 21st century for the Swiss Alps, among others, indicate the same (IPCC, 2013, 2021; Etter et al., 2017 ). However, the pronounced loss of snow water resources over the past few decades in the Alps causes less negative economic impacts than in other, drier mountain regions (e.g. California - Christian-Smith et al., 2015 ). On the foothills of the Sudetes, where spring and summer droughts are common and their frequency has been increasing in recent decades (Urban et al., 2022 ), decreasing water resources in snow cover may exacerbate the deficit of surface and groundwater in this area. On the other hand, in higher locations, the persistence of snow cover is conditioned by higher winter precipitation, with the consequence that maximum surface runoff remains unchanged or tends to increase (Dankers and Feyen, 2009 ). This confirms that there are no clear-cut trends in maximum runoff from melting snow, and the variation in trends contributes to the spatially uneven and difficult-to-predict risk of snowmelt floods under a changing climate (Wang et al., 2016 ). Public early warning systems for snowmelt floods can be based on estimates of the spatial distribution of SWE at the basin scale, which in the mountains is currently the most important unsolved hydrological problem (Dozier et al., 2016 ).   4 Summary and conclusions SWE is strongly positively correlated with HS. It is therefore possible to estimate SWE values on the basis of HS. The analysis of SWEi and its changes in the Western Sudetes in the winter seasons 1961/62–2020/21, considering exposure and altitude, confirms the research hypotheses and authorises the following statements:1. The adopted method for estimating SWE (simple regression equations) is a good and easily applicable method for climatological studies of SWE. The method shows point average differences from actual values in the range of about 3–29 %. The overall average difference was 16.8 % and is comparable to the average difference for other mountain areas in Europe. The differences obtained are comparable to the differences in SWE estimation in the catchments of the Western Sudetes using advanced measurement techniques.  2. Average snow depth and its SWEi gradually increase during the season, reaching maximum values in February or March, after which it decreases markedly. Snow density, on the other hand, usually reaches an average monthly maximum in April.  3. The mean and maximum seasonal SWEi values show negative trends, ranging from approximately −0.1 to −1.3 cm / decade and −0.2 to −2.5 cm / decade, respectively. These are statistically significant at many locations.  4. The average date of maximum SWEi occurrence in the summit-ridge zone falls at the beginning of the second decade of March, in slope areas during the first and second decades of February, and in the lowest locations at the end of January. In most stations, it is characterized by a non-significant decreasing trend (maximum SWEi appearing earlier), not exceeding 2.5 days per decade.  5. SWEi values, at locations at similar altitudes, are greater at stations with a southern macro-exposure than a northern one.  6. The rate of change of SWEi with altitude is similar on north and south macro-exposure slopes  7. Since SWEi values are characterised by a positive asymmetry of differences in terms of SWE, it can be assumed that the actual SWE values are smaller than SWEi and the amount of water stored and subsequently released into the environment from snow cover is decreasing.  8. Further detailed research on snow cover and refinement of the method for estimating SWE is needed, taking into account, for example, freshly fallen snow and diurnal changes in air temperature.  9. The results obtained regarding changes in SWEi in the Western Sudetes correspond with those of other mountain areas in Europe. They are symptomatic of a warming climate, particularly intense in recent decades.     Author statement The attached paper is original research paper and reports the results of original research. The obtained results have not been previously published elsewhere and are not under consideration for publication elsewhere. Its publication is approved by all authors. If accepted, it will not be published elsewhere in the same form, in English or in any other language, including electronically without the written consent of the copyright-holder.
